column36: Drug resistance mechanisms in the human pathogen Leishmania
column37: The control of parasitic diseases is an important public health problem and the emergence of drug resistance is a major complication. In the last years we have studied the mechanism of resistance to antimonials that are used in the treatment of parasites responsible for kala-azar and leishmaniasis. These diseases are caused by the parasite Leishmania which is distributed worldwide and affects several million people including soldiers in Irak and Afghanistan. Resistance to antimonials is a major problem in some part of the world and we are proposing to define the mechanisms of resistance using a state of the art technological approach. A better understanding of resistance is important to circumvent or overcome this important clinical and public health problem.

column36: Translational control in eukaryotic development
column37: Translation is the process by which proteins are produced using the information found in genes. We are interested in how translation of a gene is initiated, and have identified and studied numerous factors required for this to occur in the fruitfly Drosophila. One of these factors, called eIF4E, is itself regulated by a protein (4E-BP) which binds to it and inhibits its activity. In the most recent term of the grant, we have found that regulation of translation by 4E-BP is necessary for an organism to resist starvation and other stress conditions. Under normal conditions, Drosophila lacking 4E-BP have a higher fat content that wild-type flies, indicating that 4E-BP has a function in metabolic regulation. As 4E-BP expression and activity increase in response to insulin in both Drosophila and mammals, our work has established a model system for understanding the fundamental causes of diabetes. The proposed work will expand and extend this study to understand more about the mechanisms by which 4E-BP activity is regulated, and to identify and characterize critical target genes whose expression is regulated by 4E-BP.

column36: Epithelial cell signalling responses to attaching-effacing intestinal pathogens
column37: Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) O157:H7 is a non-invasive pathogen, which results in both sporadic cases and outbreaks of bloody diarrhea (hemorrhagic colitis) and kidney failure (hemolytic-uremic syndrome) in humans. Current therapy is limited to supportive care, because antibiotics likely increase the risk of harmful consequences, due to the release of bacterial-derived toxins. Improving future management options is likely to be based on a better understanding of how this bacterial pathogen causes disease. We have demonstrated subversion of signal transduction responses in host cells infected with EHEC. The current application will focus on three complementary study aims to further characterize three inter-related signal transduction responses to EHEC, and the related murine enteric pathogen Citrobacter rodentium, following challenge of epithelial cells of human and mouse origin, respectively. We will: 1) determine whether nucleotide-binding domain-like receptors (Nod1 and Nod2) mediate EHEC- and C. rodentium-induced inhibition of the transcription factor, nuclear factor (NF) kappa B, 2) define bacterial and host factor(s) mediating bacterial inhibition of the interferon-gamma - Jak1,2 - Stat1 signal transduction cascade, and 3) delineate the role of atypical isoforms of protein kinase C (PKC) present in cholesterol-enriched microdomains of the plasma membrane in EHEC- and C. rodentium-infected epithelia. The model systems we employ have proven effective for testing the benefits of novel intervention strategies that are currently under development, and will define new target molecules and therapeutic approaches for use in managing this infectious disease. This research program will advance knowledge in the area of intestinal inflammation induced by a bacterial infection that causes both serious short-term disease and death and has the potential to induce chronic illnesses, including irritable bowel syndrome, in affected Canadians.

column36: Aging, neurofunctional reorganization and communication abilities
column37: This research program is about how the brain reorganizes itself to support the preservation of communication abilities during successful aging. The components of communication that will be studied are important for everyday life as they include the ability to use and process the meanings of words, to understand narratives and to understand the non-literal meanings of utterances such as indirect requests. Using the most powerful neuroimaging technologies -- including functional magnetic resonance and optical imaging -- this study will allow to describe the patterns of neural networks for communication associated with successful aging. At the same time, the impact of education and the relationship with cognitive abilities will be explored. Overall, this program will allow us to identify the optimal functional reorganization that sustains successful communication with increased age as well as the most suitable rehabilitation strategies for elderly who have to live with communication deficits due to a brain lesion.

column36: A Novel Method for Pharmacosurveillance: Combining an Electronic Prescribing and Drug Management System and Administrative Database
column37: Medications are the most frequent causes of preventable adverse events including illness, and death. Drugs do not have complete information on safety and effectiveness at the time of market approval. Present-day adverse drug reaction monitoring systems rely on health professionals to report and miss more than 90% of adverse drug reactions. There is an urgent need to develop better methods of monitoring the safety and effectiveness of drugs after they enter the market. The use of health administrative and electronic prescribing and health record data are two new approaches that could be used to provide a more timely and accurate detection of adverse drug effects. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the accuracy of administrative data in detecting adverse drug events, and the improvement in the accuracy of detection with the addition of electronic prescribing data. We will assess these new methods of post-market surveillance in a cohort of 2,300 patients within the primary care practices of 104 physicians using electronic prescribing systems. Patients who are newly prescribed drugs for hypertension, depression and pain will be included, as these medications are commonly prescribed and implicated in adverse drug events. We will use patient interviews and chart review to collect information about adverse effects during a 6 month follow-up period. We will use electronic prescribing orders for drug discontinuation due to adverse effects, as well as diagnostic codes in administrative records of medical visits and hospitalizations to determine whether these two sources of information can accurately detect the adverse drug events. The results of this study will be used to evaluate whether these new sources of information-administrative and electronic prescribing data-could be immediately used to institute a more effective means of monitoring the safety and effectiveness of drugs in Canada.

column36: Using Novel Canadian Resources to Improve Medication Reconciliation at Discharge
column37: People who are hospitalized often already take many medications. Many of these medications will be stopped or changed during a hospital stay. When patients are discharged from hospital and return home, they can sometimes get ill from the medications they were given because of problems in communication between the hospital treatment and their community-based health care providers. This study will test the advantages of using available information from provincial drug plans and community pharmacies to provide better information about community medications patients are taking at the time of hospital discharge, and improve the communication of changes made during a patient's hospital stay back to the community pharmacists and doctors. Computerized lists of community medications will be used to help patients and health professionals check which medications are being prescribed and taken. Doctors, pharmacists and nurses in the hospital will then be able to make sure new hospital and previous community drug lists are correctly matched and that the information is shared with the community doctors and pharmacists. This study will take place in three hospitals which are part of the McGill University Health Centre. There are a total of 28 medical, surgical and psychiatric units that provides treatment to 1.3 million Quebecers living in the western part of the province, spanning the area from Montreal to James Bay. We will randomize half of the hospital units to a discharge medication reconciliation and communication module, and compare these units to usual care to find out if the use of these computerized tools will decrease the number of people getting ill from medication problems that make them come back to hospital after they have been discharged home.

column36: Evaluating the Accuracy of New Methods of Pharmacosurveillance: Computerized Administrative Data and Electronic Prescribing and Drug Management Systems
column37: Prescription drugs play a rapidly expanding and important role in the prevention and treatment of common health problems. Over 60% of adult Canadians have used at least one prescription drug in the past 6 months, and six or more drugs are taken by 18% of the older population. While there are considerable benefits from modern drug therapy, the frequent occurrence of adverse drug-related events and the uncertainty about effects of drugs after they enter the market have highlighted fundamental shortcomings in the ability to actively monitor drugs after their approval. Electronic health records, computerized prescribing and automated patient follow-up systems are health information technologies that are being increasingly used to improve the quality of care around the world. These new health information technologies provide an unprecedented opportunity to develop an active surveillance system that will monitor and provide patients and physicians with real-time feedback on the comparative safety and effectiveness of new drugs. Conducting active surveillance on a collaborative international scale will provide more rapid information about drug safety and effectiveness from users around the world as well as permit more personalized risk/benefit analysis for subgroups where drugs may have a different risk/benefit profile. The purpose of this project is to develop state-of-the-art methods of i) monitoring, and ii) analyzing the comparative risk and benefit of new drug therapies, in real-time, through an international prospective surveillance system, and iii) communicating this information to clinicians to inform treatment decision-making at the point-of-care.

column36: Randomized Trial Comparing Radical Hysterectomy and Pelvic Node Dissection vs Simple Hysterectomy and Pelvic Node Dissection in Patients with Low Risk Cervical Cancer Defined as Lesions Measuring Less than 2 cm with Less than 50% Stromal Invasion
column37: Cervix cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in women. Most recent statistics estimate that almost 500,000 women globally will be diagnosed with cervical cancer each year and more than 270,000 annually will die from it. Due to effective screening strategies in developed countries, the incidence of cervical cancer has decreased but the proportion of young women presenting with low-risk early-stage disease has increased. The traditional treatment for these women is radical hysterectomy. This is a very effective procedure and has a high cure rate, but is associated with potentially severe and long-lasting side-effects. These include impairment of bowel, bladder and/or sexual function and infertility, which may lead to poorer quality of life. Some gynecologists who specialize in cancer surgery believe a less extensive surgical procedure (simple hysterectomy) will provide the same cure rate as radical surgery and will reduce the chances of the adverse effects described above. However, no studies have directly compared the effectiveness and the short and long-term side-effects of simple and radical hysterectomy in women with low-risk early stage disease. There is a need to determine which procedure is optimal and to standardize treatments. The proposed trial, CX.5, will be led by an established network of Canadian cancer investigators known as the NCIC Clinical Trials Group and will include participation of other international groups. The objective of CX.5 is to determine whether simple hysterectomy is as good as radical hysterectomy in preventing cancer from recurring and better in preventing the side-effects associated with surgery. Important secondary outcomes include evaluation of quality of life, measures of sexual health, and cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses. The trial will include 700 women from across the world, including 135 from Canada and will take 8 years to complete.

column36: Executive Functioning in Children and Adolescents with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD)
column37: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) leads to physical, mental, behavioral, and learning disabilities as a result of prenatal alcohol exposure. Children with FASD have difficulties with executive functions (EF) including planning, thinking flexibly, problem solving, and working memory (cool EF) as well as tasks involving emotion and decision making (hot EF). Individuals with FASD also display adverse outcomes including behavior problems, mental health issues, delinquency, and substance abuse, as well as problems adaptive to society. The goals of the proposed project are to examine: 1) the pattern of hot and cool EF difficulties in children and adolescents with FASD compared to control children 2) how both hot and cool EF contribute to adverse outcomes; 3) whether EF can be improved with targeted cognitive interventions. Participants will include children and adolescents (aged 11 to 17 years) with FASD and non-exposed controls. They will complete tests of cool and hot EF and their parents/caregivers will complete various rating scales regarding the participants behavior. Next, two groups of children with FASD will receive a targeted intervention: one focused on working memory and one focused on self-regulation, the third group will serve as a waitlist control. We hypothesize that children with FASD will have deficits in both hot and cool EF, but that they will have greater impairment on hot EF measures. We also expect that EF (and particularly hot EF) will be associated with adverse outcomes in FASD. Finally, we expect that the EF interventions will lead to improvements in EF. The research will inform our understanding of EF in FASD and thus has implications of the health and development of children and adolescents with FASD.

column36: Repeat Emergency Department Visits Among Long-Term Care Residents in Ontario
column37: Long-term care (LTC) residents are a vulnerable segment of the older population. They have a high burden of dementia and other illnesses as well as significant limitations in their independent functioning. Because of this, they are at high risk for emergent health problems, such as a serious fall or an acute complication of an existing chronic condition (like diabetes), that results in a visit to the emergency department (ED). While these ED visits are often necessary, they also represent the health system's inability to respond to residents' needs before they become a serious health crisis. Equally as problematic are findings that suggest that many residents make multiple ED visits because their underlying needs were not addressed during the first visit resulting in additional ED visits. To date, there is little research that describes such repeat ED visits by LTC residents, the consequences of these visits, or how to target interventions to reduce their occurrence. In our research, we will use data from Ontario to identify all LTC residents and follow them for up to one year. All ED visits during this time will be counted so that we can estimate the frequency of repeat ED visits. Advanced statistical methods will allow us to comprehensively describe patterns of repeat ED visits, identify resident risk factors, and estimate the contribution of each the LTC and hospital sectors to repeat ED visits. Our results will help to focus quality improvement efforts aimed at safely minimizing ED use by identifying opportunities for intervention in both LTC homes and hospitals.

column36: Cerebral and psychomotor development in babies with infantile spasms
column37: Infantile spasms (IS) is one of the most devastating and treatment-resistant epileptic syndromes in infancy. It affects one in every 2,000 babies. IS is characterized by three main symptoms: halt or decline in psychomotor development (crawling, walking, talking, social interaction, etc.), epileptic spasms, and abnormal electrical brain activity seen in the electroencephalogram (EEG). The first spasms usually appear between age 3 and 7 months. Most cases are treated successfully with hormones or anticonvulsive drugs. However, the developmental outcome remains poor in most of these infants. Mental retardation is a serious consequence of IS, and has been reported in 71% to 88% of patients. Of the children who have normal overall intelligence and are able to attend regular school, most have specific deficits such as motor, memory, or language problems, as well as learning difficulties. Previous studies have shown that early diagnosis and treatment of IS may improve the developmental outcome. The main aim of this research program is to prevent and minimize developmental and psychomotor deficits in infants with IS by conducting three sets of studies: 1) identification of predictive markers for IS to allow for earlier diagnosis, 2) development of a new, noninvasive technique for IS treatment monitoring to better understand the effects of anticonvulsive drugs on the developing brain, and ultimately, to enable earlier adjustments in treatment, and 3) investigation of specific developmental profiles and psychomotor outcomes in children with IS in relation to age at onset, causes of IS, and IS treatment. Early detection and treatment of IS should help prevent cognitive and developmental deficits, thus improving the quality of life of these patients and their families.

column36: The expression and role of soluble IL-7 receptor alpha in HIV-HCV co-infection
column37: An immune response that effectively clears a viral infection depends on the actions of cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells (CTL). Cellular messengers known as cytokines, particularly interleukin-7 (IL-7), are very important in generating such responses. In progressive HIV and hepatitis-C virus (HCV) infections, CTL function is impaired, and similarly, IL-7 and its receptor CD127, have reduced activity. We have detected increased levels of a soluble form of CD127 (sCD127) in HIV+ individuals, which may function to alter IL-7 activity and contribute to immune impairment. Furthermore, in HIV-HCV co-infected individuals, a co-morbidity affecting approximately 30% of HIV+ individuals, sCD127 may contribute to HIV/AIDS progression. Studies will investigate expression and functions of sCD127 in both HCV mono- and HIV-HCV co-infection. This research could lead to be better understanding of how sCD127 influences anti-viral responses, thereby building the foundation needed for the development of novel immunotherapeutics and vaccine adjuvants to fight HIV and HCV infections.

column36: Gender in Measurement and Rehabilitation of Musculoskeletal Work Disability
column37: Problems with bones, muscles, joints and other tissues that make up our musculoskeletal (MSK) system can be affected by activities that we do at work or home. Painful MSK problems can make work difficult and affect our overall health. The tasks we do at work can cause or aggravate these problems. Women and men are very different when it comes to developing these problems or recovering from them. Women tend to have MSK problems more often, and can have more difficulty returning to their normal work activities. We are not sure if this is because of biological differences between men and women; or because men and women tend to have very different work and life roles. It may be a combination of these factors. Women's muscles, bones and joints are different and exposed to different hormonal influences. Women usually have different roles at work and at home, than men. These can involve different stresses like posture and repetitive activity. Workplace relationships, lack of control of work tasks or environment, and family life balances can also affect these problems. Jobs that women perform are often different than men-sometimes even with the same job title. Women perform more unpaid work roles caring for others. Unfortunately, there are not many researchers who study how work affects health differently between men and women. The purpose of this chair is to dedicate a researcher's time and attention to answering questions about how men and women are different in terms of developing and recovering from MSK health problems. The researcher will also train a new generation of researchers to increase the number of people and research directions that focus on solving these problems. The chair will develop new research teams, develops new tools for measuring symptoms and work problems, determine how differences in work tasks and environments affect men and women, and develop strategies for care to be more sensitive to these differences in the future.

column36: Neurophysiology of 3-D Gaze and Head Control
column37: Diseases and disorders of the nervous system make up the largest class of medical problems in the world. One way to address this huge problem is study basic brain mechanisms so that we can then try to understand how they are affected by multiple diseases. For example, sensory-motor transformations underlay most aspects of daily living, work, and leisure, and are affected by nearly all diseases, disorders, and injuries to the brain. Most of what we know about such basic brain processes comes from animal studies. Despite advances in human brain science, it is still very limited in what it can test, for example it cannot differentiate between different neurons in an area of the brain, and it often forces unnatural behaviors, like fixing the head in place or making subjects lie down. For this reason neural recordings in monkeys are still needed, because they are very close to the human in brain and behavior. However, monkey studies have often times been limited by the need to test very simple behaviors in rather unnatural conditions, and by two-dimensional approximations to the real three-dimensional (3-D) motion. Here, we propose to use a monkey model to examine some of the most fundamental questions of sensorimotor control with the use of a new method for analyzing neural activity recorded during naturally variable 3-D behaviors (especially with the head free to move naturally). This will enable us to describe how visual signals are processed, stored and converted into neural commands for eye and head movements. We will also study how the brain encodes future sequences of coordinated movement, and we will test, for the first time, if a specific part of parietal cortex is involved in sensorimotor integration for head control. Importantly, this new work will allow us to obtain very precise quantitative measurements from more natural behaviors that should therefore apply more closely to real-world situations than most previous neural recordings of this type.

column37: A lack of vitamin D has been linked to several types of cancer including breast cancer. In earlier studies we have shown that vitamin D blocks the production of another hormone called parathyroid hormone related protein or PTHrP. PTHrP is produced by the great majority of breast tumors and when overproduced accelerates the development of bone metastases. Based on these observations we believe that we can target this vitamin D-PTHrP axis to counter the development of bone metastases. The majority of breast cancer patients who have a recurrence will develop cancer spread to the skeleton, which causes considerable suffering and morbidity. Bone metastases are currently treated with bisphosphonates that inhibit osteoclast bone lytic activity. Unfortunately, bisphosphonate treatment is not a cure and the number of patients experiencing skeletal complications is reduced by only 20%, which exemplifies the need for improving the efficacy of bisphosphonate therapy. Recent evidence points to the existence in tumors of a small population of multi-potent therapy-resistant cancer stem cells (CSC) that survive treatment to regenerate tumors locally and produce metastases. One aspect of this proposal is to examine the possibility of countering breast cancer metastatic spread to the skeleton by targeting of the CSC population through the vitamin D-PTHrP axis. We believe that the combination of vitamin D therapy, specific blockade of PTHrP activity, and bisphosphonate treatment in a co-targeting strategy will create an enhanced treatment addressing all levels of metastatic spread from breast to the skeleton. Another aspect of this proposal is to improve the efficacy of vitamin D by targeting specific signaling molecules that render the cancer cells resistant to the effect of vitamin D. Overall our goal is to develop pre-clinical models of vitamin D-based therapies. If successful, these strategies will constitute proofs of principle for therapeutic intervention.

column37: Chronic pain affects as many as 1 in 5 people worldwide. Over the next two decades, as the population ages and modern medicine allows people to survive serious illness, the number of people affected by chronic pain is expected to rise to 1 in 3. Chronic pain can be debilitating, isolating, dehumanizing, and all too frequently, can turn deadly. Understanding the molecular basis of pain is key to the discovery of novel analgesics. Pain transducers are membrane proteins specifically sensitive to the danger signals heat, cold, chemical irritants or ATP. ATP receptors belonging to the P2X ion channel family have been shown to be involved in chronic pain in rodents and primates and they are candidate therapeutic targets for pain treatment without the negative side effects of morphine and pregabalin. P2X3 is expressed exclusively in the pain-sensing neurons located in spinal and trigeminal ganglia. P2X4 is upregulated in spinal microglia following nerve injury and P2X4 activation has been shown to contribute to neuropathy-associated pain hypersensitivity. We propose in this research program to investigate the function and integration of P2X3 and P2X4 receptors in sensory pathways, by understanding how other receptors talk to P2X receptors and by developing novel selective tools to probe P2X function. Our work will generate novel data to assess the potential of P2X receptors as valid targets for the pharmacological treatment of inflammatory and neuropathic pain.

column36: Evaluating Collaborative Care for Postpartum Depression in Pediatric Primary Care Settings (EPDS Trial)
column37: Last year over 49,000 Canadian mothers experienced depression in the first year following childbirth, putting at least 80,000 children at risk for poor developmental outcomes. International experts have clearly identified exposure to maternal depression as a major childhood adversity and have suggested that effective interventions to address this condition are one of the most important preventive strategies we can implement to reduce long-term negative developmental outcomes among children. Unfortunately, postpartum depression often remains undetected and untreated. Collaborative care is an approach to treatment that is highly effective for the management of depression in primary care settings. Part of the success of this approach is that it actively promotes treatment initiation and adherence while addressing patient preferences and perceived barriers. However, this approach has not been evaluated for the treatment of postpartum depression and no systematic or evidence-based approach for postpartum depression management in primary care exists in Canada. The purpose of this trial is to evaluate the effect of a collaborative care intervention on postpartum depression among mothers attending well-child visits in an early childhood primary care practice. Women with depressive symptomatology will be randomly allocated to either an intervention group (usual postpartum care plus collaborative care) or a control group (usual postpartum care). A research assistant blinded to group allocation will telephone all mothers at 6, 9, and 12 months post-randomization to collect maternal outcome data; child outcome data will be obtained from trained staff at each practice. The study is novel, important, and timely, as it will provide data to advance our understanding of how to deliver optimal mental health care for mothers in the postpartum period while also offering information about how improving depression treatment outcomes serve to prevent adverse outcomes in children.

column36: Defining the burden and managing the effects of psychiatric comorbidity in chronic immunoinflammatory disease
column37: This Team Grant will create a multi-disciplinary team with complementary expertise. Our team will focus on the problem of psychiatric comorbidity (such as depression and anxiety disorders) in persons with chronic immuno-inflammatory diseases including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), multiple sclerosis (MS) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The research program has several objectives. First, we will identify the frequency of psychiatric comorbidities among persons with IBD, MS, and RA as compared to the general population, determining how this varies according to age, sex, region and socioeconomic status. Second, we will assess the impact of psychiatric comorbidity on MS in three ways. By focusing on health care utilization, mortality and health-related quality of life we will gain a broad perspective on how psychiatric comorbidity influences health. By focusing on work disability we will gain an understanding of how psychiatric comorbidity influences participation in work and social roles. Finally, we will work with primary care and specialist physicians to determine the best way to diagnose and treat psychiatric comorbidity in persons with chronic immuno-inflammatory diseases. We will partner with primary care physicians, advocacy groups including the Crohns and Colitis Foundation, MS Society of Canada, and Arthritis Society to ensure that our findings are widely disseminated. We will develop information materials for patients and their families regarding the management of stress, depression and anxiety. Anticipated benefits from our population-based research program include better recognition of the magnitude of psychiatric comorbidities and their impact on IBD, MS and RA; development of strategies to manage these comorbidities; and development of generalizable research strategies to evaluate and manage comorbidities in chronic immuno-inflammatory diseases.

column36: Brain Dysfunction in Chronic Inflammatory Disease: Reciprocal Effects of CNS and Periphery Crosstalk
column37: Chronic inflammatory diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, hepatitis and inflammatory bowel disease share many common features. Among the most significant of these are changes in the brain that lead to behavioral symptoms of fatigue, depression, cognitive dysfunction and social withdrawal. Such debilitating symptoms markedly diminish the quality of life of hundreds of thousands of Canadians living with these conditions. One might think, of course a patient with inflammatory bowel disease, liver disease, or rheumatoid arthritis will be depressed, anxious and distracted; who wouldn't be? We contend that these behavioral changes are not a response to disease. Rather, a fundamental alteration occurs in the way in which the brain functions in the face of a chronic inflammatory disease. Despite the impact of these symptoms, the mechanisms of brain dysfunction in chronic inflammation are not well understood. Furthermore, there is an increasing appreciation that altered central nervous system function has considerable consequences for disease progression; this too has not been explored. We wish to address these shortcomings by understanding how persistent inflammation may cause disturbances in the brain and how chronic immune-mediated inflammatory diseases reprogram the brain to alter neuronal function, precipitating co-morbid behavioral dysfunction, which influences the disease processes. To effectively examine these important problems we have assembled a trans-disciplinary team of experts in the management of chronic inflammatory disease: neuroscientists, psychiatrists and imaging experts who are fluent in understanding brain-body communication and plasticity of brain function. Our unique basic-clinical-translational research team is poised to facilitate the discovery of common central mechanisms underlying the neurological and psychological conditions associated with chronic inflammation. Translating our discoveries to improve patient outcomes is our ultimate goal.

column36: A Multidisciplinary Approach To Target Chronic Inflammation Of The Gut, Liver And Joint.
column37: The liver and gut forms an important partnership to digest, absorb and process harmless food particles (antigens). To perform this function successfully both organs need to be able to be tolerant of food antigens whilst retaining the ability to mount vigorous immune responses to ingested harmful bacteria and viruses (pathogens). Disruption of this balance with increased inflammation and reduced tolerance is at the root of most common gut and liver diseases. This includes conditions ranging from simple food intolerances to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and severe liver disease in the form of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC). In some individuals, inflammation spreads from the liver and gut to include the joint and leads to long term disability and pain. The cause of all 3 diseases is hypothesized to be a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental factors that triggers an overactive immune system. Recent work has demonstrated that inflammatory liver, gut and joint diseases are remarkably similar as they have shared genetic susceptibility genes and respond to similar biological therapies. Thus in this grant we aim to understand in detail how these diseases are linked genetically and define shared biological pathways and common environmental triggers of disease such as smoking, pollution and obesity. We will then link all this data with clinical disease features and responses to treatments to define genetic and biological markers that can be used to predict disease features, complications or responses to treatment to make the best possible care decision for each individual. The strength of this this proposal lies in our intend to call on the collective experience of experts in IBD, liver disease and joint inflammation to combine forces to accelerate knowledge of the factors that link these three organs to cause disease and how we can modify them to the benefit of patient care.

column36: NADPH oxidase function in the pathogenesis of pediatric IBD and JIA
column37: Chronic inflammatory diseases in children can have a severe impact on one's quality of life and are associated with high costs for treatment and lost productivity, including missing school. Two such diseases are Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) and Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA), which cause inflammation of the intestine and joints of very young children, respectively. The causes of JIA and IBD are unclear, but unfortunately the number of kids with these diseases is rising rapidly in Canada. Although environmental factors are suspected, including nutrition and infections, their impact and the ways that they contribute to these diseases remains unclear. In this grant we will look at some of these environmental factors. It is also known that people who get IBD or JIA share some common genetic traits that make them at risk for developing the disease. In this proposal we will study genes that make up the NADPH oxidases, enzyme systems that normally play an important role in fighting infections. We will study a group of IBD and JIA patients and determine which ones have mutations in NADPH oxidase genes, and how these mutations affect the patients' immune system and the microbes in their intestine (since these microbes impact greatly on our physiology). We will also determine if patients with mutations in NADPH oxidase genes manifest disease because of specific environmental triggers, and also define the most effective treatments for these patients. Our study will help to determine how our genes and our environment combine to causes IBD and JIA. This information will provide important information leading towards improved treatment of these diseases.

column36: PRECISION: Preventing Complications from Inflammatory Skin, Joint and Bowel Conditions
column37: Thanks to better treatment, people with inflammatory diseases of the skin, joint or bowel are now more likely to die from complications of the disease than the disease itself. The complications appear to be similar across the diseases, suggesting that low grade ongoing inflammation may be the culprit. The diseases we will study affect over 5 million Canadians. They include psoriasis (a skin disease); rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and lupus-like diseases, ankylosing spondylitis, gout and osteoarthritis (joint diseases); and Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (bowel diseases). We focus on complications that occur in a greater frequency than would be expected by chance, including heart attacks, strokes, blood clots in the legs and lungs, severe infections, hip fractures, selected cancers, diabetes, and chronic lung disease. We will do the following: 1. Find out how common these complications are and their true impact on individuals, including the financial costs. 2. Find out whether inflammation is in fact the cause of the complications and whether there are other factors that can either increase the risk of the complications or eliminate them. More than 500,000 Canadians (1 in 10 of those affected) will be studied. 3. Develop patient-centred approaches to reduce or eliminate the frequency and consequences of the complications. With prompt diagnosis and more knowledge, prevention is possible; five million Canadians could live better, longer lives and money will be saved by not treating complications that do not occur. Our team of over 30 scientists and patients have been working for a decade on identifying the complications and doing test runs that show this is doable. Four patients have been involved in every step of the study design. They have surveyed another 636 patients to assist in making sure the questions asked are truly relevant to all Canadians with these diseases. This research has the potential to save lives.

column36: Restitution Enhancement in Arthritis and Chronic Heart disease
column37: Many diseases share common pathways through which they cause damage. This is particularly true of diseases which result from inappropriate or uncontrolled immune system activity and tissue damage in a process known as inflammation. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory disease that affects millions of people worldwide with varying severity. In some people, the disease improves either spontaneously or following only simple initial treatment while in others, disease persists and worsens leading to disability. Myocardial fibrosis, resulting from inflammation and ineffective healing responses, can lead to reduced heart function and death after an initial heart attack has been treated. In some people these diseases improve, either spontaneously or after initial treatment, while in others, disease persists and worsens. In this project, a team of medical doctors and scientists from Canada, Finland and the United States have come together to study patients early in disease so we can identify the clinical features as well as the cells and chemicals in the body that cause or allow the inflammation to get better in some patients with either heart disease or arthritis. This information can then be used to help doctors identify, very early, those patients who need, or don't need, more extensive or aggressive treatment. The information on cells and chemicals will allow us to identify the pathways we need to modify in order to potentially prevent ongoing damaging inflammation in more patients. Using this information, we will work together to begin to examine ways to better treat and prevent these and other inflammatory diseases. column36: Insights into Parkinson's disease, Crohn's disease, and leprosy: a common role for LRRK2
column37: The immune system has increasingly been shown to play a role in various disease states, though the manner by which the immune system responds is complex and not fully understood. To achieve this we have assembled a multidisciplinary team with expertise in LRRK2 biology, genetics, and the immune system. Together, these three disorders represent an incredible burden on health care costs and human suffering worldwide. The identification of commonalities related to immune dysregulation could lead to unique therapeutic strategies, and has the potential to transform clinical outcomes of patients suffering from these conditions.

column36: Development and application of new tools and assays to enhance discovery and translation in cancer genomics
column37: Cancers result from a collection of spelling errors ("mutations") that accumulate in our genetic material over time. Individual mutations that recur in cancer can lead us to key cellular apparatus that malfunctions in this disease, which, in turn, can guide the development of new treatments that may be more effective and less toxic than standard therapies. Discovering such mutations requires sophisticated methods that can efficiently "read" the genetic code of our cells ("DNA sequencing") and interpret the mutations that are likely to alter cellular function. My research aims to apply DNA sequencing to understand why certain tumours do not respond to current therapies and sometimes migrate to additional locations (i.e. become "metastatic"). In general, this process involves sequencing many tumours from individuals who were not successfully cured and identifying the individual genes that are significantly mutated in these tumours. Owing to the increased complexities in working with relapsed tumour samples, this research will also require the implementation of improved analytical techniques for mining these data. My research will also pursue new approaches that, using the knowledge of mutations present in tumours gleaned by sequencing, can detect the presence and relative abundance of tumour cells using a blood test. Such methods may ultimately provide means for the non-invasive monitoring of changes to tumour over time and thus more accurate methods for assessing treatment response and relapse.

column36: Non-invasive treatments to improve disease symptoms and cartilage health for knee osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is one of the leading causes of physical disability in adults worldwide and is associated with a significant personal and economic burden. It is estimated that 1 in 8 Canadian adults currently have OA which results in 27.5 billion dollars in annual economic burden to individual Canadians and the healthcare system. Most commonly affecting the knee, OA is characterized by the breakdown of articular cartilage - a smooth lining at the ends of bones that permit ease of movement and shock absorption. It is believed that high magnitude and poorly distributed loads that pass through the knee joint play a strong role in the development and progression of knee OA. Thus, improvements in pain, physical function and quality of life can be achieved by developing treatments that effectively reduce and more evenly distribute these loads. My research program will focus on the use sophisticated motion analysis equipment and techniques as a way to measure the loads experienced by the knee joint during movement. Specifically, the research will focus on two methods to reduce and more evenly distribute loads within an arthritic knee: gait modification and shoe orthotics. These treatments are designed to be non-invasive (non-surgical and non-pharmacological) and delivered with minimal resources or expense in order to improve patient safety while reducing healthcare costs. The focus on non-invasive treatments is in stark contrast to the majority of current OA research which is in the areas of surgery or drugs. Thus, the research will provide effective treatment alternatives that also have lower costs of delivery, less side effects of treatment, and higher availability to patients. Additionally, the development of new treatment strategies that minimize joint loads have great potential in improving symptoms and slowing the rate of disease progression, thereby reducing the economic costs in the long-term and significantly improving the quality of life of those affected.

column36: Functions of platelets and microparticles in inflammation
column37: According to the tale written by Quintus Smyrnaeus, Ulysses had the idea of building a wooden horse inside which 30 men from his elite army were hiding. The Trojans, excited to see the wooden horse, which is the emblem of the city of Troy, decided to wheel the trophy inside the fortified city, leading to its destruction. A Trojan Horse is thus the stratagem that causes a recipient to invite an enemy into a securely protected setting. This research project is to some extent inspired by this story. Platelets are blood cells that play major roles in the prevention of bleedings, and the transfusion of platelets is a life-saving medical procedure for patients undergoing a major surgery, with massive bleedings, for subjects with abnormal platelets (not fully functional) and those with diseases like cancers or low platelet counts. Unfortunately, platelet transfusion sometimes triggers adverse reactions, with similarities with infections. In fact, approximately 1 in 100 platelet transfusion induces adverse reactions, among which 1 in 4000 are considered severe. Of importance, in Canada transfusion-induced acute lung injury (TRALI) is the third leading cause of death during transfusion. In our laboratory, we are interested by a highly pro-inflammatory component derived by platelets. Like in the tale of the Trojan Horse, we believe that this component contained into the donor platelets is thus transported inside platelet concentrate storage bags. Once inside the platelet concentrates, platelets themselves release this inflammatory mediator, promoting the adverse reactions in patients upon transfusion. In this research project, we want to determine what are the most optimal methods for the preparation and conservation of platelet concentrates to limit the release of this overlooked component. We also aim to understand by which mechanisms this novel mediator can trigger adverse reactions, including TRALI, during transfusions.

column36: The control of interlimb coordination in health and disease
column37: After a spinal cord injury, maintaining an upright posture during walking and attaining and sustaining even moderately fast walking speeds is difficult. These impairments could be partly the result of a defective coordination between the four limbs, also termed interlimb coordination. Despite this simple fact, the structures and pathways within the central nervous system involved in coordinating the four limbs are poorly understood, particularly in the injured spinal cord of adult mammals. This is mainly because we lack an effective model to study interlimb coordination after spinal cord injury. Our objective is to better understand the control of interlimb coordination during walking and its recovery following spinal cord injury. We will study interlimb coordination in an adult mammalian model (feline) of spinal cord injury using a treadmill that can independently control the walking speed of each limb, called a split-belt treadmill. Using novel experimental paradigms, we recently showed that interlimb coordination is flexible during locomotion and that centres within the spinal cord play an important role in coordinating the left and right sides. This proposal will directly build on and expand our recent findings by providing more details on the neural pathways involved in coordinating the four limbs. These pathways could be targeted by therapeutic strategies aimed specifically at strengthening interlimb coordination after spinal cord injury, which could directly improve functional recovery.

column36: Improving Outcomes After Major Non-Cardiac Surgery: An Integrated Research Program
column37: More than 10 million people have major medical problems after surgery every year. I am leading 2 studies to help prevent these problems. The first study will help better identify people with poor fitness before surgery. It is believed that such people are at risk for heart attacks, difficulty breathing or other problems after surgery. At present, doctors judge fitness by asking patients about what activities they can do. For example, patients may be asked if they can climb stairs. However, this method (called "subjective assessment") is not good at identifying patients who have problems after surgery. I lead a study (called the METS Study) of 1312 patients in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the UK to compare subjective assessment against 3 other methods to measure fitness. These other methods are an exercise test (called CPET), a questionnaire about physical activities (called DASI), and a blood test (called NT pro-BNP). Before surgery, each patient will undergo a subjective assessment of their fitness, complete the exercise test, answer the questionnaire, and undergo the blood test. We will then follow them for 1 year after surgery to determine which method is best at identifying people who have problems after surgery. The second study will compare hospitals in Ontario to identify ones where fewer people having problems after surgery. I will compare these "high-performing" hospitals against others to understand how they take care of patients differently before, during and after surgery. By learning this information, these high-performing hospitals can serve as examples for other hospitals to learn from, both in Ontario and other regions. If other hospitals can learn to take care of patients in the same way, their patients may also have fewer problems after surgery. By helping to better identify high-risk patients before surgery and organize their care for surgery, these studies will make surgery safer for millions of people around the world every year

column36: New neurons, stress and memory: behavioural functions and cellular mechanisms.
column37: The discovery that neurons are added to the adult brain of nearly all mammals examined, including humans, has profoundly changed our understanding of the potential for plasticity in the brain. One region of the adult brain that has high levels of adult neurogenesis is the hippocampus, a structure critically involved in learning and memory. In the hippocampus, new neurons are better at forming connections and are more active than pre-existing neurons, suggesting that they may preferentially contribute to memory processes. Consistent with this possibility, animals that lack adult neurogenesis show a variety of memory-related impairments. However, the hippocampus also regulates and is highly sensitive to stress. Stress prevents the addition of new neurons and drugs and experiences that protect against stress, such as antidepressants, environmental enrichment and exercise increase the addition of new neurons. Furthermore, animals lacking neurogenesis are more vulnerable to the negative behavioural and hormonal effects of stress. Since memory is also heavily regulated by stress it is likely that stress impacts memory through its effects on neurogenesis, although this has never been explored. This proposal will therefore examine the effects of stress on learning-related properties of new neurons. First, we will examine whether stress alters the ability of new neurons to form connections in the brain, which is thought to be an essential biological component of memory. Second, we will identify whether a dysfunctional response to stress underlies the memory impairments seen in animals that lack neurogenesis. Given the contribution of stress to a broad array of mental health disorders it is expected that these results will directly contribute to novel treatments for people suffering from memory and mood disorders.

column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating inflammatory responses in atherosclerosis
column37: A quarter of all deaths in Canada are caused by complications associated with cardiovascular disease. The main cause of vascular disease is atherosclerosis, or build-up of plaque in the arteries. Atherosclerosis is an inflammatory disease. One subset of inflammatory cells, macrophages, play an important role in the development of atherosclerosis. How these cells gather in plaques, however, is not clear. Macrophages can appear in plaques through recruitment of their monocyte precursors from the bloodstream. Our recently published data shows macrophages also proliferate or divide locally within the plaque. We are currently pursuing 3 main research streams: 1. Investigating the role of lesional macrophage proliferation in atherosclerosis. Which process - monocyte influx or macrophage proliferation - is more important? What are the mechanisms that drive proliferation? How does the balance between the two processes change with co-morbidities and treatment? Does one process influence the other? Which of the two is the better therapeutic target? The answers to these question are likely to identify new therapeutic targets in treating atherosclerosis. 2. column36: Understanding and Responding to HIV Vulnerability Among Disadvantaged Populations in Canada and Globally: A Program Science Research Agenda
column37: HIV is a major public health problem. Since the start of the HIV epidemic, there have been over 30 million people infected with HIV and 30 million related deaths. In Canada, 71,000 people are estimated to be living with HIV. My research aims to identify and respond to gaps in the HIV prevention and treatment continuum, using a Program Science framework. Although developing and developed countries are different, the underlying drivers of the HIV epidemics are similar, as are the vulnerabilities faced by marginalized populations. As well, lessons learned in either setting can benefit each other. I have three central projects in my research agenda: Study 1 aims to understand the HIV risk and vulnerability faced by young women as they transition into sex work in Kenya, Ukraine and India. Female sex workers (FSWs) experience a much higher risk of HIV than the general population, and programs targeted to FSWs are a critical component of HIV prevention. The goal of this research is to estimate HIV risk, and characterize the behaviours that influence this risk, during the transition period from first sex until self-declared entry into sex work and during the early period of sex work. The findings will contribute significantly to our understanding of HIV risk and will inform the strategic design of HIV prevention programs. Studies 2 and 3 of my research plan focus on HIV care outcomes. These studies establish cohorts and use a combination of clinical and provincial health care data in Manitoba. Study 2 aims to identify where there have been missed opportunities for earlier diagnosis of HIV. This will identify where to expand testing options in order to ensure earlier diagnosis and linkage to care. Study 3 builds on this with the development of a prospective cohort of HIV positive persons across Canada to understand health care patterns and explore models of HIV care. Through these cohorts, we will better understand the health care needs of this vulnerable population.

column36: Mechanisms of opioid analgesia in the central nervous system
column37: Chronic pain is pervasive, insidious, and afflicts 1 in 5 adult Canadians. Treating pain in these individuals is notoriously difficult and often requires opioids, one of the most powerful and effective classes of drugs used for controlling pain. However, a major problem with opioid use is the loss of pain relieving effects (opioid tolerance) such that higher and more frequent doses are necessary to achieve the same level of pain relief. The struggle to maintain adequate pain control decreases the quality of life for chronic pain sufferers and complicates many conditions including cancer, stroke, diabetes, traumatic injury and a host of other diseases. The need for escalating amounts of opioids puts patients at risk for unwanted side effects such as constipation, respiratory distress, and drug dependence. Despite the potential side effects, opioids remain the pharmacological cornerstone of modern pain therapy. Our research focuses on improving the effectiveness of opioids in relieving pain as well as decreasing the side effects associated with opioid therapy. This proposal examines the inner workings of microglia, which are important immune cells in the brain and spinal cord. We will focus on a molecule that is critical for microglia pain signaling in the spinal cord - the P2X7 receptor - and its unique ability to alter communication between cells leading to loss of opioid pain control. By dissembling the cellular machinery that inhibits the ability of opioids to alleviate pain, we can begin to target core components of this machinery to enhance current opioid therapy or help create new options for chronic pain sufferers.

column36: Investigating the effects of sound on movement
column37: Music and movement are intimately tied. We often observe this in daily life, when people spontaneously tap their toes or nod their heads to the beat in music. The link is so strong that several cultures do not even have different words for music and dance. The effects of music or a steady beat are sometimes used therapeutically to help patients with movement disorders (such as Parkinson's disease). However, we know little about how music alters movement, and what characteristics of music are most effective in influencing movement. The proposed project examines how different aspects of music can alter movements in young and older healthy volunteers as well as in Parkinson's disease patients. Specifically, we examine the contribution of the following musical factors: the strength and clarity of the beat, the enjoyment of the music to the listener, how much the music induces a desire to move, and how good the listener is at 'feeling the beat'. We will focus on the speed of movement, but will also measure other aspects of movement, such as how quickly a movement is initiated and whether balance is affected. Finally, we will use neuroimaging to determine the brain responses that lead to music's influence on movement in healthy volunteers and in patients with Parkinson's disease. The outcomes will inform our basic understanding of how sound affects movement systems in the brain. The findings will also be important for optimizing musical interventions in therapies targeted at movement disorders.

column36: Molecular determinants of small airway obstruction in COPD
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is currently the fourth leading cause of death in Canada and is the only disease where mortality rates continue to climb. This is due to Canada's aging population being at greater risk of developing COPD, as the "Baby boomer" generation grew up when smoking rates were at their peak and smoking is the number one risk factor for COPD. COPD patients have difficulty breathing as their airways - the tubes that carry air in and out of the lung - become partially blocked and damaged. Importantly, there are no cures for COPD, which makes the disease so deadly. The structural cells that line the airway tubes respond to smoke exposure by promoting inflammation and thickening of the airways, termed fibrosis. Our research is focused on understanding how these cells respond to smoke and promote fibrosis in the 20-30 percent of individuals who smoke. The goal of our study is to identify the disease drivers that cause airway fibrosis in COPD patients and to identify new therapies to prevent the disease. Our work leverages a unique set of donated human lungs which will be analyzed with new computed tomography (CT) scanning methods to understand how the physical damage and airway fibrosis occurs over time within COPD lungs. We will then use lung cells isolated from smokers with and without COPD to test if the disease-drivers we identify can be modulated with new or existing therapies. This research will allow better understanding of smoke-related airway disease, and should lead to improved measures to protect Canadians exposed directly or indirectly to smoke exposure.

column36: Identifying Genetic Determinants of Human Sleep and Circadian Rhythms
column37: Sleep and circadian rhythms (24-hour biological rhythms regulated by an internal biological clock) have a huge impact on human performance and biology. However, our knowledge of the genes influencing human sleep and circadian biology is incomplete. Moreover, while small-scale animal and human experiments suggest that sleep and circadian disruption (as experienced, for instance, in shift-work and jet-lag) may have a major impact on brain function, their impact on neurological disease at the population level is only partly understood. The overall goal of the applicant's research plan is to identify genes influencing human sleep and circadian function, and to explore the impact of sleep and circadian disruption on common and important human brain diseases in aging such as dementia and stroke. Toward this end, the applicant has developed a number of analytical approaches to facilitate large-scale at home measurement of sleep and circadian rhythms, and to measure brain genetic rhythms from collections of brain tissue obtained from organ donors. He will apply these tools to several large existing studies in Canada and the United States, as well as to an existing collection of donated brain tissue to identify genes influencing human sleep and circadian rhythms and the mechanisms whereby they act, and to assess the influence of sleep and circadian disruption on human brain diseases in the community. This work may lay the foundation for new treatments to manipulate sleep and circadian function to combat the adverse brain effects of jet lag or shift work as experienced by millions of Canadians. It may also lead to genetically guided optimization of the scheduling of neurological therapies to optimize clinical outcomes. Finally, it may lay the foundation for sleep or circadian interventions as a potential strategy for decreasing the burden of stroke, dementia, and other brain disorders in the aging Canadian society.

column36: Sexual desire emerges from arousal: Testing a model of responsive desire in women with and without sexual difficulties.
column37: Sexual health is an integral component of physical and mental quality of life. Sexual arousal and desire problems affect up to one third of women, yet effective and safe treatments do not yet exist. Recently, changes to the way sexual arousal and desire problems are conceptualized have been proposed by sexuality researchers, such that sexual arousal and desire are no longer distinct experiences where desire leads to arousal. Instead, sexual desire is triggered by, or emerges, from experiencing sexual arousal. This new model of sexual response may be beneficial to women's health because it more accurately captures women's experience of their sexuality and better explains women's experiences of sexual difficulties. This model has not, however, been scientifically tested to determine which aspects of sexual arousal trigger sexual desire, and whether these aspects differ for women with and without sexual arousal and desire difficulties. Our primary objective is to understand the relationships among sexual arousal, sexual desire, and sexual health in women. We will assess sexual arousal in women with and without sexual arousal and desire difficulties using physiological, psychological, and hormonal measures. We will then follow women after participation and collect behavioural and self reported measures of their experience of sexual desire. Understanding the relationship between sexual arousal and desire will create gender-specific knowledge about women's sexuality and about the causes of women's sexual dysfunctions. This outcome is vital given the unsuccessful history of applying male based models of sexual functioning to women. The proposed research will have direct implications for identifying risk factors for sexual arousal and desire problems, inform treatment decisions, and decrease the burden of sexual dysfunction and its negative impacts for Canadian women.

column36: Mouse Models to study Intervertebral Disc Development, Health and Disease
column37: Low back pain as a result of intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration is a cause of major disability and constitutes the leading musculoskeletal disorder responsible for days lost from work. Studies show that chronic back pain is increasing at an alarming rate; to the degree that backache has a lifetime prevalence of over 80% in Canada. Our ability to effectively treat disc disease is hampered by an incomplete understanding of IVD development and function. One molecule that has been suggested as a regulator of disc health is connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). Previous studies have shown that CTGF contributes to skeletal development in mice, and has benefical effects on IVD cells in culture. The exact role played by CTGF in IVD development, health and disease has however yet to be established. To explore the role of CTGF, our lab has begun to investigate when and where it is expressed in the spine. We have established that in early stages of development, CTGF is expressed in the notochord, the embryonic cell type that gives rise to the central tissue of the IVD (nucleus pulposus). Using a novel transgenic mouse, we also show that loss of CTGF in notochord-derived cells deregulates embryonic disc formation and also accelerates age-associated disc degeneration. We therefore propose that CTGF is essential to IVD formation, health and disease and have developed three aims of study to examine this hypothesis using complimentary mouse and cell culture models. These studies will gain new insight into the role of proteins within the IVD tissue environment, specifically CTGF, in maintaining IVD health or accelerating disc disease. In the long term, these studies will identify candidate molecules that could be used as biological treatments to minimize or reverse disc disease and associated back pain.

column36: Optimizing the performance of our Primary Health Care System
column37: Primary health care is the care delivered by family doctors, nurses, and other health professionals to individuals and families in a community. A strong primary health care system effectively meets the needs of its population, resulting in healthier communities and lower costs. Canada has invested billions of dollars in an effort to make its primary health care system more accessible, effective, and fair. Despite these investments, the Canadian health care system still has a number of gaps in which certain groups receive below average care. The goal of my research program is to produce evidence about what approaches can help address these gaps so that we can invest in them and improve our system. Over the past decade, a number of provinces and practices have introduced several innovations to help improve the quality of their primary health care. For example, some practices moved from paper to electronic medical records, some doctors adopted a new payment structure that is intended to incentivize better care, and some practices opted to incorporate nurses, pharmacists, and other health professionals in order to provide more comprehensive care. Some of these efforts have likely achieved their intended goal, while others have not. I will study the large variability in Ontario's primary health care practice structure to understand what innovations have likely contributed to optimizing care. I will also work with regional decision makers and primary health care practices to identify the problems in access to primary health care, which groups are most affected by these problems, and the barriers they face. I will then draw on evidence in Canada and internationally to select the most appropriate approaches to address these barriers, implement the chosen strategies in my region, and assess whether they achieved their goal. By ensuring that our investments are well directed, Canada stands to gain healthier populations and save money.

column36: Identifying and modifying transdiagnostic risk and resiliency variables for anxiety and pain
column37: Anxiety and pain are common human experiences that cause significant distress or impairment for almost 1 in 5 Canadians with annual costs exceeding $60 billion. Successful treatments are available, but such treatments are costly, there is limited access to qualified providers, and even with the best available care many people still receive only limited symptom relief; moreover, the overwhelming tendency is to provide treatment rather than prevention. My overarching goal for the next 5 years is to develop inexpensive and broadly deliverable assessment, treatment, and prevention methods for anxiety and pain. I believe this can best be accomplished by identifying the underlying mechanisms and constructs (i.e., vulnerabilities) that are common to different anxiety disorders (e.g., social anxiety disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder) and to different pain experiences. Once identified, methods can be developed for reducing vulnerabilities and, therein, treating and even preventing anxiety and pain. My research suggests differences in attention are an important vulnerability that can be modified using simple computer tasks that can be administered inexpensively online. My current CIHR-funded research is testing the effectiveness these tasks for patients with chronic pain. Similarly, how well people cope with uncertainty appears to be a critical factor in developing and maintaining clinically-significant anxiety; as such, I am researching methods to increase our ability to tolerate uncertainty. I will apply for CIHR funding to test the effectiveness of delivering those methods online. Finally, I believe prevention is the best treatment, which is why I am leading an international team of experts in testing a method for preventing posttraumatic stress disorder in RCMP. Overall, my research results will support Canadian mental heath care by producing timely, inexpensive, and broadly deliverable methods for assessing, treating, and preventing anxiety and pain.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 2nd leading cause of cancer mortality in Canada, with 9,200 deaths annually. column36: Interactive Technologies for Mental Health in Primary care

column36: Improving patient important outcomes for hemodialysis patients using pharmacological and dialysis-based strategies
column37: Over 2 million people worldwide receive kidney dialysis because of kidney failure. Although dialysis sustains life, patients who require dialysis often suffer from chronic pain, nausea, fatigue and other symptoms that substantially reduce their quality of life. Recent research by our group, and others, suggests damage to the heart and potentially other body organs occurs during dialysis and may cause them to feel unwell. In addition to making patients feel unwell, this damage during dialysis may contribute to high rates of death experience by patients that require dialysis - only half of dialysis patients in Canada survive over 3 years. We will conduct a series of studies to determine how often the heart and brain are damaged during dialysis. We will also identify ways in which dialysis is done that can be changed to both reduce patient's symptoms and improve their chances of survival. Finally, we will conduct studies to determine if treatments that prevent heart and brain injury in non-dialysis patients are also safe and effective in dialysis patients. Together, these studies will reveal important information about why so many dialysis patients have poor quality of life and high mortality rates and will help us identify treatments that will improve their quality of care.

column36: Microfluidic Technologies for Cell Separation and Cell Biomechanics
column37: This proposal describes a research program in medical technology development comprising of three projects. The first project aims to develop technologies for the isolation of circulating tumor cells. Approximately 90% of all cancer related deaths is a result of metastasis, or the spread of cancer from one part of the body to another. Circulating tumor cells are the seeds of this process that first detaches from a primary tumor, circulate in the bloodstream, and reattach to a different tissue. The capture, identification, and analysis of these cells have the potential to enable major advances in the research and treatment of many types of cancers. Specifically, the presence of circulating tumor cells can provide an early indication of disease, while the number and status of these cells can be used to select personalized drugs and dosage levels to most appropriately treat each patient. The second project aims to develop technologies for evaluating the quality of stored blood used for blood transfusions. This capability can potentially enable the Canadian Blood Services to optimize storage practices to maximize storage time and ensure maximum health benefit to each transfusion recipient. The third project aims to develop technologies to study malaria infection. Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite transmitted by mosquitoes to humans. Globally, there are between 200 and 500 million cases of malaria per year, resulting in approximately 1 million deaths, the majority of which are small children. Our technology aims to be a simple tool for physicians and researchers to study growth of the parasite and its response to drugs.

column36: Responding to the health crisis among street-involved youth in Canada: evidence to inform interventions and policy responses
column37: Street-involved youth are extremely vulnerable to experiencing health-related harms for a variety of reasons, such as high rates of illegal drug use, poverty and neglect, as well as precarious living conditions, either on the street or in risky relationships. Approximately 40% of the street-youth in several Canadian cities report injection drug use. As a result, street youth are increasingly being recognized as among those at highest risk for drug related harms including HIV and hepatitis C (HCV) infection. Unfortunately, data to inform strategies to prevent injection initiation are extremely limited and injection initiation and HCV transmission dynamics among young people are not well understood. Another alarming trend among youth is the rapidly increasing misuse of prescription opioids (POs). After marijuana, POs are consistently identified as the most commonly misused drug among Canadian youth. There are signals that PO use may promote transitions into heroin use and initiation into drug injection; however, longitudinal evaluations of this phenomenon are lacking and our knowledge is limited to retrospective and cross-sectional studies. To address these gaps, the proposed research plan focuses on: a) evaluating the impact and intersection of evolving drug use patterns and a range of individual, social, structural, and environmental factors on injection initiation, and HCV incidence among street-youth; and b) generating a body of evidence that will inform policy responses to address the crisis of PO misuse among at-risk youth. This research plan is based on an existing cohort of 700 street-involved youth who use illicit drugs, the At-Risk Youth Study (ARYS), and the creation of a nested cohort of 200 newly recruited youth who misuse POs. The overall objective of the research plan is to generate evidence to inform and evaluate interventions to address critical health and social harms afflicting at-risk youth who use illicit drugs including prescription opioids.

column36: Protein Mediated Regulation of the Myocardial Na+/H+ Exchanger
column37: Ischemic heart disease and heart hypertrophy remain as key health problems debilitating or killing thousands of Canadians every year. We are studying a protein of the heart involved in both these pathologies, the Na+/H+ exchanger isoform 1 (NHE1). The Na+/H+ exchanger is a protein that removes acid from inside heart cells. The cells of the heart use food such as glucose and fat, to produce energy for the heart so that it can contract and pump blood. When this occurs, they produce waste products, and one of these is acid. Too much acid is bad for the heart. It inhibits the ability of the heart to pump blood. There is a protein called the Na+/H+ exchanger removes the excess acid from inside the cells of the heart. It turns out, that in ischemic heart disease and heart hypertrophy, the Na+/H+ exchanger activity is too activated and this tends to exacerbate these diseases. We are studying how this occurs. The Na+/H+ exchanger has a long intracellular tail. Proteins bind to the tail and this affects and regulates the activity of the Na+/H+ exchanger. We found that two proteins, calmodulin and B-Raf, bind to and regulate the Na+/H+ exchanger. We are characterizing how and when this occurs in the healthy and diseased heart. We are also investigating what other proteins bind to and regulate the Na+/H+ exchanger in the diseased heart. Our study will give novel insights into why Na+/H+ exchanger activity damages the heart and how this can be prevented.
