column36: Endoplasmic Reticulum Function in Heart Health
column37: Cardiovascular disease is one of the major health burdens in developed countries at the estimated cost of ~over $340 billion of total healthcare spending. The overall rate of death attributable to cardiovascular diseases is 230 per 100,000 (1 death every 40 seconds). Responses to stress are an integral part of cardiovascular physiology and pathology. For example, the Western-style diet commonly consumed in industrialized societies and significantly increases risk of heart disease. The Western-style diet is high in saturated fat (e.g., from palm oil) and refined sugar (fructose). Excess of fructose may be the key factor leading to heart disease. We study a cardiac membrane system called the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), which under stress conditions reacts by developing specific stress responses inside the heart that may prevent or lead to cardiac pathology. Our research focuses on understanding of Western-style diet-induced cardiac stress and on the development of basic and clinical tools to control stress responses in the heart. This will provide new targets for drug discovery and treatment of heart disease.

column36: Investigating the role of Cystatin C in multiple sclerosis.
column37: Scores of genes and proteins are increased in the brains of multiple sclerosis (MS) patients but the function of most of these molecules is poorly understood. These factors may contribute to development of the disease, progression of disability or attempts for repair, and understanding their roles may lead to the discovery of novel treatments for MS. Cystatin C gene is increased in the brains of people with MS as well as in mice with experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE), a model of MS. The function of this protein in MS and EAE is unknown and conflicting evidence exists as to whether it could be a protective or detrimental molecule. Previous work had hailed CysC as a biomarker for MS but the results could not be replicated. On the other hand, CysC has been shown to be protective in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA). Since CIA is an autoimmune disease like MS, we hypothesized that CysC may also be a beneficial molecule in MS. To our surprise, our preliminary data suggests that CysC may in fact be a detrimental molecule in MS since it enhances disability in animals with EAE. This grant aims to clarify the function of Cystatin C using the EAE animal model as well as immune cells from MS patients.

column36: Sodium, Claudin-14 and the (Patho)Physiology of (Hyper)Calciuria and Kidney Stone Formation
column37: One in ten Canadians will pass a kidney stone in their lifetime. Passing a stone is painful and the numerous Emergency and Operating Room visits required for treatment is expensive. Moreover, emerging evidence from my research program and others has identified an increased risk of chronic kidney disease, dialysis and heart disease in people with kidney stones. The risk is greatest for women under the age of 50. Therapies aimed at preventing and/or dissolving kidney stones already present in the kidney are lacking. The main therapy is to increase water ingestion and decrease sodium intake. In some individuals a water pill can be used, but it is poorly effective and has significant side effects. The main risk factor for developing kidney stones is having urine with a high calcium content. A large majority of people with kidney stones display this attribute. We do not know why this is. The purpose of the proposed research is to try and understand why and how people excrete too much calcium in their urine. We know that sodium intake increases calcium excretion in normal people and people with kidney stones. Our work will identify molecules and pathways responsible for this association such that new therapies can be developed targeting this pathway. We have recently described a novel pathway in the kidney whereby higher levels of calcium in the blood cause increased calcium excretion in the urine in normal people. Our research will identify all the molecules in this pathway, so that drugs targeting it can be generated. Finally, we have found a genetic alteration in a gene central to this latter pathway in people who form kidney stones. We wish to understand how this mutation affects calcium excretion in these kidney stone formers such that specific therapies can be designed for them. Together, these studies will delineate molecules and mechanisms that increase urinary calcium excretion, providing novel targets for much needed new kidney stone therapies

column36: Delineating the Role of Polyphosphate in Regulating Complement Activation Pathways
column37: When a person sustains an injury, the major risks to their well-being are excess bleeding and overwhelming infection and inflammation (swelling, redness, pain). Fortunately, we have systems in our blood that reduce the bleeding through the formation of blood clots and prevent the spread of infection and inflammation ("complement system"). These systems cooperate to maintain normal functioning of our organs (e.g. the kidneys, heart, liver, lung and joints) and to promote healing. Alterations in the control of the coagulation and/or complement systems predispose patients to bleed excessively (e.g. in hemophilia), to clot too much (e.g. in deep vein thrombosis or heart attacks), to succumb to mild infections, or to develop inflammatory diseases such as atherosclerosis (inflamed and damaged blood vessels), arthritis (inflamed joints), colitis (inflamed bowels) or nephritis (inflamed kidneys). Unfortunately, these disorders are common and inadequately treated due to an incomplete understanding of how the coagulation and complement systems are controlled. To overcome this, we are focusing our research on "polyphosphate" which is a long string of the metal ion, phosphate. Polyphosphate is released into the blood when injury or infection occurs. Recent studies in our lab show that polyphosphate controls the complement system. Our new and intriguing findings hold promise for the design of novel polyphosphate-based strategies to treat many of the diseases mentioned above. Using biochemical and molecular biologic techniques and genetic mouse models of human disease, we will study the complement pathways in the blood to determine which steps are controlled by polyphosphate and how it works. The information gained will provide us with insights to develop new therapies that modulate the effects of polyphosphate on complement, with hopes of improving the health of many patients.

column36: Assembly of the Anthrax Toxin Protein Translocase
column37: Anthrax toxin is comprised of two toxic enzymes and a third protein, PA, which assembles into a nanomachine that delivers the toxic enzymes to the interior of human cells. We are studying two critical steps in the assembly of this translocation machine. The first step we will study is the binding of PA to receptors on human cells - this allows the toxin to target susceptible cells. We have discovered that the extracellular part of the receptor exists in two different conformations and that only one of these conformations is able to bind toxin. Furthermore, we have shown that another region of the receptor, located inside the cell, is able to bind the cytoskeleton protein actin. It is the binding of actin to the receptor that switches the receptor from the conformation that binds toxin to the conformation that does not bind toxin. We propose to study different parts of the receptor to determine how the binding to actin inside the cell is able to change the conformation of the receptor outside the cell. The second step in the assembly process we will study is the insertion of the toxin into the cell membrane. This is an essential event because membrane insertion forms a hole through which the toxic enzymes pass to the cell interior. The receptors stabilize the toxin until the toxin reaches an acidic region of the cell; the acidity breaks an interaction between the toxin and its receptor, which allows membrane insertion. We will study how the receptor controls insertion of the toxin and the interactions that allow insertion to occur in a highly efficient manner. The work described in this proposal elucidates fundamental aspects of protein function and regulation. The information obtained will be useful for the engineering of protein translocation nanomachines and will impact drug delivery systems.

column36: The ocular endocannabinoid system: Pharmacology of an endogenous lipid signaling system.
column37: Increased pressure in the eye is a major risk factor in glaucoma, an age-related blinding eye disease that results in death of neurons in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Abnormal blood flow and inflammatory responses in the eye may also contribute to glaucoma. Our research is examining drugs that target the ocular endocannabinoid system. This important biological system regulates key processes in the body, including blood flow and inflammation. Evidence suggests that the endocannabinoid system is part of the body's autoprotective machinery, with increases in the activity of this system acting to reduce tissue damage. Cannabinoid drugs, which include naturally occurring chemical constituents of the cannabis plant and their synthetic derivatives, act on components of the endocannabinoid system. Cannabinoids are able to reduce eye pressure and may have additional beneficial effects on ocular blood flow, immune responses, and neuronal survival. These chemicals mimic the actions of natural compounds found in the eye called endocannabinoids. We want to determine how cannabinoids and endocannabinoids work in the eye and whether the ocular endocannabinoid system constitutes a therapeutic target in the treatment of glaucoma and eye disease.

column36: Skin cell therapy for the long term treatment of alopecia areata
column37: Alopecia areata (AA), defined as a non-scarring autoimmune hair loss disease, has a serious impact on the quality of life for AA patients worldwide. It is well established that infiltrated immune cells, known as CD4+ and CD8+ lymphocytes, target the hair follicles of AA patients. Various therapeutic regimens are currently used for the treatment of AA; however, none of them can prevent or cure the disease. Our preliminary results generated from an AA mouse model revealed that none of the mice received skin cells producing an immunosuppressive factor known as IDO developed AA while 80% of control animals developed extensive AA within 8-16 weeks after transplantation of AA affected skin. Here we hypothesize that IDO expressing skin cell therapy can prevent the progression of AA by suppressing the CD4+ and CD8+ cells attacking hair follicles. To address this hypothesis, we will test 4 different objectives through which 1) The potential role of skin cell therapy not only in prevention but also in progression of AA in those patients who already suffer from this disease will be evaluated, 2) The factors that affect the capacity of IDO producing fibroblast therapy in reversing the autoimmune AA disease will be tested and finally 3) The last 2 objectives will reveal the mechanism by which this cell therapy improves or even cures this disease. In conclusion, we strongly believe that, if it is proven to be true, our novel cell therapy approach would overcome the AA autoimmunity and prevent the progression of AA. Potentially this may be a long lasting, possibly permanent treatment for patients who suffer from this devastating skin disorder.

column36: Language ability and structural brain development in preschool children: predictors of reading readiness
column37: Problems with language and reading are common in children, and can lead to lifelong difficulties in school and adult life (i.e., career). Structural brain abnormalities are associated with reading problems in school-aged children, and these abnormalities might exist before reading begins. However, very few studies have examined brain development in young children, and it is not known how brain structure and language are related during early childhood. Our objective is to investigate the relationships between language abilities and brain structure in young children (2.5-6.5 years), and how they are associated with early reading ability at school age (4.5-6.5 years). We think that brain areas known to be associated with language and reading in older children will be more mature in young children with better language abilities than in children with poor language ability. We also think that faster brain development will predict better early reading ability when children start school (age 4.5-6.5 years). To test this, we will measure language ability and brain structure using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in children aged 2.5-6.5 years. We will follow these children twice a year for two years, and measure their early reading skills at age 4.5-6.5 years. Understanding relationships between language, early reading, and structural brain maturation in young children will help identify times when treatments may be most effective. We hope that, ultimately, this will support healthy development in children and improve outcomes for children with language and reading difficulties.

column36: Imaging Brain Iron in Multiple Sclerosis: Development, Validation and Clinical Implementation
column37: Multiple sclerosis is the most common disease of the central nervous system among young adults and has a high prevalence in northern countries such as Canada, with highest incidence in Alberta. The cause is unknown and there is no cure yet. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) has been used for diagnosing and following multiple sclerosis in the clinic for over a quarter century. MRI is very helpful for diagnosing multiple sclerosis by looking at lesions, but less effective for following the disease progression after diagnosis, because lesions do not always relate to the clinical symptoms of the patient. New MRI methods are needed that can provide a better objective measure of the disease to help in patient management. Our overall goal is to provide new MRI methods for the clinic to follow the individual MS patient. We will invent new MRI methods that are sensitive to brain iron accumulation, which may be a marker of brain damage or neurodegeneration. These MRI methods will have a much closer correspondence to patient symptoms as measured by a disability scale. The invention takes place by evaluating the underlying MRI physics to determine more effective imaging methods. The methods that will be developed are then carefully tested and validated in a research setting before being used in our clinic to measure changes in patients over time. The clinical work involves collaboration with medical doctors who are specialists in multiple sclerosis and clinical imaging. The end product will be a transformation in the way MRI is used to follow multiple sclerosis, by providing an objective means to track disease progression using the new MRI methods.

column36: Molecular characterization of EpoR regulation in cancer progression
column37: Mutation in von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) gene causes VHL disease, which is characterized by the development of multiple tumours in multiple organs including the brain, spinal cord, retina, pancreas, adrenal gland, and kidney. We and others have shown that VHL protein promotes the degradation of a transcription factor called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). HIF maintains cellular oxygen homeostasis or balance, which is a vital organizing principle for human development and physiology. Moreover, dysregulation of oxygen homeostasis is associated with the development and/or progression of major human diseases, including cardiovascular and chronic pulmonary diseases and cancer. One of the key proteins upregulated by HIF under compromised oxygen availability is erythropoietin (EPO), which binds to EPO receptor (EPOR) to stimulate the production and expansion of oxygen-carrying red blood cells or erythropoiesis. Recently, we discovered for the first time that EPOR protein stability is regulated by oxygen and VHL, which raises the possibility that EPOR regulation is involved in cancer biology. Moreover, over the past two decades, human recombinant EPO has been administered to cancer patients to alleviate the symptoms of anaemia. However, recent randomized controlled trials in cancer patients have indicated that EPO treatment during chemotherapy increases the rate of cancer progression and death. In this proposal, we will elucidate the novel molecular mechanisms governing EPOR signaling and interrogate this new insight in the context of normal erythropoiesis as well as EPO-induced cancer progression model.

column36: Investigation of the role of PHACTR1 in the vascular endothelium and its impact on myocardial infarction risk
column37: The blockage of the coronary arteries, that is the main blood vessels that supply the heart in oxygen, can lead to myocardial infarction, also known as heart attack. Several factors influence the risk to suffer from a heart attack: sex, age, blood lipid levels, blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, etc. Whether or not close relatives had heart attacks is also an independent risk factor for the disease. This indicates that our genetic make-up (or DNA sequence) can predispose or protect someone from this heart condition. Previous human genetic studies have identified DNA sequence variation on chromosome 6 that influences myocardial infarction risk. My laboratory has linked these genetic variants to the activity of a gene called PHACTR1 in the cells that form the inner layer of blood vessels (endothelium). Using molecular, cellular and genomic methodologies, this project aims to characterize how PHACTR1 influences the endothelium, and consequently heart attack risk. In the long-term, this effort may guide the development of novel therapeutic strategies for cardiovascular diseases.

column36: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) and multifactorial diseases
column37: A sequence variant in an important enzyme of folate metabolism, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), increases risk for neural tube defects and may increase risk for several common diseases, including pregnancy complications and neuropsychiatric disorders. MTHFR is critical because it generates methyl donors for methylation reactions. The common variant is present in 5 to 20% of populations. We generated MTHFR-deficient mice to study complex disorders and identify ways to prevent or treat these common conditions. A second important goal is to evaluate the potential deleterious effects of high dietary folate since North Americans are ingesting much more folate following food fortification with folic acid and the extensive use of vitamin supplements. In recent studies with mutant mice, we identified motor and cognitive impairments with disturbances in metabolism of choline, an alternate methyl donor when folate is deficient. In folate-deficient mice, we observed lipid disturbances in liver which may also relate to decreased choline; these abnormalities can lead to fatty liver disease. We have shown that female mice that consume high levels of folate during pregnancy have delayed embryos, embryos with heart defects, and neonatal pups with cognitive impairment. In this application, we shall determine whether MTHFR deficiency in mice fed different diets (control, low folate, high fat) leads to liver disease. We shall also examine the impact of MTHFR deficiency and low folate or high folate diets during pregnancy on brain development in young pups. The mechanisms for these processes will be assessed by histological analyses, metabolite measurements, gene expression studies, and behavioural testing. We shall attempt to ameliorate negative outcomes with choline supplementation, since deficiency of this nutrient appears to contribute to liver and brain dysfunction.

column36: Mechanisms of genome instability induced by RNA splicing defects
column37: Cancer is a disease caused by mutations in normal genes. Due to so-called 'genome instability', most cancers have an increased frequency of mutations compared to normal cells. The yeast model system has proven to be a valuable tool in defining mechanisms of genome maintenance. My research program will define the causes and consequences of genome instability in yeast as a means to understand how cancers develop and how they can be selectively targeted with therapies. Specifically, we have shown that genes involved in a fundamental activity called RNA splicing were unexpectedly important for genome maintenance. Focusing on RNA splicing factors that have been linked to genome maintenance in both yeast and human cells, we will define how genome instability occurs when these splicing functions are disrupted. Some of the human counterparts of these splicing factors are frequently mutated in leukemia, breast, and other cancers. Therefore, another aim of the research will be to specifically test the consequences of these tumour-associated mutations on splicing function and genome maintenance.The work is of fundamental importance to defining the biological networks that normally protect our cells from genome instability and to understanding potential causes of genome instability in human disease.

column36: Central roles for Cdx in organizing the vertebrate embryo
column37: The development of the vertebrate body, including the neural tube and the spinal column, begins during early development and involves complex interactions between a number of different cell populations. Defects in any one of the many events essential to the successful completion of these processes can lead to devastating congenital malformations common in the human population, such as neural tube defects. A number of signaling molecules have been implicated in normal development, including the vitamin A derivative retinoic acid. Such molecules ultimately function by regulating the expression of target genes which then dictate cell behaviour. Work from our group has led to a hypothesis that such signaling pathways function in development in part through complex interactions with the Cdx family of transcription factors (Cdx1, Cdx2 and Cdx4). Indeed, the Cdx transcription factors are emerging as essential regulators of a number of fundamental events essential for normal vertebrate development. However, how these Cdx proteins function and the full scope of their roles in the developing embryo is poorly understood. Novel mouse models developed by our group have revealed new roles for the Cdx transcription factors. In the present application, we propose further analysis of these novel roles, with particular emphasis on defining the critical pathways that are regulated by Cdx members. The information forthcoming from these studies should have important bearing on our understanding not only of fundamental processes related to embryonic development, but may also shed light on the basis for certain congenital defects prevalent in the human population as well as several types of cancer in which Cdx mis-function has been implicated.

column36: Calcium-signalling and gene expression in human fibroblasts
column37: Millions of Canadians suffer from chronic diseases in which one of the main features is the destruction of body organs and excessive scarring of the tissue (fibrosis). Thousands of these people die each year from fibrotic diseases: in fact, it has been estimated that half of all deaths in the developing world occur as a direct consequence of fibrosis of body organs. Fibroblasts are cells embedded in the skin and walls of the organs: these are not only able to produce scar tissue, but also to contract and thereby modulate tissue stiffness. Changes in ion concentration including calcium have marked effects on fibroblast function. We want to investigate if these ion changes have a direct influence on the tissue strain and organ wall composition, and if correcting abnormal calcium levels in or around fibroblasts have a beneficial effect on chronic disease. We know that fibroblasts demonstrate very interesting calcium responses when they are stimulated by growth factors. So we want to look at the relationship between changes in calcium inside the cells and production of the scar tissue proteins (gene expression). We are able to get human fibroblasts from lung tissues removed during surgical procedures. We can then separate out the fibroblasts and study them using our special microscopes (confocal, laser-illuminated, fluorimetric microscope) in order to see the changes in calcium under various experimental conditions. column37: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects about 95% of the world's population. Although EBV doesn't cause serious problems in most people, EBV is the cause of a number of important cancers including Burkitt lymphoma, which is the most common childhood cancer in much of Africa. EBV also causes infectious mononucleosis ("mono") in substantial fraction of all adolescents and young adults in the developed world. Mono is not lethal, but results in enormous health care costs and missed school/work. A vaccine to prevent EBV infection or its associated diseases would be an invaluable global health intervention. A study clinician went to each of these family's homes every week for a year, tested the infants and their family members for EBV infection, examined the baby, and asked extensive questions about risk factors for infection and symptoms of illness. This represents the most comprehensive study of EBV infection ever performed. We precisely determined the time the babies became infected with EBV to within one week, and will be able to analyze what demographic and behavioral factors increase the risk of infection, and describe what symptoms of illness occur. Now we propose to go further, and use samples that were collected from these families to examine the genetic variation of the EBV strains that they were infected with, and to study what immune factors might prevent EBV infection or help to control the infection once it occurs. This type of information is essential to deciding what kind of EBV vaccine might be most effective, and to have the best chance of preventing EBV-related illness and cancer.

column37: Ligand-gated ion channels are membrane proteins stimulated by chemical compounds. They consist of two modules responsible for the binding to the ligand and the ion conduction, respectively. This will help to develop more effective drugs to alleviate the symptoms of migraine. Technically, we will use voltage-clamp fluorometry (i.e. simultaneous measurements of function and structural rearrangements), single molecule fluorescence and fluorescent unnatural amino acids in combination with molecular biology to establish links between structural and functional data

column36: Control of Movement: Reticulospinal circuits
column37: Perhaps the most fundamental thing we do is move - whether in speaking, in playing the piano or dancing, or lifting weights. Large parts of our central nervous systems are wired to ensure that we move appropriately for the task at hand. But how are we wired to move? There are multiple brain circuits involved. Some do the planning, make the decision, and select the appropriate movement. These circuits tell "command" neurons in the brain stem which movement to perform, and these neurons inform our organising circuits in the spinal cord that in turn tell our motor neurons how strongly to activate muscles. In this application, I propose to study command circuits - those between the brain stem and the spinal cord. These neurons live in a crowded place in the brain stem, the reticular formation. Some of these neurons are wired to prevent movement, whereas others are wired to cause movement. For example, prevention of movement is necessary when we dream, so reticular formation neurons that prevent movement are activated in REM sleep. Others are activated to initiate walking. I will use a variety of techniques (for example: genetic manipulations, electrical recordings, advanced microscopy of living tissue) to study the organisation of such "OFF" and "ON" systems, with the aim of better understanding how we move. As many neurologic diseases and injuries affect movement - for example, spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, dystonia, stroke, movement disorders, and other neurodegenerative diseases - this work has broad implications. This research does not aim to cure any specific disorder, but rather to develop strategies to improve the quality of life of people with any neurological diseases or injuries that affect movement. At the end of the proposed 5 years, we will have enhanced understanding of the organisation of motor command neurons in the reticular formation, and of the relationship between moving and not moving.

column36: Regulation of ETS Transcription Factors
column37: Transcription factors are proteins that help read the genes encoded within our DNA. These factors are like "lego-blocks," with three-dimensional shapes that enable them to join other proteins and build the molecular machines that interpret our genetic code. In a precisely choreographed dance, the shapes of these lego-blocks can change, causing them to change their partners and thereby control when and how different genes are read. These shape changes result from chemical modifications, such as phosphorylation, that occur in response to cellular signals. Cancers can result when this dance is directed improperly. Our broad research goal is to understand how gene reading by a family of transcription factors, called ETS, is directed in normal and cancerous cells. In particular, we are investigating how several family members can inhibit their own ability to bind DNA as part of the control process for gene reading. We use NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) spectroscopy as a "molecular microscope" to determine the shapes of these factors with atomic detail. Excitingly, we have found that the ETS proteins are not rigid lego-blocks, but rather, are more jello-like, flickering between shapes that can or cannot bind DNA as required for each step of this dance. Indeed, the power of NMR spectroscopy lies with uncovering how protein shapes change with time. Collectively, our research will help provide the molecular "blueprint" of a cell necessary for developing methods to diagnosis, treat, and prevent ETS-related cancers.

column36: Masculinities, Lifetime Violence and Health
column37: Violence is a major public health problem. The harmful health effects of violence have been well studied in women. Men also experience and commit violence at home, in workplaces, and in public. Rates of public violence such as assault and homicide are greater for men. Yet we know little about the health effects of lifetime violence for men. In Canada, men die earlier than women and are more often disabled from accidents and chronic health problems such as heart disease and depression. These major causes of death in men (e.g. accidents, heart disease, suicide, homicide) can be linked to violence through injury, stress effects, or behaviour such as risky substance use. Beliefs about what it means to be a man also shape men's health. Common thinking is that to measure up to being a man (independent, tough, fearless), men take part in risky actions that lead to disease or harm. But not all men think of being a man in the same way. In this study, we will examine how men see themselves as men, their patterns of lifetime violence and health outcomes. A community sample of 600 English-speaking New Brunswick men ages 19 to 65 will be asked to take part in a survey by internet, phone, or in person. We will ask about their current health, the nature and extent of violence exposure they have had in their lifetimes, and how they see themselves as men. Blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, weight and height will be measured for some men who take part. Using this information, we will explore the links among lifetime violence, ways of being a man, and health, specifically mental health, chronic pain and risk for heart disease. To better understand these links, we will ask 50 men to talk to us about their health, violence experience, and view of being a man. The findings of this study will be useful for programs and policies promoting and managing men's health.

Thus, the HPA axis must be both tightly regulated and equally responsive to the demands of stress. Studies in humans and rodents have shown that when exposure to the same stimulus is repeated in a predictable manner, the magnitude of the glucocorticoid response can decline or habituate to successive stimulus exposures. Moreover, impaired HPA axis habituation and maladaptive behavioral coping styles have been proposed as leading causes for mood disorders in humans. Converging data from our rodent models suggest that stress habituation is met by an increase in the activity of AVP-containing pathways and V1A receptors in the brain. Thus, rats bearing central injections of a V1A receptor antagonist fail to show a decline in glucocorticoid secretion during repeated stress. This finding may be linked to changes in testosterone secretion during different times of the lifespan. We found that animals robbed of testosterone exposure at birth, as well as in adulthood, express a lower capacity for HPA axis habituation. We also have evidence to show that coping styles are positively correlated with AVP expression in brain regions known to regulate behavioral and hormonal responses to stress. We hypothesize that changes in central AVP and V1A receptor function play a critical role in stress adaptation. Experiments are proposed to make novel inroads on these mechanisms, certain to increase our understanding why some individuals are vulnerable to stress.

column37: The barriers that protect the cell from its external environment and divide the cell into regions or zones are called membranes. Many different types of lipids (ie. fats) are assembled together to make these membranes. In order for a cell to duplicate or change into another type of cell, specific types of lipids must be made to form new membranes or other structures in the cell. The most abundant lipid required for this purpose in phosphatidylcholine (called PC). The conversion of normal cells into cancer cells is accompanied by increased production of PC that allows these cells to survive and grow rapidly into tumours. This rapid production PC allows cancer cells to make more membranes that are required for growth and cell division. Similarly, increased production of PC occurs when cells are converted into fat storage cells called adipocytes. We will study how PC is made in cancer and fat cells, and identify common mechanisms that control the production of PC. These studies will provide fundamental insights into the relationship between fat metabolism and cell growth that could be used in the treatment or management of cancer and obesity.

column36: The Baby & Microbiota of the Intestine Project (Baby & Mi)
column37: There are many microorganisms that normally grow in the gut and keep us healthy. Babies are born without gut organisms but pick them up early in life, usually by coming into contact with microorganisms from their mother, which creates a gut flora, or mixture of microorganisms. Our study will determine if different birth experiences and exposures early in life change how the microorganisms in the gut develop after the birth. We think that if the baby grows a gut flora early in life that is different than usual it may stay that way into later life. Other research has shown that people with obesity and with diabetes have gut flora that is different than normal. It is possible that changes in the gut flora in the early days of life may be associated with conditions later in childhood such as obesity. We will test if babies who develop unusual gut flora in the early days and weeks of life still have unusual flora when they are one and three years old. We will also test if the gut flora is related to health outcomes at 3 years. About 240 pregnant women, planning to have a vaginal birth will be enrolled in this study along with their babies. Women will provide 8 diapers that contain stool from their babies in the first 3 years of life in order for the gut organisms to be analysed. We will also monitor the growth of each baby until they are three years old. A small number of studies of the early gut flora have been done by others but none have been done with this many babies, or collected as much detailed information as our study will collect. Many studies looked only at one stool sample. We will be able to examine changes over the first three years of life for a moderate size group of babies, which will strengthen our findings. Our study will be important in helping care providers understand the importance of how babies are born in terms of the influence it might have much later in life. These findings could change the way we practice.

column37: Leukemia and lymphoma (T cell malignancies) are among the fastest rising cancers in North America. Furthermore, their treatment with chemotherapy is limited because of the development of drug resistance. The proposed studies will involve clinical samples from patients with T-ALL and the use of animal models of T cell leukemia. Findings from these studies are likely to further our understanding on how T-ALL cancer cells develop. In addition, our studies may lead to the discovery of novel therapeutic strategies and to the identification of novel biomarkers, which can predict the therapeutic response and clinical outcome of T-ALL patients.

column36: Neural mechanisms of duration tuning in the mammalian inferior colliculus.
column37: Communication is a large part of what makes us human and is vital to personal health. Impediments to communication have consequences to one's confidence, perception of the world, and inclusion in employment and social activities. At times communication for healthy individuals can be challenging, but imagine the difficulty for someone with an auditory deficit. Understanding the brain's code that is the precursor to hearing can mean opening up a whole new world of communication for persons with a hearing disorder. The goal of my research is to understand the rules the mammalian central nervous system uses to encode and process acoustic information. The projects are aimed at discovering mechanisms underlying a specialized form of auditory temporal processing--neural tuning to sound duration--and to relate these mechanisms to behaviour. The auditory midbrain (inferior colliculus) contains neurons with responses highly tuned to signal duration; however, the mechanisms and pathways that create these duration-tuned neurons are still unknown, as is their role to normal hearing. The proposed experiments involve behavioural studies, recording electrical potentials from duration-tuned neurons to sound stimulation and documenting response properties, computational studies and informational analyses of the responses, and the use of drugs to block synaptic inputs and biological dyes for tracing anatomical connections to reveal the circuitry underlying duration tuning. Understanding the neural mechanisms of duration coding addresses broad issues, such as why there are multiple parallel processing pathways in the central auditory system and what role they play in hearing. The foundational knowledge gained from my research will be of enormous benefit to understanding behaviour as diverse as speech recognition and music perception, and ultimately it should have broad applications for the diagnosis and treatment of sensorineural hearing loss and language disorders.

column37: There is strong evidence that the mother's nutrition, health, and environment during the earliest stages of pregnancy immediately after conception can significantly affect the health of the embryo and the fetus and placenta into which it develops. Also, the treatment of human infertility by assisted reproduction technologies (ART), in which multiple eggs are obtained from women, fertilized, and cultured for an extended period before being transferred into the uterus, has been very effective and produced millions of babies, but there is increasing evidence that how eggs and very early embryos are handled during ART can cause health problems in the fetus, placenta, and offspring. In this work, we will be investigating mechanisms that may be important in causing such problems, concentrating on one set of biochemical pathways that we have studied in embryos that may be involved in setting up patterns of gene expression in the fetal/placental unit that can then last throughout life. This pathway involves "methyl groups." Methyl groups are transferred to many other compounds in cells including DNA (the genes), and such "methylation" is instrumental in determining which genes are active. We have found that the methyl groups in embryos come not only from folic acid like in most cells, but also from a compound called betaine. We hope to show that creating the conditions in which these pathways can function normally in eggs and very early embryos will prevent some of the problems that arise in fetuses and placentas during pregnancy, and in babies.

column37: Obesity and obesity-associated diabetes are projected to overshadow all other health problems in the coming decades. Obesity is a metabolic condition wherein excess calories are converted into fat and stored in the abdomen and other parts of the body. Theoretically, regulating calorie intake by eating quality foods and increasing physical activity will help to tackle obesity. However, implementing this seemingly simple solution is deterred by lifestyle and socioeconomic factors. Moreover, while motivation and life style changes are effective in treating moderately obese individuals, their use is limited in extremely obese patients with diabetes and other complications, who need medical treatment. The inflammation induced by the excess fat is a major culprit in the development of obesity related diabetes. Recent advances have suggested that burning the fat by generation of heat by the body can be a useful mechanism to fight diabetes and obesity. However, our knowledge on how inflammation regulates the generation of heat is minimal. We have identified interleukin-15 (for short IL-15) as one of these inflammatory factors. We have used mice lacking IL-15 as a model system to study the role of IL-15 in obesity. Our findings show that these mice fed with high fat diet do not become obese, whereas normal mice rapidly gain weight. We have observed that these mice have increased capacity to burn fat by generating heat. We propose to study how IL-15 enables weight gain in these mice and obese human patients. This knowledge could help in developing new strategies to treat obese patients.

These studies will provide fundamental insights into the role of these lipid transfer proteins in cells, and their importance in prevention of abnormal accumulation of cholesterol and other lipids that contribute to disease.

column37: The small resistance arteries that supply blood to the brain are able to react to changes in blood pressure by changing their diameter to maintain appropriate levels of blood flow under varied physiological conditions. Vessel diameter is altered through the contraction, or relaxation of smooth muscle cells within the vessel wall in response to increased, or decreased blood pressure. Accumulating evidence indicates three major cellular mechanisms control the level of contractile activation of the smooth muscle cells. The big unanswered question is how these mechanisms are activated by increased blood pressure. We will test the hypothesis that specialized surface membrane sites of connection between the extracellular fibres that hold tissues together, and the internal cytoskeleton of the smooth muscle cells, called integrin adhesions, are responsible for converting the mechanical stimulus of blood pressure into a physiological response, in this case, smooth muscle contraction. The molecular basis of the response and the role of integrin adhesions as the mechanotransducer will be studied in normal rats, and in a rat model of type 2 diabetes in which the blood pressure-dependent mechanism for control of smooth muscle contraction is dysfunctional. To accomplish this goal, we will monitor blood vessel diameter and the activation state of key adhesion and contractile proteins in the smooth muscle cells at varied pressures in small segments of arteries kept in short term culture. Understanding the basic mechanisms responsible for this fundamental physiologic mechanism and how alterations in these mechanisms contribute to dysfunction will provide guidance in the development of novel therapies to correct blood flow to the brain. The basic principles identified in this study will have wider implications because an identical dysfunctional control of blood flow is present in other situations, including stroke, Alzheimer disease and aging.

column37: Opioids are the most effective analgesics known but their clinical use is limited by severe side effects such as respiratory depression, constipation dependence and tolerance. This information can be then used in the production of novel analgesics with longer lasting therapeutic actions.

column37: Aboriginal people in Canada are aging faster than the overall Canadian population, and report more chronic conditions earlier in life. Metis seniors also report lower health status than First Nations. Very little is known about the aging experiences, aspirations, and support needs of Aboriginal seniors overall, and even less about under researched Metis peoples. In partnership with the Metis community of Ile-a-la-Crosse, SK, and guided by Aboriginal ecological epistemology, this population health intervention research project will fill the knowledge gap and provide evidence of the effectiveness of current and emerging program and policy interventions promoting aging well for Metis and other Aboriginal peoples. Over a five-year period, this project will reveal concepts and experiences of healthy aging in discussion groups, interviews, and photo projects with children, adults, and seniors. Seniors will also complete activity, diet, and quality of life measures at regular intervals. Finally, formal and informal supports and services available to seniors in the community will be systematically identified, with a selection undergoing evaluation. Along with effectiveness of selected interventions, gaps and overlaps between them will be identified. Our analysis will consider sex and gender to better understand the specific needs of men and women for a healthy aging experience. Graduate student and community trainees will be involved in all stages of data collection, and in the design, piloting, and evaluation of mini interventions. The findings will enhance aging well strategies in the research community, and more broadly in other Aboriginal communities, looking to improve the health status of this growing population in Canada.

column36: Specific inhibitors of ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases
column37: Effective strategies to treat cancer patients rely on our ability to interfere with cellular processes that are deregulated in cancer cells. In recent years, abnormalities in protein turnover states are frequently observed in many types of cancer. In most cases, this can be attributed to the misbehaviour of a cellular machinery employing a small protein called ubiquitin, which attaches to target proteins and acts as a signal for their destruction. Therefore, ubiquitin ligases (that add ubiquitin to proteins) and deubiquitinases (that remove ubiquitin from proteins) have attracted increasing attention as novel targets for drug development. These enzymes are crucial mediators of key intracellular processes and manipulation of them will have profound impacts on protein activity, localization, and life span. Unfortunately, the lack of selective molecules to prevent functions of these enzymes, called inhibitors, has severely hampered attempts to manipulate them for therapeutic benefits. The goal of this project is to develop highly specific and potent inhibitors for oncogenic ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases. Using protein engineering technology, we propose to make ubiquitin-like molecules that will associate tightly with these enzymes in a manner that will block its catalytic function, and thus, act as inhibitors. We will validate their inhibitory function in cancer cell lines using established biological assays. Additional structural analyses of critical contacts that mediate specificity and affinity will further aid the design of chemical inhibitors. In conclusion, this work will generate invaluable tools to understand and modulate activity of ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases in human cancer cells and will shed light on effective cancer therapy.

column37: Breast cancer is a significant health concern in Canada, with an estimated 23,800 women being diagnosed and 5,100 dying from the disease in 2013. column37: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a highly familial, severe recurrent mood disorder that affects 2-5% of adolescents and adults. Offspring of parents with BD can help us learn about the causes of this illness before symptoms appear. For reasons yet unknown, people with BD and their unaffected relatives often have brain circuitry problems. If our predictions are accurate, this study may suggest the need to begin thinking of, and treating, BD as a multi-system disorder that affects both brain and body.

column37: Being born too early (preterm) is one of the leading causes of major disability. Babies born preterm often develop motor, language and learning problems, and frequently do poorly at school. Our work shows that when a preterm baby experiences repeated pain, the baby's brain develops less well and language and learning problems are increased in childhood. Different NICUs treat pain in different ways, and comparing these methods can show us the better (and possibly best) ways to treat pain in preterm babies. To see if this is true, we will compare pain treatments in preterm babies in three NICUs to see if there is a relationship of pain treatment with the baby's brain and longer-term development. We will follow the babies from birth to 3 years of age. We will use magnetic resonance imaging to measure important aspects of brain development so that we can study how it may be affected by pain treatments a baby receives. We will determine if there are NICU pain treatments that are bad for brain development, and if so, provide evidence to minimize use of these treatments. Our results will help hospitals, doctors and nurses make better decisions about NICU practices and improve the health of these children.

column36: Penetrating wound induced epileptogenesis
column37: Immediate response to brain damage is a generation of seizure activities. These seizures are reasonably well controlled by drugs and if untreated they terminate within days. Thereafter the patient recovers (at least in terms of seizures). However, months or years after penetrating brain wounds occur, about 70% of patients develop epilepsy characterized by spontaneous generation of unprovoked seizures. These seizures are not well controlled by drugs. The process between brain damage and onset of epilepsy is called epileptogenesis. The mechanisms of epileptogenesis are largely unknown and therefore, there are no effective therapies against epileptogenesis. Prevention of epileptogenesis will prevent epilepsy. We obtained preliminary data showing that in adult but not young cats and mice penetrating cortical wounds lead to development of epilepsy. How epileptogenesis happens: hypothesis? The normal brain has some level of excitability, which is a balance of excitation and inhibition. Brain damage reduces mainly excitatory influences. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms up-regulate network excitability to bring it to initial level. That what is happening in young animals. In adult animals the same up-regulation of excitability occurs, but it does not stop when a sufficient level of excitability reached and therefore, it brings network to hyperexcitable state - epilepsy. What do we want to do? Basically two things: (1) To describe physiological processes taking place during epileptogenesis and (2) Based on understanding of changes in network activity and starting from the moment of trauma to stimulate traumatized cortex aiming to increase excitability and to prevent epileptogenesis.

column37: Des etudes rapportent que l'exposition au stress chronique au travail (contraintes psychosociales) contribue au developpement de problemes de la memoire (fonction cognitive) avec l'age. L'inflammation et l'oxydation sont deux mecanismes d'action impliques dans le vieillissement. Des marqueurs d'inflammation et d'oxydation sont mesurables dans le sang. Des travaux ont observe que certains marqueurs inflammatoires seraient associes a des problemes affectant la fonction cognitive. D'autres suggerent que les contraintes psychosociales au travail seraient associees a des marqueurs d'inflammation. Les telomeres sont des marqueurs d'oxydation et d'inflammation dans le sang. Les telomeres constituent la partie terminale protectrice des chromosomes, et leur raccourcissement a ete associe au stress psychosocial et au vieillissement cellulaire. Il est donc raisonnable de penser que les marqueurs inflammatoires et les telomeres pourraient etre impliques dans la relation entre les contraintes psychosociales au travail et la fonction cognitive. Notre etude vise a evaluer l'effet d'une exposition chronique aux contraintes psychosociales au travail sur les concentrations sanguines de trois marqueurs, deux inflammatoires (CRP et IL-6), et un davantage oxydatif (la longueur des telomeres) et la fonction cognitive. Ce projet sera mene aupres d'environ 4500 personnes recrutees en 1991-93 pour une etude sur les contraintes psychosociales au travail. Les donnees sur les marqueurs inflammatoires, les telomeres et la fonction cognitive seront recueillies en 2015-18. Les contraintes psychosociales au travail sont considerees comme une priorite dans les politiques de prevention en sante puisqu'elles touchent une proportion importante de travailleurs (20%) et qu'elles peuvent etre ameliorees. Notre etude pourra contribuer a identifier des facteurs menant a des problemes de fonction cognitive plus severe comme la maladie d'Alzheimer, permettant ainsi d'agir en prevention de cette maladie.

column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a global health problem that affects 3% of the world population, including over 300 000 Canadians. Recently, a drug used to sequester this microRNA in HCV-infected patients was demonstrated to have long-lasting suppression of HCV, with no evidence of viral resistance or adverse side effects. column37: In 2008, approximately 17 million deaths worldwide were attributed to diseases of the cardiovascular system by the World Health Organization. It is predicted that by 2030, almost 23.6 million people will die from heart disease and stroke. Furthermore, these problems are increasing in prevalence in both women and the developing world, making cardiovascular health an increasing significant target to improve the health and well-being of society. In the late 1990s, a small protein hormone, named apelin, was discovered in the human body which has a wide variety of physiological functions; notably a pivotal role in the regulation of blood pressure. Apelin has been shown to have potent vasodilator activity, which effectively widens blood vessels and lowers blood pressure. Recent work on apelin has shown that it additionally plays a significant role in the recovery of damaged heart and arterial tissues after heart attacks, leading to improved chances of survival in mouse models. Despite all these beneficial cardiovascular effects, this molecule only has a short lifespan of a few minutes in the bloodstream before other proteins in the blood cut it into smaller fragments. We propose to use chemical synthesis to make analogues of apelin that retain similar shape (conformation) of this natural hormone, while altering the specific sites that are cut by proteins in the bloodstream. The slight variations in structure introduced will allow the apelin analogs to become more resistant to being cut, thereby prolonging the beneficial physiological effects. This will provide stable long-lasting drug candidates for further development and testing as therapeutic agents.

column36: Tinnitus, Chronic Stress and Auditory Cortex Plasticity
column37: It is well known that excessive exposure to loud noise can result in permanent hearing loss. A common corollary to this noise-induced hearing loss is tinnitus, the subjective perception of a phantom sound which is often described as a "ringing in the ears." For ~10% of the general population, tinnitus is a persistent disturbance that can lead to sleep problems, difficulty concentrating and, in some cases, severe forms of depression, all of which can negatively affect one's quality of life and productivity. Unfortunately for tinnitus sufferers, a lack of understanding of the brain changes responsible for the phantom perception has hindered efforts to devise effective treatment. Also, it remains puzzling why only a subset of individuals exposed to loud noise go on to develop persistent tinnitus. The present proposal will use a combination of neuroanatomical techniques, recordings of brain activity and behavioral testing in a rat model to investigate the neural basis of tinnitus, and to determine whether chronic stress prior to noise exposure represents a significant risk factor for developing tinnitus. Rats will be trained in a behavioral task to report the presence/absence of tinnitus, and electrodes implanted in their brain will record the neural activity associated with the phantom auditory perception. By tracking each rat's behavioral performance and how its brain activity changes following noise exposure, we will be able to determine the neural basis of tinnitus. Additional experiments will induce chronic stress in rats using an established protocol in the weeks prior to noise exposure to determine whether chronic stress increases tinnitus susceptibility. A final series of experiments will investigate how chronic stress alone affects the brain's ability to process sound. Collectively, this proposal will provide important information as to how the brain is affected by two common conditions in modern society: excessive noise exposure and chronic stress.

column37: The demographics of our aging population present alarming future economic and social challenges for our health care systems. Effective therapies are not available to reduce the burdens of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's. column36: The cause and mechanism of oocyte elimination during meiotic prophase progression in the mouse
column37: Women are born with finite numbers of oocytes (immature eggs), and continually lose them with age, thus limiting their reproductive life span. When the oocyte reserve reaches a threshold, hormones are not properly produced by the ovary; and menopause ensues. The oocyte reserve in mammals is limited because all germ cells (the precursor of oocytes) stop proliferation and enter meiosis (a specific cell division which produces the haploid genome) to become oocytes in fetal life, and, in addition, more than half of the initial oocyte population is eliminated before birth. During this period, paternal and maternal homologous chromosomes pair, synapse and recombine; these events are essential for securing proper chromosome segregation in oocytes and generating genetic diversity in the offspring. We hypothesize that a failure in meiotic synapsis or recombination (asynapsis) in oocytes initiates a cascade of cellular events leading to elimination of oocytes carrying asynapsis, thus minimizing the risk of aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number) in embryos. Aneuploidy is the major cause of embryonic death, stillborn, and live-born infants with chromosomal anomalies. Consequently, problems with proper oocyte elimination during Meiotic Prophase I could influence a woman's fertility and the health of her offspring. To test our hypothesis, we propose (1) to delineate the mechanism regulating the apoptotic (programmed cell death) pathway leading to oocyte elimination, (2) to identify the mechanism by which persistent chromosome asynapsis leads to apoptotic elimination of oocytes, and (3) to evaluate the chromosomal integrity of oocytes that survive when apoptotic elimination is circumvented. The results of these studies will clarify the role of oocyte elimination during normal ovarian development and provide insight regarding the genetic mechanisms that underlie an increased risk of aneuploidy.

column36: Cognitive outcome in children born very preterm; longitudinal measures of brain structure & function from birth
column37: Every year in Canada more than 4,000 babies are born premature, 2 months or more before their due date. At least half of these preterm babies will have academic and behavioural problems when they start school, which is a concern for families, the education and health care systems. We have studied 100 very preterm born babies from birth, using advanced brain imaging, four times over their first 4 years of life. No other research team has this extensive experience, comparing brain and behavioural data in the very preterm-born children. The current study will determine (i) what markers recorded in the first weeks of life predict cognitive and social difficulties for that infant when he/she reaches school age; and (ii) with the proposed additional brain imaging studies, why they have these problems. Our brain imaging studies in the newborn period have provided important new information on the early brain development in these babies that we can relate to their outcome. We propose to study advanced thinking abilities (mental flexibility, inhibition and emotional processing), which are important for school and social skills, at 6 and 8 years of age in this cohort that we have been following from birth. We will use a technique that measures brain function, magnetoencephalography (MEG), in preterm and term-born children. We will also analyse the brain structural changes over the life-time period of the preterm-born children. This research will enable us to link brain imaging in infancy, and the MEG measures of brain function, to cognitive and social abilities as these difficulties emerge at school age. Therapies for children born very preterm can be successful, but are intensive and expensive; the knowledge from studies such as ours will help decide which children should be enrolled in these targeted interventions, which will allow the reduction or elimination of the cognitive and social challenges that this vulnerable group of children experience.

column36: Optimizing physician training in motivational communication (MC) skills for health behavior change
column37: A cluster of poor health behaviours or lifestyle factors (i.e., smoking, poor diet, drinking, physical inactivity) have been identified as major causes of chronic disease (e.g., heart and lung disease) and premature death. As a result, the demand for training in MC has risen drastically. Despite the fact these programs are being widely offered across Canada, we know very little about how successful they have been at teaching physicians the skills of MC. Ultimately, the results of this study will be used to better inform the design of MC programs offered to physicians across Canada. column36: Genomic analysis of cholera transmission and microevolution
column37: Vibrio cholerae is a waterborne pathogen that causes 3-5 million cases of cholera and over 100,000 deaths annually, mostly in Bangladesh. The increasing burden of cholera, the inability to achieve benchmarks for sanitation and safe water, and the emergence of pandemic strains of V. cholerae with increased virulence and environmental persistence underscore the need to understand and interrupt the transmission of cholera. Current cholera vaccines are only ~60-85% effective, and immunity lasts for only 2-3 years. Several lines of evidence suggest that V. cholerae was introduced into Haiti by asymptomatic carriers, but the reasons why some infections are asymptomatic, and other highly virulent, are still poorly understood. Also poorly understood is the relative importance of person-to-person (as opposed to waterborne) cholera transmission, and how V. cholerae evolves and adapts within individual infected patients. This research proposal will use whole genome sequencing of V. cholerae strains from cholera patients and their healthy household contacts in Bangladesh and Haiti in order to track the transmission and evolution of V. cholerae in real time. On an applied level, this research may lead to the identification of V. cholerae mutations associated with more severe disease and more effective transmission. These mutations could then be used to design field surveillance tests to identify strains with pandemic potential before they spread - both within endemic regions like Bangladesh, and also globally. Mapping and predicting immune-escape mutations will facilitate the design of a much-needed next generation of cholera vaccines capable of dealing with V. cholerae within-patient diversity and escape mutants. Finally, if person-to-person transmission is found to be an important factor in cholera transmission, this would suggest that more aggressive prophylactic treatment of household contacts may be a highly effective means of controlling epidemics.

column36: Pavlovian alcohol cues and relapse to alcoholism
column37: Remaining sober is a significant problem faced by treatment-seeking alcoholics. Relapse rates are high, and the factors that provoke relapse are poorly understood. Clinical research suggests that relapse can be facilitated by craving for alcohol, which is a conditioned response elicited by cues in the environment that signal alcohol availability. A better understanding of the psychological and biological processes that control responses elicited by alcohol-predictive cues would undoubtedly benefit treatment strategies aimed at preventing relapse. To this end, we use animal models to study the behavioural and neural mechanisms that mediate the formation and expression of learned associations between environmental stimuli and alcohol. On the basis of our prior research, we propose that glutamate in the basolateral amygdala is critical for the expression of alcohol-seeking behaviour elicited by Pavlovian alcohol cues. To test this hypothesis we will use established neuropharmacological techniques to comprehensively investigate the contribution of glutamate receptors in the basolateral amygdala to cue-induced, alcohol-seeking behaviour. We will also use cutting-edge optogenetic tools to study how afferent projections from the prefrontal cortex and ventral hippocampus to the basolateral amygdala mediate responses elicited by Pavlovian alcohol cues. By pinpointing the neurobiological mechanisms that control responding to alcohol cues, we hope to arrive at a better understanding of how to prevent the capacity of alcohol cues to induced relapse.

column37: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGFB) is a cytokine that acts as a tumor suppressor but in lung tumors it switches roles and stimulates tumor metastasis. column36: Inhibitory control of hippocampal inhibitory circuits: cellular mechanisms and function
column37: The everyday life of humans and animals relies on spatial navigation and the recollection of previous experiences and information. These critical types of behavior are accomplished via the activation of several cortical structures, including the hippocampus. In freely moving rodents, two classes of hippocampal neurons are active during spatial navigation: excitatory pyramidal cells and inhibitory interneurons. There is ample evidence that pyramidal cells code for specific locations in an environment, whereas interneurons coordinate the activity of pyramidal cells by providing well-timed inhibition. Hence, hippocampal interneurons are considered as "traffic lights" responsible for the proper routing of information during navigation. However, this raises an important question: if inhibition is fundamental for hippocampal computations, are there specific inhibitory mechanisms that control the activity of interneurons themselves? Earlier anatomical reports indicate that a higher-level inhibitory circuitry specialized in innervating interneurons exists in the hippocampus. We discovered that some cells that express the vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) exhibit a remarkable and highly selective connectivity with hippocampal interneurons. These "VIP members" of the hippocampus control the activity of different inhibitory circuits, thus allowing the coordination of the whole hippocampal network. Moreover, alterations in interneuron inhibition occur in the elderly and in several pathologies, including epilepsy, traumatic brain injury, and Alzheimer disease. To find ways to prevent several disorders, we aim to understand the cellular and functional organization of the VIP circuitry, such as the number of different subtypes of VIP cells residing in the hippocampus, the nature of their targets, the mechanisms of their recruitment during network activity, and their functional role for hippocampal computations under normal conditions and during epileptogenesis.

column36: Multimodal Assessment For Predicting Specific Pathological Substrate in Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration
column37: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the most common cause of dementia before the age of 60. It is characterized by progressive impairment of behavior (behavioral variant FTD or bvFTD) or language (primary progressive aphasia or PPA). Three other clinical entities strongly linked to FTD at a clinical and pathological level are corticobasal syndrome (CBS), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and FTD-Motor neuron disease. Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), the underlying pathology responsible for the different clinical syndromes is heterogeneous with molecular abnormalities in three different proteins implicated: Tau, TDP-43 and Fused in Sarcoma (FUS). It is difficult to predict the underlying pathology in many of these syndromes but the emergence of protein-specific treatments warrants accurate diagnosis of the clinical syndrome as well as the causative protein. Although some syndromes are more often associated with one protein abnormality, in many cases, it is still impossible to predict the underlying pathology with certainty. With the development of a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) Tau ligand, it will be possible to diagnose Tau invivo. Unfortunately, PET is not readily available and the relationship between PET Tau binding and MRI as well as cerebrospinal fluid levels of neurodegenerative markers is unknown. The overall goal of this project is to use a multimodal approach that includes clinical, neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid data to predict the underlying pathology and thus guide treatment.

column37: Pre-menopausal women are less likely to suffer from heart disease than are men, but this advantage disappears with age. column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a rare inherited disorder in which the abnormal gene codes for a protein (mutant huntingtin, mHtt) that over time accumulates in the brain, killing nerve cells and causing disease. This disease typically occurs in mid life, progresses to death over 10-30 years and is incurable. To date the problem in HD has been thought to be due to nerve cells producing their own, genetically coded for, abnormal mHtt which then causes them to dysfunction and die. Recently though, we have found in HD patients - who were transplanted with fetal tissue designed to replace cells lost to the disease process - that the abnormal mHtt could be seen in the transplant. This mHtt could only have got into the transplant from the patient as the grafted tissue was from unaffected donors. This unique observation forms the basis of this application as we now investigate the theory that mHtt can be transferred between cells either via host nerve cell connections and/or from circulating immune cells that can deliver the mHtt into the brain via inflamed, leaky blood vessels. This will be investigated using a range of techniques including studies with animals genetically engineered to carry the HD gene, cell cultures, state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques that allow to visualize cells within living tissue in real time, and blood and brain samples from HD patients. If true this new theory would have wide ranging implications not just for HD, but other similar diseases, and bring with it a totally new therapeutic approach to this currently incurable condition.

column37: At its core, cancer is a problem of uncontrolled cell multiplication. Because genes that promote this unregulated cell division are carried on chromosomes, losing or gaining extra copies of some chromosomes is one of the most frequent ways by which cancer cells acquire the ability to grow without restraint. In particular, we propose to remove the negative tags on condensin and determine how this affects the ability of cells to maintain chromosome structure and to allow effective separation of chromosomes during cell multiplication. We also want to understand how these negative charges affect condensin functions at the molecular level. The characterization of this novel mechanism will likely provide crucial insights into the specific causes of cancer, how we can detect them better and, finally, how we can treat them more efficiently.

column37: Pre-eclampsia is high blood pressure developing in mid-pregnancy that makes the mother unwell and leads to premature delivery or death of the developing baby. The placenta connects the developing baby to its mother and is mostly responsible for this disease. To date the only cure is delivery to remove the placenta. The high blood pressure is due to spasm of the mother's blood vessels; normally these vessels relax in pregnancy to reduce blood pressure. This proposal is designed to understand how the placenta stops the mother's blood vessels from relaxing. Maternal blood from the placenta is filtered by her lungs. Whatever causes her blood vessels to spasm must cross her lungs, either as very small particles or as protein signals in her bloodstream. Many different types of cells make these particles. They contain signals to be taken up and used by the target cells. These particles are called exosomes. They are of great interest because they contain genetic information that changes the behavior of the target cell. In pre-eclampsia we suspect these placental particles are shed into maternal blood, cross her lungs, and enter the endothelial cells lining her blood vessels (arteries) that control blood pressure. Once inside endothelial cells, we suspect the exosome signals stop her blood vessels from relaxing - causing high blood pressure. Our work is important because the blood-thinner drug heparin stops some women getting severe pre-eclamspia. column36: Role of scleraxis in cardiac fibrosis and wound healing
column37: The walls of the heart are strengthened by a supporting framework ("extracellular matrix") made primarily of a protein called collagen. In response to stresses such as high blood pressure, cells in the heart called myofibroblasts make additional collagen to strengthen the damaged heart wall and help the heart to maintain its function. After heart attack, a collagen-rich scar is formed to prevent rupture of the heart. However, matrix production is a double-edged sword - too much causes the heart walls to stiffen, impairing heart contraction and relaxation. Excessive collagen accumulation ("fibrosis") is a significant clinical challenge, affecting millions of patients worldwide. Drug treatments targeting fibrosis are lacking, due in part to the fact that we do not fully understand the fibrotic process. Designing drugs to target fibrosis requires a better understanding of how excess collagen is made. Our previous research indicates that a protein called scleraxis is an important new regulator of collagen synthesis. Our work shows that scleraxis directly activates the gene encoding a key cardiac collagen that is largely responsible for fibrosis. Furthermore, we have found that interfering with scleraxis leads to blockade of collagen production in isolated cells. The current proposal will expand on these discoveries by determining whether the loss of scleraxis will blunt collagen projection in animal models of high cardiac pressure and heart attack. This information is critical if we are to target fibrosis without affecting scar formation. We will test whether mice that lack the scleraxis gene become resistant to fibrosis, and whether lack of scleraxis impairs scar formation. We will also identify other genes regulated by scleraxis, and will determine how this regulation occurs. Our work will thus confirm scleraxis is a critical player in the progression of fibrosis, and a potential target for therapeutic anti-fibrosis drug design.

column37: Each year 40,000 Canadians have a cardiac arrest. Death ensues within minutes if the heart rhythm is not normalized by a shock to reset the heart. Participants are randomly assigned to standard care or standard care plus an ICD. The majority of funding for the study is being provided through unrestricted grants from Medtronic Inc., an ICD manufacturer, GE Healthcare, a Holter manufacturer, and the Alberta government. Funds from the CIHR are being requested to support study management (University of Calgary) and data coordination (Montreal Heart Institute).
