column36: Evolutionarily conserved functions of GRKs in Hedgehog signaling
column37: Hedgehog (Hh) family proteins are important growth factors that are secreted from specific groups of cells within tissues and convey information to neighbouring cells in a process known as cell-cell communication. These proteins play a critical role in controlling the growth and organization of embryonic and fetal tissues in species ranging from flies to man. They are also important for stem cell function, and consequently for maintenance of adult tissues. Due to their central role in these processes, misregulation of Hh activity can result in congenital birth defects and cancer. Much of our understanding of the mechanism of action of Hh proteins comes from studies in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster. These studies have shown that binding of Hh to its receptor at the surface of a cell triggers an intracellular signal in that cell that is initiated by a protein called Smoothened (Smo). Upon exposure of cells to Hh, Smo becomes active, moves to the cell surface, and signals through a series of downstream proteins to regulate gene expression in the nucleus. We have been studying a protein called G-protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (Gprk2) that is required for Smo to become fully active in flies and mammals. We have identified regions in fly Smo that become modified by Gprk2 through a process called phosphorylation. The same phosphorylated regions are found in Smoothened proteins in all animals, suggesting that Gprk2 phosphorylation represents an evolutionarily ancient mechanism for regulating Smoothened activity. We are proposing to define the molecular mechanisms by which Gprk2 promotes Smo activity. The results of this work will provide important new insights into how Hh signaling controls gene expression not just in flies but also in humans, with the goal of identifying potential therapeutic targets for the treatment of Hh-dependent cancers.

column36: The changing balance of neural inhibition vs. excitation during auditory system development
column37: When sensory areas of the brain develop, there are certain structures and basic mechanisms that form before birth, and thus in the absence of environmental stimulation of the senses. For the hearing system, the sensory cells (hair cells) of the ears connect up with the central brain before birth. However after birth, sound stimulation of the ears causes activation of the central brain pathways involved in hearing. At this time many more connections between brain cells (nerve cells or "neurons") are established, and networks of neurons form which can code different types of sound. As a result of these mechanisms our hearing develops. Some neurons link up to cause activation of other cells; we call this "excitation". Other neurons reduce the activity in cells they link up with; this we call "inhibition". This research is about the balance and interaction of this excitation and inhibition, and how this balance changes during early periods of brain development. The research can help us understand how normal hearing develops and also how hearing loss and deafness in infants can interfere with normal development. Nous voulons aussi obtenir de l'information sur les changements structuraux qui se produisent lorsque le recepteur AT1 passe de l'etat inactif a l'etat actif. This project aims to define the characteristics of stem/progenitor cells in the ovary, and to identify some of the mechanisms that control their behaviour. column37: Drug addiction is a chronic and debilitating disorder that has an immense social and financial impact on individuals and society. Substance abuse accounts for the highest number of preventable illnesses and deaths each year in Canada and places a significant social and financial toll on individuals, families and society. In 2006, the estimated cost of substance abuse in Canada was estimated to be $39.8 billion, with illegal drugs accounting for $8.2 billion. Drugs of abuse are believed to elicit changes in neural circuits that ultimately manifest themselves in a variety of self-destructive behaviors. Emerging evidence indicates that synaptic plasticity of glutamatergic inputs to key reward structures is critical for functional changes of neurons in addiction; however, the various molecular mechanisms involved are only partly understood. Here we investigate how TNF modifies circuit properties in reward-relevant parts of the brain. We then investigate how drugs of abuse engage the TNF signaling system, and the impact of TNF-mediated synaptic changes on the physiological and behavioural changes induced by chronic cocaine administration. Lastly, we will test if augmenting this compensatory response has potential as a therapeutic treatment.

column37: Epilepsy is a serious neurological disorder. About 54,000 Canadians have seizures that cannot be controlled by anti-seizure medications. Our new techniques offer unprecedented sensitivity and precision and will allow us to accurately identify the seizure focus. Once the studies have been completed, we will conduct a large, multicentre clinical trial to formally assess whether our MRI techniques can direct epilepsy surgery and improve surgical outcome.

column37: Our genome is organized into long pieces of DNA, called chromosomes. Cancer is caused by the accumulation of changes in DNA (mutations) that result in the activation of "oncogenes" and the inactivation of "tumor suppressors". In the context of tumour development and progression, mutations are believed to accumulate owing to compromised DNA repair functions. In this project, we will investigate a protein domain called Cut repeat that is present in a number of proteins and help accelerate the DNA repair pathway that fixes damaged bases in DNA. There are two ways by which our work can ultimately be helpful to cancer patients. First, we will generate unique tools -reagents and methods- that can serve as predictive indicators that will be used in diagnostic laboratories to predict the response of specific tumors to particular treatments and therefore help the patient and the clinician decide what is the best course of action. Secondly, our work will identify proteins and enzymatic reactions that can be controlled with a drug. We will thus have identified suitable targets for future therapeutic strategies.

column36: Will mild vs. moderate physical activity suffice to abate the progression of subclinical atherosclerosis in sedentary adults?
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the number one cause of death and sickness in Canada, killing 1 in 3 Canadians. The underlying cause behind CVD is atherosclerosis (fatty thickening of artery walls that blocks/slows blood passage). Atherosclerosis is a process that begins silently very early in life, long before the usual risk factors appear (high blood pressure, diabetes). We were shaken to discover atherosclerosis in up to 80% of young men before their 30th birthday, before any of the tell-tale symptoms (chest pain/angina) or risk factors (high blood pressure, etc.) revealed themselves. As it grows, usually by age 50 or more, atherosclerosis in the heart finally does reveal itself and causes heart attacks, or when localized to the brain causes stroke. Prevention of hidden atherosclerosis in all young adults should therefore become a priority to keep it from causing heart attack/stroke decades later. A potentially powerful way to prevent atherosclerosis is with physical activity. Unfortunately, only 15% of Canadians follow the recommendations of 150min/week of moderate activity (brisk walk/jog). Adopting a "some is better than none" approach and to avoid discouraging patients, recently some health advocates have suggested that less physical activity may be enough to prevent CVD. Being cardiologists ourselves, however, we want to give our patients the best advice: if less exercise is as effective in preventing atherosclerosis then we/and our patients should be fine with less. But if less exercise is simply not as effective than more, then we need to know the truth and encourage and motivate our patients to stick with the more stringent recommendations. column36: The role of RanBP2 and sumoylation in regulating the translation of secretory mRNAs
column37: Gene expression begins in the nucleus where DNA is transcribed into RNA, which is then processed into mature messenger RNA (mRNA). mRNAs are then packaged into large messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes, which are exported from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, where they are transported to their proper destination. For example, mRNAs that encode secretory and membrane-bound proteins are translated on the surface of the endoplasmic reticulum, a large organelle that is dedicated to secretion. Once localized, these mRNAs are translated into proteins. We have demonstrated that a large majority of mRNA encoding secretory proteins share an element, called the ALREX-element, which promotes the nuclear export and efficient translation of these mRNAs, likely by influencing how the mRNP is built and matured. In the nucleus these mRNAs are assembled into mRNPs within nuclear speckles. Then, after these mRNPs are exported, they interact with RanBP2 through their ALREX-elements. RanBP2 is a large protein that is localized to the cytoplasmic face of the nuclear pore. RanBP2 is known to attach the small peptide SUMO to protein substrates. We believe that RanBP2 sumoylates mRNP components in order to prepare the mRNA for translation. Mutations in RanBP2 are associated with acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE1) a condition caused by the hyper-secretion of cytokines. To further advance our understanding of how these mRNAs are regulated we will: 1) Dissect how RanBP2 recognizes ALREX-elements 2) Determine whether sumoylation regulates the translation of these mRNA 3) Determine how RanBP2 alters mRNPs 4) Determine how mRNPs are assembled onto mRNAs that contain ALREX-elements By dissecting how ALREX-elements function, we will gain insight into physiological pathologies where secretion in misregulated, including type 2 diabetes, and ANE1. This work will provide knowledge that will lead to novel therapeutic treatments for these debilitating illnesses.

column36: COMPLETE Trial: Complete revascularization versus optimal medical therapy to treat residual multi-vessel disease in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.
column37: Background: In patients experiencing a heart attack, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) promptly relieves the blockage in the "culprit" coronary artery that caused the heart attack. However, in one-third of patients, doctors discover additional "non-culprit" narrowings that did not cause the heart attack. These patients are at high-risk and have a much worse prognosis compared with patients who only have a culprit narrowing. However, doctors are not certain whether opening these additional narrowings with further PCI is beneficial versus just treating with proven medications alone. Some studies in non-heart attack patients have suggested that there is no advantage for an additional PCI procedure, whereas other smaller studies have suggested that there may be a benefit. Unfortunately, there have been no randomized studies large enough to address this very common question. As a result, doctors have widely varying opinions on how to treat these high-risk patients. Methods: The COMPLETE trial is a large, multinational, randomized clinical trial designed to determine whether opening residual narrowings or blockages with an additional PCI procedure is beneficial compared with just treating with medications alone. After the culprit narrowing has been treated with PCI, we will randomly assign patients to either PCI to the additional narrowings or optimal medical therapy alone. We will enroll 3,900 patients and will follow them up for an average of 4 years to determine whether additional PCI saves lives or prevents more heart attacks. Significance: COMPLETE will be a definitive clinical trial that will determine whether additional PCI to non-culprit narrowings is superior to optimal medial therapy alone in reducing subsequent death or recurrent heart attacks. This landmark international trial, designed and led by Canadian researchers, has critical implications for the optimal care of high risk patients experiencing a heart attack in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Few studies are specifically designed to address health concerns relevant during pregnancy. The consequence is a lack of evidence on best clinical practice. This includes mothers and their babies when pregnancy is complicated by an abnormally fast heart rate up to 300 beats per minute due to supraventricular tachyarrhythmia (SVA) in the unborn baby (fetus). Since the late seventies, it has been possible to detect and monitor fetal disease by ultrasound images and to treat fetal SVA with pharmaceuticals administered via the mother. To this day, physicians need to make decisions about the management of such pregnancies without any evidence from controlled clinical trials on drug efficacy and safety. This study will address the knowledge gap. Fetal SVA carries significant risks because the unborn baby can tolerate fast heart rates for only a short period before heart failure, shock or even death occurs. Premature delivery and perinatal death are frequent adverse outcomes of babies with heart failure and uncontrolled SVA before birth. Pharmacological treatment either with digoxin, sotalol, or flecainide is offered to most mothers to normalize the fetal heart rate and prevent or treat fetal heart failure, ideally allowing the pregnancy to continue to term with a normal delivery. One would expect that the more effective the drug therapy, the lower the disease-related morbidity, mortality and health care utilization will be. Aims of this prospective study will include the comparison of the efficacy and safety of different antiarrhythmic drug therapy regimens to provide much needed evidence to guide the future treatment of fetal SVA to the best of care.

column36: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Entry Receptors and Signalling
column37: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the leading cause of hospitalisation of infants in North America. RSV causes respiratory infection of the lungs leading to flu like symptoms, severe cough and pneumonia. Despite the severity of this particular infection there is no vaccine available and the only medication against RSV is a very expensive drug called palivizumab, that can only be used to prevent infection. This means that when a patient is suffering from RSV infection there aren't any specific treatments available to treat the infection itself. In summary, we need to learn more about RSV infection so that we can develop new drugs to treat it. We are researching the steps that RSV takes to enter and infect lung cells. In order for infection to happen the virus must first cross the outer membrane that surrounds the cell, which is called virus entry. We are studying the entry stage of the virus replication cycle so that we can develop the basis of new drugs that block RSV infection from happening. The biggest hurdle with developing drugs against RSV entry into cells is that very little is known about this phase of the RSV life cycle. However, recently (2011) our group shed new light on RSV entry by discovering a cellular entry receptor for RSV. Virus receptors are molecules made by the cell that a virus binds to in order to enter the cell. The ultimate purpose of our studies is to understand the RSV-receptor interaction so that we can develop drugs that block this interaction. Drugs that bind to the virus-receptor binding site on the virus act as receptor decoys that effectively soak up the virus before it has a chance to infect a cell. In summary, we are discovering the cellular factors that RSV uses to infect cells as the basis of new drugs to block RSV infection

column36: Diagnosis, pathophysiology and treatment of adult somnambulism
column37: Despite almost 5 decades of clinical and laboratory investigations of sleep disorders, relatively little is known about the mechanisms which give rise to sleepwalking (somnambulism). Sleepwalking occurs in 4% to 17% of children and is far more common in adults (approximately 4%) than commonly acknowledged. Patients suffering from this sleep disorder often consult due to a history of aggressive and/or injurious behaviour during sleep. In a significant number of cases, patients report having suffered serious injuries (e.g., contusions, fractures to limbs, rib cage, multiple lacerations) and/or having attacked a bed partner during an episode. Diagnosing sleepwalking with objective instruments such as sleep laboratory assessments is often difficult as episodes rarely occur in the laboratory. Establishing a correct diagnosis is vital for the patient's proper treatment as well as in light of the growing number of medico-legal cases of sleep-related violence. One aim of the proposed research program is to develop an investigative protocol that will allow researchers and clinicians to establish a laboratory-based diagnosis for sleepwalking. The infrequency with which episodes occur in the laboratory has also hampered the study of physiological variables associated with sleepwalking. In a series of studies, we showed that sleep deprivation significantly increases the frequency and complexity of somnambulistic events recorded in the laboratory. A second aim of the proposed research is to elucidate our understanding of sleepwalking by recording sleepwalkers' brain activity during sleep and wakefulness both before and after a period sleep deprivation. We also plan to study underlying brain processes during the episodes themselves. Taken together, these studies should a) lead us to a better understanding of why some people suffer from sleepwalking, b) help develop an objective protocol for its diagnosis, and c) guide future clinical treatments.

column36: Neural mechanisms of real-time decisions in a constantly changing world
column37: Deficits in decision-making behavior are a major aspect of many brain disorders, including diseases such as Parkinson's and maladaptive conditions such as addiction. Understanding the neural bases of decisions is therefore critical to developing more effective therapies that act at the sources of the deficit without disturbing other brain functions. Most research investigates the neural mechanisms of decision-making by studying how we make choices using static information about explicit predictable outcomes, such as choosing between two jars of peanut butter in a grocery store. However, during the brain's evolution animal behavior was dominated by decisions about actions in a constantly changing world, such as choosing which way to run away from a predator. Such "embodied decisions" still dominate our lives, whether we're playing a sport, walking through a crowd, or maneuvering through a store to get to the peanut butter aisle. Because these kinds of decisions have been so central in evolution, their study is needed to provide insights into mechanisms of decision-making at the neural level. This project aims to understand how the brain makes decisions in situations that are changing over time, and how a commitment is made to an action choice. It involves recording neural activity in the cerebral cortex and subcortical regions of monkeys trained to perform reaching tasks in different changing and ambiguous situations. It tests specific predictions of a general hypothesis that during natural behavior, the brain continuously specifies multiple potential actions currently available in the environment while at the same time collecting information for selecting one of them for execution at a given moment. Because the hypothesis proposes specific functional roles for specific brain regions, it is expected to help explain the deficits associated with damage to these regions and to suggest how these deficits may be alleviated.

column36: Cell of Origin and Tumor Initiating Cells in Serous Ovarian Cancer
column37: Serous ovarian cancer (SOC) is the most deadly subtype and sixth leading cause of cancer death in women. Surgery and chemotherapy often result in lack of detectable tumor, yet disease usually recurs and causes death. Why some SOC cells resist therapy is unclear. One reason is that SOC is very unstable genetically, and different genes can be altered in different parts of the tumor ("molecular heterogeneity"). There also might be cellular heterogeneity in SOC, such that only some cells, often called "cancer stem cells (CSC)," can divide indefinitely and give rise to the other ("bulk") tumor cells. A third source of heterogeneity could be the cell in which SOC starts ("cell-of-origin"). Indeed, "ovarian cancer" is a misnomer: many start in the fallopian tube. All of these mechanisms could contribute to the marked heterogeneity between and within individual SOC patients, and help explain disease recurrence/treatment resistance. A paucity of good experimental models has hampered SOC research. We have developed methods to quantify tumor-initiating cells in patient samples and identified cells with CSC properties, but could only purify them to a limited extent. Purifying such cells is key for understanding their biological properties and ultimately, finding ways to kill them. We also obtained from collaborators a new mouse model for SOC that lets us turn on the genes that cause the disease in different types of cells. We now propose to: (1) use new separation technology to refine CSC identification, purify them, and determine their biological properties and drug sensitivities; (2) test the CSC model in mice; and (3) use this model to turn on cancer-causing genes in different cell types, probe the cell-of-origin for SOC and ask if imposing the same gene defects on different cells-of-origin causes distinct tumor behavior. Our studies should provide new insight into the origin and pathogenesis of SOC and suggest new therapies for this deadly disease.

column37: Antibodies are proteins that are naturally made by the body to fight infections and disease. Like a lock and key, antibodies have the unique ability to specifically recognize and bind one, and only one, target. In addition to their central role in immunity, this amazing specificity also makes antibodies an extremely effective class of drugs that can be used for targeted therapies with improved effectiveness and minimal side effects. For this reason, antibody-based drugs are currently the fastest growing class of therapeutic and are being used in the treatment of many diseases including cancer, autoimmune disorders, inflammation, and infection. However, finding antibodies with desired therapeutic properties remains one of the most serious obstacles to advancing new therapies. column36: Sleep and motor learning consolidation and reconsolidation
column37: Human memory can be subdivided into different components: memories for facts and events (called declarative) and memories for knowing how to execute newly learned skills (named procedural). Contemporary theories advocate that new memories undergo off-line transformations, which allow the initially labile trace to become consolidated into the physical structure of the brain. Previously, such models proposed that for each trace, the process starts and ends only once. This concept, however, was challenged in recent years. It has been demonstrated that the reactivation of a consolidated memory trace is sensitive to interference, and thus that the later needs to be reprocessed in order to persist, a phase referred as the reconsolidation process. Importantly, there is ample evidence that consolidation of memories depends on sleep, but very little is known whether sleep is also critical for the reconsolidation of memories. Also we do not know whether the same, or different, sleep stages and oscillations are at play during both consolidation and reconsolidation. Finally, it has been proposed that the reactivation of memory traces during the night following learning is an essential mechanism for consolidation of memories to occur in humans, but again there is no data on whether similar processes are playing a role during reconsolidation, and on the specific sleep stages that may contribute to this mechanism. In this project, we now plan to use electroencephalographic recordings alone or combined with brain imaging techniques to determine the nature of the sleep oscillations that are related to the reconsolidation of procedural and declarative memory, and how these relate to the sleep processes mediating the initial consolidation of these memories. We also aim to test the role of the reactivation mechanism during sleep in the consolidation and reconsolidation of these two types of memory traces, and to determine the specific sleep features that facilitate these two processes.

column36: Molecular control of germline apoptosis in C. elegans
column37: Reproductive tissue called the germline produces gametes that give rise to the next generation. The genomes of these gametes need to be protected to ensure fitness of the next generation. Similarly, stem cells in tissues of adult organisms must be protected from internal and external stresses that threaten the stability of their genomes. For example, mutations in the DNA of these cells can inactivate genes necessary for survival and cause these cells to transform into tumors that ultimately kill the organism. Organisms have therefore acquired mechanisms that detect damage to their genomes and dictate whether to repair this damage or die by a suicide process called "apoptosis". While much has been learned about the nuts and bolts of apoptosis very little is known about how the organism as a whole controls these life or death decisions. All cells in an organism reside within neighbourhoods (tissues), and there is a great deal of communication between different tissues that determines if they live or die after encountering stresses that attack their genomes. We have taken advantage of the powerful genetic tools of a simple organism called Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode worm, to discover new genes and signaling cascades that multicellular organisms use to communicate these survival and death signals across tissue boundaries. In this grant application I propose to discover the genes that communicate these survival and death signals from the somatic (body) tissues to the germline (reproductive stem cells). We will focus our investigation on a gene we found to be a central component of this cascade called kri-1, which is homologous to a human CCM1/Krit1, frequently mutated in the neurovascular disease cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM). Understanding these fundamental cross-tissue signaling mechanisms will help us develop new ways to treat diseases in which these signalling cascades have been disrupted, such as cancer and CCM.

column36: Interventions to Support Long-term Adherence aNd Decrease cardiovascular events post-Acute Coronary Syndrome (ISLAND-ACS)
column37: Patients who have had a heart attack have high rates of repeat cardiac problems and even death. Fortunately, there are medications that help to reduce this risk. In addition, people who have had a heart attack can further reduce their risk by participating in cardiac rehabilitation programs where they exercise and learn about a healthy lifestyle and the importance of taking medications. However, only 30-40% of patients participate in cardiac rehabilitation and by one year only 50% of patients continue to properly take their cardiac medications. We will conduct a randomized trial to test strategies to increase the proportion of patients who continue to take their medications and who participate in cardiac rehabilitation. Patients who have a heart attack and undergo an angiogram showing blockages in their coronary arteries as part of their normal clinical care will be eligible. Eligible patients at each cardiac centre across Ontario will be randomized to one of four options: a) usual care, where no reminders are sent; b) a series of postal letters; c) letters plus a series of automated phone calls; or d) letters and automated phone calls with nurse telephone follow up of patients who have stopped their medications. All reminders will be sent on behalf of the cardiologist who performed the angiogram. We will contact patients after one year to determine whether they are still taking all their medications and whether they participated in cardiac rehabilitation. We will also determine health care use including the rates of repeat heart attacks in each group. We will then compare the costs and benefits of each strategy. This project integrates the decision makers and policy makers in all aspects to ensure that the findings can lead to sustainable policies. We anticipate that this project will lead to improved outcomes for patients and contribute to the science regarding how to change the patient behaviour.

column36: Preventing Work Disability through Accommodation
column37: Work disability is becoming a global health problem with the worldwide aging of the working population. Supervisors of injured workers play a key role in preventing prolonged work absences. Providing supervisors with tools to improve their response and ability to accommodate musculoskeletal and other workplace injuries may improve worker health and disability outcomes. The purpose of the proposed 5-year research program is to prevent work disability through the provision of work accommodation. The program of research will focus on three specific research questions: 1) how can stakeholders identify or develop accommodations for workers trying to return to the labour force? 2) how can workplaces and employers support the use of workplace accommodations? 3) how do we measure and demonstrate the health and economic impacts of workplace accommodation for all stakeholders? The purpose of the included CIHR-funded research proposal is to determine if a supervisor training program can improve work disability outcomes for injured workers. The project will involve at least one large employer in Canada and one in the US. Work units within the companies will be randomized to either receive the training or not. All supervisors within those work units randomized to receive the training will be given 2 two-hour sessions of supervisor training. The goals of the training program consist of increasing opportunity for problem solving to reduce injury rates, improving supervisor response to prevent or decrease work disability, and improving communication between supervisors, employees and health care providers. Worker outcomes, to be determined from workplace records, include number of lost-time injuries, duration of lost-time injuries in days, and number of days of sick leave. Results from this program of research have the potential to decrease work disability though the identification of accommodated work and save billions of dollars in direct and indirect costs.

column36: A mixed-methods approach to reduce the burden of illness due to fracture
column37: A fragility fracture is one that occurs after a slip, trip, or fall from standing height or less (for example, slipping on ice and breaking a wrist). In general, this type of fracture predicts future fractures and is a sign of poor bone health that requires treatment. Treatment, which includes vitamin D, calcium, and often medication, is known to reduce the chance (or risk) of future fractures. However, fracture patients often do not receive or follow recommendations for bone health treatment. There are many possible reasons for this. One reason may be that the concept of fracture risk is new and patients and health care providers are not familiar with the levels of risk. Another reason may be that patients who need bone heath treatment have other conditions that are perceived to be more serious and compete for their attention. The proposed research aims to study these reasons in order to understand how we can encourage individuals to follow treatment recommendations for bone health after they have had a fracture. Ultimately, this research will inform the development of future programs to improve bone health. For example, programs might address how we communicate fracture risk to patients or what advice we give to patients who have several chronic conditions. It is important that patients who have had a fragility fracture be treated for their bone health because appropriate treatment could prevent future fractures such as hip fractures; this will alleviate fracture-related health care costs in Canada including admissions to hospitals, extended care facilities, and nursing homes.

column36: A Community Based Research Program Focused on "Adding Life to Later Years"
column37: Background: In 2011, an estimated 5.0 million Canadians were 65 years of age or older, a number that is expected to double in the next 25 years to reach 10.4 million seniors by 2036. The majority of older adults prefer to stay at home for as long as possible. However, for many, receipt of home care services is the only option that enables them to remain independently and safely in their home. At present, more than 1.4 million Canadians receive publicly funded home care services annually. As the Canadian population ages and with earlier discharges from hospital, the need for home care and associated costs continue to escalate. To 'age in place' older people also require community and built environments that facilitate their health and mobility. As health and function decline with aging, older adults' ability to engage with challenging physical environments (e.g. poor street lighting or long distances to amenities) diminishes. Advancing knowledge in this emerging field is key to planning and developing effective strategies that allow older adults to grow old at home. Research Goals and Objectives: The overarching goal of my program of research is "adding life to later years" so that older adults can live independently in their homes for as long as possible. Thus, my research focuses on enhancing the health and mobility of older adults across two settings: 1. delivery and receipt of home care services and, 2. the neighbourhood built environment. My specific five-year research objectives are to: A. examine the experiences of older adults and home support workers in the delivery of home care services with specific attention to issues of worker and older adult safety; B. evaluate features of the built environment that facilitate or impede older adults' mobility, social and physical health. Ultimately, I seek to improve the quality and utility of evidence for policy and practice change that will enable older adults to age in place.

column36: Strengthening transitions in pediatric care
column37: Children and families experience many transitions in care when they interact with the health care system. Transitions in care occur when a child moves between health care providers or when they move from one care setting to another. Poor transitions in care create serious patient safety, quality of care and health outcome concerns. This program of research will use a theory-based, mixed methods approach to identify and examine gaps in transitions in care for children and families in emergency practice settings. Over 87% of children who visit Canadian emergency departments are discharged home to their place of residence. Following discharge, many children and their caregivers are unable to list their diagnosis, recount the name and purpose of medications they received, outline the recommendations for care at home or know when to return to seek medical advice. There are no national guidelines or policies related to discharge communication in Canadian pediatric emergency departments. We will conduct a series of observational studies to examine discharge communication across a range of emergency practice settings and patient conditions. We will begin by conducting focus groups with parents and physicians and nurses across six Canadian emergency departments. We will then analyze video recordings of discharge communication between families and health care providers in a pediatric emergency department. Finally we will conduct follow up telephone interviews with parents after discharge from the emergency department. Results from these studies will be used to design interventions to improve transitions from the emergency department for children and families. Interventions will be further developed through feasibility testing before evaluation in a multicentre randomized control trial. Findings from the observational work will also inform recommendations for national policies and guidelines to support discharge communication.

column36: A Clinical Trials Research Program in Biomedical HIV Prevention and HIV/STI Co-infections
column37: Despite decades of traditional prevention efforts, Canada continues to see unacceptably high rates of HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as syphilis and herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), with a disproportionate burden among men who have sex with men (MSM). As an infectious diseases specialist physician and clinical epidemiologist, my research program focuses on clinical trials of novel strategies for the prevention, detection and management of HIV and STI co-infections. First, I lead an interdisciplinary team investigating a safe, effective new approach to HIV prevention known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). PrEP involves daily use of anti-HIV medications by people at high, ongoing risk of HIV, but there are concerns about its acceptability, the ability of users to adhere, and other clinical issues. I am launching a pilot PrEP trial among high risk Toronto MSM that will gather preliminary data on these issues and inform the design of a future nationwide trial. My related studies in this area address other ways to optimize the clinical and public health impact of PrEP in the future. Second, given the exceedingly high burden of syphilis in HIV-infected MSM and the many negative interactions between these pathogens, I am co-leading a clinical trial of new approaches to diagnosing syphilis in HIV-infected MSM that will inform future strategies for controlling these STIs. Third, I am co-leading an international randomized controlled trial in the area of HIV and HSV-2 co-infection, studying whether the anti-herpes medication valacyclovir can slow the rate at which HIV disease progresses. column36: Mathematical Modelling and Epidemiology of HIV/STIs for Program Science
column37: Epidemics of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are costly - they cost lives, health, and money. With shrinking funds, difficult choices are being made about how best to protect the most vulnerable from HIV/ STIs. Mathematical models can help decision-makers by reproducing epidemics with computer simulations and letting us run what-if experiments to (a) characterize local epidemics; (b) to compare the potential effectiveness and cost-effectiveness (health benefit per additional cost to the health system) of different HIV/STI prevention strategies; and (c) to identify the most important data we should collect to better understand and monitor local epidemics. Over the next 5 years, I will work with public health decision-makers, community-researchers, and data scientists, and use the best available local data to build models of HIV and STI epidemics and address the following specific objectives: (1) to characterize the syphilis and HIV epidemic among men who have sex with men (MSM) and estimate the potential effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of different syphilis control strategies in reducing syphilis and HIV among MSM in Canada; (2) to characterize and understand the role of early HIV risk in fueling HIV epidemics among Canadians born in Africa or the Caribbean, and among female sex workers in low- and middle-income countries; and (3) to examine the influence of individual and health system characteristics and uncertainties in the data on model projections in order to optimize HIV/STI surveillance. Potential impact: This research program will provide an important, transparent, and reliable evidence base for policy-decisions and for the design of efficient and sustainable HIV and STI programs in Canada and other settings. Research results have the potential to dramatically improve how we currently deliver these programs, and thereby improve the health and well-being of people with and at risk of HIV and STIs.

column36: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Personalized Pain Medicine
column37: Chronic pain is a global public health problem of enormous social and economic impact. One in five Canadians - more than 6 million people - suffers from chronic pain. Their annual health care costs are estimated at over $10 billion, more than cancer, heart disease and HIV combined. The most common forms of chronic pain are osteoarthritis, cancer, migraine and back pain, whose prevalence increases with age, reaching 50% in the over 65s. The latter will be one quarter of the Canadian population in less than 20 years and chronic pain will severely impair their quality of life and place pressures on those upon whom they depend. Current treatments for chronic pain are unsatisfactory and existing analgesics are often not effective because the underlying genetic mechanisms are poorly understood. The research program of this CERC will focus on the genetic mechanisms of pain, searching for targets for chronic pain therapies and the development of personalized therapeutic strategies. These are currently the top priorities of increasing numbers of research and health organizations as well as of the pharmaceutical industry. The projects will focus on the identification of molecular mediators of chronic pain states using genome-wide genotyping and sequencing of DNA and RNA and evaluating these variables in populations of chronic pain patients. Identified targets will be validated through molecular and cellular techniques and through gene targeting, animal behavior and, ultimately, clinical trials. The Chair will also lead efforts to expand our current training programs in personalized pain medicine. The CERC candidate will join a team at McGill University with a 40-year tradition of excellence in pain research. The CERC will foster a qualitative change by breaking new ground in human pain genetics to ensure that McGill and Canada remain among the world's leading centers of excellence in pain research for years to come.

column37: Over 75% of mental disorders begin in early adolescence or young adulthood. When untreated, mental disorders can have serious negative consequences for youth, cause immense suffering for youth and families, and have high costs to society. Outcomes for most mental disorders have remained generally poor for many years. It is estimated that only 20-25% of youth with mental health challenges in Canada receive help. A major reason for this are inadequacies in the manner in which mental health services are provided to youth. Current services often do not offer "best-practice" treatments in a readily accessible way. Other obstacles include long wait times and difficulties encountered in navigating a complicated mental health care system. Also, traditional mental health services often do not sufficiently engage youth, resulting in high drop-out rates. ACCESS is a network including youth, families, mental health clinicians, researchers, policy makers and community members. Our goal is to conduct an in-depth, innovative transformation in the way youth are cared for by mental health services in the "real world", and to evaluate what worked. At sites across Canada, this transformation will target urban, rural and Aboriginal youth, and vulnerable populations including youth who are homeless, under youth protection or in contact with the criminal justice system. Our major aims are: -To identify more youth in need, sooner, through improved mental health awareness, well-publicized means of entry, open referral and rapid response (within 72 hours) -To offer the youth appropriate, optimal care with seamless navigation through various services -To create cultures of care that feature youth-friendly treatment, an optimistic tone, sustained youth and family participation at all levels, shared decision making and improved work/educational outcomes -A final important goal will be to sustain the positive changes in mental health services that produce better outcomes for our youth

column36: Evaluating a Population-Health HIV Treatment as Prevention Intervention
column37: The expansion of access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) has led to a dramatic reduction in HIV-related death and disease and transformed HIV into a chronic manageable illness. Now, the potential of HIV Treatment as Prevention (TasP) suggests that earlier and more aggressive treatment will extend the personal benefits of ART to produce important population health benefits, particularly in decreasing the number of new HIV infections. A world where HIV is no longer a global public health emergency can be envisaged, even in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Since 2001, the Academic Model Providing Access to Healthcare (AMPATH) program, headquartered in Eldoret, Kenya, has enrolled >150,000 HIV-infected patients across a swathe of western Kenya. AMPATH has already conducted widespread door-to-door HIV testing and is now undertaking to test/re-test (Find) >95% of all eligible adults and children in its catchments, Link to care >80% of those found to be positive, Treat 100% of those who are eligible according to current treatment guidelines, and Retain 95% of those treated. This population-health intervention, called FLTR (Find-Link-Treat-Retain), aims to improve health and health equity across the lifespan of both the general population of these catchments as well as Most At-Risk Populations (MARP), including high-risk youth, commercial sex workers, pregnant women, and adult men (all at high risk of acquiring HIV and/or less equitably accessing HIV prevention, care, and treatment services). The primary objective of my program of research is to evaluate the impact of this population-health intervention of HIV testing, care and treatment in an HIV endemic region of East Africa. The primary outcomes are a reduction in HIV incidence, and improved equity in, access to, and outcomes from HIV care. The implications and applications of this population-health intervention are far-reaching for both low- and high-income settings, including Canada.

column37: Oral health is an important part of overall health. Oral health problems in childhood can influence well-being throughout the life course. More than half of Canadian children are affected by caries (tooth decay). Surgery for caries is currently the leading reason for day surgery among children under age six in Canada. Caries are generally preventable, and one means of prevention is fluoridation of drinking water. However, an increasing number of Canadian cities are opting to stop fluoridating their drinking water ("fluoridation cessation"). Fluoridation cessation may have important implications for oral health; however, research is extremely limited. In particular, there is only very limited knowledge about the impact of fluoridation cessation on children's oral health, what attitudes members of the public hold about fluoridation and fluoridation cessation, and how decisions are made about fluoridation cessation. This program of research aims to fill these knowledge gaps. Research findings will be important in terms of identifying the best ways to improve oral health in the population, especially because dental health is not included as part of our health care system. This research involves a collaboration between the University of Calgary and the Provincial Oral Health Office at Alberta Health Services.

column36: Policy, Location, and Access in Community Environments (PLACE): A Program of Population Health Intervention Research
column37: Recent research on programs and policies, or "interventions" to support health suggests that understanding a community's environment is important for the intervention to be successful. This means that it is important to understand how the places where program and policy initiatives occur affect the interventions, and ultimately, people's health. The built (or man-made) environment, the social environment (people around us), policy decisions, and an individual's characteristics and behaviours all impact health. Each of these factors shapes the opportunities and barriers for individual and community health. Where a person lives, when and how they access the things they need in their daily life, and the policies that create their social, political, and economic environments all matter. Therefore, understanding the relationships between people, policy, and place is essential for health promotion and public health. The purpose of the Policy, Location, and Access in Community Environments (PLACE) research program is to contribute to a better understanding of the people-policy-place relationships in chronic disease interventions and prevention initiatives. Work in the PLACE lab involves community-based participatory research, qualitative and quantitative methodologies, and GIS mapping to implement and evaluate interventions, in partnership with governments and other community stakeholders. PLACE population health intervention research activities span two areas: (1) implementing and evaluating built environment interventions and their impact on health and health equity; and (2) implementing and evaluating healthy public policy initiatives, including a policy practitioner tool and provincial and national policy intervention initiatives. Collaborations with practitioners and decision-makers are at the core of every project. This fosters effective knowledge translation and exchange (interactions between research and practice) to support real-world knowledge sharing and use.

column36: Interventions urbaines et sante des populations
column37: Dans de nombreuses villes, les decideurs cherchent a modifier le cadre bati pour ameliorer les conditions de vie et la sante des populations. Cette ambition est souvent portee par un desir de developpement durable, et rejoint generalement les preoccupations de sante publique d'agir sur les determinants de la sante pour favoriser les saines habitudes de vie, ameliorer la sante, et reduire les inegalites sociales de sante. Cependant, la recherche interventionnelle sur le cadre bati est peu developpee et doit etre renforcee, d'une part pour mieux comprendre quels effets ces interventions ont sur la sante, et d'autre part pour mieux outiller les decideurs de sante publique et ceux oeuvrant dans le reamenagement de nos villes. Dans la region montrealaise, on assiste depuis quelques annees a une effervescence dans les orientations strategiques des instances municipales et autres organisations qui faconnent le territoire, avec une ambition forte de transformer les environnements de vie pour ameliorer la qualite de vie et la sante des populations. En travaillant en etroit partenariat avec la Direction de Sante Publique de Montreal, et en particulier avec les gens du secteur Environnement Urbain et Sante et leurs partenaires dans les villes, instances metropolitaines et ONG, la chaire en sante des populations et interventions urbaines proposee vise a analyser comment certains types et contextes d'intervention populationnelle sur les environnements urbains contribuent a transformer la sante des populations et a reduire les inegalites sociales de sante, en identifiant les mecanismes d'operation et les conditions de reussite. Les travaux de la chaire seront utiles aux decideurs pour batir des villes plus favorables a la sante et a l'equite au Canada et ailleurs. La chaire, qui s'appuiera par ailleurs sur un laboratoire de recherche sur les environnements et la sante existant, integrera par ailleurs des expertises diverses requises a l'analyse de ces enjeux complexes.

column36: Methods and Applications Group for Indirect Comparisons
column37: In this proposal, we outline a strategy to merge 3 existing Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR) Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) network meta-analysis (NMA) teams into one collaborative, efficient collaborating centre called the Methods and Applications Group for Indirect Comparisons (MAGIC). MAGIC includes investigators and collaborators from across Canada with internationally-acknowledged expertise in NMA and knowledge synthesis, including biostatistics; knowledge translation; health economics; pharmacoepidemiology; and pharmacogenomics. Our Collaborating Centre also includes clinical experts from a range of health care disciplines such as geriatric medicine, pediatric medicine, internal medicine and its subspecialties and primary care. Building on the success our previously funded NMA teams, we will work with Canadian policy makers to appropriately answer their questions about drug safety and effectiveness and these results will directly inform their decision making. We will improve pharmacovigilance in Canada using rigorous knowledge synthesis methods, and thereby strengthen the healthcare system and improve the health and wellness of Canadians.

column36: Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) is a national study of adult development and aging that includes 50,000 individuals between the ages of 45 and 85 from across Canada to be followed over 20 years. The ultimate aim of the CLSA is to find ways to improve the health of Canadians by better understanding the processes and dimensions of aging. Over the past 5 years, the CLSA research team has planned and implemented the study and recruited more than 38,000 of the 50,000 participants who have completed baseline assessments including telephone interviews, face-to-face interviews, as well as visits to specially designed data collection sites. The data provided by the 20,000 individuals who completed telephone interviews are now ready for release to researchers, who meet the CLSA requirements for access and are approved through a formal evaluation process. All 50,000 individuals will have completed their baseline assessment by the spring of 2015. The first follow up of the CLSA participants is scheduled to begin in the early summer of 2015 taking place 3 years after the baseline assessments. As part of the follow up participants will undergo repeat assessments and will be asked to complete additional components that have been selected based on recommendations from expert researchers to enhance the information collected and expand the science of the study. In this application, we are requesting funds to enable the CLSA team to plan and complete the first follow up and to plan and begin the second follow up. The need for information collected over time to inform decisions and design interventions and policies to improve the health and well-being of today and tomorrows seniors is widely recognized by researchers, and federal, provincial, and territorial governments. The CLSA was conceived to fill this information gap and to provide solid evidence to inform health and social care policies in Canada.

Furthermore, it is not always clear which of the alternative medications, available to treat a given disease offer the maximum benefits to the patients. column37: The research proposed will test whether the Community Health Assessment Program in the Philippines (CHAPP) will be effective in decreasing the number of people who have high risk of having the diabetes. The CHAPP is a community program which will be implemented by trained volunteers. In the program, the volunteers will invite community residents to attend CHAPP sessions where the volunteer will ask the residents questions about their health practices and also check their blood pressure, weight and height. The information of the residents will be entered into a computer and the computer program will show if the residents have a high risk of having diabetes. Those who have high risk of having diabetes will be seen by the public health midwife present during the CHAPP session to check the blood sugar of the resident. Residents who have high blood sugar will be asked to come back to have a repeat blood sugar check after they have fasted for 8-hours. If the residents consent, all information collected during the CHAPP sessions will be given to the public health office to help those who are at risk of having diabetes. In the first year of this research, the researchers will check how to best make the CHAPP fit in the community setting. In the second year, the CHAPP will be tested in 2 communities to check if there are problems in running the program. In the third and fourth year, the CHAPP will be tested if it decreases the number of people who have high risk of having the diabetes in 20 communities. If the CHAPP is effective, the fifth year will be used to inform government officials and health workers about how CHAPP can be implemented long term and in other communities. column37: Women who have had gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), which is a temporary diabetes that develops during pregnancy, are at high risk of getting type 2 diabetes sometime after their pregnancy. Research has shown that increasing physical activity, eating a healthier diet and losing weight, can prevent the progression to long term diabetes. This research study involves developing and evaluating an innovative intervention for the South African health system that will help prevent women with previous GDM from developing type 2 diabetes in the years after pregnancy. The study setting is in the cities of Cape Town and Johannesburg and will specifically target women at risk from poor communities who use the public health system. The proposed intervention will consist of offering the women a special test to see whether they have diabetes 6 weeks after delivery, along with counselling about a healthy lifestyle from a trained counsellor at the clinic and in a community venue. Currently, no such test, information or counselling support exists for these women after they have had their babies. The intervention will be introduced at primary care clinics, where mothers usually go to have their babies vaccinated during their first year of life, in order to make it convenient for them to access the service. This also offers an opportunity to test a post-partum intervention which addresses the mother's and child's health and nutrition together, rather than separately as is current practice. Before and during the implementation of the intervention, research with women, healthcare providers and health service managers will help to ensure that the proposed components of the intervention are suitable and practical in the real life clinic and community setting. If the intervention proves to be effective in preventing diabetes, further research and advocacy activities will explore the opportunities and barriers to extending the intervention across the SA health services more broadly.

column37: Morbid obesity(MO) coupled with metabolic syndrome(MSx) increase risks of cardiovascular disease, stroke, fatty liver & sleep apnea, which left unchecked are inevitably fatal and at enormous cost to Canada. RYGB causes massive weight loss in all patients but remarkably improves type 2 diabetes(T2D) & insulin resistance(IR) before the weight loss. The altered surgical anatomy of RYGB causes unforeseen changes in the gut contributing to these beneficial effects. A major change is the fecal bacterial community (intestinal microbiota-IM) & resulting bacterial genes (metagenome), shown in animal models to influence an excess assimilation of nutrients & many organs' responses- brain satiety, liver & fat accumulation, and body inflammatory responses, the latter related to many obesity-related diseases. These findings haven't been translated to human. This presents an opportunity for an entirely new therapeutic platform whereby clever use of the IM post-RYGB by fecal microbiota transplantation(FMT) serves as a 'medical' bypass strategy that can independently improve MSx & induce weight loss, perhaps reducing the need for RYGB. Our aims are: 1. Track changes in IM & metagenome of MO patients undergoing RYGB and determine the independent associations between specific changes & improvement in IR, T2D & weight loss. 2. Determine if FMT of stools from MO patients from Aim 1 vs FMT from lean subjects into a MO mouse model could reduce IR, obesity & other MSx features. We'll determine the specific candidate microbial species or genes that account for the beneficial effects on specific organs (fat, liver, insulin secretion) independent of the RYGB. 3. Test the effect of FMT of lean subjects into MO patients; assessing if the resulting IM is similar to post-RYGB IM to account for the beneficial effect

column37: For most severely obese patients, bariatric surgery is more effective than medical treatment or lifestyle modification to induce long-term weight loss with durable remission of metabolic diseases. Various types of surgical operations are available. These surgeries promote weight loss through two general mechanisms according to the type of surgery: 1) restrictive surgeries limit the amount of food consumed by reducing the size of the stomach; 2) malabsorptive surgeries limit the absorption of nutrients by reorganizing or bypassing portions of the small intestine. Better knowledge on each of the procedures will help in identifying the right surgery for the right patient. We hereby propose to investigate the determinants of metabolic recovery after restrictive or malabsorptive/restrictive surgical procedures in humans and relevant rodent models. The proposed research team involves investigators across Canada in 3 provinces and 8 universities as well as collaborators from the US and Europe. In sum, we have an increasing body of knowledge on the clinical effects of each surgical paradigm, but we do not yet have a clear understanding of the mechanisms that contribute to sustained weight loss and long-term metabolic recovery following surgery. The selection of a specific surgical approach in a given clinical context is faced with many unanswered questions that call for a better understanding of these mechanisms.

column37: The Canadian Critical Care Trials Group: We are a group of Canadian health care professionals from coast to coast who care for patients in the intensive care unit (ICU). Over the past 25 years, we have performed high quality research to enhance the care of critically ill patients and their families. For example, we have asked whether it is safe to transfuse less blood to critically ill adults and children? Yes! We showed that patients had the same chance of survival and fewer complications when we gave less blood. This practice has now been adopted worldwide. Should we cool children who suffered a severe brain injury? No! The labour-intensive therapy of cooling did not improve the outcome of these critically ill children. Consequently, cooling is no longer advocated for brain-injured children. Our research saves lives, improves the way critically ill or injured patients are cared for, and reduces costs to our healthcare system. Our work has changed the practice of critical care medicine world-wide. Our plan: Over the next 5 years, we plan to build a new infrastructure to enhance our research, expand our mentorship, and increase our impact on the outcomes of critically ill children and adults. We will accomplish this by forging new relationships, creating more innovative studies and providing resources to our researchers. This means engaging patients and healthcare policy-makers to help us develop the most relevant research programs, then evaluate them carefully. We will study the quality of care provided in the ICU, and develop tools such as common databases and standardized procedures to facilitate cost-effective research. We will investigate novel ways to ensure that important research findings are translated into better care more quickly. We will improve training for our junior colleagues, formalize the community mentoring they receive, and ensure that our more experienced investigators remain competitive, to sustain our legacy into the future.

Diagnosis of an inherited cancer susceptibility can determine whether patients and family members are at risk of cancer and both the patient and at-risk family members may benefit from increased screening, surveillance and/or prophylactic cancer prevention measures. Clinical and research practices regarding the management of potentially clinically significant incidental genomic findings are evolving. column36: CRISM-Quebec-Maritimes: Research on interventions in drug misuse
column37: Substance misuse remains a significant global public health problem which carries a heavy burden for abusers and their families alike. This disorder is indeed associated with suffering and severe health problems in patients, distress among family members, as well as tremendous costs to society. Unfortunately, prevention strategies still need to be effectively implemented and only a minority of addicted individuals receives adequate treatment. Moreover, conventional treatment strategies are often insufficient in treating addiction and no medication is yet available for a number of substances such as stimulants and cannabis. It is now widely accepted that research that could address these needs should involve not only scientists, but also clinicians, policy-makers and affected individuals. While individuals interact with each other at various levels (clinical, administrative), this is rarely as part of a cohesive interdisciplinary group. Substance users are for the most part absent of the knowledge generation and transfer processes. The overarching goal of this Node proposal is to provide a dynamic research environment where partners are engaged to identify crucial needs and priorities, and work together toward the development and implementation of intervention research in the area of substance misuse. The integration of regional research activities will facilitate national and international high quality, integrated, multisite research projects. Initial priorities will focus around development, evaluation and dissemination of interventions along four themes: i) substance-specific and poly-substance use problems; ii) substance misuse and mental health comorbidities; iii) substance misuse and pain; and iv) substance misuse and medical comorbidities.

column36: Father's lasting influence: Molecular foundations of intergenerational transmission of the paternal environment.
column37: We know that maternal exposures can affect child health, but recent disturbing findings suggest that the effects of environmental exposures can be transmitted by fathers, causing adverse birth outcomes and disease in their children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. A possible mechanism for paternal transmission of environmental information is via his sperm epigenome. The epigenome is a group of tags on DNA that signal genes when to turn on or off. We will use state-of-the-art approaches and build on existing research investment with international teams to study the father's role in transmitting the effects of his exposures to his future generations. There are international rules restricting organochlorines (e.g. PCBs and some pesticides, including DDT) because they persist in the environment, but DDT is still allowed in many parts of the world where malaria is a danger, such as South Africa. Due to natural weather currents, organochlorines bioaccumulate in the Arctic where they have never been used. Thus, Inuit populations have a high body burden of environmental contaminants through air, water, soil, and food, which may contribute to the major health disparity between them and non-aboriginal Canadians. We will examine the sperm epigenome of Inuit and indigenous South African men to assess abnormalities due to organochlorine exposure. Using a rat model, we will try to fix the damage caused by contaminants using folate, a common vitamin that is prescribed to pregnant mothers to prevent birth defects. We hypothesise that folate will prevent and repair the damage to fathers' sperm epigenome and protect his future generations. We will collaborate with teams in Europe and South Africa. Our team includes people from Health Canada, the Institut national de sante publique du Quebec, the Public Health Agency of Canada and the Micronutrient Initiative, who will communicate our research to Canadians to improve the health of men, boys and their future generations.

column36: Understanding health risks and promoting resilience in male youth with sexual violence experience
column37: This Team grant tackles the hidden problem of sexual violence (SV)victimization among male youths, from early adolescence to young adulthood. SV reflects a range of unwanted, coercive and non-consensual experiences, from sexting to rape. SV (including terms as childhood sexual abuse/CSA, sexual coercion in dating relationships, sexual exploitation of adolescents and emerging adults) represents a human rights, public health, and gender-based issue. Global population estimates of male CSA (8%) are in-line with Canadian national estimates (5.8% before age 16), and provincial estimates (e.g., 8.3% in Ontario).In US Justice data, where assaults were reported to police, in about 7000 incidents reported over a 5 year period, <9 years old was the peak age, followed by the 10 - 19 year old group. These took place most often in a residence, but also in a commercial place, college, and jail. Males experiencing SV present to varying service systems - child welfare, street services, residential care, mental health and substance abuse services, emergency services - yet, may never have their victimization recognized, and trauma-focused services may be required, but do not exist or may not be made available. Further, some victims may be asymptomatic and function well in daily living. Importantly, this Teams' projects target both contexts of challenge (rural/remote Aboriginal; child welfare; homelessness etc.), as well as contexts of resilience (high school or university attending). With stakeholders, this team seeks to fill in gaps on the level of SV among male youths; the processes underlying both impairment and resilience, and promising interventions.

column36: Shape the Path: Targeting the Health and Mobility of Older Men through Key Community Partnerships
column37: Our project title 'Shape the Path' refers to efforts to pave the way for older men to maintain mobility in a range of ways (personal, social, health settings, physical environment). Shape the Path aims to lessen the substantial burden of mobility-disability in older men. To do so we will examine factors (e.g. ethnicity, gender, environment, socioeconomic status) that influence older men's ability to 'go where they want to go, when they want to go there, and how they want to get there'. If one considers mobility as a 'capacity' then it facilitates older men's independence and their quality of life. We will assess capacity in a number of ways based on what men can actually do ( 'enacted capacity') and what they think they can do ('perceived capacity') across 3 distinct settings: community, home care and residential care. These settings represent different levels of mobility. We will use a variety of research methods to develop an in-depth understanding of men's experiences and other factors related to participation in physical activity as this is closely linked with their mobility. We will combine those new understandings with existing knowledge to intervene with a novel program that promotes (i) physical activity in community-dwelling older men. Next, we will determine the mobility characteristics of older men who receive home care support and intervene with a model that aims to enhance men's capacity (called re(ablement)) in home care. Finally, we will identify the mobility limitations of frail older men in residential care using novel sensor and video technology. This will be the basis for new strategies for promoting safe mobility for men in residential care. Importantly, we work closely with committed community stakeholders who guide the questions we ask. Together we deliver our findings back out to those who might benefit the most from what we learned, through dissemination of relevant programs, practices and policies.

column37: The present proposal aims to promote reproductive health among men in the general population and address the specific needs of two groups of men facing infertility concerns: 1) men undergoing assessment and treatment for infertility; 2) young adult cancer survivors whose diagnosis and treatment may have adversely affected their fertility. These are men who are at high risk for both physical and emotional problems, and whose specific needs are seldom addressed in research. Since men are less likely than women to seek treatment for physical or emotional issues, there is an urgent need to develop new ways to promote health and wellness in these men. Mobile health, the practice of medicine and public health on mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets, may be a promising way to do so. In order to develop a mobile health intervention, we will review existing educational resources on the Internet and from medical clinics, to see if they meet quality standards. We will survey men in our target groups about their knowledge of health risks associated with infertility and ask them about their information and support needs based on their experiences with the health care system in the assessment and treatment of infertility and fertility preservation. We will also ask health professionals about the types of educational and support resources that are available, and what is needed. This information will help us to develop a mobile health (mHealth) application (app) to provide easily accessible information, support, and tools to promote a healthy lifestyle in men facing fertility concerns. We will evaluate the effects of this type of intervention on quality of life, patient empowerment, psychological symptoms and mental wellness, physical activity and diet, and patient satisfaction.

Increase research capacity for HIV prevention for gbMSM in Canada by training community members, students, and scientists, and building research capacity in smaller cities and rural areas. 4. Increase the amount and quality of information provided by research to health providers and the community through conferences and events on HIV prevention and sexual health of gbMSM.

column36: Impact of paternal age on the health of gametes: risk of potential adverse outcomes
column37: Over the past 20 years, there is a clear trend for men to start having children at an increasingly older age. It is well-recognized that there is an association between maternal age and decreased fertility, higher incidence of abnormalities and diseases in their children; however, we are only beginning to grasp the impact of paternal age on fertility and progeny outcome. The objective of this Team Grant application is to examine how the trajectory of aging presents health challenges faced not only for older men but also for their children. Men older than 40 years of age take a longer time to make their partner pregnant and have a higher rate of infertility; partners of these men have a higher incidence of miscarriage. Paternal age is also linked to a higher risk for progeny to develop complex multi-gene diseases, such as autism, schizophrenia, and bipolar disease. Since sperm continue to be produced in men constantly throughout adult life at a rate of about 1000 sperm every heartbeat, decreased sperm cell function is likely to be associated with decreased sperm quality and not number. The central hypothesis underlying this Team Grant is that the trajectory of aging alters the quality of the sperm being delivered to the oocyte and that there is a direct relationship between infertility, paternal age, chromatin quality, epigenetic marks, and progeny outcome. The proposed studies represent a unique approach. There has been little attention to the quality of men's sperm as men move along their aging trajectory. The consequences of increased paternal age are only beginning to be demonstrated in studies from other countries. Our team has gathered the essential complementary expertise to make significant advances in this field. Our results will not only have positive consequences for men as they appreciate the link between aging and sperm chromatin quality but will also serve to decrease the health burden on future generations.

column36: The HPV-SAVE Study Team: HPV Screening and Vaccine Evaluation in men who have sex with men
column37: Infection by certain high-risk (HR) types of human papillomavirus (HPV) is the major cause of several serious cancers in men, including anal, penile and head and neck cancers. Anal infection by HR-HPV is much more common in men who have sex with men (MSM), particularly HIV-positive MSM. We also know that rates of anal cancer in the general population are increasing, and that HIV-positive MSM are at much higher risk. In fact, rates of anal cancer in HIV-positive MSM are estimated to be significantly higher than the rates of cervical cancer in women, prior to the adoption of routine screening with Pap smears. Our own work has previously shown that the prevalence of HR-HPV infection of the anal canal in Ontario MSM exceeds 90%. However, despite these alarming statistics, optimal protocols to screen for, and treat, anal HPV and pre-cancerous lesions have not been established. Further, the role of HPV vaccination in this community is unclear, as there has been very little experience with it. Finally, not only does HPV directly cause important disease in men, but infection enhances the sexual transmission of HIV through mechanisms that are unclear. This proposal brings together community and internationally-recognized experts in HPV disease and mucosal immunology to better understand these important issues, and to better define the optimal approach to HPV screening and management in HPV-positive MSM. It also aims to shed light on how this common infection impacts HIV transmission. All together, our team hopes to provide critical information to improve the health of HIV-positive MSM, and will provide an additional rationale for the provision of timely interventions (e.g. HPV vaccination) to help combat HPV's effects in this highly impacted community.

column36: Reducing HIV Vulnerabilities and Promoting Resilience Among Heterosexual Self-Identified African, Caribbean and Black Men in Ontario

Our mixed methods approach will include multiple methods of recruitment, data collection and analysis, and KTE. Our research program will address the programming and policy gaps affecting heterosexual ACB men in Ontario, reduce HIV-related and other social stigma, enhance HIV prevention messaging in ACB communities, and strengthen ACB men's involvement in community responses to HIV.
