column36: Promoting Appropriate Body Weight and Optimal Dietary Intake to Pregnant and Postpartum Women in the Context of Community-Based Organizations in Alberta
column37: Gestational Weight Gain (GWG) and dietary intake are important predictors of pregnancy outcomes. Inadequate or excessive weight gain during pregnancy increases the risk of pregnancy complications and long-term risk of chronic health problems for both mother and baby. Historically, inadequate GWG represented a great health concern, but now, with the rise of overweight and obesity rates in Canada and worldwide, the proportion of women entering pregnancy with a higher Body Mass Index has significantly increased, which has translated into an increased risk for excessive GWG (approximately 56% in Alberta). The same shift from inadequate to excessive GWG has been observed among low-income women who have been found to be at a greater risk for excessive GWG, and parity-associated obesity. This project aims to promote maternal health through supporting attainment of appropriate body weight and optimal dietary intake, during pregnancy and postpartum, among low-income women who access Community-Based Organizations (CBOs), partially funded by the Canada Prenatal Nutrition Program in Alberta. The research will use a knowledge translation framework to: 1) describe the web of factors that influence low-income women's body weights and diets during pregnancy and postpartum, 2) examine needs, gaps and opportunities within services currently delivered through CBOs during these vital life cycles, and 3) translate findings into practice by developing and implementing selected strategies that promote appropriate body weight and optimal dietary intake to pregnant and postpartum, low-income women in the context of CBOs. This project has the potential to improve maternal health by elucidating the complex web of factors that affect gestational and postpartum body weights, dietary intake and overall health. Given the importance of pregnancy for both women's and infants' health, this is a unique opportunity to positively impact the health of future generations.

column37: Autoimmune diseases occur when the patient's immune system attacks and destroys the body's tissues. Over time, inflammation damages the lining of the gut leading to diarrhea, pain, bleeding and other symptoms as well as increased risk for colorectal cancer. Currently, patients with IBD are treated with immunosuppressive drugs, anti-inflammatory medications, and surgery to remove the most severely affected portions of colon. Each treatment comes with a risk of harmful side effects, and none can cure the disease. IBD is lifelong and often progressive. Our goal is to develop a unique therapy that uses specialized immune cells, called 'regulatory T cells' or Tregs, instead of drugs, to treat the inflammation. Tregs regulate the immune response by preventing over-active immune cells from attacking one's own body. In IBD, certain factors make immune cells hyperactive which results in gut inflammation. We plan to design Tregs to recognize one such factor so that they will get activated in the gut, leading to remission of the disease. We will test our approach in isolated Tregs in the laboratory and in mouse models of IBD. Using mouse models we can show that the therapy works, and is safe, before potentially putting humans at risk. This novel therapy will be patient-specific and significantly reduce the risk of side effects. Over 200,000 Canadians have IBD, representing a $2.8 billion financial burden to our society. Research to treat and cure IBD will not only improve each patient's life, it will also reduce financial burdens on the Canadian health system and by giving the patients the ability to participate in a normal work life. In the future, Tregs could also be designed to recognize other molecules and treat other autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, or prevent rejection of transplanted organs.

column36: Wearable sensors to promote arm use post-stroke
column37: The lifetime risk of stroke is 1 in 5 after age 55 and 70% of these individuals will have difficulty using their arms and hands. Even though they have the ability, people often do not use their affected arm and hand when they are discharged from rehabilitation because they learn to compensate with the less affected arm. This is troubling as patients are often being discharged home in the first month or two after stroke when the greatest neural recovery is expected and not using their arm will limit their recovery. Furthermore, decreased arm use can lead to weakened muscles, pain, osteoporosis and decreased quality of life. Studies have shown that using pedometers to track walking steps can help people become more physically active. The aim of this study is to determine whether a treatment that utilizes an arm pedometer may increase stroke-affected arm use among people undergoing outpatient therapy. With help from engineers, we have developed a new arm pedometer that can track how much the arm and hand is used. Occupational therapists who treat upper limb dysfunction after stroke will determine how much patients in the study use their arm by asking them to wear the arm pedometer for one week at home. Patients will then be randomly assigned to 1 of 2 groups. One group will receive standard outpatient therapy and the other group will receive standard therapy plus the arm pedometer program. The pedometer group will be asked to increase their use at home by a certain amount each week and will be asked to create goals that outline the types of tasks they will perform with their stroke-affected arm. After 8 weeks, we will compare the arm movement, use and weekly pedometer readings between the 2 groups. Findings from this study will help us improve treatments for the stroke-affected arm and may reduce the harmful effects associated with not using the arm. These treatments may ultimately improve arm recovery and the quality of life for people who have had a stroke.

column36: Dysfunction of the orbitofrontal cortex in diet-induced obesity

column36: An Evidence-Based Online Intervention to Promote Adherence to a Gluten-free Diet Among Adults with Celiac Disease
column37: Celiac disease is an autoimmune dysfunction that requires strict adherence to a gluten-free (GF) diet in order to prevent detrimental health outcomes including bloating, diarrhea, constipation, and increased risk of intestinal cancers and osteoporosis. Following a strict GF diet is difficult given that gluten is added as a preservative or binding agent to many foods. Findings from a recent review suggest that as few as 42% of people with celiac disease report strict adherence to a GF diet. As such, poor adherence to a GF diet is an emerging health concern for people with celiac disease. Currently there is limited existing literature on evidence-based strategies to improve this dismal adherence to a GF diet. The goal of this research program is to develop and implement an evidence-based online intervention to improve adherence to a strict GF diet and quality of life among adults with celiac disease. The intervention material will teach people self-regulation and self-compassion skills. Self-regulation is considered a crucial skill necessary for successful adherence to a medical regimen (such as following a GF diet) among people with chronic disease. Self-compassion improves the ability to cope with chronic disease and is associated with greater quality of life. Study 1 will involve development, pilot testing and refinement of a 6-week online intervention to improve adherence to a GF diet and quality of life. Findings from focus groups with 16 individuals with celiac disease will be used to revise and refine the intervention material. In Study 2, 200 individuals with celiac disease will be randomized to an intervention or an attention control condition. It is expected that compared to the control condition, after completing the intervention, participants will report greater adherence to a GF diet and quality of life. Findings from this work will be used to inform evidence-based guidelines for the treatment and long-term care of people living with celiac disease.

column36: Using electronic health records linked to a DNA biobank to characterize relationships between mental and physical health
column37: Specific language impairment (SLI) is a learning disability found in 7% of kindergarten children and is defined as language difficulties in the absence of other developmental defects. Little is known about the causes of SLI, except that it is more common in boys than in girls, and that genetics play an important role. My research aims to identify the genetic causes of SLI by using emerging data on gene activity. Gene activity varies across tissues within an individual and between males and females, and abnormal gene activity can cause disease. Massive efforts are underway to explore the factors that regulate gene activity, and my project will use data from the Genome Tissue Expression database, which is characterizing regions of the genome that regulate gene activity in 40 different cell types and in 1000 individuals. SLI is a neurodevelopmental disorder that is more common in boys than in girls. I therefore hypothesize that the risk of SLI will be affected by regions of the genome that regulate gene activity in the brain, as well as regions of the genome that regulate gene activity differently in both sexes. I will use biostatistics to test these hypotheses, and results will help us better understand the underlying biology of SLI, the first step towards developing new treatments. Results may also be relevant to developmental disorders in which language impairment is a core feature (e.g., autism, cognitive impairment), and my methods could serve as a framework for investigating the role of gene activity in many different human diseases.

column36: Regenerative approaches to enhance recovery following cervical spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) are devastating with limited treatment options available to patients. Stem cell therapies aimed at re-establishing neuronal communication across injury sites has shown promise in animal models. Significant barriers to further recovery are our lack of understanding of the cells produced after stem cell transplant, and the formation of glial scar after injury. My work aims to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human cell-based therapies and the barriers to regrowth of neurons across injury sites. In particular, I will use a well-established rat model to determine what types of cells are produced after human stem cell xenograft, the importance of myelin regeneration in these therapies, whether removing glial scar can improve stem cell graft rates and functional outcomes. This work will create a roadmap for research on human stem cells and bring us closer to providing 1.4 million North Americans with an effective treatment option for SCI.

column36: ResistanceOpen: Developing a Global Map of Regional Antimicrobial Resistance
column37: The Public Health Agency of Canada, the World Health Organization, and the Centers for Disease Control recognize antimicrobial resistance, including resistant 'superbugs', as one of our greatest health threats worldwide. Rates of infections due to antimicrobial resistant organisms appear to be on the rise in many countries, however, there are significant gaps in our ability to track antibiotic resistance. Existing surveillance programs are limited by small sample sizes and poor geographic resolution. Understanding community level antibiotic resistance patterns is essential to understanding the risk of developing many types of antibiotic resistant infections. Currently, a public system of tracking regional (community level) antimicrobial resistance patterns across a diversity of pathogens does not exist. Through a partnership between the University of Toronto, Division of Infectious Diseases and the Harvard Centre for Biomedical Informatics, we intend to develop an open, collaborative, global database of antimicrobial resistance. This will be achieved through the use of publicly available antibiograms (indexes of resistance) as well as, through a web-based collaboration supporting open-source uploading from laboratories and hospitals in Canada and around the world. Antibiotic susceptibility will be displayed through an interactive web-based map, and will change in real-time based on user-defined selections. This will be the first open-collaboration database ('Map') of local antimicrobial resistance patterns in Canada and globally, and will (1) support clinicians in making important antibiotic treatment decisions, (2) drive a global effort into the development and spread of antimicrobial resistance, and (3) support detailed community level surveillance.

column36: Mobilizing the healthcare community towards an integrated approach to improving outcomes of patients with sleep disorders - Canadian Sleep and Circadian Network (CSCN)
column37: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects over 1 million Canadians. OSA leads to significant cardiovascular and metabolic health problems and patients with untreated OSA are at higher risk of stroke and Alzheimer's disease. The vision of the Canadian Sleep and Circadian Network (CSCN) is to mobilize the healthcare community to adopt an integrated approach towards improving outcomes and treatment of patients with OSA. Patient centric research: The CSCN has established three scientific objectives: 1) Identify biomarkers to detect OSA patients at high risk for adverse health outcomes. This research will focus on vulnerable patient populations such as severe OSA patients, obese children, and shift workers; 2) Identify the impact of OSA in neurodegenerative disorders; 3) Evaluate alternative models to improve access for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with OSA, and for improved adherence to treatment. Translation of research discoveries: CSCN will deploy a national plan of knowledge exchange between patient groups, researchers, the healthcare community and industry to provide affordable home-based diagnostic technologies, clinical practices guidelines and provide lay information to patients on research outcomes and therapies. Integration of patient's expertise: The CSCN will consult with OSA patients to focus research on patients' priorities, reinforce participative research, facilitate knowledge translation, and ensure strong links with community-based groups. Training and career development: CSCN will also create a national multidisciplinary training program integrating innovative approaches (e.g. online portal system, webinars). Outcomes: The anticipated outcomes include: i) identification of OSA patients at greater risk of adverse cardiovascular, metabolic, and cognitive effects; ii) earlier OSA diagnosis in vulnerable populations; iii) development of personalized OSA treatments;and iv) improvement strategies for patient adherence to OSA treatment.

column36: Socio-economic risk environments and health among people who use illicit drugs
column37: Socio-economic drivers of health risk are multi-dimensional and complex, and the broader socio-economic risk environment for marginalized people who use drugs (PWUD) has not been fully examined. Further, social and structural interventions to address these impacts are rare, as are examinations of how the socio-economic risk environment shapes research participation. My program of research will examine and develop strategies to mitigate the negative impacts of socio-economic risk on the health of marginalized PWUD across three interconnected lines of inquiry. First, using data from ongoing prospective cohorts of HIV-positive and HIV-negative PWUD, observational studies will examine the health impacts of key components of the socio-economic risk environment on health outcomes, including high-risk drug use; HIV and Hepatitis C-related outcomes, and mental illness. Second, I will implement social and structural intervention studies that test innovative strategies to mitigate the negative health impacts of socio-economic risk. Two RCTs will initiate this line of inquiry: (1) an RCT to test whether altering the distribution of social assistance decreases individual and community harm associated with escalations in drug use around the monthly distribution of social assistance; and (2) an RCT testing the efficacy of an intervention designed to expand access to low-threshold employment opportunities to improve employment uptake, drug use, HIV risk-behaviour and HIV treatment outcomes. Finally, to maximize the ethical and effective conduct of these and other RCTs, a third line of inquiry seeks to identify the individual, social and structural factors that affect recruitment, retention, and protocol adherence in addictions RCT research. This research innovates by linking observational, intervention and research participation studies to produce robust evidence for strategies to improve socio-economic security and health outcomes for people who use drugs.

column36: Genito-pelvic pain in women and couples: Causes, consequences and treatment
column37: Genital and pelvic ("genito-pelvic") pain is a common condition that negatively affects couples' quality of life by severely disrupting their sexuality and relationships. There are significant gaps in knowledge with respect to the biological, psychological and social predictors of genito-pelvic pain, as well as couple-based treatment. My 5-year research goals are to: 1) complete and share the findings from three CIHR-funded projects; 2) seek out funding and begin novel studies that will follow directly from this work; and 3) supervise a greater number of student trainees, thereby contributing to the training of future leaders in this important field. The three primary projects in my plan are: a) a two-month daily diary study examining the role of women's own and their partner's sexual goals in her pain during intercourse and the psychological and sexual adjustment of both members of the couple; b) a randomized clinical trial to examine the success of cognitive-behavioural couple therapy (CBCT) in treating genito-pelvic pain by testing it against a 'standard medical care' treatment (lidocaine) at post-treatment and 6-months later; c) a longitudinal study to examine the prevalence, symptom profile and biopsychosocial predictors of genito-pelvic pain from mid-pregnancy to 24 months postpartum. Data collection is underway for the first two projects, and the third project is under human ethics review. I have multidisciplinary collaborators who will ensure that my research program is clinically informed and results could be readily included in the health care system. The immediate benefit of this research is to empower women and couples to better manage genito-pelvic pain. Health care providers may change their clinical practice by inviting a more active role for women's partners and expanding treatment options. The long-term benefit is to decrease the burden of this condition by informing preventative and treatment intervention efforts.

column36: Family-based obesity prevention: Identifying effective strategies through epidemiologic research and intervention trials
column37: The overarching goal of my research is to improve the health of Canadian children by developing effective family-based obesity prevention interventions. To achieve this goal, my research plan is to conduct epidemiologic research to identify modifiable family factors that influence children's obesity risk (Aims 1 and 2) and translate that knowledge into obesity prevention interventions (Aim 3). Aim 1 is to identify how parental feeding practices influence children's dietary intake and weight. Most prior feeding research is cross-sectional and based on parental self-report, providing little understanding of how traits of the parent, child, and environment interact to affect dietary intake. To address this gap, I will conduct a longitudinal study that uses direct observation to explore how parental feeding practices influence children's intake and weight. Aim 2 is to identify how the general family environment influences children's weight. There is a paucity of research exploring how the general family context, e.g., family functioning, influences children's weight related behaviours. I have started to address this gap through my NIH-funded study exploring how general family factors influence adolescent behaviour. I aim to extend this research to explore these associations among families with young children through the Guelph Family Health Study, a family-based cohort study. Aim 3 is to test family-based obesity prevention interventions. Intervening among young children requires changing the behaviours of their parents. However, most obesity interventions have been unsuccessful in engaging parents. Using findings from Aims 1 and 2 and building on the success of my previous interventions, I will test the effectiveness of a tailored, family-based obesity prevention intervention. By determining the most effective ways to change behaviours of young children, the results of this research will optimize childhood obesity prevention and pediatric care in Canada.

column36: Fostering healthy habits of regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour in the early years
column37: The early years (under 5 years) mark the most critical period of overall development throughout the human lifespan. Regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour (e.g., TV viewing) in the early years are important for healthy growth and development, and for preventing chronic diseases. However, 75% of Canadian children in the early years do not meet national guidelines for both behaviours. Evidence is needed on the most important intervention targets and strategies unique to this age group in relevant settings (home, child care, neighbourhood). Such evidence will support achievement of appropriate doses of regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour. The overarching goal of my research program is to effectively promote healthy habits of regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour among children of the early years. Achieving this goal will foster healthy growth and development, life-long active living, and the maintenance of a healthy weight status to prevent chronic diseases. Over the next five years I will address three main research questions in parallel. Answers to these questions will provide the necessary foundation to address my overarching goal. Research Question One: What are the dose-response relationships between physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and important health indicators in the early years? Research Question Two: What are the determinants of physical activity and sedentary behaviour that are unique to the early years in the home and neighbourhood settings? Research Question Three: What role does child care policy play in promoting regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour in the early years? I will conduct several innovative research projects to address these questions. The combined outcomes of my research program will provide practice and policy evidence that can be directly applied by stakeholders to ensure a healthy start for our youngest Canadians.

column36: Magnetic resonance imaging of pediatric brain development
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders are becoming increasingly more prevalent. Some of the more common disorders include dyslexia (affecting approximately 5-17% of children), fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (2-5%), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (3-11%) and autism spectrum disorder (~1.5%). All of these can negatively affect a child's quality of life by limiting school success, career prospects, and social interactions. Therefore, supporting healthy brain development in childhood and adolescence, and thereby maximizing a child's potential, remains an important goal. My research uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to understand structural brain development, and how it relates to cognitive and behavioral development in healthy children and those with neurodevelopmental disorders. My specific research goals over the next 5 years are to: (1) examine language and structural brain development in preschool-aged children, (2) use advanced imaging techniques to understand healthy white matter development in childhood and adolescence, and (3) identify brain abnormalities in children and adolescents with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. This work will identify key periods of brain plasticity and highlight brain abnormalities, laying the foundation for future studies to develop appropriate interventions for developmental disorders. Ultimately, this research will enable programs that can support healthy brain development in children and adolescents.

column36: Strategies for Optimal Lung Ventilation in ECMO for ARDS: The SOLVE ARDS Study
column37: Artificial life support with a respiratory (ventilator) may be life-saving for patients with lung failure, especially those with the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). However, in recent years, doctors have recognized that the ventilator itself can worsen lung failure, particularly in the sickest patients. As a result, there has been a growing interest in the use of an artificial lung device called extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for the management of patients with severe ARDS. While being supported with ECMO, the lungs can rest and potentially avoid additional injury from the ventilator. However, it is currently unclear how best to set the ventilator to minimize any further damage to the lungs of patients with severe ARDS supported with ECMO. This study will help to determine the optimal settings for the ventilator in these critically ill patients on ECMO to avoid any ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI). The results of this study may help inform clinicians caring for patients with severe ARDS supported with ECMO on how to further improve outcomes in these patients.

column36: The role of Glutathione in Glutamatergic system dysregulation in Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a chronic, progressive mental illness that affects up to 1% of the population and is the 5th leading causes of disability in industrialized countries. Unfortunately, the current treatment for schizophrenia with antipsychotics are not working in about 20% to 35% of the patients. Glutamate is a substance or neurotransmitter normally present in the brain; it is the most prominent excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain and plays an integral role in every brain's function. Glutathione is a major antioxidant in the brain. It is involved in the neutralization of free radicals that may damage the cells in the brain. In addition, and relevant for our current research, Glutathione can modify the levels of Glutamate in the brain and the 'potency' by which Glutamate works in the brain. Decreased levels of Glutathione have been found in schizophrenia and increasing Glutathione levels have improved some of the symptoms in schizophrenia. However, no research has been performed to investigate the levels of Glutathione in the brains of those patients who do not respond well to antipsychotic treatment and no research has directly investigated the relationship between Glutathione-Glutamate in schizophrenia. We will recruit patients with schizophrenia with no response to antipsychotic medications, patients with full remission of symptoms of schizophrenia after antipsychotic treatment, and healthy volunteers. Glutamate and Glutathione levels will be measured in several brain regions associated with schizophrenia using a non-invasive technique called Proton Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy and will be compared across the three groups of participants using mathematical models. If our hypothesis is correct, and we are able to demonstrate abnormal levels and altered relationship between Glutamate-Glutathione in patients with treatment resistant schizophrenia, the results will help to guide new future treatments and increase understanding of anomalies in schizophrenia.

column36: A research program on migration as a social determinant of HIV, STIs, & HCV among marginalized women
column37: Migration is a globally recognized social determinant of HIV, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and Hepatitis C (HCV). Yet, little is known regarding how migration patterns and experiences impact transmission, risk, and prevention of these infections in high-income settings such as Canada. Women in sex work often face high prevalence of HIV/STIs and are highly mobile, yet little is known regarding the ways in which migration patterns influence health outcomes and access to care for migrant sex workers. In Canada, as in other settings, migration patterns generally relate to unequal social and economic opportunities, which attract women from other countries, provinces, and communities to urban areas such as Metropolitan Vancouver. Among women of Aboriginal (First Nations, Inuit, and Metis) ancestry, migration between Northern BC and Vancouver is embedded within a legacy of colonization and racialized policies, yet has received little attention in relation to HIV or HCV. Despite efforts to scale-up access to the continuum of care in BC (e.g., the STOP HIV/AIDS program), migrants, sex workers, and populations of Aboriginal ancestry remain disproportionately impacted by HIV, STIs and HCV. This research is investigating how migration influences HIV, STI and HCV risks and prevention among sex workers (e.g., exposure to new working conditions, violence). Based on a cohort study of 1000 female sex workers in Vancouver, including 600 non-migrants and 400 migrants, the research described in this application is evaluating and informing policies and programs to improve the health of migrant sex workers, including international migrants as well as internal migrants who move within Canadian or provincial borders. It will establish a broader program of innovative research and training in Migration and Global Sexual Health to facilitate comparative work with marginalized migrant women across international settings, including Canada, Mexico and Central America, and elsewhere.

column36: Addiction Research Program to Reduce Costs and Improve Health
column37: In Canada, social costs due to substance abuse are estimated to approach $40 billion annually. Specifically, intravenous drug use, including illicit opioids (e.g., heroin) injection, is associated with an array of health and social harms for individuals and communities, including high rates of overdoses and infectious diseases via the sharing of injection equipment. Unfortunately, some of Canada's most vulnerable populations, including Aboriginal peoples, are hardest hit by these harms. While some interventions, including opioid substitution therapies (e.g., methadone maintenance therapy), have proven effective in reducing injection drug-related harms, Canada is now experiencing a new epidemic of prescription opioid (PO) misuse, and little is known about how existing interventions can be optimized to address rising PO misuse, particularly among people who inject drugs. While many opioid users are also known to use cocaine, there are no approved pharmacotherapies for the treatment of cocaine addiction, necessitating urgent research efforts in this area. Lastly, while provinces have recently initiated new opioid addiction-related services, the impact of new service delivery models on PO misuse and other drug-related harms have not been fully evaluated. My proposed research builds on my past work focused on illicit drug use and aims to reduce healthcare costs and improve health by focusing on PO misuse and polydrug users (i.e., users of opioids and cocaine). Specifically, my primary research objectives are: (1) to investigate and address the impact of emerging PO misuse and concomitant crack cocaine use on patterns of injection drug use and drug-related harm; (2) to evaluate the efficacy of a novel addiction treatment option to treat polydrug users; and (3) to evaluate the impact of new structural interventions that are relevant to polydrug users.

column36: Understanding and exploiting genome instability in cancer
column37: Cancer is caused by specific DNA mutations that can arise spontaneously over time. Conditions that increase DNA damage or which inhibit DNA repair can have a strong cancer-promoting effect. Old age and environmental stresses, such as exposure to radiation or carcinogenic chemicals, damage DNA and favour cancer formation. In addition, predisposing genetic factors that affect a cells' ability to protect and repair DNA promote cancer formation by causing so-called genome instability, defined as an increase in the frequency with which mutations are passed to daughter cells. Genome instability is a recognized contributor to cancer formation but can also serve as a therapeutic target by sensitizing cancer cells to treatment with DNA-damaging radiation or chemotherapies. My lab is taking a multi-level approach to understand genome instability and its application to cancer. My group has been funded to work in two broad areas over the next 5 years. First, we have received significant funds to study how alterations in a fundamental process called RNA transcription may ultimately lead to genome damage and mutations. In certain mutant cells RNA binds to genomic DNA and this hybrid DNA:RNA molecule prevents many of the normal transactions that maintain genome stability. We are studying which mutations lead to an increase in DNA:RNA hybrids, how and where those hybrids form, what is their relevance to mutant cancer cells and how can DNA:RNA hybrids, and the conditions that cause them, be exploited for cancer therapy. Second, we have received funding to study how proteins that normally respond to DNA damage are produced by cells. When a protein is made, it must fold into a three-dimensional structure and assemble with other biological molecules to perform its function. How protein folding and assembly occur for several important DNA damage response proteins is under study in our lab. These projects intersect as they describe the causes of and cellular responses to DNA damage.

column36: Epidemiology and treatment of maternal mental illness
column37: Maternal mental illness affects up to 10% of women, with negative effects for women & their children. The vision of my research program is to optimize care for mothers with mental illness, with focus in two key areas: (1) Novel interventions that aim to increase treatment acceptability for mothers with mental illness; and (2) Population-level studies that inform us about course of illness, risk factors, and safety & effectiveness of existing treatments for mothers with mental illness. Over Years 1 and 2 of the New Investigator Award, I will complete two ongoing pilot treatment studies: (1) An electronic patient decision aid (PDA) that aims to optimize decision-making around antidepressant medication use in pregnancy; and (2) Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), an effective brain stimulation treatment for depression that is focal, and does not induce any systemic effects (making it an ideal treatment option for pregnant women). I will also complete ongoing population-level studies, and set up an enhanced data platform for future research where Ontario health data is enriched with information about psychosocial context (e.g. marital status, domestic violence), use of non-physician services (e.g. midwifery, postpartum public health nursing), and maternal-fetal exposures (i.e. drugs, substances). In Years 3 to 5, I will move on to definitively evaluating the PDA and tDCS interventions in larger groups of women; and to new studies with the expanded data platform that will allow us to better identify at-risk women & children, understand effectiveness of existing supports and services, and guide recommendations about medication use in pregnancy. Taken together, the studies in this research program will enhance our ability to intervene prenatally and in early motherhood to improve maternal and child outcomes. The program infrastructure also creates significant capacity for training junior researchers, and for addressing future research and policy questions.

column36: Statistical integration of biomarker data leads to a new understanding of aging, with direct clinical implications
column37: Aging is one of the least-understood areas of biology, with hundreds of theories but no consensus. Many researchers now agree that multiple mechanisms operate simultaneously, but there is little understanding of how they might work in concert. Our recent research has demonstrated that aging is due at least in part to breakdowns in how large numbers of molecules interact with each other. We have shown how to measure this "dysregulation" accurately and simply, confirming the importance of studying integrated aging physiology at an organismal level. These findings have many implications, both applied and theoretical, and over the next five years we will pursue as many of these implications as possible. Specifically, we will: (1) Develop, validate, and implement clinical tools to calculate a patient's dysregulation profile and to guide clinicians in adjusting treatments incorporating this information. This work will be conducted using one of the world's largest and best clinical databases, ResearchOne. (2) Study how changes in diet affect changes in dysregulation during aging, and use the results to develop nutritional recommendations that can be personalized based on an individual's nutrition and dysregulation profile. (3) Team up with researchers studying several chronic diseases to understand how dysregulation of specific physiological systems underlies chronic diseases and to develop better clinical measurement/diagnostic techniques for the underlying problems. (4) Continue mathematical and theoretical research on dysregulation in order to better understand the biological underpinnings of aging, physiological organization, and evolution. Our work to date suggests a new paradigm for how to successfully integrate physiological complexity into research across many disciplines. While aging cannot be stopped, our results represent one of the most promising avenues yet to slow the progression of its negative consequences.

column36: Endosomal control of autophagy in intestinal diseases
column37: The digestive system is complex and by consequent is the site of multiple diseases. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affect 1 in 150 Canadians, while colorectal cancer is among the most common and lethal malignancy. Although these two diseases are different, they both are linked to a cellular mechanism called autophagy. Autophagy is the process by which cells degrade and recycle their own constituents. Autophagy is induced by different stresses. In intestinal cells, autophagy helps in the removal of pathogenic bacteria. On the other hand, cancer cells grow very rapidly in environments lacking proper nutrients supply. Hence, cancer cells will rely on autophagy to stay alive. Cells of the body are composed of multiple types of membranes. These membranes are highly controlled and the mechanisms regulating them are collectively called 'membrane trafficking'. Autophagy is vastly controlled by membrane trafficking events. Thus, understanding how membrane trafficking regulates autophagy is important to find new therapeutic avenues for both IBD and colorectal cancer. My work has uncovered regulators of membrane trafficking necessary for autophagy. I found that their role is temporally controlled and that activation and recruitment of specific effectors is important for autophagy progression. In this proposal, I will characterize how one regulator of membrane traffic is activated and inhibited by certain proteins, and how it controls autophagy. I will also study how these regulators and effectors assemble into protein complexes (molecular machines) to control membrane trafficking. Importantly, I will test the newly identified components and aspects of their temporal regulation for their roles in autophagy in normal intestinal epithelium and for their requirements in colorectal cancer cell growth and in IBD models. This work will represent a key step in understanding how we can specifically control autophagy to prevent IBD or to target and eliminate colorectal cancer cells.

column36: Understanding the mechanisms of stem cell lineage development and tumour suppression using freshwater planarians
column37: Humans owe their longevity and their ability to fix tissues throughout their lives to the activity of a specific cell type called "adult stem cell". Adult stem cells exist throughout the life of an organism and when they divide, they renew themselves and also produce a daughter cell in order to replace cells that are lost due to aging or injury. For example, human blood stem cells will replace the millions of blood cells we turnover every day. In addition, humans have stem cells in most of our tissues, especially tissues which turnover rapidly such as the skin, blood, lungs, and intestines. Interestingly, those tissues are also the most common sites of tumour formation, which suggests a connection between adult stem cells and the development of cancer. In addition, cancers often have their own stem cells, called cancer stem cells, which behave very similarly to normal adult stem cells, but simply in a less-regulated fashion. Therefore, it stands to reason that if we can learn more about the biology that drives normal stem cells, we will understand how this biology goes awry during cancer development. Here we will use a non-traditional model system, the freshwater planarian, to investigate the role of cancer-causing genes in normal adult stem cell biology as well as discover new mechanisms that regulate stem cells. Planarians possess a large population of adult stem cells that can be easily manipulated and studied in the adult. We propose to use the advantages of planarians to discover new stem cell regulators in the hopes that any new molecule found may be a potential target for future therapies in human cancers.

column36: Optimizing exercise for improving cardiometabolic health and inflammation in individuals with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes

column36: AMPK regulation of macrophage cholesterol metabolism in atherosclerosis
column37: Heart disease is a condition that affects more than one million Canadians, and costs the Canadian healthcare system almost 21 billion dollars annually. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of cholesterol and immune cells in the lining of the arteries (atherosclerotic plaque), and is a leading cause of heart attack and stroke. In addition to heart disease risk factors such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, the way that our body handles the build up of cholesterol in the arteries is also very important. Specialized immune cells called macrophages are able to take up and store excess cholesterol, protecting the artery wall in the process. These macrophages have specialized pathways to then transfer the cholesterol they scavenge to the circulating lipoprotein "HDL", which then carries the cholesterol to the liver, where it can be safely removed (this is why HDL-cholesterol is called the "good" cholesterol). This is known as reverse cholesterol transport. However, when this process is overwhelmed, cholesterol builds in macrophages, turning them into foam cells and causing atherosclerosis to progress. We have discovered that an important metabolic regulator called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), activates reverse cholesterol transport in macrophages, but the mechanisms involved are still unknown. The objective of this proposal is to determine how AMPK causes this beneficial removal of cholesterol from macrophage foam cells. We will use genetically engineered mice that are lacking the AMPK gene, as well as therapeutic compounds that specifically activate AMPK to test our hypotheses. The goal of our research is to investigate and uncover novel mechanisms that contribute to atherosclerosis and heart disease in the hopes of developing more effective prevention and therapeutic strategies.

column36: Improving the outcome of rehabilitation following rotator cuff tendinopathy
column37: Shoulder pain is common and associated with substantial functional limitations. Rotator cuff (RC) disorders accounts for 50% to 85% of all shoulder complaints. Regardless of intervention, clinical trials suggest that the long-term outcome is negative for more than 30% of patients with RC disorders. The overarching aim of my research program is thus to improve the outcome of interventions for this population. To reach this aim, the present proposal includes 3 projects needed to fill some knowledge gaps. Individuals with RC disorder present movement deficits that lead to the compression of RC tendons and pain. In Project 1, the reasons they start moving differently will be investigate by exposing healthy individuals to experimental pain or fatigue and see how it influences shoulder movements. This project will improve our understanding on the development of movement deficits associated with RC disorders. One way of improving the outcome of interventions is to optimize shoulder movement by relearning a normal movement using training. However should pain be avoided during training? Project 2 will look at how well healthy individuals (experimental pain) and individuals with RC disorders learn and retain what they have learned if they are in pain. Subjects will be exposed to a force field applied to the upper limb, and will have to adapt to retrieve a normal movement. If pain interferes with learning, it would suggest that the same intervention would be less effective in the presence of pain. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; low current delivered to the brain) has been shown to enhance learning associated with training. Project 3 will investigate the effects of combining tDCS and training to improve rehabilitation outcomes. Individuals with RC disorders will be randomly assigned to one of two intervention groups: training with tDCS or same training with sham tDCS. This project will determine if tDCS should be used in this population to improve the outcome.

column36: The impact of environmental pollution on cardiovascular disease development and global health transitions
column37: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading causes of death in both high-income and lower-income regions of the world. There is an urgent need to find effective solutions that can prevent the development of cardiovascular and other chronic diseases. Almost half of the word's population cooks or heats their homes with traditional wood or coal stoves that produce air pollution levels that are 40-50 times higher than international safety guidelines. Research by myself and others shows that exposure to solid fuel smoke increases people's risk of developing cardiovascular disease. In the next five years, I will continue with this area of research with the goal of identifying environmental interventions that can effectively reduce air pollution exposures for large populations and prevent cardiovascular diseases. I will form interdisciplinary teams to evaluate the health and environmental benefits of improved household energy, better housing conditions, and improved transportation. I will develop and assess new tools to assess air pollution exposures and people's vascular function. I will also analyze urine and serum samples to identify key molecular or cellular features that may link pollution exposure and cardiovascular risk from birth to older ages. This research program uses novel methods and measurements to identify high quality environmental solutions, measure their health benefit, and shed light on the human biological processes that occur when air pollution enters the body. This work has the potential to benefit the billions of people exposed to poor environmental conditions.

column36: Precise and Rapid assessment of collaterals using multi-phase CTA in the triage of patients with acute ischemic stroke for IA Therapy (PRove-IT)
column37: Stroke is the 3rd leading cause of death in North America and a leading cause of disability in Canada. Most strokes are caused by a blood clot blocking supply of blood to the brain. Collaterals are small connections between arteries in the brain that maintain blood flow to the brain beyond a blocked artery until full flow can be restored by "clot-busting" drugs. The network of brain collaterals is the body's own tool to minimize damage caused by stroke. Patients with poor collaterals do not benefit from acute stroke treatment. Our new brain scan measures collaterals quickly and reliably, immediately identifying patients who will benefit from treatment. This study tests whether this new brain scan is capable of predicting who will benefit from acute stroke treatment. In addition, we can improve our understanding of why some patients have good collaterals and some not. If we can better understand how to keep this natural system (collaterals) strong and healthy we can reduce the effects of stroke. This study involves patients arriving at the Emergency Room with stroke symptoms. Patient information gathered then, such as medical history, blood test results and brain scans, will be analyzed and compared with each other and with information gathered later, such as a follow up CT scan (1 to 7 days later) and the patient's health in 3 months. There has been very little research into understanding collaterals. This study will tell us whether measuring collaterals using our new brain scan helps doctors treat patients faster and better. This study will also tell us why some patients have good collaterals. This knowledge can be used to develop techniques that improve collaterals in patients without them. Supporting blood supply to the brain when it needs it most will help stroke patients significantly. This study will therefore advance our ability to lessen brain damage due to stroke.

column36: Integrating clinical, functional and chemical genomics to understand lung cancer biology
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide, suffering from a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis and a paucity of effective therapeutic strategies to treat advanced tumors. However, with our increasing understanding of lung cancer biology has come the advent of targeted therapies to combat this devastating disease. These therapies target mutated components of key cellular pathways on which tumors have become dependent on for survival, yielding drastic initial response rates without the major side effects of traditional chemotherapies. Despitethesesuccessestwomajorproblemsremain:first,themajorityof lung cancer patients have tumors without mutations in targetable genes and; second, all patients eventually develop resistance to treatment with these targeted agents. In addition, since lung tumors commonly have hundreds of mutated genes, it is difficult to pinpoint those that are responsible for tumor growth and resistance to therapy, creating a clear bottleneck in the translation of laboratory findings to a clinical setting. I propose an integrative strategy to address these issues. Through analysis of the genomic profiles of human lung tumors, I aim to identify novel genes and pathways that are altered during lung cancer development. Furthermore, by combining this information with the characterization of mice genetically engineered to develop lung tumors, I attempt to elucidate the key genes driving lung cancer initiation, progression and response to therapy. Lastly, by screening libraries of chemical compounds across lung cancer cells, I aim to characterize novel inhibitors of these identified genes and their corresponding pathways that show promise for use as targeted therapies. Together, this work will further our understanding of lung cancer biology and create insight toward the development of new approaches to diagnose and treat patients suffering from this disease.

column36: Computational pharmacogenomics for drug repurposing in cancer
column37: Current therapies are ineffective in many aggressive cancer types. Despite the fact that thousands of drugs are being tested in clinical trials, the approval rate by the FDA decreased during the last decade. This is partly due to the fact that the mode of action of these new drugs is often poorly characterized and the subset of patients for which they might be effective remain largely unclear. Properly matching individual patient to the best therapeutic option is therefore extremely challenging, although crucial for the efficient implementation of personalized medicine. Recent advances in biological and computational technologies make it possible to discover new treatments for aggressive cancer types, such as medulloblastoma, pancreatic, breast, ovarian and lung cancers. Indeed, data have been recently generated to characterize the biological features of cancer cells (DNA mutations or levels of gene expression) and how these diseased cells respond to a large panel of drugs. These 'pharmacogenomic' studies offer a unique opportunity to identify which drugs might be effective to kill cancer cells, and which biological features these cancer cells must harbour to ensure significant therapeutic effects. However, due to the complexity and sheer amount of such data, current computational approaches mostly failed to repurpose existing drugs or identify new ones that were successfully validated in (pre)clinical studies. My vision is to identify new drugs with high therapeutic potential, to identify new indications for existing drugs and to build robust predictors of their response. The overarching goal of my research program is to develop novel computational approaches leveraging large pharmacogenomic datasets to enable high-throughput drug repurposing and drug response prediction in cancer. These new therapeutic strategies hold the promise to significantly advance the Canadian health care system through fast translation into clinical practice.

column36: Role of Fatty Acid Energy Metabolism in Age-Related Macular Degeneration
column37: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of blindness in adults over fifty. But little is known about the drivers of new blood vessels that invade the retina in blinding AMD. We do know however that abnormal blood lipid levels and mutations in mitochondria (the cell's powerhouse) are associated with AMD. We therefore suggested that a primary disorder in lipid energy production in the eye might drive abnormal vessel growth, as an attempt to bring more fuel to the retina. Our hypothesis challenges two dogmas in biology: (1) that sugar is the only source of fuel to the eye and, (2) that lack of oxygen is the main driver of blood vessel growth. The eye consumes more energy than any other organ and the retina is a fatty tissue. All enzymes required for energy production from fat are present in the eye. Also, Very low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR) is abundant in the eye. VLDLR facilitates the uptake of fat into cells and is expressed in high energy consuming organs able to use fat as a source of energy, such as the heart. Interestingly, Vldlr knockout (ko) mice develop vascular lesions that mimic a form of AMD. It is a good model in which to test our hypothesis. Vldlrko mice have elevated blood lipid levels because of poor fat uptake. Fat and sugar-derived energy productions are interdependent and regulated in part through lipid receptors. The lipid receptor, GPR40, is highly present in the retina, where its role has not been explored. Our preliminary results suggest that GPR40 controls energy production in the retina. Excess circulating lipids in Vldlrko mice signal through GPR40 to lower sugar uptake resulting in an energy crisis and abnormal vessel growth. Two major gaps in our understanding of AMD are explored. First, the role of lipids as an alternative fuel for the eye. Energy production may be a driving force of AMD. Second, the role of GPR40 as an energy switch in the retina and a possible therapeutic target in AMD.

column36: An Arf-GEF pathway for cytoskeleton control and tissue development
column37: Our proposal addresses fundamental aspects of molecular, cellular and developmental biology relevant to our understanding of human disease. We are determining how molecular complexes control the architecture of the outer membrane that surrounds each individual cell found in the body. This outer membrane is critical for the cell shapes and cell-cell interactions underlying the development and maintenance of tissues and organs. The outer membrane is controlled by cellular signals that organize molecular cables to pull on the membrane from within. By pulling the membrane inward, cells can divide to grow tissues, and they can pull on neighbouring cells to re-shape tissues. We recently discovered a novel molecular mechanism for keeping these molecular cables in check. We hypothesize that this restraint mechanism physically removes the cellular signals for cable formation from the outer membrane. In this way, abnormally strong pulling forces can be avoided so that cells divide and interact properly. To test this hypothesis we are using the experimental work-horse Drosophila melanogaster (the fruit fly). The molecules that organize cells and tissues in Drosophila are equivalent to those that organize cells and tissues in humans, and Drosophila has major advantages experimentally. Thus, Drosophila is an important model for discovering and studying molecules that contribute to human disease. The molecules we study are conserved from flies to humans and have been implicated in cancer progression. The cellular processes we study are also relevant to cancer. Abnormal cell division leads to gene loss or gene gain with changes to gene expression that can promote cancer growth. column36: Advancing primary care for people with and at risk for HIV
column37: The number of people living with HIV in Canada is increasing. This is in part because new infections continue to occur, primarily among vulnerable populations, in particular people who use drugs, and in part because people with HIV who receive antiretroviral therapy are living longer. The goal of this program of research is to use a primary care approach to address priorities in the care of both these populations - that is, people who use drugs who are at risk of HIV, and people already living with HIV. In the first study, I focus on the fact that people with HIV are developing other conditions associated with aging, such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes, which make their health care increasingly complex. There are several ways in which people with HIV obtain care from specialists and/or primary care physicians, but we do not yet understand the best way to care for this population in the primary care setting. I will address several challenges in the management of HIV including: the way specialists and primary care doctors communicate; the way chronic conditions and health promotion activities are managed; the way people with HIV access care in rural and remote areas; and the engagement of people who are not yet accessing care. This team brings together diverse collaborators across 3 provinces (MB, ON, NL) in order to improve care for this population. In the second study, I recognize that most current options for care among people who use drugs focus on addiction recovery. I will build on a community-based research study of people who use drugs in Ottawa to better understand which health and social services are required to create a more comprehensive and integrated approach to care. I will implement and study a self-management workshop for people who use drugs, and will explore their experience of care in existing easy-to-access settings. This study brings together policymakers, providers, advocacy groups, and people with lived experience and their allies.

column36: PKCs as molecular memory traces
column37: An experience changes the brain and leaves a trace behind. This trace is what we call memory. The goal of my lab is to understand the trace at the molecular level. Different experiences lead to different molecular traces that last for different periods of time. Our understanding of memory rests on identifying these molecular traces. We study memory at a fundamental level, identifying the simplest system in which we can examine the memory trace. One model is the marine mollusk Aplysia, because in this system the neurons that hold the memory trace have been identified. This is a valuable system as seen by the Nobel Prize awarded to Dr. Eric Kandel in 2000 for his work on memory in this system. In this model system the connections between neurons (synapses) that change during memory formation have been identified and one can study those synaptic changes in a simple preparation. Once we define an important molecular trace, we use the rodent system to determine the role of this trace in a vertebrate memory model. In this application, we study how memories are maintained and explore the hypothesis that the connections between neurons that maintain memory ('memory synapses') are fundamentally different than other synapses. We are testing the hypothesis that 'memory synapses' are labile and require persistent maintenance by a set of proteins called PKMs that persistently modify proteins at memory synapses. When these proteins are inhibited, memories are erased. We are studying both how PKMs are formed and how they maintain changes at 'memory synapses'. Understanding how memories are formed has important health implications both for pathological conditions such as mental retardation, and physiological conditions such as aging. A better understanding of how memories are formed is important for developing strategies for improving memory in both healthy and diseased populations.

column36: Developmental programming of cardiovascular function by iron deficiency: early mechanisms and therapeutic interventions
column37: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional disorder in the world, affecting an estimated 66-80% of the global population (WHO 2003), with pregnant women being the most susceptible subgroup. We and others have shown that offspring that were iron deficient during pregnancy are at a greater risk of developing heart disease and obesity in later life. Due to its prevalence and tendency to affect pregnant women, iron deficiency is poised to contribute substantially to the health care burden caused by chronic disease. Despite the magnitude of the problem, little is known about how iron deficiency impacts the development of the fetus, and without this knowledge, devising and testing new treatments is not possible. The objective of this work is to study how oxygen transport and free radical production in the fetus are altered by feeding pregnant dams a diet low in iron, and how these impact blood vessel and kidney development. We will be studying blood vessels and kidneys in an animal model because these tissues are known to be vulnerable to dietary insults during pregnancy; furthermore, kidneys and blood vessels play important roles in cardiovascular function, and problems with their development can lead to a life-time of health complications. We will also study the offspring at various ages to see how blood vessel and kidney dysfunction progresses through life, and how these programmed tissues cope with secondary stressors such as increased dietary sodium intake. The ultimate goal of this work is to build a framework of detailed information with which we can test the safety and efficacy of prenatal treatments for future use in humans, so that we can prevent the long-term health consequences of pregnancy complications like iron deficiency. With this goal in mind, a final objective of this work is to test the safety and therapeutic benefit of the nutraceutical resveratrol- a natural plant-derived polyphenol known to confer many cardiovascular health benefits.

column36: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial of group transdiagnostic cognitive-behaviour therapy for anxiety disorders in primary care
column37: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental disorders in community settings, and they are associated with significant psychological distress, functional and social impairment. Although pharmacological and psychological treatments for anxiety and depression have existed for several years now, only a minority of anxiety disorder sufferers are treated according to guidelines. Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) is the most consistently efficacious psychological treatment for anxiety disorders, but implementation of CBT in primary care is challenging due to limited resources. Recent studies indicate that group CBT for multiple anxiety disorders could be a promising alternative to individual CBT in primary care. The aim of the study is to examine the effectiveness of group CBT for anxiety disorders as a complement to usual care by family physicians. The clinical trial will be conducted in four Health and Social Services Centers in the province of Quebec (i.e. Sherbrooke, Monteregie, Laval and Quebec). Patients will be French-speaking adults with anxiety disorders, and they will be randomly assigned to one of three treatment conditions: a) Transdiagnostic group CBT (12 weekly 2-hr sessions), b) Support group (12 weekly 2-hr sessions), c) usual care. The transdiagnostic group CBT will be offered as a differed intervention to participants in groups (b) and (c) after the 12-month follow up. A qualitative study comprising individual semi-structured interviews with patients and therapists will be conducted to gain a deeper understanding of results. The primary study results will include improvement on a questionnaire on anxiety symptoms and a clinical assessment. The evaluation of group transdiagnostic CBT in the real world will provide invaluable information to decision makers, health care managers, clinicians and patients. Widespread implementation of group CBT could lead to better outcomes for a large number of patients living with anxiety.

column36: Overt responses during covert orienting: novel biomarkers for the oculomotor system in health and disease
column37: Humans are predominantly visual animals. Our dependency on vision necessitated the development of a refined oculomotor system to re-orient our line of sight. The oculomotor system is distributed over a network of brain areas, and includes both the low-level machinery that rapidly moves our line of sight, and the high-level circuits that implement the flexible strategies needed to operate in a complex world. These low-level and high-level circuits overlap within the superior colliculus (SC), which also coordinates a diverse orienting response via projections that distribute to many different targets in the brainstem and spinal cord. The orienting response includes saccadic movements of the eyes, head, and/or body to rapidly move the line of sight, and also includes more subtle changes in neck muscle activity, pupil diameter, or very small eye movements called microsaccades. The key hypothesis of my work is that information sent out by the SC can recruit some components of the orienting response without saccades, because of potent inhibition that is selectively applied to saccadic circuits downstream of the SC. Because of this, neck muscle activity, pupil diameter, and microsaccades may provide novel biomarkers of the orienting response that reflect covert, developing SC activity well before any saccade. The research outlined in this proposal aims to: i) establish the relationships shared amongst these non-saccadic biomarkers and with simultaneously-recorded SC activity (Project 1), and ii) to examine what happens to these biomarkers when a key cortical input to the SC is manipulated (Project 2). From the perspective of human health, these non-saccadic measures are accessible in the motor periphery, and with improved technology, may provide the next generation of oculomotor biomarkers which could be applied to the characterization or early diagnosis of many development or neurodegenerative disorders.

column37: Every day, humans have to cope with a large number of compounds from environmental and dietary sources, many of which being detrimental to human health. Glucuronidation is mediated by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGT). It is the prevailing mechanism to inactivate potentially harmful molecules such as drugs and food carcinogens as well as endogenous molecules such as hormones and facilitate their elimination from the body. This process is particularly active in the liver, but also in other excretory organs, such as kidney, small intestine, and colon. We have recently discovered a new regulatory mechanism of detoxification by UGTs. We have found nine new UGT proteins in human cells and demonstrated that they interfere with glucuronidation activity. In addition, our research has further revealed that these new proteins could control cellular fitness and contribute to the development and progression of cancer. This discovery clearly represents a new paradigm for the regulation and function of drug-metabolizing enzymes. Our goal is now to study how the new UGT proteins regulate the inactivation of drugs, toxic molecules and hormones and to understand their contribution in regulating cell metabolism. We will use complementary approaches to study human tissues involved in drug metabolism as well as cellular models that will be exposed to drugs, hormones and carcinogens. The findings generated from these studies are likely to have an important pharmacological and clinical impact because UGT protein activity is directly related to the elimination of toxic compounds and drugs, thereby modulating not only the effectiveness of drug treatment and side-effects, but also the development and progression of cancer.

column36: Defining and Blocking the Production of the Nickel-Containing Hydrogenase Enzyme in Bacteria
column37: The aim of this research is to determine how bacteria make a nickel-containing protein called hydrogenase. This protein is essential in many microorganisms, including pathogens such as Escherichia coli, which causes gastrointestinal illnesses, and Helicobacter pylori, which causes ulcers, gastritis and gastric cancers. Hydrogenases are vital because they allow bacteria to use hydrogen gas as energy, and if the hydrogenase protein is not correctly produced the bacteria get sick and fail to grow. For hydrogenase to function it requires a nickel ion, and this metal is specifically imported into the bacteria cell and delivered to the hydrogenase protein through the coordinated activity of helper proteins. The purpose of this grant is to understand how bacteria produce hydrogenase, with a focus on nickel acquisition and delivery. We will define the key steps of this fascinating system, revealing the mechanisms of the underlying processes. We will also identify molecules that block hydrogenase production; such compounds can be used as investigative tools and may serve as lead compounds in the design of new antimicrobial therapies. This study will contribute to our knowledge of how nickel is used in biology, a fundamental aspect of life. Furthermore, the production of proteins with complex metal centers occurs throughout Nature, and the hydrogenase biosynthetic proteins serve as an excellent model system to understand these types of processes. Finally, humans do not require nickel, so the systems that make the nickel-containing hydrogenases will provide unique targets for selective antibiotics. Despite the huge advances in antibiotic development, bacterial infections remain a serious health problem, and new types of treatment are needed. In order to realize the potential of a new strategy for antimicrobial agents a detailed understanding of these multi-faceted nickel systems is essential.

column37: Diabetes is a serious metabolic disease that affects over 360 million people worldwide. Obesity and diets high in sugar and fat contribute to type 2 diabetes by putting extra demand on the pancreatic beta-cells to secrete insulin, a hormone that normally maintains normal blood sugar (glucose) levels. Often the body can initially adjust to the increased demand for insulin, and keep glucose levels in control, by increasing in the function and number of beta-cells. However, under continued stress these important pancreatic cells eventually fail and die. As a result, too little insulin is released, glucose levels stay too high, and diabetes develops. It remains a critical unanswered question how the switch from beta-cell adaptation to beta-cell dysfunction happens, and how failure and death of the cells can be prevented. Our research group recently found that two related proteins, called Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL, not only promote beta-cell survival but also regulates normal insulin secretion. In this project we will clarify if and how the Bcl proteins control beta-cell stress levels under conditions of high glucose and fat, and we aim to determine if the Bcl proteins influence the loss of glucose control that precedes diabetes in obese mice. Answering these research questions will provide important new information of how beta-cells function, and what causes the loss of insulin secretion that ultimately leads to diabetes. This knowledge will help identify new ways to protect the pancreatic beta-cells and treating this serious disease.

Such disruptions are often associated with various metabolic, endocrine, and behavioral disturbances that contribute significantly to stress, poor health and loss of quality of life. To understand and treat the underlying causes of circadian dysregulation in these populations, it is important to first understand fundamental mechanisms that help to regulate them. In mammals, circadian rhythms are controlled by a master brain clock located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and by subordinate oscillators present in other brain regions and in peripheral organs. My research is concerned with the study of the mechanisms that contribute to the regulation of subordinate oscillators in forebrain areas important in motivation and emotion. In recent work we obtained evidence that the neurotransmitter dopamine, which has important roles in a broad range of motivated behaviors and neuropsychiatric disorders, is involved in the control of clock gene oscillations in the striatum, a brain region important in motivation, emotion, and motor control. The aim of the proposed research is to elucidate the function of dopamine in the control of a core clock protein, Per2, in the striatum and to study the role that this protein plays in mediating the effect of dopamine on motivated behaviors. Results from these studies will provide a new way to explain how changes in midbrain dopamine functioning associated with normal behaviors and experiences, and with disorders such Parkinson's disease and addiction, might disrupt clock gene oscillations in the striatum leading to a broad spectrum of behavioral and cognitive disturbances.

column36: Role of SIX family transcription factors in proliferation and tissue regeneration.
column37: The repair of skeletal muscle after injury depends on the function of undifferentiated muscle precursor cells called satellite cells. Satellite cells are undifferentiated and deeply quiescent in healthy tissue. Upon injury, they become activated, engage in rapid proliferation, and eventually differentiate into mature, contractile muscle cells to repair the damaged muscle, while a small fraction of the cells will self-renew by avoiding differentiation and returning to the quiescent state. Two key problems in the field are that we don't fully understand how these fates (quiescence, activation, differentiation, self-renewal) are established, or what mechanisms determine which fate a cell will adopt. Our research is addressing these fundamental questions. Using a combination of functional genomics, bioinformatics and molecular biology techniques, in vivo and in cultured muscle cells, we are studying how gene regulatory proteins Six1 and Six4 control muscle precursor/satellite cell function. We focus on how they control the proliferation and differentiation of muscle precursors, and look into molecular details how they accomplish this task.

column36: Novel mechanisms underlying ciliogenesis, planar cell polarity and cystic kidney disease
column37: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is the most common life-threatening syndrome that can be inherited from one generation to another. It afflicts approximately 1 in 500 people, and 50% of these individuals will ultimately lose all kidney function. Treatments for cystic kidney diseases are exceedingly costly (patients often require dialysis and kidney transplantation), and there are no current therapeutic drugs or preventive strategies. PKD therefore represents a crucial target for clinical and experimental research. Mutations in many different genes can cause cystic kidney disease. However, each gene appears to control the formation and/or function of cilia - small antennas that are present on almost every cell, and which allow cells to sense and respond to their surroundings. Mutations in these genes also appear to disrupt cell "polarity". Polarity allows cells to distinguish up from down, left from right, and back from front - essential information when cells need to come together to form complex organs like the kidney. One of the outstanding challenges in the field of PKD lies in understanding this apparent link between cilia and cell polarity. My lab uses zebrafish, a small aquarium fish, as an experimental organism for determining how genes control cilia and cell polarity. Zebrafish embryonic development is remarkably similar to humans. However, zebrafish embryos are transparent, easily grown and manipulated under a microscope, and we have developed powerful techniques for watching, in real time, how mutations in genes that cause PKD affect kidney formation. Recently, we discovered new genes that could provide the missing links between cilia, cell polarity, and PKD. In the proposed studies, we combine cell biology, experimental embryology, and classic genetic approaches to fully define the function of these genes. Our results will provide fundamental new insights into what causes cystic kidneys, and how we might ultimately treat human disease.
