column36: Investigating the link between cilia function and adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
column37: Scoliosis is a complex genetic disorder characterized by rotational deformity of the spine. Congenital scoliosis is apparent at birth, whereas Idiopathic Scoliosis (IS) develops later during adolescence and afflicts 3% of children worldwide. If left untreated, severe IS can produce chronic back pain, cosmetic disfigurement and functional disability. First described by Hippocrates, scoliosis is the oldest birth defect known to humankind. However, despite decades of intense scientific investigation, the specific causes of IS have not been identified. Our poor understanding of the basic biology underlying scoliosis largely stems from a lack of appropriate animal models for study. Most animals are quadrupeds and the structure/biomechanics of their spines radically differ from humans. Induction of IS-like deformities thus requires drastic surgical interventions that preclude relevance to human disease. Scoliosis, however, is common among fish, which experience spinal loads similar to humans. In particular, zebrafish have emerged as a powerful animal model of human disease. A wealth of genetic resources have been developed to induce pathogenic states. Moreover, the external development and optical clarity of zebrafish embryos facilitates embryological manipulation and permits live imaging of spinal cord formation at a cellular and even molecular level. In the following proposal, Dr. Ciruna's team will exploit these inherent advantages to determine the cause of late-onset spinal curvatures in zebrafish models of idiopathic scoliosis. These mutants are among the first and only genetically defined animal models of IS, and can be used to predict the causes of human disease. With these invaluable resources in hand (tractable to both physical and genetic manipulation), Dr. Ciruna has a unique opportunity to define the cell-biological mechanisms underlying scoliosis. His studies will translate into novel strategies for the diagnosis and treatment of IS.

column36: Evaluation of a cognitive psychophysiological treatment for Tourette syndrome and tic disorders
column37: Chronic tics are involuntary muscle spasms which can occur in any part of the body but mostly the upper torso (e.g., face, neck, shoulder). In Gilles de la Tourette syndrome, the muscle tics are accompanied by vocal tics such as barking, throat clearing or swearing. Tics affect as many as 300 000 Canadians and cause social, occupational and interpersonal distress. Tics peak at age 11-12 but continue into adulthood, and if untreated can cause severe disability. A current behavioural treatment option teaches tic control through a series of competing actions designed to tense muscles opposed to the tic and so reverse tic onset. Finding competing actions for complex tics can be difficult and the procedure does not generalize to all tics. Our team has developed a treatment model termed the Cognitive Psychophysiological treatment (CoPs) which specifically targets abnormal planning processes characteristic of people with tics. These targets include addressing psychophysiological regulation of action by cognitive and behavioural restructuring of the way people with tics prepare for action and build up tension prior to tic onset. Our treatment has shown positive results in small scale studies and in a recent larger open trial. The aim here is to conduct a randomized controlled trial (the gold standard for establishing a treatment of choice) over a 5-year period. Seventy-two adults and 72 children will be allocated randomly to one of two treatment modalities: the new treatment (CoPs) or the current behavioural treatment. Both treatments will be administered by specialized clinicians over a comparable 10 week period with assessment following treatment and home practice at 1-month and 6-month follow-up. This study will impact on the optimal treatment guidelines for children and adults with tics and also inform on whether intervention should focus on individual tics or address underlying processes to reduce tics and improve functioning.

column36: The state of play: Socio-ecological perspective on children's outdoor play
column37: Our fondest childhood memories are often of play. Whether jumping in a pile of leaves, catching bugs, or climbing a tree, children are often happiest when playing freely outdoors. Play is a childhood need so basic, it is enshrined in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, yet time for play has been increasingly eroded. Increasing evidence indicates the importance of outdoor play time for children's health and well-being. Our research seeks to gain the perspective of children aged 10-13 years and their parents on why they are motivated - or not - to play outside. We will use children's and parents' perspectives to develop an index of the playability of outdoor environments - the extent to which a given environment is friendly for outdoor play. An environment with high playability is easily and safely accessible and contains stimulating play opportunities. Girls and boys prioritize different aspects of their environment for play, so we expect to develop different indices of playability for girls compared to boys, and parents vs. children. We will test the relationship between the playability index and the health and well-being of children living in cities across Canada. The playability index will be useful for designing our urban environments to meet children's needs and positively influence their health.

column37: Proper function of the immune system is essential for protection against infectious disease and maintaining human health. We will also test the hypothesis that a group of proteins known as filamins mediate the release of cytokines from platelets. In this context, an improved understanding of platelet function could have important implications for rational treatment of inflammatory diseases, including periodontitis.

column36: The role of Glutathione in Glutamatergic system dysregulation in Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a chronic, progressive mental illness that affects up to 1% of the population and is the 5th leading causes of disability in industrialized countries. Unfortunately, the current treatment for schizophrenia with antipsychotics are not working in about 20% to 35% of the patients. Glutamate is a substance or neurotransmitter normally present in the brain; it is the most prominent excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain and reported to be increased in the brain of patients with schizophrenia. Glutathione is a major antioxidant in the brain and is involved in the neutralization of free radicals that may damage the cells in the brain. In addition, glutathione can modify the levels of glutamate in the brain and the 'potency' by which glutamate works in the brain. Decreased levels of glutathione have been found in schizophrenia and increasing glutathione levels have improved some of the symptoms in schizophrenia. However, no research has been performed to investigate the levels of glutathione in the brains of those patients who do not respond well to antipsychotic treatment. Further, no research has directly investigated the relationship between glutathione and glutamate in schizophrenia. We will recruit patients with schizophrenia with no response to common antipsychotic medications and healthy controls for comparison. Glutamate and glutathione levels will be measured in several brain regions associated with schizophrenia using a non-invasive technique called Proton Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy and will be compared across the groups of participants using mathematical models. If our hypothesis is correct, we are able to demonstrate abnormal levels and altered relationship between glutamate and glutathione in patients with treatment resistant schizophrenia. The results will help to guide new future treatments and increase understanding of anomalies in schizophrenia.

column36: An Integrated Real-time Modeling and Surveillance Decision-support Framework to Inform Public Health Emergency Preparedness
column37: Globally, the threat of Emerging Infectious Diseases (EID) is on the rise. Significant resources have been invested, albeit sometimes reactive, for the development of pandemic preparedness plans. During recent pandemics, we were challenged to ensure public health and security, quickly and with little information about the new EIDs. Following these incidents, some of the gaps in these plans were apparent. Post pandemic consultations with international experts from across pandemic planning research and decision-making, we better understand how to improve our pandemic plans and responses. We have compiled their recommendations to address the knowledge gaps in planning for pandemic outbreaks and public health emergencies. The most prominent recommendations include developing the methods to combine emerging infectious disease surveillance data with dynamic demographic mathematical models to quickly understand an EID. This will allow researchers to understand how quickly the EID spreads and generate real-time options for policy makers. The mathematical model, looks at the specific characteristics of the BC population to determine exactly what options would best stop the spread of disease in this province. In parallel, we will conduct a complementary project in a public health agency to learn how this new research becomes the basis for new policy during such an emergency situation. This will ensure the most efficient flow of research to the policy makers for future public health emergencies. With appropriate regional demographic and surveillance data, these advanced plans can be implemented in other regions both nationally and internationally. By focusing on real-time pandemic management options and knowledge translation networks, we will provide tools to control EIDs in a coordinated and effective way, reducing both the health and economic burden of these diseases.

column37: Le taux de cesariennes ne cesse d'augmenter au Canada. Depuis les annees 2000, il est passe de 21,2 a plus de 26%. L'indication d'antecedent de cesarienne contribue a elle seule a plus de 30% des cesariennes totales. Chaque annee, environ 30 000 femmes au Canada avec un antecedent de cesarienne auront a faire un choix difficile lors de leur prochaine grossesse : a) planifier une nouvelle cesarienne ; ou b) tenter un essai de travail (EDT) pour en arriver a un accouchement vaginal (AVAC) et accepter un risque significatif, mais rare, de rupture uterine. La rupture uterine est une des pires urgences obstetricales et constitue la principale complication de la tentative d'AVAC. Cependant, bien qu'elle puisse permettre d'eviter la rupture uterine dans la majorite des cas, une cesarienne repetee reste associee a un risque plus eleve de complications pour la mere et son enfant. L'augmentation du taux de cesariennes repetees constitue plus que jamais une importante question de sante publique a l'heure ou la cesarienne est de plus en plus percue comme une intervention routiniere et ou les professionnels hesitent, en raison du risque medico-legal, a recommander un essai de travail en l'absence d'une methode validee de prediction du risque de rupture uterine et de reussite d'AVAC. Le programme PRISMA integre une formation professionnelle aux pratiques optimales et s'articule autour d'outils ciblant le processus de decision pour un EDT ou une cesarienne. Les principes cles dans la mise en oeuvre de cette strategie sont : 1) evaluation des preferences initiales des femmes ; 2) evaluation echographique du risque de rupture uterine ; et 3) evaluation des chances de succes d'AVAC. Les resultats permettront de mobiliser les professionnels pour adopter un programme d'evaluation du risque, faciliter la prise de decision, standardiser les pratiques cliniques, et ainsi contribuer a diminuer les risques de complications par une selection optimale des femmes souhaitant avoir un EDT.

column36: The role of mRNA conformational dynamics in stimulating translational recoding
column37: Proteins are assembled in the cell based on the genetic code, but this code can be altered by shifting the frame in which it is read. In viruses like HIV, SARS, and many others, such recoding is programmed into the genome using specific structures in the RNA message. Using drugs to alter this recoding presents an attractive approach to develop anti-viral therapies which is being actively pursued. However, the molecular mechanism by which the recoding works remains controversial, hindering efforts at drug discovery. We recently discovered that the dynamical properties of RNA structures play an under-appreciated role in recoding of the genome, by using laser tweezers to manipulate RNA structures mechanically and probe their dynamics. We will extend these initial studies to investigate how recoding mechanisms depend on the dynamics of the structures in messenger RNA that stimulate the recoding. Our goal is to understand what properties of the RNA determine the efficiency of recoding, and how the RNA interacts with the protein synthesis machinery to trigger a recoding event. We will study single RNA molecules with structures that stimulate recoding, taken from a variety of viruses including HIV and SARS, not only in isolation, but also in the presence of the ribosomes which synthesize proteins. We will also investigate the effects of putative drugs that have been found to alter recoding efficiency and reduce infectivity, to determine their mechanism of action. We expect this work to lead to improved understanding of recoding mechanisms and the discovery of new targets for anti-viral drug development.

column36: Exploring the cognitive underpinnings of hoarding
column37: Hoarding disorder is a newly defined diagnostic category that affects as many as 1.5 million Canadians. Although hoarding appears on the surface (and perhaps on TV shows) to be a simple problem of poor housekeeping, the disorder involves substantial functional impairment including severe social isolation and inability to sustain minimal standards of home maintenance. Seniors and low-income renters are particularly vulnerable to threat of eviction and accidents in the home. The hallmark symptom of hoarding disorder is extreme emotional distress about, and avoidance of, discarding objects most people would let go of. As a result, the home becomes too full to use some or all of the rooms for their intended purpose. Possessions in the home become extremely disorganized, with important (e.g., passport) and unimportant (e.g., out-dated sales flyers) items mixed together. Intervention for hoarding is complex, and the most effective intervention tested thus far has shown only modest effects despite an enormous investment of resources. Limited understanding of the cognitive processes involved in decisions to acquire and discard possessions in turn limits the degree to which treatment can effectively target these processes. This research will determine the cognitive underpinnings of two key features of hoarding: excessive valuing of objects and extreme disorganization of the home. Five studies are proposed to investigate aspects of cognitive functioning as they relate to hoarding behaviour. In relation to the psychology of ownership, we focus on attention and memory as well as specific types of judgment and decision-making. We also examine whether hoarding involves deficits in executive functioning (e.g., concept formation, impulse control). The results will directly impact the development of more efficacious and cost-effective approaches to treatment as well as provide clues into the neuroscience behind hoarding and related disorders.

column36: Functional Organization of Auditory Cortex Following Cochlear Implant
column37: In Canada, hearing impairment is the most common sensory disability in adults (affecting 26% of those >45 years old) and deafness is the most common birth defect. Cochlear implants are extremely useful tools in providing auditory sensations to the profoundly deaf and have restored hearing to >400,000 people worldwide. At the present rate of implantation, over 1 million people will benefit from cochlear prosthetics by 2020. The use of cochlear implants in the profoundly deaf makes speech comprehension possible. In hearing subjects, acoustic input shapes the development of the auditory cortex of the brain. However, in deaf individuals the auditory cortex has no acoustic input. Other senses, such as vision and touch, exploit the unused "deaf" region of cortex for their own purposes. This commonly results in the enhanced visual or tactile abilities reported in the deaf. The question remains - if the dormant auditory system is then activated by a cochlear implant, how does "deaf" auditory cortex respond? Does all of "deaf" auditory cortex begin to process sound? Does the visual and/or tactile processing that invaded "deaf" auditory cortex retreat? Do different areas within auditory cortex begin to perform the same functions identified in a hearing subject? By better understanding the brain's potential for change following cochlear implant, it will be possible to develop implantation strategies to better exploit the plasticity of the brain and improve cochlear implant efficacy and hearing restoration success. The greatest benefit of cochlear prosthetics has been found in young children. Therefore, in the proposed studies, cochlear prosthetics will be implanted in young animals. We will examine auditory cortical function in the congenitally-deaf cat (the only natural model for human congenital deafness) following cochlear implant. The results of these studies will be directly applicable to clinical studies examining functional outcomes of cochlear implants in children.

column36: Epigenetic Regulation and Noncoding RNA in Prostate Cancer Progression
column37: About 1 man in 6 will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during his lifetime in North America. Prostate cancer remains the second leading cause of cancer death in man in the United State and the third in Canada. While localized prostate cancer has been successfully treated by radiation therapy and radical prostatectomy, the more advanced metastatic prostate cancer is subjected to hormone deprivation therapy through surgical or chemical castration, in which case resistant inevitably arises resulted in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) that is often lethal. A few new therapeutic options including abiraterone acetate and enzalutamide have been developed recently for the treatment of CRPC, however, these treatments can only retard progression and CRPC still remains incurable. New therapeutic option thus is in urgent need. Majority of the CRPC is driven by androgen receptor (AR), and recent progresses reveal both genetic mutations and epigenetic reprogramming related to androgen receptor signaling in CRPC. While genetic changes are almost impossible to reverse, epigenetic alterations are potentially reversible. Key Epigenetic regulators that control epigenetic reprogramming in CRPC may present as new therapeutic targets, and drugs that target these epigenetic regulators have potential as effective new therapies for the treatment of CRPC. We hypothesize that the lysine-specific demethylase 1A (KDM1A/LSD1) is critical for epigenetic reprogramming of AR and is an epigenetic driver of CRPC. We propose to decipher the functional role of LSD1 in epigenetic regulation in CRPC, which involves the interaction with long noncoding RNA. We will develop LSD1-lncRNA signature as biomarker for metastasis and CRPC, and will develop pre-clinical therapeutic models to facilitate clinical translation of LSD1 as a therapeutic target in CRPC.

column36: Regulatory B-cells inhibit Allergic Airways Disease: Role of Semaphorin 4C
column37: Severe asthma is a disease with significant mortality, morbidity and pharmacoeconomic impact. Severe asthma is an inflammatory disease and is often associated with allergies and very high levels of IgE, the primary allergy antibody. Lung biopsies from severe asthmatics often have significant antibody forming cells known as B-lymphocyte in their lungs which is not found in to the same extent in milder asthmatics. Semaphorin 4C (Sema4C) is a member of a family of molecules which play an important role in development of the nervous system and blood vessels, and recently has been found to be important in regulation of the immune system. Our laboratory has found that Sema4C is highly expressed on human and murine B-lymphocytes in allergic inflammation. Moreover, mice who have had the Semaphorin 4C gene removed (Sema4C Knock-out mice) have severe bronchospasm, exceedingly high levels of IgE and increased B-lymphocytes in their lungs, all signs of severe asthma. Moreover, severe asthmatics from the McGill Severe asthma program have much lower Sema4C in their airways than mild asthmatics. In this proposal my laboratory will determine how Semaphorin 4C regulates B-lymphocytes in allergic and asthmatic pathology and thus understand a potential new direction for the therapy of severe asthma.

column36: Regulation of gene expression by protein sumoylation
column37: Many proteins in all eukaryotic cells are subject to modification by the SUMO peptide, in a process referred to as sumoylation. This modification plays important roles in regulating multiple cellular processes under normal conditions, but abnormal levels of sumoylation have been detected in many tumours. The cause and consequences of elevated sumoylation in cancer are not known. We previously determined that proteins found on actively expressed genes are heavily modified by SUMO. Towards comprehending how abnormal sumoylation might alter gene expression, as observed in cancer, this project aims to determine the effects of SUMO modifications on the specific functions of these proteins, as well as on gene expression as a whole. The results of our work will add significantly to our understanding of how cells regulate gene expression in normal conditions, while revealing the potential consequences of cancer-related abnormal sumoylation levels on gene regulation in tumours.

column36: The neural basis of cataplexy
column37: Narcolepsy is a debilitating sleep disorder that can impair a person's ability to socialize, work, and drive safely. The symptoms of narcolepsy include relentless sleepiness, disturbed sleep, inability to move after waking-up (sleep paralysis) and vivid dream-like hallucinations while falling asleep (hypnagogic hallucinations). But, the most intriguing and bizarre symptom of narcolepsy is cataplexy - the sudden uncontrollable onset of muscle paralysis or weakness during otherwise normal wakefulness. Cataplexy is debilitating because it leaves the affected individual awake, but either fully or partially paralyzed. The cause of cataplexy is unknown, but is thought to result from the same process that causes muscles to relax while asleep. Cataplexy can occur spontaneously, but is usually triggered by positive emotions such as laughter or delight. Even though the link between positive emotions and cataplexy was identified 130 years ago, the processes by which emotions trigger muscle paralysis is unknown. This research is important because it aims to understand how the brain causes cataplexy. It is carried out in genetically engineered mice that exhibit all the symptoms of human narcolepsy, including cataplexy. This research will identify the brain regions and brain cells that cause cataplexy. Results from this research will be used to develop better treatments for cataplexy and hopefully discover a cure for narcolepsy.

column36: Characterization of a novel clinical marker of endometriosis.
column37: Endometriosis is a chronic, painful, progressive, disease that has a profoundly deleterious effect upon social functioning, emotional well-being, vitality, and employment of affected women. The annual costs associated with surgically confirmed endometriosis in Canada are approximately two billion dollars. Moreover, the health care costs associated with endometriosis are similar to or greater than other chronic diseases such as Crohns disease, diabetes, asthma, migraines, and rheumatoid arthritis. Sadly, women with endometriosis experience significant delays of up to twelve years before a definitive diagnosis is achieved. The gold standard for diagnosis remains laparoscopic visualization of endometriotic implants followed by confirmation of disease by a pathologist. Thus, there is an urgent need to identify novel clinical markers of endometriosis. Our preliminary data suggest that the plasma concentrations of BDNF are significantly higher in women with endometriosis compared to a control population of women without endometriosis. Therefore, we hypothesize that this protein is a potentially valuable candidate clinical marker of endometriosis. Consequently, we propose a pre-clinical discovery phase project to better characterize the concentrations of BDNF in the blood as a diagnostic test for endometriosis. We further postulate that blood concentrations of BDNF could be used to monitor disease progression and patient response to treatments. Finally, we plan to employ our animal model of endometriosis to assess the efficacy of a novel therapeutic agent in the treatment endometriosis and determine if this agent preserves fertility. Successful completion of this aim will provide a novel treatment for infertile women with endometriosis who currently are forced to choose between treating their endometriosis or refusing medication in order to achieve pregnancy. Therefore, we propose that results of this project will provide important advances for women with endometriosis.

column36: Molecular mechanisms orchestrating epithelial cell polarity
column37: Epithelia, composed of epithelial cells, delimit the frontier between the external environment and the inside of complex organisms. Therefore, epithelial cells cover the surface of the body (e.g. skin) and line internal cavities of organs (found in the intestine, liver, lungs, etc). An important function of epithelia is to selectively transport specific molecules to adjust the chemical composition of the different compartments of the body. This function relies on the asymmetric distribution of many cellular constituents, a structural organization referred to as epithelial polarity. The polarized architecture of epithelial cells is also required to maintain tissue homeostasis, as loss of epithelial polarity is associated with cancer and blindness. Mechanisms linking polarity defects with progression of cancer and loss of sight are still poorly understood. We have previously identified genes important for the establishment and maintenance of epithelial cell polarity. Mutations in these genes result in tumor formation and are associated with retinal collapse. The aim of our research program is to delineate the mechanisms by which these genes control the normal physiology of epithelial cells and define how alteration of their function contribute to cancer progression and sightlessness. By doing so, our research program will further define the normal functioning of epithelial cells and identify potential therapeutic targets to fight cancer of epithelial origin and blindness.

column36: Mechanisms and Neuromodulation of Network Coordination during Reinforcement Learning
column37: Humans and other primates in particular are capable to rapidly adapt to new situations and learn how to make good choices. This fast and flexible learning is achieved by the interplay of millions of brain cells that are organized in distinct parts of the brain. These cells are not centrally controlled. Rather, brain cells coordinate their contributions to solve a new learning problem indirectly in a decentralized way. But the mechanisms of decentralized coordination have remained a fundamental scientific puzzle. This research proposal aims to solve this puzzle by measuring and manipulating cell activities in the three key brain areas contributing to this fast and flexible learning. One brain area is the hippocampal complex where cells rapidly associate sensory events and contexts with reward when we make choices. Cells in another brain area, the prefrontal cortex, uses the memories from the hippocampal complex to actually make a choice. Cells in a third brain area, the anterior cingulate cortex, track the learning success over longer time scales. These cells evaluate outcomes of a choice based on the history of choices in the immediate past. Such a longer term memory is suited to control the other two areas, preventing them to repeat making a bad choice. Thus, this brain area seems to act like a gate keeper that prevents bad and unimportant memories from the hippocampus to influence a choice in the prefrontal cortex. This outlined scenario predicts a specific sequence of brain cell activities unfolding within and between three brain areas. Understanding this unfolding of coordinated activity is the focus of this grant, aiming to understand why weak linkages of the network causally relate to multiple psychiatric syndromes suffering from Attention Deficits, Motivational Dysfunctions, and severe Affective Imbalances. In summary, this proposal emphasizes a true network approach to understand how fast learning and adaptive behavior is achieved in the brain.

column36: The role of human intestinal microbiota in dietary gluten metabolism and inflammation
column37: Gluten-related disorders (GRD) include all diseases triggered by dietary gluten. The best characterized condition is celiac disease, a severe inflammation of the small intestine. The only current treatment for celiac disease is a strict gluten-free diet, which has some limitations, as this is a restrictive and expensive diet. An increasing number of people are sensitive to gluten with one in 100 Canadians suffering from celiac disease. The reason for the increase in inflammatory and symptomatic reactions to gluten is unclear, but may relate to changes in dietary and hygiene habits that affect the bacteria that normally inhabit our gut. One of the main problems with gluten is that it consists of proteins that are difficult to break down by our digestive enzymes. Gut bacteria are armed with a variety of enzymes and can completely or incompletely digest gluten. Complete degradation of gluten would be beneficial, but incomplete degradation by gut bacteria may increase the chances to develop celiac disease. In this proposal I will explore the role of gut bacteria isolated from patients with celiac disease and non celiac people in the digestion of dietary gluten and in the modulation of inflammation produced by this common protein in our diet. I propose that the bacteria that inhabit the gut of celiac patients have impaired capacity to digest gluten and that their enzymes produce toxic peptides from gluten that contribute to inflammation. Thus, celiac disease may be prevented, or better treated, by inhibiting these bacteria or their products.

column36: The Role of the Hexosamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Diabetes-Induced Accelerated Atherosclerosis
column37: The prevalence of diabetes is increasing rapidly across Canada and around the world. If you have diabetes your risk of having a heart attack or stroke is 2-4 fold greater than if you do not have diabetes. In fact, three out of every four people with diabetes will die of heart attack or stroke. The ultimate goals of our research are; 1. To understand why people with diabetics are a greater risk, and 2. To find ways to protect people with diabetes from heart disease. We have established unique cell and animal model systems to help us attain these goals. Using these systems we have recently found that high levels of sugar in the blood (hyperglycemia) can damage to the cells of the blood vessel walls. Specifically, the blood vessel cells take in the glucose and convert it to a compound called glucosamine. It appears that the high level of glucosamine is responsible for the vessel damage. In fact, when we give high levels of glucosamine to a mouse, we can induce atherosclerosis - a major underlying cause of heart attack and stroke. Our results suggest that if we can block the conversion of glucose to glucosamine, or if we can block the effects of glucosamine on the cells, that we can protect the blood vessels from atherosclerosis in our diabetic models. The experiments described in this grant proposal are designed to increase our understanding of this potentially important mechanism in cells and mouse models. We are especially interested in finding new targets that can be used to block disease progression. These studies are important because they are examining new and potentially more effective strategies to treat and/or prevent the cardiovascular complications of diabetes.

column36: Chemically-assisted discovery and investigation of antifungal drug leads
column37: Fungal infections are very difficult to treat. There are relatively few good antifungal drugs and many fungal pathogens possess resistance mechanisms that render these few drugs relatively useless. One source of new drugs is the 'secondary metabolism' of the streptomycetes bacteria. More than 70% of the existing antibacterial drugs come from this source as well as a much smaller number of antifungals. Our research demonstrates that there are many more antifungals to be discovered from this source than has ever been appreciated before. However the compounds are difficult to purify and study because they are not produced during laboratory culture. To address this problem we have developed a chemical trigger that can be added to growth medium to activatethe genes for these secondary metabolic pathways. We have demonstrated that we can identify and purify potent antifungals using this approach and that many of them are novel molecules. Our aim in this proposal is to purify a collection of 45 candidate activities that we have discovered, solve their structures and understand how they work. This will involve both the investigation of their molecular mechanism of action and their possible efficacy as antifungal drugs using animal models of infection. Our aim is to have a transformative effect on the discovery of new drugs in academia and the pharmaceutical sector.

column36: Low back pain: from mechanism to therapeutic intervention
column37: Back pain is one of the most predominant health complaints, effecting nearly 15% of Canadians. In addition to significant economic costs due to healthcare expenses and reduced productivity, back pain has a debilitating effect on an individual's physical and mental health, functional capacity and overall quality of life. Progressive degeneration of the intervertebral discs in the spine is frequently associated with low back pain. Unfortunately, our understanding of how the disc degeneration develops, progresses and can be treated is still limited. As a result, treatment is based on trial and error and invasive produces, including surgery, are performed with inconsistent clinical benefits. A deeper understanding of the pathological mechanisms will contribute to improved treatment for people living with back pain. We propose a series of complementary, pre-clinical and human studies combining our unique, well-characterized SPARC-null mouse model of disc degeneration-related back pain with clinical data and tissue samples obtained from human patients. Conducting analogous pre-clinical and clinical studies guarantees that the results of the proposed studies will be clinically-relevant.

column36: Mechanisms controlling iron efflux and accumulation in the nervous system: role in health, injury and disease
column37: Iron is essential for life. Iron is required for the normal functioning of cells and for the generation of energy to power various activities within cells. However, iron can also generate toxic substances called 'free radicals' that can damage cells. Although iron accumulation results in free-radical-mediated cell death, lack of iron can also lead to cell death. In the nervous system, iron is required for the survival and functioning of nerve cells; and for the formation of myelin, which is the insulating material that surrounds nerve fibers, which is essential for proper conduction of nerve impulses. How iron is delivered to different cell types in the nervous system is still not fully understood. The aim of this proposal is to study the role of a molecule called ferroportin that transports iron out of cells in the nervous system. In particular to study the role of ferroportin in health, injury and disease of the nervous system. This work has important implications for diseases such as multiple sclerosis, for damage following spinal cord and brain injury, and for regeneration of nerve fibers after damage.

column36: Discovering Spatial Epigenetics
column37: In order to fit inside the small volume of a nucleus, mammalian genomes must be tightly packaged in vivo. Genome folding and organization is important not only to reduce the length of chromosomes but also because it represents a novel type of gene regulation mechanism. For example, it was found that gene expression could be controlled by the formation of DNA loops. Interestingly, these DNA loops were found only in cells expressing the target genes, indicating that genome organization is tissue-specific and important for proper gene expression. This notion is reinforced by the discovery of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in cancers that create novel enhancers acting long-range to activate distal genes through DNA looping. Thus, how a genome is organized is functionally relevant not only because it can reflect its transcriptional state, but also since the way it folds can determine which long-range contacts are possible by promoting or restricting physical proximity between chromatin segments. For this reason, defining how genomes are organized is essential to understand how correct expression is obtained. To address this question, we suggest mapping genome organization during cellular differentiation to identify genome architectures that contribute to cell type specificity. Our hypothesis is that cellular differentiation occurs with changes in the three-dimensional organization of chromosomes, and that these changes determine whether genes can be regulated long distance by control elements.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of complex dietary carbohydrate metabolism by the human gut microbiota
column37: The human gut is colonized by a vast population of microorganisms, known collectively as the microbiota. When in balance, this complex ecosystem positively affects human health by enabling us to obtain energy from the otherwise indigestible complex carbohydrates known as "dietary fibre", while at the same time providing protection from pathogens and disease. And although it is clear that the breakdown of dietary fibre both fuels the microbiota and provides up to 10% of our daily calories, very little is actually known about this process on the molecular level. Large-scale gene sequencing is currently providing an increasingly detailed picture of which organisms are abundant in healthy gut microbiota and what genetic information they possess. However, our understanding of the complex interplay of proteins and enzymes encoded by this genetic information, which are the biocatalysts ultimately responsible for turning dietary fibre into simple sugars, is only in its infancy. Indeed, the pathways by which many of the most common dietary polysaccharides are metabolized by the gut microbiota are currently not known. This research program will address this knowledge gap through detailed biochemical, protein structural, and genetic analysis of coordinated systems of genes from predominant human gut bacteria, which are implicated in dietary fibre metabolism. The key outcomes of the research will include providing new insight into the basic function of the microbiota in our bodies. In turn, this will inform novel strategies to improve human nutrition and health through specific dietary intervention or microbial treatments to upgrade or "reboot" our natural microflora.

column36: Shining light on the architecture and dynamics of the eukaryotic replisome
column37: Our life starts as the gametes of our parents fuse into a single cell. The progeny of this cell will divide thousands of times as we develop and grow, transferring from mother to daughter cells the instructions to make us at every cell division. These instructions are coded in molecules of DNA, and a large molecular machine, called the replisome, works in our cells to duplicate DNA through the coordinated activity of numerous protein factors. Failure to transmit genetic information reliably can lead to the generation of genetic diseases, like cancer, and this is why replisome has evolved to have outstanding fidelity at copying DNA and is capable of linking together millions of DNA building blocks without introducing a single mistake. Despite its importance, we still lack key information on the molecular architecture of replisome and on how do its components function together. In this work, we propose to exploit recent advances in genetics and microscopy in order to observe replisome as it works in live cells. This is a novel approach that, in contrast to other methods used in the past, will allow us to extract the information while preserving cells alive, bringing us closer to understand how this cellular processes really happen. We aim to obtain important information on the regulation, composition and function of replisome. Furthering our knowledge on DNA replication will eventually explain its link to the generation and progression of genetic diseases and will help in developing treatments for them.

column36: Molecular mechanisms guiding the formation of a functional retinal architecture
column37: The retina is the neural tissue at the back of the eye that contains the light-sensing neurons that allow us to see. In order for light information to be captured and processed to make a visual image, the neurons that make up the retina must be generated in their proper numbers and reach their correct destinations. Like other regions of the nervous system, the neurons in the retina have a very specific organization. We study how the neurons that make up the retina are generated in their proper numbers, and then how these neurons migrate to their proper positions in three-dimensions. Understanding these fundamental features of retinal development are essential for the future design of regenerative strategies, which aim to replace lost retinal neurons in patients who have lost their sight. We have made great strides in elucidating the molecular and cellular pathways that control retinal cell number and retinal cell positioning, and our goal is to further our understanding of these events in this proposed research project.

column36: Analysis of the role of genetically-defined interneurons in the operation of the locomotor CPG.
column37: Locomotor behaviour (i.e. walking, flying, swimming) requires a complex pattern of muscle activation. Neural networks located entirely within the spinal cord are responsible for generating much of the timing and pattern of these locomotor movements. These neural networks are known as central pattern generators (CPGs) and are composed of multiple interneuron cell types. Little is known about the interneuronal components of the locomotor CPGs in walking mammals, primarily because of the difficulty in identifying their intrinsic interneuronal components. Recently, a genetic approach has been successful in identifying distinct populations of genetically similar interneurons in the ventral portion of the spinal cord based on transcription factor expression. Preliminary work on these cells has shown that they comprise essential components of the locomotor CPG. I propose to characterize and assess the function of specific interneuronal populations and determine how they are interconnected within the spinal cord to produce functional locomotor outputs. These studies will mark an essential step in understanding how locomotor CPGs are assembled and function, and will help to devise therapies aimed at enhancing the functional recovery of movement after spinal cord injury.

column36: Characterization of a novel function for PABPN1: the product of the oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy disease gene.
column37: Muscular dystrophies are genetic disorders that afflict more than 50,000 Canadians and for which there are currently no cures. Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) is an adult-onset form of muscular dystrophy that is found worldwide, but that is more frequent in the French Canadian and Jewish populations. OPMD is a disorder of skeletal muscle cells that is primarily associated with eyelids drooping, swallowing difficulties, and proximal limb weakness. The underlying genetic defects of OPMD are small GCG insertions in the PABPN1 gene that expands the amino terminal polyalanine tract of PABPN1 from 10 to 12-17 residues. To date, the underlying mechanism by which short GCG insertions in the PABPN1 gene causes OPMD remains completely unknown. Furthermore, limited knowledge exists about the cellular functions of PABPN1. The objective of this application is therefore to provide better understanding about the mechanistic function of PABPN1. The central hypothesis of our research project, which is based on our preliminary findings, is that PABPN1 functions in a specialized nuclear pathway of gene regulation. We propose to make use of two innovative and complementary experimental systems to characterize this novel PABPN1 function. The first is the yeast S. pombe, where we have identified the homolog to human PABPN1. This simple yet powerful model organism is widely used to study mechanisms of gene regulation. The second involves cultured human cells, which allow for detailed cellular studies of human PABPN1. In addition to shedding new, fundamental knowledge into the role of PABPN1 in gene regulation, our studies are expected to further the understanding into the molecular basis of OPMD. As such, our studies may ultimately address why OPMD is restricted to specific skeletal muscles, and therefore, lay the groundwork for developing much needed therapies.

column36: Randomized Controlled Trial of the Meaning-Making Intervention (MMi) in Patients Newly Diagnosed with Advanced Cancer: Full Trial
column37: Background: The initial news of having a life-threatening illness is typically traumatic, shocking, devastating, and very frightening, confronting patients with many important losses and evoking existential/spiritual issues such as the meaning of their cancer diagnosis, of their life and of Life, feeling a loss of control, a fear of dying, and a sense of disempowerment. Feeling their lives threatened, advanced cancer patients (ACP) ask themselves difficult questions such as "Why me?", "What is the meaning and purpose of my life now?", and "How do I cope with knowing that I will die soon?". The Meaning-Making intervention (MMi) was developed to help patients adjust more quickly and adaptively to a new cancer diagnosis. However, it is not known whether: 1) it is efficacious for people recently informed that they have advanced cancer; 2) it increases a sense of meaning in life; 3) its impact lasts beyond the end of the intervention; or 4) the effect shown is due to the MMi or whether a similar effect can be obtained by having someone listen empathically for the same amount of time as it takes to administer the MMi. Project description: Based on our previous successful CIHR-funded pilot, this study will test whether the MMi plus usual care increases the sense of meaning in life newly diagnosed ACP (any type of advanced cancer), compared to similar people who receive 1) usual care alone or 2) usual care plus visits from an empathic visitor, at 2 months after randomization to one of these treatments. We will also evaluate whether any effect is present at 4 and 6 months post-randomization, and the MMi's impact on anxiety/depression, quality of life (QoL), existential wellbeing, and posttraumatic growth. To answer our research questions 471 newly diagnosed (<6 months) ACP (stages III or IV) will be studied. Clinical implications: An early, psychologically growth-promoting intervention is especially important for ACP to prevent existential suffering and enhance their QoL

column36: Regulation of biomineralization by osteopontin
column37: In bones and teeth, small calcium phosphate crystals deposit within a scaffolding of proteins called the extracellular matrix. Protein-crystal interactions in bones and teeth define properties of the mineral phase making the tissues strong and hard. Our work is relevant to understanding the decreased mineralization that occurs in osteomalacias - diseases where bone is incompletely calcified, soft and deformable and/or prone to fracture. The research is also relevant to pathologic calcification diseases of normally "soft" tissues. Compelling evidence indicates that a protein called osteopontin (OPN) controls mineralization in most tissues. Also important is that processing of OPN by enzymes leads to mineralization-inhibiting protein fragments (peptides) with different potencies. We investigate whether processing of OPN defines a control mechanism affecting biomineralization in different tissues. Here we propose to examine this possible regulation, guided by the general hypothesis that OPN in bones, teeth and other tissues, and peptides derived from enzymatic processing of OPN, controls mineralization by binding to crystal surfaces in a way that modulates crystal growth. We will investigate these mechanisms in cell-free systems in which calcium-phosphate crystals are grown in the presence of OPN/peptides (in cell culture models, and in mouse models) using biochemical measurements, microscopies, high-resolution imaging approaches, biophysical methods to characterize mineral, and computational modeling to simulate atomic-scale binding. Such work should provide insight into keeping bones and teeth strong and healthy, and may suggest ways to treat patients where these tissues are defective.

column36: Deciphering the role of NR4A3 in dendritic cell biology and infection
column37: The immune system of an individual is devoted to fight infectious agents. The immune system possesses two arms to control infection. The innate arm of immunity consists of non-specific recognition of the infectious agent by specialized cells types that are able to engulf the pathogens and to produce effectors substances that will kill the infectious agent. In some circumstances, this arm of the immune system will not be able to fully control the infection. When this happens, innate cells will communicate to the other arm, the adaptive immune system. This adaptive arm of the system induces a specific recognition of the pathogen by two types of white blood cells, T- and B-cells. These cells are able to specifically recognized foreign substances that are expressed by microbes. This recognition will then be very efficient to eliminate the infectious agent. The induction of the adaptive immune response critically depends on a subset of innate cells named dendritic cells. These dendritic cells are very important to induce adaptive immunity since they are very efficient at presenting the foreign substances of pathogens to T cells. Various types of dendritic cells exist in the body but the events regulating their generation and their specific role during infection is still not fully understood. In this proposal, we will characterize the role of the molecules Nr4a3 in the differentiation of dendritic cells and in their response to infection. A better understanding of dendritic cell biology is pivotal to develop better strategies to fight infectious agents

column36: RUNX2-related Pulmonary Artery Remodeling and Calcification in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is characterized by the progressive increase in pulmonary artery pressure and right heart failure. PAH predominantly affects young people between 20-60 years of age. The progressive obstruction of pulmonary vessels is related to the intense proliferation of cells in the walls of pulmonary arteries. We previously demonstrated that the proliferation of these cells is related to a reduction of microRNA-204. MicroRNA are molecules that regulate the effects of genes. The proposed experiments will demonstrate that RUNX2, a factor that is activated by the reduction of microRNA-204, is central to PAH progression as it promotes cells proliferation and calcification. Through several experiments in humans and rats, the current proposal will not only demonstrate the importance of RUNX2 in PAH progression and severity, but will also open the door to new avenues of investigation and potentially to future therapies in PAH.

column36: Investigations on 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinoline (HAQ) derivatives produced by Burkholderia and Pseudomonas
column37: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a prevalent opportunistic human pathogen. Individuals who are immunocompromised or have breaches in normal barriers are especially susceptible to P. aeruginosa infections, such as cancer patients and those with indwelling medical devices. Moreover, P. aeruginosa is the primary cause of mortality among individuals suffering from the fatal genetic disorder cystic fibrosis (CF). The genus Burkholderia comprises more than 70 species that inhabit remarkably diverse ecological niches. The pathogen B. pseudomallei is the causative agent of melioidosis, a cause of human pneumonia that can turn into an often fatal septicemic infection. This bacterium is now considered a potential biothreat agent. Also, a number of Burkholderia species are increasingly prevalent opportunistic human pathogens, especially in CF. Burkholderia species are notoriously highly resistant to antibiotic treatments. <<Quorum sensing>> (QS) is an intercellular communication system used by bacteria to regulate virulence factors and modulate their interactions with hosts. P. aeruginosa and Burkholderia control the expression of a wide spectrum of virulence/survival factors through QS. Because of their adaptability, persistence and multi-resistance to antibiotics, P. aeruginosa and B. cepacia complex species, are virtually impossible to eradicate. Furthermore, the potential severity and difficulty of treatment of melioidosis pose a bioterrorism threat. It is therefore imperative to better understand how these bacteria cause infections and search for new therapeutic approaches. We have been uncovering a remarkable mechanism required for the full virulence of P. aeruginosa. This new intercellular communication system is based on the production of 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines (HAQs). We have also identified HAQ-like molecules in Burkholderia species and initiated their characterization. We believe HAQ signalling is a target for antiinfection therapeutics against these pathogens.

column36: Novel mechanisms controlling muscle attachment and myofibril assembly
column37: We work on the last steps of muscle development, the establishment of strong muscle attachments and development of the contractile apparatus inside muscles. This may pave the way for novel therapeutic interventions to better treat muscle disorders in the future.

column36: Effects of shear stress on atherosclerotic plaque regression
column37: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis, a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibres in the wall of arteries. Clinical data show that regular physical exercise is strongly cardioprotective. Beneficial effects of exercise are related to reduced blood pressure, glucose and lipid levels, but also to increased blood flow. In fact, high blood flow is greatly protective in the vasculature. Vessel segments exposed to high flow are typically devoid of atherosclerotic lesions. On the contrary, vessel segments exposed to low or oscillatory blood flow are prone to atherosclerotic plaque formation. High blood flow has even been associated with plaque regression in patients. Our objective is to understand why high blood flow is so protective, and how it leads to plaque regression. We have created an original surgical mouse model to increase blood flow in a specific artery. First, we feed the mice with a high fat diet so that they develop atherosclerosis. Then, after 12 weeks, we do the surgery. In preliminary tests, we found that the plaques in the artery exposed to high flow gradually get smaller, whereas plaques in other arteries (or in other animals without the surgery) keep getting bigger. In this application, we propose to identify what differs between progressing and regressing plaques. We will look at entry and exit of different cells in the plaque, because some cells may better at removing the fatty deposits in plaques than others. We will also verify if the fibers in the plaque prevent effective removal of these deposits. Our hope is to discover the molecular mechanisms whereby high blood flow imparts its cardiovascular benefits.

column36: Functional characterization of the type VI secretion system in Aeromonas hydrophila
column37: Protein secretion systems play a pivotal role in bacterial pathogenesis and interspecies interactions. Many human pathogens employ the type 6 secretion system (T6SS) to deliver toxic protein effectors to target cells. Aeromonas hydrophila is a ubiquitous waterborne bacterium that can cause severe septicemia and necrotizing fasciitis (flesh-eating disease) in humans, and is recognized as an emerging pathogen by Health Canada. Previous reports showed that T6SS is important for virulence of A. hydrophila but the mechanism is not fully understood. My preliminary data show that A. hydrophila employs its T6SS to kill other bacterial species, suggesting the delivery of antimicrobial effectors. I hypothesize that T6SS is important for the virulence of A. hydrophila by delivering both antimicrobial and anti-eukaryotic effectors. column37: Influenza virus is one of the top ten leading causes of death in Canada, and remains one of the gravest threats to global public health due to its propensity to cause pandemics. To combat seasonal influenza epidemics, massive annual vaccination programs are carried out at tremendous expense to the healthcare system. The ability of influenza virus to cause seasonal epidemics is conferred by its capacity to rapidly evolve in order to escape pre-existing immunity. This in turn necessitates that influenza virus vaccines be reformulated on a nearly annual basis. Frequently, the strains of influenza virus that actually circulate do not perfectly resemble the strains included in the vaccine. Due to the exquisitely strain-specific immunity that current vaccines elicit, vaccine efficacy can suffer substantially when imperfect matches occur. More importantly, current vaccines offer little to no protection against the emergence of a novel influenza virus pandemic. Therefore, there is a tremendous need to develop new influenza virus vaccines capable of inducing broad and long-lasting protection. The recent discovery of broadly-neutralizing antibodies that bind to the stalk domain of hemagglutinin has raised the hope that development of a "universal" influenza virus vaccine may be within reach. While many studies have addressed how these antibodies function in isolation, little is known about the way that broadly-neutralizing antibodies are generated and function in the context of the polyclonal responses that are naturally elicited by vaccination and infection. Our studies will define the mechanisms that govern the generation and function of broadly-neutralizing antibodies in the context of the polyclonal response to infection and vaccination. The knowledge gained from these studies will be used to advance the development of "universal" influenza virus vaccines and therapeutics which have the potential to substantially reduce the global burden of influenza-related illnesses

column36: New approaches to evaluating frailty in solid organ transplantation
column37: Solid organ transplantation is a life-saving treatment for people with organ failure, but organ donors and recipients must be chosen carefully since transplants are risky and donor organs are so scarce. In recent years, transplant programs have been accepting older donors and recipients with more chronic health problems. It is possible that some of these patients are frail - in other words, their bodies are less able to withstand stress - and this may lead to poor outcomes after transplantation. We do not know how best to measure frailty in organ transplant candidates and recipients. Without appropriate tools to measure frailty, we do not know if frail patients get as much benefit from transplantation as non-frail individuals, or how to help frail patients with organ failure have longer and better lives before and after transplantation though exercise or other treatments. We also do not know whether organs from frail people can safely be used for transplantation. The objective of this study is to develop and test the usefulness of a new tool to measure frailty in donors and candidates for heart, lung, kidney or liver transplantation. We will determine whether frailty is associated with worse health outcomes before and after transplantation. The results of this study will help transplant programs better predict benefit from organ transplantation, will improve our understanding of the aging process and how it is affected by transplantation, and may lead to strategies to reduce frailty and improve the medical care of individuals with advanced organ failure.

column37: Heart disease and stroke are the leading causes of major illness and death in the Western world and result from atherosclerosis, which occurs when blood vessels become inflamed and narrowed. Progressive narrowing occurs when white blood cells from the bloodstream and muscle cells from the outer vessel wall migrate into the inner layer of the blood vessel where they cause injury. White blood cells also engulf lipid that is present, causing them to release harmful chemicals that worsen atherosclerosis. In heart attack and stroke, blood vessels supplying the heart and brain become critically narrowed and blocked by blood clot formation. Clot formation itself worsens inflammation in the blood vessel wall, fuelling the entire process. At the cellular level, each event described above contributes to atherosclerosis. Traditional therapies and preventative strategies focus on targeting individual events or on lowering blood levels of lipids. These strategies have been largely unsuccessful. Recent work from our laboratory suggests that Slit2, a molecule originally described in the developing brain, can potentially block recruitment of white blood cells, and blood clot formation. Our recent studies further suggest that Slit2 can prevent uptake of lipids by white blood cells. Indeed, Slit2 is not a synthetic medication, but rather, a molecule normally produced by blood vessel cells in the body, whose levels fall when vessel injury has occurred. We will use a combination of cutting-edge biochemical, molecular, and cell biology techniques to define how Slit2 prevents blood vessel injury in atherosclerosis. We will use animal models of atherosclerosis to test Slit2's ability to prevent blood vessel damage in the living organism. By understanding the molecular details, these studies will allow development of completely new strategies for preventing and minimizing the damage from heart attack and stroke.

column37: Acute Otitis media (AOM) is a common and costly condition in young children.4 By age 3 years, 84 % of children have had at least one episode of AOM and 46 % have had 3 or more episodes. It will allow us to understand how different stages impact the available workforce and to understand how these women maintain their work-life balance while managing their career and personal life. Our research will recommend policy changes that will ultimately increase the number of working midwives and provide improved maternity care to Canadian women.

column37: In response to viral infection, infected cells defend themselves by activating several families of cellular proteins known as transcription factors. These proteins have a role of messenger within the infected cells and will dictate if a particular gene will be used (induced) or not. Of these transcription factors, proteins named or called IRF3 and IRF7 play a key role as once turned-on or activated, they are responsible for the induction of genes with antiviral activities (known to impede pathogens' survival in the host). The latter are potent antiviral agents and powerful immunological modulators and understanding the cellular mechanisms by which infected cells produce these antiviral agents is required to identify novel cellular targets for future antiviral therapies. Discoveries in this particular field of research have demonstrated the essential roles of enzymes controlling the activity of IRF3 and IRF7. Notably, proteins called TBK1 and TRAF3 were shown to be of paramount importance in the establishment of an anti-viral defense system. Studies have demonstrated that cells infected with viruses are equipped with sensors that detect in incoming pathogens and relay this information to TRAF3, which is required for the activation of TBK1. Once activated, TBK1 is in turn responsible for the activation of IRF3 and IRF7. This type of regulation is referred as an activating signaling cascade, which control the induction of genes with antiviral activities. Albeit these important discoveries, how TRAF3, TBK1 and other "yet to discover key players" orchestrate and fine-tuned the antiviral cellular response is still largely unknown. Our endeavor in understanding the roles of TRAF3 and TBK1 in antiviral immunity as allowed us to discover other proteins with antiviral activity, namely TFG and mTOR. The propose research program will thus verify the implication of these proteins, which we believe to be essential effectors essential to fine-tune the antiviral cellular response.

column36: Personalizing Radionuclide Therapy of Neuroendocrine Tumours
column37: Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are cancers that arise from the endocrine and nervous systems. They are most commonly found in the digestive tract and the lungs. While there are many kinds of NETs, they are treated as a single group of tumours as they share common features, such as secretion of various hormones. NETs are the second most common type of cancer of the digestive tract and their incidence has been constantly increasing over the past few decades in Canada and abroad. NETs are generally slow-growing tumours that often present at an advanced stage, when they cannot be treated by surgery, and when conventional medical therapies have limited efficacy. A newer kind of therapy using radioactive drugs targeting specifically NET cancers has shown encouraging clinical results in patients suffering from NET. These include tumour regression, symptomatic relief and prolonged survival. However, since the therapy has been administered in a standardized, "one-size-fits-all" fashion to all patients, outcomes vary widely because each patient is different. We believe that the results of this therapy can be substantially improved by customizing treatment for each patient. Such an approach will allow physicians to maximize the quantity of radiation delivered to the cancer and minimize the chances of adverse effects from the therapy. This project involves the use of standard nuclear medicine imaging techniques to determine the distribution of the radioactive drug through the body of the patient receiving the therapy. Methods will be developed to process these images and to combine them with other patient data to allow physicians to tailor the therapy to the specific needs and characteristics of each individual patient. Such image-based therapy plans will maximize the likelihood of successful treatment while maintaining a very low likelihood of any adverse effect. The goal of this research is to improve the lives of Canadian patients with NETs, through personalized medicine.

column37: Osteoporosis is characterized by low bone mass and deterioration of bone tissue. column36: Co-targeting parathyroid-hormone related protein (PTHrP) signaling and osteoclast activation to counter breast cancer metastasis to bone
column37: Skeletal metastases appear as complications in up to 70% of breast cancer patients. Once bone tumors are established, they are usually incurable. In advanced cases, the skeleton often bears the major tumor burden, causing considerable suffering and morbidity due to hypercalcemia, pathological fractures, cord compression and intractable pain. The current therapies against skeletal invasion use anti-resorptive agents such as bisphosphonates, but these compounds are not curative and new targets must be identified in the fight against bone metastases. Breast tumors and other types of cancer are composed of two main populations of cancer cells. The bulk of a tumor is composed of cells with limited proliferation capacity that are sensitive to conventional anti-cancer therapies. There is also a small population of long-lived cancer stem cells (CSCs) that are resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy. A notoriously difficult-to-treat cancer is the CSC-driven triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). TNBCs have very poor prognosis because they currently lack effective therapies. Traditional cancer therapies can effectively de-bulk tumors but fail to produce long-term remissions and prevent metastases, possibly due to their inability to eliminate CSCs. Our laboratory has identified a novel target known as the parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), previously implicated in the development of bone metastases, but which has never before been associated with CSCs or TNBC. We have produced an anti-PTHrP antibody that blocks PTHrP action and is highly-efficient against breast cancer growth and metastases. column36: A Genetic Model for Neurofibromatosis Type II
column37: Neurofibromatosis Type II (NF2) is a crippling cancer, mostly of the nervous system. The chance of developing NF2 depends on the genes you inherit. For example, NF2 patients are often born only one functional copy the NF2 gene instead of two. If that functional copy was mutated, tumours may repeatedly develop in the brain and spinal cord. The NF2 gene encodes a protein named Merlin. Merlin acts as a tumour suppressor, a name for proteins that instruct cells not to divide. This activity may be related to a second function for Merlin: it helps cells to "stick together," which is crucial for forming various organs within our bodies. Our laboratory is determining why Merlin is found in almost all cells of the human body, but mutations in the NF2 gene mostly induce cancer in just the brain and spinal cord. Other researchers that study the Merlin protein mostly work with isolated human cells for simplicity, but that approach makes it more difficult to determine how Merlin causes cells to adhere to one another to form tissues like the brain. Animal models such as mice would be vastly preferable for tissue studies, but they are more difficult to work with than isolated cells. At the crossroads between cells and mice is the commonly studied laboratory animal Drosophila or the fruit fly. The fly brain is a reduced version of the human brain, with the same types of cells acting in the same ways. Using flies, we have shown that Merlin needs to work with other proteins to perform its tumour suppressor and cell-adhesive functions. Notably, some of these other proteins are found only in brain cells. We plan to determine how these proteins assist Merlin activity in the fly brain. We already know that related forms of these proteins are found in the human brain. Our goal is to understand how these proteins function with Merlin to control how cells grow and stick together in the nervous system. Our results will aid the development of improved diagnosis and therapies for NF2 tumours.

column37: The impact of diet and body condition on the father's reproductive health and that of his offspring has been relatively under-explored and under-emphasized. Over the past two decades male fertility is declining as measured by lowered sperm counts, increased DNA damage in sperm and rising rates of testicular cancer. Other factors contributing to increasing male infertility are the increase in chronic diseases that are widespread including, obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders. While we know each of these factors can negatively impact sperm counts and quality, what is even more alarming is the emerging evidence from the field of epigenetics which suggests these factors are not limited to just damaging male fertility, but may passed on to influence the health of children and perhaps even grandchildren. So how does sperm transmit information concerning diet and body condition across generations? It involves a biochemical set of information that is hereditary just like DNA, but sits on top, or within the DNA and controls whether a gene is turned active or not. The overall research question we address is: Does a father's diet and body mass index predispose his offspring to chronic disease or developmental defects and how is this information related to the sperm epigenome? The mechanisms underlying transmission of environmental memory from parents to offspring is far from understood. In prior studies we demonstrated that a folate deficient diet altered the sperm epigenome and that these changes were associated to genes implicated in development and chronic disease. In humans fast food diets, obesity and its metabolic sequelae are known to alter folate metabolism. Using data from murine models and human samples collected from a fertility clinic we will determine how folate and body mass affects the sperm epigenome, its association with markers of chronic disease and the consequences for offspring.

column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an incurable cancer that often effects otherwise healthy young people. Despite aggressive treatment, outcomes for patients with glioblastoma remain dismal. Patients inevitably succumb to their disease in just over one year. One hallmark of GBM is its highly vascular nature. Tumour growth depends on angiogenesis, or new blood vessel formation. The initial experience with the angiogenesis inhibitor, bevacizumab (Avastin), appeared to justify this interest: it improved survival in patients with progressive GBM from 3.3 to 8.1 months. It has been speculated that an analogous alternative mechanism for angiogenesis is responsible for progression of breast and colon cancer through Avastin therapy. In our previous work, we identified a molecule involved in normal blood vessel maturation, which has been coopted in GBM to allow cancer cells to become blood vessel cells. This process, known as vascular mimicry, has been described in melanoma, but only recently found to occur in GBM. In a GBM mouse model, inhibition of this molecular, which we named LIVE, inhibited new blood vessel growth and resulted in tumour regression and prolonged survival. Our findings suggest that LIVE modulates alternative angiogenesis in GBM. In this project, we will determine if LIVE-mediated vascular mimicry is a mechanism of Avastin resistance, and if so, if LIVE inhibition enhances survival in GBM. If successful, these studies could open a new venue for treatment of patients with GBM, and in other cancers in which vascular mimicry plays a role in therapeutic resistance.

column37: Developing dementia is one of the greatest fears of aging. In fact, many fear it more than cancer. Furthermore, we will explore how each exercise type improves cognitive function as such information may lead to new discoveries and therapies. Given the immense health and financial burden imposed by dementia, our proposed study could have major impact in Canada and internationally; the results may positively reshape the path experienced by older adults with mild cognitive impairment.

column36: Defining the mechanisms and therapeutic potential of ShcA-mediated angiogenesis and metabolism that fuel breast tumorigenesis
column37: Cancer cells grow uncontrollably and are unresponsive to the checkpoints that restrain the growth of normal cells. In order to support such rapid proliferation, cancer cells must substantially increase their ability to acquire nutrients and oxygen by generating a new blood supply (neo-vascularization) and also to generate the energy (ATP) for cancer cells to divide. Our research focuses on a particular class of proteins, called receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), which substantially increase the ability of cancer cells to recruit a new vasculature and generate ATP. Adaptor proteins bridge these RTKs to downstream effector pathways, which are critical for their biological function. Our research has shown that one adaptor protein, called ShcA, is a central hub downstream of many RTKs to fuel breast tumor growth. We have generated extensive data to show that breast cancer cells with high ShcA activity substantially increase breast tumor vascularization and ATP production, leading to increased tumor growth. Herein, we will address the molecular mechanisms by which ShcA regulates tumor vascularization, energy production and cell proliferation, each of which contribute to tumor aggressiveness. The advent of targeted therapies have revolutionized clinical management of breast cancer patients. Despite the availability of a plethora of such therapies, the remaining challenge is to choose the treatment that has the best chance of success to manage the disease in advanced breast cancer patients. Our data suggests that the activation status of ShcA can alter the sensitivity of breast tumors to pharmacological inhibitors targeting pathways that promote tumor vascularization, ATP production and cell growth. We will examine whether measurement of the ShcA activation status of breast tumors can serve as a predictive biomarker to determine whether the tumor is more likely to be more sensitive to one type of therapy over another. This is the cornerstone of personalized medicine.
