column36: Stress and Obesity: the Ghrelin connection
column37: Obesity is related to a variety of pathologic conditions that include cancer, heart disease, diabetes, and renal insufficiency, all of which can lead to an early death and poor quality of life. In Canada, the rate of obesity and the health and economic issues associated with this condition have reached alarming levels. While it is clear that there are genetic factors that are closely associated with obesity, environmental factors also play an important role the behavioral and physiological responses that lead to body weight alterations and ultimately in obesity and metabolic syndrome. Stress, for example has been associated with a number of metabolic changes that ultimately can lead to obesity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease. Interestingly, a number of symptoms that are seen following exposure to different types of stressors are also seen in animals exposed to chronically elevated levels of the hormone ghrelin. Ghrelin, a stomach derived hormone, is commonly associated with the stimulation of appetite and food intake (particularly the intake of high calorie foods), as well as the accumulation of body fat. Ghrelin appears to be released following exposure to stressors, and produces many of the behavioral and metabolic alterations that are seen following chronic stress paradigms. This proposal is aimed at deciphering the mechanisms by which ghrelin does this, including the potential for drugs that block or reduce ghrelin secretion to attenuate the metabolic effects of chronic stress. The results from the proposed studies will lead to a better understanding of the hormonal mechanisms by which stress responses alter behavioral and metabolic processes.

column36: Bringing together the nutritional and glucocorticoid hypotheses of fetal programming: Does nutrition buffer the effects of stress?
column37: Many studies have shown that children who were exposed to maternal stress and poor maternal diet during gestation are at risk for impaired brain development (e.g., problems in attention and memory, problems regulating their emotions and behaviours). Even subtle impairments in brain development have long-lasting effects on children, including their success in school and their success as adults in social relationships, career, and ability to generate income. Children are not, however, equally affected by prenatal exposure to stress and nutrition. Some children exposed to prenatal stress do not seem to suffer negative effects. One reason for this may be that nutrition can change the way that the prenatal stress signals get passed on to the developing fetus. Specifically, nutrients like choline and long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids may reduce the amount of 'stress signals' like cortisol that are passed on to the fetus when a pregnant women becomes stressed. This idea offers the exciting possibility that specific nutrients can be used to prevent or treat the negative effects of exposure to maternal stress during pregnancy. In this study, we will investigate the role of prenatal nutrition as a protective factor that prevents or reduces the negative effects of maternal cortisol on children's own stress response systems and their cognitive ability. Our goal is to generate new insights into the relationships among maternal psychological stress and nutrition in the prenatal period that will inform prevention and intervention programs and policies to improve child health in Canada.

The number of Canadians living with or are at risk of developing kidney disease is estimated to be 2 million. Although progress has been made in understanding how kidney disease develops, there are still large gaps in our knowledge. The role of highly specialized kidney cells, the tubular epithelium in disease generation is now increasingly recognized. Chemicals released by immune cells or the epithelium itself alter epithelial function and initiate harmful responses. Importantly, the intactness of the cell architecture, the so called cytoskeleton, is vital for normal functions, and its disruption is an early step in many diseases. The objective of this proposal is to investigate how the chemical named Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) alters tubular cell functions and causes injury in the kidney. This molecule plays an important role in kidney disease, and affects tubular cell architecture and functions. We will study the molecular events that lead to activation of molecules involved in the regulation of cell architecture, integrity of junctions and many other vital functions including injury repair. We will focus on the cellular molecules called RhoA and their regulator GEF-H1, as these have central roles in many cell functions. They are regulated by harmful stimuli, but the details of the ensuing events are not well known. Therefore, we will use various biochemical, cell biological and fluorescent microscopic techniques in kidney tubule cell lines to study these molecules. We will also test our findings in animal models of kidney diseases. These studies will provide new information about the mechanisms of chronic kidney disease, with the hope of finding novel targets for designing drugs for these currently untreatable conditions.

column36: Cesarean section: impact on infant gut microbiota, childhood obesity and allergic disease
column37: The World Health Organization recommends that the rate of Cesarean section (CS) should be no higher than 15% and that infants should not be fed anything other than breast milk for the first 6 months. Currently in Canada, 27% of births are by CS, up from 18% in the mid 1990s. Also, only 14% of Canadian infants are strictly breastfed for the first six months of life and less so if they are born by CS. The consequences of decision-making around birth method and infant feeding should not be underestimated. Beyond risks to the mother and infant at the time of delivery, long term health effects are associated with CS birth, including allergy, asthma and overweight. Breastfeeding provides health benefits to the child by reducing the risk of these conditions. It is thought that health outcomes related to CS and breastfeeding may be due to changes in the bacteria living in the intestinal tract, called the gut microbiota. This community of beneficial bacteria evolves in response to the bacterial environment of the infant. Normally, the first exposure to microbes is the bacteria encountered in the birth canal. In a CS-delivered infant, exposures come from the mother's skin and hospital environment. Antibiotic treatment to prevent infection in CS may also affect the development of infant gut microbiota. A clearer understanding is needed of how the gut microbiota is affected by birth method and early feeding, and how these changes affect the health of the child later in life. The main goal of our research in 3,300 healthy Canadian infants is to understand long term child health outcomes arising from changes in the development of the infant gut microbiota in response to CS delivery. A secondary goal is to determine how other factors, like breastfeeding and antibiotic use, alter the effects of CS on the infant gut microbiota. This will help parents and physicians make more informed decisions about birth method and infant feeding.

These findings should guide us towards novel therapeutic approaches not only against this virus but against the entire herpes family of viruses.

column36: Microtubule dynamics and age-related aneuploidy in mammalian oocytes
column37: At fertilisation a new individual is created by the fusion of the sperm and the egg, each of which contributes half of the genetic material (chromosomes) for the offspring. However, for reasons that are very poorly understood, the development of the egg is error-prone, such that unfertilised eggs frequently possess the wrong number of chromosomes. This is particularly the case as women get older. These chromosomally abnormal ('aneuploid') eggs are the cause of developmental conditions such as Down's, are a leading cause of miscarriage, and are the leading reason for age-related infertility. We will investigate the cause of aneuploidy in eggs, particularly focussing on the spindle, the part of the cell responsible for ensuring that chromosomes are correctly divided between cells (called chromosome segregation) during the final cell division which occurs as part of egg development. Using state-of-the-art microscopy we will compare spindles in eggs from old mice and young mice, to determine precisely why the spindle in the developing egg from older mothers is more prone to chromosome segregation errors. Our preliminary data suggest that the kinesin-13s family of proteins, which are important for correct chromosomes segregation in many cells, may be defective in old eggs. We will test the role of kinesin-13s in developing eggs, and establish which of these proteins are the most important for preventing chromosome segregation-errors. Moreover, in collaboration with clinical colleagues, we will perform some of the first such studies in human eggs, and determine whether kinesin-13s are important for preventing aneuploidy. Our experiments will provide key information as to why developing eggs are likely to mis-segregate chromosomes, particularly in older mothers, and thus will help explain why pregnancy establishment becomes more difficult as women become older.

column37: Bullying in schools is a severe problem in many countries. In Canada between 20% and 25% of girls and boys are bullied by peers at some point during their school years. Understanding this association is crucial, because mental health problems during young adulthood have profound implications for the quality of later life. It is also critical to identify the bio-physiological mechanisms through which peer victimization gets "under the skull, skin and cells" and leads to mental health problems in young adult women and men. By accounting for the role of genetic influences, this design is ideal for understanding the influence of adverse environmental experiences on health. Together with the previously collected data, the proposed research will provide unique insights into the long-term effect of peer victimization and offer empirically-based resources for health professionals concerned with promoting a healthy transition to adulthood for female and male victims of school bullying.

column36: Fundamental processes impacting Campylobacter jejuni pathogenesis
column37: Campylobacter jejuni (Cj) is the leading cause of bacterial food poisoning in the developed world. Yet, its mechanisms of pathogenesis remain mysterious. Through screening and selection, we have identified means by which this pathogen is so successful. One is its shape. Cj is helical/corkscrew in morphology, and this abets its ability to burrow into the mucosa of both susceptible and commensal hosts. We have, for the first time, identified gene products involved in the cell envelope (peptidoglycan; PG) required for this shape, and logical candidates for further study. Using a rounded genetics and biochemical approach, we will perform gene deletion studies, protein localization, exploration of newly identified factors, investigation of how these factors interact with each other to control helicity, and studies of PG factors involved in the natural shape-change processes of cell division and coccoid formation as the bacteria age. Also through genetic screens, we identified and defined the Cj hyperosmotic stress response. Surprisingly, this revealed significant heterogeneity within wild type Cj 'clones', at a frequency significantly outweighing standard single nucleotide polymorphism and phase-variation. This type of heterogeneity may be what underlies the ability of Cj to infect and survive in so many diverse environments despite fragile growth requirements. We are investigating the role of purine metabolism in this process, exploring a novel regulator, and identifying and characterizing new hypervariable genes. We are excited to continue studies linking this variability with our bacterial cell shape findings, which also yield heterogeneity in a wild type population. Ultimately, we hope that the combination of traditional microbiology, genetics, and biochemistry, together with newer next-gen approaches, will finally provide insight into how and why Cj is such an important human pathogen, and clues to its eradication.

column36: Des institutions et des femmes : Evolution du nursing psychiatrique au Quebec, 1912-1974
column37: Encore aujourd'hui, dans les universites quebecoises est propagee l'idee qu'au Quebec, jusqu'en 1960, les soins dispenses aux malades mentaux etaient exclusivement reserves aux communautes religieuses et que les asiles etaient strictement des institutions de gardiennage, des lieux d'hebergement, d'abandon et de deshumanisation. Afin de deconstruire cette conception de la genese du nursing psychiatrique, nous entendons, dans le cadre de ce programme de recherche, mener une enquete historique au sein de trois institutions psychiatriques d'importance au Quebec : l'Hopital Saint-Michel-Archange (Institut universitaire en sante mentale de Quebec); l'Hopital Saint-Jean-de-Dieu (Institut universitaire de sante mentale de Montreal) et l'Institut Albert-Prevost qui etait une institution privee montrealaise. Egalement, les femmes a la tete de ces etablissements psychiatriques ont toutes ete evincees de leur poste de direction pour etre remplacees dans les annees 1970 par des psychiatres modernistes soutenus par l'Etat. A l'heure ou le reseau de la sante mentale doit travailler a l'integration judicieuse de nouvelles infirmieres specialisees, notre etude contribuera activement a la creation de connaissances qui permettront de mieux comprendre les origines des pratiques nursing en psychiatrie, le role determinant des femmes a la tete d'institutions de premier plan et l'importance d'une formation universitaire specialisee. Ainsi, nous serons en mesure de developper, pour ces infirmieres psychiatriques, des strategies pedagogiques efficaces qui participeront a l'amelioration de la prestation de soins de sante mentale au pays.

column37: All of our genes are arranged on large pieces of DNA called chromosomes. The chromosomes are huge molecules that must undergo multiple levels of compaction to fit into the cell. At the same time, the genes characteristic of that cell type must remain accessible for activation. In a stem cell the chromosomes are loosely packaged and many genes are poised for activation. When the stem cell commits to becoming a specific cell type (eg. neuron) it must tightly package and silence those genes that are not required and fully activate those genes that will be turned on. When this process is defective, cells cannot divide, differentiate or initiate gene expression effectively. Indeed, recent work has shown that mutations in chromosome regulating proteins cause a variety of human diseases, including developmental disorders with severe intellectual disability and numerous types of cancer. Despite this success, our understanding of how these chromosome regulatory proteins coordinate which genes to turn on or off,when to turn them on or off, and in what order remains poorly defined. The main aim of this research is to delineate the roles of two closely related chromosome organizing proteins, Snf2h and Snf2l that appear to have complementary roles on neural stem cell function during brain development. Defining this fundamental process is critical for us to understand how a stem cell commits to a specific cell fate and how it maintains an organized chromosome. A thorough understanding of these processes is a prerequisite to determining how these complex disorders develop, progress, and for engineering novel treatment strategies.

column36: Autophagy regulation of T effector cell metabolism and survival
column37: A central idea in immunology is that an infection must stimulate the immune system to make special cells called memory T cells. As the name implies, these cells remain in the body for the life of the individual and when the same infection is encountered, these memory T cells generate a strong immune attack to prevent the infection from taking hold. In fact, this is the basis of vaccines and is arguably one of the most successful achievements in modern medicine. Yet the precise way memory T cells are made and ways to improve the function of these immune cells remain unknown. Using our initial CIHR-funded grant, we developed a new mouse model to study the factors that are necessary to generate memory T cells. We genetically removed a gene called Atg5, an essential gene for a normal cell survival program called autophagy. Immune cells lacking Atg5 failed to survive through an infection and subsequently do not go on to produce memory T cells. We showed that immune cells that cannot survive in the absence of Atg5 display abnormal metabolism. Because metabolism is the most fundamental process of a cell, we believe this is the reason why immune cells cannot survive to become memory cells. The purpose of this proposal is to investigate how autophagy controls metabolism and the survival of T cells during an immune response. We also plan to examine whether there is a role for autophagy in controlling memory responses to human vaccines. This is an important step forward that will provide fundamental knowledge on the key events that shape memory T cells. The need for additional effective vaccines highlights the far reaching implications of our work and how to best to exploit the immune system to develop more effective immune responses and vaccines against human diseases like HIV/AIDS and cancer.

column36: The blood-epididymis barrier, a key determinant of male fertility
column37: Infertility afflicts between 12 and 15% of couples. Male infertility accounts for half of these cases. The goals of the present study are to demonstrate whether or not basal cells are in fact multipotent stem cells, how these are regulated, to determine their role in the differentiation of the epididymis, and to assess their clinical significance with regards to epididymal sperm maturation.

column36: Understanding the thoughts and emotions of others: neuroimaging measures of typical and atypical development
column37: Children with autism experience great difficulties with social interactions. Several ideas have been put forth to explain the brain mechanisms underlying these social difficulties. It may be that children with autism have a hard time understanding the thoughts and intentions of others (referred to as 'Theory of Mind'), or they may not be able to discern emotional expressions on the faces of others ('abnormal emotional processing'), or they are unable to inhibit behaviours that are socially inappropriate ('abnormal inhibitory control'). All of these abilities (theory of mind, emotional processing, inhibitory control) are learned by typically developing children over time, and do not mature until adolescence and young adulthood; however, this maturation does not seem to happen normally in autism. We propose the use of a brain imaging technique that tracks brain processing with millisecond precision (magnetoencephalography) along with a technique that takes high resolution pictures of the brain (MRI/DTI) while children with autism perform tasks that require theory of mind, emotional processing and inhibitory control. Using complex analyses developed in our lab, we can see exactly when a certain part of the brain is working on the task. By comparing between children with autism and typically developing children, we will understand how brain processing differs on these tasks and what underlies these social deficits. With this understanding, we may find that certain sub-types of autism are identifiable by specific brain dysfunctions which are tied to certain social difficulties which we will also be measuring. This knowledge will allow us to develop tailored interventions that are targeted for a child's specific deficits.

column37: Patients with severe burns need to recover in a hospital burn unit for a long time and are at high risk of developing infections and dying. column37: The loss of muscle mass, referred to as muscle wasting, is a hallmark of many chronic disease such as cancer. column36: Investigating electroretinography(ERG) as a new method for predicting conversion to psychosis in youth at clinical high risk.
column37: The importance of discovering reliable biomarkers of psychiatric illnesses is on the rise. A specific psychiatric disease is often not easily recognizable at onset and therefore a biomarker is needed to shorten the diagnostic procedure and target the proper treatment promptly. One major obstacle facing research in psychiatry and neurosciences in general is the investigation of the living brain in humans using non-invasive techniques. The retina has been tagged as an approachable part of the brain due to its common embryonic origin. Fortunately, it is possible to investigate retinal function using a non-invasive tool, namely the electroretinogram (ERG). Studying 105 patients affected by schizophrenia (SZ), we have recently discovered that the ERG parameters could identify SZ with high accuracy (90%). These discoveries have built upon our previous finding of some ERG anomalies in children having one parent affected by a psychiatric disorder. The finding of ERG deficits in these non-medicated healthy youths enhanced the potential of the ERG as a biomarker of SZ by upraising the utility of the ERG in early detection and prevention. However, it remains to see whether the ERG can recognize SZ right at the onset of symptoms. This will be verified in our proposed prospective study of youths and young adults at Clinical High Risk (CHR) for psychosis. At entry, each subject will obtain a probability of being a SZ case according to his/her ERG profile. Subjects will be seen again three years later when the diagnosis is stabilized. The ERG predictions will then be confronted with reality. We postulate that the ERG will have accurately predicted, three years earlier, the "correct" clinical diagnosis characterizing the patient three years later. Hence, our study will allow the validation the ERG as a new technology capable of quickly identifying SZ, thus avoiding the actual delay due to the instability in the natural course of clinical symptoms.

column36: Function and regulation of Numb protein isoforms in cancer.
column37: In a normal cell, growth and proliferation is regulated by signals that come from the surrounding tissue and neighboring cells. Signals from outside are interpreted by protein receptors that span the limiting membrane of the cell (half inside and half outside). A signal received outside is transmitted inside by the receptor which then passes the signal on to molecules in the cell that control cell behavior. Once a receptor molecule is activated it is quickly pulled inside the cell where it is destroyed and the signal is terminated. This is process called receptor down regulation. In some cancers, this control mechanism is lost, and the receptor stays at the surface of the cell, and continues to send signals. As a result the cell continuously divides, or migrates and invades surrounding tissue inappropriately. The focus of this proposal is a molecule called Numb that controls the down regulation of receptors. There is evidence that the function of the Numb molecule is lost or altered in human breast lung and ovarian tumors. We hypothesize that these changes in the Numb molecule disrupts the normal down regulation of receptors causing tumor growth and metastasis. In this proposal we will use biochemical, cell biology, and animal model studies to: 1. Investigate what causes the altered forms of Numb observed in cancer cells. 2. To determine how changes in normal Numb activity affects the growth and survival of human breast cancer cells. This information will allow us to evaluate whether changes in the Numb molecule occurs in tumors that have a failure of receptor down regulation. This is could impact cancer treatment as new cancer drugs specifically target cell receptors in an effort to shut them off. In addition, it will also give us specific information on how Numb becomes altered in human cancer, and whether restoration of normal Numb activity is useful and potentially achievable therapeutic goal.

column37: The kidney is an important physiological "filter" that allows us to eliminate all waste products, while retaining vital components. One vital molecule is bicarbonate, which we must retain to compensate for the acid produced while processing food. Some individuals with mutated bicarbonate transporter kAE1 are unable to properly retain bicarbonate in their kidneys, thus bicarbonate is expelled instead of reabsorbed. To reach these goals, we will use an animal model mimicking the pathology seen in these patients, complemented with in vitro analyses to dissect these mechanisms at the cellular level. column37: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a severe mental illness affecting tens of thousands of Canadians. It is the 6th most important cause of disability according to the World Health Organization. column36: B cell intrinsic mechanisms of germinal center reaction
column37: Germinal center (GC) is a small lymphoid structure in spleen and lymph nodes. Under normal circumstance, GC reaction can generate differentiated B lymphocytes called memory B cells and plasma cells, the latter produce antibodies that are responsible for neutralization and elimination of various viral and bacterial pathogens. However, abnormal GC reaction may lead to immune deficiency, autoimmune diseases, and even GC-derived B lymphomas that compose the majority of B cell tumors. During pathogen infection the incoming pathogens first activate B cells through B cell antigen receptors (BCR), The activated B cells then migrate to GC where they may proliferate multiple rounds, modify their antibody coding genes, and differentiate into either plasma or memory B cells. While it has become clear that coordination between B cells and other immune cells appears to be essential for GC reaction, molecular mechanisms that control B cell differentiation inside a GC remain not entirely clear. We found that Cbl proteins, a group of similar protein modifiers, play a critical role in GC reaction. We showed that Cbl proteins deficiency disrupts GC formation at multiple stages and severely impaired antibody production. We also identified that the impairment is caused by several defects, including loss of coordination between B and other immune cells and alteration of B cell function to produce high affinity antibodies (termed affinity maturation). In addition, Cbl deficient mice develop high incidence of lymphomas after immunization, indicating that they may function as tumor suppressors. The current proposal aims at understanding how Cbl proteins regulate GC reaction and antibody affinity maturation, and elucidate how Cbl deficiency contributes to B lymphoma genesis. Completion of this project will not only bring new insight in our understanding of GC reaction but also provide clues in the prevention and treatment of various immune system disorders.

column37: It is now well established that B cells are important in MS, but we know very little about how they contribute to disease. Clusters of B cells have recently been identified in the inflamed MS brains and spinal cords. The appearance of these clusters correlates with more severe disease, and they are often found next to regions of serious damage to the tissue. Therefore, it is thought that these clusters are locations from which B cells exert their disease-promoting mechanisms. We know little about the types of B cells found in the inflamed central nervous system, and therefore we don't know how they drive disease. We have tools to track both "autoimmune" (disease causing) and "normal" T and B in a mouse model of MS. We will use these to learn what kids of B cells get into the spinal cord, what their history is, and if they are selectively autoimmune. A promising new therapy targets and destroys B cells, but we don't know if the cells in the spinal cord are susceptible to this depletion and this is something that we will test. Further, we will explore the molecules that B cells use to get into the spinal cord. Another new therapy for MS is thought to work by blocking immune cell recruitment to the brain and spinal cord in MS and we will determine if this drug blocks B cell access and shrinks clusters, or if some other target is more effective. Finally, B cells are know to collaborate with another type of cell called a T cell through direct interactions with each other. These interactions are essential to initiate a new immune response in a lymph node and similar interactions likely occur in the inflamed brain and spinal cord in MS, perhaps within the B cell clusters. We will use cutting edge microscopy techniques to directly observe these interactions and test specific targets to block them, with the goal to prevent B cells from promoting ongoing disease.

column37: In Canada, about 86,000 people live with a spinal cord injury (SCI), and more than 4,300 new cases arise every year. For SCI individuals, limitations in sensorimotor activities such as walking and posture severely affect their quality of life. In most cases, patients have an incomplete injury that spares some connections between the brain, which initiates movements, and the spinal circuits, which generate them. This places brain structures with partial connectivity to the spinal cord in a particularly favorable position to compensate for the lost function. Specifically, the motor cortex offers significant and unappreciated opportunities for recovery of walking and is a potential target for treatments. My main goal is study the role of the motor cortex in the recovery of locomotion after incomplete SCI. We will use a well-established rat model of SCI in which hindlimb locomotion is progressively re-expressed over five weeks. While this short time course does not mimic recovery in humans, it facilitates exploration of the underlying biological mechanisms. By combining innovative paradigms to manipulate cortical activity with behavioral, electrophysiological and neuroanatomical techniques, we will study the mechanisms by which the cortex affects the spinal circuits that generate stepping after SCI. We will then tap into these mechanisms to foster and enhance recovery of walking by testing cortical stimulation protocols. Our experiments will provide a comprehensive examination of the role of the motor cortex and the mechanisms through which it influences locomotor recovery after SCI. This proposal has the potential to expand our knowledge on the neural basis of recovery after SCI. Activity-based neurorehabilitation and brain stimulation protocols can be developed to harness cortical activity that may catalyze functional recovery, e.g. walking and posture, following SCI.

column37: The cells in our body are constantly exposed to environmental factors (e.g. UV light, chemical carcinogens in the air, food, or cigarettes) that could do major damage to our DNA. If the cell did not do anything about it, the damaged DNA would be passed onto subsequent generations of cells, and could eventually lead to cancer development. To prevent this from happening, the cell uses a protein called p53 that acts as a policeman. Upon DNA damage, this protein tells the cell to immediately stop growing, allowing time to repair this damage; or, should the damage be too severe, to commit suicide by triggering a cellular process called apoptosis. In either case, the damaged DNA would not be passed onto future cell populations. P53 therefore serves a very important function, and loss of p53 itself or its function has been found in over 50% of all human cancers. How p53 carries out all these important tumour suppressing functions has been an area of intense research as it may reveal how we get cancer and how we can control cancer. At the molecular level, the chain of command from p53 down has been well studied, however, major gaps in knowledge remain. The proposed research is based on our recent discovery of a new protein whose synthesis is under the control of p53, and that this new protein, called Nmnat2, can in turn loop back and control p53's cell killing function. We consider this to be a major revelation in the p53 field, and propose a series of experiments that will define the precise relationship between Nmnat2 and p53, which should in turn shed light on the mechanism whereby p53 controls cancer development as well as other metabolic processes in the cell. The long term objective of this study is to determine if any human cancers and metabolic disorders can be traced to defects in the Nmnat2-p53 regulatory loop, and to develop specific strategies against such diseases.

column37: Cilia are cellular 'antenna' that enable many essential physiological and developmental processes. For example, motile cilia clear respiratory airways of debris and allow sperm movement. The aim of the research is to provide new fundamental biological insights and to increase our understanding of the links between cilia and disease. To achieve our objective, we propose using innovative approaches to uncover and analyse novel components of the gate. Multiple complementary strategies will be used to help define the molecular organisation of transition zone components, and to probe the molecular functions of the gate. The studies will involve the use of the nematode C. elegans, a powerful, genetically-manipulable model system. This organism allows us to take advantage of cutting-edge resources and experimental tools not readily available for researchers using vertebrate/mammalian systems. Lastly, collaborations with human geneticists will facilitate our discovery and analysis of novel disease genes associated with cilia defects (ciliopathies). Together, our findings will help us make significant strides towards understanding fundamental mechanisms of cilium formation and function-seen as increasingly relevant to human health and disease.

column37: In the neck region near major arteries, 'receptor' cells in tiny organs help maintain blood chemicals at particular levels via the control of breathing. These 'receptor' cells sense blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity, and send electrical signals to the brain that help correct any major disturbances. Abnormalities in this reflex pathway can have fatal consequences. For example, changes in 'receptor' cell properties are associated with clinical conditions such as obstructive lung disease (COPD), sleep apnea (where breathing stops periodically), hypertension, and congestive heart failure. These conditions are associated with fluctuations in blood oxygen levels, which can lead to hyper-activity in the reflex pathway, compromising blood pressure regulation and heart function. Our investigations aim to understand how these 'receptor' cells work, how they communicate with the brain, and how their properties change in disease states. To simplify the system, in one approach we isolate these 'receptor' cells from rats and grow them in tissue culture dishes alone, or with the nerve cells that contact them in the animal. Recent studies have shown that these rat 'receptor' cells behave similarly to those in humans. We grow the cells in an incubator under different oxygen levels, thereby mimicking the environment experienced in disease conditions. Also, we can expose live animals (rats) to environments where oxygen levels can be varied in precise patterns, so as to mimic the above clinical conditions. We can then apply various techniques (e.g. recording of electrical activity, imaging, molecular biology) to help understand how the 'receptor' cells communicate with nerve cells, and how their properties change in different oxygen environments. This understanding will help in the design of new drugs to target and correct abnormalities that arise in the aforementioned clinical conditions.

It occurs in older patients, associated with diabetes and hypertension. Most concerning is the fact that to date, we don't yet have a good diagnostic tool, nor effective therapies for the condition. Interestingly, IGFBP7 appears to accelerate aging, and may lead to the changes in the heart we find in diastolic heart failure. We would like to find out if this is indeed the case. We want to (1) check if risk factors for heart failure accelerate the aging process in the cells that make up the heart chamber; (2) see if IGFBP7 produced in this process will lead to the heart failure process, and whether the different heart cell types will enhance each other in response. We also want to (3) find out if we blocked this molecule's presence in the heart, whether it would benefit the patient. There is thus an opportunity that our research is opening new windows in this enigmatic disease, and potentially can change the lives of patients affected by this condition.

column36: Oncology's metaknowledge networks: an investigation of the collective dynamics of bio-clinical innovation
column37: In the last four decades, oncology has shifted from a small, marginal domain within biomedicine to one of the largest, most central and successful. It is now second only to cardiovascular medicine in terms of practitioners, research activities, biopharmaceutical investment and market size. Oncology has pioneered the most innovative recent approaches to translational research. In spite of its staggering expansion, a relatively small number of oncologists-the oncology "core set"-appear to define the international research and treatment agenda, with unknown consequences for medicine and human health. Given the dominant position of oncology at the frontier of biomedical innovation, our project proposes to achieve a deep understanding of how the organization of oncology researchers shape how the system of oncology as a whole "thinks"-what it attends to and how it searches the space of possible diagnoses and treatments in pursuit of advance. Contributions from our effort will include conceptual and empirical contributions to medical sociology, science studies, as actionable insights for health and science policy. To gain this understanding, we will deploy a "metaknowledge" approach that draws on digital archives and new computational tools to trace research teams and collaboration networks, investigative and clinical technologies, the myriad recombinant elements under investigation-tissues, cells, genes, proteins, biomarkers-and the changing landscape of institutions that hosts them. Specifically, we will use machine learning, natural language processing, network analysis and Bayesian modeling approaches, linked with qualitative and historical investigation of oncology's emergence and development. Together, these tools and data will allow us unprecedented, intregrative insight into how oncology "thinks", how it followed its particular path of innovation, and the possible consequences of that path for biomedical insight and human health.

column36: Therapeutic potential of small-molecules targeting the toxins of Clostridium difficile
column37: Clostridium difficile is a superbug that can causes serious diarrhoea in hospitalized patients, potentially resulting in death. The number and severity of infections has grown in the last 15 years because of the emergence of more virulent strains. Current antibiotic treatments for Clostridium difficile are inadequate, and new strategies are needed. Toxins produced by the bacteria are the primary cause of disease. We propose here a new method to inactivate these bacterial toxins in the intestine, before they provoke injury. This research has the potential to transform the treatment of this alarming infection.

column36: Kinematics and Muscle Activation of the Cervical Spine During Impending Head First Impacts in Motor Vehicle Rollovers
column37: Vehicular rollovers are a significant source of major injuries. Specifically, rollovers can cause neck injury, through head-first impact when an occupant "dives" into the roof during roof to ground impact. Rollover neck injury mechanisms are poorly understood and although cadaver studies have been used to study rollovers, they lack muscles and because rollovers take several seconds to develop, muscles are important to the spine posture during rollovers. We plan to study spine posture and neck muscles in human volunteers during simulated rollovers. We have developed techniques previously to record neck posture with x-ray movies and neck muscle activation with electromyography (small needles that are inserted into the various neck muscles to record their electrical activity). We have also done these studies in a rig that allowed us to study people that were strapped into a car seat and hung upside down. We will modify this rig so that it moves similarly to a vehicle during a rollover and use the same x-ray and electromyography techniques to study the volunteers necks during our experiments. This information will allow us to validate existing computational models of the neck during rollovers and we can use it to develop new seatbelts, roof panels and other novel safety devices to prevent these injuries from happening as frequently as they do now.

column36: The role of RCAN1 in Alzheimer pathogenesis
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder leading to dementia in the elderly population. Patients with diabetes have a greater risk to develop AD and a majority of AD patients also have hyperglycemia. The mechanism linking diabetes to AD remains undefined. Progressive neuronal loss is one of the pathological features of AD. People with Down Syndrome having extra copy of chromosome 21 develop characteristic AD neuropathology after middle age and several genes on chromosome 21 including APP and the regulator of calcineurin 1 (RCAN1) are implicated in AD pathogenesis. Our preliminary studies suggest that RCAN1 promotes neurodegeneration and our working hypothesis is that abnormal RCAN1 expression and function contribute to Alzheimer pathogenesis. This proposal seeks to elucidate the molecular mechanism of RCAN1's effect on Alzheimer pathogenesis and define its role in linking diabetes to AD. The results will be of clinical significance and provide evidences for targeting RCAN1 in AD treatment.

column36: Close encounters of a Natural Killer kind: Understanding how NK cells protect against HIV infection.
column37: Some people remain HIV uninfected despite multiple exposures to this virus. The term HIV exposed seronegative (HESN) has been used to describe such individuals. By comparing HESN to HIV susceptible subjects we previously identified two genotypes coding for variants of Natural Killer (NK) cell receptors (NKR) and their ligands (the molecules recognized by NKR) that were associated with protection from HIV infection. NK cells are part of the innate arm of the immune system, which means that they are primed and ready to kill HIV infected cells, and secrete factors with anti-HIV activity. As such they have the kind of functional profile needed to act early to prevent the establishment of HIV infection. In this project we will continue our examination of how NK cells and autologous HIV infected cells (i.e. cells from the same person) interact to stimulate NK cells for anti-HIV activity. We will investigate the NKR profile of the NK cell subsets activated by autologous HIV infected cells, what ligands for NKR are induced by HIV infection and what stage of the HIV life cycle NK cell inhibit. We will also explore the potential and limitations of an NK cell function that links the innate and adaptive arms of the immune response. This function, if better understood, may be exploited to trigger protective immunity in a vaccine setting.

column36: Functional and genomic clonal analysis of human glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM), a lethal cancer, is very heterogeneous, containing mixtures of different cell types. A critical barrier to effective GBM treatment is that it is very difficult to kill the varied cell types that make up the tumour mass. We have developed a method to isolate and expand single GBM cells from patient tumours into multiple pure populations or clones. We found that individual GBM samples from patients have multiple different clones that have very different genetic mutations and responses to treatment. We have identified gene expression patterns in single clones that correlate with responsiveness to the standard chemotherapy drug temozolomide, suggesting new treatments. Our methods allow us to characterize rare and previously unknown aggressive clones that may be responsible for failed treatment of a patient. In this project, we will isolate multiple clones from single patient GBMs, identify the most aggressive ones, and their mutations, study their evolution in time and space, and then develop new treatments that target the clones that drive disease progression.

column36: Targeting TAZ and YAP: a new approach to anti-fibrotic therapy in the kidney
column37: Scarring is a major cause of chronic organ failure, accounting for up to 50% of all deaths in the developed world. In the kidney, scarring is the final common pathway of damage activated by nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. If left unchecked, kidney scarring can lead to kidney failure, an increasingly common, costly, and life-threatening condition requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival. Unfortunately, no safe and effective anti-scarring treatments exist. Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) is the main stimulus for scar production. Drugs that block TGF-beta are not widely used as anti-scarring agents because TGF-beta not only promotes scarring, but also controls many other important non-scarring functions in the body. Following injury and especially with scarring, organs become stiffer. Recent studies have demonstrated that fibroblasts, the main source of scar tissue in the kidney, can sense this increased stiffness, and react by augmenting their responsiveness to TGF-beta. We have identified two proteins named TAZ and YAP which play a critical role in regulating stiffness-dependent fibroblast scarring responses. TAZ and YAP are activated when fibroblasts are grown on a stiff surface reminiscent of an injured, fibrotic kidney, and inactivated when fibroblasts are grown on a soft, healthy kidney-like surface. We have shown that active TAZ and YAP may promote fibroblast scarring responses to TGF-beta, and that inactivation of these proteins seems to block these scarring responses. The proposed studies will explore how TAZ and YAP are activated by kidney stiffening, how they promote TGF-beta-induced fibroblast scarring responses, and using specialized gene-modification strategies will test whether loss of TAZ and/or YAP can prevent kidney scarring in animal models of chronic kidney injury. Ultimately these studies aim to identify new safe and specific anti-scarring agents for the treatment of patients with chronic kidney disease.

column36: Splicing Defects in Human Hereditary Disease
column37: In order to function properly, genes need to undergo a process known as pre-mRNA splicing, where exons are joined together and non-protein coding intronic sequences are removed from the mature transcript. Several human genetic diseases are caused by mutations in splicing factors - proteins involved in splicing. We have recently identified several novel splicing factors that are mutated in specific human diseases. In this project, we will use genomic approaches to investigate the downstream effects of the mutations and attempt to identify key genes whose splicing is disrupted by the mutations. This research will help us understand the molecular mechanisms of the RNA splicing process and how its dysregulation results in the phenotypic defects observed in the patients.

column36: Mapping the microcircuits of attention in the primate brain
column37: The human brain has a limited capacity to process the overwhelming amount of information entering the senses at a given time. The mechanism of attention overcomes this limitation by selecting signals relevant to behavior for further processing, while filtering out irrelevant signals. Deficits of attention are core symptoms of mental disorders such as ADHD, Autism and Schizophrenia. For example, children with ADHD cannot effectively focus attention on specific people or objects but instead attend to every salient item in the environment. This diverts cognitive resources from important information and causes learning disabilities, complicates social interactions, and impairs memory. Our incomplete knowledge of how attention is implemented in the brain is a central obstacle to the treatment of these deficits. The long-term goal of my research is to unravel the mechanisms of selective attention in the primate brain, as well as how failures in such mechanisms can cause disorders of attention in humans. We have demonstrated that attention modulates brain activity amplifying signals that are important and suppressing unimportant ones. We have further demonstrated that the lateral prefrontal cortex, a specialized region of the primate brain, plays a fundamental role in this process. Importantly, evidence from imaging studies in humans indicates that the same area is dysfunctional in patients with mental disorders characterized by deficits of attention (e.g., ADHD, Autism, and Schizophrenia). Such a dysfunction may originate from abnormal connectivity patterns within the area that affect the way brain cells interact with one another to process information. The research proposed here will first explore how neurons in the lateral prefrontal cortex interact to implement the function of attention. Second, we will manipulate such interactions using drugs and brain stimulation techniques to produce different attentional states that resemble the one in affected individuals.

column36: Mechanisms of Protective Immunity in Ovarian Cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is a challenging disease with unacceptably high mortality. Despite this, about 30% of patients "beat the odds" and live for many years after treatment. Why do some patients do so well? In the past decade, it has become well established that some ovarian cancer patients mount strong immune responses against their tumor. Tumors from such patients are densely packed with killer T cells, a type of white blood cell that fights viral and bacterial infections, as well as cancer. Importantly, patients with large numbers of killer T cells in their tumor have markedly higher survival rates. This is a very promising finding, as it shows that the immune system can have a profound influence on survival from ovarian cancer. With better understanding of the immune response, it will be possible to design new treatments such as vaccines that enhance tumor immunity and increase patient survival. However, to do this intelligently, we need to better understand how the immune response works. Although killer T cells are important for fighting tumors, they do not work alone. We recently showed that tumors containing both T cells and B cells are associated with even higher survival rates than seen with T cells alone. In this study, we will investigate the mechanisms by which T cells and B cells work together to promote tumor immunity. We will pay particular attention to how the immune system adapts to changes in the tumor during standard treatment and progression. We envision our work will lead to a major re-think about cancer immunotherapy: instead of simply trying to activate killer T cells, we also need to find effective ways to activate their team mates, the B cells. With better understanding of how T cells and B cells fight cancer, we can design new forms of treatment that enhance the patient's natural defences.

column36: Investigating Host Defense of the Lung Microvasculature By Patrolling Sentry Neutrophils In Vivo
column37: The lung directly contacts the environment via a huge collection of air-filled sacs called alveoli. The disadvantage of this interaction is the constant exposure of the host airways to airborne pathogens. As well, the lung alveoli are richly supplied with blood, which results in a massive surface area of blood vessels in close proximity to potential pathogen portals of entry. Certainly, microbial pathogens can penetrate from the lung alveoli into the circulation and rapidly disseminate to other vascular beds and tissues. Bacteremia, or bacteria that has entered the blood stream, has important clinical implications as affected patients require longer courses of intravenous antibiotics, longer hospital stays and have higher mortality rates. Being at the forefront of pathogen interactions, the lung plays a critical role in containing pathogens before they spread, however it remains unclear if, and how, the lung deals with microbes that breakthrough the barrier and make it to the blood circulation. The overarching hypothesis of this grant proposal is that pre-positioned lung neutrophils in the blood vessels act as vascular sentries by performing surveillance and capture of any blood-borne bacteria. We are utilizing state-of-the-art microscopy for intravital lung imaging, which allows for greater cellular and molecular resolution of pulmonary intravascular immunity, in live animals, in real time. Understanding the role that lung neutrophils play in protecting us from harmful pathogen entry into the blood will allow rational therapeutic design to enhance this process in severely infected humans.

column36: Role of protein tyrosine phosphatase-epsilon in cysteinyl leukotriene receptor signaling
column37: Le leucotriene (LT) D4 est un puissant mediateur de la reaction asthmatique, causant la constriction des bronches et l'inflammation pulmonaire qui caracterisent cette maladie. Les actions du LTD4 sont possibles grace a des recepteurs presents sur diverses populations de cellules sanguines et pulmonaires. Deux recepteurs du LTD4 (CysLT1R et CysLT2R) sont exprimes differentiellement sur diverses cellules. Or nous avons recemment decouvert qu'une phosphatase, la PTP epsilon, est un partenaire d'interaction du CysLT1R et qu'elle est capable de moduler certaines fonctions de ce recepteur. De plus, des donnees epidemiologiques indiquent une association entre des mutations dans le gene de cette phosphatase et le developpement de l'asthme. Le but de ce projet de recherche consiste a etudier en detail les elements structuraux de cette interaction PTP-CysLT1R et les mecanismes par lesquels la PTP epsilon est capable de moduler les fonctions du CysLT1R et ses voies de signalisation. Nos donnees preliminaires nous indiquent aussi que la stimulation du CysLT1R par le LTD4 augmente l'expression de la PTP epsilon. Nous allons donc etudier les mecanismes regissant cet effet qui servirait possiblement de boucle de retroaction negative sur les actions du LTD4. Enfin, nous emettons l'hypothese que les cellules immunitaires des personnes qui portent une mutation du gene de la PTP epsilon presenteraient une reponse exageree au LTD4, ce qui serait en correlation avec leur phenotype asthmatique. Cette recherche nous aidera a definir le potentiel de cible diagnostique et therapeutique eventuelle de la PTP epsilon dans le traitement personnalise de l'asthme.

column36: Atomic resolution pharmacology of anti-epileptic drugs
column37: Epilepsy is one of the most common and severe neurological conditions, characterized by frequent seizures due to abnormal excessive electrical activity in the brain. Although many drugs are currently available for the management of epileptic seizures, a surprisingly large number patients fail to respond to these treatments. As many as 30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to current treatments, and many others suffer significant side effects from these drugs. Also, many of the drugs used to treat epilepsy are decades (or even centuries) old. Taken together, these observations suggest that new approaches are needed. A principal reason for the unmet need in seizure therapy that many existing drugs are redundant - they act on similar ion targets in the brain. However, genetic studies have identified dozens of proteins in the brain that may regulate electrical activity and seizures. Our study will focus on a recently introduced anti-epileptic drug named retigabine (also known as Ezogabine, Trobalt, or Potiga). This drug was approved for use in Canada in 2012, and is unique because it is the only anti-epileptic drug that targets a class of protein called voltage-gated potassium channels in the brain. These voltage-gated channels alter their activity when the drug binds, helping to suppress seizures. Our study applies several cutting edge approaches to study the specific chemical forces that allow retigabine to interact with its target, and to unravel the changes in protein function that take place after retigabine binds. Since retigabine is the first drug of its class that has been developed to treat epilepsy, we anticipate that our research project will identify changes that can be made to improve the potency and effectiveness of the drug.

column36: Development and validation of Canadian health literacy measurement tool for chronic disease management
column37: Within the context of health care, the importance of literacy is evident because all chronic disease management strategies require the transmission of information from caregivers and other sources to patients, and also because this transmission must be developed with an awareness of the potential presence of reduced HL levels in patients. column36: Impaired regulation of sinoatrial node function and atrial arrhythmogenesis in the diabetic heart
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a growing epidemic that is associated with a number of severe cardiovascular complications that ultimately result in death in as many as 65% of diabetic patients. Included amongst these are cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (which results in an inability to properly regulate heart rate) and atrial fibrillation (the most common cardiac arrhythmia). Our objective is to determine how and why abnormal heart rate regulation occurs in diabetic patients. We also aim to determine the mechanistic basis for atrial fibrillation in diabetes. Heart rate is determined by specialized 'pacemaker cells' in a region of the heart called the sinoatrial node (the natural pacemaker present in everyone's heart). Although often attributed to damage to the nerves innervating the sinoatrial node, our work demonstrates that improper regulation of heart rate in diabetes is also associated with abnormal sinoatrial node function, independently of the nerves. This represents an important new way of looking at cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. We have also uncovered novel insight into how atrial fibrillation occurs in the diabetic heart. This involves alterations in the muscle cells of the atria as well as the presence of scar tissue in the atria. Our proposed studies will greatly advance our understanding of abnormal heart rate regulation and the occurrence of atrial fibrillation in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. This will be accomplished using a range of powerful experimental approaches in intact diabetic mice, as well as in isolated hearts and isolated cells from the sinoatrial node and the atria. My laboratory is one of only a handful worldwide that can study the sinoatrial node in mice, which uniquely positions us carry out these highly important studies. We are also highly experienced in studies of atrial fibrillation. The ultimate goal of our work is to identify new therapeutic targets for the treatment of cardiovascular disease in diabetics.

column36: Computation and theory to predict structures and mechanisms for protein misfolding in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
column37: As we age, we begin to face an onslaught of threats to our health that evolution has not protected us against. Many of these include degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Lou Gehrig's disease or ALS. It is up to us to design strategies for slowing, stopping, or reversing the progression of these currently incurable diseases. To do this involves understanding the causes of the disease, which are due fundamentally to proteins behaving badly. Here we will investigate the molecular origins of how proteins malfunction in ALS, a neurodegenerative disease, to elucidate at the atomic level what may be going wrong in the cell. Malfunction often involves proteins that have misfolded, and as a consequence have aggregated together. Misfolding may be exacerbated by oxidative damage to proteins, which generally occurs as a natural consequence of aging. Most cases of ALS strike sporadically, with no known hereditary link, with the likelihood increasing as we age. What goes wrong in the cell? We will focus on how oxidative damage may be a cause of sporadic ALS. We will investigate how oxidative damage may destabilize proteins and render them susceptible to misfolding. We have previously developed a computational method that is capable of predicting how long a patient will live once diagnosed with ALS, given they have an inherited form of the disease. We propose here to extend our computational method to the much more prevalent sporadic form of the disease, by investigating the role of oxidative damage in the aging brain. We have previously developed a novel computational method that allows misfolded protein to be specifically targeted. Developing and applying our methods to describe the mechanisms and consequences of protein misfolding in ALS will allow us to rationally predict critical protein targets that may stop the progression of this currently fatal, misfolding-related degenerative disease.

column36: Streptococcal Superantigens in Colonization and Disease
column37: We study the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes. S. pyogenes causes a variety of common human infections including 'strep throat' and skin infections, but S. pyogenes can also cause more severe and invasive infections such as the 'flesh- eating disease'. column37: Over a century ago, Santiago Ramon y Cajal postulated the law of dynamic polarization according to which dendrites represent a receiving apparatus of the neuron specialized in integrating and processing the vast majority of synaptic inputs. Since then, the large structural diversity of dendritic arbors in different types of neurons has captivated the imagination of scientists. In addition to morphological complexity, dendrites exhibit a highly complex functional organization. They are endowed with multiple ion conductances, which are able to control the integration and propagation of local and global dendritic signals in a highly dynamic manner. Two types of signals are generated in dendrites: electrical and chemical. Both can be highly compartmentalized within individual dendritic branches and synaptic specializations, providing a means for the highly selective integration and modification of incoming information. However, despite the tremendous progress in dendrites research, we still do not understand the nature of computations performed by neuronal dendrites and, more importantly, their relevance to the operation of a particular neuron within its local circuitry. Here, we will use a combination of optophysiological, optogenetic and computational tools in brain slices and in behaving animals in vivo to determine the relationship between the distribution of dendritic conductances and the function of dendrites in a genetically defined population of cortical inhibitory interneurons that play a crucial role in the generation of brain rhythms and are affected in epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism. We will establish the rules of dendritic integration and the role of dendritic computations in the operation of interneurons during behavior in animals navigating in virtual environment. The results of the study will be important to connect the computations performed by single neurons to the operation of its local network, and higher-level brain function and malfunction.

column37: My lab investigates genetic mechanisms that contribute to cancer in the mammary gland or the breast. column36: Structure, dynamics and function of non-membranous organelles
column37: If you ask most biomedical researchers how molecules are organized in the cell to do specific tasks they'd likely resort to the metaphor of a factory. As in the components of a factory, the molecules that do the work in cells, like robots and humans on an assembly line, are logically arranged in time and space to perform their roles in a complex process. This description has served as a helpful and meaningful metaphor for biochemical machinery. But what if you were told that sometimes molecules are organized in the cell the way that people and airplanes are organized at an airport? Recently, such molecular organizations have been discovered in cells and they may serve a number of important cellular functions and underlie neurological diseases, including Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases and ALS, among others. Molecules in the discovered structures are arranged like oil droplets in water; loosely organized and exchanging rapidly with the cell. How many such structures, called non-membrane organelles (or NMO), could exist in the cell and what are their functions? What happens if NMOs are disrupted? These are the questions we address in this proposal. The central aim of our proposal is to create a compendium of NMOs in a model of the eukaryotic cell; the bakers yeasts. Yeast is an ideal model because it shares many genes with humans, notably those that are most primordial and those become dysfunctional with age and in diseases such as cancers, and neurodegeneration. We have shown how certain types of cell regulation including gene function and spatial organization of large cell structures depend on NMOs. The compositions of NMOs are surprisingly rich in protein molecules that when mutated, are known to underlie neurodegeneration. We hope to define how these mutant proteins cause dysfunction, perhaps by disrupting the normal functions of NMOs, and what kinds of strategies could re-stabilize them.

column37: Under normal conditions, cells require signals from their surroundings in order to grow, to move, or just to survive. These processes are essential for normal development, but they can be hijacked in cancer cells, allowing the disease to grow and spread. We are interested in a molecule called RET, that resides at the cell surface and helps convey these messages (signals) from outside the cell as part of its normal roles in development of a number of tissues. However, in some cancers, such as tumours of the pancreas, RET can also help tumour cells to spread by following a trail of signals that lead them to surround nerves lying close to the tumour (perineural invasion), causing pain and making the disease hard to treat. The RET molecule comes in two main forms, but our studies suggest that one form, called RET51, is more able to cause cancer cells to spread because it is enriched at the cell surface, thereby increasing its response to signals, which makes it an attractive target for therapies in several hard to treat cancers. Thus, our goals are to elucidate mechanisms that concentrate RET51 at the cell surface and determine how these contribute to its roles in the growth and spread of human cancers. We will do this by identifying the location of RET51 within or on human cancer cells and its abilities to induce these cells to move away or to invade their environment, particularly along nerves. Using an array of visualization methods and molecular tools we have developed we will explore the key mechanisms and protein interactions by which RET51 can promote cancer cell motility and invasiveness. Finally, we will characterize the expression of RET in prostate and colon cancers, where perineural invasion is linked with poor outcomes, to see if RET plays a role in this process. Our studies will clarify the mechanisms of RET-mediated tumour cell dissemination and provide additional tools with which to target this complicated system to combat human cancer.

column36: Engineering Adipogenesis for Soft Tissue Regeneration
column37: The proposed research program involves the development of an engineered fat tissue substitute for use in plastic and reconstructive surgery. Damage or injury to the fatty tissues underlying the skin results in scar tissue formation, which causes deformity, can limit mobility, and can have devastating psychological consequences. Our research team is developing new tissue substitutes for soft tissue reconstruction, including breast reconstruction following tumour removal, the correction of birth defects, and soft tissue repair following trauma, to improve patient quality of life. The long-term objective is to minimize scar tissue formation, while promoting the natural regeneration of the patient's own healthy tissues, to fully restore the natural shape and volume. One common strategy is to design a scaffold that defines the desired tissue shape, and to seed it with cells that can promote regeneration, such as stem cells. In the proposed research, our team will investigate adult stem cells isolated from fat, termed adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs), within scaffolds fabricated from proteins isolated from fat that has been discarded as surgical waste. Our previous studies have shown that our unique bioscaffolds naturally promote fat formation. However, a deeper understanding of the mechanisms involved in ASC-mediated regeneration in these scaffolds is critically needed in order to design soft tissue substitutes that fully restore the defects with healthy soft tissues. The proposed research will make significant progress towards identifying the key factors that regulate tissue regeneration, to engineer optimized tissue substitutes that could be clinically translated for reconstructive applications.

column36: Anaerobic eukaryotic microbes and the human microbiome: a genomic and metagenomic study
column37: Protozoan parasites infect literally billions of people worldwide each year, and are responsible for the deaths of millions. Many of these parasites colonize oxygen-poor environments in the human body such as the gut and urogenital tract. Most of these species are understudied and their basic molecular biology and roles in the human 'microbiome' are poorly understood, despite their high prevalence in both affluent and developing world populations. Using powerful high-throughput next-generation genome sequencing approaches and sophisticated computer-based analyses, we will address how select groups of protozoa: (i) adapted to life without oxygen, (ii) acquired the ability to parasitize humans, and (iii) influence the healthy and diseased human gut. We will explore how these species have acquired new biochemical pathways suited to low-oxygen habitats and investigate other ways in which the genomes of single-celled parasites have changed to allow them to live within their hosts. The roles of a number of these organisms in the human gut will be investigated using novel computational methods applied to DNA-sequence data obtained from gut samples, both from healthy subjects and from patients suffering from inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). There are several potential practical benefits of this project. Our examinations of common human gut parasites and relatives of serious human pathogens will reveal unique aspects of their biology that could help identify new drug targets. By understanding the mechanisms by which free-living organisms become disease-causing parasites, we may better evaluate risks associated with the emergence of new pathogens. Our DNA sequence databases can also be used to efficiently detect parasites in fecal samples. Finally, our research has the potential to reveal links between the whole gut microbiome and human health that would have been impossible to discover previously, when the protozoan part of the microbiome had not been considered.

column37: The brain shrinks with age, and faster if the aging person has coronary artery disease (or ischemic heart disease). column36: The role of DEPTOR in Energy Balance Regulation
column37: Obesity is a major public health issue leading to major costs emerging from the treatment of cardiovascular, metabolic (type 2 diabetes) and respiratory diseases. Obesity is characterized by an imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure, which is incidentally in agreement with the latin root of obesity "obedere", meaning "to eat in excess". Despite the progress made in our understanding of the mechanisms involved in the regulation of energy balance, there are still several aspects of that regulation, which need to be elucidated. One aspect that deserves attention is the mechanism whereby the brain controls energy intake and energy expenditure, which are the two inescapable determinants of energy balance. The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a protein that senses nutrients and growth factors and regulate anabolic processes in various organs, including the brain. mTOR nucleates distinct multiprotein complexes termed mTORC1 and mTORC2. Hypothalamic mTORC1 is capable of influencing food intake and certain components of energy expenditure such as brown adipose tissue thermogenesis. Its activity is reduced by fasting and induced by refeeding, whereas anorectic signals such as leptin, insulin and ghrelin require mTORC1 activity to exert their inhibitory effects on feeding. Recently, we have identified DEP-domain containing mTOR-interacting protein (DEPTOR) as a key modulator of hypothalamic mTORC1. We have evidence that DEPTOR may be sensitive to variations in energy stores and therefore could play a significant role in the regulation of energy balance. Whether DEPTOR could affect the metabolic profile of the obese by modulating mTOR activity has never been tested. This research proposal aims to investigate the role DEPTOR in the regulation of energy balance using molecular approaches, genetically-engineered mice and advanced molecular imaging methodologies.

column36: Systematic characterization of the Hsp70-regulated proteostasis network
column37: Proteins are major macromolecules of the cell that have incredibly versatile functions. Some are enzymes, others transport molecules inside the cell or in the bloodstream, yet others make sure our immune system stays alert. But to be able do so, each protein needs to adopt its unique shape that determines its function. Starting as a linear chain, proteins fold into intricate shapes like cellular origami. But when this process goes awry, the result can be a disease like Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease or even cancer. Because protein folding is such a fundamental process for all living organisms, cells have evolved special machines (themselves also proteins) whose function is to make sure proteins fold correctly. These proteins are aptly called chaperones. In this project, we will study how these chaperones can associate with thousands of diverse proteins but, at the same time, provide unique support to each of them. In particular, we will characterize how so-called co-chaperones, which constantly regulate the function of chaperones, provide specificity to the chaperone machinery inside the cell. We will systematically identify the proteins that each co-chaperone associates with, and use this knowledge to understand how drugs in clinical use affect these associations. The results from this study will help researchers to understand the chaperone/co-cochaperone network in unprecedented detail, biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies to understand how their drugs affect cells, and, ultimately, patients to benefit from more specific and more potent drugs against diverse diseases.

column36: Biology of Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy: Imaging QTLs and Multivariate Methods
column37: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is a common form of epilepsy affecting young adults for which there is no cure. People with JME experience different types of seizures, need to take medicines for decades, and often experience depression, anxiety or other psychiatric complications. JME is caused by a combination of genetic variations that are usually inherited. So far it has been hard to find these genes for a variety of reasons, including the lack of statistical power, failure of different laboratories to find the same results, and the variation of the disease between patients. It is generally agreed though that finding the genes would be a huge advance and a first step to curing the disease. In this project we will try to overcome the shortcomings of previous research in two ways. First, we will conduct a genetic association analysis comparing gene variants across the entire genome in 1000 JME patients and 2000 matched non-epilepsy controls to see if variants in genes, singly or in combination, among particular biological pathways that are important in brain function play a part in causing JME. Second, we will collect and analyse electroencephalographs (EEGs or brainwave tracings) of 20 JME patients and their family members. The EEGs contain information about how electrically excitable their brains are, and an increase in excitability is a fundamental property of the brains of people with epilepsy. Interestingly, some relatives of JME patients also have electrically quite excitable brains even though they don't have epilepsy, suggesting that they have inherited part of the tendency for seizures. Using this excitability measure gives us vastly more statistical power to find genes for JME within the whole genome than just using the label of having JME. We will also look at the association between the excitability measure and behavioural and cognitive profiles in relatives.
