column36: Regenerative neuronal reprogramming: elucidating and enhancing intrinsic neural repair programs
column37: Sensory neurons relay information between our body, spinal cord and brain via peripheral nerves. When these nerves are injured, they turn on repair programs that we have shown are critically dependent on signals received from the injury site and a molecule called brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). However, regeneration of these nerves is a clinically challenging scenario that can result in incomplete repair and/or pain states. We have identified a therapeutic intervention, brief electrical stimulation of the injured nerve/axons that results in more robust and accurate nerve repair, including increases BDNF expression and in preliminary work we show that it also favorably impacts the associated immune response. But, the underlying early cell and molecular events linking electrical stimulation of the injured nerve and to an improved regeneration state are largely unknown and the continued focus of our research, as they will likely provide novel therapeutic targets. More specifically we are trying to (i) understand how early injury signals instruct the injured neuron to begin regrowing an axon, form a growth cone and cope with the cellular stress these events impose; (ii) how electrical stimulation heightens this response and (iii) whether we can exploit what we have learned in a manner that advantages the more clinically challenging delayed nerve repair scenario. We believe that learning how to optimally manipulate the internal repair programs in sensory neurons will vastly improve nerve repair outcomes for Canadians.

column36: How does rapid drug delivery promote compulsive drug use?
column37: Addiction is the most common psychiatric disorder of our era. It accounts for 12% of deaths worldwide, and costs Canadians nearly $40 billion per year. In spite of much research, medications approved for drug addiction are lacking. This is in part because preclinical tests are typically conducted in animals that take drugs, but that do not show addiction-like traits. Animals that simply take drugs are not necessarily 'addicted'. The reliance on such animals to study addiction might have misled us regarding the neurobiology of addiction. With CIHR funding, we have refined a new model whereby rats taking rapid intravenous cocaine injections show excessive motivation to obtain the drug, whereas rats taking slower injections do not. Thus, by varying the speed of drug delivery, we have in our hands a powerful model whereby two groups of rats take cocaine, but only one group shows an addiction phenotype. Studying these two groups represents a unique window of opportunity to hone in on a fundamental question; what is the difference between a drug-taking brain and a drug-addicted brain? Based largely on studies using animals that self-administer drugs, it has been suggested that addiction might involve a hyperactive orbitofrontal cortex (a brain area involved in the evaluation of rewards) and changes in the activity of two molecules in the downstream dorsal striatum (a brain area involved in the pursuit of rewards). These molecules are the neurotrophin BDNF and the neurotransmitter glutamate. But are these changes truly linked to addiction, or are they simply a consequence of taking drugs? Here I propose to use our unique model to address this. In essence, we will use variation in the speed of drug injection as a tool to parse the neurobiology of addiction from the neurobiology of mere drug taking. This is certain to better our understanding of how addiction evolves, and how it might be treated.

As arrhythmias during ischaemia are a common disorder that occurs alone and in many heart diseases, this project is directly relevant to a large number of patients. By discovering processes that contribute to these deadly arrhythmias, new treatments may be developed. This ultimately will help to reduce the high incidence of death due to regional ischaemia, thus saving the lives of countless Canadians who suffer from this deadly condition.

column36: The role of regulatory T cells in HIV infection: implication in host-virus interaction
column37: AIDS remain one of the world's most serious health challenges. Globally, 35 million people are living with HIV including 70,000 in Canada. HIV infection is characterized by a progressive loss of a subgroup of white blood cells named CD4 T-cells and by chronic inflammation. column36: Endosomal control of autophagy in colorectal cancer
column37: Cancer is the first cause of death in Canada. Colorectal cancers are among the most common and lethal malignancies. This cancer has a poor prognosis in advanced stages due to its resistance to conventional therapies. Cancer cells have developed means to resist to treatments and one of them is called autophagy. Autophagy is the process by which cells degrade and recycle their own constituents. Importantly, autophagy is induced by the lack of nutrients, and cancer cells often grow in environments lacking proper blood supply. Hence, a large proportion of cancer cells rely on autophagy to stay alive. Cells of the body are composed of multiple types of membranes. These membranes are highly controlled and the mechanisms regulating them are collectively called 'membrane trafficking'. Autophagy is vastly controlled by membrane trafficking events. Thus, understanding how membrane trafficking regulates autophagy is important to find new cancer therapeutic avenues. My work has identified regulators of membrane traffic necessary for autophagy. I found their function to be temporally controlled. Their activation and the recruitment of specific effectors (molecular helpers) is important for autophagy progression. Moreover, I identified regulators of membrane trafficking and autophagy required for the growth of colorectal cancer cells. In this proposal, we will characterize how one regulator of membrane trafficking is activated and inhibited by specific proteins, and how it recruits specific effectors to control autophagy. Importantly, we will test the newly identified components and aspects of their temporal regulation for their roles in autophagy in normal cells and for their requirements in colorectal cancer cell growth. This work will represent a key step in understanding how we can specifically target and eliminate colorectal cancer cells through the modulation of membrane trafficking.

column37: The poor prognosis for lung cancer (LC) patients is typically associated with a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis, highlighting the need for effective methods for early detection. Recently, it has been demonstrated that low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening of patients at high-risk of developing LC reduces mortality by 20%; however, issues remain, including determining what to do when LDCT screens detect lung masses that may or may not be cancerous. Currently, surgical resection is the only proven treatment option for these patients and there is an urgent need for efficient, non-invasive treatment strategies to resolve suspicious lung nodules detected through LDCT screening to improve patient outcomes. The immune system provides a key line of defense against LC development; however, as investigation in patients is difficult, the specific immune cells that respond and how cancers evade destruction by these cells remain unknown. Here, we aim to perform the first comprehensive assessment of the immune response to LC using mice genetically engineered to develop lung tumours. These "model" systems will allow us to identify the immune components necessary to prevent nodules from becoming tumours and determine the way cancers circumvent this process. Furthermore, we will confirm our findings from mice in human patient samples using unique resources and methodologies, develop new compounds to help identify lung nodules most likely to develop into LC, and determine if modulating the immune response prevents LC progression. It is our hope that this work will enable the design of effective treatment strategies that bolster immune system recognition of cancer cells in patients undergoing LDCT screening, preventing their development into more advanced tumours without the need for surgery. If successful, this will lead to the optimization of LC screening through more effective management of patients, ultimately improving the survival rates of this disease.

column36: The NEUROlogically-impaired extubation Timing Trial (NEURO-ETT)
column37: Thousands of patients suffer severe brain injuries every year, from causes such as trauma, stroke, and infection. Many of them will have impaired consciousness and therefore be unable to keep food or mouth secretions from entering their lungs (called aspiration). To protect against aspiration, these patients require artificial respiration and intubation with a temporary breathing tube inserted through the mouth into the lungs. After the early phases of illness, doctors can use a test called a spontaneous breathing trial to assess when artificial respiration can be discontinued. Many patients with severe brain injury, however, pass this test yet still have impaired consciousness and an ongoing risk for aspiration. Unfortunately, little evidence exists to guide decisions about when to remove the breathing tube in these patients. There are different approaches that are commonly used in this situation. One approach involves simply discontinuing artificial respiration and removing the breathing tube, accepting that aspiration may still occur but reducing the potential for harm associated with prolonged artificial respiration. The other treatment is to perform a tracheostomy. A tracheostomy involves neck surgery to insert a new tube directly into the trachea, replacing the temporary breathing tube. The usual clinical practice is often just to keep the patient on artificial respiration for longer in the hope that the patient will wake up before removing the tube, or performing a tracheostomy if they don't wake up. Each strategy has risks and benefits, and uncertainty about the best approach often leads to prolonged use of the temporary breathing tube. This randomized controlled trial will test whether removing the temporary breathing tube as soon as possible after the patient passes a spontaneous breathing trial leads to better patient outcomes compared to performing a tracheostomy, or to the usual approach of waiting longer.

column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is 150 times more common in children with Down syndrome (DS). We already know a key marker that can be found in these leukemia cells. column37: Diseases of the cardiovascular system, such as coronary heart disease and stroke due to atherosclerosis, are known to start in the cells that line blood vessels, the vascular endothelium. What we inherit from our parents, or what one cell passes on to two cells when it divides, represents the "nature" side of the equation. These processes are influenced by the environment. We are among the first to study these concepts in the cardiovascular sciences. We believe that the principles we uncover in endothelial cells will teach us about blood vessel gene regulation in general. Our understanding of these newer concepts offers the hope of innovative approaches to preventing and treating the underlying problem in diseased blood vessels of patients. In our preliminary work we have generated mutant mice that lack GPC6, and we have shown that these mice display the typical features of patients with Recessive Omodysplasia. Our goals are to provide definitive molecular and genetic proof that GPC6-null mice display reduced Hegehog activity in the developing bone, and to uncover the molecular mechanism by which GPC6 stimulates Hedgehog activity. In addition, we will try to develop a treatment for patients with Recessive Omodysplasia. Significance: This study will generate critical knowledge not only on the molecular basis of Recessive Omodysplasia, but also on our basic understanding of the mechanism by which glypicans regulate Hedgehog activity. In addition, this study may contribute to the development of a treatment for omodysplastic patients.

column37: Severe, anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody associated vasculitis (AAV) is a serious disease of the immune system that affects approximately 34,000 Canadians. However, we will not know much about the long term effects of plasma exchange and prednisone on AAV and patient health. We will also not have much information on how subsequent treatments for AAV after plasma exchange and prednisone, affect the outcomes for these patients. We will continue to follow PEXIVAS patients for between 5 and 10 years after their first treatment. This will help determine the effect of plasma exchange and prednisone on recurrences of AAV, kidney function, heart health, cancer and death in the long-term. It will also help determine the effect of the treatments given after plasma exchange and prednisone on these health outcomes.

column36: Mechanisms and impact of genome modifying processes in immunity and cancer
column37: A unique way that the immune system boosts its response to pathogens is through introducing changes in the genes of some of its responding cell types. The focus of my research is to understand the mechanisms of processes which introduce these genetic changes, the principles that regulate their activity in immune cells vs. other cell types, and the detailed pathways by which their activities regulate biological outcomes including immune response, tissue differentiation and cancer. These studies are essential in order to understand how a system whose job is to help immunity can actually result in cancer. Our results and future studies outlined in this proposal have direct implications on strategies for treatment of cancers.

column37: Cancer is a multistep process that drives pathophysiologic changes leading to the establishment of cellular alterations that transform normal cells into malignant cells. Several pathways have been shown to contribute to the acquisition of cancer traits, however, the cause of their deregulation is dependent on multiple regulatory circuits, many of which remain to be identified. RanBPM is a protein that acts as a tumour suppressor by blocking cell growth, and promoting the death of cancer cells. RanBPM is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (called RanBPM/CTLH complex). Our work has determined that RanBPM functions to control the activation of several cellular pathways that are known to contribute to cancer development. We found that RanBPM was necessary for the activation of cell death pathways that are normally initiated when the cells' DNA is damaged. We have also determined that RanBPM controls several genes and pathways that are often found deregulated in many cancer types and cause increased cancer cell proliferation and migration. The present study proposes to characterize the function of the RanBPM/CTLH complex, a novel and uncharacterized E3 ligase complex which component RanBPM has known tumour-suppressive activities, and determine the identity of the cancer-promoting proteins that it targets for elimination. These studies will reveal novel mechanisms that restrict aberrant activation of cancer-promoting cellular pathways, leading to a better understanding of the mechanisms involved in cancer development. Moreover, it will also result in the identification of new components of cancer-related signaling pathways and as such pinpoint new regulations that could help develop diagnostic and therapeutic approaches aimed at improving cancer treatment.

column37: The most important clinical factor associated with poor survival during breast cancer progression is the appearance of metastases. Globally, this project aims to develop strategies to interfere with AXL function in metastatic breast cancer cells with the ultimate objective of moving toward the identification of anti-metastatic strategies.

column36: The Pathophysiological Role of Adrenergic Antibodies in Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
column37: Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is a chronically disabling disorder of autonomic nervous system function ("dysautonomia") with cardiovascular dysregulation, yet their causes remain largely unexplained. POTS is characterized by an excessive increase in heart rate on standing, and characteristic symptoms on standing that are relieved by lying down, including palpitation, chest pains, tremulousness, blurred vision and mental clouding. POTS affects up to 0.33% of the population, mainly women of childbearing age. Patients have very poor health-related quality of life (comparable to heart failure). The mainstay of pharmacological therapy for POTS includes Beta-blockers (e.g. propranolol) to control the excessive heart rate, and midodrine, a vasoconstrictor. It has long been suspected that POTS may be an autoimmune disease, but this has been hard to prove. We recently found that the blood of some POTS patients has antibody activity against "adrenaline receptors" that regulate heart rate and blood vessel tone. This is a newly discovered pathophysiological mechanism in POTS that could explain the symptoms in this disorder. We propose a series of translational studies with the ultimate goal of personalized medical treatment for POTS patients. We will build on the preliminary work and assess the physiological significance of these antibodies in POTS patients. By using pharmacological drug "probes", we will determine if these antibodies affect POTS patients' responses to commonly used drugs. These innovative aims could bring an antibody guided, personalized medicine approach to the management of POTS patients. We will also test "proof of the concept" that clearing these antibodies will reverse the pathophysiology in ("cure") POTS patients. Taken together, these highly innovative translational studies could create novel treatments for patients with POTS.

column36: Development of Novel Methods for Analyzing the Structure and Connectivity of the Human Basal Ganglia, Thalamus and Brainstem
column37: Major advances in brain imaging have resulted in improvements in diagnosis and surgical treatment of diseases of aging, including Parkinson's disease. However, even the best brain scans (e.g. MRI), especially those in practical clinic use cannot visualize individual areas (nuclei) deep in the brain that have distinct functions. In order to treat Parkinson's disease by surgical means, it is crucial to obtain better brain maps for these areas. We will design an atlas for Parkinson's brain that will be derived from post-mortem brains studied by advanced imaging methods, and examined using modern staining tools for delineating individual nuclei. A road-map of brain structures will be created by anatomists, and computer engineers will then integrate the roadmap into a template high resolution MRI scan, appropriate for normal ageing brain or patients with Parkinson's disease. Using methods already developed, the reference roadmaps will then be individualized for patients by integrating with patient MRIs prior to surgery. Surgeons will therefore have customized roadmaps when targeting structures deep in the brain, increasing safety and efficacy of surgery. The enhanced roadmap will be validated at surgery using traditional "goal-standard" methods for identifying deep brain nuclei, including electro-physiological mapping. In addition, advanced imaging tools will be used to identify connections between brain structures, which will also be cross-validated with the road-maps from postmortem brain structure, allowing development of non-invasive tools for determining how different parts of the brain communicate with each other, and how they may be damaged as a result of Parkinson's disease. This research will therefore use imaging methods and advanced brain processing methods to provide a unique validated roadmap of deep nuclei and connections of the Parkinson brain, and result in improved understanding the system that controls normal movements and treatment of its disorders

column36: Structural Biology of DNA Damage-Dependent PARPs
column37: The DNA that composes our genetic information is susceptible to damage that must be repaired in order to maintain the integrity of the genome and the health of an organism. Correspondingly, cells have extensive DNA repair mechanisms that detect and correct the damage that arises from environmental agents such as ultraviolet radiation and through normal cellular processes such as DNA replication. Several human deficiencies in DNA repair are associated with genomic instability and cellular transformations that can lead to cancer, thus underscoring the need to understand at a detailed molecular level the mechanisms of DNA repair. Our research focuses on a family of proteins called poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases, or PARPs. Several PARP family members are integral to the DNA damage response, where they detect damage and facilitate repair. PARP inhibitors are under clinical development to treat various cancers. An exciting aspect of PARP inhibition is the ability to selectively target cancer cells with known DNA repair deficiencies (e.g. BRCA1/2 deficient cancers). Our research group uses a structural biology approach to study how the PARP proteins recognize DNA breaks and how binding to these breaks turns on their catalytic activity to coordinate DNA repair. In particular, we use x-ray crystallography and other structural biology techniques to obtain detailed three-dimensional structures of PARPs that allow us to understand their function and mechanism at the molecular level. We further use cell biological and biochemical analysis to advance our understanding of PARP contribution to DNA repair, and to identify novel ways of inhibiting PARPs for cancer treatment.

column37: Chronic inflammation is a characteristic feature of several chronic diseases including arthritis. It arises when activation signals in cells of our immune system predominate over inhibitory ones. Inhibitory signals are driven by proteins on the surface of immune cells known as inhibitory receptors. These proteins dampen the inflammatory response by switching off activation pathways rendering them attractive therapeutic targets. Even though inhibitory receptors play an important role in the immune response, we know very little about the role these proteins play in chronic inflammatory diseases. Our findings indicate that the inhibitory receptor MICL plays a key role in chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. We reported a potential genetic association between MICL and rheumatoid arthritis. Also, our analysis of MICL in patient samples strongly suggest a role for this protein in this chronic disease. The goal of this proposal is to determine how MICL controls cell activation, in part, by identifying the signals it sends into the cells. These findings will help us determine the role of MICL in rheumatoid arthritis through the analysis of patient samples as well as studies in various cellular systems. column36: ED Ultrasonographic Regional Anesthesia to Prevent Incident Delirium in Hip Fracture Patients (EDU_RAPID)
column37: Hip fractures are common, costly and affect older people - Canadians spend 1 billion dollars to treat hip fractures each year. Unfortunately, as many as two-thirds of hip fracture cases suffer a complication known as delirium, or acute confusion. Patients with delirium may become frightened and agitated. This in turn leads to other serious problems. Having delirium doubles the chances of dying or can increase the need for admission into a nursing home. People with delirium spend an extra week in hospital on average. Using ultrasound to locate and 'freeze' or block specific nerves can stop hip fracture pain almost immediately, and use of this technique is known to reduce delirium when administered by Anaesthetists to patients at the time of their hip operation. Unfortunately, patients with hip fractures commonly wait hours or even days in the Emergency Department (ED) prior to their operation. Currently, these patients are given narcotic pain killers like morphine to dull their pain, as most ED physicians have not been trained in using this 'freezing' technique and Anaesthetists are rarely able to leave the operating room to administer freezing to patient in the ED. The EDU-RAPID study will test whether training ED physicians on how to use the nerve freezing technique will reduce the number of patients who develop delirium after a hip fracture. To study this, we will train ED physicians at 6 hospitals in small groups every 6 weeks over 18 months. We will look at how patients who are treated by ED physician who has been trained compare to patients treated by a ED physician who has not yet been trained. We will see if our training motivates ED physicians to use the block regularly. If we are correct, this study could significantly improve the comfort, quality of life, and independence of patients who suffer a hip fracture. In addition, if the study shows a reduction in delirium rates, this could represent a significant cost reduction to the health care system.

column36: Operative versus Non-operative Treatment of Acute Unstable Chest Wall Injuries: A Multi-Centred Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Major trauma to the chest from a motor vehicle accident or fall can result in multiple fractured ribs and severe instability of the chest wall. This instability can significantly impair the mechanics of breathing and is termed a "flail chest". Patients who sustain a flail chest injury have substantial rates of death (over 30%) and prolonged pain and suffering. These patients can often require mechanical ventilation for days/weeks and suffer high rates of pneumonia, systemic infection, and extended stays in the intensive care unit (ICU). In addition, these patients often report long term problems with breathing function and chronic chest pain. The current standard of care for the treatment of flail chest injuries involves non-surgical management with supportive measures. Recently, in an attempt to improve outcomes several investigators have studied the use of surgical methods to fix the multiple rib fractures and stabilize the chest wall in patients with these injuries. Several recent, small studies have suggested that surgical fixation may result in improved outcomes for these patients. Unfortunately, the studies conducted to date have had small numbers of patients, involved single centres, and have used inconsistent surgical methods. Our goal is to compare surgical fixation of flail chest injuries with non-surgical management in a large scale trial involving multiple trauma centres across Canada. The aim is to compare outcomes of the two treatments, with our most important result being the number of days a patient requires mechanical ventilation. We hypothesize that surgical fixation will result in improved patient outcomes over conventional non-surgical management. This study has the potential for global impact across the many health disciplines that care for patients with flail chest injuries and will likely lead to improved treatments and outcomes in these severely injured trauma patients.

column36: Mechanisms of GnRH action
column37: Human fertility depends on the coordinated activities of many organs in the body. These organs communicate with each other via chemical messengers called hormones. In general, hormones produced by one organ travel via the bloodstream to control the function of other organs. In the case of the reproductive system, the brain synthesizes and secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which controls production and release of two other hormones, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), by the pituitary gland. The pituitary sits at the base of the brain and secretes FSH and LH into the bloodstream following GnRH binding to its receptor on specific pituitary cells. If we think of GnRH as a key, then its receptor serves as the lock in to which this key uniquely fits. Once secreted, FSH and LH act on the ovaries in women and the testicles in men to control the production of eggs and sperm as well as the synthesis of steroid hormones like estrogen and testosterone. These steroids then feedback to the brain to control their own production by inhibiting GnRH secretion. Though we have a general understanding of where and how each of these hormones acts, fundamental questions remain unanswered. In this application, we address three general questions about how GnRH functions. First, does GnRH activate common or distinct pathways in pituitary cells to stimulate the synthesis and secretion of FSH and LH? Second, do pituitary cells make a protein that helps GnRH preferentially stimulate LH? Finally, does the GnRH receptor have unique features that enables it to preferentially control LH versus FSH synthesis? The answers to these questions will not only advance our knowledge of the hormonal control of reproduction, but will also identify novel causes and treatments for human infertility and other disorders of the reproductive system, including polycystic ovarian syndrome.

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is the most potent angiogenic factor and its administration has been shown to increase the development of new vessels in ischemic tissues and to be essential for the formation of blood vessels inside cancerous tumors. A better understanding of the angiogenic process and of the intracellular signaling molecules involved in its regulation could allow for the development of new therapeutic approaches to favor the formation of new blood vessels in ischemic tissues or, inversely, interfere with aberrant vessel growth in the retina or v in tumors. An essential event for the induction of angiogenesis is the increase in permeability of the vasculature to blood macromolecules. The opening of intercellular contacts between ECs initiates the angiogenic process and detachment of ECs allows them to migrate to form a vascular network in an area deprived of oxygen. The overall objective of our research program is to understand intracellular signaling events in ECs that control vascular development and angiogenesis. We will investigate if intercellular contacts control the effects induced by factors that act on ECs to promote angiogenesis. First, we will define if the release of nitric oxide (NO) by ECs influences endothelial intercellular contacts and controls the migration of cells. We will also determine if NO acts directly on a protein localized at cell-cell contact points, beta-catenin, to alter its function. A better understanding of the molecular events that control angiogenesis will help in the development of novel therapeutic approaches where the formation of new vessels is central to disease progression such as in ischemic tissues and vascular retinopathies.

column36: Development, validation and benefits of a genetic risk model for antipsychotic-induced weight gain
column37: Antipsychotic medications are used extensively for treatment of schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders. One of the most debilitating side effect is antipsychotic-induced weight gain (AIWG) which can result in obesity and related medical conditions (e.g. diabetes and cardiovascular diseases) leading to a high risk for premature death. In addition, patients who are obese will create substantial additional costs to the health care system. Thus it is essential to investigate mechanisms of AIWG and develop prediction tools that reduce the occurrence of obesity in these vulnerable patients.Family and twin studies strongly support genetic factors being involved in the occurrence of AIWG. In our previous studies funded by CIHR,we have contributed extensively towards identifying first important gene variants associated with AIWG. However, further work is needed incorporating more advanced strategies which consider recent advances in biotechnology and biostatistics. In this study we aim to expand our investigations by detecting new gene variants associated with AIWG by sequencing mitochondrial DNA and to perform genome wide analyses. Our main goal is to develop a genetic risk model to predict AIWG. In addition, the clinical utility of the model will be investigated in a large sample of antipsychotic-treated patients. These represent important steps towards clinical application of genetics of AIWG. In summary, a better understanding of genetic risk factors for AIWG may help clarify the biological mechanisms and help the clinician choose the best medication for an individual patient. In addition, it may provide novel targets for future drug discovery. This increased standard of care through individualized treatment will also help to reduce health care costs and therefore be beneficial for Canadian patients and the health care system.

column36: Role of autotaxin bound to platelet-derived microparticles to development of vascular damage in arthritis.
column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are common among people with autoimmune diseases with arthritic symptoms. People affected by rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have a greater risk of early subclinical atherosclerotic disease due to accelerated development of atheromatous plaques. Biologically active lipids such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), play a role in RA pathophysiology. In particular, high levels of autotaxin (ATX), the enzyme that produces LPA, were detected in synovial fluids and sera from RA patients compared to osteoarthritis patients. LPA levels in synovial fluid and expression of several LPA receptors in the RA articular tissue were also increased. To date no research team has paid attention to elevated plasma levels of ATX in arthritis. Upon activation, platelets can shed minuscule particles, named microparticles. Elevated levels of platelet-derived microparticles are associated with many diseases state including RA and SLE. Since ATX can bind to activated platelets we monitored the presence of platelet-derived microparticles positive for ATX and discovered a new class of microparticles abundant in plasma from SLE patients but not from healthy individuals, the ATX-associated microparticles was identified. According to our hypothesis microparticles serve as a vehicle to transport ATX into the vascular wall, thereby disseminating inflammation within the vascular tissue. The main goal of the research proposal is to characterize and study the role of these microparticles-associated ATX in RA and SLE. The abundance of these microparticles might correlate with development of atherosclerosis and may become useful clinical marker for increased risk of CVD in arthritis.

column36: Impact of Early Repolarization on Long QT Syndrome: Canadian Genetic Heart Rhythm Network
column37: 30,000 Canadians die suddenly every year. Some of these deaths are in young and seemingly healthy individuals, who have inherited a condition that causes irregular heart rhythms. The most common condition is Long QT Syndrome (LQTS), named for the abnormally long pause as the heart muscle prepares to contract, which can be seen on an electrocardiogram (EKG). LQTS can cause fainting and sudden unexpected death (SUD), but may not be identified with routine cardiac testing, as patients' EKGs are not always abnormal. Accurately diagnosing LQTS and screening potentially affected family members is crucial to preventing SUD. This project hopes to discover better methods of detecting LQTS by studying the relationship of LQTS to the entire human genetic code, developing teaching tools for healthcare professionals, and improving public awareness. An anonymous computerized database of LQTS patient information (including EKGs, test results, genetic screening and family history) will be created. The data will help identify which tests are most useful in diagnosing LQTS and which treatments are best suited for the condition. Blood samples for genetic research will also be collected and analyzed. The applicant has researched genetic heart rhythm conditions for 15 years and is a national leader in the field. He has previously established a national network of inherited heart rhythm experts, whose work has been recognized at scientific meetings nationally and internationally. This study will be unique for its national collaboration and ability to gather a large quantity of quality information all in one database about this rare and complex condition. Often the first signs of LQTS are fainting or SUD, and this project will combine healthcare with human genetic code information to improve healthcare provider's ability to recognize LQTS in individuals and families, and provide treatment that will save lives.

column36: A novel regulation of the hERG channel and its role in long QT syndrome and sudden cardiac death
column37: Background: The cardiac electricity-generating protein, named "HERG", is important for normal heart rhythm. A reduction in the amount of HERG protein disturbs heart rhythm and causes sudden death. Diseased conditions such as insufficient blood supply to the heart muscle (ischemic heart disease) is a common cause of irregular heartbeat and sudden death. Presently, it is not well understood how ischemic heart disease causes irregular heartbeat. Objectives: We aim to establish (1) that a special region of the HERG senses a reduced level of potassium in the blood to cause HERG to break down. (2) that this same region of HERG is easily broken down by biological molecules (named enzymes) released from heart cells as a result of insufficient blood supply. (3) a novel strategy using small synthetic molecules (peptides) to protect HERG and prevent sudden death in patients suffering from ischemic heart disease. Description of the research project: We have obtained evidence showing that a special region of HERG plays an important role in breaking down HERG in the heart when the blood potassium level is low or when blood supply to the heart muscle is insufficient. Ischemic heart disease increases the abundance of enzymes that selectively break down HERG. We will study which enzymes released from heart cells break down HERG. We will use cultured cells as well as heart cells from rats and rabbits. We will also make a rabbit model that mimics human ischemic heart disease. Importantly, we will design synthetic HERG-binding molecules to shield the special region and thereby protect HERG against breakdown. Significance: Ischemic heart disease is the leading disease in our society, and it causes irregular heartbeat and sudden death. The proposed research can potentially lead to novel drugs for treating irregular heartbeat and preventing sudden death in patients with ischemic heart disease.

column36: The synergistic integration of ephrin and Netrin signals in the developing nervous system.
column37: We now know quite a bit about how external chemical signals control the functions on the inside of cells. Such cues are prominently used in the developing embryo, for example, to instruct a progenitor cell to keep dividing to increase the size of an organ, or to make a cell stick to another to build a tissue, or to connect a neuron with its synaptic partner. Such individual signals and their receptors on the surface of cells have been identified, as have been the relay pathways that transmit those signal from the receptor to other compartments inside the cell or neuron. Many of these have been implicated in various diseases and drugs targetting such signalling events are being sought. What is also unclear is how pathways activated by different signals might work together to integrate the information about the extracellular environment. To answer this question, we are proposing to work in the developing nervous system, to understand the how signals from two very different families of secreted molecules are integrated. We gathered a lot of evidence that netrin and ephrin signals are important in the development of connections between neurons. We also discovered that when ephrin and netrin are presented simultaneously, nerves develop in a very different manner compared when each signal is presented alone. We propose to examine how this happens in neurons made from neuronal stem cells in vitro, using biochemical fractionation and protein complex formation measurement. Ephrin and netrin signals have been implicated in many diseases such as cancer and neurodegeneration. In the long term, once we understand ephrin-netrin signal integration, we would search for drugs that might boost or disrupt it.

column37: Psoriasis is a major health problem affecting up to 3 % of the population. The disease is characterized by an abnormally excessive and rapid growth of the epidermal layer of the skin. Skin cells are replaced every 3 to 5 days in psoriasis rather than the usual 28 to 30 days. Psoriasis affects both sexes, can arise at any age and to any ethnic groups. In addition, nearly 30% of the psoriatic patients will develop a debilitating arthritis form of the disease. There is no cure currently available for psoriasis, but various treatments such as topical application of corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues can help to control the symptoms. However, when these treatments are inefficient, UV radiations are then recommended or the patients are treated by a compound named methotrexate that is used against leukemias and rheumatoid arthritis. However, methotrexate and other drugs referred to as "biologics" are toxic and must be administered under very close medical attention. In such a context, new efficient and less toxic drugs are dearly required to better control the symptoms of the disease. To this end, we developed new molecules that have exhibited efficient activity on in vitro models by controlling the proliferation of the cells responsible for psoriasis. In addition, these drugs are not toxic. The objectives of our research program are two-folds. The first one is to study the mechanisms by which our drugs are controlling skin cell proliferation and differentiation both in vitro and on a mouse model of psoriasis. The second is to prepare new compounds suitable for clinical trials that will improve the quality of life of psoriatic patients. Toward this goal, our project will harness the power of computer sciences, molecular pharmacology and chemistry to tailor drugs that are more potent, more selective and less toxic.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of natural killer (NK) and innate lymphoid cell (ILC) development and function in health and disease
column37: The innate immune system protects us from pathogenic bacteria, viruses, and cancer, and also helps to maintain normal tissue function at mucosal barriers, such as the skin, gut, and lungs. Natural killer (NK) cells are a subset of type-1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC) that can detect and eliminate infected, cancer, and transplanted cells. In addition, there are two other major ILC subsets: type-2 ILC, which regulate allergy, especially in the lungs; and type-3 ILC, which regulate normal gut function, including maintenance of intestinal tissue and support for commensal microflora, our 'good' bacteria that help digest food. How NK and ILC cells perform their functions requires understanding of how they develop properly, the molecules they use to sense what is harmless or dangerous, and how these molecules assist in the decision to ignore a healthy cell, or respond to a pathogenic cell. We have identified a receptor-ligand family (NKR-P1:Clr) that contributes to NK cell and ILC immune recognition at the molecular level. Some of these NKR-P1 receptors are inhibitory, so normal cells express the Clr ligands to regulate or prevent NK cell responses ("healthy-self"), while infected and cancerous cells lose Clr expression and are eliminated by NK cells ("missing-self"). This supports a role for the NKR-P1:Clr interactions in fighting cancer and infectious disease. However, malignant cancer cells and viral pathogens can evolve ways to subvert this immunity and become pathogenic. In addition, there are stimulatory NKR-P1 receptors that recognize abnormal proteins and directly activate NK cells ("induced-self"). We propose to advance our understanding of innate immunity by studying how these cells develop, how their function supports our immune defenses in fighting cancer and infection, and how pathogens can evade this immune recognition. This knowledge could lead to therapies in cancer treatment and control of infectious disease.

column36: Molecular control of the delta-opioid receptor signaling and functional selectivity by sodium
column37: Delta-opioid receptor agonists have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of pain, depression, and Parkinson's disease. However, drugs targeting this receptor induce side effects including seizures, respiratory depression, tolerance, dependence and immunosuppression, among others. Over the last decade, pharmacological concept has evolved remarkably after the finding that different ligands, at the same receptor, can selectively activate and prefer certain signalling pathways among all pathways activated by balanced ligands. This intrinsic property of ligands, known as "functional selectivity", is conferred by the differential engagement of the ligand with the receptor, leading to the notion that the fine-tuning of receptor function can be achieved through the use of functionally selective ligands. This new paradigm has opened up the way for the generation of pharmacologically distinct drugs with enhanced therapeutic potential, while reducing their deleterious side effects. We recently discovered a cavity housing a sodium ion in the core of the delta-opioid receptor. Our findings clarified observation made more than 40 years ago showing that sodium negatively regulates agonist interaction with this receptor. Our works also highlighted the unexpected role of this cavity in controlling receptor functional selectivity. These findings lead to the hypothesis that this cavity could serve as a target site to design a novel generation of drugs with reduce side effects and increase therapeutic potential. My works aim to study and understand the mechanism by which this novel cavity and the sodium ion controlled the selective activation of the receptor-signaling outcome. I also pursued the objective of looking at the druggability of this unique site with the long-term goal to design drug that will specifically target this cavity to generate novel therapeutic avenues for the treatment of debilitating disease such as pain, depression and Parkinson's disease.

column36: Cerebral cortical neural mechanisms of motor and non-motor decisions.
column37: The world constantly bombards us with sensory inputs about many possible motor actions. Imagine walking along a breakfast buffet table. Sometimes, the input is clear and the action is obvious - you see a glass of orange juice, reach to it and put it on your tray. Other times, the situation is uncertain or even conflicting - you see pancakes and waffles and like both; which should you take? The 1st aim of this proposal is to study how premotor and prefrontal cortical areas use conflicting sensory inputs about different actions to select one action to make, using neural recordings in non-human primates that perform conditional motor tasks. We do not respond slavishly to every sensory input. Instead, voluntary behaviour is flexible and often involves arbitrary stimulus-response (SR) rules that we learn by experience. Normal interactions with the world involve selective and often conditional context-dependent responses to only some stimuli, such as the sequences of arm and leg movements elicited by green, yellow and red traffic lights while driving to work. The 2nd aim is to study how neurons in those cortical areas apply arbitrary SR rules to control action. Failure to impose rule-based control on behaviour leads to problems for both the individual and society, including impulsive, inappropriate and even criminal behaviour. We also often use rules to assess the "rightness" or "wrongness" of observed events. We know we should stop when the light is red, so when we see someone drive through an intersection on a red light, we know that what they did was wrong. The 3rd aim is to use MEG imagining methods to determine whether premotor cortical areas in humans can use SR rules to help assess the "correctness/wrongness" of observed sensory events that they watch on a monitor while a computer performs conditional tasks correctly or incorrectly. This would implicate nominally motor cortical circuits in higher-order cognitive processes not associated with action planning.

column36: Mechanisms of RNA Degradation by Autophagy
column37: Mutations in genes that activate a waste recycling program in cells, called autophagy, or "self-eating" are one cause of cancer and are implicated in neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). When autophagy is inhibited, excess waste consisting of damaged or old cellular components accumulates. In most cases we don't understand which specific type of cellular waste accumulates and causes disease when autophagy is inhibited. Our lab has been at the forefront of research on a new class of molecules degraded by autophagy called RNA. RNA is one of four major types of substrates in cells and is required for genes in our DNA to build cellular components and allow them to respond to their environment. Early studies had shown that autophagy degraded large amounts of RNA when cells were stressed, as in infection or disease. Now, our results demonstrate that autophagy uses an unusual mechanism to mark large clusters of RNA for degradation by autophagy. Fascinatingly, these RNA clusters are a defining feature of ALS that is believed to cause progressive motor neuron death and paralysis in this disease. Strikingly, genetic mapping studies suggest that mutations in genes that cause either inappropriate formation of RNA clusters or block their elimination by autophagy may cause ALS. We will investigate the surprising mechanisms underlying the ability of autophagy to recognize and degrade these RNA clusters in cellular and mouse models of ALS. Using mouse models, we will test whether autophagy-activating drugs used in patients to treat other diseases, could be an effective new treatment for ALS. This research therefore aims to understand a novel and fundamental process involved in ALS and help devise new means to treat this devastating disease.

Understanding how the immune system respond to viral infection in mucosal tissues represents a central question for HIV-infected individuals. However, vaginal and rectal mucosal tissues are quite distinct in anatomy, physiology, and immunobiology, and these characteristics can dramatically influence the efficiency of controlling HIV dissemination. Recently, successful control of several STV infections has been associated with the presence of sustained local immune response related to a novel leukocyte population called tissue-resident memory (Trm) CD8 T cells. However, dynamics and functions of this novel cell population in mucosal tissues have never been addressed in the context of HIV infection. In this study, we propose to characterize this population in mucosal tissues compared to non-mucosal tissues including peripheral blood, lymph nodes and spleen. As it is essential to determine their changes early after viral exposure, we will conduct this project using non-human primate models comparing pathogenic rhesus macaques, which develop AIDS and non-pathogenic African green monkeys, which are resistant to AIDS. These models offer a unique opportunity to analyze deep tissues, which are not easily accessible in humans, particularly early after infection. The findings obtained during this project are of considerable interest in order to better understand mucosal immunity in HIV-infected individuals since this novel population represents a potent new immune effector cells involved on STV control in mucosal tissues, the first sites of HIV viral exposure.

column36: siRNA Therapy for Leukemia: Synthetic Biomaterials to Deliver siRNA and Curb Uncontrolled Growth of Leukemic Cells
column37: Leukemias are a significant cause of death among cancer patients. Great strides have been made in understanding the factors causing leukemia and numerous new types of drugs are being continuously explored for therapy. However, the traditional chemotherapy is still the treatment of choice for most leukemias, but it is rarely curative and it loses its effectiveness on the long-term therapy. The main reason for this is that the leukemic cells adopt and become resistant to chemotherapy. This project is intended to develop a new approach for therapy of leukemia by developing a new type of drug for therapy. Engineered biomaterials effective for silencing will be paramount to accomplish the desired goal. Animal models will be utilized to determine the effectiveness of the proposed biomaterials. If successful, our approach will introduce a new treatment modality for leukemia.

Les Unites locales d'evaluation (UETMIS), comme les unites internationales (INAHTA) liees a des etablissements de sante specifiques, partagent traditionnellement des criteres d'evaluation semblables: securite, efficacite et economie de couts. Pour d'autres, l'evaluation ethique est necessaire dans la mesure ou les soins et les services prodigues sont charges de valeurs individuelles, professionnelles, institutionnelles et sociales, certains jugeant irresponsable l'absence de methode integrant explicitement des criteres ethiques a meme leur processus d'evaluation. La litterature rend fortement compte, depuis une quinzaine d'annees, du besoin des acteurs en ETMIS a cet egard. Ce besoin n'est donc pas nouveau ni les efforts consentis pour tenter d'y repondre; sans succes jusqu'a maintenant car les approches developpees sont jugees non operationnelles par les acteurs. Ce projet de recherche vise a relever ce defi. Tirant profit des echecs passes selon la litterature ainsi que selon les groupes d'acteurs qui collaborent a ce projet, notre equipe de recherche interdisciplinaire composee de chercheurs et d'acteurs en ETMIS entend developper une methode d'evaluation ethique integree au processus d'evaluation en ETMIS qui soit rigoureuse, operationnelle pour les acteurs et transferable d'une instance a une autre au Canada et a l'etranger.

column37: The rapid entry of calcium ions into nerve cells is mediated by a class of protein that responds to electrical signals by opening a calcium selective pore (called calcium channels). The results suggest that genetic mutations preferentially affect only a fraction of the possible channel subtypes and our current proposal aims to investigate the underlying basis as to how each variant distinctly cause pathophysiological aspects relevant to disease. column36: Exploitation of host ubiquitination pathways by pathogenic E. coli
column37: Pathogenic E. coli strains cause life-threatening diseases manifesting by recent outbreaks in Canada and worldwide. The ability of these pathogenic bacteria to establish infection in humans and animals depends on combined function of defined set of specific pathogenic factors called "effectors" that are delivered inside the host cell by a specialized syringe-like multiprotein complex called type 3 secretion system. The largest family in E. coli effector arsenal constitutes so-called NleG effectors, of which there are 14 members in enterohamerrhagic E. coli (EHEC) strains. We have recently characterised a conserved part of NleG effectors to share the structural fold and functionality with protein ubiquitin ligases also known as E3 enzymes. This diverse class of proteins perform a critical step in a process termed 'ubiquitination'; the addition of a small protein 'ubiquitin' to lysines of a target protein. Ubiquitination is highly conserved across all eukaryotes and is critical in protein turnover, protein localization and cell signaling processes. The E3 ligase are major determinants of specificity for ubiquitination process. Although our preliminary data linked the function of NleG effectors to host ubiquitination, their function remains unknown. In the current proposal we aim to identify the host targets of NleG effectors and establish their role in E. coli pathogenesis process using combined structural, biochemical and in vivo analysis. This will significantly advance our understanding of molecular aspects of infection by this important bacterial pathogen and open up the possibility to design novel antibacterial therapies.

column36: Understanding a novel molecular mechanism controlling structural development of neurons
column37: About 200-300 newborn infants in Canada are affected by stroke each year. There are very limited treatment options and currently no pharmacological interventions. Reorganization and rewiring of connections between brain cells following injury can promote recovery. My lab has found a new protein called Pannexin 1 that regulates these changes. Pannexin 1 forms pores in the cell membrane that control passage of certain molecules. If we block these pores, or remove Pannexin 1 altogether, the cells extend processes called neurites, structures that are critical for rewiring of connections. Recently, we also discovered a physical interaction between Pannexin 1 and another protein called "collapsin response mediator protein 2" (Crmp2). Crmp2 promotes the growth of neurites. We predict that, during normal brain development, Panx1 'keeps the brakes' on neurite outgrowth by sequestering Crmp2. This prevents the formation of aberrant connections. When a stroke occurs in the newborn, recovery is hindered by Panx1 sequestration of Crmp2 because this limits rewiring. We therefore propose that blocking the Panx1/Crmp2 interaction will improve perinatal stroke recovery by enhancing rewiring. To investigate these predictions, we will perform a series of studies using a Pannexin 1 knockout mouse as well as a molecular tool we engineered to interfere with the interaction. Essentially, we will study how structural changes in cells during development and after injury are affected if Pannexin 1 is taken out of the equation entirely or if we prevent it from interacting with Crmp2. The primary goal of this research is to bridge key gaps in knowledge of the role of these proteins in creating structural changes in brain cells. Successful outcomes of this work will ultimately lay the groundwork for the development of novel therapeutics that could be used to improve health outcomes in patients affected by acquired brain disorders such as stroke and cerebral palsy.

column37: There is inconclusive evidence that particulate matter (PM) air pollution exposure during pregnancy may affect brain development. In this proposed study, we aim to extend observation of these children from birth to age four to evaluate relationships between prenatal exposure and brain development, respiratory health, and allergic symptoms. column36: Effects of Sex Hormone Treatment on Brain Development: A Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study of Adolescents with Gender Dysphoria
column37: Adolescence is a time of rapid brain growth that is partly influenced by sex hormones. This project will use state-of-the-art magnetic resonance imaging techniques to better understand how sex hormones guide brain development. Specifically, we will examine how the brains of transgendered adolescents, who strongly experience themselves as the opposite gender, differ from those of typically-developing adolescents. One truly unique aspect of this project is that it will document how the adolescent brain responds to sex hormone therapy. Because sex hormone therapy directly influences the sex hormones that are already in the body, this project will provide insight regarding how sex hormones affect the adolescent brain. Surprisingly, even though sex hormone therapy is widely used to help transgendered adolescents change from one gender to the other, its impact on brain development during this critical stage is largely unknown. Our research will also examine a very popular biological explanation of transgenderism, namely, that certain brain structures are shifted in the direction of the opposite sex. An additional unanswered question we will investigate is whether sex hormone therapy substantially reduces the gender-related distress these youth experience.

column36: Fast cholinergic transmission in the visual system:from single synapses to behavior
column37: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a principal neurotransmitter in the nervous system. In the peripheral nervous system (PNS), including the neuronal signals to our muscles, ACh has a rapid and direct action on muscles onto which it is released. In the central nervous system (CNS), ACh is also implicated in plethora of brain functions including, attention, learning and memory and sensory function. In contrast to the PNS, in the CNS ACh appears to be released in a diffuse slow manner triggers long-lasting, widespread changes in neuronal excitability. Thus, ACh appears to act as a neuromodulator, rather than a fast excitatory transmitter as it does in the PNS. However, there is mounting evidence that fast, point-to-point cholinergic synaptic transmission may also play a significant role in the CNS, similar to that observed in the peripheral nervous system. However, addressing the role of long range cholinergic transmission is technically challenging and thus the impact of fast cholinergic transmission on specific neural computations has not been explored. In this proposal, we aim to understanding the fundamental properties of cholinergic neurons and how they affect specific neural computations. We will probe cholinergic neurons in the retina, which is the most accessible part of the CNS.Understanding cholinergic function has the potential to provide important insights into the visual changes associated with a decreased ACh in the retinas of Alzheimer's patients and also the side effects of anticholinergic treatments commonly used for diseases such as Parkinson's and myasthenia gravis.

column36: Characterization of molecular events controlling nuclear envelope/chromatin interaction.
column37: Understanding the molecular basis for many acute and chronic diseases is a daunting challenge facing the biomedical community today. It is clear that comprehending processes that control cell growth and differentiation is central to this goal, and we strive to understand how gene expression controls these processes. Many factors contribute to controlling gene expression including the environment in which genes are stored. In every eukaryotic cell, including humans, genes are housed within a spherical, membrane-enclosed compartment, termed the nucleus. The membrane shell that surrounds the genome is termed the nuclear envelope (NE). In recent years it has become clear that the NE organizes chromatin and participants in defining how certain genes are controlled. We have shown that structures present in the NE can grab on to genes and, like puppeteers, they can alter their structure and, in this way, control whether a specific set of associated genes are turned on or off. Using state-of-the-art techniques, we are investigating how the interactions of genes with the NE are regulated and identifying the signals that control these events. As the NE is highly conserved in structure and function in eukaryotes as diverse as humans and yeast, these studies can be conducted in a yeast model system where powerful genetic and biochemical approaches can be used to investigate NE/chromatin interactions. It is clear that defects in NE proteins lead to diseases including heart abnormalities and cancer. Understanding their functions in nuclear organization will provide us with a critical understanding of the underlying causes of these diseases and provide an avenue for eventual rational intervention.

column37: Infectious diseases are a major cause of morbidity, mortality and reduced economic productivity in Canada and the world. Vaccination remains the most effective public health measure to prevent infectious diseases. However, there are few vaccines against chronic infectious diseases and no vaccines against chronic parasitic diseases. Often, pathogens that establish chronic infections either manipulate their host environment or take advantage of conditions to ensure their long-term survival. Therefore, even in settings of slowly progressive chronic infection, a vaccine must mediate a rapid immune response at the outset of infection in order to prevent these pathogens from manipulating the host environment to their benefit. This project is focused on understanding the initial events of the infectious process in settings of known protective immunity. The information gleaned from this research will be employed to develop novel and unconventional vaccination strategies against chronic infections of global health importance.

column37: Male-factor infertility affects up to 40% of couples struggling with fertility treatments in Canada. What causes this condition, however, remains unknown in many cases. column36: System Immunobiology of S. aureus pathobiosis: Role of the AhR Gene Program
column37: Under healthy conditions, our bodies carry trillions of bacteria. These bacteria usually have a positive effect on the development and function of our immune systems. Some of these bacteria are, in fact, superbugs: highly lethal bacteria with broad antibiotic resistance. The question we want to answer is how do bacteria go from living on our bodies without causing disease to becoming lethal microbes. Understanding how this happens may hold the key to new ways of treating infections and inflammatory, immune-mediated diseases like multiple sclerosis and diabetes and preventing transplant rejection. Our team is tackling this question by studying the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. This microbe is carried by more than 25 per cent of healthy individuals without causing serious infections. However, under certain circumstances, it can cause severe infections and death, an outcome that carries a high health burden (estimated at US$9 billion/yr in the USA alone). Using advanced technology to map out the expression of genes and proteins in microbes and in immune cells during the different stages of S. aureus and human host interaction, we have identified a gene program known as AhR program that is highly controlled by the microbe through the human immune system. We propose here to delineate the whole gene program and the steps that turn it on and off. In doing so, we will have a target to develop new drugs that modulate inflammation and immune function.

column36: Investigating the regulation of lymphocyte function by metabolic reprogramming
column37: T lymphocytes, or T cells, are the "soldiers" of the immune system; they function primarily at the front lines of infection to identify and clear infected cells or eliminate pathogens and protect the host from infection. The ability of T cells to successfully respond to an infection depends on the T cell having enough energy and building blocks to complete the task. To meet these demands T cells display fundamental changes in their metabolism - the biochemical processes cells use to generate energy - to allow them to grow and divide and ultimately defeat foreign invaders. Our previous work has established that T cell function is very sensitive to changes in their metabolism. As T cells differentiate during an immune response they move from lymphoid organs to sites of infection or inflammation, where oxygen, nutrients, and growth factors may become limiting. Our hypothesis is that T cells actively adapt their metabolism during immune responses to maintain their function and promote immunity to pathogens. This proposal uses in vitro and in vivo experimental systems to study how cellular metabolism influences T cell function to ensure proper immune function. Ultimately we would like to determine whether manipulating T cell metabolism could be a suitable therapeutic avenue for the treatment of inflammation, autoimmune disease, or transplant rejection.

column37: Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) is a deadly heart rhythm disorder that may account for up to 30% of the 450,000 sudden cardiac deaths each year in North America. Even following a successful resuscitation, many victims of VF often experience re-initiation of VF (or ventricular refibrillation). Novel treatment strategies are needed to prevent or treat VF and refibrillation to improve the outcome for these patients. Such therapies cannot be invented without our knowledge on mechanisms that cause VF in the first place (early VF), VF that continues over a long duration of more than 3 min (long duration VF), and refibrillation. Over the course of our previous CIHR operating grant, we demonstrated that there are regional differences in dynamics during VF and they relate to rotor formation (circular pattern of heart activation), and that ion channels found on cardiac cell membrane modulate VF during its early phase and inhibition of these channels leads to termination of early human VF. In the current proposal, we plan to investigate if specific fibers responsible for electrical conduction in the heart (Purkinje fibers) maintain long duration VF. Furthermore, following up on the mechanistic insights we have gained on what ion channels might contribute to human VF, we plan to apply specific drugs to modulate these ion channels so as to prevent or halt fibrillations, and most importantly, help resuscitate human hearts from VF. This operating grant is crucial for retaining the research team I have assembled. Our unique expertise, and previous experience, and the experiments proposed in this renewal grant will allow us to better understand human VF.

column36: Implicit Measurement of Motivations for Non-Suicidal Self-Injury
column37: The act of intentionally injuring oneself can be hard to understand, and yet, this behaviour is related to considerable personal suffering, risk for suicide, and a substantial toll on the healthcare system. The development of innovative ways to understand what makes people vulnerable to self-injury will help health professionals to improve the care and treatment of people who engage in this behaviour. The primary aims of this research are to develop and examine innovative ways to evaluate and understand peoples' motives for self-injury (or, why they self-injure). Although we know that people often self-injure to experience emotional relief, punish themselves, or communicate emotional pain, much of the research has simply involved asking people why they self-injure. Such an approach may be less useful in clinical settings due to impression management, or for individuals who have limited awareness of why they self-injury. Implicit measures (a measure of intentions or associations that are not fully conscious) of motives for self-injury are less subject to these types of biases. Moreover, the use of such measures may help us uncover factors that continue to place people at risk for self-injury over time. For a previous CIHR grant, we developed and validated an implicit measure of the association of emotional relief with self-injury. Currently, we aim to develop additional implicit measures of the association of self-injury with interpersonal motives and self-punishment. We hypothesize that these new measures will relate to the daily experiences of people who self-injure and predict self-injury in the future. We also wish to examine whether those with borderline personality disorder have especially strong motives. Ultimately, this research will (a) clarify factors contributing to self-injury risk over time, and (b) suggest individualized avenues for treatment (e.g., treatment might involve communication skills for someone with strong interpersonal motives).

column36: Endothelial progenitor cell adhesion to biomimetic vascular substitutes
column37: Heart disease is a condition where the arteries nourishing the heart become too narrow. A common procedure to treat heart disease is to implant stents to reopen the blood vessels. Over 50 000 coronary artery interventions are performed in Canada each year. To reduce the risks of complications such as sudden heart failure years later, a normal cell lining should be re-established on the stent surface. The endothelial cells that cover our healthy blood vessels secrete molecules that inhibit blood clotting and vessel narrowing. To restore this cell lining, the stents can be coated with antibodies that capture endothelial progenitor cells from the blood stream. These cells can generate large numbers of endothelial cells in vitro. Studies have shown that stents that capture the circulating progenitor cells become covered by endothelial cells. However, this did not improve the performance of the stents. We hypothesize that this is due to the lack of a natural microenvironment to help cell growth and maturation. More mature endothelial cells should produce higher amounts of the molecules that inhibit blood vessel obstruction. We therefore propose to engineer stents that mimic the normal endothelial cell environment. To do so, we will coat the stents with combinations of molecules involved in endothelial cell adhesion, growth and maturation. We will also use stents that slowly dissolve over time. These stents would provide the transient support needed to reopen the vessel and recruit cells with regenerative potential. The use of biodegradable materials will avoid leaving a foreign body behind once the stents have served their purpose. These engineered materials could help restore a normal vasculature at the implant site. The stents developed during this project could help patients suffering from heart disease live without the constant fear of a recurrent heart failure or other complications.

column36: Dementia in the population: Trajectories of disease, health care use, and places of care
column37: Dementia is severe and disabling disease, touching many Canadians. Existing research has identified a number of potentially modifiable risk factors for dementia, such as exercise, participation in social activities, diet, and drug therapies. However, it is difficult to tell which factors are the most important for Canadians to address. They organize their genetic material so that parts that will be used are easy to access, while parts that aren't needed are stashed away. column36: Next generation patient-derived, genetically-defined kidney and bladder cancer xenograft models for anti-cancer drug development
column37: Over 13 thousand people are diagnosed with kidney (5,900) and bladder (7,900) cancers each year and more than 36 hundred patients die of these cancers annually (1,750 and 1,900 respectively) in Canada. New effective drugs to treat late-staged kidney and bladder cancers are highly demanded in clinic. One essential component in anti-cancer drug development is the drug evaluation models. Currently, such drug evaluation task is commonly carried out with preclinical cancer research models that consist of special, immune-deficient mice carrying grafts of cultured, commercially available human cancer cells. While such commercial cancer cell line models have merits for basic cancer research, the cell lines used in research have evolved biologically during generations of cultures and do not properly represent patients' cancers and consequently do not adequately predict efficacy of anticancer drugs in the clinic. Even when new anticancer drug candidates have successfully passed all stages of efficacy testing performed with commercial cancer cell line models, only about 5% gets approval for clinical usage by the US Food and Drug Administration. The high number of ineffective new drug candidates entering clinical trials indicates an urgent need for better ways of predicting clinical drug efficacy before drugs are tested in humans. Drs. column36: Aripiprazole Long Acting Injectable (ALAI), its potential enhancing effect on memory and associated neural structures: A longitudinal brain imaging study in first-episode psychosis
column37: Our proposed study explores the association between antipsychotic treatment and changes in memory performance and hippocampal volume. Both human and animal data suggest that aripiprazole may improve memory function as well as the brain structures supporting memory functions, notably the hippocampus. Data from our own large longitudinal study on neuroimaging in a sample of first episode psychosis (FEP), provides the first evidence in humans that aripiprazole may increase hippocampal volume. In order to pursue this new direction of research further, we now propose to conduct a new longitudinal study over a 5-year period in order to determine unambiguously whether or not aripiprazole is related to improving memory and increasing hippocampal volume in early psychosis over a 21-month period. 90 well-characterized FEP patients, followed over a 2-year period, will be put on a second generation antipsychotic based on a choice for safety and effectiveness. More precisely, they will be treated with oral aripiprazole, oral risperidone-paliperidone, aripiprazole long-acting injectable or Paliperidone palmitate long-acting injectable. In this naturalistic and open-label study, we propose 4 time-points for brain imaging (months 3, 9, 15, 21). We will use high-resolution protocol on a 3T MRI scanner at the Douglas Institute to image specific hippocampal subfields and other brain regions involved in memory. At each time point, we will also administer a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment of memory and other cognitive functions. Having multiple time-points will make it possible to describe the dynamic interplay between antipsychotic use and brain structures and functions. We hypothesize that aripiprazole will enhance memory performance and increase hippocampal volume. We will be able to examine these effects controlling for multiple possible confounders such as, substance abuse, severity of illness given our well-established clinical assessment protocol (PEPP-Montreal).
