column36: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Neurophotonics
column37: Psychiatric disorders represent a major public health problem, accruing enormous socioeconomic costs. The available treatments remain largely insufficient. Advances in the field are impaired by the lack of proper tools to conduct adequate biological measurements to guide diagnosis and treatment. This is particularly critical given evidence that early treatment of psychiatric disorders, before the onset of debilitating symptoms, leads to significantly improved clinical outcomes.The CERC in Neurophotonics proposes to fill this gap by developing and exploiting advanced photonics technologies to probe brain cells and tissue function non-invasively with high spatial and temporal resolution. The aim is to identify novel biomarkers of psychiatric diseases; in particular, to identify in children within affected families, early biomarkers reflecting a high risk of later developing psychiatric diseases.Optical technology developments that will be pursued include:1) Coherent imaging techniques, such as digital holography quantitative phase microscopy (DH-QPM), to study the structure and dynamics of cells at nanoscale levels (protein content, nanoscale membrane fluctuations, water movements). DH-QPM will be combined with other imaging and spectroscopic approaches (fluorescence, Coherent Anti-Stokes-Raman Scattering, High Harmonics) for multimodal optical interrogation of cells and tissue.2) Incoherent imaging methods will also be developed including multi-fiber, miniaturized optical probes (optiprobes) to extract spatia-temporally resolved reflectance spectra in small tissue volumes. This will yield structural and functional (neurovascular/neurometabolic) information for in vivo biopsies performed during cognitive tasks with previously inaccessible temporal resolution.Diagnostic potential will be validated using different paradigms:A) in vivo measurements in brain tissue to explore pathophysiological mechanisms inanimal models reproducing certain features of psychiatric disorders;B) non-invasive photonics-based structural/functional measurements in volunteers, psychiatric patients (e.g., schizophrenia and bipolar disorders) and high risk children during cognitive tasks and neurophysiological tests;C) in vitro measurements to study the structure, dynamics, metabolism and stress response of neural cells generated from volunteer- and patient-derived stem cells.The proposed research offers extraordinary translational perspectives for personalized medicine for the prevention and treatment of psychiatric diseases.

column36: Better understanding of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and intervention guides
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the 4th cause of mortality and it is projected to move up to the 3rd rank by 2020. Mortality has increased and COPD results in higher rates of hospitalization than heart failure, angina and other chronic diseases. COPD remains under diagnosed and undertreated, and under prioritized by policy and decision makers. We are proposing a new model of research, the Canadian Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (CanCOLD) project that will position COPD research for strong leadership and partnership (with COPD community, academic institution and industry), and alliance opportunities at National and International levels. CanCOLD as a research project provides unique and exclusive feature including sampling in the population that can better mirror the population of COPD patients at large, longitudinal assessment with repeated measurements (3 years and beyond) and extensive characterization of men and women with early disease. CanCOLD will allow identifying clinical subgroups 'phenotypes' and how factors can affect outcomes in patients, with assessment of other determinants than smoking that might impact on disease progression, and comorbidities. CanCOLD as a network platform gives access to a comprehensive dataset and a centralized tissue bank (blood storage for measuring biomarkers, DNA, RNA). It has led to high profile transdisciplinary collaboration involving researchers from most universities across Canada and collaborative engagement with industry to maximise value to COPD community with several substudies inspired by practical considerations. Through these studies, the industry partner will contribute to enhance academic research output and generate university benefits; in particular, new research findings and knowledge will likely be more rapidly applicable to practice.

column36: Methods for the economic evaluation of personalized medicine: a case study in advanced colorectal cancer
column37: Personalized medicine -- the tailoring of care based on individual characteristics -- has grown rapidly in recent years, particularly for cancer treatment. There is significant variability within cancer types, and with tumour testing many new therapies can be targeted to the patients most likely to respond to the drug. However, the cost of these drugs and of the testing required is a significant obstacle to their use. A challenge facing health care systems is how to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of personalized therapies. Data from clinical trials can be limited, and may not reflect how the drug is used in practice. The real-world effectiveness and costs of a drug can be evaluated using comparative effectiveness research methods, using data from patients being treated with the drug in real clinical settings. However, these methods have a limited ability to account for variability between patients, and in the case of personalized medicines understanding this variability is essential to understanding the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the drug. This project will look at analytic methods to compare the benefits and costs of personalized medicine, using data on advanced colorectal cancer treatment as a case study. Two drugs, cetuximab and panitumumab, targeted to colorectal cancer patients with a specific gene, were adopted in British Columbia in 2009. This study will use real-world data for patients treated for advanced colorectal cancer at the BC Cancer Agency to calculate the cost-effectiveness of these two drugs, and compare conventional evaluation methods to methods that account for the personalized nature of this therapy. These research methods can be used to generate better evidence for policy decisions around personalized medicines, ultimately improving health at the individual and population levels while using scarce healthcare resources more efficiently

column36: Evaluating the Unintended Effects of an Intervention Combining Performance-Based Financing with Social Protection in Burkina Faso
column37: The low quality of healthcare and the presence of user fees in Burkina Faso contribute to low utilization of healthcare services and high levels of mortality. To improve access to high quality healthcare, national authorities have implemented an intervention that combines performance-based financing (PBF) with social protection strategies. However, the body of evidence on the implementation and effectiveness of PBF is not well established. There is an urgent need to examine if this intervention causes unintended effects. The objectives of this study will be 1) to conduct a systematic review of the literature on the unintended effects of PBF in low-income countries, 2) to determine, from empirical data, whether the different components of the intervention resulted in unintended effects and 3) to identify adaptation strategies to improve the intervention. We will use multiple sources of quantitative and qualitative data (e.g., interviews, observations, administrative data). The results of this study will help the global health community understand the unintended effects resulting from this complex intervention to improve the health of the population.

column36: The National CIHR Hepatitis C Network (NCHCN)
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a global health problem. In Canada, it is estimated that 242,500 individuals are infected with the incidence of approximately 4,000 new cases per year. The majority of newly infected individuals develop persistent infection and chronic liver disease over many years including liver cancer. Liver disease due to chronic HCV infection is the leading cause of liver transplant in North America. There is no vaccine for HCV and new infections remain a problem among vulnerable populations like people who inject drugs (PWID), aboriginals, men who have sex with men (MS) and in developing countries. New highly effective direct acting antivirals (DAAs) have offered new hope for eradication of HCV. However, these new drugs remain expensive and their long-term effects on reversing the epidemic of liver disease related to HCV and its associated economic burden remain unknown. In response to the CIHR call to create a National Research Network on Hepatitis C, we propose to establish a continuous pipeline from discovery to implementation to reduce HCV transmission, cure and improve the quality of life of persons infected with HCV, and to work towards the eradication of HCV infection in Canada. Our overarching goal is to conduct innovative and interdisciplinary research, build research capacity, and translate evidence for uptake into practice and policy, to improve HCV prevention and health outcomes of Canadians and contribute to the global effort to reduce HCV burden worldwide. We gather basic, clinical, and population health research expertise to tackle three major themes: 1.Prevention: To improve strategies and interventions to reduce HCV prevalence and HCV incidence in the Canadian population 2.Treatment: To elaborate strategies to improve treatment access, treatment uptake and adherence, and treatment outcomes 3.Outcomes: To generate evidence-based data on health outcomes of people living with hepatitis C to guide decision making.

column36: Dynamics of cell-to-cell mediated HIV-1 spread in the lymph node
column37: The human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) epidemic has infected approximately 75 million people worldwide, of which more than 35 million have died from acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-related complications. The development of antiretroviral therapy has been a great achievement of modern medicine, significantly prolonging the life span of infected individuals and reducing AIDS-related mortalities. However, ART is not curative, as evidenced by the rapid rebound in viremia seen in patients after therapy interruption, despite months of undetectable viremia. One possible explanation is that viral replication may persist at low levels in tissues where drug bioavailability is suboptimal. Indeed, recent findings show that antiretrovirals are largely ineffective at suppressing HIV infection when it is transmitted through cell-to-cell contact between infected and uninfected cells. Given the densely packed nature of lymphoid tissues, where explosive viral replication occurs, it is thus conceivable that cell-to-cell HIV transmission plays an important role in viral dissemination in humans. In this proposal, we will test this hypothesis, using innovative in vitro and in vivo imaging approaches, to study the cellular dynamics of contact-mediated viral spread. The implications are that the development of new therapeutic strategies must be able to remain effective against, or specifically target, this form of transmission.

column36: Proteinase-Activated Receptors as a therapeutic target in allergic inflammation
column37: Asthma affects more than 3 million Canadian, causing significant morbidity and high cost for the health care system. Although we have some excellent medications to treat airway inflammation, the majority of asthmatics remain poorly controlled. Developing a treatment strategy that minimizes discomfort and side effects will be of immense significance. Asthma is characterized by airway hyper-responsiveness, which is an exaggerated response of the airways to irritating stimuli, and airway inflammation, which is evident by the presence of large numbers of eosinophils in the airways and excessive mucus secretion. We have shown in mouse models that airway inflammation is dependent on the presence of specific molecules called serine proteinases. These molecules can activate a receptor on the surface of the airway epithelium called Proteinase Activated Receptor-2 (PAR-2). We will study the functions of this receptor in allergic airway inflammation using mouse models of asthma and airway epithelial cells isolated from human airway. We will also study PAR-2 expression on a type of blood cells called monocytes. Our data indicate that reagents that block PAR-2 activation have tremendous potential to become new therapeutic options for asthma. Our data also show that measuring the levels of PAR-2 in blood monocytes may be useful in predicting the severity of disease.

column37: The primary care system in Newfoundland & Labrador today looks much the same as it did 20 years ago, but the need for more comprehensive care among the residents of NL has been steadily increasing. The province is facing high rates of chronic diseases like diabetes, and a large proportion of the population is approaching retirement age. The Primary Healthcare Research and Integration to Improve Health System Efficiency (PRIIME) Network brings researchers, clinicians and policymakers in the province together with patients and their families to find ways to improve the way primary healthcare is delivered in our communities. PRIIME has significant expertise in health systems research, experience in using technology to improve care, an appreciation for the unique challenges faced by our rural and remote communities, and a dedication to pursue research outcomes that matter to patients. With the commitment of key decision-makers across NL, PRIIME has an opportunity to support major changes to the primary care system that will provide better care for patients from birth to death, particularly complex patients whose needs haven't always been met. The Network's leadership is dedicated to finding new ways to care for patients in community-based primary care while making efficient use of limited resources. PRIIME will look at changes to primary care that have worked in other parts of Canada, such as care teams that include doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other allied health practitioners working together to support their complex patients. The goal is to build a sustainable system of community-based primary health care in a way that will meet the needs and improve the health of Newfoundlanders and Labradorians.

The development of antiretroviral therapy has been a great achievement of modern medicine, significantly prolonging the life span of infected individuals and reducing AIDS-related mortalities. However, ART is not curative, as evidenced by the rapid rebound in viremia seen in patients after therapy interruption, despite months of undetectable viremia. One possible explanation is that viral replication may persist at low levels in tissues where drug bioavailability is suboptimal. Indeed, recent findings show that antiretrovirals are largely ineffective at suppressing HIV infection when it is transmitted through cell-to-cell contact between infected and uninfected cells. Given the densely packed nature of lymphoid tissues, where explosive viral replication occurs, it is thus conceivable that cell-to-cell HIV transmission plays an important role in viral dissemination in humans. In this proposal, we will test this hypothesis, using innovative in vitro and in vivo imaging approaches, to study the cellular dynamics of contact-mediated viral spread. The implications are that the development of new therapeutic strategies must be able to remain effective against, or specifically target, this form of transmission.

column36: Proteinase-Activated Receptors as a therapeutic target in allergic inflammation
column37: Asthma affects more than 3 million Canadian, causing significant morbidity and high cost for the health care system. Although we have some excellent medications to treat airway inflammation, the majority of asthmatics remain poorly controlled. Developing a treatment strategy that minimizes discomfort and side effects will be of immense significance. Asthma is characterized by airway hyper-responsiveness, which is an exaggerated response of the airways to irritating stimuli, and airway inflammation, which is evident by the presence of large numbers of eosinophils in the airways and excessive mucus secretion. We have shown in mouse models that airway inflammation is dependent on the presence of specific molecules called serine proteinases. These molecules can activate a receptor on the surface of the airway epithelium called Proteinase Activated Receptor-2 (PAR-2). We will study the functions of this receptor in allergic airway inflammation using mouse models of asthma and airway epithelial cells isolated from human airway. We will also study PAR-2 expression on a type of blood cells called monocytes. Our data indicate that reagents that block PAR-2 activation have tremendous potential to become new therapeutic options for asthma. Our data also show that measuring the levels of PAR-2 in blood monocytes may be useful in predicting the severity of disease.

column36: Canadian Epigenetics, Environment and Health Research Consortium Network
column37: The DNA that makes up the genome is tagged with various chemical marks that are attached either directly to the DNA or to its packaging proteins. These marks, collectively called the epigenome, act as a kind of molecular mark-up language that tells the cell's proteins which genes to activate and which to silence. Unlike the genome, which remains largely the same throughout life, the epigenome changes with age, in response to environmental influences, and in many types of disease. The field of epigenomics has seen explosive growth in recent years, due in part to a series of discoveries linking the epigenome to environmental risk factors and disease progression. Altered patterns of epigenomic marks help to explain how environmental influences can affect an individual's risk of chronic disease; for example, tobacco smoke exposure can alter the epigenome in lung cells. Epigenomic changes are pervasive in many cancer types, and may even be one of the first changes to take place in some pre-cancerous cells. While recent technological advancements have allowed scientists to study the epigenome at unprecedented resolution, these techniques demand expertise and resources that have thus far limited their uptake in the Canadian research community. Through this proposal, we aim to establish a pan-Canadian network that links together existing Canadian Epigenetics and Environment Health Research Consortium components with Nodes of Genome Canada's Genomics Innovation Network and other research labs to drive epigenomic research forward in Canada, and to provide outreach and training resources to the broader research community. Funding provided by this initiative will ensure that Canada remains a world leader in epigenomics by giving Canadian researchers knowledge of, and access to, emerging epigenomic technologies and data that are essential to realize the promise of epigenomics research for future generations of Canadians.

column36: The role of the immune system in obesity related insulin resistance and metabolic disease
column37: Obesity is associated with a metabolic syndrome characterized by high fat and sugar in the blood, and is linked to type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. Obesity associated metabolic disease is a major health concern, affecting more than 20% of Canadian adults, with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes alone affecting at least 10 million Canadians, and costing our healthcare system more than $10 billion. Despite this burden on Canadians, the underlying mechanisms of disease are poorly understood. The Winer lab and others have shown that low levels of inflammation lies at the core of metabolic disease. When people become obese, inflammation blocks the body's ability to respond well to insulin, called insulin resistance (prediabetes), and this process leads to high blood fatty acids and sugar, triggering type 2 diabetes and liver disease. The Winer lab has identified inflammation in the fat surrounding internal organs as a major cause of insulin resistance. In particular, fatty tissues in obese mice and people contain high amounts of white blood cells, including T and B cells that cause inflammation. These cells produce inflammatory molecules called cytokines, which cause insulin resistance. The identification of immune cells in fat controlling metabolic disease is considered as one of the "breakthroughs of the decade" in metabolic research. The goal of the research program is to build on this work, and investigate how the immune system drives insulin resistance in fat and in other organs like the liver and gut. The lab will also understand how insulin affects immune system function. The program will utilize the latest in high resolution and robotic equipment, mouse models, and metabolic assessment, with aim to translate findings in humans. This program may lead to new ways to prevent, diagnose, and treat diabetes. Moreover, it is only through study of the immune system will vaccines with the ability to prevent diabetes altogether become a future reality.

column36: Inherited susceptibility to cancer: from gene discovery to mechanisms to clinical applications
column37: Cancer is a common disease which is typically the result of genetic changes that lead to aberrant growth and behaviour of affected cells, which then produce tumours which can spread throughout the body. Some individuals are at higher risk for cancer because of a family history of the disease. In these families, critical genetic alterations are inherited from one generation to the next in cancer predisposition genes. A better understanding of these predisposing genetic changes is not only useful to help the individuals who are mutation carriers, but it also improves our general understanding of how cancers develop in everyone else in the population by better understanding which genes are involved and how. The work performed in our laboratory for the past 20 years has focused on the study of inherited cancers in high risk families. This work led us to identify a number of new cancer susceptibility genes where genetic alterations can cause disease. In addition, we have also identified very specific changes, referred to as founder mutations, which are observed at higher frequency in our local Quebec populations. There are several reasons to continue this important work. 1) The discovery of novel cancer susceptibility genes / mutations provides at risk patients with surveillance and prevention options for their cancers. This can improve the odds for patients to survive their cancer and can also improve their psychological well-being by giving them a measure of control over their disease. 2) The establishment of population-specific screening panels provides cost effective avenues for genetic screening tailored to local populations, making screening more financially accessible to the health care system providing this service locally. 3) Identification of mutations can allow physicians to choose more effective treatment options for some cancers by using targeted treatments based on the molecular profile of the patients and the tumours they harbour.

column36: Harnessing chemical biology to control pathogenic bacteria and regulate the gut microbiota
column37: Bacteria have the ability to either harm or help us. Harm comes from pathogenic bacteria that can cause infections. Help comes from beneficial bacteria, such as those that live in the human gut, that help to digest food and prevent infection. To eliminate harmful bacteria and promote the growth of beneficial bacteria, we must first study the underlying chemistry and biology that controls their growth and function. The proposed research program will study bacterial chemistry and biology in two ways: 1) we are developing new antibiotics against bacteria that cause infections; and 2) we are studying the biochemical pathways that enable beneficial bacteria to survive in the human gut. A brief summary of both components is provided below. The first part of the proposed research program aims to develop antibiotics to treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics are chemicals that specifically kill bacteria. Since the discovery of antibiotics, these chemicals have become essential medicines to prevent and cure infections. A key challenge for using antibiotics, however, is the emergence of drug-resistance, where bacteria acquire the ability to survive despite the presence of the antibiotic. We are developing new antibiotics to treat antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The second part of the proposed research program aims to understand how certain bacteria survive in the human gut. Babies are born with a sterile gut, and gradually acquire a complex community of bacteria through interaction with the environment. These gut bacteria help digest food and prevent infections by pathogenic bacteria. Many diseases are caused by 'microbial imbalance,' where the composition of bacteria and other microorganisms in the gut deviates from normal. We will investigate how the underlying chemistry and biology enable certain bacterial species to survive in the human gut. This knowledge could ultimately enable the development of probiotic and nutritional supplements to prevent and treat disease.

column36: Enteric neural and glial control of gastrointestinal function in health and inflammatory disease.
column37: The function of your digestive system is key to good health. During digestion food moves from the stomach to the small intestine, where absorption of nutrients occurs, and finally to the colon for elimination. Movement of food through the intestines requires precise control. Not only does the gut move and digest food, but while doing so it must protect the rest of the body from ingested pathogens and from the microbes that live in its lumen. These microbes are essential for health, but must remain in the intestine or they can cause harm. Thus the gut has a dual role: digestion and defense. Digestion and defense are sufficiently complex that a "brain" is required to regulate and control them. This brain in the gut is called the enteric nervous system (ENS). The ENS is composed of nerves and specialized cells called enteric glial cells. Enteric glial cells were originally thought to be passive support cells, but through my research we know that nerves and glial cells actively communicate with each other by releasing chemical messengers. This bi-directional nerve-glial communication is important for the ENS to control the movement of food through the gut and for defense. Alterations in chemical communication in the ENS appears to be responsible for many of the symptoms of gastrointestinal disease. The vision of my research program is to discover new ways to alleviate the symptoms of gut disorders through studies of enteric nerve-glial communication. I will study the movements of the gut in the normal state and establish how nerves and glial cells communicate to regulate them. I will build on this information to find new ways to correct the abnormal gut movements that occur in disease. I will also focus on how microbes in the gut influence the neural and glial regulation of gut functions in health and disease. My ultimate goal is to develop better treatments for debilitating conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and irritable bowel syndrome.

column37: The current proposal is founded on the discovery of a new approach for the treatment of autoimmune disease (occurring when the white blood cells of our immune system mistakenly recognize and attack natural components of our own tissues). Traditionally, vaccines have been used to expand white blood cells affording protection against viruses, bacteria or cancer, or to delete white blood cells causing autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes (T1D) and multiple sclerosis (MS). We have developed a new type of 'vaccine' based on nanotechnology (using particles thousands of times smaller than the size of normal white blood cell) that can stop anti-self immune responses by selectively expanding what we call 'autoregulatory' white blood cells. These 'autoregulatory' white blood cells put the brakes on the disease-causing autoimmune attack, by inhibiting the activation of all the disease-causing white blood cells, resulting in their complete suppression. As a result, these nanomedicines can blunt highly complex autoimmune responses in mice, including T1D, MS, primary biliary cirrhosis and arthritis, without causing generalized suppression of the immune system. Importantly, we have established that human disease-relevant nanomedicines can effectively trigger the expansion of human autoregulatory white blood cells in 'humanized' mice (mice carrying white blood cells from patients), indicating that this approach is applicable to humans. Here, we will dissect the cellular origin of the disease-suppressor cell type triggered by our nanomedicines, as well as the mechanisms and the downstream cellular targets through which it suppresses disease. Furthermore, we will use mice 'humanized' with white blood cells from T1D patients to select the corresponding drug candidates for clinical development. We anticipate that these studies will open new lines of inquiry in immunity and autoimmunity and will propel a promising new therapeutic avenue for autoimmunity to the clinic.

column37: My team discovered and characterized a family of 9 enzymes, known as the proprotein convertases (PCs), key molecular scissors involved in producing the final forms of active proteins. Abnormal (higher/lower) activities of these enzymes can result in severe biological disorders, and hence PCs are prime targets for therapy in a number of human diseases. We are world leaders in understanding the role of PCs in pathologies, including cardiovascular diseases resulting from high levels of the bad cholesterol (low density lipoprotein, LDL), cancer, viral infections, brain dysfunctions such as in Alzheimer's disease and those resulting in increased anxiety and depression. Resulting in large part from our pioneering work on this protein, new injectable treatments using antibodies to block PCSK9 have been developed and shown in early clinical tests to lower LDL by as much as 60% in high-risk patients. However, this approach has some limitations and our own research suggests that serious long-term effects could result from a general blockade of PCSK9. Our goal is to fully describe the molecular mechanisms through which PCSK9 acts and to use this knowledge to develop more effective and better-targeted drugs against PCSK9. 2-The engineered PC7 inactivation in mice results in much reduced anxiety, depression and emotional fear. In humans, lower PC7 levels are also associated with a more efficient iron metabolism, higher levels of the good cholesterol high density lipoprotein (HDL) and lower levels of the bad triglycerides. We will study the biology of PC7 in mice and humans and develop PC7 inhibitors that should find new therapeutic clinical applications for the above indications.

column36: Muscarinic cholinergic modulation of cognition in primates
column37: Changes in normal cognition are a characteristic feature of schizophrenia. These problems can be seen in a reduced attention span, difficulties to memorize things, poor judgment skills, and in difficulties to plan and prioritize everyday life. Although our current drugs are quite successful in treating hallucinations and delusions, they largely fail in treating these cognitive deficits. Cognitive deficits can easily be tested with simple eye movement tasks. For example, we have long known that people who suffer from schizophrenia show telltale eye movements under certain conditions. Told to look away from a flash of light, they are unable to resist the automatic urge to glance at the stimulus. Subjects without the disorder can override the impulse. In my research program, we will train monkeys to perform these simple, yet powerful eye movement tasks to find drugs that have effects on brain activity and task performance. We will focus on drugs that act on muscarinic acetylcholine receptors which have been proposed as a novel way to treat cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. We will record the activity of individual brain cells in different areas in trained monkeys, manipulate their activity through the application of drugs that act on different muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and measure brain-wide changes in activity and communication using functional imaging techniques. My goal is to understand the role of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in cognition from the level of single brain cells to the communication in the entire brain. By understanding how brain areas interact and how certain drugs can improve cognitive processes, we hope to identify drugs that will improve the cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

column37: Circulating in the blood is a myriad of cells with different functions that are critical for our health, including red blood cells that carry oxygen, platelets that help to stop bleeding and immune cells that fight off infections and cancers. These circulating blood cells are not immortal, but rather are constantly being renewed by a continuous repetition of the process that led to their initial specialization. In this complex process, banks of genes are turned on and off in precursor cells to "steer" their differentiation toward one specialized cell type or another. This occurs primarily through the action of proteins called transcription factors, which reside in the cell nucleus and can regulate the activity of thousands of genes simultaneously. Not surprisingly, mistakes sometimes occur in this complex process and can lead to a number of very serious diseases. My own research has focused on identifying the critical components in normal blood cell differentiation and in characterizing the molecular defects that lead, in particular, to bleeding disorders and blood-borne cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma. Over 20 years ago, I co-discovered two transcription factors (Gfi1 and Gfi1b) and was the first to determine the role of Gfi1 in blood diseases including leukemia. More recently, I discovered the role of another transcription factor and co-factor of Gfi1, called Miz-1, in blood cell formation and leukemia. My goal is to understand how key blood formation processes are controlled on a molecular level and how deficiencies in these processes that lead to diseases can be fixed. Over the next few years, we will bring together clinical expertise and the most advanced biomedical research techniques to address two blood cancers: acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) as well as inherited platelet disorders (IPD) that lead to blood clotting problems.

column36: Thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self
column37: Self/nonself discrimination by T lymphocytes is a fundamental requirement of life in vertebrates and is implicated in most fatal diseases in humans. Indeed, i) nonself recognition is essential for elimination of microbes and cancer cells, while ii) immune responses against self antigens cause classic autoimmune diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis) and are instrumental in chronic inflammatory diseases, hypertension and atherosclerosis. T lymphocytes learn how to distinguish self from nonself in the thymus. Importantly, the thymus ages more rapidly than all other organs, and by the age of 45 y, 75% of the thymus is lost in humans. Thymus senescence decreases the ability to recognize new antigens and responsiveness to vaccines, and increases the risk of infection, cancer and autoimmune diseases in ageing people. Hence, it is a sobering thought that our understanding of the molecular composition of the immune self is very rudimentary and that we do not understand the mechanisms of thymic involution. Accordingly, the two main themes of my research program are thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self. My specific objectives are i) to discover the molecular composition of the immune self, ii) to uncover how the immune self is perturbed in cancer cells, iii) to understand the rules governing T lymphocyte education in the thymus, and iv) to find a strategy to rejuvenate the thymus. Answers to these questions will be instrumental in i) treating thymus atrophy, the most common cause of immune deficiency in humans, ii) understanding the molecular bases of self-tolerance and enabling molecular evidence-based treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, and iii) discovering cancer-specific antigens that can be used as personalized vaccines for cancer treatment.

column37: Stroke and Parkinson's disease are devastating neurological disorders with devastating personal, social, and economic consequences. Stroke affects 15 million people a year worldwide and is the third leading cause of death. Parkinson's disease, a movement disorder, affects 10 million people worldwide and is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. We now realize that there are incredibly sophisticated processes that govern the death of brain cells in these conditions. Our work is focused on understanding these complex processes and blocking the signals that lead to death thereby eliminating or reducing the brain injury in these conditions. While seemingly simple in concept, this strategy is incredibly difficult. For example, multiple signals likely control the death process, some of which work in parallel to control the long-term survival of brain cells. Also, how/whether manipulation of these signals ultimately lead to a proper functioning brain circuit is unclear. Finally, because it is difficult to actually work in humans to manipulate these signals, the development and use of appropriate animal models of study are critical. Our research program takes all these complex issues into consideration to systematically work through the issues that are impeding effective therapeutic strategies to treat stroke and PD. We have exciting and novel insights into the complex network of events that occur in a brain damaged by stroke or in PD. We will critically test whether these signals effectively lead to improved brain circuitry and animal behavior in these diseases. Together with a team of researchers and clinicians, we are working to define the appropriate strategies to treat these devastating neurological conditions. Our work is central to this important effort.

column37: High blood pressure (hypertension) is an important silent killer that can cause heart attacks and stroke. Not only is hypertension a deadly disease, it also cost $76 B last year in the US alone. Current drugs used to control hypertension are costly, can induce unwanted side-effects and they are not always effective in controlling blood pressure (BP) in all hypertensive patients. Having a food that will control BP represents a less expensive intervention than drugs. We have recently completed a major tightly controlled trial in which patients with peripheral arterial disease were supplemented daily for one year with flaxseed in their diet. Patients who entered the trial with high BP were the most affected by dietary flaxseed and systolic BP decreased by 15 mm Hg, an effect comparable to most hypertensive drugs available today. This decline in BP would lower the incidence of heart attacks and strokes by more than 50%. In the Foundation grant, we will continue our research with an on-going CIHR clinical trial to determine if flaxseed will lower BP in patients with high BP but without secondary disease. We will also study if flaxseed can delay or reduce the need for anti-hypertensive drugs. In a separate line of study in animal models, we will also examine the potential for dietary flaxseed to reduce damage to the heart after a heart attack has occurred. The mechanisms responsible for the anti-hypertensive action of flaxseed as well as its effects on heart protection from heart attacks will be studied. Providing low cost alternatives to drug therapy that can be used alone or in conjunction with medication has enormous appeal for the Canadian health care system. Even more importantly, this low cost alternative to expensive medication for high BP represents an appealing choice for third world countries and poor communities everywhere that cannot afford the drugs they need to lower BP and protect themselves from heart attacks and strokes.

column37: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides unparalleled insight into human disease. Through continued technical innovation, we will further its utility by advancing image acquisition, quantitative analysis, and physics knowledge. Our novel brain MRI methods will be applied to stroke patients, where current MRI protocols are insufficient for accurate diagnosis in some patient subgroups (e.g. transient ischemic attack, wake up strokes). These MRI methods will also provide insight into typical brain development with age, a process important for 'normal' cognitive and behavioural maturation that may also provide clues about vulnerability to neurological or psychiatric disorders. In addition, advanced MRI will capture the lifelong impact that prenatal exposure to neurotoxins (e.g. alcohol) can have on the brain and its development. The outcomes of this research are: (i) Technical Innovation of Brain MRI - advanced quantitative MRI methods with higher spatial resolution and greater specificity to metabolic and microstructural changes in brain. (ii) Better MRI Diagnosis of Stroke - improved lesion detection in cases where clinical symptoms suggest stroke but conventional MRI lacks sufficient image resolution to confirm diagnosis, stroke onset time estimation to allow treatment for patients who wake with symptoms, and the discovery of the mechanisms behind the sensitivity of MRI for stroke. column36: Ultra-high field Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Brain Structure and Function in Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Canada's multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence rate is amongst the highest in the world at 240 per 100,000 population, for reasons we don't understand. Fortunately, there are drugs that can reduce the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease, but these drugs are very expensive. The lifetime cost of these drugs for a single MS patient is about $1 million. If we could come up with a way to decide when, and what dose of drug to deliver to each patient, we could save the health care system billions of dollars. The goal of our research program is to develop and use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods to inform such decisions, by measuring biomarkers of the disease. MRI has been used for many years as part of the diagnosis of MS. However normal MRI findings have not correlated well with clinical symptoms and have not demonstrated significant ability to predict the course of the disease. This may be related to the fact that conventional MRI visualizes only some of the lesions and damage seen by pathologists in brain slices. Ultra-high magnetic field MRI systems have the potential to be more sensitive to the microscopic changes in tissue properties that occur as MS begins and progresses. MRI machines at such magnetic field strengths are undergoing approvals for clinical diagnostic use. Using a 7 Tesla (140,000 times the earth's magnetic field) human MRI system, we will develop MRI techniques that can characterize MS in patients on a microscopic scale. This could lead to earlier diagnosis of MS, and therefore the ability to intervene sooner with drug treatments. Earlier intervention results in better patient outcomes and lower treatment costs

column36: Canadian Program for Monitoring Overuse in Injury Care

column36: Molecular and Genetic basis of heart development and disease
column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 1-5% of the population and represents the largest class of birth defects. It is the leading cause of death in infants during the first year of life. It is also an independent risk factor for premature onset of adult cardiovascular disease including degenerative valve disease, myocardial infarction and sudden death. It is well established that CHD is a heritable trait, i.e. it 'runs in the family'. However, its transmission does not follow simple Mendelian inheritance and is influenced by other genetic as well as environmental factors. Despite great advances over the past decade, the genes responsible for the majority of human CHD remain unknown. A better understanding of the genes required for normal heart development will immensely advance our understanding and detection of CHD. It will also improve care for individuals with CHD and help prevent cardiovascular complications. During the past decade, our lab has proudly contributed to this area thru our discovery and characterization of several genes essential for normal heart development such as GATA4 and GATA5. Alterations in these genes are associated with several types of human CHD, including bicuspid aortic valve, atrial and ventricular septal defects as well as rhythm abnormalities. Using our unique tools and animal models of human disease, we wish to pursue our studies aimed at understanding the genetics of normal and abnormal heart development. We will also use our animal models to gain a better understanding of how cardiac birth defects make the heart more vulnerable to other cardiovascular problems. Such knowledge will help design therapies for prevention and treatment that are presently unavailable. The results of our research will continue to impact diagnosis and care of individuals with heart disease or with a family history of the disease.

column36: A Rapid Analytics Platform for Influenza Vaccine Evaluation and Translational Research
column37: Influenza remains a major cause of death and illness in Canada and globally. "Seasonal" flu vaccines remain the mainstay of flu control, but their field effectiveness, especially among the sick and elderly who need them the most, is questionable. Newer expensive vaccines with limited data have mushroomed raising the cost and complexity of vaccine programs. Flu vaccine effectiveness (VE) is influenced by vaccine potency and uptake; viral strain, infectivity and virulence and by host characteristics; factors that often vary by season, product and population. Flu VE cannot be understood using one-off studies limited to specific seasons, populations and outcomes, and interpreted in isolation of viral and host characteristics. Our challenge is to design effective & sustainable strategies of continually and comprehensively evaluating conventional and novel flu vaccines and understanding their complex interactions with viral, host & environmental factors. I envision a safe and effective societal response to both seasonal epidemics and& pandemics. To this end, I propose to further develop our rapid analytics platform built on a continually updated comprehensive data warehouse and use it to address knowledge gaps, guide decision-making and develop new vaccine research methods. This research program will create methods and tools to create data warehouses and automate rapid analysis of their data which can be shared with other provinces and to develop an integrated rich data to facilitate research and quality improvement initiatives. column36: Wearable technology to assist with hand and finger function

column36: The biology and clinical significance of the tumour microenvironment in B cell lymphomas
column37: Lymphoid cancers are the fifth most frequent cancer in humans, affect patients of all ages, and despite generally effective treatments, a significant number of patients still die of their disease. In certain subgroups of lymphoid cancers, the malignant cells are surrounded by normal immune cells, yet these cells are unable to muster an effective immune attack against the tumor. In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in understanding how the malignant cells are evading the immune system. However, this improved knowledge has not yet been successfully translated into better treatments for patients. My proposed research program focuses on two related subtypes of lymphoid cancer - called Hodgkin lymphoma and Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma - that often affect adolescents and young adults. Furthermore, we will focus on the development of genetic tests that predict therapy resistance in childhood and adult Hodgkin lymphoma and identify patients at high risk of relapse. Our studies will be very important for physicians and patients as our research will develop clinical tests that provide information about the individual prognosis of lymphoma patient and will help developing new drugs and personalized treatments. Ultimately, these treatment improvements will lead to higher cure rates and fewer side effects for patients suffering from malignant lymphomas.

column36: Tuberculosis: From Genomics to Control
column37: As a doctor and a scientist, I ask why many people are exposed to the bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but only a minority develop the disease tuberculosis (TB). To understand these variable outcomes, I have established CIHR-funded programs of research that study the spread of this bacterium (epidemiology) and the fundamental biology of the disease (looking from both the perspective of the bacterium and that of the human host). The present application brings together three themes of TB research that share conceptual and methodologic synergies. In molecular epidemiology work (theme 1), our group makes a DNA 'fingerprint' of bacteria to track chains of transmission. This information, integrated with Public Health data, will define better ways to intervene with antibiotics in settings with drug sensitive and multidrug resistant settings. In bacteria-based studies (theme 2), our group compares the bacteria that causes TB with related bacteria that live in the environment and do not cause a contagious disease. These studies will uncover bacterial targets to neutralize in a new vaccine. In host-based studies (theme 3), our group studies how a part of the immune system, called innate immunity, recognizes Mycobacterium tuberculosis and how this translates into effective control of the infection. These studies will define host responses to be enhanced by a new vaccine. Together, these studies, carried out at the level of human populations and within a laboratory setting, will identify critical bacterial- and human-determinants of disease. I am one of very few TB researchers in the world who has the necessary training and a track record of success to lead this combination of studies. The information gained will drive the best application of existing antibiotics, to better control TB, and inform the development of a new vaccine, to eliminate TB.

column36: Insomnia: Research Innovations to Optimize Treatment Outcome in Primary Care
column37: Sleep problems are among the most common health complaints, with insomnia affecting 20% of adults at least occasionally and 10% on a chronic basis. Insomnia is characterized by difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep associated with distress and impairments of daytime functioning. Chronic insomnia produces significant psychological (increased risks of depression), physical (increased risk of hypertension), and economic burdens (reduced productivity and increased absenteeism). Despite some recent progress in insomnia research, there are still some major gaps in understanding and treating this sleep disorder. First, little is known about its risk factors and long-term consequences. Secondly, although chronic sleep disturbances are often associated with co-existing medical and psychiatric conditions, the specific role of psychological and biological factors in insomnia is still poorly understood. Thirdly, despite its high prevalence, insomnia often remains untreated and when treatment is initiated, it is usually limited to prescribed or over-the-counter drugs. Long-term use of sleep medications is often problematic due to their adverse effects and risks of tolerance and dependency. Behavioural therapies for insomnia are effective and well accepted by patients, yet they are not readily available and are infrequently used in practice. The main objectives of this research proposal are to: a) document the natural history, risk factors, and long-term health consequences of insomnia; b) develop more efficient and cost-effective therapies; and c) examine how we can make these interventions more accessible to those who need it (i.e., patients and health care practitioners). This research program is likely to have practical implications by producing new knowledge that will improve our understanding of insomnia and how best to treat it in clinical practice, hence reducing the individual and societal burden of this important public health problem.

column36: The pancreatic islet in human health and diabetes
column37: I am a world-leading expert on the insulin producing pancreatic islets of Langerhans. The result is an impaired regulation of metabolism that leads to an increased risk of stroke, heart disease, kidney failure, blindness, and amputation. Diabetes affects nearly 3 million Canadians and costs our healthcare system $17 billion annually. My group is ideally positioned address key questions about insulin secretion in clinically relevant tissue samples from patients with and without diabetes. To achieve this I have established a human pancreas tissue program, allowing us to study clinically relevant tissue from organ donors with and without diabetes. My group combines this with molecular, imaging, and cell physiological approaches to study: biochemical connections linking cellular metabolism with insulin secretion; the organization of insulin release at the cell membrane; and processes that underlie insulin secretory dysfunction in human T2D islets and animal models of diabetes. My lab is making important inroads in these areas, leading to a better understanding of insulin secretory function in health and diabetes. This work is informing drug development and testing through partnerships with industry, and providing new insights into how secretory dysfunction in T2D may be reversed.

column36: Immune Regulation during Chronic Disease
column37: Persistent viral infections are a global health concern, with over 500 million people infected with HIV and hepatitis B and C viruses. column36: Materials and Mechanisms for Understanding and Controlling Hemorrhage
column37: Uncontrolled bleeding is a leading cause of death in Canada and worldwide, particularly in young healthy adults. While there are a range of therapies for stopping blood flow, they are still ineffective in the most severe cases of hemorrhage. My research program aims to develop new therapeutics that can be used in severe bleeding, by exploring novel mechanisms that could explain why current therapeutics are ineffective in these scenarios. Specifically, we will investigate three possible approaches; 1) Improve the penetration of blood clotting agents to wounds using delivery vehicles that can move against blood flow, which otherwise washes away factors that promote clotting, 2) Increase the ability of platelets to induce clotting, as these cell are first-wave responders that naturally help blood clot, and 3) Increase the strength by which blood clots adhere to injured blood vessels. Each strategy is based on biochemical insights and drug delivery techniques that my lab has already developed, and the research program will focus on applying these techniques to understanding and treating severe bleeding. My lab is uniquely poised to address this issue due to our extensive experience in both blood biochemistry and biomedical engineering, as well as the extensive support we have received from clinicians and the industry, which will allow us to translate laboratory findings into the clinic. The short-term goal of this program is to identify limiting factors that prevent the successful treatment of severe bleeding with current therapeutics, and then use these insights to develop novel technologies that enhance blood clotting. In the long-term, this program will lead to new clinical tools for treating severe bleeding, and has the potential to reduce death and related complications from uncontrolled bleeding in Canada and abroad.

column36: Chromosome instability and synthetic lethality in yeast and cancer
column37: Effective cancer therapy exploits specific biological differences between cancer cells and normal cells. Cancer cells often have defects that reduce the efficiency of chromosome transmission. Indeed, mutations in cancer cells that cause chromosome instability (CIN) are now widely recognized to be an important driver in cancer initiation and progression. These CIN mutations also represent tumour specific genetic vulnerabilities that could be exploited in developing new cancer treatments. Because the same building blocks are used to construct organisms as diverse as yeast, worms, and humans, "model organisms" provide powerful experimental tools for investigating the mechanistic basis of disease and for developing potential therapeutic interventions. The goals of our work are to understand the mechanisms of chromosome transmission at the levels of genes, pathways, and networks using yeast and the nematode worm as models, and to directly relate our studies to cancer and the development of new cancer therapies. Using yeast genetic techniques, in particular, global synthetic lethality analysis, we will identify yeast genes, and the corresponding human gene counterparts, that define potential therapeutic targets for selective killing of cancer cells relative to normal cells. We will use yeast to rapidly test millions of possible combinations of tumour-associated defects, drug targets, and chemotherapeutic agents to identify effective combinations, and will prioritize them for further testing in tumour cell cultures. The results of our proposed research will provide a basic understanding of the mechanisms of normal chromosome transmission, and of the corresponding defects associated with cancer pathology. Our results will also lead to the identification of new drug targets and will enable the identification of new small molecule inhibitors and combination therapies that could be used for the selective killing of cancer cells in patients.

column36: Molecular regulation of muscle stem cell function in regenerative myogenesis
column37: I am interested in understanding the mechanisms that control stem cell function and applying this knowledge to improve health. Our studies are focused on muscle stem cells and how they function in the growth and repair of skeletal muscle. The research is critical for developing novel treatments for many muscle-wasting diseases, for example Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). Our studies have already transformed our understanding of the mechanisms that control muscle stem cell function and have led to the development of a protein called Wnt7a as a novel therapy. Second, we will define the mechanisms that regulate the division of muscle stem cells as this is a central control point that governs regeneration efficiency. We will investigate these control mechanisms with the longer-term goal of identifying targets and hence drugs that could be used to stimulate muscle stem cell function. Third, we will map the regulatory networks of proteins called transcription factors that control the expression of genes in muscle stem cells from healthy versus diseased tissue. This information is key to understanding how these stem cells function. Finally, we will identify new drugs capable of stimulating muscle stems cells to enhance muscle regeneration. In parallel, we will validate our findings on human muscle stem cells to transition our therapeutic strategies into the clinic. In conclusion, the research will advance our knowledge of stem cell function and lead to novel treatments for diseases involving wasting of skeletal muscle. Importantly, this work will improve the health of patients, and also benefit the families and care givers that are affected by these devastating diseases.

column36: Bridging the Gap in Paediatric Traumatic Brain Injury: Environmental, biological and clinical markers associated with preschool concussion and TBI
column37: Concussions and other traumatic brain injuries are a frequent cause of death and disability in youth, and children under the age of 6 are at particularly high risk. Older children with brain injuries often suffer serious mental, psychological, social, and behaviour problems. Even mild injuries have the potential to cause lasting problems in children because of subtle changes in how the brain works. Recently, international teams have been working to better understand the course of recovery in children with concussion or brain injury; however, children under 6 have generally been excluded from this research. This is extremely problematic because of the high prevalence of brain injuries in toddlers and preschoolers and because they are particularly vulnerable to the effects of brain injury. Indeed, injury to the brain disrupts normal development and critically affects acquisition of new knowledge and skills. Currently, we know very little about the consequence of brain injuries in young children, or what initial signs and symptoms might help us predict development in later years. This research program will investigate the functioning of young children after they sustain brain injuries and determine how we can predict their outcomes. We will also determine whether functional problems are associated with changes in the integrity of the brain or particular genetic predispositions. The results will help us to better understand how problems develop after brain injuries in the youngest and most vulnerable age group. In turn, these findings will lead to the development of clear guidelines for doctors and health practitioners to follow when treating young children after a concussion or brain injury. We will also be able to quickly identify preschoolers who are at-risk for problems after brain injury and provide them and their families with the resources needed to prevent problems before they occur and to foster their development and quality of life.

Via these strategies, this research will identify the gene variants that cause and influence outcome of two prototypical autoimmune diseases and elucidate the mechanistic pathways that link such variants to disease. column37: Bacterial infections are major threats to human health. In the last century, antibiotics have served as our arsenals to fight bacterial infections. However, unfortunately, bacteria have since evolved resistance against virtually all known antibiotics, in several cases only a few years after a new antibiotic was introduced. We therefore urgently need to develop novel strategies if we are to prevent the spread of antibiotic resistance, and to discover sustainable antibiotic reagents (i.e. for which resistance cannot easily evolve). I envision that I will lead the field to pioneer new antibiotic strategies to improve our healthcare system by employing "evolutionary approaches" to predict and prevent the evolution of antibiotic resistance. Second, using laboratory evolution and engineering, I will generate novel anti-virulence reagents, e.g. enzymes to degrade cell-to-cell signaling molecules and therefore inhibit biofilm formation. Targeting such molecules is a potentially sustainable antibiotic strategy as it is unlikely that bacteria can easily evolve resistance. My research program will create powerful new approaches and tools to combat multi-drug resistant pathogenic bacteria. My strong expertise in laboratory evolution and engineering, and established collaborations with structural biologists, microbiologists and computational biologists will enable me to effectively tackle this challenge. My CIHR Foundation program will lead us to the development of novel antibiotic strategies and reagents to battle against antibiotic-resistant pathogenic bacteria.

column36: Towards new therapeutics through manipulation of glyco-enzymes
column37: The surfaces of every cell in the human body are coated with specific sugars. These play several roles, principally providing a way for the cell to interact with other cells and their components. Invading bacteria and viruses also use these sugars as an entry point, thus an understanding of these interactions and of how the specific sugars are built and degraded, can lead to new therapeutics. An example is the influenza virus drug Tamiflu, which blocks the critical viral enzyme that cuts a sugar off our cell surfaces and allows the virus to spread. Our recent research has shown that some of the enzymes used by disease-causing bacteria and parasites in order to infect human cells are unlike any enzymes present in human cells. This allows us to design and synthesize new classes of drug to either specifically block these enzymes, as with Tamiflu, or to liberate toxins specifically within the invader. Using such approaches, in collaboration with microbiologists, we shall develop new strategies for treatment of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, as well as the parasites that cause Chagas disease in South America. In a second part of our work we shall use enzymes to modify these cell surface sugars for a variety of applications. In one case we use enzymes to cut specific sugars off the surface of red blood cells, thereby changing their blood type from A or B (or AB) to the "universal donor" Type O. Using an approach that mimics the process of natural evolution, but accelerates it, we shall engineer these enzymes to speed them up for clinical use. This work should greatly improve our supply of blood for transfusions. In a second case we shall use enzymes to improve the performance of increasingly important protein-based drugs such as antibodies and growth factors. Most such proteins have sugars on their surface that play important roles. We shall engineer enzymes to add sugars in a highly controlled manner, yielding drugs of improved performance.

column36: Neurovascular and neuroimmune interplay in retinal vasculopathies
column37: Loss of eyesight is the most feared ailment in North America after cancer. The part of the eye that senses visuals scenes and transmits them to the brain is a structure rich in nerve cells and blood vessels called the retina. This structure is biochemically part of the brain. In debilitating diseases of the retina such as the sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity and age-related macular degeneration, the degeneration of blood vessels precipitates loss of nerve cell function. These retinopathies are the leading causes blindness in the industrial world and account for over 25 million cases of compromised vision in North America. The degeneration of blood vessels in the retina prevents nutrient and oxygen delivery and leads to a constellation of biochemical changes that deregulate cellular function. While the body attempts to repair and restore blood vessels, there are a number of yet unknown factors that hinder reparative vessel growth and consequently aggravate the loss of nerve cell function. Current treatment paradigms are largely inefficient and focus on destroying diseased blood vessels instead of repairing those that provide oxygen and essential nutrients. An attractive alternative approach would be to regenerate functional vessels into zones of the retina where vessels were damaged. In this proposal we outline a therapeutic strategy that would restore healthy blood vessels to the retina in retinopathies. This approach will help design new medications and be achieved by molecularly altering the response of retinal nerve cells to vascular injury.

column36: Targeting the dynamics and genomics of clonal evolution in cancer patients
column37: Cancers evolve over time and the gene mutations driving them can change. A major bottleneck in the treatment of epithelial cancers is a lack of diverse therapeutic / treatment options. Our studies have the potential to answer specific questions about how breast cancer arises, progresses, and becomes resistant to treatment. These findings will have a global impact within the cancer research community, allowing the design of improved and more effective therapies. In short, the practical application of cancer cell genetics will become a reality in the clinic -- representing a significant step forward in direct translational benefits for patients.

column36: Epigenetic Approaches to Enhance Cancer Immunotherapy and to Target Cancer Initiating Cells
column37: The premise of Cancer Immunotherapy is to stimulate the patient's immune system to attack the tumour cells. Recent progress in cancer immunotherapy protocols has led to a transformation in the treatment of several types of solid tumours. However, the majority of Colorectal Cancer (CRC) patients do not respond to immunotherapy, suggesting the need to combine immunotherapies with other anti-tumour strategies. Unfortunately, chemotherapy - the mainstay of cancer treatment for over 40 years - is immunosuppressive and not suitable for combination with immunotherapy. The source of therapeutic resistance is due to a rare group of cells within the tumour called cancer-initiating cells (CICs, also known as cancer stem cells) that are responsible for the continued tumour self-renewal. These CICs are highly resistant to chemo- and radiation therapy. Evidence from mouse models of cancer and human clinical trials indicates anti-cancer therapies select for and increase the number of CICs in tumours, which explain why tumours tend to be more resistant following the initial rounds of therapy. We have found that DNA demethylating agents can target colorectal CICs. We will explore a strategy of targeting CICs using epigenetic therapy and how it can be used to avoid tumour recurrence with the ultimate aim of curing this disease.

column37: Sexually transmitted infections (STI) are a major public health concern among Canadians. Screening for early signs of cancers caused by HPV, such as Pap tests for women, can ensure proper follow-up to prevent cancer development. Solutions will specifically address communities that may be harder to reach due to stigma and poverty. First, we will find out why people do or do not get vaccinated or tested for STIs and cancers caused by HPV. Next we will test new ways to offer vaccination & screening to see which are most effective and practical. Finally, we will follow our progress over the long term to ensure that chosen strategies protect the health of Canadians for years to come. Globally, 1 million people acquire an STI each day. column36: Living Kidney Donation: Improving Safety, Access, and Outcomes
column37: Kidney Failure: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Living Kidney Donation: It is safe for a living person who is healthy to donate one of their kidneys. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often volunteer to donate one of their kidneys. With advances in transplantation, the donor and recipient do not have to be related or be of the same gender, race, or age. Canada and other countries are looking for ways to safely increase living kidney donation. Barriers to Living Kidney Donation: Unfortunately, many patients who would benefit from a kidney transplant do not receive one. There are many reasons for this. Doctors do not always talk to their patients about transplantation. Patients are often uncomfortable discussing living kidney donation with family and friends. Many people do not realize that it is safe to donate a kidney; some are told they are too old to donate despite new research showing it is safe if they are healthy. As well, donor evaluation often takes a year to complete (when it should only take 3 months). A long evaluation process has negative consequences for both donors and recipients. Safely Increasing Living Kidney Donation: My research team is working with living kidney donors and transplant programs to develop and test solutions to overcome barriers to living kidney donation. As well, we are studying a large group of living kidney donors over many decades to confirm long-term safety. Information from our studies will enable more patients with kidney failure to safely receive transplants, and will help candidates make informed decisions about becoming living kidney donors.

column36: New Resources for Chemical Genomics and Metabolomics in Biomedicine
column37: Small molecule compounds such as drugs, nutrients and pollutants affect our health in many ways. Nutrients are needed to sustain life, drugs are needed to cure us of illnesses, while pollutants can kill us. Millions of these compounds exist. The complete collection of these compounds is called the "metabolome" -- derived from the word metabolite (a substance produced by metabolism). The study of how the metabolome affects us is called metabolomics. While metabolomics is a relatively new field, scientists have been collecting detailed information about metabolites for ~100 years. Unfortunately, most of this data is scattered in millions of textbooks and journal articles. The lack of centralized databases or electronic resources for metabolomics means that we still know very little about the chemical universe around us. My long-term research goal is to develop the resources needed to address these problems. Using advanced methods in information technology and analytical chemistry, my lab has created a number of databases and software tools that are helping to answer some of these questions. Our plan is to greatly improve these resources by using the latest techniques in artificial intelligence. By using computers to automatically identify and harvest vast amounts of data from the literature and learn from that data, it should be possible to develop far better resources that will allow us to better characterize, predict and exploit the chemical universe around us. column36: Families Overcoming Risks and Building Opportunities for Well-being (FORBOW): Early Intervention Targets Psychopathological Antecedents to Pre-empt Severe Mental Illness in Youth at Risk
column37: Severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression, tends to develop in late adolescence. Once the illness is established, available treatments cannot cure it. Early intervention before the illness develops may avoid years of suffering and disability. Families Overcoming Risks and Building Opportunities for Well-being (FORBOW) tests a novel type of pre-emptive early intervention that aims to prevent severe mental illness. In addition to youth from the general population, we include children of parents with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression, who are themselves at high risk of developing a mental illness. This risk is increased further among those who show antecedent symptoms like mood lability, anxiety and unusual sensory experiences. We focus on assessing these symptoms as well as using genetic tests to identify individuals who may benefit most from pre-emptive early interventions. In those aged 9-17 who have one or more antecedent symptom, we test the Skills for Wellness (SWELL) intervention, which helps young people learn skills that not only address their present problems, but also equip them to deal with future challenges. Half of the eligible youth are randomly selected to be offered the SWELL intervention. We monitor all participants annually to assess their health and development. We test the effects of the intervention by comparing those who were offered SWELL against those who were not offered the intervention. We also want to find out whether a genetic test may help select individuals who are most likely to benefit from the intervention. Our vision is to provide timely personalized interventions to maximize the benefits for mental health of the next generation.

column36: Multimodal strategy to identify novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets in lung and pancreatic cancer
column37: My research program focuses on lung and pancreatic cancer, the first and fourth most common cause of cancer deaths among Canadians. These two cancers account for 16% of new cancer cases in Canada in 2015, but disproportionately account for 33% of all cancer deaths. Currently, only 16% and 5% of lung and pancreatic cancer patients are expected to survive beyond 5 years. During the last decade, major advances in the treatment of lung cancer have been achieved through the discovery of genetic changes that transform airway lining cells into cancer cells. Mutations in cancer causing genes result in increased activation of their cell growth/survival pathways, to which the cancer cells become dependent on. New drugs developed to shut down the activities of these mutated genes cause dramatic tumor shrinkage in high percentage of patients whose tumor harbor the target mutations. This personalized cancer treatment strategy has generated tremendous excitement in oncology, even though the numbers of patients who may benefit from these new drugs remains a small proportion of lung cancer patients in Canada. However, a similar initial success has not been achieved for pancreatic cancer patients. Due to the complexity of cancer genetic and biology, our understanding of critical cellular and molecular pathways driving cancer cell growth and spread is still superficial, and drug response and resistance mechanisms remain to be explored. During the last few years, my laboratory has identified novel genes that play such important roles. We have also developed new experimental models and resources to investigate their biology and clinical relevance. The goals of my Foundation program are to gain greater understanding on how these novel genes drive the malignancy of lung or pancreatic cancers, and to develop new agents targeting some of these genes for improving the diagnosis and treatment of these two deadly cancers.

column36: Transforming chronic kidney disease care:A personalized, patient-centered approach
column37: Approximately 1 in 10 adults have chronic kidney disease (CKD), a condition that is associated with poor health outcomes and poor quality of life. Patients with earlier stages of CKD are cared for by family doctors, while those with more severe disease are cared for by nephrologists in special clinics.
