column36: Non-communicable Diseases in Obstetrics: Improving Quality of Care and Maternal-Infant Outcomes through an Obstetrical Research Network
column37: The rising incidence of non-communicable diseases (NCD), including diabetes, hypertension and obesity, remains one of the greatest challenges to global health. The incidence of NCD in pregnancy mirrors this global pattern, and has a major impact on short- and long-term maternal and infant health, including preterm birth, fetal growth restriction and perinatal mortality, as well as predisposition of the infant to future obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Unfortunately, information regarding the optimal management of pregnancies complicated by NCD is lacking. Studies on the management of these pregnancies requires large-scale collaborative efforts to identify risk factors for adverse outcomes and to evaluate the impact of interventions on maternal and neonatal outcome in pregnancies complicated by NCD. Our aim is to establish a multi-disciplinary research team that will utilize a unique infrastructure of an existing obstetrical research network to improve maternal and neonatal health in pregnancies complicated by NCD. The Southern Ontario Obstetric Network (SOON) is a unique, recently established, network of 9 academic and 11 non-academic hospitals that account for over 60,000 births per year, and is committed to sharing resources, data and knowledge to create best practices/guidelines and conduct research. We plan to use this platform in order to conduct a series of studies that will address the following questions: 1) Assess the impact of NCD on preterm birth and maternal and neonatal health; 2) Identify risk factors for preterm birth and adverse pregnancy outcome in pregnancies complicated by NCD, 3) Identify knowledge gaps and variation in care of pregnancies complicated by NCD; and 4) Explore the ability of medical and educational interventions to improve maternal and neonatal outcome in pregnancies complicated by NCD.

column36: Collaborative Obesity in Pregnancy Research Group: Supporting a Team to Investigate Placental Adaptations to Obesity.
column37: Canada, like most developed nations, is in the midst of an obesity epidemic: one in four adults is currently classified as obese, with this number expected to increase to one in three in the next two decades. In London Ontario, 45% of births are by overweight or obese mothers, posing significant management challenges for obstetrical providers. Pregnant women with obesity have a 2 to 3-fold increase in pregnancy complications related to preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. In addition, the obstetrician has significant difficulties in obtaining and interpreting results from routine tests that screen for pregnancy complications and work well in the pregnancy without obesity. Through their Collaborative Obesity in Pregnancy Research Team, Drs. de Vrijer and Eastabrook, early and mid-career Maternal-Fetal Medicine clinician-researchers, propose to develop new tools to address the unique needs of the obese pregnant woman in prevention of adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preeclampsia, and fetal growth restriction. The proposal will target the mother's cardiovascular and metabolic health and the effect of the associated chronic stress effect on the placenta and fetus, using novel technologies such as MRI (IDEAL and BOLD), assessment of metabolic stressors (metabolomics), placental response to stress (autophagy) and maternal blood vessel stiffness (pulse wave analysis). Support is sought for the Collaborative Obesity in Pregnancy Research Team, which includes well established clinical and basic scientist collaborators, to build the administrative, educational and research infrastructure to make this group successful in knowledge translation and future grant applications. This group has found excellent mentorship in Drs. Han and Lala, renowned clinical and basic science researchers (respectively) and will be supported by the University of Western Ontario, the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology and Western's Children's Health Research Institute.

column36: Equipe de cliniciens-chercheur sur la Recherche en prematurite : vers un depistage precoce et une prise en charge personnalisee.
column37: La naissance prematuree, c'est-a-dire qui survient avant 37 semaines de grossesse, touche environ 1 naissance sur 10. C'est une cause importante de deces des nouveau-nes. La prematurite a un impact important pour les couts de la societe et pour les familles. Il y a deux causes principales de prematurite : celle dite 'spontanee', par exemple un travail pre-terme, et celle dite ' medicalement induite', par exemple quand le travail est provoque pour une pression arterielle elevee et grave pour la mere et son bebe (une condition nommee pre-eclampsie). Notre projet d'equipe est axe sur la prematurite. Nous voulons mieux comprendre ses causes et pouvoir proposer des traitements adaptes aux patientes dans le but de prevenir l'accouchement pre-terme et les consequences parfois graves pour le nouveau-ne. Notre equipe est composee de trois cliniciens-chercheurs qui seront guides durant toute la duree du projet par deux mentors tres experimentes dans le domaine de la prematurite. L'equipe de recherche inclut aussi des experts indispensables pour repondre aux questions qui seront etudiees et pour transmettre les conclusions aux medecins et aux patientes. Il y a trois projets principaux proposes et les questions portent sur 1) une approche de traitement (pessaire et progesterone) pour prevenir la prematurite, 2) l'evaluation d'un test urinaire (podocine) pour predire la pre-eclampsie, et 3) la validation d'une methode pour mieux classer les differentes causes de la prematurite et evaluer leur impact sur la sante du nouveau-ne. Ces projets sur la prematurite se derouleront dans trois centres de soins et de recherche situe au Quebec (villes de Sherbrooke, Montreal et Quebec). Il y a un total de pres de 14 000 naissances/an dans ces 3 centres. Ce grand nombre permettra a notre equipe de pouvoir repondre plus rapidement aux questions sur la prematurite et ameliorer les soins aux patientes suivies durant leur grossesse.

column36: Gene Environment Team on Brown/beige Adipose Tissue (GET_BAT)
column37: More than 5 million Canadians have the chronic interrelated diseases of obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) and their incidence in the population are rapidly increasing. Obesity is an important risk factor for developing NAFLD and T2D which contribute to the development of liver cancer and heart disease. Therefore, designing new ways to treat or prevent T2D and NAFLD are important. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is an organ which has long been known to exist in rodents and infants but remarkably only in the last 5 years has been discovered in adult humans. BAT has the unique capability, compared to any other organ in the body, to burn large amounts of sugar and fat and effectively dissipate this energy as heat due to the presence of unique protein called uncoupling protein 1. Thus BAT is frequently characterized as the body's furnace. The activation of BAT in rodents has been shown to reverse obesity, T2D and NAFLD. In addition recent studies have shown that by exposing humans to cold you can increase BAT activity and lower blood sugar levels suggesting that increasing BAT activity may represent a viable therapy for treating T2D. Unfortunately, in individuals with obesity or T2D the ability to switch on BAT is compromised. Determining why BAT activity is reduced and identifying new ways to switch it on has generated world-wide scientific and clinical excitement around developing a new therapy for obesity, NAFLD and T2D and is the focus of the current proposal. In this proposal we will conduct studies in cells, mice and humans to examine how agricultural and food processing practices may regulate BAT metabolic activity directly or indirectly by altering the billions of bacteria that reside within our gastrointestinal tract. These studies will help us develop new strategies to enhance BAT activity that may be effective for treating and preventing obesity, NAFLD and T2D.

column36: The diet-microbiota-gut axis in pediatric IBD
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) describes a group of chronic conditions of the digestive system whose hallmark is unrelenting inflammation of the lining of the intestines. Crohn's disease (CD) and Ulcerative colitis (UC) are the two main subtypes of IBD. There are no cures for IBD and the ultimate cause also remains unknown. Accurate early diagnosis and effective treatments are important in reducing suffering and complications. The identification as to why these diseases develop may lead to ideas and ways about how to prevent and treat them. For instance, how the bacteria (microbiota) normally work together in our intestines is believed to play an important role in keeping us healthy but its disruption can lead to IBD. It is well accepted that the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in breaking down the food we eat into important nutrients that are essential for human health. In addition, what we eat is also known to affect which bacteria are present in our intestines and what they do. Based on this knowledge, we propose to assess the contribution of diet in the development and unrelenting continuation of the inflammation that defines IBD. This research program will investigate the complex interactions among diet, the gut microbiota and the host and provide information that may be important for personalized dietary and microbiota changes needed to keep people with IBD healthy. We propose to characterize the impact of the diet on the activities of intestinal bacteria to understand whether and how specific diet components or food consumption habits may lead to IBD and contribute to the ongoing inflammation or reasons why current treatments fail in some children. This study will generate the information required for the development of methods to improve bacterial activities in our intestine as treatment for IBD patients. This research will have important implications for the quality of life of people with IBD everywhere.

column36: The impact of the gut microbiome and environment on the development of colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. Although significant efforts have been employed to understand the cause of this disease, the mechanism remains elusive. Drs. Alberto Martin and Catherine O'Brien are leading a team of international recognized researchers to investigate the role of bacteria that reside in the gut in the development of colorectal cancer. The previous and proposed research from this team show that gut bacteria is at the root of colorectal cancer; its manipulation of dietary nutrients such as complex carbohydrates and the subsequent impact on metabolic processes within the gut promotes the development of colorectal cancer in mice and humans that are genetically-predisposed to develop this disease. The research has the capacity to develop diagnostics if a specific bacterial species is identified as the causative agent in colorectal cancer. In addition, the research will lead to the development of preventative protocols for colorectal cancer using alterations in diet or specific antibiotics that displace or out-compete "pathogenic" strains.

column36: The Developmental Origins of Obesity and Obesity-related Complications in Children
column37: Obesity is the fastest growing chronic illness in Canada, not only among adult men and women, but also in pregnant women and children. Pre-pregnancy obesity is a factor that increases the likelihood that a woman will develop diabetes during pregnancy. In turn, exposure to diabetes during pregnancy influences the risk for obesity development in children, according to recent findings. Our understanding of how a mother's diabetes during pregnancy influences the development of obesity in children is incomplete. We plan to study populations of children and their mothers in combination with rodent models of diabetes during pregnancy, to determine how the maternal environment influences the development of obesity in their children. Our research aims to identify new biomarkers of obesity risk that could be used to prevent the extensive health and financial burden of obesity in children and future generations.

column36: Exploring Biomarkers of Violence and Aggression in Vulnerable Psychiatric Populations across the Lifespan
column37: Human violence is a common phenomenon that takes a large toll on society and affects people of all ages. Although most individuals with psychiatric illness are not violent, some mental disorders are associated with increased risk of aggression toward oneself and others. Persistent violence may relate to underlying brain abnormalities. Hence, research that strives to understand the brain differences of people who engage in repeated aggression could lead to new treatment tools and violence prevention strategies. We propose using state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques to examine brain chemistry and functioning in psychiatric patients who are habitually aggressive. Because violence affects people of all ages, we will study adults and youth. The overall goal of the research is to identify brain chemicals linked to adult aggression that could be targeted by new medications and to learn how youths' brain functioning improves when they receive talk therapies aimed at decreasing violent behavior. The knowledge generated by these studies could stimulate new treatments for persistent violence and ultimately lead to improved health outcomes for both perpetrators and victims of violence.

column37: Death from cardiovascular disease is the number one killer in the Western World with associated cardiac arrhythmias causing ~50% of cardiovascular deaths. AF severely impairs heart function, contributes to heart disease progression and is the major cause of stroke. Although exercise provides enormous cardiovascular benefit, excessive exercise can also induce AF. Our studies will determine the molecular and genetic mechanisms involved in AF induction by cardiovascular disease, reveal the modulating influences of exercise, and identify novel approaches for treating and preventing AF.

column37: More and more Canadians are affected by chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive lung disease, diabetes and mental illnesses. Many of these conditions have their origins in early life (conception, pregnancy, infancy and childhood) and a number of very good Canadian pregnancy and birth cohort studies have been implemented to explore hypotheses related to such Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD). column37: Over the last decade, the notion that tissue regeneration or healing is maintained by organ specific stem cells, the so-called "tissue stem cells", has created great excitement in the medical community. Tissue stem cells are characterized by the ability to give rise to multiple cell types as well as have self-renewing ability. Despite the clear importance that tissue stem cells play in normal homeostasis and disease states, the identification of these cells has proven challenging as they are not readily distinguishable from other cells. In the rapidly proliferating gastrointestinal epithelium, stem cells that are long-lived are responsible for tissue regeneration, but also remain the most likely cell of origin for cancer. Recent work has demonstrated that the protein leucine rich repeat containing G-protein coupled receptor-5 (Lgr-5) marks a group of actively dividing stem cells known as the crypt base columnar (CBC) cells. Their identification has created considerable enthusiasm in regards to understanding how the gastrointestinal epithelium regenerates in response to injury and our identification of the cellular origin of cancer. More recently, our studies show unequivocally that Krt19 marks radioresistant colonic stem cells, distinct from Lgr5+ cells, and give rise to tumors. Furthermore, we have shown that another protein Dclk1 identifies unique quiescent and long-lived cells within the gut that serve as facultative stem cells. Unlike Lgr5+ and Krt19+ cells, Dclk1+ tuft cells do not divide, even in the context of genetic mutation, yet become cancer initiating cells only upon inflammatory insult. Thus, in the following studies, we propose to use our novel mouse models and in vitro human culture systems to characterize these stem cell populations so that we may better target the cellular origin of cancer.

column37: Proper function of the immune system is essential for protection against infectious disease and maintaining human health. During the onset of infection, white blood cells and platelets release signaling molecules known as cytokines, which orchestrate a protective inflammatory response. column36: Inflammation, Microbiome, and Alimentation: Gastro-Intestinal and Neuropsychiatric Effects: the IMAGINE-SPOR chronic disease network.
column37: 40% of Canadians suffer from gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms of abdominal pain and a change in bowel habit. The commonest causes for these symptoms are inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (affecting 0.5 million) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) (affecting 6 million). Canada has the highest rates in the world for these diseases and they cost the health care system $7.7 billion per year. IBS can occur at any age and IBD typically first presents in teenagers and young adults but then lasts life long as there is no known cure. IBD patients often need powerful drugs to suppress the immune system and sometimes surgery to remove part of the bowel. Mental health issues such as anxiety and depression affect IBS and IBD sufferers more than normal. The cause of these disorders is unknown and it is unclear why they are connected to mental health problems. We are now are beginning to understand the role our gut bacteria play in GI and mental health. Our intestines would occupy the area of a football field if stretched outside our body. This vast area is teeming with bacteria that outnumber our own body cells 100:1 and yet the intestines also have to stay permeable so that we can absorb the nutrients that we eat. It is astonishing that we are not ill all the time and we stay healthy because most of our immune system is focused on our GI tract. This is a delicate balancing act and disease may arise because the equilibrium between our gut bacteria and our immune system is disturbed. This concept has been proven in animal experiments that show IBS, IBD, and psychiatric disorders can be linked to changes in gut bacteria. We have developed a network of researchers across Canada that will study the gut bacteria and diet of IBD and IBS sufferers compared to those that are healthy. We will use this information to develop changes in diet, probiotics, fecal transplants or antibiotics to improve IBD, IBS and mental health. With this network we can start to IMAGINE a cure for these diseases.

column36: SPOR Network in Diabetes and its Related Complications
column37: Individuals with diabetes fear suffering from blindness, limb amputations, kidney and heart failure, and low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). These complications are influenced by genetic risk, life-style, sex/gender, socioeconomic and cultural (e.g., Indigenous) status, geography (rural) and co-morbid disease (e.g., arthritis). Patients and non-researcher health professionals have joined our SPOR Network to redefine methods for earliest diagnosis and treatments that will transform the health outcomes for all with diabetes. With primary care and specialist health networks across Canada, we will establish a national diabetes patient registry to evaluate best methods for screening of complications and relevant health determinants. We will design a smart-phone app, Risk Calculator, to aid patients and healthcare providers in their shared decision-making about care paths customized to address unique risk. By linking clinical information with other biological factors (genetics, medical imaging of affected organs), we will identify why some individuals have higher risk than others for complications. This knowledge will guide our development of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions to be applied before clinical signs of complications appear. To achieve best glucose control and prevent hypoglycemia we will develop and test innovative external artificial pancreas therapies in conjunction with smart-phone apps to monitor glucose control, physical activity and other modulators. We will evaluate novel diagnostic tests and therapies discovered by our scientists for diabetic heart, kidney, eye and nerve disease, along with user-friendly web-based tools to assess lifestyle (diet, physical activity) and effectiveness of personalized behaviour-modifying interventions. By aligning biomedical, clinical, population health and health services research and education with what matters most to patients we will bridge the knowledge translation gap with real impact on chronic disease outcomes.

column36: Listening, Learning, Leading: Canadians Seeking Solutions and Innovations to Overcome Chronic Kidney Disease (Can-SOLVE CKD)
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects nearly 4 million Canadians, particularly Indigenous peoples, children and the elderly, and patients with CKD have a quality of life similar to those with advanced cancer. Treating people with CKD and kidney failure is very expensive, costing the health system nearly $50 billion per year in Canada. Kidney disease is very common in people with diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, and kidney disease increases the risk of dying in such patients by two to eight-fold. The Canadians Seeking Solutions and Innovations to Overcome Chronic Kidney Disease (Can-SOLVE CKD) Network is a national partnership centered around patients and involving all key stakeholder groups: patients, caregivers, health practitioners, policy-makers, and researchers. Our Network will create new national core infrastructure that can support research, knowledge translation and training for years to come. Over the last three years, we have worked with patients with CKD and policy-makers to determine their top research priorities. We then developed a research program around these projects, which focus on three themes: Theme 1: Identify Kidney Disease Earlier and Support Those at Highest Risk of Negative Outcomes; Theme 2: Define Best Treatments to Improve Outcomes and Quality of Life; and Theme 3: Define the Optimal Ways to Deliver Patient-centered Care in the 21st Century. Over the next 5 years, our research program will find and test new discoveries. Evidence will be translated into practice and care to benefit patients. We will build capacity among junior scientists in patient-oriented research, and will also educate patients and policy-makers about this type of research. Our vision is that by 2020, every Canadian with, or at high risk for, chronic kidney disease will receive the best recommended care, experience optimal outcomes and have the chance to participate in studies of novel therapies, regardless of age, sex, gender, location or ethnicity.

column36: Understanding the interaction between methionine metabolism and epigenetics in cancer
column37: Cancer cells have distinct metabolic features that allow them to achieve uncontrolled proliferation, survival, and long-term maintenance. Cancer cells are known to have increased consumption of glucose for fermentation, namely the Warburg effect, but other metabolic pathways altered in tumorigenesis are largely unexplored. This proposal is to investigate the functional relevance of one carbon metabolism, particularly methionine in tumor growth. The study will focus on the interactions among methionine metabolism, tumour growth and cancer epigenetics. The methylation status of histones and DNA referred to as epigenetics determines cell state through regulating gene expression. The epigenetics, coupled with genetic sequence, determines gene expression and function and further contributes to physiological phenotypes and pathological symptoms. Epigenetic modifications are deregulated in cancer, demonstrating global DNA hypomethylation, but paradoxically hypermethylation of certain specific genes that are likely to be tumor suppressors. Enzymes modulating epigenetics are currently targets of many drug development efforts. However, the relevance of metabolism to methylation is largely unexplored. Dietary methionine provides direct substrate for generating the universal methyl-donor S-adenosylmethionine that further mediates cellular methylation reactions. Recent studies show the beneficial effects of dietary methionine restriction on obesity and longevity, two phenotypes closely related to anti-tumorigenicity. Our prior studies have also linked alterations of methionine metabolism with changes of histone methylation. This proposal will follow up to explore the effects of methionine restriction on tumour growth and cancer epigenetics through methylation. The outcome will determine the potential of methionine restriction as a cancer therapy, and will possibly uncover a new role of methionine metabolism in epigenetics that will be targeted for cancer therapy.

column36: Investigating the socio-structural context and impact of new Canadian legislation and criminal policies (C-36) on HIV/STI risks among sex workers and their clients
column37: In Canada and globally, sex workers continue to experience high rates of HIV/STI (sexually transmitted infection), violence, and poor access to health care services. Despite the significance of socio-structural factors (e.g., laws, stigma, social support) in influencing the HIV epidemic, large research gaps remain in our understanding of how these factors affect HIV/STI risks for sex workers. For the first time in Canadian history, new sex work legislation (C-36, implemented December 2014), criminalizes purchasing (clients) and advertising the sale of sexual services, while the selling of sex remains legal. These policies have been adopted in Canada despite the lack of evidence supporting this legal framework and an absence of research on health impacts and HIV/STI risks for sex workers. The aim of the proposed study is to investigate the impact of new sex work laws and enforcement-based policies on HIV/STI risks (e.g., drug use patterns, violence, condom use, access to care) among sex workers and clients in Vancouver, Canada. This project will draw on empirical survey data gathered from a larger longitudinal cohort study of women sex workers in Vancouver and will employ advanced social epidemiological modelling techniques to make use of the longitudinal data before and after the legal reforms. This work will be complimented by in-depth interviews with sex workers and clients recruited through a paired cohort study of men who purchase and sell sex. Given the high HIV/STI burden among sex workers and lack of research on the health impacts of criminalization of sex work in Canada and globally, there is a critical need to translate the findings into health policy and practice. Knowledge translation of the research findings to local community and international partners will help to inform ongoing developments in public health policies to reduce the risks for HIV, as well as provide evidence for upcoming Charter challenges.

column36: Teaching Indigenous health using anti-racist pedagogy: Exploring the experiences of medical school instructors with the two-eyed seeing framework
column37: Stereotypes create a significant barrier for Indigenous people when they interact with Canada's healthcare system. In recent years, the nursing and medical professions have been examining not only the role they play in perpetuating such discrimination but also what can be done to make real and effective changes. One way to address racism is through education. The Indigenous Physicians Association of Canada, in partnership with the Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada, have developed guidelines for teaching about Indigenous health to physicians in training, and these are currently being implemented in Canada's medical schools. Including discussions about racism in the classroom presents challenges for the instructor. Students may be reluctant to engage in this topic or exhibit strong emotional responses. Although researchers in other fields, such as teacher education, have been studying this phenomenon, very little is known about medical school instructors' experiences of teaching about racism's impacts on Indigenous people. For the last two years, the medical school at the University of Manitoba has been including racism as a central topic in its Indigenous Health course. My research study will involve interviewing the instructors of this course to understand their experience of teaching medical students about the racism. In doing this research, I hope to learn more about the challenges these instructors face, as well as the supports that help them in their work. As a researcher who is of both Cree and European ancestry, I aim to incorporate both points of view in my research project. Using this 'two-eyed seeing' approach, the traditions of Cree storytelling as well as mainstream research methods will help me to gain a multifaceted understanding of the instructors' interviews. The results of my study may be useful for other Canadian medical schools to address the challenges of teaching about racism and Indigenous people.

column36: Ethnobotanique des peuples premiers d' Amerique: l'impact de l'alimentation traditionnelle dans le maintien de la sante et la securite alimentaire.
column37: Les maladies chroniques comme l'obesite et le diabete, connaissent une hausse alarmante dans les communautes autochtones du nord du Quebec. Ces problemes de sante seraient associes a des changements encore recents dans les habitudes alimentaires, soit, le passage d'une alimentation composee principalement de produits traditionnels a une consommation croissante d'aliments de marche pauvres en elements nutritifs et hautement calorifiques. Or, plusieurs etudes demontrent l'apport nutritif benefique qu'apporte la nourriture traditionnelle. Cependant, le role qu'elle joue dans le maintien de la sante en lien avec les maladies chroniques est peu connu. Les objectifs de ce projet sont de 1) mieux comprendre comment l'alimentation entre dans la conception de la medecine traditionnelle, 2) identifier les plantes comestibles percues pour leurs proprietes benefiques sur l'obesite et autres maladies chroniques, et 3) evaluer leur action dans le metabolisme des graisses. Afin de verifier l'hypothese que ces aliments ont un impact positif dans la gestion des problemes de sante chroniques, une demarche integrant diverses approches est employee avec la collaboration etroite de communautes autochtones et leurs services de sante. A l'aide d'entrevues dans des communautes innues, cries et inuites du Quebec, les plantes de l'alimentation traditionnelle seront identifiees aux fins d'une analyse approfondie portant sur leur activite medicinale. Des techniques de laboratoire en pharmacologie seront utilisees pour evaluer leurs capacites d'inhiber l'absorption des graisses dans le tractus intestinal. Finalement, des techniques en chimie analytique seront employees pour identifier les molecules actives d'une plante biologiquement importante et elucider davantage son mode d'action. Dans le but d'augmenter l'accessibilite a l'alimentation et la medecine traditionnelle, cette etude servira a sensibiliser et informer des professionnels et administrateurs de la sante quant a ces traditions.

column36: The impact of chronic inflammation on susceptibility to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
column37: Pneumonia is a significant cause of death and hospitalization in the elderly in Canada. Following pneumococcal infection the elderly may experience accelerated development of dementia, respiratory, circulatory, and digestive disorders. The elderly are at increased risk of developing pneumonia because their immune system deteriorates. The aim of this proposal is to determine the factors causing the decline in immune function with age. Mounting evidence from our lab suggests that age-associated changes in immune cells occur in response to chronic inflammation. Aging is associated with chronic inflammation, which is linked to increased rates and severity of pneumonia. Macrophages are immune cells central to the removal of Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is the leading bacterial cause of pneumonia. We believe that when macrophages are exposed to chronic age-associated inflammation their anti-bacterial activity is fundamentally altered. Ultimately this research project will determine whether modulating chronic inflammation can restore macrophage anti-bacterial activity and decrease susceptibility to pneumonia. Although there are pneumococcal vaccines available for the elderly, their efficacy is low. The research proposed here will help us create novel vaccines and therapeutic strategies that work within the confines of the aging immune system. column36: Investigating the role of adherent-invasive E. coli in the pathogenesis of Crohn's disease
column37: Crohn's disease (CD) is a lifelong, debilitating illness which is notorious for causing wide variety of symptoms anywhere along with intestinal tract. Canada has one of the highest rates of CD in the world and the disease has a substantial financial burden on the healthcare system. Genetic and environmental risk factors have been associated with CD along with increased levels of bacteria known as adherent-invasive E. coli (AIEC). Our lab has developed a model for long-term AIEC infection in mice which results in intestinal inflammation similar to Crohn's disease in humans. While AIEC are found in most CD patients, AIEC can also be found in healthy patients suggesting that additional factors such as the patient's genetics or intestinal flora are needed for disease expression. My objective is to use our mouse model to determine the impact of known genetic and environmental risk factors on AIEC infection and associated inflammation. I hypothesize that different host genetics and xenobiotics influence AIEC colonization and therefore impact disease expression. I have already shown that one genetic risk factor for Crohn's unexpectedly appears to reduce AIEC colonization, indicating that indeed host genetics does play a role in AIEC colonization behaviour. I will also test how antibiotic exposure and other xenobiotics currently used in CD therapy influence AIEC colonization and host response. This research will lead to a better understanding of how various CD risk factors converge on host biology and will influence future new therapies for CD.

column36: The Effects of Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids on the Infant Microbiome and Immunity
column37: During infancy, the gastrointestinal tract is colonized with microbiota, a community of microorganisms, which play a significant role in the development, regulation, and maintenance of immune functions. Fish oil, rich in n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), are thought to be anti-inflammatory and consequently may increase susceptibility to infection by hindering their body's ability to produce an adequate inflammatory response in defense against infectious disease. Currently, women in Canada are supplementing their diets with n-3 PUFA during gestation and lactation despite their being conflicting clinical evidence regarding the beneficial effects on infant development. It is currently unknown how maternal fish oil supplementation impacts the offspring's gut microbiota and immune functions. Considering that diet influences microbiota and maternal microbiota is passed from mother to infant, we hypothesize that maternal fish oil supplementation will affect their offspring's gut microbiota and immunity. To approach this, we have completed a meta-analysis and systematic review summarizing clinical trials which have investigated the effects of maternal fish oil supplements on infant development and immune outcomes. In addition, the Gibson lab, has recruited 109 infants and mothers so I am able to evaluate the effects of postnatal n-3 PUFA supplementation in breast-milk on the fecal microbiome in infants. Finally, in collaboration with the McMaster Gnotobiotic facility, we will determine if the resulting microbiome from the infants born to mothers supplementing with fish oil, has an effect on immunity by transplanting the microbiota into germ-free mice, and examining responding immunity and susceptibility to enteric infectious disease agents like Citrobacter rodentium. This research could result in strategies to manage immune susceptibility by regulating maternal dietary intake during gestation and breastfeeding.

column36: Making SPARX Fly in Nunavut: Testing A Computer-based Cognitive Behaviour Therapy Intervention for Inuit Youth Experiencing Depression
column37: Over the past number of years in Nunavut, the amount of teenagers with depression and thoughts about suicide has seen enormous growth. This growth has been a major concern for Canada generally, and for the Government of Nunavut specifically. With so many Aboriginal teenagers suffering from mental health concerns, it is now more important than ever to look at how services can be better provided to small communities that are often located far away from mental health resources. SPARX will be tested in 25 communities across Nunavut with the goal of helping Inuit adolescents to develop strategies that will make managing their sadness and thoughts of suicide easier.

column36: Grossesses adolescentes au Nunavik: quels sont les facteurs de risque?
column37: Au Nunavik, les jeunes femmes agees entre 14 et 19 ans ont 3,6 fois plus de grossesses qu'au Quebec. Au Canada, le pourcentage de jeunes ages de 15-16 ans ayant des relations sexuelles etait de 4% en 2002 et de 6% en 2010. Les facteurs de risque associes aux grossesses adolescentes sont : l'activite sexuelle precoce, l'inutilisation de contraceptifs, les echecs scolaires, la consommation de substances et les caracteristiques familiales. Plusieurs efforts de prevention regionale au Nunavik ont echoue dans la reduction des taux de grossesses adolescentes. column36: Evaluating an on-reserve methadone maintenance therapy program for First Nations peoples
column37: 82% of First Nations people rate alcohol and drugs as the most significant issue faced by their community. Evidence suggests that First Nations clients better utilize culturally relevant services and these services show superior outcomes. To assess culturally relevant treatment for opioid addiction for First Nations communities within Canada we have partnered with an on-reserve addiction treatment centre. This treatment centre is currently the only one of its kind in Canada. This methadone maintenance program was developed in response to health and safety issues faced by local residents, including limited access to services, as well as high rates of HIV and opioid dependence among community members. Preliminary evaluation of the program indicated that 80% of clients decreased drug use and high-risk behaviours, 70% improved their housing condition, and 77% improved their family support since admission to the program. Preliminary evidence suggests that this program is effectively reducing substance use among clients and improving access to services among First Nations people experiencing opioid-related harms. However, to date, a comprehensive evaluation of this program with a comparison group has not been completed. A thorough investigation into the differences between those receiving treatment and those awaiting treatment may help demonstrate the effectiveness of this treatment approach. The purpose of this study is to compare First Nations clients on a methadone program with a wait list group of clients on a number of indicators including things like criminal activity involvement, drug use, employment status, physical and mental health, and quality of life. It is estimated that those in the therapy program will have lower criminal activity involvement and drug use, and greater employment status, physical and mental health, and quality of life compared to those awaiting treatment, and that those in treatment will improve each month they are in treatment.

column36: Contribution of the gut microbiome to the metabolism of oral anticancer drugs
column37: The human gut is home to trillions of microbes, called the gut microbiome, which have a profound impact on human health including playing a significant role in the therapeutic success of drugs. However, it remains unresolved how variations in microbial communities across patients impacts host physiology and drug therapy outcomes. Even though anticancer therapies have experienced major advances in the past few decades, there are still a number of obstacles associated with chemotherapy, including high variations in drug responses, metabolism and toxicity. We propose that inter-individual differences of the gut microbiome contribute to variations in anticancer drug metabolism. An understanding of the gut microbiome's contribution to drug metabolism will lead to innovative strategies to enhance chemotherapy and move us closer to personalized medicine.

column36: Epigenetic changes in host cells mediated by Salmonella proteins
column37: Bacteria that cause disease use a wide variety of mechanisms to control their environment. In particular, bacteria that invade host cells and use them to replicate, such as the bacterium responsible for the majority of food-poisoning cases in Canada, Salmonella, are adept at modifying their environments. Salmonella must subvert the routines of immune cells of the host that would normally prevent infection. As part of this subversion, salmonella alters normal host cell signaling pathways, preventing immune functions. Disruption to host signaling pathways often results in increases or decreases in expression of immune response genes. One method the host uses to alter expression of its own genes is to modify the chromosome at specific genes, either by modifying the chromosome itself, or by modifying the proteins that package the chromosome, called histones. Such modifications to chromatin are referred to as the "epigenetic code" of the host. Some bacteria produce proteins that can interact with the host chromatin to make additional changes to the epigenetic code of the host, and therefore generate a more favorable environment for replication. I hypothesize that salmonella are also able to modify the host epigenetic code, and that these modifications are important for salmonella survival and replication in the host. I will show that salmonella infection induces changes in the epigenetic code, and that these changes are the direct effect of salmonella proteins.

column36: Triggering of sleep slow waves in human neocortex using intracranial electrical stimulation
column37: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological disorders, affecting more than 3 million people in North America. Although antiepileptic drugs help control seizures in most patients, many individuals have pharmacoresistant epilepsy. These individuals have poorer quality of life, and more than twentyfold greater risk of death when compared with the rest of population, and it often occur during sleep. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is among the major factors contributing to seizures in epilepsy patients. By causing nocturnal episodes of intermittent hypoxemia (abnormally low blood oxygen) and sleep fragmentation, OSA may exacerbate seizures occurrence. Sleep apnea is also a well-known risk factor for cognitive deficits. Whether OSA in epilepsy patients is associated with worse cognitive functioning is poorly understood. Though, it is well established that consistent and accurate treatment of OSA with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy may reverse some of the cognitive deficits. However, whether CPAP therapy might improve cognitive functions in patients with epilepsy and sleep apnea has never been studied to date. The goal of the present study is to determine the cognitive burden of sleep apnea in patients with epilepsy, as well as explore the effects of 4 months of treatment with CPAP therapy on cognitive functioning and seizures occurrence. We predict that epilepsy patients with OSA will show worse general cognitive functioning and that use of CPAP therapy in those patients will lead to improved cognitive performance and seizure control after 4 months of treatment. Our findings will lead the way to a better understanding of the mechanisms triggering seizures and cognitive impairments in epilepsy, and are likely to have a very high impact on morbidity, mortality, and quality of life in those patients. This study will certainly highlight the importance of early treatment of sleep apnea in epilepsy patients to prevent further cognitive difficulties.

column36: Development of hyper-polarized 129Xe gas magnetic resonance imaging based Alzheimer's disease early detection biosensor
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease which affects nearly 12 million people across the world causing personality changes, memory loss and requires an inordinate amount of care diverting government and family resources towards the affected individual. Currently no known cure or preventative treatment exists and treatment only delays the onset of symptoms by a few months. The symptoms of AD are believed to be caused by the protein amyloid-beta which has been shown to form structures called amyloid oligomers which are believed to cause small pores in brain cells and predate the onset of AD symptoms. Current tests are unable to predict the onset of AD except to confirm its existence. I am proposing the development of a biosensor (molecular probe) which can be injected into the patient which binds to these amyloid oligomers. The patient can then undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies which will show the presence of these biosensor, and hence, the presence of amyloid oligomers. The detection of these oligomers will provide advance notice of impending Alzheimer's symptoms allowing patients to undergo preventive Alzheimer's treatment which is currently being developed by other researchers. This will slow the onset of AD, providing more independence for Alzheimer's patients, reducing the care giving burden on the families of the patients, and allowing economic resource to be allocated in ways of greater benefit to society.

column36: Hairy nanocelluloses for visualized drug delivery
column37: Almost a century ago, when Paul Ehrlich, a German immunologist, attended an opera in which spirits possessed an extraordinary ability to achieve their goals regardless of the difficulties they faced, no one would think that he would come up with the idea of targeted drug delivery. When a drug is administered directly into the body, it leaves toxic footprints and will be eliminated rapidly. This issue has intrigued a broad community of scientists and propelled them to design small vehicles to carry and deliver drugs specifically to infected organs within the human body. Although synthetic materials have performed well, their toxicity and side effects have posed serious health risks to patients. Thus, recent years have witnessed a growing interest in developing cost-effective natural nanocarriers possessing acceptable biocompatibility, biodegradability, and functionalizability. In this research, cellulose, the most abundant biopolymer in the world derived from trees, is engineered to yield a new class of small vehicles bearing crystalline (ordered) and amorphous (disordered) regions, called hairy nanocrystalline cellulose (NCC). While the hair provides a drug conjugation capacity that is more than 10 times greater than conventional NCCs, the crystalline part retains its mechanical endurance and provides a versatile medium to attach a dye. These safe nanovehicles enable us to visualize the delivery pathway to make sure that the drug is localized in such affected sites as cancerous tumors. We are hopeful in our endeavor to design and synthesize a ubiquitous platform for drug tracing based on wood fibres, owing to hairy NCC's superior shape, morphology, and functionalizability. This technology will pave the way towards green and sustainable nanobiomedicine based on Canada's main natural resources, which will have a resounding impact on public welfare, especially for the patients suffering from chronic diseases.

column36: Mecanismes moleculaires et cellulaires du facteur de risque genetique pour la maladie d'Alzheimer, CD2AP, dans la reponse cerebrovasculaire et cognitive a un protocole d'activite physique chez les personnes agees.
column37: La maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) est responsable de 60 a 80% des cas demence. Environ 5% des cas de la maladie sont associes a des mutations genetiques. Pour les autres 95%, plusieurs evidences suggerent qu'une diminution de l'apport sanguin au cerveau pourrait contribuer a l'initiation du processus neurodegeneratif. En effet, des facteurs de risque de la maladie tels que l'age avance, le genotype de l'apolipoproteine E, le diabete de type 2 sont associes avec une diminution de l'afflux sanguin au cerveau. L'hypoperfusion cerebrale peut contribuer a reduire l'apport en oxygene et en glucose ainsi que d'autres nutriments essentiels au bon fonctionnement du cerveau. Par consequent, les interventions visant a maximiser l'apport sanguin cerebral representent des options therapeutiques interessantes pour la MA. Dans cet ordre d'idee, l'activite physique (AP) represente une option de traitement interessante. En effet, la pratique d'AP a ete montree par plusieurs etudes epidemiologiques comme un facteurs protecteur pour la MA et permet d'augmenter le debit sanguin de meme que l'oxygenation cerebrale. Toutefois, certaines interventions chez les patients atteints de la MA ont montre des resultats mitiges, suggerant que d'autres facteurs pourraient compromettre le succes des protocoles en AP chez les patients. Plusieurs facteurs de risque genetiques ont ete identifies pour la forme tardive de la MA, dont les polymorphismes de la proteine CD2AP. Il existe tres peu de connaissances a l'heure actuelle sur le role de CD2AP dans le cerveau. Toutefois, certaines etudes proposent que la proteine pourrait avoir un role sur la memoire ainsi que sur l'integrite de la barriere hemato-encephalique. Il est donc probable que les polymorphismes de CD2AP puissent moduler la reponse a un protocole d'AP. Notre projet visera donc a etudier la relation entre les polymorphismes de CD2AP et la reponse cognitive et cerebrovasculaire a un protocole d'AP chez des personnes agees.

column36: From Singing to Speaking: Facilitating the recovery of post-stoke patients with nonfluent aphasia
column37: There are an estimated 50,000 strokes in Canada each year, costing the Canadian economy $3.6 billion a year in physician services, hospital costs, lost wages, and decreased productivity. Stroke survivors with a left inferior frontal gyrus lesion generally receive a diagnosis of non-fluent aphasia (i.e. difficulties with the production of speech), and typically do not respond well to traditional speech therapy. Because it has been shown that patients with severe nonfluent aphasia are better at singing words than they are at pronouncing them, several researchers have proposed using sung words instead of spoken words to help them recover their language abilities. Indeed, the brain regions dedicated to singing are mainly located in the right hemisphere (opposite to the lesion) and the recruitment of these brain regions, as part of a therapy, often allows a certain recovery (e.g. an improvement of their language abilities). Unfortunately, these melodic therapies are generally carried out several months after a stroke, and are very costly in time for both the therapist and the patient. Thus, we propose that an intensive singing intervention performed during hospitalization (i.e. when the brain is most malleable) is ideal to facilitate language recovery in aphasic patients. Singing is natural and very easily done in hospitals, at minimal costs. The proposed project will attempt to demonstrate the effectiveness of this intervention by quantifying the language improvements, and observing the cerebral changes associated to them. Moreover, the collected data will allow for the identification of patients for whom an intense singing intervention would be optimal, based on the location of their injury. Ultimately, this project will provide probative evidence to justify an intensive singing intervention with aphasic patients.

column36: Antipsychotic medication prescription in a Canadian offender population: A longitudinal analysis of drug safety and effectiveness
column37: Severe mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are vastly overrepresented among offender populations worldwide. Treatment with antipsychotic medication is the cornerstone of therapy for these conditions. However, adherence to these medications is a well-established challenge, complicated by often severe side effects. Previous research has found that antipsychotic medications are heavily prescribed while prisoners are in custody, but that their ongoing use is frequently disrupted during the transition from custody to community settings. Low adherence leads to an increased risk of relapse and repeat involvement with the justice system. Clinical trials of clozapine - often known as the gold standard of therapy - and long acting injectable antipsychotic drugs have shown particular promise for improving outcomes. However both are under-utilized. The proposed study is the first of its kind to investigate the impact of clozapine and long acting injectable antipsychotics in a very large sample (>250,000) of offenders. column36: Elucidating the Effect of O-GlcNAc Modification on Protein Thermostability
column37: The glycosylation of proteins with O-GlcNAc is a ubiquitous post-translational modification found throughout the metazoans. Deregulation of O-GlcNAcylation is implicated in several human diseases including type II diabetes, Alzheimer's, and cancer. However, the basic biochemical role of O-GlcNAcylation remains poorly understood. Several recent studies have demonstrated a clear link between O-GlcNAc and cellular thermotolerance. We hypothesize that a basic function of the O-GlcNAc modification is to prevent the thermal unfolding or aggregation of target proteins. To elucidate its role in protein thermostability we propose a series of biochemical and biophysical experiments to probe temperature dependent effects of O-GlcNAc on protein unfolding, folding, and aggregation. Furthermore, we will assess the role of O-GlcNAc modification on the heat-induced aggregation of proteins in cells. The proposed work will improve our knowledge of how the druggable pathway of O-GlcNAcylation influences cellular health, enabling the development of new therapeutics.

column36: The effects of running on knee cartilage measures in people with and without knee osteoarthritis
column37: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a highly prevalent musculoskeletal condition among Canadians which can be responsible for persistent pain and activity limitations, and eventually decreased quality of life. Exercise therapy has been widely recognized as an efficient treatment modality for this condition. Even though activities involving impacts, such as running, may be beneficial in maintaining knee cartilage health of healthy young adults, it remains unclear whether knee cartilages would react the same to running at an older age, and in the presence of knee OA. In this research project, we will explore if knee cartilages of older healthy runners react the same to a bout of running as those of younger runners. A mechanistic approach will be combined to imaging techniques to study if cartilage measures are influenced by running mechanics. Then, we will compare the effects of running on knee cartilages measures of older people with and without OA. Such studies are much needed in order to clarify if impaired cartilage has the ability to adapt to loading just like healthy cartilage. If cartilages of older people with and without knee OA show a similar behaviour to healthy younger adults, longitudinal and intervention studies could be designed afterwards to explore the potential of running in the prevention and treatment of knee OA.

column36: Using aerobic exercise to enhance motor learning, function and brain plasticity after stroke
column37: After stroke, a high number of Canadians (85%) suffer from long-term motor impairments hindering daily function and decreasing quality of life. Understanding the underlying structural, neurophysiological and genetic mechanisms of motor recovery after stroke may allow for improved and individualized upper limb motor learning and adjunct therapies (e.g. aerobic exercise) to maximize recovery. The beneficial effects of aerobic exercise on brain health and cognitive function are becoming widely known. Work from our lab, and others, show that the beneficial effects of aerobic exercise are not limited to cognitive function. A single session of lower-limb aerobic exercise increases excitability areas in the brain that control movement for both the arm and leg, improves neuroplasticity (the brain's ability to reorganize itself) and enhances upper-limb motor learning. This suggests that aerobic exercise potentially enhances widespread brain excitability and learning. However, the potential beneficial effects of aerobic exercise on neuroplastic change and motor learning is not known in stroke. This has led to the proposed research examining whether aerobic exercise performed immediately prior to motor practice will 'prime' the brain for structural and neurophysiological plastic change after stroke. The objective of the proposed work is (1) to determine whether a single session of aerobic exercise can 'prime' the brain to enhance motor learning and neuroplasticity after stroke, and (2) to consider how repeated pairings of exercise impacts brain excitability, neurobiology, motor learning and arm function. This work represents an essential first step in advancing understanding of how priming exercise may alter the neurobiology of the brain and impact capacity for motor learning. This research may serve as a starting point for enhanced adjunct therapies to optimize recovery after stroke, and ultimately lead to better health related quality of life for Canadians with stroke.

column36: Pannexin 1 in swelling-induced neuronal death
column37: Brain swelling is a major cause of mortality following insults such as stroke and traumatic brain injury. This condition is often caused by an underlying swelling of neurons in the brain, leading to cell death. We currently have limited capacity to replace these neurons, and therefore must devise strategies to reduce the swelling-induced cell death. Recent evidence suggests that an ion channel protein, called Panx1, is involved in this process. Ion channels act essentially as conduits between cells and the external environment. These proteins pass important signalling molecules to co-ordinate cellular responses, such as cell growth, movement, or death. In this project, I will test whether Panx1 conduits promote cell death following neuronal swelling. I will also examine the mechanisms through which Panx1 channels are activated during neuronal swelling. Early experiments indicate that harmful molecules known as reactive oxygen species, which are created within swollen cells, might play a role in this Panx1 activation and neuron death. Reactive oxygen species cause damage to all cellular components, including proteins. Therefore I will also examine whether these molecules activate Panx1 conduits by modifying parts of the protein structure. This work contributes to unraveling the complex and still largely unknown mechanisms underlying neuronal swelling and death, and will guide future studies on therapeutic interventions for brain edema and neuronal death.

column36: Treatment of paediatric anxiety disorders using reconsolidation update mechanisms: implications of executive functioning
column37: Paediatric anxiety disorders are frequent, can be extremely impairing and may lead to increased risks for adult anxiety disorders. Exposure-based therapies (including cognitive behavioural therapy [CBT]) are the first-line treatment for paediatric anxiety disorders. However, some children do not adequately benefit from treatment, and some experience a relapse of symptoms following treatment cessation. There is clearly scope to enhance the efficacy and durability of exposure therapy in paediatric anxiety disorders. The reconsolidation update mechanism suggests that following initial encoding, a memory is stored, but does not necessarily remain stable. When the memory is reactivated, it becomes labile and sensitive to change for a window of time. New information presented during this window can disrupt the reconsolidation of this memory, updating the original memory trace with new information. Augmentation of the fear memory may improve the maintenance of treatment gains following exposure therapy, because the memory can be modified and replaced with a less anxiety-evoking one. Besides, deficits of executive functioning, that is, the cognitive functions allowing for goal achievement such as planning, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility, have been extensively reported in anxious individuals, and have been associated with treatment response. Moreover, enhancement of executive functioning has been observed after successful CBT. The present study aims to test the hypothesis that incorporating reconsolidation update mechanisms to exposure-based therapy will improve treatment response in anxious youths aged 9-17 years old. We will also investigate executive functioning in our sample and potential contributions to treatment response. Our results will contribute to ameliorate exposure-based therapy protocols, will allow identifying the most at-risk youth, and may lead to the development of better targeted interventions.

column36: Identifying projection-specific changes in reward circuit activity that underlie behavioral changes and reward-seeking driven by cocaine
column37: Drug addiction is a serious health issue in Canada and throughout the world. A major goal of addiction research has been to identify the circuit-level changes in activity caused by drugs of abuse that 'hijack' the normal processes underlying reward learning in the brain, leading to compulsive drug-seeking behaviour. Key pathways implicated in addiction are the projections from dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The release of dopamine from these projections is increased by drugs of abuse such as cocaine, but direct observation of native neural activity within these pathways has remained elusive. The recently developed 'fiber photometry' technique now allows for optical recording of specific neural projection pathways within the brains of awake, behaving animals. In the present study, we propose to use fiber photometry to analyze changes in the activity of DA projections to the NAc and mPFc during different forms of cocaine-mediated reward learning. This approach will allow us to elucidate circuit-level alterations in the reward pathway of the brain which underlie behavioural changes induced by cocaine. We will also be able to identify causal patterns of activity that precede the initiation of drug-seeking behaviours, a potentially crucial aspect of addiction in humans. The results from this study will therefore be of broad interest both to neuroscience researchers and to clinicians studying the effects of cocaine on the brain, and have the potential to inform future therapeutic strategies for drug abuse.

column36: Control of human cell survival proliferation and lineage identity by synthetic gene circuits
column37: Stem cells hold huge promise for regenerating damage from both disease and injury. Their use is restricted, however, by difficulties in getting and growing them. They also often behave unpredictably, in part because the instructions they follow are only partially understood. Recently invented methods have made editing the cellular instruction manual, their DNA, possible. This makes the creation of cells with similar properties and known controls feasible. The first part of our proposal is to develop new controls for cell survival and growth using editing techniques. Controlling cell survival and growth is a critical safety measure to make sure that any cell therapy doesn't become cancer. Specifically, we will place proteins capable of killing the cell under the control of a defined chemical, and proteins which prevent the cell from growing under the control of light. This will make the cells unable to form a tumour inside the body, and able to be killed using a known drug if it should be needed. We will also use these edited cells to stress test our control mechanisms and improve their reliability. The second part of our proposal is to make stem cell-like cells that are simple to grow and can be easily converted into useful cell types. To do so we will take normal cells that can be grown without difficulties, and install switches into them that activate the proteins necessary to make them into brain, heart, and liver cells when exposed to specific chemicals. We will also characterize how efficiently these switches work both when on their own, and when put together. Finally, we will put these same switches under the control of proteins that they might encounter in the body. This would be a first step in making cells able to automatically detect damage and effect repair. Overall, this project will provide proof-of-concept for the creation of designer stem cell-like cells with novel therapeutic properties.

column36: Elucidating the circuit-level anatomic and molecular mechanisms that mediate locomotion in neuroprosthetic rehabilitation after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury is a devastating disease that affects individuals physically, emotionally, and economically. Currently, there is no cure for spinal cord injury. However, promising research in our laboratory has demonstrated the ability to restore voluntary motor control after severe spinal cord injury via spared nervous system circuits with a strategy termed neuroprosthetic rehabilitation: a combination of immediate motor control with electrochemical spinal cord stimulation and subsequent neuroplasticity developed with long-term training regimens. Despite these positive results, how this strategy enables control centers above the injury to use formed connections with spinal circuits below the level of injury to mediate locomotion remains unknown. The aim of this project is to elucidate the circuit-level mechanisms that mediate this process by anatomically understanding the residual connections below the level of injury then determining the functional contribution of these pathways to motor control after injury both in the short-term and in the long-term after neuroplasticity has occurred. This understanding will help with the future design of interventions that target the identified neural circuits as well as provide a stronger basis on which these interventions, including neuroprosthetic rehabilitation, can be translated into human trials to help individuals with spinal cord injury.

column36: Advancing Person Centered Care in the Faculty Context: A Creative Knowledge Translation Approach
column37: Young children rely on their parents to make health decisions and manage illness on their behalf. However, one in three Canadian parents struggle to find, understand and use health information and services, a problem known as low health literacy. Low health literacy contributes to poor illness management, higher health care use, and increased costs to the health system. Finding ways to clearly and meaningfully communicate health information to parents is urgently needed to improve health literacy and quality care for children. Stories and pictures are powerful ways of communicating with low literacy groups, but research is needed on how and why these approaches work. This research responds to this knowledge gap by developing a transferable explanatory theory about how, why, when, where and for whom story and picture-based communications impact parent's health literacy, which can later be used to inform future research and policy. First, the complex concept of health literacy will be analyzed to create a clear understanding of the term. Second, a panel of experts will be convened to provide input on potential theories about story and picture-based communication strategies. Using data from these first two steps, a literature review known as realist synthesis will be conducted to identify how, why, when, where, and for whom stories and pictures work to impact parental health literacy. The result of this research is a transferable theory on story and picture-based communication strategies for parental health literacy, which will be later used for (a) developing and testing communication interventions for various childhood conditions and contexts and (b) developing and testing interventions to improve how receptive a particular setting is to the story and picture-based strategy. This research forms the foundation for a program of research on clear, creative communication strategies to help parents understand and use health information in decision making in Canada.

column37: Over 2.5 million Canadians are currently living with type 2 diabetes (T2D), a highly destructive condition that results in many long-term health complications. Current T2D treatments provide incomplete disease control and cause undesirable side effects, indicating a strong need for new and effective therapies. T2D occurs when the body cannot produce sufficient levels of insulin, a hormone that acts to reduce blood glucose (sugar) levels, or when cells cannot properly utilize available insulin. Within the pancreas, specialized cells (beta cells) produce insulin, and other cells (alpha cells) respond to insulin, and together their actions regulate blood glucose levels. In T2D, both alpha and beta cells become stressed and dysfunctional. This results in decreased insulin levels and action, which results in high blood glucose levels and the onset of disease. The proposed project is focused on preventing or reversing alpha and beta cell stress as an attractive approach to restoring normal pancreatic cell function and preventing T2D. It was recently discovered that the naturally produced molecule interleukin (IL)-22 is a powerful suppressor of pancreatic cell stress. Importantly, IL-22 treatment restores normal blood glucose levels in obese mice; however, the mechanisms and cell types through which IL-22 treatment functions are unknown. The goal of this project is to identify key genetic targets of IL-22 action in pancreatic cells and determine the significance of these targets in the beneficial effects of IL-22. Additionally, by examining mice that are deficient in IL-22 action in alpha or beta cells, and measuring their ability to develop metabolic disease, I will determine which cells mediate the protective effects. Together, these studies will provide fundamental information on the role of IL-22 in health and disease and ultimately will lead to the development of novel therapies for the prevention and treatment of T2D.

column36: Mental health morbidity during pregnancy among mothers with a chronic somatic illness and its impact on children
column37: The rise in maternal age in industrialized countries has resulted in an increase in women with chronic illnesses during pregnancy. As pregnancy can be a time of heightened stress, it can place an additional strain on women suffering from a pre-existing medical disorder. Women with a chronic illness are also likely to experience more fatigue, anxiety and depression than healthy women. In my doctoral thesis, I showed that multiple sclerosis among parents leads to substantially higher levels of mental health disorders and postpartum depression, and such mental health impairments in parents adversely affect the mental health of children and adolescents. Although the prevalence of chronic disorders during pregnancy is increasing, there is a lack of knowledge about its potential impact on the mother's and child's mental health. Therefore, I aim to determine the risks of mental illness during pregnancy among women with a chronic condition and its potential effect on the development and mental health of children. Chronic illnesses of interest will include, but will not be limited to, diabetes, hypertension, (morbid) obesity, multiple sclerosis, and congenital heart disease. I will analyze de-identified data from Sweden, including information on doctor and hospital visits, dispensed drugs, and births for the entire Swedish population. This will be the first study to explore this issue in a large national database. Findings from this research will help healthcare providers understand the psychological and psychiatric effects of a pre-existing maternal chronic condition. Furthermore, this research will provide evidence that will improve pregnancy experience and outcomes and potentially identify appropriate interventions that could alleviate stress and mental health morbidity caused by chronic illnesses in pregnant women.

column36: Evaluating the pathways linking adverse psychosocial work factors to diabetes and cardiovascular diseases among men and women - a 16-year prospective study among 5,700 Canadian workers
column37: Diabetes and cardiovascular diseases are two major public health burdens worldwide. The psychosocial work environment may contribute to the development of these diseases. column36: Examining the role of bystanders and laypeople to prevent and address opioid overdose and other health emergencies: a mixed methods study
column37: Opioid overdose is now the leading cause of accidental death in North America, causing more fatalities than motor vehicle collisions. One approach to address this epidemic is to teach laypeople to identify overdose and give first aid, including calling 911 and giving naloxone, an opioid reversal agent. From its origins in public health settings, this intervention is expanding into Canadian emergency departments, hospitals and clinics. But little is known about how well this intervention works in clinical settings. This research program will explore the role and effectiveness of this intervention. First, a feasibility study will assess brief overdose training and naloxone distribution increases rates of satisfactory bystander resuscitation performance in a high-fidelity simulated opioid overdose. We hypothesize that simple training can equip laypeople to deliver essential life-saving interventions in an opioid overdose. Second, we will complete the first Canadian analysis of out-of-hospital near deaths associated with drug toxicity. Understanding the epidemiology, patterns of care, and prognosis in drug-related OHCA are prerequisites for improving the prehospital management of these patients. Third, we will conduct a systematic review of the effects of engaging laypeople in the delivery of emergency care in vulnerable and underserviced populations. This research will lay the foundation for effective overdose prevention programs in clinical settings, and deepen our understanding of the role of laypeople in the delivery of essential emergency healthcare interventions.

column37: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) describes a collection of squamous cell cancers (SCC) arising in the head and neck region. HNSCC is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to the fact that treatment options for patients with late-stage metastatic disease are limited to radiation and chemotherapy. New and effective therapies are urgently needed to help improve the lives of individuals with HNSCC. Development of novel therapeutic options relies on understanding the mechanisms that contribute to progression of HNSCC. Recent evidence indicates that interactions between tumor cells and cells of the immune system, including antibody-producing cells (B cells) and cells with direct and specific killing function (T cells), may play a role in the development of HNSCC. For example, our previous studies revealed that antibodies secreted from B cells promote the development of SCC in mouse models. In addition, it is now known that the presence of molecules that suppress the killing activity of T cells have been associated with tumor progression. The studies proposed here use mouse models of SCC as tools to study HNSCC. We will examine the hypothesis that new therapeutic approaches that target the tumor-promoting properties of B cells and also inhibit T cell suppression can improve chemotherapy responses and reduce tumor burden. Results from our research may reveal novel therapeutic targets for treatment of HNSCC. Importantly this pre-clinical modeling is being performed alongside a phase 2 proof-of-concept clinical trial evaluating whether therapeutic targeting of both B and T cell pathways slows tumor progression in patients with advanced HNSCC. We anticipate that data generated from these studies will be crucial for identifying biomarkers that stratify patients based on their likelihood to respond to therapy and will guide clinical trials by aiding the ability of clinicians to monitor disease progression, regression and/or remission.
