column36: Hyperplastic inhibitory interneurons (HINs) in fear learning
column37: Approximately 12% of Canadian adults suffer from some form of anxiety disorder. These illnesses are typified by inappropriate fear responses, often including the maladaptive generalization of fear, which occurs when fear elicited by one cue extends to other, similar cues, and can result in worsening anxiety in response to a large range of stimuli over time. Generalization is, at its core, a problem of signal specificity. Yet how it is regulated within the basolateral amygdala (BLA)-a key brain region in fear learning where associations between cues and outcomes are processed and stored-remains a largely open question. Among the BLA's numerous neuronal subpopulations, hyperplastic inhibitory interneurons (HINs) are unique in sharing many of the features that grant new, adult-born neurons the ability to rapidly integrate into memory circuits where they enhance signal specificity. In contrast to new neurons, however, existing evidence suggests that HINs may be able to de-mature/de-integrate from circuits as well, granting them an unparalleled level of flexibility. HINs may therefore be able to mimic the behaviour and function of new neurons even in regions that don't produce any. The purpose of this study is therefore to characterize how HINs in the BLA contribute to fear learning and generalization, and to explore how these cells are regulated at the molecular level. Using genetically-modified mice in which light can be used to activate or silence HINs in real-time (called optogenetics), we will be able to track changes in HIN structure, de-/integration, and gene expression as a function of both activity and the cue-specificity of learned fear. In addition to identifying how HINs are regulated and how they modulate BLA function, we expect this work to provide significant insight into the molecular control of circuit maintenance, a topic central to a wide variety of psychiatric and neurological conditions.

column36: Discovery and alteration of striatal microRNA targets to reduce compulsive eating and weight gain in obesity
column37: Imagine enduring every day the consequences of heart disease, diabetes, kidney failure, cancer, and the difficulties of breathing and moving. Imagine seeing people's lives taken away well before their life expectancy, and the families who must endure this grief. This is the impact of obesity on our society. We believe that targeting chronic disease at its root cause, ie: obesity and poor eating, is the most effective solution. However, despite attempts to lose weight and eat better, why are so many unsuccessful long term? The solution to this global epidemic may lie within the brain. Scholars believe that many suffer from a condition called "compulsive eating" or "food addiction"; that is to seek and eat large quantities of high calorie food despite the negative consequences, and to display symptoms of withdrawal and relapse during times of restriction. Compulsive eating has many similarities with other compulsive behaviours such as addiction to drugs, alcohol, and cigarettes. Recently, similar brain alterations were seen in those addicted to drugs and those with compulsive eating and obesity. To find solutions, we will look at the region of the brain that controls motivation, reward perception, and reinforcement. We aim to further characterize how this brain region changes during times of compulsive eating and weight gain. Using advanced genetic models and newly designed therapeutics, we aim to reverse the detrimental changes in the brain caused by compulsive eating to a non-addictive state in order to reduce obesity and chronic disease. The outcome of this research may not only be applicable for weight management and the reduction of associated diseases, but also for the millions with addictive tendencies toward cigarettes, alcohol, and substance abuse. This research has a vast impact and may benefit not only the 2 billion individuals living with obesity worldwide, but their families, healthcare providers, our economic security, and generations of tomorrow.

column36: Modeling changes in cervical cancer screening performance in the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine era and the determinants of HPV transmission
column37: Cytological screening is highly effective at preventing cervical cancer. However, the value of screening is less certain for the increasing number of women vaccinated against the human papillomavirus (HPV). A lower prevalence of carcinogenic HPV will reduce the performance of screening, with more false positives and overtreatment. Changes in screening practices are being considered to retain the preventive benefits while minimizing negative health outcomes. Using dynamic mathematical modelling, I will first simulate changes in screening performance, and assess the benefits of different protocol changes which may be considered such as increasing age at screening initiation, extending screening intervals, or targeting women at higher risk of cervical cancer. Dynamic models are the most rigorous method of evaluating uncertainty around potential long-term benefits and harms of health interventions. The results will be highly valuable for policy-makers seeking to provide evidence-based recommendations for cervical screening. Individuals with multiple HPV infections are at higher risk of developing cervical precancer. Sexual behaviour, acquired immunity, and genetic predisposition contribute to individuals' infection risk, but it is difficult in epidemiological studies to determine the relative importance of each factor due to measurement error and confounding. My second objective is to develop dynamic models of HPV transmission calibrated to data from a biobank of over 40,000 biological samples collected in epidemiological studies (HITCH, McGill-Concordia, Ludwig-McGill, CCCaST) to evaluate the relative importance of sexual behaviour and acquired immunity for HPV transmission, and analyze whether epidemiological observations are consistent with our understanding of HPV natural history. This research will identify the most important determinants of infection, which will help understand inter-individual variation in the efficacy of HPV vaccination and screening.

column36: Supporting evidence-informed public health decision making in breast cancer prevention
column37: The purpose of this project is to investigate ways in which to best support the use of high quality research evidence on cancer prevention into decision making, policies and programs for cancer prevention within various public health organizations across Canada. Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada. Despite continued advances in early detection and treatment, prevention of cancer is the best way to reduce the number of cancer diagnoses and deaths due to cancer. There are many ways for individuals to reduce their cancer risk, such as physical activity, healthy eating and avoiding tobacco and alcohol, however this knowledge has not been well-translated into programs within the public health system in Canada. Through enrolment of public health professionals from various organizations across Canada, we will implement various knowledge translation strategies (tailored email messaging, educational webinars, and social media) to increase the uptake of high-quality research evidence on cancer prevention. column36: Investigating the role of exercise in the workplace to boost resilience among older workers with knee osteoarthritis: An assessment of osteoarthritic symptoms and muscle quality
column37: Chronic knee pain is debilitating. Knee osteoarthritis (OA), an important source of knee pain, is the most common arthritis faced by Canadians as they age and is worsened by obesity and muscle weakness. This "wear and tear" condition damages knee tissues, causing pain and immobility. This disease also burdens the aging worker by reducing productivity and limiting the ability to work, thereby promoting absenteeism, and early retirement. Fortunately exercise reduces pain as effectively as medication. However, the effect of exercise on worker resilience (ability to adapt to stress) and the possible differential effects for men and women, are unknown. This research will establish whether exercise delivered within the workplace can reduce pain, and improve mobility, leg strength and work resilience. We also aim to show that these improvements are related with improved muscle quality. Men and women over 45 years with knee OA, working in sedentary jobs, will be randomly assigned to either 1) a control group, who is asked to maintain their current activity level; or 2) a 12-week strengthening exercise program designed specifically for knee OA. Questionnaires focused on ability and work resilience, and mobility tests will be performed before and after the intervention. The exercise group will also complete magnetic resonance imaging scans to evaluate fattiness within the thigh muscles relative to leg strength to characterize muscle quality, before and after the intervention. The control group will be offered exercise following the study. It is anticipated that exercise delivered within the workplace will improve all of the symptoms of knee OA, and improve muscle quality, for women in particular. Further, we believe that exercise at work will boost the ability and resilience for work. This work has high potential for advancing exercise to promote resilience among the hundreds of thousands of older Canadian workers affected by persistent, debilitating knee pain due to OA.

column36: Investigating cell-cell fusion mechanism using optogenetics
column37: Cell-to-cell fusion is critical for human development and health. For example, in the event of fertilization, a sperm and an egg meet and fuse together to become one cell that develops into a fetus. Similarly, many organs, such as muscle, bone and placenta, are established by cell-cell fusion. Such fusion events have been also observed in cancer, wounded and immune cells. However, we know very little about cell-cell fusion mechanism. If we do, we may be able to alter it to cure or enhance such human conditions. Fruit fly embryos contain muscle progenitor cells that also fuse to make muscle, and it has been an excellent organismal model to study cell-cell fusion with the powerful genetic tools available in this system. Studies using fruit fly embryos have identified several evolutionarily-conserved genes required for muscle progenitor cell fusion, but more fusion regulators are yet to be discovered. However, when identifying and examining the fusion regulators in embryos, conventional genetic approaches, such as mutant embryo analysis, are often hampered by the normal gene products inherited from the mother fruit fly. Intriguingly, the recent development of "optogenetics" has enabled light-inducible protein disruption using genetically-inserted light-responsive tags. My goal is to implement this optogenetic tools to remove protein function precisely when and where needed in fruit fly embryos. I will first show the effectiveness of the two distinct optogenetic strategies by disrupting a novel fusion protein in fruit fly embryos. I will compare the resulting effect of light-induced protein disruption to the mutant embryos. Then, I will apply optogenetics to disrupt other potential fusion regulators, whose mutant embryo analysis may have suffered from its essential maternal contribution. This revolutionary approach will greatly facilitate cell fusion studies, but more importantly, it will represent a unique enabling technology for broad fruit fly research community.

column36: The Impact of Emergent Biophysical Properties of Tumor Boundaries on Tumor Progression and Metastasis: Insights from in vivo, in vitro, and Computational Studies
column37: The occurrence of cancer metastasis (spread of cancer) in distant organs is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths, however it is unclear how cancer cells escape their primary sites and disseminate to other sites in the body. The crucial first step for cancer to spread is its invasion into the surrounding tissue. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms that initiate cell invasion is of fundamental importance for targeting aggressive tumors. Notably, tumor progression is associated with marked reorganization of the tumor surrounding area, called the matrix microenvironment. In normal tissue, the matrix provides barrier that hinders inappropriate cell invasion, however in tumors the matrix can be 're-modeled' to create a scaffold that favors invasion. In addition to being a biological problem, the movement of cancer cells and matrix is also a physics problem. This complexity means we currently have only an imprecise mechanistic understanding of how tumor cells interpret and maneuver through the complex matrix microenvironment of different tissues and organs. This highlights that there is a need to use methods from many disciplines to understand the various effects of matrix microenvironment on cancer invasion. The proposed research program aims using multidisciplinary approach combining ideas and methods from both biology and physics. Biophysical measurements and multi-scale mathematical modeling will be used to investigate in vitro and in vivo models of tumor cells, normal cells, and natural matrix microenvironments. In particular, I want to understand how the matrix environment changes at the point that cancer begins to invade. Ultimately, this work will enhance our comprehension of invasion and help to identify new strategies for predicting the spread of cancer and managing disease that has started to invade.

column36: "No research about us without us": Transforming disability research through fostering innovative and inclusive partnerships to drive knowledge implementation
column37: Moving research results into practice is a major social issue; an estimated $200B of research funding is wasted since evidence gets lost in the knowledge to action gap. This lack of knowledge application is similar in the field of disability research. One in five Canadian youth live with a disability. It is important for researchers to work with knowledge users, in this case youth with disabilities (YWD), to better understand respective needs and reasons for committing to collaborative research partnerships. This will help create research that is more likely to be used in practice to appropriately meet the needs of YWD and enhance service delivery within the Canadian healthcare system. To date, no studies describe in detail the interactions between YWD and researchers. The goal of this study is to examine YWD and researchers' perspectives on experiences and satisfaction with participation in research partnerships. This research is important as it responds to the call of citizens and ministries for consumer engagement in research to address their needs and preferences in order to facilitate application of evidence in practice. This study has two theory-driven phases. First, YWD and researchers will be interviewed to explore both parties' experiences, preferences, and levels of satisfaction in research partnerships over time. Results will assist in identifying key factors that enhance or impede partnerships. These key factors will be organized using a proven theory relevant to disability. Second, a literature review will identify current tools used to assess YWD and researcher partnerships in order to identify how this process is evaluated. Combined results from these two studies will provide new insights and knowledge on YWD and researchers' needs and can be used to enhance research partnerships thereby resulting in more relevant, useful and timely research that can be moved more quickly into practice and policy.

column36: Molecular Mechanisms of the Regulation of Eukaryotic Ribosome Biogenesis by Las1-mediated Protein Interactions
column37: Ribosomes are essential for life because they are the cellular factories for protein production. Defects in ribosomes cause ribosomapathies where patients exhibit bone marrow failure, developmental abnormalities, and increased cancer rates. The cell generates 7500 ribosomes per minute in mammals. To achieve this high-demand, the cell requires over 200 assembly factors and over 50% of its energy resources for ribosome biogenesis. The last 60 years of research has revealed the composition and structure of the ribosome, but the regulation for its assembly is still unclear. Las1 is an essential ribosome assembly factor; yet, we do not understand what role Las1 plays in ribosome production. Las1 has been shown to interact with two other proteins, Grc3 and the IPI complex, which are also crucial for ribosome assembly. Together, defects in Las1, Grc3, and the IPI complex have been associated with congenital lethal motor neuron disease, X-linked intellectual disability, prostate cancer, and breast cancer. The specific aims of my research is to identify the roles of Las1, Grc3, and the IPI complex in ribosome assembly and understand how environmental stress, such as heat shock, acidosis, and hypoxia, derail the assembly pathway. Targeting abnormal ribosome assembly for anti-cancer therapeutics is a growing field; however, this strategy has only recently come to fruition with a new drug, CX-5461, that is currently undergoing human clinical trials. Consequently, it is paramount to understand the regulation of ribosome assembly so that we may tap into this novel anti-cancer strategy. The long range goal of this work will be the development anti-cancer therapeutics targeting prevalent cancers such as prostate and breast cancers which impacts 1 in 8 Canadian males and 1 in 9 Canadian females, respectively.

column36: High-throughput identification and characterization of novel compounds that increase splicing inclusion of neural-specific "micro-exons".
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is the most common neurodevelopmental disorder in Canada and can severely impair a child's ability to communicate and socialize with others. Despite recent improvements in behavioral and communication therapies - which help manage the symptoms of ASD, there are still no effective treatments that target the underlying molecular pathways misregulated in this disorder. Consequently, the development of new therapeutic strategies that target the underlying biology of ASD is a critical step towards creating new and effective treatment options. In a recent scientific breakthrough, researchers at the University of Toronto discovered that "micro-exons" - small, neuron-specific segments located within particular genes - are frequently misregulated in the brains of individuals with ASD - uncovering a novel and potentially important mechanism underlying this disorder. Working in the laboratory of Dr. Benjamin Blencowe, the goal of my CIHR post-doctoral research is to identify new chemical compounds that stimulate micro-exon inclusion in the brain, and assess the potential of these compounds to treat ASD. To accomplish my goals, I will utilize a state-of-the-art, high-throughput drug screening technique to monitor the effect of tens of thousands of small molecules on micro-exon inclusion in parallel. The newly identified compounds will then be characterized in mice that are deficient in a key regulator of micro-exons and that display autism-like characteristics, in order to assess their capacity to rescue neurological changes associated with ASD, as well as behavioral changes such as reduced social interaction. This project represents a critical step towards identifying novel chemical compounds that increase micro-exon inclusion in the brain, and will investigate the potential of these compounds to treat ASD and other related neurological disorders.

column36: Role of NLRP6 in intestinal barrier protection
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic inflammatory disorders that affect the entire digestive tract; main forms are Crohn's Disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). IBD has a tremendous impact on quality of life and Canada has one of the highest rates of CD in the world, with an incidence on the rise. There is an unmet medical need to better understand CD pathogenesis since current treatment strategies calm inflammation but do not cure CD. Indeed, an elaborate balance between immune responses and tolerance to intestinal microbiota is required to maintain intestinal homeostasis. Intestinal epithelial cells represent an important physical barrier separating the intestinal lumen with its associated microbiota. Microbiota in the gut constitutes a heterogeneous microbial ecosystem and dysregulation of the homeostasis between intestinal immune systems and microbiota has been associated with the development of IBD in genetically susceptible populations. This physical barrier has several functions and plays a unique role in innate immunity. Receptors, like NOD-like receptors (NLRs), are key players in this surveillance. It is becoming clear that one of these receptors, NLRP6, plays roles in maintaining intestinal homeostasis by promoting mucosal self-renewal and proliferation. NLRP6 is relatively highly expressed in the intestine in mice and more studies are needed to further understand its function. The present proposal will focus on identifying a role of NLRP6 in the small intestine using ex vivo cultures of murine small intestine enteroids combined with in vivo models of ileitis. These studies will identify the significance of NLRP6 in the development of ileitis and will delineate the potential mechanisms involved. Results from these studies will set the stage for the development of improved therapies or the potential to uncover novel drug targets that are the cause of inflammation in the intestine and improve the quality of life of Canadian living with IBD.

column36: CoPILOT: Collaborative Powered mobility Innovative Learning OpporTunity
column37: Age related changes to our physical and cognitive capacities can have a substantial impact on our ability to be independent. As a result, aging impacts both our mobility and our ability to learn and problem solve. In many cases a powered wheelchair (PWC) could be provided to compensate for the mobility changes. However, PWCs might be overlooked based on an assumption the necessary skills would be too difficult to learn. This assumption should be challenged, as there is evidence that learning is possible for those with cognitive impairment. We know it is important to provide the opportunity to learn using techniques which minimize the potential for error and provide opportunities for success. Unfortunately, error minimized training techniques have never been explored in the context of powered wheelchair skills. This is largely because clinicians who provide training to use powered wheelchairs have not had access to technology which could facilitated error-minimized learning. CoPILOT is an innovative approach to address the learning needs of individuals with cognitive impairment. CoPILOT is a shared control approach (similar to the use of a dual controlled car for driver training) which uses new remote control technology to control a PWC. Using this technology, the clinician can demonstrate skills, and provide the learner with low risk opportunities for practice and feedback. CoPILOT is designed to promote safe and independent driving skills, and may improve the quality of powered wheelchair training by offering a graded learning experience in real world environments. With this graded approach, clinicians can focus on progressive training which builds on success, while ensuring safety for the learner, trainer, and others around them. CoPILOT training may provide mobility independence to those who have previously been considered unable to learn, enhancing opportunities for social participation, and ultimately improving quality of life.

column36: The Influence of Psychosocial Stressors on Indicators of Cardiometabolic Risk in the Transition to Young Adulthood
column37: Adolescence and young adulthood are critical periods for disease prevention. Indicators of cardiometabolic risk (CMR) already show predictive variability in adolescence and the early identification and implementation of healthcare strategies can have significant long-term health benefits. CMR refers to a set of indicators that increase an individual's risk for diabetes, heart disease, or stroke (i.e., body mass index [BMI], systolic and diastolic blood pressure [BP], and waist circumference). Much of what we know about CMR comes from studies with adults and research focusing on younger age groups is needed. For the proposed research, data from the Victoria Healthy Youth Survey (V-HYS) will be used to describe the number of young adults (ages 22 to 29) exceeding established cut-offs for non-invasive CMR indicators. In addition, psychosocial factors may contribute to these risks and may also contribute to the effectiveness of prevention programs beyond individual-level health behaviours such as diet and exercise. However, these are rarely studied. Thus, how stress (i.e., depressive and anxiety symptoms and interpersonal problems) effect CMR across the transition to young adulthood will be examined. To add, gender differences will be investigated. The V-HYS is a six-wave, 10-year longitudinal study that surveyed youth (Time 1 N = 662; ages 12 to 18) biannually from 2003 to 2014. In-person measurements of CMR (BMI, systolic and diastolic BP, waist circumference) were collected in wave 6. Measurements of internalizing symptoms and interpersonal stress were collected at each wave. Findings will provide important information about the health of Canadian youth as well as identify new targets for the prevention of CMR. The results will also inform guidelines for early identification and preventative healthcare.

column36: Metastatic Epidural Spinal Cord Compression: Development of Clinical Prediction Rules to Assess Health-Related Quality of Life and Survival in Surgically Treated Patients
column37: If left untreated Metastatic Epidural Spinal Cord Compression (MESCC) leads to debilitating pain and irreversible neurological deficits. It affects up to 10% of cancer patients. In 2015, over 86,000 Canadian cancer patients suffered from MESCC. Modern spinal surgery and radiotherapy improve Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in MESCC patients. While surgery is offered to MESCC patients with a life expectancy of at least three months, physicians tend to inaccurately estimate survival in cancer patients. Thus, statistical techniques applied to systematically collected data may improve clinical prediction. Clinical prediction rules (CPRs) are a formal combination of patient data that can be used to appraise the probability of a given patient of developing a specific outcome. Although both survival and HRQoL outcomes are crucial aspects to consider in selecting surgical patients, to date, HRQoL outcome has not been included in any MESCC-related CPR. First, we will conduct a systematic literature review and a survey to identify key preoperative predictive factors of survival and HRQoL. We will then investigate our hypothesis that survival and HRQoL can be predicted in surgical MESCC patients by using prospectively collected data on over 300 surgically treated MESCC patients to develop CPRs to predict survival up to 12 months after surgery and HRQoL for patients surviving no more than 3, 6, and 12 months. These CPRs will then be externally validated using a separate dataset. Because CPRs incorporate evidence-based data into clinical decision-making, they are highly clinically relevant. These CPRs of HRQoL and survival that are novel tools which will help clinicians deliver accurate predictive information to patients and their families, aid communication, manage patients' expectations, and assist clinicians and patients make informed treatment decisions.

column36: "Kill-switch" enabled, immune-silent, non-cytopathic, and persistent paramyxovirus vector for respiratory gene therapy.
column37: There is a need for effective lung-tropic viral gene delivery vectors for treatment of genetic lung disorders like Cystic Fibrosis, or for prophylactic delivery of broadly neutralizing antibodies against human respiratory pathogens (e.g. influenza or RSV) directly to the lung where they can be of greatest benefit. Such gene therapy is straightforward in concept, but challenging in application, due to issues with safety, host immune responses, and sufficient levels of gene expression in the right place. Sendai virus is a mouse Paramyxovirus with no known pathogenesis in humans. It is, however, fully capable of infecting the human respiratory tract, has no risk of integrating into the host genome or causing cancer, and has capacity to express high levels of foreign genes. Thus it is an excellent candidate for gene delivery to the respiratory tract, which is generally non-permissive to infection by other commonly-used virus vectors. Previously, inefficient systems for recombinant paramyxoviruses have limited the use of Sendai virus as a therapeutic vector, but recent advances in my sponsoring lab have overcome these barriers. I will take a combination of approaches to refine Sendai virus into an ideal viral vector. First, I will place the virus under selection pressures designed to render it immune-silent, so it does not induce an immune response that can cause pathology in the patient; and persistent, so that it can continue expressing the gene of interest for long periods of time. Second, I will engineer a "kill-switch" into the virus, so that if it is used in an immune-compromised patient, or there are unexpected complications from the virus or gene it bears, patient can be treated with an already clinically-available drug to eliminate the virus. Combined, these approaches will produce a Sendai virus vector that is safe, biologically-contained, capable of long-term, non-pathogenic infection, and is therefore ideal for respiratory gene delivery.

column36: Understanding p53-status in modulating the crosstalk between the immune microenvironment and pancreatic cancer
column37: Everyday, about 540 Canadians will be newly diagnosed with cancer. Despite this staggering statistic, majority of individuals will not go on to develop cancer. The following protection is largely contributed by our immune surveillance system. In addition to fighting off bacteria and viruses, our immune system has also evolved to monitor and eliminate cancerous cells. Importantly however, cancerous cells have developed mechanisms to counteract, evade and suppress our immune response. Although the genetic mutations underlying pancreatic cancer are well characterized, it remains a devastating disease. Treatments to date have failed and pancreatic cancer has the lowest five-year survival rate among patients. Better understanding of the dynamic interplay between cancerous cells and immunity will allow us to develop novel targets for pancreatic cancer treatments. Indeed, successful breakthroughs in the treatment of another cancer, melanoma, have come from targeting tumour-induced immune suppression. Therefore, our studies of cancer immune-suppression in the context of genetics will allow us to further harness the natural anti-tumour action of our immune system to combat pancreatic cancer.

column36: Studies of the Regulation of Muscle Mass and Function by Osteocalcin
column37: Skeletal muscle is needed for adaptation to exercise and plays a central role in regulating whole-body energy homeostasis. The progressive age associated loss of skeletal muscle mass and function often referred to as sarcopenia has a negative impact on the ability to perform daily activities and to perform exercise. Comorbidities of age-related sarcopenia include osteoporosis, metabolic syndromes, obesity and diabetes, loss of physical function and independence. In Canada, sarcopenia is thought to affect 30% of individuals over 60 years of age and more than 50% of people over 80 years. Recent estimates indicated that approximately 40% of the older Canadians are affected by sarcopenia. Maintaining the independence and physical function not only preserve the quality of life of older individuals but will also save billions of dollars in health care costs. Therefore, improving our understanding of the endocrine and molecular mechanisms regulating muscle mass and function is critical. Bone is another organ of the body severely affected during the aging process. Recent studies suggest that bone may be a determinant of organismal aging through the function of osteocalcin (OCN), a bone-derived hormone. OCN favours functions such as glucose homeostasis, male fertility, brain development and cognitive functions. The level of circulating OCN declines sharply with aging, raising the prospect that OCN is necessary to maintain physiological functions of the body. Moreover, OCN level has been found to be increased in human following aerobic exercise. As a result, elucidating potential involvement of OCN in regulating muscle mass and function will be an interesting frontier of research. The ultimate goal of the project may lead to identify novel mechanisms in treatment of sarcopenia and age related complications.

column36: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments and age-related aneuploidy in mammalian oocytes.
column37: One of the major causes of pregnancy loss and birth defects such as Down Syndrome is a defect with the woman's egg, whereby the egg has too few or too many chromosomes. The chance of a woman's egg having the wrong number of chromosomes increases as she gets older, and thus is the primary cause of female infertility in women of advancing maternal age. However, why eggs from older women are more prone to having an abnormal number of chromosomes than eggs from younger women is unknown. This study will test whether age causes problems with the way in which chromosomes interact with the spindle, the structure within the egg that physically binds to the chromosomes. To do this, we will use eggs from old mice, which exhibit very similar age-related defects in chromosome number as women in their 40s, thus serving as an excellent model to study human infertility. We will directly manipulate specific proteins essential for spindle mechanics to see if we can affect the old eggs to make sure they have the correct number of chromosomes. A major bottleneck in reproductive biology research is the inability to translate findings to the clinical setting, due largely in part to the precious nature of reproductive samples. Excitingly, this proposal will directly translate our findings from mice to humans, as we will have rare access to human eggs obtained from our newly established collaboration with an in vitro fertilisation clinic. As the age at which women are choosing to start a family in Canada has risen substantially over the past 30 years, and this trend is set to continue, the results of this proposal will therefore have a significant impact upon fertility and child health over the coming decades.

column36: Ribosomes in regeneration: rapid translational activation in wound healing and repair.
column37: Gene expression is controlled at multiple steps to ensure that proteins are made in the correct time and place. The production of proteins from mRNA blueprints depends exclusively on large molecular machines called ribosomes. Until recently it was believed that ribosomes act in a rote manner to translate mRNAs into proteins. However, our lab showed that cells possess specialized ribosomes with a unique composition that allows them to select when and where certain mRNAs are made into proteins. These specialized ribosomes control the production of a surprising number of master regulators of the cell suggesting that this novel level of control may allow cells to rapidly and directly remodel gene expression. Such rapid remodeling is especially important in the context of wound healing and regeneration where cells must quickly repair, reform and re-pattern damaged tissues while contending with a broad dampening of normal cellular function that accompany acute injury. Studies of protein abundance reveal that limb regeneration in species like the axolotl, a highly regenerative salamander, is accompanied by dynamic expression of distinct ribosome proteins suggesting that injured cells may rapidly assemble specialized ribosomes to mitigate tissue damage. To test this hypothesis, I will use the well-established limb axolotl amputation model to assess changes in protein translation and ribosome composition during limb regeneration and the role of these changes in wound healing and repair. This work will not only define how cells use specialized ribosomes to rapidly respond to injury and stress but also directly identify the core proteins that constitute the tool kit for vertebrate regeneration providing a firm foundation for further studies into how this tool kit may be deployed to promote better wound healing and organ repair due to chronic and acute injuries and degenerative diseases in humans.

column36: The role and regulation of pannexin ion channels during cytotoxic edema.
column37: A primary and often fatal consequence of stroke, traumatic brain injury, and other brain insults is edema: an increase in brain tissue water content. Cytotoxic edema is a component of this process and occurs when excess ions and water enter across the neuronal plasma membrane -the semi-permeable barrier separating the intra- and extracellular space. This increase in cell volume causes membrane swelling and ultimately results in cell death. Presently, the cascade of events by which neuronal swelling triggers cell death remains obscure. Preliminary evidence from Dr. Brian MacVicar's lab (the host) indicates that swelling triggers cell death by activating pannexins- a class of large transmembrane ion channels. Following activation, pannexins form large pores in the membrane and allow ions and small molecules to diffuse between the intra- and extracellular compartments. Consequently, pannexins can initiate cell death by collapsing the transmembrane electrochemical gradient and/or promoting the loss of essential cellular components. The precise mechanism by which swelling triggers the opening of pannexins is unknown. Interestingly, membrane stretch leads to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS)-a group of harmful chemical agents that are implicated in activating pannexins. For the present proposal, I will test the hypothesis that pannexin activation is a crucial step underlying cell death during cytotoxic edema. Furthermore, I hypothesize that pannexins are activated by neuronal swelling through the production of ROS. These hypotheses will be tested in acutely prepared rat brain slices using advanced microscopy/imaging and electrophysiology techniques. As there are few effective treatments for edema, this research could reveal new avenues for therapeutic intervention following a variety of brain insults.

column36: Novel Metabolic Role of BRCA1 in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
column37: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer and the third most common cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Rising incidence of HCC has been linked to growing prevalence of obesity, largely due to its strong association with the development of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) that can lead to liver injury, inflammation, and subsequently HCC. Moreover, increasing evidence suggest a potential role of metabolic factors in predisposing to the development of HCC. However, how metabolic factors and NAFLD promote HCC remains largely unknown. Breast cancer susceptibility gene 1 (BRCA1) is a well-known tumour suppressor which coordinates a diverse range of cellular processes including DNA damage repair, cell replication and death. Disruption of BRCA1 can cause increased susceptibility to DNA damage and trigger p53-dependent cell death. In addition, BRCA1 may have a role in metabolic control through regulation of genes involved in lipid metabolism. Therefore, we hypothesized that BRCA1 may be critical in regulating genomic stability and lipid metabolism such that liver cell-specific BRCA1 loss leads to p53-mediated death of cancer-prone cells and reduced accumulation of fat in liver, thereby providing protection from DNA damage- and NAFLD-associated HCC. To understand the role of BRCA1 in development of HCC, we will generate a new mouse model that lacks BRCA1 specifically in the liver. First, we will subject these mice to a chemical carcinogen to test if BRCA1-deficiency protects against DNA damage-induced HCC. Next, these mice will be fed high fat diet to mimic conditions associated with obesity to test if BRCA1-deficient mice are protected from NAFLD-associated HCC. The proposed research is significant because it is expected to identify factors that contribute to HCC pathogenesis. Ultimately, such knowledge may lead to novel therapeutic strategies for prevention and treatment of HCC.

column36: Dementia in the population: Trajectories of disease, health care use, and places of care
column37: As the number and proportion of seniors continue to grow in Canada, the burden of dementia has become a national concern. This stems from the observation that the incidence of dementia is strongly associated with increasing age. In the 2010 report commissioned by the Alzheimer's Society of Canada - "Rising Tide: The Impact of Dementia on Canadian Society" - it has been predicted that dementia prevalence will more than double in the next 30 years and the cost of care will increase by ten-fold. As the prevalence of dementia increases, the need for home support and specialized housing to care for those living with the disease will likely rise in tandem. Given its implications on health care spending, as well as the health outcomes of older adults with dementia, transitions between care settings is often used as a measure of health system performance. For frail seniors, poor transitional care and multiple transitions are associated with adverse events, low satisfaction with care, and higher re-hospitalization rates. The severe cognitive deficits and responsive behaviours of older adults with dementia further increase the burden of transitions for patients and their families. Despite these issues, no previous studies have examined the full care trajectory of those with dementia, by following these patients from being in a healthy state to disease diagnosis, need for home care, admission into nursing homes, and death. In this study, we will examine transitions across health states and care settings among older adults with dementia. Results from this study will aid the development of provincial and national dementia planning models, and for the first time, to consider transitions to dementia from preventable risks and patients' progression through our health care system. This knowledge will be critical to the designs of provincial and national dementia care strategies currently under consideration.

column36: The role of oxidative stress on multidrug tolerance and antibiotic lethality in the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa
column37: This project focuses on how defenses against oxidative stress protect the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa against killing by antibiotics. For such, we are analyzing how antioxidant defenses are modulated in a stringent response-impaired mutant (SR-null), which has low tolerance to antibiotics. We are using a series of bacterial genetics, molecular biology, transcriptomics and biochemical tools to correlate the impairment of antioxidant defenses with the low antibiotic tolerance in SR-null, as well as evaluating how the impairment and modulation of individual redox defenses impact antibiotic tolerance. We expect that the results of this project will shine light on molecular mechanisms underlying antibiotic tolerance to serve as targets to counter this grave clinical problem, which results in treatment failure and contributes for the arising of antibiotic-resistant strains.

column36: Glucocorticoid Regulation of T Lymphocyte Signalling and Development
column37: Lung and respiratory diseases make up 3 of the top 10 causes of death worldwide, and are common across low- and high-income countries. In many cases, such as severe infection or allergy, lethality results from an excessive immune response, while in other cases, lethality results from a reduced immune response and secondary infection. Appropriate regulation of immune activation in the lung is therefore critical in treating infectious and allergic lung disease. Among the most powerful immune regulators are glucocorticoids, stress hormones produced by the adrenal glands. Interestingly, recent work has shown that different tissues, such as the intestine and lung, are also able to produce their own glucocorticoids. Such local production could allow tissue-specific regulation of immunity while avoiding the negative side effects that result from elevated glucocorticoids throughout the body. My research aims to 1) Identify how inflammatory signals cause glucocorticoid production in the lung. 2) Test the mechanisms of lung glucocorticoid production. 3) Test if lung glucocorticoids control the immune response to influenza virus infection. 4) Test if lung glucocorticoids increase the risk of bacterial pneumonia during influenza infection. 5) Test if lung glucocorticoids can be induced to treat allergic asthma. Using mouse strains with genetically altered lung glucocorticoid production, I will examine the effects of infection and allergy on lung tissue and lung-infiltrating immune cells with laboratory techniques including cell culture, gene expression assays, histology, and flow cytometry. These studies will aid our understanding of how immunity is normally regulated in the lung, and will investigate pathways to stimulate lung glucocorticoid production. Stimulation of lung glucocorticoid production could be an effective mechanism for treatment of respiratory infections, allergy, and chronic inflammatory lung diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

column36: Identifying cancer vulnerabilities secondary to DNA repair deficiency
column37: Few treatment options exist for patients with cancers that spread to the brain (known as brain metastases), and these patients often die within months. Despite that brain metastases occur in up to 17% of cancer patients at an incidence of about 20,000 Canadians per year, little is known about how cancers spread to the brain. We are beginning a 'basket' clinical trial for brain metastasis patients in which we identify genetic mutations in cancer samples from the patients. The mutations identified in each patient are used to inform the choice of FDA-approved, targeted drugs so that the right drug is used on the right patient when standard treatments have failed. This project will further develop bioinformatic methods to use the data from this trial to understand key mutations that cause cancers to spread. Using this knowledge, we will guide precision medicine for current patients and facilitate the development of new drugs for future patients.

column36: Socio-environmental determinants and functional health outcomes of physical activity changes over time: Informing the development of effective physical activity interventions among older adults.
column37: Higher levels of physical activity are associated with better health outcomes. It remains unclear however which factors predict declines in physical activity and which factors should be leveraged to achieve the greatest increases in physical activity. Identifying these factors is necessary for the development of physical activity interventions that will facilitate individual and population-level reductions in non-communicable disease risk. The aim of my research will be to generate knowledge (e.g., identifying the environmental determinants of declines in physical activity) that will inform the development and evaluation of interventions that will promote increases (or prevent declines) in physical activity among older adults. My research will primarily use data collected as part of the European Prospective Investigation of Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk Study - a large prospective population-based observational cohort study. Adults (n= 25,639) were recruited between 1993 and 1998 from 35 outpatient clinics in Norfolk, England. Since then four additional follow-up assessments have been completed. Socio-demographic factors and variables identified a priori as important potential confounders/covariates (e.g., age, gender, education) were assessed using a standardized questionnaire. In the last two follow-up assessments (2004-2011; 2012-2016), physical activity was assessed for seven consecutive days using hip-worn accelerometers (ActiGraph GT1M/GT3X+) and characteristics of home neighbourhoods were assessed using a combination of self-reports and Geographic Information Systems. In the last assessment (2012-2016), Global Positioning Systems were used to track physical activity locations, which will allow for the estimation of the associations between environmental exposures and physical activity. Statistical models will be used to estimate the cross-sectional and prospective associations of physical activity with social and environmental factors and markers of cardiometabolic health. The knowledge that will be generated through my research will give clinicians and health agencies (e.g., the National Health Service and Health Canada) novel insights into how they can help improve the health of our aging populations.

column36: R-loop and Transcriptional Profiles in Individual Hypothalamic Neurons following Augmented Maternal Care
column37: Early life experience shapes an individual for a lifetime. While risk factors for mental health disorders are frequent in the population and intensely studied, much less is known about protective factors that allow for resilience in the face of adversity. Interestingly, enhanced maternal care in early life is associated with resilience to stress and improved learning and memory throughout life. Enhanced maternal care is capable of altering gene expression and the resulting epigenetic code in the hypothalamus of the brain. By studying a well established rodent model of enhanced maternal care with state-of-the-art technologies it will be possible to precisely map these protective epigenetic changes in individual neurons and begin to understand the molecular mechanisms behind them. Once identified, these changes can then be targeted by modern biotechnology and eventually be translated as a novel treatment for human mental health disorders.

column36: Ketamine-induced NMDA receptor hypofunction in nonhuman primates as a model for cognitive deficits in schizophrenia
column37: Most patients suffering from schizophrenia have cognitive problems. One especially debilitating problem, the working memory deficit, is the impairment in their ability to hold information temporarily on-line for planning, making decisions and interacting with others. While drugs currently available are successful at treating hallucinations and delusions, they fail to ameliorate the cognitive deficits. These severely limit the patients' independence, productivity and quality of life, laying heavy burdens on their families and the health care system. Because drugs that block the action of the neurochemical glutamate mimic the symptom of schizophrenia so closely that not even psychiatrists can tell the difference, we utilized this fact to model the working memory deficit in rhesus monkeys. First, we devised a task which successfully detected the working memory deficit in patients comparing to healthy people. In this task, the participants first see one of two cues: one instructs them to look towards a subsequent object while the other requires them to look away, without knowing where that object would be. As a result, during the delay period after the cue and before the object appears, either the 'look towards' or 'look away' rule must be kept in working memory. Subsequently, we found a similar impairment in the same task in rhesus monkeys after the administration of low dosage of ketamine, a drug that blocks glutamate action via the NMDA receptors. This model allow us to study the suboptimal ways in which cells in certain brain regions function under the effect of ketamine, as they may reflect the key differences between a normal brain and one affected by schizophrenia. Furthermore, understanding these changes in brain activity will help identify drugs that may rectify them, thereby offering potential treatments for the debilitating cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

column36: Improving outcome of neurocritical care by bedside monitoring of cerebrovascular health
column37: The normal function of the brain is reliant on blood flow for a continuous supply of oxygen and nutrients. Therefore techniques for monitoring brain blood flow are extremely valuable, particularly for patients with major brain injuries such as stroke. Despite the existence of a number of advanced imaging methods like computed tomography and magnetic resonance, the biggest limitation which medical doctors have to deal with is the fact that these techniques do not allow for continuous, bedside measuring. To overcome this limitation, there is a great deal of interest in portable light-based technologies that potentially could enable physicians to perform brain monitoring in all types of patients. Despite its clinical potential and the fact that a number of commercial devices have even been developed, clinical acceptance has eluded optical technologies for brain monitoring. The originality of this proposal centers on an alternative approach for tackling the main weakness, which is isolating the optical brain signal from the substantial signal coming from scalp and skull. The approach is based on the use of an optical contrast agent to provide greater signal contrast and the ability to measure brain blood flow and the integrity of blood vessels in the brain. The goal of this proposal is to demonstrate that our contrast-enhanced optical method can accurately measure these parameters in critically ill patients. Initial studies will focus on verification using an animal model and healthy controls before transporting the system to the critical care unit to obtain measurements in patients. At all stages, established imaging techniques will be used to validate our optical method. Ultimately, we believe that the ability of this technology to detect impaired brain function at the bedside will help doctors improve the outcome for critical-care patients with serious brain injuries.

column36: Transient Depletion of Innate Immunity Provides a Two-step Approach to Improve the Delivery of Tumour Targeted Nanoparticles
column37: The ability to design nanoparticles that are a billionth of the size of a human hair to carry drugs and minimize their toxic side-effects remains highly advantageous toward the development of new chemotherapeutics. The chemistry of the nanoparticles can be designed to improve biocompatibility and to offer controlled and systemic release of a drug at a tumor. The challenge with most nanoparticles is that they are sequestered by the resident immune system of the liver and spleen. These organs contain white blood cells or macrophages that remove nanoparticles from the blood stream and limit their accumulation in a solid tumor. We have developed a strategy to improve the delivery of chemotherapeutics to a solid tumor by temporarily removing a portion of these macrophages at a dose that does not compromise the patient immune system. For some of the engineered nanoparticles, a forty-fold increased accumulation in the tumour was seen using this approach. This two-step delivery strategy will greatly improve the efficacy of nano-chemotherapeutics for the treatment of cancer without compromising patient susceptibility to infection.

column36: Mismatch repair and its role in cancer predisposition
column37: Just like the spell checker in Word, cells have "spell checkers" of their own when copying their genome to ensure proper fidelity in the DNA. The spell checker that I study is called mismatch repair, which is composed of four proteins encoded by the genes MSH2, MSH6, MLH1 and PMS2. These proteins function together to correct incorrectly paired or mismatched DNA. When mismatch repair is defective, mutations like "spelling mistakes" occur in the DNA and accumulate with each cell division, paving the way to cancer. Individuals who have inherited a mutation in one of their two copies of a mismatch repair gene are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer - cancers that often arise in adults. When an individual inherits mutations in both copies of a mismatch repair gene, a more severe condition results leading to extremely high levels of mutations, causing a heightened risk of brain, blood, colon, and other cancers - which arise early in life; as children. Moreover, many tumor types eventually suffer defects in mismatch repair. Such defects are linked with tolerance to widely-used chemotherapeutic agents, and can lead to futile treatments and tumor relapse. I will be using human cell lines with inherited mutations in mismatch repair genes to study the molecular mechanisms that initiate cancer development. Specifically, I would like to understand how mismatch repair deficient cells further incapacitate their "spell checker" function allowing them to progress towards tumour development. Understanding these pathways may lead to new cancer prevention therapies to halt DNA damage and cancer progression as well as targeted therapies for mismatch repair deficient tumours.

column36: Primary Care Follow-Up of Patients After Hospital Discharge
column37: Patients who have just been discharged home following a hospital stay are vulnerable; 10-20% will return to hospital within thirty days as a result of worsening symptoms, complications from treatment, or new medical problems. Early follow-up with a primary care provider may be one way to help patients during this high-risk period. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effect of a fee code to incentivize early primary care provider follow-up after hospital discharge. Such a fee code was introduced to Ontario in 2006, yet we do not know if it succeeded in improving follow-up rates or affected other outcomes, such as hospital readmissions. Our study will answer this question. In addition, we will examine the care of patients discharged from hospital during the December holiday period. Due to decreased access to follow-up with primary care providers, patients discharged from hospital during this time may be especially vulnerable. The methods will involve identifying patients discharged from Ontario hospitals between 2002 and 2014. We will obtain information on patients and physicians from the multiple linked administrative databases at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences. Hospital admissions, emergency department visits and visits with primary care providers will be captured using hospital codes and physician billing claims, respectively. This study will identify barriers to follow-up and evaluate the effect of a fee code on follow-up and patient outcomes. This information will contribute to improving continuity at care transitions, thus bettering the health of all Canadians. This study aligns with the strategic priorities of CIHR's Institute for Health Services and Policy Research, which include "Healthy Aging in the Community" and "Health System Financing, Funding, and Sustainability".

column37: Maternal obesity and/or excess gestational weight gain are primary risk factors for childhood obesity and metabolic compromise, perpetuating a feed forward cycle of chronic disease risk for future generations. In this program we ask, how is it that exposure to an obesogenic environment in utero gives rise to children that are destined to become obese, and what are the signalling pathways? Excess adipose is associated with chronic inflammation, which has been implicated in many chronic diseases such as diabetes. It is also associated with significant changes in gut health; where changes in the composition of intestinal bacterial communities are associated with inflammation in metabolic tissues. We hypothesize that similarly, during pregnancy, excess adiposity changes the bacterial populations in a mothers gut and that these changes could cause placental inflammation modifying placental and/or fetal development, predisposing offspring to obesity and chronic disease. In this integrative multidisciplinary program we will evaluate basic biological pathways that regulate gut health and immunity in pregnancy, and whether these pathways are impaired in pregnancies characterized by excess adiposity. We will use both animal models to understand molecular mechanisms and human studies to investigate relationships between adiposity, pregnancy weight gain and the maternal gut bacteria to uncover novel pathways that mediate the early origins of childhood obesity. We will take our data, and translate it into an informative community-based, fully-developed, intervention program to support diet and lifestyle improvements in women before and during pregnancy, with a special focus on high risk populations.

column37: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among 15-24 year olds across Canada, and 10-20% of youth are affected by some kind of mental illness. However, it is estimated that only one in every five children in need of mental health services actually receives such services. Indigenous Cree youth face additional challenges to accessing services due to their remote setting. The Cree also face a legacy of colonial persecution, which has disconnected them from traditional healing methods and culturally relevant forms of support. A pan-Canadian initiative is currently underway to improve access to mental health services across the country, and the Cree community of Mistissini has been selected as one of the sites where new strategies will be developed and tested. This represents a unique opportunity to evaluate new mental health strategies as they are being rolled out. It also means there is a crucial need for youth input to ensure that these strategies address their needs and concerns. My research aims to generate a better understanding of how Cree youth think about mental illness, the reasons they decide to access or avoid mental health services, and their reactions as new strategies are taking place. I will work with Cree youth as equals throughout the research process, empowering them to think critically about the mental health challenges and resources in their community. In addition to informing the ways that mental health services can best engage youth in the Cree community, the research will generate recommendations for scaling up youth-friendly services in other communities throughout the country. By approaching the issue of mental health service access from the youth perspective, I aim to generate innovative solutions to mental health challenges that will alleviate suffering in the Cree community and beyond.

column36: Deciphering the metabolic signatures of the metabolic syndrome (MetS) in young children
column37: Babies who are born with a high amount of body fat carry this excess fat through childhood. Children who are obese often have excess abdominal fat, high blood sugar, elevated cholesterol and blood pressure, which increases their risk of diabetes and heart disease as adults. When these are present together, it is called the "Metabolic Syndrome". These risk factors may begin to develop early in life and are influenced by both "nature" (e.g. genetics) and "nurture" (e.g. a mother's diet during pregnancy, childhood diet, and physical activity). Measurement of dietary intake using questionnaires have some limitations and new biological measures have greater specificity to reflect dietary intake. We have brought together 4 multi-ethnic Canadian cohorts of pregnant mothers and their babies. The goal of our research program is to uncover markers in the blood of the pregnant mother, and child (from birth through 5 years), that reflect dietary intake and can forecast a child's likelihood of developing the "Metabolic Syndrome", a strong risk state for future diabetes and heart disease. We anticipate that these findings will strengthen the scientific evidence underpinning dietary guidelines for pregnancy and early childhood. It will also provide novel data to guide future research, and have direct relevance for clinical practice, and public health policy aimed at the prevention of heart and lung disease, and their risk factors in early life.

column36: How the early environment interacts with prenatal adversity and genetic susceptibility to moderate the risk for anxious and depressive disorders from infancy to early adolescence - the moderating effect of maternal care and the mediating effect of temperament
column37: The precocious and chronic course of depression makes it the disease with the leading cause of disability, an effect marked by a 2-fold difference in the rate for girls and women as of early adolescence. The pace of reduction in the prevalence of anxious and depressive disorders has failed to keep up with those of other chronic disorders. Arguably what is missing is not a list of risk factors, but rather a precise knowledge of how factors interact to predict those at higher risk. Findings associating prenatal experience and psychopathology provide interesting directions. Differences by gender in the response to stress are well document in early emotional development but evidence is needed in older children and adults. Genetic differences in susceptibility to prenatal events are also important. Finally, the early environment as seen in early maternal care might be a significant positive or negative influence on the effect of prenatal, gender and genetic risk. For cost-effective interventions to exploit the higher neuroplasticity in children, such a complex developmental approach is needed to identify those at risk. This is more poignant given the availability effective individual and family interventions. We will examine these important questions by means of a collaboration of 4 prolific international longitudinal cohorts, in Canada (Maternal Adversity, Vulnerability and Neurodevelopment), the United Kingdom (Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children), the Netherlands (Generation-Rotterdam) and Singapore (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Health Outcomes). With samples of 590-15,290 subjects with comparable data on prenatal exposure, genotype, early mother-child interactions and temperament as well as anxious and depressive psychopathology, we will develop a complex model of prediction of anxious and depressive psychopathology in early adolescence which would support efforts for prevention and early identification and intervention of this chronic disorder.

column36: Programmatic research to understand how modifiable environmental factors interact with the genome in the development of asthma.
column37: Lungs are for life, and we don't think about them much. Yet even small babies and children can have serious lung diseases, like asthma. In fact, asthma is the most common long-term illness that starts in very early life, and if it starts in childhood, it is a life-long problem. In asthma, the breathing passages (airways) become red, swollen and "twitchy" so they sometimes go into spasm, making it very hard to breathe. Asthma has no cure. Even if they feel fine, people with asthma still have the disease and it can flare up at any time. In Canada, about 1 in 3 people has asthma. It isn't clear why only some people get asthma, but we think it is probably due to a combination of environmental and genetic (inherited) factors. Our goal is to understand environmental and genetic factors that cause asthma in children. We will use samples and data from a large Canadian study, where the mothers and babies were assessed in pregnancy, at birth and up to age 5 years. We will determine effects of 4 carefully-chosen environmental factors predicted to be related to asthma in children: traffic pollution and the amount of green space in neighborhoods; types of bacteria living in our intestines; stress families experience during pregnancy and in the early life of a baby; and breastfeeding. We hope to gain new understanding to create better tools to predict who will get asthma and find ways to prevent asthma from developing in the first place.

column36: Determining the genetic and environmental factors associated with metabolic phenotypes across Canada
column37: The Canadian Partnership for Tomorrow Project (CPTP) is the product of $150+ million dollar investment to create a first class infrastructure to support health research internationally. It is Canada's largest population cohort with detailed data on 300,000+ adults, and a vast collection of biospecimens. The leaders of CPTP have teamed-up with scientists from a range of disciplines from air pollution science to genetics and endocrinology to enable a deeper understanding of how air pollution and the surroundings where people live interact with genes to influence cardiometabolic health. The program capitalizes on existing data and resources to address highly relevant questions for public health authorities, researchers, and health practitioners. The focus is on metabolic syndrome (MetS), a cluster of medical conditions that are common in aging adults, including: obesity, hypertension, high cholesterol, high blood sugar, and insulin resistance. Because people with MetS are more likely to develop diabetes and cardiovascular disease, this disorder represents a substantial burden on healthcare systems. MetS results from the interaction of many genes, lifestyle and the environment, including air pollution, but these mechanisms are not well understood. The activities of this program are: (1) To quantify the effect of air pollution and built environment on MetS; (2) to study the effect of air pollution on molecular changes in DNA that regulate gene activity, and to determine if these changes are associated with MetS; (3) to map differences in the DNA code that regulate the expression of genes, and see if their effect are modified by environmental factors. There are no studies on the genetic and environmental risk factors of MetS at this scale in terms of size, richness of health and genomic data. Neither is there any program that has the infrastructure to return and share data with researchers to facilitate discovery; making this an invaluable return on investment.

column37: Chronic lung diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are very common illnesses in Canada and around the world. column37: Indigenous and allied scholars agree that effective HIV prevention for Aboriginal women must be community driven, with leadership by HIV-Positive Aboriginal Women (PAW). Three decades into the epidemic, Aboriginal women continue to be disproportionately impacted by HIV. Despite the obvious social determinants of HIV for Aboriginal women, public health approaches overwhelmingly emphasize behavioural determinants and employ a 'one-size-fits-all' approach that sacrifices cultural diversity and hinders Aboriginal self-determination. The proposed project is informed by Visioning Health I (VH I): Using the Arts to Understand Culture and Gender as Determinants of Health for HIV-Positive Aboriginal Women (PAW), a multi-site, strengths-based, culturally-grounded, arts-informed, and participatory community-based pilot project. Using a phased approach and building on the success of VH I, the goals of this study are to: 1) contribute to the nascent strengths-based literature on PAW perspectives of health, culture and gender; and 2) assess the process, preliminary outcomes, and sustainability of Visioning Health as an HIV intervention/health promotion program for PAW, using participatory Indigenous evaluation methods. Informed by a decolonizing and social determinants of health lens, and grounded in Indigenous knowledge and ceremony, as well as the GIPA (Greater Involvement of People Living with HIV/AIDS) principle, we propose an arts-informed and community-based participatory approach to evaluate and assess the feasibility of Visioning Health.

column36: Using bacteria-phage interaction networks as a metric for stability in the human microbiome
column37: This research proposes to combine two recent and remarkable advances: the first, the advent of powerful tools to study bacteria that reside in the human body, and the second, the recent discovery of an amazing bacterial adaptive immune system against phages, viruses that infect bacteria. Organisms that call the human body home, collectively called the human microbiome, have been linked to many serious health effects such as cancer and gastrointestinal disorders. Studies of the human microbiome have documented high variation in the types and abundances of organisms, making it difficult to determine what it means to have a healthy microbiome. I propose to develop a metric of microbiome health by studying the interactions between phages and bacteria in the human microbiome. The ongoing war between bacteria and phages has powerful effects on microbiomes, and previous work to study interactions has relied on difficult experiments limited by the fact that most microorganisms cannot be grown in a laboratory at all. I will use a pervasive bacterial immune system that records a "memory" of phage infections to construct bacteria-phage interaction networks using publicly available genetic data, overcoming the constraints of direct experiments. I will then analyze these networks for patterns that remain consistent across many individuals to develop a better understanding of the features of healthy microbiomes. This research will shed light on important unknowns about the consistency of microbiomes across many individuals, an essential milestone in the quest to understand the microbial communities that impact humans.

column36: Why is sexual communication challenging for couples? Understanding the consequences of sexual versus nonsexual communication
column37: Couples in romantic relationships may avoid engaging in critical sexual discussions because they view them as threatening to their relationship. Studies show that partners speak more tentatively to each other during sexual (as compared to nonsexual) discussions, perhaps in an attempt to reduce conflict that can arise from sexual conversations (Rehman et al., in prep). As concealing one's emotions requires mental effort, sexual communication may be mentally taxing for couples (Richards & Gross, 1999). The first goal of my doctoral dissertation is to examine whether sexual discussions are more mentally draining for couples than nonsexual discussions. Second, I explore whether sexual communication can be made less challenging for couples using a technique called cognitive reappraisal, defined here as changing one's beliefs about a concept by highlighting its benefits. In Study 1, I will examine the cognitive costs of sexual versus nonsexual discussions. Couples will be randomly assigned to discuss a sexual issue or a nonsexual issue and then complete a cognitive task. I expect that couples who discuss a sexual issue will perform worse on the task than those who discuss a nonsexual issue. In Study 2, I will examine whether cognitive reappraisal can be used to make sexual discussions less mentally challenging for couples. Couples randomly assigned to a reappraisal condition will read about the benefits of sexual communication, while those assigned to a control condition will read about the benefits of a healthy relationship. All couples will then discuss a sexual issue and complete a cognitive task. I expect that couples in the reappraisal group will perform better on the cognitive task than those in the control group. This research seeks to clarify and resolve issues that interfere with vital sexual discussions between partners. As open sexual communication fosters intimacy, this research aims to improve the quality of romantic relationships for Canadian couples.

Dans la derniere annee, les denonciations du sexisme sur le web ont marque la blogosphere quebecoise. L'anonymat relatif du web permet d'exacerber les prejuges puisqu'il n'y a pas de responsabilite immediate pour les positions tenues ou de systeme de filtrage des commentaires. Tous les jours, des femmes quebecoises y recoivent des commentaires haineux associes a leur genre, leur identite sexuelle, leur origine. Le web quebecois offre neanmoins des safe space comme lieux de ressourcement pour les militantes feministes qui luttent contre le cybersexisme. Comment s'incarne la violence faite aux femmes dans le cyberespace? Comment la violence faite aux femmes faconne-t-elle les rapports de domination dans le cyberespace? Comment la violence faite aux femmes propagee dans le cyberespace se distingue-t-elle de celle qui s'exprime sur d'autres medias? Une telle recherche s'impose en originalite dans un contexte ou la cyberviolence a l'egard des femmes est encore un phenomene relativement nouveau. Depuis quelques annees seulement, notamment depuis l'avenement du plus grand reseau social qu'est Facebook, les rapports sociaux de sexe se produisent egalement dans le cyberespace.Sujet d'actualite qui alimente les debats, c'est aussi une question fondamentale qui doit faire l'objet d'une analyse plus systematique. Or, pour le moment, cet enjeu important n'a pas ete particulierement aborde au sein du monde universitaire.
