column36: "Talk the talk but can you walk the walk?" The role of inter-group dialogue programs in mobilizing young adults for peace
column37: Policy makers, researchers and activists argue that civil society is vital determinant of peace. There is limited understanding however of how do people in conflict-ridden societies mobilize for the peacebuilding effort. Farther, number of studies found that in countries characterized by intractable conflicts civil society participation in peacebuilding is actually declining. In my dissertation project I seek to examine the effectiveness and utility of efforts at the grassroots level to promote conflict resolution and peace building. A tool often applied by civil society for grass-roots-level peace building is inter-group dialogue programs. I use the Israeli-Palestinian inter-group dialogue programs as study case to examine whether participation in such projects mobilizes university students from conflicting groups to actively engage in civil society. The study examines diverse sample of programs to accommodate variability in contents, duration and structure. The research design combines quantitative methods, longitudinal survey, and qualitative methods, interviews and participant observation, to provide a thorough and comprehensive account of the various factors contributing to the success or failure of grassroots programs in mobilizing civil society activism. Insights obtained by the research can contribute to reconciliation and peacebuilding efforts among groups in protracted asymmetrical conflicts, as well as groups engaged in latent or nonviolent conflict. Canada is a multi-cultural and diverse society, it can therefore profit from lessons on initiatives that mobilize young citizens to meaningful civic engagement and effective approaches to conflict resolution. Systematic examination of mobilization as an indicator of individual change is a methodological contribution to ongoing scholarly discourse regarding the assessment measures of programs aimed to create social change.

column36: Thinking with trees to see the forest: Huayruro and the lived experience of deforestation in San Martin, Peru
column37: Without a radical rethinking of our relationship to forests, conservation efforts will be unable to address the rapid disappearance of the world's forests. This is important not only because of species loss, but because of the reality of climate change and a warming world. In Peru, forest loss causes 33% of national carbon dioxide emissions (MINAM 2014b). In the Amazon basin, and in Peru in particular, the largest cause of deforestation is the expanding agricultural frontier. The Peruvian Andean Amazon region of San Martin consistently has the highest rate of forest loss in the country, despite also having the greatest biological diversity. This anthropological research looks at peoples' lived experiences of deforestation by focusing on Amazonian peoples' use of the tree "huayruro" (Ormosia coccinea, Ormosia sunkei). The hardwood tree is used in construction, and its vibrant red and black seeds are used both in souvenirs and as a powerful good luck talisman. Artisans who use the seed to make jewelry note that it is no longer as readily found in the forests as before. Amazonian peoples, the Kichwa-Lamista and Awajun in particular, recognize each tree and plant as having a spirit and as being an individual. For them, knowledge comes from nature - primarily through ingestion of strong medicinal plants. How do these histories of intimate engagement with forests, and recognition of the animacy and power of plants, translate into ordinary interactions with a non-medicinal tree species? Why is the huayruro considered to be powerful for people living in the Upper Mayo and Lower Huallaga watersheds? And how can Amazonian peoples' use of this tree as both a timber and a non-timber product help us understand the lived reality of deforestation?

column36: The Michif language continuum: Supporting language vitality in Metis communities of Manitoba and Saskatchewan through language documentation and sociolinguistic study
column37: The Michif language continuum presents a fascinating linguistic case. A truly mixed language, Michif incorporates Canadian French nouns and Cree verbs, with some lexical borrowings from other indigenous languages such as Ojibwe and Dene. French Michif, a variety of Michif, has a Canadian French foundation with significant Cree influences. The origin of how the Michif languages came to be is still not well known and there are now approximately 650 speakers left in Canada. As Michif is disappearing, steps towards revitalization need to be taken: these include efforts to document the language from remaining speakers to study language variation and assessments of speakers' attitudes towards their language. The goal of this research project will be to address these steps and explore the following questions: how important is the Michif language to the identity of the Metis people of Canada and how crucial is its preservation to the well-being and prosperity of its communities? The project will be a collaborative project with community members and speakers of Michif in Manitoba and Saskatchewan Metis communities and an opportunity to be attentive to their needs. It will also explore social and economic issues that impact language perceptions, transmission and vitality. As well, it will consider accounts of the origin of French Michif and Michif, which is still not well understood. Among the many contributions that can be made by the study of Linguistics, none is more important than the preservation and promotion of endangered languages, such as Michif. After all, a language is the voice of a culture and a people. I believe that valorization of a language is a means of giving importance to the history and the stories that it tells, to a way of thinking and a way of life. The uniqueness and richness of the Michif language and culture are one of the jewels of Western Canada's heritage and identity. To see it preserved and revitalized would benefit everyone.

column36: Therapeutic interventions to impact lung inflammatory responses induced by exposure to environmental pollutants
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a term that encompasses a number of diseases such as chronic bronchitis & emphysema, is a progressive inflammatory condition of the lungs predominantly caused by inhalation of ambient pollutants such as cigarette smoke and air pollution. COPD is a worldwide public health problem that has been projected to be the 3rd leading cause of death and 5th leading cause of disability by 2020 worldwide. Recent epidemiological studies have shown that subjects with COPD and asthma taking statins to control high blood cholesterol suffer fewer exacerbations of their lung disease. We have shown that in animal studies, statins reduce lung inflammation caused by exposure to ambient urban air pollutants. Statins are known to have anti-inflammatory properties, and we suspect that these qualities are responsible for the beneficial effect in subjects with inflammatory lung diseases. Here we propose to directly test the effect of these medications on lung inflammation in subjects with COPD. We will target the lung macrophage, one of the pivotal cells in the lung responsible for processing and clearing the inhaled toxins and particles from the lung. We will use novel state-of-the-art technology to explore the effects of statins on lung inflammation in COPD and specifically on lung macrophages. In addition, it has recently been shown that the lung has its own microbiome (bacterial flora) and several studies have shown that this microbiome is closely linked to the inflammatory response in the lung. Here we will also investigate the impact of statin treatment on the lung microbiome of subjects with COPD. New treatments for COPD are urgently needed and these studies will test statin treatment as a new therapeutic approach to impact lung inflammatory pathways in COPD.

column37: The application focuses on two lethal brain cancers: adult glioblastoma and poor prognosis ependymoma. The application demonstrates inclusion of a pan-Canadian program and collaborations with industry and education. Brain tumors represent the solid cancer for which the role of cancer stem cells is the most clearly demonstrated. The development of improved models in brain tumor stem cells with well characterized genomics, epigenomics, and metabolomics with drug response will be useful not only in brain cancer, but also other solid cancers. Brain tumors rank among the most lethal of all cancers and this application can be leveraged for other cancer types.

column36: Leukodystrophy: A Translational Research Program
column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of rare genetic diseases affecting previously healthy children and leading to progressive disabilities and death over months to years. Unfortunately, no curative treatment is available. It is estimated that 30-50% of patients remain without a precise diagnosis despite multiple tests. The first step to discover a treatment is to understand the causes of the diseases and therefore, to identify the causal genes. Leukodystrophies are characterized by abnormal white matter (myelin) of the brain. Myelin is responsible for the insulation of brain cells (neurons), allowing fast electric conduction in the nervous system. Leukodystrophies are classified as hypomyelinating (lack of myelin formation) and non-hypomyelinating (abnormal myelin maintenance) based on features seen in brain scans. My research program focuses on hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, and more specifically on one disorder called POLR3-related or 4H leukodystrophy. Children with this disease develop progressive difficulties to walk, talk, swallow and see (myopia). 4H is caused by mutations in 3 genes that are important for survival of the cells. Using 4H as my primary disease of interest, my comprehensive research program aims at describing these diseases, including their evolution over time and their impact on patients and their families, finding causal genes and explaining how mutations lead to disease (pathophysiology) in order to improve medical care for the patients and families, find new treatments and prepare for the upcoming clinical trials.

column36: The influence of neurogenetics and stressful experience on emotionally-biased attention and learning
column37: Individuals vary hugely in the aspects of the world they perceive and remember: Some filter their environments through rose coloured glasses to perceive sources of pleasure, while others are overly tuned to signs of threat. Such affective biases in attention are distorted in emotional disorders such as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) as well as in addiction. It has been estimated that mental health disorders, including PTSD, anxiety, depression, and addiction disorders are the second leading cause of disability and premature death in Canada, costing the Canadian Health Care system ~$51 million annually. Given such costs, focused research on individual differences influencing neural circuitry and behaviours that contribute to such symptoms is essential. Yet much remains to be learned about neural mechanisms underlying such biases, and the factors that influence their potential for change. This study will investigate how common variations in genes that influence the activity of neurochemicals, or brain chemicals that influence how the brain functions, influence such biases, and how these can go awry in major depression and PTSD. Understanding these patterns will allow us to better predict why certain individuals may be more vulnerable to emotional disorders and addiction than others in the face of life's stresses. It will also help us to determine how different people may respond to specific treatments differently, where what helps one person harms another, to aid in developing individually tailored treatments.

column36: Role of Embryonic-Derived Cardiac Macrophages in Tissue Repair
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death not only in Canada, but worldwide. After heart tissue is injured, immune cells become activated and are both required to repair injured tissue, but also can themselves cause tissue damage. It was unclear how immune cells could possess such opposing roles. Our new work has revealed that prior to birth, primitive immune cells called macrophages enter the heart and remain there into adulthood. These primitive macrophages help experimental animals heal after heart tissue injury. In contrast, macrophages that arise in adults also can enter the heart after injury and promote tissue damage. Over the next 5 years our lab will investigate how these different immune cells are related to heart disease in animals and humans in order to improve the ability of heart tissue to repair itself after injury.

column36: Towards the use of Epigenetic Therapy as a Primer for Cancer Immunotherapy
column37: The main premise of Cancer Immunotherapy is to stimulate the patient's immune system to attack the malignant tumour cells. Recent progress in cancer immunotherapy protocols has led to exciting clinical results in several types of solid tumours. However, for some cancer types, such as Colorectal Cancer and Ovarian Cancer, the majority of patients do not respond to this type of anti-cancer approach, suggesting the need to combine immunotherapies with other anti-tumour strategies. Unfortunately, chemotherapy - the mainstay of cancer treatment for over 40 years - is immunosuppressive and not suitable for combination with immunotherapy. On the other hand, the new class of therapeutics called epigenetic therapies hold great potential for enhancing anti-tumour immune response and for potential use in combination with immunotherapy. We have found that DNA demethylating drugs can activate immunogenic signals in cancer cells, such as those that engage the interferon and antiviral pathways. We will investigate how this process happens and how it can be used to increase the tumour cell immunogenicity and to improve the immune response against the tumour. We will also evaluate new epigenetic therapeutic strategies that can improve the efficacy of anti-tumour immunotherapy.

column36: Targeting Epigenetic Mechanisms in Prostate Cancer
column37: Prostate Cancer (PCa) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men in Canada. Although cure can be accomplished when the cancer is detected at its early stages, there is currently no curative treatment when the cancer has metastasized, a phenomenon that is accompanied by the appearance of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). The major clinical challenges in PCa are thus the lack of biomarkers that can distinguish early stage, indonent from more aggressive forms of PCa, and the lack of effective treatment for the CRPC. PCa is one the most heritable disease, and more than one hundred genetic variants have been found to increase the risk of PCa -cumulatively explaining 33% of the familial risk for PCa. Understanding of how the genetic variants predispose PCa provides opportunities to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. A few of the risk genetic variants affect genes that translate into protein, but the majority of them don't. About 1.5% of the human genome encodes protein-coding genes, and about 70% encodes genes that do not translate into protein, which are named as noncoding RNAs. Noncoding RNAs function through epigenetic regulation. Unlike genetics that is irreversible, epigenetics can be reversed by various approaches. Through computational analysis, we have identified sixty noncoding RNAs affected by more than half of the genetic variants in PCa. We propose to further investigate how these genetic variants affect noncoding RNAs, and through what epigenetic mechanisms these noncoding RNAs promote PCa development and progression. Finally, we will target these epigenetic mechanisms to improve the treatment of PCa. By revealing the functional nature of specific genetic variants our proposed research may identify specific genetic and lncRNA biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This will favor personalized/precision medicine where therapies are tailored to the unique genetic identity of each patient.

column36: Image-based evaluation of orthopaedic devices and surgical procedures
column37: New orthopaedic implants are routinely introduced by device manufacturers, and are implanted in over 100,000 Canadians per year. Yet a recent study found no benefit from the introduction of any new implant design over a five-year period, with a third of those devices performing worse than the ones they replaced. This has led to device recalls, thousands of revision surgeries, and multi-billion dollar lawsuits. Even with well functioning devices, one in five knee replacement patients are dissatisfied with the procedure, for reasons that are indeterminate with currently available tools. There is a clear need to better identify appropriate targets for innovation, and properly select the patients who could benefit from that innovation. I have developed new techniques to measure hip and knee implant wear using high resolution CT scanning (micro-CT) for preclinical imaging, and video x-rays (fluoroscopy) for clinical imaging. Over the next five years, I will build on this experience, expanding my research to include upper extremity joints and implementing sensor technology alongside these advanced x-ray imaging techniques. The goal will be to measure domains that limit implant performance and patient outcomes, including implant wear, joint instability, and patient activity. Imaging tools will be shared with collaborating researchers at other institutions, and knowledge surrounding specific devices and surgical techniques will be provided to surgeons.

column36: Investigating pathogenesis of blood-borne infections among people who use illicit drugs
column37: The substantial toll from the intertwined epidemics of addiction to illicit drugs and infection with viruses like HIV and hepatitis C remains a leading public health concern in Canada. column36: The Development of Novel Therapeutic and Preventative Strategies for Kidney Stone Disease
column37: This research will prevent urinary tract infections in patients with ureteral stents, as the attachment of bacteria to these tubes is a common cause for hospital acquired infections. Ureteral stents are commonly used by a urologic surgeon in the treatment of kidney stones or other issues causing the ureter to become blocked. Urinary devices account for >80% of hospital acquired infections which are difficult to treat. In addition to increased mortality, these complications add millions of extra health care costs. Currently, antibiotics are our only method of attempting to deal with these infections, but they do not work well due to bacteria forming large communities on the surface of these devices, called biofilms, that can not be penetrated by antibiotics, therefore making them highly resistant. The project included in this application is based on the latest breakthroughs by the Lange, Straus, Kizhakkedathu, and Hancock laboratories at UBC on the development of a novel universal method to coat these devices with novel short broad spectrum anti-bioflim peptides (ABPs) designed to prevent proteins and other components from urine as well as bacteria from attaching to the surface of ureteral stents, thereby decreasing the number of infections caused by these devices. We anticipate that the technologies developed will help the more than 3 million Canadians who need urological intervention each year. The project will establish a strong collaboration among natural science, and medicine, and provide unique HQP training opportunities. The novel anti-infection coatings will also provide a general method for preventing infections associated with other medical devices.

column36: Leaving the Familiar Behind: Predictors of Friendship Formation and Social Integration in New Communities
column37: Social connections and social support networks are essential for physical and mental health. In fact, how long people live is better predicted by the quality of their social relationships and how well they are integrated in their community, than it is by how much they smoke and drink, or whether they are obese. Loneliness, on the other hand, is strongly associated with negative health outcomes including depression, poor sleep quality, more hospital and doctor visits, and compromised immune system functioning. My research investigates the processes involved in successful social interactions with strangers, friendship formation, and social integration. I focus on questions including: What motivates people to seek social contact, and why do some people have a harder time making friends than others? How do people cope successfully with social stress and social setbacks? How do people develop a larger sense of belonging when they move to a new community? These are timely topics, given that North American cultures are characterized by high rates of immigration and residential mobility. Specifically, I will examine whether and how genetic variants, psychological beliefs about oneself and others, and specific behaviours such as eye contact and mimicry, influence the outcome of social interactions. I will also investigate the long-term consequences of neurobiology, beliefs, and behaviour on the social integration outcomes of people moving to a new community. Moving to a new community can be highly stressful, and successfully establishing a new social support network during this transition has substantial long-term effects on health. Indeed, social support is one of the most important buffers against the detrimental effects of stress. In the long term, I plan to use the findings of this research to identify people who are likely to experience difficulty transitioning into new environments and to develop strategies for promoting healthy coping and socialization.

column36: Molecular And Cellular Mechanisms Leading To Pancreatic Cancer Heterogeneity
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. This cancer has been called a "silent killer" because it often does not cause symptoms until very late stages of the disease. At this point, treatment options are limited because the tumor is very resistant to chemotherapy and surgery is often not an option. There are, however, documented cases of patients responding exceptionally well to therapy. This variable therapeutic response emphasizes that there are differences between tumors, which is also known as heterogeneity. Pancreatic cancer heterogeneity has also been observed through differential expression of genes between tumors, but it is unclear what molecular or cellular mechanisms underlie the development of this variability. To improve disease outcomes, we need to better understand what causes this heterogeneity so that we can identify diagnostic tools to robustly identify tumor subtypes. If we can identify tumor subtypes, we can then develop effective treatments against those subsets. To begin to understand heterogeneity, we will use animal models to manipulate characteristics underlying tumor initiation and examine their impact on tumor heterogeneity. Briefly, we will examine whether combinations of different initiating cell types or gene mutations result in differences in tumor appearance, gene expression, or the type of additional mutations present in the tumor. We will then determine whether key differences identified in our models identify subsets of human tumors with distinct clinical outcomes. These studies will expand our understanding of factors underlying the development of tumor heterogeneity and also provide preclinical models to test novel therapeutic strategies potentially revealed by our studies. The knowledge generated by this research will aid identification of molecular markers that can reproducibly identify human PDAC subtypes with distinct therapeutic responses and clinical outcomes.

column36: Understanding the contribution of long chain omega-3 balance in brain health
column37: The brain develops until approximately 6 years of age, and is the tissue with the highest lipid concentration, after adipose tissues. Between the ages of 20 and 100, the brain undergoes physiological changes with the loss of nearly 20% of its weight - mostly in lipids. The brain is especially rich in long-chain fatty acids such as docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid (ARA). Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) intake seems to be efficient in animal studies to promote neurodevelopment and prevent onset of cognitive decline but there is controversy towards this strategy in humans. My hypothesis is that DHA plays a role in human brain functions and cognition but this is conditional to DHA efficacy. In this program, we will investigate three conditions which we have found to alter DHA efficacy: aging, the presence of the APOE4 allele (most important genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease), and diabetic pregnancy. From this new starting point, I aim to answer these questions: what are the conditions needed to achieve efficacy, by which means could DHA supplementation benefit human brain function, does it necessarily involve cerebrovascular health? For this, we will complete our current randomized control trial (300 participants), we will test whether there are breakdown in the cerebrovascular system of APOE4 mice during aging, we will test the relation between DHA supplementation and cerebral oxygenation and vascular functions in humans and we will evaluate DHA transfer to the fetus during diabetic pregnancies and evaluate whether this is linked with neurodevelopment evaluated by electroencephalography. This program focuses on two of the most vulnerable populations suffering from brain diseases - the babies and the elderly - with the ultimate goal of promoting brain health throughout the entire life span.

column36: Integrating innovative interventions promoting social participation to foster health in aging Canadians
column37: Social participation, which involves activities that meet fundamental needs for interactions and self-actualization, is seriously challenged in aging and a major intervention target. Although included in health orientations, few social participation interventions are implemented in Canada. Our recent research demonstrated the feasibility and positive impact of clinical interventions in increasing seniors' functional autonomy, social participation and quality of life. However, to reach a substantial number of seniors, population interventions are also needed. Over the next five years, we will continue to develop, implement and evaluate clinical and population interventions targeting the social participation of older adults. Specifically, we will evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of two clinical interventions with older adults from pilot communities: the Personalized citizen assistance for social participation (APIC; Obj.1) and the Lifestyle Redesign(R) (Obj.2), in helping community organizations and clinicians target social participation. In parallel, one population intervention, the Index of Social Participation Potential (IPPS), will be developed, implemented and evaluated (Obj.3) to guide municipal stakeholders in identifying policies, services and structures that best foster social participation among seniors. Development of the IPPS will be enriched by exploring how age-friendly key components foster positive health, social participation and health equity of aging adults across Canada (Obj.4). These innovations, i.e. APIC, Lifestyle Redesign(R) and IPPS, will be optimized and integrated in one multicomponent intervention, implemented and evaluated in other communities (Obj.5). Our preliminary results suggest that this multicomponent intervention will foster social participation in aging. Since most chronic diseases can be prevented or delayed by an active lifestyle, our results point to one of the most promising avenues to live longer and better.

column36: Developmental Coordination Disorder: Integrating Brain Imaging and Rehabilitation to Improve Outcomes
column37: Developmental coordination disorder (DCD) is a common condition that affects 5-6% of school-aged children, or 1-2 children in every Canadian classroom. Children with DCD find it hard to learn motor skills and perform everyday activities, such as getting dressed, tying shoelaces, using a fork and knife, printing, riding a bicycle, or playing sports. Children with DCD often feel lonely, depressed or anxious, and may have low self-esteem and problems with peers. They also tend to avoid physical and social activities, which further affects their friendships. DCD is a life-long condition that affects school performance, vocational choices, and leisure activities. Up to 50% of children with DCD will also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which further compounds the difficulties that these children face in daily life. We do not know what causes DCD, but we think there are differences in brain development and brain function in children with DCD compared to typical children. Our previous studies have shown that children with DCD use different brain areas to perform and learn motor skills compared to typically-developing children. Having a better understanding of other brain differences will help to explain why children with DCD struggle to learn motor skills. We can then determine if we can change the brain and improve motor skills through rehabilitation. In this study, we will use MRI to compare images of children's brains to accomplish two goals: (1) determine how the brain differs in children with DCD and children with DCD+ADHD compared to typically-developing children; (2) determine if rehabilitation can change the brain and improve motor function of children with DCD+/-ADHD. This study is the first of its kind and will advance our understanding of DCD and hopefully improve outcomes of affected children. Findings will provide evidence for current treatment approaches or offer insight into developing alternate interventions.

column36: Developing Adequate Protein and Energy Recommendations for the Prevention and Treatment of Sarcopenia in Cancer
column37: Two out of five Canadians will develop cancer in their lifetimes. People with cancer lose significant amounts of muscle mass due to the disease itself or its treatment. column36: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Cardiac Toxicity in Patients Receiving Cancer Therapy - An "Onco-cardiology" Initiative
column37: Advances in cancer treatment over the past 25 years have allowed patients to survive well beyond their cancer diagnosis. Unfortunately, the drugs used to treat these cancers can cause heart damage resulting in heart failure (HF). The need to better understand the mechanism of heart damage and its prevention has resulted in a new field of research called "Onco-cardiology". The proposed research program addresses important knowledge gaps in this field through 3 studies. The first study will generate Canadian data on the risk factors and rate of HF in patients with breast and blood cancers treated in Ontario between 2007 and 2012. This will be done using data linkage of administrative data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences and Cancer Care Ontario. This study will help doctors better identify patients at risk and more accurately inform their patients of their HF risk. The second study, in 136 women with breast cancer, will test a novel hypothesis that swelling of the heart (edema) detected by heart MRI is an early marker of heart injury during cancer treatment and that it predicts subsequent HF. If our hypothesis is proven, we can then study various protective strategies at an early stage to prevent HF. The third study is a randomized controlled trial that will examine whether an approach to following high risk patients receiving cancer therapy with heart ultrasound-measured strain, followed by initiation of heart medications when strain falls, can better prevent HF compared to the current standard of care. This study is based on recent knowledge that a fall in strain is an early marker of heart injury during cancer therapy. The proposed studies will allow doctors to personalize the care of each cancer patient, improving their health by allowing them to live free of heart disease after surviving their cancer. Our work will help lessen the burden on the health care system by preventing heart complications from cancer therapy.

column36: Novel health informatics solutions for improving the management of nursing resources and patient safety in acute care hospitals
column37: Adverse events (AEs) occur in 2.9% to 16.6% of all acute care hospitalizations and are responsible for 44,000 to 98,000 deaths each year. Moreover, it is estimated that 30% to 58% of all AEs are preventable. Recent studies suggest that understaffing and certain nurse staffing policies, such as the use of less qualified nursing staff and of overtime hours to meet peak staffing demands, could significantly contribute to the occurrence of preventable AEs. To meet this need, longitudinal studies are required to systematically examine the relationship between various nurse staffing policies and the occurrence of AEs, as well as to define safe staffing policies. Until recently, the detailed data required to conduct such an investigation were not easily accessible. With the advent of electronic health records and the digital capture of nurse staffing data, there is now an exciting opportunity to optimize the management of nursing resources in acute care hospitals. The goal of this program of research is to determine if: a) nurse staffing policies are associated with an increased risk of AEs, b) the risk of AEs in relationship to nurse staffing policies is modified by the complexity of patient requirements and, c) optimal nurse staffing thresholds can be established by level of patient complexity. An important prerequisite to answer these important questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals is to have access to accurate measures of AE occurrence. For this reason, a fourth objective of this program of research is to pursue the development and the validation of such measures.

column36: The Molecular Mechanisms that Regulate Immunological 'Exhaustion' in Chronic conditions
column37: A certain immune cell type, killer T cells, play an important role in controlling chronic infections such as HIV and cancer. My group has discovered that certain killer T cells are genetically different in a very small percentage of people with HIV. These people have natural immunity that prevents disease progression to AIDS. The killer T cells continue to function at a high level and destroy HIV infected cells to ensure that the virus cannot reproduce to the extent of full blown AIDS. However, in most of people these cells become dysfunctional and unable to eliminate infected cells and tumor cells in the course of chronic infections and cancer. My research focuses on better understanding why these killer T cells become dysfunctional and how we can restore their functionality. I will be developing novel immunotherapy approaches to use person's immune system to fight back chronic infections and cancer. Until recently, most cancer immunotherapies did not work for most patients, or caused severe side effects. The dream of a successful cancer immunotherapy only came to life in the last few years. Science, one of the top scientific magazines named this new approach 'breakthrough of the year' for 2013. This breakthrough approach targets a way to re-start the immune system, using immune checkpoints' inhibitors. These immune checkpoints' inhibitors jump-start a patient's immune system to recognize and kill infected cells and tumors. They are game-changers for chronic infections and cancer. Using immune checkpoints' inhibitor therapy is revolutionizing cancer treatment by manipulating a person's immune system to fight their infected cells and cancer cells. I aim to understand how killer T cells become dysfunctional in the context of HIV and cancer in order to develop novel immunotherapy drugs. I will identify and develop novel immunotherapy approaches to target these immune checkpoints to allow killer T cells to stay protective and kill infected cells and cancer cells.

column36: Understanding the generation and protective functions of broadly-neutralizing humoral immune responses against influenza A virus
column37: Influenza virus is one of the top ten leading causes of death in Canada, and remains one of the gravest threats to global public health due to its propensity to cause pandemics. To combat seasonal influenza epidemics, massive annual vaccination programs are carried out at tremendous expense to the healthcare system. The ability of influenza virus to cause seasonal epidemics is conferred by its capacity to rapidly evolve in order to escape pre-existing immunity. This in turn necessitates that influenza virus vaccines be reformulated on a nearly annual basis. Frequently, the strains of influenza virus that actually circulate do not perfectly resemble the strains included in the vaccine. Due to the exquisitely strain-specific immunity that current vaccines elicit, vaccine efficacy can suffer substantially when imperfect matches occur. More importantly, current vaccines offer little to no protection against the emergence of a novel influenza virus pandemic. Therefore, there is a tremendous need to develop new influenza virus vaccines capable of inducing broad and long-lasting protection. The recent discovery of broadly-neutralizing antibodies that bind to the stalk domain of hemagglutinin has raised the hope that development of a "universal" influenza virus vaccine may be within reach. While many studies have addressed how these antibodies function in isolation, little is known about the way that broadly-neutralizing antibodies are generated and function in the context of the polyclonal responses that are naturally elicited by vaccination and infection. Our studies will define the mechanisms that govern the generation and function of broadly-neutralizing antibodies in the context of the polyclonal response to infection and vaccination. The knowledge gained from these studies will be used to advance the development of "universal" influenza virus vaccines and therapeutics which have the potential to substantially reduce the global burden of influenza-related illnesses.

column36: Comprehending epigenomic changes in gene dysregulation and cancer using machine learning
column37: To diagnose and treat a broad range of patients using sequence data, we must understand how genomic and epigenomic differences lead to changes in gene regulation and phenotype. Changes in gene regulation often underlie the mechanism of genetic disorders and cancer. These changes can arise from variation in genomic DNA sequence. They can also come from alterations in epigenomic properties, such as DNA methylation, chromatin packaging, histone modifications, or 3D chromosome conformation. New sequencing technology reveals a forest of genomic and epigenomic variation, but we are hindered by insufficient understanding of the variation's consequences. As a result, we can apply these data to diagnosis or personalized drug therapy only in limited cases. My research program addresses this gap in knowledge to understand interactions between genome, epigenome, and phenotype in human cancers. My program applies a systematic framework to create and validate predictive models of (1) how genetic variants cause epigenomic changes, and (2) the effect of epigenomic changes on gene regulation and phenotype. First, we start with data from collaborators or public resources, using cancer cell lines and cancer patient primary tissue. Second, we develop machine learning models of how a genomic or epigenomic input leads to an epigenomic or phenotypic output. Third, we perturb input data and predict changes in output. Fourth, we validate predictions with targeted experiments. Our research will yield better understanding of the impact of epigenomic changes in cancer. It will also deliver new software and annotations to help biologists and clinicians assess changes in the noncoding sequence and epigenome of cancer patients.

column37: Tumours are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists by several changes they exhibit compared to normal cells. One member of the RTK family of particular interest is named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). Much has been learned about how EGFR functions to control the behaviour and growth of cells, mostly by identifying the other proteins in a cell required for EGFR to do this. However, much like knowing the name of dancers does not tell us much about the dance that they will perform, we need to know more than the identify of proteins that work with EGFR to control cell growth and spread: we need to understand their choreography. In molecular terms, we need to understand the organization of EGFR and other key proteins in space and time. We have recently discovered that EGFR signals must be organized in structures called clathrin-coated signaling microdomains to control cell growth and movement. Using advanced microscopy that allow us to 'see' the movement of EGFR and other key proteins (dancers), we aim to understand how these clathrin-coated signaling microdomains work in normal cells and how they are disrupted in cancer cells. Understanding how these structures control the "dance" of EGFR required to dictate cell growth and movement has the potential to allow the development of new therapies aimed at changing the "beat" to control how RTKs drive tumour growth and spreading. Hence, our research aims to help uncover novel strategies to treat certain types of cancer that are difficult to treat with existing therapies.

column36: Preventing Injecting by Modifying Existing Responses (PRIMER)
column37: Injection drug use remains a primary source of HIV transmission globally, and people who inject drugs (PWID) have been shown to play a key role in the initiation of others into injecting. However, no interventions to prevent injecting initiation are proven effective. Importantly, ongoing exposure to injecting increases the risk that street youth and other 'at-risk' populations might initiate injecting, and data suggest that the majority of non-injectors are initiated into injecting by PWID. Reducing the exposure of street youth to injecting is therefore likely to reduce their risk of initiation into injection. This multicountry, mixed methods project will therefore investigate whether a range of interventions and factors that influence injecting among PWID (opioid substitution therapy, supervised injection facilities, stable housing, incarceration environments, public injecting, and gender) may also influence the risk that they initiate others into injecting. This study will seek to: 1) determine how often PWID initiate others into injecting; 2) assess factors potentially influencing the risk that PWID initiate others into injecting; 3) investigate drug scene roles (i.e., drug dealer) that increase the risk that PWID might initiate others into injecting; and 4) test the impact of an existing structural or biomedical intervention on the risk that PWID will initiate others into injecting. To accomplish this, we will conduct a multi-site study of 3,050 PWID across North America and France employing quantitative and qualitative data from five separate ongoing observational studies of PWID (San Diego, STAHR; Tijuana, El Cuete; Vancouver, VIDUS/ARYS; Toronto, HHiT, Bordeaux/Marseille/Paris, COSINUS). This project is the first study to investigate structural approaches to reducing HIV risk by preventing injecting initiation. This novel approach addresses a major gap in HIV prevention programming.

column36: Reducing Cancer Screening Inequalities for Marginalized Populations: Moving from Knowledge to Action
column37: The main goal of this research program is to reduce cancer screening inequalities for marginalized populations. So far, this research program has identified the problem of screening inequalities among foreign-born persons, low-income persons, and those with disability, identified screening barriers and facilitators, and adapted knowledge to local contexts. Objective 2: I will evaluate the success of these interventions. Objective 3: Knowledge use will be monitored by data analyses that assess uptake of interventions, and changes in screening rates for target groups. This research program builds on a solid foundation of previous research. It is also supported by strong collaborations with respected mentors and knowledge users. Accordingly, knowledge translation strategies have been and will be well integrated into the research program. This research program will have a significant impact on existing cancer screening inequalities through clear, tangible outputs: sustainable, innovative interventions applicable widely (primary care, public health) that have been rigorously evaluated and are tailored toward marginalized groups.

column36: Stiffness as a novel biomarker and therapeutic target for kidney fibrosis
column37: Scarring is a major cause of organ failure, accounting for up to 50% of all deaths in the developed world. In the kidney, scarring is the final common pathway of damage activated by nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. If left unchecked, kidney scarring can lead to kidney failure, an increasingly common, costly, and life-threatening condition requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival. Unfortunately, clinicians have no safe and effective ways to diagnose or treat kidney scarring currently. Following injury and especially with scarring, organs stiffen. My lab has been working on ways to take advantage of this knowledge to better diagnose and treat kidney scarring, to identify those patients at highest risk for kidney failure and to treat these individuals with new anti-scarring treatments. In the first set of studies described in this application, we will take advantage of our discovery: (1) that fibroblasts, the main producers of kidney scar tissue, can sense stiffening after injury, and (2) that this stiffening makes them more sensitive to pro-scarring stimuli. We will explore how fibroblasts sense kidney stiffening, to develop new treatments that block the ability of fibroblasts to recognize that stiffening is occurring, and therefore that shut off the scarring process. In the second set of studies, we will take advantage of our recent development of new MRI techniques that can image the stiffness of a kidney without needles or surgery. Our goal is to test: (1) whether MRI measures of kidney stiffness are accurate, (2) whether they correlate with kidney scar measurements as determined by gold standard analysis of kidney biopsies, and (3) whether they predict if kidney function will decline. Given the importance of scarring to kidney disease, our expectation is that these studies, through improving the care of kidney scarring, will ultimately improve the lives of patients with kidney disease.

column36: MOM-LINC: Mechanisms, Outcomes, and Mobilization of maternally-Led Interventions for Newborn Care
column37: Mothers have been crucial to infant survival and well-being through time, yet now they are minimally involved in critical care settings. The aim of this program of research is to improve the way that healthcare is delivered to infants requiring intensive care by enhancing maternal and family active contribution to their child's care. More specifically, the research focuses on three areas. The first is how maternally led interventions can improve outcomes in at-risk newborns related to stress, pain and neurodevelopment. The second is to understand the mechanisms that underlie immediate effectiveness and potential protective longer lasting outcomes of these interventions. The third area focuses on ways to improve the uptake of these interventions by both parents and health care providers. Within this research focus, there are two inter-related content areas: skin-to-skin contact as a pain relieving strategy and breastfeeding in neonatal populations. Overall, the goal is to advance the current evidence to more fully integrate mothers and families as active participants to improve outcomes of at risk newborns that will have direct implications for newborns immediate physiological stability, later emotional and cognitive development, their families, and the health care system. Whereas much of the past neonatal research examined what was provided to families, this research seeks to identify what parents can contribute to optimizing their child's outcomes. In sum, health outcomes of Canadians and the efficiency of health systems will be improved as a result of this research.

column36: Impairments of cortical GABAergic interneurons in epilepsy
column37: Epileptic encephalopathies (EE) are severe childhood-onset epilepsies with developmental delay or intellectual deficiency. These disorders were of unknown etiology up to recently. The advent of next-generation sequencing has revolutionized our ability to identify the cause of EE in many patients and to discover new candidate EE genes in most of the other patients. My work focuses on the identification of the genetic causes of EE and on the discovery of new candidate genes using whole-genome sequencing in a large cohort of children with unexplained EE. Furthermore, I have developed means to selectively repress or mutate these new genes of interest in developing mouse brain cells. This will enable me to study the role of these new candidate genes on neuronal development and function. I am particularly interested in the roles of these genes on the generation, migration, maturation and synaptic function of cortical GABAergic interneurons, the inhibitory cells of the cortex. Indeed, my recent work has demonstrated that altered development or function of cortical interneurons leads to severe epilepsy in mice, reminiscent of that seen in patients with EE. My preliminary results on some of the new candidate genes I identified in children with EE suggest that these genes are indeed fundamental regulators of interneurons migration or function. My work should therefore widen our understanding of the molecular etiology underlying EE and of the cellular and network mechanisms causing the disease. A better understanding of these mechanisms will be critical to our ability to develop new and better-targeted therapies for children with EE and to improve these children's long-term neurological outcome. This personalized medicine approach will undoubtedly improve care for children with EE and their families.

column36: Improving Outcomes in Frail Older Adults with Cardiovascular Disease
column37: The aging population has redefined the field of heart disease from single-system disease-oriented care to multi-faceted patient-oriented care. Frailty is a syndrome seen mainly in older adults that is central to the patient-oriented care model as it reflects the individual patient's reserves and resiliency to stressful events such as surgery. My research has shown that frail patients suffer a 3-fold increase in death, complications, and poor recovery of physical function after heart surgery and other invasive heart procedures. However, existing tools to measure frailty are limited by low specificity in hospitalized patients and ambiguity about their actionable ramifications - this is a critical barrier that has stifled the advancement of treatment strategies. The solution that I am proposing is to use a different marker to measure frailty, one that has the potential to be treated in clinical practice, namely - sarcopenia. Sarcopenia, "the biological substrate of frailty", is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Various criteria exist to define it, some using special scales and others using bone density scanners, but these have not been adequately assessed in patients with heart disease who may have issues such as fluid retention that can cause inaccurate measurements. Thus, I will compare the accuracy and prognostic value of various criteria to determine how we should optimally diagnose sarcopenia in patients with heart disease. Then, I will identify patients who are referred for heart surgery and have low muscle mass and strength (sarcopenia) to test a targeted treatment - a specialized protein supplement beverage - which was designed to stimulate muscle building in older adults, and, I hypothesize, will improve their recovery of physical function and other outcomes after the heart surgery procedure.

column36: Investigating eHealth innovations to improve access and quality of mental health services for youth
column37: The majority of Canadian youth experiencing mental health problems do not have access to the mental health services they need. They navigate a tortuous pathway to mental health care with long delays to assessment and treatment, high rates of service disengagement, and ultimately poor outcomes. Barriers to care include stigma, geography, competing time demands (e.g., school), limited availability and skills of human resources, limited choices in modalities for receiving care, and disconnected services (in-person and online). eMental Health, the use of online technologies to deliver or enhance mental health care, has been identified as a promising avenue to address some of the barriers that young people face in accessing services. Yet, despite its potential, the integration of online technologies in the Canadian youth mental health care system is in the infancy stages of research, policy, and practice. My research program will generate evidence and provide critical insights on how technological innovations can be leveraged and integrated into the mental health care system to improve outcomes for youth. The program will address research gaps in the field, and through training and knowledge translation initiatives, it will also build capacity for research and practice in eMental Health for youth. Research activities will take place at the Youth eMental Health Research and Innovation Hub, a cutting-edge, state-of-the-art living lab, under my scientific direction, centrally located at the University of Montreal's new Hospital Research Centre (CRCHUM) in downtown Montreal's 'Quartier Sante.'

column36: Seniors- Adding Life to Years (SALTY)
column37: Late life is a time when older adults and their caregivers (family and friends) are faced with health and social issues that can impact their well-being. Everyone wants to live well in their final years but this is a challenge, particularly for people in residential long term care settings such as nursing homes. Seniors - Adding Life To Years (SALTY) is a project developed by researchers, care providers, care administrators, policy makers, older adults and their families from across Canada. SALTY aims to add quality to late life for people living in nursing homes and for their caregivers, including family, friends, and volunteers who support their care. SALTY's focus on late life care in nursing homes makes this project unique and urgently needed. Nursing home care in late life is under-researched and undervalued. As a result, care practices, care relationships, effectiveness of innovations, and policy contexts are not well understood. The SALTY team will evaluate promising programs, practices and policies that are being used in nursing homes in four provinces (British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, Nova Scotia). We will develop innovative strategies to understand and assess impact on quality of care and quality of life, with the aim of spreading effective approaches within and across jurisdictions. SALTY's research is organized into interrelated streams: Monitor Care Practice, Map Promising Approaches to Care Relationships, Evaluate Innovative Practice, and Examine Policy Context. We give special attention to issues of dementia, gender and underrepresented voices in this research. SALTY directly engages decision makers, knowledge users, residents and their caregivers in developing our research, to keep our research findings relevant to policy and practice and to improving quality of late life for nursing home residents and their caregivers.

column37: ABSTRACT: As society ages, increasing numbers of older patients are being admitted to Intensive Care Units (ICU) for life-sustaining treatments. Historically, older critically ill patients have been systematically excluded from many clinical trials so there is very little evidence to inform what best practices should be for this population when admitted to ICU. We have conducted several observational studies of older adults suffering from critical illness and determined that there are many problems with communication and decision-making, and that the care provided is often not based on patient/family wishes or values. In some cases, this leads to a poor end of life care, a prolonged dying experience and family dissatisfaction. Moreover, older patients who do survive their critical illness often have poor recoveries. Our team proposes to generate new evidence and synthesize existing evidence in order to create a family-partnered care pathway to define the best care that older patients should receive in ICU, and as they recover from their critical illness. Our focus is on improving communication and decision-making with these patients and their families and ensuring that optimal rehabilitation practices are being realized for those that survive and optimal end of life practices for those who die. We will work actively with our stakeholder groups, including patient and family representatives, researchers, clinicians and healthcare administrators to build knowledge translation (KT) capacity to ensure care is informed by best evidence. We will test this pathway in the province of Alberta and subsequently implement nationwide. The knowledge we generate has the potential to impact quality care for older, sick, vulnerable patients and their families in Canada and, working with our partners, can significantly impact care worldwide.

column36: alpha-cell glucagon secretion: regulated exocytosis, dysregulation & rescue of type-1 diabetes
column37: In the pancreas, alpha-cells release glucagon (which causes blood sugar to go up) and beta-cells release insulin (which causes blood sugar to go down). In type-1 diabetes, beta-cells are destroyed by inflammation. Glucagon release however also does not work properly, which can cause life-threatening low blood sugar after insulin injections. No treatment has been developed to regulate glucagon secretion. Dr. Herbert Gaisano is examining pancreatic alpha-cells to: 1) determine how glucagon is normally released which is surprisingly unclear, 2) why glucagon is not released properly in type-1 diabetes, and then 3) determine if there are ways to fix this process. To do this, his laboratory has devised unprecedented imaging technologies to visualize alpha-cell glucagon secretion as dispersed single cells, and also alpha-cells within the intact pancreas in health and in type-1 diabetes. In diabetes, alpha-cells are profoundly influenced by lack of secretion from neighboring beta-cells (destroyed) and excess secretion from delta-cells (somatostatin that inhibits alpha- and beta-cells). Knowing precisely how neighboring islet cells normally communicate with each other, and become unneighbourly to alpha-cells in diabetes will reveal new paradigms in treating diabetes.

column37: Most pharmacological principles used in psychiatry have been discovered by serendipity in the 1950s and 60s. Identification of the primary targets of these first generation drugs has led to an explosion of psychopharmacology blockbusters in the late 20th century. However, psychiatric drug development has since stalled mostly due to a lack of significant new drug targets. Mood stabilizers like lithium are drugs used to manage bipolar disorder, an important mental illness affecting 2% of the population. Research conducted within this project will allow tackling the contribution of FXR1P to the action of mood stabilizers. This will result in a better understanding of the action of existing psychoactive compounds and provide new avenues for the development of more effective approaches for the treatment of bipolar disorders.

column36: Molecular Brake Mechanisms that Regulate Brain Plasticity and Disease
column37: Memory formation requires the production of new proteins that modify connections (synapses) between neurons in the brain. These proteins support long-lasting changes in the strength and size of synapses within neural circuits. Improper control over protein synthesis results in memory impairments and is implicated in synaptic dysfunction/loss in brain diseases including Alzheimer's disease (AD). The overall goal of this project is to define specific protein synthesis mechanisms that determine where, when, and how specific mRNAs are translated into protein at synapses to support their plasticity and utilize these mechanisms to alleviate cognitive deficits in diseases such as AD. To achieve this goal, we will study a pathway we uncovered involving the molecule Fragile X Related Protein 1 (FXR1P). The FXR1P pathway is unique in its ability to selectively restrain the synthesis and activity-dependent delivery of the glutamate receptor subunit GluA2 to synapses in order to control synaptic plasticity and memory formation. Our Objectives are to: 1) Demonstrate how FXR1P regulates structural/functional plasticity of individual synapses, and 2) Determine how regulation of FXR1P and GluA2 can be used to mitigate synaptic deficits and memory impairments in AD models. This research will reveal new concepts regarding the healthy and diseased brain, and potentially identify a strategy for improving memory loss and rescuing the lost potential of individuals with cognitive impairments.

column37: Rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease are chronic conditions that affect all ages. Both conditions are caused by the body's immune system attacking healthy cells in different parts of the body. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the joints, resulting in joint swelling, pain, and difficulty moving. In Crohn's disease, the gastrointestinal tract or intestines are affected, resulting in pain, diarrhea and weight loss. Both conditions have a large impact on patients' quality of life. There is no cure for either disease, but fortunately many treatment options are available for both. Choosing the right treatment for the right patient requires an understanding of what is important to people living with these conditions. Some treatments may work better but have potential side effects. Some medications are taken as pills and others as injections at home or infusions through a vein in a clinic. Currently, treatment recommendations for both conditions are made primarily based on research evidence alone. In this program of research, we will perform multiple studies to understand how treatment decisions can be best aligned with research evidence and patient's unique disease characteristics and preferences. column36: Optimizing the delivery of HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis with Text Messaging Services and Nursing Support
column37: HIV Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is an HIV prevention modality where uninfected persons take 28 days of antiretroviral medications (ARVs) shortly after an HIV exposure to minimize the risk of acquiring HIV. PEP is highly efficacious and is considered the standard of care on medical and ethical grounds. Unfortunately, implementation challenges have limited its clinical and public health impact in Canada. At present, access to PEP is inconsistent and the quality of care varies nationwide. We seek to address two major issues with PEP delivery: First, retention in care after nPEP initiation is a major challenge as only 50% of our patients complete follow-up at the required 3-4 month time point. Mobile phone-based text messaging may offer a simple, innovative solution to address this problem. The 'WelTel' text messaging platform has proven been to improve health outcomes in prior randomized controlled trials but has never been studied in nPEP. Second, the costs associated with nPEP are high, in part because care is usually provided by specialist physicians. However, nPEP patients could readily be followed by trained nurses, since it is administered according to strict protocols and because most patients are healthy. Nurses in public health clinics are ideally suited to this role, being experienced with sexual health and available in health units nationwide.. We propose a pragmatic randomized controlled trial using a 2x2 factorial design to determine whether the proportion of nPEP patients that successfully complete follow-up: a) is higher among those receiving mobile phone-based text messaging support via WelTel than among those receiving standard care; and b) is non-inferior among those receiving care from a sexual health clinic nurse compared to those receiving hospital-based physician care. Our data will provide important information on how to strengthen retention in care and reduce costs to the healthcare system for PEP delivery.

column37: In northern Indigenous populations, rates of chronic disease have risen sharply in recent decades due to a combination of rapid acculturation to Western lifestyle and economic development that lags behind that of other Canadians. My research program conducts ongoing assessment, intervention, health policy research with the goal of reducing chronic disease in northern populations. Assessment research examines how patterns of child growth and nutrition are changing; Canadian Inuit children are no longer shorter than southern populations, for example, and if they continue to grow at the current rate, they will be the tallest generation of Inuit ever to live in Canada. Adult bodies are also changing in response to their environments. Younger Inuit no longer consume a large portion of their diet in the form of fish and marine mammals, a fact which may lead to increased risk of diabetes and heart disease in the coming years. It is important to monitor these changes in growth and dietary patterns in order to provide health promotion and treatment programs tailored to the particular needs of the Inuit population. Interventions are already underway in many northern communities. My research evaluates whether programs to promote healthy lifestyles, including school-based games and young harvester training programs, are doing a good job of exposing children and youth to the healthful benefits of traditional Inuit practices. Early results show that these programs are producing positive effects that go beyond increasing physical activity and exposing children to a wide range of nutritious, healthy, traditional foods. Participating in culturally-derived activities is increasing Inuit children's confidence and self-esteem, promoting responsibility and sharing behaviour, and increasing ties between family and community members. Children are becoming valued carriers of positive health messages, a fact that underscores the importance of investing in child and youth development.

This program of research will close the gaps of current inequities by working authentically alongside Indigenous community partners to address priority needs and concerns that have emerged in each context. This process, named antibody diversification, carries however the risk of deleterious chromosomal rearrangements that favor the development of malignancies, including lymphoma, leukemia and multiple myeloma. Thus, it is imperative that we fully understand how DSBs are regulated to elicit a functional immune response while preserving DNA integrity and limiting cancer development. Ubiquitin, a small regulatory protein, plays a major role in DSB signaling/repair. Several ubiquitylation events catalyzed by E3 ubiquitin ligases take place during the DSB response and have been implicated in antibody diversification. However, less is known about the importance of deubiquitylation events, the process of cleavage of ubiquitin, in B-cells. We are particularly interested in a specific deubiquitinase named OTUB1, which has been previously linked to the DSB response. We are currently characterizing the role of OTUB1 in B-cell biology and the emergence of B-cell malignancies in vivo using an Otub1 knockout mouse model. Understanding OTUB1 functions in vivo will provide insight into B cell biology and carcinogenesis. It may also provide a rationale for the development of therapeutic approaches targeting OTUB1. This work will have broader implication for immunology and cancer biology due to the central role of DSB repair in these fields

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma affect over 6M Canadians. These chronic diseases are typically progressive, debilitating and punctuated by sudden, worsening of symptoms or "lung attack" requiring immediate medical care and hospital admission. COPD and asthma lung attacks account for the vast majority of Canadian hospital admissions and represent a staggering burden that is under-appreciated. The enormity of this becomes apparent by recognizing that in 2008-2011, 1 in 4 Ontario hospital beds was occupied by a COPD patient, equivalent to filling 250 of the 1000 hospitals in Canada with COPD patients alone. Asthma and COPD are commonly diagnosed using a breathing test that measures the volume of air that can be forcefully exhaled in 1 second (forced expiratory volume in 1 second or FEV1). Because of this, current treatments are mainly directed towards improvements in FEV1. Unfortunately, this lung measurement cannot identify the specific location or severity of the abnormalities that we know are responsible for symptoms and lung attack. Recently however, using medical imaging methods and measurements that my lab has discovered and developed, we identified the specific abnormalities that were the source of asthma and COPD lung attacks and the symptoms that affect day to day activities and quality of life. Therefore, the objective of this research is to develop and make clinically-available new imaging tools and measurements to improve personal health and the health of vulnerable adults and children who are susceptible to chronic lung disease. column37: In high-income settings such as Canada, the United States, and the European Union, HIV infection is increasingly being managed as a chronic disease. Our proposed study accounts for the role of key factors affecting mortality and morbidity in the population living with HIV/AIDS, including demographic (e.g., age, gender, ethnicity), life-style (e.g., illicit drug and alcohol use, smoking) and treatment-related factors (e.g., type of HIV treatment). column37: Defining the fundamental mechanisms that underlie precise neuronal assembly during development and regeneration are critical not only for understanding all brain functions, but also for various developmental (e.g. Autism spectrum) and neurodegenerative disorders (e.g. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's etc.) that are met in clinical practice. column36: Structural and Functional Changes in the Retina and Optic Nerve in Experimental Glaucoma
column37: Optic nerve diseases such as glaucoma lead to visual disability and blindness, and are a significant health concern. This research has direct value towards guiding clinicians in how to monitor glaucoma in patients.

column37: Lung cancer is the most common cancer, killing 1.6 million people each year worldwide. Once the ranges of bleeding rates responsive to our proposed medicines and novel treatments are established we can test these in humans using existing imaging sequences that measure rates of bleeding. column36: The impact of disclosing personalized depression risk information on high-risk individuals' outcomes
column37: Major depressive episode (MDE) is one of the most prevalent and disabling form of mental illness in the general population. Despite increased mental health services and antidepressants use in the past 10 years, there has been no measurable change in the prevalence of MDE in the Canadian general population, which motivates the search for additional strategies for reducing the burden of MDE. One strategy that has been successful in the fields of oncology, cardiology and diabetes is early identification and prevention - identifying people who are at high risk and taking preventive actions to lower the risk so as to prevent symptoms from progressing into a MDE. The proposed study stems from a project funded by an operating grant from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR). With the CIHR support, the team developed and validated sex-specific prediction algorithms for MDE. As risk prediction is at very early stage in psychiatry and MDE is still highly stigmatized, to facilitate the future implementation of the developed risk prediction algorithms, the proposed study seeks to answer the following research questions: (1) Does disclosure of personalized depression risk information promote high-risk individuals to take preventive actions? (2) Will disclosure of personalized depression risk information negatively affect high-risk people's mental health status in terms of increased psychological distress? To answer the questions, we planned to conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with an embedded qualitative component. The proposed study will develop an evidence base for guiding the disclosure of personalized risk information and understanding the process of risk communication and consumer empowerment, contributing to the advancement of early prevention of MDE in Canada.

column36: Structural composition and regulation of electrical synapses in the CNS
column37: Numerous neurotransmitters are used by nerve cells in the brain to communicate with each other at chemical synapses. However, over the past 15 years, surprising discoveries by us and others have shown that another mode of neuronal communication mediated by electrical synapses is also prevalent in the mammalian central nervous system. These synapses are critical for information processing related to cognitive, sensory and motor functions of the brain. Such synapses are formed by structures called gap junctions that are located at close appositions between neurons, and are composed of the gap junction-forming protein connexin36 as well as a growing list of accessory proteins. Our work shows that these structures are complex, with many protein components supporting their assembly, maintenance and neurotransmission functions. Identification of those components and their functions is essential for understanding the normal operation of electrical synapses and how their malfunction could contribute to brain disorders. With our past and more recent discoveries of some of their key protein components (ZO-1, MUPP1, AF6, cingulin, N-cadherin, nectin-1, alpha-catenins and beta-catenin, SynGAP1), we aim to determine how these proteins are organized and regulate electrical synapses. Our finding of the protein SynGAP1 at these synapses is particularly intriguing, because it is already known to be important for regulating communication at chemical synapses and may be equally important at electrical synapses. Further, mutations in the gene coding for this protein were recently found to cause significant intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy in people. We expect that our work will reveal entirely new concepts on cellular mechanisms that govern the activities of electrical synapses, which will ultimately be important for considerations of how these synapses could potentially malfunction and contribute to neurological disorders.

column37: The retina is a light-sensitive layer of cells lining the back of the eye that help us to see. When babies are born too early, the blood vessels on the retina are not fully developed. column37: The circadian timing system generates biological rhythms in physiology and behaviour that are synchronized with the environment. Biol., 2008; Krupp et al., Neuron, 2013). column37: Over the last decade impressive advances have been made in our understanding of spinal cord injury (SCI) and identification of possible therapies. column36: A biopsychosocial investigation of Persistent Genital Arousal Disorder (PGAD) in women
column37: Persistent genital arousal disorder (PGAD) is a highly distressing, yet poorly understood, health concern in women, affecting an estimated 1-6% in the general population. column37: Malaria is one of the greatest threats to human health today. Globally, there are approximately 200 million cases per year, resulting in approximately 600,000 deaths, the majority of which are small children. Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite transmitted from mosquitoes to human hosts. Once inside the host, the parasite invades red blood cells to consume nutrients from the host in order to develop and multiply. The treatment, control, and eradication of malaria have long been impeded by the ability of the parasite to rapidly develop resistance to antimalarial drugs. Therefore, it is imperative to develop new drugs that act through molecular mechanisms distinct from existing drugs to control the disease and combat the spread of drug resistance. Due to the complex biochemical interactions between the drug, parasite, and human host, identification of the molecular target of potential antimalarial drugs is an enormous challenge requiring years of intense research. An emerging approach for identifying the molecular target of antimalarials is to sequence the genome of parasites that have developed drug resistance in order to identify the responsible genetic mutations. This project aims to develop a new technology to isolate these drug-resistant parasites in order to sequence their genome to rapidly identify the molecular target of antimalarial drugs. This work leverages a recent discovery made by our research team that found all antimalarial drugs dramatically reduce the deformability of infected red blood cells, which aids the clearance of the infected cells from the host. Using this characteristic, our technology will separate infected red blood cells based on mechanical deformability in order to isolate cells drug-resistant parasites from those containing drug-sensitive parasites. Once separated, we will then sequence the genome of mutated parasites in order to identify the molecular target of potential antimalarial drugs.

column36: Characterization of the proteostasis decline upon aging
column37: Aging is a complex process characterized by a progressive decline of the ability of tissues to retain their functional integrity. At the cellular level, aging has been associated to a reduced capacity to maintain the integrity of the proteome (which is the ensemble of proteins present in the cell).
