In this project, we will specifically identify which proteins become misshapen and tend to clump in brain tissues of aging mice. Our hypothesis is that clumping proteins share similar characteristics that make them more susceptible. We will employ a computational approach to identify these features and thereby rationalize why the identified proteins are more affected upon aging. This study will lead to unique and novel fundamental knowledge that could potentially reveal how proteostasis (i.e., maintenance of a balanced proteome) is affected upon aging, and provide a first glimpse of how the cell landscape is affected when things "start to go wrong". With the current ageing society, it becomes critical that we address this knowledge gap, and identify biomarkers related to cellular aging. These age-related biomarkers could be used in the future to guide studies aiming at delaying cellular aging and stop the progression of age-related diseases.

column36: The roles of WT1 in fibrosis development
column37: Loss of tissue or organ function due to abnormal scarring, also called fibrosis, contributes to about 40% of all deaths in the Western world. Once fibrosis has commenced, none of the available treatments consistently prevent its progression or recurrence. To design more effective treatments, we need to gain a better understanding of this disease process and to identify the events that cause normal tissue and organ repair to deviate toward fibrosis. The focus of this application is a gene called WT1. This gene is well known for its roles in promoting cancers. Increased activity of this gene has been recently noted in non-cancerous fibroses of the lung, liver, heart and hand. We have found that molecules secreted by the immune system potently induce the activity of WT1 and we hypothesize that chronic exposure to these molecules induces sustained WT1 activity, disrupts normal tissue repair and enhances fibrosis development. Rather than testing this hypothesis in animals that do not normally develop fibrosis, we will take the novel approach of "bioengineering" the fibrotic process in our laboratory using cells derived from human tissues. This approach allows us to use genetically identical cells from the same patients before and after fibrosis development. As members of the Roth|McFarlane Hand and Upper Limb Centre, the largest specialist surgical unit of its kind in Canada, we have direct access to the tissues we need to maintain these models. The aims of this project are to determine if increased WT1 activity 1)Disrupts tissue repair processes, and 2)Enhances fibrosis progression. If increased WT1 activity induces fibrosis, there is real potential to target it with treatments and prevent fibrosis. Treatments that target WT1 in cancers have already been proven to be safe and clinical trials of these treatments are currently underway. This project will determine if it is feasible to cross-purpose these treatments to prevent tissue and organ fibrosis.

column36: Regulatory mechanisms of innate T cells in skin homeostasis and disease
column37: Our skin is not only critical for maintaining core body temperature and fluid homeostasis, but also protects us from invasion by pathogenic microbes in our everyday environment. Immediate results from these studies will lead to a greater understanding of intercellular communication in the skin to promote the health of this critical barrier site. Our long-term goal is to harness our discoveries to improve the treatment of patients with immune-mediated skin diseases.

column36: Cell Response and Wound Healing Through Electrical Stimulation Mediated by Conductive Scaffold
column37: Electrical activity commonly exists in our body. It transfers information through nerve and activates our muscles. So there are cells that are sensitive to electricity and are responsive to electrical stimulation. Based on this, we have been studying how to use electricity to change cell activities in order to help the repair of wound. Instead of using metals to conduct electricity, we use conductive polymers. Conductive polymers are manmade organic materials that allow electricity to pass. The advantages of using conductive polymers but metals are that polymers are more like natural tissues such as in softness and elasticity. Polymers also do not get corrosion that may produce metal ions toxic to cells. Organic materials can also be degraded. In previous years we have successfully produced three categories of conductive polymers, the composite with biodegradable polymers and the composites with biostable or biodegradable textiles. We grow human cells on such polymers and then connect electricity to the polymers. In such a way the cells are exposed to electricity. We found that under some types of electrical stimulation, human cells become more active, growth faster, move faster, and produce chemicals and proteins that accelerate the repair of wound. We have presented our results in about 30 scientific articles and many scientific conferences, which makes our group the international leader in this research field. In the next five years, we will expand our research to look at the mechanisms about how electricity affects cells, and to develop protocols to find out how the electrically activated cells can heal the wound in animals. We will use our electrical stimulation model to study the interactions between the cells that made up our skin and blood vessel. Our project combines material science, electrical engineering and biosciences, providing an excellent environment to train students.

column36: Intermittent vs. Continuous Oxygen Saturation Monitoring in Infants Hospitalized for Bronchiolitis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Hospital care accounts for the largest portion of health care spending in Canada. Common childhood illnesses, such as bronchiolitis, are the leading causes for hospitalization and together account for a large portion of hospital costs. To date, there has been a lack of high quality research that answers questions about the best ways to diagnose and treat these conditions. We are proposing to launch a Canadian child hospital research network to study these conditions, so we can improve the health of children and reduce waste in the system. To launch this network, we will conduct a study around the best way to monitor infants hospitalized with bronchiolitis, the most common lung infection and a leading reason for hospitalization in infants. Infants with bronchiolitis have breathing difficulties and are provided supplemental oxygen if their oxygen levels are low. However, there is uncertainty regarding how to best monitor oxygen levels. A probe placed on the hand or foot can be used to monitor oxygen levels all the time (continuous oxygen monitoring) or just every 4-6 hours (intermittent oxygen monitoring). Research has suggested that placing infants with bronchiolitis on continuous monitoring results in unnecessary use of oxygen and infants staying longer in hospital. However, due to the lack of high quality research, its unclear which strategy is best and practice varies. The objective of this study is to conduct high quality research across 5 hospitals to determine whether intermittent compared to continuous oxygen monitoring will reduce the length of hospital stay in infants hospitalized with bronchiolitis. We will also compare safety and cost. The results of this study will inform bronchiolitis practice standards and the best use of health care resources. Furthermore, this proposal will help develop a child hospital research network focused around these common and costly conditions to ensure that children receive care based on the best scientific evidence.

column37: Thousands of dental and orthopedic implants are placed each year to address the ravages of bone degenerative diseases such as osteoporosis, osteoarthristis, osteonecrosis and periodontal disease. This project will provide scientific insight that can guide the design of improved biomaterials and of loading protocols to improve the quality of life of Canadians, and reduce morbidity, the number of implant-related deaths, and the overall health care burden to the Canadian society.

column37: Recent clinical trials have convincingly demonstrated that immunotherapy with anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can induce impressive clinical responses in children and adult patients with refractory B cell acute lymphocytic leukemia. Most importantly, these responses are often durable and long-lasting. Encouraged by this, CAR T cell therapy has been tested in various blood cancers and solid tumors. However, despite limited progress, CAR T cell therapy targeting surface molecules other than CD19 has not yet reached the same level of success. One molecule that might be the answer to this challenge is the Wilms tumor 1 (WT1) protein which is found in many leukemia cells. We have recently found that a fragment (peptide) of the WT1 protein is presented on the leukemia cell's surface by another protein called the HLA class II molecule. This suggests that immunotherapy with CAR T cells can potentially recognize and kill the leukemia cells by targeting these WT1 peptide/class II complexes on the cancer cell. In this grant proposal, we will make CAR T cells targeting the WT1 peptide/class II complex and study their antileukemia activities. The work proposed will use human cells from healthy donors and from leukemia patients to ensure that the results will be able to be brought to the clinic as soon as possible. It is already known that acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) cells often express the WT1 protein and HLA class II molecules. We hope that this study will lay the groundwork to use our innovative CAR T cells targeting the WT1 peptide/class II complex in the clinic to treat patients with AML in the near future.

column36: Therapeutic strategies for improvement of airway epithelial repair by targeting CFTR defect and bacterial infection in cystic fibrosis patients
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF), the most common genetic disease among Caucasians, is due to mutations in the gene coding for a protein called CFTR. Although CF affects many organs, the progressive lung damage due to bacterial infections remains the first cause of mortality in CF patients. Several years ago, we thus decided to devote our efforts to identify novel therapeutic strategies to promote lung repair in CF patients. We first discovered that the capability of airways to repair after injury is less efficient in CF patients than in healthy subjects, due to both the CFTR dysfunction and the presence of infections. Our work also unveiled that CFTR rescue with new compounds called correctors significantly enhances airway repair, but this CFTR rescue and repair improvement are dampened by bacteria. Importantly, we have new data supporting that lung repair could be improved by targeting products released by bacteria and using combinations of CFTR modulators. Using both airway cells and bacteria collected from CF patients, our aim is now to dissect the mechanisms whereby CFTR and infection regulate epithelial repair. Then, we will precisely define the bacterial products responsible for the deleterious effect of infection on airway repair and CFTR rescue. Finally, our aim is to evaluate the most effective strategy, with CFTR modulators and compounds interfering with bacteria, to reach the highest level of CFTR rescue and CF airway repair improvement, despite the presence of infection. Our project will allow better understanding of the contribution of the CFTR defect and bacterial infection in the failure of the CF airway to repair after injury. Our data will also give novel insights to predict the efficiency of CFTR correctors in the presence of infection and to define the best strategy to improve lung repair in infected CF patients.

column36: Regulation of muscle satellite cell self-renewal and differentiation by CCAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein beta: Implications in disease pathogenesis.
column37: Skeletal muscle has a remarkable ability to repair itself after injury or exercise, a feature that can be attributed to resident stem cells called satellite cells. After injury, satellite cells begin to divide to produce daughter cells. Of these, the majority will mature into myocytes that can fuse to one another or to damaged muscle fibers to initiate repair. The remaining daughter cells remain as satellite cells, ensuring that the muscle retains its capacity to repair over the lifespan of the organism. Understanding, on a molecular level, what makes a cell decide to mature or to remain a stem cell can help understand how disease arises in muscle and can help us develop better stem cell-based therapies. My laboratory has discovered that the protein C/EBPbeta regulates entry into myogenesis, promotes stem cell marker expression, and is necessary for maintaining the satellite cell population. In the absence of C/EBPbeta, satellite cells precociously differentiate and don't self-renew, resulting in bigger muscle fibers and a smaller stem cell population that cannot support muscle repair long term. In healthy muscle, C/EBPbeta can be found in satellite cells but once these cells become activated to repair muscle, C/EBPbeta levels drop but reappear at the late stages of new fiber formation. C/EBPbeta is misexpressed in skeletal muscle in cachexia and during aging where muscle wasting occurs. While we know that C/EBPbeta is important to prevent satellite cell maturation, it is unclear how C/EBPbeta regulates self-renewal or what its function is in new myofibers. The proposal will concentrate on answering these questions with the ultimate goal of understanding how C/EBPbeta contributes to muscle disease, and how this can be converted into novel therapies for muscle wasting.

column37: Parasitic Helminths (PHs) are major human pathogens. They include the giant roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides as well as whipworms and hookworms. PHs infect over 2 billion people worldwide causing tens of thousands of deaths per year and widespread sickness. PHs are thus a major global health problem and, while there are a few available drugs, resistance is rapidly emerging and there is therefore a great need for new drugs. How can we treat PHs? To do this effectively, we must kill the infecting PH without harming the human host. This means that we need to exploit crucial differences in the biology of humans and PHs. column37: Chronic pain, including neuropathic pain (NP), affects 1 in 3 Canadians and costs ~$650 billion/year in North America. Rational combination therapy with different NP drugs has shown potential for measurable improvements in pain relief, quality of life and healthcare utilization. Pregabalin (PGB), a sedating anticonvulsant, is proven effective for NP and the antioxidant, alpha-lipoic acid (ALA), is the only non-sedating systemic agent proven effective for NP. We will conduct a clinical trial to compare a PGB-ALA combination to monotherapy for NP. We expect that a PGB-ALA combination will be superior to monotherapy and this difference will be greater than with combinations of 2 sedating agents. Our core expertise comes from a closely functioning multidisciplinary team with proven excellence in chronic pain assessment/treatment, trial design, biostatistics, psychometrics and knowledge translation. Our recently funded CIHR SPOR Network in Chronic Pain will provide opportunities for confirmatory trials and knowledge translation across Canada and beyond.

column37: Parasitic infections pose a major threat to global human health. Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium falciparum, the causative agents of toxoplasmosis and severe malaria, respectively, are particularly important due to their widespread distribution and disease outcomes. Toxoplasmosis is highly prevalent in the developed world and is a leading cause of food-borne illness related deaths in the United States. Toxoplasma infections can lead to a variety of disease outcomes and, if congenitally transmitted, can result in abortion, neonatal death and fetal abnormalities. Children that survive prenatal infection are likely to suffer significantly reduced quality of life with neurological deficiencies such as mental retardation. Nearly 3.4 billion people live in at risk zones for malaria resulting in more than 200 million clinical cases and half a million deaths per year, 85% of which are young children. Given the clear impact of these parasitic diseases on human health and the current challenges in effectively controlling them, novel treatments are desperately needed. To establish infection and cause disease, these parasites must invade the individual cells of a host. To accomplish this, they rely on a sophisticated motility system driven by a unique molecular "motor". However, very little is known about the inner workings of this motor and thus the overall process of parasite motility is poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we will use cutting edge biophysical and biochemical techniques to dissect the motor complex. These studies will provide crucial insight into how these globally devastating pathogens invade host cells, which we will, in turn, leverage to identify novel targeted therapies.

column36: The structural basis of plasmid segregation by bacterial actins
column37: In addition to their chromosomes, bacteria possess small pieces of DNA called plasmids. Plasmids play a vital role in human health and disease because they encode genes for antibiotic resistance, virulence machinery, pathways to digest unusual substances and synthesize toxins. Since plasmids are small, they often get transferred between bacterial cells and thus contribute to the ever-growing problems of antibiotic resistance, infection and disease, nutrient indigestion, and food poisoning. With this project we focus on plasmid segregation systems driven by bacterial actin, a distant relative of the cytoskeletal filament actin of eukaryotic cells. To understand the molecular mechanism that drives plasmid segregation, we will integrate cutting-edge structural and biochemical approaches aimed at bridging single molecules to macromolecular assemblies in the cell. Understanding how the machinery of plasmid segregation works at the molecular level and within the cell will provide opportunities to effectively disrupt the process in drug-resistant pathogenic bacteria.

column36: Restoring useful function to complete and permanently denervated skeletal muscles
column37: Skeletal muscles regulating movements such as walking, hand grasping, breathing and swallowing are controlled by cells in the nervous system called motoneurons. Motoneurons controlling individual muscles often die after a spinal cord injury. Motoneuron death causes the affected muscles to become paralyzed because they are permanently disconnected from the nervous system. There is currently no known way to restore meaningful function to these muscles. However, previous studies from my lab showed that muscles can be genetically modified to express a light activated protein known as channelrhodopsin 2 (ChR2). Muscles expressing ChR2 contract when exposed to bright light even when there are completely disconnected from the nervous system. Here we propose that this technology can be further advanced to restore function to paralyzed muscles without the use to genetic manipulation. For example, paralyzed skeletal muscles will be injected with muscle stem cells that were forced to express ChR2 using viral technology. We propose that the muscles stem cells will become incorporated with the paralyzed muscles causing them to express ChR2. Once they express ChR2, the targeted skeletal muscles can be controlled in a meaningful way with small light emitting diodes (LEDs). We believe these studies will lay the foundation for using this new technology to restore meaningful movement such as hand grasping, or breathing, to individuals whose hand muscles or diaphragm were permanently paralyzed due to motor neuron death after a spinal cord injury.

column36: Imaging cerebral perfusion and energy metabolism at rest and during functional activation by hybrid PET/MRI
column37: Despite only making up 2% of the body's weight, the human brain consumes 20% of the body's energy. Because it has no stores of its own, the brain tightly controls its own blood flow in order to supply sufficient oxygen and glucose to meet the continual changes in energy demand associated with variations in brain activity. The consequence of insufficient energy supply is readily evident by the impact of stroke. However, there is growing evidence that subtle age-related alterations in energy supply contribute to the development of dementia, particularly Alzheimer's disease. Imaging methods using radio-labelled oxygen and glucose (i.e., PET imaging) have played a central role in our understanding of brain energy metabolism. However, these methods are slow (typically taking 30-45 min) and invasive since the activity in arterial blood must be measured, which limits the number of studies that can be performed. The goal of this study is to take advantage of the recent development of imaging systems that combine PET with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Our aim is to demonstrate that the unique features of this combination can reduce imaging times to roughly 5 min and make the procedure completely non-invasive, only requiring subjects to inhale a single breath of radio-labelled oxygen. With these advantages, the method could be used to acquire images under different conditions to provide a more complete picture of how brain energy metabolism is affected by age and disease. The specific aims of this proposal are focussed on validating the proposed MRI/PET method by comparison to the established PET-only approach and to assess its ability to measure brain metabolism in healthy subjects at rest and during a functional task that increases energy demands. These aims will be critical for demonstrating the accuracy and feasibility of the technique prior to clinical studies involving dementia patients.

column36: Acquisition of malignant phenotypes in tumour cells mediated by the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint
column37: Important hallmarks of cancer are the ability of tumour cells to evade rejection by the immune system, ability to spread, and resistance to therapy. One way tumour cells avoid immune rejection is by inactivating immune cells through the interaction of specific cell surface molecules, a mechanism referred to as "immune checkpoint". One of these immune checkpoints involves the interaction of a molecule on immune cells, the Programmed Death 1 (PD-1) with another molecule, the Programmed Death Ligand 1 ligand (PD-L1), on tumour cells. This interaction results in the inactivation of immune cells that would otherwise kill the tumour cells. Thus, exciting new therapeutic approaches are designed to interfere with the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint in order to control cancer. Some of these approaches have shown unprecedented and highly encouraging clinical responses in patients with various advanced cancers. We have evidence that, independently of its effects on immune cell inactivation, interaction of PD-1 with PD-L1 also promotes malignant properties (drug resistance and invasiveness) in the tumour cells. Hence, this immune checkpoint has a dual effect: it inactivates anti-tumour immune responses and endows tumour cells with aggressive properties. We plan to test the hypothesis that PD-1/PD-L1 signalling in tumour cells contributes to metastatic ability and resistance to chemotherapy. We will conduct studies that will lead us to an understanding of the mechanism by which PD-1/PD-L1 leads to aggressive properties in tumour cells. We plan to accomplish this using animal and cell culture models in which we will manipulate (stimulate or block) the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint and determine how such manipulation affects metastatic ability and drug resistance. These studies are important because they could help us improve therapies designed to target the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint.

column36: Investigating the role of eIF2beta in translation reprogramming in cancer
column37: mRNA translation is a process during which proteins are synthesized by translation machinery based on the information stored in messenger RNAs (mRNAs). Abnormal mRNA translation is common in cancer. Alterations in mRNA translation provide proteins necessary for neoplastic transformation (a process during which normal cells become malignant), as well as tumor progression and dissemination. However, understanding of the role of translation in cancer remains incomplete. This hampers development of therapeutic strategies to target translation machinery in cancer. The mammalian/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is considered to be the major pathway that controls mRNA translation in response to changes in the cellular environment. mTOR function is elevated in the vast majority of cancers. Through CIHR funded research, we demonstrated that mTOR together with CK2, another regulatory cellular protein implicated in numerous malignancies, activates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2) by phosphorylating its eIF2B subunit. eIF2 is a pivotal translation regulator that has a crucial role to deliver the very first transfer RNA carrying amino acid methionine (initiator tRNA) during the initiation step of translation. Activation of eIF2 constitutes a previously unrecognized way of how mTOR may stimulate mRNA translation. Persistent eIF2B phosphorylation leads to increased protein synthesis, proliferation (increase in cell number) and neoplastic growth, which are all characteristics of cancer cells. Based on these findings, we propose to establish the role of eIF2B phosphorylation in inducing changes in mRNA translation that favor production of cancer-promoting proteins. Considering that the changes in translation, mTOR and/or CK2 signaling are commonly detected in the vast majority of cancers, we expect our findings to yield new strategies to target translational machinery in malignant tumors.

column36: Studies on novel anti-tuberculosis agents
column37: The incidence and severity of tuberculosis (TB) have increased dramatically in recent years posing a major global health challenge. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), TB kills more adults per year than any other single pathogen worldwide and could become a major global epidemic including North America and Europe if is not controlled. There were more cases of TB in 2008 than at any point in history. Close to 5000 people die globally from TB every day. TB is the most common infection among people living with HIV/AIDS and kills one of every three of them. A disturbing fact is that TB is the only opportunistic infection of HIV (and other immune compromised patients), which is a public health threat because it spreads through coughing, laughing and sneezing. Each person with TB infects ~10-14 more individuals/year. Most alarmingly, multi-drug resistant TB (MDR-TB) with a mortality rate of ~89%, and deadly extensively-drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) and totally-drug-resistant TB (TDR-TB) with 100% mortality, have put this disease on high alert. XDR-TB has been reported in >50 countries including USA, Japan, Canada and Europe. The growing number of cases of MDR, XDR and TDR-TB worldwide and treatment failure, is of utmost concern. Consequently, there is a real unmet need to discover novel anti-TB drugs. We have made an innovative discovery of new classes of agents that exhibit potent activity against various pathogenic mycobacteria, including drug-resistant strains, and work by a novel mechanism distinct from the current drugs. In the proposed work, we will investigate anti-mycobacterial properties of these promising molecules in cell cultures and in animal models. The proposed studies will contribute significantly to the knowledge and understanding of new treatments for TB infections. Promising agents will emerge from these studies as a new generation of drugs for TB and MDR/XDR/TDR-TB that improve the life expectancy and quality of life of people worldwide

column36: Pre-Existing Immunity Prior to Heparin Exposure Increases Susceptibility for Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
column37: Platelets are small cells in the blood that help control bleeding. Heparin is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) used in major surgeries, such as heart surgery, and to manage heart attacks and strokes. Patients receiving heparin may have an allergic-type reaction called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Patients with HIT have low platelets (thrombocytopenia) and can develop severe clotting (gelling of blood so it no longer flows) causing loss of limbs, heart attacks, stroke and even death. So this drug (heparin), which usually helps patients, can actually cause more strokes and heart attacks in some people. HIT is a serious problem because it causes catastrophic effects in patients. The problem starts because some people develop attack proteins (antibodies) when they are given heparin. Some of these dangerous HIT antibodies attack platelets. However, other antibodies look the same but do not attack platelets. Testing if people have HIT is a major problem because most tests cannot tell the difference between the dangerous antibodies and the antibodies that do not cause HIT. Our first goal will be to find ways to determine ahead of time who will react to heparin and who will not. If we know that a patient will react to heparin, then the doctor can avoid its use. Our second goal is to understand why some patients develop HIT while others do not. We will study specific cells in patients to see if there is a change during HIT compared to the ones that do not have HIT during major heart surgery. Our group has the knowledge and the equipment to carry out all planned experiments. We are a HIT testing centre for many hospitals across Canada and we are located in an area that specializes in both heart- and blood-diseases providing us with ongoing access to patients with HIT. Once we understand why some patients get HIT and others do not, we will be able to provide better tests and better patient care while avoiding the disease.

column36: Modeling connexin-linked disease
column37: It is a general requirement for normal tissue function that adjacent cells communicate directly with each other through special channels called gap junctions. In over 15 distinct human diseases the genes that encode the proteins (connexins) used to make gap junction channels contain mutations that inhibit their normal function ultimately resulting in disease (e.g. developmental anomalies, skin diseases, deafness, neuropathies). There are 21 connexin genes in the human body and multiple connexins can be expressed and intermix in the same cells, leading to a complex array of gap junction channel types within tissues and organs. The most prominent connexin in the human body is Cx43 and when mutations occur in this molecule, patients exhibit oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD) causing them to suffer from bone and cartilage deformities in addition to multiple other developmental problems that often increase in severity with aging. In this study we will use ODDD patient cells and mutant mice that mimic ODDD to investigate how mutations cause disease in some tissues where Cx43 is found (e.g., bone) but not in others that also contain Cx43 (e.g., heart). Importantly we will use state-of-art strategies to develop and utilize human stem cells that carry the Cx43 mutations and repair the gene mutations prior to cells being specialized into cells of the skeleton. Once it is better understood how connexin mutations cause diseases and deformities that often intensive in aging it is anticipated that these findings could be translated to pre-clinical studies and possible treatments of gap junction-linked diseases.

column36: AMPK regulation of macrophage cholesterol metabolism in atherosclerosis
column37: Heart disease is a condition that affects millions of Canadians and costs the Canadian healthcare system almost 21 billion dollars annually. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of cholesterol and immune cells in the lining of the arteries (atherosclerotic plaque) and is a leading cause of heart attack and stroke. In addition to risk factors such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, the way that our body handles the build up of cholesterol in the arteries is critically important. Specialized immune cells called macrophages are able to take up and store excess cholesterol, protecting the artery wall in the process. These macrophages have specialized pathways to then transfer the cholesterol they scavenge to the circulating lipoprotein "HDL", which then carries the cholesterol to the liver, where it can be safely removed (this is why HDL-cholesterol is called the "good" cholesterol). This is known as reverse cholesterol transport. However, when this process is overwhelmed, cholesterol builds in macrophages, turning them into foam cells and causing atherosclerosis to progress. We have discovered that an important metabolic regulator called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), activates reverse cholesterol transport in macrophages, but the mechanisms involved are still unknown. The objectives of this proposal are to determine how AMPK causes this beneficial removal of cholesterol from macrophage foam cells and to test if this is enough to slow or prevent atherosclerosis. We will use genetically engineered mice that are lacking the AMPK gene, as well as therapeutic compounds that specifically activate AMPK to test our hypotheses. The goal of our research is to investigate and uncover novel mechanisms that contribute to atherosclerosis and heart disease in the hopes of developing more effective prevention and therapeutic strategies.

column36: Targeting cellular aneuploidy through modulation of Ran GTPase in epithelial ovarian cancer
column37: In women, ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America and the second most common gynecological cancer. With few early symptoms, over 70% of patients with ovarian cancer are diagnosed with widespread disease where five year survival rates are low. Our goal is to improve current treatment modalities for ovarian cancer to ensure better outcomes with improved quality of life. We have developed over the last 20 years a rich resource of tissues and cell lines representing the disease. We know that most ovarian cancer cells an abnormal number of chromosomes and our research has shown that this distinct feature can actually be exploited as the 'Achilles heel' of these abnormal cells. We are using our resource to develop new therapeutic agents, in particular small molecules that target a protein called Ran. We have shown that blocking Ran in cells with an abnormal number of chromosome leads to their death but that normal cells can tolerate the loss of Ran. We have shown that targeting Ran would also benefit patients with recurrent disease. This research builds on the strong models we have generated, on an extensive infrastructure between the laboratory and the clinic, and leaves us poised to impact significantly on the lives of women with ovarian cancer.

column36: Testing the Effectiveness of a Brief, Peer Support Intervention to Facilitate Transition from Psychiatric Hospitalization
column37: Among severe mental illnesses, which are responsible for 3.8% of hospital stays in Canada, schizophrenia is one of the most costly and difficult to treat. Multiple hospitalizations are common and, for many, the period of time immediately after discharge from inpatient hospitalization is one of heightened risk as they shift from a very high level of support to much less support in community settings. We propose to examine the effectiveness of a brief intervention that might better facilitate the transition into the community for people with schizophrenia - one that has in preliminary research been found feasible and associated with positive outcomes. The intervention is called the Welcome Basket. It involves Peer Support Workers (individuals with lived experience of mental illness working as supports) connecting with hospitalized individuals in the days before discharge and again in the community in the weeks immediately following discharge. The intervention involves two elements: (i) The 'Welcome Basket', which provides individuals with a small package of staple supplies and comfort items to support their move along with orientation to community resources and, (ii) environmental supports, which are items such as calendars, alarm clocks, reminders and organizers, that assist people with engaging with community activities and routines. Peers also facilitate the connecting of inpatient and outpatient clinical staff and engagement with services. Building upon initial success with implementing this approach, a test of effectiveness will be conducted. This will involve comparing the outcomes of discharge from hospital as usual with the full 6 week version of the welcome basket and a preliminary test of an abbreviated version of the intervention. Engaging in this research is an important step in determining how well this intervention works and facilitating its uptake in clinical settings where it might have an impact.

column36: Nuclear receptor regulation of ovulation
column37: The processes of ovulation and consequent formation of the corpus luteum are essential for providing the gamete for fertilization, for transport of the embryo to the uterus and for implantation and successful gestation. The third goal is to address the mechanisms by which Lrh-1 modifies transcriptional events via cofactors to induce the multiple changes in ovarian somatic cells. The fourth goal is to explore the expression of Lrh-1 and Sf-1 and their targets in ovarian cells from infertile patients to better understand ovarian dysfunction.

column36: Applying unique zebrafish models to elucidate and functionally validate the molecular genetic causes of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
column37: Idiopathic scoliosis (IS) is a complex genetic disorder characterized by three-dimensional spinal curvatures that typically arise during adolescence in otherwise healthy individuals. IS afflicts 3% of children worldwide and, in severe cases, can produce chronic back pain, disfigurement and functional disability. First described by Hippocrates, scoliosis is the oldest birth defect known to humankind. However, despite decades of intense research, the cause of IS remains unknown. As a result, treatment is limited to prolonged bracing and/or invasive corrective surgery. Our poor understanding of IS stems largely from a lack of appropriate animal models. Human upright posture, with cranial-to-caudal spinal load, contributes greatly to IS progression. However, most laboratory animals are quadrupeds and the structure of their spine, center of gravity, and biomechanics of spinal loading differ radically from humans. Consequently, induction of scoliosis-like deformities requires drastic systemic and surgical interventions, which have little relevance to human disease. Fish, however, experience spinal loads similar to humans (cranial-to-caudal), generated as a function of swimming forward through dense media (water). The zebrafish, in particular, has emerged as a powerful organism for modeling human congenital defects and disease, and we recently characterized multiple, independent zebrafish mutant strains as faithful, genetically defined, developmental models of IS. Using these invaluable resources (tractable to both biological and genetic experimentation), we have now discovered the elusive biological causes of IS. Here we apply the unique insights gained from our zebrafish models to instruct clinical next-generation sequencing studies into the genetic causes of human IS. Proposed studies will identify, for the first time, specific molecular mechanisms underlying spinal curve formation and identify novel targets for therapeutic treatment.

column36: Understanding HIV-mediated innate immune dysregulation: the role of the immune inhibitory protein LAG-3
column37: HIV is known to cause defects of the immune system which are the hallmark of HIV disease. Despite the increasing availability of antiretroviral therapy (ART) to treat HIV infections, we are still unable to completely restore the function of the immune system in people who are infected with the virus. One part of the immune system that does not recover in individuals taking ART is called the innate immune system, and the reasons why the innate immune system remains non- functional are not well understood. Over the course of many years of an HIV infection, constant exposure to the virus causes cells of the immune system to begin to display markers on their surface that inhibit their function. This project focuses on the expression of one of these markers, called LAG-3, and its expression on cells of the earliest phase of immunity called the innate immune system. Our published data indicates that LAG-3 is at least partially responsible for some of the defects that occur in innate immunity, regardless of whether someone is taking ART or not. The goal of this proposal is to determine exactly what role LAG-3 is playing in inhibiting the immune system, and whether its effects can be blocked in order to boost the immune response. It will also determine what causes LAG-3 to be expressed on immune cells, and which immune cells produce more or less LAG-3. This research will allow us to test whether blocking LAG-3 could be part of new treatment options for HIV infection.

column36: HIV antiretroviral exposure in early pregnancy - assessing the impact on progesterone mediated decidual development and function.
column37: It is now recommended that all HIV-positive (HIV+) women take HIV medications during their pregnancy. In Canada, most HIV+ women begin HIV medications before they become pregnant or early in pregnancy. Taking HIV medications reduces the risk of HIV transmission to the baby to almost zero. However, these medications have side effects: they have been associated with a higher risk of having a miscarriage, a preterm birth, and a low birth weight baby. We don't fully understand how HIV medications cause these side effects, or which HIV medications have the fewest side effects when taken during pregnancy. Our lab discovered that some HIV medications cause the levels of progesterone, the "pregnancy hormone", to decrease in HIV+ pregnant women. Progesterone is very important in maintaining pregnancy by helping form the placenta, an organ shared by the mother and the fetus. In particular, the maternal side of the placenta, called the decidua, relies on progesterone to form properly. If progesterone levels are lowered by HIV medications, the decidua may not form properly, possibly affecting the success of the pregnancy. To examine this possibility, we will investigate how different HIV medications affect the formation and function of the decidua. We will use a test-tube model and an experimental model of pregnancy to test how HIV medications affect the growth of blood vessels in the decidua, an important developmental process to ensure that enough maternal blood is available to provide oxygen and food to the fetus. We will also use advanced imaging techniques to compare decidua blood vessels in HIV+ pregnant women on HIV medications with those from uninfected women. Finally, we will test whether supplementing with progesterone will reverse the effects of HIV medications on the decidua. Our findings will inform the selection of safer HIV medications to use in pregnancy and help identify therapies to use in combination with HIV medications to improve pregnancy outcome.

column37: Obesity and eating disorders are known to lead to pathological changes in metabolism, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and are significant and growing health problems in western societies with a very high burden on individual health and the health care system (http://www.cdc.gov/obesity/data/facts.html). Despite intensive investigation and steady advances in our knowledge about the ways in which appetite and eating are regulated by the brain, we still do not fully understand how these behaviours are controlled, nor why and how this control can go wrong and then lead to disease. Consequently, there are currently very few effective treatment methods. Further study and new insights are necessary to combat this escalating health problem. The objective of this proposal is to investigate detailed cellular mechanisms that underlie a central and essential pathway in the brain - the melanocortin pathway - that controls eating behavior. Our proposal takes advantage of very recent discoveries in my laboratory that suggest a completely new way in which the melanocortin pathway works inside cells of a particular region in the brain, called the hypothalamus. We have shown that when a special protein that transports calcium out of brain cells, NCKX4, is not working in mice, those animals eat much less and weigh less. We have also shown that this is because the receptor protein, MC4R, that starts signaling in the melanocortin pathway, uses calcium to work. With these new ideas as a starting point, we will test exactly where and how the melanocortin pathway works. The experiments proposed here will lead to an in-depth understanding of the cellular signals that control feeding behavior, satiety and obesity. This information will be critical in understanding normal feeding behaviour and the events that underlie its dys-regulation. This information has the potential to lead toward the development of novel, much needed, therapeutic agents for eating disorders.

column36: Fetal Origin of Endocrine Dysfunction: The Plasticizer Model
column37: Reduced testosterone has been linked to obesity, cardiovascular diseases, erectile dysfunction and infertility. Adrenal dysfunction can lead to changes in blood pressure. Phthalate esters are used as plasticizers to add softness and flexibility to polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastics, used for a wide variety of products, including personal care products, toys, food wrappings, medical devices, and building and household products. DEHP is the most commonly used phthalate in industry. Because it is not covalently bound to the PVC polymer, it leaches into the environment and comes into contact with humans mainly through dermal exposure, oral ingestion, and inhalation. Active metabolites of DEHP are found in humans of all ages, from fetus to adulthood, and have been shown to decrease fetal testosterone production in animals. In men, there is an inverse correlation between DEHP metabolites and circulating androgen levels. In rats, fetal DEHP exposure results in reduced circulating testosterone and aldosterone levels in the adult offspring, affecting blood pressure and adipose tissue function. Recently, a new plasticizer DINCH has been introduced to replace DEHP in medical devices, toys and food packaging. Based upon preliminary data we hypothesize that in utero exposure to low doses of DEHP as well as DINCH leads to changes in testicular and adrenal function in the adult offspring, and that the altered endocrine physiology results in increased vulnerability to additional exposures to drugs and pollutants. We propose to determine the endocrine and metabolic changes occurring in adult males following in utero exposure to relevant doses of plasticizers, and to identify the mechanisms underlying long-term effects on androgen and adrenal steroids. It is critical to determine whether plasticizer exposure could be a risk factor in the origin of reproductive and metabolic disorders and identify targets for the potential pharmacological reversal of their detrimental effects.

column36: Regulation of steroid hormone biosynthesis
column37: Steroid hormones are critical for the maintenance of the organism's homeostasis, adaptability to the environment, developmental and reproductive functions. Changes in the rate of steroid formation in response to genetic defects, metabolic disorders, and/or drug or environmental exposures can result in life-altering diseases. Reduced testosterone has been linked to infertility, erectile dysfunction, obesity, osteoporosis and cardiovascular diseases. Adrenal cortisol synthesis is involved in stress-response and adaptation; changes in adrenal aldosterone production can lead to changes in blood pressure and thus cardiovascular diseases. Adrenocortical tumors produce excessive amounts of cortisol, and androgen and ovarian tumors produce androgen and estrogen, all leading to endocrine disorders and potentially to pathological conditions. Changes in circulating steroids in peripheral tissues and brain have been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders. The adrenals, gonads and placenta form steroids from cholesterol. The steroids exert their functions throughout the body. Other tissues, including brain, adipose, prostate, and skin can also form steroids that fulfill local needs. For over 50 years, steroid levels have been as indicators used to diagnose various diseases, e.g. Cushing's syndrome, Addison's disease, congential adrenal hypeplasia, hypogonadism, precocious puberty, etc, and steroids have served as drugs for the treatment of endocrine, reproductive and metabolic disorders. These conditions span from early development to aging. Despite the widespread use, and abuse, of steroids, there are major gaps in our knowledge of the mechanisms regulating their production, and the effects of hormones and drugs on their synthesis and function. The goal of this project is to understand the mechanisms underlying steroid hormone biosynthesis and regulation, and thus pave the way for the development of novel pharmacological strategies to control steroid formation.

column36: The International HIV Adaptation Collaborative: harnessing host and viral genetic data globally for HIV-1 vaccine design
column37: Ending the HIV-1 pandemic will require effective vaccine(s). To date however, no HIV-1 vaccine candidate that has reached advanced clinical testing has been able to elicit protective cellular immune responses. Improved T-cell immunogen designs capable of overcoming HIV-1's extensive capacity for mutation, genetic diversification and adaptation to host populations are thus urgently needed. Vaccine concepts guided by analysis of large-scale human/viral datasets represent a promising novel approach. Towards this goal, we have assembled a global team of computational, molecular and clinical biologists with expertise in HIV-1 adaptation, viral fitness, and vaccine discovery and who lead unique HIV-1 cohorts globally. The fundamental premise of our proposal is that large-scale, integrated analyses of host genetic, HIV-1 genetic and HIV-1 functional data can inform the design of novel HIV-1 T-cell vaccine immunogens for both prophylactic HIV-1 vaccines (to protect people against infection) as well as "personalized" immunotherapeutic approaches (to eliminate HIV-1 from those already infected). Importantly, our proposal features both basic and translational aims. Specifically, it seeks to extend our signature evolution/function- guided approaches to elucidate pathways of immunodeficiency virus adaptation within human populations and across species barriers with the goal of identifying universal versus host/viral context-specific HIV-1 epitopes for vaccine inclusion. It also describes how we will apply existing knowledge of HIV-1 adaptation to design - and test - personalized vaccines for HIV cure. We believe that results have the potential to significantly advance HIV-1 vaccine and cure research.

column36: Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes of Prenatal Stress
column37: Prenatal stress is suggested to be a primary cause of adverse pregnancy outcomes. We hypothesize that adverse consequences of prenatal stress (both generational stress and multiple stresses) can be passed on through generations to lead to poor pregnancy outcomes, especially preterm birth, and adverse developmental trajectories in the offspring. Using three distinct rat models of prenatal stress and state-of-the-art immunological, behavioural and epigenetic assessments, we will (1) study effects due of generational stress (transgenerational and multiple generational) and two-hit stress to mothers and fathers and correlate to adverse pregnancy and newborn developmental outcomes; (2) study both paternal and maternal transmission of stress to offspring and (3) study mitigating effects of enriched environments and inflammatory receptor antagonists. This work is expected to lead to the development of an animal model of transgenerational programming of pregnancy outcomes and associated biomarkers. We will identify mechanisms including how the brain translates stress to alter pregnancy health and identify markers of prenatal stress that translate to future human studies as early biomarkers of risk assessment. Further, we will determine if environmental enrichment and drug treatment are able to reverse preterm birth risk and improve maternal and newborn long-term health outcomes. Our goal is to develop new treatments that promote healthy futures for our children and next generations.

column36: Anti-CD11d immunotherapy for CNS trauma
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) are catastrophic, giving rise to lifelong disabilities. While the primary causes of SCI and TBI may differ, they both trigger robust acute inflammatory reactions that negatively impact recovery and may lead to the development of long-term chronic inflammation and further loss of neurological function. Neuroinflammation is driven by nervous system-specific processes and compounded by the recruitment of blood-dervied pro-inflammatory cells to the lesion site. The priority of any treatment strategy must be to minimize damage to the neurons not affected by the initial trauma. The need for a neuroprotective therapy for acute brain and spinal trauma is clearly unmet. The Spinal Cord Injury Team's (SCIT) research at the Robarts Research Institute has focused on developing an anti-inflammatory neuroprotective treatment for SCI and TBI. This anti-inflammatory strategy uses an antibody to CD11d to block blood-derived pro-inflammatory cells from entering into the spinal or brain lesion. CD11d participates in the mechanism that allows blood cells to migrate into spine and brain lesions. This reduces the overall inflammation in the lesion, protects against the loss of additional neurons and increases the overall rate of neurological recovery. Our goal is to advance the CD11d antibody strategy for use in human SCI or TBI clinical trials. We now have available five candidate CD11d antibodies with anti-inflammatory activity in rats that bind to CD11d on the surface of human blood cells. To progress toward human treatment, we will determine which of these candidate antibodies promotes the best neurological recovery and prevents human blood-derived pro-inflammatory cell infiltration into a CNS lesion in appropriate rodent models. Based on these results the best CD11d antibody will be selected for a Phase I Clinical Trial in either SCI or TBI.

column36: The collaborative ideal in Canadian healthcare delivery: Its rise, practice and future
column37: Collaboration is widely touted as a solution to healthcare's challenges, from fatal errors to escalating costs. Canadian governments, institutions of higher education and hospitals have acted on this rhetoric, and invested time, money and personnel resources to improve collaborative practice. Decades after the initial calls to improve care delivery through collaboration, the literature connecting these investments with positive patient care outcomes remains exceedingly sparse and inconclusive. We know that failures of collaboration and communication often harm patients, but educating providers for collaborative practice has proven to be very difficult, and rarely leads to improved patient care. The goal of this project is to draw on historical and social scientific evidence to transform how we teach healthcare professionals to collaborate. In contrast with the pre-existing literature, we see collaboration as a social construction: an idea that was championed by individuals and organizations who successfully integrated it into education and policy. This new framing will help us reach two related aims. First, it will make the development of the idea of collaboration visible through a historical case study. Second, it will allow us to document the impact of the rise of collaboration as a solution on current patient care practices. Providers will be interviewed about their views on collaborative healthcare delivery, on how collaboration has changed practices in their work environments, and on how education for collaboration could be improved. They will also be observed as they work, to help identify the factors that facilitate teamwork. By engaging healthcare professionals and leaders at every step of our project, we will ensure that we maximize the reach and impact of this project. This grant will thus help us prepare the next generation of healthcare professionals for collaboration through evidence-based education.

column36: Prohibitin: a circulating mitokine involved in the Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Syndrome.
column37: Patients with pulmonary hypertension (PHT; high blood pressure in the lungs) have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. These cells proliferate like cancer cells and create an obstruction of the vessels, making it difficult for the blood to go through. Their right chamber of the heart fails as it has to pump against increased pressure, causing many symptoms like shortness of breath, poor exercise capacity, and eventually death. They also have evidence of inflammation in their blood, similar to patients suffering from infections. Although we know that this inflammation is detrimental to the blood vessels and the heart, we do not know its cause in PHT. Finally, evidence of insulin resistance has been found in patients with PHT like in diabetic patients, and again without known cause. All these organs have something in common: they display the same abnormal way to produce energy (metabolism). We therefore hypothesized that factors circulating in the whole body could be responsible for this overall aberrant metabolism seen in organs otherwise unconnected. We were particularly interested in Prohibitin (PHB), a circulating factor that has been found increased in the serum of patients with cancer, another disease with multi-organ metabolism abnormalities. We propose to study the role of circulating PHB in PHT. We will determine 1) whether PHB levels are increased in the blood of humans and animal models of PHT; 2) the potential of PHB to change arterial cells' metabolism, proliferation and survival, and to induce PHT in animals; 4) the mechanisms by which circulating PHB acts; 5) whether the inhibition of these mechanisms improve PHT in human cells and animals. If this is proven to be true in humans, it will have a tremendous impact on our knowledge regarding how PHT starts and progresses and may reveal new ways to treat the disease.

column36: Lymphatic vessel function in atherosclerosis
column37: High blood cholesterol is an important risk factor of cardiovascular disease such as atherosclerosis. High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is called ''good cholesterol'' because it transports cholesterol away from tissues, such as the blood vessel walls, carrying cholesterol through the blood circulation for eventual excretion into intestines. Unfortunately, the clinical outcomes aiming at increasing levels of circulating HDL (or "good cholesterol") have not been as successful as expected, suggesting that raising HDL may not lead to an increased cholesterol clearance capacity or prevention of coronary heart disease. Expressed differently, more cargo ships (cholesterol transporter) leaving from the harbour docks (blood vessel wall), have not led to more merchandise delivered (cholesterol clearance). Thus, a better understanding of the cholesterol clearance process has become necessary to efficiently modulate the progression of atherosclerosis. In this regard, we provided unprecedented insight into the path that cholesterol trapped in peripheral tissues takes during cholesterol mobilization for eventual excretion (Martel, JCI 2013). We demonstrated that cholesterol (merchandise) gets out of tissues (harbour docks) and reaches the bloodstream (sea) by first entering so-called lymphatic vessels (canals). As the lymphatic system - lymph, from Latin lympha, meaning water - generally governs the transport of macromolecules from the tissues to the blood and, accordingly, peripheral lymph contains cholesterol transporters (HDL), a role in cholesterol transport seemed logical. Therefore, we view that improvement of the delivery efficiency would rely on enhancing the navigation conditions, instead of the number of cargo ships per se. The main objective of our emerging research team aims to understand the mechanisms connecting abnormal lymphatic function and atherosclerosis progression, to ultimately lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets.

column36: Development of drug combinations in acute myeloid leukemia
column37: Treatments in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) consist of standard chemotherapy which has been unchanged in the last 30 years and showed limited therapeutic benefits for the majority of patients. Moreover, long-term resistance to these drugs is the main cause of relapse in patients. Recent studies on the evolution of tumour cells suggest that, although the failure of single-agent therapies is almost inevitable, combination of therapies might effectively cure many cancers. However, the mechanism of action of most anticancer drugs is poorly characterized, which makes the rational design of combination therapies extremely challenging. Moreover, due to the large number of possible drug combinations, it is not feasible to test them all experimentally. There is therefore a dire for innovative computational approaches to better explore the large space of drug combinations with the aim to direct in vitro and in vivo testing of the most promising therapeutic strategies. In this project, we propose to address this issue by leveraging large amounts of pharmacogenomic data measuring how drugs affect cancer cells in order to identify efficient drug combinations in AML. We will develop an innovative computational pipeline to explore the large number of possible combinations of thousands of drugs, and to build companion tests predictive of their response in individual patients. We will validate our most promising candidates in the laboratory to test their therapeutic potential in AML cells in a dish and in mouse models. Upon successful validation, our novel therapeutic strategies and associated companion tests will also allow to avoid overtreatment and unnecessary toxicity by selecting the best drug combinations for each individual AML patient. Since we will enrich our drug combinations for FDA-approved drugs in our discovery pipeline, this will allow repurposing of existing drugs and will provide a mechanism to rapidly translate the results of our project to the clinic.

column36: Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Approaches to Stargardt Macular Degeneration
column37: Inherited retinal degenerative diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders that are a major cause of blindness in Canada and the developed world. They are typically characterized by progressive loss in vision resulting from mutations in genes encoding proteins essential for the survival of rod and cone photoreceptor cells. Stargardt macular degeneration (STGD1) linked to mutations in the membrane transporter ABCA4 is the most common monogenic inherited retinal degenerative disease. Affected individuals typically experience loss in central vision in their first decade of life often progressing to total blindness in later years. Mutations in ABCA4 are also associated with other severe retinal diseases including retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration. My lab has shown that ABCA4 functions in the removal of vitamin A derivatives known as retinoids that are produced as part of the visual process. Disease-associated mutations cause a loss in the ability of ABCA4 to remove retinoids. As a result toxic retinoid compounds accumulate causing photoreceptor cell death and a loss in vision. The goal of this research is to further understand the molecular structure and function of ABCA4 and determine how mutations in this protein cause a loss in vision. This information together with our expertise in retinal degenerative diseases will be used to design and develop novel pharmaceutical agents (drugs) as promising treatments for STGD1. column37: Obesity is a serious health problem in Canada. Lipolysis is carried out by proteins called lipases. We are researching one of these lipases called arylacetamide deacetylase (AADAC), which is present only in liver and small intestine. We are proposing experiments that will show that AADAC decreases fat levels in liver and intestine and therefore also the production of particles carrying "bad" cholesterol. AADAC might also metabolize certain drugs, including flutamide. Flutamide is used in treatment of cancer and polycystic ovarian syndrome and hence it is important to determine whether AADAC is indeed responsible for the harmful side effects in patients taking this drug. We have developed technology that will allow us to determine the importance of AADAC in fat and drug metabolism. column36: Characterization and cytoskeletal regulation of nucleocytoplasmic traffic and expression of mechanosensitive transcription factors. Relevance to organ fibrosis.
column37: Organ fibrosis or progressive scarring of vital organs such as kidney, lung liver and heart is a failed healing attempt in response to chronic injury. Fibrosis is the final common pathway leading to organ failure in many common diseases including diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis and substance abuse. It is a striking but lesser known fact that fibrosis is a major component of mortality, being responsible for 45% of all deaths in the Western World. Despite its paramount medical importance, fibrosis has no cure; currently there are no means to stop or reverse the disease process and the only temporary hope is organ replacement therapy. It is therefore critically important to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the initiation and progression of organ fibrosis. Fibrosis-associated changes are brought about by altered gene expression in various cells. This is due to chemical and mechanical injury-induced activation of transcription factors. These factors need to travel to the cell's nucleus where they turn on target genes. However we do not understand how this process happens and how it can be inhibited or exploited to lessen fibrosis. Our previous work shows that cellular stress induces robust remodeling of the cell's skeleton (cytoskeleton), which may be a key regulator of the nuclear traffic of transcription factors. Therefore, the overall aim of my research is to understand the molecular and cell biological mechanisms underlying the general and cytoskeletal regulation of fibrosis-inducing transcription factors. We will use this knowledge to develop new antifibrotic molecular therapies, such as antifibrotic viruses to halt or reverse fibrosis. To achieve these goals we will create a new molecular toolkit to study and alter the traffic of transcription factors. In summary, these studies will provide fundamental insight into a new area of cell biology, and use the acquired knowledge to combat a common, currently incurable disease.

column36: Impact of chronic infections on hematopoietic stem cell function
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), or blood forming cells, are found in the adult bone marrow, where they are essential for the continuous generation of circulating blood cells, including the cells of the immune system. Their function is normally tightly regulated, and the different types of blood cells are being produced in balanced quantities. In a situation of stress, such as an acute infection, HSCs become activated and they will multiply and change the proportions of the different blood cells being produced with the goal to better respond to the infection and eliminate the infectious agent. Once the infection is resolved, the HSCs will go back to their normal, dormant state. However, it is not known what happens to the HSCs when the infectious agent cannot be eliminated. Some chronic infections lead to bone marrow failure, or the loss of new blood cell production, which can be fatal. There is very little information on how this happens or how it could be prevented. The goal of our research therefore is to better understand how HSCs react during chronic infections using two well-established mouse models. We also propose that the infectious agents (virus or parasite) may actually use the HSCs to escape the immune response by inducing the HSCs to produce one type of blood cell over another. After the completion of our studies we expect to have sufficient new information to identify new targets to treat and hopefully cure chronic viral or parasitic infections.

column37: The insula is one of the least understood brain areas. This is mostly due to its deep location, which makes it less accessible than other structures. By identifying the enzymes produced by tumor cells & inflamed human tissues and by determining the ways that enzyme-induced inflammation in our animal models can be blocked, our data will identify new potential therapeutic targets for treating multiple inflammatory diseases (e.g. atopic dermatitis, arthritis, colitis) & cancer.

column36: Structural and functional investigation of arrhythmia-associated mutations in calmodulin
column37: Cardiac arrhythmias are life-threatening conditions whereby the heart beats irregularly and blood flow to the brain can be temporarily restricted. This can lead to fainting or, in worse cases, to sudden death. Knowing which type of arrhythmia someone has is absolutely key to adjust the lifestyle appropriately and to receive the proper treatment. Many arrhythmias have a clear genetic cause, and typically certain genes are linked to very specific types of arrhythmia. We know that mutations in specific genes can lead to cardiac mutations, but in most cases we don't know how. We simply know that 'somehow a mutation in gene X or Y triggers this or that particular arrhythmia'. In this project, we wish to solve this problem, by investigating the direct mechanisms of individual mutations. In particular, we will investigate several mutations in a gene known as 'CALM'. These mutations have been found in various patients worldwide that have cardiac arrhythmias. Surprisingly, depending on the exact mutation within the CALM gene, the arrhythmia is different. We wish to pinpoint exactly how each mutation works, and how it affects the electrical properties of the heart. Almost every gene in our DNA forms a code to make protein. Ultimately, it is the protein, and not the gene, that plays the actual role in our bodies. A mutation in a gene thus leads to a slightly different protein, which could then result in differences large enough to cause a serious disorder. One problem is that proteins are so small that they are hard to visualize via regular microscopy. We therefore use a highly advanced technique, known as 'X-ray crystallography', whereby we can easily see differences smaller than a 10-billionth of a meter. Here we will compare normal and diseased forms of the protein encoded by the CALM gene. This will yield important insights into the exact mechanism of the disease.

column36: Understanding lysosomal secretion in neurons: a novel mechanism responsible for beta-amyloid release.
column37: A hallmark of Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the deposition of amyloid plaques composed of beta-amyloid peptide in the brain. Although beta-amyloid has been subjected to intense study, the mechanism of beta-amyloid secretion is poorly understood. The goal of this project is to understand a new neuronal system that secretes beta-amyloid called lysosomal secretion. Beta-amyloid is produced by the cleavage of the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) by secretase enzymes. Recently we have shown that these cleavages may occur in a compartment called the lysosome. Although lysosomes are normally viewed as digestive organelles, many cells use lysosomes to secrete specialized contents, including the thyroid, lung, liver, platelets, T-cells, eosinophils, and neurotophils. We have data that shows that neuronal lysosomes contain Beta-amyloid and they are capable of secreting. We will demonstrate lysosomal secretion using a special microscopy technique called Total Internal Reflection Microscopy (TIRFM), which allows us to look at structures very close to the cell membrane (100-200 nanometers). We load cells with fluorescent dyes and use are use this microscope to create videos of lysosomes secreting their contents. We will demonstrate that this process occurs in human neurons. We will then examine several of the regulatory proteins that control this process in non-neuronal cells. Finaly we will demonstrate that beta-amyloid is secreted from lysosomes. Because many other intracellular protein aggregates are also secreted like beta amyloid, this mechanism will likely be broadly applicable across neurodegenerative diseases. An understanding of these processes will aid in the design of therapeutic strategies for AD and neurodegenerative disease.

column36: A new therapeutic target in multiple sclerosis to attenuate neuroinflammation and neuropathology: the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans
column37: Despite the introduction of several immune-modulating therapies in relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis, treatment for many patients remains inadequate. There are also no treatments for patients with the progressive forms of Multiple Sclerosis. Thus, it is important to identify hitherto unrecognized factors that might promote inflammation and neurodegeneration in Multiple Sclerosis, and which are not currently targeted by medications. The Yong Laboratory has identified alterations in the extracellular matrix in the brain of patients with Multiple Sclerosis and in animals afflicted with a Multiple Sclerosis-like pathology. Specifically, there is the accumulation of a group of chemicals named chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPG) in the brain matrix particularly in regions called perivascular cuffs, which are sites where immune cells gather before entering the brain. In preliminary experiments, CSPGs promote immune cell activity in tissue culture studies. Thus, the current research proposal seeks to define the roles of CSPGs in the disease process of Multiple Sclerosis. Moreover, the projects seek to invent and test new medications to reduce the production of CSPGs in lesions of Multiple Sclerosis. In summary, the goal of this proposal is to develop a new treatment for patients with Multiple Sclerosis through the identification of a novel factor in the pathogenesis of inflammation and neurodegeneration, the CSPGs.

column36: Metabolic Adaptations During Breast Cancer Metastasis
column37: The ability of breast cancer cells to spread from the primary tumor to distant sites in the body, a process called metastasis, is the most deadly aspect of this disease. Recent research has focused on how cancer cells meet the energy and building block requirements needed for rapid primary tumor growth. What has been less studied, is how cancer cell metabolism changes during metastasis. In addition, how the environment at distinct metastatic sites, such as the liver, influences breast cancer metabolism is unknown. We demonstrate that breast cancer cells increasingly rely on glycolytic metabolism as they progress from being tumorigenic to becoming highly metastatic. We hypothesize that in order for breast cancer cells to successfully metastasize, several metabolic adaptations must occur which engage different pathways in the cell. Metabolites refer to cellular by-products that can ultimately be used to fuel and stimulate breast cancer growth. We will assess whether metabolites produced by resident cells in the liver can fuel the growth of breast cancer cells that have metastasized to this organ. We will also address whether breast cancer cells can stimulate the production of such pro-tumorigenic metabolites from liver cells, which feed back to the tumor cells themselves. We have also identified metabolic regulators within breast cancer cells that may be targeted to reduce breast cancer metastases to the liver. Thus, this project will investigate the utility of targeting altered cancer cell metabolism as a means to impair metastasis.

column36: Dynamic 3D MRI of the fetus: a new method for detecting abnormal blood flow and oxygenation during pregnancy
column37: During pregnancy, disruption of the supply of oxygen to the baby is a common cause of injury and death. Early delivery is a treatment option, but this must be weighed against the risks of premature birth such as infection and poor organ development. New treatments are emerging to improve fetal blood flow during pregnancy, but selecting the appropriate therapy and monitoring its performance requires accurate tools for measuring the flow of blood and its oxygen content. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a versatile non-invasive technology which offers unprecedented possibilities for evaluating the fetal circulation. Our group is a world leader in the development and application of advanced MRI methods for measuring fetal blood flow and oxygen content, and we have applied these methods to study fetal heart disease and other conditions that affect fetal growth. However, our work has focused on fetal health late in the pregnancy when babies move less. Fetal motion during traditional MRI scans can ruin the images. Thus, the goal of our proposal is to develop fast, motion insensitive MRI methods to reliably measure fetal blood flow and oxygen supply. This will enable scanning earlier in pregnancy, when the fetus can move more easily, and reduce the length of fetal MRI examinations. The first aims of this proposal are the technical development of fast, three-dimensional (3D) fetal MRI. These methods will provide 3D images of the fetal anatomy, blood flow, and oxygen content of blood. Initial development will be done using computer simulations and testing in non-pregnant adult volunteers. The methods will then be applied to healthy and at-risk pregnancies. The MRI methods created through this project will provide a comprehensive assessment of the fetal circulation, enabling physicians working at this frontier of medicine to monitor the fetal circulation and its response to therapy.
