column36: Preventing bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants by adding glutathione to their parenteral nutrition, a translational study
column37: The goal of the study is to prevent or reduce the low sites of gas exchange (alveolar) development in lung (bronchopulmonary dysplasia, BPD) in preterm infants who are on parenteral nutrition (PN), an intravenous way of alimentation. All preterm infants less than 29 weeks of gestation need PN. Our previous studies in animals and in preterm infants showed that peroxides contaminating PN, contribute to the development of BPD. A deficiency in glutathione, an endogenous antioxidant, in newborn guinea pigs on PN and in preterm infants, limits their capacity to detoxify these peroxides. We recently showed in animals that correcting this deficiency, by adding glutathione into PN, prevented the biochemical cascade leading to the loss of alveoli. The proof of concept is achieved in animal. It remains to determine the optimal plasma concentration of glutathione to obtain the highest efficiency in our animal model and test it in preterm infants. Specific Objectives: In animals: 1) To find the lowest plasma concentration of glutathione to obtain the best prevention of alveolar loss in lungs of guinea pigs on PN. 2) To investigate the long-term safety of adding high concentration of glutathione in PN (a concentration needed to reach the highest normal value in plasma). In premature infants: 3) To determine the amount of glutathione to be added in PN to reach the plasma glutathione level defined in objective 1. 4) To confirm the feasibility of adding glutathione in PN to prevent BPD. Pertinence: With the increased incidence of prematurity, BPD represents a very important health care challenge with high economic burden at both individual and public level. This study will help advancing the efforts made to decrease this important complication related to prematurity. Expertise: We have all expertise, scientific and technical knowledge, to lead this study with high success. During the last two decades we have published more than 50 articles on this subject.

column36: Multiple-Case Study of Primary Healthcare Teams with Nurse Practitioners in an Integrated Healthcare System
column37: The province's healthcare system underwent important changes in 2015 to better integrate services across the care continuum. The restructuring may influence how healthcare teams function. Quebec introduced primary healthcare nurse practitioners (NPs) in 2008 with plans to add 2000 NPs over the next ten years to improve access to and the quality of primary care delivered in different settings including primary care offices, long term care and home care. Although studies have documented that NP consultation times are longer than physician consultation times, an in-depth description of what NPs do and how patient and provider roles in teams with NPs develop are lacking. We propose to examine the practice of six teams with NPs providing primary care in different settings (e.g., office, home care, long term care). We will complete organizational surveys to describe the settings; time and motion studies (n= 240 hours) to document precisely how care is provided by NPs; patient/family (n= 600) surveys and provider and decision-maker (n= 60) interviews to describe how roles develop and care is provided by teams with NPs. We will identify how different factors (e.g., type of practice, rural or urban location) influence role development of patients and providers and care is provided by teams with NPs. Patients and families are placed as central members of the healthcare team. We will identify the key components of an effective team and the most useful strategies used by teams with NPs to optimize roles in teams. This information will be used to develop and pilot-test an intervention to optimise patient and provider roles in teams. The study can fill a gap in our knowledge of the care provided by teams with NPs in different settings and inform the implementation of these new roles in Quebec's healthcare system. Decision-makers and clinicians will have a better understanding of the factors that influence consultation times. This can facilitate health human resource management.

column36: Design, Production and Testing of Cladosporin Analogs to Destroy Plasmodium and Other Protozoan Pathogens by Selective Inhibition of Lysyl-tRNA Synthetases
column37: Parasitic protozoans are one-celled organisms that cause a host of human diseases, including malaria (e.g. Plasmodium falciparum), toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii), leishmaniasis (e.g. Leishmania donovani) and amoebic dysentery (e.g. Entamoeba histolytica) among many others. Although these diseases predominate in tropical countries, they can affect Canadians as a result of travel or contact with visitors. Some like toxoplasmosis infect ~23% of the US population and usually produce only mild symptoms, but can severely harm immunocompromised persons or a fetus exposed in the 1st 2 trimesters. In contrast, the World Health Organization estimated 198 million cases of malaria worldwide with >500,000 deaths in 2013. Recently, cladosporin, a fungal metabolite we studied, was shown to inhibit a key enzyme in some of these parasites (lysyl tRNA synthetase) that is required for their protein synthesis. Cladosporin does not inhibit the corresponding human enzyme and is promising lead for development of new pharmaceuticals. However, it is not very water soluble and requires modification to become a useful drug. Our group recently identified the genes for cladosporin production and also made some analogs by both chemical synthesis as well as by biochemical transformation. We propose to extend these studies to make water soluble cladosporin analogs and to test their activity initially against the malaria-causing Plasmodium falciparum (in collaboration with Dr. Elisabeth Winzeler at University of Calfornia San Diego). We also propose to test the target proteins from at least two other parasitic protozoans to determine if they are inhibited by our cladosporin analogs. The results will provide significant amounts of drug candidates for study and will allow their assessment as possible therapeutic agents for malaria and other protozoan diseases. It will also reveal whether the lysyl tRNA synthetase enzyme target is appropriate to prevent such diseases without harming mammals

column36: Comparing the efficacy of CBT for anxiety sensitivity to disorder-specific CBT in reducing mental health symptoms: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Many Canadians with a mental health problem struggle to access effective services. This may be because they live in a rural area with limited services and no clinicians who treat their condition, or because they live with symptoms of more than one disorder (e.g., social anxiety and depression) and our current methods of treating co-occurring conditions (e.g., undergoing two treatments) are not always effective or practical. Such situations have promoted interest in transdiagnostic treatment. This treatment targets underlying risk factors shared by several disorders. By treating shared risk factors, people might get relief from symptoms of multiple disorders. Similarly, one clinician can be trained to deliver treatment to people with a range of disorders. One risk factor that might be targeted in this type of treatment is anxiety sensitivity. Anxiety sensitivity is a fear of arousal-related sensations (e.g., rapid heart rate, breathlessness) that arises from beliefs that these sensations will have serious physical, psychological, or social consequences (e.g., heart attack). Research has shown that high anxiety sensitivity is linked to several mental health problems including anxiety, depression, and substance abuse. We know that a type of psychotherapy called cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) reduces anxiety sensitivity. Thus, the purpose of the proposed study is to compare the effects of CBT for anxiety sensitivity to disorder-specific CBT (e.g., CBT for social anxiety) on mental health and addiction symptoms for people with high anxiety sensitivity. Knowledge obtained from this research will help us understand if treatment targeted at anxiety sensitivity can reduce symptoms of multiple disorders within an individual to the same or a better degree than traditional disorder-specific treatment in the short- and long-term. If effective, this transdiagnostic treatment could increase access to a simple, effective, practical, and cost-effective treatment for Canadians.

column36: Inhibitors of viral pathogenic deubiquitinases
column37: Effective strategies to treat viral disease rely on our ability to interfere with viral infection and/or replication. In recent years, abnormalities in protein turnover states have been frequently observed in various human diseases caused by viral pathogens. This can be attributed to the misbehaviour of a cellular machinery that employs a small protein called ubiquitin, which attaches to target proteins and acts as a signal for their destruction. Therefore, pathogenic effectors that mimic human deubiquitinases (enzymes that remove ubiquitin from proteins) have attracted increasing attention as novel targets for drug development. Unfortunately, the lack of selective molecules to block the function of these enzymes has severely hampered attempts to manipulate them for therapeutic benefits. The goal of this project is to develop highly specific and potent inhibitors for viral deubiquitinases. Using protein engineering technology, we propose to make ubiquitin mimics that will associate tightly with these enzymes in a manner that inhibits function. We will validate their inhibitory function in mammalian cells using established biological assays. Additional structural analyses of critical contacts that mediate specificity and affinity will further aid the development of chemical inhibitors as drugs. In conclusion, this work will generate invaluable tools to understand and modulate activity of pathogenic deubiquitinases and will open new routes to effective antiviral therapy.

column36: Deciphering breast cancer HER2-negativity with regard to HER2-targeted therapy
column37: Breast cancer is the type of cancer with the highest incidence, and it represents the second cause of death in women. Several biomarkers such as hormone receptor status expressed in the breast tumors could predict to a certain level the aggressiveness and potential of development into invasive cancer. The Human Epidermal Growth Factor 2, HER2, is a prognostic marker of clinical outcome in breast cancer. High expression of HER2 occurs in 20-25% of breast tumors and has been associated with a more aggressive clinical behavior. Anti-HER2 agents are administered only to patients with HER2-positive (HER2+) breast tumors. Therefore, patients with HER2-negative (HER2-) breast tumors receive no personalized treatments. These women have higher rate of recurrence, and when this happens a change in HER2 status is often observed (i.e. HER2- at primary diagnosis to HER2+ at breast recurrence). Such tumors could therefore benefit from anti-HER2 treatments at time of diagnosis, which currently are not provided for a primary HER2- tumor. This study will establish a breast cancer gene signature that will identify women in whom an anti-HER2 treatment in prevention (i.e. at breast cancer diagnosis) would be beneficial to prevent a breast cancer recurrence. Through lack of better options, these patients are currently treated with aggressive chemotherapeutic agents only. We can thus expect our research to have an impact not only on the incidence of breast cancer recurrence and prognosis, but on response to treatment as well, hence impacting greatly on their quality of life.

column36: Medication adherence in multiple sclerosis: a model for other chronic diseases?
column37: Only one in every two people with a chronic illness takes their medication as it was intended. This is referred to as medication adherence. People with poor medication adherence often have more health problems. They are also more likely to be hospitalized and are more likely to die. Poor medication adherence is very costly, and is estimated to cost the Canadian health care system $8-10 billion every year. Recently, we looked at information about everyone with multiple sclerosis (MS) from 3 Canadian provinces. We found that adherence to the disease-modifying therapies (DMT) for MS was much higher than what has been reported for other chronic diseases. We think this might be because of the training and support programs provided to individuals receiving DMT. If this is true, we believe MS will provide an excellent model for improving medication adherence in other diseases. However, the only studies available to compare our results to came from very specific groups, included few people, or used varying definitions for adherence. These factors can affect adherence results, so we want to test our theory by comparing our results to the adherence levels we calculate for several other diseases. We will do this the same way as we did for MS. We will also look at adherence to non-DMT medications in our MS group. This will further test our theory that the high levels of adherence are related specifically to the support programs offered with DMTs. There are no support programs for other medications in MS. This study is important for several reasons. First, it will give information about adherence for several common chronic diseases. This information is not known at the population-level, but is important to clinicians and policymakers. Second, the results will identify a possible model or intervention to improve adherence that may be applied to other diseases. Identifying ways to improve adherence will provide significant benefits to patients, and to the healthcare system.

column36: The relationship between iNKT cells & the microbiota in the control of intestinal inflammation
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) likely result from deregulated immune responses to the indigenous microorganisms that reside within the intestine, collectively termed the microbiota, in genetically susceptible hosts. The intestine contains a large number of different immune cells that have the delicate task of fighting off pathogens while "keeping the peace" with the resident microbes. Of these immune cells, T cells are central to maintaining the status quo, and deregulated T cell responses are believed to be at the core of IBD. This past decade has revealed the importance of the microbiota in health and disease, and how it influences the immune system, including the function of different types of T cells. Invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells are a type of T cells that can regulate immune responses during numerous diseases such as cancer, autoimmunity and inflammation. Specifically, iNKT cells play protective or deleterious functions in animal models of Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), respectively. Moreover iNKT cell defects have been found in CD patients. These cells are particularly well equipped to recognize microbes and therefore protect from pathogens. However, their interaction with the commensal microbiota remains elusive. Our previous research has shown that mice deficient in iNKT cells have an altered and pro-inflammatory microbiota. This research project will build on these findings to explore how iNKT cells and the microbiota influence each other, and the impact of this bidirectional relationship on the establishment of intestinal inflammation. Identification of these mechanisms may lead to new therapeutic strategies targeting iNKT cells for the treatment of IBD.

column36: Efficacy of physiotherapy for stress urinary incontinence in women with a known avulsion injury of the puborectalis muscle: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Childbirth is a major risk factor for pelvic floor muscle (PFM) trauma. In one third of women, stretching of the PFM will result in an avulsion injury (i.e. disconnection of the muscle from its insertion points on the pubic symphysis). Recent advances in imaging have led to the discovery of this previously unknown major injury and further research now enables its diagnosis with readily available techniques. Avulsion injury has alarming consequences because it has been associated with a higher rate of stress urinary incontinence (SUI) in the postpartum period as well as the long-term development of other major urogynecological conditions such as pelvic organ prolapse and anal incontinence. Women with avulsion are not only confronted by severe symptoms with significant related impacts on physical activities, overall well-being and quality of life, but they also present a higher rate of surgical failures. Moreover, it is still unknown whether the most recommended first-line treatment for SUI -PFM physiotherapy- is effective in women with this major trauma. Until now, only a pilot study conducted by our team supports the rationale and the efficacy of physiotherapy for improving PFM function in women with avulsion, despite their major muscle injury. The proposed study aims to further investigate the efficacy of physiotherapy for SUI in this sub-population with major obstetrical injuries. Women with an avulsion injury will be randomized either to receive physiotherapy or to be in a waiting-list control group for which treatment will be available after a 9-month follow-up. The current proposal addresses the urgent need to evaluate whether or not women with an avulsion -a prevalent and debilitating long-term condition- could benefit from physiotherapy treatment as a first-line intervention. It will enable women with avulsion to be directed to appropriate treatment options and, if proven effective, PFM physiotherapy could be proposed as a cost-effective first-line treatment.

column36: Functional investigation of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex in neuronal development and function.
column37: Recent technical innovations in the field of genomics have lead to rapid discovery of many mutations associated with human disease. For neurodevelopmental disorders like Intellectual Disability (ID), there are now over 700 known causative genes. Stemming from this tsunami of new information is an increased need to understand the function of these genes in a relevant biological context. Among the 700+ known ID genes, there are several biological processes that are over-represented. This includes chromatin modifiers and epigenetic regualtors, which affect gene expression through biochemical modifications that do not directly alter the DNA sequence. My lab is focused on understanding the role of chromatin regulation in neurons. This project focuses on a specific chromatin remodeling complex, known as SWI/SNF, which is one of the most overrepresented complexes in ID. My lab has initiated a systematic analysis of SWI/SNF components in regulation of learning and memory in Drosophila. Our initial studies have identified a role for SWI/SNF subunits in development of specific brain regions that are required for memory. The main aims of this project are: (1) To investigate whether SWI/SNF complexes also play a role post-development, in adult-specific processes involved in learning and memory. We use a multidisciplinary approach that combines spatiotemporal genetic manipulation, with high-throughput behaviour and cell-type specific genomics. These studies will begin to elucidate the role of the SWI/SNF complex in regulation of neuron development and function. This is a critical starting point toward understanding the human neurodevelopmental disorders associated with mutations in genes encoding SWI/SNF complex members.

column36: An integrated knowledge translation approach to examining a model of volunteer navigation (NCARE) to support older adults living with advanced chronic illness in the home.
column37: For older adults living with advanced chronic illness, aging in place is key to quality of life but without adequate support can result in heavy symptom burden and social isolation. Older adults may not be aware of health and social resources available in their communities, so an innovative model was developed to provide navigation services. In this person-centered approach, trained volunteer navigators advocate, facilitate community connections, coordinate access to services/resources, and promote active engagement of older adults with their community (NCARE: Navigation, Connecting, Accessing, Resourcing, and Engaging). Pilot work indicates this model provides important support to older adults while developing meaningful roles for volunteers. The purpose of this project is to enhance the quality of life of older adults living with advanced chronic illness at home by implementing, evaluating, and planning a sustainable volunteer navigation model using an integrated knowledge translation approach. Eight hospice societies from rural, remote, and urban contexts in BC, AB, and NS are project partners. Hospice volunteers and older adults living with advanced chronic illness will be recruited in each community. Volunteers will receive training and then provide navigation services to assigned older adults, visiting in the home every 2-3 weeks for 18 months. They will be supported by a nurse navigator coach, a hospice society volunteer coordinator, and a local healthcare provider. Evaluation data will be gathered from older adults, families, volunteers, and other stakeholders. At project conclusion, a tool-kit will be created to enable hospice societies across Canada to implement volunteer navigation. Anticipated contributions to Canadian healthcare are significant: older adults will have better quality of life, volunteers will have enhanced roles that build hospice capacity, and supportive care will be implemented early for those living with advanced chronic illness.

column37: Recognizing the critical importance of children's environment to their lifelong health and development, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child's (CRC) reporting system is intended to help State Parties to identify and correct weaknesses and deficits in government service that impact children. column36: Transgender youth in clinical care: A pan-Canadian cohort study of medical, social and family outcomes
column37: Recent media reports have increased awareness of medical interventions to delay puberty and alter physical sex characteristics to align with inner gender identity. As a result, youth whose gender identity does not match the gender they were assigned at birth have been increasingly referred to pediatric clinics that provide this type of care. Rapidly increasing numbers of referrals to nine clinics that provide such treatment in Canada reflect international trends. However, while these treatments are generally considered safe, there is very little research on the short- and long-term social and medical experiences and outcomes of youth undergoing clinical care. This project will study 300 youth (puberty to age 16 at enrolment) who have been referred to these nine clinics for puberty suppression and/or hormone therapy for gender identity issues, as well as their parents/caregivers. We will collect data at the start of the study and over two years of follow-up using youth and parent surveys, as well as youth medical information from the clinics. As a result, we will know much more about the youth who are referred for gender issues and their families, including their previous care, gender identities, family dynamics, social stressors, and factors that affect their health and well-being. We will understand more about medical and mental health outcomes for youth undergoing puberty suppression and other medical interventions, and identify factors that may result in better outcomes, for example age at which treatment is started, type of treatment, or level of parental support. We will also learn about treatment side effects. We will know more about gender and sex development among these youth, and how their physical, mental and social health develops. In addition, we will study how family functioning and parent/caregiver's well-being may change over time. We expect our study will result in changes to medical care, social services, and youth and family decision-making.

column36: Multimorbidity in Children and Youth Across the LIFEcourse (MY LIFE)
column37: Nearly 15% of youth less than 18 years of age are affected by both a physical and mental health problem, a situation known as 'multimorbidity'. This combination of problems can lead to compromised life quality, hardship for families, and considerable burden on the healthcare system. However, given the normal challenges of childhood and adolescence and stress of having a chronic physical condition managing multimorbidity in youth is difficult, but critical. We will determine how and why some youth develop multimorbidity, while others do not, because this knowledge is essential for establishing interventions to improve outcomes. Building on our successful feasibility study, we will document the course of mental health symptoms over time, as well as identify individual, family, and community predictors of mental disorder among 504 youth with chronic physical conditions. We will also examine whether the effects of these predictors are amplified or act through other psychosocial and biological variables such as poverty or physical activity. Furthermore, we will assess the extent to which multimorbidity increases the amount or alters patterns of psychiatric services usage among youth. We will enroll youth aged 2-17 years with a variety of chronic physical conditions (e.g., asthma, diabetes, epilepsy) receiving outpatient care at McMaster Children's Hospital and follow them for 24 months. We will also enroll a subset of age-matched healthy sibling controls. We will use provincial health care data to confirm psychiatric diagnoses and service use. Advanced statistical modeling will be used to estimate trajectories of health outcomes. With rare exceptions, previous studies were cross-sectional and none examined the extent to which youth multimorbidity impacts the amount of psychiatric services youth access. Preventing youth multimorbidity is essential to improve youth trajectories, strengthen families, and in turn, improve care and reduce costs.

column36: Unraveling the genetics of malignant hyperthermia
column37: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a severe, life threatening reaction that occurs upon exposure during surgery to certain anesthetics. While there are treatments for MH if it is recognized in time, response is often incomplete and individuals are left with significant potential disabilities. Thus the best strategy is primary prevention (i.e. avoiding these anesthetics in susceptible individuals). Primary prevention is dependent on correctly identifying who is susceptible, which is accomplished in most situations through genetic testing. A key existing barrier is that not all of the genes associated with MH are known. In fact, it is estimated that 30% of the genetic burden is currently not understood. In this proposal, we seek to identify all of the remaining genetic causes for this life threatening condition. To accomplish this, we will identify mutations in a large MH cohort through the combination of state-of-the art genetic tools (such as whole exome and whole genome sequencing) and novel methodology for evaluating the resulting genetic data. Successful completion of our project will enable accurate genetic diagnostics for MH, and offer the possibility of potentially eliminating the condition through primary genetic screening. In addition, the data from our study will greatly add the general knowledge of muscle function and muscle response to stress.

column37: Diabetes is a very common cause of kidney failure, leading to scarring of the filtering units of the kidneys. column36: The role of anillin in modulating the cytoskeleton of dividing and differentiated cells
column37: Cells adopt different shapes to efficiently carry out specific functions. Cell shape changes are caused by rearranging internal networks of proteins collectively called the cytoskeleton. When the cytoskeleton adopts the wrong shape at the wrong time the cell cannot carry out its function. One important example in human disease is that disruption of the cytoskeleton disrupts cell division and can lead to tumors. Other cytoskeleton rearrangements are required for cell migration, important for metastasis, and the production of cilia, the cell's antennae which are needed for correct kidney function. Therefore understanding how the cytoskeleton is dynamically reorganized at the molecular level will provide new platforms for drug discovery and therapeutics to treat diseases such as cancer and ciliopathies. Our proposal focuses on the protein anillin that binds to and regulates the cytoskeleton. As anillin interacts with many cellular factors, we propose that anillin accepts different incoming cellular signals and translates them into changes in the cytoskeleton. We have discovered a new mechanism whereby anillin regulates the formation of new cytoskeletal elements during cell division. We propose to determine how this new process regulates cell shape changes during cell division and determine if this mechanism operates in other cell shape changes during cell migration. We have also made a new and exciting discovery that anillin is required for making cilia. When cilia are disrupted the cell cannot function and, especially in the kidney, this leads to disease. Mutations in anillin are linked to kidney disease and we will determine how anillin role in making cilia. We expect our studies to identify new regulatory mechanisms that control cell shape during cell division, cell migration and ciliogenesis. This information will be important for the development of new therapeutic strategies in human disease, in particular cancer.

column36: Mechanisms of Inflammation, Immunity and Islet Dysfunction in Diabetes (MI3D)
column37: Over the last 50 years, multiple chronic diseases have seen a dramatic rise in frequency in childhood. They include type 1 diabetes (T1D), type 2 diabetes (T2D), inflammatory bowel diseases and asthma. These diseases share a common feature - they involve the immune system. This system normally functions to protect the body from pathogenic organisms. In diabetes, excessive immune responses towards normal cells that drive tissue inflammation and damage. The recent increase in frequency of these diseases likely reflect dynamic changes in our environment, including our diet, physical activity, hygiene, and use of antibiotics in agriculture and medicine. In the human intestine, resident communities of microbes ("the microbiome") extract energy from the food we eat, and control our immune system function. An altered microbiome may raise our risk for chronic diseases including diabetes. We will test the idea that individuals prone to T1D and T2D share a key risk factor: abnormalities in their intestinal microbial communities that provoke inflammation and damage insulin-secreting and the insulin-responsive tissues. We aim to understand how microbiome disturbances control diabetes development. We will analyze fecal bacteria from children with high T1D or T2D risk to identify how they elicit inflammation. The children's bacteria will be transferred into mice to determine if they cause inflammation and diabetes. We will study the effects of the bacterial products on insulin production and function. With integrated studies in humans, mice and isolated cells, we will identify the interaction between the microbiome, metabolism and immunity during diabetes progression. Because the intestinal microbiome can be changed with diet, medications or probiotics, identification of bacterial products can reveal new therapies to prevent or delay both the forms of diabetes that afflict so many persons in Canada and abroad.

column36: Imaging Tools for Quick and Appropriate Triage of Stroke Patients
column37: Stroke, mainly caused by a blood clot blocking a brain artery, is the leading cause of morbidity in the developed world. Removing the clot quickly saves at-risk brain tissue, improving the patient's chance of a good outcome. A current clinical method for removing blood clots is giving a drug that dissolves clot (clot-buster); however, this method only works 15-25% of the time for larger clots, and may cause bleeding into the brain in some patients. A more recent method of clot removal is to pull it out mechanically using a catheter inserted through an artery in the groin. This technique has a much higher success rate, but is only available at large hospitals and requires a talented surgeon. This procedure is therefore not available in community hospitals. When treating a patient with stroke, a community physician therefore needs to know if the clot in the patient's brain blood vessel dissolves quickly with the clot-busting drug or will the patient need to be sent to a larger hospital where the clot could be pulled out with a catheter? The community physician has to make decisions on treatment and transfer fast as every minute counts with stroke treatment. On the other hand, decisions have to be appropriate and correct, as otherwise some patients may be harmed while others who do not need the catheter-based procedure may be transferred unnecessarily to the bigger hospital. Moreover, the community physician sees a small number of patients with stroke each year and therefore lacks expertise in interpreting brain scans and making these decisions. To address this gap in expertise between large hospitals and community hospitals, we propose to develop an automated imaging-based triaging decision support tool that can help community physicians make clinical decisions on triage of patients with acute ischemic stroke at any time of the day or night quickly and correctly. We will automate many important imaging concepts we have developed until now for this purpose.

column36: Investigation of the role of HIV-Envelope specific antibody dependent innate immune cell functionality in HIV control.
column37: Antibody (Ab) molecules have an Fab region, which binds antigen specifically and an Fc region, which binds to various Fc receptors (FcR) on many types of innate immune cells. Fc-FcR interactions can activate FcR+ innate immune cells and induce anti-viral activity. Which FcR an Ab Fc region binds and the strength of the binding interaction depends on the Ab immunoglobulin class, the amino acid sequence of the Fc domain and the composition of added sugars (i.e. Fc biophysical features). These Fc features in turn determine which innate immune cells are activated for functions that can kill or clear pathogens (i.e. function). The pattern of HIV-specific Ab Fc functions and features differs in recipients of protective versus non protective HIV vaccines. Remarkably, the rare subset of HIV infected individuals, known as Elite Controllers (ECs) have patterns of Fc functions and features that differ from those seen in progressors suggesting that Ab dependent anti-HIV activity can control HIV. The proposal will investigate this hypothesis by considering the degree of HIV control as measured by HIV viral load (VL) and cellular HIV reservoir size and how these correlate with Fc dependent parameters. HIV+ ECs and those starting treatment in acute infection (AT) can achieve similarly low HIV viral loads and HIV reservoirs unlike those left untreated or who start treatment late in infection. But AT loose HIV control when treatment is stopped. We will investigate whether and which patterns of HIV-specific Ab Fc parameters distinguish EC from AT. The goal will be to better understand the link between Ab dependent activity and HIV control. The field of Ab therapeutics is developing ways to deliver and engineer Abs having desirable characteristics for particular disease outcomes. The information learned from this project will characterize the Ab Fc parameters that support HIV control thus potentially providing a benchmark for therapeutic Ab design for control of HIV infection.

column36: PROSPECT: Probiotics to Prevent Severe Pneumonia and Endotracheal Colonization Trial
column37: Probiotics are commercially available live bacteria thought to have health benefits when ingested. Studies have shown that probiotics may prevent 25% of all pneumonias when patients are on a breathing machine, 18% of all other infections, and 65% of serious bowel infections. However, previous studies were small and potentially biased; therefore, whether probiotics are truly helpful remains unclear. We have completed a randomized controlled pilot trial in critically ill ventilated patients in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) to test the feasibility of doing a larger trial. We demonstrated that we can enroll patients, follow the protocol, and that infections in the ICU are common. We are proceeding to investigate whether L. rhamnosus GG (a common probiotic) given during critical illness prevents infection (pneumonia, bowel infection with Clostridium difficile, and other infections), as well as diarrhea and overutilization of antibiotics. We will enroll 2650 adults admitted to the ICU who need a breathing machine. Patients will receive either the probiotic or a placebo, twice daily given down a feeding tube into the stomach. This novel intervention is key to the ongoing search for more effective and inexpensive strategies to prevent serious infections in the ICU. Probiotics may be an easy-to-use, readily available, affordable approach to help future critically ill patients around the world.

column36: Identifying integrative biomarkers of risk and resilience to childhood psychopathology
column37: Mental disorders constitute the largest contributor to the global burden of disease as measured using the disability-adjusted life years index. The most common mental disorders, including major depression and conduct disorders show a peak age of onset in later childhood and adolescence thus derailing the quality of life and productivity of individuals over entire lifetimes. However, by identifying at risk children at an early age we have an opportunity to intervene and prevent many of such mental disorders. The challenge is in effectively identifying truly vulnerable children to be able to intervene in a timely manner. Current programs for identifying at risk children are constructed on evidence linking early life adversity, such as poverty or birth outcomes, and the risk for mental illness. These factors predict mental illness at the level of the population, but are inefficient at the level of the individual due to the considerable variability in outcomes: many children born early, small, or into poverty are healthy and productive. The goal of this project is to identify robust and predictive biological and psychological measurements that help to predict which children are at risk early on. In particular, by assaying molecular markers that capture the biological mechanisms associated with specific psychiatric outcomes, we will identify factors that differentiate those who do and do not succumb to childhood mental illness given the same set of known early life risk factors. This study will thus inform targeted, and personalized interventions aimed at both reducing the severity of onset of these disorders and the negative outcomes that accompany them, such as suicide and substance abuse.

column36: Elucidation of the molecular mechanisms governing currently untargeted RAS effector pathways towards novel therapeutic approaches for the most refractory human cancers
column37: Cancers are driven by abnormal changes to the genetic material of various cell types in the human body. These changes frequently result in the production of mutated proteins, or an overproduction of proteins, leading to unregulated cell growth. The protein RAS has long been recognized as a key driver of human cancers with fully 30% having mutations in RAS genes, and significantly more showing high activity of associated pathways. RAS has thus been a vitally important target for drug development, but efforts have so far proven unsuccessful. Indeed, a lack of effective therapies for RAS-driven cancers is the major reason why lung, colon, and pancreatic cancers remain the most refractory to available treatments. Improved technological approaches, however, should allow a better understanding of mutant RAS and its associated proteins, and have massively revitalized interest in developing RAS-targeted therapeutics. I have developed new methods to study RAS function, and its connections with other proteins in cells. Targeting such associations is finally proving effective in treating some cancers, yet important relationships between RAS and some partners remain completely unstudied. This includes proteins that regulate the ability of cells to move, linked to metastasis, and proteins that lead to self-directed cell death, which I believe could be exploited as a novel cancer therapy. I use leading-edge techniques such as NMR spectroscopy and X-Ray crystallography to gain insight to the structure of proteins at a molecular level, and complement these data with studies in human cells to observe how mutations lead to cellular transformation. I propose to identify and characterize new therapeutic targets in the RAS pathway, and these efforts will be complemented by the drug discovery capabilities at IRIC. These studies are highly significance to many patients, particularly those with currently untreatable cancers such as pancreatic adenocarcinomas and lung NSCLCs.

column36: A randomized controlled effectiveness trial of urine CXCL10 chemokine monitoring post-renal transplant
column37: End-stage kidney failure (ESKF) is common (41 931 Canadians in 2013), increasing (by 35% since 2004) and costly (>$1.3 billion/yr). Transplantation is the therapy of choice for many patients (42.5% of ESKF) due to improved survival & quality of life and it has cost-savings of $33-84K/patient/yr after the first year compared to dialysis. A major challenge in transplantation is how to optimize anti-rejection therapy to balance the risk of rejection from under-immunosuppression against the risk of infections/cancer from over-immunosuppression. The ideal regimen would provide the minimum therapy to avoid complications while being sufficient to prevent rejection. In the 1st year post-transplant, 30% patients have rejection of which 2/3 is not detected by clinical markers. Accurate non-invasive tests are required so rejection can be treated early and anti-rejection therapy optimized. We have identified new urine diagnostic (detect rejection) and prognostic (predict outcome) tests in kidney transplantation. We showed that urine CXCL10 detects rejection better than standard-of-care tests. The primary goal of this multi-center, randomized clinical trial is to evaluate the effectiveness of urine CXCL10 to detect early pre-clinical rejection and determine if treatment improves important kidney transplant outcomes. Urine CCL2, CXCL10 & CXCL9 also predict late kidney transplant outcomes. Thus a secondary goal is to independently validate their performance. Early prognostic markers may be useful to identify patients at high risk of losing their transplants so they may undergo more intensive therapy and avoid minimization/withdrawal of their anti-rejection medications. This trial is the first of its kind to evaluate the impact of an early rejection marker on transplant outcomes. These new urine tests may be used to personalize medicine and improve patient and transplant outcomes. Finally, strategies that improve transplant outcomes may result in long-term health care savings.

column36: The impact of perturbations in T cell migration on the spatio-temporal dynamics of CD4 T cell homeostasis and effector cell differentiation
column37: In our global society, many of us travel to and from work, fly between cities, or even set up residence somewhere new. Along the way, we might bump into others, exchange information, and learn new things that inform our behaviour. Hence, what we learn during our travels can have a dramatic impact on our lives. T lymphocytes have a similarly cosmopolitan lifestyle within the body. The job of T cells in the immune system - to detect and stop the replication of a pathogen or cancer cell as quickly as possible - makes it essential for them to commute continuously between the blood and secondary lymphoid organs. Within lymphoid organs, T cells make critical interactions with other cells that dictate their function and fate. During infections, such interactions can license them to enter tissues and even set up residence there, protecting from reinfection. To understand the implications of the jet-setting behaviour of T cells on their function, we use advanced microscopy to track their movements within tissues in real time. This approach enables us to investigate a number of important questions. How do the interactions T cells make with other cells keep them alive? Why do pathogens or gene defects that prevent migration lead paradoxically both to severe immune deficiencies and to immune-mediated disease? In the long-term, answers to these questions will contribute to the design of better therapies for immunological diseases, such as allergy and autoimmunity, and allow us to harness the function of T cells to improve our ability to treat or prevent infections, from Ebola virus to HIV and beyond.

column36: The Influence of Acute Bouts of Aerobic Exercise on Neuroplasticity and Motor Learning after Stroke
column37: Recovery from stroke is most often incomplete and requires large amounts of practice that are expensive and often not feasible. Because of this it is important to develop new ways to speed learning after stroke. One approach that is promising is to prepare or "prime" the brain for learning by pairing exercise with skilled practice of movement tasks. Past work showed that pairing single sessions of exercise with skilled motor practice enhances learning. Our work demonstrated that the short bout of exercise primes or prepares the brain for learning by lessening inhibition which then facilitates brain plasticity. However this intervention has only been tested in healthy controls. Further, at this time we have only tested single sessions that pair a short bout of priming exercise with skilled practice. As such we do not know what the effect of multiple sessions that pair priming exercise with skilled practice would be on motor learning. The present study is designed to test the effects of priming exercise on motor learning as an intervention that is designed to enhance motor learning after stroke. This is important as such an intervention could be used to enhance the effects of rehabilitation after stroke. In total we will test two main aims: 1)We will determine if the effect of priming exercise is to lessen inhibition in the brain after stroke. 2)We will deliver repeated sessions of priming exercise paired with skilled motor practice to see if compared to a group who rests before motor practice, the exercise group shows greater learning. Our data will illustrate a new way by which learning could be enhanced after stroke. Exercise could easily be incorporated into rehabilitation settings. As such our findings can be rapidly translated to the clinical setting to promote the recovery of Canadians with stroke.

column36: Development and Validation of a Patient-Reported Measure of Compassionate Care
column37: Background & Importance: What we know and what is needed Compassionate care is increasingly recognized as an essential ingredient of quality healthcare by patients, family members, healthcare providers, decision makers, and researchers. Despite mounting evidence that it positively impacts patients' healthcare experiences and outcomes, compassion is fading from our hospitals and healthcare training programs. The consequences are significant, as a lack of compassion has repeatedly been identified as a major issue in recent high-profile healthcare inquiries. A major barrier to the development, evaluation and improvement of compassionate care is the lack of a tool to measure patients' experiences of such care in their healthcare interactions This study will produce a valid, clinically relevant, patient-informed measure of compassionate care by building on our team's previous work on compassion in healthcare, which produced the first patient-informed conceptual model describing the various components of compassion Methods: How will we accomplish this? This study will occur in 4 care settings (acute, home, residential & hospice) in Calgary, Winnipeg and Vancouver. Measure development will be accomplished by addressing the following objectives: 1. Ensure our compassion model makes sense to patients 2. Develop questions to include in the measure 3. Verify the questions with patients and experts 4. Test the completed measure in a large group of patients 5. Work with our research, education, policy and practice partners to incorporate the measure into healthcare Impact: How this will make a difference? A tool to measure patients' experiences of compassionate care will provide the means to study, assess, evaluate and improve this vital aspect of quality healthcare. In addition to its immediate impact on patient care, a compassionate care measure will allow healthcare educators and organizations to integrate compassionate care into both healthcare training and policies

column36: Evolution of evidence-based practice: evaluating the contribution of individual and contextual factors to optimize patient care
column37: There is strong research evidence on the effectiveness of rehabilitation (i.e. occupational therapy (OT) and physical therapy (PTs)) interventions for improving important outcomes such as morbidity, mortality and quality of life in individuals with high burden conditions such as low back pain, stroke and cancer. The process by which clinicians apply results from research to make decisions in their daily practice is referred to as evidence-based practice (EBP). Unfortunately, the application of research results in clinical practice is critically lacking in these professions. Though academic rehabilitation programs in Canada are designed to promote competence in EBP, the EBP outcomes at graduation (what new graduates "look like") and over time (whether EBP declines, improves, or remains the same) as well as the factors that influence clinicians' use of EBP following graduation and over time are poorly understood. The goal of this research is to understand how individual (e.g. knowledge, attitudes, confidence, behaviours) and contextual factors (e.g. resources) impact EBP, and how these change from graduation to clinical practice and over time. Using questionnaires targeting EBP (attitudes, knowledge, confidence and behaviours) as well as interviews and focus groups with groups of clinicians, this research will follow new graduates (class of 2016) from professional OT and PT Master's programs across Canada for the first 3 years post-graduation to measure and understand changes in EBP. This research is vital for designing curricula that better prepare graduates for the evolving clinical contexts, for designing organizational supports to stem any decline in EBP, and for informing continuing professional development programs aimed at maintaining clinical competence, ensuring that clinicians are offering state of the art evidence-based services.

column36: Modulation and effects of IGFBP-2 on brown adipose tissue thermogenesis
column37: Obesity results from an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure. Finding novel means to increase the burning of excess calories is an important area of research for the development of innovative therapeutic solutions against obesity and type 2 diabetes. The molecular mechanisms of action of IGFBP-2 will be further assessed by pharmacologic and genetic treatments using mice, cells in culture, and molecular techniques. We expect this research to generate important novel health-related knowledge and to result in innovative and translatable discoveries.

column36: Challenges to the vulnerable child in the transitions from preschool to grade school in a pregnancy cohort
column37: How is it that 10-15% of school children end up with mental health problems? We know that most of these children showed early signs in preschool, and many risk factors were evident in the perinatal period. So something could be happening in between preschool and school age that impacts these children's vulnerabilities. Some suggest that the challenges of having to rapidly adapt to a more structured and demanding environment such as formal school will be very stressful for vulnerable children, depending on the support they will receive from family and school environments. Further, a mismatch between child and environment could not only worsen symptoms to the status of disorders, but also spill over into additional problems. We need to take a close look at what happens in school and home during that transition to identify possible levers of intervention. But some also suggest that what accounts for being vulnerable to this transition is "programmed" as early as the perinatal period. Taking all of this into account would allow prevention science to be informed about opportunities to intervene between pregnancy and grade 2. To do this we designed and collected data on a pregnancy cohort across three trimesters and in the perinatal period. There is little research on how children navigate the transition to school. We will now follow the children, families and schools yearly for four years, before, during and after the transition. We will carefully and more intensely assess cortisol, a stress hormone, in a subsample. Because several of the children we follow will be developing childhood mental health problems, this is a very time-sensitive project that needs to be done now as they enter this important transition phase.

column36: Improving post discharge care after acute kidney injury
column37: Sudden decreases in kidney function (known as acute kidney injury or AKI), are frequently seen in hospitalized patients. AKI is an increasingly common problem, complicating 4 to 7% of all hospital admissions, and affecting more than 180,000 Canadians each year. Patients who develop AKI while in hospital have a high risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiovascular events (heart attack and stroke), and kidney failure requiring dialysis after hospital discharge. Some, but not all patients who have AKI may benefit from seeing a kidney specialist after hospitalization, however at present we don't know who should care for these patients, and whether receiving specialized care reduces the risk of worsening kidney function after hospitalization. Given the large number of Canadians affected by AKI, and the limited number of available kidney specialists, it would be helpful to be able to identify those patients who need specialized care at the time of discharge. We have developed a simple risk calculator that can accurately determine whether patients who had an AKI episode are at high risk of developing chronic kidney disease. In this program of research we will evaluate the use of this tool at the time of hospital discharge to flag high risk patients, and evaluate several strategies to determine how to best care for these patients once they have left hospital. The results of this research will allow us to identify how to optimize care for AKI patients in the community.

column36: Extension of the COMPASS Study: building on our current success shaping the direction of youth health
column37: COMPASS is the world's largest and most comprehensive longitudinal school-based primary prevention project. Our team then takes this new evidence of what programs or policies work and we feed that information back to each participating school annually with customized tools to inform them of the best prevention interventions specific to their school population. There are 2 key benefits to extending COMPASS for 5 more years. First, maintaining this internationally unique study is critical as it is just now starting to provide sufficient waves of longitudinal data to generate scientifically robust evidence of what programs or policies work over time to help prevent chronic disease related behaviour among youth. Second, by building on the existing research infrastructure, we are saving valuable prevention resources, especially when COMPASS is the only study that can: -evaluate the 100's of changes that occur in COMPASS schools annually, -evaluate the impact of emerging provincial prevention initiatives (e.g., the Healthy Kids Community Challenge or the Smoke-free Ontario Strategy), or -explore how changes to federal policies (e.g., the potential legalization of marijuana in Canada or changes to e-cigarette product regulations) impact youth behaviour over time.

column36: Influence of high dietary sodium chloride on blood vessel dysfunction in the genesis of chronic kidney disease and stroke.
column37: Two of the major health problems caused by a high salt (sodium chloride) diet are kidney disease and stroke. People with a high salt diet develop high blood pressure and this puts stress on their kidneys. We found that high salt made kidney disease worse by producing inflammation, protein in the urine, and kidney scarring. The high salt can also damage the blood vessels through inflammatory processes. column36: Role of inflammation in experimental post-traumatic epilepsy
column37: Severe traumatic brain injury leads to epilepsy in up to 50% of survivors. There are medications used to treat seizures after epilepsy has started, but none to prevent the development of epilepsy in the first place. Inflammation is a biological process initiated by the body's immune system after brain injury to try and protect from ongoing harm. However, inflammation can also have detrimental effects and is a significant mediator of ongoing secondary injury, which occurs as an indirect result of brain trauma. Secondary injury, including inflammation, has been implicated in the development of post-traumatic epilepsy. Our hypothesis is that inflammation after traumatic brain injury is necessary for the development of post-traumatic epilepsy, and can be modulated to prevent epilepsy from developing later on. In order to demonstrate a causal role, the proposed studies will measure inflammation after experimental brain injury and look for the later development of epilepsy in the same individuals, which has not been previously done. This will also determine whether the inflammatory response to brain injury can predict the later development of post-traumatic epilepsy. We will also use drugs to increase the amount of inflammation at the time of brain injury, to show this leads to increased rates of epilepsy later on and to determine which inflammatory mediators are involved. Other studies will use medication to decrease the amount of inflammation after injury to try and prevent epilepsy. The proposed projects will determine whether people with severe traumatic brain injury may benefit from acute anti-inflammatory treatment in order to prevent the development of epilepsy. This could have a huge impact not just for post-traumatic epilepsy, but also more broadly within the field of epilepsy, as it would represent a significant change from currently available treatment options for patients at risk of developing epilepsy.

column36: Improving Periphery Lung Cancer Detection by Endoscopic Laser Raman Spectroscopy
column37: Early detection is crucial to increasing the survival rate of lung cancer and reduces the cost of treatment. If lung cancer can be detected early in the pre-invasive stage, the 5-year survival is >90%. However, with conventional diagnostic techniques, lung cancer is generally asymptomatic until it has reached an advanced stage, when the treatment outcome is poor. In the past decade, great progresses have been made for improving central airway lung cancer detection due to the development of new optical technologies for endoscopy. However, these optical technologies have not been applied to the detection of periphery lung cancers due to technical challenges. Periphery lung lesions are usually spotted by X-ray computed tomography (CT) as nodules on the images. Then radial ultrasound imaging (under bronchoscopy/virtual CT guidance) plus biopsy are conducted to determine if a nodule is malignant or benign. In this project, we will focus on an optical technology called Laser-Raman spectroscopy (LRS). LRS (based on inelastic light scattering) probes molecular vibrations and gives very specific, fingerprint-like spectral features and has high accuracy for differentiation between malignant and benign cells/tissues. We hope to develop LRS into a new clinical tool for improving periphery lung cancer diagnosis, potentially without the need of biopsy or with significantly reduced number of biopsies. column36: Promoting neurovascular recovery following focal ischemic stroke
column37: In the healthy brain, neurons, glia, and vessels work in concert so that blood flow adjusts in proportion to the level of neuronal activity. In stroke, a blockage of a major artery results in a sharp decline in blood flow, damaging the neurons and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. If the blood clot is dissolved rapidly, a complete recovery is possible. However, because the currently available treatments are safe and effective only when applied rapidly following the stroke onset, only ~10% of patients receive them; most suffer significant disabilities, and up to a third are institutionalized. Uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes needed for full recovery of brain function is a major factor preventing the development of more widely applicable therapies. It has become clear that recovery is strongly affected by changes that occur in the neurons, glia and blood vessels in the peri-infarct zone, the impaired, but potentially salvageable brain region surrounding the site of stroke. Using advanced imaging in live rats, we will track the function of peri-infarct neurons, glia, and vessels in the weeks following stroke. We will treat the animals with specific drugs, delivered directly to the perilesional tissue, to raise the activity of the surviving neurons while providing them with increased metabolic support, so as to bolster the remapping of lost function to these neurons. We will develop these interventions first in the young rats and then tailor them to the middle-aged rats suffering from metabolic syndrome (e.g. high cholesterol, diabetes) that are common in humans and known to impede stroke recovery. These experiments will establish the ways by which brain functioning can be affected in the chronic stage of stroke so as to improve recovery. The insights obtained will spur the development of new treatments that are effective in the chronic stage following stroke and thus stand to benefit the vast majority of patients.

column36: Cannabis smoking and psychotic experiences in adolescents: A longitudinal brain Imaging study
column37: Cannabis smoking increases the risk for psychosis. Although the effects are small at the population level, growing evidence indicates that they are large in those with premorbid vulnerabilities and those who initiate cannabis use in early adolescence. What remain unclear are the biological mechanisms involved. Important clues are provided by the core characteristics of schizophrenia. Indeed, schizophrenia is associated with aberrant emotion processing, a disturbed sense of self and deficits in working memory. In schizophrenia patients and young adults at risk for psychosis, functional imaging studies show that the neural pathways underlying these functions are impaired. Notably, cannabis smoking impairs these brain networks, indicating that there is a significant overlap between the neural effects of cannabis and the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Despite this, no functional imaging study has examined the neural effects of cannabis smoking in psychosis-prone adolescents. Here, we propose to perform a 3-year longitudinal neuroimaging study examining the neural effects of cannabis smoking in psychosis-prone adolescents using tasks assessing emotional processing, self-reflection and executive function. We hypothesize that "at risk" adolescents will have impairments in the targeted neural pathways, which will be further impaired by the growth in cannabis use during adolescence. The project will be embedded in an ongoing 5-year clinical study involving 3850 adolescents, providing the unique opportunity to recruit an uncommon though vulnerable group of teenagers. The current study will shed new light on the mechanisms underlying the cannabis-psychosis association. Such inquiry is of the utmost importance given that cannabis use is highly prevalent in Canada and schizophrenia is one of the top 10 causes of disability. With the ongoing debate on cannabis legalization, the study of teenagers experiencing cannabis-related signs of clinical deterioration is timely.

column36: Contribution of circulating microRNAs to the etiology of vascular disease
column37: Heart diseases (including atherosclerosis) are a major cause of death and debilitation in Canada. Atherosclerosis results from blocked blood flow to the heart muscle due to the thickening of the vessel wall by the growth of a plaque, which mostly contains inflammatory white blood cells. During the early stages of disease, the cells lining blood vessels (endothelial cells) send signals to inflammatory cells in the blood to enter the wall of the blood vessel. In advanced stages plaques can burst, resulting in heart attack or stroke. It would benefit patients if we had a better way to diagnose heart disease at early stages and if we could determine the best treatment for a particular patient. This may be achieved by measuring biomarkers, which indicate aspects of the disease that are not easily seen by a doctor. It has been found that small nucleic acids known as microRNAs are found in the blood and the level of particular microRNAs may be useful as biomarkers for heart disease. We have found that endothelial cells secrete microRNAs into the blood, which can be taken up by inflammatory white blood cells. This microRNA uptake decreases the ability of monocytes to enter the vessel wall and produce plaques. Our proposal will test whether this communication between endothelial cells and inflammatory cells is disrupted during the development of heart disease. We will also measure differences in the types of microRNAs that are transferred between these cells during disease. While certain types of microRNAs are beneficial in health, the microRNAs present during heart disease may have damaging effects and actually promote atherosclerosis. Finally, we will develop methods to deliver helpful microRNAs to inflammatory cells to prevent these cells from forming an atherosclerotic plaque. Our studies will provide important new insight into the diagnosis and treatment of heart disease.

column36: Novel mediators of thioredoxin-interacting protein in diabetes complications.
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a common disease affecting 5-10% of Canadians and is associated with complications such blindness, kidney failure and nerve damage. While chronic exposure of tissues to high glucose (HG) is known to be the cause, the cellular and molecular changes are not completely understood. There is no effective treatment for these complications. Our laboratory has discovered that a protein called thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP) is markedly increased by HG and mice which lack TXNIP are protected from developing diabetic nephropathy (DN). We believe that this way TXNIP contributes to DN is by inhibiting thioredoxin (trx), a cellular component that functions as an oxidoreductase which protects proteins from being altered by processes called nitrosylation and oxidation stimulated by HG. One target protein is an enzyme, glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) which regulates glucose metabolism. HG alters its activity from an active enzyme to injure cells. Thus, TXNIP would block Trx from maintaining GAPDH in its normal state to promote cell damage. These studies are designed to prove the key role of modified GAPDH in mediating DN and that TxNIP is critical in regulating this action by its inhibition of Trx. These novel findings would lead to new approaches to treatment and prevention of diabetes complications.

column36: Predicting the impact of mutations in intrinsically disordered regions
column37: Current "personalized medicine" projects are identifying all the mutations in every patient, and we need to know which of those mutations are likely to cause diseases. About 1/5 of known disease mutations occur in enigmatic protein regions known as intrinsically disordered regions. When we discover new mutations in disordered regions, we currently can't tell which are harmful (drivers of disease) and which ones are benign (bystanders). Evolutionary analysis can point to biological function because functional sequences are preferentially preserved during evolution. If mutations in disordered regions disrupt features of disordered regions that have been preserved over evolutionary time, we predict that these are more likely to affect function and cause disease. Based on this principle, we propose to develop new bioinformatics to better predict the impact of mutations in disordered regions. To understand why disrupting the conserved features is harmful, we will test the impact of engineered mutations in yeast cells, because they are simpler and easier to study than human cells. In the end, we hope to develop better methods to predict the impact of mutations in disordered regions, and also understand why the mutations in these regions lead to disease.

column36: Elucidating the role of the V-ATPase "a" subunit in targeting and function: a novel therapeutic target for bone-loss pathologies and cancer
column37: Many essential 'housekeeping' functions in the body require acid to be pumped across the membranes of cells and tissues. Acid is pumped into lysosomes, cellular recycling bins that break down old cell components into reusable building blocks, and it is pumped into urine to rid the body of the excess produced during physical activity. Bone repair requires that specialized cells (osteoclasts) secrete acid to dissolve the bone surface prior to its being replaced by new bone. In all these cases, variants of one ubiquitous acid pump, known as V-ATPase, perform the job. Genetic mutations that impair V-ATPase activity are known to cause diseases, such as cutis laxa (wrinkly skin disease), renal tubular acidosis (too much acid in the body), and osteopetrosis (heavy, brittle bones). In contrast, abnormal increases in V-ATPase activity can also lead to diseases, such as osteoporosis (thin, fragile bones) and inflammatory arthritis (eroded joints). In tumours, V-ATPases can acidify and degrade the surrounding tissue, helping cancer cells to detach and spread to other parts of the body. Our goal is to investigate aspects of V-ATPase structure and function that are still poorly understood: the structures and organization of its protein constituents, the variations that cause it to be sent to different locations within cells of the body, factors that control its activity to match its location, and how genetic mutations in V-ATPase genes cause disease. Understanding these factors will reveal new strategies to manipulate the V-ATPase acid pump activity in a manner that is required to alleviate disease. These strategies will enable specific targeting of bone cell or cancer cell V-ATPases without affecting the acid pumps that are engaged in vital housekeeping functions. Specific targeting is a crucial requirement for developing new drugs for the prevention of bone loss in osteoporosis and inflammatory arthritis, or the spread of cancer, without causing serious side effects.

column37: HIV/AIDS continues to impact the health of millions of people worldwide. Advances in the treatment of HIV infection have dramatically reduced the death rate from AIDS and improved the quality of life of many HIV-infected patients. Despite this unquestioned success, effective therapy does not eradicate HIV and requires life-long adherence. In addition, the possible long-term toxicity associated with antiretroviral therapy (ART), resistance, stigma and cost all contribute to the necessity of finding a cure. In infected individuals taking ART, HIV persists in a small number of cells that can survive for the lifetime of the infected host. This pool of persistently infected cells, usually referred as the "reservoir for HIV infection", is the main barrier to HIV eradication. The overarching goal of this project is to develop therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing the size of the reservoir, with the ultimate objective of finding a cure for HIV infection. Multiple gaps still exist in our understanding of the basic mechanisms involved in the maintenance of the HIV reservoir. We propose to identify the cells in which HIV persists in the blood and tissues (such as the gut) of HIV-infected individuals taking ART. We will isolate the cells carrying HIV from these anatomical reservoirs. This will allow us to characterize the mechanisms by which HIV is able to persist in these cells. We will then test the ability of several drugs at interfering with HIV persistence in these cells and identify combinations that will lead to the death of the reservoir cells. Our goal is to identify a combination of drugs that can eliminate all latently infected cells in HIV-infected individuals. The results from these studies will constitute the basis for the design of a clinical trial aimed at eradicating HIV.

column36: Preclinical approach to improve testing of immuno-oncology combination therapies for early or late stage metastatic disease
column37: The proposed Project Scheme has two major complementary aims. One is designed to leverage what is the most promising development in cancer therapy since the discovery of chemotherapy: the impact of new drugs which harness the body's immune system ability to fight cancer. The other is to develop improved mouse cancer models to better predict the clinical impact of immune therapy drugs when used in combination with other selected therapies to treat early or late stage distant metastatic disease. These other therapies are antiangiogenic drugs which target a tumor's blood supply, or chemotherapy given in a less toxic, continuous low dose ('metronomic') manner. The overall rationale is twofold. First, while the clinical impact of new immune therapies is remarkable, only a minor subset of patients (eg. 10-15%) derive dramatic benefits. So strategies are needed to improve these figures, e.g. to combine immunotherapy drugs creating 'cocktails' with different anti-cancer drugs - especially those where there is a sound underlying rationale. Second, initial assessment of new therapies is almost always done in mice - usually by treating localized 'primary' tumors - an approach historically poor in predicting what later happens in patients with distant metastatic disease. Dr. Kerbel's lab instead has focused on the development of postsurgical models of metastatic disease of different cancers to model "adjuvant" antiangiogenic drug or chemotherapy treatment of either early stage or advanced metastatic disease. His results have helped contribute to the initiation of phase II and III clinical trials, a number of which have now shown positive results. However, the models - which have been distributed to numerous investigators around the world - involve growth of human tumors in immune suppressed mice. This does not allow testing of immune therapy. So the next step is to develop a similar resource using immune competent mice for studying promising combination based immunotherapies.

column36: Understanding and harnessing the therapeutic potential of VISTA: a PD-1-like negative immune checkpoint regulator
column37: Activating or dampening immune responses are events that are triggered by the binding of co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory molecular partners expressed on T cells, antigen-presenting cells and cancer cells. The uncontrolled activation of immune responses can manifest itself as inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease. In contrast, the suppression of immune responses directed at tumor cells reflects the fact that such cells are perceived as being normal cells by presenting a complement of "self antigens", allowing cancer cells to growth in an uncontrolled fashion. Altering the interaction of co-inhibitory molecules with their respective ligands [immune checkpoint pairs such as PD-1:PD-L1 and CD200:CD200R1] can be used to re-tune immune responses. For instance, clinical trials have recently demonstrated that blocking the binding of PD-1 to PD-L1 with either anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies represents a powerful way of restoring immune responses for treating late stage patients with melanoma and other cancers. Dampening inflammatory responses can also be achieved by using for instance CD200Fc or agonists of its receptor CD200R1 present on immune cells. We have found that VISTA, a newly identified immune checkpoint regulator, can be engineered to act as a powerful anti-inflammatory agent. Here, we propose to identify VISTA's receptor on T cells and cancer cells. Another aim is to evaluate the anti-inflammatory properties of our designed VISTA homolog in several mouse models of inflammation. Finally, we also plan to generate VISTA blockers that will be evaluated in tumor models as agents able to restore immune responses against tumor cells. This proposal will open-up a new area of research in immunotherapy leading to tailored VISTA-blocking agents to treat cancer patients as well as VISTA-like molecules to reduce inflammatory responses in patients with acute and chronic inflammatory diseases.

column36: Oscillatory mechanisms of sensorimotor integration
column37: Vision is of primary importance to humans, and yet we only see things clearly when we look directly at them. We therefore need to move our eyes to gather information about our surroundings. Although we are mostly unaware of these eye movements, they occur with great frequency - most people make around three eye movements per second. Interestingly, these eye movements occur at regular intervals, as if the eyes are following a rhythm. Moreover, the rhythmic nature of eye movements appears to be related to rhythmic electrical signals in the brain, which oscillate at particular frequencies. In this research, we will determine how oscillating activity in the brain is related to the rhythms of visual exploration during eye movements. We will use this oscillating activity as a means of studying key brain circuits responsible for vision and its interaction with other functions, such as memory and attention. Because these functions are known to be impaired in certain mental disorders, we will develop animal models to pinpoint the precise nature of these impairments, with the goal of informing future diagnostic and treatment protocols.

column37: Asthma is a major public health problem that is caused by environmental conditions associated with westernization of society.
