column36: The Health Effects of Prenatal Maternal Stress from the 1998 Quebec Ice Storm
column37: Background. Many studies show that a major stress in pregnancy has negative effects on the unborn child's cognitive and health outcomes. However, those studies have a variety of weaknesses, mostly because researchers cannot randomly assign pregnant women to experience stress. But disasters can. We began Project Ice Storm soon after freezing rain in January 1998 knocked out power in southern Quebec for >3 million people. We recruited women who had been pregnant during the storm and assessed their stress levels. Over the past 17 years we have observed persistent effects of that stress on their children's cognitive development, metabolic, immune and mental health. Although Project Ice Storm shows strong effects of stress in pregnancy, we cannot make conclusions about effects of the storm on the population because we have no unaffected control group, our participants are mostly upper class, and the sample size is relatively small. Objectives. Our goal is to determine the magnitude of the effects of the ice storm on the health of the unborn children from the hardest hit region. We will then estimate the economic impact of the storm on the province's children who were born in 1998. Methods. We will compare population data from three Quebec regions: one that was hard hit by the ice storm, and two others that were untouched. Health outcomes will be compared between youth born in 1998 and those born in the 3 years before and 3 years after 1998. We will obtain data on birth outcomes, health diagnoses and prescriptions, and educational testing from provincial administrative data. Importance. Although the US public health and safety agencies have procedures for protecting pregnant women during disasters, Canada does not. This study will provide the Canadian evidence needed to lobby for greater recognition of pregnant women and their unborn children as vulnerable populations during disasters, and justify providing specific care that will protect their unborn children.

column36: The impact of political conflict on the dynamics of sex work and the HIV/STI and HCV epidemic in Ukraine
column37: Female sex workers (FSW) often bear a high burden of HIV and in order for HIV, sexually transmitted (STI) and Hepatitis C (HCV) prevention programs to effectively control these epidemics, they need to understand how sex work operates so they can design and deliver interventions that match the needs of those most at risk. Sex work is not static; it is constantly adapting to the local context. At times of conflict, the organization, pattern and practice of sex work may change; and as a result, the HIV/STI/HCV risks faced by FSW and their clients may also change. The goal of this project is to examine the impact of the conflict in Ukraine on sex work and the spread of HIV/HCV in the FSW/client populations. This project will be conducted in Dnipropetrovsk (DNK), 200km from the conflict zone in the eastern region of Ukraine. DNK is a strategic location as frontline Ukrainian forces regularly pass through this city. DNK has also recently become a destination for many internally-displaced people. Moreover, having the highest HIV rates in Europe, a further rise in HIV cases in Ukraine will have important implications beyond its borders. There is very limited data about how conflict affects FSW and their HIV/STI/HCV risks. Building on our previous work which examined early HIV risk among young women and FSW in DNK (a project that was ongoing when conflict first erupted), our team is uniquely positioned to carry out this 5-year study. We will use complementary methods to characterize how conflict shapes FSW's daily lives and influences sex work and HIV/STI/HCV risks, and to estimate the extent to which conflict alters the spread of HIV and HCV among FSW and clients. Our study will generate important information for our Ukrainian partners who design and implement HIV prevention programs in DNK as well as address an important knowledge gap globally.

column36: Modulating the in utero environment to prevent later life insulin resistance
column37: There is strong evidence that children who were born from a pregnancy complicated with a poorly functioning placenta, resulting in intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) or low birth weight (LBW), have an increased risk of developing childhood obesity and diseases such as Type-2 diabetes (T2DM). T2DM and its precursor disease, insulin resistance, are chronic diseases that develop when the body does not respond correctly to insulin, a hormone released by the pancreas, and leads to high glucose levels in blood which overtime damage body tissues. The risk of developing insulin resistance in IUGR/LBW young adults is significantly higher than that of normal birth weight babies over time. The origins of this insulin resistance are believed to occur prior to birth. Alterations to the genes that regulate the way the muscle uses nutrients for growth lead to the unborn child's muscle to become unresponsive to the actions of insulin. The underlying mechanism for this change is thought to be 'epigenetic', affecting the way the genes that control the way a muscle cell uses oxygen and other nutrients are switched on or off. These changes may initially protect the fetus and promote survival inside the womb, but when they persist after birth are inhibitory to normal insulin sensitivity and lead to childhood obesity and T2DM. The unifying theme of this research project is to demonstrate whether a novel bioactive compound, pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) found in cocoa and breast milk, can reverse this process early in life, while still in the womb or breastfeeding, to prevent insulin resistance and childhood obesity in IUGR/LBW babies as they age.

column37: Two million Canadians suffer from uncontrolled asthma (Asthma Society of Canada www.asthma.ca, 2016). Asthma is an inflammatory disease resulting in airway narrowing due to excessive smooth muscle contraction. Several factors trigger the production of inflammatory mediators that presumably in turn enhance the contraction of the airway smooth muscle. The current treatments for asthma are either very specific but cannot cope with all the possible inflammatory mediators or broad-spectrum like the corticosteroids but have undesired side effects. We have developed a unique technique to study the muscle from human lung small airways so we will be able to address the contractility of the affected tissues directly. With these tissues, and the inflammatory cells purified from the donors' spleen, we will reproduce in vitro, the environment that the airway muscle bathes in. With state-of-the-art biophysical measurement equipment, we will measure the contractility changes, and the mechanisms behind those changes, of the airway smooth muscle when exposed to the inflammatory cells observed in the asthmatic airways. column36: Effect of environmental contaminants and methylome of breast adipose tissue on aromatase inhibitor efficacy in breast cancer
column37: Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are considered gold-standard therapy against hormone-dependent breast tumors which make up 80% of all breast cancers (BC). This treatment significantly reduces the risk of BC recurrence and mortality. However, about 10-15% women will experience early cancer recurrence within 5-years of diagnosis. AIs lower estrogen level by blocking estrogen synthesis from androgens but in some women this mechanism will be inadequate. Obesity has been suggested to contribute to decreased AI efficacy; however, not all obese women will fail to respond to treatment. Therefore, it is likely that other exposures may be involved in interfering with the drugs' effectiveness. AIs may be less effective against external sources of estrogens like environmental contaminants. These have been shown to alter the levels of circulating estrogens and correlate with other BC risk/prognostic factors (obesity, breast density). They have also been linked with inducing epigenetic changes through alterations in DNA methylation. By assessing the levels of environmental contaminants and methylation in a cohort of BC survivors and following their treatment response, our findings will help to further elucidate the mechanisms of AI nonresponse as they relate to these factors. These have never been investigated before in this context even though AI-treatment nonresponse remains a major obstacle to optimal BC management. Currently, nonresponding patients are unable to reap the benefits of first-line targeted therapy and experience significant morbidity due to delayed appropriate treatment. A better understanding of factors driving treatment inefficacy is necessary to spare women the consequences of ineffective treatment, and to inform treatment approaches in high-risk women early in the disease trajectory. Lastly, if environmental contaminants desensitize AIs through methylation, a modifiable DNA event, therapies aiming to reverse this process can be exploited.

column36: NLRX1 in the control of epithelial proliferation and intestinal tumorigenesis
column37: Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. The cause of colorectal cancer is likely due to a combination of factors, and has been linked to genetic mutations, diet, inflammatory processes, and bacteria that exist in the gut. Although significant efforts have been employed to understand the cause of this disease, the mechanism remains elusive. Dr. Stephen Girardin has established a research program to investigate the role of a new protein (NLRX1) in the development of colorectal cancer. NLRX1 belongs to a family of proteins that control intestinal inflammation and have been implicated in colorectal cancer. column37: Our objective is to better understand the initial processes that lead to Alzheimer's disease (AD), a neurodegenerative condition that evolves silently for decades before it can be clinically diagnosed using current methods. Identify molecules implicated in the development of an evolving 'silent' AD pathology is crucial, as such early pre-symptomatic stages are likely more responsive to therapy than treatment during symptomatic AD stages when the brain has already suffered extensive and irreversible damage. In the pursuit of this objective, we will focus our studies on early CNS inflammatory processes that we have shown to occur well before amyloid plaques are established; this early inflammation is different from classical late CNS inflammation that responds to toxic amyloid plaque formation. Using animal models with modified brain genes to reproduce key features of the human AD pathology, we will examine which types of brain cells exhibit the first signs of inflammation and when this process begins. Further, we will investigate the presence of early inflammation in post-mortem human brain tissue from healthy individuals and individuals at different stages of AD to determine how inflammation coincides with the presence of other early AD hallmarks and cognitive status. Finally, we will determine how inflammation changes with time and disease progression in blood and cerebrospinal fluid of people at high risk of developing the disease, such as individuals with a family history of AD and Down syndrome sufferers. column36: Direct Funded Home Care for Older People in Ontario
column37: Canadian home care systems are urgently in need of an overhaul.[1] There is increased demand due to aging demographics and because cultural norms now support home and community-based care over long-term residential care. This project will also consider whether DF programs attend to inequalities related to disability, gender, racialization and immigration. The team includes seven established and emerging interdisciplinary qualitative health researchers, three community partners and one government collaborator. The knowledge created through this project will have value to Ontario policymakers to refine the program being studied and other DF programs, community organizations to inform their members, academics working around care theory, and individuals exploring their home care and work options.

column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common lethal genetic disease of Canadians. A vicious cycle of lung infection and inflammation develops leading to airways destruction. Understanding these infections and how to effectively treat them is key for those with CF to live longer, healthier lives. Decades of research have focused on treating a few select bacteria infecting CF lungs including; Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus and Cepacia. However, clinicians have long recognized that the response of patients poorly correlate with the presence of these bacteria (patients may fail to respond to antibiotics which kill these bacteria and/or respond to antibiotics which these organisms resist and survive). We propose a unique approach to better understand and treat CF lung disease based on the CF microbiome. To do so, we plan to work backwards to identify factors associated with lung disease progression and treatment response. Our group maintains a massive, one-of-a-kind collection of sputum samples (lung secretions) from individuals with CF spanning twenty years. This "biobank" is linked with patient outcomes. Historical samples can therefore be analyzed to identify factors associating with future outcomes. We aim to determine: -What organisms/populations of organism contribute to disease progression and which are protective. - If established CF treatments act on the microbiome, and whether the microbiome can be used to predict treatment response. Our group of clinician-scientists have the expertise and skill in both molecular biology and outcomes research to take full advantage of this extraordinary resource, and improve our understanding and future management of CF lung disease.

column36: The unrecognized importance of smooth muscle foam cells in atherosclerosis development and treatment
column37: Heart attacks and strokes are caused by a buildup of fats, including cholesterol, as well as inflammation in arteries. This buildup is known as atherosclerosis. These diseases are the leading cause of death and decreased quality of life in Canada and worldwide, as well as an enormous economic burden on the healthcare system. Until now it was assumed that most of the cholesterol that builds up in coronary and other arteries occurs in a type of white blood cell called macrophages. However, recently while studying human hearts donated by people having a heart transplant, we discovered that the majority of cells that accumulate excess cholesterol in human coronary arteries are actually smooth muscle cells. These cells were already known to be the main cell type in the 'plaques' that build up in arteries, but their importance as the main place cholesterol deposits had never been recognized until now. This information provides a whole new way of looking at how atherosclerosis develops, and how to design new treatments to reduce the death-toll and poor quality of life it causes. The goals of this research are to understand: 1) the exact contribution of smooth muscle cells to total cholesterol overload in plaques; 2) whether mouse models used to study atherosclerosis have the same buildup of cholesterol in smooth muscle cells as humans and are therefore good models to study this problem; 3) what the reasons are for the loss of a key cholesterol exporter that we also discovered in the plaque smooth muscle cells; and 4) how to overcome this cholesterol accumulation problem in these cells, either by increasing this exporter or by bypassing it to get the cholesterol out of the cells. Our recent findings are groundbreaking, and the results of this further research stand to revolutionize how we prevent heart disease and stroke, for the benefit of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: The scope and functional significance of metabolic enzyme localization in the nucleus
column37: About 200 enzymes involved in metabolism are not found in a single location in the cell. That is, some molecules of each of these enzymes occur in the cytoplasm, and some occur in the nucleus (the cell part containing the genes). It has long been known that metabolic enzymes can occur in the nucleus. We know little, however, about what they are doing in the nucleus. For example, there has never been a comprehensive study to determine which enzymes are actually active in this part of the cell. This is a striking shortfall in the field of cell physiology given the evidence that metabolites control the expression of genes in the nucleus, including genes of high relevance to cancer. We will mount the first study to address this knowledge gap. These experiments will be performed using cells of heart, lung, pancreatic and ovarian origin. We will employ state-of-the-art methods for detecting metabolites in nuclei that have been obtained from cells in a way that perfectly preserves their content of metabolites. Nuclei will be incubated under conditions that permit metabolic reactions to occur. By determining what metabolites are made and consumed, we will be able to infer which enzymes are active in the nucleus. We will also study one specific enzyme called IDH1. IDH1 is mutated in some brain cancers and in this form produces high levels of a metabolite that can drive tumorigenesis. Because some cells in patient tumors have mutated IDH1 in the nucleus, and the metabolite it produces interferes with gene expression in the nucleus, we suspect that cancer formation is more aggressive when mutated IDH1 is in the nucleus. We will test this hypothesis with a view to possible future development of a test for cancer aggressiveness based on how much mutated IDH1 is in tumor cell nuclei. Collectively these studies will uniquely contribute to a better understanding of how metabolic enzymes are controlled in normal and cancerous cells.

column37: All viruses go through an important stage during their life cycle called translation where viral proteins are synthesized from a viral RNA. Numerous viruses such as HIV and coronavirus (i.e. SARS) use recoding mechanisms to expand coding capacity. Thus, this proposal will not only shed light into the biochemical mechanisms underlying this novel viral IRES recoding mechanism but also provide a unique and powerful model for understanding how other viral IRES and recoding mechanisms work. Understanding these fundamental mechanisms are important for human health; it provides a framework for understanding viruses that infect humans and gains useful knowledge that may reveal novel targets for antiviral therapy.

Our work has defined novel mechanisms by which Gp78 and AMF control interaction of the endoplasmic reticulum with mitochondria, the energy producing organelle of the cell. These interactions control the movement and destruction of mitochondria and limit the production by damaged mitochondria of toxic chemicals that contribute to cancer progression. Further, interaction between ER and mitochondria play important roles in cell death. We propose that by preventing Gp78 proximity to mitochondria, AMF controls whether or not Gp78 prevents cancer formation. We will now study how AMF controls Gp78 localization to the mitochondria-associated ER and how it impacts Gp78 function in breast and other cancers, i.e. whether Gp78 prevents tumor formation or rather drives tumor malignancy. Our proposed mechanism of AMF control of Gp78 function in the endoplasmic reticulum is quite novel and suggests that targeting AMF outside the cell will induce Gp78 tumor suppressor activity. Once validated, these studies will lead to the development of specific therapeutics to prevent AMF control of Gp78. We expect our knowledge translation approach will enable new mechanistic understandings leading to new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to better treat these potentially terminal cancers and provide better prognoses for cancer patients.

column36: Deciphering the mechanisms underlying synaptic dysfunction at the neuromuscular junction in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder caused by progressive dysfunction, and later death, of motoneurons innervating skeletal muscle fibers. MNs are the part of the nervous system that control muscles involved in movements such as walking and breathing. They do so because they physically contact muscles where they signal them to contract by releasing a chemical at a site on the muscle known as the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). As the disease progresses, connections between the nervous system and muscles become fewer causing the muscle to become progressively weaker to a point where they are paralyzed. Patients usually succumb to ALS within 2-3 years of diagnosis as a result of an inability to control respiratory functions such as coughing and breathing. There is no cure for ALS and treatment options are limited. ALS occurs sporadically, with no known cause, in 90% of the cases. The other 10% are caused by genetic mutations. Despite this diversity, one of the shared features of the disease is the progressive withdrawal of the motoneurons from the NMJ prior to cell death. This withdrawal speeds up the rate of paralysis and contributes to MN death. This proposal will examine why motoneurons withdraw from the NMJ in ALS. We will combine mouse genetics with electrophysiological, anatomical, biochemical and behavioral techniques to examine whether a group of proteins known BMPs are involved in stabilizing the NMJ in mice (similar proteins are well known to stabilize the NMJ in fruit flies). Furthermore, we will examine how BMPs are misregulated in ALS mice in order to determine how this misregulation affects disease progression. Ultimately, we believe that results will provide a foundation of knowledge to later develop pharmacological interventions that will stabilize the connections between motoneurons and muscle in ALS and thus improve muscle strength and quality of life for those living with the disease.

column36: Study of pathogenesis and reversibility of central and peripheral airway remodeling in an equine model of asthma
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic inflammatory disease of the respiratory tract worldwide, and 5-10% of patients are severely affected and poorly responsive to current medications. Among those, patients with neutrophilic lung inflammation represent a major health concern has they require high healthcare costs due to the severity of the disease and the poor response to therapy. The severity of asthma is considered to be a consequence of ongoing damage (remodeling) to the lungs. However, currently, the causes, functional consequences, and the possible reversibility of remodeling remain poorly characterized. This is primarily due to ethical considerations limiting lung biopsies in patients, particularly of the peripheral airways, due to their invasiveness. Thus, the study of airway remodeling in animal models of asthma is critical in better understanding the disease and developing effective therapy. The aim of the proposed research program is to investigate the contribution of neutrophilic inflammation to airway remodeling of the central and peripheral asthmatic airways, and their response to therapy with macrolides, a class of antibiotics that has been used to treat neutrophilic asthma, due to their anti-inflammatory properties. Horses, similarly to humans, spontaneously develop a condition (equine asthma) that has most of the clinical, functional, and remodeling features of human asthma. Using this unique animal disease, combined with cell culture, a novel tissue engineered 3D bronchus, and decellularized asthmatic and healthy airways, we will investigate the cells and the signaling pathways contributing to airway remodeling and response to therapy in the asthmatic lung. The proposed research will substantially advance knowledge of the role of neutrophils in asthma, the signaling pathways contributing to the airway remodeling in neutrophilic asthma, and the efficacy of macrolides at controlling airway neutrophilic inflammation and reversing remodeling.

column36: Targeting Triple Negative Breast Cancer: Role of KISS1R
column37: Breast cancer, the most common cancer among Canadian women killed 5000 women last year. In particular, triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) represents 15-20% of all breast cancers that occurs commonly in younger women (<50 yrs of age). TNBC remains the most difficult subtype of breast cancer to treat. TNBC tumors are defined by a lack of estrogen receptor (ERalpha), progesterone receptor and human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2, aka ErbB2) and so TNBC patients do not benefit from drugs used to treat other breast cancer subtypes, that target hormone receptors or HER2. TNBC patients have poor prognosis and are typically high grade and metastatic. Additionally, drug resistance to chemotherapeutics is a major problem in TNBC. Thus, an urgent need remains to identify new molecular targets for effective treatment in TNBC. We have found that in TNBC cells, kisspeptins (KPs) promote TNBC cell invasion. KPs are blood-borne secreted peptides that signal upon binding receptor proteins called KISS1R, that are highly expressed in TNBC cells, compared to normal breast cells. We found that the gene that codes for KPs (called KISS1) is highly expressed in TNBC primary tumors. The proposed work will determine whether plasma KP levels increase in TNBC patients compared to healthy patients, thus potentially identifying a prognostic biomarker for disease progression. We will determine whether KISS1R protein levels are higher in TNBC primary tumors, compared to normal breast. Our new data indicates that KISS1R signaling confers drug resistance to chemotherapeutics. Using various models (cells, pre-clinical animal and clinical samples), we will determine whether targeting KISS1R inhibits metastasis and drug resistance, and the underlying mechanisms by which this occurs. Thus, our 'bench to bedside' studies may identify KISS1R as a novel anti-cancer drug, targeting of which will inhibit metastasis and improve the effectiveness of chemotherapy that TNBC patients currently receive.

column36: Cerebral cortical neural mechanisms for feedback vs feedforward contributions to motor skill learning
column37: When our arm is perturbed by an external force or obstacle during a movement, the brain possesses neural circuits that rapidly detect the error and make a corrective adjustment to complete the movement as intended. This is called feedback control. If the same perturbation occurs repeatedly, the brain gradually learns to anticipate the effect of the perturbation and adjusts the motor command for the next movement to reduce its effect. This is called predictive feedforward control. Similarly, when we try to learn a new motor skill, we make many mistakes at first but gradually reduce our errors as our skill improves. Motor control theory had long proposed that the errors sensed by feedback circuits were used to "teach" the feedforward neural circuits that plan and execute movements what to learn and how, but the feedback circuits did not change. As the feedforward circuits changed, errors decreased and the motor system increasingly functioned in feedforward mode. However, a recent study found that both feedback and feedforward circuits change while subjects learn to compensate for external force fields; they collaborate as partners during both motor learning and skilled performance, rather than only as teacher and student. This project studies the neural mechanisms in motor cortical areas of non-human primates that play a key role in detecting and correcting errors while learning a new skill, and cause adaptive changes both in the feedback and feedforward circuits to permit skilled motor performance. A better understanding of how the cortical motor system learns new skills will help in the development of new rehabilitation procedures for patients with motor control deficits. It will also lead to improved design of neuroprosthetic controllers that use neural signals about desired movements recorded in the brains of paralyzed patients to control robotic devices, thereby greatly improving their independence and quality of life.

column37: Zika virus (ZV) is an emerging pathogen that is transmitted by mosquitoes. Until recently, circulation of this virus was limited to Africa and Asia. column36: Understanding and exploiting lysine polyphosphorylation as a new post-translational modification regulating cell growth
column37: Background: Essential processes in our cells are controlled by molecules called proteins, which are comprised of individual building blocks called amino acids. These can be modified by chemicals in the cell in different ways that tell a protein what to do and when to do it. We can think of these modifications as sets of instructions. For example, instructions might tell a protein to promote cell growth or, in other circumstances, to repair damaged DNA. Project Goals: The overarching goal of this project is to determine the function of a brand new and poorly understood chemical modification called polyphosphorylation. As their name suggests, polyphosphates are long chains of individual molecules called phosphates, which cells use in a number of metabolic processes to keep us healthy. A recent study made the surprising but fascinating observation that these chains can be attached to amino acids in proteins to regulate their functions. Our own work suggests that they serve as instructions to a set of proteins that are essential for cell growth. Project Objectives: In this project we will first determine if polyphosphorylation is an important regulator of cell growth using a combination of directed experiments and cutting-edge genetic analyses. We will then use novel protein analysis tools to determine how polyphosphate chains instruct proteins on what to do. Project Outputs: The major outputs of the project will be the identification of new targets and pathways regulated by polyphosphorylation, and mechanistic insights on how polyphosphorylation impacts protein localization, stability and interaction with other constituents of the cell. Health Impact: Since cell growth is required for tumour formation, understanding polyphosphorylation will afford us new opportunities to treat cancer. Our long-term vision is to re-establish control over processes gone awry in cancer cells by artificially modulating the length of polyphosphate chains on modified proteins.

column37: Heart attacks represent the leading cause of death worldwide, including in Canada. The immune system plays a major role in both the initial injury that occurs after a heart attack, but also how the heart repairs itself after injury. column36: Functional and evolutionary dissection of vascular endothelial cell responses to Inflammation
column37: The cardiovascular system is composed of a network of arteries, veins and capillaries. These blood vessels deliver oxygen and nutrients to the body and are the main communication channel that connects the heart, the brain and other vital organs. The cells that form their inner lining, known as endothelial cells (ECs), are vital to maintain health. They can detect danger signals in the blood. When they do, they become inflamed. For example, ECs react to infection and to risk factors for cardiovascular disease such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol. In fact, one of the root causes of cardiovascular disease is EC inflammation. Inflammation results in build up of plaque in arteries of the heart, a disease known as atherosclerosis. When plaques rupture, blood clots can form and block the flow of blood to the heart and brain, resulting in heart attack and stroke, respectively. During the inflammatory response the cell orchestrates the expression of a network of genes. To identify and inform people who have genetic risk factors for cardiovascular disease, we need to find the DNA sequences that control when, where and how much of these genes are made by ECs in response to inflammation. In this project, we will find the DNA sequences that control inflammatory genes in ECs obtained from the hearts of humans and other species. In order to catch regulatory DNA in action, we will treat these ECs with substances that cause inflammation. A necessary second objective of this study is to find the regulatory DNA that is the most important for disease. To do this we will look for regulatory DNA in ECs that is activated in a mouse that rapidly develops heart disease (atherosclerosis) when fed a high cholesterol diet. Finding regulatory regions that are activated by heart disease in the mouse will help us find the regions of DNA that are important for human atherosclerosis and other diseases involving cardiovascular inflammation.

column36: Chromosome 16q, a Cancer Suppressor Chromosome Arm
column37: Patients with estrogen receptor positive (ER+) breast cancer (BC), including those with lobular tumors, show a relatively good prognosis on the five-year horizon. However, unlike triple negative breast cancer (estrogen receptor negative, progesterone receptor negative and Her2 negative, aka TNBC), which is typically either lethal or cured within five years, ER+ BCs can progress and recur decades after what appeared to be successful treatment. Over the past 35 years, a great deal of effort, and resources, has been spent on identification of genetic alterations that cause ER+ BC. This has led to the discovery of specific growth promoting "oncogenes" that are mutated or amplified in up to 30 or 40% of cases. In addition, a number of "tumor suppressor genes" (TSG) have been identified, whereby both chromosomal copies of these genes are destroyed in some ER+ tumors. The oncogenes and TSG are relatively easy to define and study. Consequently, the vast majority of genetic, cell biological and biochemical analyses have been focused of these genes. Unfortunately, the eight hundred pound gorilla in the room, gains and losses of entire chromosome arms in BC, has been ignored for a lack of tools to approach it. Indeed, almost 100% of estrogen receptor positive breast cancers have lost one copy of chromosome 16q. Nobody knows why this happens, if this represents an important driver of tumor formation and progression, or if this feature can be exploited by targeted therapy. We have combined the two most frequently mutated genes in human lobular breast cancer to generate the first mouse model for this disease. More recently, we have used state-of-the-art CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing technology to generate a mouse model for 16q loss that can now be applied to define how this event might drive ER+ BC formation (including both lobular and ductal forms) and to find drugs to kill tumors with only one copy of chromosome 16q.

column36: Development and Validation of a clinical prediction rule to guide and improve the treatment of female stress urinary incontinence
column37: Urinary incontinence (UI) afflicts 1 in 3 women 18 years and over. The most common type is stress UI which is accidental urine leakage during coughing, sneezing and physical activity. UI can lead to significant social problems, embarrassment, and negative self-perception; reduces social interactions and physical activities; and, among older women, increases nursing-home admissions. UI interferes with quality of life and healthy aging; left untreated, it can also lead to the need for surgery. The treatment of UI and related problems alone adds $1.9 billion to Canada's burgeoning healthcare costs. Pelvic floor muscle (PFM) training, taught to women by a specially-trained physiotherapist is effective, cost-effective and is recommended as the first-line treatment option for stress UI. Consequently, many women are steered towards more costly and potentially risky surgical options. Other women may be offered PFM training when ultimately surgery is required. Based on previous research, this study aims to develop and test a clinical prediction rule to help researchers and clinicians identify before treatment, those stress UI women likely to benefit from PFM training, increasing their chances of conservative treatment success. The rule will use information from demographic, clinical and biomechanical data to make the predictions. 465 women with stress UI will complete a pre-treatment UI assessment, then 12 weekly 1-hour group-based PFM training sessions. One-year after, the women's UI will be reassessed. Using the post-treatment results as an outcome, a clinical prediction rule will be developed to inform clinicians on the pre-treatment factors which best distinguish women who will or will not benefit from group-based PFM training.

column36: Identifying reflex sympatho-excitatory targets in heart failure to improve exercise capacity
column37: A heart that cannot pump blood efficiently leads to incapacitating symptoms, shortens life, and is the most common reason older Canadians come to hospital. Heart failure (HF) patients most likely to suffer worsening symptoms and early death are those with an overactive sympathetic nervous system (which releases noradrenaline, increases heart rate, salt and water retention and constricts blood vessels) and limited exercise capacity. We were the first to record muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) in HF from the opposite limb during 1-legged cycling. We discovered that unlike healthy people whose MSNA decreases to enable more muscle blood flow during exercise, when HF patients cycle MSNA increases. We will invite HF patients and age and sex matched healthy people to participate in a study where we test their exercise capacity and then determine the function of 3 nervous system reflexes activated by exercise that behave abnormally in HF. Patients will be restudied after a standard 6 month exercise rehabilitation program to learn if training improves exercise capacity by lowering MSNA and to determine which, if any, reflexes are improved. HF guidelines recommend exercise training but only a minority of Canadian patients is referred for cardiac rehabilitation. Fewer patients still complete these programs due to HF symptoms. If we can identify the most abnormal reflex we can then test new exercise prescriptions to target this. Sharing our discoveries will have individual and societal health benefits: more patients will be referred to cardiac programs for focused and achievable exercise prescriptions. To do this research we have assembled a team with unique expertise in heart failure, MSNA recordings, exercise, and rehabilitation of HF patients.

column36: The Aging Brain: Circadian, Transcriptomic, and Epigenomic Dimensions
column37: One of the most important questions of biomedical research is "why do we ail as we age?". This may be in part due to a breakdown of the body's circadian rhythm - the physiological process that tunes up or down various bodily functions during the 24 hr cycle. Another aspect of our biology that changes in response to the aging process is the epigenome. This is an additional layer of information attached to DNA that regulates and directs how and when genes should be expressed, or transcribed, in each cell. This layer of information is not copied as accurately as DNA and is susceptible to environmental factors, which causes it to change gradually as people age. This is such a well characterized phenomenon that we can now predict someone's biological age, vs. their chronological age, based on the state of their epigenome and even gauge their survival in late-life. Preliminary results from our group show that the underlying molecular infrastructure of our circadian rhythm is in part directed by changes in the epigenome. Given the concurrent deterioration of the epigenome and circadian rhythm during the aging process, it seems conceivable that well characterized alterations to the epigenome during the aging process are disrupting our circadian physiology and likely playing a significant role in our declining health in old age. To investigate this idea, we are proposing to collect brains from mice of 5 different ages, from adolescence to old age, over the course of 24 hours in each separate group to: 1) fully catalogue all the transcriptional and epigenetic components of the circadian rhythm, in different parts of the brain, 2) identify the ones that are affected by age, 3) analyze how these may be related to aging brain diseases, so that this effort can contribute towards a remedy.

column36: Correction of brain triglyceride metabolism in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Clinical trials for Alzheimer's disease (AD) have thus far not succeeded, highlighting an urgent need to better understand how this disease develops. Over the past 5 years, our research program has been focused on identifying the missing links that determine AD progression. In a recently published discovery that received extensive international media attention, we reported that the post-mortem brains of Alzheimer patients exhibit a striking accumulation of triglycerides (stores of fatty acids) on the brain's internal ventricular surface. This project investigates the therapeutic potential of correcting defects in how the AD brain processes triglycerides. We will use an array of novel animal-based experiments to gain insight into why these triglyceride accumulations happen, whether these accumulations are modifiable by lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise, and whether preventing their occurrence is beneficial in Alzheimer's. Answering these questions may reveal new treatment strategies for this devastating disease.

column36: Understanding the function of DIXDC1 in normal and abnormal brain development
column37: The establishment of neuronal connections, called synapses, is a major milestone in human brain development that is necessary for cognitive processes such as learning, memory and motor function. Synapses are specialized connections that allow nerve cells (neurons) to communicate. Abnormalities in their structure and function underlie neurodevelopmental disorders (eg. Autism Spectrum Disorder [ASD]) and psychiatric disease (eg. Bipolar Disorder and Schizophrenia). These disorders negatively impact the daily lives of affected individuals, causing an economical and social burden, but due to a poor understanding of their biological mechanisms, there are no cures. This underscores the need to better understand how abnormal brain development causes disease. There is strong emerging evidence that molecules belonging to a class called Wingless (Wnt) signaling in the brain play a significant role in disease. Furthermore, there are multiple lines of evidence (human genetic studies, animal models and medications used in the clinic) that indicate disrupting Wnt signaling causes profound synaptic defects and ASD-like pathologies. This suggests studying Wnt signaling molecules may reveal new mechanisms underlying disease pathophysiology. In this study, we examine a new candidate molecule named Dix domain containing 1 (DIXDC1) to determine its role in neuronal growth, synaptic development and ASD pathophysiology. This project will examine DIXDC's role as a new molecular player in synaptic function, and explore a novel signaling pathway regulating DIXDC1 function. Importantly, we have discovered new ASD-linked mutations in DIXDC1 using next-generation sequencing, and we will examine how these human mutations cause brain dysfunction. Together, our experiments will provide new information that will help us understand how Wnt signaling molecules are involved in normal synaptic development, and how their disease-associated abnormalities leads to ASD pathological consequences.

column36: Mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contacts and cristae dynamics in health and disease
column37: Metabolic flexibility is a key feature of cellular function; it consists in switching back and forth between glucose and fat oxidation, matching the energetic and biosynthetic needs of the cell to the type and amount of nutrients that are available. For the cell, the ability to adapt to metabolic shifts means survival; but for the mitochondrion, which is the powerplant of the cell, this consists in adapting to periodic shifts in carbon combustion rates and to switches between alternative fuels according to nutrients availability. The goal of our research program is to understand how mitochondria secure metabolic flexibility to the cell. The function of the mitochondrion depends on its unique ultrastructure: the cristae and the MERCs, which are the sites of contact with another organelle, the endoplasmic reticulum. Recently, we published a paper in PNAS, the prestigious journal of the US National Academy of Sciences, showing that the cristae and the MERCs change in shape, number, size, and thickness every time that the hepatic metabolism switches gear (which is something that happens after a meal or upon feeling hungry). This study gave us the idea is that when metabolism shifts, a nutrients-sensing pathway instructs mitochondria to adapt their functional output to the needs of the cell by activating a molecular mechanism that simultaneously changes cristae and MERCs structure, which, together, control mitochondrial bioenergetics. In other words, we hypothesize that changes in the organelle's ultrastructure are behind its ability to secure metabolic flexibility to the cell, and failure to do so is central to the development of metabolic syndromes and diseases. To address this model we shall: 1) identify the nutrients-sensing pathway that activates MERCs and cristae remodeling in vivo; 2) reveal the mechanisms governing mitochondrial ultrastructure remodeling during metabolic shifts; 3) link MERCs and cristae dynamics to liver physiology and disease

column37: The cells that line our intestines have many functions, including making and releasing mucus. Mucus is made up of proteins that are covered with sugars, and it creates a thick and slimy layer that coats the whole inner surface of our intestines. The mucus layer is our "first line of defense" against food and water-borne disease causing bacteria - such as the dangerous "Hamburger disease" causing E. coli bacteria that cause bloody diarrhea and kidney failure. To inflict disease, these bacteria have to move across the mucus layer and enter the body. We propose that intestinal mucus plays an active role in determining whether dangerous bacteria can infect their hosts. We have found that during infection, intestinal cells make more mucus and they also increase the content of certain sugars found on the mucus. This led us to predict that these mucus changes may (a) protect the host by pushing the bacteria away from the intestinal lining, and/or (b) the mucus may provide additional nutrients (the sugars) for the dangerous bacteria, reducing their need to invade and damage the intestine to obtain food. In this project, we will investigate the role of mucus, by studying how the immune system causes these changes in the mucus. We will also study what parts of the mucus layer are most important in providing protection, and what happens to dangerous bacteria when the mucus layer is missing. We will also test whether changing the ability of the E. coli bacteria to use sugars as food, or changing the availability of these sugars affects how much damage the bacteria cause to the intestine. This project addresses an understudied, yet critical aspect of intestinal defense and will test if modifying the levels of sugars in mucus offers a new way to fight dangerous gut infections by targeting bacterial pathogen nutrition.

column36: Prevention of primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation; a bench to bedside approach
column37: Lung transplant patients are at risk of developing injury immediately after surgery-a condition called primary graft dysfunction. Patients with this condition are also at greater risk of poorer long term health. Unfortunately, there are no drug treatments available to combat primary graft dysfunction, even though researchers have found some potential therapies in scientific lab settings. The main reason why these findings have not been tried in humans is a lack of a pre-clinical model that would most closely mimic and predict treatment in these patients. Our research team will use a pre-clinical model that will let us test new drug therapies before using them in the patient clinic. We are also the developers of a new technology called Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion, where we can keep donor lungs at normal body temperature and provide it with oxygen and nutrients while outside of the body. This allows the surgeon to carefully inspect the health of the working lung before transplant. This technology also allows us to apply drug therapies before transplant, in an attempt to improve donor lung health. We will work with CSL Behring, a world-class drug company, who will support our project. We will investigate the use of two experimental drugs: alpha-1-antitrypsin and delta-V1-1 delivered with gold nanoparticles. We have previously shown in cell and small animal models that these two drugs helped to prevent primary graft dysfunction. Together, we will develop a new way to bring safe drug therapies to the patient bedside, and help future researchers develop more therapies using our pre-clinical model. Outcomes will lead to a future clinical trial in further testing these drugs for hospital use. column36: Computer-aided detection of pulmonary tuberculosis on digital chest x-rays: its role in the detection of active tuberculosis in a high burden setting of low HIV prevalence
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of death from infectious disease as it killed 1.5 million people in 2014. This is mostly because each year, 3.7 million people with TB are not diagnosed or treated. An important reason why so many people with TB are never diagnosed, is that in poor countries where TB is common, tests to diagnose TB are too expensive to use on everyone that might have TB. A possible solution is to first test people with a low-cost triage test-to know which people need to have the more expensive tests. A candidate triage test, is a digital chest x-ray (DXR) automatically analyzed by software for detecting TB (CAD4TB). To assess this, we will enrol 2272 people with symptoms of TB who go to a public hospital in Pakistan-a country where TB is common, and HIV is rare. (This is relevant as almost 90% of people with TB don't have HIV.) All participants will undergo DXR read by CAD4TB. All will also have sputum tested with the best TB test, culture. Culture will tell us which patients truly have TB, and which ones don't. This will allow us to calculate the proportion of people with TB, whose x-rays CAD4TB correctly flagged as abnormal. It will also allow us to calculate the proportion of people without TB, that CAD4TB correctly did not flag. We will then know if CAD4TB meets minimum recommendations for accuracy. We will also calculate the cost-effectiveness of DXR analyzed by CAD4TB. To do so, we will estimate 3 things for an approach where DXR with CAD4TB is used as a triage test: 1) total costs of diagnosing someone with TB, 2) number of TB cases diagnosed, 3) number of people that die from TB. These same things will be estimated for status quo approaches, i.e. that don't use DXR and CAD4TB. We will then determine how much extra does DXR with CAD4TB cost and how much does it help in diagnosing more persons with TB, and even saving more lives. This study will advance our understanding about this promising new tool in the fight against TB.

column37: People living with end-stage kidney disease need dialysis or transplantation in order to stay alive. This illness and treatment significantly impact peoples' health, emotions, work and relationships. To promote person-centred care, healthcare professionals should be asking patients about what matters to them and using this feedback to plan and deliver care. Patient-reported outcome and experience questionnaires (jointly referred to as PROs) allow patients to provide information about their quality of life, symptoms and experiences with care. However, PROs administered via paper questionnaires have been perceived as cumbersome, difficult to integrate with other health information and do not provide immediate feedback. In this research, home dialysis patients will have the opportunity to complete electronically administered PROs (ePROs) and healthcare professionals will receive education about how to use PRO information. The goal is to learn how to support healthcare professionals to routinely use this information to inform patient care, and see if this makes a difference in patients' health, quality of life and satisfaction with care. Learning what matters most to patients is essential for healthcare professionals to provide person-centred care. This research will address the gap in our understanding of how to best use patients' reports in healthcare. Findings of this research may ultimately improve the quality of healthcare for Canadians living with end-stage kidney disease.

column36: Syncope and the subsequent risk of motor vehicle crash: A population-based analysis
column37: Motor vehicle crashes result in 1.3 million deaths and 78 million injuries worldwide each year. Some individuals have a higher crash risk because medical conditions such as sleep apnea and seizures may briefly impair driving ability. Once a potential risk has been identified, patients, doctors and regulators can work together to develop driving recommendations that protect all road users without unduly limiting patients' independence. Syncope (commonly known as "fainting") is responsible for 1% of all North American emergency department visits. Tens of thousands of these patients will have a repeat episode within a year. A crash is likely to result if syncope recurs while driving, potentially resulting in harm to the patient and other road users. International guidelines recommend that patients at higher risk of syncope recurrence stop driving for one or more weeks, yet these recommendations are based on small, uncontrolled studies whose results are not applicable to most patients. No studies provide reliable estimates of the absolute or relative crash risk after syncope. BC's provincial health and driving insurance databases provide a unique opportunity to assemble the largest group of patients ever evaluated to determine the relationship between syncope and subsequent crash risk. This study will compare the records of 10,000 patients with an emergency department visit for syncope to those of 40,000 patients with a visit for another condition. After adjusting for differences in health and driving history, we will determine if crash risk is higher in the syncope patients. We will also determine which groups of patients are at highest risk. This study will generate the first robust evidence on the risks associated with driving after syncope. The results will have immediate implications for licensing authorities, road safety policy, and international clinical practice guidelines and have the potential to avert thousands of crashes annually worldwide.

column36: PTP Alpha in Normal and Tumor Cell Motility
column37: One of the biggest challenges in cancer treatment is preventing metastasis, the process by which cells from a tumor spread to other sites in the body and form secondary tumors that cause most cancer deaths. Tumor cells have acquired special properties that allow them to spread; notably the ability to invade tissues. Developing treatments to prevent cancer cell spreading requires better understanding of the mechanisms that enable this invasive ability. Cancer cell invasion is mediated by cell structures called invadopodia. These organized structures protrude from the cell body and produce enzymes that degrade the surroundings, clearing a path for the tumor cell to move. Growing knowledge of the molecular regulation and biology of invadopodia has been informed by research into similar but clearly distinct cell structures that regulate normal cell movement. In normal cells, related but non-invasive structures called focal adhesions (FAs) control interactions with their surroundings and cell migration. We discovered that a molecule called PTPa is present in FAs and plays key roles in the molecular communication that regulates FA function and normal cell movement. In our proposed research we will identify interactions between PTPa and other FA molecules, and elucidate how the outcomes of these interactions control cell movement. In parallel, we will investigate the roles of PTPa in cancer cell invadopodia, using breast and colorectal cancer cell lines as models. Our findings suggest that PTPa is involved in regulating the formation of these structures. We will investigate this, and determine if PTPa is required for invasive activity of invadopodia and how PTPa co-ordinates with other molecules to control this. Our research will provide new knowledge of the molecular connections and functions of PTPa that promote normal cell movement and tumor cell invasion. This will increase opportunities to develop targeted molecular therapies to combat cancer metastasis.

column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a fatal disease in which most muscles, including the diaphragm and other breathing muscles, are progressively destroyed and replaced by scar tissue. One practical application of personalized medicine can be summarized as "Giving the right drug to the right patient at the right time". Unfortunately, the current drug management of DMD is based on a "one size fits all" approach. Therefore, in addition to assessing the effectiveness of these drugs, we will also try to identify new blood tests called "biomarkers" that help to predict which drug works best at a given stage of the disease. The majority of outcomes in our studies will be determined in the diaphragm because it is the most severely affected skeletal muscle in our mouse model of DMD with respect to fibrosis and muscle weakness, and it most closely resembles what is found in human patients. We will also do preliminary exploratory studies of our biomarkers by taking blood samples from DMD patients in our clinic. The risk of the medications we are studying is low relative to their potential benefit and especially compared to the major adverse effects associated with the current standard treatment (corticosteroids). All of these drugs could be rapidly moved to the clinic for use in DMD patients if our studies are successful.

column37: Biofilms are slime-covered communities of microbes that stick to each other and to surfaces. This prevalent form of microbial life accounts for many chronic infections that defeat the immune system and are highly resistant to antibiotics. My work seeks to understand a process called signal transduction. All living cells use this process to sense external stimuli and trigger a chain of chemical events inside the cell, resulting in physiological adaptation to the environment. This project centers on signal transduction that coordinates biofilm growth. In many bacteria, biofilm signal transduction depends on a key intracellular molecule, cyclic diguanylate (c-di-GMP). I study c-di-GMP in the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This organism infects medical devices, the urinary tract and burn wounds. It also forms biofilms in the lungs of people suffering from cystic fibrosis (CF), causing life-threatening infections that can last for years. Nearly 4,000 Canadians suffer from CF. While a lot is known about how enzymes "make and break" c-di-GMP, little is known about the environmental stimuli that activate and inhibit these enzymes. This is a key research area because bacteria must use c-di-GMP signaling to sense and respond to host stimuli to build biofilms. C-di-GMP is a promising therapeutic target because it is absent in mammals. My lab has discovered that some isolates of P. aeruginosa have a protein that makes c-di-GMP in response to body heat. My 5-year project aims to understand - at a molecular and biophysical level - how this protein functions as a thermosensor and modulates virulence. Bioinformatics predict that this thermosensing protein is widespread among pathogens. My vision is that this research will guide the design of inhibitors targeting heat-sensing proteins that bacteria use to cause infection. Finally, I propose that these heat-sensing proteins can be reverse-engineered, enabling the design of thermally-activated proteins for biotechnology.

column36: Video-Feedback Interaction Guidance for Improving Interactions Between Depressed Mothers and their Infants
column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a major public health issue. Known as "the thief that steals motherhood" since symptoms obstruct a mother's capacity for understanding and enjoying her baby, PPD affects approximately 1 in 5 moms. Built via "serve and return" interactions (e.g. baby smiles, mom smiles back), sensitive and responsive exchanges are the foundation for healthy child development but are diminished by PPD, resulting in interactions that place children at risk for behavioural and cognitive problems. Infants perceive PPD as stressful; stressors stimulate the brain's hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis (HPA) and trigger stress hormone (cortisol) release, which, in turn, negatively affects developing infant brains by decreasing brain volume. Infants' critical periods of brain development are vulnerable to long-term effects of cortisol, explaining some of the problematic developmental outcomes observed in children of depressed mothers. How can we support depressed mothers and their infants? By improving interaction quality, depressed mothers may be motivated to engage in more play and, in turn, infants who appear interested and ready to interact are more likely to elicit positive, enjoyable experiences from mothers. column36: Tissue-resident mesenchymal progenitors and aging
column37: Adult stem and progenitor cells play fundamental roles in tissue homeostasis, renewal and regeneration, and when these cells become dysfunctional, they likely increase the pace of aging. My laboratory is particularly focused on one type of adult stem/progenitor cell termed a mesenchymal progenitor (MP) and their role in tissue renewal, regeneration, and aging. In accelerated aging conditions such as Hutchinson Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) it has been suggested that aberrant MPs make a substantial contribution to this disorder. HGPS is associated with a single base mutation in the Lamin A gene, and mice harboring this mutation also exhibit signs of accelerated aging. Numerous research groups have also shown that progerin accumulates in our cells during the course of normal aging. Using recently created novel mouse lines we will directly test the hypothesis that progerin expression in MPs contributes to aging. If this can be demonstrated, these studies will provide critical experimental evidence supporting a prominent role for MPs in aging. This information will lead to a better understanding of the aging process, while also providing a foundation to support therapeutic strategies aimed at enhancing healthy aging.

column36: Development and Validation of a New Method for Measuring Cartilage Load Using Upright Open MRI
column37: The goal of this project is to develop a new method for measuring loaded deformation of knee cartilage, for application in studying prevention and treatment of osteoarthritis. This is important because osteoarthritis, which affects 1 in 10 Canadians, is triggered by abnormal joint mechanics. Slowing or reversing the disease requires changing joint mechanics with approaches like surgery and bracing. It is difficult to study the effectiveness of potential joint protection approaches because there is currently no method for studying how load is distributed in the knee joint. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) makes measurements that are sensitive to the deformation of the cartilage due to load and may be useful, but work so far has been limited because most MRI scanners don't allow people to load their knees. We have an extraordinary opportunity to study a new potential MRI measure for loaded deformation of cartilage because we have access to an upright, open MRI scanner, which allows us to image participants standing up, while they load their knees. Our objectives are to develop this new method, determine how accurate and repeatable it is, and try it out in a study of patients with damaged joint structures that may cause abnormal loading in the joint. The significance of this work is that it will provide a tool to identify the mechanical causes of osteoarthritis and to assess how well treatments (surgery, physical therapy, activity modification) correct mechanical disorders in the joints. This knowledge is essential to reducing the burden of osteoarthritis.

column36: Applying Behavioral Economics to Predict Alcohol Trajectories during the Transition to Adulthood
column37: Alcohol misuse remains a major public health problem in emerging adults (age 18-25) in Canada. Although many emerging adults 'mature out' of alcohol misuse over time, others exhibit persistently high levels of problem drinking and the process of maturing out is not well understood. Integrating psychology and economics, the field of behavioural economics (BE) is increasingly used to study alcohol misuse and is highly relevant to maturing out. In particular, two novel BE indices have been consistently associated with alcohol misuse in emerging adults in cross-sectional studies. These are alcohol demand and proportionate alcohol-related reinforcement, two different strategies for measuring how much a person values alcohol. These indices may predict maturing out of alcohol misuse over time, but no longitudinal studies have been conducted to date. This study will systematically test the hypothesis that these BE measures will predict changes in alcohol misuse during the transition to adulthood. The study has two primary aims. The first primary aim is to predict changes in alcohol misuse from age 22-25 using the novel BE measures, both individually and in the context of established risk factors. The second primary aim is to examine mechanistic interrelationships among these variables. This includes examining whether the BE variables cause changes in alcohol misuse over time or, alternatively, whether their influence is caused by the established risk factors. In addition, the study will examine whether there are systematic differences in the predictive relationships based on biological sex, university student status, and the use of other substances. For exploratory purposes, the study will also identify the most salient periods of change and psychosocial factors that increase or decrease the value of alcohol. Taken together, the study proposes to leverage recent advances in BE to substantially increase the understanding of maturing out of alcohol misuse.

column37: The precocious and chronic course of depression makes it the disease with the leading cause of disability, an effect marked by a 2-fold difference in the rate for girls and women as of early adolescence. The pace of reduction in the prevalence of anxious and depressive disorders has failed to keep up with those of other chronic disorders. Arguably what is missing is not a list of risk factors, but rather a precise knowledge of how factors interact to predict those at higher risk. Findings associating prenatal experience and psychopathology provide interesting directions. Differences by gender in the response to stress are well document in early emotional development but evidence is needed in older children and adults. Genetic differences in susceptibility to prenatal events are also important. Finally, the early environment as seen in early maternal care might be a significant positive or negative influence on the effect of prenatal, gender and genetic risk. For cost-effective interventions to exploit the higher neuroplasticity in children, such a complex developmental approach is needed to identify those at risk. This is more poignant given the availability effective individual and family interventions. We will examine these important questions by means of a collaboration of 4 prolific international longitudinal cohorts, in Canada (Maternal Adversity, Vulnerability and Neurodevelopment), the United Kingdom (Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children), the Netherlands (Generation-Rotterdam) and Singapore (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Health Outcomes). column36: Developing agonistic therapeutic strategies for lung cancer based on synthetic lethal oncogene interactions
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide, suffering from a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis and a paucity of effective drugs available to treat advanced tumours. Despite a greater understanding of the genetic basis of lung cancer development, discovery of new therapeutics has been slow as the activities of genes implicated in this disease are difficult to inhibit while new agents targeting lung cancer cells have been ineffective due to drug resistance. Therefore, new strategies are urgently needed to develop effective therapeutic strategies for lung cancer patient therapy that yield robust responses and improve long-term survival rates. The current approach to drug discovery mainly entails identifying a gene that is mutated in lung tumours, determining if its modulation impacts cancer growth and then screening or designing drugs to inhibit gene function. An alternative approach would be to use information about what genes are never activated in lung tumours to uncover potential avenues for therapeutic intervention. The idea is that the reason these genes are not activated in lung tumours is because they were incompatible with cancer growth. With this in mind, we assessed lung tumours from over 600 patients and discovered two genes that were never activated together. When we engineered lung cancer cells to have activation of both of these genes, we found that the cancer cells died in robust fashion. The goal of this proposal is to understand why co-activation of these two genes kills cancer cells and determine whether drugs that can mimic this scenario offer an effective way of inhibiting lung tumour growth. We also aim to test candidate drugs in mice that develop lung cancer to gain insight regarding their potential use in the treatment of human patients. Thus, this work will offer true progress towards developing new agents for the treatment of lung cancer, ultimately leading to improved survival rates for patients.

column36: Molecular regulation of the kidney filtration barrier
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major public health issue that continues to rise coincident with increased longevity and the obesity, diabetes and hypertension epidemic, and ~3 million Canadians are already living with this devastating illness. Presently, dialysis and transplantation are the only forms of treatment for advanced kidney disease, and these approaches are associated with considerable morbidity, mortality and healthcare costs. Despite the burden of disease, the molecular and cellular basis of CKD is poorly understood, limiting opportunities for development of new therapies. Fundamental discoveries over the past decade have highlighted the key role of the podocyte in the pathogenesis and progression of CKD. These cells are a crucial component of the glomerular blood filtration barrier, and their function is closely tied to their unique morphology. Podocytes extend a series of interdigitating actin-based foot processes that are bridged by specialized signaling junctions known as slit diaphragms (SD). One of the earliest features of kidney disease is remodeling of podocyte foot processes and collapse of the actin cytoskeleton, resulting in disrupted filtration and proteinuria. Our lab provided some of the first evidence that signaling from the SD directly regulates foot process morphology, and we have since validated the importance of such signaling in podocyte injury and repair. These discoveries provide a molecular foothold to help understand the basis of podocyte function, and the underlying hypothesis of our research program is that perturbations in SD signaling are the initiating cause of podocyte injury progressing to CKD. Leveraging a series of novel mutant mouse models and complementary cell-based tools, the goal of this proposal is to identify molecular and cellular processes that are coordinated by the central SD protein nephrin. Our long-term objective is to translate this knowledge to the bedside to identify new podocyte-specific therapies.

column36: Regulation of mRNA stability and translation during human neurodevelopment
column37: Development of brain circuitry is affected in Rett syndrome and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene while ASD is associated with mutations in hundreds of different genes. Genes function by making RNA that is then "translated" into proteins. We discovered that the MECP2 gene makes RNA in human stem cells but it is not stable and is actively degraded. The ability to translate MECP2 RNA into MECP2 protein is also inhibited in stem cells. These two layers of regulation ensure that stem cells do not make too much MECP2 protein until they mature into nerve cells. We predict that many ASD risk genes are regulated in the same manner as MECP2 in stem cells because these RNAs would otherwise promote premature differentiation into nerve cells. We propose to expand our MECP2 gene findings into deciphering a more comprehensive understanding of RNA regulation in human stem cells as they develop into nerve cells. In OBJECTIVE 1 we will define changes in RNA translation. Our experiments will identify which RNAs are making proteins in stem cells and neurons by associating with factories called ribosomes. We will discover how translation of ASD risk genes is controlled and identify proteins that are misregulated in Rett syndrome nerve cells. In OBJECTIVE 2 we will define changes in RNA stability. Our experiments will identify which RNAs are rapidly destroyed in stem cells but not in nerve cells. We will discover how the RNA is targeted for degradation in stem cells, and how it is protected in nerve cells. In both aims, we will test the ability of RNA from ASD risk genes to promote stem cell differentiation or nerve cell maturation. The expected outcomes will be the elucidation of RNA regulation of genes that can be applied to improve directed differentiation of stem cells for regenerative medicine, and may unveil misregulated proteins for future drug development.

column36: The Surviving Opioid Overdose with Naloxone Education and Resuscitation (SOON-ER) trial: a randomized study of an opioid overdose education and naloxone distribution intervention for laypeople in ambulatory and inpatient settings.
column37: Overdose deaths from opioids like heroin, oxycodone and fentanyl have reached record levels in North America and account for over 100,000 deaths per year worldwide. Overdose often affects young people, resulting in more years of life lost than HIV, pneumonia or influenza in Ontario. Overdose education and naloxone distribution (OEND) is a promising way to address this epidemic. OEND programs train laypeople to recognize overdose and give first aid, including the opioid antidote naloxone. Conventional OEND programs are mainly available through non-clinical community harm reduction centers, involve lengthy patient training, and do not reach many of the patients at risk of overdose. OEND is being expanded to hospitals, clinics, and emergency departments, but little is known about how to offer OEND in these settings effectively. We do not know if this intervention affects patient knowledge or outcomes, and OEND programs have not been well evaluated in clinical practice. This project will generate tools and evidence to extend OEND into clinical care in emergency departments, family practices, opioid substitution clinics and inpatient settings. Scientists will work with design experts and community members to create an OEND toolkit that allows brief patient training with a new naloxone delivery device, and test the toolkit using a randomized trial. We will recruit patients at risk of opioid overdose in the emergency department, family practices, opioid substitution clinics and inpatient settings to be trained using the new toolkit or referred to a conventional community OEND program. Then we will compare their performance in a mock opioid overdose with a manikin. We will work with affected communities to share project results in Canada and abroad. The study will let us examine other effects of OEND including deaths, hospital admissions, and cost. The project will transform care for thousands of Canadians by incorporating overdose prevention into routine clinical care.

column36: Glycosylation of hydroxymethylcytosine in mammalian genomes - distribution and functional roles.
column37: Proteins are expressed from the genes contained within the DNA of our chromosomes. The regulation of gene expression in humans controls a wide range of processes, spanning from cellular growth and development through to wound healing and adaptation to variations in diet. Inappropriate regulation of gene expression leads to cancers and hinders adaptation to changes in diet and environment. One central molecular mechanism for governing gene expression is the modification or "marking" of cytosines in genomic DNA with methyl groups, as well as oxidized forms of these methyl groups. (Cytosine is the C in the 4 letters (A, C, G, T) that make up the sentences (genes) of DNA.) These "chemical marks" are particularly important for regulating cell growth and proliferation, as well as the fate of stem cells in our bodies. We have just identified a previously unknown DNA modification in which a specialized sugar is attached to cytosines carrying an oxidized methyl group. In this proposed research program, we aim to identify the precise locations in the genomic DNA of mammals where this sugar modification occurs, uncover its functional consequences on the structure of DNA and on the ability of proteins within the cell to "read: these genes, and establish how the addition and removal of this modification is regulated by other proteins as well as in response to diet. The comprehensive understanding of this newly discovered DNA modification that will result from our studies is an essential step toward being able to monitor and manipulate gene expression for beneficial medical and biotechnological applications.
