column36: Development of an animal model, a protective vaccine and monoclonal antibodies against Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus
column37: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is the cause of a severe viral hemorrhagic fever that affects thousands across Asia, Africa, and parts of Europe. The disease is spread by bites from infected ticks, or by contact with the blood or body fluids of infected animals or individuals. The case-fatality can be as high as 40%, and even with medical attention there is significant chance of mortality. Risks for small or large-scale outbreaks include laboratory accidents, bioterrorism, and imported cases from countries where the disease is endemic, combined with the projected expansion of the niche of the ticks that carry the disease due to climate change. Moreover, individuals can remain asymptomatic for anywhere from 3-6 days, increasing the potential for the disease to spread as a result of travel. At present, our understanding of the disease is limited by the lack of suitable animal models that accurately mimic human disease. As no vaccine or post-exposure therapy exists for CCHFV, our proposal seeks to address these areas of need by a multifaceted approach. Specifically, the objectives of this proposal are the following: 1) Develop animal models of CCHFV pathogenesis and transmission, and test as systems for evaluating therapies. 2) Generate, through cloning, protective monoclonal antibodies from B-cells isolated from the convalescent plasma of CCHFV survivors, and validate these in our animal models. 3) Evaluate a DNA plasmid-based vaccine against CCHFV. This proposal will further our understanding of CCHFV, as our animal models will provide insights into transmission and pathogenesis, and will aid in the development of pre- and post-exposure therapies. Our group has an established track record of translational research that has lead to these types of therapies, currently under clinical evaluation. Collectively we anticipate that the findings from this study will have the potential to transform the way this disease is treated, and improve patient outcomes

column36: Bacteremia Antibiotic Length Actually Needed for Clinical Effectiveness (BALANCE): A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial
column37: Bloodstream infections are a common and serious problem, affecting 15% of critically ill patients, increasing length of hospital stay by 2-3 weeks, adding $25,000-40,000 in excess hospital costs, and tripling the risk of death. At the same time, antibiotic overuse is also a common and serious problem, in that 30-50% of antibiotic use is unnecessary or inappropriate, and results in avoidable drug side effects such as kidney failure, Clostridium difficile infection, increased costs, and spiraling antibiotic resistance rates. The greatest contributor to antibiotic overuse is excessive treatment duration. Shorter duration antibiotic treatment (= 7 days) is as effective as longer duration treatment for ear infections, bladder infections, and pneumonia, but this question has not been directly studied in the setting of bloodstream infection. Our team's systematic review of the medical literature, national survey of Canadian infectious diseases and critical care physicians, and multicentre retrospective study (N=1202) all support the need for a randomized controlled trial comparing shorter (7 days) versus longer (14 days) antibiotic treatment for bloodstream infections. Our CIHR-funded multicenter BALANCE Pilot trial, has established the feasibility of this trial design, with excellent recruitment rates, and adherence to treatment duration protocols. In this proposal for the main BALANCE trial, we will definitively determine whether 7 days of treatment is associated with non-inferior survival rates as compared to 14 days of treatment. By defining the duration of treatment for bloodstream infections, our research program will help maximize the clinical cure of individual patients, while minimizing their risk of drug side effects, C. difficile, and antibiotic resistance. Since this intervention would require no new technology, and would reduce (rather than increase) health care costs, it would offer immediate benefits to patients and the healthcare system.

column36: Systemic immunity: the missing link between gut microbiome and asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways currently affecting more than 300 million people worldwide. It is now the most common childhood disease in Western countries. Asthma has a genetic component, but genetics offers only a partial explanation for the dramatic rise in prevalence over the last five decades. Accumulating evidence points to environmental factors as key contributors. One such factor is the microbiome, the collection of microorganisms that inhabit our body. Using stool samples collected from children enrolled in the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) Study, we recently demonstrated a connection between gut microbiome alterations in the first 100 days of life and an increased risk to develop asthma. We also found that low levels of specific intestinal bacteria in asthmatic children are linked to low levels of microbial products (metabolites) known to regulate essential immune functions. However, the immune status of those children was not determined, and the mechanisms by which an altered microbiome and metabolites functionally link to asthma is unknown. Based on the role of the immune system in asthma, we hypothesize that specific changes in the gut microbiome contribute to the development of childhood asthma by producing metabolites that modulate the host immune response. We will test this hypothesis as follows. First, we will leverage the CHILD cohort to study the immune and metabolic signatures that correlate with clinical asthma. Second, we will determine the interrelationships among the infant gut microbiome, microbial metabolites, immune system status, and asthma. Third, we will validate those interrelationships in a mouse model of asthma. This project will provide important new understanding of how asthma develops, and it will identify ways that we might prevent or treat asthma, potentially using probiotics.

column36: Vaginal Surgery for the Pelvic Floor: A Randomized Trial of Synthetic Mesh Versus Synthetic Sutures
column37: More than 4 million women in Canada suffer from pelvic floor diseases. Pelvic floor muscles, nerves and ligaments can tear and stretch, mainly from vaginal deliveries of babies and aging. Women experience urine or stool leakage and pelvic organ prolapse or bulging of pelvic organs through the vaginal opening. These problems usually come together and are very common. They affect women's ability to lead normal lives, be physically active and enjoy normal sexual relations. Many become depressed and isolated. Surgery for prolapse often fails and symptoms come back. Surgeons thought that plastic permanent mesh behind the vagina would offer a more durable repair. Unfortunately, mesh kits were commercialized without much study. They caused many unexpected complications of pain, discharge, exposure of the mesh to the surface of the vagina, and did not cure prolapse. Most were taken off the market. Women who currently want vaginal surgical repair have the option of permanent sutures to hold the vaginal wall in place. This technique is not perfect because it can tension the vagina too much and can still cause pain and return of prolapse. We know, from successful surgeries with slings for urine incontinence, and from other small studies, that vaginal mesh is safe if introduced in small amounts, deep in the pelvis, without tension. Therefore, we propose to study 2 surgeries for vaginal repair of prolapse, using small mesh arms versus permanent sutures. We think that surgery with mesh may be more durable than surgery with sutures, but we cannot know for sure until we perform our study. Women will be randomly assigned to one of the two surgeries and followed for 2 years. We will study women's opinion of how the surgery worked for their prolapse, their other pelvic symptoms, pelvic exam and their sexual health. We hope to solve the controversy about vaginal mesh for prolapse and investigate a new procedure that may be a better, more durable option for women with prolapse.

column36: Post-transcriptional regulatory networks coordinating developmental gene expression in the human pathogen Leishmania
column37: Leishmaniasis is one of the 17 neglected tropical diseases impacting over 1 billion of the world's poorest populations. The disease is caused by the protozoan parasite Leishmania and transmitted to humans by the bite of infected sandflies. The parasite can cause a broad spectrum of diseases, and in the worst cases leaving its victims disfigured for life or causing death. Public investment in prevention and treatment would decrease the burden of leishmaniasis and also help to alleviate poverty. However, there is currently no vaccine available, actual treatments are toxic or ineffective due to resistance, and the disease receives little attention from the media, pharma, and international organizations. Within mammalian macrophages, Leishmania replicates in the harsh environment of the phagolysosome to establish disease. Intracellular development of the parasite relies on post-transcriptional regulatory networks that control the expression of thousands of genes in a very dynamic and coordinated manner. My laboratory is at the leading edge of research in the field of Leishmania gene regulation and has made major discoveries that significantly advanced knowledge in this area. It has also pioneered the use of reverse genetics and Leishmania genomics and has developed various tools to help advance the field that are largely used by the community. As a follow-up of previous studies in my lab, our research program aims at investigating timely questions on how this intracellular pathogen regulates gene expression inside macrophages to ensure its survival and to establish disease. Outputs from this research program could lead to the identification of promising targets for the development of novel therapeutic and preventive strategies against this important human pathogen, hence impacting the health sector and foresee Canada as a main contributor to global health efforts. It will also contribute to job creation and training of highly qualified personnel.

column36: Socio-cultural Contexts and Young Men's Sexual Lives
column37: STI/HIV incidence continues to rise, particularly among subgroups of young men who have sex with men. New STI/HIV interventions are being launched in order to address the escalating needs of young men; however, few studies have examined how features of socio-cultural contexts affect young men's uptake of new and unfolding STI/HIV interventions. For example, for today's young men, the availability of effective treatment for HIV infection is a potential "game changer" and the socio-cultural contexts in which they launch their sexual careers are profoundly different from those experienced by previous generations. In the BC context, we are studying three intervention programs designed to reduce young men's STI/HIV risks: (i) the BC Centre for Disease Control's GetCheckedOnline; (ii) YouthCO's Mpowerment YVR; and (iii) the BC Ministry of Health's Provincial Strategy for STI Prevention, Testing and Treatment. The data generated from the proposed study will inform the effective and ethical adaptation and scaling up of these interventions in ways that enhance their capacity to positively affect the sexual health of young men at risk for STI/HIV.

column36: Insights from Rare Overgrowth Syndromes for Common Diseases
column37: Rare diseases are common. There are more than 6000 rare diseases, and though each affects fewer than 1 person in 2000, together they affect between 6% and 8% of the population. This means approximately 500,000 Canadian children and youth live with a rare disease. Rare diseases that are not fatal in childhood often lead to long-term complications in adulthood. These can include increased risk for common adult-onset diseases such as cancers and diabetes. Most rare diseases have a genetic cause, but the majority of sufferers will need multiple medical tests over many years until they get a final diagnosis. Currently, 25% of rare disease patients wait 5-30 years for a diagnosis, 40% initially receive a misdiagnosis, and half will never receive a diagnosis. This "Diagnostic Odyssey" is notorious for being time-consuming, emotionally draining and expensive for health care systems and for the families. A subset of rare diseases affect growth, causing the person to be unusually short or unusually tall. Tall stature syndromes often cause overgrowth elsewhere in the body, leading to large head size and obesity. We want to diagnose patients with these rare overgrowth syndromes by finding new molecular causes of disease. Our goal is to understand how changes in these genes and pathways damage the body's organ systems, so we can design better treatments and care. Furthermore, because overgrowth disorders in particular have an increased susceptibility to a variety of childhood- and adult-onset cancers, we believe that our insights from these rare diseases will also help us understand how common cancers arise and evolve into more aggressive forms.

column36: Promoting Health Equity for Indigenous and non-Indigenous People in Emergency Rooms
column37: Emergency Departments (EDs) in Canada often operate over-capacity and are under increasing pressure. Consequently, despite intentions to uphold principles of fairness, particular groups of people continue to experience inadequate and inequitable treatment in EDs, including Indigenous people, racialized newcomers, people with mental illnesses, facing homelessness, experiencing interpersonal violence or using substances. Stigma and discrimination operating in health care can discourage access to care, result in reliance on EDs, interfere with effective care delivery, and increase human and financial costs. This project will develop a framework for health equity interventions to promote the provision of equity-oriented care (EOC) in Emergency Departments (ED). Through an integrated knowledge translation approach consisting of a three-way collaboration among health researchers, Indigenous leadership and health care leadership we will produce a framework to promote equity for Indigenous people in ED that can be applied beyond the context of ED and beyond promoting equity for Indigenous people. The framework will integrate evidence-based strategies to address stigma and discrimination faced by both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people including that related to racism, gender and heteronormativity, substance use, housing instability, commercial sex work, or mental illnesses. We will work with three EDs in different settings: an inner-city, a large suburban area and a rural serving regional centre to develop, test and refine the framework. This research has great potential to promote equitable health care and health systems, and dramatically improve health outcomes by targeting people who have the greatest health challenges and unmet needs, contributing to repeat ED visits. The research is innovative in its implementation and testing of tailored interventions at an organizational level, leadership structure, and meaningful collaboration across professions and sectors.

column36: The physiological role of the axo-myelinic synapse
column37: Multiple sclerosis, stroke and spinal cord injury are common and devastating human disorders. The central nervous system is composed of two different types of tissue: gray matter, which comprises the nerve cell bodies, and white matter, which represents the nerve fibers connecting nerve cells to each other. Nerve fibers in the brains of mammals are highly specialized, being very thin (to pack millions of fibers into a small volume) and wrapped by an insulating fatty material called myelin to prevent short circuits. How this all-important myelin is damaged in human neurological disorders, and how the nerve fiber tells the myelin to start wrapping and insulating it, remain mysteries. This ongoing project has focused on chemical communication between axons (nerve fibers) and their myelin sheaths. We discovered that axons signal their myelin sheaths using chemical transmitters in a way that is very similar to how nerve cells communicate: through a chemical "synapse". This new axon-myelin synapse causes damage to myelin when excessively activated, and may be the first step in myelin loss in MS for instance. This project will explore the purpose of this axon-myelin synapse: why do axons need to talk to their myelin sheaths? What might myelin do for its axon when it senses a lot of electrical traffic traveling down the axon? We propose that myelin supports its axon by physically transferring material essential for the axon's long term survival. A breakdown of this communication and transfer may underlie diverse diseases such as MS, cerebral palsy and even psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.

column37: We have found a unique and never-before-seen type of diabetes in a young woman who has a mutated EP300 gene. column36: Statins for Venous Event Reduction in patients with venous thromboembolism (The SAVER Pilot Randomized Trial)
column37: Venous thromboembolism is the medical term used for blood clots in the veins. Blood clots in the veins of the legs are called deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and blood clots in the lungs are called pulmonary embolism (PE). These blood clots are common and affect more than 50,000 Canadians every year. Many individuals who have a blood clot are at increased risk of having another blood clot in the future. They are commonly prescribed medication to prevent a future blood clot. Rosuvastatin is a medication that belongs to a family of drugs called statins. They are prescribed for patients with elevated cholesterol levels and have been found to decrease events such as heart attack and stroke. It is possible that statins may also be useful for the prevention of blood clots in the veins and for prevention of complications in the legs following a blood clot. However, little research has been done to investigate this potential. We plan to conduct a large international study with over 3000 patients at 34 hospitals. The objective of the study is to test if rosuvastatin is effective and safe for preventing future blood clots. This application is for a smaller study called a pilot study. The objective is to prove that the large study can be completed. Another objective of our pilot study is to see if rosuvastatin reduces painful complications in the legs following a blood clot. We plan to include 312 people from 4 Canadian hospitals in the pilot study. All participants will have had a blood clot in their leg or their lungs. They will be randomized (like flipping a coin) to either the treatment group or the control group. The treatment group will receive one tablet of Rosuvastatin every day for 6 months. The control group will receive one placebo tablet (sugar pill) every day for 6 months. All participants will be followed for 6 months to check for side effects of the medication, new blood clots, and leg complications after a blood clot.

column37: Fifteen percent of Canadian youth have serious mental health problems, a leading cause of health-related burden for youth, and the leading cause of disability for adults worldwide. Most adult mental health problems begin in childhood and thus reducing the burden of illness in childhood should have a notably positive impact on adult mental health. The proposed study focuses on reducing mental health problems by studying one important and often neglected root cause- bullying. Bullying is a systematic abuse of power occurring at an alarming rate, with 35% of Canadian youth reporting being bullied occasionally and 10% reporting being bullied every day. column37: Intervertebral disc degeneration is a progressive disorder which affects about 60% of the population by age 70, often resulting in a debilitating low back pain. column37: In many diseases, our own body produces antibodies directed against our own tissues and organs. This phenomenon of autoantibody production is called autoimmunity, which is responsible for diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Autoimmunity is not well understood for a chronic lung disease like asthma. Eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, are a characteristic feature in asthma. Most difficult-to-control eosinophilic asthma patients are treated with a drug called prednisone (glucocorticosteroid) to control the underlying inflammation and prevent symptoms and attacks. In other diseases where certain peroxidase levels are increased such as thyroid peroxidase (autoimmune thyroiditis) and myeloperoxidase (Granulomatosis with polyangitis), autoantibodies are detected against the peroxidase itself, that lead to disease. In fact, we have recently found evidence of autoantibodies against eosinophil peroxidase, in the sputum of patients with severe form of eosinophilic asthma requiring high dose corticosteroid treatment and susceptible to recurrent lung infections. We propose that asthma, in some patients, may also be an autoimmune disease. We need to better understand why and how these autoantibodies develop and how they make the disease worse. We also hope to find the connection between infections and generation of autoantibodies. Hopefully, investigating these questions will help us identify patients at risk of developing this autoimmune type of asthma, find ways of managing them with current available therapeutics or finding avenues to develop new.

column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) occurs when the kidneys are not functioning properly. CKD causes a great deal of suffering, especially for people whose kidneys fail. column37: Patients with diabetes are 20 times more likely to have a lower limb amputation than the general population. This amputation rate is even higher when the patient has a diabetic foot ulcer. We will then test our early warning device in a group of patients who have normal blood flow, blocked blood flow, and in patients with foot wounds. By early recognition and screening, we may be able to save limbs and lives.

column37: Cancer is a devastating disease defined by genetic changes that activate proteins supporting cell growth, or are inhibitory of cell death. Modern oncology aims to specifically target these tumour drivers, which, unlike chemotherapy, has the secondary benefit of leaving normal cells unharmed. Recently, the field has produced a number of specific oncogene inhibitors, yet the results are underwhelming; most targeted therapies show an initial benefit, followed by the development of resistance. Our approach aims to first identify new 'helper' drug targets that, upon inhibition, improve the efficacy of first generation targeted therapies. Importantly, we are focusing our screens on cell surface proteins, as they are acutely accessible by antibodies. Experimentally, identifying 'helper' drug targets entails systematically removing each cell surface receptor in isolation from cancer models, then treating these modified cells with a drug. After measuring cell death and proliferation, we can then assess which removed receptor increases drug efficacy. A huge challenge in cancer therapeutics involves surmising whether inhibiting these candidates with drugs can mimic the complete removal of the enzyme, as this is not feasible for treating humans. Our second aim will assess candidate druggability and involves the development of therapeutic antibodies, which are engineered versions of naturally occurring human proteins that can be trained to bind and inhibit cancer targets. Newly designed therapeutic antibodies will be tested for their ability to increase targeted therapy efficacy, hopefully establishing novel approaches for cancer treatment and positively impacting those who suffer from this terrible disease.

As the old adage says, "the enemy of my enemy is my friend." Turning the tide of battle towards a pathogen's challengers may one day represent a promising strategy to prevent outbreaks and limit our exposure to microbial disease.

column37: Approximately half of female and a third of male Canadians will suffer an osteoporotic fracture. The financial burden of these fragility fractures currently exceeds $2.3 billion per year in Canada and will increase with the rapid ageing of our society. Osteoporosis is a highly heritable condition, which is controlled by the genetic factors that we inherit from our parents. Doctors measure bone mineral density (BMD) in order to predict a person's risk of fracture and BMD is an important criterion for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. Through large-scale international collaboration we have identified dozens of novel regions of the genome that influence BMD, and some of these influence fracture risk. These regions are highly enriched for the known drug targets for osteoporosis therapies and therefore, the novel regions we have identified will likely also contain novel drug targets for the treatment of osteoporosis. The drugs we currently use to treat osteoporosis act predominantly by increasing BMD. This is clinically helpful, but we know that most people who have fragility fractures, do not have a BMD low enough to be diagnosed with osteoporosis. This is because susceptibility to fracture is influenced by both bone quantity (as measured by BMD) and bone quality. What we therefore need in the clinic are new drugs that can prevent fracture by improving bone quality. column36: Engineering a broadly cross-protective vaccine that confers sterilizing immunity against Haemophilus influenzae.
column37: Haemophilus influenzae is responsible for a substantial proportion of respiratory infections in humans, including ear infections, sinus infections and pneumonia, as well as invasive infections such as meningitis. This bacterium lives in the human upper respiratory tract, not in other animals or in the environment. While most bacteria cannot live in human tissues because there is no free iron, which is essential for life, H. influenzae binds and removes iron from the iron transport protein in human blood, transferrin (Tf). Because this is an essential process, and because the Tf binding proteins (Tbps) must be accessible at the bacterial surface, these receptor proteins are ideal targets for vaccination to produce antibodies that protect against infection. In contrast to other H. influenzae vaccine targets, the Tbps are shared by both groups of pathogenic H. influenzae for which vaccines are needed. This means that a single Tbp-based vaccine could protect against both the respiratory tract and invasive infections. Moreover, we have recently demonstrated that Tbp-based vaccines prevent bacterial colonization of respiratory tissues, so that they provide 'sterilizing' immunity that should ultimately allow elimination of the bacteria rather than just protecting against clinical disease caused by infection. The purpose of this project is to apply our established approaches to understand the structure, function and sequence diversity of H. influenzae Tbps and then use protein engineering to create vaccine antigens that are capable of preventing colonization by all known strains of H. influenzae. Then, our novel, integrated vaccine design and evaluation pipeline approach, which includes the use of a 'humanized' mouse model for colonization, will be used to confirm how well the engineered antigens work and refine the composition of engineered antigens to produce a safe, effective and broadly protective vaccine.

Our optimal expectation is that there will be a reduction in the movement impairments and the less a-syn accumulation in animals that received both the ultrasound and gene therapy.

column36: Regulation of retromer in health and disease
column37: Every cell is like a busy city: it has to coordinate information flow, perform thousands of different tasks, and move materials, like fats and proteins, to where they are needed. Like cities, cells have a complex internal transportation system that controls traffic. This system works well most of the time, but can get disrupted, and persistent disruptions can cause dysfunction and disease. This project focuses on an important part of this cellular transportation system called "retromer". Problems with retromer cause neurological disorders such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, but to develop effective treatments for these conditions, we first need to understand the fundamental causes of disease. Many of the traffic signals and pathways linked to human disease are also found in yeast, a simple one-celled organism. Studying retromer in yeast allows us to use different genome-wide technologies to uncover pathways and machinery on a very large scale and allows us to make discoveries that would be difficult or impossible in complex organisms. In fact, retromer was first discovered in yeast, and many important discoveries about retromer are still being made in this cell system. Recently, we discovered that a family of "VPS9-like" proteins regulates retromer assembly in yeast. One of these proteins, called "VARP", was also found to be important for retromer function in human cells. This gives us the unparalleled opportunity to use yeast to study VARP and establish exactly how it regulates retromer. Once we have made discoveries in yeast, we can transfer this knowledge to the study of cells from mice or humans to test if increasing VARP function can overcome the retromer defects seen in Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease. In the longer term, our research is expected to identify new drug targets that will help in the development of new treatments for these neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Blockbuster Diagnostics? The political economy of diagnostic innovation in comparative perspective
column37: How do new diagnostic tests find their way into practice? What are the relative roles of industry and the public sector in the discovery, development and adoption of new biological markers of disease? Completion of the Human Genome Project has encouraged the belief that a major transformation in our understanding of the causes of health and disease is underway, leading to fundamental changes in clinical and public health practice related to the early detection and diagnosis of disease - termed 'personalized medicine'. Though major change may not be imminent, it is clear that we are facing a new era of potentially 'blockbuster' diagnostics, sold at high prices and in relatively large quantities. This is new, and suggests that important shifts may be taking place in the way new diagnostics are discovered, developed and adopted in clinical practice, with a growing role for the industry in research and development, new business strategies within the diagnostics industry in developing and delivering their tests, and new regulatory efforts by governments aimed at managing test adoption. Increased industry involvement may enhance the capacity to develop and validate new tests and bring them to the clinic, but it may also encourage overly aggressive marketing of tests with limited value at unsustainable prices. To date, changes have happened in ad hoc ways, so sustained research is needed to guide public policy in supporting the development and adoption of valuable diagnostics whilst guarding against poor quality tests. Using a comparative approach focused on Canada, the US and UK, we will explore discovery, development and adoption processes for novel molecular tests in three clinical areas: colorectal cancer, lung cancer and the detection of fetal anomalies. Because the potential to detect disease early holds particular promise for both public health and industry, we focus our analysis on medical screening.

column36: Assessing the Effectiveness of an Interactive Virtual Reality Intervention, Story-Telling Medicine, in Reducing Perioperative Anxiety in Children Undergoing Elective Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Preoperative anxiety (PA) affects up to 5 million children in North America each year and is associated with many adverse medical, psychological, and behavioural effects. In fact, children who are highly anxious often require more medications during surgery and afterwards, and take longer to recover. While many attempts have been made to reduce PA in children, existing interventions (e.g., medications and complex psychological preparation programs) are limited by their expense and time-intensive nature. The current lack of effective and efficient tools for reducing anxiety in children before and after surgery has prompted us to develop and test a new interactive, tablet-based Virtual Reality program, Story-Telling Medicine (STM), to help reduce anxiety and its associated negative effects in children undergoing surgery. STM is an age-appropriate, customizable program that simulates the children's hospital environment by guiding them through all of the settings they will encounter prior to surgery. This study will compare STM given in addition to usual hospital procedures (known as Usual Care (UC)), to UC alone in reducing anxiety in children undergoing surgery. We predict that children in the STM group will have lower levels of anxiety and fewer other negative effects prior to and after surgery compared to the UC group. This study provides an important opportunity to assess the effects of a simple, new, and inexpensive tool to reduce surgical anxiety in children. If effective, STM will improve children's and families' experiences with surgery and reduce mental and physical health problems in both the short and long term. This tablet-based application can be customized to virtually any surgical setting and so has the potential to be used in hospitals across Canada and beyond.

column36: Chronic stress, synaptic remodelling and neuroendocrine adaptation
column37: Chronic stress is a strong risk factor for serious mental illnesses including major depression and many other disorders in mood and cognition. These stress-related disorders are now the fastest growing category of disability insurance claims in Canada, costing an estimated $31 billion each year in lost productivity, and billions more in direct medical costs. Despite its tremendous impact on our health and society, we know surprisingly little about how stress leads to mental illness. This lack of knowledge is a major obstacle in the search for better treatments and prevention of stress-related disorders. An emerging view is that neuroplasticity is important for successful coping with stress, and that severe stress disturbs this process and leads to stress-related disorders. We hypothesize that neuroplastic mechanisms are important for fine-tuning the levels of stress hormones (i.e. corticosteroids) during chronic stress. This project will use an animal model of chronic stress to first study the neuroplasticity that occurs when the animal adapts to chronic stress. We will then investigate how this adaptation to chronic stress fails when the animal receives a more severe form of stress that causes dysregulation of the hormonal stress response. Using state-of-the-art techniques that enable us to study communication between neural cells at high temporal and spatial resolutions, we have conducted a pilot study, which has found stress-induced plasticity within a brain area that regulates the hormonal stress response. We seek to further investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which this plasticity becomes dysregulated during severe chronic stress. These experiments will identify specific brain mechanisms for stress adaptation, promising targets for future therapeutics and prevention of stress-related disorders. This project will also provide outstanding opportunities for trainees to be immersed in this emerging field along with sophisticated technologies.

column36: Development of a Novel Platform to Treat Neuropathic Lysosomal Storage Diseases
column37: Lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) are a group of approximately 50 disorders that result from inherited defects in proteins that reside in specialized compartments of cells throughout the body called lysosomes. LSDs are characterized by the accumulation of undigested or partially digested macromolecules within lysosomes, which ultimately results in cellular dysfunction and clinical abnormalities. Encouragingly, it has been shown that injecting a functional copy of the missing protein into patients, referred to as enzyme replacement therapy, can restore function to many cells in the body. Unfortunately, these injected proteins cannot penetrate the protective sac that surround the brain called the blood-brain-barrier (BBB), and thus enzyme replacement is not available to restore the function of cells in the brain. As a result, we are unable to treat the devastating symptoms of approximately half of all LSDs, which have a neurological component. In this proposal, we are taking advantage of a protein fragment produced by certain bacteria that naturally crosses the BBB and enters the brain as part of its normal function. column37: It is estimated that 6-10% of children have developmental, behavioral or cognitive problems. This will be assessed in cord blood that had been collected at birth and specimens obtained at 3 years old. We also study if BPA exposure affects boys and girls' brain development differently. column37: When cancer is caught early, the treatments are easier and the cancer can often be removed and cured. column37: The hippocampus is a brain structure that has been implicated in many different neurological conditions including epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease, where it plays a role in both diagnosis and treatment. Uncontrolled epilepsy remains a burden on the healthcare system and this work could increase eligibility for surgery can potentially improve outcomes for patients that undergo surgery. column36: Neuroimaging Predictors of Response to rTMS in Late-Life Depression
column37: Canadians aged 60 and older are the fastest growing segment of the population. Depression is a very common illness later in life and is a major contributor to high rates of disability, poor quality of life, caregiver burden and poor health outcomes. Unfortunately, up to 77% of individuals treated for late-life depression (LLD) either do not respond to treatment or respond and then relapse. Strategies for managing treatment resistance in older adults are problematic due to increased sensitivity to side effects and higher rates of prescription drug use for other medical illnesses. There are very few safe and effective options for treating patients who do not respond to antidepressants. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) involves stimulating the brain with a series of magnetic field pulses. A standard course treatment is administered daily, five days per week, for 45 minutes for 6 weeks. A newer form of rTMS called theta burst stimulation (TBS) capitalizes on the natural frequencies of brain waves and offers a more efficient way of stimulating. Specifically, a treatment session with TBS takes less than 5 minutes compared to the 45 minutes of a standard treatment. Underlying brain network dysfunction is thought to underlie depression in older adults. Functional brain imaging has the capacity to map brain network dysfunction. Certain patterns of brain network dysfunction may help to predict who is likely to respond to rTMS. By using brain imaging to predict who will respond to rTMS and exploring the effectiveness of TBS we will be able to greatly improve access and outcomes when using rTMS in older adults with depression.

column37: OBJECTIVES We have designed a new drug (STK-01) specifically for delivery into the bladder of patients with bladder cancer. Here we will test STK-10 for the first time in patients. The goal of this trial is to set the foundation for larger trials with STK-01 that will allow the drug to be used in routine clinical practice. BACKGROUND Drugs are delivered into the bladder of patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) in order to reduce the risk of the cancer coming back or developing into a more threatening cancer. This structure enables docetaxel to stick to the inner surface of the bladder better, thereby increasing the time it stays in the bladder and the depth that it can penetrate into the bladder wall. First we will determine the maximum dose that can be given safely to patients as a single dose. We will then test multiple administrations of this maximum dose. This will establish the safety of multiple doses and provide an early sign of the effectiveness of the drug. IMPACT Bladder cancer is the 5th most common malignancy in Canada, but no new therapies have been established in at least two decades. Intravesical STK-01 promises to improve the therapy of NMIBC and thereby enhance patient quality of life, minimize treatment burden and reduce cost.

column36: Impact of rewarming on the brain health of cooled neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
column37: Birth asphyxia due to lack of oxygen at birth is the leading cause of death in term newborns. Half of survivors fail to fully develop their language and motor skills and may present epilepsy later in life, which pose significant burdens on patients, families and society. The current practice is to cool these newborns for the first three days of life to protect their brain. Yet, studies on asphyxiated animals showed that rapid rewarming after cooling can abolish or reduce benefits of cooling. Remarkably, no systematic studies investigated the reaction of human brain to rewarming. We demonstrated, using non-invasive bedside brain monitoring, that asphyxiated newborns may experience worsening of their brain activity and seizures on rewarming. Moreover, we developed non-invasive bedside tools that detect insufficient brain oxygen consumption in these neonates during cooling. We think that brain oxygen consumption abnormalities precede neurological deterioration on rewarming. In this study, we propose to use sophisticated methods of analysis and state-of-the-art brain imaging tools to study how rewarming affects brain health in cooled asphyxiated neonates. We will evaluate whether brain oxygen consumption abnormalities contribute to the worsening of brain activity and seizures on rewarming. We will also study whether these measures are related to abnormal findings on advanced magnetic resonance brain images, and predict increased risks of epilepsy and abnormal development. Hence, asphyxiated newborns will be closely followed through cooling and rewarming phases using non-invasive bedside brain imaging tools. They will continue to be followed through infancy and their development will be evaluated at 18 months of age. This study will help understand how rewarming affects the brain of asphyxiated newborns. It will allow the development of new interventions to protect the brain of neonates at high risk of adverse neurological outcomes.

column36: Computed tomography perfusion for neurological death determination: a prospective Canadian multicenter diagnostic test study
column37: For many patients with terminal heart, lung, liver and kidney disease, organ transplantation is the treatment of choice and most often their only hope for survival. Organs retrieved in patients after a process called the neurological death determination (NDD) represent the principal source of organs transplanted in Canada. To ensure appropriate care for such patients, and also for the potential benefit of patients in urgent need of an organ, it is of uttermost importance to accurately identify potential patients in a state of neurological death and to proceed in a humane, accurate, timely and cost-effective manner to NDD. Situations however happen when the physician can have difficulties to timely or accurately confirm neurological death because of important facial trauma or the use of medications, for example. In such situations, doctors have to rely on additional tests. Unfortunately, currently available tests in NDD raise particular diagnostic challenges where several tests on the same patient are often used, most of which are not recommended or imprecise and hard to interpret. This often lead to rejection of organ donors and loss of potential organs for transplantation. CT-perfusion has many of the characteristics of an ideal test for NDD but has not been rigorously studied for NDD. We propose to conduct a large Canadian multicenter diagnostic test study to rigorously validate CT-perfusion compared to complete clinical evaluation for NDD. This research study will inform the different stakeholders in the fields of neurocritical-care and organ donation regarding ways to improve the diagnosis of brain death by validating an ideal test to help doctors diagnose brain death. We hope that this study will, by improving the NDD process, help ensure the most appropriate care to patients with neurological death and thus minimize the loss of potential organs for transplantation.

column37: We have recently discovered a previously unknown disease in which both the heart and the gut progressively lose their pacemakers. We can show that this defect is due to a mutation in a gene called SGOL1 and we now suspect that SGOL1 is a novel master gene regulating how the heart is formed. Surprisingly, we have important pieces of evidence suggesting that the novel disease we found could be caused both by a loss and a gain of SGOL1 gene function at the same time. In this project, we aim to study the role of SGOL1 in the formation of the heart and its pacemaker during very early steps of development. It is possible to genetically engineer mice so that they either gain or lose a certain amount of this gene. Sophisticated tools allow us to control in which parts of the heart this loss or gain occurs, and also at what time. Since an early loss of the function of SGOL1 leads to the death of the embryo at early stages of development, we will intervene at later stages. This allows to obtain more meaningful results for later development, similar to what we see in patients with the novel syndrome who become sick either as children or as young adults. Another surprising fact from our preliminary studies is that the role of SGOL1 was totally unsuspected. This gene was known to have other functions, such as very early cell divisions that lead to the formation of eggs and sperm, a process called meiosis. We suppose that SGOL1 plays different functions in the developing heart, but may still be involved in helping developing cells decide whether they should divide more or start to specialize as heart cells. The mouse models we will develop will help to tease out the role of SGOL1 in heart formation and will be broadly applicable not only to the patients with the recently discovered pacemaking syndrome, but also to patients suffering from related diseases, such as anomalies of the heart beat or valve disease.

column36: Phase II study to assess the safety of non-operative management (NOM) for low rectal cancer (LRC)
column37: Background: Current treatment of low rectal cancer (LRC) is chemotherapy and radiotherapy (CRT) followed by surgery and involves creating a permanent colostomy (bag). In 30% of patients the tumour goes away after CRT, which is called a complete clinical response (cCR). For this study, we want to follow patients who have a cCR instead of operating. This is called a non-operative management (NOM) approach. The benefit is that patients with LRC may be able to safely avoid surgery and a permanent colostomy, thus leading to an improved quality of life. While physicians across Canada would like to offer NOM to patients with LRC, they do not feel comfortable doing so unless there is a standardized clinical protocol so that patients are properly informed of the risks and benefits and the outcomes are collected and measured in a standardized way. Objectives: Therefore the objective is to conduct a pan-Canadian Phase II trial to assess the safety of NOM for LRC. Methods: Patients with LRC who have achieved a cCR following CRT will be invited to participate. Patients who participate will undergo active follow up with regular clinical visits, physical exam, endoscopy and imaging assessments at regular intervals for 2 years to assess for tumour re-growth or spread to the liver and lungs. The primary outcome will be the rate of local re-growth. The NOM approach will be considered safe if the rate of tumour re-growth is <10%. Relevance: These results have the potential to change the management of future rectal cancer patients and have significant impact on quality of life as 30% of patients with LRC would be able to safely avoid surgery and a permanent colostomy. This study is of high priority to patients and strongly supports patient-centred care. Our Patient & Family Advisory Council that consists of 30 patients with rectal cancer and family members across Canada indicated that this study is a research priority and expressed interest in being involved in this study.

column36: Investigating Parkinson disease-linked genes in brain health following infections.
column37: It has been 53 years since the introduction of dopamine replacement therapy for Parkinson disease (PD). It remains the gold standard of clinical care but does not stop disease progression. Sadly, we do not yet have any cause-directed treatment options for our patients. Parkinson's is considered a complex disease in which both genetic risk and an environmental factor (or several) are required for disease initiation. The identity of these 'environmental hits' remains unknown. We have made critical discoveries over the last three years linking the environment and genetics in brain health in our model systems. Mutations in the LRRK2 gene increase the risk for PD; however, in itself a LRRK2 mutation rarely causes disease, suggesting that a second factor is required. We hypothesize that the second hit is environmental, specifically, microbial in nature. This is based on our finding of a critical role for LRRK2 in the immune system. We found that LRRK2 protects nerve cells from damages during a viral brain infection. Furthermore, we discovered a second PD-linked gene that also protects the brain during the course of an infection. The goals of the studies proposed in our application are to: 1) identify how these two genes act in an integrated response to protect the body and brain from infection; and 2) test a new understanding of PD development. There is growing recognition of the role of inflammation and the immune system in PD and related neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's. These studies will inform current drug trials (note, LRRK2 is the lead therapeutic molecule for PD) and have the possibility to open an entirely new field of targets for drug discovery that are rooted in the immune response. The results of our work will have concrete impacts on the translation of health research for better clinical outcomes for Canadians with Parkinson's.

column36: Anatomy of leptin sensing
column37: Obesity is a major health threat due to its strong association with diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and cancer. As obesity has reached pandemic proportions interventional strategies are urgently needed. Obesity is based on an excessive increase in the body's fat mass. Key to fat mass regulation is the hormone leptin, which is produced by the fat cells and in order to keep a constant body weight, circulating leptin acts on brain areas that control feeding to trigger a reduction in food intake. While the weight lowering effect of leptin has been known since its discovery some 20 years ago, we still do not know where and how leptin enters the brain to exert its weight lowering effect. However, understanding of this process is important as obesity is usually associated with leptin resistance, i.e., while circulating leptin levels increase in proportion with fat mass, leptin seemingly looses its ability to reduce appetite in obese individuals. We have recently discovered a novel structure within the nerve cells that respond to leptin. We found that this structure, a specific bulbous enlargement in the nerve cell's filaments, to be typically located close to blood vessels and it could thus serve a sensing function for circulating leptin. We wish to study this structure in much greater detail, to establish if and how it senses leptin. We want to determine if the leptin resistance associated with mouse models of obesity is due to a selective functional impairment or degeneration of the bulbous structure we discovered. Elucidating its functional role in the context of body weight control, may critically help to develop targeted therapeutic interventions aimed at 're-sensitizing' the brain to leptin, which would lead to reduced food intake and thus weight loss.

They regulate essential functions of the human body and insufficient or excess production is associated with various pathological conditions. Steroid hormone synthesis in these cells is mainly regulated by the pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH). In Leydig cells, LH will triggers activation of proteins called kinases that modify other proteins which ultimately leads to alteration in the expression of genes involved in steroid hormone synthesis. On the other hand, very little is known about the proteins that are targeted by CAMKI and AMPK. The goal of the present project is to identify the proteins targeted by CAMKI and AMPK and to determine their roles in steroid hormone production. A better characterization of these CAMKI and AMPK target proteins could lead to novel treatments for numerous hormone-dependent pathologies.

column36: Validation of a clinical decision rule integrating the use of biomarkers for early detection of persistent symptoms after a MTBI
column37: Cerebral concussions are common and they can affect anyone. Some populations are more at risk, especially teenagers and young male adults. Each year in Canada, about 500-650/100 000 people sustain a concussion (mild Traumatic Brain Injury) and it is suspected that many of them do not even seek medical attention. The management of these patients varies a lot, notably by geographical regions. Most of the data regarding concussion is based on expert opinion. Those patients are rarely admitted and conducting robust and structured studies to recruit a large cohort of patients is difficult. Moreover, 10-56% of patients are at risk of developing persistent symptoms for more than three months after the trauma. It is crucial to target those patients and to monitor them closely. Because of a lack of scientific evidence, no validated guideline has been proposed for the detection of those at-risk patients. There is an urgent need for health care providers to have access to a simple, quick, and reliable clinical decision rule, which could predict if complications/persistent symptoms are to be expected. Our research team is already working to develop tools to better predict the evolution of these patients. Our previous studies have identified significant risk factors for developing persistent symptoms after the injury and we have suggested some predictive models. However, these models are solely based on clinical factors (e.g. age, post-traumatic amnesia, etc.) and do not identify high-risk patients specifically enough. Along with this, none of the different biomarkers (e.g. protein S100B, C-Tau, etc.) studied so far can predict patient evolution on their own. A model integrating clinical criteria AND biomarker(s) would help to better identify patients at risk for persistent symptoms after a concussion. column36: Antigen-specific functional properties and molecular profiling of autoreactive T-cells in individuals at risk for type 1 diabetes.
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease, resulting from the destruction of the insulin-producing beta- cells in the pancreas by the T-cells of the immune system. In recent years we have discovered over forty places in the genome, where genetic variants inherited from the individual's parents determine the probability that the individual will develop T1D. Normally, T-cells whose receptor recognizes parts of self either die or become inactive thanks to a variety of successive roadblocks, collectively assuring immune self-tolerance. Autoimmunity happens when a small number of T-cells evade these roadblocks and multiply to reach numbers sufficient to do the autoimmune damage. In the past few years, we have discovered a large number of places in the human genome that contain genetic variants, inherited from an individual's parents that can weaken self-tolerance. Self-tolerance is assured by the regulatory T-cells, a subset of the immune system that protect normal tissues while the rest of the T-cells attack bacteria and viruses. The delicate balance between defense from microbes and "collateral damage" to one's own body parts is occasionally broken by rogue T-cells or by a weakening of the regulatory cells. Until recently, distinguishing between these two categories of cells was difficult. Thanks to the discovery of novel markers by Dr. Piccirillo, this distinction can now be made and the cells can be separated and studied. We now wish to use this breakthrough to study whether the progression from antibody positivity to T1D is due to an overactive immune system or to weakening of the regulatory component. Moreover, we have also the technology to separate T-cells that are directed against insulin, from other cells that do their normal job in fighting infection. This powerful combination of methodologies will allow us to isolate the cells directly involved in the development of T1D and study them with the powerful genome-wide methodologies of the CAG.

column37: Evidence suggests that children with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are particularly vulnerable to cardiovascular disease (CVD). Little is known regarding what factors predispose children with T1D to CVD, hindering efforts at prevention. In order to address these gaps, studies using technology capable of detecting the earliest changes associated with CVD, specifically cardiac MRI (CMR), while documenting potentially modifiable risk factors are critically needed. The objectives of this study are: 1) To compare established markers of CVD (such as abnormal cholesterol and blood pressure) with newer measures including CMR, in adolescents with T1D and in healthy normal weight adolescents; 2) To determine the association between established measures and the newer measures in these two groups; 3) To compare, across both groups, the association between cardiac measures derived from CMR with: i) physical activity; ii) dietary intake ;iii) sedentary behavior; iv) sleep. For the proposed project, 100 participants aged 15-18 years with T1D will be compared to 100 healthy normal weight controls. Height, weight, and waist circumference and blood pressure will be measured for each participant. Physical activity will be measured using a special device called an accelerometer worn at the waist for 7 days. Sedentary behavior and sleep will be measured using self-report and using accelerometer data. Dietary intake will be assessed using three 24hr recalls. Cholesterol levels will be measured after a 12-hr fast. Each participant will undergo a CMR to examine the heart structure and function. Our study provides a unique opportunity to establish the earliest detectable changes of the heart heralding CVD in adolescents with T1D, and determine how these relate to lifestyle habits, critical information for the development of effective and targeted preventive strategies.

column36: When should systematic reviews be replicated, and when is it wasteful?
column37: Replication is a corner stone of the scientific method yet replication of systematic reviews is too often overlooked, done unnecessarily or done poorly, as identified by Francis Collins, the Director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Excessive replication - doing the same study repeatedly - is unethical and a cause of 'research waste'. There is a lack of guidance for when or why to replicate systematic reviews. Overarching Aim: The proposed research will use an evidence-driven, transparent process and implement consensus approaches to develop value-added guidance on: a) when to replicate and b) when not to replicate systematic reviews. Objectives: We propose three sequential objectives: 1.To assess the extent of replication of systematic review topics and explore reasons for replication as well as issues such as discordance, agreement and bias. 2.To develop consensus-based recommendations on when to replicate systematic reviews of effectiveness (and when not), taking into account the needs of the various stakeholder groups. 3.To identify strategies for disseminating and implementing these recommendations to key stakeholder groups (e.g. patients, clinicians, journal editors, systematic review authors, systematic review users, systematic review organizations (such as CAMARADES, Campbell, Cochrane, Joanna Briggs Institute), guideline developers, research funding agencies, KT researchers). To achieve these objectives we will: assess evidence about when to replicate systematic reviews, document characteristics of overlapping systematic reviews, survey and interview authors of replicated systematic reviews, consult with global experts on replicability guidelines, prioritize and seek consensus on items for systematic review replication guidance, and develop collaborative knowledge translation plan including practical tools for specific knowledge users.

column37: Contexte: A l'echelle mondiale, les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) constituent la 1ere cause de mortalite et les problemes de sante mentale (PSM) constituent la 3ieme cause de morbidite. Les fractions attribuables (FA) aux contraintes psychosociales au travail seront calculees. Les FA seront appliquees au nombre de cas incidents et aux couts associes. Ces connaissances nouvelles sont indispensables au gouvernement et aux decideurs des milieux de travail pour prioriser les actions de prevention en sante au travail dans les entreprises. Un dialogue continu entre chercheurs du projet et utilisateurs des connaissances assurera que ces recommandations soient adaptees aux besoins des decideurs. column37: Advances in transplantation of human insulin producing tissue (islets) have established the proof-of-concept for this therapy to emerge as a treatment for patients with type 1 diabetes. The hope for a cure from islet replacement is, however lessened by the decline in insulin independence rates seen in clinical islet transplantation. This decline is currently not fully understood, but likely involves reduced islet survival and immune rejection. Strategies to maximize survival of the transplanted islets and reduce the immune response are likely to have a major impact in enhancing long-term clinical outcomes. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) reside in many tissues such as bone marrow and have shown potential as a regenerative medicine therapy for many degenerative diseases and immune disorders. Taken together, we hypothesize that MSCs combined with islets will improve and prolong islet function and that when co-transplanted with human islet will improve longer-term islet survival by locally secreting growth factors that promote cell survival or regeneration. Notably, with Edmonton's Clinical Islet Transplant program, along with Korbutt's $26 million stem cell facility for the clinical grade production of cells for diabetes therapy, this team is well positioned to rapidly transfer findings to clinical trials.

column36: One size does not fit all: Tailoring exercise prescription for brain health based on BDNF polymorphism
column37: The size of Canadian population aged 65 and older is growing, so will the number of individuals with dementia. Exercise is a viable dementia prevention strategy. To maximize the utility of exercise (e.g., by providing personalized exercise recommendations), it is vital to determine factors that influence its effectiveness. Exercise type and a person's genotype are factors that require further investigation. There are 2 main types of exercise, aerobic training (AT) and strength training (ST). Both have benefits for brain health, but do so using different biological pathways. Specifically, AT appears to largely rely on the release of a particular protein called brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). In contrast, ST is not BDNF-dependent, but relies on another protein. Understanding how both AT and ST benefit the brain is important because in ~35% of the population, there is an alteration within the BDNF gene that results in less secretion of BDNF. Thus, we believe this BDNF gene variant may determine the degree of benefit an individual will receive from AT. Specifically, we speculate that persons with this BDNF gene variant will not experience the same degree of brain health gains from AT as those without this gene variant. Thus, for individuals with this BDNF gene variant, ST may be the more appropriate form of exercise training to promote brain health. For our research, we will examine how this BDNF gene variant may modify the degree of brain health benefits from 6 months of 3 times per week AT or ST, in older adults at risk for dementia. Our study is critical to understanding how genes may influence the cognitive response to different types of exercise training. Given the immense health and financial burden imposed by dementia, our proposed study could have major impact in Canada and internationally as the results will contribute to evidence-based, personalized exercise recommendations for dementia prevention.

column36: Long-term impact of mild and unilateral hearing Loss in children
column37: Permanent hearing loss affects 2-4 per 1000 children and usually interferes with typical language acquisition. Newborn hearing screening has been implemented worldwide to give children with hearing loss a better start in life. Almost half of children present with a milder hearing loss (mild loss in both ears or loss in one ear) at initial diagnosis. Prior to screening, these children were identified late and many experienced difficulty in school. Our recent research shows that screening lowers the average age of identification of these losses from 5 years to 9 months of age. We have also shown that up to a third of children with hearing loss experience deterioration in hearing. Therefore, there is considerable uncertainty about whether screening programs should try to detect and treat these losses in early childhood. Study Plan. This study will provide detailed information about the consequences of mild/unilateral hearing loss and therefore guide clinical care and decision-making.

The brain capillaries that form the blood-brain barrier (BBB) have a special role in maintaining the proper brain environment. However, for many brain related diseases and disorders, the limited BBB permeability of drugs presents a substantial obstacle to effective treatment. This is certainly the case for glioblastomas, the most commonly occurring brain tumor in adults. Those nanoparticles with the best response in cell culture will be examined for effectiveness in an animal model of glioblastoma. In addition, the effects of the magnetic nanoparticles on normal cellular function in the brain will be examined. The ultimate goal of these studies is to provide a new method for the safe and effective treatment of brain tumors and potentially other brain related diseases.

column36: Restoring binocular vision in amblyopia by through engagement of stimulus-specific adaptive compensatory mechanisms
column37: Amblyopia is characterized by the loss or attenuation of vision in one eye despite the eye being normal and healthy. Currently, most approaches to understanding amblyopia treat this disorder as one where all vision in the amblyopic eye is suppressed. This idea holds insofar as it describes the main symptoms of amblyopia, but it does not explain the many ways in which vision in the amblyopic eye is integrated with that of the dominant eye. For example, peripheral vision is largely unaffected in amblyopia, as is vision for more blurred patterns or moving patterns. We propose a different paradigm for understanding amblyopia--we propose that amblyopia involves the selective integration of information from the two eyes, a process we call adaptive compensation. The process is adaptive because it requires suppression to be modulated by the specific stimuli present in a given scene, and compensatory because it seeks to make up for vision lost in the amblyopic eye. The adaptive compensatory model explains many features of amblyopia and makes important predictions as to how vision in amblyopia can be improved through training.

column36: Microvascular injury and blood-brain barrier dysfunction as novel biomarkers and targets for treatment in traumatic brain injury
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability around the world. While long-term neurological and cognitive complications and disability are a major concern,to this date there are no means to accurately predict such complications nor therapies for their prevention. An emerging consensus points to the critical importance of including new means for the identification of brain pathological events in order to allow efficient prevention. In this proposal we address this unmet need by investigating traumatic microvascular injury (TMI), an established but understudied TBI pathology with a potential as a candidate diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is a prominent feature of TMI and often obtained in animal TBI models as well as in human pathological specimens. The BBB is a unique structural and functional barrier allowing the normal function of the nervous system. Our previous studies confirmed a direct role for BBB pathology in inducing brain dysfunction and damage. The goals of this research are (1) to test a new imaging approach to detect, localize, and track BBB pathology in animal models of TBI; (2) to test new therapeutics that target TMI and follow BBB pathology; and (3) implement a similar imaging approach in humans to evaluate the prevalence and spatio-temporal dynamics of BBB pathology in human subjects after acute TBI. We strongly believe that the proposed pre-clinical and translational approach will result in the first objective,quantitative and reliable diagnostic approach for the identification of TMI.

Our results will allow governing agencies to better assess the amount of protein provide by CG in the diet to meet the needs of the world's population. column36: Ketone-Mediated Epigenetic Modulation of Mitochondrial Function in Epileptic Brain
column37: Epilepsy is a common neurological problem affecting approximately 1% of the general population. While current medical treatments are effective in two-thirds of patients, there are associated short-term and long-term side-effects of drugs that pose potentially serious health risks. Moreover, the remaining third of patients with epilepsy continue to have seizures that impair quality of life and increase the risk of brain damage and even sudden unexpected death. Hence, there is an urgent need to identify new treatments that can both increase effectiveness, but also minimize undesired side-effects. A remarkable non-drug treatment for difficult-to-control epilepsy is the ketogenic diet, a high-fat and low-carbohydrate regimen that often works when medications fail. While we do not yet fully understand how this diet works, there is increasing evidence that ketone bodies - chemicals produced by the liver as a result of this diet - may be critical players. Specifically, we hypothesize that ketone bodies produce beneficial changes within the energy factories of cells (called "mitochondria") that prevent both seizures and cell death. Our preliminary studies indicate that ketone bodies increase the activity of a specific enzyme family known Sirt3 (i.e., sirtuin 3) and that these enzymes alter the chemical structure of an important protein within the mitochondria called cyclophilin D (or CypD) which helps determine whether cells live or die. The major goal of the proposed studies is to identify the precise mechanism of how ketone bodies produce anti-seizure effects, and in so doing highlight novel targets within mitochondria that can be exploited for the development of better treatments for medically intractable epilepsy. Specific experiments will be conducted to show that the hypothesized mechanism is relevant to multiple types of epilepsy in laboratory models, a necessary step before new treatments emerging from this research can be tested in humans.

column36: Regulation of Neutrophil (PMN) Inflammatory Function by Caspase-8 Phosphorylation
column37: With the widespread availability of antibiotics to kill bacteria, and of intensive care units (ICUs) to support patients with otherwise life-threatening vital organ failure, the major threat to survival for critically ill patients is the adverse effects of the immune response to infection; this deleterious host defense process is called sepsis. Circulating white blood cells called neutrophils (PMNs) play a key role in both the initial response to infection and in the lethal organ injury that results from that response. PMN activity - both beneficial and detrimental - is critically impacted by the capacity of the PMN to undergo cellular suicide through a process called apoptosis. My laboratory has found that the ability of the PMN to undergo apoptosis is regulated by subtle and inducible changes in caspase-8, the enzyme responsible for initiating apoptosis. The simple addition of a phosphate molecule to caspase-8 transforms its function from pro-to anti-apoptotic, and results in the activation of pro-survival and pro-inflammatory mechanisms in the PMN. Our work seeks to understand how this process, known as phosphorylation, is regulated, and how it might be targeted to improve the survival of patients with sepsis. We will first determine the role played by caspase-8 phosphorylation in the initial response of PMN to bacteria and their products. We will then study the mechanisms that support or block the phosphorylation of caspase-8. Finally we will determine how these changes impact key elements of PMN function. Our studies will use PMN from critically ill septic patients to understand mechanisms, and experimental models in zebrafish and mice to study the consequences of modifying the caspase-8 phosphorylation state. In aggregate they will both shed light on a novel mechanism involved in the regulation of inflammation, and provide a rational basis for treatments for sepsis based on accelerating the resolution of inflammation.

column36: Time-Lapse Quantification of Protein Synthesis in Single Cells In Vivo
column37: Protein molecules are what are created when genetic information is translated into a real world molecular actor that can affect change within a cell. Too much or too little of a protein can harm a cell and lead to diseases such as cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, or autism spectrum disorders. Unfortunately, little is known about how the production of proteins within a cell changes over time and in response to external factors. For example, when a brain cell learns something new, how does the production of specific proteins change? How fast does this happen? Where in the cell does this happen? To answer these questions, our project will track and measure protein production in single cells in the living animal to watch in real time how it changes and under different conditions. We will use cutting-edge molecular genetics and imaging techniques to tag and watch these molecular events. These experiments will give us unprecedented insight into the inner workings of the most important and final step when a gene is translated into action. Accomplishing this will allow us to understand what happens when protein production goes wrong in a disease state, and what the outcome for the cell is. This will give researchers more accurate targets and knowledge for interventions and therapies for these diseases.

column36: Carotid body potentiation in sleep apnea: identification of novel causes and solutions
column37: Sleep apnea is a serious respiratory disease affecting millions of Canadians. Medical devices for the treatment of sleep apnea continue to improve. However, the ability to comply with device-based treatments over long periods remains mixed. Sensory organs in the neck, the carotid bodies, are likely critical to the pathology of sleep apnea. When breathing is insufficient to supply enough oxygen to the body, these organs tell the brain to increase breathing and deliver more blood to tissues; when the reverse is true, they tell the brain to reduce or stop breathing. Usually, oxygen and carbon dioxide are tightly regulated, but in sleep apnea the carotid bodies become sensitized. This leads to exaggerated breathing responses to changes in oxygenation, destabilizing breathing and causing high blood pressure. Important questions regarding the treatment of sleep apnea patients are thus, why are the carotid bodies sensitized, and how can this be reversed? This proposal addresses both questions with the aim to identify novel and/or repurpose existing drugs to treat sleep apnea. Our preliminary data identify novel mechanisms of carotid body sensitization caused by fluctuating oxygenation and signalling molecules resulting from inflammation, both associated with respiratory disease. In addition, our data suggest that the effects of these mechanisms on carotid body activity can be reversed by somatostatin. This is significant because somatostatin analogues are already approved for treatment of acromegaly, circumventing the most expensive and time-consuming drug development stages. We propose to confirm the above data, investigate receptors involved, and test if somatostatin analogues can be used to treat sleep apnea. This project will help us understand carotid body function and its involvement in respiratory disease. Importantly, this project will also test feasibility of repurposing clinically-approved somatostatin analogues while identifying new targets for drug discovery.
