column36: Defining Activated Stromal Signatures and Targeting the Tumour Microenvironment of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most aggressive malignancies with a 5-year survival of < 5%. Interestingly, these tumours contain a large stromal component that can comprise up to 90% of the tumour. The tumour-associated stroma provides a microenvironment to support tumour growth and progression, and has been shown to significantly hamper effective treatment of these cancers. It has been shown that the stroma may have some protective benefits, therefore complete stromal depletion may be detrimental. There is a need to identify whether more specific stromal depletion or modulation methods are possible, with the goal of improving drug delivery and improving patient survival. The PDAC-associated stroma is hypothesized to derive from pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs), which represent tissue resident mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). During our studies related to PSC biology, we have discovered a cellular program that appears to be important in regulating PSC activation and cell-cycle entry. The overall objective of this project is to utilize novel mouse models to identify key genes expressed in the tumour stroma- specifically in the PSCs. Novel therapeutic targets will be validated in a large cohort of well-annotated patient specimens, and druggable targets will be prioritized utilizing in vitro culture systems and a collection of patient-derived mouse models (xenografts). Collectively, this research plan will allow us to answer several questions regarding the contribution and fate of activated PSCs in the pancreas, and will enable us to identify novel mechanisms and rational therapeutic combinations for modulating the activated stroma in pancreatic cancer.

column36: A virtual reality and field training toolkit to enhance community ambulation and participation in stroke survivors
column37: Mobility problems are very common after a stroke. Only 50% of stroke survivors manage to walk in the community (eg. ambulating in local stores or shopping malls) at the end of the rehabilitation process, with two-thirds presenting limitations that necessitate assistance or supervision. We believe that this ability to ambulate in the community can be enhanced with a rehabilitation intervention targeting intensive and repeated practice of important skills required for functional community ambulation (e.g. speeding up, walking longer distances, avoiding pedestrians, recalling shopping items while walking, etc.). We thus propose to develop a new intervention combining virtual reality (VR) with field training (FT) to enhance functional walking and participation to community walking in persons with stroke discharged from rehabilitation. The project comprises of three phases. In Phase 1, we will develop the combined VR and FT intervention and use the feedback of persons with stroke and clinicians to refine it. In Phase 2, persons with stroke with different levels of ability (in terms of walking, visual perception and cognition) will engage in a 4-week training program that consists of VR training in the clinic and the practice of community ambulation skills in the community. Functional walking, balance & mobility and participation to community walking will be measured twice before the intervention, right after the intervention and at a 1-month follow-up. Adherence, safety and acceptability will be documented. In Phase 3, instructional materials concerning the intervention will be developed and validated using clinicians' feedback. The unique rehabilitation toolkit that will be developed and tested in this project will provide an opportunity for stroke survivors to practice the different skills that are essential for community ambulation. The combination of VR and FT training should further optimize the transfer of skills practiced in VR setting to the real world.

column36: Individually- and Environmentally-Targeted Interventions to Improve Healthy Eating and Physical Activity across Urban Contexts: Implementation Considerations
column37: Cardiovascular diseases, cancer, and mental health issues are among the major causes of morbidity and mortality in Canada and create a heavy burden on individuals and society. Many cases could be prevented if a greater number of Canadians adopted healthy eating and physical activity. Existing research shows that health promotion programs aimed at individuals and transformations of built and social environments could help Canadians adopt more healthy lifestyles if implemented jointly. In order to implement health promotion programs and transformations of built environments to promote healthy eating and physical activity, public health officials, governments, and their partners require a keen understanding of their potential reach and acceptability by populations. Right now however, little is known about how willing populations are to participating in health promotion programs. Further, it is unclear to what extent populations are supportive of changes to the built and social environments that might make healthy eating and physical activity easier lifestyle choices. We propose to conduct surveys of adults living in the 21 largest urban areas in Canada in order to discover the potential reach of health promotion programs, to learn more about the acceptability of transforming local built and social environments, and to understand how potential reach and acceptability are associated with different socioeconomic and health characteristics. The survey data will be linked to geographic information about the services and amenities available in the vicinity of the survey participants' homes and workplaces. This will allow the team to better understand where to invest in unfolding health promotion programs, where to mobilize communities about healthy lifestyle issues, and what issues require advocacy on the part of public health officials. We plan extensive dissemination activities to share the information with public health officials and the public in general.

column36: A genome-wide search for exonic variants affecting translational efficiency
column37: Susceptibility or resistance to most common diseases is determined by the type of genes we inherit in our parent's DNA. The DNA is 99.9% identical between any two unrelated individuals and it is the 0.1% that determines differences between individuals. These inherited small variants modify the DNA, the blueprint that determines how our body is built and how it functions. The DNA encodes proteins, the building blocks of the body. The variants sometimes change the protein itself but, more often, what varies among individuals is how much of the protein will be expressed, when and under what stimulus. This is done in many cases by modulating transcription of DNA into RNA. RNA carries the DNA instructions to the ribosomes, the cell's protein-production factory. In 1997, our lab discovered one of the first such effects, of a variant of the insulin gene in type 1 diabetes and now thousands of such effects are known. A much less-well studied level at which genetic variants can determine protein production is the translation of RNA variants into protein. Proteins are much harder to study than RNA but we have developed a method that quantifies how much RNA is associated with ribosomes as an indirect but powerful way of identify proteins whose production is affected by variants in the RNA sequence, and validated it in a small number of subjects. We now propose to apply this method to a much larger sample of individuals to discover all common variants that affect association of RNA with ribosomes. The method will then be validated by using targeted protein quantification using targeted methods of modern proteomics. Significance: Thousands of variants are known to affect susceptibility to various diseases but, to translate this into understanding of disease and therapeutic targets, we need to define the mechanism of the genetic effect.

column36: Preventing cognitive and functional decline among seniors at risk: A community-based randomized controlled trial.
column37: The proposed project explores the effectiveness of Real-World Strategy Training (RWST), an individualized intervention designed to promote independence in everyday life, on older adults who identify cognitive complaints. Evidence suggests that 25-50% of community-dwelling older adults report cognitive difficulties, such as reduced memory or concentration, in the absence of any diagnosed condition. Cognitive skills are crucial to living independently and performing activities of daily life such as managing finances, medications and schedules. Adults who report cognitive complaints have an elevated risk of later experiencing more significant cognitive and functional decline, including dementia. With our growing aging population this represents a significant public health issue and signifies an urgent need for interventions that delay or even reverse cognitive difficulties. To date, many interventions have been proposed to reduce cognitive decline, including cognitive training programs and physical activity programs, but there is limited evidence that the skills learned are transferred to other aspects of everyday life - we cannot be sure they improve everyday independence. We plan to examine RWST in a randomized controlled trial. Based on our successful pilot study, we hypothesize that this training, which combines education on healthy lifestyles and problem solving training to address everyday life difficulties, will be effective in improving and maintaining independence for older adults.

column36: Nucleic acid-binding ligands as modulators of repeat instability for therapeutic benefit against neurological and neuromuscular diseases.
column37: 40 neuromuscular/neurodegenerative diseases are inherited where symptoms become more evident through family generations and become worse as individuals age. These diseases are caused by mutations in repeated DNAs. If one considers a gene as though it were a sentence such as THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT, typical mutations would be spelling errors, like THE GAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT. This mutation would be the same in all family members, all with the same symptoms. In repeat diseases the mutation would be THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT, and their children would inherit a further mutation; THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT and have more severe disease than their parents. These mutations continue as the patient ages, in affected tissues; progressively getting larger making symptoms worse as they age. This project focuses on modulating this mutation to treat affected families. Being able to arrest or reverse this repeat mutation represents a therapeutic pathway to reduce disease progression and severity. Over the past two years, we collected a variety of compounds able to bind the mutated sequence, or the structures that this sequence can form. We will screen this pre-selected library of compounds for their capacity to modulate repeat instability, highlighting therapeutic treatments by arresting or reversing the expansion mutations (THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT down to THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT).

column36: Role of Wnt Signaling in Cardiac Arrhythmogenesis
column37: Cardiac arrhythmias (irregular heart beats) affect over one million Canadians and are a major health issue in the country. Up to 50% of deaths in patients with heart failure, a condition affecting 600,000 Canadians, are attributed to cardiac arrhythmias. Current anti-arrhythmic drugs are not effective in most patients and limited by their toxicities. Therefore, novel, more effective therapies are critically needed for better management of cardiac arrhythmias. Ion channels are proteins on heart cell membrane and determine the rhythm of heart beats. Cardiac arrhythmias are mostly caused by reduced ion channel levels. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms for ion channel reduction in heart disease would allow the design of novel therapies to restore normal ion channel expression and transform the management of arrhythmogenic heart disease. The Applicant, Dr. Liang, recently (2015) made the important discovery that a specific cell signaling pathway (Wnt signaling, which is activated in heart disease) causes changes in ion channels that underlie arrhythmias. The proposed research will enable Dr. Liang's team to gain further insights into the novel role of Wnt signaling in the dysregulation of ion channels and abnormal rhythm of the diseased heart, and to explore new avenues for therapy. The establishment of this project, with the CIHR support, will potentially improve outcomes for over one million Canadians affected by cardiac arrhythmias, as well as reduce health care costs and increase industry and job opportunities in Canada.

column36: Molecular pathology of SLC25A46, a degenerate mitochondrial carrier protein causing early onset neurodegenerative disease
column37: All cells in the body require a steady source of chemical energy to carry out their normal physiological functions. The majority of this chemical energy, which is packaged as a compound called ATP, is produced by the oxidation of carbohydrate and fat in a biochemical process called oxidative phosphorylation. This process takes place in a compartment of the cell called the mitochondrion, and is carried out by several large protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Respiratory chain dysfunction interferes with the normal supply of energy, and this produces a wide variety of different diseases, the nature and severity of which depend on the exact genetic defect. The genetics of respiratory chain diseases is complicated by the fact that some components of the system are encoded in nuclear genes, others in a small genome that is contained within the mitochondria themselves. Diseases caused by nuclear gene defects generally produce the most severe phenotypes (neurodegeneration, heart or liver failure) with onset at birth or during early infancy, and are usually fatal. One of the most common clinical presentations of mitochondrial disease in infants is called Leigh Syndrome. This is a severe neurodegenerative disease that nearly always fatal in early life and for which there is no treatment. This proposal is aimed at investigating the mechanism by which a mutation in a gene that codes for a protein that is a member of the family of proteins that normally transport metabolites into mitochondria causes the disease. Characterization of the function of the genes in which we identify mutations provides biological insight into the normal assembly and function of the respiratory chain, and this we hope will ultimately permit us to devise treatments for these devastating disorders.

column36: The distinctive neuropathology underlying abnormal cognitive decline in remotely concussed former athletes
column37: The annual prevalence of sports concussion has reached epidemic proportions, making any long-term consequence of the injury sizeable in both human and economic terms. Important questions regarding susceptibility and resistance to the long term effects of sports concussion and precisely what they are and how they evolve atop the dynamic substrate of the brain abound. Any discussion of these downstream consequences inevitably leads to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the neurodegenerative disease that is widely believed to be the signature pathology of injuries involving recurrent blows to the head occurring during the practice of contact sports. However, from a scientific standpoint, there are several important gaps in what is known about CTE, making causal links premature to say the least. Typically, when a new disease/pathology is discovered, the natural progression is to move toward prospective research designs where covariates are accounted for. The current research program proposes a longitudinal investigation aiming to assess the predictive value of in vivo markers of neurodegeneration in the rate of progression and specificity of cognitive/behavioral decline in remotely concussed former athletes. This proposal aims to establish the distinctive neuropathology underlying abnormal cognitive functioning in remotely concussed former athletes. Knowing about the signature pathology of the long term effects of concussion will ultimately help us design optimal treatment and prevention strategies aiming to maintain/restore the quality of life of millions of former athletes with a history of remote concussions.

column36: Developing Longitudinal Indicators for Population-Scale Monitoring of Health Care Trajectories
column37: Health system managers track the health of Canadians using health indicators; one example of an indicator is the number of people admitted to hospital with COPD (a severe lung condition). Although the COPD admission indicator can identify hospitals or regions with more admissions than average, it does not help us understand why or, more importantly, what can be done to prevent those admissions. Many cases of severe illness can be traced back to a lack of appropriate and ongoing follow-up health care. To help understand the long-term causes of severe and preventable illness, we need to understand not only how many patients have severe illness, but also what their "care path" or "trajectory" was before they ended up with severe illness. Clinical governance organizations, such as the INESSS in Quebec, have made it a strategic priority to monitor patient trajectories. Until recently, it was very difficult and costly to collect the patient data from paper-based records, making it impossible to efficiently track patient trajectories. With the advent of electronic health records, we can now collect patient data automatically. The patient data is still, however, very complex; to identify patient trajectories automatically, we need new statistical methods. In this project, we propose to develop new statistical methods to identify patient trajectories and improve the care of COPD patients. Specifically, we aim: 1. To develop the statistical methods to cluster patients into health care trajectories; 2. To explain population-level variations in trajectories; 3. To optimize clinical care strategies by using health care trajectories for dynamic treatment decisions. Our team includes experts in informatics (Buckeridge, Verma), statistics (Stephens, Luo), clinical care (Bourbeau), and health system governance (Candas). The research activities in this project will be directly translated into practice through our partner at INESSS (Roy).

column36: Molecular characterization of radiation induced meningiomas
column37: The most common type of childhood cancer is leukemia and brain tumors, specifically glioma and medulloblastoma. These conditions often require cranial radiation to cure children afflicted with these cancers. While effective, cranial irradiation has long-term negative consequences, amongst which is the formation of radiation-induced meningiomas (RIMs). Meningiomas are brain tumors caused by over growth of the covering of the brain called the meninges. After radiation in childhood, these tumors appear many years later in adult life and will require surgery and not infrequently repeat surgical intervention given their multiplicity. Why such tumors form as a consequence of childhood radiation is not known. We also have a limited understanding in how radiation induced meningiomas compare to aggressive malignant meningiomas and in this project we will compare the molecular profile of sporadic malignant meningiomas to radiation induced meningiomas. Understanding the biology of radiation-induced meningiomas is important for identifying therapeutic targets and prevention of these tumours, but more importantly this proposal may shed light on the bigger picture of molecular alterations that occur in the brain in response to radiation therapy. Overall knowledge gained from this project will inform on the molecular signature of meningiomas that have an aggressive clinical behaviour, have the potential to shed light on the molecular alterations that are induced by radiation on the brain and identify possible mechanisms to mitigate the negative side effects of cranial radiation.

column36: Systems biology of cell size homeostasis
column37: A central and longstanding problem in biology and biomedicine is the deceptively simple question: how do cells establish and maintain the constant size that is characteristic of each tissue in the body? Despite the study of this problem for over 100 years, we still do not understand how cells determine their size. Complex networks of molecular interactions ensure that the many trillions of cells that make up our bodies divide at the appropriate time. This "decision to divide" depends on the growth of cells to an appropriate size, termed the cell size threshold. The threshold appears to operate in all eukaryotic species, from yeast to humans. We have used the simple single-celled yeast as model to identify hundreds of genes that control size. We have found that the machinery that produces the proteins in the cell (the ribosome), the organelle that produces energy for the cell (the mitochondrion), the organelle that degrades and recycles cellular components (the vacuole) and the system that generates membranes and secretes proteins (the endoplasmic reticulum) are all critical regulators of cell size. However, it is not known how all these processes are coupled to the division machinery to set the size threshold. We will now use systematic functional genomic approaches to investigate how these size control networks operate in yeast as a simple model, and we will use this knowledge and advanced genetic and biochemical methods to decipher how the analogous processes work in human cells. The coupling between cell growth and cell division goes awry in many human diseases including diabetes, mitochondrial disorders, cancer and aging. Once we understand growth and division, we will be in a position to devise means to identify and ultimately correct the defects that underlie these and other diseases.

column36: Selective imaging of matrix metalloproteinase-13 to identify vulnerable plaques in atherosclerosis
column37: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Canada and worldwide and also includes chronic diseases such as heart failure and atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is a disease of the arteries that remains asymptomatic over its development, but can lead to severe conditions such as ischemia, and complications including heart attack and stroke. These occur when plaques formed in the arteries, containing unstable deposits of lipids and cholesterol, become inflamed and rupture, giving rise to a thrombus or blood clot. Currently, it is difficult to detect and accurately predict plaque instability and rupture and it is therefore challenging to identify patients in need of treatment before a serious cardiovascular event. The goal of this project is to develop a molecular-targeted imaging probe that will be useful for specifically identifying vulnerable plaque burden at high risk for rupture to better inform and guide physicians and patients in need of intervention. This probe will allow us to quantitatively measure the density of enzymes that degrade the fibrous cap of atherosclerotic plaques and contribute to their destabilization and increase the likelihood of rupture and thrombus formation. In addition to diagnosis, the probe to be developed could be used to assist in development of therapies targeting these enzymes and to monitor patient response to treatment.

column36: High resolution profiling of phosphoproteome dynamics in normal and mutant cells defective in mitotic kinase activity
column37: Most physiological processes in cells are regulated by enzymes known as protein kinases. These enzymes act by adding a small negative charge on proteins, a phosphate group. A large fraction of cancers are caused by misregulation of protein kinases. We propose to study the role of two families of protein kinase known as Polo-like kinases (PLKs) and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which are strongly associated with cancer development in humans. We have developed a novel way to precisely modulate the activity of CDK and PLK in living cells. This will allow us to identify all the proteins that CDK and PLK modify by phosphate addition during the process of cell division. We will perform this experiment at very high temporal resolution -in the scale of minutes- while cells divide to determine which proteins are favourite targets of CDK and PLK, and which ones are low priority targets for these kinases. We will achieve this objective by using a combination of genetic and biochemical experiments in a model organism. Ultimately, this project will identify which targets of CDK and PLK are more crucial for the process of cell division, and how misregulation of these "high priority" targets can lead to cell division errors and cancer formation.

column36: A New Mechanism Regulating Synapse Function in the Brain
column37: The day to day function of the nervous system depends on the ability of nerve cells to communicate with each other. Neuron-to-neuron communication is possible through synapses, highly specialized structures that allow transfer of information from one cell to another. Synapses are constantly changing and they are dramatically altered in neurodegenerative diseases. A long-term focus of my research program is to understand how synapses are formed, how they change and how they can be maintained in the aging and injured brain. We recently discovered that a family of proteins named netrins is essential for synapse formation during development. Importantly, we also found that netrins are made in the adult brain and play a crucial role regulating memory. Exciting new studies in humans have identified mutations in the genes encoding netrins and netrin receptors in individuals affected by Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings open up the possibility of recovering neuronal function, learning and memory through the modulation of netrin activity. A major roadblock towards this goal is that very little is known about how netrins work in the adult nervous system. To gain an in-depth understanding of how netrins promote synapse function and modulate communication between neurons in the aging and diseased brain, we will identify the consequences of genetic deletion of netrin-1 from neurons in the mouse brain. We will determine if neuronal activity regulates the function of netrin at synapses, and investigate the contribution of these mechanisms to deficits associated with early stages of Alzheimer's disease. My laboratory has developed experimental tools and animal models that place us in a unique position to make groundbreaking discoveries. The proposed studies will create new knowledge of how synapses are maintained and modified and will identify therapeutic targets to prevent loss of function in aging and disease.

column36: Environment-specific maternal genetic effects in orofacial clefts
column37: Cleft lip and cleft palate are birth defects that occur when a baby's lip or mouth do not form properly. These orofacial clefts are among the most common birth defects worldwide. column36: Investigate The Role Of mRNP Structure In Translation And RNA Metabolism
column37: In all living organisms, the genetic information stored in DNA is copied into mRNA molecules before translated into proteins, the functional molecules the perform most cellular functions. The flow of information from DNA to RNA and proteins is termed the gene expression pathway and regulating the expression of its genes is an essential task for all cells. Mis-regulation, for instance by mutations in factors acting along the gene expression pathway, results in various pathologies, including cancer predisposition, development and progression and a multitude of neurological disorders. RNA has a central molecule of this process, and consists of a copy of an DNA sequence, forming a long polymer of several hundreds to several thousand nucleotides in length. However, RNA does not exist as a linear molecule but is packaged into a 3D assembly with the help of proteins that bind to RNA. The structural organization of the RNA-protein complexes influences many aspects of what happens with an RNA in cells, including whether an RNA is translated into proteins. For example, the two extremities for an RNA have to be in close proximity to allow translation. Inhibiting this interaction inhibits translation of many RNAs and reduces cell growth, and drugs interfering with this process are used as anti-cancer drugs. Understanding how the cell assures the communication between different regions of these long RNA molecules, however is not understood. Furthermore, in general, we completely lack understanding on the structural organization of the RNA polymer. In this project, we will determine how mRNA molecules are organized and how the binding of proteins to the RNA changes the 3D organization of mRNA molecules. This will reveal important insight into the role of mRNP conformation in regulating translation, sensitivity to anti-cancer drugs and RNA metabolism in general, which, in turn, will allow the development of better tools for diagnosis and treatment.

column36: The PREvention Program for Alzheimer's RElated Delirium (PREPARED) Cluster Randomized Trial
column37: By the year 2038, over a million Canadians are expected to have Alzheimer's disease, a type of dementia. Dementia increases the risk of nursing home placement among the elderly more than fivefold. Given the exceptionally vulnerable nature of this patient population, there is a pressing need to ensure that the clinical care they receive is evidence-based, tailored specifically for them, and meeting the high standards of quality that would be expected in any other health-care setting. Delirium is a sudden and severe change in brain function that can cause a person to appear confused or disoriented, have memory loss, and have difficulties maintaining focus. It is an urgent care issue facing elderly patients residing in nursing homes, or long-term care (LTC) facilities. Delirium is a significant cause of illness and mortality, affecting between 10%-89% of LTC patients, but little research has focused on delirium prevention in the LTC setting. This study will assess the effectiveness of a LTC Multicomponent Delirium Prevention Program (MDPP). The MDPP is an educational intervention provided to nursing staff working in LTC facilities that consists of four components: a decision tree, an instruction manual, a training package, and a toolkit. The feasibility and acceptability of the MDPP has already been successfully demonstrated; however, a thorough and well-designed large scale study is needed in order to confirm its ability to reduce delirium among LTC residents. In this study, at least 16 LTC facilities will be randomized to either receive the MDPP or to receive usual care. At the end of the 4-year study period, we will be able to demonstrate the degree to which the MDPP intervention reduces: 1) the number of new cases of delirium; 2) delirium severity; and 3) the duration of delirium episodes. This study will provide the blueprint of a program that can be transferable to LTC institutions across Canada.

column36: Accuracy and generalizability of using automated methods for identifying adverse events from electronic health record data
column37: Adverse events (AEs) are injuries caused by medical management rather than by the underlying condition of the patient. AEs are estimated to occur in 2.9% to 16.6% of all acute care hospitalizations, and studies have suggested that 30% to 58% of all AEs are preventable. Preventable AEs are a leading cause of death, resulting in 44,000 to 98,000 deaths each year. AEs are also very costly, with total annual costs estimated to range between USD $17 and $29 billion. For these reasons, preventing AEs is a high priority in acute care hospitals worldwide. An important requirement to evaluate the success of preventive measures is to have access to accurate, timely and efficient methods for monitoring AE rates. Moreover, with the growing emphasis on benchmarking and public reporting of AE data, these methods must also allow for valid inter-institutional comparisons. However, at present, there are no such methods. With the advent of electronic health records (EHR), and the development of automated methods for encoding and classifying EHR data, there is an exciting opportunity to identify potentially better methods of AE detection and monitoring. Taking advantage of this new opportunity, the objective of this research project is to assess the accuracy and the generalizability of using automated methods for detecting three of the most common AEs affecting hospitalized patients: 1) hospital-acquired pneumonia, 2) ventilator-associated events and, 3) central line-associated bloodstream infection. It is expected that this research project will result in more accurate and efficient measures of AEs. These measures could be used to assess the incidence rates of AEs, evaluate the success of interventions aimed at improving patient safety, and track progresses in patient safety through time. Lastly, automation has a strong potential to standardize AE monitoring, both within and across institutions, which is an important prerequisite to valid public reporting of AE data and benchmarking.

column36: Understanding the treatment benefits of novel antiviral agents for hepatitis C: quality of life, health utility, cost, and return to work
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) has been identified as having the highest health burden of any infectious disease pathogen. Direct-acting antiviral agents (DAAs) are new drugs that offer the promise of cure and substantially improved tolerability. Because of the expense of these DAAs, and the large number of untreated people, access to DAAs is arguably the most challenging drug reimbursement problem in developed countries in 2016. A critical, but missing, part of the evidence required to formulate HCV treatment policy relates to patient perspectives. We propose to measure the patient burden of HCV. Measuring patient burden involves measuring health related quality of life, the effect of HCV on workplace productivity, and costs to patients. We will interview two groups of patients in two hospitals and two community clinics in Calgary, Toronto and Montreal. The two groups of patients include patients who are being treated with one of the new drugs, and patients who have late-stage Chronic hepatitis C (CHC). Patients will fill out questionnaires and answer questions about their quality of life, out-of-pocket costs, and time they spend on CHC treatment. We will use these results to determine the costs and benefits (cost-effectiveness) of the new drugs in patients with CHC, and to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of screening people in Canada for CHC. The information from our study will play a critical role in determining whether new drugs are offered to patients with CHC. It will be used by a national agency and provincial drug formularies to guide these critical and expensive decisions. The results of our study will also play a critical role in guiding decisions around CHC screening.

column36: Global Vaccine Logics
column37: The West African Ebola outbreak exposed the need to better understand the various factors that influence the acceptance of emergency interventions, and the importance of their alignment with the priorities of national governments and local communities in low and middle income countries (LMIC). Distrust and uncertainty about the safety of medicines and vaccines continues to challenge effective immunization and public health strategies. This translational research will explore two major Canadian contributions, the mobile lab response units and the successful Ebola vaccine effectiveness trial in Guinea. The interactions between diverse rationales and practices (logics) of global, national and local communities surrounding these critical events will be explored to develop an analytical decision-making framework that will aid future interventions. Working collaboratively with the World Health Organization, national government officials, scientists and community health workers, this research will produce a framework to guide national decision-makers in the integration and evaluation of evidence from diverse knowledge holders. Clinical-scientists, health officials, governments, industry, international organizations, and citizens will utilize our framework to plan, select and implement health interventions that effectively engage local community health workers in disease detection, surveillance and future response. Grounded in the qualitative perspectives of anthropology, science studies, technology assessment and humanitarian practice and in conjunction with clinical science, this framework will feature the knowledge that reflects local context needs, regional priorities, and scientific capabilities and limitations. This study will help strengthen LMIC health systems by creating a universal integrated platform for research, emergency response training and preparedness for future disease outbreaks.

column36: A Randomized Trial of Regional Radiotherapy in Luminal A Breast Cancer
column37: Studies have shown that radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes following mastectomy and radiotherapy to regional nodes after breast conserving surgery reduces the risk of recurrence and breast cancer mortality in women with node positive breast cancer. While these benefits are important, it is recognized that there is a large group of patients with node positive breast cancer who are unlikely to recur or benefit from radiotherapy. Biomarkers are increasingly used to identify breast cancers that are likely to recur or respond to treatment. The luminal A breast cancer subtype has a low risk of recurrence and is less likely to respond to chemotherapy. Recent evidence from MA.20 a randomized trial of radiotherapy to the regional nodes supports that such cancers were less likely to respond to radiotherapy. This suggests that regional radiotherapy may not be necessary in patients with node positive luminal A breast cancer. The objective of this study is to determine if radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional lymph nodes following mastectomy or radiotherapy to the regional nodes following breast conserving surgery can be safely omitted in women with 1-3 positive axillary lymph nodes and luminal A cancer. An international multicentre randomized trial will be performed. Patients treated by mastectomy will be randomized to radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes or not. Patients treated by breast conserving surgery will be randomized to radiotherapy to regional nodes or not. Radiation following surgery is associated with significant short-term and long-term side effects. The luminal A subtype of breast cancer accounts for up to 40% of patients with node positive breast cancer. If regional radiotherapy could be avoided in this group of patients it would have substantial benefits not only for women with breast cancer and their families, but the health care system at large.

column36: Regulation of TGF-beta action in chondrocytes: signaling via ALK1 versus ALK5 pathways
column37: Arthritis refers to several related conditions that affect joints, causing pain, inflammation and swelling. Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and occurs when there is damage in and around the joints, which the body cannot repair. Currently there is no cure for OA and its progression significantly affects an individual's quality of life. OA affects nearly 4.6 million Canadians and is expected to increase to about 7.5 million by 2036. Despite much research effort, the causes and factors involved in OA are not fully understood. Transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta is a protein made in many tissues of the body and there is ample evidence to indicate that its abnormal action in cartilage is involved in the OA disease process. Our research has shown that TGF-beta can have both beneficial and harmful effects on cartilage cells (chondrocytes) depending on the type of "receptor" it uses. In particular, we have shown that TGF-beta will promote healthy cartilage by acting through one type of chondrocytes receptor (known as ALK5) but gives rise to OA-like features when acting through another receptor (ALK1). We have also shown that certain molecules such as TGF-beta co-receptors can influence whether TGF-beta acts through ALK5 or ALK1 receptor. Thus we will examine the role of two co-receptors called endoglin and CD109 in regulating the activity of ALK5 and ALK1. Our goal will be to unravel the mechanism involved in the abnormal action of TGF-beta in chondrocytes and to manipulate the activity of proteins (such as ALK1 and co-receptors) to regulate TGF-beta action, in order to promote cartilage repair. The experiments will be performed using cell and animal models of OA. We expect that findings from the proposed research may lead to the development of innovative therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this debilitating disease.

column36: Caracterisation et representations de l'accessibilite physique aux jeux de hasard et d'argent au Quebec: un outil pour la prise de decision et la creation d'environnements favorables.
column37: La pratique des jeux de hasard et d'argent peut engendrer des problemes de sante pour les joueurs et leurs proches. Au Quebec, plusieurs recherches ont demontre que l'offre de jeu etait plus importante dans les quartiers defavorises et que cela contribuait a generer un environnement moins favorable a la sante de la population. Officiellement, aucun critere sanitaire n'est pris en compte pour configurer l'offre de jeu au Quebec. Dans ce contexte, un portrait a jour et une analyse de l'accessibilite physique au jeu au Quebec sont necessaires afin de soutenir la creation d'environnements favorables a la sante des populations. La presente etude a ete concue pour repondre a ce besoin de connaissances. Ce projet vise a : 1-Realiser une revue de litterature mettant a jour les connaissances sur l'influence des milieux de vie sur la sante et sur les liens entre les environnements de jeu, la defavorisation et les prejudices lies au jeu. 2-Dresser un portrait de l'accessibilite physique de l'offre de jeu au Quebec qui rende compte des niveaux de defavorisation et des impacts du jeu par secteur geographique. La realisation d'une cartographie et son analyse seront les methodes utilisees pour y parvenir. 3-Realiser des entrevues aupres de joueurs pour comprendre comment l'offre de jeu presente dans leur milieu de vie agit sur leur parcours et habitudes de jeu. 4-Elaborer des recommandations et valider leur pertinence et leur faisabilite aupres d'experts et de decideurs des domaines concernes. Les resultats fourniront des indicateurs indispensables a la prise de decision sur le deploiement de l'offre de jeu et la creation d'environnements plus favorables a la sante. En matiere de prevention, les resultats permettront d'identifier des zones geographiques sensibles au Quebec et d'y developper des initiatives preventives mieux adaptees. La specification des declencheurs de jeu est aussi susceptible d'orienter les interventions dans les services de traitement du jeu problematique

column36: Characterization of the TGFbeta microRNAome - implications for new biomarkers and therapeutic targets in human cancer
column37: Proteins are synthesized as a result of gene expression and play a critical role in maintaining normal cell function. When expression of proteins is deregulated, diseases such as cancer can arise. We focus on the action of microRNAs (miRNAs), which are micromolecules naturally synthesized by the body and capable of regulating the production of a large proportion of proteins. MicroRNAs are interesting because given the nature of their structure, they are easy to synthesize in a laboratory setting and non-toxic to cells, hence offer a valuable therapeutic option. TGFB is a growth factor capable of promoting or inhibiting critical miRNAs. Indeed, we found that when we expose a cell to TGFB, the expression of these miRNAs changes, and that as a consequence, the expression pattern of proteins within the cell will also change. Interestingly, TGFB can prevent the formation of tumors in healthy cells and early cancers, and promote metastasis (i.e. cancer dissemination) in more advanced cancer cases. With our current research, we want to identify the miRNAs that are regulated by TGFB, and investigate how modulating their expression affects tumor suppression and progression. With our newly acquired knowledge, we will determine if the abundance of our identified miRNAs is of relevance in differentiating between normal versus tumor tissue and between different types of tumors, and if they can be an indication of prognosis or response to treatment. column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) like Crohn's disease and Ulcerative Colitis affect nearly 250,000 Canadians, and more than 10,000 new cases are diagnosed every year. IBD is characterized by periods of extreme gastrointestinal dysfunction, which significantly impacts patient quality-of-life. IBD patient care involves multiple drugs and may require invasive surgeries if drug intervention is unsuccessful. Collectively, the impact on Canada's economy, in work force and health care costs exceeds $2.8 billion annually. Although the exact cause of IBD is unknown, current treatment strategies aim to suppress the inappropriate and hyperactive intestinal immune responses. However, these immunoregulatory treatments can increase susceptibility to viral infection, a side effect that further diminishes patient quality of life and contributes to IBD-related hospital admissions. New treatment strategies are necessary, and ideally would result in successful control of disease symptoms without increasing the risk of infection. The goal of this research is to test the efficacy of newly discovered family of compounds (called ascarosides) to limit IBD-like symptoms. Ascarosides are natural by-products of intestinal worms. Notably, intestinal worms can prevent IBD in mice and are currently being tested as a new IBD treatment for humans. Our new preliminary data suggests that ascarosides can ameliorate IBD symptoms by altering the disease-associated hyperactive immune response in the intestines but do not impair the ability to clear viral infection. Using ascarosides could by-pass the need to utilize live worms as therapy, which is both unappealing to patients and has unknown side effects. Ascarosides have the potential to be highly efficacious and cost-effective small molecule drugs, with minimal adverse effects. Investing in Canadian research that aims to pioneer the pre-clinical drug testing for this product has the potential to considerably improve IBD patient quality of life.

column36: The dopaminergic ultradian oscillator and psychopathology
column37: Sleep and wake follows a 24hr rhythm, which is controlled by an internal timing system, the circadian clock. However, our daily life is also influenced by rhythms of arousal which cycle approximately every 4 hours. We have now identified the timer that generates these rhythms and it critically relies on the brain chemical dopamine, which is known to promote arousal. We found that increasing brain dopamine levels in mice can drastically lengthens the timing of a single arousal cycle and, intriguingly, the resulting patterns of rest:activity appear strikingly similar to the abnormal sleep:wake behaviour observed in individuals suffering from bipolar disorder or schizophrenia. We now wish to confirm that these sleep/wake abnormalities are indeed due to an imbalance of the dopamine clock we have discovered. We will do this by creating novel mouse models based on gene mutations that have strong links to these psychiatric conditions. We further plan to perform experiments aimed at uncovering the precise brain location of this timer as well as the mechanism of rhythm generation. The proposed studies will improve our understanding of this new biological clock but may also inform the underlying causes of mental illness, thereby paving the way for novel strategies of disease identification, prevention, and treatment.

column37: The advent of new interferon-free hepatitis C virus (HCV) Direct-Acting Antiviral (DAA) therapies has the potential to transform the health outcomes of HCV-infected individuals. These new treatments can be completed in as little as 8-12 weeks, with few side effects, and very high cure rates (e.g., >95%). Since March 2015, British Columbia (BC) has increased the availability and provision of DAA HCV treatment, and is among the first Canadian settings to do so. To achieve the equitable scale-up of DAA interventions at the population level, reductions in HCV incidence and prevalence must be achieved under challenging "real-world" conditions among key populations - and, concerted efforts to avoid reinfection must be sustained over the long term. These challenges are particularly relevant for people who inject drugs (PWID) - a population who also encounters a variety of social and structural barriers to accessing health care. The proposed study will inform the development of DAA HCV treatment policies and service delivery practices (including clinical and provincial guidelines), to optimize treatment outcomes and prevent reinfection over the long term. We will undertake a 3-year qualitative study using annual, in-depth semi-structured interviews with 60 PWID and 20 key stakeholders (including care providers, policy makers, and community organization representatives) in Vancouver. column36: Resolution of inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity in DLBCL using mass cytometry
column37: Recent work has shown that patients with cancer often have tumors that are composed of several different types of cancer cells, each with a slightly different set of genetic mutations. This variability, or "heterogeneity", means that successful therapy must target not just one, but perhaps several different cancers at the same time. As well, there is renewed appreciation for the importance of the patient's own immune system in defeating cancer, and some therapies are even focused at reawakening the patient's immune cells to attack the cancer. Thus, cancer can no longer be regarded simply as an overgrowth of one particular type of cell, but may better be considered as a complex ecosystem with multiple interconnected and constantly evolving parts. In order to diagnose cancer more accurately and to treat it more effectively, it is important that we understand the full complexity of the tumor ecosystem. We propose here to use a cutting-edge technology called mass cytometry , or "CyTOF", to examine patients' tumors one cell at a time in order to get an ultra high definition, widescreen picture of the problem at hand. We will also use the most up-to-date genomics tools to understand which genes are mutated in which cells and how those cells are functioning abnormally. We will use this information to develop a new, cost-effective, same-day test that can be provided to each and every patient and will help doctors to better understand what sort of tumor is present, if and how well the patient's immune system is responding, and what the best treatment options may be.

column36: Brain imaging biomarkers of recovery from sport concussion
column37: Concussions are a growing health concern, with over 4 million occurring annually in sport and recreation in North America. These injuries are associated with a variety of impairments in thinking (confusion, feeling "slow"), emotion (anger, depression) and physical function (dizziness, nausea). Currently, medical clearance (a "clean bill of health") is based on resolution of symptoms and performance on tests measuring thinking ability. These assessments do not directly measure the severity of brain injury. This is a significant concern, as athletes are at risk for significantly worse outcomes if they are re-injured before brain recovery is complete. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a versatile tool that can measure aspects of brain anatomy, function and blood flow. However at present, it has seen limited use in medical assessment of concussion. In this research project, we propose to use advanced MRI techniques to scan university athletes with and without concussion. For concussed athletes, we will perform scanning at key time-points in the recovery process, including while symptomatic (<7 days), time of medical clearance, and 1 month after clearance. This will enable us to visualize brain changes in concussed athletes, and to determine if the brain has recovered or is still healing at the time of medical clearance to return to play. This research will provide novel information about the brain's recovery from injury. It may be used to develop safer guidelines for concussion management, and in the future, will lay the groundwork to develop better measures of brain health and recovery.

column36: Adult neurogenesis and delay-based decision making
column37: We are continually faced with choices and must consider the benefits associated with making one particular choice over another. However, we do not always choose the most beneficial option if the payout is very hard to obtain or if we are unsure about its availability. Another cost to consider is the time required to benefit from our actions. Often is it advantageous to forego something that immediately satisfying and wait for something better. For example, despite the short-term pleasure of consuming junk food, we may instead opt for healthy food knowing that the long-term benefits will be greater. Many disorders, such as schizophrenia, depression, drug addiction and Alzheimer's disease are associated with impulsive preference for immediate rewards. We are interested in the possibility that newborn neurons that are added to the adult brain could reduce impulsivity and promote preference for delayed, advantageous rewards. New neurons are continually added to the brain of all animals, including humans. They are largely added to the hippocampus, and they contribute to hippocampal functions in memory but their exact role remains unclear. Current evidence indicates that the hippocampus is important for mentally recreating past experiences and for creating mental representations of possible future experiences. The hippocampus may reduce impulsivity by enabling individuals to envision possible future experiences and choose the behaviors that lead to long-term beneficial outcomes. However, a role for new neurons in impulsivity has never been investigated. To test this role for new neurons we will block neurogenesis in rats and assess their ability to choose a large delayed reward over a small immediate reward. We will also examine how learning to choose delayed rewards activates circuits of new neurons, to see if their functions are different from older neurons. These findings will be important for developing new treatments for disorders of impulsive decision-making.

column36: The Longitudinal Course of Intracortical Myelination and Cognitive Function in Bipolar Disorder
column37: Bipolar disorder is a mental illness that severely hampers healthy living and work productivity and affects more than 2% of the Canadian population - or more than half a million people. It is associated with episodes of depression (e.g. low mood, sadness) and mania (e.g. agitation, impulsive behavior), interspersed with periods of relative symptom relief between depressive and manic episodes. But even when their mood symptoms are absent or minimal, 60% of individuals with bipolar disorder show problems with attention, concentration and memory (also called "cognitive dysfunction"). This means that the majority of sufferers are chronically impaired. However, the exact causes of these brain deficits in bipolar disorder are unknown and there are no proven treatments for cognitive dysfunction in this population. We seek to investigate for the first time whether a loss of a specific substance, called myelin, in the outer part of the brain (the cerebral cortex) accounts for poor brain function in bipolar disorder. To that end, we will combine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine myelin with clinical testing to assess brain function in 100 individuals with bipolar disorder and 100 individuals who have no mental illness. They will be recruited at five sites across Canada and followed for two years. Our project will probe the link between myelin loss and poor brain function, which could suggest an important mechanism to improve brain function in those with bipolar disorder. In turn, this could guide new interventions to ameliorate their difficulties with thinking, concentration and memory.

column37: Rationale: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is one of the most common and debilitating injuries to the knee and many injured patients go on to develop post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA). Abnormal knee motions and joint biology changes after ACL injury likely disrupt the structural integrity of cartilage reducing its load bearing capacity. Such weakened cartilage may be at an increased risk of mechanical wear during activities of daily living and experience significant and progressive cartilage loss. Critically, there are no accurate clinical diagnostics sensitive to early PTOA changes. This gap prohibits optimal prevention of longitudinal cartilage degradation. Goal: We propose to address the unmet need for a novel "mechanical marker" that will use dynamic imaging techniques to assess the mechanics of the knee with respect to the structural and compositional changes of the knee joint cartilages at the very early stages after injury, and potentially identify those at high risk of OA following knee injury. Using state-of-the-art non-invasive, in-vivo biomechanical and imaging approaches, for the first time, groups will be compared using information of cartilage load-bearing capacity (i.e. mechanical marker), regional cartilage thickness changes, knee joint soft tissue structure and composition, dynamic knee joint movements, joint morphology change and knee function. Follow up assessment of ACL injured individuals and healthy controls will provide the means to identify how these measures interact and clarify the mechanisms of early PTOA progression. Outcomes: This unique project will address the burden of OA by informing research on clinical OA diagnostics and clinical practice, enabling monitoring of the effects of interventions on patient outcomes, and advancing a novel diagnostic tool for early PTOA assessment.

column37: This project concerns thrombocytopenia, a disease of blood coagulation caused by low counts of blood cells called platelets or thrombocytes. A person with this disease may also complain of fatigue and general weakness with or without accompanying blood loss. The immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is caused by production of antibodies against platelet proteins causing capture of platelets by white blood cells, macrophages. column36: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: etiology involving troponin mutations
column37: Familial hypertrophy cardiomyopathy (FHC) is a congenital heart disease which causes the walls of the heart to thicken (hypertrophy) and disrupts the organization of the heart's contractile machinery. As a result of this disease the heart restructures itself not just on a gross level that can be seen by echocardiography but also on a microscopic level, often resulting in irregularities in contraction and electrical disturbances (arrhythmias). We believe that mutations in the troponin complex which is made up of three protein including troponin C which are associated FHC alter the manner in which molecule interacts with calcium and we will test this hypothesis. We will address the idea that sudden cardiac death in patients with FHC is due to factors which increase the risk for SCD and precede the development of hypertrophy. The work will be undertaken at many different levels of organization from a detailed structural analysis of the thin filament which houses the troponin molecule, all the way to comprehensive studies on possible changes in the structure and function of the heart that occur as a result of the mutations engineered into this molecule. We believe that because sudden cardiac death is often the first symptom of abnormality for these individuals, it is critical to understanding the underlying cause of this disease.

column37: Multi-morbidity is the most common condition affecting older adults. As a result seniors in most countries now take around 7 medications daily. Death and illness rates from drug side effects in seniors are as high as those from many chronic diseases and affect falls, thinking, nutrition, fatigue and mobility. Taking 5 or more drugs ('polypharmacy') results in adverse drug effects requiring medical care affect in 13% of Canadian seniors: 1/3 are thought preventable. These are costly to those individuals, and costly to health systems. Canada's health care system lacks a systematic approach to minimizing these negative effects in routine care. We trialed a systematic method of patient centred reduction in medication burden in 70 seniors. This was safe, and the results suggested improvement in health and quality of life. We also tested the effect of discontinuation of single drugs in patients using over a long period to assess benefits and side effects and reviewed methods for asking patients with multiple conditions about their overall priorities for use of drug treatments, finding few tools that help incorporate these into research and clinical care. This program of research will develop these complimentary themes of generation of research evidence around drug discontinuation, and integration of patients' priorities for care. These will be drawn together in a new preventive framework for clinical care, aiming to minimize the harms of treatments in polypharmacy by patient centred discontinuation ('deprescribing'). We will test this intervention in large trials across Canada, assessing the important effects on patients and the healthcare system and will be using insights from patient's and prescriber's experiences of the process of drug discontinuation to provide tools for both. Our aim is to embed reduction of medication burden through medication review and 'deprescribing' as part of regular preventive care in older adults.

column36: Studies on novel immune-surveillance mechanisms underlying cancer elimination
column37: Cancer is a devastating disease and is the number one killer in Canada. The immune system is the body's primary defence against cancer and is tasked with the elimination of tumour cells. During the emergence of cancerous cells, they can undergo mutations altering their genetic code and enabling the cells to divide rapidly. These cells form the primary tumour that grows in one location of the body and can be medically treated. However, newly formed tumour cells may acquire further mutations that mask them from the immune system. This immunoevasive phenotype allows them to covertly enter the blood and lymph vessels and travel to distant organs. This type of cancer is classified as metastatic upon the successful colonization of these alternative sites in the body. Metastatic cancer is considered the final stage of the disease, and survival of patients with this form of cancer is significantly reduced due to the difficulty of treatment. Recently, researchers have discovered methods that can predict the turning point in cancer where the disease moves from the primary to the metastatic form; by examining the gene mutations that are present in the patient's tumour cells. We have conducted studies on metastatic tumours and have identified a key gene that is involved in metastatic progression. This gene controls the recruitment and activation of a newly described type of white blood cell and our data implies that this novel cell type plays an unidentified role in immunity to cancer cells. This observation has been validated in prostate and kidney cancer patients. Through the use of mouse studies, we will further validate the ability of this gene and the new type of white blood cells it induces, to reduce tumour burden and prevent metastasis. These novel and exciting discoveries will be explored as entirely new immunotherapies for cancer patients and could prevent metastasis.

column36: Transfusion in traumatic brain injury (TSiTBI Trial)
column37: The incidence of anemia (a decrease in the quantity or quality of red blood cells) is frequent among critically ill patients. Because red blood cells, through the molecules of hemoglobin, are oxygen carriers, a decrease in the availability of oxygen to the different organs is often to fear. In patients with traumatic brain injury, mechanisms regulating oxygen delivery to the brain are affected by the injury. The development of anemia may thus potentially worsen lesions to the brain and blood transfusion may correct anemia. However, clinicians are currently restricting the use of blood transfusion in traumatic brain injury making inferences with non brain-injured populations. Few evidence-based data help clinicians treating patients with traumatic brain injury to determine what minimal red blood cell levels (hemoglobin levels) can be tolerated before a blood transfusion is required. This project aims to conduct a pan-canadian multicenter clinical trial to compare a liberal transfusion strategy (transfusion when the red blood cell levels are not too low with the objective to keep it high) to a restrictive transfusion strategy (transfusion when red blood cell levels are low with the objective to keep it low). We believe that liberal transfusion strategy will allow better oxygen delivery to the brain, prevent secondary cerebral lesions and will improve long-term outcomes. This project is part of a vast research program aiming to identify when and under what circumstances should we give red blood cells following traumatic brain injury.

column37: Adolescence is a sensitive period for engagement in health-risk behaviors (e.g., substance use, physical inactivity, poor nutrition, risky sexual activity), which can have life-long repercussions. This project assesses the prominent Dual Systems model of adolescent brain development, which suggests that adolescent sensitivity to health-risk behaviors is due to the asynchrony between an early maturing reward-seeking system (likely due to puberty) and a slower maturing impulse control system. Research in this area is limited by reliance on cross-sectional designs, short-term effects, small samples, and a focus on only one or two aspects of development. We will address these gaps through a 5-year longitudinal study of health-risk behaviors across adolescence that includes assessments of brain activity, genetics, endocrine status, physical fitness, personality, and environmental factors. Taking a biopsychosocial approach, our transdisciplinary team of researchers will examine how these factors interact to explain stability versus change in health-risk behaviors. Participants will include 600 boys and girls (ages 8-13 at Year 1) who will be followed for 5 years. Participants will complete an annual self-report survey and a three-year lab component. This project will provide 1) an integrated investigation of the development of youth health-risk behaviors, 2) evidence-based support (or lack of support) for the Dual Systems Model of adolescent brain development and its implications for youth vulnerabilities and opportunities, 3) annual updates of precipitating factors that impact on on health-risk behaviors and brain reactivity over time that are best to target in prevention/intervention programs, such as activities that enhance impulse control and positive lifestyle choices, and 4) a timely and widespread application of findings given the strong team of researchers, partners, and integrated knowledge translation strategies.

column36: New statistical methods for cohort studies of adverse effects of medications
column37: The number of medications available to treat various health problems increases steadily. Most new drugs help improve patients' health, their quality of life and life expectancy, but some may have important unintended side effects while other may be less effective than existing, often less expensive, 'older' medications. Thus, an accurate assessment and comparison of the safety and effectiveness of alternative medications has become one of the primary objectives for both public health agencies and patients' organizations. Accordingly, considerable resources are invested in research attempting to link data on the use of specific medications with both intended and unintended health outcomes. In Canada, such research endeavors are largely facilitated by the existence, in several provinces, of large, administrative databases that contain complete information on both health outcomes and prescriptions received by individual subjects. However, to draw scientifically valid and rigorous conclusions from the analyses of population-based studies of drug safety or effectiveness, we have to address several methodological challenges. For example, patients prescribed a new drug may be more likely to have a more advanced disease and additional risk factors than those not given any drug or prescribed a less expensive older drug. If not accounted for, such differences in the characteristics of drug users may lead to biased results and incorrect conclusions. In addition, differences in the treatment duration and dose of drugs used by different patients, possibly due to treatment non-adherence, may also affect the accuracy of the results. We propose several new statistical methods that will address the above challenges and will permit more accurate assessments of the safety and effectiveness of different drugs used by Canadians. Our new methods may also help designing more rational treatment regimens, to maximize health benefits while reducing the risks of serious adverse events.

column36: Characterization of the genes and gene regulatory mechanisms that control motor neuron stability and neurotransmission in a Drosophila model.
column37: How neurons maintain structural and physiological stability of synapses (contact points) is poorly understood, even though synaptic degeneration is an established hallmark of most neurological disorders. An important clue has come from work in the fruit fly, Drosophila, which revealed that bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) secreted from muscle activate BMP signaling in motor neurons. Loss of BMP signaling (or BMP regulated gene expression) in motor neurons severely destabilizes synaptic morphology and reduces neurotransmission. Follow up work confirmed that BMPs play the same role in mammalian motor neurons, and disrupted BMP signaling has become implicated in motor neuron diseases such as ALS. It is now clear that BMP signaling controls a battery of novel genes required for morphological and physiological stability of motor neuron synapses (and other synapses) from Drosophila to humans. Most of these genes have not been identified. Our preliminary data has taken the first important step by identifying all BMP regulated genes in fly neurons (by RNAseq). With these in hand, this project can now address two, important knowledge gaps: 1) How does BMP signaling control those genes' expression? We will determine which transcription factors, resident in motor neurons, enable the BMP pathway to control gene expression in motor neurons. 2) What is the function of those genes? We will determine the function of ~100 of these novel genes that we postulate play novel conserved roles in synaptic stability of morphology and neurotransmission in humans. We address these questions in Drosophila. The mechanisms under examination are extremely well conserved from Drosophila to humans, and Drosophila offers the only genetic toolset able to complete these goals in 5 years. As this project will reveal how a novel gene network is regulated and deployed to control synaptic stability, our work will revolutionize our ability to combat synaptic degeneration in neurological disorder

column36: Predicting occurrence and lifetime expression of a major recurrent copy number variation
column37: Babies born with a genetic deletion (missing piece of DNA) on one of the pair of chromosomes 22 are known to be at high risk of having birth defects and, later on, learning difficulties and schizophrenia. Some are severely affected and some have better outcomes, even though they have the same deletion. The deletion can be found in up to 1 in 1000 pregnancies, and is usually a change that is new to the family. New commercially available tests can now screen for this genetic deletion in pregnancy. Families, healthcare providers, and researchers want to anticipate and ultimately prevent the most disabling outcomes. There is evidence that additional changes elsewhere in a person's DNA are important to specific expression and outcomes of the deletion. By studying 100 Canadian adults who have this deletion on chromosome 22 and their 200 parents who do not have this deletion we will first determine how the parents' traits, like intellectual level, may modify outcomes. Then we will use the latest technology, whole genome sequencing, to sequence the entire genome (DNA) of these 300 people. This will enable us to identify and interpret other genetic changes, both new and inherited, that make it more (or less) likely for individuals with the deletion to develop specific features that affect lifelong outcome. To start, we will compare those with and without schizophrenia. Some new genetic changes may cluster together in the genome. We will examine whether these clusters are associated with poor outcomes, and/or with the occurrence of the deletion event itself in the family. The results promise to help identify factors that shape important outcomes in individuals with this deletion, so that we can intervene early and help to prevent major disabilities. This study will also advance our understanding of common diseases like schizophrenia, and of the many genetic conditions that are similar to this specific genetic deletion.

column36: Epigenetic Signatures of Successful Aging
column37: Aging is a complex process that involves a host of physiological changes. Approximately 25% of the variation in human lifespan is attributed to genetics, with the remainder proposed as being associated with life style or environmental exposure. Epigenetics is the study of how experiences can "get under the skin" by acting as a mediator between environmental influences and genetics. DNA methylation is the most well studied epigenetic mark, and has the potential to influence how certain genes are turned on or off in association with environmental or life styles exposures, such as stress or smoking. We aim to assess DNA methylation in the longevity population of Costa Rica, the Nicoya Peninsula, to characterize an epigenetic blueprint of healthy aging. Our preliminary pilot study results suggest that age-related DNA methylation trends are different in high longevity populations when compared to individuals from adjacent control regions. We propose to expand our sample size in Nicoya, and investigate two other longevity populations: Sardinia, Italy and Ikaria Greece. We then propose to compare these findings with the DNA methylation profiles of Canadians from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. The characterization of biological aging will not only aid in understanding the etiology of age-related disease but will contribute to eventually extending the number of healthy and mobile years Canadians spend in old age.

column36: Individual differences in autobiographical memory: cognitive, behavioural, and neural correlates and their relationship to aging
column37: The notion that people differ with respect to memory abilities is accepted in the general public. Recently, people with extreme profiles of memory abilities have been discovered. Individuals with highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) have an uncanny ability to access details from personal past events regardless of the nature or importance of the event. Individuals with severely deficient autobiographical memory (SDAM) have normal learning and memory for factual information, but do not recollect details of personal events at all. These extreme memory syndromes may reflect the ends of a normal continuum of memory abilities that would be expected based on introspection and comparison with others. Yet when studying memory, researchers calculate averages across groups of people, ignoring such individual differences. In this research, we will contrast groups of individuals with HSAM and SDAM to better understand the nature of their memory function. We will test specific hypotheses regarding memory abilities and their relationship to brain structure and function that will shed light on the entire range of memory ability, not just the extremes. We will also examine how individual differences in autobiographical memory play out with aging. Memory impairment is among the commonest cognitive complaints in aging and is considered a cardinal sign of neurodegenerative disease, such as Alzheimer's disease. Yet no one has examined how such complaints and abilities relate to individual differences in autobiographical memory. It may be that individuals with high or low autobiographical memory abilities have differential susceptibility to aging and neurodegenerative effects. This research will contribute to the creation of new memory assessment tools that will be important to diagnosis and intervention in individuals with memory changes due to aging or age-related disorders.
