(3) combine the data into a nutrition - microbiome - serum metabolite axis which is indicative for a healthy nutrition and/or human health in general. With our approach, we are extending the biomarker research on the human gut microbiome, which is heavily influenced by diet and therefore might be more suitable as a biomarker for nutrition and health compared to serum proteins. Also, we are not focusing on one certain bacterium (like on one certain serum protein) but on biopatterns of metabolites of microbiome populations indicating a symbiotic homeostasis of humans and microbes as a marker for health.

column36: The Built Environment and Active Transportation Safety in Children and Youth
column37: The Convention on the Rights of the Child states that "...children have the right to the highest attainable level of health and the right to a safe environment, free from injury and violence." Active transportation (AT), such as walking and biking, is a healthy way for children to explore their environment and develop independence. However, children can be injured while walking and biking and these injuries can be severe when children are hit by motor vehicles. Many Canadian cities make changes to the built environment (e.g., traffic calming features, separated bike lanes) to try and keep people safe. There is some research on how effective these changes are in preventing adult pedestrians and bicyclists from getting hurt, but very little research has been done to show how safe various environments are for children and youth. We propose a research program to study how features of the built environment affect whether kids walk or bike to school and whether or not certain built environment features increase or decrease their likelihood of getting hurt. Our program is unique because we are partnering with injury prevention professionals, provincial governments, environmental organizations and traffic safety professionals who are in a position to help us better understand what features of traffic environments are dangerous or safe. Our research will be very useful in making walking and biking much safer for children and youth.

column37: How our cities are designed, including roads, houses, and neighourhoods influences how much physical activity people get. column36: Climate Change and Indigenous Food System, Food Security, and Food Safety (Climate Change IFS3)
column37: A changing climate will affect food through a range of effects on agriculture, livestock, water systems, and wildlife, which have implications for food security, foodborne disease, and malnutrition. Indigenous populations who rely on the environment for livelihoods are considered highly sensitive to these impacts. The Climate Change and Indigenous Food System, Food Security, & Food Safety (Climate Change IFS3) research program addresses a significant deficit in understanding the food-related health (agri-health) dimensions of climate change among Indigenous populations globally. The research program has created a multinational intersectoral team to characterize the vulnerability and resilience of Indigenous food systems to climate change to inform, enhance, and expand climate change adaptation interventions and adaptation planning. The program responds to needs identified by communities, public health units, Indigenous organizations, governments, and the United Nations through ongoing partnerships with Inuit (Canada), Batwa (Uganda), and Shawi (Peru) populations. Working within these regions, the program has 3 research pillars: 1) Community-driven environment and health surveillance, 2) Projecting climate change impacts on agri-health outcomes, and 3) Developing place-based adaptation pathways. Within the foci of food and climate, we will examine how culturally defined gender roles and age impact vulnerability and resilience, and highlight the importance of Indigenous Knowledge. Comparative analysis is an explicit goal and is built into program design through the use of consistent methodologies across regions. Our participatory, community-based approach will offer best practice guidance for other initiatives, will create community and scientific leaders with expertise in Indigenous agri-health and climate change, and demonstrate the importance of Indigenous Knowledge for adaptation, seeking to empower communities to manage the agri-health effects of climate change.

column36: Multisectoral Urban Systems for health and Equity in Canadian cities
column37: At the end of the 19th century, confronted by epidemics of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis or gastroenteritis, public health authorities began collaborating with municipalities to improve urban environments. Major works were undertaken to install drains and eliminate unhealthy housing, notably by prohibiting dwelling units in basements and windowless rooms. These efforts were very successful as infectious disease rates decreased and did so well before the advent of antibiotics. Initially in developed countries and now in developing nations, there have been major increases in chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and several cancers. At the beginning of the 21st century, to counter these threats to population health, Public Health Departments have forged new alliances with major Canadian cities. Together, they are working to create environments that foster the supply of healthy and affordable food, enhance active transportation, and reduce the risks of bad housing conditions. Our research program aims to study these cross-sector partnerships, which involve collaborations between health practitioners, municipalities, representatives from civil society, housing authorities, and actors from other sectors. We will study partnerships aimed at transforming built environments to increase the availability of fruit and vegetables, promote public transport and physical activity, and improve availability of affordable housing. We will also look into how these partnerships take into account social and gender inequalities and pay special attention to children and youth. To carry out these studies and make comparisons, we will rely on the active participation of the Directors of the Public Health Organizations in Montreal, Saskatoon, Toronto, and Vancouver. Ultimately, we will identify the factors that lead to success in forward-looking initiatives aimed at preventing the new epidemics of chronic diseases.

column36: FiberTAG: TAGging dietary Fiber intake and their interest for health by measuring biomarkers related to the gut microbiota.
column37: The scientific rationale of recommendations in dietary fiber (DF) intake comes from the recognition of their benefits for health based on studies published many years ago. It remains unclear which key physiological effects are generated by DF in view of the diversity of the food components considered as DF, the relevance of their classification as soluble versus insoluble, and from the recent discoveries putting forward their interactions with the gut microbiota. The FiberTAG project will establish biomarkers to meet two objectives. First, the consortium will use existing cohorts to investigate the link between DF intake, gut microbial signature (composition and metabolites), and key gut biological functions. The second objective will be to develop innovative approaches to evaluate the health interest of novel insoluble DF, prone to interact with the gut microbiota. One of the existing cohorts is the Alberta FYBER study. In this study, we systematically investigate the effects of different types of fibre on inflammation and measures of metabolic health in overweight and mildly obese people. We will also look for links between different types of dietary fibre and the composition and function of each person's gut microbiota. This will allow us to test whether microbiome patterns in individuals predict the effects of the fibre. To achieve this, we will begin with an exploratory clinical trial that compares the effects of three types of fermentable dietary fibre with the effects of non-fermentable cellulose. We will measure how fibre type and microbiota composition and function affect specific health outcomes such as reduced inflammation. Overall, the FiberTAG study will aim at refining the concept of dietary fiber based on novel biological effects that can occur upon gut microbiota-nutrients interaction.

column36: Fundamentals on Telomere and Telomerase Functions
column37: One could compare our genome to a large library that contains numerous shelves, each with an extraordinary large number of books. The combined information contained in all the books represents our genetic information and is required to make us who we are. In this paraphrase, the bookshelves represent our chromosomes. Due to the heavy use of the books and because the whole library, including the shelves, need to be duplicated each time a cell divides, there is continued wear and tear on the terminal bookends on the shelves. Without continued upkeep and repair, the bookends will eventually become dysfunctional, causing books to fall off the shelves and get lost. The telomeres and the telomerase enzyme that we study are, respectively, the bookends and the maintenance operator for the bookends. In real life, it is essential to ensure the integrity of the ends of our chromosomes. The telomerase enzyme is composed of several subunits; two of which, one protein and one RNA molecule are required for the enzyme to work in a minimalistic test-tube system. Inadequate supply of any of the components, causing instability of the chromosomes, is associated with aging and human disease, foremost cancer, but also dyskeratosis congenita (DKC) and other congenital disorders now called telomeropathies. Using a simple but powerful model system, we propose to investigate the biology of telomeres and the telomerase enzyme. In particular, we plan to identify all the components, learn more about how they interact, are regulated and localized. Most importantly, we will determine when and how telomerase operates at its most important location, namely on telomeres. Given that telomere and telomerase function and regulation are highly conserved across many species, from yeast to humans, our studies will provide critical clues and input into how telomere biology could be exploited for the benefit of human health.

column37: Socioeconomic marginalization (SEM) is a key driver of drug use and drug-related harm, resulting in excess morbidity and mortality among people who use drugs and a significant social and economic burden in Canada and internationally. My overall goal is to reduce drug use and related harm through effective interventions that address SEM among people who use illicit drugs. Using linked observational, intervention and randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluation studies, the specific objectives of my CIHR Foundation program are to: 1) Conduct observational research that identifies elements of SEM to be targeted via social and structural interventions; 2) Implement social and structural RCTs that test public health solutions targeting SEM; and 3) Evaluate how social and structural drivers of SEM affect addictions RCT recruitment, retention and experiences from local and comparative national perspectives. Through qualitative, quantitative, experimental and mixed-methods approaches, this work will yield a robust evidence base for strategies to reduce drug use and drug-related harm driven by SEM. Parallel iKT initiatives will promote the integration of public health objectives into social and welfare policy, thereby reducing the human and health system costs of SEM among people who use drugs.

column37: Aggressive induction chemotherapy produces complete remission in ~70% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but most ultimately relapse, at least in part, due to the persistence of dormant stem cells that are resistant to standard chemotherapy. column36: Molecular and cellular biology of T regulatory cells
column37: The goal of my research is to understand how our immune system regulates itself and to use this information to develop new ways to treat patients with immune-related diseases, such as autoimmunity or transplant rejection. A healthy immune system must strike a balance between attacking infectious or dangerous substances while not reacting to our own cells and tissues. This delicate balancing act is called immune tolerance. Both autoimmune diseases and transplant complications are caused by disrupted immune tolerance. At present, immunosuppressive drugs are our only treatment for these conditions. Yet these drugs suppress all immune responses, putting patients at risk of infection and cancer, often without controlling their disease. We need to find better ways to prevent harmful immune responses. I am an expert is the study of a type of white blood cell called T regulatory cells, or Tregs, which coordinate immune responses and maintain immune tolerance. My work has defined how Tregs develop and function, and led to clinical trials to test use of Tregs as a cell therapy in transplantation and autoimmunity. I developed methods to monitor the presence of Tregs in blood and tissues, allowing more precise measurement of immune tolerance. If used as a treatment, Tregs could control pathological immune responses without altering healthy immune balance. Towards this aim, the next stage of my research has 3 goals, to: 1) create "designer" Tregs that are engineered to be active only in the presence of a transplant and test their ability to prevent transplant rejection and preserve normal immunity; 2) design new ways to alter Tregs so their function is tailored to specific disease contexts; and 3) identify biological pathways that regulate Tregs, so that they can be targeted for new treatment options. My research will enable new Treg-based therapies to prevent and treat the many chronic diseases that are caused by a failure of immune tolerance.

column37: Canada leads the world in gender and health research policy. column36: Functional Protein Dynamics in Health and Disease
column37: Protein molecules play critical roles in cellular function and they catalyze many of the biochemical reactions that are necessary for life. The three-dimensional shapes of these molecules are necessary for guiding proper function and they can change with time due to interactions with other molecules, during the process of carrying out specific functions, or simply the result of random fluctuations. Although very detailed static pictures of protein molecules have been produced using traditional biophysical tools, macromolecular function and misfunction is, in many cases, intimately coupled to flexibility; knowledge of molecular motions therefore becomes critical. Thus, static pictures of proteins that have been generated to date often do not completely explain results from functional biological assays, nor do they necessarily illuminate the path for engineering new functions or for rational drug design. The goal of this research is to develop new Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy based techniques for studying motional processes in proteins and for relating these to function and to apply the methodology to important protein systems that are implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration and amyloidosis. The insights obtained will augment the structure-function paradigm that has dominated our understanding of how proteins work to include the important role of molecular dynamics. They will inform how function can be manipulated by changing how parts of proteins move in relation to each other and provide clues about how to design, in a rational manner, new classes of drug molecules. Advances that are made in the laboratory will be translated into potential drugs through collaborations with leading medicinal chemists and clinician scientists.

column36: Regulation of postsynaptic expression and function of ionotropic neurotransmitter receptors
column37: Normal function of the brain depends on tightly regulated communication between neurons. The neurons communicate with one another through junction sites called synapses via "synaptic transmission". During this process, neurotransmitter molecules are released from presynaptic neurons and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic neurons. Deregulated synaptic transmission is believed to be at the root of many brain diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, epilepsy, and stroke. I believe that by better understanding the mechanisms controlling the efficacy of the synaptic transmission among neurons there is the potential to identify targets and thereby to create better therapeutics for these brain disorders. Theoretically, the strength of synaptic transmission can be regulated by altering either the presynaptic neurotransmitter release or the responsiveness of postsynaptic neurotransmitter receptor. Research in our laboratory has focused on the regulatory mechanisms which determine the responsiveness of postsynaptic ionotropic receptors. Strong evidence accumulated from our work and other labs suggest that both function and number of these receptors may be rapidly altered. These rapid changes may be responsible for the pathogenesis of many brain disorders. Currently, we are proposing experiments to investigate how rapid changes in the function and number of postsynaptic receptors, therefore synaptic transmission strength, is regulated. The main objective of our research is to identify molecular processes underlying the regulation of the efficacy of synaptic transmission. Through these fundamental investigations we aim to identify new therapeutic targets and develop new drugs to treat brain disease. Since inter-neuronal communication is a pivotal component of brain function and the alteration of this process underlies many disorders, our proposed studies can be expected to lead to better treatment for these diseases

column36: Alternatives to antibiotics: New strategies for treating multi-drug resistant infections
column37: Antibiotics are the most successful medical intervention in human history. They are critical for preventing and treating life-threatening infections. A lack of effective antibiotics would lead to difficulties with major surgeries, chemotherapy, transplantations, and early-term births; even minor injuries could become infected and deadly. Thus the relentless and concerning increase in multi-drug resistance to antibiotics in the face of a inadequate pipeline for new antibiotics has caused great concern for public health officials and the general public. Indeed, in Sept 2016, all 193 member countries of the United Nations declared antimicrobial resistance "the biggest threat to modern medicine". Here we will investigate the mechanisms of adaptive, multiple-antibiotic resistance in the important pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, one of the most difficult to treat bacterial "Superbugs" in our society. Adaptive resistance is a feature of specific bacterial "lifestyles" that are triggered during growth in patients; we will investigate the mechanisms of such resistance in the context of growth circumstances that occur during infections. To tackle adaptive and acquired resistance and provide new therapies that address the poor success of modern antibiotic discovery, we will then develop three alternatives to antibiotics: 1) Novel anti-biofilm peptides to treat adaptive multiple-antibiotic resistance due to the growth of bacteria on body surfaces as multicellular colonies termed biofilms (representing two thirds of all hospital infections); 2) Peptides that enhance the anti-infection properties of the immune system; and 3) Compounds that will reverse the inability of the immune system to respond to pathogens in patients with sepsis (causes 8% of all deaths worldwide). A feature of these strategies is that they will assist in making available antibiotics work better. Our research will move our discoveries to clinical testing during the funding period.

column36: Leveraging Essential Genes and Genetic Networks to Cripple Human Fungal Pathogens
column37: The impact of fungal pathogens on human health is devastating. They infect billions of people around the globe, and kill more than 1.5 million each year. The most vulnerable are people with reduced immune function, such as those with HIV or those undergoing immune suppressing treatments for cancer or organ transplants. One of the leading fungal pathogens of humans is Candida albicans. It kills ~40% of people suffering from bloodstream infections. Treating these infections is extremely difficult, as fungi are closely related to humans and there are very few drugs that kill the fungus but not the host. With the emergence of drug resistance, it is now critical to develop new therapeutic strategies. To address this important clinical need, it is critical to uncover the genes and genetic networks that are required for the pathogen to survive and cause disease. We are one of the first academic labs to obtain a powerful resource that will allow us to test the function of almost every gene in the C. albicans genome. Through collaboration with a pharmaceutical company, we now have access to the largest library of C. albicans mutants, which enables genetic depletion of ~40% of genes in the genome. We will use sophisticated computational approaches to predict essential genes, and will expand this resource to cover them all. This resource provides an unprecedented opportunity to identify which genes are essential for the pathogen, and to determine their molecular function and interactions. We will use this platform to characterize the impact of reducing the dosage of each gene on growth, cellular physiology, and traits associated with the capacity to cause disease. We will perform state-of-the-art screens to identify new molecules that target essential genes, and will evaluate their therapeutic potential. This research will reveal new approaches to cripple the pathogen, and enable development of novel therapeutic strategies to improve clinical outcome for millions of people.

column37: Projections indicate that by 2050 drug resistant bacteria will kill more people than will cancer. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is one of many emerging new bacterial infections arising from drug resistance. The viability of Caesarean sections, chemotherapy and transplant surgery depends on antibiotics being able to treat infections. Bacterial resistance is increasing at a dramatic rate. There is a limited choice of drugs available to manage infections from drug resistant bacteria. This indicates that there is a strong need to develop new antibacterial drugs, yet pharmaceutical companies are exiting the infectious diseases discovery arena. The goal of this research project is to rationally design novel chemical entities (NCEs) for bacterial infections combining chemical and enzymatic approaches. These NCEs are designed to target a specific biosynthetic pathway found in Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria and mycobacteria thereby making it an attractive target for the development of a broad-spectrum anti-infective. This pathway is not targeted by any currently approved drugs, nor by any known natural products, nor is there any significant work in the literature regarding the inhibition of this pathway, nor is the pathway present in mammalian cells. Our inhibitors are designed using knowledge of enzyme mechanism and structure. We have synthesized NCEs that bind multiple enzymes in the pathway. column36: Investigation of a new approach for treatment of deprivation-induced vision impairment
column37: Brain regions that support visual perception complete their development early in postnatal life when visual experience informs the proper development of neurons and their connections. Disruption of normal visual experience during this formative postnatal period, as can happen with cataracts, refractive errors or misaligned eyes, alters the development of neural connections and can result in the leading cause of vision impairment in children called amblyopia. We have recently demonstrated fast and complete recovery from amblyopia in kittens reared in complete darkness for 10 days. Our preliminary investigation of the molecular changes underlying this recovery suggests that darkness reverses the accumulation of proteins called 'molecular brakes' that attenuate the capacity for neural plasticity and recovery. We have also recently observed a similar remarkable recovery from amblyopia following temporary binocular retinal inactivation. Successful treatment of amblyopia with darkness or retinal inactivation represents a potential breakthrough in visual health research. Experiments in this proposal will provide a better understanding of the optimal treatment parameters for both treatments, and will investigate potential mechanisms engaged to enable recovery. We will address key issues important for the translation of these treatments to human benefit, including examination of the time window within which they promote recovery, the consequences of different lengths of treatment, and the importance of post-treatment binocular vision. We further propose to provide a more thorough mechanistic understanding of the molecular events that enhance neural plasticity and promote visual recovery, with focus on a collection of proteins known to restrict the capacity for neural modification. The overarching goal of this proposal is build up to a proof of principle study on a clinical population of human amblyopes.

column36: Optogenetic visualization and manipulation of neural activity
column37: Life on the earth's surface is bathed in the white light of the Sun. This light provides energy to support life through photosynthesis, but life on earth has evolved to harness light in a myriad of other critical ways. For example, receptors in our eyes respond to certain wavelengths of light, such as those reflected from the corals of a tropical reef. The receptors send electrical signals to our brain that we perceive as colour. We are harnessing light as a research tool to understand how our nervous systems work. Light-based tools will advance our understanding of many nervous system disorders, such as neurodegenerative diseases, brain damage from stroke, and chronic pain. Biologists can now borrow natural systems that interact with light and transplant them in mice and other organisms that serve as models of human disease. These transplanted systems are called "optogenetic tools," and they have revolutionized our ability to visualize and manipulate biology in live animals. They have a particularly big impact in neuroscience. Optogenetic tools now help neuroscientists to watch the electrical signals from thousands of individual neurons in a model animal's brain. They also let researchers effectively write a memory into a mouse brain using light - a capability that was in the realm of science fiction until just a few years ago. Knowledge that we gain from these studies in animals with optogenetic tools can be applied to treating nervous system disorders in humans. My research program develops new optogenetic tools for neuroscience research. My speciality is borrowing the proteins that give coral their colour and altering them to create innovative research tools. One theme of my research is equipping neuroscientists to visualize the chemical communication between neurons of the brain that increases or decreases neuron activity. Another theme is creating more subtle and specific methods to activate key biochemical processes in neurons with light.

Our studies will provide novel information for how serious human pathogens, like S. aureus, can obtain iron and thereby cause serious infections. column37: Our goal is to control the changes in brain excitability that follow a precipitating event and lead to mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE); this process is known as epileptogenesis. column36: Pre-Clinical Translation of Circadian Biology to Benefit Treatment of Heart Disease
column37: Body processes in mammals cycle with a 24-hour day-night (circadian or diurnal) rhythm, which is controlled by molecular clocks in the brain and other tissues such as the heart. Our cardiovascular system appears to follow a day-night rhythm as well. For example, heart rate and blood pressure are highest during the day when we are awake and lowest at night during sleep. Heart disease also exhibits a rhythm, as heart attacks and sudden cardiac death are more likely to occur in the morning than at night. In earlier and preliminary studies we used murine heart disease models and showed that the circadian mechanism underlies time of day variations in the genes and proteins in the heart, cardiac structure and function, and pathophysiologic responses to disease. Several of our high impact murine experimental studies reveal clear translational potential for applying circadian biology to benefit treatment of heart disease. 1) Timing drug therapies to the body's physiologic and molecular rhythms can improve drug efficacy and benefit outcome of heart disease. 2) Minimizing circadian rhythm disruption in the first few days of critical illness can improve healing - this especially has implications for intensive care units and multi-bedded wards where daily rhythms are disturbed. Here we intend to pursue the insights gained from our most promising circadian rhythms research studies, and apply them to the treatment of clinically relevant myocardial ischemia-reperfusion (mI/R, heart attack). We will demonstrate efficacy and uncover the direct role of the circadian mechanisms in rodent mI/R models, followed by vital testing in our new pre-clinical centre with state-of-the-art imaging relevant to humans (echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging). Reconsidering how we practice medicine, by translational application of circadian biology to clinical cardiology (and medicine in general), is a fundamental new approach to understanding and treating heart disease.

column36: Determining the pathways, components and functional niches that define specialized ribosomes.
column37: Ribosomes are the cellular protein synthesis machinery, and highly conserved from bacteria to humans. They are complex molecular machines made up of four ribosomal ribonucleic acids (rRNAs) and 80 ribosomal proteins. Until recently it was believed that ribosomes are the exact same in every single cell within an organism, from a liver cell to a neuron. However, recent studies showed that there exists a small pool of 'specialized' ribosomes that can be found either in specific cells or tissues, such as testis or oocytes, and which appear to be involved in the biosynthesis of very specific proteins. Moreover, genetic mutations in components of ribosomes, resulted in highly specific diseases affecting the blood, skeleton or cancer predisposition, and established themselves often during early development, suggesting that these components, and 'specialized' ribosomes, may have an important role. While some of the differences between 'normal' and 'specialized' ribosomes have been uncovered, the proteins they are to synthesize as well as how specialized ribosomes are produced and fine-tuned themselves have not. Ribosome biogenesis, the process of making ribosomes, involves the coordinated function of over 200 proteins, and understanding the mechanisms that define making and function of specialized ribosomes will be of great importance to understand human development and disease on a molecular level. The main aim of the proposed research is to determine the events that distinguish different populations of ribosomes and their activity within different cell and tissue types. This will allow us to gain insight into how specialized ribosomes, and mutations within them, can affect the development of certain diseases as well as the fate of cells and organs during human development as a whole.

column37: CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) provide major protection against infection and cancer. Upon infection, CTLs undergo a three-phase developmental program, wherein they first rapidly proliferate in the expansion phase and differentiate into effectors that kill infected cells. Then, the majority (~90-95%) of CTLs die by apoptosis in the contraction phase, and the remaining surviving cells (~5-10%) become long-term memory CTLs in the memory phase. However, what mechanism determines CTL die or survival remains unresolved. Since the goal of vaccination is to prevent diseases by immunological memory, a detailed understanding of the molecular basis for CTL fate and memory is critical to vaccine design. T cell-surface mannose-6-phosphate receptor (M6PR) is a multifunctional receptor that can uptake cytolytic molecule called granzyme-B (GzmB), leading to T cell death. We demonstrated that CTLs with low M6PR -expression (M6PRlow-CTLs) survived because GzmB could not bind to and kill these M6PRlow-CTLs. We also demonstrated that interleukin (IL)-7 cytokine was able to down-regulate CTL M6PR-expression, thus leading to M6PRlow-CTL surviving the contraction phase and becoming memory CTLs. In this project, we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms or pathways regulating T cell fate and memory in IL-7-stimulated CTLs. Therefore, we can incorporate our findings in rational vaccine design to develop potent vaccines with less contraction, but enhanced CTL memory and in new drug development for infectious and cancer diseases.

column36: Microbial Biofilms: Molecular mechanisms to therapeutics
column37: Bacteria typically live as collections of cells attached to a moist surface surrounded by a slimy coating. This mode of growth is called a biofilm and is beneficial to bacteria because the self-produced slimy coating protects them from antibiotics and our immune system, and provides a perfect environment for them to evolve and acquire antibiotic resistance. This protection and the bacteria's ability to grow on a large range of different types of moist surfaces, including human cells, make biofilms a major medical problem. Biofilms are responsible for ~80% of all infections in the body. This includes infections of the inner ear, urinary tract and pulmonary system, and those associated with contaminated medical devices such as catheters, heart valves and prosthetic joints. The failure of current antibiotics to clear biofilm infections results in serious health complications for patients and highlights the urgent need for effective new therapies to treat these often-fatal infections. A critical component of the protective biofilm coating are long chains of sugars units. Biofilms cannot form if the bacteria are unable to produce these sugar chains or when the chemical composition of the sugars is altered. Our goal is to understand how the bacteria make these sugar chains and to use this knowledge to develop novel anti-biofilm therapeutics. Our goal is to develop two types of therapeutics: the first would be used to prevent biofilm formation and hence eliminate the life-threatening complications that frequently occur; while the second would be used to treat and clear biofilms, thus improving health outcomes for individuals suffering from chronic infections.

column36: Pathogenic Strategies of the Lyme Disease Spirochete
column37: Lyme disease is an emerging infectious disease caused by a spiral-shaped bacterium (Borrelia burgdorferi) that is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick. Incidence of the disease is increasing, triggered in part by global warming. The disease can result in a wide variety of symptoms, mimicking other medical conditions, often making diagnosis difficult. The focus of this project is to investigate two important strategies used by B. burgdorferi to mount a successful infection. 1) Antigenic variation. This is a process by which the pathogen continually changes the sequence of the major component of the outer coat that is recognized by antibodies. The outcome is a continual wardrobe change for the pathogen that keeps it one step ahead of host recognition resulting in persistent infection. Antigenic variation occurs by continual DNA rearrangements in the gene for the major surface protein, VlsE. We will study this process in detail using next generation sequencing. We will also study the DNA regions involved in the rearrangement process and the protein molecules that promote the DNA rearrangements. 2) Vascular transmigration. The reason why B. burgdorferi can cause such a large number of different symptoms is because the organism disseminates through the circulatory system and can exit the vasculature in virtually any part of the body. The result is varying symptoms depending upon where B. burgdorferi exits the bloodstream. The process of vascular transmigration is mediated by interactions between B. burgdorferi and endothelial cells lining small blood vessels. We will investigate these interactions and the changes they cause in blood vessels that allow B. burgdorferi to exit. We will also study the proteins and signaling pathways involved and the molecular changes occurring to the endothelial layer that unlock the door for escape. Details uncovered on these important processes may be useful for future development of clinical interventions.

We are studying a large family of more than 700 transcription factors known as the zinc finger proteins. We have unexpectedly discovered that the zinc finger proteins almost always recognize RNA as well as DNA and propose to identify the sequences that they recognize. This will enable better understanding of human disease and help us to better predict both what diseases might occur and how best to treat those diseases. We are also studying several proteins in which mutations cause three devastating and fatal neurodegenerative diseases, spinal muscular atrophy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; also as known as Lou Gehrig's disease) and fronto-temporal dementia, as well as another protein important for the growth of many kinds of cancer cells. We propose to determine how the zinc finger proteins control the splicing together of RNA fragments to form contiguous segments that code for protein, as well as how the zinc finger proteins, the neurodegeneration proteins, and the cancer-promoting protein determine where RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that reads human genes, stops at the ends of genes. We will also try to identify chemicals that prevent RNA polymerase II from stopping and might be developed into new kinds of anti-cancer drugs.

column36: Characterizing Arm Recovery in People with Severe Stroke (CARPSS)
column37: Every year, over 50,000 new strokes are reported in Canada. Recent advances in acute care have increased the likelihood of surviving a large stroke and have resulted in up to 30% of all stroke survivors living with severe upper limb disability. Stroke survivors with severe arm disability have the poorest prognosis, lowest health related quality of life, incur the greatest costs to the healthcare system and receive the least amount of intensive rehabilitation. While some people with severe disability show little recovery, others attain a substantial amount of functional recovery. This highlights a need to be able to identify people with severe upper limb disability who have the most potential to show recovery. Additionally, there is currently poor understanding of what an individual with stroke considers to be meaningful recovery. Thus, the main aims of the proposed research are to: 1) track individuals with severe upper limb disability across the first year post stroke to determine which factors best predict recovery of function, 2) establish a definition of meaningful recovery using data from stroke survivors themselves in combination with clinical and brain based measures, and 3) test a novel algorithm that predicts the degree of functional recovery. Determining reasons why someone with severe upper limb impairment achieves meaningful recovery after stroke is an important question; this information will help to develop novel interventions for the growing and under-served group of people living with severe upper limb disability. Also, understanding how recovery occurs in people with severe arm impairment will enable the appropriate delivery of individualized rehabilitation interventions and better outcomes for Canadians with stroke.

column36: Structural Biology of Tankyrase Activity and Regulation in Cell Signaling
column37: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) create the posttranslational modification poly(ADP- ribose) to regulate a wide variety of cellular programs, such as DNA damage repair, gene transcription, cell death signaling, and metabolism. The PARP superfamily has 17 members with a diverse set of regulatory domains attached to the conserved catalytic domain that creates the ADP-ribose modification. A more detailed understanding of the specific biological pathways regulated by PARPs has emerged recently. However, there remain fundamental gaps in our knowledge of how the catalytic activities of the different PARP family members are regulated, and this limits our understanding of how several important cellular programs are regulated by ADP-ribosylation. Tankyrase is a PARP enzyme that is involved in a number of cellular pathways, including telomere maintenance, glucose homeostasis, Wnt signaling, mitotic progression, and RNA processing. How tankyrase selects cellular target proteins for modification is poorly understood, in part due to limited structural information, and in part due to a paucity of biochemical analysis. Based on our preliminary structural and biochemical work, the proposed studies will provide important advances in our understanding of how tankyrase selects and modifies target proteins. Several PARP enzymes, including tankyrase, are the targets of small-molecule inhibitors used for the treatment of cancer. Current PARP inhibitors lack isozyme specificity and are therefore limited in their ability to serve as specific biological probes of PARP function. The proposed studies will build toward a mechanistic understanding of tankyrase activity and regulation that will contribute to the design of tankyrase-specific inhibitors as chemical probes, and potentially as new anti-cancer compounds.

column37: Asthma is characterized by excessive constriction of the airways and inflammation in the lung. Traditional drugs target two aspects of the disease; inflammation and airway constriction. Fatal asthma-attacks usually result from failed response of airway muscle to relaxant drugs. The fact that muscle relaxants and anti-inflammatory drugs do not cure asthma suggests that they are not targeting the root cause of asthma. Recent research in our laboratory has revealed a new drug target that may be related to the root cause of asthma. We have found that the stiffness of the relaxed airway muscle contributes to the overall stiffness of the airways, and is partially responsible for the reduced airway distensibility found in asthmatic patients. Interestingly the muscle stiffness does not respond to the traditional muscle relaxants, which is effective only on activated muscles. We found that a new class of drugs targeting the structural integrity of airway muscle cells is effective in reducing the cell stiffness, and in the presence of mechanical stretches similar to those experienced by the muscle in a breathing lung, the relaxant effect of the drugs on airway muscle is synergistically enhanced. In this application we propose to identify new drug targets that "soften" the airway muscle cells, making them more responsive to mechanical stretches imposed by breathing, which further softens the cells, leading to improved airway distensibility and dilation. The goal of our research is to provide a better alternative for treating asthma.

column36: Does providing a brief Internet intervention for hazardous alcohol use to people seeking online help for depression reduce both alcohol use and depression symptoms among participants with these dual disorders? Randomized controlled trial

Further, there is evidence that excessive alcohol consumption among this group can make their depression worse. There are effective Internet interventions that target hazardous alcohol consumption or depression separately but none that combine these online interventions without the involvement of a therapist. This will allow us to capitalize on the strengths of Internet interventions - 24-hour access, wide availability, and cost efficient delivery of health services. This project proposes to recruit 986 hazardous alcohol consumers with current depression from recent registrants of MoodGYM - the most widely evaluated Internet intervention for depression. Participants will be assigned by chance to receive just MoodGYM or to receive MoodGYM plus an extensively evaluated brief Internet intervention for hazardous alcohol consumption - Check Your Drinking. Participants will be contacted 3 and 6 months after receiving the interventions to assess changes in drinking and depression status. It is predicted that participants receiving the Check Your Drinking intervention in addition to MoodGYM will reduce their alcohol consumption to a greater extent than those who just received MoodGYM. Further predictions include the impact of receiving Check Your Drinking on improvements in depressive symptoms. This research will yield the crucial first steps in developing lower-cost and efficacious Internet interventions for people suffering from depression who also drink in a hazardous fashion - promoting the widespread availability of care for those in need.

column36: Sustaining evidence-based chronic disease management
column37: Canada is a nation of pilot projects, with a lot of resources spent on implementation but failure to address sustainability. If the KT interventions are effective, how do we then sustain (or adapt) them across hospitals? Thus, failure to sustain implementation has implications for cost and patient care and diminishes trust and support for future implementation. This research program is targeted to address this challenge; specifically, our team of clinicians, patients, caregivers, policy makers and researchers will complete research to sustain effective KT interventions to optimise care of older adults with chronic diseases. column37: Up to 80% of schizophrenic patients show disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms. Clinical observations have suggested that the schizophrenia pathology can lead to circadian disturbances, but also that these disturbances can in turn worsen schizophrenia symptoms, and constitute a risk factor for the disease. Here we plan to identify the mechanisms underlying this gene-environment interaction, and to test its impact on cognition and relationship to neurodevelopmental risk factors of schizophrenia. Our work will have a translational potential in developing novel strategies, taking circadian rhythms into consideration, for improving cognition in schizophrenia and other psychiatric conditions.

column36: Optimizing cardiac energy metabolism to treat heart disease
column37: The very high energy demands of the heart are met by continous metabolism of sugars, fatty acids, ketones and amino acids. Normally, there is a balance between the use of these fuels. However, in clinical conditions such as heart failure, myocardial ischemia (i.e. such as following a heart attack), obesity or diabetes, energy production in the heart switches towards an excessive use of fatty acids. This excessive use of fatty acids causes the heart to be less efficient at using energy, which can compromise heart function. Our research has shown that a major contributor to this excessive use of fatty acids is due to changes in the levels of a molecule called malonyl CoA within the heart muscle, and due to an increase in a process caused post-translational acetylation. The studies proposed in this grant application will determine the cellular mechanisms responsible for how malonyl CoA levels and acetylation are regulated in the heart, and how alterations in these processes alters fatty acid use by the heart. We will also determine if preventing the switch from sugar to fatty acid metabolism, can be used as a therapeutic strategy to protect the heart in heart failure or following myocardial ischemia. We will also examine the molecular mechanisms responsible for the maturation of cardiac fatty acid oxidation following birth, and what impact congenital heart defects (that are seen in approximately 2% of infants) has on this maturation of energy metabolism. These experimental studies will be translated into clinical studies in which energy metabolism is optimized to improve heart function in patients with heart failure. Understanding how energy metabolism is regulated in heart should lead to the development of therapies that optimize energy use by the heart and decrease the severity of heart disease.

This might be because researchers test strategies without allowing them to fit with the real-world environment. The goals of this research program are to produce high-quality, relevant knowledge to allow us to design better strategies to improve survivors' follow-up care and to test a strategy based on this knowledge. The focus will be on survivors who have completed their cancer treatment (i.e., surgery, chemotherapy, and/or radiotherapy) and are now cancer-free. Follow-up care is delivered during this period. The research program will involve 4 studies. The first three studies will be carried out to gather information about: (1) what stakeholders' think are the important outcomes during follow-up care; (2) the various strategies that have been used to try to improve outcomes during follow-up care, and how these strategies can be applied in the real world to maximize their benefit; and (3) stakeholders' views on the factors that hinder or help the delivery of follow-up care. Together, this information will inform the development of study 4 - specifically, the design and testing of a follow-up care strategy to improve the outcomes important to stakeholders. Survivors and other key stakeholders will be involved in the entire research process to make sure the studies and findings are relevant to them. This program will help us design cancer survivorship care that is more responsive to stakeholders needs' and more likely to be taken up in practice and policy.

column36: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-host interactions: from mechanisms of viral persistence to infection control
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) remains a global health challenge. Despite the significant advances made over the past decades with respect to our understanding of how HIV causes AIDS, the hope for a definitive cure has been frustrated by the seemingly endless propensity of HIV to subvert host defenses and to persist in long-lived viral reservoirs (VR) that cannot be eliminated by current antiretroviral therapies (ART). While ART have dramatically improved the prognosis for infected individuals, they are not curative because of the persistence of VRs. HIV eludes host immune defenses and establishes VRs in part because it encodes a set of small accessory proteins, whose function is to overcome various types of antiviral immune response. My Team discovered and characterized two of the six accessory proteins encoded by HIV and we are world leaders in understanding the role of these virulence factors in HIV transmission, pathogenesis and persistence. Given their crucial roles in overcoming host defense mechanisms, these accessory proteins are attractive targets for the design of HIV cure strategies aimed at eradicating persistent HIV infection. Our research program will focus primarily on two of the accessory proteins encoded by HIV-1, namely Viral protein U (Vpu) and Viral Protein R (Vpr), to unravel the full spectrum of their activities and better define their functions in HIV persistence, to elucidate how they operate at the molecular and cellular levels and to identify new areas of their biology that are applicable to therapeutic intervention. This work will uncover viral and host targets for HIV persistence reversal and provide new insights that will inform and guide HIV cure strategies. While conducting these studies, our dynamic and forward-looking training and mentoring program will provide trainees with a conceptually and technically deep experience and skills that are sought by employers in academia, government and the private sector

column36: Innate immunity and its disruption by microbial and genetic factors
column37: Approximately 1/150 Canadians have Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD) like Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis. These diseases devastate affected individuals and their families, and significantly burden our health care system. IBD are caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors, including how our bodies interact with bacteria. Genetic studies link IBD to innate immunity. Innate immunity encompasses the tissue and cellular defenses that protect us from infection. Innate immunity allows us to co-exist with the many 'good' bacteria in our guts, and to kill the 'bad' bacteria that we encounter. The factors that regulate innate immunity and its alterations in IBD are not clear. Our research will examine innate immunity in three ways. First, we will study a critical component of innate immunity that is linked to IBD, called autophagy. Autophagy is a process that delivers cellular contents to specialized compartments called lysosomes, where they are broken down. This process protects our cells during stressful conditions like bacterial infections. We will build 'maps' of how the autophagy machinery interacts with other cellular components under normal conditions, and how it changes in IBD. Second, we will study how two bad bacteria, Salmonella and Listeria, hide inside our cells during infection. These bacteria use toxins that disrupt our innate immune defenses, and can teach us how innate immunity is regulated. Third, we will study genes linked to IBD, and ask how they change autophagy and other innate immune defenses. Our studies will advance scientific understanding of how innate immunity controls our interactions with bacteria, and will provide knowledge that can be used to develop new ways to treat IBD.

column36: Neighbourhood Design and Physical Activity: Generating Evidence to Inform Healthy Public Policies
column37: Creating health supportive environments has the potential to improve population-level health, including increasing physical activity participation in Canadian adults. Findings from previous studies suggest that urban planning policies that inform the design of the neighbourhood built environment are associated with physical activity behaviour. These previous findings have had, for the most part, a positive impact on current urban planning policy and practice however, these studies have several major methodological issues, one of which includes the over-reliance on cross-sectional designs that do not allow the temporal direction of associations between the built environment and physical activity to be established. These studies have also typically relied on self-reported measures of physical activity that can over-estimate physical activity levels. Moreover, there is a lack of evidence on the economic value of creating physical activity-supportive neighbourhood environments. Building on my previous research, I will lead a research program that will deliver rigorous causal and economic evidence in a form that can be used by policymakers to create better built environments that support health for all individuals regardless of their socioeconomic circumstances or life-stage. This 5-year research program will: 1) Characterize the relations between neighbourhood design and physical activity, and; 2) Generate evidence on the economic value of neighbourhood design to inform physical activity-supportive urban policies. This research will incorporate natural experimentation with mixed methods and economic analyses, and will advance previous research on neighbourhood design and physical activity by using recent technological advances in physical activity and built environment assessment. The research findings will inform economically sound evidence-based urban policy to improve population health by reconfiguring neighbourhood design to support physical activity.

column36: Mechanisms underlying vulnerability of selective neuronal circuits following early life seizures
column37: One of the most frequent problems in the neonate is the occurrence of lack of oxygen for a short time in the uterus (prenatal period) or during birth (perinatal period). A lack or reduction of oxygen during birth, or birth asphyxia, can often result in lifelong neurological consequences such as learning problems, lower IQ and increased vulnerability for disorders such as cerebral palsy (a disorder of movement and posture), epilepsy or schizophrenia. This problem occurs in approximately 1-6/1000 live births and despite many years of research, there are no available drug therapies to protect brain neurons from ongoing damage once birth asphyxia has occurred. We propose to use new, cutting-edge techniques, which have been recently made available in the neuroscience field to study the cellular and molecular mechanisms that link birth asphyxia to the occurrence of lifelong neurological problems. The neocortex, the outer region of the brain, is composed by two main types of neurons (specialized brain cells): excitatory and inhibitory neurons, that produce glutamate and gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), respectively, as neurotransmitters (a chemical that facilitate communications between brain cells). GABAergic cells are very important for the regulation of brain function and excitability. This group of cells displays a stunning diversity of shapes, functions and ability to change following environmental stimuli. Our hypothesis is that birth asphyxia alters the development of specific types of GABAergic cells. We further hypothesize that these differential effects are in part responsible for the lifelong neurological consequences in adults that experienced birth asphyxia. We propose to study the molecular mechanisms that lead to specific GABAergic cell deficits following birth asphyxia using transgenic mouse models.

column36: Optimizing Combination Strategies for GPNMB-expressing Triple Negative Breast Cancers
column37: BACKGROUND: Breast cancer can be sub-divided into distinct molecular subtypes, including triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), which is associated with the poorest patient outcomes. Unlike other breast cancer subtypes (luminal, Her2+ breast cancer) that have targeted therapeutic agents, TNBCs are treated by surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. GPNMB is a cell surface molecule that promotes tumor growth, invasion and metastasis in human and murine mammary carcinoma models. However the precise molecular mechanisms by which GPNMB induces these effects are largely unknown. Interestingly, we have shown that GPNMB is most highly expressed in TNBC. CDX-011 is a GPNMB-targeted antibody-drug conjugate that has shown robust clinical activity in late-stage clinical trials for breast cancer. Data from clinical trials with CDX-011, as a single agent, reveals that response rate is directly linked to tumoral GPNMB expression. Our preliminary results show that TNBC cells treated with chemotherapy agents, such as Doxorubicin, or targeted inhibitors (MEKi) display increased GPNMB levels. Thus, we hypothesize that that treatment-induced up-regulation of GPNMB will sensitize TNBC cells to CDX-011. OBJECTIVES: We will 1) elucidate intrinsic mechanisms that promote GPNMB-induced breast tumor growth and metastasis, 2) determine how therapeutic stress induces GPNMB expression in TNBCs and 3) assess the efficacy of combining chemotherapy or MAPKi with CDX-011 for treating TNBCs. SIGNIFICANCE: These studies will provide important information regarding how GPNMB promotes breast tumor growth and metastasis. We will also devise effective combination therapy strategies involving CDX-011 that may increase the efficacy of current therapies used to treat TNBC. The research proposed in this application will produce the necessary data to support clinical trials to test such therapeutic combinations.

column36: Cellular and molecular characterization of T cell development for immune-reconstitution
column37: The proposed research focuses on blood cell development, and, in particular, on how a subset of white blood cells, known as T lymphocytes, are generated. T cells are important effectors and master regulators of the immune system, which protects us from cancer and infectious diseases. The thymus is where T cells are generated from progenitor cells that arrive from the bone marrow. The proposed research program aims to understand the molecular controls that initiate and regulate the development of T cells. We have made important breakthroughs by identifying the key molecular interactions (Notch signaling) for inducing T cell development in the thymus, which led to the creation of a simple tissue culture system for the generation of T cells from any source of stem cells. Our work has provided a deeper understanding of the signaling cascades employed during normal thymocyte differentiation, in particular at a stage when T cell lineages bifurcate. Lastly, as mutations in components of these signaling pathways may result in primary immunodeficiencies or lead to oncogenic events, the research to be carried out has clear clinical implications. The overall research program direction is also guided by our recent work showing that transplanting in vitro-generated human progenitor T cells along with bone marrow stem cells into immunodeficient mice results in a dramatic increase in the ability of stem cell-derived cells to give rise to new T cells in the host thymus. This is an important discovery given that stem cell transplants in humans typically fail to regenerate new T cells. The proposed work will ensure that we continue to make important fundamental discoveries as to how Notch signals induce and regulate T cell development, improve upon on how to employ those insights for the generation of human T cells from stem cells, and enable us apply our advances to realize important cell-based immune-reconstitution and immune-therapeutic clinical applications.

column36: Targeting Interferon-beta in leukemia immunotherapy
column37: Dr. Spaner is trying to develop methods to improve the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy. Chemotherapy is the main form of treatment for cancer but cannot cure most types of cancer. Immunotherapy is another form of treatment that tries to stimulate cells of the body's immune system, called T cells, to kill cancer cells. Unfortunately, cancers may become resistant to T cells in the same way they learn to resist chemotherapy. This resistance is due largely to cytokines and other factors that are associated with cancer and suppress the immune system. A drug called Ibrutinib, which is used currently to treat blood cancer patients reduces production of these immunosuppressive factors and helps T cells kill cancer cells. Unfortunately, cancer cells are still able to survive in the presence of Ibrutinib. Dr. Spaner's group has found that Ibrutinib causes the production of a cytokine called Interferon-beta that can continue to suppress the immune system. In this project, Dr. Spaner will try to learn more about how Interferon-beta suppresses T cells and if using drugs that prevent interferon-beta from acting on cancer cells together with Ibrutinib can be a safe and effective way to improve immunotherapy. He will study cancer cells from patients with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), the most common leukemia in Canada, as it is easy to obtain large numbers of cancer cells for experiments, unlike most other cancers. The results of this project are expected to justify using Ibrutinib and Interferon-signaling inhibitors to treat CLL. This approach is expected to increase cure rates with immunotherapy in CLL and also many other forms of cancer.

column36: Pathogenic Pathways and in-vitro modelization of Intracranial Aneurysms in populations of Inuit and French Canadian descent
column37: Intracranial aneurysm (IA) is a common cerebrovascular disorder that can lead to sudden and unpredictable severe complications with devastating consequences for the patients and their families, and implicate huge costs for the health system of Canada. Genetic predisposition has been considered as one of the most significant risk factors for IA based several independent studies. Previous epidemiological studies have shown that certain isolated populations, such as Inuits, are particularly at high risk to develop IA. Over the past 10 years, we have identified 50 individuals with definite brain aneurysm belonging to 25 families from 8 different villages in Nunavik. We have also collected a second cohort of French Canadian people diagnosed with IA, originating from Quebec City. Within this cohort, we have identified and collected 80 families with IA (total of 144 affected individuals and 180 unaffected first-degree relatives). A cohort of 500 sex- and age-matched control individuals has been collected as well. Genetic studies using next generation sequencing was undertaken in order to characterize the specific genetic vulnerability to IA in both Inuits and French Canadians. These two populations, in which founder effect has been well documented, offer advantages for gene mapping of heritable disorders by reducing both the genetic and the environmental heterogeneity. The pathogenecity of genetic DNA variations, identified through next generation sequencing analyses, will be biologically validated using our unique in vitro tissue-engineered patient-derived vascular and microvascular models. We expect to identify and validate a number of genes conferring susceptibility to IA, and to gain insight into the mutational mechanisms and pathogenic pathways of this disease. Also, this approach could provide unique tools to identify "at risk" patients, which would be able to be followed in a timely fashion, allowing the prevention of the devastating outcome of aneurysm rupture.

column36: A clinical decision support tool for diagnostic imaging use for low back pain
column37: Objective: To develop a tool to help doctors make appropriate decisions about the need for diagnostic imaging for patients with low back pain. Rationale: Low back pain is one of the most common and disabling health problems in Canada and the world. In most cases, low back pain resolves without requiring diagnostic imaging (x-ray) and with little treatment. Yet, diagnostic imaging is frequently used for low back pain contrary to recommendations from clinical guidelines. This is despite evidence that diagnostic imaging is of limited value in most cases - exposing patients to unnecessary radiation, increasing health services use and worsening patient outcomes. Currently, no clinical decision support tool is available. Clinical guidelines describe 'red flags' - characteristics of serious cause low back pain such as fracture, or cancer - where diagnostic imaging may be appropriate. However, few studies have evaluated these red flags, contributing to inconsistent recommendations across guidelines. A clinical decision support tool will improve the delivery of appropriate clinical care, and create opportunities for improved patient outcomes and reduced healthcare costs. Methods: Our study population will be patients presenting to five Canadian emergency departments with low back pain, assessed at their emergency department visit, then 3 and 12-months afterwards. We will develop a statistical model to determine which low back pain patients should or should not receive diagnostic imaging. We will then work with clinicians and hospital administrators to convert the statistical model into an easy to use clinical decision support tool. The tool will enable quick and accurate assessment of the need for diagnostic imaging for low back pain. Team: Our team brings extensive expertise in clinical tool development, low back pain research, the clinical management of back pain patients, and implementation science. We regularly consult with a diverse group of Low Back Pain Advisors.

column36: Targeting sleep to optimize brain recovery and slow neurodegeneration
column37: Breakthrough discoveries in rodents have revealed that sleep is crucial for generating neurons, strengthening synapses, and clearing brain waste products. Considering the high prevalence of sleep disorders in the general population, it is now urgent to assess how these new discoveries translate to the human brain. The Foundation grant will allow me to determine whether and how sleep could be a target for slowing down neurodegeneration and optimizing recovery after brain damage in humans. I will achieve this goal by studying 2 clinical populations with vulnerable brain health and sleep disorders: older individuals with obstructive sleep apnea and younger patients with traumatic brain injury. Obstructive sleep affects 20% of individuals after the age of 65. It produces hundreds of awakenings per night and chronic intermittent hypoxia. Sleep apnea impacts brain structure and function in older individuals. How sleep apnea affects long-term brain health with age and whether sleep apnea treatment can slow down neurodegeneration are topical questions. Traumatic brain injury affects mostly young adults and is the main cause of disability in that population. It destroys brain structures and connexions that need regeneration. We found that patients have severe sleep disturbances while they are hospitalized. We need to test whether sleep disturbances inhibit recovery and identify causes of acute sleep disturbances that we could use as a target for treatment. In the next 5 years, I will identify patients with sleep apnea at risk of neurodegeneration. I will produce new evidence regarding the neurodegenerative profile of treated vs. untreated patients. I will identify causes of sleep disturbances occurring after traumatic brain injury and characterize the link between sleep disturbances and brain recovery. My research program has the potential to transform and improve clinical care protocols by including sleep management among treatment priorities.

column36: Non-coding RNA in diabetic kidney disease
column37: Kidney disease caused by diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure in Canada. Currently, the main treatments to stop kidney disease from getting worse in diabetes are medications that lower blood sugar levels and medications that lower blood pressure levels. Although these medications are helpful, they are only partly effective and we need new treatments. RNAs are small molecules that are present in all cells. It has been known for several decades that RNAs pass the genetic code from the DNA in our genes to make proteins, the workhorses of our cells. DNA carries the code for RNA and RNA carries the code for protein. More recently it has come to be appreciated that a large amount of our DNA makes RNA that does not carry a code to make proteins. These RNA molecules are called non-coding RNAs and they can be classified according to their length: long or short. Although long non-coding RNAs do not code for proteins they do have important roles in cells, like helping to turn genes on or off, acting as scaffolds or helping other RNA molecules to make proteins. Long non-coding RNAs often go wrong in disease but their contribution to the development of diabetic kidney disease is essentially unknown. Through our earlier work, we have discovered that the amount of a particular long non-coding RNA, called HOTAIR, is increased in diabetic kidney disease and that blocking its actions helps protect special kidney cells, called podocytes, from damage caused by high sugar levels. In this project, we will conduct a series of experiments to explore the role of HOTAIR in the development of diabetic kidney disease and to determine whether blocking HOTAIR can protect against kidney damage. These studies will provide important new information about the previously underappreciated actions of non-coding RNA in diabetic kidney disease, with long non-coding RNA blocking therapy being a plausible new treatment for the condition.

column36: Role of HMG CoA reductase protective and risk variants in the pathophysiology and treatment of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
column37: The brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) begin several years before the onset of cognitive changes; there is currently no prevention and no cure for the disease. This proposed study will use resources from the Centre for Studies in the Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease and the Douglas-Bell Brain Bank in Montreal to examine the neurobiology and the mode of action of a series of novel genetic variants in a gene called HMG CoA reductase, which were found to either accelerate or slow down the progression of the disease in the years prior to diagnosis. column37: The two most common inherited bleeding disorders, von Willebrand disease (VWD) and hemophilia A (HA), are the result of deficiencies and/or dysfunction of two critical proteins in the human blood clotting system - von Willebrand factor (VWF) and factor VIII (FVIII). We will continue studies that have been ongoing in our group for the past 25 years aimed at understanding basic and translational aspects of VWF and FVIII. We will use genetic approaches to determine the basis for the 35% of type 1 VWD patients in whom mutations in the VWF gene have not been identified, and will investigate whether the VWF propeptide has an independent clotting function. The second area of focus will evaluate risk factors for the development of an adverse immune response to FVIII therapy in HA, a complication of treatment in ~30% of these patients. We will determine the influence of VWF on FVIII immunity, and will explore the role of the host gut microbiome as a risk factor for FVIII antibody development. In the final phase of this proposal, we will conduct two complementary series of experiments that address the safety and efficacy of gene therapy approaches for the treatment of HA. Using our unique canine hemophilia resource, we will first determine the vector integration patterns following long-term adeno-associated viral vector gene transfer, and will then compare these outcomes with a novel foamy viral vector-based approach.

column36: Novel Approaches Directed to Prevention and Treatment of Huntington Disease
column37: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited brain disease that affects approximately 1 in 7300 people in the Western world. HD is caused by a mutation in one copy of the HTT gene, which produces a toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This mutant protein disrupts many vital cellular functions and is ultimately responsible for the brain cell death associated with HD. There is no treatment for this disease. We propose targeting different steps of the disease process, including suppression of the mutant HTT gene, increasing clearance of the mutant protein, and inhibiting its toxic effects to advance complementary therapies for treating HD. One therapeutic strategy to prevent production of mHTT is to silence (or turn off) the mutant HTT gene using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeted to genetic variations found in mutant HTT. Our goal is to develop multiple ASO drugs targeting the most common genetic variations in HD patients, maximizing the number that could be treated through gene silencing of mutant HTT. ASOs are unable to enter the brain when delivered in the blood and must be injected directly into the fluid that bathes the brain. This procedure is invasive, and ASOs delivered this way do not reach all susceptible areas of the brain. Therefore, we are developing new non-invasive ways to enhance delivery of ASOs to the brain. Another strategy is to reduce levels of mHTT protein by increasing its degradation in the cell through a process called autophagy. Autophagy is abnormally reduced in HD which may be due to altered protein modifications of mHTT. We will target specific mechanisms that could increase clearance of mHTT from the cell and reduce its toxicity. Our final therapeutic strategy is to target pathways that are disrupted by the presence of toxic mHTT. We are investigating the effect of modifying molecular components of these pathways using small molecules to promote protection and survival of brain cells, and in the long run improve patient outcomes.

column36: Seeking Molecular Signatures for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
column37: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a unique cancer of the head & neck region, wherein most diagnosed patients are relatively young (peak incidence between 40-45 years) and have advanced disease; the 5-year overall survival rate of such patients is a dismal 65%. These patients typically die from the distant spread of their cancer, known as distant metastasis. Currently, we do not have any clinically useful biomarkers to distinguish patients who will develop metastasis versus those who will not. Furthermore, we do not understand why some patients respond to treatment yet others do not. Our group recently identified a potential "molecular signature", based on the analyses of biological molecules called "micro-RNAs" that are produced by the tumor. The signature is capable of predicting which patients will develop distant metastasis. The objectives of this proposal are to: 1. Validate the molecular signature on a separate group of NPC samples to confirm its clinical applicability; 2. Incorporate other types of biological molecules (DNA, mRNA) into the molecular signature to identify their usefulness; 3. Discover the underlying mechanisms by which the molecular signature works; and 4. Evaluate the utility of blood-related molecular signatures as a way to assess NPC aggressiveness. At the completion of these proposed studies, we will have developed the most informative molecular signature in terms of predicting metastasis for NPC patients and evaluated the underlying biology. This molecular signature may then be used to aid in the clinical management of future patients; patients who will experience metastasis may be treated with more aggressive therapies, while those who will not relapse may be spared the side-effects of harsher treatments. All the generated data will be shared with the medical community. Ultimately, this project will advance our goal of personalized cancer therapy for NPC patients, which will have significant national and global impact.
