column36: In vivo regulation of stem cell division and self-renewal
column37: The human body is composed of billions of cells that largely have specialized properties, allowing them to sustain the normal function of the organs and tissues where they reside. Among these, stem cells are unique in that their divisions are important to regenerate the various tissues of our organs. Stem cells must divide in a way that enables tissue regeneration without loss of the stem cell pool, a process known as self-renewal. Proper regulation of stem cell division and self-renewal must be tightly controlled, because defects in these process can have deleterious consequences to an organ's function and thus be a primary cause of disease. For instance, stem cell division without self-renewal can lead to the atrophy of an organ or tissue, and thus compromise its function, while stimulating uncontrolled proliferation in stem cells can result in cancer. Understanding the fundamental aspects of stem cell division in an in vivo context is therefore crucial to identify the critical steps that govern their properties and devise novel strategies to exert control over their self-renewal. The objective of this project is to study how stem cells divide in vivo and understand what molecules control this process. I tackle this problem using a small nematode worm as experimental model, allowing me to use various methods that are not feasible in humans. The stem cells of this nematode worm divide very much like human cells and use essentially the same building blocks to go through the process, and therefore our findings in this model organism will greatly inform on human stem cells. As such, they help to guide the experimental design of approaches aimed at the development of novel therapeutics for cell proliferation-based diseases in humans.

column36: Protease-activated receptor (PAR)-2: A novel effector of mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel diseases
column37: The inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, affect over 200,000 Canadians. These are lifelong, debilitating conditions that have no clear cause, no cure, and which have significant costs to the health care system and patient quality of life. For unknown reasons, Canada has the highest incidence of IBD in the world. Unfortunately, current therapies are costly, ineffective for some patients, and can have serious side effects. We need to understand the underlying causes of IBD so that we can develop better treatments and, ultimately, find a cure. Our research team is studying the epithelium, the layer of cells that lines the intestinal wall and which provides an important barrier between the trillions of bacteria in the intestinal lumen and the immune system of the intestine. Over-activation of the immune system by gut bacteria plays an important role in IBD. We know that the epithelial barrier breaks down in IBD, and we think this may be an important contributor to these diseases. We hypothesize that a specific type of protein receptor on epithelial cells, protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2), may play a role in the resolution of the inflammatory response and speed healing. In this proposal, we have set three aims to test our hypothesis. First, we are going to measure the enzymes that activate PAR2 in IBD tissue. We will then see if they act through PAR2 to turn on genes that control the healing process. Second, we are going to use new cell culture methods in epithelial cells derived from mouse intestine and intestinal biopsies from consenting IBD patients to determine how PAR2 alters epithelial cell behaviour, especially cell migration, to speed healing. Third, we are going to test these PAR2-mediated effects in mouse models of disease, to see if they are appropriate targets for therapy. Ultimately, our proposed research will identify avenues for the development of new treatments for IBD.

column36: Beyond the Exome: Decoding the Next Frontier of the Rare Disease Genome
column37: Around 7000 rare genetic diseases (RDs) affect more than 1 million Canadians, most of them children. When considered together, RDs are a common cause of disability, early mortality, and healthcare costs. Over the past several years my research program has efficiently examined the protein-coding portion of the genome (~1%) to understand the cause of many RDs; however, as many as 60% of patients remain undiagnosed after this analysis. These patients often undergo a diagnostic journey involving multiple specialist consultations, imaging studies, invasive investigations, and other laboratory and genetic tests; a slow (5 to 30 years for 25%) process referred to as the diagnostic odyssey. These families are faced with significant uncertainty surrounding treatment, prognosis and the chances of future children or other family members also being affected. The goal of my research is to understand the genetic cause of unsolved RDs to end the diagnostic journey for as many Canadians with RD as possible. Given the rarity of all of the diseases we study, my program will help design and employ international RD patient data-sharing so that we, and indeed all RD scientists, can readily identify families with the same disease and changes in the same gene to prove causality. To look more broadly, my program will use the latest and most comprehensive technologies to examine a person's entire genome to identify the genetic cause of unsolved RDs. Finally, my program will develop new tests to determine whether a given genetic change has an impact on protein function. The outputs of my RD research program will lead to new insights into human biology in health and disease, develop novel diagnostic tools and tailor management to improve the care for Canadians with RDs, while enhancing global synergy, thereby ensuring continuing Canadian leadership in this realm.

column36: Regulation of hippocampal network and memory by inhibitory interneuron synaptic plasticity
column37: GABAergic interneurons are the major inhibitory cells in the brain and they play a crucial role in controlling the excitability of projection cells in neuronal networks. They are multiple types of inhibitory interneurons which regulate neuronal activity in distinct ways. They are essential for normal brain function and are implicated in many CNS disorders, including epilepsy, autism, Rett syndrome, anxiety disorder, Tourette syndrome, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. However the specific role of the different types of inhibitory interneurons has been difficult to elucidate because of the large diversity of these cells. The hippocampus is an excellent model system to determine the role of inhibitory interneurons in cortical networks because of its highly ordered, well-defined anatomical architecture and its known function in learning and memory. We take advantage of new transgenic mice and molecular biological approaches that allow cell-specific manipulations in certain subtypes of interneurons. We build on our previous work and carry out a comprehensive study of the function of a specific class of GABA interneurons that provide dendritic inhibition and regulate hippocampal network plasticity underlying memory consolidation. Identifying and elucidating such network contributions of identified interneurons shed new light on the inhibitory control of neuronal networks in the brain at the molecular, cellular, network and system levels. These are necessary first steps in developing new approaches to tackle the important health problems associated with CNS disorders implicating memory deficits and GABAergic interneurons.

column36: Identifying translational regions underlying synaptic plasticity

column36: Targeting GABA-A receptors to mitigate postanesthetic cognitive deficits
column37: General anesthetics are an essential component of modern medical care. Each year, millions of patients undergo anesthesia worldwide. Despite their widespread use, general anesthetics are inherently unsafe and their molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Such lack of knowledge has stalled the discovery of safer anesthetics and the development of treatments for their adverse effects. Our research program addresses three questions that have perplexed scientists for over a century: How do anesthetics depress brain function? What are their adverse effects? How can such adverse effects be treated? We discovered a mechanism and potential treatments for a major adverse effect: persistent postanesthetic cognitive deficits. The results are important because many patients experience long-term cognitive deficits and delirium after anesthesia and surgery. Such cognitive deficits are associated with poor long-term outcomes, increased mortality, and higher healthcare costs. The causes are unknown, and no effective treatments are available. We showed that anesthetics target both astrocytes (the most abundant support cells in the brain) and neurons. Activation of anesthetic-sensitive sensors in astrocytes may cause both the desired, acute memory-blocking effects of anesthetics and the undesired, persistent cognitive deficits. Anesthetics stimulate astrocytes to release soluble factors. These factors modify the function of neurons, which causes persistent cognitive deficits that last long after the anesthetics have been eliminated. We will determine how astrocyte-neuron crosstalk causes both the desired and undesired effects of anesthetics. We will also develop new treatments based on our patented drugs and other newly discovered compounds. Overall, this research program will advance our understanding of anesthetic mechanisms and will allow the development of new treatments to ensure that patients don't simply survive anesthesia but thrive in the postoperative period.

column36: Role for metabotropic glutamate receptors in Huntington's disease
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a devastating autosomal dominant inherited neurodegenerative disorder that is characterized by progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric impairments. In addition, the proposed experiments will allow us to examine the role autophagy in HD, as well as help determine whether huntingtin aggregates are contributory to the HD disease process.

To do our research, we will use cultured cells, mouse brain slices, mouse behavior testing, electrophysiology, microscopy and biochemical assays to identify the SAP102 mechanisms controlling the crosstalk between D1 and glutamate receptors. It is hoped that our research will improve our knowledge of the crosstalk between the SAP102, the D1 receptor and the glutamate receptor in normal and diseased brains. We believe that our research will help developing novel drugs that target specifically the cross-talk between these three proteins to restore normal dopamine and glutamate function in individuals suffering from mental illnesses such as Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia.

column37: Our ability to encode, store and retrieve past experience in rich contextual details (episodic memory) declines with age and can be an early sign of Alzheimer's disease (AD).Our previous fMRI research showed that context memory tasks are more sensitive than recognition memory tasks at detecting early signs of episodic memory decline with healthy aging. Importantly, midlife is a time of transition from pre/peri-menopause to menopause in MA females and is associated with decreased endogenous estrogen levels, which can negatively impact memory. In our prior work, 70-80% of our MA samples were females. As such it is not clear if our prior findings generalize across the sexes and what aspects of our previous results may have be driven by the menopausal status of females. Moreover, given that there are more females diagnosed with AD compared to males, after controlling for sex differences in life expectancy, it is also important to explore if known risk factors for AD, i.e. having and apolipoprotein E e4 allele (+APOE4), differentially impacts females vs. males at midlife. The goal of the current study is to extend our prior work on midlife brain aging and episodic memory and investigate how biological sex, menopausal status, and +APOE4 status impacts the neural correlates of episodic memory in MA using functional and structural magnetic resonance imaging methods. This work is significant because our results will help determine if +APOE4 impacts memory and brain structure/function in females > males by midlife, and if this effect interacts with female menopausal status. This data will ultimately help refine our ability to identify adults at risk of developing AD at an age when intervention may be most beneficial

column37: Dr. Mona Loutfy is recognized as a national and international leader in the area of women, reproductive health, and HIV. She founded the Women and HIV Research Program in 2006, which uses community-based research to carry out research that is deemed most essential to women living with and at risk of HIV. This Foundation Grant will move the Research Program to exciting new areas with three goals: 1) finalizing a new model of care (the Women-centred HIV Care Model) aimed at optimizing the health and wellbeing of women with HIV in Canada, particularly those at increased risk of HIV including Indigenous women and trans women; 2) disseminating created knowledge on Reproductive Health and HIV (i.e. the 2018 Canadian HIV Pregnancy Planning Guidelines); and 3) mentoring and training the next generation of researchers, clinicians and community partners that will focus on health equity for women with and at risk of HIV. A novel aspect of this Grant is the building of a Canadian Trans Women and HIV Research Initiative - a timely endeavour given the current climate of trans health and the Prime Minister's submission for the inclusion of gender identify, Bill C-16, in the Canadian Human Rights Act in 2016. Another exciting component of this Grant is the partnering with Indigenous researchers and leaders to further research for the wellbeing of Indigenous women living with and at risk of HIV. This will be done using the principles of Truth and Reconciliation of Canada, Indigenous ethical guidelines including First Nations, Inuit and Metis guidelines and "Two-eyed Seeing" research methods. Dr. Loutfy has worked as an ally to Indigenous researchers and leaders for a decade and is committed to continuing this work by contributing to strength-based and culturally-grounded research with Indigenous women. This will include working with Elders and Knowledge Keepers and Indigenous women themselves. She successfully did similar work with racialized Black women for the prior 12 years.

column36: Impact of transitioning to secondary schools on health behaviours associated with obesity and academic related outcomes: A socio-ecological perspective
column37: In developed countries, including Canada, rates of being overweight and obese in children have increased substantially. Lack of physical activity, too much sedentary time, and poor dietary habits all contribute to unhealthy weight trajectories. Adolescence is a period when many unhealthy behaviours emerge or escalate. Most notably, we and others find that these problems are exacerbated during the transition from elementary to secondary school. Our goal is to examine factors that influence adolescents' physical activity, sedentary time and dietary habits as they transition from elementary to secondary school. We will use qualitative and quantitative methods (interviews, surveys & direct measures) to determine changes that occur in the school, household and social settings during this transition to identify how they influence adolescent health behaviours. We will also determine if health behaviours relate to academic performance. First, we will collect health and related data in grades 7 and 8 (before/after the transition to a new school) from 736 students/parents from 49 schools in BC. We will assess health behaviours (physical activity, sedentary time & dietary intake) and school (access, availability, opportunity, environmental context), household (modeling, access & availability, parenting practices & styles, family environment), and social (modeling, co-participation, norms) influences. Then, to better understand and interpret data from questionnaires and direct measures, we will interview 40 student/parent pairs before and after the transition. Our findings will provide new insights into how school, household and social environments contribute to health behaviour during the transition to secondary school. In future, our data can be used to develop targeted programs to address these factors and encourage more positive behaviours at adolescence. Ultimately, we aim to alter the current trajectory towards increased health risk among Canada's youth.

column36: Promoting Brain Health to Prevent Dementia: Roles of Covert Vascular Brain Injury and Cognitive Reserve in Age-Related Cognitive Decline
column37: Dementia is Canada's largest, and growing, public health problem, affecting more than 500,000 Canadians and costing more than either cardiovascular disease or cancer. There is encouraging evidence that, for persons of a given age, the risk for dementia has decreased somewhat. Other scientists have proposed that this is because people's brains are healthier (that is, that they have more cognitive reserve) or that they are less like to get silent strokes (small strokes seen on brain scans in people at risk for cognitive decline), but without proof. Meanwhile, the risk for Alzheimer's disease has probably not changed, and it remains incurable. My Foundation program is designed to identify the factors that promote healthier brain aging and lower risk of silent strokes, and to explore new ways of diagnosing and monitoring symptomatic patients. My background in neurology, epidemiology, and neuroimaging has prepared me well for this work. At the University of Calgary I have established one of the world's largest brain MRI analysis centres. Leading a national team of Program Experts, I will examine risk for stroke and cognitive decline in persons recruited from the community in two studies (with 9,700 and 1,500 participants) all of whom have had a brain MRI. We will repeat the brain MRI in six years in 1,500 to see who has had new silent strokes or excessive brain tissue loss (i.e., atrophy). We will look at many potential protective factors including education, occupation, income, diet, physical activity, social activities, and stress levels. In another study I will examine markers of disease-related brain changes in persons with Alzheimer's disease and a related blood vessel condition called cerebral amyloid angiopathy. These studies will point to effective strategies to promote brain health and to diagnose and monitor symptomatic patients.

column36: Targeting the Mammalian Mitochondrial Interactome to Dissect Macromolecular Assemblies and Pathways in Health and Disease
column37: Mitochondria (mt) generate the majority of a cell's energy supply, which is consumed by neurons in the brain to execute diverse cellular functions. Beyond its essential role, defects in mitochondrial protein (MP) function can cause or contribute to neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), for which no effective long-term cure currently exists. This is likely owing to the central involvement of MPs in a myriad of interconnected essential functions in neurons, including the quality control (QC) systems that support cellular homeostasis by maintaining healthy mt for proper neuronal function and integrity. However, impairment in QC during energy demands causes accumulation of damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria, resulting in neuronal death. Despite detailed mechanistic investigations of individual MPs, our understanding of the relationship between how all human MPs globally function and interact together at the level of complexes and cellular pathways still remains incomplete. Emerging evidence suggests that QC systems play a key role in the development of Parkinson's disease (PD), and potentially influences mt homeostasis and neuronal death. While this presents an avenue for therapeutic development, the intricate network of interacting MPs in complexes/pathways is not yet fully understood, hindering progress. My proposal aims at addressing the aforesaid gaps by drawing on our recent advances in proteomic and genetic platforms to provide the first high-resolution view on the molecular organization and mechanistic operation of human MP assemblies, and to uncover the pathway-level relationships for genes encoding the components of QC machineries linked to PD. This work will yield molecular models for new binding partners in mt processes, provide valuable data resources for the community, facilitate discovery of potential new therapeutic targets for NDs, and inspire further research into novel treatments for sustainable health care.

column36: Porphyrin Nanomedicine for Cancer Imaging and Therapy
column37: Despite decades of research, applying cancer nanomedicine for patient care still faces many challenges including inefficient nanoparticle delivery to tumours, safety concerns associated with inorganic nanomaterials, the diverse architecture of tumours, and over-complexity in nanoparticle design. In 2011, we discovered first-in-class organic nanoparticles, termed porphysomes, with the ability to address these limitations. They are non-toxic, being made from lipid (i.e., fat) and natural pigment porphyrins (i.e., chlorophyll in plants and heme in blood). Furthermore, they are simple in design, yet can exhibit multifunctional imaging and therapeutic properties, stemming from a single porphyrin-lipid building block. These diverse properties include the ability to bind metals, and transform locally delivered light energy into heat, sound waves or chemicals toxic to cancer cells. In this Foundation Project, we will build upon porphysomes' inherent multifunctionality to expand knowledge and address key issues in cancer nanomedicine, phototherapy, and drug delivery through the creation of a new generation of porphyrin biomaterials: 1) porphyrin microbubbles and biomimetic porphyrin nanoparticles able to effectively target brain tumour therapy beyond the blood-brain barrier; 2) porphyrin nanoparticles that harness the immune system to enhance lung cancer therapy; 3) stimuli-responsive porphyrin nanoparticles that improves phototherapy efficacy and safety; 4) nanoparticles made of expanded porphyrin molecules with the ability to bind metals for nuclear and radiation medicine. The clinical translation of these materials will be facilitated via our fifth Program pillar, which establishes clinical safety and efficacy of prototypical porphysome. Ultimately, the outcome of this program will be the development of clinically relevant materials that realize the potential of cancer nanomedicine in improving current cancer therapy regimens.

column36: Improving health equity for LGBTQ youth in Canada and globally: Addressing the role of families and culture
column37: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, Two Spirit and queer (LGBTQ) adolescents face persistent health gaps compared to their straight and cisgender peers in Canada and globally. Is it getting better? Our Stigma and Resilience Among Vulnerable Youth Centre at UBC has developed leading evidence to answer this question: some health gaps are narrowing, but only for some LGBTQ youth (mostly gay boys) and these trends are not yet documented for rural or ethnoculturally diverse LGBTQ youth. Likewise, families are important sources of support for adolescents, but trends show parental support for LGBTQ youth is not improving. Interventions are needed to help all families better support their LGBTQ youth, and to reach youth and families in rural areas. Our Vision: to reduce stigma, foster resilience, and improve health equity for LGBTQ youth in Canada and throughout the world. Our 7-year program of research has 4 primary aims: 1) to track trends in health and health disparities for LGBTQ youth from diverse ethnocultural groups in Canada, Europe, and New Zealand; 2) to identify how families reject or support LGBTQ youth in different cultural groups in these same regions, and examine the link between family support and LGBTQ youth health; 3) develop and test new culturally-relevant on-line and smartphone-based interventions to build parental support and lower family rejection of LGBTQ youth; and 4) develop & test similar technology-based health promotion interventions for diverse and rural LGBTQ youth. Our participatory mixed-methods approaches will use population-based surveys, on-line focus groups, longitudinal research methods, and pilot tests of on-line and text message interventions. With our team of experts from Canada, the USA, New Zealand, and Europe, we will identify culturally-specific knowledge to improve clinical care of LGBTQ youth and families, and create new, culturally relevant family and youth interventions, to narrow the health gaps for LGBTQ youth.

column37: Over half of Canadians are overweight or obese. Obesity leads to higher levels of blood insulin and glucose. These are features of prediabetes, which leads to type 2 diabetes. Diabetes has serious consequences to our health and economy. Even prediabetes contributes to over 2 million annual deaths worldwide. Existing treatments help control blood sugar usually by increasing insulin. However, existing treatments focus on glucose, but do not address the root cause of prediabetes progression during obesity. Higher insulin can accelerate obesity and promote "insulin resistance". The discovery of insulin has saved many lives by controlling blood sugar. Now we need to stop the progression of prediabetes. After every meal or snack containing sugars, insulin is secreted and then cleared from the blood. Obesity slows clearance of insulin, exposing the body to more insulin. This can add up over time to further worsen obesity and prediabetes. Drugs that change insulin clearance all the time (not just after a meal) have failed and we still do not have good weight loss drugs that change eating behaviour or the body's ability to burn more energy. It is very important to discover ways to reduce the repeated exposure of the body to prolonged insulin after each meal. A key problem was that we did not understand enough about what changes insulin levels after eating. My lab discovered that bacteria in the gut produce factors that can lower insulin. The trillions of bacteria in our gut are an untapped source of new drugs. My lab has already found one part of bacteria that makes insulin work better. The next step is finding out how bacteria are sensed by the immune system to alter insulin. This research will combine unique resources across Canada to find out which parts of bacteria can be used to stop or slow prediabetes. This research may lead to new ways to target insulin and the development of prediabetes, which are different from the current drugs that focus on blood glucose.

column36: Origins, Consequences and Outcomes of Neuroprogression in First Episode Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is an illness that causes a high degree of personal disability, caregiver burden, and societal impact. Despite the advances in medical, psychological and social aspects of care in the last 60 years, less than 1 in 7 people with schizophrenia achieve paid employment. Existing treatments have a good effect on reducing 'positive' symptoms of schizophrenia (hearing voices, having false beliefs), but currently, there are no treatments to reduce the 'negative' (reduced motivation, interests, and activity) and 'cognitive' symptoms that are central to the persistent disability seen in many patients. We lack understanding of what brain processes, when affected, produce these resistant symptoms. One promising area is to look at the process of continuous loss of brain tissue that occurs in this illness. Patients who have poor outcomes have a higher rate of brain tissue loss; abnormalities in brain's innate defense mechanisms against infection may contribute to continued tissue loss. We now have very sophisticated brain-imaging facilities that allow us to study this over the course of illness using the magnetic field. As these brain scans are non-invasive and do not involve harmful radiation, we can repeat them multiple times. We propose to study patients experiencing the first episode of schizophrenia and follow them up over 1 year to assess the course of change in brain tissue and symptoms. The objective of this study is to develop an insight on the triggers of tissue loss and how it eventually leads to a poor outcome, enabling us to discover treatments to reverse this process. There are several protective treatments that can prevent brain tissue damage, but we must first identify the right patients to treat. Treating intractable cognitive, negative and persistent positive symptoms could potentially result in a reversal of functional deterioration to an appreciable extent and promote patients' journey towards recovery from this debilitating illness.

column36: Behavioural, neuroimaging, and connectome studies of the medial temporal lobe in healthy and epileptic brains
column37: The medial temporal lobe (MTL) is a brain network that plays an important role in memory, spatial navigation, and social cognition. Pathology of this region has been observed in several neurological conditions, including temporal lobe epilepsy, the most common drug-resistant epilepsy in adults. In addition to seizures, epileptic patients often present with difficulties in memory and emotional wellbeing, likely due to damage to the MTL. Many patients undergo surgery to treat the seizures. However, some may show further memory deficits and emotional problems after the operation, which may ultimately impact their quality of life. This research program is centered on assessing whether these problems can be understood through a comprehensive evaluation of the anatomy and wiring of the different elements in the MTL. We will integrate high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging of MTL microstructure, function, and connectivity, and relate these markers with memory and emotion regulation scores obtained in behavioral studies. By studying epileptic patients before and after surgery, we can evaluate consequences of temporal lobe resection on brain networks mediating these cognitive and affective skills. The program builds on my expertise in studying the MTL and my experience in assessing how neuroimaging markers relate to cognitive outcomes in healthy and epileptic populations. It will provide a foundational account of how impairments following surgery can be understood and prevented. In particular, integrated investigations of the functional and psychological aspects of MTL anatomy will advance theoretical perspectives concerning the role of this brain network in memory and emotional processing. Our framework may help to predict surgical outcomes in epileptic patients, and identify candidates suitable for targeted rehabilitative therapies.

column36: Nouveau paradigme de traitement optimise par corset de la scoliose idiopathique de l'adolescent
column37: La scoliose est une deformation de la colonne vertebrale affectant 2-4% des adolescents. Le traitement par corset est le seul traitement conservateur efficace pour limiter la progression de la deformation. C'est un traitement difficile pour les jeunes (inconfort, atteinte de l'image de soi, limitation des activites) qui doivent porter cette orthese rigide 20 a 23 hres/jr durant toute la croissance. L'efficacite du traitement est reliee au temps de port du corset. Toutefois, il existe un probleme inquietant de participation au traitement car en moyenne, le corset n'est porte que 12 hres/jr. Cette non-participation du patient a porter son corset mene assurement a l'echec du traitement. Les objectifs de ce projet sont de mieux cibler les sujets a traiter; offrir un corset plus efficace pour corriger la deformation; developper un questionnaire de mesure de qualite de vie et de confort du corset et mettre en place une equipe d'intervenants pour encourager une meilleure adhesion au traitement. Notre equipe travaillera a changer radicalement le traitement par corset en selectionnant mieux les candidats a traiter en evaluant le risque de progression de leur scoliose afin d'eviter de porter un corset inutilement, et en offrant un corset plus efficace pour les patients qui sont a risque de progression. Nous analyserons aussi les resultats du questionnaire pour verifier sa capacite a informer le personnel sur les raisons du refus au traitement et nous interviendrons aupres du patient non-adherent selon ses besoins. Cette nouvelle approche ameliorera la correction apportee par le corset afin d'amener un meilleur taux de succes au traitement qu'obtenu precedemment. Notre nouveau corset devrait etre plus confortable, mieux tolere et donc apprecie des patients. Finalement, l'equipe transmettra les outils developpes dans ce programme afin que les technologies et les interventions demontrees efficaces soient disponibles pour tous les patients dans les centres specialises.

column36: Ubiquitination of histone H2B in B cell immunobiology and cancer
column37: The immune system plays a major role in protecting humans from bacteria, viruses, and toxins (known as antigens). One of the ways that the immune system accomplishes this is by producing antibodies that bind to and neutralize these antigens. Antibodies are small molecules made by B cells. Each B cell makes only one type of antibody which will bind to only one antigen. By changing the antibody stalk, the properties of the antibody are changed. For example, IgM antibodies can be changed to IgG antibodies which can be used by macrophages to engulf bacteria that are coated by these antibodies, or to IgA antibodies that can be secreted into mucosal tissue and can neutralize pathogens in the lung or the gut. Changing the antibody class is accomplished by the class switch recombination process, and the key enzyme that initiates this process is called AID. Much still needs to be investigated about how class switch recombination is accomplished in B cells and the enzymes that are involved. We have recently identified novel genes that function in class switch recombination, namely RNF20, RNF40, and USP22, and propose to investigate how these genes function in this process using cell lines. Our current work suggests it functions by repairing DNA breaks that occur in B cells. We have also made mice where we can specifically delete USP22 in any tissue of our choice. We will specifically delete USP22 in B cells to determine whether B cell development and class switch recombination require USP22. Hence, our proposed work will allow us to determine how an effective antibody response is generated. Since enzymes involved in DNA repair are typically found to suppress tumor development, and because AID and the class switch recombination process are linked to the development of lymphomas, we will also test whether USP22 is critical for the development of lymphomas and colon cancer.

column36: Novel therapy for Hyperkalemic Periodic Paralysis (HyperKPP)
column37: Hyperkalemic Periodic Paralysis (HyperKPP) is a neuromuscular disease that is characterized by periods of myotonia weakness and paralysis. Few treatment options are available to patients suffering of HyperKPP, and in many cases they lose efficacy over time. Using a HyperKPP mouse model, we first found that HyperKPP muscles are weaker than normal; i.e., they generate less force. Then, we found that activating two proteins in the cell membrane, an ion transporter and one ion channel, can provide a novel therapy that fully restores force development back to normal levels. There is also evidence that the activity of two of these proteins can be increased using a drug that activates protein kinase A (PKA). This is advantageous because a single drug can be used to activate PKA instead of two drugs, reducing the extent of side effects. More importantly, it is proposed to test the efficacy of three already Federal Drug Administration (FDA) approved drugs that are used to treat various diseases via an activation of protein kinase A. In a first series of experiments, we will determine in vitro how effective each of three drugs is at increasing force generation in HyperKPP muscles toward that of normal muscles. In a second series of experiments, we will treat HyperKPP mice with the most effective drug to determine how effective they are at improving force generation over long period of time; i.e., to make sure they do not lose effectiveness over time. If successful, the ultimate aim will be to initiate clinical trials.

column36: Cortical and basal ganglia mechanisms in movement disorders
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the commonest neurodegenerative diseases. It is due to dysfunction of parts the brain known as the basal ganglia and the cortex, and different parts of the brain are abnormally connected to each other. Theme 1 of the research program will use several state of the art techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging, magnetoencephalography and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to determine how the connections in the brain are altered in PD. We will develop novel treatment to normalize these connections. Theme 2 will define the inhibitory functions of the basal ganglia that are particularly relevant to impulse control disorder and gait disturbance in PD. Electrical activities of the basal ganglia will be directly recorded from deep brain stimulation (DBS) electrodes implanted in the basal ganglia and with stimulation applied at selected times during inhibition tasks to define the role of the basal ganglia in inhibitory functions. Theme 3 will promote changes in the brain by combining a surface magnetic brain stimulation technique (TMS) with DBS, and will test this approach as a novel treatment for PD. Theme 4 will determine how electrical activities in deep brain structures are related to different clinical states of PD patients. We will use this information to develop new DBS systems that will automatically adjust stimulation parameters depending on the clinical status to produce the optimal stimulation effects. This will lead to new and improved DBS treatment for PD. The program will be conducted by the Program Leader with a group of Program Experts who are established investigators with diverse expertise. It provides an excellent training environment for future researchers. The findings will advance our knowledge of PD, and lead to improved treatment for PD patients.

column37: At present, there are 4.6 million Canadians living with the pain of arthritis for which there are inadequate drug treatments. Current medications provide only limited pain relief and most drugs have significant negative side-effects. Thus, there is an urgent need to discover novel, more effective analgesics with low toxicity. During arthritis, enzymes are released into the joint which cause damage to the cartilage, bone and ligaments. In addition to the digesting effects of these enzymes, they can also signal pain and inflammation by acting on specific targets called PARs. We have shown that these PARs are present on nerves in the joint and we believe that one mechanism by which enzymes signal pain is by stimulating these PARs. We hypothesise that PAR activation can lead to nerve damage and consequently arthritis pain. In this project, we plan to identify the enzymes responsible for joint nerve injury and pain. We will also test drugs that block PARs to see if we can protect joint nerves from further damage and uncover a new way of alleviating arthritis pain.

column36: Improving Transition of Care and Outcomes of Cardiovascular Disease Using an Innovative Big Data Approach
column37: Heart disease continues to pose a significant burden on healthcare systems in Canada and around the world. Each year, more than 600,000 patients present to the emergency department for chest pain assessment, more than 80,000 patients are hospitalized with a heart attack, and more than 60,000 patients undergo coronary angioplasty to treat heart blockages in Canada. Although there have been significant advancements in the prevention and management of heart disease, patients continue to be at risk for serious events. For example, heart attack patients have a ~10% chance of dying and ~40% chance of being readmitted to the hospital in the first year after their initial events. Emerging data suggest many adverse events occur because the care during transitions of patients from hospital to home, or from the emergency department, is suboptimal. This proposal consists of a series of innovative, large-scale projects that will close the gap in the quality of care received by heart disease patients during care transitions. We will examine how to measure care properly, assess the current level of care, and understand what the drivers of these deficiencies are. Next, we will create tools to help patients and clinicians in order to improve the quality of care. Lastly, we will create a Learning Health System so that we can align the priorities of patients, clinicians and policy makers. The ultimate goal of this research program is to build capacity and sustainability to continue to improve the care and outcomes patients with heart disease.

column36: Identification and Characterization of Human Hematopoietic and Leukemia Stem Cells and Elucidation of their Role in Regenerative Medicine and Disease
column37: Blood is the most regenerative human tissue with a trillion cells produced daily. The dozen mature cell types that compose adult blood originate from rare hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Only HSCs have the capacity to give rise to other HSCs while regenerating the entire blood system. When the mechanisms controlling normal blood development go awry, it can lead to leukemia, a form of blood cancer. Our lab was the first to show that acute leukemias possess a hierarchical structure similar to that of normal blood development. We discovered that cancer stem cells (CSCs) are at the apex of this hierarchy and possess the ability to self-renew and produce all of the cells of the tumour. CSCs are responsible not only for initiating and maintaining acute leukemias, but also for therapy resistance and recurrence of disease after treatment. Through CIHR's Foundation Program, we will identify and study the molecular mechanisms underpinning the unique properties of HSCs and CSCs, especially those that enable CSCs to resist treatment and cause relapse. Our research findings will lay the foundation for the development of new methods to enhance HSCs from cord blood, making them more amenable for transplantation. HSC transplantation is an effective treatment for many diseases; however, two thirds of patients who require a transplant cannot receive it because they lack a matched donor. Findings from our Foundation program will also lead to the development of new prognostic and predictive biomarkers for leukemia and identify new therapeutic targets to eliminate leukemia CSCs while sparing normal HSCs. Although most adults with acute leukemia (B-ALL and AML) respond initially to conventional therapy, 50-75% of patients experience a relapse and >60% of adult patients succumb to their disease. We will work with our clinical and industry partners to ensure that our research findings are translated to improve the health of Canadians.

column36: The predictive values of novel metabolic markers for early knee osteoarthritis changes
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, affecting about 10% of the world's population aged 60 years or older. It is the major source of joint pain and disability, and imposes substantial socioeconomic burden on society with a cost estimate between 1.0% and 2.5% of gross domestic product. Presently, available treatment is entirely directed at controlling the pain associated with OA with joint replacement for end-stage disease. This is unlikely to change in next few years, reinforcing the relevance of targeted interventions at early stage of the disease or even before the development of symptoms. As a result, clinicians have a challenging task of identifying those at highest risk of developing severe OA in a timely manner. However, the prediction of OA risk is still in its infancy. Using a metabolite profiling method, we identified seven novel metabolic markers that are related to knee OA with greater power to discriminate OA patients from controls than any other biomarkers identified so far. Given that OA manifests first as abnormal joint tissue metabolism before any structural changes can be detected, these novel metabolic markers would have great potential for early diagnosis of OA. We therefore propose to examine the predictive values of these novel metabolic markers for knee OA early changes in well-established longitudinal cohorts. The results will provide a better understanding of how these novel metabolic markers predict early OA diagnosis and OA worsening. These novel metabolites could also be potential novel targets for drug development for OA.

column36: Regional specificity of aortic aneurym: Cell specific function of disintegrin and metalloprotease-17 (ADAM17) in thoracic versus abdominal aortic aneurysm
column37: Aortic aneurysm (focal dilation of the aorta) is a serious vascular disease and a great health concern with fatal or devastating outcomes. Aorta is the largest artery in the body which carries the blood from the heart to the rest of the body. In aortic aneurysm, an area of the aorta becomes enlarged (bulges out). The wall of the aorta loses its elastic property (like an old rubber band) and unable to squeeze the blood along (forward) to different body parts/organs. When an old rubber band is subjected to high pressure (blood pumped from the heart), it can snap (i.e. aortic rupture) which results in a large amount of blood loss which can often result in death (if in the chest), or lower body paralysis (if in abdominal area). So far, there have been no treatment for this devastating disease. ADAM17 is a an enzyme located in the cells withing the aortic wall. It can clip membrane-bound molecules and release them initiating (or inhibiting) their activity. ADAM17 is increased in the aortic wall during aneurysm formation, but it is unknown whether it contributes to disease progression, or if it is simply a by-stander. In addition, it could have different functions in the thoracic versus the abdominal aorta. Our lab is among the few labs (world-wide) that has developed models of aortic aneurysm (in thoracic and in abdominal aorta, independent from atherosclerosis). We will use genetically modified mice that with cell-specific ADAM17-deficiency (in smooth muscle cell or endothelial cells) and models of thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm to determine the role of ADAM17 (in different cell types in the aorta) in aortic aneurysm formation and progression. We will use aorta specimens from patients with aortic aneurysm to confirm our findings from our mouse models. The findings from this study will reveal novel function of ADAM17 in aortic aneurysm which can also be beneficial for patients with other aneurysms (e.g. brain aneurysm & stroke).

column36: Oncohistones in Cancer
column37: Histones package our genetic information (DNA) and regulate all processes needed for a cell to grow or differentiate. There are several changes in the histone tail that act in concert with other factors (epi-genome) to govern gene activity states and the overall function of our genetic identity. Indeed, the epigenome is like the symphony of our cells, the partition that makes sense of the musical notes (DNA). Therefore, aberrant histone and chromatin modifications disrupt these normal cellular processes leading to the development of cancer. Our ground-breaking discovery of mutations in these histone genes (oncohistones as we named them with mutations at three specific residues in the histone 3 tails) in deadly brain cancers in children has linked human normal development and what we now know are epigenetic-driven cancers. We also recently uncovered oncohistones in other bone or muscle cancers, leukemia and head an neck cancers. We aim in this program to understand how this new mechanism of cancer promotes aberrant growth, identify targets amenable to therapy, provide relevant models to test the effects of these therapies prior to rapidly translating them by using our collaborative network to clinical trials at the bedside. Ultimately, if successful, our program will positively change the bleak outcome of oncohistone-associated cancers.

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the 3rd leading cause of death worldwide and affects 1 in 4 adults. Asthma affects about 1 in 3 and is the most common chronic disease of children. Previous studies have shown that women, people of some ethnic backgrounds, people with some comorbidities, immigrants, indigenous people and other groups are vulnerable to asthma and COPD and/or their poor health outcomes. COPD and asthma practice guidelines and health policy, however, are based on evidence obtained from studies that enrolled mostly white participants in controlled settings with little consideration of these factors. This is not sufficient for Canada's diverse, multicultural population where studies in diverse real world populations are needed to customize approaches for those most vulnerable to disease burden. The main objective of my program is to determine the best COPD and asthma care for affected Canadians of different sexes, ages and other backgrounds. My program will use big data from millions of Canadians containing information on age, sex, ethnic background, immigrant status and other patient characteristics as well as health behaviours (eg. smoking), medical information (eg, medications), lung function, air pollution and other factors to answer the question: What is the best way to prevent acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD in people of diverse backgrounds? Our will be translated into an online risk calculator whereby patients entering their characteristics can determine their own risk of asthma or COPD exacerbation, as well as receive customized, detailed education on how to reduce this risk. This tool will be expanded and adapted to provide clinicians, educators, program leaders and government aggregate information on the diverse populations they provide care or set policy for. Once we have perfected these methods for asthma and COPD, we plan to expand them to other respiratory diseases.

column36: Role of ADAM15 in cardiac remodeling and heart failure: Discovery of its novel myocardial substrates
column37: Despite the significant progress in heart disease management and treatment, American Heart Association announced in 2015 that after a decade of decline, death due to cardiovascular diseases is on a rise accounting for 1 out of every 3 deaths in North America. The World Health Organization reports that cardiovascular diseases continue to cause the death of 17 million people each year, with ischemic and hypertensive heart disease as the leading causes of heart failure. We have identified a molecule (ADAM15) that is present in the heart, and its levels are markedly elevated in the diseased heart. But the role of ADAM15 in progression of heart disease has so far been neglected. We have the mouse model to investigate the function of ADAM15 in two common types of human heart diseases, heart attack and dilated (enlarged) hearts. These mouse models will allow us to monitor the role of ADAM15 in progression of heart disease in early and advanced stages of heart disease. Moreover, through collaboration with clinician/scientists (cardiologists/cardiac surgeons) at U of Alberta, we have access to human heart specimens from heart failure patients (who received new healthy hearts, and donated their sick heart to research). We will confirm our findings from mouse models, in the human hearts, and in cells isolated and cultured from these hearts. We have recently purchased a state-of-the-art echo-ultrasound imaging system to measure and monitor the heart function in mice before and after (throughout the progression of) heart disease. Uncovering the function of ADAM15 in heart disease will add one more piece of the puzzle towards getting the full picture of all the factors involved in heart disease. This will be of significant importance in developing novel and effective therapies for heart disease.

column36: Structural and Functional MRI in Preclinical Models of Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia
column37: It is estimated that 27,000 Canadians are survivors of preterm birth, many reaching adulthood and afflicted with chronic lung diseases related to prematurity. Since the fetal lung develops more slowly than other organs, preterm babies often have difficulty breathing and require additional oxygen, causing further injury. Up to 40% of extremely premature infants suffer from bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), a lung disease which incurs significant healthcare costs, second only to asthma among childhood illnesses. Furthermore, BPD is associated with chronic lung diseases later in life such as asthma that result in frequent visits to the hospital and can be fatal. Although there is currently no cure, newer therapies are offering hope that BPD can be treated or even reversed if detected early enough. However, conventional diagnostic tests often look normal in early BPD and cannot be used reliably to determine if a treatment is required or whether it is working. There is a need for better tools to detect and diagnose early BPD in order to develop better treatments and determine those infants that stand to benefit from existing therapies. In this proposal, we will use Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to detect early BPD and response to treatment. MRI can pinpoint how well the lung is working without the need for radiation, making it safe and potentially useful for assessment of BPD in premature infants. We will test our approaches in newborn animals (rats and rabbits) with lung lesions that mimic human BPD to determine how and when to best detect and treat early disease. Animals grow quickly compared to children and will allow us to study BPD early and throughout the life span and investigate treatments that could be used in humans in future. The development of MRI as an effective tool for animal models of BPD will enable translation of these findings to the clinic for improved acute care of the lungs of premature infants and reduced chronic health consequences due to BPD.

column36: Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms of pituitary development, function and disease
column37: The gene expression program of a cell defines its identity, i.e. it tells us, and the cell itself, who it is, what is its role and how to play it in complex organisms like ours. We study mechanisms for the control of gene expression and their misregulation in disease. The blueprint for this control is in our DNA and changes in this blueprint result in mutations. In addition to studying this genetic level of gene regulation, we also investigate epigenetic mechanisms, ie mechanisms that govern the wrapping of genetic material (DNA) into chromosomes. Both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms orchestrate the complex development of a functional human and their deregulation cause diseases. We use a hormone-coding gene of the pituitary gland as our model system and throughout the years we have discovered new regulators and new mechanisms that account for normal processes but also disease states. We have thus predicted a form of hormone deficiency that is lethal to neonates, explained it and provided a treatment that fully recovers the lethal outcome of this condition. The new frontier in the field is the epigenetic level of regulation and we are exploring this with state-of-the-art high-throughput massive DNA sequencing technologies. We also identified mechanisms involved in development of the pituitary tumors that cause Cushing disease. This disease is particularly deleterious because of excessive uncontrolled hormone production leading to hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, and metabolic disruption. We have partly explained the resistance to hormone feedback that characterises these tumors and we now seek to determine how cell growth is deregulated in order to develop novel treatment approaches.

column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating the progression of atherosclerosis: exploiting macrophage reverse transendothelial migration as a therapeutic strategy
column37: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of arteries and remains the principal cause of death in our society despite effective cholesterol-lowering therapies. Atherosclerosis develops silently for decades before causing heart attacks and strokes. My research focuses on cells and genes that participate in atherosclerosis. Currently, there are no therapies targeting cells in the artery wall to inhibit the formation and progression of atherosclerosis. These therapies would benefit patients with risk factors, such as high blood cholesterol. Dendritic cells (DCs) are white blood cells and important components of the immune system. DCs are found in the inner artery wall of healthy humans and animals, in areas where atherosclerosis develops. DCs in mice with high cholesterol engulf lipid and become "foam cells". This is the first step in the formation of atherosclerosis, and is followed by other white blood cells entering the artery and becoming foam cells. Recently, we discovered a novel protective mechanism by which up to half of DCs in the normal artery exit into the bloodstream in response to inflammatory stimulus or exposure to bacteria. However, engulfed lipid blocks DC exit. Our goal is to elucidate the mechanisms underlying DC exit from the normal arteries so that we can determine the changes that shut off this process in foam cells. This is an important endeavor since we believe that in the future we can overcome these inhibitory mechanisms so that accumulated lipid can be removed from the artery wall by exiting lipid-loaded foam cells. This could become a unique approach to reduce both the lipid burden and foam cells. In atherosclerotic lesions, the number of foam cells increases with time in part due to cell division. Moreover, after DC exit their numbers recover within a day because remaining cells divide. Thus, therapeutic strategies that promote foam cell exit from aorta must also target molecules that promote cell division.

column36: Immunological memory of innate lymphoid cells and allergic lung inflammation
column37: We have previously identified a unique population of lymphocytes, called group 2 innate lymphoid cell (ILC2) in mouse lungs. Although ILC2s do not directly recognize allergens, they are activated by inhaled allergens and produce a set of allergy-inducing proteins. We have shown that ILC2s are important for the development of allergic lung diseases including asthma. More recently, we have found that ILC2s remember previous activation by allergens and become memory ILC2s, which are more readily activated by allergens than naive ILC2s. We will also study whether activation or inhibition of lung ILC2s in very young ages affect the functions of lung ILC2s and allergy development in adulthood. Our knowledge of memory ILC2s will likely lead to novel treatments of asthma by inhibiting the generation of memory ILC2s or their functions.

column36: Engineering stem cell fate and function
column37: Regenerative medicine (RM) offers an opportunity to address the root causes of chronic diseases, which typically result from the breakdown of tissues maintained by stem cells (SC). In Canada, chronic disease consumes 67% of direct health care costs, with approximately $68 billion attributable to treatment costs. Canada is a leader in SC-based RM and my group has contributed to discovery and innovation in this sector. Early RM technologies focused on the transplantation of cells from the same individual. RM is now at a stage where cell products, such as blood SC, are manufactured for clinical testing. My proposed program is building the next generation of RM therapeutics - living cells and tissues designed to treat specific indications. My vision is to understand, at a fundamental level, the mechanisms by which complex tissues develop from SC, and to use this understanding to advance new cell therapies and regenerative medicines. Our approach is based on three complementary thrusts. First, we are developing computer simulations of normal and diseased human tissue development. These simulations allow us to connect the genetic coding inside SC to the environment that influences SC growth. These simulations will one day dramatically shorten the time it takes to develop new therapies for degenerative diseases. Second, we are rewiring the genetic code in, and the environment around, SC to understand the key requirements of SC-based tissue development and to increase the quantity and quality of SC-derived cells produced. Third, with our partners, we are moving promising discoveries towards the clinic using advanced models of disease, with a focus on testing specialized blood cells as blood cancer and autoimmune disease therapeutics. Our work will reveal new rules that govern tissue development, generate new technologies for RM applications, and yield new SC-based therapies. Our work contributes to the CIHR mission to improve the health and welfare of Canadians.

column36: Structural Biology of Calcium-Dependent Cellular Processes in Health and Disease
column37: As the most abundant mineral in the body, calcium has long been recognized as vital to the formation and maintenance of living systems. Bones, where calcium is stored in the solid state, continuously release ions or salts of this mineral (i.e., Ca2+) into the body, and this soluble form of calcium plays a central role as a messenger within cells. We call this the biological calcium signal. However, too much Ca2+ (or too much calcium signal) is detrimental to cells, and uncontrolled calcium levels in our body are life-threatening. In cancer, the calcium signal is largely deregulated for the advantage of cancer cell growth. In order to understand how normal and cancer cells produce and respond to calcium signals, we will investigate the molecular details of the calcium-dependent cellular processes that we think are most relevant to cancer. In this proposal, we attempt to answer key questions: (i) how is the calcium signal generated and how does it become deregulated in cancer?; (ii) how does the calcium signal influence other signaling circuits that drive the growth and proliferation of cancer cells?; and (iii) how does the calcium signal affect the proper cell adhesion of normal cells, and contribute to metastatic properties of cancer cells? Part of this program is also relevant to immunodeficiency, as genetic defects (mutations) in the calcium signal generators we study (called STIM/ORAI) cause severe combined immune disease or SCID. The proposed program will contribute to a better understanding of how cancer cells use the calcium signal circuits to promote their survival and growth, as well as how immune cells battle infectious agents in the human body. Deeper understanding of the calcium signal transduction system will provide new clues for novel therapeutic strategies to treat patients with immunodeficiency and cancer.

column36: Addressing gender-based health inequities among immigrants to Canada
column37: Despite progress towards gender equity in the last decades, age-old patriarchal structures and attitudes that promote male dominance are still the norm in many countries. Canada increasingly receives large numbers of immigrants and refugees from countries where the status of women is lower than that of men. Gender inequities manifest in various health disadvantages for girls and women over the life span across the world. These include female-selective abortions, excess child mortality for girls, poorer quantity and quality of healthcare, dating and intimate partner violence, and fewer opportunities to achieve their full potential compared to males. However, little is known about whether such patterns persist among immigrants settling in Canada and how their health, development and wellbeing are affected. To fill these critical knowledge gaps we will use state-of-the-art methods to analyze rich information obtained by linking multisectoral databases encompassing all immigrants arrived to Manitoba and Ontario in the last three decades and their offspring born in Canada. This research program will generate valuable information to assist with a healthier integration of immigrants to the Canadian society and help advance gender equity initiatives in Canada and beyond. This research program brings together a multidisciplinary and interprofessional team of researchers, government and immigrant community partners who will collaborate to ensure that the research findings translate into improved programs, policies and services for the benefit of children, women and families in the affected minorities and in the population at large.

column36: Evaluation of the effect of cannabis legalization on road safety.
column37: Marijuana is the second most widely used recreational drug in the world after alcohol. It impairs the skills required for safe driving, and increases the risk of car crashes. The Canadian federal government will introduce laws to legalize marijuana in Apr 2017. It will then take approximately 18 months for the laws to be passed and put into force. Legalization of marijuana may result in more car crashes caused by drivers who are impaired by marijuana and this potential problem should be evaluated. Since 2011, the CIHR funded "Cannabis and Motor Vehicle Crashes" (CMVC) study has collected data on how often injured drivers in British Columbia test positive for marijuana, alcohol, and other drugs. This presents a unique opportunity. column36: Mechanisms Coordinating Polo Kinase Activity and Localization in Cell Division
column37: Cancer is the excessive division of cells in the body. To duplicate, cells must separate two identical sets of chromosomes during mitosis and divide correctly. This process requires the coordinated activities of several proteins that have been conserved between species during evolution. The Polo kinase protein (Plk1) is necessary for cell division by interacting with and modifying other proteins. Several types of cancer cells become addicted to elevated Polo activity. Thus, if Polo is inhibited partially, cancer cells die while healthy cells can still live and divide. Efforts have been deployed to obtain molecules capable of blocking the catalytic activity of Polo. Some of them are in clinical trials for the treatment of various cancers and have given promising results. However, the toxicity and side effects of these drugs limit their use. Our goal is to gain new knowledge of how Polo functions and how the cell responds to interference with Polo. This information will help design more effective and less toxic therapies targeting Polo in cancers. Recent findings by us and others have indicated the existence of previously unrecognized levels of regulation of Polo. The proposed research will build on these discoveries to uncover the precise molecular mechanisms controlling Polo activity in space and time during cell division so that it can fulfill its functions. For this part of the project, we will use the fruit fly Drosophila as a model system allowing a powerful combination of approaches. The new knowledge will provide basis to efforts in the development of compounds that interfere with specific aspects of Polo functions to kill cancer cells but not healthy cells. We will also use the new CRISPR technology to search for genes that become essential in the presence of low doses of Polo inhibitors in human cells. This information will direct the development of combinatorial therapies simultaneously targeting Polo and synergic mechanisms in cancer cells.

column36: Heterogeneity through space and time drive the clinical behaviour of childhood medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Medulloblastoma is really made up of four diseases, of which two types, Group 3 and Group 4, account for the majority of cases, as well as the majority of children who are dying of their disease. The main tumor 'lump' in the cerebellum is called the 'primary tumor'. The primary tumor can spread (metastasize) to cover other regions of the surface of the brain and spinal cord. The most damaging therapies for children with Group 3 and Group 4 medulloblastoma (radiation) are necessary to treat the metastases. The dream of curing cancer through precision medicine has entailed sequencing cancer genomes to identify tumor specific mutations, which could in turn be targeted by pathway specific drugs that are lethal to the tumor but harmless to a child's normal cells. While this model is showing early success for some adult cancers, it holds limited promise for treatment of medulloblastoma; recent results from our lab have shown that most medulloblastomas harbor few of these tumor specific mutations and that the tumours differ greatly both across a given 'lump' and between the primary tumor and the metastases. Instead, medulloblastomas appear to be driven by large deletions or insertions of genes. We now also know that some of these differences are seen regularly in medulloblastomas and the metastases and this makes them an excellent choice for the development of targeted therapy. We have begun developing new tools, and aim to use these tools to study these differences which occur in the tumours and between the primary tumor and the metastases-we strongly believe this is the best, and perhaps the only way to improve survival for children with medulloblastoma.

column36: Inhibition of Netrin-1 Dependence Receptor Binding as a Targeted Approach for Cancer Therapy
column37: Dependence receptors are cell surface receptors that determine cell fate dependent on the availability of their extracellular ligand, called Netrin-1 (NET1). Know functions of NET1 include cell guidance, adhesion and regulation of cell survival. We focus on the structure and function of NET1 and how it orchestrates its unique interactions with individual dependence receptors, such as UNC5 and DCC. Most remarkably, if the NET1-dependence receptor complex is interrupted- a programmed cell death is triggered. However, to date it is not known how NET1 orchestrates on a molecular level this complex set of signals. We aim to perform an integrated structural biology approach, combining protein X-ray crystallography in conjunction with SAXS, AUC/DLS/SEC-MALS and in-depth biochemical and functional assays. When combined, these tools create a detailed molecular understanding of how NET1 acts on its receptors, and how the activated receptors together work to influence the cell physiology. This research proposal aims to define the molecular basis of NET1-UNC5 and NET1-UNC5-DCC complex interactions and to unravel the structural basis for relevant signaling pathways. In these studies we will seek to develop new therapeutic targets with the overall goal to interrupt NET1-mediated dependence receptor complexes and thereby causing apoptosis in tumor cells.

column37: Breast cancer is the most common female cancer. column36: Cell volume regulatory mechanisms in oocytes and preimplantation embryos and their role in development and embryo health
column37: Early embryos are extremely sensitive to conditions that disturb their cells' size. This implied that regulation of cell size is critical to early embryo development. We previously found, using the mouse as our model, that early embryos have a unique mechanism for maintaining cell size that relies on accumulation of high levels of the amino acid glycine inside embryonic cells. Glycine is needed to replace some of the salts that the embryos, like other cells, routinely take up to quickly correct deviations from their preferred size. Embryos appear to be very sensitive to having too much salt inside them, and need to replace it with something benign like glycine. We also found that cell size regulation first arises in the egg, beginning when they are ovulated from the ovary. We do not know how the glycine mechanism is turned on at ovulation or how these processes are regulated in eggs and embryos. We also have little information about the effects of disruptions of these normal processes on the health of later embryos and the resulting offspring. In this project, using the mouse model, we will determine how the egg switches on the mechanism that uses glycine. Finally, we will find how disruptions of the unique cell size-regulatory mechanisms in eggs and embryos affect the health of offspring. Increasingly, infertile couples (more than 15% of couples in Canada) are treated by assisted reproduction technologies (ART) that include in vitro fertilization (IVF) and the extended culture of eggs and embryos outside the woman's body. Fertility preservation for cancer patients similarly relies on ART. In addition to important knowledge about eggs and embryos, our project will potentially lead to better understanding of what can go wrong during ART and effects on the health of the children that are born, and lead to safer ART techniques.

column37: My work focuses on viruses that infect bacteria, called phages. Bacteria have developed "immune" systems to protect themselves from attack by phages. The advent of this technology has opened the possibility of curing human disease. My laboratory has discovered naturally occurring proteins that can potently inhibit CRISPR-Cas9 systems. These proteins will be used to improve CRISPR-Cas9 methods to make them safer for human therapeutic purposes. We will also investigate mechanisms and other uses for CRISPR systems. My laboratory also investigates structures that form parts of the phage particle itself. In particular, we work on phage tails, which bind to bacterial cell surfaces and inject the phage DNA into cells. Naturally occurring bacterial machineries, called tailocins, are closely related to phage tails and can be used to kill bacteria in a highly specific manner. We are developing methods to engineer these tailocins to kill any desired bacterial strain. These engineered tailocins will be used to manipulate the human microbiome to alleviate disease conditions, such as Crohn's Disease. Tailocins also have the potential to treat antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections.

column36: Pinpointing pathways for pathogenesis and therapeutic intervention by identifying disease modifiers
column37: Genetic modifiers are factors that improve or worsen the presentation of a disease. Knowledge of modifiers reveals pathways for disease pathogenesis, predicts disease outcome and provides an ideal starting point for treatment. However, gene modifiers are hard to find in humans. Identifying genetic modifiers in a model organism allows for their validation and translation to humans. I carried out a modifier screen in a mouse model for Rett syndrome, a neurological disorder, which uncovered missing pathway members, revealed new genetic interactions, and pinpointed new drug targets. Greatly improved health in Rett mice that carry modifiers from two pathways suggests that combination therapy will confer amazing improvement. Outcome-predicting biomarkers, identified through our studies, will be employed as we inform strategies for clinical trials with our company ArRETT. Our approach is paradigm-shifting, because it illustrates the power of unbiased modifier screens to discover therapeutic targets, providing proof-of-principle for a modifier approach to be considered for other rare disorders, which currently have no treatment options. The knowledge will impact the health of Canadians by broadly informing clinical outcome of neurological disorders, reducing the financial burden on the health care system.

column36: Synaptic alterations underlying major brain disorders.
column37: BROAD GOALS The overarching theme of this research is to establish the molecular mechanisms by which synaptic transmission is modulated in the CNS and how errors in this process contribute to major brain disorders. We will focus on the process known as long-term depression (LTD), which we will study at synapses within the rodent hippocampus. BACKGROUND Information is stored in the brain via a process known as synaptic plasticity. The two most extensively studied forms of synaptic plasticity are long-term potentiation (LTP) and LTD. Increasing evidence suggests that errors in these processes may cause or contribute to many of the most severe neurological and psychiatric disorders. Our working hypothesis is that the cognitive deficits that are associated with these disorders are due, at least in part, to an exaggerated LTD process. It is now believed that LTD is a normal physiological process that is necessary for synaptic development and for learning and memory throughout the life-span. LTD involves the weakening of synaptic transmission and can lead to physiological synaptic elimination (pruning). We believe that LTD is normally tightly regulated but that in numerous brain disorders this regulation breaks down, due to environmental and or genetic causes. Aggressive LTD may explain the initial cognitive deficits and synapse loss. RESEARCH AIMS 1. Discover the key missing components in the process of hippocampal synaptic plasticity, with a focus on LTD. 2. Determine how hippocampal synaptic plasticity, in particular LTD, becomes altered in rodent models of neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. 3. Identify new drug targets and develop new compounds with novel actions on synaptic plasticity, as part of the process to develop better treatments for major brain disorders.
