column36: Mitochondria are a critical regulator of enteric epithelial-bacteria interaction
column37: The bacteria that colonize the human intestine are a critical determinant of health and susceptibility to disease such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and neurological disorders. The epithelial lining of the gut is the primary point of contact with these bacteria and hence knowing how the epithelium acts as a barrier to exclude the entry of bacteria into the body and how the epithelial cells respond when bacteria penetrate them or cross the epithelial barrier is central to health and well-being. Mitochondria are the cells' power-station, generating the energy needed for the cell to function and are generally described as a discrete organelle - both positions are overly simplified: mitochondria form a complex, dynamic network that remodels by the controlled processes of fission and fusion, and they produce signaling molecules (mainly reactive oxygen species) that direct many cellular events. We showed that epithelial cells with deranged mitochondrial activity have reduced barrier function and actually internalize bacteria: both events have implications for health and disease management. Loss of epithelial barrier function could precipitate local inflammation and potentially sepsis, and bacteria inside the epithelial cells are likely a threat requiring mobilization of immune activity that could result in tissue damage. There is surprisingly little information on how mitochondrial function regulates epithelial-bacteria interaction and how bacterial pathogens or pro-inflammatory signals regulate mitochondrial form and function, particularly fusion and fission: the latter promoting cell death which would contribute to loss of epithelial barrier function. We have developed a novel study with leading edge technologies to precisely examine how mitochondria mould the epithelial-bacterial relationship in the gut. With this knowledge we will be better positioned to advance approaches to maintain digestive health and treat (or cure) gut problems such as IBD.

column37: A human brain consists of numerous neurons that communicate with each other. Using a small animal model called C. elegans, whose nervous system contains only a few hundred neurons, we have discovered new genes that are critical for either the structural development, or activity tuning of neuronal communication. Through collaboration with other biologists, human geneticists, and neurologists, we have demonstrated that not only do these genes function similarly in other animals, human mutations that cause their functional anomalies lead to neurological disorders. Here we continue to use the C. elegans model to uncover genes and pathways that are critical for brain development and function. A specific question that we aim to address is how development impacts function. Like all animals, we continue to grow after birth. The ability for animals, humans included, to sense signals from the environment, and select and execute meaning motor responses is essential for the viability of both individuals and the specie. This ability, called sensorimotor function, is governed by a nervous system that changes structure and property after birth. How does a nervous system coordinate growth and functionality? We will address this question through comparing the structure and function of neural circuits during development. Applying already acquired insights, we have established C. elegans models for several human neurological disorders, whose cognitive and functional defects have fundamental developmental origins. By applying similar interrogations to these models, our studies will not only shed light on fundamental mechanisms that define the dynamic changes of the nervous systems, but also address the physiological and developmental origins of neurological disorders.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of antibody-mediated QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias
column37: Autoimmune disease affects more than 20 million people in North America. Autoantibodies such as anti-Ro52 are present not only in autoimmune disease patients but also in 0.6-2.7% of the general population. In addition, monoclonal antibody drugs such as rituximab are a fast growing area of drug development with a multi-billion market. Emerging clinical evidence suggests that certain antibodies (e.g. anti-Ro52 and rituximab) can cause a heart electrical disorder called long QT syndrome, and cardiac arrhythmias. The rhythmic heartbeat is controlled by specialized proteins in the cell membrane called ion channels. Among them the potassium channel "hERG" is the common target for various medical conditions. Dysfunction of hERG is the primary cause of medical condition-induced long QT syndrome. We hypothesize that certain antibodies (e.g. anti-Ro52, rituximab) damage hERG function and thus cause long QT syndrome. Our project has three aims. 1. We will determine whether and which specific antibodies impair hERG function in hERG-expressing cell lines as well as in heart cells isolated from neonatal rats. 2. We will perform detailed investigation on how hERG function is impaired by antibodies using state-of-the-art biomedical techniques in hERG-expressing cell culture systems. We will also investigate novel strategies to prevent antibody-mediated impairment of hERG channels. 3. We will induce specific antibodies in a live rabbit model via immunization and verify the idea that the induced antibodies disturb the heart rhythm. We will investigate how to prevent antibody-mediated heart rhythm disturbances using biological and pharmacological approaches. This project reveals a novel cellular pathway that underlies antibody-mediated heart rhythm disturbance, and explores novel means for its prevention and treatment. The novel information will also be important for pharmaceutical companies to develop safer drugs to avoid antibody-drug-induced heart rhythm disorders.

column36: Innovative biomechanical and molecular strategies to fight fibrosis
column37: Different precursor cells are activated to rapidly repair injured tissues. Examples for injury are skin trauma or burn wounds, infarct or chronic overload of the heart, lung epithelium damage, liver infection or alcohol abuse, and kidney damage because of high blood pressure. The activated cells are called myofibroblasts (MFs) because they secrete fibrous collagen matrix ("fibro") that is contracted ("myo") into mechanically stabilizing scar tissue. Although MFs are essential to restoring mechanical integrity of damaged tissue, they never truly regenerate organs and scar formation comes at the cost of reduced organ function. Worse, MF deregulation leads to excessive tissue and organ scarring - a condition called fibrosis. Fibrosis contributes to ~45% of deaths in industrialized nations by causing malfunction and failure of vital organs, such as heart, liver, kidney, lung, and vasculature. Fibrosis promotes tumor progression in the stroma reaction, leads to implant failure in foreign body responses, jeopardizes mesenchymal stem cell therapies by turning stem cells into scar cells and disfigures skin. MFs are key pharmaceutical targets but anti-MF therapies have not yet been translated to clinical treatments of fibrosis. Identifying the joint mechanical and biochemical regulators of MFs, which are incompletely understood, will be essential to promote healing with intervention therapies. Our unrivalled, state-of-the-art research will provide new insights into understanding disease progression, establish novel markers for wound healing therapies, enable the production of innovative technology for use in mechanobiology cell studies, and develop industry-standard drug screening devices. New drug targets, screening tools, biomarker and treatment strategies have tremendous commercial potential/value and will improve the quality of life of fibrosis patients in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Explaining activation changes during the early stages of Alzheimer's disease and promoting processes of compensation and brain plasticity
column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) starts with a long "silent" phase during which the disease is present in the brain, but symptoms are minimal. This may explain why up to 200 medications to treat the disease have failed in the last 30 years, as all of them have been introduced "late", missing this early silent phase. Understanding what is happening in the brain during this phase of the disease, and predicting which mildly impaired individuals will progress to AD is crucial to our development of cures. This early period may represent a critical time for pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions intended to halt the progression of the disease or to mitigate symptoms. Many older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or with a subjective complaint decline (SCD) stand in this early stage of the disease. Thus, studying these individuals might provide the precursor markers of AD. This program proposes to identify their brain and clinical symptoms using advanced neuroimaging and cognitive techniques. We have previously found hyperactivation during that stage, i.e., greater brain activation than healthy older adults. We want to better understand this phenomenon, as it may provide insight into how the brain attempts to counteract the effects of neurodegeneration. We will test the hypothesis that hyperactivation is due to intense compensatory neuroplastic processes. We will also follow subjects longitudinally to see if a combination of functional imaging and other measures can accurately predict who will progress to dementia. Finally, we will assess if cognitive training programs can increase neuroplastic compensatory processes during that early phase of AD and identify the optimal program and dose and the type of training that is most adapted to different individuals. If successful, this program will allow for an earlier diagnosis of AD and develop novel approaches to non-pharmacological prevention strategies for older Canadians who are at risk of cognitive decline.

column36: Mechanism for high fat diet-induced activation of MCH neurons and its role in obesity
column37: Obesity is a major health problem worldwide, as it increases the risk for cardiovascular diseases, type II diabetes, certain cancers etc. The main cause of obesity is excess intake of high-calorie food and sedentary lifestyle. As the brain controls food intake and energy expenditure, in particular a region called the hypothalamus, it is important to understand how high fat food affects the hypothalamus to promote weight gain. It has become clear that high fat diet (HFD) induces inflammation of the hypothalamus. Importantly, this inflammation causes excess food intake and obesity. However, how hypothalamic inflammation affects body weight regulation remains poorly understood. One key cell population in the hypothalamus is melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons that promote food intake. Our preliminary study using rodent models suggests that a certain inflammatory mediator (prostaglandin E2; PGE2) is induced by HFD and activates MCH neurons. This results in more food intake and weight gain. Based on this exciting finding, we propose to address the hypothesis: "HFD-induced hypothalamic inflammation increases food intake and body weight by directly activating MCH neurons". Aim 1: We will elucidate the effect of HFD on PGE2 production in the hypothalamus. This will be the first study to investigate the role of hypothalamic PGE2 in diet-induced obesity. Aim 2: Cellular mechanisms underlying HFD-induced changes in MCH neurons will be investigated, with a focus on PGE2 signaling. Aim 3: We will test whether blocking PGE2 signaling in MCH neurons can alleviate diet-induced obesity. The proposed study will explain why HFD-induced inflammation induces obesity. Given the prevalence and impact of obesity on our health and society, it is important to determine the consequences of diet-induced hypothalamic inflammation and discover novel therapeutic targets for obesity.

column36: Ultrasound detection of placental pathology based on hemodynamic pulse wave reflection
column37: The "after-birth" or placenta, connects the developing baby to the inside of the mother's womb to supply it with nourishment and oxygen to stay healthy and grow into a full-term healthy baby. Poor baby growth inside the uterus affects at least 1 in 20 pregnancies, and is mostly due to the placenta either not forming properly, or being damaged. This "placental insufficiency" disease can be difficult for doctors to recognize and as such developing babies are lost to stillbirth. Doctors use ultrasound "scans" to follow baby size and Doppler ultrasound to measure blood flow in the umbilical cord arteries, that connect the developing baby and its placenta. The problem with these Doppler ultrasound scans is that they are not accurate enough to find all babies at risk of stillbirth from placental disease. Most growth-restricted babies, especially in the last month, have apparently normal results, yet after delivery their placentas are not normal. If we can improve Doppler scans in pregnancy, we can plan the delivery of at risk pregnancies to avoid stillbirth, and when the tests are normal we can let the pregnancy continue normally until natural birth. Our research group has developed a new type of ultrasound test that we believe, from preliminary experiments, can accurately identify pregnancies with placental insufficiency. However, much is still unknown about how this test works and how to interpret the results. We would also like to extend the use of the test so that a greater range of placental problems can be detected. Our plan for this work is to use pregnant mice where we can reliably produce different types of placental problems and evaluate how the test results change. If our research is successful, we will have extended a safe and accepted ultrasound method to become much more accurate and therefore worthwhile to use in identifying and providing safe care to at-risk women whose pregnancies are affected by "placental insufficiency".

column36: Mechanisms of ERK-dependent tumor suppression
column37: Cellular senescence is a stable cell cycle arrest triggered by stresses that can cause cancer. Some cancer causing genes can activate this program in normal cells. The prototype senescence inducer is oncogenic RAS, a gene that is mutated in 30% of human cancers and up to 90 % of pancreatic cancers. We discovered that the strength of RAS signalling through the ERK MAP kinase pathway is the most important factor regulating oncogene induced senescence. RAS induces senescence both in cell culture models and mouse models of pancreatic cancer. Tumors can only form when this senescence barrier is overcome. Attenuation of ERK signalling allows cells with oncogenic ras to bypass senescence and progress into malignant tumors. We propose to counteract the attenuation of ERK signalling in pancreatic cancer by hyperactivating ERK using both genetic and pharmacological tools. Our preliminary data shows that this strategy works both in cell culture and in mice restoring the senescence tumor suppressor response. We will investigate the mechanism by which hyperactive ERK signaling suppress tumor progression in pancreatic cancer cells and identify biomarkers that characterize this tumor suppressor response. We will also conduct genetic studies to identify new targets that can improve ERK-dependent tumor suppression for the eventual treatment of pancreatic cancer.

column36: Neuronal correlates for body-centered and world-centered representations of spatial self-motion
column37: Whether running to catch a ball or turning to reach for a coffee cup, our ability to interact with the environment depends critically on knowing our motion and orientation in space. As we move, the brain combines multiple sensory signals to compute estimates of our motion that we use to maintain balance, navigate, plan actions and maintain clear visual perception. This poses a challenge because different types of motion estimates are required for different tasks. For example, to keep our eyes on target as we move requires estimates of our head motion along axes centered in the head. However, when running to catch a ball, tasks such as estimating our heading direction, maintaining balance as we run, and reaching accurately to grasp the ball require estimates of the axes along which the body is moving and their orientation with respect to gravity. Because no individual sensor provides such estimates they must be computed by transforming and combining information from multiple sensory sources. The aim of this work is to investigate how brain circuits transform and combine multisensory signals (vestibular, proprioceptive) to compute the types of motion estimates that are essential for tasks such as postural control, spatial navigation and voluntary reaching. Despite the importance of these estimates for the majority of tasks we perform every day, our understanding of how and where they are computed and the nature of the motion representations encoded remains rudimentary. Spatial disorientation, balance and dizziness disorders are particularly common in the elderly for whom the result is often loss of balance and falls resulting in significant injury or even death. By providing a better understanding of how the brain computes and uses self-motion estimates for tasks such as navigation, postural control, and goal-directed action it is hoped that this research will lead to improved diagnostic tools and rehabilitative strategies to counteract these debilitating problems.

column37: Blood vessels control blood flow by altering their diameter. In the brain, this process ensures that every region receives enough blood for its metabolic needs. We have identified a protein, named the "cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR)" that under normal conditions keeps blood vessels in an open state. Currently, these medications are not used in heart failure patients (they are exclusively used to treat cystic fibrosis). Our objective is to show that these medications restore blood vessels to their normal size in heart failure and understand how they do it. If these medications work as predicted, we should see better brain blood flow in heart failure patients. Some of our experiments will use genetically modified mice, which are expected to behave differently by not responding to the drugs. If successful, we will introduce a new therapy for a serious heart failure complication. Our research advances fundamental concepts in how blood vessels in the brain work. By doing so, this research will improve the health of Canadians with heart failure.

Increasing our understanding of how the immune system works will provide insight into how to effectively control and eliminate infections and devastating diseases such as HIV, multiple sclerosis and cancers.

Proteins do not work in isolation; instead they form components of highly complex molecular machineries such as protein complexes or biochemical pathways. Understanding how the proteins are organized within the context of these machines allows the identification of those that play the most critical roles. Here we propose a sophisticated biochemical separation strategy to build a global roadmap that describes how parasite proteins work together as molecular machines to allow the parasite to invade host cells and disseminate to other hosts. Through pilot funding from CIHR, we have already constructed a draft map for a related parasite Toxoplasma - providing a wealth of novel information on the processes that allow these parasites to infect and cause disease. Over the next five years, we will capitalize on this initial investment to construct high quality roadmaps for Plasmodium. Exploiting these maps, we will identify parasite proteins that are essential for infection. Working with colleagues at the forefront of drug development, our findings will translate directly into drug screening pipelines that attempt to identify novel anti-parasitic therapeutics.

column36: Understanding bacterial ribosome biogenesis to enable antimicrobial discovery
column37: Emergence of antibiotic resistance among organisms responsible for infectious disease has outpaced new antibiotic development posing a serious health problem in Canada and globally. Significant efforts must be focused on developing new antibiotics if we are to avoid the return to a pre-antibiotic era of healthcare, when infection control did not exist - people at the mercy of microbes, the elderly dying from pneumonia, more children dying in infancy and treatments such as heart surgery or chemotherapy no longer possible. This proposal focuses on the assembly process of the bacterial ribosome. Ribosomes are essential enzymes for all bacteria, including major pathogens for humans. They are complex molecular nanomachines made up of over 50 components that synthesize all proteins in the cell. Their assembly pathway has tremendous potential but that has not been explored as a target for antimicrobials. We propose to determine the function of three essential proteins RbgA, YphC and YsxC, which precise molecular functions in the maturation of the ribosome remain to be elucidated. We will use an electron microscope to directly image these proteins to gain insights into how they work and how they interact with assembling ribosomal particles. Recent advances in electron microscope instrumentation provide an opportunity to see these structures at high resolution. Our work promises to give an unprecedented view of this essential bacterial enzyme. In addition, RbgA is widely distributed and homologs are found also in eukaryotes (including humans). Therefore, the proposed work will inform on ribosome assembly not only in bacteria but also in humans. Importantly, recent work has highlighted the importance of defective ribosome assembly in the development of blood cancers. Thus our work may also have relevance for development of cancer treatments.

column36: Defining the Roles of the Overgrowth Syndrome Genes NSD1, Setd2 and EZH2 in Shaping the Epigenome and Transcriptome in Early Embryonic Development
column37: Human overgrowth disorders such as Sotos syndrome are characterized by pre- and postnatal increased growth, intellectual disability and facial anomalies. These diseases result from mutations in genes that encode enzymes that turn off other genes by changing the structure of DNA. These genes include NSD1, most frequently mutated in Sotos Syndrome patients, and SETD2. Both encoded enzymes chemically modify a specific amino acid on a specific protein associated with DNA called histone H3. Other patients with overgrowth syndromes have mutations in the gene Dnmt3a, which encodes an enzyme that chemically modifies the DNA itself. Interestingly, the modifications of histone H3 influences the activity of the protein that modifies the DNA, as well as that of another protein, EZH2, which chemically modifies histone H3.The ezh2 gene is mutated in the related overgrowth disorder called Weaver Syndrome. These observations suggest "cross-talk" between these enzymes and in turn the genes they regulate. However, a systematic study of the consequences of disrupting these regulatory proteins has not been conducted. Here, using the mouse as a model system, we will study the interplay between these enzymes and the marks they deposit, by mutating these "overgrowth syndrome genes" in the mouse and studying the consequences of such mutations in the early mouse embryo, where these genes are first active. This "genome-wide" study, using state-of-the-art sequencing technology and mouse genetics, will lead to a better understanding of the molecular basis of several human overgrowth syndromes including Sotos and Weaver, potentially leading to new avenues for treatment of these diseases.

column36: Evaluating the Potential of ACE Inhibitors in Alzheimer's Disease
column37: AD is the most common cause of dementia in the aging population for which there is no cure. Recently, studies have reported a significant reduction in the incidence of AD among some subjects taking ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs). Both ACE (Angiotensin Converting Enzyme) and the Angiotensin Receptor (AR) are part of the renin-angiotensin system known to regulate blood pressure. What is clear is that unraveling the mechanisms of action of ACE inhibitors & ARBs would provide insight into which patients could benefit from these drugs and have immediate impact on the treatment of this devastating disease. Drosophila has proven to be an excellent model system to study neurodegenerative diseases. The short life span of flies coupled with powerful genetic approaches has made it possible to generate models of disease that faithfully recapitulate many features observed in patients. Once a model has been generated it can also be used to rapidly evaluate the effectiveness of various drugs. We have established several models of AD in Drosophila and shown that these flies exhibit progressive neurodegeneration and defects in synaptic plasticity and memory. We have also shown that ACE inhibitors & ARBs can suppress many of these defects. Our goal is to take advantage of these fly models to: 1) Evaluate the therapeutic potential of these drugs; and, 2) Determine how these drugs work by identifying their molecular and cellular targets. Altogether, these studies will determine the mechanism by which ACE inhibitors and ARBs are effective in AD and which patients are most likely to benefit from this novel therapy.

column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is an age-related movement disorder whose familiar features of tremor and rigidity result from the loss of neurons in characteristic regions of the brain. There is a growing body of evidence that these symptoms are preceded by other abnormalities that may arise decades before the movement issues become obvious. Notable amongst these abnormalities are a diminished sense of smell and persistent constipation, which are attributable to a loss of function of neurons in the nose and gut respectively. It has been postulated that PD is actually initiated at these sites by the exposure of neurons to some environmental agent (viruses or pesticides, for example) which promotes misfolding of a critical protein in susceptible individuals. The misfolded protein (alpha synuclein) may aggregate and spread from one neuron to another and act as a template to promote the misfolding of additional molecules of alpha synuclein. Over the course of decades the misfolding problem may reach the brain, having traversed neuronal connections from the distant sites of disease initiation. If true, this mechanism would provide a large window of opportunity for interventions to delay or eliminate the disease. We propose to test the hypothesis using a mouse line that we have created specifically for this purpose. We have engineered this line such that the aggregation of the misfolded protein generates a fluorescent signal that can be detected by microscopy. We will use known genetic or environmental triggers to initiate the process, and determine where in the gut or nasal lining the fluorescence is first detected. We will follow the fluorescent signal over time and determine if there is spread to the brain. We will also use clinical samples to determine whether the forms of misfolded alpha synuclein that are present in subtypes of human neurodegenerative disease initiate spread in our mouse model.

column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a fatal disease that preferentially targets young women in their 30s and 40s. PAH involves a loss of blood vessels in the lung. This loss leads to increased stress on the right side of the heart and eventual death due to heart failure. Although there is a well-appreciated link between PAH and immune disorders, there is currently little understanding of how changes in the immune system lead to disease in the lung vasculature. Our previous research has shown that particular immune cells, known as Natural Killer (NK) cells, are impaired in PAH patients and animal models of disease. We have also found that genetically modified mice lacking either NK cells or a specific molecule on the surface of NK cells both develop PAH. The current project will use these mouse models, as well as NK cells from PAH patients, to determine exactly how NK cell impairment contributes to disease. This work will focus on identifying the proteins that NK cells use to regulate blood vessel structure in health and disease. Recent studies have also shown that NK cells in humans are diverse. The specific subsets of NK cells that regulate blood vessels will also be identified. Despite the approval of several new treatments, the the annual mortality rate of PAH remains high (~15%), in-line with that of stage 3 breast cancer. This poor survival is linked to the fact that available therapies primarily treat the symptoms of PAH and do not address the underlying factors driving disease progression. Such treatments are also extremely expensive, placing a large burden on the Canadian health care system. The proposed work will help to clarify the role of NK cells in PAH, with the goal of developing new treatments for this devastating disease.

column36: Advancing Mental Health Care by Improving the Delivery of Therapist-guided, Internet-delivered Cognitive Behavioural Therapy in Clinical Practice
column37: Depression and anxiety are prevalent and disabling conditions that often go untreated. Internet-delivered Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (ICBT) is a relatively new approach to treatment that is a convenient way for patients to access care. ICBT is highly standardized and involves patients reviewing weekly lessons over the Internet. Patients also receive brief weekly support from a therapist via secure emails or phone calls. Past research shows that ~75% of patients complete ICBT and report large symptom improvements. Although these results are very promising, research also suggests that ICBT could potentially be improved by being more personalized in terms of treatment duration and amount of therapist contact, especially for clients with more severe symptoms. We will conduct three studies to evaluate personalized ICBT. The first trial will involve therapists who work in a clinic that specializes in ICBT. Over 18 months, we will randomize 440 patients with depression and/or anxiety to either receive standardized (5 lessons completed in 8 weeks; weekly therapist contact) or personalized ICBT (5 lessons; personalized duration and therapist contact). In the second study, 440 patients will be treated by therapists working in five community mental health clinics in Saskatchewan. We will compare outcomes of 220 patients treated with standardized ICBT in one year to outcomes of 220 patients treated with personalized ICBT the following year. In both trials, we will compare patients who receive personalized and standardized ICBT on outcome measures, intervention usage, satisfaction measures and costs. In the third study, we will interview therapists and managers to learn about strengths and challenges of delivering personalized ICBT. The research will ultimately advance how ICBT is used in clinical practice and is expected to lead to improvements in mental health outcomes and mental health care delivery.

column36: Tumour Acidification Treatment: Optimization using pH-Weighted MRI
column37: Cancer remains the leading cause of death in Canada and more effective treatments are needed. column36: Regulation of receptor mobility and spatial organization: Key factors in B cell activation
column37: Activated B cells make antibodies that protect against infection. However, people with autoimmune diseases make antibodies that attack parts of their own body. Hence the ability to modulate B cell activation has significant implications for health and disease. Each B cell has B cell receptor (BCR) proteins on its surface that determine what molecule it responds to (i.e. the antigen). Binding of antigen to the BCR triggers intracellular signals that cause B cell activation and antibody production. However even in the absence of antigen, the BCR continually generates a low-level of antigen-independent "tonic" signaling. The strength of this tonic BCR signaling determines whether a B cell is in a resting, partially activated (primed), or activated state prior to encountering antigen. We showed that bacterial components drive B cells into a primed state in which they are more sensitive to antigen and need less to become activated. Understanding how B cells become primed in this way may help us design better vaccines. Conversely, B cells from autoimmune patients are hyperactive and may require little or no antigen to become activated and make damaging antibodies. Reverting these cells to a resting state could prevent autoimmunity. Our project builds on new ideas about how BCR signaling is controlled by the movement and organization of the BCR within the cell membrane. To signal, BCRs must form clusters with each other, interact with other membrane proteins that organize signaling machinery, and move away from negative regulators. New advances in microscopy have allowed us to visualize the movement and clustering of the BCR in the membrane, as well as its interactions with positive and negative regulators. Our goal is to elucidate how BCR mobility, organization, and interactions are controlled, and how this determines the strength of tonic BCR signaling. This may suggest new ways to modulate B cell activation in order to improve vaccines and prevent autoimmunity.

column37: One of the most common causes of disability and death during aging is metabolic bone disease, which includes osteoporosis, bone disease due to cancer, hyperparathyroidism, and osteomalacia. We are studying three major hormones, parathyroid hormone (PTH), PTH related peptide (PTHrP), and vitamin D which regulate normal bone metabolism, but can also contribute to the development and progression of metabolic bone disease. Calcium itself can act as a hormone by interacting with a calcium sensing receptor (CaSR), which has been identified in several tissues including parathyroid (which produces PTH), kidney and bone. Activation of CaSR can lower PTH and CaSR activators, called calcimimetics have been developed to control hyperparathyroidism. Although continuously high levels of blood PTH, as occur in hyperparathyroidism, can destroy (resorb) bone (producing "catabolic" effects), in contrast, intermittent PTH administration forms bone (an "anabolic" effect) and is therefore used in osteoporosis therapy. Vitamin D has also been reported to have both anabolic and catabolic effects on bone but the precise mechanism is also unclear. Wnt is a growth factor which is a potent stimulator of bone formation, and can be inhibited by a bone-derived protein called sclerostin. Our goal is to understand how PTH, PTHrP and vitamin D exert their anabolic effects on bone. We will use genetically modified mouse models to examine the ways PTH and PTHrP act to form bone, determine if CaSR activation can influence the anabolic effects of PTH on bone, and determine if vitamin D stimulates bone by interacting with sclerostin. These studies should improve our understanding of how these hormones influence bone, and how to develop improved anabolic therapies for important diseases of the skeleton.

column36: Determining the role of histone modifications in mediating transcriptional consistency in beta-cells and in diabetes pathogenesis
column37: During the development of type 2 diabetes immune cell induced inflammation and metabolic stress induce insulin secreting beta-cells to lose their normal functionality. In part this is because the beta-cells have reduced levels or critical genes that help maintain them as fully functional cells. Restoring the levels of these critical genes can restore beta-cell functionality and is a possible therapeutic approach to treating type 2 diabetes. Despite this the mechanisms by which the levels of these factors become reduced in beta-cells during T2D progression is not clear. Our recent data shows that the structure of the chromatin around these genes plays a key role in regulating their expression, which dictates the levels they are present in in the cell. Specifically, we have found a unique type of modification that can occur to the chromatin can help reduce the variability of a genes expression in different cells, as genes with these modifications have reduced cell to cell variability than genes that do not have it. However, we find that in patients with T2D genes with these modifications become just as variably expressed as genes without these modifications. This not only results in an overall reduction in the levels of these genes in the beta-cells of T2D patients, but also means that some beta-cells exist in these patients with much lower levels than the average. We believe these cells become highly dysfunctional, and are a critical component of how T2D progresses. In this work we intend to determine how age and T2D increase transcriptional variability in beta-cells in both mouse models and in humans. We will assess whether these factors directly affect the chromatin modifications we believe control gene expression variability, and generate mouse models to understand the role these modifications play in maintaining normal gene expression. This work stands to generate significant novel insight into T2D progression, and may implicate novel therapeutic approaches.

column36: Dissecting NF1 signaling in melanoma
column37: Unlike the majority of cancers where the rate of newly diagnosed cases and deaths are declining, melanoma rates have been increasing significantly in both men and women. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in Canada, and in 2015, melanoma was responsible for 70% of skin cancer-related deaths. Much progress has been made in the development of treatment options for melanoma patients based on basic science discoveries. For example, from focused gene sequencing studies, we know melanoma is caused by mutations in two genes, BRAF and NRAS, that lead to uncontrolled growth of melanocytes in about 70% of patients. These findings led to the development of targeted therapies, so-called "smart drugs", designed against BRAF and targeting NRAS in an indirect way. Unfortunately, many patients that are given these "smart drugs" eventually develop resistance. Furthermore, targeted therapy options for patients that lack BRAF and NRAS mutations are limited. In contrast, other immune-based therapy that harness the power of a patient's immune system have shown incredible clinical utility for melanoma patients. However, over 50% of melanoma patients do not have durable long-term responses to immune therapy. It is still unclear why some patients respond to immune therapy and why others do not. With the advent of next generation sequencing technology, we recently gained the ability to sequence all genes in many melanoma patient samples. Our studies revealed half of patients that lack mutations in BRAF and NRAS possess mutations in a gene called NF1. However, it is still unclear how we can use this information in the clinic to treat patients. Our preliminary work suggests that NF1 regulates components of the immune system that may have implications for immune therapy response. The goal of this project is to understand how NF1 promotes melanoma and modulates the response to immune therapy, as well as to develop novel therapeutic strategies to treat this melanoma subtype.

column36: Does Mechanopluripotency Enhance the Derivation and Expansion of Naive Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells?
column37: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer huge potential for regenerative medicine. Being pluripotent, they can be differentiated to any cell or tissue in the body. Pluripotency is one component of stemness; the other is the ability to self-renew. In order to meet the anticipated demand for high quality iPSCs, we have been developing bioprocesses for expanding them as aggregates in computer controlled vessels called stirred suspension bioreactors (imagine a smaller version of an upright washing machine). Recently we made international headlines when we demonstrated that we could generate mouse iPSCs 1000-fold more efficiently in bioreactors compared to static culture. Our research has led us to the discovery of a new phenomenon, mechanopluripotency, wherein mechanical forces caused by bioreactor stirring promote pluripotency. In this project, we plan to study if mechanopluripotency occurs in human iPSCs and if it can be used to improve and standardize hiPSC expansion culture. Our study focuses on the newly characterize naive hiPSCs, which more closely resemble their mouse counterpart. We will determine if mechanopluripotency operates in naive hiPSCs and by what mechanism. We will determine if mechanopluripotency allows hiPSC expansion without a requirement for pluripotency maintenance factors and chemical inhibitors. This move will not only lower iPSC expansion costs, it will also increase cell quality since inhibitors are suspected to have negative consequences on quality. Finally, we will determine if mechanopluripotency allows the efficient derivation of hiPSCs in bioreactors, a goal which has previously eluded us.

column36: Molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern the development of cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM)
column37: Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCM, also referred to as Cavernous Angiomas) are dilations that form mainly in the blood vessels of the brain. CCM are surprisingly common, with roughly 0.5% (1 in 200) of the population having at least one such lesion. CCM result in leaky vessels that can lead to symptoms ranging from a mild headache to seizure and even hemorrhagic stroke. A CCM diagnosis can only be achieved at present via detailed MRI, something a patient would not have until the symptoms have become very severe. The only "treatment" available at present is surgical removal of CCM, however in severe cases lesions are either not accessible to surgery or they are too numerous to remove. Because CCM are diagnosed late, we do not understand how they first arise and then develop to full-blown leaky lesions. This knowledge is critical to designing therapies that can prevent worsening or new development of CCM in patients or people from at-risk families. To address this, we will use complementary approaches in roundworm (C. elegans) and vertebrate (zebrafish) animal models to dissect the events that lead to CCM. C. elegans is a genetic powerhouse, which has been used to discover many genetic pathways that regulate human development and disease, notably cancer. Zebrafish have a brain vasculature much like our own, and as their embryos are transparent, we can use microscopy to watch the vasculature at high resolution as disease develops in real time. Using C. elegans and zebrafish, we will uncover the key players in CCM disease progression, identify what goes wrong in vascular cells in CCM, and examine the ability of different interventions to stop CCM onset and progression. This will lay the foundation for future clinical work aimed at preventing severe neurological damage in patients suffering from CCM.

column36: Reactivation of occult hepadnaviral infection and hepatitis in the woodchuck model of hepatitis B
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) belongs to the most deadly human microbes. It causes life-threatening liver diseases, such as chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis and liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). More than 2 billion people (~1/3 of global population) show evidence of HBV infection, while 240-370 million have symptomatic chronic hepatitis B of which up to one million die annually. In Canada, ~270,000 individuals have chronic hepatitis B. We discovered that, in addition to symptomatic infection, HBV in humans and woodchuck hepatitis virus (WHV) in woodchucks cause asymptomatic (occult) chronic infection that can also culminate in development of HCC. This occult infection under certain conditions, like immunosuppression or anti-cancer therapy, can reactivate and cause sever hepatitis, liver failure and death. The mechanisms of this reactivation are unknown. Because HBV infects only humans and higher primates and the caused liver disease cannot be studied in cultured cells, the use of an appropriate animal model is essential. We developed a unique research facility at Memorial University in which woodchucks susceptible to WHV infection are studied. We also devised models of occult HBV infection in woodchucks. In this study, we want to reactivate occult infection in woodchucks by commonly used drugs, such as dexamethasone (corticosteroid) and a drug against rheumatoid arthritis and B cell lymphoma. We want to identify factors that predispose to development of severe hepatitis in occult infection and molecular mechanisms involved. By doing so, we can learn how to predict if reactivation may occur and what to do to prevent it. Also, the preclinical model for testing of new drugs for their HBV reactivation abilities will be established. In addition, we will learn about mechanisms of reactivation of other silent (latent) viral infections which complicate current treatments.

column36: Improving Clinical Decision Making for Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects 1 in 10 Canadian adults, and can lead to kidney failure requiring dialysis. In most cases, CKD remains stable, and can be safely managed by a family doctor. However, for some patients, it can progress quickly and needs specialist care. In 2011, we developed an equation that accurately identifies patients at the highest risk of progression. We are now proposing national studies that will test how our equation can be integrated in patient care. First, we want family doctors to use the equation to talk to their patients about their risk of kidney failure and how to reduce it. Doctors will use the equation to determine whether a patient needs to see a kidney specialist or not. Second, we want kidney specialists to use the equation to plan for dialysis or transplantation, but only for patients at the highest risk of kidney failure. These studies will help ensure patients are involved in making health care decisions with their doctor and will help provide clinical care specific to each patient. In the next 5 years, these studies will transform care for CKD in Canada and beyond our borders.

column36: Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Monoamine Oxidase B in Major Depressive Disorder With and Without Comorbid Traumatic Brain Injury
column37: 50% of clinical depression cases are treatment resistant, most likely because clinical depression is composed of multiple biological changes, and these changes may vary from one case to another. These are the first definitive studies of MAO-B in clinical depression and clinical depression with comorbid head injury. If we find that elevated MAO-B predicts clinical response to the treatment that shuts down MAO-B, this could be developed as a new way to match specific treatment to specific biology in clinical depression so as to get better treatment outcomes.

column36: Predicting the onset of bipolar disorder: A longitudinal high-risk study
column37: Bipolar disorder is a severe psychiatric illness that runs in families and onsets in adolescence - a critical time of brain and emotional development. Bipolar disorder is a high-ranking cause of disability and premature death worldwide. Currently there is no way of predicting who will develop bipolar or related mood disorders in those with a positive family history. Bipolar disorder is likely the result of a number of susceptibility genes triggered by exposure to multiple social, psychological, and biological risk factors. This proposal builds on prior funded research and requests funds to study the most promising risk factors that may be amenable to treatment in adolescent and young adult high-risk offspring of parents confirmed to have bipolar disorder over a 5-year period. At the end of this study, we will be able to develop a predictive model - a first of its kind - that will estimate the likelihood and timing of illness in individuals with variable sets of risk factors. We will also collect saliva and blood samples for future studies of changes in gene activity associated with risk exposure and illness onset. This information will improve identification of individuals at familial risk who are most likely to develop mood disorders and advance the development of specific innovative preventative and early intervention approaches. Ultimately, this work will result in a major leap forward in understanding genetically-mediated causal pathways leading to bipolar disorder and help to change the trajectory of this illness through informing strategies to prevent onset and progression.

column37: CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA (CLL) is the most frequent leukemia of adults in Western countries. Most cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia are found through routine blood tests. However, CLL is a heterogeneous disease and the clinical course of CLL varies considerably in which the disease progresses rapidly in some patients and slowly with symptoms that develop gradually in others. This results in clinical heterogeneity in terms of patient survival rates whereas variable response to therapy has also been observed between patients. It is thus essential to find appropriate prognostic factors as well as strategies to overcome resistance to current treatment and new therapeutic targets. This project is based on very exciting observations of a link between the expression of a gene named UGT2B17, CLL poor prognosis and drug resistance. This gene is involved in cell metabolism but an intriguing feature is the fact that current data also point towards a potential role of UGT2B17 beyond its usual metabolism function in the cell. This proposal will serve to better understand the function of this novel prognostic marker in CLL as well as its role in resistance to anti-cancer therapy. Eventually, poor prognostic factors such as UGT2B17 could be used to select patients for future clinical trials and identify subgroups that would most benefit from better therapeutic options and likely to relapse after treatment, the mainstay for first line treatment in CLL.

column36: Biopsychosocial predictors of postpartum genito-pelvic pain: A two-year follow-up
column37: During pregnancy and after childbirth, many women experience pains that can significantly interfere with their lives. Pain in the genital or pelvic region ("genito-pelvic") is particularly poorly understood, often misdiagnosed or ignored, and viewed as shameful by the women who experience it. Yet this pain may be very common, with average estimates of 27% at 3 months, 24% at 6 months, and 16% at 1 year postpartum. It can negatively affect women's sexuality, psychological wellbeing, and relationships. There is a critical lack of research describing the symptoms and persistence of genito-pelvic pain after childbirth, as well as the potential predictors that may help identify women who are at risk. The goal of this study is to examine the prevalence and biopsychosocial predictors of women's genito-pelvic pain and couples' psychological and sexual wellbeing from mid-pregnancy to 24 months postpartum. We will follow our established cohort of women (assessed at 20 and 32 weeks gestation, 2 weeks, 3- and 6-months postpartum) to 12 and 24 months postpartum and involve partners. We expect that breastfeeding and labour characteristics (e.g., tearing) will be associated with greater pain and sexual and psychological problems in the first year after birth, but their impact will decrease by the second year. We also expect that certain psychological and social variables in pregnancy, such as a greater fear of pain, will be associated with more pain and problems after childbirth. Finally, we expect that greater empathy in the postpartum period will be associated with women's lower pain and both partners' greater sexual and psychological wellbeing. Findings will improve our understanding of how postpartum genito-pelvic pain develops and why it persists for some women. Results will also aid in identifying novel intervention targets, as well as the most critical time points for best preventing and treating genito-pelvic pain and its consequences.

column36: Small nucleolar RNAs as regulators of gene expression
column37: Small RNAs form several large families of biomolecules emerging as essential regulators of fundamental cellular processes. While miRNAs, a large family of cytoplasmic small RNAs regulating transcript stability on widespread levels, have been extensively characterized, nuclear small RNAs are also emerging as fundamental regulators performing varied roles. The conserved family of small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a group of such nuclear small RNAs. SnoRNAs have been well-characterized as guiding the chemical modification of ribosomal RNAs, an important step in ribosome biogenesis and ultimately in protein synthesis. However, over the past 5 years, many independent reports have identified specific snoRNAs as involved in diverse other functions ranging from the maturation of pre-messenger RNAs to the response to stress in the cytoplasm. By analysis of deep-sequencing datasets of small RNAs of several human cell lines, we identified groups of snoRNAs differing in terms of their protein binding preferences and terminal sequences, suggesting they could play different regulatory roles in the cell. In light of these recent findings, we propose to characterise specific families and subgroups of small RNAs and to define their role in the regulation of essential nuclear processes, using computational and experimental methods. Many small RNAs display significantly deregulated expression in cancer and a subset have been shown to play an important role in cancer development and maintenance. This study will shed light on a large group of nuclear regulators of gene expression that have been generally ignored in this role, significantly increasing our understanding of the multi-layered regulation of gene expression.

column36: Telephone-Based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Post-Operative Bariatric Surgery Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Bariatric (weight loss) surgery is the most effective treatment for extreme obesity, but surgery does not treat underlying psychological and behavioural issues. Currently, psychotherapy ("talk therapy") for eating problems is not routinely offered with surgery, and many people start to regain weight one year later. Objective: This study will examine if adding a convenient and accessible psychotherapy by phone one year after surgery will lead to increased weight loss two years after surgery. Primary Hypothesis: Relative to the Control group (who will get routine care), the group of individuals who get psychotherapy will have lower weights 2 years after surgery. Secondary Hypotheses: Relative to the Control group, the psychotherapy group will report significantly less maladaptive eating behaviours and medical burden, and significantly greater quality of life. column36: Consequences of ultraviolet light-induced aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling on intestinal immunity
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) affect 1 in 150 Canadians, one of the highest incidences worldwide. Risk factors include genetic predisposition, smoking, hygiene, diet, gut pathogens, and environmental factors, including sun exposure. Extensive public health data have revealed an inverse relationship between incidence of Crohn's disease, latitude and sun exposure. Notably, moderate exposure of skin to UV irradiation produces a molecule called FICZ, which can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). The AhR is abundant in several organs, including the gut, and is implicated in protection against IBD. The capacity of the AhR to be activated by molecules of dietary and environmental origin may be key to its protective actions in IBD. We have compelling evidence that molecules produced in skin by moderate UV exposure activate the AhR in several peripheral organs including the gut and influence immune signaling. The core goals of this application are to understand the consequences of activation of the AhR by UV light on intestinal immunity and how this protects against IBD. We will also study the effects of activation of the AhR on microbial components of the gut. Our working hypotheses are that (i) moderate UV exposure produces molecules that act to reinforce immune signaling by the AhR in peripheral organs, and (ii) that AhR signaling induced by cutaneous UV exposure influences the microbial composition of the intestine. These studies provide a mechanistic link between sun exposure and reduced incidence of IBD.

column37: Women who had gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) during pregnancy are at high risk of future type 2 diabetes, which can be prevented with lifestyle programs that improve diet and physical activity. We have trained 10 diabetes educators to deliver the program, and our pilot data has shown good uptake and feasibility so far. Our project will provide novel information on effects of lifestyle interventions on early markers of diabetes risk in a well-defined, high-risk population of young women to support the implementation of a targeted diabetes prevention program.

column36: Practice, policy, and ethical implications of Canadian nursing roles in medical aid in dying: A knowledge synthesis and qualitative investigation.
column37: On June 17, 2016, amendments to the Canadian criminal code (Bill C-14) made it possible for nurse and medical practitioners in Canada to administer or prescribe a substance that results in death for eligible persons. This practice is referred to as medical assistance in dying or MAiD. Under Bill C-14, nurse practitioners may provide MAiD and registered nurses will play key supportive roles. In light of these developments, Canadian nursing policy and regulatory bodies have been working to construct frameworks to support nursing practice in the context of MAiD. This work will continue into the foreseeable future as provinces and territories develop additional legislation and policies. Synthesizing existing knowledge about nursing implications from other countries where MAiD is legal, and gathering empirical evidence about nurses' experiences as MAiD is implemented in Canada, is critical to informing this ongoing development. The purpose of this project is to conduct a knowledge synthesis of the practice, policy, and ethical implications of MAiD for nursing from (1) empirical literature, (2) grey literature, and (3) primary qualitative work. In phase one, we will conduct a knowledge synthesis of the literature on nursing and MAiD. In phase two, we will obtain an in-depth understanding of the distinctive social, moral, practical, and clinical implications of nursing involvement in MAiD in the Canadian context using a qualitative investigation of the experiences of Canadian nurses who have cared for patients receiving MAiD. In phase three, we will synthesize this knowledge using meta-summary, meta-synthesis, and ethical reflection. Outputs will include practice recommendations, a policy analysis, and ethical resources to support nursing practice. Evidence from this project will support the development of nursing practice, policy, and research toward the ultimate goal of providing high quality care to Canadians seeking MAiD

column37: The WHO describes obesity in children under 5 as an 'exploding nightmare.' In Canada, the high rate of overweight (15%) and obesity (6%) among preschoolers is a significant public health concern. To halt the obesity epidemic, interventions must begin early in life. However, few successful models exist for early life obesity prevention, in large part because existing interventions had minimal family involvement. To overcome this limitation, we propose intervening within the home. A home-based approach engages the entire family and provides a tangible window into families' behaviours that are only an abstraction in clinic or community settings. Costs, including medical costs and productivity losses experienced by the families, will also be compared between the 2 groups. This study will test a novel and promising approach to obesity prevention - an approach that engages young children and their families at home, where they eat, play, and sleep. Our interdisciplinary team with expertise in randomized trials, behaviour change, and health economics has partnered with knowledge users in public health and primary care to develop and deliver this intervention. As a result, this research could provide a sustainable model for early life obesity prevention, leading to long-term improvements in health and reductions in costs to the health care system and society as a whole.

column37: In Canada, as in most developed countries, atherosclerosis is one of the leading causes of illness and death. According to the most recent data, one in five deaths in Canada is due to atherosclerosis-associated cardiovascular complication. Despite great medical advances, therapies are urgently needed to improve the cardiovascular function in atherosclerosis. Endothelial cells, which line the innermost layer of blood vessels, play important roles in maintaining blood vessel function, thereby understanding the mechanisms underlying abnormal endothelial function may serve to uncover novel therapeutic approaches to treat atherosclerosis and associated cardiovascular dysfunctions. DNA is the genetic material present in every cell type, and is prone to damage by various stressors. BRCA2 is a protein molecule, which maintains the DNA integrity by repairing the damaged DNA. We want to investigate if there will be increased atherosclerosis-associated endothelial dysfunction and endothelial cell death after feeding these animals with high fat diet. Our study will delineate a new role of BRCA2 in atherosclerosis, which may help identifying a potentially new therapeutic target to treat cardiovascular diseases. Our study may point to an increased possibility of developing cardiovascular diseases in breast and ovarian cancer patients with mutation in BRCA2 gene.

column36: Activation of Pyruvate Kinase M2 as a Novel Therapy for Chemotherapy-Induced Cardiotoxicity
column37: Chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity (CIC) is a very common complication of many anti-cancer agents and although cancer therapies maybe suppressing tumor growth, these patients begin to develop heart failure. Therefore, a better understanding of the signalling pathways involved in CIC are desperately needed, as there are currently no therapies that prevent the onset of this condition and most patients eventually die of either cancer or heart failure. One of the challenges in designing appropriate therapies to prevent CIC is selectively protecting the heart without preventing the benefits of cancer therapies against tumors. An intriguing difference between the heart and the tumor environments are the levels of oxygen (the molecule we breathe and required for life). The heart is present in an area of high oxygen levels, while the tumor can survive in areas of low oxygen. Therefore, screening for oxygen-sensitive proteins that may be induced by CIC agents in the heart may provide targetable therapies that are selective to the heart, without interfering with the anti-cancer effects of promising cancer therapies in the tumor. We have identified a candidate oxygen-sensitive protein called pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) that is induced in the heart by CIC agents. Intriguingly, drugs that activate PKM2 has previously been shown to suppress tumor growth, however, PKM2 function in the heart remains elusive. We show that activating PKM2 in the heart, where oxygen levels are high protects against CIC, but maintains and in some cases even enhances cancer therapy-mediated regression of the tumor, where oxygen levels are low. The therapeutic implications of this project may provide drug discovery platforms that could directly prevent CIC, which are desperately needed, but may also be applicable to other metabolic pathologies, including other forms of heart failure, cancer and diabetes.

column36: Mechanism of Ribosomal RNA Gene Silencing and Its Roles in Pluripotency and Cancer
column37: Building the cell's protein factories is a complex job involving many hundreds of components and takes up much of a cell's efforts to grow. For cancers to grow, they must find ways to make more of these protein factories than surrounding normal tissues. So, if we could find ways to limit the manufacture the protein factories, known as ribosomes, we could control cancer. In fact, we have recently demonstrated that targeting the genes that make the RNAs of the ribosome kills cancer cells while leaving normal cells untouched. Several "tumour suppressor" proteins prevent cancer by doing just this. For example, the ARF and TP53 tumour suppressors are very important in limiting ribosome production and either or both are inactivated in 80% of cancers. We recently discovered that highly proliferative cancer cells show an unusual "epigenetic silencing" of the Ribosomal RNA genes. Epigenetic silencing is one means by which genes are selectively inactivated to establish different tissues such as skin, bone, blood, intestine, etc. We found that silencing of the Ribosomal RNA genes is lost in some cancer cells and closely resembles the situation in the embryonic stem cells that will create all the different tissues of the body. We discovered some years ago that the ARF tumour suppressor regulates a protein called TTF1. This protein is known to determine epigenetic silencing of the Ribosomal RNA genes. We hypothesize that the changes in ribosomal RNA gene silencing may allow pre-cancerous cells to grow rapidly, but more importantly cause the type of chromosome rearrangements that lead to full-blown cancer. Our lab. is trying to understand how this happens in the hope of discovering novel and more effective ways of treating cancer.

column36: Mind the gap: Duration of protection from measles maternal antibody in Canadian infants - generating evidence to update policy
column37: Measles is the most infectious vaccine-preventable disease. Although measles no longer infects us routinely in Canada, recent outbreaks have raised concerns that some population groups may not be adequately protected against the disease. Of particular concern are infants, who are born with antibodies transferred from their mother during pregnancy. We previously assumed that infants are protected by their mothers' antibodies until they are capable of making their own through vaccination at 12 months. However, recent evidence suggests that in settings like Canada, where most mothers are immune to measles through vaccination, levels of maternal antibody are lower since vaccination results in less robust immunity than natural infection. This results in a shorter duration of protection in infants, potentially leaving them susceptible to measles. This study aims to determine the duration of time that infants are protected from measles in their first year of life, between the time their maternal antibodies are no longer protective until they receive their first dose of measles vaccine at 12 months. This study will help to answer critical practical public health questions related to measles prevention and control. Specifically, updated Canadian data are required to evaluate whether current recommendations for immunization of infants at 12 months need to be reassessed. column36: Structural and Functional MRI Assessment of Treatment Response in Early Cystic Fibrosis Lung Disease
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common genetic disorder affecting children and young adults in Canada. While life expectancy for CF patients has improved in recent decades, recurrent and persistent infections are major causes of lung function decline that ultimately lead to death. New treatments are becoming available that can slow the long term rate of decline in lung function. However, conventional breathing tests often look normal in young patients with early CF lung disease and cannot be used reliably to determine if the treatment is working. Therefore, the medical community needs tests that can better assess the lungs of young CF patients, especially to follow the effects of treatment. A picture taken of the lungs, or medical imaging test, would allow doctors to see and properly treat the lungs of children with CF at an early stage, before disease is severe. X-ray imaging is one such approach but is generally not able to measure the effects of CF treatments and also involves unwanted radiation, a particular concern for repeated scans in younger patients. In this proposal, we will investigate a novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique called xenon-MRI (Xe-MRI). Xe-MRI provides clear pictures inside of the lungs and involves no radiation so can be used repeatedly in children. Xe-MRI has been used successfully to diagnose several lung diseases but has not yet been investigated for monitoring lung disease treatment in children with CF. We will test the ability of Xe-MRI to detect improvements following treatment of early CF lung disease, not demonstrated by conventional breathing tests. By showing that Xe-MRI is useful for detecting and following the treatment of early CF lung disease, this test could also be used for the development of new improved treatments for children with CF in future. Furthermore, this test would likely also be useful for assessing other lung diseases such as asthma.

column36: Targeting molecular scaffolds for the treatment of obesity and metabolic disease
column37: As a risk factor for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, obesity has been steadily increasing in society at alarming rates. Approximately 25% of Canadians are either over-weight or obese. Anti-obesity therapies have varying degrees of effectiveness, but no therapies actually target fat cells, which are key in the development of obesity. Fat cells, or adipocytes, grow through a complicated roadmap of signals that need precise direction. It is currently not known what are the proteins in fat cells that direct these signals needed for fat cell growth, but specialized proteins called molecular scaffolds could be the key players. One type of molecular scaffolds are 14-3-3 proteins, which we previously found to control the growth of fat cells in mice. We previously studied one member of 14-3-3 proteins, 14-3-3zeta, and mice that were genetically modified to have no 14-3-3zeta in all cells had less fat than normal mice. When mice were made to have more 14-3-3zeta in every cell, they actually gained more weight when fed food high in fat. It has been found that fat samples from obese individuals have higher levels of 14-3-3zeta. Combined with our mouse data, this raises the question of whether having more 14-3-3zeta in fat cells is enough to promote the development of obesity. Therefore, the aim of this proposal is to see if 14-3-3zeta can be a suitable target in the fat cell for treating obesity. This will be tested in mice that do not have 14-3-3zeta in their fat cells and to see if this protects them from developing obesity. Studies will also try to understand what 14-3-3zeta does in a fat cell and also if new drugs can be developed to block the actions of 14-3-3zeta in fat cells. Collectively, these studies will examine if 14-3-3zeta can be a suitable drug target to treat obesity, which continues to grow at alarming rates throughout the world.

column36: Discovery, validation, and pre-clinical development of novel strategies to prevent anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.
column37: Background: A staggering 42% of childhood cancer patients develop disabling/life-threatening adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Anthracyclines are widely used for the treatment of ~70% of adult and childhood cancers. However, anthracyclines cause serious heart damage in 5-16% of patients, resulting in death or life-long disability. Currently prevention is limited to reducing the dose of anthracyclines or using a second drug to protect the heart, dexrazoxane. However, dose reduction reduces anti-cancer effectiveness and dexrazoxane is restricted to adult patients with advanced cancer receiving high anthracycline doses, and dexrazoxane is not approved for use in pediatric patients due to risks of secondary cancers. Our goal is to prevent anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We identified that the RARG gene is related to anthracycline-cardiotoxicity in a large children's cancer study (Nat Gen, 2015). Building upon these findings, we will pursue two prevention strategies: 1. Develop a novel cardioprotectant that disrupts the RARG pathway. We will screen a panel of targeted drugs in a human cardiac cells, followed by evaluation in well-established animal models of anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We have now demonstrated proof-of-principle for 2 drugs exhibiting up to 95% cardioprotection in cultured cardiac cells and these were more effective than dexrazoxane. 2. Identify new genetic risk factors to pre-emptively identify patients at higher risk of anthracycline-cardiotoxicity. We have collected DNA from a large group of adult patients for high-throughput genomic analyses. We will combine pediatric and adult studies to improve the study. Validated factors will be incorporated into a predictive test and explored as additional candidates for strategy #1. Expected Outcomes: A new safe and effective anthracycline-cardioprotectant will be primed for clinical evaluation in patients. New genetic risk factors will be transitioned to a clinical testing program.

column36: Imaging use for low back pain by primary care practitioners
column37: Low back pain is one of the biggest public health problems in Canada. Clinical practice guidelines consistently recommend that diagnostic imaging (for example x-rays, MRI and CT scans) is not performed routinely on people with low back pain because imaging is expensive and offers no help in diagnosing the cause of the pain in most patients with low back pain. In addition, these unnecessary tests lead to wasted resources and even potential harm to people from radiation exposure. It also raises the chances that people will go on to receive further unnecessary tests or treatments, or even invasive and harmful treatments. Despite these guideline recommendations, primary care clinicians frequently ignore these recommendations and order imaging. This project will quantify the extent of unnecessary diagnostic imaging for people with low back pain who visit a primary care practitioner in Ontario, including family physicians, physiotherapists and chiropractors. The project will also explore why these practitioners order diagnostic imaging, and determine whether reasons occur at the patient level, the practitioner level, the system level, or a combination of these. The information gathered will help us develop innovative strategies to reduce unnecessary diagnostic imaging. These strategies could lead to improved use of limited healthcare resources and reduce harm to the substantial number of Canadians who seek care for low back pain.

column36: Mechanisms of insulin resistance in podocytes and diabetic nephropathy
column37: Clinically evident kidney failure eventually develops in patients with type 1 (T1D) and type 2 (T2D) diabetes, and continues to progress despite receiving intensified glycemic control and renal protective drugs. Moreover, up to now, we have only a diffuse understanding of why some diabetic patients develop nephropathy whereas other patients never progress to dialysis. Elevated glucose and saturated fat (FFA) levels may cause local factor changes affecting podocyte survival, an important vascular cell in kidney, which are not easily reversed. I made a very interesting finding on a potential target called SHP-1 that is elevated with high glucose concentrations in diabetic kidney of rodent animals. SHP-1 is a member of the protein tyrosine phosphatase family that downregulates the activity of important growth factors such as insulin, VEGF and nephrin, which are crucial for podocyte survival and function. Interestingly, insulin resistance caused by FFA is triggered by the activation of the protein kinase C (PKC)-alpha. Thus, unwanted abnormalities of renal podocyte function causing insulin resistance in T1D and T2D can be regulated by the activation of two independent pathways: SHP-1 and PKC-alpha. The aim of the present proposal will characterize and explore the role of SHP-1 and PKC-alpha activation producing biological abnormalities such as podocyte death and insulin resistance. To accomplish this aim, we will use several methods to specifically manipulate the protein expression level of SHP-1 and PKC-alpha in podocyte cell line and evaluate their impact on insulin and nephrin actions. Moreover, I will use genetically modified tissue specific mice of SHP-1 to characterize its cellular mechanisms implicated in diabetic nephropathy using a T1D and T2D mouse models. We believe that this proposal will help us better understand the mechanisms underlying renal cell dysfunction related to kidney failure in T1D and T2D.

column36: Neural circuitry for detection of texture boundaries
column37: Our rich and effortless perception of the complex mixtures of objects and surfaces comprising our everyday world is one of the most remarkable achievements of the human brain. A key early step in the required neural processing is separation of the retinal image into regions corresponding to distinct surfaces of different objects. In natural images we can effortlessly perform such "figure-ground segmentation" of borders defined by differences in a variety of local image properties, for example differences in luminance, colour, contrast, or texture. This segmentation process necessarily precedes higher-level visual functions such as object recognition, and is fundamentally important to normal visual perception. Analysis of complex visual patterns begins in the early visual cortex, areas V1 and V2. The responses of single neurons in these cortical areas are highly specific, or "tuned", to particular kinds of visual stimuli. An understanding of the nature of stimulus selectivity of these neurons forms a critical basis of our current understanding of human visual perception. This research program has three specific objectives: to evaluate and extend our recently discovered model of the neural circuitry for detecting luminance and texture boundaries in early visual cortex; to explore whether there might be two different kinds of such neural processing; and to examine the relationship to detection of colour boundaries. The outcomes of this work will yield fundamental, health-related knowledge that may facilitate the future design of diagnostic tests and therapies for visual disorders.
