column36: Microparticles in Diabetes
column37: People with diabetes are far more likely to suffer a heart attack than nondiabetics. Diabetes causes changes to the blood vessels and this is believed to responsible for the increased risk of heart attacks and stroke. This project seeks to expand our understanding of how diabetes causes damage to the blood vessels. Microparticles are tiny pieces of cells that are released from dying cells in the body. Recently it has been found that the levels of microparticles in the blood are increased significantly in diabetes. Increased microparticles can predict a risk of a heart attack or death due to heart problems. The goal of this project is to determine how microparticles are formed in diabetes and how they may cause damage to blood vessels. We anticipate that by understanding the proteins carried by microparticles and the signaling that microparticles activate in diabetes we will be able to develop new drug treatments that can be used to reduce risk of heart and kidney problems in diabetes.

column37: Inactive lifestyles have a huge cost - to Canadians' health, our healthcare system and our economy. Comparing children who do/do not receive extra PA counselling will tell us if the "tool kit" helps children with heart problems to be more active, giving them access to the physical and mental health benefits of PA. column36: Mitigating Illness and Raising Wellness at the Human-Dog Interface in Northern Canada
column37: Dogs have been an integral part of the physical, social and cultural environment of Inuit and First nations but also can be a source of health risks in contemporary Northern communities. Attacks, bites, injuries, sometimes death, and the transmission of deadly rabies and probably other microbes are part of the reality in Northern communities. All these dog-related health issues are exacerbated by the lack of, or limited access to, veterinary services, the presence of free-roaming dogs and dog overpopulation, which remain chronic issues in Northern communities. The project's ultimate goal is to improve the health and wellness of Inuit, Naskapi, Cree and Westerners living in Northern Canada by mitigating dog-associated health risks and by supporting the role of dogs on wellness in these Northern communities. The Inuit, Naskapi, Cree and Western knowledges and perspectives on health and dogs will be mobilized during the course of the project as they are essential in contributing to a comprehensive understanding of the health effects at the human-dogs interface in the Northern communities and to inform the most successful sustainable interventions to protect human health and support human wellness. The primary project outcome is the reduction of the dog-related threats to human health and wellbeing in the North (i.e., attacks, bites, potential rabies case management, death), as well as supporting the positive dog-related health and cultural roles following the implementation of community-based, sustainable solutions during the course of the project.

column36: Functional organization of the human brain for colour and form vision: from LGN to extrastriate cortex.
column37: The understanding of human colour vision is a challenge that has interested scientists for over 300 years. The core of the problem is to understand how the spectral differences across the visual scene in the physical world are translated by the brain into the neural signals that represent the wide array of colours that we see in our perceptual world; in other words, how the human brain sees in colour. It is well known that there are two major subdivisions in the human visual system. The dorsal pathway is dedicated to visual guidance of our actions and motion through the visual world, whereas the ventral pathway encodes what we see in terms of the shapes and objects in the visual scene. In this proposal I investigate the role of the ventral pathway in the encoding of form and colour. I aim to identify which pathways and brain areas are used to encode colour as compared to the achromatic (black & white) components of the visual image, and how colour, form and shape analyses are combined within the brain. The research uses the latest techniques, including fMRI of the human brain and brain stimulation (TMS), to identify how the brain regions and pathways are functionally organized to deconstruct the visual image and then reform it into global percepts, enabling us to see the coloured version of the visual world that we so easily take for granted.

column36: Efficacy and Safety of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in patients with mild vascular cognitive impairment
column37: Despite promising leads, to date clinical trials of medications to halt or reverse dementia have failed. Consequently, treatment interventions for dementia are now focusing on those with cognitive problems who are at high risk of progressing, to intervene before there is irreversible damage to the brain. Cognitive problems are common in patients with heart disease and those who experience cognitive difficulties are more likely to develop dementia. While exercise can help many people maintain cognition, many people do not achieve cognitive benefits. Our research has provided the first evidence that oxidative stress may limit the benefits of exercise on brain function and cognition. Recent research suggests that reducing oxidative damage in the brain may possibly be an effective way to prevent the brain changes that lead to the cognitive deficits and functional impairment in dementia. N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a widely available and safe supplement, has powerful antioxidant effects, which may be beneficial to boost cognition. This study will test whether the antioxidant supplement NAC is safe and effective to improve cognition in patients with heart disease who show early memory problems, known as vascular cognitive impairment-no dementia (VCIND). In the current study, patients will be randomized to NAC supplements or placebo orally for 24 weeks while participating in a supervised exercise program. Standardized neuropsychological testing will be used to compare cognitive performance between the placebo and NAC groups. We will use new techniques to accurately measure the amount of oxidative stress damage in blood and evaluate whether the treatment is more efficacious in individuals with certain brain characteristics on MRI scans. If positive, these results will be important for the design of a longer term trial to investigate whether NAC can delay the onset of dementia.

column36: Sleep and circadian rhythms in men and women
column37: Women are up to twice as likely to suffer from insomnia as men. For a similar sleep schedule, we find that young adult women's circadian clock causes them to fall asleep and wake up earlier than men. These results in naturally cycling women are helping us understand why women are more likely than men to wake up earlier in the morning and feel tired after a night's sleep. After menopause, the risk of sleep disturbances increases substantially and affect 25-50% of women. Yet, almost nothing is known about the changes that occur with the circadian system regulating sleep and waking during menopause. In the present study, we propose to recruit postmenopausal women, aged 45 and older. From this group, 14 will be healthy sleepers and 14 will suffer from chronic insomnia. Each participant will be studied twice in time isolation for 3 consecutive days. During each visit, they will undergo a special procedure of multiple naps designed to test how their circadian clock controls sleep, waking, and mood. Saliva samples will be collected in order to assess internal biological time by measuring their content in the hormones cortisol and melatonin. Sleep will be recorded during naps and performance will be tested during waking episodes. Results will be compared between healthy sleepers and insomniacs in order to clarify how the circadian clock and melatonin affect sleep and waking in postmenopausal women. The present study will help understand the role the circadian system plays in the greater female susceptibility to sleep-wake disturbances. Future studies will pursue similar questions in men.

column36: Evaluation of My-HEARTSMAP, a self-reporting youth mental health assessment & management tool.
column37: Approximately 30% of all youth who seek health care in the emergency department (ED), have underlying mental health (MH) concerns. Unrecognized, MH issues may exacerbate the severity and frequency of youth's physical symptoms, their therapeutic needs, and hinder responses to treatment. Screening youth to detect and address MH concerns early, also helps improve MH outcomes. However, the ED is a busy place where clinicians are often preoccupied with more visible health problems, resulting in missed opportunities to optimize care in the ED. We recently adapted a clinical tool for families and youth to self-assess their MH status. This tool is called MyHEARTSMAP. It addresses 10 areas: home, education, alcohol & drugs, relationships & bullying, thoughts & anxiety, safety, sexual health, mood & behaviour, abuse, and professional resources. The severity and urgency of concerns across each category is assessed and then linked by an embedded algorithm to recommendations for services that families and youth can access. Our study goal is to evaluate MyHEARTSMAP with families and youth. First, using a set of fictional scenarios, we will determine if MyHEARTSMAP is a reliable tool for youth and families to use. Second, we will determine if MyHEARTSMAP is a valid tool. To do this, we will recruit families and youth (age 10-17) in the ED to use MyHEARTSMAP to self-assess the youth's mental health status. The families' self-assessment will then be compared to that of a clinician. Our project aims to provide a reliable and valid self-assessment MH tool for use in the ED, which will identify youth that could benefit from early intervention, to help optimize their ED care, and appropriately link families to resources. Because the tool relies on youth and family self-reporting, it allows for families' increased ownership over their health, while creating a more patient-centered and individualized care plan, but with minimal impact on ED flow.

column36: Hippo Regulation of Hepatocyte Identity and Function
column37: The term "liver disease" comprises over 100 types of disorders. However, the most common form of chronic liver disease is Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), which affects an estimated 30-46% of the population in the US. In Canada, over 2,000 deaths per year are due to liver disease and a further 1,700 deaths from liver cancer. As in the US, obesity is the leading cause of liver disease, with over-exposure to common chemicals or medications and viral infections such as hepatitis, being major contributors. Regardless of the initiating factor, chronic liver disease can cause permanent liver damage and scarring that will progress to cirrhosis, poor liver function and eventually may advance to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Currently, there is no cure for cirrhosis. Treatment focuses on slowing progression and minimizing complications, such as portal hypertension. When it is no longer possible to manage the complications, a liver transplant is required, but demand for transplants far exceeds available donor tissue. Recent advances in the differentiation of human pluripotent cells (hPSCs) into hepatocytes has excited researchers by providing a potential source of cells for liver transplants, drug testing and bioartificial liver devices. However, current methods of growing liver from hPSCs do not yet result in fully functional cells. Thus, methods to improve donor tissue expansion or the derivation of liver tissue from hPSCs require a better understanding of the factors that promote and maintain liver cells proliferation and differentiation. Our reserach will focus on how cells communicate and regulate the expression of genes in the liver. Using mouse as a model system, we will study how the different cell types in the liver are made and allow the liver to grow.

column36: Regulation of DNA double-strand break repair pathways in multiple myeloma
column37: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is the second most common hematological malignancy in Canada. Due to its heterogeneity, a large portion of patients affected by MM is refractory to or relapses from first line therapies, including the proteasome inhibitor (PI) Bortezomib. Therefore, it becomes crucial to better understand the pathobiology of MM and the resistance mechanisms of this malignancy. MM are characterized by recurrent chromosomal aberrations and aneuploidy. These features have been correlated with dysregulation of the DNA damage repair pathways. However, little is known about the exact mechanisms driving genomic instability in MM. We are particularly interested in one type of DNA damage, called DNA double-strand break (DSB). DSB is a highly dangerous DNA lesion that can result, if improperly repaired, in deleterious chromosomal rearrangements characteristics of MM. We are currently characterizing the major two DSB repair pathways, classical non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination, in different MM cell lines. Our goal is to determine at what level these pathways are dysregulated, thereby contributing to the heterogeneity and aggressiveness of MM. Understanding DSB repair pathways in MM will provide targets for the treatment of this pathology. It may also provide novel biomarkers to predict the risk of relapse/refractory MM.

column36: Predictors and consequences of long-term functional trajectories of older men: The Manitoba Follow-up Study
column37: Older adults travel different pathways as they approach the end of life. Some enjoy good health right up to the end, while others are ill or incapacitated for a long period of time, and then just slip away. The ability of a person to perform their normal activities of daily living (a.k.a. "functional capacity") is key to the lives of older people, since researchers have found it to relate to important things like death, nursing home admissions, and hospitalization. That said, the research on functional capacity as we get progressively older is sparse. Important questions remain, such as how different chronic diseases (and combinations thereof) affect our late-life pathways; and how being on diverse pathways can have different implications for health and well-being. The Manitoba Follow-up Study (MFUS) is one of the longest-running studies of health and aging in the world. MFUS has been following the same group of 3,983 men since 1948. column37: Understanding how cells grow and divide is a fundamental question in biology. During animal development the proper regulation of cell growth is essential for controlling organ and organism size. While in cancer, deregulated cell growth is often an early event in tumor formation. The processes that control growth are remarkably similar across different species. For example, in both humans and fruit flies similar genes regulate growth and mutations in these genes often lead to cancer. These similarities allow us to use the fruit fly as a simple, yet powerful genetic system to study what genes and molecules controls growth. We made the striking discovery that overproduction of a single molecule, called transfer RNA, can accelerate growth and increase body size in fruit flies. Transfer RNA plays a critical role in the synthesis all of the proteins and enzymes in a cell, including those essential for growth. Our goal in this grant is to understand how the production of tRNA is controlled and how increase in the production of transfer RNA can drive growth. Abnormal production of transfer RNA is often seen in cancer cells, therefore our work in fruit flies may provide clues to help us understand the runaway growth that makes this disease so devastating.

column37: With HIV vaccines unlikely to be available for years, marginalized populations in low income countries represent "hotspots" where specialized interventions are required to prevent transmission and support engagement in care. Four million young people aged 15-24 living with HIV globally are a critical group experiencing multiple barriers to care, however few studies have provided evidence for development of interventions. Acholi young women impacted by Northern Uganda's civil war are among the most neglected populations in East Africa. Complex societal processes contribute to vulnerability in this post-conflict environment and can drastically escalate susceptibility to HIV, other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and early death. Young women in Northern Uganda are faced with the challenges of return migration, poverty, mental health, lack of health infrastructure, and insufficient services. They also experience increased opportunities for HIV exposure via untreated STIs, sexual violence, and sex work. Epidemiological data that characterizes the impact of war and the post-conflict environment on both vulnerability and resilience of young women in Northern Uganda are scarce. Little is understood about how to support young women's access to HIV care: treatment retention, adherence, and viral suppression. We will initiate a study addressing HIV vulnerability among young conflict-affected women aged 13-24 years in 3 Northern Ugandan districts - the areas most severely impacted by the protracted war between the Government of Uganda and the Lord's Resistance Army. Using ethnographic and epidemiological methods over 3 years, we will: 1) estimate prevalence/incidence of HIV and syphilis and identify risk factors; 2) investigate associations between post traumatic stress, resilience, and depression with HIV incidence, and; 3) pilot the feasibility and acceptability of using mobile phones to support engagement in HIV care.

column36: Roles of the PRP19 complex in the Maintenance of Genome Stability
column37: Our cells are constantly subjected to stress that can damage their genetic material and cause mutations. Mutations can lead to the development of diseases such as cancer. To prevent the occurrence of deleterious mutations, our cells harbour signaling pathways that detect the DNA structures associated with damage and protect our genomes from degradation. Cancer cells often have defects in these protective pathways and are thus more sensitive to stress and accumulate mutations more readily than healthy cells. This is leveraged by doctors to destroy tumors through the use of chemo- and radio-therapy which cause unsustainable levels of damage to the genetic material of cancer cells. In an effort to identify novel therapeutic targets that could help in the fight against cancer, we have recently identified many new proteins that can recognize the structures found at broken regions of the genome. Amongst these factors, PRP19 is particularly important for the resistance to chemotherapeutic drugs and irradiation which tells us that PRP19 helps cells repair their DNA. PRP19 works by modifying other proteins in the cell such as RPA, an essential guardian of our genome. Our work will help us understand how the modification of RPA and other proteins by PRP19 and additional PRP19-like proteins called ubiquitin ligases allows our cells to protect their DNA. We will thus examine how PRP19 works with other proteins to remove the toxic DNA lesions that may appear when cells replicate their genetic material. This new information will improve our understanding of the complex pathways that protect our DNA and guide us in the elaboration of novel strategies that will improve the efficiency of current anti-cancer treatments.

column36: Translational studies into human colon motor dysfunction
column37: Colonic motility disorders, ranging from Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) to chronic constipation and pseudo-obstruction, impose a heavy personal and economic burden affecting 7 million Canadians, with a health care cost of >$8 billion /year and >$8 billion/year in lost productivity. Children with chronic constipation experience depression and stunted education. Treatments are often not beneficial because we do not have a complete understanding of how motility is controlled and we do not know what is actually wrong with the colon of patients because we do not measure it. I propose inherently translational studies aimed at understanding mechanisms underlying colonic dysmotility, generating novel therapeutic approaches. My first aim is to understand the mechanisms by which the colon creates normal or abnormal motility with a focus on the critical role of interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC), the pacemaker cells of the gut that orchestrate most motor patterns. I am internationally recognized as a leader in this field and ICC abnormalities are the most common pathology finding in constipation. My second aim is to measure and understand motility dysfunction in patients, using 84-sensor high-resolution manometry. Parallel animal and human studies will allow me to identify optimal stimuli to be used in the assessment so that I can translate abnormal responses to stimuli into causes of dysmotility. My third aim is to understand pathophysiology. In animal models, and in patients through mucosal biopsies, I will reveal relationships between abnormal motility, abnormal bacterial composition and abnormal microbe-derived metabolites. As outcome I will obtain optimal diagnostic testing of colonic dysmotility in patients, a better understanding of the underlying pathophysiology to allow for better management of each patient to increase health-related quality of life. Elucidation of the nature of the dysmotility will allow the development of new treatments and reduce hospital costs.

column36: Imaging of cerebral vascular adaptation following traumatic brain injury
column37: The blood vessels that supply the brain with oxygen and nutrients form a complex and highly organized network whose proper functioning is essential for our survival. Disease or injury to the brain may damage this network and disrupt the transport of blood and the mechanisms that regulate how much oxygen and nutrients are delivered. As the brain recovers from injury, new blood vessels are added, others are removed, and existing blood vessels may change in dimensions or even move. How these changes occur is poorly understood yet is thought to be essential to recovering healthy brain function. The goal of this project is to understand this adaptation process for the purpose of developing better methods to monitor and promote recovery following brain injury. Our research strategy is to use experimental mice that receive an injury to the part of the brain that is responsible for controlling movement. Advanced 3D optical microscopy methods will be used to directly observe the changing blood vessel network following injury. Magnetic resonance imaging will be used to assess how blood is being distributed within the brain and the capacity of the brain to elevate blood flow when needed. A subset of the mice will undertake voluntary exercise to evaluate whether this improves recovery. We will use these observations to identify beneficial patterns of blood vessel remodelling following traumatic brain injury and to assess when and if exercise can be used to promote recovery. Finally, we will evaluate a new ultrasound diagnostic technique in the mice to monitor changes in how blood is supplied. Together these findings could lead both to better methods to promote recovery following brain injury and to new diagnostic methods that could be used clinically to monitor the progress of treatment.

column37: The immune system of an individual is devoted to figth infectious agents. This is achieved by white blood cells that patrol the organism to eliminate pathogens. column36: Toward a Paradigm Shift in Rehabilitation for Adults and Children Living with HIV in Sub-Saharan Africa: Development, Implementation, and Evaluation of a Novel KT Intervention
column37: THE ISSUE: Improved access to treatment in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) means that people are growing up and growing older with HIV as a chronic illness. These adults and children are now experiencing diverse HIV-related disabilities. Physiotherapists (PTs) and occupational therapists (OTs) can deliver rehabilitation to address these disabilities, but pilot research exposed a gap in HIV care among PTs and OTs in Kenya and Zambia. OUR IDEA: We plan to develop, tailor, implement, and evaluate a novel knowledge translation (KT) intervention in four diverse settings in SSA with the goals of improving knowledge, attitudes, and self-efficacy about HIV and encouraging rehabilitation students to become HIV and rehabilitation advocates. OUR TEAM: The team is co-led by longstanding colleagues, Nixon and Myezwa. Nixon (researcher) pioneered HIV and rehabilitation in Canada in the 1990's. Myezwa (knowledge user) is a leading HIV and rehabilitation advocate in SSA. The project includes a "KT science team" of Canadian KT leaders and four "site implementation teams" of rehabilitation educators and senior leaders at the training sites in SSA. OUR APPROACH: This three-phase project will (1) develop, (2) tailor and implement, and (3) evaluate a KT intervention at four diverse rehabilitation training programs in SSA. A realist evaluation approach will be used to establish what works, for whom, and under what circumstances in order to (a) enable tailoring and implementing the KT intervention across sites and (b) improve knowledge, attitudes, and self-efficacy in HIV and rehabilitation advocacy among rehabilitation students. IMPACT: This study builds on CIHR research that integrated rehabilitation into HIV in Canada. A similar change is needed in SSA but on a greater scale: Canada has 75,000 people living with HIV; SSA has 24 million. This study will enable us to expand this intervention throughout SSA, creating a critical mass of HIV and rehabilitation advocates to promote health.

column36: Efficacy of cognitive behavioural and skills training therapy of adolescents with ADHD
column37: Attention Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common childhood psychiatric condition,which often persists into adolescence. In adolescence ADHD is associated with poor academic, social, and emotional functioning, other psychiatric problems, substance abuse, and antisocial behaviour. Although medication effectively reduces symptoms such as hyperactivity and inattention, it does not directly address academic, social, emotional, and behavioural problems. Overcoming these would require building skills in organization, time management, problem solving, emotional modulation, stress management and interpersonal rapport. Yet, psychosocial treatments targeting such skills in adolescents with ADHD have been little studied and are scarce in the community. The proposed study will evaluate cognitive behavioural and skills training therapy (CBT+S) for adolescents with ADHD. Adolescents will be randomly assigned to 14 sessions of either manualized group CBT+S or manualized supportive group therapy (SGT, control condition). An additional treatment-as-usual group will be evaluated to control for repeated measurements. CBT+S will focus on skill acquisition in common problem areas for adolescents with ADHD, such as organization and time management, distractibility, impulsivity, and social skills. A coach will call each participant twice a week to help practice the learned skills. Parallel groups will be provided for parents of CBT+S and SGT participants focusing on education, support and sharing experiences. If CBT+S proves to benefit adolescents with ADHD, it can be made widely available to these adolescents in the community. This would help them improve their academic, social, and emotional functioning and ultimately their long term outcomes.

column36: Genetic mosaicism in human development
column37: A growth restricted fetus is more likely to be born premature or with birth defects and is at increased risk for adverse neonatal, childhood and adult health outcomes. Poor growth is most often linked to a placenta that does not deliver oxygen and nutrients efficiently tot eh developing baby. One cause of poor placenta function, present in ~10% of pregnancies with pathologically small babies, is a chromosome (genetic) abnormality found in the placenta that is not present in the baby. This is referred to as confined placental mosaicism. In the past only large chromosome errors could be tested for in the placenta, but with advances in diagnostic technologies, smaller genetic changes can now be detected. These likely also account for a portion of small babies. Our goal is to determine the incidence of genetic abnormalities confined to the placenta and how often they explain why a baby is born too small. This genetic data is also important for interpreting prenatal testing; increasingly, prenatal testing is done by analyzing cell-free DNA derived from the placenta that circulates in maternal blood. Our goal is to fill the major gap in knowledge concerning the incidence and impact of placental mosaicism on fetal growth and development.

column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death globally and in Canada, where it kills more people than breast, prostate, colorectal and pancreatic cancers combined. Unfortunately for the majority of Canadians diagnosed with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) today, the prognosis remains the same as it did 20 years ago, a dismal 15% five-year survival. Yet the data suggest these mutant genes do not act on their own: they require additional cooperating genes for tumors progression malignancy. One such gene is the tumor suppressor P53, which is mutated in 70% of NSCLCs. This proposal aims to uncover how the tumor suppressor P53 works at molecular level and when it is important in the evolution of a fully malignant metastatic cell - both of which are paramount to discovering new and effective cancer treatments. Genetically modified mouse models (GEMM) are presently the gold standard for whole organism cancer modeling. We will make use of our novel GEMMs of human lung cancer where we can control the site, the number and the timing of specific genetic events. This enables us to query fundamental questions regarding the genetics of tumour initiation, progression, maintenance and ultimately, metastasis. Furthermore, these GEMMs of human lung cancer provide platforms for both the engineering and validation of targeted therapies with the goal of developing new therapies to alleviate suffering inflicted by this dreaded disease

column36: Studies of the functional role of pancreatic stellate cells (PaSCs) during islet differentiation, regeneration and diabetes.
column37: A major problem for people with diabetes is the loss of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas. Repopulating beta-cells requires a thorough analysis of the factors that regulate their growth and maintain their function. One important cell type near by the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas is the pancreatic star-like cell (PaSC). PaSCs required maintain pancreatic structure and exocrine function is well-studied, whether it has effects on the beta-cell is unknown. We carried out a preliminary study of these cells in the human fetal pancreas and found that the PaSCs proliferate rapidly and show changes in gene and protein expression during development. In contrast, in the adult pancreas, PaSCs were found to be activated following pancreatic organ injury and to be involved in repair of the damaged tissue. In the diabetic mouse pancreas, there was activation of the PaSCs within beta-cell clusters. These pilot studies indicate that PaSCs likely have a role in the pancreas during development and following injury or the onset of diabetes. column36: Therapeutic targeting of immune-inflammation pathway via IL23-IL17 axis in Endometriosis
column37: Endometriosis, characterized by growth of endometrial lining outside of the uterus, is the most prevalent global cause for hysterectomy, infertility and pelvic pain. It affects 6-10% of reproductive age women and 35-50% in women with pelvic pain/unexplained infertility. Despite its staggering economic impact ($1.8 Billion/year Canada; $22 Billion/year USA), endometriosis remains misdiagnosed, misunderstood and ineffectively treated. Diagnosis relies on invasive laparoscopy procedure to visualise lesions. Current treatments transiently alleviate but do not cure endometriosis. Growth of endometriotic lesions depend on abnormally levels of estrogen combined with pronounced inflammatory environment in the peritoneal cavity. Indeed, we provided striking evidence that endometriotic lesions are major regulators and promoters of inflammation. From our preliminary data and published papers, IL23-IL17 axis emerged as a major pathway in regulation of pain and inflammation. However mechanisms and molecular drivers of IL23-IL17 axis that modulate inflammation and pain in endometriosis is unidentified. Using endometriosis patient samples, cell lines and our established mouse models, we will: 1) Determine the basis for endometriosis associated immune dysfunction and how it contributes to susceptibility and progression of endometriosis.2) Identify and validate immune-inflammatory mediators (e.g., IL-17/IL-23 axis) contributing to the pathogenesis of endometriosis and for their diagnostic/therapeutic potential. 3) Conduct pre-clinical evaluation of IL-23-IL17 axis for therapeutic targeting in mouse model of endometriosis. Our research will provide novel insights into how complex immune networks are involved in the pathogenesis of endometriosis and deliver real-life solutions for improved diagnosis and better management of endometriosis patients.

column36: Mechanisms underlying schizophrenia
column37: Clinical Issue: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a debilitating mental disorder affecting young adults. SZ symptoms include early social isolation, cognitive decline prior to episodes of auditory hallucinations, false beliefs and associated anxiety and depression. Current treatments targeting the dopaminergic system remedy psychosis but not other schizophrenia symptoms. The goal is to identify therapeutic targets dysregulated early in the disease process to provide better outcomes for SZ. We have recently discovered a new mouse model of SZ in which the phosphatase enzyme PTP1B is hyperactive in the brain. We also found that in two other commonly used experimentally induced mouse models of SZ this enzyme activity is increased in the affected brain regions. Our previous work showed that hyperactivity of this enzyme disrupts the function of important glutamate receptors on neurons. This can lead to malfunction of dopaminergic circuitry and cause psychosis in humans. Moreover, we reported that hyperactivity of this enzyme also impairs the production of one of the body's own cannabis-like substances (endogenous cannabinoid). Since cannabinoids control how much neurotransmitters are released from neurons, this would further lead to aberrant neuronal activity. Dysregulated levels of cannabinoids in the serum and the cerebrospinal fluid are observed in SZ patients. Our hypothesis is that elevated PTP1B activity is the central mechanism that accounts for functional deficits in the SZ brain. We will test whether targeting this enzyme with a selective inhibitor called Trodusquemine will ameliorate SZ symptoms in two preclinical mouse models. Significance: In Canada, about 1% of the population (~350,000) has SZ. Successful validation of targeting PTP1B to improve SZ in preclinical mouse models can rapidly move to clinical trials since Trodusquemine has already undergone phase 1 clinical trials to treat obesity.

column37: The early years of life are critical to establishing healthy behaviours. Sadly, the majority of preschool age children are not meeting both Canadian physical activity and screen time guidelines and have poor motor skills. Childcare centres are important settings as more than half of children attend childcare and spend a large proportion of their days and weeks there. In a sub-set of centres, we will also measure children's physical activity, sedentary behaviour and motor skill competencies. The findings will inform future policies and enhance our understanding of how policy action supported by communication and capacity-building strategies influences the environment of childcare centres.

column36: Ultrasound based pedicle screw navigation: an intraoperative image guidance system without radiation exposure
column37: Each year more than 28,000 Canadians are treated surgically for lower back pain. Many of these cases require instrumentation with pedicle screws, which requires some form of X-ray imaging like fluoroscopy or intra-operative CT thus exposing patients and operating room personnel to significant amounts of harmful radiation. This project will adapt and clinically test a new intra-operative ultrasound-based navigation system that is an inexpensive, radiation-free alternative to intra-operative X-ray imaging. This novel technology allows for precise identification of the bony surface of the vertebrae without exposing the spine by merging the pre-operative CT and intra-operative ultrasound images. Such 3D renditions of the spine improve patient-to-image registration facilitating image-guided spine surgery. The novel system will be validated as a safe, accurate, and novel method for intraoperative guidance to perform instrumented lumbar spinal fusion and decompressions. The immediate benefits of this system compared to current standard intraoperative X-ray-based imaging technology are: 1) Elimination of all intraoperative radiation exposure to patient and operating room personnel 2) Real-time navigation at every level of the spine with intuitive visualization. 3) Increased accessibility (in terms of lower costs, smaller footprint, less cumbersome) of navigated spine surgery for all surgeons. 4) Decreased operating room time and thus decreased morbidity of spine surgery. 5) Improved accuracy of navigation through better registration. 6) Decreased numbers of malpositioned screws and consequently, reduced numbers of revision surgeries. And finally, 7) unlimited levels of fusion may be performed with the novel navigation method. This is of particular importance in scoliosis cases where current technology only captures 5 to 6 segments at a time and dose constraints limits the number of X-ray based images.

column36: MRI parenchymal enhancement and risk of breast cancer: A population-based study of women screened in the Ontario Breast Screening Program
column37: The Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) High-Risk Screening Program includes women between the ages of 30 and 69 years who have a very high risk of breast cancer. As part of this program, women undergo breast screening every year with both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and mammogram. Because of their very high risk, these women are also frequently considered for preventive surgeries (e.g., having their breasts and/or ovaries removed). While potentially reducing a woman's risk of breast cancer, these surgeries can seriously impact their quality of life. New markers of breast cancer risk that can identify the women who would benefit the most from these interventions are needed. This will help provide personalized recommendations for both breast cancer prevention and screening. Mammograms generate an image of the breast where fat appears white and breast tissue appears dark. The amount of breast tissue a woman has is called mammographic density (MD). Having high MD is known to strongly increase a woman's risk of breast cancer. This relationship is well known in average-risk women but it is not known if it is also true for high-risk women. Another characteristic of the breast that might tell us about a woman's risk of breast cancer is seen on MRI and is called background parenchymal enhancement (BPE). Small studies have shown that having high BPE may increase a woman's risk of getting breast cancer. Dr. Brooks and her research team will examine the relationship between MD and BPE and risk of breast cancer in women being screened in the OBSP High-Risk Program. This study will be the first to look at the relationship between BPE in an established screening program. This study will provide us with information that will better determine a woman's risk of getting breast cancer, helping to guide recommendations for breast cancer screening and preventive interventions. This could significantly impact how high-risk women are screened and treated in the future.

column36: Developmental origins of childhood obesity: tracking the causal epigenetic changes programming adiposity in children
column37: Obesity now affects up to 1 in 5 children in Canada. Obese children are more likely to stay obese as adults and this has profound impacts on their long-term health. Indeed, obesity increases risk to develop diabetes and heart diseases among many other diseases. Events during pregnancy are suspected to play a role in 'programming' whether a child develops obesity, but we still do not know much about the mechanisms involved. Scientific and medical observations strongly suggest that "epigenetic" factors are important. The term epigenetics refers to chemical modifications of the genes that act as a change in the software reading the genetic information (hardware). Maternal conditions - such as diabetes in pregnancy - influence the environment in which the foetus develops. The environment of the foetus in the womb can affect the epigenetic marks with profound effects on the reading and expression of the genetic information throughout life. Such long-term changes involving genes implicated in weight control will have an impact on the risk to develop obesity and related chronic diseases. For this reason, the so-called epigenetic mechanisms have a real potential to explain why some unfavourable environment within the womb affecting foetal development during pregnancy may predispose newborns to develop obesity early in their life as well as diabetes and heart disease later on. Our primary objective is to identify epigenetic marks observed at birth that predict which child will become obese. Then, we will determine which specific pregnancy events, whether maternal obesity or diabetes during pregnancy, cause these epigenetic changes. Finally, the impact of these epigenetic changes on gene expression levels will be assessed. Our study will help to understand the biological mechanisms linking epigenetic events occurring during pregnancy and the increased risk for children to develop obesity.

column37: Rationale: Progressive degeneration characterizes muscle disorders (e.g. Duchenne muscular dystrophy [DMD]) and age- or disease-related declines in muscle mass/function. Poor blood flow (ischemia), inflammation and fibrosis are profound in these diseases, generating an environment that prevents muscle repair. New strategies must improve this environment to impact the lives of patients. A promising approach that is believed may improve the muscle environment uses vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to improve blood flow. However, contrary to this approach, our group has now demonstrated in a preclinical mouse model of DMD that delivery of VEGF is not sufficient to reduce ischemia, and in fact increases muscle inflammation and fibrosis! Our hypothesis is that the vasculature in DMD is abnormal. Thus, our overarching objective is to rescue abnormal vasculature in DMD by administering a factor that stabilizes it, Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1). Specific Aims: 1.To characterize abnormal vasculature in detail, in (a) preclinical mouse models of DMD and (b) skeletal muscle tissue samples from DMD patients. These data will allow us to critically identify a window of opportunity to intervene with delivery of Ang-1 as a therapeutic. 2. To provide laboratory-based proof of concept in DMD mice for the administration of Ang-1 to improve muscle repair. 3. To develop a novel, targeted Ang-1 delivery approach that will allow for the precise regulation of Ang-1 delivery that will be essential for future clinical use in patients. Significance: Without an approach to improve the muscle environment, and prevent/reduce ischemia/inflammation/fibrosis, it is unlikely that the benefits of therapeutics for muscle regenerative disorders can ever be fully realized. Our vascular-targeted strategy will reduce medical costs, prolong ambulation and longevity, and improve quality of life for patients not only affected by muscle degeneration, but perhaps by any vascular defect.

column36: The role of RhoA/mDia1 pathway in salt-sensitive hypertension
column37: Hypertension is the prevalent treatable risk factor contributing to cardiovascular diseases, which remain the most common cause of death in industrialized countries taking the lives of over one million people every year in the U.S. alone. In Canada, over 20% of adults are diagnosed with hypertension, and an estimated 9 in 10 people who live an average lifespan will develop the condition in their lifetime. Excessive dietary salt intake is strongly correlated with cardiovascular diseases such as myocardial infarction and stroke, and is regarded as a major contributing factor to hypertension. While the link between salt and hypertension is well established, the mechanisms by which high salt intake leads to increased blood pressure remain unclear. Consumption of salt in a meal increases the levels of salt (sodium) in the blood, causing activation of specialized brain cells that release a hormone called vasopressin. Vasopressin leads to retention of water in the kidney in order to decrease blood sodium levels back to normal. Vasopressin also affects blood vessels causing them to constrict. These effects of vasopressin can lead to the elevation of blood pressure. Our hypothesis is that chronic exposure to excessive amounts of salt causes a hyperactivation of vasopressin-secreting brain cells. These cells have a specialized cellular skeleton that determine their shape (just like the shape of the body is determined by its skeleton). This cellular skeleton becomes denser and stiffer when the cells are chronically exposed to high salt levels. As a result, the cells become overly activated and secrete excessive amounts of vasopressin, leading to a sustained blood pressure increase and hypertension. We propose to study the mechanisms by which high salt causes the modification of cellular skeleton in the brain cells thereby leading to hypertension.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an incurable, severely debilitating disease with suboptimal therapy and no cure. Canada has the highest incidence of MS in the world with 291 cases per 100,000 people. MS is most commonly diagnosed in young adults and patients suffer progressive and irreversible damage to the brain. The root causes and risk factors for MS are still unknown. As such, current therapies are limited to treating symptoms, rather than the root cause. Other incurable diseases that lead to progressive loss of quality of life, and death, include the occupational respiratory diseases; which are caused by breathing in toxic materials such as asbestos and silica. These diseases commonly affect our firefighters, miners and military personnel. MS and occupational respiratory diseases are caused by chronic inflammation of the brain and lung respectively. Although the brain and lung have very different functions in the body, they share some common features during inflammation. One common feature is that the inflammatory protein IL-1 is made by cells locally and leads to excessive inflammation and tissue damage. It is well known that if we limit IL-1, we can protect from MS and occupational respiratory diseases; but we don't fully understand how and why IL-1 is made. We have exciting new evidence to suggest that a recently found digestive protein in immune cells triggers the release of IL-1 in both the brain and lung. Mice that don't have this protein are protected from experimental models of MS and respiratory disease caused by silica. Interestingly, this protein was recently identified by other scientists as being a possible risk factor for MS. Our research will determine how this protein brings about IL-1 release and inflammation in the brain and lung. This will allow scientists and doctors to better understand how chronic inflammation develops and potentially formulate new strategies to treat diseases such as MS and occupational respiratory disease.

column36: Getting Older adults OUTdoors (GO-OUT): A randomized controlled trial of a community-based outdoor walking program
column37: The ability to walk outdoors is key to participating in the community. Walking outside the home is a universally accessible form of physical activity with multiple health benefits. Walking can help reduce the risk of heart disease, hypertension, stroke, diabetes, osteoporosis, depression, and falls. Practice walking across roads, slopes and curbs, while talking, and dealing with crowds and traffic, is safe and feasible and can improve confidence and walking ability. Walking outdoors in nature appears to improve mental health more than walking indoors. Despite these health benefits, the majority of older Canadians infrequently walk outside. Barriers include fear, physical disability, inappropriate footwear and walking aids, challenging physical environments, such as uneven pavement, and poor weather. The best strategy for getting people to walk outdoors regularly is unknown. At the workshop, participants will learn about appropriate footwear, walking aids, equipment, and goal setting, and practice skills to increase outdoor walking. In the outdoor walking program, groups of 9 participants will meet for one hour, twice a week, to practice increasingly challenging activities in parks and built environments. The effect of the workshop and outdoor walking program compared to the workshop plus reminders on improving outdoor walking activity, physical activity, participation, and health-related quality of life, will be evaluated. Each participant will complete four evaluations: before the intervention and 3, 5, and 12 months later. We will interview select people at 6 and 12 months to ask their opinions of what worked and didn't work. Increasing outdoor walking is expected to improve health and well-being, and help people live independently in the community for longer.

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and a huge burden on health care globally. Despite worldwide efforts, all clinical trials on AD to date have failed. These disappointing findings demonstrate that our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of AD is far from complete, and that novel and effective treatments for AD are urgently needed. It is thought that the accumulation of amyloid-B (AB) in the brain is a primary driver of AD. However, an unresolved question is what causes the accumulation of AB. We recently discovered that genetically suppressing the activity of ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2) dramatically reduces AB level and blocks memory impairment in a mouse model of AD. This exciting finding indicates that RyR2 plays a major role in AD pathogenesis. The goals of this project are to determine RyR2's contributions to AD pathogenesis and to develop novel RyR2-targeted treatments for AD. To achieve these goals, we will determine the role of RyR2 in AB accumulation, neuron loss, and memory impairment in AD mice. We will define how genetically suppressing or enhancing RyR2 activity affects Ca regulation in AD neurons. Further, we will establish if pharmacological RyR2 inhibition suppresses AD pathology. We have developed the necessary tools and obtained key preliminary data demonstrating the feasibility of our approaches. We expect to reveal for the first time direct evidence that RyR2 plays a major role in AD pathology. We also expect to reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanism underlying abnormal Ca regulation in AD and identify the first RyR2-targeted potential treatment for AD. These proposed studies will advance health-related knowledge and improve health outcomes by uncovering novel fundamental mechanisms and developing novel treatments for AD.

Such characteristics allow neural crest cells to colonize several regions of the developing embryo and generate a wide array of cell types such as peripheral neurons and glia, pigment cells, craniofacial bone cells as well as specific cell subsets of the heart, inner ear and thymus. Because of the large number of neural crest cell derivatives, distinct structures/cell types (isolated or in combination) are affected in each neurocristopathy. The most important issue in this research field is that the underlying genetic cause and associated pathogenic mechanism of most cases of neurocristopathy are poorly understood. To address this problem, we use the mouse as a model organism and take advantage of the state-of-the-art methods of genomic modifications and analyses. Such studies are complemented by more classical techniques of molecular and cellular biology. Importantly, through established collaborations with researchers working in a clinical setting, we also validate our findings in children affected by the studied neurocristopathy. Notably, this work allowed us to identify a new gene for which the mutation can cause CHARGE syndrome - a neurocristopathy with a very complex clinical presentation and which can be fatal for many young children. The main objective of the current project is to understand the function of this new gene (Fam172a) in both normal and pathological conditions. This work is expected to significantly improve the way children suffering from CHARGE syndrome - as well as their families - are currently being taken care of.

column36: Tau: a novel target to prevent early neuronal dysfunction and death in glaucoma.
column37: Sight is essential for humans to gather critical information about their surroundings. The fear of going blind has been reported to be more powerful than that of having cancer or heart disease. Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, affecting >60 million people worldwide. There is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the death of retinal ganglion cells, the neurons that convey visual information from the retina to the brain. High intraocular pressure is the most significant risk factor for developing the disease, but the mechanisms by which ocular hypertension damages retinal ganglion cells are unknown. A major roadblock towards developing effective therapeutics for glaucoma is that very little is known about the early pathological alterations that lead to retinal ganglion cell dysfunction and death. Our recent work has identified a new and intriguing role for tau, a microtubule binding protein implicated in Alzheimer's disease, in ganglion cell neurodegeneration. We showed that tau undergoes substantial alterations early in glaucoma including abnormal phosphorylation, aggregation and missorting. In this application, we will determine the role of tau in the earliest pathological changes in glaucoma, namely retinal ganglion cell dendrite retraction and anterograde axonal transport impairment. This project is unique and timely because it will provide new insight into the molecular mechanisms that govern glaucoma pathogenesis, and it will serve as a springboard to identify new therapeutic targets and potential diagnostic tools for this blinding disease.

column36: Studying microbial load and antibiotic resistance genes in source and drinking water from First Nation Reserves
column37: Data from the past two decades indicate that approximately 1 in 5 First Nation communities in Canada are under a drinking water advisory at any given time. Most of the drinking water advisories are due to microbial contaminants. Many First Nations homes rely on cisterns (water-holding tanks) for home storage of drinking water and Canadian experts identified in 2013 the urgent need for science research on these systems. In a pilot study carried out by us in a First Nation community, we found significant numbers of coliforms, E. coli, and also antibiotic resistance genes drinking water supply. In this project, we will expand our study to four different communities and compare piped and cistern water distribution systems using state-of-the-art analytical chemistry and molecular biology methods to provide for detailed water quality measurements. Water samples collected along distribution pathways will be analyzed on a seasonal basis for chlorine concentrations, the presence of coliforms (indicator of fecal contamination), total microbial community, and also for the presence of antibiotic resistance genes. In addition, an alternative in-house water treatment technology will be tested. This Project Grant application is a research collaboration between academic researchers, First Nations leaders, and four First Nations communities. These researchers have collaborated in preliminary studies (2014) that led to the development of the proposed research plan that will improve the drinking water quality in the participating communities and in other First Nations. Safe drinking water will not only improve the health of individuals and families in First Nations communities but will also result in reduced heath-care costs for Canada. It will also provide for greater opportunities for First Nation socio-economic development since most businesses require clean water.

column36: Elucidating the role of alpha 11 integrin in mediating cardiac fibroblast-extracellular matrix interactions in health and disease
column37: When the heart is damaged, the body responds by laying down scar tissue. In the early stages, this is a good thing and helps to keep the heart pumping. After some time though, the scar tissue causes the heart to stiffen and it becomes more and more difficult for the heart to both pump, and fill up, with blood. The cells which produce the scar tissue are called fibroblasts, and they "talk" to the scar tissue so that they put the right amount down in the right place. However, this process often goes wrong, and that can cause the heart to fail even sooner. The proteins which help the cardiac fibroblasts "talk" to the scar tissue are called integrins. Our group has identified an integrin, which we don't know much about. It is called the "alpha 11 integrin". Research by our team has shown that when this integrin is missing, the hearts become stiff and the cells look small and thin. This research project will study how this protein "talks" to scar tissue, and what role it plays in the normal heart, and after the heart suffers damage. Given the fact that about 45% of all deaths in the world occur as a result of chronic scar tissue formation, it is vital that we understand exactly how scar tissues and cells work, so that we can one day develop new treatments to stop people dying not only of heart disease, but also other diseases where scar tissue is a problem such as liver disease, lung disease and kidney disease!

column36: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy: Seizure induced brainstem hypoxia
column37: People with epilepsy often die suddenly and unexpectedly. In fact they are 27 times more likely to do so compared with the general population. This unfortunate occurrence is called Sudden Unexpected Death in EPilepsy (SUDEP) and it is the leading cause of death in persons with epilepsy. SUDEP most often occurs where an individual with a history of epilepsy is found dead with evidence of a prior seizure. From the few studies on patients in a hospital setting, that would have died if not for medical intervention; we know that SUDEP is ultimately caused by failure to breathe either during a seizure or very soon after a seizure ends followed quickly by heart failure. What we don't know is what causes the failure to breathe. My laboratory has recently discovered a period of severely low oxygen levels (hypoxia) during and following a seizure. The hypoxia is found only in brain regions involved in the seizure and is severe enough to cause behavioural dysfunction. I hypothesize that SUDEP occurs when seizures invade the breathing centers in the brainstem and local tissue oxygen falls below a critical level impairing the function of those areas which leads to breathing failure and death. We will first determine the relationship between seizure activity and local oxygen levels in brain breathing centers on breathing behaviour. To do this we will use an implantable device that continuously measures the absolute levels of oxygen in awake behaving mice. We will next determine more drugs that can prevent seizure-induced hypoxia. We have previously identified two kinds of drugs that prevent the seizure-induced blood vessel constriction and low oxygen levels. We will use these to determine the effect of preventing the seizure-induced hypoxic period on mouse breathing and survival. We believe that SUDEP is preventable and that the knowledge generated by these proposed studies will ultimately save lives.

column36: Monitoring and Management of Burn Injuries Using an Intelligent Multifunctional Wound Dressing
column37: Burn injuries represent a major life-threatening and life-altering event that impact the quality of life of many Canadians each year and place enormous demands on the national and global health care systems. Damages caused by burns are painful and can catastrophically compromise the integrity and protective function of the skin and establish an active portal for infections. Inadequate oversight of infected sites can lead to cellulitis (cell inflammation) and ultimately bacteremia and septicemia, both of which can significantly increase the mortality and morbidity rate. The overarching goals of the current research proposal are to fabricate a modular intelligent multifunctional wound dressing (SmartDerma) and utilize it for the treatment of burn injuries. Such platform is capable of measuring the wound environment and delivering drugs to the wound. SmartDerma will autonomously monitor the condition of the wound and the dressing itself and relay information to a nurses' station using a wireless link. The performance of SmartDerma will be evaluated in vitro and in vivo as critical steps towards the clinical applications of this technology. We envision that SmartDerma will revolutionize current practice, which involves time-consuming and manual removal of a dressing and visual inspection of the underlying wound. This process is uncomfortable for the patient and disturbs the natural healing process. Our hi-tech dressing will generate significant savings in healthcare costs, due to reduced clinical inspection time and shorter hospital stays as a result of faster wound healing.

column36: Interrogation of drug and toxin mechanism of action by a matrix of chemogenomic profiles in human cells
column37: This project aims to exploit a new technology that will enable drug and toxin mechanism of action to be determined directly and systematically in human cells. This approach, called chemogenomic profiling, is based on a revolutionary new method called CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, which allows all genes in the human genome to be simultaneously assessed in a single experiment. Large pools of human cells in which every gene has been individually disrupted in a targeted manner by CRISPR/Cas9 are grown in the presence of a drug, toxin or any other chemical to reveal the genes whose loss confers either sensitivity or resistance to the drug when compared to a non-treated control pool. Analysis of such chemogenomic profiles provides direct genetic evidence for how a drug or toxin affects the cell. We propose here to apply this method to 1000 drugs and toxins of high priority to Health Canada. The type of information revealed by this technology has never been available previously and will transform our ability to establish specificity in early stages of drug development and assess the absence of unintended side effects for approved drugs. The technology will enable the cost-effective and rapid determination of toxin mechanism of action without the need for expensive animal studies. This information will enable extensive current lists of known or suspected toxins to be triaged for more detailed toxicological studies, and thereby save a great deal of time and cost in the assessment of chemical exposure, both to the general public and within specific industries. The retrospective investigation of established toxins will also suggest future means to mitigate the risks of exposure. The ability to rapidly assess drug and toxin effects by chemogenomic profiling will facilitate the development of new drugs and improve environmental safety for the benefit of all Canadians.

column36: Long QT syndrome in Northern British Columbia: Gene-gene interaction, life course differences, and implications for safe management
column37: Usually rare, LQTS is a treatable hereditary heart rhythm condition, which if unrecognized may cause sudden cardiac death. Northern BC First Nations likely have the highest rate in the world, 15 times higher than expected. For over 10 years, our team has partnered with the Gitxsan Community to understand the effect of the common KCNQ1 gene mutation, identifying more than 140 carriers, and enrolling more than 800 community participants. We have learned that other genetic factors can increase risk, and certain times in life may have higher risk than others. Our data suggests young women of childbearing years have the highest risk for sudden death. However, children over a year of age may be spared from the fatal effects until they reach adulthood. Treatment with beta blockers is used in all ages to prevent risk of sudden cardiac death. The problem is that this standard treatment to reduce risk may have the side effect of predisposing to low blood sugar, especially in young children. Furthermore, another genetic factor common in the population (CPT1A P479L) may also increase risk of low blood sugar. A third risk factor is the KCNQ1 mutation causing LQTS can also lead to increased insulin secretion in the pancreas, further risking low blood sugar. Four children in Northern BC have now presented with severe episodes of low blood sugar, all with LQTS and CPT1A P479L, while on treatment with beta-blockers. This emerging information has implications for safe management of infants and children with LQTS in Northern BC. Priority attention will be focused on infancy, childhood, pregnancy, and for all women of childbearing years for 1) risk of cardiac event 2) evidence of treatment complication resulting in potentially damaging low blood sugar. We will also focus on children to explore their lived experiences with the condition and its management. Information from this study will provide evidence for the development of effective and acceptable management strategies.

column36: Genetic mechanisms of arterial calcification
column37: Calcification of the heart's (coronary) arteries occurs as a result of atherosclerosis and increases the risk of dying. Normally, the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the artery wall release calcium but also produce specialized proteins that bind to calcium and prevent calcification of the arteries by promoting calcium removal by macrophages. Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is heritable and common genetic variants on chromosome 9 (at 9p21.3) increase the susceptibility to atherosclerosis and accelerate CAC through an unknown mechanism. We compared human arterial SMCs with 0, 1 or 2 copies of the 9p21.3 risk variants and found that the most differently expressed gene is statherin, a tiny protein known to block calcification in the saliva but not previously tied to this function in SMCs. SMCs with 2 copies of the risk variants expressed almost no statherin, were susceptible to calcification in culture, and could be rescued from calcification by over-expressed statherin. Importantly, we detect statherin in the blood and find lower levels in patients with atherosclerosis and CAC. Our hypothesis is that loss of statherin is the reason 9p21.3 risk variants accelerate CAC. We propose 3 Aims: 1) We will confirm in patients with coronary artery disease that coronary calcification is tied to lower active (phosphorylated ) or higher inactive (dephosphorylated) plasma levels of statherin. 2) We will determine how statherin affects calcium crystal uptake and inflammation of macrophages. 3) We will use a transgenic mouse expressing an active form of human statherin to reverse arterial calcification caused by atherosclerosis or by a genetic defect. Significance: 75% of the world population carries the 9p21.3 risk variants. Therapy targeting statherin to block progression of arterial calcification could reduce mortality in many people.

column37: Preeclampsia is a serious and prevalent disease of pregnancy. It is clinically diagnosed by severe, sudden-onset high blood pressure and blood vessel damage that can lead to organ dysfunction and death in pregnant women. Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal and infant illness and death in Canada and worldwide, with up to 76,000 maternal and 500,000 infant deaths attributed to the disease globally, and there is no known cure. The major cause of preeclampsia is defective development of the placenta, which is the organ that embeds itself into the mother's uterus and is responsible for nourishing the baby throughout pregnancy. We know little about why the placenta does not develop properly in these pregnancies. Without this knowledge, devising better management strategies and interventions is not possible. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that abnormal behaviour of a unique subset of highly abundant uterine immune cells has a causative role in disrupting placental development. We will also examine whether the absence of these immune cells can improve placental and fetal health. Collectively, this project will test the applicability of targeting uterine immune cells to improve placental development, and will form a foundation by which we can decrease or prevent the incidence of preeclampsia.

column37: Our lungs are relentlessly bombarded by foreign particles and must continually work hard to discriminate between dangerous and harmless ones. Considering the volume of allergen-filled air inhaled every day, the prevalence of inflammation and lung diseases is surprisingly low. Interestingly, no increase of CD200 on these cells was observed in allergic asthmatic animals. To investigate whether CD200 is important in protecting against asthma pathogenesis, we treated allergic asthmatic animals with a synthetic CD200 prior to allergen challenge. This treatment effectively reduced their asthma symptoms. In view of these results, this proposal aims to confirm our preliminary data and further investigate the mechanisms involved in the protective role of CD200, through the use of both acute and chronic asthma models. We will also determine the relevance of our data by studying CD200 expression on human macrophages with and without allergic asthma, and also, before and during the allergy season. A better understanding of CD200 protecting functions may highlight new targets for asthma therapy, leading to improved control of this lifelong disease.

column36: Developing a framework for the ethical design and conduct of pragmatic trials to improve the quality and value of health care systems and practices
column37: The randomized controlled trial is the gold standard method for evaluating medical interventions. However, the majority of trials are conducted under laboratory-like conditions, which limits their applicability to the real-world clinical setting. There is therefore an urgent need for so-called pragmatic randomized controlled trials, which are undertaken in the routine clinical setting. Pragmatic trials can provide patients, doctors and policymakers with more reliable information as to which treatments and strategies are best for patients. But whilst ethical guidelines exist to protect participants in research -their applicability for pragmatic trials is not straightforward. This has led to confusion, where some trials have been carried out with inadequate protections, and in others, strict enforcement of current guidelines have posed unnecessary obstacles, undermining scientific quality and impeding improvements in the quality of healthcare. Our goal is to clarify this situation by developing novel ethics guidance to help researchers and research ethics committees conduct and review pragmatic trials. Questions addressed will include: Should pragmatic trials comparing accepted and routinely available medical treatments be classified as research and therefore receive extra scrutiny or should they be considered within the scope of usual medical care (as some have suggested) and fall under the rules of the doctor-patient relationship? Do patients always need to be informed about pragmatic trials and be required to provide informed consent? What information about risks and benefits should be disclosed to patients? We will answer these and other questions through extensive analysis of ethics documents and national and international regulations. We will also build a database of completed trials and examine practices; survey researchers, research ethics committees and patients; organize a consensus meeting to generate guidance; and disseminate our work to stakeholders.

column37: The flow of blood in uninjured vessels and the rapid conversion to an insoluble clot following injury are essential for maintaining life. Conversely, inappropriate clot formation (thrombosis) in intact blood vessels causes heart attacks and stroke. Drugs that prevent blood clotting are frequently employed to treat patients at risk of such diseases. However all of the currently used drugs either increase the risk of bleeding in patients or are ineffective in certain populations. New drugs that prevent thrombosis but do not increase the risk of bleeding are needed for better patient management. Blood cells called platelets are important initiators of thrombosis. It is believed that blocking platelet function by inhibiting sensors on the surface of these cells is a strategy for preventing thrombosis without increasing the risk of bleeding. We have identified a new drug (RAG8) that acts on one such platelet surface sensor called PAR4. By blocking PAR4 with RAG8 we prevent very specific cellular events to disrupt the formation of large disease causing clots, without affecting the formation of smaller platelet aggregates. This should reduce the risk of bleeding in patients taking this drug. In this project we aim to better understand how PAR4 works and test the ability of RAG8 to prevent heart disease in a mouse model that mimics human disease. Two groups of mice, one with RAG8 and another with an inactive drug, will be monitored over time and the development of heart disease in the two groups of animals will be studied. We will also use blood isolated from healthy human volunteers and study the effect of RAG8 on releasing factors that lead to the formation of large clots. Combined these studies will generate data that will help advance this drug to human clinical studies and give us a clear understanding of mechanisms that contribute to formation of heart diseases and stroke causing blood clots.

column36: Our Ancestors Are in Our Lands, Waters, and Air: Sharing Stories about Two-Eyed Seeing in Health Research for Healing, Reconciliation, and a Shared Future
column37: For the Mi'kmaq of Pictou Landing First Nation (PLFN), the estuary adjacent to our community, known as A'se'k (and now known in English as Boat Harbour), and the surrounding landscape have provided us with the foods, medicines, transportation, shelter, and tools we have needed to survive and thrive since time immemorial. But for 50 years, a nearby mill has been piping its effluent directly into the waters of A'se'k and pumping its particulate matter out the stacks into the prevailing winds, which directly target PLFN. Concerned about our children's health, the Pictou Landing Native Women's Group (PLNWG) mobilized in 2010 to undertake community-based participatory health research. We were concerned for our community's physical, mental, emotional and spiritual health in relation to the industrial pollution. Bringing academics in, our team has worked together since then to implement a Two-Eyed Seeing approach to research the women's question: "Are we getting sick from Boat Harbour?" To date we have been researching the mill's health impacts using a number of Indigenous and western research methods to meet this goal. Throughout, we have been documenting our journey by collecting film footage for the production of a documentary film. Now we want to share our novel health-related knowledge vis-a-vis a documentary film about our integrative research. Using the film as a catalyst, we want to investigate how university-based and community-based researchers across disciplines, professions, and sectors can begin to conceptualize a Two-Eyed Seeing approach in their own research in the spirit of healing and reconciliation in Indigenous health. Our overarching goal for this Project is to foster a Two-Eyed Seeing approach across the four health pillars at CIHR that will ultimately translate into improved Indigenous health knowledge, services, and outcomes in Canada, and move us all towards reconciliation and healing for a shared future.
