column36: Deciphering the signalling cascades controlling cell-cell fusion
column37: Cell-cell fusion is a regulated cellular process, occurring only in a few cell types, which is essential for development. During embryogenesis, the most frequent type of cell fusion is myoblast fusion, which joins the membranes of two different muscle cells to form a small muscle fibre. This process is repeated thousands of times until the muscle fibre reaches its correct size. Abnormal cell fusion is also a feature of muscle diseases, such as Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophy. However, signalling cascades controlling cell fusion remain largely undefined. Therefore, the objective of this project is to uncover the mechanisms underlying cell fusion has it is not only important for basic biology, but will also contribute the knowledge essential for its manipulation in therapeutic settings, such as promoting regeneration in muscle diseases. Genetic studies in the fruit fly revealed the identity of some genes controlling fusion. Interestingly, the majority of them are involved in controlling the actin cytoskeleton, which is a structure that defines the cell's shape. We are expert in studying cytoskeletal dynamics. The conserved proteins governing cell fusion in vertebrates remained unknown until we discovered Dock1 as the first protein essential for myoblast fusion in mice. We next uncovered a signalling pathway essential for fusion composed of a receptor called Bai3, a signalling molecule called Elmo that binds Dock1, and their target Rac1. Here, we propose to characterize the mechanisms that ensure controlled activation of Bai3 at the right time for myoblast fusion to take place. Next, we outline experiments that will define the role of Elmo in myoblast fusion in muscle development and regeneration. Finally, we identified a protein that is selected by Rac1 to induce cell fusion. We found that this protein is tightly linked to a number of proteins involved in helping cells define their direction in a tissue, and we will determine how Tanc1 orchestrates cell fusion.

column37: With the discovery and use of the first antibiotics during the 1930's, the mortality or morbidity associated with infectious diseases have considerably decreased. However, over the years the use, abuse and misuse of antibiotics have selected for "superbugs" resistant to a wide spectrum of, and in some cases all known antimicrobial drugs. Multidrug resistant bacteria cause untreatable and hard-to-treat infections associated with high mortality rates and increased healthcare costs. Because microorganisms are increasingly resistant to antibiotics, and the pipeline of discovery and development of new antibiotics is slowly drying out, the World is now facing the risk of returning to a pre-antibiotic era, when even the most common infection was potentially fatal. It is now recognized that the emergence and propagation of "superbugs" are largely fueled by exchanges of genetic material (DNA) between microorganisms. The most potent mechanism of transmission of DNA between two bacterial cells is called conjugation. During conjugation, a multidrug resistant donor cell injects parts of its genome into a sensitive recipient cell and converts it into a multidrug resistant "superbug". The goal of our research project is to characterize key elements of the "syringe" and "needle" used by the donor cell to promote the injection of its DNA into the recipient cell. Understanding the molecular aspects of the mechanism promoting the exchange of antibiotic resistance genes will provide us with new targets for the rational design of new drugs aimed at blocking gene transfers to curb antibiotic resistance transmission between microorganisms causing infectious diseases in human and animals.

column36: Diet, physiological dysregulation, and aging: understanding longitudinal links through trajectory analysis
column37: It may seem obvious that what we eat affects how we age, but how diet might affect underlying aging processes remains largely unknown. In light of recent studies showing that vitamin supplements are mostly not helpful and may even be harmful, it is increasingly clear that molecule-by-molecule approaches to guiding nutrition are insufficient. How then can nutritional guidance for older adults be more precise than simply "eat well"? There is very little scientific understanding of how nutrition affects the physiology of aging, in part because the cellular and molecular links are complex and the fundamental mechanisms of aging remain controversial. Addressing this problem is not simple. We need to (1) find appropriate ways to simplify and accurately measure the complexity of what people eat, and of how our bodies age; (2) use data sets that permit us to see how one affects the other within aging individuals over many years; and (3) use sophisticated analytical approaches that let us examine how both nutrition and underlying biology change with age, and how each of these changing systems affects the other as it changes. Our team has this broad expertise, and we will use NuAge, the only cohort study in the world with sufficiently detailed data on both nutrition and biomarkers during aging to tackle these questions. Innovative and validated analytical methods will identify key signals from complex data on nutrition and aging biology, and then assess how these trajectories interact during an individual's lifetime. Our preliminary results have already identified dietary changes that appear to slow aging. The results of our study will (a) help establish how nutrition impacts biological aging processes; and (b) allow us to develop dietary strategies for aging adults exhibiting specific biological aging signatures, measurable through biomarker profiles.

column37: Rett syndrome is a debilitating genetic condition predominantly affecting females for which there are currently no effective treatments. There is hope, however, as work in mouse models of Rett syndrome show that even at very severely symptomatic stages, the condition can be rescued. Unfortunately, the procedures used to show this reversibility can not be employed in the clinic. Thus, while there is evidence the condition can be treated, we now must find a legitimate target for interventions that can be translated into the clinic. This requires the identification of alterations in Rett syndrome that can be hypothesized to contribute to the disease, and can be targeted with drugs. We have now identified one robust and reproducible deficit that meets these criteria, namely a deficit in the way neurons transport material to and from their processes. Using a drug to correct this deficit, we found that several Rett-like features of the Rett syndrome mouse model could be improved. These encouraging results provide the rationale for the current study, where we propose to identify how the transport deficit arises in Rett syndrome neurons, and test the degree to which the chronic administration of the drug that improves the transport deficit will also improve Rett syndrome mice.

column36: Understanding the Plasma Membrane as a Barrier to Drug Accumulation and Nutrient Absorption
column37: We have recently made an exciting discovery that impacts our understanding of how the plasma membrane (the membrane that encapsulates a cell) of animal cells interacts with molecules in the environment, including nutrients and drugs. For our studies, we use a nematode worm, called C. elegans, to better understand animal biology. For over 40 years, the study of this worm has lead to many discoveries that directly impact our understanding of human biology. In animals, the plasma membrane (PM) is composed of four different fat-like molecules called lipids. One of these lipids, called sphingomyelin (SM), is made by a SM biosynthetic pathway. Through our investigation of how chemicals interact with the worm, we discovered that the activity of this pathway is a key determinant of how molecules interact with the PM. When the SM pathway operates normally, large fat-loving molecules are able to associate with the PM, and smaller molecules are unable to pass through the PM. When the SM pathway is defective, the fat-loving molecules cannot associate with the PM, and smaller molecules can pass through the PM barrier. These observations impact our understanding of how drugs and fat-like nutrients get absorbed by cells. In AIMs 1 and 2 of this proposal, we describe our experiments to investigate this process in detail. One of the enzymes that we think operates in the SM biosynthetic pathway is called PGP-14. Evidence suggests that PGP-14 provides the SM pathway with a precursor, called phosphatidylcholine (PC), for SM synthesis. The human version of PGP-14 is called ABCB4, which provides PCs in the liver so that the body can absorb fats. When ABCB4 doesn't work, children develop an incurable liver disease called PFIC3 and require a liver transplant to survive. In AIM3 of this grant, we use PGP-14 worm mutants as a tool to find drugs that will make up for the lack of PGP-14/ABCB4 biochemical activity in the hopes of providing a cure for children suffering from PFIC3.

column36: Sweet and Stiff: How diabetes activates YAP and TAZ to trigger kidney fibrosis
column37: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure in Canada. Although significant treatment advances have been made, many patients with diabetes still develop significant kidney injury, ultimately progressing to kidney failure. One of the main reasons why diabetic kidney disease still progresses is that scarring, a critical cause of kidney injury in diabetes, remains poorly understood and thus not well treated. Historically, researchers have focused on chemical triggers of scarring such as high blood sugar levels. As scarring develops, however, the kidney also progressively stiffens. We recently found that this kidney stiffening is an important mechanical trigger for further scarring. How cells respond to diabetes-induced chemical and mechanical stimuli to cause kidney scarring has so far remained a mystery. We and others have recently found that: (1) YAP and TAZ are two important proteins that respond to high sugar (chemical) and kidney stiffness (mechanical) injury stimuli, and (2) YAP and TAZ are important drivers of kidney scarring. In this proposal, we will test whether cells use YAP and TAZ as final common injury sensors to trigger kidney scarring in diabetes, and examine how YAP and TAZ use high sugar and kidney stiffness stimuli to activate scar production. These studies will provide important insights into how kidney scarring begins early in diabetes, and progresses at later stages. Early in diabetes, sugar levels are increased but the kidney is soft because it is not yet scarred. We hypothesize that YAP and TAZ are activated only by high blood sugar in this setting. Later, sugar levels remain increased, but because the kidney has now become scarred, it has stiffened. At this stage, YAP and TAZ are activated both by high sugar levels and the stiffened kidney. Most importantly, if successful, these studies will establish anti-YAP and TAZ treatments as a way to effectively treat both the early and late stages of diabetic kidney disease.

column36: Peptide-based Inhibitors of Bacterial Drug Efflux Pumps
column37: Multidrug resistant bacteria are becoming increasingly widespread, creating an urgent societal need for improved infection treatment and control. A major mechanism of multidrug resistance in bacteria involves protein 'pumps' that remove antibiotics by rapidly pumping the drugs out. These proteins are embedded in the membranes that encircle the bacteria, where they must assemble into unique 3-dimensional structures to produce the pathways ("holes") in the membranes through which the antibiotic molecules are excreted. In research to-date, our laboratory has learned key details as to how one such pump performs its drug pumping action. Using this information, we designed, synthesized, and tested novel peptide (small protein) molecules, and showed that they significantly block ("inhibit") the protein's pumping activity by penetrating the bacterial membrane and interacting with it in a specific manner that disables its pumping mechanism - thus trapping the antibiotics inside the bacterial cell and restoring the drug's intended bacterial killing action. As well, we have recently discovered that this pump works by a virtually identical mechanism in most of the common infectious bacteria. Now, the top priorities of our proposed project are to improve the structures and antibacterial activity of these peptide-based molecules to produce new broad-spectrum agents that will be highly active against a wide range of bacteria. We also propose to extend the approach to inhibit another major drug pumping protein. Our best molecules can be used not only directly to kill bacteria, but also in combination therapies with existing antibiotics to improve treatments, such as for cystic fibrosis, and as additives to decontaminating chemicals to create powerful "double action" antibacterial solutions. In the longer range, our research will generate a novel class of peptide inhibitors for clinical use as a strategy for overcoming a major source of bacterial resistance.

column37: Statement of Health Problem: Atrial Fibrillation (AF) is a heart rhythm disturbance that affects over a million people in Canada and the United States. AF can cause strokes, heart failure, poor quality of life and premature death. People with AF not benefiting from medications may need to undergo a heart procedure using catheters. Objective of our Clinical Trial: We have a devised a new method to perform the catheter procedure that will potentially reduce the chance of AF recurrence. The University of Ottawa Heart Institute has funded a pilot trial to evaluate our innovative method of catheter ablation. Our initial experience with this method in 40 subjects has shown that this is a safe procedure and does not increase the cost of the procedure. We wish to find out if the new method is superior to the currently used catheter ablation procedure. Subjects with AF have found our research meaningful and are eager to participate in the study. Our colleagues in 10 Canadian centres have found this innovative method of catheter ablation very promising and have expressed their desire to participate in this trial. Our goal is to recruit 396 subjects to our trial with the help of research funds from the CIHR. Impact of our Clinical Trial: We expect significant reduction in AF recurrence as a result of our innovation. This should directly improve patient satisfaction along with reduction in AF related health care costs. At an individual level, we hope to improve quality of life, exercise capacity, mental health and AF related symptoms. At a societal and health care system level, reduction in AF recurrence will potentially decrease AF related hospitalizations and emergency department visits. This will result in reduction of health care utilization (direct impact) and "days lost at work due to AF" leading to increased productivity (indirect impact)

column36: Modulation of Adolescent TBI via the Orexin System, Sleep, and Glymphatic Function
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the most under-addressed and expensive pediatric health problems in Canada. Mild TBIs account for the majority of these brain injuries and incur national costs well above $3 billion/year. Adolescence is a particularly vulnerable time for mild TBI, and in particular repetitive mild TBI (RmTBI). Despite the fact that adolescents demonstrate heightened sensitivity to mild TBI, and are at increased risk for RmTBI, adolescence is a scarcely studied population within this context. A recently discovered waste clearance system for the brain, the glymphatic system, has been linked to functional recovery from brain injury and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. This waste clearance system is much more effective during sleep, essentially disengaging while the individual is awake. Given that 70% of patients with mild TBI report sleep disturbances and adolescents are significantly more likely to be sleep deprived, we hypothesized that RmTBI in adolescence impairs sleep and glymphatic system function, resulting in increased risk for short and long-term neurological consequences. Using a clinically relevant animal model of mild TBI, this project proposes to 1) explore the short- and long-term neurological outcomes associated with RmTBI in adolescents using behavioural, epigenetic, and MRI techniques; 2) determine how RmTBI in adolescence disrupts circadian rhythms, sleep and the glymphatic system; and 3) remediate pathology associated with adolescent RmTBI with a pharmacological agent that improves sleep and targets the glymphatic system. We believe this project will capitalize on exciting and novel innovative mechanisms like the glymphatic system and sleep to vastly improve our understanding of RmTBI in the adolescent brain. Pharmacological treatment of the RmTBI with a sleep-promoting agent will provide mechanistic insight into mTBI pathology and provide new therapeutics for treatment of RmTBI in adolescents

column36: Exploring the role of the circadian clock in regulating HIV replication and viral reservoir reactivation in Th17 cells
column37: Despite major advances in the past three decades, HIV-1 infection remains a major health problem, with a total of 36.9 million infected people worldwide and 2 million new infections in 2014. In Canada, new infections continue to occur among young men having sex with men as well as within the First Nations communities. Current antiretroviral therapies (ART) are highly efficient in controlling HIV replication. However, viral eradication is not achieved and ART interruptions are followed by rapid viral rebounds. The cost of life-long ART together with drug toxicity and resistance, as well as stigma, justifies the need for an HIV cure. Accordingly, the focus of this translational research proposal is to generate knowledge for the rational design of new cell-specific therapies to reduce HIV persistence and boost immune restoration. The T helper 17 (Th17) cells represent a subset of CD4+ T-cells that play a critical role in the immunity against pathogens at barrier surfaces. Studies by our group and others provided solid evidence that Th17 cells fuel HIV infection and viral reservoir persistence during ART. Briefly, i) Th17 cells are preferential infection targets and their virus-induced depletion from mucosal sites causes non-AIDS co-morbidities; ii) Th17 cells express drug efflux pumps that may render the intracellular concentrations of ART suboptimal; and iii) a fraction of Th17 cells are long-lived and harbor replication-competent HIV reservoir. This project builds on our unique expertise in the identification of molecular mechanisms governing HIV replication in Th17 cells. Specifically, our studies will explore the role of the biological clock within Th17 cells as an "Achilles heel" that could be targeted by specific drugs to prevent HIV infection and the subsequent viral reservoir reactivation. This will contribute to the ultimate goal of HIV eradication in the ART era. The feasibility of our studies is ensured by our team of experts.

column37: Preeclampsia is a potentially life-threatening hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, to which there is no cure. column37: Over the last few decades, neuroscientists have tried to better understand the different phases of memory. column37: Cardiac arrhythmias are electrical disturbances that can prevent the heart from working properly. Currently, the therapeutic options for the treatment of AF have limited effectiveness and adverse effects can often be encountered. In order to develop an improved therapeutic approach for AF, there is a critical need for a detailed understanding of the mechanisms responsible for the higher male susceptibility to this arrhythmia. This information would not only provide valuable insight onto how and why men are more at risk of developing AF than women, but it would also lay foundation for enhanced and sex-specific therapies for the disease. Accordingly, the primary objective of this proposal will be to identify the basic mechanisms responsible for the higher prevalence of AF in men. These studies will be realized using combination of electrophysiological and biochemical techniques while using mouse and human tissues. This work will help to better understand sex-related differences in the pathogenesis of AF. Ultimately, understanding the mechanism responsible for sex differences in cardiac arrhythmias may help to develop improved strategies for the prevention and the management of cardiac arrhythmias in both men and women.

column36: Functional and morphological remodeling of mitochondria and associated endoplasmic reticulum by flaviviruses
column37: Infections with flaviviruses constitute a major global public health concern worldwide. Notably, Dengue virus (DENV) causes the most prevalent mosquito-borne viral disease with estimated 400 million infections per year. More recently, the Zika virus (ZIKV) outbreak in the Americas brought a lot of attention notably because infection of pregnant women can lead to congenital transmission and eventually cause microcephaly in the infant. Other neurological complications such as Guillain-Barre syndrome can be observed in infected adult individuals. Moreover, ZIKV is sexually transmissible adding another challenging layer for the control of disease, and the World Health Organization has predicted 3-4 million infections per year in the Americas. Most importantly, no antiviral therapies treating these diseases or vaccine against ZIKV are currently available. This unmet medical need is partly due to the fact that very little is known about the molecular mechanisms governing the replication of DENV and ZIKV within infected cells. More specifically, much is to learn about how ZIKV and DENV "reprogram" many important functions of the infected cell (such as pathogen sensing leading to innate immunity) to create an environment favorable to viral replication. Based on our recently published work and expertise on flavivirus biology, this proposal aims at identifying novel cellular pathways co-opted by DENV and ZIKV. More specifically, we will focus on how these viruses exploit mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell, by changing their morphology, composition and relationship with other cellular compartments in order to inactivate antiviral immunity, to regulate the cell death program and to modulate metabolic functions. Ultimately, this project may pave the way to the identification novel drug target for therapeutic treatments of both Dengue and Zika fevers and associated complications.

Our findings will help clinicians and the health care system develop targeted interventions and policies that can more effectively manage emotional distress of Pakistani women both in LMIC and in Canada. Our understanding of psychosocial pathways to PTB will inform future research to examine how psychosocial interventions reduce risk of PTB.

column37: The Hippocampus is a brain structure that plays a fundamental role on memory formation. It is one of the most profoundly and early affected brain regions in patients with Alzheimer Disease, other dementias, and Schizophrenia, all characterized by profound memory and cognitive deficits. However, our knowledge of Hippocampus function and mechanisms of memory formation in humans remains superficial. Addressing this issue is fundamental in order to advance our understanding of many brain diseases. Two main theories have dominated the field of hippocampus research over the last decades: a) that the Hippocampus plays a fundamental role in spatial navigation, pioneered by studies in rodents, and b) that the Hippocampus plays a fundamental role in the formation of associative memories, pioneered by studies in humans and non-human primates. First, we test the hypothesis that the Hippocampus possesses a cognitive map of spatial and non-spatial variables that encode associative memories. Second, we will test two different hypothesis of the role of rhythmic oscillations and eye movements in memory formation in the Hippocampus. Finally, we will manipulate neural activity in different parts of the Hippocampal network and determine the effect of the procedure on memory formation. We will use a novel combination of electrophysiological recordings, optogenetics activation/inactivation of neural activity and behavioral measurements of eye movements and performance in non-human primates performing complex navigation tasks in virtual reality environments. The results will be relevant for advancing our basic knowledge of Hippocampal function, searching for the causes of core symptoms of mental disease and for generating interventions to ameliorate and/or prevent such symptoms.

column36: NETs in complement-mediated TMA
column37: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a disease, in which blood clots block small blood vessels. Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a form of TMA, caused by defects in the immune system that affects the kidneys. Available treatments are dialysis or kidney transplants, but even transplantation is not a guaranteed cure, because the disease can recur in the graft. aHUS eventually leads to clot formation in multiple organs and death. We need new treatment approaches for aHUS, which will require a better understanding of how this disease develops. Factors that predispose to the development of aHUS include genetic mutations that interfere with the normal function of the immune complement system (50%). The commonest factors that trigger aHUS are infections (>60%). How these "predispositions" and "triggers" combine to produce aHUS is not well understood. We also do not understand the cause for this disease in the rest of the patients. Our new idea is that a type of immune blood cells, called neutrophils, is altered in these patients. Neutrophils can form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). These toxic traps, akin to fishnets, can damage the inner lining of the blood vessels and promote blood clot formation. Our goal is to understand the combined effect of NETs and complement in triggering and worsening aHUS. These studies are important, as current treatments that are directed to stop complement problems are way too expensive for most patients. We also propose to identify new genetic mutations to improve the diagnosis of aHUS and treatment options. Our research group has a longstanding interest in understanding what controls the actions of complement and NETs, pioneering treatments for aHUS, and identifying disease-associated mutations. This project holds great promise for advancing the understanding of aHUS and of other diseases involving the immune system and blood clots. We have all reagents, patient groups and expertise to successfully complete these studies.

column36: The role of intestinal B cell responses in celiac disease
column37: Celiac Disease (CD) is a complex intestinal inflammatory disorder induced by dietary gluten, which development is controlled by a combination of environmental and genetic risk factors. CD is highly prevalent in North America with around 1% of the Canadian population affected by the disease. The only effective treatment currently available for CD is a lifelong gluten free diet (GFD), yet persistent symptoms and intestinal tissue damage are commonplace among celiac patients that adhere to a GFD. Thus, there is an urgent need for non-dietary therapies that improve patient health and alleviate the social and personal constraints associated with following a GFD. The development of new therapies has however proven challenging because of our incomplete understanding of the mechanisms underlying CD pathogenesis. It is well recognized that T lymphocytes play a central role in CD by causing tissue destruction, however, B lymphocytes - specialized cells involved in the secretion of antibodies and autoantibodies - are also likely very important. Indeed, autoantibodies against the enzyme tissue transglutaminase are produced in CD and their titers have been shown to correlate with intestinal damage. Here we propose to study the contribution of intestinal B cell responses to the pathogenesis of CD and to evaluate in vivo the biological role of autoantibodies in a mouse model of CD that recapitulates all the main features observed in CD patients. We will capitalize on the use of our unique mouse model together with human serum samples to decipher the contribution of B cells to CD immunopathogenesis and to characterize the impact of autoantibodies on the development and/or exacerbation of the disease. In addition of a considerable gain of knowledge on the immunopathogenesis of CD, our work may lead to the identification of novel targets that might guide novel therapeutic strategies.

column36: A Multi-Method Approach to Exploring Prescribing Cascades
column37: Prescribing Cascades occur in healthcare when the side effect from a medication is interpreted as a new condition - and a second drug is prescribed to "treat" the side effect. Prescribing cascades are important because they can be prevented. Our team invented the concept of the prescribing cascade in the late 1990's and now, twenty years later, it is an idea that is widely accepted but not well understood. Although lists of serious prescribing cascades are available to physicians, pharmacists, and other health providers, we do not know how common prescribing cascades truly are. In particular, how and why they develop and continue, what is their impact on patients, and/or how they can be prevented or reversed are all unknown. Our research will address these gaps in knowledge. We will analyze health care databases with information on more than 1.8 million older adults, as well as conduct interviews with individual patients, caregivers, health providers and knowledge users. We will use these different sources of information to inform our answers. We will examine community and long-term care settings and explore differences between women and men. We have incorporated individuals and organizations that can help us to create change throughout our research process. Our findings will result in practical tools that will inform clinical and policy strategies and prevent and/or reverse prescribing cascades. Our research evidence will be shared widely, and will include activities intended for researchers, as well as those designed to educate patients, caregiver and health providers to prevent prescribing cascades and their complications.

column36: Dissecting the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory integration
column37: We perceive the world through our five senses. A central questions of neuroscience is how nervous systems integrate information from multiple sensory modalities to make such decisions. Although recent research suggests that many neurological conditions (e.g., autism, schizophrenia) affect the capacity for such multisensory integration, our current understanding of this process has not yet yielded tangible benefits to society. column36: Using C.elegans to learn to predict the personal severity of mutant phenotypes
column37: Why do people have different risks of getting specific diseases? In part, the answer lies in their genes. We know hundreds of mutations that cause genetic diseases e.g. inheriting mutant forms of the CFTR gene causes cystic fibrosis. However, even in well-known examples, the situation is complex - two people inheriting the exact same mutation can have very different severity of symptoms. At present we do not understand the basic mechanisms underlying this. Our goal in this project is to use the powerful genetic tools available in the nematode worm C. elegans to examine systematically why the same mutation can have different effects on different individuals. We will compare how changing each of ~1400 genes affects 10 different worm strains - these 10 strains are as different as 10 different people. This study will yield the first view of the effect of genetic variation on mutant phenotypes in any species and will tell us how to predict this. We already measured the mutant phenotypes of ~1400 genes in 2 worm isolates in a pilot study. We found that ~20% of genes had different mutant phenotypes in this pair of worm isolates showing that genetic differences between individuals often have a major effect on mutant phenotypes. Crucially, we find that we can predict some of these differences in severity, a major step - this study yielded two high profile publications. We now propose to extend this study to 10 worms - comparing 2 worms was just a start. This will give us much more power to investigate the causes of the differences in severity of mutant phenotypes. It will also give us a large enough dataset to begin to build models that will predict the severity of a mutant phenotype in any individual. Ultimately, uncovering the basic principles that govern why the same mutation can have such different disease outcomes in different people will have a key impact on our understanding of genetic disorders in humans.

column36: Characterization of novel HIV-1 latency-modulating pure natural products
column37: While combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) has significantly reduced HIV-1 morbidity and mortality, cART is not a cure. This is because HIV is capable of persisting in a dormant or "latent" state in a small number of cells throughout the body. These cells, called "HIV reservoirs", can become re-activated at a later time to produce infectious virus; thus, cART must be maintained for life. Towards the goal of achieving durable HIV remission (or the ultimate goal of a complete cure), two opposing strategies have been proposed: reservoir elimination and reservoir containment. The former involves the use of latency reversal agents (LRAs) to "activate" HIV reservoirs, after which they can be eliminated naturally or therapeutically - whereas the latter involves the use of pro-latency agents (PLAs) to permanently maintain HIV reservoirs in a dormant state. However, the few LRAs and PLAs that have been discovered and tested to date have shown only limited clinical success. Thus, discovery of new agents and combinations are urgently needed. Natural products are a rich source of distinct chemical compounds. We screened >400 unique compounds derived from marine natural products and African traditional medicines and have identified 7 new compounds with LRA activity and 2 with PLA activity in vitro. Initial mechanistic studies suggest that at least 3 of these compound classes target HIV reservoirs by processes distinct from those of existing agents, suggesting their potential to synergize with existing therapies. In this project, we propose to assess these compounds' toxicities, their abilities to target HIV reservoirs from patient-derived cells, and to elucidate their mechanisms of action. column36: Aldehydes, Antioxidants, and Atherosclerosis: Translational prognostic molecular imaging with novel prognostic and companion diagnostic agents.
column37: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of death in Canada, resulting in as many as one in five deaths due to the various forms of this disease. Atherosclerosis is the hardening of arteries and narrowing of blood vessels through the build up of a fatty substance called plaque. While significant improvements in the management of atherosclerosis have been made, fundamental challenges towards its detection and treatment still remain. Both the ability to differentiate stable (benign) from unstable plaques (more prone to fatal cardiac events), and the role of antioxidants as therapeutics are still under developed. Tackling these issues is challenging, but could result in a substantial improvement to the life span of Canadians susceptible to atherosclerosis through earlier diagnosis, and better and safer treatment. To this end, this proposal seeks to develop and implement new diagnostic tools compatible with current medical imaging practice that can predict the stability of these plaques and to evaluate novel antioxidants that could improve disease outcomes. Our imaging agents rapidly and specifically bind to aldehydes, molecules associated with biological stress that have been shown to be strong molecular predictors of disease outcome in humans. By quantifying these stress molecules early on, we hypothesize that we can predict the severity of atherosclerosis in the individual patient non-invasively with medical imaging. Furthermore, we will investigate antioxidants that have been shown to outperform nature's best agent: vitamin E. The success of this proposal will result in a novel medical imaging agent and a novel therapeutic that could both see rapid clinical application and begin to improve the cardiovascular health of Canadians.

column36: Identification and testing of novel inhibitors of pathological eye angiogenesis
column37: In disorders causing blindness, such as retinopathy of prematurity, diabetic retinopathy, and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), sprouting of new blood vessels (angiogenesis/neovascularization) that mainly occurs in the embryo leads to death of the nerve cells of the retina. These neovascular disorders place a substantial burden on patients and the health care system. AMD alone affects approx. 100,000 Canadians over the age of 50, while diabetic retinopathy is the most common cause of blindness in people under 65. Understanding the molecular basis of these diseases is the best hope for developing new medications to tackle them. Nerve cells in the retina require nutrients and oxygen provided by two distinct vessel beds: retinal vessels that support the optic nerve cells of the inner retina, and the choroid vessels that sustain the light-capturing photoreceptors of the outer eye. In neovascular eye disorders, the existing vessels sprout and new, leaky vessels extend within the vessels beds. The leakage leads to swelling in the eye that disrupts the nutrient and oxygen supply, and vision loss occurs as retinal cells degenerate. Current approaches to block new blood vessels from forming are not effective in all patients and they may have serious side-effects. We urgently need an effective way to prevent these faulty new blood vessels from forming, without affecting the health of retinal nerve cells or the normal blood vessels. This proposal addresses this gap by providing fundamental knowledge of a novel mechanism to prevent new blood vessels forming in the eye. We have identified a mechanism that normally controls eye vessel growth in the embryo that is implicated in pathological blood vessel growth in the adult eye. In this project we will define these mechanisms of normal and pathological eye blood vessel formation, informing the development of new treatments for neovascular eye disorders.

column37: The use of prescription opioids has increased markedly in recent years, and Canada is now the second leading consumer of opioids per capita in the world. This has been associated with a dramatic rise in rates of dependence, addiction, and overdose death involving these drugs. This public health crisis has becoming a priority for provincial and national governments, and population-based research in this field has been an important tool for policymakers developing strategies to address this growing threat to public health. Historically, most research has been limited to government-reimbursed prescriptions. However, because most Canadians do not receive government-funded drug coverage, large gaps remain in our understanding of opioid prescribing and its consequences. The introduction in 2012 of Ontario's Narcotic Monitoring System (NMS), which captures all opioid prescriptions in Ontario regardless of payer, offers a novel opportunity to explore opioid prescribing in a truly population-based fashion. Through linkage of this dataset to a broad repository of health care data, we will describe provincial patterns of opioid prescribing, evaluate the real-world impact of existing programs, quantify indicators of inappropriate prescribing and misuse, identify populations at highest risk of overdose and death, and inform policies likely to impact on this crisis. All work will be overseen by a steering committee comprised of patients, researchers and policy-makers to ensure broad relevance, uptake and dissemination. As Canadian decision-makers struggle to develop evidence-based policies to address the growing national opioid crisis, this work will provide a picture of the current state of the opioid epidemic in Ontario and potential areas for change. This research will generate evidence to help inform and evaluate prescribing policies that will have broad implications for public health.

column36: Identifying genes and regulatory pathways that control sex differences in lipid storage using Drosophila as a model.
column37: In Canada, >10 million people are affected by metabolic diseases associated with excess fat storage (e.g. cardiovascular disease, obesity). Approximately 40% more men suffer from diseases of fat storage than women and drugs used to treat abnormal fat metabolism often work better in one sex (e.g. fenofibrates); yet, knowledge of how men and women differ in fat storage is incomplete. While lifestyle and sex hormones contribute to sex differences in fat storage, therapies based on lifestyle changes are difficult to maintain, and sex hormone therapy has undesirable side effects in both sexes. The next step forward in developing better treatments for abnormal fat storage is to identify the genes that control fat storage in each sex. Targeted therapies will reduce the burden and cost of diseases associated with fat storage (currently >$20bn). My research is at the forefront of discovering genes that drive sex differences in fat storage using fruit flies as an innovative model. Importantly, the genes that regulate fat storage are the same in flies and humans, and our work has shown that sex differences in fat storage faithfully reproduce male-female differences in mammals. Thus the genes involved in sex differences in fat storage we identify in flies will advance our understanding of this problem in mammals. Our use of flies has allowed excellent progress in 18 months: we identified fat storage genes that are regulated differently between the sexes. We hypothesize that this regulation explains why the sexes differ in fat storage. The goal of our project is to discover which of these genes is essential for fat storage in each sex, and to understand how these genes are regulated differently in males and females. We will advance health-related knowledge by identifying a pool of genes that control sex differences in fat storage, providing an essential starting point for researchers to develop new therapies for tackling metabolic disease that will work in men and women.

column36: Stromal Gene Expression Predicts And May Drive Metastasis in Prostate Cancer
column37: Men with low to intermediate risk prostate cancer (PCa) face vexing decisions regarding treatment. The tumour can remain indolent and will not impact the patient within his lifetime, or it can progress to become life threatening (metastatic tumour). A holy grail of PCa research is the identification of prognostic biomarkers, which are biological factors that are associated with the disease outcomes, that can be used to improve patient risk stratification at time of diagnosis and guide treatment decisions. We have created patient-derived PCa tumour mouse models with different metastatic potential that fully recapitulate the transition of a patient tumour from indolence to metastasis. In an effort to identify the mechanisms that drive the growth of a metastatic tumour in these models, we have identified a rich source of prognostic biomarkers in the mouse stroma, which is the tissue supporting tumour growth. We have been able to identify a group of 93 genes only active in the mouse stroma associated with metastasis. We called this group of genes the Stromal Metastatic Signature or SMS. In collaboration with GenomeDx Biosciences, a Vancouver-based company, we confirmed our preliminary observations; that the SMS is strongly prognostic for predicting metastasis in human tumour. The purpose of this very innovative proposal is to seek funding first to further validate the SMS using additional large human tumour cohorts, second to improve the SMS prognostic value by integrating existing tumour-based signatures, and finally to test the hypothesis that the stromal compartment drives metastasis using a novel therapeutic agent developed in our research centre. This very innovative project represents a unique opportunity to apply novel and exciting research findings to the advancement of an important health issue.

column36: Exploring the causes and consequences of falls across the continuum of care in Canadians with spinal cord injury
column37: Most people living with spinal cord injury (SCI) fall at least once/year. Falls result in injuries, hospital admissions and reduced quality of life. In people with SCI, very little is known about the causes and consequences of falls. Our goals are to understand why falls occur among individuals with SCI, and how falling impacts their quality of life, independence, and participation in work, social activities and family life. This study has two parts. In Part 1, 64 adults who recently suffered a SCI will participate. The research team will follow participants for the first six months after leaving the hospital to track any falls they experience. When a participant falls, he/she will complete a fall survey to note how and why the fall occurred. With this information we will describe the common circumstances surrounding falls in people with SCI. Participants will also complete questionnaires about quality of life, independence in daily activities, confidence in balance and mobility, and participation in life roles. Scores on the questionnaires will be compared between participants who fell and those who did not fall, telling us how falling impacts the quality of life, independence and participation of people living with SCI. In Part 2, 24 participants who reported a fall in Part 1 will complete a photo assignment. They will take photographs of situations, places and things that show how falling impacts their lives. The photographs will then be discussed in individual interviews and group meetings to identify common contributors to falls and explain how falling impacts daily living. Information from the photographs, interviews, questionnaires and fall surveys will be brought together to address our research goals. This research will allow us to understand the causes and impact of falls on the lives of those with SCI. We will learn more about how falls can be prevented, and how the quality of life of people with SCI can be increased.

column36: Understanding the Role of the Family Physician in Early Psychosis Intervention: A Mixed Methods Study
column37: Psychotic disorders have a profound impact on the lives of young people. The symptoms of psychosis may include delusions, hallucinations, and erratic or unusual behavior. The onset of these symptoms usually occurs in adolescence and young adulthood. This has a big impact on a person's social, educational, and career development. People with psychosis have better outcomes if we identify and treat them soon after symptoms begin. But Canadian research shows that many people with first-episode psychosis have difficulties accessing specialized treatment programs, and some people receive ongoing mental health care from their family doctor. This project will use data from electronic medical records of family doctors, as well as interviews with young people with first-episode psychosis, family doctors, and clinicians at specialized programs. Our aim is to understand whether people seek help from their family doctor for the early symptoms of psychosis. We will look at how many cases of early psychosis are detected in primary care, and how the family doctor manages these patients. We will also look at whether some groups, such as immigrants or those living in rural areas, seek care more or less often from their family doctor. The findings from this project will allow us to understand the role of the family doctor in the care of young people with early psychosis. It will also allow us to identify specific groups in the population who might face more barriers to accessing specialized mental health care. This information will inform strategies to support family doctors in their important role in providing care for these young people. It will also help administrators and policy makers to deliver mental health services that are accessible to everyone. We hope that by increasing access to care for young people with first-episode psychosis, we can improve outcomes, prevent delays in educational and career development, and ease the distress of those affected by the disorder.

column36: Concussion & You: A peer-led approach to raising concussion awareness in Canadian high schools
column37: Concussion is a common injury amongst Canadian youth with high school students being the most at risk. Post-concussion symptoms can have a significant impact on youth participation in daily activities and overall health. To improve health outcomes of youth we must provide them with the tools and resources to recognize that they have had a concussion and how to manage their injury. The 'Concussion & You: Peer Educators in Action' program aims to meet this need. This program will enable Canadian high school students to engage in three components to raise concussion knowledge, awareness and reporting behaviour: 1) Concussion Awareness Council - champion students will be trained and supervised to deliver educational resources to classmates; 2) peer-led Concussion Awareness Campaign - champion students will be coached to develop and run an annual awareness campaign using creative approaches; 3) peer-led Concussion Awareness Campaign Showcase - awareness campaigns completed by students will be celebrated at an annual 'virtual' event. This project aims to: 1) share concussion knowledge, raise awareness and improve concussion reporting behaviours amongst Canadian high schools; 2) explore the impact of a peer-led service learning approach. This program will be supported by the development of an online Concussion Awareness Toolkit and Web Portal. During the study, this toolkit/web portal will provide a platform to share knowledge with and support participating high schools. After the study, this toolkit/web portal will be made available to the general public to allow for broader access to evidence-based, relevant and engaging concussion education and awareness materials, and to promote the sustained delivery of peer-led concussion education in Canadian high schools. This project will provide insight into how to best raise concussion awareness and improve concussion reporting behaviours in high school students and provide a foundation for a much needed national strategy.

column36: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD): Defining the Impact, Severity and Natural History of NAFLD in Canadian First-Nations and non-First Nations Communities
column37: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) is a chronic liver disease resulting from excess amounts of fat in the liver. It is the most common liver disease in Canada, affecting 25% of the population and causing substantial liver-related morbidity and mortality. Despite the importance of this condition there are no community-based studies describing the burden of NAFLD in Canada and in particular the First Nations (FN) populations, who are at a significantly higher risk of developing NAFLD due to the high rates of diabetes and obesity (established risk factors for NAFLD) in this population. To address this knowledge gap, we will conduct surveys of ~2,000 adult residents in FN and non-FN communities using portable ultrasounds. Persons with NAFLD will be assessed for disease severity by clinical, biochemical and radiologic (FibroScans) features and followed for 5 years with biannual clinical visits to monitor the course of the disease. Those without NAFLD at baseline will be reassessed with repeat ultrasounds at the end of the 5-year follow-up period to determine the incidence of new cases. This study is designed to improve the awareness, understanding and ultimately, provide more effective care for Canadians with NAFLD. While documenting the extent and severity of the condition in rural and FN communities, the researchers will work with community leaders and elders to develop educational programs, prevention strategies and identify lifestyle changes that would be of therapeutic benefit. The research findings will also inform and assist in health policy planning aimed at decreasing risk factors, improving early detection, predicting outcomes and identifying resources for NAFLD care in this country. Finally, the results will form the basis for an envisioned national NAFLD study that will address the unmet needs of a large segment of the Canadian population.

column36: La modulation des ganglions de la base par les afferences neurochimiques du tronc cerebral: implication dans la physiopathologie des troubles du mouvement
column37: Les ganglions de la base forment un ensemble de structures cerebrales profondes impliquees dans le controle du mouvement. Le fonctionnement harmonieux de ces structures depend d'un equilibre fragile entre plusieurs systemes de natures neurochimiques variees. Les donnees que nous avons obtenues au cours des cinq dernieres annees suggerent que certains groupes neuronaux situes dans le tronc cerebral modulent de facon synergique l'activite des ganglions de la base et que leur debalancement genere des troubles majeurs de la motricite. Notre projet de recherche vise donc a elucider les caracteristiques morphologiques et neurochimiques de l'innervation serotoninergique, dopaminergique et cholinergique des ganglions de la base en provenance du tronc cerebral et a caracteriser la reorganisation de ces circuits neuronaux dans la maladie de Parkinson et les dyskinesies induites par son traitement pharmacologique a la L-Dopa. Grace a l'originalite de notre approche experimentale et a une equipe de recherche dynamique possedant des expertises complementaires et uniques au Canada, notre projet permettra de faire la lumiere sur les changements neuronaux qui surviennent dans la maladie de Parkinson et qui sont responsables des troubles moteurs et cognitifs associes. Les connaissances generees par cet ambitieux projet de recherche translationnel, combinant des etudes chez l'animal et l'homme, conduiront a une meilleure comprehension de la vulnerabilite selective de certains neurones face aux processus neurodegeneratifs de la maladie de Parkinson. De plus, elles permettront de developper de nouvelles avenues therapeutiques afin d'attenuer les symptomes moteurs et non-moteurs du parkinsonisme ainsi que les effets secondaires causes par son traitement pharmacologique.

column36: Statutory Regulation and Emerging Traditional/Complementary Health Care Professions
column37: As in many jurisdictions worldwide, Ontario's health care system is undergoing a significant change by granting state sanctioned self-regulated status to practitioners of traditional, complementary and alternative medicine (TCAM). Surveys will gather quantitative data about newly-regulated TCAM practitioners, which will be compared to data gathered before the regulations came into effect. Semi-structured qualitative interviews with TCAM practitioners and regulators will allow an in-depth exploration of how the regulations may (or not) be impacting practice. Documents will be analysed to provide important context for both quantitative and qualitative findings. The proposed project will provide practical feedback for policy makers, practitioners and patients as to the impacts of, and challenges associated with regulating TCAM health care providers. This is an area that to date has been understudied, and - as the World Health Organization has emphasized - whose urgency is increasing as patients across nations increasingly seek out TCAM care that is both safe and effective.

column36: The HNE mouse: a new model of cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's Disease that displays neuronal and vascular pathologies
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) affects approximately half a million Canadians, and is the most common form of age-related dementia. There continues to be an urgent need for the development of new therapies that slow or reverse the underlying disease process and relieve the symptoms of AD, and also of new animal models that mimic age-related disease progression and provide better predictive validity. The majority of currently used mouse models of AD exhibit pathological changes dependent on the overexpression of mutant human genes linked to early-onset, familial AD that account for only a small proportion of AD cases (1-2%). However, the study of lateonset/ age-related AD (98% of AD cases) has been hampered by the lack of such animal models. The research described in this proposal focusses on the use of HNE mice, a new, oxidative stress-based model of age-related cognitive impairment with AD-like pathologies. Validation of an age-related model of AD that complements current rodent models will allow greater insight into the pathogenesis and molecular/cellular mechanisms of AD. It will allow identification of targets for early intervention, and will be useful in assessing the efficacy of therapeutic agents for improving memory and for slowing, preventing, or reversing the synaptic failure and neurodegeneration associated with AD.

column36: Using Herpesvirus Proteomics to Identify Mechanisms of Cellular Regulation
column37: Most people are infected with three different herpesviruses; herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). These life-long infections can be asymptomatic or can lead to a variety of health problems including oral lesions, mononucleosis, cancer and life-threatening illnesses in immune suppression. These viruses persist and cause disease through the action of the numerous proteins that they encode, which bind to and manipulate the functions of some cellular proteins. However the functions and cellular targets of most of the viral proteins have not yet been determined. This project uses comprehensive protein interaction methods and a unique library of HSV-1, EBV and CMV proteins to determine the cellular targets of the viral proteins. We are particularly interested in cellular proteins that are targeted by all three viruses as this would reflect the importance of these cellular proteins for viral infection and cellular regulation in general. This work will provide insight into how viruses manipulate cells to cause disease and enable life-long persistence, and will identify potential drug targets for antiviral treatments. It will also identify new mechanisms of regulating important cellular processes.

column36: Therapeutic Alliance Tensions and Repair in Psychotherapy Practices: A Psychotherapy Practice Research Network (PPRNet) Proposal
column37: This study will look at improving the relationship or alliance between therapists and patients who are receiving psychotherapy. The study focus was determined by the research priorities identified by a large practice-research network of psychotherapists in Canada. Psychotherapy is the treatment of choice for many mental disorders, yet there is a gap between research and practice. Research indicates that: the therapist-patient alliance is important to reduce patient symptoms, alliance tensions are detrimental to patients, and those therapists who identify and repair alliance tensions can improve patient outcomes. In this study we will use state of the art research to train community-based therapists in evidence-based interventions to identify and repair alliance tensions. Trained therapists and their patients will be compared to therapists who provide usual care to their patients. We will measure improvement in therapists' skills in identifying and repairing alliance tensions and how this is associated with better patient mental health outcomes. We will also interview trained therapists to identify the best ways of improving the training and disseminating the findings to psychotherapists across Canada. Research to improve practicing therapists' ability to identify and repair therapeutic alliance tensions will result in better mental health outcomes for patients.

column36: Locus coeruleus in Alzheimer's pathology: its impact on early neuroinflammation and amyloid pathology
column37: The onset of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. AD pathology develops silently for decades before its clinical presentation. During such phase, there should be a progressive accumulation of toxic proteins (amyloid-beta and tau) in the brain. We also recently characterized an early, disease-aggravating, pro-inflammatory process using genetically modified (GM) animal models of the disease. The Locus Coeruleus (LC) is a structure located deep in the brain which releases noradrenaline (NA), a neurotransmitter with anti-inflammatory properties. In AD, LC neurons degenerate particularly early-on due to tau pathology. Little is known about the downstream consequences of LC degeneration on the AD evolution. We aim at elucidating how LC pathology affects the earliest AD brain inflammation. We postulate that LC degeneration exacerbates such early inflammatory process which in turn potentiates and aggravates the amyloid pathology. To address this, we will use GM rats that replicate the progressive amyloid pathology observed in humans and also display pre- and post-plaque neuroinflammation. We will manipulate the LC of these GM rats to create an early dysfunction (by either triggering tau accumulation or lesioning LC nerve cells) or, in opposition, stimulate the LC to release NA. This will allow us to assess the direct impact of an inactivation or activation of the LC, respectively, on inflammation and amyloid pathology. These investigations will contribute significantly to the understanding of the early disease-aggravating pathological events occurring at pre-diagnostic stages of AD. The findings should offer new clues to halt the progression of AD before irreversible brain damage and thus may provide new targets for development of novel early therapeutic interventions.

column36: Pregnancy Specific Anxiety Scale (PSAS): Instrument Development and Psychometric Testing
column37: There is a well-identified need in the literature to develop a reliable tool to measure anxiety specific to pregnancy to identify women suffering from this condition. The purpose of this study is to address this gap by developing a valid tool. A detailed understanding of pregnancy anxiety is essential for tool development. Thus, we conducted a comprehensive review on previous research to define anxiety and its characteristics during pregnancy. We also conducted several interviews with pregnant women during different stages of pregnancy to supplement these findings. In this project, building on this knowledge, the initial structure of the tool and its items will be developed. A group of experts will review the items to examine their clarity and readability; the degree of agreement among the experts will be tested to determine the need for further revisions. Next, a small group of pregnant women will complete the new scale to evaluate its clarity and consistency. Then the performance characteristics of the new tool will be further evaluated using standard scale assessment protocol among two separate large samples. Identifying and managing anxiety during pregnancy is important because women with high levels of anxiety are at increased risk for alcohol consumption, having premature births, and experiencing depression after giving birth. Additionally their children may develop behavioral and mental health problems later in their life due to this early anxiety. Identifying women with anxiety during pregnancy and referring them to appropriate services can improve pregnancy postpartum and child outcomes and enhance the quality of life for women and their families.

column36: Vascular stabilization of cerebral small vessels
column37: Cerebral Small Vessel Disease (CSVD) is estimated to cause 25% of all stroke and arises from defects in the small vessels of the brain (arterioles, capillaries and venules). Each year, ~16,000 Canadians die from stroke, of which ~4000 have CSVD. CSVD doubles the risk of a future ischemic stroke and therefore understanding its pathogenesis is urgent. However, we are limited in understanding the CSVD mechanism by the lack of technology to image small vessels in the human brain. It is only once damage reaches a threshold that MRI imaging detects the lacunar infarcts and white matter defects characteristic of CSVD, but this is relatively late in the disease progression. Long-term morbidity is high and we lack specific treatments. CSVD is suspected to have a strong genetic component, although causative genes have been elusive in the general population. My lab develops animal models of vascular stabilization and has joined forces with an international team that has identified genetic risk factors for CSVD in humans. In this proposal I exploit animal models and human genetics collaborations to identify mechanisms by which mutations in a novel CSVD genetic risk factor, Foxf2, increases CSVD risk.

column36: The Canadian F.I.G.H.T. (Fluorescence Image-Guided Help in Treating) Breast Cancer Surgical Trial
column37: Breast cancer, the most prevalent cancer in women, is treated by breast conservation surgery (BCS), where tumor is removed while preserving the maximum amount of healthy tissue. Under standard white light visualization, tumor borders are difficult for surgeons to visualize. Despite current best practice to guide optimum tumor resection, ~23% of Canadian women require a second operation to remove remaining cancerous tissue that wasn't detected during the initial surgery. Thus, there is an urgent clinical need for a new imaging tool that improves tumor visualization and guides the surgeon towards complete tumor removal in real time - during the first surgery. To address this need, we developed a new Health Canada-approved handheld fluorescence imaging device (called PRODIGI) which we have clinically evaluated in combination with a safe clinically-approved tumor localizing imaging agent called 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) to detect breast cancers during surgery, based on the tumor's red fluorescence signal which is produced by ALA-induced protoporphyrin IX (PpIX), a natural molecule in the body. Based on encouraging initial results of our current single-center feasibility trial, we now propose a prospective multicenter randomized controlled trial (RCT) over 5 years conducted by a multidisciplinary team across breast cancer centers at 7 Canadian health institutions in 4 provinces (ON, AB, SK, NS). The primary goals of this RCT will be to definitively determine the effectiveness of this new intraoperative imaging approach in reducing re-excision rates and disease recurrence, while identifying potential impact on the quality of life for breast cancer patients and health economics, compared with the standard of care. If successful (and nationally adopted), we expect to eliminate >3000 second surgeries in Canada over 3 years, reduce surgical wait times, be deployed rapidly into surgical practice, especially in resource-limited areas, and reduce variability in BCS outcome.

column36: The FL.I.G.H.T (Fluorescence Image-Guided Healing Trial) for Diabetic Foot Ulcers: A Single Centre Phase II Trial
column37: Lower extremity complications such as chronic diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a major risk for Type II diabetes patients. Minor injuries that would normally heal without consequence in non-diabetic individuals are at greater risk of bacterial infection and progression to non healing (chronic) wound status in diabetics, largely due to a loss of sensation in limbs (neuropathy) and decreased blood flow (vascular disease). If not treated efficiently and effectively, DFUs can have serious complications e.g. amputation, sepsis and death. We propose to address this significant unmet clinical need using a novel commercial handheld fluorescence imaging product called the MolecuLight i:X (MolecuLight Inc.) which images clinically-significant wound bacteria without contrast agents or patient contact. Evidence in animal models of chronic wounds and multiple published clinical trials (mainly DFUs) have shown significant clinical potential for fluorescence imaging to detect potentially harmful bacteria in wounds otherwise invisible to doctors. We have shown that clinicians can easily, objectively and more accurately determine the likelihood of bacterial infection than the standard of care. Moreover, published clinical evidence has shown fluorescence imaging enables more accurate microbial wound sampling and guides more targeted debridement of wounds to reduce bacteria levels. Our pilot data also show that when used like this, the i:X device accelerates DFU wound healing, compared with current methods. Thus, we propose to expand the current pilot studies through a statistically-powered 3 y randomized controlled trial to test the therapeutic benefit of fluorescence-guided treatment for DFUs in a larger group of patients. A successful trial could help reduce DFU healing times compared with standard practice (using a new Canadian product) and improve patient quality of life, reduce amputation risk and alleviate health care costs for diabetes complications in Canada and beyond.

column36: Hepatic signalling of glucose and lipid metabolism in vivo
column37: More than 25% of Canadians are obese. Obesity is the major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which affects approximately 8% of Canadians. Elevated levels of circulating and tissue fat predispose obese individuals to develop type 2 diabetes. Furthermore, fatty liver is nowadays the major cause of liver disease and excess circulating fat predisposes obese individuals to develop cardiovascular disease. Our objective is to investigate the mechanisms of fat-induced abnormalities in sugar and fat handling in the liver, which is a very important organ for the maintenance of normal blood sugar and fat levels. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that sugar and fat handling by the liver are regulated by two different pathways that branch from the same fat-activated molecule. We will measure liver production of sugar and fat and liver fat accumulation under fasting conditions and after challenging with fat administered by vein or diet. This will be done in mice that lack key molecules of these two pathways and their activating molecule, and in control mice. Liver tissue, which cannot be obtained from humans, will allow us to assess these two pathways and their activating molecule. Thus, we will delineate a roadmap of interest for manipulation by the pharmaceutical industry. By understanding the mechanisms of fat-induced abnormalities in sugar and fat handling by the liver, we will identify targets for nutrient and drug intervention to prevent type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and cardiovascular disease. Thus, our investigation will help mitigate the public health impact of obesity.

column36: Examining the role of helper T cell immunity in Clostridium difficile infection
column37: Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is the leading cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea in developed countries and a major source of morbidity, mortality, and health care costs. CDI classically develops following ingestion of spores spread from other patients (usually in the health care setting) plus antibiotic treatment, which depletes normal bacteria in the gut, although community-acquired cases and cases without preceding antibiotics are becoming more common. Illness due to C. difficile is caused by two toxins, TcdA and TcdB, with the latter likely more pathogenic in patients. Even though CDI can be successfully treated with specific antibiotics as many as 30% of people develop spontaneous relapses, where the symptoms return after treatment. Each relapse raises the risk of subsequent relapses, and sometimes patients can only be cured by fecal microbial therapy (FMT or "stool transplant"). It remains impossible to accurately predict relapsing CDI, and as a result newer, expensive treatments that can reduce relapse risk are seldom utilized. The immune system probably plays an important role in helping people recover from CDI. Naturally occurring antibodies against TcdA and TcdB are predicted to protect against infection and relapse, but studies examining this effect have been inconsistent. Moreover, CD4+ T cells, also known as helper T cells, are required for robust antibody generation, but have never been studied in CDI. In preliminary studies, we have developed a new test that can measure and characterize CD4+ T cells that specifically recognize TcdA and TcdB. Using this test, we have found high levels of TcdB-specific T cells in patients with recurrent CDI. Our goal is to better characterize these cells and compare their function in patients with recurrent versus new-onset CDI, to be able to better predict clinical outcomes in CDI, and help guide the development of new treatments and vaccines for this important illness.

column36: Curing Hirschsprung disease with neurotrophic factors
column37: Hirschsprung disease (HSCR) is a potentially fatal congenital malformation where the enteric nervous system (ENS) is missing from the end of the bowel. Because the ENS controls patterns of intestinal contraction and relaxation, the segment without neurons remains constantly contracted, resulting in blockage and accumulation of fecal material (megacolon). The ENS also controls several other intestinal functions, explaining why children with HSCR have vomiting, growth failure and a high likelihood of dying from systemic bacterial infection. HSCR affects 1 in 5000 newborn infants and current treatment consists of painful surgical removal of the segment that lacks enteric neurons followed by re-connection of innervated bowel to the anus. Unfortunately, many children continue to have problems after HSCR surgery including life-threatening bowel inflammation (enterocolitis), stool leakage, constipation, bowel perforation, hospital re-admission and repeat surgery. A therapy that could really cure HSCR children is clearly warranted. Based on our new preliminary data, we now believe that a non-surgical regenerative medicine approach to treatment might be possible for children with HSCR. Specifically, we found that neurotrophic factors can induce the formation of new neurons in the bowel of two HSCR mouse models as well as in human colon removed from children with HSCR as part of their routine care. Induced neurons significantly improve bowel function, preventing death of our two HSCR mouse models. During the next 5 years, in addition to addressing safety concerns, we will use several other mouse models that mimic human HSCR as well as supplemental colon tissues removed from HSCR patients to determine if treatment outcome may vary as a function of genetic mutations. These studies should lead to future human clinical trials that could provide valuable alternative treatments for children with HSCR and perhaps other intestinal motility disorders.

column37: At its most basic level, our nervous system is an intricate circuit of specialized cells called neurons. Neurons convey information using electrical signals, which result from the controlled movement of charged ions across the neuronal membrane. This process relies on a class of proteins embedded in the neuronal membrane called ion channels. Due to their role in electrical communication, ion channels are key components of our nervous system. Mutations in ion channel genes are implicated in numerous human diseases, including Alzheimer's and schizophrenia; and aberrant ion channel function in the brain leads to cognitive impairment, thus ion channels are the targets of a wide variety of drugs. Therefore, insight into ion channel structure, function and mechanism is not only fundamental for a molecular understanding of the nervous system; it is also immediately relevant to human health. The proposed research will provide mechanistic insight into ion channel functions associated with cognitive impairment, which will be leveraged to guide the design of new and improved drugs. The result will be better mental health for Canadians through the development of novel, next-generation pharmaceuticals.

column36: Blood-based detection and molecular imaging visualization of cancer using reporter gene vectors called tumor-activatable minicircles
column37: One in 4 Canadians will die from some form of cancer. The ability to effectively help these people relies heavily on our ability to detect tumors that have spread around the body when they are smaller, less abundant, and more responsive to therapies. For decades, both blood tests and imaging tests have been developed but the tests currently used by doctors suffer from an inability to see the smallest of tumors, dramatically affecting patient survival. These issues are largely due to the fact that these tests typically target the detection of molecules that are not expressed by all tumors and are often expressed by normal organs, which clouds the ability to say if a person has cancer or not. We desperately need new technologies to better detect cancers anywhere in the body in order to stem the loss of life caused by these terrible diseases. To address these critical needs, Dr. Ronald and his team are developing an entirely new way to detect and visualize cancer that focuses on forcing tumors, but not normal organs, to produce molecules called reporters that can be easily detected with either blood or imaging tests. This new technology is called tumor-activatable minicircles and is essentially tiny and safe DNA rings that when injected into the body are silent when someone is healthy but begin to produce reporters when they encounter a tumor. Importantly, this brand new technology has many safety features, so once we more fully develop and test it in animal studies, we predict it will have a high likelihood of future testing in cancer patients. We strongly feel this cutting-edge technology has the potential to revolutionize cancer detection in the future.
