column36: Dissection of medial entorhinal microcircuits in health and Alzheimer's disease
column37: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) is a high-level cortical structure that generates a neural code for location, similar to a GPS. Individual neurons in the MEC 1) create a grid of repeating spatial fields (grid cells), 2) signal the proximity to borders of the environment (boundary vector cells), or 3) respond to a particular direction in space (head direction cells). Together these cells create a rich and detailed representation of space that is important for navigation and spatial memory. We propose a strategy to determine how these different codes are generated within the MEC. Importantly, these neurons exhibit unique coding differences based on their anatomical location; differences in neuronal responding are observed across the six cortical layers, as well as along the dorsal/ventral axis. This heterogeneity in response has led to circuit-level computational models that simulate how each neuronal group contributes to generation of grid cell firing. Here we propose to combine recordings of grid cells with targeted inactivation of each component within the MEC microcircuit. This strategy will help to reveal how grid cells are generated in the MEC, and more broadly will contribute to our understanding of how information is processed in the neocortex. The second goal of this project is to characterize which parts of the microcircuit exhibit dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Here, we provide preliminary data that grid cells are indeed disrupted in the J20 mouse model of AD. We propose to characterize the spatial cell types throughout the MEC in J20 mice to reveal which cell types and lamina are disrupted in AD. Together, these goals will strengthen our understanding of spatial processing in the MEC in health and disease.

column36: Addressing Recent Trends in HIV Among Gay, Bisexual, and other Men Who Have Sex with Men in Vancouver, British Columbia
column37: New HIV diagnoses are 71 times higher among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM) than other men in Canada. Since 2010, BC has adopted Treatment as Prevention (TasP) as a policy to increase HIV testing and treatment in order to reduce HIV transmission. However, new diagnoses among GBM in BC remain stable with an increase among young GBM. HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a new prevention tool, was approved for use in Canada earlier this year although uptake in BC remains limited. We wish to examine the differential impact of PrEP and TasP on HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention and transmission among younger (<30 years) versus older (30+ years) GBM in Metro Vancouver with 3 study aims: 1) To measure significant HIV risk behaviour over time that considers use of TasP and PrEP; 2) To determine cumulative STI incidence and the affect of PrEP and TasP; and 3) To understand attitudes about HIV, challenges with HIV prevention and treatment, and changes in sexual negotiation and practices. We will conduct a 3-year mixed method study to collect and triangulate rich data sources. To address Aim 1 and 2, we will enrol 700 GBM (including 250 young GBM) into a prospective bio-behavioural cohort study. Participants will be followed every six months to complete computer assisted self-interview questionnaires and provide biological specimens for HIV and other STI testing. To address Aim 3, we will conduct in-depth qualitative interviews with 50 GBM who were recently diagnosed with HIV, are currently using PrEP, or who report significant HIV risk with no TasP or PrEP use. Situated within the world-renowned BC Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS, our experienced research team includes public health and service organization leaders. This research will inform population-specific, age-relevant public health policy, programming, and interventions to reduce the burden of HIV and STIs for GBM, especially young GBM.

column36: Mechanisms underlying novel pro-survival peptides in neuroprotection
column37: Brain cell death following injuries or stresses often lead to permanent disabilities; this is largely due to the poor abilities of brain cells to re-grow. In contrast, the adult nerve cells of Lymnaea stagnalis, a freshwater pond snail, show a greater ability to survive and to spontaneously regenerate following injury. Thus, it is likely that the snail nerve cells carry the message essential for cell survival and for nerve regeneration. This message may be carried by novel proteins which are not found in mammals. This brings about one innovative approach to identify the novel invertebrate proteins that promote cell survival and nerve re-growth and test whether insertion of this novel protein into mammalian central neurons, such as mouse and human neurons, can rescue nerve cells from cell death. We have recently found a number of novel snail proteins that are required for nerve cell growth and regeneration following injury in snail. In this study, we characterize the effects of caltubin, one of these novel proteins, on property of mammalian neurons and investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms of caltubin in cell survival and nerve re-growth of these cells. We hypothesized that caltubin regulates the stability of the nerves thus prevents cells from death after injury. We will identify specific regions of this protein that are responsible for the effects of caltubin in mouse brain cells, and create new small caltubin peptides to promote cell survival and reserve cell integrate following injury or stress conditions. We will use multiple advanced molecular, biochemical and optical imaging techniques in combination of cell culture and animal models in this study. We anticipate these experiments will assist us to develop new drugs for neuroprotection in the future. This study highlights the potential of an innovative strategy for developing new neuroprotective drugs against cell death in neurological diseases.

column36: Role of NBEAL2 in blood platelet maturation
column37: Megakaryocytes are large bone marrow cells that can each shed thousands of tiny platelets into the bloodstream. There are over a million platelets in a drop of blood, and when they encounter cuts they initiate clotting to stop bleeding. Since ruptured atherosclerotic plaques and inflammation can trigger the same response, platelets are also responsible for the clots that cause heart attacks, strokes and other internal damage. Platelets also contribute to wound healing and immunity, and to plaque development and the spread and growth of cancers. These wide-ranging impacts of platelets on health and disease are linked to their ability to roam the bloodstream and respond to a variety of situations in different ways. They can undergo physical changes and directly interact with other cells, and platelets can also release an assortment of proteins packed in structures called a-granules. My group has identified several proteins involved in granule development, including NBEAL2, which when lost by mutation leads to the production of platelets that are abnormally large and lacking in a-granules in a condition known as Gray Platelet Syndrome (GPS). Discovering the cause of this condition helped several patients I see regularly in clinic at SickKids, together with their families. The aim of my project is to determine how NBEAL2 ensures the normal development of platelets and a-granules by identifying proteins and cell structures that this protein interacts with at various stages of megakaryocyte and platelet development. We will do this using approaches and techniques where my research group has gained internationally-recognized expertise, such as microscopy imaging and the development of animal and cell models of GPS. Our results will advance understanding of platelet biology, which will assist ongoing efforts to control the negative impacts of platelets on health and enhance their positive roles. We will also open up new avenues of research.

column36: Development of a multi-mechanistic virus-based therapeutic platform for pancreatic cancer
column37: The cure rate for Pancreatic cancer remains less than 6% and 75% of patients die within the first year of diagnosis. Sadly, these statistics have not changed in the past 3 decades despite tremendous progress in our understanding of the genetic causes of pancreatic cancer and the complexity of its tumour microenvironment. Currently, surgical resection provides the only potential long-term cure for pancreatic cancer; however only 15% to 20% of patients have tumours that are amenable for this highly debilitating procedure. Furthermore, pancreatic cancer is partially characterized by early metastases, which severely limit the success of surgical resection. Oncolytic viruses are a new and exciting class of anti-cancer therapeutic agents due to their specific predilection to infect and kill cancer cells. Virus-based therapies are showing moderate but promising benefit to pancreatic cancer patients in early clinical trials. Yet resistance due to the unique biology of pancreatic tumors is one of the biggest challenges for developing breakthrough therapies against pancreatic cancer. One of the most active areas of research to overcome such resistance is the use of combinatorial approaches aimed at stimulating the patient's immune system to fight against cancer cells while also inducing a potent and selective cytotoxic effect in the tumor. Successful execution of this project will lead to the generation of an oncolytic virus platform suited not only to kill pancreatic cancer cells but also to sensitize the tumor environment to targeted anti-cancer drugs. We expect that the combination of virus-based immunotherapy and anti-cancer drugs is an effective two-pronged attack that enhances direct killing of cancer cells and also breaks the tolerance of the immune system for pancreatic cancer, leading to a novel and potentially effective therapeutic approach for patients who currently have little hope of long-term survival.

column36: Discovering the transcription regulatory networks that control uterine contractions
column37: The uterus is composed of the smooth muscle layers and epithelial tissue required for multiple reproductive functions in women. The activity of the smooth muscle component, the myometrium, generates the force needed to expel the fetus at birth. To initiate contractions, individual smooth muscle cells within the myometrium express a repertoire of genes in response to hormonal and inflammatory signals. In many patient cases, however, this multiple cell-coordinated contractile response occurs prior to term; women can consequently enter labour too early, which results in the delivery of underdeveloped infants at high risk of death or complications later in life. Recent research has identified genes up-regulated in term labour and preterm labour myometrium; however, the mechanisms that activate these genes remain unclear. To understand the basis of preterm labour and develop new preterm labour therapies, we need to find the molecular players involved in activating these genes in both term labour and preterm labour. In this project, we will find the genomic sequences and proteins that activate the expression of genes required for preterm labour in mouse and human myometrial tissue. To uncover the important regulatory sequences driving labour-specific gene activation, we will generate and compare the myometrial epigenetic profiles associated with gene regulatory sequences at different time points during pregnancy. We will next find the regulatory sequences activated in preterm labour using infection- and hormone-mediated mouse models as well as patient samples. Finally, we will find the critical regulatory sequence binding proteins needed to activate labour-specific genes in both labour types. Uncovering the suite of genomic regions and regulatory proteins that underlie the labour process will provide new targets for the development of therapeutic treatments for preterm labour, preventing complications that occur when babies are born preterm.

column36: Establishing chloride intracellular channel CLIC1 as a therapeutic target for pediatric brain tumor
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The conventional treatment that combines surgery, irradiation and chemotherapy is highly toxic to normal brain cells and produces life-long side effects such as lowered intelligence, early aging, and increased chance to develop other cancer. Therefore, identifying the molecules that fuel aggressive MB growth but are largely dispensable for normal cells is key to develop cancer-specific therapy. Ions, such as potassium and chloride, are essential constituents of human cells. Ion channel proteins form tiny pores to control ion to move in or out of cells. The movement of ions can change the electrical and physical properties of the cells, which control many biological processes including tumor growth. We recently found a potassium channel named EAG2 that is required for MB growth but not normal brain development. We discovered an old drug as a novel EAG2 blocker and found that the drug had strong efficacy in a human MB patient. Therefore, we pioneer in identifying ion channels as novel regulators for brain tumor and developing channel-targeted therapy. In order to effectively treat MB, a combinatorial therapy, in which multiple tumor-specific molecules are targeted, is necessary. We found that a chloride-permeating channel named CLIC1 is abnormally accumulated in MB cells, and inhibiting CLIC1 slowed MB growth in mice. We hypothesize that CLIC1 as a novel regulator of MB can be blocked to suppress tumor growth. We will reveal the tumor stage in which CLIC1 is required for MB growth and define the mechanism by which CLIC1 regulates MB, knowing which will instruct the logical designing of a CLIC1-targeted therapy. Completing these studies will solidify our research program, which is based on a unique scientific niche in brain tumor therapeutics by targeting ion channels. We will innovate cancer therapy by targeting ion channels to treat the devastating brain tumors.

column36: Single-cell characterization of viral transcription- and translation-competent HIV and SIV reservoirs
column37: A vaccine against HIV is crucially required worldwide to limit the spread of this virus. The major HIV-infected (HIV+) cell population, a type of white blood cells known as CD4 T cells, comes in multiple different "flavours", each with different functions. In order to develop a vaccine that can teach the immune system how to target and kill HIV+ cells, scientists must first understand which flavors of CD4 T cells are infected. However, currently available technologies have made it difficult to visualize these HIV+ cells in great detail. Previous work has relied on looking at the relative numbers of HIV+ cells in different populations, rather than the individual HIV+ cells, or studying HIV infection using cells and viruses grown in the lab. The interactions between these "in vitro" cells and viruses may be very different to the events occurring within a HIV-positive individual. To address this important issue, we have developed a novel assay that, for the first time, allows very rare HIV+ cells to be visualized at a single-cell level. We will perform in-depth analysis of individual HIV+ cells from the blood of patients who are infected with HIV. We will also use an animal model of HIV, SIV in non-human primates (monkeys), to image the infected cells in important tissues and organs. This will provide researchers with a highly detailed picture of HIV+ cells and guide development of a vaccine. In addition to a vaccine, a cure is required to treat those individuals that are HIV-positive. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is not a cure for HIV; as long as a patient takes their medication the virus is forced into hiding, but it can reappear when ART is stopped. Specialized drugs (known as latency reversing agents or LRAs) have been developed to kick the virus out of its hiding place. We will investigate how different flavors of CD4 T cells respond to LRAs, and use this knowledge to inform studies working towards a cure for HIV.

column36: An optogenetic approach for rewiring thalamocortical circuits to restore function after stroke
column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult disability in North America, often robbing its victims of the ability to perform even the most basic sensory-motor tasks (dressing, eating, brushing teeth, driving) that we take for granted in daily life. Since many patients fail to recover adequately with existing treatment options, there is a great need to develop a deeper understanding of what happens to sensory circuits after stroke and use this knowledge to develop new treatments that will maximize recovery. One brain region that plays a crucial role in processing sensory information is the thalamus. After stroke, it is thought that the connections from this region are either damaged or are dysfunctional thereby disrupting how our brain processes sensory information. Surprisingly little is known about what happens to these connections after stroke and to what extent can they recover normal function. The first goal of this research project will be to use imaging technologies to assess the structure and functionality of thalamic connections after stroke. Since our preliminary data suggest that stroke does indeed make these connections less excitable, we will then use a powerful new experimental approach to promote the excitability of these connections. This approach involves genetically modifying cells to make them more excitable by expressing proteins (derived from algae) that can be activated by light (called "optogenetics"). We will then determine the impact of optogenetic stimulation on neural circuit rewiring and recovery of sensorimotor function. And finally, since we have pilot data proving the feasibility and utility of this experimental stroke therapy, we will explore what molecular mechanisms mediate its beneficial effects. Ultimately, the proposed project will generate critical foundational data regarding the effects of stroke on sensory circuits and will test a new therapeutic approach to improve recovery of sensori-motor function in a rodent model of stroke.

column36: Characterization and modification of Bordetella lipid A
column37: Bordetella pertussis, the causative agent of whooping cough can alter a component of its surface structure called lipid A to either increase or dampen host responses to it. We will investigate the mechanisms by which small changes in B. pertussis lipid A influence how it is engaged by the host cell and how this interaction affects signaling responses and the production of immune molecules called cytokines. The amount and pattern of cytokines produced can shape the outcome of an infection. We will also examine the influence of engineered lipid A changes on B. pertussis pathogenesis in a humanized mouse model of infection. This work also has implications for improving the whooping cough vaccine. There is a growing concern that the duration of protection from the current protein-based whooping cough vaccines does not last very long and this may be attributed to the complete removal of lipid A, something that was done to eliminate the endotoxicity of the whole-cell vaccine. Manipulating B. pertussis to produce an altered lipid A may ultimately result in an inexpensive, killed whole-cell vaccine that produces fewer fevers yet is potent enough to elicit a longer lasting immune response to stop the spread of whooping cough.

column36: Vitamin D In the prevention of Viral-induced Asthma of preschoolers (DIVA): a multicentre randomized controlled trial
column37: Colds are the main cause of asthma attacks in preschoolers, an age group with the highest rate of visits to the emergency room because of asthma. The best strategy to prevent asthma attacks caused by colds is still unclear. Most children with asthma have low blood levels of vitamin D and this has been linked with more frequent asthma attacks and higher use of corticosteroid drugs. In recent studies, children and adults who took daily vitamin D supplements have less colds and less asthma attacks. To rapidly increase and maintain the amount of vitamin D in the body early in the fall and throughout the winter, we propose to give a high dose of vitamin D by mouth in the clinic, once every 3 months, along with a standard daily dose. This approach safely and effectively increases and maintains the level of vitamin D in the blood of children. In this 7-month randomized controlled trial, children aged 1-5 years with asthma attacks triggered mostly by colds, will receive a high dose of vitamin D or a placebo every 3 months during their usual clinic visit. They will also take a daily dose of vitamin D. This study will test whether if children receiving vitamin D have less severe and less frequent asthma attacks compared with the placebo. The study will also document the safety profile of this strategy. Vitamin D may prove an effective means to prevent moderate and severe asthma attacks triggered by colds in young children. If positive, results of this study may offer an effective means to prevent asthma triggered by colds in young children.

column36: Personalized medicine from theory to health practice: making dynamic treatment regimes more accessible
column37: Personalized medicine provides treatment decisions tailored to each individual patient, maximizing the chance of the best possible health outcomes. Dynamic treatment regimes formalize this idea. These are sequences of rules which, based on a patient's medical history, suggest which treatment to prescribe at particular times to give patients the best results. A 'regime' can be as simple as giving one drug to men and another to women, or a long list of options that update over the treatment of a lengthy illness. There are, however, many unanswered questions in this area, and this project will address some of most importance to health researchers studying the treatment of long-term conditions. The project will cover three areas. One will consider different definitions of the 'best' outcome for a group of patients. Usually, we pick treatment rules that give a population the best overall average result, but sometimes we may want something else. For example, in a health setting we care about avoiding especially bad outcomes (such as death, or major complications), and so might prioritize this above all else. How to do so requires further study. A second topic will look at assumptions researchers must make to carry out analyses, studying the impact of these assumptions and how to check if they're met. A final aim is to compare some of the more popular methods for finding the best treatment decisions. There are a number of methods available, with 'better' ones often more difficult to use. This last area will aim to identify when simpler methods can compete with more complex ones in practice. All new methods developed will be made available through software. With a focus on real-world, practical concerns, this project will make dynamic treatment regimes far more accessible and useful. In turn, this will further the study and understanding of personalized medicine, leading to better health outcomes for society as a whole.

column36: The Epinephrine Randomized Optimal Versus Current Dose (EpiROC) Canada Trial
column37: Each year in Canada, there are over 40,000 people who collapse from cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest is a sudden stoppage of the heart. This life threatening problem is treated by paramedics with CPR, shocks and drugs, including the routine use of adrenaline. The worldwide standard dose of adrenaline is 1mg every 3 to 5 minutes with no total limit. Although the standard dose of adrenaline can help restart the heart, half of these patients die in the hospital from irreversible brain injury and brain death. Despite decades of use, there is no proof that the standard dose of adrenaline is effective at improving survival out of the hospital and there is growing evidence suggesting that the standard dose of adrenaline may be harmful to the brain, particularly with higher total doses. Adrenaline increases blood flow to the heart to improve its chances to restart but when more than 2mg total of adrenaline is used, there is decreased blood flow to the brain leading to brain injury and brain death. We believe and would like to test how effective are low (optimal) doses (up to 2mg total) of adrenaline compared to the current standard doses (no total limit). We also want to test whether the low dose of adrenaline is better than nothing (placebo). We will test these three treatments in a large group of patients treated in an existing world-class Canadian out-of-hospital resuscitation research network called the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) consisting of central and southern Ontario, and all of British Columbia. This will be the first clinical trial to test the effects of low dose adrenaline, the standard dose of adrenaline, and placebo in cardiac arrest. This research may improve patient survival and brain function after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, and change the way in which cardiac arrest is treated worldwide.

column36: Genetic and acquired defects in islet prohormone processing in diabetes
column37: The pancreatic beta cell produces not only insulin, but also another peptide hormone called islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) or amylin. Both insulin and IAPP are released from beta cells in response to high blood sugar or following a meal, and can be measured circulating in the blood. Insulin and IAPP, like other hormones, are first made as larger precursor proteins that are cut by enzymes in the beta cell, and sometimes undergo other modifications before they are packaged into small compartments in the cell awaiting the signal for their release into the bloodstream. There is strong evidence that the precursor forms of IAPP and insulin (called proIAPP and proinsulin), as well as other modified forms of these proteins, are altered or increased in diabetes, perhaps even prior to disease onset. In this proposal, using genetically engineered mouse models, clinical samples from patients with diabetes, and human islets from organ donors, we aim to identify forms of proIAPP and proinsulin that are altered in disease, how these forms might contribute to loss of beta cells in diabetes, and whether measuring these proteins in blood could help predict disease.

column36: Indigenous Doulas as a Culturally Based Health Intervention to Improve Health and Birth Outcomes for First Nations Women in Remote Communities Who Travel for Birth
column37: Most women in rural Manitoba First Nations communities travel to tertiary centres to deliver their babies. The impacts of being alone and unsupported include a range of psycho social stress resulting in poor health outcomes for mom and babies such as preterm birth, low and high birth weights, infant and neonatal mortality. Having support during pregnancy, delivery and postpartum can alleviate some of these poor health outcomes. Doula care is about supporting women during labour and birth and has shown considerable efficacy with women from marginalized groups or transcultural climates. column36: Reconciling the legacy of mercury: learning from historical exposure to improve delivery of health and social services in the Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek (ANA) community
column37: Fish, a highly nutritious food that can also accumulate mercury, is a mainstay in First Nations' traditional diet. In the 1970's, the Medical Service Branch of Health Canada (MSB-HC) undertook a surveillance program to assess First Nation's mercury exposure; blood or hair samples of 38, 571 persons from 514 First Nation communities were analyzed. The highest concentration (660 mu g/L) was in blood from Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek (ANA), also known as Grassy Narrows, whose rivers and lakes had been contaminated in the 1960's by a choralkali plant that dumped 9 tons of mercury into the Wabigoon-English river. Because of the resulting high concentrations of mercury in fish and humans, MSB-HC collected and analyzed 4000 blood or hair samples and 184 cord bloods from ANA. Scientists from Japan with expertise in Mimamata Disease (MD), a neurologic disorder resulting from high levels of mercury exposure, examined ANA residents and identified over 30 cases of MD. However, there has never been an epidemiologic study on the long-term health effects of mercury in ANA despite growing knowledge on the deleterious effects of pre and post natal mercury exposure on children's neurodevelopment, on adults' motor and the visual functions and on the cardiovascular system. The ANA community, with support from the Ontario and Canada Ministries of Health, is currently carrying out a community health assessment (CHA) survey of all of its members. We have the unique opportunity to link the historical mercury data with the CHA results. We will (i) constitute the historic databank; (ii) examine the effects of pre-natal exposure (cord blood samples) on health and well-being in adulthood; (iii) examine the effects of past mercury exposure on aging and health of elders; This study is carried out in collaboration with ANA and with the support of Chief and Council. Our findings will help to improve health and social services and education in this and other First Nation communities.

column36: Modelling the Tuberous Sclerosis-related neoplasm Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
column37: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a Tuberous Sclerosis-related lesion of the lung, similar to a cancer, which only affects women. LAM cells produce enzymes that destroy the lungs of the patients. The only treatment is the drug Rapamycin that slows down the progression of the disease until the patient can receive a double lung transplant, which carries a lot of risk. A major obstacle for LAM research and the development of new LAM treatments has been the difficulty in isolation of LAM cells from patients to study LAM or to perform drug screens. When LAM cells have been isolated, these cells don't behave like LAM in the culture dish or they stop growing. To solve these problems we have made LAM-like cells from both female and male human stem cells and we have developed a gel that has many of the properties of a human lung so that we can grow LAM or LAM-like cells in a 3D lung-like environment. We found that TSC deficient, LAM-like cells behave differently in 2D (normal) and 3D culture. In this proposal we will use our LAM-like cell lines and our 3D lung tissue like culture system to tease apart why Rapamycin only slows down LAM but does not stop it and to explore why mutations in TSC2 predispose a woman LAM more than mutations in TSC1. In addition, we will perform a drug screen of nearly 1300 FDA-approved drugs to identify drugs that can work alone or in concert with Rapamycin to preferentially kill LAM cells or to stop their production of MMPs, which destroy the lungs of LAM patients. In addition, since we are using both male and female cells, we may learn why LAM only strikes women.

column36: Deciphering the transcriptional control of cytoprotective responses to identify new therapeutic targets
column37: All of our body's cells have systems, collectively called "cytoprotective factors", that protect the cell's components from damage. These factors help maintain cell health, and thus help prevent many diseases, such as neurodegenerative disease (e.g. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, etc). However, when erroneously activated, cytoprotective factors also allow cancer cells to thrive and to resist treatment with chemotherapies. In cancer, disrupting hyperactive cytoprotective systems is therefore a potential therapeutic approach. Our research focuses on the 'Mediator', a molecular machine that is required to read and transcribe genetic information. Mediator is present in all organisms from yeast cells to humans. This means we can study it in animals like roundworms to make new discoveries that can help improve human health. In my lab, we use the tiny worm called Caenorhabditis elegans to study how Mediator works in cells. We discovered that one particular Mediator protein acts like a cytoprotective factors: it helps cells remove foreign substances like drugs and toxins, and making whole animals resistant to such stress. Moreover, this protein interacts with others that are known to help cancers become drug resistant. Therefore, targeting this one Mediator protein could be a new cancer treatment. However, we do not yet know how this works at the level of molecules, which prevents us from targeting this specific protein to improve human health. Our goal is to determine how this Mediator protein works, thus laying the foundation for developing new Mediator-targeting cancer drugs.

column36: Personalized MRI-based predictive models to guide VT therapy
column37: Ventricular tachycardia (VT), a fast heart rhythm, is a common and potentially lethal complication in patients who suffer a heart attack (i.e., infarct) and later develop chronic scars. The current diagnostic procedures are highly invasive, precluding many patients to undergo the VT inducibility test in the electrophysiology (EP) lab and often failing to detect the VT foci in those undergoing the test. Furthermore, radio-frequency ablation (RFA) therapy has a low success in scar-related VT patients. Thus, there is a clear need to develop better tools that can help clinicians to effectively improve the diagnostic procedure and the treatment success (i.e., destruction of foci). While recent research efforts from our group have been focused on employing exquisite MR imaging methods to identify the structural hallmarks of these foci, here we propose an innovative complementary approach by developing computer heart models that offer a comprehensive '3D look into the heart' and allow us to non-invasively predict using simulations the electrical impulse propagation in the presence of scars. Our focus is to customize preclinical heart models using high resolution MR images and electrical data obtained in vivo in a translational pig model of chronic infarct. Specifically, we will aim to: 1) develop a novel minimally invasive technology able to accurately simulate in silico the typical clinical VT test; and 2) determine via simulations the critical sites for RFA, thereby informing the operator where precisely to place the ablation lesions to achieve a complete destruction of suspected foci and a higher success rate of RFA. We envision that these personalized MRI-based heart models will hold the unique capability to simplify highly invasive EP studies, predict the VT inducibility and precisely guide the therapy, leading to a substantially improved VT treatment outcome and, ultimately, to a higher quality of life in a large population of Canadian patients with scar-related VT.

column37: Children with rare inherited metabolic diseases (IMD) are among the small number of children who have disproportionately high needs for care, both in the hospital and in the community. Work together with families and providers to develop approaches that have the strongest possibility to resolve the challenges we have learned about. Comprehensively studying challenges in the delivery of health care services for children with IMD will allow us to design a set of highly promising interventions to improve care and outcomes for these children and their families.

column36: In vivo two-photon imaging of cell type-specific reorganization of inhibitory circuits during motor learning in awake and behaving mice.
column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult disability and the third leading cause of death in Canada. In addition to having potentially devastating effects on quality of life, stroke is estimated to cost the Canadian economy more than $3.6 billion a year in treatment, physician services, hospital costs, lost wages, and decreased productivity (Statistics Canada, 2012). The primary motor cortex in the brain is responsible for voluntary movement. It has also been proposed to be one of the sites for motor memory formation and storage, also known as motor representations. Therefore, when the motor cortex is damaged following a stroke, we lose the ability to execute movements that were formerly part of normal daily life. One hypothesis to achieve true recovery is to re-initiate motor learning in the brain and establish new representation to replace the destroyed ones (Murphy and Corbett, 2009). Hence, a determination of the basic molecular mechanisms underlying motor learning will enhance our understanding of post-traumatic rehabilitation in brain injury and disease. Our lab has developed a novel forelimb lever-press task for head-fixed mice, permitting us to perform chronic two-photon imaging and follow learning-related dynamic changes among various neuron subtypes in the motor cortex of behaving mice over weeks of training. Here, we propose a series of experiments employing in vivo two-photon imaging combined with the lever-press task to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying learning-driven inhibitory neural circuit modifications essential for the structural and functional plasticity with motor memory formation in the awake brain. By deciphering the basic mechanisms underlying motor movement acquisition in normal heathy brains, our work will have immense potential to understand dysfunction in circuits altered by stroke and aid in the development of novel therapeutic targets for stroke recovery and other brain injuries impairing motor function

column36: Identification of HP1a as a key regulator and a novel therapeutic target for neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is a currently incurable, lethal subtype of prostate cancer that can develop from the disease following prolonged hormonal therapy. Unfortunately, there are few treatment options available for NEPC and new therapeutic targets and more effective treatments are urgently needed to improve its management. A state-of-the-art pre-clinical model of NEPC, developed in our group, is giving us unprecedented levels of accuracy in monitoring how NEPC progresses. In our pilot study, these findings were further validated in clinical samples. Furthermore, we also observed increased HP1a is an early event during NEPC development and a reduction in HP1a expression was found to lead to inhibition of cancer cell growth. These results suggest HP1a may play an important role in NEPC development. In the proposed study, we hypothesize that 1) HP1a impacts multiple aspects of cancer biology and is functionally important in NEPC development; 2) reduced HP1a expression in cancer cells will significantly suppress NEPC growth; and 3) reagent targeting HP1a can be used as a novel therapy to treat NEPC. The ultimate goals of this project are to have a better understanding of the function of HP1a in NEPC and to produce potential therapeutics designed to target HP1a and hence suppress NEPC development. When successful, this study will improve our understanding of mechanisms underlying the development of NEPC and also provide new insights for the personalized treatment strategy for prostate cancer patients. Identification of novel therapeutic agents in this study will lead to more effective therapy and better quality of life of prostate cancer patients.

column36: The lungs as HIV reservoirs: Interplay between disrupted respiratory immunity and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
column37: AIDS remains one of the world's most serious health challenges. Globally, 35 million people are living with HIV including 75,000 in Canada. Despite intense efforts to cure HIV, HIV reservoirs are a main barrier to eradication. A reservoir refers to a place (either a cell type or anatomical compartment) where HIV "hides" from the immune system. The lungs have many features which make them ideal reservoirs for HIV, and HIV has been detected within the lungs of individuals even after several years of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Having HIV within the lungs is associated with several imbalances in chemicals affecting interaction and communication between cells. Furthermore, as people with HIV are living longer due to the success of HAART, they are suffering from more chronic diseases associated with aging, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is the 3rd leading cause of death in the general population in North America. People living with HIV show signs of COPD more often than people without HIV (20-60% vs. 7%). Like in the lungs of people living with HIV, people with COPD have disturbances in lung immune cells. Furthermore, it is possible that having HIV within cells changes genetic material within the cells (ribonucleic acid or "RNA" and deoxyribonucleic acid or "DNA") and influences cell functions, making lungs more susceptible to develop COPD. We plan to study the interaction between immune cells and HIV reservoir size in the lungs of people living with HIV, both with and without COPD. We also plan to study the genetic characteristics of lung cells in relation to the amount of HIV they contain. These findings are important for understanding how HIV may contribute to chronic lung disease such as COPD. Ultimately, these findings are important for the development of strategies to reduce chronic diseases associated with HIV infection and improve quality of life.

column36: A novel memory prosthetic: From neuroscience to rehabilitation
column37: Memory loss is the most common and debilitating cognitive impairment resulting from Alzheimer's disease (AD) and from the mild cognitive impairment (MCI) which often precedes AD. The numbers are staggering. Currently 564,000 Canadians live with AD or a related dementia, costing $33 billion annually (a figure set to rise to $293 billion by 2040). Memory loss diminishes one's sense of identity and autonomy, leading to a vicious cycle of social isolation and depression, which in turn exacerbates memory loss. Digital Memory Augmentation (DMA) is an approach to mitigate memory loss in which portable devices capture information about everyday episodes, allowing for later review and recollection. DMA has already been shown to produce memory benefits - even more so than common strategies such as keeping a diary. However, prior DMA approaches have not been informed by our understanding of brain function; moreover, the benefits of DMA for brain health and for everyday function have not been carefully quantified in a large group of older individuals. This project aims to develop a new kind of DMA that optimally reduces memory impairment in MCI/AD. This will be the first memory device designed based on our understanding of how the brain internally "reminds" itself of prior events. The device will mimic important functions of the hippocampus - a brain area damaged in MCI/AD- by replaying and reorganizing movies of an individual's life to help stabilize and retrieve memories. This project will produce: (i) an optimized memory prosthetic device and a publicly available App that mimics the internal memory strategies of our brains; (ii) reliable data on the device's efficacy for mitigating brain deterioration and daily function in people with memory impairments. Overall, this project translates cognitive neuroscience research into a practical and non-invasive solution to a problem profoundly affecting millions of Canadians.

column36: A new approach to preserving female fertility
column37: A woman's fertility declines sharply beginning at about 35 years of age. In large part, this is due to a decrease in the quality of her oocytes, meaning in their ability to give rise to a healthy baby. Although scientists have identified specific defects in oocytes of reproductively aged women, we do not understand when or how these defects arise. If we knew why oocyte quality decreases as women age, we might be able to prevent this process and preserve her fertility. Our preliminary experiments suggest that the problem originates not in the oocyte itself, but in its interaction with cells of the follicle that provide essential nourishment to the oocyte as it grows. Our objective is to discover why interaction becomes disrupted. This will allow us to develop methods to maintain this essential interaction, so that the follicle cells can properly nourish the oocyte. column36: Exercise Training in Patients with Persistent or Permanent Atrial Fibrillation
column37: This clinical research program is concerned with a serious irregular heart-beat condition and how to improve the quality of life of those suffering from it through a special kind of exercise. The condition is called atrial fibrillation, or AF, a heart rhythm disorder which is a major health problem in Canada. AF sufferers have a poor quality of life (palpitations, laboured breathing, dizziness) with risks of stroke, bleeding complications and death, and their difficulties in exercising can lead to obesity and worsening overall health. Exercise is not prescribed for AF, though moderate-intensity continuous exercise, or MICE, is for other heart diseases. Unfortunately, this latter regime tends to be onerous, the health benefits problematic and it is time-consuming. Our aim is to test AF patients to see if another regime of high-intensity interval training (or HIIT, alternating periods of hard exercise and rest) is better than MICE in improving quality of life and exercise capacity. We will recruit 132 people with AF. We will first measure the parameters outlined above then randomly assign people to usual care, MICE or HIIT. The MICE and HIIT groups will exercise 3 days per week for 12 weeks. The MICE group will exercise on a stationary bicycle for 40 minutes at 60% of their maximal effort. The HIIT group will exercise on a stationary bicycle for 16-minute interval-training blocks of 30-seconds at 100% of their maximal effort interspersed with 30-seconds of recovery. We will measure outcomes at the beginning of the project and again after 12 weeks. Scores for people in the groups will be compared. HIIT has never been evaluated as an alternative to MICE or usual care in people with AF. If our clinical trial shows that HIIT helps these people to improve their quality of life and exercise capacity over their usual therapeutic regimes, then doctors caring for people with AF will have a new, improved treatment option at their disposal.

column36: Impacts of City-Wide Bicycle Infrastructure Investment on Population Health & Health Equity
column37: Governments are making major investments in transit, cycling, and walking infrastructure to alleviate the pressures of traffic congestion, car pollutant emissions, and population growth. The City of Victoria, together with province, have committed $9M to build a connected network of cycling facilities that separate bicycles from motor vehicles. This is an unprecedented opportunity to study the impact of building a city-wide network designed to attract people of all ages and abilities to cycling in a mid-sized Canadian city. We will assess impacts of this intervention on population health, comparing Victoria with two other mid-sized cities. We will assess active transportation and safety-related outcomes, using data collected through population surveys before, during, and after the intervention. We will map the access to cycling facilities, and changes in safety impacts, especially within disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Finally, we will calculate the health-related economic benefits of cycling. The outcomes of this project will be: preliminary evidence on whether investment in an 'all ages and abilities' network can induce a shift in travel behaviour and safety, both overall and across population groups; evidence on the impact in terms of access to cycling routes and safety; and an economic assessment of the health-related benefits, which can be used to contextualize the investment. We will provide actionable evidence to guide decision making on public investment in active transportation, in study cities as well as the many other North American cities facing growing transportation and population health challenges.

column36: Children And Teens in Charge of their Health: A feasibility study of solution-focused coaching to foster healthy lifestyles in children and young people with physical disabilities
column37: Many Canadian children find it hard to lead healthy lifestyles in today's world, but children with physical disabilities (CWPD) are more likely to be inactive and have a poorer diet than their able-bodied peers. They are also 2-3 times more likely to be classified as overweight or obese. Unhealthy lifestyles may follow them into adulthood and affect their health and quality of life. CWPD usually cannot join mainstream health promotion programs, because they need activities tailored to their particular needs. Unfortunately, we know these programs are often unavailable. Our study will ask CWPD to take part in health coaching sessions, in which a specially trained health professional provides one-on-one help so that children can use their existing abilities and work towards physical activity and diet goals the child feels are realistic and important. We want to know whether this coaching helps children lead healthier lifestyles. We will randomly put 30 CWPD into one of two groups. All children will receive their regular health care. Half of the children will receive simple written information. The other half will work with a health coach for 6 months. After the first face-to-face session, children will 'meet' with their coach online. All children will be assessed 4 times over 12 months to assess their lifestyles. The coaching group will also be interviewed at the end of the study to tell us what they liked and didn't like about the coaching, as well as any differences they think the coaching made to their lifestyle. To help them talk, they will take photographs to show what their life is like after the coaching finishes. This study will help us understand what works best when trying to help CWPD lead healthy lifestyles, and will lead to bigger research that can help children with and without disabilities to understand how to lead a healthy lifestyle. Knowing how we can help children address these problems will improve health and quality of life in child and adulthood.

column37: RATIONALE Parents with low socioeconomic status (hereafter SES) usually have a low level of literacy. This study is born from a partnership between Web editors of 'Naitre et grandir' (N&G) and 'AboutKidsHealth (AKH), and researchers who developed and validated the Information Assessment Method (IAM). N&G and AKH are popular websites with high quality comprehensive information about child development, health and well-being. The IAM allows parents to assess online information and provide feedback to Web editors. High quality online consumer health information improves knowledge, self-efficacy and health. However, as suggested by pilot data we collected since June 2014, low SES parents underuse N&G and IAM. Yet, it is these very parents who are more likely to report decreased worries and increased confidence as outcomes of using N&G information. Thus, there is a need to improve online child information for low SES parents, and interactions between low SES parents and Web editors, and to explore how parents and children experience these health and well-being outcomes. METHODS We will conduct our study in four phases. Phase 1. We will interview low SES parents to identify barriers and facilitators to using N&G information and to interacting with N&G editors via IAM. Phase 2. We will integrate Phase-1 findings to revise IAM and N&G, and implement a new version: IAM+N&G+. Phase 3. We will compare the use of the original (IAM/N&G) and new (IAM+N&G+) versions. Phase 4. We will interview low SES parents who will have received the N&G+ newsletter and rated it using IAM+; and create life histories to describe how perceived outcomes are experienced by parents and children. IMPACT Results will be applied by two popular resources: N&G and AKH. Thus, they will directly benefit Canadian low SES parents and children. In addition, results will lead to develop a free toolkit for all Web editors that will help improve health interventions to better support and empower low SES parents.

column36: From Patient to Policy: Using data to drive TB elimination in Canada's foreign born population
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is the world's leading infectious disease killer. This disease affects over 10 million people each year and causes 1.8 million deaths. The World Health Organization has made TB elimination a priority and is calling for new programs that prevent and treat TB. Unfortunately, progress towards TB elimination in Canada has stalled in recent years and our national TB elimination efforts are far from complete. This is in part due to persistently high rates of TB in Canada's growing foreign-born population. To accelerate TB elimination efforts in Canada, new strategies for TB prevention in migrant populations are needed. The most promising approach to TB prevention is to detect latent (asymptomatic) TB and treat it before the disease develops and spreads. This approach is potentially effective but is extremely resource intensive, so broad latent TB screening and treatment of the 6.8 million foreign-born residents of Canada is impractical. Instead, we need to create a screening strategy that balances the public health benefits of TB prevention with the system resources required for such a program. Using health databases from BC, Ontario, and Quebec--the three largest migrant-receiving provinces, we aim to develop evidence that will help guide TB screening and preventative therapy in the foreign-born population of Canada. First, we plan to develop a TB risk calculator that quantifies an individual's risk of active TB. We then plan to examine the impact of screening in different populations, including understanding the most cost-effective screening approaches. This research directly addresses the three key themes highlighted by the federal government's plan to enhance Canadian TB elimination. Our findings will generate valuable to inform public health policies and screening programs aimed at tackling TB.

column36: Novel signaling mechanisms leading to pain in irritable bowel syndrome
column37: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is characterized by abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. It is extremely common, affecting over 10% of the adult population in North America and exerts a tremendous societal impact. For example, it is among the most common reasons for workplace absenteeism and in Canada, costs over $1B annually for diagnosis alone. Despite this, the mechanisms that underlie IBS remain poorly understood and as a result, the available treatments are not very effective. The most debilitating symptom is abdominal pain, and we have evidence that inflammatory mediators in the gut, known as proteases, can activate pain-sensing nerves in the gut and intensify the IBS patient's pain. Our previous studies and preliminary data have revealed that: 1) in IBS patients, multiple proteases are released and trigger sustained activation of pain-sensing visceral nerves; 2) changing the diet of IBS patients can alter the activation of inflammatory cells called mast cells (an important source of gut proteases); and 3) in germ-free mice inoculated with the microbiome of IBS patients, we can recapitulate the increased pain signaling and protease activity when we feed these mice diets comparable to those in humans. Based on these findings, we believe that multiple proteases lead to sustained pain signaling in IBS and that dietary factors sustain this abnormal neuronal activation. Using human biopsies in animal IBS models, we will define the protease profile released in response to changes in diet, and examine if the microbiome of a given patient influences the degree of protease-induced pain. We will also investigate how these proteases, once triggered, can sustain excitation of gut pain-sensing nerves and determine whether protease signaling is amplified by other mast cell mediators, such as histamine. Together, our work will clarify how proteases trigger and prolong pain signaling and in doing so, identify novel targets for treating IBS pain.

column36: Healthy public policy through engagement: Promoting the mental health of Canadian children
column37: Mental health problems are the leading health challenge facing young Canadians, with 13% of children aged 4-17 years, or nearly 700,000, experiencing clinically-significant mental disorders at any given time. To more effectively address this issue, children's mental health leaders argue for a public health approach including promotion, prevention and treatment within a "healthy public policy" framework. However, while advances have been made in prevention and treatment, promotion has yet to receive sufficient attention. This study will address critical gaps in children's mental health policy in Canada. Collaborative research approaches will be used in British Columbia and Alberta study sites to engage young people to: 1) enhance understanding of the factors influencing children's mental health; 2) build children's capacity to engage in policymaking processes; 3) develop a testable framework for collaborative policymaking with young people; and 4) explore feasibility of proposed approach. Mixed methods incorporating qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis will ensure a comprehensive approach to addressing study objectives. This study will address Canada's children's mental health shortfalls - by contributing new evidence on processes for engaging young people in developing new policies to promote children's mental health outcomes.

column36: Control of Breathing during Sleep: Brainstem Mechanisms of Respiratory Control
column37: Approximately one in four Canadians is affected by significant sleep problems that can diminish their health, alertness, safety and quality of life. The most common and serious of the sleep disorders have impairments of breathing as their root cause. One example is sleep apnea, which affects up to 20% of adults and is thought to be involved in some cases of sudden unexplained death in infancy. Sleep apnea is defined as cessation of breathing during sleep, and is typically caused by closure of the air passage in the throat in sleep due to relaxation of those breathing muscles (e.g., the tongue) whose activity normally keeps this air passage open. Episodes of breathing cessation in sleep can occur hundreds of times per night, each resulting in temporary suffocation that causes major sleep disruption. Understanding the brain mechanisms causing sleep apnea is important because of the adverse medical, societal and economic costs of this common disorder, such as increased strokes, angina and heart attacks, debilitating daytime sleepiness, increased traffic and work-related accidents, impaired work performance and decreased quality of life. Our research will identify the brain mechanisms that cause changes in breathing across wakefulness and sleep. Research will also identify how commonly used prescription and non-prescription sedating drugs (such as anesthetics, sleeping tablets, painkillers and alcohol) can also depress breathing and the waking-up responses to respiratory distress. This information will identify common mechanisms causing the prevalent problems of sleep and sedation-induced depression of breathing, and will guide pharmacological approaches aimed at preventing or reinstating breathing when it is depressed or fails.

column36: Regulation of the hepatic fibrogenic response by Suppressor of cytokine signaling (SOCS) proteins
column37: The liver is constantly exposed to toxic chemicals from food and medication that cause inflammation. Normally, the liver is able to fend off these insults and repair itself quite rapidly. However, when the onslaught is chronic, for example, during chronic alcohol abuse or infection by hepatitis viruses, the inflammation persists and outpaces the normal repair process. This results in persistent liver damage, leading to a condition known as liver fibrosis, which can progress towards cirrhosis, wherein the vital liver functions are compromised and often leads to liver cancer. Liver cancer ranks as the fifth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related death. Most liver cancer patients die within one year due to late diagnosis and lack of effective treatment. While the liver cancer is difficult to treat, early detection of fibrosis and development of anti-fibrotic interventions could prevent the advancement of disease and its progression towards cancer. Inflammation in general is mediated by a group of proteins called 'inflammatory cytokines', which have a normal function as long as their activity is controlled. This is achieved by a variety of mechanisms, of which the control exerted by a family of proteins called 'Suppressor of cytokine signaling' appears to be very important. This is supported by data from human patients who do not express the SOCS1 protein in the liver, and from our own studies using mice lacking SOCS1. We propose to use this mouse models to gain a better understanding of how SOCS1 regulates liver fibrosis. This knowledge could lead to development of new therapeutic approaches to treat liver fibrosis, and thus diminish patient suffering and healthcare burden from cirrhosis and liver cancer.

column36: gp130 cytokines and IL-33 in progression to chronic lung fibrosis
column37: Buildup of scar tissue in chronic lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) results in local events in lungs that compromise lung function. These include the accumulation of inflammatory cells and decreases in oxygen exchange, and IPF patients have an average survival time of 3 years after diagnosis. Although multiple molecules may collectively determine the severity of disease, we believe that certain hormone-like molecules termed cytokines play a crucial role in the development of this lung pathology. Our novel proposal hypothesizes that one of these cytokines in particular, a gp130 cytokine family member Oncostatin M (OSM), is up-regulated in lung fibrosis and interacts with cells to induce a partnering cytokine called IL-33. These two molecules can orchestrate a variety of inflammatory functions that cause progression to severe and chronic fibrosis. We will test specifically how these two cytokines regulate actions of both mouse and human lung cells in tissue culture, test for ways to inhibit their function, and use mice that are deficient in the IL-33 gene to determine if our hypothesis holds true in mice. We will also determine the spectrum of genes that are increased in severe fibrosis of our established animal models involving OSM and IL-33, and correlate with the spectrum of genes we can detect that are regulated in human IPF samples of stored lung biopsied tissue. We predict that these studies will demonstrate the importance of OSM and IL-33, and the gene signatures they induce, in models of severe respiratory disease in order to define a framework for new approaches in treatments for lung fibrosis.

column36: In vivo interrogation and control of genetically-identified somatosensory neurons in neuropathic pain pathways
column37: Chronic pain affects as many as 1 in 5 people worldwide. As the population ages and modern medicine allows people to survive serious illness, the number of people affected by chronic pain is expected to rise to 1 in 3. Chronic pain can be debilitating, isolating, dehumanizing, and all too frequently, abuse of opioid painkillers can turn deadly (see the current crisis of fentanyl overdoses). Developing new tools to study pain and develop new avenues for analgesia is critical. Previous approaches to activate pain pathways used chemical, thermal, mechanical, or electrical stimulation. These stimuli lack spatial and/or temporal control and often involve invasive procedures. Our goal is to design novel genetic tools that ensure highly precise control on the activity of peripheral pain pathways, and therefore pain perception. Our data provide evidence that optical analgesia can be achieved in freely moving rodents without noxious stimuli or injury. Our approach relies on transgenic mice expressing light-sensitive proteins (opsins) into a specific group of genetically-identified sensory neurons called nociceptors. When exposed to light, light-sensitive proteins are activated, triggering or inhibiting the propagation of electric signals from the periphery to the brain, where pain is perceived. In this project, we propose the development of preclinical models in which pain can be modulated and remotely controlled without any tissue damage. The high sensitivity and specificity of our approach resulted in measurable behavioral responses of the transgenic transducer-expressing mice, following exposure to activators (nociception) or inhibitors (analgesia). Opto/chemogenetic stimulation or inhibition of the sensory pathways in vivo will allow us to investigate the critical role of specific neuronal populations in peripheral pain circuits, facilitating the development of analgesic drugs and gene therapy for the treatment of chronic pain.

column36: Electromechanical signaling in the cerebral circulation: Basic mechanisms to disease application.
column37: Many blood vessels must work together to match blood flow delivery with brain activity. Coordinated blood flow is important for nutrient delivery and its loss diminishes brain function. Recent research has suggested that this coordinated control might be tied to electrical charge moving along vessels. This vital process has never been studied in a critical organ like the brain and thus we know little. The goal with this research is to understand blood vessel communication in the brain and to determine its basis, regulation and importance to biology. The three objectives will: 1) Determine where communication resides in brain blood vessels; 2) Determine whether blood vessel communication impacts stroke injury; and 3) Determine whether blood vessel communication can be modified. We believe this research will provide the first evidence of vascular communication in brain blood vessels. Vascular communication requires pores called gap junctions and we think that if you impair them, blood flow will be compromised and brain injury intensifies. We begin our research with computer modeling and key experiments (microscopy, patch clamp electrophysiology, cell imaging) are performed on animal and human vessels. Our idea that communication controls blood vessel coordination is unique and to foster translational impact we collaborate with neurosurgeons who provide us with human brain vessels. We also work with stroke neurologists who help us design experiments and assess whether vascular communication impacts stroke severity and the brain's ability to recover from this leading cause of adult disability in Canada.

column36: Optimizing insulin basal rate adjustments to prevent exercise-induced hypoglycemia in patients with type 1 diabetes using insulin pump therapy
column37: In type 1 diabetes (T1D), secretion of insulin, a vital hormone to reduce blood sugar, is lost. Thus, patients with T1D need life-long intensive insulin therapy using multiple daily injections or insulin pump therapy. Because patients with T1D lose normal reduction of insulin during exercise, their blood glucose levels may fall rapidly thus increasing the risk of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar with malaise and risk of convulsion & coma). This risk is not only increased during exercise but also for up to 24 hours following exercise when the body reconstitutes its stores of sugar. We have shown that fear of hypoglycemia is a major limitation for physical activity for patients with T1D. Various strategies have been proposed to reduce the risk of exercise-induced hypoglycemia such as reduction in insulin dose in the hours preceding the exercise and food intake containing sugar but none fully reduces the risk of hypoglycemia. Insulin pump therapy allows more flexible treatment than multiple injections since it allows suspending or reducing insulin infusion before, during and after exercise. However, very few studies have investigated how patients should implement this strategy. Therefore, to reduce the risk of exercise-induced hypoglycemia, the objective of this application will be to determine in 3 complementary trials 1) the best timing to initiate a reduction in insulin infusion (how long before exercise?); 2) the optimum insulin infusion reduction (how much during exercise?) and 3) the best strategy to control post-exercise glucose levels (prolonged insulin reduction or snack?). We believe that the results of these trials will identify new strategies to prevent hypoglycemia and thus encourage patients with T1D to practice regular physical activity. Increased physical activity should improve quality of life and could reduce the risk of obesity and cardiovascular disease.

column36: Dendritic mechanisms for cortical associations in layer 5 pyramidal neurons from a mouse model of Fragile X syndrome.
column37: Fragile X mental retardation syndrome (FXS) is the most common known cause of autism. Studies in the mouse model of FXS (Fmr1-KO mice) have demonstrated defects in the cerebral cortex at cellular and circuit levels. A key function of the cerebral cortex is its ability to associate external sensory information with an internal representation of the world in order to make predictions about the future. One particular type of cortical neuron, the layer 5 (L5) pyramidal neuron, is believed to be the main associative neuron integrating sensory inputs in their proximal dendrites (dendrite=the receptive surface) with contextual information at their distal dendrites. Recently, it has been shown in Fmr1-KO mice that the distal dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons have an enhanced summation of excitatory inputs, while in our preliminary data we show that proximal dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons from Fmr1-KO mice have a diminished summation of excitatory inputs. Hence, we hypothesize that these cellular impairments can lead to an underrepresentation of sensory information and an overrepresentation of contextual information, which alter the firing and encoding of information of L5 pyramidal neurons from Fmr1-KO mice. Hence, we will examine synaptic transmission and integration of excitatory inputs in proximal and distal dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons from control and Fmr1-KO mice, and study the functional consequences that these defects have in the association of sensory and contextual information in the Fmr1-KO mice. Lastly, we will uncover the specific mechanisms responsible for the altered synaptic integration found in the distal and proximal dendrites of Fmr1-KO L5 pyramidal neurons. To perform this work we will use cutting edge imaging, genetic, and electrophysiological tools. Our prediction is that these defects will affect the encoding of information in single neurons and the circuit they reside on; representing one of the mayor cortical defects associated with FXS.

column37: First Nations people have shown considerable strengths and resilience despite experiences of significant trauma and stress due to the effects of colonization. The primary goal of this research is to use a strengths-based approach to evaluate how and for whom strengths and resilience resources mitigate the negative health impacts of trauma and stress on mental health and substance use challenges. We propose to conduct analyses of rich qualitative and quantitative data previously collected in two Ontario First Nations, supplemented with additional qualitative data. First, in-depth interviews as well as Photovoice data (i.e., photographs and corresponding narratives) from individuals who have lived experience with mental health and substance use challenges, will be analyzed to illuminate how strengths and resilience resources affect the process of recovery. Second, informed by findings from the qualitative analyses, quantitative analyses of general population survey data will identify unique patterns in the use of different sources of strength/resilience. We will also determine how strengths and resilience resources such as cultural identity and community strengths buffer the impact of trauma and stress on mental health and substance use outcomes. Together with community partners, we will integrate and synthesize the findings and develop key recommendations for strengths based programming. By integrating both qualitative and quantitative data, and partnering closely with community stakeholders in the analysis and interpretation of these data, this initiative will derive a deeper understanding of strengths and resilience resources and how they can be enhanced and reinforced to address mental health and substance use challenges in First Nations communities.

column37: The presence of new blood clots in the veins of legs and lungs decreases the quality of life of patients and may cause death. Current blood thinners are given by injection and orally, but they require taking frequent blood samples to adjust the medication dosing to prevent bleeding. Recently, new blood thinners that are taken orally have been developed. Two of these new blood thinners prevent recurrent clots very well and do not require injections and blood samples for dosing. These new blood thinners are approved in Canada and are currently recommended treatment options for patients with clots in the veins of legs and lungs. A problem however, is that studies are not clear which of these two new blood thinners results in fewer bleeding complications. Since excessive bleeding is a limitation for the use of these new blood thinners, doctors are unsure which drug will be the best blood thinner to use in these patients. We propose to study patients with clots in the veins of legs and lungs who are fit to receive these two new blood thinners. We will determine which of the two new blood thinners results in less bleeding events. This study will help to determine the safest new blood thinner.

column36: Pannexin 1 channels as novel regulators of malignant melanoma
column37: Malignant melanoma is becoming more prevalent each year. Although it accounts for only 4% of all skin cancers, it is responsible for 79% of skin cancer-related deaths. There were 1,150 deaths from melanoma in Canada in 2015. Therefore, it is imperative to look for new therapeutic targets. In this proposal, Dr. Silvia Penuela will determine if a novel protein that allows cells to communicate through channels, called Pannexin 1 (Panx1), might be involved in regulating the aggressiveness of malignant melanoma, and may be a novel target for melanoma treatment. Dr. Penuela will use a number of different mouse and human tissues and cells to assess if these Panx1 channels are acting to promote cancer progression. About 15 years ago, the pannexin family of proteins that forms channels on the surface of human cells for communication was first discovered. We and others have found that these channels, when present at low levels are important in releasing and ingesting small molecules that tell cells how to behave. In mice, we found that these channels are extremely abundant in aggressive melanoma cells, suggesting that they give melanomas a survival benefit enhancing their ability to grow, migrate and enter other organs ultimately causing death. In this proposal we will explore the expression of Pannexin 1 in human melanoma biopsies from different stages of disease progression. We will evaluate the susceptibility of mouse models that are lacking Panx1 to develop tumours after inoculation with melanoma cells. Finally, we will use mouse models to determine how Panx1 causes tumor cells to grow and move to form metastasis, and we will test several chemicals and new compounds that have been shown to block Panx1 channels, as potential new therapies to be used in the fight against malignant melanoma.

column36: Gait as a clinical marker to predict progression to dementia syndromes in MCI
column37: A decrease in walking speed (gait slowing) is a common problem in older persons that is frequently overlooked; however, it is a strong predictor of future cognitive disability, and adverse events. Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a transitional state between normal cognition and mild dementia, although not all older individuals with MCI will progress to dementia. A recent Canadian consensus on dementia called for better characterization of MCI emphasizing the need to identify potential clinical, imaging, and biological changes that may serve as predictors of further dementia. To date, the predictors identified are difficult to apply in clinics. However, since an association between gait slowing and dementia has been established, gait itself might be able to serve as a clinical predictor. This study will build upon the previous Gait & Brain Study, which has demonstrated that a greater slowing on walking speed under a dual-task condition (e.g., walking while talking) is associated with accelerated cognitive decline in MCI. We will also look for physical changes in the brain that are associated with slowed gait speed under a dual-task condition. We hypothesize that a high dual-task cost in older people with MCI will predict future progression to dementia. Furthermore, we will test combinations of dual-task test with clinically available variables to improve prediction. If our hypothesis is confirmed, conducting practical walking assessment in clinics may help detect who will eventually progress to dementia. We believe that combining simple gait testing with available clinical information (age, sex, and cognitive testing) will improve dementia prediction in MCI. A better detection of those with MCI who will progress to dementia will help the Canadian health system optimize available resources by identifying who may benefit from additional testing, and help implement early strategies and interventions to improve quality of life.

column37: About a quarter of middle aged Canadians are hypertensive and mounting evidence suggests these people are at a risk of exacerbated AD progression.
