column36: MicroRNA-218s and their regulated signaling networks in placental development and preeclampsia
column37: Preeclampsia (PE) is a major disorder of human pregnancy, characterized by high blood pressure and presence of proteins in the urine. PE is not only the leading cause of maternal death and still birth, but also affects the health of mothers and children later in their lives. The cause of PE is not well understood; however, insufficient invasion of placental cells into the uterus and subsequent failure to modify uterine blood vessels is thought to be the initial event of PE. This results in insufficient blood supplies to the placenta, causing an abnormal secretion of factors from the placenta into the blood to affect the functions of cells lining the blood vessels, known as endothelial cells. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that have important roles in controlling the levels of proteins being made in cells. We have recently discovered that miR-218 levels are lower in placentas of PE patients than those of healthy women. Our preliminary data showed that miR-218 has potent effects in promoting invasion of placental cells to the uterus and to dilate the maternal blood vessels. We also found that miR-218 may regulate the function of endothelial cells. These novel findings suggest that miR-218 plays important roles in maintaining the proper development of the placenta and that insufficient production of miR-218 in the placenta contributes to the development of PE. The major objectives of this grant are to further investigate the role of miR-218 in placenta development; to identify which key molecules are regulated by miR-218; and to determine how abnormal production of miR-218 may lead to PE. We will use cells derived from placenta, placental organ culture and placenta/uterus co-culture systems, as well as endothelial cells, to study the functions of miR-218 and the key molecules regulated by miR-218. The proposed research will improve the understanding of PE and may reveal novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets for this disorder.

column36: Functional and Molecular Characterization of Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts in High Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer
column37: High grade serous ovarian cancer is a highly aggressive and lethal cancer. Our project is focused on gaining a better understanding of the biology of the different types of cells present within ovarian cancers in the hopes that doing so will lead to identification of new therapies. In addition to the cancer cells, tumors contain normal cells from the body called fibroblasts. We believe that fibroblasts provide an environment that promotes the survival of the cancer cells, as well as promoting other cancer properties such as the ability to spread to other parts of the body. It is possible that by blocking the interactions between fibroblasts and cancer cells, we may be able to interfere with cancer progression. The major goal of this application is to understand how fibroblasts support the growth of ovarian cancer, and to develop ways to interfere with that support. We have already developed methods to separate out the fibroblasts and cancer cells from patient tumors and have analyzed them to determine what genes each cell type is expressing. From this we have generated a list of possible mechanisms for how the fibroblasts are functioning. In this project, we will test whether blocking fibroblast-cancer cell interactions can slow down or stop tumor progression, allowing us to develop new strategies to treat ovarian cancer patients in the future.

column36: Dissecting early and progressive leukemogenic impairments in the hematopoietic hierarchy and function using pre-leukemic inherited bone marrow failure syndromes as human disease models
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a blood cancer with a bleak outlook despite treatment with intensive chemotherapy and bone marrow (BM) transplant. Tools for early detection and prevention are desperately needed. Yet, it is unknown how AML evolves because patients is generally not tested before they become ill. The purpose of this study is to decipher how BM progresses from a non-leukemic state to leukemia, while discovering BM defects in patients with high leukemia risk, namely, inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFSs). Fanconi anemia (FA) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) are IBMFSs that start with deficient formation of blood cells in the BM during childhood and progress to pre-leukemia (early signs of cancer), which, if untreated, culminate in AML. Patients with FA and SDS die from either low blood counts (causing infections and bleeding) or leukemia or from the treatments' side effects. Since patients with FA and SDS annually undergo BM testing to check if they develop leukemia, samples for research can be obtained from consenting patients before, during pre-leukemia and overt leukemia. Such samples provide a unique opportunity to study how leukemia develops and identify early changes in BM that indicate treatment. In this study we will analyze BM cells from patients with SDS and FA at three stages: no-leukemia, pre-leukemia and leukemia. We will identify BM cells that grow fast (like leukemia cells), discover genetic mutations that indicate early leukemia and determine why early leukemic cells grow in excess. Last, we will use specially prepared cells from IBMFS patients called pluripotent stem cells as a model to insert mutations that we identify and study which mutations turn the cells leukemic. The results of our study can be used for early detection and prevention of leukemia in IBMFSs, and for discovery of drugs that correct the early damage. The principles learned will likely apply to other cancers, though the specific defects may vary.

column36: Quantitative electroencephalography in rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep: an early marker of cholinergic neurodegeneration in mild cognitive impairment
column37: The prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia is increasing at a rapid pace. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent cause of dementia. The Alzheimer Society of Canada states that 747,000 Canadians had AD in 2011 and that the current estimated costs of dementia for Canada is around $33 billion annually. The degenerative process leading to AD is believed to start decades before the onset of dementia. This long and progressive period is called mild cognitive impairment (MCI) but not all individuals with MCI will develop AD. The identification of earlier markers to detect which MCI individuals will progress to AD is urgently needed for the development and assessment of preventive and therapeutic strategies. Up to now, promising markers measuring brain activity have been identified in awake patients. We propose that rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep is a more sensitive state than wakefulness to detect early neurodegeneration in MCI patients. Indeed, during REM sleep, the activity of the acetylcholine system, which is affected early in MCI, is not masked by other systems that are active during wakefulness. The goal of this project is to predict, in individuals with MCI, those who will develop AD three years later by studying REM sleep characteristics. We will also validate that REM sleep is linked to the integrity of the cholinergic system using brain imaging. If our hypotheses are confirmed, REM sleep characteristics have the potential to become a reliable non-invasive and low-cost tool to help identify MCI individuals at high risk of progressing to AD and test the efficacy of preventive treatments.

column36: Next Generation Antithrombotics: Safer Inhibitors for Thrombosis that Targets Procoagulant Polyanions
column37: Thrombosis- clotting of the blood in blood vessels- is the leading cause of death in Canada and in the Developed society. Blood clot formation in arteries (blood supply vessels) is a major cause of majority of heart attacks and stroke. Blood clot in veins (venous thromboembolism (VTE)) is the third leading cause of death in world after heart attacks and stroke, and is one of the leading cause of death in patients with cancer. Current treatment of these diseases includes the use of drugs which can prevent platelet (a type of blood cell) activation and aggregation, and the use of anticoagulants (blood thinners). However, none of these therapies are perfect due to inherent bleeding side effects associated. Importantly, none of these treatments target the fundamental cause of pathological thrombosis in veins and arteries. Recent studies discovered that biomolecules such as polyphosphate released by platelets and extracellular nucleic acids released by the damaged or activated cells in the blood vessels initiate blood coagulation and cause pathological thrombosis. Thus, in this proposal we are developing novel molecules that can directly neutralize the activity of these potent thrombus generating polyanionic biomolecules by selectively binding them and forming a complex thereby preventing the thrombus formation. This novel drug molecules will also have no or minimal bleeding side effects unlike the current drugs used in the management of thrombosis. This research is based on a recent discovery of a patented novel class of dendritic polymeric inhibitors in our laboratory. This novel therapeutic approach will change the way clinicians treat the patients suffering from blood clot problems and will save the lives of millions of people, and improve their quality of life.

column36: Core Outcome Set Development for Effectiveness Trials of Interventions to Prevent or Treat Delirium (Del-COrS)
column37: Delirium is a condition also known as acute confusional state. Patients have altered consciousness level, sleep disturbance, memory problems, and are unable to focus attention or concentrate. Delirium is common, serious, and potentially preventable. Delirium impacts nearly all patients from the critically ill to elderly living at home. Delirium can result in death, complications, prolonged hospital stay, and loss of independence resulting in long-term care placement. For these reasons, studies of treatments to prevent or reverse delirium have risen considerably. To determine the effects of treatments, researchers measure outcomes, for example quality of life, symptoms, or complications. At present, there is no consistency in outcomes studied by researchers for methods to prevent or treat delirium. This creates problems as we cannot compare or combine study results, making treatment decisions difficult. One strategy to overcome this problem is to agree upon a set of main outcomes for a health condition, called a core outcome set (COS). We aim to develop COS for studies of methods to prevent or treat delirium for critically ill and hospitalized patients, those requiring palliative care, and older adults at risk of delirium. We will review the evidence base to determine outcomes already used. We will interview patients and families about outcomes important to them. We will conduct a Delphi study (consensus building exercise) to seek opinion from patients/family with experience of delirium, clinicians, and researchers and to reach agreement. We will test in this Delphi study if the way we provide information influences the results. We will hold a meeting to establish the final COS. Engagement in research projects may be hard. We will interview our patient/family participants to find out what was hard, what worked well, and recommendations to inform similar studies in the future. Finally we will use the same methods to decide the best tools to measure COS outcomes

column36: Repeated Demyelination as an MRI Marker of Progressive Multiple Sclerosis
column37: In multiple sclerosis (MS), brain lesions form when the immune system attacks healthy tissue. This results in damage to the myelin insulation surrounding nerve cells - a process called demyelination. The subsequent partial repair of the myelin is called remyelination. In previous work, using advanced MRI and image processing methods, our group demonstrated that both demyelination and remyelination occur when new lesions form. Pre-existing lesions can also undergo repeat demyelination. Such "repeat" demyelination is difficult to observe on normal MRI scans, since the tissue already looks abnormal on MRI. Furthermore, repeat demyelination is not repaired as well as damage in new lesions, and brain injury accumulates. Interestingly, repeat demyelination is also three times more common in people with progressive MS compared to those with relapsing remitting disease. The goal of this project is to test the idea that damage in new lesions is usually repaired well enough that the brain can function normally again. In progressive MS, however, we hypothesize that the repeat demyelination cannot be repaired well enough, resulting in a progressive worsening of clinical symptoms. This information has the potential to help researchers look for new ways to treat progressive MS. As well, looking at the number of repeat lesions on an MRI may enable doctors to better predict patients who are at risk for progressive MS.

column36: ULK1 (most upstream autophagy inducer) as a potential therapeutic target in Osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and major cause of disability worldwide. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms by which OA can be prevented or treated remains to be determined. Cartilage is the most critical tissue in our joint that is destroyed during OA. Cartilage consists of only one type of specialized cells called chondrocytes and during ageing these cells tend to die faster resulting in destruction of the cartilage and joint tissues. In order to stop cartilage destruction, it's essential to identify key biological processes that can increase the survival of chondrocytes in the cartilage. Our studies using animal models and human OA cartilage samples have identified such biological process of cell survival called autophagy. During ageing and OA, this process does not function very well i.e. this process is weaker resulting in decreased cell protection and increased cell death. The central factor that controls autophagy in the cartilage is unknown. Our studies suggest that a biological factor called ULK1 is a central factor that controls autophagy and maintains chondrocyte survival as well as controls destructive activity within the cartilage. Based on our preliminary data, our hypothesis is that during OA, ULK1 function decreases and as the result autophagy decreases resulting in greater cell death and cartilage destruction. Thus delivering ULK1 in joints will increase chondrocyte survival and halt further cartilage degeneration. To prove this hypothesis, we have generated mice in which ULK1 is specifically absent only in the cartilage, allowing us to specifically identify the role of ULK1 in OA disease process. Furthermore we have also created a method of delivering ULK1 in knee joint of mouse OA model to see if ULK1 therapy can stop chondrocyte death and stop cartilage destruction. Data obtained from this study has the potential to show that ULK1 therapy can be used to stop cartilage destruction and halt OA disease.

column37: Concussions are common pediatric injuries and symptoms include headaches, nausea, difficulty concentrating and paying attention, and confusion. They can also cause several emotional symptoms, such as anxiety, depression, irritability, and changes in sleeping patterns. We found that 12% of youth presenting to a concussion program developed a new psychiatric disorder, worsening symptoms of a pre-existing condition, or suicidal ideation during concussion recovery. column36: The pricing of generic drugs and its impact on market structure, competitiveness and security of supply
column37: A generic drug is identical to a brand name drug in terms of dosage form, strength, safety, quality, performance and intended use, but its price is much lower. In Canada and worldwide, regulations setting the maximum allowable price for a generic drug, relative to its branded counterpart, have been used to make generic markets more competitive and to reduce costs for individual consumers and publicly-funded drug plans. In 1998, Ontario imposed a 70/90 price cap which meant that the first generic had to be priced at =70% of the associated brand-name price, and subsequent generics had to be priced at =90% of the first generic. The price cap was subsequently lowered to 50% in 2006, and 25% in 2010. Other provinces soon followed suit, with similar price-cap regulations. On April 1, 2014, a nationwide generic pricing framework developed by the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance (pCPA) was introduced, which requires new generic drugs to be priced at 75% (85% if no product listing agreement with brand), 50% or 25% of the brand name price, depending on the number of generic competitors. Furthermore, 18 commonly-used generic drugs have now been priced at 18% of brand. Our study will be the first to evaluate the performance of these new Canadian generic drug pricing policies. This research is important because setting the maximum allowable price at the wrong level can lead to the inefficient use of public funds, such as high provincial drug plan expenditures in the case where a generic drug price is still too high. On the other hand, setting prices too low might create drug shortages, since fewer new generics would enter the market while other generics would cease production. Our goal is to assess the impact of price-cap regulations on different Canadian generic drug market outcomes and especially the supply and availability of generic drugs. The findings will be used to guide policy-making to ensure fair pricing and reduced risk of generic drug shortages in Canada.

To date no cause for this increased risk has been identified. Some researchers have proposed that this potential transfer of maternal vaginal bacteria may be prevented by a caesarean delivery. This may result in altering the establishment of the infant's own bacterial community. However a clear link between delivery type and the infant's bacterial community has not been established. As a result of this idea the practice of "vaginal seeding" has emerged, where a newborn delivered via caesarean section is swabbed with the mother's vaginal secretions to transfer the mother's vaginal bacteria to the infant, mimicking what the infant would have been exposed to during vaginal birth. However the benefits of "vaginal seeding" have not been evaluated and the safety of this practice has not been proven despite it coming into clinical use. The goal of our study will be to determine if the maternal bacterial community is actually transferred to the infant during delivery and if the different types of deliveries alter this transfer. This study will use advanced gene-based methods to profile the bacterial communities present in women who deliver vaginally or via caesarean section and connect these to the infant gut bacterial community in the first 3 months of life. This research will lead to a deeper understanding of the potential role of the maternal bacterial community on the infant gut bacterial community.

column37: Many proteins expressed by cancer cells are modified with carbohydrate chains. However, we have recently discovered that VAR2CSA also binds a similar placental-like CS structure broadly present in human cancer. It is therefore tempting to speculate that tumors re-express placental-type CS to accommodate these important cellular processes. In this project we will elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind CS reconfigurations in human prostate and bladder cancer, and establish the role of these CS modifications in tumor cell growth and survival. Our work will provide new insight into the regulation and function of cancer-associated carbohydrates, essential for developing effective therapeutic strategies targeting human cancer.

column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rhythm disorder that causes one out of six strokes. Prevention of strokes in AF is achieved through the use of blood thinners such as coumadin. These patients will be treated in the usual manner except for this small procedure which has been shown to be quite safe. Having successfully recruited 2300 participants into the trial supported by multiple seed and bridge grants, we now seek full funding to complete recruitment to the full 4,700 participants required to know if left atrial appendage closure works. The LAAOS III trial will determine if closing the left atrial appendage can reduce stroke and other complications in addition to usual therapy. A positive study will change the way heart surgery is performed on patients with AF and result in a large reduction in the number of strokes in Canada. column36: Opposite roles of MYCN and YAP in cancer initiation
column37: Retinoblastoma is a rare childhood cancer of the eye. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a common and very lethal adult tumor caused by smoking. It kills more people than any other cancer. These cancers have much in common, including frequent loss of the RB tumor suppressor gene. Dissecting other shared features that drive these cancers will illuminate new strategies to prevent and treat both diseases. Retinoblastoma arises from cone photoreceptors in the embryonic retina, the cells we use to detect colour. They are hypersensitive to RB loss because they have naturally high levels of MYC, a pro-cancer protein. Why do they need such a dangerous protein? We discovered that MYC is potent at forcing cells to become cones. Cones make other pro-cancer proteins, so by driving this cell fate, MYC inadvertently facilitates tumor formation. Remarkably, we find that MYC also promotes formation of the lung cells that give rise to SCLC. MYC regulates gene expression, so we will identify the targets it controls that promote formation of the tumor-prone cell types in retina and lung. In related work, we discovered that the YAP protein blocks retinoblastoma and SCLC. This is also surprising, because in many other tumor types YAP drives cancer. Our data suggests that YAP impairs retinoblastoma by inhibiting cone formation (and so MYC production). Here, we will examine more closely whether YAP does this in the embryonic human retina, and whether it also blocks the formation of the cells that give rise to SCLC in the lung. YAP is switched off in retinoblastoma and SCLC, so reactivating this gene could be a potent new therapy. To test this idea we will ask if inducing YAP blocks SCLC progression in the mouse lung. If it does, this result would justify extensive efforts to identify drugs that reactivate the silent YAP gene in RB-deficient cancers. SCLC treatment has changed little in decades, but our insights offer hope for new therapies.

column36: The Evolution of the Most Lethal Human Malignancy: The Genetic Progression of Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer
column37: Thyroid cancer is the most common endocrine malignancy with 6500 new cases in Canada each year. Most thyroid cancers are well-differentiated (non-aggressive) types that are almost always cured with standard thyroid surgery with or without radioactive iodine therapy. Indeed, the chance of dying from these thyroid cancers is less than 5%. In contrast, anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is rare, accounting for only 1% of thyroid cancers, however it is perhaps the most lethal human malignancy with an average survival of 3 to 6 months. Only 10% of patients are alive one year after diagnosis. Its presentation is dramatic, with the rapid onset of airway and esophageal blockage and frequent spread to the lungs. It is intriguing that the same organ can harbor both the most indolent and most aggressive cancers (ATC). Interestingly, 21-79% of ATCs have coexisting areas or a previous history of well-differentiated cancers. Although this suggests a progression from well-differentiated cancers to ATC, to date there is little molecular conformation that such a progression exists versus de novo generation of ATC. As anaplastic thyroid cancer is extremely rare and most cases are inoperable, there are a paucity of tissue samples for study at any one center. The Global Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer Initiative (GATCI) led by Dr. Paul Boutros at the Ontario Institute for Cancer Research and Dr. Anthony Nichols at Western Univeristy has brought together 14 institutions to pool samples for analysis. Over 300 samples are available including 50 with matched well-differentiated and anaplastic components. We will utilize this internationally unique resource to study cancer progression at the molecular level using cutting edge genetic techniques. The novel genes found to be unique to the aggressive tumors will then be studied in cells and mouse models to identify which of the genes are truly important to cancer progression.

Cadherin and a-catenin localize at the cell membrane of epithelial cells, preventing those cells from leaving the epithelium to form metastases. This is of particular significance as app. 85% of all forms of cancer derive from epithelial cells and are called carcinomas. The maintenance of epithelial tissue integrity, to which cadherin and a-catenin make major contributions, plays a pivotal role in the prevention of metastatic development in carcinomas. We use the fruit fly Drosophila as a stand-in for humans to investigate how cadherin and a-catenin govern cell behaviour. The main work in the Tepass laboratory focuses on a-catenin, which links cadherin to the cytoskeleton of the cells, an interaction that is essential for cadherin function and currently only poorly understood. Insights into how cadherin and a-catenin work normally is expected to inform us about the role of these factors in cancer, and ultimately will help develop better tools for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

column36: Maternal and infant health in association with household food insecurity
column37: Household food insecurity, the inadequate or insecure access to food due to financial constraints, affected 12.6% of Canadian households in 2012. Food insecurity among pregnant women is concerning because food insecurity is associated with poor health and increased health care costs. It may pose serious risks to the health of newborns, negatively affecting their health through childhood and beyond. However, in Canada, there has been little research examining food insecurity during pregnancy or early life. This research into the origins and implications of food insecurity for pregnancy and child birth in Canada will importantly help to set priorities and identify directions for interventions in the future. Our research findings will also be used to develop guidelines for physicians and other health care providers to help them respond more effectively to women who are food insecure during pregnancy.

column36: A novel BAFopathy syndrome: Functional genetics using human stem cells and gene editing technologies
column37: Certain molecular complexes are required for brain cells to mature properly. In mammals including humans, a complex called BAF is known to be essential for brain development. BAF is made up of several subunits, some of which are already associated with childhood brain disorders including intellectual disability and disorders on the autism spectrum. BAF functions to bind to DNA and to turn genes on and off. We previously performed genome sequencing on a family with two children with the same severe neurodevelopmental disorder and identified mutations in ACTL6B, a gene which makes a protein that is a subunit of the BAF complex and which has never been associated with disease before. We have identified four unrelated cases with mutations in this gene and with a similar clinical profile, strongly suggesting that mutations in this gene cause disease. Using the index case, we have made stem cells from skin, and turned these skin cells into brain cells, and have done the same in healthy controls. We have performed whole genome gene expression analysis and mapped the binding sites of the BAF complex using similar technology. We have also made isogenic control cells with CRISPR/Cas9 technology where we have repaired the patient mutation and deleted the gene itself, two ways to generate excellent comparison data for rare diseases. In this proposal, we plan to make stem cells from all patients with an ACTL6B mutation, to assess gene expression and BAF binding to DNA at multiple neurodevelopmental timepoints, and to compare human data with mouse knock-in data, where we will generate mice with the patient mutations. column37: Habiter un quartier pauvre, enclave, dont le parc locatif est en mauvais etat, dispendieux, voire insalubre, ou les epiceries sont eloignees, les emplois de pietre qualite, ou l'amenagement est peu securitaire, avec peu d'espaces verts, ou la circulation abonde, c'est habiter un environnement defavorable a la sante. Or, pour ameliorer leur sante, les Canadiens doivent trouver ce dont ils ont besoin dans leur voisinage. Mais comment ameliorer un environnement defavorable a la sante? Une voie de solution reside dans l'action intersectorielle locale qui consiste a reunir les acteurs d'une meme communaute pour qu'ils priorisent et agissent ensemble sur des conditions de vie (logement, alimentation, transport, etc.) afin de les rendre plus favorables a la sante. Notre projet vise a rendre explicite comment se produisent les effets de transformation de milieu associes a l'action intersectorielle locale. Il s'appuie sur les resultats d'une etude en cours (ROH 211-215), qui a permis de developper un outil d'analyse des processus et effets de ce type d'action, et de relier les uns aux autres, sous forme de chaines de production d'effets. Le present projet permettra 1) de valider ce developpement de connaissances novateur (notre outil) sur un grand nombre de cas (n=40) et 2) d'identifier des regularites dans les chaines conduisant a des effets observables tout comme dans celles n'aboutissant pas a des effets. Cette recherche est realisee par une equipe chevronnee reunissant trois chercheurs (deux de l'Universite de Montreal et un de l'Universite du Quebec en Outaouais) et quatre utilisateurs de connaissances, directement concernes par l'action intersectorielle locale (Ville de Montreal, Direction de sante publique de Montreal, Centraide et Coalition montrealaise des Tables de quartier). column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of genetic diseases affecting previously healthy children and leading to progressive disabilities and death over months to years. Unfortunately, no curative treatment is available for these children, a situation only exacerbated by the fact that an estimated 30-50% of patients remain without a precise diagnosis despite multiple tests. Finding the cause of these diseases, the erroneous gene, is the first step toward finding a cure. Leukodystrophies are characterized by abnormalities in the white matter of the brain, whose main component, myelin, is needed to insulate brain cells (neurons), protect them, and allow fast electric conduction necessary in the nervous system. Leukodystrophies are classified as hypomyelinating (lack of myelin formation) and non-hypomyelinating (unhealthy myelin) based on distinguishing features seen in brain scans. This research project focuses on identifying new causal genes for hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and understanding why mistakes in these novel genes lead to disease. Children with these disease-causing genes develop progressive difficulties that affect their walking, talking, and swallowing, among other things. This project will allow patients and their families to have a proper diagnosis, obtain genetic counseling and make family-planning decisions, as well as open the door for the discovery of treatments.

column36: Neurophysiological biomarkers of insomnia treatment response: towards personalized therapeutic approaches in chronic insomnia
column37: Insomnia is a frequent problem in the general population and is associated with physical and mental health problems. It is still difficult to treat insomnia. Indeed, sleeping pills have side effects and tend to lose efficacy over time in many people with insomnia. Psychological treatment for insomnia - called cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-I) - is effective in a majority of people with insomnia, even in the long term, but requires access to qualified therapists. In addition, up to 40% people will still have insomnia symptoms after treatment. In order to provide the treatment option that is the most likely to work for each specific person, it is important to be able to predict which individuals will respond better to CBT-I. Brain electrical signals measured with electroencephalography (EEG) during sleep (particularly a type of brain signal called sleep spindle) tend to vary from one person to another, but remain stable from one night to the other in a specific person; for this reason, they are considered as a 'trait', i.e. a fingerprint characterizing a specific individual. Some of our preliminary work shows that insomniacs with less sleep spindles tend to benefit less from CBT-I treatment. This means that sleep spindle could be used to predict if people will be likely to have their sleep improved after CBT-I before it is used. In this project, we now wish to confirm these results on a larger group of insomniacs, using more detailed measures of sleep spindles. We also wish to define reference values of sleep spindles - adjusted for age and sex - that will allow identifying insomniacs likely to respond to CBT-I. The findings from this research will allow evaluating if a brain electrical measure such as spindles can be used to predict the efficacy of the recommended first-line treatment option for insomnia, and can thus be used as a tool to guide which treatment to recommend in a specific person.

column36: Timing Deficits in Developmental Coordination Disorder: Understanding the Role of Auditory-Motor Interactions and Implications for Therapies
column37: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) affects 5-6% of school-aged children and is characterized by difficulties in activities of daily living. These children are of normal intelligence but show slow and inaccurate gross and/or fine motor movements. Without intervention, the deficits continue into adulthood in the majority of cases. This population is at high risk to develop anxiety, depression, and obesity; these children are at generally increased risk for physical and mental health problems because DCD affects children's ability to interact socially. One of the core deficits in DCD is poor motor timing. Rhythms and timing are fundamental to biological organisms. In humans, breathing, heart beats, walking, and perceiving speech and music rely on the ability to extract timing regularities in auditory signals and/or to produce regular movements. Remediation treatments for DCD have focused on movement therapies. However, recent work from our group and others on understanding how time and rhythm information is processed in the brain shows that the perception of auditory rhythms is accomplished through interactions between auditory and motor (movement) areas of the brain. Simply hearing an auditory rhythm sets up oscillatory brain rhythms we can measure with electroencephalography (EEG) involving both auditory and motor regions. Thus, we hypothesized, and pilot data corroborated, that children with DCD also show timing deficits in the perception of sounds. The research program aims to (1) understand these auditory perceptual deficits in DCD from both a brain and behavioural perspective and (2) investigate benefits of adding auditory rhythmic cuing to existing movement-training therapies to improve outcomes. The research is significant in furthering our understanding of sensorimotor timing deficits underlying DCD and applying this knowledge to improve treatment programs.

column36: Development of small molecule modulators of Ras signaling
column37: Activating mutations in Ras genes are among the leading drivers in human cancer. The prevalence of Ras genetic lesions is especially high in pancreatic (>90%), colorectal (50%), and lung (30%) cancers. We propose herein a two-pronged strategy to develop small molecule modulators that will block Ras activity in human cancer cells and therefore provide drug candidates for several deadly cancers. We recently identified a series of chemical inhibitors by high-throughput screening with an assay detecting the interaction of Ras with its effector RAF. These molecules were found to inhibit oncogenic signaling and proliferation in Ras-mutant cancer cell lines. We now need mechanistic characterization of these compounds in order to further optimize them and improve their effectiveness. More specifically, we will confirm the binding of these compounds to Ras-ERK pathway components and we will assess their selectivity by biophysical, biochemical and genetic approaches. In a second approach, we will develop compounds mimicking a synthetic protein, named NS1 that binds to Ras with high-affinity. NS1 was recently developed by our collaborators and was shown to block oncogenic signaling and the proliferation of cancer cells (Spencer-Smith et al. Nat. Chem. Biol.). We will exploit this privileged information to rationally design and synthesize Ras inhibitors. The NS1 crystal structure with Ras will be used as a template for computer-assisted molecular modeling. Mimicking protein-protein interactions with small molecules has historically been challenging. We therefore propose to synthesize larger molecules, named macrocyclic peptides, designed to interact over an extended surface while retaining drug-like properties. The two aims of this proposal represent innovative strategies to inhibit Ras function in human tumors. It can be expected that compounds emerging from these approaches will form the ground of effective treatments for many common cancers bearing activating Ras mutations.

column36: Tumor suppressor mechanisms of SOCS proteins in hepatocellular carcinoma
column37: The liver carries out many vital functions such as metabolism of dietary nutrients, storage of vitamins and iron, synthesis of blood proteins and formation of bile. Besides, the liver purifies blood to prevent toxic substances from reaching other vital organs. Hepatocytes, which are the main cell type in the liver, detoxify and eliminate toxic substances that enter blood. During this process, hepatocytes may get injured and undergo death, which prompts adjacent normal cells to proliferate regenerate a functional liver mass. However, repeated/persistent assaults (e.g., alcohol abuse, hepatitis virus infection) induce chronic inflammation and liver 'fibrosis', leading to 'cirrhosis' - characterized by replacement of loss of liver tissue with fibrous tissue, resulting in reduced liver functions. In livers with cirrhosis, hepatocytes undergo recurrent proliferation to restore liver functions. This causes the formation of liver nodules, within which cells accumulate genetic lesions and may become cancerous. While liver failure caused by cirrhosis ranks among the top 10 causes of death in the western world, liver cancer remains the 3rd leading cause of cancer death. Understanding the molecular basis of abnormal hepatocyte proliferation following liver injury is essential to develop more efficient treatments for liver cancer. The key mediators of hepatocyte proliferation are cytokines and growth factors. Normally, their actions are tightly controlled by diverse mechanisms, one of which is mediated by the 'Suppressor Of Cytokine Signaling' (SOCS) family of proteins. The genes coding for SOCS1 and SOCS3 proteins are frequently inactivated in liver cancer biopsies, indicating that they play important roles in preventing hepatocytes from becoming cancerous. Our goal is to understand how these SOCS proteins function in the liver using mouse models of liver cancer so that this knowledge could be used to develop rational strategies to treat liver cancer.

column37: The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) and the Functional Annotation Of Mouse (FANTOM) consortiums reported that there are far more transcripts than initially anticipated. Surprisingly, it turned out that coding transcripts represent only <3% of the total genome, whereas the majority of other transcripts have no coding potential. The existence of the large number of noncoding transcripts has been disregarded as junk DNA and transcript noises for some time, but increasing evidence suggests that a significant part of such noncoding transcripts are in fact functionally active RNA molecules. Importantly, the biological function of noncoding RNAs is thus primarily determined by their structure and their interactions with protein partners. Among these non-coding RNAs are riboswitches, which are structured elements typically found in the 5' untranslated regions of mRNAs. Riboswitches regulate gene expression by altering their structure upon binding to small cellular metabolites. Similarly to the majority of non-coding RNAs, very little information is known regarding how the structure of riboswitches is used to modulate genetic expression. As a result, it is imperative to employ novel high-resolution methods to characterize RNA structures under conditions closer to the in vivo context, most preferably allowing to study the structure of nascent transcripts. A major goal of our research is to unravel the molecular mechanisms by which riboswitches perform ligand binding during their transcription (i.e., co-transcriptionally) to control gene expression. Our research could be used to design novel general antimicrobial drugs based on riboswitch ligand analogs, which would be selectively toxic to bacteria carrying these RNAs. The knowledge obtained from this research will also be generally applicable to study more complex systems, such as long non-coding RNAs associated to cardiovascular diseases and several types of cancer.

column36: Molecular Therapeutic Targeting of Malignant Gliomas
column37: Malignant gliomas are highly aggressive cancers with a survival expectancy of less than 2 years despite surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Over the past 30 years, limited progress has been made in treating this aggressive cancer despite our increased understanding of the molecular genetics and basic biology of these tumours. Accordingly, new treatment strategies are desperately needed. Malignant gliomas are comprised of a central glioma core (GC) of cancer cells which are rapidly dividing to increase the size of the tumour mass. Intrinsic resistance mechanisms of these cancer cells in the GC prevent chemotherapy and radiation therapy from being effective. In addition, malignant gliomas are characterized by highly invasive cells which are not rapidly dividing but are capable of migrating a considerable distance away from the central core in a zone of infiltration (ZOI). These invading glioma cells are somewhat protected by an intact blood brain barrier (BBB) which prevents chemotherapy from effectively reaching the ZOI. In this proposal, we will use novel therapies based on our recent studies to treat the rapidly dividing glioma cells in the GC. We will focus on metabolically reprogramming glioma cells in the GC to reduce their proliferation, and to inhibit glioma cells from following pro-survival pathways in response to cellular stresses such as hypoxia, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. In addition, we will target the invading glioma cells in the ZOI using novel inhibitors of cell invasion, and magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound to break down the BBB around the GC to facilitate contact of these inhibitors with the invading glioma cells. We expect that simultaneous precision targeting of the GC and ZOI with potent drugs and advanced delivery strategies will provide therapeutic and survival benefit to patients suffering from this lethal cancer.

There are two unique aspects to our proposed study. Firstly, we are among the first to produce a stable expression construct allowing long-term studies of the circular RNAs. The second unique approach is our inhibitor system that is designed to block the function of individual circular RNAs in both cell and animal models. These allow us to specifically study individual circular RNAs, and better understand any causal relationships. Our proposed experiments will help us explore the regulatory roles of circular RNAs in both cardiac aging and other cellular repair contexts. The agents developed may be used as tools in understanding the role of circular RNAs in heart development, aging, disease-associated injury and tissue regeneration. With these approaches, we hope to design therapies to intervene against the adverse remodeling associated with age-related heart disease.

column37: Lupus is a systemic autoimmune disease, in which the immune or defensive system attacks the body's organs/tissues because it fails to differentiate between these and foreign, potentially dangerous materials (like microbes). This leads to inflammation in various organs and the development of signs and symptoms that are different from one person to another. Its course is unpredictable, defined by relapses and remissions. column36: Chloride dysregulation and neuropathic pain: Linking molecular mechanisms with altered pain processing via identification of cellular and circuit level changes
column37: Imagine gentle touch causing excruciating pain. Such pathological pain develops in up to 1 in 15 people because of insults to the nervous system. Despite identification of many "pain" molecules, so-called neuropathic pain remains hard to treat. The slow pace of developing better pain medications reflects gaps in our understanding of how molecular changes impact the operation of cells and neural circuits. Pain perception ultimately depends on the functioning of complicated neural networks that involve many cells and molecules interacting in complex ways. Neural circuits in the spinal cord are known to play a crucial role in pain processing. Certain spinal neurons are responsible for inhibiting other spinal neurons, thus controlling what sensory information gets relayed to the brain. Too little inhibition results in neuropathic pain. Many different molecular changes can compromise inhibition but reduced expression of a molecule known as KCC2 is particularly important; in fact, downregulation of KCC2 is necessary and sufficient to explain many forms of neuropathic pain. Yet it remains unclear in what cell types KCC2 is downregulated and precisely how this affects those cells and the circuits they form. In the proposed study, we will use rodent models to determine which spinal cell types experience pathological changes in KCC2 and how this impacts cell function. We will also study how pain processing by spinal circuits is affected. Lastly, we will integrate these results by building a computer model that simulates how spinal circuits normally process pain signals and how that processing is altered by the disinhibition caused by reduced KCC2. This basic scientific understanding - formalized in a computer model - will rectify critical knowledge gaps and explain precisely how a molecule like KCC2 can cause neuropathic pain. That information will be used to explore how therapeutic strategies can reduce neuropathic pain by mitigating the effects of KCC2 downregulation.

column36: Probing the spike initiation properties of primary somatosensory neurons using optogenetics
column37: Nerve cells, or neurons, generate electrical pulses known as spikes. Spikes are used to transmit information over long distances, e.g. from your fingertip to your spinal cord. Generating too many or too few spikes can have serious consequences. In some types of chronic pain, for example, sensory neurons that generate too many spikes cause gentle stimuli to be mistakenly perceived as painful. Understanding the spike generation process is therefore an important goal of neuroscience research. However, the part of the neuron that transmits spikes is a very fine fiber called the axon. Because it is so fine, axons are difficult to study using standard tools, forcing researchers to study spike initiation in the bigger and more accessible cell body. But sometimes, as in the case of neurons responsible for sensing touch, the cell body is far from where spikes normally originate. It is uncertain whether spikes originating in axon terminals in the skin arise through exactly the same process as spikes studied in the cell body, and whether spikes originating at each location are similarly affected in conditions like chronic pain. We have overcome the challenge of studying axonal spiking by capitalizing on a new technology known as optogenetics. Optogenetics allows us to manipulate neurons using ion channels that are sensitive to light. Specifically, by making axons express a light-sensitive ion channel known as channelrhodopsin, we can shine light on different parts of the axon to study how spikes are initiated in each part. We can also then study if the spike initiation properties of any axon region are altered by a certain drug or disease process. Based on computer simulations and past experiments in cell bodies of neurons, we will use this new light-based approach to study spike generation in previously inaccessible parts of the axon. This information will help ongoing efforts to correct changes in spike initiation that contribute to chronic pain and other diseases.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory disease of the brain leading to paralysis, that mostly affects young adults. The majority of patients will present with a relapsing-remitting (RRMS) form of the disease in which the occurrence of symptoms (relapses) is followed by periods of partial or complete recovery (remission). In primary progressive MS (10-15%), which affects mainly men, there is a steady worsening of neurological function without intermittent recovery. Affecting more than 100, 000 Canadians, women 2-3 times more often than men, research into the exact cause and disease mechanism of MS is essential to find an effective treatment. Current treatments can temper, but not cure RRMS and no therapy is available to treat the progressive disease. The current and common mouse models for MS lack some essential disease features i.e. gender differences, spontaneous disease development, progressive disease phase and involvement of various inflammatory cells, making them inadequate to study this disease in vivo. Our goal is therefore to use a new mouse model, named the TCR1640 model, that thoroughly reflects the clinical features of MS to fully elucidate the exact disease mechanisms, that are so distinctive for MS, and to find novel specific therapeutic targets for every disease phase. We will first investigate the relationship between gender and disease development. Next, we will elucidate how different disease phases occur (relapse and progressive) and resolve (remission) from an immunological and neurological point of view. Finally, we will use this mouse model to test new therapeutic strategies for all types of MS. After this, we can look forward to implement these in MS patients. Therefore, using a mouse model that clinically and immunologically reflects human MS disease is essential to shed light on disease development, gender differences and on the untreatable progressive disease phase to find an effective treatment for all disease courses.

column37: Broken bones in the hand are one of the most common injuries seen in emergency departments. Current common practice is to provide people who have a broken wrist/hand with a prescription for opioid pain medications to help manage their pain. Secondary outcomes will be: grip strength, pinch strength, total active range of motion of the wrist/hand, the McGill Pain Questionnaire and patient satisfaction. Secondary outcomes will be measured at baseline, during the first 3 weeks and 6, 12, and 24 weeks after the fracture. Statistical analysis will determine whether the groups are different at any time point. We will also test whether the treatment responses are affected by gender or age. This information will allow doctors to pick the type of medicine that is both effective and safest for future patients.

column36: Getting Ready for Vision Therapy in Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders
column37: Our goal is to identify therapies for a group of genetic diseases, the Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders (PBD). Progressive retinal degeneration leading to blindness is one of the major, untreatable handicaps in this condition and correcting vision would vastly improve the quality of life of these individuals. PBD are due to mutations in PEX genes, whose protein products are required to assemble peroxisomes- intracellular organelles vital for complex fat metabolism. Most persons with PBD have a common mutation in the PEX1 gene, that encodes a misfolded protein, PEX1-G843D, with significant residual function. These children and adults have a condition characterized by progressive tissue damage due to ongoing peroxisome dysfunction over time. Importantly, there is a window of opportunity to intervene and halt this progression. We have now identified two promising drugs (approved for other purposes) that recover peroxisome function in patient cell lines by acting as 'chaperones' to improve PEX1-G843D function. We also have a mouse model with the equivalent mutation that has a retinal degeneration similar to patients. A recent pilot study showed that our candidate drugs recovered retinal functions in the mice by electroretinogram studies. In this project, we will study the murine retinal disease to determine the best time points to intervene for therapy and accurate clinical endpoints to measure response. Expanding our patient cohort, we will also carefully study and compare the human retinal disease to ensure we can translate this therapy to patients. If successful, this will be the first targeted therapy for PBD and address a devastating feature, blindness. The information we gather on the course and pathophysiology of the disease, will also enable and accelerate all future, independent avenues for correction of the retinal disease in PBD. Finally, we expect that these chaperone drugs will also be able to treat other body systems involved in this disease.

column36: What is the cause of chromosome segregation error in the mammalian preimplantation embryo?
column37: The health of the newly fertilised embryo is an important determinant of fertility. One problem commonly experienced by women undergoing fertility treatments is that the early embryo has cells with the wrong number of chromosomes - termed 'aneuploid' cells. Embryos with aneuploid cells are considered unlikely to give rise to a healthy baby. Indeed, many clinics use the presence of aneuploid cells to discard bad-quality embryos rather than transfer them back to the patient. The presence of aneuploid cells in the early embryo indicates that errors have taken place during chromosome segregation - the process of sharing the chromosomes between the daughter cells at the time of cell division. However, despite the clear importance in human fertility, the cause of these chromosome segregation errors in early embryos is unknown. Our laboratory specialises in the use of state-of-the-art imaging approaches to observe and investigate the process of chromosome segregation, and we have developed an assortment of techniques for observing these processes in embryos. Here we will perform some of the first examinations of how chromosome segregation works in the early mammalian embryo, and try to understand why this process goes wrong so often. Most of our experiments will use mouse embryos, with some experiments using human embryos that can no longer be used for treatments. This work will shed light upon the causes of chromosome mis-segregation in the embryo, helping to explain the problems experienced by many fertility patients, and we hope that our experiments will directly lead to improved methods for selecting embryos for transfer to patients in the clinic.

column37: Febrile seizures are the most common seizure disorder to affect children who are at a high risk of developing intractable epilepsy. The mechanisms of febrile seizures are unknown which has limited the development of prophylactic treatments. There is strong evidence supporting that febrile seizures occur when children have fever-induced increases in breathing associated with an infection that leads to respiratory alkalosis and subsequent decreased seizure thresholds. Indeed, shifts in acid-base balance are well recognized to alter brain function such that alkalosis leads to hyperexcitability and decreased seizure thresholds, and acidosis producing the opposite effect. Transient receptor potential vanilloid type 1 receptors (TRPV1) are heat sensitive receptors that play an important role in thermoregulation and responses to inflammation. Importantly, TRPV1 has been localized in the vagus nerve which is a key driver of the fever-induced increases in breathing linked to respiratory alkalosis. The overall goal of this proposal is to test, in an inflammation-based model of febrile seizures established in my laboratory, the link between TRPV1, inflammation and fever-induced increases in breathing accounting for respiratory alkalosis and consequent increased risk of febrile seizures. The results of this study will provide a molecular target upon which, currently unavailable, prophylactic treatments for febrile seizures can be developed and made available for use in clinical practice.

column36: De-Adopting Low-Value Practices in Critical Care Medicine
column37: Frequent failure to implement best evidence into patient care practices is arguably the largest deficiency in modern healthcare, resulting in suboptimal patient care, preventable medical errors, and increased morbidity and mortality. There is a growing body of literature which suggests that the removal of ineffective (i.e. low-value) or harmful clinical practices (i.e. de-adoption) is integral to both the delivery of high quality care and the sustainability of our healthcare system. To improve our understanding of the process of de-adoption, members of our team have reviewed the literature, resulting in a conceptual framework for de-adoption. Results from this background work revealed that few studies have actually examined how to successfully de-adopt an intervention that is already integrated into clinical practice. column36: Molecular Rules in Brain Cell Microcircuits in Health and Disease
column37: Maintaining the balance between excitation and inhibition is a fundamental attribute of brain function that is necessary for information processing and higher functions, such as affect and cognition. The maintenance of this balance occurs through the constant fine-tuning of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission on multiple time scales, from milliseconds to weeks and months. Much has been learned about short-term functional adaptations (seconds to hours) at the cell contact level; however how the different cell types of brain microcircuits synchronize their functions on longer time-scales (weeks to months) to maintain optimal function, while allowing plasticity, is less well-known. Our data suggest a predominant role for inhibitory cells in mediating adaptive changes during brain aging. We and others show similar inhibitory changes, albeit out of synchrony or exaggerated, in the context of depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Hence we predict that (1) changes in gene function, specifically in inhibitory neurons, maintain long-term adaptations during life-long brain aging, and that (2) changes in the same cell-dependent gene programs occur in several brain disorders. Using molecular biology and computational methods, we will test this hypothesis directly in the human post-mortem brain, using samples from midlife and older subjects. Similar approaches will be used in rodent models to investigate mechanisms and conservation of processes across species. We will then determine the extent of changes in the same cells and pathways in the context of diseases, using human samples from bipolar depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's patients. This novel dimensional approach across species, lifespan and brain disorders has the potential to reveal the molecular mechanisms and rules that govern long-term homeostatic processes across the main cell types of brain cell microcircuits in health and brain diseases.

column36: Disclosing a psychiatric condition in the workplace: Evaluation of stigma and work outcomes
column37: Job tenure is a significant issue for individuals with a severe mental disorder, as successful employment and the economic self-sufficiency it provides are important to recovery. Supported employment (SE) programs help people with severe mental disorders obtain employment. However, job tenure for people with a severe mental disorder is often brief. One of the best predictors of job tenure is the implementation of work accommodations. However, accessing accommodations in the workplace requires disclosure of the mental disorder, and fear of stigma may lead employees to choose not to disclose. Decision-making about disclosure at work is thus a complex process, as disclosing can have both positive (e.g., work accommodation) and negative (e.g., stigma) outcomes. We will specifically be exploring disclosure to the immediate supervisor, as the supervisor plays a significant role in the implementation of work accommodations and relevant employment outcomes (job satisfaction, job tenure). Participants (n=300) will be recruited from SE programs in Ontario and Quebec. We will collect both quantitative and qualitative data, over multiple time points. Participants will be enrolled in the study at the time of gaining competitive employment. We will follow up with participants 6 months after study enrollment to collect data on disclosure and outcomes, including work accommodations, job satisfaction, stigma, work productivity, and job tenure. A subsample of participants (n=45) will be invited for an in-depth interview in which they will be asked about disclosure decision-making and the experience of disclosing, if applicable. Our study will provide a deeper understanding of the impact of disclosure on stigma and work outcomes (e.g., implementation of work accommodations), allowing organizations to enhance inclusivity, leading to increased job tenure, enhanced recovery and well-being for individuals, and increased productivity and reduced disability claims costs for organizations.

column37: The bone marrow (BM) makes millions of blood cells every day via a complex multistep process. White blood cells fight infections, platelets prevent bleeding and red cells deliver oxygen; all are crucial to sustain life. Reduced blood formation is a common problem caused by infections, toxins, cancer treatment or genetic conditions. Current treatments include blood transfusions, BM stimulants or BM transplants. Unfortunately, these treatments frequently cause serious side effects or are ineffective. Developing better treatments requires deep understanding of how the BM forms blood cells. Our understanding of blood cell formation has been advanced. Yet, most studies used animals such as mice that have significant limitations due to major differences between mouse and human BM cells. Inherited BM failure syndromes (IBMFSs) are rare genetic diseases in which one or more types of BM blood-producing cells are impaired, leading to infections, bleeding and heart failure. The study of IBMFSs can not only help develop cures for these patients, but also help understand how the human BM normally works and overcome the critical limitations of animal research. The goal of our study is to advance our understanding of how the human BM functions, while deciphering why blood cell formation is disrupted in IBMFS patients. We will analyze patients' BM and identify cells that are reduced in number. To determine why the affected BM cells are reduced, we will determine the type of genes that are activated or inactivated in these cells, the cells' growth properties and ability to survive various stresses. Last, we will use specially-prepared cells from IBMFS patients called pluripotent stem cells as a model to correct the blood defects. Our study will close critical gaps in our understanding of how human blood cells are formed. This information is crucial for developing effective and safe ways to improve blood formation in various conditions including IBMFSs, infections and cancers.

column36: The Role of Kidney Injury Molecule-1 in Renal Transplantation
column37: Kidney transplantation is the ideal treatment for patients with end-stage kidney disease. Despite better drugs to suppress the immune system, however, the long-term survival of the transplants remains suboptimal. Damage of the kidney due to the lack of blood flow during organ procurement and cold storage before transplantation (ischemia-reperfusion injury, or IRI) is believed to be a major contributor to the limited lifespan of transplants. The tissue injury is further compounded by rejection episodes in the transplanted kidney. There is also growing evidence to suggest that IRI may interact with immune factors worsening graft injury. Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) is a protein produced by native and donor kidneys following injury. Using mice genetically engineered to be deficient in KIM-1, we previously showed that KIM-1 protects the native kidneys of mice from tissue damage and kidney dysfunction following IRI. Paradoxically, however, KIM-1 can also promote chronic kidney disease and scarring. Whether KIM-1 protects or is harmful in transplanted kidneys is unknown. In this project, we will use a mouse model of transplantation to help determine if KIM-1 in the transplanted kidney can protect it from tissue damage from IRI as well as from acute rejection, or whether KIM-1 leads to long-term scarring and premature graft loss. We will also test the therapeutic potential of a new molecule called AIM, which we have shown can protect native kidneys from the damaging effects of IRI via a KIM-1 dependent pathway, in improving the lifespan of transplanted organs. The findings from our proposed studies will advance our understanding of why transplanted kidneys fail prematurely, and help us to develop new potential treatments to prolong their lifespan.

column37: The leading cause of irreversible vision loss in developed countries is Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD). column36: Cocaine Addiction: Epigenetic Studies in Living and Postmortem Brain
column37: The overarching goal of this research is to understand how interactions between inherited genes and early drug use can affect vulnerability to addictions. We are starting with the study of addictions because understanding better the causes of addiction could help us develop effective treatment and prevention strategies. And the need for new treatments is urgent. Substance use is associated with economic costs greater than all other psychiatric disorders combined, and the present research is expected to identify critical genes, enzymes, and brain pathways that could serve as important therapeutic targets. column36: Role and therapeutic potential of ERK3/ERK4 MAP kinases in acute kidney injury
column37: MAP kinases are a family of enzymes that play important roles in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation, migration and adaptation. column37: Microtubules (MTs) are protein polymers that form a cable-like network of transport super-highway to move important cargoes around inside a cell. One of these cargoes is our chromosomes, the genetic material that makes us what we are. It turns out that these cables need to grow and shrink all the time to perform their functions such as capturing and transporting chromosomes, especially when cells are dividing. A clinically proven strategy to stop cancer cell proliferation is to perturb the growing and shrinking dynamics of MT polymers. In fact, MT-targeting drugs are among the most successful chemotherapeutic agents currently used in the clinics. However, their success is hindered by adverse side effects and the development of drug resistance in cancer patients. To address these shortcomings, we propose to further exploit this proven approach through an alternative route - by targeting the protein enzymes that control the MT polymers. Using a high-throughput screening approach, our lab has already identified chemical agents that modulate these MT modifying enzymes. Importantly, these agents exert a potent growth suppressive effect on cancer cells, but seem to spare non-cancer cells. However, the precise molecular mechanism how these molecules work is still not known. In the proposed project, we aim to use modern cutting-edge technologies to understand the following: 1) How these chemical agents affect the MT-regulating enzymes at the molecular level; 2) how this in turn affects cancer cell proliferation; and 3) how to improve the specificity and efficacy of this new class of potential chemotherapeutics. Our ultimate goal is to validate this new strategy in order to develop the next generation anti-cancer drugs.

column36: Defining the molecular basis of chemoradiation sensitivity in HPV+ head and neck cancers.
column37: Human papillomaviruses (HPV) infect undifferentiated stem cells of our skin. Furthermore, our unbiased approach to identify genes that promote resistance to treatment is likely to provide therapeutic targets that can be exploited to treat HPV+ OPC patients that resist current therapies. Finally, our project has the potential to reveal new biomarkers to measure the responsiveness of HPV+ OPCs to treatments.

column36: On the road to promoting mobility and health after driving cessation among older adults
column37: Mobility is a broad concept that can be understood as the ability to move oneself within environments that include one's residence and neighbourhood. This study will identify factors that promote health among older adults after driving cessation and will be used to develop interventions and policies to facilitate a healthy transition to non-driving.

column37: In Thailand, as in Canada and globally, young men who have sex with men (YMSM) and young transgender women (YTGW) are at high risk for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Despite this, YMSM and YTGW are largely excluded from existing Thai HIV outreach efforts: these primarily target older MSM and TGW at gay bars and clubs, with a minimum age of entry of 20-years-old. Additionally, many YMSM and YTGW do not publicly identify as gay or TGW, and do not feel comfortable using HIV services delivered by gay or TGW community-based organizations (CBOs). This convergence of high HIV risk, lack of access to HIV prevention programs, and lack of evidence to support interventions tailored for these populations, is a public health emergency. The goal of this innovative project is to culturally adapt and evaluate an evidence-based HIV prevention program with YMSM and YTGW in Thailand. We will work with YMSM, YTGW, a Community Advisory Committee, local CBOs and service providers to build on a peer outreach model with demonstrated effectiveness in reducing HIV risk among YMSM in North America, by culturally adapting (such as matching slightly older with younger YMSM and YTGW, more appropriate in Thai culture than same-age peers) and testing the model in Thailand. In addition to evaluating program outcomes, we will use participatory methods, training YMSM and YTGW in digital storytelling to represent their experiences, and share findings with other YMSM, YTGW, CBOs, policymakers and the public in Thailand and internationally. Results from this culturally adapted HIV prevention program will advance health knowledge and health outcomes for sexual minority youth, and support a replicable model for use with other youth in the Global South who are highly impacted by HIV.

column37: Radiotherapy plus hormonal treatment is the recommended form of treatment for men with high risk prostate cancer. column37: Receptors located at the surface of the cell integrate the extracellular environment towards cellular functions such as cell survival, proliferation and migration. To efficiently control extracellular signals, cell surface receptor levels and turnover is tightly regulated. This process is orchestrated by the Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery, composed of several cellular proteins. Importantly, ESCRT components are essential for the attenuation of the cell surface signalling. Impairment in ESCRT function leads to receptor stabilization, persistent signalling, and cancer promotion. The identification and characterization of these tumor suppressors is essential to develop new cancer therapies. Our previous work identified HD-PTP, a new member of the ESCRT complex, as a novel tumor suppressor. Indeed, inactivation of HD-PTP in mice leads to development of lung cancer and lymphoma. Interestingly, we have shown that UBAP1 and Endofin, two novel ESCRT components and HD-PTP binding partners, share HD-PTP functions. Therefore, we hypothesize that HD-PTP and its binding partners (UBAP1 and Endofin) exert tumor suppressor functions. This research project aims to characterize the physiological function of HD-PTP/UBAP1/Endofin-containing novel ESCRT complex and to determine their role in tumor development. Moreover, since ESCRTs play a central role in a wide range of signaling pathways activated downstream of numerous cell surface receptors this project might have significant implications in the development of new therapeutic strategies that would be applicable to a wide range of cancers.

column36: Targeting novel acid stress resistance mechanisms in cancer cell metabolism
column37: In all cancer cells, a series of fundamental metabolic changes occur that enable growth and spread of tumours throughout the body. Hence, these metabolic changes are important potential therapeutic targets in the treatment of cancer. An important metabolic change that occurs, called the Warburg effect, is related to how cancer cells generate cellular energy to feed their growth and survival. A consequence of the Warburg effect is accumulation of damaging intracellular acid, and cancer cells must have systems in place to counter acid accumulation. The only known system involves turning on acid pumps to pump the acid out of the cell into the surrounding tumour environment, and drugs are currently being developed against this limited set of targets. Using a discovery-based approach we have identified over thirty new potential targets of acid stress in cancer cells. The objective of this grant proposal is to validate roles for these targets in growth and survival of cancer cells and to test them as potential therapeutic targets using animal tumour models. Identifying additional systems that cancer cells use to survive acid stress will provide insight and facilitate novel approaches in the treatment of cancer, and will potentially lead to development of new classes of anti-cancer drugs.

column36: Making I-SPARX fly in Nunavut
column37: Inuit youth in Northern Canada face extreme adversities, leading to concerning mental health needs, and the highest adolescent suicide rates in the world. Despite their increased risk, remote Northern communities are often without resources for early prevention and intervention programs. A strong focus needs to be placed on creating intervention tools that will be accessible in Northern communities. Furthermore, little prevention or intervention research has been conducted with Inuit adolescents who are at risk for depression in Nunavut. The extent, severity and idiosyncrasies of Inuit adolescent depression need to be studied, and suitably tailored interventions evaluated. Cultural relevance, with regard to Inuit and adolescent culture, should be paramount in the selection of approaches. Making I-SPARX fly in Nunavut strives to enhance resiliency and increase mattering by empowering youth who are at risk for depression with skills to foster their own mental health and positively contributing to the collective welfare of their communities. This project evaluates a holistic, multi-generational intervention that brings together cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), emotion regulation support (ER), culture identity and community processes to foster resilience. Included in the intervention is the use of an award-winning computer program, SPARX which uses CBT and ER skills to teach the user how to cope with negative thoughts and feelings. The proposed intervention will be anchored in the youth-driven design of an Inuit version of SPARX (I-SPARX), supported by Elders. This design will aim to integrate the six integral principles of Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit. Additionally, youth will take on activities that engage their communities in the dissemination and practice of I-SPARX teachings. SPARX- once adapted to Inuit culture and with Nunavut youth making the program their own - may become a useful tool for both Nunavut youth at-risk for depression and for those working with them.

column36: Formulation of a vascular regenerative niche within implantable human decellularized adipose tissue bioscaffolds
column37: Stem cell transplantation to prevent amputation in patients with critical limb ischemia (CLI) is under intense investigation. However, new blood vessel formation requires contributions from at least 3 distinct cell lineages; endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) that represent the building blocks of vessels, hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPC) that stimulate vessel growth, and mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) that form vessel-wrapping cells called pericytes. Understanding how these cells can be used to form new blood vessels remains the key to translating the potential of stem cells into a curative cellular therapy for CLI. Using readily available human umbilical cord blood (UCB) samples, we have pioneered the selection and expansion of HPC, EPC and MSC lineages to generate the large cell numbers required for regenerative therapies in humans. Importantly, each subset retained complementary vessel building functions after expansion. HPC abundantly secreted protein signals that accelerated the recovery of blood flow after implantation into the ischemic limbs of mice. EPC spontaneously formed tube networks in lab cultures and integrated into vessels after transplantation. MSC demonstrated vessel-wrapping function and improved vessel stability. Despite these promising findings, donor cell survival was limited after direct injection into the ischemic limb and improved delivery methods are required to prolong benefit. By combining expertise in stem cell biology with advanced bioengineering, we aim to develop an effective treatment for CLI using UCB-derived progenitor cells delivered within implantable, 3-D bioscaffolds derived from human adipose (fat) tissue. We hypothesize that co-delivery of UCB-derived progenitor cell subsets within cell-supportive 3-D bioscaffolds will improve donor cell survival and function to permit stable human blood vessel formation. These studies will provide proof-of-concept for the development of novel cell therapies for the treatment of CLI.
