column36: Exploring structure-function relationships between dietary fibre and the gut microbiome: Towards predicting and personalizing nutritional strategies.
column37: Being overweight significantly increases risk for numerous diseases that have been linked to the microbial populations that inhabit our gastrointestinal tract. The exact role of the gut microbiota in human health appears to depend partially on diet. A diet high in fat can trigger inflammation when harmful molecules are produced by gut bacteria and taken up into the body. On the other hand, gut bacteria can ferment dietary fibre to produce short-chain fatty acids, molecules that have anti-inflammatory properties. However, we do not yet understand all the consequences of microbial fibre fermentation in the gut to healthy functioning of an individual. We also do not know how individual differences in types of bacteria that compose each person's gut microbial community influence how we can ferment different chemical types of dietary fibre. With such knowledge at hand, it would be possible to adjust an individual's diet based on the configuration of the microbes in our digestive tract. We propose to systematically investigate the interactions between fiber chemistry, the genetic make-up of the gut microbiota, and metabolic and immunological measures of health in overweight and mildly obese people. We will also look for links between different types of dietary fibre and the composition and function of each person's gut microbiota. This will allow us to test whether microbiome patterns in individuals predict the effects of the fibre. To achieve this, we will begin with an exploratory nutritional trial that compares the effects of three types of fermentable dietary fibre with the effects of non-fermentable cellulose. We will measure how fibre type and microbiota composition and function affect specific health outcomes such as reduced inflammation. This new knowledge can be used to improve dietary strategies for preventing obesity, develop strategies to modulate a person's gut microbiota for better health outcomes, and lay groundwork for personalized human nutrition.

column36: The population health and healthcare burden of poor dietary patterns and potential strategies for reducing mortality, morbidity and healthcare use in Canada
column37: Chronic diseases are major causes of reduced quality of life, increased hospitalization, and premature death. Poor diet is a common preventable risk factor and likely plays a significant role in morbidity and premature death in Canada. This project will describe dietary patterns of Canadians and how these patterns have changed over time. The study will also calculate the impact of unhealthy dietary patterns on chronic diseases (cardiovascular diseases), death and healthcare use. The health and healthcare benefits of strategies to improve dietary patterns will also be examined. Culturally-relevant dietary patterns will be "reverse engineered" to examine how to reduce health and healthcare burden and inequalities among Canadians. This study will use the nutrition focused Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) 2004, and the forthcoming 2015 cycle. The CCHS 2004 is unique worldwide; it is the largest population-based dietary survey linked to health and health care outcomes. These data allow very detailed assessment of health and social outcomes. Robust population health policy models will be created to support evidence-based nutrition policy for reducing the burden of poor dietary patterns. Policy actors will be involved in model development to ensure that models address questions of real-world policy relevance. Health calculators (risk-assessment tools) will be created from the policy models. These calculators can be used by individual Canadians and their clinicians to increase awareness of health risks from poor dietary patterns. This project will provide the first evidence on dietary patterns and health and healthcare outcomes at the national population level, an essential component for development of nutritional guidelines and policies. The models and supporting data linkages will create a lasting infrastructure and will position Canada as a world leader in population health assessment of nutrition policy.

column36: Ectopic calcification of spinal tissues: etiology and potential therapeutic targets
column37: Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH) is a disease characterized by aberrant mineralization of soft connective tissues in the spine. It is a relatively common condition, with prevalence around 25% in men and slightly less in women over the age of 50 in North America. Symptoms include pain and stiffness in the thoracic spine and, in severe cases, dysphagia and compression of the spinal cord and nerve roots leading to paralysis. Importantly, the cause of DISH is unknown and there are no specific treatments. This proposal uses a genetically modified mouse model which develops ectopic calcification of spinal tissues with remarkable resemblance to DISH in humans. We will use state-of-the-art imaging and molecular approaches to define the underlying mechanisms related to the development of DISH, and confirm candidate effectors in human DISH spine tissues. Our proposed studies promise to provide breakthrough insights into the etiology of DISH, and will permit the development and preclinical testing of novel therapeutics to prevent or delay the progression of this debilitating disorder. These studies may also generate important information on related disorders of spine calcification, such as ossification of the posterior spinal longitudinal ligament (OPLL).

column36: Hippocampal-neocortical interactions and the precision of human memory in aging
column37: Memory underlies virtually every aspect of human cognition, including the ability to perceive and interpret the world, to maintain a sense of identity and continuity with the past, and to adapt to an ever-changing environment through the acquisition of new knowledge. For more than 50 years we have known that the hippocampus is central to the human ability to encode and remember experiences; and when this brain structure decays from age or disease, memory falters. The hippocampus is the computational engine of human memory, it contains the codes and algorithms that make new learning and remembering the past possible. It is only through its interaction with the distributed fields in the neocortex that the hippocampal engram becomes fully realized as a conscious episodic memory. We still know very little about this fundamental interface between the hippocampus and the association cortices of the cerebral mantle and how it is affected by the aging process. We will use high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to investigate how information is represented and transformed as it moves from the neocortex to the hippocampus during tasks that require the kind of precise memory representations that decline with age. The proposed research will not only advance our fundamental neuroscience understanding of human memory, but also has clear translational potential in developing a more nuanced and precise probe of the human memory system that has implications for brain health in aging and in patients with neurodegenerative diseases. Indeed, the paradigms developed in this proposal can be used in trials of memory-enhancing therapeutics to assess their impact on hippocampal and neocortical signatures of precise memory storage and retrieval.

column37: Heart attacks resulting in dead and damaged tissue within the heart are the most common cause of premature death in the developed world. Major advances in medicine have reduced the number of people that die immediately after a heart attack; however, the death rate due to heart failure - a gradual disease in which a person's heart eventually cannot pump enough blood to sustain the body - in the years following a heart attack or other heart injury remains high. In fact, of people who are diagnosed with heart failure, 30-40% will die within one year. New methods to understand why the heart fails, and to improve diagnosis and treatment of the disease, are urgently needed to improve this situation. Recently, evidence has suggested that metabolic changes (i.e. changes in the way the heart produces chemical energy from the fuel sources from our diet) contribute to tissue damage and the progression towards heart failure. There is some evidence that drugs that make metabolism more efficient can improve the heart failure patient's chances of survival and quality of life.

column36: REVISE: Re-Evaluating the Inhibition of Stress Erosions in the ICU
column37: Patients who are critically ill in the Intensive Care Unit, especially those who need breathing machines, can develop ulcerations in the stomach that bleed. To prevent bleeding, most critically ill patients around the world receive a daily drug called pantoprazole that suppresses acid production. However, today, compared to decades ago, patients appear less likely to develop gastrointestinal bleeding, perhaps due to earlier feeding, modern medicine and better resuscitation. Studies of acid suppression are old and of poor quality such that their results are being questioned. There are also harms associated with acid suppressing drugs, including lung infections (pneumonia) and bowel infections (Clostridium difficile). Therefore, it is difficult to know whether pantoprazole does decrease stomach bleeding these days, or whether the dangers of lung and bowel infections are actually more common and serious. The goal of this international study is to determine if, in critically ill patients needing breathing machines, pantoprazole is effective in preventing bleeding from stomach ulcers, or whether it increases the risk of pneumonia and Clostridium difficile, or whether pantoprazole has no effect at all. Whether the harms are worth the benefits, and whether the benefits are worth the costs, will be determined by an economic analysis to inform patients, families, clinicians, and healthcare systems globally.

column36: Investigating the Role of RECQL in Breast Cancer Susceptibility
column37: Our team recently discovered that a gene named RECQL is a breast cancer susceptibility gene. We found that mutations in this gene, although rare, are strongly linked to the onset of breast cancer in two populations of women from Poland and Quebec, Canada. This proposal outlines the research we plan to conduct to expand our understanding of the role that the RECQL gene plays in breast cancer etiology. First, we will determine the RECQL pathogenic mutation frequency among women in Ontario (including breast cancer patients and healthy women), as well as the risk of breast cancer diagnosis and survival among women with RECQL mutations compared to women without these mutations. Then, we will look at how RECQL and other genes are expressed at the tumor level in breast cancer patients with RECQL mutations, in order to better understand how tumor cells thrive in these patients. Finally, we will use animal models for establishing the susceptibility to breast cancer in presence of defective RECQL gene. By doing this study, we will determine the mutation frequency of RECQL and the associated risk of breast cancer in women in Ontario, all of which will inform genetic testing policies for breast cancer in the province. We will also get a better understanding about how carrying RECQL mutations biologically predisposes women to breast cancer. This knowledge will be critical for both preventing and treating breast cancer among mutation carriers.

column36: A functional surfaceome map of human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) ensure the lifelong production of all essential blood cells in the organism, and transplantation of these cells is used for the treatment of certain types of cancer of the blood system. HSC transplantation (HSCT) requires a stem cell source, typically peripheral blood or bone marrow from a compatible donor, however, such a donor is not available for 40% of patients in need of a graft. HSCs present in cord blood (CB) represent an interesting alternative for these patients since donor compatibility requirements are not as stringent as for other types of grafts, however, the low numbers of HSCs present in CB units prevent their widespread use for HSCT. In an attempt to improve the situation, our group has discovered a novel molecule, UM171, which expands CB HSCs in culture. The benefits of expanding CB HSCs with this molecule for HSCT are currently being studied in a clinical trial. The study of HSCs and the development of additional HSC agonists to further improve their expansion and reduce time to engraftment, the major challenge associated with HSCT, is limited by our inability to isolate pure HSC populations from CB, which would be greatly improved by the identification of novel stem cell markers. Our group has recently optimized a proteomics approach that allows the identification of markers at the surface of cells. This method will be used to identify specific HSC markers, with the goal of improving HSC purification from heterogeneous CB samples and develop novel strategies for their expansion. Ultimately, our findings should help optimise HSCT and provide a better prognosis to patients affected by acute myeloid leukemia and other blood diseases.

column36: Symptom screening and early palliative care in patients with advanced cancer: a randomized trial
column37: Palliative care is defined as care by a team of specialists that increases quality of life (QOL) for patients with a life-threatening illness. Four large randomized controlled trials showed that when patients with advanced cancer were referred early to specialized palliative care teams, they had improved QOL and greater satisfaction with their cancer care. Although it is known that patients with the most severe physical and psychological symptoms have the greatest need for palliative care, these patients are often not referred to palliative care teams. Therefore, it has been suggested that there should be a triage system to identify patients who have the greatest need. Our research team has developed a system that identifies patients with high symptom burden in order to offer them access to the palliative care team. This system, which uses information patients already report about their symptoms at each oncology clinic appointment, is called STEP (Symptom screening with Targeted Early Palliative care). We propose to run a trial at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre and Kingston General Hospital comparing STEP with regular symptom screening in oncology clinics. Patients are eligible to participate if they have advanced cancer and a life expectancy of at least 6 months. Consenting patients will be assigned randomly (by chance) either to receive STEP or to follow routine symptom screening. Patients in both groups complete symptom screening on computers in the waiting room of oncology clinics. For patients in the STEP group, if one or more of their symptom ratings are higher than the defined cut-off, a nurse will be alerted to call them to offer an appointment in the palliative care clinic for assessment and follow-up. All patients will complete questionnaires measuring outcomes of QOL, depression, symptom control and satisfaction with care at recruitment, 2, 4 and 6 months. We will measure the impact of STEP on these outcomes, compared to screening alone.

column37: Stimulant use is a key driver of morbidity and mortality, including mental health challenges (e.g. psychosis, suicide), infectious diseases (e.g., HIV, hepatitis C), and other health harms. Despite the significant health burden associated with stimulant use, there are currently few evidence-based treatments for stimulant use disorders (SUD) and little attention has been paid to the integration of these interventions across healthcare and recovery systems. Recent advancements in psycho-social interventions (e.g., contingency management) have shown promise in the treatment of SUD, and several pharmacotherapies (e.g., dexamphetamine, cannabinoids) are being explored. However, there has been a lack of research into the acceptability and feasibility of prospective treatment interventions among stimulant-using populations, and the preparedness of healthcare and recovery systems to implement these interventions. Building upon our extensive experience in examining contextual influences on the health of adult persons who use drugs (PWUD) and drug-using street-involved youth (SY), this project aims to: (1) examine social, structural, and environmental influences on the implementation and effectiveness of current strategies for the management of SUD among PWUD and SY; (2) examine the acceptability and feasibility of prospective pharmacotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of SUD among PWUD and SY; and, (3) explore individual and contextual influences on readiness to adopt prospective pharmacotherapeutic interventions and evidence-based practices for the management of SUD across the health system. This study will be nested within the research and training infrastructure of the BC Centre for Substance Use, and will leverage the relationships of this centre to translate findings into improvements in health planning and systems in relation to stimulant use.

column36: An "Inducible" Gene Therapy for Glaucoma: A Novel Approach to Prevent Loss of Vision
column37: Glaucoma is considered the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. The increased intraocular pressure (IOP) has been established as the main risk factor for the development of glaucoma. Unfortunately, currently approved therapies for glaucoma that target IOP are unable to prevent the detrimental course of the disease, raising the need for novel treatments that can prevent or stop the progression in glaucoma. A family of enzymes that degrade proteins, called proteases, are activated in glaucoma. Abnormal activation of these proteases in glaucoma can cause inflammation by releasing harmful molecules in the eye. Recently, we have developed a special protein that replaces those in the cell so that instead of harmful factors, special therapeutic factors are released. The long term goal of this novel and first-in-class strategy is to have the retinal cells release the special, therapeutic proteins during the first signs of glaucomatous damage in the eye. Our proposed "inducible" therapeutics will be positioned in retinal cells in advance of disease, and will work as needed to reduce the negative systemic and off-target effects frequently associated with current therapies for eye diseases. The know-how gained from these studies can lead to development of novel gene therapies for treatment of other brain diseases such traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

column36: Improving Healthcare Utilization by Frequent 911 Callers: The Community Paramedicine at Home (CP@home) Trial
column37: Frequent calls to emergency services (911) for preventable reasons are a burden on the healthcare system and its limited resources. These calls are often for "Lift Assist" (older adults who fall and cannot pick themselves up) or for health issues that have not been properly managed by the family physician. In these cases, simple interventions that reduce the risk of falls and avoid complications due to chronic disease (e.g. diabetes) and poor mental health may have a significant impact on how these individuals use healthcare resources. Community paramedicine (CP) is a new role for paramedics in Canada. CP@home is a CP intervention where community paramedics visit the homes of frequent 911 callers to conduct assessments for mobility, pain, chronic disease, and mental health. Based on their findings, they provide health education and refer the individual to available community services (e.g. fall prevention programs). A report is also sent to their family doctor to keep them informed. The paramedics follow-up with the individual on two more occasions to make sure the intervention is working and to make adjustments if needed. The proposed research study aims to evaluate the CP@home intervention and determine if it is effective in reducing the number of 911 calls from these frequent users, as well as improving their health and quality of life.

column36: Augmented Renal Denervation for the Prevention of Cardiac Arrhythmias.
column37: Heart rhythm disorders (HRD) are the most common cause of sudden death following a heart attack. High sympathetic nerve activity (SNA) is known to cause HRDs. Inhibition of SNA may be an effective preventive treatment for HRDs. Renal denervation (RDN) is a relatively new medical procedure performed to de-activate nerves along large blood vessels at the kidneys. Originally developed to treat high blood pressure, RDN was found in recent studies to also reduce irregular heartbeats. Our preliminary study demonstrated that RDN reduced spontaneous HRDs following a heart attack. However, the clinical use of RDN was halted on the basis of inconclusive results regarding the true benefits of this treatment, with its failure in clinical trials attributed to methodological concerns and the regeneration of renal nerves, as well as the inadequacies of the currently available technology for the RDN procedure. The lack of tools to monitor nerve activity during the nerve de-activating procedure is particularly glaring. New accessories are needed to improve the technology before RDN can be defined for therapeutic use. RDN has thus far been delivered blindly, without the means to verify if therapy has truly been delivered at the nerves and if SNA has been impacted. It is important to understand how adequate deactivation of nerves can be assessed and the mechanisms by which RDN may reduce HRDs following a heart attack. Recently, we have developed a specialized catheter to measure renal nerve activity during the RDN procedure. In this proposal, in an in-vivo pig model of heart attack, we aim to explore the effects of heart attack on renal SNA and the long-term effects of repeated RDN on cardiac arrhythmias. We will also demonstrate how our novel catheter can be deployed to address the glaring need for nerve monitoring and improve the RDN procedure for future clinical use.

column36: Genetic Insights to the Causes of Cerebral Palsy
column37: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common cause of physical handicap in children. CP describes a group of diseases that affect the brain in early life. We are now starting to understand that our genetic code plays an important role in causing CP. Genetic testing is not done routinely for all children with CP. To change practice, we need more proof that genetic testing brings important information to a lot of families with CP, and how this information affects families. We will invite 200 children and their parents participating in the Canadian CP Registry (CCPR), living in the Greater Montreal and Toronto areas, Calgary and Edmonton, to give a blood sample. From their blood, we will read all of their genetic information, using a method that has been used in many other genetic disorders but has never been used before in CP research. We will look for genetic mutations that are present in the child but not seen in their parents. We will also ask families to complete two questionnaires to see how they feel about this testing, and if it makes a difference to their lives. We will see if the effect of genetic testing on families is different by type of CP and also by parent characteristics. With a more complete understanding of the genetic causes of CP, doctors will be able to identify CP earlier, have better ways of preventing CP, develop new therapies and better understand the causes of CP. Also, with more information on the impact of genetic testing on the family, doctors will be better able to support families after they get their test results, decrease the family's level of stress and have a patient-centered approach to care.

column36: Brain oxidative stress and disability progression in multiple sclerosis
column37: The cause of chronic progression in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains a mystery. One cause, which is suspected by many experts, is so-called oxidative stress. This refers to the generation of abnormally increased amounts of highly reactive molecules that oxidize many other molecules and damage cells, particularly nerve cells, leading to their premature death. Cells have intrinsic mechanisms in place to deactivate/detoxify these highly reactive molecules. One of these, and perhaps the most important, is to produce the anti-oxidant molecule, glutathione (GSH). It is now possible to measure the amount of GSH in the brain of living subjects by implementing special sequences on MRI scanners to perform magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) that is specifically designed to measure GSH. For this project, we propose to use one such special sequence to measure GSH in the brain of patients with MS. This will allow us to answer a number of important questions related to the role of oxidative stress in driving disease progression in MS, and also allow us to calculate the number of patients that would be required to use this technique to assess the ability of drugs to treat oxidative stress.

column36: The great escape: Improving the activity of chemotherapeutics delivered by antibody-drug conjugates with integrated endosome escape and nuclear-directional trafficking control capabilies
column37: The image of the 'therapeutic missile' commonly used to present targeted drug delivery agents emphasizes precision, control, and efficiency. For the next evolution of cancer treatment, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a great representative of this concept. ADCs home to tumor cells with exquisite precision and control. However, upon landing on tumor cells, ADCs lose their precision, control, and efficiency for effectively delivering and accumulating the drugs inside the cell. ADCs travel in an intracellular route that is controlled by the cancer cell that transports ADC back outside the cell or respond in ways that kick the delivered drugs out. Without the drugs reaching effective cellular concentrations, cancer cells are able to resist and survive and patients soon relapse and die. We will develop ADCs that take control of their intracellular travel by incorporating our new Canadian technology (ACCUM) that mimics how viruses travel inside the cell. ACCUM attaches easily to ADCs enabling them to take control of their travel, which consists of a more efficient route to deliver their drugs. The result is that ACCUM-empowered ADCs are able to deliver their drugs with better efficiency inside target cancer cells than current ADCs. The increased accumulation has resulted in more effective cancer cell killing. The goal of this project is to further mature this technology for use in patients with invasive bladder cancer (IBC) - a worldwide problem without any life saving medications. We performed a clinical study and discovered a target (IL-5Ra) for IBC and developed rodent models that mimics the growth of human IL-5Ra-IBC. The research experiments designed in this proposal are to optimize conditions for clinical translation by optimizing ACCUM-ADC formulation and IBC cell killing. We will then determine the tumor killing effectiveness in our rodent models. This research will place Canada in an ADC leadership role and provide effective treatment for IBC.

column36: Atrial Fibrillation in the Emergency Room (The AFTER Study): Prospective validation of the clinical decision instruments
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an abnormal heart rhythm that, untreated, can lead to a stroke and/or heart failure. With the aging of the population, the number of people with AF is expected to increase dramatically: 250% by the year 2050. ER visits for AF already increased by 88% between 1996 and 2004. In Ontario we admit 40% of these ER patients to hospital. However if the number of ER AF patients increases by 250%, the healthcare system is likely to begin to fail if we continue to admit the same percentage of this much larger pool of patients to hospital. Most patients can receive the care they need at office visits; most tests and therapies don't require a hospital stay. They have very few bad outcomes (e.g. stroke, death) after their ER visit: in context with the high (40%) admission rate, there appears to be an opportunity to safely send more of these patients home from the ER, IF the high-risk patients can be reliably identified in the ER (so that they receive the in-hospital care they need to avoid bad outcomes). We have created tools to help ER physicians to identify these patients. The tools perform well so far, but this needs to be confirmed in another group of patients, in order to be scientifically rigorous and safe. Our project objective is to perform the final test of the tools. We will enroll AF patients from 11 ERs, where ER physicians will enter the components of the tools (e.g. patient age, lab results, etc.) into a password-protected website. The data will be sent securely to our research institute for analysis, where we have records of all deaths, hospitalizations, and ER visits in Ontario. If the tools prove successful they will safely allow more people with AF to go home, will reduce subsequent deaths, and will identify predictors of return ER visits. These tools could safely reduce the number of patients who are being hospitalized by up to half, which would in turn preserve the safety of the hospital system for patients who need it most.

column36: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease categorization using cardiovascular risk and levels of inflammatory mediators: a way toward more personalized care
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a condition in which cough, constant secretions and shortness of breath steadily decrease patients' quality of life. But the lung is not the only organ affected. In fact, in COPD patients, heart disease is often the cause of hospitalization and of death. COPD and heart disease are strongly related. Studies suggest that the risk for suffering from a heart problem is greatly increased when COPD patients experience a worsening of their respiratory symptoms (known as acute exacerbation). Unfortunately, the risk for future heart disease is not routinely assessed in COPD patients and we do not have the tools to detect COPD individuals at high risk. Sustained inflammation has been identified as a big culprit linking heart disease and acute exacerbations in COPD patients. A family of mediators of inflammation, the alarmins, is currently being studied for its roles in both, COPD and heart disease. The particular feature of these mediators is that they act only after being released from damaged tissue. This unique research project will assess cardiovascular risk and measure the levels of several inflammatory mediators (including the alarmins) in a large population of COPD and non-COPD individuals. These mediators could represent signs of "alarm" that, if detected at early stages, it is believed that they may be used to predict future risks in COPD patients. We will then study the specific mechanisms that lead to the production of these molecules in the lung. Our results will reveal new tools to identify COPD subjects at risk for future adverse events, namely heart disease and exacerbations. Furthermore, these tools will help us to implement strategies to prevent these events in COPD patients. Finally, our results will lead to the identification of potential targets to decrease inflammation in COPD.

column36: Role of Gene Expression Changes in the Mechanism of Action of Long-acting Beta2-adrenoceptor Agonists in COPD
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) - commonly referred to as chronic bronchitis or emphysema - is a progressive and debilitating disorder of the lungs. In most cases, it is caused by long-term exposure of susceptible individuals to tobacco smoke. Typically, COPD is characterised by persistent inflammation of the lungs leading to difficulty in breathing and, ultimately, premature death. An acute attack of COPD, known as an exacerbation, describes a rapid worsening of a patient's disease above normal day-to-day variability. Such attacks can be life threatening, are one of the leading cause of hospitalizations in North America and have a detrimental impact on ease of breathing and quality of life. Treatment of COPD is limited and mortality remains high. However, it is known that patients with COPD who experience exacerbations derive benefit from a class of drugs collectively known as LABAs. It is believed by many investigators that LABAs protect against exacerbations by opening the airway passages. However, recent research from our laboratory suggests that the beneficial effects of LABAs may also be due to their ability to switch-on a variety of genes in the lungs that, together, suppress inflammation, improve breathing and reduce the severity of attacks. To test this idea, we will explore the biology of candidate genes switched-on by LABAs using lung cells from normal healthy subjects and smoking individuals with COPD. We will also conduct a clinical study to measure the effect of a LABA on gene expression changes in the lungs of patients with COPD to confirm results obtained with isolated cells. We believe this research is important because acute attacks of COPD are associated with a considerable risk of death. The work proposed here should improve our understanding of how LABAs benefit patients with COPD and identify novel genes that could be exploited therapeutically.

column36: The IMPACT of food environment policies on the Canadian food supply, dietary intakes and health: evidence to inform policy action
column37: More than two-thirds of the Canadian diet comes from packaged, processed food items and food consumed away from home in restaurants and fast-food settings, which are typically of little nutritional value, and can lead to weight gain and chronic disease. Poor diet and obesity increase a person's risk of developing many health conditions such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer, and also reduce the overall quality of life and number of years a person will live. There are a number of proposed food environment policies that will impact the nutritional quality of the Canadian food supply, including guidelines for the food industry to reduce sodium in processed foods, and the addition of calorie information to restaurant menus. Our findings will inform policies to improve food environments, helping consumers make healthier food choices. In this research, we will look at changes in the nutritional quality of the food supply before and after these two policies have been put into place. For example, we will look changes to the amount of sodium and calories in packaged and restaurant foods. We will also look at what Canadians are eating and how their diets might change, as a result of the changes to the food supply. Finally, we will also try to understand whether these changes to the food supply and dietary intakes could result in fewer diseases and deaths in the Canadian population. We have created a group of leading Canadian scientists and policy collaborators from government and professional organizations who will use our research to help develop policies, programs and educational tools to improve the health of Canadians.

column36: Immigration and work disability in the Canadian context
column37: Immigration defines our nation and, for the majority of immigrants and their families, work is a cornerstone to successful integration into Canadian life. Within the Canadian context, we know much about the health outcomes and the employment patterns of immigrants, but less about the impact of work on health, in particular on work disability experiences and the longer term health consequences of work disability. Emerging evidence suggests that immigrants to Canada have different experiences to Canadian-born workers. Longer disability durations for immigrant workers may be attributed to more severe work injuries in higher risk jobs; and to barriers navigating health care, employer and insurance benefits systems for optimal return to work outcomes. Evidence also suggests important differences in work disability experiences for women and young workers immigrating to Canada. Using a unique research opportunity that will merge immigration data with workers' compensation and medical services data for the working population of British Columbia, the purpose of this study is to describe differences in work disability experiences, along the continuum from injury to rehabilitation to return-to-work and to longer term health outcomes, among immigrant workers compared to Canadian-born workers. Evidence of different experiences and of determinants of these differences, are necessary inputs for discussions and ultimately decisions by policy makers, employers and regulators/insurers to reduce barriers and health inequities, and improve return-to-work outcomes for all workers, including immigrants.

column36: Peripheral regulation of PPAR Nuclear Receptors in energy metabolism
column37: Vascular diseases impose the greatest burden upon our national health care system and are predicted to remain the leading cause of death and disability in Canada. column36: Protein and Exercise to Reverse Frailty in OldeR Men and women undergoing TAVR: The PERFORM-TAVR Trial
column37: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has emerged as a less invasive option for relieving symptoms and prolonging life in high-risk older adults with severe aortic stenosis. The number of TAVRs performed is rising steeply, estimated to grow worldwide from 71,000 in 2015 to 289,000 in 2025. While technical advances have enabled remarkably high rates of 97% implantation success and 96% in-hospital survival, 2 out of 5 patients still suffer non-favourable outcomes at 1 year; defined as death, poor quality of life, progressive disability or persistent limiting symptoms. I recently led the CIHR-funded Frailty-AVR study that prospectively enrolled 1,010 patients and found frailty to be among the most powerful predictors of suffering a non-favourable outcome after TAVR. Frailty is a geriatric syndrome characterized by low muscle mass and strength that affects a staggering 50-75% of TAVR patients. I will now transition from measuring frailty to treating frailty in order to improve outcomes. Based on my systematic review of the literature, I found that two interventions had consistently been proven to increase muscle mass and strength and counteract frailty - physical activity and protein supplementation. Therefore, I will conduct the PERFORM-TAVR multicenter randomized trial to determine whether a supervised home-based physical activity program combined with a protein supplementation beverage taken for a period of 3 months will yield beneficial effects on physical functioning in frail older adults recovering from TAVR. The home-based intervention has a high potential for sustainable clinical implementation due to its accessibility, low cost, promotion of self-care behaviors, and a track record of safety and efficacy in geriatric patients. This trial is the first of its kind with the potential to change practice by altering the way we care for frail older adults after a TAVR procedure to optimize patient-centered outcomes.

column36: Addiction treatment trajectories among street-involved young people who use opioids: Responding to a public health emergency in Vancouver
column37: In 2016, the British Columbia Provincial Health Officer declared a public health emergency due to dramatic increases in fentanyl related overdose deaths in the province, including among street-involved young people. Addiction treatment is a cornerstone of addressing the overdose crisis, and Vancouver is in the process of rapidly expanding its efforts to create a comprehensive addiction treatment system for adolescents and young adults. In 2015, the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority (VCH) issued new clinical guidelines that make Suboxone a recommended first line treatment for opioid use disorders among young people. VCH anticipates the addition of 17 youth dedicated residential addiction treatment beds over the next year. Vancouver is also in the midst of scaling up efforts to coordinate healthcare service delivery for vulnerable, drug using populations through the Downtown Eastside Second Generation Strategy. With these changes, street-involved young people's access to Suboxone, residential treatment beds, and continuity of addiction care promises to reach unprecedented levels. However, many urgent questions remain regarding how to most effectively deliver these interventions, in ways that are congruent with the complex, everyday lived experiences of these young people, as well as those who provide addiction treatment and care to this population. The proposed study will address this knowledge gap by describing street-involved youth's addiction treatment trajectories and outcomes in the context of Vancouver's expanding efforts to address the overdose crisis. Through interviews and ethnographic fieldwork, we will document the evolving experiences of these young people and their service providers, in relation to a transforming system of services in this setting. Our goal is to create new knowledge that will directly inform ongoing efforts to deliver innovative youth addiction treatment services in Vancouver.

column36: VAST-MAP: Vascular Stiffness Mapping for Aging Analysis Using High Frame Rate Ultrasound
column37: About six million Canadians are now at the age of 65 or older. For these people, their age is inevitably a major risk factor for contracting cardiovascular diseases. One well-recognized vascular hallmark in aging subjects is the stiffening of arteries, and it has been regarded as a predictor for future cardiovascular events. Recognizing the clinical significance of such a vascular biomarker, this project will seek to facilitate mapping of local vascular stiffness levels by engineering a novel non-invasive imaging technology that is based on: (i) High-frame-rate ultrasound (HiFRUS) with >1,000 fps frame rate capability; (ii) Analysis of pulse wave propagation dynamics, where each heartbeat sends a wave of blood (i.e. pulse) through the arterial network (the stiffer the artery, the faster the pulse wave travels). The new HiFRUS-based vascular stiffness mapping tool will be referred to as VAST-MAP. Four objectives have been set forth to devise and apply this technology to vascular aging investigations: 1) Design a suite of robust computing algorithms for VAST-MAP; 2) Calibrate the experimental efficacy of VAST-MAP by conducting laboratory experiments; 3) Assess the practical effectiveness of VAST-MAP by applying it to young and aged human subjects; 4) Pursue the first application of VAST-MAP in vascular aging intervention studies. The key expected outcome of this project is that a new imaging tool (VAST-MAP) for local arterial stiffness quantification will become available for use in vascular aging research. This will pave way for the development of new diagnostic routines to complement the existing risk scoring system for prediction of future cardiovascular events.

column36: Imaging, understanding, and managing radiotherapy inflammation and radiation necrosis
column37: In brain cancer, patients usually receive a treatment in the form of targeted radiation rays (radiotherapy). Radiotherapy has evolved, and we can now give brain tumors a huge dose of radiation while the rest of the brain is relatively unharmed. However, regions close to the tumors can still take quite a beating. Sadly, this can cause severe side effects, going all the way from drowsiness to dementia. To prevent these side effects, we must understand better why these occurs. We know that these effects are partially caused by inflammation. Inflammation is the normal reaction of the body to damage - a response that include sending specialized cells - the white blood cells - where damage is detected. Inflammation is very important for wound healing, but if it does not subside in time, it can cause more damage than the wound itself. Prof. Lepage and his team will be working on how we can use current imaging methods - scanners that can see inside you - to predict and detect inflammation. Using this knowledge, we will be able to test methods to reduce side-effects, and methods to use inflammation to our advantage to better cure brain tumors.

column36: Oral mucosa as a source of cells with regenerative potential in skin
column37: Scar formation following injury to skin is a common, unwanted outcome of the wound healing process. Clinically, scars can range from fine lines to expansive, disfiguring hypertrophic or keloid scars. Regardless of the type of scars, they lead to considerable psychosocial impacts or physical complications or both for the individual involved. At least 45 million patients in the United States alone undergo procedures that could benefit from therapies that reduce scar formation, resulting in a $4 billion anti-scarring therapy market annually. During the past decades, using various animal models, steady progress has been made to identify factors that may reduce scar formation. In spite of these advances, no effective therapy to predictably prevent scar formation exists today. Intriguingly, studies from several laboratories using rodent models have indicated significantly faster wound healing in oral mucosa than in skin. Our findings using a validated pig model have provided the first systematical evidence that oral mucosal wound healing also results in significantly reduced scar formation as compared to skin wounds. Importantly, connective tissue cells, called fibroblasts, in skin and oral mucosa have different properties that may contribute to the different wound-healing outcomes. In this preclinical study, we will develop novel bioengineered skin substitutes carrying oral mucosal fibroblasts to test whether they can be used to promote wound healing and prevent scar formation in skin using the pig model. This study will pave the way for the development of novel clinical applications for humans to promote fast and scarless wound healing in skin by using oral mucosal fibroblasts.

column36: What works best to protect public health? An international comparison of post-market regulatory risk communication on prescription drugs
column37: Medicines provide important health benefits but can also lead to harm, and are a major cause of emergency department visits and hospitalization. Much of this harm is preventable through appropriate use of the safest available treatment option. When new safety concerns arise, Health Canada and other national regulatory agencies put out warnings to health professionals and the public, with the aim of supporting safer medicine use and avoiding situations that can lead to harm. When and how warnings are issued can differ considerably between countries, but no research has compared the effectiveness of different approaches. This study compares safety advisories on medicines in Canada, the United States, the European Union (United Kingdom and Denmark), and Australia from 2005 to 2016. The focus is on new safety concerns for which the decision to communicate, methods used, or key messages differ between countries. We will develop a database of advisories on serious safety concerns in the five countries from 2005 to 2016. At a population level, we examine whether recommended changes to prescribing, other health-related behaviours, and health outcomes have occurred to a greater extent in countries with safety advisories than in those without advisories, The study also includes policy analysis and interviews with clinicians and patient groups to better understand factors that enhance the effectiveness of safety advisories and how awareness and medicine use are affected. The aim of the study is to identify best practices in regulatory risk communication on medicines, in terms of effects on medicine prescribing and use, and ultimately on public health.

column36: Cortical mechanisms of 3-D scene and object recognition in the primate brain
column37: We have no trouble recognizing objects around us but computers are generally very bad at this. The key difference between us and computers is that for us, an object stays the same even if the lighting, colours, viewing angles, or textures of the object change. Another key difference is that our brain can use the 3-D shape of the object, which stays the same even if the scene image changes. The studies proposed here are aimed at understanding how the 3-D shapes of objects are represented in the brain. The results are fundamental for an understanding of how the brain represents objects, faces, and scenes, which together form the very basis of our visual experience. The knowledge gained here will guide both computer models and algorithms for object recognition, as well as treatments for acute and chronic neurological disorders that affect face and object recognition.

column37: Lung transplantation is a life-saving intervention for people with end-stage lung disease. Currently, a large proportion of donors have infectious diseases such as the Hepatitis C virus (HCV). Despite otherwise good quality organs, lungs from HCV donors cannot be used due to exceedingly high risk (>90%) of transmission to the transplant recipient. Previous reports have shown poor survival of recipients when this practice was applied. The emergence of new direct-acting antiviral drugs suggests a high chance of cure for HCV; nevertheless this has never been evaluated in the context of lung transplantation. If this proves to be successful, a large source of new donors will become available for patients with lung failure.

column36: Investigating Pharmacogenetic Mechanisms of Doxorubicin-Induced Cardiotoxicty in Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Cardiomyocytes
column37: Many anti-cancer drugs cause side effects that damage the heart. Doxorubicin is one of the most commonly used anti-cancer drugs and is used to treat breast cancer, lymphoma, and many childhood cancers. However, up to 26% of patients who receive this drug experience cardiotoxicity, which can lead to heart failure, heart transplantation, and death. Currently, we lack the ability to predict which specific patients are at risk of this adverse drug reaction, and we have no effective methods to prevent it. The goal of this study is to investigate the function of specific genes that have been associated with doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity. By understanding if these genes directly impact the response to doxorubicin, and what biological mechanisms are involved, we could potentially use these genes as genetic tests to predict which patients are most likely to develop cardiotoxicity from this drug. We will study the role of these genes in heart cells generated from human stem cells. My lab has recently described a new way of studying doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity using such stem cell - derived heart cells. We will introduce the specific gene variants of interest using a state-of-the-art gene editing technology called CRISPR. We will compare heart cells with or without these gene variants to determine how they respond to doxorubicin. We will also isolate stem cells from the blood of patients that have suffered from doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity, turn these stem cells into heart cells, and study how they respond to the drug, in the presence or absence of the specific gene variants. If we can identify the patients at highest risk of drug-induced heart damage, we could take steps to prevent or mitigate this devastating adverse drug reaction. Ultimately these efforts will result in safer and more effective drugs and will allow Canadians to stay healthier and experience fewer side effects.

Our research project will evaluate how the ACE program implemented and improved care transitions for the elderly at these hospitals. We will also evaluate how the Wiki-suite helped adapt and apply the ACE program in participating hospitals.

column36: Rational optimization of CFTR modulators and assessment of predictive potential of novel cystic fibrosis (CF) airway epithelial models for clinical outcome
column37: The cystic fibrosis (CF) protein (CFTR) resides at the cell surface and ensures normal water and ion composition of the liquid that lines the airway. CF mutations impair CFTR function and the composition of the airway surface liquid layer. This leads to lung infection and uncontrolled inflammation, the primary cause of premature death in CF. Robust correction of these defects has been achieved for only 9 rare mutations, by ivacaftor, representing a small subset of >2000 mutations, corresponding to ~5% of the CF patient population. The recently approved FDA drug combination of lumacaftor and ivacaftor (Orkambi) targets the most common mutation with variable clinical benefit: 50% of patients gained >5% (FEV1) lung function, while the others showed no or only very modest benefit, indicating a substantial variability of responsiveness. Importantly, the drug susceptibility of most other CFTR mutations, which may be correctable, is still unexplored. To overcome the limited efficacy of the available drugs, there is unmet need for authentic and validated model systems for preclinical investigations. We will implement novel "primary" cell based models derived from noninvasively collected nasal epithelial cells. Based on our preliminary data, this model will maintain patient specific hallmarks of airways cells expressing rare CF mutations. To complement this approach, we will generate 60 of the rare mutations in respiratory epithelial cell lines and use these models for testing approved drugs and optimizing novel combinations of investigational CF drugs in functional and biochemical assays. Promising combinations will be validated in human airway cells and their effect will be compared to their clinical benefit to identify mutation and patient specific treatment protocols.

column36: Genetic Determinants of Individualized Islet Responses to Dietary Macronutrients
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) impacts more than 3 million Canadians and 385 million people worldwide. Obesity, which increases the risk of T2D, has also reached epidemic proportions, impacting ~30% of the population. Despite numerous treatment options many obese and/or T2D patients suffer from a decreased quality of life. Defects in the insulin-secreting beta cells are critical for the development of obesity/T2D. Elevated fasting insulin (hyperinsulinemia) is a pre-requisite for the development of obesity. Interestingly, obesity and its complications can be prevented in mice that are genetically protected from diet-induced hyperinsulinemia, suggesting that a reduction in insulin levels is beneficial to the metabolic health of an individual with obesity/T2D . While glucose is the main driver of acute insulin release, other dietary macronutrients can also potentiate insulin secretion. However, insulin release in response to these macronutrients is different between individuals. This could explain why 'low-carb' diets that aim to keep insulin levels low are only effective in a subset of the population. Thus, the goal of our study is to understand these variations, and identify pathways that determine the sensitivity of individuals to various macronutrients. We will characterize human islet functional responses to dietary macronutrients by measuring insulin release. The responses will be compared to the unique genetic profile of the donor. Multi-scale modelling will used to predict obesity and diabetes risk. We will also use glucose-responsive insulin producing cells (that have been generated from human embryonic stem cells) as a controlled cell model system to identify the molecular mechanisms that influence insulin secretion in response to nutrients. The proposed final outcome will be the development of a model that will allow us to predict, based on a person's genetics, whether they will be an insulin hypersecretor in response to any macronutrient.

column36: Gonococcal subversion of classical neutrophil functions
column37: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ngo) is a bacterial pathogen that causes more than 100 million cases of the sexually-transmitted disease gonorrhea in the world each year. In addition to the copious male urethral or female endocervical discharge that are the hallmark of gonorrhea, Ngo infections can progress to cause scarring of the reproductive tract, chronic pelvic pain and dangerous ectopic pregnancies in women, or blindness of children born to infected mothers. Critically, Ngo has recently attained 'superbug' status because it has acquired resistance to all clinically relevant oral and injectable antibiotics, making the threat of untreatable gonorrhea a looming reality. This has led to a global urgency to develop new strategies to halt the spread of Ngo and/or to treat established infections caused by this dangerous microbe. It is clear that the damage associated with Ngo infection is caused by an overzealous response of a single type of white blood cell, known as the neutrophil. What is disconcerting is that the neutrophil is the immune system's most potent bacterial-killing immune cell type, yet the massive numbers of neutrophils that enter Ngo-infected tissues are not capable of clearing the infection. Moreover, the neutrophil response is clear evidence that the immune system has been alerted to the presence of a dangerous bacterial intruder, yet it does not develop an effective immune 'memory' response that would otherwise protect against subsequent infections. Notably, recent work has revealed that different types of neutrophils exist, with functions ranging from the promotion of inflammation to the suppression of effective immune responses. This paradigm-shifting finding clearly contradicts the classical belief that all neutrophils are the same. column36: Mechanisms controlling estrogen receptor alpha expression and activity in breast tumorigenesis
column37: Breast cancer is a prevalent world-wide disease but its manifestations are heterogeneous, necessitating treatment regimen adapted to the main tumor subtypes currently identified. Two thirds of tumors overexpress the estrogen receptor alpha (ER) compared to normal tissues and are candidates for targeted treatments that block estrogen signaling. These tumors are associated with the best prognosis. Estrogen receptor-negative tumors on the other hand are not sensitive to these treatments and, for a significant proportion of them, can be treated only with chemotherapy. Further, ER-positive tumors can become resistant during tumor progression. Thus, understanding why some tumors gain or lose expression and/or activity of this important therapeutic target is crucial to improving the appropriate classification and treatment of this disease. To address this question, the applicants have initiated large-scale screens in breast cancer cell lines that express ER. Through suppression of expression of each individual gene in the genome, they have identified candidate proteins that are thought to modulate the expression and/or activity of ER using a surrogate assay that measures the activity of this protein. In this application, they will use a recent and sensitive technology for modulation of gene expression called CRISPR-Cas9 to validate current candidates and identify new ones. In addition, candidate ER regulators identified in current and future screens will be characterized for their capacity to modulate ER expression and/or activity. Finally, whether defects in these ER regulators arise during breast tumorigenesis will be investigated using archived breast tumor samples, and the impact of these proteins on the tumorigenic properties of breast cancer cells and their response to ER-targeted treatments will be investigated in cell line and animal models.

column36: Probing biased recognition of flu hemagglutinin by precursors of broadly neutralizing antibodies to the HA stem
column37: Influenza virus remains a serious threat to public health. Superior vaccines would be desirable that confer immunity against a broader diversity of flu strains, especially given the pandemic-causing potential of flu. Influenza vaccines stimulate our immune system to produce antibodies that help to protect against viral infection. For reasons that are not fully clear, broadly reactive antibodies (brAbs) can be elicited in some individuals by seasonal vaccination, as evidenced by the occasional recovery of such antibodies from select individuals. Developing a vaccine formulation that purposely is able to elicit such brAbs would constitute a significant advance. Understanding how the development of such brAbs is best triggered and promoted would likely help to inform new vaccine design strategies. The brAbs that we focus on in this project target a fairly invariant area on the flu protein hemagglutinin (HA), which is functionally important and displayed abundantly on the surface of the virus. Studies show that brAbs to this region originate from just a few antibody genes, suggesting that brAbs deriving from the same gene share a particular bias in how they initial recognize HA and that they may evolve along similar genetic pathways to turn into brAbs. This project will determine if early versions of potential brAbs indeed share common features in their development towards broad recognition of flu HAs and investigate if HAs from certain flu strains are preferentially bound by early versions of such antibodies. To probe these questions thoroughly, we will use novel genetically engineered animals with capacity to produce human-like antibodies, thus providing a surrogate readout system for antibody responses in humans. We expect the results of our work to further the development of better flu vaccines with capacity to evoke antibodies that offer broader protection than those produced by current seasonal vaccines.

column36: An examination of forebrain circuit activity that promotes hedonic reactions to palatable food consumption
column37: Approximately 10% of Canadian adults will experience major depression at some point in their lives. One of the core symptoms of this psychiatric disorder is a pronounce absence of pleasure in most activities. This research proposal seeks to identify neural circuit activity that promotes the sensation of pleasure. We focus on one very specific cause of pleasure, the consumption of highly palatable food. The pleasure derived from eating, at least as measured by positive facial reactions in rodents, can be driven by mu opioid receptor signaling in a particular forebrain area: the rostral nucleus accumbens shell. In humans, neural activity in this region correlates with the pleasures of food, sex, addictive drugs, music, and art. Mu opioid receptor signaling here is believed to alter the balance of activity between different types of output neurons, but the details and mechanisms of this effect are unknown. The principal aim of this grant is to identify in rodents how positive facial reactions to food consumption arise from mu opioid receptor signaling in the nucleus accumbens. We will use a combination of tools to record and manipulate specific cell types and circuits to identify what specific balance of activity in this area is the cause of mu opioid receptor-induced positive facial reactions to feeding. We will also try to enhance positive feeding reactions in an enduring manner through long lasting circuit manipulations. A better understanding of this particular source of hedonic reactions will provide a framework for a more general understanding the neural underpinnings of pleasure. Insights gained from these kinds of circuit analyses have already been used in the development of highly specific therapeutic interventions designed to improve the lives of patients afflicted by mental illness.

column37: Supporting older Canadians through home care is a health policy priority in Canada. However, there are still significant gaps in access to care and quality of services that are provided. As a result, those who receive home care sometimes experience undesirable and potentially preventable health outcomes, such as hospital stays, emergency room visits, early entry to nursing homes, or even death. Part of the challenge is the underfunding of home care; this is why the Canadian government had recently promised to invest $3 billion dollars in enhancing the care provided in this setting. An equal part of the challenge is a lack of evidence in what types of care people need and how much care is required to reduce adverse outcomes. This grant will use rich population-level data for those who are receiving home care to, first, describe the needs of home care recipients (e.g., disease and disabilities). We will also aim to explain the differences in the level and types of home care services provided in Ontario, and across several provinces in Canada. Finally, we will use statistical techniques to identify the mix (i.e., personal support workers, nursing) and intensity (i.e., hours per week) of services that may be required prevent unwanted outcomes for different types of home care users - paying special attention to people are are frail and may be nearing the end of life. We will build tools that will map out and predict how we can prevent these undesirable outcomes. The tools will be designed for patients, their family and caregivers to inform care planning, but could also be used by health care planners and policy makers to improve care for the entire population. Our goal is to generate knowledge and tools to inform current and new investments for home care, and can support interventions to improve care for Canadians, especially those who are frail and may be nearing the end of life.

column36: Stimulating Functional Networks to Enhance Stroke Recovery
column37: Currently ~400,000 Canadians live with the after effects of stroke and stroke is the number one cause of disability. Despite often not having a full recovery from stroke, most people will have a remarkable improvement in function in the absence of any therapy. The problem is that this only occurs in the first few months after a stroke. This fact suggests that the brain has the ability to temporarily heal itself "naturally" through repairing and rebuilding connections between the cells in the brain called neurons. During recovery from a stroke regions of the brain reorganizing on their own. This suggests that we can enhance stroke recovery by stimulating new, active group of neurons. New treatments are being tested in patients that aim to strengthen the formation of new sets of neurons by stimulating the brain. These treatments appear promising yet only some patients get better. One reason why stimulation therapy may not always work is that we do not know which particular neurons need to be stimulated. This project will identify which neurons reorganize naturally during recovery and test if stimulating these neurons can improve recovery. Our work will be performed in animal models of strokes since there is no non-surgical method that allows us to manipulate or visualize individual neurons after a stroke in humans. We will determine which specific neurons participate in recovery from stroke and identify the timeline of brain reorganization following stroke. We are well suited to accomplish this task using special mice that allow us to 1) label and visualize individual neurons to see what neurons are active at any given time and 2) stimulate neurons in a live animal that is performing a behavior task. Thus, this fundamental study will not only shed light on the underlying mechanisms of stroke recovery, but also allow us to design better treatments for stroke recovery, so survivors will struggle less with disability and enjoy a better quality of life.

column36: Viral Control of Autophagy to Reprogram the Host Cell Secretome
column37: Viruses are incredible tools that teach us how our cells work. In my lab, we study the virus, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). This virus causes a rare skin cancer called Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). My lab is interested in how this virus changes cells that comprise blood vessels, called endothelial cells, to make them secrete proteins that are called inflammatory cytokines, that promote the cancer KS. I have discovered that KSHV targets granules called processing bodies (PBs) that play an important role in controlling inflammatory cytokine production (Corcoran et al. 2015 PLoS Path. 11:e1004597). My lab now has exciting new evidence that connects the disappearance of PBs to the process of autophagy, which literally means 'self-eating'. Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that permits cells to survive the stress of starvation by promoting the degradation and recycling of a variety of cellular structures, thereby providing essential cellular building blocks and energy for survival. Autophagy has also been shown to regulate inflammatory cytokine production; however how this occurs is not clear in most cases. My compelling preliminary evidence connects autophagy increases with the disassembly of PBs and increased inflammatory cytokine production. This is the first evidence suggesting the coordinated regulation of autophagy and PBs controls inflammation in our cells. Impact and Significance: My lab has made a fundamental discovery about how inflammatory cytokine expression is regulated. Inflammatory cytokines are aberrantly produced in many disorders in addition to KS, such as rheumatoid arthritis and many other cancers. Increasing our knowledge of how autophagy and PBs are functionally linked will help develop new treatments to limit inflammation in many situations.

column36: Mobilizing a land-based culturally appropriate active living intervention among Indigenous youth
column37: The benefits of physical activity (PA) are far-reaching, and individuals with high PA have better mental, physical and emotional health. However, our population is more inactive than ever and to tackle this health issue it is important to act early, especially in populations that are most vulnerable. In Canada, one of the most marginalized groups is Indigenous youth. Even though they are Canada's fastest growing group, Indigenous youth have poorer health outcomes than others. As PA's benefits are numerous, we propose to develop sustainable ways to improve PA in Indigenous youth and thus, ultimately increase their chances of leading a healthy life. The answer lies in adopting culturally appropriate ways to integrate to PA into the daily lives of Indigenous youth. We have devised an intervention that is not only culturally appropriate, but also novel. In our 5 year intervention we will invite youth from our partnering communities to spend 5 days/year at a tipi camp. In this tipi camp we will teach youth to take advantage of living on the land, and combine this approach with introducing them to active arts-based theatre games. We have done a similar tipi camp in the past and observed that being in the tipi camp improved not only their PA, but also their mental health and overall wellbeing. After the tipi camp we will follow up with active arts-based programs through the schools of these youth. We will assess their PA and overall wellbeing in three different seasons every year throughout the intervention period. We aim to demonstrate that this novel intervention will allow Indigenous youth to lead a healthier, active life. We believe that if we generate evidence that establishes the importance of culturally appropriate active living, it will change the current state of affairs, where Indigenous youth are left to fend for themselves. We ultimately aim to show that this is an effective and economical approach to address a wide range of health issues in Indigenous youth.

column36: Bifunctional non-secosteroidal vitamin D analogues as novel cancer therapeutics
column37: We have developed a novel class of molecules as potential cancer therapeutics that possess two distinct but complementary biochemical (or drug) activities within a single molecular backbone - essentially acting as two drugs in one. We previously found that molecules that mimic the action of vitamin D (VDR agonists) in combination with drugs (HDACi) that inhibit the activity of enzymes called histone deacetylases (HDACs) strongly cooperate to kill cancer cells. As individual drugs can be cleared by the body at different rates, complicating therapy with drug combinations, we sought to develop single molecules that act both as VDR agonists and as HDACi; i.e. functioning as two drugs in one. These "bifunctional" molecules represent a novel class of therapeutics. Our work over a number of years combining chemical synthesis with characterization of molecular function led to the production of series of molecules that acted as both VDR agonists and HDACi. Moreover, these molecules could be assembled in relatively few and simple steps of chemical synthesis. Our goals in this grant application are to understand in detail how our hybrid molecules produce their therapeutic effect and to further develop their potential in preclinical studies to identify molecules with the potential to be used as actual drugs. The work essentially entails three parts. (i) We will use cancer cells in culture to understand the molecular details of how the two drug activities combine to produce a therapeutic effect. (ii) We will produce new hybrid molecules with improved properties. (iii) We will study the therapeutic potential of our lead molecules in several mouse models of cancer for which there has been relatively little therapeutic advance in the last few years, including advanced squamous carcinoma of the head and neck and so-called "triple-negative" breast cancer.

column36: Lipid homeostasis regulation by brain glucagon signalling
column37: Background: A key feature of diabetes and obesity is an abnormal level of fats ("lipids") in the blood. High blood levels of lipids made by the liver increase the risk of damaging bodily systems that serve to maintain our metabolism. Thus, it is important to discover and understand mechanisms that affect how lipid production and balance is controlled by our bodies and work towards the goal of lowering lipid levels in the blood, to reduce the risks of health problems associated with an imbalance in metabolism. Objective: Our research aims to unveil novel actions of glucagon, in the brain, that alters whole-body balance of lipid levels. Research project: We will test how glucagon, a hormone made and found in the body, is used by the brain to control liver lipid production, and consequently lipid levels in the blood. We will assess the action of glucagon in the brain under normal conditions and in obesity (from high calorie feeding) and in diabetes. We hypothesize that the brain, by specific pathways controlled by this hormone, alters lipid production and output by the liver. Hence, glucagon action in the brain will affect blood lipid levels. We hypothesize that nutrient excess impairs glucagon's action in the brain, which contributes to an over-production of lipids by the liver. Hence, targeting this defect will help restore blood lipid levels in conditions of obesity and diabetes. Impact: Insights gained from the proposed research will reveal new pathways and mechanisms to regulate blood lipid levels. The research will advance our current understanding of how glucagon affects lipid metabolism, not just by its known effects on tissues like the liver, but also by its novel actions in the brain. These findings will reveal putative new targets, which can help lower blood lipid levels in diabetes and obesity, and thus improve the quality of life of people affected by these conditions. This also helps to reduce the collateral effects on health care and spending.

column36: Developpement d'un traitement selectif de l'endometriose : Etude du potentiel du premier inhibiteur irreversible de la 17beta-HSD1 chez le primate
column37: L'endometriose touche environ 10% des femmes pre-menopausees et a des consequences tres importantes sur le plan personnel, professionnel et socio-economique. Les principaux symptomes sont la douleur chronique, la dysmenorrhee et la perte de fertilite. Les therapies pharmacologiques actuelles ont pour effet de limiter les symptomes associes a cette maladie, mais ne peuvent malheureusement pas la guerir. Une recurrence elevee de la maladie est egalement observee chez les patientes traitees. La seule therapie curative actuellement disponible est l'ablation radicale par chirurgie des lesions d'endometrioses. De nouvelles therapies curatives moins invasives et moins couteuses sont donc requises. Nous avons developpe au cours des dernieres annees un inhibiteur de la 17beta-HSD1, une enzyme capitale pour la production de l'estradiol, l'hormone la plus puissante chez la femme. Cet inhibiteur de la 17beta-HSD1, nomme PBRM, vise a reguler localement les niveaux d'estradiol dans les lesions d'endometrioses sans affecter la production systemique des estrogenes. Cette action selective laisse entrevoir un avantage important compare aux autres traitements hormonaux actuellement utilises qui provoquent un blocage global et non specifique de la production ovarienne, ce qui est incompatible dans le cas de femmes en age de procreer. Compte tenu des resultats preliminaires in vitro et in vivo tres prometteurs que nous avons obtenus avec le PBRM et de ses avantages lies a son mode d'action unique, nous sommes maintenant interesses a verifier son efficacite chez le babouin. Ce singe est l'espece de primate reconnu comme le modele par excellence pour etudier l'endometriose et le modele le plus pres de l'humain. Cette recherche aura donc un impact capital pour demontrer l'utilite de notre technologie pour le traitement selectif de l'endometriose et permettre son avancement vers les etudes cliniques chez la femme.
