column36: Wireless neurophotonic probes for the interrogation of neurons in memory circuits
column37: As the average age of the population of Canada and the developed world rises, neurodegenerative conditions will become increasingly prevalent and a growing burden on the healthcare system and economy. A major neurodegenerative disease is Alzheimer's disease (AD), which causes memory and cognition loss. AD and dementia affect roughly 1.1 million Canadians and incur an economic cost of $10.4B per year in Canada. Currently, there is no cure or effective treatment. The Lancet Neurology Commission recently stated, "an effective therapy for AD is perhaps the greatest unmet need facing modern medicine." This project addresses the challenge of understanding neuron circuits in the brain involved in memory, with the goal of improving the efficacy of neurostimulation therapies for AD and dementia. Such treatments would stimulate specific brain circuits to promote memory encoding and/or retrieval in patients with AD or dementia. The project will create a new type of wireless, implantable deep brain probes for rodent experiments on memory loss rescue that uses optical stimulation and electrical stimulation+recording of specific groups of neurons. Importantly, these brain probes will be made using the same processes and infrastructure as semiconductor microelectronics to ensure compatibility with volume manufacturing and a viable technology translation path that will widely benefit neuroscientists and clinical researchers. This project brings together world-class expertise from around the globe in photonics, electronics, neuroscience, and deep brain stimulation. In addition to the Canadian team members, the project involves collaborators in France and United States who will provide complementary expertise in the design, fabrication, and testing of the neural probes. The results of this international project will benefit the health of Canadians and lead to high-value neurotechnology products that are designed and integrated in Canada.

column36: Age-related differences in brain activation in the default-network during successful memory formation
column37: Healthy aging is accompanied by a reduction in performance in standard laboratory tests of memory. Moreover, older individuals worry about declines in their memory and report that reductions in memory functioning negatively impact their quality of life. Thus, it is critical to gain a better understanding of age-related differences in memory, particularly since current demographic trends predict an increase in the proportion of older adults in Canada in coming years. Previous studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a commonly used brain imaging technique, indicate two consistent age-related differences in brain activation during memory formation (e.g., learning a list of pictures). First, older adults under-activate regions of visual cortex compared to young adults, which has been interpreted as a reduction in processing of visual details with age that contributes to decreased memory. A second pattern of age-related differences is that older adults over-activate a set of regions known as the default-network compared to young adults. The significance of this age-related increase in activation in default-network is currently unclear. Previous research has implicated the default-network in internally-directed cognitive processes, such as focusing on thoughts and feelings. Based on this prior work, the current research project will test the hypothesis that age-related differences in brain activation reflect a change in attention during learning, such that older adults focus more on the personal relevance and meaning of learning material at the expense of specific perceptual details. This study will be important in uncovering the brain mechanisms underlying the finding that older adults focus more on personal relevance, and that they may learn information better if it is presented in a way that is meaningful to them.

column36: Biosynthetic alternatives to human donor corneal transplantation
column37: The cornea is the outer window to the eye that transmits light to the retina for vision. Permanent transparency loss, due to disease or damage, can result in vision loss and blindness. Transplantation of human donor corneas is the only widely accepted treatment, but it is overshadowed by a worldwide shortage (only 1 donor cornea available for every 70 needed) and functional limitations (sub-optimal optical results, rejection, and graft failure), particularly in very sick eyes with inflammation and infection. Our goals are (1) to overcome the donor shortage and to improve surgical outcomes by developing biosynthetic alternatives to donor corneas, and (2) to revolutionize cornea surgical methods so that patients can be treated by removing only the damaged tissue and filling the resulting tissue gap with a transparent, injectable hydrogel that will be polymerized in situ instead of a full transplantation, somewhat like dental fillings. In regenerative medicine, biomaterials are used as scaffolds to promote tissue repair. Our approach consists in designing collagen mimics at the nanoscale level and allowing these to self-assemble into full size 3-D scaffolds after injection into the diseased cornea. We will then use light to start the crosslinking reaction, to form a stable, transparent graft. Our proposed new treatment comprising of a new surgical paradigm and new biomaterials will offer a minimally invasive and unequaled alternative for sight restoration. Our approach will have a tremendous impact in patients who currently have very poor prognosis with traditional corneal transplantation.

column36: CLEAN Meds RCT: Carefully seLected and Easily Accessible at No charge Medications
column37: Canada is the only developed country where people access healthcare services care by doctors for free but more than half of medications are paid for out-of-pocket. We are measuring the effects of providing adult family practice patients with free and convenient access to a carefully selected set of medications. This is a randomized controlled trial. People who have had trouble affording medications are recruited at routine family practice visits. Each person is randomly assigned to either receive usual access to medications or to receive access to a carefully selected set of essential medications without copayments, dispensing fees or deductibles - in other words, "for free" at the point of service. The list of medications to which patients would have access is based on the World Health Organization's model list of essential medicines that everyone in the world should be able to access. The medications will be dispensed through a centralized pharmacy model that involves patients receiving medications via mail. We measure how often people take their medications and how well chronic conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes are controlled. We also assess cost impacts to the healthcare system. We will compare these outcomes between people who have usual access to medications and people who get the essential medications for free. The study is being conducted from family practices throughout Ontario, including northern and rural communities. Patients, community representatives and policy makers have been involved in designing the study, and in developing the program of drug delivery and the communication of our findings. A community guidance panel has helped us design parts of the study. We hope that our involvement of community members in the research process will help improve the involvement of the community in future research studies. The results of this research could led to improvements in medication access for people in Ontario.

column36: Innovation in Pediatric Clinical Trials
column37: Clinical trials use real patients under carefully controlled situations to measure how well a medication works and how safe it is. Knowledge gained from trials helps doctors choose which medicines to prescribe. Clinical trials for children are difficult to do, because they get sick less often than adults, and parents are understandably protective and reluctant to enroll their kids in a trial. Also, many hospitals need to be involved to study enough patients, which is expensive to coordinate. As a result, doctors don't have enough solid evidence for prescribing medicines to kids, which means a lot of guesswork. We are using new methods of study design to see if they will make clinical trials in children easier and better. We will create resources for trial design, management and analysis that can be used by researchers across Canada to make clinical trials for children easier, less expensive and more informative. These resources will be known as KIDSCAN, a Canadian effort for safe drugs in kids. We will be testing these new methods and resources in 4 clinical trials conducted in 6 pediatric emergency departments across 4 provinces. The medical conditions and treatments to test were chosen by researchers in pediatric emergency medicine because they are common, and include breathing problems, stomach upset, and pain from an injury or procedure. We will use statistical methods that will determine what information already exists that a trial can build on, and what information we might still need in order to change what doctors decide to do. As well, we will use centralized systems and services to conduct the trials and manage the data. To determine if these new methods and resources were successful we will look at the cost of the trial, the quality of the evidence generated, and the changes in procedures used in the pediatric ED. We hope to show that these new methods and resources will mean doctors will have more and better information on which to base their decisions.

column36: The BedMed Initiative - Making better use of existing therapeutics
column37: High blood pressure (present in 1 out of every 5 Canadian adults) increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Blood pressure lowering pills reduce this risk - but we may not be using these drugs optimally. A study conducted in Spain suggests that using blood pressure pills at BEDTIME, instead of taking them in the morning (when they are most commonly used), reduces death, heart attack, and stroke by more than 50%. If true, a switch to bedtime prescribing would have more impact on the health of Canadians with high blood pressure than whether high blood pressure is treated at all - increasing life expectancy an estimated 5.5 years. Surprisingly, this study has yet to change how high blood pressure is treated. This is because 1) many health care providers feel it is "too good to be true" (i.e. don't know if they can believe it) and 2) because the RISKS of bedtime blood pressure lowering haven't been explored. Examples of potential risks include more falls and fractures in older adults who might feel lightheaded late at night, and worsening of vision in patients who are at risk of glaucoma. In this project, volunteer patients and their primary care providers will be conducting a large treatment trial designed to 1) establish whether heart attacks and strokes really are reduced by switching blood pressure medications to bedtime, and 2) determine who might be put at risk if the timing of blood pressure pills changes. In pursuit of answers to these pivotal questions we will 1) leverage 7 electronic health databases spanning three provinces, 2) introduce new technology that will assist the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network (CPCSSN) to conduct clinical trials, and 3) expand the reach of the Pragmatic Trials Collaborative (Canada's largest practice-based research network www.PragmtaticTrials.ca). The BedMed trial will forge a novel tri-provincial pragmatic trials network and serve as a template for future comparative effectiveness work.

column36: An Integrated Platform for Innovative Pragmatic Cluster-Randomized Registry Trials in Hemodialysis
column37: . Dialysis is a life-saving treatment for people whose kidneys have stopped working. However, this treatment is difficult. Patients must be connected to a dialysis machine three times a week and the chances of dying are extremely high. One in three patients will die within a year of starting dialysis. Heart attacks and strokes are the most common cause of death. Dialysis patients also suffer from many unpleasant symptoms and may be unable to work or live independently. For several reasons, it has been difficult to do clinical trials testing promising treatments for patients receiving dialysis. As a result, we don't always know what treatments work well. However, we have developed several strategies to conduct clinical trials in new ways to help dialysis patients. We've brought together 50 people including patients, doctors, and scientists who are working together to make these trials meaningful and efficient. Over the next four years we will conduct two trials and also prepare for two future trials. By testing promising treatments in this way we hope to identify treatments that help dialysis patients live longer better lives.

column36: The SuDDICU study- A study of the impact of preventative antibiotics (SDD) on patient outcome and antibiotic resistance in the critically ill in intensive care
column37: Antibiotic resistance, driven by the overuse of antibiotics, represents a huge threat to public health in Canada and worldwide. At the same time infections are a major cause of death for Canadians and significantly increases health care costs. Critically ill patients are particularly susceptible to infections caused by antibiotic resistant organisms and have an even higher mortality. Significant tension exists between avoiding inappropriate antibiotic use and preventing life-threatening infections. One intervention used to reduce infections and prevent deaths is selective decontamination of the digestive tract (SDD), a preventative antibiotic regime. The evidence supporting the use of SDD for saving lives is reasonably strong but health care professionals have refrained from using SDD due to fears that increased use of antibiotics drives antibiotic resistance. Whether these fears are justified is unknown. Currently, we deny patients a potentially life saving preventative therapy out of concern for the potential impact of antibiotic resistance on subsequent patients. Therefore, further study is imperative to determine the balance of benefit and harm before embarking on wider antibiotic use. In this study we plan to undertake- 1. A large-scale clinical trial examining the effect of antibiotics on the number of patients who die from infections. 2. A large study of antibiotic resistance patterns in modern ICUs including answering whether such antibiotics drive resistance The study of antibiotic resistance will be our key focus in Canada. If the benefits of this treatment are realized without driving antibiotic resistance, this study could have global impact through lives saved and infections prevented as well as reducing health care expenditure. The controversy surrounding SDD is such that only a definitive study is likely to resolve the debate, and without this study the opportunity to establish a life-saving measure as standard of care may be lost.

column36: Using big data to conduct innovative cardiovascular clinical trials
column37: Traditional randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have provided extremely valuable information on medical therapies (e.g., statins) and procedures that have changed the way cardiovascular diseases are treated. However, despite their contributions, traditional RCTs are costly, their findings may not be applicable to patients unlike those in the study, and the use of trial findings may be infrequent. These limitations may be addressed by the field of 'big data.' Novel and efficient methods can be developed using big data to conduct clinical trials by facilitating recruitment of patients, measuring patient characteristics and follow-up of patient outcomes in large 'real-world' populations. While Canada has some of the world's best population-based health databases, much work remains to be done to determine how best to use these data in clinical trials. Our multi-disciplinary team of 30+ researchers, health care professionals, decision makers and patients will undertake two studies which will test the potential of using big data to: a) increase use of cholesterol-lowering statin drugs aimed at preventing heart attacks and strokes, and b) accurately identify the occurrence of cardiovascular hospitalizations in clinical trials. By leveraging big data, this project has the potential to transform how clinical trials are conducted and dramatically lower costs, making Canada a world leader in innovative clinical trial methodologies and attracting more clinical research to this country.

column36: Cost-effectiveness of single family room care in a Canadian NICU: A randomized controlled trial
column37: We save the lives of more preterm babies than ever before, but there have only been small improvements in how healthy these babies are after going home. Caring for these babies costs over half a billion dollars a year. Researchers in Sweden find that building hospitals where every family gets their own room helps babies go home sooner, and reduces their chances of developing serious lung disease. Other studies suggest that caring for babies in their own rooms might have a number of other benefits including improved breastfeeding, and reduced infections. Unfortunately, single rooms do not improve outcomes for every baby, and may actually result in harms to some. Researchers believe that benefits of single rooms come through increased parent presence and involvement in care; Parents in the original Swedish study spent 24 hours a day in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). We have little idea of what types of social and financial burdens are born by parents when units switch to single family room designs, and high visitation rates might not be feasible for all Canadians. Before encouraging changes in all of Canada's 177 NICUs we need to be sure that pursuing them does not create new disparities or make us miss opportunities that would make a bigger difference. This research will explore how much benefit is associated with a switch to single family room care, and at what cost to the healthcare system and parents. We will randomly assign families to either a single family room or open bay bed, and track how babies do in both types of rooms. We will also calculate costs incurred by the hospital and parents. Ours will be the first study to provide high quality evidence for what a switch to single family room designs means for the healthcare system and parents. Results will be able to be used by health leaders to help make decisions about whether they should make a switch, and what sorts of family and hospital factors they should consider.

column36: Engineering the Type Six Secretion System as a Novel Antimicrobial Therapy
column37: Increasing instances of antibiotic resistance highlight the need for new ways to treat infectious diseases. It was recently discovered that bacteria can use a molecular version of a 'poison-tipped spear' to stab and kill one another, and the poison on the tip is crucial for this process. This weapon has great potential for killing bacteria but a major challenge of harnessing it as an antimicrobial tool is targeting it only towards harmful microbes, called pathogens, while not hurting human cells. The goal of my project is to genetically engineer this spear to only target dangerous bacteria by replacing the poison on the tip with the molecular equivalent of a precise pair of scissors. I will use particular 'scissors' that can be customized to specifically cut and detoxify harmful genes that only pathogens carry, such that they render those bacteria harmless without affecting human cells. I will do this by first demonstrating that these targeted scissors can be placed on the spear and that they can be delivered into the target bacteria. Then I will ensure that they are active and can specifically affect pathogens. Finally, I will ensure that the scissors are inert towards human cells, and moreover that they can effectively protect human cells against attacks from harmful bacteria. This project is greatly significant because it will produce a completely new way of fighting pathogens that can target antibiotic resistant bacteria (and render them sensitive again) as well as act in a specific and customizable way that targets only harmful microbes, a feat that even the best antibiotics are not capable of. In summary, this project proposes to develop an entirely novel antimicrobial technique for the treatment of infectious disease.

column36: Cost-effectiveness of modified-return-to-work after a musculoskeletal injury
column37: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) such as sprains and strains are the second most common cause of disability worldwide. Disability rates due to MSDs increased 45% from 1990 to 2010. MSDs are a major problem in the workforce, and account for the highest disability costs (yearly almost $15 billion) in Canada. Workplace interventions that aim to reduce disability duration for people with work-related MSDs show only limited effects. Policies that mandate certain workplace practices may be important to reduce work disability. Modified return-to-work (MRTW) is a key policy to prevent and reduce the work disability due to MSDs. MRTW gives workers the opportunity to gradually increase working hours and work load, and to limit or modify work tasks while recovering from in injury. Many Canadian employers offer MRTW, but its effectiveness is unknown. I have the opportunity to use unique data with information from workers in British Columbia (BC) with a MSD to investigate the effectiveness of MRTW to increase successful and sustainable RTW. I will perform this project in three phases: 1) define individual RTW processes during one year after injury, 2) investigate the relationship between worker characteristics and the RTW process, and 3) assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of MRTW in the RTW process. The ultimate goal is to improve the implementation of MRTW and reduce the duration of work-disability for more successful and sustainable RTW. The research will be conducted at The Partnership of Work Health and Safety at the University of British Columbia (UBC). The Partnership brings together policy-makers, researchers and data resources from the UBC and the provincial workers' compensation system. They address current and emerging issues of work-related health in BC, which ensures the impact of the study results on policy.

column36: Gender, sexuality, and the prevention of initiation into injection drug use
column37: In the context of growing opioid misuse in Canada, a critical public health priority is to prevent - rather then simply respond to - the transition of individuals into injection drug use (IDU), given its many harms. As IDU is a socially communicable phenomenon, efforts must focus on preventing the involvement of people who currently inject drugs (PWID) in initiating others. As North American PWID disproportionately identify as sexual or gender minorities, and up to one-third are estimated to be female, such interventions must consider how gender and sexuality shape IDU initiation events. Both women as well as sexual and gender minorities (SGM) face structural and interpersonal vulnerabilities that increase their risk of drug-related harms once they begin injecting, but little is known about how this social context contributes to IDU initiation. This project will contribute to preventing IDU initiation among women and SGM by identifying how gender and sexuality shape initiation events, and how gender dynamics impact the effectiveness of health system interventions to reduce the risk that PWID initiate others into IDU. This mixed-methods research will draw on quantitative and qualitative data from Preventing Injecting by Modifying Existing Responses, a five-year multi-site study pooling data from four observational cohorts of people who inject drugs in Canada, the United States, Mexico, and France. Additional original qualitative data will be collected from SGM who inject drugs in the Tijuana-San Diego border region. This study will be the first to examine pathways to IDU for SGM. Employing integrated knowledge translation, this study will move the research field from identifying gender and sexual orientation disparities related to injection drug use towards intervening to reduce them. It will also help to ensure that the prevention benefits of current and emerging injection prevention interventions are fully realized for Canadians of diverse genders and sexualities.

column36: Mechanisms and Markers of Reduced Penetrance in LRRK2 Mutation Carriers using Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
column37: Parkinson disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder affecting movement and cognition. The greatest burden is to patients and families, affecting over 100,000 Canadians with >2.5 billion dollars. The main drug treatment is L-dopa which helps the motoric symptoms but fails to halt the progression of disease. Development of treatment to halt disease progression has been limited. The most common pathogenic mutation that causes sporadic and familial PD is LRRK2 (Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) p.G2019S. LRRK2 mutations accounts for up to 40% of sporadic PD in Tunisia. However, the penetrance of LRRK2 p.G2019S is highly variable. Given the relatively high rate of occurrence of LRRK2 mutations, finding markers for and elucidating mechanisms of reduced penetrance has a high imperative. I have previously identified DNM3 (Dynamin 3) as a potential genetic modifier of disease penetrance in LRRK2 p.G2019S carriers. I now hypothesize that biological mechanisms including dynamin-related proteins can modulate the phenoconversion of LRRK2 p.G2019S and the identification of these mechanisms will provide insight for developing treatments for patients. We propose that there are large genetic and biological influences that explain the differences in age-at-onset in families with LRRK2 p.G2019S. We will select skin cells from specific individuals to make induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs) to differentiate into human neurons. Molecular, cellular and physiological studies of LRRK2 p.G2019S human will be characterized at a high-throughput 'omics' level.

column36: Simple Machines on a Nanoscale
column37: Important secreted-protein signaling loops exist in several cancers that sustain their growth and promotes cancer cell proliferation. Evidence suggests that persistent DNA damage due to genome instability in certain cancers results in cytoplasmic DNA that causes persistent activation of cellular signaling proteins called cGAS and STING. cGAS is an enzyme present in the cytoplasm that binds cytoplasmic DNA and catalyzes the formation of a small molecule called cGAMP. cGAMP can bind to the adaptor protein STING, which results in the activation of immune signaling and cytokine protein production. There are several cancers, such as multiple myeloma, fibrosarcoma, malignant astrocytoma and a mouse melanoma, that require the constant presence of certain cytokine or growth factor proteins to survive and/or proliferate. From our unpublished and preliminary data, we have discovered that in certain biological contexts the cGAS-STING pathway can cause constant production of some of the same cytokines and growth factor proteins that the aforementioned cancers require. We propose that in several cancers, the cGAS-STING pathway is critical for tumor-promoting protein-secretion loops. Verification of our findings could identify previously unknown signaling network relationships and will suggest the viability of new cancer therapy drugs that block the cGAS-STING pathway.

column37: In response to stresses such as heart attack or high blood pressure, the heart grows through an enlargement of the heart muscle - a process called cardiac hypertrophy. Although cardiac hypertrophy initially helps the heart pump blood more effectively, long term cardiac hypertrophy ultimately leads to heart failure. Patients with heart failure have shortness of breath, fluid retention and an inability to exercise. Furthermore, someone who has heart failure has a ~40% chance of dying within 5 years of the diagnosis. This research proposal is designed to more clearly define the molecular mechanisms that control cardiac hypertrophy, with the long term goal of developing new drugs to treat humans with heart failure.

column36: Impact of co-abuse of alcohol and cannabis on cognition: Identifying the roles of the dopamine and endocannabinoid systems
column37: Abuse of cannabis or alcohol causes profound harm to the brain, resulting in impaired cognitive functioning. These harms may be exacerbated when these drugs are abused together, which typically happens for the first time during adolescence. Since the brain does not fully mature until young adulthood, adolescent boys and girls who co-abuse alcohol and cannabis are vulnerable to developing impairments in memory and impulse control. These cognitive functions are supported by a network of brain regions, where specific signaling mechanisms (e.g., the dopamine and endogenous cannabinoid systems) can be disrupted by drug abuse. It is unknown how co-abuse of cannabis and alcohol impacts the development of these systems, and how cognition is compromised as a result. In view of the impending legalization of cannabis in Canada, it is critical that the associated harms be identified. This research will characterize the long-term cognitive impairments caused by the co-abuse of cannabis and alcohol during adolescence, using male and female rats as a model. During a developmental period that corresponds with human adolescence, rats will be exposed to either the psychoactive ingredient of cannabis (e.g., THC); alcohol; THC plus alcohol; or no drugs at all, each day for three weeks. After two weeks, the degree of cognitive impairment in impulse control and memory will be assessed using touchscreens, a method that is analogous to cognitive tasks used in humans. Using imaging techniques, the impact of drug exposure on the dopamine and endogenous cannabinoid systems will be quantified and correlated with the changes in cognition observed. This research will identify the cognitive impairments caused by the co-abuse of cannabis and alcohol during adolescence, and their neural foundations. These findings will advise policy-makers and the general population of the potential consequences of simultaneous alcohol and cannabis use.

column37: Over 235,000 Canadians are homeless annually, and more than 5,000 are homeless on any given night in Toronto. Homelessness is associated with high rates of mental illness, such as psychotic illness, drug dependence, major depression, and personality disorders. The pan-Canadian research project At Home/Chez Soi showed that homeless mentally ill people tend to be high users of acute mental health services, such as hospitals and emergency departments. These public services, plus shelters, ambulances, police, and jails, are estimated to cost nearly $53,000 per homeless person per year. Meanwhile, the same people are also less likely than their housed counterparts to seek care in the community in the form of appointments with a family doctor or a psychiatrist. There are multiple explanations for the preferential use of acute care settings in comparison with outpatient settings, such as competing priorities, stigma, and barriers to care. Our study will be the first to analyze the social and clinical situation of homeless people suffering from mental illness on the scale of a whole state or country. No study has yet investigated the kind of care the homeless receive directly after their discharge from a psychiatric hospital. I will use health administrative data to examine all patients discharged from an Ontario psychiatric hospital during a three-year period. My main hypothesis is that upon their discharge from a psychiatric hospital, people who are homeless will be less likely to receive a physician follow-up and more likely to be rehospitalized or to revisit the emergency department. They will also have a higher mortality rate. Evidence found in this study will help with planning and designing programs that will improve access to care for homeless people.

column36: Callous-Unemotional Traits in Children with Severe Disruptive Behaviour: Identification of Treatment Mechanisms
column37: Widely used treatment programs for children with behavioural problems include parent and child components to improve problem solving and emotion regulation skills. However, these programs are not effective for a significant number of children. This study will identify child-specific factors that contribute to diminished treatment effects and pilot a promising treatment in order to better intervene with these factors to improve outcomes. Empathy is a prosocial emotion that is associated with healthy childhood social development. However, children who have problems understanding and expressing empathy tend to show more persistent and severe behaviour problems compared to their peers. They are also particularly difficult to treat. Working with parents to help children develop empathy may be an effective route to reducing children's aggression and improving their social behaviour. For example, research demonstrates that when a parent shows more warmth, their child has fewer problems expressing empathy. As such, intervening to help parents teach empathy skills by facilitating parental warmth is a promising avenue for intervention. The objective of this study is to understand how parenting with warmth affects children's expressions of empathy and behaviour problems over the course of treatment. The first part will look at these relationships in an ongoing treatment trial for children with behaviour problems aged 6-12 years. The second part will recruit a sample of children with low empathy skills who do not show sufficient response to the original treatment. These children will be randomly assigned to either receive the additional treatment or to a wait-list condition (whereby they receive the treatment after 8 weeks). This project will provide important information on child factors that contribute to the severity of children's behaviour difficulties and that interfere with their treatment response; this will identify new avenues to improving treatment outcomes.

column36: Delineating the relationship between posttraumatic stress disorder and alcohol consumption: Examining in-the-moment processes and genetic moderation
column37: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a pernicious and debilitating mental health condition. The annual cost of AUD among Canadians is estimated at 14.6 billion and, globally, alcohol is among the leading contributors to disability and premature death. High rates of co-occurrence between AUD and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) have been firmly established. Furthermore, co-occurring AUD/PTSD renders individuals more vulnerable to a host of poorer outcomes. AUD has been theorized to develop following traumatic event exposure through attempts to alleviate emotional distress and cope with symptoms of PTSD. Genetic factors and deficits inhibiting responses in the presence of alcohol cues have also been implicated as contributing to AUD/PTSD. However, our understanding of AUD in relation to PTSD is limited due to a reliance on self-report measures of alcohol use. This research will extend the literature by using laboratory-based experiments involving self-administration of alcohol to increase our understanding of associations between trauma exposure, PTSD symptoms, and alcohol-related problems and use. Specifically, an established alcohol self-administration task will be coupled with a PTSD-specific stress reactivity protocol to uncover mechanisms associated with AUD/PTSD. This is the first study to evaluate alcohol consumption using a self-administration protocol among individuals with PTSD. This is also the first studies to investigate a polymorphism of the serotonin transporter gene among humans with AUD/PTSD. The findings of this research are necessary to elucidate our understanding of the development and maintenance of AUD in relation to PTSD, and to identify Canadians at greatest risk for AUD/PTSD. Moreover, these results may guide the development of prevention strategies and inform the most efficacious and parsimonious intervention efforts for individuals with AUD/PTSD, ultimately improving the health of Canadians.

column36: Identification and network-based characterization of molecular biomarkers associated with treatment outcomes in major depressive disorder.
column37: Depression is a serious mental condition which affects individuals of all ages, and with more women affected than men. According to WHO rankings, depression is the fourth leading factor of disability worldwide. As a result, depression also poses a significant burden to healthcare systems. Although there are numerous antidepressant drugs available, finding the right medication for the right patient has remained challenging. It is known that depression and drug response are genetically mediated, however, more research is needed using well-characterized samples. A confounding factor has been that a large proportion of depressed patients respond to placebo, but placebo effects have remained understudied with only a few genetic studies conducted. My research aims to evaluate computational models that will be used to predict which patients are likely to respond to treatment by investigating genomic DNA, clinical, and demographic characteristics. To achieve this goal, I will use a large and well-characterized sample composed of 450 individuals treated with an antidepressant or placebo. I will use the most advanced computational models to develop algorithms that will predict response to either treatment. The proposed study is part of the larger CAN-BIND (Canadian Biomarker Integration Network in Depression) program. In addition, I have access to a second large and well-characterized cohort of patients treated for late-life depression, which will serve as my independent sample and independent placebo-treated sample (n=257). The proposed work has the potential to significantly broaden our knowledge on the genetics of treatment response in depression. Detailed knowledge about genetic determinants of drug response represents the first steps towards personalized medicine and tailored treatment for individual patients.

column36: Monoamine Oxidase B in Major Depressive Disorder
column37: According to the World Health Organization, in countries like Canada, clinical depression is the leading cause of death and disability. Four per cent of Canadians suffer from clinical depression, and in half of these cases the clinical depression is treatment resistant. We think that one cause of treatment resistance is that commonly used current treatments which raise a brain chemical called serotonin miss key brain changes in clinical depression. We think the approach to overcoming treatment resistance is to discover these key biological changes and to carefully match treatment to such changes so as to improve rates of treatment response. We have begun to discover a new biological change in clinical depression, which is increased levels of a protein in the brain called MAO-B. MAO-B has several properties, including having an effect opposite to antioxidants, and removing brain chemicals that support normal mood. In this study, using a unique brain imaging technology only available in Toronto, we will determine whether MAO-B level is increased in brain regions that influence mood during clinical depression and treatment resistant clinical depression. Then we will study whether cases of clinical depression with elevated MAO-B levels will preferentially respond to a special antidepressant that shuts down MAO-B. These are the first definitive studies of MAO-B in clinical depression. If we find that elevated MAO-B predicts clinical response to the treatment that shuts down MAO-B, this could be developed as a new way to match specific treatment to specific biology in clinical depression so as to get better treatment outcomes.

column36: Characterizing the roles of RIF1 and 53BP1 in DNA double strand break repair pathways in the context of PARP1 inhibition
column37: Women carrying mutations in the BRCA1 gene has over 50% chance of developing breast cancer. A recent class of chemotherapeutics, poly ADP ribose polymerase 1 (PARP1) inhibitors, has shown promising results in BRCA1-mutated breast cancer. However, several resistance mechanisms to PARP inhibitors have been observed. The BRCA1 gene product, along with the 53BP1 protein, determines how cells repair DNA double strand breaks. Since normal 53BP1 function is required for PARP1 inhibition, which induces DNA damage, understanding its functions in DNA damage repair is essential for characterizing and mitigating chemotherapy resistance. This proposal focuses on analyzing how 53BP1 interacts with its effector RIF1 to prevent BRCA1 recruitment to DNA damage sites. The binding interface consisting of the RIF1 HEAT repeats and phosphorylated 53BP1 will be analyzed by mutational analysis and structural biology approaches. Effectors of RIF1 in DNA damage repair pathways will be identified by comparative mass spectrometry identification of RIF1 binding partners in normal and DNA damage conditions. Mutations and proteins identified by these approaches will be tremendously useful for specifically probing RIF1 and 53BP1 function and characterizing the different DNA damage repair pathways in the cell.

column36: Breaking the chain of maternally transmitted obesity: oligofructose supplementation during gestation and lactation and its impact on muscle function in offspring
column37: In 2015, the Canadian Medical Association declared obesity to be a chronic medical disease requiring enhanced research, treatment and prevention efforts. Early life events are now recognized to play an important role in lifelong susceptibility to obesity. One important risk factor for childhood obesity is having a mother who is obese during pregnancy and lactation. In turn, children with obesity have a high likelihood of becoming adults with obesity. A successful obesity intervention must break this cycle. The high energy demands of skeletal muscle give it great potential to help prevent and treat obesity and associated metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes. However, skeletal muscles are structurally and functionally impaired in obesity, with greater content of fat and fibrotic material and reductions in insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake. Additionally, obesity is associated with a lower capacity for muscle to produce force when controlling for muscle size. This would make physical activity more difficult, and may encourage sedentary behavior. Our collaborator, Dr. Raylene Reimer, has a well-established rat model of maternally-transmitted obesity in which female rats are fed a high fat, high sugar diet throughout pregnancy and lactation. Importantly, she has shown that supplementing the diet of mother rats with oligofructose (a prebiotic, soluble dietary fibre) during pregnancy results in offspring with lower body fat and improved insulin sensitivity. My research aims to 1) understand the cause of the muscle weakness associated with obesity, and 2) determine if maternal oligofructose supplementation can improve muscle structure and function in offspring. This work will be done in the lab of Dr. Walter Herzog, who has the best equipped lab in the Western Hemisphere in which to study muscle structure and function. This research has a strong chance of identifying an intervention that can protect young muscles from the negative influence of poor maternal diet.

column36: Oncolytic rhabdovirus vaccines as an adjuvant to adoptive T cell therapy for paediatric metastatic rhabdomyosarcomas: Precision targeting, expansion and trafficking
column37: A childhood cancer diagnosis is a tragic, seemingly unfair, reality for nearly 1000 families in Canada each year. Innovations in treatment have been able to increase the odds of beating a paediatric cancer, but this success is a double edged-sword. Many of these treatment make kids unimaginably sick. These therapies can be so toxic that they result in life-long disabilities in cognition, fertility, and even the formation of cancer again. Further, some children's cancers we are just not good at treating at all. For example, rhabdomyosarcomas that have travelled to other parts of the body have an expected survival as low as 20%. We believe that childhood cancer can be combatted more effectively, and without long-term toxicities, by implementing a new form of cancer treatment called immunotherapy. Cancers form when tumours are able to shut-down the immune system. Immunotherapy is a treatment that re-educates the body's immune system to fight the cancer by reactivating immune cells. In some adult cancers, immunotherapy is producing unprecedented durable responses (aka 'cures'). It is these types of responses that is pushing immunotherapy to the forefront of cancer treatment. In this research, we will evaluate if these responses can be achieved in childhood cancers, starting with metastatic rhabdomyosarcomas. Viruses are powerful tools in our arsenal against cancer. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are live viruses engineered such that they specifically infect and kill cancer cells. Decades of work has now demonstrated that OVs are also potent activators of the immune system. However, research also demonstrates that OV therapy alone is insufficient. This proposed research will evaluate OVs as a 'booster shot' for another immunotherapy, adoptive T cell therapy (ACT), to rapidly direct immune responses to the cancer. "OV-ACT" has the potential to become an effective, non-toxic, therapy for rhabdomyosarcoma and likely other childhood cancers.

column36: Structural mechanism of Plk1 activation by Aurora A and the phospho-protein Bora: implications for cell cycle regulation and therapeutic intervention in human cancers
column37: Cell division is a biological process in which a mother cell divides into two daughter cells. This natural phenomenon is indispensable for the development of organisms and for the regeneration of cells within damaged tissues. The precise control of cell division in space and time is essential for the survival of an organism and defects in the control of cell division can lead to human diseases such as cancer. Cell division is carried out by a myriad of proteins including a class of enzymes called protein kinases, which act by transferring a tag called phosphate onto other proteins. The proposed research is focused on the protein kinase Plk1 (Polo-like kinase 1). Plk1 is essential for cell division but too much leads to cells that grow and divide uncontrollably. Indeed we see that Plk1 is present at exceedingly high levels in a wide range of cancers and these high levels correlate with poor outcomes for patient survival. Therefore, understanding precisely how Plk1 is turned on and off in a controlled manner will be essential for understanding its contribution to cancer formation and potentially cancer treatment. Two additional proteins under investigation in this proposal are Bora and the protein kinase Aurora A. Both participate in turning on Plk1 but how they do so is a mystery. I propose to study how Bora and Aurora A work together to turn on Plk1 by looking at how they interact with one another using a technique called X-ray crystallography. This technique allows us to visualize the three proteins in action at the level of the atom. By seeing how these three proteins work together, it will reveal ways to turn off the process with drug like molecules which would provide a starting point to develop real drugs to treat and cure human cancers.

column36: Timing of referral to nephrology care and impact on kidney failure, hospitalization and mortality in people with chronic kidney disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects about one in 10 Canadians and is associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease and kidney failure. In an attempt to lower these risks, guidelines recommend early referral to kidney specialist services for people with CKD. However, the studies supporting this recommendation are of low quality and may have led to biased conclusions. Specifically, existing studies include only people who eventually started dialysis, as opposed to the vast majority of CKD population not yet treated with dialysis and whose family doctors must decide whether to refer to a kidney specialist, and when. In addition, the observation in existing studies that longer pre-dialysis nephrology care leads to better patient outcomes following dialysis start could be explained by the fact that people who have rapidly progressive kidney disease tend to require dialysis sooner making the length of pre-dialysis care is shorter. These people tend to be sicker and are therefore more likely to have poor health outcomes. In contrast, people who are healthy and have kidney disease that progresses more slowly tend to be followed for a longer time in pre-dialysis clinics. It is unclear if longer pre-dialysis care is a marker for a healthier patient, or if the care provided in pre-dialysis clinics leads to improved patient outcomes. The proposed research will take these factors into account and leverage detailed Alberta provincial data sources to assess the impact of timing of referral to kidney specialist services on kidney failure, hospitalization and death in people with CKD. Given the large patient population, the widespread practice of early referral and limited health care resources, this unique work is expected to provide high-quality evidence to inform referral guidelines and health policy, identify areas of clinical focus to improve outcomes, and stimulate future research.

column36: Mechanistic underpinnings of fetal programming: How maternal bisphenol exposure gets translated into changes in the developing brain.
column37: The hypothalamus is a critical brain region for regulating behaviour, appetite, and mood, and also controls numerous hormone signaling pathways leading to effects throughout the body. However, the specifics of how this region organizes in the developing fetus remain poorly understood. This is increasingly important, as altered hypothalamic development is thought to underlie psychological and developmental disorders including depression, autism, and even schizophrenia. Using a common lab fish species for preliminary studies, our lab discovered that bisphenols such as bisphenol A (BPA), the molecule found to leach from plastics, can disrupt neuron formation in the hypothalamus, even at extremely low doses that match those found in a major river in Alberta. Here, I will determine if the BPA effects observed in the fish hypothalamus are also applicable to mammals, specifically mice, as a necessary precursor to applying the findings to human health and development. We will feed pregnant mice BPA-laced food and examine the brains of offspring for altered development. We will also isolate fetal mouse brain cells and apply BPA directly to them in tissue culture and measure changes in cell division. BPA is an endocrine disrupting chemical, meaning it mimics hormones in the body. We expect it will work through hormone pathways and a key goal of this project is to identify exactly how BPA modulates hormone pathways in the developing brain and what effects this may have on behaviour, mood, and health later in life. We will also study mice born to mothers exposed to BPA, as well as multiple future generations, to model how BPA causes changes transgenerationally. Altogether this study will provide important evidence as to the dangers of maternal exposure to BPA on fetal brain development in mammals, with a specific focus on the hypothalamus, the key hormone regulator that when malformed, can lead to major developmental and behavioural disorders later in life.

column36: Tailoring antigen-specific regulatory T cells for use in transplantation
column37: Transplantation is the best and sometimes only treatment for end-stage organ failure. In the last ten years, the lives of more than 20,000 Canadians have been improved, extended, or saved by donated organs. Immunosuppressive drugs make transplantation possible, but since these drugs cannot suppress just the cells reactive to the transplanted organ but suppress the entire immune system, these drugs come at the price of an increase in infection and cancer risk. The drugs are also not perfect; many organs are still lost to rejection. Our goal is to improve the success of transplantation, by finding ways to re-educate the recipient's immune system to tolerate the transplanted organ. Our strategy is to harness the natural immunosuppressive properties of a type of white blood cell called T regulatory cells (Tregs). Tregs naturally regulate immune responses by ensuring the immune system attacks infectious or harmful substances without over-reacting to self or non-harmful foreign proteins. In the last 10 years, research has shown that Tregs could be used as a cell-based therapy to induce immune tolerance and prevent organ rejection. The efficacy of Treg cell therapies can be significantly enhanced if the cellular product is enriched for Tregs that recognize an target that is specific to the transplanted organ. Dr Levings' lab developed a method to improve the potency of Tregs by engineering them to express a protein that activates them when they are in the presence of a transplant. My goal is thus to study the potential of those engineered Tregs to control allograft rejection and lower the chances that transplant recipients will reject the donor organ.

column37: This program of research will produce practical tools for evaluating the readiness for sustainable integration of a mobile health intervention, the PIERS app, in a low-resourced health system setting. This app is currently being evaluated in a cluster randomized controlled trial to determine impact of its use on maternal and perinatal mortality and major morbidity. column36: Novel mechanisms for the regulation of G-protein coupled receptors in hypertension
column37: The primary objective of the proposal is to understand how hormones that circulate in the blood to regulate blood pressure alter the activity of the receptors that are expressed in blood vessels. We are interested in horomone called angiotensin II that activates angiotensin receptors. Angiotensin receptors are on the surface of cells that form blood vessels and the activation of these receptors leads to blood vessel constriction, hence, they are important for maintenance of normal blood pressure and heart function. Alterations in the receptor activity of angiotensin II has been shown to be associated with hypertension and congestive heart failure. Our goal is to better understand how other proteins expressed in blood vessels regulate the activity of these receptors under normal conditions and how changes in regulation of receptor activity lead to disease. We will investigate the effects of a loss in the expression of an enzyme called G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2), known to phosphorylate and inactivates the receptor. The loss of GRK2 results in altered angiotensin receptor signaling in blood vessels and leads to the development of hypertension in mice, but the exact mechanism remain largely unknown. We will utilize these hypertensive mice to understand the role of GRK2 in angiotensin II receptor signaling. We will also study a protein called Rab4 that controls the movement of receptors between different compartments in the cell. Therefore, we will assess the effect of changing Rab4 expression on angiotensin receptor delivery to the cell membrane via testing whether the overexpression of a malfunctioning Rab4 protein will generate hypertensive mice. Understanding the mechanism(s) by which angiotensin signaling is regulated is crucial to delineate the underlying pathways for the development and/or progression of hypertension. A better understanding of these pathways is key for the generation of novel approaches for treating cardiovascular disease.

column36: Alloantigen-specific regulatory T cells generated with a chimeric antigen receptor: ability to prevent the humoral alloimmune response
column37: Pathologies linked to end-stage organ failure represent the second cause of morbi-mortality worldwide and have major socio-economic consequences. Transplantation, which consists in the substitution of a defective organ by a functioning graft retrieved from a donor, is the best therapeutic option. Because the donor is from the same species but genetically different from the recipient, immune system of the latter inevitably recognizes donor-specific determinants expressed by the graft. The immune response that develops against donor-specific determinants is responsible for tissue damages, which lead to allograft dysfunction, a process called rejection. Organ damage is caused either by T lymphocytes, a process named cellular rejection, or by donor-specific antibodies(DSA), a process named antibody-mediated rejection (AMR). It is now widely acknowledged that AMR is the main cause of long-term organ loss. This is explained by the lack of reliable therapy to prevent DSA formation. Developing new approaches to prevent AMR has become one of the main challenge of transplantation medicine. Pr Levings' group (BC Children's Hospital Research Institute, Vancouver, where the project will take place) has just recently developed an innovative method of cell therapy to prevent allograft rejection. In this approach, recipient's T cells with tolerogenic properties (regulatory T cell, Treg) are genetically engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) and recognize donor-specific determinants. The group has obtained robust experimental evidence that these "educated" Treg have a remarkable ability to prevent cellular responses when transferred to recipients. In the present project, we will test for the first time the ability of donor-specific CAR Tregs to prevent AMR. We will try to potentiate inhibition of DSA formation through specific in vitro manipulations of CAR Tregs. This project could lead to a novel therapeutic approach to prevent antibody-mediated rejection.

column36: Neuroprotective effects of upper extremity skilled learning in people with multiple sclerosis
column37: Approximately half of people with multiple sclerosis (MS) report impairments in hand function. These individuals have difficulty performing everyday tasks, such as using eating utensils, and buttoning clothing. Challenges in activities of daily living can result in reduced community involvement. Inactivity not only leads to a decreased quality of life, but also affects disability development on a neurological level. While natural MS disease progression worsens neurological function, high levels of inactivity and disuse of the hands can advance the formation of lesions and declination of myelin in the brain. Therefore, new therapies that increase hand use are essential to the overall health of people with MS. Our proposed project will involve learning a new motor skill with both hands. Putting a golf ball or shooting a basketball are examples of skills; they involve performing movements to achieve a goal. Acquiring a skill is the key ingredient to our rehabilitation therapy. Learning a skill produces positive changes in brain tissue, such as myelin. To investigate the effects of practicing a skill, individuals will perform an at home-based therapy that requires goal-directed hand use. We believe encouraging individuals to learn motor skills will improve brain and hand function in people with MS.

column36: Ethical Guidance and Regulation of Pharmaceutical Direct-to-Consumer Communication: Building Consensus between Industry Decision-Makers and Public Policy-Makers
column37: Direct-to-consumer communication (DTCC) of pharmaceutical drugs refers to all messages sponsored by a pharmaceutical company, disseminated mostly through television, magazines, and the Internet. Although visions may be highly polarized about its benefits and risks, both proponents and opponents agree that DTCC has strong potential to shape treatment-seeking behaviours and influence interactions between patients and their healthcare providers. Thus, ethical guidance and regulation are needed. However, current national and international regulation of DTCC is deficient in two ways. First, it lacks consistency between countries, causing citizens of countries with strongly prohibitive regulation to receive unregulated communications that transcended national boundaries. Second, regulation lags behind industry practices, allowing new means of communications such as social media and mobile applications to remain unregulated. Various stakeholders have different visions of how to regulate DTCC and there is a need to better understand the sources of their disagreements and the rationale for current regulations. Historically, there has been very little discussion between various stakeholders, locally in a given country, or globally between various countries to ensure consistency. This project aims to initiate an international conversation between industry decision-makers and public policy-makers, as a means to generate consensual ideas to 1) bring DTCC ethical guidance and regulation up-to-date with current and emerging technology use, and 2) improve coherence in ethical guidance and regulation between countries. Ultimately, this project will contribute to improving patients' experience of healthcare delivery because a smarter and better coordinated approach to DTCC regulation will enable respect of the values at the very root of regulation, that is, the duty to protect public health and enable patients to make fully informed and autonomous decisions.

column36: Multimodal characterization of airway remodeling with label-free nonlinear optical imaging and spectroscopy
column37: Direct costs of asthma, which include medical/nursing care and medication, in Canada are estimated at $600 million per year, currently use 14% of Canadian health care funding, making it the second most expensive disease to treat. Unfortunately, around 200 Canadians die from asthma each year. We now understand that structural changes within the airway of asthmatic patients, termed airway remodeling, are currently unresponsive to existing asthma medications. The healthy lung is able to inflate and deflate as we breathe due to a net of collagen and elastic fibres. However, in asthma patients, the airways within the lung are continually injured. This constant injury results in a build-up of scarring due to non-elastic fibres, such as collagen,which reduces the normal lung capacity. Our objective is to use a new type of microscope called nonlinear optical microscopy (NLOM), for the first time on asthmatic and non-asthmatic lungs. The NLOM will help us to understand the 3-dimensional changes in the lung tissues (e.g. elastic and collagen fibres) with disease. Changes, such as fiber length, thickness, and alignment, can be quantified by examining nonlinear optical (NLO) images using mathematic models. Using these tools, our data suggests that collagen and elastic fibers are more disorganized and disrupted in asthmatic subjects. Furthermore, the cells responsible for collagen and elastin production seem to be defective in asthmatic airways. The ultimate goal of this research is to provide researchers and clinicians with important information, from which medications to repair collagen/elastin fibers to prevent scarring of the lung could be developed in the future.

column36: Rejuvenating aged muscle stem cells by targeting aberrant biophysical signalling.
column37: Progressive skeletal muscle wasting with age, also known as sarcopenia, is detrimental to the quality of life and overall health of seniors. This is attributable in part to the deterioration and loss of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) required to repair tissue damage. MuSCs isolated from aged muscles show an altered molecular response to environmental cues, leading to poor proliferation and defective regeneration. However, mechanistic understanding of how aged MuSCs integrate signals from their microenvironment remains unknown. By deconstructing the cross talk between biophysical and biochemical signaling, we propose to elucidate how aged MuSCs sense their environment. Moreover, we will study how these aberrant biophysical signalling affect the repair functions of aged MuSCs and target these changes to enhance regeneration in aged muscles. These studies will identify novel mechanisms of MuSC aging that can be targeted as therapies to delay or reverse the loss of regenerative function in the aged.

column36: The impact of aging on the biology of endurance exercise-derived exosomes
column37: Canada's population aged 60 years and older will nearly triple within 50 years, and those older than 80 represent one of the fastest growing subpopulations in the country. Currently, they represent ~15% of the population but account for ~40% of hospital services in provincial and territorial health care spending. The impact of aging on muscle health and general well-being is broad and multi-faceted, including impaired function, increased morbidity and reduced quality of life. Exercise is a fundamental component of human health, as regular physical activity has been shown to reduce the risk of physical disability, chronic diseases, and extend the functional lifespan. The benefits of endurance exercise appear to be systemic, as they occur not only in muscle but across many other tissues as well. The term 'exerkines' can be used describe factors released in response to exercise without indicating a specific tissue or organ of origin, contained within cellular packages called exosomes. These complex systemic signals, responsible for these metabolic benefits following exercise, have not been elucidated. Understanding these factors in the context of aging is crucial to the development of therapeutic interventions and strategies in order to reduce age-related co-morbidities and disease. Thus, the aim of this study proposal is to use a human exercise model to describe the exercise-induced factors that provide systemic benefits and further our understanding of how they are transported to the muscle, organs and other tissues in the context of aging. To investigate this, we will compare the biology of exerkines following short- and long-term exercise in older as compared to young individuals. Thus, our main goal is to identify how the aging process affects the biology of exerkines in response to exercise. Our findings will further our understanding of exercise physiology, helping inform and develop therapies to help mitigate the various comorbidities of human aging.

column36: Design and Implementation of a Novel High-Throughput Screening Platform to Subvert Serum Survival Strategies of Antibiotic Resistant Bacteria
column37: Infections cause by antibiotic resistant bacteria, or 'superbugs', have become one of the greatest threats to our healthcare system. Infections that were once considered relatively benign and easy to treat are now becoming life-threatening due to our inability to prescribe effective antibiotic therapy. As antibiotic resistance spreads, our current arsenal of antibiotics is rapidly becoming obsolete. Although the obvious solution to this problem is to develop new antibiotics, no novel class of antibiotic has been approved in the last 30 years. One approach to modern-day antibiotic discovery involves screening thousands of natural or synthetic chemicals to identify those which kill bacteria in rich growth medium. Unfortunately, antibacterial molecules identified in this way rarely translate into clinically successful antibiotics. Creative strategies to increase the likelihood of identifying new and effective antibiotics are urgently needed. To this end, this proposal aims to identify antibacterial molecules through an innovative screening approach that specifically targets bacteria that cause bloodstream infections. Bloodstream infections (BSI) caused by antibiotic resistant bacteria are life-threatening, and in some circumstances can result in death of 50% of patients. Although blood contains antibacterial activity, pathogenic bacteria have developed strategies that allow them to survive and grow in human blood. These survival strategies are not targeted by current antibiotics, and thus represent an untapped potential for the development of novel therapies. By screening for molecules that inhibit bacterial growth in blood, but not rich growth medium, I believe that these survival strategies can be subverted. I aim to develop such a platform to screen thousands of small molecules in order to identify molecules that specifically inhibit the ability of bacteria to survive in blood. This research could pave the way for new treatments for BSI.

column36: Hormonal Contraceptives, the Vaginal Microbiome, and Susceptibility to Sexually Transmitted Infections
column37: When it comes to gender, not all things are equal. In terms of reproductive health, women are at a higher risk than men for a number of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Women are at an increased risk of Herpes and Chlamydia, and they are at a 2-5 times greater risk of acquiring Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) than men. There are several reasons for this including anatomy, hormones, and the menstrual cycle. Recent research has shown that another reason why women are at increased risk of STIs might be the bacteria that live in the vagina, that play a central role in protecting against infections. The bacteria are controlled by hormones, which are also the active ingredients in birth control. In fact, there are many studies that show that women may be at an increased risk of getting HIV from sexual contact if they are on the injectable birth control (Depo-Provera). In this proposal, we want to know if Depo-Provera is increasing diversity of the bacteria in the vagina, and making it easier for STIs like HIV to infect women. The goals of this project are to 1) look at how Depo-Provera affects the bacteria living in the vaginal tract which serve to protect against infection, 2) determine if giving Depo-Provera to mice with a human immune system increases bacterial diversity in the vagina and increases their chances of an HIV infection, and 3) show that an experimental change favouring more diverse bacteria in the vagina makes it easier for HIV to infect humanized mice. We want to understand if women on Depo-Provera have more "unhealthy" bacteria in their vaginal canals, and if Depo-Provera and/or "unhealthy" bacteria make it easier for HIV infection to occur in a humanized mouse model of infection. There are over 100 million women world-wide who use contraceptives, and this research will help better understand STIs in women and identify new factors that affect the risk of STIs. This will allow women to make more informed choices about their birth control method

column37: The health of mothers and children internationally is an important priority for the Canadian government. Using accurate research to make decisions about where to spend health dollars is essential because it ensures that monies are well spent and have the biggest impact for mothers and children. The information gained from this study will ensure that decisions about international health spending are fair, effective and ultimately improve the health of mothers and their children.

column36: Chemical-genomics approach to identify new targets for antibiotics in Salmonella Typhimurium
column37: Antibiotic drug resistance has reached crisis levels, in part because modern drug discovery attempts have failed to identify new antibiotics. The solution to this crisis requires a paradigm shift from traditional drug discovery platforms. Most antibiotics target a small number of bacterial processes, including ribosome function, cell wall synthesis, and DNA topology. Many small molecule screening campaigns employ reductionist approaches focused on a small number of validated target proteins. Traditionally, genes that are required for bacterial growth in standard laboratory conditions were pursued as drug targets. However, in the course of an infection bacteria encounter many harsh environments that are a component of the natural host defence against microbes (innate immunity). Bacteria such as Salmonella evade the innate immune response and in some cases use innate immunity as a signal to promote pathogenesis. I propose that the genes and bacterial processes involved in subverting the immune response are suitable candidates for development of fresh antibiotics. In the work proposed here I will use high-throughput genetic arrays to find genes and pathways in Salmonella that allow this pathogen to subvert the host immune response. I will use this knowledge to develop a screen of 50,000 natural products, pre-approved drugs, and chemically diverse small molecules to identify new leads for the development of antibiotics. This pilot screen can be scaled-up to include ~500,000 compounds. This research will help us begin to unravel the complex genetic interactions that govern bacterial pathogenesis and could identify new leads for antibiotics targeting Gram-negative bacteria.

column36: Applying novel genomics approaches to infectious disease epidemiology: shared rare variants for inferring transmission of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
column37: Gonorrhea is a sexually-transmitted infection that affects over 100 million people world-wide. Due to widespread antibiotic resistance, only one treatment approach is still effective against the causative bacteria (Neisseria gonorrhoeae). Recent studies are inconclusive; some suggest it is mainly acquired during antibiotic treatment, while others suggest it is mainly transmitted from person to person. Experimental data using animal models suggest some resistant strains are more fit, potentially making it easier for them to be transmitted than sensitive strains. Understanding these factors is critical to develop effective public health interventions. To address this, I will examine the genome (DNA) of N. gonorrhoeae from persons diagnosed in Australasia between 2013-2015. First, I will develop the bioinformatics workflow to analyze this genetic data. In order to determine how much drug resistance is due to transmission of already-resistant bacteria, I will then identify or refute transmission between individuals by considering how closely related their bacteria is to one another, their drug resistance profile and epidemiological contact. Next, I will apply these methods to a public health surveillance project for Victoria, Australia, wherein epidemiologic data (e.g., sex, HIV, number of sexual contacts) will be collected along with corresponding bacterial DNA. Using these data, I will identify who infected whom and use regression to assess potential differences in the number of secondary cases (people infected by others) between persons with resistant and sensitive strains, accounting for patient-level risk factors for transmission. This study will contribute to our understanding of transmission of drug-resistant strains. If there is evidence of greater transmissibility of drug-resistant strains, independent of patient characteristics, this will further support the need for rapid antibiotic testing and help public health prioritize contact investigation.

column36: Detection of cognitive impairment with high frame rate ultrasound (HiFRUS) estimation of carotid wall shear stress in older adults
column37: Recently, there has been growing interest on the link between arterial health and the risk of cognitive impairment in older adults, with previous research focused on arterial markers such as brain blood flow, the stiffness of central arteries and plaque accumulation in the carotid artery. While these methods are promising for the early detection of cognitive impairment, they have technical limitations, which makes it difficult to apply them in routine practice. Recently, a high frame rate ultrasound (HiFRUS) system was developed, capable of capturing video at >1000 frames per second, which allows very high quality measurement of complex blood flow information and artery wall shear stress (i.e., the force of blood against the wall of the artery). Low blood forces in the carotid artery have been shown to promote development of arterial plaque, potentially leading to cognitive impairment (e.g., poor memory, attention), although this has not previously been studied. Therefore, the purpose of this study is twofold: 1) to determine whether measurements of HiFRUS blood forces are different in older adults with cognitive impairment; and 2) to determine whether HiFRUS blood forces are better related to cognitive impairment than other measures of cardiovascular health, such as arterial stiffness. This study will take place at the Schlegel-University of Waterloo Research Institute for Aging, with recruitment of a large sample of 160 older adults occurring in the surrounding community and the long-term care and retirement facilities of Schlegel Villages. The proposed study will be one of the first to apply this non-invasive technique in humans, and will seek to further explore the role between complex arterial blood forces and cognitive impairment in a large number of older adults.
