column36: A quasi-experimental study comparing prevalence and patterns of cannabis use among youth and young adults in Canada, with US states where cannabis use is illegal and in US states where cannabis use is decriminalized, before and after cannabis legalization in Canada.
column37: Cannabis is the most used illegal drug in the world. Although recreational cannabis use in Canada is illegal, 24% of under-25's reported using cannabis in 2013. Canada, however, will soon legalize cannabis use and there are concerns that this may increase use among young people. Although cannabis use is not associated with the levels of harm that come with tobacco or alcohol, cannabis use at an early age is associated with greater risk of damaging health outcomes. The Canadian Health Minister stated that a primary objective of legalization would be to "enhance the safety of youth"; however, the existing evidence on the potential effects on young people is mixed. The Canadian policy is therefore one of the best opportunities to assess the impact of cannabis legalization on young people, with important implications for public health policy. My dissertation will examine the impact of cannabis legalization on the prevalence and patterns of use of young people in Canada, and US states where cannabis is illegal and where it is decriminalized. Young people will be surveyed at three time points: before implementation and at a 12-month and 24-month follow up. An anticipated outcome is that there will be modest changes in prevalence of use and a modest increase in experimentation, with no significant changes in frequent or problematic use. The study allows for comparisons 'within-Canada' over time, as well as comparisons between Canada and US states where legislation varies. The results of the study will contribute to the body of evidence assessing the impact of cannabis legalization on young people and resulting public health policies. Furthermore, this research will be important to other countries reviewing their own cannabis legislation. The Canadian government will review this policy and my research will provide evidence about the impact of cannabis legalization. This is a one-time opportunity to capture a rare snapshot of the implementation of such a radical policy.

column37: Drug treatments are essential for the survival of cancer patients. Unfortunately, medications needed for treatment can also cause permanent disabling side effects, severely impacting on the quality of life of patients already suffering the devastating consequences of cancer. Although platinum-based drugs, such as cisplatin, are highly effective and are the most frequently used class of cancer medications, they are also accompanied by severe side effects. In fact, 40-60% of children and 10-25% of adults treated with cisplatin lose some ability to hear, while more than 70% of children and 30% of adults experience kidney injury when taking this drug. If clinicians were able to predict which patients are most likely to experience these side effects before prescribing cisplatin, they could take measures to avoid their occurrence. Pharmacogenomics, the study of how genetic differences influence why we respond differently to medications, aims to provide clinicians with this predictive information. My research aims to investigate both pediatric and adult patients receiving cisplatin to identify the genetic and clinical variables that are associated with high risk of kidney failure and hearing loss. I will use these results to guide the development of predictive tests and novel treatment strategies. The culmination of this work will allow for the implementation of personalized treatment strategies, which provide maximum benefit and minimal harm to cancer patients.

column36: Probing the role of phosphorylation of the cardiac Ryanodine Receptor: a target for arrhythmia-causing mutations
column37: The beating of our hearts is a complex biochemical event. It relies on electrical signals, which can sometimes be disturbed, resulting in potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias. One of the key component involved in the contraction of heart muscle is a small ion known as calcium. Just prior to the contraction, calcium rushes into heart cells and triggers the contraction. Having the right amount of calcium at the right time is thus key for our regular heart rhythms, and too much or too little entry of calcium can be potentially fatal. The different compartments within the heart muscle cell are separated by membranes, which form barriers for many molecules. The calcium ions required for contraction of the heart muscle cells must pass through special gates. The sites where it all happens are formed by highly specialized protein channels that can open and close, thus determining the amount and timing of calcium release from one compartment to another. The most important of these so-called 'calcium channels' is a large protein with the name 'Ryanodine Receptor'. The gene that encodes this protein is among the largest genes known with literally hundreds of mutations documented to cause arrhythmias. In collaboration with several cardiologists who specialize in arrhythmias, we aim to determine how exactly the various mutations in this gene lead to the arrhythmias as a step to developing therapeutics. In order to do this, it is necessary to know the overall 3D structure of the calcium channel. To do this, make use of a highly specialized technique termed "X-ray crystallography". By shooting X-rays at crystals of the channel and analyze the way these rays scatter off the atoms in the crystal, we can figure out via complex calculations, what the 3D structure looks like. By comparing structures of the calcium channels of normal and diseased individuals, we can directly observe the mechanisms of the disease-causing mutations and discover potential therapeutic strategies.

column36: The Role of Granzyme B in Cutaneous Leishmaniasis
column37: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is a skin infection that leads to blistering. Caused by protozoan Leishmania parasites, CL is transmitted by the bite of infected phlebotomine sandflies. This produces up to 200 lesions, typically on exposed parts of the body, such as the face, arms and legs, causing serious disability. In addition, lesions can leave permanent scars, which are often the cause of social prejudice. An estimated 1.3 million new cases are reported annually, with 30,000 of these resulting in death. Currently, there is no cure for CL. Granzyme B (GzmB) is a protein-degrading enzyme present in normal skin at minimal amounts. However, GzmB becomes elevated in skin that is cut, burnt, damaged by the sun or afflicted by various skin diseases. Here, GzmB prevents the skin from repairing itself and this leads to scarring. Previously, wounds in laboratory mice where GzmB was genetically knocked out showed improved healing and reduced visible signs of skin damage. In collaboration with viDA Therapeutics, the Granville Lab are developing novel inhibitors of GzmB that can be applied topically to the skin, showing emerging evidence of improved healing outcomes. Recent studies now indicate GzmB is elevated in the skin lesions of CL patients. Importantly, GzmB appears to be drastically more elevated in CL lesions than reported elsewhere in cuts, burns and other skin diseases. GzmB is therefore predicted to have an important role in the severity of CL. The aim of the current study is to investigate the contribution of GzmB to the development, severity and healing potential of CL lesions. We propose that the inhibition of GzmB, using topically applied drug formulations, will reduce lesion severity and improve visual appearance. CL is of major concern to the World Health Organization, and listed as one of the top 5 neglected diseases. The development of new therapeutic options for CL would have an enormous public health benefits.

column36: Adolescent drug use: Neural dynamics and network connectivity
column37: Smoking is arguably a developmental disease, with 70% of smokers starting before the age of 15. Smoking remains prevalent worldwide, with 20% of the population smoking regularly. Human neuroimaging studies have identified changes in connectivity between brain regions in smokers, however whether these differences are a result of smoking or reflect predispositional differences that helped initiate smoking require the use of animal models, which have a long history and utility in addiction research. Here, I will employ a preclinical model of adolescent nicotine exposure to study the longitudinal impacts of adolescent drug exposure on brain function and circuitry using neuroimaging together with behavioural testing. These measures will address whether adolescent exposure to nicotine produces a unique brain state, characterized by changes in neurotransmitter systems, connectivity and behaviours. The employed neuroimaging techniques will include functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), to determine connectivity and network strength, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). MRS quantifies brain metabolites, such as the main excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, glutamate and -aminobutyric acid (GABA) respectively, which show extensive developmental changes throughout the adolescent period. Once the developmental consequences of adolescent nicotine exposure have been quantified, I will implement a technique for viral delivery of designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs (DREADDs) to specifically target glutamatergic and GABAergic neural populations to determine the causal role of these neurotransmitter systems in this disease state. This research proposal offers an opportunity, unique to animal studies, to understand the longitudinal impact and preceding mechanism of adolescent nicotine exposure on brain circuitry and function. It will contribute to our understanding of adolescent development and its vulnerability to early drug exposure.

column36: The maladaptive effects of wood smoke on Granzyme B expression and abdominal aortic aneurysms
column37: Due to climate change, the number of annual forest fires over the past 40 years has continued to rise. Although cigarette smoke is one of the greatest risk factors for cardiovascular disease, the effect of wood smoke is currently unknown. Firefighters have been found to be at a higher risk for having a cardiovascular event as compared to other emergency response personal. In fact, firefighters are at greater risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than from burn injury. Although smoke exposure is thought to play a role in firefighter deaths, the mechanisms by which wood smoke promotes cardiovascular disease is unknown. Granzyme B is an enzyme that degrades extracellular matrix and adhesion proteins that are important in sustaining tissue structure and function. Human and mouse models of abdominal aortic aneurysms have demonstrated increased Granzyme B expression and aneurysm rupture. Granzyme B inhibition prevents aneurysm rupture and increases survival in mouse models. Cigarette smoke is the number one risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysms. While smoking is associated with increased Granzyme B levels in COPD, the link between wood smoke, Granzyme B, and aneurysms is not known. Likewise, while Granzyme B expression is seen in pro-inflammatory mast cells in aneurysms, the mechanism by which Granzyme B is induced in such cells is unknown. Our objective is to investigate the role of wood smoke on Granzyme B expression in mast cells in the onset and progression of abdominal aortic aneurysms. We will use the ApoE-/- angiotensisn II mouse model and determine what, if any, effect that wood smoke has on aneurysm formation and progression. In isolated primary human peripheral blood mast cells, we will examine the effect that epigenetic and microRNA regulation has on Granzyme B expression in mast cells, cells which do not normally express Granzyme B. This research may lead to the development of new drugs to target Granzyme B and treat abdominal aortic aneurysm.

column36: Characterization and development of a live, attenuated Streptococcus pneumoniae vaccine
column37: Streptococcus pneumoniae, also called the pneumococcus, asymptomatically colonizes the nasopharynx of young children. However, the pneumococcus can eventually spread to the lungs and cause a life-threatening respiratory illness called pneumonia, which is a major killer of young children in developing countries. Vaccination is the best strategy to fight the disease by preventing initial bacterial colonization. Two pneumococcal vaccines are currently available; however, both rely on a single bacterial component called the capsule. Several drawbacks are associated with capsule-based vaccines. Notably, they do not prevent pneumococcal colonization of the nasopharynx and do not provide universal protection. In addition, they are difficult and costly to manufacture. An improved vaccine is therefore greatly needed. We developed a novel vaccine that has the potential to circumvent these limitations by using live but weakened pneumococci. However, before such a vaccine could be clinically tested, we need to 1) determine its impact on the immune system, 2) determine which bacterial components are important for establishing protection, and 3) determine if antibiotic treatment in conjunction can alter the efficacy of the vaccine. The reservoir for pneumococci is the nasopharynx of asymptomatic humans. We therefore believe that blocking colonization in the first place would reduce its overall dissemination in the population. It would also prevent the development of pneumococcal-related diseases. Our vaccine has the potential to provide such protection. Its development and eventual implementation could reduce the global burden and also reduce morbidity and mortality associated with pneumococcal infections. Preventing pneumococcal carriage would also alleviate treatment-associated medical costs. In conclusion, development of an improved pneumococcal vaccine would be highly beneficial for the global population, both in the developed and the developing countries.

column36: Immune constraints on the evolution of clonal heterogeneity in ovarian cancer
column37: Cancer therapy fails when cancer cells evolve resistance during treatment. Understanding the selective pressures that limit this evolution through the course of disease is therefore essential, but has been hampered by the immense complexity of the genetic landscape of cancer. Recent advances in genomic techniques that reconstruct the past evolutionary trajectories of cancer within a patient are, for the first time, now allowing direct tests of the ways that different factors constrain this evolution. In particular, the patient's immune system is now known to be potent factor that can limit cancer progression, and is expected to be a strong selective force shaping tumor evolution. We will couple high-resolution data on anticancer immune responses with genomic reconstructions of cancer evolutionary history to test the ways that patient immunity constrains evolution in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) - a highly lethal disease in urgent need of improved treatments. We aim to understand how HGSC genomes evolve in response to pressure from the immune system. This will allow us to predict new targets for immunotherapy, deploy immunotherapy to help limit the evolution of treatment resistance, and delineate the evolutionary potential of individual HGSCs to improve treatment strategies.

column36: The co-occurrence and impact of PTSD and chronic pain in youth: neural activation patterns as a mutually maintaining mechanism
column37: Chronic pain, defined as pain occurring constantly or frequently for 3 months or more is highly prevalent, disabling, and poses enormous costs to society (11.8 billion/year). Indeed, chronic pain during childhood and adolescence can lead to persistent pain problems and mental health disorders into adulthood. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a mental health condition characterized by prolonged distress following exposure to a traumatic event (e.g. serious injury, sexual violence). PTSD and chronic pain have been found to co-occur at high rates in both adolescent and adult populations, and are linked to heightened impairment and disability. Comorbid chronic pain and PTSD has been explained by the presence of shared affected brain regions, and cognitive (attention/memory biases) and behavioural (sleep disturbance) vulnerabilities that lead to the development and/or maintenance of both conditions. There are a number of brain regions where pain signals and responses to threat converge and interact to affect brain responses. However, brain activation patterns among children and adolescents with chronic pain and PTSD have not yet been examined. Therefore, we will assess PTSD symptoms in 30 youth with and without chronic pain. Moreover, we will use state-of-the-art neuroimaging methods to assess their brain responses to neutral, happy and fearful facial expressions. Comparing how the brain processes information in youth with chronic pain and varying levels of PTSD symptoms to those without chronic pain has the potential to lead to early identification of risk for pediatric chronic pain and mental health comorbidities. This study will also help to inform the development of tailored interventions to address these symptoms and improve health outcomes.

column36: Decision making impairments in psychiatric disorders: testing the trans-diagnostic role of interoception.
column37: The ability to make optimal decisions is often altered in mental health conditions such as autism, eating disorders, substance addiction and depression. This impairment could contribute to the rigid and maladapted behaviours sometimes observed in these conditions. For example, persons with these conditions might favour high risk - high reward choices instead of the more advantageous low risk - moderate reward alternatives. Recent theoretical models suggest that our ability to make decisions often rely on our ability to perceive our own body. Indeed, bodily perception, also called interoception, can make one's aware of subtle emotional cues that are useful to guide decision making (e.g. increased heart rate, faster breathing). It is therefore possible that impaired bodily perception is responsible for the decision-making difficulties observed in these conditions. The current proposal aims to test this hypothesis by measuring interoception and decision-making abilities in a large non-clinical sample and in multiple clinical groups. Decision-making abilities will be measured using tasks in which participants are requested to make choices involving different consequences for them and others (e.g. receive a reward while their partner receives a punishment) or to make choices with a different risk/reward trade-off. Interoceptive abilities will be measured using tasks that require participants to count their heartbeats, to assess the strength of their respiration or to assess the temperature of a liquid in their mouth. This project has the potential to identify a common explanation for decision making difficulties observed in several psychiatric conditions. This could in turn lead to significant changes in our conception of these conditions and to new therapeutic approaches aimed at improving interoception in these patients.

column36: Genetic tools for precise manipulation of the human gut microbiome
column37: The gastrointestinal tract is home to trillions of microorganisms, collectively called the gut microbiome, that have a profound impact on human health. It remains unclear, however, the extent to which these microbes can interfere with the treatment of human disease by metabolizing therapeutic drugs within the gut. One particular species of bacteria that can be present in the gut, Eggerthella lenta (E. lenta), is able to inactivate the cardiac drug digoxin, interfering with its efficacy in the treatment of patients with heart disease. We propose to use this organism, and its drug metabolism ability, as a model for developing tools to target specific bacteria or activities in the gut. To do this, we will engineer viruses to carry elements that interact with the E. lenta adaptive immune system to inhibit drug metabolism, and subsequently use the viruses to infect E. lenta within the gastrointestinal tract. We hope to show that the strategy used for E. lenta and cardiac drug metabolism can be generalized, and that other species, strains, or activities in the gut microbiome can be manipulated in this manner for therapeutic purposes. This work is important in the gut microbiome field because there is currently no tool for specific targeting of bacterial species or activities within this complex environment. The development of a method to easily manipulate specific microbes or control their metabolism could improve treatment outcomes for patients who carry drug-metabolizing strains of bacteria, bringing us closer toward the goal of precision medicine.

column36: Determining the Mechanism of Myelodysplastic Syndrome Progression and Resistance to Azacytidine Therapy Using Single-cell DNA Methylation Sequencing
column37: Myelodysplastic syndrome is the most common form of blood cancer, with an estimated 60,000 to 120,000 cases in the United States. Sufferers of MDS have imbalances in their kinds of blood cells, eventually leading to bone marrow failure, or a more rapid and deadly blood cancer. There are no drugs which cure MDS, but one drug, azacytidine, helps alleviate symptoms in about two thirds of patients. Nevertheless, even among those patients for whom azacytidine is effective, the disease eventually becomes resistant. Evidence suggests that MDS originates among blood-producing stem cells in the bone marrow gone wrong. We are able to sort out those stem cells from bone marrow samples, and examine each cell's DNA methylation (a kind of molecular switch which controls the cell). Many cancers disruptiively increase DNA methylation to turn off anti-cancer genes. Azacytidine does the opposite and decreases DNA methylation and decreases DNA methylation effect -- it decreases DNA methylation, and, it is believed, switches anti-cancer genes back on. By examining DNA methylation in cells from patients who were responsive to azacytidine and comparing it with those who became resistant, we hope to uncover the mechanism of azacytidine resistance. This could quickly lead to new or complimentary therapies which would help patients to live longer, and with better quality of life.

column36: Access to HIV treatment and prevention services and injection initiation among people who inject drugs in North America
column37: The increase in prescription opioid misuse and subsequent initiation of injection drug use (IDU) is a public health concern across North America (NA). IDU remains a key driver of the HIV epidemic in all three countries of NA. There is evidence that syringe distribution, supervised injection facilities and opioid substitution therapy are effective in preventing HIV transmission and may also decrease the initiation of other people into drug injection. Appropriate scale-up and expansion of such services varies across socioeconomic and geopolitical settings. It is therefore critical to have HIV services for people who inject drugs (PWID) tailored to respond to factors driving HIV transmission and injection initiation across diverse socioeconomic settings. The proposed project would therefore investigate the suite of available HIV services (i.e., testing, treatment, and prevention) for PWID in three different socioeconomic settings across NA: Tijuana, Mexico; San Diego, USA; and Vancouver, Canada. It will analyze how socio-structural services such as housing and access to welfare mediate HIV service uptake and HIV risk behaviors across settings. This project will also investigate the association between HIV service uptake and the risk that PWID initiate others into injection drug use. In addition, it will not only inform under-resourced settings on Canadian health policies but it will also inform efforts to optimize and scale up HIV services for underserved populations in low- and middle-income settings across North America that have been disproportionately impacted by IDU-driven HIV epidemics, including Mexico's northern border region as well as rural and remote indigenous communities in Canada.

column36: Establishing the role of SP140 in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a chronic condition characterized by severe inflammation of the intestine. There are two main forms of IBD: Crohn's Disease (CD) and Ulcerative Colitis (UC). 1 in 150 Canadians is living with CD or UC, one of the highest rates worldwide. IBD disrupts an individual's ability to digest food, absorb nutrition and eliminate waste in a normal manner, placing enormous health and financial burden on individuals. There are currently no specific treatments for IBD. SP140, a protein that recognizes modifications on the proteins packaging the DNA, has been recently shown to have important ramifications in CD. A single nucleotide mutation found in SP140 was significantly associated with CD risk in a study analyzing control and CD patients. The role of SP140 in CD pathogenesis has never been previously studied and is the objective of our study. Given it is highly expressed in immune cells and has various domains for DNA recognition, this protein holds promise to critically regulate inflammation in CD. We will assess the role of SP140 in CD in healthy control and CD patients. We will further investigate what each of the different domains in the SP140 protein is responsible for. Lastly, we will study the role of SP140 in a preclinical model of CD in order to clearly establish its role in modulating immune responses. SP140 belongs to a family of proteins that have received a lot of attention in their role to regulate inflammation. Inhibition of these proteins have been shown to be therapeutically relevant in the setting of inflammation. The proposed research will further our understanding of the mechanisms underlying IBD and present potentially novel therapeutic strategy which will be critical in tackling the increasing IBD incidence in Canada.

column36: Normalizing Memory and Cognitive Changes in Rehabilitation
column37: Experiencing changes in ones' memory and concentration due to aging or brain-related conditions can make an individual feel less capable or competent relative to his/her previous self or peers. Aging individuals report 'being panicked' or feeling 'mentally ill' because of these changes. Group rehabilitation programs help these individuals by making them feel more normal about their memory and concentration changes. Normalizing one's experiences and emotions provides a powerful source of relief and facilitates individuals in accepting and adjusting to their new lives. These experiences seem to maximize actual and perceived memory improvements, treatment progress, and functional outcomes from rehabilitation programs. Since a sense of feeling normal seems to be a critical component of memory rehabilitation improvement, there is a strong need to develop a tool that measures this feeling. Thus, for my dissertation I will develop and validate a questionnaire called the Psychological Normalization Inventory (PNI) that assesses an individual's sense of feeling normal in regards to their memory and concentration issues. This tool will then be used to (a) determine whether a new online memory intervention program fosters a sense of feeling normal and (b) examine whether this feeling positively affects rehabilitation outcomes. Through this research and the development of the PNI, I will help clinicians understand their clients' psychological experiences and facilitate them in assessing whether a rehabilitation program fosters a sense of feeling normal. Moreover, by assessing whether normalization influences rehabilitations outcomes, I will gain insights that will facilitate the ultimate goal of maximizing memory and functional improvements from rehabilitation programs that aim to improve memory and concentration.

column36: Self-Management of Adolescent and Young Adult Survivors of Childhood Cancer
column37: Children from low-income households and ethnic minority groups are less active than other children. These children are at a greater risk of developing health problems as they get older. We need to find a way to increase their physical activity levels at an early age so that they can become active and healthy adolescents and adults. So far, physical activity interventions have not been able produce long-term changes in physical activity and we believe this is because they do no teach children how to be efficient and confident movers. In this study, we will have 30 low-income community preschool classrooms participate. 15 of the classrooms will be taught a movement-based instructional program where we will teach the children many different motor skills (throwing, catching, jumping, hopping) and build their movement confidence. The other 15 classrooms will participate in their usual free play activities at recess. The instructional program will occur 30 min/day, 4 days/week for 30 weeks. We will measure motor skills, movement confidence and physical activity in all children before the program, right after the program is finished and then once a year for the following 3 years. column36: Trans-synaptic co-ordination of GPCR signalling-complexes in the striatum
column37: GPCRs represent a superfamily of proteins that facilitate cell-to-cell communications and participate in the regulation of all aspects of human physiology. GPCRs play a central role in human disease with 40% of prescribed pharmaceuticals having GPCRs as targets. Much of the effects of glutamate, the major neurotransmitter of cellular communications in the brain, are mediated by mGluRs: a subset of GPCRs that modulate learning, memory, and adaptability of the brain and have been increasingly implicated in neuropsychiatric disease. The striatum is a region of the brain at the nexus of both mGluR activity and neurological disease. It co-ordinates complex tasks including decision-making, reward, and motor control, and has been implicated in the pathology of depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease. We recently discovered a family of cell-adhesion proteins (ELFN1 and ELFN2) that specifically interact with mGluRs on adjacent neurons. Mutations in ELFN1 have been associated with ADHD and epilepsy in humans and loss of ELFN1 in mice similarly results in hyperactivity, seizures, and abnormal response to psychostimulants suggesting the involvement of the striatum. Yet, virtually nothing is known about the mechanism of ELFN1/2 action in the striatum. We hypothesize ELFN1 and ELFN2 physically synchronize communications between neurons in the striatum. We will utilize precise genetic tools to remove ELFN1/2 from distinct neuronal populations in mice and perform behavioural evaluation to determine which disorders can be pinpointed to ELFN1 in the striatum. We will investigate the functional bias of ELFN1/2 action on mGluRs and dissect the possible mechanisms of disease-causing mutations in ELFN1. Finally, we will investigate the potential for a novel mechanism for synchronization of neuron-to-neuron communications by fully characterizing the assembly of ELFN1/2-containing protein complexes at cell junctions and their druggability for disease.

column36: Finding Antibiotics Targeting Bacterial Proteases
column37: Our ability to treat infections is critically threatened by the spread of antibiotic resistance. Resistance has emerged to all clinically available antibiotics and is combining in multidrug-resistant superbugs for which there are few, if any, treatments. In order to avoid cross-resistance and develop antibiotics effective against these pathogens, antibiotics with novel targets are required. Proteases, enzymes that degrade proteins, offer one such underexploited target. One family of molecules known to target proteases are acyldepsipeptide antibiotics (ADEPs). These compounds work by activating a protease known as ClpP to indiscriminately degrade proteins, thereby killing the cell. While this mode of action has numerous advantages, poor pharmacological properties and low efficacy against some pathogens limits ADEP's use. My project aims to overcome these limitations in two ways. First, improved ADEP derivatives will be made using enzymes capable of making modifications to the core ADEP molecule. Second, novel classes of antibiotics will be discovered using a high throughput screen designed to find protease activators. In these ways, novel antibiotics targeting bacterial proteases will be discovered and developed. These antibiotics with a novel molecular target will be vital to combating infectious diseases as the threat of a post-antibiotic era continues to grow.

column36: The causes and consequences of paediatric multiple sclerosis: A population-based study
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease that affects the brain and spinal cord. Most persons develop MS during adulthood, but about 5% have their first symptoms in childhood. This is a particularly devastating form of the disease for patients and their families. The cause of childhood MS (and MS in general) is not known, nor are the longer-term consequences. This leads to major uncertainties in the management of the disease. Sweden has a unique population-health program which has the potential to answer these questions. In Sweden, there is a long tradition of collecting detailed health information from all citizens. As such, Sweden has one of the largest groups of persons with childhood MS in the world, including nearly 900 cases. Beyond MS-specific information, we would also have detailed information about the birth, family history of disease, genetics, general health, education, and income of these persons. All of this data is private and names are removed. Firstly, we will look for possible environmental factors which might increase the risk of MS in children. A previous study has shown that low sunlight exposure during pregnancy increases the risk of MS in the child. We would explore other maternal factors, such as drug exposure and illness during pregnancy, and mode of delivery which might influence the risk of MS in the child. Understanding what causes MS is central in preventing new cases. Secondly, we will explore the long-term impact of childhood MS on disease progression, education, employment, income, and mental health. All of these are important components of a person's quality of life and we expect that they will be affected by their illness. Childhood MS is challenging to treat because very little is known about the effects of medication on children. We will explore the longer-term side-effects and effectiveness of MS drugs in children. Ultimately, the goal of the proposed study is to improve care for people growing up with MS.

column36: Preclinical assessment of a novel Chlamydia vaccine
column37: Chlamydia trachomatis infections are the most prevalent sexually transmitted bacterial infections in many developed countries, including Canada. Globally, the World Health Organization estimates that 130 million new cases of C. trachomatis infection occur each year, with the highest incidence occurring in the most impoverished regions of the world, where adequate control programs are significantly lacking. C. trachomatis infections in women can lead to a number of complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility. Alarmingly, studies have shown that asymptomatic infections occur in up to 90% of women, leaving them even more susceptible to developing serious complications, as they do not have an impetus to seek medical help. The high rate of asymptomatic infections, taken together with the severity of the infection induced pathology, suggests that controlling C. trachomatis infections requires a vaccine, despite the availability of antibiotics. The type III secretion (T3S) system is used by some pathogenic bacteria to ensure successful infection, and are excellent vaccine candidates due to the nature of their structure and function. Recently, we have shown that animals immunized with chlamydial T3S components were protected against infection and disease. Given the success of this study, it would be prudent to further explore the use of T3S components in a vaccine against C. trachomatis using more relevant animal models. In that model, we aim to 1) optimize our vaccine strategy, 2) understand the nature of the immune response elicited by our vaccine, and 3) identify the immune correlates of protection. Our research could advance our understanding of Chlamydia infections and help bring new C. trachomatis vaccines into clinical trials.

column36: DNA damage responses in cells of the developing brain
column37: This research aims to understand the cellular and the molecular events that cause mental decline and secondary brain cancers after anti-brain tumor radiation therapy in children. Radiation therapy is an important treatment for childhood brain cancers. While radiation helps to cure these brain tumors, it also causes deficits in mental functioning and contributes to the development of secondary, radiation-induced brain tumors. These "late effects" of radiation therapy worsen in severity the younger a patient is treated. Radiation therapy eliminates tumor cells by irreversibly damaging their DNA. However, healthy brain cells also receive radiation during treatment, and how well these cells recognize and repair damaged DNA is not known. This project will investigate how the different types of brain cells in a child's developing brain respond to radiation therapy. We hypothesize that specific types of immature brain cells present in a child's brain might be sensitive to radiation because of differences in how these cells recognize and repair DNA damage after radiation therapy. To investigate this, we will assess whether all types of brain cells have the same levels of molecules that repair DNA damaged by radiation, and whether these levels change with age. Then, we will examine whether any differences in the levels of these DNA repair molecules have any impact on how different types of brain cells respond to radiation. This research may identify strategies to prevent mental decline and secondary brain tumors after pediatric radiation therapy. It may also identify markers that might distinguish individuals particularly susceptible or resistant to these late effects. Understanding the cellular and molecular responses to radiation in a child's brain is necessary to match brain cancer patients to the safest and most effective treatments. These therapies will then not only cure brain cancers, but will reduce or eliminate the long-term impact on a child's brain.

column37: Background: Cardiovascular disease accounts for the deaths of one third of all Canadians, and costs the health care system over $20 billion each year. Despite these benefits, the way the heart adapts to exercise training is poorly understood, and it remains to be determined how to maximize the beneficial effects associated with exercise. This research will evaluate ways to further improve the effectiveness of exercise, and the mechanisms by which the heart improves to the training. Understanding the ways in which the hearts function improves, and ways that these adaptations can be enhanced will lead to more effective exercise recommendations. Ultimately, this research has the potential to decrease the burden currently imposed by cardiovascular disease, and contribute to creating healthier Canadians.

column36: Prehabilitation intervention to improve patient-centered outcomes post-colorectal surgery for cancer: A multicenter randomized controlled trial
column37: Colorectal surgery is a common surgery for the treatment of colon and rectal cancers as well as other bowel diseases. Recovery from colorectal surgery is difficult, especially when compared to other general surgeries, because of the many potential negative side effects. These side effects include surgical complications, long hospital stays, and slow recovery of pre-surgery fitness. It usually takes several months for patients to recover the strength required to return to their typical daily activities. A new field of study, known as prehabilitation, has helped patients experience better surgical recoveries by preparing them for their operation with personalized nutrition, anxiety reduction, and exercise counseling in the weeks before surgery. These positive results justify larger-scale trials to evaluate whether widespread adoption of prehabilitation into surgical care guidelines is within the best interest of patients and health care services. The proposed study is designed to test whether prehabilitation improves the recovery of strength and fitness of colorectal cancer surgery patients in a multicenter randomized controlled trial. We expect that patients who take part in the prehabilitation program will have better surgical recoveries, which includes earlier discharges from the hospital, fewer surgical complications, fewer hospital re-admissions, and earlier recovery of activities of daily living. We will also assess the potential cost-savings of the program. Finally, a unique aspect of our study is that patients who participated in the prehabilitation intervention will be invited to discuss their experiences and help us, as partners, improve the design of the prehabilitation intervention so that it is most acceptable to future patients. Altogether, the study will inform health care decision makers by evaluating a program that is designed to effectively improve patient care for surgery, be acceptable to patients, and use health care funds judiciously

column36: Examining Neighbourhood Socioeconomic Status, Anxiety during Pregnancy, and Preterm Birth
column37: In Canada, one in every twelve babies is born premature. Premature birth is defined as the birth of a baby prior to reaching 37 weeks of pregnancy. One in three deaths of newborn babies is related to premature birth. Among survivors, breathing problems, vision and hearing problems, and learning issues are common. Pregnant women living in disadvantaged neighborhoods tend to have higher rates of premature birth. Disadvantaged neighborhoods are defined as areas where many people are less educated, poor, and unemployed. It is known that pregnant women living in those neighborhoods are more likely to be anxious due to financial hardships. Thus, being anxious during pregnancy may play a role in the increased occurrence of premature birth in those neighborhoods, although this has not been examined. This research will use data from two community-based studies in Calgary that includes 5,588 pregnant women. Information about characteristics of pregnant women, their anxiety, and premature birth will come from those studies. Information about neighborhood characteristics (income, education, and employment) of those women will come from the 2011 Canada census data. This information will be used to look at whether living in a disadvantaged neighborhood and being anxious during pregnancy contributes to premature birth. This research is important because it will add new knowledge on who is at most risk for premature birth. The findings will be beneficial to the public, health professionals, research community, and policy makers. Determining who is at highest risk for premature birth can inform policy makers to design and implement public health programs targeting those populations. This leads to decrease premature birth and its related deaths and health problems in children.

column37: Sepsis is a lethal syndrome of organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated immune response to infections including pneumonia, meningitis and influenza. Sepsis affects 250,000 Canadians each year and kills 35,000; children and older patients face a particularly increased risk. Sepsis is difficult diagnose and treat. Current medical management is entirely supportive; many survivors are left with severe disability and worse long term health outcomes. There is an urgent need for effective new treatments and diagnostic tests. Neutrophils (PMN) are white blood cells that play a key role in sepsis. While PMN combat infections, they can also harm healthy cells, leading to injury of the heart, lungs, liver, and kidneys and the need for life support in an intensive care unit (ICU). How PMN regulate their functions in sepsis is poorly understood. In this proposal, I aim to understand a novel mechanism underlying PMN dysfunction. We recently identified a PMN protein, TARM1, which can activate PMN anti-infectious functions, and is closely related to a previously described protein, SIRL1, that has inhibitory functions. Both are expressed on septic PMN and so may work together to regulate PMN responses. This study aims to 1) understand how changes in TARM1/SIRL1 expression on septic PMN influence their anti-microbial functions, 2) to determine how TARM1/SIRL1 activate intracellular signals for survival and functional activity in septic PMNs and 3) correlate TARM1/SIRL1 expression on PMNs with clinical outcomes in sepsis. Success in these studies will identify new approaches to identify, monitor and, importantly, tailor novel treatments to improve outcomes for septic patients.

column36: Identifying novel determinants of adult stem cell identity and maintenance
column37: Skin-the largest organ in our body-forms a crucial barrier between our internal tissues and the external environment. It is also the site of skin appendages, such as hair follicles and sweat glands, that are necessary to allow us to survive in changing climates. In particular, the mammalian hair follicle undergoes serval cycles of growth, destruction and rest, which necessitates multiple rounds of hair generation. A key component of all adult tissues, including hair follicles, are stem cells that retain the capability to become any of a number of more differentiated cell types. In the adult hair follicle, stem cells are responsible for giving rise to the differentiated hair in each round of hair generation, as well as contributing to wound healing when the skin is damaged. These are the cells that are also the origin of squamous cell carcinomas, a common and potentially life-threatening cancer. Despite the absolute importance of these cells, currently we have an incomplete molecular and cell biological picture of how skin stem cells are specified and maintained, and how this goes awry in disease states. This proposal aims to expand our knowledge of this important field in the hope that the biology elucidated may translate into functional insight into the establishment and maintenance of adult stem cells in normal and disease states. To achieve this, I have devised a loss-of-function genetic screen to assess the importance of each candidate specifically in hair follicle stem cell identity. I have also designed a second rapid way to conditionally knockout my top candidates from the screen and test them rigorously for their long-term functional relevance in normal hair cycling. Together, this will allow me to define novel molecular mechanisms that determine adult stem cell function, which in turn can be investigated for their impact on disease.

column36: Investigating bacterial pathogenesis mechanisms and host subversion strategies
column37: Due to increasingly widespread antibiotic resistance, it is predicted that by 2050 bacterial infections will be causing more deaths than cancers. Bacterial pathogens subvert host processes by injecting protein virulence factors (effectors) into host cells to modify the behaviors of specific host proteins, thus causing disease. However, there has been limited success in elucidating effector roles and, correspondingly, pathogenesis mechanisms. This limits the development of new treatment strategies, which are becoming essential in view of increasingly widespread antimicrobial resistance. Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm) is one of the best-studied and understood model bacterial pathogens. It causes different diseases in humans and mice. It has been the target of intense scientific investigations for decades. However, its pathogenesis mechanisms are still poorly understood and cellular targets have been identified or predicted for only about half of STm's 45 effectors. The proposed project will systematically identify host proteins interacting with each of the 45 effectors and map downstream changes to protein complexes, occurring as a result of the bacterial infection in human and mouse cells. The resulting data will be used to predict effector roles and to identify disease determinants that are associated with each type of disease and outcome. Successful implementation of the proposed project will represent a significant step forward in knowledge discovery about bacterial pathogenesis. In addition to making significant scientific discoveries, it will provide important resources and tools for future studies, thus speeding up future investigations and helping shape how bacterial pathogenesis mechanisms for a variety of pathogens are investigated in the future. In the long term, it will contribute to reducing healthcare costs and combatting the rise in antimicrobial resistance.

column37: Antibiotics are used to help combat infection with harmful bacteria. Unfortunately, antibiotics can also have off-target effects and kill helpful bacteria that reside in our gut. The community of bacteria in the gut, also called the microbiome, plays an important role in restricting the growth of harmful bacteria. This function is termed colonization resistance. Colonization resistance is reduced when antibiotics disrupt the microbiome. Klebsiella is a potentially harmful bacterium that can take advantage of reduced colonization resistance to expand to high levels in the gut following antibiotic treatment. This expansion is a significant clinical problem since having high levels of Klebsiella in the gut puts patients at an increased risk of both a dangerous spread of the bacteria into the body and pneumonia. Identifying these factors could lead to treatments that block the initial expansion of Klebsiella in the gut, or the increased risk of infection in other parts of the body that results from that expansion.

column36: Frailty and Cardiac Rehabilitation: Do sedentary and physical activity behaviors improve outcomes?
column37: Complications affecting the heart and blood vessels (cardiovascular diseases) are the leading contributor to overall disease burden in older adults. This information is troubling, considering that the number of older adults in Canada is expected to double over the next two decades. However, not everyone at the same age is as impacted by these complications as others. These differences in health even at the same age describes someone's level of frailty. A person who is frail cannot respond or recover as well as others to stressors, such as an illness, surgery, or other serious health events. Research shows that frailty makes complications of cardiovascular disease worse, which means that it is important to provide health care that will improve frailty and the overall health of older patients. Increasing physical activity and reducing sedentary time is shown to improve frailty, as well as improve cardiovascular disease health outcomes. Therefore, programs that promote an active lifestyle are appropriate to target both conditions. Cardiac rehabilitation is the standard of care for patients who have experienced a serious event such as a heart attack in order prevent another event from happening by promoting a healthier lifestyle, including physical activity. column37: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a psychiatric disorder that affects up to 2% of the global population. With an estimated quarter million people in Canada suffering from schizophrenia, the disorder poses a significant burden on society, estimated at $6.85 billion CAD in 2004. The disorder is characterized by a range of complex behavioral abnormalities, including a debilitating deficit in reward processing and motivation. These symptoms not only affect daily functioning, but they also tend to worsen with most antipsychotic medications. The mechanism underlying schizophrenia is largely unknown, but there is emerging evidence that viral or bacterial infections during pregnancy play a key role. Activation of the fetal immune system is thought to disrupt the normal development of the fetal brain. Such prenatal immune activation is thought to cause structural and functional abnormalities in the brain, yet the exact mechanism remains unknown. Microglia, the resident immune cells in the brain, were recently demonstrated to play a key role in the shaping of neuronal networks during development. We hypothesize that, given the central role of microglia in both immunity and brain development, activation of microglia during infection may compromise their role in modulating the formation and maturation of neuronal networks. This may cause the behavioral alterations, such as motivational deficits, that become evident in adulthood. For my PhD project, I will use a mouse model to explore the effect of maternal immune activation on the development and function of an area of the brain that has previously been associated with the reward and motivation deficits seen in schizophrenic patients. This will allow me to show, for the first time, that maternal infection during critical stages of neuronal development alters brain wiring in an area of key importance for reward processing and motivation. This study will be an important step towards understanding the development of SCZ.

column36: Impact of provincial primary care reforms on the management of persons with Alzheimer's disease and on associated health care use and cost
column37: Alzheimer's disease is a devastating illness for patients and their families. It robs those affected of their memory and independence and eventually leads to death. As the population in Canada is aging, the number suffering from Alzheimer's will double to 1.4 million with a projected health care cost of $800 billion over the next 20 years. To address this crisis, Canadian provincial governments have implemented reforms to provide better care to patients with Alzheimer's by increasing the role of family doctors. By doing so, governments hope to also reduce the burden of this disease on our health care system. While these publicly-financed reforms have been ongoing for several years, there has been no systematic study to assess whether they have been effective. My study, part of a Canada-wide research program on Alzheimer's disease, will be the first to provide this information. I will examine the impact of these reforms by analyzing government data on all patients with Alzheimer's disease in Ontario and Quebec over the last two decades. These datasets will allow me to access almost 2/3 of the Canadian population with Alzheimer's disease and study the trends in care and health service use before and after the reforms. Using innovative statistical models, I will examine whether more people with Alzheimer's are being diagnosed and regularly followed by family doctors. I will also determine whether the reforms have decreased the number of emergency visits, hospital stays and nursing home care needed for patients with Alzheimer's. My analysis will give provincial health officials, researchers and Alzheimer's patient groups much needed data on what parts of the reforms are working and what needs to be improved. Overall, my study will help provinces achieve a sustainable and effective health care system capable of meeting the needs of patients and families affected by Alzheimer's disease, ultimately leading to a better quality of life for this vulnerable population.

column37: Major depression is a mood disorder that has a negative impact on quality of life. Depression screening, which involves using short questionnaires to identify people who may have unrecognized depression, has been suggested as a way to improve the detection, management, and treatment of depression. Depression screening is recommended in the United States and in certain medical guidelines in Canada (e.g., stroke guidelines), but is not currently recommended in Canada's main primary health care guidelines due to concerns that screening tools do not accurately distinguish between patients with and without depression. Only approximately 20-40% of patients identified as depressed by current screening tools truly have depression. In my project, I will combine original patient data from published depression screening studies to create a very large database that can be used to determine more accurate ways to assess and appropriately identify patients with depression. My project will allow us to determine the probability that a specific patient is depressed by considering the patient's individual depression score along with specific characteristics, such as age, sex, and medical diagnosis, which are associated with depression. This method will be more accurate than current procedures that only classify patients as "likely" or "not likely" depressed. To implement my findings, I will develop a free online calculator that allows healthcare professionals to use the results of my research with actual patients in practice. This project will improve the effectiveness of depression screening, which depends on accurate screening questionnaires. In collaboration with Canadian guideline-makers, findings from my project will be applied in hospitals and health clinics to facilitate effective depression screening programs, improve the management of depression, and set Canada apart as a leader in depression research and practice.

column36: The neuroepigenetic link between childhood abuse and suicide: a single-cell type sequencing approach
column37: It is estimated that approximately 30% of adult mental illness may be due in part to a history of severe childhood abuse. A major question, then, is by what mechanisms does abuse predispose a survivor to psychopathology in adulthood? Our goal is to investigate this question using the field of epigenetics. Epigenetic modifications, such as DNA methylation, result in changes in the expression of one's genetic code without altering its underlying sequence. Studying DNA methylation is an interesting way to address our question of interest as this modification contributes to brain development/plasticity and is responsive to environmental experiences. In this project we plan to investigate DNA methylation and expression across the entire genome from cortical brain tissue of subjects who were abused as children and died by suicide as adults. In the past, researchers asking similar questions ignored that the brain is composed of a heterogeneous mixture of cell populations that can be differentially affected by our environment. Our project advances the field by using methods that allow us to study abuse driven changes in a single population of brain cells. We've chosen to study pyramidal cells due to evidence of their dysregulation in animal models of depression and post-mortem human brain tissue from depressed subjects who died by suicide. As a result, our research will allow us to identify pyramidal specific epigenomic and transcriptomic networks biologically disrupted by childhood abuse.

column36: Prospective memory functioning following traumatic brain injury: Vulnerability to mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is defined as a set of cognitive deficits that do not yet meet criteria for dementia. However, patients who meet the diagnostic criteria for MCI may progress to dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, at a much greater rate than the general older population of Canadians above the age of 60 (26% vs. 3%, over a three-year period). To facilitate early identification and treatment of those who may be at greater risk of MCI and Alzheimer's, it is essential to understand the nature of cognitive deficits that may be implicated, particularly among those who may be more predisposed to developing dementia. For instance, traumatic brain injuries are commonly reported by older individuals and have been shown to contribute to the development of MCI and Alzheimer's disease. Prospective memory, which refers to memory for future planned actions, such as taking medication at a specific time, has been shown to be disrupted among survivors of traumatic brain injuries, but also among those with MCI and Alzheimer's. In fact, this relationship has been so frequently found that prospective memory impairments have been suggested to be an early clinical indicator of Alzheimer's disease. The proposed research therefore has several important aims: 1) to better understand the nature of prospective memory deficits among survivors of traumatic brain injuries; 2) to investigate whether prospective memory performance, following traumatic brain injuries, may better identify those with MCI and Alzheimer's disease; and 3) to determine whether prospective memory performance and previous traumatic brain injury may predict further cognitive decline, including MCI and Alzheimer's diagnoses over a three-year follow-up period. Using data collected from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, this study will allow for the better understanding of those who are at greater risk of developing dementia following traumatic brain injuries, to better inform early interventions.

column36: Identifying components of the mitochondrial electron transport chain as potential therapeutic targets for pulmonary hypertension
column37: The body responds to changes in oxygen during development and adaptation to inadequate oxygen supply (hypoxia). Pulmonary hypertension (PH) affects thousands of Canadians. Like cancer, PH is marked by excess cell growth and impaired cell death, due in part to impaired oxygen sensing and metabolism. The majority of PH treatments target the vasospastic component of this disease. Understanding the mechanism of oxygen sensing and targeting impaired oxygen sensing in PH could provide new therapeutic targets. Nearly all blood vessels dilate in response to sudden-onset hypoxia, ensuring maximum blood flow and oxygen delivery to the organs. However, small pulmonary arteries (PA) in the lung constrict in response to even mild hypoxia, a process called hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV). HPV optimizes oxygen uptake by diverting blood flow to well-ventilated lung segments. HPV occurs through a rapid, reversible process that is intrinsic to the pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMC), and vasoconstriction is initiated by cellular changes that inhibit voltage-gated potassium channels and activate calcium channels. Elevation of cytosolic Ca2+ leads to vasoconstriction. It is thought that a sensor within the cell converts PO2 into a secondary messenger that regulates ion channels, enzymes and vascular tone. Prior research identified the mitochondrion (the powerhouse of the cell that generates energy) as the probable oxygen sensor in the PA and shown that changes in electron transport chain (ETC) function controls pulmonary vascular tone through alterations in cellular signalling. The goals of my research are to identify the molecular subunits of the mitochondrial ETC that respond to hypoxia and the differences between the mitochondria of PA and renal arteries, and investigate how these differences are linked to cell function. Identifying ETC subunits that mediate oxygen-sensing will provide novel therapeutic targets for PH and other diseases of impaired oxygen sensing.

column36: Characterizing the genome-wide burden of rare variants in developmental disorders
column37: Developmental disorders (DD) are a group of complex conditions that primarily impact neurodevelopment, beginning in infancy or childhood and persisting across the lifespan. Individuals with DD often suffer from impairments in various areas of development, including growth, language, learning, and sociability. DD includes conditions such as intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Collectively these conditions affect about 3 of every 100 people in the world and place considerable strain on affected individuals, families, and society. There is significant evidence to support the association between rare genetic changes in regions of the genome that code for proteins (called a "gene") and DD. However, the majority of research to date has only focused on new (not present in either parent) genetic changes in a single gene. This type of genetic change, called a de novo mutation, can only account for about 30-35% of DD cases. The aim of this study is to determine what percent of DD cases can be explained by rare inherited variants (from either or both parents) in two or more genes. Our goal is to provide families of those with DD with a genetic diagnosis, which can help tailor health care decisions, inform future reproductive choices, and advance the design of new treatments.

column37: Autophagy is a word originating from the Greek words auto, meaning "self", and phagein, meaning "eating". It is a process used by cells to degrade and recycle damaged structures, to trap and destroy invading bacteria and viruses, and to break down non-essential cellular components to re-use them as energy during periods of starvation. An inability to properly carry out this process can result in numerous diseases including various neurodegenerative diseases, heart diseases, infections and cancer. Autophagy begins with the cell rapidly encapsulating the material to be degraded within a specialized compartment called the autophagosome (a process lasting about 10 minutes). How the cell regulates the formation of this capsule is largely unknown due to technical difficulties associated with studying such rapid events. This proposal aims to develop and employ new technologies to make studying the autophagosome easier. We will use specially designed chemicals to rapidly relocate proteins to and from the autopahgosome and watch how this impacts formation of the capsule in real-time using live-cell microscopy. Understanding how the capsule is formed will help us figure out how the inability to properly carry out autophagy leads to disease and ultimately identify new therapies for those diseases.

column37: In an era of highly effective antiretroviral therapy, access to care remains an important barrier to HIV outcomes. Geographic discrepancies in healthcare access in Canada have been documented for many illnesses; however HIV data are limited. Furthermore, the impact of stigma, transportation barriers, and lack of gender autonomy for women living in rural/Northern areas can overlap, creating even greater barriers to health. This study aims to better understand factors that can lead to poorer HIV health outcomes for women living with HIV in rural/Northern Ontario (ON) and British Columbia (BC). This study will look at different ways to categorize rural and Northern regions of Canada and how these categorizations help explain geographic differences in health outcomes. This information will be used to determine the best geographic categorization to be used in the subsequent phase. Next, this study will look specifically at women living with HIV in ON and BC through the Canadian HIV Women's Sexual & Reproductive Health Cohort Study. We will look at how geographic barriers (living in rural/Northern regions) interact with other factors such as socioeconomic status, racism, sexism and HIV stigma to impact health outcomes for women living with HIV. Data from this study will be used to identify gaps in care and direct recommendations for targeted interventions to improve the health and wellness of women living with HIV in rural/Northern Canada. This study will be guided by community-based research principles and will engage community members in rural/Northern ON and BC throughout the research process. As many women with HIV in rural/Northern Canada are Indigenous, Indigenous community partners will be meaningfully engaged, adhering to principles of cultural safety. column36: How microglia and complement inhibitory molecules shape synaptic plasticity
column37: During development, a process called synaptic pruning removes inappropriate neural connections. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, have recently been implicated in synaptic pruning. Very little is known about why certain synapses are spared while others are pruned. This work will aim to answer the question: How do certain synapses become destined for elimination by microglia? There is evidence to suggest that the complement system, a part of the immune system that enhances the ability of antibodies and white blood cells to clear invading organisms and dead cells, plays a role in synaptic pruning. To protect host cells from aberrant complement attack, healthy host cells express proteins that inhibit complement. Whether these molecules also protect properly wired synapses from microglial synaptic pruning, is not known. We hypothesize that strong synapses that have wired correctly will express higher levels of complement inhibitors and thus will be protected from microglial removal. The first goal of this work will be to provide definitive evidence that microglia are involved in synaptic pruning. Next, we will examine whether synapses are stabilized by complement inhibitors. Finally, we will examine if neuronal activity increases levels of complement inhibitory molecules on the surface of synapses. Determining how complement proteins determine which synapses should be removed will lead to a greater understanding of our current mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and the neurobiology of learning and memory. Additionally, synaptic dysfunction is a defining characteristic of many neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. Increasing our understanding of how synapses are pruned will allow us to explore how this mechanism may become overactive in diseases such as autism, Alzheimer's disease, and schizophrenia.

column36: Structural and functional exploration of the misfolded protein sensor, UGGT
column37: Proteins are essential macromolecules that need to fold into their proper shapes to carry out their biological functions. Helper proteins called chaperones exist in human body to help ensure that proteins achieve their correct three-dimensional conformations. Errors in protein folding lead to diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's disease and cystic fibrosis. UGGT is a key chaperone, responsible for sensing improperly folded proteins. It acts as a gatekeeper in human cells and marks misfolded proteins by attaching a glucose residue to the protein. This glucose residue is a signal the sends the protein back into the refolding process. Despite over 30 years of study, we do not understand how UGGT distinguishes between well folded and unfolded proteins. By an unknown mechanism, UGGT recognizes unfolded proteins as distinct from the millions of different shapes of folded proteins. My research aims at understanding how UGGT specifically recognizes unfolded proteins. The approach I propose to visualize UGGT is cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM). Recent advances in cryo-EM have made it possible to resolve the structures of proteins at a scale never before possible. I will observe how UGGT interacts with unfolded proteins and selectively modifies them with glucose. The knowledge gained will set the stage for developing drugs to modify the activity UGGT in the treatment of misfolded protein diseases.

column37: CRISPR-Cas, a recently discovered gene-editing technology, is a game-changer. Not only is it more precise than previously developed gene-editing tools, but it is also cheaper, faster, and easier to use. These qualities have made CRISPR-Cas extremely attractive to researchers around the world and across a wide range of specialties. As a result, this gene-editing technology has been quickly adopted for use in biological, agricultural, veterinary, and medical research to create, for example, hardier crops and new cancer treatments. The lab where I will be conducting my research was the first in the world to discover anti-CRISPR proteins, which stop CRISPR-Cas from functioning. They were also the first to figure out how some anti-CRISPR proteins perform this important task. I will be continuing this work by asking key questions, such as: "What do anti-CRISPR proteins look like?", "Are they common and widespread?", "Do anti-CRISPR proteins carry out their work in different ways?", "Is stopping CRISPR-Cas from functioning their only job?", and "Can I design a computer program that will quickly and accurately categorize new anti-CRISPR proteins based on their predicted functions or structures?" In the laboratory, I will perform a high-throughput screen to look for binding partners (potential anti-CRISPR proteins) to the Cas proteins. In the office, I will write a computer program to interpret the laboratory results and to use information from other research groups to categorize and summarize our current knowledge of all known anti-CRISPR proteins. This work should provide us with a better understanding of how anti-CRISPR proteins work to stop CRISPR-Cas from functioning and anything else they might be doing. The results of my study may also lead to the use of anti-CRISPR proteins in combination with CRISPR-Cas as tools for biomedical research.

column36: Exploring new mechanisms of lysosomal dysfunction and alpha-synuclein aggregation in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the second most frequent neurodegenerative disease, affecting 2% of population by age 65. PD is a progressive disease, which mainly manifests as motor dysfunction, but also leads to dementia in 20% of cases. This disorder strongly affects the capacity of patients to perform everyday tasks, such as writing or pouring a glass of water, making emotionally difficult to manage for patients and their families, and financially costly for the society. Current therapies only partially and temporarily correct motor difficulties, but they become inefficient as the disease progresses. New ways to treat the disease are needed, which can target the disease at the root to not only provide palliative but also curative treatment. One molecular basis for most PD cases is the abnormal accumulation in the brain of an otherwise harmless protein present in our cells, called synuclein. Normally, cells will get rid of excess synuclein through their waste-management facility, the lysosome. But in PD patients, the lysosome is dysfunctional for unclear reasons, causing synuclein to accumulate. Some mutations in the DNA of PD patients alter the correct function of lysosomes, but why these mutations cause PD is unknown. The present project aims at understanding how these DNA mutations cause waste-management defects, synuclein accumulation, and ultimately PD. This project is new and ambitious, because despite their clear implication in PD, the DNA mutations we want to study have been mainly disregarded by PD research community. Ultimately, our project will uncover new mechanisms that explain waste-management defects in PD. This will allow the design of novel and promising ways to increase waste-disposal capacities in the cells of PD patients, get rid of excess toxic synuclein, and prevent or even revert disease progression.

column36: Translating Epigenetics in the Canadian Regulatory Environment: A 3-Round Delphi Study to Identify Consensus and Dissension among International Experts about the Ethical, Legal and Social Implications of Epigenetics and Prioritize Policy Requirements
column37: Epigenetics is a promising field of study which is shedding light on biological mechanisms responsible for gene regulation. While variations in the DNA sequence play a critical role in disease susceptibility, some biochemical modifications "over" the DNA sequence ('epi'-genetic) also contribute significantly. Interestingly, the socio-environmental contexts in which people are born, grow up and live (e.g., exposure to pollutants, familial context, social adversity) may affect the "epigenetic programming" of some genes in the long term and sometimes for future generations. Epigenetic research is ethically sensitive because it points to some stakeholders, for instance, polluting industries and misbehaving parents, who may be found morally responsible for wrongful epigenetic programming. Concerns over the possibility that misuses of epigenetic information may lead to stigmatization or unjust discrimination have also emerged in recent years. Two hypotheses of my research project are listed as belows: 1) Currently, epigenetic research, findings, and information are not sufficiently taken into account in existing laws, policies and guidelines, including those developed in the context of genetics research; and 2) Early engagement of scientific experts and bioethics scholars in discussions about the implications of epigenetics for policy making purposes could provide credible foresight for responsible governance. The objective of this research project is to better understand how epigenetics findings should be integrated into laws, policies and guidelines from experts' perspective. Using a 3-round survey, I will collect and analyze qualitative and quantitative data, build a consensus about most imperative issues and provide solutions. Further analysis of the current Canadian regulatory environment will be performed to identify gaps and flaws. The results will provide timely guidance for policy-makers to integrate epigenetics into sustainable health care and public policies.
