column36: Neurobehavioral correlates of vascular risk factors and depression
column37: In modern societies, where average life expectancy is high, determining which factors compromise successful aging is a major goal for scientists and for clinicians. Vascular pathologies (e.g., hypertension and obesity) and depression represent two factors that put us at greater risk for suffering general disability and cognitive impairment in older ages. Moreover, these factors are not completely independent, rather, they seem to interact with each other in complex manners. As such, depression increases the odds for suffering vascular pathology, while the presence of vascular pathology augments the chances for developing depression. However, the exact ways in which these factors interact with each other and compromise brain structure and function remain elusive. The present project is aimed at examining the links between vascular pathology, depressive symptoms and their association with alterations in brain connectivity and cognition. Our working hypothesis is that vascular risk factors and depressive symptoms can statistically predict alterations in brain connectivity and in cognitive outcomes. We will analyze data from the UK Biobank, a large-scale open access dataset with approximately 10,000 participants aged 40 to 69 years old. We will use structural equation models to examine the complex associations between (i) vascular pathology, (ii) depressive symptoms, (iii) brain connectivity, and (iv) cognition. Our results will inform public health policies and clinical strategies aimed at preventing cognitive decline in older ages. Further, the present project will provide a broad conceptual framework that will be easily transferable to the study of neurodegenerative conditions - e.g., Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment and vascular dementia.

column37: Histone proteins act as spools around which our DNA is wound to form nucleosomes that organize our genome. Gene expression is regulated by enzymes that mark the histones in ways that change biological function. column36: Evaluating the efficacy of neuromodulation for the detection of consciousness in unresponsive patients
column37: Many patients in intensive care and complex continuing care are behaviourally unresponsive (e.g. unable to move and/or speak) as a result of severe trauma or disability. These patients include those in a minimally conscious state (MCS) or unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS; previously referred to as vegetative state). Distinguishing between MCS and UWS is important, as individuals in MCS have some degree of consciousness and subjective experience, while individuals in UWS do not. However, the current clinical gold standard for detecting consciousness is based solely on the patient's behavioural responses, which causes the presence of consciousness to go undetected in nearly half of patients. Misdiagnosing unresponsive patients can have major implications for prognosis and treatment, impacting the level of care obtained by patients. The goal of this study is to develop a bedside system that can accurately detect an individual's level of consciousness. More specifically, we will test whether modulating brain networks through anaesthesia and brain stimulation can enable the detection of neural markers of consciousness. Through the assessment of the connectivity in brain networks, we will assess whether neurological patterns of consciousness in UWS respond to anaesthesia and brain stimulation in a similar manner to neurologically compromised individuals with known consciousness (e.g. those in MCS). We hypothesize that anaesthesia and brain stimulation will be able to identify UWS patients that possess "covert consciousness". This study will enable the development of an accurate system for the bedside assessment of consciousness, providing a neurophysiological basis for decision-making and enabling evidence-based treatment decisions and improved quality of care. Ultimately, we aim to provide an accurate diagnosis and care to unresponsive patients, which will decrease the emotional and economic burden associated with their care, and improve their quality of life.

column36: Early life-influences on suicidal ideation, suicide attempts and suicide mortality: a life-course perspective to inform prevention
column37: Suicide and suicidal behaviours (suicidal ideation and suicide attempt) are among the leading public health concerns, especially among youths (second cause of death in Canada). Most prevention programs aim to identify and help individuals made vulnerable to suicide by a difficult time in their lives (unemployment, relationship problems). However, contemporary research is showing that early-life influences, such as events occurring before or around birth and family characteristics (birth order, parental age, family size, birth weight, birth length), can influence later susceptibility to suicide. For instance, the fourth-born child is 200% more at risk to commit suicide in adulthood than the first-born child. This project is interested in these early factors, and the way to prevent their later effect on suicidality. The objectives are: (1) to review and summarise the current literature on this topic; (2) to study the association between early-life influences and suicidal behaviours in 3 large cohorts: the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development, including 2120 children, followed from 5 months to 17 years; the National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youths, including 16903 children, followed from 1 to 25 years; the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Kindergarten Children, including 3018 children, followed from 6 to 29 years; (3) to determine why early-life influences convey a higher risk of suicide. Indeed, it is possible that this risk is not due to these factors per se, but to other intermediate factors. Our hypothesis is that early-life influences have an effect on some intermediate factors, which in turn increase the susceptibility to suicide. Especially, we will examine the role of 3 potential intermediate factors: parenting practice, parental stimulation/attention toward the child, and mental health problems in adolescence. Knowing the intermediate factors linking early-life influences and suicidal behaviours will highlight new avenues for prevention.

column36: Analysis of breast cancer REaCT (Rethinking Clinical Trials) data
column37: Telomeres are sections of DNA found at the ends of our chromosomes. Telomerase is an essential component of the makeup of our genetic information. It helps to assemble and protect our DNA in our telomeres from damage. Since telomerase possesses such a critical role for our cell's health and make-up, it's dysfunction can result in devastating effects to our well-being. Cancer is a disease characterized by the rapid and uncontrolled division of cells. As a cell begins to become cancerous, it divides more often, and its telomeres become very short. If its telomeres get too short, the cell may die. However, these cells can escape death by making more telomerase, which prevents the telomeres from getting even shorter. Cancer cells contain active telomerase to enable them to become 'immortal' and continue dividing uncontrollably. When compared to normal healthy cells in our body, the levels of telomerase are greatly increased in cancer cells. This observation, which is found to be true for a wide number of different cancer types, can be exploited to develop new cancer therapies which specifically target the out-of-control telomerase. If telomerase activity was switched off in cancer cells, their telomeres would shorten until they reached a 'critical length'. This would, prevent the cancer cells from dividing uncontrollably to form tumours. Further research into the different processes which control telomerase levels and activity, once identified, can be exploited as targets for cancer therapy. Based on these findings, compounds can be developed which specifically target this out-of-control cellular process, and tested on human cancer cells to determine their efficacy in slowing the progression of cancer.

column36: Reorganization of basal ganglia circuits by drugs of abuse
column37: Drug abuse is a major health issue, but we continue to lack long-term, effective treatments for addiction. This is due to a lack of understanding of how addictive drugs leave long-lasting changes in our brains. Drugs of abuse act in the brain by increasing dopamine release, which alters the connectivity of neural circuits that are responsible for reward processing. The nucleus accumbens is an important brain region for the learning and expression of reward behaviours, but the specific ways in which drugs of abuse alter circuit connections into and out of the nucleus accumbens remains unknown. The goal of my postdoctoral research is to examine how drugs of abuse change the connectivity of nucleus accumbens neurons to promote aberrant forms of drug seeking behaviour. The results of these experiments will give new insight into the mechanisms by which repeated exposure to drugs of abuse alter the brain and should inspire more targeted approaches for the treatment of addiction.

column36: Von Willebrand Factor to Guide Management of Paravalvular Regurgitation during TAVI in Real-Life Practice - REVITALISANTE TRIAL
column37: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI) is a less invasive technic to achieve the replacement of diseased aortic valve compared to standard surgery (open heart surgery). Indeed, this procedure does not need extracorporeal circulation or opening the chest and the heart and is increasingly performed under conscious sedation instead of general anesthesia. TAVI procedure my however be complicated by the presence of paravalvular regurgitation or leakage (PVR) due to an incomplete sealing around the implanted prosthetic valve, a serious complication that is associated with increased risk of death following TAVI. This complication may be identified using different imaging modalities (echo, angiography...) and then corrected. However, these imaging modalities are not enough accurate to quantitate severity of PVR. Consequently, PVR severity may be underestimated and miss-corrected (with a poor prognosis) or overestimated leading to the use of futile and dangerous corrective procedure (risk of aorta rupture, stroke). The objective of this study is to use a simple blood biomarker of Von Willebrand factor known as CT-ADP that have been recently shown to be extremely affected by the severity of leakage and then can be used to identify severe leakage and to select patients who will really need additional corrective procedures. Yet, the utility of this biomarker in real life need further validation. This study aims particularly to investigate whether the monitoring of CT-ADP during the procedure changes decision making in the management of the leakage and if its measurement at the end of the procedure improves prediction of patient prognosis following TAVI. The validation of this tool will be helpful to accurately detect the main complication of the procedure (leakage), select patients who will need additional corrective procedures following TAVI, and to avoid a considerable number of unjustified diagnostic tests and futile, dangerous, and expensive therapeutic procedures.

column36: Novel signal transduction-based precision therapies for Gq (GNAQ)-driven human malignancies
column37: Ocular melanoma is the most common type of eye cancer in adult. Half of the patients with ocular melanoma will develop liver metastasis within 15 years after diagnosis. The median survival time is then only 2-8 months, independently of the successful treatment of the primary tumor. Clearly, new care options are urgently required to help cure these patients. It has been recently established that genes encoding Gq proteins (GNAQ and GNA11) are mutated in 83% of ocular melanomas, unveiling the existence of G protein-driven human malignancies. However, the molecular mechanisms by which these mutations can promote tumor progression remain poorly understood. The objective of our project is to decipher the Gq oncogenic signaling network, with emphasis on a novel downstream target, FAK, in order to find new therapeutic options. To do so we will combine functional and genomic information obtained from standard cell lines, genetically defined mouse models, and cell lines derived from ocular melanoma to understand how Gq activates the tyrosine kinase FAK, and the role of this activation in promoting malignant cell growth. Finally, we will endeavor to translate this deeper understanding of signaling circuitry in ocaular melanoma into new precision cancer care by investigating the pre-clinical outcome of targeting the Gq-FAK pathway. To this end, we will generate a mouse model for ocular melanoma metastasis to evaluate the effect of FAK inhibitors as a monotherapy or in combination with already known and novel chemotherapy agents.

column36: Targeting Cell Death Signaling Pathways in the heart
column37: Doxorubicin is one of the most widely used chemotherapeutic agents for treating human cancers, including breast, lung and lymphomas, however, its propensity for inducing necrotic cell death and heart failure has profound implications for individuals treated with this agent. In fact better diagnostic tools for early cancer detection has resulted in an insurgence of individuals treated with doxorubicin at risk for developing heart failure. Therefore, there is an immediate and impeding need for discovery of therapeutic interventions that will mitigate doxorubicin cardiotoxicity and heart failure. Preliminary work by the mentor's has identified a protein call Bnip3 (Bcl-2 Ninteen Kilo Dalton Interacting Protein) is activated in the heart following doxorubicin treatment. Notably, Bnip3 promotes injury resulting in mitochondrial damage and cell death. The underlying mechanisms by Doxorubicin promotes cardiac injury and cell death remains unknown. Hence, the focus of this proposal is to elucidate how doxorubicin promotes cardiac cell death and the role of Bnip3 in this process. The long-term objective of this research is directed toward improving the quality of life of patients treated with doxorubicin by developing new drugs that will decrease the incidence of heart failure. The spin-off benefit to this research would be realized by a substantial reduction in costly medications and need for long-term patient care. It can be seen that this research will have a major and positive impact on society and Canada's health care system in particular.

column36: Synthetic biology-enabled identification of novel antibiotic resistance mechanisms using de novo proteins to screen for emergent activities
column37: Antibiotic resistance remains one of the most pressing crises facing modern medicine. We use antibiotics as weapons against bacteria, while bacteria find ways of deflecting our attack. Existing forms of resistance make current antibiotics nonfunctional, and newly emerging resistance makes even our best new antibiotics stop working. Currently, our only option when we encounter resistance is to switch to a different antibiotic, and we're rapidly running out of good ones to use. This is because resistance is widespread and frequently develops spontaneously. We need to understand resistance better to "hit back" when we encounter it. By counteracting resistance we can protect the usefulness of antibiotics and continue to treat the patients that suffer from antibiotic-resistant infections. The tools of synthetic biology can help, using libraries of de novo proteins - proteins that have never before existed in nature. I will develop a method to predict the emergence of new antibiotic resistance activities by screening vast libraries of proteins for new antibiotic resistance activities. Proteins that produce resistance will indicate mechanisms of resistance that could also emerge in clinical bacteria. These proteins will teach us about the way a bacterium escapes antibiotics, so we can learn to counter that resistance even before we introduce that antibiotic into patients. Once I have identified proteins that produce resistance, I will determine the chemical mechanism the proteins use to make the bacteria resistant. This information will help us better understand the likely causes of resistance when we use an antibiotic in the clinic. Thus, using this broad screening method for antibiotic resistance, we will be able to better predict and anticipate where resistance will come from. We can even apply this strategy for the newest antibiotics as they are discovered. For the first time, we will be prepared when we find resistance and be able to immediately fight back

column36: 3D Bioprinting of Tissues and Organs
column37: An enormous clinical need exists for the development of technologies to facilitate the regeneration of injured or diseased tissues and organs. Tissue engineering involves mimicking the extracellular matrix (ECM) of a tissue or organ for clinical use, research and drug discovery. Generally, the production of 3D structures with complex geometries by printing is being applied in industry. This process can also be applied for the formation of 3D scaffolds of biological materials, tissues and organs. In 3D bio-printing, layer-by-layer precise positioning of biopolymers, bio-chemicals and living cells, with spatial control of the placement of functional components, is used to fabricate 3D functional living human constructs with structural, biological and mechanical properties that are very similar to those of native tissues. The overwhelming challenge in 3D bio-printing field is to ensure sufficient vascularization and innervation of the engineered construct, which are essential for the long-term viability of any bio-printed tissue construct. Currently such constructs often tend to be avascular, aneural, thin or hollow, and they are nourished by diffusion from a host vasculature. 3D bio-printing shows great promise for efficient generation of biomimetic tumor models with excellent reproducibility to further advance and accelerate cancer research. The objective of this research will be to design, fabricate 3D bio-printed living tissues, which will possess morphologically, mechanically, and biologically suitable properties to mimic the ECM of the native tissue with sufficient vascularisation and innervation within the 3D constructs. This will overcome clinical complications associated with the lack of donor organs, with testing of drug toxicity and with the modeling of cancerous tumors.

column36: The role of microbial sphingolipids in the initiation, progression and treatment of inflammatory bowel disease
column37: A healthy mammalian gastrointestinal tract is shaped by a co-evolution between the immune system and molecules derived from our resident gut microbes, the gut microbiome. Despite the wide array of mechanisms working to promote intestinal homeostasis, breakdowns in this relationship can result in chronic inflammation and Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). IBD is likely due to abnormal host immune responses to the gut microbiome in genetically susceptible individuals. While we know there is an alteration in the intestinal microbiome of IBD patients correlating with disease status, many specific mechanisms as to how our gut microbiome can influence IBD remain unresolved. Here, we aim to fill this gap in knowledge by analyzing which microbial products can interact with the host to initiate inflammatory disease. Specifically, we are interested in specialized membrane lipids called sphingolipids which are abundant in human cells, and altered in abundance during IBD. Recently, we discovered that certain bacterial species in the intestine can also produce sphingolipid metabolites, of which many have unknown functions and could feed into inflammatory pathways triggering IBD. We hypothesize these microbial sphingolipid metabolites can impact the initiation and progression of IBD. To study this, we have developed a protocol to isolate sphingolipids from clinically relevant strains of bacteria and screened these lipids in immune cells for their impact on IBD associated pathways using RNA sequencing. This screen will aim to identify novel bacterial sphingolipids that can activate pro-inflammatory signalling events in immune cells. Further, using gene-knockdown strategies, we will determine which receptor any novel sphingolipid can interact with on immune cells to trigger inflammation. We plan to further investigate these observations in animal models and human biopsies to determine the relative impact microbial sphingolipids have on IBD.

column36: Gut-peptide based polypharmacy for the treatment of obesity and anxiodepressive behavior: the role of astrocytes
column37: Obesity and high-fat regimen lead to brain functions impairment such as altered feeding behavior and development of anxiety- and depressive-like behavior. There is a strong link between obesity and depression in humans and animals alike and high-fat diet-induced brain inflammation is suspected to be that missing link. A novel drug has been generated in the lab of Dr Tschop to correct obesity and brain inflammation. This compound is a combination of a GLP-1-like molecule, mimicking drugs already on the market to treat type 2 diabetes, and dexamethasone, a well-known anti-inflammatory molecule. Diet-induced obese mice treated with this novel compound exhibit massive weight loss, better insulin sensitivity and reduced neuroinflammation. Our aim is to understand if this novel compound can further improve feeding behavior, anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors, and to better understand the role of specific brain cells -known as astrocytes- in mediating these beneficial effects. This project has a strong translational potential and will also help understand the role of non-neuronal cells in the brain with respect to obesity and high-fat regimen-induced brain inflammation. We will use mouse models and treat them with this novel drug or a control solution and then assess their responses using state-of-the-art behavioral testing. We will also explore the role of astrocytes in their response using various genetically engineered mouse models allowing us to discriminate the effects linked with astrocytes direct or indirect actions and allowing us to artificially activate or repress astrocytes activation in a context of drug treatment. We believe this study will further solidify the potential of this new GLP-1-dexamethasone compound as a anti-obesity & anti-brain inflammation therapy, in addition to shedding light on the cellular mechanisms behind its actions.

column36: Novel therapies for surfactant protein deficiencies causing neonatal death and childhood lung fibrosis: Alveolar epithelial cells (AECs) derived from induced pluripotent cells (iPSCs) in therapy
column37: Lungs are made of pipes (conducting airways) that deliver oxygen to millions of air sacs (alveoli) where oxygen is taken up by the blood and distributed to the rest of the body. These air sacs are coated with surfactant produced by lung cells. Surfactant keeps the air sacs wide open to insure exchange of oxygen. Surfactant is made out of a mixture of proteins and lipids. Amongst these surfactant proteins (SP), SP-B and SP-C decrease lung surface tension to keep the alveoli open. Unfortunately, there are rare, but lethal genetic diseases in which SP-B is abnormal. Babies born with SP-B deficiency have trouble breathing at birth because the alveoli are crumpled and can't open. These babies usually die or develop lung fibrosis (scarring). Currently, there is no therapy. Our body contains stem cells, a pool of cells that have the ability to become any type of cell (i.e. bone, muscle or lung cell). The "best" stem cells known so far are the embryonic stem cells (ESCs) because they can become any type of cells in the body, but there are ethical, social and technical issues with ESCs. A major discovery was achieved in 2006 (and rewarded with the Nobel Prize in 2012) when researchers showed that one could turn a skin cell into an embryonic-like stem cell. These cells are called "induced pluripotent stem cells" or iPSCs. It is now possible to make stem cells from any patient with a genetic disease. The objective of our project is to correct the genetic defect in iPSCs from patients suffering from SP-B deficiency. We will first test if we can fix the mutation in iPSCs from patients with SP-B deficiency. In a second step, we will take human iPSCs, turn these into lung cells that produce surfactant, and deliver these to SP-B deficient mice. Then we will verify if these cells are safe and restore normal breathing and produce surfactant. The novel technologies represent a promising and innovative way to discover a new treatment for these devastating genetic disorders.

column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a devastating disease that affects millions of people worldwide. column36: Investigation of mechanisms of iron overload induced cardiomyopathy
column37: Currently around 25% North Americans suffer from a condition known as metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is defined as a cluster of abnormalities including obesity, insulin resistance and increased blood pressure which together substantially increase risk of developing cardiovascular diseases, such as heart failure. Among patients with metabolic syndrome around 13.4% of them also have increased levels of iron. Several research studies have shown that increased iron levels can have a detrimental effect on the health of these individuals. While there have been studies investigating the role of increase iron in other tissues and conditions, we contend that iron is still an underappreciated factor in the development of heart failure in patients with metabolic syndrome. First, using isolated heart cells and establish cell lines, we will confirm our preliminary data that increased iron causes insulin resistance. Further, we will investigate and determine the role that autophagy and the NRLP3 inflammasome play in the development of insulin resistance when there is an increased iron present. Secondly, based on the results of the cell culture experiments, we will investigate these mechanisms in mouse models which lack either autophagy or the NLRP3 inflammasome to determine their effects on the heart. Taken together we aim to conduct a focused and in-depth analysis of mechanisms responsible for development of cardiovascular diseases under conditions on increased Iron. New knowledge from studies such as this are needed to pave the way for development of improved therapeutic strategies for treating patients with cardiovascular disease.

column36: Zebrafish models for pyridoxine dependent epilepsy research; drug discovery and pre-clinical validation
column37: Rare diseases (RDs) are often life threatening conditions caused by mutations in our genetic material. Although individually rare (<1 in 2,000 individuals), collectively RDs affect an estimated 1 in 12 Canadians, impacting families, society and the health care system. One such RD is pyridoxine dependent epilepsy (PDE), caused by a genetic defect in the breakdown of lysine, one of the building blocks of proteins; the condition is characterized by seizures and progressive intellectual disability. This defect in lysine breakdown leads to the accumulation of a toxic biochemical; this compound is believed to cause PDE and thus its reduction may have therapeutic benefit lessening seizures and neurodevelopmental problems. My work has led to the identification of drug candidates that, by two different pathways, may lower the levels of the toxic metabolites in cells isolated from PDE patients. We believe that one or both compounds may have a beneficial impact on PDE patients; importantly one of these is a safe widely used medication. An important step to translate what I have shown in patient cells into actual clinical trials is testing the drugs in an animal genetically engineered to have PDE. I propose here the generation of such an animal, specifically a zebrafish that will have the same mutations as our PDE patients. Zebrafish have emerged as an important epilepsy model, as they often display seizures that resemble the ones observed in humans. Engineering these fish to have the same lysine degradation defect as PDE patients may also result in them also displaying spontaneous seizures, we also believe they will accumulate the toxic metabolites. The animals will therefore not only help yield answers on how the seizures occur, but also be used to test the drugs candidates and perform drug screens. If successful, the zebrafish research shall lead directly clinical trials in PDE patients providing them a better quality of life.

column36: Relationships between lifestyle behaviours and obesity in Zimbabwean children: a search to understand lifestyle transitions in a developing country
column37: Results from the International Study of Childhood Obesity, Lifestyle and the Environment revealed that key outcomes for children from Kenya (the only low-income country in the study), were different from others. These findings led to speculation, without confirmatory proof, that Kenya's low-income status may have had an influence. However, there was no other country out of the 12 in the study (including Canada) that was comparable to Kenya. In addition, none of the sites had data from a rural sub-sample which may also have different characteristics. Relying on results from only urban and peri-urban populations of mostly medium-to-high income countries for making global policy decisions or for intervention strategies may be misleading and inappropriate. The project being proposed will help address this problem by collecting data among school-children from Zimbabwe (a low-income country comparable to Kenya), using a similar protocol as done before but adding a rural sub-sample and some additional measures. The project will fill an important and country-specific gap in research data on prevalence estimates of childhood obesity and its relationship with lifestyle and environmental factors. The data will also enable international comparisons of these relationships, and provide evidence of similarities or differences which are important for structuring accurate public health messages and intervention strategies that are informed by relevant research evidence. Furthermore, comparing children across cultures and regions will help researchers and policy makers borrow ideas that are applicable to all country contexts but also develop separate ones where needed. Accurate estimates of the magnitude of childhood obesity and how it relates to other factors is very important in the efforts to reduce or prevent non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular and other chronic diseases, while elevating awareness of the importance of a healthy lifestyle during childhood.

column36: Modifications de l'epissage alternatif par le virus du papillome humain : fondements moleculaires et implications dans les cancers oropharynges
column37: A l'echelle mondiale, on estime que plus de 10% de tous les cancers sont relies a des infections virales. Cependant, pourquoi et comment les virus causent le cancer, ainsi que pourquoi certaines infections vont devenir des cancers alors que d'autres non, necessitent plus d'etudes. De maniere interessante, il a recemment ete demontre qu'un phenomene deregule dans le cancer et de nombreuses autres maladies tels que la sclerose laterale amyotrophique et la maladie de Parkinson, peut aussi etre modifie par des virus. Ce phenomene, nomme epissage alternatif, aurait donc un potentiel pour participer au processus de developpement de cancer lors d'infections virales. Ce projet de recherche vise a etudier la deregulation de l'epissage alternatif dans le cadre d'infections virales qui peuvent causer des cancers. Nous allons particulierement etudier ce phenomene chez le virus du papillome humain (VPH), qui est un facteur etiologique important des cancers cervicaux et oropharynges. Ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre par quels mecanismes les virus modulent l'epissage alternatif, dans quels buts ils le font mais surtout quel est l'impact sur le developpement de cancers. Ultimement, ces etudes ouvriront la porte a l'identification de nouvelles avenues therapeutiques par lesquelles les evenements d'epissage alternatif pourraient etre modules. Un traitement pour prevenir le developpement de cancers lors d'infection par des virus pourrait meme etre envisage.

column36: A biopsychosocial conceptualization of persistent genital arousal disorder (PGAD): Investigating the impact of PGAD on genital sensitivity, physiological arousal, psychosocial, sexual, and relationship functioning in women.
column37: Persistent genital arousal disorder (PGAD) is a highly distressing condition that affects approximately 1-6% of women. PGAD is characterized by symptoms of physical sexual arousal (swelling and/or sensitivity of the genitals and nipples) that are described as distressing, intrusive, unwanted, and sometimes painful. Individuals with PGAD frequently report feelings of worry, stress, and depression. Although awareness has been growing, there continues to be a lack of research on this condition, and its causes remain unknown. Little is known about how PGAD impacts mental health, sexuality, and interpersonal relationships. With more information about these factors we may begin to understand how treatments can target both mental health and physical concerns associated with PGAD. The main goal of the proposed study is to improve our understanding of the complex nature of PGAD by examining psychosocial function, sensory characteristics (including sensitivity to touch and heat), and blood flow processes in a controlled study framed by the biopsychosocial perspective. The investigation of these elements will be undertaken using a multimethod approach: 1. Measures assessing psychosocial function and the impact of PGAD; 2. Quantitative Sensory Testing to explore genital and non-genital sensitivity to gain understanding of underlying nerve fibre involvement; and 3. Laser Doppler Imaging to investigate genital and non-genital blood flow processes. This research will provide much-needed information related to the development and maintenance of PGAD. In addition, this information will help inform health professionals in selecting effective treatment options while increasing medical and public recognition of this debilitating condition.

column36: Game of Clones: Investigating genetic & immune drivers of myeloid leukemogenesis
column37: In the last few years, researchers were surprised to find that we can detect mutated, pre-cancerous blood cells in >10% of people over the age of 65. These people have a ten-fold increased risk of developing leukemia, an aggressive blood cancer. Moreover, even after undergoing chemotherapy, these mutated pre-cancerous blood cells often persist in the patient, suggesting that they may be the source, or "root" of the new cancer when the patient relapses. We do not know how these roots develop, expand, or how to eradicate them. However, new data suggests that these roots alter or thrive in a certain kind of "soil": an inflammatory environment in the bone marrow and blood. Therefore, I hypothesize that the mutated pre-cancerous roots interact with the degree of inflammation in their environment, and this enables them to expand. To test this idea, I am using highly sensitive DNA sequencing to detect various pre-cancerous mutations in the blood of 400 otherwise healthy people over the age of 65 (recruited through Baycrest and Sunnybrook Hospitals). I am also quantifying markers of inflammation in these patients, and have found that certain mutations (e.g. in genes called "TET2" and "DNMT3A") are associated with more intense inflammation. I will also be testing how much these roots with certain gene mutations expand in mice. Interestingly, my preliminary analyses show that a specific inflammatory marker in the soil is more intense with these certain gene mutations, and I will test if blocking that intense signal causes the roots to regress. My work will enable earlier cancer surveillance for blood cancer development and its re-emergence. For Canada's aging population, this may facilitate a paradigm shift toward more targeted, preventative medicine. This means that aggressive, often unsuccessful cancer therapies could be avoided in an already frail population, which would improve individuals' quality of life and the healthcare burden overall.

column36: The neuromuscular function as a diagnostic tool and a therapeutic target in an ALS mouse model
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a late-onset neurodegenerative disease, leading to paralysis and death in 2 to 5 years after the diagnosis. In this disease, the specific connection between the motor nerve and the muscle is lost prematurely, leading to progressive difficulties in performing daily activities like moving, walking, eating and talking for example. Unfortunately, no cure is currently available. This specific connection between the motor neuron and the muscle is called the neuromuscular junction, and its destruction is one of the first events in the disease process, which highlights the importance of studying this variable. Alterations have been previously characterized at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) in various animal models as well as in humans, even before symptoms onset, but several questions about NMJ and muscle function remain ill-defined. In addition, the role of glial cells during disease progression, a special type of cells that are present at the NMJ, also needs to be addressed. First, this project has the goal of understanding neuromuscular function in two different types of muscle, using a slow and progressive ALS mouse model. We also want to study muscle strength and contractile parameters of the muscles, in order to highlight early differences in the mutant mice that could lead to the development of a new diagnostic tool, if adapted for humans. Furthermore, a second aim of this study is to test potential drug therapies at the NMJ that could restore motor function and potentially lead to a cure if revealed efficient in humans. Finally, a third aim of this study is to gain insight on the role of the special glial cells at the NMJ during disease progression and their possible involvement in the pathologic process of ALS. These glial cells exert numerous important functions for the maintenance and health of the NMJ that could be impaired or perturbed in ALS, and could therefore represent a promising therapeutic target as well.

column36: DTI Reconstruction of Language Pathways of the Brain: Refining their Respective Specific Functions and the Effect of Bilingualism on their properties
column37: Studies suggest that learning a second language impacts the white matter structure of the brain and that this effect would be modulated by age of acquisition of the second language and its proficiency level. However, the exact nature of these white matter changes and how they are associated with language abilities remain unclear. The left Superior Longitudinal Fasciculus (SLF) is a major white matter language processing pathway of the brain and has been subdivided into three branches according to which brain areas they connect. The temporo-frontal extreme capsule fasciculus (TFexcF) is another recently discovered language pathway. A few studies have been able to dissect the SLF branches and the TFexcF in humans using Diffusion Imaging Tractography, but these are often mixed up with other nearby pathways, such as the arcuate fasciculus, and their specific role in language processing and their contribution to second language learning remain poorly understood. The present project aims to study two groups of bilinguals, simultaneous bilinguals (who learn two languages from birth) and sequential (who learn a second language after the first). We will use anatomical and diffusion (white matter) brain imaging to reconstruct the three SLF branches and the TFexcF in each bilingual participant. Behavioural measures of different aspects of language performance will be used for correlations with quantitative measures of these white matter tracts. The effect of age of acquisition of a second language will be investigated by comparing the white matter tracts of the two bilingual groups. Refining the structural definition of these language pathways and their specific functions has potential clinical implications to identify specific impaired connections in lesions or stroke and for language rehabilitation. This project will also help understand the neural biomarkers for predicting language learning success or impairments, as in developmental conditions.

column36: Anatomo-functional connectivity subtypes in age-related neurodegeneration
column37: As the population ages, neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD) are reaching epidemic levels. Scientists are racing to find drugs that can slow down or even prevent the progressive loss of brain cells. Because the brain has the ability to adapt and compensate for injury (up to a point), by the time cognitive symptoms such as memory loss become evident, many brain cells have been lost. Since "time is brain", new treatments are increasingly being tested on people with mild or even no clinical symptoms, but who are at risk of developing AD. To be able to demonstrate that a drug works within the relatively short timeline of a clinical trial, doctors need to find individuals who are at high risk of symptoms developing or worsening in the near future. Selecting appropriate participants is very challenging, because the evolution of symptoms is highly variable across individuals. I propose that differences in the organization of brain connectivity across individuals will shape how soon symptoms will appear, and how fast they will progress. In other words, for a given level of brain injury, the severity of clinical symptoms experienced by different people will depend on how each person's brain is wired. I will characterize individual functional and structural brain networks using cutting-edge, magnetic resonance imaging methods to identify "subtypes" of brain connectivity that are highly associated with varying levels of impairment on different clinical assessments. I then will apply "machine learning" techniques from computer science to find the combination of functional and structural connectivity subtypes that most correctly identifies each subject's category of cognitive impairment (from cognitively normal to AD). Subtype analysis of brain functional and structural connectivity promises to become an important new tool to help doctors identify individuals most likely to get cognitively worse, and therefore to benefit most from treatment.

column36: A longitudinal randomized controlled trial investigating improvements in verbal memory and multimodal brain connectivity in schizophrenia following treatment promoting semantic encoding strategies
column37: Remembering a grocery list, an appointment, or to take one's medication at a certain time of day are skills that most people take for granted; however, individuals living with schizophrenia have severe difficulty with these typical daily tasks. This can make it difficult for them to live independently, and they often must rely on their loved ones and health professionals for many aspects of everyday life. Psychological interventions, such as cognitive remediation therapy, are computer-based training programs targeting memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities. These types of psychological treatments have been shown to improve cognitive functioning, including memory, as well as social and occupational functioning in schizophrenia. Importantly, these interventions also improve brain structure and function, providing evidence that they have wide-ranging positive effects in people living with schizophrenia. However, these beneficial effects are generally modest and may not have a significant clinical impact in patients' lives. It is, therefore, of utmost importance for researchers to identify the best targets for treatment and improve the effects of these training initiatives. The proposed research aims to do so by targeting specific memory impairments in severely impaired patients, and will involve a long-term clinical trial. Patients with severe memory impairment will take part in one of two brief psychological interventions and will be assessed on symptoms, memory, and brain connectivity immediately before and after treatment, as well as at 3 months follow up. We hypothesize that those who take part in the specific memory-based intervention will show stronger improvements in overall memory and brain function, and that these benefits will remain at follow up. This research will help clarify the equivocal findings of previous research, and will provide support for the benefit of a brief psychological intervention on memory and brain function in schizophrenia.

column36: Assembly of inhibitory circuits in the normal and premature cerebellum
column37: The brain depends on connections of nerve cells. These connections can be excitatory or inhibitory and the balance between the two is essential for brain function. Abnormal development of inhibitory nerve cells and their connections plays an important part in many disorders including epilepsy and autism. Babies born prematurely or who do not get enough oxygen at birth are more likely to develop these problems - possibly because their inhibitory circuits are not formed correctly. In this project, I am looking at a group of inhibitory nerve cells that are born later in pregnancy - beginning around the time babies can survive outside the womb. I will identify the events that help the cells become the correct type of nerve cell and form the right connections. I will also see how injury around the time of birth (low oxygen, infection) affects the normal development of these cells. Finally, I will see if treatments during and immediately after injury can help damaged brains regain their normal wiring. The knowledge from this work will help us learn how inhibitory connections form in the brain and how premature birth and damage can affect this wiring. In the future, this can be used to change treatment of premature infants and to offer preventative strategies for serious pediatric neurological disorders.

column36: Associations between fitness, activity intensity, and time: the influence of novel risk for chronic disease in Manitoba
column37: It is well known that lifestyle factors, such as physical activity and nutrition are associated with the risk of chronic conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease. These lifestyle factors are often the target of strategies that affect the majority of adults. It is estimated that a savings of hundreds of millions of dollars annually in health care costs could be realized by 2020 in Manitoba by increasing the number of individuals meeting the Canadian Physical Activity Guidelines. However, providing one-size fits all recommendations has not been successful, as only 15% of the adult population are meeting the current activity guidelines. There also exists individual differences in the way that people respond to physical activity interventions. Recently, relationships have been found between the level of participation in physical activity, as well as the health benefits attained through activity with the specific genes. As well, the human gut is home to a complex community of over 100 trillion microbial cells. These cells may also influence or be influenced by lifestyle factors, such as physical activity, and thereby also influence the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions. I will explore these complex interactions and how they relate to risk factors for chronic conditions. My research will create information to customize specific physical activity strategies that will hopefully improve the health of Manitobans in a personalized fashion.

column36: Therapy development for pediatric diseases by gene correction in vivo
column37: Type 1 hereditary tyrosinemia (HT1 is caused by lack of the enzyme fumarylacetoacetase (FAH) needed to metabolize tyrosine present in the protein intake of our food. By-products of this amino acid build up, lead to a variety of symptoms including liver and kidney dysfunctions, cancers and death. Birth incidence of HT1 is 1/100,000 worldwide but startling in some regions of Quebec where it affects over 1/1,846 individuals. For genetic diseases that manifest at a young age with irreversible consequences, such as HT1, early treatment is critical and essential. Neonatal gene therapy using viral vectors has the potential advantage of achieving therapeutic effects before disease manifestation and the vector faces a relatively immature immune system. However, treatment of infants faces a major challenge because the loss of episomal vector genomes during liver growth results in the rapid extinction of therapeutic genes expression. In this work, We are going to use a CRISPR/Cas9 based genome editing to induce the integration of a therapeutic FAH gene in a genomic self harbour situated in the albumin gene locus. Experiments will be done in vivo using a mouse model having a lack of the FAH enzyme. Our goal is to translate an innovative genome editing technology into a novel class of human therapeutics that enables precise molecular modification of a genetic defect. Our long-term objective is to develop gene therapies using genome-editing technologies to treat rare inherited metabolic diseases affecting children, such as HT1. We are also interested to improve our knowledge on mechanisms of gene repair. Importantly, this strategy represents a generic approach. HT1 is a well-described model of liver disease; hence we suggest that our approach could be translated to other metabolic diseases for which no treatment exists. Ultimately, this research proposal may lead to significant improvements in quality of life for children and their families affected by rare diseases.

column36: Place-Attachment and the Maternal and Neonatal Health of Inuit in Nunavut: "What was, what is, and what could be"
column37: Inuit in Canada experience the highest infant mortality rate in the country, as well as significantly higher rates of preterm births, stillbirths, and maternal health issues, as compared to the non-Inuit population. These differences are attributed, in part, to the lack of availability and type of obstetrical care women receive. Most women are required to fly out of their communities to Iqaluit or Ottawa for birth, and may have to remain in distant hospitals for weeks or months (referred to as obstetric evacuation). This obstetric evacuation can have serious impacts on the overall health and well-being of a mother and child, but also that of her family and community, who find it challenging to connect emotionally with a newborn after missing the birthing event. Few studies have examined how Inuit psychological, emotional, and spiritual connections to the land influence both their health outcomes and childbirth experiences. The proposed research will explore how the health of mothers and infants may vary based on birth location, and how Inuit experience the health system, given the reality of obstetric evacuation. A cross-sectional study will be used to determine the prevalence of maternal and infant health issues among women who give birth at home, Iqaluit, and Ottawa. Interviews with Inuit mothers, family members, and Elders will be opportunities to hear Inuit perspectives on their historic and current childbirth experiences. Results will be shared with policy-makers and primary healthcare workers, and will include Inuit-identified recommendations for improving health policy and healthcare for mothers and infants, such that Inuit have access to the type and extent of care they have reason to value. This research provides critical information intended to inform policy and programs to reduce the rates of maternal and infant health issues among Inuit in Canada, and enhance the responsiveness of the health system to Inuit needs, preferences, and culture.

column36: Impact of epigenetic markers of breast adipose tissue on the efficacy of aromatase inhibitors treatments.
column37: Breast cancer and obesity are both major health concerns in developed countries. Obesity results from complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors, and is now well recognized to increase breast cancer risk and mortality. In fact, after menopause, fatty tissue is the main source of female hormones, particularly estrogens, and about 80% of breast cancers are hormone dependant, i.e. breast cancer cells need estrogens to grow and multiply. One of the standard treatments for these types of breast cancers, called aromatase inhibitors, blocks the production of estrogens in fatty tissues. Thus, obesity may interfere with efficacy of this hormonal treatment. Actually, differences in hormonal treatment efficiency have been observed, particularly in obese women, and this phenomenon could be explained by differences in genes activation in their breast fat tissue. Genes can be activated by several mechanisms called epigenetic events. Epigenetic events are reversible chemical modifications of DNA that regulate activity of genes depending on the function of the cell and its environment. Obesity may affect breast cancer treatment efficiency through these epigenetic events, especially through a mechanism called DNA methylation. Interestingly, this mechanism can be reversed, making it an appealing target for breast cancer treatment. However, nothing is known about how patterns of this DNA methylation mechanism in breast fat tissues may relate to hormonal treatment efficacy. The objective of the present project is to address the hypothesis that breast fat tissue of women before treatment contains a number of hypo-methylated or hyper-methylated genes that can predict response to hormonal treatment. Therefore, by studying differences in genes activation markers in breast fat tissue of several breast cancer patients, we aim to develop personalized treatments that could increase hormonal treatment efficacy and eventually improve breast cancer survival.

column36: Enhancing immunogenic cancer cell death through the novel combination of oncolytic viruses and photodynamic therapy
column37: The immune system is designed to recognize and kill cancer cells. Therefore, cancers have had to develop strategies to evade a patient's immune system. Biotherapies represent a safe and effective new strategy to treat cancers by manipulating natural biological systems to enhance tumour-specific immune responses. It is now known that cancers can die in one of two ways: immunogenic or non-immunogenic cell death. Immunogenic cell death (ICD) induces cancer-specific immune responses that can kill tumour cells anywhere in the body. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) represent a particularly promising type of biotherapy. These are naturally occurring viruses that do not cause disease. They take advantage of the fact that most cancers shut down antiviral mechanisms as part of the process of evading cell death. OVs typically cause no harm to normal cells but can infect and kill cancerous cells throughout the body. The ability of OVs to cause ICD is highly variable and there is much room for improvement. Therefore, we propose to enhance ICD by combining OVs with photodynamic therapy (PDT). Specifically, PDT uses a light-sensitive drug that concentrates inside a tumour. An external light source can then be safely applied to the cancer site to activate the drug, which then kills the local cancer cells. PDT can only be applied to superficial cancers, such as skin cancers, but since it causes ICD, the ensuing immune response can target cancer cells anywhere in the body. Traditionally, PDT was limited to treating tumours within millimeters of the surface of the skin. We propose to use cutting-edge technology to penetrate up to several centimeters depth, allowing cancers such as breast tumours to be treated. We hypothesize that OVs and PDT will be complementary, resulting in potent immune responses that can kill cancer cells anywhere in the body that escape the initial direct effects of each monotherapy. Our initial targets of this therapy will be melanomas in the brain and breast cancers.

column36: Arts-Based Knowledge Translation of Health Research
column37: Knowledge translation (KT) is the element of research that focuses on sharing findings with the people that will use the knowledge. Often, this involves health care professionals and patients. Without this integral connection between health research and implementation, new knowledge may not lead to wide spread implementation, or have an impact on health. For these reasons, CIHR includes KT as part of its mandate. The proposed study will assess the outcomes of an arts-based method of KT to disseminate health research. Specifically, a dance-based event will take place to share the mounting research suggesting dance is a useful form of therapy for people with Parkinson's disease (PD). The event will also be livestreamed so participation may take place virtually. The target audience will include people with PD and health professionals. Three main research questions will be explored: Does participation in an arts-based, KT event (1) influence health professionals' referral practices to recommend dance to PD patients?; (2) influence people with PD's perspective on dance as an accessible/worthwhile form of therapy?; and (3) does live versus virtual participation impact outcomes of the KT event? Outcomes of the event will be assessed using both survey and interview data to determine if arts-based KT is an effective way to share health research.

column36: Help Seeking Behaviours, Access to Care and Suicide among Rural and Urban Populations in Ontario, Canada
column37: Previous research has indicated that those living in rural areas may have increased risk of suicide compared to their urban counterparts and research from the United States suggests that those living in rural areas are less likely to seek help from mental health care professionals prior to suicide. The primary aim of this study is to compare help seeking behaviours prior to suicide and suicide attempts among rural and urban populations. Factors that are associated with rurality and that may predict these help seeking behaviours will also be examined such as travel time to the nearest mental health service centre and nearest general health service centre, having a family physician, and prevalence of health professionals in the nearest town. This study will be completed using health services data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Research. We hypothesize that lower rates of help seeking will be associated with increasing distance to nearest hospital or mental health services centre, lower prevalence of mental health care professionals and other health professionals and lack of primary care physician. This research contributes new knowledge because previous research comparing suicide rates in Canada is based on 1996 data and does not evaluate health care service utilization prior to suicide.(1) Additionally, help seeking prior to suicide attempts have not yet been compared in an urban versus rural setting. This research is important because rural populations are vulnerable and historic trends suggest increased risk of suicide.(2, 3) My background growing up in a rural setting living and working on a farm, previous epidemiological research involving rural populations, my undergraduate degree in Psychology and my experiences as a suicide phone line volunteer are reasons why I am an ideal candidate to conduct this research.

column36: Predicting Impact of DNA and RNA Variants in Cancer on Three Dimensional Protein Structure
column37: Cancer is primarily a result of changes in our genetic makeup, also known as DNA. According to a fundamental principle in biology, DNA encodes the instructions for generating proteins - the functional and regulatory components of our body. Therefore, changes in DNA subsequently alter the structure of the protein they encode. Because protein functionality is directly linked to protein structure, my goal is to develop a tool that predicts the change in protein structure that results from specific DNA changes. This will be accomplished by combining detection of DNA changes with physical chemistry measurements and predictive statistical models. The tool will be developed specifically exploring prostate cancer, however, once completed it will be applied to cancer types comprehensively. With this information, we will be able to better understand the aberrant functions of cancerous proteins allowing for improved detection and treatment of a broad-range of cancers.

column36: The Mechanistic Function of SARM1 and NLRX1 in Apoptosis and Cell Death in the Nervous System
column37: Cells of the body are constantly dying while new ones are being formed. Too much or not enough cell death leads to a wide spectrum of diseases, depending on where the imbalance is found. Given the complex nature of the brain and the incidence of neurodegenerative disease and brain injury, it is essential to start investigating mechanisms that lead to the death of brain cells. Recently, a protein named SARM1 has been found to be essential for cell death specific to the brain. The action of SARM1 also leads to more general cell death, although the mechanism and extent is poorly understood. Additionally, the protein NLRX1 has been identified as a regulator of this general cell death. Further study has shown NLRX1 and SARM1 interact, but it is unknown whether there is an effect of such interaction. The goal of this project is to uncover the mechanism of how these two proteins regulate the death of brain cells and other types of cells as well. Using mice to model disease, we will perform experiments in specific cell types and entire brains collected from them. Such experiments will involve characterizing the localization of NLRX1 and SARM1 within the cell, how brain cells respond to different death signals, and whether mice lacking either NLRX1 or SARM1 differ from normal mice in their brain cell death profiles following injury. SARM1 is now known to play a major role in brain injury. By uncovering the mechanisms of SARM1-mediated brain cell death, we gain an understanding of the causes of neurodegenerative disease and traumatic brain injury which can be taken forward into the clinical setting to focus therapeutic efforts.

column36: Identifying social determinants of nutrition and evaluating the effectiveness of preconception multiple micronutrient supplementation on growth among adolescent girls in rural Pakistan
column37: Undernutrition is an underlying cause of millions of deaths among women and newborns in resource-limited settings, where food may be inadequate in both quantity and quality. The risk of undernutrition is even higher for adolescent girls, given their increased nutritional requirements during puberty. Improving nutritional status using multiple micronutrient (MMN) supplements and identifying factors among those at the greatest risk for undernutrition could help to reduce the number of girls with deficiencies, and other poor health outcomes. In the context of a randomized control trial in rural Pakistan, we hypothesize that providing adolescent girls (15-19 years) with MMN supplements during the period before pregnancy begins (preconception) will more effectively improve their nutritional status compared to participants who receive the standard of care (no supplements during preconception). Stemming from this study, the objectives of my dissertation will be to (1) describe the dietary intake of adolescent girls at enrolment; (2) identify social determinants of nutritional insufficiency from dietary and biomarker data for iron, vitamin A, and vitamin D among adolescent participants at enrolment; and (3) determine whether MMN supplementation for 1 year improves growth measures compared to no intervention from height and weight data collected at 3 time points (after 0, 6, and 12 months). Investigating the association between the social determinants of health and nutritional status measures could allow us to better target nutrition interventions to those adolescent girls at the highest risk of undernutrition through nutrition programmes. As the unique nutritional requirements of adolescents have not been adequately acknowledged within international nutrition policy guidelines, study findings will help to fill this critical gap.

column36: Development of a digital microfluidic platform to identify and target single cells from a heterogeneous cell population for lyses in an ultra-low volume
column37: Genetic abnormalities are a leading cause of death among Canadian newborns and infants. The standard-of-care for prenatal diagnosis of genetic abnormalities is (1) maternal blood tests and fetal ultrasound to screen for "high-risk" pregnancies, followed by (2) a diagnostic test on fetal cells requiring either insertion of a needle through the abdomen or vaginal surgery to confirm the results. The latter procedures carry a risk of miscarriage, require experienced medical personnel, are very expensive, and do not provide results until late in the pregnancy. There is clearly a need for safe (less invasive), less expensive prenatal diagnostic techniques that are able to provide relevant information at earlier stages of pregnancy. Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH) in Toronto runs the largest prenatal diagnosis center in Canada and one of the largest in North America. Scientists and physicians at MSH have developed a method to collect and isolate fetal cells non-invasively, using a technique similar to a routine PAP smear. In this proposal, techniques will be developed to rapidly and reproducibly isolate and analyze these cells for prenatal diagnosis of genetic abnormalities using microfluidics and genomic analysis. If successful, the techniques described here could completely transform the way prenatal diagnosis is delivered in Canada and around the world. That is, risk-associated, expensive, invasive diagnostics available after 12-15 weeks of pregnancy would be replaced with safe, inexpensive, non-invasive diagnostics available as early as after 5 weeks of pregnancy. This will result in higher coverage of the population, reduced patient anxiety, increased medical options for at-risk pregnancies, and significant reductions in health care costs. Canadians will also benefit from the formation of a promising prenatal diagnostic startup company, attracting investments and bringing job opportunities into Canada's burgeoning high-tech/biotech sector.

column36: Porphysome Mediated Drug Delivery and PET Imaging to Enhance Adoptive Double Negative T-cell Therapy for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treatment
column37: Since the leading cause of cancer death worldwide is lung cancer and its 5 year survival rate is <20% adjuvant treatments are needed. Immunotherapy is promising because it can improve patient survival. However, to improve immunotherapy, we need to understand where immune cells migrate to and overcome immune cell deterioration. To address these issues, we propose the use of nanoparticles, called porphysomes. Our lab has shown that: 1) porphysomes can be attached to radioisotopes and then used in imaging, and 2) porphysomes can carry and locally deliver drugs to tumors to reduce systemic drug toxicity. This project will combine these aspects of porphysomes to address the problems associated with one form of immunotherapy, called adoptive cell therapy (ACT), for the treatment of lung cancer. In ACT, immune cells are removed from humans, grown ex vivo, and injected into patients, for targeting and killing of tumor cells. Firstly, we will track the migration of immune cells in a lung cancer mouse model, by radiolabeling porphysomes and then attaching porphysomes to an immune cell called the double negative T-cell (DNT). DNTs from a healthy donor do not attack normal cells of the recipient, and are safer. Porphysome conjugated DNTs will be imaged via positron emission tomography. Next, we will load porphysomes with an "immune booster" and attach porphysomes to DNTs. The immune booster will be slowly released from the porphysomes, and be locally delivered to the DNTs. This continual stimulation of DNTs will improve their killing ability. Results will firstly, improve our understanding of the localization of immune cells during ACT and enable us to optimize parameters to improve its efficacy. Secondly, porphysome-mediated local delivery of an immune booster should prevent immune cell deterioration and systemic toxicity. Successful proof-of-concept will allow for loading other immune regulating agents into nanoparticles and improve immunotherapy for other cancers.

column36: Early injecting careers: Implications for health, HIV risk behaviours and clinical care
column37: Injection drug use among youth is a significant public health concern that is associated with severe harms among youth including, fatal drug overdose, violence, and risk of HIV and Hepatitis C (HCV) incidence. However, initiation of injection drug use among early injecting careers remains understudied. While there is growing recognition that contextual factors play a central role in determining youth's high-risk drug using behaviors, little is known about initiation into injecting, early injecting careers, and potential interventions that may help prevent initiation into injecting. Furthermore, our understanding of factors that determine early cessation or predict sustained injecting among recent initiates remains very limited. Therefore, this study proposes to employ longitudinal data analyses to characterize early injecting careers, with a focus on the individual (e.g., childhood trauma, drug use patterns) and social-structural (e.g., homelessness, incarceration) factors that shape injection initiation, early cessation of injecting, and sustained injecting. Findings of this study are essential to developing meaningful and effective policy and program interventions that seek to prevent early injecting careers from progressing to sustained injecting.

column36: The role of humoral immunity in the acquisition, transmission, and clearance of human papillomavirus infection in heterosexual couples.
column37: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection; over 200 HPV types exist. Most HPV infections clear within a year, but some persist and may result in cervical, vaginal, penile, anal, and mouth and throat cancer. Despite the introduction of costly screening and vaccination programs, HPV is estimated to contribute to 5.2% of the worldwide tumor burden. Hence, HPV prevention needs improvement. Considering that most infections disappear spontaneously, the immune system may have a major role in preventing and clearing HPV infections. It produces antibodies against HPV in response to natural infection or vaccination. Much about this immune response remains unknown: we do not know what triggers the immune system against specific HPV types, its ability to prevent new infections, or how an immune response affects HPV transmission from/to his/her sexual partners. Further, it remains debated whether antibodies against HPV in an individual predict persistent infections or future risk of cancer, or are simply a consequence of past infections. Answers to these questions are important, as (1) they may aid in developing new prevention strategies against HPV-related cancers, and (2) as Canadians become increasingly aware of their HPV status by HPV testing, they would want to be informed about the consequences of an infection. To answer these questions, I will analyze data from the clinical study HITCH, a CIHR-sponsored study of over 500 young, newly formed couples conducted between 2005 and 2013. Baseline demographics, sexual behaviour and HPV infections on genitals, mouth and hands were recorded for 2 years; blood samples were also taken. With these data, I will measure antibody levels against HPV and study their correlation to past, present and future HPV infections, and identify biosocial factors that may affect the immune response. Hence, this study will improve our understanding of the immune response to HPV infections.

column36: Developpement d'un systeme de retroaction en temps reel pour prevenir les atteintes musculosquelettiques du membre superieur chez les travailleurs.
column37: Les atteintes aux membres superieurs d'origine professionnelle sont frequentes et affectent la qualite de vie des personnes qui en sont atteintes. Elles peuvent etre egalement associees a une perte de productivite en entreprise, donc a des couts pour l'employeur, mais egalement a des depenses importantes en soins de sante pour la societe. Malgre tous les efforts deployes depuis les dernieres annees en prevention, le nombre de blessures de ce type est en constante augmentation. De plus, les professionnels ne disposent pas actuellement d'outils d'evaluation permettant de determiner la reelle demande des emplois. Dans ce contexte, il est difficile d'offrir des interventions qui seront, a la fois, adaptees aux exigences de l'emploi et aux capacites de l'individu. Le present projet vise au developpement d'un appareil mesurant les exigences physiques d'un emploi (la force necessaire et les mouvements effectues) afin d'offrir une retroaction au travailleur pour qu'il evite les situations dans lesquelles il se mettrait a risque de blessures. Cet appareil pourra egalement etre utiliser par les cliniciens dans le cadre de leurs interventions pour leur permettre de formuler des recommandations claires et adaptees a la condition de chacun des travailleurs.

column37: B-cells play a key role in establishing a protective immune response by synthesizing antibody molecules to recognize and neutralize invading pathogens. During their development and maturation, B-cells rearrange their genetic material that encode for antibodies. This process named class switch recombination requires B-cells to undergo programmed DNA double strand break (DSB). DSBs are particularly dangerous as they compromise genomic integrity. In case of a faulty DSB repair B-cells may not elicit a functional immune response and are prone to become malignant. Therefore, B-cells have developed a complex DSB response to ensure that these DNA lesions are properly repaired. It is primordial to fully understand how DNA repair occurs in B-cells to provide genetic diversity while avoiding triggering B-cell malignancies including lymphoma and leukemia. My work will focus on the role of Ubiquitin in the repair of DSBs in B-cells. The dynamic ubiquitin system has an important regulatory role in different cellular functions including DSB signaling/repair. The E3 Ubiquitin ligase RNF168 is critical in signaling DSB. Mutations in RNF168 result in an immunodeficiency syndrome called RIDDLE. Recently, a deubiquitylation enzyme OTUB1 has been identified as an important regulator of RNF168 activity during the DSB response. OTUB1 is overexpressed in several B-cell lymphomas and could be a promising target for their treatment. The goal of my project is to study the role of OTUB1 in B-cells, in particular the repair of DSBs during antibody diversification. In this regard, I will characterize different mouse models where Otub1 has been deleted and determine the impact of its loss for B-cell biology, DSB repair, and the emergence of B-cell lymphoma. This project will provide insight on OTUB1 role in B-cell biology. It will also help elucidate DNA repair mechanisms in B-cells. Finally, it will shed light on the implications of improper DSB repair for the development of B-cell malignancies

column36: Combining mathematical models and machine learning for the identification of novel neuroimaging biomarkers for disorders of neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration
column37: Disorders of brain development and degeneration, including Autism Spectrum Disorder and Alzheimer's disease, cost the Canadian healthcare system billions of dollars every year. The identification of new measures of disease progression or severity using brain scans can enable the development of new therapies, reduce the cost and length of clinical trials, and allow doctors to better track the progression of brain disease. The recent creation of large collections of brain images has provided researchers with access to more medical images than ever before. This creates a challenge because now researchers need to develop new ways to use this complex data. Once new methods are developed, it could allow us to better understand normal brain development and any changes to the brain caused by disease. Recently, success has been made in identifying methods of measuring brain disease progression using machine learning, an approach to artificial intelligence that is good at recognizing complex patterns. In addition, mathematical models have allowed for a better understanding of how diseases progress in the brain. This project will develop new ways to identify measures of disease progression by combining mathematical models and machine learning techniques. This project could contribute to the understanding of the underlying mechanisms of multiple disorders, enable doctors to better monitor patients, allow doctors to better predict how patients will respond to treatment, and lead to the development of new treatment options.
