column36: Identification of Novel Receptors Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs) Regulating the Hippo Signaling Pathway in Tumorigenesis
column37: Lung cancer kills 1.6 million people each year worldwide and is the most fatal cancer for Canadian men and women. Despite major progress in our understanding of the causes of lung cancer, more than 85% of lung cancer patients still die within 5 years after diagnosis. The poor prognosis associated with lung cancer is in part due to lack of effective drugs and "druggable" targets, or can be due to the development of resistance to drugs after initial treatment. Therefore, there is an urgent need to determine what cellular changes cause lung cancer to spread and develop drug resistance, and to identify new druggable targets. Our research group and others have recently discovered that changes in the Hippo signalling pathway are critical for the development and spread of lung cancers and also for their resistance to therapeutic drugs. However, the precise ways in which Hippo promotes cancer growth and metastasis is not completely known and there are currently no drugs available that can directly target Hippo for lung cancer therapy. For this project, I have developed a light emission-based biosensor tool, to detect interactions between un-known proteins involved in Hippo signalling. This powerful tool allows us to discover novel regulators of the Hippo pathway, which are capable of promoting cancer cell proliferation and metastasis in cancer cells. We are the first group in the world who have used this approach to find novel regulators of cell proliferation in lung cancer. Results from this study will identify new cellular pathways that interact with the Hippo pathway, thereby contributing significantly to the Hippo pathway research field and will have the potential to provide us with novel targets for cancer therapy. In the future, I will use different strategies to further determine the connection between these candidates and cancer, thus providing a new therapeutic strategy for successful cancer treatment.

column36: Network modeling of Alzheimer's disease progression: Using multimodal neuroimaging to test whether Alzheimer's pathology spreads through existing brain networks
column37: Amyloid-beta (AB) plaques and tau tangles are pathologies that are present in large concentrations in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Additionally, AD is also characterized by loss of large amounts of brain tissue. Neuroimaging techniques allow scientists to measure these disease markers in living humans. By combining information from several different types of neuroimaging measures, complicated relationships between normal brain processes and disease process can be better understood. These "multimodal" analyses have led recently to the hypothesis that disease processes spread from one part of the brain to another over time, and that the pattern of spread is not random. Specifically, brain regions that are more affected by different pathologies also have a greater number of physical connections in the brain. Recent research has used mathematical models to test whether this hypothesis is valid, and to try to predict the ordering of biological events that leads to dementia. One such model, called the Epidemic Spreading Model (ESM), has used data from multiple neuroimaging tools to predict the spreading of AB in the brain. The model identifies an "epicenter", or a starting point of disease spread, and simulates where and when AB will move from this epicenter to other brain regions, based on how connected the regions are to one another. The ESM predicted the spread of AB with unprecedented accuracy, however a more complete picture of the biology of AD will require modeling the other hallmarks of the disease, namely tau and loss of brain tissue. The current project will adapt the ESM to neuroimaging techniques that measure where tau and brain tissue loss occur. Applying the ESM to these additional disease markers will help us empirically test, a) do these disease markers indeed spread through connected brain regions over time, b) if so, which specific brain networks are the most vulnerable and when, c) what areas are affected first.

column36: Social Impacts of Biomedical HIV Prevention: PrEP Implementation among People who Inject Drugs
column37: In 2016, Health Canada approved the first preventative medication for use among HIV-negative individuals to protect against the transmission of HIV. This drug, called Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis ("PrEP"), has the potential to revolutionize the HIV/AIDS epidemic and has gained widespread endorsement around the world. But for social scientists, critical questions remain regarding the social and ethical implications of medicating people who are not sick but are simply "at risk." In addition, existing PrEP research and interventions have focused primarily on men who have sex with men and have ignored the needs of other groups with high rates of HIV transmission, particularly people who inject drugs. In my research, I will address these issues by exploring willingness to use PrEP among people who inject drugs, potential barriers and motivators to using PrEP, and how PrEP interventions can be designed ethically and responsibility to meet the specific needs of people who inject drugs. As Canada begins to incorporate PrEP into HIV prevention initiatives, this research will guide healthcare providers and policymakers as they design PrEP interventions for people who inject drugs and other hard-to-reach and marginalized populations. Further, as new medications are prescribed to "treat" risk factors, this data provides empirical evidence to theoretical discussions of medicating risk and mere potential for illness.

column36: Aberrant expression of the platelet aggregating cell surface protein podoplanin by acute promyelocytic leukemia blasts may explain the bleeding complications associated with this disease.
column37: Acute promyelocytic leukemia or APL represents 10% of newly diagnosed patients with acute myeloid leukemia. A portion of patients still die from the important bleedings that uniquely characterize this subgroup, and bleeding complications are more frequent and severe when diagnosis is delayed. The full understanding and early diagnosis of APL thus represent a clear unmet medical need. No specific therapy currently exists for this complication. I have recently identified a gene called podoplanin, which is uniquely expressed in APL and not in other forms of leukemias. Podoplanin has the capacity to bind and deplete blood platelets, which are essential components of blood clots. My hypothesis is that the abnormally high expression of podoplanin on the surface of APL cells leads to the depletion of circulating platelets in this disease and represents a key component of the bleeding manifestations specifically observed in these patients. To confirm our initial observations, we now propose to analyze podoplanin expression in a large collection of APL patients and in other leukemia samples, and verify its utility as a rapid and reliable diagnostic test. Moreover, we will determine if podoplanin expression levels predict the severity of bleeding in these patients (aim 1). We will also test the hypothesis that platelet aggregation (leading to their depletion from blood) is directly triggered by podoplanin expression on the surface of APL cells (aim 2). In aim 3, we will identify drugs that can modulate podoplanin expression in APL cells with the possibility of providing a solution for the bleeding disorder of such patients.

column36: Impact of IL-15 on T cells in MS and its animal models
column37: Multiple sclerosis is a neurological disease affecting numerous patients; more than 2 million people are affected worldwide. Despite many years of research, the cause of this illness is still unknown. The immune system usually provides protection against microbes. However, the immune system in multiple sclerosis patients shows abnormalities and it attacks components of the brain as if they were foreign microbes. The purpose of our study is to identify molecules present in the brain of multiple sclerosis patients that are used by the immune system to attack it. We hope to identify new molecules and cells that could eventually be targeted by future treatments. Our group observed that one particular molecule called interleukin-15 is present in abundance in the brain of patients with multiple sclerosis but not in other patients. Moreover, this molecule is also more elevated in the blood of patients than in healthy volunteers. Our goal is to analyze how this molecule increases the capacity of the immune system to cause damage in the brain of multiple sclerosis patients. A better understanding of the impact of this molecule could help us design a new therapy to treat patients with multiple sclerosis.

column36: Can trophic cascades transcend nearshore habitats and link marine and terrestrial ecosystems?
column37: Carnivores can change entire ecosystems through a trophic cascade. A simple, three species trophic cascade occurs when a carnivore affects the abundance of plants by limiting the herbivores that previously grazed the plants. Sea otters are an example of a predator that causes a trophic cascade. On rocky reefs, sea otters limit sea urchins. Because sea urchins eat kelp, when otters are present ecosystems switch from being urchin-dominated to kelp-dominated. Sea otters were once hunted to near-extinction, and their recovery has provided a natural experiment with equivalent areas differing only in whether sea otters are present. Sea otter recovery might also affect terrestrial communities. Kelp growth facilitated by otters might increase the amount of kelp that washes up on shore. This kelp provides a nutrient source to insects, birds, and mammals on land-a boost that could lead to healthier or larger populations. I will test if the presence of sea otters increases the biomass of invertebrates and small mammals on adjacent land by increasing kelp deposits on shore. Such a connection would link marine and terrestrial ecosystems through a nutrient subsidy created by sea otters-furthering our understanding of community ecology. Another way sea otters might affect nearshore communities is by switching their diets. Once otters have eaten the easily available urchins, they eat clams and crabs in sheltered habitats. I will investigate how and when re-colonizing sea otters switch to these sheltered habitats and how this switch affects soft-bottomed ecosystems. Understanding how top predators structure ecosystems is a key component of community ecology. My research will contribute to the advancement of ecological theory and help to evaluate management tradeoffs as sea otters recover in areas they were previously extirpated from. Such studies are increasingly important as humans learn to coexist with recovering apex predators around the world.

column36: Integration du controle a la source et du controle en temps reel comme mesures de reduction des debordements de reseaux d'egout unitaires
column37: Dans de nombreuses villes du Canada et ailleurs dans le monde, l'eau usee et l'eau qui ruissele lors d'evenements pluvieux se jettent dans le meme reseau d'egout. Ce melange d'eaux contaminees est ensuite transporte et traite avant son rejet dans l'environnement. Toutefois, par temps de pluie ou de fonte des neiges, la capacite du reseau peut s'averer insuffisante, ce qui entraine des debordements d'eaux usees dans les cours d'eau. Ce phenomene de debordements de reseaux d'egout unitaires, est associe a de graves problemes environnementaux, la perte d'usages recreatifs et la degradation visible du milieu. Les solutions disponibles pour contrer cette problematique comprennent les mesures de controle de l'eau pluviale a la source telles que l'implantation de surfaces vegetalisees ou la construction de reservoirs. Alternativement, le controle optimal de l'ecoulement de l'eau pluviale au sein du reseau par l'ajustement instantane des infrastructures hydrauliques est un autre type de solution possible. Toutefois, les connaissances sont limitees quant a la maniere optimale de reduire le nombre et la quantite des debordements de reseaux d'egout unitaires, d'autant plus que l'impact des changements climatiques et l'influence du climat continental froid et humide doivent aussi etre consideres dans l'evaluation des solutions disponibles. Pour repondre a ce defi, l'utilisation d'outils de modelisation hydrologique et hydraulique combines a des calculs d'optimisation mathematique permettra d'estimer le potentiel d'integrer a la fois des solutions de controle du ruissellement a la source et en reseau sur un meme territoire. La recherche vise en particulier a proposer des solutions optimales en termes de cout et d'efficacite pour des reseaux d'egout de differentes tailles. Les resultats escomptes appuieront ainsi les municipalites, les gouvernements et les scientifiques dans le developpement d'outils de gestion durable des eaux pluviales et de preservation de l'environnement.

column36: Molecular mechanisms mediating a positive calcium balance during development
column37: Calcium has multiple essential roles in the body including forming the foundation of bone structure. Bone growth occurs rapidly in infancy and continues throughout childhood, with bone mass peaking in early adulthood. It is, therefore, crucial to build strong bones during childhood. Unfortunately, many infants and children are at increased risk of poor bone health due to factors including prematurity, bowel disease, and kidney disease. Calcium balance in the body involves interactions between the intestines, kidneys, and bones. If inadequate calcium is absorbed from the intestine, it is sacrificed from the bones. Unfortunately, mechanisms leading to a positive calcium balance for appropriate growth are not clearly understood. Our first objective is to understand these mechanisms. We use mice at different ages to measure gene expression and protein levels of molecules and hormones involved in calcium absorption in intestines and kidneys. We then directly measure calcium movement across intestine sections of mouse intestine to investigate the role of non-typical intestinal sections during growth. To date, our results suggest the finding of a new pathway of absorption in some sections of the small intestine that only exist in young mice. The results of this research thus far challenge the current understanding of calcium absorption. These studies will have a significant impact on scientists and non-academics in this field. Given the important role of calcium in the body, understanding how it is absorbed from the diet will inform adequate calcium intake for humans and animals, aid in optimising infant formulas, and create potential targets for new therapies to prevent poor bone health later in life.

column36: Broke but not Broken: Examining Agency and Resistance Among Homeless Canadian Youth
column37: By engaging in in-depth interviews, focus groups, and arts-based methods with homeless and street-involved youth in Ottawa, Montreal, Vancouver and Halifax, this doctoral research will explore how homeless Canadian youth negotiate and/or overcome their marginalization through agency, empowerment, and community during their lives on the street. I will explore the following three core questions: (i) In what ways do young homeless and street-involved adults (age 18-30) experience street life as an empowered choice? (ii) How do personal experiences of trauma, stigma, and marginalization shape how young homeless people view, conform to and/or resist pressures to engage in formal education, paid work or traditional living situations? And (iii) how do they speak about and experience past and present challenges to conforming to mainstream societal expectations and authority? Because many youth do not access shelters and other homeless services due to their reluctance to conform to the rules and obligations required, such as sobriety (Finley 2010; Kort-Butler & Tyler 2012; Shillington et al. 2011), they are a difficult population to access. There is an urgent need for scholarly literature that explores their lived experiences and modes of resistance (Marshall et al. 2008) to aid in developing public policy recommendations and improving services for homeless youth. Discovering how youth use agency in their interactions with authorities will help inform policy makers and scholars how to better engage homeless youth and provide services that respect their autonomy, while improving relationships with the police and the broader community.

column37: Cette recherche vise a identifier les mecanismes qui font des marches financiers un agent de transformation des rapports sociaux et du rapport a la nature. Dans une demarche alliant philosophie sociale et sociologie economique, ce projet s'appuiera sur l'experience vecue des salaries endettes, dans le but de formuler un diagnostic critique sur le pouvoir grandissant de la finance. La relation de pouvoir entre le debiteur et son creancier sera reexaminee, a la lueur des nouveaux produits financiers qui se sont introduits dans ce rapport social. La generalisation des dettes sous diverses formes, permise par les marches financiers, est susceptible de discipliner de maniere inedite les comportements sociaux et merite, pour cette raison, une attention particuliere. Le transfert massif de l'epargne des travailleurs sur les marches financiers invite egalement a evaluer les implications des fortes exigences de la sphere financiere sur les entreprises et les travailleurs eux-memes. Enfin, l'analyse de la prise en charge financiere de la gestion de la nature permettra de questionner le developpement d'une nouvelle representation commune de la nature. Cette recherche sera determinante pour la sociologie et la philosophie sociale dans la mesure ou elle permettra de saisir les ressorts concrets du pouvoir de la finance. Elle est susceptible d'interesser tous les citoyens soucieux de mieux comprendre les mecanismes de l'economie dans le but d'avoir une plus grande emprise sur celle-ci.

column36: A mixed-methods analysis of the experience of post-war displacement and psychological resilience in Sri Lanka
column37: Individuals in post-conflict settings have experienced not only direct exposure to violence but also secondary traumatic events associated with displacement such as interrupted school attendance, loss of family and community, lengthy and dangerous journeys, and inadequate resources or shelter (American Psychological Association, 2010). Following a 26-year civil war, Sri Lanka has tens of thousands of internally displaced persons (IDPs), including many born during the conflict (Siriwardhana & Wickramage, 2014). Despite living in adverse circumstances, a growing body of literature points to vital protective factors such as support networks and a sense of community that are important in recovery post-conflict. There is increasing awareness of the importance of social and cultural dimensions of resilience that extend beyond the individual. While some literature exists on risk and protective factors in displaced populations, there has not been an explicit exploration of the intersection between age at displacement, return migration, and resilience in a post-conflict setting. Using a mixed-method design, this study will explore: (1) which factors of the environment in a post-conflict situation are important to the maintenance and promotion of resilience in return migrants, and (2) how resilience is conceptualized in returning IDPs born prior to and those born during the conflict in Sri Lanka. The Conservation of Resources Theory (COR), an integrative model that considers both environmental and internal processes in resilience research (Hobfoll, 1988, 1989, 1998, 2015), will provide a framework for analysis. The theoretical contribution of this study will be adding a cohort perspective to Hobfoll's COR theory in a post-conflict setting. Additionally, understanding how age at displacement plays a role in the development and maintenance of resilience and psychological wellbeing can inform community-based mental health interventions for displaced communities globally.

column36: The Emergence of New Street Level Bureaucrats: How Formal Policy is Re-Shaped and Implemented by Non-State Contracted Agencies
column37: My research will focus on how non-state agencies (private firms and NGOs) and their employees, that are contracted by the state for the purpose of supplying public social services (health, education, employment, etc), re-shape public policy entrusted to them, through the process of policy implementation. I will use the theoretical framework of "Street Level Bureaucracy" approach, used by researchers over the last 30 years to examine actions of public servants (teachers, social workers, school nurses, police officers, public defenders etc.), responsible for implementation and enforcement of public policy. This approach attributes a pivotal role to street level bureaucrats in the process of policy implementation, in virtue of their discretion and autonomy. It has not yet been applied to explore actions of non-state agencies that supply public services. My research will close this significant gap in literature. Understanding ways in which public policy is re-shaped by non-state agencies, will further our knowledge on ramifications of privatization and outsourcing, and will contribute to this on-going public debate. My research will explore comparative case studies - in Israel and in Canada, in areas of public health and employment programs. First stage will explore formal policy (as crafted in government and entrusted to these agencies), through a comprehensive formal policy document analyses (such as cabinet decisions, legislation and public tenders). Second stage will focus on characterizing factors shaping the actions of employees in contracted agencies. For this I will use qualitative methods often utilized in Street Level Bureaucracy research, such as interviews with employees and managers in these agencies. My research will explore how personal, organizational, and professional factors of street level bureaucrats (employment structure, motivation, work ethos etc,), may differ when considering non-state agencies, and effect the process of implementation.

column36: Mentoring new patient-oriented researchers in innovative HIV e-care
column37: HIV medications are getting better but for many HIV-infected Canadians taking their lifelong medication is a serious challenge. Current HIV care insufficiently addresses this. Better consideration of the patient's perspective during medical visits could help. Dr. Lebouche's research program centers on the development and testing of a new measure, a questionnaire about factors that patients believe make it hard for them to take their HIV medication. It aims to ensure that care is more patient-centered and responsive to these factors. This measure will be filled out on an electronic tablet prior to patients' regular clinic visits and scores will be shared with their doctor so that any difficulties can be discussed and addressed. Dr. Lebouche is consulting with both patients and HIV doctors to create this measure to ensure that it is relevant to them and he has several clinical trials planned to evaluate it. We utilize real-world, pragmatic methods to take into account personal preferences and characteristics that help move us towards personalized whole-person care. We work in multidisciplinary cancer care teams to integrate research knowledge seamlessly into clinical practice. column36: Dual Targeting of Combination Therapy to Breast Cancer: A New Strategy to Overcome Drug Resistance
column37: Human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 positive (HER2+) breast cancer (BC) is an aggressive subtype of BC associated with high recurrence rates and poor survival. The combination of the chemotherapeutic agent paclitaxel (PTX) and HER2 antibody targeted agent trastuzumab (TmAb) has been the gold first line therapy in advanced HER2+ BC for nearly two decades. However, the majority of patients develop TmAb resistance within the first year of treatment. Additionally, the conventional PTX formulation currently used (Taxol(R)) has been associated with dose-limiting neurotoxicities and severe hypersensitivity reactions. The use of mamalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors, such as everolimus (EVER), has been shown to overcome TmAb resistance and increase sensitivity to PTX. Importantly, administering this combination at the synergistic ratio could allow for reducing PTX dose, thus, improving the toxicity profile of the drug. Polymeric nanoparticles designed to deliver cancer therapies to BC tumors have been explored, successfully demonstrating the use of this delivery system to reduce systemic toxicity and improve the antitumor effects of anti-cancer drugs. Furthermore, recent studies suggest that TmAb resistance is associated with and enhanced by an increase in expression of the epidermal growth factor receptor 1 (EGFR). Therefore, the goal of this research is to develop a novel polymeric nanoparticle formulation, actively targeted to both HER2 and EGFR receptors, to specifically deliver a combination of the cytotoxic agent PTX and EVER at their synergistic ratio to TmAb resistant HER2+ BC models. We believe this novel formulation will make for a powerful therapeutic for treatment of advanced HER2+ BC including TmAb resistant tumors, reduce the toxicities of PTX, thus, improving survival rates and the quality of life of patients with advanced HER2+ BC.

column36: HIV Risks, prevention and HIV criminalization: Optimizing Continuum of Care to Reduce HIV risks among Black African and Caribbean Communities in Ontario
column37: The overly broad application of HIV-related criminal case laws continues to stifle public health and HIV prevention efforts. Since 1990s, the Canadian Criminal Justice System became involved in cases of perceived HIV exposure and/or transmission, prosecuting persons living with HIV for engaging in behaviors deemed "risky" in terms of possible HIV transmission. Canada continues to enforce these laws despite evolving scientific evidence on HIV transmission and the lack of empirical evidence to demonstrate that HIV-related case laws are effective at preventing HIV transmission. The African, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities are disproportionately burdened by HIV and HIV-related criminal laws. Despite the significance of these laws in influencing HIV epidemic, large research gaps still remain in understanding how HIV criminalization impact HIV risks, HIV prevention efforts and healthcare engagement for the ACB Communities. The aim of the proposed study is to examine the impact of HIV-related criminal and public health laws on HIV prevention and healthcare engagement among ACB communities at risk and living with HIV (undiagnosed and diagnosed) in Ontario, Canada. This qualitative research will utilize Community Based Research approach, intersectionality, Syndemics theory, and socio-ecological framework to examine and analyze the contextual, individual, cultural, social and structural factors that currently drive health disparities and HIV risks, and undermine HIV prevention and healthcare engagement. This is a multi-level research project that will employ critical discourse and intertextual analysis, in-depth interview and focused group discussions, and participant observations. Knowledge translation and exchange of the research findings to local and transnational partners will inform the ongoing development of public health policies to reduce health disparities and HIV risks, as well as provide evidence for enactment of alternative approaches to criminal laws.

column36: Skeletal Muscle Ketone Body Metabolism & Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Obesity puts people at huge risk for developing diabetes. Current research has spent a major effort on understanding how the increased sugar and fat in our diet has negative actions on the skeletal muscle that cause obesity-related diabetes. However, this approach has not resulted in any successful new drugs for this disease. We will take a different approach, and investigate how a different nutrient energy source, the ketone body, may be a critical factor responsible for obesity-related diabetes. Ketone bodies are a less common fuel source in the body. They are made in the liver during starvation, and used as an energy source by the brain, and other organs such as the heart and skeletal muscle. The situation of diabetes is commonly referred to as "starvation in the midst of plenty," to suggest that the body of a patient with diabetes thinks it is starving, even though their bodily organs are being supplied with a high amount of sugar and fats. Thus, we believe this "starvation in the midst of plenty" environment that diabetic patients live with provides a horrible situation where ketone bodies are continually being made and used for energy, even though these patients are not starving. In order to test our hypothesis, we will create genetically modified mice that have reduced metabolism of these ketone bodies only. We will test whether our genetically modified mice are protected against the development of diabetes, when fed a diet enriched in fat and sugar that causes significant obesity over time. In addition, we will use specialized techniques to increase metabolism of ketone bodies in lean and healthy mice, and test whether increasing ketone body metabolism can cause diabetes. In summary, our research may lead to the discovery of new drugs that can treat and/or prevent obesity-related diabetes.

column36: Exploring the barriers, enablers, and perceptions of a First Nation school's nutrition policy
column37: First Nations children have a high prevalence of obesity and obesity-related chronic diseases. School nutrition policies have the potential to improve the diet and health of First Nations children by guiding food and drink choices and promoting nutrition education within schools. Research concerning the unique enablers and barriers of nutrition policy implementation in First Nations schools is needed to move policy action forward. A First Nation school in Alberta implemented a school nutrition policy as a strategy to improve nutrition for children. This mixed-methods study aims to understand the 1) perceptions of students and parents of the policy, 2) school, student, and family factors acting as enablers and barriers to its implementation, and 3) adherence to the policy. Findings from surveys and interviews with parents and students and participant observation of the school nutrition environment will be integrated to increase the depth of understanding, and the reliability and credibility of the conclusions of the evaluation. The outcome of this research will be a strengthening of the school nutrition policy so that it is reflective of the health perceptions and beliefs of the community; has limited barriers to implementation; and ensures that the school environment provides children with access to healthy food choices. Results will be shared with the Alberta Project Promoting active Living and healthy Eating (APPLE) Schools, which will help to define effective ways to create, support and sustain healthy First Nations, Metis, and Inuit APPLE Schools in Alberta. With the knowledge gained from this research, it may be possible to promote meaningful changes to the food environment within schools across Canada with a high Aboriginal population, potentially leading to a reduced prevalence of obesity and obesity-related chronic diseases in First Nations, Metis, and Inuit children in Canada.

column36: Examining how patients and providers bridge Indigenous and Western healing paradigms in the Northwest Territories
column37: Indigenous people in Canada experience a disproportionate number of health issues compared with their non-Indigenous counterparts. Although studies show that the quality of health services offered to and taken up by Indigenous patients is negatively impacted when Western approaches to health and healing are prioritized over Indigenous approaches, Indigenous healing paradigms and practices are excluded from institutionalized healthcare in most parts of Canada. In an attempt to improve the quality of care for Indigenous people, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) has called for greater collaboration between Indigenous and Western healers. Currently, however, there are very few hospitals in Canada that work to bridge Indigenous and Western approaches to healing. In the Northwest Territories (NWT), the need is particularly great. Despite NWT's high proportion of Indigenous residents (51%), there are few initiatives in hospitals that incorporate both Indigenous and Western healing practices. Furthermore, there is a gap in knowledge about how patients and providers currently experience Indigenous and Western healing paradigms in practice. In order to address the TRC's calls for action and improve the quality of health services for Indigenous people and communities in the NWT, it is critical to fill this knowledge gap. My PhD research will use community-based qualitative research methods and the 'two-eyed seeing' approach to (1) examine how healthcare providers and patients in the NWT understand and experience the interaction between Indigenous and Western healing paradigms in hospital settings, and (2) illuminate the assumptions and values underlying these paradigms, which inform the quality of health service provision. Working in partnership with Dene Elders, this project aims to inform the creation of government health policies and programs in the NWT and to improve the quality of healthcare for Indigenous patients and communities.

column36: A New Framework for Addressing Aboriginal Health Issues: A Participatory Approach in Two First Nations Communities Using Frontline Worker Input
column37: Aboriginal peoples face multiple health challenges and a significant health gap exists between Aboriginals and non-Aboriginals. The decrease of health issues in Aboriginal peoples can contribute to the reduction of health inequities, an important public health concern and priority research area. There have been various approaches used to address health issues within Aboriginal communities that have produced mixed results. A review of knowledge-to-action models and frameworks found community engagement, cultural considerations, and different knowledge types crucial for intervention success. However, no model was found that encompassed all the characteristics that support health equity. This review also identified the importance of frontline worker input in all phases of the intervention process, but many of the frameworks did not include this essential group. Currently, there is no comprehensive framework for those working in Aboriginal communities to decrease the burden of health challenges that includes the recommended features from the literature and frontline worker input. Based on findings from the literature and frontline worker input, a participatory action research approach will be used to develop a new framework to incorporate frontline worker experiences addressing multiple health issues within Aboriginal communities. Through the development of this framework, health outcomes can be improved, creating a healthier overall population.

Phase two will build upon phase one insights by working in partnership with Indigenous community members, clinicians, and health care leaders, to identify barriers to child health equity. The multiple perspectives will highlight the processes that contribute to unfair differences in Indigenous child health outcomes and identify strategies for dismantling them.

column36: Impact des conditions de logement sur la sante des familles et le developpement des enfants autochtones dans les regions nordiques du Canada
column37: Les conditions d'habitation dans lesquelles vivent les peuples autochtones figurent parmi les preoccupations de sante publique les plus importantes a l'heure actuelle. Une grande proportion des logements du Nord canadien sont surpeuples et necessitent des reparations majeures. Ces pietres conditions de vie, la promiscuite et le manque d'intimite qui en decoulent engendrent des tensions familiales et peuvent declencher des episodes d'abus et de violence, dont les enfants sont parfois temoins ou victimes. Plusieurs etudes suggerent des liens entre les conditions d'habitation et la sante mentale des familles, particulierement celle des femmes, et le developpement des enfants. Pourtant, un tres petit nombre d'etudes s'est interesse a l'impact des conditions de logement sur la sante des populations autochtones. Mon projet doctoral comprend deux volets. Le 1er volet profite d'une initiative ayant permis la construction de 360 logements au Nunavut et Nunavik. Il vise a evaluer l'impact de demenager dans un nouveau logement sur la sante mentale des meres (evaluee a l'aide de questionnaires avant-apres le demenagement) et sur la dynamique familiale (decrite lors d'entrevues individuelles aupres de 24 meres avec jeunes enfants). Le 2e volet vise a evaluer l'impact des conditions de logement sur le developpement moteur, cognitif et socio-emotif des enfants (0-11 ans). Pour ce faire, j'utiliserai les donnees quebecoises de l'Enquete regionale sur l'education, l'emploi et la petite enfance chez les Premieres Nations (3540 repondants), une enquete developpee par et pour les Premieres Nations. Les deux volets de mon projet seront developpes en etroite collaboration avec les communautes autochtones. Mon objectif au final est de fournir des resultats permettant d'informer les prochaines politiques de logement en contexte autochtone autour d'enjeux juges pertinents par les familles autochtones, permettant d'ameliorer la sante des familles et le developpement des enfants.

column36: Etude exploratoire descriptive sur les strategies d'adaptation utilisees par les jeunes Inuit du Nunavut a risque suicidaire
column37: L'incidence des suicides au Nunavut est 10 fois plus elevee que dans le reste du Canada. Dans l'objectif de sauver des vies, il est important de s'interesser a la resilience dont fait preuve certaines communautes inuites avec des taux de suicide plus bas. L'ambition de cette etude est de dresser un portrait exhaustif des strategies d'adaptation, composantes inherentes de la resilience, utilisees et valorisees par les jeunes Inuit a risque suicidaire, afin d'enoncer des recommandations sur les actions a prioriser pour ameliorer le bien-etre au Nunavut. column36: The effects of chronic HIV infection and antiretrovirals on cellular aging and mitochondrial health in immune cell subsets
column37: Over 37 million people live with HIV globally. In Canada, there are over 75000 persons living with HIV, with a new HIV infection every 3 hours. HIV is currently treated with combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), a mixture of three different anti-HIV drugs. This allows people with HIV to live longer and prevents death from Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). However, despite successful treatment, people with HIV are still more likely to suffer from diseases that usually occur with old age. These include heart, bone, and liver diseases, as well as certain cancers. A rapidly-aging immune system is suspected to lead to these age-related diseases, but it is unclear whether this results from the virus (HIV) or the treatment (cART). Although people with HIV are known to have older immune cells, it is unknown which types of immune cells are affected. In addition, approximately 1% of people with HIV are "non-progressors", and remain healthy without treatment. We do not know how the virus affects aging in their immune systems. I will separate blood samples from 400 participants into specific types of immune cells, and measure parameters that are related to cellular aging. Then, I will compare the results between HIV+ (treated and untreated) and HIV- people, while examining other factors that may predict the age of their immune cells (such as age, amount of HIV virus in blood, and other viral infections). I will also determine if the virus affects non-progressors the same way, and whether they should get treatment even if they appear healthy. Our findings will clarify how HIV accelerates immune system aging, something that may predict many diseases. In North America, most people with HIV will be over 50 years old within 5 years, which means more will struggle with HIV and age-related diseases than ever. This study will provide a deeper understanding of how HIV may lead to these diseases and how to better care for people living with the virus.

column36: Improving prescribing practices in primary care: treatment of depression in obese and overweight patients.
column37: People who are very overweight (considered obese) often suffer from depression. Similarly, people with depression are at risk for becoming obese. Both obesity and depression are very common among Canadians. Family practitioners are usually the first health professionals that people visit to help deal with depression. In patients with depression, excessive weight may make the treatment less efficient because fat can interfere with the action of the drug. Yet, it is not clear if family practitioners prescribe drugs against depression differently for obese patients to account for this fact. It is also unclear whether these ways of prescribing may influence a person's general health. The goal of our study is to evaluate how primary care practitioners prescribe antidepressants for overweight and obese people, and to assess how this influences a patient's general health. For our analysis, we will use two data sets: a large healthcare data set based on the primary care-based electronic medical records from several Canadian provinces, and a database on Quebec residents diagnosed with depression. Our study will help us understand if primary care practitioners prescribe antidepressants differently for patients of different weight groups, and whether it affects treatment effectiveness and patients' general health. This study will help improve policies for prescribing antidepressants for obese and overweight people in primary care.

column36: IL-37 recruitment of SIGIRR: A novel mechanism to suppress intestinal epithelial cell driven inflammation and microbial dysbiosis in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
column37: Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) suffer bouts of extreme gut inflammation that disrupt the population of bacteria in their intestines. Thus IBD patients often have fewer beneficial bacteria and suffer an overgrowth of potentially dangerous bacteria. In healthy individuals, such responses are typically prevented by SIGIRR, a protein made by the cells that line the gut. SIGIRR acts by suppressing mechanisms that drive inflammation. We have shown that loss of SIGIRR dramatically increases inflammation and drives bacterial imbalance. The inflammation can become so severe that gut tissue can become necrotic. We do not have a way to promote the beneficial actions of SIGIRR in the gut, but recently, a newly recognized anti-inflammatory compound called interleukin (IL)-37, has been shown to interact with SIGIRR to inhibit inflammatory responses in human cells. In this project, we plan to test whether IL-37 stimulates SIGIRR to: i) control inflammation and suppress bacterial killing responses in the cells that line the gut; ii) protect mice from experimentally-induced IBD; and iii) promote normal gut microbe balance. Ultimately, my studies will explore the potential for IL-37 to act as a new therapeutic for patients with IBD.

column36: Transformation of the human cell protein landscape by Enteropathogenic and Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli during infection by rewiring host phosphorylation signalling
column37: Diarrheal disease affects 1.7 billion people every year, killing around 760 000 children. A leading cause of this are the "attaching-and-effacing" (A/E) pathogens, including enteropathogenic (EPEC) and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC - the agent of "hamburger disease"). EPEC and EHEC's ability to cause disease relies on manipulating the human gut in order to create an environment where they can thrive. They achieve this by secreting "effector" proteins directly into host cells using a sophisticated molecular syringe. These effectors then manipulate host signalling proteins to take control of processes like gut cell survival and immune signalling away from the host. One way in which effectors achieve this is by altering how chemical phosphate groups are added to host signaling proteins. EPEC and EHEC also secrete a number of phosphorylating effectors (kinases) into host cells, which may have redundant or even antagonistic functions. The role of phosphorylation in disease is poorly understood, but in many other systems regulates how proteins interact. I propose to show that EPEC's ability to manipulate phosphorylation of host proteins triggers dramatic changes in the way they behave and bind to each other, and that this is essential to infection. I first will use a newly developed technique to identify which host proteins are specifically phosphorylated by the effectors of EPEC, and which are phosphorylated as a general consequence of infection. I will then monitor how the interaction partnerships that host proteins participate in change as a consequence of this phosphorylation. Finally, I will investigate whether interfering in these EPEC-manipulation of host protein interaction blocks infection. This will be the first ever whole cell host-pathogen "interactome" study, and will develop a methodology for studying host-pathogen relationships, aiding development of better antibiotics in an age of increasing bacterial resistance.

column36: Improving Medication PRescribing for Ontario's Vulnerable Elderly High Cost Healthcare Users (IMPROVE-HCU)
column37: High cost healthcare users (HCUs) are a small group of patients that use a disproportionate healthcare resources compared to the average patient. In 2011, 5% of Ontarians used 65% ($19.8 billion) of total measurable public healthcare expenditures. Most HCUs are seniors with multiple chronic conditions taking multiple medications. With costs expected to double in 20 years, the current approach to HCUs has been deemed unsustainable by leading economists and there is an urgent need to design interventions to improve their health outcomes and costs. Our proposed research program seeks to better understand the impact of prescribing quality and drug use in senior HCUs. It is currently unknown whether HCUs are using optimal drugs and whether savings can be found through more cost-effective drug use. In Study 1, we will be using health administrative databases to investigate the current quality of prescribing and drug use in senior HCUs. We will be using the STOPP-START screening tool to look for potentially inappropriate prescribing that should have been stopped or started based on high quality scientific evidence. We will also explore the cost-savings if the government adopted a policy known as "reference-based pricing" for select high cost drugs with cheaper, equally effective alternatives. In Study 2, we will test the feasibility of conducting a large randomized trial to test the effectiveness of a new strategy to optimize drugs for hospitalized seniors HCUs to reduce their risk of death, re-hospitalization and healthcare costs. This project will demonstrate the impact of optimizing medications for Canada's high need, high cost seniors. It is the first of its kind internationally and it will help clinicians, hospitals and government develop new strategies to address the healthcare sustainability crisis. If only 10% of HCU expenses could be avoided or delayed, an additional $1.7 billion would be available in Ontario alone to fund better care for these seniors.

column36: Integrating Patient Preferences into Quantitative Benefit-Risk Assessment of the Sodium-Glucose Transport Protein 2 Inhibitors
column37: Optimal treatment decisions surrounding drug therapies rely on information about the trade-offs among benefits and harms. Moreover, the selection of an appropriate drug therapy is very patient specific and should take into consideration not only the potential benefits and harms, but also patient preferences. There are currently no standardized approaches that take these three factors into consideration to allow for a quick comparison across treatment alternatives. My research will use advanced methods for quantifying the relationship between effectiveness, safety and patient preference. Specifically, I will study the newest medications approved in Canada to treat type 2 diabetes called the sodium-glucose transport protein-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors. The SGLT-2 inhibitors work by blocking the kidney from reabsorbing sugar back into the bloodstream thereby lowering blood glucose levels. These drugs are effective in managing diabetes and have even been shown to reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes in high risk patients. There are however several safety concerns including higher rates of infections, kidney disease and bone fractures. The manner in which patients make trade-offs between these benefits and harms are not understood. My doctoral dissertation will consist of four studies: the first will summarize the clinical evidence and rank the safety and effectiveness of the SGLT-2 inhibitors compared to other common diabetes medications; the second will evaluate the reasons why patients prefer certain diabetes medications over others; the third and fourth studies will use findings from the first two studies to calculate a summary measure regarding the overall trade-offs of the potential benefits and harms for the SGLT-2 inhibitors using two different approaches. My research aims to improve patient safety and lead to better health outcomes and lower healthcare costs.

column36: Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies (CEMT)
column37: The term epigenome refers to chemical modifications of DNA and proteins that control the structure and regulation of the "genome", a term referring to all the DNA within our cells. In contrast to the genome, which changes very little if at all over the course of an individual's life, the epigenome is dynamic and changes during normal development, aging, disease challenges and in response to various external stimuli. Such epigenome changes can result in significant differences in how genes, and thus how cells, behave. Thus, an understanding of the epigenome and how it works in different cell types is critically important to understanding many aspects of human health and disease. The Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies (CEMT) has established a track record of leadership in the International Human Epigenomic Consortium; in the generation of reference epigenomes from a broad spectrum of normal and diseased human cell types; in the development and testing of technology for broader future applications; and in making such technology rapidly available to Canadian scientists. The CEMT is designed as an integrated unit composed of internationally leading biologists and clinicians with specialized access to, and knowledge of, the normal and diseased cell types we will analyze. The collaborative team effort described herein will transform our understanding of the relationship between the dynamic nature of the epigenome and how genes are turned on and turned off, and lay the foundation for larger studies to revolutionize our understanding of the role played by the epigenome in health and diseases, and from there how to more effectively manage the health of our populations.

column36: Does One Size Fit All? The Implications of Gender for OR Team Performance, Teamwork Interventions, and Equitable Patient Outcomes.
column37: Effective teamwork in the operating room (OR) is essential to surgical patient safety and improved health outcomes. Interventions to promote evidence-based practice have been shown to effectively improve teamwork in the OR to some degree. Yet, investigations of OR teamwork have overlooked the role of gender in OR teamwork, despite evidence from other areas of healthcare demonstrating its relevance to team interactions, practice patterns, care delivery, and patient outcomes. Without this knowledge, interventions to optimize teamwork have remained "gender neutral" (i.e. have not considered how gender may influence teamwork skills as well as barriers and facilitators for attaining these skills). The study of gender and teamwork in the OR has largely been limited by the practical challenges associated with obtaining high-quality OR data. Our group belongs to the international Surgical Safety Network, which uses OR Black Box technology to improve practice in the OR and obtain the best possible outcomes for all patients. Like black boxes used in aviation, the OR Black Box is an innovative tool that records detailed information from the surgical environment (e.g. audio, video, patient vitals). We plan to use the OR Black Box as part of a mixed methods study to: (1) describe variation in teamwork by gender and its impact on patient outcomes, and (2) determine the impact of gender on teamwork skills, barriers, and facilitators to enhance the effectiveness of teamwork interventions in the OR. This novel contribution will increase our understanding about how gender influences OR teamwork and its barriers and facilitators, and the findings will inform future interventions to improve teamwork through incorporating a gender perspective. Our study is a critical first step to the responsible implementation of teamwork interventions that consider gender and will enable comparisons of effectiveness between these interventions and those that do not take a gender perspective.

column36: Transforming the practice of KT: Embedding gender
column37: Knowledge translation (KT) is about how we to use research in healthcare. Its goal is to improve the care that patients receive through use of the best available research evidence. Unfortunately, researchers and those who do KT have not done a good job of thinking about sex, gender, and identity. Many KT methods involve using frameworks. A framework is a set of items or factors that may influence why people do things or why things happen. For example, a framework may have a list of factors (e.g., knowledge, skills, emotion, etc.) that may make an individual for or against using research evidence to improve the health care system. So far, no KT frameworks include factors related to gender and identity. It is possible that gender may influence an individual to be for or against using evidence to improve the health care system. In this study we will develop and evaluate existing KT frameworks will be improved by adding in elements of individual identity. We will conduct a study that includes 3 parts. In part 1, we will ask people who do KT to pick which steps in the KT process would benefit from including identity-related factors and do interviews with people who develop interventions to find out about their personal barriers to considering identity in their KT work. We will then use this information to pick KT frameworks and update them to include identity-related factors. We will also create a training course for people who develop interventions to learn how to use these updated frameworks. In part 2, we will evaluate the training course, comparing it to an existing training course that has no content on identity. In part 3, we will pilot the updated frameworks in 6 KT projects to see how they have used the updated frameworks.

Notre recherche participative fait appel a des methodes mixtes et comprend trois grandes etapes: 1) co-construction d'une formation aux professionnels de la sante et d'une intervention AC axee sur les personnes qui integre l'analyse comparative fondee sur le sexe et le genre; 2) evaluation de la formation et de l'intervention AC dans le cadre d'un projet pilote mettant en oeuvre une etude de cas multiples basee sur trois sites, 1 au Quebec, 1 au Nouveau-Brunswick et 1 en Ontario ou seront comparees l' intervention AC ou le genre est pris en compte a une intervention AC ou il ne l'est pas); 3) recommandations et perennisation des partenariats developpes dans le cadre de la recherche et dissemination des resultats. Ce projet permettra la creation de la premiere equipe interdisciplinaire, intersectorielle et pan canadienne engagee a produire des strategies d'AC efficaces axees sur le genre et le sexe des personnes en contexte francophone afin d'optimiser l'appropriation des connaissances issues de la recherche par les usagers et usageres des services de sante et services sociaux dans ces contextes et la reduction du gaspillage au niveau de la recherche et des services sociaux.

column36: Integrating and measuring the effect of sex, gender and gender transformative approaches to substance use treatment, prevention and harm reduction in Canada
column37: In the midst of a serious opioid crisis, emerging cannabis legalization, ongoing binge drinking patterns, and the introduction of e-cigarettes, there is an immediate need to understand sex and gender related implications of these trends, and how to respond to them in practice. This Team will develop and test the impact of incorporating sex, gender and gender transformative variables and principles into existing substance use treatment, harm reduction, and health promotion/prevention materials and programs in three settings in Canada. The substance use system is underdeveloped with respect to the inclusion of sex and gender in its approaches, materials and messaging, and the application of gender transformative principles is scarce. All genders are affected by gendered norms, stereotypes, relations and power distributions but we do not currently have an evidence-based gendered response to opioid overuse, cannabis, e-cigarettes or binge drinking. We will work in three settings to co-develop a set of interventions that incorporate sex, gender and gender transformative principles into programs, messages, staff education and materials. The implementation of these approaches and their effectiveness in shifting knowledge, attitudes and practice will be measured. These efforts will rely on ongoing systematic reviews, knowledge translation approaches in training, education, program design and prevention messaging, in conjunction with practice wisdom from three organizations. Gendered approaches to knowledge translation that address equity are a key challenge for treatment, harm reduction and prevention programs. This Team will translate and tailor evidence in: education of staff and clients; client-practitioner interactions; program design; and enhanced messaging. This is essential to adequately address root causes and health inequities associated with substance use in Canada

column36: Modeling an approach to gender-conscious participatory action-oriented research and knowledge transfer favouring equality, equity and occupational/environmental health
column37: Participatory approaches which integrate knowledge users from the beginning and throughout research (integrated knowledge transfer, or iKT) have been shown to garner better results in terms of uptake of knowledge and health outcomes. When this participatory approach also includes specific attention to sex and gender (s/g) it can further improve relevance and results, but runs certain risks, such as stereotyping. This proposal pulls together a well seasoned team, with experience in participatory research on sex and gender going back to the 70s, and emerging scholars of environmental and occupational health. Studies and iKT projects conducted by team members include subjects such as seasonal workers' health, work-family interface, occupational health & safety training, and influences of sex and gender on environmental effects in the immune system. The goal of the project is to closely examine past and current research with an aim to producing reproducible strategies for best practices in the integration of sex and gender in iKT. We will undertake an analysis and evaluation, in collaboration with our partners, of the mechanisms underlying successful partnerships, obstacles to the uptake of research results for gender and health, and training approaches. The results will improve researchers' ability to successfully include sex and gender considerations in their KT projects, with demonstrable improvements on personal and public health ensuing.

column36: A gender transformative approach to improve outcomes and equity among persons with Traumatic Brain Injury
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability in Canada and globally. The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging indicates that one out of four Canadians report a history of TBI. The Public Health Agency of Canada reported that TBI is among the most costly neurological conditions, set to cost 8 billion by 2031. Concussions, the most common form of TBI, are now a federal priority. Traumatic brain injury is considered a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and has been associated with increased rates of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and sleep disorders which further compromise long-term health and social isolation, unemployment, homelessness and criminalization. Interventions addressing these challenges exist but consumers report a lack of tailored approaches. In particular, sex and gender related differences in acute injury, rehabilitation and community re-integration impact health, access to supports and preferences for care. Research has focused on men creating a significant knowledge gap about TBI in women, leading to misdiagnosis and inadequate treatment and support. Addressing this gap, this project will generate evidence about whether applying sex and gender based analysis to knowledge translation interventions involving persons with TBI improves effectiveness. The project examines the impact of a sex and gender approach on existing evidence, knowledge translation efforts and interventions. A pilot project utilizing our knowledge-to-action framework will identify facilitators addressing gender roles, gender identity, gender relations and institutionalized gender. An implementation intervention will be tailored to address sex, gender and other identity or diversity related characteristics identified in the barriers assessment.

column36: The Canadian HIV Stigma Index CBR Project
column37: Stigma persists as a profound stressor in the lives of people living with HIV affecting access to care, treatment, and employment. HIV stigma can be perceived, directed at individuals and groups or systemic; it varies across lifespans, gender and sexual spectra, contexts and structures and ranges from single micro-aggressions to general stereotyping. The proposed national community-based research study will implement The People Living with HIV Stigma Index in Canada. It will recruit 1,200 adults living with HIV in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic provinces in order to: 1) better understand the social determinants of HIV stigma such as gender, cultural milieus and socioeconomic status, 2) map out HIV stigma across lifespans, contexts, structures and systems such as the workplace, the legal system, the educational system and the health system, and 3) mobilize local and national actionable solution(s) to support people living with HIV (e.g. local policy change efforts). This data and process will be used by people living with HIV, community-based AIDS service organizations, policy makers, health care providers and researchers to implement evidence-informed local activities. The education and KTE process rests on a successful learning model for delivery of content, skills and experience; a model that is a) "blended" (in-person, online, a/synchronous), b) "convenient" (traditional, electronic and mobile learning), and c) multimodal (including social and traditional media, conventional and online events. This is a strong community-academic partnership between communities and researchers across Canada. It includes a governance based on regional leadership-the Canadian HIV Stigma Index Steering Committee comprised entirely of people living with HIV-with national coordination. It includes networks of people living with HIV, academics, people from private and community-based sectors, and when available, government decision-makers.

column36: Checking Out the Drug, Checking In On Life and HIV Prevention: A Community Responds
column37: The increasing incidence of non-fatal overdose events and overdose-related deaths is emerging as a significant public health concern in Canada. One known contributor to the rising rates of both fatal and non-fatal overdose is the issue of unknown drug quality and/or contents. In Ottawa, the number of calls in 2016 to paramedics to attend to non-fatal overdose events has more than doubled since 2012. Additionally, current methods of issuing drug alerts have proven inadequate, as they are often delivered after adverse events have already occurred, rendering them less effective as an overdose prevention strategy. Furthermore, the high prevalence of HIV and HCV in this community, combined with high reported rates of drug-use equipment-sharing suggests increased rates of HIV and HCV acquisition and transmission could occur if no intervention takes place. This project will involve implementing a drug analysis service (in partnership with Carleton University) at Oasis, a harm reduction program located in the Sandy Hill Community Health Centre. Clients will be able to anonymously drop off samples of drugs for analysis, allowing for timely surveillance and reports regarding drug quality to be issued to the community. In this way, we aim to proactively make people who use drugs (PWUD) aware of adulterated substances before adverse events occur. We anticipate that this service will act as an alternate gateway for clients to be connected with other HIV prevention and harm reduction services that they may not otherwise have accessed, potentially reducing the incidence of HIV and HCV among PWUD in Ottawa, while simultaneously extending and improving the quality of life of PWUD already living with HIV.

column36: Through our own eyes and in our own words: Women, HIV, Criminalization and Prison Exposure
column37: Women living with HIV are over criminalized and overrepresented in Canadian prisons. This is especially true for women living with HIV who also face additional health and social inequities, including poverty, housing instability, racism, and substance use. Criminalization and criminal justice involvement are highly gendered with marginalized populations overrepresented including Indigenous and racialized women, trans and two-spirit individuals and marginalized youth. Through meaningful partnership with women living with HIV, there is an urgent need to collaboratively document the lived experience of criminalization and prison journeys for women living with HIV to gain a better understanding of how to improve continuity of HIV care and prison HIV care provision, including post-release transitions. The proposed community-based research project aims to use participatory qualitative and arts-based research with women living with HIV community, policy and research experts to: 1) gain a better understanding of how the law that criminalizes HIV non-disclosure uniquely shapes the experiences of women living with HIV, including HIV related stigma, access to care, and experiences of violence; 2) characterize the journeys of women living with HIV through the prison system, with the aim of identifying policies and practice that better support women living with HIV during and post incarceration; 3) build community-based research capacity among women living with HIV, HIV service organizations and academic researchers to examine criminalization of HIV and prison health. Women living with HIV will be engaged in all aspects of this project from planning, data collection, writing and dissemination and are represented as co-investigators, collaborators, knowledge users, Peer Research Associates, and interviewers.

column36: A community-based cohort study of HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in Ontario
column37: Canada continues to see unacceptable rates of HIV, particularly among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, trans- and cis-gender women, and African, Caribbean and Black (ACB) communities. A new strategy called PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis, the daily use of anti-HIV medication by those at high risk) holds great promise to help address this challenge, and is already being prescribed in Canada. However, PrEP remains controversial due to uncertainty about whether its HIV prevention potential is counterbalanced by increases in risk behaviour and sexually transmitted infections, whether users will be able to adhere and stay engaged in care, and whether user experiences such as PrEP-related stigma impact on use. In addition, there is great concern among communities that PrEP access has been inequitable. To address these issues, we will study 800 PrEP users in Ontario in a cohort study over three years. Our fundamental questions are, "Is PrEP having the intended impacts on the health of at-risk populations in Ontario? What are the 'real world' benefits and challenges of PrEP rollout? How can we optimize PrEP delivery and access?" We will: 1.Gather real world data on key biological, behavioural, experiential, and engagement in care outcomes over time, in a diverse cohort of PrEP users in Ontario 2.Characterize multiple measures of PrEP access within the cohort 3.Compare PrEP outcomes according to key characteristics of PrEP users. Because some of the key populations affected by HIV have been underrepresented in PrEP studies, we have reserved spots within the cohort for transgender women, cisgender women and ACB persons. In conjunction with our recruitment activities, we have developed a detailed plan for outreach with at-risk populations and the providers that serve them to raise awareness about PrEP and provide advice on PrEP access. Our findings will directly inform future efforts to optimize PrEP rollout and improve PrEP access in Canada.

column36: Connections With the Land: Developing Gender Appropriate Two-Eyed Seeing Land-based Wellness Interventions, Wise Practices, Research Methodologies, and Knowledge Translation and Exchange for Indigenous People With Lived HIV and/or HCV Experience
column37: This research project is a response to many sustained calls from the Indigenous community for more culturally relevant and land-based healing programs for Indigenous people living with or affected by HIV. Since time immemorial, Indigenous people have been using connections with the land, cultural practices and other aspects of ceremony in order to prevent illness, treat disease and maintain wholistic wellness. The focus of this project will be on introducing practical skills and initiating transformative experiences through a series of land-based healing retreats for 100 to 120 Indigenous people living with or at-risk for HIV/AIDS over three years. Diverse, land-based cultural wellness retreats are typically multiday excursions that take place on the land and involve a variety of traditional practices based in Indigenous knowledges, spirituality and ceremony. These retreats seek to meet individuals "where they are at" in terms of their unique life circumstances. Activities and ceremonies vary depending on the time of year, physical location and needs of the retreat participants. Potential resultant health outcomes from these interventions will consist of improvements in wholistic wellness, as well as improvements in resilience and empowering participants to self-advocate for their own health care needs. Multiple sharing circles with the same participants will be conducted at various points in time, before and following land-based healing activities, as well as during retreat activities. As a research tool, sharing circles are adept at gathering stories and capturing people's experiences, and have been used by Indigenous communities to teach culture and tradition, promote and research health, and provide spiritual counselling and healing.

column36: The GIPA Homefire: Understanding APHA Leadership towards a Wholistic Response to STBBIs
column37: Since the beginning of the epidemic, Aboriginal People living with HIV and AIDS (APHAs) working collaboratively alongside allies, have been integral in the response to the disproportionate impact of HIV and AIDS within First Nation, Inuit and Metis populations in Canada. As a community-driven movement, leadership by 'Aboriginal Peoples for Aboriginal Peoples' is valued as essential for a meaningful and effective response to HIV and AIDS. This grant brings together a team of experienced and dedicated APHAs, academic and community researchers to explore the concepts of the Greater Involvement of People living with AIDS (GIPA) and APHA leadership. Recognizing that current models of GIPA do not incorporate culture and therefore have not 'fit' well for mobilizing leadership with Indigenous Peoples in Canada, this grant aims to 'Indigenize' the GIPA Principles. We will also look at the health benefits of APHA leadership, as well as the factors that may lead to negative health impacts due to involvement in leadership activities. We will apply a mixed methods approach to this work, emphasizing Indigenous ways of knowing, decolonizing research methodologies, Two-Eyed Seeing and the principles of Community-Based Research.

column36: Implementing the "Patient's charter of tuberculosis care" in high incidence Indigenous communities and across jurisdictional borders
column37: Among Indigenous Peoples in the Prairie Provinces TB occurs in focal pockets of incidence, such that most communities have little to no TB while a few others are very high-incidence. High incidence communities tend to be clustered together and are bound both by their geographic proximity and through kinship to members of other nearby communities. As such, in Component I we proposed the development of a cross-border, regional coalition to advocate for better population and community health supports that would have the downstream effect of reducing TB transmission and progression to disease. TB elimination cannot be met in isolation, but instead requires that interests of the region at large and the people living therein be considered and promoted. In Component II, this regional committee would support the implementation of two locally specific TB elimination strategies across diverse, yet interconnected, communities. Our team has identified two interrelated strategies that we will implement and evaluate in component II. These two TB elimination strategies are: 1) improved, regional, surveillance and translation of those surveillance data back to relevant community members, and 2) an expanded program of outreach that has as its primary focus "wellness".

column36: Nishtam Niwiipitan (My First Teeth): A Multi-Pronged Approach for Improving Mother and Child Oral Health in Aboriginal Communities
column37: Early Childhood Caries (ECC), or tooth decay in baby teeth, is a serious burden on Aboriginal communities across Canada. Most ECC cases are severe and require teeth extractions or fillings under general anesthesia (GA), forcing families to seek specialty treatment in hospitals, often a plane flight away. Culturally appropriate preventive interventions promise to be effective and cheaper in reducing ECC rates and the need for dental surgery under GA. The study's primary aim is to work collaboratively with on- and off-reserve Aboriginal communities in Ontario and Manitoba to strengthen the effectiveness and scalability of a multi-pronged ECC preventive intervention through community-informed enhancements/adaptations. The intervention includes oral health Anticipatory Guidance (AG), delivered to mothers by trained community-based researchers using Motivational Interviewing (MI), and fluoride varnish treatments for their infants and toddlers. The intervention enhancements will be developed by the communities in an initial, qualitative phase of the study. Qualitative phase results will then inform a second, quantitative phase when these new elements are placed into an experimental trial with a larger sample. The idea is that these enhancements will improve the existing multi-pronged approach, grounded as they are in the experiences of community participants. Knowledge Sharing Learning Circles will develop community relevant outcome measures for mothers and their children that fully synergize with local ways of knowing, so that effectiveness/scalability is measured through the lens of the community. The third and final phase of the project will report on the outcomes and impact of the community-enhanced oral health approach. Using a mixed methods exploratory sequential design, researchers and community partners will combine a range of intervention enhancements to reduce ECC and bring about tangible improvements in Aboriginal children's oral health and wellbeing.

column37: Children with cancer and hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients suffer from severe and bothersome symptoms because treatments are intense. Participants will be children with cancer or HSCT recipients who are 8-18 years of age and who are expected to be in hospital or in clinic daily for 5 days. In our future vision, symptom control will become a metric by which to judge the quality of healthcare. In order to realize this vision, we need a feasible mechanism by which children with cancer and HSCT recipients can be enabled to report and track symptoms and for this information to be readily available to clinicians. This approach will lead to improved symptom control and better QoL for children receiving cancer treatment.

column36: Development of a safe, effective and clinically acceptable VSV-based HIV vaccine
column37: Over 36 million people are currently infected with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and approximately 1.8 million new people are infected annually. While drugs exist to help treat an infection, there is currently no vaccine available to prevent the infection. We propose to improve upon a vaccine made by Dr. Chris Parks from the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI). This vaccine uses a modified animal virus (VSV), which does not cause disease in humans, as a vehicle to safely deliver a part of an altered protein from the HIV virus. The altered HIV protein interacts with the body to stimulate immune defenses that protects against HIV infection. We will modify further the altered HIV protein to have it be present in greater numbers on the surface of the VSV delivery vehicle and therefore make it better at inducing immune defenses. Once the modifications are complete, we will test these new vaccines in mice and rabbits to see which work best. The best vaccines will then be tested in small rhesus monkeys (macaques) to see if they can protect these animals from an infection. We will also work on making these vaccines in a manner that is compatible with future testing and application in humans.
