column36: Accessing chromatin interactions by high-resolution analyses of correlated regulatory element variation
column37: Disease and development are reflected in chromatin states and their interactions in regulatory space. As opposed to developmental processes, it is anticipated that the genetic and epigenetic predisposition in disease is based on subtle alterations in chromatin conformation. Translational studies of altered chromatin structure are currently hampered by inflexible technologies. Direct "chromatin conformation association studies" require methodology that is scalable, tunable, and robust to variable quality of biological materials. We have charted CpG methylation variation in high-resolution across hundreds of population samples and observe significant enrichment of allelic and non-allelic methylation variation correlations in genomic regions shown to directly interact by conventional chromatin conformation assays. Preliminary data also points to preferential location of informative CpGs at boundaries of regulatory regions. We now propose the generation of a resource and framework to utilize interacting differentially methylated regions (iDMRs) applicable in large-scale studies to assess phenotypic importance of chromatin looping variation. We leverage methodologies we developed for targeted bisulfite sequencing to allow very high-resolution analyses for iDMRs as well as a unique cellular panel of human mesenchymal stem cells and their differentiated derivatives where standardized reference epigenome maps are generated in parallel. The full spectrum of chromatin conformation variation ranging from inter-individual to developmental differences are represented in this dataset serving as the optimal platform to develop analytical approaches for iDMR discovery. Conventional approaches for detecting and disrupting chromatin conformation in same cells serve to benchmark iDMR specificity and sensitivity. The resource and methods developed here will pave the way for systematic interrogation of chromatin conformation in new areas of population health and complex disease risk.

column36: Improved delivery of respiratory health care services using a metabolomic approach
column37: Asthma is the most common disease of children and is a leading healthcare cost for people of all ages. Asthma is caused by airway narrowing from abnormal inflammation. When people can't breathe then come into hospital. This is scary for kids (and adults) and it is expensive for the healthcare system. Other diseases cause airway obstruction, but the inflammation is different and the treatment is different. Doctors want to select the right drug at the right time to decrease airway inflammation and prevent hospital visits. Unfortunately, measuring airway problems and inflammation is difficult in a typical doctor's office. A noninvasive test is not available, especially for doctors taking care of small children. Instead, doctors give out trials of therapy, a strategy that wastes money and often does not always help the patient. Metabolomics is the study of small molecules generated from cellular metabolic activity. Diseases like asthma have different cells in the lungs compared to other respiratory diseases (e.g. viral infection). This creates different metabolites. Sicker lungs stress the body more causing different metabolites. Urine is an excellent biological fluid because it's easy to collect and it's rich in chemical composition. We have been studying urine in adults and kids with various lung diseases, and we believe we are close to a non-invasive urine test to measure these metabolites, which will diagnose and manage these diseases better than the current approach. We now need to study larger groups of people with respiratory diseases to validate the test. There are saved urine samples from adults and children with different airway diseases like asthma in Canada. Funds from this grant will allow us to study these samples and confirm that we have a test for asthma or asthma like diseases. We could then run clinical trials using the test to show how treatment could be better targeted to the right person at the right time. This would prevent hospital visits.

column36: Influence of Sex Hormones on Association CRTh2 Gene Variants and Asthma in Women
column37: Inhaled glucocorticosteroids (GC) are the main treatment for asthma and yet responses vary greatly across the population. Those that continue to have symptoms despite being on high dose GC are called severe asthmatics. These patients represent roughly 10% of the asthma population, but are estimated to cost the healthcare system 4 times more than the other 90% of asthmatics. Understanding the pathways modulating GC responses will help us determine how to treat this subtype of disease. We recently observed that blood levels of Th2 cells (a type of T lymphocyte), are higher in severe compared to non-severe asthmatics and that patients taking the highest doses of GC had the most Th2 cells. Importantly, when stratified by sex we realized higher % Th2 cells were observed in severe asthmatic women, not men, and tracked with more healthcare visits and medication usage. In vitro we found that GC actually increased expression of CRTh2, a gene that promotes Th2 cell survival. Genetic changes in CRTh2 are associated with increased risk of developing asthma, yet no one has looked at whether their effects differ in men and women or influence GC responses. We found that the GC-induced effect on CRTh2 was enhanced by estrogen receptor activation. This could explain why women exhibit less anti-inflammatory effect from GC than men and suggests a role for genetic variation in genes regulating estrogen signaling in asthma. This catalyst grant will i) determine whether CRTh2 gene variants exhibit sex-specific effects on asthma, GC usage and % Th2 cells; ii) explore the influence of genetic variation within the estrogen signaling pathway on development of asthma, GC usage and % Th2 cells. These results will improve our understanding of differences between men and women and determine if sex-specific treatments should be considered. Future work will involve testing these findings in a clinical trial(s) as well as delving more deeply into mechanisms of action.

column36: The derivation, validation and implementation of an international risk prediction tool in IgA nephropathy
column37: IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is a type of kidney disease that results from the immune system attacking the kidney, and can only be diagnosed using a kidney biopsy. Although there are effective treatments, they have many side-effects and should be used only in patients at the highest risk of progressive loss of kidney function. However, this requires the ability to identify patients at high risk, and there is currently no established method to do this. Previous efforts at creating prediction tools to identify high-risk patients have been limited because they were not validated in different ethnic groups, were very inaccurate, did not include findings from the kidney biopsy to improve accuracy, and were not designed for easy use in clinical practice. This project is a large international collaboration of prominent researchers in IgAN that merges 7 different databases from North America, Europe, China and Japan to create a new prediction tool in IgAN with improved accuracy, that includes kidney biopsy findings, and that is validated in different ethnic groups worldwide. We will convert the prediction tool into an app for use on mobile devices and a web-based calculator so that it can be easily used. In addition, patients with IgAN and physicians will be interviewed to determine ways in which the prediction tool, mobile app and web calculator can be created so that they are easy to use in clinical practice and address the needs of physicians and patients alike. This project will create the first prediction tool that can reliably identify high risk patients so that treatment can be given only to patients at highest risk, while lower risk patients can be spared the side effects of unnecessary therapy.

column36: An app-based intervention to empower self-management for people with rheumatoid arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis is a major cause of severe chronic pain and disability. To live well, people with rheumatoid arthritis need skills and support to manage their symptoms and treatment use, be physically active, and know when to seek help. But sometimes they struggle with interpreting their symptoms in relation to their treatment and daily activities. This makes it challenging for them to decide if and when to seek help from health professionals. We will develop and test a program with self-tracking technology to address this challenge. The program will include a mobile app for self-recording symptoms and treatment use. It will also be paired with a Fitbit wristband to automatically track physical activity levels and show them side-by-side with the self-recorded information such as pain, disease activity, fatigue, stiffness and stress level. This means patients will be able to see how their treatment and lifestyle affect the disease over periods of time. The app will send an automated prompt when there appears to be a disease flare based on their own recording. In the next two years this project will achieve three aims. First, we will partner with patients, health professionals and an e-health company to build and launch the app. Second, we will invite 15 patients with rheumatoid arthritis to help us test how well the app functions in a lab and in their own environment. Feedback will be used to refine the app and user instructions. Finally, we will recruit 60 patients to test how feasible it is for the program to be delivered in the community. We will assess if it shows promise of being successful to improve physical activity and health outcomes. This project will be a catalyst for a better understanding and future research in the use of self-tracking technology to support self-management. The connections of our team members will allow us to efficiently communicate the results to the public, health professionals and other researchers.

column36: Medication adherence as a predictor of morbidity and mortality in patients with chronic respiratory diseases
column37: Adherence to long-term drug therapy is essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes in patients with chronic diseases. Nevertheless, its levels often falls below 50% in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients. The ultimate goal of our project is to provide tools to physicians and patients that will allow them to assess the long-term risks associated with non-adherence to prescribed medications in order to facilitate shared treatment decision-making. The aims of this project are to develop 3 predictive models based on medication adherence in order to: 1) predict the 1-year risk of asthma and COPD exacerbations, as a function of adherence to all controller medications taken; 2) predict the 5-year risk of all-cause morbidity, as a function of the adherence to all medications prescribed concomitantly for chronic use; and 3) predict the 5-year risk of mortality, as a function of the adherence to all medications prescribed concomitantly for chronic use. A large sample of patients with asthma and COPD will be obtained from Quebec health administrative databases between 2000 and 2016. Adherence to medications will be assessed over one year using prescription refills. By applying high-performance statistical modeling, we will develop prediction models which will estimate the long-term risk of exacerbations, morbidity and mortality based upon patients' adherence to all their medications prescribed for chronic use, and sociodemographic characteristics. Ultimately, the predictive models will be incorporated in electronic medical records, thus allowing an easy and quick access to physicians and patients in routine clinical practice. The prediction models will have the potential to enhance decision-making on medication prescribing, help physicians target high-risk individuals, and discuss personalized strategies to promote treatment adherence with their patients. They will also motivate high-risk patients to modify their medication adherence.

column36: The role of genes and sex in determining therapeutic responses in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common medical condition that affects 1 in 5 Canadians over the age of 40. COPD is the number one cause reason Canadians become hospitalized. The most effective drugs to reduce "lung attacks" that lead to hospitalization are bronchodilators (drugs that open up the breathing tubes) and azithromycin, an antibiotic, which is taken once daily. Based on previous research, we know that these drugs don't work on all patients (in fact, only 1 out of 6 patients receiving any of these drugs will experience benefit; 5 out of 6 will receive no benefit or experience just side effects). In this study, we will determine whether the genetic make-up of patients with COPD is important in predicting which patients respond to these medications and which patients don't. We will also see whether men and women respond the same or differently to these drugs. The results of these study will help researchers to develop genetic tools to help doctors to give these drugs to only those patients who will benefit. This will save money and prevent side effects.

column36: Characterizing Sexually Dimorphic Drug Metabolism Using Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell Derived Hepatocytes
column37: Sex differences in drug metabolism can negatively affect individual responses to drugs often leading adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Several drugs used to treat mental health disorders, have been found to have a disproportionate number of ADRs in women. A major player in drug metabolism are the superfamily of enzymes known as the cytochrome P450s (CYPs). These are mostly found in the liver and are responsible for breaking down foreign chemicals. With the advent of human gene sequencing, the field of pharmacogenomics has arisen, which promises to predict ADRs based upon an individual's CYP gene sequencing profile. Because this approach focuses on individual variability in CYP gene coding sequence, it has only proven to be only 7% effective at predicting drug responses. What is missing is a measure of CYP gene expression and enzyme function, which is difficult to perform because of the near-impossibility of procuring patient liver cells. Recently, however, methods have been developed to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from an individual's blood or cheek cells, which in turn can be expanded and differentiated into liver cells. Using liver cells derived from male and female patient iPSCs, we will compare sex and hormone differences in specific CYP abundance, activity, and ability to metabolize known adverse drugs in mental health. Derrick Rancourt (UCalgary), an iPSC expert, will generate iPSC liver cells. Ayman Al-Kadi (UAlberta), a human CYP expert, will characterize CYP function from said liver cells. Doug Demetrick of Calgary Laboratory Services is an end-user of our approach. Two Alberta-based core facilities, Gene Expression Profiling and Metabolomics, will support our research. Through our approach, we hope to develop new empirical methods to better support pharmacogenomics. Our ability to study drug metabolism both male and female liver cells will enable better stratification of ADRs based upon sex.

column36: Do men and women differ in how pharmacogenetics optimizes smoking cessation therapy?
column37: Cigarette smoking is a leading cause of preventable illness and death in Canada; strategies to optimize smoking cessation success are key to improving healthcare delivery and reducing tobacco-associated economic and personal costs. There are three medications to aid cessation: nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, and varenicline. Genetic variation in specific enzymes and transporters that act on these medications influences drug levels, treatment response, and adverse effects. There are also sex differences (via hormones) on the activity of these enzymes and transporters as well as sex and gender differences in response to and success of cessation therapies; for example, women have lower quit rates on nicotine replacement therapy and bupropion, and higher quit rates on varenicline, compared to men. This proposal will examine, for the first time, sex and gender differences in the known impact of genetics on treatment response, providing a better understanding of how sex and gender can be integrated into genomics-based strategies for personalizing smoking cessation. We propose to analyze existing data from ~1,700 smokers (822 males and 873 females) that participated in our placebo-controlled clinical trials involving the nicotine patch, bupropion, and varenicline. Participants have been genotyped for key genetic variants in relevant metabolism and transporter genes, and drug levels have been assessed. The current project will explicitly test (using biostatistical tests) whether genetic effects on enzyme activity, treatment drug levels, and smoking cessation (and adverse effects) differ for men and women. We will also examine sex and gender differences in the genetic effects on withdrawal/depressive symptoms and smoking cessation-associated weight gain. Our studies will improve the tailoring of smoking cessation treatment in both men and women, which will reduce the extensive morbidity, mortality, and economic costs associated with cigarette smoking.

column36: Early INterventions to Support Trajectories for healthy lifE in INdia (EINSTEIN)
column37: The health and economic burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is increasing rapidly worldwide and falls disproportionally on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where almost 75% of the global deaths from NCDs occur. Undernutrition is a very significant problem in India, and low birthweight occurs in ~25% of the 26 million babies born each year. Further, the prevalence of stunting, wasting, underweight and anaemia is very high in children under 5. At the same time, obesity is also increasing in India, with estimates that 19% of children and adolescents and 15% of women of reproductive age are overweight or obese. An estimated 65 million people live with diabetes and a further 77 million are pre-diabetic, making India one of the diabetes capitals of the world. The rising burden of cardiometabolic disease is accompanied by a growing recognition of the burden of neurodevelopmental and mental health disorders in India, with 13% of children aged 1-16 years experiencing mental health problems. Research has shown that maternal undernutrition and low birth weight have a detrimental impact on fetal development leading to an increased susceptibility to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and impaired learning. A multidisciplinary team of experts from India and Canada will investigate how exposures in the preconception period and during pregnancy, infancy and childhood impact life-long trajectories of health and development in Indian children. The research team will recruit young women from Mysore who intend to have a child within the next two years to establish a preconception cohort and evaluate the impact of a package of interventions on children's health, cognitive and behavioural outcomes. The team from the EINSTEIN project will engage with community and policy makers to ensure that the information that will be generated can be applied to policies and practices in India and potentially other LMIC to enhance the life-long health and wellbeing of children.

column37: The burden of non-communicable diseases in low and middle income countries (LMICs) is significant and increasing due to several risk factors including undernutrition at early age, sedentary behaviour, poor diet, and heredity. It is recognised that prevention of obesity in women of reproductive age is critical both for their health and for that of their children but efforts to address the paradoxical challenges of stunting in early childhood and escalating obesity have been largely unsuccessful. To date, interventions in overweight pregnant women have not produced appreciable impact on pregnancy and birth outcomes. This suggests that the pre-conception periods may be key windows of opportunity to intervene to prevent obesity and contribute to the survival and wellbeing of newborns throughout their lives. This project will begin laying the foundations for healthy trajectories by improving women's health prior to and during pregnancy and reinforcing optimal health in the infant. A team of experts from South Africa (SA) and Canada will focus on a longitudinal analysis of how early-life exposures in the preconception period and during pregnancy, infancy and childhood impact life-long trajectories of health and development of children in SA. The research team will recruit women of childbearing age from Soweto, a historically disadvantaged urban area of Johannesburg, to establish a preconception cohort and evaluate the impact of a package of interventions on children's health, cognitive and behavioural outcomes. The team will engage with community and policy makers to ensure that the information that will be generated can be applied to policies and practices in SA and potentially other LMICs to enhance the life-long wellbeing of children.

column36: Developing a stroke-specific comorbidity index to predict mortality and disability in a population-based study
column37: Stroke occurs when a blood vessel in the brain is blocked. Many patients die after a stroke. Survivors may live with disabilities. They may have difficulty doing simple things like bathing or cooking and may no longer be able to live in their home. Knowing the risk of being disabled is very important to patients, but doctors have difficulty predicting who will be disabled and by how much. Because every patient is different, the goal of our project is to find a tool to help doctors and health policy decision-makers calculate each patient's risk of dying or being disabled after a stroke. Recovery after stroke takes time. After leaving the hospital, patients often need to go to a rehabilitation centre. Some patients need to temporarily live somewhere where extra help is available. We will measure disability by calculating the number of days a patient spends in their own home in the first 90 days after a stroke. Not many researchers have studied this number. We want to study it because going back home is important to patients. Understanding the risks of dying or disability helps patients. In the hospital, doctors can help patients and their family members understand how much the stroke will affect them after leaving the hospital. From the health system's point of view, being able to tell who is at risk of dying or being disabled is important for finding out if the treatments doctors give are helping patients. We can compare groups of patients to see if all patients are being helped: women, different ethnic backgrounds, immigrants, and very old or very young patients. We can also make report cards comparing different hospitals or provinces. The results of our study will help make stroke care more personalised to each patient's needs so that each patient receive the best care, regardless of who they are or where they are in Canada.

column36: Development of a telemonitoring app for management of patients with multiple chronic conditions within an integrated care model
column37: About 75% of healthcare dollars are spent on caring for patients with chronic illnesses. Many of these patients have multiple chronic conditions (more than one chronic illness) and they are the most costly to the healthcare system. Patients with multiple chronic conditions often don't know how to best take care of themselves and their conditions are usually taken care of separately by different doctors without much communication. These patients end up getting readmitted to hospital over and over again. The requested funding will be used to enhance an app, named Medly, which is used to monitor patients in their homes. Medly has been used to manage single chronic illnesses, such as heart failure. The enhanced Medly will be a platform that can be used to manage patients with multiple chronic conditions. Each patient will take measurements at home, such as blood pressure, that are important for their specific combination of chronic illnesses. Medly will send instructions to the patients based on their measurements and their healthcare provider will also be alerted when needed. This enhanced Medly will help patients in a more holistic way, including having added features to deal with mental health and videoconferencing for them to communicate with their providers. Our health technology partner, Celltrak, is a company that has mobile technology that providers use to access patient information. By combining Medly as the technology that patients use, a telemonitoring system will be created that can meet the needs of both patients and providers. CellTrak will also help commercialize and disseminate Medly. Part of the requested funding will be used to pilot Medly at William Osler Health System's Integrated Chronic Disease Management (iCDM) Clinic. This will be an ideal setting to pilot Medly because the iCDM Clinic will have a team of healthcare providers working together to care for their patients with multiple chronic conditions.

column36: E-health intervention for cardiac rehabilitation: Pilot implementation and feasibility assessment
column37: Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is designed to increase healthy behaviours (e.g. physical activity, healthy eating, smoking abstinence) and reduce risk factors (e.g. high blood pressure & cholesterol) in order to improve quality of life and health among people with heart disease. Unfortunately, few patients attend CR, often reporting several barriers to access including travel distance, parking fees and lack of time. Advances in technology have the potential to improve accessibility and delivery of CR programs, and improve patient empowerment. The University of Ottawa Heart Institute has developed an e-health program called the Virtual Cardiac Rehabilitation Program (VCRP); an online cardiovascular health management system (website & Smartphone app) that provides strategies for the control and management of risk factors. The goals of VCRP are to: empower and educate patients; foster better communication between patients and their health care team; stimulate shared decision-making; and, facilitate care coordination leading to better health outcomes. The VCRP provides patients with: real-time access to their health information, as well as tracking of risk behaviours and factors through integration with devices; a wellness plan; access to a personal on-line health coach; goal-setting notifications; on-line community forums; and, circle of care access to information. The aim of this project is to evaluate the effects of VCRP (with integrated fitness tracker) compared to a standard, home-based CR program. The study will look at changes in: patient empowerment; health behaviours; risk factors; quality of life; clinical outcomes; and, costs. The study will improve our understanding of: patient and provider needs; program usability; and shared decision-making. Results will inform the use of e-health programs such as VCRP into healthcare settings to improve patient empowerment, shared decision-making, and the ability to integrate wearable monitors to improve health behaviours.

column36: Subtypes of Major Depressive Disorders as Predictors of Incident Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Depression is a well-established risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D). Specific depression subtypes are more relevant for T2D than others. For example, an atypical depression subtype might be associated with an increased risk of developing T2D. The atypical subtype is characterized by increased appetite, weight gain, obesity, and hypersomnia. The aims of the proposed study are to a) investigate the role of depression subtypes (e.g., atypical depression, melancholic-anxious depression, and major depression without anxiety/atypical symptoms) on the onset of T2D incidence in a Canadian community sample; and b) evaluate whether including depression subtypes improves predictive value of the previous developed Canadian Diabetes Population Risk Tool (DPoRT). We propose to combine survey data (Canadian Community Health Surveys (CCHS) 2002 and 2012 for Ontario residents) with a validated population-based diabetes registry (Ontario Diabetes Database). We will validate our results in a different cohort (CCHS 2002 and 2012 for Quebec residents and administrative data in Quebec (RAMQ)). The results might inform the development of strategies for prevention at the individual level (i.e., depression subtypes with the highest risk of T2D) and might have the potential to contribute to the development of tailored treatments for depression, which, in turn, might lead to improved diabetes prevention.

column36: A Novel Asthma eHealth Application for Self-Management, Improved Health Literacy, and Shared-Decision Making
column37: Asthma affects 8.3% of Canadians, leads to serious respiratory symptoms, and costs our health system $1.8 billion per year. Health-related smartphone apps can provide patients with personalized health information anytime and anywhere, allowing them to better manage diseases like asthma. Health providers can also benefit from electronic tools to improve the efficiency and quality of asthma care. We previously built the Electronic Asthma Action Plan System (eAAPS) to help doctors to produce an asthma action plan (AAP) - a written form given to patients, with instructions on what to do when symptoms worsen. The system required patients to complete a questionnaire about their asthma on a tablet device in the waiting room and this information was processed and transmitted to their doctor's computer along with a computer-generated personalized AAP. Our pilot study of this tool showed that it does improve care, however less than one third of patients completed the tablet questionnaire. This study aims to improve the system by developing and testing an asthma care app that will: 1) allow patients to complete the questionnaire on their own devices; and 2) provide a tool to help manage their asthma, including displaying the AAP, education about asthma (focusing on confusing health language and concepts), and a "decision aid" that will help patients and doctors to make shared decisions about medications. We will then integrate this app with the eAAPS such that both systems share all data, and test the updated system to see if and how patients actually use the app, if they are satisfied with it, and how it affects their health behaviour. If successful, our unique approach may be a model for the design of similar technologies for the care of other chronic diseases. Ultimately, we will seek to implement our app and asthma care system across Canada to improve not only the way that healthcare is delivered, but also the everyday health of Canada's 3 million asthma sufferers.

column36: Security and authentication for large scale deployment of disease-specific applications for patients with serious and complex renal disease.
column37: Patients with serious and complex renal diseases are at high risk for progressive renal injury leading to end stage renal failure, major cardiovascular event or premature death. They often have disease-specific and patient-related characteristics that make treatment difficult. Such patients are generally followed at specialty outpatient renal clinics. Their condition requires close monitoring between regularly scheduled clinic visits to proactively identify and resolve emerging problems. However, community-services are often ill-equipped to provide resource-intense monitoring for such patients, leaving them vulnerable and anxious. With new technology, it is now possible to continuously monitor care remotely, support self-care activities and greatly improve communication between patients and their healthcare providers. Technologically-driven care innovations can fill the gap between clinic visits, build confidence and strengthen trust in prescribed treatments. Our research team built a smartphone-based app system for patients with complex chronic diseases to support patient self-care and promote shared decision-making. The features and strengths of our app system are well-documented in top-ranked, peer-reviewed international medical journals. A key component is the use of algorithm-driven automated feedback to provide patients with real-time actionable messages, vital for behavioural change. The purpose of this proposal is to expand the app system's capabilities and facilitate large scale deployment to specialty renal clinics across the Province of Ontario. This will be achieved by expanding and testing app features for renal patients with serious and complex diseases and incorporating new security measures to permit retrieval of personal health information from the government-operated data assets such as ConnectingOntario, which enable patients to use their own smartphone anywhere without compromising their personal health information.

column36: Sex and genetic determinants of direct-acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC) efficacy and adverse outcomes
column37: Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are a new type of blood thinners widely used to prevent stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), a disorder associated with irregular heartbeat, or venous thromboembolism (VTE), a harmful blood clot in a deep vein that can also travel to the lung. Even so highly effective and well tolerated, there remains concern relating to the overall safety of DOACs. Recently, it has been reported that women treated with DOACs for VTE are at higher risk for bleeding compared to men, whereas the reverse was seen for patients with AF. At present, the underlying mechanisms for these differences are poorly understood. We recently observed higher blood levels of two DOACs, apixaban and rivaroxaban, in female compared to male patients, while weight and genetic makeup contributed in part to the variation. Studies in healthy subjects show that the amount of DOACs present in the blood stream is linked to their effect, yet little is known regarding implications for treatment or adverse response in patients, and sex-related differences are not considered in current dosing guidelines. We speculate that sex, clinical factors and genetic variation determine DOAC blood level; patients with higher than intended levels are at greater risk for bleeding, while those with lower levels may lack protection from stroke. In this research proposal we plan to study clinical and genetic factors that may explain differences in DOAC level between women and men in a large number of AF patients followed in routine care. To examine differences in adverse outcomes, we will access administrative databases (i.e. OHIP) to obtain data concerning hospitalisation or ER visits due to bleeding after DOAC prescription via the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES). Findings from this research will provide new insights concerning sex-related differences, and help better tailor DOAC therapy thereby enhancing therapeutic effect while minimizing toxicity risk.

column36: Automated screening, triage, and follow-up to facilitate proactive, personalized postpartum mental health treatment for new parents.
column37: Mental health symptoms - especially depression and anxiety - are very common in new parents, affecting close to 20% of mothers and at least 10% of fathers. When such symptoms progress to severe levels, they can be more difficult to treat. Early identification of symptoms and prompt treatment are ideal. Despite broad awareness that mental health symptoms in new parents are common, few systems are in place to automatically assess and monitor such symptoms. Evidence-based symptom surveys that can identify parents at risk for postpartum mental health disorders exist, and effective medication and non-medication treatment options are available. Yet, most primary care settings do not have systems in place to ensure that parents with mental health problems (and especially fathers) are identified and treated. This study will use a digital app with tablet computers and email integration to engage parents in assessing their mental health symptoms within weeks of the birth of their new baby. Electronic symptom surveys, sent on behalf of the family doctor, will be used to support proactive, personalized postpartum mental healthcare (P3MH). Responses will be used to enable a tailored care plan for the patient, including advice about options for referrals, treatment, and local community-based psycho-educational and/or social supports. This eHealth intervention includes a web-based application for parents and seamless integration in the electronic medical record, so that when the family doctor sees the patient in clinic, relevant information is ready to be discussed. In this study, we will carry a co-design process with patients and health professionals to refine this eHealth intervention, and determine the usability, user experience, and perceived value of this process in terms of whether it enables mental health symptoms to be caught early and managed in the best way possible for each parent. We will also pilot the procedures for a future large-scale evaluation.

column36: Using Individual Patient Data Meta-Analyses to Develop Individual Prediction Models for Depression Screening
column37: Depression screening is controversial, and the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care recommends against depression screening. A major concern is that depression screening tests are not sufficiently accurate. All existing studies have used a cutoff method, where all patients who score above the cutoff on a depression screening questionnaire are considered positive screens and possible cases, whereas those below the threshold are considered negative screens. This method is not accurate, and information from actual patient screening scores is lost by dichotomizing simply into positive and negative screens. Datasets collected in primary studies are too small for developing individual risk models for depression. We will use very large datasets (e.g., > 20,000 patients) that we have synthesized for screening with three commonly used screening tests, the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (primary care settings), the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (hospital settings and medically ill), and the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (perinatal care), to develop individual risk models. We will use actual screening questionnaire scores, along with patient demographic and medical characteristics, to estimate risk compared to a gold standard diagnostic interview. Results will be used to develop an easily accessible app for use in practice.

column36: Harnessing the Quebec Pain Registry and the Quebec health administrative databases to improve the management of chronic non-cancer pain in women and men
column37: Chronic non-cancer pain (CNCP) affects 1/5 Canadians and its human and economical burdens are enormous. CNCP is poorly managed, with medications such as opioids being one of few tools available to family doctors who do not have easy access to multidisciplinary teams. Nonetheless, little good quality data exist on who benefits from opioid therapy or is at risk of opioid abuse. In parallel, the ongoing opioid crisis referring to waves of opioid overdoses in North America has led clinicians and governmental instances to adopt an increasingly conservative approach to the use of opioids. This however is not without consequence for CNCP patients. These elements have led this research team to propose in depth examination of opioid therapy in CNCP patients using a unique methodology that combines Quebec health administrative data banks with an existing registry of 8,650 patients with CNCP (Quebec Pain Registry). While individually none of these data banks can adequately answer certain questions about the impact of opioid crisis on CNCP patients, their combination will provide rich and unique data. Most notably, this pairing will provide accurate and precise information on opioid prescriptions, pain diagnosis, pain severity, quality of life, and mood. We will use advanced statistical methods to (a) identify different patient subgroups who are most and least likely to benefit from opioid therapy and identify predictors of treatment response, (b) examine the frequency and risk factors of opioid doctor shopping behaviors (one form of opioid abuse), and (c) examine the impact of the opioid crisis on opioid prescriptions and related serious adverse events in Quebec. Identifying factors associated with opioid treatment response and risk of abuse can lead to significant improvements in pain management practices and in the condition of CNCP patients while providing a safe and responsible framework for the use of opioids as a therapeutic tool.

column36: Modeling the Health and Treatment Trajectories of Persons with Terminal Gastrointestinal Malignancies to Enhance Patient-Centered Care
column37: Patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer often need to make important decisions regarding their care soon after their diagnosis. column36: Pregnancy Complications and the Risk of Subsequent Cardiovascular Disease
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of disability and death in women. Nonetheless, the risk of CVD remains poorly understood in women. Over the last ten years, the rates of pregnancy complications such as hypertension in pregnancy and gestational diabetes have steadily increased. Previous studies have shown that women with a history of complications of pregnancy are at higher risk of future CVD. However, tools currently used by physicians to predict CVD risk do not consider complications of pregnancy and the corresponding earlier onset of CVD risk factors. Furthermore, these tools were developed over 20 years ago in older adult populations that are not representative of the general population or current clinical practice. There is therefore a need to develop a method to predict CVD that accounts for complications in pregnancy. We will develop two predictive models to determine the 5-year risk of CVD (including stroke, heart attack, or blocked arteries) among women who have recently given birth. The first model, which will be developed using a database from the United Kingdom called the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, will include extensive clinical information to answer this question. The second model, which will be developed using the British Columbia Perinatal Data Registry, will be a simplified model that will be more easily used in routine clinical practice. These models will allow for contemporary assessment of CVD risk in women and assess the value of pregnancy-related information when determining CVD risk. This study will provide physicians with the information needed to better predict CVD risk in women and to identify which women would benefit from the closer monitoring and the early initiation of CVD prevention. Given the clinical and economic consequences of CVD in women and the availability of effective interventions to prevent CVD, the results of this study will have substantial clinical and population health implications.

column36: Postpartum depression Action toward Causes and Treatment (PACT) - Canada: Predictive Analytic Models for Postpartum Depression Risk
column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) is the most common complication of childbirth, affecting up to 1 in 5 women in the year after delivery. It is associated with long-term maternal morbidity, child emotional, cognitive and behavioural difficulties, and even maternal and child mortality. The long-term cost of PPD and related perinatal mental illnesses is estimated at ~1.4 billion Canadian dollars per one-year cohort of children. Prevention of postpartum depression could avert a significant amount of this burden. Specific psychosocial and psychological interventions can prevent PPD, especially when delivered in the early postpartum (as opposed to in pregnancy) and in high-risk women. Yet, there is no evidence-based tool in common practice that can accurately predict the level of risk for PPD in an individual woman. The aim of this catalyst grant is to create a clinical risk index, to be used around the time of delivery, for determining the probability that a woman will develop depression in the first year postpartum. We will harmonize and analyze linked population-based clinical and health administrative datasets comprising key PPD risk factors in ~400,000 Ontario women, create a statistical model that predicts who will develop PPD, and convert the final model into a clinical tool that can estimate a woman's PPD risk. Stakeholders, including women with lived experience, public health nurses, primary care and antenatal care providers will help create a clinically useful tool to optimize future integration into the health care system. To our knowledge, this will be the first research in Canada, and the largest and most comprehensive worldwide, that attempts to create a personalized tool for determining PPD risk, thereby making a significant contribution to knowledge and practice.

column36: Predicting neurodevelopmental disorders from childhood trajectories of endophenotypes and genetic determinants in children born to an affected parent
column37: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder affect 3% of our populations. The two disorders have common etiologies as expressed in shared common genetic determinants and clinical observations. Our group and others have identified a clustering of indicators such as cognitive deficits and attenuated symptoms of psychosis, as forming risk clusters that are better predictors of later conversion than individual indicators alone. It is also known that males have more severe illness, an earlier age of onset, poorer response to treatment and poorer prognosis. Our long-term objective is to develop a predictive tool involving genetic risk scores and risk indicators to be used in primary care clinics for discriminating the most at risk among the high-risk children-adolescents born to a parent affected by schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. We will take advantage of the longitudinal follow-up of children from Eastern Quebec kindreds densely affected by schizophrenia and bipolar disorder to build prediction models, and validate them in a cohort of children from the Horizon Parent Enfant (HoPE) translational program recruiting children born to an affected parent in the Quebec City area.

In order to be able to offer exercise programs to patients living with the consequences of a stroke, new technologies such as interactive video games, or virtual reality, that are monitored remotely, using telerehabilitation, could allow patients to continue their recovery at home using increasingly readily available equipment. The novelty in this study would be to combine a gaming environment with real-time communication systems, known as telerehabilitation, that would allow audio-visual communication between a therapist and the patient at home. The feasibility, safety and efficacy of this program will be evaluated. This modality would allow the clinician to verify and correct the exercises the patient is performing. The patient would be expected to perform the exercises daily on the interactive console over an 8-week period, while the clinician's real-time periodic monitoring would occur once or twice a week. In addition, the clinician would be able to remotely modify the exercises in such a way that they remain challenging as the patient's performance improves.

column36: PainQuILT: A patient-centred e-health solution to empower older adults and improve pain assessment and management
column37: PainQuILT is an online tool that helps patients with painful conditions to visually communicate and track their pain (http://painquilt.com). It uses a library of simple pictures to help patients describe what their pain feels like, such as a matchstick for 'burning pain' and a hammer for 'pounding pain'. Patients can also show where and how much it hurts using a virtual body map. All of this information is tracked over time, and can be used to talk with clinicians and help make decisions about pain management. Our team has completed studies showing that PainQuILT is useful and valid for children and younger adults with chronic pain. Since we have involved patients in all stages of developing PainQuILT, it is also preferred by a majority of patients compared with other ways of expressing and tracking pain. As people get older, their risk of developing certain types of chronic pain increases. Older people's pain is sometimes poorly managed, which is often caused by poor assessment. It is important to find ways to improve communication about pain between patients and their healthcare providers so that older patients can be more involved in decisions about how to manage their pain. A simple, visual tool like PainQuILT may be a good way to give older patients more control over how they talk about their pain. It may also help clinicians to better understand the pain experiences of their older patients over time. This study will evaluate PainQuILT among English- and French-speaking older adults with pain who live in the community and in nursing homes. This study will help us understand whether PainQuILT can help to improve pain communication, decision-making, and pain management in older adults

column36: Developing a wearable device and a mobile application that aids patients in self-management of their COPD by providing biofeedback, education and guidance
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a deadly, prevalent and disabling chronic disease that incurs high cost to the health care system. Even with optimal treatment, people with COPD frequently experience exacerbations or worsening of their condition and need admission to hospital. Wearable technology such as smartwatches may be able to accurately monitor physiologic parameters such as coughing, heart rate and physical activity which may change with exacerbations of COPD. These parameters may both be able to accurately detect early acute exacerbations but also engage patients in their condition. We have developed a smartwatch application that records physical activity, heart rate, and respiratory sounds such as coughing. Our feasibility study found older patients with COPD will wear them, and we can collect accurate information data from the smartwatch sensors such as coughing. To achieve our goal of improving the care of patients with COPD, we will design, build and evaluate an e-Health application that will help patients with COPD manage their condition. This app will help patients monitor their physiologic parameters and will provide guidance for COPD self-management, including what actions to take when a COPD exacerbation occurs. This mobile application will also try to persuade patients with COPD to adopt healthier behaviour such as increasing their physical activity or stopping smoking. It will also be a platform to communicate with their health care provider. From our experience to date, elderly patients with COPD want to take control of their health. Paired with our smartwatch application, an e-Health app may improve their self-management and help them manage their COPD exacerbations earlier and at home. This would reduce the negative and costly experience of requiring a hospital admission. Incorporating this affordable wearable technology into the usual care of patients with COPD care could then help improve the health of the COPD population.

column36: Analytical mobile application to support shared decision making for pregnant women
column37: A difficult decision faced by all pregnant women and their partners is whether or not to undergo prenatal screening to assess the risk of certain genetic conditions in the fetus, and deciding among available tests. Decisions resulting from these tests may involve preventive surgery on the fetus, termination of pregnancy, or major lifestyle changes. Few pregnant women are aware of the benefits/risks of such tests, including the risk that taking the test will have little or no impact on their long-term health. To be involved in these decisions (shared decision making), they need information and support. Objective: To develop and test an app that will help women and their partners make informed decisions about prenatal screening with their healthcare providers, and to promote its use in population-based prenatal screening programs in Quebec province. Impact: This app could improve delivery of information, shared decision making, best use of prenatal screening tests, and health outcomes for pregnant women in Quebec and ultimately Canada. Our research will help women and their partners by providing them with an easy, mobile and enjoyable way to prepare to make their prenatal screening decision, using information based on scientific evidence and presented in an understandable way that is relevant to their daily lives and longer-term life choices. As this is a highly value-laden decision, our proposed app will also take an ethical, person-centred approach. It will help users consider their values and preferences into account, too, in making the decision. Not all pregnant women and their partners, once informed by best evidence, will want to do the test. In summary, this study will allow us to design an effective and accessible app to inform pregnant women and their partners about prenatal screening, pilot test the app, and explore how it could be used on a much larger scale, i.e. in population-based prenatal screening programs.

column36: Sex differences in the treatment of heart failure
column37: Heart failure (HF) arises when the heart muscle cannot pump sufficient blood to meet the body's needs for blood and oxygen. For example, a heart attack or high blood pressure can leave the heart too weak or stiff to fill and pump efficiently. Symptoms of HF include shortness of breath, fatigue and swelling. HF is divided in two categories; depending on which heart problem causes the HF. "Systolic HF (also called HF with reduced ejection fraction or HF-REF)" occurs when the heart cannot contract strongly, indicating a pumping problem. Many medications are effective to treat this type of HF. "Diastolic HF (also called HF with preserved ejection fraction or HF-PEF)" occurs when the heart cannot relax, leading to a filling problem. Treatment options are much more limited for this type of HF. Women are more likely to develop HF-PEF, while men are more likely to develop HF-REF. Moreover, women with HF have generally a better survival than men with HF. Currently, little information is available to know if some genes influence the risk of developing HF or the efficacy of its treatment. Because genes contain the information that makes all individuals unique, we hypothesis they could be used to personalize the management of HF. As part of this research project, we propose to evaluate whether women and men with HF show differences in genetic risk factors of HF. Moreover, we plan to investigate whether these genetic factors influence the risk of mortality and hospitalisation differently between men and women and the effects of drugs. To do so, we will use multiple studies of patients with HF. The identification of such genetic factors will not only lead to a more personalize evaluation of the risk of HF and its treatment, it could also lead to the identification of new treatments for this disease.

column36: Development, validation, and dissemination of an individualized prediction tool for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a very common disease of the lungs. COPD patients frequently experience episodes of worsening of their disease, referred to as acute exacerbations or 'lung attacks'. Severe exacerbations of COPD are the number one reason (aside from child birth) for hospitalizations in Canada. The burden of COPD is comparable to that of other common diseases such as diseases of the heart. Despite this, patients and care providers do not have access to the required decision tools that are available for such diseases (such as Framingham Risk Scores that can be used to estimate the risk of future heart attacks). Such decision tools can be used for shared decision making such that both the patient and the care provider appreciate the level of risk specific to the patient and adjust the level of therapies according to patient preferences. To fill such a gap in COPD, our group has recently undertaken a major step by creating an individualized prediction tool (and associated eHealth platform - a Web App) for lung function decline in COPD (Zafari et. al. CMAJ, 2016). We propose to create an individualized prediction tool for COPD exacerbations. To achieve this, we will 1) use data from several studies (clinical trials and cohort studies) to develop and validate an individualized prediction model for exacerbations; 2) implement the model into a freely accessible Web App; 3) demonstrate the application of the App in helping patients and physicians decide on antibiotic therapy for preventing exacerbations. The Web App will be professionally designed and will be combined with our previously-developed Web Apps to create a suite of eHealth tools for Precision Medicine in COPD. The engagement of both patients and care providers as team members ensures the eHealth tool will be optimized from both perspectives. We have systematically engaged influential organizations as knowledge users to ensure the final product receives widespread visibility.

Evaluation of HEAL-C's influence on improving personal outcomes will then be evaluated in a pilot trial. column36: Explaining Increased Bleeding Risk in Women with Cardiovascular Diseases: a Sex-Drug-Gene Approach
column37: Women aged 55 years and younger who suffer from acute coronary syndrome (ACS) have been known to have poorer health outcomes and higher death rates than men. Prior research has shown that women have a higher risk of major bleeds (requiring medical treatments) compared to men. Also, many drugs that are prescribed to decrease clot formation, like clopidogrel, are associated with increased risk of bleeding in women compared with men. The digestion of these drugs in humans is regulated by many genes. In particular, various CYP genes are known to play a role in the metabolism of drugs including Clopidogrel. Any mutation in these genes can alter the digestion of these drugs leading to either excessive or poor metabolism causing higher risk of either bleeding or less of a beneficial effect on the formation of clots in blood vessels. The understanding of factors underlying increased risk of bleeding in women as compared to men on these drugs is still incomplete. Therefore we propose to examine differences in drug-gene interactions between male and female clopidogrel users as a possible factor explaining these differences. We believe that interaction of the CYP genes responsible for metabolism of these drugs, in men vs. women could help explain the increased risk of major bleeding in women as compared to men. Our cohorts GENESIS-PRAXY (GENdEr and Sex DetermInantS of Cardiovascular Disease: From Bench to Beyond Premature Acute Coronary SYndrome) and the Recurrence and inflammation in the acute coronary syndromes (RISCA) study are prospective cohorts of patients hospitalized for Acute Coronary Syndrome. We propose to enhance our PRAXY and RISCA cohorts through expanding data analysis to genotyping in order to identify differences in sequencing at the single nucleotide level. A better knowledge of these differences could lead to the development of better therapies tailored the patient sex.

column36: Personalizing the Prevention of Osteoporotic Fracture
column37: Problem: Osteoporotic fractures are a major health burden for Canadians - one in three women and one in five men suffer at least one osteoporotic fracture in their lifetime. There are 30,000 costly hip fractures per year in Canada and that number is expected to quadruple by 2030. The current approach to preventing osteoporotic fractures is an "one size fits all' approach. Antiresorptive therapies, such as bisphosphonates, at standard dosing are used first-line for women and men at high risk of fractures, regardless of other factors. The emergence of atypical femur fractures (AFFs) in some postmenopausal women (especially Asian women) who have been on long-term antiresorptive therapies calls into question this "one size fits all" approach. Physicians' and patients' fear of this rare side effect led to inadequate prescribing and poor patient compliance. As a consequence, a huge care gap exists: even those who have had fractures are not treated to prevent future fractures. Objective: To develop predictive analytic models that can identify patients who are at increased risk of having AFFs. Predictive models will test and identify sex-race-drug-gene relationships associated with increased harm. Study Design: A case and nested-control study of 350 cases of AFF and 700 controls without AFF using linked datasets including clinical data, diagnostic imaging, genomic data, data on health of collagen, and physical activity instruments, from the Ontario AFF Cohort, the Quebec AFF registry, the Canadian Multicentre Osteoporosis Study, and genomic data from Harvard University. To test the hypotheses, we will develop various predictive models. Significance: Findings from this project will accelerate our understanding of AFFs, improve risk stratification, target individuals at increased risk of osteoporotic fracture for antiresorptive drug therapy while minimizing drug-related adverse events, and advance personalized medicine approaches in the field of osteoporosis and fracture

column36: Personalized medicine for ankylosing spondylitis
column37: Back pain is one of the two top causes of disability according to the Centre for Disease Control and affects 20% of Canadians. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common inflammatory arthritis causing back pain affecting over 300,000 Canadians. The cause of AS is not completely understood. Treatment options for AS are not uniformly effective and are associated with potential side effects. Sex and gender influences diagnosis, prognosis and treatment responses. If we can predict which patients are likely to safely respond to a particular drug, we can reduce unnecessary delays in treatment and reduce both adverse events as well as cost associated with treatment. Different cell populations have been postulated to play a role in the pathogenesis of AS. Thus studying these cell populations individually may be more informative. Our research program has a strong clinical, laboratory and imaging database with stored biological samples including cells. Patients with stored cells and who started biologic medications will be initially studied. Cell specific genetic data will be generated by categorizing the peripheral blood cells into specific subpopulations. The RNA extracted from each individual cell population will be analyzed to generate genetic information. This information will be combined with existing clinical data to develop an algorithm that can predict treatment response and adverse effects. New patients starting biologic drugs will be enrolled for analyzing and comparing similar data obtained from freshly isolated cells. The new algorithm/prediction rule will be compared to data obtained from traditional whole blood RNA analysis.

column36: Improving the health of infants and children through research that links large health administrative databases with clinical, screening, and laboratory data
column37: Acute Lower Respiratory Illness (ALRI) continues to be a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in young children, and respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the most common pathogen implicated in ALRI. It infects virtually 100% of infants by age 3, with 10% requiring medical attention, and 1 to 2% experiencing illness severe enough to require hospitalization. Currently, the only treatment that can reduce RSV risk is palivizumab, a drug which contains RSV antibodies. Palivizumab is extremely costly and is limited to specific high-risk populations (e.g. congenital heart disease, preterm birth), so it is presently provided to less than 2% of Ontario children at a yearly cost exceeding $20M CAD. Our research has shown that between 2006 and 2013, there were about 1500 hospital admissions per year for Ontario infants, or approximately 10% of non-birth-related admissions before age one. Our findings demonstrated that more than 85% of these infants do not have one of the major risk factors that would make them eligible to receive palivizumab. In order to reduce the burden of severe RSV, there is an urgent need to improve the identification of high-risk infants in order to better target treatment to those infants most likely to benefit. By linking together health administrative data, newborn screening metabolite data, lab tests, palivizumab prescription data, pregnancy and birth registry data, and additional data sources, our proposed project aims to develop a much more accurate prediction model that can get medicine and information to the parents and doctors caring for infants at highest risk, and result in reduced illness, reduced burden on infants, parents and the health system, as well as reduce health system costs.

Some cancer treatments may reduce the chance of having children and currently many young adults do not receive enough information to make informed fertility decisions before treatment. More young adults are surviving cancer and the inability to have children due to their cancer treatment can cause negative emotions and lower wellbeing. Making a fertility decision before cancer treatment is hard and young adults may feel conflicted because the fertility options may delay treatment, be costly, and do not guarantee the ability to have children after treatment. Our research team has created a paper decision aid called the BEFORE (Begin Exploring Fertility Options, Risks and Expectations) for young Canadian breast cancer patients to help them weigh the risks and benefits of each fertility option allowing for an informed decision that is made in partnership with their health care providers. The goal of this study is to build on the work to offer a BEFORE app version of the decision aid and expand the decision aid to all young adults with any cancer needing to make fertility decisions. This app will allow young adults to learn more about the cancer treatment that can affect their fertility, fertility options available before and after cancer treatment, provide a personal exercise to help consider which options are right for them, provide resources for extra information and support, and sample questions to ask their health care team. The field of cancer and fertility is growing and to address this we will ensure the BEFORE app can be easily updated to include new fertility options and changes in recommendations as they occur. The BEFORE app will help to begin fertility conversations between young cancer patients and their health care providers to ensure patients make informed fertility decisions that reflect their values before starting cancer treatment.

column36: The Role of Sleep Quality and Emotion Regulation in Predicting Depressive Symptoms
column37: Adolescence is characterized by changes in emotionality and cognitive control, and heightened risk for depression. Depression is a debilitating disorder affecting 20% of the population and incurring a significant financial burden on the health care system. Depression in adolescence is associated with risk of suicide, and increased rates of mental health problems in adulthood. Understanding what places individuals at risk for depression during adolescence is critical. Investigating emotion regulation may provide an opportunity to understand key processes that relate to risk for depression, as difficulty regulating emotions has been identified as a key feature of depression. A second factor that should be considered during this period is sleep dysfunction, which is common in adolescence and is associated with both depression and emotion regulation difficulty. The proposed study aims to investigate the role of sleep dysfunction and emotion regulation ability in predicting depressive symptoms in adolescents. The current study will assess emotional processing using the late positive potential (LPP), a direct measure of brain electrical activity. It is hypothesized that sleep dysfunction will be associated with increased depressive symptoms, an enhanced LPP to emotional pictures and decreased down-regulation of the LPP to negative pictures. Moreover, it is hypothesized that the association between sleep dysfunction and depressive symptoms will be modulated by decreased down-regulation of the LPP to negative pictures. Adolescence is a key and understudied period of neurodevelopment, difficulties regulating emotions may be a critical process related to sleep dysfunction and emerging symptoms of depression. Clarification of factors that contribute to depression may help in the early identification of those at risk, and foster prevention and targeted treatments.

column36: Nursing Adaptation, Organizational Resilience and Providing Safe Healthcare
column37: Every year, errors harm 1 in 10 Canadians who receives healthcare in a hospital. The cost of these errors exceeds $1 billion annually. Recently, in safety research, there is a new trend, shifting away from studying what goes wrong, to understand how healthcare systems adapt safety under pressure. This safe adaption is called organizational resilience. It is hoped that by increasing organizational resilience, it will be possible to have fewer errors in hospitals. The proposed study will investigate how nurses adapt safely to pressures at work, and protect patients through their actions. This research will be conducted by a nurse researcher, who will observe nurses working in a hospital, for a period of approximately 6 months. Nurses will be asked to think out loud during parts of their work, to demonstrate how they are adapting their nursing practice. The researcher will use this information to understand how nurses can be supported at work, through policies and education. The goal is to increase the number of times that things go well, and reduce errors that harm patients.

column36: Investigating the role of microRNA-7 in the hypothalamic control of energy homeostasis
column37: The hypothalamus is a region of the brain that controls food intake, energy expenditure, and utilization of glucose and fats in the body. When the brain senses changes in energy status (e.g. after overeating, fasting, or exercising), the hypothalamus responds by switching specific genes on or off and coordinating brain circuits to tightly manage fuel storage in the body. In obesity and diabetes, the pattern of gene expression becomes disturbed and leads to metabolic dysfunctions. MicroRNAs (miRs) are RNA molecules that control biological processes by shutting off specific genes. MicroRNAs are essential to maintain energy balance, as mice lacking microRNAs in the hypothalamus become severely obese. One microRNA in particular, called miR-7, is one of the most highly and specifically expressed miRNAs in the hypothalamus. It plays a crucial role in brain development, but it remains unknown if miR-7 is also needed for the brain to control metabolism. We are studying gene-edited mice with either a lack of, or excessive expression of, miR-7 in specific hypothalamic cells. We will measure their body weight, lean and fat mass, food intake, and energy expenditure. We will also monitor their blood glucose levels, glucose tolerance and insulin tolerance. If we detect metabolic abnormalities, we will study the cells which lack or overexpress miR-7 to identify the genes being targeted and shut off by miR-7 and causing the dysfunctions. We will also collect hypothalamus samples into a culture dish and manipulate the target genes to study their specific functions. To understand how miR-7 responds to energy status changes, we will measure miR-7 levels in mice after high-fat feeding, prolonged fasting, and exercising, as well as in obese and diabetic mice. This study aims to define a new mechanism involving miR-7 in the brain that may be manipulated as a therapeutic strategy to combat metabolic diseases.

column36: Evaluation of novel cancer immunotherapies that combine the potency of chimeric antigen receptors and the intracellular targeting of T-cell receptors
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada and in many developed countries around the world. Recently, progress in the field of immunology has allowed for the development of "immunotherapies" against cancer. These allow doctors to use a patient's own immune system against their cancer. This can be done in three different approaches. One approach involves 'checkpoint' blockade drugs that decrease immune inhibition, leading to better-activated immune cells throughout the body and allowing immune cell-driven cancer cell killing. This strategy is most effective in tumours with a high number of mutations, such as melanoma, but due to the blanket nature of activation of the immune system this approach often leads to side effects. Another approach involves collecting tumour-associated immune cells surgically, treating them in the lab to strengthen them, and re-injecting them back into the patient. Finally, a third approach involves collecting a patient's immune cells and modifying them with an alternative targeting system, re-targeting them to the cancer. This re-targeting can be done with optimized natural receptors or with synthetic proteins - chimeric antigen receptors (CARs). In addition to re-targeting the cells, CARs also include co-stimulatory components, strengthening their anti-tumour response. This latter approach has so far been very successful in the clinic, and in a relapsed B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia trial at MSKCC, it induced an 88% "overall complete response" rate. A limitation with CARs compared to naturally-occurring receptors is that they must target cell-surface targets and cannot, currently, target intracellular proteins. This makes designing tumour-specific therapies difficult. My project aims to evaluate three different ways of resolving this limitation by combining the intra-cellular scanning ability of naturally-occurring receptors with the higher efficacy of CARs, expanding the number of CAR-treatable cancers.

column36: Using a novel Pan-Canadian mobile immunization platform to assess and improve national vaccine coverage
column37: In Canada, significant gaps exist in the capacity and infrastructure of immunization programs to collect data on vaccine coverage, limiting ability to guide resource investment and delivery of interventions aimed at addressing gaps in immunization coverage. Leveraging ImmunizeCA, a free, mobile and web-based immunization application the overall objectives of my research will be to comprehensively assess vaccine uptake amongst ImmunizeCA users. I will first synthesize current evidence-based literature on the effectiveness of personalized technological interventions for improving vaccine uptake and series completion in both paediatric and adult populations. From here, seasonal immunization coverage rates amongst ImmunizeCA users will be aggregated and interpreted alongside known infection outbreaks. Data will be combined as a 'coverage map' to provide contextualization and visualization of vaccination and outbreak data in the form of a Canadian Adult Immunization Coverage Map. Demographic data of the ImmunizeCA user population, will then be used to determine predictors of seasonal vaccinations. Using modelling strategies, special populations with highest and lowest risk of vaccine preventable diseases will be determined. Lastly, in a randomized controlled trial, I will assess whether tailored reminders delivered via email, text messaging and locally through the app improve on time adult seasonal vaccinations. The findings of this research will be used to provide local public health units and provincial and territorial governments with information on the effectiveness of their vaccination programs. Further, findings will be used to engage knowledge users and guide decision makers on the utility of digital technologies for guiding clinical care and public health investments in digital infrastructure.

column36: Building a systematic, ecological model of risk and protective factors for intimate partner violence against women: The role of long-term community exposures
column37: The most common form of violence perpetrated against women is intimate partner violence, which is the act or threat of physical, psychological, or sexual harm by a current or former partner. Intimate partner violence has severe negative health outcomes, particularly for female victims, including death, injury, psychological disorders, unintended pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, and increased risk of chronic diseases. This research aims to inform the prevention of intimate partner violence against women in the first instance. To do this, I will first systematically review published and unpublished evidence of the causes of intimate partner violence against women. This will indicate which are the strongest causes of intimate partner violence that should be targeted in preventive interventions as well as where further research is needed. It will also highlight which groups of women are most affected and thus for whom the delivery of interventions should be prioritized. Second, I will investigate how the communities within which women and their partners live may affect the experience of intimate partner violence, of which very little is known. Targeting high-risk communities may be an effective intervention strategy that balances reaching women in need with available resources. Using over 20 years of data from the United Kingdom's Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children, I will test whether greater exposure to community violence and disorder leads to the experience of intimate partner violence in young adulthood and whether this exposure exacerbates individual risks for intimate partner violence such as mental health problems. I will also look at whether the effects of communities vary based on whether a person is male or female or the victim or perpetrator of violence. These findings will inform interventions to prevent intimate partner violence and its negative health outcomes, a matter of critical importance both in Canada and abroad.
