column36: Defining Synthetic Lethal Genes in YAP/TAZ-Dependent Breast Cancers
column37: Breast cancer, the most common cancer in women worldwide, is the second leading cause of female cancer death in North America. Despite advances in therapy, breast cancer remains a significant cause of mortality, and improved treatments utilizing novel approaches are needed. One characteristic of breast cancer cells that distinguishes them from normal cells is that they are often tetraploid, a condition where cells harbor twice the normal number of chromosomes. Normally, tetraploid cells fail to proliferate. However, our lab recently demonstrated that inactivation of a cellular pathway termed the Hippo pathway restores proliferative ability to tetraploid cells. The Hippo pathway controls cell proliferation by regulating two proteins, YAP and TAZ, which can enter the nucleus of a cell and activate growth-promoting genes. When the Hippo pathway is active, it prevents these proteins from entering the nucleus and thus restrains cell division. Conversely, when the Hippo pathway is inactivated, YAP/TAZ accumulate in the nucleus to turn on pro-growth genes. Breast cancer cells frequently show abnormally high levels of YAP/TAZ in their nucleus. This suggests that a common, and perhaps requisite, feature of breast cancers is that they inactivate the Hippo pathway to drive growth. However, whether these cells are dependent on YAP/TAZ for their survival is unknown. In addition, the genes turned on by YAP/TAZ that are critical for tumour growth are poorly resolved. Our proposal aims to find new drug targets in YAP/TAZ-driven breast cancers. To this end, we will characterize YAP/TAZ dependency across a cohort of breast cancer cell lines and identify key genes that differentially drive the growth and survival of YAP/TAZ-dependent cell lines. These genes represent novel drug targets whose identification holds the potential to enable the selective killing of tetraploid breast cancer cells dependent on YAP/TAZ, while sparing the non-cancerous diploid cells around them.

column36: Identification of autoantigens using T cell traps
column37: Autoimmune disorders result from the targeted destruction of tissues by dysregulated immune cells. The specificity of this response is mediated by immune reactivity towards particular disease-promoting proteins, such as insulin in the case of type I diabetes. While targeted therapies have been developed to overcome issues of non-specificity associated with conventional treatments, their translation to the clinic has yet to gain traction. Part of the problem is that we do not know the identities of many of the disease-promoting proteins associated with autoimmune cells. Moreover, the scarcity of these cells in the blood and the inaccessibility of diseased tissues (where they are most prevalent) prevent their analysis. Thus, a strategy to enrich autoimmune cells would facilitate their study and the identification of disease-promoting proteins. Previously, we developed an implantable scaffold capable of "trapping" autoimmune cells; however, only a minor fraction of the trapped cells were autoimmune cells. Here, we aim to design an injectable material to improve trapping of autoimmune cells and identify their protein specificities. The material will be chemically or biologically modified to maximize enrichment of autoimmune cells and minimize inflammatory cell infiltration. We will evaluate the efficiency of autoimmune cell trapping using transgenic animal models and the specificity of the material system to trap autoimmune cells in the context of various autoimmune disease models. To identify the protein specificity of the trapped autoimmune cells, we will use single-cell sequencing and modified epitope prediction algorithms to predict, then validate potential disease-promoting proteins. This strategy will enable researchers to study autoimmune cell populations in various diseases and identify disease-promoting proteins. Knowledge of these proteins will facilitate the design and clinical translation of targeted medicines for treating autoimmune disease.

column36: A Cognitive Bias Modification Intervention for the Psychological and Sexual Functioning of Women with Childhood Sexual Abuse
column37: Up to 35% of North American women experience childhood sexual abuse (CSA; Putnam, 2003). Women with CSA often show difficulties in their sexual and mental health (e.g., inhibited sexual arousal, post-traumatic stress disorder; Noll et al., 2003). Many treatments that have been useful for women without CSA have been shown ineffective for treating women with CSA. One of the maintaining factors of the sexual concerns in these women, is an anxious-avoidance of sexuality. The current study looks to investigate a computerized-intervention, that was found to be effective in treating anxiety and addictions, for reducing the anxious-avoidance in these women and mitigating their sexual and psychological concerns. In study one, we examine the sexual avoidance biases of women with and without CSA using an approach-avoidance task (AAT) that assesses the automatic processing of information that occurs before our conscious processing. Individuals will be exposed to sexual images and, depending on the tilt of the image presented (e.g., 30 degrees left or right), will use a joystick to push the image away (i.e., avoidance behaviour, the image gets smaller on the screen to mimic its movement in space) or pull the image towards themselves (i.e., approach behaviour, the image gets larger until it fills the screen). Reaction times and accuracy of responding to the image tilt of the sexual vs. neutral images will demonstrate automatic biases in processing the sexual images as something to avoid (i.e., push away) or approach (i.e., pull toward). In study two, we will implement a two-week training program for women with and without CSA using the same AAT but manipulating the tilt of the sexual images to have more pull actions, thus training less avoidant responses to sexuality in these women. We predict that the reduction of these anxious-avoidance biases will increase the overall sexual and mental health of these women.

column36: Evaluation of Clinical Utility and Cost-effectiveness of Genome-Wide Sequencing in the Canadian Rare Genetic Disease Clinic
column37: Rare diseases affect as many as one in twelve Canadians. Many of these individuals experience a diagnostic odyssey; they are evaluated by multiple medical professionals, but lack an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan. Rare diseases are often caused by mutations in an individual's DNA. Currently, these patients are evaluated in the Medical Genetics clinic and between one and ~50 genes which may be responsible for their clinical symptoms are tested for mutations. However, this testing is expensive and is often unsuccessful as there are over 3,500 genes currently linked to disease. New technologies have been developed which can simultaneously test every gene in the genome in a cost-efficient manner. These technologies have been highly successful in research to diagnose rare disease patients, and are now being tested for use as clinical testing. This project will evaluate the success rate and cost effectiveness of these new genome sequencing technologies for the diagnosis of rare disease patients. For patients, an accurate genetic diagnosis informs patient care and facilitates the development and use of more targeted effective treatments. Within the healthcare system, accurate diagnoses bypass the waste of health care resources on unnecessary treatments and continued diagnostic testing. Overall, establishing the effectiveness of this new technology as a diagnostic tool for rare diseases will improve the care of these patients and make better use of the limited resources within our publically funded healthcare system.

column36: Development of pharmacokinetic models for factor VIII and factor IX for use in individualization of dosing
column37: Hemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency in a certain clotting factor resulting in spontaneous bleeds and eventual joint damage. Treatment typically consists of regular infusion of the missing factor to maintain a sufficient level of factor at all times. Dosing is typically based on the patient's weight but patient response is highly variable, meaning that under-dosing and over-dosing often occur. This suggests that an individualized approach to hemophilia treatment is optimal. The classical approach to individualization requires rigorous blood sampling and complex calculations, making it difficult to apply in a clinical setting. However, the population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) approach harnesses data from a large population of patients to identify sources of variability (e.g. age, weight, sex) and reduces the number of samples required to obtain an accurate prediction of the individual's response. The Web Accessible Population Pharmacokinetics Service - Hemophilia (WAPPS-Hemo) aims to establish a web-based service to provide dosing recommendations using PopPK models and individual data submitted by clinicians. Brand-specific PopPK models will be developed in the software NONMEM using richly sampled data from industry sponsors. Before being incorporated into the WAPPS-Hemo platform, the models will be extensively evaluated using typical strategies such as graphical analysis and data-splitting methods. The development and evaluation of models for use in individualized dosing has the potential for high impact with respect to the patient, who will benefit from safer and more effective treatment, and with respect to clinicians, who will benefit from integrated knowledge and guidance that is both reliable and easy to incorporate into routine practice.

column36: The Development of Caregiver-child Attunement: Child age and Context-related Patterns
column37: Learning how to self-regulate strong emotions later in life develops from early experiences with your caregiver in distressing situations. Early in life, infants learn how to calm down through coordinating their stress reactivity and regulation behaviours and physiological states with their caregiver. Continued exposure to co-regulation in stressful contexts shapes infants' capacity to regulate their negative affect. Currently, researchers and clinicians lack a basic understanding of how caregiver-infant physiological co-regulation develops over the second year of life. The second year is very important as infant-caregiver distress regulation patterns (i.e. attachment style) becomes reliably demonstrated at this time. The goal of my project is to better understand the development of caregiver-infant cardiological co-regulation (across age and different distress situations) and to determine the relationships between co-regulation and broad infant mental health indicators. The present study will follow caregiver-infant dyads at 12-, 18-, and 24-month vaccination appointments (high distress situation), with an additional lab-based appointment at 24-months. The laboratory visit will involve a mild distress situation (inappropriate puzzle) and a moderate distress situation (separation from caregiver task). The heart rate of the caregiver and infant will be simultaneously recorded at each immunization and lab visit 3-minutes prior and following the distress tasks. Additionally, infants will be tested on a gold standard infant development battery and parents will fill out questionnaires about their and their infant's mental health. The findings from this study are relevant to both researchers and health professionals. My program of research will provide novel and foundational knowledge about the development of physiological co-regulation between toddlers and parents and its role in predicting suboptimal mental health at the end of the second year of life.

column36: When rare meets common: burden and impact of rare genetic variants in primary psychiatric populations
column37: Genetic diseases are individually rare but collectively common. Many genetic conditions can mimic mental health disorders and the psychiatric symptoms can be difficult to treat with regular medications. Most people are not aware that many genetic conditions are treatable. Treating a genetic disease can cure the associated psychiatric symptoms or help regular medications work better. Discovery of rare genetic diseases in psychiatric patients would reveal specific treatment options, and give information about the chances of other family members being affected. We will use sophisticated genetic testing to determine how often rare genetic diseases occur and how best to diagnose them in psychiatric patients. We will test DNA samples from thousands of schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BPD) and major depressive disorder (MDD) patients to determine how often treatable genetic diseases occur so that we can develop a test to detect these diseases in psychiatric patients. We will also test these DNA samples for clinically well characterized syndromic copy number variants (CNVs) - changes in the amount of genetic material - and determine whether they are overrepresented in psychiatric patients. This will help us understand how important CNVs are in causing symptoms seen in SCZ, BPD and MDD. Our research will be the first to define the types and frequencies of rare genetic syndromes in SCZ, BPD and MDD populations. Discovering genetic diseases in psychiatric patients will shift how health care is delivered to these vulnerable patients by addressing underlying conditions rather than masking symptoms with medications. Treating genetic diseases that cause psychiatric symptoms will especially help patients who don't respond to regular medications. This will lead to significant cost savings to the health care system. Our research will help doctors diagnose rare genetic diseases in psychiatric patients, so that they can receive the best treatments to optimize overall well-being.

column36: Phenomic approaches for the functional characterization of drug targets
column37: Drug development is time-consuming and very expensive. One of the solutions to alleviate the problem is the repurposing of approved drugs for new disease indications. Successful examples of such drug repurposing, however, often emerge from coincidental discoveries and there is room for improvement. In this project, we propose to use a novel approach that uses large genetic datasets for the repurposing of drugs. More specifically, we will do this by studying the genes that encode the proteins that are targeted by cardiovascular drugs. Recent studies have shown that individuals with mutations in drug targets can have clinical manifestations that mimic the action of the medication. For example, statins are one of the most prescribed drug classes in Canada for the reduction of cholesterol. Individuals with mutations in the gene encoding the drug target of statins were shown to have lower blood cholesterol levels and lower coronary artery diseases, similar to statin users. Following on this concept, in our study we propose to search for clinical presentations in individuals that have mutations in drug targets of cardiovascular drugs. We will use data from 150,000 individuals to the UK Biobank and over 10,600 participants to the Montreal Heart Institute Biobank, which are observational cohorts that include detailed medical information along with large genomic datasets. We will also develop the informatics tools necessary for such studies and we will make them available to the research community. Replication and validation of our findings will be possible by using data from over 27,000 participants to clinical drug trials that include patients using the tested cardiovascular drugs. This approach leverages a large collection of clinical and genomic datasets to discover new clinical uses for existing cardiovascular drugs.

column36: The Hepatitis C Revolution: Evaluating the Impact of Direct Acting Antiviral Therapy in a HIV-Hepatitis C Co-Infected Population
column37: The Hepatitis C virus (HCV) causes serious liver damage, that can lead to premature death. This process is accelerated considerably among people co-infected with both HIV and HCV. To reduce the growing clinical and healthcare burden of advanced liver disease, this population needs to be treated and cured of Hepatitis C. Fortunately, cures for Hepatitis C now exist, however at an extraordinary cost, up to $120,000/treatment. Clinical trial results show these drugs are well tolerated and cure most people of HCV. However clinical trials do not always reflect what happens in the "real world". My doctoral thesis, will evaluate the "real world" health and economic impacts of treating HIV-Hepatitis C co-infected individuals with these new treatments. I will use a large cohort of participants, representing approximately a quarter of the total co-infected population in care in Canada. Details on demographic, risk, treatment and clinical data have been and will continue to be collected for the next 5 years. By 2017 I expect close to 400 people in this cohort will have received Hepatitis C treatment. Based on this data I will: (1) Describe the need for "real world" data; (2) Evaluate the different provincial policies regarding Hepatitis C therapy across Canada; and describe who initiates therapy by various risk profiles (People who inject drugs, people of Aboriginal decent, Women, and Men who has Sex with Men); (3) Estimate, short and long term health and economic impacts of treatment. When using observational data oppose to clinical trial data, being able to identify an unbiased result requires a comprehensive understanding of epidemiology. This is why I will explore different epidemiological methods to estimate the impact of these new drugs. Although cures are now available, due to the costs access to treatment is limited. I hope the results from my thesis will improve clinical care and avoid health inequalities in this vulnerable population.

column36: Comparative Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Medical and Surgical Interventions for Pituitary Tumors
column37: Health care costs continue to steadily increase in Canada. Current health policy helps to worsen the health care crisis by increasing both access and cost to an inefficient system and fail to address the basic problem: an inability to deliver better patient outcomes at a lower total cost. This has led to a growing demand to identify ways that increase the cost-effectiveness of health care delivery in Canada. Establishing appropriate funding models for health care requires a full understanding of the link between cost and health system outcomes. This project will investigate health care costs and benefits from a surgical point of view. To this end, I will be performing a comparative check for the cost-effectiveness of trans-sphenoidal surgical resection of pituitary adenomas by endocrinologic subtype versus medical therapy. The study will involve a detailed review of the literature, as well as a multi-national, multi-institutional breakdown of the predictors and outcomes of pituitary tumor surgical intervention. Finally, the research study will involve the development of computerized analytical models to evaluate value of care for patients with pituitary adenomas by treatment strategy.

column36: Modulation de la vigilance et de la cognition via la lumiere bleue chez les personnes agees avec ou sans remplacement du cristallin par une lentille intraoculaire
column37: Plusieurs etudes ont montre que l'exposition a la lumiere, particulierement a la lumiere bleue, peut augmenter la vigilance et la performance des jeunes a plusieurs types de taches cognitives. D'ailleurs, les reponses a la lumiere pourraient etre diminuees chez les personnes agees vu le jaunissement du cristallin. Ce jaunissement diminue considerablement la quantite de lumiere (surtout la lumiere bleue) atteignant la retine. Par contre, cet impact sur les effets de la lumiere chez les personnes agees n'a jamais ete evalue. Lors de la chirurgie des cataractes, le cristallin affecte est remplace par une lentille intraoculaire qui est aussi claire que celle d'un jeune adulte. Ainsi, l'objectif de cette etude est d'evaluer les effets de la lumiere sur la vigilance et la cognition des personnes agees avec ou sans lentille intraoculaire de remplacement. Nous posons l'hypothese que comparativement a une condition de lumiere blanche tamisee, qui correspond a une mesure de controle, la condition de lumiere bleue ameliorera la vigilance et la performance cognitive des personnes agees principalement chez celles ayant une lentille intraoculaire de remplacement. Nous etudierons 30 participants ages (65 a 80 ans; 15 avec lentille et 15 avec cristallin naturel) en bonne sante physique et cognitive. Les sujets seront exposes a deux conditions de lumiere (Bleue et Tamisee) lors de deux sejours en laboratoire, avec un intervalle de deux semaines entre les conditions. Les mesures de vigilance et de performance seront prises une heure avant le debut des expositions de lumiere jusqu'a une heure apres la fin de celles-ci. La presente etude fournira des renseignements cles sur la facon d'utiliser la lumiere comme intervention imple, non invasive et peu couteuse pour ameliorer la cognition et la vigilance chez les personnes agees. L'etude fournira egalement des informations cruciales sur les consequences du remplacement de la lentille concernant les effets de la lumiere.

column36: Effets d'un protocole de stimulation non-invasive du cerveau sur la douleur rapportee et le systeme moteur des patients orthopediques ayant subi un traumatisme cranio-cerebral leger concomitant.
column37: Le traumatisme cranio-cerebral leger (TCCL) est frequent chez les personnes qui ont subi une fracture isolee, bien qu'il passe souvent inapercu. De recentes etudes ont demontre que le TCCL nuit au retablissement orthopedique, notamment en augmentant la douleur percue (et la duree de celle-ci), important facteur de risque de chronicisation, en plus de tripler le temps requis afin d'effectuer un retour au travail. Des protocoles de stimulation non-invasive du cerveau ont recemment propose une alternative prometteuse dans le traitement contre la douleur. En effet, la stimulation par Theta-Burst (TBS) proposee permet de reduire la douleur percue chez les personnes atteintes de blessures musculo-squelettiques en stimulant la region du cerveau qui commande les actions des membres blesses. Pertinemment, cette region du cerveau est egalement atteinte suite a un TCCL et est responsable de certains symptomes observes suite a cette blessure, dont les symptomes moteurs (perte d'amplitude dans les articulations, diminution de la force et de la vitesse d'execution motrice). Ainsi, ce projet de recherche propose un protocole d'intervention, incluant 10 sessions reparties sur deux semaines, visant a reduire tant la douleur percue que les symptomes moteurs communs au TCCL et au trauma orthopedique (TO) pour ainsi optimiser le retablissement tant orthopedique que cerebral. Ce projet de recherche propose donc une avenue therapeutique prometteuse, d'importance clinique capitale, considerant a la fois la forte prevalence du TCCL et des TO, mais aussi leur fardeau personnel et societal incalculable chez cette population clinique trop souvent jeune, blessee durant les annees les plus productives de leur vie.

column36: Preclinical imaging platform for assessing a novel anti-amyloid therapy
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that is characterized by multiple pathologies of abnormal aggregates of misfolded proteins: amyloid beta (Ab) and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT). In 2014, the number of people living with dementia worldwide was estimated to be 44 million and this number is expected to grow to 135 million by 2050. However, there is no effective treatment or preventive measures yet and such catastrophic projection has promoted the academics and pharmaceutical companies for a collaborative effort in discovery of an effective drug. Insofar, a handful of clinical studies that have completed targeted Ab aggregates as the Ab abnormality is believed to initiate the AD and its progression at early stages of the disease. Unfortunately, the therapeutic drugs have been effective in decreasing the Ab aggregates but unsuccessful to show improvement on the cognitive domains. This is largely due to the lack of selectivity and heterogeneity in the pathology and cognition of the patients. Also, they did not meticulously identify where the clearance of Ab was localized in the brain. At various stages of AD, Ab abnormality spreads from local brain regions to the global level. And there are AD vulnerable regions that show higher level of pathology and play a crucial role in the cognitive function. Here, my project will examine the efficacy of a novel drug, Kal-ABP, developed by National Research Council selectively targets Ab aggregates. My project will quantify the Ab load and neuroinflammation using positron emission tomography (PET) and structural and functional changes using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before and after the therapeutic treatment. This is a unique opportunity and first preclinical study to profile the efficacy of the drug under multi-modal translational neuroimaging platform. This will allow better understanding of the target engagement and regional association to improve cognition.

column36: Targeted delivery of tropomyosin receptor kinase A agonists to the brain using magnetic resonance image-guided focused ultrasound
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) affects over half a million Canadians. AD is characterized by a gradual decline in cognition, which arises in response to several pathological changes in the brain including degeneration and dysfunction of nerve cells. At present, there is a critical need for AD therapies that enhance neuronal survival and function. Neurotrophins are proteins in the brain that induce neuronal survival and function, and can potentially halt cell loss observed in AD. In particular, nerve growth factor (NGF) has significant potential for the treatment of AD. The main challenges in clinical trials for NGF have been delivery to the brain in sufficient doses to impact cell function and controlling its delivery to specific brain areas to minimize off-target effects. Novel therapeutic agents with more favorable pharmacological properties than native NGF have been developed to address these limitations. These molecules are classified as tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TrkA) agonists which stimulate neuronal survival and activity by interacting with TrkA present on neurons. Moreover, a promising strategy for the non-invasive delivery of therapeutics to specific brain areas is magnetic resonance imaging-guided focused ultrasound (MRIgFUS) combined with microbubbles given intravenously. The interaction of ultrasound with circulating microbubbles allows for drugs injected intravenously to enter the brain at MRIgFUS-targeted areas. In this project, we will use animal models to establish the efficacy of TrkA agonists delivered to the brain using MRIgFUS. We expect that this treatment will improve neuronal health and cognition, while minimizing side effects. Overall, this research will provide key milestones in animal models prior to clinical translation for AD patients.

column36: "Breathe into Pain" - The Role of Parasympathetic Activation in the Development of Chronic Pain 3 Months After Thoracic Surgery
column37: STUDY SIGNIFICANCE Significant numbers of patients undergoing major surgeries develop chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) every year. CPSP can be so severe, stressful, and intractable that it can require extensive medical care long after the initial surgery. Since stress intensifies pain, many nonpharmacological pain interventions involve eliciting one's relaxation response to "turn down" pain signals. However, pre-existing difficulties in eliciting one's relaxation response to cope with pain-related stress may be a risk factor for developing CPSP. Previous research has shown that breath-focused mindfulness meditation is effective for reducing pain symptoms and eliciting relaxation. Using an innovative, hospital-integrated assessment protocol, my proposed dissertation research will test the relaxation response as a risk factor for developing CPSP. STUDY METHODS The relaxation response is primarily activated by the vagus nerve, a major parasympathetic nerve involved in decreasing heart rate and pain signals. Patients undergoing thoracic surgery at the Toronto General Hospital will be assessed for vagus nerve activity using non-invasive heart rate variability measures during rest, pain-induction, and mindful breathing. The assessments will take place ~1 week before and 3 months after surgery on a total of 60 patients; n = 30 with CPSP, and n = 30 without CPSP. We will test whether vagus nerve activity predicts the onset of CPSP 3 months after surgery, and also examine differences in vagus nerve activity between patients with and without CPSP. IMPACT ON PATIENTS & HEALTHCARE Thousands of Canadians undergo surgery yearly to treat major illnesses and ~10% will develop moderate-to-severe chronic postsurgical pain. Results from this study will promote future research on how relaxation response data can be used to predict CPSP, and inform preventive treatment strategies for CPSP and other pain conditions to be implemented into perioperative and outpatient care settings.

column36: Biofeedback-enhanced movement-based video game therapy for children with cerebral palsy
column37: Active video games like Wii-Fit and Xbox's Kinect Sport are engaging ways to practice skills from home. Similarly, new technology like Fit-Bit and the Myo Armband give information about how people move. These technologies provide 'biofeedback' that, when combined with active video games, can be a motivating, fun and effective home-based therapy. This is especially promising for the 1 in 400 kids born with Cerebral Palsy (CP). These children often have difficulty using their hands and spend many hours in rehabilitation programs. This research aims to add biofeedback into active video games and test how it helps kids with CP make better use of their hands. We will achieve this goal in three steps. First, we will review how biofeedback has been used before to help people with CP. This will help us know the best way to use it in the active video game. Second, in partnership with Paris-Saclay University (France), we will add biofeedback into an active video game we have made. We will use the Myo Armband to give information about arm movements and muscle activity. During this development phase, we will get feedback from families to refine the game and find the most helpful ways of cueing movement strategies. In the last step, we will test how biofeedback in active video games helps to improve hand and arm movements. Ten children with CP from Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital (Toronto, Canada) and Fondation Ellen Poidatz (Saint-Fargeau-Ponthierry, France) will participate. They will play active video games with biofeedback repeatedly over several weeks, and we will measure how well they can use their hands and arms before, during and after they play. With biofeedback-enhanced active video games, we can offset the burden of intense rehabilitation by providing home-based, fun and effective ways to help kids with CP use their hands more effectively.

column36: The Effects of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation on the Brains of Tobacco Smokers
column37: In Alzheimer's disease (AD), several factors might accelerate the formation of clumps of tau proteins in the brain. Some studies have provided evidence that anesthesia and/or surgery might be such factors and increase the risk of AD. One of the problems is that, for obvious reasons, it is impossible to dissociate the effects of anesthesia from those of surgery in human. Another problem is the confounding effects of other perioperative factors. In this context, dissecting the effects of anesthesia and surgery on AD pathology, while controlling for other factors, is important since tau pathology shows a strong relationship to dementia in AD, and to memory loss in normal aging and mild cognitive impairment. The overall goal of this project is therefore to clarify the impact of different anesthetics, of their method of administration, of surgical procedures, and of the management of perioperative factors on tau pathology in transgenic mice models.

column36: Evaluation of the human burden of disease from third generation cephalosporin resistant Escherichia coli and Salmonella infections and the contribution from antimicrobial use in food producing animals
column37: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections that can be serious and in some cases fatal. They have saved countless lives and have extended life expectancy since their discovery in the early 20th century. Unfortunately, their widespread use also contributes to the development and spread of antibiotic resistance in illness-causing bacteria, with the result that antibiotic treatment becomes ineffective. The problem is a serious 21st century global public health crisis and steps need to be taken urgently to preserve the effectiveness of these precious medicines. Many types of antibiotics are used both in humans and animals. While it is known that antibiotic use in food animals can lead to antibiotic resistance, the extent to which this use contributes to resistant bacterial infections in humans is unknown. This research will address this important need by determining the impact of antibiotic resistance in enteric (gut-related) bacteria on human health in Canada and the contribution from antibiotic use in animals, focusing on 3rd generation cephalosporin resistance in Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Salmonella. There are three components to the research: 1) determination of the human health impact of antibiotic resistance in selected E. coli and Salmonella human infections; 2) identification of the proportion of these antibiotic resistant infections involving animal sources; and 3) mathematical modelling of antibiotic resistance selection by antibiotic use in animals, spread of resistant E. coli and Salmonella through contaminated food and environment to humans, and resultant risk of human illness from antibiotic resistant infection with these bacteria. The results from this research are essential for improvement of veterinary antibiotic use policy in Canada and around the globe. All Canadians will benefit from improved and appropriate antibiotic use that will preserve current antibiotic effectiveness and reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistance.

column36: Trajectories of executive dysfunction in youth with pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis: A mixed methods approach to assessing cognitive outcomes
column37: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic disease of the central nervous system that has a prevalence rate in Canada that is among the highest worldwide. MS can also occur in children and adolescents, with up to 10% of patients diagnosed prior to age 18. Cognitive impairment is common for these youth, with particular impact on executive functions. These are a range of skills which play a role in mental control and self-regulation, and allow for engagement in goal-directed behaviours. Deficits in executive function may result in poorer academic function, difficulties in social relationships, reduction in autonomy, greater risk-taking, and challenges in planning to achieve goals. Although these youth fare worse than their peers on executive function tasks, it is not known whether MS leads to slower development, a lack of development, or an actual loss of these functions over time. We also don't know whether children who are younger at their first MS attack are at greater risk of having these cognitive difficulties as the disease progresses. We aim to investigate how executive functions develop differently in youth with MS, and whether one's age at disease onset influences how these functions mature. As performance on typical paper-and-pencil tasks of executive function have not fully mapped on to skills in daily life, we will also explore the experiences of these youth as they encounter real-life challenges that require executive function. This will be done through questionnaires and interviews with the patient and their family. This research will help us to understand cognitive outcomes for patients with pediatric-onset MS. We also hope to gain insight into the real-life consequences of executive dysfunction, to help health care practitioners and families develop strategies for accommodation and rehabilitation around these deficits.

column36: Relating Genomic Aberrations in Prostate Cancer to Tumour Hypoxia and Response to Treatment
column37: The major goal of my research is to personalize cancer medicine by applying computational models to big data. Each year, ~1.4 million men around the word are diagnosed with prostate cancer and ~290,000 die from the disease. Localized cases are classified as low-risk, intermediate-risk or high-risk using clinical measurements to help guide treatment decisions. However, these groupings are not precise: for example 30-50% of intermediate-risk patients suffer relapse of their disease after radiotherapy or surgery. One reason for differing response to treatment is the cellular and molecular heterogeneity of tumours (i.e. not all tumours are the same). Tumour cells also exist within an environment that has gradients of oxygen levels. Patients with hypoxic tumours (i.e. tumours with low oxygen) can rapidly fail treatment. Focusing on 548 prostate cancer samples, I have shown that important genes (e.x. PTEN and RNLS) have an increased frequency of having a DNA copy number change under hypoxia. We also see more point mutations in important genes (e.x. TP53) in samples that were hypoxic. My goal is to further link tumour genomics, microenvironment and response to treatment. I will relate hypoxia to mutational trinucleotide signatures and epigenetic changes. I will also examine fusion genes and changes in splicing under hypoxia. Next, I will spend four months at the Wedge lab (Oxford University, UK) to look at how tumour evolution changes under hypoxia. Finally, I will use machine-learning to link these data and create a tool that can be used in the clinic to guide more precise treatment of prostate cancer. With the computational facilities at the Ontario Institute for Cancer Research, I am well equipped to do this work. Better understanding this relationship is critical to improving the lives of the ~25,000 Canadian men diagnosed with prostate cancer each year.

column37: Les risques du stress pendant la grossesse sont connus des chercheurs, mais celles qui en beneficieraient le plus, les femmes enceintes, n'en savent rien ! C'est un probleme puisque les meres et les futures meres voudraient obtenir le plus de connaissances possible pour faire face aux changements qu'engendre la grossesse dans leur quotidien. Il existe en fait un delai d'environ 17 ans entre le moment des decouvertes scientifiques et leur utilisation dans la pratique clinique. Determiner le meilleur moyen d'informer les femmes enceintes n'est pas une tache facile. En informant les femmes enceintes des risques du stress pendant la grossesse sur le developpement de leur enfant, il se peut que nous ayons sur elle l'effet que l'on cherche a prevenir, c'est-a-dire les stresser encore davantage. Une strategie de communication particuliere doit donc etre elaboree afin que de l'information pertinente soit transmise aux femmes enceintes de facon efficace et adequate. Les professionnels de la sante (obstetriciens et sages-femmes) sont des experts en lesquels les femmes enceintes ont confiance et ont le role d'informer ces dernieres pendant leur grossesse. Ce projet cherche donc a ameliorer la strategie de communication des professionnels de la sante pour que les femmes enceintes recoivent l'information relative aux risques du stress pendant la grossesse. Pour ce faire, une synthese des resultats de la recherche scientifique sera remise aux professionnels de la sante. Par la suite, ils prendront part a un groupe de dialogue pour echanger ensemble leur point de vue et repondre a la question qui nous interesse : Comment peut-on ameliorer la strategie de communication des professionnels de la sante aupres des femmes enceintes au sujet des risques du stress pendant la grossesse sur le developpement de l'enfant ?

column36: Early structural brain connectivity changes in stroke patients: Potential early biomarkers of language recovery and impairment
column37: Every year 62,000 Canadians have a stroke. The loss of language abilities is highly prevalent among stroke survivors and 100,000 Canadians are living with chronic language impairments. The sudden loss of the ability to communicate has a heavy impact on the life quality of patients and their families. While some stroke survivors show good recovery of their language abilities a few days after the incident, others show poorer recovery and will continue to live with language impairments months after the stroke. Previous research seems to suggest that dynamic changes take place in the brain a few days after the stroke. White matter fibers, which are connections between grey matter areas in the brain, can be damaged by the stroke. However, they sometimes spontaneously regenerate. This phenomenon could be behind good early language recovery found in some patients. Moreover, atrophy (i.e. loss of brain cells) can be found in remote regions connected via white matter to the brain area affected by the stroke. However, these early brain changes after a stroke and their contribution to language impairment and recovery are largely unknown. In this project we will examine stroke patients with language impairments within the first 2 weeks after a stroke, in order to assess the patterns of progression of their language impairments and their relation to brain changes using neuroimaging techniques. We will establish the relationship between white matter regeneration and the degree of early language recovery. Then, we will determine whether patients with poorer recovery show atrophy in brain regions connected by white matter fibers to the location of the stroke-induced brain damage. A better understanding of the changes in the brain's connections in the early phases after a stroke and their contribution to the progression and recovery of language impairments can eventually lead to improved diagnosis, prognosis, and rehabilitation of this devastating consequence of stroke.

column36: Role de la sphingosine-1-phosphate dans la biologie des tissus lymphoides tertiaires pulmonaires et les effets pathobiologiques associes
column37: L'air n'est pas un environnement sterile; certains agents biologiques infectieux ou inoffensifs y circulent librement. Malheureusement, l'exposition repetee a ces agents peut causer des problemes au niveau pulmonaire tels que l'asthme, la rhinite allergique ou les pneumopathies d'hypersensibilite. Les maladies d'hypersensibilites surviennent lorsque le systeme immunitaire considere l'inhalation de particules, meme si elles sont totalement inoffensives, comme une attaque et induit une reponse immunitaire. Cette reponse immunitaire se caracterise par le recrutement de globules blancs, ainsi que par la formation de structures lymphoides s'apparentant a des ganglions lymphatiques directement au niveau du poumon afin de defendre l'organisme. Cette defense peut entrainer une modification de la structure du poumon et une difficulte a respirer chez le patient. Il n'existe actuellement aucun traitement efficace contre les maladies d'hypersensibilite excepte le retrait complet de l'individu du milieu qui le rend malade. Eviter l'exposition a l'agent biologique peut parfois etre difficile lorsque la source de la maladie n'est pas identifiee ou lorsque le retrait du milieu d'exposition nuirait aux activites quotidiennes de l'individu. Dans cette optique, il est primordial de comprendre comment la reponse immunitaire se met en place afin de trouver de nouvelles cibles therapeutiques. Mon projet s'efforce donc de comprendre comment certains lipides presents de facon physiologique dans le corps humain peuvent venir reguler cette reponse des globules blancs. Les resultats preliminaires montrent que ces lipides interferent avec la formation de structures lymphoides, ce qui conduit a une diminution des symptomes d'hypersensibilite. Ces resultats supportent un potentiel therapeutique pour les modulateurs de ces lipides qui sont d'ailleurs en phase clinique pour le traitement de certaines maladies inflammatoires dont la sclerose en plaque et la colite ulcereuse.

column36: Haptic Simulation in Cerebral Angiography: Establishing New Clinical Competency Targets
column37: Brain aneurysms can occur in populations of all ages and often go unnoticed until they require medical intervention. With an occurrence of 3.2%, approximately 1.1 million Canadians live with unruptured aneurysms. Brain aneurysms found in almost 2% of all MRI scans, coupled with 22 000 patients with burst aneurysms, lead to a large population seeking medical attention. The best method for their treatment is angiography which uses catheters to access the aneurysm from inside the blood vessels and treat them. These procedures allow the patient to be treated and released the same day, but require extensive training on the clinician's side. As trainees access the blood vessels in the patient through their leg, they need to be able to navigate in 3-D space while twisting a catheter at the level of the thigh, use snapshot x-raying to update their position within the body, and be able to fill an aneurysm in the brain with electrolytic coil. This complicated array of skills is only learned through an operating room-based fellowship program which results in unnecessary patient risks, high healthcare costs and inefficient skill development opportunities for novice fellows. Furthermore, the standard of skill the learner needs to reach is not standardized at all. The goal of my research is to show that these skills can be learned outside of the operating room using modern simulation and, subsequently, be standardized for performance and patient outcome across the board. I have already been able to show that using diagnostic simulation training lowers total operating time and radiation exposure by at least factor of 4. In addition to this, these improvements are a direct result of the trainee's lower number of mistakes. Our upcoming research will provide exciting data on how to better train future interventionalists conducting these procedures and establish concrete expectations for their performance.

column36: Accepting imperfection: Exploring the effectiveness of a dialectical behavior therapy skills training intervention for university students high in perfectionism and suicide ideation
column37: Throughout the world, suicide is a major problem. Moreover, amongst Canadians aged 15-24 suicide is the second leading cause of death. Research has shown that maladaptive perfectionists, individuals concerned with living up to high expectations and with intense self-criticism, are at increased risk of committing suicide and are especially resistant to treatment. Importantly, within the highly competitive university environment, maladaptive perfectionism is notably high. Yet, there are no well researched treatments for maladaptive perfectionists that are at-risk of committing suicide. Research has also shown that both maladaptive perfectionism and suicide are associated with having difficulties managing emotions. Therefore, a treatment that targets difficulties with managing emotions appears to be the ideal method for reducing instances of suicide amongst maladaptive perfectionists. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) is a treatment specifically focused on managing emotions, and it was specially designed for treatment of suicidal individuals. Adapted from DBT, DBT Skills Training (DBT-S) is a short-term and cost effective treatment that effectively treats university students. However, DBT-S has not yet been used to treat maladaptive perfectionists. This study will therefore explore the effectiveness of DBT-S for treating maladaptive perfectionism and suicide-risk amongst university students. Participants will complete measures of maladaptive perfectionism, suicide-risk and difficulties managing emotions prior to treatment, immediately after treatment and 4 weeks after treatment. Statistical tests will explore whether DBT-S results in significant reductions in maladaptive perfectionism and suicide-risk and whether these changes are due to improved ability to manage emotions. This project will be the first to examine a treatment that is easily accessible and cost-effective for this high-need population, as well as inform future research and mental health programming.

column36: Effets des ortheses plantaires sur la biomecanique du membre inferieur chez des patients ayant une instabilite chronique de la cheville
column37: Les entorses de la cheville sont parmi les pathologies musculosquelettiques les plus frequentes. Or, une grande partie de ces entorses causent une instabilite de la cheville. L'instabilite de la cheville peut etre decrite comme etant une cheville instable, qui est plus a risque de subir a nouvelle entorse. L'instabilite de la cheville cause notamment des deficits ligamentaires et musculaires. Bien que quelques auteurs aient etudie les effets biomecaniques d'une instabilite de la cheville sur le controle de la posture statique, peu ont evalue ses effets lors d'une tache de marche. C'est pourquoi, dans ce projet de these, les effets biomecaniques d'une instabilite de la cheville seront mesures a la marche. Par ailleurs, il a ete demontre que les entorses et les instabilites de la cheville representent un grand fardeau financier au niveau des soins de sante et ont un impact negatif sur la qualite de vie des personnes atteintes. Il devient alors primordial d'optimiser le traitement de ces pathologies pour diminuer la recurrence. En pratique clinique, les ortheses plantaires sont frequemment utilisee pour traiter l'instabilite de la cheville avec generalement des bons resultats. Par contre, dans les etudes scientifiques, peu d'auteurs ont evalue les effets des ortheses plantaires sur cette pathologie a la marche. Il y a donc un besoin important de faire de la recherche pour optimiser l'efficacite du traitement orthesique. Dans ce projet de these, nous effectuerons une revue systematique de litterature dans le but de faire une synthese des etudes disponibles sur le sujet. Par la suite, nous ferons deux projets de recherche qui consisteront a determiner les differences biomecaniques de participants souffrant ou non d'instabilite de la cheville lors de la marche avec et sans ortheses plantaires.

column36: Comparing Self-reported and Rater-assessed Clinician Fidelity to Cognitive Processing Therapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
column37: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a chronic and disabling condition associated with severe negative effects on individuals' emotional, occupational, and social functioning. Approximately 75% of Canadians will experience a traumatic event in their lifetime, and about 9% will go on to develop PTSD. Despite the existence of several supported treatments for PTSD, research indicates that only a small minority of clinicians use these treatments in practice, leaving many patients untreated or inadequately treated. Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) is recommended as a first-line intervention for PTSD and studies indicate that a therapist's competence in delivering treatment is associated with patient outcomes. However, assessing therapist competence in treatment is costly and resource intensive. Another method suggested is to have clinicians rate their own competence, but there is little research examining if this method is reliable. This study will examine how clinicians' ability to rate their own competence compares to expert-rated competence in CPT. The results of this study will indicate if clinicians can accurately assess their own competence in delivering CPT, and determine if they can identify the need to seek additional consultation and resources to support the treatment, which ultimately leads to better care for the many Canadians suffering from PTSD.

column36: Interplay between peripheral signals, behaviour and the central clock
column37: Circadian rhythms have evolved to anticipate and adapt animals to the constraints of the earth's 24-hour light cycle. Notably, they can provide anticipatory benefits, such as promoting water intake prior to sleep to mitigate the impact of reduced water intake during sleep. Most circadian rhythms are orchestrated by the body's mater circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus; however, little is known about how pathophysiological perturbations might alter the activity of clock neurons to beneficially adapt rhythms to new physiological conditions. The vascular organ of the lamina terminalis (OVLT) is a specialized brain area that is capable of detecting dehydration and the presence of molecules present in the blood during systemic infection. Owing to these characteristics, the OVLT is in a prime position to inform the clock of changes in physiological status, and drive changes in clock neuron activity that can adapt central rhythms to the new condition. My preliminary data shows that clock neurons are inhibited when OVLT neurons are excited by hypertonicity (as in dehydration). Since the electrical activity of clock neurons is low during the awake-period and high during the sleep-period, I hypothesize that dehydration will inhibit the activity of clock neurons via OVLT neurons that release the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and prolong the awake-period in mice to promote water-seeking behaviour. Conversely, I hypothesize that bacterial endotoxin (an infection molecule) will excite clock neurons via OVLT neurons that release the excitatory transmitter glutamate to promote sickness behaviour (e.g. sleep). Gaining a specific understanding of the mechanisms regulating circadian rhythms could provide important targets for therapeutic intervention in diurnal disorders or for adaptation to shift-work or jet-lag.

column36: Quality vs. quantity: Identification of genetic determinants of osteoporotic fracture that are independent of bone quantity.
column37: Approximately half of women and a third of men in Canada will suffer an osteoporotic fracture. The financial burden of these fragility fractures currently exceeds $2.3 billion per year in Canada, for just hip fractures, and will increase with the rapid ageing of our society. Osteoporosis is a highly heritable condition that is controlled by the genetic factors that we inherit from our parents. In order to predict a person's risk of fracture, doctors measure bone mineral density (BMD), making BMD an important criterion for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. The drugs currently used to treat osteoporosis act mainly by increasing BMD. This is clinically helpful, but we know that most people who have fragility fractures do not have a low enough BMD to be diagnosed with osteoporosis. This is because susceptibility to fracture is influenced by both bone quantity (measured by BMD) and bone quality. What we therefore need in the clinic are new drugs that can prevent fracture by improving bone quality. Through large-scale international collaboration we have identified dozens of novel regions of the genome that influence both BMD and fracture risk. Several drug therapies for osteoporosis that focus on improving BMD target proteins coded by these fracture-associated regions. Therefore, the new regions we have identified will likely contain novel drug targets for the treatment of osteoporosis. In this study, we will address the clinically relevant question of identifying drug targets for osteoporotic fracture that affect bone quality and are independent of BMD. We will use human genetics, a highly reliable tool for identifying novel drug targets, and then we will use a suite of statistical and biologic tools to validate them. By identifying and validating genetic characteristics that directly contribute to fragility fracture, we will help prevent the burgeoning epidemic of osteoporotic fractures and provide needed drug targets for an entirely new class of osteoporosis medications.

column36: Enhancing the Effects of Written Exposure for Generalized Anxiety Disorder via Imagery Training
column37: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a highly prevalent, chronic, and difficult-to-treat condition characterized by excessive worry and anxiety. Research has shown that people with GAD avoid thinking about feared situations in a clear way in an attempt to keep anxiety and other uncomfortable emotions at bay. However, this avoidance is actually counterproductive because it intensifies worry and anxiety. Past research has shown that an intervention called written exposure (WE) improves worry. In WE, people counteract their avoidance by fully imagining and processing clear, vivid thoughts of their worst fear coming true. This is accomplished by writing repeatedly and concretely about their worst fear. This study will examine a way to optimize the WE intervention; specifically, whether the addition of an imagery-training (IT) phase can further enhance WE's beneficial effects. Research in other clinical populations has shown that those who have better imagery abilities show larger symptom improvements within exposure-based treatments. For individuals with GAD, imagery ability may be even more important because these individuals report difficulties generating vivid images of their worst fears. Individuals with GAD will be assigned to one of two conditions: (1) WE with imagery training or (2) WE without imagery training. Both conditions will engage in 20-minute WE sessions on 3 consecutive days, but participants in the IT condition will also receive a 15-minute imagery training each day prior to engaging in WE. During IT, individuals will be trained to engage in imagery through different exercises. We hypothesize that the addition of imagery training to WE will lead to greater improvements in GAD symptoms, worry and worry-related difficulties than WE without imagery training. WE has considerable promise as a brief, inexpensive treatment for Canadians with GAD and the proposed experiment examines a novel enhancement of it.

column36: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Chromatin: the Circadian and Aging Connection
column37: This project is dedicated to understanding of how genes are regulated in the cell's nucleus. We will investigate not only spatial parameters of such regulation but also temporal ones: how molecules surrounding DNA change during the 24 hour period (circadian cycle) as well as over months and years in the aging cells. This interdisciplinary research project combines three loosely associated fields - chromatin architecture, circadian biology, and aging. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study exploring aging- related changes in chromatin architecture from the circadian perspective. Our intuitive and testable hypothesis may help to prove that ageing is, at least to some extent, deterministic. We will generate the first circadian map of interaction of regulatory elements, which will help understanding the 4D regulation of gene expression and other functional aspects of the nucleome. Our effort may show that spatial aspects of nuclear organization are inseparable from the temporal dimension, and that 'spacetime' is a critically important concept not only in physics but also in life sciences. This basic molecular biology study may have innovative translational implications. Establishing a relationship between aging and circadian rhythmicity may allow us to leverage circadian pathways to delay or reverse aging and aging- related diseases, such as cancer, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Building the relational ethics of health for adults with disabilities using the lynchpin of capacity hearings
column37: Despite decades of health care advances and human rights enlightenments, health promotion and maintenance needs of adults with disabilities (AwD) continue to be inadequately understood and addressed. This project is about promoting the health of AwD by informing their legal capacity - which plays out as part of their relationships - to direct their own lives. AwD are often determined to have diminished legal capacity and correspondingly, have substitute decision makers appointed to make health, financial, or legal decisions on their behalf. However, we believe the legal capacity of AdevD has been assessed too simplistically. In this project, we will treat legal capacity not as a property inherent to an individual, but as a process that occurs in relationship with others and thus, must be understood using relational approaches. We will study processes of determining legal capacity for AdevD by gathering and examining evidence of the ways in which capacity hearing decision-makers do, and can, respect what we are calling a "relational ethic" of health promotion and maintenance through the very processes by which they determine the capacity of AdevD. We will conduct conversation analyses of capacity hearing processes, as well as content analyses of capacity hearing experiences and decisions, in two Canadian provinces, Alberta and Ontario, to learn about the ways in which capacity hearing tribunal members practice a relational ethic in their interactions with tribunal actors, namely AwD, support-providing family members and friends of AwD, and fellow tribunal members, on topics related to health and other decision making. Our purpose is to inform understandings of capacity determination processes with, and for, AwD, and use these understandings to create scholarly and practice-relevant resources that promote relational ethics in the determination of the health promotion and maintenance "capacity" of AwD to direct their own lives.

column36: Selling Health: How do pharmacists consider their ethical conduct in relation to front-of-store stales?
column37: In nine provinces, tobacco sales are banned from pharmacies because pharmacists' roles as health care providers is seen as incompatible with selling tobacco. Recently, removal of sugary drinks in pharmacies has made news for the same reason. Regulatory agencies and national pharmacy associations have called for pharmacists to expand their roles in population health. This is important since pharmacists are the most geographically accessible health care providers, are highly trusted in Canada, and products sold in pharmacies can imply approval by the pharmacist. The proposed 3-phase research study will examine community pharmacists' perceptions of factors that drive front-of-store (non-drug) sales in light of the ethical and legal frameworks within which they operate. This is especially relevant now, with decreasing revenues from drugs and increasing revenues from front-of-store sales. In Phase 1, we will undertake comprehensive ethical and legal analysis to examine the responsibilities of pharmacists as health care providers and as retailers, with a focus on front-of-store products. In Phase 2, we will conduct up to 40 pan-Canadian interviews with pharmacists to explore factors driving front-of-store sales and how pharmacists see themselves as health promoters, and to explore whether any tension exists between their roles. In Phase 3, working with a multi-sector advisory group, we will conduct a policy analysis to synthesize findings from Phases 1 and 2 and provide policy options for facilitating healthy retail environments in pharmacies. In addition to papers and conference presentations, we will create fact sheets based on our findings that we will share with three key audiences: community pharmacists, provincial regulatory authorities and the pharmacy industry. This research will help to determine ways community pharmacies can support health promotion efforts in Canada.

column36: Elaborating The Epistemic Conditions that Ethically Justify Randomized Clinical Trials
column37: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are essential to acquiring new medical knowledge. However, an RCT is not required to answer every clinical question, nor is every RCT ethical. Therefore, there must be certain conditions that, when satisfied, render RCTs scientifically and ethically justifiable. This study explores the interplay between ethical (value-based) and epistemic (knowledge based) issues in medical research. The central questions of this research project are: 1.Under what epistemic conditions are RCTs ethically justified? 2.Do current regulatory processes adequately assess whether RCTs have fulfilled these conditions? We will seek to answer these questions by performing two phases of data gathering: 1. A Systematic Qualitative Review of the philosophical, bioethical and research literature on the epistemic conditions that justify RCTs 2.A series of Semi-Structured Interviews with decision-makers at national regulators (HealthCanada, FDA, etc.) and research ethics boards (REBs) about the processes by which they perform the epistemic evaluation of RCTs The main hypothesis of this research program is that the epistemic conditions that justify RCTs are difficult to establish without specialized knowledge in the area of the research question. Moreover, we hypothesize that such expertise is generally lacking from the process by which RCTs receive regulatory approval. This work has implications for the way RCTs are evaluated by national regulators and by local REBs. It represents one piece of an ongoing research program intended to explore and rationalize ethical-epistemic issues surrounding RCTs.

column36: Networks of Centres of Excellence (NCE) - "Global Network in Strategic Health Sector Supply Chain Innovation" (SCI-Net)
column37: Growing demands for patient care are exceeding system capacity to deliver services, and costly medical error is now the third leading cause of death in North America behind heart disease and cancer (Makary & Micheal, 2016). A key determinant of sustainability and safety in other industries has been the implementation of supply chain best practices that track and trace products and processes from manufacturer to end users to create efficiency and ensure safety. Health systems in Canada, and indeed around much of the industrialized world, have not implemented supply chain best practices to enable either the tracking of products (e.g., medications, devices, implants), care processes, or patient outcomes. Health systems have also not achieved supply chain efficiencies and cost savings through automated inventory management to ensure patients have access to the safest products available at the lowest cost. In addition, there is no health system in the world able to track and trace products and care processes from manufacturer to patient health outcomes to reduce medical error, and create safer health systems for populations. This lack of strategic supply chain management in today's healthcare systems makes it virtually impossible for Canadian health leaders and their global counterparts to increase efficiency and manage cost in the face of growing demands, while at the same time reducing the high rates of medical error for patients in healthcare settings. The Global Network in Strategic Health Sector Supply Chain Innovation ("SCI Net") will mobilize knowledge of strategic supply chain best practices to inform Canadian, American, Australian and European (UK, Netherlands) health systems, and position Canada as a global leader in health sector supply chain innovation that leverages supply chain practices to reduce medical error and achieve safer health outcomes for patients.

column36: Voice Adaptive Training for older adults with Aphasia
column37: Older adults are the fastest growing segment of our society and several common chronic conditions present a risk to older adults' health and wellness. Stroke is a chronic condition, which is the leading cause of disability throughout North America and Europe. Nearly one third of individuals who have a stroke will present with aphasia, a communication impairment that affects the ability to speak, understand, read and write. These persistent language impairments can have a negative impact on all aspects of daily life, and people who live with aphasia often report that this negative impact is worse than is reported even in cancer or Alzheimer's disease. The aim of the project is to empower older people with aphasia to improve their communication abilities. We will do this by developing an app for communication and everyday life support called VoiceAdapt. We will apply innovative speech-sensitive technology to the app in order to develop a system that detects and adapts to the language difficulties of the person with aphasia. The system will have built-in features that personalize and adapt to an individual's communication difficulties in specific locations in order to provide individualized exercises to facilitate therapy and recovery. First, the input and feedback of users, including people with aphasia, speech-language therapists and others, will be incorporated into the design and development of the app. Second, the app will be tested in a trial where one group of people with aphasia will receive the VoiceAdapt app for six weeks and another won't. We expect that the group that practices the individualized exercises in VoiceAdapt will have improved language, communication and well-being compared to the other group. It is hoped that the unique features of this technology will help to improve the communication abilities of people with aphasia.

column37: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) Calls to Action highlight the importance of Canadian post-secondary institutions in increasing the number of Indigenous health professionals and scholars. PIKE-Net's strategies are and will continue to be informed by the recommendations of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, inspired by the Manitoba's universities, colleges and public school boards' commitment to action on reconciliation, and dedicated to ensuring that First Nations, Metis and Inuit mentees have access to all opportunities accessible in partners institutions, in a culturally safe learning environment. We have an established history of providing a world-class mentorship program (2001-current). During this time, we supported 227 student and early-career professionals in Indigenous health research. We propose an approach informed by Willie Ermine's concept of ethical space, by focusing our relational mentorship program in three strategic areas: 1) Culturally-grounded mentorship; 2) Multiple domains of success across all 4 research pillars; and 3) Systemic interventions. We propose: a mentor support program, mentor matching, an Annual Mobile/Virtual Summer Institute, international learning opportunities, monthly webinars, community outreach, and advocacy within the universities to break down systemic barriers. It is through these activities that we will improve recruitment and retention of Indigenous students; increase and improve the quality of training opportunities for those students; increase networking opportunities (including international networks); increase the number of Indigenous students who are awarded outside funding (i.e. provincial or national funding); improve the quality and quantity of knowledge products; and continue to identify and address individual/systemic barriers for Indigenous students.

column36: Alberta Indigenous Mentorship in Health Innovation Network (AIM-HI Network)

column36: Neuroprotective agents for cerebral malaria
column37: Malaria is the third leading cause of death in children globally. In Canada, we see about 400 cases per year, especially among new immigrants and travellers returning from the tropics. It mostly affects young children in sub-Saharan Africa, who are at risk of severe disease, death, and mental disability following infection. Cerebral malaria is a deadly complication which occurs when the brain is involved. Despite the world's best antimalarial drugs, the mortality rate is still about 20%, meaning that one in five children with cerebral malaria will die of their infection. Furthermore, 25% (one in four) children who survive cerebral malaria will be left with lasting brain problems. New treatment strategies are needed to reduce the number of deaths as well as the long term effects of cerebral malaria on the brain. We think that some newly licensed drugs for cancer and brain disorders can be used for an entirely different purpose: to protect the brain in cerebral malaria. This surprising re-purposing of new medications makes sense because these drugs target molecules which govern the leakiness of vessels and brain swelling. By targeting these molecules, we think that we can improve outcomes in cerebral malaria. We want to test these drugs in 2 ways: a model of the blood brain barrier using cells in a "petri dish," and an animal model of disease. We will test these drugs to see if they can protect the brain by stabilizing the "blood-brain barrier" which separates the brain cells from the bloodstream. If we find promising molecules, this will be significant because it will suggest new treatments that could be tried in clinical trials of children with cerebral malaria.

column36: Early movers: The role of physical activity and sedentary behaviour in the healthy growth and development of infants
column37: The first five years of life are a dramatic period of growth and development. These early years lay the foundation for life-long health. Regular physical activity and minimal sedentary behaviour, such as screen time, strengthens healthy growth and development. I was one of the leaders in developing new Canadian guidelines to support healthy active lifestyles during these first five years. These guidelines will be released in 2017 and include recommendations on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. In developing the guidelines, we found gaps in the information available. For example, we found few long-term studies on young children, especially infants. Few studies looked at how physical activity and sedentary behaviour affect a child's development of motor skills, thinking skills, and social skills. My research study will fill these gaps in information. I will examine the long-term associations of physical activity (tummy time) and sedentary behaviour (screen time, reading, carriers, car seats, high chairs, strollers, swings) in infants with their gross motor skills and their achievement of gross motor milestones in the first 18 months of life. In partnership with Alberta Health Services, 250 parents of infants in Edmonton, Alberta will fill out a questionnaire when their infant is 2, 4, and 6 months old. They will tell us about their infant's physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and gross motor skills. They will also record the gross motor milestones that their infant reaches over the first 18 months of life. A sub-sample of 115 parents will also complete a more detailed questionnaire at 2, 4, and 6 months and their infant's gross motor development will be directly measured at 6 months. Our findings will fill gaps in knowledge and help update Canada's guidelines with the best information. Findings will also be useful in programs that target physical activity and sedentary behaviour in our youngest Canadians, to support their healthy growth and development.

column36: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome: determining post-discharge outcomes, the effect of early diagnosis, and identifying inflammatory signatures to better understand disease mechanism
column37: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) affects children of all ages with a severe lung injury needing respiratory support in the intensive care unit (ICU). It has a mortality rate of 18-27%. Because children are still developing, long-term consequences of PARDS are highly significant. However, only a few small outdated studies have looked at the long-term outcomes of PARDS survivors. While most of these studies looked at lung function, none focused on issues that may be important to patients and their families such as breathing problems, quality of life, mental health symptoms, and health care resource use. Given that PARDS is a heterogeneous syndrome, clinical and biological data may be used to identify distinct subgroups of children within PARDS, who may have different treatment responses and outcomes. Not only this would be useful in understanding disease mechanism, but importantly, it may also identify subgroups of children with worse outcomes and ultimately allow for the design of targeted treatments. Finally, delays are common in the diagnosis of PARDS and compliance with current management guidelines is poor. Novel techniques such as decision support systems may help physicians in the management of these children. In this study, we aim to better characterize the outcomes of PARDS survivors, to examine whether subgroups of children with PARDS can be identified, and to determine whether an earlier diagnosis of PARDS using a computerized decision support system will improve the care of these children. We will also build a database containing information on children with PARDS linked to biological samples for future research. The results of this study will provide insight into the long-term outcomes of PARDS survivors and the mechanisms underlying this condition, and may change the way PARDS is currently diagnosed. Finally, the creation of a PARDS database will be a valuable tool for future interdisciplinary studies in this field.
