column36: Transcriptional control of cancer metabolism
column37: Cancer cells need specific nutrients and to transform these nutrients using specific biochemical pathways to generate enough energy and building blocks to sustain their growth and rapid division. My research program is centered on understanding how cancer cells adapt their metabolism to favor their proliferation and resistance to therapeutic intervention. More precisely, our team is investigating changes in the expression of specialized genes that modify the metabolic program of cancer cells. These changes in gene expression often result from the aberrant activity of proteins known as transcription factors. The normal function of transcription factors is to respond to cellular needs by modulating gene expression so that the cells have the necessary tools to perform their normal activities during the development and lifespan of the organism. However, cancer cells highjack transcription factors to promote tumour growth and their metastasis to distant organs. The abnormal action of transcription factors in cancer is best-exemplified by a class of proteins known as nuclear receptors, which include the estrogen and androgen receptors that promote the growth of breast and prostate cancer, respectively. In recent years, my research program has been focused on studying the roles played by nuclear receptors and other transcription factors in regulating energy metabolism, notably how cancer cells differentially process nutrients such as amino acids, sugars and lipids to fuel their growth. Our goals are to find differences between the action of transcription factors in normal and cancer cells and to exploit these differences to induce metabolic vulnerabilities in tumours, thus making them more responsive to anti-cancer drugs. The ultimate outcome of this program should be improvement in the treatment and quality of life of cancer patients.

column36: Investigating the pathophysiology of atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome caused by DGKE deficiency
column37: Blood vessels are like roads that can reach any cell of our body. We call the cells that line blood vessels "endothelial cells". Blood flows fast in normal blood vessels, but it is slow when there is damage. It forms a blood clot. This is similar to a "good traffic jam": it helps repair injured blood vessels. The body must control the machines that help with repair to avoid "bad traffic jams". Healthy blood vessels don't need blood clots. In the lab, we study the function of endothelial cells in the kidneys. We work on a disease called "atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome". For simplicity, we call it "aHUS". Patients with aHUS get kidney failure. Why? Blood clots form in the blood vessels of the kidneys. These clots prevent normal blood flow in kidneys. Blood flow is important to deliver food and oxygen to the kidneys. We found that mutations in the gene DGKE can cause aHUS. Each cell in the body contains DNA, a code made of genes. Genes make proteins-the building blocks of cells. Mutations are changes in the DNA that cause abnormal function of a protein. For our patients, the mutations prevent DGKE from working well. DGKE is an enzyme that works on fats. DGKE stands for "diacylglycerol kinase epsilon". Diacylglycerol is also called DAG. Enzymes are like machines that do specific tasks in cells. For example, a kinase adds a phosphorus group to its target. DGKE is a kinase that targets one type of fat named DAG. Cells use DAG as a signal to turn on specific functions. It is like a light switch. When DGKE modifies DAG, it turns off the signal. When DGKE can't work, it is as if the light switch is left on too long. When that happens, patients cannot prevent blood clotting in their kidneys. These patients develop kidney failure, and we have no treatment to offer.

column36: Novel Type 1 Cannabinoid Receptor Allosteric Modulators
column37: The type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) is present at high levels throughout the brain and other parts of the body. CB1R is activated by the body's own cannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol), synthetic cannabinoids, and cannabinoids from marijuana (e.g. THC and cannabidiol). CB1R is considered a potential target for the regulation of appetite and the treatment of addiction, pain, spasticity in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, epilepsy, post-traumatic stress disorder, and anxiety. Despite its potential as a therapeutic target, we are still learning how the many naturally occurring and synthetic cannabinoids that exist affect CB1R and how CB1R in turn produces distinct effects in the body. To this end, new compounds known as allosteric modulators are being developed that can increase or decrease CB1R's response to the body's cannabinoids, but lack intrinsic activity and will not, therefore, produce the intoxicating effects associated with other cannabinoids. The goals of my research are: (1) to develop allosteric modulators of CB1R that alter the body's response to its own cannabinoids, (2) test those modulators in animal models, and (3) to apply the knowledge gained from goals 1 and 2 to specific disease states where cannabinoids might be therapeutically beneficial. This research project will provide insight into the mechanisms of CB1R activity, important considerations for the use of cannabinoids as a medicine, and lead to the development of new drug compounds.

column36: Aligning industry incentives with AMR control goals: Exploring the feasibility of an antibiotic susceptibility bonus for drugs to treat Gram-negative infection
column37: High prices create incentives for industry to develop new antibiotics, but also incentivize firms to promote their products to maximize sales volume. Similarly, the Market Entry Rewards proposed by the O'Neill Commission and others will, if introduced, help to get new drugs to market but do not directly address the problem of antibiotic overuse leading to emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) (O'Neill 2016). The multidisciplinary study proposed here explores the feasibility of a finance-based intervention intended to directly re-align pharmaceutical industry interests with the minimization of AMR and with the overall prolongation of antibiotic efficacy through time. The proposed intervention allows pharmaceutical companies to qualify for staged bonuses if pathogen susceptibility to their antibiotic remains above a given threshold, despite a certain minimum volume of usage. This Antibiotic Susceptibility Bonus may help maximize efforts towards good prescribing practice and towards minimizing the risk of acquisition, development and transmission of antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. The lure of a bonus greater than expected revenues from unit sales could help align efforts behind antibiotic stewardship and infection prevention efforts in hospitals, communities, agriculture, and the environment, bolstering public and private AMR initiatives across One Health sectors. The project proposed here will evaluate the feasibility of the Antibiotic Susceptibility Bonus - from the intricacies of representative susceptibility sampling, to calculating optimal bonus magnitudes based on market considerations, true product "usefulness", and access-related factors, and ultimately how each of these could be constructively applied to 2-3 case studies of late stage (Phase III) candidate antibiotics and an existing product with particular antimicrobial features - each targeting multi-resistant Gram-negative bacteria.

column36: Development of a microRNAs-based panel for early prediction of gestational diabetes mellitus
column37: Gestational diabetes is a condition diagnosed between the 24th and 28th weeks of pregnancy. It originates from a problem in glucose transport into cells. This condition affects up to 26% of pregnancies and is known to increase the risk of complications. Recent data shows an increase of gestational diabetes cases over the last 20 years. This condition is now considered a real public health concern. Unfortunately, the tools we use only enable us to diagnose and treat elevated blood glucose once it is present and thus only after it has started to affect the health of the mother and her baby. Accordingly, the World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends that gestational diabetes should be detected and treated earlier. In that context, microRNAs can play a big role and unlock many possibilities. MicroRNAs are small genetic sequences that regulate numerous aspects of our biology and that can travel from one organ to another in the human body. They could thus reveal early losses of biologic equilibrium such as those that occur before gestational diabetes develops. Recent studies have revealed their enormous potential as markers to monitor the development or progression of diseases including diabetes. Our pilot data strongly suggests that this also applies to gestational diabetes and supports new promising possibilities to develop innovative prediction panels based on miRNAs detectable in the first trimester of pregnancy. Based on our exciting preliminary findings, we thus propose to develop a miRNAs-based panel for prediction of gestational diabetes during pregnancy. Our project takes root from the most modern techniques available to seek microRNAs in maternal blood and aims at finding the best candidates for the prediction of gestational diabetes. These findings will later enable us to understand and intervene before the appearance of elevated blood glucose during pregnancy and its harmful health effects on the mother and her child.

column36: Antimicrobial Resistance Manure Intervention Strategies
column37: Livestock animals consume the majority of antibiotics globally. These antibiotics and their active degradation products together with antibiotic resistant bacteria are partially excreted into the environment via manure. Manure is one of the major sources of bacteria resistant to antibiotics in the environment, and, as exemplified by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), it may significantly contribute to their spread in food, water and air, with subsequent exposure of humans. To date, no study has investigated the reduction of antimicrobial resistance (antibiotics, bacteria and genes) by different manure treatments, such as anaerobic digestion and aerobic composting. In this study, we will measure the effectiveness of different manure treatment procedures on antimicrobial resistance reduction throughout the manure processing chain and assess relevant parameters in this reduction. We will focus on major bacteria, including extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacteriaceae, vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE), MRSA, and the corresponding antibiotic resistance genes and residues in large-scale (centralised) treatment as well as small-scale (farm) systems, in different national contexts and varying resistance prevalence. Culture-dependent and culture-independent methods and metagenomic studies will be used to evaluate the abundance of selected antibiotic-resistant bacteria and their concomitant resistance genes (and mobility) at different steps of the manure treatment process. Risk assessment studies will be conducted and outcomes will be communicated to improve risk awareness, to guide intervention prioritization and to improve understanding of exposure risks. Knowledge on the effects of manure processing on antibiotic resistance transmission may contribute to a reduction of the impact of the livestock industry on antibiotic resistance.

column36: Intervention of antimicrobial resistance transfer into the food chain
column37: Soil and water have been identified as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and the food chain as the most likely mode of AMR transfer into human and animal pathogens. Manure is reused as soil fertiliser in which food plants grow and is a source of AMR. We hypothesise that pre-treatment of manure will reduce and remove the abundance and diversity of AMR genes and pathogenic bacteria of high priority from entering the food chain. Alleviating AMR elements from entering the food chain will reduce the transfer and uptake of mobile AMR genes and pathogens by human and animal bacteria. This project will focus on chicken and pig manure as both have been demonstrated to carry a wide variety and abundance of mobile AMR genes of clinical relevance. Our intervention is to pre-treat the manure in order to reduce or remove the burden of AMR in the manure prior to reuse as fertiliser. The microbiomes of chicken and pig manure differ, but the AMR genes and mobile elements overlap. Our study will investigate if the same pre- treatments will reduce or remove AMR prior to application and if these reductions or removal are maintained on the food plants or grass, and in the soil. Reducing or removing the threat of AMR at the start of the food chain will reduce the potential for selection and transfer of such AMR genes and pathogens further along the food chain. By stopping or reducing the continuous transfer of AMR genes and mobile elements along the food chain we will reduce the burden of AMR in pathogenic bacteria.

column36: OPEN Stewardship: An Online Platform for Expanding Antibiotic Stewardship
column37: Antibiotic resistance is a mounting public health threat calling for action on global, national and local levels. Antibiotic use has been a major driver of increasing rates of antibiotic resistance. This has given rise to the practice of antibiotic stewardship, which seeks to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use across different care settings. Antibiotic stewardship has been increasingly applied in hospital settings, but adoption has been slow in many ambulatory care settings including primary care of humans. Uptake of antibiotic stewardship in veterinary care has been similarly limited. Audit and feedback systems of antibiotic use coupled with patterns of antibiotic use and best practice guidelines have proven useful in outpatient settings, but scale-up is limited by heterogeneous systems of care and limited resources. We aim to develop an open web-based system that allows for advanced stewardship interventions in the form of feedback and benchmarking as well as sharing of best practice guidelines and antibiotic resistance patterns. The proposed model can be rapidly expanded across health systems, countries, and sectors (animal vs. human), with minimal resource expenditures. We will build upon an existing platform for monitoring antibiotic resistance, and pilot these interventions with international providers in both medicine and veterinary medicine, in the form of an interrupted time series analysis. Outcomes will focus on platform development, interface usability, and prescription patterns during the study.

column36: A foundation grant for bridging the mutation and interactome landscapes of the eukaryotic cell
column37: Every two individuals are genetically different due to mutations inherited from their parents or new mutations that have accumulated during their lifetime. Most of these mutations have no noticeable consequences. Yet, a small number have strong effects and lead to inherited diseases and somatic ones, such as cancers. Some healthy individuals can tolerate the complete loss of genes, while others develop diseases in response to these mutations. The difference between benign and harmful mutations comes from the organization of the cellular machinery and the interaction between this organization and the thousands of mutations that make everyone unique. For instance, the human genome contains hundreds of genes with multiple copies and having these backup copies could be a strong determinant of the resilience of the cell to otherwise harmful mutations. Here we propose an innovative research program that will elucidate these mechanisms of resilience and sensitivity to mutations of the eukaryotic cell. Our approach will involve cutting edge technologies in genome sequencing, high-throughput screening, genome editing and bioinformatics to determine what are the effects of disease and non-disease mutations directly on the inner organization of the cell. Our discoveries will shed light on the mechanisms of resilience and fragility to mutations in addition to providing mechanistic details on how human disease mutations alter the inner cell machinery. This will lead to more powerful approaches for the prediction of disease susceptibility and outcome from genome sequences, as well as to the development of knowledge-guided drug development.

column36: Physical Activity and Cancer Outcomes: Generating Practice-Changing Evidence
column37: My research program focuses on physical activity (PA) in cancer patients. Specifically, I am interested in how PA may help cancer patients prepare for treatments, cope with treatments, recover after treatments, and improve long-term survival. The long term goal of my research program is to reduce the negative impact of cancer by ensuring that all cancer patients have access to high quality exercise programs. Research has shown that PA improves fitness and quality of life in cancer survivors but clinical practice has not really changed. I have argued that the chances of PA being offered in clinical oncology practice would be greatly increased if PA was shown to improve survival. The overall aim of my proposed research program is to find out if PA can actually improve survival in cancer patients. I am proposing to study this question with 5 projects including: (a) the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Study, which is the first study examining the associations between objective PA, fitness, and breast cancer survival in 1,500 newly diagnosed breast cancer patients, (b) the Colon Health and Life-Long Exercise Change (CHALLENGE) Trial, which is the first experimental study examining the effects of a 3 year exercise program on survival in 962 colon cancer patients, (c) the Intense Exercise for Survival (INTERVAL) Trial, which is the first experimental study examining the effects of a 2 year exercise program on survival in 866 patients with advanced prostate cancer, and (d) 2 smaller studies in rectal cancer patients receiving combined chemoradiation therapy and prostate cancer patients receiving no treatments. PA is a low cost, low risk intervention that improves fitness and quality of life in cancer survivors but it has not been put into practice to help cancer patients. If PA can be shown to improve cancer survival, it would likely be offered to all cancer patients in Canada and around the world as part of their standard care.

column36: Replication stress and pulmonary hypertension: Role for checkpoint kinase 1
column37: Patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. Like cancer cells, PAH cells are characterized by exaggerated capacity to multiplicate and resistance to death resulting in a progressive narrowing or obstruction of the vessels. Indeed, if the blood vessels tighten up, making the space for the passage of blood narrower, it takes greater pressure to get the same amount of blood through to its destination. The heart has to work harder to pump blood through those arteries. The heart progressively fails causing shortness of breath and poor exercise capacity, which rapidly culminate in death. In spite of recent progress in our understanding of the mechanisms involved in this disease, no substantial modification of the rapid progression and fatal course of this disease has been achieved, leaving lung transplantation as the only treatment in end-stage PAH. Therefore, the identification of new therapeutic targets is a pressing need. Although exposed to stressful conditions that jeopardize their survival, PAH cells continue to multiplicate indicating that these cells have developed adaptive protective response allowing them to survive. Nevertheless, the factors implicated in this pathological protective response remains largely unknown. In the present proposal, we hypothesize that a factor called CHK1 known to confer resistance to harmful stress conditions is overexpressed in PAH cells leading to the development of PAH. To test the validity of our hypothesis, we will 1) determine whether CHK1 is increased in PAH cells and contributes to PAH cells' anomalies; 2) decorticate the mechanisms by which CHK1 acts; and 3) assess whether inhibition of CHK1 improve PAH in animal models.

column36: Short term benefits but long term harm? Assessing the consequences of antenatal corticosteroid administration for child neurodevelopment
column37: Antenatal corticosteroids are medications given to pregnant women who are at risk for preterm labour to help their babies' lungs develop faster. The medication is known to lower the chances of newborn death or serious breathing complications at birth. However, there are growing concerns that this effective medication may also harm children's longer-term brain development, and doctors are becoming reluctant to use the medication without a better understanding of its long-term safety. Our study will establish if antenatal corticosteroids have harmful consequences for child brain development, such as lower kindergarten assessment scores, cerebral palsy, or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. We will link the medical records of over 12,000 preterm births in British Columbia, Canada, 2000-2013, to standardized provincial kindergarten test results, doctors' visits, and medication prescriptions. We will compare the health outcomes of infants born immediately before and immediately after the gestational age that antenatal corticosteroids are recommended (up to 34 weeks of pregnancy, but not after). These babies, born as little as hours apart but with a very different chance of receiving corticosteroids, will help us to isolate the effects of the medication on child health from other potential causes of poor brain development. The results from this research will help to ensure that women and their doctors are able to make fully informed decisions on use of this effective medication to balance both short and longer-term child health.

column36: Genetic-epigenetic interactions in lactase non-persistence
column37: One of the most consistent findings in biomedical research is that overwhelming majority of human diseases have inherited risk. Surprisingly, such genetically predisposed individuals do not display any pathology soon after birth, and it takes decades before the first appearance clinical symptoms. For example, the most common age-of-onset for schizophrenia is between 18-25 yrs, 15-30 yrs for bipolar, and 20-29 yrs for Crohn's diseases. We asked how these individuals with genetic risk factors can live 'symptom-free' for many years. To understand the basic principles of delayed age-of-onset, we studied a normal developmental trait of milk lactase non-persistence. Every infant can digest milk at birth and during breastfeeding, however, this ability is lost by adulthood in individuals who carry DNA-variants for milk intolerance. We found that chemical additions (epigenetic factors) on the key gene for milk digestion (lactase) were involved. As lactose digesters and non-digesters aged, the number of epigenetic factors "landing" on the lactase gene were different and this was controlled by DNA variation. Thus, we hypothesized that the age-of-onset of milk intolerance will be earlier with a greater number of accumulating epigenetic factors which depends on DNA variation. However, our findings are limited to two DNA variants. There are several ethnicity-specific DNA variations that may "attract" different numbers of epigenetic factors with age, which may explain the differences in the age-of-onset of milk intolerance across ethnicities. In this project, we will use mice to investigate how different types of DNA interact with epigenetic factors, and how their interactions can explain different latency of inability to digest milk. Our effort to uncover the mechanisms of gradual transition from milk tolerance to intolerance will open very promising avenues in research of a wide variety of diseases, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and inflammatory bowel disease.

column36: An epigenetic link between the gut microbiome and the immune response in asthma
column37: Asthma has become the most common childhood disease in developed countries, with major social and economic consequences. The causes of asthma are complex and poorly understood. We and others have recently shown an association between the gut microbiome and asthma. Subsequently, in mouse experiments, we found that butyrate, a fermentation product of the gut microbiome, dampens TH2 skewing of the immune system. Mice lacking exposure to butyrate early in life, due to gut microbiome dysbiosis, have a pro-inflammatory immune phenotype with heightened TH2 response in a model of asthma. In a preliminary experiment, we successfully transferred the phenotypes of both heightened and dampened TH2 skewing via bone marrow (BM) transplants to irradiated recipient mice. Epigenetic analysis strongly suggests an epigenetic mechanism is involved in these immune phenotypes. The main objective of the proposed project is to conclusively determine if and how the epigenome functions in regulation of the immune system in response to exposure or lack of exposure to butyrate. In transfer experiments, we will determine whether hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC), or other cell types, can confer the immune phenotypes. We will conduct comprehensive epigenetic analyses of HSPC, or other cells that confer the immune phenotypes, in transfer recipients. Bioinformatic analyses of epigenetic profiles will predict immune function. We will more comprehensively characterize the immune phenotypes of the recipient mice, focusing on predicted functions. The results will be validated by exposing mouse and human HSPC to low concentrations of butyrate and subsequently determining their epigenetic profiles and the phenotypes the cells confer to recipient mice. This project will provide understanding of a novel epigenetic process linking the microbiome and the immune system, which will have potential practical applications in the prevention and treatment of asthma.

column36: Harnessing Neuron-Astrocyte Communication for Promoting Brain Health
column37: A common feature in nearly all brain disorders and diseases is a breakdown in brain homeostasis. Key to brain homeostasis are highly specialized cells called astrocytes. Astrocytes play fundamental roles in brain function including controlling extracellular ion and neurotransmitter levels, brain energetics, and cerebrovasculature. Astrocytes perform diverse functions through their complex molecular, functional, structural properties. However, the mechanisms that create and sustain differences among astrocytes that allow them to fulfill unique physiological roles in the brain remain poorly understood. We discovered a completely new mechanism involving neurons for making different types of astrocytes in the brain. Communication between neurons and astrocytes enables astrocytes to produce key molecules including neurotransmitter transporters and receptors, adhesion molecules, potassium channels, and water channels. Thus, neurons in the mature brain control astrocytes to ensure that astrocytes acquire and maintain specialized properties that are precisely tuned to associated brain circuits. In this grant, we will determine how different astrocytes are created and maintained in the brain to support neuronal health and circuit function and identify how the properties of astrocytes can be harnessed to mitigate brain disorders and diseases.

column36: Translating DNA methylation-based signatures into molecular diagnostics for human epigenomic disorders
column37: Our proposal focuses on disorders that are caused by changes (mutations) in epigenes. Epigenes are genes that control the expression of other genes, through epigenetic marks; by inserting or removing these marks, genes can be turned on or turned off. To date, there are about 60 genetic disorders caused by mutations in specific epigenes, with more being identified every year. We studied 4 such disorders and showed that each disorder is associated with a specific pattern of epigenetic marks. We call each unique pattern of marks an epigenetic 'signature' and have shown that these signatures have the potential to be used as diagnostic tools. Typically, to confirm the diagnosis of a genetic disorder, one relies upon the ability to detect the specific gene mutation through sequencing the genetic code (DNA). However, sequencing has many challenges, most notably, the common finding of DNA sequence changes of unclear significance. We found that our epigenetic signatures have the power to determine which DNA sequence changes cause disease and which ones do not, thereby providing a definitive answer for changes of unclear significance. As a result, they could also be used instead of DNA sequencing to diagnose genetic conditions. This grant outlines a plan to translate epigenetic signatures into diagnostic tests for complex disorders caused by epigenes. We will test our currently identified epigenetic signatures on a platform that can be utilized by diagnostic laboratories around the world. We also plan to identify new epigenetic signatures to increase the number of disorders that could be tested using this platform. We anticipate that translation of these signatures into diagnostic tests will revolutionize testing for genetic disorders. The diagnostic platform could also be used in future to test for epigenetic changes caused by environmental exposures or drug treatments.

column36: Integrated Nanotechnology and Biomedical Sciences Laboratory
column37: Many researchers are developing drugs for the treatment of cancer. These drugs are administered in to the body and they kill cancer cells as well as healthy cells because the drug can go all over the body. This leads to excruciating side effects. Nanotechnology involves the use and design of structures, particles, or materials that have at least one dimensions smaller than 100 nm. Many researchers and companies are developing strategies to package drugs into a nanotechnology that can be further engineered to target and release the drug at the cancer cells in the body. The successful achievement of this would lead to increased therapeutic outcome and reduce side effects. The Chan group's research showed that 7 out of 1000 administered nanotechnology can target the solid tumour, 3 out of 100,000 can reach the cancer cells, and only 2 out of 100 cancer cells will be targeted by the nanotechnology. Thus, the delivery efficiency to each of the cancer components is low because the body is a hostile environment with biological traps such as the liver that removes the nanotechnology and prevents them from targeting cancer cells. With the funding from the CIHR Foundation grant, the Chan lab is aiming to solve the problem of delivery for nanotechnology. This will be achieved by studying how the nanotechnology interacts with each of the biological traps. These studies will allow us to develop a blueprint to build a nanotechnology that can escape them and identify strategies to increase the delivery efficiency to greater than 10% in the solid tumour. We will finally correlate the delivery efficiency with therapeutic outcome and side effects. Beyond seven-years, we will examine the optimized strategy derived from this study in human patients. The outcome of this research will create a pipeline of nanotechnology for treating patients with cancer.

column36: Epi-Radiomic Signatures of Prostate Cancer Progression in Men on Active Surveillance
column37: Over 25,000 Canadian men are diagnosed with prostate cancer each year, most with tumours that have not spread outside of the prostate gland. Many of these will never threaten a man's life and can be safely monitored (known as 'Active Surveillance') without requiring surgery or radiation therapy. While this reduces the occurrence of severe side-effects such as incontinence and erectile dysfunction, which are associated with these treatments, one-fifth of men on Active Surveillance eventually need treatment for cancer that has progressed over time. Unfortunately, there are no effective tools to accurately identify which men have a cancer that will progress. If it were possible to identify cancers that will progress, doctors could confidently recommend Active Surveillance to men with a very low risk of progression, leading to fewer unnecessary treatments and side effects and reducing anxiety for patients concerned about whether their disease will become life threatening. Men with a more aggressive disease would also be helped by this tool by ensuring that they are treated earlier and without delay. We will study 500 men whose cancers either did or did not progress on Active Surveillance. First, we examine cancer biopsies from these men to determine if a process called DNA methylation, which is often turned on inappropriately in life-threatening prostate cancer, is altered in tumours that ultimately progressed and required surgery. Second, we will study the blood of these men to see if these processes can be detected non-invasively. Finally, we will quantify the benefits for both individual patients and the healthcare system as a whole of adopting these biomarkers in routine clinical practice. Through this work, we will develop a tool that will allow men and their doctors to make more informed, accurate decisions about whether to elect for definitive treatment or whether a man's cancer can be safely monitored by Active Surveillance.

column36: Measuring what Matters: Integrating Patient-Reported Outcome Measures into Clinical Practice
column37: The success of pediatric solid organ transplantation can no longer be defined on the basis of objective clinical outcomes alone. Subjective evaluation of the burden of disease or/and treatment from the patient's perspective has become increasingly important. Patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) have the ability to engage patients meaningfully, give them a voice in their healthcare, and capture their varied experience and attitudes. The overarching objective of this research is to establish how to integrate validated PROMs systematically and effectively into clinical practice to improve the care and outcomes of pediatric transplant patients and families. While there is emerging evidence to guide effective integration of PROMs into patient care, many operational questions must be answered. To address a number of necessary methodological and practical decisions, our study design includes a three phased approach including: (1) a systematic review to identify PROMs utilized within the field of pediatric solid organ transplantation; (2) interviews with patients, caregivers and healthcare providers to elicit their perspectives surrounding the implementation of PROMs; and (3) a consensus meeting to examine practice and systems-based facilitators and barriers to implementing PROMs. This research will enable us to address the key operational issues so that we can successfully integrate PROMs into clinical practice and evaluate their impact on outcomes and overall well-being of pediatric transplant patients and families.

column36: Prognostic value of urinary renal and vascular biomarkers in hypertensive pregnant women
column37: Preeclampsia is a life-threatening condition of pregnancy for both mother and baby. For the mother, symptoms include high blood pressure. Higher amounts of protein are also found in the urine of women with preeclampsia. This is known as proteinuria. Preeclampsia can damage the mother's kidneys making them leak more protein than usual into her urine. It can also lead to other organ damage. Complications for babies can also be severe, including preterm birth and very low birth-weight. The accurate measurement of proteinuria is therefore crucial to the healthcare of women evaluated for preeclampsia. Important medical decisions such as hospitalization, drug prescription, and time of delivery all take into consideration proteinuria laboratory results. It is recognized that methods currently used to measure proteinuria during pregnancy need to be improved. One way is to measure albumin, one of the many proteins contained in urine. This is called albuminuria. Albuminuria has been shown to be preferable to proteinuria in many clinical settings outside of pregnancy. Here, we will show that is also preferable for pregnant women. Because special kidney cells called podocytes were recently found in the urine of women with preeclampsia, we will also assess the potential of podocyturia and compare it to the other two methods. We think that podocyturia used in combination with albuminuria may be a simple and effective way to know whether preeclampsia and its complications will occur. Finally, a protein linked to placenta and vessel health in pregnancy called Placental Growth Factor can also be easily measured in the urine and we plan to study this protein as well. Our goal is very straightforward: to improve urinary tests in hypertensive pregnant women by providing simple and accurate laboratory methods. This is crucial to prevent complications for mothers and their babies. Our project will also ensure Canadian leadership in this field.

column36: Immune regulation of placental blood flow and fetal health.
column37: Preeclampsia (sudden-onset high blood pressure in pregnant moms) and intra-uterine growth restriction (IUGR; poor growth of baby in the womb) are leading causes of sickness and death of pregnant moms and babies in Canada. My lab's goal is to determine underlying causes of preeclampsia and IUGR in order to improve management and therapeutic strategies. The major cause of these diseases is defective development of the placenta. The placenta is the organ that embeds itself into the mother's uterus during early pregnancy, and nourishes the baby throughout gestation. We know little about why the placenta does not develop properly in preeclampsia and IUGR. Without this knowledge, devising better management approaches and interventions is not possible. Therefore, the objective of this project is to determine underlying factors that cause placental maldevelopment during early pregnancy. Our lab and others have provided compelling evidence that aberrant behavior of immune cells in the uterus is involved in causing the placental maldevelopment that precipitates preeclampsia and IUGR; but the nature of their involvement is not yet known. Thus, this project will test the role of these uterine immune cells in placental development, and will determine whether aberrant activity of these cells is involved in causing placental dysfunction. Collectively, this project will test the applicability of targeting uterine immune cells to improve placental and fetal health, with the ultimate goal of devising strategies to enhance maternal and neonatal health in pregnancies at-risk of developing preeclampsia and IUGR.

column36: Sleeping soundly: Understanding the translation of sleep promotion at school to sleep behaviours at home. Insights from children and parents
column37: Sleep is increasingly recognized as a behaviour that plays a vital role in achieving a healthy lifestyle, and is also crucial to children's development. Research has shown that inadequate sleep is associated with an array of physical and psychosocial health deficits including obesity, physical inactivity, poor nutrition, anxiety, depression, suicide risk, impaired concentration, ability to retain information, hyperactivity, impaired motor sills, and poorer overall health and immune function. Further, shorter sleep duration and poorer sleep quality are linked to poorer academic outcomes. The home and school are recognized as critical environments to shape healthy behaviours, and as such, health promotion efforts have increasingly focused on the school setting. While several school-based education initiatives have been implemented to support improved sleep among children, it is unknown if sleep behaviours are being translated home. The overall aim of this proposed research is to understand how school-based sleep education translates to sleep behaviours at home. Children are often viewed as change agents for health behaviours, thus this research will examine if and how children act as change agents and initiate sleep behaviour changes in the home. Parents also influence children's sleep behaviours, therefore this research will examine parents' perspectives regarding sleep and how parental support in the home environment reinforces school-based learning. Findings from children and parents will inform and strengthen existing school-based sleep education through an extensive stakeholder consultation.

column36: Dissecting the function and mechanisms of the Mediator Kinase module
column37: The control of gene expression is key to all cellular processes. One universal player in this regulation is the Mediator complex. Mediator plays a central role in the regulation of gene expression acting as a bridge between the so-called general transcription factors (involved in the regulation of all genes) and the gene-specific transcription factors. Mediator is frequently mutated or present in abnormal level in many cancers and genetic diseases. Mediator contains a built-in regulator, an enzyme that adds phosphate groups on Mediator and other proteins, allowing for fine tuning its activity. This regulator module (called CKM) within Mediator is the most frequently Mediator component affected in cancers. Because it is an enzyme, the activity of CKM is in principle "drug-able" but before this can be achieved, a better understanding of how it works is required. In this project, we will use the power of budding yeast as a model system to dissect the mechanisms and function of CKM. This knowledge will leverage our capacity to mine strategies to re-equilibrate Mediator activity in diseases.

column36: Elucidating novel mechanisms of extracellular nucleic acid recognition, internalization, trafficking and signaling: implications for infection, inflammation and autoimmunity.
column37: Extracellular or circulating nucleic acids derived from infected or damaged cells can be of virus or self origin. Once recognized and taken up by healthy cells, these nucleic acids rapidly and potently lead to the production of cytokines, including interferon. While interferon is important to protect against infections and cancer, inappropriate interferon responses lead to a variety of diseases, including autoimmunity. While class A scavenger receptors (SRAs) are required for binding and internalization of circulating nucleic acids, little is known about how individual SRA family members carry out these functions. Surprisingly, little is also understood about the cellular trafficking or localization of different nucleic acid species following uptake by SRAs. We have uncovered several unexplained anomalies in how different forms and lengths of nucleic acids traffic within cells and induce interferon following uptake by SRAs. In this grant, we will study the internalization, trafficking and signaling of various forms and lengths of nucleic acids to understand the mechanisms of how they activate cytokines such as interferon. Given that interferon can either prevent disease or cause disease, depending on its regulation, understanding basic mechanisms of interferon production in response to circulating nucleic acids is of critical importance.

column36: Beyond diarrhea, to disability and death: uncovering the hidden health consequences of foodborne infections
column37: Each year, over 4 million Canadians develop a new infection because of the food they eat; short term symptoms, like diarrhea, alone result in 2.5 million days of work missed, and $400 million in health care and other costs. And although these infections can have serious consequences, including miscarriage, arthritis, kidney failure, and death, just how many Canadians go on to experience such consequences, and what this costs our healthcare system, is unknown. Without this knowledge, policy makers struggle to protect Canadians, unable to adequately argue for sufficient investments to make food safer, and clinicians do not have the evidence they need to avert such serious consequences in their patients. Previously, the approach required to accurately determine the serious consequences of foodborne infections across the population was lacking. Now, with decades of population-wide electronic health records, including sufficient details on foodborne infections, we are finally able to address this issue. The province of BC is uniquely positioned to support this novel work. BC's rich collection of health records allows us to seamlessly explore the various medical consequences experienced by everyone in BC who tests positive for a foodborne infection. Thus, we will conduct a longitudinal cohort study, across the population of BC, determining what fraction of people develop serious consequences following a foodborne infection, what this costs the health system, and what risks infected Canadians face (e.g., of miscarriage, death), regardless of whether or not they are already vulnerable (e.g., young, old, pregnant). This work will uncover the real risks faced by the >4 million Canadians infected from food each year. This knowledge will allow provincial and national policy makers to invest in making food safer, and physicians to better diagnose and treat patients, which will ultimately prevent foodborne infections, and their serious consequences, among Canadians.

column36: Post-translational protein arginylation in skeletal muscles
column37: Muscle contraction is a basic function of life, responsible for body movements, hear beating, breathing, to cite a few. Contraction is regulated by a variety of processes, including biochemical pathways that may change the way muscles work. Such changes may improve or inhibit contractions, and may eventually lead to weakness and muscular diseases, such a muscle dystrophies. The goal of this proposal is to investigate one regulatory mechanism called arginylation, a process by which muscle proteins receive arginine (Arg) from tRNA. We have pilot data showing that arginylation is a strong regulator of muscle contraction, and that lack of arginylation leads to muscle weakness and dystrophy. We will use novel and accurate methods that include sub-cellular structures and single molecules isolated from muscles to test the mechanism by which arginylation regulates muscle contraction. We will also test the effects of potential treatments for muscle dystrophy caused by lack of arginylation. This research will provide information that is needed for the understanding of the basic mechanisms of muscle contraction in health and disease, and may have implications for everyday life.

column36: Epithelial alpha-v-beta-6 integrin: critical regulator of periodontal inflammation
column37: A large segment of the adult population suffers from periodontal diseases (PDs) that can result in loss of teeth, a financial burden, and potentially contribute to many systemic conditions. The pathogenesis of PDs is a complex process in which intricate subgingival bacterial biofilm induces inflammation that leads to tissue degradation and bone loss. In health, junctional epithelium (JE) links the gingiva to the tooth enamel, creating a seal and preventing bacteria from entering the gingival tissue. In PD, bone loss develops around the teeth with periodontal pockets and the JE transforms into pocket epithelium (PE). However, it is not clear how JE/PE participates in the regulation of periodontal inflammation. In the inflammatory infiltrate, the outcome of the cytokine response is regulated by the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that are countered by anti-inflammatory cytokines. These cytokines need to be activated for biological function. An integrin known as alpha-v-beta-6 can activate them. Mutations in this integrin cause PD in mice and humans. We have shown that JE constitutively expresses this integrin and these anti-inflammatory cytokines. In PD, the expression of this integrin in PE is strongly downregulated, resulting in "acquired integrin deficiency." This integrin-mediated cytokine activation in JE appears to be crucial for the maintenance of periodontal health and preventing systemic inflammation. The factors leading to the downregulation of this integrin expression in PE cells are not known. In the present proposal, we will determine the mechanisms through which this integrin expression is downregulated in JE/PE in periodontal disease and how this integrin "deficiency" regulates cytokine expression in epithelial cells. The long-term goal is to determine the molecular mechanism of periodontal inflammation and use this information for preventive therapies.

column36: TEMPO-2 - A randomized controlled trial of TNK-tPA versus standard of care for minor ischemic stroke with proven occlusion.
column37: Most minor strokes are due to lack of blood getting to a part of the brain. When this occurs, patients get sudden loss of function in that region of the brain. This might mean inability to move a limb or inability to speak. In the luckiest case, this dysfunction resolves rapidly by itself and we call it a transient ischemic attack (TIA). If less lucky, the disability persists due to a minor stroke. Minor stroke and TIA account for about 50% of all strokes in Canada. Most physicians think that patients with minor stroke or TIA do not need aggressive treatment with clot busting drugs because the risk of bleeding in the brain is greater than any benefit. However, we believe that this judgment is incorrect. We have shown that minor stroke and TIA patients with evidence of a blocked blood vessel on a brain scan are at a very high risk of being left disabled with conservative treatment. This subgroup of patients can benefit from aggressive therapy with clot-busting drugs. The usual clot-busting drug usually used in Stroke is called tPA. A newer drug used in patients with heart attack called TNK works faster and is safer than tPA. In the TEMPO-2 clinical trial, we will determine if TNK, given as a single dose, is better than usual care for patients with minor stroke with a proven blocked artery. Patients will have a 50:50 chance (i.e. like the toss of a coin) of getting either treatment or usual care. Patients will be assessed 3 months after the event for evidence of disability. column36: The VANISH2 Trial: Ventricular Tachycardia Antiarrhythmics or Ablation in Structural Heart Disease 2
column37: Background: The VANISH2 trial is designed to determine the best treatment for people who have life-threatening abnormalities of heart rhythm. Heart attacks leave scars in the heart muscle. The scars can interfere with the normal signaling within the heart that controls the heart beat. In some cases, the interference can cause a very dangerous abnormal heart rhythm known as ventricular tachycardia (VT). This rhythm is the most common cause of sudden death in Canada. When patients are at high risk for recurrences of VT, a defibrillator (ICD) can be implanted which can shock the heart back to normal rhythm from a cardiac arrest. These devices are life-saving but do not prevent the abnormal rhythm, they just provide a rescue when it occurs. In order to prevent dangerous arrhythmias, doctors use strong rhythm control drugs or a procedure called catheter ablation. An ablation is performed by advancing wires through the blood vessels into the heart, using X-rays and other imaging to see where they are and the short circuits within the scar can then be identified and interrupted (ablated). Neither the drugs nor the ablation procedure work perfectly and both carry risk. This trial is designed to determine which treatment is the best. Study design: Patients who have had heart attacks and develop VT will be randomly allocated (50:50) to be treated either with rhythm control drugs or catheter ablation. All patients will receive an implanted defibrillator. We will enroll a total of 366 patients and follow them for at least 2 years to see which group does the best with respect to recurrent abnormal heart rhythms and survival. Expected Outcomes: This trial will determine whether the best treatment for VT is heart rhythm drugs or catheter ablation. This evidence will permit more optimal treatment for many thousands of patients worldwide.

column36: Adequate intake of choline in pregnancy may be critical for MTHFD1 synthetase deficiency, a common genetic variant in folate metabolism
column37: Folate and choline are important nutrients required to support healthy pregnancies. Inadequate intake of these nutrients before and during pregnancy can increase the risk of birth defects and other pregnancy complications. Folate is a critical vitamin that provides the building blocks for DNA (e.g. purines) and methyl groups for a host of biosynthetic reactions. Choline is required to produce important components of cell membranes, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Choline becomes even more important when folate metabolism is disturbed, because it replaces folate for certain functions. Although most Canadian women are aware of the importance of folate and reach the recommended intakes due to folate fortification programs and use of folate supplements, 85-90% do not have adequate choline intakes. Gene variants in folate metabolism, such as MTHFD1 R653Q, may also increase risk for neural tube defects, heart defects and other pregnancy complications. About 20% of Canadians have the QQ genotype, which we have shown to impair MTHFD1 function and decrease purine synthesis. Some studies have suggested that QQ women are more sensitive to low choline intake. Our goal is to determine whether inadequate choline contributes to the reproductive complications associated with the 653QQ genotype, and whether supplementation with choline or choline metabolites can overcome the effect of the genetic defect. We will examine human placentas from women with the 653RR and QQ genotypes with high and low folate intakes to assess the effects of diet and genotype on choline metabolism. We will use our mouse model for the variant to determine if low choline diets impair embryonic development and see if different types of choline supplements improve pregnancy outcomes. Our research will highlight a neglected aspect of nutrition during pregnancy and lay the groundwork for personalized dietary recommendations based on R653Q genotype to prevent reproductive complications.

column36: Improving responsiveness across the continuum of kidney health care in rural and remote Manitoba First Nation communities (I-KHealth)
column37: Manitoba First Nations (MFNs) have the highest documented prevalence and the second highest incidence of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in Canada. Those living in rural/remote locations and requiring care experience significant barriers. Although preventable, nephrologists heard FN patients, especially from "renal families" (where other members have chronic kidney disease, CKD/ESKD), report that ESKD is inevitable. These statements likely reflect limited opportunities for maintaining health in the face of barriers including racism, perpetuating risk factors and undermining prevention efforts. This partnership-based program of research brings together community-based researchers from the Nanaandawewigamig Diabetes Integration Program (hereafter DIP, a part of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs), FN patients with lived experience of renal disease, University of Manitoba (UM) university-based researchers and members of the MRP (nephrologists, nurses, dietitian, social worker). We propose a 5 year program of research with 2 broad objectives: 1. To improve access to effective PC-based care for patients identified at being at low and medium risk of CKD; and 2. To expand the number of dialysis modalities available to FNs through the development of a FN-centric assisted PD model (APD), developed in partnership with FN communities. ESKD/CKD continues to fundamentally impact the lives of Indigenous patients, their families and communities. Despite repeated reviews and the implementation of a range of renal service plans, access to dialysis (in varied forms) in Manitoba rural and remote communities, including MFN communities, remains poor and still results in family dislocation. The critical questions outlined in this application remain unanswered, and stand to make a significant impact on primary care, treatment options and outcomes.

column36: Targeting Key Autophagy Proteins/Pathways for Treatment of Human Leukemia
column37: Blood cancer (leukemia) is common, with ~55,000 cases expected in the United States and Canada in 2017. The National Cancer Institute (US) calculated an overall 5-year survival rate of 56% for various blood cancers. This is because drug resistance and relapse pose significant challenges. Life-long treatment is required, with potential side-effects and a high cost. Blood cancer cells generally respond to drug therapy at the onset, but the drugs lose their effectiveness after 6-12 months. We and others have discovered that this is mainly due to the inability of current therapies to eradicate blood cancer stem cells, which maintain the potential for relapse. There is thus an urgent need to develop new therapies that specifically target blood cancer stem cells so that these cells can be eliminated, leading to a cure. We have found that ATG4B, a novel drug target and key driver in autophagy, displays abnormal activity in blood cancer stem cells, particularly in drug-resistant patients. However, there is currently no drug that blocks autophagy in a specific and potent way, nor any related drugs for autophagy inhibition that are approved as therapeutics. We have identified several promising new drugs that specifically target ATG4B in blood cancer stem cells. Combining these with current anti-cancer drugs more effectively inhibits blood cancer stem cell growth in culture than single drug treatment; this treatment strategy also doesn't have side-effects on normal blood stem cells. This study will thus investigate if this combination therapy will more effectively eradicate blood cancer stem cells obtained from drug-resistant patients, using our established animal cancer models. This will provide ultimate proof-of-concept for the development of more effective therapies with fewer side effects than currently used therapies. More immediate economic benefits are also expected from the commercialization and drug development that will be fuelled by this research.

column36: Airway smooth muscle tone on asthmatic airway hyperresponsiveness
column37: Asthma is a lung disorder caused by diverse environmental triggers, such as allergens, viruses, pollutants and cold dry air. Despite constant effort in research, asthma continues to be highly prevalent in Canada. It currently touches approximately 8% of the population, a great proportion being children. Asthma can be debilitating for many patients and can progress into more severe forms, especially when not treated properly. It also represents a serious burden for the society in term of direct medical costs, as well as indirect costs, such as the loss of productivity at school or at work. Medications that are currently approved to treat asthma fall short, as it is estimated that the symptoms are not adequately controlled in as much as 50% of patients. In fact, some patients are poorly responsive and sometimes totally refractory to asthma medications. Plus, some of these medications can engender side effects. Together, this suggests that there is a serious need to keep improving the treatment of asthma. Since it is barely impossible to avoid the development of asthma, owing to the variety of environmental triggers involved, a part of research in that field must be dedicated to the relief of respiratory symptoms. It is well understood that the contraction of the muscle within the wall of the airways contributes to asthma symptoms by narrowing the passage of air in and out of the lung. Numerous studies have also demonstrated that the force of that muscle can increase rapidly in response to different molecules found within the lungs of asthmatic patients. An increased force of that muscle certainly plays an important role in the manifestation of asthma symptoms. Blocking this gain in force is thus a promising quest in order to relieve asthma symptoms. The goal of this research project is to understand the mechanisms by which the force of the airway muscle is enhanced in asthma. The hope is to identify key pathways for which targeting will improve asthma treatment.

column36: Implementation of a Stepped Care Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia in Routine Cancer Care
column37: An abundance of psychosocial interventions has been developed and found to be efficacious in clinical trials conducted in academic settings to reduce psychological symptoms and improve quality of life of cancer patients. However, these interventions are not typically integrated in routine care thus resulting in a huge gap between the massive research evidence supporting their usefulness and what is actually done in the real-world. The consequence is that cancer patients do not receive the best available psychological interventions. Our research team is an international leader in the psychological treatment of cancer-related insomnia. In 2005, we published the first clinical trial supporting the efficacy of cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) in cancer patients, a finding that has repeatedly been replicated since then. Despite the available evidence showing several beneficial effects associated with CBT-I, this treatment remains rarely offered. Recently, we developed a stepped care model in order to increase the use of CBT-I in routine care. It begins with a web-based CBT-I followed if needed (only if the patient still suffers from insomnia) by up to 3 sessions with a psychotherapist. Our findings indicate that this stepped care approach is as efficacious as a more standard face-to-face CBT-I while being much less costly. It is now time to implement this approach widely in routine cancer care. The main goals of this study are to ascertain factors that make it easier/harder to implement our stepped care CBT-I in 5 hospitals providing care to cancer patients, to evaluate the extent to which health care providers use it and administer it competently after it has been implemented and to assess its effects on patients' well-being. A pre-implementation quality study (Phase 1), a clinical trial (Phase 2) and a post-implementation quality study (Phase 3) will be performed.

column36: Cell cycle regulation of human pancreatic endocrine cell development.
column37: Diabetes occurs when the insulin-producing pancreatic B-cells die or stop functioning resulting in uncontrolled blood sugar levels. Current treatments for diabetes include replacing the function of these cells either through insulin injection or the use of oral drugs that help control blood sugar levels. However, often these therapies fail, resulting in extended periods of high blood sugar levels that can be damaging to nerves, eyes, and organs. Alternatives to injectable and oral therapies, including improving the function of insulin-producing cells or transplanting replacement insulin-producing cells, have been shown to reduce the damage caused by high glucose. Unfortunately, not enough is known about how normal B-cells work and not enough transplantable donor tissue is available to treat the increasing number of people with diabetes. Currently, we are able to form cells that resemble B-cells from stem cells but in order to improve the efficiency of this process we will need to better understand human pancreas development. In addition, we are unsure whether these stem cell-derived B-cells will function normally after transplantation into those with diabetes or if they will return to being stem cells. In this project we aim to study how the cell cycle, the process where a cell grows and divides to produce copies of itself, controls human B-cell formation. This study will be the first to investigate the role of the cell cycle during human pancreas development and will improve our understanding of how human B-cells are formed and are maintained. This knowledge could lead to new approaches to generate treatments for the over 10 million Canadians that are living with diabetes or prediabetes.

We will work closely with key stakeholders (e.g., bar owners, bar-goers, sexual violence prevention/treatment professionals, police, college/university representatives) to use the findings in developing preventive interventions and policies to reduce ASHA in bars/clubs.

column36: Targeting platelet-specific molecules in periodontal disease
column37: Periodontitis, or gum disease, is a very common infection of the mouth that causes inflammation of the gum tissues and also destroys the connective tissues and bone that support the teeth. In addition, platelets control blood coagulation (clotting) but also release cytokines that can promote inflammation. The goal of this grant application is to study platelet-specific cytokines and to determine whether shutting down the function of these molecules might help to prevent tissue damage caused by gum disease. column36: Ubiquitin-mediated regulation of membrane proteins
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada, with 1 in 2 Canadian developing cancer in their life time and 1 in 4 dying from it. Breast cancer is the most prevalent cancer in women. Over the past decade, major efforts have been devoted to tailor drug treatment to each cancer patient (personalized medicine). This is enabled by routine sequencing of tumor DNA to identify the mutations that cause or enhance tumor growth, and tailor drugs to the abnormal protein discovered; most often this involves targeting abnormal modification of the protein by a phosphate, a process called phosphorylation. Equally important is ubiquitination, a process where a small protein called ubiquitin is attached to a target protein to mark it for destruction. This process is abnormal in many cancers, yet so far, with the exception of one drug used to treat one type of blood cancer, there are no drugs that interfere with ubiquitination. My lab is working towards closing this huge gap, focusing here on investigating the role of the ubiquitin system in cancer and develop drugs to target its components. My lab has made seminal contributions to our understanding of the ubiquitin system over the past 20 years, focusing on a family of enzymes (proteins) of the ubiquitin system called the Nedd4 family. Using both cells and animal models, we have learned that this family is important for regulating both normal animal development and growth of cancer cells and tumors. We plan to now investigate how the Nedd4 family enzymes work, what regulates them, and how they regulate tumor growth (focusing on breast cancer). Moreover, we plan to perform drug screens to find drugs that can alter the function of Nedd4 proteins, with the ultimate goal of using these drugs for cancer therapy.

column36: Developing and testing quality indicators for palliative care using existing data
column37: Dying is something that will happen to everyone and good quality of care at the end of life is a basic human right. From the survey questions we will define a set of quality indicators that look at things like pain, trouble breathing, depression, caregiver distress and falls. These indicators will be reported as a percent (e.g., percent of people with pain) so we can compare different health care providers from across Canada on these measures. By looking at these indicators, palliative care providers can see how they are doing and how they compare to other places. In this way, they can figure out where they might need to make some changes in order to improve the quality of care that they provide.

column37: Our body can tell time of day: light, which is detected by our eyes, sends a signal to our brain and then throughout our body through hormones. We have done experiments which show that intestinal healing occurs with a day/night rhythm. In this proposal, we will study circadian rhythms in intestinal stem cells that heal diseased tissues. We will find out how and why light in our environment shapes our health. This work is a new area of research. Our artificial environments constantly interrupt natural light/dark cycles. Do we disrupt important healing rhythms when we stay up all night? When we travel, we often irritate and affect our digestive systems. Shift workers have more intestinal disease, but it is not clear how this happens. The research proposed here will test how changes to lifestyle (ie. by shift work, or frequent travel) are risk factors that make the intestine heal poorly. Translating this research may be as simple as avoiding frequent sleep interruptions. Our work will also affect the timing of therapies and the use of stem cells in regenerating the intestine and colon of colitis patients. Knowing whether time of day affects healing will be useful in choosing the right time to perform many therapeutic treatments.

column36: RAS-MAPK signal transduction in normal and cancer cells
column37: RAS proteins are key regulators of cell division. Significantly, over a third of human cancers are associated with activating mutations in RAS genes, which makes them the most frequently mutated oncogenes. Yet, despite considerable efforts, there are still no approved drugs that suppress directly hyperactive RAS. Important advances have nonetheless been made in recent years by targeting RAS effector proteins. My lab has a long-standing interest in a group of proteins (RAF, MEK, and MAPK) that transmit RAS signals in normal and cancer cells. Markedly, inhibition of these proteins by pharmacological means curtails tumor growth. While this path has yielded some clinical successes, severe limitations emerged, including drug resistance and toxicity. We recently brought to light a central mechanism underlying RAF activation by RAS, which contributes in part to resistance to RAF inhibitors. We propose to extend our understanding of this mechanism and, based on learned principles, develop new classes of RAF inhibitors to evade drug resistance. Innovative strategies to directly inhibit RAS function will be also explored. Using the fruit fly model organism, we also found unexpected mechanisms that selectively control MAPK protein levels. We will study these mechanisms to identify novel means to manipulate RAS-MAPK activity. Given the high degree of evolutionary conservation of the pathway, these mechanisms will also be studied in human cells as they will provide alternative entry points for therapeutic intervention. Cancer research is a long and intricate process and it is only through multi-pronged approaches that valuable therapies will emerge. We have generated knowledge, tools, and partnerships with other groups that place us in a unique position to make major contributions to the cancer field. Given the high incidence of RAS-MAPK dependent cancers, we expect that efficacious compounds targeting this critical pathway will bring enormous benefits to human health.

column36: Assessing the effectiveness of an approach based on the meanings of vocal behaviours in older people living with Alzheimer's disease in long-term care facilities: DECIBELS Project
column37: Between 13 and 60% of older people who live with Alzheimer's disease (ADRD) in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) manifest vocal behaviours (VB) that may seem inappropriate, e.g. moaning, screaming, calling out. These behaviours may indicate ill-being, disturb others, create feelings of powerlessness in family and formal caregivers, and lead to inappropriate medication. Previous efforts to reduce VB have been largely ineffective. Our team developed a new approach based on finding the underlying reasons for VB through a partnership between family and formal caregivers. The goals are to reduce VB, enhance older people's well-being, and increase family and formal caregivers' empowerment. We tested the approach in a pilot study of 14 triads comprising an older person living with ADRD, a family caregiver and a formal caregiver. The results were promising; overall, it is feasible to implement the approach in LTCF and it has positive effects on older people, family and formal caregivers. Now we propose to assess the clinical and economic impact of the approach in 18 LTCFs with 108 triads like those in the pilot study. The approach will be implemented in 9 randomly selected "experimental" LTCFs; the other 9 (control group) will continue with their usual practices. We will measure VB frequency and the well-being of the older people before, two and four months after starting the implementation. We will also measure the perceived disruptiveness of VB for family and formal caregivers, their ability to work in partnership and their empowerment relative to VB. We will compare data between the control and experimental LTCFs, and calculate cost-effectiveness based on changes in VB frequency. Our proposed three-year project aims to improve the well-being of all involved in LTCF by promoting a better understanding of VB and implementing a solution to optimize care. We believe the findings will provide evidence to justify the wider implementation of our approach in LTCF.

column36: macroH2A shapes self-renewal properties in glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. It is incurable, with average patient survival of about 14 months even with an aggressive therapeutic regimen consisting of maximal tumor resection, and concomitant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. One of the reasons for therapeutic failure is the complex functional heterogeneity in this brain tumor. In fact, not all cells are functionally identical in GBM, but a small population has properties reminiscent of normal stem cells, whereby they are uniquely responsible for tumor growth and recurrence. We call these specialized cells "cancer stem cells," or tumor-initiating cells. Whereas current treatments are relatively successful at targeting the other cells in this tumor, cancer stem cells have ways of evading current therapeutic intervention. We have recently shown that one feature that distinguishes cancer stem cells from the other cells in GBM is the way DNA is packaged. Cancer stem cells have regions of highly compacted DNA, which is caused by low levels of a protein that binds the DNA and relaxes its architecture. This protein is called H3.3. We have now identified macroH2A as another protein that may play a role in DNA packaging in cancer stem cells. We will characterize macroH2A, its function in orchestrating DNA packaging in cancer stem cells, and the way it affects the dynamics of tumor growth. These data will be used to rationally deploy a new generation of drugs that can affect DNA packaging. By changing the architecture of the DNA in cancer stem cells, we may be able to kill them or reprogram them into less lethal cell types that can be targeted by standard therapies. Eliminating cancer stem cells with novel techniques will be key to obliterating the ability of a tumor to grow and recur.

column36: Cooperation between DIMs and motor proteins in DSB mobility-dependent repair
column37: Our DNA is under constant assault from environmental and internal factors. Fortunately, our cells can repair damaged DNA thereby preventing human illnesses such as cancer and premature aging. DNA repair mechanisms are evolutionarily conserved, from yeast to human. In fact, owing to its ease of manipulation, studies conducted in yeast have revealed numerous of the key players and processes mediating human DNA repair. One of the major DNA repair mechanisms is called homologous recombination, in which damaged DNA is replaced by DNA sequences copied from another intact sequence elsewhere in the cell. Importantly, we had found that for yeast cells to repair damaged DNA by homologous recombination, the damaged DNA must be transiently targeted to DNA hospital-like structures called nuclear pore complexes. This transient targeting is dependent on a DNA ambulance-like motor protein complex called Kinesin-14, another ambulance-like motor protein whose identity remains illusive, and protein filaments called microtubules [Chung et al. Nature Commun. (2015)]. This is puzzling as microtubules are typically not located in the part of the cell that contains the DNA and is called the nucleus. Yet, a similar dependence of DNA repair on motor proteins and microtubules was then reported in mammals and shown to impact the efficacy of anti-cancer drugs [Lottersberger et al. Cell (2015)]. Here we pursue new data revealing the formation of street-like microtubule filaments inside the DNA-containing nucleus. Thus, we will take advantage of the power of yeast genetics to test if these DNA damage-induced intranuclear microtubules (DIMs) act like roads that are driven onto by ambulance-like motor proteins to transport damaged DNA to and away from hospital-like sites of DNA repair. Overall, we will decipher a highly sought-after DNA repair mechanism that is critical to human health and longevity.
