column36: Mobilizing anti-tumor microglia/macrophages with niacin to improve the prognosis of glioblastoma: Bench to clinical trial and back.
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly malignant brain tumor where less than 5% of patients survive beyond five years. This dismal prognosis calls for fresh ideas and new treatment regimens. Recently, brain tumor initiating cells (BTICs), also called brain tumor stem cells, were discovered and they exploit the immune system (macrophages and microglia) by suppressing their activity or by eliciting growth factors to sustain brain tumor growth. An important and novel approach would thus be to rejuvenate or mobilize the compromised macrophages and microglia to contain BTICs. The collaboration between Drs. John Kelly (neurosurgeon/glioma biologist), Jeff Dunn (magnetic resonance imaging, MRI) and Wee Yong (neuroimmunologist) has uncovered generic medications with the capacity to stimulate macrophages/microglia. These include an anti-fungal medication, amphotericin B, and vitamin B3 (niacin). Amphotericin B is poorly tolerated in humans so the group has developed niacin further. Impressively, the group has found that in mice with brain tumors, treatment with niacin mobilizes the compromised immune cells, reduces tumor volume as detected through MRI and histology, and significantly prolongs the lifespan of mice. Remarkably, the life-extending impact of niacin exceeds that of the current front line therapy for GBM, temozolomide, and the combination of niacin and temozolomide has even better outcomes. To bring the laboratory findings to the clinic, the team now includes two neuro-oncologists, Paula de Robles and Gloria Urgoiti. Together, the team will determine how niacin stimulates immune cells to contain brain tumor growth, how best to further mobilize the activity of niacin, and conduct a Phase I/2 trial of niacin as an immune stimulator in GBM patients. Collectively, this team seeks to uncover new insights of GBM and translate therapeutics from the bench to bedside to mobilize the normally protective immune system to improve the prognosis of GBM.

column37: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder that is fatal and has no cure. The prevalence of this disease in Canada is estimated at 13.7 per 100,000, thus the need to understand the biological basis of the disease for the development of therapeutic treatments and a cure is of paramount importance. Huntington's disease is primarily characterized by progressive motor incoordination and involuntary movements that result from neurodegeneration of a region of the brain called the striatum. The overall objective of the proposed work is to understand the biological basis of the cognitive and behavioural impairments in the hippocampus, in particular those related to learning and memory. Our goal is to identify molecular targets that can be exploited therapeutically to (i) slow disease onset, and (ii) reduced cognitive dysfunction that will both improve patient quality of life and reduce caregiver burden.

column36: Vibrissa motion: motor strategies and facial expressions
column37: The brainstem contains genetically programmed circuits for the expression of life-sustaining orofacial functions, such as breathing, suckling, licking, sniffing, and whisking in rodents. These behaviors meet the need of basic physiological functions such as breathing and nutrient ingestion. Orofacial activities also serve to explore the environment and communicate emotional states through facial expressions and vocalization. In rodents, vibrissa movement is an important component of orofacial activities. In the present proposal we seek to identify brain circuits that control vibrissa motion, and determine under which behavioral conditions these different circuits are recruited. Toward this goal, we use virus-based methods to trace neuronal circuits, and to activate or inactivate specific regions of the brain stem that are involved in the control of vibrissa motion. Electrophysiological recordings are also carried out in alert rats to correlate neuronal activities with vibrissa motion that are associated with exploratory activities or with emotional reactions. Despite the behavioral importance of facial expressions in social communications in man and mammals, the neurophysiological basis of these activities remains poorly understood. Our research program might open new perspectives on this aspect of animal and human behavior.

column36: Structural studies of neurodegenerative diseases
column37: The brain is the most fragile organ both physically and biochemically. Brain cells do not regenerate so they have to last a lifetime in face of wide range of stresses: physical, chemical, and biological. To deal with these, neurons have evolved protective mechanisms. The goal of our research is to understand these defences and develop new therapies to treat or prevent the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, which are an increasingly serious public health problem. We are focusing on Parkinson's disease, which afflicts some 60,000 Canadians, and a genetic disease, ARSACS, first identified in Quebec. Both diseases involve perturbations in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, part of the cellular recycling machinery that is used to identify and remove damaged proteins and organelles. The approach we are using is to visualize protein complexes in the ubiquitin-proteasome system using the tools of structural biology. Seeing how the proteins work will allow us to design therapies. Parkinson's disease can be caused by mutations in a quality control system for mitochondria. In healthy neurons, a protein kinase PINK1 detects damaged mitochondria and then signals Parkin, a component in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, to start the degradation process. Defects in either step cause a genetic, early onset form of Parkinson's disease. The second disease, ARSACS, is caused by loss of Sacsin, a protein chaperone that helps mitochondria split apart (mitochondrial fission). Through mechanisms not yet understood, this leads to a slow progressive loss of Purkinje cells, which control movement. Understanding and developing treatments for these diseases will also help in the treatment of other dementias. There is evidence for impaired mitochondrial function in Alzheimer's, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The proposed studies of the ubiquitin-proteasome system will set the stage for the development of new drugs for neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Saturation Transfer MRI as a biomarker of tumour response to radiation treatment in patients with glioblastoma multiforme
column37: Glioma is the most common and aggressive form of brain cancer. The current standard of care is surgery followed by radiation treatment (XRT) and chemotherapy. A major challenge with XRT is determining tumour response, which is currently done by assessing changes in tumour size. It may take weeks before significant changes in tumour size occur, by which time the therapeutic window is often lost. Clinically, early identification of non-responders may significantly improve outcomes by allowing the oncologist to change the treatment. We developed new MRI techniques to characterize tumour environment which have the potential of predicting tumour response to XRT. This study has two major goals: 1.To assess tumour response to XRT with novel MRI sequences and to identify the optimal MRI protocol to distinguish between responders and non-responders. 2.To differentiate radiation necrosis or pseudo-progression from tumour progression with MRI. Our preliminary data has shown that: 1.MRI can predict tumour response as early as two weeks after the start of the XRT. 2.MRI characteristics of brain tissue are significantly different than in normal controls. 3.MRI features of white matter have the potential to predict tumour response before the treatment. We aim to find the earliest time-point and the optimal MRI protocol that allow for robust tumour response monitoring. 110 patients will be recruited for this study. These patients will be MRI scanned immediately before treatment and then will be monitored by MRI during the course of XRT. We are proposing novel MRI approaches for non-invasive characterization of cancer therapy. It will also offer the means to evaluate treatment effects relatively early so appropriate changes in patient management can be made. Our proposed methods are not limited to glioma. They can be used for many cancers and treatment regimens.

column36: Sticky money: Exploring the acceptability of a sugar-sweetened beverage tax among Canadian Indigenous populations
column37: Evidence suggests that pop contributes a lot of sugar to the Canadian diet, which is linked to increasing levels of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Consequently, an increasing number of jurisdictions globally are adopting a pop tax to curb intake, as recommended by the World Health Organization. Canada has not yet adopted the tax, but its merit is being widely debated. In Canada, the burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes is greater among lower socioeconomic groups and Indigenous populations while pop intake is higher within these same groups. These realities underscore the need to understand the perceived impact of a pop tax on intake among low socioeconomic groups and Indigenous populations to improve population health outcomes. However, previous experience with tobacco taxes have demonstrated that taxes are not effective policy levers in reducing smoking rates among low socioeconomic groups, thus suggesting that a similar tax on pop may also be ineffective. Tobacco taxes were also not implemented in most First Nations communities. In this research, we have four objectives: 1) to describe how pop intake has changed in Canada from 2004 to 2015 among Indigenous, low income, rural/urban, and food insecure people; 2) to examine how middle-class Canadians living in Winnipeg perceive a pop tax; 3) to examine how First Nation people living in the Island Lake First Nations (on-reserve) perceive a pop tax, should one ever be implemented; and 4) to examine how Indigenous people living in Winnipeg (off-reserve) perceive a pop tax. What we learn by doing this research will help us understand the pros and cons of implementing a pop tax in Canada. This research will also inform recommendations concerning effective strategies for public health messaging that might accompany such a tax and suggestions for use of tax revenue that are acceptable to populations who may be most burdened by a proposed pop tax.

column36: Role of Prohibitins and SUMOylation in Osteoarthritis Pathogenesis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of joint disease and the major cause of chronic disability in adults. It is commonly assumed that multiple factors, including genetic and developmental, metabolic and traumatic factors can trigger OA. Although OA affects more than 300 million people worldwide, a clear understanding of its causes is still lacking. Moreover, the early stages of OA progression are not well understood mainly due to the difficulties in assessing these events in aging humans. We have discovered that cartilage forming cells from OA patients cannot produce a protein, termed PITX1. PITX1 proteins are essential during the development for the formation of cartilage joints and hind limb bones but its disappearance during adult life could cause knee or hip joint OA. The team led by Dr. Alain Moreau has discovered that loss of PITX1 in cartilage and bone is caused by an aberrant accumulation of a protein termed Prohibitin (PHB1) and depletion of a related family members (PHB2) in nuclei of bone and cartilage forming cells of patients suffering of knee or hip OA. This research project will investigate the causes by which nuclear accumulation of PHB1 and depletion of PHB2 occur in OA. Notably, we will examine the contribution of SUMO (small ubiquitin-like modifier) proteins given that when they attach to other proteins (a process called SUMOylation), they contribute to trap PHB1 in the nuclei of bone and cartilage forming cells in OA through their physical interactions with a SUMO-binding module presents in PHB1 protein. Our preliminary data showed an elevation of SUMOylation activity in primary OA. Elucidation of these mechanisms could be important for the development of effective treatments for OA and may lead to the development of better molecular tools to assess the risk of developing OA and monitor disease progression.

column36: The checkpoint receptor PD-1 inhibits Natural Killer cell responses to cancer.
column37: The body has an extraordinary weapon against cancer: the immune system. Unfortunately, tumors often learn how to evade the immune response. Our goal is to understand the inhibitory circuits that suppress the immune system in cancer in order to develop new strategies to activate our own immune cells against tumors.

column36: Improving Mitochondria in Aged Hearts Following Ischemic Injury with Novel Epoxy Lipids
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in older individuals. As people age there is an increased risk and incidence, with aged individuals comprising greater than 75% of patients presenting with CVD. Ischemic heart disease is a major contributor to CVD yet the development of successful therapies has remained elusive. Heart damage begins to occur after it has been deprived of oxygen (ischemia) for an extended period of time. Ischemic injury can significantly affect key components of the cell, such as mitochondria. In the heart, mitochondria provide about 90% of the energy for cardiac function. Natural decline in cardiovascular function with age has been well established but our understanding of the mechanisms is limited. Evidence indicates deterioration of mitochondria over time plays a critical role. Mitochondria are critical to cardiomyocyte survival and heart function, so maintenance of a healthy mitochondrial population is essential for the preservation of healthy cardiac muscle. Dietary sources of essential fatty acids have a significant effect on cardiovascular health. The overall goal this project is to investigate the cardioprotective role of novel metabolites produced from omega-3 fatty acids, which are found in dietary sources. Proteins within a cell metabolize these fatty acids into active molecules called epoxy lipids. These molecules are involved in regulating different functions in the body. Our research has demonstrated they can limit mitochondrial injury. Thus, the objective of this grant is to understand how this occurs in young and aged hearts, as well to target these molecules as viable therapeutic strategies to prevent and/or treat mitochondrial damage caused heart disease. We aim to identify new regulatory mechanisms and advance our understanding of mitochondrial function in aged hearts.

column36: Regulation of acute nausea: Cannabinoid/Serotonin interactions in the interoceptive insular cortex
column37: Nausea is a distressing condition that occurs commonly and is very hard to treat. Currently available treatments for nausea and vomiting more effectively control vomiting than nausea. Overall, nausea is currently reported as the most distressing side effect of chemotherapy, and one that often leads patients to discontinue treatment. Nausea is reduced by the active ingredient in marihuana, delta-9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), by its action on cannabinoid 1 (CB1) receptors. The CB1 receptors are naturally activated by chemicals produced in the brain, called endocannabinoids. The action of endocannabinoids, however, is very short, because enzymes break them down rapidly. Drugs which inhibit these degrading enzymes dramatically prolong the action of the endocannabinoids and also suppress nausea in rats. The area of the cerebral cortex that regulates nausea is the interoceptive insular cortex, a region that receives neural input from the gut. Serotonin in this region triggers nausea and drugs that act on CB1 receptors in this region reduce nausea. The primary effect of activating CB1 receptors is to reduce the release of neurotransmitters, including serotonin. As well, the primary non-psychoactive cannabinoid in marihuana, cannabidiol (CBD), also reduces nausea by reducing forebrain release of serotonin. We will test the hypothesis that the sensation of nausea is triggered by serotonin release within the interoceptive insular cortex, and the anti-nausea effect of endocannabinoids and CBD is the result of "turning off" the release of serotonin in this region. The results of these experiments will provide a better understanding of the neural regulation of nausea, and will lead to new treatments of this difficult to control condition.

column36: Do Land-Centered Mitigation Strategies Positively Impact Indigenous Health and Wellbeing in subarctic Canada?
column37: Indigenous Knowledge is a body of knowledge and beliefs transmitted orally, being both cumulative and dynamic. During the 1970s, Indigenous knowledge gained credibility on the international stage. When there is more than one way of knowing, all ways should be used to contribute to a more complete understanding of complex environment-and-health issues, such as, development on Indigenous traditional homelands. The proposed project will use Indigenous knowledge and mainstream science as complementary ways of knowing and doing, in order to evaluate land-centered mitigation strategies related to development projects on Indigenous homelands. It is well recognized worldwide that Indigenous groups have significantly lower standards of health compared to their non-Indigenous counterparts, and although many closing-the-gap programs have been initiated, this gap remains. Recently, there has been a movement away from this deficit model with more attention being paid by governments and researchers to the importance of time on the land as related to health and wellbeing. The proposed project will evaluate two existing land-centred mitigation programs. To evaluate the programs, we will use both quantitative and qualitative methods. We are trying to identify the key elements of these land-centered mitigation programs that promote health and wellbeing in Indigenous homelands, in the context of development. We want to develop a best practices framework that can be used to help inform future negotiated agreements between governments (or other proponents of development) and Indigenous groups, and also inform other government-administered programs. The proposed study will provide Indigenous communities, health care professionals, development proponents, and policy makers with new information on health and wellbeing, with respect to land-centered mitigation strategies.

column36: FANS: Building Evidence to Inform Policies and Programs for Food and Nutrition Security in Manitoba Youth
column37: Food insecurity occurs when people do not have reliable economic or physical access to a sufficient quantity of affordable, nutritious food. Nutrition insecurity occurs when diets are not adequate in terms of variety, diversity, nutrient content, and safety to meet needs for a healthy life. Although food and nutrition insecurity have been identified as public health issues in Manitoba, there is a lack of current, detailed data for program planning and policy development to address these issues among Manitoba youth. This is especially concerning for Indigenous and newcomer youth, who are more vulnerable because of lower socio-economic status. Food and nutrition insecurity exacerbate inequities and increase risk of poorer future health and education outcomes. Working with over 15 partners, this integrated knowledge-translation study will assess food and nutrition insecurity in Manitoba youth, and how the intersection of these conditions impacts health and education outcomes. Aims: 1) describe patterns of food and nutrition insecurity, and associated dietary intakes and behaviours, in youth; 2) examine whether food bank usage and income can be used as a proxy measures for food and nutrition insecurity in youth; 3) examine the relationship between determinants of health, food/nutrition security status, and health/educational outcomes; 4) develop empirical evidence to inform food and nutrition security programs and policies. These aims will be achieved by: surveying the food/nutrition security status, and dietary/food behaviour patterns of grade 9 students; analyzing food bank use data; linking results with administrative data; and sharing results with stakeholders and decision-makers. The research will contribute to reducing disparities by generating important information which can be used by education, government and community experts to design and implement programs/policies (e.g. income security; housing support; school food and nutrition programs; surveillance).

column36: Targeting the EphA2 receptor in triple-negative breast cancer
column37: Targeting tumor-specific molecular alterations is crucial for optimizing cancer treatment and finding new targets is essential for the development of novel, more efficient therapeutic approaches. Previous work has implicated a cell surface molecule called EphA2 in enhancing aggressiveness of multiple malignancies, including breast cancer. In fact, EphA2 is overexpressed in the majority of breast tumors. We recently found that human triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) tumors could be suppressed in mouse models by targeting EphA2 with a synthetic anti-EphA2 antibody. However, a small percentage of tumor cells remain resistant to this treatment. To improve tumor elimination, we plan to use a novel approach called "Synthetic Lethality" (SL), where an inhibition of a SL gene selectively kills resistant cancer cells. Identification and validation of these SL genes would trigger the development of new efficient combination therapies, co-targeting EphA2 and SL genes, which is expected to eradicate TNBC tumors. This is important, as currently there is no effective therapy for TNBC and it is associated with a high rate of patient mortality. In addition, we will use our anti-EphA2 antibody for developing tumor-imaging reagents that would allow to apply non-invasive procedures to identify patients expressing EphA2 in their tumors, who are most likely to benefit from anti-EphA2 treatment. This will help to personalize anti-EphA2 TNBC therapy based on EphA2 expression profiles and thus, optimize its clinical application. Overall, our work will to help to develop new personalized combination therapies that should significantly improve survival of patients affected by TNBC.

column36: Evaluating innovations in transition to adult care: Transition Navigator Trial
column37: Transition to adult care is a challenging and complex time for adolescents and young adults with chronic health conditions. Many patients and families struggle to adapt to adult health care settings, and report difficulties accessing needed services to manage their health conditions into adulthood. Similarly, adult care providers feel unprepared to care for transferred pediatric patients with chronic health conditions, and lack necessary resources and time to manage the complexity and diversity of their psychosocial and medical needs. As a result, transferred patients experience difficulties navigating an unfamiliar adult health care system, and some experience significant and irreversible health deterioration. These gaps in transitional care undermine the long-term benefit of significant investments made in child health. Limited studies to date evaluate the effectiveness of interventions to improve transitional care across multiple health care settings. We propose to evaluate the impact of a patient navigator service to coordinate transition to adult care of adolescents and young adults living with a chronic health condition in Alberta. Our primary outcome of interest is emergency room/urgent care visits. We will also conduct interviews and focus groups to develop an in-depth understanding of participants' and their families' perceptions about the patient navigator role to reduce modifiable barriers to care. We will also create a comprehensive cost model to determine the net health care cost impact attributable to the patient navigator intervention. This study will provide urgently needed data to guide pediatric and adult health care providers and policy makers regarding optimal transitional care delivery and will benefit the growing population of young adults living with chronic health conditions.

column36: Participatory action research for the development of a tailored pediatric-adult transition program
column37: As adolescents with chronic health conditions enter adulthood, they need to be prepared to move from child-centered healthcare services to adult-focused healthcare services. A recent review of research about transition programs found that most of them focused on helping young people transfer to adult centers of care, but few offered support and information to prepare them and their families to address issues beyond the management of their health condition. This situation creates significant challenges for young people who may also benefit from information about managing other aspects of their lives including making healthy lifestyle choices, understanding their reproductive health, negotiating independence from parents, while experiencing the loss of services for children and the relationships they built in the child-centered system. To date, research on health care transition programs does not yet offer a full picture of how well different transition programs achieve goals of successful transition. Additionally, because research is limited, it is difficult to know what aspects of these programs benefit the global well-being of young persons. For these reasons, it is essential to support the development of services that seek to understand and meet the needs of patients during the transition period and to test their actual ability to promote the well-being of children in real-world contexts. We propose a specific kind of study (called "Participatory action research") aiming to engage all stakeholders (such as youth, parents and clinicians) in the development of a patient-oriented transition program. This study design implies that all these stakeholders will be considered as full partners in identifying priorities for developing and implementing a set of transition services. We hope that this original strategy will ensure that the knowledge generated will be useful for those who will use it and that it will help engage them in their institution.

column36: Novel Live TB Vaccines to Replace BCG
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the top 10 causes of death worldwide. In 2015, there were an estimated 1.4 million TB deaths, and an additional 0.4 million deaths resulting from TB disease among people living with HIV, 480,000 new cases of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) were reported, and cases of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) were detected in 105 countries. Because of these situations, effective vaccines are urgently needed. BCG, an attenuated live bacterium, is the only available vaccine against TB. Over 90% of children worldwide are vaccinated with BCG and >120 million doses of BCG are administered annually, making it the world's most widely used vaccine. However, BCG is not an ideal vaccine and has a limited effect against pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults. We have recently identified several molecular factors that affect the vaccine properties (safety and effectiveness) of BCG. Based on these findings, I have developed two strategies to construct new TB vaccines to replace BCG. Firstly, we have constructed a novel recombinant BCG by genetically manipulating regulatory proteins PhoP-PhoR to enhance the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of BCG. Secondly, we have constructed an attenuated live vaccine strain of M. tb (lsr2 deletion mutant), which has the ability to induce macrophage apoptosis and promote antigen presentation. We have made substantial and promising progress on each of this strategy. I describe in this proposal a number of experiments to complete the studies of our promising lead candidates. The outcome of our study will provide more effective TB vaccines to replace BCG, which will help to end the TB epidemic.

column36: The cellular and molecular basis of susceptibility to enteric bacterial infection
column37: Intestinal infection with bacterial pathogens is a major cause of illness, hospitalization, and death, around the world. Food-borne bacterial pathogens can cause food poisoning (gastroenteritis), with symptoms including abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and vomiting. Further, bacterial infection is a potential trigger of inflammatory bowel disease, and a known cause of disease relapse. To identify those at the greatest risk of bacterial infection, and design preventative treatment strategies, it is important to understand the basis of susceptibility to infection. Our intestines have several defence mechanisms to prevent infection with bacterial pathogens. Our immune system can kill or force the expulsion of invading bacteria. Further defence is provided by the thousands of species of non-harmful bacteria that under normal circumstances live in our intestines (the microbiota). Our intestinal microbiota help to prevent infection with bacterial pathogens by competing with them for space and nutrients and by stimulating our intestinal immune defences. Our research uses mouse infection models to understand how disruptions to the intestinal immune system and microbiota can influence susceptibility to pathogenic bacterial infection. We have shown that mice infected with intestinal parasitic worms are highly susceptible to intestinal infection with pathogenic bacteria. This provides us with an excellent model system for understanding how an altered intestinal environment can result in susceptibility to bacterial infection. We will investigate how altered immune activation and disruption of the microbiota during parasitic worm infection alters the ability of pathogenic bacteria to infect the intestine. We expect that our work will contribute to strategies to control bacterial-driven intestinal disease, including gastroenteritis and inflammatory bowel disease, as well as predicting and controlling the adverse effects of parasitic worm infection.

column36: Towards a framework for assessing intolerable suffering: determining eligibility for MAID in Quebec and Ontario
column37: On December 10, 2015, an Act respecting end of life care came into force in Quebec while at the federal level, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to other Acts (medical assistance in dying) took effect on June 17, 2016. Both laws give patients access to medical aid in dying (MAID) under certain circumstances. Among these is that the person experiences intolerable physical or psychological suffering related to a medical condition. Determining if a patient fulfills the eligibility requirements must be done by two physicians or nurse practitioners. Research in other countries with similar requirements suggests that clinicians find assessing suffering to be very difficult and the way they go about doing so varies considerably between clinicians. Furthermore, because the Quebec and federal laws are not identical, there is potential for differences between provinces. In this project, we want to investigate what clinicians are doing in practice when they evaluate the suffering of patients requesting MAID. We will then use this knowledge to propose a method for doing such evaluations. This project has three parts. The first is to compare the methods used to determine intolerable suffering by clinicians who have assessed patients requesting MAID in Quebec and Ontario. The second part is to compare Canadian practices to standards of care and real practice in countries that have similar eligibility criteria to Canada. The third part is to propose an approach for assessing suffering of patients who request MAID. The goal is to provide guidance to clinicians who undertake these evaluations so that they are better equipped to deliver good care in these clinical situations.

column36: Regulation of chromosome cohesion and genome stability by a novel Histone modification
column37: Approximately one in two Canadians will develop cancer during their lifetime. However, cancer treatments have changed little in the last 30 years. The recent success stories of GLEEVEC and similar drugs has generated considerable interest in generating more inhibitors that work in the same way, although they sometimes lack specificity and tumours can become resistant to them. An alternative approach that is gaining momentum is to target cancer cells specifically while they are dividing, causing cancer-specific cell death as a result of massive chromosome segregation errors. This approach would be not only more effective, but would considerably decrease side effects as lower doses of each drug would be required, and would decrease the chance of acquiring resistance, when used in combination therapy. With this mind, my lab is interested in investigating how this approach could be used to target molecules involved in cell division, a process that is invariably disrupted in cancer. We are studying the mechanisms of how the key proteins that guard the integrity of the cell division process are deregulated in cancer cells and how they can be potentially targeted to specifically kill cancer cells and not the healthy neighboring tissue. Our work thus focuses on the basic biology of cancer, but we are also screening for drugs that target some of the proteins we are studying with the ultimate aim of developing new cancer therapeutics. Our research in the basic biology of cancer is therefore directly leading to new advances in the science behind cancer development and translating to tangible benefits for the Canadian public.

column36: Therapeutic potential of resolvins for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe disease characterized by progressive and irreversible muscle wasting. Dystrophic patients display ambulatory dysfunctions in early childhood that quickly degenerates into respiratory dysfunctions and premature death in young adult. The disease is caused by a genetic mutation leading to the loss of expression of dystrophin, a structural protein important for muscle fiber stability. Moreover, we recently showed that dystrophin also regulates the function of muscle stem cells (also named satellite cells), which are responsible for muscle repair. Therefore, muscle wasting observed in Duchenne muscular dystrophy is not only caused by fragile muscle fibers, it is also attributable to poor muscle healing due to impaired muscle stem cell function. Thus, new therapeutic approaches must target muscle stem cells to mitigate the disease. To date, glucocorticoids are the only drugs that can temporarily slow down muscle wasting in Duchenne muscular dystrophy by dampening the chronic inflammatory process; however, they also have detrimental side effects that impair muscle stem cell function and stimulate long-term muscle wasting. Therefore, there is room for improvement and for the development of a more efficient therapy for this severe disease. Our research program investigates the impact of a new class of omega-3 derived mediators for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. These molecules have a potent ability to resolve inflammation, without the harmful side effects, and they could directly stimulate muscle stem cell activity and promote muscle healing. With their ability to dampen inflammation and simultaneously restore muscle stem cell functions, these mediators have the potential to preserve dystrophic muscle function overtime, improve the quality of life and the life expectancy of the patients suffering from Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

column36: The Influence of Age on Driving-Related Cannabis Effects: Exploring Cannabis Use Frequency and Related Factors
column37: Legalization of recreational cannabis use in Canada will have important implications for road safety. In 2012, collisions in Canada caused by cannabis resulted in estimated costs of over $1 billion. Evidence suggests that legalization in some jurisdictions has led to increases in driving under the influence of cannabis (DUIC). While collisions and fatalities caused by DUIC have been most common among young drivers, the increase in DUIC following legalization appeared to be a result of increases in DUIC among older drivers compared to youth. Several impaired driving countermeasures (e.g., graduated licensing) are designed specifically to target young drivers. If legalization results in larger numbers of older cannabis-using drivers, it is important that we understand how cannabis affects driving in both young and older drivers in order to target countermeasures appropriately. It is well known that alcohol increases collision risk among young drivers at a faster rate than among older drivers, which has been attributed to inexperience with both alcohol and the driving task. Evidence regarding possible differences in cannabis use frequency in young versus older populations has varied; but, across populations, use frequency impacts the drug's cardiovascular and cognitive effects and the subjective drug high produced. This study will assess age differences in the effects of smoked cannabis on simulated driving and will explore factors that may significantly affect these differences. Young (19-25 years) and middle-aged (35-45 years) occasional and frequent cannabis users will smoke a cannabis or placebo cigarette in each of two sessions. Before and after smoking, participants will operate a driving simulator, complete cognitive/psychomotor tests, and provide oral fluid and blood samples. Results of the study will have immediate implications for impaired driving prevention, legislation and policy, including standards by which enforcement officers judge driver impairment.

column36: The oral health and dental care pathways of humanitarian migrants: Advancing a mixed methods program of research
column37: There are over 21 million refugees and 3 million asylum seekers in the world today. Canada actively seeks these humanitarian migrants for resettlement. Over 80,000 refugees were resettled between 2015 and 2017, with an additional 58,000 awaiting their asylum requests. Studies indicate that the general health of humanitarian migrants is fragile, especially for those having lived through war, famine, poverty and spent years in refugee camps. Oral health is one area where health research has not yet developed for this population. According to the World Health Organization, there is an urgent need to develop research in this neglected area. Tooth decay (cavities), periodontal disease (bone loss around the teeth), tooth loss, oral cancers, HIV/AIDS-related oral disease and dental trauma are major public health problems. Further, research is increasingly demonstrating important connections among oral health, general health and quality of life (e.g., pain, disability, stigma, loss of taste and smell, inability to eat, smile or communicate). Many general diseases (e.g., diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, cancer) have oral manifestations which then in turn increase the risk of oral disease. Importantly, oral health follows a gradient of socioeconomic status (SES): those with the lowest SES demonstrate the worst oral health, least service use, and poorest treatment adherence. This study is designed to better understand the oral health of newly-arrived humanitarian migrants in Canada and their pathways to finding dental care. This is the first project in Canada to take a systematic approach to the oral health of this population. This study is necessary to provide baseline data from which to develop targeted interventions through a longitudinal program of research on the oral health of humanitarian migrants in Canada.

We identified a protein called Par6, which is frequently up-regulated in advanced breast cancers. Importantly, we could identify these changes in some of the earliest pre-cancer lesions. We hypothesize that Par6 may be a marker to help predict lesions that have the highest likelihood of progressing to cancer. In this project we have four aims to test this hypothesis. 1) We will examine a large number of samples from breast cancer biopsies and determine if changes in Par6 correlate with patient outcomes; 2) We will identify whether different Par6 expression patterns correlate with different signaling pathways that could contribute to cancer progression; 3) Determine the consequence of different Par6 expression patterns on breast cancer progression using novel mouse models.

column36: Mechanisms driving prefrontal cortex development in adolescence
column37: Adolescents are more likely to experience mental health disorders than individuals in any other age group. In Canada 50% of mental illnesses begin during the teenage years and about 1 out of 4 youth meets criteria for a psychiatric disorder. Several strategies are being launched to identify high-risk groups and to improve treatment and prevention programs for the youth. Yet, research on the biological causes of the heightened risk for psychopathology in adolescence is still very much needed to guide these initiatives. My research is concerned with the neurobiology of the developing adolescent brain and its susceptibility to psychopathology. I investigate whether and how environmental factors known to increase or to protect against psychiatric disorders alter adolescent brain development. My ultimate goal is to identify therapeutic targets for early intervention. My work focuses on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a region that develops until early adulthood and undergoes dramatic changes during adolescence. The PFC mediates higher cognitive processing, including decision-making, planning, and motivation. Interestingly, its function is compromised in psychiatric conditions with an adolescent onset, including depression, substance abuse, and schizophrenia. Through studies in rodents and humans, my team identified a set of genes that controls PFC development specifically in adolescence and that are tightly associated with these disorders. My research project seeks to determine (1) how these genes control PFC development, (2) whether they are modulated by adverse experiences, and (3) whether they could serve as biomarkers of vulnerability. My research will have significant implications for the development of early prevention/intervention strategies.

column36: Exercise intensity matters: a window of opportunity to promote neurorecovery and cardiovascular health in stroke
column37: Participating in regular exercise is important for improving walking speed and endurance after stroke. Typically, cardiovascular exercise is performed at moderate intensities in a continuous manner, but if higher intensities can be reached, greater improvements in recovery and function may be achieved. Intensity appears to be a key ingredient in exercise programs for improving both brain health and cardiovascular health. However, high intensity exercise may be challenging for people with stroke, especially if it needs to be sustained for long periods of time to achieve a training effect. It is important to find creative ways to help these individuals exercise at higher intensities that will lead to better recovery and health after stroke. High-intensity interval training is a form of exercise that combines short bursts of intense exercise with periods of active recovery or rest. This type of exercise may be more feasible for individuals with stroke because high intensities do not need to be sustained for long periods of time since breaks are allowed. High-intensity interval training has been shown to be safe and beneficial to many areas of health and function in healthy adults and people with heart disease. To date, only a few studies have examined the effects of high-intensity interval training in people living with stroke, and have mostly focused on improvements in walking ability. Brain health and cardiovascular health are perhaps the two most important aspects to improve stroke recovery and to reduce the risk of future strokes, respectively. High intensity exercise has the potential to improve both of these areas. This will be the first study to investigate the effects of high intensity interval training on brain plasticity and cardiovascular health in people living with stroke.

column36: Reactivating spinal locomotor circuits by non-task-specific sensory feedback from the limbs after complete spinal cord injury
column37: After a spinal cord injury, walking is often impaired and in the most severe cases, the limbs are paralyzed. However, in animal models of complete spinal cord injury, the legs can recover an involuntary walking pattern after a few weeks of treadmill training. This remarkable recovery, first shown in cats, is due to the presence of a centre within the spinal cord that generates the basic walking pattern without descending commands from the brain. During treadmill training, receptors in the legs that respond to weight support and muscle stretch send signals to the spinal cord. These signals in turn reactivate the centre that controls walking. Treadmill training has been shown to improve walking in people with spinal cord injury. However, whether it is more effective than other treatments has been questioned. Treadmill or locomotor training is based on the principle that mass practice of the desired movement must be made to engage the appropriate neural circuits. In other words, if you want to restore walking then you must practice walking. However, our preliminary results show that applying manual pressure to the calf muscles for a few weeks restored walking in our cat model of complete spinal cord injury. These results suggest that when it comes to restoring walking, training does not need to be specific to the task. The goal of this project is to confirm our preliminary results in a larger group and to determine the neural and muscular mechanisms involved in this remarkable recovery. The results could have an important impact on the rehabilitation of walking in people with spinal cord injury because rhythmic manual stimulation of muscles/skin could complement or replace locomotor training. Many people with spinal cord injury cannot engage in locomotor training or other types of rehabilitation approaches because of pain and/or other musculoskeletal injuries. However, people with spinal cord injury could easily receive manual therapy from a trained therapist.

column36: Mechanistic studies of the SMX tri-nuclease with direct links to genome stability
column37: The preservation of genetic material is essential for survival. However, cells are continuously exposed to a plethora of DNA-damaging agents (e.g. sunlight, chemicals). If not repaired, damaged DNA can lead to deleterious consequences, ranging from mutations and chromosomal aberrations to cell death. Cells contain sophisticated DNA repair pathways to preserve genome integrity. Our understanding of the mechanisms that underpin these networks is incomplete. This knowledge is of utmost importance since defects in DNA repair lead to various diseases, including neurological defects, immunodeficiency, and cancer. In order to determine how and why errors in DNA repair lead to these pathologies, we first need to understand the fundamental mechanisms of DNA repair and genome stability. Most DNA repair pathways require nucleases, which are molecular scissors that cut damaged and abnormal DNA structures. This is a critical activity because the failure to remove such structures compromises genome stability. In humans, a protein called SLX4 orchestrates the assembly of a large multi-nuclease complex called SMX. I have recently shown that SMX removes DNA structures that would compromise normal cell function. My work highlights an essential role for SMX in DNA repair and genome stability. However, key questions about SMX structure, assembly, and nuclease activity remain to be addressed. The overarching goal of our research is to understand how the SMX complex operates in human cells. Complementary biochemical and cellular approaches will be used to elucidate the molecular interactions that promote SMX assembly and nuclease activity. These studies will provide a solid framework for understanding how the SMX tri-nuclease functions in DNA repair and genome stability. Likewise, this research will significantly advance our understanding of the essential cellular pathways that go awry in a spectrum of human diseases, including cancer.

column36: Increasing the effectiveness of weight loss programs for emotional eaters: Training emotional eaters to use acceptance-based techniques for weight loss and maintenance
column37: Currently, over 15 million Canadian adults are overweight or obese. Standard behavioral treatment programs are right now the most effective way to achieve lasting weight loss. Emotional eaters lose less weight in such programs and easily gain it back. Emotional eating is defined as overeating in response to negative emotions. The current proposal aims to find ways to make weight loss programs more effective for emotional eaters. We propose to do this by using Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) techniques. ACT techniques are increasingly recognized as tools to avoid emotional overeating and help emotional eaters lose weight. Rather than trying to control negative emotions through change or problem solving (which has been shown not to work for emotional eaters), ACT techniques teach individuals to accept their negative emotions and to react to them in other ways than by eating. We propose to further strengthen the effectiveness of the weight loss program by training the emotional eaters to habitually apply ACT techniques when they have the urge to eat in response to emotions. We will assign overweight or obese emotional eaters randomly to either a standard behavioral treatment weight loss program or our ACT program. In the ACT program, participants will use concrete action plans (if-then plans) to apply ACT techniques to deal with negative emotions that would normally make them eat. In the standard program, participants will use if-then plans to apply cognitive behavioral techniques. We expect that the ACT program will lead to (1) greater and more sustained weight loss than the standard behavioral treatment program and (2) a greater reduction of weight-related risk factors for diabetes and cardiovascular diseases than the standard program. Further, we expect that (3) the greater weight loss is due to higher distress tolerance, better emotion coping habits, and less emotional eating.

column36: The crosstalk of myeloid cells and innate lymphocytes at mucosal surfaces
column37: The gastrointestinal tract is the body's largest mucosal surface. The number of microorganisms seeding this environment vastly outnumber the body's own cell numbers. The intestinal epithelium, a single layer of tightly connected cells, is the first physical barrier to these microbes, while the inner and outer mucus layer serve as chemical barriers and contain antibodies and anti-microbial peptides. Breaching of these barriers by microbes results in inflammation, tissue damage, organ failure and death. It is thus an obvious task to maintain the intestinal barrier function whilst avoiding overriding immune activation. This task demands about 60% of the body's total immune cell mass and further emphasizes the importance of maintaining the homeostasis of the intestinal tract. Macrophages (MP) and Dendritic cells (DC), also termed mononuclear phagocytes (MNP) are the body's major sentinel cells. Their key function is the phagocytosis of foreign antigens, its processing and presentation to T cells as an MHC-peptide complex. This process requires contextual interpretation of the local microenvironment to initiate an inflammatory response against pathogens, or immunologic tolerance towards commensals and food. The molecular cues required to interpret the intestinal microbial composition are poorly defined. It is further completely enigmatic how immunologic tolerance to this vastly great number of bacterial antigens is achieved. The quest for the molecules and mechanisms initiating this process are of great importance, as a growing number of autoimmune pathologies are associated with alterations in the intestinal microbial community. This proposal aims to understand the fundamental signals and mechanisms that are required to initiate the crosstalk of innate immune cells of the intestine, to ultimately control immunity to luminal antigens.

column36: FER as a novel therapeutic target in breast cancer
column37: Cancer is a complex continuum of diseases caused by dysregulated expression of the genes controlling cell proliferation and survival. Unfortunately, many genes can be involved, which explains why cancers are so diverse in clinical behaviour and response to treatment. More effective treatments require more knowledge of the defective regulatory pathways in individual cancers and new therapies to regulate these pathways. In practical terms this means that more effective cancer treatments will involve combinations of therapeutic agents and greater understanding of how their targets regulate normal and cancer cell behaviour. In our previous work we have studied the function of an enzyme called FER in the hope that it might represent a potential novel therapeutic target in breast cancer. To test this, we genetically engineered mice to no longer produce functional FER and found that they are overtly healthy, suggesting that humans might also tolerate inhibition of FER without serious toxicity; an important consideration for any therapeutic target. When these FER-deficient mice were bred to a strain of transgenic mice which develop breast cancer, we observed a significant attenuation in tumor development. We also learned that FER-deficient tumor cells have greatly reduced potential to spread from the site of tumor origin to other organs. These exciting result suggests that FER might represent a novel therapeutic target in breast cancer, and potentially other cancers as well. We have learned a great deal about how FER contributes to cancer cell behaviour, including metastasis and sensitivity to specific therapeutic drugs currently used to treat breast and other cancers. We now propose to validate FER as a therapeutic target in breast cancer, begin developing inhibitors of FER suitable for clinical use, and determine which drugs to combine with FER inhibitors to achieve maximum therapeutic effects.

column36: Examining the consequences of child abuse on cerebral myelination
column37: Child abuse, defined as childhood sexual, physical or emotional abuse or neglect by a parent or caregiver, causes lasting pain and hardship for millions of Canadians. The aim of this research is to understand the nature of the white matter alterations that have been described in people with a history of child abuse. White matter in the brain consists of myelinated axons, which are analogous to insulated electrical wires allowing brain regions to communicate with each other. Neuroimaging studies have found alterations in the organization of white matter in people with a history of child abuse. Unfortunately, the resolution offered by such brain scans in not sufficient to understand the cellular and molecular nature of these alterations. Postmortem human brain samples make it possible to scrutinize the fine neuroanatomy and molecular composition of white matter. Having both the expertise and a direct access to well-characterized postmortem brain samples from the Douglas-Bell Canada Brain Bank, we propose to conduct this research by comparing brain tissues from individuals having suffered from severe child abuse to matched controls. In two major white matter tracts involved in the regulation of mood and emotion, we will isolate myelin-producing cells and determine their molecular and epigenetic profiles. We will also characterize the fine morphology of myelinated axons in these tracts. This research will provide novel insights regarding the cellular and molecular nature of altered brain connectivity associated with child abuse. This may in turn help identify novel therapeutic targets, and better inform public policies aimed at preventing child abuse or minimizing its impact on mental health.

column36: Alternatives to current Chimeric-Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy in acute lymphoblastic leukemia
column37: The technology of Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) is a promising new therapeutic tool in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. Usually, patient's own immune cells (T cells) are modified to express the CAR that allows the T cells to both target and kill the patient's own leukemic cells. Despite the efficacy of this treatment in some chemotherapy-refractory patients, 50% of patients do not respond to therapy or will relapse because CAR T-cells get exhausted and do not persist in the patient. This improved therapy will: 1) increase efficacy; 2) reduce adverse-effects; 3) eliminate graft-vs-host disease risks associated with classic bone-marrow transplant; 4) open the opportunity to have CAR-NK cells from universal donor without compatibility risk. column36: Endothelial Progenitor Cell Exosomes and MicroRNA Transfer as Therapy for Acute Kidney Injury
column37: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious condition in which kidney function falls rapidly (often over minutes to hours), commonly because of loss of blood flow. AKI is frequent, affecting about one out of every twenty people in hospital. In severe cases treatment includes dialysis, but kidney function recovers in only about one half of patients, and mortality is high. Unfortunately, there are no treatments to improve kidney repair after AKI. Use of stem cells may help kidneys recover from AKI. Recently, we isolated "progenitor" cells from human umbilical cord blood and infused them into mice with AKI caused by temporary blockage of blood flow to the kidneys. While the cells reduced kidney damage, they did not incorporate into the kidneys, but rather appeared to release factors that stimulated recovery. In fact, the cells shed tiny membrane particles ("exosomes") that contain a substance called "miR-486-5p". Injection of mice with the exosomes strongly protects them from kidney injury, and the benefits may relate to transfer of miR-486-5p. Use of exosomes may be preferable to cell treatments, since exosomes have a low risk of immune "rejection", and are not likely to cause abnormal cell growth. However, several questions must be answered before exosomes can be given to humans with AKI. Do infused exosomes target specific kidney cells to promote repair, and does miR-486-5p transfer to these cells? How does transfer of miR-486-5p from exosomes reduce kidney injury, and what other effects may occur in the kidney with this treatment? Do exosomes protect against other causes of AKI, such as due to kidney toxins? In this grant, we will conduct animal studies to address these key questions. Detailed animal studies will also be performed to determine the effects of exosome dose, timing of administration, and differences in response according to sex. Our proposal represents the critical next step in developing exosome treatments that could help humans with AKI.

column36: Including Patient Voice in Healthcare System Performance: Development of Patient-Centred Care Indicators
column37: In Canada, efforts are increasingly being made to move healthcare research and policy towards a patient-centred care (PCC) model. PCC is defined as care that is respectful and responsive to individual patient preferences, needs and values, and ensures all clinical decisions are guided by patient, family caregiver values. Traditionally, the quality of healthcare has been driven predominantly by policy makers and evaluated through the lens of healthcare professionals, with limited attention to the perspectives of patients and family caregivers. Recent policy recognizes that patient views about their health and well-being not only complement healthcare provider perspectives, but also enhance the effectiveness and quality of care being provided. Inclusion of both patient and family caregiver views is essential to achieve high quality healthcare. Currently there are no Canada-wide mechanisms to measure and monitor PCC at the system level across the continuum of care. The development of patient-centred quality indicators (PC-QIs) represents a key step towards ensuring that healthcare systems remain responsive to the needs and preferences of patients. Our objective is to develop a set of PC-QIs that will be evidence-based and informed and prioritized by patients, ultimately driving care improvements that patients need and deserve. Patients and family caregivers will be involved throughout the study. The long-term goal is to implement these indicators to measure and monitor PCC across the healthcare system in all patient care settings. We plan to develop PC-QIs through 1) a scoping review, an environmental scan of indicators previously reported in various settings and countries and obtaining input on experiences with the healthcare system from patients and family representatives; 2) consensus of indicators from patients and family representatives, clinicians and decision makers; and 3) assessing the feasibility of implementation of PC-QIs.

The most common cognitive complaint in children born VPT is attention difficulties, which are estimated to affect 30-40% of children. In early childhood, attention skills mature rapidly and help children to succeed as they start schooling. In children born VPT, however, difficulties in attention have been linked to lower academic success. It is therefore important to better understand what puts children born VPT at risk for attention problems and to find ways to support the development of attention skills in young children. Based on our previous research, we believe that there may be alterations in brain networks in children born VPT that predispose them to attention difficulties. To test this, we will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure brain networks in children aged 4-6 years, and a battery of cognitive tests to measure attention skills. These data will be analyzed to better understand how differences in brain networks make children born VPT vulnerable to attention difficulties. column36: Understanding the assembly, trafficking and signalling of G protein-coupled receptor dimers.
column37: Most of the drugs currently used to treat heart failure and related diseases (including beta-blockers) are directed against the largest family of cell surface receptors (which transduce signals outside of the cell into activity inside the cell), the so-called G protein-coupled receptors or GPCRs. These drugs target ligand-binding sites, i.e. the site where endogenous compounds interact with the receptor. Drugs thus act as either agonists, mimicking the effects of the natural ligand or as antagonists, which block the effects of the natural ligand. The problem is that all of these drugs produce significant side effects. This, in part is due to the fact that targeting the ligand binding site may not be specific or selective enough to elicit or block only the desired effect. This is likely due to the nature of the receptor and how it's downstream signalling pathways are organized. These receptors do not as previously believed interact with their signalling partners in a random fashion as a result of agonist stimulation. Recent data has shown that 1) each single receptor can be coupled to multiple signalling pathways in the same cell ; 2) receptors are physically and stably associated with their signalling pathways even before they are activated and 3) these complexes form during biosynthesis, i.e. before the receptor gets to it's final destination in the cell membrane. How then, can we make drugs that are more specific and have less side effects? This project is aimed at characterizing individual receptor signalling complexes, their organization and specificity and how they are assembled. Once we know 1) what is in any given signalling complex in specific cell types and 2) how it is assembled and localized in the cell we can in principle, we can thus reduce the number of side effects seen with current therapeutic approaches to diseases such as cardiovascular disease.

column36: Optimizing outcomes in survivors of childhood, adolescent and young adult cancer
column37: With modern cancer therapies, most children and teenagers diagnosed with cancer will become long-term survivors. Unfortunately, the treatments that lead to their cure also cause significant long-term health problems in many of these individuals. All cancer survivors require life-long medical care that is focused on preventing, or detecting and treating, these long-term side effects of therapy in order to maximize both the length and quality of their lives. My clinical research program is focused on defining Precision Survivor Care: how to ensure that survivors of childhood and teenage cancer receive the most appropriate health care based on their specific long-term risks by considering different clinical settings and health care providers, and how to deliver these services in a way that is most cost-effective for Canada's health care system. To achieve our research goals, we will take advantage of several large North American databases that contain detailed information on over 40,000 survivors of childhood and teenage cancer treated over the last 40 years. We will 1) explore which clinical settings and health care providers lead to the best health outcomes for survivors; 2) develop tools that help us to predict which survivors are at greatest risk for serious health problems, such as heart disease and new cancers, so that we can appropriately screen these individuals; and 3) conduct a study to find out how we can ensure that the greatest number of survivors follow guidelines for screening. The findings from this research will have direct impact on the health and quality of lives of cancer survivors across the country and will inform provincial cancer systems about how best to care for this growing population of young Canadians. This program will also create many opportunities to train the next generation of researchers and health care providers who will focus on ensuring the best possible outcomes for children and teenagers diagnosed with cancer.

column36: T-cell signaling and cancer immunotherapy
column37: T-cells of the immune system recognize and eliminate foreign pathogens. Over the past decade, it has become clear that the same cells can recognize and kill tumor cells responsible for cancer. T-cells express stimulatory and inhibitory receptors that determine how they will respond to tumors. Positive receptors include the T-cell receptor (TCR) and a co-receptor called CD28, while inhibitory co-receptors CTLA-4 and PD-1 reduce T-cell responses. Blockade of these inhibitory co-receptors with antibodies in 'immune checkpoint blockade" (ICB) and the generation of chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) in immunotherapy has now revolutionized the treatment of cancer patients with unprecedented response rates against certain tumors. Despite this success, most patients are not cured, and some cancers are unresponsive. New modalities will depend on an understanding of the make-up of signaling pathways in T-cells engaged by receptors on their cell surface. This grant proposes to discover new pathways that regulate specific T-cells, to uncover how they operate mechanistically and to apply this knowledge to the development of new immunotherapies against cancer. We propose to take a multipronged approach by uncovering the signaling mechanism used by T-cell co-receptors to promote anti-tumor immunity, to 'stop or arrest' T-cells in tumors so that they accumulate to kill the tumor and to block the expression of inhibitory PD-1 and CTLA-4 with small molecules that have therapeutic advantages over present therapies.

column37: Malnutrition remains a main contributor to global child mortality. Approximately, half a million children die each year from severe malnutrition. Severe malnutrition requiring inpatient management is challenging to treat despite the universal use of international treatment guidelines with a mortality of up to 30% of cases. These guidelines are, for the most part, not based on scientific evidence and our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the poor clinical outcome is limited. Only by understanding these basic cellular processes will we be able to provide innovative interventions for critically ill malnourished children. Reports have shown that metabolic disturbances, such as low blood sugars are related to poor outcome and suggest impaired function of liver. In recent studies, we found that, in severe malnutrition, liver cells lose specific cell components called peroxisomes and show poorly functioning mitochondria. In order to achieve our aim, we will perform studies in an established mouse model of severe malnutrition where we can manipulate the degradation of cell components. In addition, we will study the role of impaired function of peroxisomes and mitochondria in severely malnourished children and its relation with clinical outcome. This project is a great example of successfully bringing together leading basic scientists and clinical researchers, with the goal of addressing severe malnutrition in children. Ultimately, insights arising from this project could lead to more effective interventions to reduce mortality in malnourished children.

column36: Autotaxin-lysophosphatidic acid signaling in obesity-related heart disease
column37: Obesity is a serious health problem in Canada. A main complication of obesity is insulin resistance, wherein the hormone insulin loses its ability to stimulate the uptake of blood sugar in tissues. Insulin resistance often leads to type 2 diabetes and can damage heart muscle cells, giving rise to heart muscle weakening. If untreated, obesity and diabetes-induced heart muscle weakening may lead to heart failure and early death. It is important to understand why people with obesity or diabetes develop heart muscle weakening and what can be done to prevent and treat this disease. The objective of this research proposal is to study what is happening in heart muscle cells of obese people with insulin resistance or diabetes that leads to heart muscle weakening. We will examine the role of a small fat molecule, lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), in this process since we have previously shown that the molecular machinery that produces LPA is stimulated in people and mice with obesity. We will test through experiments on animal cells and obese mice with obesity/diabetes, whether high LPA levels and heightened communication between LPA and heart muscle cells cause heart muscle weakening and how this occurs. We will test whether LPA hinders insulin function in heart muscle cells and changes the use of sugar and fats as energy source in the heart. We will also test whether high LPA reduces the function of mitochondria, powerhouses of heart muscle cells. Finally, we will test whether blocking LPA communication to heart muscle cells can protect from obesity-induced heart muscle weakening in mice. This research will allow us to better understand obesity and diabetes-induced heart muscle weakening and develop new and better ways to treat this disease. In doing so, our research is expected to help lower the burden of obesity and diabetes on the Canadian health care system.

column37: Studies into the removal of 'old' cells in mice have shown that this results in a stunning reversal of aging where the mice lived longer and healthier. These mice however were genetically engineered such that their 'old' cells can be triggered to die by ingesting an antibiotic drug. How can we find these 'old' cells in a normal mouse and ultimately human without the aid of such genetic manipulations? This proposal is about engineering a cell to follow these signals to the 'old' cells. Once at the site, the engineered cell will release a biological chemical that kills the 'old' cells. The engineered cell has a suicide gene that converts a particular antiviral drug that is normally not toxic to a form that is very toxic. Hence, after ingesting the antiviral drug, the engineered cell will die. This type of therapeutic intervention is similar to what happens when the cells of our immune system are functioning at their best. Immune cells adeptly detect disease conditions and then respond specifically and locally to minimize side-effects.

column36: Role of Hey2 in heart progenitors and cardiac regeneration
column37: Heart disease remains the major cause of death in North American adults. Lost heart muscle is not replaced following events such as heart attacks. The heart compensates for this to maintain sufficient pump function in a way that ultimately leads to heart failure. Further, congenital heart defects occur in close to 1% of live births, and can have a severe impact on the health and mortality of children. Despite many years of research, little is known about the stem cells that go on to form the different types of cells found in the heart. These cells are called cardiac progenitors. As they are the "building blocks" of the heart, cardiac progenitors are an ideal vehicle to fix the damaged heart. We study this in zebrafish embryos, which allow live and direct visualization of all stages of heart development. Further, the adult zebrafish heart can fully regenerate, a process we seek to understand in order to allow human cardiac repair. In this project, we aim to uncover how a gene called Hey2 regulates the way in which cardiac progenitors make the components of the heart. We have found that Hey2 acts as a master "brake" on stem cells, with cardiac progenitors dividing more and adding more cells to the heart in the absence of Hey2 function. Further, during adult heart regeneration, Hey2 expression is turned off immediately after injury, suggesting that again it is a master brake that must be relieved to allow regeneration. Learning how Hey2 regulates embryonic development and adult heart regeneration are critical first steps towards finding means to drive repair of the human heart. This knowledge will be used to devise therapies based on activating regenerative pathways to heal the damaged heart, and using zebrafish embryos to screen for potential drugs to alleviate the burden of congenital heart defects. Discovering how zebrafish cardiac progenitors are made and develop will therefore drive future efforts to repair what is at present irreparable heart disease.

column36: Let's Stop OA: Development and feasibility testing of an intervention to manage knee osteoarthritis risk factors after anterior cruciate ligament injury
column37: Fifty percent of people who injure the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) develop knee osteoarthritis (OA) in 6-10 years, even if the ACL is surgically reconstructed. Less known by the public, however, are the available ways to reduce the risk of developing knee OA after ACL injury. These include staying active, preventing another knee injury and keeping a healthy weight. Recovery from an injury represents a teachable moment for people to learn about and start practising skills to prevent knee OA. In this project, we aim to develop a new self-management program specifically designed for people to learn about ways to decrease knee OA risk after an ACL injury. Our research questions are: 1) What do people know and do 2 to 3 years after ACL injury to decrease the risk of OA? 2) What are the experiences of people with knee OA symptoms 6 to 10 years after an injury? 3) What makes a self-management program useful, engaging and timely for the target population? 4) Is this program feasible for real-world testing in the community? To answer these questions, we will do a survey of Canadians who recently recovered from an ACL injury to find out what they know and have done to reduce OA risk. We will also interview patients who have developed knee OA about their experiences since the first injury. The results will be used to develop a 'draft' program, which will be shared with 30 to 35 health professionals and patients for feedback. We will then refine the program and launch a pilot test to confirm that the program is feasible for a full-scale testing in the community. This project represents an important step to prevent knee OA. Not only will it add new knowledge to benefit a population that has a high risk for future OA, our research plan will also ensure success in the future testing and real-world use of the self-management program. This will contribute to shortening the well-known "17-year delay" between scientific discovery and tangible benefits for patients.

column36: Identification of molecular determinants of pathological pain in rodent and human spinal cord
column37: Chronic pain affects approximately one in five individuals in Canada. Despite the personal, social, and economic challenges associated with poorly managed chronic pain, there is a lack of efficacious therapeutics. To develop better treatments, the specific sequence of molecular events that leads to dysfunctional pain output need to be determined. We have assembled a multidisciplinary health professional and basic science research team to tackle the challenge of identifying which molecular players are critical for spinal pain pathology. This collaborative effort includes the preclinical biochemistry expertise of the Lombroso lab, the spinal pain research expertise of the Hildebrand and De Koninck labs, and the clinical expertise of the Tsai lab. Importantly, all four of these independent research groups have past experience in translational neuroscience. Using biochemical, electrophysiological and behavioural approaches, our team will identify how protein activity and neuron excitability change in rodent models of pain produced by pain amplifying signals as well as by inflammation. By altering specific molecular processes in these pathways, we will determine which targets are required for increased spinal pain transmission and pain hypersensitivity. Unlike the vast majority of basic science pain research programs, we will also test whether our findings from rodent models of pain translate to conserved pathological mechanisms in human spinal cord tissue, in both males and females. This research plan is anticipated to lead to the identification of specific molecular targets (candidates include Fyn, GluN2B, KCC2, STEP61, and GluN2D) and potential therapeutic strategies for the treatment of intractable human pain.

These studies represent the next major step in the path to translating our findings from stem cell biology to new therapies. Cell-based therapies will represent a fundamental change in our approach to treating blood, heart and liver disease and will dramatically improve the quality of life of Canadians who suffer from them.
