We are studying how these machines are recruited to specific messenger RNAs, and how, once recruited, they shut down protein synthesis. We are also interested in understanding how these machines are themselves being regulated as cells respond to different stimuli. Understanding these fundamental mechanisms that regulate protein synthesis may ultimately allow us to design new molecular diagnostics for screening diseases and potentially target these diseases through novel therapeutic avenues.

column36: Overcoming immune resistance in Gram-negative bacteria
column37: Just like antibiotic resistance genes render bacteria unresponsive to traditional antibiotic therapy, there are bacterial gene products that have evolved to weaken our natural host defenses. These anti-immunity genes carried by bacteria confer intrinsic susceptibility to individuals during infection because of their neutralizing effects on our normally robust systems of immunity. This Project Scheme application builds on 10 years of research towards a comprehensive understanding of how enteric pathogens overcome host immunity by integrating a spectrum of virulence and fitness genes during host infection. Born out of our pioneering work on regulatory evolution as a mechanism of pathogen emergence, we have identified bacterial virulence proteins that inhibit natural host defense systems. Importantly, we have shown that these immune antagonists can be blocked to restore natural host immunity, even against drug-resistant organisms. Therefore, we believe there are strategies to re-sensitize pathogens to our innate immune system and create novel opportunities in anti-infective medicine. Using new technologies in genomics and microbial chemical biology, we are creating an unprecedented opportunity for insight into the interface of human and microbial biology that is informing novel strategies to combat infections and drug resistance. This knowledge base creates opportunities for innovative drug target discovery with tangible impact into public health.

column36: Novel therapies for thrombosis
column37: Thrombosis, blood clots in arteries or veins, is responsible for 1 in 4 deaths in Canada and worldwide. Thrombosis causes heart attacks, strokes and deep-vein thrombosis (DVT), clots in the deep leg veins. Vein clots can dislodge and travel to the lungs producing fatal pulmonary embolism (PE). Clots forming on medical devices such as heart valves can break off and cause PE or stroke. We aim to reduce death and disability from thrombosis by developing safer anticoagulants (blood thinners), manufacturing coatings to prevent clotting on medical devices, and raising awareness about thrombosis. Anticoagulants are a cornerstone of thrombosis treatment. The goal of such therapy is to prevent clotting without causing bleeding. Currently available anticoagulants do not meet this goal and cause bleeding, which can be fatal. Therefore, we need safer anticoagulants. We identified factor (F) XI as a target for safer anticoagulants by showing that an agent that lowers FXI levels is effective and safe for DVT prevention after knee replacement surgery. However, this agent takes several weeks to work. Therefore, we have developed faster acting FXI inhibitors that we will test at the bench, in animals, and in surgical patients. Clotting on medical devices leads to device failure or to PE or stroke. Devices trigger clotting by activating FXI. We have coatings that block this process and we will test them at the bench and in animals before moving to humans. Global awareness about thrombosis lags behind that of disorders such as cancer and AIDS. To overcome this, we launched a year-long educational program culminating in World Thrombosis Day to enhance awareness so that patients can advocate for thrombosis prevention and treatment. We have 1000 partners and a global reach of 2.7 billion and plan to further increase our reach. Therefore, by raising thrombosis awareness and developing novel strategies to prevent and treat it, we will reduce death and disability from thrombosis.

column36: Understanding Schwann cell heterogeneity for improved nerve repair
column37: Traumatic injuries to nerve and other disorders affecting nerve (called neuropathies) are common conditions, resulting in severe paralysis, sensory loss and pain in many Canadians. Techniques to repair nerve injuries to date allow some recovery of function, but most patients continue to have significant neurological dysfunction and debilitating pain. We propose a cell-based therapy to improve outcomes. The adult skin, which can be obtained from patients with minimal side-effects, contains unique stem cells (skin-derived precursors, or SKPs) that can be differentiated into a repair type of cell that normally provides support to nerve cells. This cell, called a Schwann cell, supports nerve cell axons, along with providing insulating myelin and growth factors, which helps axons regenerate following injury. We have already developed techniques to rapidly generate skin Schwann cells (SCs) from human skin, and have preliminary data on their ability to repair nerve and to produce some myelin. In this proposal, we aim to optimize SCs for repair potential and then validate their effect after delivery in a rodent nerve injury model. The optimization of SCs will include approaches to genetically re-program cells and the use of advanced cell identification and sorting techniques to isolate and then expand cells that are most potent for repair. We will deliver the optimized SCs via an approved for human use nerve guidance conduit, leveraging state-of-the-art innovation from a partner company, to examine the functionality of these cells in nerve injury and repair in rodents. We have put together a dynamic team with expertise in nerve surgery and repair (Midha), stem cell biology (Biernaskie) and neural development and genetic reprogramming (Schuurmans) and have some promising preliminary results. This research has the potential to improve the way in how nerve injury is managed, thereby positively impacting the health and well-being of many Canadians.

column36: Control of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling by clathrin signalosomes
column37: Tumours are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists by several changes they exhibit compared to normal cells. Some of these changes involve alteration in the abundance and function of proteins found on the outer surface of the tumour cells. These changes in the function of cell surface proteins are required for tumours to grow and spread throughout in the body (metastasis). Hence, obtaining a better understanding of how cells control the function of proteins found on their outer surface has the potential to provide new ways to treat cancer. One of the types of cell surface proteins altered in cancer cells is hormone receptors, in particular one named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). EGFR signals to cells to grow and migrate and when uncontrolled, these traits can lead to cancer and metastasis. The cell surface is like that of a soccer-ball in that it is made up of "patches". As the hexagonal patches on a soccer ball are of different colours, the "patches" on the outer surface of a cell, termed microdomains, also have unique properties. We have discovered that a particular type of microdomain on the cell surface, called a clathrin signalosome, determines how a cell responds to certain hormones. The hormone receptor EGFR is found within the clathrin signalosomes on the surface of a cell, yet how clathrin signalosomes control hormone receptors such as EGFR remains a mystery. To uncover how clathrin signalosomes control the function of EGFR and thus cancer progression, we will use several different approaches including advanced microscopy of cells engineered to contain fluorescent versions of specific key proteins, allowing us to "see" EGFR within microdomains. This research will reveal how clathrin signalosomes work within healthy and cancerous cells to control EGFR function. Since alterations in the normal function of EGFR cause cancer cells to grow and metastasize, this work may reveal new ways to treat various types of cancer

column36: Experiential learning at the Saint John Human Development Council
column37: The Saint John Human Development Council (HDC) is the only social program planning council in the province of New Brunswick. Established in 1979, the mission of the HDC is to plan, develop, coordinate, and promote social development in greater Saint John. The HDC has been asked to host a new initiative (i.e., the Local Immigration Partnership (LIP)) aimed at improving health outcomes for Saint John's newcomers (i.e., immigrants, refugees), and in turn, its health system. One-year federal funding was provided with the potential for annual renewal for up to three years. The LIP aims to facilitate the development of local, comprehensive, intersectoral partnerships to: 1) integrate newcomer needs into the strategic planning process; 2) identify newcomer and community priorities; and 3) implement a strategy and action plan to improve newcomer (health) outcomes. This limited funding has been awarded at an opportune time. In the past two years, Saint John welcomed over 500 Syrian refugees and New Brunswick had the 5th largest provincial sponsorship of Syrian refugees in Canada. The increase of newcomers presented new and unique challenges to Saint John's health system resources; including a spiked demand on health care professionals due to a lack of a coordinated care approach for newcomers and newcomers' difficulties navigating the health system. With the City and several community organizations, the HDC will work to establish and coordinate a comprehensive intersectoral partnership strategy. The HDC's current budget cannot sufficiently fund a highly skilled project manager (i.e., PhD-trained) and adequately resource its initiative. Thus, HSI funding would provide invaluable assistance to help build capacity in the HDC and its partners, and improve the likelihood of a successful LIP.

column36: Enhancing Nurses' Role in Opioid Stewardship - Implications for health policy, practice (advocacy) and patient safety
column37: Multiple national strategies have been developed address the opioid crisis, however, Canada still remains the second largest consumer of prescription opioids. These drugs can have negative effects on consumers because they have addictive properties so therefore consumers may become addicted to these drugs if there are not taken as prescribed. For other drug classes such as antimicrobials, there have been programs developed to improve prescribing and hence patient outcomes. These programs are collectively called antimicrobial stewardship programs and usually promote cooperation between health professionals. However, most programs do not specify how nurses can promote safe prescribing and they usually are under-utilized in these programs, although it has been shown that these programs lead to better patient outcomes e.g. reduced hospital-acquired infections. For opioids, the concept of stewardship is quite ill-defined so not surprisingly nursing roles in opioid stewardship are also under-utilized. Since, the Canadian Nurses Association is advocating for prescribing by registered nurses (RNs) and nurse practitioners (NPs), this project aims to propose a nurse opioid stewardship framework. Step 1 involves an examination of published studies and other documents produced by governmental bodies to identify what nursing roles have been proposed and which ones currently exist. Step 2 involves stakeholder engagement with policy makers, decision makers, health professionals and patients to obtain their perspectives and recommendations of how opioid management could be improved. Step 3 involves conducting direct observations with NPs and RNs to further understand their role and to see how the recommendations from Step 1 and 2 could be incorporated opioid stewardship.

column36: Improving the Care of Palliative Oncology Patients and the Frail Older People living in the North Toronto Sub-Region of the Local Health Integrated Network
column37: Caring for cancer patients as they approach their final year of life needs to be improved. Many patients are not receiving timely or appropriate symptom relief. Despite preferring to die at home or in hospice, patients die in the hospital or in the emergency department. By breaking down silos, and integrating care across the community and with the patient, we can improve care during the final stages of life. We propose to do this by increasing communication and integration with our family physicians, specialists, hospitals and ambulance services (by electronic records, or telecommunication) such that patients can avoid a hospital admission. Electronic records would include patients' wishes outlined in their advanced care plan. We also propose to improve processes for patients to be directly admitted to hospice, palliative care units or necessary hospital admissions. Our goal is to have patient management aligned with their preferences and to decrease the number of hospital admissions, emergency department visits and associated wait-times.

column37: This Health Systems Impact (HSI) Fellowship will base a current postdoctoral fellow of McGill's Participatory Research at McGill at CIETcanada. Both institutions will provide an invaluable experiential learning environment through their concern in harnessing evidence-based strategies and local knowledge to address real world challenges. Indeed, the overarching goal of CIET is to move epidemiology's center of gravity from universities in rich countries toward places and situations where it is needed most: in developing countries, in emergencies and among marginalized populations. CIETcanada is an affiliate of CIETinternational, which recently established a branch office in Guatemala to address the "last mile" challenge of healthcare in Guatemala's large historically marginalized indigenous-Mayan population, which faces some of the worst maternal and child health statistics in the world. The "last mile" refers to the gap keeping formal health services out of reach for the world's most physically and socially remote people - most particularly women, with important repercussions on maternal and child outcomes. The Fellow will lead CIET's Safe Birth initiative to integrate an evidence-based, participatory, community-led intervention for vulnerable women into Guatemala's formal maternal health programs in collaboration with key local partners, and test its acceptability, feasibility and impact on maternal health and wellbeing. She will also pave the path for scaling up the intervention throughout Guatemala and possibly other contexts worldwide. She will oversee and strengthen the operations of CIET and partners in Guatemala, including capacity building in participatory research, critical thinking and evidence-informed health systems improvement. This Fellowship hence emphasizes health system impact and aims to develop professional experience and transferrable skills that can benefit and constructively engage some of the world's most marginalized populations.

column36: Process Evaluation of the Canadian Blood Services' Cord Blood Bank: Managerial and Donor Perspectives
column37: The goal of this 2-year project is to develop and conduct a qualitative process evaluation of the implementation and outcomes of the Canadian Blood Services' Cord Blood Bank (CBS CBB). An integral component of Canada's public health care system, CBS manages the national supply of blood, blood products and stem cells, and related services for all the provinces and territories (excluding Quebec). Umbilical cord blood (blood collected from the umbilical cord and placenta immediately following birth) is rich in stem cells that are used to treat over 80 diseases. Launched in 2015, CBB is part of the Canadian Blood Services OneMatch Stem Cell Network that aims to match and coordinate delivery of cord blood units to patients. The CBB faces the critical challenge of effective donor recruitment to ensure the program's success. In part because this program is new, detailed understanding of the barriers to, and experiences of, donor participation is lacking. A key impact goal is to optimize the operations of the CBB with a focus on the successful recruitment and participation of donors. The proposed project directly addresses the impact goal and critical challenge of CBS by developing and implementing an evaluation framework to identify and assess the challenges and facilitators that impact the successful recruitment and participation of donors. This project will have two phases. Phase 1 will develop an evaluation framework based on managerial/staff perspectives to identify and clarify the CBB's operations, goals, and challenges related to the overall system and donor recruitment. Phase 2 will apply and refine the evaluation framework based on donor/potential donor views and experiences of CBB's recruitment and donation processes.

column36: Canadian Communities of Practice in Global Health: meeting the SDG challenge
column37: Canada's commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) has implications for both domestic and foreign policy in a complex, shifting, and interdependent global health system crowded with multiple actors and stakeholders. The array of activities involved with global public health practice necessitates engagement with health policy and systems research (HPSR), and Knowledge Translation (KT) is critical to bridging the gap between knowledge generated through research and the knowledge that is used to inform policy, practice, and programs. My proposed two-year Fellowship, with the Canadian Society for International Health (CSIH) and the University of Ottawa, advances KT through deepened engagement with the Canadian global public health community for the integration of SDGs within health systems in Canada and internationally. I will work with CSIH to promote engagement within the Canadian global health community between its annual conferences, bridging the current gap in sustained dialogue in an interdisciplinary global health community that is otherwise not formally connected. Drawing from CSIH's rich membership base and its efforts for collaborative action to achieve SDG implementation in health systems, I will establish two Communities of Practice under this Fellowship: one focusing on Canadian health actors engaged in international health system strengthening abroad, and one drawing together those with a focus on how Canadian health systems are engaging with the SDGs, a topic which, to date, has been largely unexplored. In addressing the dominant themes in SDG research, policy, and practice among Canadian actors in global health, I will coordinate a special issue of an international peer-reviewed journal as part of the dissemination associated with this Fellowship.

column36: Modeling the Transmission Dynamics of Chikungunya Virus: Climate Change and Emerging Viral Threats in Canada
column37: The goal of the fellowship is to contribute to projects of the Public Health Agency of Canada's (PHAC) program on assessing risk of emerging infectious diseases with climate change. Specifically, the fellow will assess the risk of transmission of exotic vector-borne diseases in Canada under current and future climate. In collaboration with the University of Guelph, the fellow will contribute to developing a generic disease risk modeling platform. Development of models to assess transmission risk of Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), a mosquito-borne alphavirus, will be used as a test bed to develop the platform. CHIKV is a globally re-emerging pathogen responsible for ~390 million cases each year and is a major public health concern to PHAC. The virus has recently expanded its geographical range and caused localised outbreaks in Europe following virus introduced by infected travelers returning from endemic countries. Over 500 Canadians acquire CHIKV each year while travelling and many return carrying the virus. However, Canada's cold climate currently limits establishment of key Aedes spp. mosquitoes, but southern regions of Canada are predicted to become suitable for the vector under predicted climate change. Such establishment would facilitate local person-to-person transmission of CHIKV. We propose to develop mathematical models to imitate the dynamics of CHIKV transmission in Canada under the projected climate change and assess the efficacy of known interventions. Assessing risk by predicting the magnitude and geographical distribution of possible CHIKV transmission in Canada and understanding the efficacy of interventions to minimize the public health impact are key elements for long-term planning for prevention of emerging infectious diseases. The ultimate aim is that the model provides a generic platform to assess the current and future risk of transmission of a range of exotic viral diseases (e.g. zika and dengue virus infection) that have the same mosquito vectors.

column36: Healthy Weights Before, During, and After Pregnancy
column37: In Peel, one in three women enter pregnancy with an overweight or obese status. Women who are overweight or obese at the start of pregnancy are more likely to experience gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, Caesarean birth and have a high birth weight baby compared to normal weight women. During pregnancy, only one in four women in Peel (in all body mass index categories) gain the recommended amount of weight. Gaining too much weight during pregnancy can increase the likelihood of Caesarean birth or having a high birth weight baby and can make it more challenging to achieve a healthy weight in the postpartum period. Gaining too little weight can increase the likelihood that baby is low birth weight. The proposed program of work will support Peel Public Health, along with key stakeholders and healthcare partners in developing a collaborative strategy to address women's weight before, during and after pregnancy. This will include a community assessment, an environmental scan, and a literature review. The anticipated results will be the creation of practice-based recommendations, which will help Peel Public Health to better understand its ethno culturally diverse community of families in order to develop equitable and sustainable interventions. The implications of the research will impact the health status of mothers, (e.g., healthy birth weights, reduced gestational diabetes and hypertension), spouses/partners, and their children, setting these children on a positive trajectory that will have life-long impacts on their health.

column36: Implementing and evaluating the scalability of COMPAS-SM: a patient-oriented quality improvement intervention targeting mental health care in primary care
column37: I will be conducting my fellowship within the Institut national d'excellence en sante et en services sociaux (INESSS), which that promotes clinical excellence and efficient use of resources in health and social services in Quebec and supports evidence-informed policy within the Ministry of Health and Social Services. My project will advance INESSS's strategic objective to promote best practices and quality improvement in mental health care in primary care settings. The aim of my project is thus to implement and evaluate an intervention designed to improve the quality of mental health care in primary care. The name of this intervention is COMPAS-SM and it builds on previous COMPAS interventions led by INESSS in the area of chronic disease care. The COMPAS intervention has three main components, namely to present regional data on quality of care to primary care providers from that same region (i.e. feedback component), to stimulate discussion and critical reflection on this data (i.e. reflection component), and to facilitate the creation of quality improvement action plans to address priority gaps in quality (i.e. action plan component). The focus of my project will be on depression care and will be conducted in two phases. Phase 1 aims to implement the new COMPAS-SM intervention by identifying and prioritizing new indicators for depression care in primary care, extracting data on these indicators from INESSS's medical administrative databases, and then preparing and holding four COMPAS-SM workshops with primary care providers from two health regions. Phase 2 involves evaluating various aspects that will help us understand how to scale up the intervention to new mental disorders and territories, including its alignment with contexts, feasibility, adoption and effectiveness. This project is a perfect blend of my interests and those of INESSS, and will spark new initiatives to improve the quality of mental health care in primary care.

column36: Research informing Canada's Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour, and Sleep Indicator Framework: Setting priorities, informing surveillance needs and integrating knowledge translation
column37: One of the Public Health Agency of Canada's central activities is to conduct public health surveillance to report on the state of Canadian's health, identify areas in need of intervention and evaluate current programs. The Agency has a history of program and policy initiatives related to health behaviours such as physical activity. More recently, the Agency has been working to update how it measures factors related to healthy living to better align with emerging research and needs of programs and policy priorities. Specifically, the Agency is looking to also include measures such as sedentary behaviour and sleep. Sedentary behaviours include, for example, the time you spend sitting while watching TV, using a computer or riding in a car and have been shown to negatively impact health. The Agency also recognizes the importance of the environments that support healthy behaviours and are also committed to providing surveillance on factors in these environments. The work proposed for this fellowship will identify the best measures to use in Canadian surveillance for measuring sedentary behaviours at home, work, in travel and during leisure time. Further, it will identify factors in the environments related to these behaviours and identify how best to measure them. The fellowship will also assess the accuracy of measuring physical activity in children as part of a new national health survey. Priority setting for the measures will be undertaken and a strategy to disseminate knowledge from the research to partners such as program and policy developers, as well as the public will be developed. The proposed research will improve the health of Canadians and the health delivery system by providing sound information on which to base decisions for policy and program develop, as well as to evaluate current programming.

column37: Heart failure affects one million Canadians, with at least 50,000 new patients diagnosed each year. Current guidelines suggest that patients with heart failure (HF) be treated in a specialized, multidisciplinary clinic. The largest of these HF clinics is located at the Ted Rogers and Family Centre of Excellence in Heart Function at the Peter Munk Cardiac Centre, Toronto General Hospital (Toronto, ON). However, there is no guideline for what constitutes the best or most necessary type of care provided by HF clinics. As such, the Centre is focusing on improving and optimizing the care they provide in the clinic. We will first understand the current state of care provided by the HF clinic at the Toronto General Hospital, then review the existing evidence, and work with patients and staff to develop and implement change ideas to improve care. Small-scale implementation of these change ideas will be tested using quality improvement methodology. Rapid cycle evaluations will focus first on implementation and process metrics, followed by patient and system-level outcomes, to ensure success. We will then develop a large-scale implementation strategy and evaluation plan to improve the care provided by the clinic, ideally redirecting limited health care resources to more effective, patient-centred care. Our project will be grounded in patient engagement and experience-based co-design, bringing patients and providers together as equals. Working together, we will identify areas for improvement and design and evaluate these change ideas, ensuring our solutions will be feasible, relevant to staff and patient-centered.

column36: Embedding Shared Decision-Making in Patient Centered Care in Community Rehabilitation Programs in Alberta
column37: The phrase "no decision about me without me" (Coulter, 2011) is central to the changes taking place within community rehabilitation programs in Alberta Health Services (AHS). Like many health systems, AHS is moving toward better patient engagement in healthcare practice and policy. Shared decision-making (SDM) is essential to patient engagement and patient-centred care. SDM recognizes patients and their values as the centrepiece around which healthcare should be planned. AHS has developed a new model for how care will be delivered in community rehabilitation that prioritizes collaborative goal setting, co-created transition planning from hospital to community, and holistic partnerships between clients, providers and community. AHS has established a program of learning and evaluation to support the system change to this new model for care delivery. The program is called Innovation Collaboratives. My research will examine facilitators and barriers to the implementation of this new care delivery model, and the Innovation Collaboratives supporting it. Using an ethnographic design, information will be gathered from rehabilitation clients and providers. This information will describe perceptions and experiences of shared decision making, patient engagement, quality of life and functional status at 2 time points. Qualitative interviews will be conducted for in-depth understanding. A feasibility study will be done first. It will clarify which community rehabilitation clinics are best suited for this study and make sure the survey instruments are reliable in this population. AHS will get a tool at research completion to aid in transforming the study findings into effective training modules and policy positions on SDM. This knowledge translation tool will be pilot-tested in community rehabilitation clinics with upcoming Innovation Collaboratives. This research project will help AHS expand their new model of care for community rehabilitation to improve SDM.

column36: Cellular mechanisms and the mechanics of a cleft-like tissue boundary
column37: The human body contains hundreds of different cell types which are uniquely organized into tissues and organs, and it is essential that cells respect the boundaries between anatomical structures. An example of a dramatic failure of boundary function is the invasion of healthy tissues by malignant cells during the spreading and metastasis of cancer. We study a specific type of boundary, cleft-like tissue boundaries, which develop in the embryo and give rise to the interfaces that separate tissues and organs in the adult organism. Here we propose to study the mechanical properties of such a boundary, to discover the general principles that underlie cleft-like tissue separation mechanisms. Some of the molecules involved in boundary formation are also known from their role in cancer progression, and by linking the function of these molecules to mechanical properties of tissue interfaces, we will make metastatic processes understandable at a new level, and add to the repertoire of possible approaches to interfere therapeutically.

column36: Investigating LKB1-mediated inflammation as a mediator of tumour progression
column37: It is now appreciated that the immune system plays an important role in controlling cancer progression. Recent work in understanding how T cells respond to the tumour microenvironment has led to transformative therapies - so called "immune checkpoint blockade" therapies - used to treat cancer by unleashing anti-tumour immune responses. However, inflammation is a double-edged sword. Tumour-associated inflammation has been shown to be an important contributing factor to cancer progression. Understanding how inflammation is regulated in the tumour microenvironment may help us to design rational therapies that circumvent the tumour-promoting effects of inflammation while maintaining or enhancing anti-tumour immune responses. Current models propose that immune cell interaction with the tumour microenvironment promotes cancer-associated inflammation. Our results indicate that the tumour suppressor LKB1, mutated in multiple cancers including lung, breast, and pancreatic cancer, can regulate tumour-intrinsic and tumour-extrinsic effects on cancer-associated inflammation. This proposal investigates the role that inflammation controlled by LKB1 has on cancer development and progression, and whether we can use existing drugs to block inflammation and reduce cancer incidence.

column36: Histone variant H2A.Z as a novel therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating form of dementia characterized by memory loss and accumulation of amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles. Developing effective therapies relies on uncovering common mechanisms that underlie memory loss and AD pathology. Here, we will test the role of a newly identified memory suppressor, histone H2A.Z, as a key contributor to memory loss and AD pathology in several mouse models of AD. We recently discovered that H2A.Z impairs memory in normal mice and that levels of H2A.Z are increased in a mouse model of AD, suggesting that therapies aimed at inhibiting H2A.Z may reverse memory deficits. We will test this hypothesis using four approaches. First, we will use genome-wide sequencing to characterize AD-related changes in H2A.Z levels and distribution across the genome, allowing us to identify key genes and gene regions affected in AD. Next, we will determine if learning-induced changes in H2A.Z binding are impaired in mouse models of AD by quantifying 2 distinct histone pools that regulate stimulus-induced changes in H2A.Z. Third, we will test the efficacy of H2A.Z and the proteins that regulate its binding for treating memory loss and pathology in mouse models of AD. We will use virally-mediated approaches to deplete genes encoding H2A.Z, or the H2A.Z-regulating proteins Anp32E and Scrap. Finally, we will validate H2A.Z as a target in human AD brains, and use human cell lines to directly test the ability of H2A.Z to reverse AD pathology. The use of multiple H2A.Z regulators allows us to test several promising new targets as potential AD therapies, with the potential to simultaneously reverse memory deficits and the underlying plaques and tangles through a novel category of histone proteins.

column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of neurogenesis in the retina: towards improved cell therapies for retinal dystrophies
column37: In retinal degenerative diseases, the progressive loss of the light-sensing photoreceptor cells eventually leads to blindness. Cell-based therapies are generating excitement for the treatment of retinal degeneration, as they offer the potential to restore vision. But this approach still faces major challenges. Photoreceptor cells are highly specialized neurons and generating them from stem cells remains inefficient. While some improvement was made in recent years to increase rod photoreceptor production from various populations of stem cells, the generation of a large number of cone photoreceptors, essential for daylight vision, remains a challenge. Our hypothesis to explain this limited success is that current protocols do not take into consideration the intrinsic identity of stem cell-derived progenitors. As in normal retinal development, we believe that stem cell-derived retinal progenitors have an intrinsic temporal identity that restricts their competence to generate specific populations of cell types produced during a given time window. Cone photoreceptors, for example, are produced at early stages during retinal development, whereas rod photoreceptors are produced late. Understanding how progenitors change over time to switch from cone-producing phase to a rod-producing phase is essential towards improving cell replacement protocols. We posit that manipulating the temporal identity of stem cell-derived retinal progenitors will increase cone production, which could be used for grafting or disease modelling. We will test this idea using human embryonic stem cell-derived retinal progenitors and provide mechanistic insights on how temporal identity is regulated in retinal progenitors during retinal development using mouse models. We will also test whether temporal factors can be used to reprogram retinal glial cells into photoreceptors, which would bypass the need for costly stem cell culture and grafting by stimulating endogenous regeneration.

column36: The subgenual anterior cingulate cortex and chronic pain
column37: Pain is a major public health issue and societal problem that affects millions of Canadians (more than those with heart disease, cancer, and diabetes combined), costs >$43B annually and is difficult to treat when chronic because it is not well understood. Brain stimulation has been used to treat chronic pain but is effective for only a minority of patients. What distinguishes responders from non-responders is not known. We recently discovered that healthy people differ in how an area of the brain called the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) communicates with the brain's pain modulation circuitry, and this difference can contribute to how they modulate pain. In this project, I will characterize neural activity within the sgACC and its communication with the brain's pain control system, and determine whether it is abnormal in patients with different types of chronic pain. I also measure the functioning of the sgACC system in patients before and after they have undergone nerve decompression surgery to alleviate chronic pain associated with carpel tunnel syndrome. This project will provide fundamental knowledge about the individuality of the pain modulation system in the brain. The project will also identify particular characteristics of the sgACC system that are present in patients prior to ineffective or effective surgery. This information could then be used to predict which patients will benefit from carpel tunnel surgery. More broadly, the information could be used to select patients most likely to benefit from other procedures that stimulate that brain that could be developed to modify how effectively the brain's pain modulation system works.

column36: SHRed Injuries: Preventing Injuries and their Consequences in Youth Sport and Recreation
column37: Injuries are not accidents; they are predictable and preventable. Injuries are the leading cause of ill health and mortality in Canadian youth. Sport and recreational (S&R) injuries account for more than 40% of this burden. One in 3 youth seeks medical attention for a S&R related injury each year. Lower extremity injuries comprise most of these injuries. Consequences of S&R injury include reduced physical activity, obesity, osteoarthritis, disability, and economic burden. The goal of my research program, "Surveillance in High Schools to Reduce Injuries and their consequences" (SHRed Injuries), is to promote a healthy and active future for youth through research in injury prevention in S&R, to reduce the public health burden of lower extremity injuries and their consequences. I will aim to 1) Reduce the number of youth lower extremity S&R injuries and associated economic burden through effective prevention programs such as through evaluating strategies such as sporting rules/policy changes, training strategies, and equipment recommendations; and 2) Enable more youth with lower extremity injuries to return safely to health and daily activities by reducing injury consequences and associated economic burden by developing and evaluating prevention strategies to prevent injury consequences. The foundation of my program will include comprehensive injury surveillance that I have developed and validated in youth sport. My research program has influenced best practice and policy through sustainable solutions that have had significant public health impact by reducing the burden of youth S&R injury. My research program will engage youth, parents, coaches, clinicians, sport organizations, educators, and policy makers across health care, education, and public health. The program will target a 25% improvement in decreasing the number of youth S&R injuries and enabling more youth to return safely to health and daily activities by reducing injury consequences and economic burden

column36: Commensal fungal metabolism in lymphoid organ development and maintenance
column37: In our intestine, there is a large cohort of microbes, including bacteria and fungi. Their presence is important for our immune system development. In germ-free mice (no microbes in the gut), lymph nodes in the host are small and incapable of mounting efficient responses against invading pathogens. For many years, we know this dependence of our immune system on those "microbial guests", but no molecular understanding was available. We previously found that a group of resident fungi called Candida tropicalis is critical for the peripheral lymph node maturation. The presence of these fungi in our gut microbiota drives a group of retinoic acid-producing dendritic cells (a type of immune cells) to leave the gut and come the growing lymph nodes, where they stimulate the structural development. They do so by inducing a particular set of molecules, PNAd, at the entry portal of lymph nodes. Interestingly, in the early weeks, lymphocytes entering those sites are educated to return to the gut to build the defense there first. This makes sense as the microbial burden is the heaviest in the gastrointestinal tract after birth. To follow up on those findings, we plan to study what types of fungal productions are driving these cells to leave the gut, and how these dendritic cells change the chemotaxis molecule expression in the peripheral lymph nodes. We also wish to study whether the homing of lymphocytes from the peripheral lymph nodes is critical to the initial gut immune homeostasis in the neonates. These questions are critical for us to comprehensively understand the interplays between our microbiota and the health of our immune system.

column36: ROS metabolism and mitochondrial function in the aging process and in age-dependent diseases.
column37: Most diseases that threaten Canadians, including cancer, heart disease, metabolic diseases, and neurodegenerative disease (such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease) are associated with age: they are much more likely in older individuals. Our goal is to understand the role that free radicals (also called reactive oxygen species (ROS)) play in the overall process of aging and in age-dependent diseases. Free radicals are chemically reactive molecules, which means that they can potentially damage cellular constituents. However, we have discovered that, rather than causing aging, the important role of free radicals as regulators of cell function contributes to longevity by helping cells and organisms to react to, and combat, various stresses. On the other hand, in aging individuals, the production and removal of these free radicals becomes much less well-balanced. It is in this situation that free radicals can be produced in excess, thus leading to damage to cells and promoting the development of disease. We are studying the role of free radicals in both situations, beneficial in young individuals and potentially deleterious old individuals, in order to learn both to harness their beneficial properties and protect from their deleterious effects.

column36: Affective heart disease and physical activity messages for women
column37: A lot of time and money is spent to create messages that try to educate women about heart disease. These messages also give information about heart healthy behaviors like being more active. Most of these messages talk about the health benefits of exercise and suggest things like setting goals to help women be more active. Women with heart disease tell us the messages can make them feel guilty, that they caused their own sickness. The emotions we feel are very important and influence what we choose to do. Researchers have suggested that messages should deliberately try to make women feel good about being active, even if they already have heart disease. This research will try to do that. The first thing we will do is create messages that try to make women with and without heart disease feel good about being active. We will ask women to comment on the messages and will change the messages based on the comments. We will test if the new messages make women feel better (for example, happier or less stressed) than messages that talk about why being active is good for you. Those messages also ask women to set goals and that can be hard for them. We will see if the women who read the emotional messages move more compared to women who read the other messages. This research tests what women think about existing heart disease prevention messages. If the new messages cause positive emotional responses then maybe heart healthy behaviours will also change. This research may impact the health of women with and without heart disease because physical activity is good for most people. If successful, this study design can also test messages about other things like smoking and diet. It might seem like a small change in how heart disease is talked about, but many people and groups can use the results. In that way, many people can be positively affected.

column36: A ONE Health approach for the prevention of MERS-CoV
column37: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a newly emerged pathogen that causes severe respiratory disease in humans. To date, more than a third (35%) of people infected do not survive. MERS-CoV is thought to be passed from dromedary camels to humans. Contact with dromedary camels is a frequent factor in initial human cases. These primary humans cases have subsequently caused large outbreaks of MERS-CoV, typically in hospitals. This has resulted in the temporary closure of healthcare facilities in order to control the spread of MERS-CoV. Here we propose to design a vaccine that stops transmission of MERS-CoV in camels, and as result transmission to humans as well. The vaccine we are designing is based on one that is already used in dromedary camels for the prevention of camelpox. This vaccine, called Ducapox, is a weakened version of the virus that causes camelpox in camels. We have introduced the gene that encodes the spike protein from MERS-CoV into this virus and propose to use this approach to demonstrate that this vaccine can prevent infection alpaca with MERS-CoV. Then, using assays that measure various components of the immune response to infection and vaccination we will determine what immune response results in protection from infection with MERS-CoV. From our previous work we know that alpacas are protected from re-infection and thus we can compare and contrast the immune response from experimental infection to the immune response to vaccination. Here we propose that an agricultural vaccine for camels can prevent infection and transmission of MERS-CoV in camels to halt MERS-CoV infections in humans.

column36: Risk prediction of sudden death in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: the Canadian ARVC registry
column37: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is an inherited heart condition associated with life threatening heart rhythm disturbances in early/middle adulthood that affects more than 10,000 Canadians. ARVC is commonly associated with cardiac arrest and sudden cardiac death. Early diagnosis of ARVC can lead to effective treatment approaches, including exercise restriction, medical therapy and selective use of implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs), a pacemaker-like device that can correct dangerous heart rhythms with a shock. Given the high risk for cardiac arrest and sudden death, and the benefit of early prevention, new methods for identifying those patients at risk are urgently needed. Our primary goal is to develop new methods for predicting which patients who have a genetic predisposition, or who have been diagnosed with ARVC, are at greatest risk of collapse and sudden death. To do this, we will use the proposed Canadian ARVC registry, which enrolls ARVC patients from 15 clinics across Canada. As a secondary goal, we will explore the impact of ARVC on the understanding, emotions and attitudes of patients and their families. We anticipate that this research will lead to: 1) The development of a risk score that can be used to treat ARVC patients, 2) An understanding of the effect of specific genes on the way in which ARVC presents and the risks of each gene finding, 3) A Better understanding of how the disease progresses, 4) Finding new factors that may modify the severity of the disease, particularly behaviors that increase the risk for sudden death (for example exercise), and 5) The ability to target the use of invasive and expensive ICDs, so they are implanted in the right people to prevent sudden death. The knowledge gained by these studies will be used to identify at-risk family members, offering earlier intervention and precise treatment to slow disease progression and to prevent sudden death.

column36: Generalized anxiety disorder in older adults : Efficacy of a self-help treatment guided by trained lay providers
column37: Few older adults receive treatment for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) despite a high prevalence in this population and significant associated health care costs. Although older adults generally prefer psychotherapy to medication for help with anxiety, face-to-face psychotherapy is difficult to access for many of them. Psychological guided self-help (GSH), which patients use by themselves at home under the supervision of a licensed mental health provider (e.g., psychologist), has been shown to be effective. However, the capacity of our health care system to respond adequately to the mental health needs of seniors has been questioned and cost-effective solutions are required. Because the therapist's role in GSH is limited to supporting the patient, it is conceivable that this role could be assumed by trained and supervised lay providers (LP) instead of licensed providers. If this approach is effective, it could help provide many older adults with much needed mental health treatment at a lower cost. The main objective of this project is to evaluate the effectiveness of GSH guided by LP for GAD in older adults. Participants will be assigned randomly to an experimental group, which will receive treatment immediately, or to a control group whose treatment will be delayed. Data will be obtained through clinician evaluations and self-assessment questionnaires. They will include socio-demographic characteristics, symptoms of GAD, variables related to anxiety, such as depression and sleep difficulties, and participants' perception of treatment. Data collection will take place at different times: before treatment begins, after treatment ends, and at 6 and 12 months after the end of treatment. The efficacy of GSH will be established by comparing the change in the two groups on the main variables. We will also identify the characteristics of patients associated with improvement during treatment and document their perception of treatment.

column36: Minimizing Lung Injury during Mechanical Ventilation
column37: Over 90,000 Canadians each year become critically ill and need a life-support device called a mechanical ventilator; this forces oxygen into the lungs through a breathing tube, and helps the patient to breathe. While mechanical ventilation saves lives there is also a serious price: forcing air into the lungs causes additional lung damage that can lead to disability or death. The current grant application builds on two novel findings in my laboratory. First, our laboratory reported that an old-fashioned 'Iron Lung' could be applied to the outside of the abdomen (not the chest) in conjunction with conventional mechanical ventilation; the effect was to selectively open up the lower parts of the lung without over-stretching (and injuring) the upper lung regions. We will understand how this works, and then by knowing which patients might benefit, will rapidly move to test the approach in volunteers and then in patients. If successful, this would represent a fundamental advance in mechanical ventilation. Second, briefly disconnecting a ventilator, a common occurrence to carry out routine patient care, can result in rapid deflation of the lung. This was traditionally thought to be without consequence. However, using laboratory models we have discovered that this may cause significant harm, and have preliminary data explaining how and where in the lung this harm occurs. We will determine the exact mechanisms and then determine if this occurs in patients, and devise approaches to its prevention. These two complementary lines of research will make mechanical ventilation safer (and more effective) and if successful, will save the lives of many critically ill patients.

column36: Characterizing RecQ helicase Sgs1 in maintaining genomic stability during aging
column37: Cancer and aging are seemingly distinct events. However, similar changes in the ability of our cells to respond to environmental challenges are observed in both aging and cancer. For example, damage to DNA, our hereditary material, accumulates in both cancer cells and older cells. Normally, when DNA becomes damaged, pathways become activated to repair the damage. These repair pathways are known to become disrupted in cancer and now some pathway components are proving to be effective targets in particular types of cancer therapy. In older cells, DNA damage accumulates, however the underlying reason for this is not known. To date, most work in cancer research has been performed in young cells, young model organisms or in human cancer cell lines. Since most cancers occur in older individuals, we believe that it will be much more relevant to study DNA repair during aging, especially since there is very little known about how these processes might change or contribute to cancer development. Confounding issues certainly arise with age, but at the cellular level, where cancer and aging biologically converge, pathways that protect our DNA from mutations clearly need to be studied in cells that have aged. My lab uses the model organism budding yeast. Over the past 60 years, work in yeast has provided a foundation of knowledge critical for understanding the molecular events leading to cancer in humans. Since yeast cells are well characterized regarding DNA repair and they also age, they represent a powerful model for rapidly asking how age is related to DNA repair. Thus, characterizing DNA repair in old yeast cells will provide important clues for why DNA repair efficiency decreases and cancer increases exponentially with age in our population.

The field of Knowledge Translation (KT) has emerged and is expanding in attempt to speed up this process. The long term goal of this project is to improve the health of people across Canada by ensuring the latest research is quickly incorporate into everyday health care practice and policies.

column37: Everyday we breathe in over 10000 liters of air just to survive. For some of us, breathing in air presents no problems. For over 3 million Canadians with lung diseases, breathing in air can lead to lung "attacks" that make it difficult to breathe, require hospitalization, and in the most severe cases, death. The air that we breathe in daily can contain substances like air pollution, allergens, cigarette smoke, fungi, bacteria, and viruses. Studies have shown that exposure to these substances can lead to lung "attacks" in those with lung diseases, but it remains a mystery as to how this happens. Our research group studies how exposure to inhaled substances can lead to inflammation in the lungs and how this leads to lung "attacks". We are studying how inflammation "leaks" out of different cells in the lung in response to inhaled substances, leading to a spread of inflammation that can grow bigger and bigger if left unchecked. We propose that plugging the "leaks" can prevent inflammation from spreading, preventing lung "attacks", and saving lives. Our experiments are designed to study a specific "leak" that is important in inflammation, determine how this "leak" is different in healthy and diseased patients, investigate how genetic differences contribute to this "leak", and to make safe drugs that can plug the "leak". Collectively our studies will increase our understanding of how inhaled substances can trigger lung "attacks" and also provide a unique new strategy for treating individuals that suffer from lung diseases.

column36: Quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Pulmonary Edema: Application in Acute Heart Failure
column37: Heart failure (HF) affects over half a million Canadians and growing. Acute HF is a leading cause of hospitalization (>65 years) and 20-30% of these patients die with 6 months, with a cost of billions of dollars a year. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (water in the lungs) is a key symptom of HF (a result of poor heart function) and is a major cause of shortness of breath. Treating edema is the primary treatment in acute HF. However, pulmonary edema is most commonly assessed with qualitative tests like a stethoscope and/or chest X-ray. There is a widely recognized need for safe tests that can quantify the amount of water in the lungs in patients with pulmonary edema, particularly for the evaluation of existing and newly developed treatments. We propose that magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an ideal teat for assessment of pulmonary edema (the source of MRI signal is water). We will develop new fast MRI methods to make lung water maps. The aims of our proposed research program are to first to develop new MRI methods that will allow fast and accurate images of the amount of water in the lungs. We will use these methods determine normal values for MRI lung water density. These values are need in order to identify which patients have elevated lung water. Second, we will study heart failure patients admitted to hospital for acute HF, who are treated primarily for their pulmonary edema. We will measure the change in lung water with standard hospital therapy (e.g. diuretic). We will show that we can directly measure the amount of water removed with therapy, and thus show that MRI is a good test to study new drugs. Finally, we will determine the relationship between elevated lung water and subsequent events, such as emergency room visits, hospitalization or death. We will show that elevated lung water will predict these events. This is important as we will be able to identify which patients need to managed more aggressively, to help avoid these future events.

column36: Structure-function relationship of peptidoglycan O-acetyltransferase, a potential new antivirulence target to combat AMR
column37: Ensuring the mechanical strength of their cell walls is essential to the viability of bacteria. This strength to the wall is conferred by a continuous (macro)molecule unique to bacteria called peptidoglycan which completely encases the cell. Given the importance of the peptidoglycan layer for bacterial survival, it is not surprising that higher eukaryotes have exploited this "Achilles heel" to combat infections. However, pathogenic bacteria have adapted to this response by chemically modifying their peptidoglycan thereby preventing its disruption. One such modification is O-acetylation. In the absence of this modification, pathogenic bacteria become extremely susceptible to host innate immune factors, particularly to the peptidoglycan-lytic enzyme called lysozyme. Additionally, this O-acetylation serves to control peptidoglycan metabolism within a bacterium by blocking the function of endogenous lytic enzymes essential for cell growth and division. Consequently, bacteria require the activity of an enzyme (named Ape) to remove blocking acetyl groups when required to permit continued PG metabolism. Inhibition of Ape prevents further growth of bacteria that require the enzyme (eg., Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and its activity is essential for survival of Neisseria meningitidis in animal models. The research plan that we propose builds on our findings to date on the specificity and structure-function relationships of the enzymes involved in both adding and removing this O-acetylation. Experiments involving biochemical, kinetic, and structural characterisations are designed to better inform the search/development of strong inhibitors of these enzymes that my represent leads to new antibacterials.

column36: Children's Street Crossing Behaviours and Pedestrian Injury Risk
column37: Unintentional injury is the leading cause of death for Canadian children 1-19 years. For elementary-school children, motor vehicle pedestrian injury is the key issue. The proposed research will address this issue by studying how children cross streets and identifying risk factors for injury. Although both environmental factors and child attributes are implicated in pedestrian injuries, few studies have explored interactive effects of these factors (e.g., Do child attributes elevate injury risk only under certain traffic conditions?). Also, research has been limited by the challenge of how to measure children's crossing behaviors in traffic without elevating risk of injury. This research will address these issues in an innovative way -- using a Virtual Reality pedestrian environment to study how children cross streets in highly realistic traffic conditions that can be completely controlled. The overall goals are to determine: (1) how individual-difference attributes interact with contextual factors (built environment features, traffic conditions) to influence children's risk of injury when crossing streets and (2) if these relations differ by child sex or age group (e.g., Can attention differences explain why boys and younger children are at highest risk for pedestrian injuries?). The knowledge gained from this research can inform: city planning about traffic flow and road design; school policies about crossing guards and guidelines about safe school routes; guidelines for parents about children's readiness to cross unsupervised; and the development of behavioral training systems to teach children safer crossing skills.

column37: Blood vessels in a healthy adult are stable and do not change very much. When diseases affect blood vessels, the cells that are contained in blood vessels can change. If we are correct, we will be able to test the idea that using drugs that act at these specific sites, rather than everywhere in the cell, we will have fewer side-effects than are seen in drugs that target these events everywhere in the cell. column37: Depression is a debilitating mental disorder affecting over 350 million people globally and is associated with high personal and socioeconomic burden. Efficacy of classical antidepressant medications, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants is compromised by extended delays to achieve therapeutic efficacy. Sadly, 50% of patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) do not obtain remission with traditional antidepressants. One of the most exciting discoveries in neuropharmacology in two decades is that a single intravenous infusion of ketamine has robust, rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in individuals with TRD lasting up to 1-2 weeks. Not surprisingly, this discovery has inspired great interest in identifying the underlying molecular mechanisms. Ketamine blocks the NMDA class of glutamate receptors, consistent with dysfunctions within the glutamatergic system and dysregulation of synaptic plasticity in the pathophysiology of depression. Systematic investigations of ketamine's effects on in vivo synaptic plasticity in animal models of depression, as well as direct contribution of synaptic plasticity changes to ketamine's antidepressant effects, are key to understanding the mechanisms by which ketamine and other candidate drugs achieve their unique effects. Proposed experiments will utilize a genetic model of depression (Wistar-Kyoto WKY rat). In preliminary experiments we observed weakness in synaptic plasticity that was rescued by ketamine. Therefore, we hypothesize that impaired synaptic plasticity in WKY rats causes depression-like deficits in motivation, cognition, and social interaction. Furthermore, we propose that restitution of synaptic plasticity is a crucial mediator of the antidepressant response to ketamine. Novel candidate compounds will be screened using the WKY model of TRD.

column36: Mechanisms of Genome Instability
column37: Before a cell can grow and divide it must duplicate its DNA. Mistakes during the copying of the DNA can lead to the kinds of changes that are frequently seen in cancerous cells (mutations, for example). These changes are important for cancer development, progression, and treatment, but there is little information about how they arise. Understanding how changes to the DNA arise could lead to improvements in cancer detection and treatment, and is also relevant to ageing, where mistakes in the DNA happen more often. We will study how proteins help copy the DNA, how proteins prevent mistakes during the copying of the DNA, and will apply this knowledge to discover new ways to prevent the kinds of mistakes that can lead to human diseases, including cancers.

column36: Predictors of poor health and functional recovery following road trauma: An emergency department inception cohort study.
column37: BACKGROUND: Each year in Canada, road trauma causes over 2,000 deaths and 10,000 serious injuries. Disability after an injury is a major public health concern, but the long term health outcome after road trauma is poorly investigated and based mostly on outdated research that does not reflect modern vehicle safety features or modern medical treatment, and largely ignored cyclists and pedestrians. In addition, there is almost no research that helps healthcare providers know which patients are most likely to have a bad outcome following a crash - making it difficult to provide them with the care they require. It is important for policy makers to know the healthcare costs and lost productivity that results from road trauma, but this information has not been well studied. Our study will provide this missing information. METHODS: We will interview patients who visit an emergency department after a car crash. The interview will ask about their general health before the crash, the injuries they had from the crash, and other details of the crash. We will interview them again at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months after the crash to find out about problems they had since the crash. The follow-up interview will ask about pain, ability to go about their usual activities, whether they have returned to work, and about the medical care they required after the crash. STUDY FINDINGS and IMPORTANCE: Our study will help doctors and nurses know how quickly people recover from their injuries and which patients are likely to have long term health problems after a car crash. We will also describe how much medical treatment these patients require and how much work they miss. This information will also help policy makers make informed decisions on how much money and resources to devote to crash prevention or to treatment programs for crash victims.

column36: Mutational mechanisms of pancreatic cancer development
column37: A diagnosis of pancreatic cancer is often fatal. This deadly tumour is highly aggressive, metastasizes rapidly in patients, and is resistant to nearly all forms of cancer therapy. This disease is expected to be the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the coming decade. Improving clinical outcomes has proven to be stubbornly difficult in pancreatic cancer and highlight an urgent need for scientific advances. This deadly disease often strikes "out of nowhere," and the cancer is usually inoperable by the time the patient experiences symptoms. The cause of pancreatic cancer's frequent appearance at an advanced stage has long been a medical mystery. Using whole genome sequencing, our group reconstructed the history of pancreatic cancer development in 150 independent tumours. Unexpectedly, we found that many of the important genetic events that cause this cancer actually occur 'all at once', similar to the idea of the 'big-bang". These results provide fresh insights into how these tumours develop and help to explain why this disease is so aggressive. These 'big-bang' type events, which are so frequent in pancreatic cancer, are rare in cancers that are not as aggressive. This leads us to believe that they play an important role in the biology of pancreatic cancer. Our goal is to evaluate the impact of these 'big-bang' events on pancreatic cancer development. Overall, we plan to determine if these events are the actual cause this cancer, how they influence metastasis, and therapy resistance. By better understanding the biology of this lethal tumour, we hope to eventually design more effective therapies to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Role of cerebrovascular abnormalities in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorders.
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) alter the child's development, affecting motor skills and social interactions. Genetic anomalies (mutations) have been identified as possible origins for ASD, leading for instance to delays in the maturation of neurons. About 1% to 2% of children worldwide have been diagnosed with ASD, but the causes of ASD remain enigmatic. Brain maturation heavily depends on a steady supply of oxygen and nutrients from the blood stream. As such, key vascular features ensure proper brain maturation: the growth of blood vessels, the maintenance of blood vessel permeability, and the regulation of blood flow. Early life impairments in these vascular features will alter the normal course of brain development. Very few studies have investigated the possible contribution of vascular deficits to this group of disorders. Several studies suggested a link between ASD and altered cerebral blood flow, and a recent postmortem study using brains of young ASD patients suggested a possible impairment in the formation of brain blood vessels. But these observations have not been thoroughly verified, nor tested in a robust animal model of the disease. As a result, involvement of the brain vasculature to the onset and/or progression of ASD remains to be elucidated. We propose to address this gap of knowledge by thoroughly investigating 1) the health of the brain vasculature in a genetically-engineered animal model of ASD, and 2) the consequences on neuronal development when only brain blood vessels (not neurons) are affected by a known, ASD-associated mutation. Our goal is to test novel questions: How do blood vessels develop in the ASD brain? What role(s) do vascular deficits play in the progression of ASD? Our research program proposes a new angle to ASD research, providing novel insight into the involvement of brain blood vessels in ASD. Identification of new players in ASD pathogenesis is essential to the develop new therapeutic strategies.

column36: SECRET: Study of rivaroxaban for CeREbral venous Thrombosis
column37: Cerebral venous thrombosis is a condition where blood clots form in the draining veins of the brain. It is a rare type of stroke but when it occurs it tends to affect younger women. 75% of patients are female and 80% are under the age of 50. People with CVT can have severe headaches, vision loss, weakness, seizures and coma. 15% are left dead or disabled, 25% cannot return to work, and over half have long-term problems with low energy, thinking or mood. Because it is a rare disease, CVT is hard to study in large trials. Treatment for the disease is based on opinion. CVT is treated with strong blood thinners, but it is not clear which blood thinner is best or how long people should be treated. We want to study which type of blood thinner for CVT is the best choice. But because it is a rare disease, first we need to make sure we can find enough people to join the study. We have teamed up with 17 stroke hospitals across the country to find patients. Patients in our study will be randomly assigned to one of two types of blood thinners. The first is a newer type called rivaroxaban that does not need regular blood tests. The second is the usual type of blood thinner which requires blood tests to check drug levels. We will see if our large national team can find 50 patients in one year for the study. We will study each patient for one year and will do repeat brain scans to see if their blood clots have dissolved, and will do detailed testing about thinking and concentration in patients with CVT. Because CVT is rarely studied, we also want to learn more about its long-term effects of CVT on patients' quality of life. We will have discussions with patients across the country about which symptoms affect their lives the most. We hope to improve the way we treat CVT, and how well we understand its long-term effects. By partnering with patients to set our top research priorities, we hope that together this will help improve their quality of life.

column36: Impact of the organophosphate ester flame retardants found in the Canadian environment on the reproductive system
column37: As part of our everyday lives we are exposed to a wide variety of chemicals derived from consumer products, such as foam, electronic equipment and plastics. Most of these chemicals are present at very low concentrations. However, exposure to even low doses of substances that disrupt hormones can exert important biological effects. In particular, exposures to endocrine disrupting chemicals are suspected of contributing to the declines in human fertility reported from the developed world. In the past decade governments across the world have regulated the production, uses and importation of specific environmental chemicals that have been shown to disrupt hormone actions. As a consequence, alternative chemicals have entered the market to fill the "gaps". However, there is often little information on the extent to which we are exposed to these replacements or on their health impacts. Our research will focus on a major group of such chemicals, the organophosphate esters (OPEs), that is in rapidly increasing use. We will test the hypothesis that exposure to these compounds is associated with adverse effects on the male and/or female reproductive systems. Cells with key endocrine functions will be used to identify genes and pathways that are disrupted by OPEs and may serve as biomarkers of their effects on fertility. Using an animal model we will elucidate the effects of exposure to the mixture of OPEs found in Canadian house dust on male and female fertility. Finally, we will assess the association of human OPE body burden with female and male infertility. These studies will enhance our understanding of the health consequences of exposure to a family of widely used chemicals for which we currently have very limited data. In addition, we expect that they will contribute to the development of policies to ensure the identification of alternative chemicals that are safer and have a reduced environmental impact prior to their use as replacements.

column36: Reducing the burden of bleeding and cardiovascular complications of bleeding
column37: Cardiovascular disease, which includes coronary heart disease and stroke, affects more than 1 million Canadians and 300 million persons worldwide, and results in 18 million death each year. One of the most effective and widely used approaches to prevent cardiovascular disease is antithrombotic treatment (e.g., aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, newer direct acting oral anticoagulants) that prevent potentially harmful blood clots from forming at the site of atherosclerotic plaques. The most important side-effect of these treatments is bleeding. The importance of bleeding has been vastly under-rated. We paid little attention to bleeding, thinking that for the most part this was easily treatable, and much less important than heart attack and stroke. We now know that bleeding is not only common, affecting thousands of Canadians with cardiovascular disease each year, but is also a powerful risk factor for heart attack and stroke, the very events that these treatments aim to prevent. My research program focuses on determining why persons with cardiovascular disease develop bleeding, and why those who bleed are at such high risk of attack and stroke after bleeding. Having identified the risk factors and mechanisms, my subsequent studies will evaluate whether targeted interventions can prevent cardiovascular events and mortality related to bleeding.

column36: Molecular and physiological understanding of the protein tyrosine phosphatome towards clinical applications.
column37: For the past 25 years, my laboratory focused on elucidating the function of a family of genes named "protein tyrosine phosphatases" (PTPs). The PTP family contains 107 different genes in humans that control a plethora of normal cell functions. PTPs have one common property: to remove a phosphate molecule added to specific tyrosine residues present in many cellular proteins, which confer, or deny, various properties to proteins. Our main purpose is to understand PTP function and to transfer this knowledge into common scientific knowledge and towards clinical applications. Herein we propose three experimental sections. Section 1 is a continuation of our recent work on PTPN1(also known as PTP1B) and PTPN2 (also known as TC-PTP) in characterizing their roles in the immune system. We plan to examine their function in a type of immune cells named "T-cell ". These comprise several subsets of T-cell with different function that kill tumor cells and maintain surveillance against cancer cells. Our proposal is to use small molecule inhibitor of PTPs to reactivate patients T- cells or improve the novel cancer immunotherapeutic approaches of CAR-T cells. Section 2 is pursuing a new system of proteins (the PRL-CNNM proteins) that we first reported in 2014. Involved in the supplies of magnesium to all higher organisms, PRL PTPs are upregulated in almost all cancers to sustain growth and invasion. By understanding their roles and preventing their binding to CNNMs, we intend to develop a novel class of anti- cancer drugs. Finally, section 3 has for objective to explore further this large and relatively still unknown gene family. Our previous data showed that most PTPs are involved in the immune system. We plan to assess the function of each one of the entire gene family towards inhibiting or activating the immune system response against cancer. We are confident that this program will contribute original and important scientific advances and novel clinical applications.
