column36: Decoding the DNA double-strand break repair pathways: from mechanistic insights to human genome instability diseases
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of mortality in Canada representing 30% of all deaths. One in 2.3 individual will get cancer and 1 in ~3.8 will die from it, incurring $1.16 trillion in direct cost worldwide in 2010. Genomic instability is a common feature of tumor cells and is thought to represent a basic mechanism to acquire the several genetic alterations required during the neoplastic process. Double-strand breaks (DSBs), the most lethal kind of DNA lesions, can be repaired by two pathways; homologous recombination (HR) or non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). The choice between NHEJ and HR involves an intricate network of resection enzymes whose interplay and hierarchy remain largely unexplored. It is becoming increasing clear that not only failure, but also misuse, of these pathways can trigger genomic instability leading to cancer, the biggest killer in Canada. Paradoxically, defects in the DSB pathways provide weaknesses that can be exploited to design new targeted cancer therapies. The DSB repair machinery can thus be seen as a double-edged sword in cancer protection and treatment, making the understanding of its regulatory mechanisms of crucial importance in the cancer research field. This proposal aims to obtain a comprehensive view of the functions of HR enzymes. By funding this Foundation Program, it will ensure that the mechanisms of these enzymes are defined. Furthermore, using novel inhibitors discovered by our group, we will inhibit the functions of these enzymes to target the vulnerabilities of cancer cells to improve patient care.

column36: Needles without tears: Inoculating children against pain and fear
column37: Not just a poke, needle pain and related fear are in fact major health concerns. All Canadian children undergo painful needle procedures; hospitalized children undergo multiple procedures daily. Pain causes unnecessary suffering, fear, procedure complications (e.g., fainting, failed procedures), and avoidance behaviours. An alarming 20% of unvaccinated 6- 18-year-old children (herein called youth) refuse vaccination due to fear of needle-related pain. This leaves them at risk of acquiring and spreading disease. My vision is to make children all over the world healthier by improving their experiences during needle procedures which will increase needle procedure acceptance. In previous work, I led the creation of a Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG) to address pain and fear and documented gaps for youth. The current project has been developed with key user groups to address these gaps using real-world solutions. Over 7 years, I will build on my successes with my CIHR-funded Help ELiminate Pain in Kids & Adults (HELPinKids&Adults) team to address key unanswered questions. Specifically, to help close the pain care gap for youth, I will: 1) identify best practices for injection techniques, 2) implement and evaluate a novel tool/game developed by youth teaching youth how to reduce pain, fear and fainting, and 3) create both an updated CPG that incorporates this new evidence and a national plan to facilitate integration into healthcare systems. I expect improvements in patient-prioritized outcomes (pain, fear, fainting and needle procedure acceptance); I estimate a 5% absolute increase in school-based vaccine uptake alone. Long-term, I expect improved health outcomes and health cost savings due to improved compliance and efficiency. Importantly, this research program engages youth and other stakeholders to address youth's most pressing concern about healthcare - the needle - and fulfills our ethical obligation to first, do no harm.

column36: Mechanochemical signalling in embryonic wound repair
column37: An outstanding question in biology is how cells coordinate their behaviours. Cells coordinate their movements to sculpt, repair, or invade tissues. A common feature of collective cell movements in development, repair, and disease is the reorganization of the cytoskeleton, the network or proteins that cells use to generate mechanical forces. However, the mechanisms that promote cytoskeletal redistribution during collective cell migration are not understood. We found that highly reactive, oxygen-containing molecules (reactive oxygen species) are critical for cytoskeletal rearrangements during collective cell movement. In addition, we and others showed that cytoskeletal proteins can be regulated by the mechanical forces sustained by cells in living animals. We will use the process of epidermal wound repair in fruit fly embryos to model collective cell movements and establish the basic molecular and physical mechanisms of cytoskeletal reorganization during collective cell migration. Fruit fly embryos are transparent, allowing visualization of coordinated cell movements with high spatial and temporal detail; they are easy to manipulate genetically, and also with drugs and lasers; and over 75% of the genes involved in human disease exist in fruit flies. We will apply advanced microscopy and image analysis to track the distribution of molecules in living embryos; mathematical modelling to develop hypotheses about how changes in chemical or mechanical signals may affect cytoskeletal protein dynamics and cell behaviour; and pharmacological, genetic and biophysical manipulations to test modelling predictions and determine the molecular pathways by which reactive oxygen species and mechanical forces affect cytoskeletal dynamics. Our results will reveal the mechanochemical signals that coordinate cell movements, and will enable subsequent efforts to manipulate cell migration for tissue engineering or cancer research applications.

column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), such as hydrocephaly, lissencephaly, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and intellectual disability affect up to 1 in 8 children born and represent a significant challenge to the health care system and resources available to Canadian families. In Ontario alone, an estimated 300,000 children are diagnosed with developmental disorders of the brain, while ASD alone occurs at a high frequency of 1/88, and is associated with a lifetime cost per individual of $5.5 million. NDDs are thought to arise from abnormal brain formation in the fetus. Yet the underlying genetic and cellular mechanisms remain largely unknown and treatment options are extremely limited. One of the key brain regions involved in NDDs is the neocortex. Its formation relies on the production of a diverse set of neuronal populations and their organization into specific networks important for cognition. Understanding what controls the differentiation and migration of neurons is crucial as alterations in brain anatomy are seen in patients with a range of psychiatric illnesses. We have identified a novel regulator of neocortical organization that when mutated in the mouse gives rise to several hallmarks of developmental disorders of the human brain, including the abnormal formation of neural circuits, enlarged ventricular spaces, reduced axonal growth, and an abnormal accumulation of cells near the ventricles. We propose to study use this mouse model to advance our knowledge of the cellular and molecular processes that contribute to the formation of the neocortex and its connections to regions of the brain important for emotion and cognition. In so doing we will identify diagnostic events and therapeutic strategies for addressing developmental disorders of the brain.

column36: The Pain Squad+ Smartphone App To Support Real-Time Pain Management for Adolescents with Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Pain negatively affects the quality of life (QOL) of adolescents with cancer (AWC), slows cancer recovery, and results in negative long-term health effects. Pain is also significant cost to the healthcare system and families. To address this problem, our team has developed and used a phased-approach to test a smartphone-based app, called Pain Squad+. Using this app AWC report the pain they have and the app provides AWC with advice on how to treat this pain based on an algorithm our team developed. An email is also sent to a nurse if an AWC reports severe pain 3 times in a row. The nurse then contacts the AWC to assist in treating pain. This project will test the effect of the Pain Squad+ app, with and without nurse help, on treating pain and other pain-related health issues and managing costs associated with pain care, when compared to AWC not using the app. We will enroll 222 AWC recruited from 9 Canadian pediatric oncology care centres into a 3-group randomized controlled trial. AWC in the experimental groups will be asked to use Pain Squad+ for 8 weeks (with or without nurse involvement) and all groups will complete pain-related outcome measures at baseline, 2-, 4-, 8-, and 16-weeks. The primary study outcome will be pain intensity. The secondary study outcomes will be (a) pain interference; (b) QOL; (c) pain self-efficacy; and (d) cost effectiveness and utility. We will use established statistical methods to analyze the health and cost data we collect over the course of this study. A real-time and cost effective way to address the problem of pain in AWC is needed. Pain Squad+ can improve pain treatment and QOL for AWC as well as decrease costs incurred by families and the healthcare system. If effective, the Pain Squad+ as a model of technology-assisted care may represent a way to improve the QOL for a range of Canadian patients by treating a variety of physical and psychological symptoms the moment they occur.

column36: Asthmatic phenotyping by microfluidic assessment of shortening velocity and contractile force of airway smooth muscle cells obtained from biopsies
column37: Two million people suffer from uncontrolled asthma in Canada. Asthma is a respiratory disease characterized by breathing difficulty caused by excessive airway narrowing. This narrowing is the result of contraction of the smooth muscle (SM) in the airway wall. While many asthmatics have increased airway SM mass, which may explain excessive airway narrowing, others do not. Thus, these latter cases may suffer from increased contractile capacity of individual SM cells. We have shown that in the horse with heaves, an animal model of asthma, the rate at which airway SM shortens is increased whereas airway SM of horses under remission exhibits an increase in stress and stiffness. Thus, we hypothesize that different subtypes of asthma are characterized by differences in airway SM contractile properties. We propose to develop a "lab on a chip" device for measuring these contractile properties from SM cells acquired by biopsy from people with asthma. Goal: To identify asthma subtypes by measuring the rate of shortening and the contractile force of airway SM from biopsies of human asthmatics and controls. Approach: Airway SM cells from biopsies will be isolated and injected into a device that we will develop from two layers of silicone, each containing a network of micro-channels. Cells will flow into separate lanes and get sucked to the floor of the lanes, which is made up of micro-pillars of known stiffness with perpendicular channels, attached to a low-pressure source, in between them. The immobilized cells will be exposed to contractile or relaxing solutions and bending of the micropillars by the contracting cells will allow measurement of the contractile force, while a sudden release of the cells will allow measurement of the rate of shortening. Significance: This study will enable differential diagnoses of asthma subtypes based on airway SM contractility, directly contributing to more effective, personalized treatments.

column36: Scaling up shared decision making for patient-centred care
column37: Most Canadians wish to stay at home in their old age, but to still have access to healthcare. With new medical technologies (such as alarm bracelets), more and more seniors can stay at home for longer and receive care from home care teams. But seniors living at home often face difficult decisions, such as "Who will look after me when I can't look after myself any more, or if I have dementia?" or "Should I move to a nursing home, or stay here?" For the caregiver, the decision may be "Can I continue to care for my loved one at home?" When more than one option is possible, home care teams can help seniors and their families who are making these hard decisions by giving them the information they need and asking about their values and preferences. This way, seniors and their caregivers can know more about their choices and choose options that reflect what is important to them. We call this 'shared decision making', and it has been shown to improve patient experiences (less disappointment, anxiety or regret) and better use of healthcare dollars. More and more, seniors will be making such decisions in consultation with their home care teams. Over the years we have developed tools and training programs to help home care teams support seniors and their caregivers in making the decision about whether a senior who is no longer independent should stay at home with more help, or move to a nursing home. However, most of our research has been at the regional level. Too many pilot projects that could benefit far more people stay hidden at the local level. So we plan to scale up the tools, programs and systems that seem to work well for one decision and one region. We will adapt and apply them to home care in other places across Canada and to other difficult decisions, so that more seniors and their caregivers benefit from shared decision making and can make decisions together that are better for their health, their pocket, and their quality of life.

column36: Molecular Targeting of Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Bone Marrow Regeneration
column37: Cancer has become a major healthcare issue for Canada, and is now the leading cause of death in our country. 1 in 2 Canadians may be afflicted with cancer, and 1 in 4 Canadians are expected to die from it. Although progress in therapy has been made in many cancers, such as breast and prostate, treatment options for other cancers remain stagnant. This is exemplified by acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a type of blood cancer where dysfunctional leukemic cells take over the blood system. Disease burden can initially be reduced by lowering the leukemic cell numbers (called remission) with chemotherapy, but the disease usually comes back within 2 years (called relapse). When AML relapses, the option is to re-treat the cancer with the same chemotherapy but at a higher dose, and for longer. Unfortunately, the disease usually becomes resistant to treatment and can no longer be controlled. However, the exact reason for AML relapse and resistance to chemotherapy remains unclear. Our program group in Hamilton, Ottawa and London has now identified rare leukemic cells that: a) survive chemotherapy and b) regrow to give rise to relapsed disease. Detailed tests on these unique cells revealed that before they regenerate AML disease, they begin to express leukemia-specific proteins that give them a growth advantage in the bone marrow space where they live. Furthermore, we have revealed that the bone marrow space itself changes to support leukemia, and is directly affected by chemotherapy. Available drugs can inhibit some changes in the bone, and our early findings indicate these drugs can reduce relapse when combined with chemotherapy. Our team of physicians, biochemists and stem cell biologists will define and test a series of new drugs that target proteins that inhibit surviving leukemic cells and change the bone marrow environment that will prevent relapse before it occurs, and activate normal blood stem cells to combat leukemia in patients in the next 7 years of support.

column36: Systematically mapping functional human sequence variation and context-dependent protein interactions
column37: There are few cases where we fully understand how DNA sequence variants impact gene function, and how these changes propagate through networks of molecular and cellular interactions to yield human disease. My team is developing genomic technology to address two distinct goals to improve our understanding of genetic disease: 1) Mapping sequence-function relationships to identify human DNA sequence variants affecting their gene product; and 2) Mapping the downstream network of macromolecular interactions, including their dynamics and context-dependence, to better understand how the connection from genotype to phenotype is mediated. Towards the first goal, we developed a hybrid experimental/computational platform for deep mutational scanning (DMS), in which the functional effects of missense variants are exhaustively mapped in specific target human disease genes. These maps have already been validated for two human disease genes: calmodulin and cystathionine beta-synthase, with the former map already in clinical use. We will continue improving the DMS technology: extending it to human cell models and experimentally detecting the impact of both intronic and exonic variation on splicing and gene function, and applying it to ~100 human disease genes over the next 7 years (approximately 2% of the ~4000 annotated human disease genes). Towards the second goal, we developed a 'barcode-fusion genetics' (BFG) strategy, enabling two reagent libraries to be coupled so that all reagent pairs are tracked via combined ('fused') barcodes. This allows efficient mapping of protein interactions under different environments and genetic backgrounds. We recently developed a prototype method, 'messenger BFG', in which fused barcodes are transcribed, sensing interaction dynamics on the time scale of minutes. We will continue developing this approach, adapting it to human cell-based protein interaction assays, and applying it at proteome scale to both human and yeast proteomes.

column37: Patients with cancer often experience noticeable weight loss, which can start prior to diagnosis and which rapidly increases when the disease reaches an advanced stage. column36: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy to Improve Patient Outcomes Following Internal Fixation of Extremity Fractures: A Randomized Controlled Trial (SPOC-CBT)
column37: Each year, over 12 million individuals in North America sustain a fracture of the extremity, many of which are managed operatively. However, outcomes are variable and many patients continue to experience persistent pain and disability at one-year after surgery. In a recent trial of patients with open extremity fractures, 67% of patients reported moderate to severe pain and 38% reported pain that interfered at least moderately with daily activities at one year. column36: Modeling antibody diversification processes through Cas9-mediated mutagenesis
column37: The immune system plays a major role in protecting humans from bacteria, viruses, and toxins (known as antigens). One of the ways that the immune system accomplishes this is by producing antibodies that bind to and neutralize these antigens. Antibodies are small molecules made by B cells. Each B cell makes only one type of antibody which will bind to only one antigen. By changing the antibody stalk, the properties of the antibody are changed. For example, IgM antibodies can be changed to IgG antibodies which can be used by macrophages to engulf bacteria that are coated by these antibodies, or to IgA antibodies that can be secreted into mucosal tissue and neutralize pathogens in the lung or the gut. Changing the antibody class is accomplished by the class switch recombination process, and the key enzyme that initiates this process is called AID. However, much needs to be learned about this process. In this grant proposal, we plan determine the types of mutations and the enzymes that are required by AID to induce class switch recombination. In addition, since AID has been shown to induce chromosomal translocations that are central to the development of lymphomas, this proposal will also examine the types of mutations and enzymes involved in the development of these cancer-causing events. Hence, the proposed work will allow us to determine how an effective antibody response is generated against pathogens, and will also characterize molecular pathways that play important roles in cancer development. This new information will in turn influence vaccine development or the generation of therapeutic agents that target lymphomas.

column36: Host cell protein substrates of enterovirus proteases
column37: Enterovirus infections are associated with several acute and chronic diseases worldwide and in Canada. Most enterovirus infections are cleared by the immune system, however, infection by certain enteroviral species and strains can be more severe. Poliovirus is the most well-known member which causes paralytic poliomyelitis. The non-poliovirus members are more common such as rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, and coxsackievirus and EV71, which are associated with more debilitating diseases such as viral myocarditis, Type I diabetes, and hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and in rare cases, meningitits. Although enteroviruses have been studied for several decades, the molecular basis of infection and the pathogenic mechanisms leading to disease are still poorly understood. One of the signature properties of enteroviruses is that the virus expresses a protein, called a protease, which cleaves host proteins in the cell to facilitate virus infection. Currently, the extent of host proteins targeted by the viral protease is not known. In this study, we will utilize a novel unbiased proteomics approach to comprehensively identify all of the targets of the proteases from coxsackievirus. Unlike other methods, this new approach is sensitive and can identify the location of the cleavage site on the target protein. The identification of novel targets will provide a catalog of the host processes that viruses affect. Importantly, the knowledge gained will allow us to identify new targets for antiviral therapy. The development of this strategy can be exploited to identify the repertoire of host targets of proteases from other viruses.

column36: Identifying Autosomal Recessive Genes for Intellectual Disability
column37: The program goals are to identify new genes for intellectual disability (ID), focusing mainly on autosomal recessive (AR) causes, to deduce their functions, to direct findings back to the clinic, and to identify therapeutic opportunities. AR forms of ID are believed to account for a large proportion of affected individuals, and are the main genetic cause of ID in countries where within-family marriage (consanguinity) is common. However, attempts to map the genes responsible have been poorly explored. We have completed studies of 192 MPX consanguineous non-syndromic ID families and identified 38 new genes. We aim to continue with >300 additional MPX, and >100 single affected (SPX) families (or proband/mother/father trios) from countries where consanguinity is common. We aim to identify causative genes/mutations in these families, using a combination of genotyping and next generation sequencing. Genes identified in consanguineous families are also relevant to outbred populations, thus we plan to survey the genes identified in >2500 ID patients from Canada. Our studies to date have already had an impact on diagnosis, and the proposed work will add significantly to this legacy. The results will also help illuminate the pathophysiology, facilitating the development of treatments. Understanding the genetics of these diseases will improve diagnosis and treatment in the long term.

column36: Thrombosis and Thrombocytopenia: Novel mechanisms and treatments
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that aggregate and are responsible for bleeding arrest (hemostasis) at sites of injury. They are also key targets in many diseases. High platelet activity may result in heart attack and stroke (thrombosis), which are leading causes of death worldwide, while low platelet number may cause severe bleeding and miscarriages (thrombocytopenia). Our goal is to elucidate underlying mechanisms of these diseases and develop novel therapeutics. Platelet surface integrin alphaIIb beta3, is traditionally thought to exclusively bind fibrinogen (Fg)/VWF and mediate cross-linking of platelets (aggregation) during hemostasis/thrombosis. My discovery of Fg/VWF-independent thrombosis, proved that unidentified proteins ("X" ligands) bind beta3 integrin to support platelet aggregation. However, these ligands and their role in thrombosis still need to be delineated. We will use chemically engineered beads coupled with alphaIIb beta3 to pull down with high purity unidentified plasma and platelet proteins that bind alphaIIb beta3 (GPIIbIIIa). Specific alphaIIb beta3-protein interactions will be measured and the roles of new ligands in platelet biology, thrombosis and hemostasis will be studied using platelet function assays. We expect these ligands may affect both facets of platelets (activation and inhibition) and may be targeted to control many diseases. Immune-mediated thrombocytopenias involve targeting of self- or non-self (e.g. fetal)-platelet antigens by antibodies leading to platelet destruction known as autoimmune (ITP) and fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT), respectively. We have shown antibodies targeting different platelet surface receptors (i.e. GPIIbIIIa vs. GPIbalpha) can lead to very different disease outcomes and response to treatment. We will continue to explore these differences between the anti-GPIIbIIIa and GPIbalpha immune response in ITP and FNAIT to enhance treatment efficacy.

column36: The Development and Genetics of the Face
column37: We study structural birth defects of the face. Upwards of 3% of children are born with either structural birth defects of the face such as cleft lip or holoprosencephaly or a genetic disease that affects the face. Both types of conditions cause suffering for affected children and their families. Individualized treatment of diseases such as birth defects is a key goal of precision medicine. Variation among individuals produces differences in responses to treatments. To understand birth defects one has to understand the causes of this variation. We aim to understand how genetic influences act through development to produce variation of the face. Ultimately, the goal is use the knowledge gained to alleviate suffering by either preventing birth defects or, when they occur, to offer the most appropriate treatment for each patient. We propose to modulate central pathways of craniofacial development to determine how they and their interactions determine variation in morphology, cellular dynamics and the expression of downstream genes. column37: Cardiac pain disproportionately burdens more women than men. Women with premature MI are often from minority groups and have low socioeconomic status and exposure to sexual abuse during childhood7. Pilote and Norris (co-investigators) reported feminine roles and personality traits were associated with higher rates of recurrent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and major adverse cardiac events (MACE) compared to masculine characteristics; posited to be explained in part by increased anxiety8. We will incorporate condition specific factors such as gender (GRS) and sex (age, race, ethnicity and risk factors) into the HEARTPAIN architecture.

column36: Unraveling sensory coding dysfunctions that underlie chronic pain
column37: Intractable pain continues to be the single most common cause of disability that impairs quality of life. Unfortunately, current pain treatments rarely achieve complete pain control, and are often associated with disabling side effects. This is concerning, since persistent untreated pain is associated with several brain disorders, including cognitive deficits, anxiety, depression and addiction. To address this medical problem, the objective of my research program is to elucidate how the nervous system processes pain signals and how this is disrupted in chronic pain syndromes. For example, what makes a normal touch be misinterpreted by the brain as signalling pain? To gain these new insights, we design and use advanced light-based technologies to view and control both healthy and diseased brain circuits; develop new tools to analyse data from physiological, cellular and molecular studies, and develop computer-based approaches to model brain functioning to address issues that are not easy to tackle experimentally. This combination of novel approaches has allowed us to identify new therapeutic targets and develop new drugs that have potential to reverse abnormal pain. We will continue to refine our drug discovery strategies so that we can ultimately help bring relief to those suffering from chronic pain.

column36: Synaptic Plasticity and Dysfunction in the Brain
column37: The development of the brain is an enormously complex task that requires the formation and refinement of trillions of connections between billions of brain cells (neurons). These connections, known as synapses, are critical for all brain functions. They control our movement and senses; they regulate our emotions and decisions. They make us who we are. Dysfunctions in the development or function of synapses are thought to be central to many brain disorders including intellectual disability, schizophrenia, autism, Alzheimer's disease and addiction. If we are to develop targeted therapeutic and behavioral interventions for brain disorders, then studying the fundamental mechanisms of how synapses form and function is crucial. The overarching goal of my lab is to elucidate specific cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying synapse formation and function, and then use this information to probe synaptic dysfunctions that contribute to diseases of the brain. In order to develop a comprehensive understanding of synapses and to modify synapse function at the molecular level, we use rodent models. Mice and rats share similar genes with humans, have related brain structures (including synapses), and can learn and remember simple tasks. My work will identify and manipulate specific molecular targets that are essential for proper synapse development and brain function. This will result in a better understanding of which disruptions in synaptic function lead to brain disorders, and set the stage for refined approaches that can be leveraged to develop new therapeutics for restoring brain function and cognition. Collectively, my work will address: the molecular and cellular mechanisms of how we learn and remember; how disrupting proper synaptic communication in the brain can lead to brain disorders; and whether improving synaptic function later in life might be a therapeutic target for restoring cognitive and functional abilities.

column36: Fatty Acid Handling and Cardiac Dysfunction
column37: The heart "burns" fat as a source of energy to help maintain its ability to pump blood efficiently. Although the use of fat for energy is extremely important in the healthy heart, evidence in animals has suggested that drugs that can partially inhibit the use of fat can prevent injury to the heart following a heart attack. However, one potential limitation of this approach is that fats can still enter the heart cells but by reducing the heart's ability to "burn" these fats, the fats can begin to accumulate within the heart cells. Of importance, having excess fat accumulate in hearts cells has been shown to lead to poor heart function. This fat-induced heart dysfunction may become even more apparent in obese individuals where levels of fats in the blood are very high and fats are already starting to accumulate in heart cells. In this instance, the use of these drugs may be even more harmful. One very important gatekeeper of fat entry into the heart cells is a fat transporting protein called CD36. We have shown that by reducing the activity of CD36, we can decrease the amount of fat that enters into the heart cell, which in turn limits how much fat can be burned for energy yet reduces the accumulation of fat. Thus, we speculate that drugs that inhibit CD36 may be much more beneficial than existing drugs that partially inhibit the use of fat. Based on this, we will test whether inhibition of CD36 function (which will decrease fat uptake into the heart as well as limit the use of fat for energy) is beneficial or detrimental to the heart in a variety of diseased states. These studies will ultimately lead to a better understanding of the importance of CD36 in the heart as well as allow us to ascertain whether drugs designed to inhibit CD36 in the heart (or related pathways that partially inhibit the use of fat for energy) may contribute to improving the performance of the heart in patients with heart disease and/or obesity.

column36: The Regulation of Alternative Splicing in Dopaminergic and Serotonergic Neurons

Differential usage of alternative splicing has served as a mechanism contributing to customizing the functions of individual brain cells. column36: A systematic genome wide effort to identify and validate targetable synthetic dosage lethal interactions of mitotic kinases in colorectal cancer cells
column37: Cancer cells often overexpress specific genes due to the effect of translocations, gene amplification, or other epigenetic modifications. Researchers have thought that directly inhibiting the function of these overexpressing genes could help to eliminate cancer cells. For example, a gene called Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) is overexpressed in multiple cancers including colorectal cancers, indicating that inhibition of this kinase could be a powerful antitumor strategy. However, efforts to inhibit this kinase showed low objective response rates, poor survival and severe toxic side effects in clinical studies. This is because these drugs were not specific enough and often resulted in off-target effects, where they targeted other members of the polo-like family. To circumvent this concern, here we propose to take advantage of a basic biological concept called "Synthetic Dosage Lethality", where cancer cells overexpressing genes like PLK1 could be killed, when another gene is turned "OFF". In other words, rather than directly inhibiting genes like PLK1, we have developed a method that can query every single gene in the genome, in a span of four weeks, and identify those target genes whose loss-of-function can selectively kill PLK1-overexpressing cancer cells. Using this approach, we will execute our investigation in colon cancer cells as it ranks third in morbidity among all other malignancies. In addition, our lab is fully equipped with all the tools and reagents required to test the effect of the target genes that we identify in this cancer. Thus the successful completion of our project has the potential to identify several new druggable targets for colon cancer treatment. Our findings are expected to trigger the development of novel targeted therapies that would improve the survival of colon cancer patients.

column36: Molecular mechanisms underlying the clinical efficacy of inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist combination therapies in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease, characterised by intermittent airways constriction and occurs in up to 10% of individuals. Regular inhaled glucocorticoids are clinically referred to as inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and dampen lung inflammation to control mild to moderate asthma. However, more severe disease and asthma exacerbations are poorly controlled by ICS and clinical guidelines recommend the addition of a long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist (LABA). These drugs enhance the effectiveness of the ICS to a level that is not achieved by increasing the glucocorticoid dose. The glucocorticoid receptor (GR), the protein target by which glucocorticoids act, is responsible for modulating gene expression to mediate beneficial effects in asthma. In the context of LABA, combinatorial effects between glucocorticoid and LABA-activated pathways result in enhanced clinical effectiveness of ICS/LABA therapies. However, the mechanistic basis, and the genes modulated, are not established and therefore cannot be selectively targeted. The current proposal will elucidate mechanisms underlying this clinically important effect. In this context, it is salient that the pharmaceutical sector is currently testing novel drugs that activate GR in ways that are different to conventional glucocorticoids. These compounds enhance some aspects of GR function relative to other activities. While, the objective is to improve the clinical efficacy of GR-based therapies, it is important to stress that we do not know which aspects of GR function are most important for synergy with LABA. There is therefore a risk of failing to identify novel GR ligands that most effectively synergise with LABAs. This will preclude maximising benefit from future combination therapies. The current project addresses this key knowledge gap by identifying mechanisms of GR action that are important for synergy with LABA. Such data will help guide the discovery of improved combination treatments for asthma.

column36: TICS: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Intervening in Children with Tourette's Syndrome
column37: Tourette syndrome (TS) is common. TS affects over 80,000 Canadian youth. Tics are the core symptom of TS. These are repetitive, sudden, semi-voluntary movements or sounds. Brain stimulation can also induce brain plasticity. We think by combining brain stimulation with habit reversal therapy, we can not only provide short-term relief, but also help retrain the brain to be better at suppressing tics at an earlier age than usually expected. (1) We think that the severity of tics will decrease with treatment. (2) We think the tic reduction will be greater in the combined treatment group. (3) We further think that we will see changes in brain function and chemistry in the target area, the supplementary motor cortex. (4) Again, we think the changes will be greater in the combined treatment group. Our team has pioneered brain stimulation in children and adolescents. By developing a way to treat TS, we can reduce the severity of tics and improve their quality of life.

column36: Beyond Transparency in Pharmaceutical Research and Regulation
column37: Making pharmaceutical safety and effectiveness evidence transparent, i.e. accessible, to physicians, researchers, healthcare payers, and ultimately patients is an essential but elusive goal. Consider the drug rofecoxib (Vioxx). It was approved in Canada and elsewhere in 1999 for treating arthritis only to be withdrawn from markets in 2004, before which thousands of patients who took Vioxx are estimated to have suffered cardiac arrest and death. Regulatory officials had prior knowledge of this safety risk but kept it confidential on the grounds that information was the drug manufacturer's property. Following Vioxx and similar cases a variety of new laws and policies were put into place to increase the transparency of pharmaceutical evidence and regulators' decision-making. Most recently, Parliament enacted Bill C-17, "Vanessa's Law", arming Health Canada with several new powers, including the ability to make drug safety and effectiveness information more transparent. However, meaningful improvements in transparency have been slow to arrive; changing the real world practices of regulators and clinical researchers, much less industry, remains a huge challenge. column37: Concussion and brain injury are recognized as a major health issue for Canadians. The group is the only one in the world with the pilot data, the team and the patient population needed for such a study. column37: The Issue: HIV is the leading cause of death for adolescents aged 10-19 years in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Uganda's 2017 HIV prevalence among adolescent girls is three times (9.1%) that of adolescent boys. Only 53.6% of adolescent girls in Uganda know their HIV status, far below the UNAIDS goal of 90% of persons living with HIV knowing their status by 2020. Uganda hosts 1 million refugees/displaced persons, and 98,000 live in Kampala, most in slums. Urban refugee/displaced adolescent girls have increased HIV risks due to poverty, violence, and limited healthcare. Yet we know little of HIV testing and prevention needs with displaced/refugee adolescent girls living in Kampala's slums. Our idea: We plan to develop, implement and evaluate an oral HIV-self testing (HIVST) intervention with displaced/refugee girls aged 15-19 in Kampala. HIVST is acceptable and properly used with adolescents in other SSA regions, yet we do not know the best way to link HIVST to HIV care. We explore how m-health (healthcare delivered on mobile-phones), congruent with how adolescents learn and socialize, can improve linkage to care with HIVST. Our Approach: Our 3-phase project involves: 1) working with refugee/displaced peer navigators to develop an m-health intervention (2-way supportive text messages; WhatsApp discussion groups); 2) implementing a cluster randomized trial with displaced/refugee girls aged 15-19 in 3 slums in Kampala (Arm 1: HIVST; Arm 2: HIVST + m-health; Arm 3: standard of care). We will assess changes in HIV testing, HIV status knowledge, and linkage to HIV care between the 3 arms. Phase 3 involves a process evaluation and participatory knowledge mobilization. Impact: We build on our CIHR planning grant that highlights the urgent need for HIV testing and prevention with urban refugee/displaced girls in Kampala. Findings will highlight optimal HIVST delivery approaches that can be expanded to other refugee/displaced adolescents in Uganda, SSA and humanitarian contexts.

column36: Effect of aberrant inflammation during pregnancy on subsequent risk of cardiovascular disease in mothers and their offspring
column37: Conditions during pregnancy can have long-term effects on the health of mothers and babies. Pregnant women who have high blood pressure and their urine contains protein are said to suffer from pre-eclampsia. Women and babies afflicted by pre-eclampsia have a higher chance of getting heart disease later in life. Babies with low birth weight (LBW) also have increased risk of heart disease later in life. Interestingly, excessive inflammation in pregnancy is linked to pre-eclampsia and LBW. We want to determine if and how abnormal inflammation in pregnancy increases the risk of subsequent heart disease in mothers and their children. To accomplish these goals, we developed a rat model of pre-eclampsia and LBW. In this model, inflammation in pregnant rats is induced by administration of a bacterial substance called lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Rats injected with LPS develop a condition similar to pre-eclampsia and their pups have LBW. We plan to monitor these rats and their pups after delivery to look for signs of increased risk of cardiovascular disease. We previously found that certain anti-inflammatory agents and exercise prevent inflammation and LBW induced by LPS. Therefore we will conduct studies to determine if exercise or treatment with anti-inflammatory agents mitigates risk of disease. Higher risk of disease in women and children who suffer from pre-eclampsia and LBW is linked to modifications in the DNA structure or in DNA-associated proteins. These modifications are called 'epigenetic alterations'. We plan to determine if inflammation in pregnancy leads to epigenetic alterations that could predict disease later in life. For this, we plan to use our rat model as well as blood samples from women and babies collected at the time of delivery. Our proposed studies are important because, if exercise and anti-inflammatories reduce the risk of disease in pregnant women and their children, this could lay the groundwork for to new treatments to prevent heart disease.

column36: Improving Depression Screening in Geriatric Patients by Reducing Bias and Generating Individualized Accuracy Estimates: An Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis of the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS)
column37: Major depression is common among elderly Canadians. Depression screening, which involves using short questionnaires to identify people who may have unrecognized depression, has been suggested as a way to improve the detection, management and treatment of depression. Some organizations recommend depression screening for elderly adults, but screening is not currently recommended in Canada's main healthcare guidelines due to concerns that screening tools do not accurately distinguish between patients with and without depression. Another concern with existing screening methods is that they do not do consider patient risk factors such as age, sex, care setting, and medical diagnoses, which may be associated with depression. Instead, they simply classify patients as either "likely" or "not likely" to be depressed. In our project, we will combine original patient data from published studies that used the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) depression screening tool, in order to create a very large database that can be used to determine more accurate ways to identify elderly patients with depression. The project will allow us to determine the probability that a specific elderly patient is depressed by considering the patient's individual depression score along with specific patient characteristics (e.g., age, sex, care setting, medical diagnosis). To implement our findings, we will develop a free online calculator that will allows healthcare professionals to use the results of our research with their patients in clinical practice. This project will improve the effectiveness of depression screening in the elderly, which depends on accurate screening questionnaires. In collaboration with Canadian guideline-makers, findings from this project will be applied in hospitals and health clinics to facilitate effective depression screening programs, improve the management of depression, and set Canada apart as a leader in depression research and practice.

column37: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) were originally identified in the seventies but were dismissed as splicing errors. column36: A pragmatic registry-based randomized trial of drug tapering in rheumatoid arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects up to 1% of the adult population and causes fatigue, joint pain, swelling and a reduced quality of life. Fortunately, the treatment for rheumatoid arthritis has advanced, and most patients can now have their disease effectively controlled with medications. After a patient's disease has been successfully treated and controlled, the usual practice is to continue with these medications for life. Emerging evidence suggests some patients may be able to successfully reduce medication once their disease is under control, but this evidence has important limitations, and more clinical trials are needed. In this grant, we will conduct a clinical trial to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a patient-centered approach for treatment reduction in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The study will be embedded within an ongoing national study of over 2000 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. From this study, we will identify patients whose disease has been well controlled for at least 6 months and ask if they would like to participate. Interested patients will be randomized to either usual care or a structured but flexible approach to reduce treatment in a shared decision with their physician. Treatment outcomes, including both benefits (ability to successfully reduce treatment) and harms (disease flares) will be compared over 18 months. column36: Role of lysosomal enzymes cathepsins B and D in neuronal vulnerability: potential implications in Alzheimer's disease pathology
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a brain disease characterized by a gradual loss of memory, followed by deterioration of higher cognitive functions such as language, calculation and judgement. The pathological features associated with AD brain include the loss of nerve cells in selected regions along with abnormal deposits of certain molecules such as amyloid beta (Ab) peptide and tau protein in structures called plaques and tangles, respectively. The brain regions which are severely affected in AD are hippocampus and cortex, whereas certain other regions such as cerebellum and striatum are relatively spared. It is believed that accumulation of Ab peptide can trigger the loss of nerve cells, but why only selected cells die in AD brains remain unclear. There is evidence that leakage of lysosomal enzymes called cathepsins B and D from their storage sites is markedly increased in nerve cells before they die in AD brains, but the role of these enzymes in the death of these cells is not fully understood. In a series of experiments, we will first establish the significance of the leakage of cathepsins in Ab-induced death of nerve cells grown in Petri dishes and the underlying cause of leakage of these enzymes from their storage sites. In parallel, we will measure the levels and activity of these enzymes in affected as well as unaffected regions of genetically modified animal models of AD and in post-mortem human AD brain samples. Subsequently, we will determine whether nanoparticles that have been shown to restore leakage of cathepsins can protect nerve cells against Ab-mediated toxicity in Petri dishes and in animal models of AD. This study will establish the role of cathepsins in the selective loss of nerve cells in AD brains. Additionally, these results could lead to identification of new molecular targets for the early diagnosis and/or development of new therapeutic opportunities such as nanoparticles in preventing the loss of nerve cells in AD brains

column36: Follicle-stimulating hormone regulation of bone physiology and pathophysiology
column37: Osteoporosis is a common and debilitating disorder of bone fragility in aging populations, which is associated with increased fracture rates. In women, the incidence of osteoporosis increases markedly following menopause. As estrogen promotes bone health, it is the postmenopausal loss of estrogen that is usually linked to osteoporosis. Indeed, many therapies target the estrogen receptor to prevent or treat postmenopausal osteoporosis. Recent observations over the past decade challenge this current dogma, attributing bone loss to the actions of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary gland. Estrogen and FSH levels in the bloodstream are tightly linked as FSH stimulates the ovaries to make estrogen. When estrogen levels fall at menopause, FSH levels rise, ostensibly to stimulate more estrogen production. However, the ovaries lack the ability to produce estrogen at this stage of life. Therefore, postmenopausal women have both low estrogen and high FSH, and some researchers have recently argued that it is the elevated FSH that is driving bone loss. In support of their view, they identified receptors for FSH on osteoclast cells in the bone. The normal function of osteoclasts is to degrade bone and FSH has been argued to increase osteoclast activity, and therefore bone loss. As a result of these observations, efforts are being made to develop inhibitors of FSH to treat bone loss in postmenopausal women. This new approach is highly controversial as many investigators question whether previous studies on FSH in bone physiology were correctly interpreted. Here, we propose to resolve this controversy using mouse models unique to our research team. The results of our work will definitely establish whether or not FSH regulates bone.

column37: Oral health is a very important public health issue. Oral health problems are common. People with oral health problems may have trouble eating, speaking, and interacting with others. When it comes to research on fluoridation and oral health, there are some important knowledge gaps. First, much of the evidence is out of date. First, we will examine the association between community water fluoridation and children's tooth decay. In previous work, we studied children's dental caries in Calgary 2-3 years after fluoridation was stopped, and compared it to Edmonton where fluoridation continues. We will build on that earlier work by 1) conducting a longer-term follow up (7-8 years after fluoridation was stopped), and 2) conducting an economic analysis, to understand whether or not the benefits of fluoridation are greater than the costs. Second, we will expand our work to consider another population: seniors living in long term care facilities. Seniors in long term care facilities are vulnerable to poor oral health, but they have not been well studied. column36: Novel Drug Targeting of the Circadian Factor REV-ERB Limits Infarct Expansion and Remodelling After Myocardial Ischemia/Reperfusion
column37: Ischemic heart disease leading to myocardial infarction (MI, heart attack) is a leading cause of death worldwide. Studies using broad approaches to reduce inflammation fail to show clinical effectiveness because they act on both beneficial and deleterious immune pathways involved in infarct healing. Specific targets are needed instead. We recently showed that the circadian system is an important mechanism regulating immunocyte recruitment to infarcted myocardium. We will use genetic circadian models to investigate the specificity of this approach. We will also demonstrate that this strategy is vital using a pre-clinical model and state-of-the-art imaging relevant to humans. This is a unique and direct pharmacological approach to limit infarct expansion and remodelling after mI/R, can be given alongside conventional therapies, and is effective for improving outcomes.

column36: Subchondral Bone Properties and their Association with Pain and Joint Deterioration in Postmenopausal Women with Knee Osteoarthritis and Varying Risk for Fractures
column37: According to the World Health Organization, osteoarthritis is 4 times as prevalent as strokes and heart disease combined. Knee osteoarthritis patients develop lesions in the bones of their knees, which have been linked to pain. However, their presence already indicates more advanced disease. One reason why pain is elevated in those with bone lesions is the buildup of pressure in marrow, triggering pain receptors. This phenomenon may be linked to micro damage in bone due to weak bones under normal loads or normal bones under high loads. While knee osteoarthritis has been linked to obesity, a condition associated with high loads, as many as 50% of patients are not obese and have normal loads. Postmenopausal women with elevated fracture risk may be at risk of having micro damage to knee bones. In fact, many non-obese individuals with knee osteoarthritis are postmenopausal women. While no tools have been developed to directly measure pressure in bone, the laws of physics indicate that pressure in a fluid is related to its viscosity and the speed of flow. In the proposed study of postmenopausal women 50-85 years of age diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis, investigators will estimate marrow fluid thickness by looking at its density and by measuring how fast fluids flow in and out of knee bones using imaging. These pieces of information will be linked to knee pain and function measured by questionnaires and examined in the context of fracture risk and osteoporosis. These correlates of bone pressure will also be linked to cartilage volume, bone structure, and other disease-related measures. If these bone pressure-related measures relate to pain and disease features, they may be good candidates for treatment targets and for tracking recovery from knee osteoarthritis in postmenopausal women with elevated fracture risk. This study could also identify a subgroup of individuals with knee osteoarthritis who may need to be treated differently than others.

column36: Cortical contributions to visually-guided locomotion in the cat
column37: This project is designed to determine the contribution of one part of the cerebral cortex, known to be involved in the planning of voluntary movements (the premotor cortex) to the planning of visually-guided gait modifications. While locomotion is sometimes thought of as a relatively automatic behavior in which the major function is to produce rhythmical, alternating movements of the limbs, it is actually a highly complex activity requiring cognitive and voluntary control under natural circumstances. On uneven terrain, for example, decisions have to be made about where to make the next step and frequently one plans a sequence of steps to avoid an obstacle. Walking in the street, one must decide how to walk around objects and people and how and when to step on and off a curb. Even indoors, one must navigate the furniture and objects on the floor. These behaviours require processing of visual information about the environment and a means to integrate this information with the immediate and long-term locomotor goals of the subject and the state of the limbs at the time of making the decision (e.g. which limb is in stance and which in swing and how do I adjust gait to most efficiently. or quickly, step over that obstacle). In the current project, I intend to test the hypothesis that the premotor cortex contributes to several essential aspects of goal-directed locomotion, including: decision processes that determine which limb will step over an obstacle; determining the parameters of the gait modification (trajectory and/or muscle activation patterns); and in more complex circumstances determining the sequence of steps required to clear a series of obstacles (e.g. a boulder field on a walking trail).

column36: Ehawawisit (With Child): Maternal and Perinatal Health Outcomes among the Metis in Alberta and the Influence of Proximal, Intermediate, and Distal Determinants of Health
column37: This project is a collaboration between the Metis Nation of Alberta (MNA) and Metis and non-Metis researchers to evaluate the health status of Metis mothers and their babies in Alberta. The Metis are post-contact Indigenous peoples. They have unique identity, values, language, and traditions. One in three Indigenous persons in Canada identify themselves as Metis. Alberta has the largest population of Metis in Canada. In contrast, there have been a few studies about Metis health. None of them have evaluated the health of Metis mothers and their babies. It is also important to know how circumstances in which people are born, grow up, and live (social determinants of health) affect their outcomes. Metis-specific research is urgently needed in this area. The word Ehawawisit in Michif language means "With Child". For the Metis, pregnancy and birth are a time of connection with their own heritage through the child. From a Metis point of view, the health of mother and baby are mirrors of the health of the community. This idea aligns with the concept of social determinants of health. Our research has three objectives: 1) to compare health status of mothers and newborns between Metis and non-Metis in Alberta; 2) to evaluate the role of social determinants of health on these outcomes; and 3) to explore from a Metis point of view how colonialism and its social effects have influenced these outcomes and Metis experiences of pregnancy and birth. We will conduct a cohort study based on administrative health data, and Metis Gatherings of knowledge holders using talking circles and storytelling. Research results will influence the planning of maternal and perinatal services for Metis women in Alberta within the new MNA Comprehensive Health and Wellness Centre, a MNA initiative to provide culturally safe, community health care to Metis in Alberta. Our work will provide knowledge to inform Metis-specific programs that address the unique challenges of Metis mothers and their babies.

column36: Functional Roles and Therapeutic Potentials of Invariant NKT Cells in Sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening illness caused by a disproportionate host response to microbes. It is characterized by early, severe inflammation followed by impaired immunity to opportunistic infections. Successful treatment of sepsis may thus require a two-step approach, namely to prevent excessive inflammation in the early phase and to boost antimicrobial immunity in the later phase. Natural killer T (NKT) cells are a tiny but powerful subset of lymphocytes with a unique ability to recognize glycolipids (molecules composed of sugar and fat). Promptly after activation, NKT cells secrete large quantities of soluble molecules called cytokines that mediate cell-to-cell communications in the immune system. Importantly, NKT cells can be manipulated to produce cytokines that either promote or suppress inflammation. The proposed research will follow 4 Specific Objectives. Objective 1 will test how NKT cell depletion in mouse models of sepsis may affect host responses, morbidity and mortality. In Objective 2, we will use glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells in a "two-hit" experimental model that simulates early and late phases of sepsis. Mice will be treated sequentially with anti- and pro-inflammatory glycolipids in the above phases, respectively, and will be evaluated for their ability to clear secondary infections. In Objective 3, we will generate mice that harbor either the entire human immune system or human NKT cells. "Humanized" mice will be rendered septic and treated with glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells. In Objective 4, we will obtain blood samples from septic patients shortly after presentation and shortly after resolution of their symptoms. Immune cells will be isolated, exposed to NKT cell stimuli and subjected to functional analyses. Collectively, the proposed studies will reveal the role of mouse and human NKT cells in sepsis, and also importantly hold the promise of introducing new and effective treatments for this dangerous and potentially fatal illness.

Canada is the second highest opioid consumer in the world and is facing a public health crisis with opioid addiction (opioid use disorder (OUD)) and death. There are relatively few treatment options for OUD and the most common is a substitution with methadone (methadone maintenance treatment, MMT), a synthetic opioid. However, MMT outcomes vary greatly, with the average patient receiving MMT for multiple years and many continuing to use opioids while on MMT. Furthermore, MMT itself carries significant health risks, including high rates of death. There is preliminary evidence that differences in MMT response are partially determined by the individual genetic makeup. Identifying how genes affect the response to methadone has the potential to substantially improve the opioid addiction treatment outcomes via a precision medicine approach. Toward this end, the proposed study will leverage innovations in genomic approaches to systematically examine individual variation in MMT response in a large sample of opioid addiction MMT patients. Our hypothesis is that MMT outcomes are significantly determined by genes that can inform future treatment decisions and the study's fundamental goal is to rigorously test this hypothesis using multiple cutting edge methodologies.

column36: Physiology and biochemistry of small regulatory RNAs
column37: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics has become a global medical concern as shown by recent reports on the rise of highly drug resistant bacterial strains. Although this resistance was predictable, research to identify new antibiotics or cellular drug target has dropped drastically. Furthermore, many of the most commonly used and often last resort antibiotics have debilitating side effects. In stark contrast, we now appreciate that microbes in human microbiomes play crucial roles in maintaining good health. It is now clear that commensal bacteria in the intestine of mammals accomplish many beneficial functions. Although symbiotic bacteria and mammals have co-evolved and adapted to each other, the ecological niche offered by the host is plagued with environmental insults, to which the bacteria need to adapt rapidly and continuously. In response to stressful environment, bacteria express small regulatory RNAs to coordinate gene expression and adapt to various stress. Our recent work with small regulatory RNAs strongly suggest there is a large amount of unknown yet significant RNA-RNA interactions within bacterial cells. These interactions might regulate virulence and pathogenicity as well as antibiotic resistance. We will map the global RNA-RNA interactions quantitatively within the model bacterium E. coli as well as the major human pathogen Salmonella. Concurrently with this long-term goal, we will investigate the most promising RNA-RNA interactions to establish novel mechanisms of gene expression. We already have established the extended interactome of a few specific sRNAs in E. coli using a novel approach that we developed in the lab. Deciphering the most critical RNA-based regulations (including sRNA-mRNA, mRNA-mRNA, tRNA-mRNA), in bacterial cells. New RNA-RNA interactions are creating specific targets to test novel RNA-based therapies for medical doctors, pharmaceutical companies and drug developers.

column36: Access to Recovery with Assistive Technology Devices
column37: There are currently no assistive technology applications (Apps) for culturally-centered substance addiction treatment supports available in Canada. Recent Canadian culturally rooted substance addictions research supports the health and wellness of Indigenous peoples, contributes to cultural renewal, and highlights awareness of the link between colonialism and substance addiction. In addition, quantitative North American evidence has validated that Indigenous culture increases wellness for Indigenous people in the domains of mental, emotional, spiritual, and physical well-being. Thus, this project aims to understand how assistive technology devices (i.e. iPad or smart phone) can be utilized to increase access to culturally-centered substance addiction treatment support for individuals and families, particularly for those who live in rural and Northern areas. This community-based research project that will include qualitative and quantitative data, reflects the principle of two-eyed seeing (draws on strengths of Indigenous and Western knowledge) and prioritizes 'culture' as intervention in substance addiction treatment that promotes a holistic model of health and wellness as outlined in the Cultural Responsiveness Framework (CRF); a framework tool that everyone can access, as the CRF aims to build capacity within mainstream health systems to gain a better understanding of First Nations culture. This project is particularly relevant to the health and well-being of Metis, First Nations, and Inuit and non-Indigenous individuals (and their families) who have both intellectual disabilities and substance addiction issues. Globally, assistive technology device-based mainstream substance addiction treatment interventions have begun to demonstrate to be cost-efficient, when compared with counselor-facilitated substance addiction treatment methods; but also appear to be as effective in the engagement and treatment of patients with substance addiction issues.

column36: Unconventional NMDA Receptor Signalling in Neocortical Plasticity
column37: Few would probably dispute that one of the most important functions of the brain is learning and memory. If you open up any modern neuroscience textbook, you will learn that NMDA receptors are critical for memory formation in the brain. It is therefore perhaps not so surprising that these receptors have been implicated in devastating neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. In recent years, however, its become clear that our understanding of NMDA receptors is incomplete. For example, they are sometimes located on transmitting instead of receiving side of neuronal connections, where they cannot function according to the standard textbook view on how learning in the brain operates. Furthermore, they sometimes signal metabotropically, i.e. in the absence of depolarising neuronal activation, which completely changes how neuroscientists think about their function. This proposal will explore tow unorthodox modes of NMDA receptor signalling: on the transmitting side, and metabotropically. This is a virtual blank on the map, and must be understood to treat major neurological pathologies such as Alzheimer's and epilepsy.

column36: Quantitative ultrasound techniques for diagnosis of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
column37: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is the most common liver disease in Western countries, due in large part to its association with type 2 diabetes and obesity. The more advanced form of this disease is known as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). If left untreated, NASH can evolve to cirrhosis, the late stage of fibrosis. Once cirrhosis is established, patients are at increased risk of developing gastrointestinal bleeding, liver cancer and liver failure that may require transplantation. Fatty liver disease is difficult to diagnose because symptoms can be vague. In some cases, the liver may already be damaged without any symptoms. Furthermore, blood tests cannot be used to definitely establish a clear diagnosis. A liver biopsy is currently needed to diagnose the severity of fatty liver disease but this is usually not indicated in asymptomatic patients. This procedure requires the insertion of a needle inside the liver to remove a small piece of tissue for examination under microscope. Liver biopsy is an invasive procedure with a small risk of major complications such as bleeding in 0.5% of cases. It is also affected by sub-optimal sampling leading to diagnostic errors. Ultrasound is optimum for screening patients with or without symptoms because it is a safe and widely available technology to scan the whole liver. Members of our team have developed advanced ultrasound techniques that provide unique information not possible with state-of-the-art techniques. Unlike liver biopsy, these techniques would be applicable even in asymptomatic patients because it is non-invasive. This research proposal proposes a novel approach for diagnosis of NASH and will be the first study to measure individual components of NASH (fat, inflammation and fibrosis) with quantitative ultrasound (QUS) scores. This study is timely because NASH is the second leading cause of liver transplantation in North America and is predicted to become the leading indication in the near future.

column36: Targeting vulnerabilities in SMARCA4-deficient lung cancers
column37: Cancer is a heterogeneous disease. Distinct subtypes of cancers from the same primary site of origin can be defined by their unique molecular pathological features. Consequently, cancer therapy is shifting towards strategies aimed at genes specific to each patient, where mutated cancer-causing genes in tumors are targeted by highly selective inhibitors. These drugs are often very effective and have minimal side effects as normal tissues do not harbor the cancer-causing mutations, which are being targeted. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer and is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in Canada. NSCLC consists of different subtypes characterized by distinct cancer-causing mutations. For subtypes with mutations activating genes such as EGFR (10-35%) or ALK (3-7%), there are potent drugs that target these activated gene products and have significantly improved patient survival. In contrast, 10-37 % of NSCLCs are deficient in SMARCA4, a known tumor suppressor gene lost in many cancer types and which to this date remains undruggable. Therefore, effective treatment of these patients remains an unmet clinical challenge. In this proposal, we will first exploit a molecular weakness of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs. We have previously uncovered a vulnerability of SMARCA4 loss in an ovarian cancer subtype, which can be targeted using an FDA-approved drug originally developed for treating breast cancers. To extend our findings to NSCLCs, we will use a variety of model systems, including cell culture, mouse preclinical cancer models, and tumor samples from lung cancer patients. Independently, we will use powerful genetic tools to identify novel vulnerabilities of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs that can be exploited therapeutically. Our goal is to provide potential treatment strategies to treat SMARCA4-deficient NSCLCs and provide a clinical benefit for cancer patients.

column36: Interrogation of genome editing applications for the treatment of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating neuromuscular disorder with no cure available. Up to 70% patients carry large deletions in the DMD gene resulting in the absence of dystrophin, an integral muscle protein. Recent advances in genome engineering technologies have the potential to develop into life-saving therapies for this condition. Building on our previous successes we have developed several gene editing strategies applicable for correcting DMD deletions and two mouse models to test these approaches. Specifically, Objective 1 is designed to assess efficacy and safety of repairing a variety of DMD-causing deletions in patient cells using different genome editing systems in order to identify a best candidate for animal studies. The overall goal of the Objective 2 is to perform detailed genetic, biochemical and functional characterization of two novel mouse models with large DMD deletions: del52-54 and del52-55. Finally, in the Objective 3, we will test the hypothesis that disease severity in the newly generated DMD mouse models can be improved via in vivo genome editing using adeno associate virus (AAV) as a delivery vehicle. We anticipate that the development and refinement of therapeutic strategies described in this project will lead to efficient expression of dystrophin to restore muscle strength and function in our newly generated animal models, recapitulating large DMD mutations found in patients. The results of this project will provide data that can be directly translated into large animal models of DMD and subsequently into clinical trials in patients with deletions in the DMD gene. Furthermore, these pre-clinical proof of concept studies will pave the way for development of therapeutic approaches for other inherited conditions caused by large genomic rearrangements.

column36: HIV-1 Nef-Host Interactions Mediating Immune Evasion and Pathogenesis
column37: Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 (HIV-1) is the human virus responsible for Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS). Specifically, the coordinated activity of multiple HIV-1 proteins results in infected patients progressing from the asymptomatic phase to AIDS. Interestingly, the HIV-1 protein Nef has long been considered a major factor contributing to disease progression even though Nef lacks any known enzymatic activity. Instead, Nef binds to human proteins to wreak havoc inside the infected immune cell. This proposal will study interactions between Nef and host proteins. Furthermore, the precise details on how these interactions mediate disease progression and the evasion of the immune surveillance system will be defined. To accomplish this, we will combine our expertise in the movement of proteins within cells and super resolution imaging techniques to define the specific localization of these protein complexes within infected cells. We will also study these molecular pathways in a patient cohort of HIV-1 infected individuals to assess how these Nef interactions mediate immune evasion and disease progression in patients. These studies will provide novel information on new interactions that can be targeted to inhibit HIV-1. Indeed, we believe that performing these studies will lead to the future design of novel drugs and therapeutic agents that will benefit patients infected with HIV-1.

column36: Comparative effectiveness of a comprehensive, patient-centered hospital discharge planning intervention for frail older adults: feasibility study for a large mixed-method randomized pragmatic trial
column37: A large number of frail older adults have difficulty performing activities of daily living and resuming former roles in the months following hospital discharge. This increases the risk of unplanned hospital readmissions and emergency visits after they return home. Comprehensive, patient-centered discharge planning has been reported to improve older adults' ability to perform activities of daily living and to reduce readmission rates after hospital discharge. However, to our knowledge, no evidence-based discharge protocol is routinely used in Canada with the frail population. An innovative discharge planning protocol called "HOME" was recently developed in Australia. The HOME intervention includes: 1) hospital-based partnership with patient and family to establish goal setting and problem solving; 2) pre-discharge home assessment to address safety issues and problems with patient and family; 3) post-discharge home assessment and in-home training to address unmet needs; and 4) follow-up telephone calls to provide ongoing support to patient and family. A Canadian version of HOME has been developed. This will be followed by a large trial to investigate if this intervention increases functioning in daily life activities and decreases hospital and emergency readmissions for frail patients who are discharged home. Our proposed study is a preliminary and necessary step to identify problems that may arise during this large trial and address them proactively. If proven beneficial, the Canadian version of HOME would be an appropriate, applicable and acceptable intervention to improve patients' experiences and outcomes as well as change health practice surroundings discharge planning with frail older adults.
