column36: Inappropriateness of Health Care in Canada
column37: We will examine inappropriate health care in Canada. We define 'inappropriate health care' as: 1) inappropriate clinical practices, meaning underuse, overuse and misuse of clinical practices or 2) inappropriate settings, meaning providing care in a health setting that does not match the patient's clinical characteristics or the practices required for his or her care. The goal of this research project is to inform quality improvement programs across Canada by conducting a systematic review of inappropriate health care in Canada. Our specific research objectives are to: 1) systematically search and critically review published and grey literature for studies of inappropriate health care in Canada; 2) estimate the nature and magnitude of inappropriate health care in Canada and in its provincial and territorial jurisdictions; and 3) inform a research and action agenda for future quality improvement activities aimed at reducing inappropriate health care in Canada. Our main output will be the first-ever evidence-based compendium of inappropriate health care in Canada. From this we will develop and distribute to provincial/territorial and national governments and leaders in health care quality detailed summary reports of inappropriate health care across Canada and in their province/territory. These reports will detail both the nature and the magnitude of inappropriate health care in the jurisdiction for three core care categories: preventive care, acute care, and chronic care. We will also bring together the key stakeholders from across the country involved in health care quality. We will share with them our findings to stimulate discussions with them to inform: i) an action agenda on how to reduce inappropriate health care in Canada, and ii) a research agenda that identifies areas where future research and/or monitoring are needed in inappropriate health care in Canada.

column37: Human chromosome ends are protected from damage by a stretch of repetitive DNA sequence known as telomeres. In healthy mortal cells, telomere DNA is gradually shortened during successive rounds of replication as a cell ages, and ultimately instructs cells to naturally terminate. In cancerous cells the enzyme telomerase ensures maintenance of a stable telomere length and therefore enables the indefinite growth and uncontrolled division characteristic of tumor formation. Active telomerase is diagnostic of cancer progression, as has been identified in the vast majority of malignant cancers. In this proposal, we seek to understand the regulation of telomerase by enzymes known as helicases that exert their effects through prevention of proper telomerase assembly. We will use an integrated experimental approach involving high-resolution structural biology, biochemical analysis, and functional methodologies. Our work aims to provide a template for the rational design of therapeutics to attenuate telomerase activity.

column36: Limiting late effects following pediatric cranial radiation
column37: Recent decades have seen a substantial improvement in the survival of children with brain cancer, the second most common cancer in children. Patients are now living into their adult years. Unfortunately, the side effects from brain tumour treatment frequently affect brain development. Survivors suffer a progressive decline in mental capacity and achieve lower levels of education, household income and full-time employment. These debilitating mental side effects impact quality of life and are strongly linked with radiation therapy. After radiation, the brain experiences loss of cells, inflammation, and reduced capacity to make new cells. We have shown that manipulation of these effects alters impact of radiation on the brain, with the exciting result that brain development can be partially restored. In this proposal, we will determine if it is possible to induce such improvements by drug treatment or lifestyle changes, so that normal brain development can be achieved after radiation. To do so, we will systematically test 11 candidate treatments in a mouse model, measuring brain growth after radiation using magnetic resonance imaging. First, each treatment will be tested individually. Next, we will test the best treatments in combination. Finally, for the most-promising treatments, we will determine how treatment affects tumour response to CRT, and measure the cognitive and behavioural benefits. At its conclusion, this work will establish a strategy appropriate for restoring brain development after radiation in children. Treatments have been selected for ease of translation (9 of 11 treatments are already used in patients for other medical conditions or are in clinical trials), so that promising results can be moved quickly to childhood cancer survivors. Ultimately, our goal is to ensure that cancer survivors have the same opportunities and quality of life as their cancer-free peers.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Our immune system changes as we age. As an example, we begin to produce more of some kinds of white blood cells (monocytes and neutrophils) and less of others (B and T cells). Since monocytes and neutrophils are required to protect us from infection, you might think that this would protect older adults from infections, but what actually happens is that these cells don't mature properly and enter into the bloodstream prematurely. These immature monocytes don't help fight infection but actually make some infections worse. Furthermore, these immature monocytes produce a lot of inflammation which also has a negative impact on our health as we age. The purpose of this proposal is to determine why we start to produce more monocytes as we get older, to determine why these monocytes do not mature properly and to identify ways in which we might be able to restore this process. To do this we will collect blood from young and older adults and assess how maturity decreases with age and determine whether this immaturity correlates with levels of inflammation. Specifically we believe that a molecule called TNF might be involved because when we aged mice that did not have TNF, they did not have any changes in the development or function of their monocytes with age. To determine if this is the case in humans, we have collected samples from humans who are undergoing anti-TNF therapy. We predict that when their TNF is high, their monocytes will be less mature and when their TNF goes down due to their therapy, their monocytes will become normal. We will use our unique colony of old mice (18-22 mo), including old mice that don't make TNF (called TNF knockout mice) to determine which cells make this TNF. The long-term goal of this project is to find novel ways to keep us healthier as we get older. Because monocytes protect us from infections but can also contribute to diseases that increase with age (e.g. cardiovascular disease), we hope these findings will have broad applications.

column36: Inference-Based Cognitive Therapy versus Exposure and Response Prevention for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A 16-Session Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a highly disabling psychiatric illness, characterized by obsessional thoughts that cause patients to perform time-consuming and distressing compulsive rituals. Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is a first-line psychological treatment of choice, which requires patients to face their fears by being exposed to feared stimuli. ERP has been shown to reduce symptoms among those who comply with treatment. However, there is still a significant portion of patients that do not improve, especially those who firmly believe their obsessions are realistic and reasonable (i.e. OCD with Overvalued Ideation). Also, a large proportion of patients refuse the treatment or drop out during treatment due to the distress provoked by ERP. That leaves at most 3-4 out of 10 people with OCD who benefit from ERP, and even then, residual symptoms often remain, or symptoms eventually reappear after treatment. One evidence-based approach to the treatment of OCD, termed inference-based cognitive therapy (IBCT) has been shown to be as effective as ERP with the potential to overcome the limitations of ERP. Since IBCT is a cognitive approach, the treatment does not require exposure to feared stimuli and likely more tolerable for patients with OCD. Also, there is evidence that IBCT is more effective than ERP for those with overvalued ideation, since it directly targets the distorted reasoning that is responsible for the intensity and persistence of the obsession. The current study aims to directly compare ERP with this promising evidence-based cognitive therapy, which is expected to be significantly more effective for those with overvalued ideation, as well as significantly more tolerable with lower rates of treatment refusal, drop-out and higher treatment satisfaction. The project is designed to maximize potential beneficial health outcomes and offer a new evidence-based treatment option for the large proportion of patients unable to benefit from ERP.

column36: CYP24A1 Enzymatic Activity in FGF23-Mediated Renal Phosphate Wasting Disorders
column37: Phosphate and vitamin D are critical for many physiological functions including skeletal development, mineral balance, energy metabolism, and proper nerve and muscle function. The kidney is a major player in the maintenance of the body's phosphate and vitamin D balance, by virtue of its ability to regulate: (i) the amounts of phosphorus it reclaims before it gets lost in the urine based on the body's needs, and (ii) the production and thereby the levels of vitamin D in blood, important for the absorption of phosphorus from the intestine. These processes at the level of the kidney are very tightly regulated mainly by two hormones: parathyroid hormone (PTH), and the more recently-identified fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Genetic diseases of phosphate and vitamin D metabolism with have high FGF23 and low vitamin D levels in the blood have been described. For the most common form, XLH, it is estimated as high as 1 in 10,000 newborns are affected. Children with XLH have rickets (bone deformities including short stature and bow or knock-leggedness) that progress to poor skeletal mineralization with soft, brittle bones, and calcification of tendons and ligaments in adulthood. Studies proposed in this application, a continuation of our previous work funded by the KFOC and published recently in a prestigious clinical research journal, aims to use transgenic mice and molecular biology techniques to understand the mechanism by which high levels of FGF23 affects bone development by altering the concentration of vitamin D locally in bone. We aim to show that, whether by genetics or by pharmacotherapy, this process can be altered to allow better bone formation to take place. Findings arising from this work will help uncover previously unrecognized targets and strategies for the treatment of patients with these genetic disorders.

column36: Metformin in Women with Type 2 Diabetes in Pregnancy (MiTy) Trial: A randomized controlled trial
column37: The incidence of type 2 diabetes is rising at a remarkable rate, and with it we see a rise in type 2 diabetes in pregnancy. Insulin is the standard of care for the management of women with type 2 diabetes in pregnancy. However, despite treatment with insulin, these women continue to face high rates of poor maternal and fetal outcomes. Mothers have high blood pressure, preeclampsia, high rates of cesarean section, while infants have preterm birth, low blood sugar, they are large, can get stuck during delivery leading to birth injury, and often require the NICU. Metformin is an oral hypoglycemic agent presently being used in patients with type 2 diabetes outside of pregnancy and in other pregnant populations, with some benefit. Our aim is to see whether the addition of metformin to standard therapy of insulin alone, will improve these poor pregnancy outcomes by conducting a multicentre, randomized trial, randomizing 500 pregnant women with type 2 diabetes to receive either metformin or placebo, in addition to their usual insulin regimen. We hypothesize that metformin use, when added to the treatment with insulin, will improve pregnancy outcomes by reducing high maternal blood sugars, high maternal insulin doses, excessive maternal weight gain and pregnancy-induced high blood pressure, all of which should reduce poor outcomes in the baby. Our primary outcome will be the reduction of a composite outcome, which will include pregnancy loss, preterm birth, birth injury, respiratory distress, low blood sugar, and neonatal intensive care admissions over 24 hours. Our MiTy Kids study (separately funded) aims to follow these children for up to 2 years of age, to see if metformin reduces the risk of childhood obesity. This study will provide critical insight into an important treatment, which will impact standard of care and clinical practice, with the potential to benefit the health of pregnant mothers with diabetes and their children, immediately and in the long-term.

column36: Role of a lipid hydrolase TGH in hepatic fat storage and lipoprotein secretion
column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a major health problem that is caused by extra fat building up in a person's liver cells. Worldwide, this disease affects about 30% of the adult population and over 70% of people with obesity. The health risk for people with NAFLD is that this disease can progress to more serious problems: -inflammation and swelling of their liver, called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) -normal liver tissue being replaced by non-living scar tissue, called cirrhosis -end-stage liver disease and liver failure, the most common reason for needing a liver transplant Having NAFLD or NASH also places people at much greater risk for type 2 diabetes, heart disease and end-stage kidney disease. Today, we have no effective treatments for NASH. My research team has discovered that a protein called TGH affects distribution and storage of fat. Our experiments show that TGH has profound effects on circulating fat in the blood and on development of NAFLD. We showed that reducing the amount TGH in mice protects the liver from developing NAFLD and NASH and improves insulin signaling. Because TGH regulates how fat is stored in the liver, this protein could be a good target for drugs to prevent or treat NAFLD and NASH. My research aims to find out how TGH regulates the amounts of fat that people store in the liver and in the blood. Understanding the mechanisms that this protein uses to regulate fat storage may lead to new treatments for NAFLD/NASH and diseases triggered by NAFLD/NASH.

column36: Medically at-risk drivers: The road to developing evidence-based fitness to drive guidelines
column37: With the aging population also comes an increase in age-related deficits (e.g. decreased vision, slowing of cognitive functions), as well as an increase in age-related medical conditions (i.e. cognitive impairment/dementia, Parkinson's disease, stroke), all of which can affect safe driving. These trends present a significant public health concern given that older adults are disproportionately (per mile driven) involved in collisions resulting in serious injury and death. Hence, determining the most effective means to identify and assess medically at-risk drivers is critical given the rapid growth in this segment of the driving population. Together with the Ministry of Transportation Ontario, the Societe de L'Assurance Automobile du Quebec (SAAQ) and the Saskatchewan Driving Licensing and Registration Office (SGI), this project entails the development of an online, web-based repository (e-repository) where data from comprehensive driving evaluations of medically at-risk drivers are captured and tracked accordingly. By establishing a large-scale database, we will be able to track drivers already referred to a specialized driving assessment centre in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan and use this data to examine the referral process and the relationship between functional abilities, on-road driving performance (i.e., pass/fail), and crashes/violations (from driving records). Ultimately, we will develop evidence based tools to assess fitness to drive which will be translated into policy and practice guidelines for health care professionals and government agencies.

column36: Novel therapies to augment neurological benefits of cellular therapies for traumatic spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a leading cause of permanent neurological disabilities affecting over 2.5 million individuals worldwide. In Canada, there are over 86,000 patients who are afflicted with lifelong consequences of SCI with approximately 4,200 new cases each year. The lifetime medical cost of each SCI patient is estimated at 1.6 to 3 million dollars. Thus, SCI has a profound impact on patients, their caregivers, and the healthcare system. Currently, there is no effective treatment for SCI and new therapies are needed to allow neurological improvement in patients. Extensive research by our group and others show that transplantation of neural stem cells offers tremendous possibility for SCI repair. Indeed, based on these experimental discoveries, neural stem cell transplantation has moved to clinical trials in recent years. Initial outcomes of these trials indicate that while neural stem cells are safe and promising for treatment of SCI, their benefit for neurological recovery of patients is only modest. We have made the same observation in our experimental evaluations, establishing a need for combinatorial therapies to augment the functional outcomes of current cellular therapies. To this end, we have discovered new therapeutic targets with the potential to harness the regenerative capacity of neural stem cells for repairing the injured spinal cord. We have identified that formation of a glia scar around the lesion and increased production of inhibitory molecules in the scar limit the benefits of neural stem cell transplantation. We show that inhibiting these factors facilitates the longterm survival of stem cells and their abilities for tissue regeneration. We are currently investigating several aspects of these strategies and importantly their potential in improving functional recovery in an animal model that clinically reflects human SCI. Our goal is to develop effective regenerative medicine strategies for improving the quality of life in SCI patients.

column36: Urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA) and its receptor (uPAR) interaction in tumor microenvironment, therapeutic implications
column37: Serine protease urokinase type plasminogen activator (uPA) and its receptor (uPAR) play an important role in tumor invasion, growth and metastasis. Targeting genes expressed by tumor cells is an attractive approach for early diagnosis and developing novel treatment strategies. Large-scale clinical studies in several cancers including those in breast and prostate cancer patients, have demonstrated increased expression of uPA-uPAR which play an important role in tumor growth and spread to different organs including skeleton which results in bone pain, nerve compression and immobility. In this proposal, using state-of-the-art models of cancer, we will elucidate the role of the uPAR and its different domains in tumor progression and metastasis to non-skeletal and skeletal sites. We will evaluate the role of uPAR in immune surveillance and determine the effects of inhibiting checkpoint protein inhibitors alone and in combination with anti-uPAR agents on tumor growth and metastasis. Using our highly selective lead anti-uPAR antibody, we will examine its efficacy alone and in combination settings to block cancer growth and spread to non-skeletal and skeletal sites using our mouse models of cancer. Collectively this research proposal will further clarify the role of the uPAR system in tumor growth and its spread to the skeleton. Results from these studies will play a key role in the optimization and clinical development of novel uPAR targeted therapeutic approaches alone and in combination setting against breast and prostate cancer growth and bone metastasis.

column36: Altered hepatic retinoid homeostasis in the initiation and progression of alcoholic liver disease
column37: Vitamin A is an essential part of our diet and is used by the body in many ways, including vision, immunity and reproduction. The liver acts as a warehouse for vitamin A: storing it and releasing it for use in other parts of the body. Vitamin A is also important in maintaining liver health, and it has been suggested that a disruption in this role promotes the development of liver disease. Alcohol abuse is a major cause of preventable death and gives rise to a significant disease burden in Canada. The main organ affected by drinking too much alcohol is the liver, with a well-described disease response ranging from fat accumulation (steatosis), to inflammation (hepatitis), scarring (fibrosis and cirrhosis) and ultimately liver failure. According to the Canadian Liver Foundation, approximately 1 in 12 Canadians drink heavily, and thousands of Canadians die every year because of alcoholic liver disease, making it a national research priority. Moreover, heavy drinking rates are double for First Nations people living on Reserves, representing a population at increased risk of alcohol-related disease. The research described in this proposal aims to establish that alcohol disturbs the way vitamin A works in the liver, contributing to hepatic disease. Through a series of complementary experiments, we will determine the mechanism through which alcohol disturbs vitamin A function at two points in the disease process: 1) the initial step of fat accumulation, and 2) the formation of scar tissue, representing the worsening of liver disease. This research will provide a better understanding of how alcohol causes liver disease by disrupting vitamin A function. The new knowledge generated by this research may be translated into improved care for heavy drinkers at risk of alcoholic liver disease by providing ways to prevent its formation, or stop it from worsening. This knowledge will also provide new insight into how altered vitamin A function contributes to other human diseases.

column36: Thermosensitive Liposome Formulation of Vinorelbine in Combination with MR-Guided High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Mediated Hyperthermia: An Innovative Approach to Treatment of Rhabdomyosarcoma
column37: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents, with the majority of cases arising in children under the age of 10 years. Following the successful treatment of the initial disease, recurrence manifests in approximately one-third of patients, with about 80% of recurrences localized at the primary tumor site. Unfortunately, with current treatments, the 5-year survival rate for these patients is only 17-28 %. In addition, due to the characteristic toxicities associated with some anti-cancer drugs for RMS, treatment of these young patients can lead to a series of long-term health complications in adult life including neurological and cardiac disorders. The current research project describes the development of a nanoparticle (termed a liposome) containing the anti-cancer drug, vinorelbine. This drug works by preventing the cancer cells from dividing and ultimately leads to cell death. Liposomes containing various drugs are currently used in the treatment of several cancers. Our liposome nanoparticles have been specially designed such that the drug is released when the temperature exceeds that of normal body temperature. We will achieve localized release of the drug at the tumor site by increasing the temperature of the tumor using an ultrasound machine. This technique will increase the amount of drug delivered specifically to the tumor site and therefore minimize drug exposure to normal tissues. We will also investigate whether the combination of vinorelbine and an increase in the temperature of the tumor has a greater tumor killing effect compared to vinorelbine alone. The potential benefits of this project for RMS patients are a greater killing effect of recurrent RMS tumors and a reduction in the short and long-term side effects, which are commonly associated with exposure of chemotherapy to normal tissues.

column36: Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction and Oxygen Sensitive Cardiac MRI in Women: A Novel Non-Invasive Diagnostic Tool
column37: Although more women than men die annually of coronary artery disease (CAD), nearly one half of women presenting with chest pain are found to have non-obstructive CAD (NoCAD). Historically, these patients were often reassured without consideration for diagnostic or treatment options. More recently, evidence has shown that nearly 50% of women with chest pain and NoCAD have occult disease in the small vessels of the heart, referred to as coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), which has been shown to carry a heightened risk for future cardiovascular events. Current characterization of patients with chest pain syndromes and NoCAD rely on invasive testing that lack standardized protocols and use pharmacological agents including adenosine, which are often poorly tolerated in patients. This has limited the use of these diagnostic tests in the evaluation of patients with NoCAD, leaving many patients with CMD undiagnosed and untreated. Recently, oxygen sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (OS-CMR) using a combination of breathing manoeuvres has been shown to be capable of identifying microvascular changes in the heart in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Given the less invasive nature of this technique, we intend to study this novel diagnostic tool to assess its ability to detect CMD in women. We will also evaluate whether breathing manoeuvres during OS-CMR can detect CMD as accurately as with the administration of adenosine. We expect that our study will show that women with CMD will have inadequate oxygenation response to breathing manoeuvres that will be identified on OS-CMR. Additionally OS-CMR with breathing manoeuvres will be able to detect CMD as accurately as adenosine. Our results will support the use of OS-CMR as a non-invasive diagnostic tool in the assessment of women with chest pain and NoCAD, which will allow physicians to better identify patients with CMD and provide the foundation for which future treatment can be studied.

column36: CONSORT Extension for Trials Conducted in Existing Data Structures, Including Researcher-generated Cohorts, Registries, Electronic Health Records, and Administrative Databases
column37: Large-scale randomized trials (RCTs) are complex and expensive to perform. Less than one-third of RCTs achieve their planned recruitment target, follow-up of participants is labor intensive, and results from trials often cannot be generalized to real-world settings. To overcome these challenges, an increasingly common approach involves conducting trials within existing data structures, including trials with participants from researcher-generated cohorts, registries, electronic health records and administrative databases. These designs, however, reflect relatively recent innovations, and published trial reports often do not adequately describe important aspects of trials, such as steps taken in recruitment and maintenance of the cohort, information provided or not provided to participants about trial participation, and how participants are selected and allocated to trial arms. Reporting guidelines increase the reporting quality and utility of research, but there is no guideline for trials embedded in existing data structures. The goal of the proposed project is to develop and disseminate a reporting guideline, as an extension of the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement for trials conducted in existing data structures, including researcher-generated cohorts, registries, electronic health records, and administrative databases. We will systematically review guidance on conducting and reporting these types of trials and review published trials to identify reporting gaps. From this, we will generate a list of potential modifications to items in the standard CONSORT statement checklist and potential new items. These will be vetted via a Delphi exercise with team members and stakeholders and at a face-to-face meeting. The CONSORT extension for trials embedded in existing data structures, which we will produce and disseminate, will contribute to transparent reporting of these trials.

column36: Treatment induced changes to bone quality: Impact on the skeletal stability of the metastatic spine
column37: Many malignant cancers can spread (i.e. metastasize) from their site of origin. A very common site of this spread is to the bone. The spine is the most common bone tissue affected. Metastatic disease in the bony spine can present as bone destroying (osteolytic), bone forming (osteoblastic) or as a mixture of the two (mixed), but all demonstrate an increased risk of fracture. In the presence of cancer, we have shown that differences exist in the quality of the remaining bone (in both its mineral and organic components) leading to compromised material and mechanical behaviour. This characterization has formed a robust foundation upon which we propose to evaluate the impact of systemic and localized cancer treatments on bone quality in the metastatic spine. This research will elucidate the complex interactions of multimodal cancer treatment on bone quality and fracture risk in the spine using state-of-the-art medical imaging, experimental and computational methods. Our work will link preclinical and clinical data sets to enable translation of this knowledge towards informing clinical practice. The ability to accurately determine the impact of treatments on structural integrity will provide an important foundation upon which to direct new and existing local and systemic treatments for spinal metastatic disease.

column36: Structural Basis of Cyclic Nucleotide Signal Translation and Inhibition
column37: Pancreatic, endocrine and cardiac tumours as well as intellectual disabilities and abnormal bone growth in children are caused by defective reading of the signal transmitted within cells by a messenger molecule called cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). Furthermore, a closely related molecule, cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), plays a critical role in the replication of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. The goals of this project are to study two proteins that bind to cAMP and cGMP, i.e. the cAMP-dependent protein kinase A in mammals (PKA) and cGMP-dependent protein kinase G in P. falciparum (pfPKG), and to: (a) elucidate the structural and dynamical changes caused by inherited mutations that lead to incorrect translation of the cAMP signal and diseases such as cancer and developmental defects; (b) to understand how to suppress the signals carried by the cAMP and cGMP cyclic nucleotides to improve current cancer and malaria treatments. We will use nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to investigate how modified molecules that resemble cAMP and cGMP, and which may serve as future cancer and malaria drugs, interact with PKA and pfPKG, respectively. Their effects on these proteins are currently poorly understood at the structural and dynamical level, and NMR has only recently been used to investigate these interactions at atomic resolution. NMR will reveal the structural and dynamical changes in PKA and pfPKG caused by cAMP and cGMP analogs, respectively, as needed to fully understand how to modulate these proteins' activities. NMR is also ideally suited to unveil how disease-causing inherited mutations alter the physiological interactions of PKA with cAMP. Elucidating the structural and dynamical changes caused by disease-related mutations and modified cyclic nucleotides will help understand the molecular origins of multiple tumours and pediatric disorders, and will also facilitate the design of improved cancer and malaria drugs.

column36: Heat Activated Liposomal Delivery of Chemo and Molecular Therapy in Combination with Radiotherapy for Treatment of Breast Cancer Recurrence at the Chest Wall
column37: In Canada, breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer in women accounting for 26% of all newly diagnosed cancers. While many therapeutic options for early stage BC can be curative (including radiation therapy, breast-sparing surgery or mastectomy), the treatment of recurrent BC (present in 10-20 % of BC patients) can be clinically challenging (and includes chemotherapy, surgery and/or radiation therapy). Novel combinations of existing therapies offer an exciting opportunity to enhance the killing of BC cells while at the same time avoiding the development of resistance to therapies, which can occur rapidly when treating patients with a single agent. In the proposed research project, two anti-cancer drugs will be encapsulated into a type of nanoparticle called a liposome. Liposomes containing various drugs are currently used in the treatment of breast, ovarian and other cancers. Our liposome nanoparticles have been specially designed so that the drugs will only be released when the temperature exceeds that of normal body temperature. We will increase drug exposure to tumor by increasing the tumor temperature using an ultrasound machine. This technique will allow for a significant amount of the two drugs to be released at the tumor site and minimize any potential side effects in normal tissues. The two drugs we are delivering, doxorubicin and alvespimycin, act on cancer cells by different mechanisms. Preliminary studies by our group have shown that the combination of these two drugs is synergistic and highly efficacious in killing a range of BC cells. Given their synergistic effect, combining the two drugs allows us to reduce the total dose of doxorubicin by at least 20 fold. This is important because doxorubicin is known to have significant side effects including cardiotoxicity. This nanoparticle therapy will also be combined with targeted radiotherapy to offer an exciting combination-based approach for the treatment of recurrent breast cancer in the chest wall.

column36: Understanding Class I MHC Receptor Control of Natural Killer Cell Memory
column37: Adaptive immune memory is one of the most powerful weapons the body has to fight infections. It is how vaccines work: the immune system sees harmful, foreign matter, and T and B cells remember it so that the immune response is stronger and faster the next time that target is encountered. Surprisingly, natural killer cells, a cousin to the T cell, can also remember these targets, in a process we do not yet understand. We have previously demonstrated that this natural killer memory relies on a specific natural killer cell protein called Ly49I. This proposed research seeks to better understand what Ly49I does that allows memory in these cells, and to identify which other proteins and which helper cells contribute to natural killer memory. Understanding natural killer cell memory is exciting because it works through different mechanisms than T cell memory, so learning how this memory works will open a whole new field of study in immunology. It is also exciting because natural killer cells are experts at killing cancer, so understanding their memory could lead to novel cancer vaccines and therapies designed to prevent the recurrence of a dormant cancer.

column36: Establishing dietary treatment with DHA as part of neoadjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among Canadian women as 1 in 9 women over their lifetime will be diagnosed with this form of cancer. In 2015, the Public Health Agency estimated 25 000 Canadian women, or approximately 480 women per week would be diagnosed with breast cancer, and over 5000 would die. The vast majority of these women would have been offered some form of chemotherapy treatment. Long chain polyunsaturated omega-3 fatty acids, found in fatty fish from cold water, have been shown to decrease breast cancer growth in laboratory animals and human cancer cells in culture (e.g. in petri dishes). Recently, studies from our group have suggested that one of these omega-3 fatty acids, docosahexanoic acid or DHA, can improve the ability of a common chemotherapy drug to kill breast cancer, but not normal cells. Our studies indicate that DHA can kill cancer cells using some of the same death signals that chemotherapy drugs use. We are proposing that treating breast cancer cells with DHA will improve the effectiveness of current breast cancer chemotherapy drugs, without increasing side effects. We are especially interested in the use of DHA during early (neoadjuvant) chemotherapy that is used to treat Stage II & III breast cancer prior to surgery and/or radiation. We will study the use of DHA in cell models, animal's implanted with human tumors and in a small clinical trial in women undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy to determine the efficacy and the effect on the tumor and the women's immune system. We anticipate that providing or feeding DHA will improve the action of the chemotherapy drug and help protect the women's immune system. Our studies will provide evidence that an inexpensive dietary treatment improves drug effectiveness without additional toxic side effects to the patient. Our work has the potential to significantly benefit women diagnosed with breast cancer

column36: Bayis Il Tus - A Strong Breath: Community-Based Research to Identify the Prevalence of and Contributors to Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease in Remote and Rural First Nations Communities in British Columbia
column37: First Nations peoples in Canada have more challenges with their lung health compared to non-First Nations people. They are often exposed to more air pollution and cigarette smoke and have a high prevalence of cough, wheeze and shortness of breath. Although there is a high use of health care services for chronic lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), this disease is not "on the radar" in many First Nations communities. This may be because we do not know how many First Nations people have COPD, especially those living in remote and rural areas. We know that cigarette smoking causes COPD, but there is much less known about the effects of household, historical/community/cultural, and work-related factors on the burden of COPD in First Nations people. This project is a new partnership between UBC, Carrier Sekani Family Services and eleven partner Nations. This study is unique in being able to address the individual, community, and historical risks of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. The goal of this study is to better understand the burden of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. Aim 1: Estimate how many people have COPD and how many people have not been diagnosed. Aim 2: Find out if there is a link between inhaled pollutants (from household, work-related, and historical/community/cultural sources) and: 1) symptoms; 2) blocked airflow; and 3) health care use. In order to do this, we will recruit adults from randomly-selected households in eleven First Nations communities in northern BC. We will collect detailed measures of lung function, symptoms, self-reported current & past exposure to lung irritants, and health care use. We will also collect indoor air quality measures from homes and community buildings. With the study results, communities will be able to better plan for health services, and create prevention strategies to reduce the chance of First Nations people developing COPD in the future.

column36: The role of victimization in adolescents' sexual health: A longitudinal study
column37: Exposure to victimization in childhood and adolescence is a widespread social and health issue in Canada. In a representative sample of more than 23,000 Canadians aged 18 years and older, the rate of child sexual abuse, physical abuse, or exposure to domestic violence was found to be 32%. Victimization is associated with a host of negative short- and long-term mental and physical health consequences, such as internalizing and externalizing problems, post-traumatic stress disorder, substance abuse, chronic pain and sexual revictimization. Although several studies have examined the consequences of childhood and adolescent victimization, progress in this area is hampered by important methodological limitations, such as the use of clinical samples, cross-sectional designs, and adult retrospective reports of victimization. Further, very little work has focused on sexuality, beyond sexual risk-taking. The proposed longitudinal study will overcome prior methodological limitations by examining the effect of different types of victimization assessed at age 14 on the sexual health of adolescents aged 14-17 over a three-year period. In their high school classrooms, 4,000 community participants will complete standardized measures at baseline as well as one and two years later. We hypothesize that victimization assessed at Time 1 will significantly predict worse sexual health outcomes at two- and three-year follow-ups. Our interdisciplinary team of psychologists, sexologists and physicians specialized in victimization, adolescence, and sexuality is well positioned to carry out the proposed research, which has direct implications for the health of Canadians. Findings will generate novel longitudinal data concerning the relationship between childhood and adolescent victimization and sexual health, and will contribute to the identification of factors to be targeted in prevention and intervention programs aimed at improving adolescents' sexual health.

This project is part of an ongoing partnership between the University of British Columbia, Carrier Sekani Family Services and eleven partner First Nations. This study is unique in being able to address the culturally-relevant treatment and education of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. We hope that in the long term, this study will increase lung-related health services to remote northern BC First Nations communities and support similar efforts in other communities.

column37: Canadian youth 16-25 are the vital future of society and their health and wellness are the concern of all Canadians. Deserving serious attention, however, is the evidence that the health of Indigenous youth living in Canada is disproportionately worse than the general Canadian population. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's Calls to Action outlined the historical processes of colonization as the most critical social determinant of Indigenous youth health, which perpetuates realities of poverty, racism, and discrimination that hinder their healthy development, particularly within urban contexts where Indigenous youth are on the 'front-lines' of experiencing the stereotypes and prejudices of non-Indigenous Canadians. The goal of our research is to move beyond descriptions of Indigenous health inequities towards participatory action interventions designed to improve health outcomes of youth in Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Thunder Bay, and Halifax. Through strong collaborations with youth and community partner organizations serving their needs, this 5-year project will: a) develop a needs, strengths, and health assessment map with and for Indigenous youth; b) design and implement culturally informed participatory action research projects that will address key social determinants of health that emerge from the needs assessment maps; and c) identify and evaluate the health and resilience outcomes for participating youth by examining changes over time. While observing variations across sties, it is anticipated that Indigenous youth who participate in action research of this kind will show significant increases on various health and resilience measures. The health related knowledge from this project will also: 1) inform effective Indigenous youth engagement strategies; 2) improve social determinants of health impacting Indigenous youth in urban contexts; and 3) guide effective program and policy interventions promoting greater health equity for Indigenous youth across Canada.

column36: RESTORE: Robot Enhanced Stroke Therapy Optimizes Rehabilitation
column37: Treatment after stroke often involves rehabilitation. Rehabilitation involves learning to move and feel again through intensive practice. It may require tens of thousands of repetitions of a particular movement to relearn it after stroke. Robots can help increase intensity as many therapists cannot help someone do thousands of repetitions of a movement in today's healthcare system. We are specifically interested in when is the best time to start rehabilitation and how much do we need to best retrain someone to use their arm after stroke? Our first objective is to determine whether one hour per day or two hours per day of robotic rehabilitation is better. Our second objective is to determine if we should start having stroke survivors work on rehabilitating their arms a few days after their stroke or wait a few weeks to begin. We think that starting early and working harder will lead to the best possible outcomes. Our third objective involves using information from brain scans and electrical measures of brain function to determine who responds best to early rehabilitation. Stroke survivors will play robotic rehabilitation games to improve their strength, sensation, range of motion and overall function in the arm. We will randomize stroke survivors to one of five groups. The first will begin working with the robot 8 days after their stroke for 1 hour per day. The second will begin working with the robot 8 days after their stroke for 2 hours per day. The third will begin working with the robot 21 days after their stroke for 1 hour per day. The fourth will begin working with the robot 21 days after their stroke for 2 hours per day. A fifth will receive standard of care treatment. At different times during the study we will measure arm function with various scales as well as brain MRI's to determine which treatment is best. The study will also help us to decide when to begin rehabilitation and the amount of rehabilitation needed to get the best result.

column36: Does the BC Farmers' Market Nutrition Coupon Program improve the dietary behaviours and psychosocial well-being of low-income adults?
column37: Healthy eating is important for good health. However, many low-income Canadians cannot afford to buy enough healthy food. The BC Farmers' Market Nutrition Coupon Program gives low-income seniors and young families 16 weeks of coupons worth $15/week to buy healthy foods in farmers' markets and teaches them about healthy eating. It is not clear if the program is meeting its goals of improving the diets, well-being and health of low-income adults because its impacts have not been studied. This research will study the impact of the BC Farmers' Market Nutrition Coupon Program on what people eat, and their social and mental well-being. It will also try to understand how the program makes these changes and how the program can be improved. We will use a strong study design that can show cause and effect. We will study these things by asking 200 adults who are in the program, and 200 adults who are not in the program, to tell us about the foods they eat, their social relationships, stress levels and general mental well-being. All of these questions will be asked before the program starts, right after it ends, and 16 weeks after it has ended so that we can understand how these things changed during and after the program. A smaller group of 40 adults will be interviewed about their experiences in the program to help us understand how any changes happened, and how the program can be improved. The BC Farmers' Market Nutrition Coupon Program is paid for by taxpayers and so it is important to find out if it is actually helping to improve people's diets and well-being. Information from this study will help the BC government and the BC Association of Farmers' Markets to understand if the program is meeting its goals, how it is doing so, and how the program can be improved. This information can also be used by governments in other provinces and countries to decide if they should start their own farmers' market nutrition coupon programs.

column36: Biological and translational implications of replication repair deficiency and hypermutation in human cancer
column37: The human cell needs to duplicate each DNA molecule to enable it to divide into 2 daughter cells. This important process is called DNA replication and is not mistake free. Indeed, up to a third of mutations which result in cancer occur during this replication phase. The human replication repair genes responsible for fixing these mistakes are therefore extremely important to avoid accumulation of such mutations. We found that mutations in the replication repair genes which result in replication repair deficiency or RRD, can be inherited or as a part of tumor formation and cause an important group of cancers characterized by thousands of mutations hence termed hypermutant cancers. These hypermutant cancers are common, can occur in all tissues and are resistant to common therapies but sensitive to novel treatments such as immunotherapy. In this project, we will extend our recent discoveries to study RRD cancers using newly developed zebrafish, mouse and human stem cell models. We will screen for compounds that can be developed into novel therapies for patients with hypermutant cancers and will test thses therapies in these models. Finally, winning combinations will be tested on our international clinical trial for which we will pefrom the clinical and molecular analysis. Completion of this project will open a new window for the understanding, our ability to diagnose and treat human hypermutant cancers.

column37: Patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) develop progressive liver disease and often require liver transplantation. Accordingly, we looked for a better tolerated antiretroviral treatments and found out that a newer class of medications called integrase inhibitors could block betaretroviral infection. Now we plan to conduct a pilot study using a combination of integrase inhibitors and reverse transcriptase inhibitors in patients with PBC to see if this regimen improves disease without undue side effects.

column36: Deciphering the mechanisms of synaptic dysfunction in a genetic model of spinal muscular atrophy
column37: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease characterized by death of motoneurons innervating skeletal muscle fibers. It is the leading genetic cause of infant mortality, but no effective treatment is currently available. SMA is caused by mutations or deletions of the SMN1 gene. In SMA, connections between nerve cells and muscles at specialized sites called synapses become fewer causing the muscle to become progressively weaker. The causes of defective synaptic connections at early stages in SMA are poorly understood, yet synapses may be an excellent therapeutic target for this untreated disease. In this proposal, we aim to understand how loss of SMN leads to synaptic defects in a zebrafish model of spinal muscular atrophy. Zebrafish are amenable to powerful synaptic and genetic analyses. We will examine the strength of connectivity at peripheral and central synapses in vivo using cutting-edge genetic and physiological techniques. We will further characterize how SMN deficiency causes synaptic defects at the cellular and molecular level. This proposed research will enhance our understanding of synaptic pathology in SMA and provide important insights to later develop pharmacological interventions that will stabilize synaptic connections and motor function in SMA.

column36: Winning pathways toward accessibility: the case of dental services for people using wheelchairs
column37: Les personnes en fauteuil roulant ont d'immenses difficultes pour trouver des cliniques dentaires physiquement accessibles; une fois dans la clinique (quand cela est possible), elles sont recues par des professionnels peu competents pour repondre a leurs besoins specifiques. Les consequences de ces situations d'exclusion sont dramatiques: leur sante dentaire se degrade, ce qui affecte une sante generale deja fragile. Cette situation n'est pas surprenante: les professionnels dentaires sont peu formes pour soigner les personnes en fauteuil roulant. Les ecoles professionnelles sont conscientes qu'il faut mieux former leurs etudiants, mais elles savent mal repondre a ces questions: Qu'est-ce qu'une clinique accessible? Quelles competences enseigner aux futurs professionnels? La litterature repond tres mal a ces questions. Voila pourquoi nos buts sont de: 1) definir un modele de clinique dentaire accessible (incluant les espaces physiques et les competences des professionnels dentaires) ; 2) developper et implanter des modules educatifs dans ce domaine dans les ecoles professionnelles dentaires canadiennes. Nous adopterons une approche appelee investigation appreciative: cette methode vise a identifier ce qui << marche le mieux >> dans les pratiques existantes, puis a s'en inspirer pour developper et implanter de nouvelles facons de faire. Ainsi etudierons-nous en profondeur 8 cliniques dentaires championnes, c'est-a-dire des cliniques ayant developpe un interet et des savoir-faire specifiques aux personnes en fauteuil roulant. L'etude de ces cliniques nous permettra de definir un modele de clinique accessible, puis de developper des modules de formation professionnelle de 1er cycle et continue. A la fin de la recherche, toutes les ecoles dentaires Canadiennes enseigneront notre modele de clinique accessible, et tous les professionnels dentaires deja etablis (incluant hygienistes et assistantes/secretaires dentaires) auront acces a notre programme de formation continue.

column36: Substance Use in Women: Pregnancy and Beyond
column37: Substance use is a major global problem. The use of opioids is rising and substance use during pregnancy is more and more a problem. Little is known about substance use among Canadian pregnant women. Canada is only second to the US in opioid use among high income countries. This is concerning as fetuses exposed to substance use during pregnancy are at risk of low birth weight, premature birth, death, and potential health and behavioral issues. Mothers with substance use may be at risk of long term health effects, even after quitting. The long term outcomes of mothers with substance use and their infants are poorly understood. Better knowledge of health issues in women with substance use is necessary for physicians to better care for patients and prevent future health problems. The aim of this project is to assess long term health outcomes of women with substance use and their infants in Quebec. We will look at hospitalization data for all women who ever gave birth in Quebec, Canada from 1989 to 2016. We will identify women with substance use before or during pregnancy and any health problems they had during delivery. We will follow the women and their children over time in the years after pregnancy to determine how substance use affects their later health. This study will provide essential information on the growing problem of substance use during pregnancy in Canada. We will provide detailed data on the long term outcomes related to substance abuse and shed light on health issues of women and children that could be prevented earlier in life. Better knowledge of long term consequences of substance use for both women and children will improve identification and clinical management of affected patients.

column36: Building Indigenous Pathways for Diabetes and Obesity Prevention and Management with Urban and Rural Communities in BC
column37: Health, government and community organizations often lack Traditional Knowledge, community leadership/ownership and cultural/gender appropriate perspectives, critical in decreasing healthcare gaps and burden of disease. In our recent Canadian Institutes of Health Research Indigenous diabetes/obesity study, three urban/rural BC Friendship Centres (FC) (Kelowna, Vernon, Williams Lake), local community members and research teams (researchers, Indigenous/non-Indigenous health providers, community members, Elders, Traditional Healers, and youth) identified healthcare gaps: access to healthcare, Traditional knowledge and practices, education in cultural safety, food security, nutrition, exercise, and cultural activities). The common goal for this study is to work with six interested BC interior urban/rural Friendship and Metis Centres to blend Traditional and Western Knowledge for optimized health and health equity in holistic patient-centred diabetes and obesity care. This 4 year community-led study, guided by local governance and ownership, values and customs will have full involvement in all aspects of study and sharing knowledge of locally blended diabetes/obesity prevention/management activities/programs. We will co-develop pathway tools/frameworks for culturally safe, equitable, strength-based, site-specific healthcare policies, research, and practice for communities of similar size, geographic and cultural distinctness, nationally and internationally.

column36: Sexual pain in endometriosis: role of somatic mutations and local neurogenesis
column37: Endometriosis affects 1 in 10 women of reproductive-age. It is defined as tissue from inside the uterus growing in other parts of the body, such as on or near other pelvic organs such as the ovary and colon. Half of women with endometriosis experience sexual pain: specifically deep dyspareunia, defined as pelvic pain with deep penetration during sexual activity. In our recent research, we identified new genetic and molecular pathways by which endometriosis may cause pain with sexual intercourse. Sexual pain in endometriosis is associated with a subtype of endometriosis known as deep infiltrating endometriosis, in which endometriosis invades pelvic organs and forms adhesions. We recently reported the existence of somatic (non-inherited) gene mutations, such as in the KRAS gene, in this type of endometriosis. These mutations may be responsible for the invasive qualities of this type of endometriosis and thus sexual pain. We also have found evidence that sexual pain in endometriosis is associated with increased nerve density around endometriosis. This nerve growth in turn may be under the influence of nerve growth factor and an immune factor known as interleukin-1b (IL-1b). In this proposal, we will validate our findings in a prospective data registry and accompanying tissue bank for endometriosis. Using this large prospective dataset, we will test whether the KRAS (or other gene) mutations are associated with deep infiltrating endometriosis and thus sexual pain. Similarly, we will test whether nerve growth factor and IL-1b are associated with nerve growth around endometriosis and thus sexual pain. We will also develop a new mouse model of endometriosis. In the future we will use this model to test new drugs for endometriosis, which either target the gene mutations, or block nerve growth factor or IL-1b. In 5-10 years of grant end, we propose a clinical trial of the most promising drug, with the aim of providing a new treatment for this common condition.

column36: STandard versus Accelerated initiation of Renal Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury (STARRT-AKI): A Multi-Centre, Randomized, Controlled Trial
column37: Background: Sick patients receiving care in the intensive care unit (ICU) commonly develop acute injury to their kidneys. This sudden loss of kidney function predisposes these patients to the accumulation of fluid and blood toxins and often leads to death. Acute kidney injury often prompts clinicians to start dialysis therapy, which involves passing a patient's blood through a specialized filter to remove excess fluid and metabolic waste. However, the right time to start dialysis is not clearly known to clinicians. Starting dialysis early or proactively can help better control fluid and blood toxin levels and may lead to a lower risk of death. On the other hand, dialysis has side effects and is expensive and if early dialysis does not improve patient outcomes, it may be best to only start it when the patient gets much sicker and the clinician does not believe there is any other choice. Aims: This study will establish which one of two strategies for starting dialysis (accelerated/early vs. standard) in ICU patients with acute kidney injury leads to a lower risk of death and non-recovery of kidney function and which approach is more cost-effective. Design: This study is an international, multicentre, randomized clinical trial comparing early vs. standard start of dialysis in 2866 critically ill ICU patients with acute kidney injury. Significance: The study will guide clinical practice and inform policy on when to start dialysis in ICU patients with acute kidney injury. The trial has enrolled 970 participants (34% target) from active 90 sites across 10 countries and has fostered extraordinary collaboration with endorsement from critical care trials groups and medical organizations around the world. These funds will enable us to complete recruitment and perform a rigorous cost comparison of these two approaches to starting dialysis in ICU patients.

column36: PURE Frailty
column37: Frailty is how vulnerable an individual is to either developing an illness, or dying if they develop an illness. Frailty increases with age. Frailty is becoming increasingly common because populations are ageing. We have already shown that low muscle strength (an important indicator of frailty), is closely related to developing illnesses and dying if an illness occurs. We need to understand what factors lead to people becoming frail, in order to develop ways to prevent frailty. This study will measure how often frailty develops and what factors put an individual at risk for becoming frail. We have already measured frailty (measured by low muscle strength, low activity levels, and unplanned weight loss) in 170,000 people from 25 countries around the world and have followed them for nearly 6 years. We propose to follow these individuals for another 3 years, when we will measure 1) how often those who are not frail become frail, 2) reasons why those who develop frailty do so, 3) the health consequences of becoming frail. Through this research, we will identify health targets that might protect people against becoming frail or protect against the negative effects of frailty.

column36: Impact of low testosterone on cardiac structure/function in aging
column37: Heart disease increases with age in men and women as sex hormone levels fall. Since a women's risk of heart disease goes up after menopause, there has been a lot of interest in the idea that estrogen influences heart disease. However, it is now clear that testosterone decreases with age not only during "manopause" in men, but in women too. Marketing campaigns focused on the benefits of testosterone have led to an increase in the use of testosterone supplements in older people. This is important, because low testosterone increases the risk of diseases like heart failure, where the heart cannot pump blood very well, but high testosterone can be harmful too. We discovered that age decreases the ability of male hearts to contract by changing the ability of heart cells to regulate internal calcium. To mimic low testosterone in aging, we removed the testes from male mice. We found that low testosterone upsets the ability of heart cells to contract and regulate calcium, just like the effects of age. Some calcium is needed for the heart to contract, but the balance needs to be right. When calcium is disrupted it can lead to diseases like heart failure. There is still a great deal more to know about how testosterone affects the heart. We plan to look at how long term exposure to low testosterone changes contraction in whole hearts and affects contractions and calcium levels in individual heart cells in males and females. We will start to look at effects in middle age (1 year old mice) and follow them until they reach 2 years of age, which is about 85 human years. We will also treat male and female mice with testosterone to find out if testosterone therapy is beneficial or harmful and if this depends on the dose used. This research project will help us understand the links between testosterone, aging and heart disease. It will help us recognize whether testosterone supplementation is good or bad in vulnerable older people with heart diseases.

column36: The role of circ-Itga9 in cardiac remodeling
column37: Cardiac diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries. Over time, as hearts age or become senescent, adverse remodelling that is initially beneficial, progressively leads to reduced cardiac functioning. Our research aims to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie this remodeling and repair. Circular RNAs are closed continuous loops of RNA that were recently detected in eukaryotic cells, and may affect cell physiology through a variety of mechanisms. Our work revealed that the circular RNA circ-Itga9 is tightly associated with heart diseases. We hypothesize that circular RNAs may regulate cell senescence and tissue repair by binding to protein regulators of cardiac senescence. To test this, we will modify cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts so that they express more of the circular RNAs in question. We can also use the reverse approach to silence circular RNA expression, and observe the changes in function. Using these approaches, in conjunction with standard experimental models, we can better understand the function of circular RNAs in cardiac diseases. There are two unique aspects to our proposed study. Firstly, we are among the first to produce a stable expression construct allowing long-term studies of circular RNAs. The second unique approach is our inhibitor system that is designed to block the function of individual circular RNAs in cell and animal models. These allow us to specifically study individual circular RNAs, and better understand any causal relationships. Our proposed experiments will help us explore the regulatory roles of circular RNAs in both cardiac aging and other cellular repair contexts. The agents developed may be used as tools in understanding the role of circular RNAs in heart development, aging, disease-associated injury and tissue regeneration. With these approaches, we hope to design therapies to intervene against the adverse remodeling associated with age-related heart disease.

column36: Cellular mechanisms of sensorimotor integration
column37: Our sensory experience of the world remains stable and predictable, even as we move through our environment and interact with it in complex ways. This is because our brains are somehow able to seamlessly integrate action and perception. Before our muscles even move, our brain is predicting the consequences of those actions on what we see, hear, and feel. This is why, for example, it is nearly impossible to tickle yourself--your brain is ready for the sensation and actively filters out the "ticklishness." When the brain systems that perform functions like this fail, the consequences can range from motion sickness and vertigo to the kinds of hallucinations and delusions that characterize schizophrenia. How the integration of sensory input and behaviour happens is only partly understood. To understand what events happen in individual nerve cells during integration, we are studying this process in a tiny roundworm. Despite its simplicity, it has to solve the same action-perception problems we do in order to successfully interpret and navigate in its environemnt. This same simplicity means that we can study molecular events, signaling between nerve cells, and behaviour all at the same time in an intact animal. Because all animals share the same fundamental biology at this level, what we learn will help us understand what happens in both healthy and dysfunctional brains to allow action and perception to work together.

column36: Epigenetic regulation of repeat expression by RB and EZH2 in cancer
column37: Cancer cells possess a number of features that distinguish them from the normal cells in our bodies. This grant application is focused on studying the remnants of ancient infections that leave behind foreign DNA sequences called repeats. Their expression can be uniquely misregulated in cancer, creating a feature that distinguishes cancer cells from surrounding normal cells. In most cases these repeat sequences are sufficiently altered that they no longer generate viruses or cause new diseases. However, some pieces of these DNA sequences can be expressed and this leads to two major outcomes for host cells. The first is that expressing these sequences creates the opportunity for repeat sequences to move to a new location in the cell nucleus. This is called transposition and it is potentially damaging to the cell as it can alter the expression and function of the cell's normal genes at its new location. From a cancer perspective this can be the source of changes in DNA sequence (mutations) that cause the disease. While this is bad, the second consequence of expressing repeat sequences is that it can lead the host cell to appear as though it has been infected. This can trigger an immune response in which our natural defence system will kill the 'infected' cell. Thus these repeat sequences are an attractive means to recruit our natural defences to help fight cancer. This grant proposal will study repetitive sequences with the aim of using this information to design more effective ways to kill cancer cells.

column36: Molecular hallmarks of breast cancer sensitivity to ErbB2-targeted therapies
column37: Many breast tumors are driven by a protein ErbB2 which they overproduce. These tumors are treated with drugs called ErbB2 inhibitors but not everyone benefits from them. The drugs can damage the heart and are costly. Hence, predicting who can and who cannot benefit from these drugs would be of great value. Breast tumor cells originate from normal breast cells forming a layer in the breast. Normal cells die when they detach from this layer. ErbB2 blocks death of cancer cells after they detach, and this allows them to form tumors and spread through the body. How ErbB2 causes these effects is not well understood. We have found that ErbB2 triggers signals causing loss of a protein Irf6 in tumor cells detached from their normal location and that Irf6 loss reduces cellular amount of a cell death-inducing protein Perp. Cells lacking Perp do not die outside of their normal location. We have also noticed that ErbB2 inhibitors increase Irf6 and Perp levels in detached tumor cells that are sensitive to these medicines but not in the cells resistant to the drugs. We will examine what signals ErbB2 induces to cause Irf6 and Perp loss in breast tumor cells and whether this loss allows the cells to form tumors and spread through the body. Some ErbB2-overproducing tumors are treated with ErbB2 inhibitors in an effort to shrink the tumor which is then surgically removed. The patient further receives these drugs to kill tumor cells that may have stayed in the body. We will test human breast tumor samples obtained before and after treatment with the drugs to assess whether the increase in Irf6 and Perp levels in the tumor after it is forced to shrink by the drugs predicts whether the patient will benefit from these medicines. This will allow the patients that are not expected to benefit from the drugs to avoid them after the surgery. Thus we expect that our work will uncover a new breast cancer mechanism and help doctors decide which patients can benefit from ErbB2 inhibitors.

column37: The majority of people who are aging and who have some conditions that affect their brain or spinal cord [stroke, spinal cord injury (SCI) experience continuous changes in blood pressure (BP). Unstable BP damages small blood vessels in the brain and leads to numerous secondary complications, including heart attack, stroke, and cognitive problems. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of disease and death after SCI, which is largely due to dysfunction of autonomic nervous system that regulates blood vessels and heart. Based on the Canada-wide data, we recently demonstrated that people with SCI are at 300-400% increased risk of stroke. This finding was alarming and has led to the realization that improving brain health after SCI is the logical and most critical next step in improving the quality and quantity of life for those with SCI. In this project I plan to apply my expertise in the field of SCI to determine why individuals with SCI experience more strokes and poor cognitive function. First, I will use an animal model to determine how and why the brain and its blood vessels become damaged due to repetitive BP elevations after SCI. Second, I will test the efficacy of cycling exercise as a potential therapy to improve the brain and blood vessel health after SCI. Our ultimate goal is to reduce secondary complications resulting from BP changes and improve the quality and quantity of life for individuals with SCI and other neurological conditions, thereby increasing the generalizability of my research. This project is also aimed at reducing the remarkable burden on the Canadian health care system; where the lifetime health care expenditures are among the most expensive of any condition (i.e. $2.9M for cervical SCI).

column36: Nicotine mechanisms contributing to tobacco smoking
column37: The societal costs of tobacco smoking are immense, with around 37,000 deaths each year due to smoking in Canada alone. Current quitting aids are of little help. Although nicotine clearly plays an important role in tobacco addiction, we have no clear idea what that role is. Oddly, when nicotine is tested in pure form, divorced from tobacco, it turns out to be a remarkably weak reinforcer (please note: in this context, a reinforcer is basically a reward). For example, neither human subjects nor animals will typically work hard to obtain injections of the drug. In this respect, nicotine is not in the same league as cocaine, amphetamine or heroin. There are, however, several less conventional ways by which nicotine could make tobacco addictive. For a start, nicotine has the ability to make other rewarding stimuli more powerfully rewarding (the so-called reinforcer-enhancing effect), which could, for example, allow nicotine to boost the effects of other addictive chemicals lurking in tobacco smoke. The proposed research will use animal models in order to better understand the addictive actions of nicotine. Unfortunately, much animal research has been done using excessively high doses of nicotine that do not translate readily to tobacco smoking; I propose to rectify this. We will investigate how nicotine exerts its reinforcer-enhancing effect (for example: is this an action of nicotine directly in the brain, and if so which types of nicotine receptor targets are involved?). We will also study whether nicotine's rewarding effects can "rub off" onto sensory cues through frequent association. We are also interested in finding ways to alleviate the unpleasant effects of nicotine withdrawal, which are often a barrier to quitting smoking. Overall, this research will deepen our understanding of the behavioural and chemical basis for tobacco addiction, which in turn should uncover new approaches to possible treatment.

column36: Early growth response 1 and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating condition that results in cognitive impairment, loss of executive functions and dementia. It is estimated that 47 million people world-wide suffer from dementia. In Canada alone, 564 000 people have dementia with 25 000 people dying as a result each year, creating an annual financial burden of $10.4 billion. In 15 years, this number is projected to double. Currently no disease modifying therapy is available and treatment of AD remains symptomatic.Tangles and plaques are the two characteristic lesions found in the brains of AD patients. Tangles are found inside the nerve cells and are formed by the abnormal hyperphosphorylation of tau protein (containing more phosphates that normal). Hyperphosphorylated tau is unable to provide mechanical support to neurons. Plaques are found outside of the nerve cells and interfere with cell communication, trigger inflammation and promote cell demise. Plaques are formed from a peptide called beta amyloid by the actions of two enzymes: beta secretase-1 (BACE-1) and gamma secretes. Studies have determined that BACE-1 is somehow over activated in the AD brain, leading to excess production of beta amyloid. What activates BACE-1 and how tau becomes hyperphosphorylated in AD patients had remained mystery Several researchers found that Early growth response 1 (Egr-1) protein was significantly elevated in the autopsied brains of AD patients. Recently, we showed that Egr-1 promotes tau hyperphosphorylation and activates BACE-1 in mouse brain. Very recently, we demonstrated that inhibition of Egr-1 in the hippocampus reduces levels of both hyperphosphorylated tau and beta amyloid and improves learning and memory in mouse model of AD. Our data indicate that Egr-1 is a potential therapeutic target for AD. More recently, we have designed a peptide derived from a physiological inhibitor of Egr-1 to treat AD. In this project, we wish to test the efficacy of this peptide in two mouse models of AD.
