column36: Improving Pain Assessment in Nursing Home Residents with Dementias
column37: The numbers of nursing home residents with advancing dementias continue to grow. However, the ways that we manage their troublesome symptoms, like pain, are still less than optimal. As a result, residents with untreated pain experience unnecessary suffering and further decline in their mental and physical function. This often increases their need for care and the cost of care. To manage their pain successfully, we must first identify it accurately. Asking residents if they have pain is considered the best way for healthcare workers to measure pain, but this is not always possible for residents with more advanced dementias. They are not able to communicate their pain in usual ways, such as talking about it. For these residents, a useful way to identify their pain is by observing them to detect their behaviours that may be related to pain (such as grimacing or crying). The goal of this research project is to develop and test a rating scale for pain-related behaviours that can be observed in nursing home residents with moderate to severe dementias. Our scale will be based on standard resident information that is regularly collected in Canadian nursing homes. Once we test our new pain rating scale fully, we will determine the best way to help healthcare workers use our scale as they observe residents in their everyday work. Our strategy to measure pain in nursing home residents with dementias is the first step in recognizing and managing their pain. Better pain management can improve quality of life for these vulnerable residents.

column36: Interactions and Assemblies of Protein Disordered States: Principles and Diseases
column37: The biological function and disease-causing malfunction of proteins are underpinned by their structures and interactions with themselves and other biomolecules. Despite tremendous progress in past decades, the basic driving forces of protein conformational changes are not well understood, limiting the application of biophysical knowledge of disease-related proteins in therapeutics development. The need for a deeper physical understanding is especially acute for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) that lack a stable structure. Comprising ~30% of the proteome, IDPs are prominently involved in cellular regulation, a role facilitated by IDPs' ability to perform dynamic, multi-site recognition of other biomolecules. Malfunctioning of IDPs causes numerous diseases, notably various forms of cancer and neurological degeneration. A remarkable recent discovery is that liquid-liquid phase-separated IDPs -- like oil droplets in water -- are a major component of functional compartments in the cell. However, the biophysical basis of individual and collective IDP properties remains mostly undeciphered. The proposed research builds on the fundamental advances we have recently made, particularly in understanding how IDP phase separation depends on their amino acid sequences. Harnessing the unique interdisciplinary expertise of our own research group as well as those of our collaborators, we endeavour to expand significantly our fundamental physico-chemical knowledge of biomolecular organization and recognition for the novel multi-site interactions and liquid-liquid phase behaviours of IDPs. Results of our investigation will enable advances in understanding disease processes and ultimately to developing new therapies.

column36: Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Cohort Study
column37: With improvements in early detection and treatment, survival rates for breast cancer have improved. Unfortunately, breast cancer treatments can cause both short and long term physical and psychological side effects. More specifically, breast cancer survivors are at a higher risk for breast cancer recurrence, second cancers, heart disease, weight gain, bone loss, fatigue, anxiety and depression. Previous research has shown that regular physical activity can improve the physical and psychological function of breast cancer survivors, help manage some short term side effects of treatment and reduce the risk of having a recurrence. However, this research has not been adopted into regular oncology practice because specific exercise advice cannot be provided regarding the type and volume of exercise necessary for improving quality of life and survival of breast cancer survivors. We initiated the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer cohort study in 2011 with a CIHR Team Grant. The aim is to determine if physical activity can help breast cancer survivors manage the side effects of treatments, enhance quality of life, reduce their risk of disease recurrence and improve survival. Study participants are asked to complete questionnaires, undergo tests for physical fitness tests and lymphedema (swelling in the arms), have their body composition measured (body fat, lean mass, bone density), give a fasting blood sample and wear devices that objectively measure their physical activity and sedentary behavior (time spent sitting) at breast cancer diagnosis and again at 1, 3, and 5 years. They are then followed for breast cancer outcomes. To date, we have recruited 75% of our cohort of 1500 and are now seeking funding to complete the recruitment and follow-up of all participants. A better understanding of precisely how physical activity and physical fitness affect breast cancer recurrence and survival will lead to improvements in exercise recommendations for breast cancer survivors.

column36: Role of CLEC12B+ macrophages in the pathogenesis of vitiligo and melanoma
column37: For the past 17 years, my laboratory has been studying skin diseases caused by abnormalities of melanocytes, the cells that produce melanin pigment that protects our skin from the harmful effects of ultraviolet light in the sun. More than 50 million people worldwide develop a severe disfiguring disease called vitiligo, which is caused by patchy loss of normal skin color due to death of melanocytes. In addition, more than 300 thousand of people develop melanoma each year in the world, which is caused by the opposite change in the melanocytes, i.e. uncontrolled multiplication of cancerous melanocytes. The exact mechanisms leading to the opposite fates of melanocytes in these two diseases are unclear. There is an urgent need to develop better therapies for vitiligo and melanoma. My laboratory recently found a new type of innate immune cells in the surroundings of the melanocytes in the skin, the CLEC12B+ macrophages. These cells are important participants of the immune response to pathogens attacking our skin, such as bacteria, allergens and viruses. They are also required for stopping the immune responses when the pathogens are eliminated, so that the immunologic balance is restored, tissue injuries are repaired, and damaged cells are replenished. My lab found that in vitiligo, there is a shortage of these cells, where as in melanoma, there is an excess. In culture dishes, these macrophages secrete growth factors that can enhance melanocyte survival, but suppress professional killer cells, such as the natural killer cells and killer lymphocytes. Therefore, I speculate that deficiency of these macrophages is the reason for vitiligo development, and that over population of these cells have the opposite effect, that is, unchecked growth of the melanoma cells. In this project, I will test these hypotheses using cultured cells in petri dishes and in animal models. The results generated will help develop more effective therapies for vitiligo and melanoma.

column37: What do we know about this topic? Cancer patients, adults and children, are greatly distressed by vomiting due to chemotherapy. Vomiting due to chemotherapy is completely prevented in most adults with cancer by giving medicines called antiemetics. Antiemetics are much less effective in children. Even when recommended antiemetics are given to children receiving chemotherapy, about half still vomit. Bone marrow transplant is the only curative therapy available for some children. Children who have bone marrow transplants receive chemotherapy. Even when these children are given recommended antiemetics, almost all vomit. Olanzapine is now strongly recommended as an antiemetic for adults with cancer. Olanzapine may also improve vomiting control in children. But, its safety and efficacy in children receiving chemotherapy are unknown. Since children respond differently to medicines compared to adults, a specific study must be done to make sure that olanzapine is safe and effective in children. How will we do this study? We will compare vomiting in two groups of children receiving chemotherapy for bone marrow transplant. The first group will receive standard antiemetics plus olanzapine. The second will receive standard antiemetics plus placebo. Children will take olanzapine or placebo on each day they receive chemotherapy and for 4 days after. Children or their parents will record when children vomit. Using a special tool, older children will also tell us how nauseated they are. We will monitor and question children and parents to see if children have side effects. Why is this study important? This study will tell us if olanzapine reduces vomiting in children receiving chemotherapy for bone marrow transplant and the side effects that these children experience. Our findings will influence the care of children undergoing bone marrow transplant and receiving chemotherapy in Canada and elsewhere. We hope to improve the health and the quality of life of these vulnerable children.

column36: Repurposing slow-release oral morphine as new oral alternative for the treatment of opioid use disorder
column37: While reversing overdoses with medications like naloxone is a cornerstone of the response to the opioid public health emergency, preventing overdoses through the development of effective treatments for opioid use disorder (OUD) is critical to addressing this epidemic. Unfortunately, in Canada, there are only two proven life-saving treatments: buprenorphine/naloxone (BNX) and methadone. However, these medications have limitations and are not acceptable for many individuals, resulting in a substantial proportion of individuals who remained untreated and at immediate risk of overdose, death and other negative outcomes. Small European studies suggest that slow-release oral morphine (SROM) may be another potentially effective treatment that is better tolerated, and is associated with greater patient satisfaction and reductions in craving compared to methadone. The goal of the proposed research is to build on these encouraging results and rigorously evaluate the relative effectiveness, safety and acceptability of SROM and methadone in real-life clinical settings in Canada. To that end, we will enrol approximately 200 adults with OUD, who are currently exposed to fentanyl, and who have tried but not benefited from treatment with BNX. Eligible participants will be randomized to receive either methadone or SROM for approximately six months, using a double-blind design where neither participants nor their physicians will know which medication they are receiving. Findings from this study will greatly increase our knowledge of the relative benefits of different treatment alternatives for OUD, and how each of them may suit different individuals' needs. Importantly, from a health policy perspective, positive results confirming SROM clinical utility could present significant potential to increase access to an additional form of evidence-based treatment for OUD in Canada, with potential to be scaled up rapidly given that SROM is already available as an inexpensive generic drug.

column37: Lymphedema is a condition of uncontrolled fluid accumulation and tissue swelling that affects ~140 million people worldwide. Lymphedema can cause discomfort, immobility and organ dysfunction. Edematous tissue in lymphedema presents a high risk of infection. The major cause of lymphedema in the world is lymphatic filariasis. In Canada, the major cause of lymphedema is the damage to the lymphatic vessels and LNs associated with cancer and cancer therapies, which impacts almost all of the cancer types that involve cancer spread via the lymphatic vessels. Currently, there is no cure for lymphedema, mainly due to the lack of mechanistic understanding of its development. Some lymphedema patients exhibit significant body disfigurement and need life long intervention with compression garments, which cause a huge psycho-social and economic impact on these patients. The lack of knowledge regarding the regulation of lymph flow has been the barrier for the disease prevention or treatment. Lymphatic vessels maintain fluid balance and transport tissue waste, pathogens and cells to lymph nodes for protection by the immune system. In the lymph node, lymph flow direction determines the time, the location and the cell types that antigens will encounter after immune stimulation. Lymph nodes are typically surrounded by fat tissue and I have found that this perinodal fat may partially compensate for the immune protection function when lymph flow via lymphatic vessels is compromised. In this study, I will determine how fat tissue around the LN participates in fluid balance and combating bacterial infection when lymphatic vessel function is compromised. Our work aims to target perinodal adipose tissue in order to develop potential therapeutic methods to reduce edema and improve host immune protection.

Basically, they involve: 1. changes in the ability of the heart to use nutrients to produce energy (energy production becomes less efficient). 2. change in the size of the heart (the size of heart cells initially increases). 3. change in the number of heart cells decreases (normally these 'muscular' cells work together to cause contraction: less number of cells means less force) and 4. a change in the balance between elasticity and stiffness of the beating heart (mainly due to changes in the 'scaffold' that normally supports the heart). Exactly WHY these various changes occur in people with obesity and diabetes has still to be fully understood. Only when we know these details will more effective therapies be developed.

column36: Comparative Safety of the Sodium Glucose Co-transporter-2 (SGLT-2) Inhibitors in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
column37: The newest medications approved in Canada to treat type 2 diabetes are called "sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors". SGLT2 receptors are mediators of glucose uptake that ensure the reabsorption of glucose in the renal tubules. SGLT2 inhibitors work by inhibiting these mediators, and thus increase the urinary excretion of the filtered glucose. Although these medications are studied extensively prior to being approved, the extent to which they cause unintended side effects, especially when they are used in real life conditions is not well known. Notably, federal regulatory agencies such as Health Canada and the US Food and Drug Administration have published warnings regarding several safety signals arising from patient reports. Given the increasing use of SGLT2 inhibitors in the treatment of type 2 diabetes, better evaluation of their post-marketing safety is required. We propose to study the real world safety of SGLT2 inhibitors using a combination of large databases from the US, UK and Canada that contains detailed healthcare records for individuals with diabetes. These databases will include information on prescription medication use, diagnoses, laboratory tests (e.g., cholesterol levels, kidney function), and information on hospitalizations and death. To evaluate the overall risk-benefit profile of these medications, we will measure the risk of acute kidney disease, renal impairment, infections (urinary tract infections, genital infections), too much acid in the blood, and amputation for individuals receiving SGLT2 inhibitors versus other oral diabetes therapies. For all of these analyses we will use advanced statistical analysis to account for differences in age, sex, and disease burden. Our study will contribute towards understanding the real world effects of the SGLT2 inhibitors and will help patients, clinicians, and policymakers assess the overall risks and benefits of these medications.

column36: Occupational Exposure to Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals and Colorectal Cancer risk.
column37: Worldwide, colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer. Men are more likely to develop colorectal cancer than women. Different environmental, lifestyle and biologic factors may explain this risk difference. Also, research is uncovering the role of estrogen, a hormone that promotes the development and maintenance of female characteristics, in preventing colorectal cancer development in women. Less is known of the role of hormones in the development of colorectal cancer in men. Similar to the evidence in women, there is support that the proper functioning of sex hormones may prevent the onset of colorectal cancer in men. Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that interferes with the proper functioning of sex hormones. We are exposed to these chemicals in the environment and in diet; however, workers in certain sectors are highly exposed to endocrine disruptors. In this research, we will examine whether exposure to endocrine disruptors in the workplace increases the risk of developing colorectal cancer. Our research will be based on an ongoing Canadian study that began in 2009. This study included men and women who have volunteered to share information on their health, lifestyle, environment and behaviours. Our research will include all men and women who were newly diagnosed with colorectal cancer since 2009. For comparison, we will select a sub-group of people, who have not had cancer at the beginning of the study. The interview asked detailed questions on the longest-held job for all participants. Using this information, we will determine whether exposure to endocrine disruptors at the longest held job was probable or not. We will compare the number of colorectal cancer cases among participants who were probably exposed to endocrine disruptors to those who were never exposed. This study offers a valuable opportunity to examine, in a short time frame and at low cost, whether endocrine disruptors play an important role in colorectal cancer risk.

column36: Regulation of neurodegeneration by chaperone proteins
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common disabling neurodegenerative disorder, affecting an increasing number of Canadians, for which we have no cure. A defining feature of the disease is degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in an area of the brainstem called the substantia nigra. The main treatments available for Parkinson's disease aim to replace or mimic the dopamine that is lost due to death of these neurons. However, these treatments only alleviate symptoms and can be associated with substantial adverse effects or limited efficacy. This deficiency is due, in large part, to the lack of treatments that target the key molecular pathways involved in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease. We have recently identified a chaperone protein that regulates the maintenance of protein quality control within cells which is affected in PD. Importantly, we have shown this chaperone protein interacts with proteins known to cause PD. In this study we propose to specifically define how this chaperone protein modulates protein quality control and cell death. We will then use an approach that combines gene therapy and specialized targeting sequences that can specifically engage this chaperone protein to test if this improves outcomes in preclinical models of PD. This work will provide the foundation to develop therapeutics that regulate chaperone proteins in the brain as a novel approach to the treatment of PD and other neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Optimizing Canada's Healthcare for REfugees (OCHRE)
column37: The world is facing an unprecedented level of migration due to violence and persecution with many countries struggling to develop best models for resettling refugees. In response to the recent Syrian refugee crisis, Canada opened its doors to over 40,000 refugees over an eighteen month period using in part its unique refugee resettlement program in which private citizens are responsible for early resettlement. Navigating the healthcare system is one important early resettlement process with repercussions for many long term health and social outcomes, yet little is known about how well primary healthcare needs are met across refugee resettlement models. In many provinces, specialized community health centres focus on vulnerable populations including refugees, and these and other primary care models often include broader mental health and social service support. How well these interdisciplinary models are accessed by refugees and whether this changes health and social outcomes is not well studied. We will use population-based data to study how refugees arriving in Ontario from 2008-2017 are accessing the primary care system. We will assess whether privately sponsored refugees have similar outcomes to those who are government assisted and we will also study whether the large number of Syrian refugees that needed resettlement services had their primary healthcare needs met. In addition, we will analyze whether refugees who seek primary care in community health centers are more likely to have recommended visits such as for cancer screening and less need for sustained social assistance. We have involved provincial and federal policymakers, as well as community organizations and private citizens in the conduct of the project so that our analyses are relevant and communicated to those who can act on the results. We want our research to enable federal and provincial policymakers to better meet the healthcare needs of refugees.

column36: Developing a culture-specific model of resilience against substance use among Canada's on-reserve Indigenous youth
column37: The cultural strengths of Canada's Indigenous communities are prominent in the midst of centuries of devastating colonization. Moreover, evidence shows that cultural connectedness inspires well-being among Indigenous youth. However, adolescence is a time fraught with uncertainty about one's identity and opportunities to drink and smoke. The objective of our project is to leverage the inherent strengths of Indigenous culture to develop a model of resilience. We aim to use a two-eyed seeing approach, in which both Indigenous and Western perspectives are used to identify factors that protect Indigenous youth from substance use. Further, we aim to translate knowledge learned back to Indigenous community youth using the traditional method of storytelling. To reach these aims, we propose a five-year study that will focus on adolescents in one Northern Quebec Indigenous community. This will be a three stage project. Stage 1 will be community listening. The research team and community members will come together to define culture and community context, and how these relate to youth substance use. Stage 2 will be an empirical study. In a school-based study, potential predictors of substance use will be assessed over a three-year period as adolescents progress through secondary school. This will permit the unique opportunity to track culturally- (community-) relevant protective factors of substance use as they unfold across formative years. Stage 3 will focus on knowledge translation and communicating what is learned back to the community. The findings will be shaped into stories of resilience that are told by community members. A compilation of storytelling will be filmed, and DVDs and an online version produced. These will be the property of the community and distributed through varied platforms, such as community events and youth programs. To summarize, this research aims to illustrate the process and product of using two-eyed seeing to address a compelling health issue.

column36: Family-administered delirium detection in the critically ill
column37: Delirium is a brain condition in which patients become very confused and lose their ability to focus attention. Over half of the patients in intensive care units (ICUs) suffer from delirium during their ICU stay. Being older makes a patient more likely to develop delirium in the ICU. Research has shown that patients with ICU delirium are more likely to die or have long-term brain problems. Family members may also notice changes in their own mental health. Although nurses and doctors have tools to measure delirium in the ICU, delirium can be very difficult to diagnose and, in some cases, may be missed. This means that some patients with delirium are not being treated. Family members may be the first to notice changes in a patient's thinking, concentration or alertness. There are tools called the FAM-CAM and "Sour Seven" that can be used by family members to measure delirium. However, neither of these tools has been used in an ICU. By doing this study, we will be able to show if the FAM-CAM and "Sour Seven" can be used by family members to accurately measure delirium in older adults in the ICU. We will also be able to evaluate the stress that family members experience while a patient is in the ICU. The results from this study may lead to changes in how family members are involved in care and in the end improve the diagnosis of delirium in the ICU. In turn, this may improve patient care and patient and family outcomes in the ICU.

column36: Targeted Therapies for Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
column37: Finding new therapies for rare diseases is an urgent need in Canada. Our research program seeks to develop effective and safe treatments for patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a devastating lung disease that causes destruction and failure of the lungs. LAM is caused by cancer-like abnormalities arising in cells (LAM cells) with genetic mutations in the 'tuberous sclerosis complex-2' (TSC2) gene. LAM also develops in ~1/3 of patients with 'tuberous sclerosis complex' (TSC), an inherited disease of mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 gene that affect ~1 in 6000 Canadians, and leads to tumours in multiple body locations. Key roadblocks in finding new treatments for LAM include the inability to grow and study LAM cells from patients, and a poor understanding of how loss of TSC2 gene function contribute to their cancer-like properties. In pilot studies, we identified the hormone 'urotensin' as a potential target for therapy that is particularly active in LAM cells. At the same time, we used stem cell technology to engineer a 'test tube' model that closely resembles LAM cells from patients, and that can be used to discover potential therapies. In Part 1 of this project, we will to use these LAM-like cells to understand the cellular mechanism(s) by which urotensin activity is altered in LAM cells, and how urotensin contributes to their cancer-like properties. In Aim 2, we will use LAM-like cells in state-of-the-art drug screening protocols to identify drug regimens that are less toxic and more effective than current therapies for LAM.

column36: Deciphering the molecular mechanism of acquired resistance in leukemia
column37: Recent findings in the area of leukemia research have led to the identification of new therapeutic approaches that are more efficient and less toxic than classical chemotherapies because they target a precise molecular event at the origin of cancer development. However, even though a large number of leukemia patients respond positively to targeted treatments at first, a significant portion of them eventually relapse. Once these patients become resistant to treatment, very few options are available to them. It is generally believed that resistance to drug treatment in leukemia patients is acquired through a process that entails the progressive modification of leukemic cells such that they acquire novel properties allowing them to escape drug treatment. However, the mechanism(s) through which leukemic cells acquire resistance while being subjected to drug treatment is unclear. Understanding this mechanism is a necessary step towards the development of therapies that are truly curative. Our lab has recently obtained new and exciting results suggesting that a specific protein (named OGT) may be at the heart of the process of acquired resistance in leukemia. In this application, we propose to fully characterize the mechanism through which OGT mediates resistance. For this purpose, we will use a variety of molecular and cellular techniques as well as unique in vivo models of disease. Successful completion of this proposal is expected to identify new therapeutic targets that could be used to prevent and/or treat relapse in leukemia patients.

column36: Transdifferentiation of astrocytes into neurons to improve neuronal network function in Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Progressive cognitive decline associated with amyloid deposition, neurofibrillary tangles, and neurodegeneration is hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD). The cognition impairment in both patients and in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease is related to temporal modulation of neuronal signaling that depends on the balance between neurons that are responsible for excitatory and those mediate inhibitory activity. In Alzheimer's disease patients and in rodent models of AD, it is the inhibitory neurons that are initially dysfunctional and ultimately lost. The loss of inhibitory signals in specific regions of the brain impairs attention and memory processing and retrieval. Furthermore, memory acquisition requires changes in signaling patterns of hippocampal inhibitory interneurons. A variety of cognitive processes including working memory is known to depend on an intact inhibitory network. Historically, the use of drugs targeting inhibitory interneurons as well as exogenous stem cell replacement to address the imbalance of excitatory-inhibitory activity have resulted in severe side-effects. Our treatment strategy to rebalance the neuronal network by induction of cellular conversion of endogenously activated astrocytes into inhibitory neurons that respond appropriately to environment signals represents a critical advance over paradigms investigated to date.

column36: Characterization of HR-Killer1 and identification of small molecules for cancer therapy and enhanced gene editing using CRISPR/Cas9-based DNA repair strategies
column37: Inherited diseases arise from mutations in our genes, and similarly genetic mutations underlie the development of a variety of cancers. These mutations arise from DNA damage that is repaired incorrectly in our cells, and ironically radiation or drugs that damage DNA are the most common form of cancer therapy. Thus, if you can manipulate DNA repair you can also enhance DNA damage in cancer cells as a means of therapy. In 2013, scientists discovered that you could efficiently edit DNA in human cells using a system from bacteria called CRISPR (clustered regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats). CRISPR represents a primitive immune system found in many species of bacteria, which provides them with the ability to "fight" viruses by cutting the viral DNA into pieces. This cutting activity is provided by the CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), which uses small guide RNAs (gRNAs) to pair with and target DNA molecules for cleavage. CRISPR/Cas9 can be applied to genome editing by using the DNA cutting activity to repair damaged genes, or to insert new genes; and for this advance, CRISPR/Cas9 was named "Breakthrough of the Year" by Science Magazine in 2015. Using a novel assay based on CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing we have identified a new small molecule inhibitor of DNA repair called HRK1, which we will characterize as a potential new cancer therapy. In addition, we have partnered with the Centre for Drug Research and Development (Vancouver B.C.) to screen for both enhancers and inhibitors of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing. Enhancers of CRISPR/Cas9 can be used to improve the efficiency of gene editing; whereas inhibitors will likely block DNA repair, and thus can be used to sensitize cancers to radiation and chemotherapy. Ultimately, the compounds we identify and characterize will provide new therapeutics for cancer and agents to enhance the efficiency of gene therapy.

column36: Reducing morbidity in critically ill children by re-evaluating the prophylaxis of stress ulcer-related upper gastrointestinal bleeding: A pilot randomized controlled trial.
column37: Reducing the adverse effects experienced by critically ill children is an urgent research priority. Acute and severe illness can cause stress ulcers in the stomach. These ulcers can cause severe bleeding. Thus it makes sense trying to prevent stress ulcers, which can be done with drugs that decrease stomach acid. Despite little testing in children, more than half of critically ill children receive these medications. These may increase the risk of infections, which may be more common than bleeding itself. A large study is needed to test if withholding these medications reduces the risk of side effects and adverse events without increasing the risk of bleeding. Such trials in pediatric critical care are exceptionally challenging to complete. We are conducting a pilot randomized controlled trial in 6 Canadian Pediatric Intensive Care Units (PICUs) to test and refine the study procedures and see if a large trial is feasible to do. Children receiving life support in a PICU can participate. They will be given either a commonly used medication (pantoprazole) to reduce their stomach acid levels or an inactive placebo while they are in the PICU. We measure important aspects of successfully completing a trial: how many children we can recruit at each PICU, how quickly we can start the study medication, adherence to study protocol, and how often the study medication is given according to our protocol. This pilot trial is a critical part of a research program needed to ensure that a large trial is successful. The large trial will tell us if giving prophylaxis or withholding it is the preferred strategy. Either outcome will allow clinicians to reduce the burden of morbidity in all mechanically ventilated children balancing the risks and benefits of prophylaxis. This pilot trial will be critical to successfully completing such a challenging trial.

column36: Marijuana legalization policy: Impact on prevalence and risk behaviours among youth and young adults in Canada.
column37: In 2018, Canada will become only the second country to legalize recreational cannabis use. Overall, the proposed research will provide a rigorous design for evaluating the impact of national-level cannabis legislation in Canada using 'within-country' and 'between-country' controls over time. column36: The impact of lesion location on contralesional plasticity and its role in motor recovery after ischemic brain injury
column37: Stroke can damage different regions of the brain. After the injury, patients often suffer the loss of functions of the hand. Time and rehabilitation can provide some recovery of function but it is usually incomplete. Better treatments are necessary, but to achieve this we need to understand the mechanisms involved in recovery. Some imaging studies report that after a stroke, the unaffected regions of the brain change their activity during recovery. This suggests that these spared areas could be involved in recovery. However, the way they can do so remains unclear. This is particularly a problem for the areas in the hemisphere opposite to the lesion, the contralesional hemisphere. Some studies suggest that this hemisphere helps the recovery while others show it hinders recovery, and this appears to be influenced by the location of the lesion. The broad goal of our project is to understand how lesion location affects changes in contralesional areas and, as a result, the role these areas undertake in recovery. To address these questions, we use monkeys because their motor areas are similar to the ones in humans. In different groups of animals, we will provoke lesions similar in sizes but destroying progressively more brain regions involved in the control of hand movements. During the recovery, we will record the activity of the neurons in the contralesional hemisphere and study how it changes. After the animal has completed its spontaneous recovery (without any treatment), we will use drugs to inactivate each contralesional area. This will reveal the new role the contralesional areas undertook for recovery of the paretic hand after different types of lesion. Finally, we will inject anatomical tracers and study the rewiring of connections of the contralesional areas. Our experiments will greatly increase our understanding of the mechanisms that allow contralesional areas to take a good or bad role in recovery and how the location of lesion affects these processes

column36: Investigating the contribution of Shank3 in Alzheimer's disease
column37: More than 740,000 Canadians are living with Alzheimer disease (AD) or related dementia, a number expected to double by 2031. Compared to other prevalent diseases, the absence of effective treatments for AD is shocking. It is of prime importance for AD patients, their loved ones and the society as a whole, that we rapidly develop new therapeutic strategies. To achieve that aim, the identification of new relevant drug targets is the key. My laboratory has always been trying to understand why neurons fail to communicate in AD and whether it is caused by loss of proteins located in "synapses", where neurons interconnect with each other. My specific interest in one of those synapse proteins, Shank3, started when I learned 5 years ago that the child of one of my close friend had mental retardation due to a lack of this protein. I could witness with my own eyes the consequence of a loss of 50% of this protein on a child's capacity to learn and memorize. If lacking Shank3 has such an effect on a child, could it do the same in AD? We then found that there is almost 50% less Shank3 in the brain of AD patients. Since we know that children born missing 50% of the gene coding for Shank3 display extensive cognitive impairments, it seems likely that a comparable loss of Shank3 protein in AD may contribute to symptoms. To test that hypothesis, we thus propose to determine whether the consequences of shutting down half of Shank3 in animal models leads to signs and symptoms similar to AD. We have used a strategy that focuses on the French Canadians of Quebec, a study population known for its contribution to medical genetics. This proposal describes our strategy for identifying and characterizing our most promising candidate genes. Understanding the role of new cancer risk genes to hereditary ovarian cancer will advance knowledge of its causation. Also, such genes have the strongest potential as genetic biomarkers that could be useful for developing ovarian cancer prevention and management strategies. column37: Accurate detection and diagnosis of breast cancer remains a major problem in today's society. Even when something suspicious is diagnosed and breast surgery is decided upon, the success of surgery depends on the doctor's ability to accurately identify (and remove!) all cancer regions within the surrounding healthy breast tissue. Unfortunately, some tumor is often left behind (as it does not look very different from healthy tissue), and surgery must be repeated at a later time. The unique combined polarimetry-guided MS instrument will draw upon the strengths of the two technologies and should prove useful as a rapid, accurate and practical method to improve the success of breast cancer surgery.

column37: Narcolepsy is a disorder characterized by excessive sleepiness: patients fall asleep during the day without being able to resist the urge to sleep. Narcolepsy is often accompanied by sudden episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotions and termed cataplexy. Research in the past decade demonstrated that daytime sleepiness in narcoleptic patients who present cataplexy is related to a lack of a substance in the brain called hypocretin. However, some patients with narcolepsy never experience episodes of cataplexy. Furthermore, other patients presenting daytime sleepiness and no cataplexy closely resemble narcoleptic patients, but they tend to sleep for longer durations during the night and during daytime naps, without feeling refreshed after naps. This disorder is called idiopathic hypersomnia. No consistent lack of hypocretin has been observed in narcolepsy without cataplexy and idiopathic hypersomnia, and the brain abnormalities responsible for sleepiness in these disorders are poorly understood. This lack of knowledge considerably limits the possibility of developing optimal treatments. In the absence of more effective interventions, many patients with idiopathic hypersomnia or narcolepsy are dramatically affected by severe daytime sleepiness, which causes threatening risks of accidents, and impairs productivity and quality of life. Our objective is to analyze complementary modalities of brain imaging in patients with narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia. This will allow us to identify brain regions and networks that are affected by these disorders, and will thus help us clarify the distinct brain mechanisms of daytime sleepiness in these different conditions. Understanding the brain regions and networks responsible for the disruption of daytime functioning in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia will be critical for developing new treatments, which will target the brain mechanisms specifically involved in each of these disabling disorders.

We will also do surveys of nurses, doctors, and other health professionals to find out what they know about carrier screening, how they feel about it, and how prepared they are to offer carrier screening to their patients. column36: Role of the insula in refractory epilepsy
column37: The insula, the fifth lobe of the brain, is a complex structure hidden by the frontal, temporal and parietal brain lobes. Despite important advances in the comprehension of frontal, temporal and parietal epilepsies, insular epilepsy remains to date a relatively neglected disease. Our group is among the few in the world to have expertise in the diagnosis and treatment of insular epilepsy. By systematically recording insular activity directly during epilepsy investigations, our group showed that a significant portion of patients suspected with other forms of epilepsy actually suffer from insular seizures. In addition, we showed that failure to recognize insular seizures can lead to wrong selection of surgical targets and dramatic epilepsy surgery failures. The main issue faced by clinicians is that they don't recognize or poorly understand insular epilepsy, thus they cannot diagnose it efficiently. In this proposal, we tackle this important challenge by addressing the following questions: 1) What are the clinical symptoms or combinations of symptoms the are highly suggestive of insular epilepsy? 2) What is the value of modern brain imaging techniques for detecting insular epilepsy, 3) How does the insula interact with other regions of the brain to generate seizures? 4) Do neural interactions between the insula and other brain regions bear predictive factors regarding the chances of success of epilepsy surgeries? Ultimately, we expect the knowledge gathered during the proposed research to bring the clinical management of insular epilepsy patients to the level reached for other forms of epilepsy. By providing clinicians with efficient tools for understanding and diagnosing insular epilepsy, in addition to uncovering new factors for insular epilepsy surgery success, better surgical outcomes will be achieved.

column36: Integrin Linked Kinase as a Novel Therapeutic Target for Heart Failure
column37: Worldwide, heart failure is the leading cause of death and disability, with only half of currently diagnosed patients surviving a further five years. Heart failure patients each receive, on average, 2.5 disease-related drugs each day. However, the vast majority of drugs are designed to address secondary symptoms and not the mechanisms that directly cause poor organ function typical of heart failure. We have shown that a protein present in heart, called Integrin-linked kinase or ILK, is a key regulator of human heart function. ILK controls heart function through unique interactions with other proteins, specifically the parvin proteins. Heart function is normally regulated by ILK:beta-parvin complexes, but in heart failure ILK:alpha-parvin complexes dominate, and reduce heart function. Our strategy is therefore to disrupt ILK:alpha-parvin complexes and thereby favour the formation of beneficial ILK:beta-parvin complexes. Through collaboration with our Industry partner (IRICoR), we discovered lead peptides (circular peptides) that can disrupt ILK:alpha-parvin complexes, and showed that these lead compounds protected the heart under stress. Cyclic peptides were pursued since they have the capacity to make more extensive binding contacts with protein complexes than traditional small molecules. The next step in drug development is to test and refine our lead compounds, turning them into true therapeutic drugs that can be given to patients. We have developed methods (assays) that allow us to examine ILK:parvin interactions at microscopic levels, up to the effect on whole animals, including the use of human heart cells (techniques we pioneered in some cases). Using our established relationship with industry-experienced chemists and drug design personnel (IRICoR), our collaborative team can ensure that our initial discoveries translate to improvements in patient care.

We also predict that chemicals promoting TRPML3 and BK activity may combat bacterial infection. To test the hypothesis, we have collaborated with multidisciplinary teams of medical specialists in the fields of autophagy and microbial pathogenesis. We have also collected substantial preliminary data, acquired experience with the proposed work and have been equipped with all the necessary knowledge, space, equipment, techniques and materials that allow us to complete the proposed work. We believe that our study will not only provide important information regarding the role of TRPML3 and BK in autophagy regulation, but also lead to new therapeutic strategies combating many bacterial infections, i.e. developing drugs targeting TRPML3 or BK.

Brain synapses undergo long-lasting changes in the strength of communication known as synaptic plasticity, which is the accepted cellular mechanism for learning and memory. Signalling via cAMP and cGMP are deemed important for the process, yet, the detailed nature of their regulation at (e.g. time course, response size and interactions) remains obscure owing to a lack of precise methods and tools. To decipher the roles of cAMP/cGMP, I will apply our newly established technologies to light-dependently control their levels in a location-specific manner by the use of advanced microscopy and engineered light-sensitive proteins. Utilizing these technologies, we will reveal how cAMP and cGMP interact to control synaptic function, plasticity and cognitive performance. The proposed research and light-sensitive technologies will advance our knowledge of brain function and provide an in-depth understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying brain function in health and disease. The work is directly relevant to understanding and treating brain disorders that affect cognitive function, including Alzheimer's disease. The expected outcomes include the development of novel optical technologies and valuable tools to elucidate the role of signalling cascades in broad research fields. cAMP, cGMP and other signals to be studied are used by all cells in the body and hence the work has applications to a wide range of medical conditions. The new knowledge will form the basis for development of novel strategies for patients afflicted with devastating brain disorders.

column37: Protection against pathogen infections and cancers is provided by the immune system. However, the immune system is responsible for the development of autoimmunity in genetically susceptible individuals. A white blood cell type critical for both immune protection and induction of autoimmunity is the T cell. During their development, T cells undergo rigorous selection processes in the thymus in an attempt to enrich the body with protective T cells and limit the presence of potentially harmful T cells. Much attention has been focused on the physical removal of T cells that recognize one's own healthy cells during development through a cell death mechanism. However, it is becoming clear that the ability of T cells to recognize one's own cells results in the generation of T cell populations that can protect against damage. Furthermore, we have evidence that, as opposed to the physical elimination of potentially harmful T cells, functional inactivation of these T cells is a more potent way to prevent autoimmunity. We propose to investigate the important events that regulate the development of protective T cell populations and to determine the relative importance of, and key molecules involved in, the functional inactivation of potentially harmful T cells during their development. Information generated from our experiments will provide valuable information into how the body normally avoids autoimmunity and will also generate insight into treatment options and therapeutics for cancer immunotherapy, chronic infections and organ transplantation.

column37: It is estimated that approximately 20% of the Canadian population is currently suffering from chronic pain. Amongst the different chronic pain syndromes, chronic low back pain (CLBP) is by far the most prevalent, and the one responsible for the most years lived with disability. Alas, we still have a limited understanding of the factors contributing to pain chronicity. Consequently, most current treatments only have modest effects on CLBP. However, in recent years, evidence has mounted to support the effectiveness of physical exercise as a treatment for CLBP. Unfortunately, we know very little of the physiological mechanisms underlying the impact of exercise therapy on CLBP. Indeed, because the backs of most CLBP patients (~85%) do not show any particular signs of pathology explaining the persistence of the pain, it has been proposed that CLBP may be principally maintained or amplified by the central nervous system (CNS, i.e. brain and spinal cord). The objective of the proposed project will therefore be to investigate the CNS mediators of the effects of exercise therapy on CLBP. More specifically, we hypothesize that physical exercise will reverse the stress-related central inflammation and hippocampal atrophy associated with CLBP. In order to test this hypothesis, 100 patients with CLBP and 100 age-matched controls will be tested before and after a 16-week long physical exercise intervention (3 x 1 hour of high intensity aerobic and muscular exercise per week). Blood draws will be taken to measure circulating levels of pro- and anti- inflammatory molecules, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) will be used to measure the volume and connectivity of several brain structures, including the hippocampus. Finally, half of the participants will start the study with a 16-week long period without exercise training in order to control for time and other non-specific effects of exercise therapy.

column37: Severe mental disorders such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder affect more than 2% of the Canadian population, especially youth. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a pro-inflammatory factor, well known to be involved in inflammation and also to play a role in regulating metabolism. Thus, we will use olanzapine as a representative atypical drug to explore the possible mechanisms of MIF in AAP induced metabolic dysfunction. Our research will include multiple techniques related to basic medicine and molecular biology. I hope to develop a novel strategy to inhibit metabolic side effects and heart disease during atypical antipsychotic treatment. We believe that MIF inhibitors will improve the clinical psychiatric treatment with atypical antipsychotics. Based on the results of these experiments, in our future studies, we are planning to extend the use of MIF inhibitors to clinical practice by collaborating with Dr. Donghong Cui in Shanghai Mental Health Center, China. column36: Sleep and Pain in Childhood Arthritis: A crossover randomized control trial comparing adequate and restricted sleep duration, and its impact on pain in adolescents with arthritis
column37: Childhood arthritis is an important cause of pain for affected children and adolescents. It is the most common rheumatic disease of childhood. Chronic pain is frequent and impactful. Many adolescents with arthritis also have trouble sleeping. They often struggle to sleep through the night, wake up earlier, and are sleepier during the day compared to healthy children. Our research group, among others, has shown a strong link between sleep and pain. One of the main questions that has not been answered by past studies is what comes first, poor sleep or pain? We want to find out if pain is caused or made worse by poor sleep, or if it is pain that leads to poor sleep. If we answer this question, we should be able to direct our treatments in a more effective way. This link is especially important for teenagers with arthritis. Adolescents often have poor sleeping habits, regardless of their health. This means that teenagers with arthritis may have even worse sleeping habits, or may be more affected by it. The main purpose of this study is to assess the impact of changing sleeping patterns on pain, and disease activity, in teenagers with arthritis. We think that better sleep will directly lead to better health. We will measure the changes in sleeping patterns for 3 weeks. The 1st week will be a baseline week. For the 2nd and 3rd weeks, participants will change the amount of time they spend in bed. One week will be a longer duration of sleep (9.5 hours in bed) and the other week will be a restricted amount of sleep (6.5 hours in bed, which is widely believed to be inadequate). Each experimental sleep condition will last for 5 nights. The other 2 nights of the week will be a break, where the participants can choose their bedtimes. Wake up times will be the same across the whole 3 weeks. We will measure sleep and pain via surveys and a pain app, and other arthritis-related variables at weekly study visits.

column37: The beneficial bacteria that live within us and the harmful bacteria that make us sick are in constant conflict with one another and the outcomes of these conflicts can determine if we acquire an infection. One of the weapons that good and bad bacteria use to fight with one another is a needle-like nanomachine called the 'bacterial type VI secretion system'. Bacteria use this molecular needle to inject antibacterial toxins into rival bacteria. The human disease-causing bacteria known as Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses the type VI secretion nanomachine to wipe out other bacteria and establish life-threatening infections in susceptible individuals, such as people with cystic fibrosis or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The goal of the proposed research is to fully understand how this bacteria-killing nanomachine works at a molecular level so that we can one day disable it, thereby giving our beneficial microbes a much better chance of warding off the deadly Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria.

column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) represent a new class of typically antibody-based agents that restores the body's natural immune response directed at cancer cells. They do so by blocking signals, often sent by cancer cells to immune cells to dampen immune responses directed at them. ICIs thus allow for the release of tumor-directed immune responses. These blocking agents, namely anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibodies, have led to impressive clinical results in patients with advanced melanoma and lung cancer, particularly when combined together or with other established cancer therapies. However, these treatments only prolong patient survival in certain types of cancers. One key reason is that our immune system has evolved many checkpoints to control its responses directed at infections or to dampen them to avoid self-immunity. One key checkpoint pathway that works in parallel with PD-1 and PD-L1 involves a molecule called VISTA. We propose to develop VISTA inhibitors since the expression of this molecule has recently been shown to increase on both immune and cancer cells of prostate cancer patients that do not respond to anti-CTLA-4 therapy. This finding indicates that tumor cells are evading recognition from immune responses by de-activating immune cells such as T cells through their VISTA pathway. We propose to develop and test several classes of VISTA inhibitors that will work with approved ICIs to restore immunity towards tumors.

column36: What will it take to decrease the burden of the HIV and STI epidemics among MSM in British Columbia, Canada? A sexual network modeling analysis, combining syndemic theory, to evaluate the impact of behavioural and biomedical interventions for HIV and STI prevention
column37: Gay, bisexual, two-spirited and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are disproportionally affected by the HIV epidemic in high-resource countries. Since 2004, in British Columbia (BC), the proportion of new diagnoses among MSM have plateaued, while those of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), especially syphilis, have been rapidly increasing, consistent with a substantial level of condomless anal intercourse. Today, there are three powerful strategies available to prevent HIV infection among MSM, including: the use of condoms, treatment as prevention (TasP), and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). In this 5-year study, our key contribution will be to develop a new methodology to forecast the consequences and benefits of emerging programs and policies for HIV and STI prevention among MSM prior to their implementation. This methodology will provide a deep understanding of the heterogeneity in sexual practices within MSM networks over time, enabling a more accurate assessment of the impact of different interventions targeting these networks. The proposed analyses accounts for the role of key factors affecting HIV and STI transmission among MSM, including demographic (e.g., age, income level), psychosocial (e.g., substance abuse, history of partner violence, childhood sexual abuse), and health-related factors (e.g., health status). Our ability to confidentially link administrative databases of all people diagnosed with HIV and at risk of acquiring HIV in BC, and assess surveillance testing data, makes this one of the first interdisciplinary research studies of how co-occurring STIs and risk behaviour are fuelling the HIV epidemic within MSM sexual networks. Importantly, this study will provide highly relevant new information for decision makers to inform resource prioritization and policies as they address the future impact of HIV, STIs and utilization of healthcare resources by HIV infected MSM in BC, Canada and internationally.

column37: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Canada. Unfortunately, there are no effective therapies available that can provide permanent solution to the problem. Identifying, new research approaches that can offer permanent therapies for this disease are needed. Patients with heart disease require constant long-term treatment and care. Therefore, it imposes a significant economic burden on Canadian healthcare system. The strategy of transplanting stem cells into damaged heart has emerged as a novel therapy for the treatment of heart disease as stem cells have the ability to transform into heart cells and replace dead cardiac cells. Bone marrow derived allogeneic (unrelated donor) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from young healthy donors have emerged as ideal candidates for cardiac repair, because these cells have the ability to suppress the host immune system and survive in the heart after transplantation. Moreover, there are no ethical issues involved with these cells. However, recent reviews of animal studies and initial clinical trials reported that allogeneic MSCs were rejected by host immune system that impaired the benefits of allogeneic MSCs mediated therapy. Therefore, understanding the cell signaling pathways that regulate transplanted stem cell survival/rejection in the heart will help in developing new therapeutic agents that could prevent stem cell rejection and enhance the benefits of stem cell therapy. The objectives of current proposal are to study the mechanisms of transplanted stem cell rejection and to find out the strategies to increase post-transplantation survival in the heart. The outcome of this research will help in interpreting the results of ongoing allogeneic mesenchymal stem cell based clinical trials, and to carefully design future trials. The long-term objectives of this research are directed toward improving the quality of life of patients with heart disease using stem cell therapy.

column37: Prostate cancer continues to be a leading cause of death for men in North America The main factor that drives the transformation that changes normal prostate tissue into cancerous lesions is the androgen receptor (AR), a molecular signalling protein, which is induced by male sex steroid hormones, such testosterone, to interact with DNA in the cell nucleus, thereby stimulating tumor growth. An "anti-dimer" compound would clearly be useful to treat such resistant forms of prostate cancer where only months of survival benefit are offered through using conventional agents. Thus, our pioneering work has the potential to inform the next model of prostate cancer treatment with novel alternative anti-cancer molecules.

column36: HEARTBiT: A novel multi-marker blood test for management of acute cardiac allograft rejection
column37: Heart transplantation is a life saving therapy for people with end stage heart failure. Acute rejection, a process where the immune system recognizes the transplanted heart as foreign and mounts a response against it, remains a clinical problem despite improvements in immunosuppressive drugs. Acute rejection occurs in 20-30% of patients within the first 3 months post-transplant, and is currently detected by highly invasive heart tissue biopsies that happen 12-15 times in the first year post-transplant. Replacing the biopsy with a simple blood test is of utmost value to patients and will reduce healthcare costs. The goal of our project is to develop a new blood test to monitor heart transplant rejection. Advances in biotechnology have enabled simultaneous measurement of many molecules (e.g., proteins, nucleic acids) in blood, driving the development of new diagnostics. Our team is a leader in using computational tools to combine information from numerous biological molecules and clinical data to generate "biomarker panels" that are more powerful than existing diagnostic tests. Our sophisticated analytic methods has recently derived HEARTBiT, a promising test of acute rejection comprising 9 RNA biomarkers, from the measurement of 30,000 blood molecules in 150 Canadian heart transplant patients. Our objective is to study a custom-built HEARTBiT test in a setting and on a technology that enable clinical adoption. We will evaluate the new test on 400 new patients from 5 North American transplant centres. We will also track patients' HEARTBiT scores over time to help predict future rejection, and explore use of proteins and micoRNAs to improve HEARTBiT. Our work will provide the basis for a future clinical trial. The significance of this work rests in that it will provide a tool to identify acute cardiac rejection in a fast, accurate, cost-effective and minimally invasive manner, allowing for facile long-term monitoring and therapy tailoring for heart transplant patients.

column36: How does frailty influence the risk and expression of dementia in Alzheimer disease?
column37: Dementia is a clinical syndrome in which impaired memory and thinking interferes with a person's daily life. The most common cause of dementia is mixed Alzheimer disease (AD) / vascular dementia. AD can be diagnosed clinically when someone is alive and, after death, by brain autopsy. Even so, not everyone who meets the autopsy diagnostic criteria for AD actually has dementia in life. Despite some study, why this discrepancy exists is still unclear. We plan to address it by looking at how overall health affects brain function. To do this, we must measure health problems, which we quantify with a frailty index. The frailty index counts the number of health problems that an individual has accumulated. Frailty increases the risk for many age-related illnesses (including heart disease, hip fracture and dementia). Now we want to know if this helps explain why brain autopsy findings alone do not account for the clinical features of dementia. We hypothesize that the frailer a person is, even though it is more likely that they will have cognitive impairment, this will be less clearly related to their brain autopsy findings. We will use data from two large, community-based, autopsy series in older people (Chicago USA; Cambridge UK). The people in those studies generously agreed to have their memory and thinking tested every 1-2 years and to donate their brains after they had died. These extremely valuable studies are well suited to what we plan to do. Our research team includes physicians who study both dementia in people and AD in brains, as well as scientists skilled in data analysis. We have team members at varying levels of their careers, from PhD student to established professor. Understanding how frailty affects brain function can improve our understanding of how dementia arises, and how it can be treated and even prevented.

column37: The overall goal of this project is to assess patterns of opioid prescription in BC in relation to serious outcomes (e.g. dependence, illicit drug use, overdose, and death) and provide evidence for do-no-harm strategies to address BC's prescription opioid crisis. In 2016 in BC, there were 978 illicit drug overdose deaths and, in the first half of 2017, another 780 deaths. This is the highest number of drug overdose deaths ever recorded and BC announced a Public Health Emergency in April 2016. Currently, many drugs sold illicitly contain fentanyl, an opioid that is many times more potent than heroin. Fentanyl detection in illicit drug deaths has risen from 4% in 2012 to 81% in 2017 to date. The dramatic increase in illicit drug deaths over time is, in part, due to policies designed to address problematic prescription opioid use. Currently, a half a million British Columbians are prescribed opioids for non-cancer pain each year and the quantities of opioids prescribed have risen dramatically over time. Numerous recommendations have been developed including prescription drug monitoring programs that help prescribers know if their patients are taking high amounts of opioids, dangerous drug combinations, or being prescribed opioids inappropriately; and accelerating requirements for tamper-resistant formulations of medications. However limited evidence suggests the possibility of unintended consequences which could increase the illicit drug death rate. Thus, recent reports have called for a better understanding of the relationship between prescription opioid misuse and illicit opioid use for informing prevention and treatment initiatives. This study will address the relationship between prescription drug use, illicit drug use, and harms secondary to drug use. We plan to evaluate patterns of opioid prescribing and drug taking behaviours in relation to serious outcomes and evaluate the effects of supply interventions, opioid agonist therapy, and public policy on changes

column36: Viral determinants of natural human cytomegalovirus transmission
column37: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection causes birth defects in >2 per 1,000 births worldwide. As such, a vaccine to prevent CMV infection is needed. Most people in the world acquire CMV during early childhood from CMV in breast milk, saliva or urine. Children are often infected with CMV by their mothers, but mothers are frequently also infected by children, and interrupting the cycle of transmission between mothers and children is the key to reducing the enormous global health burden from CMV. Our study will guide the development of a CMV vaccine by characterizing the specific viral variants and modes of transmission between mothers and children. We have shown that only one or very few individual viruses that are able to successfully establish infection, which we call transmitted/founder (T/F) viruses. We are able to capture CMV transmission events between mothers and children, and determine the precise time of infection. Because CMV is highly genetically variable, we can use next-generation sequencing (NGS) to distinguish viruses from different individuals, as well as between compartments (e.g., breast milk, saliva, or urine) in the same individual. Thus, we are able to determine the exact source of a CMV infection. We can also measure the number of viruses present, and sequence of the entire genome of T/F viruses that initiate CMV infection. We will enroll a prospective cohort of 100 pregnant Kenyan women and their children, and collect samples of breast milk, saliva, urine, and blood to measure CMV viral loads and sequence the T/F viruses that infect infants and mothers. Our project will be conducted in Nairobi, Kenya, where our team has worked for >20 years on maternal-child viral infections, and brings together experts in epidemiology, virology, genomics, and mathematical modeling. This work will be invaluable for defining optimal CMV vaccine targets and evaluating vaccine strategies to prevent the transmission and morbidity of CMV.

column36: Updating Needs and Network Meta-analyses for the Canadian Guidelines for Chronic Rhinosinusitis
column37: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS), also called chronic sinusitis, is a very common life-long disease affecting over 5% of the Canadian population, and this number increases with age. The annual cost of chronic sinusitis for Canada is estimated at $1.3 billion while the government pays an estimated $860 million yearly for chronic sinusitis treatment. Past research has shown the quality of life in CRS sufferers to be comparable to that of patients with poorly controlled asthma and kidney failure requiring dialysis. CRS sufferers have also been shown to miss considerable amounts of work, suffer from more depression and require more mental health care visits and healthcare resources than the average person. Guidelines provide doctors information for treating diseases. Canadian guidelines for CRS were last updated in 2011, and since that time more than 50 new research studies of relevance have been published. Systematic reviews (i.e. reviews which assess the totality of relevant evidence) are a vitally important study design in the practice of evidence based medicine, which are commonly performed to inform the development of clinical guidelines. Given the vast amount of new evidence, there is an imperative need to update the information used to inform recommendations for CRS management in Canada using a systematic review approach. These efforts will establish new levels of evidence for CRS interventions, thereby improving the health of Canadians and reducing variation in clinical practice. This research program will use rigorous systematic review methodology and will directly incorporate input of the Canadian CRS guidance panel to inform the update of the Canadian guidelines in 2018-19.

column36: Identification of therapeutic targets for pediatric acute megakaryoblastic leukemia
column37: In Canada, nearly one quarter of childhood cancers are leukemias. Encouragingly, many of these pediatric leukemias are now treatable with a variety of anti-cancer drugs. Nonetheless, leukemia still accounts for an alarming ~25% of cancer-related deaths in children. One of the most aggressive forms of leukemia is known as "acute megakaryoblastic leukemia" (abbreviated as AMKL), and the particular form of AMKL we are focusing on responds very poorly to current treatments. Indeed, 80% of afflicted children succumb to this type of AMKL within 5 years after diagnosis. In view of this shocking statistic, we have assembled a diverse team of investigators spanning fundamental science and clinical expertise with the common goal of identifying novel treatments for this aggressive and often fatal form of pediatric AMKL. Importantly, we have developed a unique way to study human AMKL in mice. Our team will exploit this new "mouse model" along with cancer cells taken from human patients and cutting edge scientific methods, to approach an important challenge in childhood leukemia research. The proposed studies have great potential to not only identify effective drugs for combating pediatric AMKL, but may also lead to new treatment options for other types of leukemia and blood disorders.

column36: Enhancing ovarian cancer immunogenicity by increasing antitumoral responses using engineered oncolytic vaccines
column37: Cancer immunotherapy is a revolutionary approach based on methods that stimulate the immune responses in our body to kill the cancer cells. Immune cells called cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) specifically recognize cancer cells to eliminate them. However, when a tumor is established, cancer cells use several mechanisms that dampen the immune system. Growing tumors establish an immunosuppressive microenvironment that renders CTLs dysfunctional. Tumors also escape from immune recognition by their ability to decrease the expression of proteins in their cell surface called major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I). In this project, we propose to combine different approaches in cancer immunotherapy to efficiently target and eliminate tumor cells. First, oncolytic virus (OV) are able to specifically replicate and kill tumor cells directly but also by stimulating CTL responses. Second, OV can be modified to make them express proteins that will empower immune cells sitting in the tumor niche. Using OV modified to express the proteins IL-15 and IL-21, tumor cells will produce a more supportive environment for CTLs to execute their killing capacities and generate a long-lasting protection against tumor cells. Third, MHC-I proteins can be increased on tumor cells by delivering NLRC5, a master protein that promotes the expression of MHC-I and other related proteins to increase tumor cell visibility towards CTLs. We have developed an infected cell vaccine (ICV) platform using tumor cells infected with the OV Maraba MG1 modified to express IL-15 and IL-21. The ICV-IL15+IL21 expressing NLRC5 will be used as a vaccine to stimulate the activation of antitumoral CTLs. Focusing on ovarian cancer, a cancer that is in dire need of more effective treatments, the combination of these three approaches should result in a treatment that generates robust CTL responses and stimulates the formation of memory that will confer long-lasting protection against relapse.

column36: Pannexin1 mediation of stroke recovery responses: Sex and sex steroid influences
column37: Pannexin 1 (Panx1) is a protein found in the membrane of various cell types, including neurons, to assist in the passage or communication of very small molecules. Ischemic injuries that deprive neurons of oxygen and glucose (e.g. stroke) can enhance the activity of Panx1 to promote cell death (apoptosis). Men and women often show differences in stroke severity to suggest a potential role for the gonadal steroid hormones, estradiol and testosterone. Because Panx1 can mediate apoptosis and inflammatory signaling responses in injured neurons, we reason that it may come to explain sex differences in stroke outcome responses. Indeed, in our brain stroke model we have evidence to show that either the loss of the Panx1 gene or its pharmacological blockade significantly reduce the amount of neuronal damage in female, but not in male mice. This striking difference underscores Panx1 as an important focal point for unmasking underlying gonadal hormone and cellular mechanisms mediating sexual dimorphisms in stroke severity, as we propose to examine in the current application. The findings of this grant promise to provide novel frameworks for sex- and age-dependent differences in stroke vulnerability and rescue.

column36: An engaging, patch-free treatment for young children with amblyopia
column37: Amblyopia (also known as lazy eye) is a vision disorder that affects approximately 1 in every 50 children in North America. Amblyopia is due to abnormal development of visual brain areas and causes poor vision in one eye along with a loss of 3D vision. The most common current treatment for amblyopia involves patching of the stronger eye to encourage use of the weaker eye. Patching improves vision in the weaker eye, however treatment compliance is problematic because children dislike wearing an eye-patch. In addition, patching does not directly treat the loss of 3D vision caused by amblyopia. Recently, an alternative approach to amblyopia treatment has been proposed that involves the use of videogames that are modified so that different parts of the game are seen by each eye. This encourages cooperation between the two eyes and leads to recovery of vision. The videogame treatment is promising, but it is not suitable for young children who cannot play the games. In collaboration with the British Broadcast Corporation (BBC), a world leader in children's television programming, we will begin to test the use of modified cartoons to treat amblyopia in younger children. We will also develop a novel computer-vision system that will monitor treatment adherence by recognising the patient's face and recording their engagement with the cartoons. As a whole, this project will provide a foundation for future, large scale, clinical testing of a new at-home amblyopia treatment. This project will lead to improved vision for young children with amblyopia both in Canada and world-wide.
