column36: Development, evaluation and implementation of genetic clustering methods for the real-time molecular surveillance of HIV outbreaks
column37: Immediate access to combination antiretroviral therapy not only drastically reduces HIV-related morbidity and mortality in people living with HIV, but also has public health benefits because it significantly reduces transmission. The global effort to eradicate the HIV pandemic has thus turned to issues of implementation: e.g., to reach populations at the greatest risk of HIV transmission for focused deployment for HIV testing and prevention resources. A person's HIV population rapidly accumulates new mutations within months of infection to become genetically unique. This means that clusters of infectious that remain very genetically similar may indicate a recent outbreak of virus transmission. Because HIV sequences are already routinely collected as standard-of-care, these large treatment databases are perpetually accumulating at clinical and research centres around the world. There is now tremendous interest in making secondary use of these databases to support public health efforts by detecting transmission outbreaks in "near real-time". We were responsible for building the world's first real-time cluster monitoring system for the HIV treatment database in British Columbia, Canada. However, HIV genetic clustering methods have seldom been examined rigorously. We recently discovered that current methods are severely biased to detect "clusters of diagnosis" - populations who tend to be diagnosed sooner post-infection than others - and fail to detect the clusters of transmission intended to be foci for public health efforts. We propose to: (1) develop a fundamentally new approach to HIV genetic clustering that focuses on transmission rates; (2) evaluate clustering methods using detailed simulation models and the retrospective analysis of treatment databases, and; (3) develop an open-source implementation toolkit and evaluate knowledge translation issues in building real-time systems in Uganda and Malaysia.

column36: Modulating peri-ischemic neuronal hyperexcitability
column37: In the healthy brain, neuronal functioning depends on continual tuning of blood flow in proportion to the level of local neuronal activity. A blockage of a major artery during stroke results in a sharp decline in blood flow, killing the neurons and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. Despite the availability of treatments for clot dissolution in the acute and rehabilitation regimens in the chronic stage, most patients suffer significant long-term disabilities and up to a third are institutionalized. Development of more effective therapies is hindered by the uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes required for complete recovery. Recent evidence suggests that the activity of the neurons in the peri-infarct zone, the damaged but potentially salvageable brain region surrounding the site of stroke, greatly influences recovery. Using advanced imaging techniques in rats, we will monitor the function of peri-infarct neurons in the hours following stroke induction. We will inject the brains of these rats with viruses that carry specific membrane channels to allow us to modulate the activity of peri-infarct neurons non-invasively, by illuminating them with light of specific wavelength. These finely controlled experiments will allow us to determine activity levels of these neurons that minimize short- and long-term functional deficits. We will then attempt to achieve comparable activity profiles by tuning the dose of locally delivered novel anti-convulsant medication. These experiments will establish the ways by which brain functioning can be affected early post stroke so as to improve neuronal function. The insights gained will guide the development of next generation, non-invasive treatments that can be readily combined with current therapies to enhance recovery from ischemic stroke.

column36: Gestational exposure to chemicals related to hydraulic fracturing in Northeastern British Columbia, and their endocrine disrupting potential
column37: In 2016, we conducted a pilot study that evaluated exposure to environmental contaminants (toxicants) in 29 pregnant women living in Northeastern British Columbia. This region is characterized by intense natural gas exploitation by hydraulic fracturing known to release contaminants in the environment. We found that exposure to a toxic solvent (benzene) in these women was four times higher than in the Canadian population; in Indigenous women, exposure to this solvent was six times higher. Exposure to toxic heavy metals was also high. This is concerning because exposure to these contaminants during pregnancy could alter fetal development. To better evaluate the exposure to these contaminants and their potential risks during fetal development, we propose to: 1) Characterize exposure to these chemicals in 100 pregnant women residing in Northeastern British Columbia using urine, hair, indoor air, outdoor air, and drinking water samples. 2) Assess the effect of these chemicals on hormone production during fetal development using in vitro tests. Disruption of hormone production during pregnancy is associated with pregnancy and birth outcomes like pre-eclampsia, small birth weights and pre-term birth. 3) Evaluate associations between natural gas development intensity and exposure levels in pregnant women. 4) Explore social inequities related to exposure to environmental chemicals in Northeastern British Columbia.

column36: Targeting of a mobile genetic element into the genome using budding yeast as a model system
column37: Mobile genetic elements are regions of DNA that copy and paste themselves into a genome. More than half of the human genome is full of repetitive elements and movement of these elements can result in cancers as well as other disorders. The elements that move in the human genome are called retrotransposons. We use the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S. cerevisiae) and the Ty1 retrotransposon, which is present in 32 copies in the yeast genome, as a model system. The yeast Ty1 retrotransposon is similar in structure and life cycle to retroviruses such as the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1), which results in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Studies of the Ty1 retrotransposon have already been important for elucidating the fundamental mechanisms of how retrotransposons/retroviruses replicate and enter the genome. In this research proposal, we will study the precise mechanism of how the Ty1 retrotransposon is pasted into a specific region of the genome. The highly conserved Ty1 integrase protein is necessary for pasting the retrotransposon into the genome but needs the help of host cellular proteins to accomplish genome entry. We will uncover which host proteins interact with Ty1 integrase and how this interaction results in targeting to a region of the genome. Because Ty1 integrase is conserved with retroviral integrases, and many yeast proteins are conserved with mammalian proteins, the knowledge we gain from our research can be applied to human cells and ultimately health care. Our fundamental research using a model organism is critical for understanding how disruptions can occur in the human genome.

column36: Examining the role of emotion regulation and arousal in co-morbid anxiety in autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
column37: Background: There are over 100,000 children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in Canada. Up to 84% of these children experience impairing anxiety that can affect the physical and mental well-being, and reduce opportunities for education and future employment. There is currently very limited understanding of factors that contribute to anxiety in ASD and potential treatment approaches. Objective: The goal of this study is to address this gap by characterizing the contribution of two known risk factors, namely emotion regulation difficulties and dysregulation of physiological arousal, to anxiety symptoms in ASD. Methods: A sample of children with ASD (n=75), typical controls (n=75), and clinical controls (anxiety disorders; n=75) will be recruited. Participants will complete baseline testing (movie watching) and a task designed to engage emotion regulation processes. During these tasks, two physiological indices of arousal (electrocardiogram, skin conductance) will be recorded using non-invasive sensors. A multi-dimensional assessment of emotion regulation will be administered to all groups (parent-reports; behavioural observation). We will use a combination of traditional statistical tools (multiple regression analysis) and machine learning techniques to examine the association between emotion regulation, arousal, and anxiety in the sample. Expected outcomes: The results of this project will advance the knowledge of factors contributing to anxiety symptoms in ASD and lead to improved health outcomes for Canadian affect by the condition.

column36: Early intensive leg exercise to improve walking in children with spastic diplegia from encephalopathy of prematurity
column37: Children born prematurely are at risk of brain injury that can result in cerebral palsy, most often affecting the both legs. Current treatment is largely passive, including leg braces, repeated injection of a paralyzing agent (botulinum toxin) in muscles that are abnormally active, and surgery as deformities occur. Active, physical therapy for weak muscles is infrequent, occurring twice a month or less. Yet, recent work in mammals show that early brain injury can be alleviated by intensive exercise therapy, but only while the animal is very young. Building on our success with early, intensive therapy for children with perinatal (around birth) stroke, we will apply intensive therapy for the legs in children with cerebral palsy involving both legs. Children (8 mo - 3 yr old) will be randomly assigned to start treatment immediately or delay treatment for 6 months. The delay period controls for improvement without treatment. The children in the Delay Group will also receive the same treatment after the delay period. The therapy will be guided by physical therapists and centred on play. Measures will be taken before, during and after the delay and treatment periods. Measures will include clinical scores of motor development, proficiency of walking, participation at home, and physiological measures of motor and sensory function. All children will be followed until they turn 4 yr old, to determine if there are long term benefits. The cost-effectiveness of the intervention will be evaluated by a health economist. We anticipate that like the children with perinatal stroke, early intensive exercise will improve mobility, facilitate earlier and better walking, and that the effects will be enduring.

column36: Vitamin K as a positive modulator of cognition in cardiovascular disease: mechanistic studies of its vascular actions
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is highly prevalent amongst Canadians and represents an important risk factor for late-life cognitive impairment (i.e. learning, memory) and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease. Conditions such as atherosclerosis (ATX) and hypertension (HT) have been linked to arterial stiffness, alterations in cerebral blood flow, and decreased brain perfusion. Initially discovered for its role in blood coagulation, vitamin K (VK) has recently emerged as an important nutrient for vascular health and brain function. In the vasculature, VK is beneficial through the actions of proteins which act as calcium inhibitor. In brain, VK is widely present and participates in the activation of a number of proteins involved in blood flow, vessel integrity, and brain cell activity. Moreover, VK has been shown to modulate cognition in both animals and humans, notably during aging. In studies by our group, feeding rats a high VK diet throughout their lives was associated with better learning and memory functions in late-life. The overreaching goal of this proposal is to provide evidence for the beneficial effect of enhanced VK status on cognition in the context of CVD and characterize its mechanism of action. Our specific aim will be to determine, using two rodent models, the potential of VK to mitigate cognitive impairment through an amelioration of the vasculature, cerebral blood flow, brain oxygenation, and brain structure integrity. Animals will be fed various levels of dietary VK and will be investigated at different life stages. Experiments will include multidisciplinary approaches including imagery studies. The proposed studies will be amongst the very few to integrate state-of-the-art imaging technology to investigate the role of a nutrient in rodent brain, and will expand the importance of VK to the context of CVD. Importantly, they will help plan future intervention studies in this group of patients who could largely benefit from this nutrient.

column36: Interference with Gli to Control Castration Resistant Prostate Cancer
column37: Prostate cancer grows and spreads under the influence of androgens (male steroids). For this reason, hormonal therapies are used to treat patients with metastatic disease. Unfortunately, these therapies are only transiently effective; eventually patients develop castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) that continues to grow and spread. While newer anti-androgens provide some respite, CRPC cells soon develop resistance to these drugs as well. We propose a highly innovative approach for better control of CRPC that targets Gli proteins in prostate cancer cells. Gli proteins regulate genes that are needed for cancer cell growth and division. Our preliminary work has shown that androgens activate Gli proteins in prostate cancer cells and that Gli activation is required for continued growth of CRPC cells. We have also developed some novel tools that interfere with Gli activation and these agents slow CRPC cell growth significantly. The Aims of our proposed work will provide proof-of-principle that androgen-activated Gli proteins are the drivers of CRPC growth and that interference with Gli activation is a rationale strategy for better control of CRPC. column37: Proteins are string-like molecules that play many vital roles in the human body. They are made up of about 20 different building blocks called amino acids, which are in a particular sequence that enables the string to fold up into its correct 3 dimensional structure. When the sequence is changed due to a genetic mutation, the protein may not fold up correctly and cause disease. Misfolded proteins are often mislocalized and degraded, but if they can reach their normal cellular location they are still functional. This is what happens in cystic fibrosis, in which the misfolded protein is called CFTR. Drugs that correct the localization and function of CFTR have been developed, but they provide only a small benefit for most patients and better drugs are needed. We have identified new compounds that bind directly to CFTR and correct it's trafficking, but to improve them we need to answer questions such as "Where do they bind? Do different drugs bind at different sites? How do they work to trigger correction? Which combination of these correctors gives the most therapeutic benefit? These questions will be addressed in this grant proposal with a view to developing better therapies for protein trafficking diseases.

column36: The Functional Improvement Trajectories After Surgery (FIT After Surgery) Study: A Multicentre Prospective Cohort Study to Evaluate the Incidence, Trajectories, Risk Factors, Impact and Healthcare Costs Related to Significant New Disability after Major Elective Surgery
column37: About 190 million people have surgery every year in developed countries. Many of them are older and have pre-existing health problems, such as heart disease. A good understanding of their risks with surgery is critical. Such information guides patients and healthcare teams on which operation is the best option, and helps identify people who need help to recover well after surgery. At present, doctors simply tell patients about their risks of death or complications within 30 days after surgery. This practice is problematic. Few patients (less than 3%) die shortly after surgery, but many more (30-40%) have major complications that lead to long-term health problems, such as heart disease or stroke. These problems can cause significant disability such that, even months afterwards, some patients can no longer take care of themselves, live in their own home, or work. Thus, understanding how often and why major disability occurs after surgery is important, especially since most people want to both survive surgery and function well. We will therefore conduct the FIT After Surgery Study to understand the risks, underlying reasons and impact of significant new disability in people who are aged 65 years or more, and having major surgery. The study will include 2000 patients having major surgery at 10 hospitals across Canada. Using special interviews and tests, participants will be followed for 1 year after surgery to find out if they develop a significant new disability. We will measure the risk and impact of significant new disability after surgery, and identify which types of patients, operations and complications are likely to lead to disability. Our study will help patients to make better-informed decisions about having surgery, and help identify patients needing help to recover after surgery. It will also identify which complications research and quality improvement must focus on. The FIT After Surgery study will thus improve the care of surgical patients worldwide.

column36: The influence of microglia on the developing hypothalamus
column37: The human hypothalamus is only about the size of an almond and yet, it is very important to our survival. Indeed, the hypothalamus is essential for regulating key physiologies such as when to eat, sleep, drink, reproduce, shiver, and even love. To control these physiologies, the hypothalamus acts as a thermostat, first by sensing cues and then eliciting a response via its many neurons. Interestingly, even during embryonic development, the hypothalamus is still responsive to its environment. Microglia are another type of sensing cell in the brain but instead of responding to external cues, microglia respond to internal ones. For example, microglia are tasked with detecting injury and trying to repair it, as well as identifying unnecessary debris (e.g., dying cells) and clearing them away. Recent studies are starting to show that microglia also influence fetal brain development. Our own work has demonstrated a unique role for microglia in the developing hypothalamus. We have discovered that microglia in the embryonic hypothalamus are particularly activated, clustering around a discrete niche of the dorsal third ventricle. We showed that hypothalamic microglia interact with progenitors and can influence normal developmental programs. Consistent with these findings, elimination of microglia during gestation caused newborn pups to be born obese, strongly supporting a role for microglia in hypothalamic development. From these data and others, we hypothesize that microglia communicate with hypothalamic RGCs to influence development, particularly tanycytes. In this proposal, we will test the intriguing notion that cells whose primary purpose is to sense insults (e.g., microglia) are used to establish the key brain region essential to sensing homeostatic cues throughout life.

column37: The adult brain contains several populations of neural stem cells. In addition to the "active" neural stem cells, which participate in processes such as learning and memory and ongoing replacement of cells in certain brain regions, there also appear to be several types of "quiescent" neural stem cells, whose biological functions remain poorly understood. We believe that these quiescent neural stem cells can be harnessed to enhance the brain's intrinsic self-repair capacity during neurodegenerative diseases and following injury. Our laboratory has recently developed an experimental strategy that allows us for the first time to directly study and manipulate one of the adult brain's quiescent neural stem cell populations. In this research proposal, we take advantage of this strategy to determine what the normal functions of these cells are, how their quiescence is controlled, and how they can be activated during normal aging and in Alzheimer's disease. Our experiments will be carried out using innovative and powerful animal models, which will provide us with fundamental new insights into how stem cells are regulated in the adult brain and can be re-activated under pathological conditions. A sub-goal is to investigate a potentially mitigating effect of NE on socioeconomically related impairments in development. The significance of the proposed project is well reflected by a highly urbanized Canadian society with declining early childhood development and increasing socioeconomic inequalities, where knowledge on healthy urban planning is urgently required. The focus on children is specifically chosen in order to provide the highest health impact across the life course and thereby contributing to a healthier Canadian society. Results from the project may contribute to solutions to current challenges for early childhood development in terms of rapidly changing living environments, harmful exposures, and stressful lives. We aim to increase the evidence for environmental exposures' relation to early childhood development and thereby support healthy urban planning with targeted environmental interventions for a vulnerable population - children, especially in socioeconomically deprived areas.

column37: Major depressive disorder is a debilitating and often chronic mental illness that affects 1 in 5 women over the lifespan. When depression is not treated effectively during pregnancy, the mother's and her child's health is at risk. Antidepressant medications are a mainstay of treatment for women whose depression is severe, or not adequately responsive to psychotherapy. Yet, it is very hard to determine when risks for relapse/ongoing depression definitely outweigh the small, but still uncertain risks of antidepressants. So, treatment decisions regarding antidepressant use in pregnancy must be guided not only by evidence about harms and benefits, but also by: (1) how a woman values the potential benefits and harms of the treatment options; (2) which option she prefers; and (3) the extent to which she wants to be involved in the treatment decision. column37: Prior clinical studies and new European guidelines have proposed that patients coming to the emergency room (ER) with chest pain can be either sent home or admitted based on one blood test (hs-cTn) result. We have published data indicating that the combination of hs-cTn and glucose (i.e., sugar in the blood) is better than hs-cTn alone in identifying patients who can be sent home or admitted in our previously funded CIHR study. The first population would be those patients who are being investigated for a heart attack in the ER and who have enrolled in our previous CIHR study. The second population would be all patients that have clinically cardiac troponin ordered, with hs-cTn measured for research purposes, in the ER in one city. The third population will be all ER patients in the province of Ontario who have hs-cTn reported. We will investigate if hs-cTn alone and interpreted with the European guidelines is better than our laboratory scores at ER presentation for predicting which patients will or will not suffer from a heart attack, or heart failure, or will die at 30-days, 1, 2-years after their visit. The findings from our study will determine the best pathway forward for using hs-cTn at ER presentation and will be a significant step towards safely discharging and admitting patients to the hospital based on a single blood draw.

In this context, the aim of this project is to conduct a multicenter randomized controlled trial assessing a lifestyle intervention in obese infertile women that continues throughout fertility treatments and pregnancy. The results of this study will provide data on the importance of lifestyle management for obese women consulting in fertility clinics, in order to improve their fertility as well as helping them to achieve a healthy pregnancy and to have a healthy baby. column36: Deciphering the entry pathway of the Ebola and Marburg viruses
column37: Outbreaks of emerging viral diseases are increasing at an alarming rate and are a worldwide concern. A notable example of emerging viruses is the Ebola virus that causes severe hemorrhagic fevers in humans and non-human primates with lethality rates that can reach 90% and against which there is currently no antiviral therapy. The threat of unpredictable outbreaks emphasizes the need for the development of therapeutic drugs against Ebola virus. However, fundamental to developing new drugs is the elucidation of the different steps of the life cycle of the virus, such as the discovery of host proteins essential for infection that can be targeted to block virus spread. We have previously identified the receptor of the Ebola virus, the protein Niemann-Pick C1, which resides in late endocytic vesicles. This discovery allowed us to propose a model of infection by which the Ebola virus attaches to the cell surface, is internalized, and is trafficked to intracellular vesicles containing essential host factors such as the Ebola virus receptor triggering entry and delivery of the viral genetic material into the host cell. The requirement of multiple host proteins for viral entry offers several targets for pharmacological inhibition. A promising target includes a protein complex involved in the turnover of endosomal phosphoinositides. Genetic manipulation and chemical inhibition of the complex activity lead to efficient block in Ebola virus infection, suggesting that these proteins and endosomal phosphoinositides are critical for infection. Here, we propose to investigate their roles of in viral trafficking and entry using genetic and chemical biology approaches. The ultimate goal of the proposed research program is the development of urgently needed antiviral therapies against Ebola virus for Canadians and worldwide.

column37: Psoriasis is a major health problem affecting up to 3 % of the population. The disease is characterized by an abnormally excessive and rapid growth of the epidermal layer of the skin. Skin cells are replaced every 3 to 5 days in psoriasis rather than the usual 28 to 30 days. Psoriasis affects both sexes, can arise at any age and to any ethnic groups. In addition, nearly 30% of the psoriatic patients will develop a debilitating arthritis form of the disease. There is no cure currently available for psoriasis, but they are treatments such as topical application of corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues that can help to control the symptoms. However, when these treatments are inefficient, UV radiations are then recommended or the patients are treated with a compound named methotrexate that is also used against leukemias and rheumatoid arthritis. However, methotrexate and other drugs referred to as "biologics" are toxic and must be administered under very close medical attention. In such a context, new efficient and less toxic drugs are dearly required to better control the symptoms of the disease. To this end, we develop new molecules that exhibit efficient activity on in vitro models by controlling the proliferation of the cells responsible for psoriasis. In addition, these drugs are not toxic. The main objective of our research program is to prepare new compounds suitable for clinical trials that will improve the quality of life of psoriatic patients. Toward this goal, our project will harness the power of computer sciences, molecular pharmacology and chemistry to tailor drugs that are more potent, more selective and less toxic.

column36: Post-ictal hypoperfusion: a novel marker of the seizure onset zone.
column37: Epilepsy is a serious neurological disorder. About 54,000 Canadians have seizures that cannot be controlled by anti-seizure drugs. In these cases, the only available strategy is removal of the brain area generating seizures, called the seizure onset zone. However, seizure cure is <50% due to incomplete identification and removal of this area. We will use an established technique called Computerized Tomography Perfusion (CTP) to better identify and remove the entire seizure onset zone and improve post-surgical outcome. In routine clinical practice, the seizure onset zone is located by electroencephalographic recordings of seizures or single photon emission computerized tomography measures of blood flow during a seizure. However, these techniques have limited spatial resolution or are very labour-intensive and costly. Recently, we showed that seizures are followed by highly significant post-seizure blood flow reductions at the seizure onset zone lasting up to 1 hour that can be precisely measured using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These exciting findings suggest that the area of post-seizure hypoperfusion may be a novel seizure onset zone marker and better target for epilepsy surgery. Measuring post-seizure blood in clinical practice is hampered by difficulty in obtaining MRI scans within 1 hr. We will therefore measure post-seizure blood flow reductions in 150 patients using CTP as CT scanners are rapidly accessible. We will determine if CTP can better detect the full extent of the seizure onset zone compared to conventional methods (Aim 1) and if it can better predict post-surgical freedom (Aim 2). Our project is directly applicable to health care as we will determine if post-seizure hypoperfusion can better identify the full extent of the seizure onset zone and predict post-surgical outcome. Our study will ultimately allow clinicians to use this measure to direct surgery and improve surgical cure rates since CT scanners are widely available across Canada.

column36: "Laser treatment for stress urinary incontinence - a randomized controlled trial"
column37: Up to a third of women lose urine involuntarily (urine incontinence). While being "wet" may dramatically impact women's quality of life, urinary incontinence is also expensive for patients, society and the health care system. The costs for both patients and the health care system are high: protective pads and treatments such as physiotherapy, medical devices and surgery. In addition, this condition may affect women's ability to work (loss of income). There is an urgent need for new low cost, effective and validated therapies to treat women with incontinence. Recently, an innovative therapy using a laser has been used to treat women with incontinence. Many private clinics in Canada are offering these laser therapies (at a cost of $2000-3000) to treat incontinence. The laser is applied through the vagina in a procedure that does not require anesthesia. This is a relatively quick procedure (< 10 minutes) with very few reported complications and risks. The heat generated by the laser is reported to change the structure of the tissue around the vagina and add support for the vagina and bladder to reduce incontinence. Although this innovative, low-risk, potentially low cost and quick procedure would seem to be a very attractive option for women with incontinence, the laser is not being widely offered to women in Canada, in part because of a lack of scientific studies showing that the laser is effective. To date, there have been no randomized controlled clinical trials ('gold standard' studies) that have evaluated the efficacy of laser treatment. It is difficult for physicians to recommend such a treatment to the many patients with urinary incontinence without such evidence. A randomized controlled trial to study how effective the laser is to treat women with incontinence will be conducted. If the laser is shown to be effective, this treatment could represent a new, innovative and potentially low-cost therapy to help the millions of women with incontinence.

column37: Females have two X chromosomes while males have only one X chromosome and the sex-determining Y chromosome. The X chromosome contains over 1000 genes that therefore have the potential to be expressed twice as much in females compared to males. To avoid this expression imbalance one X chromosome is silenced in females. We have discovered that the gene that initiates this silencing process is located on the X chromosome and named XIST for X-inactive-specific-transcripts, because, unlike all other genes, it is only expressed from the inactive or silent X chromosome. In addition, XIST, does not make a protein, rather it is the founding member of a class of genes who functions as a long RNA. We believe it does this by binding proteins and bringing them to the inactive X and in this work we will identify these proteins and how they act to silence the X. This will help us understand silencing, and also some of the sources of differences between males and females.

column37: Hospitalizations, deaths and costs from hepatitis C are increasing in Canada due to undiagnosed and untreated cases. Hepatitis C virus infections can cause chronic infection of the liver that is silent for 20-30 years before about a fifth of infected people develop liver failure or liver cancer. Newly available treatments are very effective in curing the virus if given before advanced liver disease develops. For these drugs to be effective, uptake at all steps along the hepatitis C care pathway (diagnosis, linkage to care, treatment and cure) needs to be high. There are no Canada wide studies on the hepatitis C care pathway however, modelling studies suggest that only half of all hepatitis C cases are diagnosed. The groups at highest risk for hepatitis C in Canada including drug users, migrants from countries with high rates of hepatitis C, and baby boomers (born between 1945-1965). Each group has different challenges accessing hepatitis C screening and treatment. Drug users have barriers accessing health care because of substance abuse and mental health, migrants have cultural and language barriers and recent guidelines have recommended not to screen baby boomers for hepatitis C. Understanding how many people in the key hepatitis C risk groups are screened or treated will help design the best hepatitis C control programs in Canada. The aim of our study is to measure the number and proportion of people screened, linked to care, treated and cured from hepatitis C in Canada and in the key risk groups. We will use these results to run models to determine which steps along the hepatitis C care pathway we should invest for each risk group. Our study results will provide decision and policy makers with information so that the most effective screening and treatment programs can be developed to prevent complications and deaths from hepatitis C and to achieve hepatitis elimination in Canada.

column36: Exploring the role of environmental factors in neuronal aging
column37: Our bodies are inhabited by thousands of bacteria. These bacteria (collectively referred to as the microbiota) are not passive inhabitants, but instead play important roles in metabolism, development of the immune system, and protection against pathogens. In addition to these roles, alterations in the bacterial makeup of the microbiota have been observed in a number of diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases. However, these studies are correlative, demonstrating alterations in already diseased patients; they do not demonstrate a causal role in disease development and do not identify specific factors that contribute to disease. Further investigation is required to determine if, and how, alterations in the microbiota contribute to the development of these diseases. To this end, we are focusing on the potential role of microbiota in influencing neurodegeneration. Our goal is to identify possible interventions that will slow the decline in neuronal function that occurs with age. The development of treatments and interventions designed to target the microbiota requires the identification of specific bacterial factors that influence disease state and an understanding of how these factors work. To accomplish this, an experimental system is needed that allows alteration of the microbiota and where genetic differences between individuals does not exist. We use a small nematode (worm), C. elegans for this purpose. Using these animals, we are able to easily generate large populations (millions) of genetically identical animals for analysis. We will determine the influence of hundreds of bacterial strains isolated from humans, on neurodegeneration using C. elegans models of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases. Using the bacteria that differentially influence neurodegeneration, we will identify specific molecules produced by these bacteria and examine changes in the expression of genes that occur in response to these factors.

column36: Characterizing the pathophysiological roles of secretory microRNAs in multiple sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic brain disease with an unknown cause or cure. At present, the drugs used for treating MS patients target the immune system and have very little effect on preventing disease progression and neurodegeneration. While cells of the immune system play a significant role in MS, we must uncover novel strategies that both protect the brain and promote repair following injury. Such strategies would not only benefit MS, but other neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer's, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and ALS. MS is a highly complex disease that involves significant cross-talk between cells of the brain and immune system. Unfortunately, many of the drugs that selectively target molecules involved in this cross-talk are ineffective in most neuroinflammatory conditions, including MS. While these drugs are clinically effective for treating several other immune-mediated diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis, we now acknowledge that cell-to-cell communication is much more complex in the inflamed brain and requires further study. Our research focuses on a newly discovered method of cell-to-cell communication that occurs via exosomes, which are small enclosed biological structures that have been implicated in inflammation and neurodegeneration. Exosomes can be detected in all bodily fluids and may have the potential to be used as disease biomarkers and/or targets of drug therapy. In MS, we hypothesize that exosomes deliver molecules called microRNAs that help to mediate inflammation, neurodegeneration, and brain repair. This research will provide a detailed characterization of the microRNAs within exosomes and identify how they can directly impact key genes and biological pathways that are implicated in MS. In the future, the ability to alter microRNA profiles within exosomes may lead to an exciting therapeutic avenue to explore in MS and other brain diseases.

column37: North America's overdose crisis has significantly impacted British Columbia (BC), leading to the declaration of a public health emergency in 2016. With fentanyl-adulterated opioids driving rapid increases in opioid-related drug overdose, new practices to prevent overdose deaths are being implemented in BC, however, they are typically designed and implemented using a "gender neutral" approach that can fail to account for the influences of a wider set of socio-structural forces (e.g., gender inequality, gender norms, colonialism) that may be crucial to effectively intervene to reduce women's risk of overdose. Although a few women-specific and Indigenous-specific interventions have been launched, including North America's first woman-only overdose prevention site, they have yet to be evaluated. Research has demonstrated that gendered power relations shape women's exposure to drug-related risks and harms. However, the relationship between gender and overdose remains poorly understood. Effective overdose-related interventions for highly-impacted subgroups of women (e.g., Indigenous women; transgender women) also must be informed by better understandings of the social experiences of women who use drugs. This 4-year study aims to generate evidence to strengthen interventions and strategies to decrease overdose-related harms, including death, among women who use drugs through an examination of the socio-structural forces shaping overdose risk, women's access to and experiences with overdose-related interventions, and the perspectives of drug-using women on potential strategies to improving overdose-related interventions and outcomes. Our innovative research aims to tackle key enduring knowledge gaps surrounding overdose-related risks and harms to women who use drugs, and to translate research evidence into practical improvements, informing the ethical delivery of effective policies, programs, and practices in BC, across North America and globally.

Stewart Tug vessel near Bella Bella, BC. Findings from each HIA highlight how current health surveillance approaches are missing critical information and vary considerably across Nations. Urgent action is needed given the number of current development projects proposed and major weather events affecting First Nations. It is the objective of this investigation to address this critical health data gap for BC First Nations by informing the development and implementation of a culturally appropriate health surveillance system. This is a basic requirement for short and long term preventative and mitigation strategies need to protect and improve health outcomes for First Nations in BC.

column37: Background: Asthma is one of the most common chronic diseases in childhood and is a leading cause of emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. Despite improvements in available treatments, ED visit and hospitalization rates for asthma remain high. Currently, children who leave the ED following an asthma exacerbation do not always receive comprehensive asthma education or get started on asthma controller medications, even though these strategies are known to prevent repeat asthma visits. This may be due to physician discomfort in prescribing these treatments or lack of asthma educators. However, these treatments are likely only needed for children who are at high risk for repeat ED visits or asthma hospitalizations. There are currently no guidelines to direct clinicians how to practically identify these high-risk children before discharge from the ED. Aims: Derive a clinical risk score to identify children who are at high risk for repeat asthma ED visits or hospitalizations within 12 months following an initial asthma ED visit. Methods: We will analyze data that was collected as part of a previous study that included all children with an asthma exacerbation who came to the ED at one of five specialized pediatric hospitals. Information on characteristics of children who participated in this previous study will be linked with provincial health administrative data in Ontario and Quebec to provide information on health care outcomes one year after their initial ED visit, and specifically whether the children were hospitalized or had repeat ED visits for asthma. This information will be used to develop a clinical score to identify high-risk asthma patients. Expected Outcomes: This study will allow us to develop a simple method to identify children at high-risk for future asthma ED visits or hospitalizations. This method can be used in future to target treatments to high-risk patients who would benefit most.

Consequently, these studies will provide clues to better treat diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer.

Complexity of human biology makes it difficult to address this challenge effectively; however, fundamental aspects of human disease had been in past and will be in future efficiently addressed through analysis of orthologous genes using experimentally tractable model organisms. The goal of my research is to combine powers of unbiased mutagen-induced modifier screens using Caenorhabditis elegans model and whole genome sequencing (WGS) in order to accelerate discovery of new disease-associated genes, modifiers of known disease-associated genes and potential Orphan drug targets. To reach these goals, I will: (1) isolate modifiers by performing forward genetic screens on orthologous genes implicated in human rare disorders; (2) identify molecular basis of modifiers using WGS, state-of-the-art bioinformatics and molecular genetics techniques, and (3) characterize the phenotypes and mode of action of the genetic modifiers. This research is of high importance as it will establish C. elegans as a model organism for systematic high-throughput heritable genetic modifier screens with high potential for direct impact on diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of rare diseases, in particular the ones with no treatment options (currently >95% of rare diseases).

column36: CYCLE: An international, multi-centre, randomized clinical trial of early in-bed cycling for mechanically ventilated patients
column37: Background: Critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are the sickest patients in hospital, and need advanced life support. People who survive their critical illness are typically very weak and disabled. Over half of them have severe leg weakness impairing their quality of life for up to 5 years. In-bed cycling uses a special bicycle that attaches to the hospital bed, allowing patients on life support to gently exercise their legs in the ICU. Objectives: The main goal of this research program is to see if patients who need a breathing machine recover faster if they receive early in-bed cycling than if they do not. Methods: Adults who need a breathing machine in the ICU are eligible. Patients will receive 1 of 2 treatments: (1) early in-bed cycling 30 minutes per day, 5 days per week while they are in the ICU or (2) routine physiotherapy. Patients will be assigned to either treatment in a manner similar to flipping a coin. Participants will receive these treatments from physiotherapists for 30 minutes/day, for 5 days/week as long as they are in the ICU. Physiotherapists will also test participants' strength throughout the study. Outcomes: We will measure patients' muscle strength and function 3 days after they leave the ICU. We will ask patients to rate their quality of life after the ICU and at hospital discharge. Finally, we will assess the costs of offering in-bed cycling to these patients. Relevance: By 2026, the demand for ICU services in Canada will increase by 40% compared to 2011. More survivors will have disability after their time in ICU, and there is an urgent need to help them recover faster and be stronger. To-date, early in-bed cycling in the ICU has not been studied in terms of how it affects health issues important to patients (e.g. walking, quality of life). The CYCLE RCT is the largest trial ever done in this field, to help patients get as strong as possible while they are recovering from critical illness.

column36: Regulation and impact of productive AID targeting during antibody responses.
column37: Antibodies are a major component of the human immune system. A large repertoire of specialized cells named B-lymphocytes, each producing a different antibody, are constantly renewed to be able to detect any of innumerable and constantly evolving pathogens. The initial recognition of a pathogen, by the antibody on the surface of a B-lymphocyte, signals the onset of changes in the genes encoding the antibody, which will allow improving its affinity and effectivity to eliminate the infection. Most vaccination strategies rely on stimulating the B-lymphocytes that produce antibodies against known pathogens so that they expand and undergo the AID-mediated antibody improvements before any exposure to the actual pathogen. The genetic mechanisms that shape the antibodies and mediate immunity are initiated by an enzyme named AID. As a side effect of changing the antibody genes, AID can also cause collateral genetic damage. This can predispose to cancer or negatively affect the B-lymphocyte's ability to multiply, which is critical for the process of generating a protective response. We study the mechanisms that balance these beneficial and detrimental effects of AID. We investigate how AID reaches the genome and how much it works once there, which have a direct impact on the antibody response. On one side, these mechanisms need to allow sufficient AID activity to produce useful antibodies. On the other hand, they need to protect the genome from excessive damage. Our results would allow explaining the cause of immunodeficiency when the mechanisms we study do not work and enable manipulations for therapeutic applications. Salient examples would be to treat autoimmune diseases mediated by antibodies, boosting the efficacy of immunization in aged people, or enhancing vaccination to increase the chances of generating infrequent antibodies, such as those that neutralize rapidly evolving viruses.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases are the number one killer in Canada. The current therapy for preventing and treating atherosclerosis (stiffening and blocking of arteries) uses statins to reduce levels of LDL (bad) cholesterol in the blood. This basic knowledge will open up new opportunities for blocking MMP14 and reducing LDL cholesterol in blood. column36: Evaluating diagnostic accuracy of tests and decision rules in the absence of a perfect reference test: Application to extrapulmonary tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is the world's leading infectious disease killer with an estimated 9.6 million new cases of TB in 2014. Though public health efforts typically focus on pulmonary TB, extra pulmonary TB (EPTB) accounts for an unknown 15%-40% of the burden and is associated with important morbidity and mortality. A key challenge to combating EPTB is the lack of a perfect diagnostic test, presenting a hurdle for disease diagnosis in individual patients, and also for estimation of disease burden and evaluation of new tests at the population level. To date most studies estimating disease burden or diagnostic accuracy have relied on naive methods resulting in biased estimates. Our objective is to address this by developing a Bayesian latent class model, which is a statistical model that acknowledges the imperfect nature of all tests and possible dependence between them. We will focus on three common forms of EPTB (pleural, lymphatic, meningitis). Our methods will be applied to large cohorts of adults with suspected EPTB from India and South Africa, two countries with a heavy disease burden. We will also use data from an ongoing Cochrane review of the accuracy of Xpert for EPTB. The results of these different latent class analyses will allow us to estimate the predictive value of composite decision rules for EPTB, allowing us to estimate for the first time the extent of overtreatment and underdiagnosis. These predictive values will be used to carry out cost-effectiveness studies. The methods we describe will contribute to addressing the major public health problem of reducing EPTB burden. This project brings together an international group whose complementary methodological and clinical expertise in latent class analysis, systematic reviews and tuberculosis, is necessary to execute it. The project will support training of graduate students. The methods and software described in this proposal will be relevevant in other disease areas as well.

column37: Each year 400,000 North Americans suffer sudden cardiac death (SCD), usually from a life threatening heart rhythm. One in five of us will die from SCD, often without any warning and where help is not available. An implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) is a special type of pacemaker that can prevent SCD. However, the current guidelines of who should get an ICD use only one measurement, the "ejection fraction" (EF), to decide if someone should or should not get one. Using this approach only 1 out of 10 patients getting an ICD actually get benefit, and more than 80% of patients who end up suffering SCD are never given one. Therefore, we must find better ways to figure out who should and should not be given an ICD. Our lab has been working for over 10 years to find features on picture of the heart that pick out people at highest risk of SCD. To date we have published 8 features that strongly predict this. We have now made a computer software that can automatically build a 4-dimensional heart model (beating 3D heart) from images taken with an MRI scanner. We believe this can find people at high risk of SCD. To do this we have partnered with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, a group of scientists that use approaches (similar to Google) to solve complex problems. We plan to teach a computer program, using a total of 1,500 MRI studies in patients sent for an ICD, what a "high risk" patient looks like. We will test the ability of this new software to predict if and when a new patient will suffer SCD. If successful, we will make this software available to the community to improve how we deliver ICDs to those patients who need them most. This work could therefore have a major impact by saving a larger number of lives in people with heart disease.

column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most commonly diagnosed non-skin cancer in Canadian men and one of the leading causes of cancer-related death. In almost all patients, the proliferation and growth of PCa is driven by the androgen receptor (AR). Given this critical role, inhibiting the AR is the standard of care following surgery or radiotherapy. The effectiveness of current therapeutics is usually temporary, with the cancer eventually developing drug resistance. There are no curative treatment options for resistant PCa and these patients have a median life-expectancy of only 20 months. Currently, all clinical anti-AR agents act by direct binding to the AR's hormone binding site. These drugs are therefore vulnerable to mutations which frequently arise at this region. Further, as they are structurally related they cannot be used in combination. There is therefore an unmet need for new therapeutics that inhibit the AR. By combining computer modeling, biological screening and structural biology, we have developed an entirely new class of anti-AR drugs that target a novel region of the AR (called BF3). Our lead compound efficiently inhibits the AR and shows efficacy in both PCa cell lines and xenograft animal models. Building off these proof-of-principle studies, this project will progress our lead compound to advanced preclinical development in preparation for clinical trials. The high incidence of PCa coupled with a relatively long disease course and the demographics of aging Canadian population, will eventually make treatment of this cancer one of the largest expenditures in the health care budget. We anticipate that these new anti-AR drugs will replace or supplement existing anti-AR therapeutics and will provide new options for treating patients with late-stage PCa. Since the emergence of resistance is the lethal end-stage of the disease, we anticipate that the proposed research will eventually have a substantial impact on patient survival.

column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada - nearly one out of four deaths in Canada are due to cancer. Advances in cancer biology and genomics have revealed a wide range of cellular mechanisms that contribute to the development and progression of cancer, as well as mechanisms with the potential to slow down or stop the progress of cancer. Among these are a group of molecules encoded by the genome, called microRNAs. Previous research has repeatedly shown that modifying the activity of some microRNAs can inhibit the growth and even lead to the death of the cancer cell. A promising strategy against cancer, therefore, is to change the activity of such microRNAs so that the cancer cell behaviour is reversed. However, for the majority of these microRNAs, our knowledge of how to manipulate them in the cell is limited. Cellular pathways are highly interconnected, meaning that one component of the cell, for example a particular microRNA, can often be inhibited or activated by manipulating another component of the cell. In recent years, researchers have used genomic technologies such as RNA-sequencing to generate terabytes of data from experiments in which various cellular pathways and proteins are manipulated. Many of these manipulations may affect specific microRNAs - however, microRNA activity is not directly observable from the data generated by these experiments. We have recently developed unique and powerful computational methods that can infer the microRNA activity from the patterns hidden in these data, enabling us to mine the massive body of available datasets to find the manipulations that affect the activity of microRNAs. Using these novel computational methods followed by in-depth analyses and experimental validation, this project aims to provide a map of the cellular pathways and proteins that can be exploited to modify the activity of microRNAs, revealing new strategies for targeting the cancer cell.

Families of potential organ donors play a central role in the consent process yet little is known about what determines whether or not they consent. Organ donation is a personal decision made by patients and/or their families. As a result, it is expected and appropriate that some families refuse. Amid continuing need for organs and the declining number of organ donors, it is critical that we investigate the factors that influence the decision-making of relatives of potential organ donors. column36: Molecular Basis of Quebec Platelet Disorder
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that help control bleeding. Our team is studying an inherited disorder called Quebec platelet disorder (QPD) that alters platelets and causes serious bleeding. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD including its genetic cause. In Canada, about 1:200,000 Quebecers has QPD and each person with QPD has a 50:50 chance of passing on QPD each of their children. QPD causes bleeding because it increases a clot busting enzyme called urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA). Persons with QPD have very high levels of uPA in platelets but not in other cells - we are trying to find out why. QPD is caused by a "duplication mutation" which means that a person with QPD an extra copy of the uPA gene and nearby DNA. In QPD cells that make platelets, uPA production is >100 times normal, which is far more than expected for having one extra uPA gene. Additionally, the overproduction of uPA occurs only in QPD cells that make platelets. We explored why and found that QPD duplicates a gene enhancer ("turn on switch") for vinculin (the next gene) - this switch is active only in cells that make platelets. QPD puts the extra copy of this switch right front of the uPA gene. We suspect this is why the gene for uPA becomes turned on too much in QPD cells that make platelets. We will use special methods, including "chromatic conformation capture methods" to test this "swtich" and if it is the reason that the uPA gene in is switched on in QPD cells that make platelets. We will also use special methods to alter genes to test if we can correct the problem in QPD cells that make platelets. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD. We have exciting new information and the technical skills that are needed to study what causes QPD. The study will give us important new information on how genes are controlled when the body makes platelets and how this is changed by QPD. The study will give us new insights on what causes platelet disorders

column36: A novel role for the breast cancer 1 protein (BRCA1) in prenatal protection against oxidative DNA damage, embryotoxicity and abnormal postnatal brain function
column37: The breast cancer 1 (BRCA1) protein is known to protect against breast cancer. However, we have discovered that during pregnancy BRCA1 also protects fetal mice from DNA damage that can cause birth defects and disorders in brain function after birth. The DNA damage is caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are normal forms of activated oxygen essential for fetal development. However, when the fetus lacks proteins like BRCA1 that prevent and repair DNA damage, or when ROS production is enhanced by drugs like alcohol (ethanol, EtOH), the damage accumulates and causes abnormal fetal development. The developmental disorders in BRCA1-deficient mice may be relevant to children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), and the exacerbated disorders with fetal EtOH exposure may be relevant to children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). To elucidate the role of BRCA1 in these disorders, we have developed a genetically altered mouse model lacking only 1 of their 2 copies (+/-) of the Brca1 gene, with a small decrease in BRCA1 protein. The progeny exhibit increased DNA damage and postnatal learning and memory deficits, which are worsened by a single low-level fetal EtOH exposure. We will use this mouse model to determine how both normal and EtOH-enhanced ROS levels and prenatal DNA damage cause birth defects and postnatal behavioural differences, and how BRCA1 protects the fetus from DNA damage. Our studies will establish a biological role for BRCA1 beyond cancer, in protecting the developing fetus from normal and chemically-enhanced ROS levels. This developmentally protective role of BRCA1 is likely important, since both copies of the Brca1 gene must be lost to increase the risk of cancer, whereas the loss of only 1 copy increases the risk of developmental disorders. Our results may identify new mechanisms and risk factors relevant to ASD and FASD, which could help in developing novel predictive and therapeutic strategies for high-risk pregnancies.

column36: Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT): A pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial of a gender-sensitized weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for men who are overweight or obese
column37: About 40% of Canadian men are overweight and another 20% are obese. Approximately 70% of men's staggering health care costs (estimated at $36.9 billion annually) could be prevented if men improved their lifestyles (i.e., got active, ate better, and lost weight); however, few men engage in lifestyle change. The apparent reluctance of men to engage in healthy lifestyle programs may reflect the fact that men with excess weight tend to be less aware or concerned than women about their overweight status. Research has shown that programs situated in a sporting context, where men have a strong sense of affiliation as a fan, are effective and lead to high satisfaction among men. Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT) is adapted from Football Fans in Training and our own HealtheSteps lifestyle prescription program. Hockey FIT is a 12-month (3-month active phase and 9-month maintenance phase) weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for middle-aged, overweight/obese male hockey fans, delivered by trained coaches in collaboration with teams in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL). Across the CHL, there are 52 teams spanning small to large urban centres, located throughout Canada. In the proposed study, 32 sites (affiliated with major junior hockey teams and local YMCA facilities) will be randomly assigned to either the intervention (Hockey FIT program) or comparator (wait-list control). At each site, 40 male hockey fans at-risk for chronic diseases will be recruited to take part in the study. Sites assigned to the comparator will offer the Hockey FIT program to their enrolled male hockey fans after 12 months. Through the Hockey FIT program, our study aims to promote weight loss, increase physical activity levels, and improve other health measures through a cost-effective solution that is acceptable and appealing to men who are overweight or obese. Indeed, findings from our pilot study indicate that Hockey FIT has the potential to achieve these goals.

column36: The effects of reward cues on risky decision making: the role of dopamine and relevance to addiction
column37: In addicted people, exposure to things like drug paraphernalia (known as contextual cues) is believed to trigger cravings, drug use and relapse. Exactly how cues promote such outcomes remains poorly understood. One possibility is that cues influence decision-making and tip the scales in favor of the maladaptive addictive behaviour, making it seem more appealing and worthwhile. Our work in both rats and humans suggests that adding sensory reward cues - similar to the lights and sounds in gambling settings - results in riskier and more disadvantageous choice on gambling-like task. In rats, these effects of cues are dependent on the neurotransmitter dopamine. Our goals are: 1) to study whether problem gamblers are particularly susceptible to risk-promoting effects of sensory reward cues - which are abundant in gambling settings; 2) investigate whether dopamine contributes to cue-driven risky choice in healthy humans and problem gamblers, and dopamine system's responsiveness to cues might be associated with problem gambling. To address these aims, we will use positron emission tomography to look at dopamine levels during decision-making in the presence versus in the absence of sensory reward cues. We will do this in a group of healthy participants and a group of problem gamblers. We expect to find that decisions of problem gamblers will be more influenced by cues than those of healthy participants. We also expect that the presence of cues will result in greater elevation in dopamine levels for problem gamblers than healthy controls.

column36: Understanding molecular control of lipid metabolism in brain aging
column37: While perturbed lipid metabolism has been implicated as a risk factor for aging-related neurological degeneration, it remains unknown how the perturbed lipid metabolism arises during the aging process. Importantly, bioactive lipids have been shown as controllers to regulate neural stem cell function that plays an essential role in learning and memory by producing adult-born neurons. To this end, we are interested in understanding molecular mechanisms that control lipid metabolism to regulate neural stem cell function in the context of aging brain with the long term goal of identifying the molecular target for drug discovery to treat aging-associated cognitive decline. Recently, we discovered a signaling-induced molecular pathway that is required to maintain homeostatic neurogenesis and new memory formation during normal aging. This molecular pathway involves the direct phosphorylation of CBP, a histone acetyltransferase, by atypical protein kinase C (aPKC). We recently identified that monoacylglycerol lipase (Mgll), an enzyme that converts endocannabinoid (2-AG) into arachidonic acid, is a downstream target of the aPKC-CBP pathway. Importantly, we observe that the attenuation of the aPKC-CBP pathway causes upregulation of Mgll expression occurring in both normal and Alzheimer's Disease aging brain of animal models. Thus, we hypothesize that deregulation of the aPKC-CBP pathway in brain aging impairs lipid composition and adult neurogenesis that culminate in the cognitive decline, a phenotype associated with brain aging. Together, our experiments will provide important new information regarding regulation of lipid metabolism and provide fundamental knowledge towards the development of therapeutic strategies fighting against the aging process.

column36: Effects of GPR55 on synapse formation and remodeling during development.
column37: Functional connections between nerve cells (called synapses) are essential to establish the architecture of the nervous system. The modification of synapses is thought to be one of the mechanisms by which learning and memory occur. It has been known for decades that cannabis consumption has a profound influence on learning and memory and that maternal marijuana smoking during perinatal period causes cognitive and social deficits that last in the adulthood of the offspring. For the moment, we do not know if these effects are mediated by the classic CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors or by other receptors such as the GPR55. Altogether, these observations led us to investigate a novel function for cannabinoids (like cannabidiol (CBD)) or other GPR55 ligands in regulating the formation and the maintenance of synapses. We have shown that GPR55 stimulation increases the synapse number and blockade of this receptor decreases it. Therefore, the main objective of this project is to identify the contribution and the mechanisms by which GPR55, and its ligands modulate the synapse number. The identification of a fundamental molecular mechanism regulating the connections between nerve cells will provide important insight into normal brain function and learning process. Furthermore, it will probably permit the discovery of new pharmacological targets and the development of innovative therapeutic strategies aiming at treating congenital or neurodegenerative diseases. This project is timely because Canadians are among the highest consumers of cannabis in the World and its consumption might be on the rise when it will be legalized in 2018. Moreover, the GPR55 system is the target of several compounds in the pipelines of pharmaceutical companies (Sativex(THC+CBD), Epidiolex, and GWP42003(CBD)). Thus, the results obtained from the proposed experiments will potentially explain some of the side effects produced by these drugs.

column36: Hippocampal contributions to approach-avoidance conflict decision-making: a cross-species investigation into the underlying cognitive processes and wider neural circuitry
column37: 'To approach, or not to approach?' Many situations in life induce a state of motivational conflict in us as to whether we should approach a seemingly attractive proposition or stimulus (e.g.,highly calorific chocolate cake), or whether we should avoid the very same stimulus as it may have negative consequences (e.g, weight gain). Very little is known about how the mammalian brain regulates this fundamental process of decision making that can potentially go awry in psychological disorders such as addiction, in which the 'approach' tendency takes predominant control, and others such anxiety, which involve heightened 'avoidance' tendencies. This will offer a new perspective on the role of the hippocampus in decision-making processes, a capacity that is currently thought to be predominantly mediated by the medial prefrontal cortex. Furthering our understanding of the neural basis of approach avoidance conflict resolution, and the identification of differential neural pathways for the control of approach/avoidance behaviour has the potential to create new therapeutic avenues for psychological disorders in which 'approach' or 'avoidance' tendencies are aberrantly dominant.

column36: Development of Viral Sensitizing Antibody Drug Conjugate and Oncolytic virus Combination Regimens for the Treatment of Breast Cancer
column37: Oncolytic viruses are safe viruses engineered to specifically infect and kill cancer cells, and can also stimulate the immune system to recognize tumors. Although they have the potential to treat a broad range of malignancies, the inconsistency of treatment response remains a major challenge and poor infection of tumors is a recognized issue. We have pioneered the development of small molecules that we termed "viral sensitizers" that are able to sensitize tumors to viral infection and potentiate the activity of oncolytic viruses. However, for these molecules to act at maximum efficacy, they currently need to be injected directly into the tumor, which is often not possible. To overcome this issue, we propose to exploit a technology that allows for targeting chemotherapeutics to tumors by piggy-backing on tumor-targeting antibodies. This strategy has notably led to Kadcyla(R), an approved chemotherapy-conjugated version of Trastuzumab(R) (Herceptin(R)) that targets the tumor protein HER2 expressed in a subset of breast cancers. Coincidentally, we have discovered that the type of chemotherapeutic conjugated to Kadcyla has viral sensitizing properties and we have gathered data in cell lines and in immune-deficient mice carrying human breast tumors that combining an oncolytic virus with Kadcyla leads to improved cancer control. This particular approach could be rapidly tested in humans, but before this, we must gather more data in mice with HER2-expressing breast cancer that have immunological characteristics that more closely resemble what we would observe in a human. Furthermore, we will attempt to modify this strategy to deliver our most promising viral sensitizing molecules, and to bypass the need for tumors to express HER2 in order to be effective. To maximize the likelihood of success and eventual impact on cancer outcomes, we have partnered with antibody-drug conjugation experts at the Centre for Drug Research and Development.

column36: Mechanisms of cell death in inherited retinal degeneration caused by rhodopsin mutations
column37: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a devastating genetic disorder of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. The gene most commonly involved in RP is rhodopsin, which produces a protein that detects light. There are large quantities of rhodopsin protein in the light-sensitive rod photoreceptor cells of the retina. Mutations in the rhodopsin gene result in death of rods. However, it is unclear how rhodopsin mutations kill rods. It is proposed that because rods make so much rhodopsin, even subtle rhodopsin defects can result in drastic consequences. We pioneered the use of genetically modified Xenopus laevis frog tadpoles to study this problem. It is easy to make numerous types of genetic changes (e.g., different disease-causing mutations) in this animal to reproduce and compare different forms of the disease. We demonstrated that there are different types of rhodopsin mutations that kill rods in various ways. Two of these ways kill rods faster if the animals are exposed to light. Although the two light-exacerbated mechanisms are caused by mutations in the same gene, and although to an ophthalmologist, patients with these mutations appear to have the same disease, we find that these are actually two very distinct forms of RP that respond differently to treatment. In fact, certain treatments that benefit one form of RP actually worsen the other form. This has important implications for patient treatment: genetic testing will be necessary to test treatments and establish which treatments to use. We propose experiments that will help us understand how these mutations kill rod cells and key ways these mechanisms differ. Our new knowledge of the underlying cell death mechanisms, the unique genetic aspects of the system, and technical advances in manipulating the X. laevis genome will be of value to the scientific community and patients who suffer from RP.

column36: Mechanisms of rod and cone disk membrane synthesis and quality control in normal and diseased retina.
column37: Retinal degenerative diseases are genetic disorders of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. Retinitis pigmentosa is a disorder causing death of rod photoreceptors, while other retinal degenerations affect both rods and cones, or primarily cones. Rods and cones are the light sensitive cells of the retina. They are named for the shapes of their light sensitive outer segment organelles, which are modified non-motile cilia. The outer segments contain a highly organized stack of non-contiguous (rods) or contiguous (cones) disk-shaped membranes that contain very high concentrations of the G-protein coupled receptor rhodopsin. The exact mechanism by which these disks form is unclear. However, it is clear that defects in biosynthesis of both the disks themselves, and disk components such as rhodopsin, are responsible for inherited human retinal disease. Disk biosynthesis is proposed to involve the proteins prcad-21 and prominin-1 which form a complex that may be involved in a step such as disk evagination or sealing. We propose to examine the roles of prcad-21 and prominin-1 in disk formation using X. laevis and D. column36: How Approaches to Care Shape the Pathways of Older Adult Home Care Clients
column37: Home care is increasingly looked to as a means of strengthening the healthcare system by addressing wait lists for residential long term care and supporting older adults to age in place. Although provincial home care policies claim a commitment to "client-centered" approaches to care, there is variation in who delivers home care services, what services are available and for how long, and what the supports are for family/friend caregivers. Regional differences in approaches to care make it difficult to assess the appropriateness of the goals of home care policies, and know if everything is being done that could be done to support clients, caregivers, home support workers and the system in achieving the best possible outcomes. Our multi-method project analyzes how approaches to care shape client pathways within, and potentially out of, the home care system in 2 provinces with similar population size but different service delivery models (Nova Scotia and Manitoba). Our overarching research question is: How do approaches to care shape older adult home care client pathways through the home care system? We will construct typical scenarios of a person's movement over time, by analyzing client data between 2011-2017. We will then interview care groups of clients, caregivers, and care providers at 3 points in time in an 18 month period to understand individual experiences. To gain a systems level understanding, we will examine how regional policies organize approaches to care by analyzing interviews with policy makers and sector representatives, and policy and practice documents. This will create research evidence that can be used to improve home care clients' experiences, and inform care practices, while taking into account individual, provider and system perspectives. We will work with our partners and knowledge users to develop workshops and webinars to share our findings and to support informed decision making at all levels of care.
