column36: Innate Defence Regulator (IDR) peptides: Regulatory mechanisms in the control of asthma
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic respiratory disease, characterized by inflammation in the lungs and narrowing of the airways, which makes it difficult to breathe. Nearly 3 million Canadians suffer from asthma. The direct and indirect cost related to asthma in Canada is around $2.2 billion annually. Nearly 10% of patients do not respond to available steroid therapies and have severe uncontrolled asthma. These patients represent the major burden of asthma and associated healthcare costs. Moreover, commonly used steroid therapies can increase the risk of lung infections, which results in worsening of asthma. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new therapies that can control asthma, without compromising a patient's ability to resolve infections. This study focuses on new molecules known as innate defence regulator (IDR) peptides, which are designed from natural molecules that play a critical role in the immune response. IDR peptides can control both inflammation and infection in the lung, with the potential to overcome side effects associated with current therapies. We have shown that IDR peptides improve breathing capacity in an animal model of asthma, and can control cellular processes linked to steroid unresponsiveness. This project is aimed at the development of IDR peptides as a new therapy for asthma. In this project, we will identify the changes that occur in lung cells after they are treated with IDR peptides. We will also study the biological effects of IDR peptides in the control of lung inflammation and fibrosis, in a mouse model of asthma. The results from these studies will allow us to identify new drug targets with the potential to alleviate unresponsiveness to steroid therapies, a condition for which there is currently no effective treatment. This project will directly support the development of a new IDR peptide-based therapy for asthma, which will have the added benefit of countering steroid-refractory asthma and controlling lung infections

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disorder that results in degeneration of the brain which leads to severe memory impairments. This is a devastating disease producing personal and societal costs that are immeasurable and growing as the "baby boomers" age. The common and central feature of AD is amyloid deposition, of which the major component is the amyloid beta peptide (Abeta). As new clinical trials focus on the initial stages of the disease, early diagnosis is now more important than ever. There is growing evidence from human neuroimaging that the preclinical stage of AD is associated with profound functional alterations of specific brain network. Recent studies using transgenic mice model of AD have shown that some brain cells become highly active in the early stages of AD when the animal exhibit normal learning and memory. In the later stages of AD, neurons become less active with an accompanying decline in animals cognitive abilities. Although the relationship between altered neuronal activity, neural network abnormalities and the behavioral consequences are less known, it is fundamentally important to understand these early brain changes as they provide a target for therapeutic interventions early in the progression of the disease before significant and irreversible brain damage occurs. In particular, this work will provide new understanding of how pathogenic forms of Abeta contribute to neuronal activity and network dysfunction and behavioral & cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease. Our hypothesis is that cellular hyperactivity in the early stages of AD is a key driver of changes in the brain that ultimately lead to the descent into dementia. The proposed work will provide evidence of where in the brain and when these changes occur, the cause of these brain changes, and a target for treatments that could halt or slow devastating effects of AD from occurring.

column36: Does traffic-related air pollution reduce the effectiveness of corticosteroids in asthma treatment?
column37: We are all routinely exposed to air pollution derived from transport and power generation, or occupationally in industries that underpin the Canadian economy (forestry, mining, oil & gas), with many Canadians exposed to unacceptable levels. The Government of Canada notes "air pollution costs Canadians and the Canadian economy billions of dollars per year". This study has the potential to enhance both prevention and therapy for Canadian asthmatics. Our results can inform physician practices and drive regulatory policies to protect vulnerable groups. Additionally, understanding how the effects of corticosteroids on lung gene expression are modified by air pollution could lead to the development of improved medications for the millions of Canadians suffering from airways disease.

column36: Predicting therapy resistance in castration-resistant prostate cancer with circulating tumor DNA
column37: The standard of care therapies for advanced prostate cancer, abiraterone and enzalutamide, are not effective in 20-40% of patients. We currently are unable to recognize this subset of patients up-front, which means they are inevitably treated with a drug that will not work: leading to unnecessary treatment side-effects to the patient and wasted time while their disease worsens. Our unique research team combines cancer bioinformatics expertise with clinical oncology to develop genomic-based strategies that better recognize patients with poor prognoses. Although it has long been known that cancers shed a small amount of their DNA into the bloodstream (known as circulating tumor DNA, ctDNA), the analysis of this DNA is only now possible through advancement of next-generation sequencing technology. Our recent work has shown that changes detected in ctDNA accurately reflect cancer itself and can therefore show the DNA changes occurring in a patient's prostate cancer before, during, and after treatment. In this project we will look at changes occurring in the ctDNA of hundreds of Canadian men with prostate cancer that are being treated with abiraterone, enzalutamide and other therapies. We will determine which changes can predict a patient's subsequent response to treatment. We are uniquely placed to perform this analysis given our strong track record of success in prostate cancer ctDNA profiling, our novel custom (and validated) methodology, and our recent establishment of a province-wide ctDNA profiling program that has rapidly accrued hundreds of patient blood samples. Success with our project will help us understand why some cancers are intrinsically resistant to the most commonly used therapies. Furthermore, we will have developed a clinically-practical framework (requiring only a blood sample, rather than a metastatic tissue biopsy) that may ultimately help prioritize patients for other therapies that have an improved chance of success.

column36: Function of Flaviviridae viral RNAs in the host cell nucleus
column37: Pathogenic RNA viruses of the Flaviviridae family include Zika (ZIKV), West Nile (WNV), Dengue (DV), and Hepatitis C (HCV). ZIKV outbreaks are occurring in more than 80 countries and in 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. DV is endemic in at least 100 countries and WHO estimates that nearly 400 million infections occur yearly, while HCV causes serious liver damage with more than 170 million individuals infected worldwide. A central tenant of Flaviviridae virus biology, and one that guides therapeutic strategies, is that the virus production cycle occurs within the cytoplasm of host cells. However, we recently discovered that the RNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV shuttle in and out of the host cell nucleus. The movement of ZIKV and HCV RNA genomes through the host nucleus has not been explored in the literature, and the functional importance of nuclear viral RNAs remains completely unknown. Critically, altering the transport of ZIKV and HCV RNAs through the nucleus negatively impacts virus production, pointing to a crucial, yet uncharacterized, role for the nucleus in Flaviviridae biology. We hypothesize that the vRNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV enter the host nucleus to (1) engage nuclear pathways that aid in virus production and (2) to regulate host cell gene expression including activition of cell defence mechanisms. We expect that our research will produce new knowledge, technologies, and methodologies that will establish an area of research with pan-Flaviviridae therapeutic opportunities.

column37: Cilia, the antenna-shaped structures found on most human cells, have recently emerged as major hotspots for genetic diseases called ciliopathies. Over 30 different ciliopathies, caused by mutations in nearly 200 genes, are currently known. Defects in the functions of cilia, which play critical roles in physiology and development, result in many clinical ailments. These include blindness, polycystic kidney disease, morbid obesity, skeletal anomalies and brain defects. Since 2003, my group has made seminal contributions to the understanding of cilia and ciliopathies. In particular, we were the first to link a multi-organ genetic disorder, Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), to defective cilia function. We discovered that several components (proteins) implicated in BBS specifically function in a process termed intraflagellar transport (IFT), which is responsible for the formation and functions of cilia. We also identified and uncovered the functions of novel IFT-associated proteins, all of which are now associated with ciliopathies. The central goal of our research proposal is to establish an experimental system in which we can decipher or 'model' the mechanisms by which different patient ciliopathy mutations cause IFT and ciliary defects. To further enhance our ability to understand how patient mutations affect IFT, we will conduct genetic, cell biology and biochemistry experiments to shed new insights into the functions and regulation of the IFT system. We will accomplish these goals by taking advantage of innovative resources and experimental tools that are either not available for, or not easily applicable to, other researchers using mammalian (e.g., human cells) or vertebrate (e.g., zebrafish) model systems. Collectively, our findings will help unravel fundamental mechanisms of cilia formation and function, and importantly, provide molecular diagnostic tools necessary to understand how IFT mutations can lead to an important and growing class of human disorders.

column37: The two basic elements of successful Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) transmission are a viable virus and a susceptible target host cell. Activated immune cells are more susceptible to HIV infection than resting cells and, once infected, they produce up to 1000 times more virus. It is known that inflammation brings activated HIV target cells to the site of irritation. Most of biomedical prevention approaches focus on either keeping HIV away (condom use) or neutralizing it once it is present in the genital tract (antiviral drugs, microbicides, vaccines). However, what has not been a focus of HIV prevention efforts, is trying to limit the availability of susceptible HIV-target cells at the genital tract. The results showed ASA reduced the number of HIV target cells in the female genital tract by 35%. In this current study, we build on those finding using detailed molecular studies to determine the molecular mechanism(s) involved in ASA's effect on the recruitment of HIV target cells in the genital tract. We will also determine if daily administration of ASA will reduce HIV target cells numbers at the genital tract Kenyan female sex workers who are at high risk of acquiring HIV. We will also determine which dose of ASA is most effective, the duration of the effect and whether there are any side-effects on the vaginal microbiome. The long-term goal of this study is to provide a novel HIV-prevention approach that is both readily available and non-stigmatizing. If we can demonstrate that ASA is able to reduce HIV target cells among women at high risk of acquiring HIV, then we will be one step closer to a much needed novel HIV prevention.

column37: Reducing or eliminating problem behaviours is a critical component to every-day healthy functioning and to the successful treatment of clinical conditions such as drug and food addiction or anxiety disorders. column37: Worldwide, 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men over 50 years of age will experience osteoporotic fractures. Current osteoporosis treatments have various shortcomings such as poor bone quality and several skeletal and non-skeletal side effects. Therefore major investments have been made into the development of more effective drugs that are less prone to side effects. Due to efforts of ourselves and many others it has been discovered that bone-degrading cathepsin K (CatK) is a highly suitable drug target whose inhibition led to increased bone quality and reduced fracture rates in clinical osteoporosis trials. Based on our previous studies on the mechanism of collagen degradation by CatK, we have developed a strategy to specifically block the collagen-degrading activity without affecting other biologically important actions of this protease. We termed this novel and innovative type of drugs "ectosteric inhibitors" and our proposed project is aimed at characterizing these substrate-specific drugs at their molecular, cellular and in vivo levels of action and efficacy as anti-resorptives. We have identified compounds that have a similar bone-preserving potency in cell assays and in an osteoporosis mouse model similar to the most advanced clinically evaluated CatK inhibitor without affecting non-bone-related pathways. This proposal introduces the novel concept of substrate-selective inhibitors that are superior to all previously developed protease drugs and aims to develop potent, efficacious, and side effect free osteoporosis drugs.

column36: Phylodynamics of HIV within hosts
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infects different parts of the body and types of cells, including cells that play an important role in our immune system. Furthermore, an infected cell can become "latent" so that it does not produce new copies of the virus, making it essentially invisible to the immune system and drug treatments, only to become reactivated months or years afterwards. The existence of these reservoirs of latently infected cells is a key reason why it is so difficult to cure an HIV infection. HIV also evolves rapidly because it makes many mistakes when copying its own genome. This rapid evolution makes it possible to infer how different copies of a virus from the same patient are related. These evolutionary relationships are usually represented by a tree or "phylogeny". Phylodynamics is a new interdisciplinary field where the shape of a phylogeny is used to reconstruct how an epidemic has spread through a human population. Methods from phylodynamics have already made enormous impacts on our understanding of HIV, influenza A virus, and the recent Ebolavirus outbreak in West Africa. Our proposal is a completely novel application of phylodynamic methods to examine the proliferation of HIV within patients. We will extend techniques from pattern recognition being developed in our lab to enable computers to extract information about HIV latency and its spread among different populations of cells from the shapes of phylogenetic trees. The key expected benefits of the proposed research are to inform the development of HIV cure strategies by reconstructing how the virus spreads among different cell types and tissues, and their respective characteristics as potential latent reservoirs.

In our study, groups of older adults together with their CCAs will complete the Home Support Exercise Program (HSEP) 5 days per week for 6 months. The older clients in the CCA's care will follow the proven HSEP version while the CCA may move to the intermediate and advanced versions. The study will include 150 older adult participants (50 in each group) and 50 CCAs from two health regions in Saskatchewan. column36: Enabling Multi-site,Tailored Feedback Interventions to Reduce Low-Value Test Ordering in Critical Care: A Systematic Approach
column37: Laboratory testing of patient blood samples is one of the highest volume activities in health care, but between 20-30% of tests ordered are thought to be low-value or entirely unnecessary. This leads to three major problems: 1) wasted spending on unnecessary tests that could be used for other healthcare purposes 2) increased health risks (e.g. blood loss causing anemia that can be particularly dangerous for the highly vulnerable patients in critical care), and 3) risk of false positive results that lead to further unnecessary testing that can be costly, anxiety-provoking, and invasive. Reducing low-value testing is often difficult, particularly in team-based settings like critical care. A potentially effective strategy is Audit and Feedback, where providers' own practice data (e.g. the number of a specific lab tests ordered over the past month) is provided back to them to spur change. Our overall goal is to develop, test and deliver feedback strategies to reduce low-value test ordering in critical care, a highly complex and team-based environment that is one of the heaviest users of laboratory testing. Our team combines 1) lab testing data, infrastructure, and expertise from the Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association (EORLA), the body responsible for all 13 million annual in-hospital lab tests in Eastern Ontario; 2) world-leading expertise in feedback and healthcare professional behavior change, and 3) critical care clinical expertise from a range of critical care units in Eastern Ontario. This project will 1) develop tools to help organizations identify low-value tests and design feedback strategies to reduce their use; 2) design tailored feedback strategies for several critical care sites, and 3) evaluate the effectiveness of these feedback strategies. This work will enable better test ordering practice, help improve efficiency of a major component of modern health care, and reduce the need for patients to be put at risk by unnecessary testing.

column36: Changing the patient-PCP dialogue: fostering trust through joint clinical decision making
column37: A patient visits their doctor with a set of symptoms hoping for a diagnostic test, a prescription, or a diagnosis. Yet, sometimes doing nothing is better. Unnecessary interventions needlessly expose the patient to harms, lengthen the wait for other patients in need of tests or therapy, and burden the health system with avoidable costs. The challenge is how to have doctor-patient conversations about clinical decisions about tests and procedures in a way that is patient-focused and maintains trust. To change the conversation, we need a better understanding of the doctor-patient interaction. We need to understand how doctors build trust with their patients, and do these strategies change if the doctor feels that the patient before them might face barriers in accessing health services. This is very important when faced with suggestions that "doing more" (tests, procedures) is not necessarily better. We need to understand how different groups of patients perceive their doctor visits, including how these might affect Metis patients compared to other Manitobans. In theory, all Manitobans, including the Metis, have equal access to the health care system, but the reality is quite varied and different. Some, by virtue of education, income, race, gender, language, and other issues might have trouble accessing health services and have poorer health outcomes. It is important to understand if there are aspects of initiatives promoting "more isn't better" that might harm some Manitoba patients, like the Metis, because of their already poorer health status. Equally important, unless the expectations of patients who are able to access the health system are met about what they need to feel assured they are getting the best care, trust in doctor recommendations may be compromised. Using interviews with doctors and focus groups with Metis and other Manitobans in Winnipeg, Brandon and Winkler, we focus on common reasons bringing patients to visit their doctor: pain or infection.

column37: In recent years, it has become clear that the beneficial non-pathogenic bacteria in our intestines, that together form our microbiota, have a strong influence on the immune system and therefore also have an effect on both health and disease. These immune cells are found in high numbers in the intestine and are important in preventing inflammation in response to the normal microbiota. It is known that the function of these immune cells is shaped by the bacterial composition of the microbiota. However, it is known whether these immune cells recognize these beneficial bacteria in the same classical way like they recognize for example a virus following infection. The proposed project uses newly developed experimental tools to study this. Furthermore, this project will also study how, in return, different activated immune cells that recognize specific bacteria change the functional properties of these bacteria. Last but not least, we will also investigate how the microbiota modulates the production of antibodies that are specific for the bacteria within the microbiota. The main aim of the project is to better understand how the microbiota can modulate these immune responses. This is important to know for the development of novel approaches to treat chronic inflammatory disorders that make use of the capacity of the microbiota to modulate immune responses.

column36: Regulation of the PCSK9 binding interaction with LDL receptor
column37: Hypercholesterolemia is associated with increased incidence of heart disease, specifically due to increased blood levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL), the so-called "bad cholesterol". LDL removal from blood requires the LDL receptor, a cell surface protein that latches onto circulating LDL particles and mediates their uptake into cells. PCSK9 is a protein in blood that also binds to the LDL receptor, but this binding causes the LDL receptor to be degraded inside cells. PCSK9 may have evolved to help maintain a balance between cell surface LDL receptor levels and production of lipoproteins by the liver, but this function is detrimental with a modern high-fat and high-cholesterol diet. We recently discovered that PCSK9 also binds to LDL particles themselves, with LDL-bound PCSK9 being less active against the LDL receptor. The project will determine how LDL binding affects the structure and function of PCSK9 and how these changes lower PCSK9's ability to bind to LDL receptors. Our aim is identify regions in the PCSK9 molecule that are necessary for its function in the blood. These protein regions would in turn represent targets for therapeutic inhibition of PCSK9-mediated LDL receptor degradation in the treatment and prevention of hypercholesterolemia.

column36: Functional Dissection of Germline Small RNA Pathways
column37: Patterns of gene expression distinguish different cell types (i.e. brain, hair, and muscle cells express different sets of genes to make them different from each other). Misregulated gene expression can lead to developmental disorders, infertility, cancer, and other diseases, thus there are many cellular safety mechanisms that regulate the process. One key mechanism for controlling gene expression involves sRNA pathways that can act in different cellular compartments and at several steps in the process of turning a gene on or off. Small RNA pathways play key gene regulatory roles in a variety of organisms, and rely on conserved Argonaute effector proteins, which utilize sRNAs to provide sequence-specific identification of target genes. Our research focuses on understanding how sRNA pathways regulate gene expression in the nuclei of cells known as germ cells (sperm and egg). The nucleus is where the process of gene expression initiates, and sRNA activities in the nucleus are currently poorly understood, especially in animals. Our studies focus on understanding the molecular mechanisms by which sRNA pathways impact chromatin (how chromosomes are packaged), using the nematode, C. elegans, as a powerful model system, and applying integrated genetic, genomic, molecular and cell biology approaches. Uncovering the molecular mechanisms of sRNA-mediated gene regulation in germ cell nuclei reveals a deeper understanding of basic cellular functions that contribute to development, differentiation, fertility and disease, and provides a more precise means to manipulate gene expression, leading to more effective sRNA-based therapeutics and laboratory techniques.

column36: Role of alternative polyadenylation in Ras-driven cancers
column37: Cancer is a disease of genes, which are blueprints for proteins that carry out the work of cells. Genes make proteins through an intermediate template called messenger RNA (mRNA). Proto-oncogenes can be thought of as gas pedals that drive cell proliferation. Mutations that convert proto-oncogenes into oncogenes push the "pedal to the metal", causing cells to over proliferate and form tumours. Oncogenes drive cell proliferation in simple organisms like worms by same mechanisms as they function in humans. Despite sequencing thousands of cancer genomes we still lack an understanding of how oncogenes drive tumour growth. Taking advantage of the powerful gene manipulation techniques of the tiny worm C. elegans we found that an oncogene called Ras cooperates with insulin signalling to promote tumour growth, which is also conserved in human tumour cells. We show that Ras requires an intact insulin pathway to sustain its oncogenic activity, and that this is achieved by dictating where messenger RNA tails are placed. These tails have sections where specific molecules can bind and put the brakes on to prevent its translation into protein. Cancer cells produce too much protein, which is required to fuel their rapid growth. We hypothesize that inhibiting insulin signalling promotes the formation mRNAs with longer tails containing sites to apply the brakes on activated oncogenes, and suppress tumour formation. To understand how this works we will combine the powerful gene manipulation technologies available in C. elegans, human cells, and mice. By exploiting these models we hope to identify new drug targets that can prevent abnormal tumour cell growth in humans.

column36: Novel targeted therapeutics against leukemia stem cells
column37: The goal of this project is to identify drugs that can target the rare cells that cause treatment failure in leukemia - leukemic stem cells (LSCs). AML is sustained in a patient by LSCs that act somewhat like normal stem cells, although cancerous, in that they are the 'root' of the disease and need to be eliminated to achieve a cure. Therapy for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) involves extremely intense toxic treatment. Even with this aggressive treatment, approximately 40% of these patients do not respond to therapy or the leukemia returns later. Therefore novel treatment approaches are desperately needed to improve outcome and reduce toxicity. We have taken data on the activity of genes in LSCs and regular leukemic cells and combined it with data sets on how drugs cause changes in gene activity to identify 152 compounds that we predict would specifically eliminate LSCs. We have directly tested 83 of these compounds and found that 12 of them do preferentially target LSCs in human leukemia. We propose to examine these 12 compounds in depth and determine how well they work against multiple leukemia samples, what exactly they do, and how safe they are. Our efforts to understand their mechanisms of action and their effectiveness in primary leukemic cells will yield novel insight into the unique functioning of LSCs. This increase in our knowledge of LSC and leukemia biology will in turn enable additional gains in prognosis, therapy and prevention.

column36: A New Entity of Cardiac Arrhythmia Associated with Loss of Cardiac Ryanodine Receptor Function
column37: In the heart, muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium from the internal calcium stores through the calcium release channel, called the ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2). It has been well established that enhanced RyR2 activity as a result of gain-of-function (GOF) RyR2 mutations can lead to irregular heart rhythm and sudden death. An increasing body of evidence indicates that suppressed RyR2 activity due to loss of function (LOF) RyR2 mutations can also cause sudden cardiac death. However, the molecular mechanism underlying sudden death caused by LOF RyR2 mutations is largely undefined. Despite their fundamental differences, unfortunately, patients with LOF RyR2 mutations are currently being diagnosed and treated the same way as those with GOF RyR2 mutations. As a result, patients with LOF RyR2 mutations are often misdiagnosed and mismanaged, which may lead to sudden death. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop effective diagnostic tests and treatments for these patients. The objective of this research proposal is to explore the mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment of heart dysfunction associated with LOF RyR2 mutations. To achieve this goal, we propose to identify and characterize LOF RyR2 mutations and their associated heart defects, to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms of their actions, and to develop novel diagnostic tests and therapeutic strategies for RyR2 LOF mutation associated diseases. These proposed studies will gain new insights into the mechanism of RyR2 LOF-associated heart dysfunction, and may lead to the development of novel diagnostic tests and treatments for this new entity of heart disease.

column36: Stem cell related genesis and maintenance of glioblastoma
column37: Brain cancers, particularly glioblastomas (GBM), are amongst the worst human cancers. The 5-year survival is <10%, effectively rendering patients with this diagnosis to a death sentence. Patients are desperate for better treatments. A major barrier to finding better treatments has been a poor understanding of the mechanisms of brain tumor initiation and growth. My research group found that GBM growth was dependent on a few cells in the tumour that have stem cell properties, these cells lie at the root of GBM growth and are also resistant to conventional therapies. We have found that human GBM stem cells depend on the Sox2 gene, which is a master gene of stem cells. These findings suggest that the Sox2+ normal stem cells in the brain may be the cells that give rise to glioblastoma, but how, when, and why they do is not known. In this proposal, we will study the role of the brain's normal Sox2 expressing cells in the genesis and growth of glioblastoma, using experimental approaches that cannot be performed with human cells, by creating tumours in the brains of mice. We will test whether normal Sox2+ neural stem cells in the mouse give rise to experimental glioblastomas and how activation or suppression of the growth activity of these cells affects the emergence of glioblastoma. We will also determine if the growth of these tumors, and their therapeutic resistance depends on subpopulations of Sox2+ cells. These studies will complement and extend knowledge derived in research of human cells by allowing us to study all stages of glioblastoma, from the earliest tumors to full-blown cancers both pre- and post-treatment. We cannot easily get access to the first steps of the disease, nor some of its worst forms, so this work in mice will fulfill areas of unmet need in the research of this cancer. We will then use these models to test preventative measures and to develop more effective therapies.

column37: Hydatidiform mole is an aberrant human pregnancy with no embryo that has fascinated scientists in all civilizations since its description by Hippocrates more than 2000 years ago. The common form of this condition affects 1 in every 600 pregnancies in western countries. Most of these moles are sporadic, not recurrent, and benign. However, up to 20% of them degenerate into malignant tumors, require single or multiple-drug chemotherapy, and may lead to the death of the patients in the absence of appropriate follow-up and treatment. Today, it is not known why some moles become malignant and not others. I, together with my team, identified a major gene, NLRP7, responsible for a rare form of recurrent moles and have made significant contribution to its current understanding. Because of the contribution of my group, patients with recurrent moles are now tested for NLRP7 and those with recessive mutations counselled that their defect lies in their oocytes and that they can have normal pregnancies and live births from ovum donation. Our most recent and important finding is that the root of this disease in patients with NLRP7 mutations stems from the placenta because it did not complete its full differentiation and that is why it keeps proliferating. This proposal aims at delineating the extent of the undifferentiated state of the placenta of recurrent moles from patients with recessive NLRP7 mutations, investigating whether the identified markers are involved in the malignant degeneration of sporadic moles, and demonstrating the roles of these markers in conferring tumorigenesis. In this application, I am seeking the CIHR support to start understanding the molecular basis of the malignant component of moles and help the most fragile patients with this condition.

column36: Synaptic, cellular and molecular mechanisms of depression susceptibility
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and existing antidepressant therapies have limited efficacy. It is well known that chronic stress can lead to depression, yet not all those who encounter stress will become depressed. Understanding what makes some people especially vulnerable to depression is essential for developing proper treatment and for possibly even preventing the disorder. Stress experienced in early life is one factor known to increase risk for depression but key questions remain unanswered. What are the enduring changes in brain function that are induced by early life stress to mediate life-long susceptibility to depression? Can neural signatures of aberrant brain function be detected before depression is observed? To answer these questions, we will employ a multi-disciplinary approach integrating advanced neuroscience techniques with robust mouse models to probe the enduring effects of early life experience on neuronal activity and the underlying changes in gene expression in a key brain circuit implicated in depression, the ventral hippocampus projection to the nucleus accumbens. We will use ex vivo measurements of neuronal connectivity, in vivo imaging of neuronal activity and post-mortem assays of genome-wide gene expression to examine how maternal separation in mice, a form of early life stress, shapes neuronal function and gene networks in the ventral-hippocampus to nucleus accumbens circuit to increase susceptibility to chronic stress in adulthood. Elucidating both the alterations in brain circuit function and the underlying gene networks that render an individual susceptible to depression will provide the knowledge necessary to develop treatments to treat and even prevent depression. This research will open the door to new interventions to regulate brain activity to mitigate susceptibility before depression emerges, reducing the enormous societal costs and improving the lives of millions of Canadians struggling with depression

column36: Lipophagy in Reverse Cholesterol Transport
column37: Atherosclerosis, a form of heart disease caused by the build-up of cholesterol deposits in the artery wall, is responsible for one in five deaths in Canada. Meanwhile, existing cholesterol-lowering drugs are only partially effective at reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. New therapies are urgently needed to combat this deadly disease. Our research team is looking for new ways to improve the removal of cholesterol from atherosclerotic plaques, stop the plaques from growing bigger, and possibly even reduce their size. We are testing whether increasing a process in cells called "autophagy"-which breaks down lipids and exports them-could achieve this. Autophagy plays a key role in recycling toxic elements from cells and promotes cell survival during periods of cell stress. Through autophagy, cellular components are delivered to organelles called lysosomes (the waste disposal system of the cell), which digest unwanted materials. Our research has already shown that autophagy can also engulf and digest cholesterol that has accumulated in the artery wall. This process helps remove cholesterol, through a process called 'reverse cholesterol transport' providing an entirely new therapeutic target to reverse atherosclerosis. Specifically, this proposal seeks to determine the role of autophagy in digesting accumulated lipid in various cell types found in atherosclerotic plaques (macrophages, vascular smooth muscle cells), and to compare the relative importance of the autophagy pathway in these cells for reverse cholesterol transport and atherosclerosis regression. By shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms of lipid autophagy, our research team hopes to identify pathway components that can be targeted and manipulated to treat heart disease. We are also looking for new targets for developing drugs that can increase cholesterol breakdown and export by cells in the artery wall.

column36: Assessing the role of adolescent hormonal contraceptive use on risk for depression
column37: Young women in Canada often use hormonal contraception (HC), and its popularity is increasing. The use of HC is highly effective in preventing teenage pregnancies and has a number of positive societal and economic consequences. However, HC was originally developed as a medication for adults, and much remains unknown about the potential side effects for teenagers of using HC. For example, because adolescence is a life stage during which major brain development is still ongoing, use of HC during this period could have effects on brain development with long-lasting consequences on young women's mental health. Our proposed research builds upon the growing evidence that relationships may exist between the synthetic hormones that are contained in HC, patterns of brain development, and mental functioning. We will conduct a three-year study of young women aged 13-18, documenting their use of HC during this period along with their stress reactivity, social competence, and depression symptoms. Thus, our study is designed to examine not only whether young women who use HC are at increased risk for developing depression, but also why such a relationship might exist, and which women may be particularly sensitive to such side effects of using HC. Women are approximately twice as likely as men to develop depression in their lives. Depression is a leading cause of years lived with disability and reduced quality of life, unemployment and lost wages, and risk for suicide. We expect that our research will advance scientific understanding about why women might be at particular risk for developing these disorders. We also hope that our research will contribute new data relevant to an important ongoing conversation in the medical community and in the public about the prescription of HC to adolescent women, ultimately promoting more informed dialogue and decision-making.

column36: Deciphering the role of DCIR in HIV-1 pathogenesis
column37: Several studies have shown that early or pre-exposure treatments help prevent HIV-1 infection and the consequent destruction of the immune system which is then able to regain some control over the infection. In link with these observations, identification of new targets for HIV-1 involved in the first stages of infection remains the best option to eradicate HIV-1 infection. Dendritic cells (DCs) are the first immune cells which recognize HIV-1 in mucosal tissue. The initial interaction between HIV-1 and DCs occurs through attachment factors and we have identified the dendritic cell immunoreceptor (DCIR) as a key receptor. The binding of HIV-1 to DCIR allows the virus to be internalized, to escape the mounting of an immune response and to be transported to the lymphoid organs, where it gains entry into CD4 expressing T cells (CD4TL) by cell-to-cell transmission from DCs. Subsequent virus replication causes severe and irreversible depletion of CD4TL, bereaving the infected person of an efficient immune response against HIV-1. We are now interested in a possible role of DCIR in the early step of infection that appear to interfere with and ultimately compromise the immune response to HIV-1. We propose to test this hypothesis in vitro and in vivo using well-characterized cell models and humanized mouse models. We hope this novel approach will constitute a springboard for the development of new innovative therapeutic strategies against HIV-1 by blocking HIV-1 binding to DCs via DCIR without affecting the specific immune responses.

column36: Roles of Alkali Cation/Proton Exchangers in Organellar Function and Neurodevelopmental Disorders
column37: The human brain has one of the highest rates of consumption of biochemical fuel (i.e., glucose) needed to sustain neuronal electrical activity. This in turn produces significant levels of metabolic ionic byproducts, such as protons (acid), bicarbonate and phosphates (bases) that must be effectively buffered, recycled for other purposes, or removed in order to maintain a suitable acid-base (pH) milieu for optimal brain function. Abnormal disturbances in brain pH balance are associated with the progression of various pathophysiological conditions, including newborn asphyxia, stroke, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and neuropsychiatric disorders - debilitating conditions that have an enormous human and economic impact on society. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that control brain pH levels are not fully understood. This project examines the roles of one major class of pH-regulating ion transport proteins called alkali cation/proton exchangers (i.e., SLC9A gene family), with a specific focus on the SLC9A6 transporter that is located in mobile membrane-bound vesicles located inside most brain cell types. Recent studies have identified mutations in SLC9A6 that cause an increasing diagnosed form of severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and autistic behaviour called Christianson Syndrome. We have isolated the SLC9A6 gene and are currently studying the effects the mutations have on neuronal function. We hypothesize that these defects impair the proper pH and functioning of vesicles that carry neurotransmitter receptors and other proteins to synapses of neurons, which in turn affects brain electrical activity and function. This assumption will be tested using a range of molecular, cellular, genetic and electrophysiological techniques in cultured cells and mouse animal models; thereby shedding new insights into the contributions of SLC9A6 to human health and disease, and identification of efficacious strategies for disease treatment.

column36: CEACAM-1 and TIM-3 interactions in HIV reservoir establishment, persistence and evasion from HIV specific immunity.
column37: No therapy can yet rid the body of HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, thus requiring life-long adherence to drugs. People on effective therapy harbour residual virus in their bodies, which can remain silent or 'latent' for many years, in areas of the body called 'reservoirs'. The main reservoir of hidden virus is within CD4 cells. It has been estimated that there are only about a million of CD4 cells in the body that contain HIV hidden from the effects of the immune cells. An immune cell called the 'cytotoxic killer T cell' can attack this reservoir. This proposal will explore new strategies to allow the immune system to 'see' the latent virus better instead of it being hidden and also improve the ability of the immune system to kill HIV infected cells better and eliminate reliance on drug therapy. Our preliminary findings suggest that two immune molecules called CEACAM-1 and TIM-3 are key to HIV's ability to hide and evade immune attacks. Our grant proposal aims to increase our understanding of the effects of these molecules on the reservoir. If successful, these studies will pave the way to new immune based therapies that can be used so that the immune system can rid the body of HIV. If successful, such treatment would benefit Canadians living with HIV as it will reduce the burden of lifelong treatments and side effects associated with them, thus improving their health and well-being.

column36: MR-Guided Management of Occlusive Peripheral Arterial Disease
column37: Occlusive peripheral arterial disease occurs when blockages in blood vessels limit the blood supply to the leg. This disease is widespread and represents a major societal burden. Approximately 20% of those over the age of 59 years suffer from this disease, which results in over 160,000 limb amputations being performed per year in the US alone. Our goal over the next 5 years is to extend the role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to increase the success rates in patients who can have this disease treated using minimally invasive percutaneous techniques using catheters and wires advanced through blood vessels. X-ray fluoroscopy, the imaging modality that is currently used to guide percutaneous procedures, has relatively poor soft tissue contrast. This makes it difficult to visualize blockages and to ensure that a revascularization device stays within the vessel during the procedure. This limits success rates and restricts minimally invasive treatment to short blockages in large arteries (which occur much less frequently than long occlusions further down the leg). Other treatment options include bypass surgery, which has substantial associated risk, and medical therapy, which has been shown to have limited effectiveness. MRI, unlike x-ray, has excellent soft-tissue contrast and with MRI it is possible to develop a detailed picture of blocked vessels and downstream tissue that can greatly aid in guiding revascularization procedures. Through a program of technical developments we plan to advance methods which will improve revascularization of blocked blood vessels. We anticipate this will facilitate less invasive treatment in a significant population that would ordinarily be subjected to more invasive surgery or to less effective treatments.

column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting more than 1% of the Canadian population. PD is marked by a progressive spread of atrophy from the midbrain to subcortical structures and eventually, to the cerebral cortex. The motor and cognitive consequences of PD are devastating, yet symptom severity is impossible to predict. Why some patients develop purely motor symptoms, while others develop affective and cognitive symptoms, remains a mystery. Recent discoveries suggest that PD may be caused by neuron to neuron spreading of an endogenous protein, alpha-synuclein, which misfolds and aggregates, causing damage and cell death. An exciting possibility is that an individual's clinical phenotype depends on which large-scale brain networks are targeted by this protein abnormality. Here we propose to integrate clinical measures, neuroimaging and genetics to predict spreading patterns of alpha-synuclein and the emergence of clinical symptoms. Key deliverables include (a) statistical methods to identify atrophy patterns and at-risk patients, and (b) computational methods to infer spreading patterns and predict future atrophy. Currently, little is known about the large-scale network mechanisms driving the spread of neurodegeneration and emergence of symptoms, so the proposed project will offer important insight into designing novel therapies to slow or divert disease progression.

column36: Regulation of stem cell proliferation in the C. elegans germ line
column37: Stem cells provide the source material for development, tissue maintenance and wound repair. They are able to provide these functions because of their unique ability to both self-renew and differentiate. Self-renewal, or the ability to make new stem cells, ensures that a stem cell population is maintained. Differentiation is the process by which these cells form the desired tissue. A balance must be maintained between self-renewal and differentiation in order for stem cells to function properly. If there is too much self-renewal, a tumour may form instead of the desired tissue. If there is too much differentiation, the stem cell population will become depleted, preventing the desired tissue from being formed in the future. We study the genetic and molecular mechanisms that control the balance between self-renewal and differentiation. As a model, we use the germ line of the small nematode worm, C. elegans. This model is one of the best-understood stem cell systems due to the vast array of investigative tools that are available. We have identified a number of genes that, when mutated, cause the balance between self-renewal and differentiation to become compromised. By studying how these genes function, we will determine the molecular mechanisms involved in regulating stem cell behaviour. Importantly, each of the genes we have identified have similar genes in humans, which are also thought to be involved in regulating stem cell proliferation; therefore, our analysis will be directly applicable to understanding human stem cell behaviour. We are also taking the next step in understanding stem cell behaviour by identifying the proteins that are enriched in stem cells. Through this exquisitely sensitive stem cell system, we will determine the proteins that provide stem cells with their unique characteristics. Understanding how specific factors regulate stem cell behaviour will bring us closer to realizing their full therapeutic potential.

column37: Anorexia Nervosa (AN) can have devastating effects upon the physical and psychological well-being of its sufferers, and has the highest mortality rate of any mental-health problem. Such realities beg for the identification of factors that cause and maintain this life-damaging disorder. AN is believed to involve the activation of certain genetic tendencies by the environment. For example, social pressures towards thinness induce people to diet intensively, and resulting nutritional factors are believed to affect gene expression. A main process involved is DNA methylation, which is influenced by one's nutritional state, and which can be measured in DNA extracted from blood. Our previous research has shown that women with AN have abnormal DNA methylation patterns, especially when they have been ill for a long time. Furthermore, we have found that treatment helps "reset" DNA methylation in some genes. To learn more about what DNA methylation levels mean for illness staging and recovery, we will study a large group of women and girls affected by AN and test whether: 1) Refeeding and weight normalization "restore" DNA methylation levels to normal. 2) Diet-induced changes in specific nutrient levels in blood underlie some of the methylation changes we see. 3) Someone's DNA methylation levels predict how well they will respond to treatment. 4) Findings differ between teenage and adult patients. We will study women and girls who currently have AN, before and after intensive treatments; women and girls who are recovered from AN for at least a year; and healthy women and girls who have never had an eating disorder. We hope that our study will promote a better understanding of the causes of AN, so as to guide improvements in preventive efforts and treatment.

column36: Deregulation of the anaphase promoting complex in human cancer
column37: The anaphase-promoting complex (APC) is an essential component of the cell that is required for cells to divide. Cancer cells particularly require activity of this complex since cells in tumours are in a constant state of cell division. Work from the lab of Dr. Teodoro has shown that some types of ovarian cancers are driven my mutations that inappropriately activate the APC. One of the goals of the proposed research is to understand how genetic mutations in the APC lead to cancers in humans. Since cancerous cells constantly require activity of the APC, targeting this complex using drugs may be an effective new manner of treating cancer. Inhibition of the APC has been shown by the Teodoro lab to selectively induce death in cancer cells while leaving normal cells unaffected. Another goal of this research project is to identify the pathways that maintain APC activity in cancer cells. It is hoped that inhibition of the APC will be an effective mechanism to arrest the growth of cancer cells that can be translated into novel chemotherapies.

column36: Testing a novel reward processing model of negative urgency in individuals with binge eating
column37: Mental illness is a significant public health concern; approximately 50% of the population will experience a mental health disorder in their lifetime. Research has led to the development of effective treatments for mental health disorders. However, psychiatric disorders commonly co-occur, and it is not always clear which disorder should be treated first. Moreover, treatments have generally been designed based on expressed symptoms rather than the bio-behavioural mechanisms that underlie symptom expression. The proposed research will focus on identifying the bio-behavioural mechanisms that explain negative urgency - the tendency to act impulsively when experiencing negative emotions. This personality trait has been linked to almost all mental health conditions (e.g., eating disorders, alcohol and substance use disorders, major depression, borderline personality disorder) and is thus a prime target for novel trans-diagnostic treatments. We will test the hypothesis that negative urgency is related to increased processing of rewards when an individual experiences negative emotions, and that emotion-enhanced reward processing explains why negative urgency relates to mental health conditions. These hypotheses will be examined in a sample of women with binge eating and eating disorders. Binge eating has a strong, specific relationship with negative urgency, and negative affect is the most common precipitant of this behavioural eating disorder symptom. If reward processing increases under negative mood conditions relate to negative urgency and binge eating, treatments for mental health conditions characterized by high negative urgency should be designed to decrease reward processing and should be administered in the context of a negative mood for maximal benefit.

column36: Identifying Therapeutic Vulnerabilities of Brain Arteriovenous Malformations
column37: Brain arteriovenous malformations (BAVMs) are a tangle of large, abnormal blood vessels within the brain. The resulting high blood flow can cause these blood vessel malformations to rupture and bleed, which may lead to severe illness or even death. BAVMs are a leading cause of bleeding in the brains of children and young adults. The main reason to treat a BAVM is to prevent a rupture. Treatment of BAVMs with surgery or radiation carries significant risk, and is both invasive as well as costly. There are currently no drugs available to treat this disorder and the cause of BAVMs is not known. We have identified spontaneous, non-inherited genetic mutations in a gene called KRAS in the majority of BAVM patients. These mutations occur in the cells that line blood vessels within BAVMs, but do not occur elsewhere in the patient. The KRAS gene codes for a protein that serves as an ON-OFF switch in blood vessel cells. When the KRAS gene is mutated, blood vessel cells are stuck in the 'ON' state and think that they are receiving cell growth and migration signals, even when they are not. In this proposal, we first aim to identify the defective genes in BAVMs that do not have mutations in KRAS, and second to understand how KRAS mutations influence the formation of BAVMs. To do this, we will introduce mutations in KRAS in blood vessel cells of mice and zebrafish; both common animal models to study blood vessel development and disease. In addition to testing whether these animals develop BAVMs, we will also use drugs to block cellular signalling pathways downstream of the 'ON' switch to determine whether we can treat BAVMs in these animal models. This may help us to discover drugs that could be used to treat this disorder in humans.

column36: Signaling and chromatin mechanisms of Paneth cell differentiation in intestinal development and disease
column37: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is one of the most common and deadly gastrointestinal diseases in human infants. With 30% mortality, it is characterized by inflammation and death of intestinal cells. Currently, how NEC initiates is unknown. As newborns become exposed to gut microbiota after birth, intestinal cells begin to differentiate into Paneth cells, a critical cell type controlling immune response. Therefore, we hypothesize that proper gut microbiota exposure is essential for intestinal cell differentiation into Paneth cells, thereby preventing NEC initiation. Indeed, our preliminary work demonstrates that gut microbiota exposure is critical for intestinal cell differentiation into Paneth cells, and its proper differentiation is critical to the prevention of NEC in early postnatal development. Interestingly, antibiotic treatment significantly reduced the number of immune cells. We will investigate further how gut microbiota promotes Paneth cell differentiation through immune cells. During cell differentiation, the chromatin structure, a massive protein complex that organizes and protects DNA, must open to make the DNA accessible to processes that will bring about major changes in gene expression. However, the chromatin mechanisms underlying Paneth cell differentiation are unknown. By analyzing chromatin and gene patterns of Paneth cells and intestinal progenitors isolated from pups treated with antibiotics, we will define the role of gut microbiota in Paneth cell-specific regulation of chromatin. By modifying chromatin, we also aim to restore Paneth cell differentiation, thereby rescuing NEC-like symptoms. Our work will provide important insight into the chromatin mechanisms of Paneth cell differentiation, identifying novel Paneth cell regulators and effective biomarkers for NEC. Additionally, this work will help advance the development of novel therapies.

column36: Contributions of the Ventral Auditory Cortical Pathway to Auditory Cognition
column37: Auditory categorization enables listeners to efficiently identify and respond to auditory stimuli. It is a computational process in which auditory stimuli are classified and grouped into sound categories based on their acoustic features, perceptual representations, or other types of information. For example, when we hear the word "fundable" from different speakers, we can categorize the sex of each speaker based on the pitch of the speaker's voice. On the other hand, to analyze the linguistic content transmitted by speech stimuli, we ignore the unique pitch, timbre etc. of each speaker's voice and categorize it into the distinct word category "fundable". Despite an important literature on the neuronal mechanisms of auditory categorization, many issues remain unknown or have yet to be fully elucidated. First, no studies have identified the sites in the brain that contain the information needed to create categorical representations. Second, and relatedly, there is not a clear understanding of distinct contributions of different brain regions to different types of auditory categorization. Finally, although our world is inherently multisensory, it is not known the degree to which the ventral auditory pathway contributes to multisensory categorization. The accomplish these goals, we combine high-density recordings within and across brain regions, rigorous and quantitative behavioral studies, and causal manipulations in rhesus monkeys to address these issues and identify the mechanisms underlying auditory categorization. These studies will provide important insights into hearing dysfunction and hearing perception. This understanding is crucial for guiding the development of more effective clinical approaches to alleviating hearing difficulties in complex acoustic environments- difficulties which are common in the elderly, the hearing impaired, and in individuals with cochlear implants or certain developmental disorders.

column36: Elucidating a new role for bile acids in protecting against C. difficile toxin pathogenesis: Implications for therapy
column37: Clostridium difficile (C.diff) is the leading cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea in the developed world. This opportunistic bacterium is a major problem in hospitals for three main reasons. The first is that C.diff is able to form highly resilient spores outside of the body that are difficult to eradicate from hospital settings. The second is that C.diff disease is triggered by antibiotics, which deplete most of the normal healthy gut bacteria, with the exception of antibiotic-resistant C.diff itself. Third, C.diff produces toxins in the gut that cause tissue damage leading diarrhea and in some cases death. Recent studies have shown that the so-called "good bacteria" in the gut (often referred to as the microbiota) also play an important role in C.diff disease. Indeed, it has been shown that a subset of bile acids produced in the gut are chemically modified by certain gut bacteria into molecules that prevent C.diff growth. We recently uncovered an entirely new role for the chemically modified bile acids - as direct inhibitors of the gut-damaging toxins. We hypothesize that in addition to modulating bacterial growth that modified bile acids play a role in preventing toxin-induced damage in healthy carriers of C.difficile. Further characterization of this new pathway will help define the specific molecules responsible for this protection and guide development of anti-toxin molecules to prevent the symptoms of disease in patients suffering a C.diff infection.

column36: Bridging Place and Social Spaces: Building Healthful Relationships Towards Indigenous Food Sovereignty in Southwestern Ontario
column37: Traditional foods harvested locally contribute to the wellbeing of Indigenous peoples. Store-bought foods tend to be processed, while foods harvested from the land are more nutritious. In Canada, research on traditional foods has mainly taken place in the north. Southern communities also experience limited food and land access. In southwestern Ontario, Indigenous communities have expressed an interest in eating more local foods. An organization in the community of Six Nations offers programming to increase food access on reserve. Urban Indigenous families and youth who frequently relocate to cities for work or school are also in need of support to reinforce these important relationships. To build on local initiatives and investigate barriers identified in this region, a participatory research project is proposed. Study objectives are to address traditional food access and knowledge barriers by profiling community examples, while exploring innovative land-based education and practices across generations. Working with a diverse set of partners on reserve, in cities, and campus, the study will be community-based and use Photovoice methodology to capture sources and stories of traditional foods in the community of Six Nations, and the nearby urban environments. Participants will take pictures where foods are harvested, hunted, or shared. Photographs will become the objects of interviews to collect stories behind the images. Distributing study results will involve Elders, parents and youth in sharing circles and the development of workshops in urban centres and out on the land. The photographs and digital stories will be displayed at local events to advocate for the continued building of relationships in support of land-based initiatives and knowledge transfer. Sharing practices, increasing food knowledge and access through increased social supports will contribute towards the health and wellbeing of individuals, Nations and Territories.

column36: Molecular and synaptic mechanisms underlying social memory and its impairments in brain disorders: role of PAK signaling
column37: Social interactions are essential to our mental health and their deficits are hallmark symptoms of many brain disorders, including autism, intellectual disability, depression and schizophrenia, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this application, we will identify the brain regions, cell types and synaptic processes governing social recognition memory and its impairments in mice. We have established a novel mouse model of brain disorders and shown that disruption of the p21-activated kinase (PAK) signaling, a key pathway linked to several neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, in the entorhinal cortical (EC) excitatory neurons leads to impairments in social recognition memory and specific deficits in synaptic strength in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. To address this hypothesis, we will examine the precise pattern of PAK expression, the specific neuronal circuit and cellular compartments, molecular substrates and their manipulations to reverse social impairments in animal models. The results of this application will reveal circuit, synaptic and molecular mechanisms responsible for social memory and will provide new strategies to mitigate social and cognitive impairments in brain disorders.

column37: Epileptic encephalopathies (EE) are pediatric epilepsies with intellectual deficiency (ID). EE are generally refractory to standard therapies, resulting in significant morbidity with major societal impacts. Identifying the mechanisms underlying EE is therefore critical to improve outcomes. METHODS: I will use a multimodal approach using gene editing in cultured cells, human stem-cell-derived neurons and mice; and electrophysiology, imaging, EEGs and behavioural assays to test the impact of novel CACNA1A mutations on Cav2.1 function and neuronal networks. Ernst) and modelling (N. D'Avanzo). Together, we are equipped to achieve our goals efficiently. column36: The risk for premature atherosclerosis in survivors of childhood cancer: A study in the Preventing Cardiac Sequelae in Pediatric Cancer Survivors (PCS2) cohort
column37: Most children newly diagnosed with cancer will survive their illness. Unfortunately, many of these survivors will develop long-term complications from their cancer treatment that can lead significant illness and even early death. Heart disease is the most common non-cancer cause of early death in these survivors. Most cardiac research in these patients has focused on heart failure which is a result of some of the common chemotherapies used to treat childhood cancer. However, there is growing evidence that many survivors of childhood cancer will develop damage to their coronary arteries that can lead to a heart attack. Little is known about who is at greatest risk for this life-threatening outcome. We will take advantage of a cohort of >1100 survivors of childhood cancer who we are following in a study of heart failure. We will recruit 250 of these survivors and 250 of their siblings to undergo an assessment of their blood vessels using several innovative imaging tools in our cardiovascular laboratory. These look at both the structure and function of their vessels. In addition, we will gather data from physical examination (blood pressure, body fat) and blood work (fats and cholesterol). This data will be combined using a novel analytical method to determine the risk and risk factors for early atherosclerosis in childhood cancer survivors. These risk factors will inform the design of a tool that can be used by clinicians that care for childhood cancer survivors (during childhood and adulthood) to determine which survivors are at greatest risk of having a heart attack. They will then be able to implement preventive measures such as lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, smoking cessation) or medical management to prevent this life-threatening consequence of cancer care.

column36: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Evaluation of NA1 Neuroprotection on Infarct Growth Following Endovascular Treatment for Acute Ischemic Stroke.
column37: Stroke occurs when there is a blockage of a brain artery which stops blood flow causing brain damage and disability. Rapid removal of the blockage with micro instruments, a procedure called endovascular therapy (EVT), has been shown to dramatically improve the functional outcome of patients with stroke. However, despite the procedure being very successful in terms of removing the blockages in the blood vessels, still 50% of patients do not recover well. There are many reasons for poor clinical outcome despite restoration of blood flow. Even in patients with small stroke, a substantial number do poorly. Animal studies suggest that under certain conditions, restoring blood flow can actually make brain damage worse. In current research, we have shown in acute stroke study treated by EVT using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) that one potential explanation is that when blood flow is restored to the stroke damage continues to grow. To address this problem, in the REPERFUSE NA1 study, we ask the question: Can we improve on stroke outcomes following endovascular treatment by reducing the growth of stroke damage that occurs following the successful restoration of blood flow with EVT? In this study using MRI we aim to show the effect of a promising a new brain protection treatment NA1 on reducing the brain damage following stroke treated by EVT. MRI will measure early infarct growth by measuring brain damage immediately after treatment and the following day, and the delayed infarct growth that occurs over 3 months. The REPERFUSE NA1 study will provide an important step to establishing whether brain protective treatment NA1 can work together with EVT to help reduce the growth of stroke related brain damage and improve stroke recovery.

column36: Levothyroxine for the Treatment of Subclinical Hypothyroidism in Pregnancy: A Population-based Assessment
column37: In Canada, there are over 450,000 pregnancies each year, including 380,00 live births and 100,000 abortions. Due to the increased demands during pregnancy, hypothyroidism or low thyroid hormone levels, are the most common endocrine disorder. Subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH) occurs in 2% of pregnancies as a result of high levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone levels but thyroid hormone thyroxine levels are normal and symptoms of hypothyroidism (such as fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, or depression) are either mild or absent. Levothyroxine is used to treat overt hypothyroidism based on previous studies supporting a higher risk of pregnancy complications (both for the mother and baby) in these women. However, the benefit of levothyroxine for SCH in pregnant women is less clear. Despite a lack of firm evidence, current recommendations suggest that women start treatment with levothyroxine at the time of SCH diagnosis. Thus, there is a need to determine the effectiveness and safety of levothyroxine in pregnant women with SCH. Our study will use a database from the United Kingdom called the Clinical Practice Research Datalink to answer this question. This database has the electronic medical records for over 14 million patients and includes a detailed pregnancy register. We will compare the chances of having a pregnancy complication between patients who use levothyroxine and those who do not use levothyroxine. The main outcomes that we will study include maternal and fetal complications, such as diabetes and hypertension during pregnancy, blood loss during delivery, maternal death, preterm birth, small birth weight, and fetal death. If we find that levothyroxine reduces the risk of pregnancy complications, our study will provide reassurance regarding the effectiveness of this drug in pregnancy. Given the increasing rates of SCH in pregnancy, this study will have important policy, clinical, and public health implications.

column36: The Effect of Exercise on Hypertension in Chronic Kidney Disease: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: High blood pressure (BP) is twice as common in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) as it is in those without kidney disease. High BP increases the risk of heart disease and is also one of the main reasons that kidney function worsens, increasing the risk of kidney failure. Medications can treat BP but are often ineffective, have side effects, and are costly. Regular exercise can lower BP but because of differences in the causes of high BP in people with CKD, it is unclear if exercise would work in this population. Consequently, exercise is not included in the routine care of people with CKD and sedentary behaviour is common. The role of exercise in CKD management is important to patients: a better understanding of the role of lifestyle interventions, such as exercise, in managing CKD is a top research priority. Therefore, the aim of this study is to test whether regular exercise can improve BP in people with moderate to severe CKD. We will measure other important outcomes, such as quality of life. We will also use this study to help design a larger study on whether exercise can slow the loss of kidney function. In this trial, we will assign 160 people with moderate to severe CKD to receive structured exercise along with their usual care or usual care alone (no exercise resources). The exercise program is 24-weeks long and includes supervised, hospital-based sessions and home exercises led by an exercise specialist. Our findings will be used to show that exercise can improve the care we deliver and will provide the basis for further studies looking at whether exercise can slow the worsening of kidney disease.

column36: Mitophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in aging muscle
column37: Mitochondria are the organelles responsible for energy (ATP) production in most cell types. This research is important for our understanding of how exercise can improve musculoskeletal health during the aging process, with important consequences for the well-being of Canadians.

T4P are thus potential targets for new antimicrobial therapies such as vaccines. Each filament is made of thousands of small lollipop-shaped proteins called pilins. The "stick" of the lollipop is very conserved and has a number of important functions. It stores pilins in the cytoplasmic membrane; forms the inner core of the pilus; and acts as a recognition domain for sensor proteins that monitor pilin inventories, so more are made only if needed. We will investigate how these monitoring systems recognize pilins, so we can fool them into shutting down even if there aren't enough pilins available. In contrast, the "lollipop" part of a pilin is diverse, making it harder to design a vaccine that will cover all possible "flavours". We are trying to understand the causes and consequences of pilin diversity, to inform the design of new treatments. We study Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), a pathogen designated by the World Health Organization as a critical priority for new therapies due to its high level of resistance to antibiotics. We searched thousands of Pa DNA sequences to find all of its pilin flavours, and constructed a panel of different pilins in a common genetic background. This unique and expandable resource will allow us to ask how the immune system "sees" different pilins - when is recognition lost? We think that diversity arises from attempts to escape from viruses that stick to the pili. Changing a pilin's sequence or hiding it with sugars blocks attachment. Remarkably, some viruses can bind to very different pilins, suggesting they see a non-obvious common feature. We will characterize how those viruses interact with diverse pilins. They are of interest as therapeutics, as they can kill multidrug resistant bacteria. Together, this work will give us an unprecedented understanding of how pilus diversity is shaped.

column37: Patients with severe cornea pathologies have a poor prognosis for recovery after cornea transplantation. Adding to this is the surgery-related risk of infection and inflammation that increases puts the patient at a high risk for graft rejection. Due to a severe worldwide shortage of donor corneas, many high risk patients are not being treated. We developed biosynthetic corneal implants based on collagen and have successfully tested these in patients, inducing the patients' own corneal progenitor cells to "regrow" corneal tissues and nerves from within. Recently we developed a newer version that is easier to handle and scaleup. However, issues or infection and inflammation still need to be solved, which is the aim of this project. We previously tested nanosilver as an alternative to antibiotics to avoid bacterial resistance and confirmed that nanosilver has anti-bacterial and anti-inflammatory properties. We also tested LL37, peptide that is part of the body's innate defence against bacteria and viruses. Here, we will engineer mesenchymal stroma (or stem) cells to produce their own LL37 and incorporate these into our implants. An alternative is using natural hyaluronan-derived nanoparticles to deliver exogenous LL37. The release of LL37 coupled with a coating of nanosilver will be tested. Their safety and efficacy will be thoroughly examined in vitro using cell and organ culture techniques. Afterwards, these combination implants will be tested in animal models for safety and efficacy. Our results offer tangible hope for high-risk patients with poor prognoses with donor corneal transplantation. These developments open the door to new solutions to the problems of corneal tissue shortage and corneal blindness worldwide.

column36: How best to engage patients in hospital service planning and improvement

column36: Modelling campylobacteriosis risk in Canada through the various environmental and foodborne sources of exposure in a climate change perspective.
column37: Campylobacteriosis is an infection of the gut caused by the Campylobacter bacteria. It is characterized by abdominal cramps, pain, fever, and watery, sometimes bloody, diarrhea. Some of them will develop severe lifelong sequelae. In addition, this infectious disease generates high costs to the food industry through quality controls and to society through medical costs and productivity losses. Campylobacteriosis is seasonal; it occurs predominantly in summer for unclear reasons. Environmental factors, agricultural activities and human behaviours are likely contributors to the seasonal increase of campylobacteriosis.
