column36: Understanding contextual factors to effectively and equitably scale up GetCheckedOnline to diverse populations and geographic settings
column37: Digital health services are thought to be cost-effective and improve access particularly in rural areas, despite limited evidence and challenges to their implementation. We need to examine the "rhetoric and reality" of these services, and understand what external factors influence their success or failure. GetCheckedOnline (GCO) is an effective program developed by the BC Centre for Disease Control to reduce barriers in accessing testing for sexually transmitted infections and blood borne infections (STBBI). Research from the Vancouver pilot phase of GCO has found the service to be acceptable and effective in reaching people with barriers to accessing testing. Our initial analysis of GCO's scale-up to other urban, suburban and rural communities in two regional health authorities (RHA) in BC has found differences from Vancouver and between expansion sites (e.g., in the proportions of first-time testers). Further scale-up in BC is planned to other RHA, and eventually to other parts of Canada. However, further adaptation of GCO may be needed to reach other populations facing barriers to STBBI testing. Our team's overall goal is produce research which leads to the best implementation and maximum effectiveness of GCO for multiple populations affected by STBBI, and that informs further scale-up in BC and potentially in other parts of Canada. We do this in order to reduce barriers to accessing testing, leading to earlier diagnosis and linkage to care for STBBI in Canada. Our research approach uses an implementation science framework to: (1) understand what works, for whom, during scale-up; (2) adapt the intervention for better impact in minority language communities, men sex workers, and people who inject drugs; (3) assess the feasibility of implementation in a different health care system (Toronto); and (4) describe external factors influencing GCO implementation and whether access is improved equitably across populations who use it.

column37: Canada is experiencing a public health emergency related to medical (prescription) opioids and, in some regions, illicitly produced opioids (e.g., fentanyl, heroin). Services are being expanded in many jurisdictions, but progress is slow and only patchworks of public health interventions and treatment services are currently in place across the country. Without scaling up evidence-based programs in different regions and among different populations, the individual and population burden of opioid use will continue to be high. This proposal was written in response to CIHR's Request for Applications to the Canadian Research Initiative on Substance Misuse (CRISM) network for a directed grant addressing the opioid emergency (https://tinyurl.com/y9sgx64x). CRISM is a unique CIHR funded national research network of researchers, system managers, people with lived experience, and decision-makers. Its purpose is to conduct research and support knowledge translation to enhance delivery of evidence-based interventions for substance misuse.CRISM will develop and execute a program in four thematic areas that have high potential for reducing the individual and population burden of opioid use: (1) scaling up public health interventions (i.e., safer consumption services and naloxone delivery); (2) optimizing opioid use disorder treatments (i.e., oral and injectable opioid pharmacotherapy); (3) improving the evidence base for withdrawal management, psychosocial and recovery-based treatment options; and (4) collaboratively developing new intervention approaches to meet the needs of high-risk target populations. The proposed implementation science program will be developed purposively, capitalizing on service innovations that are rapidly being deployed at the regional level; strategically, by developing effective longer-term working relationships with groups disproportionately affected by the opioid emergency; and collaboratively, through a structured process to engage CRISM member expertise and people with lived experience of opioid problems. The overall aim is to inform and support the implementation of an improved national intervention continuum to address this complex health challenge.

column36: Endoplasmic Reticulum Proteostasis to rescue Alpha1 AntiTrypsin Deficiency (acronym ERAAT) This is a proposal to the -Rare Joint Transnational Call for Proposals 2017 "Transnational Research Projects for Innovative Therapeutic Approaches for Rare Diseases"
column37: Alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency (ATD) is a rare disease caused by mutations in the alpha1-antitrypsin (A1AT) genes leading to improperly folded protein products unable to be secreted, and that in some instances aggregate in hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The normal function of A1AT is to be transported to the lung where it acts as an inhibitor of neutrophil elastase. Z mutant alpha1-antitrypsin (ZA1AT) is retained in the ER by cellular quality control mechanisms and aggregates in this compartment. The consequences are severe health issues such as a loss-of-function defect in the lungs leading to lung emphysemas and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) due the lack of circulating active A1AT. In the liver, the accumulation of ZA1AT through loop-sheet polymerization of soluble monomers leads to a proteotoxic gain-of-function, subsequently linked to deficient export from the ER. This aggregation can cause liver fibrosis and cirrhosis and subsequently hepatic failure. The current therapeutic option for ZA1AT is transplantation. To date, there exists no other effective pharmacological treatment alternative for ATD. Research from the Chevet laboratory showed that selected activation of the IRE1 arm of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) improved the secretion of functionally active ZA1AT. This provides the proof of principle supporting the hypothesis that increasing ER proteostasis is a novel strategy to decrease proteotoxicity in the liver and to neutralize proteolytic activity in the lung in ATD.

column36: Allele-specific lowering of mutant polyQ proteins as treatment for Huntington disease, spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 and spinocerebellar ataxia type 7
column37: Polyglutamine (polyQ) diseases are a group of monogenic, autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorders caused by a polyQ encoding CAG triplet repeat expansion in the disease causing gene with pathogenic consequences. The most prevalent polyQ disorders are Huntington disease (HD) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), while spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7) shows some unique features for development of therapeutics. All three diseases begin in young adults, cause severe disability and lead to premature death. Currently, there is a complete lack of disease modifying treatment for any of these disorders. Targeting specific mechanisms that are thought to be relevant to human disease pathogenesis is very challenging as the disease genes are often pleiotropic and there is only scant data from human studies to prioritize biological mechanisms. Our project bridges these challenges by specifically targeting the causative mutant gene or its transcript and testing for efficacy of three promising gene-suppressive strategies: ASO, RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9, in multiple unique and suitable model systems. Specifically, we will 1) use population genetics to identify targets of greatest therapeutic potential to design novel gene silencing molecules for these targets, 2) evaluate the efficacy of novel, optimized ASOs, RNAis and sgRNAs in in vitro and in vivo models, 3) develop potential biomarkers of brain target protein levels and 4) apply novel MRI / NMR methods as potential imaging biomarkers for disease progression and evaluating therapeutic efficacy.

column37: More than 25% of Canadians over the age of 15 care for family members or friends. Caregiving has a significant impact on their physical and mental health, with males and females reacting differently. Digital technologies such as mobile applications and home monitoring systems have been developed to assist with caregiving activities. However, sex and gender considerations are largely ignored in the design and evaluation of these technologies. To address this, our research program will develop a sex- and gender- based technology evaluation framework (SAGS-TA). We will develop SAGS-TA through several activities. First, we will review existing knowledge and literature about technology and caregiving to identify the major sex and gender gaps. We will then work with informal caregivers, technology developers and policymakers to develop a prototype framework for addressing sex and gender in technology development. We will do this by presenting findings from the first step and inviting people to share how these relate to their personal experiences of caregiving. We will analyse their responses to generate sex and gender evaluation themes for each stage of the technology creation, testing and implementation process. We will then gather feedback on the sex and gender themes in a second discussion session to complete the SAGS-TA framework. Finally, we will apply the SAGS-TA framework to a current technology development project to test its effectiveness. This pioneering project is pivotal for realizing sex and gender customized technologies to support informal caregivers and advance research and policy-making.

column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is the most common form of heart valve diseases, affecting almost 3% of the population older than 65. Our team has identified a particle carried in the blood called lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) as one of the strongest risk factor for CAVS. Our second objective is to investigate the role of the proteome of Lp(a) (other proteins that are carried by Lp[a]) in key steps of valvular calcification. Our team has been working in collaboration with Ionis pharmaceuticals, a pharmaceutical company that is currently developing a compound that has recently been shown to lower Lp[a] levels by 80%) to identify patients with high Lp(a) levels and CAVS. Our objective is to take advantage of this partnership with the industry and the Lipoprotein(a) Foundation to further expand this unique cohort to families of affected individuals and to gain new valuable knowledge into the biological mechanisms that link high Lp(a) with CAVS.

column36: Sticky money: Exploring the acceptability of a sugar-sweetened beverage tax among Canadian Indigenous populations
column37: Evidence suggests that pop contributes a lot of sugar to the Canadian diet, which is linked to increasing levels of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Consequently, an increasing number of jurisdictions globally are adopting a pop tax to curb intake, as recommended by the World Health Organization. Canada has not yet adopted the tax, but its merit is being widely debated. In Canada, the burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes is greater among lower socioeconomic groups and Indigenous populations while pop intake is higher within these same groups. These realities underscore the need to understand the perceived impact of a pop tax on intake among low socioeconomic groups and Indigenous populations to improve population health outcomes. However, previous experience with tobacco taxes have demonstrated that taxes are not effective policy levers in reducing smoking rates among low socioeconomic groups, thus suggesting that a similar tax on pop may also be ineffective. Tobacco taxes were also not implemented in most First Nations communities. In this research, we have four objectives: 1) to describe how pop intake has changed in Canada from 2004 to 2015 among Indigenous, low income, rural/urban, and food insecure people; 2) to examine how middle-class Canadians living in Winnipeg perceive a pop tax; 3) to examine how First Nation people living in the Island Lake First Nations (on-reserve) perceive a pop tax, should one ever be implemented; and 4) to examine how Indigenous people living in Winnipeg (off-reserve) perceive a pop tax. What we learn by doing this research will help us understand the pros and cons of implementing a pop tax in Canada. This research will also inform recommendations concerning effective strategies for public health messaging that might accompany such a tax and suggestions for use of tax revenue that are acceptable to populations who may be most burdened by a proposed pop tax.

column36: The SURV1VE-Trial - Sustained inflation and chest compression versus 3:1 chest compression to ventilation ratio during cardiopulmonary resuscitation of asphyxiated newborns - a randomized controlled cluster trial
column37: When newborn babies are born without a heartbeat the clinical team must provide breathing and chest compressions (what we call cardiopulmonary resuscitation) to the newborn baby. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation only happens in about 1% of deliveries. Despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation approximately one million newborn babies die at birth every year and newborn babies surviving cardiopulmonary resuscitation at birth have high rates of death and neurological impairment. The poor prognosis raises questions as to whether we can improve cardiopulmonary resuscitation methods and specifically adapt them to newborn babies to improve outcomes. Currently we use a 3:1 ratio, which equals 3 chest compressions to one rescue breath to resuscitate a newborn baby. This means that we stop chest compressions after every 3rd compression to give one rescue breath. We believe that this interruption of chest compressions is bad for the newborn baby and that chest compressions should be continued without interruption while rescue breaths are given continuously. We believe that this approach will allow us to reduce death and long-term burdens in newborn babies born without a heartbeat. The submitted proposal is a multi-center clinical trial, which will be performed at several sites across Canada and the rest of the world. In the delivery room of participating centers infants will be randomized to two different chest compression techniques to assess which technique improves their care. Our approach represents a unique way of delivering chest compression and rescue breaths for newborn infants. We hope that our approach will reduce death and long-term burdens in newborn babies born without a heartbeat. If validated, this will represent an important and novel approach for neonatal resuscitation, which can be adopted by clinicians in delivery rooms around the world. In summary, the results of this study could benefit many babies each year.

column36: Sleep controls hematopoiesis and regulates atherosclerosis: a novel neuro-immune axis
column37: Humans spend one third of their life asleep. Despite its importance, we know surprisingly little about why we sleep and what impact it has on disease. Today, largely due to advances in electronic devices and instant communication systems, busy modern lifestyles promote work and social demands at the expense of rest and sleep. In this proposal we will study how sleep impacts the immune system and the risk of developing cardiovascular disease (CVD). Recent clinical studies have demonstrated that people with poor or insufficient sleep have a higher risk of CVD compared to those with a healthy sleep pattern. The reasons for this correlation have not been studied. We have established two innovative mouse models of sleep disruption. Our preliminary data suggest that sleep disruption activates the stem cells in the bone marrow that give rise to white blood cells. This results in an increase in the number of white blood cells in the sleep disturbed mice and an overall increase in inflammation. These white blood cells enter the walls of arteries which gives rise to fatty plaques, CVD and eventually heart attacks. We will study how sleep alters the biology of stem cells and white blood cells in detail. Using innovative mouse models and sophisticated genetic techniques we will track stem cell activation, function and movement. In addition, we will study how stem cells and white blood cells from sleep disturbed mice alter CVD progression and healing of the heart after a heart attack. This work will be conducted in collaboration with a team of renowned scientists and doctors at the Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Our work will not only identify novel biological functions and new targets for CVD therapeutics but will also influence public policy. Governments and organizations can use our data as evidence to promote a healthy lifestyle that includes sufficient sleep.

column36: Patellofemoral osteoarthritis: evaluating risk factors and mechanisms of structural features with or without pain
column37: In Canada, knee osteoarthritis (OA) affects over 4.4 million individuals, and costs upwards of $27.5 billion each year. Literature suggests that knee OA most commonly begins behind the knee cap, or patellofemoral (PF) joint. PF OA is highly prevalent and is associated with knee pain and disability. It thus represents an important and potentially impactful target for knee OA research. Current understanding of PF OA pathology, aetiology, and risk factors remains poorly understood. Moreover, a discordance between structural features and pain exists that continues to perplex researchers and clinicians. There is thus an urgent need for research aimed at better understanding risk factors for PF OA, as well as mechanisms and features of symptomatic PF OA that can inform and guide novel treatment approaches. Emerging evidence suggests a personalized-medicine approach (subgrouping knee OA based on these factors) may enable more tailored, and thus effective, treatments. The aim of this fellowship is to: (i) identify risk factors for PF OA, in particular those that can be modified with treatment; (iia) create individualized biomechanical models to evaluate mechanical faults that may contribute to knee OA and pain; and (iib) explore other non-mechanical features (e.g. inflammatory, psychosocial) that may explain why some individuals with knee OA experience pain and others do not. Additional aims are to: (iii) review the evidence to identify best treatments currently available, and identify gaps in the literature regarding treatments; and (iv) develop and validate simple tests for measuring key mechanical faults in a clinical setting. Combined, the results of this fellowship will provide a knowledge foundation to improve the design and methodology of future clinical trials aimed at treating knee OA.

column36: The Endocannabinoid System in Glucocorticoid-Induced Metabolic Outcomes: A Focus on Genetic Variants of Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase
column37: Chronic stress, with the coordinated rise in stress hormones known as glucocorticoids (GCs, cortisol in humans), is a major risk factor for obesity. Evidence suggests that GC actions underlie the effects of chronic stress on energy balance. Yet the relationship between stress, GCs, and energy balance is highly complex. For example when confronted with stress, some individuals gain weight, whereas others lose weight. It is believed that an individual's response to stress and GCs is moderated by genetic variants. Nevertheless, genetic risk factors at the interface between energy balance and stress regulation remain elusive. In humans, there is a common genetic variant in the gene for fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), present in ~38% of Europeans. This genetic variant (C385A) reduces levels of FAAH. This reduction in FAAH ultimately affects the endocannabinoid system since FAAH breaks down the endocannabinoid ligand anandamide. Indeed anandamide regulates energy balance and the stress response. Importantly, the low-expressing FAAH variant (A-allele carriers) has been associated with improved stress coping and increased rates of obesity in humans. Thus, the FAAH variant is positioned to moderate stress-induced metabolic outcomes. The proposed project will be the first to examine whether genetic variants of FAAH predict individual susceptibility to obesity in response to chronic GC exposure. We will employ a mouse model, which recapitulates the common human mutation in the FAAH gene (C385A), to investigate the effects of differential FAAH expression (between C- and A-allele carriers) on feeding and energy expenditure. This project has the potential to establish a molecular link between energy balance and stress, and help to explain why diverging metabolic outcomes arise when confronted with stress. Together, the outcomes of these studies may have implications for obesity prevention, via lifestyle modification (stress reduction) in genetically susceptible individuals.

column36: Comparing how fee-for-service and salary-based specialist physician payment affects patient selection, visit frequency, delivery of recommended services, and health care costs of Albertans with chronic disease
column37: Chronic diseases, like diabetes, heart disease and kidney disease, account for two-thirds of health care expenditures in Canada. How to manage the growing economic burden of chronic disease care is a pressing question for health systems and provincial and federal policymakers. How specialists are paid may affect their behaviour and, in turn, the treatments that patients receive, as well as health care quality and costs. Since 2004 many specialists in Alberta have been paid a salary, rather than fee-for-service (FFS). Yet, FFS remains the dominant model in Alberta and nationally. FFS encourages higher volume of services and may discourage care coordination. Thus, FFS may not be ideal for chronic diseases where multidisciplinary, team-based care has a central role. The objective of this research program is to assess the effect of salary-based specialist physician payment compared to FFS on selection, visit frequency, delivery of recommended services, and health care costs of patients with chronic diseases. We anticipate patients with salaried specialists will have a lower frequency of visits, higher quality care, and lower costs. We will use a Chronic Disease Data Repository, including lab, pharmacy and physician claims and inpatient, emergency department and outpatient visits for all Albertans. We will examine two samples: 1) adults with diabetes and early kidney disease (since preventive management is similar) newly referred to specialists and 2) adults with advanced kidney disease initiating dialysis. We will also conduct interviews with specialists to assess their perspectives on payment models, which may engage them in development of future payment reforms. There are limited rigorous studies comparing FFS and salary-based payment models and no formal studies of Alberta's salary-based model. This study offers an opportunity to evaluate the merits of salary-based payment models and contribute to future physician payment policy--an Alberta Health priority.

column36: Leptin revisited: role of melanocortin neurons in glucose and leptin regulation
column37: Obesity and type 2 diabetes have now reached epidemic proportions worldwide. This situation is alarming considering that these pathologies are intimately linked to the development of important health issues including insulin resistance, cardiovascular diseases and cancers. Improvements in our understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating energy balance (food intake and energy expenditure) and glucose homeostasis are needed for the development of new tools to treat obesity and related diseases. The brain, specifically a region called the hypothalamus, regulates food intake and other aspects of metabolism. Complex neuronal circuits within the hypothalamus respond to metabolic signals secreted in the body, such as leptin (a hormone produced by adipose, or fat, tissue) and insulin (a hormone produced by the pancreas), to regulate body weight and glucose levels. Despite the tremendous number of studies investigating the mechanisms of leptin action and regulation in the past decades, these mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we developed novel transgenic tools to tease apart the specific neurons responsible for responding to metabolic cues and determine how these signaling pathways affect metabolism. The specific goal of this project is to elucidate the neural, molecular and transcriptional mechanisms of leptin action and production. This research project is aimed at 1) dissociating the effects of leptin on energy balance versus glucose homeostasis, and 2) discovering the pathways that regulate leptin synthesis. These findings could have important therapeutic implications for people with obesity and diabetes.

column36: Prenatal stress investigation at the single-cell level: a multi-omics study in the cerebral organoid model
column37: Mental illnesses like anxiety and depression affect more than 20% of the Canadian population, and lead to an economic burden at the population level of an estimated $51 billion per year. A common risk factor for these conditions is adversity or abuse during early life. Interestingly, even during prenatal development, exposure to stress or adversity in the mother can be transferred to the fetus brain, and subsequently can permanently affect how the stress hormone system is regulated. Given the prevalence of mental illnesses and the role of stress in causing them, it is imperative to learn more about the biological mechanisms involved and the system components where intervention is possible. Some progress has been made in elucidating the neurobiology of stress, but many questions cannot be addressed with current tools, which include animal models and 2-dimensional human cell culture systems. This proposal aims to establish 3-dimensional culture systems called cerebral organoids or "mini-brains" - stem-cell derived tissues that mimic the human brain - as research models for developmental psychiatric disturbances. Stress will be simulated in these cerebral organoids by manipulating the main hormone associated to stress, cortisol. Molecular mechanisms will be investigated comparing 'stressed' and 'unstressed' conditions in cerebral organoids by studying specialized cells types. This is important, because the human brain is very complex, and very different processes occur from cell to adjacent cell (i.e. neurons, etc.). Comparing findings from this model to evidence from brains of individuals who experienced severe adversity during early childhood and subsequently suffered from depression in adulthood, will allow placement of our findings into the clinical context. The outcomes from this research have the potential to expedite identification of at-risk populations, and even guide development of intervention strategies.

column36: Role of brain injury in the induction of Alzheimer's disease in a humanized mouse model
column37: Animal models expressing high brain levels of mutated human amyloid-beta (AB) and/or tau proteins, the two main hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease, have provided substantial insight into the understanding of the disease process. However, all clinical trials of candidate drugs developed using current models have been unsuccessful to date. These experimental models may be unpredictive due to the excessive expression of AB and tau, which artificially enhances the formation of protein aggregates to cause early memory dysfunction, and because of the absence of environmental factors accelerating risk. Therefore, new models with endogenous expression of the proteins which yield slowly developing and weaker manifestations of the disease may have greater validity. I propose that a more reliable model of Alzheimer's disease can be created by subjecting mice expressing normal levels of mutated human AB and human tau (humanized mice), to environmental risk factors commonly associated with dementia such as traumatic head injury. To demonstrate this, I will characterize the humanized mice with respect to Alzheimer's disease manifestations. The animals will then be subjected to mild and repeated traumatic head injury (chronic concussion) and monitored for the appearance of protein aggregates, neuronal dysfunction, and memory disorders. Finally, to study the molecular mechanisms by which chronic concussion might promote Alzheimer's disease, I will investigate the role of mGluR5 and Fyn, two key regulators of neuronal activity. The interest of this proposal is twofold: first, it will help us to design an innovative experimental tool with which one can probe deeper into Alzheimer's disease pathology; second, it will allow a better grasp of the role chronic head injury might play in the development of dementia.

column36: Dairy product plasma metabolites and cardiovascular disease
column37: Dietary intervention has been established as one of the most important strategies for cardiovascular disease prevention. Dietary guidelines around world advocate the consumption of dairy products as part of a healthy diet. Indeed, there is a substantial body of evidence reporting that milk consumption is inversely associated with the risk of hypertension, that cheese consumption is inversely associated with the risk of stroke, and that yogurt consumption is associated with a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes. However, biological mechanisms underlying the health effects of dairy products remain unknown. The objective of this research project is to identify mechanisms through which the consumption of different types of dairy products influences cardiovascular disease risk. This study will build on recent advances in nutritional biochemistry that allow to measure a broad spectrum of small molecules in the blood reflecting different biological mechanisms. In the study, metabolite profiling will be conducted among 7,000 subjects from the Nurses' Health Study and the Health Professional Follow-up Study who have been followed for more than 30 years. The association between dairy products consumption and blood concentrations of metabolites will be evaluated to identify the metabolic signature of dairy products as well as the cardioprotective mechanisms induced by the consumption of these foods. This study will represent the most comprehensive assessment of the metabolic pathways responsible of the cardioprotective effects of dairy products. The study will provide strong evidence to support public health recommendations and the place of dairy products in dietary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Finally, this study represents one of the most extensive application of systems epidemiology in nutrition where traditional epidemiologic methods are coupled with modern technologies in order to identify biological mechanisms underlying the health effects of diet.

column36: Modulating bacterial cell metabolism to enhance the efficacy of antibiotics
column37: Antibiotics kill bacteria by poisoning their cellular machines, which perform essential functions like copying DNA, making proteins, or building a cell envelope. Bacteria can survive antibiotic treatment by (a) mutating the drug target so that the antibiotic cannot stick to it, (b) degrading the antibiotic so that it is not active, or (c) pumping the drug out of the cell. However, less well appreciated are the cases where bacteria survive antibiotic treatment by simply going to sleep and turning off their machinery. These cells, called bacterial persisters, become inactive until the antibiotic goes away, and then they start growing again - it's an ingenious trick to avoid being killed when bacteria do not have antibiotic resistance genes. Worryingly, we have recently come to find that bacteria often become persisters on the road to full-blown antibiotic resistance, highlighting the importance of figuring out how to kill these sleeping cells before it's too late. But how do you kill bacteria that aren't doing anything? You wake them up! Here, I propose to use state-of-the-art technologies to develop ways to jump-start bacterial cell metabolism to sensitize bacteria to antibiotics. To do this, I am first going to understand precisely what components of cell metabolism are required to fully activate different antibiotic targets. Once this is complete, I am going to take both growing bacteria and persisters, and treat them with antibiotics in combination with the necessary metabolites (cellular food) to maximally activate specific parts of the cell, such that the antibiotic can efficiently kill bacteria regardless of their sleepiness. Through this research, I aim to increase the utility of our most precious antibiotics to treat infections, as well as take advantage of the diverse metabolism of different bacteria to make species-specific antibiotic therapies capable of killing bad bacteria while keeping our good bacteria happy.

column36: Are neurobiological features defining subtypes of brain dysfunction in major depressive disorder trait or state? Characterizing the determinants of familial risk and treatment remission in neurobiologically-derived subtypes of major depressive disorder.
column37: 13-16% of Canadians will develop an episode of major depressive disorder (MDD), and conventional treatments have low recovery rates. One of the most significant barriers to improving these rates is that we lack a robust understanding of the differences between MDD patients. MDD presents differently patients, and some treatments work for some patients but not for others. In the spirit of understanding the biological differences between MDD patients, we developed a novel method to define MDD subtypes. We showed in a large multisite sample that MDD patients can be subdivided into four subtypes defined by unique patterns of brain circuitry ("biotypes"). These biotypes predicted responsiveness in subjects who received non-invasive brain stimulation. What we do not know, however, is whether subtype specific features of brain dysfunction predate MDD onset, nor do we know which biological features improve when MDD treatments work, and do not. Identifying such features will potentially help treat MDD two ways: first, by identifying factors that can be targeted to prevent a MDD episode; and second, by identifying residual features of brain dysfunction after treatment that can be targeted to maximize clinical efficacy. The first aim of this proposal is to identify features of brain dysfunction in healthy individuals with a high familial risk for MDD, and to use these features to prospectively predict MDD onset at 5 and 10-years follow-up. A second aim of this proposal is to identify predictors, changes and constancies in brain dysfunction that accompany treatment response to a widely used first-line antidepressant, and to relate residual brain dysfunction to persistent clinical symptoms after treatment. I will leverage two large, pre-existing, multisite datasets with repeated measures rich with clinical, neuroimaging and psychological information to address these aims.

column36: Developing an entirely new anti-vascular therapy approach to treat metastatic cancer by targeting vessel co-option
column37: One in two Canadians will develop cancer in their lifetime and one in four will die, mostly due to tumours spreading to other sites of the body (metastasis). Cancer therapies that inhibit the growth of new blood vessels into tumours have known, but limited effectiveness when treating patients with metastasis. This is partly due to tumour cells bypassing the need of creating their own blood supply and instead hijacking the existing blood vessels in organs with a rich vasculature such as the lung - one of the most common sites of metastatic disease in cancer patients. This process is called "vessel co-option" and in the lung leads to the striking phenomenon of tumour cells filling up the air spaces to exploit the organ's existing blood supply. We propose strategies to target such co-opted vessels in lung metastases. There is a high probability that since co-opted vessels are exposed to many changes brought about by the tumour, they express proteins that are not normally found on healthy blood vessels, and which may be therapeutically targetable. We have developed a mouse model of breast cancer metastasis that mimics cancer observed in human patients. In this model vessel co-option happens exclusively when metastasis occurs in the lung. To determine differences in co-opted versus normal vessels, cells of the co-opted blood vessels will be isolated from lung metastases and undergo gene expression analysis in comparison to vessels from normal healthy lungs. Drugs will be generated that target these differences on hijacked vessels with the goal of destroying them. There are also a number of carefully selected existing drugs and experimental therapies which may have the property of targeting vessel co-option, and these will be evaluated. Such vessel co-option targeting therapies could be used in combination with drugs that stop the growth of new blood vessels to block two major ways a tumour gains a blood supply, in turn starving the tumour and arresting its growth.

column37: Severe asthma accounts for a large majority of hospital visits and admissions in Canada and this has enormous costs for the asthma patient, their caregivers and employers and the health care system. Unfortunately, for many patients with asthma, current therapies do not improve their symptoms or their risk of disease worsening, necessitating hospital visits, lost work/school days and poor quality of life. New treatment options are emerging for asthmatics who have a high disease burden. However, currently there is no way to predict those patients who will respond favorably to the different therapies now available and under development. My recent research has shown that our understanding of asthma can be dramatically improved by harnessing the power of medical imaging and computer programs. To decrease the staggering burden on patients and the health care system, we want to develop new imaging measurements of asthma that can be used to improve patient outcomes. Therefore, for the first time, I am developing and evaluating the clinical utility of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based measurements of asthma. We think that MRI can be used to "personalize" treatment selection in individual asthmatics resulting in the correct treatment course, for the right patient and at the right time. Ultimately leading to better patient outcomes. My research will develop, clinically validate and integrate pulmonary MRI into asthma patient care. Our advances are very likely to impact asthma management and how new treatments will be developed, delivered and evaluated. Based on the enormous burden on the health care system, the vastly diminished quality of life, and increased morbidity of patients with asthma, the MRI measurements we develop will have high clinical and economic impact in Canada.

column36: Investigating the structural, biophysical and biochemical properties of large-scale protein association and liquid-liquid phase separation in neurological disorders.
column37: Brain function is poorly understood and there are no effective drugs for major neurological diseases, such as autism, Lou Gehrig's and Alzheimer's diseases, costing many billions of dollars to our society every year. Most of these diseases arise from genetic mutations leading to malfunction of proteins, the molecular machines that perform most biological functions. Some proteins have stable structure but others, called intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), are highly flexible. This extreme flexibility, or disorder, is very abundant in brain proteins, particularly those associated with neurological diseases, as it is advantageous for protein interactions essential for regulating key biological processes. Using unique methodologies developed in my laboratory, I propose to study IDPs and define a new paradigm for protein binding relying on dynamic interactions. This work will change the way proteins interactions are viewed, including those between two, multiple or even huge numbers of protein molecules, which can come together in a process called phase-separation to form liquid droplets involved in organizing the cell. A new paradigm focusing on dynamic interactions of disordered proteins will allow novel approaches to the study of neurological diseases. I propose to study disordered disease-associated proteins, such as caprin1 and G3BP1, which are directly linked to autism and Lou Gehrig's disease. As proteins are never isolated within the cell, I will investigate the disease-associated proteins in large-scale complexes with their cellular interaction partners. I will apply multidisciplinary expertise and powerful methods to key disordered proteins involved in brain function and diseases. I hypothesize that loss of regulation and rigidification of dynamic complexes of these disordered proteins leads to pathology in the brain. This study will yield insight enabling novel therapeutics for a variety of neurological diseases.

column37: Research in animals and humans has linked maternal prenatal stressors to longitudinal mental health outcomes in offspring, suggesting that the in utero environment affects fetal development. One of the earliest behavioral markers of prenatal stress exposure in infants is negative emotionality, a temperamental indicator of heightened stress reactivity, characterized by irritability, sadness and fussiness. Although it is appreciated by developmental psychologists that temperament, and its underlying biological components, are shaped by the interplay of genetics, experience, and normal processes of maturation, research is highly lacking that actually demonstrates how the environment becomes biologically embedded in relation to child temperament. An intriguing, nascent area of research in child development has identified an epigenetic marker in children, in the form of DNA methylation, informative of the developmental history of the interplay of biology and environment. DNA methylation can act upon the genome to guide the expression of genes into biological material and is proposed to be involved in the biological embedding of salient environmental exposures, including prenatal factors. In this proposal, I test the hypothesis that DNA methylation patterns bridge the link between prenatal stress exposure and infant negative emotionality at 6 months of age.

column36: Circulating tumour DNA as a precision oncology tool for metastatic bladder cancer
column37: Metastatic bladder cancer is a lethal and under-studied disease. Chemotherapy has historically been the most effective treatment for metastatic disease, but long-term survival has been a rarity. Recently, new drugs including immunotherapies are showing significant promise, but only a small proportion of patients respond to these treatments and we have no reliable way of predicting who the responders will be. During the first three years of my faculty appointment I have worked closely with clinical collaborators to develop a blood test that can identify tumour DNA present in a small blood sample (called circulating tumuor DNA, ctDNA). We can therefore use ctDNA to evaluate the genetic changes (mutations) in metastatic cancers that correspond to treatment response or resistance. Our preliminary work suggests that mutations detected in ctDNA accurately reflect cancer itself, meaning that we can profile a patient's metastatic bladder cancer before treatment without the need for a tissue biopsy. In this project we will identify mutations in the ctDNA of hundreds of Canadians with metastatic bladder cancer that are being treated with chemotherapy or immunotherapy. My research team will determine which mutations can predict a patient's subsequent response to treatment using our rare combination of cancer bioinformatics and clinical oncology. We are uniquely placed to perform this analysis given our strong track record of success in metastatic cancer ctDNA profiling, our novel custom methodology, and our recent establishment of a province-wide ctDNA profiling program that is rapidly accruing hundreds of patient blood samples. Success with our project will help explain why some metastatic bladder cancers are intrinsically responsive or resistant to the most commonly used therapies. Furthermore, we will have developed a clinically-practical framework (requiring only a blood sample) that may ultimately help prioritize patients for therapies with the best chance of success.

column36: Crisis and opportunity: how are social-ecological transformations scaling-up?
column37: Transitioning to a sustainable and equitable planet requires not just incremental improvements but transformational changes at all scales. Yet we know little about how such transformations happen nor how do they scale up. In this postdoctoral project, I will study already embedded solutions found in pre-existing sustainability initiatives - or seeds - that innovate to provide place-specific responses to existing social-ecological challenges. Through a comparative case-study of food-related sustainability initiatives in Athens and Montreal, this postdoctoral project will further our understanding of how social-ecological transformations happen and ways to foster sustainability pathways. More specifically, this project asks: how are small sustainability initiatives - or seeds - affecting wider social-ecological transformations (i.e. scaling up)? And how do these seeds change the way people relate to and manage ecosystem services? This project will integrate a focus on transformations to research on ecosystem services to better assess the sustainability of these emergent sustainability pathways. The first case-study, Montreal, provides an example whereby seeds have managed to institutionalize social-ecological innovation notably by collaborating with formal political structures to create new policies to promote social economy and sustainable development. The second case study, Athens, provides an example of radical new social-ecological innovations that emerged after a major economic crisis in opposition to the state. The project will adopt a mixed methods approach - combining interviews, an online survey, and a social network analysis to an ecosystem services assessment-to assess how seeds in the two case studies scale up and steer (or not) social-ecological transformations. The project will generate a set of lessons learned to aid policy and grassroots efforts and also contribute to advancing theory related to social-ecological transformations and ecosystem services.

column36: L'interpretation du meilleur interet de l'enfant dans les expertises et jugements en matiere de garde et de droits d'acces
column37: Dans le processus judiciaire menant a une decision concernant la garde et les droits d'acces d'un enfant apres une separation, des experts (travailleurs sociaux et psychologues) sont regulierement interpelles afin d'eclairer la Cour. Il est reconnu que les recommandations de ces professionnels sont generalement suivies par les juges ou que l'avis d'un expert incite bien souvent les parents a trouver une entente. Ces professionnels (juges et experts) se trouvent donc a l'origine de decisions cruciales pour le futur d'enfants et de familles particulierement vulnerables, car souvent aux prises avec des conflits chroniques et severes. Durant ce processus, tant les experts que les juges devront avoir le meilleur interet de l'enfant (MIE) pour objectif, car il s'agit du seul critere relatif a la determination de la garde en droit canadien. Or, ce critere a ete maintes fois critique en raison de son caractere subjectif et indetermine. S'appuyant sur la theorie des representations sociales, ce projet a pour objectif d'eclairer la pratique future des juges et des experts en examinant comment le MIE est interprete dans les rapports d'expertise et les jugements concernant la garde (poids accorde aux differents elements presents dans les dossiers, tendances actuelles qui influencent les decisions des juges et des experts et risques de biais). Pour ce faire le contenu de 43 expertises et jugements finaux concernant la garde et les droits d'acces (tires d'un echantillon de dossiers judiciaires de 2000 justiciables dans quatre districts judiciaires au Quebec et en Ontario) sera analyse. A terme, ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre l'utilisation de la preuve psychosociale par les tribunaux et de proposer un cadre d'analyse pour l'interpretation du MIE. Ces avancees sont d'une grande importance pour la prise en charge des dossiers comportant des conflits severes de separation, ces derniers beneficiant d'un arrimage plus fluide entre les services psychosociaux et judiciaires.

column36: "Through the veil": Revealing Mysteries of San Rock Art
column37: Rock art is one of the most ancient expressions of the human mind, and is found across the world, ranging from the Late Pleistocene to the present day. It raises several questions: When was it first produced? How was it made? Who created it? In this project, such questions are intended to be answered for San rock art, also called Later Stone Age (LSA) rock art, one of the longest traditions in the world. Thanks to detailed interpretative work using the extensive San ethnographic studies available, the meaning of LSA rock art is well known. In contrast, little is understood about how the paint itself was made or what it was made from, while the age of these paintings also remains mostly unknown. However, this information is critical to interpreting rock art and apprehending the changes in the art and, by extension, societal and spiritual changes among the San groups that may have occurred when they were in contact with sedentary populations and then Europeans. We aim first at studying San rock art: its representations, the techniques used by the artists, the provenance of raw materials, and detailing its changes through time. Second, we seek to explore changes in San spirituality and to assess whether they are linked to societal changes. To deal with these questions, San rock art will be characterised and dated and the same will also be done for portable art and objects with traces of pigments such as grindstones. This will be the first time that such comparisons are considered in the study of San rock art, though they are crucially needed to assess whether societal changes are linked to changes in the art. The main strength of this project is its interdisciplinary aspect, as it combines chemistry, geology, geochemistry, archaeology, material culture, and the history of art. All of these complementary fields are linked together to give new insights into the San groups, well-known by their art, but still mysterious in their beliefs and aspects of daily life

column36: Cellular senescence in diabetic retinopathy
column37: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most prominent complication of diabetes and the leading cause of severe visual loss. Diabetic retinopathy has largely been perceived as a microvascular disease given its overt vascular phenotype. Yet over the past years, considerable evidence suggests that central neurons in the retina also contribute to disease progression and hence DR presents salient feature of neurodegenerative disease. Current dogma on neurodegenerative diseases dictates that once a central neuron cumulates damage and ceases to transmit sensory stimuli, it degenerates and dies an apoptotic death. Yet, from an evolutionary standpoint, survival advantage would be gained from a mechanism triggered to help weather stressors and preserve nervous tissue integrity, eventually allowing for repair and restoration of function. My host lab (Dr. Sapieha Lab's) has recently identified a new stress response system in DR, where retinal neurons, microglia and endothelial cells enter a state of premature cellular senescence. This state of the retina contributes to disease progression through generation of a series of inflammatory mediators collectively termed the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. On the other hand, why retinal neurons enter a state of premature senescence during diabetes and whether this is a protective mechanism is not understood. In the proposed research program, we explore a novel paradigm of neuronal dormancy, where retinal neurons enter a state reversible senescence to weather diabetic and ischemic stressors. This challenges two dogmas: 1-Cellular senescence is irreversible. 2- Central neurons such as retinal ganglion cells in the retina have the inherent capacity to enter a state of dormancy to activate programs of cellular repair. Understanding the fundamental mechanisms that lead to the induction and reversal of cellular senescence may have broad implications for diabetes, and that beyond the retina.

column36: Integrating person-centered and precision psychiatry in the clinical assessment of depression
column37: Depression is now the leading cause of disability around the world. However, the range of syndromes subsumed under the label of depression remains broad. This heterogeneity has led to a crisis of diagnosis and poor treatment outcomes. In the face of this ongoing challenge, there is an urgent need to develop novel, more specific diagnostic tools and treatments. Assessment of depression is hampered by the growing divide between an increasingly neuroscientific view of this disorder and the importance of affirming the whole person of the patient in light of their individual life history, sociocultural specificity and subjective illness experience. Providing optimal diagnosis and treatment in psychiatry requires addressing individual pathology in all its dimensions: biological, mental, social, and environmental. My research will integrate the latest neuroscientific and sociocultural advances in psychiatric research to tackle this pressing health challenge. With the support of a Banting Fellowship I will develop and evaluate a novel integrative toolkit to assist clinicians in diagnosing and treating patients with symptoms of depression. My research will leverage the conceptual framework of 'precision' psychiatry (which emphasizes individual neurobiology and genetics) to complement recent efforts in 'person-centered' psychiatry (with its focus on experiential and social-cultural context). The project will produce a toolkit that helps clinicians integrate neuroscientific and sociocultural dimensions in their patient assessment. In a second stage, I will study how the implementation of the toolkit impacts clinical practice and treatment outcomes. Ultimately, this project will provide a basis for the continued development of patient-focused research and clinical care that does justice to the neurobiological, psychological and social specificity of individuals.

column36: Deciphering the adaptive and encoded drug response in ovarian cancer with single cell sequencing and scalable statistical modeling
column37: High grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) is the hardest to treat ovarian cancer with around 2800 cases in Canada each year. Despite its severity, little is known about the mutations to each tumour's DNA that allows it to spread and ultimately lead to mortality. These tumours can be treated with chemotherapeutic drugs but over time they become resistant to treatment. Discovering the molecular features that allow tumours to evade chemotherapy and what is unique about the subset of patients in which this happens would allow us to design novel therapies to prevent this. The lack of progress in understanding these DNA mutations has been in part due to difficulty measuring them. However, in the last two years the technology has sufficiently advanced (pioneered by researchers at BCCA) to measure both DNA mutations and RNA expression (a proxy for each cell's behaviour) in individual tumour cells. Researchers in the Shah group will apply these techniques to HGSC tumours over time as the tumours are exposed to different chemotherapy drugs to uncover the mutations that accompany chemotherapy resistance. However, this wealth of data will be impossible to interpret without a new statistical framework. We will create methods that allow us to reconstruct the "tree of life" for each tumour sample - allowing us to work out which cells mutated from others and in doing so tracking the sequences of mutations that confer resistance to chemotherapy. We will extend this methodology to understand mutations over time as cells are perturbed by the applications of various drugs and to work out the relative contributions of the cells' innate resistance (mutations) and adaptive resistance (by changing their gene expression behaviour) to chemotherapy resistance. This research has strong potential to impact clinical care as it will lead to new understandings of why certain patients don't respond to chemotherapy and could culminate in new treatment methods to suppress chemotherapy resistance.

column36: Defining the Roles of Overgrowth Syndrome Genes in Shaping Developmental Gene Networks in Early Embryos
column37: Human overgrowth disorders such as Sotos syndrome are characterized by pre- and postnatal increased growth, intellectual disability and facial anomalies. These diseases result from mutations in genes that encode enzymes that turn off other genes by changing the structure of DNA. These genes include NSD1, most frequently mutated in Sotos Syndrome patients, and SETD2. Both encoded enzymes chemically modify a specific amino acid on a specific protein associated with DNA called histone H3. Interestingly, the modifications of histone H3 influences the activity of the protein that modifies the DNA, as well as that of another protein, EZH2, which chemically modifies histone H3. The Ezh2 gene is mutated in the related overgrowth disorder called Weaver Syndrome. These observations suggest "cross-talk" between these enzymes and in turn the genes they regulate. However, a systematic study of the consequences of disrupting these regulatory proteins has not been conducted. Here, using the mouse as a model system, we will study the interplay between these enzymes and the marks they deposit, by mutating these "overgrowth syndrome genes" in the mouse and studying the consequences of such mutations in the early mouse embryo, where these genes are first active. This "genome-wide" study, using state-of-the-art sequencing technology and mouse genetics, will lead to a better understanding of the molecular basis of several human overgrowth syndromes including Sotos and Weaver, potentially leading to new avenues for treatment of these diseases.

column36: Molecular mechanisms of neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease is a disabling neurological disorder that is increasing in prevalence and thus having a growing impact on the Canadian population. This disease results from a process called neurodegeneration in which vulnerable nerve cells in the brain die more rapidly than normal. Neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease causes the clinical symptoms referred to as parkinsonism which include tremor, rigidity, slowness of movements, and postural instability. There are therapies which can alleviate these symptoms but they are associated with significant side effects. Furthermore, none of our current treatments for Parkinson's disease can slow or stop the death of nerve cells. This is due, in large part, to our limited understanding of the molecules that cause neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease. The goals of the proposed research program are to elucidate the critical molecules responsible for neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease and to discover drugs that target these molecules. The research plan is based on three main aims: 1) to understand how the protein alpha-synuclein is linked to the neurodegenerative process in Parkinson's disease; 2) to identify chemical compounds that target alpha-synuclein as potential novel drugs for Parkinson's disease; and, 3) to investigate the molecular pathways of protein homeostasis that regulate neurodegeneration. The overall outcome of the proposed research will be the elucidation of key molecular mechanisms involved in Parkinson's disease and related disorders. This work will lay the foundation for future studies aimed at developing new treatments for people with Parkinson's disease and thereby lead to improved health outcomes for Canadians affected by this disease.

column36: Defining the dynamics behind Ryanodine Receptor function using Malignant Hyperthermia mutant channel
column37: Some individuals have a single mutation within their skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor (RYR1) resulting in Malignant Hyperthermia (MH), a life-threatening complication associated with general anesthesia. The RYR1 is a channel responsible for the rapid, but controlled, release of calcium from internal stores within the cells of our skeletal muscles that triggers muscle contraction. These individuals, only when exposed to general anesthetics, show uncontrolled contraction of their muscles and body temperatures that reach over 40.6 degrees Celsius. While considerable advances have emerged regarding our understanding of RYR1, there is still much to learn about the relationship between the protein's structure and how small molecules like anesthetics can significantly alter their normal function. Our objective is to use techniques from chemistry and biology as well as a novel combined strategy to identify the binding sites for anesthetics within normal and MH mutant RYR1 in order to determine and compare the consequence of binding on RYR1 structure. To accomplish this we will employ photoactive analogs of the anesthetics isoflurane and sevoflurane to 'photolabel' their binding sites within both RYR1s. We will determine the affect of anesthetic binding on the structure of the ion channel using a novel strategy that couples cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) with the photoactive analogs in order to obtain a snapshot of the anesthetic interactions with the channel. Preliminary studies have indicated a potential anesthetic binding site within a unique region of RYR1 that would have long-range effects on the structure within other channel regions. Ultimately this investigation will provide 1) a strategy for the advancement of scientific methods and 2) define the transitions that occur within RYR1 and the impact of anesthetics on the channel's function.

column36: Illuminating the structure and dynamics of the proteasomal Rpn1 protein in unfolded client recognition by methyl-TROSY NMR
column37: Human health relies on the ability to properly degrade old proteins when they are no longer needed. The degradation of proteins is carried out by an enormous protein machine called the proteasome. When protein degradation is impaired, neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) can occur. The proteasome contains two major pieces denoted as the core and regulatory particles (CP and RP respectively). The CP resembles a barrel with pores at each end where proteins enter for degradation. The RP is involved in recognizing and pushing old proteins into the CP to be recycled. Specifically, the RP contains a highly dynamic and multi-functional protein called Rpn1 which is crucial to recognizing and moving proteins marked for degradation into the CP. Rpn1 has been suggested to bind unfolded proteins, acting as a bridge for protein folding and degradation at the proteasome, however the details of this possibility remain unknown. A robust understanding of Rpn1 function, and therefore protein degradation, is predicated on site-specific studies of the interactions of unfolded proteins with Rpn1. We will use solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to investigate how Rpn1 recognizes unfolded proteins. This information will shed new light on the proteasome mechanism and will benefit the development of drugs that prevent neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Moving knowledge to practice: developing, implementing and evaluating in-hospital physical activity practices to enhance health for children during treatment for cancer
column37: Over 80% of children diagnosed with cancer will survive the disease. However, most will experience negative effects that can greatly reduce their health and quality of life. In-hospital physical activity (PA) during treatment is one strategy that can reduce negative physical and psychosocial effects and enhance quality of life in the short- and long-term. Though in-hospital PA practices (ie, recommendations, education, opportunities) are advocated for children during treatment, hospitals in Canada do not provide PA practices as part of usual care. Consequently, most children with cancer are not active enough to receive the health benefits PA can offer. Further, PA remains low for years or decades following treatment. In select countries internationally, in-hospital PA practices are part of usual care. Research suggests improved care and enhanced health and quality of life in the short- and long-term at these centres. To address the gap in childhood cancer care in Canada, this research program will develop, implement, and evaluate in-hospital PA practices for children undergoing treatment for cancer. To do this, healthcare professionals (eg, oncologists, nurses, physiotherapists, child life specialists), childhood cancer patients and their caregivers, and experts (ie, researchers and healthcare professionals who have successfully implemented in-hospital PA practices in their centres) will be consulted. These individuals will help identify strategies for implementing in-hospital PA practices into usual cancer care. Once identified, these practices will be implemented and evaluated in the Alberta Children's Hospital and Stollery Children's Hospital. If successful, the outputs from this project have the potential to improve existing care and enhance health and quality of life in the short- and long-term for children undergoing treatment for cancer in Canada.

column36: Spatiotemporal resolution of the contributions of pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms to synapse-specific transmission variability and synaptic plasticity
column37: Activity-dependent changes of synaptic efficacy are the cellular basis of learning and memory. Synaptic plasticity bidirectionally modifies synaptic strength by enhancing or depressing transmission, effected through a complexity of mechanisms that act pre- and postsynaptically, over different time scales, and in response to different stimuli. Despite decades of intensive research, the fundamental question of how changes in synaptic efficacy are ultimately expressed during plasticity remains to be unequivocally answered; that is, to what extent and over what timescales do plasticity events modify respectively presynaptic neurotransmitter release and the number or function of postsynaptic receptors? This outstanding question represents a fundamental gap in our knowledge about how synaptic plasticity is evoked to modify the function of neuronal networks controlling behaviour. The rapid and dynamic regulation of AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPAR) surface mobility constitutes a major mechanism underlying synaptic plasticity. However, it is also apparent that the recruitment or removal of AMPARs by exo- and endocytotic mechanisms postsynaptically, and changes in neurotransmitter release probability presynaptically, are also involved in synaptic modulation during plasticity. Here, I propose to use a multi-level approach combining electrophysiology, genetically-encoded optical reporters, innovative molecular tools to control AMPAR trafficking, and state-of-the-art super-resolution imaging approaches to determine how the dynamics of AMPAR surface mobility postsynaptically, and synaptic vesicle release presynaptically, define the functional properties of synaptic transmission during both basal and plastic states. This work will shed new light on the fundamental mechanisms of synaptic transmission, plasticity and specificity, and advance our knowledge of the etiology of numerous psychiatric, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders that are linked to AMPAR dysregulation.

column36: Mechanotransduction in the central nervous system: elucidation of the role of Piezo1 in microglia
column37: Mechanotransduction consists of sensing and transforming physical tensions on the cell membrane into intracellular signals. Piezo1 and Piezo2 are mechanically-activated ion channels that play crucial roles in sensory transduction as well as cardiovascular and developmental regulation. In the central nervous system (CNS), Piezos haven't been reported. My preliminary data reveal Piezo1 responses in microglia, known as the resident macrophages of the CNS. These highly dynamic cells maintain CNS homeostasis, respond to damage and invading pathogens, and underlie many neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases. Piezo1 may be essential in regulating mechanosensitive processes that characterize microglial function under resting and pathological states. Therefore, we sought to validate the functional expression of Piezo1 in microglia, identify the physiological mechanisms affected by Piezo1, and test the behavioral effects of Piezo1 loss- and gain-of-function in the appropriate animal models. My preliminary results show Piezo1-mediated calcium signals in cultured microglia, a response that is greatly up-regulated in activated microglia. This suggests an important role of Piezo1 in mechanosensitive phenomena that occur under activation, such as morphological alterations, migration, and phagocytosis. The relevance of Piezo1 in these processes will be investigated in vitro and in vivo by comparing control mice to Piezo1 loss- or gain-of-function transgenic models. Once a Piezo1-dependent process is identified, the appropriate mouse disease model will be tested to check for behavioral phenotypes and gain insights on the clinical relevance of microglial Piezo1. This work would present the first evidence of the presence of Piezos in the CNS and may reveal critical roles of mechanotransduction in microglial function underlying neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Neuroimaging Biomarkers for Transition to Mental Illness in Youth
column37: Mental illness is a major cause of disability worldwide, and most of these illnesses develop during adolescence. Like most illnesses, mental health issues are more manageable if they are identified and treated early. However, two issues have prevented the delivery of effective mental health treatment to adolescents. The first issue is that many youths experience symptoms and behavioural disturbances but these symptoms are neither pronounced nor persistent enough to warrant a diagnosis. The second issue is that only some of the youths who experience these symptoms will develop a mental illness. As a result, it is difficult to correctly identify targets for intervention and support. The goal of this project is to use brain imaging, along with psychiatric tests, to create a model that can predict the development of a mental illness. In order to achieve this goal, we are currently recruiting and following youths between the ages of 12-25, the majority of whom are at high risk of developing mental illness, either because they have experienced symptoms, or because of a family history of mental illness. Participants will perform brain imaging experiments and other tests over the course of a year, in order to determine which are best at predicting whom will go on to develop a mental illness. For the brain imaging experiment, we are using a reward task, as this has been shown to differentiate various mental illnesses. The model we propose to develop will allow targeted interventions that can lessen disease impact and foster healthier outcomes.

column36: Multi-regional neuronal dynamics of short-term memory
column37: Short-term memory is a core cognitive function for animals. Imagine solving a Rubik cube, we first recognize the configuration of the cube, maintain the configuration in short-term memory while devising a plan, and then carry out the plan seconds later. In our daily lives, maintaining information in short-term memory is important for reasoning, decision making, and motor planning. Although short-term memory is recognized as a critical function in everyday function, and is impaired in diseases such as schizophrenia, how the brain represents and uses short-term memory is not fully understood. Previous studies only examined single brain areas under one task condition and failed to identify a single area that stores short-term memory. Like almost all brain functions, short-term memory is likely maintained in a circuit across multiple regions of the brain, and we require simultaneous measurement from multiple regions to identify the neuronal substrates. The proposed research aims to use new electrophysiology technology to simultaneously record the activity from hundreds of neurons in multiple regions, and perturb the activity to establish function. We propose to study two different behaviors in mice that involve short-term memory. In the first task, mice need to maintain short-term memory during a delay period. We will record and perturb activity across approximately 50 brain regions, selected based on connectivity data. This will generate a complete functional map of neuronal activity underlying short-term memory. In the second task, the mice must route the short-term memory to the upcoming motor plan to correctly perform the task. The second task will allow us to see how the activity map is used in different behavioral context. The successful completion of the map dynamics for short-term memory will guide the development of computer models of the brain and gives a window into the potential dysfunctions that are responsible for cognitive and motor diseases.

column36: Dentate mossy cell gating of seizure generalization in temporal lobe epilepsy.
column37: It is unclear why some seizures spread beyond the brain region of origin to recruit more widespread networks, a process known as seizure generalization. This is troubling because seizures are not adequately controlled with medication in a third of people with epilepsy and seizure generalization results in convulsions that can cause injury or death. It is important to understand why seizures generalize to treat and avoid these detrimental convulsions whose effects extend well beyond seizure termination. Using cutting-edge techniques, it is now possible to isolate and observe the contributions of distinct cell-types to the function of a larger brain network. Utilizing these techniques to study epilepsy enables me to track the activity of specific cell populations during seizures that either remain within the epileptic network or spread to cause convulsions. Upon understanding how activity patterns of key cell-types lead to seizure generalization, treatments that disrupt these patterns can be selected to prevent convulsions. A basic understanding of this phenomenon could lead to treatments that dramatically improve quality of life and reduce the risk of death in poorly controlled epilepsy.

column36: Deep Cellular- and Immuno-Biology of Alzheimer's Disease Progression - A Framework for Mechanistic Understanding
column37: A continually growing aging population comes with increasing health risks for Canadians. Approximately 750K Canadians are currently living with Alzheimer's disease (AD) or other dementias, and this number is projected to double in 20 years. Current AD research focuses on treatment of patients after development of AD. However, high dimensional neuroimaging will lead to untapped knowledge on disease progression mechanisms of AD, giving us a platform to develop groundbreaking, proactive solutions to AD management. Neuroimaging is critical to better understand the clinical progression of Alzheimer's disease, and understanding processes in the brain and the interplay between pathology and immunology in the onset of AD would better identify: (1) risk factors for AD, (2) therapeutic targets to manage the disease, and (3) understanding of the disease progression mechanisms. The primary aims of this proposal are to understand: (1) what the brain looks like of people with and without AD at a cellular and subcellular level, (2) whether the immune system has a role in disease progression and pathogenesis, and (3) to develop utility of therapeutic targets based on the findings. To answer these questions, we will use multiplexing technologies in order to characterize, phenotype and image the brains of donors. These multiplexing technologies include mass cytometry (CyTOF) and multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI), they will allow us to analyze a large number of proteins (>40) in biological samples at the (sub)cellular level. Current technologies are limited in allowing us to only look at 2 or 3 different proteins that we believe have a role in AD; however, CyTOF and MIBI will allow us to look at >40 proteins which have a potential role in AD, and how they interact with one another. This approach will allow us to understand multiple pathways leading to AD pathology, and potentially identify therapeutic targets for the development of novel drugs to manage AD.
