column36: YOUTH WELLBEING IN CHINA AND CENTRAL AMERICA:IMPLEMENTATION OF AN INTEGRATED PREVENTION AND INTERVENTION PROGRAM
column37: High rates of mental illness and addiction (often associated with self-harm) have been reported in China and Central America. Stigma, poor mental health knowledge, and limited awareness and/or accessibility to health services lead to low help-seeking, further compounding the problem. Thus, there is an urgent need for strategies to promote mental health knowledge to enable early identification and treatment and to improve help-seeking behaviour. The aim of this 5-year project is to implement and evaluate a multi-level, integrated mental health education, screening, and intervention program to improve functioning and well-being in youth in China, Honduras and El Salvador. About 5000 students in China, 2000 students in Honduras and 2000 students in El Salvador will be recruited. Participants will receive a 12-week mental wellness and leadership program (MWL) online (at universities) or in class (at vocational/technical schools). Curriculum topics will include mental health education (illness and stigma, help-seeking, stress management), social responsibility (prejudice, violence, gender-based violence), and leadership (values, skills). Students will be assessed on psychosocial function (e.g.distress, coping, stress, academic performance) and physiological measures of stress (saliva and hair cortisol) before and after MWL completion. An open-access phone app will be created to screen for emotional difficulties and addictive behaviours and will be available to MWL and non-MWL students. Those students who screen positive for significant emotional difficulties, as well as those with depression, anxiety and/or addictive behaviours who are referred by health professionals, will receive one of two forms of an 8-week internetbased cognitive-behavioural therapy (iCBT) program. The iCBT emotional well-being program will target mood and anxiety symptoms, and the iCBT addictions program will target substance abuse (including alcohol and tobacco) and problematic internet use. Students will be assessed on symptom and functional improvement as well as on physiological measures of stress before and after program completion. This project offers the opportunity to implement and evaluate the broad benefits of a novel integrated prevention and psychological intervention program for youth in culturally differing regions. The program will be adapted and incorporated into existing postsecondary institutions in the three countries with measurement of cross-cultural acceptability, efficacy, fidelity of implementation, and sustainability. It is proposed that the project will improve the mental wellness of transitional youth with good sustainability in two distinct global regions, and furthermore, it offers an opportunity to objectively evaluate to cost and benefit of this implementation.

column36: Implementation research: community intervention to prevent repeated suicide attempts in Ningxia China and Nunavut Canada
column37: BACKGROUND: Suicide is the most serious outcome of a variety of mental illnesses, including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, eating disorders and substance abuse. Reducing suicide mortality is an important objective of the World Health Organization's 2013-2020 Global Mental Health Action Plan and the United Nation's 2015-2030 Sustainable Development Goals. A prior suicide attempt is the most important risk factor for death by suicide, but regular brief community follow-up after an attempt can prevent repeated suicidal behavior. AIMS: This 5-year implementation science project will develop methods for adapting the WH0 SUPRE-MISS intervention for suicide attempters in parallel projects in Ningxia, China, and among Inuit in Nunavut, Canada. These methods for adapting SUPRE-MISS will then be promulgated in Inuit and other indigenous populations, other parts of China, other low- and middle-income countries, and other low-resourced settings in high-income countries. METHODS: PHASE 1. Conduct focus groups with local stakeholders to identify local factors that need to be considered when developing a location-specific version of SUPRE-MISS that provides a brief educational intervention about suicide prevention to individuals who have recently made a suicide attempt and periodic social support and access to emergency services to these highrisk individuals. PHASE 2. Pilot-test the adapted intervention in a small number of settings for one year. PHASE 3. Revise and then scale-up the intervention to more settings for 30 months and continuously collect outcome measures, process measures, and resource utilization measures (for cost-effectiveness assessment). PHASE 4. Conduct post-intervention focus groups with stakeholders to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the intervention. Integrate these qualitative results with the quantitative results (e.g., rates of repeated suicidal behavior) to prepare a report on the process of implementing the SUPRE-MISS intervention in low-resource settings. Work with administrators and policy makers in China, Nunavut, and other locations to develop policies that will widely promulgate the use of this approach to suicide prevention. FEASIBILITY: A strong multidisciplinary team with extensive experience in suicide prevention in the target communities has been assembled and the active support of local administrators and policy makers who can provide practical support for the project and develop policies to promote its results has been obtained. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: This project will develop methods that can be widely disseminated to help achieve the United Nation's ambitious goal of reducing suicide mortality by 1/3 by 2030. Combining findings from parallel projects in a low-middle-income country with those from a low-resource setting in a high-income country will provide a unique case example of how implementation science can be used to address complex mental health problems in different low-resource settings.

column36: Enhanced Measurement-Based Care Effectiveness for Depression (EMBED): A Canada-China Implementation Project
column37: Depression affects 300+ million people globally and is now the leading cause of disability and burden of disease worldwide. In China, the National Mental Health Work Plan 2015-20 specifies improving the ability of healthcare facilities to identify depression and increase the treatment rate by 50%. Measurement-based care (MBC) - the routine use of validated outcomes such as the PHQ-9 depression questionnaire to guide clinical decision-making - is a simple evidence-based practice (EBP) that may help meet these objectives. However, there is still a significant care gap in the implementation of MBC in China and elsewhere. In Canada, we have adopted the concept of enhanced MBC (eMBC), in which technology can engage both patients & physicians in using MBC; eMBC enhancements include web and mobile app tools for patients to track their own progress with the PHQ-9, and an evidence-based, lowcost, low-intensity psychological treatment (guided self-management with telephone coaches) that has embedded patient measurement and feedback to physicians. EMBED: a Canada-China implementation project, proposes to develop a novel EBP implementation strategy by adapting, implementing and evaluating eMBC in diverse community mental health clinics in Shanghai, modeled on programs implemented in Canada. EMBED addresses 4 broad aims: 1) identify contextual enablers & barriers to MBC implementation; 2) explore physicianand patient-level factors as mediators for an EBP implementation; 3) provide clinical & health economic outcomes to establish effectiveness of eMBC; and 4) build knowledge & capacity for scale up of eMBC in China and beyond. Our hypothesis is that physician & patient factors that are barriers for implementation of standard MBC will be enablers for implementation of eMBC. To achieve these aims, we will first conduct a Situation Analysis to determine the key barriers & enablers for MBC implementation in Shanghai. We will adapt a Canadian eMBC program for the Chinese context, then will use a hybrid implementation-effectiveness design (an adaptive cluster randomized evaluation) to compare eMBC with standard MBC implementation in 12 community clinics, 240 physicians, and 1200 patients. We hypothesize that eMBC implementation will lead to superior implementation, patient and costeffectiveness outcomes, compared to standard MBC. EMBED will advance the international literature on MBC broadly by focusing on the understudied role of patients in implementation of MBC. EMBED will also further implementation science by creating new knowledge on contextual factors, including mediating effects of physician- and patient-level factors, together, on EBP implementation outcomes. Moreover, the unique partnership of the EMBED team with the APEC Digital Hub for Mental Health will ensure a pathway for integrated knowledge & policy translation so that findings will have significant scale-up and spread potential in other regions in China, the Asia-Pacific and worldwide.

column36: Linking Hearts: Advancing Mental Health Care of University Students Through Interdisciplinary Collaboration (in Jinan)
column37: Young people are vulnerable to the onset of mental illness. Research shows that delayed treatment of mental illness leads to negative outcomes. In China, prevalence of depression among university students is as high as 20 to 30%. However, 9 out of 10 people diagnosed with a mental disorder never sought mental health care. Stigma and low mental health literacy are among the most important help-seeking barriers. Further, mental health services, largely at specialized hospitals only, are overstretched, while community and informal levels of care are underdeveloped. To address this, the study will examine the implementation of an evidence-based intervention, Acceptance and Commitment to Empowerment - Linking Youth and 'Xin' (hearts) (ACE-LYNX), to: (1) decrease stigma (attitude), (2) increase mental health literacy (knowledge), and (3) promote individual well-being (outcomes) and the collective capacity to collaborate (action) to promote mental health and form an integrative network of care for students. ACE-LYNX consists of two components: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a mindfulness-based cognitive-behavioral intervention, and Group Empowerment Psychoeducation (GEP), psychoeducation integrated with principles of equity, empowerment, and social justice. The study will take place in three regions of Jinan, Shandong, China. We will engage one hospital and two universities in each region. We will begin with an assessment of contexts, consisting of a university student survey (n= 600), student focus groups (n=144), and stakeholder and professional focus groups (n=144). The data will inform intervention adaptation. Using a train-the-trainer model, we will train 90 interdisciplinary professionals to become ACE-LYNX-Pro Champions. They will in turn train the "2nd generation" ACELYNX- Pro Champions (n=270) and students to become ACE-LYNX Student Champions(n=360) with a lay version of the intervention. All champions will form a collaborative integrated mental health care network supported by a community of practice through a Learning Management System and Weixin (WeChat). The champions will be followed over 6 months for their outreach and health promotional activities, including using Weixin to form a Student Mental Health Virtual Network. The RE-AIM framework will be used to examine Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance/Sustainability of ACE-LYNX and the integrated network. Psychometric measures will track the intervention's impact on attitude (CAMI), knowledge (MAKS), empowerment (Bulls-Eye, monthly activity logs), and mental health outcomes (DASS-21, AAQ-II), while service volumes and Social Network Analysis will be used to examine the functioning of the real and virtual networks. We will apply an Integrated Knowledge Translation framework to engage key stakeholders throughout the study to ensure maximal impact and dissemination with the aim of system transformation at the micro, meso, and macro levels.

column36: Shared Care for ADHD in Children and Youth: Merging the Canadian and Chinese Experiences
column37: In the context of modern China, children experience a tremendous pressure to perform at high levels. This stressful environment is associated with depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation and attempts in adolescence. Children with a diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are highly inattentive, restless, impulsive, and therefore at high risk, despite a normal intellectual potential. ADHD is easy to diagnose and treat, but difficult to diagnose and treat well. The treatment effects are dependent on the quality of care and on the coordination of different interventions, planned according to individual needs. The first main barrier to treatment is the shortage of qualified clinicians. In response, our main strategy will be to implement a shared care between general practitioners (GPs) and specialists. The second barrier is the lack of training in GPs. We will implement a focused ADHD training targeted to the needs of GPs. A third barrier is the lack referral process. We will implement stepped care in which the patient is treated at the most appropriate level of care, depending on complexity or outcome. We will adapt the Canadian shared care model for ADHD to the Chinese context. To test its flexibility, it will be implemented within the pediatric care system in two districts of Shanghai and within the mental health care system in one district of Beijing. We will first assess how ADHD guidelines are used, and the existing collaboration between GPs and specialists. After a Consensus Conference, we will implement a shared care pathway and we will produce actionable findings in a formative evaluation to improve implementation. At the end of the setup phase, we will assess the use of guidelines, the deviation from the intended protocol, how its members evaluate the care process, examine the effectiveness with regard to ADHD outcome, and functioning of the pathway, in terms of patient flow and timing. Once the shared care model is functionally implemented, we will scale up the care system horizontally by linking it progressively with schools selected randomly in the target districts. Using already established collaborations with the educational psychologists, we will first survey the knowledge and perceived needs of teacher, then implement a screening strategy for ADHD problems in the schools, as well as web-based effective strategies to educate parents and teachers about ADHD and mitigate its impact. We will assess the effectiveness of the intervention, and how it changes the perception of ADHD and the help-seeking process, as well as the rate of referrals into the shared care system. These two steps will allow defining the scalable unit that could be used in further implementation of the model. A costeffectiveness analysis is integrated in the project in order to support its scalability. Beyond ADHD, this shared care model will be able to respond to various mental health treatment challenges, both in children and adults.

column36: Screening and management of perinatal depression within primary care
column37: Depression during pregnancy and after an infant's birth is more common in China than in high-income countries and can harm the mother, infant, and family. Chinese women's mental health needs are unmet given lack of investment in mental health, unequal distribution of mental health services, and few specialized healthcare providers to support mental health issues. Our goal is to create an effective perinatal depression screening and management (PDSM) program that will be sustainable within the maternal and child healthcare system in China. Our implementation strategy is guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and RE-AIM (Reach x Efficacy, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance) and includes 2 Phases: (1) Pilot in Ma'anshan City, Anhui Province during which we will, through stakeholder engagement, adapt current evidence and test the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted screening guidelines and psychosocial intervention (internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy; iCBT) by healthcare providers and women. We will use mixed-methods to (a) identify and evaluate various implementation strategies (e.g., individual, organizational) to promote uptake of the screening guidelines and iCBT; (b) evaluate acceptability (i.e., knowledge, attitudes, and behavior) before and after implementation of guidelines and iCBT; (c) evaluate reach by determining the degree to which the population that is eligible to benefit from the program actually received it; (d) evaluate treatment fidelity by determining the extent to which the screening guidelines and iCBT was implemented as designed by monitoring adherence, dosage of delivery (i.e., the number of weeks completed), and program quality. (2) Scale-up to Hefei (capital and largest city), Bengbu (mid-sized urban city), and Fuyang (urban city) adapting the screening guidelines and iCBT based on Phase 1, and using steps (a)-(d) to promote uptake. Our monitoring and evaluation plan includes evaluating impact, effectiveness, and quality (i.e., public health impact) in both the Pilot and Scale-up phases. Our project is jointly supported by Chinese and Canadian researcher, focuses on implementation research related to depression, an affective disorder that will become the second leading cause of disease by 2010. It also, addresses women's mental health during pregnancy and following birth when vulnerability to depression is intensified, and promotes uptake screening which promotes use of mental health service and iCBT a psychosocial self-administered intervention with support from a trained mental health care provider that promotes reduction in depressive symptoms. Our study will enable integration of PDSM into the maternal and child healthcare system with flexible guidelines that considers context, ensures mental healthcare is personalized and responsive to Chinese women's needs, and promotes implementation outcomes of acceptability, reach, and fidelity.

column36: Standardizing the treatment, prevention, and management of depression in China: a multi-disciplinary approach
column37: Depression is a common mental disorder affecting approximately 350 million people worldwide and representing the third leading contributor to the global disease burden (World Health Organization [WHO], 2012). However, much of the literature on the depression derives from studies conducted in Western Europe and North America. Consequently, there is a need for novel depression research in low- and middle-income countries, including China. In China, depression is highly prevalent but is not treated in existing community mental health programs, limiting many residents' access to mental health care and contributing to the large treatment gap. Currently, mental health care for depression exists at urban mental health centres; additionally, there is a lack of integration between primary and mental health care and the absence of mental health training for primary care physicians. Collectively, these factors hinder access to mental health care in rural and urban areas, and across communities of various socioeconomic backgrounds, languages and dialects. Thus, the development of community mental health prevention and treatment programs for depression would increase access to mental health care for residents of China in both rural and urban areas. Additional barriers that contribute to the treatment gap include culturally ingrained negativistic attitudes towards mental disorders that contribute to social- and self-stigma, and lack of education about mental disorders and their treatment. Consequently, our research endeavors, involving coordination between Canada and China, are as follows: (1) to help develop community-based mental health services for the early identification of individuals with depressive symptoms and prevention of clinical depression, (2) to improve access to mental health care and the management of patients with depression in community- and hospital-based settings, and (3) to establish international psychosocial networks or systems to monitor the quality of care. In addition, we aim to implement prevention and intervention strategies that address the aforementioned barriers to improve the quality of depression management and increase willingness to seek mental health care. Studies have reported that screening individuals with depressive symptoms and the subsequent provision of psychological therapy to prevent the onset of clinical depression is a cost-effective intervention, compared to treatment after depression onset. If depression prevention strategies become a standard part of mental health services, unnecessary suffering due to depression will be greatly reduced.

column36: Effects of shoe-worn insoles on pain, function, and joint biomechanics in people with knee osteoarthritis: A randomized controlled trial.
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common disease affecting the muscular and skeletal system. It causes pain and disability in nearly 5 million Canadians and costs the Canadian health care system over $10 billion annually. There is no cure and with our ageing population, these number will only continue to grow. Conservative treatments (non-surgical and non-pharmacological) such as exercise or shoe-worn insoles can improve pain, function, and potentially slow disease progression. Therefore, they remain the most recommended treatment for patients with OA in joints such as the knee. However, the success of these treatments can be quite varied between patients, as some patients respond very well and others respond poorly. The research conducted by Dr. Kobsar during his PhD was the first to discover that it is possible to identify individual patients more likely to respond to a given treatment prior to beginning it. Similarly, Dr. Hunt has recently identified a shoe-worn insole that may be an effective treatment for many people with knee OA. Therefore the proposed project is the logical extension and combination of Dr. Kobsar and Dr. Hunt's recent work. Specifically, the primary purpose of the study is to determine the effect of a shoe-worn insole on pain, function, and knee mechanics in patients with knee OA. A total of 102 knee OA patients will be randomly given either a customized insole or a standard insole (control group) to wear for a period of 9 months. The results of this study will determine the effect of a customized insole on pain, function, and knee mechanics. The study will also examine the characteristics of these knee OA patients in relation to their response in order to predict and prescribe this treatment to future individuals who are most likely to respond favourably. Identifying inexpensive methods, such as insoles, and prescription guidelines can provide a safe and effective way to reduce the substantial personal and economic burdens associated with OA.

column36: Platform technology for blood diagnostics integrating microneedle blood sampling and quantum-dot based multiplexed assays
column37: Blood is the most useful sample fluid for lab medicine and diagnostics. It is most often obtained by inserting a needle in a vein in the arm (venipuncture). In the US, over 2 billion venipunctures are performed annually and is a technique that requires skilled personnel. Venipuncture is often associated with pain, discomfort and bruising, and is most difficult in persons with small, fragile, or "deep" veins (e.g. obesity), in babies, and when repeated sampling is needed. We propose an alternative that will minimize discomfort and bruising, will not require highly skilled personnel, and will be safe and easy. Our project combines an array of tiny needles (microneedles) that can be placed as a "patch" on the surface of the skin to collect small amounts of blood. The microneedles cause little discomfort, have a very low risk of causing bruising, and can be applied by the patient or a non-medical person. As the blood is collected, it will flow into a "lab-on-a-chip-on-a-phone" device, where the blood tests will automatically be performed using new and highly sensitive fluorescent probes. These tests will include immunoassays for protein biomarkers associated with cardiovascular disease, partially in collaboration with our industry partner, as well as assays of the activities of blood coagulation factors. Results from this platform can be immediately and electronically sent to the patient and physician. This research builds on successful preliminary applications with the microneedle arrays and fluorescent probes separately. We will now further develop and combine these innovative methods for a much-needed medical use, make comparisons to the standard venipuncture approach, and ultimately plan to perform many tests simultaneously with the devices. The benefits over current methods will be substantial: a painless, safe and user-friendly way to draw and test blood, with rapid reporting of results to health professionals and patients.

column36: Understanding Diagnostic Pathways of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Towards Improving the Timely Identification and Care of Girls and Women
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is reported to be four to five times more common in boys than in girls. The methods and criteria for diagnosing ASD, however, are largely based on studies with boys, which recent research suggests may overlook girls and women who present differently. Indeed, girls and women with ASD are at a greater risk of being identified at a later age and, as a result, often miss critical opportunities to access early interventions and timely supports. Many women report that they go undiagnosed or are misdiagnosed with other psychiatric conditions (e.g., psychosis, anxiety, personality disorders) before receiving their ASD diagnosis; however, no research to date has systematically examined this issue. The proposed study aims to better understand why girls and women with ASD are often under-recognized, as well as their associated healthcare needs. To do this, I will conduct a two-phase mixed methods study. First, I will use Ontario health administrative and billing data to examine the diagnostic pathways (i.e., the "routes" leading to diagnosis) of women who received their ASD diagnoses as adults. Next, I will compare the health outcomes (e.g., clinical profiles and service use patterns) of women with ASD who received their diagnosis as children with a) women with ASD who received their diagnosis as adults; b) equivalent groups of men with ASD; c) women and men without ASD. Finally, to help contextualize the quantitative results, I will conduct qualitative interviews with front line primary care providers (e.g., family physicians, paediatricians) as well as referral-based specialists (e.g., psychiatrists, developmental paediatricians) concerning current ASD assessment and care practices for females. This research will generate much-needed information to reduce sex/gender diagnostic and care biases and will assist in creating training materials to help clinicians better identify and care for girls and women with ASD.

column36: Identifying the neural correlates of social cognitive performance in schizophrenia spectrum disorders: A dimensional, data-driven approach
column37: Impaired social functioning is often a defining feature of individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). These patients exhibit deficits in social processes such as identifying emotions and understanding things from the perspectives of others. Such impairments are profoundly debilitating and have been linked to the ability to function in daily life. To date, investigations in SSDs tend to compare patients versus healthy individuals, and often include small sample sizes and patients with different levels of impairment, impeding the identification of consistent treatment targets. Indeed, there are currently no approved treatment options for these symptoms. Two circuits in the brain have been implicated in key social abilities affected in SSDs. However, early data from our lab suggests that subgroups of individuals may activate these brain circuits differently, which may result in different profiles of social behaviour and function among these groups. Thus, brain circuit abnormalities may differ in subgroups of people showing different levels of social impairment. In the present study, patients with SSDs and healthy individuals complete social tasks during brain imaging, as well as social and cognitive measures outside the scanner. We will take advantage of the range of social impairment seen in patients with SSDs, determining for the first time whether activation in these social brain networks predicts social performance across a very large sample of patients and healthy individuals. Novel methods will also be used to identify uniquely informative subgroups of participants generated based on these brain-behaviour associations. Critically, these findings should accelerate the identification of treatment targets and inform development of biologically based treatments for social deficits in individuals with SSDs.

column36: Development of a Mobile-based Application for Monitoring Functional Gains and Maintenance After Treatment for Youth at Risk of Psychosis
column37: Mental illness typically develops in adolescence, causing serious disruptions in youth's interaction with peers, family members, and their ability to perform well at school or at work. Current research has already been able to identify early possible signs of psychosis e.g. confusion about what is real or imaginary or feeling suspicious. These youth are considered to be at clinical high risk (CHR) for developing psychosis. Several studies have followed these youth over the years to see how many of them will develop psychosis, and to explore possible reasons for this to happen. One of the major concerns among these CHR youth is a decrease in their ability to function in social situations, at school or at work, and it is important to address them to avoid starting a spiral of loneliness and detachment from peers, discontinuation of hobbies, school, and impairment in work-related activities. To tackle such difficulties, we are currently conducting with CHR youth who have difficulties in social and school or work functioning to participate in a group treatment study that is testing the short-term effectiveness of a specialized treatment to address social functioning. Expert clinicians help youth to practice social skills, improve problem solving and learn new strategies. Given youth's enthusiasm for new technologies, we propose to assess the maintenance of the skills learned in the group through a mobile-based application that will be developed for this treatment and used at the end of the group treatment. This method of follow-up will provide continuously available support to the study participants, and it is anonymous, non-stigmatizing and gives researchers real-time information. One of the features of the tool is the provision of feedback on participants' social and school or work functioning by showing visual charts on a daily basis. We believe the feedback will improve the maintenance of the skills gained through the group intervention.

column36: The role of pericardial macrophages in cardiac repair
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. 14,000 Canadians die every year from a heart attack, which is 1 person every 40 minutes. Furthermore, the individuals that do survive typically live with a heart that does not function as efficiently and over time will fail. This dramatically impacts the quality of life of these individuals and is also associated with high costs to the Canadian economy. We are trying to understand what goes on in the heart after an injury to find better ways to treat patients. Inflammation, which is driven by our immune system, is known to play an important role in the healing response after a heart attack. Different cells of the immune system can contribute differently to healing in the body, with some promoting while others blocking repair of the injured area. The balance between these two sides during the inflammatory response will ultimately determine how well the heart will function and whether failure will occur. To better understand what is happening at the level of the injury we will be using high-powered microscopes to see the immune system in action within the heart. This will provide us with key information on how different components of the immune cells interact with one another and other cells of the heart to influence the healing process. Our aim is to identify key cells and molecules that are crucial to promoting optimal repair of the heart. This in turn could lead to designing new treatments that will help preserve the function of the heart and ultimately delay or prevent failure in patients who have suffered a heart attack. This collectively will contribute to saving lives and improving the quality of life of Canadians as well as minimizing the financial burden associated with heart disease.

column36: Quantitative imaging of fluorescent Cav3.2 T-type calcium channel biosensor: a novel tool for studying processing of pain signals.
column37: The proper communication between neurons is an important determinant of nervous system function. Malfunction in the communication system between nerve cells can lead to a number of disorders, including chronic pain. Chronic pain is a prevalent problem and it is considered a debilitating condition that affects up to 1.5 Billion people worldwide and bears a tremendous socioeconomic burden. Many chronic pain conditions are not easily treated and new therapeutic avenues are needed. Cav3.2 T-type calcium channels have a key role in regulating electrical pulses in sensing nerve cells and they have emerged as an attractive therapeutic target to treat inflammatory and neuropathic pain. However, to date in vivo studies have been hampered by our inability to record Cav3.2 channel activity at nerve terminals in the spinal dorsal horn. The research outlined in this application explores the contribution of Cav3.2 T-type channels currents to inflammatory and neuropathic pain in vivo using a strategy that combines molecular biology, genetic engineering, electrophysiology, optogenetics and microscopy. We will report, using real time resolution, for the very first time the activity of Cav3.2 T-type channels in the spinal dorsal horn in vivo, thus gaining unparalleled insights into the processing of pain signals. By understanding the regulation of Cav3.2 T-type channels in the spinal dorsal horn, we will shed new light on the cellular mechanisms that give rise to inflammatory and neuropathic pain are present. In the long term, this in turn can be exploited towards new avenues for treatment of chronic pain.

column36: Development and evaluation of a remote robotic ultrasound clinic model to improve access to medical imaging in northern and Indigenous communities
column37: Ultrasound imaging is essential for many medical diagnoses; however, this imaging modality is not available in many northern and remote communities because of a lack of on-site sonographers and radiologists. An emerging solution to increase access to ultrasound imaging is telerobotic sonography. Telerobotic ultrasound systems allow sonographers or radiologists based at a central site to remotely perform ultrasound examinations, allowing patients to receive the care they need in their home community and avoid transport to another facility. The objective of my research is to determine whether a robotic ultrasound clinic is a viable model to increase access to ultrasound imaging for patients in northern and remote communities. I will explore the lived experiences and perceived needs of northern Indigenous community members in accessing ultrasound imaging through interviews. I will then use these findings to inform the design and implementation of a pilot remote robotic ultrasound clinic in a northern Canadian Indigenous community which does not have access to local ultrasound services. I will evaluate the effect of this clinic on patient management and ultrasound imaging utilization, determine best practices for establishing a robotic ultrasound clinic, and conduct a cost analysis comparing a robotic ultrasound clinic and a conventional ultrasound clinic to which patients must travel. Finally, using provincial ultrasound imaging utilization data, I will use spatial analysis and GIS mapping to determine where additional supports for ultrasound imaging are most needed, with a view to scale up the proposed robotic ultrasound clinic model. Findings from this research will inform the development of robotic ultrasound clinics, enabling more patients to receive ultrasound imaging in their home community. This may reduce time to diagnosis and treatment, improve health outcomes and patient satisfaction, reduce strain on major referral hospitals, and reduce healthcare costs.

column36: The Impact of Altered Nutrient Intake or Metformin Treatment on Genome Structure and Function in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) Fibroblasts
column37: Hutchinson Gilford-Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) is a rare premature aging disease affecting 1 in 4 million live births. Children with HGPS exhibit parallel but highly accelerated features of aging, including; hair loss, loss of fat deposits under the skin, arthritis and brittle bones. These children usually succumb to heart attack or stroke at ~14 years of age. HGPS is caused by a mutation in the laminA/C gene, generating the toxic protein Progerin. Progerin accumulates within the cell, disrupting the function and organization of the patient's genetic material (the genome), causing cells to become "old" (senescent) at a faster rate. No effective therapeutic strategies exist for the treatment of HGPS; however, the immunosuppressant rapamycin has been reported to stimulate Progerin degradation. Although promising, potential severe side effects of rapamycin have generated concern over its use as a treatment for HGPS. The aim of this project is to explore alternative treatment strategies that promote Progerin degradation and restoration of normal genome function and organization. Depletion of the essential amino acids leucine and arginine, glucose restriction as well as treatment with the anti-diabetic drug metformin function similarly to rapamycin but with fewer side effects. As metformin is already used to treat type 2 diabetes and is safe in humans, it is a logical choice as a potential HGPS treatment. The aim of this proposed research is to determine if depleted levels of amino acids/glucose or metformin can: 1) stimulate Progerin degradation, 2) decrease rates of cellular senescence and 3) re-establish normal function and organization of the genome within HGPS cells. These findings will not only provide alternative treatment strategies for patients with HGPS, but also -as increased levels of Progerin have been detected in aged cells from healthy humans-provide novel understanding of the underlying biological processes of aging.

column36: Novel 3D bioprinted human cardiac tissue models for drug safety and efficacy testing.
column37: During human clinical trials, a large percentage of candidate drugs fail because they are unsafe or ineffective. Even when pre-clinical cell and animal studies seem positive, problems occur because tests done with drugs on these models are often not predictive of what happens in humans. Much of this is due to significant differences in biology between species. For instance, ion channels (membrane proteins through which heart cells conduct electrical currents) can vary between humans and animals. Many drugs, including non-cardiovascular drugs, target these ion channels in the heart, which can potentially result in lethal arrhythmias. Thus, it is critical to use preclinical models that can closely reproduce what happens in humans to better predict drug safety. To streamline the therapeutic development pipeline, we will develop a novel 3D bioprinted human cardiac tissue model which will improve the translational science process for predicting whether drugs will be safe and effective in humans. The goal is to develop 3D human cardiac tissue structure(s) that closely model the electrophysiological properties of the human heart, relevant to impulse conduction and arrhythmia generation. We will use commercially available human induced-pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes and novel microfluidic based 3D bioprinting technology and methodologies to build the 3D cardiac tissue. Ultimately, these models are expected to replace the use of animals to screen drugs for safety and efficacy. To validate our models, we will evaluate the cardiotoxicity potential of a range of known compounds, and compare the outcome with data obtained using current standard assays. It takes on average over $2.5 billion to develop and gain marketing approval for a new drug. About $100 million is required to complete the pre-clinical studies alone. Using novel bioprinted models of cardiac tissue is expected to significantly cut the cost and time of bringing a new drug to market.

column36: Using a Brief Psychological Intervention to Facilitate Social Integration and Improve Mental Health Among Mostly Heterosexual Young Adults During the Transition Into College
column37: Despite their invisibility, mostly heterosexual (MH) people outnumber the sum of gay, lesbian, and bisexual people. MH refers to heterosexual people who sometimes have same-sex sexuality. It is estimated that 11-16% of women and 2-6% of men are MH, and that this proportion peaks in young adults. To date, no research has studied MH young adults in Canada. Alarmingly, however, MH people in the U.S. report more mental disorders than exclusively heterosexual (EH) people. This finding suggests that in Canada, there is likely a large group of young adults being overlooked by health researchers and professionals. In two studies, I propose to (1) investigate the mental health of MH first-year college students, for the first time in Canada, and (2) facilitate social integration and reduce mental health problems among them, using a brief online psychological intervention. Study 1 will prospectively examine mental health disparities between MH and EH first-year college students, as well as the underlying roles of social integration and internalized homophobia. Study 2 will use a one-session online video intervention, adapted from prior successful self-affirmation interventions, to ease transition into college and to narrow the mental health gap of MH young adults. The findings from this research can be used to develop healthcare policies and allocate resources to a disadvantaged group of Canadians who have been previously underrepresented. Our psychological intervention has the potential to reduce mental health disparities in stigmatized Canadians who experience same-sex sexuality.

column36: Young adulthood, 'coming of age' in lifecourse epidemiology? Uncovering how transitions towards adulthood contribute to social inequalities in health across age and time
column37: Young adults (ages 18-25) are facing increasingly worrying trends with regard to health-related practices such as smoking, problem drinking, poor diet, substance abuse, unsafe sexual practices, and health care services underuse after adolescence. Their implications are further obfuscated by recent changes in young adults' transition through education, employment, family, and housing arrangements. Better understanding how these current trends intertwine is crucial because we know very little of the consequences that these will play on the rest of these individuals' lives as they become full-fledged adults. The period of young adulthood is, therefore, increasingly understood as a key period in the development of health and health inequalities across the life-course. While an important scholarship addressing these issues has emerged at the crossroads of psychology, sociology, and demography, there is still a paucity of work inside public health developing a comprehensive understanding of the experiences and needs of young adults today. In response, this project seeks to advance our understanding of young adults' transitions and health-related practices during young adulthood and midlife. This project will investigate these issues using four renowned British studies spanning three generations: the (1958) National Child Development Study, the 1970 British Birth Cohort, the Next Steps study and the Understanding Society study. This project will contribute to develop a stronger scholarship able to inform how public health research, policy, and practice should understand young adults and address their needs. This project will start in Fall 2018 in collaboration with Professors Amanda Sacker and Ingrid Schoon at the "International Center on Lifecourse Studies in Society and Health" at University College London (UCL) in London, UK.

column36: The Role of Material Security in Improving Health for People Who Use Drugs
column37: It is well known that access to sufficient and stable income promotes health. Material security (e.g.,housing, food, and service access) may operate distinctly from income security yet may also be critically important to health. column36: Prediabetes in youth: understanding the role of prenatal and early childhood dietary behaviors
column37: Type 2 diabetes in children and youth is on the rise, largely due to increased rates of obesity and unhealthy lifestyle. Prediabetes is defined as abnormal blood sugar levels associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes and it affects one in every six overweight adolescents. Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents are serious conditions which are poorly understood, which limits the development of effective preventive strategies. We aim to study the influence of mothers' diet during pregnancy and childhood dietary quality on adolescent prediabetes and future risk of developing diabetes. Project Viva is a unique study including over 1000 mother-child pairs for whom data is available during pregnancy, at birth, during infancy (6 months), at early childhood (3 years), mid-childhood (8 years), and early adolescence (13 years). Data was collected in both mothers and children and include: lifestyle (detailed dietary information, physical activity and sleep), metabolic profile based on collected blood samples, socio-demographic data (income, education, etc.) and body weight. This project will allow us to gain a comprehensive understanding on the role of diet, both before and after birth, in the risk of diabetes in adolescents. Diabetes in the pediatric population is a growing public health concern because they carry the burden of diabetes for many more years, leading to greater risk of complications and at an earlier stage of life. Identifying individuals at greater risk for life-long diabetes at an earlier stage could contribute to the development of efficient preventive strategies.

column36: Engineering flagellin-specific Tregs to restore intestinal homeostasis in IBD
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of severe, incurable chronic conditions which affect approximately 1/150 Canadians. IBD results from uncontrolled inflammation in the gut, causing symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bleeding and weight loss. IBD is driven by an imbalance of various types of immune cells which are normally present in specific proportions. I am interested in two cell types: effector T cells (Teff) which help fight infections, and regulatory T cells (Treg) which control Teffs and prevent healthy cells from being accidently attacked. In IBD, too few Tregs are present in the gut thus uncontrolled Teffs end up attacking intestinal tissues. Studies in humans have demonstrated that injecting large numbers of Tregs can help restore the balance of Teffs and Tregs in the gut and inhibit IBD. However, obtaining enough cells to accomplish this is difficult. In this project, I will investigate whether Tregs can be made more potent such that the number of Tregs required to treat IBD is reduced. Research has shown that Tregs which specifically recognise intestinal molecules are better at inhibiting IBD. This is partially because intestine-specific Tregs stay in the gut instead of circulating throughout the body. A molecule often found in the gut which is expressed by E.coli and commonly attacked in IBD patients is "flagellin". In this project, I aim to increase the therapeutic potency of Tregs by genetically modifying them to recognise flagellin. I will investigate whether flagellin-specific Tregs suppress IBD development/progression more effectively than unmodified Tregs in three models of IBD, including a humanised mouse model. I will then re-engineer this approach to be suitable for clinical use. Overall, I expect my findings to critically inform the future clinical investigation of flagellin-specific Tregs for treating IBD. This work can potentially transform how IBD is treated, offering a highly desirable cure with minimal side-effects.

column36: Towards healthy environmental assessment in British Columbia, Canada: Incorporating health imperatives and the determinants of health into natural resource governance
column37: Resource development both positively and negatively influences the determinants of health in resource-dependent communities, many of which are located in rural and remote locations across northern British Columbia. Despite being an identified pillar of environmental assessment (EA) regulation in British Columbia, health is typically analyzed through the lens of biophysical exposure risks and direct health impacts as part of a 'desktop review' of baseline data. Indeed, the limited inclusion of the determinants of health in EA processes has been documented provincially, nationally and internationally due to limitations of capacity and expertise, poor intersectional and disciplinary collaboration, and the need for transparency and efficiency in assessment. This project takes a "health in all policies" approach to consider how the social and ecological determinants of health can be better accounted for in EA processes to promote upstream drivers of health and well-being. Through a combination of policy analysis, surveys, interviews and capacity-building workshops with diverse sectors involved in EA certification (e.g. First Nations Lands officers, industry proponents, EA practitioners, health authority staff, and a variety of other provincial ministerial contacts), this research seeks to promote a new generation of intersectoral engagement in resource governance processes. Specifically, it leverages lessons from across sectors to enhance collaboration during EA certification, bolster monitoring and surveillance of the determinants of health in the EA process, and thereby improve capacity of the many actors examining and responding to population health and health equity impacts of resource development.

column37: Ovarian cancer is one of the most serious cancers for women, and although it ranks as only the 5th most common women's cancer, its average 5-year survival rate is only 45%. It is well accepted that early diagnosis is the key to extend survival in ovarian cancer patients. CA 125 is a protein existing in most ovarian cancer cells which can be measured in blood, and therefore is widely used in the clinic for screening of primary ovarian cancer and of cancer recurrence. However, it has been estimated that with the current technology for measuring blood CA 125, the tumor cannot be detected until it has grown for more than 10 years, to a few centimeters, because the existing blood assay is not sensitive enough to detect the protein at very low concentrations. There is an urgent need for low-cost, effective (evidence-based), and easily accessible interventions targeting middle-age men's SSE and CSE, as part of the overall effort to decrease melanoma-related mortality in this population.

column36: Delineating BRCA1-driven Breast Cancer With Single Cell Genomics
column37: Breast cancer is one of the most prevalent forms of cancer in women worldwide. Despite recent advances in understanding the initiation and progression of breast cancer, prognosis still remains poor. Detection and diagnosis of precancerous lesions and tumors early have the potential to improve treatment and reduce cancer-related deaths. Heterogeneity within the cell population is a striking feature of many tumors. Malignant disease may be mainly driven by rare subpopulations of tumor cells, and tumor cell heterogeneity may complicate therapies due to resistant clones within the population of cells. The goal of this interdisciplinary project is to develop a systems-level analysis pipeline to study cell heterogeneity during early tumorigenesis and advanced stage breast cancer in unprecedented resolution. We will implement a recently developed single cell RNA sequencing platform to reveal the gene expression within individual normal human breast epithelial cells and compare the spectrum of cellular heterogeneity to that of tissue of early stages of breast cancer and in more progressed triple negative breast cancer. We will apply and develop identify distinct ell types and states, their specific markers, and how they relate to each other within their path of cancer development. In doing so, we will unravel early systematic changes that occur in breast cancer. Understanding the systems-level changes during breast tumorigenesis in single cell resolution stages may will lead to the identification of novel biomarkers for early cancer detection and may form the basis for the development of therapeutic approaches to prevent breast cancer from progressing into a life threatening condition.

column36: Contribution to neuroinflammation of immunometabolic reprogramming of resident microglia and infiltrating macrophages
column37: Macrophages are tissue-resident cells that fulfill homeostatic functions, notably in the central nervous system. Following assault, they become activated and secrete mediators that lead to a local inflammation (neuroinflammation). Moreover, large numbers of infiltrating macrophages exert inflammatory effects that contribute to neuroinflammation. Even though resident and infiltrating macrophages may have differing immunological functions and roles, these are dependent on their metabolism (a phenomenon called immunometabolism). As such, metabolic reprogramming can modulate macrophage functions, and subsequently their role, including their inflammatory activities and participation in the development of disease. While controlled inflammation is required to resolve an assault and repair damage, its exacerbation can result in permanent damage and debilitating disabilities. Indeed, exacerbated neuroinflammation is responsible for numerous life-threatening diseases whose burden on human health in Canada is extensive. However, information regarding the contribution to neuroinflammation of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming remains largely unknown. Consequently, the goal of this project is to study this contribution using a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Firstly, the metabolic processes of resident and infiltrating macrophages modulated during neuroinflammation, in comparison with homeostasis, will be identified. Thereafter the role of this reprogramming on the immunological functions of macrophages will be evaluated using cells isolated from mice deficient for key metabolic pathways and/or specific checkpoints previously identified. Finally, the contribution of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming to neuroinflammation and the development of and outcome of disease will be assessed using these same deficient mice. In summary, this project aims to dissect the contribution to neuroinflammation of macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming

column36: Developing resilience to obesogenic food environments through food literacy
column37: More Canadians now die from diseases caused by poor diet than from smoking-related illnesses, and diets low in fruit and vegetable intake cost Canadians 3.3 billion dollars a year. The food environment profoundly influences diet and is associated with diseases such as obesity and diabetes. This environment has evolved so that children and adolescents are constantly fed cues to consume unhealthy foods. Nutrition "knowledge" may come from social media or advertisements and slick marketing may shape food preferences. All of these factors affect current and future dietary practices. Food literacy is the foundation of healthy dietary practices and provides youth with an opportunity to build resilience to unhealthy food environments. Yet, we know very little about how food literacy is acquired and the level of literacy needed to make healthy dietary decisions. The proposed research will address these knowledge gaps. The purpose of this study is to examine the connections between food literacy, food environments and health indicators among youth. To address the knowledge gaps, we will conduct 1) an environmental scan of food literacy learning opportunities for children and adolescents (consisting of a scoping review, interviews with practitioners followed by a survey) and 2) a cross-sectional survey on food literacy, food environments and health indicators among youth. Results will be translated to practitioners and policy makers through guidelines for enhancing food literacy to promote optimal health. Food literacy will equip youth with the abilities, knowledge and self-efficacy to make healthy food choices, which will reduce risk for diseases and decrease healthcare costs. This research will strengthen Health Canada's healthy eating strategy to improve healthy eating and protect vulnerable populations by understanding how to improve food literacy and make healthy dietary choices in unhealthy food environments.

column36: Impact of Food Production Compounds on Human Microbiota & Metabolic Health
column37: Obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) impact over 25% of adults in Canada and cost the health care system over $20B annually. The gut flora is involved in all three of these metabolic diseases. Our food supply has been affected by changes in agricultural production, food additives, and food packaging over the past several decades. These toxicants in our food supply may modulation of the gut flora and thus alter metabolic activity and contribute to metabolic disease. I aim to identify and characterize how food production compounds and additives contribute to altered metabolic activity in obesity, T2D, and NAFLD, through regulation of the gut microbiome. I will create a rapid screening system to determine bacterial response to our toxicants library of food additives and contaminants. I will then culture the gut flora and screen for bacteria that respond to our toxicants library. The most responsive bacteria will be used to colonize mice that are initially free of any bacteria (germ-free) with and without exposure to the toxicants. We will measure the metabolic outcomes, allowing me to make the connection from gut bacteria to metabolic disease. We will compare results from these mice to uncolonized germ-free mice that are treated with the same chemicals or additives to concretely indicate a causative role for the microbiome. This research will identify chemical exposures through our diet that may be implicated in metabolic disease. Identifying these compounds will provide necessary information to create change in government policy regarding their use in the food industry. Improving food production and understanding metabolic alterations in response to toxicants will improve public health and spur novel therapeutic avenues for the treatment of increasingly prevalent metabolic diseases.

column37: Optimal early brain development is vital to health and success in life. Since development of the brain begins at conception, maternal health problems, dietary imbalances, and physical inactivity in pregnancy can lead to emotional and behavioural problems in offspring early in life. Many Canadian women consume an unhealthy diet and/or fail to get enough exercise during pregnancy. It is not surprising then that up to 40% of women enter pregnancy overweight and that up to 75% gain too much weight during pregnancy. Despite these facts, no studies in humans have examined if interventions that optimize maternal diet and exercise during pregnancy can improve brain development in offspring. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a study that will follow the children born to the 400 women that will be enrolled in a study of a nutrition+exercise intervention in pregnancy. The nutrition component consists of a nutrition plan tailored to women's needs, as well as sessions with a dietitian. Our exercise intervention involves women engaging in a structured and monitored walking program. In this study, half of the women will receive our nutrition+exercise program and the other half will receive treatment as usual by their healthcare providers. Our objective is to determine if fetal exposure to the nutrition+exercise intervention leads to improved emotional and behavioural development in offspring in the first 36 months of life compared to women who receive usual pregnancy care. We hypothesize that emotional and behavioural functioning will be superior in the offspring of women exposed to the intervention and the function of an area of the brain that is very important to the development of emotional coping will be optimized. If offspring brain development and behaviour can be improved via a nutrition+exercise program during pregnancy, it could be used to prevent or reduce the severity of emotional and behavioural problems in offspring with benefits across the lifespan.

column36: A Generic Rating of Allograft Function after Transplantation (GRAFT)
column37: Deceased organ donors provide many organs for transplant to individuals with failing hearts, livers, kidneys and other organs. Optimal care of deceased donors in the intensive care units may increase the number of available organs, and promote their long-term survival. For future users, we will develop user-friend organ-specific guidelines and test the inter-rater reliability. The development of our tool will better facilitate the conduct of future research to improve the care of deceased organ donors and increase the availability and function of donated organs.

column36: Beyond Function: Exploring Participation in Life Roles in People with COPD
column37: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a lung condition that makes it hard for people to breathe. Treatment for people with COPD usually focuses on helping them walk for longer and manage their breathing problems. A patient's ability to participate in life roles by visiting with friends and taking care of loved ones is another important part of health. Unfortunately, this is an area not often considered in people with COPD. In fact, people with COPD often say they feel alone and like they have lost their identity. In order to find ways to increase participation in people with COPD we need to start by finding an accurate and valid tool to measure it. Objective: We will test the ability of a questionnaire to measure participation in COPD. We will also see if our usual treatment has any effect on participation. Method: One hundred people with COPD in Toronto and Hamilton will complete a few questionnaires and physical tests. We will ask some of those people to complete the questionnaire a second time within one week. People with COPD who are starting a rehabilitation program will complete the participation questionnaire and some related tests at the beginning and end of their programs. This will tell us if the participation questionnaire measures what it should, if it can detect any change in participation that happens with rehabilitation and if there is meaningful change in participation during the program. Importance: This will be the first study to show the measurement abilities of this questionnaire in people with COPD. It will also be the first study to show if the usual treatment for people with COPD does anything to change participation. These projects will help us develop new treatments to increase participation in people with COPD. Being able to participate in life roles is important to patients so this will have a positive impact on their lives.

column36: Improved Cancer Immunotherapy for Breast Tumours
column37: Breast cancer is a disease that accounts for almost one quarter of all cancers in women. Though current treatment regimens have shown success with early stage primary tumors, there are few to no treatments that can successfully treat aggressive forms, prevent metastasis or completely cure advanced metastatic disease. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) (a subtype negative for hormonal biomarkers) holds an overall dismal clinical outcome due to lack of expression of targets for therapy and as such, patients routinely undergo aggressive regimens of chemotherapy. These regimens come with a multitude of side effects, including high levels of toxicity and an increased risk of developing other forms of cancer later in life. Immunotherapy, a form of therapy that boosts the immune system to fight cancer cells, has gained increasing prominence in recent years largely due to its safety and astonishing success rates. Some chemotherapies can be classified as immunotherapies when administered at low doses, as they stimulate the immune system. Checkpoint blockade is another form of immunotherapy that uses antibodies to initiate the death of cancer cells. It is clinically approved for various forms of cancer and has become a first line treatment for melanoma. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are another promising form of immunotherapy that selectively kill cancer cells, showing little to no toxicity in healthy cells. They have exhibited excellent clinical tolerability, even when used at high viral doses. For our work, we propose to exploit and improve upon accumulating clinical knowledge in the development of immunotherapies for TNBC. The proposed studies will focus on clinical relevance and translation in order to generate a new treatment regime that displays minimal toxicity and simultaneously exerts anticancer effects on both primary and metastatic lesions. Although this proposal is specific to breast cancer, the underlying concepts can be applied to many other forms of cancer.

column37: Introduction: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) accounts for more than one-third of total global deaths. Although there has been a decline in CVD over the last three decades, the rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are expected to rise in high-risk ethnic communities. Also, recent evidence suggests that the development of CVD risk factors is influenced by pregnancy-related factors. To better understand these factors, the Aboriginal Birth Cohort (ABC) and South Asian Birth Cohort (START) are recruiting mother-baby pairs from the Six Nations reserve and Peel region, respectively. In parallel to high quality research, it is vital to create accessible avenues for meaningful knowledge translation. Because pregnancy is a time period where women feel especially motivated to make positive lifestyle changes, it makes for an optimal time for knowledge translation. Objectives: In my PhD program, I seek to develop and test novel knowledge translation tools to improve the knowledge of pregnancy-related T2DM risk factors in high-risk communities (Indigenous and South Asian). Methods: A mixed-methods approach of quantitative and qualitative methodologies will be used to develop and test a knowledge translation intervention. Descriptive statistics will be used to compile existing data from two birth cohort studies (START and ABC, both being conducted by my supervisor) on the causes and consequences of these risk factors. A qualitative approach will be used to thematically explore knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and behaviour change. Participants for the qualitative study will be purposely sampled and recruited via the cohort studies' regular clinic visits. Integrated KT methodology will be used to distill the research data to develop products alongside key stakeholders. Conclusion: Now more than ever, it is imperative to integrate knowledge translation approaches to warrant the application of research results to practice and support the improvement of primary care.

column36: A systems approach for enhancing perinatal care regionalization

Maternal, fetal and neonatal morbidity and morbidity rates will also be assessed especially in rural and remote communities. The project will identify problems with regionalization of perinatal care and ascertain lacunae in the organization of services. Recommendations will be formulated in collaboration with provincial/territorial stakeholders. This initiative has the potential to significantly enhance the care of mothers and babies in Canada.

column36: Understanding the mechanistic influence of early colonizing microbes on immune development and disease
column37: Asthma is the most common childhood disease within developed countries. Asthma occurs when the immune system mistakenly targets lung tissue with an inflammatory response. Typically, asthma symptoms do not arise until 3-5 years of age, however, growing evidence suggests that events that happen much earlier in life play a pivotal role. Immediately after birth, infants are colonized by a diverse set of microbes that collectively make up the microbiota, and early colonizers have a profound effect on the developing immune system. Four members of the microbiota, Faecalibacterium, Lachnospira, Veillonella, and Rothia (FLVR), are present within the first 100 days in infants who are protected from asthma. These microbes can also provide similar protection in mouse models of asthma. Introducing FLVR to children at risk of developing asthma has the potential to be an effective preventative treatment, however it is important to first understand how these microbes are influencing the developing immune system. Microbes interact with the immune system by producing proteins and metabolites that act as messages. I aim to determine which messages FLVR are sending to immune cells to prevent harmful targeting of lung tissue. Additionally, children with asthma often develop allergies as well. I aim to determine whether FLVR therapies can be expanded to protect against two common food allergies, egg and peanut. column36: Developing a wellness focused self-management program for colorectal cancer survivors using a patient-oriented research approach.
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second most common cancer in Canada. Through more aggressive treatments and earlier diagnosis, more people are living after a diagnosis of CRC. CRC and treatments, can have negative long-term effects including poor quality of life, changes to physical health (fatigue, bowel changes, poor sleep, poor physical functioning) and changes to mental health (fear of recurrence, anxiety, depression, social isolation). CRC patients also need to navigate the health system for ongoing follow-up. Current models of care focus on detection of disease recurrence lack a holistic and coordinated approach. Chronic disease models of care, including self-management strategies, although successful in other populations have not been widely adopted in cancer. Self-management can empower and enable patients to maintain their health and wellness and understand how to navigate the system. The aim of this research is to examine health outcomes and health needs of CRC survivors to inform the development of a self-management program. The research has three objectives. 1. To use Alberta Health administrative databases to evaluate patient-reported and clinical outcomes in CRC patients. 2. To evaluate the efficacy of cancer self-management interventions. 3. To explore CRC patients' and clinicians' perspectives on health care needs and self-management. This study is significant because its addresses a gap in the care currently provided to CRC patients and will provide novel information on effective strategies for CRC patient care. Information from this research will inform the development of a self-management program for CRC patients tailored to their unique needs. With numbers of CRC patients expected to increase, and diminishing health care resources, optimal wellness may be realized through patients managing their own health and understanding how to navigate the system.

column36: Interactions between cilia and folic acid during craniofacial development
column37: This research aims to better understand the relationship between craniofacial birth defects and epigenetic factors, of which folate is one. Birth defects are highly variable, even amongst children with the same genetic mutation, likely resulting from epigenetic modification. These epigenetic changes are changes that affect how genes are expressed, without changing the genetic sequence itself. Folate, a folic acid derivative, was added to the Canadian grain supply in 1998 to reduce spinal cord closure defects such as Spina Bifida. Folic acid appears to change how the DNA is expressed. Fortification has reduced the number of infants born with spinal cord defects. It is not understood how folate prevents these types of birth defects, though it may be due to epigenetic effects. Further, the links between folic acid and other birth defects, such as craniofacial birth defects, remains unclear. Importantly, recent data suggest that in some cases folic acid may actually increase the severity of spinal cord defects in mice. Paradoxically, this may reduce the apparent frequency of defects at birth by increasing mortality in utero, possibly by increasing the kinds and severities of the defects. These specific cases involve a structure called the cilia, which helps transmit signals within and between cells. Our preliminary data show that alteration of cilia in the mouse generates variation in how the embryo grows and develops, and alteration of cilia genes can increase variance in the shape of the face and lead to birth defects. We propose to examine how folate and cilia interact during development of the face and to examine how folate can affect birth defects in the face.

column36: INSIDE-OUT: Unveiling predictors of childhood asthma
column37: Lungs are for life, and we don't think about them much. Yet, even small babies can have serious lung diseases, like asthma which is a life-long problem. In fact, asthma is the most common long-term illness that starts in very early life. In asthma, the breathing passages becomes red, swollen and "twitchy" so they sometimes go into spasm, making it very hard to breathe. Asthma has no cure. Even if they feel fine, people with asthma still have the disease and it can flare up at any time. In Canada, asthma is the most common and burdensome chronic non-communicable disease affecting young Canadians. This is a segment of the population deserving special attention given their age, vulnerability and the burden at the societal and economic level: 1-in-3 Canadians will be diagnosed with asthma in their lifetime. It isn't clear why only some people get asthma, but we think it is probably due to a combination of environmental and inherited (genetic) factors. The goal of the proposed research is to understand environmental and genetic factors that cause asthma in children. We will use samples and data from a large Canadian study, where the mothers and babies were assessed in pregnancy, at birth, and up to age 5 years. We will determine effects of carefully-chosen environmental factors predicted to be related to asthma: traffic pollution, neighboring green spaces, and types of bacteria living in our intestines. Early life is a critical period to shape the later life health, especially through epigenetics mechanism: changes in the function of our genes in relation to environmental influences provide a basis to explain how and why asthma and allergies exist and progress. We hope to gain new understanding to create better tools to predict who will get asthma and find ways to prevent asthma from developing in the first place.

column36: The proteomic and metabolomic characterization of clear cell ovarian carcinoma: towards better management strategies
column37: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death for women from cancers, with about 25,000 women diagnosed in North America each year. Ovarian cancer is divided into subtypes based on molecular characteristics and clinical outcome. Although we have understood ovarian cancer as many diseases, the treatment has remained the same for the past 30 years for all subtypes - untargeted platinum-based chemotherapy. Clear cell ovarian cancer (CCOC) is the second most common subtype of ovarian cancer affecting many women. At late stage, it is more aggressive and resistant to current chemotherapy compared to other subtypes. Although deadly, CCOC is still not well understood and lacks effective targeted therapy. Existing molecular and genomic studies suggest that it is a metabolically driven malignancy, but its metabolic profile has not yet been studied. This research will be the first characterization of a large cohort of clinical cases of CCOC using protein expression in conjunction with global metabolite profiling. Understanding of the altered metabolism in CCOC will revolutionize the ovarian cancer research community and provide strong foundations on which to build further discoveries. Most importantly, we hope that identifying targetable metabolic pathways will guide the development of more effective therapies to help patients with this deadly disease.
