column36: Examining the role of sexual relationship power inequity on multi-levelled drivers of HIV vulnerability for young women in an HIV hyper-endemic setting of South Africa
column37: On average 2,000 young women (YW) in South Africa acquire HIV every week, representing the highest new infection rates globally. Emerging research has begun to examine and act upon the multiple-intersecting factors that place YW at increased risk for HIV. High-levels of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and immature vaginal lining make YW more biologically susceptible to HIV. HIV risk for YW is also elevated due to social factors. Our previous work has found that YW experience high-levels of sexual relationship power inequity (SRPI), which compromises their agency to negotiate safe sex, impacts mental health, and heightens their risk of STIs/HIV. Evidence is needed to examine how socio-relational factors intersect with biological risk. As such, this proposed research seeks to examine and explore measures of SRPI and how SRPI influences biological, relational, and structural HIV vulnerabilities for YW growing-up within HIV hyper-endemic settings. Using prospective data from a youth-centered sexual reproductive health study conducted among South African youth aged 16-24 over an 18-month period, the objectives of this proposal are to 1) examine how SRPI influences STI treatment uptake, partner notification and STI incidence, 2) explore the pathway from SRPI to heightened biological susceptibility through it's influence on markers of stress and inflammation and 3) explore how SRPI is measured, conceived and influences the sexual decision-making practices and health-seeking behaviours of young men and women. As international targets aim to achieve an AIDS-free generation by 2030, this research merging biological and socio-behavioural data to examine the factors impacting heightened HIV-risk for YW living at the epicentre of the HIV epidemic is extremely timely. Moreover, the proposed research is in line with and can be used to inform the Canadian governments new feminist approach to international aid that prioritizes advancing and promoting equal rights for women.

column36: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease contributes to a tumour-promoting microenvironment and the development of lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Inflammation is a well-known cause of cancer, and inflammatory lung diseases (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)) have been associated with an increased risk of developing lung cancer. While the two diseases share known risk factors, the reasons why COPD airway damage leads to lung cancer are unknown. This includes the understudied role of inflammation in inducing damage, which could be an important factor in cancer development. We believe that COPD-related damage promotes cancer formation by causing gene expression changes in both airway cells and immune cells. Further, we believe gene expression changes crucial to cancer growth will be shared between the damaged tissues and the tumours themselves. We will test our theories by assessing the lungs of 15 individuals with COPD and lung cancer (rare samples collected at St. Paul's Hospital). We will identify changes in gene expression, along with differences in immune cell content, throughout the lung, and compare them to tumours in order to identify the changes most associated with cancer formation. This will reveal previously unknown gene expression changes and immune cell responses that are most likely driving cancer development. Additionally, we will build off the work our lab has previously conducted on the airways of COPD patients with and without lung cancer. We will first see if gene disruptions observed in the airways of COPD patients with lung cancer are also found in this rare lung tissue dataset. Second, we will determine if these genes can initiate cancer in normal lung cells by using CRISPR and virus-based gene editing techniques. Finally, we will test whether inhibition of these genes in mice can prevent the development of cancer. My project will lead to scientific discoveries that will help explain why COPD predisposes patients to lung cancer, and will reveal new targets for cancer therapy and methods of cancer prevention.

column36: Epigenomic Dysregulation in Synovial Sarcoma
column37: Synovial sarcoma is a highly aggressive soft-tissue cancer that predominantly affects adolescents and young adults. This malignancy, which accounts for 10% to 20% of soft-tissues sarcomas in such a young population, has limited sensitivity to conventional chemotherapies and thus a poor survival rate. Synovial sarcomas are characterized by a unique chromosomal abnormality that ultimately dysregulates critical genes via epigenetic modifications. Epigenetic modifications are essentially changes in the control of genetic material that do not alter the genetic code itself. For example, these modifications include the addition or removal of chemical tags on genetic material and change how the genetic material is regulated. In synovial sarcoma, we believe there are abnormal additions and removals of these tags - abnormal epigenetic modifications. The exact mechanism of how this aberrant process occurs in synovial sarcoma is poorly understood and controversial. To shed light on this mystery, it is prudent to examine what these epigenetic differences are and how they transform normal cells into cancer. To study this, I will use synovial sarcoma tissue samples from patients to profile the epigenetic changes that occur in these tumors, look for patterns using computational techniques, and carry out validation studies using mice. By understanding how epigenetic changes drive synovial sarcomas, we hope to guide the use of emerging epigenetic therapeutic agents in the treatment of this deadly disease. Additionally, synovial sarcoma is closely related to a number of other soft-tissue cancers that affect adolescents and young adults. Like synovial sarcoma, these cancers have limited treatment options, leaving numerous young patients in face of high mortality rates. In the long-term, we hope that a better understanding of synovial sarcoma can also reveal novel therapeutic approaches for these related cancers.

column36: Connecting the Microbiome and Neurodegenerative Dieseases
column37: The microbiome consists of trillions of bacteria, viruses and fungi that co-exist with humans in sites such as the intestines, nose and mouth, and is important to most aspects of health. My project will explore links between the microbiome and Parkinson's (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) and the conditions that often accompany these diseases, such as depression and anxiety. PD leads to loss of motor control and affects 100,000 Canadians. Studies have shown that the intestinal microbiome differs between those with and without PD. Interestingly, most patients experience constipation and loss of smell years before motor symptoms; these early symptoms take place at sites densely populated by microbes. AD is the leading cause of dementia, which affects 400,000 Canadians. Animal studies have found that the microbiome is important in AD; therefore, this is a key area to explore in humans. My first aim is to compare the microbiome of PD and AD patients versus controls. We will see whether a microbial "signature" exists for each disease and associate microbiome findings with disease severity. A second aim is to see whether probiotics improve depression, anxiety and fatigue in PD, as these conditions are also associated with microbial imbalances. As most patients have intestinal problems, we hope that shifting their microbiome to a healthier state could improve these symptoms. Finally, any discoveries will be further explored in the lab to understand the mechanisms connecting microbes to brain diseases. This will include seeing whether different microbial populations can modify PD/AD symptoms in mice, and examining how molecules made by microbes impact cells such as neurons and immune cells. The goal of my research is to provide new understanding of how the microbiome is important in neurodegenerative disease, and ultimately to work towards non-invasive interventions such as diet changes or carefully-designed probiotics that might help treat or even prevent these diseases.

column36: Evaluating the Long-Term Efficacy of Affective Mental Contrasting Interventions for Promoting Physical Activity Behaviour and Psychological Well-Being among New Mothers
column37: The transition to motherhood is typically associated with substantial decreases in physical activity levels. New parents are also at an increased risk of compromised psychological well-being. Since moderate-to-vigorous physical activity reduces symptoms of depression in new mothers, increasing physical activity levels has the added benefit of promoting psychological well-being. This study proposes to test the long-term effectiveness of implementing a novel physical activity intervention for new mothers that is designed to increase their physical activity levels and psychological well-being. Specifically, this study will evaluate the effectiveness of a mental contrasting strategy, which involves having new mothers focus on the best outcome of achieving future physical activity goals, while also identifying their biggest potential barrier that may prevent them from achieving these goals. Since the enjoyable aspects of physical activity have been found to be more motivating than the long-term health benefits, the proposed interventions will focus on the former. It is expected that the goal setting intervention targeting participants' perceptions of enjoyment will result in increased health-enhancing physical activity levels among new mothers six months and one-year following the intervention, compared to an intervention focusing on health benefits or an intervention that focuses on neither enjoyment nor health benefits. Further, it is hypothesised that these increased physical activity levels will result in improvements to participants' psychological well-being. The results of this study have the potential to inform scalable interventions for new Canadian mothers.

column36: The growing crisis of overly big babies: Comparing prevalence, outcomes and risk factors in midwifery v physician care
column37: A bigger than average baby (called macrosomia) is generally accepted as an adverse outcome in maternity care. About 10% of all babies in Canada are macrosomic. This is a significant public health concern as macrosomia has been linked to higher rates of cesarean or forceps delivery, severe birth trauma, excess bleeding, infant birth injury and infant death. Macrosomia is increasingly common worldwide, in part due to increases in obesity, excess weight gain and diabetes among childbearing women. A surprising recent finding indicated that 18% of all midwife-involved births in Ontario were macrosomic babies. Midwifery is a rapidly growing profession in Canada and outcomes are understudied. Reasons for these elevated rates of macrosomia among midwifery clients is unknown. Further, the impact of macrosomia on severe health outcomes is also unknown and it may differ for midwifery vs physician care. This study proposes to address this serious research gap by examining two cohorts of births in BC and WA state who were attended by midwives and physicians. The study findings will clarify the extent of macrosomia and associated severe outcomes among midwife v. physician births. Further, this will identify individual factors, aspects of prenatal or labor (adherence to specific obstetric guidelines from the Society of Gynecologists of Canada), or differences in training of midwives or gestational diabetes screening methods which could reduce severe morbidities among bigger babies and their mothers. Study findings can be used to propose evidence-based interventions, updated guidelines or policies to improve health for larger babies and reduce adverse outcomes such as cesarean delivery, birth trauma, or newborn birth injury.

column36: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein as a novel regulator, predictor, and therapeutic target of sepsis
column37: 1 in 18 Canadians die from sepsis (the body's response to a severe infection), each year. One of the challenges in treating sepsis is that it is very hard to predict which patients with an infection will need intensive treatment versus which patients will recover uneventfully. My research supervisor's laboratory has recently shown that patients' levels of high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (the "good cholesterol") drop quickly during sepsis. Importantly, the greater the drop in HDL levels, the greater the chance that a patient will die or suffer from serious organ failure. What is unknown is what controls the drop in HDL during sepsis, and whether genetic variation (differences in the DNA sequences among people) plays a role. My project is aimed at exploring the genetic mechanisms of HDL levels during sepsis. My preliminary data has identified a new gene variant that appears to play a major role in controlling the drop of HDL levels during sepsis. To complete my work, we will examine the DNA of patients with sepsis whose HDL levels drop very low, compared to patients whose HDL levels do not drop as much. Through my supervisor and his collaborators, we have access to large cohorts of patients with sepsis that have been collected from previous studies. We will also examine the function of the gene variants that we identify by introducing these variants into cells and examining the function of the gene products. This work is important for several reasons. Firstly, this work could lead to "personalized medicine" approaches to sepsis, by predicting which specific patients will develop the most dangerous consequences of an infection based on their genetics. Secondly, this project may lead to new ways to treat severe infections by targeted HDL levels. Ultimately this work will lower the burden of death from sepsis and severe infections among Canadians.

column37: Within the last 30 years, the rate of suicide amongst young Inuit men and boys has increased exponentially. This project will provide much-needed knowledge about the applicability of masculinity theory in non-Western populations.

column36: Elucidation of the phosphorylation regulated mechanisms that control kinetochore-microtubule attachment stability by quantitative mass spectrometry
column37: Many established cancer therapies target the process of cell division in order to kill cancer cells. These therapies prevent the separation of chromosomes from the mother cell into the two daughter cells. There have been recent gains in the understanding of how such therapies kill cancer cells, but the processes that regulate the separation of DNA to the daughter cells remain poorly understood. The kinetochore is a large protein structure that attaches the DNA to the mitotic spindle. The spindle then exerts a pulling force to separate the chromosomes into the two daughter cells. During cell division, many of the proteins that comprise the kinetochore are modified by the addition of phosphate to alter their behaviour in response to different stimuli. We intend to use a technique called mass spectrometry to measure and define the phosphate modified proteins at the kinetochore. The objective of this project is to define at a systems level how such changes occur during normal cell division and also in cells targeted with anti-cancer therapies, thus leading to a greater understanding of the process of cell division.

column36: Developing An Unconscious Neural-Reinforcement Therapy for Common Fears
column37: Can 'hardwired' fear responses, e.g. for spiders and snakes, be reprogramed unconsciously in the human brain? Currently, exposure therapy is amongst the most effective treatments for anxiety disorders, but this intervention is subjectively aversive to patients, and rates of premature attrition have been reported to be as high as 70%. We developed a fully unconscious method to bypass the unpleasantness in conscious exposure using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) neurofeedback. Using this method, the similarity between the current brain activity and the brain representation of a feared object is computed in real-time and fed back to participants. Over the course of multiple trials, participants learn to generate brain patterns increasingly similar to the pattern of the feared object. I have previously shown that this intervention leads to a decrease in physiological fear responses without exposing patients to feared objects. In a double-blind fMRI neurofeedback protocol, participants will be trained to activate the whole-brain neural representation of one of the two feared animals, while the second animal will act as a control. We hope to observe a specific decrease in clinical symptoms, physiological fear responses and behavioural avoidance of real animals, for at least 6-8 months. column36: Elucidating the interaction between Ail and vitronectin at the atomic level to determine the mechanism of Yersinia pestis pathogenesis.
column37: Yersinia pestis is the causative agent of the plague, and is responsible for the death of millions of people during massive pandemics. It is highly pathogenic as it can prevent the host's immune response and overwhelm it with massive growth. In combination with easy dissemination and potential weaponization of drug-resistant Y. pestis strains, there is a need to understand the mechanism of infection for medical countermeasures. Ail (adhesion invasion locus) is a membrane protein on the cell surface of Y. pestis and is a key virulence factor. Ail is thought to contribute to the pathogenesis through interaction with Vn (vitronectin), a serum protein that regulates various physiological processes including blood clotting and immune system. Their interaction can enhance bacterial attachment to human cells, suppress host immunity, and inhibit coagulation. Despite being important players of pathogenesis, the exact mechanism of Ail and Vn interaction is unknown. My work will, thus, focus on elucidating their interaction at the atomic level, where I will characterize the molecular structure of Vn then identify Ail-binding motifs on Vn and Vn-binding motifs on Ail through biophysical techniques. All of these interactions will be tested and validated using biochemical assays and cell-based assays. This transdisciplinary project will identify essential binding motifs to provide key targets for drug development and further advance our understanding of mechanisms behind Y. pestis pathogenesis.

column36: Treating advanced retinal degeneration - rebuilding multiple co-dependent retinal layers with stem cells
column37: Despite dozens of clinical trials (and countless animal trials) to regenerate the retina with stem cell transplants, none have solved the challenge successfully. This is because the retina has many layers, and all layers are necessary in order to permanently restore vision in patients with advanced retinal degeneration - ~1 million patients in Canada and >50 million worldwide. This results in a staggering amount of suffering and considerable global economic burden of 1/3rd of a trillion dollars (USD) annually for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) alone (not including the millions of patients that suffer from advanced, diabetes-related or inherited, retinal degeneration). Current stem-cell suspension transplants can only replace a single retinal layer. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplants can delay further degeneration, but they cannot replace dead photoreceptors. Photoreceptor transplants indeed restore vision, but only briefly since the diseased RPE cannot maintain the new photoreceptor graft. Current scaffold- or sheet-based transplants can be multi-layered. However, they provide limited retinal coverage, result in higher levels of surgical trauma than suspension injection, form inappropriate graft structure, and cause additional cell death - in many cases destroying the layer they were designed to regenerate. Given this, there is considerable need for simple, atraumatic replacement of multiple retinal layers. Here, we propose to continue development of new technology that organizes subretinal graft (including RPE and photoreceptors) into correct orientation and layering with wide coverage. This therapeutic is administered using standard outpatient surgical techniques and infrastructure. We have attained dual-graft stratification in: in vitro, pig ex vivo, and rabbit in vivo models. The next critical step towards the clinic is larger-scale animal trials assessing vision benefit.

column36: Primary and secondary emotions in cognitive therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder: A search for treatment moderators and mechanisms
column37: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a disabling condition that affects some Canadians after traumatic events. It interferes with one's ability to work, and is linked to greater physical and psychological problems, and suicide. Even frontline PTSD therapies are not effective for everyone, and these treatments must be improved to decrease the suffering that comes with the disorder. PTSD is associated with many negative emotions, which come in two different forms: primary emotions (e.g., fear/terror) occur directly in response to traumatic events, whereas secondary emotions (e.g., shame, guilt) occur because of how someone interprets the event and their experiences following it (e.g., self-blame for an attack). Secondary emotions are linked to more severe PTSD and may influence how someone responds to treatment, but this has not been tested thoroughly. This project examines whether individuals with PTSD with different primary and secondary emotions improve at different rates, if at all, over the course of cognitive therapy for PTSD (CT-PTSD), a frontline PTSD treatment. It also examines whether changes in these emotions during CT-PTSD influence improvement in PTSD symptoms. PTSD symptoms, primary emotions, and secondary emotions were measured weekly in 268 individuals receiving CT-PTSD. We will use this data to examine whether specific primary and secondary emotions at the first week influence how PTSD symptoms change during treatment. We will also assess whether decreases in specific primary or secondary emotions influence later changes in PTSD symptoms. These findings will reduce the personal, societal, and economic costs of PTSD in Canada by revealing whether individual's emotions can be used to predict if and how they benefit from treatment, and thus if they may need treatment changes to get better, faster. They also indicate which specific primary or secondary emotions, if any, therapists should target to help the treatment work best.

column36: Defining stromal immune suppressive mechanisms in ovarian cancer
column37: I aim to find strategies to overcome immune suppression in the tumor environment of ovarian cancer in order to create more effective immune-based treatments for patients. Current treatments for ovarian cancer, consisting of surgery and chemotherapy, are initially effective in most cases. However, most patients develop chemotherapy-resistant relapses, resulting in an unacceptably low survival rate of about 30% at 5 years. Encouragingly, the immune system has a strong influence on survival in ovarian cancer. Tumors that have a dense infiltration of T cells (a type of immune cell) are correlated with a markedly higher survival rate. However, a significant proportion of patients lack these dense T cell infiltrates. Instead, T cells are trapped in the surrounding stromal regions of the tumor and fail to make direct contact with tumor cells. I hypothesize that suppressive mechanisms inhibit the infiltration of T cells in these stromal areas and that, with better understanding, these mechanisms can be reversed by immunotherapy. In Aim 1, I will determine whether T cells that are trapped in stromal regions are nonetheless capable of recognizing tumor cells. If so, then these T cells have the potential to recognize and eradicate tumors. In Aim 2, I will attempt to identify and then block the signals by which stromal cells carry out suppressive functions. I will assess the effects on T cell infiltration and tumor regression. This project will facilitate the development of new treatments that release T cells from the suppressive effects of stroma to launch more powerful attacks against ovarian cancer and related malignancies.

column36: Optimizing opioid agonist treatment: Novel therapies and models of delivery in the management of opioid use disorder
column37: Overdose death rates have increased dramatically in Canada in recent years. These deaths have been driven largely by the inadvertent use of powerful opioids, including fentanyl, that have been added to street drugs such as heroin. In British Columbia (BC), a record number of overdose deaths led the provincial government to declare a public health emergency in 2016. Strategies to address the overdose crisis have therefore become an urgent public health priority. One such strategy that has recently been introduced in BC is the expansion of treatment options for opioid use disorder, including injectable treatments. Previous research conducted under idealized clinical conditions has found that such treatments may be beneficial for individuals with opioid use disorder who have not had success with oral treatments such as methadone. However, little is known about the effectiveness of injectable treatments for opioid use disorder under "real world" conditions. This is an important gap in understanding given that medications found to be effective under idealized conditions often perform differently once translated to real world populations and general practice settings. The proposed research will use prospective methods to monitor and evaluate the uptake and impacts of injectable opioid treatments as these are expanded in BC. Specifically, this research aims to identify barriers and facilitators to access to and retention on injectable treatments, as well as how retention in these treatments shapes health outcomes, including reductions in drug use and risk of overdose. This project will also seek to determine how healthcare models of injectable treatment delivery (e.g., pharmacy models; health clinic models) can be best adapted to address the needs of different populations of patients. It is hoped that the proposed research will make important contributions to understanding and improving treatment for opioid use disorder, both in Canada and internationally.

column36: Validation of the innovative clinical endpoint capture methods in the pragmatic multi-center randomized trial "Aspirin Dosing: A Patient-Centric Trial Assessing Benefits and Long- term Effectiveness (ADAPTABLE)"
column37: Clinical trials of good quality are necessary to assess the efficacy and safety of new medical treatments. However, long-term follow-up of patients treated with novel therapies is often complex and expensive, hindering the implementation of high-scale research initiatives. To optimize research efficiency, decrease its costs in the perspective of judicious allocation of resources, and, more importantly, to make patients benefit earlier from potential new treatments, innovative research methods are necessary to obtain follow-up. The so-called "registry-based randomized trials" have the potential to simplify follow-up by using pre-existing registries embedded in clinical care, without unnecessary medical outpatient visits. The purpose of the study is to evaluate the validity of the data obtained through this innovative method, compared to the more costly traditional methods. For this purpose, data from the ADAPTABLE trial will be analyzed. The primary objective of this trial is to identify the best dose of aspirin for prevention of severe cardiovascular events. For this purpose, 20,000 patients will be followed-up for up to 30 months, and data will be collected through electronic health records, without unwarranted medical visits for the patients. This is the largest study of this type ever performed in North America. In a sample of these patients, the traditional method of follow-up (through direct medical contact with the patients) will be performed, and compared to the innovative and less costly method (through pre-existing electronic registries), to assess the validity of the latter method. If it provides follow-up data of good quality, as we expect, this will be an incentive for the development of platforms for registry-based trials adapted to the specific Canadian reality. The ultimate goals are to improve patient care, and to alleviate clinical researchers in all fields of medicine from a significant logistic and administrative burden.

column36: Planned missing data designs for health research
column37: Missing data can create significant problems for researchers throughout the health sciences. Missing data arise when participants drop out of a study before completing it, as in longitudinal studies when people move away or become too busy to continue in a study, or when participants skip questions on a survey or parts of a test, because they are bored, or tired, or do not want to answer sensitive or difficult questions. Traditional statistical analysis methods are designed to be used with complete data, so researchers often delete whole cases (participants) who have missing data points. This practice, however, frequently leads to biased results. As such, unplanned missingness can be a serious problem for research generalization. Planned missingness, on the other hand, has tremendous (and for the most part unrealized) potential. With new statistical methods that produce unbiased results, planned missing data designs are an efficient way to manage cost, improve data quality, and reduce participant fatigue and practice effects. To date, however, there is little guidance for researchers on how to design such studies: how to choose the variables which will have missing values, what percent of data should be missing, how large a sample is needed, and to what extent the model will be able to detect meaningful effects. The present proposal aims to provide comprehensive guidance to researchers for using planned missing research designs in longitudinal research. The results will educate researchers on when, how, and why to use planned missing elements in their research designs. Planned missing data designs will increase the validity, generalizability, and cost-effectiveness of applied health research.

column36: Hypoxia-selective inhibitors of DNA repair
column37: The proposed work involves the development of a drug that will improve the effectiveness of radiation therapy. column36: Global and national impact of child restraint legislation on variation in child occupant fatalities
column37: Road traffic crashes are an important cause of deaths for children in the world, especially in low- and middle-income countries, which accounts for more than 90% of road traffic fatalities. column36: Repenser l'ergotherapie au soutien a domicile pour favoriser la participation sociale des aines (REPAIRS): vers le deploiement et l'implantation d'un continuum d'interventions innovantes
column37: Les personnes qui ont une vie sociale active sont en meilleure sante et vivent plus longtemps. Or, en vieillissant, une personne sur deux est a risque de vivre de l'isolement social et de la solitude. Heureusement, il est possible d'agir efficacement pour reduire l'isolement social des aines et les aider a s'integrer plus facilement dans la communaute. En effet, les cliniciens, dont les ergotherapeutes, peuvent offrir un eventail d'interventions demontrees economiquement rentables pour ameliorer la vie sociale des aines. Par exemple, les ergotherapeutes peuvent batir des liens avec des ressources de loisirs de la communaute ou offrir aux aines des interventions en groupe, en plus de suivis personnalises pour les aider a avoir une vie sociale pleine de sens pour eux. Cependant, ces interventions sont actuellement peu offertes dans les services d'ergotherapie a domicile aupres des aines, notamment en raison d'un manque de soutien pour les implanter. Ce projet de recherche permettra a des chercheurs, des decideurs, des membres de la communaute et des ergotherapeutes de documenter l'implantation d'interventions qui favorisent la participation sociale des aines. Les chercheurs inviteront d'abord un groupe d'ergotherapeutes a choisir, parmi un eventail de possibilites, les interventions qu'ils desirent implanter. Les chercheurs consulteront egalement les ecrits scientifiques afin d'identifier les strategies a privilegier pour faciliter l'implantation de ces interventions. Grace a ces connaissances, les ergotherapeutes integreront ensuite les interventions a leur pratique reelle. Les participants decriront finalement les conditions qui expliquent l'implantation reussie ou non des interventions choisies et les defis associes. Ces recommandations seront utiles pour guider les cliniciens, les decideurs et les membres de la communaute dans l'implantation de services a domicile qui ameliorent durablement la sante et le bien-etre de la population vieillissante canadienne.

column36: Vulnerable young women in Botswana co-design solutions to improve access to government support programs: a structural approach to HIV prevention
column37: Botswana's HIV prevalence is one of the highest in the world, disproportionately affecting young women (15-29 years). Those who are unemployed and out-of-school are among the most vulnerable and at high risk of HIV infection. Conventional HIV prevention messages that promote abstinence, monogamy, and condom use, have failed to stop the spread of HIV. That is in part due to structural factors, such as poverty, lack of education, and sexual violence. These structural factors undermine the ability of young women to negotiate safe sex. Access to government programs that support small businesses, return to education, or opportunities to gain work experience, could empower young women and decrease their HIV risk. However, designed for private sector development, these programs currently do not reach vulnerable young women. This research project is part of INSTRUCT, the first national-level trial that uses a structural approach to HIV prevention. My research goal is to improve access to government support programs by vulnerable young women in Botswana. I investigate individual and system-related obstacles to program access and delivery. As vulnerable young women and service providers are deeply familiar with these obstacles and their underlying causes, they are best suited to identify ways to overcome them. They will therefore co-design solutions to improve access to support programs. To facilitate policy change, the evidence and co-designed solutions will be presented to national policy makers. The larger INSTRUCT trial will assess the impact of several structural interventions on HIV prevalence. Implemented by Botswana NGO CIET Trust and the National AIDS Coordinating Agency, INSTRUCT is fully supported by the government of Botswana. Within this enabling environment I hope my project will demonstrate that active participation of vulnerable young women in policy design can generate innovative local solutions to reverse the global HIV epidemic.

column36: Depression as a gut feeling: The gut microbiome as a mediating factor in the dysregulation of the gut-vagus-brain epigenome in the context of depression.
column37: We live our lives engaged in a biochemical conversation with trillions of intestinal microbes. It is known that this gut 'microbiota' can modulate the intestines, and that neurons in our intestines can 'talk' to neurons in our brain along the vagus nerve, as part of a larger bidirectional signaling system called the gut-brain axis. Recent research has suggested that microbial signals can be transmitted up the gut-brain axis to modulate mood, and may be a factor in the development of mental illnesses, such as depression. However, the exact mechanisms by which the gut microbiome alters gut-brain signaling and depression risk are still unclear. Depression is strongly associated with disrupted stress response pathways. Gene regulatory processes known collectively as epigenetic mechanisms have been shown to be key mediators in this disruption. Interestingly, gut bacteria produce many of the chemicals that epigenetic processes require, and changes in the levels of these chemicals in mice have been associated with specific epigenetic changes in host cells. Thus, the gut microbiome may be an important epigenetic modulator. In addition, some of the gut microbiota-associated mood alterations disappear in animals if the vagus nerve is severed, suggesting that some moods begin in the gut. I therefore hypothesize that gut microbiome mediated epigenetic processes increase depression risk in humans by altering the gut-vagal-brain axis. My PhD project will identify depression-associated changes in epigenetic regulators in the gut microbiomes of depressed people who died by suicide, and clinically depressed populations. I will test whether specific gut microbe species predict the epigenetic changes in neurons along a gut-vagal-brain pathway. As the first investigation of the gut-microbiome-brain epigenome, this project will further our understanding of microbial-host interactions, which may be a factor in multiple other diseases and an important target for future intervention

column36: The Gut Microbiome as a Key Regulator of Early Life Stress Induced Depression - A Translational Mouse Model
column37: Early life stress increases vulnerability to a number of illnesses, including psychiatric illness such as depression, in adulthood. However, the mechanism for this is unknown. The gut microbiome (the collection of over 100 trillion bacteria and small organisms in our intestinal tract) is an interesting target of research in this regard since it is involved in the development of depression following adult stressors. Indeed, the gut microbiome, on top of its roles in processes such as digestion, interacts with both the central nervous system and the immune system to ultimately modulate stress reactivity and risk for psychiatric illness. However, the effects of early life stress on gut microbiome composition have yet to be explored. Consequently, we hypothesize that early life stress disrupts the composition of gut bacteria to promote the progression of disorders that involve the immune system and the brain, including depression. To test this, we are using mice exposed to early life stress or no stress and measuring gut microbiome composition, intestinal inflammation, brain-immune interactions, and depressive-like behaviours. To determine whether the gut microbiome is causally involved in mediating early life stress induced depression, we are conducting microbiome transplants between stressed and non-stressed mice. In humans, we are examining post-mortem intestinal tissue from depressed suicides or healthy individuals who died of other causes. Through forensic interviews, our lab can assess early life histories of these post-mortem individuals, placing us in a unique position to translate findings from our early life stress animal cohort to a clinically relevant population. The ultimate purpose of this integrative project is to further our knowledge of how different systems (brain, immune, gut) interact to promote the development and progression of depression, a leading cause of disability in Canada.

column36: Investigating the link between mild traumatic brain injuries and aggressive behaviour: an advanced structural neuroimaging study of brain injured children
column37: Mild traumatic brain injuries, or concussions, are a pervasive and exceedingly common condition, affecting up to 600 per 100,000 Canadians every year. A proportion of concussed individuals display aggressive personality changes after their injuries. These changes are associated with several negative outcomes, including impaired social integration and criminality. Concussions in children are especially troublesome, as they are associated with worse outcomes. Research suggests that aggressive behavior is controlled by a circuit of the brain composed of an area called the orbitofrontal cortex, a structure called the amygdala, and a connection between the two called the Uncinate Fasciculus. Current theories suggest that the amygdala is involved in detecting threats and mobilizing the brain for an aggressive response, and the orbitofrontal cortex is involved in suppressing these responses via the Uncinate Fasciculus. However, there are many unanswered questions about the role of concussions in aggressive behaviour. Does damage to one or more parts of this circuit lead to increased aggression, and if so, which parts? Are there any other brain areas involved in aggression? Can post-concussive aggression be predicted through brain scans? The impact of this research will be to better understand the neural basis of aggressive behaviour, as well as the potential to predict which children will display post-concussive aggression. With the vast number of concussions that are sustained by children every year, being able to predict personality changes has important implications for prevention.

column36: Role of the HNF-1aG319S Polymorphism in Early-onset Type 2 Diabetes in Oji-Cree Youth
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by high blood sugar due to the reduced ability of the body to respond to insulin and the insufficient release of insulin from pancreatic islets. Youth onset T2D is the fastest growing disease among Indigenous children of Central Canada, the majority being of Oji-Cree heritage. This is a serious concern because 50% of youth living with T2D will develop complications such as kidney failure within 15 years of diagnosis. The combination of a change in the DNA of the HNF-1a gene (HNF-1aG319S) and dramatic dietary changes likely contribute to the recent appearance and immense increase in T2D observed among Oji-Cree youth. As a result, we need to decipher how these environmental and genetic factors interact to affect the development of T2D. HNF-1a is a transcription factor, meaning it works to control the expression of other genes within a cell. We have created the first mouse model reflective of the HNF-1aG319S variant using state-of-the-art gene editing technology. Male and female mice that carry zero, one or two copies of the G319S variant will be fed one of three experimental diets: a standard mouse diet, a diet similar to the traditional Oji-Cree diet, or a diet similar to the modern Oji-Cree diet. We will assess markers of diabetes development including whole-body glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity from birth to old age. The pancreatic islets will be isolated to define the cellular and gene expression mechanisms through which the G319S variant impairs insulin secretion and pancreas development. This will be the first detailed investigation into the relationship between genetics, diet, and diabetes in the Oji-Cree population. Our study will provide an in-depth description of the cellular pathways that are disrupted due to the G319S variant, as well as their functional impact at a whole-body level. This model will serve as a foundation to develop culturally-appropriate therapeutic strategies in the future.

column36: Connectome-based brain biotyping and in-silico network simulation in neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: Accumulating evidence has led to the reconceptualization of mental illnesses as syndromes of 'miswired brain connectivity' during brain development. To transform such insights into clinically useful deliverables, however, we need a precise delineation of disease-specific properties. Unfortunately, the current 'symptom-based' diagnosis fails to explain commonly encountered overlaps in clinical presentations as well as their heterogeneity. The key to address this level of complexity may lie in the creation of an objective, data-driven classification system based on an underlying biology. In the proposed research program, I will develop a novel 'disease subtyping' framework based on the brain network derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). I will conduct my research based on the community-referred 'Healthy Brain Network Biobank', an ongoing initiative that collects multimodal MRI and behavioral data from 10,000 youth who may have psychiatric symptoms. My study targets >680 children affected by mental illness including attention-deficit/hyperactivity, anxiety, conduct, and autism spectrum disorders. Two analyses will be performed: 1) connectome-based disease subtyping and 2) computational network simulation. In the first analysis, I will extract the latent pathological components from functional networks underlying developmental disorders and cluster them to find more homogeneous subgroups. Multimodal profiling will then comprehensively evaluate the differences in behavior and brain organization across the identified subgroups. In the second analysis, a computational network simulation will estimate hidden biophysical features related to neurodynamics in order to probe disease mechanisms. Data-driven disease subtyping will provide objective transdiagnostic boundaries that mirror underlying biological processes. The proposed framework holds promise for the development of effective targeted therapies in multiple developmental conditions.

column36: Engineering immunomodulatory exosomes derived from human mesenchymal stem cells for treatment of acute inflammatory conditions
column37: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and sepsis are among the leading causes of death in Canada, especially for critically ill patients. These devastating conditions are characterized by severe inflammation in response to an insult or infection. In ARDS, inflammation localized to the lungs impairs normal gas exchange, which can lead to respiratory failure. For sepsis, overwhelming inflammation throughout the body leads to failure of vital organs such as the kidney, heart, and brain if not quickly treated. Despite decades of research, there are no specific therapies for ARDS and sepsis and current treatment consists mainly of supportive care. The Stewart Lab has completed the first clinical trial using a stem cell type called mesenchymal stem cells to reduce damaging inflammation in septic shock. However, delivery of cells can potentially cause serious adverse events including formation of tumours and blood clots. I believe that small membrane-bound particles released by mesenchymal stem cells, known as exosomes, may have similar beneficial effects in inflammatory diseases, without the risks of cell delivery. Hence, exosomes represent a potentially safer "cell-free" treatment option. The aims of this project are to evaluate the ability of exosomes to treat ARDS and sepsis in relevant animal models, to identify the biologically active cargo contained in these tiny particles that may be mediating this protective property and, given this insight, explore ways to genetically modify this cargo to enhance the therapeutic effects of exosomes. The findings from this research proposal will be a crucial first step in establishing the therapeutic potential of exosomes for treating acute inflammation. If exosomes are proven beneficial in ARDS and sepsis, our research group is ideally positioned to move this potentially life-saving treatment into clinical trials, and provide a novel approach for treating these vulnerable patient populations in Canada and around the world.

column37: Diabetes is a disease that affects over 11 million Canadians. High blood sugar from diabetes causes damage to cells throughout the body. column36: Connecting Cell Cycle Progression to Invasion: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Development in Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
column37: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare lung cancer that predominantly strikes women during reproductive years. In LAM patients, cancerous cells invade the lungs, causing destruction of essential tissue and leading to respiratory failure. LAM is driven by genetic mutations which alter molecular pathways and allow the LAM cancer cells to grow, live longer, and cause severe damage. Unfortunately, the current treatment regime for LAM has limited efficacy and is unable to rid patients of disease. Thus, the goal of this project is to develop an improved therapeutic option. I additionally seek to better understand the molecular pathways driving the cancerous properties of LAM cells. Recently, it was discovered that blocking the protein CDK2 can kill LAM cells and prevent cancerous invasion. While CDK2 is commonly known for its involvement in cell replication, its role in invasion remains elusive. I will better understand the function of CDK2 in LAM invasion by deleting this gene and examining changes in the LAM cells' cancerous abilities. Using molecular and computational techniques, I will explore the array of genes and proteins that effect, and are affected by, CDK2. Equipped with an improved understanding of LAM invasion, I will then investigate a new LAM treatment option by testing a Health Canada-approved drug which blocks CDK2. First, I will inject human LAM cells into mice to create an accurate model of the disease. I will then treat the mice with the drug to assess therapeutic efficacy. Changes in mouse lung function and the extent of LAM cell elimination will be measured. The anticipated success will allow this treatment to be rapidly brought to human clinical trials. This work will lead to a better understanding of the cause of LAM cancerous invasion and its connection to the cell cycle system. Importantly, this project will rapidly advance essential therapeutic options for LAM patients and provide key insights into cancer and other invasive diseases.

column36: Investigating Inflammatory Cell Death Mechanisms during Pulmonary Exacerbations in Cystic Fibrosis
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is one of the most common genetic diseases in Europe and North America. In CF, there are mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene (CFTR), which results in defective chloride transport in cells, creating fertile ground for infection with chronic opportunistic pathogens. Up to 80% of CF patients become infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacterium, which causes a decline in lung function. Many CF patients experience recurrent episodes of rapid impairment in lung function, called "pulmonary exacerbations", requiring medical attention and hospitalization. While overt activation of the immune system (i.e. inflammation) that responds to pathogens in the lungs is considered to be a key driver of the decline in lung function, the precise mechanisms in the context of CF have remained unclear. The aim of this project is to identify the most toxic inflammatory signaling mechanisms that result in the rupture and death of host cells during stable disease and pulmonary exacerbations of CF patients. To do so, I will use P. aeruginosa that is isolated from CF patients' sputum during pulmonary exacerbations and stable disease to evaluate their ability to activate different inflammatory responses upon interacting with various types of immune cells. I will also use normal cells and cells with a CFTR gene mutation to determine the mutation's impact on inflammatory cell death signaling during infection. Finally, due to the potential association between viral infections and pulmonary exacerbations, I will delineate this impact in a mouse model. Ultimately, this work will shed light on the mechanisms behind pulmonary exacerbations based on pathogen and patient factors, leading to the identification of new potential therapeutic targets and approaches for patient management. In doing so, these new therapies could greatly impact the CF patient population by helping preserve lung function and significantly improving their quality of life.

column37: Serious mental illnesses (SMIs) are devastating conditions that can lead to immeasurable suffering. Peer support workers are persons with SMIs who help others with SMIs recover. In addition to fostering recovery, peer support workers may also foster generativity, or experiences of contributing towards the betterment and well-being of others. Examples of generativity are caregiving or engaging in political participation. In addition to adding meaning to one's life, generativity may also foster recovery. This project was developed, and will continue being developed, through collaborating with persons with SMIs. First, we will interview persons with SMIs receiving peer support to explore experiences of generativity, facilitators of generativity, and the role generativity plays in recovery. Findings from the interviews will be organized according to common and important themes. We will then distribute questionnaires to a larger number of persons with SMIs receiving peer support. Our choice of questionnaires will be based on what participants say during the interviews. We will then analyze findings from the questionnaires to determine what factors might lead to generativity, as well as to determine if generativity is related to recovery. Findings from this project may illuminate the ways persons with SMIs contribute to society and help peer support workers develop interventions aimed at increasing generativity in their clients.

column36: Maintaining mobility for high risk home care clients: Development and validation of a new fracture risk assessment tool and care planning guide for home care
column37: People receiving home care often experience broken bones, like a hip fracture, which may affect quality of life, make them move into a nursing home, or they may die within 1 year. It is important to be able to decide who is at a high risk for fracturing to prevent them from experiencing these negative events. Current tools used to assess fracture risk are not helpful for home care clients because they need information that is often not available (e.g., bone mineral density values), assume that the person will live for another 10 years (many home care clients pass away within 1 year), and do not include important information such as dementia. The proposed projects will develop a new fracture risk assessment tool appropriate for home care clients. For the first part of the project, I will use a routinely collected assessment that is already used in home care, the resident assessment instrument - home care (RAI-HC), and hospital records to decide which risk factors are most important for predicting if someone will fracture or not. Based on statistics and expert panel input, I will then create and validate a tool that will calculate the home care clients' risk of fracture within 1 year using the routinely collected information. For the second part of the project, I will do a large literature review to put together recommendations for what home care providers should do once they have the home care clients' risk calculated. I will review the literature about exercise, behavioural interventions, calcium and vitamin D, and medications. I will describe the effect of each of the interventions on fracture prevention, and make recommendations for what could be done for each risk level. The proposed projects will develop a fracture risk assessment tool and recommendations that can be used with already existing and routinely used assessments. These assessments are done in many countries across the world, so the tool and recommendations will be able to be used internationally.

column36: Investigation of the role of ventral hippocampal and amygdalar circuits that control fear discrimination among threatening and non-threatening contexts
column37: Traumatic experiences that threaten our safety, such as natural disasters, physical assault, terrorist attacks, or military combat, are events that can lead to the development of psychiatric conditions, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). "Re-experiencing" is a PTSD symptom that can occur when a patient is in an environment that is similar to the traumatic one. The similarity between the environments can cause the individual to re-endure the same psychological and physiological arousal that occurred during the original trauma. Re-experiencing represents a major hurdle for clinicians in the treatment of PTSD because the defined neuronal circuits of this phenomenon are unknown. The formation, storage, and retrieval of contextual memories largely depends on the hippocampus (HPC). The HPC contains "place cells" that are preferentially active in discrete areas of a context and together form a neuronal ensemble that generates a cognitive map. In a world full of similar contexts, the HPC has the challenge to compare cognitive maps to determine whether contexts are the same or different from each other. Our goal is to understand how the HPC discriminates safe and dangerous contexts when they are similar to one each other. We will record HPC place cell activity in behaving rodents during discrimination of safe and dangerous contexts to determine how place cell activity influences downstream neural structures responsible for emotional processing. Moreover, we will use techniques allowing for sub-second precise inhibition and excitation of place cells during the critical time windows of context discrimination to investigate the causal role of these cells in context fear discrimination. In summary, we will use a multidisciplinary approach to unravel the basic circuit mechanisms responsible for encoding the discrimination of safe and dangerous environments and further our understanding of the neuronal processes underlying symptoms of PTSD.

In fact, several PARPi have been approved by Health Canada for treatment of BRCA1/2-deficient breast/ovarian cancers. However, while initial response is often positive, PARPi-resistant cancer cells eventually emerge thus limiting the long-term efficacy of the treatment. It was recently shown that BRCA1-deficient cells overcome PARPi sensitivity by rewiring their DDR to bypass the need for BRCA1 in a way that is increasingly reliant on another DDR protein, ATR. Strikingly, the Zou laboratory demonstrated ATR inhibitors (ATRi) re-sensitized PARPi-resistant cells to PARPi. This highlights a promising combinatorial (ATRi/PARPi) approach for cancer treatment. However, our knowledge of the underlying molecular mechanisms is incomplete. We therefore aim to comprehensively elucidate the molecular basis of ATR function to understand how ATRi can be used for the treatment of breast and ovarian cancers.

column36: Enhancing methods for analyzing and interpreting patient-reported outcome measures in clinical research and evidence-based decision-making
column37: In deciding whether to use a particular treatment for conditions such as depression, arthritis, or heart disease, doctors and patients must balance the benefits against the side effects and burden. To make this trade-off, they must understand the likely degree of benefit in symptoms and wellbeing. These outcomes are typically measured from directly asking patients using questionnaires in which patients describe how they are feeling. We call such questionnaires patient-reported outcomes (PROs). PRO measures (PROMs) are increasingly used in clinical trials and systematic reviews to evaluate health care interventions. Information obtained from PROMs can guide clinical decisions and inform shared-decision making. However, the use of PROMs involves challenges, the most important of which is deciding if a particular treatment effect is trivial, small but important, moderate or large. For instance, without further information, clinicians may find it difficult to grasp the importance of a three-point difference on a questionnaire that aims to assess health-related quality of life in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. One way to make this judgment is to consider the minimal important difference (MID), the smallest change in a PROM score that is important enough that patients would consider a change in treatment to achieve that benefit. Over the past 3 decades, researchers have developed statistical methods to estimate MIDs for various PROMs. However, the studies using these methods are not planned or conducted equally well. Though the MID is an alluring concept, there is much we are still learning about MID methodology. We plan to lead two projects that will further advance MID methods and optimize the presentation and interpretation of results from PROM in clinical trials, systematic reviews and clinical practice guidelines to inform evidence-based decision-making in clinical practice, ultimately enhancing quality of care and patient outcomes.

column36: Determining how microbes lower blood glucose and insulin after bariatric surgery.
column37: Half of the Canadian population is obese or overweight, which predisposes to serious health problems, such as high blood glucose and insulin, elevated blood lipids/cholesterol and hypertension. Obesity leads to type 2 diabetes (T2D), stroke and other chronic diseases that have high costs to public health care. However, we still do not understand why some obese people have high blood glucose and others do not and what actually causes the progression of prediabetes. The bacteria inhabiting our gut (i.e. gut microbiota) is now recognized as an important player controlling host metabolism. Bariatric surgery, the most efficacious intervention to cause remission of T2D, is associated with changes in the type of gut bacteria. Bariatric surgery also lowers blood glucose and insulin BEFORE weight loss. Nobody has fully tested HOW gut bacteria within a bariatric surgery patient change glucose and insulin control. We will use new ways to grow and identify bacteria from the same patient before and after 3 different types of bariatric surgery. We will also transplant the bacteria to germ free mice and determine how these microbes can lower blood glucose without the need for weight loss. We will look for novel species and bacterial molecules that can be used in the treatment and diagnosis of T2D.

column36: Sirtuin 6 and Inflammatory Vascular Diseases
column37: Aging is an inevitable process that affects all life forms as we know it. In human health, aging is linked to many diseases like cancer, arthritis and heart disease. Common to many of these age-related diseases is an underlying abnormal activity of increased inflammation. However, we do not yet know what controls healthy aging or unhealthy inflammation that may lead to illness. Therefore, more information is needed to improve our treatments. Sirtuins are a recently discovered family of proteins. They slow aging in various organisms like yeast, worms and even small animals such as mice. This has inspired recent human studies, which identified certain sirtuin proteins associated with increased longevity. Interestingly, sirtuin proteins also regulate the activity of inflammation within organ tissues. So far, research in mice have shown that animals that do not produce enough sirtuin proteins in their body age faster and die younger than those with a normal level. Work in our laboratory over the past few years discovered that lack of nutrients that support sirtuin proteins cause blood vessel weakening and early cardiovascular disease in research mice. My research will focus on the roles of sirtuin proteins in regulating inflammation of the cardiovascular system during health and illness. I hope to discover novel pathways that help us understand the shortcomings of our current therapies. The ultimate goal is to provide innovative personalized treatment options for patients. Broadly, improving our knowledge of blood vessel aging and inflammation will help patients with vascular diseases, while having a profound impact on how we view other age-related diseases like cancer, arthritis and metabolic syndromes.

column36: Kinome Profiling of Triple Negative Breast Cancer Cells to Reveal Predictors of Response to Targeted Therapy
column37: Fortunately, oncologists have access to specific drugs that target and treat most breast cancers, but not triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), the most aggressive type of breast cancer So far, this cancer can only be treated with non-specific chemotherapy too often accompanied by terrible side effects. I will set out to uncover new ways to treat TNBC more effectively and reduce the side effects. Some TNBC cells over-produce the protein osteopontin (OPN), making the cancer cells "addicted" to two other proteins, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and hepatocyte growth factor receptor (Met). My initial findings suggest that triple negative breast cells that overproduce osteopontin are "addicted" to these receptors. Furthermore, the triple negative breast cells can be killed by drugs such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) that target receptors of epidermal growth factor and hepatocyte growth factor. I will explore this by measuring how the amount of OPN produced by the cancer cells determines how many cancer cells survive after chemotherapy. We will determine if other proteins like EGFR and Met, (additional kinases), are more active (often because they are more abundant) and compensate when cancer cells are treated with EGFR and Met target drugs. Our research will use "omics" methods to investigate all the kinases from the cancer cells before and after drug treatment by measuring the amount and activity of all kinases. The main outcome should allow oncologists to measure OPN levels in their patient's blood which will predict which TNBC tumors will be effectively treated by the TKI drugs and life for TNBC patients should become significantly enhanced.

column36: Development of a lung ultrasound therapy system for acute respiratory distress syndrome
column37: Treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a common disorder in intensive care units with a mortality rate approaching 40%, is a considerable challenge. In ARDS, the lungs are filled with fluid resulting in patients drowning in their own fluids. ARDS is one of the most difficult conditions to treat because of its patchy distribution, where the fluid-filled regions of the lung are interspersed within the normal lungs, causing conventional treatments to preferentially affect the normal lungs rather than the injured regions. For instance, mechanical ventilators, although life-saving, preferentially inflate the normal regions of the lung resulting in overdistension and injury of the normal lung itself. Similarly, medicines given by inhalation or injection preferentially affect the normal lungs or other organs in the body. Here we propose a revolutionary form of "personalized and targeted medicine" to treat ARDS based on ultrasound technology and microbubbles (tiny gas bubbles already used clinically for diagnostic purposes). While the normal regions of lung scatter ultrasound waves (because ultrasound is blocked by air), the ultrasound waves are able to penetrate the injured (fluid-filled or collapsed) regions, allowing enhanced delivery of drugs like antibiotics to the damaged lung. This approach is a revolutionary form of "personalized medicine", since it will allow the delivery of medicines and genes exactly where they are needed in each patient. In this project, we will develop a clinical prototype of an ultrasound therapy system specifically for the lungs and optimize treatment protocols using large animal models of ARDS. At the end of the project, we will translate the study to a Phase I clinical trial in humans.

column36: Developing and testing strategies to identify and support patients with chronic kidney disease in a disadvantaged Ontario primary care population
column37: Chronic kidney disease is a medical condition where people have reduced function of their kidneys. In some case this can lead to kidney failure, which requires costly treatments to survive, such as dialysis or a kidney transplant. Many patients may never reach kidney failure, especially if their family doctor can diagnose their condition early and provide the appropriate treatments. However, there are usually no symptoms until the later stages of the disease, so many patients may have chronic kidney disease but their doctors are not aware of it. Also, among patients with known chronic kidney disease, many are still not receiving the recommended treatments from their family doctors to prevent their kidneys from failing. We will develop a new tool within the electronic medical records of community care access centres in Ontario, Canada (107 primary care facilities) to help the care team diagnose patients with chronic kidney disease earlier and provide the necessary treatments. We will test the tool within a few centres to see if it is helping to improve care and if the care team finds it useful before we provide it to the remaining centres. This research will lead to improved care for patients with early chronic kidney disease, preventing patients from reaching kidney failure and dying.

column36: Dissection of a novel pathway for cellular error correction
column37: Understanding the mechanisms by which individual cells within an organism overcome stress and damage throughout their birth, growth, and lifetimes is critically important for our understanding of human development and disease. Cells in the early embryo are incredibly robust to sources of damage, including DNA mutations. The responses of cells to damage during embryogenesis mirror the mechanisms that occur in cancer cells, allowing them to survive and proliferate in the presence of deleterious mutations. The Schier lab has recently identified a new population of cells within the early embryo using a combination of computational and genetic experiments (Satija et al, Nature Biotech, 2015). These cells respond to DNA damage by activating a novel cellular mechanism related to programmed cell death (apoptosis). Because they avoid cell death in the presence of damage, the Schier lab coined these the 'seven-sleeper' cells. They were named after the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, who took cover from prosecution in a cave before emerging once the danger had passed several years later. I propose to completely dissect the developmental origin, function, and ultimate fate of these cells. I will use a combination of genetic, pharmacological, imaging, and computational tools to characterize the 'seven-sleeper' cells. I aim to answer questions about why this program is activated during embryogenesis, how it relates to known mechanisms of apoptosis, and dissect exactly how it works to protect damaged cells. Observations made by me, and results I generate can be translated, and my long-term goals are to add to our understanding of the cellular mechanisms of DNA repair and the regulation of cell death in cancer and other diseases.

column36: Caregiving for dementia: determining the population-level physical and mental health consequences using administrative data
column37: Most dementia care occurs at home, often with the support of informal caregivers who assist with basic needs. An increasing number of these caregivers are taking on more complex roles such as medical care at home, and navigating health and long-term care systems. With the number of Canadians living with dementia expected to double in the next 15 years, there will be significant increases in the demand for informal caregiving. Caring for persons with dementia is extremely demanding. Among Canadian informal caregivers, more than a quarter provide over 21 hours of care per week. This caregiving is a chronic stress experience, with small studies reporting severe and long-term physical and psychological impacts on dementia caregivers. The larger population health impact of dementia caregiver stress is unknown, as is its impact on the wellbeing of the person with dementia who is receiving care. This doctoral research will involve three distinct but interrelated projects. The first project will involve a literature review synthesizing the available evidence on the impact of informal caregiver stress on the person with dementia receiving care. The next two projects will use de-identified administrative databases that capture publicly-funded health care claims in Ontario and Manitoba. The Ontario database will be used to investigate the impact of caregiver stress on health care utilization and psychotropic medication use among persons with dementia receiving home care. The Manitoba database will be used to assess health outcomes of Manitoba family caregivers looking after persons with dementia. We anticipate this research demonstrating a significant impact of dementia caregiving on population-level health outcomes. These findings will be of substantial interest to the 564,000 Canadians living with dementia and their caregivers. We hope this research increases awareness about the impact of caregiver burden in dementia, thereby motivating increased caregiver supports.

column36: Use of Multi-Site Interviews to Understand and Reduce Barriers to Postmastectomy Breast Reconstruction across Ontario
column37: Breast reconstruction (BR) can be offered to breast cancer patients after mastectomy and aims to surgically restore the breast form. BR may provide long-term quality of life improvements as well as psychological benefits for breast cancer patients. As breast cancer is the most common cancer in women affecting 1 in 9 Canadian women during their lifetime, BR has the potential to impact many lives. Despite these potential benefits, BR remains significantly underused in Ontario as it fails to be consistently integrated as part of the treatment of breast cancer patients. To prepare for the proposed project, I first performed a systematic literature review. I found that patient factors such as increased age, immigrant status and non-Caucasian race; tumor characteristics such as larger tumours; as well as negative physician perceptions of BR were associated with low rates of BR. Canadian studies highlighted a significant problem, that access to BR in Ontario is not universal. These studies fail to explain in detail the relationship between these factors and low rates of BR, specifically, why and how these factors can lead to low rates of BR. Meaningful discussions with patients, clinicians and administrators are therefore needed to increase our understanding of the relationship between these different barriers and poor access to BR in Ontario. In my study, I will first conduct interviews to increase our understanding of the local barriers to access to BR in Ontario, and then use this knowledge to design interventions that target these barriers and aim to improve access to BR in Ontario. The ultimate goal of my project is to address the inequity and inaccessibility barriers faced by breast cancer patients in Ontario, and to advocate for breast reconstruction to be offered to breast cancer patients in an equitable, timely, and accessibly manner in the future.

column36: Redefining care for patients with advanced non-cancerous disease - identifying quality indicators near the end of life.
column37: Canada's population is aging in part due to the longevity of life afforded by advances in medical care. Because of this, the number of individuals living with chronic diseases like heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, end-stage renal disease and dementia are also increasing. These chronic illnesses take their toll on patients, their families and the healthcare system. Chronic illness demands high quality end-of-life care, to treat distressing symptoms but not many patients receive it. Only one-third of people with chronic illness have access to formal end-of-life care, and most of them have cancer. The delivery of quality end-of-life care requires multiple different health professionals and a broad approach to address the complexity of care near the end of life. Defining what "good" care for these individuals looks like requires the alignment of financial, organizational and care delivery mechanisms with patients' informed preferences. This ensures that decisions for care are based on high-quality shared decision making that incorporates the goals of care of patients and their families. Presently, there is a lack of defined standards for high value end-of-life care in non-cancerous disease states. I intend to complete three critical research projects during my four years as a PhD student, which will review the current knowledge state and actual practices of providing quality end-of-life care in Canada. I will then use this understanding to create an evidence-based set of guidelines (called "quality indicators") for patients with advanced non-cancerous disease nearing the end of life, using a panel comprised of patients, their caregivers, policy makers and clinical experts. By presenting these standards nationally, these quality indicators will help standardize and ensure the delivery of high quality end-of-life care to all Canadians at the provincial and national level.

column36: Developing functional and genomic tools and identifying driver mutations of mismatch repair deficient cancers to improve diagnostic efficiency for Biallelic Mismatch Repair Deficiency Syndrome
column37: Biallelic Mismatch Repair Deficiency Syndrome (BMMRD) is the most fatal pediatric cancer syndrome in which children develop multiple aggressive cancers and do not survive into adulthood. BMMRD occurs when children are born with mutations in their DNA that make their cells unable to repair errors that occur when cells replicate. Many different mutations can cause BMMRD, and many of these mutations are still unknown. This has made it extremely challenging to diagnose patients and ensure they receive appropriate treatment. Therefore, my goal is to develop new, reliable methods for diagnosing BMMRD. My first objective is to develop a test that measures the ability of cells to repair errors in DNA. As DNA contains the instructions for creating proteins, I will develop an artificial piece of DNA with an error that prevents it from being able to produce a protein. I will put this DNA into cells, and as BMMRD cells cannot repair DNA errors, they will not be able to produce the protein, whereas cells from other individuals will. Therefore, this test will be able to reliably identify BMMRD. Secondly, due to their inability to repair errors, BMMRD patient cells develop many additional DNA mutations. I will measure the number of mutations in BMMRD cells to allow this mutation number to act as a unique identifier of BMMRD and be used for diagnosis. Finally, I will uncover new, unknown mutations causing BMMRD in order to help better diagnose patients. I will obtain data on thousands of cancers that resemble BMMRD, and analyze their DNA using bioinformatic tools to identify these new mutations. My work will produce revolutionary approaches to diagnosis that will, for the first time, make it possible to diagnose all cases of BMMRD. This work can also be leveraged for the diagnosis of adult cancers with similar features. My work will also deepen our understanding of the genetics of BMMRD, and yield valuable insights into future investigations of this serious disorder.
