column36: Self-Adjuvanted Nanoparticles as an HIV Vaccine Platform
column37: Over the past 25 years, efforts have failed to develop a vaccine capable of broadly protecting against HIV. In response to HIV, the human immune system seems generally unable to respond effectively, providing limited protection to the infected individual. Past HIV vaccine candidates have been met with similar challenges, where they are unable to elicit a broadly protective response. Thus, improvements must be made to increase specificity and breadth of the immune response to an HIV vaccine. Towards this goal, subunit HIV components (antigens) displayed in high-density have been demonstrated to be more effective in activating the immune system in comparison to monomeric antigens, due to their ability to activate several receptors on immune cells (B cells) simultaneously. In order to improve current HIV antigens and create an improved immune response, I propose to design a novel platform based on self-assembling protein-based nanoparticles to co-deliver multimers of HIV antigens and immunomodulatory proteins to the immune system. I will then test these nanoparticles in vitro in B cells and in immunization trials with animal models to determine their potential for immune activation and antibody production. It is predicted that the development of protein nanoparticles as an immunomodulatory platform for HIV antigens will enable broader reactivity and enhanced immunity to vastly improve the efficiency of current HIV vaccination strategies.

column36: Improving the Quality of Life of Patients with Parkinson's Disease using Deep Brain Stimulation and Magnetoencephalography
column37: Parkinson's disease is the second most common degenerative brain disorder and affects over 100,000 Canadians. Patients suffer from tremor, rigid muscles and slowed movement and when medications are no longer effective in treating these symptoms patients receive a treatment called Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS). DBS is a surgical procedure which involves the insertion of a 'brain pacemaker' through the skull. This device is programmed to send electrical signals to certain areas of the brain to relieve symptoms. Despite the widespread use of DBS, the mechanism by which it works is unknown; as a result, conventional DBS programming is subjective and requires multiple patient visits. My project involves the integration of computers and brain activity to optimize DBS settings in patients with Parkinson's disease. Since every patient has a unique set of symptoms and response to DBS, I will examine how individual brain activity responds to different DBS settings. Brain activity will be measured in the form of magnetic fields and compared to tremor activity and motor function. We expect that the optimization of DBS settings based on patients' brain activity will improve symptom relief and reduce side effects, thereby improving patient quality of life through increased mobility and independence. Fewer clinical visits to adjust DBS settings will also benefit patients and their caregivers and result in lower healthcare costs. There is a growing need to improve the efficiency of DBS programming using technology since DBS is becoming more popular in Parkinson's disease. Our group is also the first to use DBS to treat depression, anorexia and Alzheimer's disease for which programming guidelines do not exist. This innovative project will improve the efficacy of DBS to provide a better quality of life to Canadians suffering from Parkinson's disease and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a lifelong brain developmental condition estimated to affect about one in 100 Canadian children. Many individuals who live with autism often have other medical, psychiatric and developmental issues. Thus, ASD represents a major public health concern with large implications for social care costs. Currently, we have no effective treatments for ASD. Thus, deeper understanding of the biology of ASD will lead to new therapeutic options that are urgently needed. Understanding ASD begins with understanding how the brain works at the molecular level. Specifically, within the brain's cells exist structures known as neuronal granules. These granules function to ensure that proteins are made at the right time and place; however, this is no longer the case in ASD. Thus, neuronal granules are a promising unexplored therapeutic target. Recently, formation of neuronal granules has been shown to be driven by a process called phase separation. An every-day example of phase separation is the separation of vinaigrette into distinct oil and vinegar liquid droplets. Now imagine this phenomenon in the cell, where vinegar droplets represent neuronal granules and the oil represents the cell environment. I propose to study how phase separation of neuronal granules changes in ASD. Insights from my work will contribute to new therapeutic interventions for ASD. My project is broken down into three stages: beginning by developing an understanding from basic principles, moving to a disease model, and then developing strategies to reverse the disease. In my project, I will understand how neuronal granules form and function, model known ASD mutations into the granules, and test if protein modifications or drug compounds can reverse the mutational damage. In my experiments, I will use FMRP, a protein involved in a common genetic cause of autism. Overall, my work will begin to unravel the mysteries of ASD which is beneficial to hundreds of thousands of Canadians.

column36: Structure-function studies of the HIF-pVHL axis: Implications for disease
column37: Take a deep breath! Just as your brain reminds you to breathe, every single cell in the human body can sense if there is enough oxygen to survive and can adapt to changes in oxygen levels thanks to oxygen-sensing proteins. This ability is necessary in all stages of life, from the formation of blood vessels during fetal development, to adaptation in high altitudes by increasing the number of red blood cells, and responding to blood vessel blockages. Yet, this process is not always to our advantage. The process of oxygen-sensing also allows for both malignant and benign tumours to maintain their impressive bulk, even as cells within the tumour become oxygen deprived. In other words, while a cell's response to oxygen levels is important for survival, these processes can also be hijacked during tumour formation to allow for rapid cell division. It is not surprising that the proteins involved in the cell's oxygen-sensing pathway are found to be defective in different types of cancer, including one major killer: kidney cancer. Our research is focused on the study of mutations found in these oxygen-sensing and response proteins, namely pVHL and HIFalpha. HIFalpha activates the oxygen-response pathway, while pVHL deactivates it. Together, these proteins fine tune the oxygen-response pathway and ensure that each cell is correctly measuring oxygen levels. However, such is not always the case. For example, pVHL is mutated in several diseases, including the polycythemia, which is a chronic condition of elevated red blood cell levels. HIFalpha is also mutated in patients with polycythemia and in tumours of the neuroendocrine system. Our studies are focused on how these protein mutations disrupt the oxygen signalling pathway. We hope that these studies will reveal why these mutations are disease-causing and can serve as a logical basis for the development of prognostic and therapeutic tools. In the process, our research will help gain further insight into how cells sense oxygen.

column36: Establishing the oncogenomic landscape of clinically aggressive meningiomas
column37: Meningiomas are the most common adult primary brain tumors. Although the majority of meningiomas are benign, subsets of these tumors are clinically aggressive and challenging to treat. These clinically aggressive meningiomas (CAMs) behave similar to cancerous brain tumors. The interventions available to treat CAMs are limited, with surgical resection and radiation therapy as the only two viable options. Even with the most aggressive available forms of treatment, patients are not cured of their tumors and the regrowth of tumors results in considerable morbidity, poor quality of life and significant loss of functional years. A better understanding of the genetic changes associated with CAMs would allow for the development of personalized treatments critical for improving the durability of response and quality of life in these patients. We plan to use multiple genetic-based sequencing techniques to establish the genetic landscape of CAMs and to identify key driver genetic mutations in these tumors. We will correlate our genetic findings with key clinical parameters and quality of life data. The key genetic alterations identified will be selected as possible targetable changes that will be examined using animal studies. Our laboratory has used and published this approach previously for a different brain and spinal tumor (schwanommas, published in Nature Genetics), and we are confident that this approach will establish the genetic landscape for CAMs and will identify new mutations for patients with CAMs that may be targeted to personalize and enhance durability of treatment. This work will establish a comprehensive genomic database harmonized with fundamental clinical and quality of life data that will be unparalleled. The most promising genetic alterations can be translated into clinical practice through Phase I/II clinical trials.

column37: Cancer affecting the brain and spinal cord is the second most common type of cancer in children, accounting for 18% of all pediatric cancers. Medulloblastoma is the most common brain cancer in children and can occur in patients in infancy through to adulthood. The current standard of care includes surgical removal of as much tumour as is safely possible, followed by aggressive radiotherapy and chemotherapy regimens to treat the cancer cells that remain after surgery. These modern treatment strategies date back to the 1990s. With this multimodal treatment strategy, survival rates have plateaued at approximately 70%. Additionally, while current treatments can achieve cures in a significant number of these patients, the effects of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy on the developing brain lead to intellectual impairment, hearing loss, short stature, hormonal dysfunction, and an increased risk of developing secondary cancers early in life. Together, the lack of improvement in survival rates over the past two decades combined with the significant quality of life impairment caused by treatment side effects in survivors creates an urgency to develop novel targeted therapies for these patients. One key discovery is that the leading cause of death in medulloblastoma patients is the spread of the cancer from the initial site. This study will focus on strategies to identify the key pathways involved in the spread of medulloblastoma. We will use emerging genetic technologies to screen for genetic weaknesses that can be exploited to selectively block the spread of cancer cells. Additionally, we will try to better characterize how cancer cells are able to move from the site of the initial tumour into distant sites in the brain and spinal cord. Finally, we will test targeted therapies in mouse models of medulloblastoma to try to prevent cancer spread within the brain and spine.

column37: During bacterial infection, white blood cells known as neutrophils mount a complex defense response to eliminate the infecting organisms. In healthy individuals, after the clearance of bacteria, neutrophils respond to internal biological signals to terminate this response by undergoing a process of controlled cell death called apoptosis. Failure to undergo apoptosis can result in bystander injury to healthy tissues, a condition known as multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS). This process is called sepsis, life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated response to infection. Sepsis is the leading cause of death and disability for patients in an intensive care unit. No specific therapies are available to treat sepsis and management remains largely supportive. One quarter of patients who develop sepsis die; survivors experience a reduced quality of life, and a higher risk of death. In this research program, I seek to understand how changes in neutrophil responses to bacterial signals during sepsis can inhibit apoptosis, and prevent the normal resolution of inflammation. Hence, this study will investigate: 1)How certain proteins within neutrophils can direct cell responses to either cell survival or death. 2)How the formation of certain protein clusters can influence bacterial recognition and cellular response by the neutrophil. 3)Whether pharmacological drugs targeting neutrophil survival can potentially be used for the treatment of patients with sepsis. Our translational studies will use patient blood samples to identify potential new strategies to accelerate the resolution of neutrophil-mediated tissue injury during sepsis.

column37: The R2TP complex is a newly identified chaperone complex involved in ribosome biogenesis and many other cellular pathways. The complex is conserved across species and was found to be upregulated in cancer cells. In humans, R2TP is essential for the assembly and proper functioning of critical protein complexes involved in cellular signaling, development and proliferation. Human R2TP is formed by four proteins: RVB1, RVB2, PIH1 and RPAP3. RVB1 and RVB2 form a hetero-hexameric ring structure and interact with proteins proven to be associated to cancer development. PIH1 interacts with RVB1-RVB2 playing a role as a specificity factor for R2TP. RPAP3 interacts with PIH1 and connects R2TP to HSP90, an essential chaperone for cellular homeostasis. Despite the critical roles played by R2TP, it is not clear how it functions in the human cell and what cellular pathways are modulated by this complex. To address these questions, an integrative analysis of physical and genetic interactions of R2TP is proposed in this project. Cellular-based assays will be performed to systematically identify proteins interacting with R2TP, either strongly or transiently. Additionally, epistatic screens will be used to map the interactions between thousands of genes and the R2TP-coding genes. This integrative approach will allow the identification of novel pathways regulated by R2TP. Deciphering R2TP functions will also provide important insights for future development of therapeutic targets to fight cancer.

column36: Who to Help? Identifying Parent and Child Needs for Intervention Prior to Pediatric Needle Procedures: A Mixed-Methods Approach
column37: Needle procedures are common throughout childhood and they often elicit pain and fear in children and parents. Unmanaged pain and fear associated with needles has health implications for the child in pain (e.g., may lead to avoidance of future immunizations) and society more broadly (e.g., may compromise community immunity). Therefore, understanding parents' and children's emotional experience and needs during needle procedures is required to reduce these negative consequences. An in-depth examination of emotions is needed, which involves capturing the individual's own descriptions of the event, and how they behave and respond physiologically to the event. Further, although there are many feasible treatment strategies to manage pain and fear associated with needles, there are no available screening tools to identify parent-child dyads that would likely benefit from such strategies. My doctoral research will address these gaps in the literature by incorporating both quantiative and qualitative information of parent and child emotional experience, including: self-ratings of emotional states, open-ended interview questions, behavioural observation, and physiological activity. This project will also inform the development of a screening tool, which will be evaluated by how well it predicts parent and child reported and observed experiences. A detailed description of how dyads feel before, during, and after the procedure might help us understand what their needs are and which strategies they think would help make needles less upsetting. The use of a simple screening tool can help health care providers identify which parents and children are more likely to need strategies to manage pain and fear. The overall goal of this work is to help make needles a more pleasant experience for families so that they are not avoided in the future.

column36: Intelligent Ureteral Stent System for Prevention of Renal Damage
column37: At least 10% of the Canadian population (>3.5 million Canadians) will develop a kidney stone in their life, resulting in significant patient morbidity and burden on the healthcare system. This problem is further deteriorated as ~50% of the patients will have a repeat episode within 5 years. Most patients are treated by placing a ureteral stent, a thin hollow plastic tube, in the ureter (the duct that bridges the kidney to the bladder) to ensure proper urine drainage past the stone that may be blocking it. Ureteral stents are also used in cancer patients to maintain urine flow through the ureter that may be compressed by growing tumor. The stent itself, however, often causes an obstruction in the urine flow, by limiting the ureter's wave-like motion to push urine down to the bladder and/or by building up crystals on the stent. In such case, the kidney swells, a condition known as hydronephrosis, which results in kidney injury and eventual failure if left untreated. This research will develop a novel "smart" ureteral stent that will continuously track renal pressure while it is indwelling, uniquely allowing for early detection of increased pressure before damaging hydronephrosis develops. This will enable non-invasive, quantitative, and cost-effective tracking that is currently not available via any existing diagnostic route. The stents will be developed to function as radiofrequency antennas, with embedded micro pressure sensors and microelectronic chips to wirelessly sense and transmit renal pressure. The device will be prototyped using microsystems technology available at UBC. This novel stent technology will allow kidney stone patients to check the status using a portable monitor at home, giving an alarm for the need of further diagnosis and necessary treatment by urologists. The research results are anticipated to promote different types of stents and other implants to acquire perceptual features for a wide range of medical applications beyond the urologic area.

column36: Injectable collagen matrices for cardiac tissue repair
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) ranks number one in worldwide mortality. In Canada, heart disease is responsible for a third of the yearly deaths. The procedures currently used to treat heart attack patients can restore blood flow to the heart, but they do not repair or regenerate the damaged tissue. As a result, patients are left with a poorly functioning heart. About 1 in every 10 patients will develop advanced heart failure, and this number is growing. These patients suffer a loss of blood pumping capacity, and heart failure has a 5-year mortality rate of ~50%. Thus, there is a need to develop a new therapy able to simultaneously prevent the onset of heart failure and promote heart repair. Cell therapy has shown promise for treating damaged hearts, but improvements are needed. Our goal is to develop a new biomaterial that can be used with cell therapy to improve repair in the damaged heart and limit the extent of damage that occurs. The material is made from collagen, a protein with an important role in supporting cells and regulating their function. It is injectable for easy delivery into the injured heart tissue. In preparation for clinical use, we aim to investigate how the physical properties of our injectable collagen materials affect their ability to repair the heart. The materials will also be optimized to enhance the function of therapeutic cells. For this, we will use animal models of heart disease, which closely mimics the human condition. This work will allow us to establish which characteristics our materials require in order to achieve the best therapeutic outcome.

column37: Dementia remains incurable and is not only a burden to patients and their families but is also a huge economic burden for public health. column36: Sex-Dependent Role of Telomeres and Cellular Senescence in Pain in Mice and Humans
column37: Telomeres are the DNA "caps" that protect the ends of chromosomes. When cells divide, the length of the telomeres decrease, and this telomere shortening has been associated with diseases of aging and mortality. Chronic pain is the most prevalent human health problem, affecting up to 25% of the Canadian population. Available treatments for pain are often ineffective and associated with side effects including addiction, and thus new pain treatments are sorely needed. One potential new avenue of pain research concerns the role of telomeres, as three published studies have associated telomere length with clinical and experimental pain sensitivity. No systematic analysis of the interaction between telomeres and pain has ever been undertaken, however. Our laboratory has amassed preliminary evidence of a bidirectional relationship between telomeres and pain in mice, one that appears to be true only in males. We have observed that injuries associated with chronic pain can shorten blood cell telomeres, that mutant mice unable to synthesize telomeres have altered pain sensitivity, and that telomere length correlates with pain sensitivity. In addition to telomeres in blood cells, we have observed one of the well-known effects of telomere changes-called cellular senescence-in cells known to mediate pain signals in the nervous system. We are proposing a set of studies to evaluate: 1) the mechanism underlying the relationship between telomeres, cellular senescence, and pain in mice; and, 2) the relationship between telomeres and pain in tissues from human pain patients (including those with fibromyalgia and low back pain). These studies will reveal the nature of the sex difference, and serve as another powerful reminder why biomedical research needs to include both sexes.

column36: Self-renewal Programs in Rhabdomyosarcoma
column37: Relapse is a major clinical problem facing pediatric patients with rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), a devastating malignancy of the muscle. In RMS, populations of undifferentiated cells with stem-like properties drive relapse and if these cells could be eliminated, tumors would regress and patients could remain relapse free. In the Langenau lab, I am utilizing zebrafish, human and mouse xenograft models of RMS to understand biological mechanisms relating to relapse. I have identified an important role for Van Gogh-like 2 (Vangl2), a core regulator of the non-canonical Wnt/Planar cell polarity (Wnt/PCP) signaling pathway in growth and self-renewal of RMS. I have discovered that VANGL2 is expressed in a majority of primary patient RMS and that VANGL2 depletion inhibits tumor cell proliferation and reduces self-renewal. Using a powerful zebrafish model of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) developed in the Langenau lab, I identified that Vangl2 expression enriches for self-renewing tumor cells and when over-expressed, elevates their number >9-fold. Further mechanistic studies reveal a role for RhoA downstream of Vangl2, identifying targetable pathways for potential patient treatment. Previous work has linked Wnt/PCP signaling to growth, invasion and metastasis. However, my work will be the first to assess Wnt/PCP signaling in the self-renewal of tumor cells, offering novel opportunities to isolate and characterize relapse mechanisms involved in human cancer.

column36: Harnessing Large Sequencing Datasets to Investigate the Contribution of Rare Genetic Variants to Monogenic and Polygenic Obesity Risk
column37: Obesity is a major health concern and a risk factor of type-2 diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease. Genetic factors influence body weight and can explain up to 70% of the inter-individual variation of body mass index (BMI). In some cases, mutations in only one gene are thought to cause obesity (i.e monogenic obesity); and in others, many different genetic factors contribute to the development of obesity (i.e polygenic obesity). Although many genetic mutations/variants have been implicated in obesity, it is still a challenge to categorize them into those that are truly "causal" and those whose function is conditional on other variants and/or environmental factors. I aim in my study to 1) calculate for each known mutation the probability that a person develops obesity if he/she is a carrier. This task was previously limited by the absence of large population datasets. I will conduct my analyses in the largest whole genome sequencing dataset, TOPMed (N > 65k individuals) as well as the Mount Sinai's biobank which has > 35k samples with sequencing data. I will also 2) seek to discover new genetic variants that influence BMI and obesity using linear and logistic regression. I will focus on genetic variants that are predicted to disrupt protein function: protein truncating variants (PTVs) and damaging missense variants. PTVs are genetic variants that lead to shortening of the protein-coding sequence of genes and are highly predicted to cause loss-of-function of a given protein. Previous work on PTVs led to therapeutic advances. We will attempt to identify novel PTVs associated with obesity and explore whether an accumulation of PTVs and/or damaging missense variants in certain genes influences obesity. We have access to two large sequencing datasets which provides the best opportunity to explore our hypotheses. This work will contribute a better understanding of the mechanisms involved in obesity and may provide new gene-based drug targets to personalize treatment.

column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in Canada. Altered expression of the protein named RET receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK), which regulates cell function, has been identified in 10-20% of patients diagnosed with the most common type of lung cancer, lung adenocarcinoma (LADC) and is associated with metastasis and reduced patient survival. However, the roles of RET in LADC progression or metastasis are not known and there are currently no RET-specific drugs for the treatment of lung cancer. Current drugs target multiple RTKs and those that also target RET have not improved overall patient survival and are associated with harmful side effects. Recent advances in molecular technologies have produced promising RET-specific drugs. Our lab has identified a novel drug, SW-01 that blocks RET activity and reduces cancer cell growth. And in partnership with Cancer Research UK's Drug Discovery Unit, we have obtained a panel of drugs designed to target RET. Our lab has developed innovative live-cell methods to assess the ability of drugs to specifically target RET, effectively block RET activity and reduce growth and metastasis in LADC cells. We will also analyze RET expression in LADC tumour samples with patient data, such as age, sex, stage and treatment, from the National Cancer Institute and the Canadian Cancer Trials Group to identify key patient traits linked to RET expression in lung cancer. Evaluation of novel drugs in lung cancer cells will elucidate RET's role in LADC tumour growth and metastasis and facilitate development of RET-targeting drugs. Integration of RET expression with LADC patient data will help physicians to create more effective personalized treatment strategies for lung cancer patients.

column36: Measurement of personal support workers' exposure to ergonomic stressors while providing care in clients' homes.
column37: Most Canadians prefer to live as independently as possible in their own homes, rather than in institutions. This requires a strong community care system. The majority of home care (70- 80%) is provided by personal support workers (PSWs), who assist their clients with personal care activities including getting out of bed, dressing and bathing. Unfortunately, these caregivers experience work-related injuries at nearly twice the rate of the general working population. Beyond an understanding that providing personal care in clients' homes involves high exposures to known injury risk factors (such as lifting heavy loads, working in awkward postures, and working alone), we know comparatively little about the specific activities and conditions that put PSWs at such high risk of injury. In the proposed work, we will use wearable sensors to record PSWs' exposures to known injury risk factors as they provide their regular client care. To preserve client privacy, only PSW movement will be tracked. We will also ask PSWs what care activities they assisted with during each visit, how hard they had to work, and whether they had the space and equipment that they needed to provide care safely. Findings from this study will be used to identify activities and conditions that expose PSWs to excessive risk of injury. We will then work with care providers to find ways to improve safety.

column36: The effects of childhood maltreatment on developmental pathways and mental health problems in adolescence: Toward shaping the future of trauma-informed targeted interventions for at-risk adolescents
column37: Exposure to childhood maltreatment including abuse and neglect is a major public health concern in Canada and worldwide. One in every three Canadians experience a type of abuse during childhood resulting in an economic cost of more than 15 billion dollars per year. Exposure to maltreatment changes the normal development and mental health of a child in several ways. Importantly, exposure to maltreatment is associated with earlier initiation, greater severity, more comorbidity, and more resistance to treatment of mental health disorders. These findings highlight the overwhelming need to make early interventions for child maltreatment a priority in Canada. In this project, I aim to (1) test novel hypotheses elucidating the relationship between child maltreatment and psychopathological outcomes; and (2) develop trauma-informed personality-targeted interventions for reducing the risk of psychiatric disorders in maltreated adolescents. The current project will be the first study to collectively investigate differential effects of maltreatment type on initial levels and pattern of growth of internalizing and externalizing personality traits, psychiatric symptoms and related brain responses using two longitudinal studies with large samples of adolescents (i.e., Co-Venture and IMAGEN studies). In addition, I will develop novel trauma-informed personality-targeted interventions and will test the efficacy of these interventions on reducing the internalizing and externalizing problems in adolescents with substantiated cases of child maltreatment, recruited from Youth Protection Services, in a pilot randomized-control trial. The findings from this project will significantly advance our understanding of the early markers of emerging psychiatric disorders in maltreated adolescents and aid transforming the culture of mental health care for this vulnerable population.

column36: Dene First Nations Youth-Led Health Messaging Program in a Community Context
column37: In Canada, First Nations are fighting devastating health issues using Indigenous healing knowledge. Health problems are most concerning for First Nations youth, who face the remnants of colonialism, cultural genocide, intergenerational trauma from residential schools, and poverty. Although many national groups have called for Indigenous youth as leaders in decision making, little action has been taken to explore Indigenous youth leadership initiatives in Canada. Researchers in the field of health risk communication, which is broadly concerned with how people communicate about the risks associated with health issues such as obesity and disease, have recently conducted some successful projects with Indigenous youth. Youth have contributed to better understandings of health problems and solutions, enhanced their strengths and health, and created positive rippling effects in their communities. A promising health intervention appears to be participatory risk communication, an approach that lets First Nations youth take the lead to create and present messages about health. At the same time, they learn Indigenous traditional knowledge skills and how to be co-researchers. This approach aims to improve youth's health, health communications, and community health outcomes, but requires further validation across various First Nations, Inuit, and Metis communities. I will conduct one case study with the Yellowknives Dene First Nations (YKDFN) in Ndilo and Dettah, NT. I will use an Indigenous community-based participatory research approach to highlight community strengths and Indigenous knowledge while identifying my connections to the community as a YKDFN member. During multiple participatory stages of health message development, based on Indigenous traditional knowledge and culture, YKDFN youth will exercise leadership, develop on-the-land skills that promote health, strategize to reduce health risk behaviors, and co-research outcomes of the intervention.

column36: Developmental programming of cardiovascular dysfunction by perinatal iron-deficiency
column37: Iron deficiency (ID) is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, and pregnant women are most at risk. It is estimated that 23% of Canadian women, and as many as 50 to 80% of women in developing nations, experience ID during pregnancy. Iron is important for oxygen transport and energy production, and therefore its deficiency during pregnancy can affect the growing fetus. This project aims to determine how ID alters development of the kidney, making these fetuses prone to long-term health issues, including high blood pressure, kidney disease and heart disease. More specifically, using a model of ID during pregnancy, I aim to determine how the mitochondria-the cell's energy powerhouse-is affected within different organs in the offspring. This project will study how abnormal kidney function changes over the lifespan. A second aim of this study is to test new treatments to prevent the kidney damage caused by ID during pregnancy. Specifically, we will test the plant-derived compound resveratrol as a natural supplement during pregnancy to reduce the damage caused by ID to the developing fetus. The model of iron deficiency during pregnancy used by our research group is clinically relevant, and promises to help many people by identifying how diseases begin and how we can use new treatments to stop these events from taking place. Because ID affects so many pregnant women worldwide, our research has enormous potential to reduce the burden of illness like heart and kidney disease, and therefore help many people.

column36: Time to Stop 'Weighting' and Start Doing: Exploring the Impact of a School-based Weight Bias Intervention
column37: Weight bias is the tendency to unfairly judge a person because of his or her weight. It has many serious physical, mental, and social health outcomes, such as depression, disordered eating patterns, and avoidance of physical activity. Indeed, such negative outcomes can lead to further weight gain. In Canada, one in four children has overweight or obesity. These children face weight bias in all aspects of their lives, including at school, where weight is the most common cause of bullying. Research on ways to reduce weight bias in children is scarce. However, one promising strategy is to address weight bias in school policies and curricula. This strategy is timely given the recent focus on creating safe and caring learning environments in schools. Partnering with the Edmonton, Alberta school community, I will lead a study to develop, implement, and assess the impact of a tailored, school-based program in reducing weight bias in Grades 1-3 students, school staff, and parents. Proposed program elements include student, school staff, and parent education and anti-weight bias policy. I will develop resources, such as lesson plans, for the program, which will be implemented for eight months in an elementary school. To assess program impact, I will examine weight bias in students, school staff, and parents before and after the program implementation period. I will also explore school staff experiences in delivering the program, in order to improve its content and design. This research is needed to create effective strategies to reduce weight bias in schools, a public health issue affecting many Canadian children. By presenting findings to key stakeholders (e.g., Alberta Education), I hope to influence policy change to address weight bias in schools and foster positive social environments that promote children's health and well-being. This program has the potential to be scaled up for students in Grades K-12 across Canada.

column36: The application of ultrasonography in type 2 diabetes: validating ultrasound in the measurement of muscle thickness and quality, and establishing its relationship to metabolic markers of disease
column37: The proportion of Canadians living with diabetes is growing: 3.4 million Canadians were diabetic in 2015, and this number is expected to increase 44% to 5 million by 2025. Compared to healthy adults, type 2 diabetes (T2D) patients experience a reduction in both the force-generating capacity of their muscles as well as overall muscularity, contributing to difficulty performing activities of daily living and lower quality of life. Clearly, a more comprehensive characterization of this growing proportion of the Canadian population is warranted. Ultrasound is a non-invasive tool with several advantages over more well-established body composition methodologies including: 1) low cost and accessibility; 2) the ability to directly quantify muscle thickness and cross-sectional area (CSA); and 3) evaluating the degree of fat and fibrous tissue contained within muscle (which are reflective of poor muscle quality). The infiltration of fatty tissue in particular may be closely associated with impairments in glycemic health (the ability of skeletal muscle to remove sugar from the blood stream). The first objective of my postdoctoral research is therefore to validate ultrasound measurements of muscle quantity (thickness and CSA) and quality (fatty/fibrotic infiltration) in T2D patients. The second objective is to examine whether these ultrasound-derived measurements of muscle quantity and quality relate to indicators of disease severity (ie. glycemic health) in blood and muscle samples taken from T2D patients. The results of this work will be especially relevant for future exercise and nutrition interventions seeking feasible and informative methods to track changes in muscle health in T2D patients. The proposed research will enhance our understanding of relationship between body composition and metabolic health in diabetes, and - it is hoped - assist in the development of novel strategies to treat and manage this highly prevalent disease.

column36: A Sensor for Early Detection of Deep Tissue Pressure Injuries
column37: Pressure ulcers are gaping wounds where the skin, fat and muscles are damaged all the way to the bone. People who use a wheelchair for daily mobility or who are confined to bed because of illness such as the elderly, patients with spinal cord injury, stroke, or the patients who undergo long surgeries, are at risk of developing pressure ulcers. These wounds take a very long time to heal and need special care. Canada spends more than $3.5 billion on treating them each year! Nurses try hard to prevent pressure ulcers. They carefully check the skin of patients to make sure they are not developing. But, many pressure ulcers develop deep in the tissue, close to the bone, and work their way out. By the time the nurses can see them on the skin, all the tissue below had died. Deep pressure ulcers usually develop around the bones we sit on and the ones we lie on in the buttocks. These pressure ulcers can be deadly; even superman (the actor Christopher Reeve) passed away from a pressure ulcer. Deep pressure ulcers can be detected using MRI or ultrasound. But, these methods are very expensive and cannot be used every day. Also, the images have to be shown to a specialist (radiologist) before we can know if a pressure ulcer is present. We want to develop a simple device that allows nurses to test how healthy the tissue deep below the skin is. If they see that a pressure ulcer is developing deep in the tissue, they can take action quickly and consult a doctor to ensure that the ulcer does not get bigger. This device can also be used by vulnerable people or their family members with minimal help. This can improve the quality of life of people and save healthcare large amounts of money.

column36: Experimental Characterization of Phosphate Dysregulation in Kidney Disease and Generation of a Clinical Tool to Identify Phosphate Dysregulation
column37: Kidney disease affects over 25 million North Americans. While kidney failure can progress to the need for a kidney transplant or dialysis treatments, people with milder kidney failure are far more likely to die of heart disease before their kidneys fail completely. This is partly due to problems with phosphate balance, which results in a build-up of calcium and phosphate in the walls of blood vessels. The urine is the major way that extra phosphate is removed from the body. We have shown in our previous experiments that the kidneys have difficulty removing phosphate even when kidney failure is only mild and well before kidney failure is recognized in the clinic by health care providers. Our animal experiments will investigate how phosphate is handled in early kidney failure and how that affects blood vessels. The results of these animal studies will help us to develop a new clinical test to diagnose problems with phosphate removal in humans at a time that is much earlier than we are currently capable of. We call this clinical test the "oral phosphate tolerance test" and it will be used to evaluate how well patients respond to a challenge of phosphate. Kidney failure will affect 1 in 8 Canadians and this number will be even higher in the future due to obesity, diabetes and an aging population. Moreover, phosphate is being used widely as a food preservative. Targeting patients at risk for phosphate imbalance earlier in the course of their kidney failure may decrease the risk of heart disease in this population.

column36: Development of a Blood Test for Colorectal Cancer based on Metabolomic Signature
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer death in the western world. Ideally, CRC will be detected early because treatments become progressively more complicated, toxic and expensive in later disease stages, and the survival is best in early stage of disease. That is the basis of screening. Currently, the gold standard screening test is colonoscopy, which is invasive, expensive and difficult to perform on large populations. One strategy is to enrich the subgroup that requires a colonoscopy by doing a stool test (called a fecal immunohistochemical test, FIT). The problem is that compliance for stool tests is less than 40% because testing stool is objectionable and inconvenient. We have developed a blood test based on the chemical composition of serum. This test is quite sensitive and it has already been tested on over 600 patients. In this project, in collaboration with Med-Life Discoveries and Innovate Calgary, as well as a multidisciplinary science team, we will further refine the test, then create a diagnostic test that can be used in a typical clinical laboratory. Software will be developed to enhance the capability to analyze test results. Finally, we will test the new diagnostic test on blood samples collected from close to 3500 individuals who had screening colonoscopies. At the end, we will have a convenient, clinically applicable test that will be tested in the future in a larger clinical trial that would inform regulatory agencies and clinicians on the value of this new test as an alternative screening tool.

column36: Biological Finger Joint Replacement
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common type of arthritis in Canada, and finger OA affects at least 6.8% of individuals over the age of 26 years. In the absence of disease modifying treatments, current therapeutic modalities are aimed at reducing pain. These treatments alleviate symptoms but do not prevent the processes that result in the changes characteristic of this disease. Failure of these treatments usually culminates in joint replacement surgery. Current studies reporting outcomes of artificial finger joint replacements have highlighted the high rate of failure and lack of efficacy in restoring hand function by such implants. We have developed an alternative biological approach to joint repair that involves formation of a personalized biological replacement designed for secure fixation by bone ingrowth while presenting a surface lined by cartilage that will mimic the native joint form. In time as the bone substitute component degrades and is replaced by natural tissues (bone), this replacement part will allow for complete joint regeneration to the desired function. The goal of this research proposal is to develop and evaluate a small joint biologic joint replacement in a pre-clinical animal model. The aim is to design a joint replacement that can be used to resurface a joint in the finger or wrist affected by either osteoarthritis or any inflammatory arthritis such as psoriatic or rheumatoid arthritis. With the results obtained from the proposed studies it will be possible to progress towards translating our approach into a clinical treatment for people with hand arthritis.

column36: Development of a Point of Care System for Automated Coma Prognosis
column37: The Problem: Coma is a state of unconsciousness with a variety of causes. Traditional tests for coma outcome prediction are mainly based on a set of clinical observations (e.g., pupillary constriction). Recently however, event-related potentials (ERPs; which are transient electroencephalogram [EEG] responses to auditory, visual or tactile stimuli) have been introduced as useful predictors of a positive coma outcome (i.e., emergence). However, such tests require a skilled neurophysiologist and such people are in short supply. Also, none of the current approaches have sufficient positive and negative predictive accuracies to provide definitive prognoses in the clinical setting. Objective: We will apply innovative machine learning methods to analyze patient EEGs to develop a simple, objective, replicable, and inexpensive point of care system which can significantly improve the accuracy of coma prognosis relative to current methods. The physical requirements of the proposed system consist only of an EEG system (inexpensive in terms of medical equipment) and a conventional laptop computer. Methodology: We intend to extend our newest algorithms and develop machine learning tools for automatic analysis and detection of ERP components. Preliminary results by the team in this respect have been very promising. The most salient features (i.e., biomarkers) extracted from the ERP will be identified and combined in an optimal fashion to give an accurate indicator of prognosis. Features will be extracted from resting state brain networks and from network trajectories associated with the processing of ERP signals. Significance: The proposed work will enable critical care physicians to assess coma prognosis with speed and accuracy. Thus, families and their health care team will be provided the most accurate information possible to guide discussions of goals of care and life sustaining therapies in the context of dealing with the consequences of devastating neurological injury.

column36: Prospective, population-based studies of antimalarials and their impact on vision loss, quality-of-life, disease activity, and mortality in patients with rheumatic disease
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and lupus are forms of inflammatory arthritis that affect at least 1 of every 100 Canadians, mainly females. Immune dysfunction leads to organ and joint damage, disability, work loss, pain, fatigue and early mortality. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), an anti-malarial drug, is also a long-term treatment for lupus and RA that improves survival. Though effective, low cost, and generally safe, one serious adverse effect of HCQ is irreversible retinopathy (damage to the back of the eye) that can lead to vision loss and blindness. Retinopathy was thought to be rare (<2% of long-term HCQ users), but in a recent study using more sensitive screening tests, many more were affected (7.5%). As a result, guidelines now call for HCQ users to have these new, more sensitive eye tests every year, to diagnose it earlier. But much is unknown about the risk of retinopathy, risk factors, and impact of earlier diagnosis on patients' vision, survival and quality-of-life. For example, detecting more cases of mild retinopathy (which may not progress) could simply increase patients' anxiety. To fill these gaps, we will use electronic healthcare data (without names or identifying information) to follow ~3,000 people with lupus and RA who have used HCQ for at least 5 years. We will use new statistical methods to estimate of the risk of retinopathy (overall, and with HCQ different doses), and risk factors, which may include female sex, increased age, kidney disease, and using higher doses of HCQ. We will also study its progression over time - we expect severe cases of retinopathy will progress to vision loss, but milder cases will not. Finally, we will also see what happens when patients stop HCQ, or reduce the dose. While that may help prevent vision loss, risk of death may increase alongside. Our findings will help clinicians and patients make more informed treatment decisions to reduce their chances of vision loss, while optimising their survival and quality-of-life

column36: Growing old: Optimizing health and aging in immigrants with health services research
column37: In Canada, we are witnessing two key population trends: our population is aging rapidly, and is also becoming more diverse. Researchers have shown that immigrants can experience unequal access to health services and receive different treatment by health providers, but we do not know to what extent this happens in older immigrants. We also know that certain countries and cultures live longer than Canadians. Because of this, our diverse aging population presents us with two opportunities to improve the health of all older adults. The first is the chance to understand if health disparities exist so that we can make efforts to correct them. The second is to study older adults of different ethnicities and cultures to learn what factors might contribute to aging well (that is, living longer, healthier lives). To do this, we will use Canadian immigration records for Ontario residents that have been linked with health records that are collected every time residents access a universally-funded health care service. We will use this information to compare immigrants with long-standing residents to see if there are differences in age, sex, geography, health status and heath care utilization (among other factors). We will also interview older adults who are members of the Retired Teachers of Ontario to learn from them what contributes to healthy aging. Results from this research can be used by policy makers to ensure that all older adults have equal opportunities to age well, especially those who are most vulnerable.

column37: An astounding 70% of Canadian adults report a history of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), such as childhood abuse and neglect. ACEs are associated with a range of poor health outcomes in adulthood, including depression. In fact, 90% of primary care patients who report depression also report a history of ACEs. The recognition and treatment of ACEs, however, remains unaddressed in most primary care settings. This study will be the first to evaluate a clinical treatment program within primary care settings that targets both symptoms of depression and the effects of childhood adversity. Specifically, this study will evaluate the effectiveness of the Skills Training in Affect and Interpersonal Regulation (STAIR) model in reducing symptoms of depression among adults with a history of ACEs. STAIR targets essential skills that have been impaired due to experiences of childhood adversity, such as the ability to effectively regulate emotions. Adult primary care patients will be eligible for the study if they report a history of ACEs and current depression. Half of the patients will be assigned to attend six sessions of the STAIR treatment program, while the other patients will receive no treatment beyond usual care from their primary care provider. All patients will complete a measure of depression at baseline, mid-study, and post-study. It is hypothesized that the STAIR group will show significant improvements in symptoms of depression as compared to the usual care group. This study will provide important information about the effectiveness of STAIR in treating depression and about the feasibility of implementing such a program within primary care settings. Findings have the potential to inform the dissemination of a widely accessible treatment protocol for Canadians with ACEs that will expand choice for patients, improve quality of care, alleviate the burdens of depression, and lower health care costs for society as a whole.

column36: The Structural and Metabolic Changes Associated with Ependymal Layer Disruption in the Age Continuum of Hydrocephalus - A Human and Animal Model Study
column37: Hydrocephalus (HC) is a debilitating disease that affects 1 in 1000 Canadians. It afflicts all age groups, with infants being the most vulnerable. HC results from an over-accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the brain. Untreated HC results in irreversible brain injury, disability and death. The only treatment is CSF diversion, typically via a shunt, 50% of which fail within the first two years. A major hurdle in the advancement of care in HC has been the limited understanding of HC's pathophysiology. As a neurosurgeon, I have seen many patients die or maimed by HC, and convicted to now devote my life's work to it. As such, I have taken a leave of absence from my clinical duties to pursue a PhD in HC scientific research, after which I will return to practice. My goal is to become a surgeon-scientist, who will pioneer translational research in HC. My PhD is a dual university collaboration, which I helped establish between the University of Calgary (U of C) and Washington University (WUSTL). The focused objective of my research is to characterize the cellular mechanisms of HC and identify molecular pathways that can be targeted for treatment. I will be using donated brains of deceased HC and non-HC patients across all age groups, from 12 centers worldwide. Recently, emerging evidence has implicated cells of the brain's ventricles where CSF is made, as a major component in the pathogenesis of HC. I will therefore leverage the resources and expertise at both U of C and WUSTL to study those cells in my samples. I will also use state-of-the-art brain imaging and CSF analysis technologies to identify potential biomarkers that may be used to diagnose and treat HC in at-risk individuals. In addition, I will create a novel mouse model of HC to cross-validate our findings, and establish it for future HC research. This multi-center study is first of its kind, and will lay the foundation for rigorously pursuing treatments that would curb this devastating disease.

column36: La reduction du risque cardiometabolique chez les Canadiens : Developpement, optimisation et evaluation d'un environnement numerique d'apprentissage intelligent en counseling sur le changement de comportement de sante aupres d'infirmiers.
column37: La prevention des maladies cardiovasculaires et du diabete est une priorite nationale de sante publique. Le counseling sur le changement de comportement (CCC) permet de reduire l'incidence de ces pathologies et leurs complications en visant les comportements nocifs (ex. diete hypercalorique). Toutefois, il y a eu peu de succes dans la conception d'interventions efficaces pour former les infirmiers en CCC. Les approches de formation actuelles en CCC sont peu accessibles et ne sont pas personnalisees a la pratique de chaque infirmier, ce qui entraine une application clinique sous-optimale. De plus, les approches de formation en ligne dites standardisees, lineaires et identiques pour tous les infirmiers, sont peu efficientes. Pour resoudre ce probleme, les environnements numeriques d'apprentissage intelligents (ENAI), utilisant l'intelligence artificielle, permettraient de fournir une formation personnalisee en considerant les connaissances, les objectifs et la pratique de chaque infirmier. Cette etude vise a developper un ENAI en CCC, puis a mener un essai clinique pour examiner son efficacite a ameliorer les resultats d'apprentissage et cliniques chez des infirmiers. Nous developperons l'ENAI en CCC, puis nous l'optimiserons en laboratoire en evaluant avec des technologies de pointe les reponses affectives et cognitives de 15 infirmiers lors de son utilisation. Nous recruterons ensuite 128 infirmiers et les assignerons soit a l'ENAI, soit a une approche de formation en ligne standardisee en CCC. Nous prevoyons que l'ENAI ameliorera l'efficience de l'apprentissage, les connaissances, les competences et l'application clinique du CCC en comparaison avec une approche de formation en ligne standardisee. Cette etude sera la premiere a developper et evaluer un ENAI chez des infirmiers. Cette recherche nous permet d'entrevoir une meilleure prise en charge des facteurs de risque comportementaux en milieu hospitalier et confortera le leadership du Canada en education en sante.

column36: Rescue Electrical Conduction of Heart Scar Tissue to Diminish Cardiac Arrhythmia
column37: Heart attacks and heart failure are the main causes of disability and death around the world and in Canada. After a heart attack, the death of muscle cells causes a scar to form in the heart. This scar stops the normal path of electrical signals that allows the heart to beat in a coordinated fashion to efficiently eject blood from the heart. In addition, the disrupted signals can induce extra inefficient heart beats (arrhythmia). Patients with abnormal conduction or arrhythmias often need a pacemaker, but electrical stimulation of the heart from the pacemaker disrupts the normal beating sequence and induces dysfunction of the heart. Both heart attack and the electrical stimulation result in abnormal signal conduction in the heart. We will create new conductive biomaterials which will repair the heart and properly conduct electrical signals across the scar following a heart attack. The new materials will enhance the transmission of electrical signals that control the pumping of the heart. The goal is to restore the normal pattern of coordinated heart contraction for heart diseases described above. One biomaterial is a gel that will be injected into the scar tissue to improve the electrical signaling propagation of the heart. The second biomaterial is a membrane which will be applied to the surface of the damaged heart. Our new materials are unique because they will facilitate electrical conduction and keep the heart beating synchronously. We will measure how well the gel and the membrane conduct electrical signals and how well they coordinate the heart beats. Our aim is to provide a new treatment for cardiac patients that will be more effective than current therapies. This new approach could allow patients to return to their normal lifestyle and remain active without the need of a pacemaker. The overall impact of our proposed research is to improve the quality of life for patients, and reduce the burden of heart disease for both patients and the healthcare system.

column36: Mechatronic Device for Multimodal Suppression of Parkinsonian Tremor
column37: Tremor, one of the most disabling symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), significantly affects the lives of patients. Traditional medicines are often ineffective and surgery is highly invasive and risky. A new approach to managing tremor includes using devices that involve either mechanical suppression via actuators (e.g., motors that apply forces), or electrical suppression (using a modulated electrical signal to stimulate the muscles involved in generating tremor). Unfortunately, the devices that have been presented in the literature are too heavy and cumbersome for daily use by patients and none are currently commercially available. Building on our previous work, the objective of this project is to develop a device that can suppress tremor motion by combining both mechanical suppression and electrical stimulation. Compared to other devices that use mechanical suppression alone, this device is expected to be more compact in size, lower in weight, and offer an extended battery life. Compared to devices that use electrical stimulation alone, this device is expected to be able to suppress motion better and to decrease pain and discomfort. To conduct this work, we will design smart control systems that adapt to the patient's ability to tolerate electrical stimulation. We will design new actuators using smart materials. We will investigate how to electrically stimulate muscle when combined with mechanical suppression. Finally, a validation experiment will be performed on individuals with PD to determine the feasibility of the device for clinical use. The expected outcome of this project will be a first prototype of a tremor suppression device that effectively incorporates both mechanical suppression and electrical stimulation. This new technology will be greatly beneficial to patients who are disabled by tremor of the wrist and fingers and is expected to significantly improve their ability to perform activities of daily living.

column36: Cesarean delivery rates and perinatal outcomes in Canada and Sweden: Identifying targets for safely reducing the cesarean deliveries
column37: The rate of cesarean delivery (CD) in Canada has increased from 17.6% in 1995 to 27.9% in 2015. High rates of CD are potentially responsible for unnecessary utilization of health resources as well as maternal and neonatal harm. The reasons for the increase in CD rates are multifactorial and not well understood. Recent data suggests that CD rates below 20% are possible, safe, and compatible with optimal health outcomes for mothers and their newborns. For instance, Sweden has had a stable, relatively low CD rate for years (16.4% in 2003 and 17.4% in 2015), along with low rates of maternal and perinatal adverse outcomes. However, direct comparisons of CD rates between populations tends to be compromised by differences in obstetric profiles and risk factors for adverse perinatal outcomes. Furthermore, there is an implied presumption that any increase in CD rates represents an adverse change which needs to be remedied. The alternative perspective on this issue is that any increase in CD rates needs to be set against potential improvements in maternal, fetal and infant health. Increases in CD rates that occur concomitantly with declines in maternal, fetal and infant adverse outcomes may potentially justify higher CD rates. Therefore, this research aims to use retrospective cohort studies with data from Canada and Sweden to 1) identify subpopulations of women responsible for the variation in CD rates between Canada and Sweden, 2) contrast these populations using analyses that incorporate important between-country differences in risk factors for CD, such as maternal age, pre-pregnancy body-mass-index and weight gain in pregnancy, and 3) evaluate differences in CD rates in Canada and Sweden within the context of maternal, fetal and infant morbidity and mortality. These issues have yet to be addressed in the extant literature and hence represent critical knowledge gaps for women, clinicians, public health policy-makers, and related stakeholders.

column36: Advanced Bioreactors for Evaluation and Systematic Optimization of Decellularization and Recellularization of the Lung and Trachea
column37: Diseases affecting the airways are an important clinical problem and for the majority of patients with end-stage disease, transplantation of lung and/or trachea has become the only life-saving option. Ideally we need access to 'off-the-shelf' replacement grafts reducing the dependency on donor organs, wait-time and risk of death. In the lung, organ regeneration is achieved by using biohybrid devices with partially synthetic or natural scaffolds. The approach is to utilize advanced bioreactors operating under optimized physiological conditions to repopulate with new cells, scaffolds in which the resident cells have been removed, and use for functional replacement of damaged tissue. While transplantation of regenerated whole lungs is a far-off goal, we exploit the simpler system of the trachea with which we have extensive expertise while addressing key issues that will set the foundation for future clinical application of whole lung grafts. At the end of the funding period, we expect to begin clinical translation of a functional tracheal biograft used to address small airway and larger tracheal defects, respectively. The optimized tracheal bioreactors developed can result in commercial products via licensing to already existing lung biotech companies or through company creation ventures with focus on enhanced organ-specific bioreactors. In addition, the development of a computational model of fluid flow using a computerized geometrical models of vascular (and airway) networks will allow in silico experimental programs to explore strategies for targeted cell delivery. Models developed here have the potential for significant impact in lung tissue engineering, and can be applied to research groups focused on other organs. Completion of this work will set in motion a therapeutic strategy with the potential to save lives and vastly improve the quality of life of Canadians suffering from end-stage lung disease.

column36: Novel technologies for engineering closure of non-healing skin wounds
column37: In normal individuals, most skin wounds close within a few days. However, in patients with diabetes or vascular problems skin wounds can stay open leading to development of a "chronic" or non-healing wound. Such wounds commonly cause tremendous psychological and physical suffering for the patient, and often result in limb amputation and even death. Despite extensive research, reproducible treatments for non-healing dermal wounds remain elusive. Skin is composed of many different protein types, which change when skin is injured. Proteins such as collagen provide structural support, but another type known as matricellular proteins are produced in the wound bed and form a scaffold that cells attach to and move on. However, these proteins provide cells the instructions on how to repair the tissue. These proteins are not normally present, but are upregulated after injury. However, our analysis of chronic wounds has found that two of these matricellular proteins, periostin and connective tissue growth factor (CCN2) are missing and no scaffold is formed in the wound, meaning it is unable to repair. Periostin and CCN2 are very important in shutting down inflammation and inducing the next phase of repair, where cells move into the wound and make new tissue. We made scaffolds composed of fibres of periostin and CCN2 and demonstrated that they caused cells to enter the wound and close it in diabetic mice. Furthermore, they helped attract blood vessels into the wounds. We have now formed a multi-disciplinary collaborative research team consisting of biologists, engineers, imaging specialists, a veterinarian, clinicians and industrial collaborators Advanced BioMatrix, to optimize maufacturing protocols and move our work into a large animal model that would be required prior to testing of the scaffolds in humans. If successful, this proposal will lead to the development of new materials that could be used to make chronic skin wounds close.

column36: Drug use geographies: a qualitative GIS study of the impacts of overlapping housing and overdose crises on women who use drugs in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside
column37: Housing is an important factor shaping health. However, due to a lack of affordable housing in cities, single room accommodation (SRAs) housing has long been 'housing of the last resort' for people who use drugs. Previous research has highlighted the negative impacts of SRA housing on health outcomes, with women facing additional harms (e.g. increased violence, adverse mental health outcomes). In Vancouver, British Columbia (BC) SRA units are among the only housing options available to people who use drugs amid a housing crisis, despite these known health-related risks, and the majority of SRAs are concentrated in the Downtown Eastside neighbourhood - the site of Canada's largest drug scene. Currently, Vancouver's housing crisis overlaps with a province-wide opioid overdose crisis, the centre of which is also the Downtown Eastside. Approximately 30% of fatal overdoses in 2017 took place in SRA housing or shelters. Indigenous women have been unduly impacted by these overlapping crises compared to non-Indigenous women. This highlights the need to understand the specific ways in which women, especially Indigenous women, are at risk of overdose. While previous research has highlighted how social, physical, political, and economic factors influence drug-related risks (e.g. syringe sharing, drug use environments), no research has examined how SRA housing creates overdose risks for women who use drugs. This project addresses this research gap by examining the unique ways in which women who use drugs experience and manage overdose risk within SRA housing.

column36: Improving the identification of retinal biomarkers of Alzheimer disease in vivo
column37: Alzheimer's disease is a slowly evolving neurodegenerative disorder that ultimately leading to dementia. We will develop methods combining multispectral retinal imaging with image processing to identify biomarkers of amyloid plaque accumulation in the retina and correlate results with brain PET amyloid imaging.

column36: Trends in the use of oral anticoagulation therapies and outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common and important cardiac arrhythmia in the world, characterized by an irregular heartbeat from quivering of the upper chambers of the heart (atria). AF is emerging as the next epidemic in cardiovascular medicine. It is estimated that 5 million patients are being diagnosed with AF each year worldwide and its prevalence is expected to double in the next 20 years. AF independently increases the risk of stroke, death, cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular events. One-fifth of all strokes are attributable to AF with significant morbidity and mortality. Substantial advances have been made in stroke prophylaxis for AF patients in the last few years including the development of new oral anticoagulants (NOAC). However, it is unclear whether these new therapies have been widely adopted in clinical practice and if this has translated into an improvement in patient outcomes. In Canada and around the world, there is great interest in improving the performance of the healthcare system. Our study will explore if there are gaps in current practice and if patients are receiving optimal care. Analysis of this real-world data will create targets for future Quality Improvements efforts in our healthcare system, which will ultimately ensure that patients are receiving the best possible care. The study results will have important implications for patients with heart disease, hospitals and policy-makers.

column36: Evaluating the impact of a financial incentive for shared decision-making on lung cancer screening rates in the Medicare population
column37: Health systems aim to encourage patients to be active participants in their care. This includes informing patients about their different treatment options, encouraging them to ask questions and discuss their concerns, and ensuring that their values and preferences guide treatment decisions. One process for placing patients at the centre of their own care is "shared decision-making" (SDM). It is a model of patient-provider communication that has been shown to increase patient knowledge and result in decisions that better reflect what matters most to patients. However, providers often say there is insufficient time to engage in SDM. One solution is to provide longer (or additional) consultations so that SDM can occur. Within a fee-for-service healthcare system like Canada, this would require paying providers for additional consultation time through the introduction of a new billing code for SDM. Canadian jurisdictions have considered this option, but as of yet none have implemented it. However, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) in the US have. In 2016, the CMS introduced a billing code for a SDM visit for high-risk patients who were considering lung cancer screening with a CT scan. Currently, only about 3% of eligible patients undergo lung cancer screening in the US. The belief is that by allocating addition time to engage in SDM, a greater proportion of patients will be screened, resulting in decreased lung cancer mortality. This study will be the first to evaluate the impact of this billing code for SDM on lung cancer screening rates. The evidence will be used to inform policy in the US, where there are established screening programs, and in Canada, where provinces are beginning to explore the potential of population-based lung cancer screening programs.

column36: Selective laser-mediated gene therapy for ocular diseases
column37: Ocular diseases affecting the cornea (front part of the eye) or the retina (image processing cells in the back of the eye) are leading causes of vision loss and affect millions of individuals worldwide. These diseases are either incurable or only transiently improved with current therapies. Emerging solutions that interfere with defective genes or supplement deficient ones have shown promise. However, there is a current void in treatment modalities that selectively target diseased cells on the eye, which has hindered the development of effective gene-therapy-based treatments. Several current gene therapy approaches call for the use of viruses to deliver genes, yet virus-based systems present a number of toxic side-effects. A safe, precise and selective gene delivery system for corneal and retinal cells would open novel therapeutic avenues to address diseases that are of major public health concern. The proposed research project aims to develop a targeted and non-viral gene delivery treatment for the cornea and the retina using lasers and FDA approved gold nanoparticles. This project will be performed by a multidisciplinary team of researchers with complementary expertise in lasers, nanotechnology, optics, corneal and retinal cell biology. Our team has developed an expertise in laser-mediated gene delivery into cells with high efficiency and very low toxicity using gold nanoparticles. Building on a filed patent and exciting preliminary data in cells, tissues and in live animals, we will expand our technical expertise to diseased eyes, with the aim to offer a new, safe, selective method and system to treat two important diseases leading to blindness in Canada: age-related macular degeneration and corneal endothelial dystrophies. The project will be performed with our Knowledge Transfer Users, Axis Photonics, experts in laser technologies and Optina, owner of a proprietary eye camera diagnostic system. Both will participate in the commercialisation of our technique.

column36: Image-Guided Molecular Optical Spectroscopy for Tumor-Targeted Prostate Cancer Interventions
column37: Confirming the location, extent, and grade of prostate cancer for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes remains challenging due to the architectural and phenotypic heterogeneity. In the case of blind systematic ultrasound-guided biopsies, this leads to more than 30% of false negative rates, while for tumor-targeted (focal) therapies such as brachytherapy, their success hinge on precise mapping of MRI cancer targets to provide the gross tumor location, but lack molecular information at the treatment location, without accurate grading of the tumor and can lead to a poor balance of toxicities. Therefore, there is no existing medical technologies addressing the timely confirmation of tumor location/grade during therapy. Our objective is to develop an image-guidance system integrating real-time molecular tissue characterization with an optical Raman spectroscopy (RS) instrument for tumor-targeted prostate cancer interventions, improving tumor localization and characterization. Specifically, we will develop and conduct first in-human studies using a real-time navigation platform technology allowing for high-precision and tumor-specific harvesting of samples during biopsy procedures. Four research aims will be completed to insure in-human translation of the technology into to our partners Elekta and Philips Canada within 3 years: (1) Develop a fiber optics RS needle device for tissue characterization to guide prostate interventions; (2) Train supervised machine-learning algorithms from spectral RS signatures to infer biological properties; (3) Implement an integrated image-guidance platform with real-time RS tissue classification and needle tracking to identified MRI targets with prostate motion compensation; (4) Conduct a pilot clinical study patients with localized PCa visible on MRI and who will undergo HDR brachytherapy. Ultimately, we will have a high-end technique clinically tested in prostate interventions for practical molecular identification and cancer detection.
