column36: Improving the reliability of cytology diagnosis with immunoplasmonic multiplex labeling.
column37: Most cancer diagnoses are first established using a biopsy, and as such, biopsies are critical to the health care of Canadians. Different types of biopsies are performed to achieve a diagnosis, but physicians do prefer fine-needle aspiration cytology, hereafter referred to as cytology, because it is associated with fewer side effects for the patients. Accordingly, the number of cytology performed annually is increasing for many organs such as lung and pancreas. Cytology is evaluated by pathologists, who are using different tools to refine their diagnoses. The objective of the most commonly used tool is to detect proteins in the cells which are specific for cancer. The multiple preparation steps that have to be performed to colour those proteins can destroy said proteins and therefore affect the reliability of the tool. Our objective is therefore to bypass the preparation steps by using metallic nanoparticles to identify the proteins without degrading them, thus improving the reliability of the diagnosis. Furthermore, we propose to use specific laser-based technologies to detect the metallic nanoparticles. This project may be considered pioneering as clinical validation on human cytology samples will ensure highly beneficial accuracy of diagnosis and optimal selection of treatment, consequently improving the health of Canadian patients. To achieve this innovative research project, we put together an excellent multidisciplinary and complementary team of internationally renowned scientists and industrial partners coming from the full spectrum of knowledge involved in this project. This team has already acquired a strong expertise in metallic nanoparticles use and detection for biological diagnostics and we are recognized by our peers as protein detection experts. Our excellence is demonstrated by multiple patents and declarations of inventions. Our industrial partner, Photon etc, completes our skills in commercialization of metallic nanoparticles and their detection.

column36: Re-engineering of the hospital sink environment to reduce transmission of multi-drug resistant opportunistic pathogens
column37: Microbes are becoming more and more resistant to antibiotics and are often found in sinks and plumbing in hospitals. Recently, there has been an increase in the number of infections caused by these organisms. Sinks and plumbing seem to play a role in multiplication and transmission of these organisms, partly due to water-saving technologies. We intend to reduce patient exposure and risk of infection associated with organisms found in sinks through improved engineering measures, design and risk management. Critical priority pathogens listed by the World Health Organization in the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance will be targeted in this study (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and Enterobacteriaceae - Serratia marcescens). Different technologies and approaches will be applied in neonatal intensive care unit rooms to prevent colonization and dispersion of these organisms to patient: self-cleaning drains, point-of-use devices and chemical disinfection procedures of the drain and sink. Our results will help pave the way for safer hospitals through optimal engineering design. As we are partnering with people who make recommendations and build hospitals, our results will improve hospital designs.

column36: Computer-Integrated Ultrasound Guidance and Mechatronics Assistance for Breast Brachytherapy
column37: Permanent-seed breast brachytherapy is a treatment in which radioactive seeds are inserted into the breast using hollow needles and can be considered as a patient-friendly and cost-effective option for women diagnosed with early breast cancer. However, it is a relatively new procedure that lacks an established surgical protocol and assist devices similar to what exists for the well-established prostate brachytherapy procedure. Issues in breast brachytherapy include difficulty and reliability of ultrasound (US) imaging and needle guidance under it, which results in inaccuracies in placing seeds within the breast. This results in uncertainties for doctors looking to adopt breast brachytherapy, which is exacerbated by the already-existing steep learning curve associated with brachytherapy in general. This is because, in practice, seed-carrying needles often do not follow their planned paths due to needle deflection and tissue deformation, resulting in seeds being placed inaccurately, which can result in an undesirable radiation dose being delivered to the breast. Many of the above concerns contribute to the reluctance of doctors and hospitals to adopt breast brachytherapy. However, these concerns can be addressed with computer and mechatronic assistance and image guidance to improve the accuracy and reliability of seed placement using accurate measurements, objective assessments, and reproducible movements. Our objective is to provide solutions to the unique issues of breast brachytherapy using mechatronic systems and computer algorithms for visualization and control of seed deposition. We will develop a US probe positioner, a hand-held needle steering assistant, and software to match images taken before and after the surgery and monitor seed placement so that the surgeon is free from many of these problems and is fully in control of the most critical action, i.e., needle insertion, and the most important outcome monitoring task, i.e., seed location tracking.

column36: Placenta on a chip: A humanized platform for testing of pharmaceuticals and environmental chemicals
column37: The human placenta is a complex organ that controls the health of the baby and also impacts the health of the mother. Signals from the cells that form the barrier between mother and fetus can "program" the babies health after it is born or control whether the baby is born prematurely. 1 in 9 babies are born prematurely and this can lead to many health problems in later life. It is difficult to study this barrier in animal models or humans because of the complexity of the placenta. Our research will develop a "placenta on a chip"; a micro-device that mimics a small section of the human placenta in 3D. We will develop special surfaces that allow the stem cells of the placenta to behave as though they were in their natural environment within the womb. This portable "placenta" will be the first example of such a device that brings together the important cells of the placenta and simulates the proper oxygen levels and blood flow that would exist in the human placenta. This device will be very useful in reducing the cost of testing drugs to see if they would be harmful to the mother or fetus and also help to reduce the number of animals that are used in drug testing. Importantly, we will also verify whether this device predicts the biological responses of actual placental tissues when treated with environmental toxins; something that no one has evaluated. We will easily and inexpensively be able to identify whether certain chemicals are causing the maternal-fetal barrier to release signals that might harm the baby or cause premature birth. We have already partnered with Evik Diagnostics, a Canadian company that is interested in diagnostic testing for conditions that affect the health of the mother and baby in pregnancy.

column36: Intergenerational transmission of child social-emotional health: Investigating the roles of socioeconomic position, community support, and infant-caregiver attachment
column37: Lifecourse health research consistently demonstrates that children's early environments have significant and enduring consequences for children's social-emotional development and future mental health outcomes. Early stressors including socioeconomic disadvantage and unpredictable or consistently low adult responsiveness can change children's biological capabilities to respond to stress, and these capabilities can be passed down across generations. Secure attachment to a primary caregiver may be one way that exposures to early adversities can be overcome, putting children on healthier lifecourse trajectories and disrupting cycles of disadvantage and compromised mental health. This study investigates how early attachment is associated with intergenerational social-emotional outcomes for offspring in the context of varying socioeconomic circumstances. Two primary objectives are to: (1) examine how early infant-caregiver attachment across generations affects children's social-emotional health (psychosocial functioning and behaviour) as well as biological markers of stress (DNA methylation); and (2) evaluate whether data can be routinely collected during 18-month public health nurse visits to identify social and structural supports available within communities that can help improve infant-caregiver attachment for the overall purpose of optimizing child mental health outcomes. This research capitalizes on two unique data sets available through the Royal Children's Hospital and Deakin Centre for Social and Early Emotional Development in Melbourne, Australia. Objective 1 will be examined using data from the Australian Temperament Project Generation 3, a multigenerational cohort study spanning 3 generations. Objective 2 will be examined using the Toddler Development Instrument, a Canadian-developed survey collecting population-level data on children's early environments, community resources, and infant developmental milestones.

column36: Engineering DNAzyme-gold nanoparticle diagnostic device
column37: Mosquitos carry many infectious pathogens that can significantly affect a patient's health as well as other people that the patients come into contact with. Currently, there is a major global scare with the transmission of the Zika virus, which has been implicated in cerebral brain malformations among fetuses and newborns. Given advances in transportation vehicles, there is a significant risk of the virus being imported back to countries where the mosquitos carry it are found. There remains an urgent need to develop simple methods to rapidly diagnose Zika virus infection as it continues to spread to new locations. Rapid diagnosis in areas with reduced access to testing laboratories will allow appropriate management of pregnant women who become infected and implement control measures as the virus spreads to new, often remote areas. Here, in this project, our aim is to develop a unique colour-based test using nanotechnology components to be able to rapidly diagnose patients that are presenting symptoms for the Zika virus, as well as two other important mosquito borne viruses, dengue and chikungunya virus. Testing of the 3 viruses is important to determine proper treatment, as patients infected with either of three viruses may present the same symptoms. We will further develop a smartphone readout system that enables the quantification and monitoring of transmission of Zika virus. A team consisting of an engineer and two medical doctors is assembled to build and test this diagnostic device. Our commercial partners have the infrastructure to build the device and reagents, test the diagnostic systems, and to globally sell and distribute the technology for use in patient care.

column36: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Augment Mobility and Cognition in Cerebral Microvascular Disease? Exploring the Temporal Synchrony of Relevant Neural Networks
column37: Cerebral microvascular disease (CMD) is a disease that affects the small blood vessels in the brain and impairs their ability to properly supply nutrients to the brain. It is common in older adults and is associated with impaired mobility (i.e., slowed walking) and increased risk of dementia. To date, there is no effective drug therapy for older adults with CMD. However, there is emerging evidence that individuals with CMD may benefit from approaches such as transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Specifically, researchers demonstrated that tDCS can improve brain function in those with CMD. This proposed study aims to expand on previous work by pairing tDCS with advanced brain imaging techniques to better understand how exactly does tDCS positively benefit brain function as well as one's cognitive function and mobility. The specific goals of the proposed project are to examine whether: 1) tDCS will improve how different regions of the brain work and coordinate with one another; and 2) tDCS-induced changes in brain function are associated with improved cognitive function and mobility. We will achieve these two goals by carrying out a study where people with CMD are assigned by chance to 1) tDCS or 2) sham. 48 men and women aged 65 years or older with CMD will be included. Both groups will undergo 10 sessions of stimulation over Two weeks. We will assess cognitive function, mobility, and acquire brain scans at the beginning and at the end of the 10-week study. To determine longer term effects, we will repeat our cognitive and mobility assessments 1 and 2.5 months after trial completion. If successful, this project will be the first study to show that tDCS can positively impact brain function and thereby enhance motor and cognitive functions in older adults with CMD. These findings will help validate tDCS as a potential solution to functional declines caused by CMD.

column36: Longitudinal analysis of incubation of cue-induced craving in individuals with cocaine use disorder: An event-related potential study
column37: One of the main challenges in the treatment of drug addiction is the high risk of relapse that can happen very early at the beginning of the abstinence period. The relapse phenomenon is accompanied by an experience of a strong urge to use drugs called craving, which can be triggered by a re-exposure to cues and contexts previously associated with drug use. Studies have shown a phenomenon called incubation of craving, which is an increase of craving in the first months after stopping the use of drugs, such as cocaine. However, these studies used self-reported methods to qualify craving, a subjective method that may be biased. Moreover, no human studies have attempted to monitor the evolution of craving over a long period of time. Therefore, this project aims at objectively evaluating how the incubation of craving evolves over a period of one year in cocaine-addicted adults. Two hundred and ten subjects will be assessed using an electroencephalographic method called event-related potentials, which measures brain activity in response to images. In this case, neutral images and images associated with cocaine use will be presented. Brain reactivity to the images as measured by a specific component of event-related potentials will be compared at different times following the beginning of abstinence (3, 6, 9, and 12 months). Finally, this study will increase our knowledge about the fluctuation of craving over time and its involvement in relapse. This project will specifically inform clinicians about the risk factors for relapse at specific moments during the abstinence period, which may also guide the development of new interventions and prevention tools in order to reduce the chances of relapse.

column36: Epigenomic characterization of early mouse intestinal cancers
column37: It is now widely recognized that while cancer is a genetic disorder, epigenetics plays a significant role in cancer progression. Epigenetics describes a set of modifications that are placed on DNA and can alter the message of the DNA sequence. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the fourth leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide, and arises as the result of genetic and epigenetic abnormalities within the cells of the intestine. While it has been thought for some time that the initiating events of CRC are genetic abnormalities of intestinal stem cells, a growing body of evidence suggests that epigenetic alterations precede and may cooperate with these genetic changes. One of these epigenetic changes is termed DNA methylation, in which the DNA message is abnormally silenced. This proposal directly tests some of the DNA methylation observations that were detected in primary human cancers by use of an innovative reporter. This fluorescence signal allows us for the first time to visualize cells that have undergone the earliest genetic changes in the path to cancer. These intestinal cells will be isolated and analyzed for their DNA methylation status, and we will then evaluate which of these changes are important for cancer progression. In summary, we aim to identify those DNA methylation changes that are essential for the earliest stages of CRC. We anticipate that the findings from this study will have a lasting impact on the understanding of colorectal cancer initiation, will inform new biomarkers of early colorectal cancer and identify new therapeutic vulnerabilities. As these epigenetic DNA modifications are reversible, we have the potential to manipulate them with drugs for the ultimate goal of tumour suppression.

column36: Genomic and ecologic insights into the spread of antibiotic resistance in nursing homes
column37: Antibiotics are vital for treating bacterial infections. However, many of these disease-causing bacteria have developed drug resistance to counter antibiotic treatment. These bacteria are often referred to as multi-drug resistant organisms (MDROs). Infections caused by MDROs are harder to treat, and in worst case scenario, can lead to death. Among healthcare facilities, nursing homes (NHs) play a critical role in providing care for older and chronically sick people. Unfortunately, NHs are also major reservoirs of MDROs, putting their already frail residents at risk of MDRO colonization (carriage without being sick) and infection. When colonized or infected NH residents go home or transfer to another hospital, they bring the MDROs with them which then can spread to other healthcare facilities and the community. To begin to put a stop to this vicious chain of events, I will study how MDROs spread within the healthcare system with a focus on NHs, and how MDROs colonize NH residents. To understand how MDROs spread, I will collaborate with a NH researcher who has collected MDROs from 18 Michigan NHs during 2010-2015. By studying the DNA of these MDROs, I can determine how similar or different they are. Similar MDROs found in different NHs suggest that these MDROs have been moving between these NHs. I will then address whether residents from these NHs visit the same hospital or are associated with the same neighbourhood, which may be where MDROs from different NHs are exchanged. Next, as my preliminary data have shown that NH residents colonized with one type of MDRO are at a higher risk of acquiring a second type of MDRO, I will examine the biological mechanism underlying these relationships, an important step for understanding the clinical implications of MDRO colonization. My proposed work will provide the first glimpse into MDRO ecology and epidemiology in NH settings, identifying the most effective points of intervention to control MDRO colonization and infection.

column36: Regulation and function of human tumor-exosome induced myeloid-derived suppressor cells in metastasis and infection.
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada, resulting in 80,000 deaths per year. In addition to the type of cancer, the main predictor of cancer outcome is the presence of metastasis. Metastasis is the presence of tumor cells at distant sites in the body. To this day, scientists do not understand exactly how metastasis occurs and medical doctors have no specific drugs to prevent it. Our current models suggest that tumors release very small packages called 'exosomes' into the bloodstream that act like 'messages in a bottle' to establish new 'homes' at distant sites in the body. Exosomes also contain instructions that increase cells that suppress the immune system. This allows tumor cells to move around the body unnoticed. One such immune cell is the 'myeloid-derived suppressor cell' or MDSC. We understand how these events might happen largely from animal models and 2-dimensional human cell culture but these have limitations when trying to develop new therapies for humans. Further affecting outcomes in cancer patients are infections, which contribute directly or indirectly to >50% of cancer-related deaths. Whether the underlying changes to the immune system that allow metastasis to occur also contribute to the >10-600-fold increased risk of infection in cancer patients is unknown. It is possible that the increased risk for infection and death in cancer patients is an underlying increase in immune suppressive MDSCs. We will determine how cancer exosomes and the immune suppressing cells they generate provide a crucial link between infection and metastasis in oncology patients. We will be using computer chip printing technology to engineer 3-dimensional human tissues. We will use these human 3D tissue models to decipher how cancer exosomes and immune suppressive MDSCs increase metastasis and infection. This approach will allow us to develop new therapies, in a human system, that target common pathways to prevent both metastasis and infection in cancer patients.

column36: Evaluating Cerebrovascular Reactivity Following Surgical Intervention of Brain Arteriovenous Malformations
column37: Brain arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a disorder in which there is a tangle of abnormal and poorly formed blood vessels. The brain has little control of blood flow through these abnormal vessels, which become weak and may burst, causing a bleed (hemorrhagic stroke). Brain AVMs are the second most identifiable cause of hemorrhagic stroke. Each AVM hemorrhage poses a 30% risk of death and 25% risk of long-term disability. There is currently no established risk assessment tool to identify AVMs patients at high risk for hemorrhagic stroke or seizures. Identification of high risk AVM patients can help decrease the incidence of hemorrhage simply by enabling more timely treatment, which would significantly reduce the impact of this disorder on population health and economics. Our aim is to better understand and quantify the extent of the brain's ability to regain control of blood flow following surgical intervention of AVMs. Using an advanced MRI method, we will quantify how well the brain regulates blood flow and delivers blood to brain cells. The method uses a unique and safe breathing device that supplies different concentrations of carbon dioxide added to oxygen while MRI brain images are collected. Control of blood flow is well regulated in the brain; breathing a small amount of carbon dioxide increases blood flow in healthy vessels whereas flow does not increase as much in unhealthy vessels. At this time, there are no standards to assess whether a patient regains control of brain blood flow following surgical intervention of an AVM. We hope to show the clinical utility of advanced MRI in identifying patients who regain control of blood flow after surgery, which could significantly reduce the time spent in the hospital. A patient treated for an AVM who is identified with persistent unhealthy control of blood flow following surgery would be considered high risk, allowing doctors to begin appropriate surgical intervention sooner.

column36: Metabolic signatures of triple negative breast cancer sensitivity and resistance to cyclophosphamide and doxorubicin in patient derived tumor xenografts
column37: Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer in women and the second leading cause of cancer related mortality. Approximately 1-in-8 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in their lifetime. Advances in breast cancer research have identified three tumor characteristics that can be used by physicians to choose appropriate therapy for targeting the cancer. However, some breast cancers are "triple negative" and lack these characteristics, causing them to be more difficult to treat. Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) accounts for 12% of breast cancer diagnosis and these patients have the highest mortality of all breast cancer patients. TNBCs are typically treated with cyclophosphamide, anthracyclines, and taxane therapy since there are currently no specific markers to target therapy. Therefore, tumors in these patients have a high rate of drug resistance. Thus, there is a need for the discovery of new biomarkers that can be used to personalize TNBC treatment and detect drug resistance, thereby increasing patient survival. The objective of this project is to identify biomarkers that detect drug effectiveness and resistance using metabolites found in TNBC patient derived tumor xenografts (PDTX). Unlike the gene mutations that cause cancer, metabolites can be released from cancer cells and measured in blood and urine. We hypothesize that tumor, plasma and urine metabolite biomarkers can be used to predict and detect drug sensitivity and resistance in TNBCs. Metabolite changes can also occur in response to drug treatment. Furthermore, metabolism can be altered in TNBCs that are sensitive and resistant to drug therapy. Therefore, identifying metabolite biomarkers of drug sensitivity and resistance prior to treating patients may allow physicians to choose more effective treatment. Moreover, early detection and rapid intervention may be possible through measuring metabolite biomarkers in plasma and urine during drug therapy.

column36: Dynamic phenotyping of pathologic mood instability across affective disorders
column37: Mood instability, defined as an emotional dysregulation, mood swings, or emotional impulsiveness, is a common feature of mood and anxiety disorders. Mood instability is associated with elevated risk of suicide and reduced treatment responsiveness in individuals with a psychiatric diagnosis. Considering its dynamic nature, traditional surveys that assess mood variability once a week or once a month may not be the best way to capture the complex picture of mood instability. Fortunately, with recent technological advances and mobile applications, it is now easy to collect, at random occasions in the day, all sorts of information from research participants such as symptoms or mood states in their everyday life. It is likely that mood instability reflects a dysfunction in the neural circuits of the brain, however, little is known regarding its associated brain mechanisms. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain allows us to capture both static information, such as the structure of brain regions, and dynamic information, such as the connectivity between regions. In this research project, I propose to investigate whether abnormalities in the structure and connectivity of brain networks are related to mood fluctuations within the day, in order to disentangle the trait (static) and state (dynamic) signatures of mood instability.

column36: Alternative polyadenylation in cancer cells: investigating the role of N6-methyladenosine
column37: Nucleic acids, such as DNA and RNA, have fundamental roles as carriers of genetic information. Genes encoded in DNA are transcribed into RNA molecules and subsequently translated into proteins, the effectors that mediate biological activities. Cancer cells undergo vast changes in gene expression that enable uncontrolled growth and increased cellular division. Untranslated regions of messenger RNAs play a crucial role in controlling these changes. In many cancers, these regions are dramatically shortened, and normal gene regulation is abolished. Yet, we still do not fully understand how cancer cells choose and regulate the length of the untranslated regions. Messenger RNAs additionally undergo diverse types of chemical modifications in cells. One such modification, the recently discovered methylation of adenines (N6-methyladenosine), was proposed to control the length of the untranslated regions of some RNAs. Interestingly, the proteins that are responsible for N6-methyladenosine are altered in lymphomas, brain and breast cancers. Thus, it could be an important mechanism by which cancer cells modulate the expression of disease-promoting genes. This project will investigate the link between the N6-methyladenosine RNA modification and the control of gene expression in breast cancer cells. Using molecular and biochemical approaches, we will remove N6-methyladenosines and measure the changes in expression of cancer-relevant genes. This work will help to better establish how cancer cells regulate gene expression at a fundamental level, with the hope that this knowledge can help us devise better and more effective treatments in the future.

column36: Defining vaccine-elicited CD8 tissue-resident memory T cell (Trm) function at the female genital mucosa in rhesus macaques
column37: A memory CD8 T cells is a type of white blood cell that remembers our body's exposure to a small portion of a pathogen called an antigen. These cells form the basis of vaccination and when they re-encounter the same pathogen or antigen, they respond by engaging our body's immune system to find and kill the invader. Most memory cells were thought to patrol our body and recirculate through the blood. Recently, however, a specialized type of memory T cell was discovered that resides in tissues including the genital tract, gut, lung, liver, etc. without recirculation. This specialized cell type is called a tissue-resident memory T cell (Trm) and is perhaps the most abundant T cell type in the body. The female genital tract is the most common portal of entry of HIV infections. In this project, we will test a novel vaccine that generates abundant CD8 Trm as well as antibodies that can target and kill a pathogen in the genital tract in mice. We will first test whether we can achieve abundant and highly functional CD8 Trm in the genital tract of rhesus macaques. We're using rhesus macaques as they are closely related to human beings and are a good model animal for HIV vaccine development. After vaccination is complete, we will test how well it functions within the animal by injecting SIV particle (monkey version of HIV) in the cervix as a model of HIV transmission. We expect our vaccine-generated CD8 Trm to respond to this SIV particle. We will thoroughly monitor many aspects of the immune response within the first two days after challenge as HIV is most vulnerable during this period. The response will be monitored not only throughout the genital tract, but also in blood, lymph nodes, and other tissues. The insights that we will gain from describing how CD8 Trm function after they 'see' antigen again may fundamentally alter our knowledge of their capacity and pave way for improved vaccine design against intractable diseases like HIV/AIDS, TB, malaria, and cancer.

column36: Socioemotional and semantic deficits and their cerebral correlates in frontotemporal dementia variants
column37: In 2016, neurodegenerative diseases were affecting the lives of approximately 564 000 Canadians. Amongst these diseases, frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the most frequent in individuals under the age of 60 years old. The very early onset and the complex nature of this disease bring significant and different challenges both in its diagnosis and management. FTD can manifest as a spectrum of clinical syndromes, and two of them, behavioral frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA), particularly pose a challenge in terms of differential diagnosis. bvFTD is characterized by prominent and progressive behavioral changes, more specifically interpersonal and emotional behavior as well as deficits in executive functioning. svPPA is characterized by a prominent and progressive deterioration of semantic memory and language. Despite these clear-cut definitions, many studies have demonstrated that there is substantial overlap between bvFTD and svPPA (both in terms of symptoms and of changes in the brain). However, the nature and the underlying mechanisms of this clinical overlap are still unclear, and several unresolved issues remain in the literature. Therefore, the aim of this project is to characterize and compare patients with different FTD variants on social cognition and semantic/language measures, and to identify the most sensitive and specific tests for a better differential diagnosis. We also aim to investigate network-based brain correlates of social cognition and semantic/language in FTD variants. This project is critical to improve the differential diagnosis in these diseases and could also help to better direct patients towards appropriate therapeutic and behavioural intervention, as well as adequate counselling of families and caregivers. With the potential development of protein-specific therapies for neurodegenerative diseases, a better understanding of the brain processes involved in these diseases is also essential.

column36: Reprogramming tumour immunogenicity with STING-Nanoparticles
column37: One hallmark of cancers is that it is capable of escaping detection by the immune system. This ability allows cancer to grow uncontrollably without triggering an immune response that would result in its destruction. Immunotherapy seeks to harness the immune system to destroy cancer by activating tumour-specific T cells. This will allow for the training of the immune system to "remember" how to detect and kill cancer cells if they return. The goal of this research is to develop an effective approach for increasing anti-tumour immune system response within cancer. Studies have shown that the stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway within the body plays an important role in the immune system's natural ability to recognize and destroy tumour cells. This pathway can be activated through the delivery of cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cGAMP) to tumour cells. However, two challenges are associated with the administration of cGAMP to patients. The physio-chemical properties of the molecule result in (i) rapid elimination from the body and (ii) toxicity. Thus, a novel STING-activating nanoparticle will be engineered to allow for improved delivery and decreased toxicity of cGAMP. The nanoparticles, tiny bubbles composed of biocompatible polymers, are called polymerosomes and can be used to encapsulate cGAMP reducing its exposure to the body. This will create a safer formulation of cGAMP, which can be tested further in animal tumour models. It is expected that this formulation will activate the STING pathway, which will result in an immune response that will destroy tumour cells and create lasting T cell memory in the case of relapse.

column36: Achieving precision in Image-guided Neurosurgery via an open source collaborative software environment
column37: Each year, thousands of Canadians undergo neurosurgery for resection of brain lesions such as tumours, epileptic foci and vascular malformations that are in close proximity to areas of the brain that are critical to movement, vision, sensation, or language. Accurate guidance information is required to balance two constraints: achieving maximal resection of pathological tissue while minimizing potential neurological deficits. Image-guided neurosurgery systems (i.e., a GPS for surgery) provide tools to visualize and interpret patient-specific volumes of anatomical, vascular and functional data to enable precise surgical interventions. Unfortunately, brain tissue can deform up to 30mm or more during surgery (known as brain shift). Over the past 15 years, Collins' NeuroImaging and Surgical Technologies (NIST) lab at the MNI has developed an open-source research image-guided surgery platform known as IBIS. Our novel contribution uses ultrasound, acquired intra-operatively, to achieve accurate patient-image registration, even in the presence of brain shift. However, our methods can sometimes be limitated in terms of accuracy, robustness, and anatomical coverage. We propose to integrate data from multiple sensors and multiple algorithms to accurately and robustly account for brain shift and allow for accurate guidance throughout surgery. To do this we will apply Kalman filters in a multi-channel registration framework. To reduce development costs and facilitate inter-lab collaborations, we will integrate our IBIS software into 3DSlicer to take advantage of a huge user base (280,000 downloads, 250+/week). Our industrial partner Synaptive Medical, a dynamic Toronto-based startup, will provide input, ensure commercial relevance and help trainees learn about development and commercialization of medical devices. Synaptive's help will facilitate translation of our image-guided technology to the operating room so that all patients can benefit from these tools.

column36: OCTSurfer - Advanced Imaging and Integrated Image Analysis Platform for 3D Optical Coherence Tomography Images of the Eye
column37: Eye doctors use lenses to look inside the back of the eye, at the retina, to search for diseases causing vision problems. With these lenses, they can only see the surface of the retina. Also, what they see is rarely recorded. Eye-witness testimony of the eye doctor is how clinical diagnosis is done at this time. A new technology called OCT can show pictures of the retina below the surface. These pictures are recorded first and then analyzed by the eye doctor. Since these devices only see a small area of the retina at a time, eye doctors prefer the old way of looking through the retina directly using lenses. We propose to develop a new OCT scanner that can record a picture of the full retina, the same or better than the area seen with lenses directly, so doctors don't miss anything. At the same time, OCT pictures show what's below the surface, like blood vessels. Since the retina pictures are recorded, these can be interpreted and discussed by more than one doctor, and event sent to another clinic for more analysis and expert opinion. We propose to develop computer programs that use equations to make measurements from these pictures. So not only can the doctor see below the retina over a wide area, they can also get measurements that let them decide if a region inside the retina is healthy or if there is some problem such as damaged cells in the retina, poor or damaged blood supply, or any other damage. The OCTSurfer technology that we propose has the potential to make it easy for doctors to find diseases by making detailed and minute measurements that are difficult to make visually. This will lower the chances of errors, like when something is judged to be a problem when it isn't, or when a problem is missed. People living far from cities can benefit by sending their images to a eye doctor in a city clinic. Optometrists could use OCTSurfer to screen for disease and refer people to eye specialists for proper diagnosis.

column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is the most common form of acute leukemia in adults and among the leading causes of cancer related deaths in the youngests of them. This will allow a better definition of the rarest AML subgroups, the discovery of new ones, as well as an increase in the chances of identifying new markers. column37: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by motor symptoms such as tremor, muscle rigidity, postural instability, slowness of movement and cognitive changes. This renders treatment management difficult, as physicians require a complete portrait of the symptomatology of patients including location and intensity of DID. Current assessment technics depicts a representation of the symptomatology at a specific point in time, in the clinic, but do not capture their variation throughout the day nor their relationship with other symptoms or specific activities. Hence, such snapshot is not fully representative of the true impact of the symptomatology on the functional mobility of a person. Inertial systems enable full-body motion capture and have the potential to be used outside laboratories, in the natural environment of a person. The current study investigates the use of an inertial system to capture the mobility of patients living with Parkinson's disease. Our work will focus on automatically detecting the symptomatology of patients based on their voluntary behaviours' performance. This study has the potential to provide a technological platform to test the efficacy of medications on the daily lives of patients in their natural living environment, providing a more representative portrait of the situation to the movement disorders specialist empowering optimal patient follow-up.

column36: The Psychobiology of Health Maintenance in Late Life: Examining Modifiable Pathways to Healthy Aging
column37: An unprecedented demographic shift is occurring in industrialized nations that will present significant challenges for individuals and society. In 2016, the number of Canadian adults aged 65+ exceeded the number of children for the first time in census history, and this older demographic is projected to double in size over the next 50 years. Although Canadians are living longer, declines in physical health and functioning remain common in old age and have significant personal and societal implications: Recent projections indicate health care spending in Canada will increase by $2 billion per year from 2014-19 due to population aging alone. This underscores the need for a better understanding of modifiable factors that can sustain health into late life. My postdoctoral research program seeks to address these challenges by identifying modifiable psychobiological mechanisms that may protect against biological dysregulation and physical disease in old age. The research will focus on whether volitional health maintenance strategies promote adaptive longitudinal changes in older adults' biological and physical health, and whether such changes are due to intervening psychosocial factors and health behaviours. My research will also examine if the benefits of health maintenance strategies differ for older adults who vary on demographic (e.g., age, sex), psychosocial (e.g., social support), and health factors (e.g., acute vs. chronic illness). Most important, my research program will develop and test a novel health maintenance motivation intervention to increase adaptive health behaviours in late life. This research may have significant implications to the extent that increasing positive health behaviours (e.g., physical activity) has the potential to improve the physical health and functioning of older adults and offset mounting costs facing the Canadian health care system.

column37: Most people are infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). This life-long infection can be asymptomatic or can lead to a variety of health problems including mononucleosis, cancer and life-threatening illnesses in immune suppression. However the functions and cellular targets of most of the EBV proteins have not yet been determined. The activities of many cellular proteins are controlled by SUMO modifications, so viruses can affect cellular processes by altering these modifications. This project uses comprehensive methods to elucidate how EBV proteins manipulate cellular SUMO pathways. The cellular proteins targeted by EBV proteins and their significance for viral infection and cellular processes will also be determined. This work will provide insight into how viruses manipulate cells to enable life-long persistence and cause disease. It will also identify cellular proteins that play important roles in various cellular processes that are altered by viral infection, and mechanisms of regulation of these processes. Finally, the viral-host interactions discovered in this project will provide potential drug targets for antiviral treatments.

column36: Association Between Allopurinol and Cardiovascular Events, Mortality and End-Stage Renal Disease in Diabetes
column37: Project Summary: Allopurinol is a medication that is traditionally used in patients with gout to lower uric acid levels. More recently it has been recognized that in addition to causing gout, elevated uric acid levels case systemic inflammation and high blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart disease, death, and kidney disease. High uric acid levels are common in people with diabetes. However, no large studies have evaluated whether people with diabetes and gout who are taking allopurinol have a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, death and kidney disease compared to those who are not taking allopurinol. The Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) collects health care data on all Ontario individuals eligible for health insurance for administrative purposes. We will use this data to study the relationship between allopurinol and heart disease, death and kidney disease in people with diabetes. Anticipated Outcomes: We believe there is a sufficient number of individuals with both diabetes and gout (high uric acid levels) in Ontario to answer the research question. We hypothesize that allopurinol is associated with a reduction in heart disease, death and kidney disease in patients with diabetes and high uric acid levels. This would be important to those with diabetes and physicians who care for patients with diabetes. Allopurinol is inexpensive, safe and would be readily available for use if a benefit were found. column37: With the risk of premature birth, mothers are often treated with glucocorticoids, a hormone involved in our response to stress. column36: Systematic identification and characterization of neuronal alternative splicing networks underlying nervous system development and disorders
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent group of neurodevelopmental disorders that impairs the ability of affected individuals to communicate and interact. ASD is remarkably heterogeneous in terms of its clinical presentation as well as its genetic etiologies. A major current challenge is to identify common molecular mechanisms and pathways that underlie ASD. Recent studies from our laboratory have shown that alternative splicing (AS) is frequently misregulated in brains of autistic individuals. AS is the process by which segments (i.e. exons) from a given gene, are differentially assembled to produce multiple gene products and thus greatly expands the RNA and protein repertoires of cells. AS is particularly prevalent in the nervous system. However, the functions of the vast majority of neuronal AS events and how these impact neurological disorders including ASD is not known. Accordingly, a major goal of biomedical research is to systematically determine the role of neural-specific exons in the context of nervous system development and neurological disorders. This aim forms the basis of this CIHR fellowship proposal. To accomplish this goal, I have developed a novel CRISPR-based screening platform enabling for the first time the systematic identification of phenotypically important exons. I will apply this technology in order to investigate the function of thousands of alternative exons in the formation of neurons. The most critical exons will be further characterized by a unique combination of genome-wide assays, biochemical experiments and animal models. The research described in my proposal represents the first systematic approach for investigating the biological function of alternative exons in nervous system development. My research is expected to provide insights into the mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD and holds promise for identifying novel therapeutic targets, which will be of considerable benefit to Canadians.

column36: Development, implementation, and evaluation of a novel physical activity maintenance program for women with cancer
column37: One in two Canadian women will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime. While survival rates for many female cancers are improving, women are living with treatment related side effects for years after their cancer treatments have ended. Physical activity has been shown repeatedly in the literature to help manage side effects and prevent recurrence. However more than 85% of female cancer survivors in Canada are inactive. ActiveMatch is a free online program that was created to try and get more women with cancer active by connecting them with other women who are also looking for support to start an exercise routine (like a dating app). Partners connect and set up activity related goals and plans. Currently no services are provided within ActiveMatch to encourage the maintenance of physical activity. This is important because more than 50% of women who start a physical activity program will return to inactive levels after the program ends. Also, unless physical activity is maintained the benefits of exercise will not persist. Therefore the goals of this project are to develop a physical activity maintenance program (PAMP), deliver the PAMP to current ActiveMatch users, and evaluate the effectiveness of this program on improving long term physical activity levels, engagement in physical activity, and quality of life. This program will include 8 sessions delivered by phone or email. It is anticipated that participants who receive the PAMP will have improved outcomes compared to those who do not. Overall, the project provides a novel approach to promote the maintenance of physical activity for women with cancer using a novel mode of application. If participants maintain levels of activity it will lead to improved management of side effects and could lessen the burden on the health care system by decreasing the need for additional health care services. Together, this can help Canadian women with cancer lead healthier and more meaningful lives after cancer treatment.

column36: How is p97 directed to its many functions? An NMR study of p97/p47 interactions
column37: Many molecular machines convert the energy from ATP hydrolysis into changes in the structures of the molecules that they act upon. As one of the most abundant machines in the cell, p97 is involved in a number of cellular functions including protein quality control, regulation of the cell cycle, response to DNA damage, as well as programmed cell death. Mutations in p97 have been linked with neurodegenerative disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer's, Huntington's and Parkinson's diseases and with a number of different cancers. p97 is able to perform many diverse functions with the assistance of over forty different adaptor molecules that chaperone this machine to different regions of the cell and change its activity. One important cellular function mediated by p97 involves the reassembly of the Golgi apparatus in cells that have recently divided, generating a functional organelle that is critical for the proper processing of synthesized protein molecules. This process requires the association of p97 with one of its cofactors called p47, but the way in which this interaction occurs is not understood. Using nuclear magnetic resonance techniques I will study and characterize the interaction between p97 and p47, providing a detailed understanding of how p47 regulates p97 function and how this regulation can be derailed in the context of p97 disease mutants.

column36: The surgical management of aortic valve disease in the era of transcatheter aortic valve replacement
column37: Aortic stenosis (AS) is the most common acquired abnormality of the heart valves, affecting 10% of people over the age of 65. In AS, the movement of aortic valve leaflets is restricted, blocking blood flow from the heart to the rest of the circulation. In symptomatic people, up to 50% will die if left untreated. Historically, open heart surgery was required to remove the damaged aortic valve and replace it with an artificial valve, an invasive procedure suitable only for healthy elderly individuals. The durability of the valve replacement surgery depends on several factors, particularly, the patient's age and the type of artificial valve placed. Failing valve replacements traditionally required a second, higher risk open heart procedure. More recently, a minimally invasive technique called transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has become the treatment of choice for patients at extreme surgical risk as well as many at moderate risk. In TAVR, blood vessels in the groin are accessed to replace the damaged heart valve. TAVR has emerged as a possible lower risk treatment for failed artificial valves. Nonetheless, in low risk and young patients, open heart surgery remains the standard treatment for AS. The goal of this research is to determine the ideal management of aortic valve disease with considerations for new minimally invasive approaches. First, we will address whether there have been changes in the types and sizes of aortic valves placed in young and low risk patients at the time of their open-heart surgery after the introduction of TAVR as this would affect their treatment options should their artificial valve fail. We will then determine the best treatment strategy for patients that previously had surgery but now have a failing replaced valve. Finally, we will determine the optimal management strategy for young and low risk patients through computer simulation models. There are currently no studies to inform the best treatment pathways for this group.

column36: Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy: Epidemiology, Healthcare Resource Utilization, and Safety, Efficacy, and Cost-Effectiveness of Decompression Surgery
column37: Spinal cord injury - the first thing most people think of is trauma, such as a car accident. However, the leading cause of spinal cord injury, far more common than trauma, is arthritis of the neck. With aging, there is wear and tear to the spine, just like the knees or hips. The difference is arthritis of the neck can cause paralysis. Arthritis narrows the spinal canal causing compression of the spinal cord, damage to nervous tissue, and resultant disability. This is termed degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM). The population burden of disease of DCM has not been studied. Further, while decompression surgery is regularly undertaken in patients with moderate or severe DCM with the objective of preventing further neurological impairment, the role of surgery in patients with mild DCM is controversial. On one hand, these patients have only minimal symptoms, and hence the benefits of surgery may be small weighted against the risks. An alternative view is these patients may actually stand to gain the most from surgery, because a proactive intervention at this stage could prevent later development of severe permanent neurological deficits. To that end, the present investigation aims to systematically study trends in the number of people afflicted by DCM and healthcare resource utilization for their care, in order to quantify the burden of disease and make future projections to inform policy makers. We will also identify high risk subpopulations who may benefit from screening measures. Further, we will study the impact of mild DCM on patients' quality of life and clarify the safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of surgery for patients with mild DCM. With the aging population in Canada, DCM has the potential to become a substantial source of disability, and this has important economic implications for our society. In anticipation of this shift, the expeditious diagnosis and treatment of DCM, so as to minimize disability, must be made a key public health priority.

column36: Etude des interactions entre les profils omiques, l'alimentation et la sante cardiometabolique au sein de familles
column37: Les saines habitudes de vie dont une alimentation equilibree jouent un role primordial dans la prevention des maladies cardiovasculaires (1). Bien qu'on ait identifie plusieurs determinants des maladies cardiovasculaires, leurs mecanismes fondamentaux demeurent incompris (2). A ce jour, aucune etude n'a integre les interactions des facteurs genetiques et de l'alimentation sur la sante cardiovasculaire au sein de familles, d'ou l'importante et l'originalite du present projet. L'objectif general, qui se veut exploratoire, est de caracteriser les interactions des facteurs genetiques, de l'alimentation et de la sante cardiovasculaire au sein de familles. Le projet compte 48 participants repartis en 16 familles, constituees au minimum de la mere et de son enfant. Les parents biologiques et les enfants devaient etre en bonne sante et resider sous le meme toit. Des prelevements sanguins, des mesures anthropometriques et des questionnaires alimentaires ont ete recueillis lors de la visite des participants a l'institut de recherche. Par la suite, il sera possible d'analyser les resultats dans le but de mieux comprendre les mecanismes par lesquels l'alimentation influence les facteurs genetiques et les maladies cardiovasculaires. Nous serons egalement en mesure de savoir si l'effet de l'alimentation sur ces facteurs et la sante est le meme chez les parents et les enfants d'une meme famille. Tout cela dans le but de mieux comprendre les mecanismes complexes regules par l'alimentation pour mieux prevenir les maladies cardiovasculaires et contribuer a ameliorer la sante des familles canadiennes. References : (1) Eckel RH et al. Circulation 2014. (2) MacLellan WR et al. Nat Rev Cardiol 2012.

column36: Risque de fracture en dialyse et transplantation renale : etude epidemiologique sur les donnees administratives de la RAMQ
column37: Introduction L'insuffisance renale chronique (IRC) cause un debalancement dans la regulation du metabolisme osseux. Cela conduit a une fragilisation des os des patients qui deviennent plus exposes a des fractures que la population generale, ce qui entrainent alors une mauvaise qualite de vie et une augmentation du risque de mortalite de ces patients. Une fois que les reins ne fonctionnent plus, les patients sont traites soit par hemodialyse, dialyse peritoneale et/ou par greffe renale. Bien que les frequences de fracture en IRC soient connues, peu d'informations sont disponibles a savoir si celles-ci sont differentes selon le type de traitement. Hypothese generale Le risque de fracture et de mortalite chez les patients souffrant d'IRC varie en fonction du type de traitement (hemodialyse, dialyse peritoneale ou greffe renale). Objectif Principal Comparer le risque de fracture et de mortalite selon le type de traitement chez les patients adultes souffrants d'IRC. Methodologie Tout d'abord nous avons effectue une revue systematique de toutes les etudes qui se sont interessees a ce sujet et avons soumis ce protocole pour publication (accepte avec modifications mineures). Nous allons maintenant developper un fichier de codes identiques a ceux utilises par les medecins pour identifier les patients souffrants d'IRC selon leur traitement dans la base de donnees de la RAMQ. Puis, nous allons comparer le risque de fracture et de mortalite selon le type de traitement depuis les 15 dernieres annees et evaluerons si ce risque a change avec le temps. Contribution a la recherche Ce projet permettra de mettre en evidence l'importance des fractures en IRC et d'identifier leurs facteurs de risques afin d'ameliorer la sante des Canadiens par la mise en place de strategies de prevention ciblees. Aussi, l'identification adequate des patients IRC sera utile pour toutes autres etudes futures sur les patients IRC au Quebec.

column36: Side effect-free cathepsin K targeting drugs for skeletal diseases
column37: Arthritic diseases affect 15 % of the population and bone cancer is a frequent metastatic side effect of the most common breast and prostate cancer. Aside from human suffering enormous financial health care costs are added to the treatment of these diseases. Current treatments have various shortcomings and side effects, which include increased cancer risks, atypical fractures, bone necrosis, infections, and vascular problems. There is clearly a need for more effective and safer treatments. Unfortunately, little progress has been made in recent years. Most treatments attack rather non-specifically entire cells or block complex pathways, which is likely causing the side effects. In contrast, the protease, cathepsin K, is solely responsible for the bone degradation and significantly contributes to joint erosion. Its inhibition has been shown to effectively reduce fracture rates in post-menopausal women. However, this treatment also had severe side effects leading to the termination of the further development of cathepsin K inhibitors. Our research has identified and verified a novel type of cathepsin K inhibitors without causing any of the side effects seen in clinical trials. Interestingly, a major source of these compounds are certain Chinese herbs traditionally used in skeletal diseases. Recently, we have shown the efficacy of one of these compounds in an osteoporosis model without any observable side effects. This project will expand this approach and will generate more potent and druggable derivatives from the herbal compounds. Compounds will be analyzed in arthritis and bone cancer mouse models. We anticipate that these compounds will have a superior efficacy with no or fewer side effects than current treatment regimes. This project requires a strong interdisciplinary collaboration between chemists, pharmaceutical scientists, biochemists, and animal model researchers and will provide an excellent opportunity for the training of students.

column36: Electron cryomicroscopy analysis of erythrocyte Anion Exchanger 1 (AE1), its interaction with erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins, and its recognition by proteins from malaria-causing Plasmodium parasites.
column37: Anion Exchanger 1 (AE1) is a red blood cell membrane protein that anchors the skeleton of the cell to its membrane, through interactions that are important for maintaining the shape and function of red blood cells. Genetic defects in AE1 and other red blood cell proteins lead to numerous disorders, including hereditary spherocytosis, a condition characterized by abnormal red blood cells that requires regular blood transfusions in moderate-to-severe cases. Hereditary spherocytosis occurs as often as 1 in 1000 to 2000 births, affecting numerous children in Canada. Our ability to develop new and better treatments for diseases like hereditary spherocytosis is limited by a lack of information on the 3D structure of AE1 interacting with components of the red blood cell skeleton. AE1 is also targeted by proteins from malaria-causing parasites during parasite invasion of red blood cells. Malaria results in the death of over 400,000 people worldwide. Current vaccines are limited in their ability to reduce infection or disease. Targeting the interaction between AE1 and these parasite proteins using structure-guided vaccine design can lead to new and more potent vaccines. In this project, I will determine the structure of AE1, its complex with red blood cell skeleton proteins, and its complex with proteins from malaria-causing parasites. To accomplish this, I will use state-of-the-art electron microscopy techniques available at SickKids. The knowledge gained will improve our understanding of how genetic defects in AE1 and its interacting partners lead to diseases like hereditary spherocytosis, and provide insight into malaria disease progression. Importantly, the structures I will determine will form a blueprint for designing drugs to treat hereditary spherocytosis, and for the development of new anti-malaria vaccines. This project has the potential to improve the health of numerous children and adults in Canada and worldwide.

column36: In-Utero Determinants of Preterm Brain Health
column37: Although survival rates of preterm babies have improved in recent decades, prematurity, which means being born before 37 weeks, remains a leading cause of childhood disability. In preterm babies, brain development is often compromised, leading to the later disability. Our overall objective is to examine the association between the fetus' environment inside the uterus and later brain development in preterm babies. Our first aim is to determine the association between the growth of the fetus inside the uterus and the baby's brain development. Using a set of preterm babies that have already been imaged with MRI, we will look back at pregnancy ultrasounds to assess the rate of fetal growth. Through MRI, we will visualize the brain's development. We expect that poor growth inside the uterus will be associated with impaired brain development and later childhood disability. Our second aim is to assess whether the size of the fetus' and newborn's brain is dependent on the reason for preterm birth. We will enroll a new set of pregnant women who are expected to deliver before 32 weeks. We will image the fetuses using MRI while they are still inside the uterus and then image the babies' brains once they are born. We will enroll women who are expected to deliver prematurely either because the fetus is not receiving enough blood flow, or because their membranes (i.e., "waters") have broken. We expect that the fetuses with inadequate blood flow will have smaller brains than the fetuses whose mothers' membranes have broken prematurely. We will also assess how the amount of blood and oxygen that the fetus receives affects brain development after the baby is born. The results of our study could help doctors and researchers optimize therapies that could protect these vulnerable brains while the fetus is still inside the uterus.

column36: The Role of Scaffold Proteins in Cytokinesis and Ciliogenesis in Human Cells
column37: Cytokinesis is the process by which a cell physically divides its cytoplasm to produce two daughter cells. This sophisticated process is carefully orchestrated by a cascade of sequential events and drives the morphogenesis and formation of a whole new organism. Misregulation of any step during the cytokinesis process is known to be associated with formation of cancer or malformation of various organs. The research in our laboratory in the cell biology program at the Hospital for Sick Children (Sickkids) research institute has provided new, fundamental insights into the mechanism underlying the cell division process. Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms mediating the cell division process is extremely important, as it can potentially lead to therapeutic approaches for various life threatening conditions caused by cell division failure in humans. I am also interested in understanding the mechanism of cell differentiation in human cells. In particular, my goal is to unravel how cilia are formed, which are hair like structures or organelles that extend from the surface of the cell and play a vital role in human development and physiology. The malfunction of cilia is associated with a number of genetic conditions such as heart disease, kidney disease, infertility, obesity and diabetes, and mental retardation. The findings of this study results in better understanding of the pathogenesis and potential treatments of such conditions.

column36: Identifying early-life nutritional determinants of neurodevelopment in very low birth weight infants: the role of donor milk and long chain polyunsaturated fatty acid intake
column37: Children born preterm face neurodevelopmental consequences when they reach school age, such as academic underachievement and behavioural issues. Good nutrition during early life can prevent some of these negative effects, however preterm infants still struggle relative to those born at term. The best source of nutrition for infants, particularly those born preterm, is mother's breast milk, however, mothers of preterm infants often have difficulty producing sufficient amounts. Recently, hospitals in Canada have begun feeding donor milk, rather than formula, in the absence of sufficient mother's milk because it reduces the risk of serious complications that can cause death or disability. Despite these critical benefits, donor milk has lower levels of many nutritional components than mother's milk because of its processing, including 50% lower levels of fat. These nutritional limitations could have negative neurodevelopmental consequences for preterm infants. In my postdoctoral fellowship, I will examine the relationship between the proportion of donor milk, compared to mother's milk that preterm infants consumed during their initial hospitalization, and their performance on cognitive tests at 18 months and 4 years of age. I will use imaging techniques, such as MRI, to see whether infants fed more donor milk have normal brain development. I will also measure the fat composition of samples of the mother's milk and donor milk the preterm infants consumed during early life, and use this data to see whether infants who ate more of certain types of fat, like omega-3 or omega-6 fats, perform better on cognitive tests, or have better brain development. These studies will help us determine whether donor milk has nutritional limitations, such as a lack of certain types of fat, that need to be addressed to support healthy brain development in preterm infants.

column36: Extracellular vesicles are key mediators of cardiac rejuvenation and repair
column37: Following a heart attack damaged tissue is replaced with a scar in a process called infarct healing. This loss of functional heart tissue leads to structural changes that promote the development of heart failure. In Canada, heart attacks are more prevalent in patients >70 years of age compared to those <50. Moreover, infarct healing is impaired with aging, which contributes to increased mortality following a heart attack. Therefore, it is essential to develop treatment strategies that are effective for aged individuals. Several approaches have been investigated to improve cardiac tissue repair including stem cell therapy and tissue engineering. Accumulated research evidence has demonstrated that secreted factors are the key effectors which act to enhance cardiac repair. This has led to a surge of interest in the use of cell free therapies using extracellular vesicles (EVs) for the treatment of heart attacks. EVs are small membrane bound vesicles that are secreted by cells throughout the body and modulate cell activity through transfer of microRNAs and proteins. With aging there is a decline in circulating EVs however, it is not known why aging leads to changes in EV profiles and whether these changes contribute to impaired cardiac repair. Moreover, it is not known whether EVs can be used in cardiac rejuvenation based therapies, which aim to improve repair mechanisms in aged individuals to that of a younger state. To answer these important questions this project will investigate: 1) how aging and cellular senescence affects EV profiles, 2) whether aged EVs transfer factors to influence cell function, and 3) whether EVs can be targeted to rejuvenate the cardiac repair mechanisms which decline with age. Collectively, these findings have important translational applications as we will establish the role EVs play in the decline of cardiac repair with aging and identify new treatment strategies which improve infarct healing in the aged population.

column36: A multi-phase clinical trial to establish biological proof-of-concept, determine safety and maximum tolerated dose, and assess efficacy of neoadjuvant ketoconazole and posaconazole in patients with recurrent high grade gliomas
column37: High grade gliomas (HGGs) are the most common and aggressive brain tumors. Among many aggressive features, they invade much farther into the brain than we can see with MRI or the microscope and so surgeons can never remove the entire tumor. That is why radiation and/or chemotherapy are used as standard of care after surgery. Despite this, currently they are considered incurable. We have no therapy that can be given before surgery to decrease their invasiveness and our current therapy after surgery has not changed in years. We desperately need treatments that can specifically target tumor cells to decrease their invasiveness and aggressiveness. HGG tumor cells grow rapidly and need a lot of energy. Normal brain cells do not survive in low oxygen environments but tumor cells do by switching the way they make energy; they grow, invade, and resist therapy by relying on the hexokinase 2 (HK2) enzyme. In our lab we have shown that HGG tumors in mice without HK2 are less invasive. After screening many drugs, we identified 2 azoles (ketoconazole and posaconazole, usually used against fungal infections) as possible blockers of HK2. When tested in mice injected with HGG tumor cells, azoles blocked tumor energy production, growth, and increased survival of mice. We now want to test this in humans with recurrent HGGs who need surgery. First, our goal is to give the lowest dose that is safe, to humans with HGGs before their surgery to show that the drugs can get into the human tumor cells and have the same effect we saw in mice. Then, in another group of HGGs patients we will keep increasing the dose to find the highest dose that is still safe. Once we find this maximum tolerated dose, we will test the drugs in a larger group of HGG patients, and compare the effects to those patients who are getting standard care, to see if giving our 2 azoles before surgery can make surgery easier, decrease the invasiveness and survival of HGG tumor cells, and increase patient survival.

column36: The role of ontologically distinct cardiac macrophage subsets in ischemic injury
column37: Heart failure is a leading cause of hospitalization and mortality in Canada and world-wide. A common initiating factor in the development of heart failure is adverse cardiac remodeling due to acute/chronic inflammation following myocardial infarction (MI). Understanding the role innate immune cells play in the initial inflammation and subsequent reparative response following injury is of critical importance. Recent observations from our group have identified a heterogeneous population of cardiac resident macrophages (MFs) which play important roles in tissue injury/repair dependent on their ontological origin. In contrast to the prevailing theory that all cardiac MFs are derived from blood monocytes we have definitively shown that cardiac MFs have two distinct origins. The majority of cardiac MFs are embryonically derived (EmbryoD-MFs) while the remainder are monocyte-derived, produced by bone-marrow hematopoietic stem cells (HscD-MF). Importantly, our preliminary data suggests MF origin drives MF function, with embryonic-derived subsets being responsible for tissue repair, while HscD-MFs promote inflammation, which may lead to pathological repair. Together, this provides a novel framework to study cardiac MF populations which we predict will have distinct and opposing roles following MI. The overall goal of this study is to define the distinct roles of EmbryoD-MFs and HscD-MFs for the first time, in order to exploit novel ontogeny-guided therapies that prevent MF-driven tissue damage while simultaneously promoting MF-driven cardiac tissue repair.

column36: Novel Delivery System for High Dose Rate Intensity Modulated Brachytherapy with Yb-169 as a Radiation Source
column37: Radiotherapy is an effective and safe treatment for cancer. Approximately 50% of cancer patients benefit from this treatment, that is, close to 100,000 Canadians with cancer each year. Brachytherapy, is a form of radiotherapy where radioactive sources are placed inside or near the tumours using thin, hollow tubes (catheters) implanted for a short period of time, giving a high radiation dose to the tumour while maintaining a low dose to surrounding healthy tissues. However, dose distribution in conventional brachytherapy is identical in all directions resulting in dose spillage to radiation sensitive healthy tissues. This proposal aims to develop a novel radiation delivery system that will manipulate the radiation dose to conform to the shape of a tumour by incorporating radiation shields inside the implanted hollow tubes, i.e. the delivery system will modulate the intensity of the emitted radiation from the brachytherapy source. The shields can rotate during the treatment, direct the radiation towards the tumour and away from healthy tissues. Developing and making intensity modulated brachytherapy clinically available, will significantly improve the potential of brachytherapy with reduced toxicity will increase the cure rates and improve the quality of life for Canadians with prostate, breast, cervical, uterine, vaginal, vulvar, head & neck and oesophageal cancers. In addition, this proposal will offer undergraduate and graduate student to work in a multidisciplinary environment with radiation oncology, radiation physics, biology, computing and engineering.

column36: Sex differences in innate lymphoid cells and asthma
column37: Asthma is one of the most common health problems in Canada. Many studies have found that adult women are more likely to develop asthma than adult men, but the precise reason for the gender difference in asthma incidence is currently unknown. Asthma is caused by over-production of a group of proteins called type 2 cytokines that induce excessive mucus production and narrowing of airway, which result in breathing difficulty. We have found a family of innate lymphocytes called ILC2 that produces large amounts of type 2 cytokines. We have also found that ILC2 is activated by a protein called IL-33, and female mice have more IL-33 in the lung than male mice of the same age. We think female sex hormones enhance IL-33 production in the lung, which makes lung ILC2 more sensitive to allergens. We will test this idea by comparing the numbers of ILC2 and the amounts of IL-33 in the lung of male and female mice. We will also test the effects of sex hormones on IL-33 production in the lung and allergen-induced ILC2 activation as well as asthma development in mice. Through this study, we hope to find out why adult women are more likely to get asthma than men. This study may result in new ways to treat asthma patients.
