column36: Amyloid beta sex specifically alters synaptic physiology
column37: With age comes wisdom, or so they say. Yet, the reality is that with age, the ability to remember declines and for many progresses to the point where individuals are no longer self-sufficient. This is the experience for over 500,000 Canadians suffering from Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other forms of dementia. The AD endemic has been growing exponentially and is predicted to affect 150 million people by 2050. Moreover, these estimates do not include the countless silent sufferers dealing with the social, emotional, and financial turmoil associated with caring for loved ones stricken by this disease. AD progresses slowly, first robbing sufferers of their short-term memories, like where they left their keys, then wiping away their long-term memories, like the names of their loved ones, and finally taking away their ability to do simple daily tasks, like taking a shower. There is no cure for AD and little progress has been made to develop new treatments. Interestingly, 2/3 of AD patients are women who have a more aggressive disease progression. This suggests that understanding the differences between male and female brains could provide important clues to new therapeutic avenues. We will study how amyloid beta, a pathological agent in AD, disrupts neuronal health and function. We have exciting preliminary data suggesting that amyloid beta affects male and female brains differently, and these differences could lead to sex-specific therapies for men and women. Our research will focus on the role of calcium, an element that plays a vital role in maintaining neuronal health and whose regulation may differ between men and women. Our data indicate that modulating calcium is a powerful tool to reestablish neuronal function and maintain brain health. We hope to open the door towards new strategies and new treatments based on a better understanding of the underlying causes of AD.

column36: The genetics of sex differences related to perinatal health
column37: Our goal is to understand why pregnancies with a female fetus are less vulnerable to infection, preterm birth and other adverse outcomes, than those with a male fetus. At the most basic level, the only difference between males and females is that males generally have one X and one Y chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. In females, most of the genes on of the two X's in are typically turned off in each cell to equalize gene dosage between the sexes; However, this process appears to be relatively sloppy in the placenta, the organ upon which the fetus depends on for normal growth and development. We expect that sex-differences in placental biology likely drive a wide-range of downstream effects on fetal health including susceptibility to infection and preterm birth. column36: Genetic variance in the endocannabinoid system and vulnerability towards the impact of early life adversity on emotional behavior and sensitivity to stress: An examination of gene-environment interactions relevant for psychiatric illness.
column37: Early life adversity (ELA; i.e. childhood trauma or abuse) is known to be a significant risk factor for development of anxiety disorder, which are among the most prevalent psychiatric conditions in children and adolescents. However, a significant proportion of individuals who experience ELA do not develop psychiatric issues later in life. This suggests that there is a gene-environment interaction that can regulate the effects of early life experience on the developing brain. The endocannabinoid system, a signaling system in the brain, is known to be involved in regulation of stress, fear, and anxiety. Interestingly, a relatively common genetic alteration in this system (present in ~38% of the population) has been shown to enhance top-down control of emotionality and promote resilience against anxiety. However, the influence of this gene alteration may depend on environmental conditions present during development. A recent report identified that individuals with this gene alteration may actually exhibit an increased vulnerability, not resilience, to develop anxiety disorders, if they were exposed to ELA. The following proposal utilizes this gene-environment interaction in order to examine the molecular, biochemical, and genetic link between ELA and anxiety disorders. Specifically, this proposal uses two well-established mouse models to investigate the effects of ELA in mice with the endocannabinoid gene alteration on: 1) activity and connectivity of specific neural circuitry (frontoamygdala circuitry, which is implicated in anxiety); 2) stress response; and 3) anxiety and stress-coping behaviour. Importantly, with the high prevalence of anxiety disorders, overrepresentation of ELA in anxiety patients, and commonality of endocannabinoid gene alteration it is likely that many individuals diagnosed with anxiety disorders have unique neural circuitry underlying their symptoms. Thus, these experiments may provide an avenue into more personalized treatment of anxiety.

column36: Causal effect of time-varying driving pressures on mortality in mechanically ventilated, adult patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome
column37: Ten percent of all patients admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) suffer from a condition known as Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). This is a form of life-threatening respiratory failure characterized by severe lung damage. ARDS is associated with a very high mortality rate, up to 50% of people may die from this condition. At present, there is no cure, and limited treatments, for ARDS. Patients with ARDS need to be placed on a ventilator (breathing machine) to support their breathing. The ventilator uses pressure to deliver breaths to patients in order to support the patient's breathing while the lungs heal. Unfortunately, if this pressure delivered by the ventilator is too high, it can also cause damage. We would like to investigate whether using a lower pressure delivered breath-by-breath by the ventilator can improve outcomes in patients with ARDS. To investigate this, we will use existing data from the Toronto Intensive Care Observational Registry (iCORE), which includes measurements from all patients admitted to one of the five University of Toronto-affiliated ICUs. Using these data, we would like to characterize the effect of higher versus lower ventilator pressure on mortality in patients with ARDS. An important aspect of our proposal is the use of novel analytical techniques (marginal structural models) to understand how the treatment affects patients while accounting for patient- and treatment-related differences. We believe that patients who receive less pressure during artificial ventilation will have a lower risk of death. If so, this could lead to a change in current practice and potentially improve outcomes for those that suffer from ARDS.

column36: Characterizing chemical pollution to support the establishment of healthier alternatives: Addressing pesticide contamination among the Cayambe Indigenous community, Ecuador
column37: Global agricultural systems are now highly interconnected. Purchases made by people in high-income countries may have an impact on the wellbeing of marginalized communities elsewhere. Chemical pollution is one of the paths illustrating this connection, as growing demand for imported agricultural goods may increase the exposure to pesticides, and the risk of developing non-communicable diseases (NCDs), among populations in the proximity of agricultural crops. Ecuador is the world's third-largest flower exporter, an industry that relies heavily on pesticide use. About half of flower farms in Ecuador are located next to Indigenous Cayambe territory, and this community has been struggling for their health and food sovereignty. Cayambe people may be at higher risk of developing NCDs, due to weak pesticide risk management and inadequate access to health care in the region. Moreover, underlying factors, such as poor nutrition and compromised immune systems, increase the risk of developing NCDs when exposed to pesticides. Though this situation raises concerns, few studies address this issue in the region and in low-income countries. The Cayambe community has raised concerns about excessive pesticide use in the region and its local government is committed to reducing exposures. Based on a long-term collaboration with Universidad Andina Simon Bolivar, and Cayambe authorities, we have a unique opportunity of working together to disentangle major sources of pesticide contamination. We will measure levels of pesticide contamination in mothers and children, risk perceptions of pesticide use, and health-related variables. Using maps generated by a drone, we will compare these variables with living and working places. This study will allow us to identify high risk areas of contamination and paths of exposure. It will also enable us to evaluate strategies to reduce environmental and human health degradation, and build healthier alternatives that could be applied to other settings.

column37: Neuropathic pain is a type of chronic pain state caused by damage to the nervous system. About 3 million Canadians suffer from such pathological condition that is associated with increased drug prescriptions and visits to health care providers. As a consequence, quality of life is significantly impaired because of poor sleep, anxiety, and depression that are frequent and severe in patients with neuropathic pain. An incomplete understanding of molecular mechanisms in neuropathic conditions makes it difficult to predict which patients will experience pain after injury and how certain patients respond to specific drugs. Thus, more effective personalized pain therapies are needed. The spinal cord is an important gateway for pain messages transmitted to the brain. Inhibitory neurons control the flow of pain messages from the spinal cord to the brain. Any disruption of that inhibition - often referred to as the "pain gate" - disrupts normal pain processing and results in neuropathic pain. Specifically, downregulation of a molecule known as KCC2 is necessary and sufficient to explain many forms of neuropathic pain. However, we still do not know what cell types in the spinal cord express KCC2 and, consequently, how they are affected by KCC2 downregulation. In the proposed study, I will use transgenic mice to determine which cell types in the spinal cord experience KCC2 downregulation and how their function is impacted. I will also explore how therapeutic strategies can reduce neuropathic pain by upregulating KCC2. By the end of this project, we will learn more about how changes in KCC2 function affect the flow of pain messages transmitted to the brain. Our improved understanding of the underlying mechanisms behind neuropathic pain will help us develop more effective and efficient strategies to alleviate neuropathic pain by mitigating the effects of KCC2 downregulation.

column36: Identifying and rejuvenating the bone marrow stem cells responsible for preventing heart failure in elderly cardiac patients
column37: After heart attack, the damaged area in the heart tissue undergoes significant changes that often result in symptoms of heart failure. These symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling and exercise intolerance. Currently, thousands of Canadians live with heart failure. Unfortunately despite the recent developments in medical and surgical therapies, only 50% of these individual survive more than five years. Current therapies for end stage heart failure include either heart transplant or the use of mechanical assist devices. However both these options are extremely limited, costly, require significant resources from the providers and reduce patients' quality of life. Cell therapy is a promising avenue for improving the function of the damaged heart. After a heart attack, bone marrow stem cells move to the heart and regenerate the injured organ. However clinically, bone marrow stem cell therapy in patients has not shown significant improvements in their heart function. A possible explanation is the reduced ability of the stem cells of older patients to repair heart tissue. In order to improve the efficiency of cell therapy in patients with heart disease, we aim to study the differences between various types of bone marrow stem cells to identify the most important cells for heart repair, investigate the effect of aging on the ability of these cells to improve heart function, and to rejuvenate old cells using novel approaches. This study will be the next step in developing better therapies to prevent heart failure in patients who have suffered from heart attack.

column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) can cause chronic hepatitis C, a treatable infectious disease that continues to contribute to liver-related illness and death. In 2011, there were over 245 000 Canadians living with chronic hepatitis C. Unfortunately, only 20% of individuals with HCV are thought to be diagnosed, as access to HCV testing is limited. Standard HCV tests are slow, costly, labour intensive, and require extensive user training, making them unsuitable for use in resource-poor areas where they are needed most critically. Early diagnosis, however, allows patients to prevent complications and obtain treatment earlier. In order to determine which HCV treatment is best suited for a patient, doctors must know the type of HCV causing the infection. Here I propose a design for a low-cost, easy-to-use diagnostic test that can identify the type and quantity of HCV using a single tablet. In my project I will use nanoparticles, materials 1-100nm in size, to detect different types of HCV. Nanoparticles colour coded for HCV type will be used in combination to identify multiple types of HCV in the same test. These nanoparticles will be encased in a tablet-similar to drug tablets that dissolve in liquids. A tablet is advantageous as it has a long shelf-life, is inexpensive, is quick to make, and is simple to use. Within minutes of mixing the tablet and patient sample, a smartphone camera can scan the sample to determine the type and quantity of HCV. Since there are over 1 billion smartphone users in the world, this diagnostic platform can increase accessibility to medical tests globally. As opposed to sending tests to distant facilities or purchasing expensive equipment, my method requires little user training, has a long shelf life, and costs less than 30 cents per test. Moreover, the design of this diagnostic test can be applied to other infectious diseases, as the rapid identification of infected individuals is essential for containing outbreaks and effectively managing disease.

column36: Molecular adaptation to allergen exposure: sex-related differences in asthma
column37: Asthma is the most common chronic respiratory disease. It is characterized by inflammation in the lungs and narrowing of the airways, which makes it difficult to breathe. Nearly 3 million Canadians suffer from asthma, and the direct and indirect cost related to asthma in Canada is around $2.2 billion annually. On average, adult females experience greater disease severity and are more likely to develop resistance to the available steroid therapies. As a result, they are more likely to have uncontrolled asthma compared to males. However, we do not understand the reasons for these differences between females and males. In order to develop better treatment strategies for asthma, we need to understand why these differences occur, and that means we must examine the cells and molecules that are found in the female lung following allergen exposure to see how this differs from males. In this study, we will identify the cellular and molecular changes that occur in the lungs following exposure to a common allergen, and assess how these changes differ between females and males. This work will employ both mouse models of asthma and direct human studies. This information will be an essential resource for future drug development studies as we work to find new ways to provide relief to the millions that suffer from this debilitating disease. If we understand why the disease develops differently in females and males, or why they respond differently to current therapies, it will help to identify new avenues of study (based on the identified molecular differences) as we work to devise new treatment regimens. It is entirely possible that we will need to develop sex-specific treatment protocols to provide the most comprehensive and efficient care for asthma sufferers. column36: Effect of trophoblast sex on uterine immune cell function
column37: The biological sex of a fetus associates with risk of having specific pregnancy disorders. For example, preterm births are more likely if the fetus is male, while the risk of pre-eclampsia is increased if the fetus is female. Moreover, male fetuses fare poorer in pregnancies afflicted by stress (i.e. infection, malnutrition). These observations suggest that the sex of the developing baby interacts with biological processes important in pregnancy. The placenta (a fetal-derived organ being of the same sex as the fetus) is essential in pregnancy for ensuring adequate maternal blood/nutrient delivery to the developing baby. The placenta also plays a central role in modifying the mother's immune response to ensure that the developing baby is tolerated. Importantly, many disorders of pregnancy associate with inadequate placenta function. Placenta function is controlled in part by specialized immune cells residing within the mother's uterus, and abnormal changes in uterine immune cell behavior associate with abnormal placenta function and disorders of pregnancy. However, it is currently unknown if the sex of the placenta or its cells differentially modifies maternal immune cell biology. This proposal aims to examine how placenta cells of either male or female sex differ from eachother with respect to the genes they express in both healthy and unhealthy women. Further, we will investigate if the biological sex of the placenta and its cells affects uterine immune cell function. This research will generate important knowledge with respect to how the sex of the fetus and its tissues interacts with the mother's immune system in pregnancy. These findings will provide critical insight into possible biological processes that are different in pregnancies with a male or female fetus that may help to provide answers as to why the sex of the baby establishes unique pregnancy outcome risks.

column36: Sex-specific investigations of Parkinson's disease mouse models: application for gonadal drugs repurposing.
column37: Both the prevalence and the incidence of Parkinson's disease (PD) are well documented to be higher in men than in women and these sex differences could be due to effects of the circulating sex hormones. Most PD patients experience gastrointestinal dysfunctions often preceding motor dysfunctions. PD might originate in the peripheral nervous system spreading later to the brain. Drugs for PD only improve motor symptoms: no drug is yet available to limit disease progression. It is thus important to identify pharmacological agents that would interfere with peripheral dysfunctions before spreading to the brain. This project will investigate two drugs to target the gut-brain axis for PD therapy: 1) dutasteride that inhibits the enzyme 5alpha-reductase, and 2) raloxifene that selectively modulates estrogen receptors. We have shown that these drugs possess anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties in a male toxin-induced mouse model of PD. We hypothesize that these drugs will have an effect as well in male than female mice but to a different extent. We will also start investigating the sex difference in an alpha-synuclein mouse model of PD with the hypothesis that alpha-synuclein accumulation is less in females due to estrogen neuroprotection. Our objectives are to evaluate A) the pharmacological properties of dutasteride and raloxifene in an early peripheral model of neurotoxin-induced PD with male and female mice to determine the contribution to the disease of male and female hormones and B) investigate the sex differences in alpha-synuclein accumulation in alpha-synuclein genetically modified intact and gonadectomized mice. This project will validate novel indications for two drugs already approved for human administration to accelerate their use by PD patients. The drug studies will be performed in a toxin-induced model of PD and we will start investigating sex differences in a genetic model of PD. This project has high translational potential.

column36: Sex-dependent effects of cranial radiation in the developing brain

column36: Long-term behavior of tailings dams after closure: implications for dam safety risk management
column37: The mining process produces slurry wastes known as tailings, which are stored in containment structures called tailings dams. Following mine closures, tailings dams are subject to natural forces, such as erosion, as the dam transitions into a landform that is compatible with the natural landscape. This poses a significant problem as tailings dams are designed to be safe during the mine's active life, which is much shorter than the lifespan of the dam. Failure of these structures can result in catastrophic consequences to the public and the environment as the tailings may escape the dam resulting in extensive environmental contamination and even fatalities. To prevent failure of these large structures after mining, their long-term behavior must be understood and incorporated into the original design. Unfortunately, there is currently little information available regarding how these structures age over time. This is problematic as there are thousands of tailings dams worldwide, many of which are located in the vicinity of urban centers. The objective of the proposed research is to describe the long-term behavior of tailings dams following mine closure to aid in risk management. The proposed research involves three main stages. First, a fault tree will be developed to visually illustrate the causes, effects, and consequences of different failure modes based on a detailed case study review of multiple tailings dams. Second, the failure modes identified in the first stage will be analyzed and modelled over time. The model will be evaluated using tailings dam case studies. Third, a risk assessment tool will be developed based on the probability and consequences of failure for tailings structures post-closure. This is expected to improve the design of tailings dams which will reduce the probability of failure and the release of tailings to the environment. Consequently, this research is expected to improve public safety and aid in environmental protection.

Pour ce faire, des parcours commentes seront realises avec les personnes elles-memes. Ces trajets a pied dans le quartier de residence des participants permettront de connaitre leur point de vue sur leur milieu de vie. En devoilant la realite de cette population la plupart du temps invisible, cette etude vise a contribuer a l'amelioration des conditions de vie offertes a ces personnes. column37: My research investigates recent political efforts by cities to confront global challenges. Specifically, it examines the efforts of two city-networks, the C40 City Climate Leadership Group and the Strong Cities Network, which address climate change and violent extremism respectively. It further asks about the conditions under which these networks are successful in achieving their policy objectives. In addition to improving our understanding of how cities are meeting the challenges of climate change and violent extremism, this examination provides insight into the changing nature of the global political order. Are cities in these networks becoming more influential, in the sense that they are writing new rules and commanding legitimacy in these issue areas? And if cities are making rules and influencing global politics beyond the state, what does this mean for our traditional system of international authority? By analyzing how contemporary global politics is functioning, we can better understand which political strategies are effective and which are not, and with that knowledge, learn more about how to overcome political gridlock on pressing global issues.

column36: Influenza immunization for all Canadians: Does One Size Fit All?

Data show that the immune system of males and females do not respond to infections in the same way. Females seem to be able to clear viruses more rapidly. column37: Pregnancy with diabetes or gestational diabetes (i.e., maternal diabetes) creates elevated blood sugar levels in the womb, resulting in a variety of birth defects, for example, congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT). CAKUT is a common medical condition in children whose kidneys are not developed properly during pregnancy and responsible for 34-59% of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in childhood and 31% of pediatric kidney failure in United States and Canada. In addition, there are lifelong consequences for the offspring-increased tendency to develop various disorders, such as metabolic syndrome, hypertension (HTN), obesity, cardiovascular disease and CKD in adulthood, and the development of those debilitating diseases varies between men and women in life. The exact reasons for this phenomenon, called perinatal programming, are poorly understood. In this proposed project, we aim to study the sex/gender regulation role of angiotensin II type 2 receptor (AT2R) which is one of key genes known to be important in the development of CAKUT, in our mouse model of maternal diabetes-induced perinatal programming. There is compelling evidence that as a potential therapeutic target for HTN, cardiovascular disease and CKD, AT2R mediates vascular and renal action via sex/gender dependent manner. Thus, better understanding of the sex-dependent mechanisms that underlie maternal diabetes-induced perinatal programming will help develop a novel sex-specific strategy to prevent programmed diseases and comorbid illness in both sexes. The goal of this project is to gain new insights and help researchers and clinicians to develop HTN and CKD prevention and treatment approaches, with a view to reducing diabetic pregnancy-associated healthcare burdens in Canada and thereby improve the quality of life of Canadians.

column36: Targeting sex mitochondrial asymmetry to elucidate sex-specific consequences of intermittent hypoxia in newborns
column37: Respiratory disorders and mortality occur at a one-third lower rate in newborn females than in newborn males. For instance, newborn females have a lower risk of developing respiratory distress syndrome at birth, a greater resistance to oxygen deprivation injuries (hypoxia), and a lower risk for sudden infant death syndrome and neurodevelopmental impairment. Our understanding of such heterogeneity remains limited. However, this relatively higher protection observed in females is especially apparent in the period in which the brain is still immature. Indeed, preterm newborns are more at risk for developing respiratory irregularities that are often manifested as apneas (suspended breathing), desaturation (decreased arterial oxygen content), and bradycardia (decreased heart rate). Such clinical signs, called intermittent hypoxia (IH), occur in 85% of preterm infants (apnea of prematurity - AoP). During adulthood, IH causes the dysfunction of mitochondria, which are tiny intracellular structures that use oxygen to generate almost all the energy required for life. Unsurprisingly, mitochondria have been implicated in several human diseases; when dysfunctional, they induce the production of aggressive forms of oxygen, known as reactive oxygen species, and pro-inflammatory cytokines, molecules that participate actively in inflammation, infection and trauma. Importantly, recent studies have shown that the mitochondrial response to brain injury at neonatal ages is sex dependent. Accordingly, in this study, we propose exposing newborn rats to IH, thus simulating AoP conditions, to assess sex-specific consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction and associated oxidative stress and inflammation. Noting that sex is seldom considered an influencing factor in newborn clinical care and that IH is persistent despite adequate treatment (caffeine, ineffective in ~50%), our results will provide a new and solid basis for clinicians to identify more effective and sex-tailored treatments.

column36: Sex-specific functional and transcriptional contributions of the cortico-striatal and -tegmental pathways in mediating stress susceptibility and resilience
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a sexually dimorphic condition affecting millions of men and women every year. Despite its highly heterogeneous aetiology, chronic stress is a recurring factor interfering with the establishment of cognitive strategies required to deal with daily-life stress. While being a major member of complex neuronal circuits involved in mediating the effects of stress, the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is known to project densely to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA). These mutually exclusive projections are involved differently in the regulation of stress susceptibility in males although their impact in females has not been studied yet. We recently showed that the transcriptional organization of gene networks in the brain differs significantly in males and females with MDD and stressed mice. Importantly, our data suggest that these changes interfere with the activity of individual neuronal populations in a sex-specific fashion. So far, it is unclear whether these populations are projecting preferentially to the NAc or the VTA and whether the activity of these projections differ in stressed males and females. Furthermore, the sex-specific transcriptional programs regulating the activity of these cells are unknown. Here, I propose a multidisciplinary approach combining viral approaches with Ca2+ imaging in behaving animals to monitor projection-specific activity following stress in males and females. I will use pharmacogenetics approaches to modulate these projections and determine their behavioral impact in males and females. Finally, I will sort out these cells and use RNAseq combined with advanced bioinformatics approaches to identify male and female-specific gene networks controlling the activity of both projections differently in males and females. Ultimately, these approaches will lead to the development of better therapeutic strategies for the treatment of mood disorders in males and females.

column36: Etude des modulations de l'expression des genes et de l'epissage des ARNm cellulaires dans le cadre d'une infection par differents Flavivirus: le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune et le virus Zika
column37: Les Flavivirus, tel que le virus Zika, le virus du Nil occidental, et le virus de la fievre jaune, sont des virus transmis par les moustiques auxquels plusieurs milliards de personnes sont exposees au niveau mondial. Ces virus sont etroitement apparentes, mais ils causent des maladies distinctes. De facon generale, tous les Flavivirus peuvent infecter le systeme nerveux et causer des inflammations du cerveau. Par contre, seulement certains Flavivirus, dont le virus de la fievre jaune, peuvent causer des fievres hemorragiques. De plus, le virus Zika est le seul Flavivirus associe au developpement de microcephalie, soit une croissance anormalement faible du cerveau chez le foetus, lorsque la mere est infectee durant la grossesse. Il est connu que les virus deregulent un grand nombre de processus cellulaires de l'hote dans le but de favoriser l'infection. Par contre, les mecanismes par lesquels les virus causent ces changements restent a etre elucides. Dans cette etude, nous investiguons l'infection de cellules avec trois differents Flavivirus, soit le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune, et le virus Zika, dans le but de comprendre comment ces virus interagissent avec l'hote. En effectuant les infections dans les memes conditions, il est egalement possible de comparer les differents virus et leurs effets sur les cellules, en plus de determiner des deregulations communes aux trois virus ainsi que des deregulations uniques a chaque virus. Ces resultats permettront de mieux comprendre comment ces virus affectent l'hote et pourquoi ils causent des maladies differentes.

column36: Quantifying the drivers of animal migration - an integrative approach
column37: Migration is the seasonal movement of animals between two distinct ranges, and is a strategy used by a variety of species worldwide to maximize reproductive success. Migration is critical for populations to thrive in changing environments. Despite this, it is among the most threatened processes on the planet, with declines in migratory behaviour attributed to climate change and habitat loss. We know little about what shapes individual differences in migratory behaviour and the relative roles of genetics, physiology (e.g., body condition), and environmental heterogeneity in shaping migration in a changing landscape. My objective is to develop a complete understanding of migration by untangling the effects of environmental conditions, physiology, and genetics on this fundamental process. Using data collected from three migratory species: moose, mule deer, and mountain goat, I will measure individual variation in migratory behaviour within each species and test multiple hypotheses about the drivers of migration. Using recent advances in technology, I will screen the DNA of all three species to determine if the same genes that control migratory behaviour are shared across species. I predict that while environmental factors will be the main factor controlling migration across species, the remaining variation in behaviour can be explained by a few genes of large effect that are shared across all three species. My project takes an original approach to understanding the drivers of migration behaviour and combines ideas and techniques from multiple disciplines in biology, including ecology, genetics, and physiology. My results will contribute to the understanding of migration behaviours in three species that are important for food security, tourism, and culture in Canada, and whose populations are at risk as their migration routes become threatened due to climate change and habitat loss.

column36: Exploring the role of sex-hormone driven natural antibody during bloodstream E. coli infections
column37: Women generally live longer than men, one of the leading causes of such female advantage in longevity relies on the sex differences in infection, i.e. women are less susceptible than men to infectious diseases caused by various pathogens. As our immune system is the arsenal providing weapons to fight microbial infection, we could imagine that there must be a sex-difference in anti-microbial immunity, which makes women better armed than men during infections. Here we report a sex difference in the production of natural anti-E. coli antibodies. Using intravital microscopy, we could directly visualize the very dynamic interaction between invading bacteria and host immune cells. We have found a critical role of these antibodies in promoting the capture of circulating bacteria by the liver, an organ which captures and clears the majority of invading bacteria during an intravenous infection. Consequently, males without these natural antibodies showed greater bacterial dissemination and more severe morbidity than females. These antibodies are made at puberty only by females and can bind specifically to E. coli, which allows immune cells to catch and kill the bacteria. They are over 10 times more prevalent in females than in males due to the selective up-regulation by estrogens. Because these antibodies are made without any immunization, it is reasonable to hypothesize they may function as a "ready-to-fire" strategy to quickly eliminate invading pathogens and perhaps to extend protection to newborns. This study reveals a novel mechanism underlying the sex-biased difference in infection, which could be instructive for treatment of infectious diseases in individual sexes and in pre-pubertal patients.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease in which the immune system attack and destroy cells in the brain and spinal cord. While there are a number of drugs that can help relieve symptoms in the early "relapsing/remitting" phase of MS, treatment option in the late "secondary progressive" phase are very limited. While women develop MS more frequently than men, the progression of symptoms occurs more rapidly in men. Understanding the role played by sex in MS could help us develop better therapies. In our lab, we study a variant of MS in mice. We find that male mice get worse disease and in fact develop secondary progressive symptoms. In this grant, we will try and understand why this is the case. Increased disease in male mice could be due to two possible reasons: either immune cells are more easily able to enter the brain/spinal cord and are more potent than in females, or the cells that make up the male brain and spinal cord are more sensitive to immune attack. We will therefore try to distinguish between these possibilities. Sex differences are often considered to be the result of sex hormones, ie. due to the fact that males produce testosterone and females produce estrogen and progesterone. However, this overlooks the fact that men and women have one chromosome that is entirely different. We will therefore use a unique genetically engineered mouse strain whose pups can uncouple sex hormones from sex chromosomes. These "4 core genotype" mice can have testes with XY chromosomes; testes with XX chromosomes; ovaries with XY; or ovaries with XX. We will examine each of these mice for their ability to develop secondary progressive symptoms. This project is important because it will help us understand why men and women show such striking differences in MS. In the future, this could help us to predict whether one sex can respond better to a given MS drug than another. This will in turn help neurologists make more informed decisions regarding MS patient care.

column37: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a blood clot that forms in a vein. VTE is a common, lethal, costly, yet treatable condition. There are effective drugs to prevent VTE but they carry an increase risk of bleeding. Our team has long-term interest in understanding what causes VTE, and how to prevent and treat VTE. We argue that we need to understand how DNA and the way it is packaged and 'read' (i.e. the epigenetic 'code') lead to disease in order to better prevent and manage VTE. The epigenetic code is the intermediate player linking a person's environment and his/her genetic make up. An individual's sex is an important variable on how the genetic and epigenetic codes impact a person's risk to VTE, and how he or she responds to treatment. In particular, we are intrigued by the fact that men and women have a similar risk of developing a first VTE, but men have more than twice the risk of a subsequent VTE after a 'blood thinner' drug treatment is stopped. We propose that sex-specific epigenetic marks underlie the protective effect against subsequent VTE observed in women after treatment with a 'blood thinner'. We will analyze patients' blood sample, biological and clinical data, and perform lab experiments, to understand the biology behind sex differences in VTE treatment. This will be the basis of new tests that will ultimately improve the standard of care received by men and women after a first VTE event. Given the importance and the risk of using 'blood thinners' to manage patients following a VTE, being able to predict who will benefit the most from such drugs and who can safely discontinue their use after initial treatment are of major importance in caring for these patients. This will also inform on novel intervention targets that could reverse the risk of VTE.

column36: Sexual differences in brain vulnerability to arterial stiffness
column37: Arterial stiffness is an important risk factor for attention, memory and learning deficits, and ultimately, for dementia. We define arterial stiffness by the loss of elasticity in blood vessels. It increases with age and this increase accelerates at the age of about 50 years old, but at variable levels between individuals. The consequence of arterial stiffness is the decrease capacity of the arteries to dampen blood pressure variations induced at each heart beat. Normaly, absorption of these fluctuations will allow a constant blood flow and a loss of pulsatility in small blood vessels. However, when this pulsatility persists in small blood vessels, it could damage the surrounding tissue. Up to date, many epidemiological studies suggest a link between arterial stiffness and brain damages. It was also demonstrated that women exhibit higher arterial stiffness than men. In addition, the mortality rate is higher in women than men for the same level of arterial stiffness. It would be thus very interesting to determine whether the brain of female mice in a menopause model is more vulnerable to arterial stiffness than males and females at premenopause. The main objective of this project is to study the difference in brain vulnerability to arterial stiffness between males and females. In particular, we will study the difference between male and female mice on the structure and elasticity of carotid arteries that carry blood from the heart to the brain, on cerebral blood flow and on cognition. For this purpose we developed a unique model to study the effects of arterial stiffness on the brain. As arterial stiffness increases during the peri- and post-menauposal periods, we will combine our arterial stiffness model to a model of accelerated menopause. This study will help to understand why men and women brain's vulnerability to develop dementia differs and to develop personalized therapeutic strategies for both men and women to prevent and cure dementia.

column36: The Impact of Sex on Kidney Metabolism. Implications for Diabetic Kidney Disease
column37: Being a man is harder on the kidney than being a woman. Male sex predisposes to the development of several diseases affecting the kidney, known as chronic kidney disease (CKD). People with diabetes are at high risk of CKD as their kidneys are injured by high levels of glucose. These patients may develop diabetic kidney disease (DKD), the predominant type of CKD. We think that the harmful effect of male sex in DKD and CKD may be due to actions that the male sex hormones (known as androgens) exert on the kidney cells. However, we are still trying to discover what happens in kidney cells when they are in contact with androgens. Understanding how androgens are able to damage kidneys will allow the clinicians to apply more personalized treatments of kidney disease, depending on the patient's sex. We discovered that androgens affected the metabolism of kidney cells. Kidney cells with impaired metabolism may not be able to take up nutrients from their environment and use them to generate energy and work properly. Kidney cells may then get injured and die. It is then possible that perturbed metabolism is the reason why androgens are bad for the kidney. Metabolism is a very complex process based on the actions of many proteins that transform the nutrients to metabolites, used to make energy and build cellular machinery. We will study which of these proteins and metabolites are implicated in the bad effects of androgens in the kidney. We will also study how sex hormones influence the way kidney cells consume glucose and oxygen. We will finally study if androgen effects observed in cells are also observed in male animals with DKD. In this project, we will discover the processes through which androgens damage the kidneys, and how we can stop them, thus preventing CKD and DKD. Our proposed research will improve public health, and may lead to sex-specific therapies for kidney disease.

column36: Enhancing and Expanding the "Know Your Status" Initiative in on-reserve Indigenous Communities in Saskatchewan: A Community-engaged Intervention to Increase Diagnosis, Linkage to Care and Prevention of HIV, HCV and STBBIs
column37: First Nations people living on-reserve in Saskatchewan have the highest rates of HIV infection in Canada, with an incidence approximately 7.3-times higher than the national average. They also have the least access to care and to life saving antiretroviral therapy. To address this need, a comprehensive on-reserve HIV testing and treatment initiative called "Know Your Status" (KYS) was launched in 2011. KYS is a community-designed and community-managed program based on partnerships and collaborations between First Nations communities and care providers. Key components of KYS include: community involvement and leadership, education, prevention, specialized nursing support, support for mental health and addictions, lab testing and accessible and culturally-safe clinical management that meets clients where they are located. Culturally supportive services, such as mentorship from Elders and traditional teachings, are also integrated within the program. Thus far, KYS has been primarily implemented to care for HIV and sexually transmitted infections on a few on-reserve communities. However, there is a need to expand the program to include hepatitis C testing, linkage and treatment, as a result of similarly high on-reserve rates. The research team, in close partnership with First Nation communities, intends to refine, adapt, and expand the KYS intervention to communities with the greatest need. Traditional experimental designs to evaluate the KYS initiative cannot be used for various reasons. Instead, the team will use practical, though rigorous, methods to evaluate the effectiveness, acceptability and sustainability of the expanded KYS program, while ensuring that community needs are met. First Nations leaders and communities, policy makers and other physicians will be engaged throughout the project to build community and provincial capacity to treat on-reserve HIV and hepatitis C, and to ensure program sustainability for years to come.

column36: ATTEMPT: Adolescent Type 1 diabetes Treatment with SGLT2i for hyperglycEMia & hyPerfilTration Trial
column37: Despite how far along we have come in advancing diabetes care, many teenagers with type 1 diabetes still struggle to meet blood sugar and HbA1c targets, which is a measure of diabetes control. In fact, over 80% of teenagers do not meet recommended Canadian guidelines for HbA1c. High blood sugar levels or HbA1c is known to affect other parts of the body causing long-term health issues. Recently, a group of medications, called sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have been used in adults with type 2 diabetes and shown to improve diabetes control and prevent long term kidney and heart issues due to high blood sugars. This study, called the ATTEMPT Trial, will look to see if the SGLT2i called Empagliflozin benefits teens with type 1 diabetes. This study was designed to include the perspectives of parents and teens with type I diabetes so the researchers can learn more about what is important to them as well as the safety and acceptability of taking these medicines as part of their diabetes care. Given that the teenage years are a challenging time, it is important that we study these new medicines early on to see if they may improve blood sugar levels and protect against future diabetes related problems, such as kidney and heart disease, in teens with diabetes.

column36: Evaluating Innovative Health Care Solutions to Improve Outcomes for Persons with Type 1 Diabetes using a Novel Electronic Data Repository
column37: Living with type 1 diabetes (T1D) is challenging in many ways. People with T1D are expected to fit self-management and regular clinic appointments into busy lives, balancing short- and long-term risks of low and high blood sugar levels. Our research aims to improve the lives of people with T1D by testing an innovative health system intervention to help patients achieve better diabetes control in a way that places less burden on individuals and is more patient-oriented. Specifically, the intervention will involve electronic delivery of health care and related support services to people living with T1D in addition to usual care, including 1) frequent, brief virtual visits with their diabetes care team to share and discuss blood sugar patterns, diabetes self-management, coping strategies, personalized goals and action plans and 2) structured online educational courses, tools and supports. Virtual visits will use videoconferencing technology that can be securely accessed free of charge from any personal device (PC, tablet, smart phone). We will test the intervention's impact on diabetes control, patient-reported experiences and outcomes, and heath care use and costs. The intervention will be tailored to two age groups: young adults 17-24 years of age and adults 25 years of age and older. It will enable "high frequency, low touch" care to patients with poorer diabetes control and at times in their lives when they are at high risk for diabetes complications. This approach will allow patients to receive more education and support than is feasible in traditional health care models based solely on in-person clinic visits, in a way that is more seamless (fewer disruptions to daily life) and tailored to individual needs (by offering an array of online educational classes, tools and resources) based on stage of life. We hypothesize that the intervention will improve diabetes control, patient experience and access to self-management education and support for patients with T1D.

column36: Improving breast cancer treatment using a combination of oncolytic vaccinia virus immunotherapy with image-guided radiation.
column37: We are studying a breast cancer treatment strategy using viruses modified to selectively kill tumours. These oncolytic ("cancer lysing") viruses both directly kill tumours and also educate the immune system to target cancer cells, helping to prevent tumour recurrence. We have modified vaccinia virus to preferentially grow in cancer cells, killing them, while leaving healthy tissues intact. In breast cancer models, our virus slows tumour growth and extends survival, however, mice still eventually succumb to disease. We aim to increase the effectiveness of virus treatment by combining it with radiation therapy (RT). RT is often used to treat solid tumours such as breast cancer. For patient treatment, sophisticated machinery exists to precisely target RT to tumours and reduce damage to adjacent tissue. One drawback is that cells at the tumour margins, or cells that have spread to distant sites (metastatic cells), evade RT, leading to the return of the cancer. We anticipate that combining RT with an oncolytic virus will allow us to achieve better control of breast cancer in mouse models. To study this, we have access to a specialized image-guided RT machine, the only one of its kind in Western Canada, which allows us to deliver RT to mice with similar precision to that used in humans. We anticipate that RT will clear the bulk of the tumour, while our virus will infect and kill any remaining cancerous cells at the tumour margins, or which have spread to other sites in the body. We also expect that when our virus is combined with radiation it will improve stimulation of the immune system to target the cancer. In this way, the virus will function as a cancer vaccine and prevent metastasis and recurrence. We anticipate that this targeted approach will offer a more effective way of treating breast cancer, while also causing fewer side effects compared to traditional approaches. This will improve the quality of life and long-term outcomes for cancer patients in Canada.

column36: The development, implementation, and evaluation of a transdiagnostic group intervention for First Nations children.
column37: Wait-lists for mental health services in First Nations' communities often make services inadequate to meet community needs. The use of transdiagnostic treatments could serve to reduce these wait-times by allowing individuals who are experiencing a wide array of difficulties (e.g., depression, anxiety, substance use) to receive services that address underlying symptoms at the same time. These treatments also provide a new framework for evidence based culturally appropriate services within First Nations' communities by incorporating strategies that align with cultural values. Working in collaboration with a community based organization serving First Nations communities in North Western Ontario, a skill based transdiagnostic group intervention will be developed and implemented. This treatment will target community specific needs through consultation with organizational staff and community members. Culturally appropriate skills, concepts, and examples will be identified and integrated into the treatment. This is the first project to adapt and assess the effectiveness of a transdiagnostic mental health treatment for First Nations children. Following an initial pilot group of the treatment, approximately 50 children aged 7-12 years will complete a revised version. It is anticipated that these group interventions will reduce difficulties in emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, behavioural avoidance, and self-care of the children while developing positive coping strategies.

column36: Developing a Conceptual Framework for Measuring the Unmeasurable: Exploring How Structural and Systemic Racism Impacts Chronic Disease in First Nations Communities in Canada
column37: First Nations people in Canada experience higher rates of chronic disease than the rest of Canadians including heart disease, cancer, diabetes and other conditions. Understanding the root causes of these high rates is complex as it requires examining known risk factors. Racism was identified as an influential, yet under-recognized, determinant of health by First Nation leadership in the province of British Columbia. While social determinants of health have been important in understanding the root causes of poor health, racism and its impact on chronic disease is still heavily underexplored. The specific aim of this research is to examine how racism impacts chronic illness in First Nations communities. This study will analyze data from two Canadian health surveys along with conducting interviews with First Nations people living with a chronic health condition to better identify the complex ways that racism can influence risk factors, prevalence, access to treatment and health outcomes. The findings of this study will be used to inform the first provincial heart health and wellness strategy aimed at reducing cardiovascular disease within First Nations in British Columbia. The knowledge generated will enable the identification of key gaps in healthcare delivery, treatment, and screening which can be used to inform the development of innovative and culturally-safe interventions to improve the First Nation health outcomes and the patient-oriented care journey.

column36: Effect of cumulative exposure to antiretroviral therapy on cancer risk in people living with HIV
column37: Background: Cancer has been a major feature of the HIV epidemic, with Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma being the first reported manifestation of AIDS-defining cancers. With the arrival of antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV has become a chronic disease and studies have shown an increase in non-AIDS defining cancers. Additionally, people living with HIV have a higher risk of developing cancer than the general population. There are 75,500 Canadians living with HIV, with the highest proportion in Ontario. In Canada, there is a lack of research assessing the cancer burden and the effect of ART on cancer risk in people living with HIV. Objectives: 1) Determine the incidence and prevalence of site-specific cancers in adults living with HIV in Ontario between 1995 to 2016; 2) Determine whether specific ART regimens show protective cancer effects; and 3) Quantify the extent to which cumulative exposure to ART lowers the risk of infection-related cancers via controlled viremia and improved immune function. Methods: Study objectives will be achieved using data from Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, Ontario Cancer Registry, Ontario HIV Treatment Network Cohort study, and Canadian HIV Observational Cohort Collaboration. We will calculate incidence rates of site-specific cancers after HIV diagnosis using count modelling techniques. Period prevalence before HIV diagnosis, at HIV diagnosis, and short-term and long-term ART exposure will be calculated. We will quantify relationships between ART use, cancer risk, immune suppression, viremia, demographic, socio-economic and behavioural factors using mediation analysis techniques. Significance: This study will bring forward the need for comprehensive HIV care and cancer control. By understanding the cancer burden and the additional hardships of this key population, medical practice and policies can be adapted to offer better long-term care, plan for resource allocation, and optimize treatment to improve health outcomes.

column36: Implementing the Chronic Care Model to improve the care of people living with HIV: The role of self-management
column37: People with HIV are living longer in Canada, mainly due to advances in care and treatment. The success of antiretroviral therapy means that people with HIV are also experiencing more diseases of aging and require ongoing care for multiple chronic conditions. These complex needs may be best addressed through primary care or community-based settings that include integrated health and social services. Care for people with chronic illnesses involves many elements, and one of these elements is support for self-management. There is evidence that self-management programs improve the confidence, knowledge, skills, and motivation people require to take care of their chronic diseases. However, it remains uncertain whether and how these programs similarly help people with HIV to manage their health. In addition, HIV infections in Canada more often affect groups who already must deal with other disadvantages (e.g., poverty, racism), thus requiring an equity lens in research conducted with this population. To address such concerns, I will engage disadvantaged groups (e.g., people who inject drugs) in all phases of this work, and attend to sex- and gender-based issues. In the first part of my research, I will review and describe the literature on the role of self-management in improving health among people with HIV. Second, I will conduct qualitative interviews with diverse individuals, including people with HIV, community-based organizations, and care providers. Results from the literature review and interviews will inform the implementation and evaluation of a sustainable chronic disease self-management program to determine its impact on physical and mental health outcomes. By using existing community partnerships and networks at the local, provincial and national levels, my research is expected to improve health care for people living with HIV. Lessons learned from this research can also be extended to community-focused care for people aging with other chronic conditions.

column36: Role of HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins variable regions in ADCC responses
column37: Around the world, it is estimated that about 37 million people live with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In Canada alone, between 63,000 to 89,000 individuals live with HIV/AIDS and there are thousands of new infections each year. In the absence of an efficient vaccine against HIV and treatments still far away from eradicating the virus, we need to find new approaches to fight this virus. Recent studies have shown that our immune system already possess potentially effective protective mechanism against HIV infection, the antibody-dependant cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) response. The findings of this study will help us to progress in finding a functional cure for HIV-infected patients by sensitizing specifically HIV-infected cells to a strong ADCC response. Moreover, some of these results might be useful at designing new immunogens able to elicit a protective response and thus decrease HIV-1 transmission.

column36: Impact of HPV-induced Immune Changes in the Anal Mucosa on HIV Transmission
column37: There are approximately 37 million people currently living with HIV in the world which, if left untreated, leads to AIDS and death. HIV infection is also a significant public health concern in Canada, particularly when it comes to at-risk populations including men who have sex with men. For instance, in Toronto, almost 1 in 4 men who have sex with men are estimated to be infected with HIV. Therefore, it is important to understand what factors are driving increased HIV risk in this population. One of the factors that have been suggested to play a role in increased HIV risk is infection with Human Papillomavirus (HPV) that can sometimes lead to anal cancer. We believe that HPV infection can increase HIV risk, because when the immune system becomes active in order to respond to HPV infection, this active immune status actually makes it easier for HIV to infect the body. Our goal is to describe this active immune status in detail, so that if HPV infection does increase HIV risk, several methods including HPV treatment and HPV vaccine can be explored to reduce HIV transmission.

column36: Metabolomics as a new strategy to understand modifiable factors for cancer prevention
column37: The Problem: The Canadian Cancer Society, as well as other health agencies emphasize the importance of a healthy lifestyle for cancer prevention. About one-third of cancers can be prevented by maintaining a healthy weight, eating a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, being physically active and limiting alcohol consumption. However, in Canada the rates of overweight and obesity remain high, consumption of fruit and vegetables has declined, less than 15% of adults meet physical activity recommendations and 80% consume alcohol. A large survey of adults found nearly 50% felt "it seems like almost everything causes cancer" and a recent study suggested the majority of cancers are due to "bad luck". An understanding of mechanisms linking preventative behaviour and cancer is critically needed to move the field forward. Metabolomics is the study of chemical fingerprints that cellular processes leave behind, specifically endogenous and exogenous small molecule profiles. New technology such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) provides robust, high throughput, quantitative measure of hundreds of unique metabolites. Hypothesis: There will be distinct metabolic profiles associated with preventive behaviours: healthy weight, fruit and vegetable consumption, physical activity and alcohol consumption. Further, metabolic profiles will differ between individuals who engage in multiple versus single or no preventive behaviours. Overall Study Aim: To use metabolomics to characterize metabolic profiles of lifestyle-related preventive behaviours in adults. Aim 1: Metabolite profiles will be characterized for each lifestyle-related preventive behaviour: healthy weight, consumption of at least 5 fruit and vegetables per day, no more than 2 alcoholic drinks (men) or 1 (women) and at least 30 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity on 5 days of the week. Aim 2: Metabolites will be compared between people according to the number of preventive behaviours they engage in. Aim 3: To determine the relevance of metabolites identified in aims 1 and 2 to cancer development. Methods: 1,200 adults without a history of cancer will be selected from the BC Generations Project (BCGP), a study of men and women aged 35-69 from across British Columbia. Between 2009 and 2014 nearly 12,000 adults completed questionnaires, had physical measurements and provided blood samples. The amount and type of physical activity was assessed from validated surveys. Adiposity measures include measured height and weight, waist circumference and % body fat from bioelectrical impedance. The number of fruits and vegetables and alcoholic drinks typically consumed were selfreported. A high-throughput, automated assay will quantitatively measure metabolites in stored plasma including metabolites from the following classes: lipids, organic acids, organoheterocyclic, organooxygen and nucleosides. The human metabolome database (HMD) contains data on ~49,000 metabolites including origin, biofunction, metabolic and disease pathways and associated disorders and diseases. Metabolites identified in aims 1 and 2 will be referenced with the HMD and prior literature to determine relevance to cancer. Significance: With the aging population, the burden of cancer in Canada will increase exponentially. There is thus a clear and immediate need for prevention to control cancer. These results may identify new biomarkers correlated with preventive behaviours that are potentially relevant for biological processes leading to cancer development. This can help guide future targeted studies that consider these metabolites as mediators or targets that impact cancer. column36: Social deprivation and environment, and risk of prostate cancer
column37: Problem: Social deprivation has been defined as a lack of participation in social relationships, lack of interaction with others and/or with society at large. Socially deprived individuals experience poorer health outcomes, including greater cancer mortality and poorer prognosis for some cancer sites, such as the prostate. Surprisingly, hardly any research has evaluated whether it relates to prostate cancer incidence more specifically. As social environments can facilitate or impede resource sharing, reinforce health beliefs as well as health behaviors, they could be expected to impact on the entire prostate cancer spectrum, including incidence and prevention. Objective: To explore the association between several indicators of the social environment (isolation, fragmentation, disorder, deprivation, etc.) and the risk of developing prostate cancer. Individual, work and neighbourhood level indicators will be investigated at several time points over the lifecourse. Methodology: The proposed analyses will be conducted on a vast, already assembled Canadian dataset, which will be augmented with relevant neighbourhood-level data. Between 2002 and 2015, the Canadian Cancer Society and the Cancer Research Society funded the largest ever and most comprehensive population-based case-control study of prostate cancer to elucidate its causes. It comprises 1,933 prostate cancer cases, including 538 aggressive cancers, and 1,994 population controls.

Over the past decade, there has been a dramatic and robust increasing trend in CRC incidence rates among young adults (aged 15-49) in Ontario, across Canada, and in other countries. It is important to understand who is at risk so that cancer prevention initiatives can be developed and targeted towards young adults, and the identification of higher risk persons (risk stratification) in the general population will enable the development of young-onset CRC prevention and screening strategies for this largely preventable disease. For the last 30 years, population-level tobacco control has aimed to decrease the incidence of cancer by reducing smoking prevalence and exposure to second-hand smoke (SHS). Indeed, significant declines in smoking prevalence have been observed in Canada since the implementation of national media campaigns, smoke-free policies and legislations, and restrictions on the sale of tobacco products. Despite this success, smoking prevalence has stagnated recently and remains unacceptably high among certain social groups, notably those of low socioeconomic status (SES). These social inequalities in smoking translate into inequalities in health, such that socially marginalized groups have a disproportionately heavier burden of smoking-related cancers. To better understand social inequalities in smoking, some researchers have examined the effects of population-level tobacco control by SES, but findings from the few published studies are inconsistent. Some suggest that tobacco control measures increase, some suggest they decrease, and others suggest no impact on social inequalities in smoking. This important knowledge gap on the impact of tobacco control policies on inequality leads us to ask the following research questions: 1) In what ways do population-level tobacco control policies affect social inequalities in smoking? 2) What are the effects of these policies on social inequalities in smoking? To address these questions, we will use a mixed-methods approach to study a tobacco control policy in Quebec entitled An Act to Bolster Tobacco Control (B44), which was implemented in 2016. B44 seeks to reduce overall smoking prevalence and protect the population from SHS by restricting tobacco use in cars with children present, on restaurant and bar terraces, in playgrounds, and in a nine meter radius of private and public building entrances. Objectives and methods. There are three specific objectives: 1) To critically examine the discourse behind B44 (i.e. make the assumptions, interests, values, and used evidence underlying B44 explicit) and to assess whether B44 addresses or not social inequalities in smoking in its discourse. This objective will be addressed by analysing 24 policy-related documents and interviewing 15 tobacco control practitioners in Montreal. 2) To describe how low SES smokers perceive and experience B44 as affecting their everyday lives and their smoking. This objective will be attained by interviewing 15-20 low SES smokers from the Interdisciplinary Study of Inequalities in Smoking (ISIS) cohort. 3) To measure changes in smoking prevalence, initiation, and cessation among adults according to SES before (2007-2015) and after (2016-2017) B44 was implemented. Data from the Canadian Community Health Survey for Quebec and other Canadian provinces as control groups will be used.

column36: Innovations for assessing occupational exposure to carcinogens in population based studies
column37: Millions of Canadians are exposed to known or suspected carcinogens at work. Recent estimates suggest that as many as 15% of new lung cancer cases each year in Canada are a result of occupational exposure to carcinogens; these cancers are preventable. Large population based studies exist in Canada with a goal of investigating cancer in relation to environmental or lifestyle risk factors. These studies provide information on risk factors that is key for targeting prevention activities, but occupational exposures are often overlooked. The burden of occupational cancer in Canada supports the need for considering occupational exposure in population-based cohort studies, but measurement of occupational exposure in population based studies is both challenging and rare. Where done, it has been undertaken in subsets of the population (i.e. nested case-control studies) with a very narrow focus. Recent technological advancements are making it possible to assess a variety of external exposures using novel passive samplers, as well as internally by measuring environmental contaminants, their metabolites or alterations to the epigenome, transcriptome or microbiome. These new technologies can be used to better estimate external and internal exposures over the working life of large and diverse groups and offer an innovative opportunity to improve our understanding of occupational cancer and how to prevent it. This proposal seeks to explore whether small, inexpensive passive samplers and high resolution metabolomics (HRM) can be used in large population based studies to assess occupational exposure to flame retardants (FR), a group of semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOC) of relevance to occupational cancer and found in electronics, household products and protective equipment. This study will answer two research questions: 1. Can simple, passive samplers be used to differentiate between adults with occupational exposure to polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) and organophosphate (OP) flame retardants, and those without? 2. Can high resolution metabolomics (HRM) be used to differentiate between adults with occupational exposure to PBDEs and OP FRs, and those without?

column36: ACHRU Community Partnership Program for Diabetes Self-Management for Older Adults - Canada
column37: Living with diabetes and other chronic (ongoing) conditions is common in older adults. These individuals have poorer health and higher use of health services compared to older adults with diabetes alone. Programs that help older adults self-manage their diabetes and other health conditions benefit both individuals and the healthcare system. The McMaster University Aging, Community and Health Research Unit developed and tested a new patient-centered, community-based program to improve the delivery and outcomes of care for older adults with diabetes and other chronic conditions. This 6-month program was developed in partnership with patients, caregivers, primary and community care providers and researchers. The program is delivered by nurses, dietitians and community providers. It involves in-home visits by nurses and dietitians, monthly group wellness sessions at community centers, and monthly team meetings. Wellness sessions include exercise, education, shared meals, and social support. Caregivers are invited to be active participants along with patients. The program was successfully implemented in Ontario and Alberta. Participants who received the program had better quality of life, self-management, and mental health at no additional cost compared to those receiving usual care. To determine how the program can best help people, more testing is needed with different communities and groups of people. We will partner with primary healthcare teams (e.g., family doctors' offices) in three provinces to adapt and test the program in a variety of real-world settings. We will assess how to best put this program into practice and measure outcomes important to patients and caregivers so study results are relevant to them. Study findings will guide the development of a plan for expanding the program to reach and benefit more older adults with diabetes and other chronic health conditions. Patients and caregivers will be involved as key partners in all aspects of the research.

column36: SPIDER-NET, A Structured Process Informed by Data, Evidence and Research-Network: An approach to support primary care practices in optimizing the management of patients with complex needs
column37: Health care costs are increasing quickly. About half is spent on a small number of people with complex health problems. We need to address this. Built on a successful model for improving care by working together, the Structured Process Informed by Data, Evidence and Research (SPIDER) contains 3 parts: 1) Build teams with family physicians, nurses, pharmacists, medical staff and patients. These teams will learn together, from each other and from experts about improving quality in practice; 2) Use information from Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) to discover what the issues in each practice are, and decide together what could be done; and 3) Start making the practice changes that were agreed to with the help of coaches. Repeatedly test, measure and improve care. We will test SPIDER to see if it helps older patients taking many medications (polypharmacy), some of which may not be necessary or may even be harmful. More drugs often mean more side effects and this is even worse as people age. The risks of side effects like confusion, dizziness and falls increases in elders. Older patients taking ten or more medications are especially complex and high risk; we can do better for them. We expect SPIDER to help family doctors and their teams deliver better care by reviewing and reducing riskier drugs for these patients. We will test SPIDER in seven centres, in five provinces. We expect that it will improve patients' quality of life and their heath; it may also save money by reducing the number of times people are admitted to hospital. Our team is made up of experts and leaders in quality improvement, audit and feedback, pharmacists, physicians, patients and researchers. All of us have experience in the parts that make up SPIDER, so we are able to do this; we will now work together to improve care for elders in our communities by reducing and improving medications, to support their health and help them reach their goals for quality of life.

column36: Screening for Poverty And Related social determinants and intervening to improve Knowledge of and links to resources (SPARK) Study
column37: The social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions and processes at an individual, family, neighbourhood, community and societal level that impact on health. Numerous studies have confirmed the central role that SDOH play in creating and maintaining health inequities. While much is known about SDOH, we lack the individual-level data necessary to target interventions, and lack rigorously evaluated interventions to meet social needs in health settings. Sociodemographic data collected at the individual level, paired with interventions to meet social needs when identified, could address this problem. Further, robust sociodemographic data linked to electronic medical records (EMRs) can support quality improvement and new care pathways at the organizational level, planning and resource allocation at the system level, and advance research on health inequities. The SPARK Study is a cluster randomized controlled trial that will rigorously evaluate a "modest" versus "intensive" intervention to help address poverty when identified. While the primary outcome of this intervention is change in income attributable to the poverty intervention, we will capture data on additional impacts, including linkage to community resources, psychological stress and quality of life. To prepare for the trial, we will develop and validate a standard tool for sociodemographic data collection and social need identification, building on our previous research. We will also pilot test our tool, EMR integration, recruitment processes and study instruments before launching the full trial. Finally, we will collect qualitative data alongside the trial to evaluate implementation and better understand how the intervention to address poverty impacts on participants. This program of research will advance the ability of health providers, organizations and systems to collaborate with patients and communities to "go upstream" and address SDOH.
