column36: Personalized Risk Assessment for Prevention and Early Detection of Breast Cancer: Integration and Implementation
column37: Breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. A woman faces a one in eight chance of developing the disease in her lifetime. Currently, women aged 50 to 74 are recommended to have a mammogram every 2 to 3 years. To maximize the benefits and reduce harms, women should be screened based on their personal risk of the disease. More precise risk assessment combining data on genomic profiling and other BC risk factors has the potential to markedly increase the proportion of identifiable high risk women. This project will provide evidence that can significantly expand the benefits of current age-based population screening programs by supporting the transition to a risk-based approach. It will also improve counseling of women with a family history of BC who are seen in cancer genetic clinics. Earlier detection of BC will allow more cancers to be detected while they are still small and curable, which in turn will save lives and bring significant health and socio-economic benefits. By studying very large cohorts of women using high throughput genomic technologies together with statistical and epidemiological methods, this project will develop a validated multi-gene panel test including genetic variants reliably associated with BC risk. This will enable individualized risk assessment and improve the counseling process by health care providers for women with and without a known BC family history. To support a framework for future implementation of a risk-based screening approach, a large population-based cohort will be assembled to evaluate the acceptability and feasibility of using a new comprehensive risk prediction web tool and a genomic profiling test within the existing health care system. The cohort will be followed to determine behavioural, psychosocial and clinical outcomes. Policies will be developed to address the socio-ethical and legal challenges for women, health professionals and decision makers associated with implementing risk-based breast screening. By providing this evidence, this project will change breast screening practice and ensure better use of human and financial resources. Women will face less invasive BC treatment with fewer complications and improved quality of life and survival, thereby reducing both the clinical and economic burden for a large proportion of Canadian women.

column36: Reducing the global burden of infectious diseases through precision population health
column37: The global rise in the prevalence of antibiotic resistant bacteria is a problem so serious that it threatens all modern medicine. We have already reached the point where half of the common bacteria that cause infections are resistant to our front-line drugs. Moreover, new superbugs have emerged that cannot be cured with any drug. Once these multiple-drug resistant organisms take hold in our healthcare setting, many of the benefits of modern medicine, including hip replacement surgery, chemotherapy, and organ transplant, will become too risky due to the chances of acquiring a deadly infection. Finding an immediate solution to this global health crisis is our moral imperative to ensure that future generations will benefit from modern medical practices. One of the primary reasons for the increasing levels of antibiotic resistance is the one-size-fits-all approach we take to treating infections, which encourages the over use of these drugs. The one-size-fits-all approach also causes unnecessary sickness and deaths. Different strains of bacteria can be dramatically different in the risks they pose to our health. However, we do not consider these risks when treating infections because of technological limitations. To solve this problem, we have assembled an international team of infectious disease experts, microbiologists, database experts, and analytical chemistry experts to develop a new approach to treating infections. Our solution is to 1) identify every significant biochemical trait that is found in the most dangerous bacteria, 2) create an automated analytical system and database for predicting the potential risks posed by each individual infection, and 3) implement a new Precisions Infection Management (PIM) strategy that will allow clinicians to match each patient to the exact level of antibiotic therapy necessary to cure infections without unnecessarily selecting for antibiotic resistant bacteria. PIM will reduce overall antibiotic use and may preserve the lifespan of our critical front-line drugs. In addition, it will help ensure people suffering from dangerous bacterial infections (e.g. "flesh-eating" strains) get aggressive therapy faster. Likewise, PIM will ensure that people infected with non-dangerous strains receive milder therapies and minimize the risks of medical complications (e.g. kidney failure). PIM allows these significant health improvements without increasing costs to our healthcare system: we predict that PIM will actually save money because of the reduced time people will need to spend in the hospital, and more importantly, it will save lives.

column36: Care4Rare Canada: Harnessing multi-omics to deliver innovative diagnostic care for rare genetic diseases in Canada (C4R-SOLVE)
column37: There are about 7,000 rare genetic diseases (RDs) that affect more than one million Canadians. RDs have a devastating impact on Canadians: two-thirds cause significant disability, threequarters affect children, more than half lead to early death, and almost all have no treatment. The cause of more than one-third of the 7000 RDs is currently unknown. Care4Rare Canada Consortium leads the world by using genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) to identify the genetic cause of RDs. However, more than one third of patients seen each year in Canada with a suspected RD remain undiagnosed and can spend years visiting specialists and undergoing unnecessary testing to explain their disease. Contributing to this gap in care is that genomic sequencing is not available as a clinical test anywhere in Canada. Thus, building on the success of Care4Rare, the goal of the C4R-SOLVE project is to identify the genetic cause for the remaining unsolved RDs while making genomic sequencing available as a clinical diagnostic test in Canada. To understand the remaining unsolved RDs, C4R-SOLVE will explore new sequencing technologies and improve data sharing world-wide, enabling the discovery of new causes of RDs. To improve access to clinical diagnostic testing, C4R-SOLVE will work with provincial ministries of health to determine the best way to include genomic sequencing as a clinical test to diagnose RDs. By achieving its goal, the C4R-SOLVE project will more than double our ability to diagnose this one third of RD patients, while building the infrastructure and tools needed to improve RD diagnosis around the world. An accurate diagnosis will benefit patients and their families as a genetic diagnosis leads to optimized care, improved family wellbeing, and new disease insights. Further, optimal delivery of clinical genomic sequencing has the potential save at least $28M per year, benefiting the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Silent Genomes: Reducing health care disparities and improving diagnostic success for children with genetic diseases from Indigenous populations.
column37: Indigenous populations face unique health challenges, inequities, and barriers to healthcare in Canada and around the world. As such, they typically have poorer health outcomes than do non-Indigenous groups. While genomics (the study of the complete set of human genes) has advanced health care by allowing medical treatments to be tailored to the specific needs of individual patients ('precision medicine'), this 'genomics revolution' is also contributing to health inequities. In particular, compared to what is becoming routinely available to other Canadians, Indigenous populations often have little or no access to genomic technologies and the research that drives them. This has created a 'genomic divide', a key component of which is the lack of background genetic variation data for Indigenous populations. This prevents accurate diagnosis because the reference data are needed when multi-gene and exome (entire genome) testing panels are used. Notably, these genomics resources are silent with respect to First Nations (FN), Inuit and Metis peoples (collectively our Canadian Indigenous populations). Silent Genomes will address the genomic divide by reducing access barriers to diagnosis of genetic disease in Indigenous children. With our First Nations, Inuit and Metis partners we will: 1) Establish processes, through an Indigenous lens, for safe governance of biological samples and genome data in the Silent Genomes project, which will lead to broader policy. 2) Address barriers to accessing genetic/genomic health care and bring genomic testing to at least 200 Indigenous children with suspected genetic disorders. 3) Develop an Indigenous Background Variant Library (IBVL) of genetic variation from a diverse group of 1500 FN Canadians and assess improvement in diagnosis for referred children. 4) Assess effectiveness of the IBVL to lower health care costs and plan for long term use of IBVL for Canadian Indigenous children and adults needing genetic/genomic health care.

column36: PEGASUS-2 - PErsonalized Genomics for prenatal Abnormalities Screening USing maternal blood : Towards First Tier Screening and Beyond
column37: The discovery that DNA of fetal origin is present in maternal blood during pregnancy has led to a new genomics-based maternal blood test called non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS), which is very reliable at screening for Down syndrome. Currently, public healthcare systems pay for this expensive NIPS test only as a second-tier screening for women who have first screened positive on less costly and less accurate biochemical and ultrasound tests. Hence, only after an initial screen has delivered a positive result is NIPS currently used to help women participating in prenatal screening programs avoid a diagnostic amniocentesis. If NIPS were used as the entry-level test for Down syndrome screening, it would benefit women by providing a higher chance of detecting an affected pregnancy and a lower chance of providing a false positive result. It would also enable women to have their final diagnostic result sooner than the current standard of care permits. As well, because NIPS can also detect other fetal chromosome anomalies, its use could enable screening for more conditions. This project aims to provide highquality evidence to inform decisions by health care organisations about using first-tier NIPS to replace traditional screening tests for Down syndrome, and potentially to screen for other fetal chromosome anomalies. We will compare the current screening approach of second-tier NIPS with the use of first-tier NIPS in a large cohort of pregnant women. We will also study the costeffectiveness of expanding screening to other conditions, and the ethical, social and legal implications of doing so. As well, we will provide strategies for scaling up shared decision making processes between couples and their health care practitioners. Finally, we will further develop the NIPS technology to lower its costs, expand the detection of other anomalies, and ensure the quality control of clinical-grade NIPS testing in Canada and worldwide. While taking into account the values informing couples' decisions about participation in prenatal screening, this project will enable publicly funded access to a promising genomics technology for all pregnant women in Canada. Further, it will ensure that couples have access to web-based tools to help their decision making, and that all health care professionals are trained in shared decision making for prenatal screening.

column36: Tackling Childhood Brain Cancer at the root to improve survival and quality of life
column37: One in every 285 children will suffer from a cancer before the age of 15 years. While overall survival and quality of life for child survivors have improved substantially over the last 3 decades for cancers of the blood (leukemia), brain cancers are still lethal and disabling. For some aggressive forms of brain cancer barely 10% of children and young adults survive 3 years after diagnosis, despite enormous efforts and costs to families and to the health care system. Those who do survive often have severe disabilities resulting from their treatment (which can include surgery, radiation therapy to the brain and the use of toxic drugs), with consequent limitations to their social and professional lives. Through previous research our team discovered that many paediatric brain tumours are driven by mutations in genes essential for regulating the development and growth of all body tissues, but which have specific roles in brain development. These findings have enabled more accurate diagnosis of the specific subtype of each paediatric brain tumour, and partly explain why these cancers are unresponsive to existing treatments. This new research aims to fast-track the use of targeted therapies against some of the mutated proteins, while continuing to identify new therapeutic targets for children whose tumours do not yet have a clear molecular diagnosis. We will do this using novel ways of interrogating the genome on the single cell level, determining how the genome is rearranged in childhood cancers, and identifying specific vulnerabilities of the cancer cell compared to the normal cell from which it originated. We will validate proposed therapies in reliable models and accelerate translation to the bedside through our network of care providers. As well, we will assess how to assign children rapidly to a personalised treatment strategy early in the disease course, based on the molecular diagnosis of each tumour. These goals will be pursued by engaging relevant stakeholders and developing an innovative business model enabling drug discovery even for rare disease sub-types. Our project promises to improve survival and quality of life for all children and young adults with brain tumours. By leading to more efficient drugs tailored to specific patients, it will enable health care providers to increase success in treating children with brain tumours, while also decreasing the burden of survivorship on patients, their families and Canada's health care system.

column36: Precision Medicine CanPREVENT AMR: Applying Precision Medicine Technologies in Canada to Prevent Antibody Mediated Rejection and Premature Kidney Transplant Loss
column37: Chronic kidney disease affects 1 in 10 Canadians with estimated costs of over $2 billion/year. Transplantation is the treatment of choice for those whose kidneys fail: it improves survival (>85% vs <50% at 5yr), optimizes quality of life (85% vs 70% of normal) and decreases health-care costs ($15,000 vs $55,000/yr) compared with dialysis. But severe graft rejection (known as "antibody-mediated" rejection or AMR) occurs in up to 30% of transplant patients causing premature graft loss, return to dialysis, and early death. We will develop a program to prevent AMR and promote lifetime survival of the transplanted kidney. Our program will employ genetic technologies to: (a) reduce the risk of rejection through better donor-patient matching; (b) monitor the immune response after transplant to predict AMR; (c) enable personalized treatment with powerful drugs to prevent rejection while avoiding infection or cancer; and (d) study the legal, ethical, societal and economic considerations of introducing these strategies into clinical practice to improve quality of life and reduce health-care costs. The program builds on our highly successful national transplant program coordinated through the Canadian Blood Services (CBS) and links 16 major transplant programs, 9 leading universities, and 14 provincial transplant organizations and laboratories. It is led by an experienced Canadian and international team of genome experts, transplant immunologists, clinical scientists, legal scholars, ethicists, and health economists, working collaboratively with patients, members of the public, health providers, provincial health organizations, national coordinating bodies and commercial partners. Our program seeks to reduce the frequency of AMR by at least 50%, with the expected benefits from preventing rejection commencing quickly and increasing annually due to increased survival of transplanted kidneys. Approximately 500 Canadian patients lose their graft every year, and return to dialysis results in a 4-fold increase in the risk of death, decreased quality-of-life and incremental costs of up to $1 million per patient over their remaining life years. The benefits of this program will consequently occur at three levels: (a) the patient and family, with a gain in survival and quality of life, reduced caregiver burden, and personal health expenditures; (b) the healthcare system, with reduced dialysis care and re-transplant needs; (c) and society, due to increased workforce productivity and decreased kidney management costs.

column36: Genomic and Outcomes Databank for Pharmacogenomic and Implementation Studies (GoPGx)
column37: The vision of Go-PGx is to save lives and improve the quality of life for patients through the prevention of serious adverse drug reactions (ADRs) - often called 'side effects'. The treatment of childhood cancer is particularly impacted by ADRs. ADRs in children are 3-fold more likely to be life-threatening and a staggering 75% of childhood cancer patients develop chronic health conditions and 42% develop disabling or life-threatening ADRs from cancer treatment. It is increasingly evident that genetic differences in patients affect one's likelihood of experiencing an ADR - studying the variability in response to medication is called pharmacogenomics (PGx). Go-PGx is an integrated pipeline of innovative research and the development of tools to facilitate these findings (usually referred to as knowledge translation) into clinical practice by implementing lab tests to predict a patient's likelihood of suffering from an ADR in pediatric cancer treatment. Go-PGx builds upon over 14 years of experience in studying ADRs with research collaborators integrated in 10 pediatric hospitals across Canada. We have collected over 6,125 DNA samples and have corresponding reports of medication use and ADR outcomes recorded in a clinical database. We will build upon this with four linked research activities: (1) We will make new research discoveries of genetic susceptibility to ADRs and (2) develop tools to educate and inform physicians and patients beginning with a prioritized focus on five severe pediatric oncology ADRs. We will generate a comprehensive ADR database of linked clinical and genetic information to provide an accessible resource for to help researchers around the world. (3) At the same time, we will start providing PGx testing in 10 pediatric oncology centers across Canada, (4) while studying important components to the uptake of ADR screening in the health care system, such as understanding what the barriers and facilitators are to making this kind of testing successful; what the perceptions of clinicians, patients and families are to this kind of testing; and understanding the economic implications of introducing this kind of testing into clinical practice across Canada. Go-PGx wants to provide this much-needed access to pharmacogenomic testing in pediatric oncology and lay the foundation for accessible pharmacogenomic testing in Canada.

column36: Deciphering the genome biology of relapsed lymphoid cancers to improve patient management
column37: Collectively, lymphoid cancers are the 5th most common cancers in men and women and affect patients of all ages. In Canada alone, 16,000 patients are newly diagnosed, and 6,000 patients will die of the disease each year. The mortality of the disease is almost exclusively linked to disease relapse when the current standard of care fails to cure the cancer. Therefore, successful treatment and symptom control of relapsed disease represents the single most important need for patients suffering from lymphoid cancers. Unfortunately, the causes of treatment failure are mostly unknown and, as a consequence, no clinical tests are available to inform on the individual prognosis of patients, likely treatment outcomes of salvage therapy, and to guide physicians and patient to use alternative therapeutic choices, such as small molecule drugs or modern immunotherapy. Moreover, treatment relapse and associated treatment cost is a major burden for the health care system with over $315 million attributed to relapsed disease in Canada alone. This means that often times expensive, but ineffective treatments are applied without guidance by adequate clinical testing. In this project, we will focus on the most common forms of lymphoid cancer, namely follicular lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia that together account for approximately two thirds of all lymphoid cancers. The main goals of our research are to develop clinical tests, alongside modern treatments available at relapse, to improve patient outcomes, quality of life, and to make tests widely available in the Canadian, publicly funded health care system. We will achieve these goals by applying state-of-the-art sequencing of patient biopsies taken at the time point of clinical relapse, performing detailed economic analyses, and engaging patients into joint decision making with their treating physicians. Our project will provide novel clinical tests in diagnostic laboratories, access to cutting-edge scientific progress, produce decision aids for patients, and help policy makers in the process of implementing personalized treatment approaches into the health care system.

column36: Genetic instability of the haploid male germ cells
column37: Genetic diversity is provided by de novo transmittable mutations and it is now known that most new mutations are male- driven. During the formation of spermatozoa, the final steps involves a major change in the way DNA is packaged and we demonstrated that this is accompanied by the formation of transient DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in spermatids of both human and mouse pointing to an evolutionary-conserved mechanism. These DSBs arise in haploid cells where there is a single set of chromosome. The repair process cannot therefore proceed using the homologous chromosome as template as in normal somatic cells and must rather rely on a end-joining process. These end-joining repair processes are less reliable and known to induce DNA deletions and insertions. Our hypothesis is that mutations can therefore be induced when the DSBs are repaired in the subsequent steps of the spermatid's differentiation process. Our goal is therefore to confirm whether this process is indeed genetically unstable and if specific regions are involved in the ethiology of genetic diseases since our first screen suggest that neurodevelopmental genes are targeted with high significance. DSBs are also observed during yeast gamete formation emphasizing the conserved nature of this transition and providing a powerful genetic tool to decipher the DSBs mechanism. These investigations may confirm the discovery of a novel mechanism contributing to genetic diversity, evolution and possibly to neurodevelopment disorders such as autism.

column36: Noninvasive diagnosis of tuberculosis through point-of-care detection of cell-free DNA in plasma and urine in HIV-positive and negative patients
column37: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis that causes significant suffering worldwide. It remains a challenging condition to diagnose, especially in patients infected with HIV, as they often have forms of disease with few bacteria to detect. In addition, children who have difficulty producing phlegm, and patients who have tuberculosis outside the lungs, also pose diagnostic difficulty. In these cases, invasive sampling (typically a needle-based procedure such as biopsy, or a sample from the lower back to obtain cerebrospinal fluid) is often required. To address this need, we have developed a simple and non-invasive laboratory test to diagnose tuberculosis from blood and urine samples. More specifically, this test is a multiplexed nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell-free DNA. The assay has thus far been tested on 126 blood samples from adult patients with tuberculosis in the lungs, and Stanford Hospital patients with tuberculosis outside the lungs and patients without tuberculosis, with an overall sensitivity of 74% and specificity of 100%. The proposed study aims to comprehensively assess and optimize the test performance characteristics of this assay in HIV-positive and negative patients, with the aim of developing it into a point-of-care test. This new test shows potential to improve timely diagnosis of tuberculosis, and thus reduce transmission of the infection to other people. It also may improve targeted anti-tuberculosis therapy by limiting treatment to those who test positive, and avoid unnecessary side-effects in those who test negative.

column36: Couple-based intervention for HIV treatment and prevention in South Africa
column37: This study seeks to develop and evaluate a couple-based intervention targeting antiretroviral (ART) medication adherence for HIV-infected South African women and their male partners. South Africa is a country with one of the highest rates of HIV infection. Since HIV is primarily transmitted through stable heterosexual contact in South Africa, working with both members of a couple is recommended. This intervention has the potential to simultaneously improve HIV-infected women's adherence to life-saving ART (used to suppress HIV) as well as bring men into care. Men's disengagement from HIV testing and treatment is a major barrier to meeting global goals of eradicating new HIV infections by 2030. Therefore, in order to work with both members of the couple and be maximally effective, one intervention must target women's ART adherence and men's disengagement from testing and subsequent treatment. To date, however, this has not been done. The proposed study will develop a couple-based intervention that targets the needs of both women and men by building off existing individual interventions (separate interventions have been developed for ART adherence and enhancing motivation for HIV testing and treatment). The study will then use focus groups with South African men and women to ensure the proposed intervention is culturally appropriate. The intervention will then be pilot-tested with 20 South African couples to evaluate whether it has the intended effect on women's ART adherence and men's HIV testing and subsequent treatment. Overall, this study seeks to test a unique intervention that has the potential to simultaneously meet the needs of South African men and women as an opportunity to both prevent and treat HIV.

column36: Efficacy of Viral RNA Processing Inhibitors in Controlling HIV-1 Replication in vivo
column37: Antiretroviral therapies (ARTs) for HIV-1 infection target the viral lifecycle and delay the progression of those infected to AIDS. However, the effectiveness of these ARTs are plagued by a rise in drug-resistant HIV strains present in over 7-24% of newly infected people in the US and Europe. This issue calls for new approaches in combating HIV-1 infection. Several studies have demonstrated that delivering agents towards this stage, which is not targeted by current ARTs termed HIV-1 RNA processing, can successfully inhibit HIV-1 growth. Two of these inhibitors (digoxin and chlorhexidine) are already FDA-approved drugs for other purposes. Although chlorhexidine is not suitable for systemic use, concentrations of digoxin required to inhibit HIV replication in T cells cultured from HIV-infected patients are within accepted dosage levels used to treat heart conditions. Furthermore, I discovered that one digoxin derivative (digitoxigenin) and compound 191 are both potent inhibitors of HIV-1 RNA processing with improved safety profiles over digoxin. All of these studies, however, were performed in cell culture and these findings may not be transferable to patients. Whether this approach can become a novel ART for treating HIV-1 infection remains to be determined. In this proposal, I plan to investigate if these HIV-1 RNA processing inhibitors are effective against HIV-1 infection in an environment that mimics humans known as "humanized mice." These mice will be infected with HIV-1 and treated with inhibitors to test their ability to inhibit HIV-1 growth in comparison to current ARTs. Successful generation of a humanized mouse model could complement drug screening efforts by supporting their validation in animal models, bringing discoveries one step closer to potential clinical trials. Moreover, this model could also support global efforts in combating other deadly diseases, particularly ones involving human immunodeficiencies, and viruses, such as Zika and Influenza.

column37: Cancer is one of the diseases most commonly associated with malnutrition. Surgery is a main treatment for cancer. column36: The role of dietary fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) in the pathophysiology of inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea and constipation are common for patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Unfortunately, these gut symptoms cause significant disruption to the daily life of patients and can affect their ability to leave the home. These symptoms can be particularly troublesome in patients whose IBD is in remission but have ongoing IBS-like symptoms. The financial and social cost is huge. For many years patients have asked their doctors if there is a particular diet that could help control their symptoms. Thankfully recent research has shown that a particular dietary therapy can be effective in reducing these gut symptoms in IBS patients. This dietary therapy is called 'the low FODMAP diet'. This diet involves avoiding certain foods containing short-chain fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) with evidence suggesting it is helpful in 3 out of 4 patients with IBS. It has been recognized that 40% of patients with IBD in remission suffer from IBS-like symptoms. There is now some suggestion that the diet also helps these patients. However, it is unclear which patients will respond to the diet, how the diet may impact inflammation as occurs in IBD, and if there are any safety problems associated with the diet. The overall aim of this research proposal is to understand the effects of fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) on inflammation, symptoms and safety in patients with IBD in remission that have ongoing IBS-like symptoms. Specifically, this research aims to assess if an individual's gut bacteria can predict who will respond to the diet; if the diet is able to improve inflammation; if the diet improves symptoms; and finally if the dietary restrictions cause any safety problems such as reduced nutritional adequacy. Findings from this research will lead to development of individualized dietary therapies to reduce the burden of gut symptoms in patients with IBD and co-existing IBS-like symptoms

column37: The development of medications to safely promote B-cell replication would be ground-breaking for the treatment of all forms of diabetes. GABA, a neurotransmitter, was shown to facilitate B-cell regeneration in mice. column36: Translating meta-analysis evidence into practice: Development of a decision analysis model and interactive decision-making tool to support diabetes quality improvement in Canada
column37: Diabetes is an increasingly prevalent chronic condition that significantly impacts the health and well being of millions of Canadians and results in a high burden of services and costs to the Canadian healthcare system. While it is possible to reduce the impact of diabetes through evidence-based care, gaps between evidence and practice remain. Quality improvement initiatives have emerged to optimize diabetes care and improve patient outcomes. Typically, such initiatives involve 'complex interventions' in which multiple components are assessed in a single intervention. Our systematic review of the effectiveness of diabetes quality improvement interventions has used innovative approaches to determine the effect of the different quality improvement components (and their combined interventions). The proposed project seeks to contextualize this evidence in light of the benefits, harms, and costs of implementing a quality improvement intervention in specific contexts for Canadian decision-makers (e.g., regional health system planners, patient associations). To do this, the study will involve three interrelated tasks: refinement of the decisional problem, the development of a decision model, and the building of front-end decision tool decision-makers can use to tailor evidence to their local setting. Such an approach will allow Canadian decision-makers to explore the impact of implementing a quality improvement intervention under alternative scenarios to inform them of the best approach for their particular setting. In addition to the potential impact on healthcare delivery and patient outcomes in diabetes, the methods of this study may be directly applicable to other syntheses of complex interventions for chronic conditions, or complex intervention research more generally.

column36: Genetic and Functional Studies in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
column37: Approximately 1 in 150 Canadians has inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and it appears to be increasing globally. It was recently reported that this increase is greatest in younger children. The suspected underlying cause of IBD is the combination of many factors including immune factors, bacteria (microbiota) and environment in children. It is thought that genetics plays a larger role in the development of IBD in younger children than in adults. Dr Muise has established the iNternational Early Onset Pediatric IBD Cohort Study (NEOPICS) network and his lab routinely performs genetic screens on young children from the IBD clinic for genetic defects which may contribute to disease. Our study will focus on young children diagnosed less than 6 years of age with very early onset IBD (VEO-IBD). In addition to poor nutrient absorption with delayed growth and development, severe intestinal inflammation leads to impaired quality of life, social and economic burdens, and even mortality. These children may have more severe forms of disease and may be refractory to conventional medical and surgical therapies. A move towards 'precision medicine', by using molecular information, including genetics, to improve the precision with which patients are categorized and treated is the next step in IBD treatment. However, precision medicine requires accurate classification (phenotyping), sequencing and ongoing gene discovery. The proposed research will aim to establish the genetic determinants, by using whole exome sequencing (WES) in VEO-IBD patients. This will allow for identification of causative mutations in known genes associated with colitis and uncover novel genetic defects and pathways. It is our ultimate goal to understand how genetic mutations cause disease and to find potential therapies to correct them for these young patients.

column36: Understanding the role of a4beta7+ Tregs in the development and treatment of inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Canada has some of the highest rates of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in the world. The causes of IBD are complex, but one likely factor is an imbalance in gut immune responses. Immune cells, specifically the subset of immune cells called T cells, are of particular importance. There are two types of T cells that have competing functions: effector cells, which generally cause inflammation, and regulatory cells (Tregs), which suppress inflammation. Under healthy conditions the effector cells are kept in-check by the regulatory cells. Evidence suggests that shifts in this equilibrium between regulatory and effector T cells may contribute to the pathogenesis of IBD; when there is an imbalance, inflammation flares up and damage to the gut can occur. T cells secrete a molecule called integrin a4B7 that helps T cells migrate to the gut; therefore, a4B7 is thought to have a role in IBD. Clinical trials of a commercial antibody called Vedolizumab (which binds to a4B7, rendering it dysfunctional) have shown a reduction in IBD symptoms after treatment. It is not known how Vedolizumab works, but it is likely related to control of inflammatory effector T cells and the function of regulatory T cells in the intestine. Both effector and regulatory T cells express a4B7, but how Vedolizumab affects their homing in the gut is unknown. The primary goal of my proposal is to study how Vedolizumab affects the homing and function of effector versus regulatory CD4+ T cells in the gut of IBD patients. In addition, I will determine if human Tregs that express a4B7 can cure IBD in a mouse model. Understanding the mechanism of action of Vedolizumab is key to understanding more about the pathogenesis of IBD and optimizing the use of this therapy to treat IBD patients. This project will also determine if the use of a4B7+ Tregs to treat IBD patients is a suitable option to reduce the symptoms of IBD.

column36: Ontario Healthcare Implementation Laboratory: A Learning Health System Approach that Leverages Data to Improve Quality in Primary Care
column37: When clinicians do not have the supports in place to help them follow best practices, patients may not reliably receive the ideal tests and treatments. As a result, they are less likely to achieve the best possible health outcomes. Providing clinicians with data on how often they follow best practices helps improve healthcare quality. This strategy is known as 'audit and feedback' and it can play an important role in directing the efforts of clinicians to improve in areas where improvement is most needed to make sure that patients have the best possible outcomes. Our team is working with provincial organizations using audit and feedback and additional supports to help primary care providers like family doctors improve patient care and outcomes in two important areas: opioid prescribing and antibiotic prescribing. Our patient partners and other stakeholders have endorsed these areas as high-priority for action. Our innovative trials will test how audit and feedback can help primary care practices improve in these areas. Conducting experiments in each area will help us learn about how to better deliver evidence-based, patient-centred primary care across a range of acute and chronic conditions. Patients will be involved in governance and will be on steering committees at every level of this research. Patients will also help co-design interventions (including educational materials that primary care providers can share with their patients). By providing education and orientation to our patient and researcher partners and evaluating our patient engagement strategy, we will build capacity in patient engagement and patient oriented research in innovative trials and implementation science. Our partnerships with provincial health care organizations will help us achieve large-scale impact during this project and beyond, ensuring the results of this research will benefit large numbers of patients.

column36: CoMFORT (Cow's Milk Fat Obesity pRevention Trial)
column37: Childhood obesity is a looming healthcare crisis with 1 in 3 Canadian children now living with overweight or obesity. The long term consequences of childhood obesity include increased risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and stroke which reduce quality of life and longevity. Cardiovascular disease currently costs Canada's health systems $7 billion annually and is forecasted to triple in the next 30 years. Since 1992 Health Canada has recommended that children older than 2 years consume reduced fat milk (i.e. 1% milk fat) rather than whole milk (3.25% milk fat) to prevent childhood obesity. Unfortunately, childhood obesity has tripled since then and whole cow's milk intake has halved leading many to wonder whether the reduction in whole milk consumption is leading to childhood obesity. New research from our group and others supports that reduced milk fat intake early in life may be promoting rather than preventing childhood obesity. Although several biological mechanisms have been proposed, the leading theory is that children may feel more 'full' after consuming whole milk and less likely to seek calories from unhealthy foods. This innovative clinical trial will compare the effect of primary healthcare recommendation for whole milk (intervention) vs. reduced fat milk (control) in early childhood in optimizing childhood growth development and nutrition at 4-5 years of age. We will use new cohort trial methods leveraging Canada's largest childhood cohort study (TARGet Kids!) to conduct this trial which will minimize cost and maximize feasibility. This trial must be conducted now to ensure that primary healthcare providers are delivering the correct nutritional recommendation and to protect the next generation of Canada's children from the long term consequences of childhood obesity.

column36: De-implementing low value care: a research program of the Choosing Wisely Canada Implementation Research Network
column37: Up to 30% of tests and treatments given to patients are not needed. This can lead to significant inconvenience and harms for these patients without any benefit. It also wastes money for patients and the health system. Choosing Wisely Canada (CWC) is engaging patients and health professionals to fix this problem. CWC has made 280 recommendations about tests and treatments that should be avoided in certain situations. But these are still happening because it is not an easy thing to change health care processes. Implementation science aims to understand the underlying reasons for health care processes and to develop and test potential solutions to improve them. This project links CWC, patient and health system partners in three provinces with leading Canadian implementation scientists to develop and test solutions for two important topics: x-rays/CT/MRI scans that are not needed for patients with low-risk back pain; and pre-operative tests that are not needed for patients having low-risk surgery. In each province, we will do preliminary studies to make sure we fully understand the different reasons for unnecessary care. Then we will develop targeted solutions using insights from behavioural and system science that support both health professionals and patients to make informed decisions about whether these tests are needed. We will test these solutions in experiments. Some health organisations (either family practices for low back pain imaging or hospitals for pre-operative testing) will receive the solution and some will not. We will determine who gets the solution using an approach similar to flipping a coin to ensure that health organisations that receive or do not receive the solution are similar. We are working with the Canadian Institute of Health Information to use the data already collected routinely to measure whether the solution worked. If our solutions work, we will engage our partners to spread and scale them across Canada.

column36: ENCOMPASS: ENhancing COMmunity health through Patient navigation, Advocacy and Social Support
column37: Some patients who have multiple long-term health conditions have significant challenges in accessing needed services despite available primary care and social services resources. Patient navigation programs may help those with complex health conditions improve their care and outcomes and if delivered by community health workers (CHWs) who have close community ties, these programs have the potential to reduce barriers to care and increase access to coordinated, person-centred care. The University of Calgary's ENCOMPASS program aims to improve the care and health outcomes for high-risk patients by linking patients with chronic disease with a CHW to help them navigate the health system, facilitate communication between patients and providers, improve patients' understanding of their conditions and treatment plans, and support patients in their self-management. In Canada, patient navigation programs have not been well studied or broadly implemented in patients with chronic disease, making a comprehensive evaluation of ENCOMPASS important. This program has great potential to improve care for patients with chronic diseases in Alberta's primary care system. A key element of ENCOMPASS is that patients have been involved in all stages from planning, to pilot testing, to implementation. Given the increasing popularity of patient navigation/CHW programs in other Canadian provinces as well as in the United States, the results of the proposed research will have value outside Alberta.

column36: Canadian Adaptive Platform Trial in Intensive Care (CAPTIC) Program
column37: More than 250,000 Canadians are admitted to an ICU each year. While most survive, the mortality rate of 10% remains high, and survivors often experience severe long term disability and a reduced quality of life. Improved ICU care has come largely from using available treatments more effectively, than from the development of new drugs. But the questions are many, and available funding is limited. We will introduce a new model of a clinical trial - the platform trial - to Canada. Platform trials study several different questions at a time and use adaptive techniques to increase the odds that patients in the trial receive the interventions that are performing better. They are potentially more efficient and cost-effective than traditional trials, but they are new and untested. We will assemble groups of key stakeholders - patients, clinicians, researchers, and policy-makers - to study the opportunities and threats of the platform trial model. We will recruit 300 patients to an ongoing international platform trial that is building pandemic research capacity. We will use these experiences to design a Canadian platform to support the research activities of the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group - the oldest and most productive ICU research group in the world. The insights gained, and the research capacity created, will affirm Canadian research leadership in critical care, and lead to better patient outcomes in a learning health care system.

column36: Reducing Diabetic Foot Complications through a Multidisciplinary Chiropodist Based Intervention
column37: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is a major complication of diabetes and can be a significant physical, social, financial and emotional burden. About 25% of persons with diabetes develop DFUs. If poorly managed, DFUs can lead to amputations, 1 of the 2 most feared complications of diabetes. The risk of DFUs can be reduced with simple preventative measures yet DFUs and DFU relapses have not declined as there is no high-quality data supporting proactive DFU treatment. Chiropodists are experts at managing foot disorders. A small study linked chiropodist care with markedly less leg amputations in people with diabetes and on dialysis. This led us to think that an intensive, structured, chiropodist-led strategy will lower amputation-related hospitalizations in those with diabetes and their need for medical, social and financial resources. In consultation with persons with diabetes, amputees and representatives from health agencies, and diabetes and DFU professional groups, we designed a novel trial to study if chiropodist care will lower amputation-related hospitalizations in those with diabetes undergoing dialysis since this group is deemed to have the greatest need and is one that administrators are most likely to effect change in funding allocation and health care systems delivery. Our study will include 2200 participants from 40 sites in Ontario, Alberta and Manitoba. The 2-year study will record amputation-related hospitalizations, deaths, cost effectiveness and perceived quality of life. Our committee includes persons with diabetes, amputees, chiropodists, a nurse, a family doctor and specialists. We have trial experts, a health care economist and statisticians who will assist in data interpretation, and individuals in the government and professional groups who will provide guidance on rolling out the findings (if positive) into clinical practice. Finally, the trainees will receive hands on experience to enrich their expertise as they carve out their career paths.

column36: Cortical Plasticity Following Deafness
column37: In Canada, hearing loss is the most common sensory disability in adults and deafness is the most common congenital sensory abnormality in children. A 2006 Australian study estimated that costs to that nation's economy from hearing loss amounted to $10.6 billion per year. On a per capita basis, this translates to a Canadian equivalent of almost $18-billion annually. Although we hear with our brains little is known about what occurs to the brain as a consequence of deafness. In this proposal we will be studying what happens inside the brain following the onset of deafness shortly after birth or in adulthood. Specifically, we will be studying the regions of the brain that normally process sounds in hearing individuals. To do this we will examine deafness in an animal model. This approach will permit us to examine the activity of individual neurons, to examine changes in brain circuitry and activity, and to examine how changes in the brain affect perception and behavior. If the part of the brain that normally processes hearing is not receiving sound, then what is it doing? Is it processing visual information? Is it processing information concerning touch? If it is processing sight, then it may very well help explain the increased visual abilities of deaf humans. Changes in the brain such as this are known as "plastic" changes, or simply "plasticity". These changes are also called "compensatory" because they help the subject enhance their ability to use their remaining senses. Therefore, the goal of this study is to examine the natural plasticity of the brain. Knowing how the brain responds to changes in its inputs in this way will help us develop appropriate therapeutic strategies to help increase brain plasticity and help patients to overcome conditions such as deafness and blindness.

column36: A Randomized, Parallel-Group, Open Label, Non-Inferiority, Pragmatic Trial Comparing Random AND Targeted Biopsies to Targeted Biopsies Alone for Neoplasia Detection During Screening Colonoscopy in Adult Persons with Colonic Inflammatory Bowel Diseases: A Pilot Study
column37: Persons with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are at increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) and require frequent CRC screening with colonoscopy. Colorectal tumours can be more difficult to visualize in persons with IBD than in persons without IBD. Therefore, IBD experts have long recommended a strategy of taking 30 to 40 random biopsies to help detect these lesions during screening colonoscopy. Oddly, there have never been high quality studies demonstrating the usefulness of this practice. Recent literature suggests that random biopsies have an exceedingly low rate of detecting tumours in persons with IBD and that improved technology and practice have made 80 to 90% of colorectal tumours visible. Since random biopsies pose potential risks, such as lower gastrointestinal bleeding and bowel perforation, and substantially increase procedural time and costs, it is important to determine whether this practice is still merited. We ultimately wish to conduct a large, multi-center randomized controlled trial to evaluate whether the practice of taking random biopsies during colonoscopy can be avoided without increasing the risk of developing CRC faced by IBD patients. However, we first propose a smaller-scale pilot study that will evaluate our ability to recruit patients, the rate at which colon lesions are detected, and adherence to the study protocol by investigators, which will inform the capacity and requirements to conduct a full-scale trial. The pilot study aims to recruit 400 patients at 12 academic IBD centers over one year. If we are able to proceed with the full-scale trial, based on the pilot study findings, it could lead to a major advance in IBD patient care. If avoidance of random biopsies during colonoscopy screening is not found to be harmful to patients in the full trial, it would enable practitioners to abandon this practice, which could substantially reduce the risks, time and costs associated with screening colonoscopy in persons with IBD.

column36: Correlates of Healthy Aging in Geriatric HIV: CHANGE HIV STUDY
column37: The population of persons living with HIV (PLWH) is aging due to effective HIV therapy and new infections occurring in older individuals. Much needs to be learned about what it means to age with HIV. Although organ diseases (like heart and brain) are increased in PLWH, aging is more complex and health evaluations must consider the impact of these conditions on a person's ability to function well. We propose to bring together this new interdisciplinary team and the CHANGE HIV (Correlates of Healthy aging in Geriatric HIV) STUDY. We will invite men and women living with HIV >65 years of age from primary care and hospital HIV clinics in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver to join. At regular clinic visits we will add tests of physical, cognitive, mental, social function and quality of life and collect data on external factors like housing, behaviors and stigma that might influence health. We will analyze the way the factors interact to identify the ones that contribute most to healthy aging well if these differ by sex or gender. From the data, we will calculate a healthy aging score that can inform care and research by assessing a person's overall health status and track changes with time or therapy. The knowledge gained will inform interventions and strategies to improve healthy aging and help us know which ones are the most important, feasible and acceptable to those aging with HIV. Our data can be used to advocate for changes to health and social policies and appropriate allocation of resources for services for aging PLWH. A program strength is to train and stimulate new academic and community investigators building future research capacity in HIV and aging. Community members will be meaningfully involved in all stages ensures our research is feasible, ethical and relevant and supports the development of knowledge that is useful to key. Our learning's will advance understanding of aging in PLWH and ultimately lead to improved clinical and community practice and policy.

column36: Healthy Living for HIV-exposed Uninfected Children - cognitive, behavioural, neuroimaging and animal studies to assess the impact of in utero exposure to HIV and antiretrovirals.
column37: The use of HIV medications in pregnancy has enabled a radical reduction in the rate of vertical HIV transmission. As a consequence, there is now a large and growing number of HIV-exposed uninfected children (HEU)-children born to women living with HIV that are not HIV infected. While most HEU children are in good health, some studies suggest that these children may experience developmental delays compared to their peers, including learning difficulties, issues with their memory, and behavioural problems. We know that the environment the child is exposed to during pregnancy (the in utero environment) can influence their long-term health. However, we don't know how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment and whether these changes affect the long-term health of HEU children. Our team will investigate how exposure to HIV and various HIV medications during pregnancy affects brain development and mental health in HEU children. We will perform cognitive and behavioural tests and brain imaging studies in a cohort of HEU and HIV unexposed children of similar age and background. We will examine correlations between their brain anatomy and behavioural and cognitive performance. We will measure various factors in the cord blood of these children (collected at the time of birth) to better understand how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment. We will perform similar tests in a mouse model where we can directly compare different HIV medications, examine how they affect brain development and behaviour of the pups, and design and test therapies that will improve outcomes. Our duty to HEU children does not stop with the prevention of HIV infection. We must understand how HIV and HIV medications alter the in utero environment and influence long-term health, so we can optimize HIV treatment in pregnancy and ensure the best health outcomes for HEU children.

column37: Scientists have made extraordinary advances in understanding and treating HIV infection over the past 20 years. The main problems when HIV-1 infects a person's nervous system are difficulties in thinking and persistent pain from damaged nerves. These problems are part of a condition called NeuroHIV. They diminish a person's quality of life, impair their sleep, reduce their ability to hold a job, affect their mood and isolate them socially. Over the past 5 years, our team has defined how often these problems occur and their severity. We have also discovered new disease processes and used that knowledge to develop and test new approaches to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. For example, we uncovered new biological markers for people who have cognitive problems and pain from NeuroHIV. We found new possible treatments for these cognitive problems and pain, and we are testing those treatments in clinical trials. We have also identified specific sex and gender factors that make some people with NeuroHIV more vulnerable to thinking problems and pain from damaged nerves. NeuroHIV causes other problems that need research. These problems are linked to sex and gender diversity, and to how aging affects people with NeuroHIV. Our team of researchers from different areas of science and health will map basic pathways in the biology of NeuroHIV. Discovering these pathways can help us to analyze symptoms and risk factors for NeuroHIV. Understanding the pathways will also lead to new ways to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. Part of our work will be to build broader community knowledge of NeuroHIV and its related problems.

column36: Action for Positive Brain Health Now
column37: Older people living with HIV worry about their memory, and with good reason. A third or more have problems with thinking or concentration, despite good control of their HIV infection. Rates of depression, anxiety and poor motivation are also high. Separately or together, these brain health problems affect function and quality of life. The causes of brain health symptoms in HIV are not fully understood, and we don't know whether brain health inevitably worsens over time. Our team has developed new ways to assess these problems in the clinic, identified the factors that relate to poor brain health in a large on-going cohort study, and provided preliminary information about whether these symptoms can be treated. Here, we build on this foundation to meet three broad aims: (1) Understand the factors that lead to poor brain health, focusing on viral, cerebrovascular, and social contributors; (2) Empower people living with HIV and the clinicians who care for them with practical tools to assess brain health and personalize treatment; (3) Act to help people living with HIV improve brain health through lifestyle changes. We will extend the existing cohort study to provide crucial information about whether brain health worsens over longer follow-up. We will add a second wave of participants, including more women, to help us provide personalized brain health recommendations suited to a wide range of people. We will implement the assessment tools that we have developed in our current study as easy-to-use apps. We will work closely with the HIV clinicians and community partners on our team to ensure these are user-friendly and clinic-ready. We will test an innovative, two-phase intervention to help people with brain health challenges pursue health goals tailored to their own priorities and risks, to improve their memory, mood and quality of life. This study will provide the knowledge and tools that people living with HIV need to take charge of their brain health now.

column36: SEARCH (active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare) & PREVENT (Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team)
column37: The debilitating and lethal consequences of severe adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are a striking failure of modern medicine. The consequences for patients who experience severe ADRs are catastrophic. In Canada, there are an estimated 200,000 severe ADRs, claiming 10,000-22,000 lives, and costing $14-18 billion each year. To tackle this complex problem requires a multi-faceted collaborative linking of scientists, clinicians and regulators sharing complementary expertise in an environment that promotes teamwork. The Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) Active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare (SEARCH) initiative was first funded in 2011, with the overarching goal of conducting active surveillance to identify important drug risks, reduce the occurrence of severe ADRs and improve drug safety in Canadians. In close collaboration with the Drug Safety and Effectiveness (DSEN) Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team (PREVENT) the work of SEARCH is strengthened through the discovery of pharmacogenomics biomarkers - that is understanding the genetic variation between patients that affects their individual drug response. This inter-individual variation acts as key predictors of ADRs for many drugs in clinical use today. Our team will build on its broad experience in active surveillance methods, pharmacogenomics expertise and its established network of ADR surveillance clinicians in Canadian health centres. These surveillance clinicians are located at 13 pediatric academic health centers and 13 adult academic health centers and their role is to identify and report ADRs, and collect DNA and the detailed clinical information that is needed to evaluate potential drug risks. This will allow SEARCH & PREVENT to continue active surveillance in areas of importance to the CIHR Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network, Health Canada and other pertinent stakeholders.

column36: Mechanisms of cell clearance during tissue homeostasis and regeneration using freshwater planarians
column37: Humans replace billions of cells every day, a process of which requires making the correct number and type of new cells, and removing old cells. column36: Role of type I interferon in B cell dysfunction associated with chronic viral infection
column37: Persistent viral infections such as those caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), the hepatitis C virus (HCV) or the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are a major global health problem. It is estimated that more than 500 million people in the world are infected with at least one of these viruses. Currently, only HBV infection can be prevented through vaccination while the development of vaccines against HCV or HIV is still a long-term goal. Although a number of highly effective antiviral drugs were recently developed against all three viruses, these are not able to cure HIV infection or have variable success rates against HBV and HCV infections. In Canada, HCV infection constitutes the most frequent indication for liver transplantation and together with HBV, these pathologies account for 1000 deaths annually while the number of people living with HIV continues to rise. There is therefore a great need for further research aimed at better understanding the fundamental mechanisms employed by these chronic viruses to escape the host immune response and establish persistence. One common feature between these three infections is the appearance of dysfunctions in the B cell response with important pathological consequences. The main objectives of this research program are therefore to better understand the mechanisms that contribute to these dysfunctions and to develop clinical interventions to restore normal B cell responses during chronic viral infections. This knowledge will prove very useful for the rational design of vaccines or improved antiviral drugs.

column37: Our muscles rely on electrical signals to contract. When our brains send out a signal, this ultimately leads to a small electrical current inside the muscle cell. Here we try to understand both the basic mechanism of the coupling, as well as the mechanism through which mutations in the specific muscle genes lead to disease.

column36: Rhinovirus induced modulation of epithelial phenotype in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic airway disease that affects 300 million people worldwide. Although all children get multiple infections with human rhinovirus (HRV - the "common cold virus") in early life, only a subset get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, and are far more likely to develop asthma by age 6. It is not clear why only some children get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, but the interaction of HRV and development of allergies may play a role. Human airway epithelial cells (HAE) are the main site of HRV infection and it is thought that HRV affects asthma by changing HAE biology. The characteristic features (phenotype) of HAE are altered in asthma, and these altered HAE interact with nearby structural and immune cells to help cause asthma. Despite the central role of HAE in regulating airway diseases, the effects of HRV infection on HAE phenotype have not been well characterized. We have found that HRV infection of HAE from normal people causes transient changes in cell biology. In this proposal, we will fully characterize the effects of HRV on epithelial phenotype and will define the mechanisms by which HRV causes these changes. We will determine if repeated infections with HRV cause greater effects in HAE than a single infection. In addition, we will test the idea that HRV infections (single or repeated) in the setting of an "allergic" environment produce more profound alterations in HAE that mimic the phenotype seen in asthma. We will compare HAE from asthmatic children to those from normal children to see if they have greater responses to HRV. Finally, we will experimentally infect normal and asthmatic volunteers with HRV to test the idea that HAE in asthmatic patients show greater response to HRV in vivo. By understanding how HRV infections alter epithelial responses, alone and in an allergic setting, we may be able to develop ways to prevent or reduce the effects of HRV in asthma in order to improve the well-being of patients with asthma.

column36: The functions of mammalian TRAPP complexes and their role in disease
column37: The Transport Protein Particle (TRAPP) complexes were first discovered in yeast. Subsequent work identified related, conserved complexes in humans. These complexes function in moving proteins between various intracellular compartments within a cell. Although they share a core of common proteins, there are unique proteins that are associated with the core to form the various complexes (three complexes in yeast, two in higher eukaryotes). While the functions of the complexes in yeast are better understood, the functions of the mammalian complexes are less clear. In addition, several of the subunits that associate with the complex in humans have been shown to have functions independent of the complex. Furthermore, recent work has led to the identification of individuals that have mutations in TRAPP proteins. Curiously, these individuals all have different phenotypes depending on which TRAPP protein is mutated. Thus, understanding the functions of the mammalian TRAPP proteins and their role in disease is a necessary next step in our understanding of these complexes. This present application seeks to understand the functions of two specific subunits called C11 and C2L. In order to facilitate this work, we are developing a simplified in vitro assay that reconstitutes transport in the secretory pathway. We will use wild type TRAPP complexes as well as complexes harboring mutations in the aforementioned proteins to assess their ability to reconstitute membrane traffic in this pathway. The results of these studies will provide insight into specific human disorders that are linked to TRAPP mutations and will allow clinicians to more quickly assess new disorders that may be linked to these complexes.

column37: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin in biphasic manner, an initial peak phase (~15 min) followed by a sustained phase (several hours), to ensure continuous assimilation of circulating nutrients into tissues. In type-2 diabetes, both phases are perturbed resulting in deficient insulin release causing hyperglycemia. Half of initial peak phase is attributed to secretory granules (SGs) predocked on calcium channels (Cav1.2/1.3) on the plasma membrane where calcium influx induces SG fusion to release insulin. Newcomer SGs (NSG) are a newly discovered SG population that account for the entire sustained phase and half of first-phase secretion. We discovered the SNARE (syntaxin-3, VAMP8) and associated proteins responsible for NSG fusion; but unlike predocked SGs, little else is known about the NSG secretory machinery. Our first hypothesis (Aim 1) is that NSGs specifically land on and undergo fusion at a new set of calcium channels (Cav2.1/2.3) which bind syntaxin-3. An undefined reserve pool must exist to continually replenish NSGs after depletion from stimulated release. We found potassium channel (Kv2.1) clusters on plasma membrane that bind NSG-syntaxin-3. Our second hypothesis (Aim 2) is that syntaxin-3/Kv2.1 clusters form complexes that serve as an accessible reserve pool for NSGs to park prior to their relocation to adjacent calcium channels. This provides a unique architecture that couples the reserve pool (Kv2.1 clusters) of SGs to SG release sites (Cav), a process that has long eluded previous investigation. This work has broad application to many endocrine cells that exhibit sustained secretion required to meet varying metabolic needs. Insights into these novel fundamental steps of secretion are a basis for development of treatment strategies to improve secretion. As proof, we will express (with virus) Cav and Kv2.1 into pancreatic islets of diabetic humans (in vitro) and rats (in vivo) to improve the deficient insulin secretion and restore glucose homeostasis.

column36: Impact of obesity-associated inflammation on breast cancer progression
column37: There is a strong association between chronic inflammation, and the risk of developing cancer. One of the most prevalent examples of chronic inflammation is obesity, which affects over 1/3 of adults in Canada/USA. Inevitably, obesity now rivals smoking as the #1 preventable risk factor for cancer. Obesity is associated with higher incidence of breast cancer metastasis (i.e. cancer spread), particularly to liver and lung. Of particular interest is lung metastasis, given the high frequency of breast cancer progression to this site in patients, and the association between obesity and multiple lung-inflammatory conditions (e.g. asthma). Despite that 1/3 of adults are overweight/obese, the vast majority of preclinical studies are focused on how breast cancer spreads in lean models. We recently determined that lung tissue becomes severely altered in response to obesity. We found that the abundance and the behaviour of certain immune cells within the lungs are drastically changed with weight gain, creating an environment that can nourish cancer cells that have spread to this organ. Importantly, we have found that weight loss is sufficient to reverse obesity-associated lung inflammation and breast cancer metastasis. These are significant findings because the lung is one of the most frequent sites of metastasis, which causes death in patients. The objective of this study is to provide a translational framework for understanding how overweight/obesity affects breast cancer metastasis, with the goal of identifying blood-based prognostic markers and new therapies. This could improve treatment methods for a large proportion of breast cancer patients, and contribute to a broader understanding of the relationship between the immune system and cancer. We hypothesize that breast cancer progresses differently in obese patients compared to lean patients, and therefore, obese patients will require different treatment considerations.

We hypothesize that liraglutide improves heart health in diabetic patients by boosting the heart's ability to burn sugar for energy. We have recently generated a unique genetically modified mouse strain in our lab, in which the ability of the heart to burn sugar for energy has been eliminated. We will carry out our plan by placing normal mice and these unique mice on a fat-enriched diet that causes diabetes. By investigating whether the drug liraglutide is able to reduce heart disease risk in normal mice and these unique mice, we will be able to determine whether liraglutide, and possibly other drugs that mimic the actions of the gut hormone GLP-1, improve heart health in patients with diabetes by boosting the heart's ability to burn sugar for energy. Therefore, our research may support liraglutide as a more preferable therapy to prescribe to diabetic patients, since this drug can improve both their high blood sugar and overall heart health.

column36: Precision Engineering of Cartilage Grafts for Nasal Reconstruction
column37: More than 3 million people were treated for skin cancers in North America in 2015. Approximately 40% of all skin-cancer cases occur on a person's nose. When cancer is diagnosed on the face, and in particular on the nose, treatment options often lead to loss of function and significant disfigurement. The nose is the most prominent and conspicuous feature of the face, making deformities difficult to conceal, which can lead to emotional distress and social isolation along with the difficulty or loss of breathing through the nose.The structure of the nose is made of cartilage. Unfortunately, when skin cancer appears on the nose, the cartilage at the site of cancer is sacrificed during radiation or surgical treatment. column36: Transforming youth mental health and addiction services by building optimal integrated service models: A discrete choice conjoint experiment modeling youth, caregiver, and agency perspectives
column37: Currently, Canadian youth have great difficulty accessing timely, youth-friendly, evidence-based mental health and addiction (MHA) services. There is increasing provincial, national and international interest and investment in developing integrated service hubs (ISHs) for MHA to address these concerns. The ISH model aims to increase agency capacity to serve diverse youth MHA needs by providing multiple services, potentially including psychotherapy, psychiatry, primary care, housing support, and other services. Given rapid expansions of ISH initiatives and extensive investments in them, it is crucial to identify the service components/characteristics most critical to their success from diverse stakeholder perspectives. When services fit with the preferences of service users and agencies, clients are more likely to use and benefit from the services, and agencies are more likely to provide services in an evidence-based way. This study will identify the core components and characteristics of ISHs for youth MHA, from youth, caregiver, and agency perspectives, using a consumer preference modeling approach. A multi-step engagement process will involve youth, families, and agency representatives in three Ontario locations (Toronto, Chatham, and Penetanguishene) to discuss their perspectives and inform the development of a comprehensive preference survey. The survey will then be administered to 500 youth, 500 families, and 500 agency representatives throughout Ontario to identify the service components considered most crucial from diverse perspectives and in diverse settings. column36: A randomized controlled trial of symptom screening by children with cancer and feedback to providers
column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. To address these gaps, we developed the Symptom Screening in Pediatrics Tool (SSPedi) specifically for children receiving cancer treatments. We also created evidence-based guidelines to help providers know how to manage symptoms. To bring identification and management of symptoms together, we created a web-based application called Supportive care Prioritization, Assessment and Recommendations for Kids (SPARK). SPARK consists of two components: (1) Symptom screening component centered on SSPedi and (2) Supportive care guideline component. The next step is to establish that these tools improve the lives of children with cancer. We will conduct a randomized controlled trial which evaluates the effectiveness of daily symptom screening by children seen in hospital daily for 5 days and feedback of symptom reports to healthcare providers with links to guidelines for symptom management. Participants in the control arm will receive the standard of care in which symptom screening with feedback is not performed. We will include English-speaking children and adolescents 8-18 years of age expected to be in hospital daily for 5 days. The primary endpoint will be the day 5 total SSPedi score which ranges from 0 to 60 (higher means more bothersome symptoms). We plan to enroll 345 children across 7 Canadian institutions over 4 years. This research will enable children to report symptoms and will help providers know how to manage symptoms using the best available evidence. Ultimately, SPARK implementation will lead to better symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column37: Antibiotic resistance is rising to dangerously high levels in all parts of the world, compromising our ability to treat infectious diseases, as well as undermining many other advances in health and medicine.
