column36: Characterization of quality control pathways that target cytosolic misfolded proteins with missense mutations for proteasome degradation
column37: Gene mutations that cause diseases often do so by causing misfolding and degradation of the mutant proteins. Protein misfolding occurs when a protein does not attain its so-called native structure, which is reached when the protein is properly folded to perform its function in the cell. Our goal is to better understand how mutant proteins that misfold are recognized by elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system. The ubiquitin proteasome system consists of groups of enzymes that first mark proteins targeted for degradation by attaching to them a small protein tag called ubiquitin. These ubiquitin-tagged proteins are then recognized by the proteasome, which eliminates them from the cell. Our main hypothesis is there are several degradation paths for different groups of proteins that misfold due to mutations. To test this idea, we will analyze using different cell-based assays a large panel of mutations that have been associated to genetic disorders or diseases. More specifically, we will focus on missense mutations that induce the change of single amino acids. First, we will identify which mutated cytosolic proteins are degraded by the ubiquitin proteasome system from a large panel of known disease-associated mutations. We will then determine which known elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system target these misfolded mutant proteins. A major question is how E3 enzymes that attach ubiquitin recognize misfolded proteins. To address this question, we will employ the identified mutant proteins as model substrates to better identify which regions or domains on E3 enzymes recognize the misfolded proteins. Finally, we will set up a screen to identify novel genes involved in targeting misfolded proteins for degradation. By better understanding how misfolded proteins are triaged within the cell, we will gain fundamental knowledge of disease mechanisms, leading to potential novel therapeutic approaches.

column37: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity" (World Health Organization, 1948). Diseases such as HIV/AIDS and Hepatitis C (HCV) thrive in conditions of poverty and marginalization. Research on the quality of life of people living with HIV/AIDS reveals that unemployed individuals report more depression, anxiety, social isolation, and low self-esteem than employed individuals. Moreover, unemployment is a key factor in the contemplation of suicide among people with HIV/AIDS. Alternatively, employment among people living with HIV/AIDS is a strong indicator of improved quality of life. A finding we confirmed in our research study (PROMPT) supporting 80 members of Ottawa's low income homeless (or at-risk for homelessness) People Who Use Drugs reduce (and in some cases quit) smoking. Many PROMPT participants repeatedly stated that boredom and a lack of meaningful social connections and employment were major hindrances in their reduction and overall recovery from smoking and drug use. With these PROMPT findings, we propose a Community-Based Participatory Action project that builds the social capital of 80 participants that identify as members of Ottawa and Toronto's low income People Who Use drugs living with or are at-risk for HIV/AIDS/HCV. The proposed multi-site project will include life-skills training, counseling, health services access (testing and treatment), and education on HIV/AIDS/HCV. Most importantly the project will include a poverty reduction intervention that connects participants with short-term work and volunteer opportunities. The work and volunteer opportunities' will be made possible with the support of local business owners and networks that support the study's poverty reduction and community building elements. The aim of project will be to demonstrate the feasibility and cost of holistic healthcare that encourages a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being

column36: The "Weaving Our Wisdoms" Study: Using a Land-Based Approach to Optimize Whole-istic Health among Indigenous People Living with HIV
column37: Lamouche (2010) notes that "break with the land is the single most important factor in health problems among Indigenous peoples". It follows that reconnecting to the land is a crucial pathway to health, including for Indigenous people living with HIV. But HIV interventions are usually based on Western ways of knowing. This study, designed by Indigenous People living with HIV, focuses on the potential for land-based approaches to promote wellness. First, we will convene "HIV olders" (i.e., Indigenous people living long-term with HIV) and other Indigenous community leaders to design a 4-6 day land-based wellness program. Next, we will implement the program with Indigenous People living with HIV from throughout Alberta and BC - we call these participants "knowledge gatherers". During this phase, we will investigate research questions about the impact of land-based approaches, the role of "HIV olders" in building the capacity of others, and about land-based research methods. In the final phase, we will "weave our wisdoms". That is, we will build on existing and new relationships with First Nations, Metis and Inuit communities across the country to explore land-based approaches to wellness. This study will be housed at the Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network, which has a long track record of successfully implementing research that is meaningful to Indigenous People living with HIV. The study is guided by four complementary approaches to research: (1) community-based research, (2) Indigenous knowledge, (3) decolonizing methods, and (4) two-eyed seeing. The overall goal is to "weave the wisdoms" of Indigenous people living with HIV to improve their own wellness while also building the capacity for wellness among others.

column36: Thrive Project: A community-driven investigation of the home and community care needs of older adults living with HIV
column37: Over the past two decades, with the advent of modern HIV treatment and a robust provincial HIV strategy across British Columbia (BC), people living with HIV (PLHIV) are now living longer, healthier lives. This has contributed to a significant demographic shift, with individuals 50 years and older now making up more than half of all PLHIV engaged in care in BC. While the aging cohort of PLHIV represents positive strides in the fight against HIV, it also necessitates an evaluation of whether health care services for older adults in the province are adequately supporting the expanding cohort of older PLHIV. This is especially pertinent given the complex physiological, psychosocial and age-related challenges experienced by older adults living with HIV. Home and community care (HCC) services, such as in-home nursing services, community care, and case management, that are responsive to the unique needs of older PLHIV have the potential to appropriately address the evolving landscape of age-related health concerns while simultaneously ensuring a high standard of care. However, evidence suggests older PLHIV are often unable to access HCC, leaving them to rely on accessing hospitals and urgent care facilities for primary care services. In this 3-year study we will undertake a comprehensive community-based research project to measure trends in healthcare utilization and health outcomes among older PLHIV, document the experiences of older PLHIV accessing HCC supports, and use novel service access mapping approaches to spatially characterize the health and ancillary care use of older PLHIV. We also aim to identify potential strategies to overcome barriers to accessing HCC services. To employ this knowledge, we will work alongside community partners and healthcare stakeholders to develop interventions that will improve health outcomes and support older PLHIV.

column36: An Examination of Resilience Against HIV/AIDS Among Middle-aged and Older Men Who Have Sex With Men: Resources, Strengths, and Protective Factors
column37: According to the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC, 2013), gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) have remained the population most affected by HIV/AIDS in Canada since the early 1980s. Although the proportion of HIV cases among MSM 30-39 years old has been decreasing since 1994, the proportion of HIV infections among MSM aged 40 years and older have been increasing since the start of the epidemic. PHAC reports that most research on HIV/AIDS among MSM focuses on their vulnerability and that research on the resilience of MSM against HIV/AIDS is wanting. It also reports that although there are available studies on young MSM and resilience, there is a lack of research done on older MSM. This suggests that resilience of older MSM against HIV/AIDS represents an area that is under-researched. Scientific literature and historical accounts provide evidence of resilience among MSM, and there has been research undertaken that highlights the challenges and coping strategies of HIV+ older MSM. However, to date, there has been no research done to examine the resilience of both HIV+ and HIV- MSM aged 40 and older against HIV/AIDS. This is the aim of our project; specifically, to examine resources, strengths and protective factors they possess that prevent further HIV transmission and allow them to thrive in a society not ready to meet the needs of a growing number of older MSM and HIV long-term survivors. We plan to recruit and include MSM aged 40 and older from the community as peer researchers and members of our advisory board so that they can provide us input and feedback during all stages of the research process. After providing them appropriate training, our peer researchers will interview HIV+ and HIV- MSM 40 and older from Ontario to achieve our project's aim. Together, we will analyze our data and share the knowledge and lessons we learn to relevant research and MSM communities through public presentations and accessible print/online materials.

column36: Preventing the spread of HIV: The critical role of addiction treatment services
column37: Addiction treatment programs play a critical role in HIV prevention because they reduce drug use, the frequency of injection, and unsafe practices. In some instances, however, people who use drugs and want treatment, do not enter treatment or stay in treatment because of the policies and practices of the program. Relatively little is known about these policies and practices, and specifically and how they might act as barriers to access and retention, in some cases, but facilitators in others. Our qualitative research will help to fill these gaps in our knowledge. The research will take place in the four Atlantic Provinces, and we will speak to people who use drugs about their perspectives and experiences of program policies and practices. In addition, we will ask about safer/unsafe drug and sexual health practices among those who do not access/stay in treatment because of policy and practice barriers. Perspectives on policies and practices will also be obtained from family of choice/family members; staff at community-based organizations providing harm reduction services; and, directors and/or physicians working at addiction treatment programs. Results from this study will be discussed in workshops and forums with people who use drugs and key stakeholders, including policy-makers. Suggestions and recommendations will be made for potential changes, modifications and/or additions to policies and practices. The workshops and forums will also provide the opportunity to discuss possible HIV prevention efforts for people who use drugs who may be at risk of unsafe practices when they cannot access/stay in treatment.

column36: Stress, Brain and Neurodevelopment in Children Born Preterm
column37: In Canada, as in other high resource countries, preterm birth (<37 weeks gestation) is the most important cause of disability. Among children born preterm >50% show significant developmental problems (cognitive, attention, behaviour, social, motor, academic) impacting family and society. While abnormal brain development is evident in these vulnerable children, persisting to adulthood, little is known about why some preterm children do well and others decline, even when born in the same gestational age range. Early stress impacts brain structure and function. Children born very preterm (<32 weeks gestation) are exposed to pain-related stress of medical and nursing procedures (~10 per day) during weeks to months in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Understanding factors that explain the wide variation in neurodevelopmental outcomes in children born preterm, and that promote stress regulation and brain recovery in children born very preterm will provide critical underpinnings for developing interventions to optimize long-term neurodevelopment in this fragile population.

column36: Targeting Exercise Activated Pathways to Counter the Side Effects of Antipsychotic Drugs
column37: Antipsychotic drugs are used to treat a number of conditions including schizophrenia, anxiety and bipolar disorders and their use has increased dramatically over the past decade. Unfortunately, these drugs have harmful metabolic side effects such as weight gain and rapid increases in blood sugar with each dose of drug. Together these effects increase the risk for developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. In recent work, we have shown that a single session of exercise prior to treatment with antipsychotics completely protected against the acute increase in blood sugar. Although exercise adherence is poor in individuals taking anti-psychotic drugs we have been using exercise as a model to identify pathways which could be targeted to reduce the metabolic side effects of these drugs. Based on preliminary data from our laboratory we have shown that the activation of an energy-sensing enzyme called AMPK confers the same protection against anti-psychotic metabolic side effects as exercise. The purpose of this project is to examine the effects of AMPK in protecting against the acute and long-term metabolic side effects of antipsychotic drugs and to determine if AMPK mediates the beneficial effects of exercise. The data generated from these studies will provide insight into new approaches that could be used to lessen the metabolic consequences of antipsychotic drugs and could shed insight into the mechanisms mediating the protective effects of exercise.

column36: Multi-centre Temporal Ultrasound Image Analysis for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer diagnosed in Canadian men, with about 25,000 new cases per year. The gold standard for PCa diagnosis and prognosis is ultrasound (US)-guided needle biopsy with pathologic grading. The biopsy procedure is not patient specific; rather, it involves taking "blind" biopsy cores, leading to frequent re-biopsy or over diagnosis of insignificant cancer. There is an acute need for patient-specific targeting techniques that have higher chance of detecting early aggressive PCa. Aggressive PCa must be diagnosed early and accurately to appropriately treat patients at higher risk of morbidity and mortality. Meanwhile, it is critical to balance against over-treatment of indolent PCa, of which is more appropriately managed using an active surveillance approach. The best biopsy technique today is to localize PCa with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and use its fusion with US to improve the detection rate of aggressive PCa. However, this method alone is not able to accurately differentiate indolent PCa and cannot reliably detect small lesions of aggressive PCa. In this project, we propose a turnkey technology, where subtle variations of backscattered US signals from a tissue location over a short time span, i.e., temporal enhanced US, are used to detect physical properties of the underlying tissue using a machine-learning framework. Our objective is to establish the efficacy of this technology in identifying clinically significant PCa in real-time US, so that accurate biopsy targeting is achieved. In a series of clinical studies, we will develop and deploy this technology across multiple institutions. This technology is expected to positively and rapidly benefit the lives of all patients suffering from PCa. Collaboration with leading investigators in Canada and USA will create an effective environment for leading international development of next generation cancer diagnosis imaging tools.

column36: Role of autophagy dysregulation in pancreatitis caused by alcohol and glucagon-like peptide
column37: Acute pancreatitis (AP) causes high morbidity and mortality, and at considerable financial costs to health care in Canada. The most common cause of AP is alcohol, affecting 10% of alcoholics. There is still no effective specific treatment directed at the pathogenesis of alcoholic AP in part because the postulated disease mechanisms could not be directly tested on human pancreatic tissue. Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, which potentiate glucose-mediated insulin secretion, is the new panacea for treating diabetes; now a multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical market. However, GLP-1 drug treatments exhibited six-fold increase in AP, the basis is totally unknown. Our overarching hypothesis is that alcohol and GLP-1 drugs can cause perturbations in autophagy, the cellular 'self-eating' process that normally gets rid of cellular garbage. Autophagy involves a series of vesicle formations that involve distinct SNARE proteins (Aim 1), which when pathologically activated (alcohol - Aim 2, GLP-1 - Aim 3), causes inadvertent protease activation (instead of physiologic degradation) which can damage and destroy acinar cells (i.e. AP). To mechanistically address these conditions in a clinically-relevant manner, we've developed the method of preparing fresh human pancreatic slices to assess autophagy processes and how their perturbations contribute to acinar cell injury. We will assess whether manipulation of autophagy SNAREs expression in rat pancreas can modify alcohol- and GLP-1-mediated pancreatic injury. This work may identify novel treatments for AP and impact current diabetes management in patients taking GLP-1 drugs.

column36: Equity in Mental Health Care for Children and Youth
column37: Mental health problems and suicide are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality for children and youth. Yet access to mental health care for children is an ongoing challenge. The principle of equity in access to healthcare is reflected in the Canada Health Act. However, equity in access to MH care is ill-defined and has rarely been examined in relation to child/youth mental health services (CYMHS). The current study will conduct a systematic review of how equity has been evaluated with respect to MH care for children and youth. Equity can be defined as equal access to services. Within Ontario and across Canada, specialized MH and psychiatric services for children and youth are delivered mainly through publicly-funded agencies and psychiatrists. Private providers (psychologists and social workers) also play a role; we have little information on the role that private providers play in the systems that care for this population. The present study will also examine the distribution of publicly-funded agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers, and the extent to which sociodemographic factors (e.g., family income) are related to the distribution of child and youth MH services. If the distribution of agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers varies by regions, this would likely result in inequity in access to care for individuals in regions with fewer agencies/providers. Second, if the distribution of agencies, psychiatrists, and private providers varies by region as a function of sociodemographic factors, it would also reflect inequities in access to care. Identification of inequity is the first step to addressing those inequities and ultimately improving the systems in place to care for children and youth with mental health problems.

column36: Functional and genetic susceptibility to progressive cryptococcal pneumonia
column37: Cryptococcus neoformans is an environmental fungus found throughout the world that causes serious disease of the lungs and brain in over one million humans each year. This pathogen is capable of infecting healthy humans and is particularly dangerous for those with weakened immune defences. Interestingly, only a minority of all individuals that are exposed to Cryptococcus neoformans will become ill. We believe that humans have natural differences that influence their susceptibility to severe cryptococcal infection and their response to treatment; however, we lack a firm understanding of the basic mechanisms that control these processes. Precise knowledge of host immune defense would be extremely valuable for diagnosis, prediction and monitoring of disease progression, and personalized therapy of cryptococcal infection. To identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control the development of severe cryptococcal disease, we use a mouse model of infection that closely resembles the human disease. We will apply cutting edge technology to analyze the function of lung cells, tissues, and organs and determine how the underlying cellular pathways and genes influence immunity. The knowledge we derive through this project will be translated into improved prevention and clinical management of serious human fungal infections.

column36: Understanding mutagenic replication-transcription conflicts in cancer-initiation
column37: Mutations in DNA are a driving force in cancer initiation, progression and therapy resistance. Some mutations arise from normal functions involving DNA. These functions include copying DNA during cell division, and transcribing DNA into RNA messages that control the production of proteins in the cell. These two independent processes, termed DNA replication and transcription, must occur at the same time on the same DNA, and therefore they can interfere with one another. We now know that these replication-transcription conflicts are a potential source of DNA damage and mutations and are thought to be influenced by breast cancer susceptibility genes. This proposal will clearly define new roles for breast cancer tumour suppressor genes in preventing replication-transcription conflicts, and survey the prevalence of such conflicts in normal cells from individuals with elevated 5-year risk for breast cancer and in early and late stage breast cancer samples. Our hope is to find new ways to selectively eliminate breast cancer cells experiencing high levels of replication-transcription collisions.

These treatments are highly effective at curing most patients with HPV-related OPSCC, but side effects from treatment can be severe and long lasting. column36: The impact of nuclear G protein signalling in health and disease

However, many recent studies have demonstrated that not all of these receptors are transported to the cell surface and may in fact be targeted to internal cellular structures such as the nucleus, ER and Golgi apparatus. column36: Establishing the importance of diet and insulin resistance in modulating immune function in obesity
column37: Obesity is associated with several risk factors (for example, high blood sugar, poor insulin response and inflammation) that increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Obesity is also associated with abnormalities in the immune system and an increased risk of infection. Specific components of the diet such as high dietary intake of fat and sugar influence not only the development of obesity but also the immune system. Therefore, it is still unclear if the immune dysfunction associated with obesity in human are attributable to 1- the excess of body fat per se and/or 2- the metabolic complications also often associated with obesity such as elevated blood glucose and/or 3- the overall poor diet quality of an individual. We are proposing a study where we will characterize, in controlled feeding conditions, the functionality of the immune system by investigating a panel of makers of the immune system (inflammation in the blood and the response of immune cells). At the end of a 4-week feeding period where participants will all consume the same standardized diet, we will compare the immune system of three groups of adults with obesity: a. obesity with normal blood glucose concentrations; b. obesity with marginally elevated blood glucose concentrations; and c. obesity with T2DM. All groups will be matched for age, sex and body mass index, and compared to a group of healthy normal weight subjects. By comparing these four groups, we will be able to gain an understanding of the immune complications associated with obesity alone (e.g. excess of body fat per se) and the association of blood sugar and diet in modulating these immune complications. This is essential to subsequently identify dietary interventions to counteract the immune dysfunctions associated with obesity.

column36: Mechanisms of REM sleep behaviour disorder
column37: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) affects 2-6% of the elderly population and is characterized by excessive movement during REM sleep. These movements are typically so violent that they result in patient injuries, which often require medical attention. However, the most alarming aspect of RBD is that 80-90% of patients eventually develop a brain disease like Parkinson's disease or dementia after being diagnosed with RBD. During healthy REM sleep, most of the body's muscles are paralyzed. However, in RBD muscle paralysis is lost, which causes RBD patients to actively move during REM sleep. Because RBD is tightly associated with brain degeneration and this degeneration begins in brain regions that cause REM sleep paralysis, it is hypothesized that RBD is caused by degeneration of the brain regions that control REM sleep paralysis. However, it still remains unclear which cells in the brainstem control REM sleep paralysis and if damage to these cell circuits underlies RBD. This medical research will be of importance to Canadians because it identifies the brain mechanisms that cause healthy REM sleep and it determines if degeneration of these regions causes RBD.

column36: Ubiquitin-KEKS: Function of a Novel Ubiquitin Isoform Coded by UBBP4, a Gene Initially Annotated as a Pseudogene.
column37: Protein degradation constitutes a major cellular function that is responsible for maintenance of the normal cellular physiology by breaking down proteins. The ubiquitin-proteasome system is one of the major mechanism responsible for protein degradation within cells. The regulation of protein stability by this pathway is critical in the molecular basis of carcinogenesis, as it is involved in the regulation of cell growth and preventing abnormal accumulation of proteins. Additionally, ubiquitin modification of target proteins signals many cellular processes other than proteolysis that are also important for the development of cancer. Deregulation of ubiquitin ligases, which are proteins involved in many biological processes including protein degradation, results in uncontrolled proliferation, genomic instability and cancer. Attempts to develop general protein degradation inhibitors for cancer therapy have been questioned because it is highly toxic, and could results in long-term effects from the accumulation of misfolded proteins that is the hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, there is great interests in identifying specific proteins involved in this process that could be targeted instead. We identified UBBP4, a gene encoding novel ubiquitins that could be involved in such specific ubiquitination of proteins. The main goal of studying ubiquitin and ubiquitin ligases is to develop drugs that specifically target these enzymes. Thus, it is crucial to identify the substrates of these ubiquitin ligases and understand their cellular functions. We will be using different innovative approaches to identify the proteins modified by UBBP4, as well as functional role for this new modification. The results obtained from the experiments proposed in this application will allow us to better understand the molecular mechanisms regulated by ubiquitin.

column36: Putting Social Citizenship into Practice: Reducing Stigma and Promoting Social Inclusion of People with Dementia
column37: PURPOSE: The purpose of this four-year study is to learn how communities can reduce stigma and promote social inclusion of people living with dementia. We are creating a team of academic researchers, people with dementia, and community partners who will work together, using the approach of "participatory action research", to meet two goals: (1) create a useful definition of "social citizenship" based on the experiences and opinions of people with dementia; and (2) show how this definition can provide practical guidance for communities to reduce stigma and promote social inclusion of people with dementia. METHODS: An action group of people with dementia will be the centre of a team that includes academic researchers and community partners. To meet the first goal, the action group will direct the team on gathering in-depth information from different groups of people in the community who are living with dementia. Methods will include focus groups, workshops, interviews, and observation. The information will be analysed to create a framework defining the concept of social citizenship and identifying ways to respect citizenship. To meet the second goal, the research team will use this framework with direction from the action group to identify, apply, and assess strategies communities can use to support social citizenship for people living with dementia. Information about the process and impact of these strategies will be gathered and analysed. IMPACT: Study outcomes will include a set of practical guidelines to provide direction for communities to reduce stigma and promote social inclusion of the growing numbers of people with dementia. We expect this to shape policy and decision-making at organizational and municipal levels. Including people with dementia in a full participatory role as co-researchers is groundbreaking in Canada, so we also expect study results to be influential for health and social care planning, and for further research.

column36: Integrated phylogenetic, molecular and functional analyses of the within-host latent HIV reservoir
column37: Thanks to the advent of combination antiretroviral therapies, HIV infection is now considered a chronically manageable condition. These drugs however do not completely eliminate HIV from the body; as such, an HIV cure is actively being pursued. HIV is able to persist in the body because the virus establishes "latent HIV reservoirs", long-lived cells that harbor a dormant copy of the HIV genome within them. HIV can persist for decades within these cells, but the virus may reactivate at any time to produce infectious particles. It is for this reason that HIV therapy needs to be maintained for life. Establishment of latent HIV reservoirs is a continuous process that begins shortly after infection. Moreover, HIV is continually evolving within a given host. Thus, by the time an individual reaches chronic infection, their latent HIV reservoir is expected to comprise a genetically diverse pool of viral sequences that constitute a "fossil record" of HIV evolution in that individual. Importantly, latently-infected cells are likely to differ in key respects including their ability to reactivate to produce infectious HIV particles and their susceptibility to recognition by the immune system. Methods to study HIV reservoir diversity and to identify key characteristics that associate with reservoir reactivation would greatly aid efforts towards an HIV cure. Our interdisciplinary team, comprising molecular biology, bioinformatics, and clinical experts, has developed an innovative genetics-based method for determining when a given HIV sequence "went dormant" within a host. We now seek to apply our method to address foundational gaps in our understanding of HIV persistence. We believe that our integrated approach will provide a versatile and potentially transformative addition to the growing armamentarium of tools in HIV cure research, towards the ultimate goal of developing strategies for HIV reservoir elimination.

column36: The CART Canadian NP mifepristone implementation study
column37: Nurse Practitioners are often the most trusted and sometimes the only health care professional available, and are well placed to provide essential sexual and reproductive health care services across Canada. Abortion is a common reproductive health procedure with nearly one third of females in Canada having at least one abortion. column36: Unravelling the contribution to the hypoxic ventilatory response of purinergic and glial signalling in the preBotzinger Complex
column37: The mammalian brain depends on a constant supply of oxygen to meet its energy needs. If this supply fails for even a few minutes permanent brain damage or death can result. A host of adaptive responses have evolved to protect brain oxygen. Prominent among these is the biphasic hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) in which a fall in blood oxygen (hypoxia) supplying the brain triggers an initial increase in breathing. If this increase does not restore oxygen levels, breathing falls in what is called the secondary hypoxic respiratory depression. Release of the excitatory neurochemical ATP in breathing centers of the brain helps maintain the increased breathing. However, this ATP is degraded to adenosine; brain hypoxia also causes widespread release of adenosine. Adenosine causes widespread depression of neuronal activity. This depression is highly adaptive in most brain regions because it reduces metabolic demand and hypoxic brain injury. However, depression of breathing is highly maladaptive because it is only through increases in breathing that oxygen levels can be restored. The net result is that the initial hypoxia-induced increase in breathing is followed by a secondary depression that is potentially fatal in premature infants who suffer from apnea of prematurity; it is also problematic in adults with sleep-disordered breathing where repeated, cyclic falls in oxygen exacerbate cardiovascular disease. Thus, there is great clinical interest in understanding the mechanisms underlying the HVR. The interaction between ATP excitation and adenosine inhibition of breathing is emerging as key in determining the magnitude of the hypoxic depression. The aim of this proposal is to use rodent models to determine the factors that control the balance between the excitatory actions of ATP and inhibitory actions of adenosine during hypoxia and develop strategies to shift the balance in favor of excitation to counteract the life-threatening hypoxic respiratory depression.

column36: Genetic instability of the haploid male germ cells

column36: Mechanistic studies of cell-free DNA and histones in sepsis: At the interface of innate immunity, coagulation, and inflammation
column37: Sepsis (ie. blood poisoning) is triggered by harmful microorganisms or their toxins in the blood or tissues. These harmful agents can cause a vicious cycle of blood clot formation and inflammation, which may lead to multiple organ failure and death even after the microorganisms have been cleared with antibiotics. In Canada, there are approximately 90,000 patients with sepsis each year. Of these, 30% to 50% of these patients will die. Many anti-sepsis drugs have been tested in humans, but all of these clinical studies have failed. This suggests that some fundamental knowledge is lacking in our current understanding of why sepsis kills patients. In recent years, neutrophils (a type of white blood cells) have been shown to release web-like structures (called NETs) to capture and kill microorganisms. NETs consist of DNA, histones, and neutrophils enzymes. However, NETs can also cause collateral damage to the body. We have previously shown that the DNA and histone components of NETs can trigger blood clotting and prevent blood breakdown. We have also shown that high levels of DNA in the blood of septic patients is a strong predictor of death. In a mouse model of sepsis, injection of DNAse (an enzyme that breaks down DNA) results in improved organ function and improved survival rates. In the current proposal, we plan to further study how DNA and histones triggers blood clots and inflammation in sepsis. We will perform studies of blood cells and blood molecules in test tubes. By comparing blood samples from septic and non-septic ICU patients, we can identify the precise biological pathways that lead to high levels of DNA in septic patients. We will also perform studies in a mouse model of sepsis to see if removal of DNA and/or histones from the blood can improve survival in septic mice. Our research thus has the potential to identify new anti-sepsis strategies that will improve the lives of septic patients.

column37: Streptococcus pneumonia (the pneumococcus) is a bacterium that often lives in the nose and throats of humans. This relationship is most often benign but this microorganism is also an accomplished disease-causing germ that can cause mild ailments, such as earaches, to lethal illnesses like pneumonia, blood poisoning, and infections of the brain and central nervous system. There are effective vaccines and medicines (antibiotics) to treat infections caused by the pneumococcus; however, this germ is constantly adapting to avoid both of these medical interventions. The human body has large amounts of carbohydrates with complex structures, termed glycans, displayed on the surface of cells and coating the surfaces of tissues (e.g. mucous). Remarkably, the pneumococcus relies on its ability to attack these glycans to colonize humans and ultimately cause disease. Our research is aimed at determining how this happens. What glycans does the germ attack? What pneumococcal factors do this? What is the outcome of destroying a host sugar? Armed with the fundamental insight from examining these questions we plan to develop and study molecules that can be used to prevent S. pneumoniae from attacking host glycans; such molecules are proving useful as research tools but may also provide a platform for developing new treatments to combat S. pneumoniae infections.

These include socioeconomic characteristics, nutritional status, smoke and drug use, physical activity, psychosocial stress and environmental exposure to name a few Furthermore, there has been increasing evidence that preterm birth also may have a genetic predisposition component. The genetic component of preterm birth appears to be transmitted primarily for the maternal side as it has been shown that a woman has an increased risk of delivering prematurely if her mother, sisters or maternal half-sisters have delivered prematurely. We have been investigating the function of a gene called Nodal and we showed that if you mutate this gene, the mother give birth 2 days before term. Thus we believe that this gene is involved in regulating term pregnancy and if we disrut its function, this lead to preterm birth. We now want to see if this is also true in humans. The identification of genes involved in preterm birth is only beginning but it offers a promising avenue to identify factors that regulate the timing of parturition and will lead to the identification of molecular mechanisms involved in regulating the timing of parturition.

column36: Mechanisms of long-term change to neuronal activity and secretion
column37: My research focuses on nerve cells from the brain. I am interested in how the bio-electrical properties of nerve cells are controlled. These properties are governed by minute holes in nerve cells called channel proteins, which pass ions (like calcium, sodium or potassium) in and out of the cell. Because ions are charged, their movement through channels results in the flow of electrical current. Nerve cells harness currents to receive sensations, code information, and signal other nerve cells, muscles, or glands. Signalling involves the release of either small chemicals or specialized proteins, termed neuro-peptides, from a nerve cell. My objective is to examine how nerve cells use channels in a coordinated fashion to release neuro-peptides and initiate behaviour. Taking a reductionist approach, I employ the brain of a sea snail, called Aplysia, which has large and identifiable nerve cells. In particular, I study the bag cells, which are motivational cells that evoke reproduction, a behaviour essential to all animals. My work concerns how, after only a very short stimulus, the action of certain channels allows these nerves cells to respond with a prolonged episode of neuro-peptide release to trigger reproduction. I will investigate the mechanisms that allow channels to remain open for lengthy time periods. This includes interactions with structures inside the bag cells, known as mitochondria, which normally act as an energy source, but in this case regulate channel function. Long-term responses are found in nerve cells from many animals, and are essential for handling sensory information, learning, movement, and controlling drinking, eating, ovulation, birth, or breast feeding. Thus, my findings will apply to processes such as perception, memory, and fundamental behaviours. Furthermore, because the channels permit a nerve cell to be active on its own, there may be implications for epilepsy, where bio-electrical properties are inappropriately adjusted.

column37: Nociceptors are sensory nerves activated by harmful stimuli such as thermal changes, mechanical force and chemical insults. The neuroinflammatory system in the lung remains ill defined. My overall hypothesis is that lung sensory nerves can detect infection and through the selective release of neuropeptides alter the neutrophil response, thereby changing the clinical outcome. To test my hypothesis I have developed mouse models that are deficient in sensory nerves and I am using sophisticated lung imaging to interrogate how these nerves regulate inflammation during homeostasis and during pneumonia. Understanding the interplay between the neuro and immune systems is essential to understanding pulmonary diseases.

column36: Behavioural profile matching: A precision medicine approach to concussion rehabilitation
column37: Concussions are very common. Although many people recover well from concussion, at least 1 in 5 will have persistent symptoms and difficulties with daily activities. How people cope with their symptoms following concussion powerfully influences their recovery. We have recently identified two unhelpful coping styles following a concussion - (1) avoidance, where people perceive activity as unnecessarily dangerous and take great care to avoid overexertion, and (2) endurance, where people engage in high levels of activity despite worsening symptoms until they "crash," requiring recuperative rest. These same unhelpful coping styles are seen in other health conditions, such as chronic pain. We believe that individuals who engage in avoidance behaviour benefit from a different type of concussion treatment than those who engage in endurance behaviour. If our belief is true, the current one-size-fits-all approach is not likely to work for everyone who suffers a concussion. We will evaluate whether assigning individuals to a specific treatment tailored to their coping style is practical, acceptable, and beneficial for their recovery. In the proposed study, patients will be recruited from concussion clinics and offered one of two treatment programs based on random assignment (like a coin toss). Both programs will be delivered by an occupational therapist and psychologist over eight weeks, using a videoconference system. We expect that the majority of patients who we approach will choose to join the study and that most of them will attend regularly, do their therapy assignments, and complete a final assessment. We will also check that the therapists are providing the treatments as outlined in a treatment manual. The information collected in this study will inform the development for a larger trial involving additional clinics across Canada, so that we can learn more definitively whether our matching approach can speed up recovery and reduce the burden of concussion.

column36: Ecological Momentary Assessment of Simultaneous Cannabis and Alcohol Use
column37: Cannabis and alcohol are widely used among young adults in Canada and both substances are often used at the same time. Rates of simultaneous use of alcohol and cannabis may increase as a result of legalization and increased access to cannabis in Canada. Combining cannabis with alcohol can increase risk for harms such as psychological and physical symptoms, social problems, and risk for substance use disorders. However, little is currently known about real-time patterns of simultaneous use of cannabis and alcohol, or how these contribute to risk for harms above and beyond using either substance alone. This study will use real-time mobile data collection to examine patterns of simultaneous cannabis and alcohol use in individuals' daily lives. Young adults who regularly use cannabis and alcohol will be asked to track their use of both substances using a smartphone app for three, 21-day periods spaced 6 months apart. On mornings following alcohol and/or cannabis use, participants will complete measures of substance use consequences. Data will be used to examine patterns of simultaneous use, including the frequency of co-use, the overall quantity of each substance used, and the temporal ordering of each substance (e.g., cannabis before alcohol or vice versa). Contextual influences on simultaneous use and the subjective effects of combining cannabis with alcohol will also be investigated. Further, the unique risks of combining cannabis and alcohol (e.g., risky behaviours, hangovers) will be examined relative to the use of either substance alone. Finally, changes in patterns of simultaneous use will be examined over a one-year period in relation to health outcomes such as symptoms of substance use disorders. The findings will improve our understanding of the unique health risks of cannabis and alcohol co-use, which will have direct implications for public health policies as cannabis becomes legal in Canada.

column36: Quantifying Brown Adipose Tissue Thermogenesis in Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Brown fat is the only organ able to burn energy to directly produce heat. This tissue allows small animals to live in cold environments without having to rely on muscle shivering. Brown fat is present in adults and can be seen using 'positron emission tomography' imaging (or 'PET imaging') with injection of a radioactive sugar label (or 'sugar tracer') that is taken up by brown fat when it is activated upon cold exposure. PET imaging with a sugar tracer is currently the standard method to measure brown fat. We have found that brown fat in adults burns energy mostly by utilizing its own fat content. We have demonstrated that PET imaging with a sugar tracer underestimates the total contribution of brown fat to energy expenditure, especially in people with type 2 diabetes. The contribution of brown fat to energy balance cannot be precisely determined using the current methods we have. As brown fat is currently viewed as a promising target for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes, it is essential to quantify its role in energy expenditure in people without and with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes. We propose here to develop and validate new methods to quantify brown fat energy expenditure by measuring its own fat utilization with a combination of PET imaging with a novel fat tracer and magnetic resonance imaging techniques. We will apply these novel techniques during cold exposure and stimulation with a drug known to activate brown fat in people. Our laboratory has made outstanding contributions to the field of brown fat research through the imaging innovations we made and our integrated approach to the study of energy metabolism directly in people. This project will lead to new standard methods to measure brown fat energy expenditure and will provide essential knowledge on brown fat as a target to prevent and treat obesity and type 2 diabetes.

column36: PARP inhibition in PAH: A Phase 1 clinical trial
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a progressive condition characterized by the chronic elevation of pulmonary artery (PA) pressure leading to failure of the heart. In spite of recent advances in approved therapies, PAH remains a serious disease with significant mortality. In contrast to the earlier belief that contraction of pulmonary vessels played a key role in PAH, it is now established that excessive proliferation of the cells within the pulmonary artery wall is a pivotal component of pulmonary vascular obliteration, a currently irreversible feature of PAH for which available pharmacotherapies have no/limited efficacy. In recently years, it has become increasingly appreciated that, contrary to normal cells, these cells are exposed to stressful conditions, jeopardizing their survival. To deal with these insults, these cells have developed pathways, allowing them to survive and proliferate and leading to intense remodelling of pulmonary vessels. Central to these strategies are the activation of the mechanisms that repair DNA. We recently documented that pharmacological inhibition of PARP1, the most important mechanism involved in DNA repair, reverses PAH in human cells and animal models of PAH. Very recently, Olaparib, an orally available PARP1 inhibitor, was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in treating cancers and was approved by Health Canada for the treatment of ovarian cancer. The time is thus right to translate our findings in human PAH. This proposal addresses a very novel and promising therapeutic avenue to treat and is one of the first step of personalized medicine in PAH. We propose an early phase clinical trial to determine whether: 1) PARP1 inhibition with olaparib is safe and effective; 2) patients' genes can predict the efficacy and the side effect profile of olaparib in adult patients with symptomatic PAH.

column36: Systematic Analysis of Post-transcriptional Regulatory Mechanisms and Functions in Drosophila
column37: DNA is copied into messenger RNAs (mRNAs), which in turn encode proteins. For most of the second half of the 20th Century it was thought that the regulation of which proteins are made in any particular cell of the body or stage of development is at the level of transcription (production of mRNA from DNA). However, it has become clear in the last decade that a great deal of this regulation occurs post-transcriptionally via control of mRNA stability, localization within the cell and/or in the translation of the mRNA into protein. These processes are regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which together with their bound mRNAs and other associated proteins, regulate these processes. In order to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms of post-transcriptional control and how the compendium of proteins in each cell type is assembled, we will use the powerful model organism, the fruit fly Drosophila, to systematically identify the mRNAs bound to each of 68 RBPs in the early embryo together with other associated RNAs and proteins. We will use experimental and computational methods to identify the binding sites for each of these 68 RBPs. Finally, we will assess the molecular functions of these binding sites in control of the post-transcriptional processes listed above. Together these studies will provide the first insights into how the 'post-transcriptional code' is read out as the compendium of proteins present in a cell. Given that RBPs and their binding sites tend to be highly evolutionarily conserved and that 90% of the closely related human RBPs have been associated with a variety of diseases, our results will lead directly to insights into the components and functions of post-transcriptional processes in other organisms, including humans.

column36: Precision medicine in smoking cessation: nicotine metabolism genetics in nine clinical trials
column37: Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable illness and death in Canada; using precision medicine genomics approaches we plan to personalize smoking cessation treatment choices. In this proposal, we seek to identify genetic factors that influence the nicotine metabolite ratio (NMR), a measure of nicotine inactivation that predicts treatment outcomes in multiple smoking cessation clinical trials. NMR is also associated with the amount smoked, dependence, reactivity to smoking cues, risk for lung cancer, and many other smoking-related behaviours; in general, faster nicotine metabolizers (higher NMR) smoke more, are more dependent, have lower quit rates, and a higher risk for lung cancer, compared to slower metabolizers. Up to 80% of NMR variability between smokers is due to genetics, however only a small fraction of this genetic variation is known. While NMR itself could be used clinically to personalize smoking cessation, this is not yet possible because measuring NMR requires sophisticated techniques; there are no commercially available NMR kits and NMR is not routinely measured. In contrast, DNA, from which genetic information can be determined, is more easily collected. Thus, using genetics to better understand NMR, and how NMR is related to smoking and illness, we will enhance quitting and reduce tobacco-related illness and death. Our goal is to sequence (i.e. read) the major nicotine inactivation gene in ~1,000 smokers to identify specific variants affecting NMR. We also have data from 9 smoking cessation clinical trials, where >5,000 smokers with NMR will be examined for the variants identified in our sequencing analyses. We will then study how these variants functionally influence NMR, smoking behaviours, and cessation outcomes using this unparalleled clinical resource. Through these analyses, we will improve our ability to genetically tailor treatment, which will ultimately improve smoking cessation rates and the mortality associated with smoking.

column37: Persons with spinal cord injury (SCI) are at risk for many chronic health conditions like diabetes, heart disease and cancer and health complications such as a urinary tract infection, pressure ulcer or pneumonia. In order to provide evidence, a study is needed to evaluate the impact of SCI&U on self-management skills, quality of life and hospital use. Prior to launching a large scale study; however, a feasibility study is needed to inform recruitment, data collection and follow-up. It is anticipated that such a program would not only reduce health complications and hospital visits, but also improve quality of life for individuals with SCI.

column36: Regulation of Salmonella pathogenesis by transposon-encoded small regulatory RNAs
column37: Gastrointestinal infections by Salmonella and related enteropathogenic bacteria can lead to severe diarrheal disease and accordingly present a serious human health problem. Infection requires passage of Salmonella from the GI tract into epithelial cells lining the lower intestine. This cell invasion process requires the expression of a large set of genes encoded on a 40 kb chromosomal DNA segment called Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1). The control of SPI-1 gene expression is complex involving a positive feed-forward cascade that includes several different transcription factors. We recently discovered that the insertion sequence IS200 encodes small regulatory RNAs (tad-sRNA for short) that contribute to SPI-1 gene expression. Part of the current proposal is focused on defining what genes in SPI-1 tad-sRNAs regulate and how this regulation occurs. Further investigation into the scope of tad-sRNA gene regulation in Salmonella led to the discovery that tad-sRNAs also regulate the expression of genes required for cysteine biosynthesis. As cysteine biosynthesis plays an important role in oxidative stress response and Salmonella needs to mount an aggressive oxidative stress response to propagate in certain cell types, we will test the possibility that tad-sRNA regulation of cysteine biosynthesis contributes to Salmonella pathogenicity. Finally, we will determine if host gene regulation by tad-sRNAs is a widespread phenomenon in bacteria. Overall, we expect results from this proposal to provide valuable new information in three important biomedical areas including: (1) how bacterial pathogenicity is controlled; (2) how the expression of a component of central metabolism (cysteine biosynthesis) is regulated and (3) why insertion sequences are stably maintained in bacterial genomes - notably insertion sequences can make major contributions to the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

column36: Role of beta-PIX and CdGAP in the pathogenesis of proteinuria
column37: Leakage of proteins into urine (proteinuria) is a hallmark of many kidney diseases. When you have a lot of proteinuria, you are more likely to progress to kidney failure. This is why it is important to find effective treatments to stop proteinuria. Current treatments are non-specific with a lot of undesired side effects and not always effective. What is blocking the discovery of specific and effective treatments is the fact that we do not know how proteinuria develops. Normal kidneys have a barrier function that allows the passage of water and waste products into the urine while retaining proteins that are essential for body function. In the kidney, cells called podocytes are maintaining this barrier function. When podocytes are injured, this causes proteinuria. The proposed research will define what is happening in podocytes when they are injured. Our recent research identified that in proteinuric kidney diseases, the molecule called Rac1 is activated in podocytes and this makes podocytes to malfunction. When the Rac1 activation is persistent, eventually podocytes are lost in the urine and that leads to kidney failure. Thus, blocking Rac1 is a promising treatment strategy for proteinuria. However, Rac1 is expressed in all the cells in the body and blocking Rac1 itself will likely harm the body. Instead, we have identified two proteins, called beta-PIX and CdGAP that regulate Rac1 in podocytes. We will study how these proteins work in podocytes and establish if they could be good therapeutic targets. The results of the research will make us understand how proteinuria occurs and allow the development of a better therapeutic approach.

column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease which can cause inflammation and damage to any part of the body. It affects 1:2000 people, women nine times more frequently than men, usually during the most productive time of their lives. Consequently, there is a significant social and economic cost associated with it. Involvement of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) by SLE results in a variety of neurological and psychiatric problems. Frequently, there is disturbance of normal cognitive function (e.g. the ability to think clearly, remember recent and past events and organize everyday tasks) which is called cognitive dysfunction ("lupus fog"). It is one of the least understood features of the illness despite its negative impact on daily function and quality of life. Dr. Hanly, who has conducted several research projects in this area, plans a study with experts in neuropsychology and neuroimaging to learn more about why lupus patients suffer from cognitive dysfunction. Patients attending the Lupus clinic at the Queen Elizabeth II Health Sciences Center in Halifax will be invited to undergo clinical testing for cognitive dysfunction. On the same day, brain imaging studies using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) will be performed to assess information flow through brain networks, something that is required for normal cognitive functioning. The function of the blood-brain-barrier, a structure the protects the brain by controlling which components of the blood diffuse into the brain, will also be assessed. The proposed studies have not previously been done in SLE and should provide new information on why lupus patients have cognitive difficulties. The results should lead to improvements in the diagnosis and treatment of this distressing condition. The investigators are well established researchers, who bring diverse and complementary skills to address this important area of clinical need for SLE patients.

column36: Iron and inflammatory regulation of hepcidin: implications for anemias and infectious diseases
column37: Iron is an essential nutrient but also a potential biohazard; therefore, its metabolism is tightly controlled. Most of body iron is utilized within red blood cells for oxygen transport to tissues. Aged red blood cells are cleared by tissue macrophages, which liberate iron and recycle it to the bloodstream for new erythropoiesis. Iron efflux from macrophages and other cells is inhibited by hepcidin, a liver-derived hormone. The expression of hepcidin is primarily regulated by iron, inflammatory and erythropoietic cues. Genetic defects in hepcidin pathways cause hemochromatosis, a disease of iron overload. Pathological suppression of hepcidin also occurs in anemias with ineffective erythropoiesis, such as beta thalassemia, and contributes to iron overload. During infection, inflammatory induction of hepcidin triggers iron sequestration from the bloodstream to macrophages. This is considered a protective response by reducing iron availability to invading bacteria but may favor growth of intracellular pathogens. Prolonged inflammatory induction of hepcidin reduces iron availability for erythropoiesis and contributes to the anemia of inflammation, the most common cause of anemia among hospitalized patients. Targeting hepcidin pathways offers new therapeutic opportunities for iron-related disorders. However, the development of hepcidin-based therapeutics requires a better understanding of mechanisms underlying hepcidin regulation. Herein, we hypothesize that the pathways for hepcidin regulation by iron and inflammatory signals are interconnected and affect the development of anemias and the outcome of intracellular infections. We propose experiments with mouse models of iron metabolism, anemia of inflammation, beta thalassemia and infection with the intracellular Leishmania parasite to investigate basic mechanisms, which is essential for the development of new pharmacological interventions.

column36: Dietary manipulation of gut microbiota to mitigate early-life antibiotic associated obesity
column37: Antibiotics are life-saving drugs that have considerably reduced the rates of human death and disease and were thought to have minimal long-term adverse effects. However, recent research suggests that when antibiotics are given in early life, either to pregnant mothers or to infants, intestinal bacteria can be disrupted and result in increased risk of obesity and asthma in later life. Intestinal bacteria are less stable in early life and therefore susceptible to their environment including antibiotics but also diet. Prebiotics are non-digestible food ingredients like fiber that selectively feed health promoting bacteria in the gut. Their intake is associated with lower body weight and fat mass, improved glucose control and reduced inflammation. Given the current epidemic of childhood obesity and the high prevalence of infant antibiotic exposure, research is needed to develop strategies to reduce obesity risk, especially when early life antibiotic treatment cannot be avoided. Given that prebiotics positively modify intestinal bacteria, there is the potential that consuming them at the same time as antibiotics could provide protection. Two situations that are highly relevant to real life will be examined. The first experiment will examine whether giving prebiotics (inulin and oligofructose) to pregnant rats at the same time that they receive antibiotics will reduce the risk of obesity in their offspring. The second experiment will examine whether giving prebiotics to very young rats at the same time as antibiotics will reduce their risk of developing obesity later in life. Fecal transplant studies will help us determine the direct role of intestinal bacteria in providing protection with prebiotics. This work will provide important insight into whether prebiotics can reverse some of the metabolic risk of early life antibiotic exposure. Overall, this work has the potential to identify a novel therapy for reducing the burden of obesity and improving longterm health.

column36: Novel therapeutic molecular targets for amyloid-beta pathology in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia in the elderly. As the world's population ages, many advanced countries including Canada face a growing burden of care for patients with Alzheimer's disease. Loss of brain cell connections called synapses is an early pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease and is strongly correlated with cognitive impairment. A protein called amyloid-beta that is deposited in plaques in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease can induce synapse loss and dysfunction. Our project aims to reveal how to prevent amyloid-beta-induced synapse pathology by uncovering mechanisms through which amyloid-beta leads to synapse loss and dysfunction. We have recently discovered that amyloid-beta oligomers interact with and disrupt the function of synaptic cell adhesion molecules called neurexins. Neurexins play essential roles in synapse formation and plasticity as well as in cognitive functions such as learning and memory. We also identified neurexin-binding proteins that may be able to protect neurexins from amyloid-beta-mediated disruption. column36: Evaluation of Diagnostic Testing for Primary Aldosteronism
column37: Hypertension affects >6 million Canadians and is a leading cause of heart attacks, strokes, and death. 1 in 4 of people with hypertension have uncontrolled high blood pressure despite taking multiple drugs. One of the most common causes of resistant hypertension is primary aldosteronism (PA), a condition where the adrenal glands make an excessive amount of a hormone called aldosterone, leading to high blood pressure. PA is important to recognize because highly effective treatment is available. However, PA is challenging to diagnose. The current process for diagnosing PA is lengthy and expensive. The first step involves a screening blood test. Patients with positive screens are sent for costly "confirmatory" testing. Further invasive testing and definitive treatment are offered to those confirmed to have the diagnosis. However, the usefulness of confirmatory testing is unclear. It is uncertain how often "normal" or "abnormal" results correspond with the truth. It is unresolved whether confirmatory testing is needed, or whether it merely adds an unnecessary step to an already complicated diagnostic pathway. In an effort to better understand the role of confirmatory testing for people with resistant hypertension, we propose to evaluate the performance of confirmatory testing compared to an established gold-standard. Individuals suspected of having PA will receive confirmatory testing and definitive treatment. The outcomes will be compared to determine how many people with PA are misclassified with confirmatory testing. We will examine for potential differences in responses between women and men. This study will help healthcare providers understand the strengths and limitations of confirmatory testing. Our results may help facilitate improved diagnosis and access to effective treatment for individuals with high blood pressure.

The remarkable capacity of tissue regeneration is illustrated by the activity of the muscle stem cell, which is normally a rare cell resting within muscle, but is rapidly activated in response to injury to expand a population of muscle cells needed for repair. Nevertheless, skeletal muscle remains affected by untreatable muscle disease. These diseases, including muscular dystrophies and muscle wasting associated with cancer or aging, are associated with a decline in stem cell function. We therefore aim to further regenerative medicine based approaches by discovering novel mechanisms regulating muscle stem cells. The central dogma of molecular biology states that DNA makes proteins through an RNA intermediate. We focus on mechanisms that regulate the final step, the 'translation' of RNA to protein (otherwise known as protein synthesis), a previously underappreciated aspect of gene regulation that is readily targetable by pharmacological strategies. We will investigate whether certain proteins are selectively synthesized to maintain the 'stemness' properties of muscle stem cells, and whether the pathways that govern protein synthesis can be targeted in regenerative medicine applications.

column36: New Quantitative MRI for Human Stroke
column37: Stroke is a very common cause of death and disability in Canada. Imaging is used to determine the type and location of the stroke, and to follow its evolution. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is increasingly used in stroke follow-up, since it is sensitive to subtle tissue changes. However, current stroke MRI has limitations and could be even more useful. We plan to develop and test new MRI methods for stroke. The base of our new methods builds on technical MRI areas where we have already made major advances and are recognized leaders. The new MRI methods will yield accurate measurements of tissue properties, and are thus quantitative methods. We expect to create new MRI for stroke to measure key tissue changes including iron and volume changes in hemorrhage, size and evolution of microbleeds, tissue decay rates, and tissue and vein oxygenation. These measures will be tested against current standards in patient research studies using a dedicated research MRI centre. Each measure opens new windows into the study of stroke evolution and future response to therapy. To gain entry into clinical MRI protocols, the methods must be very fast or make use of current clinical MRI techniques in new ways. Methods that require no extra scan time will also be tested in our local MRI clinic. This research involves an MRI physicist, two stroke neurologists, and a neuroradiologist. The end result of this research will be new MRI methods that can provide greater insight into stroke and have the potential to change future use of clinical MRI for stroke follow-up.

column36: Neurotrophins in megakaryocytes and platelets
column37: BACKGROUND: Platelets are small cells that circulate in blood. They form a plug to prevent bleeding in case of injury in the blood vessel. Platelets then take on a role in wound healing. Platelets can discharge many proteins around the wound, including growth factors that help the vessel grow new cells to close the wound. Surprisingly, platelets also contain brain growth factors, which they also discharge when they respond to injury. There is 100 times more brain growth factors released by platelets than from brain cells. However, what brain growth factors do in the blood vessels remains unknown. WHAT WE HAVE DONE: We have isolated platelets from the blood of healthy volunteers to study their ability to release a specific brain growth factor named the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). We have found that platelets release large amounts of BDNF, as well as its parent molecule proBDNF. We have also found that both BDNF and proBDNF are able to stimulate platelets to stick together, form a clot and release more of their cargo. We do not know how BDNF and proBDNF act on platelets or on blood vessels. WHAT WE WILL DO: We will identify which pathways BDNF and proBDNF use to induce clot formation. We will block different pathways to determine which ones are the most important. We will pinpoint which receptors (locks) respond to BDNF and proBDNF (keys). Taken together, these experiments will allow us to understand the biology of brain growth factors outside the brain. POTENTIAL BENEFITS: By better understanding how platelets respond to brain growth factors, we will be able to encourage platelet to release of their useful cargoes and help vessels heal. This might be particularly important in the vessels that nourish the brain, where damaged blood vessels could lead to stroke and dementia. Platelets may be a new avenue of treatment for these crippling diseases.

column36: Brain Function and Connectomics Following Sex Hormone Treatment in Adolescents Experiencing Gender Dysphoria
column37: Adolescence is a time of rapid brain maturation that is partly influenced by sex hormones. We are currently using magnetic resonance imaging to assess the influence of sex hormones on brain structure. This project will take us one step further and use state-of-the-art functional magnetic resonance imaging techniques to better understand the influence of sex hormones on brain function. Specifically, we will examine how brain functioning of transgender adolescents, who strongly experience themselves as the opposite gender, differs from that of typically developing adolescents. One truly unique aspect of this project is that it will document how the functioning of the adolescent brain responds to sex hormone therapy. Because sex hormone therapy directly influences the sex hormones that are already in the body, this project will provide insight regarding how sex hormones affect the functioning of the adolescent brain. Surprisingly, even though sex hormone therapy is widely used to help transgender adolescents change from one gender to the other, its impact on brain function during this critical stage is largely unknown. Our research will also examine a very popular biological explanation of transgenderism, namely, that brain function is shifted in the direction of the other sex. Additionally, we will investigate whether there is a relationship between the structure of the brain and patterns of brain activity, as well as whether brain structure and function change together during sex hormone therapy.

column36: Elucidating the role of the Alzheimer risk factor CD2AP in brain capillary endothelial cells & vascular functions
column37: The human brain requires adequate blood flow to perform its many functions. A complex network of arteries, capillaries and veins called the cerebrovasculature direct important nutrients throughout the brain. In structure, this network can be described as resembling the many branches in a tree. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating brain disorder and the most common form of dementia in the elderly. An estimated 60-90 % of AD patients have cerebrovasculature abnormalities; this means that their brains fail to receive all the necessary nutrients from the blood. Individuals with diabetes and hypertension have an even higher risk of developing AD. It is thought that these diseases directly damage the cerebrovasculature. Unfortunately, we still do not understand why the cerebrovasculature fails to do its job in AD. Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels and they are surrounded by endothelial cells. Together with other cells called pericytes and astrocyte endfeet, brain capillary endothelial cells form the blood-brain-barrier. This barrier is vital: It oversees the exchanges between the brain and blood, and controls brain vascular functions. CD2AP is a protein that we have found to be highly enriched in the cerebrovasculature, particularly in brain capillary endothelial cells. Genetic studies show that abnormalities in this protein contribute to AD. Levels of CD2AP are also altered in patients who died with AD. Our research studies will investigate the roles of CD2AP in brain capillary endothelial cells, as well as its contribution to the blood-brain-barrier and how it functions. We intend to shed new light on the causes of AD, particularly on the associated vascular defects. This new health knowledge will serve to develop treatment of the impaired cerebrovasculature in AD patients.

column36: Integrated muscle protein turnover and mechanisms underpinning muscle loss in healthy and sarcopenic older men and women
column37: As we age we lose muscle and strength. This phenomenon is known as sarcopenia and it, like osteopenia is to osteoporosis, is a precursor to significant health problems. In the case of osteopenia and osteoporosis we know that one's risk for fracture increases. However, with sarcopenia there is no corresponding sarcoporosis, but instead we begin to lose strength and muscle function. Eventually the loss of muscle function can become so bad that we lose the ability to conduct activities of daily living and tasks such as getting into and out of chair are significantly compromised. People with more advanced muscle and strength loss are at high risk for the development of full disability, which oftentimes leads to full time institutionalized care. Nonetheless, we know that eating an appropriate amount of protein, containing the right amount of amino acids (the building blocks of protein), can help in preserving muscle mass. We also know, based on previous work from our group that the protein needs of older persons are higher, likely by 50% or more, than those of young persons. Regrettably, this evidence is not incorporated into professional practice. In fact, advice to consume less protein, particularly from high quality animal proteins may be, if followed, unwittingly resulting in accelerating muscle loss in older persons. Thus, the aim of this project is to combine two highly innovative methodologies using what are know as stable isotopes (non-radioactive isotopes) to determine just how much protein older men and women need to maintain their muscles. We are studying men and women separately since there are important sex-based differences. Importantly, we will focus on how much protein their muscles need to slow muscle loss as they age. We will also study older men and women who have sarcopenia to see what has happened in their muscle that led to them developing sarcopenia.
