column36: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and Cardiovascular Development from Childhood to Early Adulthood
column37: A toxic childhood environment including physical, sexual, and emotional abuse, exposure to violence and crime in the home or neighbourhood, severe household dysfunction such as substance abuse, serious mental illness, separation from parents and family, severe neglect, material disadvantage or homelessness, and natural disasters, serious illnesses, accidents or injuries has been linked to many adult physical health issues and disease as well as other negative outcomes including poor school performance, mental disorder, criminality, substance abuse, and general life instability.[1-3] Collectively referred to as adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), recent reviews have found strong links between an accumulation of these experiences and adult cardiovascular disease (CVD).[4-11] It is largely perceived that child abuse, neglect and severe household dysfunction and other ACEs are rare occurrences and their effect on the overall health of the population is minimal. However, child adversity is common, with recent Canadian prevalence estimates of child abuse at 27% to 32%,[12-14] and severe household dysfunction at 49%.[13] Since CVD is a leading cause of death in Canada,[15] the potential effect of ACEs is far more significant than previously thought based on these prevalence rates.[12,13] Yet how ACEs amplify the risk for CVD later in life remains unclear. Recent reviews all conclude that CVD risk factors such as smoking, physical activity, nutrition, obesity, diabetes, hypertension and family history cannot adequately explain this connection. Instead, they direct future research to focus on the interaction between psychosocial factors and physiological systems. As such, the primary objective of this project is to examine the role of ACEs on preclinical measures of cardiovascular health and development from childhood to early adulthood and to examine how both psychosocial factors and physiological mechanisms combine to explain this relationship.

column36: Pharmacological Strategy to Prevent Ischemic Mitral Regurgitation: Preventing the Effects of Serotonin on Heart Valves.
column37: Mitral valve role is to prevent the blood going backward as the heart pumps forward. In many cardiac diseases, the heart enlarges and becomes too big relatively to the valve size. The valve is distorted by the enlarging heart and can't close completely: the blood starts to go backward in the lungs instead of going forward. This condition is called "functional mitral regurgitation" and is a major complication that accelerates the heart disease, increasing deaths and hospitalisations. There is no good treatment available. After a heart attack, a substance named serotonin is released in the blood. We believe that serotonin can interfere with valve adaptation to the enlarging heart by causing abnormal scarring in the valve, and ultimately contributes to the valve leak. Our research goal is to demonstrate that serotonin can interfere with mitral valve function after a heart attack. We want to test a drug named cyproheptadine, which is known to prevent the effect of serotonin in the body. We want to demonstrate that cyproheptadine can prevent abnormal scarring in the mitral valve and ultimately help to prevent mitral valve regurgitation after a heart attack. We will use animal experimentations to answer our questions. Because we want to study conditions similar to what happens in human, we will work with sheep since their heart is of similar size and shape compared with human heart. We will create heart attacks in the animals; one group will be treated with cyproheptadine, and another group will not be treated. We have tested this drug in sheep before and we know it is well tolerated. We will use imaging techniques such as echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance and cardiac computed tomography to measure the heart size, valve size and mitral regurgitation in both groups to assess the effects of cyproheptadine. We will also analyse the valves after the experiments to evaluate parameters of valve growth and abnormal scarring

column36: Characterizing the functional organization of the human cerebellum and cerebro-cerebellar communication
column37: The cerebellum ("little brain") is a highly folded brain structure that communicates tightly with the cerebrum ("big brain"). While it was traditionally thought that the cerebellum was only important in the coordination of movement, research over the last 30 years has made clear that it is involved in a much wider range of functions, including memory, attention, emotion, and social cognition. Furthermore, many researchers have proposed that disrupted communication between cerebrum and cerebellum is one of the root causes of disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and dyslexia. Potentially, we should be able to detect disrupted organization using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technology that allows researchers and clinicians to observe neural activity in the whole brain in awake humans. Despite the great promise of this approach, it has proven difficult to pinpoint specific cerebellar deficits. One obstacle is that we currently do not have a full understanding of the functional organization of the healthy cerebellum or of the normal communication between cerebrum and cerebellum. The goal of the project is therefore to develop a comprehensive functional map of the human cerebellum and of cerebro-cerebellar connections in healthy adults. Moreover, the project will develop a simple and time-efficient procedure for measuring this functional organization within a single individual. Having such an instrument will allow researchers to more easily detect abnormalities of cerebellar function in psychiatric and developmental disorders. Ultimately, the research project will contribute to our ability to predict disorders such as schizophrenia, dyslexia and autism to evaluate the outcome of novel treatments.

column36: Emotional cascades and nonsuicidal self-injury among undergraduate students
column37: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), which refers to the direct and deliberate destruction or alteration of bodily tissue in the absence of suicidal intent (e.g., self-cutting, burning, severe scratching) is a widespread and significant mental health concern among university students. As many as 1 in 5 undergraduate students has engaged in NSSI, and students who engage in NSSI are at increased risk for other mental health concerns across the university years (e.g., depression, anxiety, suicidal behaviour). Although mounting research and theory suggest that NSSI is a form of coping behaviour used by students to reduce overwhelming negative emotions (e.g., stress, anxiety, anger), it is unclear why students engage in NSSI rather than other coping behaviours (e.g., talking to a friend, going for a walk) to reduce their distress. To clarify the emotional context in which NSSI occurs, and to identify ways to help students resist NSSI urges when distressed, the proposed study will examine associations among emotions, NSSI, and coping behaviours among undergraduate students who self-injure. In the first phase of the study, 280 students with a recent history of NSSI will complete multiple assessments each day for 14 days using a smart phone app, reporting on mood, NSSI urges and behaviours, and use of alternative coping behaviours. A subsample of participants (n = 20) also will be invited to participate in follow-up in-person interviews about their experiences with NSSI. The proposed project will advance health-related knowledge and theory by providing new insight into the processes through which NSSI occurs and is maintained. Moreover, identifying alternative behaviours and strategies students who self-injure can use to resist NSSI urges will equip mental health practitioners with strategies to help students reduce (and ultimately extinguish) the use of NSSI as a primary coping behaviour.

column36: SIGIRR: Preserving Gut Defense by Suppressing Epithelial TLR/IL-1R Signaling
column37: The human gut is normally filled with 'good' bacteria that help us digest our food. They also help defend us from 'bad' bacteria that cause food poisoning. It is important that our immune system does not attack these 'good' bacteria, since this would lead to chronic intestinal inflammation, pain and diarrhea. However it is also important that our bodies can fight off any invading 'bad' bacteria, in the event they defeat our good bacteria and try to escape our intestines and cause disease. We are studying the cells that line our guts, since we believe they are key to our body's ability to properly decide when our intestines are under threat by dangerous bacteria. We have identified a protein, called SIGIRR that helps these cells make the correct decisions, since if it is missing, the intestine becomes very aggressive, attacking bacteria even when the threat of infection is low, and actually increasing the risk of developing severe food poisoning. By studying SIGIRR, we hope to develop new ways to reduce the risk of gut infections, as well as stop the chronic gut inflammation seen in patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease.

column36: Physiology and mechanisms of adipocyte creatine energetics
column37: The pandemic increase in obesity is leading to serious obesity-related complications including diabetes, stroke, heart disease, infectious disease and many cancers. Two types of fat (adipose tissue) exist: white fat and brown fat. White fat store excess energy, while brown fat burns energy (thermogenesis). Impaired brown fat activity causes obesity in preclinical models and is associated with obesity in humans. Therefore, understanding the molecular determinants that control brown fat activation holds great promise in the fight against obesity. This proposal seeks to understand the underlying molecules that control a newly identified metabolic pathway in brown fat. Furthermore, the the health benefits of this pathway will be examined at the whole body level by using genetically engineered mouse models and by exploring the association of this pathway to human obesity. We have previously shown that creatine metabolism supports energy expenditure and is necessary to combat diet-induced obesity. However, the underlying mechanism that controls the anti-obesogenic action of creatine metabolism is not fully understood. This work will identify the molecular determinants that control creatine-dependent energy expenditure and will examine the role of these new molecules in regulating thermogenesis and providing protection from obesity. The proposed research has tremendous potential to discover new molecules that can be exploited therapeutically to combat obesity. Importantly, thermogenic brown fat has been found in humans, and so understanding how to activate this tissue has direct implications toward human health and well-being. The findings that come out of this proposal hold promise for improving the health of individuals and the population.

column36: A Pragmatic Cluster, Randomized, Crossover, Registry-Embedded Clinical Trial of Proton Pump Inhibitors vs. Histamine-2 Receptor Blockers for Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis Therapy in the Intensive Care Unit (PEPTIC Study)
column37: Patients receiving care in Intensive Care (ICU) are at risk for developing stomach or duodenal (small intestine) "stress" ulcers. Stress ulcers occur commonly when life-support (a breathing machine) is required or when a patient develops a bleeding tendency due to their illness. Stress ulcers may cause serious bleeding. Given stress ulcers are common and associated with adverse outcome, most patients are routinely given one of two types of drugs, a 'proton pump inhibitor' (PPI) or a 'histamine-2 receptor blocker' (H2RB) to prevent them. While prevention is vital, these drugs can have adverse effects, including risk of certain infections. This study will establish which of these routinely provided drugs to prevent stress ulcers leads to lower risk of serious bleeding, prolonged ventilation, C. difficile infection and hospital death. The study is a 'randomized cluster, crossover registry' trial comparing two standard of care drugs used for the same purpose. In this study, all data is already routinely collected via existing care systems. There will be two phases. In phase one, half the ICUs will be randomly (like a coin toss) assigned to use PPIs to prevent ulcers while the other half will use H2RBs. In phase two, each ICU will switch to the opposite treatment. For any given patient, if there is a specific indication for either PPI or H2RB, the indicated treatment will be given irrespective of treatment assigned to that ICU at the time. In other words, patients will always receive the treatment that clinicians believe to be in their best interests. In addition to the direct benefit of comparing ulcer treatments, the study utilizes an innovative and pragmatic design that may transform how future trials are performed in ICU. Such a design using existing data sources, imposing no added health record access, could provide opportunity to efficiently detect small, but clinically important treatment effects at comparatively lower cost than conventional randomized trials.

column36: Derivation of a clinical decision rule for emergency department head CT scanning in seniors who have fallen.
column37: There is very little research on diagnosing serious head injury (brain bleeds) in the elderly. One in three seniors experiences a fall each year and half of these people are treated in the emergency department. Almost all serious head injuries in older adults are caused by falling, and one case in six is fatal. Although falls are common for seniors, only 5% of those who are seen in the emergency department have a brain bleed. Over half of the seniors who go to the emergency department after a fall have a head CT scan. Currently, very few head scans done in the emergency department are positive for a brain bleed and the diagnosis is initially missed in 1 in 5 patients with a brain bleed. Ordering a head scan can prolong the emergency department stay by several hours. The emergency department can be an unpleasant and uncomfortable environment. We will create a new test (a clinical decision rule) which tells emergency doctors whether a head scan is needed or not. We will ensure that this new rule is safe. The rule will identify everyone who has a brain bleed, but will also lead to fewer head scans overall. This will allow patients with brain bleeds to receive the care they need and avoid unnecessarily long waits in the emergency department for those who do not have a brain bleed. Our study will follow 4000 people over the age of 65, who are treated in emergency departments across Canada after a fall. The emergency doctor will collect information about the risks of having a brain bleed and will follow a protocol for ordering a head scan. We will follow each patient for 6 weeks, to determine whether they are diagnosed with bleeding in the brain or not. We will use this information to develop a simple and safe test designed to guide emergency head scanning and improve the quality of care offered to seniors.

column36: Role of enteroviral infection in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a devastating disease marked by the deterioration of nerve cells that control muscles, leading to paralysis and ultimately death. ALS afflicts approximately 30,000 people in North America; however, there is currently no cure for this disease. ALS can be genetically inherited or can occur sporadically in people without any apparent history of the disorder in their family. The cause(s) of sporadic ALS remain(s) unknown. Infection with enteroviruses, a family of RNA viruses that include poliovirus, coxsackievirus, enterovirus-A71, and enterovirus-D68, has been proposed as a possible factor because they can target muscle-controlling nerve cells and polio survivors have been reported to experience new weakening in muscles that were previously affected by viral infection. However, definitive evidence of the role of enteroviruses in sporadic ALS is lacking. We recently made an exciting discovery that enteroviral infection results in the hallmark molecular and pathological features of ALS. In the present project, we will examine whether enteroviral infection induces ALS-like symptoms in normal mice and/or accelerates disease onset and progression in mice that are genetically susceptible. We will also test whether application of anti-enterovirus drugs can lessen the development of ALS. Moreover, we will investigate the possible mechanisms involved, with an emphasis on the RNA metabolic pathway, the host disposal system for damaged proteins and organelles, and the spreading mechanisms of ALS. We expect that the results of this project will not only uncover a potentially powerful new factor that contributes to the development of ALS, but also will allow for the development of novel forms of treatments for ALS.

column37: The human heart continuously beat over a person's lifetime at a regular pace (more than 2 billion heartbeats in a 70-year lifespan). For the heart to function properly, its upper (atria) and lower (ventricle) chambers must fill with and pump blood in an organized manner. This is achieved through an intricate network of electrical signals. Electrical signals are propagated through specialized proteins called ion channels. Each ion channel must fulfill a very specific function to ensure that the electrical impulse is transmitted normally. By bringing in the cell the calcium ions necessary for the heart contraction (beating), the L-type calcium channel is one of most important proteins for the heart function. Change in the function of the channel will affect the amount of calcium ions coming in the cell. Excess calcium ions in the cell trigger a series of maladaptive reactions that could ultimately result in fatal heart failure. It is therefore paramount to understand how calcium ions transit through the ion channel. L-type calcium channels are made from multiple proteins or subunits that ensure the controlled passage of calcium ions from the circulation to the cardiac cell. This project investigates the role of the "Cavalpha2delta1" subunit in bringing in calcium in the cell. Too many calcium ions will kill the cell and not enough calcium ions will make beating impossible. We are identifying the hotspots of the "Cavalpha2delta1" protein that are critical for incoming calcium ions under normal physiological conditions. We are further investigating the variations in the expression of "Cavalpha2delta1" in pathological settings, using rat models of heart failure. We use molecular tools that label regions of "Cavalpha2delta1" and we track their role by measuring the electrical activity of the protein. This knowledge will provide valuable insight into future gene and pharmacological therapies to target the active sites and design improved calcium channel blockers.

column37: Research shows that poor diet is linked to diseases such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer. Smartphone 'apps' may provide a major opportunity for resolving this public health issue because they are increasingly popular and they have the capacity to deliver individually targeted information and activities. Third, we will conduct focus groups with participants to gain insight into their experiences using the app to enhance the product for future versions. We will also be considering how low-income youth and youth at risk for health issues (e.g. diabetes or obesity) benefit from using the app. This will provide a model on how to use smartphone technology for promoting healthier diets and behaviours.

column36: ICOS signaling in T cell tolerance and gut homeostasis
column37: Our immune system works under two major rules: i) recognize and destroy pathogens ii) do not harm body's own cells. Failure of the first rule causes immunodeficiency whereas breach of the second rule leads to autoimmune diseases. White blood cells termed "T cells" play important roles in enforcing these rules. To perform this duty, T cells are guided by a group of cell surface sensors including "ICOS (inducible costimulator)". Highlighting the importance of ICOS in promoting immunity, humans lacking ICOS suffer from severe immunodeficiency repeatedly coming down to infections. However, some patients are affected by both immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. It has been puzzling how the lack of ICOS increases the chance of autoimmune attack in patients whose ability to fight pathogens is weakened. Using genetically modified mouse models, Dr. Suh's research team began to understand why: on one hand, ICOS supports "helper T cells" that facilitate immune responses against pathogens; on the other hand, it promotes a particular subset of "regulatory T cells" whose role is to stop autoimmune T cells from erroneously attacking body's own cells. Building up on these observations, Dr. Suh's team will elucidate what biochemical events ICOS evokes inside T cells and how those change T cells' behavior ultimately leading to immune disorders. This study will not only advance basic T cell biology but also help devise new ways to treat immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases.

column37: Hundreds of millions of people world-wide are exposed to the natural element arsenic in their drinking water. This has resulted in a global public health crisis because arsenic causes cancer in humans. In Canada, arsenic "hot-spots" naturally exist with levels in well water potentially exceeding acceptable levels. As a waste product of industry (especially mining), arsenic is also a serious Canadian concern. While reducing human exposure to arsenic should be a major priority, evidence suggests that humans are susceptible to arsenic-induced disease for decades following cessation of chronic exposure. Furthermore, in many regions, removing exposure is not economically feasible. Thus, strategies for the treatment and prevention of As-induced disease, in addition to exposure reduction, are necessary. Selenium is an essential trace element which is toxic in excess. Selenium reduces the toxic effects of arsenic in laboratory animals by increasing its elimination from the body. Low blood selenium levels in humans chronically exposed to arsenic have been associated with increased risk for arsenic-induced disease. Clinical trials for testing the ability of selenium tablets or selenium-enriched diets to prevent arsenic-induced disease have been initiated in arsenic-endemic regions. The study of how selenium modifies the toxicity of arsenic in human tissues has been largely ignored. Furthermore, selenium comes in many different chemical forms and the best form for supplementation and prevention of arsenic-induced disease is not known. The overall goal of this research is to understand the influence of different forms of selenium on arsenic metabolism and transport in human liver and red blood cells. Ultimately, this information is critical for optimizing human selenium supplementation and for the prevention and treatment of arsenic-induced disease.

column36: Influence of visual and proprioceptive feedback during voluntary motor actions
column37: A basketball player must make split second decisions on how to avoid her opponent as she drives for the net. Even if the opponent bumps into her, skilled players rapidly make adjustments to score the basket. This ability to move and interact in a complex world is a key aspect of voluntary control. The present proposal will apply mechanical disturbances (small bumps to the arm) and/or visual disturbances (shift a cursor representing hand position) and observe how monkeys generate motor corrections under a range of behavioural contexts. Critically, we will also record in primary motor cortex (M1), a key region involved in voluntary control, to understand how it supports rapid motor corrections. The first project will modify specific features of the environment (target shape or presence of obstacles) to observe how neural activity in M1 of monkeys and corresponding motor corrections change based on these features of the environment. Preliminary observations highlight how M1 responses to a visual disturbance increase when the monkey must generate a more vigorous correction to attain a small target as compared to a large target. Our second project addresses the fact that we can use different types of feedback (visual or proprioceptive feedback of the limb) to make motor corrections. The question is how do you combine these different types of feedback. We use mathematical models that consider features of sensory feedback (noise and transmission times) to predict how each sensory signal should contribute to online control. Preliminary data highlight how feedback from the limb has a much more powerful influence on motor corrections than vision. Examination of the pattern in M1 of activity associated with different types of sensory feedback highlight that these sources of sensory feedback are broadly distributed across this motor region. The results will provide important properties on brain circuits control that support our ability to move and interact in the world.

column37: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic Sclerosis, and Sjogren's Disease, are all Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases (SARD). These conditions share many clinical, immune, and genetic features, including high blood levels of antibodies that react against the nucleus of the patient's own cells, called anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA). These antibodies can be seen in SARD patients many years before development of symptoms. Although this finding suggests that it may be possible to identify people that are going to develop SARD prior to the onset of symptoms, high levels of autoantibodies can also be seen in healthy people who will never develop SARD. Because the SARD conditions at disease onset can already be associated with extensive inflammation and damage of various organs, the ability to identify people at high risk of developing SARD prior to the onset of organ damage would improve the prognosis of these conditions. However, to do this we need to have blood tests that accurately identify those individuals who will develop clinical disease and a better knowledge of what immune pathways would be best to target with drug treatment. In previous work, we identified several immune changes that are seen in individuals with ANAs who have no SARD symptoms or insufficient symptoms to make a diagnosis, and compared them with patients with new onset SARD. This has led us to propose a model for the critical immune events that lead to SARD development. In this study we seek to further develop this model and to determine whether it accurately predicts the individuals with a positive ANA test who will progress to clinical SARD. This will allow us to develop a biomarker panel that more accurately predicts individuals who are at high risk of developing SARD and to determine the best treatment to prevent and/or delay disease onset.

column36: Impact of temporary lesions of frontoparietal cortex on feedback processing during voluntary motor actions
column37: We take for granted our ability to perform simple daily activities such as reaching for a cup of coffee. Impressively, if we are accidentally bumped while reaching we automatically make swift and agile corrections to reach and grasp the cup. These motor corrections require the brain to quickly process sensory information about the body and the world around us, and convert this information into patterns of muscle activity to attain the goal. While cerebral cortex has been known to be involved in planning voluntary motor actions, recent studies suggest cerebral cortex may play a more prominent role in processing sensory feedback from the limb during voluntary movements. In Project 1, we will directly test this idea by transiently reducing neural activity (by cooling the cortical surface) in one of two key cortical regions in monkeys and quantifying how motor corrections to unexpected disturbances of the contralateral arm are altered during voluntary motor actions. Our preliminary data demonstrate that inhibiting neural activity in one of two brain regions, dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) or parietal area 5 (A5), alters the ability of the animal to generate motor corrections, demonstrating their causal role in feedback control of the arm. We develop mathematical models that highlight the patterns of errors associated with each cortical region are similar to that expected if PMd is involved in generating motor commands, and A5 is involved in sensory processing for online control. In Project 2, we will explore whether these cortical areas also influence feedback corrections with the ipsilateral arm by observing how cooling of PMd and A5 bilaterally or unilaterally impact motor corrections to unexpected limb disturbances. This work provides important new knowledge on the role of cerebral cortex in voluntary control that will guide our ongoing clinical studies quantifying motor impairments associated with various brain injuries and diseases.

column36: Understanding and managing the limits of physiological tolerance in heat vulnerable individuals during rest and physical activity
column37: Canada is entering unchartered territory as it experiences record high temperatures. However, our understanding of the effects of heat exposure on vulnerable Canadians remains incomplete, limiting our ability to make evidence-based decisions on the best strategies to implement to protect the most vulnerable. Recently, we showed that the body's response to heat is impaired in healthy adults as young as 40 years. This impairment is worse in older adults and in those with even well-controlled diabetes. In these individuals, heat tolerance is reduced as the body is unable to cool itself via the evaporation of sweat, placing them at increased risk of heat-induced illnesses or death. Further, we showed that commonly recommended exposure limits such as the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists Threshold Limit Values (TLV(R)) to manage the health and safety of individuals during exercise in the heat do not protect middle-aged and older adults from potentially dangerous increases in body heat storage and therefore core temperature. Our project will build on this work by using our air calorimeter (a device to accurately measure the heat dissipated and stored by the body) to assess how the presence of hypertension in older adults, with and without type 2 diabetes, may affect the body's ability to lose heat. Using this gold-standard method we will define the heat thresholds where age- and disease-related impairments in the body's capacity to dissipate can lead to dangerous increases in the amount of heat stored in the body (and therefore core temperature) during simulated exposures to hot weather conditions at rest and during exercise. Our project findings will enable 1) the identification of age- and disease-specific 'high risk' weather and exercise conditions, and 2) the development of short-term (heat advisories, work/exercise exposure limits, etc.) and long-term (heat adaptation strategies) heat protection measures to safeguard health during hot weather.

column36: Population-based longitudinal cohort study of femoroacetabular impingement of the hip using magnetic resonance imaging outcomes
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis. Hip OA on x-ray occurs in 19.6% of adults over age 50 and 14.3% of people over the age of 60 have hip pain. Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a condition where a bony bump in the hip region leads to pressure on different tissues in the hip. This is thought to be exacerbated by physical activity. FAI can be identified on x-rays. It has been proposed that FAI is the single most common cause of hip OA. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the only modality that can assess different joint tissues in detail, including cartilage and bone, and can detect early stage OA, often decades before it shows up on x-ray. With novel techniques, such as contrast-enhanced MRI of cartilage, we can see damage in cartilage even earlier. We have previously recruited a randomly selected cohort of 182 people with and without FAI, with and without hip pain. Subjects were evaluated in detail at baseline with questionnaires, including a life-time physical activity questionnaire, x-rays, MRI, contrast-enhanced MRI and blood/urine samples for future biomarker analysis. We propose to reevaluate this cohort 6 years after baseline. The objectives of this study are to determine whether 1) those with FAI, compared to those without, are at increased risk of worsening of cartilage damage and early hip OA on MRI; 2) physical activity is a risk factor for early hip OA on MRI and whether this risk is exacerbated with FAI; 3) biomarkers predict early hip OA. This study is unique. For the first time, in such a well-defined cohort, we will determine the risk of FAI and of physical activity on early hip OA. Our results will be generalizable to the population at large. Understanding the role that these factors play in the development of hip OA over time is a key step in future prevention strategies, to improve treatment of this disabling condition and thereby reduce the burden and health care costs of this disease in Canada and world-wide.

column37: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), also referred to as Axial Spondyloarthritis, imposes immense burdens on Canadians with this disease in terms of function and quality of life. We will also define the genetic signature of the white blood cells which are activated in AS and which maintain the inflammation in the joints. The outcome of our research can have significant impact on the treatment and diagnosis of patients with AS. First, identifying the molecules which direct white blood cells from the gut to the joint sets the stage for novel treatments to block such cell traffic. Secondly, identifying receptors on the critical white blood cells opens the possibility of identifying what activates these cells and what innovative approaches could interrupt the activation of these inflammatory cells. Finally, the addition of genetic profiling of T cells to currently known risk factors could contribute to earlier diagnosis of AS.

column36: Trans PULSE Canada: A National Study of Transgender Health
column37: Transgender (trans) persons are those whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth. This project builds on our success in Trans PULSE Ontario (2005-2014), a trans health study that documented major inequalities and changed social and health care policies. column36: Uncovering the structural basis for the mechanical properties of elastin
column37: The proper function of many human tissues, such as major arteries, lungs, and skin, depends on their capacity for elastic extension and recoil. The protein called elastin is responsible for these vital properties, and defects in the elastic matrix formed by elastin lead to various cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases. In addition, biological techniques have made it possible to generate artificial materials with mechanical properties resembling those of human elastin, with important potential applications as biomaterials for tissue repair and drug delivery. However, to understand the role of elastin in health and disease and to design useful materials with tuneable mechanical properties, we must first understand how elasticity is controlled at the molecular level. In this project, we will use a combination of computer simulations, NMR spectroscopy, and other biophysical approaches to uncover the molecular basis for the mechanical properties of elastin. We have developed simplified model systems that encapsulate the key properties of the entire protein and enable us for the first time to obtain detailed information about how this protein imparts critical mechanical properties to elastic tissues. In particular, we will investigate how the molecular structure of elastin controls extensibility and elastic recoil (how spring-like these materials are), resilience (how much heat is dissipated in every stretching and recoil cycle), and stress relaxation (how much energy it takes to keep them extended). This work will provide critical insight into the factors underlying susceptibility to highly-prevalent vascular diseases such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and aneurysms. Ultimately, this insight will also guide the rational design of biomimetic materials of high significance to the health and well-being of Canadians, with potential for use in artificial skin for burn victims, vascular grafts for heart patients, or in scaffolds for growth of artificial tissues and organs.

column36: Workplace exposures and prostate cancer: analysis and reporting on a Canadian population-based study
column37: Each year, more than 21,000 Canadian men are diagnosed with prostate cancer. Because its causes have not yet been identified, ways to prevent it remain unknown. There is compelling evidence that the environment plays a role in the development of this cancer. Several chemicals are themselves carcinogens or act as hormone modulators, and could be at play. The workplace is a preferential window for studying environmental chemicals. Most workplace chemicals eventually find their way into the general environment so studying them bear relevance to the population at large. However, there has been very little research based on strong methodological protocols in this area. Benefiting from the support of several Canadian funding agencies, the largest and most comprehensive study ever conducted on workplace risk factors for prostate cancer was initiated in Montreal in 2002. Some 4,000 men were recruited and interviewed to elicit information on a wide range of sociodemographic, lifestyle and medical factors. Lifetime work histories, representing 15,727 detailed job descriptions, were collected and translated into exposure to hundreds of specific chemical agents. Using state-of-the art methodological approaches, we assembled an unparalleled occupational database enabling to study the role that lifetime exposure to occupational chemicals, night work and physical activity/inactivity play in prostate cancer development. The coding of this colossal occupational component was completed in 2015, but funding available could not support its analysis. CIHR funding is sought at this time to leverage this large effort and investment, to support the primary data analysis and dissemination of findings on 19 sub-groups of environmental exposures assessed in the workplace. Workplace research is a major driver of environmental protection. Study findings will serve as important evidence for establishing preventive measures against prostate cancer in Canada, and elsewhere in the world.

column36: Neurocognitive effects of osteocalcin in type 2 diabetes
column37: As they age, people with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) suffer a faster decline in memory and thinking abilities, allowing dementia to set in on average 2 years earlier than in people without T2DM. As people live longer with T2DM, strategies to protect the brain from the debilitating and costly cognitive complications of T2DM are urgently needed. Current medications for T2DM improve blood sugar control, but they do not fully correct the hormone changes seen in T2DM. New evidence suggests that lower levels of a particular hormone released from bone during exercise, osteocalcin, is associated with brain changes and thinking abilities in older people. This hormone is 35% lower in people with T2DM, but it remains to be seen whether it can explain the deficits in memory that commonly occur in T2DM. We aim to show that lower levels of osteocalcin in the blood predict poorer memory and thinking abilities in people with T2DM. We also aim to show that the benefits of a 6 month exercise program are limited in T2DM by low osteocalcin levels. We will follow people with T2DM as they undertake either 6 months of exercise or an education intervention, to see if exercise increases osteocalcin levels. We will also compare the exercising T2DM group to a control group without T2DM of similar age, gender and body weight undertaking the same exercise intervention to see if people with T2DM can attain the same increases in osteocalcin and cognition when they exercise as people without T2DM. Overall, this study will determine if the body uses osteocalcin to protect against cognitive decline, and if T2DM blocks these benefits. The study will determine whether the osteocalcin system could be targeted with new drugs to prevent cognitive decline in people with T2DM.

column36: Bioengineering a finger joint replacement
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a disease of joints which are composed of soft tissue (cartilage) covering the ends of bones. It is the most common type of arthritis in Canada, and finger OA affects 10% of women and 7% of men. In the absence of disease modifying treatments, current therapeutic modalities are aimed at reducing pain. These treatments alleviate symptoms but do not inhibit the processes that result in the changes characteristic of this disease. Failure of these treatments usually culminates in joint replacement surgery. Current studies reporting outcomes of artificial finger joint replacements have highlighted the high rate of failure and lack of efficacy in restoring hand function by such implants. We have developed an alternative biological approach to joint repair that involves formation of a personalized biological replacement designed for secure fixation by bone ingrowth while presenting a surface lined by cartilage that will mimic the native joint form. In time as the bone substitute component degrades and is replaced by natural tissues (bone), this replacement part will allow for complete joint regeneration to desired form and function. The goal of this research proposal is to develop and evaluate a biologic small joint replacement in a pre-clinical animal model. The goal is to design a finger joint replacement that can be used to resurface a joint in the hand or wrist affected by either osteoarthritis or any inflammatory arthritis such as psoriatic or rheumatoid arthritis. With the results obtained from the proposed studies it will be possible to progress towards translating our approach into a clinical treatment for people with hand arthritis.

column36: Premature carotid atherosclerosis evolution and plaque vulnerability assessed by quantitative ultrasound biomarkers in HIV-infected individuals
column37: Atherosclerosis development is multifactorial and involves the accumulation of lipids within the artery wall. At the early development stages of the disease, the cross-sectional area of the artery is not modified as only an inward vessel wall thickening is observed. With more advanced progression of the disease, partial and total artery blockage may occur thus impacting the flow of oxygen and nutrients to downstream organs. An occluding artery is known in the medical field as a stenosis, whereas the thickening of the artery wall at the origin of this flow obstruction or stenosis is labeled a plaque or an atherosclerotic plaque. Carotid arteries are particularly prone to atherosclerosis and the rupture of a plaque by mechanical stresses (due to the blood pressure and cyclic pulsation of the artery) can lead to the formation of a blood clot, its migration within the arterial system of the brain, leading to a subsequent stroke. Although knowledge on characteristics defining carotid plaques at risk has advanced, predicting rupture is very challenging. A few imaging methods have been developed for this objective, namely magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray computed tomography, positron emission tomography and ultrasound imaging. These technologies provide imaging biomarkers of risk but none of them aim imaging biomechanical stresses at the origin of plaque rupture. We developed a method that can directly image the deformation of the artery wall likely contributing to the initiation of plaque rupture. We are also developing quantitative ultrasound imaging methods to study plaque structural characteristics. The objective of our proposal is to further develop these methods to provide a computer platform to process ultrasound images and extract these new mechanical and tissue biomarkers for clinical evaluation of HIV patients at higher risk of atherosclerosis evolution and stroke.

column36: The everyday experiences of minorities in the health professions: 'Strange faces in the hallways'
column37: Researchers, educators and professional bodies have argued that we need greater presence of underrepresented minority groups in the health professions to meet the needs of changing populations. Evidence shows minority health care professionals are more likely to work with marginalized populations, and minority patients are more likely to seek care from them, and be satisfied with that care. While numbers of minorities have slowly risen in the health professions, there are still significant problems of recruitment and retention. Little is known about the day-to-day experiences of minority individuals who do enter the health professions, experiences which may shape where and how they practice, how long they stay in the profession and the extent to which they may be able to fulfill the potential for reducing health inequities. Thirty to 35 professionals will be interviewed from each of three health professions that differ in history, social status and degree of autonomy: medicine, nursing and occupational therapy. They will be from groups marginalized by race and ethnicity, Indigeneity, class, disability, and/or sexual/gender identity. Interviews will inquire about experiences of belonging and marginality, 'invisible work' such as deciding about disclosures, and strengths such as social networks, community relationships, values and beliefs, and connection with patients. This research will illuminate potential losses if efforts to increase diversity are not accompanied by efforts to reduce marginalization within the professions. It may inform the recruitment and retention of skilled health professionals, highlighting the resources minority group members bring to the professions as well as challenges they face. Ultimately, the results may help ensure that efforts to diversify health care reach their full potential.

column36: Initial vancomycin taper for the prevention of recurrent Clostridium difficile infection
column37: Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is a diarrheal illness that often comes from taking antibiotics or being in the hospital. It affects 37,000 Canadians a year with an estimated cost of $281 million. CDI can cause complications such as hospital admission, difficult to treat diarrhea with dehydration, kidney injury, and sometimes even surgical removal of the colon or death. Even with proper treatment, more than one quarter of patients develop another episode, called a recurrence, within a few months. There is an urgent demand for strategies to prevent these recurrences. Despite this pressing need, the evidence for the best initial treatment of CDI is limited. There is some evidence that taking vancomycin for longer and at decreasing doses (tapering) may reduce the risk of recurrence. Oral vancomycin is inexpensive and if tapering decreases CDI recurrence this would be a major finding. We will conduct a randomized controlled trial of an additional 14 days of vancomycin as compared to a placebo and evaluate for a reduction in the rate of recurrence. This trial will involve community-dwelling and hospitalized adults at one of 17 hospitals across Canada (affiliated with the Universities of British Columbia, Ottawa, Sherbrooke, Toronto, Queen's and McGill). The primary outcome will be recurrence between 14 and 56 days of initial treatment. We will also look at whether patients are less likely to die, be admitted to hospital, or need rescue therapies like stool transplantation or surgical removal of the colon. This project will provide important scientific evidence for or against vancomycin tapering for the prevention of recurrent CDI. This study has never been performed and right now doctors and patients rely on historical practice and small, limited studies to make decisions. Public funding for this study will help our team determine the best treatment to prevent patients from developing CDI a second or third time, eliminating a sizable burden of disease.

column36: Cryobiology of Cardiomyocytes and Engineered Living Cardiac Tissue
column37: Heart failure occurs when damaged heart muscle cells cannot pump enough blood and is the cause of over 30% of deaths worldwide. Heart muscle cells, called cardiomyocytes, have almost no ability to replace themselves. Promising treatments involve replacing dead cardiomyocytes with live cardiomyocytes, either as cells or as engineered (lab-grown) tissues. Co-Investigator Radisic's group has developed a new type of tissue from cardiomyocytes, called "Biowires". These can be used as a substitute for heart muscle tissue in research, for example, to test how well new heart drugs work or to test whether other drugs are toxic to heart tissues, a major reason for drug recall. A critical obstacle to the use of cardiomyocytes and Biowires is the inability to store them and keep them alive until needed. Cryopreservation uses temperatures as low as that of liquid nitrogen (-196 C) to preserve biological materials and is the only way to store mammalian (including human) cells and tissues long term. Cryopreservation is used routinely in medicine; cryopreserved stem cells are used to treat blood disorders and cryopreserved heart valves to replace faulty valves (heart valves are not made of cardiomyocytes). Despite the need for cardiomyocytes, there has been no comprehensive research on cryopreserving them. This study will develop procedures to cryopreserve heart muscle cells and engineered heart tissues in such a way that live and functioning cells are recovered when thawed. Principal Investigators Elliott and McGann will use their cryobiology and cryopreservation expertise to carry out the first comprehensive cryobiological study of cardiomyocytes with the outcome of making cardiac cells and tissues available on demand. This collaboration between Canada's leading cryobiology centre at the University of Alberta and Canada's leading tissue-engineering centre at the University of Toronto will advance Canada's international reputation in regenerative medicine and biotechnology.

column36: Pre-dementia at-risk states: a longitudinal study of cognition and neuroimaging biomarkers in Mild Behavioural Impairment (PARADIGM)
column37: Early detection of dementia is essential to implement preventative interventions and optimize treatment. The current approach to detection is to identify overt impairment in memory and thinking as a marker of dementia. However, the vast majority of treatments at this stage have not been successful, with the explanation that disease course is too advanced by the time cognitive impairment is recognized. A new approach to detecting dementia risk earlier involves assessing the emergence of changes in behaviour or personality in later life as potential indicators of brain dysfunction leading to dementia. A neurobehavioural syndrome called Mild Behavioural Impairment (MBI) has been described by an Alzheimer's Association consensus group, which identifies later-life onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS- eg. changes in behaviour or personality, onset of apathy or social disinhibition) as a high-risk group for developing dementia. For some, NPS may be the earliest manifestation of dementia, first noticed by family members and caregivers. Often, these changes in behaviour and personality are attributed to a psychiatric illness, and the connection to dementia is not appreciated. Further, the neuroanatomy of these symptoms is poorly understood. We will recruit people with MBI and perform brain scans and cognitive testing, at baseline and at 2 year follow up. We will compare brain scans in these patients to those collected in other studies funded by Brain Canada and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research to determine the neural signatures of MBI. We will also compare the rates of cognitive decline in MBI to those without MBI, and progression to dementia. This study will help identify symptoms for early diagnosis of dementia and potential targets for early treatment. It will also help us understand the importance of monitoring for emerging changes in personality and behaviour in older adults, as a cost-effective method for identifying people with a high risk of dementia.

column36: Intracrine endothelin signalling in heart cells
column37: Enlargement and stiffening of the heart occurs when the heart is continuously exposed to conditions such as elevated blood pressure and/or increases in the amount of certain molecules, such as hormones, in the blood. Certain factors, including endothelin, also stimulate the heart to enlarge, or hypertrophy, by acting on cardiomyocytes - the muscle cells of the heart. In addition, fibroblasts, another type cell in the heart, become activated, increase in number, and make the walls of the heart stiffer and less able to relax. Relaxation of the heart with each heartbeat is essential for the heart to fill with blood for the next contraction. We are investigating how endothelin, a naturally occurring regulatory protein, is involved in fibroblast activation and cardiomyocyte enlargement. If the underlying cause for these processes (e.g., increased endothelin release, high blood pressure) continue to be present, a point is reached where the heart can no longer function properly. In this proposal, the means by which endothelin stimulates the cells (cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts) of the heart are being studied. There are many steps in the chain of events initiated by endothelin acting upon heart cells. The first step is the interaction of endothelin with specialized proteins, dedicated to binding endothelin, called receptors. The final results include changes in the growth and function of the heart. The cells of the heart contain two types of endothelin receptor. These receptors activate a network of signalling systems, similar to a telephone network, within the cell. In this project, the function of endothelin receptors that are located on the cell nucleus will be studied to determine their role in regulating the growth and function of muscle cells in the heart. The goal of this research it to identify novel targets for the development of drugs to be used to prevent or treat heart diseases.

column36: The Role of Ketones in Heart Failure
column37: Although advancements in therapies to treat cardiovascular disease have reduced the number of deaths of cardiac patients, these treatments/interventions have ultimately increased the number of people who eventually go on to develop another clinical condition called heart failure. Simply stated, heart failure is a condition that is defined by poor heart function that prevents the heart from pumping enough blood to the rest of the body. For decades, it has been established that one of the contributing factors of the failing hearts poor performance is the heart's inability to generate enough energy to beat properly. Recent studies have shown that a major fuel for the heart is ketones. Ketones are molecules that are produced by the liver from fats and can be used in the heart to produce energy. Of importance, recent work has suggested that the failing heart (in both mice and humans) increases the amount of ketones used to produce energy in what is thought to be an attempt to increase energy production. However, whether or not this increase in ketone use by the heart is beneficial or detrimental to the failing heart is still unknown and future research into this area is clearly needed. Using 2 mouse models of heart failure, we will investigate the role of ketones in heart failure and determine if they are good or bad for the heart. We hypothesize that increased ketone use by the failing heart is beneficial and propose that providing even more ketones to the heart can be used as a potential new therapeutic approach for the treatment of heart failure. Together, our studies will contribute to increasing our knowledge about heart failure and further test new treatment strategies for heart failure.

column36: Characterizing cerebral thrombus composition with Phase-based MRI
column37: In Canada, over 50,000 people suffer a stroke every year. Of those, 85% are ischemic - i.e. caused by a clot that blocks an artery in the brain. Not all clots are the same, and studies have shown that knowing the composition of the clot can help doctors plan the best therapy. For example, some clots can be removed to restart blood-flow and thereby improve patient outcome. Clot composition can also help to infer the source of the clot (i.e. did it come from the heart or break off from a large artery); this is important to determine the best post-stroke treatment to prevent a second stroke. Unfortunately, there are no current methods that can be used to determine clot composition in stroke patients. We have developed a fast new MRI method that that - for the first time - can create different types of images, which are sensitive to the different components of stroke-causing clot (i.e. red blood cells, platelets, fibrin, lipid, calcifications). We plan to determine the relationship of the different MRI parameters and clot composition by first imaging clot samples that have been removed from patients with a stroke (as part of treatment) and correlating these images against histological measures of composition. We will then image patients who have suffered a stroke and still have the thrombus in their brain vessels. Using a combination of MRI parameters we will be able for the first time to distinguish between strokes caused by clots that have come from the heart versus clots that have broken off from a large artery. Knowledge of the source will enable doctors to more appropriately treat patients who have a clot from a cardiac source (usually related to irregular heart rhythm) earlier by giving blood thinners, that results in preventing repeat strokes. Ultimately, our new method can also be used in the emergency department, to determine the best treatment option for each patient's stroke.

column36: Cellular mechanisms regulating the pathogenesis of secondary progressive CNS autoimmunity
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease in which the insulating sheath that surrounds nerve cells of the brain and spinal cord begins to degrade. This can ultimately lead to significant impairment of movement and cognitive decline. Canada has one of the highest rates of MS incidence in the world, and thus it is crucial that we study the causes of, and potential therapies for, this disease. In particular, the "secondary progressive" SP form of MS affects a little less than half of all patients, yet there are no treatments for this form. MS is complex disease in which many different types of cells can contribute. In this research project, we focus on two cell types, the CD4+ helper T cell and the CD8+ killer T cell. Data indicates that both are involved in MS, but their exact role is not well understood. Here, we aim to better understand the molecular signals that make CD4+ and CD8+ T cells cause damage to the nervous system. To help us do this, we developed a new experimental model in which mice develop SP-like MS at a frequency similar to that seen in humans. We will use gene knockout and gene therapy techniques to understand the role of specific genes to the disease process. These efforts will help identify drug targets, and may also help generate tools with which we can better predict disease progression.

column36: Precision diagnostics in childhood diabetes; therapeutic implications
column37: Our research aims to address the problem of certain uncommon forms of diabetes that are often incorrectly diagnosed and, as a consequence, prescribed a treatment that is not the best for the specific patient. There are different causes of diabetes but, in children, the most common form is type 1 diabetes (T1D) that results from autoimmune destruction of the beta cells in the pancreas that produce insulin. Insulin by injections or by pump is the only treatment. Type 2 diabetes, due to obesity and sedentary life, can rarely be seen in teenagers but in a non-obese individual under the age of 18, a high blood sugar is automatically diagnosed as T1D and treated with insulin injections. This is correct in most cases but about 1% of children diagnosed as T1D have uncommon genetic forms of diabetes. These patients have the same symptoms as T1D and are clinically indistinguishable from T1D but they have intact beta cells that only need some "help" and can be treated with pills. We propose that the percentage of these cases is higher than 1%, because we have evidence that not all genes whose mutations cause these uncommon forms have been discovered. In our cross-country collaboration, we will test 5,000 Canadian children and we will select about 1,000 who are the best candidates for a whole exome sequencing, a state-of-the-art technology that allows a thorough examination of all 18,000 known human genes. With the new genes that we will discover, we expect that the total number of such cases will be considerably more than 1%. The number of cases is small, but across Canada there are as many as 3,000 or more patients that can benefit from this life-changing diagnosis. More important than pills vs. injections is that the pills allow much better control of the blood sugar that helps prevent the long-term complications of diabetes (blindness, kidney failure, amputations)

column36: Understanding persistency in the high-cost category among mental health and addiction patients
column37: It is a well-known fact that a small number of patients incur a relatively large amount of health care costs. This finding has attracted the attention of policymakers who are generally interested in finding ways to decrease costs. There has been some research on these patients but very little on high cost patients with mental disorders and addictions. There has also not been much research that has tried to understand why mental health and addictions high cost patients continue to be high cost users for many years. Using health care data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences in Toronto Ontario, we will investigate how persistent mental health and addictions high cost patients 18 years of age and older use the health care system. We will define mental health and addictions high cost users as all patients with 50% or more of mental health and addictions-related costs and provide a description of this patient group. Our model will help us understand why some patients remain in the high cost category over time. It will also help us know whether this experience differs by sex, age group, income level and administrative health region. A more detailed understanding of what makes these individuals an expensive population to treat may help reorganize the health care system so that we can address their health needs in an effective and timely way. For example, information on who remains in the high cost category over time can help understand which individuals are more likely to be hospitalized or use the health care system more frequently. This work may also help us design appropriate prevention policies to target different groups of patients with mental disorders and addictions.

column36: Process Evaluation of the SuDDICU trial: An international randomized cluster crossover trial of the impact of a preventative antibiotic regimen (SDD) on patient outcome and antibiotic resistance within intensive care
column37: To understand if treatments such as drugs or procedures effect patient outcomes (e.g. symptoms, quality of life, survival), medical researchers conduct studies comparing outcomes of patients that receive the treatment to outcomes of patients that do not. However, because many treatments are complex (involve multiple parts and/or people), it can be difficult to understand the meaning of study results due to local differences influencing the way the treatment being studied was introduced and delivered. A process evaluation is a type of study that occurs alongside the main study and enables understanding of factors influencing how a treatment was introduced and maintained over the duration of a study as well as how much of the treatment was delivered as planned. We will conduct a process evaluation of a multi-centre study studying if a regimen of antibiotics (drugs that kill bugs) given to prevent rather than treat an infection to critically ill adults during admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) reduces death, antibiotic usage, and antibiotic resistance rates (drug is no longer effective for a certain infection) - The SuDDICU study. We will conduct surveys, interviews, audits, and observe practice in ICUs taking part in the trial to understand: (1) how the treatment was introduced at each ICU and maintained over time; (2) if the treatment was delivered as planned; and (3) what this information can tell us to understand the results of the main trial. Our process evaluation will enable us to better understand if these preventative antibiotics saves lives and reduces antibiotic usage as well as the impact on antibiotic resistance. It also will give us information about whether we could expect the same findings if we introduced the intervention into other ICUs after the study and how best to do this.

column36: Alberta oil sands development: impact on reproductive health
column37: The oil sands in Northern Alberta have undergone intense development over the past decade. There are widely opposing views of the industry with oil sands supporters highlighting the significant economic benefits for Canadians, and critics raising concerns regarding environmental and human health impacts of oil sands development. The people who are most affected by the oil sands industry are the First Nations communities living in the Peace-Athabasca Delta. Elders and community members are concerned that chemicals produced from oil sands activity are contaminating the water supply and harming the health of wildlife and humans. One of the major areas of concern is related to reproductive health. Oil and gas contaminants have the potential to impact fertility of Indigenous men, women and children as well as the unborn generations. In addition, reduced reproductive success in wildlife means population declines which impact the cultural, economic and social well-being of Indigenous communities through the erosion of the trust they have in their natural environment, and as a consequence, impacts on their ability to harvest and consume traditional foods. The goal of this project is to determine the impact of chemicals from oil sands activity on reproduction in mink, a culturally and economically significant species. These results will also provide insight about the effects of these chemicals on human reproductive health.

column36: Neural and Molecular Basis of Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression
column37: Opioid medications are widely used in pain management, but present the side-effect of respiratory depression that can be lethal with overdose. Opioid drugs induce sedation, i.e. loss of consciousness, and considerably reduce breathing. When overdosed, opioids can shut down the nervous system, completely stop breathing, induce severe hypoxemia and patients may eventually die. The current epidemic of opioid overdoses is resulting in over 2,500 in Canada according to the Public Health Agency of Canada. Opioid drugs are responsible for thousands of emergency visits every year, causing a severe health and financial burden. Nevertheless, opioids remain the pharmacological cornerstone of modern pain therapy and there are currently no treatments to prevent respiratory depression by opioids without reducing their analgesic properties. The current opioid antagonist naloxone is very effective at blocking mu -opioid receptors, i.e. the receptors that mediate respiratory depression by opioid drugs, but it also blocks opioid analgesia so it cannot be used as a preventive treatment. The development of new therapies has been hindered by a lack of knowledge about how opioid medications alter brain activity and what mechanisms underlie respiratory depression by opioids. This research program proposes to identify the mechanisms underlying respiratory depression by opioids and to find new therapeutic solutions to prevent it. Without a preventive treatment to reduce the severity of respiratory depression, opioid medications will continue to present severe health issues and the death toll associated with opioid drugs will continue to rise.

column36: Stress Hydrocortisone in Pediatric Septic Shock (The SHIPSS trial)
column37: Septic shock accounts for up to 8% of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admissions worldwide, carries significant morbidity and has a mortality rate between 5% and 40% depending on the geographic region in which it occurs. Mainstays of treatment involve antibiotics, fluids and medications to improve blood pressure. However, the high morbidity and mortality of pediatric septic shock have led physicians to consider corticosteroids for unstable patients since corticosteroids are inexpensive and widely available. However, although the use of corticosteroids for septic shock has been widely debated for over 40 years, there is no clear evidence for or against this practice. Some pediatric studies have reported an improvement in blood pressure and organ function with corticosteroids while other studies have suggested an increase in blood sugar and the inability to fight infection. We therefore plan to conduct a randomized controlled trial to determine if hydrocortisone (a corticosteroid) compared to placebo improves outcomes (as measured by mortality and quality of life) in children with septic shock. This study will enroll 1032 patients in 30 centres across Canada and the US. Eligible children will include those from age 1 month to 17 years, with a severe infection and need for medications to support their blood pressure. We will exclude patients that have a known reason for receiving corticosteroids, who have malaria or a fungal infection and those who do not wish to participate. We will also assess organ function, potential side effects and healthcare costs in the hydrocortisone and placebo groups. Our study will be the first pediatric septic shock trial that is large enough to assess the potential benefits of corticosteroids and the first trial to assess the effect of a treatment for septic shock on quality of life. The results of this study will provide evidence on which to base recommendations for corticosteroid administration in pediatric septic shock.

column36: The physiology of adult neural stem cells
column37: Since the beginning of the 19th century, the adult brain was considered as an organ deprived of any regenerating capacity. This dogma was, however, shaken by the discovery of neural stem cells in certain regions of the adult human brain and their ability to produce new neurons. This discovery raised an exciting possibility of using endogenous brain regenerative capacity to cure brain damage and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, although promising, the use of neural stem cells to heal these devastating diseases is far from reach. The main reason for this is that endogenous neural stem cells in the human brain are found in their quiescent "dormant" state and in order to induce brain regenerative capacity we need to understand what are the signals and mechanisms that control the transition of stem cells from their quiescent to proliferative states. In this project using mouse models, advanced imaging and genetic tools, in vivo monitoring of stem cells activity, and pharmacological interventions we will study intrinsic mechanisms underlying maintenance of quiescent state and their entry into the proliferative phase. Our study will allow better understanding of the mechanisms that maintain stem cells quiescence and control their proliferation. This, in turn, will provide new strategies to increase neurogenesis and "turn on" brain regenerative capacity to heal devastating neurodegenerative diseases and brain trauma.

column36: Targeting RIPK3 as a key regulator in the development of SLE
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that affects approximately one in every 1000 Canadians, and can result in life-long suffering and premature death. Individuals with SLE develop an immune response against their own cells, but it is not known how or why this abnormal immune response arises. Treatment of SLE often involves broad suppression of the immune response, with consequences for the patient's resistance to infection. A better understanding of how SLE arises will lead to more selective drugs that target the specific biological processes that cause SLE. The aim of the proposed research is to investigate how SLE originates. Using an animal model of SLE developed by us, we identified an important protein called "RIPK3". RIPK3 regulates cell death and inflammation, and is essential for the development of SLE in our animal model. In this study, we will determine whether RIPK3-dependent effects on cell death or inflammation, or both, are responsible for murine SLE. We will then use drugs (pharmacologic agents) to specifically block these RIPK3-dependent processes. Our research in animal models will provide proof that targeting RIPK3-dependent mechanisms may lead to the prevention or improvement of SLE. Our findings with human cells will indicate whether RIPK3-dependent cell death is important in human SLE. In summary, our proposed research has the potential to generate a novel innovation that can impact both knowledge about SLE and patient care. An improved understanding of SLE will ultimately result in better treatment and prevention of this chronic and debilitating disease.

column36: The Hsp70 chaperone system and protein quality control
column37: Age-related diseases are a growing medical challenge for an aging population. These include neurodegenerative diseases which have no known cure, such as Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and which are characterized by the accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates. Normally folded proteins can become damaged by mutation or stress, leading to misfolding and aggregation. The chaperone proteins are critical cellular defenses against aggregation. They bind misfolded proteins to promote folding, or help remove permanently damaged proteins by degradation. Nevertheless, damaged proteins build up during aging and are thought to overwhelm the chaperones. Hsp70 is one of the most important chaperones, as it has key roles in protein folding and prevention of aggregation. The different functions of Hsp70 are determined by its regulatory co-chaperone proteins. Recently, another role of Hsp70 was found, in the solubilization of proteins out of aggregates. We propose that disaggregation of proteins is an important pathway for their degradation by proteasomes, which may have an advantage over the slower degradation of aggregates by autophagy. We will examine Hsp70-mediated disaggregation using purified proteins and in live cells, to determine its biochemical mechanisms. A focus will be the co-chaperones and chaperones required for disaggregation. Next, we will address the importance of disaggregation and proteasomal degradation in models of ALS, caused by mutations in the SOD1 protein leading to its aggregation. We will then address other cellular proteins that are at risk of aggregation when the Hsp70 system is impaired. Post-translational modifications on Hsp70 that regulate its function under different stress conditions will be identified. Our project will explore how Hsp70 acts and fails in protein aggregation diseases, and the possibility of enhancing its function towards future therapies.

column36: Pol II and its R-loops in the control of rDNA and genome stability
column37: The human body is composed of trillions of cells, the longevity of which is dependent on the balance between forces that promote or stall growth. On one hand, early cell stalling is known as senescence and it can lead to premature cellular aging if kept unchecked. On the other hand, uncontrolled cell growth can lead to cancer. Critical to the cell's ability to strike the right balance between growth and senescence are highly repetitive DNA regions known as ribosomal DNA (rDNA) repeats. These rDNA repeats harbour genes from which molecules known as ribosomal RNA (rRNA) are produced. rRNA production is critical to general protein production and cell growth. In contrast, DNA damage at rDNA repeats can lead to premature senescence. How cells strike the right balance between the impact of rDNA repeats on growth and senescence remains unclear. Here, we pursue new findings suggesting that a new protein complex localizes to poorly understood spacers located between rDNA units in order to optimize protein production and growth while limiting DNA damage and cell senescence. We have two main objectives. First, we wish to decipher the rDNA-regulatory role of this complex at rDNA in order to reveal new mechanisms that are critical to the regulation of growth and senescence in human cells. Second, we will exploit the new knowledge of this mechanism to preferentially induce early senescence and limit tumorigenic potential in breast cancer cells. Overall, this work will uncover key health-related knowledge pertaining to the balance between cell growth and senescence while revealing how it can be exploited to combat deadly human diseases.
