column37: Blocked arteries reduce blood supply to the heart causing chest pain. Doctors use two procedures to restore the blood flow. Bypass surgery creates a new path around the blocked artery. Stenting reopens the blocked artery by inserting a tiny mesh tube, called stent. In clinical trials, bypass surgery had better results than stenting for treating multiple arteries. Therefore, doctors may suggest surgery rather than stenting for multiple blocked arteries. However, these trials did not include patients who had to wait for many weeks before receiving the treatment. We study results of bypass surgery and stenting done at various times after treatment decision. We want to find out whether waiting for bypass surgery is better than having immediate stenting. We use a patient registry to find results of bypass surgery and stenting in BC. First, we obtain registry data for patients with multiple blocked arteries. Second, we select those who did not need emergency treatment. Third, we link these data to hospital records and vital statistics. Then, we compare the frequency of treatment results in three groups of patients. The first group consist of patients who had bypass surgery by the time recommended by doctors. The other two groups are patients who had bypass surgery after the recommended time and those who had stenting. The proposed study will help strengthen health care in Canada. Our research will add new data from a large number of patients treated at various times after treatment decision. The data will help doctors to compare delayed surgery and immediate stenting. When recommending bypass surgery or stenting, doctors are concerned about unintended results of the treatment. The study will determine whether results of delayed bypass surgery are better than results of immediate stenting. This knowledge will help physicians decide how to treat blocked arteries when patients have to wait for surgery. The study will also advance methods for studying access to cardiac care.

column36: Oriented cell division in prostate stem cell homeostasis and cancer
column37: Prostate cancer is one of the most common and most deadly cancers in males. Over the years, research has mostly focused on the identification of treatments against advanced forms of prostate cancer. In this grant proposal, we rather aim to understand the cellular environment that promote cancer initiation, to eventually devise preventative treatments aimed at maintaining a healthy prostate tissue organization. Such approach is not currently available for prostate cancer. Our recent results in mouse models show that when the cells of the prostate divide in the plane of the tissue (horizontal), they maintain a proper tissue architecture made of one layer of basal cells and one layer of luminal cells. However, when the cells divide vertically, they create an aberrant layer of cells that lose their polarity, proliferate more and harbor stem/progenitor cell characteristics. We believe that this cellular environment promotes the birth and growth of tumor initiating cells. Here, we will study how cells defective in the orientation of cell divisions generate this abnormal cell population and will identify new regulators that promote vertical divisions. We will also generate cancer initiating cells (single cells missing the tumor suppressor Pten) and identify the detailed characteristics in the cellular environments that promote their growth. We expect the normal prostate epithelium to suppress cancer initiation but the aberrant depolarized cell populations to promote it. We will corroborate our results in premalignant human tissues obtained from our clinical collaborators and link these results to disease outcome. Together these results will greatly advance our understanding of oriented cell division and the maintenance of tissue architecture. More importantly, it will identify the characteristics of premalignant lesions that are associated with cancer initiation and progression. These results will be critical to develop interventions aimed at preventing prostate cancer.

column36: Neuroimaging Prodromal Neurodegeneration in Synucleinopathy
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) have a long prodromal interval, meaning that symptoms have started but the disease is not yet fully developed. This interval is key to developing new preventative treatments, because they can be used at a stage when they are most likely to work. Studying prodromal PD and DLB was limited until the discovery that >80% of people with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), a disorder in which people act out their dreams at night, actually have prodromal PD/DLB. This means that studying people with iRBD gives a rare opportunity to directly observe the earliest stages of disease. Although routine clinical scans in PD/DLB are normal, there have been major recent developments. PET and SPECT scanning can find loss of the dopamine system which underlies motor parkinsonism. We have developed a new PET scan of the cholinergic system, to help understand cognitive loss. Also, there are new MRI scan techniques with exciting potential to identify early PD/DLB. We will recruit 40 iRBD patients and 20 controls. They will have a comprehensive clinical prodromal marker assessment as part of our ongoing cohort study (our center has the largest cohort of iRBD patients in the world). All patients will have three different brain scans: a cholinergic PET scan, a dopaminergic PET scan, and an MRI scan that includes three new markers of prodromal PD/DLB. We will follow patients each year, to see the scans predict development of disease over time. So with this study, we will: 1) See if the acetylcholine system is abnormal in early-stage PD/DLB, and if this might explain some of the cognitive changes that happen to our patients. 2) Test three new MRI markers to diagnose early-stage disease. 3) Be able to continue the world's leading cohort on prodromal PD/DLB, so we can follow-up the many key prodromal markers we've already assessed and test new ones as they are discovered.

column37: Parkinson disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder in the developed world. column36: Kir Channel Regulation by Membrane Lipids: An Enabler of Hemodynamic Sensing in the Cerebral Circulation
column37: Brain arteries control how much blood is delivered to nerve cells. To ensure the right amount of blood is delivered, cells in the artery alter their electrical activity using "ion channels". As their name suggests, ion channels allow sodium, chloride, potassium and calcium to move across a membrane and there are many different types. One, called the inward rectifying K+ (KIR) channel is unique as it breaks away from expectations, leading us to raise key questions. Is KIR a simple channel or is it regulated in a way we haven't defined? What is the function of this unique channel and what impact does disease have on it? We propose that KIR channels in brain blood vessels are regulated by plasma membrane lipids. Specific lipids allow KIR channels to sense blood pressure and flow and when cholesterol rises, this channel is compromised. Goal, Aims: We will examine KIR channels in brain blood vessels and determine the chemical agents and stimuli which control them. There are three aims and they include: 1)Defining whether membrane lipids regulate KIR. 2)Defining whether blood pressure/flow regulate KIR. 3)Defining whether high cholesterol impairs KIR. Methods, Expertise: We will test ideas in cells and brain blood vessels from rats, genetically altered mice and humans. We will use computer models, measure the electrical activity of isolated cells, see how vessel size changes and quantify brain perfusion. Our work is supported by a network of collaborators. Impact: This grant challenges the idea that KIR is a boring background channel. We argue that KIR is uniquely regulated by membrane lipids, enabling them to sense blood pressure/flow, the dominant factors setting vessel size and tissue perfusion. We incorporate Knowledge Translation by working with neurosurgeons who provide brain arteries so that we can validate our ideas in humans. We also use animal models of high cholesterol to see whether this lipid impairs KIR and consequently blood vessel size.

column37: Chlamydia is the leading cause of sexually transmitted bacterial infections and the most common cause of infectious blindness worldwide. Rates of Chlamydia infection are increasing steadily worldwide, including in Canada and the US. The proposed research will use this newly developed RLDIs mouse model to investigate the immune responses and immunological mechanisms involved in each step of the disease. The results of this research will advance greatly our understanding of the Chlamydia-induced disease process. Our study has a strong potential to translate the design and evaluation of vaccines and novel therapies from animal model to humans. Our work can also be applied to understanding other infectious diseases.

column37: Optimal self-regulation, the ability to set limits and manage one's own emotions, attention, and behaviour is vital to health and success in life. The nutrition component of this intervention consists of an individualized nutrition plan that is tailored to women's needs, as well as educational sessions with a dietitian. Our exercise intervention involves women engaging in a structured and monitored walking program. In this study, half of the women will receive our nutrition+exercise program and the other half will get treatment as usual from their healthcare providers. The main objective of this study is to determine if fetal exposure to our maternal intervention leads to improved self-regulation in offspring at 48 months of age compared to women who receive usual pregnancy care. If we are able to show that offspring self-regulation can be improved via our structured and monitored nutrition+exercise program during pregnancy, it could be used to prevent or reduce the severity of behavioural, emotional, and cognitive problems in children early in life.

column36: Molecular characterization of VHL-HIF axis in cancer
column37: Oxygen homeostasis or balance is a vital organizing principle for human development and physiology. A universal response to compromised oxygen availability involves a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which accumulates during low oxygen levels or hypoxia to trigger the expression of numerous genes including those that promote new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), anaerobic metabolism, and the production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells to facilitate adaptation and survival in hypoxia. We and others have shown that von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumour suppressor protein targets HIF for oxygen-dependent degradation. Mutations in VHL cause VHL disease, characterized by the development of tumours in multiple organs including the kidney, as well as a chronic condition called polycythemia where patients produce too many red blood cells. Notably, kidney cancer remains to be the leading cause of both morbidity and mortality for VHL patients. More recently, mutations in HIF have been reported to cause certain types of cancers also observed in VHL patients as well as polycythemia, revealing a new class of HIF-driven disease. However, it remains unclear what drives the metastatic process of kidney cancer and why certain HIF mutations cause cancer while other HIF mutations cause polycythemia. This proposal, based on our promising preliminary data, aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying these mysteries with important clinical implications.

column37: Epidemiological data shows that the majority of mental illnesses have their onset in early life, and point toward early life stress as a major predictor of mental illness later in life. Early life is also marked by the maturation of select brain circuits which are implicated in mental illness and are particularly sensitive to stress. column36: Crystalloid FLUID Choices for Resuscitation of Hospitalized Patients: A Pragmatic Comparative Effectiveness Trial (FLUID)
column37: Patients who are acutely ill and admitted to a hospital will likely receive salt fluids to help improve blood pressure, and maintain vital organs (ex: heart and kidney) and the circulatory system. Two salt fluids most commonly used for these purposes are normal saline and Ringer's lactate. Both salt fluids have been used for several decades. Until recently, it was thought the fluids are essentially equivalent other than some minor differences related to the concentration of salt components and buffers that are contained to reduce acid in the blood. Normal saline is the dominant fluid used and contains more sodium and chloride than Ringer's lactate. In contrast to normal saline, Ringer's lactate contains a buffer as well as a small amount of potassium and calcium. Recent data suggests that salt fluids that contain less chloride like Ringer's lactate, may cause less acid in the blood, and less kidney failure and death. But Ringer's is more expensive than saline and previous studies have been small or had weak designs. To answer this question with confidence, it requires many patients to be recruited into the trial from many hospitals, using a process of randomization. Such a large sample size is required when the expected differences in study outcomes between the two fluids are small. Our research team will conduct a novel pragmatic randomized trial in 16 hospitals where each hospital stocks exclusively one type of fluid for 3 months and then switches to stocking the other fluid for another 3 months. We will determine if Ringer's lactate versus normal saline reduces death and re-admissions to hospital, emergency department visits, need for dialysis, surgical re-operation or re-intubation, and discharge to a facility other than home. Our team will also conduct a costing analysis. The information gained from FLUID will have a significant impact on fluid therapy practise and is relevant to patients, clinicians, and the Health Care System.

column36: Microglia response to chronic sleep restriction
column37: Chronically insufficient sleep is common in our society and is increasingly recognized as a cause of health and safety problems with significant economic costs. We only have a limited understanding of the mechanisms underlying the health and cognitive impairments associated with chronic sleep loss. It is crucial to develop improved strategies to deal with these negative consequences by understanding the mechanisms underlying impaired health due to chronic sleep loss. Towards this goal, we have developed a rat model of chronic sleep restriction. Our recent findings show that 4 days of insufficient sleep activates microglia (immune cells in the brain) and that this activation persists for at least one week following sleep loss. We propose to use this model to examine the mechanisms underlying the effects of chronic sleep loss, with a focus on the role, if any, of microglia. As there can be sex differences, we will use both male and female rats. To examine whether microglia activation is involved in the changes in sleep patterns observed during chronic sleep restriction, microglia will be inhibited using an antibiotic that blocks microglia functions, and sleep patterns will be recorded. We will also assess the response of microglia to chronic sleep loss and examine the anatomical relationship between microglia and neurons involved in sleep regulation after chronic sleep loss. In addition, we will determine whether chronic sleep loss sensitizes microglia to produce an exaggerated immune response in the brain to inflammatory stimuli that are subsequently administered. Insights gained from the proposed research could have significant health and economic impacts since sleep is so important, yet so often sacrificed for other activities. Ultimately, the proposed research will help us develop innovative strategies for coping with the negative impacts of reduced sleep and help reduce the adverse impacts of chronic sleep loss on the health of both men and women.

column36: Hormone therapy induces reprogramming to drive aggressive prostate cancer
column37: Targeting the androgen receptor (AR) has been the cornerstone of treatment for men suffering from prostate cancer, essentially starving tumors of the fuel they need to grow and survive. For these men who progress to this deadly form of prostate cancer called Neuroendocrine Prostate Cancer (NEPC), the only treatment option is a highly toxic chemotherapy however the survival is only measured in months. Toward this end, we discovered a protein called BRN2 that is essential for the growth and survival of NEPC. Moreover, we have developed drugs that can inhibit BRN2 and display potential to inhibit NEPC progression. The current proposal outlines the following strategies: - Understand BRN2's role in structural changes in the genome and how that causes treatment resistance as well as this transformation to NEPC. - Test our first-in-field BRN2 inhibitors on human patient derived NEPC tumors that are grown in mice. - Test the efficacy of the BRN2 inhibitors in combination with current AR inhibitors. column36: Novel therapeutic targeting for cognitive deficits in depression and aging
column37: Cognitive deficits, including impaired attention, learning, memory and problem solving, occur in the majority of depressed patients and are a hallmark of normal aging. They greatly reduce the quality of life for affected individuals and their family, and significantly impact the health care system and society's productivity. Notably, cognitive deficits are not treated, and in some cases are negatively affected by current drugs, and persist in periods of remission. In normal aging and depression, we previously reported biological changes affecting a subtype of brain cells that provide chemical inhibition, namely somatostatin (SST)-positive GABA neurons. Preclinical rodent models confirm the alterations in SST-neurons and support a causal role in cognitive deficits. SST-neurons signal through a5-GABA-A receptors (a5-GABAA-R), suggesting that augmenting brain inhibition through a5-GABAA-R may have pro-cognitive effects. Over the last 10+ years we and colleagues have developed and optimized a series of compounds that activate a5-GABAA-Rs and that display drug-like properties and therapeutic efficacy in mouse models of cognitive deficits in depression and during aging. A patent application was submitted and conversations are on-going with biotech companies. Here we will select the best candidate among our optimized leads, based on drug-like profile and therapeutic efficacy (Aim 1). We will then complete studies under regulatory guidelines to submit a new drug application to health care regulatory institutions (Aim 2). Finally, we will develop in parallel a non-invasive neurophysiological tool to measure brain inhibition in human subjects (Aim 3). This tool will be used to stratify patients based on pathological severity, and to facilitate subsequent clinical trials. Industry partnership will be sought throughout the project. At completion, this project will deliver the first potential cognitive enhancer drug and a companion diagnostic tool to test it in humans.

column36: Apoptotic control of urinary tract morphogenesis by the IAP pathway
column37: In recent years, we have shown that proteins called LAR-family phosphatases are necessary for the normal maturation of the connection between the ureter and the bladder. When these genes are inactivated in the mouse, urine is produced but the obstruction between the ureter and the bladder prevents it from reaching the bladder, which results in severe renal damage. We found that this defect occurs because a group of cells should be eliminated to allow for the ureter-bladder connection but in mouse embryos mutant for the phosphatases, these cell are not eliminated correctly. Hence, LAR-family phosphatases are necessary for a form of cellular suicide called programmed cell death (or apoptosis). We have now identified that LAR phosphatases regulate cell death through Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (IAPs) and obtained evidence that this pathway may be also be involved in malformations of the urogenital system. In this proposal, we layout our plan to elucidate precisely how LAR-phosphatases, tyrosine kinases and IAPs regulate apoptosis. We will explore the role of dead cell removal in tissue formation and will further determine whether the regulators of programmed cell death we identified in the mouse are responsible for developmental defects in humans. For this, we established a collaboration with a pediatric nephrologist who collected the DNA from patients suffering from ureter-bladder connection problems. Using this DNA we found that some of these patients seem to carry mutations in the programmed cell death pathway we identified. We will characterize further these mutations and validate them in mouse models. In addition to shed light on the newly identified link between LAR-phosphatases and programmed cell death, these results will impact our understanding of renal malformations in newborns and help physicians determine the best course of action to ureter-bladder connection defects with the least stress and invasive procedures for children.

column36: Improving Access to Specialist Care through eConsult for Patients Living with Chronic Pain
column37: One in five Canadians suffers from chronic pain, a debilitating condition that requires prompt access to care for effective treatment. Individuals with chronic pain report the lowest health-related quality of life among all patients with chronic conditions. Unfortunately, these patients often wait months or even years for treatment, causing anxiety and reducing their capacity to participate in daily activities. Innovative solutions are needed to provide these individuals with prompt access to the care they need. One such innovation is the Champlain BASE (TM) eConsult service, which allows primary care providers and specialists to communicate electronically. By providing a channel for primary care providers to contact specialists with questions about their patients' care and receive a quick reply-often in as little as two days-eConsult can improve access to specialist advice for chronic pain patients. Since its launch in 2009, eConsult has shown its ability to improve access to specialist advice. This includes chronic pain specialists, who feature among the 109 specialty groups the service offers. Building on our past success, we are now proposing to expand the eConsult chronic pain services in three provinces: Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec. We will begin by looking at the unique needs of patients in each province and adjusting the service to best address them. Next, we will launch the service in select regions within each province and identify any challenges we face. Lastly, we will expand the services provincially, measure their outcomes on patients' care, and create a series of communication tools that can be used by others looking to launch eConsult in their own regions. Our team includes experts in eConsult and chronic pain care, as well as patient partners who will review the entire process and have a say in how the project is run. Together, we will work to ensure that all patients have quick access to high quality chronic pain care.

column36: Organization of the Cerebellum
column37: The majority of neurons (up to 85%) in the brain are found in the cerebellum. The cerebellum integrates information from various sensory systems and is involved in numerous processes including motor control, learning and cognition. How the cerebellum organizes information from the various senses is still poorly understood. The cerebellum has a unique organization: some neurochemicals are expressed as "stripes" throughout the cerebellum. The most thoroughly studied of these neurochemicals is the enzyme aldolase C, also known as zebrin. Although the exact role of zebrin is not clear, it is expressed in the same way in all vertebrate species studied, indicating that it is essential for cerebellar function. The organization is such that there are stripes of neurons that express zebrin alternating with stripes of cells that do not express zebrin. The goal of the proposed research is to understand how these stripes relate to function and processing of information in the cerebellum. We use a part of the cerebellum known as the vestibulocerebellum as a model. This is an area where visual, vestibular and spinal information is integrated in order to control eye movements, posture, locomotion, and balance. To understand how information is organized with respect to the zebrin stripes, we will determine how the visual, vestibular, and spinal connections are associated with particular zebrin stripes in the vestibulocerebellum. Moreover, we will record from neurons in particular zebrin stripes to determine the nature of sensory processing within each stripe. These studies will provide basic information about the principles of fundamental sensory organization in the cerebellum. This is critical for understanding diseases of the vestibulocerebellum that cause disturbances of visuo-motor behaviour (e.g., oscillopsia, oculomotor abnormalities, vertigo), and diseases that affect the cerebellum in general such as Wernicke's encephalopathy, Alzheimer's disease and autism.

column36: Dissecting mechanisms by which Excitatory Amino Acid Transporters (EAATs) contribute to CNS function and neurological diseases
column37: The brain has two main cell types - neurons and glia - and interactions between them are crucial for many processes involved in brain development and information processing. For example, their two-way communication regulates the number and types of cells that are produced, and influences how neurons communicate chemically with one another at their sites of contact called synapses. There is still much to learn about the interactions between neurons and different types of glia. We are particularly interested in how glia use Excitatory Amino Acid Transporters EAATs) to take up important chemical transmitters like glutamate from synapses, and to act as channels for the passage of chloride ions in and out of cells. Defects of EAATs are a common feature of a variety of disorders such as ataxia, stroke, epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases. Historically there has been a dearth of tools to study and manipulate glial subtypes in the laboratory. We have spent several years generating and collecting such tools, and we have launched new approaches to study neuron-glial interactions. In particular we are using a genetically tractable model organism, the fruit fly, because it has a simple yet sophisticated brain and central nervous system (CNS) in which neurons and glia perform many of the same functions they do in humans. It is also easy to study how the CNS controls behaviors like movement and sleep. The fruit fly has two EAATs that predominate in two distinct subtypes of glia. In this proposal we are specifically addressing the following questions: What is the role of the EAAT1 chloride channel? How do mutations of the EAAT1 cause episodic ataxia? How is EAAT2 different from EAAT1, and what is the role of EAAT2 in controlling sleep?

column36: Molecular based approach for discovery and improved outcome for children and young adults with low grade glioma
column37: Brain tumors are the most common cause of death and long term disability in children, and adolescent/young adults (AYA). Low grade gliomas (LGG) are the most common brain cancer in this age group. Childhood and adult LGG have very different biology and patient outcomes. Most children with LGG have excellent survival rates but have suffered from long term sequelae of over-aggressive therapy. This has led to new treatment strategies (targeted therapies with use of oral pills) and rarely using aggressive surgery and radiation. In contrast, adult LGG typically transform to high grade glioma resulting in very poor outcome even with aggressive therapy. Importantly, some AYA LGG behave like childhood LGG and unfortunately get unnecessary toxic treatments. Similarly, some childhood LGG behave as adult LGG and die from their tumor. Figuring out which is which is still an extensive research gap. To address this issue, we established the LGG taskforce, which includes major pediatric centers in Canada, US and adult centers in Toronto. Our group played a key role in uncovering many of the common mutations in childhood and adult LGG. Based on these data we plan to use novel genomic diagnostic tools to find all the mutations driving childhood and AYA LGG. We will use new tools to detect these mutations in blood and other body fluids thus avoiding the need for surgery to diagnose and monitor response to LGG. We will then the right new therapy to fit the right mutation. Finally, we will treat these children and AYA with targeted therapies which will replace the current toxic surgery and chemo-radiation approaches. Completion of this project will transform our way of treating these children and young adults to improve survival rates for these patients. This study can serve as a model for other cancers in this vulnerable age group.

column36: Academic health centers in Canada: Prospects and challenges for learning health systems
column37: Health care organizations are being criticized for their low ability to adapt and improve at a sufficient pace to meet patients' needs and expectations. Recently, a new form of organization, namely Academic Health Centers (AHC), have emerged with promises of being incubators for innovation. Hence, bringing together three core components of education, research and delivery of care, these organizations are supposed to continuously improve their practices. These promised are also rooted in the digital revolution that is underway, where electronic data open new doors for learning about the actual outcomes of care. In Canada, huge investments have been made to create AHCs, but little is known on their actual ability to support innovation. This is where this project will make a contribution: by analysing what are the ingredients for AHC to become incubator for innovations in the Canadian health systems and ultimately to improve care. Our research is structured around three phases: 1) An exploratory study throughout all 17 AHC in Canada will be conducted to identify key innovations, and essential ingredients for their emergence and scaling up. Documents analysis on innovations, as well as interviews with CEO and key stakeholders will be performed. 2) Case studies will be conducted in purposefully selected sites to understand dynamics of innovation within these organizations. Various sources of data (e.g. internal reports, interview with key informants) will be used to analyze in-depth processes of innovation and their relationship with organizational and policy contexts. This phase will allow for the elaboration of critical pathways and identification of key ingredients for innovation in AHC. 3) These pathways and ingredients will be validated through a consensus with experts from Canada and other jurisdictions using a Delphi method. It will culminate in recommendations for policy makers and managers to increase the value proposition of AHC in Canada.

column36: Frailty rehabilitation: A community-based program to promote healthy aging
column37: Frailty is an important clinical state that contributes to falls, hospitalization, institutionalization and death. When an individual simultaneously has many health problems, a frailty "tipping point" may be triggered by even a minor stressful event such as adding a new drug or urinary tract infection. Our research suggests that approximately 23% of Canadians over age 65 are frail, and by age 85 this estimate increases to over 40%. As we learn more about frailty and its consequences, there is an urgent need to develop community-based interventions that will prevent or delay frailty in older adults. Our proposed study will examine if frailty rehabilitation program is an effective community-based intervention to promote healthy aging. We will recruit 324 frail community-dwelling older adults (aged 70+) into three groups: Group 1: will receive twice-weekly socialization program Group 2: will receive twice-weekly group exercise program Group 3: will receive the multimodal frailty rehabilitation program including twice-weekly group exercise, and additional frailty management (nutrition assessment and medication review plus protein supplementation, as needed). We will examine how effective frailty rehabilitation is by tracking changes in physical function and frailty status at 0, 6 and 12-months. We will also examine healthcare by tracking emergency department visits, hospitalization and institutionalization for 1-year after the intervention. Results of this study will help us to understand the best ways to keep older adults healthy, independent, and active for as long as possible. Our research team are international leaders with expertise in healthy aging, rehabilitation, geriatric and family medicine.

column37: Lung cancer is the second most common cancer in both men and women and the number one cause of cancer related death in North America. Lung cancer is rarely detected at the early stages of disease because symptoms tend to be mild and non-specific. When diagnosed, 60-75% of patients have advanced disease and are considered incurable. For the large group of patients with advanced disease, survival is only 12-15 months after treatment. Therefore, even a small improvement in treatment, is significant for these patients. Lung cancer treatment is based on damaging the DNA of cancer cells with chemotherapy and radiation. Many patients do not benefit from this treatment because their tumors have strong DNA repair systems. Our aim in this project is to develop new drugs that can block DNA repair in lung cancer but do not affect normal cells, so that the toxic effects of DNA repair inhibition is not observed in normal cells. We have already found "hit" molecules that block specific DNA repair pathways in human lung cancer cells through chemistry and modelling of their interactions with the DNA repair pathways. The newly developed "hit"s were shown to be effective in killing cancer cells of specific genetic defects (known as PTEN deficiency, which is reported in up to 70 % of lung cancer cases) in petri dish or in animals. In addition, the "hit" inhibitors of DNA repair were found to sensitise cancer cells to DNA damaging chemo and radio therapy. In this proposal, we will develop nano-carriers with specific signal molecules on their surfaces that bind to lung tumor cells but not to normal cells. These nano-carriers will direct the inhibitors of DNA repair to lung tumors, so that their activity can be enhanced,. They will also reduce drug exposure to normal cells so that their toxic side effects are reduced at the same time.

column36: When Expertise Collides: Using Experience-Based Co-Design to Enhance Care Experiences for Children with Medical Complexity in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit
column37: The goal of this project is to improve care for hospitalized medically fragile children and their families. The care of these children is a high priority for our health care system because of their growing numbers, and the challenges their care poses for families and health care professionals. To improve care, we will partner with parents and children with medically complex conditions admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), and critical care health providers. Our approach places the experiences of parents and children at the heart of efforts to improve care. We will video/audio-record interviews with children and their parents to collect their stories of PICU care. Seeing and hearing these stories firsthand is a powerful mechanism to help others understand the lived experiences of these children and families. We will produce a 30-minute film of the highlights of those families' PICU experiences and use it to inspire groups of children, parents and health care professionals (doctors, nurses, and others involved in their PICU care) who will work together to design ways to enhance PICU care. We will then make changes necessary to improve PICU care for children with medically complex conditions and their families. This approach is called Experience-Based Co-Design (EBCD), and it places the family's experience at the centre of the design process. Lastly our team will explore and evaluate peoples' experiences with EBCD, and whether or not this approach contributes to lasting improvements in PICU care. Our team will work with parent and professional stakeholders to share the study findings broadly, and influence care across the country.

column36: CAreful Ventilation In Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (CAVIARDS)
column37: Each year almost 40,000 Canadians receive mechanical ventilation for a a diffuse inflammation of the lung caused by infection, flu or trauma and called acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Mortality is still unacceptably high >40% : this can be improved by making ventilation more protective for the lung. Mechanical Ventilation is indeed life-saving but, paradoxically, can cause further inflammation and injury in the remaining healthy lung. There is ample evidence that current mechanical ventilation is not sufficiently lung protective. We think we can provide a safer ventilation based on bedside measurements which we previously described to make ventilation non injurious and safe. Positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) is one of the cornerstone of the treatment but it needs to be based of the lung response to pressure: we want to avoid exposing non responders to high pressure. We have designed a technique which can determine the individual response and the need for high or low pressure. Maximal distension of the lung is currently not well assessed at the bedside. We have described a technique using esophageal manometry to determine the distension of the most exposed regions of the lung, at higher risk of injury: this offers a limit for protection. We also showed that this distension can be used during spontaneous assisted breathing. We want to show that all these measures, which we call respiratory mechanics can feasibly and safely guide ventilator management and improves physiology. We want to perform a pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) to assess the feasibility of our approach (Respiratory Mechanics-directed ventilator management), aand show it is safe (minimal signal for harm) and feasible.160 patients will be enrolled in 2 arms over 18 months. It will be compared to a standard protocolized approach. The results will inform a definitive study.

column36: The influence of heme on the gut microbiota and colon carcinogenesis
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 2nd most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canada, with an average of 72 Canadians being diagnosed with CRC every day. A link between red meat consumption and the development of CRC has been documented by many studies, and has been partially attributed to the presence of heme in the red meat. Heme, an essential part of the protein hemoglobin, is an iron-containing molecule that serves to bind oxygen. An important role in the development of CRC has also been attributed to the gut microbiota, the complex community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that live in the digestive tract. Because bacteria compete for iron, an essential metal indispensable for their growth, and not all bacteria are equipped with the necessary tools to capture and utilize heme iron, we think that heme may change the gut microbiota composition by promoting the growth of certain bacteria over others and cause a bacterial imbalance (dysbiosis). We have generated preliminary results suggesting that dietary heme induces dysbiosis, aggravates inflammation of the colon (colitis, as seen in Inflammatory Bowel Disease), and promotes CRC development in rodents. The overall goal of our research is to determine the role and the mechanisms by which dietary heme modulates the gut microbial composition. In addition, we will test different strategies based on natural and engineered probiotics to reverse the non-beneficial effects of heme-induced microbiota shifts. The high incidence of CRC in Canada compared to other countries has increased the need for preventive measurements, for which it is critical to understand contributing mechanisms. This project will further our understanding of the link between heme, microbiota, and CRC, and how to reverse gut microbiota imbalances (dysbiosis), opening novel avenues for CRC prevention. This project builds on our team's unique expertise in iron metabolism, microbiology, and bioengineering as well as specialist platforms in the institute.

column36: Cholinergic influence in aging and brain pathology
column37: Canada faces significant aging of its population as the proportion of adults 65 years of age or older increases more rapidly than all other age groups. Since the incidence and prevalence of dementing disorders such as Alzheimer's disease increase with advancing age, the number of persons with dementia is expected to increase as the Canadian population grows older. It has been estimated that by the year 2031 there will be approximately 1.4 million Canadians with dementia. Degeneration of a group of brain cells that release the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, named cholinergic neurons, is a key feature in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and correlates with pathology and dementia. However, the precise relationship between decreased function of these cholinergic cells and pathology in AD is still elusive. Importantly, ACh signaling seems to be important to modulate inflammation as well as aging of cells however, the molecular mechanisms are not completely understood. Our goals in this proposal are to determine how cholinergic neurons influence brain inflammation and cellular senescence and to investigate different alternatives to bypass cholinergic failure and improve brain inflammation. Importantly, results from these studies are highly translational and could reach the clinic in a foreseeable future.

column36: Studying inflammatory bowel disease etiology: a life course approach
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease is a chronic disease of the gut. It affects digestion and absorption of food, and elimination of waste. Its causes are unknown. After many studies, researchers have only been able to identify a few risk factors with certainty. They include family history of the disease and cigarette smoking. The causes of this disease are still unknown, but some researchers think that certain times in life could be more critical for the development of the disease. Our goal is to clarify the causes of disease, and identify which ones could be targeted by prevention program. We will study medical, lifestyle, and psychosocial factors from the time of birth until adult years. We will determine if they are linked to the development of the disease. These factors are for example: prematurity, breastfeeding, antibiotic use, diet, smoking, stress. We will also study carefully when these factors occur during a person's life. For this research, we will use a cohort of about 400,000 persons born between 1970 and 1974, in the province of Quebec, Canada. We created this cohort for a previous study by linking together some provincial administrative databases. Data on medical services and hospitalizations for inflammatory bowel disease were obtained until 2014 and will be used to determine who is affected by the disease. Then, we will ask about 2600 persons of the cohort to complete a web survey to obtain additional information. Among the participants, we will compare persons who have the disease to those who do not, and evaluate what are the key moments throughout their lives when these factors could increase the risk of the disease. This research will help understanding which factors increase the risk of inflammatory bowel disease by detecting if there are certain times in a person's life that are especially important. We will produce crucial information to establish prevention programs.

column36: Home to Stay: An integrated monitoring system using a mobile app to help reduce readmissions following colorectal surgery
column37: Background: Colorectal surgery includes surgery for colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease and other benign diseases such as diverticulitis. In Canada, approximately 21,000 colorectal surgeries are performed each year. Patients undergoing colorectal surgery face high rates of unplanned hospital visits including readmission to hospital and Emergency Room (ER) visits. These unplanned hospital visits lead to significant distress and anxiety for patients and increased health care costs. Research Aims: The goal is to evaluate the use of an integrated discharge monitoring system with a mobile application (app) to support colorectal surgery patients at home following discharge from hospital. Methods: The study will include 3 hospitals across Canada. Patients will be assigned to either a control group or intervention group. Control group patients will receive standard follow up care after going home following surgery. Intervention group patients will be enrolled in an integrated discharge monitoring system using an app to monitor their progress at home following discharge after surgery. The main outcomes are to measure the number of patients with unplanned hospital visits within 30 days of discharge following surgery, the quality of patient recovery and confidence managing one's own health care. Patients are eligible if they are being discharge home after having elective colorectal surgery, are 18 years or older and speak and understand English or French. At the end of the study, the outcomes between the control group and intervention group will be compared to look for important differences. Expected Outcomes: It is expected that the results of this study will show that the integrated discharge monitoring system will lead to a significant improvement in the quality of patient recovery and self-confidence with one's own health care, as well as significantly reduce the number of unplanned hospital visits for patients undergoing colorectal surgery in Canada.

column36: Developing evidence-based recommendations to prevent falls and improve safety during bathing transfers
column37: Bathrooms are common locations of slips and falls for older adults, with a significant number of injuries occurring in tubs or showers. Grab bars, bathmats and other assistive devices can improve safety when used during bathing, and are commonly recommended by healthcare professionals to help those with mobility limitations to safely enter and exit tubs and showers. Current clinical recommendations for bathing safety equipment are not based on evidence of their effectiveness for fall prevention, but rather on clinical experience and client perceptions of safety and ease of use. Proactive installation of grab bars has also been recommended to reduce fall risk in non-clinical populations (who also experience high rates of slip and falls in bathrooms), but information is lacking on where these should be installed to maximize effectiveness. With focus on aging and disability, this study will take a comprehensive approach to understanding and improving the safety of bathing transfers using rigorous laboratory evaluation of current and innovative practices to determine effectiveness of bathroom assistive devices for fall prevention. This important research is actively sought by two main stakeholders: clinicians who advise on bathroom safety and advisory members for building codes currently debating whether bathroom grab bars should be mandatory in newly-built homes. The former group seeks biomechanical evidence to guide client recommendations on the comparative effectiveness of bathroom safety devices. The latter group requires evidence to inform deliberations on the expected costs and benefits of requiring grab bars to be installed in home bathrooms. Our team will work with leading clinicians and policy makers to provide an evidence base to inform clinical practice and building code development. Preventing falls through improved evidence-based environmental design is of paramount importance to the health of Canadians and to support aging-in-place strategies.

column36: Cancer Therapy exploiting Conditional Synthetic Lethality based on Genotoxic Stress levels
column37: Because cancer cells have lost checkpoints that healthy cells have, they have increased levels of DNA damage. This DNA damage causes particular problems during replication, when cells make a copy of their DNA. (When a cell divides, both cells should have a complete set of the DNA.) Cancer cells therefore have higher stress levels than healthy cells and they rely on certain remaining pathways to survive this stress. An important signaling pathway after replication stress is initiated by a protein called ATR. Another important signaling protein is Wee1. Our unpublished studies indicate that cancer cells strongly rely on these two proteins to survive, and inhibiting the function of Wee1 or ATR by selective drugs is harmful to the cancer cells. But if both, ATR and Wee1, are inhibited, the cancer cell killing is stronger than one would expect from just an additive effect of each drug alone. We call this "Synergy". This promises to get a much better therapy response with a novel treatment combining the two drugs. Furthermore we see the synergistic killing in cancer cells at doses well tolerated by healthy cells. This is important to avoid side effects which are due to killing of healthy cells. In our preclinical studies, using human cancers grown in mice, we will test the combination treatment targeting ATR and Wee1 for the ability to inhibit tumour growth and prevent metastasis. In addition we hope to understand which tumours are most likely to respond to the combined inhibition of Wee1 and ATR inhibition. Because the Wee1 and ATR inhibitors we are using for our studies are drugs already being tested in the clinic (on their own, not in combination), our knowledge could soon find application in actual patient treatment. Because our lab focuses on breast cancer, we first will study that type of cancer. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in Canada and worldwide.

column36: The Role of Electrophysiology Testing in Survivors of Unexplained Cardiac Arrest: The EPS ARREST Study
column37: Sudden cardiac death (SCD), defined as an unexpected death due to a presumed cardiac cause within 1 hour of symptom onset, remains a major cause of mortality in developed nations despite aggressive efforts to reduce its societal burden. Within Canada, SCD is estimated to impact 30,000 individuals annually, with an approximate survival rate of 10%. The majority of cases of SCD in older individuals occur secondary to heart attacks and various forms of structural heart disease, while genetic cardiac conditions account for a significant proportion among young adults. Although always tragic, SCD is particularly devastating when it occurs in young otherwise healthy individuals. Among individuals that survive a near fatal event, when the initial coronary angiogram and echocardiogram fail to identify the underlying cause, the diagnosis remains unexplained despite extensive additional clinical and genetic investigations in approximately 50% of individuals. Failure to identify a cause generally leads to a diagnosis of idiopathic ventricular fibrillation and insertion of an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD). An inability to arrive at the correct diagnosis often precludes administration of optimal medical care, not only for the patient, but also for family members, given that these conditions often having an underlying genetic origin.

column36: PINK1 Inhibition as a Novel Therapeutic Strategy to Target Acute Myeloid Leukemia Stem Cells
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive type of blood cancer that kills over 1,000 people every year in Canada. Current treatments are often not effective in curing patients because they fail to kill a special type of cells known as leukemia stem cells (LSCs). These cells are resistant to chemotherapy and can give rise to relapsed disease. New treatments that kill LSCs are much needed in order to improve the long-term survival of AML patients. We made a novel and unexpected discovery that we can change LSCs into non-dividing harmless cells by shutting down the function of a protein known as PINK1. This protein controls the quality of mitochondria inside cells. Importantly, normal blood cells do not appear to be affected by inhibition of PINK1. In this proposal, we will explore 1) how PINK1 inhibition change LSCs into harmless cells, and 2) whether PINK1 inhibition can prevent leukemia development in mouse models of human AML disease. If successful, our proposed studies will help establish PINK1 inhibition as a new way to treat AML and the basis for future efforts to identify drugs that block PINK1.

The global aim of this application is to understand the biological functions of ERalpha and ERbeta in prostate cancer cells.

column36: A randomized controlled trial comparing Avatar Therapy to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in Schizophrenia with treatment refractory hallucinations
column37: Schizophrenia is associated with long-lasting health, social and financial burden for patients, families, caregivers and society. According to the World Health Organization, this burdensome illness is one of the top 10 causes of disability in developed countries. The costs associated with hospitalization, lifelong treatment and loss of productivity lead to a great economic burden. In Canada, the total annual costs associated with schizophrenia are over $10 billion. The main reason for this heavy burden is that 25-30% of schizophrenia patients respond very poorly to antipsychotic medication. Moreover, psychotherapeutic treatment alternatives are very limited for this suffering population. This unmet clinical need requires innovation and action. Psychotherapeutic treatment alternatives such as Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT) are very limited and provide at best moderate results. Virtual reality (VR) opens new exciting avenues to treat this illness. With immersive VR, we recently tested a novel psychotherapeutic intervention, Avatar Therapy (AT), where the therapist engages in a dialogue with the patient through a virtual representation of their distressing voice. This relational and experiential approach offers a unique opportunity to help patients gain control over their voice. The preliminary results of our randomized-controlled trial (RCT) pilot showed a large effect on auditory verbal hallucination for AT and a moderate effect for CBT. The main goal of the currently proposed RCT study will be to show that AT is superior to CBT for the treatment of chronic auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia. As evidence-based therapeutic options are limited for this burdensome illness and provide only modest symptomatic relief, the current trial will contribute to the validation of a novel approach answering a fundamental clinical need. The demonstration of the superior efficacy of AT would be a great breakthrough and will open new avenues to clinical treatment.

column37: Maintaining independence in our communities is a priority to ensure healthy, active and meaningful lives for our growing senior population and persons with disability. While home environments can be easily adapted to changes in one's unique needs, an overhaul of shared public spaces within our cities would require leadership and policy change from our governments - a challenge to implement unless sufficient evidence is provided. In outdoor spaces, pedestrian street crossing is a particularly challenging task for many older adults and persons with impairments. This is due in part to the physical design of the intersection and/or signaling features. These challenges are worsened during winter, as the accumulation of ice, snow and slush can create slippery conditions which impact safety and create physical barriers for ambulatory individuals and wheelchair users. The objective of our research is to understand and address current barriers to safety and accessibility at pedestrian street crossings, with a specific emphasis on winter travel. Focus groups with different user groups representing older adults, and persons with mobility, visual and hearing deficits, will be conducted to identify current barriers to accessibility and safety at intersections. We will then present innovative solutions to address the identified features of concern, to be constructed and evaluated in our simulation winter lab. In this manner, we will be able to uniquely evaluate the impact of each modified feature of the intersection individually and as part of a "whole" design. Our results will define a new standard for pedestrian crossings, addressing barriers to community mobility in winter. Our team will work with cities and policy makers to inform transportation standards and propose changes that reflect more suitable intersection designs for Canada's four-season climate. Findings will support an inclusive, age-friendly built environment, prevent injuries, and promote overall health

column36: Targeting airway cells for gene-editing to correct genetic diseases
column37: The main objective of the proposed research is to test a novel strategy for gene therapy to treat lung diseases, using cystic fibrosis (CF) as a model. CF is the most common fatal genetic disorder in the Caucasian population and is caused by mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. Multiple organs are affected by this disease, including pancreas, liver and and intestine, but lung failure due to chronic infection and inflammation is responsible for most CF-related morbidity and mortality. Despite the recent success in the development of new drugs that target mutated CFTR, these drugs are not available for most patients with CF and often result in limited improvement of CF lung disease. Thus, new therapeutic options are needed. Taking advantage of newly advanced gene-editing tools as well as our unique expertise in the fields of gene therapy and CF research, we plan to conduct preclinical tests of our therapeutic approach for treating CF lung disease. Previous lung gene therapy trials demonstrated the challenge of sustained expression of delivered genes due to the lack of efficient delivery vehicle and methods as well as strategies to avoid host immune responses. Our group has developed the most efficient vehicle and methods for gene delivery into airways. There are several advantages of our unique vector system over traditional gene carriers, such as large gene-carrying capacity, high transduction efficiency and the capability of reaching airway stem cells. In addition, our system, when used for delivering gene-editing tools, does not provoke a host immune response attacking the gene-edited cells. Our team has extensive experience in gene delivery to large animal models and gene functional analysis in patient primary cells. Considering the experience of our team and the resources in our CF Center, we are in an ideal position to conduct the exciting preclinical research we propose.

column37: Lupus is a life threatening, chronic disease that can affect many different parts of the body. One of the most common and severe forms of lupus involves the kidneys. Lupus kidney disease is more common and more severe among certain racial/ethnic groups than others, suggesting genetic differences are important factors in who will get kidney disease, and what the outcome of the lupus disease will be. We know from genetic studies in healthy people that genes determine in part how well kidneys function. But we have yet to discover all of the genes that influence a person's risk of developing kidney disease caused by lupus. This gap in knowledge is due in part to the fact that previous genetic studies of lupus did not have access to detailed information on kidney function measures from both blood and urine, and how they change over time within a person with lupus. We propose a powerful approach to identify genetic factors important to the development of lupus kidney disease and kidney function in people with lupus. In this project, we will use genetic differences and repeated measures of kidney function from blood and urine, to identify genes influencing kidney function and kidney disease in both children and adults with lupus. Our aims are to examine how (1) genetic differences, and (2) predicted amounts of gene products in different cells and tissues, relate to kidney disease and kidney function over time in lupus. We propose to study continuous, kidney measures from blood and urine, obtained at multiple times over the course of disease, in 638 children and 3,371 adults with lupus, from around the world. This project will discover genes causing lupus kidney disease. These new insights into lupus biology will help identify those at highest risk of developing kidney disease caused by lupus, predict progression to kidney failure, and enable individualized therapy. Ultimately these discoveries will improve care and outcomes for all patients and families with lupus.

column36: Understanding the complexity of dopamine transmission: Specific role of the neurons co-expressing D1 and D2 receptors.
column37: Synthesized in a few restricted nuclei in the brain, dopamine (DA) is a major regulator of motor and cognitive functions. The importance of DA neurotransmission is highlighted by its direct implication in neurological and psychiatric disorders, such as Parkinson disease, Tourette syndrome, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorders, Schizophrenia or addiction to drugs of abuse, to refer to the most established. Altogether, these disorders share in common a disturbance of DA transmission, however with either increase or decrease transmission, and sub-specific regional origins. With the development of novel genetic and molecular approaches in the last decade, it appears more and more that the DA transmission system, far from being homogeneous, is actually composed of distinct neuronal sub-populations. Whereas most research studied the complexity of DA neurons themselves, less attention is given to study the neurons that actually receive DA inputs. Our proposal will focus on a subpopulation of neurons in the striatum under the DA control that are regulating motor functions but also emotional and addictive behaviors. We do have strong evidence for considering that 10-20% of these neurons, which are expressing the two main DA receptors, called D1 and D2 dopamine receptors, are filtering the DA input at large. Such role was totally unsuspected; its study will bring a novel understanding on the regulation of brain function in normal and pathological conditions. It will also allow to rationalize the development of new and specific therapeutic approaches for several brain disorders.

column36: The use of autologous cell extracts to repair injured salivary glands.
column37: Among the Canadian population, each year 4,000 new head and neck cancer patients receiving radiotherapy treatment suffer from injured or destroyed salivary glands leading to permanent dry mouth (xerostomia). These patients suffer greatly due to discomfort in chewing and swallowing, tooth decay, sore throat, taste loss, and oral infections. While these patients can constantly sip water to reduce their discomfort a little, there are no curative treatments to date. The aim of our research is to offer these patients a practical and effective cure. Our research involves the use of a human bone marrow cell extract (BMCE) which is collected by freezing and thawing the patient's own bone marrow cells, thereby releasing their intracellular contents including molecular factors such as proteins and growth factors. Advantages of cell extract therapy includes reduced risk of immune rejection and thromboembolic complication, ease of obtaining cell extracts, long-term storage, and low cost of production. As human BMCE therapy is a novel technique, we would like to perform further testing in the following areas: #1) assessing its safety to repair salivary glands damaged by irradiation and reducing its cytotoxicity, and #2) substantially simplifying its mixture of molecules while enhancing its efficacy and biological activity. This research will be tested on human salivary biopsies and in mouse models with irradiated salivary glands. The potential impact of regenerating lost salivary tissues is enormous. We hope that through this research, we will be able to provide millions of patients worldwide with a curative therapy using a cell extract drawn from their own tissues to restore normal functions to their impaired salivary glands.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling the phase behavior and biosynthetic activity of the nucleolus
column37: Living cells are divided into specialized compartments called organelles. Typically, membranes form a selective barrier between organelles and the cytoplasm, such that each compartment can maintain a distinct biochemical composition that is tailored to its function. By concentrating substrates and isolating reactions, membrane-bound organelles increase the rate and efficiency of cellular metabolism. However, cells also contain organelles that are not enclosed by membranes. With no physical barrier, molecules can freely exchange between these compartments and the surrounding cytoplasm or nucleoplasm. Recent progress has focused on the composition and assembly of membraneless organelles, but their function remains poorly understood. The proposed research aims to establish how the unusual structure of membraneless organelles impacts their function. To answer this question, we will use quantitative imaging to visualize the nucleolus in the model organism C. elegans. The nucleolus is a membraneless organelle that produces ribosomes, molecular machines that a cell needs to grow. Indeed, cancer cells, which experience uncontrolled growth, have enlarged and hyperactive nucleoli. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that links neurodegenerative disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's disease, to changes in the fluidity and activity of stress granules and other membraneless organelles. Thus, understanding the relationship between the fluidity and activity of the nucleolus in the worm has the potential to advance the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of human disease.

column36: Role of endogenous remyelination after spinal cord injury
column37: Myelin is the fatty insolation layer surrounding nerve fibres that enables the fast conduction of electrical impulses. This layer also plays a role in the nutrition and maintenance of the nerve fibres themselves. Loss of myelin occurs in diseases like multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury. The nervous system can repair myelin (by a process called remyelination) but remyelination is incomplete and fails with increasing age. We hypothesize that this ultimately leads to the degeneration of the nerve fibres in the spinal cord. We further propose that this degeneration is responsible for the age-dependent functional decline after chronic spinal cord injury regularly seen in people. Using mouse models that allow us to visualize, inhibit and stimulate myelin repair we will provide proof of concept for this novel approach to treat chronic spinal cord injury and possibly aging of the brain.

column36: An integrated strategy to identify inhibitors of protein-protein interactions as potential therapeutics for Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease is a common and disabling neurological disorder that is increasing in prevalence and thus having a growing impact on the Canadian population. The disease results from a process, called neurodegeneration, in which certain brain cells die more rapidly than normal. Neurodegeneration leads to the clinical features of Parkinson's disease including motor symptoms (such as tremor, rigidity, slowness of movements, and postural instability) and non-motor symptoms (such as dementia, psychiatric symptoms, and sleep disturbances). Currently available treatments alleviate some of these symptoms, but they are associated with complications and limited efficacy. Furthermore, these treatments are not disease-modifying in that they cannot slow or stop the neurodegenerative process. The discovery of disease-modifying therapies is of paramount importance for the future of Parkinson's disease therapy. Our project combines a wide range of expertise and utilizes a truly integrated approach for Parkinson's disease drug discovery. We propose a novel strategy to target pathways that regulate the protein alpha-synuclein, a key contributor to neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease. We will screen for inhibitors of these pathways, validate hits in a battery of cell-based tests, and directly test lead inhibitors in animal models. This work will lay the foundation for our future studies aimed at developing the much-needed disease-modifying treatments for people with Parkinson's disease.

column36: Dynamic molecular and cellular mechanisms driving epithelial cell ingression
column37: Most cells that give rise to cancer in the skin, breast, lung, colon or many other organs have a common feature: they are epithelial cells. Epithelial cells have to lose their characteristic cell shape either partially or completely to initiate tumor formation or invade other organs to form metastases. This process is called epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and is a key step in cancer progression. We will study EMT in a novel unique model to gain insight into cancer formation that will ultimately help to diagnose and combat cancer. Epithelial cells are held together by a molecular glue called adherens junctions. These structures prevent epithelial cells from excess proliferation to form tumors or from migration to other organs to form metastases. It has been established that the loss of adherens junctions occurs during EMTs and is a key early step in promoting cancer. We have established a model in which the loss of adherens junctions during EMTs can be investigated with unprecedented clarity, and is analyzed with computational tools that reveal details of the process that have not been seen before. The application of state-of-the-art live imaging approaches has greatly advanced our understanding of how cell change shape and molecules control cell behavior in recent years. EMTs occur in cancer but also in normal development, and the underlying mechanisms are believed to be essentially the same. Cells in the fruit fly embryo that give rise to the nervous system undergoes an EMT-like process in a context that is uniquely accessible to advanced live imaging methods. Fruit flies are a proven model in cancer research; combining the powerful genetic and molecular tools available in the fly with our state-of-the-art imaging capabilities, and the ongoing development of computational tools for image analysis will give us novel insights into a core process in cancer progression.

column36: Effects of Neurodevelopmental Exposure to Cannabinoids on Prefrontal Cortical Function: Implications for Neuropsychiatric Disorders
column37: Marijuana use for recreational and therapeutic purposes has increased exponentially over the past several years. Furthermore, levels of delta-9-tetrahydrdocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive component of marijuana, have risen dramatically. Canadian teens are among the most frequent marijuana users in the industrialized world. These trends are significant from a mental health perspective as numerous epidemiological reports link adolescent marijuana exposure to increased risk of psychiatric symptoms in later adulthood. However, although epidemiological reports show correlations between marijuana exposure and increased rates of schizophrenia in young adulthood, it is difficult to ascertain causal relationships between marijuana exposure and the emergence of these problems in later adulthood. The most effective way to address this issue is to conduct controlled, pre-clinical studies allowing us to precisely control neurodevelopmental THC exposure during a defined window of adolescent brain development. Our research program uses rodent models of cannabinoid exposure to examine how neurodevelopmental cannabinoid exposure may lead to persistent affective and cognitive deficits in adulthood. We have recently made a series of discoveries showing that adolescent THC exposure causes molecular, neuronal and behavioural abnormalities resembling certain schizophrenia-like pathology. For example, chronic adolescent THC exposure causes molecular adaptations in a region of the brain called the 'prefrontal cortex' and strong dysregulation of the brains dopamine system, a neurochemical pathway that is severely disrupted in schizophrenia. Our project will examine how adolescent THC exposure may induce functional disturbances in neuronal activity within the PFC and characterize how these effects may lead to dysregulation of dopamine transmission and associated disturbances in affective and cognitive processing resembling those observed in schizophrenia.

column36: Investigating the relationship between HER2 and ATG4B in breast cancer.
column37: Approximately 20% of breast cancers have amplification of the ERBB2 gene, which codes for HER2, the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2. HER2 is a protein that promotes cell growth and proliferation. While there are therapies designed specifically to treat HER2 positive cancer, treatment resistance presents a substantial challenge for patients and clinicians. We recently discovered a novel association between HER2 and another protein called ATG4B. We found that HER2 positive breast cancer cells require ATG4B to survive under stress conditions. We also discovered that ATG4B inhibition sensitizes treatment resistant HER2-positive breast cancer cell lines to anti-HER2 treatment. These observations warrant further investigation, so in this study we propose to investigate the clinical relevance and therapeutic potential of ATG4B. To do so, we will examine ATG4B expression in human breast tumor specimens and determine ATG4B function in mouse models of HER2 positive breast cancer. We will also study the mechanistic links between HER2, ATG4B and treatment response. Understanding how HER2 influences ATG4B could lead to the identification of new targets or combination targeting strategies. Together, these studies have the potential to validate ATG4B as a new therapeutic target to help overcome treatment resistance in HER2 positive breast cancers.

column36: Mapping the Anatomy of Decision-Making
column37: We make decisions, large and small, every single day. When we choose food from the grocery store shelves, or mark our X in the ballot box, what is happening in our brains? How do we make the best choices when faced with many options, which may vary in many ways? Understanding which regions of the brain are critical for making decisions, and exactly how they contribute to this complex process, is important for understanding why decisions sometimes go wrong. Why do people with psychiatric or neurological illnesses, such as dementia or schizophrenia, often show poor judgment? Why do even healthy people choose the cake when they are supposed to be dieting, or the cigarette when they mean to quit smoking? This project studies the basic components of human decision-making, focusing on the contributions of specific parts of the frontal lobes, and how these regions interact with the rest of the brain. We will work with people with focal brain injury, testing which regions and circuits are critical for normal decision-making. This work will shed light on the brain mechanisms that allow us to find the best option in a crowded decision landscape and help us understand how emotional and motivational influences colour how we see the world around us. It will yield new ways to understand clinical symptoms like low motivation and poor judgment, opening the door to better tests of these abilities, and better approaches to treat or prevent impairments in these domains.

column36: Epidural stimulation to neurorehabilitate the sympathetic nervous system and improve cardiovascular health after spinal cord injury
column37: The sympathetic nervous system regulates a number of critical physiological functions. Spinal cord damage leads to severe sympathetic dysfunctions, including a loss of blood pressure control. The loss of blood pressure control underlies the #1 cause of death in people with spinal cord injury, which is cardiovascular disease. The clinical options for managing these life-threatening swings in blood pressure are limited. While drugs can be used to increase or decrease blood pressure, the slow and long-lasting effects obviate effective management of the rapid changes in blood pressure occurring after spinal cord injury. Over the past decade, electrical stimulation of the spinal cord has shown remarkable promise for improving voluntary movement after injury by restoring nervous system connections. We will use novel electronic device, that when implanted onto the spinal cord, can specifically target neural circuits responsible for cardiovascular and blood pressure control. Here, we propose to harness this intervention to neurorehabilitate sympathetic control of blood pressure after spinal cord injury. Moreover, we will deploy a judicious combination of cutting-edge scientific methods to identify the mechanisms underlying the immediate and long-term effects of this intervention, with an emphasis on the health of the cardiovascular system and the rehabilitation of normal circuits with in the sympathetic nervous system. Our ultimate objective is to establish a novel non-pharmacological therapy to rehabilitate sympathetic function after spinal cord injury that will prevent blood pressure instability, improve heart and blood vessel health, and thus enhance and extend the lives of people living with this condition.
