column36: Hypoxia in tumour-draining lymph nodes as an indication of immune activation and immunotherapy response
column37: Over the past several years, a new treatment option called immunotherapy, which stimulates the patient's own immune system to kill cancer cells, has been approved to treat several different cancer types. Tumours generally survive by evading attack from the immune system, and immunotherapy works best in patients with tumours that are more easily detected by the immune system. While immunotherapy can produce outstanding responses in 10-20% of patients with some tumour types, many tumours are harder for the immune system to recognize as harmful, and immunotherapy works in only a small fraction of patients with these cancers. A critical unmet need in immunotherapy research is a reliable way to predict which patients will benefit from this promising treatment option. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped organs located throughout the body, where immune responses to bacteria, viruses, and cancers develop. We have discovered that when a tumour is recognized by the immune system, nearby lymph nodes display regions of low oxygen (hypoxia) and we predict that cancer patients with hypoxic regions in their lymph nodes will benefit the most from immunotherapy. In this proposal, we will test whether the oxygen levels in lymph nodes can predict responses to immunotherapies currently used in the clinic. We will also determine how this low oxygen environment affects the ability of the immune system to kill cancer cells, and we will analyze the oxygenation status of lymph node samples from patients with breast cancer. This proposal will lay the foundation for future clinical studies to help oncologists direct immunotherapies to patients that are most likely to benefit from this remarkably effective therapy.

column36: Identification of molecular events enabling vacuole escape of Shigella: an avenue toward novel therapeutic strategies
column37: Infectious diseases are still among the most frequent causes of deaths. Fortunately, antibiotics save millions of lives every year. However, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), antibiotic resistance is a major threat to public health. The rapid spread of antibacterial resistance highlights the need to globally combat this problem. Compounding things, the pace of novel antibiotic discovery has plummeted to a level not seen since the 1940's. Thus, the discovery of novel antibiotics is critical. This project aims to identify novel anti-infective agents that will replace classic and failing antibiotics. Our research focuses on bacterial pathogens that intimately interact with human tissue because current antibiotics do not specifically target these. The focus of this proposal is the bacterium Shigella, which on a global scale is responsible for hundred of millions infections each year. The outcome for roughly 1 million of these cases is death. According to the WHO, Shigella is one of the bacteria for which novel antibiotics are urgently needed. Shigella is a pathogen that lives within human intestinal cells. Normally, human cells can recognize intracellular bacteria and destroy them, however Shigella is capable of evading detection and destruction. This project will identify the mechanisms used by Shigella to hijack human cellular factors. This deeper understanding of Shigella pathogenesis will facilitate the design of novel therapeutics stimulating the host defense and inhibiting Shigella hijacking mechanisms. Because of their specificity, these novel therapeutic strategies will be less prone to resistance than classical antibiotics. As a result, this work will impact both Canadian and global communities, and translation of the acquired knowledge to new treatments will open the door to collaboration between basic scientists and clinicians.

column36: Sex and Gender-related Differences in Access to Care for Premature ACS: Does the Health Care System Matter?
column37: Women still struggle to achieve high-quality equitable cardiovascular care. Recently, there has been growing attention to young women (=55 years) with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), who experience worse recoveries and higher mortality compared with similar aged men. Moreover, the rising incidence of ACS in young is of immediate concern. Despite recent advancements in understanding premature ACS outcomes, important questions remain. Access to high-quality care which may differ across health care systems (private/public) could explain the suboptimal care and poorer outcomes in young women post-ACS. Gender-related factors (e.g. socioeconomic status) have been associated with poorer access to timely cardiac procedures among women, independent of sex. The impact of sex and gender on access to care along the continuum of care for premature ACS, including how it varies across health care systems requires further investigation. Accordingly, our objective is to examine sex differences in the trajectory of access to care from pre-ACS to post-ACS setting among young patients and whether gender-related factors are associated with access to care. We hypothesize that female sex and gender-related factors traditionally ascribed to women are associated with poorer access to care in young and the magnitude of such disparities depends on health care system. To test this, we will merge data on two largest prospective cohorts of young patients with premature ACS to date: GENESIS-PRAXY and VIRGO studies. A sex and gender-based approach to address the unmet health care needs of premature ACS is much needed. It will help identify factors for targeted interventions aimed at improving women's access to high-quality health care. Merging these cohorts across 4 countries (US, Canada, Spain, Switzerland) will provide an opportunity for high-impact international research on sex and gender differences on access to care and for accessing the generalizability of results across health care systems.

column36: Unravelling the role of primary cilia in the control of male fertility
column37: Because more than 30% of male infertility cases are of unknown origin, it is crucial to identify the molecular factors controlling the male reproductive system. The epididymis is a long tubule located downstream of the testis in charge of the acquisition of sperm fertilizing ability. It is therefore an exquisite model for studying sequential events that transform an immature sperm cell into a fully motile and fertile spermatozoon. Recently, primary cilia have been found associated with epithelial cells of the epididymis. These organelles are unique antennae that emerge on the surface of cells and are mediators of many signaling pathways involved in differentiation, proliferation and cell migration. In Human, primary cilia dysfunctions are associated with a broad spectrum of defects, including male infertility, that are commonly referred to ciliopathies. Since primary cilia are essential to maintain the physiological functions of most organs, our research project aims at unravelling the role of primary cilia in epididymis development and homeostasis. This innovative project combines complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches on cell lines and mouse models. Considering the importance of epididymal functions in the control of sperm fertilizing abilities, carrying out this research will help decipher the cellular functions that may be impaired in some cases of male infertility.

column36: Deciphering the function and mechanism of long noncoding RNAs in lung cancer
column37: Non-small cell lung carcinoma is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide with activation of KRAS signaling being one of the most prevalent oncogenic events. Current efforts to understand the genetic and molecular interactions contributing to KRAS-induced tumors have focused mostly on protein coding genes, leaving the noncoding genome vastly under-explored. We now know that a large fraction of the genome is transcribed and generates thousands of long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) that do not encode proteins. Accumulating evidence point to lncRNAs as risk factors frequently dysregulated or mutated in a variety of human cancers. Amongst the few lncRNAs that have been characterized, some were found to affect processes relevant to transformation, such as proliferation and genomic stability. Yet, most studies have been limited to cell line-based assays or remain correlative. Thus, whether lncRNAs contribute to the formation or progression of lung cancer in vivo and how they may affect oncogenic pathways such as KRAS still remains poorly characterized. Recently, downregulation of the lncRNA Tug1 was found to correlate with poor prognosis in human non-small cell lung carcinoma. Our preliminary experiments indicate that loss of Tug1 collaborates with activated KRAS signaling to promote cellular transformation. Using genetically engineered mouse models, we propose to characterize the putative tumor suppressor function of Tug1 in vivo and determine which pathways involved in cellular transformation are affected. We will also decipher its mechanism of action in KRAS-induced lung cancer and use xenograft models to determine whether its function is conserved in human. This project will uncover novel lncRNA-based mechanisms contributing to the formation and progression of lung cancer in vivo. It will also provide potential new therapeutic avenues by revealing new aspects of KRAS signaling, one of the most frequently activated pathway in lung cancer.

column36: Assessing the certainty of evidence about patients' values, preferences and utilities
column37: People need to weigh benefits against harms when they make a healthcare decision. Knowing how much importance a patient puts on one outcome versus another is essential when decision makers are weighing the benefits and harms for a given treatment. We have developed a broad framework to assess how certain one can be about the evidence of outcome importance to patients when considering the overall body of evidence in health guidelines. However, for this field more specific guidance is needed to assess a body of evidence and very little work has been done to determine a valid approach to assess individual studies that make up that body of evidence. For example, researchers lack tools to assess limitations of studies and ways to measure how well the studies apply to a certain patient population. Based on existing research, this project will develop tools to assess limitations and how the evidence from patient values and preference studies can be applied. The tools will then be used in studies and the resulting assessments will inform, in consultation with health decision makers, guidelines and patient decision aids. Information about patient preferences and the value patients place on outcomes is critical for health decision making. The development of methods to properly assess this information will help to ensure patient values and preferences are considered appropriately in health guideline development and will promote considerations of patient values and preferences into the design and conduct of research studies.

column36: A Primary Care Online Appointment Scheduling Platform for Emergency Departments: Improving the Care Transition between Emergency and Primary Care
column37: With the aging of the population the number of people living with chronic diseases is going to go up dramatically. When these patients have flares of their disease, they go to the ER. After treatment in the ER, many of these patients could go home to their own beds (instead of being admitted to hospital), IF reliable, timely outpatient followup care was available. Unfortunately, there is no real 'system' of care between ERs and family doctor (FD) offices; in fact, patients themselves constitute the current system, arranging their own followup care. For older patients in particular, this can be challenging, and they are the people at the greatest risk of poor outcomes. To solve this dilemma the PI conducted a CIHR-funded meeting of leaders from the government, hospitals, and FD offices. They chose an online FD appointment system as the best solution to this problem. ERs can login and give patients being discharged from the ER an appointment at their FD's office in real-time, before they leave the ER (24h/day). Because the emergency doctor knows when the patient is going to be seen next, he or she feels safe discharging the patient (rather than admitting them to hospital), and the patient doesn't have to call the FD office, nor try to explain the diagnosis and importance of follow-up care to the office receptionist. We have 3 ER test sites, and we will engage FD offices in the surrounding areas to upload several open appointments per week to the online system. We have created a similar scheduling system at our hospital using hospital clinics. If early followup is improved for patients at these ERs, we can use the techniques learned in this project to efficiently roll-out to all of Ontario's EDs and FD offices, and eventually to all of Canada. Our partners at eHealth and Ontario government will help us do this. We believe that we can dramatically improve continuity of care for ER patients, resulting in less deaths, hospitalizations, and return ER visits for them.

column36: Comprehensive Ontario Microbiology laBoratory Administrative daTa for AntiMicrobial Resistance (COMBAT-AMR)
column37: The United Nations, the World Health Organization, and the Public Health Agency of Canada have each declared the rise in drug resistant infections to be a global threat to health due to the rapid increase in resistance and decline of new drug development. Combatting resistance is an international priority but surveillance of drug resistant infections is challenging due to the large number of bacteria, antibiotics, and laboratories involved, combined with suboptimal reporting mechanisms. In most jurisdictions, current surveillance systems rely on manually completed surveys submitted voluntarily by hospitals, meaning that the system is slow, labour intensive, prone to bias, and unable to measure the resistance in long-term care and outpatient settings. The COMBAT-AMR project will use the newly developed Ontario Laboratory Information System (OLIS) which is an electronic compilation of all patient test results from all laboratories in the province. Using OLIS, we will identify antibiotic resistance from the summary reports of all clinical microbiology culture specimens in the province. By linking OLIS to Ontario population databases, we will be able determine the total extent to which antimicrobial resistant infections contribute to hospitalization and death in Ontario by creating the Clinical Antibiotic Resistance Index (CARI). The CARI will be broken down by bacterium, region, healthcare sector, patient characteristics such as age and sex, and time, thereby revealing important bacteria and population subgroups where antibiotic resistance is of primary concern. The CARI will be the first index that accounts for the importance of antimicrobial resistance from the patients' perspective and will provide crucial evidence to inform clinical decisions and government policy for combatting resistance.

column36: The COMPAS+ project: Evaluating the impacts, implementation and scalability of a provincial quality improvement collaborative for the management of chronic diseases in primary care
column37: Primary care is largely viewed as the ideal setting for the prevention and management of common chronic diseases. Quality improvement collaboratives (QICs) have emerged as a popular and effective strategy for accelerating quality improvement (QI) processes and reducing gaps between best and current practices in chronic disease care. Currently, a large-scale QIC initiative known as COMPAS+ is being undertaken in the province of Quebec to improve the quality of chronic disease care in primary care settings. The overall aim of this study is to evaluate the impacts, implementation and scaling-up of the COMPAS+ QIC. Our main objective is to evaluate the impact of COMPAS+ on QI processes, interprofessional collaboration, chronic disease prevention and management, and patients' care experiences and health outcomes. This study will use a mixed methods evaluation approach. It will involve multiple integrated health and social service centres. COMPAS+ is expected to be an important catalyst of new QI activities surrounding the prevention and management of chronic diseases in Quebec primary care settings, thus contributing to the adoption of more evidence-based practices and to better health outcomes.

column36: Deciphering the role of the nuclear receptor LRH-1 in the establishment of a specific transcriptional program in triple negative breast cancer.
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in Canadian women. The majority of breast tumors at primary diagnosis are positive for the estrogen receptor ERa. These types of breast tumors generally have a better prognosis and respond well to antihormone therapy. While this treatment is beneficial for the majority of patients, some of them still develop locally recurrent or metastatic disease. Breast cancers called "triple negative" (TNBC), which represent nearly 15% of breast cancers, are generally very aggressive, present a risk of higher recurrence and development of metastasis. Since TNBC cannot be treated with conventional breast cancer antihormonal-based or trastuzumab-based treatments, it is of the utmost importance to develop effective new treatments by defining new therapeutic targets in TNBC. In this research project, we are particularly interested in 1) elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which LRH-1 controls TNBC cells progression and metastasis; and (2) confirming the LRH-1 as a potential therapeutic target in TNBC. We will use genomic approaches and molecular and cellular biology techniques that will help to reveal the functions of LRH-1 and to evaluate its potential as therapeutic target. The results obtained from these studies should lead to new insight that will be directly relevant to the understanding, treatment and prevention of breast cancer.

column36: Peers4Wellness: Indigenous Approaches to Wellness Support and Research for Indigenous Women with HIV and HCV in British Columbia and Saskatchewan
column37: Peers4Wellness is an Indigenous research study, which is peer-led and community-driven. It is focused on Indigenous women (cis-and trans-gendered) who have lived experience with HIV and/or hepatitis C (HCV). Our goal is to help these women with their HIV/HCV wellness and health care needs by developing Indigenous-grounded supportive care. In Canada, the rates of HIV and HCV, respectively, are 3 and 5 times higher among Indigenous people, and Indigenous women in particular, than non-Indigenous people. Yet, Indigenous people have lower HIV/HCV health care utilization than non-Indigenous people. This pattern is a result of the barriers which Indigenous people experience when accessing HIV/HCV care, including the lack of Indigenous ways of wellness and health care. Peer navigation programs, which train peers as support health workers, are shown to help people with their health and getting health care. These programs are not widely used for HIV and are almost lacking for HCV. Importantly, existing peer navigation programs do not have systematic, explicit and robust approaches to address the unique needs of Indigenous people. Because peer navigation is a promising approach to better health care, this study is focused on extending the scope of research and practice on peer navigation to include HCV and Indigenous people, particularly Indigenous women. This study will develop a wise practice peer navigation toolkit for providing culturally safe and responsive supportive care to improve the engagement and retention of Indigenous people in HIV/HCV care. Peer navigation will serve as a springboard to further develop Indigenous models for supportive HIV/HCV care. This study's current focus is Indigenous women in two priority provinces: British Columbia and Saskatchewan. The model will be gender and context adaptable. We expect that the implementation of this innovative model will improve HIV/HCV outcomes for Indigenous people in Canada, and Indigenous women in particular.

column36: A Paper-based Microfluidic Platform for Automated Point-of-Care Diagnosis of Laryngopharyngeal Reflux
column37: Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), also known as "silent reflux", is the back flow of gastric juice into larynx and pharynx, and affects 20-60% of population in developed countries. Rapid quantification of the digestive enzyme, pepsin, in saliva or laryngeal surface secretion could allow accurate diagnosis and thus effective treatment of LPR. Currently, only lateral flow strip based tests are available for pepsin tests at the point of care (POC), which is limited in detection accuracy and sensitivity. This project aims to develop a novel paper-based microfluidic platform for rapid and accurate detection of LPR protein markers in an automated "sample-in-answer-out" fashion. The platform can perform multiplexed enzyme-linked immunosorbent arrays (ELISAs) of pepsin and two other LPR markers on a paper-based microfluidic chip, and automatically regulate the transport of reagent solutions on the chip, and accurately quantify colorimetric readout signals of the assays. It will be integrated into a handheld device, and does not require human intervention during operation. We will study the correlation of concentrations of LPR biomarkers in saliva and laryngeal surface secretion with conventional diagnostic outputs in individuals with and without LPR, and confirm the most relevant biomarkers for LPR diagnosis. We will evaluate the effectiveness of our microfluidic platform using patient samples, and compare it with the standard laboratory ELISA tests. This project will lead to the next generation of POC diagnostic technology for LPR with high sensitivity, which will facilitate doctors to identify LPR patients without going through time-consuming laboratory tests and thus improve the life quality of the large population of LPR patients.

column36: Understanding dermal progenitor cell biology towards improved skin wound healing.
column37: More than 14 million severe skin wounds (burns, trauma, ulcers) are treated each year in North America. The consequence is chronic pain, immobility, disfigurement and in many cases infection leading to further medical complication or death, particularly in the elderly. The annual societal cost of wound care in Canada alone is estimated at $4 billion. One of the primary reasons that wounds do not heal is due to an inability to regrow healthy dermis and a tendency to form fibrous scar tissue. The dermis provides essential nutrients and mechanical support to the overlying epidermis and skin appendages (hair follicles, glands, nerves, blood vessels) embedded within it. Strategies to regrow new functional dermis and its appendages are desperately needed to reduce health care costs and to restore quality of life after skin injury, particularly in the elderly. An attractive approach is to stimulate stem cells that reside in adult skin. Our preliminary studies identified two different populations of dermal stem cells that are activated in response to injury and are recruited into skin wounds where they typically form scar. However, under some circumstances, these same cells can become regenerative, rather than scar-forming, even initiating formation of new hair follicles and healthy fat cells within the wound. Thus, enhancing dermal stem/ cell function could limit formation of scar and improve skin healing. To realize this clinical potential, we will: 1) Characterize the signals within the wound that drive regenerative versus scar-forming stem cell responses 2) Identify mechanisms to effectively stimulate and recruit dermal stem cells after injury 3) Determine how old age changes dermal stem cell response to injury. Our goal is to identify drug targets that could be used to modulate dermal stem cell response after injury in order to improve the quality of wound healing, thereby improving functional outcomes for Canadians suffering severe skin injury or disease.

column36: Developing a transdiagnostic group intervention for First Nations children and youth
column37: Wait-lists for mental health services in First Nations' communities often make services inadequate to meet community needs. The use of treatments that target behaviours and thought patterns that are similar across disorders (i.e. transdiagnostic) could serve to reduce these wait-times by allowing individuals who are experiencing a wide array of difficulties (e.g., depression, anxiety, substance use) to receive services that address underlying symptoms at the same time. These treatments also provide a new framework for evidence-based culturally appropriate services within First Nations communities by incorporating strategies that align with cultural values. Working in collaboration with a community-based organization serving First Nations communities in Northwestern Ontario, a skill-based transdiagnostic group intervention will be developed and implemented. This treatment will target community specific needs through consultation with organizational staff and community members. Culturally appropriate skills, concepts, and examples will be identified and integrated into the treatment. This is the first project to adapt and assess the effectiveness of a transdiagnostic mental health treatment for First Nations children. An initial pilot group of the treatment with approximately 8 children aged 7-12 years will be implemented, after which the adjusted full treatment protocol will be implemented with 5 groups of 8-10 children (N = ~50). It is anticipated that these group interventions will reduce difficulties in emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, behavioural avoidance, and self-care of the children while developing positive coping strategies.

column36: Gene Therapy to Prevent Blindness in Patients with Congenital Aniridia
column37: Aniridia is a rare eye disorder caused by half the normal amount of the protein paired box gene 6 (PAX6). It affects both sexes and is not known to be influenced by gender. Individuals with aniridia are typically born with low vision, and because there is no effective treatment, subsequently lose all vision. Thus, there is a therapeutic window available to prevent vision loss. This application will take advantage of recent advances in the fields of both traditional gene therapy and CRISPR gene therapy. Traditional "augmentation" gene therapy methods allow us to directly increase the amount of missing protein in affected cells to treat disease. CRISPR gene therapy allows us to modify DNA in affected cells to alter the behavior of the cells and treat disease. The broad goal of this proposal is to develop a gene therapy to treat patients with aniridia and to engage with the aniridia patient community. We hypothesize that using both traditional gene therapy and CRISPR gene therapy we can increase the amount of PAX6 protein and improve eye function in a mouse model of aniridia. We will also undertake a patient engagement initiative, which will include an analysis of Canadian policies on gene sequencing, characterization of patient motivators and barriers to gene sequencing, and generate a fact sheet regarding sequencing for aniridia. This work builds on Dr. Simpson's expertise in both mouse models and aniridia, and Dr. Robillard's expertise in patient engagement. By the end of the proposal, we will have completed the preclinical work in mouse and positioned the therapy for commercial investment. In addition, we will have given the tools we developed to not-for-profit companies for world-wide availability to researchers. Finally, we will have disseminated a fact sheet illuminating issues surrounding patient engagement in future clinical trials.

column36: Epigenetic changes affecting muscle stem cell function in the aging population
column37: Building and maintaining our muscle mass is an ongoing battle between the stem cell-based processes that build muscle, and the degenerative processes that cause muscle loss. In our youth, stem cells have the upper hand in the battle where they make muscle faster than it is broken down. This allows for growth and increased strength in young healthy individuals. Unfortunately, as we age our stem cells get worn down and become less efficient at building new muscle. This allows the degenerative processes to get an edge in the battle leading to the loss of 1% of our muscle mass each year after the age of 40. Evidence in mice suggest that epigenetic processes contribute to age-related decline in stem cell function that leads to muscle loss. As epigenetic processes are reversible, this suggests that we may be able to find ways to extend the functional lifespan of our muscle stem cells to prevent muscle loss as we get older. In this project, we will use the latest technologies in the study of epigenetics to identify the changes taking place in muscle stem cells of aging humans. From these studies, we expect to identify specific factors we can target therapeutically to help ensure that our aging population is able to enjoy mobility and good quality of life while reducing the costs on our health care system.

column36: Epigenetic reorganization and differentiation of glioblastoma
column37: Brain cancers, particularly glioblastomas (GBM), are amongst the worst human cancers. The 5-year survival is <10%, effectively rendering patients with this diagnosis to a death sentence. Patients are desperate for better treatments. The Dirks group found that GBM growth was dependent on a few cells in the tumour that have stem cell properties, these cells lie at the root of GBM growth and are also resistant to conventional therapies. Reminiscent of normal stem cells, these specialized GBM cells divide to replenish themselves (a process called self-renewal) and can generate more mature cell types that lose the ability to sustain tumour growth, through the process of differentiation. We have recently identified that GBM stem cells have a unique packaging of their DNA, or "epigenetic state", that facilitates self-renewal and blocks maturation. We also found that about half of GBM patient tumors have GBM stem cells (GSCs) that can be more easily coaxed into a much more mature state, by activation of a gene ("ASCL1") that normally controls brain cell maturation into functioning nerve cells (neurons) during development. ASCL1-expressing GSCs can be treated with drugs causing them to turn into cells that resemble mature brain neurons, meaning they lose ability to divide and stop the tumour from growing. Key to this transition is a reorganization of the epigenetic state from one that is pro-self-renewing to one that is pro-differentiating. In this program, we will investigate the balance between epigenetic states of self renewal and differentiation in GBM. We will explore the potential for epigenetic reorganization and differentiation-based therapy for GBM by testing clinic-ready pro-differentiation drugs, testing novel classes of compounds that modify epigenetic states, and by using-editing technologies to discover new ways of differentiating GSCs. This project will usher in a completely new area of GBM research, which could have massive impact for patients.

column36: Early detection of cancer in high-risk patients through profiling of circulating tumour DNA
column37: Across Canada, 1 in 10 cancers occur in people with an inherited strong family risk of cancer (hereditary cancer syndrome: HCS). These families have multiple members affected with similar cancers, often at a younger age. When a family member with cancer is detected with an inherited faulty version of a gene, some healthy relatives will also share the faulty gene. These cancer "previvors" often refer to themselves as a ticking cancer time bomb. As such, they often enroll in intensive cancer surveillance programs that include colonoscopy, mammogram, and magnetic resonance imaging. These programs are costly ($94.5M/year in Ontario alone), not personalized and do not detect all potential cancers. As a result, many patients show up with late-stage cancer or cancer of an organ that is not screened. Lifetime treatment costs are substantial (Ontario averages are $76,000 for breast, $58,000 for ovarian and $70,000 for colorectal cancer), and often with poor outcome as 40% of cancer patients die within 5 years. The key to preventing these tragedies is early detection of disease. Circulating tumour DNA analysis is a promising method for detecting DNA from cancer cells in the blood. We will develop this method to detect early signs of cancer in previvors, people with HCS but not yet a cancer diagnosis. This will enable prediction of cancer onset so that patients and their doctors can make decisions to treat or prevent their cancers. We will recruit HCS patients from across Canada to provide blood samples before and after they develop cancer. In parallel, we will build a test to detect early stage disease, and work with provincial health authorities to determine cost-effectiveness. Doctors and their patients will help us establish recommendations for use in the broader health care system. Lessons learned from our project can be extended to cancer screening programs for all Canadians.

column36: The Longitudinal Study of Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) in Patients with Advanced Cancer
column37: There have been enormous changes in Canada over the past decade in public attitudes about medical care at the end-of-life. Palliative care has become much more accessible and medical assistance in dying (MAiD) was legalized in June 2016. Since that time, over 2000 Canadians have received assisted death, of whom more than 60% had advanced cancer. The physical, psychological and social factors that lead to the desire for death and requests for MAiD, and the stability of this desire over time has not been studied in countries where MAiD is legally available. This study will identify patient, disease and treatment-related factors that drive the desire for death and for MAiD in patients with advanced cancer. We will study whether these factors can predict the desire for death and for MAID and will compare results with our Will to Live (WTL) study in advanced cancer that was completed 10 years ago. We now propose a five year study that will assess 1000 patients at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (PM) from diagnosis of advanced cancer to death. We will collect survey information and interview patients every six months on: (1) the desire for death and attitudes and desire for MAiD; (2) psychological and physical suffering and quality of life; (3) social support; (4) communication with health care providers about MAiD; (5) psychosocial and palliative care treatments; and (6) advance care planning. We will collect information from the UHN MAiD database on MAiD approval and completions, and reasons for not receiving MAiD. The findings from this study will help healthcare providers have conversations about MAiD and the desire for death with patients, guide legal changes being considered to permit MAiD as an advanced directive, and inform health systems to ensure appropriate access to MAiD and to alternative supportive treatments for patients with advanced cancer.

column36: Molecular and biomechanical studies of bacterial-vascular adhesion mechanisms and their contributions to Lyme disease
column37: Blood-borne spread of bacteria via the cardiovascular system (dissemination) is responsible for most death due to bacterial infection. A key dissemination step is bacterial adhesion to the cells lining blood vessels (endothelial cells), which permits bacteria to slow down and escape from the bloodstream to infect new tissues. Bacterial interaction with blood vessels is challenging due to the force generated by flowing blood. Defining the physical mechanisms allowing bacteria to stick to blood vessel surfaces under flow is crucial for understanding how bacteria disseminate, and may lead to the development of strategies for slowing or preventing bacterial dissemination. However, the vascular adhesion mechanisms of most pathogens are largely unknown. The bacterium that causes Lyme disease, Borrelia burgdorferi, is a highly invasive pathogen that disseminates to most organs and tissues. Blood vessel and flow properties vary widely in different tissues and organs, generating unique, postal code-like conditions in each vascular bed that affect how bacteria disseminate to these tissues. Since B. burgdorferi disseminates to many tissues this pathogen may produce many adhesion molecules facilitating vascular interactions under diverse conditions. Vascular interaction mechanisms are better-understood for B. burgdorferi than most other pathogens, largely because we and collaborators have developed powerful methods to study dissemination in living mice and artificial systems mimicking blood vessels. We have identified several Borrelia, endothelial cell and blood molecules contributing to B. burgdorferi-endothelial interactions, although many molecules and mechanisms supporting B. burgdorferi dissemination to different tissues remain unknown. These studies will examine the repertoire of molecules and mechanisms supporting Borrelia dissemination to diverse tissues, and will provide the groundwork for exploring dissemination mechanisms of other bacterial pathogens.

column36: Examining the epidemiology, treatment, and outcomes in young-onset colorectal cancer (EXPLAIN-yCRC)
column37: Colorectal cancer is the second most common form of cancer in Canada. The disease frequently strikes in adults 50 years of age or older. Our goal is to better understand the growing problem of young-onset colorectal cancer using British Columbia's rich data sources. First, we will calculate the number of individuals who are currently living with young-onset colorectal cancer as this will help inform the ongoing care of survivors of this condition. We will look at differences between women and men and different age groups. Second, we will examine how young-onset colorectal cancer is being treated, for example, how long from a diagnosis does treatment start and what types of treatment are used. We will also study whether there are differences in treatment between men and women. Third, we will calculate the cost of caring for young-onset colorectal cancer. We will also compare the risk of dying from young-onset colorectal diagnosed at less than 50 years of age as compared to colorectal cancer diagnosed at 50 years of age and over. We will also examine potential differences in outcomes between men and women. Altogether, by explaining the growing problem of young-onset colorectal cancer, our research will help improve understanding, treatment, and outcomes of young-onset colorectal cancer.

column36: Novel 3D personalized bladder cancer model on demand: A new era for personalized medicine.
column37: Bladder cancer (BC) is the 5th most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canada. It is usually manifested as 'superficial' BC. However, 25% of patients progress to a more aggressive and potentially lethal state. Recent studies of BC have revealed several distinct subtypes emphasising the need for an individualized approach. Our group has successfully established a bladder cell removal (decellularization) protocol. These acellular bladders have been seeded with normal bladder cells and grown for up to 1 month showing adequate cell survival. These preliminary results proved to us the feasibility and great potential of engineering bladder tissues. Here we propose to develop a 3D BC model, on demand, using acellular bladder scaffolds as a platform, which will enable us to recreate a BC of a specific patient to test and/or develop drugs. The development of this model will potentially make a step forward on how we currently test anti-cancer drugs. Each 3D BC tissue constructed, will be identical to a specific patient undergoing bladder cancer. This approach will have the potential to simultaneously test multiple anti-cancer drugs before giving the appropriate one to the patient, avoiding sequential unnecessary treatments and reducing side effects which will ultimately improve patient's quality of life. Our model system is a novel approach that will aid in: the mechanistic studies of cell-cell interaction; provide a platform to test and develop new drugs; reduce the number of animals used for experimentation; and, provide a model for preclinical treatment evaluation before deciding on a personalized therapy. At the conclusion of this project we hope to have developed a new tool that will significantly impact the way we currently treat bladder cancer patients.

column36: Coordination of inhibition and excitation underlying neural computations
column37: Nerve cells in the brain communicate with each other via chemical synapses. Generally, each nerve cell releases either an excitatory or an inhibitory neurotransmitter onto its postsynaptic partner. Excitatory neurotransmitters activate postsynaptic neurons, increasing the probability that they fire action potentials; while inhibitory neurotransmitters do the opposite. The efficiency of most computations rely on 'balanced' excitation/inhibition (E/I), where on the gross scale these opposing forces are always in competition. It is the fine imbalances in E/I that in fact controls the level of neural activity. Despite its central importance, measuring the fine balance between E and I is not easy. This is inhibitory and excitatory inputs are made throughout the neurons dendritic tree, where they interact. Current methods do not allow us to easily measure electrical activity in the dendritic trees. Instead, electrodes are usually placed at the soma, which collects the average I/E throughout the dendritic tree. While, results from such measurements have provided a framework for understanding E/I balance, the lack of insights of how E/I interacts in the dendritic tree strongly limits our understanding how neural computations occur in the brain. In this proposal, we aim to understanding how E/ I shape a specific computation that underlies our ability to compute the direction of moving objects, performed by neural circuit that lies at the back of the eye, in the retina. Our experiments will use a multidisciplinary approach including molecular, electrophysiological and two-photon Ca2+ imaging techniques, which allow us to view synaptic activity throughout the intricate dendritic trees of neurons. We hypothesize that the E/I is finely modulated in space and in time, which enables the circuit to compute direction with speed and extreme precision. This allows us to accurately perceive the direction of rapidly moving objects, which of course, is crucial for our survival.

column36: Developing functional beta cells for diabetes treatment
column37: Diabetes is characterized by the increase in sugar levels in the bloodstream due to the lack of beta cells in the pancreas or due to their malfunction. Beta cells can lower blood glucose levels by sensing the increase in sugar in the blood and releasing insulin in response to that increase. Patients with type 1 diabetes and those with type 2 that are insulin-dependend need to monitor the sugar levels and administer exogenous insulin via injection or pump several times a day. As an alternative to insulin administration, pancreas or islet transplants can be used to treat patients with type 1 diabetes, however the shortage of donors and the need for immunosuppressants limit this treatment to fewer people. Stem cell derived pancreatic cells could be transplanted in lieu of a pancreas or pancreatic islets, eliminating waiting lists and the need for donors. In this proposal, we aim to develop safe pancreatic cells from stem cells by purifying the cells prior to transplanation using a specific marker found on their surface. Our hypothesis is that the purification step will eliminate the risk of tumors without affecting the survival and functionality of the pancreatic cells and their efficiency at restoring normal sugar levels in the blood.

column36: Mind the Gap: Disparities in Perinatal Health among Foreign-born Women in Canada
column37: Migration is a gendered process with differential exposures to health risks for women at different stages of immigration. Premigration risks for female migrants might include greater exposure to gender violence, economic precarity, and less access to basic rights and healthcare services because of women's lower social position in migrants' origin countries. Childbearing age immigrant women are a unique population in terms of health challenges because of the added vulnerability that occurs during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Research shows that maternal health is particularly poor among immigrants in Canada. Immigrant women have worse self-rated health, more postpartum health complications, and higher rates of perinatal depression than Canadian-born women. Immigrant women also do not consistently have better pregnancy outcomes compared to Canadian-born women. To examine potential health service gaps for childbearing immigrant women, we will use linked administrative and vital statistics databases maintained or created by Statistics Canada to estimate non-delivery antenatal hospitalization rates for immigrants and Canadian-born women. Antenatal hospitalization is a well-established indicator of maternal morbidity. We will also examine the association between mother's country of birth and perinatal health outcomes (preterm birth, stillbirth and infant mortality) to determine if some immigrant subgroups are more susceptible to poor health. Finally, we examine whether gender inequality affects immigrants' perinatal health.

column37: Muscular dystrophy is a life-threatening muscular disorder, to which there is no cure. column36: Influenza detection and innate defenses in the reservoir host
column37: Bird flu continues to circulate in wild and domestic birds in Asia and Africa. Occasionally it can infect humans, and is extremely deadly and has killed half of the 850 people that have been infected in the last 10 years. There is real concern that this virus can recombine with other strains and create a new pandemic strain. Also, when ducks make a protective immune response, we wonder what genes they turn on, and how those proteins work to prevent harm from flu. Finally we plan to put the duck innate sensor in chicken cells and experimental chickens to allow direct comparison of the contribution of this pathway to flu defences.

column36: Do you really know what I want?: Voices of people with dementia in shared decision-making about living well to the end of life
column37: Many researchers are now emphasizing the need to listen to the voices of people living with dementia (PWD), especially to their expert knowledge of living with the illness, their perspectives as health service users, and their thoughts about living well with dementia to the end of life (EOL). This project adopts the lenses of shared decision-making, feminist care ethics and social citizenship to look at how PWD could become active collaborators in shaping EOL decision-making. The study goals are to explore and PWDs' perceptions of what it means to live well to the EOL and to develop effective methods of sharing these findings and creating dialogue with the Canadian public. The study will involve in-depth interviews with persons with early-moderate stages of dementia and an informal caregiver and a series of visioning workshops where participants will use arts-based methods (such as collage, painting or creation of poetry) to explore their values and preferences for living well with dementia to the EOL. The works created will be exhibited in spaces where the public, policy makers, and healthcare providers can engage in dialogue about 'having the EOL conversation' and about what it means to live well with dementia to the EOL. This work will enhance understanding of the views of PWD in discussions about living well to the EOL and contribute to the development of approaches that support PWD in communicating about their preferences.

column36: Spit for Science 2: Genetic and environmental influences on behaviour and cognition in childhood neuropsychiatric disorders
column37: Many mental illnesses begin before age 18 and can have devastating effects throughout life. Three of the most common and impairing childhood-onset mental illnesses are attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Genes play an important role in these disorders but the specific genes are unclear. Spit for Science 2 (S2) continues the work of the Spit for Science (S1) by using alternative approaches to identify risk genes for childhood-mental illness. Instead of focusing on clinical diagnoses, which are complex and vary considerably from person to person, we are examining behavioural (e.g., inattention) and cognitive traits (executive functions - how you control behaviour to reach your goals) linked to the disorders and that cut across disorders. Patients are at the extreme of these traits but these traits vary widely in the population (attentive to inattentive). We will also examine how environmental factors like air pollution and marginalization affect how genes influence traits. To understand the genetics of mental illness in youth, we will recruit 30,000 children and adolescents from the Ontario Science Centre. They will provide DNA via spit, mental health trait information and complete an executive function cognitive task (Stop-Signal Task). Environmental risk data will be extracted from postal codes. Combining S2 and S1 data will create the largest pediatric mental health genetic sample in Canada providing sufficient statistical power to identify genetic signals. We will use a range of cutting-edge genetic methods to identify and validate genetic risk variants for these traits, understand which genetic risk are unique and shared across traits and disorders and test gene by environment interactions. We hope to identify novel genes involved in childhood mental illness which could potentially lead to early detection, better treatments and improved treatment-outcomes for Canadian youth.

column36: Strengthening the implementation of "Health in All Policies" at the county/municipal level in Ontario and Quebec using realist explanatory case studies and knowledge mobilization
column37: A growing number of local governments in Canada are having all of their departments - such as health, housing, education, and transportation - working together to improve the conditions for health in their communities. These governments are trying what has been called "Health in All Policies" (HiAP). HiAP works best when federal, provincial/territorial, and local governments work together to develop healthy policies. But there is little evidence to support the use of HiAP. This team includes academic researchers working closely with people using HiAP in local governments across Quebec and Ontario. Our goal is to create knowledge that directly supports people in government in using HiAP. We will use a series of case studies to examine the causes of positive and negative experiences with using HiAP, while trying to understand how provincial governments can effectively support HiAP at the local level. We will conduct around six case studies - three in each province - and our data will include 16 interviews with politicians, civil servants from health and non-health sectors, and non-governmental partners working on HiAP locally. We will also analyze documents describing HiAP experiences in case settings that we obtain from government (e.g., meeting minutes), academic journals, and other sources. To ensure that our findings help support improvements to the use of HiAP locally, we will work with our policymaker partners to: (1) host a regular meeting with knowledge users to facilitate on-going discussion on how to improve HiAP efforts; (2) writing and sharing a series of policy briefs that describe our findings about each case in plain language; and (3) designing and hosting a series of workshops in each case setting to discuss our findings and what they mean for improving the use of HiAP locally. Later, we will check whether or not and why these three steps had any impact on the use of HiAP in case settings.

column36: Structural Drivers of Iatrogenic Opioid Misuse in Alberta First Nations: Understanding Prescribing Patterns to Address Medicine's Role in the Opioid Crisis
column37: Rates and impacts of opioid misuse among Indigenous communities are difficult to quantify, a task complicated by the challenge of not perpetuating a deficit lens (i.e., victim-blaming, moralization) when identifying drivers of negative opioid-related outcomes among under-served and racialized populations. This study seeks to contextualize structural drivers (i.e., factors embedded in wider social, political and health systems) that shape opioid-related health disparities among First Nations (FN) in Alberta. Together with 4-5 FN partners connected to the research team through the Alberta First Nations Information Governance Centre, the mixed methods study will mobilize administrative data around access to prescription opioids among non-cancer FN patients, linking these to patient, family, community & provider experiences collected in sequential focus groups and interviews. Once quantitative and qualitative data are integrated, FN stakeholders will engage in a consensus-building process to prioritize key areas and opportunities for enhancing provider capacity for responsible prescribing. Data sources include prescription insurance claims made by dispensers to the Non-Insured Health Benefits program, medical college prescription surveillance data from Alberta's Triplicate Prescription Program (TPP), and potentially Alberta Health practice data. Analysis for structural drivers will focus, for instance, on physician parameters (e.g., prof. & educ. background, patient panel sizes), as well as system, social, and political resources supporting or impeding chronic disease and pain management. The study positions the team for future partnership with Primary Care Networks to identify the influence of patient panels (e.g.,size, composition, geographic range) & health utilization data (e.g.,duration of visits, access to allied health professionals for pain). Evidence developed will orient FN & research partners to develop and evaluate interventions for responsible prescribing.

column36: Women, Victimization, and Homelessness: Towards a conceptual model to advance trauma- and violence-informed research, policy and practice
column37: Despite several decades of research documenting the scope and impacts of violence against women in the general population and internationally, the victimization of women who are homeless has received comparatively less attention. This is important given women are one of the fastest growing subpopulation of homeless persons today. Moreover, violence is identified to be a key cause and consequence of homelessness among women. Evidence suggests that women who are homeless often experience many forms of violence over the lifespan including childhood abuse, domestic violence, street-victimization and exploitation (e.g., street predators, drug/survival sex-trade), discrimination and stigma, and histories of colonization among Indigenous women, for example. However, the nature and extent of violence and its impacts among women who are homeless has yet to be synthesized and embedded in prevention and intervention policies and practices. Thus, we propose to conduct a systematic review of the published literature to date to assess the prevalence, nature and severity of violence experienced by homeless women over the life course to understand violence in this population. The review will be guided by trauma- and violence-informed frameworks and include mixed-methods research to shed light on the key risk, protective and broader socio-structural factors that shape victimization and its effects in this population. The primary purpose of this review is to establish the foundational knowledge base needed to inform a conceptual model for gender- and trauma-responsive policy and practice, and guide future research directions. Our team is uniquely positioned to directly apply the results via key government and community stakeholders and national networks actively working to eradicate homelessness and gender-based violence across Canada.

column37: Investigators of common diseases & traits in human populations can now measure genomic variation at an unprecedented level of detail using advanced technologies, but analytic capacity to integrate & interpret the complex underlying relationships remains limited. Because variation in disease risk depends on many factors acting in combination, our objective is to find better ways to search through the enormous number of potential genetic variants that could possibly be involved in causing disease. We will evaluate approaches that assemble the variants into natural groups that are likely to be working together and can be studied more effectively. Advanced modelling techniques are likely to help distinguish among alternative genetic disease mechanisms. Some genomic differences between people determine differences in levels of a risk factor for disease but are incidental to differences in disease susceptibility or progression. Other genomic differences between people determine differences in disease outcome through another unidentified pathway. We aim to develop new models to provide evidence about such alternatives & identify circumstances where they can be most useful. The methods we develop will be applied & tested in studies of the development of complications of diabetes, in comparisons of individuals with and without cancer, and in studies of other health outcomes. The aim is to identify genes and biological mechanisms that can be targeted for therapy or prevention.

column36: Microfiltration of Circulating and Disseminated Tumor Cells in Ovarian Cancer: From Monitoring Therapeutic Response Towards Predicting Disease Outcome
column37: Circulating and disseminated tumor cells (CTCs, DTCs) that dissociate from the primary tumor, can be found, respectively, in blood and ascites of ovarian cancer patients, and could be used to monitor the response to therapy, and help track the tumor state. CTCs and DTCs are very rare and present in low numbers, and isolating them has been a great challenge and has prevented using them more broadly for cancer disease management. As CTC isolation technologies have progressed, subpopulations of CTCs with various metastatic potentials have been identified. Very recently, aggregates of CTCs, callled CTC clusters, have been discovered, and they were found to have an approx. 50 times higher metastatic potential. Our team developed a microfiltration system which we believe outperforms other CTC isolation systems as when we analyzed a small ovarian cancer patient cohort in a pilot study, we observed CTCs and clusters in every patient, whereas previously they were only rarely found. Our method is also simple to use, potentially low cost if mass produced, and hence could be adopted for clinical use in the future. Here, we propose to use our microfiltration system to monitor the response to therapy in ovarian cancer patients by taking blood and ascites before surgery, after surgery, and at different time points during chemotherapy. We will isolate CTCs, DTCs and clusters, and analyze the number of cells and clusters, their morphology, and different molecular markers that are expressed and which have been linked to cancer metastasis and resistance to therapy. This study will validate our technology in a clinical context, and provide insight into the mechanisms of tumor response and resistance to therapy in ovarian cancer. It will set the foundation for future studies to help stratify patients and establish disease prognostics, and perhaps identify groups that might benefit from targeted, precision therapies, both for ovarian and other cancers.

column36: Structure and Dynamics of Adenosine A2A receptor - Gs Complexes
column37: A family of approx. 800 different G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in our cell membranes controls most of our physiology by sensing hormones, neurotransmitters and chemical signals, which result in the modulation of signaling pathways. More than a third of current prescription drugs target GPCRs. The adenosine A2A receptor is a prototypical GPCR and an important drug target for a wide spectrum of diseases including oncologic, inflammatory, Parkinson's and cardiovascular diseases. GPCRs can adopt different shapes (conformations), of which only active conformations couple to G proteins and modulate intracellular signaling. Detailed molecular insight into receptor shape changes and G protein coupling will provide new avenues for pharmaceutical intervention. How G proteins are activated by adenosine A2A receptors and modulate intracellular signaling can be uncovered with paramagnetic resonance techniques like EPR and DEER spectroscopy, where small labels are covalently attached to the individual proteins which allow us to "visualize" GPCR conformations. The effect of pharmaceuticals on the A2A receptor and its subsequent interaction with intra-cellular binding partners, like G proteins, can be interrogated using the labels as environmentally sensitive antennas. Measuring distances between two labels attached to a protein allows the "visualization" of conformational changes. Our research centre is the sole facility in Canada for these vital and complex spectroscopic techniques, allowing us to monitor the responses of pharmaceutical compounds on the dynamic interplay between A2A receptor and G proteins. We wish to enhance our understanding of A2A receptor-mediated G protein activation to improve our still limited knowledge about this crucial drug target and GPCRs in general.

column37: Anxiety and related psychiatric issues are often comorbid with many inflammatory diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease, although the mechanisms of this inflammation-related anxiety are not well understood and there is currently no primary therapeutic approach that manages these symptoms. This grant proposes to investigate if the development of anxiety associated with peripheral inflammation involves a change in endocannabinoid function, and if elevating endocannabinoids could be a suitable strategy to treat these comorbid issues associated with inflammation.

column36: The importance of connector hubs in focal epilepsy: a multimodal investigation
column37: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder that affects 1% of Canadians. The main treatment is longterm drug therapy, to which more than 30% of patients are refractory. Fortunately, surgery may be considered in cases of drug resistant epilepsy in which we can define a focal area of the brain responsible for the seizures. The goal of surgery is the resection of brain tissue that generates seizures, without causing functional loss. However, there are no noninvasive techniques able to measure precisely when (on a millisecond time scale) and where (on a millimeter spatial scale) epileptic activity occurs in the brain. Some techniques are dedicated to answer "where" (good spatial resolution) in the brain, whereas others can identify "when" (good temporal resolution). Most neuroimaging techniques have been developed in order to be sensitive to different brain signals: (1) direct measurements of neuronal bioelectric activity (from scalp recordings) and (2) indirect measurement of brain activity through hemodynamic processes providing oxygen to the active neurons and glucose metabolism. The objective of our work is to combine these imaging techniques, to study whether the network organization of brain underlying activity during rest could exhibit some specificity that would allow us to characterize the disease of a patient. Such patient specific characterization should be possible, accounting for only few minutes recordings of resting state activity, even when no transient epileptic discharges could be recorded. We expect these findings to be relevant to investigate new therapeutic approaches for these candidates for epilepsy surgery.

column36: Molecular evolution of self-nonself discrimination by paired NKR-P1 receptors, self ligands, and viral immunoevasins
column37: The innate immune system protects us from pathogenic bacteria, viruses, and cancer, and also helps to maintain normal tissue function at mucosal barriers, such as the skin, gut, and lungs. Natural killer (NK) cells are a subset of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) that possess cytotoxic/killer cell function and can detect/eliminate infected, cancer, and transplanted cells. How NK cells perform these functions requires understanding of the molecules they use to sense what is harmless or dangerous, and how these molecules assist in the decision to ignore a healthy cell, or respond to a diseased cell. We have identified a receptor-ligand family (NKR-P1:Clr) that contributes to NK cell recognition at the molecular level. Some NKR-P1 receptors are inhibitory, so normal cells display "self" Clr ligands to prevent NK cell responses ("healthy-self"), while infected cells lose Clr expression and are killed by NK cells ("missing-self"). This supports a role for NKR-P1:Clr interactions in fighting cancer and infectious disease. However, malignant cancer cells and viral pathogens can evolve ways to subvert innate immunity and become pathogenic, including abnormal display of self ligands, or the evolution of decoy proteins or surrogate "non-self" ligands, respectively. In addition, activating NKR-P1 receptors can recognize some of these abnormal proteins and directly activate NK cells ("induced-self"). We propose to advance our understanding of innate immunity by studying how NK cells use receptors to see "self" ligands, and how viruses use immune evasion proteins to subvert NK detection. Detailed knowledge about how pathogens evade normal immunity, specifically details about how structure-function relationships evolve between host and pathogen, will ultimately lead to advanced therapies in cancer treatment and control of infectious disease, in turn supporting our immune defences to cancer and infection.

column36: Qanuikkat Siqinirmiut? A community-based study of southern Quebec Inuit health and wellbeing
column37: Our project begins with a question "Qanuikkat Siqinirmiut?" or "How are the people in the south?" The number of Inuit living in southern cities is increasing rapidly, with just over 27% (17,695) now living outside the traditional territories of Inuit Nunangat. In contrast to those in the north, very little is known about the health of Inuit in the south. It is clear that Inuit in the north and the south experience significant health disparities when compared to the majority population. In southern Quebec the development of services for health promotion, prevention, and the treatment of illness is limited by a near complete absence of data on the health of the population. This project is intended to build a knowledge base on the health and wellbeing of Inuit in the south through the development and implementation of a population health survey. The project is uses a culturally-adapted Community-Based Participatory Research research strategy to , A collaboration between the Southern Quebec Inuit Association and a group of university-based researchers, the team includes researchers, community members, service providers, students, and political and social organizations who are poised to act on the findings of the research. Qualitative interviews, ethnographic and participatory visual research techniques will bring context and depth to the understanding of Inuit health and wellbeing. The survey tools used in from other studies of Inuit health will be adapted and expanded with the results of the qualitative methods in order to reflect the realities of those in the south. Additional Scientific outcomes include a better understanding of urban Inuit health and its relationship to northern health issues. Our goals are to develop an understanding of community health and wellbeing that is based in Inuit experience order to build capacity to address health disparities and community need.

column36: Indigenizing harm reduction in response to the opioid crisis: A scoping review and community-based research projects with First Nations in BC
column37: Since April 2016, British Columbia (BC) has been in a state of public health emergency due to opioid-related overdoses and deaths, in which Indigenous people have been disproportionately affected. The First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) assumed the responsibilities of Health Canada's First Nations Inuit Health Branch-Pacific Region in 2013 and is governed by First Nations individuals and communities across BC. Responding to the opioid crisis has been a top priority for the FNHA since the start of BC's opioid crisis. Harm reduction is an effective way to reduce stigma and harms associated with opioid use and other licit and illicit drugs. An Indigenous approach to health research and health care service delivery is critically needed to develop effective practices for Indigenous Peoples in Canada. However, an Indigenous approach to harm reduction for opioid use has not been studied extensively, and there is limited literature on community-based harm reduction practices for First Nations in Canada. The main objectives of this project are to: 1) synthesize current Indigenous approaches to harm reduction for opioid use using a Western scoping review that includes Indigenous storytelling methods, 2) refine and/or implement and measure Indigenous harm reduction interventions in all five health regions in BC, and 3) develop an Indigenized harm reduction model for opioid use. First Nation communities will lead the research with the support and guidance of project team members as needed. A multidisciplinary research team with experience exploring substance use, mental health and wellness, and harm reduction will work together to implement this five-year project. Results will be used to improve harm reduction initiatives and better support Indigenous people who use opioids, ultimately informing the FNHA's health programs and services and other harm reduction initiatives across Canada.

Yet, about 844 million people in the world lack access to a basic drinking water source. While we often assume these sorts of problems `only' occur in developing countries, intra-regional variation in middle and high income countries reveals water-sanitation crises in our most vulnerable populations. Aligning with CIHR IPPH's research priorities on intersectoral action and health equity, and building on my on-going work in developing countries, my research program is aimed at developing a viable research agenda to reduce the negative outcomes associated with waterborne diseases in low-income areas of both Canada and Mexico. column37: My work focuses on examining the burden of infectious diseases, including vaccine-preventable diseases, at the population level, focusing on important subgroups of interest and the impact on the healthcare system in Ontario. Having recently transitioned from a doctoral program in epidemiology to a position as an independent researcher, I have maintained my interest in working in applied public health research, but have the opportunity to expand my areas of interest and networks. I am in the process of developing my research program, but am focusing on using administrative data to estimate the burden of infectious disease in Ontario, incorporating data based on laboratory confirmation where possible. I am also aiming to incorporate an additional focus of providing relevant information for diseases for which there may be upcoming preventive measures (e.g. new vaccines) or expanded policy opportunities (e.g. expanded use of current vaccines) and to evaluate the impact of relevant interventions that have already been implemented. column36: Identifying Subgroups and Risk Among Frequent Emergency Department Users: Whose needs can safely be met elsewhere?
column37: Emergency Department (ED) costs make up an increasing proportion of Canadian healthcare spending. Patients who use EDs frequently account for 4.5-8% of all ED patients, yet make up almost 30% of the visits. Those patients whose visits to the ED do not result in hospitalization, or whose visits involve care that could more efficiently be provided elsewhere, could likely have their needs met elsewhere at lower cost. Frequent ED users include many different types of patients, for example, those with chronic disease, mental health issues, and substance misuse. Some are more likely to be hospitalized and die compared to non-frequent users, but the risk is not the same for all frequent ED users. For instance, the most extreme frequent ED users (18 or more yearly visits) are admitted and die less often than more moderate frequent users, indicating that they could probably be diverted safely from the ED. My goal is to identify and describe groups of frequent ED users with unmet health needs who can safely be treated outside of the ED. I will do this by linking large databases that collect information about ED visits, admissions, physician billing information, prescription drugs, home care, nursing homes, and provincial deaths. I will start by identifying different frequent ED user groups based on their ED visit patterns and other patient characteristics like age or various illness categories. I will then examine whether these different frequent user groups have different risks of having poor health outcomes (dying or being hospitalized). My results will allow me to identify and target appropriate patient groups for ED diversion, and will inform the development of lower-cost interventions (which will vary by patient group), allowing regions, hospitals and EDs to plan interventions to reduce ED use among these groups. In future studies I will apply the same methods to identify frequent ED user groups in other provinces, and will refine and test developed interventions.

column36: Canadian Donation and Transplantation Research Program (CDTRP): Maximizing benefits through national infrastructure and sustainability planning
column37: Transplantation is used much more broadly to treat diseases than most Canadians realize. No longer is it restricted to people with organ failure. Instead, it is poised to become the preferred treatment for many chronic diseases and blood cancers. Nonetheless, challenges remain, such as the 50% transplant failure rate and the risk of complications and cancer from immunosuppressive medication. Even though 90% of Canadians want to be organ donors, few succeed: nationally, there are only around 750 deceased donors per year. As a result, only 33% of Canadians on waitlists receive transplants. The others wait-or die waiting. In 2013, the Canadian National Transplant Research Program (CNTRP) was created to increase the number and quality of transplants in Canada by uniting the donation, solid organ transplant and bone marrow transplant research communities. Building on CNTRP's success, in the renamed Canadian Donation and Transplant Research Program (CDTRP), we are now restructuring the projects into broader themes that will forge new collaborations, strengthen existing ideas and create new ones, and lead to innovations that maintain our position as a global leader in donation and transplantation research. We are also shifting from centralized funding to supporting research through grant competitions funded by partners according to their priorities. Our program infrastructure will support research, training and knowledge transfer, and will catalyze collaborations across disciplines, stakeholders and researchers nationwide (and beyond) to advance research in donation and transplantation, and promote equity and diversity in these fields. This grant will allow us to transition towards a more self-sustaining national network in which we can achieve our long-term vision: that Canada fulfills every donation opportunity and realizes the full potential of transplantation as a cure for many chronic diseases and blood cancers.

column36: Age-related changes in standing balance: evidence of contributing factors from across the life course
column37: From getting out of bed in the morning to standing, sitting and walking throughout the day, balance is a crucial component of everyday life. It underlies nearly every physical movement at all stages in life from infancy to older age. Despite this universal truth, balance is a frequently overlooked aspect of physical health. There is strong evidence that cognitive ability plays an important role in successful balance, by combining sensory and motor signals. The MRC National Survey of Health and Development offers a unique opportunity to study these relationships. Data on health and life have been collected from over 5,000 individuals in the UK since their birth in March 1946. The proposed project will examine how factors across life, with a specific focus on cognition, are associated with standing balance in mid and later life. Project findings could help shape primary prevention and health policies by identifying what contributes to poor balance and subsequent fall risk. Helping maintain independence with ageing at the individual level should directly impact on increasing costs associated with age-related impairments at the population level.
