column36: Modelling the cardiovascular health impacts of urban policies in Accra, Ghana
column37: Cities can promote or harm the health of the populations that live within them. In low-income settings, especially those in Africa and Asia, urban dwellers are exposed to many things, including household and community air pollution and noise pollution. The increasing prevalence of these health-harming exposures, as well as the rise of urban populations, has contributed to the increasing burden of cardiovascular diseases and mortality in many low and middle-income settings. However, cities can also use the powers and assets available to them to create healthy environments by creating and implementing health-promoting policies and regulations that affect urban form and services (e.g., transportation, housing, energy). My PhD research is part of a larger multi-country research program that is comparing the trade-offs and health benefits of different pathways for urban development. My PhD research will use innovative machine learning, statistical, and epidemiological, techniques to measure and characterize the spatial patterns of environmental exposures in Accra, Ghana, and simulate the impacts of different policy scenarios on levels of blood pressure and body-mass index. Policy scenario's, such as increasing bus rapid transit (BRT) options, subsidizing cleaner household cooking fuels, banning the import of old, diesel fuel, cars, or improving housing quality in slums, will be refined and amended with local stakeholders in Accra through in-country workshops and meetings. The data I will use will be from emerging (e.g., satellite images), existing (e.g., publicly available population-based surveys), or new (e.g., I will collect on the ground noise-pollution measurements) sources. My research will provide researchers, urban planners, and public health experts in Ghana with the tools and information to make informed decisions on the potential cardiovascular health benefits of changes to urban environments and services.

column36: Clinical infectious disease sequencing for antimicrobial resistance detection and antibiotic stewardship
column37: Since Sir Alexander Fleming's discovery of penicillin in the earliest twentieth century, antibiotics have been the silver bullet used treat bacterial infections. In recent decades however, antibiotics have become less effective, because bacteria have evolved resistances to their effects. Unfortunately, it is currently impossible to access resistance profiles without isolating the relevant bacteria from the patient and growing it in culture, which costs either valuable days of delayed treatment, or overuse of antibiotics, leading to even stronger and more wide-spread resistance. Resistance profiles can easily be accessed through DNA sequencing, and the advent of portable, real-time sequencers is steadily making bedside sequencing a realistic and practical clinical test. I plan to use sequencing to combat antibiotic resistance in two ways. Firstly, I will use and develop algorithms to examine raw signals from the sequencer in order to detect potential resistance to antibiotics directly from human samples. In this way, even the time-consuming step of translating these signals into DNA sequence may be skipped. Secondly, I will use this same data to gain deeper insight into how resistance to antibiotics develops and spreads among bacteria and their hosts at a genetic and epigenetic level, in order to better inform antibiotic stewardship policies. Ultimately, these efforts will help curtail the crisis of antibiotic resistant infectious diseases, and avoid a health systems setback to the pre-twentieth century era, where medicine had no answer to deadly bacterial infections.

column36: Soft Robotic Diaphragmatic Assist Device for the Treatment of Mechanical Respiratory Failure
column37: The diaphragm is the large, dome-shaped muscle responsible for breathing. Diaphragm failure occurs in a variety of conditions including phrenic nerve injury, congenital diaphragmatic hernias (CDH), and many degenerative neuromuscular diseases. In phrenic nerve injury, the diaphragm doesn't properly contract because it isn't receiving the proper signals, and in patients with CDH and muscular dystrophies, the muscle lacks the ability to contract properly. Regardless of cause, diaphragm failure ultimately causes the patient to struggle to breathe. The constant struggle to breathe can cause chronically low oxygen, muscle fatigue and even respiratory failure. When these cases are severe, patients often got on a noninvasive ventilator, which involves a face mask that covers the nose and mouth and forces air into the lungs. Because noninvasive ventilation options hinder freedom of movement, speaking, and eating, noninvasive ventilation is generally only used overnight during sleep, which only provides temporary relief for fatigued respiratory muscles. We propose the development of an "implantable ventilator" that would help push the diaphragm into a normal breathing motion. This device would allow the patient to go about their life freely, unhindered by bulky face masks. This ventilator can be operated at all hours of the day, providing the therapeutic effect of proper ventilation around-the-clock. Our proposed device is inspired by our previous work on a soft robotic heart sleeve developed for heart failure. Similar to a blood pressure cuff, the heart sleeve was wrapped around the heart and when inflated, the sleeve would squeeze the heart. An external control box automatically inflated and deflated the device in time with the normal heart beat, aiding the hearts failing pumping ability. Using a similar technology, we plan to use soft robotic technology to create a device that pushes the diaphragm into its normal motion, allowing patients to breathe properly again.

column36: Investigation of factors that enable National Essential Medicines Lists to improve or hinder access to essential cardiovascular disease medicines: case studies in Kenya and Uganda
column37: The human right to health is challenged for many people worldwide due to a lack of access to essential medicines. The factors that support or impede the effective implementation of National Essential Medicines Lists (NEMLs), as a policy tool to ensure accessibility and affordability of essential medicines are currently poorly understood, particularly in low and middle-income countries. Disparities in access to medicines for cardiovascular disease (CVD), the number one cause of death worldwide, are a major human rights and equity concern as the poorest populations in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) bear the highest burden of disability and death from CVD, and at younger ages. Therefore, this study seeks to investigate the social, political and economic factors that enable or impede the successful implementation of National Essential Medicine Lists to improve availability and affordability of essential CVD medications in both the public and private health sectors in LMICs. A health policy analysis will be conducted focused on national level policy implementation processes in Kenya and Uganda. This cross-country comparative study between Kenya and Uganda will make it possible to distinguish social, political or economic contextual factors influencing the successful implementation of NEMLs. The aim of this study is to supply evidence to governments, United Nations Agencies, and civil society organizations that will deepen our understanding of factors that enable or hinder successful implementation of National Essential Medicine Lists. This evidence will be of great use to various actors on the path toward improving access to affordable CVD medicines and reducing preventable morbidity and mortality from CVD, in LMICs as well as developed nations such as Canada. The evidence will also be useful for understanding how to expand access to essential medicines in other disease areas.

column36: Identifying glucocorticoid receptor mediated mechanisms of polygene-environment interactions in depression.
column37: Depression is a common psychiatric disease, affecting nearly one in five individual during his or her lifetime. According to the World Health Organization, depression is currently the primary cause of disability worldwide, and is expected to become the leading cause of global burden by 2030. Despite these significant social and economic costs, the biological and genetic underpinnings of depression are not well understood. Both environmental and genetic factors contribute to depression risk, and these factors likely interact. For example, stress and exposure to stressful life events are the strongest risk factors for depression. Yet not everyone who is chronically stressed or experiences a stressful life event develops depression, indicating there are additional factors, such as genetics, that are at play. Previous research from our lab discovered that common genetic alterations could increase an individual's sensitivity to stress and consequently increase his or her risk of developing depression. The goal of my project is to determine the molecular mechanisms by which these alterations increase one's sensitivity to stress and thereby depression risk. First, I will investigate how these genetic alterations cause differences in the functioning of an important receptor (the glucocorticoid receptor). Secondly, I will look at how these variants may cause regions of DNA to interact differently with each other. Changes in both of these factors cause changes in gene expression and protein production, which ultimately modify brain networks that are altered in depression. If these mechanisms are successfully identified, they could represent novel therapeutic targets for the pharmacological treatment of depression. Additionally, understanding the role of stress and stressful life events on depression risk could help identify high risk populations, such as those exposed to trauma, so that early and effective social and preventative programs could be delivered.

column36: Dietary phytoestrogen intake, weight change, and the risk of gout
column37: BACKGROUND: Gout, the most common inflammatory arthritis in Canada and the US, is a metabolic condition caused by too much uric acid (a chemical in the blood). Gout has been shown to be associated with many other conditions, including obesity, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol levels. These conditions are also associated with an increased risk type-2 diabetes, a serious metabolic condition that also poses a substantial public health burden in Canada and the US. Although it's plausible for a relationship to exist between gout and type-2 diabetes, research to date has shown conflicting results. Specifically, studies have shown that having gout can increase the risk of developing type-2 diabetes, while having type-2 diabetes can actually decrease or have no impact on the risk of developing gout. Moreover, little is known about how diet, an important modifiable risk factor for type-2 diabetes, may also impact this risk of developing gout. OBJECTIVES: Using three large prospectively-collected datasets containing detailed medical, lifestyle, and dietary intake data, I propose to investigate the relationship between gout and type-2 diabetes. Specifically, I will: 1) Investigate the bidirectional association between gout and type-2 diabetes; and 2) Develop a dietary urate index using an established metabolomics dataset and examine this dietary index in relation to the risk of developing gout and type-2 diabetes. SIGNIFICANCE: Collectively, these investigations will help to identify individuals who are at an elevated risk of developing gout and type-2 diabetes, and will also identify modify dietary factors that may help reduce the risk of developing these serious conditions.

column36: Diagnostic, treatment, and health-related outcomes of depression screening in primary care and family medicine: a natural experiment
column37: Depression is a common problem that affects up to 15% of patients in primary care settings. Without proper treatment, depression can lead to increased disability, pain, and somatic symptoms, beyond that caused by comorbid physical conditions. Screening has been proposed as a method of increasing the detection of depression. However, policy makers and researchers have been hesitant to support widespread implementation because little is known about whether screening increases access to mental health care or improves health outcomes. The gold standard of evidence in health research is from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), but evidence for depression screening using this study design is very limited. Natural experiments, which are commonly used to examine the effects of policy changes, provide the next best source of evidence. The proposed project is a natural experiment using administrative data from clinics and hospitals in the Johns Hopkins network in the United States. Over a year ago, Johns Hopkins mandated depression screening for adults at all points of care within their network, but implementation has not been uniform across clinics or among providers. This scenario presents the ideal environment in which to conduct a natural experiment. In conjunction with the Johns Hopkins network, we will aggregate and clean electronic health record data and preform analyses of services use and health-related outcomes. We will compare the rates of depression diagnoses, of referrals to mental health care, and of treatment with medication or psychotherapy between patients who receive screening versus usual care. Furthermore, we will compare long-term mental and physical health outcomes between those diagnosed with depression via screening versus usual care. The results from this project will be used to inform national preventative health guidelines on the care and management of depression in medical settings.

column36: Functional Mechanisms of Adult Neural Stem/Progenitor Cells during Post-stroke Recovery
column37: Stroke is caused by an impairment of blood flow to the brain resulting in death and dysfunction of affected tissue. Millions of stroke survivors worldwide are afflicted with significant disabilities in day-to-day function. Unfortunately, the brain's ability for repair and recovery is somewhat limited and impairments caused by stroke are often permanent. However, stem cells in the brain, especially in a region called the subventricular zone, offer a potential source for endogenous brain repair. It is understood that these stem cells proliferate after stroke and other brain injuries, sending newborn progenitor cells towards the injured area in order to aid recovery, but the precise functions of these new cells are unclear. Using a mouse model of stroke, we will investigate how neural stem and progenitor cells influence various recovery and repair processes. These processes include: reorganization of blood vessels to re-establish blood flow and promote recovery of tissue surrounding the infarct, formation of scars that surround the damaged tissue to limit the spread of injury and protect surviving cells, and synaptic plasticity of surviving neurons, which is crucial for recovering lost functions. Importantly, these processes will be related to functional recovery using sensitive behavioural assays in order to identify which are best predictive of functional improvement. This research will define the functional mechanisms of newborn cells after stroke. In addition to revealing fundamental aspects of brain repair, findings may aid efforts directed at exploiting the benefits of stem cells in order to improve recovery from stroke.

column36: Catechins as Adjuvants in the Treatment of Alzheimer's Disease: Enhancing the Response of Microglia to Amyloid Beta
column37: One of the main causes of neuronal death in the brain of Alzheimer's Disease (AD) patients is the formation of toxic assemblies of the amyloid beta protein. In healthy individuals, amyloid beta mostly remains as monomers. However, genetic mutations and aging cause amyloid beta monomers to grow into larger ensembles or oligomers that are toxic to cells. One particular group of cells that are affected by the amyloid beta oligomers are microglia, "spider-like" cells that scavenge their environment and clear harmful factors. The depression of the protective effect of microglial cells by amyloid beta oligomers in AD is one of the main mechanisms through which amyloid beta self-association leads to neuronal death. Hence, amyloid beta aggregation inhibitors provide a potential therapeutic option to restore healthy microglial cells in AD patients. One such inhibitor is the green tea extract epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG). We have recently shown that EGCG remodels existing toxic amyloid beta oligomers into non-toxic structures by coating the surface of these oligomers and inhibiting their growth. However, it is still unclear which amyloid beta oligomer-cell interactions are down-regulated upon addition of EGCG. Understanding this is critical for turning EGCG into a viable drug-like molecule. We speculate that the EGCG-induced coating prevents the interaction of amyloid beta with healthy cells, such as microglia, and arrests its toxic effects. To test this hypothesis, we plan to monitor the interaction of amyloid beta oligomers with microglia in the absence and presence of EGCG, using NMR and fluorescence spectroscopies combined with confocal microscopy. This study will provide a better understanding of the EGCG inhibitor mechanism and will facilitate the development of new inhibitors of amyloid beta aggregation.

column36: Therapeutic Alliance in Cognitive Behaviour Therapy for Children with Autism
column37: Approximately 70% of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) have considerable emotional and behavioural challenges, meeting criteria for at least one mental health disorder. Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) has been shown to be helpful in reducing these problems, but only a portion of children with ASD significantly improve as a result of therapy. It is, therefore, critical to identify what leads to treatment success. Differences in treatment outcomes can partially be explained by the collaborative relationship between therapist and patient, known as the therapeutic alliance. This relationship is recognized as a significant predictor of treatment success for both children and adults involved in CBT. For children with ASD, many factors may impact the therapeutic alliance, such as severity of ASD and mental health symptoms, and their motivation to participate in therapy. At the same time, therapist skills, and their ability to accommodate the specific needs of children with ASD may also influence the therapeutic alliance. Little research has focused on how child and therapist factors influence the quality of therapeutic alliance in CBT for children with ASD. The purpose of my proposed research is to improve therapeutic outcomes for this group of children, by determining how child characteristics and therapist skills influence therapeutic alliance, and if therapeutic alliance predicts treatment success. There is a great need for effective mental health interventions for children with ASD. This study will be the first to identify the child and therapist factors that impact the therapeutic alliance, and will provide information about how therapeutic alliance leads to successful outcomes following CBT for children with ASD. The findings from this study will be used to educate therapists on the skills needed to develop a strong alliance, and ultimately maximize the benefits of mental health intervention for this population.

column36: Child's Behavioral Problems: Prenatal Anxiety Programming Effects and Moderation by Maternal-Child Attachment Security and Child's Sex
column37: Prenatal anxiety is a major mental health issue that affects approximately 2 in every 10 pregnant women. To date, research has largely focused on the detrimental influence of perinatal depression on children's behavior; however, prenatal anxiety may be even worse for children's development. Prenatal anxiety is thought to result in a "programming" effect on fetal brain, and may contribute to the later behavior problems in children. It is known that behavioral problems in children as young as 12 months of age are associated with subsequent adolescent and adult psychopathology. Thus, it is important to prevent these behavioral problems from arising by lessening or alleviating prenatal anxiety. The security of a child's attachment to his or her mother is foundational to child's social and emotional skills in later life, and is linked to better behavioral adjustment in children. Maternal-child attachment may thus buffer the negative influence of prenatal anxiety on children's behavioral problems. Further, boys and girls exposed to prenatal anxiety are prone to different behavioral problems, with girls more likely to be anxious and depressed (internalizing behaviors), and boys more likely to be aggressive and hyperactive (externalizing behaviors). A better understanding of how both prenatal (anxiety) and postnatal (maternal-child attachment) factors impact child's behavior has important implications because prenatal anxiety and maternal-child attachment security may be modified by interventions. Ultimately, the findings of this research will inform targeted interventions to prevent anxiety during pregnancy and foster maternal-child attachment, which will improve the health and well-being of families across Canada.

column37: Certaines personnes sont plus susceptibles que d'autres a des maladies causees par des bacteries comme des pneumonies ou des bronchites. Ces gens doivent souvent prendre des antibiotiques, mais ceux-ci ne sont pas toujours efficaces. Alors comment controler leurs infections ? Augmenter les effets du leucotriene B4 serait une solution. Qu'est-ce que le leucotriene B4 ? Il s'agit d'une molecule produite normalement par nos globules blancs et qui les stimulent a eliminer les bacteries. Aider ces globules blancs a mieux eliminer les bacteries en augmentant les effets du leucotriene B4 aiderait grandement les gens susceptibles aux bacteries. Mais comment augmenter les effets du leucotriene B4? Augmenter, en meme temps, sa quantite et ses effets est notre solution. QUEL EST LE BUT DE MON PROJET ? Mon projet vise a comprendre 1) comment augmenter la quantite et les effets du leucotriene B4 et 2) confirmer si cette strategie rend nos globules blancs plus performants. QU'EST-CE QUE MON PROJET APPORTERA ? Dans le futur, nous croyons qu'un medicament permettant d'augmenter la quantite du leucotriene B4 pourrait etre utilise pour aider les globules blancs a eliminer bacteries, diminuer les infections et la prise d'antibiotiques chez des gens qui souffrent d'infections repetitives. POURQUOI C'EST IMPORTANT ? Certaines personnes souffrent d'infections repetitives, comme les personnes atteintes de fibrose kystique. Pour traiter leurs infections, la prise d'antibiotiques est la meilleure solution utilisee aujourd'hui. Cependant, de plus en plus d'antibiotiques ne sont plus suffisamment efficaces pour tuer les bacteries. Mon projet pourrait donc amener une solution alternative pour traiter les infections, et ainsi ameliorer la qualite de vie chez les gens souffrant d'infections repetitives.

column36: Microglial Activation across Major Depressive Disorder and Effect of Minocycline Treatment
column37: According to the World Health Organization, clinical depression is the leading cause of death and disability in moderate to high income nations, affecting up to 5% of Canadians at any one time. Current treatments often help, but half of clinical depression cases do not adequately respond. We think that there are multiple brain changes in clinical depression, some of which are missed by common treatments. We think that brain inflammation may be one of those brain changes that could contribute to clinical depression and affect treatment response. Our site has a special brain imaging tool to detect inflammation. Inflammation is the body's response to infection or trauma, like the redness after a scrape on the skin. In 2015, our research site discovered that brain inflammation happens in medication-free clinical depression. We also discovered that brain inflammation is present in commonly co-occurring psychiatric illnesses, such as obsessive compulsive disorder. It is possible that brain inflammation could contribute to multiple psychiatric illnesses. Our present study is the first to see whether there is brain inflammation in treatment resistant depression (clinical depression that does not respond to treatment). It will also be the first study to see whether we can reduce the brain inflammation with an anti-inflammatory medication, minocycline, which is currently on the Canadian market for another indication. If brain inflammation is detected in treatment resistant depression, new treatments could be developed to change the inflammation to make it more curative or to get rid of the inflammation. If minocycline reduces the brain inflammation, this might result in an entirely new treatment direction for treatment resistant depression and other commonly co-occurring psychiatric illnesses.

column36: Novel vaccine strategy to enhance mucosal immune responses against HIV-1 and STIs in the female genital tract
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a major global health issue, with 36 million individuals infected worldwide and over 1.5 million deaths occurring due to infection each year. With no cure currently available, an HIV vaccine is urgently needed. This is especially troubling for women, who are at higher risk for infection with HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) compared to men. The aim of this research project is to develop a vaccination strategy for HIV that will generate better protection in the female genital tract (FGT), the primary site of infection during heterosexual transmission. We believe we can achieve this by using estradiol, a female sex hormone which has shown to be protective against susceptibility to STIs. Based on previous studies done with herpes infection, another viral STI, we predict that estradiol will increase tissue-resident memory T cells, a newly described subset of cells, and improve antibody responses against HIV. Tissue-resident memory T cells are generated following immunization, and are programmed to remain within the FGT. As a result, these cells are readily available to help control infection and provide rapid protection. To test our vaccination strategy, we will immunize mice using a novel HIV candidate vaccine, and examine the immune response generated to determine the effect of estradiol treatment. We will also characterize these novel memory T cells in human endometrium and cervix tissues from pre- and post-menopausal women, to determine how hormone levels can influence these cell populations. The knowledge generated from this project will fundamentally improve women's reproductive health by: 1) offering an efficacious vaccination strategy for STIs, and 2) emphasizing the need to keep sex-specific immune responses in consideration during vaccine development.

column36: Investigating how amino acid polymorphisms in the contemporary outbreak strains have influenced Zika virus fitness
column37: The ongoing Zika virus (ZIKV) outbreak in Latin America has garnered attention due to the growing evidence that ZIKV causes birth defects. ZIKV was identified 70 years ago, historically causing low levels of mild illness. However, recent ZIKV outbreaks have been characterized by a rapid geographic expansion, and only recently has ZIKV been associated with neurological complications such as Guillain-Barre syndrome and fetal microcephaly. We hypothesize that the recent increase in viral transmission and disease severity are the result of evolutionary acquired mutations in the ZIKV genome. To test this hypothesis, in this proposal, we will compare ZIKV strains isolated from the current outbreak to historical ZIKV strains in human and mosquito cells. We will then determine the region(s) of the ZIKV genome responsible for conferring increased fitness seen in the contemporary strains, and introduce mutations from the current outbreak strains into the historical reference ZIKV strain and measure the resulting changes in viral infectivity, replication, and induction of the host immune response. We anticipate that these studies will identify regions of the ZIKV genome that have contributed to the rapid spread and increased disease severity seen in ongoing ZIKV outbreaks, provide insight into the function of ZIKV proteins in viral pathogenesis and be an important step in the development of ZIKV-specific vaccines and antiviral therapies.

column37: Depuis vingt ans, il y a eu des progres considerables en greffe renale. De nouveaux agents immunosuppresseurs ont diminue considerablement le taux de rejet dans la premiere annee suivant une transplantation. Or, la survie a long terme n'a pas autant augmente, en partie en raison du rejet tardif, en particulier celui cause par les anticorps contre le greffon. Le specialiste en transplantation est confronte a un probleme lorsqu'il traite ce type de rejet : s'il n'y a pas assez d'immunosuppresseurs il y aura un rejet tandis qu'une trop grande quantite expose le patient aux infections et cancers. Pour gagner le combat contre ce rejet, il faut comprendre comment il se developpe dans le greffon et elucider les composantes immunitaires impliquees. Dans certains cas, les anticorps produisent des dommages en promouvant la coagulation dans les capillaires du greffon. Pour d'autres, des anticorps specifiques attirent des lymphocytes T CD8+, pour endommager la greffe. Finalement, dans certains patients, le rejet, que nous croyons du aux anticorps, serait cause par des cellules sanguines specialisees appelees monocytes, que nous savons activees lors des rejets. L'objectif de notre projet est de dechiffrer les differentes sequences d'evenements par lesquelles les anticorps peuvent endommager le greffon. Dans le laboratoire, nous utilisons des cellules reproduisant les micro-vaisseaux presents dans le compartiment renal, le glomerule. En utilisant ce modele pour etudier les cellules immunitaires, nous esperons atteindre notre objectif et esperons que ces connaissances aideront au developpement de protocoles efficaces et securitaires pour traiter le rejet et augmenter l'esperance de vie chez les greffes renaux.

column36: Is a new patient-centred joint-protection program able to enhance fidelity, intention and adherence in people with hand osteoarthritis? A randomized trial of 2 delivery formats.
column37: The most common location for osteoarthritis (OA) is the hand. Hand OA is responsible for pain and limitations in hand function that can limit peoples' ability to work or remain independent. As hand OA progresses, the joints become deformed. Joint Protection Programs (JPP) were developed in the 1980's to help people with hand OA do tasks in daily life, alleviate pain, and prevent joint deformity. JPP teach people how to change, or pace tasks, and how to use devices that reduce joint loading. Although studies have shown these programs can be effective, many people do not fully understand or use JPP. The JPP in use today have not been updated to reflect the life tasks and tools of the 21st century. Much has changed - like how we use our phones. We can do better for people with arthritis. We will update the JPP to better address the important daily tasks that people do, and work with patients and engineers to find the best solutions. In Stage 1, we will develop JPP modules about the principles of joint protection, better ways to do tasks, how to use using assistive devices/technology and ways to adapt JPP to personal goals. The new JPP will use engineering data on hand forces in life tasks, and feedback/priorities of patients. We will develop written guides and video versions with patients demonstrating JPP. Each module will be relevant, easy to understand and give practical examples. In Stage 2, 40 people with arthritis will be randomly allocated to complete either the written guide or video program over a 2-week period. Everyone will complete standardized tests of joint self-protection during life tasks, grip strength, pain, hand function, satisfaction, and their intention to continue to use JPP in the future. Interviews with patients will define their experiences, facilitators and barriers to using JPP. This study will lead to more useful, accessible and effective JPP that help people with hand OA avoid pain and prevent joint deformity.

column36: Les troubles psychotiques chez les victimes d'agression sexuelle a l'enfance : une etude prospective de cas-controle apparie
column37: Des milliers d'enfants canadiens sont victimes d'agression sexuelle chaque annee. L'agression sexuelle a l'enfance implique des consequences deleteres sur la sante mentale des victimes, pouvant mener a des troubles psychologiques tels le stress post-traumatique et l'anxiete et meme, selon les recentes etudes a ce sujet, aux troubles mentaux graves tels les troubles psychotiques. Des etudes realisees aupres d'adultes ayant un trouble psychotique indiquent que pres du tiers d'entre eux ont ete agresses sexuellement a l'enfance. Certains auteurs proposent que les repercussions psychologiques de l'agression sexuelle, tels le stress post-traumatique et le recours a la dissociation en tant que mecanisme de defense, peuvent expliquer le developpement d'un trouble psychotique. Effectivement, le fait de s'adapter a un evenement traumatique en se detachant de soi et de ses emotions negatives serait lie aux experiences psychotiques. Ces hypotheses sur le developpement des troubles psychotiques suite a une agression sexuelle n'ont toutefois jamais ete testees ni demontrees. L'objectif general de cette etude sera de documenter les trajectoires developpementales des troubles psychotiques aupres d'adolescents et de jeunes adultes ayant vecu une agression sexuelle a l'enfance en comparaison a la population generale. Les trajectoires de sante mentale des deux groupes seront comparees en fonction des diagnostics de stress post-traumatique, de dissociation et de troubles psychotiques obtenus lors de consultations medicales ou d'hospitalisations. Il est primordial de determiner les mecanismes psychologiques impliques dans l'association entre l'agression sexuelle a l'enfance et les troubles psychotiques aupres d'adolescents et de jeunes adultes. Une meilleure connaissance de ces mecanismes permettra d'offrir un meilleur suivi et des traitements plus adequats aux jeunes victimes, en plus de contribuer a la prevention des troubles psychotiques aupres des populations a risque au Canada.

column37: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) act at the cell surface, relaying chemically-encoded messages delivered by hormones or drugs to a network of intracellular proteins resulting in physiological effects. For instance, adrenaline binds to adrenergic receptors causing an increase in heart rate and opening of the airways. These receptors are thus important targets in drug discovery and development as we modulate their function by administering drugs. Drug-induced receptor activation leads to a reorganization of receptor "shape", thought to be a key determinant in dictating downstream physiological effects. Certain drugs can stabilize specific conformations leading to desired biological outcomes while others also generate unwanted side effects. It may be possible to regulate a drug's effect to tailor drug responses for a specific need. The main focus of my research centers around the beta2-adrenergic receptor (beta2AR), an important target for the treatment of pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases, conditions that many Canadians suffer from. My goal is to understand the link between receptor "shape" and function and to uncover ways that receptor shape or conformation can change in response to environmental factors. For this purpose, we engineered conformation-sensitive biosensors as part of a pharmacological toolkit to report on changes in beta2AR conformation adopted upon drug binding. These biosensors provide us with tools to study the conformational landscape of the beta2AR as well as a method to identify which drugs or associated signaling partners influence its conformation. Altogether, these biosensors will allow us to gain a more complete understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms that govern receptor conformation and function. Our approach will allow 'fine-tuning' of drug responses as we will gain information on how to better target the beta2AR in a therapeutic context.

column36: Complex and concurrent disorders in the provincial Correctional system in British Columbia: a retrospective cohort study of over 200,000 cases over 10 years
column37: It is well known that people with severe and persistent mental disorders and substance use disorders are overrepresented in jails and prisons. Researchers have identified a subgroup of individuals with complex and concurrent mental disorders and substance use disorders (CCD) and associated psychosocial and behavioral challenges that often cycle through criminal justice and health services in an ineffectual and costly pattern. After release from custody, people with CCD are at higher risk for reincarceration, unemployment, homelessness, physical illness/injury, and death than people without CCD. Approximately 15,000 adults come into contact with the Corrections system per year in British Columbia. Little is known about the prevalence, incidence, and trajectories of people with CCD. The current study aims to fill this gap by conducting a retrospective analysis of a large cohort of people with CCD. Data from comprehensive mental health intake assessments to inform placement and treatment planning will be collected for all inmates from 2006-2016 (over 200,000 records). The primary aim of the study is to compare inmates with and without CCD. We hypothesize that people with CCD have higher prevalence and incidence of reincarceration (including violent reoffending), poorer social well-being, and poorer health outcomes than people without CCD. To test this hypothesis, we will compare: 1. Reincarceration (time to reincarceration, severity of offence); 2. Health outcomes (physical and mental health issues, self-harm); and 3. Social wellbeing (living situation, employment), for inmates with and without CCD. This information has important implications for policy and planning related to mental health services for justice-involved people. An understanding of the demand for services among BC inmates is critical, given the link between mental illness and poor outcomes, and the potential for treatment to contribute to successful re-integration and reduce adverse outcomes.

column36: The Role of Loricrin In Aggressive Periodontitis
column37: Aggressive periodontitis (AgP) is a severe, rapidly progressive form of periodontitis (gum disease) that occurs in adolescents and young adults. Current research suggests that there may be multiple different causes for AgP. Some data pinpoint issues with patient immune defense mechanisms, others target features of the bacteria and some studies focus on the cornified epithelium (CE), which is the outermost layer of the skin and oral mucosa and has an important role in barrier function. The CE protects against dehydration and pathogen invasion. Loricrin is the most abundant CE protein and its decreased presence has been linked to many skin related disorders; it is considered to be a key protein in the barrier function of the CE. A recent study showed decreased loricrin expression (7x) in patients with AgP compared with those with chronic periodontal disease. We will use human primary skin cells to test the impact of loricrin decrease on barrier function in vitro and later in a mouse model. The objective of our research is to determine if a change in oral epithelial barrier function is a common mechanism in patients with AgP and responsible for the extreme host response that leads to excessive inflammation, bone and tooth loss. Revealing the underling mechanism in AgP will dramatically change early diagnosis of this complex disease and ensure that susceptible patients are treated promptly to reduce long term morbidity and quality of life issues. Mechanistic insight will also enable development of new interventional strategies.

column37: Periodontal disease is a common inflammatory condition of the tissues responsible for supporting the teeth. This disease affects the vast majority of the North American population during their lifetime and can negatively alter physical appearance and chewing efficiency through tooth loss. Unfortunately, the management of this disease is associated with a significant consumption of health care resources in Canada. While the effects of this condition appear confined to the mouth, periodontal disease has been associated with the development of diabetes, heart disease and cancer. The literature suggests that periodontal disease is regulated by complex relationships between the wide variety of bacteria which inhabit the oral cavity and the earliest responding cells of the immune system known as neutrophils. It is now accepted that neutrophils are no longer a uniform group of cells which are merely responsible for fighting infection. At this time, however, it is unclear as to how differing groups of neutrophils vary in function and how these cells influence systemic health in the setting of periodontal disease. This project will strengthen our understanding of neutrophil biology by focusing on the genetic and functional variations between differing neutrophil populations in states of health and inflammation. We will utilize animal models of abdominal cavity infections and periodontitis to identify the potential mechanisms by which periodontal disease influences systemic health. Identifying differing neutrophil subsets may also serve as a biochemical test to monitor periodontal disease progression and treatment effectiveness in populations affected with this condition. Finally, knowledge of the functional capacities of differing neutrophil subsets may allow for the development of novel treatments which dampen immune system within the oral cavity, thereby reducing the damage associated with periodontal disease and potential worsening of existing systemic health conditions.

column36: Real world gait analysis and modification of people with knee osteoarthritis using a novel instrumented shoe
column37: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common chronic disease associated with pain, loss of mobility and reduced quality of life. There is no cure for OA, and treatment for many people involves expensive surgeries or life-long drug regimens, both carrying high risk of side effects. New treatments, including changing the way people walk - termed gait modification - have been developed to slow disease progression and improve symptoms, while reducing patient risk. However, delivery of gait modification has mainly been limited to expensive and inaccessible laboratory settings. Recent technological advances using sensors worn on the body (wearable sensors) have become a realistic option to monitor walking in natural settings and for longer durations, something not previously possible in a lab. This is important to understand how people walk in the real world, and whether or not treatments are effective and feasible outside of controlled laboratory settings. My research will explore gait modification for knee OA out in the community, utilizing the Smart Shoe. The Smart Shoe is a sensorized athletic shoe that measures foot rotation. First, participants will wear the shoes for 4 weeks to assess normal walking patterns outside the lab. Participants will also take part in training sessions to modify their foot rotation, providing insight into how people learn new movement patterns in real-world conditions. Finally, participants will undergo a 3-month gait modification program using instant feedback from the sensors. This study will provide the first analysis of gait modification for knee OA in real-world settings. Transferring walking analysis and treatment outside of the laboratory will significantly reduce delivery costs, while improving the accessibility to those affected. Additionally, gait modification using wearable sensors paired with a smart device will improve treatment outcomes and patient quality of life, ultimately reducing the economic burden of this disease.

column36: Enhancing motor recovery in a non-human primate model of chronic stroke by inhibiting pro-death neuronal signaling
column37: Stroke is a disorder with staggering emotional and socioeconomic impact. It is a leading cause of death in Canada and leaves the majority of survivors with long-term disabilities that significantly diminish their autonomy and quality of life. Motor recovery following a stroke is critically dependent upon the survival of mature and newly born neurons in brain areas adjacent to the injury. In fact, the degree reallocation of motor function to adjacent areas has been shown to be related to the proficiency of motor recovery. Recovery can be hindered by the fact that in the days to weeks following a stroke, neurotoxic signaling resulting from physiological stress from the initial injury increases and can cause neuronal death. Classes of molecules that inhibit neurotoxic signaling pathways may have neuroprotective properties and promote pro-survival signaling. The drug NA-1 is one such inhibitor and its administration in the days following a stroke could promote neuronal survival and improve motor recovery. We will assess the motor function of Cynomolgus macaques using behavioral tests and determine baseline brain connectivity using functional imaging. The animals will undergo a transient medial cerebral artery occlusion to induce a stroke and will be given injections of either NA-1 or placebo during recovery. We will continuously assess motor function and brain connectivity throughout recovery to determine whether NA-1 can significantly improve neuronal survival, functional connectivity, and motor control. The findings of the proposed research has important implications for the efficacy of such drugs in improving stroke recovery which can lessen the socioeconomic burden and the emotional and physical strain of stroke related disabilities.

column36: Muddy molecules for pandemic protection: A prospective longitudinal survey using genomic analysis of wetland sediment for the detection and characterization of avian influenza viruses in wild waterfowl in the Fraser Valley, British Columbia, Canada
column37: Avian influenza (AI) is a viral disease that can cause serious human and animal health consequences. The recent outbreaks of H7N9 and H5N1 AI strains, along with the possibility for AI to change into new strains with improved human-to-human transmission, leads to concerns that AI could cause the next global pandemic. Certain AI viruses are considered to be higher risk for causing disease, particularly H5 and H7 strains. The surveillance for AI is crucial to the prevention of its devastating impacts. AI normally circulates in wild waterfowl hosts who are the targets for AI surveillance; however, these hosts typically carry the virus without showing signs of disease. Additionally, our current AI surveillance techniques in wild waterfowl is focused on testing individual birds, which is labour intensive and makes it difficult to obtain a representative sample of the whole wild host population. This is problematic as we may not be detecting many AI strains circulating in the wild hosts. A solution to this problem is to test environmental samples. As wild birds excrete the virus in their feces and many individual birds defecate in wetlands, taking samples of wetland mud allows for the detection of AI viruses deposited by many birds within the population. This project will be the first study to evaluate the use of wetland sediment for the ongoing surveillance of AI, and will evaluate the effectiveness the environmental method against the gold-standard. The two-year study will have monthly surveillance on 3 wetlands, where the diversity, rate of positivity, and timing of AI viruses in sediment is compared to those circulating in live waterfowl birds (the gold-standard method). Data will also be collected on related wetland ecological variables such as water temperature and waterfowl abundance. This project will provide human and animal health officials with a more efficient and accurate signal of seasonal AI risk and help to prevent future surveillance failures.

column36: MicroRNA-9 Promotes Immune Cell Activation Through Targeting Negative Regulators of gene expression
column37: Dendritic cells (DCs) are important cells in the human immune system which are critical for targeting the immune response against specific threats. When a DC senses a threat , it becomes activated which leads the cell to move into the lymph node and direct T-cells against the specific threat. Both DCs and T-cells control whether or not they become activated to be sure they only activate with the right signals. This control is important otherwise these cells could activate by themselves , causing your immune system to attack the body, or to not activate properly causing improper immune responses against bacteria. Our lab is trying to figure out the exact way that DCs and T-cells control their activation, and have found that both of these cell types increase the amount of microRNA-9 when they are activated. MicroRNAs are a way for cells to repress the expression of genes specific for each microRNA, which leads to less of that gene's products in the cell. We believe microRNA-9 repress' the genes of various repressors of activation, and thus more microRNA-9 leads to more activation. If that is the case then perhaps this pathway can be enhanced to increase the activation of these cells or be blocked to stop your immune system from attacking yourself. Overall this research will shed some light on how both DCs and T-cells control their activation and can lead to better understanding of how this can go wrong in autoimmune diseases such as diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.

column36: Etude des hyperactivations cerebrales dans le prodrome de la maladie d'Alzheimer par le biais de l'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle
column37: Le diagnostic de la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) se fait a la phase de demence, c'est-a-dire lorsque l'autonomie au quotidien de la personne atteinte est compromise. Ceci dit, les recentes decouvertes dans le domaine nous ont montre que certains changements cerebraux surviendraient plusieurs annees avant l'apparition des premiers symptomes. La presence de mecanismes cerebraux compensatoires pourrait expliquer cette periode ou les symptomes sont minimaux, voire absents. Des hyperactivations cerebrales, c'est-a-dire des niveaux d'activation superieurs a ceux d'individus cognitivement sains, ont ete observees dans le trouble cognitif leger, une phase qui precede generalement le stade demence. Ces hyperactivations pourraient etre un marqueur precoce de la maladie et sous-tendre de tels mecanismes compensatoires. Toutefois, le moment d'apparition de ces hyperactivations est meconnu, puisque la plupart des recherches ont etudie des individus trop atteints par la maladie. L'etude d'individus presentant une plainte de memoire pourrait fournir des indices precieux pour repondre a cette question. Ensuite, on ne sait pas comment ces hyperactivations changent avec la progression de la maladie, puisque la plupart des etudes n'ont pas evalue leurs sujets a plusieurs reprises dans le temps. Aussi, peu d'etudes ont examine la relation entre les hyperactivations et les pertes neuronales dans les stades precoces de la MA, ce qui limite les connaissances sur la relation entre ces types d'alterations. Enfin, on ne sait pas s'il existe des facteurs individuels (education, style de vie) pouvant favoriser la mise en place de mecanismes cerebraux compensatoires, ce qui pourrait guider le developpement d'interventions cognitives. Ce projet vise donc a etudier les hyperactivations cerebrales chez des individus ayant soit un trouble cognitif leger, soit une plainte de memoire en examinant leur relation avec les dommages neuronaux, la progression de la maladie, et les facteurs individuels.

column36: Integrated Knowledge Translation in Child Health: Advancing Evidence and Contributing to Pediatric Readiness of Canada's Emergency Departments
column37: Not using the best available evidence is common in the field of child health. Past research has found that as many as 4 in 10 children receive care that is not based on latest evidence and that 1 in 4 may receive care that may even be harmful. Knowledge Translation (KT) is often used to help move this research into practice. Yet, in child health and beyond, we still experience challenges to close this gap between what we know and what we do. It has long been thought that developing partnerships between those who produce and those who use research is the solution, as it ensures we ask research questions that are important to those who have to apply it. This joint way of conducting research, called integrated KT, is in its early scientific days with several important gaps that remain. No studies have looked at whether integrated KT efforts are working or not. Also, many of these studies measure and report differently on their interaction with end-users, making it difficult to compare and summarize the effects of research. The long-term goal of this project is to improve our understanding of how well integrated KT projects have worked to date in the field of child health, understand researchers and end-users experiences with practicing integrated KT, and to engage in and learn from an applied integrated KT project. The secondary goal of this research will be to measure baseline pediatric readiness of facilities across Manitoba and assess barriers and facilitators to achieving readiness status using an applied integrated KT approach.

column37: Mitochondria are structures within our cells that are responsible, among other things, for the production of energy. Genetic Mitochondrial Diseases affect the proper functioning of mitochondria. Organs with high-energy demand, such as muscles, heart and brain, are more susceptible and become dysfunctional. The French Canadian Variant of Leigh Syndrome (LSFC) affects 1/2000 child in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region of Quebec and there is no available cure to treat them. Recently, many studies revealed the multiple beneficial effects of stem cell. After a single injection, stem cells circulate in the body and home in the affected organ to heal it. Stem cells are currently used in clinical trials in humans to treat various diseases and we think they are an interesting option for the treatment of mitochondrial disorders. To better understand the mechanisms underlying mitochondrial diseases, our research group has developed a genetically modified mouse mimicking LSFC. The goal of this project is to study how the proper functioning of the mitochondria is altered in a model of LSFC. Afterwards, we will treat the LSFC mouse with stem cells collected from healthy mice. We will repeat our previous measurements to validate how this treatment improves the outcome of mitochondrial diseases. Our work will greatly contribute to the knowledge on mitochondrial disease, help with diagnosis and patient care, and potentially propose a curative therapy for patients.

column36: The Kusamala Program: an interactive counselling program for primary caregivers of children hospitalized with severe acute malnutrition in Malawi
column37: Kusamala means "to take care" in the native language of Malawi, a Southern African country with a high burden of malnutrition. When children have severe malnutrition and an illness, they require hospital treatment and have a high chance of dying during or after their treatment. Fortunately, due to advances in research and healthcare, the mortality rate is decreasing. This means that we have to turn our attention to what happens when these vulnerable children leave hospital. How can we ensure that children grow and develop properly once they return to their homes? We believe that the answer is to teach and empower caregivers, who are mainly mothers, with specific messages of how to take care of their children. There is a valuable opportunity to do this while caregivers wait in the hospital during their children's treatment. With this in mind, we developed an interactive counselling program called the Kusamala Program. The program is four days long, with one and a half hour sessions each day taught by hospital nurses. It covers three different topics which could improve growth and development of children: 1) nutrition and feeding; 2) water, sanitation, and hygiene; and 3) play. The first topic is important to help children to gain weight and grow. The second topic is to reduce the chance of children getting sick again. Finally, past studies have shown that play is necessary to improve development of the brain and motor skills. Play is commonly forgotten as a component of care of children in Malawi, where caregivers often have many other essential priorities like making money for their families, looking after several children, and tending to the home. However, if caregivers are made aware of the significance of playing with their children, we believe it is possible for caregivers to add play to their day. Ultimately, the Kusamala Program for caregivers could have profound impacts on their children's future by allowing children to reach their potential.

column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI), which involves an injury to the brain caused by an external force, is a leading cause of death and disability in children. Approximately 70 to 90% of TBI can be classified as mild in severity. Although most children recover quickly from mild TBI, some suffer negative long-term consequences, such as physical, cognitive, emotional and behavioral complaints, often termed persistent post-concussion symptoms (PPCS). Functional status, or the ability to participate in and carry out daily activities, is another area of potential difficulty after mild TBI. Multiple measures of functional outcomes are available (i.e., Functional Disability Inventory, Pediatric Injury Functional Outcome Scale, Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory, Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended). Predictors of functional outcome will include acute symptom burden, neuropsychological test performance, and functional neuroimaging (i.e., default mode network connectivity). The study findings will be important because mild TBI is a significant public health problem, with millions occurring annually in children in North America. A better understanding of functional outcomes and their predictors after mild TBI will help us to identify children who are likely to struggle with their recovery and to identify potential therapeutic targets for such interventions, so we can intervene effectively as soon as possible to prevent poor outcomes.

column36: Placental mosaicism in fetal growth restriction
column37: In up to 10% of pregnancies, the baby does not grow to its full potential. These growth-restricted babies are more likely to be born early or with birth defects, and they are at increased risk for poor infant, childhood, and adult health outcomes. Fetal growth restriction typically occurs when the placenta, the organ that transfers oxygen and nutrients to the developing baby, does not work efficiently. One cause of poor placenta function is genetic abnormalities found in the placenta but not the baby. Previous research in this area only focused on large chromosome errors in the placenta, but with technological advances, we can now detect deletions or duplications of smaller sections of the chromosomes, called copy number variants. These copy number variants likely also account for poor placenta function, and as a result, poor fetal growth. Using DNA samples collected from the placenta and the baby's umbilical cord from 30 pregnancies with evidence of poor fetal growth and from 30 pregnancies with a healthy baby, I will: 1) Determine how frequently copy number variants are found in the placenta but not the baby 2) Assess if copy number variants confined to the placenta are more frequent in pregnancies where the baby is born too small 3) Determine what effect these copy number variants have on the function of the placenta The results of my research will be important for both understanding the causes of poor placenta function and for the interpretation of prenatal testing. Increasingly, prenatal genetic testing is done by analyzing DNA from the placenta that is found in the mother's blood. This project will help us to understand how often a genetic abnormality may be present in placental DNA but not actually present in the baby, which is important for pregnancy counselling. Overall, this project will address the major gap in our knowledge about the incidence and impact of copy number variants in the placenta on fetal growth and development.

column37: There is increasing evidence that early-life stressors (either before or after birth) are an important risk factor for the development of eating disorders later in life. There is also evidence that children and adolescents with weight-related concerns, such as being overweight, have a greater risk for developing eating disorders, and lower chances of recovery. Children who are victim of bullying based on their physical appearance are at particular risk for developing an eating disorder. However, little is known about the specific mechanisms through which these risk factors may increase vulnerability to disordered eating. Also, since most of the research has been done in individuals with advanced cases of eating disorders in clinical settings, it is unknown whether these factors predict an even greater amount of eating disorder symptoms in the general population. In our first study, we will investigate how early stressors predict risk for eating disorders in adolescence. We will also look at how childhood weight and eating behaviors (such as over-eating, picky eating and irregular eating) influence this association. In our second study, we will specifically look at how bullying based on physical appearance affects the brains of victims who have lived such experiences. We will perform brain scans in young adolescent girls with and without a history of bullying. While in the scanner, they will look at stimuli (words) relevant for eating disorders. We will then compare both group's brain reactivity to this information in specific brain regions that are involved in emotional regulation. We will also assess the activity of specific genes in both groups. With these studies, we hope to better understand specific behavioral and biological pathways that might explain risk for disordered eating in the general population. This will help the development of prevention and intervention strategies aimed at reducing the impact of weight concerns on risk for eating disorders.

column37: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a mental illness characterized by intense mood changes. During mania, a person with BD will experience increased energy and poor self-control, often leading to risky decision making with consequences for themselves or their families. During depression, they will experience feelings of worthlessness and a loss of interest in things they once enjoyed. BD develops in late teens to early 20s and affects the individual for the duration of their life. Detecting and treating individuals at risk for BD at an early stage is critical in reducing onset of illness and the associated disability. As part of an existing study that has assessed over 375 youth at risk for severe mental illness, we will select 9-16 year olds who have a family history of BD or show early milder symptoms of the disorder and offer them 3 months of pre-emptive skill building therapy. We will study the effect of therapy by comparing both the symptoms and brain function before and after the intervention. We expect that giving these individuals the skills for managing emotions, impulses, and stress will lead to less symptoms in the future and to an improvement in the emotion regulation areas of the brain. The proposed research will tell us if early intervention improves the outcomes of at-risk youth and if it the improvement can be measured at the level of the brain, paving the way for better diagnosis and use of personalized prevention methods for BD.

column36: Genetic determinants of complex lipid and lipoprotein phenotypes
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the primary cause of death globally, and is responsible for one-third of deaths in Canada. With its expected rise in prevalence due to the obesity epidemic, CVD will continue to strain the health-care system and economy-over $20 billion is lost annually through hospital costs and decreased productivity. There has been an intense focus on identifying and attenuating CVD risk factors: lipids are a classic example, with low levels of "good" cholesterol (HDL-C), and high levels of triglyceride (TG) increasing CVD risk. While HDL-C and TG levels are influenced by lifestyle, they are also driven by genetic mutations. In this research project, mutations that influence levels of HDL-C or TG will be identified in individuals with extreme lipid profiles, either high HDL-C, low HDL-C, or high TG. The primary aims of this project are to: 1) identify single mutations with large effects on HDL-C or TG levels, and 2) determine if the accumulation of multiple mutations-each with small lipid-altering effects-can produce a cumulatively large effect on HDL-C or TG levels. By identifying lipid-altering mutations, not only can we provide a genetic explanation for patients with extreme, unexplained HDL-C or TG levels, we may also uncover novel insights into HDL-C or TG genes and mechanisms, allowing for new drug targets. For example, a study looking at the genetics behind high levels of "bad" cholesterol (LDL-C) found mutations in a gene that has since become a novel drug target: the drug has passed clinical trials and reduces both LDL-C levels and cardiovascular events. Further, looking at the accumulation of mutations could translate into a prediction tool for extreme HDL-C or TG levels in patients. If this tool is utilized early enough, depending on the prediction, additional preventative measures could be taken to attenuate CVD risk by specifically altering lipid levels through lifestyle alterations or medications.

column36: The Efficacy of Functional Electrical Stimulation (FES) Cycling for Improving Mobility in People with Multiple Sclerosis with Severe Mobility Impairment
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects Canadians at a higher rate than anywhere else in the world. One of the most devastating and poorly managed consequences of MS is walking impairment. Current therapies for managing MS do not prevent long-term accumulation of walking impairment, ultimately resulting in a negative impact on employment, participation in everyday activities, and overall quality of life. Additionally, there are significant socioeconomic costs of MS related walking impairment that all Canadians must incur. Consequently, there is a demand for effective strategies that prevent or slow walking impairment in people with MS. Exercise training is one approach that has been effective for improving mobility in people with MS. These benefits have been primarily reported in people with MS who do not experience major walking impairments. Unfortunately, individuals with severe MS experience significant mobility impairment and are often excluded from exercise training studies. These individuals require specialized approaches to exercise training that are adapted and physically accessible. One such approach is functional electrical stimulation (FES) cycling. This rehabilitation-based therapy provides mild electrical stimulation to weakened muscle groups to produce/enhance leg cycling movement and the capacity for exercise training. The proposed thesis research will test the effects of 24-weeks of FES cycling exercise in people with MS who experience walking impairment. Participants enrolled to this study will be involved in either FES cycling or passive leg cycling for 24 weeks. This thesis project will assess the ability of FES cycling to improve walking ability (walking speed, walking endurance, and agility). We expect that FES cycling will promote improvements in walking ability or slow the progression of walking impairment for these participants.

column37: RATIONALE Low education low income parents (parents with low socioeconomic status, hereafter SES) usually have a low level of literacy and health status. High quality online consumer information improves health, quality of life, and participation in healthcare, for low SES parents. I will interview 30 parents to understand what outcomes they experienced after using N&G+. IMPACT Results will directly benefit low SES parents and children. column36: Using a combined approach of meta-analysis and pharmacoepidemiology to assess the safety of SGLT2 inhibitors (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2)
column37: Approximately 15% of people living in Canada have type 2 diabetes mellitus ('diabetes'). Patients with diabetes have abnormally high levels of glucose in their blood. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are a new class of oral medications that lower blood glucose by facilitating excretion of glucose into the urine. While clinical trials have demonstrated that these drugs work effectively, there is limited information about their safety since the clinical trials had relatively few patients and were fairly short in duration. I plan to study the safety of these drugs using a variety of study design methods. One such method is through conducting a systematic review and meta-analysis. Specifically, I'll review the existing literature about these medications and summarize, both qualitatively and quantitatively, their overall safety. The other study design will involve "real-world" data. Real-world data are drawn from health care use outside of the traditional clinical trial experimental setting. These data can come from electronic medical records, insurance claims, and registry studies. The benefit of real-world data is that it reflects real-world use and generally contains a lot of participants (i.e., thousands to millions) which allows the detection of rare side-effects. Since SGLT2 inhibitors can lower bone density and affect calcium and vitamin D levels, I want to study whether they increase a patient's risk of breaking a bone. Assessing the risk of fracture for these medications is important, since patients with diabetes are prone to fractures. I will analyze the risk of fractures for patients who newly started SGLT2 inhibitors compared to patients who newly started another type of medication for diabetes. Our study will include over 200,000 participants from three databases (two US databases and one Canadian database) and has the potential to provide timely and highly-relevant information for both patients and their prescriber.

column37: Emotional eating is the tendency to overeat in response to negative emotions, such as stress or anxiety. It has been associated with weight outcomes, namely weight gain over time, and difficulties with weight loss. Despite this association, there are also many normal weight individuals who engage in emotional eating, however the ways in which they maintain their weight are not known. The proposed research aims to better understand and address the relationship between emotional eating and weight. The first stream is a pilot weight loss intervention that uses Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) techniques to target and reduce emotional eating, with the aim of improving weight loss outcomes for overweight and obese emotional eaters. The second stream examines emotional eating in normal weight individuals, to gain an understanding of the compensatory or regulatory strategies they may engage in, in order to maintain their weight. This research will contribute to our understanding of the relationship between emotional eating and weight, and importantly test the effectiveness of interventions designed to target emotional eating to improve weight loss outcomes.

column37: Problematique: L'echographie est maintenant un outil indispensable au suivi de la grossesse et a la prevention de nombreuses complications. La restriction de croissance foetale intra-uterine (RCIU) est une complication majeure de la grossesse affectant environ 5 a 10% de celles-ci. Dans les cas les plus severes, elle est associee a des naissances prematurees, a des retards neuro-developpementaux et constitue la cause principale d'environ la moitie des morts foetales in utero. Au cours des dernieres decennies, de nombreux outils echographiques ont ete developpes pour depister, diagnostiquer et predire les complications liees a la RCIU. Malheureusement, il n'existe pas de consensus sur l'approche a privilegier en regard de ces nouveaux outils offerts et cette situation amene une importante variation dans la pratique medicale et dans la qualite des soins offerts. Objectif de recherche: Evaluer les facteurs associes a l'efficience de l'echographie du 3e trimestre dans le depistage des RCIU. Methodologie: 4 projets seront realises. 1. Une revue systematique sur l'echographie du 3e trimestre pour le depistage des RCIU. 2. Une enquete aupres des specialistes en medecine foeto-maternelle du Quebec permettra de caracteriser les pratiques actuelles et de sonder les pratiques jugees optimales relatives a l'utilisation de l'echographie du 3e trimestre pour le depistage des RCUI. 3. Une cohorte de femmes enceintes suivies au CHU de Quebec ou Ste-Justine. Les caracteristiques des echographies du 3e trimestre et la prise en charge suivant l'echographie seront evaluees. 4. Une etude cas-cohorte de RCIU pour lesquelles les outils recents seront etudies en regard du developpement neonatal. Impact potentiel: Ce projet pourrait permettre d'identifier les facteurs ameliorant l'efficience de l'echographie du 3e trimestre dans l'evaluation de la croissance foetale. Ainsi, il permettra d'optimiser le depistage des RCIU qui pourront beneficier d'un suivi adequat et d'interventions appropriees.

column36: Inhibitors of PNT domain polymerization as a novel therapy to target ETV6 chimeric oncoproteins
column37: I am studying cancers that result when the protein segment called PNT, encoded by the ETV6 gene, becomes improperly fused to another gene fragment that encodes a protein tyrosine kinase (PTK). This phenomenon is called a chromosomal translocation, and the PNT-PTK chimera is an oncoprotein (a protein that leads to tumors). The specific PNT-PTK protein I am studying, called ETV6-NTRK3 (EN), has been implicated in a multitude of different cancers affecting many different demographics. These oncoproteins self-associate (bind to themselves) within our cells and cause unregulated stimulation of cellular signals. This in turn leads to aberrant cellular growth and ultimately cancers, such as congenital fibrosarcoma and secretory breast carcinoma. My goal is to find a compound that prevents this self-association, thus making the oncoprotein inactive and preventing unregulated cellular growth. I will use high-throughput screening tests to search extremely large chemical libraries for molecules that prevent this self-association. I will also test the binding of small compounds to the PNT domain to use as "building blocks" to design an inhibitor. I will characterize the effects of these candidate inhibitory molecules using techniques including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), Initially, these inhibitors will help us understand the mechanisms of cellular transformation that occur in cancers arising from ETV6 chimeric oncoproteins such as EN. However, my long-term goal is to optimize the pharmacological properties of these inhibitors in animal models as a step towards developing new therapeutic against ETV6-related cancers.

column36: Discovering Novel Blood-Based Biomarkers to Identify a Patient's Risk of Cancer and Cancer Prognosis.
column37: In many cases early detection of cancer results in a favourable prognosis. There are several blood-based measures (or biomarkers) such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) which predict future cancers and can also be used as screening tests for existing cancers. In some cases these biomarkers can be used to identify high risk individuals, while in others, they can be used to screen for early cancers. Research to date has shown that fluctuations in certain biomarkers such as serum, iron and platelet counts can predict future cancers. These biomarkers have also been shown to predict a cancer prognosis. The objective of my research will be to identify and validate novel biomarkers for cancer risk and prognosis using recently introduced Ontario laboratory data and novel analytical techniques. We will use data from the Ontario Laboratories Information System (OLIS) which was recently added to a large Ontario health data reservoir at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES). It has been proposed that artificial intelligence applied to electronic databases can be exploited to identify novel biomarkers for cancer risk. We will analyse selected biomarkers using traditional epidemiological methods as well as novel machine learning algorithms. With data from millions of Ontario residents at our disposal we will conduct high powered studies capable of detecting small variations in blood-based biomarkers prior to cancer detection. This study will be the first of its kind in Ontario, and may have implications toward the detection and treatment of certain types of cancers. Variations in blood-based biomarkers could help understand the physiology and etiology of cancer in its earliest phases. Further, biomarkers that predict cancer risk and prognosis could improve patient outcomes through early detection and improved treatment decisions.
