column36: Developing comprehensive predictive models of postoperative outcomes to improve surgical performance and perioperative care
column37: Surgery is never without risks. Complications such as wound infections, blood clots and even death are not only possible but still common. The cause of these complications generally falls in three main categories: the patient's medical conditions, the surgeon's skill during the operation, and the care the patient receives after the surgery. Science has come a long way in reducing these risks, but there is still work to be done putting these areas together. In this study, we ask how medical conditions, surgical skill and care after the surgery intersect to cause complications. Currently, before surgery, a patient's risk of complications or death is calculated using a risk score, which assesses their medical conditions alone. Risk scores generally stop at the door to the operating room: they do not take into account the surgeon's performance or the care afterwards. The surgeon, therefore, generally does not know how to tailor her skill or postoperative care to provide her patient with the best outcomes. Programming techniques in the field of machine learning are capable of finding these connections between medical conditions, surgical skill, and care after an operation, to discover ways for surgeons to tailor care and improve their patients' outcomes. We plan to use our large existing database of surgical videos in the field of bariatric surgery and urology to provide insight into surgical skills, and combine this with data from the medical record system at St. Michael's Hospital to get information about patients' health, postoperative care and outcomes. The objective of this project is to build a tool that will teach surgeons how to better care for each individual patient, as certain health conditions may cause their needs to vary. By finding care pathways that are customized to individual patients, this project could change the way surgeons operate on and care for their patients, and in so doing reduce patients' complications and improve their quality of life.

column36: Integrative approaches for resolving the biological complexity of the cardiovascular complications associated with end-stage renal disease
column37: An estimated three million Canadians have or are at risk of having chronic kidney disease. End-stage renal disease (ESRD), the last stage of chronic kidney disease, is a serious life-threatening condition in which the kidneys do not work well enough for survival without treatment. With the aging population, a growing number of people are developing ESRD. Cardiovascular problems are the leading cause of death in ESRD patients. Although there are some known risk-factors associated with cardiovascular mortality in ESRD, the biological pathways that are changed prior to cardiovascular events are severely understudied, making it difficult to identify which patients have the highest risk, and how best to treat them. To better identify, inform, and treat ESRD patients who have an increased risk of cardiovascular mortality we need to understand which biological pathways are changed. To address this gap in knowledge, I will utilize genetic sequencing and protein identification to discover biological pathways that are changed in patients with cardiovascular complications. Combining previously collected clinical data with these uncovered biological pathways will allow us to build an integrative risk-prediction model for the cardiovascular complications of ESRD. I expect this research will lead to the development of a tool physicians can use to better assess and treat patients with ESRD. In addition, knowing which molecular mechanisms cause cardiovascular complications will allow researchers to better understand how current therapies work and how more effective ones can be developed in the future. This may, as a whole, aid in decreasing the global health and economic burden of chronic kidney disease.

column36: Modifiable school determinants of youth substance use
column37: Canada has the highest rates of youth cannabis use across 43 countries, which is of salient concern due to the impact on brain development. Evidence indicates substantial variation across schools in levels of youth substance use, above individual risk factors, suggesting that schools may serve as important settings for prevention efforts. However, the mechanisms by which schools influence youth substance use are not well understood. The objective of this program of research is to gain a deeper understanding of the extent to which school settings influence youth substance use, with the ultimate goal of identifying modifiable factors within this setting to serve as targets for preventative efforts. These goals will be achieved by: conducting a systematic review of the literature that identifies factors in schools that can serve as intervention targets; obtaining accurate school effects, by accounting for the inter-dependent effects of families and neighbourhoods; exploring the mechanisms of school effects (such school climate, sense of belonging, and availability of resources) and if these effects moderate other risk factors; and examining whether school settings have long-lasting effects on substance use patterns in adulthood. These objectives will be met through secondary analysis of two CIHR-funded studies: the 2014 Ontario Child Health Study, which includes over 10,000 youth, and the School Mental Health Surveys, which includes over 32,000 elementary and secondary school students across Ontario. We will use the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, a study in the United States of elementary and secondary students followed from 1994 to 2009, to examine whether school settings have long-lasting effects on substance use patterns. The results of this study will help identify modifiable school contextual factors that are associated with youth substance use for potential intervention in the face of the changing cannabis culture in Canada.

column36: The impact of dietary lipids on disease activity, immune responses and the gut microbiome in colitis
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that affects 1 in 150 Canadians. The incidence continues to rise, yet prevention and treatment options are limited. Diet plays a key role in our immune system through changes to the gut microbiome. For example, what we eat encourages the growth of beneficial and harmful bacteria in our gut. An imbalance in the bacteria, called dysbiosis, is linked to chronic diseases like UC. Scientists agree that high fat diets promote dysbiosis, however recent evidence suggests that the type of fat we consume may contribute to inflammation and lead to dysbiosis in our gut. The Gibson lab has demonstrated that monounsaturated fats (olive oil) are beneficial to gut inflammation while n-6 polyunsaturated fats (corn oil) are harmful, and n-3 polyunsaturated fats (fish oil) are beneficial when combined with saturated fats (dairy). Based on these results, the blend of fats in the Mediterranean Diet (MD) is believed to be beneficial to colitis. I hypothesize that a MD will reduce clinical disease activity in UC and reduce the development of colitis in mice. I will perform a diet study where patients with UC in remission will receive a MD or control diet for 12 weeks. Disease activity, symptoms and quality of life will be assessed through questionnaires taken at various time points. To evaluate changes to the gut microbiome, stool samples will be collected/analyzed. To understand if the MD influences colitis in mice, the mice will be fed a high fat diet (40% total fat) where the fat is derived from either corn oil, olive oil, milk fat or MD (blend of fat) for 5 weeks. Tissues and stool will be obtained from the mice and examined for immune responses and dysbiosis. Little is known about how dietary fat impacts the immune system and the gut microbiome. Understanding the relationship between diet and the gut microbiome will inform new dietary treatments and create novel strategies for managing IBD.

column36: Impact of altered TDP-43 function on stress granule formation and microRNA processing
column37: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease targeting motor neuron cells within the brain and spinal cord tissue, which leads to loss of mobility, and is fatal within 2-5 years of diagnosis. Currently, there are no satisfactory treatments to ease the progression of the disease. The majority of ALS cases have no known genetic cause, and thus environmental factors-including stress-are likely major contributors to the disease progression. Cells, including motor neurons, have mechanisms in place to respond and recover from stress via the formation of stress granules (SG). SGs are crucial regulators of gene expression, and are required during stress to express the genes necessary for stress recovery. Interestingly, TDP-43 is a protein responsible for SG formation; however, in ALS, TDP-43 is drastically altered either through mutations or mislocalization within motor neurons, leading to this protein being dysfunctional. TDP-43 dysregulation appears in 97% of all ALS cases. Thus, it is hypothesized that altered TDP-43 function in ALS results in changes to SG formation causing motor neurons to be highly sensitive to stress, increasing the risk of cell death. Using both cell and mouse models of ALS, it will be determined how altered TDP-43 function impacts SG formation. Further, changes observed in these two ALS-models will be correlated with changes seen in ALS patients. This is the first project that combines cell and mouse models with ALS patient data to further our knowledge on cellular stress and its link to ALS disease progression. The data produced from this research will determine exactly how SG formation is affected in ALS, and could provide potential biomarkers and drug targets that will allow for earlier diagnosis and treatment of patients in the future.

column36: Cytomegalovirus-driven natural killer cell responses in HIV infection
column37: Over the course of our lifetime, we are exposed to many different types of virus infections, and our own healthy cells can transform into cancer cells. Though many viruses only cause transient infection, some viruses (i.e. human cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis) cause lifelong persistent infection and have great medical and socioeconomic repercussions. Natural killer (NK) cells identify and destroy cancer cells and also fight virus infection. In response to a common herpesvirus infection (CMV), NK cells adapt and become superior killers of infected cells. Our work explores how the pressures of CMV and HIV co-infection affects adaptive NK cell formation and function, and whether we can harness the potential of these adapted NK cells against virus infection or malignancies. One way NK cells recognize and kill infected or cancerous cells is by attaching to antibodies that adhere to cells. We hope to guide these superior NK cells toward infected or transformed targets using specific antibody therapy. Greater insight into the basic mechanism and biology that drives the development of NK cells with heightened activity would facilitate the progress of new strategies for therapeutic targets to control a broad range of infections and malignancies.

column36: The Nutrigenomics, Overweight/Obesity and Weight Management Trial (The NOW Trial)
column37: Nutrigenomics is a science that explores how individual genetic variation changes the way in which foods, beverages, and supplements are processed in the body and how different processing can affect health outcomes. For example, this science helps to explain why some people respond well to a high-protein diet for weight loss, while others respond better to a low-fat diet. The nutrigenomics, overweight/obesity and weight management trial is a study that aims to first, determine if receiving a personalized nutrition and activity weight loss plan based on genetics improves body fat percentage more than a general, population-based nutrition and activity weight loss plan. It also seeks to explore if genetic testing for personalized weight loss alters attitudes towards behaviour change, results in greater dietary and/or physical activity changes, more muscle mass, and/or greater overall pounds of weight lost compared to a standard, general weight loss plan. Participants in this study include overweight or obese patients from a rural Ontario community (study 1) and transplant recipients who are overweight or obese (study 2). Half of the participants will be randomly selected to complete a genetic test and receive personalized nutrition and activity advice for weight loss. The other half will receive a standard weight loss plan based on current population-based guidelines. Body fat, muscle mass, weight, dietary intake, physical activity and attitudes will be assessed at the very beginning of the study, and 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months after receiving the weight loss plan. This research is important given that rates of overweight and obesity continue to climb, both in the general population and the transplant population, and new strategies are needed to help people better manage their weight. With increasing knowledge about how the human genome alters our response to different dietary strategies, we can use this information to improve upon weight loss plans.

column36: Identification of Genetic Variants Causing or Predisposing to Hereditary Essential Tremor.
column37: Essential Tremor (ET), the most frequent type of tremor in humans, is up to 20 times more prevalent (2-4%) than Parkinson's disease (PD). Often confused with PD, ET is characterized by an involuntary oscillation of a body part, primarily the upper limbs, during postural control and voluntary motion. While not life threatening, involuntary tremor can produce disabilities with basic daily activities such as eating, driving and writing as well as be a source of social embarrassment. Current diagnosis is solely based on clinical findings, which poorly differentiate ET from other types of tremor. Current therapies do not effectively control or cure tremor symptoms. Like many other common human diseases and traits, ET is known to cluster in families and it is believed to be influenced by several genetic and environmental factors. Genetic variants that are associated, or the cause, of ET have been sought for over a decade and have provided valuable insights into the complexity of the genetic architecture of the disorder. Despite these recent advances, causative variants yet explain only a small proportion of ET cases. Given the highly heritable nature of ET, we hypothesize that individually rare and inherited genetic variants might contribute to disease risk in ET. In order to test this, we propose to use a combination of DNA sequencing and high-density genotyping arrays to test for the disease segregation of rare inherited variants in a cohort of 13 well-defined ET families. By focusing on rare variants in a familial cohort, we hope to explain a significant portion of the missing heritability in ET, as well as open new avenues to investigate aspects of the disease mechanisms. Moreover, understanding genetic basis may contribute to better prevention, diagnosis and treatment of the disease. Overall, this study will provide new insights for the entire field of movement disorders.

column36: The Identification of the Amino Acids on Platelet Factor 4 That Bind Pathogenic Antibodies in Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
column37: At least 30% of patients admitted into the hospital will be exposed to the common anticoagulant, heparin. 1-3% of these patients develop heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): an adverse drug reaction that can lead to amputations, strokes, and death. HIT remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients receiving heparin if not diagnosed and treated in a timely manner. Therefore, there is a need to develop a rapid and accurate diagnostic test for HIT that will improve the management of HIT patients. HIT occurs when patients who receive heparin form antibodies which subsequently results in an immune response but most of the antibodies formed in patients do not cause HIT. HIT only develops in those patients who produce immune complexes that cause intense platelet activation, low platelet counts, and clotting. Current rapid and available diagnostics tools cannot distinguish between antibodies that can or cannot cause the disease. Prompt diagnosis and treatments mitigate the life-threatening complications of HIT. However, the presence of these clinically insignificant antibodies greatly increases the over-diagnosis and mistreatment of patients thought to have the disease, increasing the risk of bleeding. To improve HIT diagnosis, we will identify the molecular differences between the antibodies that cause HIT and those that do not. This will be done by developing mutants of the protein that binds HIT antibodies and test the ability to incite platelet activation. From this, we can develop a new diagnostic assay that will be able to dictate whether the antibodies found in patients are specific for HIT. This development of a rapid and accurate diagnostic test will improve the management of HIT patients.

column36: Marginalizing Migrants: Exploring the Precarity of Migrant Health in Prairie Canada
column37: Within the context of globalization, workers-particularly from the global South-are encouraged to be mobile and flexible in their labour market participation. Over the past few decades, the share of migrants moving from developing countries in the global South to participate in low-wage work in the global North has grown dramatically. Through cross-national trade agreements, the Canadian government supplies a steady stream of transnational workers to Canadian employers who demonstrate labour shortages through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TWFP). In western Canada, Manitoba is a critical hub for a large population of migrant workers. In southwestern Manitoba, aggressive recruitment campaigns by the hog-processing industry (targeting would-be migrants from Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia), have driven population growth in smaller urban centres and towns. The town of Neepawa and the city of Brandon are prime examples of communities that employ a large number of Temporary Foreign Workers (TFWs), usually with limited English or French language ability and possessing limited rights and protections under the current TFWP. In particular, work permits tie TFWs to a single employer, leaving them vulnerable to employer abuse and the under-reporting of workplace injuries and illnesses due to the threat of deportation. As 'non-citizens' of Canada, migrant workers often work under conditions that would be deemed unacceptable to Canadian workers. For this reason, WHO has emphasized the need to draw linkages between migration, health and human rights. This is especially relevant within the context of the Canadian prairies where we know little about the health problems facing transnational migrants. column36: Development of an adjunct behavioural weight management intervention in bariatric surgery
column37: Obesity, defined as having a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or above, is a critical international health care issue with the rates of obesity and morbid obesity increasing worldwide. Morbid obesity (BMI of 40 kg/m2 or above) is associated with an increased risk of multiple serious medical conditions including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, respiratory disease (e.g., asthma) and certain types of cancer. Bariatric surgery is the gold standard of treatment for morbid obesity. While bariatric surgery is associated with important reductions in body weight, weight-related health conditions, and mortality, a significant proportion of bariatric patients experience suboptimal post-surgical outcomes, including consistent and rapid weight regain, even in the short-term (e.g., within 6 months after the surgery). There are a variety of interventions which have been used to try and enhance the effects of bariatric surgery on longer-term weight maintenance through changes in lifestyle behaviours (i.e., physical activity, sedentarity, diet). However, many of these have been poorly developed and not well tested. This has resulted in varied rates of success with little knowledge of how to improve the overall intervention package (combination of intervention components or strategies included in the intervention). The ultimate goal of this project is to develop an appropriate trial protocol to assess the efficacy of different behavioural weight management strategies to improve long-term weight maintenance after bariatric surgery (identify the best combination(s) of intervention components and strategies for certain bariatric patients). Central to achieving this objective is working with key stakeholders (patients, health care professionals, health administrators/policy makers, and researchers) to identify the most pertinent behavioural weight management intervention strategies that should be used before and/or after bariatric surgery to enhance outcomes.

column36: Investigating the role of post-event processing in the maintenance of social anxiety symptoms
column37: Many people experience anxiety in social situations at some point in their lives, whether it be dreading doing a presentation in class or at work, or talking with other people. When this social anxiety persists and becomes very distressing or impairing, among other criteria, a diagnosis of social anxiety disorder (SAD) may be considered. To help improve treatments with the goal of providing access to better care, social anxiety research examines how symptoms develop and how they are maintained. For example, we know that people tend to review all the distressing and embarrassing events that happened to them following a social situation. This tendency to repeatedly think about the negative aspects of an event is called post-event processing (PEP), and this repetitive negative thinking increases social anxiety. However, we do not know if and how thinking about the positive aspects of a situation can help social anxiety symptoms and be utilized in treatment. In addition, the memories we keep of past social situations may be affected by PEP. For instance, if a person concentrates on the negative aspects of a social interaction for a long time, they may find it difficult to then think of something positive that had happened in that same situation. The goal of this proposal is to see how negative and positive PEP influence social anxiety symptoms following a social interaction. I plan to also explore whether PEP does indeed change how a high socially anxious person remembers this social situation. Focusing on the positive rather than on the negative may help decrease social anxiety symptoms. It might also help make memories of social situations that are more positive and less negative. The results from this proposal will help us better understand social anxiety and why it persists. It will also provide information that will be used to help people who live their lives with social anxiety and SAD.

column36: Quantifying Modifiable Risk Factors for Premature Cardiovascular Mortality in India
column37: Every 2 seconds, one person is killed by heart disease or stroke. These diseases cause the highest number of deaths every year, and they are increasing particularly in South Asia. One of the hardest hit countries is India: heart disease and stroke kill 2.4 million Indians each year, and this could cost $2.2 trillion in economic losses from 2012 to 2030. Our research will help save lives by discovering why so many of these deaths are occurring in India. We will conduct the first national study to quantify how conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure cause heart disease and stroke. We will analyze death patterns of 1 million people across India to discover valuable information about which areas of the country are doing well and understand the factors behind their success. Additionally, we will reveal the gaps that exist in areas that require improvement. Our findings will provide a valuable road map to directly enable our partners at the Indian Council of Medical Research to save lives and reduce the impacts of heart disease and stroke. Our study is important to Canada because it will serve as a model of research that can be applied to benefit the health of Canadians. We will develop new research techniques that can be used to save lives, especially in underserved areas in northern Canada. What we learn about heart disease and stroke in India may also be applied to enhance the health of 1.1 million Indo-Canadians. Overall, this research proposal achieves the goals of the CIHR to increase Canadian leadership in global health research initiatives, and to apply the knowledge gained to inform solutions in Canada.

column36: Developing and refining TEENSAID: A bilingual, clinical tool to optimize communication and goal-setting between health care providers and teens with obesity
column37: Obesity in the teenage years is difficult to manage successfully. In order to provide teens with the best care possible, we need to better understand how their lifestyle habits influence their weight and health. We also need to provide them and their health care providers (HCPs) with educational tools that can be used in clinical settings. My research includes two related studies. Study 1 (Part 1) is a qualitative study that includes 1-on-1 interviews with teens with obesity (n~30) from weight management clinics in Edmonton (English) and Ottawa (French). I will explore their perspectives on factors that make it easy or hard for them to maintain healthy lifestyle habits. Once collected, teens will prioritize these factors from most to least important, which I will use subsequently to develop a bilingual tool (TEENSAID) that HCPs can use in counseling teens with obesity (Part 2). Study 2 is designed to refine and pilot test TEENSAID via a one-group posttest only design. While waiting for their weight management appointment, teens from Edmonton and Ottawa will choose up to 3 barriers and/or enablers that are relevant to them. Next, teens will share their choices with their HCP during the appointment, which will include discussing their priorities and goal-setting to enable behaviour change. Both teens (n~30) and HCPs (n~10) will complete a survey after the appointment, which will include questions related to their perceived likeability, applicability, acceptability, and feasibility of TEENSAID. HCPs will also participate in focus groups (n=2) to gain richer insight. The results of these two studies will have a direct impact on what and how health services are offered to teens with obesity in Canada. Next steps of my thesis include testing the effectiveness of TEENSAID using a randomized controlled trial.

column36: Dissecting RNA binding protein-directed control over hematopoietic stem cells by CRISPR-based genetic screening
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain an individual's life-time requirement of all the cells that compose the blood system. To achieve this HSCs must balance multiple functions, including the generation of functional blood and immune cells in appropriate frequencies and the enduring potential to recreate identical versions of itself (self-renew). Dysregulation of the balance that defines the HSC program largely underlies cancerous and non-cancerous blood pathologies. Often, HSC transplants are required, life-saving therapies. The success of transplants is limited by the scarcity of HSCs in donor bone marrow samples. As such, a major goal has been to expand functional HSCs prior to transplant. This has proven challenging due to our very limited understanding of the genetic and molecular mechanisms that control the HSC program. Molecular mechanisms depend on the molecules that exist and cooperate within a cell. Notably, genes in a cell are first turned on in the form of RNA molecules that undergo many decisions before they are turned into a final product, often a protein molecule. To date, much effort has been directed to understanding the first step when genes are turned on (transcribed) in HSCs. By contrast, very little is known of the specific decisions made to generate the final products in HSCs, a process termed post-transcriptional control. At the cornerstone of post-transcriptional control lies RNA binding proteins (RBPs), which are involved in making decisions regarding whether a final product should be made and how, when and where this should occur in a cell. This research aims to use state-of-the-art screening to systematically identify RBPs that are required for HSCs to function properly and subsequently to identify by unbiased techniques how these RBPs control the HSC program. We anticipate the insights from this research can advance the clinical application of HSC transplants and inform the design of improved therapeutics for blood pathologies.

column36: Targeting GABA-A receptors to mitigate persistent cognitive deficits induced by inflammation and general anesthetics
column37: Every year, millions of patients undergo surgeries with general anesthesia; and most of them are safely discharged. Unfortunately, a proportion of these patients experience short- and long-term cognitive deficits after their operations. Although these deficits range in severity, they are associated with poor long-term outcomes including loss of independence and premature retirement, as well as high healthcare costs. Currently, our understanding of the mechanisms of these impairments is limited, and no effective treatments exist. I aim to understand how two factors that are often concurrent at the time of surgery interact to lead to postoperative cognitive impairments. Specifically, the factors are inflammation (the body's natural immune response) and the anesthetic drugs. Work from my lab has showed that both these factors can lead to cognitive impairments independently, through similar mechanisms. Specifically, both inflammation and anesthetic drugs increase the activity of "memory-blocking" receptors in the brain. In the case of anesthetics, this increase is known to last for many days, leading to persistent cognitive deficits. Our preliminary results show that inflammation makes the brain more vulnerable to these anesthetic-induced cognitive deficits. Through my work, my goal is to understand the mechanism by which inflammation causes this vulnerability, and to develop novel treatments to mitigate these deficits. If successful, my work will ensure that patients not only survive surgeries, but also thrive after their operations.

column36: Potentiating Gram-Positive Antibiotics in Gram-Negative Bacteria
column37: The World Health Organization has revealed a list of 12 groups of bacteria that pose the highest risk to human health for which new treatments are needed. A vast majority of the bacteria on this list are classified as Gram-negative, a type of bacteria that possess an outer membrane structure. This outer membrane protects the bacterial cell from chemicals in the environment, including antibiotics. Many of the antibiotics in clinical use are not effective against Gram-negative bacteria, as they cannot penetrate the outer membrane barrier. Altering outer membrane integrity is important for allowing these antibiotics to enter impermeable Gram-negative cells and treat these bacterial infections. Our research group has previously uncovered 41 genes involved in resistance to vancomycin, an antibiotic that cannot penetrate the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli). We are undertaking a large-scale study to examine which genes, when deleted in combination with those 41 genes, will allow entry of the impermeable antibiotics vancomycin and rifampicin through the outer membrane to kill E. coli cells. Upon discovering which pairs of gene deletions compromise outer membrane integrity, we will screen 1,600 Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved drugs to find molecules that target those gene pairs. Our goal is to find a combination of molecules that enable antibiotic penetration through the Gram-negative outer membrane. This would open up new treatment avenues through combination therapy for these hard-to-treat, intrinsically resistant infections.

column36: Effects of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) on Cannabis Use and Cognitive Outcomes in Schizophrenia
column37: Background: Cannabis is the most commonly used drug in schizophrenia, posing as a barrier to overall quality of life. Cannabis use disorders (CUD) in these patients is associated with earlier onset and worsened symptomatology and cognitive/functional impairments that have been shown to improve with cannabis abstinence. Moreover trending legalization of cannabis in 2018 poses a significant threat to this population for which there is no satisfactory treatment. Brain stimulation techniques like repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) directed to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are well-tolerated and may have potential to address co-morbid CUD in schizophrenia, while improving psychiatric symptoms and cognition. Objective: To assess effects of rTMS as a treatment for CUD in schizophrenia patients. Methods: A total of 40 individuals meeting criteria for schizophrenia and CUD between ages of 18-55 will be recruited from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) in Toronto. Participants will be randomized into either active (n=20) or sham (n=20) high frequency rTMS (20 Hz) groups in a 6-week, double-blind, randomized, parallel controlled trial. All patients will receive contingency management and drug counselling interventions to facilitate 28-day cannabis abstinence trial endpoint, also monitored by THC levels from urine samples. Outcomes: The primary outcome will be trial endpoint self-reported cannabis use assessed by timeline follow-back and confirmed by cannabis urine toxicology. Secondary outcome measures will include cognitive outcomes (verbal learning, working memory and mismatch negativity), cannabis craving and withdrawal, and psychosis symptom ratings (Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale for Schizophrenia, Calgary Depression Scale for Schizophrenia). Significance: The proposed research may improve the health of patients suffering from schizophrenia and comorbid CUD with use of rTMS as a treatment, thereby improving functional outcomes.

column36: Electroencephalographie quantitative en sommeil paradoxal : un marqueur precoce de la neurodegenerescence cholinergique dans le trouble cognitif leger
column37: La maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) est le trouble neurodegeneratif le plus courant qui affecte les personnes agees et constitue un probleme de sante publique croissant. Le processus degeneratif de la MA debute plusieurs annees avant l'apparition de symptomes cliniques. Cette periode longue et progressive se nomme le trouble cognitif leger (TCL), bien que cela ne soit pas tous les individus avec un TCL qui progresseront vers la MA. Le manque de marqueurs fiables pour identifier quels individus avec un TCL progresseront vers la MA represente un obstacle majeur pour le developpement et l'evaluation de strategies preventives et therapeutiques. Plusieurs marqueurs mesurant l'activite cerebrale a l'eveil semblent prometteurs. Nous proposons que le sommeil paradoxal (SP) soit un etat plus sensible que l'eveil pour detecter les changements precoces de l'activite cerebrale dans la MA. En effet, lors du SP, l'activite du systeme cholinergique, lequel degenere a un stade precoce de la MA, n'est pas masquee par d'autres systemes qui sont actifs lors l'eveil. Ceci offre la possibilite d'etudier l'integrite du systeme cholinergique alors que les autres systemes sont plus silencieux. L'objectif de ce projet est d'evaluer, chez 100 patients avec un TCLa et 30 participants en sante (65-85 ans), la valeur predictive de mesures d'activite cerebrale obtenues lors du SP, comparee a celles obtenues lors de l'eveil, pour determiner qui sont les individus ayant un TCL et ceux etant cognitivement sains. Ceci sera accompli a l'aide d'analyses sophistiquees et de techniques de classification avancees. Grace a l'imagerie cerebrale, nous verifierons aussi, dans un sous-echantillon (i.e. 20 TCL et 20 controles), que le SP soit lie a l'integrite du systeme cholinergique. Si nos hypotheses sont confirmees, les caracteristiques du SP ont le potentiel de devenir un outil fiable, non invasif et peu couteux qui pourrait etre deploye a grande echelle pour le depistage precoce de la MA.

column36: A Good Story, Well Told: Understanding the Creation of Digital Stories in Health Care Settings
column37: Patients and their family members have an intimate knowledge of the health care system through their personal experiences. Modern health care systems have increasingly focused on engaging patients and family members in the design, delivery, and evaluation of health care. The emerging medium of Digital Storytelling shows great promise meaningful patient engagement tool. A Digital Story use photos, videos, music and individuals' own voices to create a 3-4 minute mini-movie about their health care experience. Despite burgoning research in the utlility of Digital Storytelling in various health care contexts, there is a paucity of published research into the expereince of the patients and families making these stories. Philosophical hermeneutics, as developed by Hans-Georg Gadamer, is a reflective inquiry with the purpose of enhancing the understanding of a phenomenon, and therefore a hermeneutic methodology is most suited to the research question of this study. It provides a mechanism for getting behind the surface phenomena and data, and using this research approach will generate a rich and deep understanding of the digital storytelling process in a health care context. Data collection for this project will involve the filming of a digital storytelling weekend workshop with 6-8 patients and family members. Data analysis will occur through careful watching and re-watching of interviews and the spontaneous story events in conjunction with writing around significant interpretations that arise. This will result the creation a 45-minute documentary and a written interpretive analysis of the full participant video interviews and the film itself. Both knowledge products will provide Patient Engagement professionals a deep understanding of the craft of digital storytelling from which they then can adapt the process to their own specific health care setting.

column36: Effect of Trans-Cranial Magnetic Stimulation on Functional Brain Networks and Cognition in Parkinson's Disease with Mild Cognitive Impairment
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 2% of people in the age range of 65-69 years and up to 10% of people over the age of 80 years. Despite the dominance of motor symptoms, cognitive (concentration, memory, and attention) deficits in PD are increasingly recognized as symptoms that are detrimental to quality of life. Diverse genetic and neuropathological factors have been related to cognitive impairment in PD. However, these factors give rise to common problems when considering brain networks. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive technique that is increasingly used to stimulate and inhibit brain networks. column36: Re-learning to reach after stroke
column37: Despite advances in the management of stroke from a medical and rehabilitation perspective, among Canadians who have had a stroke, overall health-related quality of life associated with chronic impaired arm and hand function is declining. This suggests a need to investigate novel approaches to enhance recovery of arm function. Successful rehabilitation of arm function depends on the ability to re-learn the motor skill of reaching. Often after a stroke, voluntary arm movement is not possible without assistance from a therapist physically guiding the impaired arm through many movement repetitions. Studies of reach training in healthy adults have not found this method to be as effective as active practice, suggesting learners require both the experience of generating the movement and the sensation of what it feels like as it is moving to retain the learned skill. This can be made possible with a new approach to guidance using a bimanual robot. I propose to use a bimanual robot, to yoke the movement of one robot arm to match the movements of an active robot arm. This allows a learner to engage in unassisted physical practice with one arm, such that it guides the yoked arm which experiences the sensation of the same movement. The rationale for this approach is supported by evidence that learning a reaching task with one arm transfers to the opposite arm in healthy adults. The proposed method will first be validated in healthy adults before being tested in individuals with impaired arm function secondary to a stroke. Performance on the reaching task will be assessed in both arms prior to and following the intervention. I hypothesize that arm movement speed and accuracy (recorded by the robot during reaching task training) of the yoked arm will improve as a result of self-guided bimanual movement training. This work could provide valuable insight and rationale for the potential use of robot-assisted therapies clinically as a tool to enhance arm rehabilitation after stroke.

column37: Colorectal cancer is the 2nd most common cancer in Canada and many who are diagnosed progress to advanced disease. The use of targeted agents to treat advanced colorectal cancer has improved patient outcomes. Cetuximab is one of the first of these drugs to be approved in advanced colorectal cancer treatment. A series of tumour mutations have been identified that can help health care providers determine the chance of controlling the disease using cetuximab. However, these predictive mutations are only useful in approximately half of patients. The hypothesis motivating this study is that it is the genes that a person inherits that influence favourable response or failure of this drug in controlling colorectal cancer. We will take a novel, comprehensive approach that simultaneously investigates many inherited genetic variants in the molecular pathways involved in how cetuximab is handled by the body and its mechanism of action, using information gathered from cellular, animal, and human sources. We will then determine which of these genetic variants are linked to either how well the drug works, resulting in longer time before the cancer starts to grow again as well as longer overall survival times, and which are associated with its side effects. Instead of evaluating each side effect separately, we will use innovative statistical techniques to look at groups of symptoms together. We have access to a unique repository of blood and tissues samples from two Canadian-led international trials. In fact, we have already identified one important genetic marker in the gene FCGR2A that helps inform on the effectiveness of cetuximab for an additional 8% of patients. These early results suggest that using a comprehensive approach will further divide these colorectal cancer patients into those who are most versus least likely to respond favourably to cetuximab, such that patients least likely to benefit from cetuximab therapy can be offered an alternate therapy or clinical trial.

column36: Novel strategies to target HER2-positive breast cancer cells while circumventing anti-HER2-induced cardiotoxicity
column37: Breast cancer is the leading form of cancer in Canadian women. About one third of breast tumors are referred to as HER2-positive. This means that the cells in the tumor have abnormally high levels of a protein called HER2. A diagnosis of HER2-positive breast cancer is associated with poorer prognosis, increased metastasis, and lower overall survival rates compared to HER2-negative breast cancer. Strategies to block HER2 in tumor cells do exist; they are commonly used in HER2-positive breast cancer patients and they can help. Unfortunately, HER2 is also found in the heart, where it has important functions. Therefore, when HER2 blockers are used to block HER2 in tumor cells, they might also block HER2 in the heart. This leads to undesirable side effects that sometimes cause the heart to fail. This project is designed to find new ways to block HER2 in breast tumor cells, while still leaving HER2 intact to function properly in the heart. Our research partners have designed new therapies to specifically block breast tumor HER2, and here, the effects of these new therapies on healthy and diseased heart muscle cells will be compared to the older HER2 blockers that are currently used in clinic. This study will also investigate whether abnormal mechanical forces experienced during high blood pressure, for example, put heart muscle cells at risk for HER2 blocker-induced damage. It is hoped that this research will contribute to the body of knowledge that will improve the care of patients diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer.

column36: Epigenetic Modulation in the Acquisition of Cancer Cell Plasticity
column37: Recurrence rates of cancer and the spread of cancer throughout the body through distant metastasis are two key determinants of cancer mortality, claiming a multitude of Albertans every year. A subpopulation of cells in tumors termed cancer stem cells (CSCs) are emerging as a significant factor in patient survival. These CSCs maintain a stem cell phenotype, much like embryonic stem cells (ESCs); and display the ability to adapt to a changing environment, which confers resistance to therapies, and the ability to re-establish the tumor post-treatment, leading to reduced patient survival. Despite its importance in patient survival, the mechanisms by which CSCs bypass regulation, acquire, and/or maintain stem cell like characteristics are not well understood. Using micro-environmental factors shown to promote CSC populations, my project aims to determine the similarities and the differences between the CSC and ESC response. This is done by growing various human cancer cell lines and embryonic stem cell line under hypoxia (low oxygen conditions) or Nodal (embryonic protein), both of which are involved in ESC maintenance and have been shown to increase CSC frequency. After the treatments, the cells will be harvested and the regulation present in ESCs will be compared to that of CSCs. Through this method, we can begin to highlight differences in how ESCs and CSCs respond to hypoxia and Nodal. The implications of these experiments will be two-fold: identifying the mechanism of dysregulation present in CSCs and determining potential targets for therapeutics. In order to completely eradicate cancer, cancer therapeutics must start targeting these CSCs in addition to the bulk of the tumor. Understanding the mechanisms by which it bypasses regulation is the first step in targeted therapeutic development. Therefore, this project has extensive consequences for therapeutic development and future cancer research that can vastly improve patient survival and quality of care.

column36: Mast cells as regulators of inflammation in heart failure
column37: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death by non-infectious disease worldwide. Damage that occurs to the heart following a heart attack can lead to the formation of scar tissue in a process called fibrosis. Scar tissue in the heart interferes with its ability to pump, which drastically decreases the ability of the heart to function and ultimately leads to heart failure. As part of the Restitution Enhancement in Arthritis and Chronic Heart disease (REACH) team, I am working to determine what conditions promote or prevent fibrosis and heart failure. I will use samples obtained from human donors, as well as several animal models of disease, to analyze this question. This research will help us to gain a better understanding of the impact of the mast cell on the environment within the heart that could promote or inhibit heart failure. Through this work, we hope to identify potential targets for future drug development, or determine ways in which we can limit the development of fibrosis in future patients.

column36: Pharmaco-epigenetics as a Novel Approach to Personalized Medicine
column37: Epigenetics is an innovative and rapidly emerging field that can be applied to psychiatric disorders in order to decrease the erratic nature of treatment outcomes that so many patients continue to experience. This project will use a large discovery data set to determine the role that the epigenetic modification known as DNA methylation plays in anxiety disorder symptoms, as well as poor response to and increased side effects of antidepressant medications. Epigenetic analyses are at the cutting edge of genomic studies and allow us to gather information beyond the sequence of DNA to examine the small chemical modifications that attach to the DNA. DNA methylation can significantly alter how a gene works. In the context of this project, the genes that are turned on (or turned off) can lead to increased risk for failure to respond to a medication, or to development of serious side effects. As mood and anxiety disorders are closely connected to the function of our stress response system, it is also important to discover how the epigenetic differences of our stress system genes may influence the effectiveness of antidepressant treatment. The project will be expanded to examine many epigenetic sites across the entire human genome to discover new targets involved in treatment outcomes of anxiety disorders, in addition to determining how DNA methylation may change over time with medication treatment. As 50% of all antidepressant treated patients fail to ever reach remission, shortening the trial-and-error process of finding effective medications for patients will significantly improve each individual patient's quality of life, reduce the costly side-effect burden, and offer substantial socioeconomic benefits to the Canadian health care system.

column36: Evaluation of an Alternative Model of Care for Stable Rheumatoid Arthritis Patients: Collaborative Nurse-Led Shared Care Model
column37: Today, one out every 100 Canadians lives with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a debilitating disease, which has a devastating impact on patients' lives and, in Canada, is associated with an annual economic burden over $5B. Currently, there is no treatment for RA. However, the disease can be controlled with medical therapy. For the best outcomes, patients require diagnosis and therapy within four weeks from the first symptoms of the disease. Next, patients require life-long monitoring for adverse effects of medications, disease flares and increased risk of comorbidities. Currently, follow-up of patients in remission (stable RA) consumes most of the rheumatologists' time and limits their ability to see newly onset and urgent patients. The follow-up of stable RA patients can be managed by non-physician care providers. For example, in nurse-led shared care clinics (NLSCCs) for RA patients, nurses take primary responsibility for stable patients' follow-up while allowing rheumatologists to focus on newly onset and urgent patients. In such clinics, besides RA management, patients receive holistic chronic disease care, which includes co-morbidity screening, education, lifestyle management, and ongoing communication between the patient, nurses, rheumatologists and primary care providers to ensure continuity of care. My research will evaluate the quality of care at the first NLSCC for stable RA patients in Alberta compared to a traditional rheumatologist-led clinic. Next, using computer simulation modeling, I will explore the effects of province-wide implementation of NLSCCs on waiting times for new onset and urgent RA patients and cost to the health care system. This research is important, as it will determine whether the use of NLSCCs for RA patients improves quality of care for stable RA patients and whether widespread implementation of this model of care has the potential decrease waiting times for new onset and urgent patients in local Alberta settings.

column36: Functional Characterization of Regulators of p53 Gain-of-Function Mutants
column37: Tumour suppressor p53 is the most commonly mutated gene in all cancers. It encodes for a protein termed p53, which is at the centre of a comprehensive regulatory network that protects our cells from becoming cancerous. More than 22 million cancer patients today carry mutated p53. Nearly half of them are caused by a single mutation in its DNA sequence, leading to a single amino acid substitution on the p53 protein. The resulting mutant proteins, termed point mutated p53 protein (mutp53), not only abolishes its original tumour suppressive function, but also gains novel oncogenic functions (gain-of-function, GOF), promoting tumour formation, growth, invasion, and chemoresistance. Therefore, to improve and tailor therapies for patients carrying mutp53, it is paramount to understand how tumours acquire these GOFs via mutp53. Through earlier work, we observed that mutp53 is preferentially stabilized in tumours but not in normal tissues; in addition, upon reducing mutp53 protein level inside the tumours, these tumours collapse. Therefore, if we can find out what are the factors that stabilize or cause the accumulation of mutp53, we could destroy these tumours. My project therefore aims at finding out these factors that regulate the mutp53 and its associated regulatory networks. To this end, I shall employ a unique gene targeting technique developed in our lab to screen and analyze the role of hundreds of genes in cancer development within a single mouse, in just five weeks. Through these functional genomics and proteomics screens, we can characterize the physiological regulatory and interaction network that is specific to mutp53. Among these regulators, I shall prioritize to validate and functionally annotate those that can be targeted by available drugs. Therefore, my overall goal is to elucidate the genetic network that drives mutp53 oncogenesis, and devise and improve therapies to treat these cancers in a more personalized manner.

column36: Effectiveness and Feasibility of Providing Postnatal Breastfeeding Support to Vulnerable Mothers as an Extension to the Canada Prenatal Nutrition Program
column37: Breastmilk is uniquely adapted to meet infant nutritional needs and support optimal physical, cognitive and immune system development. This research will test a community-based model of postnatal breastfeeding support which could be implemented on a large scale, contributing to significant improvements in the health and development of infants born to vulnerable families in Canada.

column36: Investigating the Role and Therapeutic Potential of Neurolysin in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer with a 2-year survival rate of 35%. Despite aggressive chemotherapy, the majority of patients relapse. AML's poor prognosis is largely due to the existence of treatment-resistant cells, called leukemic stem cells, which cause cancer reoccurrence. New therapies that specifically target leukemic cells and stem cells provide a promising and more effective alternative to the harmful effects of chemotherapy. Mitochondria are important components of the cell that produce energy. It has been shown that AML cells and stem cells have unique mitochondrial characteristics compared to normal blood cells, highlighting a potential therapeutic vulnerability. Mitochondrial function and structure is maintained by a group of enzymes called mitochondrial proteases. We have recently discovered that a specific mitochondrial protease called neurolysin (NLN) is highly expressed in a subset of patients with AML. We have also shown that reducing NLN levels inhibits leukemic disease propagation and disrupts mitochondrial function. However, the role of NLN in the mitochondria is unknown. Moreover, the effects of inhibiting NLN to stop the progression of leukemia have not been studied. The impact of this project is to understand NLN's function in the mitochondria and investigate its potential as a novel therapeutic target in leukemia. Specifically, it will expand our knowledge on targeting the unique metabolic properties of cancer cells and stem cells, with the goal of developing more effective treatments without the toxicity of chemotherapy.

Study participants diagnosed with heart disease will be invited to participate in a psychological impact evaluation survey to determine the impact of a heart diagnosis through PPS to ensure optimal support in those diagnosed. This research will guide physicians and sporting organizations to determine which athletes are at risk and how to screen to prevent SCD and ensure safe sport participation. This will be the first prospective, longitudinal, large-scale (800 athletes) study in Canada examining cardiovascular risk, incidence of heart disease and examination of comprehensive screening tools in recreational and competitive athletes.

column36: The Discoidin Domain Receptor-1 Acts as a Mechanotransducer to Promote Vascular Calcification
column37: Cardiovascular diseases are the second leading cause of death in Canada and constitute a significant economic burden. Atherosclerosis is the most common vascular disease and is characterized by the formation of a plaque on the vessel wall, restricting the flow of blood. Vascular calcification is a complication observed in late atherosclerosis that increases the risk of death, and is characterized by the mineralization of the plaque by bone-like cells. These bone-like cells originate from smooth muscle cells (SMCs) that change cell type. There is a lack of effective treatments for vascular calcification that do not affect bone health. Our lab is interested in the Discoidin Domain Receptor-1 (DDR1) protein and its role in vascular calcification. We have found previously that loss of DDR1 slows vascular calcification in mice. It is known that cell differentiation into bone cells is promoted by high stiffness of the cell micro-environment. Scarring of the plaque with the progression of atherosclerosis can cause stiffening. DDR1 has been implicated in stiffness sensing, and thus DDR1 may promote calcification by aiding SMCs sense increases in stiffness. My results showed that DDR1, SMC, and bone protein levels increase with stiffness. DDR1 loss prevented this response to stiffness. Cell contractility is known to increase with stiffness. SMC contractility increased with stiffness, whereas it did not with DDR1 loss. Finally, SMC calcification was found to be stiffness-dependent, whereas DDR1 loss reduced calcification and calcification no longer responded to changes in stiffness. My results suggest that DDR1 allows SMCs to sense and respond to increasing stiffness thus promoting calcification and changes in SMC identity. This study is one of the first to examine how stiffness influences SMC identity. With my findings, I look to identify targets for new treatments of vascular calcification and to better our understanding of how cell identity is regulated.

Preventing these diseases rely on accurately predicting future risk in order to determine the need for preventive medications. Current risk prediction tools have been derived and validated in the younger population. It is thus unclear how reliable they are in the older adult population. Because older adults are not all the same, the construct of frailty has been developed to capture differences in older adults in their risk of mortality, complications, disability, and institutionalization. The purpose of our research is to assess whether frailty influences and modifies the accuracy of risk prediction for heart disease, vascular disease, and stroke in older adults. Our goal is to improve risk prediction and to better individualize preventive therapy for older adults.

column36: Reimagining Research-Based Theatre: An Arts-Based Approach to Engaging Health Care Providers, Patients and Family Members in the Co-Design of an Educational Intervention to Improve Shared Decision Making in Primary Care
column37: There is a growing number of people who are living with chronic conditions (e.g. diabetes, heart disease) and their health depends on good self-management. Self-management is having the knowledge, skills, and support needed so the person with the chronic condition can slow or stop it from getting worse. To do self-management well, health care providers (e.g. doctors, nurses, dietitians) need to work with patients so everyone shares their knowledge (e.g. patient shares they prefer walking over a gym, doctor shares exercise recommendations) to create a personalized self-management plan (e.g. walk 3 times a week after dinner for 30 minutes). Self-management plans need to adapt to life changes and this requires an ongoing partnership between health care providers and patients. "Shared decision making" is a way to create this partnership, but is currently rarely done. My work aims to increase shared decision making in primary care with the following plan of action: (1) Create a theatre play using research, patient stories, and advice from patients and health care providers; (2) Perform the play to show common problems to shared decision making and allow the audience to see different perspectives (e.g. patients see what the doctor is thinking, doctors see how life context impacts self-management). The audience will then work together with actors and myself to identify changes and tools needed to increase shared decision making; (3) Create a course with interested audience members that combines the play with activities to train health care providers based on work in (2), and (4) test the course with health care providers to get their feedback on areas to improve and to test if the course does what it is expected to do (e.g. change attitudes towards shared decision making). This work is important because the research will use theatre in an original way that gives us a new method to meaningfully include patients and families in the design of the care they receive.

column36: Comparing Opium Tincture (OT) and Methadone for Medication-assisted Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Double-blind Controlled Clinical Trial
column37: Harms related to the use of opioids (heroin, morphine, fentanyl, etc.) such as AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome), hepatitis C and overdose have caused major public health consequences to date. However compared to its burden, range of treatments for opioid use disorder (OUD) depending on the country is often narrow. Opium tincture (OT) is a preparation of opium (herbal extract of opium poppy) with water and alcohol. In recent years, there has been a growing effort in treating OUD with OT in Asia and especially Iran due to cultural acceptability, its availability, and low cost. Because of lacking clinical research, it is not tested whether OT is effective and safe for this indication. Therefore, we started to conduct a clinical trial (RCT) to test whether OT is as effective as methadone for treating OUD in terms of keeping patients in treatment. Clinical trials are the standard ways to test if treatments work for certain health conditions. The study is an international collaboration between the University of British Columbia, Canada and Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Study will recruit 240 participants in 3 outpatient clinics and follows them for 12 weeks. If effective, OT will increase the range of available treatments OUD. Increased range of treatments can play an important role in addressing the current overdose crisis in Canada and preventing future similar crises in Canada and other parts of the world. In addition, successful execution of this project will improve the quality of addiction research in Iran which has a unique profile of OUD (highest frequency of OUD and opioid seizures globally, opium being the most commonly used illicit drug, contamination of opioids with lead and a very dangerous form of opioids unique to this region called crack heroin). Improved research infrastructure in this region will eventually improve the quality of care for patients with this condition in Canada and around the world.

column36: Exploiting RP1L1 as a Uniquely Insightful Model of Photoreceptor Degeneration
column37: Degeneration of the light-sensitive cells within the eye (photoreceptors) results in irreversible vision loss, and inherited photoreceptor degenerations affect ~1/3000 individuals. Typically, degenerations impact either cone photoreceptors (responsible for daytime/colour vision) or rod photoreceptors (responsible for dim-light vision). Specific mutations in the gene Retinitis Pigmentosa 1-Like 1 (RP1L1) have been found to cause a rare cone degeneration, Occult Macular Dystrophy (OMD). Conversely, loss of RP1L1 leads to a rod degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa (RP); RP is the most common photoreceptor degeneration. The underlying disease mechanisms causing photoreceptor death when RP1L1 is mutated or lost are not known, which makes intervention to prevent vision loss challenging. How and why disease can lead to death of one photoreceptor type and not the other is unclear, which makes the development of photoreceptor type-specific therapies difficult. This work will provide unique insights into the fundamental differences between rods and cones and how this impacts disease. Zebrafish are an ideal model for studying photoreceptors, as they have a diversity of cones similar to that of the human retina and many tools available for photoreceptor study. Zebrafish models of RP and OMD will allow for characterization of disease progression, including early disease indicators, and elucidation of disease mechanism(s). This project will explore what RP1L1 is doing in healthy rods versus cones, how this changes in disease models, and what makes rods and cones distinct. Appreciating disease mechanism, as well as the molecular distinctions between rods and cones that make them differentially susceptible to disease, will allow for targeted intervention. Information about the fundamental differences between rods and cones and how this impacts disease can be applied to a broad range of photoreceptor diseases, allowing for development of new therapeutics.

column36: Promoting Responsible Governance of Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy in Canada.
column37: Mitochondrial diseases are a group of rare inherited disorders that can be present at birth or manifest later in life. They cause devastating physical, developmental, and cognitive impairments that are progressive and have no available cure. The number of people affected with mitochondrial diseases is difficult to assess, since the range of conditions is wide and have diverse symptoms. Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy (MRT) is a type of in vitro fertilization (IVF) that aims to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial diseases to next generations. As mitochondrial DNA is passed down from the maternal line, MRT replaces a mother's mutated mitochondrial DNA with mitochondria from a healthy egg donor. MRT in Canada is considered a criminal offence by the Assisted Human Reproduction Act (2004), which prohibits any practice that modifies the genome of a human being or in vitro embryo. In order to provide Canadian policymakers with informed policy options for the rapidly evolving context of assisted reproductive technologies, I will conduct a systematic literature review of relevant academic sources which characterize the socio-ethical implications and scientific advancements of MRT. I will also review and assess pertinent legislation, policies, and ethical guidelines, in both the research and clinical contexts, in Canada, the US, the UK, and Mexico. Based on the knowledge obtained from the two aforementioned steps, I will interview Canadian stakeholders (scientists, clinicians, policymakers, ethicists, couples with affected children as well as those who are carriers and wish to have biological children and egg donors) with regard to MRT in order to seek a more thorough perspective of their needs and worries. Finally, I will analyze my results by applying an ethics of care theory in order to produce key policy principles to help bioethicists and regulatory bodies alike develop policies better suited to the Canadian health care context.

column36: Motives for Desired or Compliant Sex for Young Adult Women with BPD Symptomology
column37: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a prevalent and serious mental illness. Symptoms of BPD include intense and rapid mood swings, unstable relationships, and engagement in self-harm or suicidal behaviors. Effective psychotherapeutic treatments for BPD have been developed, such as dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). There is still, however, much room for improvement when it comes to alleviating key interpersonal problems in BPD. Therapeutic interventions that increase self-compassion (reacting to one's own suffering with kindness and understanding) may improve the treatment of these interpersonal difficulties. This study will evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of adding self-compassion training to DBT skills groups and will explore whether the added self-compassion training impacts interpersonal functioning. Participants diagnosed with BPD will be randomized to complete either thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training, or thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training modified to include self-compassion training. Feasibility and acceptability of the programs will be assessed post-treatment and compared between the two groups. Outcome variables, including interpersonal functioning, will be measured pre-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and at follow-up thirteen weeks later. It is anticipated that there will not be differences in acceptability and feasibility between groups, and participants that receive self-compassion training will show greater improvement in interpersonal functioning. This research will determine whether self-compassion training is a potentially useful addition to evidence-based care for BPD. Furthermore, this research has the potential to reduce the significant personal suffering and healthcare toll of BPD by informing improvements in treatment.

column36: The Role of Proteinases in the Progression of Osteoarthritis Neuropathy and its associated Pain.
column37: Arthritis is ranked as the number one cause of disability in Canadian women, and number three in men. Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common type of arthritis, affecting 1 in 10 Canadians. Remarkably, 60% of OA patients cite inadequate pain relief with current treatments. This is possibly because a third of arthritis patients develop neuropathic pain where the nerves innervating the affected joint are damaged. This type of pain is poorly controlled by drugs commonly prescribed to arthritis sufferers. We believe that the joints nerves are damaged, in part, by serine proteases-which are pro-inflammatory mediators found in arthritic joints. Using an injury model of OA, I will study the progression of knee joint damage and nerve injury, and determine if the use of drugs targeting serine proteases can provide pain relief once nerve damage has occurred. The activity of pain sensing nerve fibres in the joint will be recorded as an indicator of arthritic pain; increased nerve activity will indicate a higher likelihood of pain, and decreased nerve activity will indicate a lack of pain. The level of serine proteinases in arthritic patient's joints will be assessed to determine if the concentration and type of proteinases present correlate with the stage of the disease. This project will enhance our understanding of OA pain and reveal novel targets for the pharmacological treatment of OA pain with a neuropathic component.

column36: Defining the role of ArpC1b and the actin cytoskeleton in macrophage migration, phagocytosis, and immunoregulation
column37: Macrophages are cells present in virtually every organ, where they play an important role in both the short-term (innate) and long-term (adaptive) immune responses. They can engulf foreign pathogens as well as clear the millions of dead cells produced by our body each day. To reach these targets, macrophages must migrate through the tissues and degrade their way through dense matrix. Following particle engulfment (a process known as phagocytosis), they can interact with lymphocytes, components of the adaptive immune system, and release pro- or anti-inflammatory substances called cytokines. Together, these reactions maintain homeostasis and can regulate the production of antibodies. Many macrophage functions require the activity of the cellular skeleton, particularly the actin-nucleating arp2/3 complex. Recently, patients have been identified with a mutation in ArpC1b, a subunit of this complex. The condition presents with recurrent infections, autoimmunity, and autoinflammation. To understand the source of these abnormalities, I propose to investigate the role of ArpC1b in the context of macrophages. We hypothesize that ArpC1b is critically required for optimal macrophage function and cannot be rescued by the analogous protein ArpC1a present in other tissues. To better determine the impact on macrophage function I will perform migration, matrix degradation, and phagocytic capacity assays. I will also compare the cytokine profile of macrophages isolated from patients and from healthy donors, to determine how the mutated protein may modulate the remainder of the immune system. This research will help us better understand the patients' condition and the role of the macrophage cytoskeleton in autoimmunity and autoinflammation.

column36: Understanding the integrative body composition and metabolic changes of older adults during two weeks of reduced ambulation and following six week of exercise rehabilitation
column37: Beginning around the 4th to 5th decade of life, we typically observe a loss of skeletal muscle tissue and a gain in fat mass. These age-related changes in our muscle and fat tissues predispose many individuals to developing health related impairments (i.e. diabetes, loss of strength, difficulties in performing daily activities). Recent evidence suggests that brief periods of inactivity, such as reducing the number of steps taken in a single day (<1500/day - which may occur from minor injuries or illnesses), accelerates these negative changes in body composition and development of impairments. What must be appreciated, is that following these periods of reduced activity, older adults may not recovery their muscle mass or reduce their fat mass. A key strategy to aid recovery is exercise. However, the extent of recovery in older adults following an exercise program, compared to returning to daily activities, after these periods of reduced activity are unclear. My research aims to determine the extent of muscle loss and fat mass gains during reduced activity (2 week of reduced steps taken in a single day) and assess the role of an exercise program on recovery of pre-inactivity health status in older adults. Alongside assessing changes in muscle health and fat mass, we will also examine how these changes alter our ability to regulate blood sugar and fat levels in our blood and perform functional tasks such as standing up from a seated position. This research will be critical for describing the extent and negative effects that periods of inactivity have on muscle mass, fat mass, and physical health of older adults. In addition, this work will be key in informing strategies to promote exercise programs for older adults following these periods of inactivity. Ultimately, this work will aim to improve independence and quality of life for older adults and promote healthy aging.

column36: A feasibility project using pasteurized human donor milk (PHDM) for medical supplementation of the general newborn population in Atlantic Canada: Policy, practice and consumer implications.
column37: Overview: Pasteurized human donor milk (donor milk) is the best nutrition for infants when they cannot access their mother's own milk. In Atlantic Canada only 3 hospitals offer donor milk to premature infants in neonatal intensive care units. I argue that other infants need access, such as those born at 34-37 weeks, with neonatal abstinence syndrome or low blood sugar, or separated from their biological mothers for social and medical reasons. Although more expensive than formula, greater use of donor milk could save costs by increasing breastfeeding and improving health. There are ethical concerns with offering some infants donor milk and not others. Understanding families' and health care providers' perceptions of donor milk for general newborn use and their response to this feasibility pilot will help identify ways to make donor milk more accessible. Anticipated outcomes: Understanding families' and health care providers' perceptions of donor milk will help me develop educational plans to support a 6-month feasibility project. The project aims to enhance understanding of and increase use of donor milk, support breastfeeding by providing a bridge when mother's own milk supply is delayed, improve outcomes, and be affordable. I will use findings to inform local and national policy and as a foundation for research to improve equality in access. Contributions to the field: This research contributes to breastfeeding medicine by identifying what values, norms and concerns promote and hinder use of donor milk, and by exploring the ethical, economic and practical issues with making it available through a feasibility pilot for the general newborn population. It contributes to knowledge translation by improving understanding of perceptions of using donor milk outside of critical care settings and how to change behaviour to improve access. I aim to find ways to support the uptake of donor milk to increase access and improve mother/infant health.
