column36: Improving the quality of life of youth with epilepsy through targeted interventions
column37: Epilepsy is a common debilitating condition characterized by spontaneous, unprovoked seizures. Mounting evidence has shown that children with epilepsy have a poorer health-related quality of life (HRQOL) relative to their peers. The aims of the proposed study are twofold. First, to evaluate how HRQOL changes over the long-term among children with epilepsy and, importantly, identify the baseline patient and family characteristics associated with poor outcomes. Second, to evaluate the effectiveness of low-cost non-pharmaceutical interventions targeted to patients and families who are at risk for poor HRQOL in the long-term. These findings will be extremely useful in preparing patients to be aware of the potential challenges they may face, identifying at-risk children and families, and offering targeted non-pharmaceutical interventions. To address the first aim, I am using comprehensive information collected from patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy across Canada to assess HRQOL at the time of diagnosis, and 0.5, 1, 2, 8, and 10 years later. Questionnaires at each time point were completed by 173 parents. To address the second aim, I propose to recruit patients and families to evaluate the impact of two low-cost non-pharmaceutical interventions, implemented over a 12-week period, relative to a control condition. At the successful completion of this study, we will have identified protective and risk factors present at the time of diagnosis, which will allow for the identification children and families who are at risk of poor HRQOL over the long-term. In addition, we will evaluate the effectiveness of two low-cost interventions that may be readily integrated in a busy clinic or offered through epilepsy support centers in the community. The long-term goal of this project is to identify children with epilepsy who are at risk of poor HRQOL in the long-term and provide low-cost targeted interventions.

column36: Influence of mental health disorders and their management on adult functioning outcomes among emerging adults with a history of out-of-home care: a quantitative and qualitative study.
column37: As youth transition out of foster care at age 19 in British Columbia they are expected to live independently with little or no support from the government or their families. The extreme vulnerability of this population has been brought to the public's attention by several high-profile deaths of youth who had recently aged out government care. A consensus has been reached across the province about the need to reform the services that support youth as they age out of care; the planning of these reforms has been initiated by relevant government agencies. Research has confirmed that youth who have been in foster care have a high risk of suffering from mental illnesses. They also struggle more than their peers to transition successfully into adulthood; for example, they are more likely to not graduate from high school, have unstable housing and employment, have low incomes, and be involved in criminal activity. Although many negative impacts of foster care have been established, there is a lack of research on how mental illnesses influence the transition into adulthood in this population. My thesis project will look at the impact of mental illnesses and how they are treated on key indicators of a successful transition into adulthood among youth (18 to 29 years) who have been in foster care. For this analysis, I will use linked databases that include indicators for the entire population of Manitoba. I will also interview youth living in Vancouver who have a diagnosed mental illness and have been in foster care. We will discuss how they think the treatment of their illnesses (or lack thereof) influenced their transition into adulthood and how the system of care could be improved to better support this transition. The evidence generated by my thesis will serve to inform the reform efforts that are currently being undertaken in British Columbia, and has the potential to significantly impact the long-term outcomes of youth who age out of care in the province.

column36: Using A Biopsychosocial Perspective To Predict Recovery From Concussion In Adolescent Athletes.
column37: Sport-related concussion is a growing concern for youth involved in recreational contact sports (e.g. hockey, football, etc.). Most individuals will recover from a concussion within a short period of time (i.e. within 30 days); however, a small percentage (~10-20%) of youth will experience post-concussion symptoms lasting beyond 30 days. Persistent post-concussion symptoms are associated with poor functional outcomes, lower cognitive performance and reduced quality of life. In recent years, investigations have focused on identifying factors related to persistent post-concussion symptoms. Factors include: young age, the female sex or gender, certain medical history factors (e.g. history of depression, anxiety or familial history of psychiatric illness) as well as a history of multiple prior concussions. At this time, few investigations have examined the affect that a concurrent mood disorder (i.e. depression or anxiety) has on recovery from concussion in young athletes. Furthermore, little is known about how a concussion impacts risk for developing a mood disorder following an injury. Athletic identity and coping abilities have also not been thoroughly examined in this regard. The proposed study will look at concussed athletes between the ages of 13 and 18 years old. Shortly following a diagnosed concussion, athletes will provide information about their age, sex and gender, sport, medical history (i.e. history of concussion, depression or anxiety), coping skills and identity as an athlete (collected once). They will also complete three questionnaires inquiring about depressive, anxiety and post-concussion symptoms; these measures will be completed at time of injury and throughout the following year. Findings will allow investigators to examine the relationship between mood, athletic identity and prolonged post-concussion symptoms in young athletes. This knowledge can in turn provide a more informed approach to the clinical management of concussed youth athletes.

column36: Exercise Response: Is Irisin a Novel Factor that Explains the Metabolic Adaptation?
column37: Over the past few years, the prevalence of obesity and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) has drastically increased, and is expected to continue to rise. This is unfortunate, as it has led to extreme costs to our health care system. Exercise has been recognized as a first line of treatment to prevent and manage these two chronic conditions; but, not everyone benefits from exercise in the same way. For example, some individuals may lose weight from an exercise program, while others who participated in the same program will not see any results. A number of factors may lead to this variation, including a hormone released from your muscles during exercise, called irisin. Irisin is a recently discovered hormone that has the potential to provide a multitude of health benefits for individuals living with obesity and T2D. However, as irisin is novel, it is not clearly understood how different forms of exercise (intensity or duration) impact the typical health outcomes usually observed with exercise. First, our study will investigate whether irisin is released at a greater extent during high intensity aerobic exercise (e.g.: vigorous bike ride) compared to moderate intensity aerobic exercise (e.g.: jogging) in adults living with obesity. Second, we will study the release of irisin in a group of individuals who did not get any health benefits from a 12-week exercise program. Then, we will see if they get exercise benefits after an additional, more challenging, exercise program that lasts 12 more weeks. This will tell us what form of exercise best stimulates irisin release and whether these changes are related to meaningful clinical outcomes in individuals living with diabetes/pre-diabetes. Results of this study will be of great importance for health research, as they will provide a better understanding of the link between irisin, exercise, and health outcomes. column36: Exploring AAA+ unfoldase conformation and interaction landscapes
column37: Proteins are the basic building block of the cell. The ability of proteins to carry out different jobs depends on their 3D shape. The basic unit of proteins is a single string-like molecule that folds in on itself, like yarn knit into a sweater, to form a specific 3D structure. In order to recycle protein components when they are no longer needed or have lost their proper 3D shape, cells have developed specialized machinery, known as unfoldases, that unravel proteins by pulling them through a narrow opening. In this project we will use electron microscopy to see snapshots of one of these molecular motors in action. We can then identify how these unfoldases recognize which proteins need to be recycled. We will determine how the unfoldases co-operate with other helper proteins to recognize and stimulate unfolding activity. This knowledge will help us understand how these unfoldases function in the cellular environment. It will also lend insight into cancers where unfoldases are overactive, and genetic diseases like familial ALS and Paget's disease of the bone, where these systems are underactive due to genetic mutations. Just like looking at a blueprint for a car motor, seeing the structure of this protein can help us to identify why mutations cause the machine to break down, or help design ways to slow down overactive versions.

column36: Advancing physical activity recommendations and their implementation among individuals with osteoporosis
column37: One in three women and one in five men will experience a fracture due to osteoporosis in their lifetime (Osteoporosis Canada, 2016). Furthermore, people with fractures, especially in the spine, have been underrepresented in most exercise studies, leaving a gap in our knowledge about the effectiveness and safety of exercise in this population. My research has three aims: 1) to complete a comprehensive review and meta-analysis to identify the effects of different types of exercise on outcomes important to people with osteoporosis; 2) to establish expert consensus on safe movement and exercise after a recent spine fracture due to osteoporosis; and 3) to develop and pilot test a community-based program to help implement physical activity recommendations among individuals with osteoporosis. column36: Nano-delivery of novel inhibitors of polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP) for tumor targeted sensitization of colorectal cancer to DNA damage.
column37: Colorectal cancer (CC) is the 4th most common cause of cancer-associated death worldwide. Surgery, chemotherapy (CT), and radiotherapy (RT) are the most common treatments for CC. However, these treatments are rarely curative and cause severe side effects in patients. Moreover, 50% reoccurrence takes place due to therapeutic resistances particularly in this type of cancer. This is mostly due to the adaptation of cancer cells by acquiring resistance mechanisms against anti-cancer treatments. RT and CT used in CC commonly act by causing DNA damage leading to cancer cell death. However, cancer cells can survive by adapting the DNA damage through expression of DNA repair mechanism. The natural ability of cancer cells to repair DNA can undermine the clinical outcome of DNA damaging chemo and radiation treatments in CC. Inhibitors of DNA repair render tumors more susceptible to DNA damage by RT and CT, leading to higher rate of cancer cell death; but may act similarly on normal cells, leading to severe toxicity in patients. Our research team has identified a DNA-repair enzyme called polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), as a new target for drug development in CC. We have synthesized several effective small molecule inhibitors of PNKP that were shown to enhance the effect of RT and CT treatment in CC. Now, our focus is on the development of nanocarriers that can specifically deliver PNKP inhibitors to cancer cells while sparing normal cells. The nanocarriers of PNKP inhibitors are expected to enhance their anti-cancer effects in CC and at the same time reduce their side effects on normal cells. Through this approach, we expect to be one step closer to the development of more effective and less toxic new treatments for CC.

column36: Breastfeeding and medically high-risk pregnancy: A mixed methods approach to examining feeding intentions, experiences, support, and outcomes
column37: Optimal breastfeeding protects women and infants against numerous acute and chronic diseases, yet three quarters of Canadian mothers do not meet the global recommendation of exclusive breastfeeding from birth to six months. In Canada, approximately one in four pregnant women have high-risk medical complications, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, placental disorders, or pre-existing medical conditions. These women are less likely to plan to breastfeed, to begin breastfeeding after birth, and to continue exclusive breastfeeding until six months compared to women without medical complications. This is worrisome because a high-risk pregnancy often leads to the delivery of a preterm or sick infant, and breastfeeding plays an important role in protecting the survival and health of these newborns. Unfortunately, explanations for suboptimal breastfeeding behaviours among women with high-risk pregnancies are lacking which makes it impossible to effectively address this problem. This research will examine the prenatal breastfeeding goals of women with high-risk pregnancies and the reasons behind these goals. We will track whether mothers begin and continue breastfeeding, as well as explore their postpartum breastfeeding experiences including the type and quality of supports that they access. Finally, we will identify what factors positively or negatively influence the achievement of breastfeeding goals among mothers, which may include demographic or social characteristics, maternal medical complications, delivery outcomes, and breastfeeding experiences. We can use these findings to collaborate with health professionals and decision makers in developing education and support services that are sensitive and responsive to the breastfeeding needs of women with high-risk pregnancies. Ultimately, this research will be instrumental in improving the number of high-risk women and their infants who receive the diverse and lifelong health benefits of breastfeeding.

column36: The pathophysiology in hypoxic ischemic brain injury after cardiac arrest.
column37: Hypoxic ischemic brain injury (HIBI) is a devastating illness that occurs after cardiac arrest (the heart stopping) and can yield irreversible brain damage, often leading to death. HIBI occurs from inadequate delivery of oxygen to the brain during cardiac arrest and in the hours and days following resuscitation. The mainstay in therapy is to optimize the delivery of oxygen to the brain to help it recover. In patients with traumatic brain injury (similar to HIBI), optimization of oxygen delivery to the brain is associated with improved outcomes. Regrettably, the benefit of this therapeutic strategy is not well delineated in HIBI. Crucial determinants of oxygen delivery to the brain including blood pressure, blood carbon dioxide levels, hemoglobin (blood's carrier of oxygen) and intracranial pressure (the pressure exerted by the brain inside the skull) are key determinants of brain oxygen delivery. We are aiming to delineate the roles of each of the aforementioned variables in how they effect brain oxygen delivery in human patients with HIBI after cardiac arrest. By doing so, we hope the findings will lead to crucial therapeutic studies in the future aimed at optimizing oxygen delivery in HIBI patients.

column36: Reactive and Proactive Mechanisms of Response Inhibition in Gambling Disorder
column37: Response inhibition refers to the ability to suppress actions that are inappropriate in a given setting and that interfere with adaptive behaviour. Importantly, impaired response inhibition has been linked to severity of gambling problems, as well as higher relapse rates in individuals with gambling disorder. Recent research separates response inhibition into two distinct, yet complimentary components: reactive (the ability to stop in response to a sudden and unexpected stop-cue in the environment) and proactive control (the ability to use cues in the environment to anticipate and prepare for a stop). Although proactive control is an essential component of successful stopping and affects the success of reactive control, no studies have examined proactive control in gambling disorder. The current study will address this gap in the research by using a relatively novel cognitive task, which unlike traditional stop-signal tasks, will allow the measure of both reactive and proactive control in 50 individuals with gambling disorder and 50 healthy controls. As an exploratory aim, we will examine whether reactive and proactive control are associated with self-reported impulsive-like personality traits. By distinguishing between reactive and proactive control, more targeted treatments can be developed to address high relapse rates by improving response inhibition in this difficult-to-treat population. Furthermore, if reactive and/or proactive control are associated with specific impulsive personality traits, treatments can be individualized for different subtypes of gamblers (e.g., some gamblers may benefit from cognitive training while others may not). The findings from the present study may lend support for the utility of impulsivity-based strategies in treatment programs.

column36: Using exercise training to promote recovery following pediatric brain injury
column37: Background: Childhood is a critical period for brain development. During this time, there is growth of important brain regions. It is also a time that shapes our abilities to think, remember, and problem solve. However, although childhood is important for healthy brain development, it is also a period when the brain can be injured in ways that cause long-term damage and disability. Two of the most serious childhood brain injuries are traumatic brain injuries and injuries caused by radiation therapy for brain cancer. Together, these two brain injuries affect more than 150,000 Canadian children. Even though they often result in lasting brain damage and make it harder for children to think, remember, and problem solve, they have no effective treatment. Based on recent studies, scientists think a potential treatment for these brain injuries is exercise training (a form of intense physical activity). Before they can recommend that children with brain injuries participate in exercise training, it is important to better understand its long-term effects, and how exercise effects the brain. The goal of this study is to learn more about both the short- and long-term effects of exercise training in children with brain injury. Methods: I will test how exercise training improves the ability of children with brain injuries to think, remember, and problem solve. I will also test if exercise training results in brain repair in these children. These tests will be performed right after children with brain injuries complete exercise training, and again 6 months later. Impact: Exercise training can help the thousands of children who live with the lasting effects of brain injuries. It may be able to repair the brain and improve children's abilities to think, remember, and problem solve. Exercise training is also a more cost-effective way to care for children with brain injuries. This can lower healthcare costs, which is helpful to patients, their families, and society.

column36: Development and evaluation of a brief online motivational interviewing intervention for clients who lack motivation to engage in Internet-delivered cognitive behaviour therapy for anxiety and depression
column37: Anxiety and depression are common and disabling conditions that are associated with large economic costs. Traditionally, these concerns are treatable with face-to-face cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT); however, Internet-delivered cognitive behaviour therapy (ICBT) has emerged as an equally effective method of disseminating care while also improving access to services and reducing therapist time and costs. ICBT involves delivering treatment material to manage anxiety and depression online using structured web-pages. While the impact of CBT and ICBT is impressive, clients experience varying responses to these treatments. Opportunities exist though to further enhance outcomes in order to maximize the effect of CBT and ICBT. For instance, motivational interviewing (MI) has been incorporated into the initial sessions of CBT and has been shown to significantly improve symptoms of anxiety and increase treatment completion relative to CBT alone. MI is a clinical tool used by therapists to help facilitate clients' motivation to change. Client motivation is important in therapy and has been shown to predict greater treatment adherence and symptom improvements. Yet due challenges associated with adapting key components of MI over the Internet, this clinical method has not been offered alongside ICBT. Developing a brief online MI treatment that requires no therapist time has the potential to serve as a cost-effective method to bolstering ICBT completion and recovery rates. The goal of the proposed study is to, therefore, develop and evaluate a brief online MI intervention aimed at increasing client motivation to engage in ICBT for anxiety and depression. The development phase will involve adapting the original MI protocol for anxiety over the Internet. The evaluation phase will involve using mixed methods to determine the value of supplementing ICBT with MI for clients who lack motivation to participate in therapy. Results will inform next steps for efficacy testing.

column36: Role of Perfusion MRI in Improving Diagnosis of Frontotemporal Dementia and Monitoring of Disease Progression
column37: Early diagnosis of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) remains a challenge since it is characterised by a wide range of symptoms which overlap with other psychiatric disorders. This ambiguity can hamper timely inclusion in clinical trials and the ability to assess treatment outcomes. Due to the tight coupling between brain activity and cerebral blood flow (CBF), perfusion imaging approaches such as positron emission tomography (PET) can assess treatment effects with greater reliability than clinical endpoints. However, widespread use of PET imaging is limited by its high cost, limited availability, and invasiveness. While arterial spin labeling (ASL) magnetic resonance imaging, is a cost-effective and non-invasive alternative, inconsistent results across FTD studies highlights the need for its optimization. The aim of this study is to demonstrate that ASL is an ideal functional imaging technique for longitudinal FTD studies aimed at assessing the benefits of emerging therapies. Our initial studies will focus on developing and validating a non-invasive approach to quantify CBF using a hybrid PET/MRI approach. Next, we will use this non-invasive approach in FTD patients and controls to assess the ability of ASL to accurately map perfusion changes associated with disease symptoms. Finally, we will assess the stability of ASL data to detect longitudinal perfusion changes in FTD patients. This ability will enable better patient stratification, such as based on the rate of disease progression or treatment response, which is particularly relevant to the FTD given the heterogeneity of the disease.

column36: De-constructing Oncogenic Effectors in a Synthetic Model of Human T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
column37: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a cancer predominantly affecting children where their immature T-cells multiply uncontrollably. This disease is linked to mutations in various genes causing higher (oncogenes) or lower (tumor suppressors) activity than normal. Some of the commonly known oncogenes implicated in T-ALL are NOTCH1 (N), LMO2 (L), TAL1 (T), and BMI1 (B). Previous researchers have used addition of single oncogenes to create models of T-ALL using mouse blood progenitor cells but so far similar efforts using human cells have been unsuccessful. Differences in mouse and human T-cell biology underscore the importance of a human model of this disease. Our lab recently developed the first human model of T-ALL by forcing human blood progenitor cells isolated from umbilical cord blood to express an 'always-on' form of NOTCH1, and to overexpress LMO2, TAL1, and BMI1. The objective of my project is to determine the importance of each oncogene individually and in combination with each other in the process of transforming healthy cells into disease propagating T-ALL cells. I will test these oncogene combinations in cord blood progenitor cells by growing them in culture to evaluate for increased cell growth and immature characteristics. I will then use sequencing technology to analyze the gene expression profiles of these cells to discover downstream genes affected by each oncogene we tested. The relative importance of these discovered effector genes in leukemic transformation will be determined by combinatorial expression in my T-ALL model. Finally, I will validate the original oncogene combinations and the discovered downstream genes by injecting the cells into immunodeficient mice and monitoring for leukemia development. These studies will help us understand the individual oncogene contributions and downstream effectors in a human T-ALL model and will facilitate discovery of new targets for therapy.

column36: The Strongest Families (TM) Parenting Program: A randomized-controlled trial of a culturally appropriate parenting program for northwestern Ontario First Nations communities
column37: The Truth and Reconciliation Report (2015) has documented the need for culturally relevant parenting programs within First Nations communities. First Nations families have requested parenting supports that meet their unique challenges, often within remote and rural communities. Strongest Families (TM) is a twelve week web-based parenting intervention that is administered with telephone support by a paraprofessional coach. This program has been modified by a First Nations research advisory group to better meet the needs of First Nations families. To determine if this program is an effective solution for First Nations communities, we will assess both how feasible and useful it is for families, by interviewing the first 15 families that complete the intervention and asking about their experiences with the program. We will also evaluate how effective the intervention is by randomly assigning 185 participants to either complete the intervention or to have access to other parenting resources. By comparing the outcomes of those that complete and do not complete the intervention, we hope to evaluate how effective the program is at reducing child behavioural concerns and parent distress. Results of this study will be used to promote the continuation of Strongest Families, and to improve parent and child mental health outcomes using a First Nations model of parenting.

column36: Elucidating the molecular mechanisms that permit sustained interferon gamma signaling to potentiate breast cancer metastasis
column37: Introduction: Metastatic breast cancer (BC) remains incurable. The spread of breast cancer to other organs such as the lungs, liver and brain occurs through a complex set of steps, our understanding of which remains incomplete. Our immune system has mechanisms to target and control early cancer development. In order for tumors to progress and metastasize they must first overcome this anti-tumor immune response. We know that while acute inflammation is a necessary component of the anti-tumor immune response, chronic inflammation can instead contribute to tumor progression and metastasis. Interferon gamma (IFNG) is a very important inflammation molecule that drives anti-tumor immunity. Yet, its role in later stages of BC remains unclear. Using a well-studied mouse model of BC, we recently revealed that IFNG, while important for delaying BC onset, actually increases BC spread to other organs. We hypothesize that this novel and unexpected finding is the result of chronic exposure to IFNG during BC development that improves the ability of these BC cells metastasize. The aim of this research project is to understand how IFNG promotes metastasis. Research methods: We will determine the specific step(s) of the metastatic process that IFNG acts upon to promote metastasis using transgenic mouse models available in our lab. Based on this we will then interrogate which of known and potential effects of IFNG signaling are responsible for promoting metastasis in our mouse model. Finally, we will screen human breast tumors from a large biobank with matching clinical follow-up data, to determine whether increased IFNG levels or signaling in these tumors is associated with increased risk of metastasis in patients. Impact: We have identified a novel role for IFNG in breast cancer. This research will provide insight into the dual and opposing roles immune molecules can play during different stages of cancer. Ultimately, this research will improve our understanding of metastasis.

column36: Explorer l'efficacite de la therapie cognitive-comportementale du trouble panique chez les patients qui presentent une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique comorbide
column37: Le TP est un trouble anxieux entrainant de severes limitations dans le fonctionnement quotidien et une importante detresse psychologique, en plus d'etre associe a un risque suicidaire accru et a une forte utilisation des services medicaux. Lorsqu'il est present en comorbidite avec une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique, le trouble panique peut etre associe a une augmentation du risque de mortalite ou d'evenement cardiaque. De plus, la presence d'un trouble panique peut nuire au traitement et a l'evolution de la maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique, notamment parce que ce trouble est associe a l'adoption d'habitudes de vie nefastes, a un evitement de l'activite physique et a une faible adhesion aux traitements medicaux. Le traitement de premier recours pour le trouble panique est la therapie cognitive-comportementale, mais des adaptations pourraient y etre necessaires afin de tenir compte de la presence d'une condition cardiaque. De plus, l'efficacite de la therapie cognitive-comportementale n'a pas encore ete demontree chez ces patients. Ainsi, compte tenu de l'impact potentiellement majeur du trouble panique sur l'evolution de la maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique, il est essentiel de determiner si la therapie cognitive-comportementale est efficace dans cette population. Ainsi, le present projet de recherche a pour objectif principal d'evaluer l'efficacite d'une therapie cognitive-comportementale adaptee aux particularites des patients qui souffrent egalement d'une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique pour traiter le trouble panique. Il vise egalement a documenter l'impact du traitement sur la qualite de vie, l'adhesion aux traitements, la detresse psychologique et l'utilisation des services medicaux. Ce projet de recherche a donc le potentiel de contribuer significativement a l'amelioration de la sante globale et de la qualite de vie des individus souffrant a la fois d'un trouble panique et d'une maladie coronarienne atherosclerotique.

column36: Deep learning-based study of the endogenous retroviral-derived immunopeptidome in ovarian cancer.
column37: Vertebrates have evolved from primitive life forms with a strategy of survival that bases itself on longevity instead of high reproductive rates. Indeed, while our specie does not produce many offspring, it has a remarkable immune system, that enables it to efficiently combat disease and therefore prolong its lifespan. At the heart of our adaptive immune system are T lymphocytes, that transit through our bodies and scan cells for indications of infection. In fact, all cells display at their surface molecules that present short protein fragments (or peptides) collectively referred to as the immunopeptidome. The immunopeptidome mirrors the processes that are happening in the cell itself. Since T lymphocytes are trained to recognize peptides that indicate infection or abnormal activity, they should be able to recognize and eliminate infected cells but also pre-cancerous cells. However, we still do develop cancers, which suggests that this recognition process is not perfect. In our laboratory, we believe that if we use the right peptides as anti-cancer targets, we could train the immune system to efficiently recognize and destroy tumors. We know that those ideal targets must generate a powerful and prolonged immune response. These targets arise from many genetic differences between tumors and the healthy tissue. Therefore, our study aims to identify tumor-specific peptides and understand their nature.

column36: The effect of a decatastrophizing cognitive restructuring intervention on sensitivity to physical activity among adults with knee osteoarthritis: a randomized experimentally controlled trial
column37: Knee osteoarthritis is a common health condition that causes pain, disability, and high healthcare costs. Best practice guidelines recommend that people with knee osteoarthritis engage in physical activity as a self-management strategy. Unfortunately, few people with knee osteoarthritis engage in regular physical activity or exercise. A common barrier to adherence is an increase in pain severity during physical activity. One treatment that may decrease pain during physical activity is a psychological technique called cognitive restructuring. Cognitive restructuring focuses on challenging unhelpful thoughts. Negative thoughts about pain have been linked to poor health outcomes for people with muscle, bone, and joint pain. This research will involve 200 adults with knee osteoarthritis. Participants will be randomly assigned to a treatment or education program. The researchers will measure participant levels of physical activity for one week prior to the treatment or education program. The treatment in this study will involve four 60-minute cognitive restructuring sessions delivered over four weeks by a trained healthcare professional. The education program will include four 60-minute sessions on knee anatomy and osteoarthritis. Through this work, the researchers will: 1) determine the extent that levels of pain during physical activity predict daily physical activity levels, 2) determine whether decreasing negative thoughts about pain reduces pain during physical activity, and 3) determine the extent that changes in pain during physical activity can be explained by reduced negative thoughts about pain. If the treatment shows a positive effect, the researchers could develop and then evaluate a new treatment that combines decreasing negative thoughts about pain and structured physical activity. The ultimate goal of this research is to develop evidence-based treatments to improve adherence to physical activity and exercise among adults with knee osteoarthritis.

column36: Circulating tumor DNA as a predictive biomarker in metastatic bladder cancer
column37: Metastatic bladder cancer is a lethal and under-studied disease. Chemotherapy has historically been the most effective treatment for metastatic disease, but long-term survival is rare. Exciting new treatment options have recently emerged, however, responses to these new therapies are highly variable and we lack a reliable method of predicting who the responders will be. Therefore, efforts are underway to develop tools to determine the ideal therapy for each individual based on their tumor's molecular features. My research aims to develop a blood-based test for identifying genetic changes (mutations) present in metastatic bladder tumors. This test relies on the fact that when cancer cells die they often shed their DNA into the circulating bloodstream (known as circulating tumor DNA, ctDNA). We can therefore use ctDNA to evaluate the mutations in metastatic cancers that correspond to treatment response or resistance. In my preliminary research, I found that most patients with metastatic bladder cancer can have their tumors analyzed in this manner. Importantly, my initial work showed that it was feasible for patients to have real-time testing of their cancer's molecular features, without the need for invasive tissue biopsy - which is often impractical, costly and can cause significant patient morbidity. In this project, I will identify mutations in the ctDNA of hundreds of Canadians with metastatic bladder cancer, and determine which mutations predict a patient's subsequent response to treatment. Success with my project will help explain why some metastatic bladder cancers are intrinsically responsive or resistant to the most commonly used therapies. Furthermore, I will have developed a clinically-practical framework (requiring only a blood sample) that may ultimately help guide rational therapy selection in advanced bladder cancer.

column36: Determining the mechanism for lung lipid defects in a Mecp2-mutant mouse model for Rett syndrome
column37: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurological disorder that almost exclusively affects females and is caused by mutations in the gene methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2). Girls with RTT reach their normal developmental milestones, but soon lose their ability to speak, use their hands, and walk. Seizures and severe breathing disturbances are also common. These symptoms are progressive, such that most patients require constant supportive care, which is a huge burden on the health care system as well as their families. Although breathing difficulties account for the death of most RTT patients, the lung is rarely studied. Using a Mecp2-mutant mouse model of RTT, our lab showed that MeCP2 bridges a lipid-regulating complex to its DNA targets; when MeCP2 is absent, fat is over-produced. This leads to increased fat content in the brain, liver, and blood of Mecp2-mutant mice. Importantly, specialized cells in the lung also synthesize lipids for lung surfactant and may be affected by the loss of MeCP2 in similar ways. I aim to understand how loss of MeCP2 in the lung contributes to breathing abnormalities in RTT. Surprisingly, I have identified perturbed lung lipid synthesis pathways in the lungs of Mecp2-mutant mice that lead to profound fat accumulation. Additionally, breathing defects in these mice improve following treatment with lipid-lowering statin drugs, implicating a role for lung lipids in RTT respiratory symptoms. Elevated fat in lung surfactant has previously been associated with respiratory distress and breathing disturbances. Therefore, a better understanding of how MeCP2 regulates fat in the lung will shed light on how and why these breathing difficulties manifest in RTT patients. Respiratory impairment is a severe and life-threatening hallmark of RTT. My findings will support the repurposing of lipid-lowering therapeutics to treat this devastating disease and greatly improve the quality of life of patients with RTT.

column36: The impact of prenatal malaria exposure on the susceptibility of offspring to psychiatric disorders.
column37: Worldwide, there are ~125 million pregnant women at risk of infection with malaria each year. Malaria infection during pregnancy (MiP) has severe consequences for the health of both mother and child. Studies have revealed a connection between infections in pregnant women and an increased risk of psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia in their children. Mental illness is a growing problem in areas with high malaria transmission, but the impact of MiP on offspring neurodevelopment has not been well studied. We have used an established animal model of MiP to examine whether MiP can prime offspring for mental illness later in life. We found that offspring born to malaria-infected mothers had abnormal psychiatric behavior in adulthood. Furthermore, brain cells from embryos of malaria-infected mice were mislocalized within the developing cortex, and exhibited an increased proportion of newly born neurons compared to unexposed embyros. The next steps of our research include further investigating the effect of MiP on autism spectrum disorder-like behaviours, as well as studying the consequences of MiP on the long-term trajectory of brain development (e.g. adult brain structure and cell types). We will also examine disturbances in other mechanisms of neurodevelopment that may underlie malaria-related psychiatric outcomes, and investigate potential therapeutic strategies to prevent neurological injury in MiP-exposed offspring. Factors that interfere with normal development of children lead to enormous financial and social costs for low-resource countries. This proposal suggests that malaria infection during pregnancy is one such factor, and one that is preventable. Since such a large number of pregnant women are at risk of malaria, this research has broad implications for global maternal-child health, as well as the potential to reduce the burden of mental illness in low-income countries.

column36: Investigation of PNP-3, a natural product antibiotic effective against multi-drug resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
column37: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multi-drug resistant bacterial pathogen deemed a top threat by both the Center for Disease Control and the World Health Organization. A. baumannii causes pneumonia, blood infections, wound infections, and meningitis in humans. To address this problem, over 100 strains of a group of bacteria called Pantoea were surveyed for antibiotic activity against A. baumannii, and two strains were identified. The purpose of this research is to attempt to isolate and characterize these antibiotics to assess their potential for therapeutic development. My objectives are to: 1) identify and characterize the genes responsible for antibiotic production in each Pantoea strain, 2) extract the antibiotics and identify the structures, 3) evaluate the antibiotic properties, and 4) explore the regulation of antibiotic production. To date, I have identified the genes responsible for antibiotic production in each Pantoea strain and found them to be identical, indicating that the same antibiotic is produced by both bacteria. The group of genes encode proteins that function to synthesize the antibiotic, transport the antibiotic, and regulate its production. I also found the antibiotic to be effective against a wide-range of human pathogens, including several multi-drug resistant A. baumannii strains, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and members of the bacterial group Enterobacteriaceae, all of which are on the World Health Organization's critical threat list. So far, several attempts to extract the antibiotic have been made; however, none have given clear results. Currently, I am attempting to overproduce the antibiotic in E. coli, which will hopefully allow for easier isolation of the antibiotic. Overall, my research highlights not only Pantoea as an antibiotic source, but also an antibiotic with potential to treat multi-drug resistant A. baumannii infections.

column36: High-throughput RNA interference screening reveals epigenetic modifier dependencies in a synthetic model of human T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
column37: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive malignancy of blood cells. T-ALL represents 15% of pediatric, and 25% of adult cases of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Current therapy with high intensity combination chemotherapies achieve 5-year survival rates of approximately 90% and 50% for pediatric and adult T-ALL, respectively. However, these therapies have a broad specificity of cellular targets, and as such, are associated with life-long cytotoxic effects. The consequences of chemotherapy can be drastic, particularly in the pediatric setting, highlighting the importance for development of targeted therapies. In order to improve patient treatment outcome and to minimize the cytotoxic side-effects associated with chemotherapy, dedicated efforts are required to identify and validate candidate therapeutic targets. High-throughput methods are needed to enable screening large classes of genes for their therapeutic potential. Furthermore, reliable models that can faithfully recapitulate the disease state are required to accurately understand disease mechanisms. Recently, our lab developed the first ever model of human T-ALL derived from normal blood cells. This model provides us with an accurate representation of human disease, allowing us to understand the pathways that lead to pathogenesis. To identify novel therapeutic targets, we propose to use our model of human T-ALL to perform high-throughput screening methodologies that assess the importance of 300 epigenetic factors in disease maintenance. Importantly, our findings may provide an avenue for targeted therapy in T-ALL.

column36: Comorbidity and TBI in older adults: A population-based analysis
column37: Traumatic Brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability. While incidence among older adults is steadily increasing, we know very little about factor affecting outcomes this fastest growing segment of the population. To address this research gap, the purpose of this study is to examine how co-existing medical conditions affect older adults with TBI and their subsequent demand for healthcare services. This would be achieved in two phases - (1) a review of current literature and (2) an analysis of existing healthcare data. Specifically, Phase I comprises of a review of current research on the topic are to examine the link between co-existing medical conditions and outcomes in patients with TBI. Based on the review findings, Phase II will involve a population-based analysis of existing healthcare data of approximately 15,000 older adults (age>65) entering the hospital with a TBI in the province of Ontario, Canada. Through statistical tests and models, we will examine the health conditions older adults with traumatic brain injury have when they are hospitalized and how these conditions affect outcomes (healthcare resource utilization, physical functioning and discharge destination). As the first study of its kind to our knowledge, findings can assist in the development of more accurate assessments of the nature and impact of co-existing medical conditions in this vulnerable population. In particular, healthcare providers will be more aware of the different common medical conditions experienced by older adults with TBI, which will guide the planning of treatments and services targeted towards these individuals. On a policy level, the findings will help address the recognized need to inform future projections regarding which interventions might be most needed for which patients, in which settings, and at what time since injury, and highlight a systems approach necessary for the management of chronic disorders such as TBI.

column36: Identifying microbial mechanisms of inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis in the human intestinal microbiota
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a lifelong, debilitating disorder of the gastrointestinal tract, affecting 200 000 Canadians with increasing incidence worldwide. While the cause of IBD is currently unknown, the human gut microbiota (the community of bacteria, viruses, and fungi in the gastrointestinal tract) is hypothesized to play a role in initiating and maintaining IBD. My project aims to understand how the gut microbiota influences inflammation and identify specific microbial factors that may lead to IBD. In collaboration with the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario, my laboratory has collected intestinal washes from hundreds of pediatric IBD patients and non-IBD controls. By sequencing and analyzing microbial DNA from these samples, I will identify bacteria, viruses, and microbial metabolites that are more abundant in IBD patients. Specific techniques will be used to isolate viruses and predict metabolites. Once these microbial factors are identified, their ability to elicit IBD will be tested using human cell cultures grown from patient biopsy samples. Specific microbes or compounds can be injected into these human cell cultures to demonstrate inflammation. Identifying and characterizing the microbial causes of IBD initiation and maintenance will improve disease diagnosis and enable the discovery of new IBD treatments.

column36: Improving weight loss among breast cancer survivors: Accounting for the intricate relationship between expectancy, motivation, and fears of cancer recurrence
column37: Due to early detection and treatment of breast cancer (BC), the number of BC survivors in Canada is growing. Many women often struggle with weight management prior to diagnosis and often treatments for BC will further contribute to weight gain. Excess weight in BC survivors has been linked to a host of challenges including poor mental health, and even increased risk of cancer recurrence. The Healthy Lifestyle Modification after Breast Cancer (HLM-ABC) program was developed by clinical-research teams at York University and The Sunnybrook Odette Cancer Centre (OCC) to address these issues. The HLM-ABC is a professionally-facilitated, online weight management group wherein BC survivors work towards improved physical activity and eating habits, in order to achieve a healthy weight and improve quality of life. Importantly, a sub-group of BC survivors with unique weight management difficulties was identified, who struggled with weight management prior to their diagnosis, which negatively impacted their participation. As well, psychological factors such as motivation and fears of cancer recurrence could either motivate or de-motivate participants during the program. We therefore adapted the HLM-ABC to meet the needs of the BC survivors with lower motivation and previous weight loss difficulties. In this study, we will look at groups of BC survivors partaking in the HLM-ABC to verify whether one's weight prior to BC diagnosis impacts weight loss outcomes, as well as further explore the associations between treatment expectancy, fears of cancer recurrence, and motivation. Through standardized questionnaires and weight measurements, we hope to better understand what accounts for effective lifestyle changes among BC survivors. If we can pinpoint the psychological factors contributing to weight loss among BC survivors, we will be able to improve effective services for the range of women attempting to improve their prognosis and mental health through healthy lifestyle programs.

column36: Investigating translational mechanisms that regulate neuronal subtype specification in the developing mammalian brain
column37: Congenital brain defects and neurodevelopmental disorders are highly common, afflicting the individual, their loved ones, and the wider community. These disorders, particularly autism, are frequently due to errors in the process of neuronal subtype specification that occur during fetal brain development. Despite the importance of this process, the mechanisms underlying the generation of different types of neurons are still largely unknown. The distinct types of neurons that build the cerebral cortex are generated from neural stem cells, and are crucial for the assembly of functional neural circuitry. This circuitry, in turn, enables us to perceive and navigate the world around us. In my work, I will address how neuronal subtype specification occurs from the underexplored perspective of translation, the process in which messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are converted into functional proteins. I propose to characterize a new model in which individual neural stem cells already contain all the necessary information to generate different types of neurons in the form of mRNA, but that these mRNAs are prevented from being translated into functional proteins until the appropriate time during development. I will do so using a combination of advanced genetic, cell biology, and microscopy techniques. This work will provide new mechanistic insights into how genetic mutations that lead to aberrant protein translation make the brain prone to developmental defects. It will also advance the field of neurobiology by challenging existing assumptions regarding how stem cells are instructed to generate all the different types of neurons that comprise a healthy, functional brain.

column36: Investigating the effects of broadly-neutralizing anti-influenza virus antibodies on immune effector cells
column37: Influenza virus causes the seasonal flu, and is one of the most prevalent viral pathogens worldwide. This virus affects 10% of adults and 20-30% of children across the world, and causes 250 000 to 500 000 deaths every year. Although current flu vaccines are the best way to prevent disease, they must be administered every year and only protect against a few strains of the virus. Influenza vaccine development must also be completed every year, and is a complex and expensive process. The major reason why current influenza vaccines offer transient protection is because the virus mutates frequently and becomes unrecognizable by our immune system from year to year. In the current study, we investigate broadly-neutralizing antibodies, which recognize portions of the virus that are less prone to mutation, and how they interact with cells in our immune system to protect us from infection. The goal of this project is to aid in the development in a universal flu vaccine, which will address the shortfalls inherent to current flu vaccines.

column36: An Inter-provincial comparison of innovative programs that help individuals and families affected by life-limiting chronic illnesses navigate end-of-life
column37: As our population gets older and the number of people living with chronic diseases rises, it will become more difficult to provide good quality care for people who live with advanced chronic disease and are approaching the end of life (EOL). Much research across Canada has shown that our healthcare systems often cannot meet the needs of these people in its current state. We need innovative ways to increase patient and family awareness of, access to, and coordination between services and supports that help people meet their needs and goals as they get closer to EOL. One potentially important approach is the delivery of community-based navigation programs that can educate patients and families, link them to critical health system and community services and supports, and support better coordination across healthcare settings. This project will identify and compare how well community-based navigation programs, put in place across Canada, help individuals and families affected by advanced chronic diseases improve their access to services and supports, and achieve their EOL goals. We will also examine how these programs can best be implemented in other places. We will get this information through several different ways, including surveys and interviews with people who work in the programs (e.g., nurses, navigators, managers) and use the programs (e.g., patients, family members). The information we receive will be used to: understand how navigation programs work, for who, under what circumstances, and to produce what types of results; and to shape recommendations about whether and how to implement such programs in other parts of our country.

column36: Scaling-up eConsult in Primary Health Care: a policy analysis in four Canadian provinces
column37: One of the most promising innovations that have been piloted to improve access to care is eConsult. eConsult is a model of asynchronous communication that allows family physicians (or nurse practitioners) to electronically consult specialists regarding their patients' medical issues. This model of eConsult was first developed and piloted in the Champlain region in Ontario and then spread throughout other regions in Ontario (ON). It is also in early stages of implementation in Manitoba (MB), Quebec (QC) and Newfoundland and Labrador (NL). To date, few strategies have been developed by the provinces to expand regional eConsult pilot projects at the health system level. However, over the past year, both professional associations and provincial growing interest in potential system-level strategies to support its expansion. Building on previous work, the aim of this comparative policy analysis project is to inform decision-making for the expansion of eConsult by supporting the development of a scaling up plan, a crucial step in the scaling-up process, in close collaboration with key stakeholders in Manitoba, Quebec, Ontario and Newfoundland and Labrador, and to foster cross-jurisdictional learning. More specifically, this study will: 1)Describe the designs of eConsult piloted in four provinces -Logic models (document analysis, validation with advisory committees). 2)Identify policy barriers and enablers to scaling-up eConsult in each province. -Policy analysis (policy documents, interviews with 10 key stakeholders per province). 3)Propose and prioritize strategies for the scale-up of eConsult appropriate to each province's context. -Nominal group in each province. 4)Share experiences across jurisdictions and learn from each province's policy issues and strategies for the scale-up of eConsult. -Pan-Canadian deliberative policy dialogue.

column36: Evaluating Older Adult Care Continuums in Alberta and Manitoba: A Comparative Analysis
column37: Older people are the main users of publicly funded care continuums comprised of home care, various types of community-based housing with health services care options (called supportive housing in this research), and nursing homes. While this basic continuum exists across Canada, provinces vary greatly in terms of the number and type of services that they offer. This is especially the case in Manitoba and Alberta. Manitoba has the second largest supply of nursing home beds in Canada but has one type of supportive housing. Alberta has the smallest supply of nursing home beds in Canada with four levels of supportive housing. No research examines how these different continuums work. We don't know (for example) how often nursing home residents in one province remain in the community in the other, or how often people have long hospital stays when transferring along the continuum. We also don't know what older people think of these care options, and how often things like high user-fees stop them from using the services they want. This knowledge is required to know how care continuums are working and also to identify where improvement is needed. This research will compare the different care continuums in Manitoba and Alberta. We will first compare the number and type of services that exist and also the policies governing their use (e.g., admission criteria, user fees). Using healthcare use records from Winnipeg (Manitoba) and Edmonton (Alberta), we will then compare how people actually use these continuums along with other healthcare services (e.g., long hospital stays as people transfer from one continuing care sector to the next). We will also conduct interviews with users and providers, to get their perspective on how well their continuum works and where improvement is needed. Our results will help planners to better understand the strengths and challenges of their own care continuum, and to see the benefits of adopting certain features used elsewhere.

column36: A National Research Network on Lyme Disease
column37: Lyme Disease (LD) is an emerging microbial threat and new approaches are required to help contain this risk to human health. LD is caused by the bacterial pathogen, B. burgdorferi that is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick. LD is of increasingly urgent concern in Canada; between 2009-2016 there was a 700% increase in the number of reported cases. Additionally, areas of Canada that were once considered to be at low-risk are transitioning to high risk as tick populations become further established due to climate change. Further research is necessary to address the many critical knowledge gaps that exist in Canada. We will establish the Canadian Lyme Disease Research Network (CLyDRN) which is composed of researchers, clinicians, patients, community members and other stakeholders with the ultimate vision of reducing the impact of LD on the health of Canadians. We will accomplish this vision by creating foundational resources and spearheading new research initiatives. This includes the creation of Canada's first repository for tissue samples from LD patients and an associated clinical database that will include detailed patient information. We will also develop national research capacity and support training of new LD researchers. These resources will support research initiatives in four areas: 1)Develop and evaluate new diagnostic tools and methods, 2)Identify preventive measures, interventions, and population health approaches to decrease risk of occurrence of LD, 3)Determine the burden and natural history of disease, clinical management and risk factors and 4)Attend to the contextual complexity through patient and community engagement, training and integrated KT research. Our Network will mobilize and build LD-specific capacity and training opportunities, improve clinical science and practice, provide best evidence in testing and patient care, improve patient outcomes and inform policy.

column36: Supporting integration through primary health care teams: A comparative policy analysis across four Canadian provinces
column37: Primary health care (PHC) models in Canada continue to change. There are still many gaps in understanding what works and what does not work as well for PHC teams to promote integration and continuity of care, especially for those complex patients with more than one chronic condition. This research will be completed in four provinces across Canada including British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, and Quebec. The goal of our research is to study provincial and regional policy documents (guiding principles and courses of action) that support health services integration for complex patients through PHC teams. We will also study patient engagement in developing and applying policies. The study will include three phases. In Phase 1, we will collect and analyze all policy documents from the four provinces. We develop individual case reports and then compare the policies across the provinces. In Phase 2, we will carry out interviews with patients from each province and then hold a discussion session with patients in each province to discuss the research results and develop actions together. In Phase 3, we will obtain feedback through online and web-based discussions from a broad group of provincial and national stakeholders including patients. We will ask these stakeholders to develop recommendations and actions based on the research results. The results of the study will provide us with a set of leading national practices for integrated health services delivery through PHC teams. The results will be helpful to participating provinces, other provinces in Canada, as well as internationally.

column36: BEhaviors, Therapies, TEchnologies and hypoglycemic Risk in Type 1 diabetes: The BETTER study
column37: Type 1 diabetes requires that patients inject themselves insulin to control the level of sugar in their blood because their pancreas cannot do it anymore. A consequence of this treatment is low blood sugar episodes. This is named hypoglycemia. Severe hypoglycemia has the potential to cause accidents, injuries, coma, and death. Patients voiced a need for better strategies to reduce those episodes. This is the focus of the BETTER program. In this program, we will test an online educational strategy to help patients who are wearing an insulin pump or are wearing a monitor to know in real time their blood sugar, to optimise their use of these devices. It will also include a peer-to-peer forum discussion to further offer social support. The program will be built in partnership with patients. It will be tested across the province of Quebec among adolescents and adults. We hypothesize that this program will help patients reduce hypoglycemia episodes. To recruit patients for this trial, we will first build a registry of patients. From this registry, we will know who is using the devices and who is having the most hypoglycemic episodes. Patients will answer questionnaires annually part of the registry. In this questionnaire they will have to report hypoglycemia, answer to questions on fear of hypoglycemia, if they feel their hypoglycemia, etc. We will also carry out small trials to improve effectiveness of the wearable device measuring blood glucose in real time, to test new strategies to correct a low blood sugar episode, to obtain the point of view of caregivers for helping during serious episodes and finally, to test an artificial pancreas system in a specific condition in which it may be harder for the system to prevent or correct a low blood sugar episode. All these trials will increase our knowledge on hypoglycemia, how to prevent and treat those episodes.

column37: More and more Canadian adults are living with more than one chronic diseases or conditions at the same time, especially as they get older. We will examine the effective elements of these programs using a framework for patient-centered care developed by researchers in Quebec (QC) and Ontario (ON). Our first step will be to identify the various programs for patients with multiple chronic conditions being offered by primary healthcare teams in NL and NS. We will interview team members and patients from these programs to map the process of care for patients. We will also do a survey of patients with multiple chronic conditions to understand their experience of receiving care from these teams. We will compare results across provinces. We will hold a meeting of the teams from all four provinces to share knowledge and develop tools that could be used by primary healthcare teams, patients, healthcare administrators and researchers. We expect that we will identify program enhancements that could lead to improvements in quality of care for patients with multiple chronic conditions. This could enable these patients to experience better health and require less emergency and hospital care.

column36: Canadian Autoimmunity Standardization Core (CAN-ASC)
column37: To stay healthy, we need to have an immune system that works properly: it needs to attack foreign cells, but leave our own cells alone. If our immune system attacks our cells, it causes an illness called an autoimmune disease. There are many types of autoimmune disease, including type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, celiac disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. Two million Canadians of all ages live with an autoimmune disease. Researchers and healthcare professionals are working hard to find new and better ways to treat these lifelong diseases. column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is the most common acute leukemia in adults. We have developed a molecule, which targets STAT%, an important driver of blood cancers. column37: Endometriosis is the presence of tissue from the lining of the uterus (womb) found outside the uterus. 10% of women will be affected by endometriosis during their childbearing years with ~1 million Canadian women affected in any given year. Symptoms can include daily pelvic pain, pain during menstruation or sexual activity, infertility and, in rare circumstances, development of ovarian cancer. The economic impact of endometriosis is ~$2 billion/yr in Canada and over $50 billion/yr in the USA, attributed to lost productivity and management of chronic disease. Nonetheless, it remains vastly understudied, leaving women with unanswered questions on how to deal with their disease and whether any treatment may be successful. Historically thought of as an inflammatory condition, endometriosis is classified based on where it presents: (1) on the ovary (endometrioma), (2) on the surface of peritoneal organs (superficial), or (3) invading into organs (deep endometriosis). Staging of endometriosis estimates the amount of disease present. Neither anatomical classes, nor staging, are reliable for predicting success of treatments or alleviation of symptoms. In 2017, my group reported a world-first discovery that 25% of endometriosis carry cancer-driver mutations despite having no risk of becoming cancer. We have since discovered that different types of endometriosis have similar mutations and some women with multiple types of endometriosis may have the exact same mutations across all lesions. To accelerate research and drive development of new management strategies we propose to examine how mutations and anatomical presentation of endometriosis influence its interaction with normal cells in the body and the immune system (the microenvironment). This study will form the basis for a new molecular-classification of endometriosis.

column36: Developmental outcomes of preterm infants enrolled in a randomized clinical trial of a parent administered sensorimotor intervention in the neonatal intensive care unit.
column37: Background: Children who are born prematurely are at a higher risk of developing developmental delays than children born at term. Early experiences in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) can influence developmental outcomes. Sensorimotor interventions as well as parental engagement have been designed with the aim of improving the development of children born preterm. Substantial evidence supports the benefits of each intervention on improving developmental outcomes. However, there remains a significant gap in the literature on the efficacy of a parent administered sensorimotor intervention (PASI) program in the NICU on infant's development. The proposed study is designed to evaluate the potential benefits of such a program on infant's development. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of a PASI program on preterm infant's neonatal and motor developmental outcomes. Study Design: A multi-center randomized block clinical trial will be performed. Method: A total of 84 preterm infants (< 33 weeks gestation) will be recruited and randomized. Infants in the experimental group will receive the sensorimotor program, consisting of tactile (whole body) and oral input for 15 minutes, one time per day, for 10 days. Infants in the control group will receive standard care. The following outcomes will be monitored time to attainment of complete oral feeds (primary outcome), rate of weight gain, length of hospitalization, and motor outcomes at hospital discharge and at 4 months corrected age. Significance: Results from this study will provide us with further knowledge on the impact of sensorimotor intervention on infants' developmental outcome as well as the effect of active parental involvement on infants' development. Provision of a PASI program is a safe and low cost effective intervention that may increase the development and quality of life of preterm born children and their family.

column37: Young babies are at high risk of severe disease from whooping cough - they can end up in intensive care in hospital, and some babies will die. Whooping cough vaccine (Tdap) has recently been recommended in Canada to be given to all pregnant women to prevent whooping cough in their newborn babies, before they are old enough to be immunized themselves. This recommendation has also been made in many other countries, however we do not fully understand how Tdap works. At the moment, we do not fully understand how much antibody is needed to protect newborn babies against whooping cough, or exactly how the antibodies protect babies. This proposed project is linked to a trial we are doing of Tdap vaccine in pregnant women with HIV in Uganda. In that study pregnant women with HIV will receive Tdap. Their immune response will be compared to pregnant women with HIV given tetanus vaccine and also to pregnant women without HIV given Tdap. In the proposed project we want to use the blood samples collected from the women in the trial, and their newborn babies, to help us to understand how Tdap vaccine works during pregnancy. We will use these samples to examine the amount of antibody produced after Tdap in pregnancy and also test exactly how this antibody interacts with the bacterium which causes whooping cough, called Bordetella pertussis. This will help us to understand how Tdap vaccine works in pregnancy, which will help to ensure we use it in the best way possible to prevent whooping cough in babies.

column37: Background: Many cutting-edge therapies rely on manipulating the adaptive immune system, which has evolved a vast diversity (repertoire) of immune receptors to recognize and remove pathogens and cancer cells. The existing iReceptor Platform uses community-developed standards to facilitate sharing of AIRR-seq data by enabling queries across a system of distributed data repositories. Research Project: The iReceptor Plus Canada-EU consortium of researchers will address several key challenges to optimally sharing AIRR-seq data among public and industrial partners: protecting patient privacy and the intellectual property of partners, performing complex analyses on data brought together from many sources, and expanding the size and number of repositories that can be integrated in the network. Benefits and Impact: The iReceptor Plus project will facilitate sharing of AIRR-seq data among multiple institutions, including biopharmaceutical companies and researchers working with human confidential data, across multiple diseases, treatments and populations. This will lead to a better understanding of the causes of infectious and autoimmune diseases and cancer, which can lead to early detection and suggest novel therapies. These improvements will reduce the social and economic burden of these diseases, advance Canada's leadership role in immunotherapy, and contribute to improved patient care worldwide.

column36: Effects of Canadian Smoking Policies on Children's Use of E-Cigarettes and Exposure to Second-Hand Smoke in Cars
column37: Rising e-cigarette use among children and their exposure to second-hand smoke in cars have become significant public health challenges. In this study, we will investigate the behavioral and health impacts of two Canadian health policies recently adopted to address these significant child health risks: 1) Provincial bans on smoking of combustible cigarettes and e-cigarettes inside private vehicles; 2) Provincial bans on the sale of e-cigarettes to children. These policies have attracted substantial attention and debate in Canada and other countries. Yet, there is still little evidence on their effects. This research will use state-of-the-art quasi-experimental methods with data from national surveys and administrative data to estimate the effects of the policies. The potential impacts of our proposed research on child health are broad and substantial. Given the high burdens of asthma and other respiratory diseases related to smoking and second-hand smoke exposure, even modest reductions in these outcomes could have substantial health benefits. Through establishing whether, and to what extent, these bans on smoking in cars and access to e-cigarettes to minors can improve health outcomes and generate economic benefits, our study will inform efforts to monitor, strengthen and fine-tune these current policies. As the federal government is considering a national e-cigarette policy (Bill S-5) that, among others, bans smoking in cars and sales of e-cigarettes to minors, evaluation of these provincial laws will also provide timely evidence to inform potential effectiveness of this federal legislation and guide its enforcement efforts.

column36: Identification of biomarkers for antenatal depression in early pregnancy and associations with Child developmental milestone achievement at 12 and 24 months of age in the All Our Families prospective cohort
column37: Antenatal depression (AD) is one of the most common pregnancy complications in developed countries. It affects about 17% of pregnancies, translating to nearly 68,000 Canadian women per year. AD is a debilitating disease for mothers, and has negative impacts on the fetus, and later infant development. The reason that AD negatively impacts infant development is not well understood. There is increasing evidence that depression coincides with inflammation in the body, and specifically elevated blood-levels of cytokines, chemicals involved in immune response. Research over the past two decades has established that inflammatory responses in the body during pregnancy, cytokines in particular, can cause damage to the brain of the developing fetus. While elevated blood-cytokines are well-documented in depressive disorders generally, similar cytokine patterns in AD are not as clear. In pregnancy, a fine immuno-regulatory balance is required to ensure the fetus is not rejected, while allowing for adequate maternal immune response to protect against infection. Normal cytokine balances thus differ in pregnancy, when compared with non-pregnant women. Little is known about healthy cytokine balances in pregnancy, making comparisons of healthy and disease-specific cytokine profiles difficult. Past studies using traditional analysis methods have been limited to comparing a small number of cytokine levels. Advanced analysis methods can identify complex patterns of cytokines and provide more information about their association with infant development. Our study will A) use advanced analysis methods to identify complex patterns of up to 43 cytokines associated with AD in early pregnancy, and B) examine associations with Infant development at 1 and 2 years of age, in a population-based prospective cohort. Our results will inform the mechanisms by which AD impacts infant development, and inform potential anti-inflammatory treatments during pregnancy to reduce negative impacts on infants.
