column36: Using telerehabilitation to support families of children with motor difficulties aged 3-8 years old. A patient-centred, mixed-method innovative pragmatic trial
column37: Background: Many children (about 1 child out of 20) have motor delays that are sometimes seen as "minor" and are not immediately explained by a specific diagnosis. These children are often underserved by existing health and rehabilitation services even though we know that they are at risk of developing important negative outcomes in the long run. The most recent scientific evidence indicates that motor delays can be effectively addressed via early interventions supporting families and stimulating the child's development. Some researchers have proposed that such interventions could be efficiently and conveniently delivered online but no patient-centred, interactive online intervention has been formally trialed in Canada for children with motor delay and their families. Objectives: The goal of this study is to determine whether an online intervention can support families of children with motor delay. We will determine whether the online intervention can improve the child's motor skills and the family's well-being, while exploring the factors that may influence the way the intervention could be included into existing health services. Description: We will recruit 100 families of children with motor delay, 3 to 8 years of age, who are not yet receiving public rehabilitation services. These children will be referred to the study by a health professional. Families will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: 1) control group (usual health care) or 2) intervention group (access to health professionals via webinars, group and private discussions, and regular one-on-one virtual meetings). This study, conducted in Quebec, will be led by researchers, telerehabilitation experts, decision-makers and patient advocates. Relevance: This study will evaluate an innovative, convenient and accessible intervention providing assistance for an important yet underserved population of children and their families.

column36: Investigating the Keys to Spermatogenic Niches Among Men with Non-Obstructive Azoospermia
column37: Infertility affects 15% of couples world-wide, and male factors contribute to half of cases. The most severe form of male infertility, termed non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) occurs where no sperm are produced due to defective spermatogenesis. An overwhelming 70% of these cases have no known cause. Treatment options are limited and involve a surgical procedure termed microTESE where a surgical microscope is used to identify dilated seminiferous tubules in the testis that are most likely to contain a degree of preserved sperm production, compared to the vast majority of collapsed tubules lacking sperm production. This technique is the last option for fertility and is only successful in approximately half of cases; thus, research is desperately needed to understand the mechanisms underlying these severely infertile men with NOA to progress care This study will investigate the mechanisms that distinguish active and defective spermatogenesis with the aim to identify novel therapeutic targets. To do this, we will compare testis tissue from men with NOA and control men with normal sperm production. We will use state-of-the-art single cell sequencing which allows us to study the precise genetic expression within each individual cell from each testis biopsy. Using advanced analysis techniques, we will identify differences in cell-type-specific gene isoforms and expression between normal controls and men with NOA including comparisons between dilated tubules (with spermatogenesis) and collapsed tubules (defect spermatogenesis). Using specialized 3-D organoid cultures, we will investigate the regulatory differences in germ cell and somatic cell interactions among the experimental groups. Results from this study will contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms and identification of novel therapeutic targets among severely infertile men with no presently available treatment.

column36: A Clinical Decision Rule to Identify Young Children at Risk for Iron Deficiency
column37: An 18-month old child is seen by her family doctor for her 18-month check-up. She was breastfed in the first year, introduced to cow's milk at 10 months, and currently drinks 1 L of cow's milk per day by bottle. Her mother describes her as a fussy eater who has poor meat and vegetable intake. As a healthy infant, this child was born with enough iron stores for the first 6 months of her life. The doctor suspects that since she stopped breastfeeding and began to eat other food, she may not be getting the recommended daily amount of iron that she needs for her brain development. Iron deficiency is very common among children between the ages of 1 to 3 years (12%) and is associated with developmental delays that can lead to permanent deficits. Early identification of iron deficiency can prevent a significant public health problem with serious consequences. Testing for iron deficiency involves a simple inexpensive blood test. Most Canadian children do not have any blood tests at their doctors' visits. Primary care doctors have to decide whether to order a blood test on children they think are at risk for iron deficiency. Our team is developing a tool called a 'clinical decision rule' that can be used by doctors to identify which children ages 1-3 years may be at risk for iron deficiency and could be confirmed with a blood test. To develop the tool, we used data from 900 healthy children 1-3 years of age visiting their primary care doctor for their scheduled visit. As members of the only child health practice-based research network in Canada called TARGet Kids!, these primary care doctors are collecting data on risk factors for iron deficiency and blood samples on children. Before our clinical decision rule can be used by primary care doctors across Canada, we need to test our clinical decision rule in a new and separate group of children.

column36: Understanding fiber fermentation within the 1-year-old infant gut microbiome

column37: One of health care's largest outstanding issues is that many patients do not respond to treatment or are harmed by a treatment. Approximately 90% of drugs are effective for less than 50% of patients, resulting in significant individual, social, and economic impacts. Variable treatment response also contributes to the rising cost of drug development, currently estimated at around $2.6 billion per drug. A fundamental driver of these inefficiencies is the variability that exists in the human genome of patients. To better understand this variability, and develop more effective drugs and customized treatment approaches, we need to better integrate the variable human genome datasets being studied globally. This proposal addresses key fundamental, internationally important, challenges to enable effective global genomic data sharing and harmonization. The project builds on existing databases and infrastructural resources, including Europe's largest controlled access database - EGA - and a worldwide collection of human genome datasets, including major cohort studies in Canada. Specifically this Canada-EU joint project addresses: federated data discovery, secure authentication and authorization to access data, and standardization of the data (in particular other contextual data associated with the genomic data which is currently poorly organized). The project will demonstrate the effectiveness of this data harmonization, enabling joint cohort analysis with targeted clinical applications. This project will also incorporate important outreach and training initiatives, and address particular ethical, legal and social issues associated with this federated data analysis. This work will address key gaps in the development of the personalised medicine vision described in the ICPerMed Action Plan and by CIHR. The analyses enabled by this project will advance scientific knowledge in ways not previously possible.

column36: EUCANCan: a federated network of aligned and interoperable infrastructures for the homogeneous analysis, management and sharing of genomic oncology data for Personalized Medicine.
column37: We propose to create the EUropean-CANadian Cancer network (EUCANCan), a federated infrastructure whose mission is to enable Personalized Medicine in Oncology by promoting the generation and sharing of harmonized genomic and phenotypic data. These reference nodes will work together in an interoperable fashion to provide the genomic oncology community with a uniform computing environment for the processing, harmonization and secure sharing of cancer genome and phenome data in the context of clinical research, enabling the discovery of clinically-relevant patterns of variation in the cancer genome such as biomarkers predictive of therapeutic response. The infrastructure will also provide a proving ground for federated genome analysis systems that may one day be integrated into national and regional healthcare systems. EUCANCan's objectives are: (1) harmonise protocols for the identification and interpretation of germline and somatic variation profiles within cancer genomes; (2) generate strategies for the flow, management, storage and distribution of data within and across EUCANCan nodes; (3) define community standards for data elements, types and formats; (4) develop an open and accessible data portals for the searching and download of EUCANCan data; and (5) define an appropriate ethical and legal frame to ensure the secure sharing of protected individual genomic and phenotypic data across countries.

column36: EUCAN-Connect: A federated FAIR platform enabling large-scale analysis of high-value cohort data connecting Europe and Canada in personalized health
column37: Rapid progress in information and biotechnologies offers the promise of better, personalized health strategies using rich phenotypic, environmental and molecular (omics) profiles of every individual. To capitalize on this great promise, the key challenge is to relate these profiles to health and disease while accounting for high diversity in individuals, populations and environments. Both Europe and Canada have long-term investments in population-based prospective cohort studies providing essential longitudinal data. These data must be analyzed in unison to reach statistical power, however, presently cohort data repositories are scattered, hard to search and integrate, and data protection and governance rules discourage central pooling. EUCAN-Connect will enable large-scale integrated cohort data analysis for personalized and preventive healthcare across EU and Canada. This will be based on an open, scalable data platform for cohorts, researchers and networks, incorporating FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) for optimal reuse of existing data, and building on maturing federated technologies, with sensitive data kept locally and only results being shared and integrated, in line with key data governance guidelines. column36: EU-CAN-SHARE: Integrated human data repositories for infectious disease-related international cohorts to facilitate personalized medicine approaches to infectious disease research
column37: EU-CAN-SHARE builds on existing infrastructures and partnerships to develop a sustainable model for the storage, curation, and analyses of the complex data sets collected by infectious disease (ID)-related cohorts. While ID cohorts collect both clinical-epidemiological (CE) and terabytes of OMICS data, storage and analysis of CE and high dimensional laboratory (HDL) data remains separate and developing the infrastructure for housing and analysing HDL data is not feasible for individual studies. In this project, we develop innovative approaches to the synthesis and analysis of CE&HDL data, and modify governance models for cloud-based repositories elaborated by and for scientists in high-income countries to meet the specific challenges of synthesizing CE&HDL data and sharing data across international cohorts and with the Open Science community. We develop data architecture and governance that link biobanks to data repositories to facilitate equitable use, collaborative, cross-domain analyses, and replicability. The team leverages partnerships with multicentre ID cohorts in the global South, and connects EU investments in OMICS infrastructures with Canadian expertise on pipeline and workflow development, biostatistical methods, and ethical and governance issues related to the establishment of repositories for CE&HDL data in resource-limited settings. Drawing from best practice and governance elaborated for similar initiatives, the repository will employ a federated model where a tiered permission system and cohort-specific hubs facilitate cohorts' analysis of their own data, cross-cohort analyses, and connections with the open science community within a clearly elaborated legal, ethical, and equitable framework. The cloud-based platform will provide analytic tools and computational power to facilitate cross-domain, collaborative analyses that inform personalized medicine approaches to diagnostic, treatment, and vaccine development in ID-focused international cohorts.

column36: euCanSHare: An EU-Canada joint infrastructure for next-generation multi-Study Heart research
column37: Personalised medicine approaches are highly needed in the domain of cardiology, as cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the major contributors to mortality and morbidity worldwide. To date, cardiovascular research has been conducted by interrogating biomedical data in single cohorts, but these are often limited to specific populations, geographical areas, or data type. These challenges call for integrated multi-cohort approaches to allow researchers to investigate established and emerging markers within and across heterogeneous populations. In Canada, CVD research has been at the forefront of multi-cohort approaches through the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) (MUHC, McGill, McMaster, ICES). The CAHHM exploited Canadian know-how in legal data (McGill) and in harmonisation and integration (MUHC) to create a centralised longitudinal super-cohort from 8 Canadian cohorts for enhanced data sharing in cardiovascular research. However, infrastructures and models to facilitate integrated sharing of information and data between Canadian and European cohorts are missing. The euCanSHare project proposes to leverage, extend and integrate two complimentary initiatives in Canada (CAHHM) and Europe (BiomarCaRE) to develop a robust ecosystem for enhanced data sharing, integration and exploitation in CVD research. In this way, existing Canadian and European tools will be put on a Common IT platform developed within euCanSHare, and will offer extensive services and functionalities. Comparative analysis of legal frameworks in Canada and Europe will be led by experts from Canada (McGill) to inform the shared automation of such services. The integrated cloud-based collection of technologies, policies and standardised procedures will reduce the cost of research, allowing efficient data management at scale across international projects.

column36: Canadian "Rare Diseases: Models and Mechanisms" (RDMM) Network
column37: Thousands of rare genetic diseases (RDs) affect one million Canadians, mostly children, and cause significant disability, lead to early death, and almost all have no treatment. Genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) has transformed our ability to identify gene mutations that cause RDs, but we understand very little about the impact of those genes and mutations on biology and health. As a result, we don't know how to treat most of these devastating diseases. Studying gene mutations in model organisms (such as yeast, worm, fly, fish, and mouse) provides important information about how mutations cause disease and can identify potential therapies. However, geneticists discovering genes that cause RD do not usually conduct research in model organisms, and model organism scientists are not usually aware of genes being discovered by geneticists. Thus, in 2014 we established the Canadian 'Rare Diseases: Models and Mechanisms' Network ('The RDMM Network') to a) connect geneticists discovering RD genes with model organism scientists able to study that gene and b) provide small grants to support collaborative research. The RDMM Network has engaged these communities, made connections for 72 RD genes, and funded 79 projects. Our research has already led to original scientific publications, successful large-scale grants, and identified two life-changing therapies. These results are very promising, and we want to expand the impact and reach of the RDMM Network. To do so we will: - Further engage the clinical and model organism communities - Enable connections when model organism expertise is not available in the country where the gene was discovered, by linking similar networks around the world - Support more projects by partnering with Canadian organizations interested in co-funding research. Building on our experience running the RDMM Network, we will support more than 50 collaborative projects to generate new knowledge that will improve the care of Canadians with RD.

column36: Disparities in congenital heart disease burden by maternal socioeconomic status and ethnicity
column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a type of heart problem that babies are born with. It is a major cause of babies' death in Canada. CHD can cause severe disability. Patients with CHD may require life time cardiac care. Previous studies have shown that the chance to have babies with CHD among poor families and certain minority groups is higher than that among rich families or other ethnic groups. However, results are vague and inconsistent. There are substantial limitations in previous studies, which make the results biased and difficult to interpret. In Canada, at least 50,000 children are born into poverty, and one in every 100 infants are born with CHD. Considering that Ontario consists of 39% of Canada's population and one third of Ontarians are visual minorities, health inequity would be a major concern in prenatal health if pregnant women from poor and vulnerable families or minority groups have an increased risk of CHD in offspring. Therefore, we plan to study if mothers from a minority group or who live in poor, less educated, or socially deprived neighbourhoods have an increased chance to have babies with CHD. We are going to link several big data sources, including the BORN Information System (BIS) birth registry data, the CIHI data, and the Census data collected by different organizations and equity index scores developed by experienced Canadian researchers. All databases are available. Therefore, no extra cost on data collection is needed. Findings from this study will help us better understand the causes of CHD and further develop strategies for the CHD prevention. The results of this study could have important recommendations for health policy to improve health inequity in Canada.

column36: Sleeping for Two: A randomized controlled trial of cognitive behavior therapy for insomnia experienced during pregnancy
column37: Sleep problems are common during pregnancy, they tend to worsen as pregnancy progresses, and they are associated with increased birth complications, higher rates of depression and anxiety and worse infant sleep. Although there are medications for short-term treatment of insomnia the majority of pregnant women say that they will not take them because of fears about the potential impact on the developing baby - this leaves pregnant women without alternative treatments for insomnia. Our research group has developed a psychological intervention called "Sleeping for Two: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) experienced during pregnancy". The intervention is a six-week psychological therapy that helps pregnant women improve behaviours and thoughts related to sleep. Initial results show that the therapy improves symptoms of insomnia during pregnancy. This proposed project is a larger trial of the Sleeping for Two intervention. The main goals of the project are to investigate if the Sleeping for Two intervention, compared to regular care in pregnancy, reduces symptoms of insomnia in pregnancy and if those gains are maintained at 6-months postpartum. Additional goals are to test if CBT-I reduces symptoms of depression, anxiety and improves infant sleep. We plan to recruit pregnant women with insomnia and assign them to receive either six sessions of in-person CBT-I or to receive regular obstetrical care. We will ask participants to complete an assessment at baseline, seven weeks later and then again when they are six months postpartum. We predict that the CBT-I intervention will reduce symptoms of insomnia and improve other important outcomes, including lowering symptoms of depression, anxiety and improving infant sleep.

column36: Closing the gap: Identifying risk and resilience factors influencing mental health and wellness among First Nations children and youth
column37: Indigenous children and youth experience poorer health and wellness compared to those in the general population. These health gaps have been attributed to the intergenerational consequences of harmful colonization practices, continued systemic discrimination, and social determinants of health that further disadvantage Indigenous peoples. In this regard, within First Nations communities in Canada very young children and youth are disproportionately dying by suicide, highlighting the importance of early identification and intervention. However, empirical evidence elucidating the factors contributing to Indigenous children and youth mental health is lacking. To address this gap, we propose a mixed methods approach to obtain an in-depth understanding of the pathways influencing the mental health of First Nations children and youth. We will examine the risk factors, such as historical and current community stressors, as well as the resiliency factors, such as community belonging, that lead to or protect against First Nations children and youth suicide and comorbid conditions. This will begin with the analyses of nationally representative surveys to examine First Nations children and youth living in reserve communities and those living in urban regions of Canada. Additionally, we will conduct a qualitative study with mental health service providers who work directly with Indigenous youth to gather a richer understanding and story of Indigenous child and youth mental health. It is expected that this work will provide an in-depth understanding of factors contributing to the mental health disparities that exist for Indigenous children and youth, with a view to inform evidence-based strategies for prevention, identification and treatment.

column36: Resolving mechanisms and biomarkers of ascending infections to prevent preterm birth
column37: Millions of genes are carried by complex communities of microbes inhabiting our bodies - together, these microbes and genes form the microbiome. The microbiome is inherited, largely from our mother at birth, forming an integral part of our unique physiological identity. My research seeks to understand how the maternal microbiome influences the success of human reproduction - both by vitally supporting human development, and by sometimes causing it harm. To this end, I am pioneering new methods of discovering which bacterial species, genes, and biochemicals are linked to pregnancy complications, with the goal of harnessing the maternal microbiome to prevent preterm birth. Our preliminary findings these organisms, known as Sneathias, may use similar mechanisms as Group B Streptococcus and other obstetric pathogens. This work could therefore suggest new ways of screening women for a higher likelihood of preterm labour and preventing preterm birth.

column36: Accuracy of general paediatrician diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder compared to multi-disciplinary team assessment
column37: Background: Increasing rates of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have contributed to lengthy waits for expert diagnostic assessment that negatively impact ASD outcomes. Many ASD diagnostic guidelines state that an expert team is needed to make the diagnosis; although some children currently receive their diagnosis from a community-based clinician, e.g. a general paediatrician (GP). There are no studies of the accuracy of GPs in diagnosing ASD. Project aims: The aims of this project are to: 1) determine accuracy of GP ASD diagnosis compared to an expert team assessment; 2) to determine child features associated with accurate diagnosis by GPs. Possible features include: child's age; sex; cultural background; ASD severity; developmental delays; and having a sibling with ASD. Methods: We will recruit 26 GPs from across Ontario, as well as 260 of their patients (10 per GP) who have been referred with possible ASD. The GP will complete their assessment and decide on a diagnosis, but will not tell the family. The ASD expert team, consisting of a developmental paediatrician and a psychologist, will also perform a diagnostic assessment without knowing the GP's opinion. The team will inform the family of their diagnostic opinion. We will determine the diagnostic agreement between the two assessments. We will then determine which of the child's characteristics (age, sex, cultural background, ASD severity, developmental delays, having a sibling with ASD) predict agreement in diagnosis. Expected Results: Results from this study will determine whether GPs can independently and accurately diagnose ASD. Future activities include refinement of educational workshops for GPs on ASD diagnosis and development of pathways to identify which children can be diagnosed in a community setting.

column36: Social Competence in Children Diagnosed with Sickle Cell Disease: An examination of risk factors
column37: Background: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a severe, genetic form of anemia that causes distorted red blood cells. The distorted red blood cells can impact almost every tissue in the body and cause a number of difficulties including pain, risk of stroke, learning difficulties, decreased quality of life and social difficulties. Children who have a diagnosis of SCD do not have as many friends as their peers. Social difficulties are a serious health risk that may be comparable to the health risks associated with drinking and smoking. Yet, we do not understand who is most at risk of experiencing social difficulties. We need to understand this in order to find the best way to treat these social difficulties. The aims of the current study are to identify some of the factors that might be contributing to social difficulties in children diagnosed with SCD. Methods: Sixty-nine children diagnosed with SCD and 69 healthy children will be invited to participate and complete some tests that will assess aspects of their social function. They will also undergo imaging of their brain (MRI) that will aim to see whether there may be brain abnormalities caused by their disease that can be linked to social difficulties. Their parents, teachers and classroom peers will also complete measures designed to assess the social function of the children diagnosed with SCD and healthy children. Expected Results: This study will identify some of the factors related to the social function in children diagnosed with SCD. This will help us learn to better identify which children may be at greatest risk of social difficulties and to design better treatments to help these children.

column36: Impact of maternal pertussis immunization on pregnancy outcome and child health

column36: Disability, Employment, and Public Policies Initiative
column37: Employment is an important channel through which individuals develop self-esteem, consolidate their social network, and secure sufficient income for retirement. Yet, it remains widely acknowledged that persons with disabilities lag seriously in employment. According to Statistics Canada, the employment rate of people with disabilities was twenty percentage points lower and their unemployment rate five percentage points higher. Women and those aged 35 and above seem particularly vulnerable.In 2001, 40% of women with disabilities aged of 15-64 years were part of the Canadian workforce, compared to 69% of women without disabilities in the same age category (Statistics Canada, 2012). Aging of the Canadian population will add further challenges to public services and programs. Data on the prevalence of disabilities are clear - rates of disability for Canadians 65 years or older are double those of the population at large, and the prevalence of disabilities increases with age for almost all types of disabilities. The later suggests that the socioeconomic impacts of disabilities will likely grow in the future as the Canadian population continues aging. This proposal contains an interdisciplinary research program aimed at developing economic policies to help persons with disabilities. Our research program covers policies to foster job search, job retention and promotion, and facilitate transition from the labor market to retirement. Our research program recognizes that existing data sources (survey and administrative data)are necessary yet insufficient to estimate econometric models capturing the complex realities facing persons with disabilities. Persons with disabilities may for example have pessimistic views of their chances on the labor market and withhold effort to search for jobs and get promoted. They may also fail to understand the complexities of public programs and their fiscal incidences.

column36: TYDE: Transitioning Youth with Disabilities and Employment
column37: Article 27 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) recognizes "the right of persons with disabilities to work on an equal basis with others... in a work environment that is open, inclusive and accessible to persons with disabilities," and compels "State Parties to safeguard and promote the realization of the right to work." In Canada, people with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to employment with only 49% of individuals with disabilities reporting work (Statistics Canada, 2012). The employment situation for people with intellectual disability (ID) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is significantly worse; working age individuals represent the most unemployed and underemployed citizens in Canada. According to the Canadian Survey on Disability (2012), only 22.3% of persons with ID or ASD indicated some kind of employment, and, when employed, these individuals received low wages, worked few hours, and often worked in segregated settings; further, when ID/ASD research considers sex/gender, females fare worse than their male counterparts. In spite of this, work is an aspiration for people with ID or ASD and is a key mechanism for social inclusion.The BC Transitioning Youth with Disabilities and Employment Project -- "The TYDE Project" -- aims to improve employment outcomes for transitioning youth ages 14 - 18 with ID or ASD in British Columbia through early interventions that target youth and their parents with particular attention paid to gender in the design, implementation and assessment of this research and knowledge mobilization (KM). Research consistently supports that intervening early when young adolescent girls and boys with ID or ASD are transitioning from school to adult life translates to positive employment outcomes. Further, research demonstrates that 1) experiences with inclusive education, 2) positive parental expectations for employment and/or post-secondary education, 3) greater levels of self-determination among transitioning youth with ID or ASD, and, 4) early work experience are predictive of higher employment outcomes. These four domains underpin our research and KM program. Through this partnership, we will:1. Develop and test The TYDE Transitioning Youth to Employment Tool; an online interactive learning environment designed to enhance employment outcomes for youth with ID or ASD by increasing youth pre-employment skills, increasing youth self-determination, and improving parental/caregiver knowledge and expectations for fostering their youth's future employment experiences.

column36: Healthy Professional/Knowledge Workers: Examining the Gendered Nature of Mental Health Issues, Leaves of Absence & Return to Work Experiences from a Comparative Perspective
column37: Mental Health (MH) related leave accounts for nearly 30 per cent of short- and long-term disability claims, yet many suffer in silence. The combined effects of absenteeism and presenteeism due to MH issues has been estimated to account for more than $6 billion in lost productivity costs.(6) Given their knowledge service role, these presenteeism and absenteeism can be uniquely challenging for professional workers. Indeed the negative consequences extend not only affect relations with co-workers and employers, but, with the broader public in terms of accessibility to and quality of services. Negotiating leaves of absence and return to work can be particularly difficult when potentially stigmatizing MH issues are involved and when work culture and structure constitute insurmountable barriers. Although MH-related presenteeism and absenteeism are areas of growing concern for professional/knowledge workers, they are seriously understudied, particularly from a comparative perspective. The role gender plays is also conspicuously absent as an explicit focus. Addressing absenteeism and presenteeism across a range of workers, we ask: - What are the mental health experiences of professional/knowledge workers causing them to take or contemplate taking a leave of absence from work? - What are the key factors causing them to leave work -- with a focus on personal, family and work context -- and which of these factors are most influential in fostering their return to work? - Which of these key factors prevent others experiencing mental health issues from taking a leave?Reflecting an explicit gender perspective, we will examine how the barriers, facilitators and experience of contemplating and negotiating leaves of absence and return to work are gendered at the level of the worker and their profession. We also ask what interventions can mediate these gendered experiences.Our Partnership will be the first interdisciplinary, collaborative, comparative research initiative investigating and addressing the gendered experiences of MH, LoA and RTW for regulated professional/knowledge workers. We bring together academic researchers, worker representatives, unions, professional associations, employers, service providers, insurers, policy-makers, and other stakeholders across the following domains: 1) healthcare, including dentists, midwives, nurses and physicians; 2) education, including professors and teachers; and 3) accountants. In addition to cutting across sectors, these groups of workers also differ by work context and gender composition. We take an explicit gender perspective in the collection and interpretation of the data gathered, which we will augment with a broader intersectionality lens and life course approach. A mixed methods approachPage 2 will capture the complexity of the issues, involving qualitative data -- documents, observations and interviews with the range of stakeholders -- augmented with quantitative data from available administrative and newly developed survey datasets. These components will inform targeted case studies and evaluations of ongoing interventions drawing upon the input from our participating stakeholders. Comparing across knowledge worker groups, locations and using mixed-methods allow us to address the complexity of the phenomena for a truly ground-breaking research program. We will integrate our partners throughout the entire research process beginning with co-developing the research foci, accessing existing and collecting new data, interpreting the findings, and translating the knowledge into more effective and equitable leave of absence and return to work policies, practices and programs. We will contribute to the development, implementation, and scale-up of evidence-based and gender-responsive interventions.

column36: Policy and practice in return to work after work injury: Challenging circumstances and innovative solutions
column37: A fundamental purpose of workers' compensation (WC) law and policy is to help people return to work after injury, to which end it creates regulatory economic drivers as incentives. However, our pilot studies, focusing on some of the most vulnerable categories of workers, suggest that such drivers often become the new purpose of the process, pre-empting the original purpose of the law. We have gathered together a multi-disciplinary team of 14 academics, 18 partners and over 20 trainees to address the overarching policy question: How can we get back to the purpose of the legislation and promote sustainable return to work (RTW) for all workers injured or made ill because of work? We focus in particular on the effectiveness of current policies as applied to three overlapping categories of potentially vulnerable workers: the precariously employed, the geographically mobile and low wage earners in Quebec, Ontario, and the Maritime Provinces. We are interested in workers suffering from either physical or mental health problems attributable to the workplace and in the roles of unions and workplaces in supporting RTW in light of the policy frameworks applicable. The proposal seeks funding for 7 research programs (A-G), to examine the scope and effectiveness of regulated RTW policies and the application of those protections to three categories of workers in particular: 1) those injured while working in non-standard employment (defined) or 2) while engaging in employment-related geographic mobility or 3) full time low wage earners. When possible we will include both unionized and non-unionized workers within the purview of our research, and partners have been chosen accordingly. Programs A-G build on our pilot projects while adding new dimensions(role of workplaces and immigration issues): A: Classic legal analysis of rules governing injured workers' rights to support for sustainable return to pre-injury employment or to the broader labour market, looking specifically at WC, occupational health and safety and human rights law; qualitative studies in B Ontario and C Quebec to document experiences of workers injured while precariously employed who attempt to return to pre-injury employment or return to the labour market. D: a mixed methods study to document experiences of mobile workers injured while working outside their home province who attempt to return to pre-injury employment or the broader labour market. E will develop tools for workplaces and unions to assist them with RTW of workers with physical or mental health problems. F focuses on immigration issues and the temporary foreign worker program as related to RTW in Ontario and Quebec. G will synthesize the results from the six research programs, to develop recommendations for policy makers and workplace actors as to types of regulatory and policy protections, and workplace practices, that work for promoting sustainable RTW for the working populations targeted by this project. All of our studies include a gender lens, seeking to ensure that academics and partners understand how policies and practices apply to men andwomen. This approach will include a consideration of work-family balance issues, at the time of determination of suitable post-injury employment, but also consideration of the segmented labour market, and the disproportionate presence of women in part time, temporary, and low wage employment. Partners supporting this application, include governmental agencies representing the interests of employers, workers, and the protection of public health and NGOs. Their participation in research design and knowledge mobilisation will strengthen the research program and facilitate recruitment of new partners while providing economic support ($957,209) for our activities.

column36: Mobilizing a Caregiver-Friendly Workplace Standard: A Partnership Approach
column37: INTRODUCTION: There are more than 5.6 million employees in Canada with adult/elder care responsibilities and 35% of them are simultaneously employed (2012). Lack of workplace support can result in carer-employees (CEs) leaving the workforce, and/or missed work days, or early retirements which can impact employers in terms of reduced productivity and avoidable costs due to a range of HR issues, such as turnover and absenteeism. Given the gendered nature of both family caregiving and the labour sector, it is incumbent upon workplaces to implement gender-sensitive caregiver-friendly workplace practices (CFWPs) to appropriately accommodate CEs whilst sustaining efficiencies in the workplace. Doing so enhances work-life balance, workforce retention, and reduces health costs. The Healthy, Productive Workplace -- Partnership Development Grant (HPW-PDG) allowed McMaster University to partner with the Canadian Standards Association, among others, to create a bilingual Caregiver Inclusive and Accommodating Workplace Organizations Standard for Canadian workplaces. This HPW-Partnership Grant (PG) will mobilize uptake of the Standard in Canada and abroad, while accruing evidence on the Standard's broader health and economic impacts.GOALS: In partnership with: (i) academic researchers; (ii) a range of diverse, committed partners - representing academia, government, non-government/non-profit, private business/service providers, and labour, and; (iii) collaborators representing various industries, the proposed partnership will disseminate and mobilize the Standard across Canada and the world. We will deliver a sex and gender-sensitive program of research to assist CEs, human resource professionals, unions, workers associations, government organizations, and a variety of employers, to implement the successful uptake of the Standard. RESEARCH PROGRAM: Led by Dr. Allison Williams, a CIHR Research Chair in Gender, Work and Health, and the Sex and Gender Champion for the PG, the proposed research program will be executed by a geographically representative group of invited partners and collaborators, together with world-class academic researchers with unmatched expertise in this field. In addition to the internationalization of the Standard (Project 1), where the Canadian Standards Association will follow a specific standards protocol, an international comparative review of CFWPs will be undertaken to provide a baseline for the global uptake. Carers Canada will lead Project 2, which includes a rigorous program of knowledge mobilization and evaluation. Project 3 involves a qualitative assessment of experts, recruited from the Conference Board of Canada, to diagnose readiness to support CEs in Canadian organizations. The results of Project 3 will inform a feasibility study (Project 4), which will be realized in partnership with Habanero Consulting Inc. Working with a host of partners representing precarious workers and cultural minority groups, Projects 5 and 6 will realize the Standard's cultural competency/ safety. RESEARCH OUTCOMES: This proposed research project, which includes a robust knowledge mobilization program, will support new thinking and behavior that will lead to improvements in the economic, social, cultural and intellectual well-being in Canada and internationally. Research capacity will be built, with 29 trainees and 2 emerging scholars integrated in all aspects of the research, governance and partnership. New knowledge about CFWPs will be generated, providing the evidence needed for continued uptake of the Standard, and informing curricula in business management/HR -- both of which will ensure ongoing sustainability of the Standard as a significant intervention in improving healthy, productive workplaces in Canada and abroad.

column36: Accommodating and Communicating about Episodic Disabilities (ACED): A partnership to deliver workplace tools and resources to sustain the employment of people with chronic, episodic conditions
column37: Central to this initiative is that many physical and mental health conditions cause episodic disability. Episodic disabilities are intermittent, often unpredictable, and may be largely invisible to others until symptoms are severe. Examples are depression, anxiety, multiple sclerosis, Crohn's, colitis and arthritis. Taken together, they are among the most common and costly chronic conditions in Canada. The nature of episodic conditions creates unique challenges for workplace disability management, particularly in implementing privacy and duty to accommodate policies. Objectives: The aim of this partnership is to enhance the work sustainability of Canadians with chronic, episodic mental and physical health conditions through the development of easily accessed, evidence-based tools, resources and training that protects privacy and facilitates communication and accommodation planning among workers, supervisors and others in the workplace. Objectives are: 1) consolidate and enhance existing evidence for toolkit development; 2) develop new evidence-informed resources, including a communication decision-making tool, interactive job analysis and accommodation planning tool, and skills training workshops for supervisors and HR/disability managers; 3) pilot test and evaluate the toolkit in diverse workplaces, including conducting cost analyses; 4) expand the evidence base to include greater attention to sex/gender, age/life course, diverse employment contexts and episodic conditions; 5) develop new researcher capacity in disability studies; 6) build new workplace partnerships for testing and dissemination.Methods: We will use a theory-driven, integrated evaluation approach that comprises researchers, partners and other stakeholders to develop and evaluate the toolkit and that follows a recommended four-stage life cycle: 1) evaluation of needs; 2) toolkit development and initial implementation; 3) mature implementation; 4) outcome and economic evaluation and dissemination. Partners: Our identification of team members is strategic and adds value compared to an approach that focuses on a single health condition or type of workplace. Research team members have expertise in psychology, economics, health sciences, ergonomics, public health, and knowledge translation. Partners are five national health charities of conditions often causing episodic disabilities and four workplace focused partners. They are: the Canadian Mental Health Association, Crohn's & Colitis Canada, Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada, Realize, The Arthritis Society, the Institute for Work & Health, the Great-West Life Centre for Mental Health in theWorkplace, Mindful Employer Canada, and the Ontario Ministry of Labour. All partners have a mandate to improve the inclusiveness of work and the employment participation of workers with episodic disabilities. They are at the forefront of progressive thinking about workplace disability policies and practices and/or are leaders in creating innovative tools and resources. Outcomes: Our partnership will produce important scholarly and social benefits, including: new tools, resources and skills training applicable to a range of episodic conditions and contexts; providing new trainees and a cadre of early career investigators with research and leadership experience in disability studies; greater understanding of the personal, social and economic value of addressing the workplace needs of individuals with chronic, episodic disabilities; knowledge mobilization and dissemination plans that will result in a lasting legacy of our partnership.

column36: Partners for enhancing healthy and productive work for young men and women with disabilities
column37: Maintaining a healthy workforce is a priority for employers, workers and policy makers. Of the 1.5 million working age Canadians with a disability, 411,000 are unemployed but want to work and their disabilities do not prevent them from doing so [1-2]. There are nearly 200,000 Canadian young adults aged 15-25 who have a disability, representing a substantial untapped pool of capable future workers [1]. Despite the strong business case for hiring people with disabilities, their employment rates are consistently half or less compared to people without disabilities [3-4]. Workplace accommodations can optimize disabled workers' labour participation [5-6]. However, despite the benefits of accommodations, employers struggle with how to accommodate employees with disabilities and the types of accommodations that will facilitate employment [7]. Although many people with a disability could benefit from accommodations, only a small proportion of workers disclose their need for accommodations due to fear of discrimination or job loss [8-9]. Little is known about the experiences of disability disclosure and workplace accommodations among young people who attempt to enter and remain in the workforce. It is critical to identify effective disclosure strategies and workplace accommodation processes because they can improve quality of life and job performance [10].This grant is linked to the "Insight" and "Connection" programs and is designed to connect academics and knowledge user partners to increase the multi-directional flow of knowledge. This five-year CIHR-SSHRC partnership grant in "Healthy and Productive Work" will allow us to develop an interdisciplinary partnership and co-create knowledge to develop, implement and evaluate the following evidence-informed, gender-responsive solutions to enhance healthy and inclusive labour force participation of youth with disabilities. OBJECTIVES: (1) to develop evidence on disability disclosure and workplace accommodations that help youth with disabilities to enter, remain healthy and productive in the workplace; (2) to implement and evaluate evidence-informed, gender-responsive solutions for effective implementation, evaluation, and scaling up of interventions (i.e., toolkits, simulations, mentoring) that enable productive work among youth with disabilities; (3) to build capacity for measuring and demonstrating the broader health and socio-economic impacts of these interventions; (4) to expand the evidence base and research capacity regarding the integration of sex and gender-based analysis with respect to healthy and productive work; and (5) to enhance inter-disciplinary partnerships through the Inclusive Youth Employment Research Coalition through inter-disciplinary collaborations between researchers and knowledge users while building capacityof the next generation of researchers. We will develop a cross-sector partnership of academics, employers, youth with disabilities and knowledge users to understand how best to provide workplace accommodations. To enable knowledge generation through engagement with these partners, the partnership also includes leading Canadian academics with expertise in child disabilities, workplace accommodations, gender, diversity, and human resources management. These individuals are committed to advancing our understanding of workplace accommodations and improving employment opportunities for young people with disabilities. KEY DELIVERABLES: The project deliverables involve the following: three toolkits; (2) interactive bi-monthly webinars and 5 workshops; (3) interactive project website; (4) infographics, policy briefs, videos; (5) publications / presentations; and (6) development of an Inclusive Youth Employment Research Coalition.

column36: Cultural Agility in Northern BC's Healthcare System: Increasing Indigenous Employment Participation and Responsiveness to Indigenous Well-Being
column37: Building on a 2016 SSHRC Partnership Development Grant (FILE #890-2016-3038) in primary partnership w/ Northern Health (NH) and the First Nations Health Authority (FNHA), the broadest goal of this 2018-2023 Partnership Grant is: to improve health sector employment environments, and the delivery of healthcare services, in Northern BC (and beyond) by researching, implementing, and evidencing "culturally agile" healthcare services especially by using community-informed decolonizing critical humanities and social science methods and methodologies. Culturally agile healthcare services in BC would: 1) support (especially Indigenous) people from northern and rural places to join and stay in healthcare employment professions and 2) ensure the healthcare system is safer for all Indigenous peoples, including employees. This goal was honed over 17 months in consultation w/ 20+ community organizations across Northern BC and in close partnership w/ NH and FNHA.Delivery of healthcare services in BC is uniquely complex: in 2005, BC First Nations (FN), the Province of BC, and the Government of Canada signed a Transformative Change Accord, agreeing to work together to "...restore, revitalize and strengthen [the health of] First Nations and their communities and families [and] to eliminate the gap in standards of living w/ other British Columbians...". This resulted, in part, in the FNHA, the first province-wide health authority of its kind in Canada. In 2013, the FNHA assumed programs, services, and responsibilities formerly handled by Health Canada's First Nations Inuit Health Branch -- Pacific Region: the FNHA's vision is to transform the health and well-being of BC's First Nations and Aboriginal people by dramatically changing healthcare for the better. The FNHA works closely w/ other Health Authorities, including NH, which, w/ over 35% of the FN population in BC, serves the highest proportion of FN people in BC. With more than 8000 employees, NH is one of the largest employers in northern BC.Indigenous people live w/ multiple health barriers, including chronic illnesses and poor mental health, w/ Indigenous women facing increased barriers. Fostering Indigenous participation in the healthcare labour force, especially as it is demonstrated to increase the health of ALL Indigenous peoples in a service delivery area, is an urgent and dynamically emerging concern. Conversations between NH and Aboriginal Health Improvement Committees (AHICs -- who are tasked w/ collaboratively addressing local challenges that manifest first at a systems level based on relationships w/ communities) established a critical need to address issues such a racism and cultural safety within NH. These conversations established needs for new tools and interventions, which are 'beyond tables and numbers' and instead'speak to the heart' and 'incorporate Indigenous ways of knowing and being'. Our Partnership Grant (PG) will extend established partnerships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous multi-sectoral and interdisciplinary stakeholders across Northern BC. We align specifically w/ SSHRC's 'future challenge area' in addressing how experiences and aspirations of Indigenous Peoples are essential in building a successful shared future healthcare workforce in Northern BC. Our team (representing Indigenous and non-Indigenous stakeholders, social and medical/health scientists, along w/ humanities scholars and health employers) will work together in developing new ways of educating and strengthening a culturally safe & agile northern healthcare workforce for tomorrow by focusing on ways decolonizing community-informed social sciences and humanities approaches to knowledge production and dissemination might be mobilized to inform or develop healthcare delivery.

column36: Transforming Nurses' Work Environments Through a Strengths-Based Leadership and Management Training Program
column37: CHALLENGES: The current healthcare system is fragmented, depersonalized, disease-centric, and costly. Patients and families often feel powerless, disconnected, and voiceless, as do the nurses who care for them. Nurses report that dissatisfaction with the work environment is sufficient to make them want to leave nursing. Nurses often experience systemic sex and gender discrimination expressed in bullying, verbal abuse, and devaluing of their contributions, impacting their physical and mental health. What is needed is a paradigm shift from the current deficit-based management approach to a strength-based approach. Strengths-Based Nursing (SB-N/C) is both a philosophy and value driven-approach to guide the actions of clinicians, leaders, and managers. SB-N/C enhances, develops, and works with peoples' existing and potential strengths to bring out the best in the person and to contain, minimize, and/or circumvent what is not working. This shift requires re-training clinical managers and leaders to work through a strengths-based lens to build communities of caring and create safe workplaces for nurses ensuring that nurses can then provide safe, quality care to patients and families. GOALS & OBJECTIVES: The overall objective is to transform nurses' work-life environments from deficit-focused to strengths-focused through developing leaders/managers who are guided by a strengths-based approach to improve their health and productivity. To achieve this, we will refine a Strengths-Based-Leadership and Management (SB-L/M) Integrated Training Program for clinical leaders and managers with 3 components: 1- create and use innovative, multi-media teaching materials for story-sharing and sharing circles; 2- refine a 12-module course that integrates the best practice of healthcare with a SB-N/C approach paying attention to sex and gender issues in the workplace; 3- develop mentorship with situated coaching to ensure implementation and sustainability. Using a mixed-methods design, we will evaluate the processes and impact of this program on clinical leaders/managers, point-of-care nurses, and quality of patient/family care. PARTNERSHIP: To accomplish the objectives requires a multi-disciplinary Partnership. Partners continuing from Stage 1 (PDG) are: McGill University, Ingram School of Nursing, the birthplace of SB-N/C and SB-L/M; Concordia University's Center of Oral History and Digital Storytelling, with considerable expertise in multi-media story-sharing, collecting and analyzing oral histories and their impact on bringing about social change; and two clinical hospitals in Toronto, SickKids and Holland-Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital. Both hospitals have robust family-centred care, a developmental approach underpinning their pediatric care, and a commitment to SB-N/C in their strategic plans. Added to Stage 2 (PG) are: Two newclinical partners in Quebec, the Jewish General Hospital, Department of Nursing and CIUSSS-Ouest-de-L'Ile-de-Montreal, both of whom are committed to SB-N/C and strengthening their nurse-managers who directly supervise point-of-care nurses; the Canadian Nurses Association, the national voice of Canadian nursing profession that advocates on policy and legislation; and Concordia University's John Molson School of Business, bringing their experience and expertise in teaching operations, management skills, and in evaluation of the program. Our team continues collaboration with an award-winning visual anthropologist, and a knowledgeable scholar in sex and gender issues. Ultimately, this Partnership will contribute to a deeper understanding of the factors that create improvements to or obstacles in nurses' work-life environments, so that we can then inform policy and legislation at local, national, and international levels.

column36: Interrelationships between prescribing practices, patterns of illicit drug use, and overdose
column37: Overdose mortality rates associated with prescription and non-prescription opioid use have risen across North America over the past decade. In 2016, BC declared the opioid overdose crisis a public health emergency and introduced a number of interventions in response to the crisis, including new safe prescribing standards for opioid medications that aim to reduce the risk of addiction and overdose by curbing prescription opioid overprescribing. However, it is unknown how the reduction in prescribing opioids may impact patterns of illicit drug use, such as the illicit purchase of prescription painkillers and transition to injection heroin use. These drug use practices place users at an elevated risk of overdose, particularly with the recent emergence of fentanyl in the illicit drug supply. The proposed study aims to investigate the potential relationship between changes to opioid prescribing and patterns of illicit drug use. Data will be extracted from two ongoing longitudinal cohorts of people who inject drugs (PWID) in BC, and additional data will be collected via qualitative interviewing. The study will also examine the implementation of the safe prescribing practices, including how aspects of patient-physician interactions and linkage to addiction treatment and/or pain management impact drug use outcomes. Finally, the impact of the prescribing changes on other care-related outcomes, such as adherence to HIV treatment, will be examined. The evidence generated through this work will inform best practices for the safe prescribing of long-term opioid treatment in and outside of BC.

column36: Neuroimmune guidance cues, MicroRNAs & Inflammatory responses: Sex differences in cardiovascular diseases (MISs-CVD)
column37: Atherosclerotic vascular disease continues to be a leader of morbidity and mortality. Although sex hormones are known to play a role in this lipid- and inflammatory-driven disease, the underlying mechanisms are largely unclear. Neuroimmune guidance cues (NGCs) are key regulators of cell movement and positioning, and have emerged as significant players in inflammation. We have previously reported a role for Netrin-1 on macrophage emigration from plaques as well as key regulation of lipid metabolism by microRNA (miRNA)-33. Recently, we have uncovered sex-biased miRNAs targeting NGCs and hypothesize that these miRNAs provide missing mechanistic links in the endothelial-monocyte interactions and macrophage retention in the vascular wall during atherosclerosis in women vs men. We now seek to fully characterize the clinically relevant sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs in monocytes, plasma and aorta specimens from healthy subject and patients with atherosclerosis. We will also use primary endothelial cells and assess direct interactions between the sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs and unravel the functional impact of promising miRNAs on endothelial permeability, monocyte and macrophage trafficking and atherosclerosis using an innovative 3D vessel-on-a-chip platform and in vivo mouse models. This ambitious interdisciplinary project requires combined expertise of molecular cell biology, bioinformatics and physiology to provide crucial understanding of the gender differences in atherosclerosis and may provide novel gender specific therapeutic avenues to combat atherogenesis in both men and women.

column36: Unravelling proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) mechanisms in calcific aortic valve disease: from aortic valve sclerosis to stenosis
column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is a fatal pathology that affects 2-3% of the population. Yet, drug therapies are ineffective, leaving the urgency to fully characterize the aetiology of aortic valve calcification (AVC) to develop innovative therapies. Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) binds to and targets the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). It was recently shown that individuals with loss-of-function genetic variant at the PCSK9 gene have low levels of atherogenic lipoprotein concentrations (LDL and Lipoprotein(a)) and reduced risk of coronary heart disease and CAVS. However, the mechanisms through which altered PCSK9 activity could protect against or cause CAVS is lacking. Our preliminary data suggest that PCSK9 plays an active role in CAVS. We will, therefore, determine whether PCSK9 is a causal risk factor for CAVS using genetic epidemiology. Further, we will shed light on the molecular underpinnings through which PCSK9 causes CAVS in humans using state-of-the-art in vivo as well as in vitro models in combination with next-generation sequencing. As a complementary and potential pre-clinical model, we will determine the role of PCSK9 in the development of aortic valve calcification in mice. The overarching aim of this research program is to provide the required biological evidence using a highly translational approach to support PCSK9 as a therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of patients with CAVS.

Clinical guidelines have been established to help clinicians determine when a patient is ready to return to physical activity; however re-injury rates remain high,suggesting a need for improved objective assessment criteria. Injury rates are also on the rise in young, active children ages 8 to 18 years old. Each year, approximately 1 in every 20 girls playing competitive soccer or basketball will injure their ACL, or in other terms, one ACL injury per team. These injuries can be devastating to a young individual and there are currently no clinical guidelines specifically tailored to this age group to help optimize their rehabilitation. The overall purpose of my research is to understand how the knee joint is controlled in children who have injured their knee. In order to understand how an injury affects the knee joint differently between boys and girls, I will also evaluate how healthy children control their knee joint. I hope to identify differences in muscle activity and movement strategies between boys and girls that will help create better rehabilitation programs that can be used to improve recovery from a knee injury and prevent other children from having these traumatic injuries.

column36: The Neural Basis of Low-Dose versus Normal-Dose Psychostimulants on Executive Functions in Youth with Attention-Deficit / Hyperactivity Disorder: A Randomised Controlled Trial
column37: Attention-Deficit / Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and deficits in executive functions (EFs). EFs, which are associated with a brain area called prefrontal cortex (PFC), include abilities like attention, self-control, reasoning, and problem-solving. Our brain cells communicate with each other via neurotransmitters. In ADHD, there are lower levels of the neurotransmitter dopamine (DA). Psychostimulants (or stimulants) are often used as treatment as they increase DA. Some 50% of children with ADHD are now medicated with stimulants. Yet, they often struggle in school. At moderate-to-high doses, stimulants block DA's transporters. The striatum (a brain region associated with behavioural problems in ADHD) relies on that mechanism but PFC does not. Thus at those doses, stimulants should help the striatum function better, but not PFC. Recent animal neuroscience studies have now shown that at low doses, stimulants specifically help PFC. Given this, we reasoned that psychiatrists prescribing the right dose to help behaviour in ADHD might be giving too high a dose to help cognition. We just completed a triple-blind study where each youth with ADHD was tested once on their prescribed dose, and once on half that. Whether the full dose was given in the 1st or 2nd session was randomised. Regardless of whether the full dose was given in the 1st or 2nd session, all performed better on EF tasks when on half their dose. For my dissertation I would like to test the neural mechanism underlying this hypothesis. Using fMRI, I aim to show in youths with ADHD that at moderately high stimulant doses, the striatum works more efficiently and performance on a striatum-dependent task is better, while at a low dose, PFC works more efficiently and performance on a classic EF test is better. This is vital as understanding how the brain works on different stimulant doses could help us change the standard of care for ADHD, improving millions of lives.

column36: Identification of converging Molecular Pathways Across Chromatinopathies as Targets for Therapy: IMPACT
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a large and heterogeneous group of disorders. Many NDD risk genes are involved in modification of DNA structure and conformation otherwise known as "chromatin". The end result is that these genes control the production of RNA by a process known as "transcription" which impacts its "translation" into protein in nerve cells. In this proposal we study five distinct NDDs that are grouped together as chromatinopathies: Kabuki, Kleefstra, Gabriele-de Vries, Helsmoortel-Van der Aa, and a syndromic type of Autism Syndrome Disorder. They are caused respectively by mutations in KMT2D, EHMT1, YY1, ADNP and CHD8, which are involved in regulation of chromatin and ultimately transcription. These syndromes share overlapping clinical features, are interconnected by the molecular role of the causative genes, which are further connected by molecular partners. We hypothesize that mutations in these five genes give rise to unique as well as common downstream effects in gene transcription and translation. In brief, we will generate stem cells with mutations in the 5 genes using a method called gene editing; differentiate them into nerve cells to study functional effects on neural connectivity and network circuitry; explore the underlying molecular mechanisms using sequencing approaches that assess chromatin states, RNA transcription and protein translation; and integrate these findings to validate common molecular targets that disrupt neural network activity in NDD. Therefore, the IMPACT collaborative project (featuring labs in Europe and Canada) will reveal common converging disease mechanisms as attractive targets for therapeutic intervention. The development of such knowledge-based therapeutic interventions across individual NDDs can potentially be useful for designing interventions suitable for multiple related rare neurodevelopmental disorders.

column36: Impact of Early life MetaBolic and psychosocial strEss on susceptibility to mental Disorders; from converging epigenetic signatures to novel targets for therapeutic intervention
column37: Each year 38.2% of the EU population suffers from a mental disorder. Extensive research on the biology of stress now shows that healthy development can be derailed by excessive or prolonged activation of stress response systems in the body and brain during fetal life. Such toxic stress can have damaging effects on learning, behavior, and mental health across the lifespan. The consortium has been built to integrate basic researchers and clinicians to work on two very relevant cohorts (offspring of obese or stressed mothers) that will be here combined in a very innovative way to ask specific questions on mental health risk factors and their potential prevention. One main concept is that maternal obesity during prenatal life can trigger similar responses to maternal stress, altering developmental trajectories and increasing the risk for mental health at adulthood. It is hypothesized that maternal stress might be accompanied by inappropriate nutrition patterns which could synergize in activating stress-response systems in the developing organism. These adverse experiences can increase the likelihood of developmental delays and later health problems, including heart disease, diabetes, and depression. This consortium will assess whether common biological signals characterise early exposure to metabolic and psychological stress, affecting the long-term expression of genes involved in brain as well as immune-metabolic function, triggering mental disorders. A special emphasis will be given to long lasting epigenetic modifications, which could alter context- and time-dependent expression of genes relevant for brain function as well as peripheral biomarkers indices of immune-metabolic function that might be used in the clinic for disease prevention and health promotion during pregnancy. The Canadian team will be responsible for mapping epigenetic modifications in human blood and brain samples.

column36: Molecular determinants of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition in ovarian cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecological cancer, taking the lives of 1% of Canadian women. While the cancer remains localized to the ovary, treatments are quite effective, but the spread of the disease throughout the body dramatically reduces efficacy. Unfortunately, most cases are diagnosed at late, metastatic stages. Understanding the molecular mechanisms ovarian cancer cells use to spread throughout the body may lead to new strategies to detect and therapeutically target these metastatic cells. It is widely-believed that in order to metastasize, cancer cells must undergo a process called an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Within tumours, cancer cells are tightly anchored to each other (a characteristic of "epithelial" cells), but to metastasize, they remove these molecular anchors and activate genes that allow them to crawl around and burrow through tissues (characteristic of "mesenchymal" cells). This is also important for many normal processes, including embryo development and tissue repair. Despite being well-studied in these contexts, modern technologies have not been applied sufficiently to completely understand the molecular changes driving the EMT. The goal of the proposed project is to apply these technologies to map the molecular determinants of the EMT in ovarian cancer. First, we will expose ovarian cancer cells to a protein-transforming growth factor beta 1-that is a potent stimulator of an EMT. We will then use a technique called single-cell RNA sequencing to measure the activity of all genes in thousands of single cells after exposure, allowing us to map their response. After identifying which genes are activated or deactivated, we will use the DNA editing tool CRISPR-Cas9 to delete each of them to see which are critical for metastasis. This would provide a complete list of targetable genes to block metastasis and may also provide markers that could be used to predict the progression of a patient's cancer.

column37: La maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) est une maladie degenerative qui, au vu du vieillissement croissant de la population, verra son incidence multipliee, entrainant d'importantes consequences socioeconomiques pour les patients, les proches aidants ainsi que la societe. Le diagnostic n'est invoque qu'a un stade avance de son evolution etant donne l'apparition tardive des premiers symptomes. Les dommages irreversibles au cerveau sont alors considerables et s'accumulent deja depuis plusieurs annees. De nouveaux outils sont donc imperatifs afin d'identifier les individus a risque de developper la MA avant que celle-ci ne se manifeste, permettant d'agir plus rapidement et d'en minimiser les impacts. L'imagerie par resonance magnetique (IRM) est une technique d'imagerie sans effet nefaste pour la sante qui pourrait potentiellement repondre a ce besoin. Dans le cadre de ce projet, je me concentrerai sur la capacite de l'IRM a detecter les changements structuraux causes par les lesions pathologiques de la MA et de ses comorbidites, avec une attention particuliere pour la proteine tau. Cette proteine s'accumule de facon anormale dans le cerveau des individus atteints de la maladie et semble etre fortement associee a la perte de volume cerebral observee chez ces patients. Je creerai egalement un outil pour evaluer la presence et la severite des changements cerebrovasculaires associes au vieillissement. Il est attendu que les mesures de surfaces, de volumes et d'epaisseurs des structures du cerveau permettront de detecter la presence et predire la distribution regionale des depots de proteines et des lesions vasculaires qui, pour l'instant, ne peuvent etre objectivees qu'au moment de l'autopsie. Ce projet novateur entrainera des retombees importantes, notamment en permettant aux cliniciens de poser un diagnostic precoce et d'intervenir rapidement, en plus de faciliter la recherche de nouveaux medicaments capables de ralentir ou meme guerir la maladie.

column36: Caring Ahead: A Mixed Methods Study to Develop and Evaluate a Questionnaire to Measure Preparedness for Death in Caregivers of Persons with Dementia
column37: Caregivers of people with dementia face unique challenges related to caring for family members. Burden and stress on caregivers increase as dementia advances and 75% of caregivers develop problems like anxiety, depression or isolation, and increased rates of cancer and heart disease. These problems do not end when the person with dementia dies. Caregivers are twice as likely to develop complicated grief (severe feelings which make it difficult to function) than the general public or other types of caregivers. Feeling prepared for death has been linked to better adjustment and well-being after death. Therefore helping caregivers of persons with dementia prepare for death is essential. However, there is currently no questionnaire to measure how prepared or ready people feel for death. We also cannot measure if practices like advanced care planning are effective in helping people feel more prepared. Therefore through this study we will develop and evaluate a questionnaire to be titled 'Caring Ahead', in order to measure how prepared caregivers feel for death and life afterwards. Caregivers, experts and community members across Canada will be interviewed to better understand what preparation for death means. The questionnaire will be developed using this information and then tested in a group of caregivers or persons with dementia. Development of this questionnaire will help researchers and health care professionals identify how prepared caregivers feel in order to guide support and care. The questionnaire can be used to examine if advanced care planning is effective in helping caregivers prepare, or if new practices are needed.
