column36: Modeling developmental trajectories of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using population level linked health data
column37: The prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is estimated at 1 in 68. Children with ASD have highly varied functional abilities yet supports are often based on diagnosis, rather than function. We also have limited knowledge of long term developmental trajectories in ASD and the factors that influence these trajectories. We know that early intervention can lead to significant improvements in some children but children who are diagnosed later may miss this opportunity. Improving our understanding of the developmental course of children with ASD may lead to an improved identification of children at risk for ASD. By classifying children based on developmental trajectories and functional abilities, we can better identify children based on needs, rather than diagnosis, reducing obstacles and stress families face in accessing services. The aim of this study is to use population-level health data and individual diagnostic and school developmental data from multiple data sources to model developmental trajectories for children with ASD. We will also compare these trajectories to children who have not been diagnosed with ASD. This study will allow us to identify early life factors that affect school aged functional outcomes, particularly in children at risk of and who have been diagnosed with ASD. Our data set includes children born in British Columbia from 2000 to 2009 with 11,000 children diagnosed with ASD. This work is highly relevant to 3 areas of child health research: developmental trajectories, child health outcomes, and systems integration. By using novel ways of looking at developmental trajectories for children with ASD at a population level, our dataset will be large enough to provide potential powerful results to help focus in on important early life factors affecting long term outcomes in ASD in the context of a child's individual developmental trajectory.

column36: What is the optimal duration of anticoagulant therapy for patients with a first episode of unprovoked venous thromboembolism?
column37: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a major cardiovascular disease comprising of blood clots in the leg veins and the lung vessels affecting more than 50,000 Canadians each year, and is third-leading cause of cardiovascular death. Unfortunately, more than 50% of VTE cases occur without an identifiable cause (i.e. unprovoked). In these unprovoked VTE patients, the optimal duration of treatment with blood thinning medications (i.e. anticoagulants) is a common and difficult question, due to the closely balanced risks and burdens from recurrent VTE (if treatment is stopped) and major bleeding (if treatment is continued). Deciding to stop anticoagulants after the initial 3 months, or to continue them lifelong is primarily governed by the poorly established, long-term risk of recurrence when treatment is discontinued. Furthermore, an economic evaluation of the dilemma between short versus lifelong duration of treatment for such patients has never been conducted. I will first conduct a systematic review of the literature to identify studies of patients with unprovoked VTE in whom treatment was stopped after at least 3 months of anticoagulation. Next, using meta-analytic technique, I will combine the study results to establish the long-term risk of recurrent VTE at 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 years after stopping anticoagulation. I will then use these results to construct a decision model of unprovoked VTE patients, adopting a lifelong time horizon, and a publicly-funded healthcare system. The model will explore the crucial tradeoffs of recurrent VTE and major bleeding to determine whether considering lifelong duration of treatment, as compared to short-term therapy, is cost-effective (provides value for money). Taken together, results from this project have strong potential to provide definitive evidence needed in the decision-making process regarding the optimal duration of anticoagulation for unprovoked VTE, and thus inform policy and define clinical practice.

column36: Application of machine learning to improve prognostic predictive model discrimination for individual patients in a primary care, learning health system.
column37: Ontario primary health care (PC) has the potential to postpone or prevent many patients from requiring hospital services. To do this PC doctors or other PC health providers need to know which patients could benefit from care before they get too sick. Our research will develop tools to help identify patients with a high chance of future poor health and to help patients and doctors work together to decide what PC programs or treatments will help the patient stay healthy enough to avoid the hospital. These tools will be designed with and for the Association of Ontario Health Centres (AOHC), which has 107 PC facilities for 580,000 Ontarians. We will first build tools for Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) using the AOHC electronic medical record database, and will later expand to other diseases and PC organizations. Our tools will rely on predictive modelling, which is a method to estimate the chance, or risk, of developing an outcome (e.g. CKD or hospitalization) within a certain amount of time. We will develop novel two-part predictive models. The first part will be a statistical model that uses common risk factors, such as age, to predict the chance of developing the outcome. This is how most predictive models are built. While this method can work well for collective group-level predictions, it does not usually work well for telling whether an individual patient will develop the outcome. We propose using artificial intelligence (AI) to improve this ability. The second part of our model will apply AI techniques to find patients in the AOHC database that are similar to the patient for whom a prediction is desired, and then will use the outcomes of the most similar patients to adjust the prediction from the first part of the model. We will compare the performance of the novel two-part model to the more traditional one-part model. Overall, our research will contribute towards personalized tools to improve identification of patients in PC with a high chance of poor health.

column36: Supporting public health decision-making for Lyme disease: Assessing health outcomes, economic burden and intervention strategies using administrative data and decision-analytic models.
column37: Lyme disease (LD) is an increasingly common vector-borne disease reported in temperate climate zones in North America. The most common symptom of LD is erythema migrans (bull's-eye) rash. However, undetected or untreated LD can result in persistent functional, cardiac and neurological complications. In Ontario, LD incidence rates have increased 10-fold since 2006, with some areas reporting the highest rates in Canada (>21/100,000). Currently, consensus on the long-term outcomes and quality of life of LD patients is lacking. Additionally, the economic impact (healthcare costs) and the value of LD treatment and prevention strategies have not been assessed in Canada. For my first objective, I will conduct a systematic review focusing on long-term health outcomes, risk factors and quality of life associated with LD by assessing primary observational studies completed in North America and Europe. For my second objective, I will complete a costing study using health administrative data. I will use a population-based cohort study design to compare Ontario residents infected with laboratory-confirmed LD and uninfected individuals to determine the attributable healthcare costs of LD. Lastly, my third objective will provide economic evidence on the cost-effectiveness of current and potential LD treatment and prevention strategies (e.g. vaccination, personal protection, and antibiotic therapy) by assessing their cost per quality-adjusted life years gained from a healthcare payer perspective using a microsimulation model. Deeper understanding of long-term health outcomes can aid clinicians and patients with LD clinical management and educate the population at risk of LD. This work will also establish the value of potential LD intervention strategies and provide high-quality evidence to support health policy decision-making in Ontario.

column36: Physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modelling of antibody-based drugs in children: Model development and population applications
column37: Children need drug therapies for cancer and other serious diseases, just like adults. However, we cannot use the same drugs at the same doses to treat both adults and children. Children are not just little adults - simply giving a lower dose based on size will not suffice. They are physiologically immature and many of the processes that govern the distribution of drugs in their bodies are not fully developed. We must account for these age-dependent differences in physiology when deriving safe and effective doses. This is especially true for cancer drugs, when side effects can be fatal. I design math models that are based on real physiology to paint a picture of the ways that drugs move and interact throughout our bodies. These models can be used to simulate the impact of certain physiologic differences on drug concentrations in the blood. For most medications, safety is linked to drug concentrations in the blood; higher concentrations lead to more side effects and poorer safety. My models simulate drug concentrations in children and enable us to make predictions about which drugs and doses are safest to use. With a strong prediction in place, fewer clinical trials are needed to explore safety and fewer children are needed to determine the "right dose." I focus on the newest class of drugs called the "monoclonal antibodies." Antibodies are targeted missiles against tumours. Each antibody's mission is to seek and destroy one specific protein that is essential for tumour growth or survival. In my future work, I will be refining a model for antibodies and trying to identify the age-dependent features in children that cause them to process these drugs so uniquely. My goal is ensure the best use of cancer medicines in children. I will strive to make cancer treatment just a small chapter in a child's life, and not the whole story.

column36: Brain-Based Evidence for Exercise as a Treatment for Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Globally, Canada has the highest proportion of people living with multiple sclerosis (MS) - a life-long disorder that damages the brain. Because there is no cure for MS, and people are typically diagnosed in early adulthood, most people require treatment for the majority of their lives. Unfortunately, many continue to experience debilitating symptoms and side effects despite medications, which cost $20,000-$40,000 per person. As a result, there is a strong need for low cost behavioural treatments that help to reduce MS symptoms. So far, there is some evidence that exercise may improve thinking skills, mood, fatigue, and quality of life for people with MS. However, little is understood about how exercise might help protect the brain in order to improve these symptoms. Our study will look at the impact of a cost-free walking exercise intervention on brain structure (using an brain imaging technique called magnetic resonance imaging) and MS symptoms. Specifically, we will look at whether exercise changes the brain in people who have MS and how these brain changes relate to thinking skills, mood, fatigue, and quality of life. This is the first study of its kind. Demonstrating the effectiveness of a free, easy-to-access exercise intervention would have a significant impact in reducing the cost of care and improving the quality of life for people with MS. A better understanding of how exercise affects brain structure and MS symptoms will help doctors better treat MS symptoms. Our ultimate goal is to help people with MS build a better quality of life (with increased thinking skills, and reduced depression and fatigue) by protecting the brain from the degenerative effects of MS through exercise.

column36: New treatments of neurodegenerative diseases involving the cellular recycling machinery
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases are among the most serious health problems facing modern society. Many of these disorders become more common with advancing age, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and many others. The burden of these neurodegenerative diseases is growing inexorably as the population ages, with enormous economic and human costs. The need for new medicines is resounding, since current treatments are only able to help the cognitive and behavioral symptoms, to slow down the disease progression, but are not able to prevent nor cure. These diseases are characterized by the accumulation of toxic proteins naturally produced by our bodies. At the same time, as we age, our recycling machinery in each of our cells starts to be less active and less efficient. We think that increasing the recycling activity in our cells transiently with drugs could clear these proteins and restore all cognitive capacities. A mouse model of Alzheimer's disease has already shown that activating this process brought complete cure. However, our knowledge about how it happened and other potential targets is very limited. We are proposing to further investigate the molecular pathways involved in cellular recycling and explore potential therapeutic drugs in worm and mouse models of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Our preliminary data shows that some already approved drugs might be used for new purpose and have a positive impact for neurodegenerative diseases. Our work will provide new insights about the disease progression and might uncover new directions for new treatments. This project has the potential of significantly improve the outcomes of many neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Brain signal variability in chronic pain patients, and its relationship to clinical symptoms and treatment efficacy
column37: One in five Canadians suffer from chronic pain. Despite its overwhelming prevalence, current pain-management strategies are not effective, and very few chronic pain patients achieve full pain relief. It is known that the brain (which processes, relays, and modulates pain), and behaviours (such as how one copes with pain) both shape how how an individual experiences pain. Thus, it is likely that individual differences in these factors underlie the large variability in disease symptoms and management. Therefore, in order to understand why some patients respond well, while others show resistance to treatment, non-invasive brain imaging techniques (e.g. functional MRI) can be used to study functional brain mechanisms that underlie disease symptoms and treatment response. Therefore, my PhD project will use brain imaging measures, as well as behavioural measures, to investigate the brain features that contribute to disease symptoms and treatment outcome. By identifying pathological brain characteristics, and investigating their relationship with patients' clinical scores (e.g. reports of pain intensity/duration), pain-related behavioural measures and psychological traits, we can begin to understand the mechansims that are responsible for clinical impairments. This multifaceted approach can uncover brain and behaviour characteristics that underlie disease manifestations which may, in turn, serve as possible targets for novel intervention strategies as part of a personalized treatment approach.

column36: Whole Genome Sequencing to identify novel loci in French Canadian ALS patients
column37: Despite over a decade of gene discovery, the genetic causes of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (also known as Lou Gehrig's disease or ALS) are not fully understood. Examining the sequence of human genes has opened many avenues of clinical research, and several genes are now known to be mutated in patients with ALS. However, the discovery rate of ALS-associated genes has not kept pace with predictions, and it is necessary to increase the scale of genetic studies. Most research has only examined small portions of the genome to look for mutations that cause ALS. Our study will use whole-genome sequencing to investigate all the DNA within a patient. We propose to sequence the entire genome of 265 French-Canadian ALS patients to discover new disease-associated mutations. Because the disease is rare, and because mutations that cause the disease occur at very low frequencies in a population, we will employ recent statistical techniques that group mutations together to increase the power to detect associations. We will also be able to find regions of the genome that contain overly-repetitive or missing sections, which may alter the function of a gene and predispose one to develop ALS. The French-Canadian patient group we will study is ideal for genetic discovery in ALS because it contains a single ethnicity in few geographic regions. This study group will help to minimize errors such as inherently distinct genetic backgrounds across different ethnicities, and various predisposing environmental factors. The treatment and prevention of ALS will ultimately depend on a complete understanding of the processes and susceptibilities to the disease, and this understanding will start with the complete characterization of the genome when one has the disease. By knowing which mutations will result in ALS, we can try to predict the disease before it begins.

column36: Stomach Cancer Trends in the North American Arctic
column37: Problem: Stomach cancer is the fifth most commonly diagnosed cancer world-wide and the third most common causing death. While declining in Canada and the United States, the burden is not shared equally. Arctic and Indigenous populations have been shown to have elevated rates of stomach cancer but up-to-date rates across the Arctic and among Indigenous People in Canada are incompletely described and differences with national and non-Indigenous counterparts have not been thoroughly examined. This gap is a significant barrier to evidence-based decision making. Vision: There is an urgent need to examine stomach cancer trends in Canada's Arctic and among Indigenous Peoples in Canada to understand geographic patterns, identify potential causes and inform cancer control priorities. Using this data, we can reverse the evidence-deficit, eliminate disparities, and create a more inclusive and forward-looking evidence-based system for all Canadians. Aims: I plan to calculate and compare rates of new cases, mortality, and survival for stomach cancer among Arctic populations to southern provincial and national comparators, and Indigenous rates to non-Indigenous counterparts using data from population-based cancer registries. Significance: Despite a universal healthcare system in Canada, Arctic populations and Indigenous Peoples are at a disadvantage. Cancer-specific information is limited for Arctic and Indigenous populations and this gap is a significant barrier to evidence-based decision making. This is the first Pan-Arctic cancer-focused analysis. This project is supported by a network of Arctic Territorial and State, Provincial and Indigenous health authorities enabling a statistically and culturally meaningful examination of trends to address regional cancer control priorities and eliminate disparities. Further, this project has the potential to be applied to Arctic regions globally.

column36: Characterizing the Role of PLAGL2 in the Establishment of Pre-leukemia and Relapse
column37: Leukemia is a serious condition which affects approximately 22510 Canadians. Despite advances in research over the last few decades, incidence of new cases and mortality rates show no sign of decline. Recent studies have identified a new population of benign "preleukemic" cells (preLSC) in leukemia, which harbor some, but not all the genetic aberrations present in leukemic cells. These preLSCs have a selection advantage over healthy cells and resist chemotherapy, potentially seeding for both de novo leukemia and relapse. One of the ongoing projects at the Hope Lab has identified PLAG1 as a potent factor for the expansion of HSPCs ex vivo. However, its overexpression was also observed to exhibit some hallmark preleukemic features such as stem-maintenance and stress-resistance. While PLAG1 transcript is not significantly elevated in clinical datasets of leukemia, its functionally similar family member PLAGL2 is. We hypothesize that the elevation of PLAGL2 commonly observed in leukemia is able to enforce a stress-resistant phenotype within HSPCs to both facilitate the establishment of a preleukemic state and sensitize the cells to future leukemic transformation. I aim to evaluate the stress-resistant, pro-survival, chemoresistant phenotype of HSPCs overexpressing PLAGL2 in both in vitro cultures and murine xenografts. PLAGL2's influence on the transcriptome will also be analyzed to deduce possible effector pathways and establish a potential "preleukemic" signature. Finally, I will screen for drugs known to target key nodes of the effector pathways in hopes of rescuing preleukemic HSPCs and sensitize them to chemotherapeutic treatment. The establishment of a preleukemic gene signature could be lead to the early identification of at-risk patients and more accurate assessment of prognosis during remission. Meanwhile, the attenuation of the unique pathways identified could also allow for the targeted eradication of preleukemic cells, decreasing the opportunity for relapse.

column36: Scaling up the Family Carer Decision Support Intervention: A Transnational Effectiveness-Implementation Evaluation
column37: Dementia is increasing across the world. The effect of the disease on families, caregivers and communities is an important global public health challenge. Family carers of dementia patients often make end-of-life decisions for their family members. But, they do not know if these decisions are what their family member would want. Also, staff at care homes do not have the skills and information to speak with family members about end-of-life care decisions. Both of these experiences can put the person living with dementia at-risk for care that they would not want. This project will try to reduce the uncertainty towards end-of-life decision making. It will do this by using a tool called the Family Carer Decision Support (FCDS) intervention. The tool will tell family members about the options for end-of-life care for a person living with advanced dementia. This tool has been used in a study in Northern Ireland. In Northern Ireland, it helped families to make decisions about goals of care at the end-of-life. When this tool was used, family members were happier with the care given to their family member. The goal of this study is to use the tool in homes within different countries and determine if it is helpful for family members to make decisions. When the tool is used in different countries, it will encourage the use of the tool across the world. It will also encourage families to make end-of-life care decisions. This new information about the tool will also help set-up guidelines for the tool's use.

column36: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell dysfunction linked to schizophrenia: from mechanisms towards new therapeutic strategies (project coordinator: Dr. Maria Cecilia Angulo, project acronym: OPCphrenia)
column37: Schizophrenia is a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder affecting 0.5% of the world population. Symptoms include hallucinations, delusions as well as impaired cognition, attention and social interactions. The underlying brain pathology is abnormal function of a particular type of neuron, the fast-spiking inhibitory interneuron. Recent findings also implicate the abnormal integrity of myelin, a fatty substance that coats nerve cell projections and is essential for efficient neuronal signal propagation. Myelin is produced solely by oligodendrocytes, a non-neuronal cell type in the brain. Schizophrenia patient studies suggest myelination impairments could be a critical determinant of the disease. Yet, the mechanisms linking oligodendrocyte lineage cell dysfunction to schizophrenia are unknown. Our team has discovered unique properties of interneuron myelination and critical forms of communication between interneurons and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs). Given their intrinsic regenerative capacity as the cell type responsible for generating oligodendrocytes in the adult brain, OPCs represent a potential therapeutic target for enhancing the repair of myelin deficiencies in schizophrenia. Notably, we recently discovered that OPCs derived from genetically-identified familial schizophrenia patients have impaired function and defective myelination potential. Thus, we propose that schizophrenia is likely to be, at least in part, an OPC disease ("OPCphrenia"), arising from aberrant interneuron-OPC communication. In this proposal, we will dissect interneuron-OPC communication and investigate potential therapeutic rescue strategies for aberrant schizophrenia-related OPC dysfunction by re-balancing the levels of interneuron-secreted factors. We will leverage novel methodological advances, mouse genetics, and human patient samples to advance the understanding of schizophrenia pathophysiology and identify new molecular targets for future therapeutic intervention.

column36: Investigating how mechanosensitive neurons contribute to allodynia in neuropathic pain
column37: Millions of Canadians suffer from chronic pain that severely compromises their quality of life. One of the most debilitating symptoms is mechanical allodynia, wherein gentle touch is perceived to be extremely painful. The fact that current analgesics are not very effective at treating allodynia emphasizes the need for better understanding of how touch becomes painful. While perception of touch occurs in the brain, this perception depends on electrical signals coming from the periphery (usually skin). The skin in innervated by mechanosensitive neurons that have the ability to convert touch into electrical signals. My project will identify changes in how those electrical signals are generated under conditions associated with allodynia. To do this, I will record the electrical activity from mechanosensitive neurons while applying different stimuli to the skin. By making those neurons express a light-sensitive ion channel, I will compare touch and light stimulation. To link the changes in electrical activity to mechanical allodynia, I will then perform behavioural experiments to measure the pain response associated with these changes. Nerve-injured animals will be used as a model of chronic pain. This research will shed light on how neural coding by mechanosensitive neurons is disrupted in chronic pain and how this disruption leads to allodynia.

column36: Understanding Pain Mismanagement in Older Adults with Dementia
column37: The fastest-growing age group in Canada is that of older adults-those aged 65 or older. As individuals age, the likelihood of experiencing painful conditions and procedures increases, as does the likelihood of developing dementia. Despite the fact that pain is more common in older adults, it is often poorly managed in this group, especially among those with dementia. Pain diagnoses are commonly missed in older adults with dementia, and the pain that is diagnosed is often undertreated. This may be because individuals with dementia have difficulty communicating both verbally and nonverbally, or because those assessing their pain are making inaccurate judgments. Though the facial expression of pain in adults is stable and can be used as an alternative method of judging pain when verbal communication is compromised, this expression may change in dementia, possibly affecting communicative ability. In addition, people with negative attitudes about aging and dementia may be less accurate in judging older adults' pain. This study investigates how facial expressions of pain change in dementia, if these changes impair communication, and how observers' negative attitudes affect judgments of the pain of older adults. Initially, we will videotape facial expressions of pain during a physiotherapist assessment in older adults with and without dementia, and compare them to determine whether the facial expression of pain changes in dementia. Next, individuals with varying attitudes toward aging and dementia will rate the older adults' pain, to determine the extent to which negative attitudes about dementia and aging affect the accuracy of pain judgment. This study could improve pain treatment by improving communication and addressing bias in judgments of older adults with and without dementia. If we are able to understand why the pain of older adults is underestimated and undertreated, we can move toward implementing education and training programs to address the problem.

column36: Integrated Parkinson Care Networks: addressing complex care in Parkinson disease in contemporary society
column37: Parkinson disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that affects 80,000 Canadians and is expected to double by 2030 worldwide. Care needs are complex. The traditional model of care delivery centred in the physician has strains and limitations. Care Integration has the potential to improve patient quality of life by tailoring the care approach, facilitating the navigation of the patient and caregiver in the complex map of care resources available in the hospital and the community. Informed by the Ontario-developed Framework for Chronic Disease Prevention and Management, we have developed an Integrated Parkinson's disease Care Network in Canada with a significant attention to the participation of patient and care partners in the design of the proposed solutions. Following this model, we are now poised to develop it in other countries partnering with seven reference Parkinson's European centers. We will start by assessing 1) What are the views and needs of people with Parkinson's and care partners in a care delivery model based at home and the community, and 2) How can the implementation of a care delivery model based at home/community be successful in different social geographies and health-economical contexts. column36: Targeting TAO2 and its downstream pathway as critical effectors of Autism spectrum disorders in 16p11.2 microdeletion patients
column37: Atypical brain connectivity is a major contributor to the pathophysiology of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) including Autism spectrum disorders (ASD). TAO2 is one of several genes in the 16p11.2 microdeletion region susceptible to ASD, but whether it contributes to NDDs is unknown. Previously, we performed behavioral analysis on a Tao2 knockout (KO) mouse and found impairments in cognition, anxiety and social interaction. Tao2 KO mice have abnormal brain size and neural connectivity in multiple regions, deficits in dendrite and synapse formation, and reduced excitatory neurotransmission. Whole genome and exome sequencing of ASD families identified three de novo mutations in TAO2. Together, these data provide evidence that TAO2 is a neurodevelopmental disorder risk gene. Therefore, it is imperative to test whether TAOK2 and its downstream effectors are critical for ASD linked to the 16p11.2 microdeletion and whether activation of the TAOK2 pathway can overcome 16p11.2-associated abnormalities. Our proposal builds upon these observations to test the exciting hypothesis that TAO2 is a molecular hub in synapse function and ASD.

column36: Somatic DNA mosaicism of the ADNP gene in cells, ADNP-mouse tissues and tissues of a post-mortem ADNP individual: An indication of how this may affect disease.
column37: Autism, characterized by highly-variable qualitative impairments in social interaction and communication skills, is a poorly understood disorder. In this proposal, we will analyze a form of autism that is caused by mutations in a single gene called ADNP. The high frequency of clustered mutations of ADNP at the stem-loop forming sequence reveal this sequence is a mutation hotspot - somatic mutations of this may account for clinical variations in affected individuals. The potential to form an unusual DNA structure may predispose the sequence to an underlying mutation mechanism involving a DNA repair defect following pausing of a replication fork at these hairpin structures, or during aberrant repair in non-proliferating tissues. It is not known if these de novo mutations in the ADNP gene were incurred in the parental germ line and/or post-natally through the development and growth of the affected individual. The latter might be expected to display some degree of somatic mosaicism for the mutant allele. We developed a novel assay using the ultra-sensitive Digital Droplet PCR (dd-PCR) to assess, with high-sensitivity, the levels of ADNP mutation in DNA extracted from teeth, hair root cells (similar developmental origin as neurons) and ADNP patient-derived iPSCs of autistic offspring. The utility of this assay will permit the assessment of the potential contribution of somatic mutations of ADNP, and other genes, to autism. This could impact our ability to assess the clinical variability amongst affected individuals.

column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are a group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by deficits in social skills and communication, stereotyped and repetitive behavior, and a range of alterations in cognitive function. In addition we will harness the potential of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) to characterize CDH13 dysfunction in patient iPSC-derived cultured inhibitory neurons at the molecular and cellular level. Understanding circuit-specific alterations caused by CDH13 deficiency in mouse and human models may ultimately help us designing targeted treatment of specific ASD symptoms.

column37: The World Health Organization "Health for the world's adolescents" report revealed that depression is the predominant cause of illness and disability and among the top three causes of mortality for adolescent boys and girls. column36: Multi-scale exploration of autoantibodies against synaptic receptors
column37: Psychotic disorders (PDs) encompassing schizophrenia and bipolar disorders, are major health problems worldwide. Growing evidence suggest that these major psychoses have a neurodevelopmental component involving in particular synaptic imbalance mostly between glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurotransmitter systems. However, due to their complexity our understanding of PDs remains limited. It is well-established that several converging factors are involved in these complex PDs, among which immune status, including autoimmunity, are particularly relevant. A role for autoimmune dysfunction in PDs, reported in schizophrenia almost a century ago, is supported by specific autoimmune responses to selfantigens identified in particular in PD. The importance of autoimmunity in major psychosis has been strongly reinforced as a number of syndromes characterized by global encephalopathy and by more focal psychiatric symptoms was found to result from autoimmune dysfunction, caused by anti-neuronal antibodies that alter synaptic transmission, such as NMDARAb in encephalitis. Thus, the role of the autoimmunity against neuronal receptor targets in the pathogenesis of PDs has gained tremendous support over the last years and urgently requires multidisciplinary in-depth investigations to unravel the molecular mechanisms underlying psychosis and offer new therapeutic strategies. We identified that almost 20% of patients diagnosed with schizophrenia are seropositive for these autoantibodies, opening therapeutical options for these patients. Here, we plan to tackle such a major challenge in a unique, complementary and synergistic consortium of clinical and basic research experts, who strongly contributed to our current understanding of autoimmunity in brain disorders. Our objective is to uncover how NMDAR-Ab underliesPDs in seropositive NMDAR-Ab patients, using a unique and multi-scale combination of experimental approaches, from pre-clinical experiments to clinical exploration.

column36: A novel paradigm for effective and safer treatment of schizophrenia: biased (ant)agonists with a characterized polypharmacological profile
column37: Schizophrenia (SZ) is a severe disease affecting 1-2% of the population. Current treatment is associated to side effects such as motor coordination problems, a feeling of the mind slowing down, abnormal electrical activity in the brain, altered heart rhythm, among many others. In addition, a high percentage of patients do not respond (30%) or only partially (additional 30%) to treatment. There is therefore a real need for developing better drugs. The drugs currently used to treat SZ are antipsychotics that act primarily through receptors that belong to a large family of proteins, the G protein-coupled receptors. They are present at the surface of neurons where they recognize and transduce the information of neurotransmitters. One of the main target of antipsychotic drugs is a receptor binding serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood control. However, these drugs are not fully selective and they also act on closely related receptors, the monoamine receptors, resulting in a polypharmacological profile. However, the relative contribution of each receptor to the beneficial and undesired effects is poorly understood. Moreover, each of these receptors control multiple cellular signaling cascades that are differentially regulated by distinct drugs. This phenomenon of 'biased signalling' is an important aspect of drug action. We therefore propose to develop chemical probes with defined biased and polypharmacology profiles to interrogate which signalling activities are responsible for alleviating the different SZ symptoms and which ones underlie the various side effects. For this purpose, we assembled an international team of experts with complementary know-how in computational and medicinal chemistry, molecular pharmacology and cell signalling as well as animal model of SZ. In addition to provide highly original insights into the mode of action of antipsychotics, these studies should open the way to the design of better and safer therapeutics for the treatment of SZ.

column37: ALS is the most common motor neuron disease. It is characterized by the death of motor neurons (MNs) in the brain and spinal cord. The disease starts in adult life and causes a progressive paralysis that is typically fatal within a few years, usually due to respiratory failure. The number of ALS cases worldwide is predicted to increase to nearly 400,000 in 2040, largely due to the aging population. Yet, no effective therapy is currently available for ALS. The current lack of treatments that can halt or reverse ALS highlights the need for disease relevant human cell-based experimental model systems to study the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the degeneration of motor circuits in ALS. In this regard, the present application seeks to develop and validate previously unavailable experimental model systems to study ALS pathophysiology based on both neuronal and glial cells derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) obtained from ALS patients or non-ALS controls. This project involves academic partners with solid expertise in ALS, iPSC technology and high-throughput ("omics") approaches. This unique combined international discovery effort will allow the assessment of the roles played by energy metabolism and immune pathways in ALS pathogenesis and their potential as therapeutic targets. Achieving these objectives will lead to new advances into the study of ALS pathophysiology and will contribute to the emerging field of ALS disease modeling based on disease-relevant human iPSC-derived cells. These are both important and timely goals of ALS research.

column37: The main aim of this project is to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying a rare form of progressive motor impairment, called dystonia, associated with mutations in the RARb gene. We have already shown that mutations found in the patients with dystonia enhance the activity of RARb in response to retinoic acid in cultured cells. We hypothesize that this increased activity of RARb disrupts the development or the function of a specific region of the brain, called the striatum, which is involved in the control of movements. Using a mouse model of this disease and patient-derived brain cells, we will investigate molecular alterations resulting from the most common mutant form of RARb with the goal of better understanding the mechanisms of the disease and developing rational treatments. The information generated in this project will allow us to build an integrated knowledge database that will provide a comprehensive blueprint of the retinoic acid receptor network function and dysfunction.

column37: Mature T-cell leukemias/lymphomas (MaTCL) are hematologic malignancies of mostly incurable prospects in light of limited efficient therapies. As a heterogeneous group of tumors, single MaTCL types are rare, which impedes large-volume biomaterial and data collections and clinical studies. Hyperactivating somatic mutations in JAK/STAT genes stand out as high-incidence aberrations across MaTCL entities. Particularly the model diseases investigated here, T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) and T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-LGLL), carry those in 50-70% of cases. This interdisciplinary JAKSTAT-TARGET consortium of immunologists, hematologists, structural chemists, and systems biologists capitalizes on unique resources such as clinical registry-linked sample repositories, new high-fidelity mouse models, pipelines of structure-based target design, and in-silico machine learning tools. We propose that targeting the JAK/STAT signalling network in synergistic combinations with drugs inhibiting inter-connected other key driver pathways will improve individualized anti-leukemic efficacy. We will achieve this by three objectives (O): O1 will address the causal T-cell-receptor and cytokine mediated impact on genome integrity and on the occurrence of JAK/STAT mutations. It interrogates the biochemical and functional consequences of the mutated and unmutated clones, and derives actionable differential vulnerabilities. O2 will study the performance of identified synergistic drug combinations using in-house developed optimized STAT-inhibitors in novel animal models and primary samples. O3 will implement drug-screen data from patient material into an ongoing clinical trial. Ultimately, with machine-learning algorithms we will integrate the harmonized data of genomic profiles, drug-sensitivity patterns, and clinical outcomes from all objectives toward multi-omics guided predictions of optimal choices for trial designs and individual-patient based therapy selection.

column36: Violence against women migrants and refugees: Analysing causes and effective policy response
column37: Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) is a major infringement of women's human rights, and an obstacle to sustainable development as set out in the SDGs. SGBV against migrant and refugee women is widespread, but often remains invisible and under-analysed both in academic research and policy-making. This research will take an intersectional approach to understand SGBV in the context of migration, analysing the ways in which discriminations and inequalities based on gender, race, nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity and age, interact to make certain women more vulnerable to SGBV and less able to access support and services for survivors than others. SGBV may be exacerbated by policies aiming to restrict migration, or to increase control of borders, which can push women into adopting dangerous routes to arrive in their country of destination. Conflict and the risks of migration may also render women vulnerable to trafficking and sexual exploitation. Conditions of reception, and policies for integration in receiving countries may also lead to increased risk of SGBV for migrant and refugee women. But these women are not just "victims", and their strategies and agency should also be explored. In sum while we know that female migrants and refugees are particularly exposed to violence we lack a systematic understanding of the underlying dynamics that (re)produce patterns of violence. It is this gap that the research seeks to fill in order to make policy recommendations for reducing these women's vulnerability to SGBV and increasing their access to services.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibres in the wall of arteries. Atherosclerotic plaques develop slowly over time. They gradually encroach onto the interior of blood vessels, and only become symptomatic when a blood vessel is obstructed by 70% or more. A more serious situation arises when the atherosclerotic plaque ruptures suddenly. This happens because the contents of the plaque include fatty deposits that provide poor resistance to daily wear and tear. If a large fatty deposit is accompanied by a thin cap (the cap forms a protective fibrous layer between the atherosclerotic plaque and the interior of the blood vessel), the risk of rupture is enhanced. When a rupture occurs, the contents of the atherosclerotic plaque are exposed to the blood flowing in the vessel, leading to the formation of a blood clot within the vessel. This may completely and suddenly block the vessel, causing heart attack or stroke. Our proposed research will investigate a new treatment option that would reinforce the plaque cap, rendering plaques less susceptible to rupture, based on molecules that influence protein synthesis within cells.

column36: MicroRNA-145 as a key regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation and CNS myelination
column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the insulation around the nerves, known as myelin, is damaged by the immune system, resulting in loss of muscle control and partial paralysis. The cell type that produces the myelin sheath around the nerve fibers is called the oligodendrocyte. This cell has to undergo morphological changes prior to being able to wrap around the nerve fibers. Our research is directed towards understanding the factors that regulate the steps leading to the morphological changes. We believe that the orchestration of gene networks, rather than single genes, are critical to the progression of oligodendrocytes to becoming myelin-producing factories. We are studying the impact of manipulating specific molecules called microRNAs that have the ability to regulate a specific set of genes implicated in this progression. This is an important step towards the development of better treatments for disorders in which this process is aberrant, such as in MS.

column36: Role, function, and regulation of the delta opioid receptor and its implications for the treatment of pain
column37: Despite the existence of a multitude of drugs with analgesic properties, the treatment of pain often remains problematic. Notwithstanding significant side effects (constipation, nausea, sedation), alkaloid compounds remain the most effective drugs to relieve chronic pain. The best known of all alkaloids undoubtedly remains morphine, belonging to the family of opiates. Morphine and its derivatives bind and activate at least three subtypes of G protein-coupled receptors, the mu (MOP), delta (DOP) and kappa (KOP) opioid receptors. Although these three receptor subtypes possess analgesic properties, the actions of the majority of opioids used clinically target MOP. In contrast to the latter, activation of DOP leads to few unwanted effects. Under normal conditions (i.e. in healthy animals), the analgesic potency of delta selective agonists is lower than that of morphine. In recent years, however, it has been shown that under certain conditions, the activation of DOP can counter the painful sensations with an efficacy close to morphine. In my laboratory we are interested in studying the mechanisms regulating the trafficking of DOP toward the plasma membrane of nociceptive neurons under conditions of chronic pain. A better understanding of these mechanisms could help develop strategies to increase the effectiveness of pain therapies and thus improve the quality of life of patients.

column36: Scaling up the Community Health Assessment Program in the Philippines (CHAP-P).
column37: The Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program (CHAP) is a community-based, volunteer-led cardiovascular risk assessment and blood pressure monitoring program with health education/promotion sessions for older adults living in the communities. CHAP was tested in Canada and has produced consistent results of improving cardiovascular outcomes. The Community Health Assessment Program in the Philippines (CHAP-P) is an adaptation of CHAP to low and middle income countries (LMICs), integrating diabetes risk assessment. Through consultations, some research studies, with the inclusion of Philippine and international stakeholders, the CHAP-P intervention was demonstrated to be acceptable and feasible to the setting. This current study aims to determine scale-up processes for implementing an expanded CHAP-P intervention one Region in the Philippines. Previous work focused in a few towns in selected municipalities of the Zamboanga Peninsula Region, Philippines. This scale-up aims to spread across the entire Region, a population of 3.6 million. This region is similar to the setting of other LMIC that has isolated areas, poor roads, several ethnic and linguistic groups, and scarce health resources. The scale-up process will include a team of partners and collaborators from the Philippines and other countries including lay volunteer health workers, researchers, health professionals, public health officials, and politicians. We will conduct several meetings to present CHAP-P; discuss the needs to prepare for its implementation including preparing materials and equipments, personnel training, and cost-sharing; and set-up ways to monitor and evaluate CHAP-P so that the community residents can benefit from the program more. We will document how CHAP-P was scaled up, identify barriers in the process and solutions to overcome them, and produce a guideline on how to scale-up CHAP-P so that other Regions in the Philippines and other countries can use what we learned in this process.

column36: Exercise as a countermeasure for inflammation processes and loss in neuromotor drive following muscle disuse: the SAFE randomized controlled trial.
column37: As evidenced in astronauts returning from a space camp mission, muscle disuse occurs in elderly and frail individuals through the same mechanisms. As the actual scientific research era hinges on patient-centered outcomes, it is equally important to develop tools that are scientifically reliable and of interest and at the patient's benefit. As muscle disuse leads to deleterious and unwanted consequences, there is a momentum to develop countermeasures to initiate prevention. As such, although exercise was proposed as a very efficient strategy to offset the impact of inactivity in those patients, reliable tools to manage its regimen and to evaluate its efficiency are still expected. The SAFE trial focuses on important surrogate outcomes of muscle wasting and loss of function. Eligible healthy participants, aged 55-65 years old, will randomly be allocated to the control (physiotherapy + psychological support) or intervention (physiotherapy + psychological support + 60 min of exercise/day) arms of the study. Trial will be conducted in the context of a bed rest laboratory, where participants will be lying down in bed on a 24/7 regimen during 14 days. Using pragmatic samples (blood and muscle biopsies), to facilitate the future implementation in the clinic, inflammation markers and neuromuscular activity and function will be assessed. Participants will be assessed at 7 days, 4 weeks and 4 months post-intervention. Conclusive evidence that the proposed markers and sophisticated measures accurately monitor neuromuscular changes would certainly change the management of these patients by physicians and therapists during space flight or in context of frailty. The success of the SAFE trial will be secured through the collaboration of a multidisciplary team composed of trainees, young, mid-career and senior researchers with expertise in aging, exercise and muscle function and biostatistics.

column36: Addiction, Health Risks and Recovery in Context of Social Precarity: How to Better Address Complex Needs Taking into Account Gender and Life Stages
column37: Vulnerable populations that experience social precarity tend to have a chronic SUD and require long-term services that are adapted to their complex care needs. The general aim of this transnational Canadian, French and Belgian study is to better understand how gender and life stages influence addiction, health risks, and recovery trajectories in order to guide the development of integrated services that address complex social and health care needs. The three specific objectives of the project take into account gender and life stages issues in order to: 1) identify specific vulnerabilities and capacities in people with SUD who experience social precarity over a lifelong trajectory of PS use and related risk behaviors; 2) understand long-term service and recovery trajectories related to SUD and health risks within this population; and 3) guide the development of long-term integrated services that better address the complex social and health needs of this population. In order to pursue these objectives, we propose to combine the following methods: semi-structured interviews on PS use, health-risk and recovery trajectories (n=270, 90 per country); a systematic literature review; and consensus development conferences with expert panels (PS users, clinicians, various key stakeholders) who have an interest in the services offered to PS users (n=3 groups of 12-15 participants, one per country). Examination of the distinct contexts related to PS use, health risks, and services in France, Belgium, and Canada will help to develop contextualized knowledge that can enhance life-stage-responsive and gender-responsive services locally and internationally, taking into account the needs of specific populations.

column36: Targeting potassium channel to disrupt the cellular hierarchy and suppress malignant growth of pediatric brain tumor
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The conventional treatment, which combines surgery, irradiation and chemotherapy, is toxic to normal brain cells and produces life-long side effects such as lowered intelligence, early aging, and increased chance to develop other cancer. Therefore, identifying the molecules that fuel aggressive MB growth but are dispensable for normal cells is key to develop cancer-specific therapy. Ions, such as potassium and chloride, are essential constituents of human cell. Ion channel proteins form tiny pores to control ion to move in or out of cell. The movement of ions can change the electrical and physical properties of the cells, which control biological processes including tumor growth. We recently found that potassium channel Eag2 is required for MB growth, discovered a drug as a novel Eag2 blocker, and showed that the drug had marked anti-MB efficacy in mice and a MB patient. Therefore, we pioneer in identifying ion channels as novel regulators for MB and developing ion channel-targeting therapy. Brain tumor-initiating cells (BTICs) are rare cells that generate multiple tumor cell types to fuel the malignant brain tumor growth. Since BTICs are insensitive to irradiation and conventional chemotherapy, they are the roots for tumor initiation and recurrence. While Eag2 regulates the growth of non-BTICs, our unpublished study identified that potassium channel Kcnb2 is present in MB BTICs. We discovered that genetic deletion of Kcnb2 reduced the number of BTICs and suppressed MB growth, but it did not overtly alter the normal development of mice. We propose to define the mechanism by which Kcnb2 regulates BTICs and MB growth, and determine the therapeutic efficacy of combining Kcnb2 inhibition and conventional therapy. By completing our studies, we will uncover the unrealized potential of targeting ion channels to treat brain cancer by attacking the root of brain tumor growth and recurrence.

column36: Building a foundation for an economic business case for models of care for patients with Inflammatory Arthritis in Canada
column37: With the aging of the population, the prevalence of chronic diseases has increased drastically. Today, about 1 million Canadians live with Inflammatory Arthritis (IA), a group of chronic diseases that lead to irreversible joint damage, pain, profound disability, and increased mortality. Patients with chronic diseases, such as IA, require care from multiple types of providers in a variety of healthcare settings and education on managing the disease over their lifetime. However, traditional healthcare systems, which were designed to provide care for acute conditions, are challenged to deliver high-quality chronic care. Thus, alternative models of care focused on chronic disease management are being currently sought. Models of care represent strategies that outline the optimal manner of care delivery for patients with a specific chronic disease, for instance, IA. These models aim to improve care delivery in order to provide the right, safe, and effective care to the right patient at the right time. Several exemplars of successful models of care for patients with IA exist in Canada, however, they are not a common practice. Costs of implementation of new models and long-term investments required to support them, such as support staff and infrastructure, represent one of the main barriers to a broader implementation of models of care for patients with IA. The proposed project aims to explore the characteristics of examples of models of care for patients with IA in Canada and to assess the associated quality of care and costs in order to identify the factors that contribute to a successful model of care in the Canadian environment. Findings of this project will be used to build an economic business case for models of care for patients with IA, which will show the value of these models to health authorities in order to facilitate a broader implementation and sustainability of such models in Canada and, consequently, improve quality of care for Canadians living with IA.

column36: Measuring the need and supply of mental health and addiction services in Canada
column37: Each year approximately 25% of Canadians experience difficulties with mental health or addiction disorders, for example depressive disorders or anxiety disorders. These disorders can result in changes to one's mood, thinking, and/or behaviour which cause difficulties on a day-to-day basis. Those who receive treatment through therapy and/or medication for mental health or addictions disorders are often able to recover from these disorders, however, services are not necessarily offered consistently throughout Canada. My proposed project will be conducted in partnership with the Canadian Institute of Health Information (CIHI), a not-for-profit organization which collects data from each province and territory to provide actionable information on its priority populations, including recipients of mental health and addictions services. My proposed project will inform the measurement of need and supply of mental health and addiction services within Canada. First, I will review current approaches to measure need of mental health and addiction services, noting their strengths and limitations. Next, I will use data from CIHI that includes information about the mental health and addictions workforce in Canada, including data about psychologists that provide therapy in hospitals and the community. Finally, I will work with psychologists to consider the role that they have in providing mental health and addiction services and compare this to what would be expected based on best practices. This project will improve our understanding of the gap between need and supply of mental health and addictions services which will inform policy and health system planning, and will support CIHI's ultimate goal of improving the health of Canadians. The results from these projects will be freely available online through a published report.

column36: Common Assessments for Repeated Paramedic Encounters: Evaluating Care Planning in Community Paramedicine
column37: Patients voice frustration about repeatedly telling their health story to multiple care providers. This happens, in part, because different care providers assess patients differently and may not adequately share the information they discover with other care providers. Following a common assessment approach can reduce this inefficiency and improve patient care. Common assessments have been implemented by multiple health care sectors in Canada. Recently, an assessment instrument that followed common assessment processes to parallel sectors of health care was developed for use in community paramedicine home visit programs. This research seeks to address the quality of this assessment instrument in terms of its ability to measure changes in patient condition over time, whether paramedics find it useful, whether it can predict outcomes or adverse events, and whether it improves coordination of information between providers. As a result, community paramedicine programs that provide scheduled visits to improve access to care will capture the appropriate information needed to facilitate coordinated care and redirect patients from accessing this care from emergency departments.

column36: Efficient Disaster Response and Integration of Health Services: Review and Recommendations for the Canadian Red Cross
column37: The Canadian Red Cross (CRC) works to improve health systems in war zones and natural disasters by providing emergency services and basic health care. The CRC is a global leader in providing healthcare to women and children in these areas. Mobile Health Units (MHUs) in Afghanistan, supported by the CRC, provide services in war zones where no other healthcare agency can go. The CRC collected data for its mission in Afghanistan through the number of MHUs in the field, the types of healthcare services provided and people involved in the delivery of these services. Another example of CRC's global presence is through supporting the Integrated Recovery Programme (IRP) focused on the health of women and children, after severe flooding in the northern areas of Pakistan in 2010. Over one thousand people were surveyed before and after the delivery of the IRP in flood-affected areas in Pakistan. Data was also collected through focus group discussions and interviews with community members and program managers. The programs in Afghanistan and Pakistan, both majority Muslim countries, with cultural and religious similarities had a unique set of challenges to the delivery of MHUs and IRP in these countries. An important barrier to accessing healthcare in these two countries was the availability of female health workers and their role in the delivery of services in the specific social and cultural context. This project will review IRP and MHU programs in Pakistan and Afghanistan to understand the extent to which of female healthcare workers can affect the delivery of health services in these countries. The review aims to provide CRC with recommendations to improve its disaster response by empowering women to get involved in the delivery of health services.

column36: Developing a health services strategy and framework for equitable primary care services for the Ontario spinal cord injury population, using visual analytics
column37: A principal aim of most health services research is gaining a better understanding of barriers to equitable care. This can be achieved by applying visual analytics to available health administrative databases. Traditional data analysis is limited due to human vulnerability to information overload. Visual analytics builds upon traditional statistical analysis by promoting understanding of data with effective visual and interactive techniques. Being interactive gives decision makers the ability to drill down data from different aspects revealing meaningful representations, that can be used for evidence-informed decision making. Visual analytics is a fast growing discipline, e.g. the Alberta Health Services' live dashboards on health services' use. This proposal is aimed at developing a strategy and framework for studying access to primary care services for persons with spinal cord injury living in Ontario. The strategy will include research questions, perspectives, and priority indicators related to access. The framework will focus on databases, operational definitions and methods. column36: Implementing and Evaluating the Effects of Standardized Electronic Health Records on Learning Health Systems and Patient Experience in Canada
column37: The prevalence of multiple chronic conditions among adults, and increasingly children, has been on the rise in Canada. Patients with multiple comorbidities are seen frequently by various health professionals and in different health care settings (e.g., hospitals, outpatient settings, emergency rooms). Most clinical settings have adopted Electronic Health Records (EHRs) for recording patient data. However, EHRs are not standardized and health information sharing among health care settings is lacking. This results in inefficiencies, including duplication of testing and data entry and lack of medication reconciliation, resulting in suboptimal patient care. Also, EHR data are not being appropriately used to inform how health systems can be improved by capturing patient data and outcomes longitudinally through a centralized digital record. There is thus a critical need to standardize EHRs to improve patient experience and create Learning Health Systems (LHS). A LHS is a health system that seeks to constantly improve performance by analyzing EHR data and applying findings to improve operational processes. This project seeks to 1) assess the different types of clinical forms (e.g., assessment, discharge, progress notes) used by health professionals to collect patients' health information in various health care settings, 2) evaluate the use of paper-based clinical forms and digital forms in EHRs by gathering health professionals' perspectives, 3) use machine learning to identify commonalities between these forms which will inform the standardization of EHRs, and 4) apply machine learning techniques to data collected through standardized EHRs to understand drivers of patient behaviours. The proposed work will allow for health professionals to intervene before undesirable patient outcomes occur, which includes hospital readmissions and adverse drug events. There is also a possibility to scale this standardization solution to other provinces and territories.

column36: Harnessing the power of technology to better assess pain in long-term care
column37: Among older persons living in long-term care homes, pain continues to be underassessed. Staff frequently report a lack of time as the reason why they are unable to assess residents' pain on a regular basis. Technology, however, may be able to provide a solution to this problem. Cameras placed in long-term care homes will send information to a computer. If a threshold for pain behaviours is crossed, a secure email will be sent to nursing staff and a light at the nursing station would flash to indicate that an email was sent. Even though technologies of this kind are being developed, the successful implementation of such technologies is not guaranteed. In fact, there are factors that may influence someone's intention to use such a technology. We propose to uncover these factors and find ways to facilitate the use of technologies that are likely to benefit older Canadians living in long-term care homes. To reach this objective, we will use data from questionnaires, interviews, and focus groups to engage with the many different people involved: policymakers, administrators, front-line staff, family members, residents. Using this data, we will develop guidelines to facilitate the use of technologies to provide care for older adults. These guidelines will be presented in the form of a booklet that can be distributed to relevant policymakers. Educational sessions about the computer vision system will be developed for those who are involved in the care of these long-term care residents. Workshops will be tailored for each of these groups to meet their needs. This workshop will aim to increase our likelihood of successfully implementing the previously mentioned computer vision system in at least two long-term care facilities in Saskatchewan.

column36: Use of emergency health services (EHS) for transporting stroke patients: what is known about when to seek emergency care and how transport decisions impact in-hospital care
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability in Canada. Scientists have observed that people who suffer a stroke and are transported to the hospital by ambulance have lower rates of death and better outcomes. Because of this campaigns, like the Face Arms Speech Time (F.A.S.T) program, have been created to increase public awareness of stroke symptoms and what to do in the event of a stroke. Still we know many people have a stroke and do not use an ambulance to get to hospital. Instead they choose to wait for symptoms to go away, drive themselves, or get others to drive them. It is unclear how mode of arrival, especially outside a large metropolitan city, affects one's hospital medical care. This represents an important gap in current knowledge because we do not fully understand factors or effects associated with calling an ambulance in the event of a stroke, specifically in smaller urban or rural areas. The purpose of this study is to understand why (or why not) people call an ambulance when they or someone in their care is having a stroke and how calling an ambulance affects medical care they receive in hospital. To answer these questions, we propose to quantitatively examine a dataset of stroke patients (19,000 cases) to determine differences in ambulance usage across British Columbia. In a smaller subset of the sample (700 cases), we will determine if mode of arrival affects time to seeing a healthcare professional and treatment including brain scan. To understand the decision-making process, we will qualitatively study stroke patients by interviewing a sample of 25 persons who called an ambulance and 25 who did not. The results of this study will be important for people at risk for stroke, their caregivers, and the general public to understand why it is important to call an ambulance when a stroke is happening. This research is also important for health organizations who can use information from this work to refine services and public awareness campaigns.

This work will help answer key questions about expanding CCT in Nova Scotia, and help the government arrive at the best solutions for "the here and now." column36: Unitization: a strategy to circumvent memory deficits in aging and amnesia.
column37: Memory is the repository of our personal histories and stored knowledge, and it is essential to planning our futures and maintaining a sense of self. By 2036, almost a quarter of Canadians will be aged 65 and older, and many will experience memory decline. As memory declines, other cognitive functions are affected, as are daily activities. To support our aging population we must develop simple, cost-effective cognitive strategies to alleviate age-related memory declines. We recently discovered that a cognitive strategy, unitization, supports memory function in older adults and even in cases of amnesia who have severe impairments in memory. Through unitization, information about multiple items is represented as a single unit through an interaction between new and existing knowledge. In order to ultimately use unitization more widely to improve cognition in memory-impaired individuals, we must first understand what level of cognitive and neural function is needed for the strategy to be successfully used. We will use neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies to examine the cognitive functions and brain regions that correlate with the successful use of unitization. This will allow us to predict which people would be most likely to benefit from unitization. Additionally, we will examine if unitization can support inference, a cognitive function that relies on memory. The ability to infer information beyond what is directly observed is essential to daily living, as it plays a role in problem solving and in guiding behavior in social interactions. Successful use of unitization to alleviate impairments in inference will show how unitization has broad potential to support declining cognition, allowing older adults to maintain their independence and quality of life for longer.

column36: Identifying priorities and actions for creating healthy built environments in Ontario
column37: The mission of Public Health Ontario (PHO), the host organization, is to enable informed decisions and actions that protect and promote health and contribute to reducing health inequities. This includes the expectation for public health units (PHUs) to promote the creation of healthy built environments (HBE) through the establishment of key partnerships and healthy public policy. column37: Le systeme de sante au Quebec, fait face au defi des soins pour une population vieillissante, soufrant souvent de plusieurs maladies chroniques a l'origine de besoins de plus en plus complexes. column36: Working with Canadian and global Indigenous, excluded and underserved populations to strengthen health systems' response to non-communicable disease inequities
column37: This Health System Impact Fellowship application for Dr. Farah Mawani, hosted by Dignitas International (health system organization) and School of Public Health, University of Alberta (academic institution), focuses on the growing Canadian and global challenge of non-communicable disease (NCD) inequities between and within countries. Worldwide, non-communicable diseases (mainly cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases, diabetes, and mental illnesses) account for 70% (39.5 million) of global deaths, and a growing burden of disease. Dr. Mawani will lead, in partnership with Indigenous, Canadian, and global health policymakers, researchers and civil society members, a program of work that will strengthen Canadian and international NCD surveillance systems so that they illuminate, rather than mask, NCD inequities within and across populations in Canada and globally. Dr. Mawani will lead a team in creating, sharing, applying, and evaluating knowledge sharing plans for a minimum set of NCD equity indicators; and a process for including Indigenous, excluded, and underserved populations in developing NCD surveillance systems. She will focus on Indigenous communities, and immigrants/refugees in Ontario, Alberta and at the national level in Canada, and share learning to enable impact beyond those communities. This is a vital step to reducing NCD inequities, and improving NCD outcomes of Indigenous, excluded, and underserved populations. Through this clear focus, Dr. Mawani will further develop professional skills including leadership, mentorship, collaboration, communication, knowledge sharing, negotiation, and change management to enable her to have greater impact on transforming health systems.

column36: Leveraging data to improve obstetrical safety in Canada: a formative evaluation.
column37: Health care services provided during pregnancy, labour, birth and the time after birth period can influence the long-term health of women and infants. There is wide variability in clinical practice and outcomes in maternal-newborn care settings suggesting there are opportunities for improvement. While the quality of obstetrical care in Canada is generally high, adverse events in patient safety continue to occur. With over 140,000 babies born in Ontario each year there are many opportunities to address patient safety issues and associated costs at individual and system level. BORN is Ontario's pregnancy, birth and childhood registry and network. Our aim is to create an online system based on patient safety indicators that will reduce the number of negative outcomes for obstetric patients in Ontario and potentially throughout Canada. This project will include the identification of indicators using research evidence and expert consensus methods. We will create a review of the evidence for one safety indicator and explore options for the design of the online system. The purpose of this research is to develop an online system that can be piloted and and ultimately implemented in Ontario and Canada, to reduce poor outcomes for maternity services patients that were avoidable through optimal care.

column36: Evidence-Based Strategic Directions to Reduce Emergency Department Patient Wait Times within the Hamilton Niagara Haldimand Brant Local Health Integration Network (HNHB LHIN)
column37: Increasing emergency department (ED) patient wait times represent a substantial challenge for health care systems in numerous jurisdictions. In the province of Ontario, there were 5.8 million ED visits in fiscal year 2016-17, a 1% increase over the volume in 2015-16. However, over the same time period, the ED wait times increased by 11% for admitted patients. Over the past few months, substantially high lengths of stay times in Ontario EDs have garnered significant media attention. Longer ED wait times are related to a greater risk of adverse patient outcomes, increased rates of patients leaving without being seen, patient dissatisfaction, ambulance offload delays, and higher levels of stress among ED health professionals. The available research indicates that ED wait times are influenced by factors at three levels: individual patient, hospital institution, and system features. In 2016-17, the HNHB LHIN had the fifth highest ED volumes at 572,770 and the highest ambulance volumes at 116,492 in the province, as well as the worst ED wait times among all 14 LHINs. This project will use a mixed research methods approach to undertake an in-depth analysis of the ED wait time situation within the HNHB LHIN in comparison to five LHINs located in southern Ontario. The findings from the quantitative and qualitative data analyses will be assessed to identify the input and output factors affecting patient throughput and increased ED wait times in the HNHB LHIN in comparison to other LHINs. These factors will be assessed in the context of the Institute of Medicine's aims for the improvement of health care. Based on this, evidence-based strategic recommendations on potential opportunities for alleviating ED pressures will be made to the HNHB LHIN.
