column36: Strengthening health system support of caregivers' readiness for engagement in autism care
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is estimated to affect 1 in 66 children, or roughly 350,000 people, in Canada. The impact is far greater when one considers the complex needs of families affected by ASD. Autism Ontario is a non-profit organization whose goal is to strengthen support for caregivers and families of children with ASD, and it works with government to understand the needs and find solutions. More and more, parents or caregivers of children with ASD are being asked to play a role in their child's intervention services and care. While research shows such involvement can be useful, the extra demands can be difficult for some caregivers for a variety of reasons. Health, education and other systems of care need a way to better understand, measure, and support parents' readiness to meet demands of engaging in care. With the right knowledge and measurement tools, such systems can tailor and adjust how they involve caregivers to be more sensitive to their unique needs and strengths. This will prepare such systems to better support family health at a critical time, promoting better outcomes. The proposed fellowship project is a partnership with Autism Ontario, and has two aims. First, the research fellow will conduct a review the literature using systematic methods to summarize what is known about the factors influencing parent involvement in their child's care. Second, the fellow will develop a new measure of parents' readiness and ability to meet these demands for involvement. Information for developing this measure will come from the literature review and from interviewing people on both sides-parents of children with ASD, and professionals that provide ASD services. The measure will then be tested to ensure it works well in a clinical setting. When ready, it will be made available, free of charge, for care providers across Canada to monitor and improve service delivery to families of children with ASD.

Ultimement, permettre au SSSS de garder le leadership necessaire qui fera de lui un acteur strategique ayant des leviers d'action necessaires pour assurer une meilleure gouvernance des innovations afin que celles-ci puissent servir a la population de maniere equitable. column36: Indigenizing harm reduction: Identifying barriers to Western systems and supporting community-driven approaches to reduce opioid-related mortalities among Indigenous people who use drugs in British Columbia
column37: As the opioid crisis in Canada continues, British Columbia is undoubtedly the epicentre with over 1,400 fatal overdoses in 2017. Government statistics indicate that First Nations people are five times more likely to die of an overdose than non-First Nations people in BC, and that this difference is greater for First Nations women and youth compared to non-First Nations women and youth. Despite an array of harm reduction and addiction treatment services in BC, First Nations people encounter several barriers to accessing and completing care and services including, racism and stigma, lack of service availability and anonymity in rural and remote communities, and trauma associated with colonization and the residential school system. In 2013, the First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) became the only province-wide First Nations health authority and since then, has been a primary player in BC's response to the crisis. As such, FNHA has identified key policy challenges that the proposed work will seek to address: prevent fatal overdoses, reduce drug-related harms (e.g., HIV), and increase service access, treatment options and culturally safe support for Indigenous people who use drugs (IPWUD) throughout the province. The proposed work will consist of 3 components with the overarching goal to develop a First Nations-led model of harm reduction that improves access and retention to supports and services, ultimately reducing opioid-related deaths among IPWUD. Part of the work will involve community-based research with 5 of BC's First Nations from each of FNHA's health regions to help articulate 'promising practices' from community harm reduction programs. The other components will identify ways to improve access, retention and cultural safety of harm reduction and treatment services in collaboration with FNHA and the provincially-mandated BC Centre on Substance Use. Findings will inform FNHA policy and programming, and be shared with health system partners in BC and beyond.

column36: Immunization on a budget: Using health economics to inform immunization policy in Alberta
column37: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) causes upper and lower respiratory tract illnesses in adults and children. While generally mild in adults, RSV can result in serious illness, hospitalization and death in infants. To date, the best method to prevent serious RSV infection is the passive immunization of at-risk children with 4-5 doses of the drug palivizumab during the RSV season. Due to the high price tag for a course of palivizumab (~$5,600 per child per season in Canada; totalling $2-3 million per season in Alberta), there is ongoing debate about the cost-effectiveness of this intervention. The Canadian Pediatric Society (CPS) recently updated their recommendations on the use of palivizumab; however, Alberta is not currently following these updated recommendations. The Alberta Ministry of Health is considering more closely aligning their RSV prevention policies with the eligibility criteria currently recommended by CPS; however, prior to making a decision they want to understand the economic and health consequences of applying different palivizumab guidelines in Alberta. To address this issue, we will determine the utilization and cost associated with palivizumab in Alberta. Moreover, we will conduct an economic evaluation of palivizumab based on current practice in Alberta, in comparison to the CPS guidelines. Finally, to help build sustainable capacity at the Alberta Ministry of Health to use economic evidence, we will produce recommendations for the Alberta Advisory Committee on Immunization to consider when reviewing and synthesizing economic analyses on immunizations.

column36: Measuring the impact of current and future harm reduction strategies in the ongoing opioid overdose epidemic in British Columbia
column37: North America is currently experiencing an opioid overdose crisis and this has been particularly pronounced in British Columbia (BC). In this jurisdiction there has been a rapid increase in overdose deaths since 2012, which has largely been driven by an increasing concentration of synthetic and more potent opioids in the illegal drug supply market. Despite a large effort within the province to reduce opioid-related harm, overdose deaths have continued to rise. This includes a scaling-up of BC's Take Home Naloxone program, a non-clinician administered therapy that is highly effective at reducing the effects of an overdose. More novel interventions have also included the introduction of opioid overdose sites, where people who use drugs can be observed and helped if they overdose. There is therefore a greatly urgent and important need to estimate the impact of these interventions and where new resources would be best positioned to have the most impact. In collaboration with the BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions (the Ministry) and with support from BC Centre for Disease Control and the Ministry of Health, I will estimate the impact of the current interventions to date as well as project the impact of future interventions and scale-up. I will combine together cutting-edge mathematical modelling and statistical techniques with provincial administrative datasets to evaluate the current provincial interventions and estimate the number of deaths averted due to current intervention scale-up and proposed novel interventions. The collaboration with both Ministries will ensure modelled scenarios will reflect policy proposals and help to support and inform their decisions.

column36: Economic evaluation and cost valuation of a province-wide quality improvement initiative: a case study of 'Call for Less Antipsychotics in Residential Care' (CLeAR) in British Columbia
column37: British Columbia has 62,000 people living with dementia and this number is expected to rise to 87,000 by 2024. A common challenge for many seniors is the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia. In October 2013, the British Columbia Patient Safety & Quality Council (BCPSQC) launched its initial cohort of care homes participating in a 'Call for Less Antipsychotics in Residential Care' (CLeAR) quality improvement (QI) initiative in response to rising concerns over inappropriate antipsychotic use in residential care. In this study, we aim to conduct a comprehensive economic evaluation and cost valuation of a province-wide QI initiative. A mixed-methods approach to economic evaluation will be embedded into the third cohort of CLeAR. Data collection and analysis will take place in three phases, starting with literature review of available economic studies on quality improvement and related patients outcomes; approximately 30 qualitative interviews with care home residents to explore their perspective in the design and execution of CLeAR; secondary data analysis to determine costs and patient-level clinical outcomes, and finally cost-effectiveness analysis to estimate cost per life year gained. Overall, our study findings will inform stakeholders and Ministry of Health about decisions on resource allocation for interventions designed to address both technical and non-technical (e.g., culture, teamwork) aspects to improve quality of care.

column36: Title: Advancing the health and wellness of BC First Nations within the hepatitis C prevention, care, and treatment cascade using integrated clinical and administrative data
column37: Hepatitis C (HCV) infection is a critical public health problem in Canada that disproportionately impacts Indigenous people, leading to higher risk for liver-related illnesses and mortality. The British Columbia Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC) and the First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) have partnered with the goal of using population-level clinical and administrative data to identify gaps in the HCV cascade of care (prevention, diagnosis, linkage with care, treatment, and cure) between First Nations and non-First Nations people in BC. The objectives of this research are to: 1) Identify and compare gaps or leakage across the HCV cascade of care between First Nations and non-First Nations in BC; 2) Work with the FNHA to identify measures within the integrated data which may serve as strengths-based wellness indicators within First Nations communities, and that support access to the HCV cascade of care, and; 3) Apply the strengths-based wellness indicators identified by the FNHA to highlight areas where HCV prevention and engagement in the HCV cascade of care may be enhanced to better meet the needs of BC First Nations.

column36: Moving beyond headcounts: improved physician workforce planning for primary care in BC
column37: Consistent access to high-quality family medicine improves the health of the population and lowers the costs of health care. Reports of family medicine shortages and of difficulties in accessing family physicians are ubiquitous in British Colombia (BC). To address shortages and access challenges, the Ministry of Health needs a clear understanding of how many active family doctors are working within provincial boarders, how many are providing comprehensive and patient-centered care, how they structure their practices, and how patients access (or do not access) the services they provide. The Ministry also needs a method to accurately estimate the future supply of family physicians and services in order to proactively design and implement policies that will address upcoming accessibility issues. These challenges are particularly salient given the upcoming rollout of team-based care across the province. To address these issues, this fellowship will integrate the results of several ongoing studies into a strategy for proactive physician workforce planning, supporting recruitment and retention efforts and the development and evaluation of new models of family medicine practice. It will provide granular data on the supply of comprehensive care, identify current and future gaps, and inform policy on training, recruitment and retention of family physicians. Ultimately, it will enhance the capacity for evidence-informed workforce planning within BC's Ministry of Health, leading to downstream improvements in access to family medicine across the province.

column36: Utilizing a syndemic approach for population level prevention, care and treatment cascades of hepatitis C virus and related epidemics
column37: Different distributions of social conditions, vulnerabilities, (e.g. drug use, mental illness) or other infections (HIV, HBV, TB), contribute to differences among populations affected by hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. The different distribution of these comorbidities drives heterogeneity in cascades of care (diagnosis, initiation of treatment, cure and retention in care). This study aims to improve HCV treatment and prevention by applying concepts of syndemic theory to improve the integration and delivery of health services among populations affected by HCV infection, such as people born 1945-65 ("Baby Boomers") and people who inject drugs (PWID). The British Columbia Hepatitis Testers Cohort (BC-HTC), which includes all individuals tested for HCV, HIV, HBV, sexually transmitted infections or TB since 1990, linked with administrative and healthcare data, will be used for this study. The study will extend the HCV cascade of care to include prevention and care related to underlying syndemic factors (e.g. drug use, mental illness and other co-infections). Gaps in HCV care cascades, and syndemic factors associated with gaps, will be identified, and factors associated with these gaps will be investigated. This will facilitate identification of avenues for shared and integrated interventions to improve prevention and care for HCV, and underlying substance use.

column36: Patient/Public Engagement Measurement and Evaluation Project (PEMEP) within the British Columbia Ministry of Health's Patients as Partners Initiative
column37: In 2010, the Patients as Partners Initiative of the British Columbia (BC) Ministry of Health began work to improve the BC healthcare system by partnering with patients to empower patients and to develop and support the implementation of sustainable healthcare policies. column36: Harnessing Health Systems to Optimize Biomedical Prevention for HIV Elimination among Gay, Bisexual, and Other Men Who Have Sex with Men in Canada
column37: Effective biomedical HIV prevention technologies such as Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis and Treatment as Prevention, combined with regular and accessible HIV testing and linkage to care, have the potential to vastly improve the health of people living with HIV and eliminate HIV transmission to HIV-negative individuals. With a cost savings of approximately $300,000 per averted HIV infection, these tools represent an opportunity for significant cost savings to the Canadian health care system. However, access to biomedical HIV testing, treatment, and prevention services remains patchwork across Canada, and HIV incidence among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) remains elevated, with gbMSM being 71 times more likely to acquire HIV than other men. This suggests that further work is needed to ensure health systems are sufficiently equipped to meet the needs of this diverse community. As such, this fellowship leverages the newly-formed Community Alliance project - a collaboration between Canada's leading gay and bisexual men's health organizations - to improve health systems access for gbMSM by (1) by developing a robust evidence base for health systems change through the identification and synthesis of regional and national data sources; (2) developing a monitoring-and-evaluation framework for measuring progress towards programmatic goals; and (3) building research and analytic capacity among community-based partners and researchers to promote ongoing data synthesis, analysis and reporting. Primary data for this project will be drawn from Sex Now - a serial cross-sectional survey of over 8,000 gbMSM across Canada administered by the Community Based Centre for Gay Men's Health (CBRC). Findings will be disseminated through the Community Alliance, which will leverage them to develop strategic partnerships for the betterment of health systems serving gbMSM, resulting in improved quality of life and health outcomes for people living with and affected by HIV.

column36: Informing Policy on School Transitions for Children with Disabilities in Alberta
column37: Children with disabilities face many problems across their lives. On average, they are less likely to go to university and work, and they earn less than others. To support these children, the government offers many programs. One issue is that these programs are often hard to use during transitions periods, such as changes between elementary and junior high school. School transitions can cause problems for these children, which include a loss of support, anxiety, and depression. This research looks at health care problems resulting from transitions across school life and how to decrease these problems. We examine data on Albertan children's (age 3 to 22) use of support programs over six years. This data shows how these children used school, disability, and health care supports. We will look at how different school transitions during these six years affect health care use. Poor health care outcomes will include an increased use of mental health services and the emergency room. First, we look at which school transitions lead to poor health care outcomes for children with disabilities. This identifies when these children may need more support. Next, we examine if the use of support programs reduces poor outcomes found during high risk transitions. Finally, we will work with partners in the government and schools to find better ways to support these children during high risk transitions. This research will provide knowledge and strategies to promote the health of children with disabilities.

column36: The social organization of Family Integrated Care (FICare): Mapping coordination of care in NICUs for effective scale and spread
column37: Babies born before 37 weeks of gestation cause serious concerns for their families, care providers, and the health system. These babies are preterm and require care in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) to grow and develop. Admission to the NICU can interfere with early parent-infant relationships and contributes to parental stress. For the most critically ill preterm babies (born before 32 weeks gestation), integrating families into their baby's care (Family Integrated Care or FICare) helps babies gain weight faster and reduces parental distress. We don't know if FICare improves outcomes for babies who are born between 32 and 36 weeks gestation and admitted to a Level II NICU. We do want to know if FICare improves outcomes for babies and their parents, reduces the length of time they are patients in the NICU, and reduces costs. If FICare is effective we want to make this kind of care common practice in all Level II NICUs. If FICare is not effective in reducing length of NICU stay for babies we still need to understand why outcomes were not improved. Therefore, we need to understand how FICare is actually working, and whether it requires adaptation before it is put into practice. Qualitative interview data about health care providers, hospital administrators, and parental experiences of FICare will be analyzed. For this project I will map activities that show how FICare is actually working, and how care is being coordinated by institutional work processes. From this analysis, I will identify the gaps between FICare and how care actually plays out in the NICU. The discoveries will inform how FICare can be adapted and implemented with integrity.

column36: Community-Based Assessment and Prevention of Tooth Decay for Children Experiencing Domestic Violence
column37: Approximately 1/2 of children in Canada experience some tooth decay. Severe tooth decay is the number one reason for day surgery in young children (less than 5 years of age), even though it can be prevented. The estimated hospital cost alone for this surgery is approximately $21 million/year. The full cost to society is much more when you add on dental and anaesthesiology fees, parents' lost work time and travel costs. Preventing tooth decay is important, but our publicly funded health system provides very little dental care, and many Canadians cannot afford dental prevention or treatment services. Canada has some publicly funded dental programs available, but vulnerable groups especially, may not make use of them for various reasons. My program of work aims to support dental health for a hard to reach group-children in families experiencing domestic violence. column36: Structural analysis of mycobacterial oxidative phosphorylation and targeting it to treat tuberculosis
column37: Cells use oxygen to convert chemical energy from diverse sources into the universal energy currency ATP before use. This process, called oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos), is performed by a series of large molecular machines that reside in cell membranes. In OxPhos, electrons stripped from fuel molecules ("oxidation") are passed between several of the molecular machines (Complexes I, II, III, and IV) with oxygen serving as the final electron acceptor, reducing it to water. During electron transfer Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from one side of the membrane to the other, establishing a chemical and electrical proton gradient. A final machine, known as ATP synthase, allows protons back across the membrane, using the energy released to make ATP. While example atomic-resolution structures have now been determined for all OxPhos complexes it is still not clear how electron transfer is coupled to the proton pumping that powers aerobic life. Understanding OxPhos has important biomedical implications. Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the organism Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a leading causes of death worldwide and an important health issue in Canada's indigenous populations. The breakthrough TB drug bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase. Mycobacterial Complexes III and IV form an unusual supercomplex (CIII2CIV2) with a dramatically different structure than the human Complexes III and IV. This structure is both unique and essential, making it an attractive target for developing TB drugs. We will determine structures for CIII2CIV2 and ATP synthase from mycobacteria. The unique CIII2CIV2, which carries out two thirds of the electron transfer pathway in a self contained stable assembly, provides a valuable tool for understanding universal principles of electron transfer. Structures of CIII2CIV2 and mycobacterial ATP synthase in complex with approved and candidate antimycobacterial drugs will provide key insights into how these drugs work and can be improved.

column36: The Impact of Physical Exercise on the Inactive Body and Brain
column37: Physical activity has multiple benefits for our health, including cognitive and brain health. Unfortunately, many adults become physical inactive with age. Studies repeatedly show that physical inactivity is associated with numerous negative health outcomes, including cognitive impairment and increased dementia risk. Older adults become physically inactive for many reasons, secondary to chronic conditions such as arthritis or lung disease, or acutely, due to bed rest as a result of injury, surgery, or hospitalization. It is important to note that bed rest is a reality for many older adults and often is a "tipping point" for subsequent decline in function and independence. Whether implementing bouts of physical exercise during periods of physical inactivity, such as bed rest due to injury or illness, may effectively mitigate the negative consequences of physical inactivity is not well established. Moreover, the exact mechanisms by which physical exercise may protect older adults' cognitive and brain health during periods of physical inactivity is not well understood. However, a better understanding will advance the development of novel interventions and rehabilitation strategies to counter the adverse effects of physical inactivity on cognitive health in older adults. Thus, maximizing on an opportunity provided by CIHR and the Canadian Space Agency, we will determine: 1) the effects of 14 days of bed rest on cognitive and brain outcomes in adults aged 55 to 65 years old; 2) the impact of daily bouts of moderate to vigorous physical exercise in mitigating the effects of bed rest on cognitive function; and 3) the mechanisms (i.e., how) by which bed rest and impacts cognitive and brain function. Given the immense health and financial burden imposed by cognitive impairment, and majority of older adults are physically inactive, our results will guide future strategies to positively shape the path of cognitive aging in health and during transitions in care.

column36: Exploring the role of phosphoinositides in the trafficking of proteins to the apical complex in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
column37: Malaria is one of the world's most common infectious diseases, with approximately 274 million cases each year and 400 000 deaths, and thus represents one of the most devastating global public health problems. The lack of an effective vaccine, the emergence of resistance to first-line drugs like artemisinines, combined with the small number of suitable new drugs against the malaria parasite demonstrate the urgent need for the development and implementation of novel intervention strategies in the form of drugs, vector control measures and an effective vaccine. Indeed, it is expected that if the trend in malaria prevalence stays on its current upwards course, the death rate could double in the next twenty years. Invasion of a red blood cell by Plasmodium falciparum parasites is an essential step in the malaria lifecycle and host response to parasite antigens are an important component of human malarial immunity. Consequently, the molecular players involved in erythrocyte invasion are key targets for both therapeutic and vaccine-based strategies to block parasite development. Several of these invasion proteins are stored in the apical complex of the parasite, a structure containing secretory organelles called dense granules, micronemes and rhoptries, and are released at different times during invasion. Because of its essential role, interfering with the generation of the apical complex represents a very attractive target for the design of a new kind of antimalarial. Our studies will focus on trying to understand how the parasite directs proteins to the different structures of the apical complex. Understanding this complex process will likely provide a wealth of new targets for the development of strategies to block apical complex generation and preventing malaria pathogenesis.

column36: Epilepsy and emotional comorbidities: Role of the endocannabinoid system.
column37: At least half the people with epilepsy have crippling levels of fear, anxiety and depression. These emotional disturbances greatly reduce their quality of life and are not effectively treated. Thus, it is critically important that we better understand the brain mechanisms that underlie these emotional disturbances and develop effective treatments. This proposal will determine the role of the endocannabinoid (eCB) system in the emotional problems caused by repeated seizures. We will identify the brain mechanisms that become altered in epilepsy and test new cannabinoid-based drugs to determine if they can prevent or reverse the high levels of fear and anxiety. My laboratory in collaboration with several colleagues have new data which shows that the endocannabinoid system becomes altered following seizures and that this is related to emotional changes in rats. We hypothesize that alterations of fear and anxiety associated with repeated seizures are caused by a persistent maladaptation of the eCB system. We will first determine the relationship between seizure activity and endocannabinoid function with changes in emotions. We will next identify drugs which alter endocannabinoid function to determine if they can effectively block or reserve the emotional changes. Finally we will determine if high levels of stress that occurs after seizures is responsible for the emotional changes. We believe that the emotional changes that lower the quality of life in people with epilepsy can be effectively treated and that the knowledge generated by these proposed studies will ultimately improve lives for persons with epilepsy.

column36: The discovery of new antibiotics derived from inhibitors of sporulation
column37: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, sepsis and various kinds of infection that result from surgery or in patients whose immune system is compromised by chemotherapy. They are therefore at the front line of virtually all aspects of modern medicine. The efficacy of these incredible drugs, mostly discovered during the period from 1940-60, is being rapidly eroded through the antibiotic resistance. As a result, new antibiotics are desperately needed if we are to sustain our current standard of care. But the classical approaches to antibiotics discovery are not working all that well. The reason for this is that all of the available molecules in the world have been tested for the inhibition of growth of pathogens. New approaches are therefore desperately needed. We have discovered that the filamentous bacteria of the genus Streptomyces provide a fascinating alternative approach. Because these bacteria are filamentous in structure, they use many elements of the core molecular machinery (cell wall biosynthesis, cell division, chromosome segregation etc) differently than rod shaped or coccoid bacteria - which include almost all of the pathogens. Many processes which are essential for viability in pathogenic bacteria are employed primarily for sporulation in the streptomycetes. Our hypothesis therefore, is that screening for inhibitors of sporulation in Streptomyces has the potential to reveal novel inhibitors of these core processes and that these inhibitors might be developed as antibiotics against "conventional" bacteria. We have tested this hypothesis and thereby discovered three novel antibiotics: EN-7, Min-1 and Fil-1. In this project we will further develop these compounds in the hopes that we can provide valuable leads for fighting infectious disease.

column36: Molecular control of neural stem cell fate decisions
column37: The neocortex is the region of the brain where higher cognitive functioning occurs, allowing us to perceive stimuli in the environment and have conscious thought. The original dogma was that new neurons could not be generated after embryonic development since there were no stem cells to replace lost neurons. However, more recent studies have identified a pool of neural stem cells that reside in the adult brain. Moreover, it has been found that these stem cells are first born in the embryonic period, persisting in an inactive state until adulthood. We have been studying how neural stem cells decide to be inactive, or divide and differentiate into neurons in the embryonic brain. These studies have focused on proneural genes, which we found mark a pool of slow-dividing neural stem cells in the embryo and adult. We now try to understand how the proneural genes control whether neural stem cells remain inactive, divide or differentiate. We have three aims in this study. In the first aim we examine how slow-dividing stem cells that express these proneural genes respond to a brain injury, and trace their embryonic progeny. In the second aim, we ask how these proneural genes can be manipulated to induce neural stem cells to produce new neurons in development and after brain injury. In the third aim, we begin to model the roles of these proneural genes in a primate system, using monkey tissue and generating brain organoids from human cells as a surrogate model system. These studies are important because re-invigoration of these dormant stem cells by manipulating the proneural genes may aid brain repair.

column37: Some 20% of youth have mental health/addiction (MHA) disorders, and adolescence is an optimal time to intervene. Yet, youth are challenged to access effective services in a timely way. Provincial, national and international efforts are under way to build community-based, integrated service hubs offering wraparound care to youth. However, these efforts are advancing in the absence of rigorous research data demonstrating effectiveness. The study will randomly assign 450 youth to receive either hospital-based care or ICCT services to compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the two service pathways for youth with MHA challenges. We have already successfully recruited 112 youth into the study as of August 2018 and have progressed to five hospitals now actively recruiting participants. As provincial, national, and international efforts to implement ICCT-type models of care advance under significant public and private investment, it is critical that robust data be collected to examine their effectiveness. By providing rapid access to integrated, collaborative care geared to youth needs and preferences in youth-friendly community settings, this project is expected to substantially improve the mental health of this population, making Ontario a leader in innovative systems of care.

column36: Repairing the brain of sick newborns: From bench to bedside
column37: At birth, some babies experienced a condition called asphyxia, which means that their brain and other organs did not receive enough blood and/or oxygen. This life-threatening condition accounts for 23% of all babies' deaths around the world, and often leads to cerebral palsy and trouble with learning and functioning in everyday life. At this time, no treatment is available to repair the brain damage in these babies. Sildenafil (Viagra(R)) already is given safely to babies suffering from increased blood pressure in their lungs for other reasons than asphyxia at birth. Our recent studies in an animal model of asphyxia at birth suggested that sildenafil may improve the damage to the brain. Also, our recent pilot study with human babies showed that it is feasible to give sildenafil to babies who suffer from asphyxia at birth. We hypothesize that (1) sildenafil can repair the damage to a baby's brain by stimulating the growth of new nerve cells and decreasing brain swelling; and that (2) sildenafil can be safely increased up to 6 mg/kg/day in these babies and may improve how their brain and heart/lungs work. We will use a rat model of asphyxia at birth to study the mechanisms involved in repairing the brain after it is damaged. We also will determine the optimal dose of sildenafil that can be given to human babies who suffered from asphyxia at birth to improve their brain, heart, and lungs. This project will enable us to understand the repair mechanisms involved in the damaged baby's brain after asphyxia at birth and to determine whether sildenafil is a promising treatment for repairing this damage. This project may provide new solutions for these babies to reduce the consequences of asphyxia at birth and improve their future life. Thus, it may help many families around the world who are dealing with this devastating condition.

column37: Background: Beyond biological sex, gender is increasingly recognized as a pivotal determinant of health. However, there are no standardized gender measurements. Aims: The overarching aims of this large Consortium are to integrate sex and gender dimensions in applied health research, to evaluate their impact on clinical cost-sensitive outcomes and patients reported outcomes related to quality of life in noncommunicable diseases including cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease, chronic kidney disease and neurological disease. We also aim to construct innovative ways to disseminate the application of gender measurement towards personalized approaches to chronic disease prevention, diagnosis and treatment. Methods: With a five-country transatlantic network comprised of 30 investigators, we will benchmark innovative solutions to measure gender in retrospective cohorts. Based on consensus, we will develop a framework to identify gender-related factors, as well as cost-sensitive and patients reported outcomes and measure their associations in 32 accessible cohorts of patients affected by cardiovascular, chronic kidney and neurological diseases and metabolic syndrome. Large database analysis and when appropriate machine learning approaches will allow the derivation of pan and within country disease specific gender scores which will be validated through e-Health and m-Health applications in prospective disease groups. Educational modules will be developed to promote awareness, implementation and dissemination. Innovation: As a five-country multidisciplinary Consortium with access to granular large databases, we are uniquely positioned to harness an innovative methodology that will provide a framework to close gender gaps in chronic disease management and promote knowledge transfer in the scientific community and clinical practice.

All steps will be integrated in a back and forth manner and reviewed and challenged by an international expert Sounding Board. Our international research team brings awareness of the impact of different cultural milieux on health (ie a varied set of cultural eyes to interpret findings) as well as the intellectual and methodological richness of multiple disciplines (social sciences, economics, medicine). In addition to scholarly papers and policy advice we will deliver a manual & two workshops for young academics on methods for studying the depth and breadth of sex/gender and health equality.

column37: Inherited heart rhythm disorders include Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Early diagnosis of these disorders can provide the most effective care, including personalized exercise restriction, personalized medications and more appropriate use of implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) to regulate heart rhythms. The primary goal of this research is to develop more effective methods for predicting who are at greatest risk of a serious cardiac event. To do this, we will use healthcare data collected from participants in the Hearts in Rhythm Organization (HiRO) research database. This includes inherited heart rhythm disorder patients from 19 specialized adult and pediatric clinics across Canada. Our additional goal is to create a patient-oriented research program that addresses the current and future needs of these patients, their families and their communities. In the long-term, we expect this research to result in improved screening practices to better identify at-risk patients and individualize their treatment to prevent and decrease the tragedy of sudden cardiac death. Involving patients in the research process will ensure that we are addressing issues that are most pertinent to their well-being. We envision that this will improve communication between the healthcare provider and patients, so that patients are well informed about their condition and ensuring that they can take an active role in managing their health and improve their quality of life.

column36: Identifying Key Prescribing CASCADes in the Elderly: A Transnational Initiative on Drug Safety
column37: Prescribing cascades occur when a health care provider misinterprets the side effect of a drug as a new medical condition and prescribes a second, potentially unnecessary, harmful drug to address the side effect. To inform tailored interventions, there is a need to understand potential sex and gender differences in how cascades develop and are managed. In this transnational study, an interdisciplinary team of experts in sex, gender, and ageing will respond to this critical gap by applying a sex and gender lens to complementary health data from four countries. We will use administrative and clinical data on older adults to calculate sex-stratified prevalence rates for three prescribing cascades prioritized by our collaborating partners. We will also interview prescribers, patients, and caregivers to explore how socially constructed gender roles contribute to the experience, presentation, and management of prescribing cascades. Findings will improve our understanding of how adverse drug events are different between older women and men and inform the development and dissemination of tailored knowledge translation products to reduce the frequency and impact of prescribing cascades.

column36: Risky decision making as a cause, consequence and treatment target for addiction.
column37: Whether someone is dependent on a chemical substance like cocaine, or has developed a behavioural addiction such as gambling disorder, the maladaptive choice to pursue the addiction at the expense of other goals lies at the heart of the problem. Indeed, individuals with an addiction disorder, or who later develop problems with addiction, score poorly on laboratory-based decision-making tests such as the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT) that involve the weighing of costs and benefits. One hypothesis is that decision-making impairments may be compounded as the addiction develops because of the way in which addictive drugs, and also engagement in addictive behaviours, affect brain function, biasing the decision-making process in favour of the addiction. Choosing to abstain from the addictive substance or behaviour then becomes really hard. We have successfully developed an animal model of cost/benefit decision making based on the IGT: the rat Gambling Task (rGT). On both human and animal tests, subjects must choose between four different options, each of which is associated with different amounts of potential reward and loss. By avoiding high-risk, high-reward options, subjects can maximise gains. Most rats develop this optimal strategy, although some animals instead favour the risky options. These risk-preferring rats are uniquely and adversely affected by taking cocaine: their decision making gets worse and they show increased drug-seeking in withdrawal indicative of greater relapse risk. Adding sound and light cues when the rats win on this gambling task significantly increases the proportion of rats biased towards the risky options. We now want to use this model to understand why the addition of these "bells and whistles" potentiates risky choice and addiction vulnerability, and harness that knowledge to pilot potential therapies for addiction.

column36: Impact of inactivity and exercise on muscle and bone marrow adiposity
column37: Inactivity increases fall and fracture risk, particularly in older adults. This may be due to bone and muscle weakness related to fat accumulation in bone marrow and muscles during inactivity as well as aging. We will test if exercise during 14-day bed rest can prevent or reduce inactivity-related fat accumulation in muscle and bone marrow and bone deterioration. We will assess if fat accumulation is linked to changes in muscle strength or bone properties. We will randomize 24 bed rest study volunteers (55-65 yrs) to an exercise group and control group. Both groups will have similar numbers of women and men. Exercise includes daily cycling and resistance exercises strengthening leg and arm muscles. We will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantify muscle and bone marrow fat in the lower leg, hip and forearm prior to and after the 14-day bed rest and during recovery. We will measure muscle strength and function of the lower and upper extremities, and obtain measures of bone properties at the same time points. We will also obtain images using a new compact MRI prototype our group has designed for the International Space Station (ISS-MRI). We will test whether changes in bone marrow and muscle fat and bone porosity differ between exercise and control groups after bed rest and during recovery. We will also assess if observed differences are linked to muscle strength or function. We will test if changes alter between body sites or sexes. We will use MRI data to optimize the ISS-MRI. Study findings will reveal if fat accumulation and bone deterioration due to inactivity can be prevented by exercise and clarify mechanisms underpinning muscle weakness and injuries after inactivity. Findings will guide future research designs and strategies for effective exercise-countermeasures. This evidence can help in securing musculoskeletal health and mobility as well as prevention of falls and fractures after space travel or other periods of inactivity.

column36: IMproved Personalized medicine through machine LEarning in MENTal disorders
column37: Psychotic disorders are severe mental illnesses with early onset, frequently chronic course and often lifelong impairment. As a consequence, they cause an enormous healthcare burden, costing close to Euro100 billion annually in Europe alone. The biology of these illnesses is insufficiently understood and no objective tools exist to aid in diagnosis or treatment selection. This leads to long periods of inadequate and ineffective treatment, significantly limiting the opportunity for achieving more optimal clinical outcomes. To address this, IMPLEMENT will develop a translational research framework that identifies biomarkers for treatment-relevant stratification of the most severe psychotic disorder, schizophrenia. Using big data approaches (n > 60,000), IMPLEMENT will explore the impact of genetic risk and neurodevelopmental processes on the formation of biological subgroups and use clinical studies of conventional antipsychotic treatment and innovative treatment approaches to tune subgroup profiles towards clinical utility. The IMPLEMENT framework will incorporate preclinical validation to leverage neurobiological understanding and optimize biological subgroup profiles. The clinical utility of these profiles will be validated in independent clinical samples and prospectively recruited subjects. IMPLEMENT will integrate these efforts with ICT development, to optimize the use of high-dimensional datasets across diverse repositories, to optimally harmonize data for personalized medicine investigations and safeguard patient privacy. Overall, IMPLEMENT will provide the basis for biologically-informed personalized medicine approaches in schizophrenia, addressing an enormous unmet medical need in an area of medicine in which currently no robust clinical stratification tools exist.

column36: Engineering of a probiotic bacterium for precise microbiome editing
column37: We propose to develop a safe-to-use, efficient and programmable conjugative probiotic (COP) as a highly innovative tool to precisely edit the microbiome and fight multidrug resistant pathogens. COP bacteria also include potent bacterial conjugation machineries for high-efficiency delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 systems into the microbiota. The CRISPR-Cas9 system can easily be programmed to cleave DNA simply by providing custom guide RNA (gRNA) spacer sequences that match the desired target sites. Targeting DNA sequences located in a bacterial chromosome leads to cell death by compromising genome integrity. The CRISPR-Cas9 system can also cure cells from plasmids carrying antibiotic resistance or virulence genes, thereby "disarming" potentially dangerous bacteria by restoring susceptibility to antibiotics. Unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics, the COP system is designed to be highly specific, with selectivity conferred by carefully chosen CRISPR-Cas9 target sequences and tuning of the host range through the selection of appropriate COP conjugative machineries. This new technology would also constitute a powerful microbiome manipulation tool for fundamental research, and to progressively advance towards clinical applications. Once established, this innovative method could have a significant impact on medicine by eventually offering a new tool to treat dysbiosis or as an alternative to antimicrobials for the prevention or treatment of many infectious diseases.

column37: Hemodialysis requires a reliable method of connecting the patient to the blood-purification machine, called vascular access. The two most common forms of vascular access are catheters and fistulas. A catheter is a plastic tube inserted into a vein in the neck; a fistula is a vein surgically connected to an artery in the arm that is accessed by needles. Many expert committees consider fistulas the preferred form of vascular access and actively promote them. However, these recommendations are based on studies that may have overestimated the benefits of fistulas and underestimated the potential risks associated with procedures required to achieve and maintain fistula patency. We do not have sufficient data to provide patients with enough information to allow them to make an informed decision about pursuing a fistula creation attempt or using a hemodialysis catheter without attempting a fistula. We cannot offer decision support to promote shared decision-making because we do not know patient, caregiver and healthcare provider decision needs. We will study people who start hemodialysis with a catheter in six large renal programs in Canada. We will follow participants from the start of hemodialysis to determine the benefits and harms associated with attempting fistula creation, and whether they vary with sex, age or presence of disease conditions. We will also assess decision needs of patients and caregivers, and healthcare providers. This project will leverage multicenter, high-quality data describing vascular access procedures and our expertise in this area of research. We will provide important data on potential benefits and possible harms of attempting or avoiding fistulas and will identify the attributes of hemodialysis access-related decisions that are important to patients and caregivers, and healthcare providers in order to inform the design of a tool to support decision-making about the vascular access for hemodialysis.

column36: Rational antiepileptic drug selection by combining gene network and ICT analysis (RAISE-GENIC)
column37: Epilepsy is a common disease affecting >70 million people worldwide. Patients with epilepsy suffer from recurrent seizures that lead to injuries, death, social stigma as well as job and driving restrictions. Epilepsy is treated with anti-seizure drugs with the aim to stop the seizures. Although many anti-seizure drugs are available, we are currently unable to predict which drug works best in a particular patient. Therefore, we must select the drugs based on trial and error. Unfortunately, though, using this approach typically means that less than one in two patients become seizure free with the first drug, which then leads to a cycle of selecting another drug, testing its anti-seizure effects for several weeks or months before another drug can be tried. It would revolutionize epilepsy treatment if we were able to predict the anti-seizure drug with the highest likelihood of success in an individual patient (personalized medicine). We aim to achieve this by combining two strategies. The first strategy examines human brain cells which are generated from skin cells of adult donors. These cells are treated with four different anti-seizure drugs (carbamazepine, valproate, lacosamide, levetiracetam) and we will investigate how specific genes respond to being exposed to these drugs. We will then look at available genetic data from 1382 patients and examine if changes in these genes correlate with a drugs's ability to stop seizures. The second approach will perform a "big data analysis" incorporating details on the patient's epilepsy, genetic data, brain wave signals and brain imaging to predict treatment effect. Using these large sources of complementary data, we will develop tools to help doctors and patients predict the effect of the different anti-seizure drugs. Subsequently, we will test in an independent cohort of 100 patients if the tool correctly predicts the best anti-seizure drug. Finally, we will prepare a clinical study to establish the tool in clinical practice.

column37: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 1 in 100 live births and is the leading cause of neonatal deaths related to birth defects. To find the missing cause of CHD, we will use whole genome sequencing (WGS) which allows exploration of the entire genome to find gene defects that cause CHD and determine if and how these gene defects predict severity of disease and outcomes. Canadian, Dutch and German partners have established a consortium that leverages DNA samples from population biorepositories to create the largest cohort of CHD for WGS. We will sequence over 1500 children and adults with TOF/TGA. Preliminary data has identified novel causes of CHD not previously reported e.g. defects in new genes, defects in multiple genes, and defects outside of genes in regions that control gene expression. Thus WGS will help unravel the genetic architecture of CHD in a way not previously possible. We will use this information to determine if type and number of gene defects predicts which patients will have a mild versus severe phenotype. This information can then be used to advise families about chances of having another affected child and potentially reduce this risk by pre-implantation genetic diagnosis. It can also inform which patients should undergo fetal interventions that prevent the heart disease from progressing to severe forms. Together, this can help to reduce the burden of CHD and to improve outcomes in this vulnerable population.

column36: Functional Genomics of Neurodegenerative Diseases: Defining Molecular Pathogenesis and Targets for Biomarkers and Personalised Therapies
column37: Neurodegenerative dementias are the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, affecting >24 million people at a cost of >US$172 billion annually. Despite a lot of effort, apart from a handful of mildly effective symptomatic treatments there are no proven ways of stopping these diseases. This proposal addresses takes an innovative approach to develop therapies that address this unmet need. The program is built upon our recent success in identifying genes that carry DNA variants that increase risk of dementia. We have noticed that these genes cluster into functional groups ("cellular pathways"). Two of the largest clusters are of particular interest. One cluster regulates the function of brain inflammatory cells (microglia), which search the brain for damaged cells and aggregated proteins. Another function of these cells is to prune unwanted nerve connections (synapses). The other cluster contains proteins that can change their conformation in order to facilitate key cellular functions (such as making proteins in synapses that are crucial for memory, or regulating the function of microglial cells). Because these clusters contain multiple different genes with DNA sequence changes that increase risk of dementia, it is clear that these clusters govern pathways that are very important in causing synaptic damage leading to dementia. A vital clue is that some of the genes in these pathways also contain variants that actually protect the patient from developing clinical disease. This clearly suggests that mimicking the effect of these protective genetic variants could be a way of preventing/slowing the progression of these diseases. The current program will therefore develop a better understanding of the components in these disease causing pathways, understand how they are regulated, and identify specific components that could be used as molecular targets for treatments that would make the pathway function normally.

column36: Personalization of Long term Treatment in Bipolar Disorder
column37: We propose a set of studies to improve the selection of long term treatment for bipolar disorder. Bipolar disorder is a severe psychiatric condition characterized by periods of mania and depression as well as by changes in brain structure and function. People with bipolar disorder have high rates of disability and are at risk of suicide if not receiving proper treatment. Long term treatment with mood stabilizing medications is the cornerstone of the disease management. However, even the most effective treatment, lithium, is effective in less than one third of all patients. To select among several available treatment options, clinicians rely on trial-and-error: different medications are given for months at a time until an effective one is found. Finding clinical and biological markers associated with good treatment response is expected to shorten this otherwise lengthy and inefficient process. To find such markers, we have established a partnership of specialized clinical programs and expert molecular-genetic laboratories. Our proposal combines novel techniques of studies of nerve cells produced from induced pluripotent stem cells and analyses of factors regulating functions of various genes (epigenetic factors). The project has three related aims: Aim 1: Confirmation of genetic predictors of response to lithium found in a study recently conducted by several of us. Aim 2: Testing the hypothesis of differences in epigenetic regulations between responders and non-responders to lithium and integrating these findings with the genetic results in Aim 1. Aim 3: Characterization of neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of patients with bipolar disorder responsive and non-responsive to lithium. Our results will 1) inform future studies of treatment response, and 2) contribute to developments of personalized clinical management of bipolar disorder.

column36: Testing a conceptual model of adjustment and compliance in couples seeking fertility treatment
column37: Infertility is a growing public health issue, affecting 12-16% of Canadian couples. Although advances in assisted reproductive technologies now allow more couples to become parents, treatment is strenuous, has limited success rates, and can disrupt both partners' psychological, relationship, and sexual adjustment. Hence, despite a favourable prognosis, 20-30% of couples choose to end treatment before achieving birth. Yet, fundamental knowledge about compliance with fertility treatment is still lacking. The most common reasons for dropout are physical and psychological burden of treatment and relationship strain. Research in this area, however, suffers from important flaws, including the use of retrospective designs and the use of general descriptors to identify causes of discontinuation. Evidence about the predictors of non-compliance is also scare. This 2-year prospective study will examine predictors of treatment non-compliance in both partners of 350 couples seeking fertility treatment. Patient, treatment, and clinic factors, as well as psychological, relational and sexual strain are expected to predict treatment discontinuation. This study will 1) provide novel prospective data about factors associated with treatment burden and discontinuation in couples seeking fertility treatment, 2) help identify barriers to treatment compliance, 3) help inform the development of interventions to guide couples through their decisional process, and 4) highlight clinical factors that could be modified to promote better patient care, prevent undue treatment termination, and improve cumulative pregnancy rates.

column36: Integrative Personal Omics Profiles in Glioblastoma Recurrence and Therapy Resistance
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the most aggressive brain tumors with a grim prognosis and median survival times of less than 15 months. Despite multimodal therapy, including surgical resection and radio-chemotherapy, recurrence is inevitable. However, time to recurrence is an individual parameter in patients and depends on genetic factors and on clinical parameters such as extent of resection. In recurrent GBM, repeated surgery can substantially prolong the lifespan if recurrent tumors are detected at early stages. Until now, recurrence monitoring is based on radiologic imaging but suffers from limited sensitivity and confounding effects. Therefore, circulating "liquid biopsy" markers predicting the time-window of recurrence are an unmet clinical need. We propose to use a spectrum of "Omics" methods to dissect the individual parameters that determine recurrence and therapy resistance in GBM. We will use a retrospective cohort of 100 patients clinically fully annotated GBM primary and recurrent samples. Abundance-based biomarkers associated with time-to-recurrence and therapy resistance will be obtained by analyzing extracellular vesicles (EVs) with respect to proteolytic fragments (mass-spectrometry based), protease actvitivies, and miRNA content. In addition, a full NGS analysis will be performed to characterise recurrent tumors in each individual patient to combine all "Omics" with clinical and imaging data. From these analyses, we propose to identify personalised easy-to-access biopsy markers so that investigation of pre- and post-surgery blood samples (at time of initial surgery) allows to faithfully discern tumor-originating molecules through their decreased abundance in post-surgery samples. We further hypothesize that multimodal monitoring, e.g. combining imaging data with molecular markers allows to establish a molecular signature of GBM recurrence which is particularly powerful for reliable prediction of GBM recurrence in a prospective patient cohort.

column36: Impact of Protein Nutrition in Critically-ill Patients
column37: Critically-ill patients admitted to the intensive care unit undergo inflammation and tissue damage, which contribute to ongoing organ malfunction. Studies indicate that increased dietary protein, or protein building blocks (amino acids), may improve their health outcomes. In agreement, studies in clinical and laboratory research studies indicate that the administration of amino acids can prevent protein breakdown. Controversy arises, however, from a number of clinical trials that failed to show an overall benefit for early nutrition in the critically-ill. This may be because the trials did not focus on protein therapy, nor did they use biological measurements to discriminate between patients who responded to nutritional therapy and those who did not. Here, we propose that the intravenous supplementation of amino acids in critically-ill patients can improve protein metabolism, and that this is associated with biological signatures ('biomarkers') that identify the patients who will most likely benefit. Our team is in a unique position to measure protein metabolism and biomarkers using state-of-the-art technologies that can be translated to clinical practice. The discovery and development of biomarkers of nutritional response is a critical step towards a larger clinical trial to establish protein nutrition as an effective therapy in the critically-ill.

column36: Pharmacological Characterization of eNOS-based Platelet Subpopulations
column37: Platelets are circulating blood particles normally responsible for stopping bleeding by forming blood clots (platelet aggregates). In conditions such as heart attack and stroke blood clots form inappropriately in sick (atherosclerotic) blood vessels. Recently, we have discovered that two types of platelets exists. One type of platelet generates the signaling molecule nitric oxide and the other type of platelet does not generate this signaling molecule. Nitric oxide is well known to inhibit platelet clot formation, and we have found that platelets that do not generate nitric oxide initiate clot formation, while platelets that do generate nitric oxide limit clot formation. Additionally, we have preliminary data that suggests that the two platelet subtypes may respond differently to (anti-platelet) drugs that are used to prevent heart attack or stroke. By the end of our studies we expect to have established that the two platelet subtypes differ in their response to antiplatelet drugs and that heart attack patients with an elevated ratio of non-NO-producing to NO-producing platelets may not fully respond to current anti-platelet therapy. These basic and translational studies of platelet biology have the potential to significantly impact the health of Canadians by better predicting risk and extent of clot formation. Lastly, these studies have the potential to inform personal anti-platelet therapy, and to potentially inform the future development of more effective anti-platelet drugs.

column36: Novel Mechanisms of Leishmania Pathogenesis
column37: Leishmaniases are a group of infectious diseases caused by parasites that infect 12 million people worldwide with 1.3 million new cases every year. Like many neglected diseases, leishmaniasis is primarily endemic to developing nations and thus presents additional socioeconomic burdens to already impoverished people. Leishmania donovani-the focus of this project-causes visceral leishmaniasis with severe morbidity and mortality. There are no effective vaccines and current treatments have limited efficacy and significant toxicities. The mechanisms that enable intracellular pathogens such as leishmania to chronically infect macrophages -pivotal cells of the innate immune system- are a focus of intense interest. Research is proposed here to investigate two novel mechanisms of leishmania pathogenesis. The first mechanism relates to investigate the roles of small, non-coding RNAs (snRNAs) in immunity to intracellular infection. These snRNAs are found in both animals and plants and some viruses and are well conserved and recognized as a vital component of genetic regulation. snRNAs have been implicated in stress, cancer, infection and innate immunity. Our hypothesis is that leishmania uses small RNA-based effector mechanisms to establish chronic infection. Research relevant to the second novel mechanism of pathogenesis relates to exploitation of host cell signaling pathway-PI3K-Akt in particular- by leishmania to create an environment which is permissive to survive inside the host. Our hypothesis is that PI3K functions as a master regulator of innate immunity to leishmania and promotes chronic infection. We will study the molecular mechanism of PI3K-Akt regulation by leishmania. column37: Cancer is a deadly disease. Despite decades of research, cancer remains the leading cause of death worldwide. As early detection and treatment can greatly improve patient outcomes, better diagnostic and therapeutic agents are urgently needed. One method physicians used to diagnose cancers is by giving patients an imaging scan called positron emission tomography. Patients receive a small dose of a radioactive agent, which selectively targets tumours and sends a signal to a detector to pinpoint their location. These imaging agents can be easily modified to carry a more potent radioactive element to kill cancer cells for therapeutic applications. While radioactive imaging/therapeutic agents designed for various cancers have been developed, these existing agents are encumbered by severe limitations. The most common problem is their high accumulation in kidneys. The high accumulation leads to very bright signal coming from kidneys, overshadows nearby small tumours, and makes it harder to detect tumours adjacent to kidneys. Similarly, the high accumulation of the radioactive agents can result in severe damage to kidneys. The goal of this proposed research is to develop a general strategy to minimize accumulation of radioactive imaging and therapeutic agents in kidneys. Most importantly, this strategy is expected to have very broad applicability, and can be used to reduce the high kidney accumulation of most of the previously reported radioactive imaging and therapeutic agents, and facilitate their clinical translation. The success of this research will generate more sensitive imaging agents for cancer detection and more efficacious therapeutic agents with minimized toxicity to kidneys. Overall, the success of this proposed research will significantly improve the diagnosis and prognosis of cancer patients in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Itch is a common features of various cancers, while cancer cells actively secrete factors promoting neuronal infiltration of tumors. The work will take place first in women with large advanced breast tumours and then in women with smaller breast cancers. At the end of the work our goal is to have an ultrasound tool that can be used to determine whether a patient is going to respond favorably to their chemotherapy. column36: Deciphering the role of the newly uncovered dopaminergic pathways to brainstem locomotor circuits in mammals: from cell to behaviour.
column37: Brainstem cells generate the walking command sent to the spinal cord to activate the leg muscles. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine cells die in the brain, resulting in walking deficits. Classically, the connection between dopamine and brainstem cells is considered as solely indirect and to involve intermediary brain regions. However, direct connections between dopaminergic and brainstem cells were recently uncovered. These direct connections promote locomotion in basal vertebrates. In mammals, such connections could play a key role in locomotor control as well. In Parkinson's disease, the loss of such direct connections could be involved in the walking deficits. However, we still do not know the functional role of such direct connections in mammals. Our goal is to identify in mice the locomotor role of the direct connections between dopaminergic cells and brainstem cells. The brainstem cells targeted by the dopaminergic cells will be identified using high-resolution examination of brain anatomy, where the different cells will appear in different colors. Using in vivo optogenetics, we will determine whether turning on these direct dopaminergic connections is sufficient to initiate or speed up locomotion. Using in vivo chemogenetics, we will determine whether turning off these dopaminergic connections impairs gait or stop locomotion. Finally, the cellular mechanisms through which dopamine controls brainstem cells will be identified using patch-clamp electrodes able to detect the electric currents underlying brain cell activities. The proposed project will provide important new knowledge on the mechanisms through which the walking commands are controlled by dopamine in the brain. This knowledge is essential to understand why the walking commands are impaired by the loss of dopaminergic cells in Parkinson's disease. This will allow us to propose new strategies to improve locomotor function in Parkinson's disease and other locomotor disorders.

column37: Invasive fungal infections affect more than 2 million people worldwide annually, and result in death for more than half of these patients. In a healthy immune system, a hormone called GM-CSF activates antifungal defenses to protect against fungal infection. One molecule that controls GM-CSF, called CARD9, appears to be highly important, because humans that have mutations that interfere with the function of CARD9 spontaneously develop life-threatening invasive fungal infections, including of the brain. Although the roles of GM-CSF and of CARD9 in protecting against fungal infections are therefore clear, HOW they protect specific organs is not understood. We believe that these molecules do so by preventing fungus in the gut from escaping into the body. When GM-CSF or CARD9 are malfunctioning, we hypothesize that macrophages in the gut are defective, which allows the fungi normally residing in the gut to escape from the gut tissue and then into specific circulating cells (called monocytes), that then carry the hidden fungus to specific organs, like the brain, leading to life threatening disease. My research aims to understand how GM-CSF and CARD9 enable monocytes and macrophages to combat fungal infections at the level of the gut, blood and brain. I will use innovative cutting-edge techniques to investigate these processes, in whole mice and in cells. This exciting research will provide important and new insights into organ- and cell-specific immunity to fungal infections, opening the door to developing new ways to treat these devastating infections.

column37: Chronic pain can develop in patients with the disease Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Because the central nervous system (spinal cord and brain) is affected in disease like MS-this type of chronic pain is referred to as 'central neuropathic pain' (CNP). CNP affects nearly half of the people with MS and is incredibly distressing. Currently there is no effective treatment for CNP. Finding a treatment that can target the spinal cord or brain directly can be very challenging and comes with the risk of unwanted side effects. On the other hand, the 'peripheral nervous system' (the nerves and cells that reside outside of the spinal cord and brain but communicate with them) is much easier to target, is often more amenable to treatment and is the focus of our proposed research. Our research to date has revealed that sensory neurons which reside in a structure of the peripheral nervous system known as the 'dorsal root ganglion' become stressed when disease affects the spinal cord and brain. Stressed sensory neurons can begin to send inappropriate signals into the central nervous system and we hypothesize that this is a major factor that establishes CNP in diseases like MS. Our studies will examine this at a variety of levels. First, we aim to understand the specific changes that arise in a stressed sensory neuron that can cause it to function inappropriately. We will then examine several novel therapeutic strategies aimed at relieving the stress on the neurons and determine if this will restore normal function and relieve CNP.

column37: In 2014, the World Health Organization labeled antibiotic resistance a "global threat" that requires urgent action. This message has been reinforced by many reports including a UK report, which predicts that if no steps are made to curtail antibiotic resistance, an extra 10 million people a year worldwide will die by 2050. The media has captured the essence of this report with the sound bite "Superbugs to kill 'more than cancer' by 2050". The present situation is indeed alarming in that there are no antibiotics to which bacteria have not developed resistance and many bacteria have multiple resistance mechanisms, making infections caused by superbugs nearly impossible to cure. Aggravating the situation is the fact that for economic reasons, the pharmaceutical industry has largely abandoned new antibiotic drug development. To address this pressing healthcare threat, a multi-pronged approach is required. Most importantly, in addition to curtailing the indiscriminate and unnecessary usage of antibiotics, one crucial aspect to pursue is to study the mechanisms by which bacteria resist the effects of antibiotics and exploit this information for the development of new antibiotic therapies that are less impacted by such resistance mechanisms. Therefore, we will examine in atomic detail how superbugs are resistant to two different classes of antibiotics. We know that these bacteria have dedicated enzymes that detoxify many antibiotics, and the research will reveal how this is exactly achieved. We will than take these insights and explore how we can slightly alter the antibiotics by chemical means so that they can no longer be detoxified, while still retaining their antibiotic properties. Complementary, we will also examine if we can prevent the bacterial enzymes from detoxifying the antibiotics in the first place, using a blocking strategy. Either avenue should provide us with new and much needed solutions for treating infections caused by superbugs.

column37: Les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) sont la cause la plus frequente de deces dans le monde occidental et representent un defit pour la recherche et la medecine moderne. Les MCV sont les manifestations cliniques de l'atherosclerose qui correspond au depot de cholesterol, sous forme de plaque, dans les parois des arteres pouvant causer leur obstruction. La rupture de la plaque atherosclerotique est impliquee dans approximativement 70% d'infarctus fatal du myocarde et/ou de mort subite. Meme si les techniques actuelles de diagnostic de MCV permettent d'evaluer l'etendue de la plaque atherosclerotique et le niveau de stenose arteriel, elles ne permettent pas d'evaluer avec precision la stabilite de la plaque. La stabilite de la plaque atherosclerotique depend fortement du niveau d'inflammation a l'interieur de la plaque. Les resultats de plusieurs travaux suggerent que l'huile d'olive, en reduisant l'inflammation systemique, permet d'augmenter la stabilite de la plaque atherosclerotique. Cependant, il n'existe pas de donnees concernant l'effet de l'huile d'olive sur l'inflammation arterielle qui reste le meilleur marqueur de la fragilite de la plaque. L'imagerie par tomographie d'emission par positrons (TEP) est une technique utilisee en clinique pour, a la fois quantifier l'inflammation au sein de la plaque atherosclerotique mais aussi pour suivre l'effet d'interventions ciblant de ce type d'inflammation. Cependant, le probleme d'accessibilite a ce type d'imagerie et les couts eleves qui lui sont associes limitent son utilisation.
