column36: Ultrasound-Mediated Drug Delivery to the Spinal Cord
column37: The brain and spinal cord have protective barriers that regulate their environment. While these barriers are beneficial in healthy individuals, in patients with brain or spinal cord disorders, these barriers prevent drugs from reaching their target. This work will investigate the use of ultrasound to temporarily open the barrier between the blood vessels and spinal cord in order to deliver drugs more efficiently. Medical ultrasound (US) has many potential therapeutic applications, one of which is facilitating drug delivery in the brain by temporarily opening the barrier between the blood and the brain. This is accomplished when the US interacts with micro-sized gas spheres that are injected in the blood stream and causes them to vibrate, stimulating the blood vessels walls. By focusing the US energy to a small volume, this effect can be directed to specific sites without impacting the surrounding tissue. In the brain, a number of anti-cancer agents have been delivered in preclinical studies using this method and have shown improved effects in combating tumors. In preliminary studies, this technique has also been used to open the barrier to the spinal cord, and recently a positive therapeutic effect was seen in an animal model. We hypothesize that US-based drug delivery can safely increase the therapeutic efficacy of drugs delivered to the spinal cord. In rats, we will examine the effects of ultrasound on the spinal cord, develop methods to safely control the treatment exposures, and test this method as a treatment for spinal cord tumors.Using benchtop measurements and experiments in a large animal model we will also investigate how the human spinal geometry will impact treatment monitoring and control techniques. If this study is successful it could lead to a noninvasive treatment option for patients with spinal cord disease and encourage the investigation of new drug interventions for these conditions.

column37: Systemic sclerosis (SSc), or scleroderma, is a rare, chronic, autoimmune connective tissue disease. Support groups are an important resource for people rare diseases, including SSc, and most support groups are led by people with the disease. Many SSc patients, however, cannot access support groups, and many existing groups are not sustainable due to factors that could be addressed by training peer leaders. Our partners, including Scleroderma Canada and our international partners, are committed to developing an infrastructure to improve the accessibility and effectiveness of SSc support groups. To do this, we have partnered to develop the Scleroderma Support group Leader EDucation (SPIN-SSLED) Program. The SPIN-SSLED Program includes 13 sessions that are delivered to groups of 5 patient group leaders at a time via videoconferencing technology, which allows us to reach leaders who are dispersed across North America and the world. column36: Advancing the methodological frontiers of adaptive treatment strategies
column37: While our current understanding of how well biomedical treatments work is based on population averages, the average effect of a treatment across a population may not be a good indicator of whether or not to recommend a particular treatment for an individual patient. This is because individual patients may respond differently to the same treatment due to their unique combinations of factors such as pre-existing health conditions, genetics, environmental factors, and lifestyle choices. Moreover, a patient may respond differently to the same treatment over time, e.g. as he/she ages. These two types of variability (between individuals and within a single individual over time) motivate the need for targeted treatment plans in which patient care is improved by using information on an individual's changing health status to adapt treatment recommendations accordingly. Examples include the management of chronic conditions, treatments that require frequent adjustments, or clinical decisions based on events such as remissions or intolerable side effects of a drug therapy. This approach, known as precision medicine, relies on "adaptive treatment strategies" where treatment plans account for between and within individual differences over time. The goal is to help physicians deliver the best treatment for each patient each time a treatment decision is made. These strategies provide answers to questions like "If a patient has not responded to an antidepressant, should the dose of that drug be increased, or should a new drug be prescribed?" While the concept of adaptive treatment strategies has existed for more than 2 decades, new statistical methods and tools are needed to gain maximum insight from contemporary "big data" datasets and to accommodate new treatments that have been developed . My research goals for the next 7 years are to advance statistical theory and develop the needed methods and tools for answering clinically relevant questions related to HIV and mental health.

column36: Frailty and the Kidney Transplant Wait List
column37: Many people with advanced kidney disease will benefit from a kidney transplant. Some people are not eligible because they are have health conditions that put them at a high risk of dying before receiving a transplant or high risk of deteriorating health after a transplant. Deciding who is able to receive a transplant involves a detailed evaluation of a person's health and a review by transplant specialists. Some people with kidney disease who are being considered for a kidney transplant have difficulties in their health, mobility or function that put them at a risk for a shortened lifespan. This is often referred to as frailty. Currently, we do not know how being frail might affect the health of those who are waiting for a kidney transplant. Knowing this information could be helpful in a number of ways. It would provide transplant specialists with information to allow them to make an informed, objective decision about whether patients should be put on the wait list and not rely solely on their clinical impression. It would also provide a more complete picture of a person's overall health in addition to the tests that are currently used to better inform patients who are deciding about being put on the wait list. In this study, we aim to examine what happens to people who are frail and wait listed for a kidney transplant compared with those who are not frail. We will use several different tools to assess frailty. We will follow patients to see if they die or are removed from the wait list before they can receive a transplant in addition to a number of other important outcomes such as being admitted to hospital or changes in their quality of life. We hope that the results of this study may lead to better allocation of kidney transplant organs and a more objective method of evaluating eligibility for the wait list.

column36: Studying telomeres maintenance by telomerase using live cell imaging
column37: In order to properly grow and divide, normal cells must maintain the integrity of their genome. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and are essential to maintain their stability. Telomere shortening leads to genomic instability and favors the rise of cancers. In most eukaryotes, telomerase is a specialized enzyme used to elongate telomeres. Most of our knowledge on telomerase relies on the detection of its activity in large populations of cells. However, little is known about the behavior of telomerase in single cells, as it acts on a single telomere. For this purpose, we developed an assay to image both telomerase molecules and telomere in single living cells, using the budding yeast as a model organism. Using this approach, the events leading to the recruitment of telomerase at a single short telomere will be studied in real time, in single cells. We will particularly focus on the role of sister telomeres cohesion during telomerase recruitment at short telomeres. We will explore how telomerase is regulated in a telomere-specific manner by focusing especially on its interaction with telomeric repeat-containing noncoding RNA (TERRA). Finally, we will use live cell imaging to study the dynamics of telomerase molecules and their recruitment at telomeres in living human cancer cells. Identifying the pathways involved in the regulation of telomerase and telomeres will help understand how tumors arise and develop into cancer, and also reveal new potential targets for cancer therapy.

column36: Ski is a negative regulator of cardiac fibrosis
column37: Patients surviving a heart attack or those with hypertension develop chronic heart disease. These patients make too much collagen in their heart muscle, wherein non-muscle cells called myofibroblasts secrete excessive collagens, which stiffens the heart. Most of the "glue" (extracellular matrix) between muscle cells in healthy hearts is made of tough collagen proteins. Too much collagen leads to cardiac fibrosis which results in weak muscle contraction and relaxation. Despite this, there is currently no treatment for cardiac fibrosis, nor are there any specific cardiac drugs approved to fix cardiac fibrosis. In recent years, we have found a new protein called Ski. Ski turns off this over-deposition of matrix, in diseased heart cells. Further, we have made progress of how Ski actually achieves this positive change. We are now poised to extend our understanding of how Ski corrects cardiac fibrosis. We discovered that Ski is able to deactivate cells that cause fibrosis, and this is associated with normal control of the extracellular matrix; but our also work shows that Ski somehow is redirected and lost in heart failure. So, we hypothesize that loss of Ski's function in sick hearts may contribute to cardiac fibrosis and speed up the onset of heart disease - our experiments will test this hypothesis directly in mice wherein we specifically turn off Ski in cells making extracellular matrix. Finally we hypothesize that Ski turns off the function of special proteins that normally promote fibrosis in sick hearts. Experiments designed to answer this will show the mechanism of Ski's beneficial effects. Thus we will tease out and develop our understanding of how Ski protein influences the progression of cardiac fibrosis, and how this work will allow us to design new Ski-based therapies to treat cardiac fibrosis, for the prevention of heart failure.

column36: Harnessing neuroinflammation to develop new treatments for multiple sclerosis and glioblastoma
column37: In response to insults, the body launches an immune response to eradicate the threat and instigate tissue repair. Unfortunately, chronic excessive inflammation leads to tissue damage while dampened immune responses may favor the development of tumors. My research programs are centered on inflammation within the brain and spinal cord, termed neuroinflammation. I focus my research activities on multiple sclerosis (MS) and glioblastoma (the most malignant and deadly form of brain tumor), where MS exhibits chronic neuroinflammation that destroys cells within the brain and spinal cord, and glioblastoma has suppressed immunity that allows brain tumor cells to escape detection and being killed. Indeed, brain tumor cells change the nature of immune cells and exploit them for cancer growth. My research programs thus seek to: 1) stop immune cells from going into the brain and spinal cord to inflict injury in MS, and neutralize the injury that immune cells can produce within the brain/spinal cord; 2) understand and harness the beneficial aspects of the immune system to facilitate the repair of myelin, particularly in aging subjects where the newly formed myelin can protect nerve fibers and thus slow the progression of disability in MS; and 3) rejuvenate the compromised immune system in glioblastoma in order that immune cells can perform their evolutionary function of fighting threats and eliminate the brain tumor. Thus, rather than considering MS and glioblastoma as distinct entities that should not be researched together, I have taken the unique approach of removing the silos from these diseases to study them together. By understanding why they lie on opposite ends of a spectrum, the lessons and drugs acquired in MS can be used to inform and treat glioblastoma, and vice versa. Thus, the overall research seeks to acquire new knowledge and enable recovery from devastating MS and glioblastoma.

column36: Cognitive Control and Vulnerability to Major Depressive Disorder
column37: Depression is a highly recurrent disorder, underscoring the need to identify risk factors for relapse. Cognitive control involves a set of cognitive processes that allow selective processing of information, which includes inhibiting irrelevant information, shifting from one task to another, and updating working memory. People with depression have difficulty exerting cognitive control over emotional information, and these cognitive difficulties are associated with functional and occupational impairment. People who have recovered from depression do not exhibit cognitive control dysfunction. However, negative mood or stress may activate depressive cognitive processes, such that during periods of mood decline, previously depressed people have difficulty controlling the processing of emotional information, thereby increasing risk of prolonged negative mood and relapse to depression. The objectives of this study are to evaluate the hypotheses that: 1) previously depressed people will show impairments in cognitive control over emotional information when in a negative mood state compared to a baseline mood state; and 2) mood-induced impairments in cognitive control will predict relapse to depression. A sample of currently, remitted, and never depressed individuals will complete computer tasks to assess the primary components of cognitive control: inhibition, set-shifting, and updating. Tasks will be administered in a baseline mood state in one study session and after a negative mood induction in a second session, which will allow us to evaluate cognitive processing in response to negative mood. Remitted depressed participants will enter a 1-year follow-up period during which they will be assessed every 2 weeks for depression. This study will test a novel cognitive risk factor for the recurrence of depression, which can help us to identify people who are most at risk of relapse, and develop targeted treatment approaches to reduce this risk.

column36: Cytoneme-mediated growth signalling in Drosophila
column37: The growth of embryonic tissues is controlled by "growth factors" that are produced by discrete populations of cells, move through the tissues, and stimulate cells at a distance to grow and divide. column37: According to the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one the largest threats to public health and economic growth. Recently, the WHO for the first time divided pathogens into three categories according to the urgency of need for new antibiotics: critical, high and medium priority. The most critical group of all includes multidrug resistant bacteria that pose a particular threat in hospitals, nursing homes, and among patients whose care requires devices such as ventilators and blood catheters. They include Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas and various Enterobacteriaceae that cause severe and often deadly infections such as bloodstream infections and pneumonia. Despite significant investments by industry and academia into antibiotic discovery and development over the past decades, no new antibiotic class with novel mode(s) of action to fight these pathogens has been approved in half a century. The reasons for this failure have been identified and are caused by the inability of current compounds to penetrate into bacteria (low permeability) and their likelihood of being pumped out (efflux). To overcome this bottleneck in antibacterial drug discovery, we plan to develop helper molecules (adjuvants) designed to enhance membrane permeability, reduce efflux of antibiotics and prevent or delay resistance development against these pathogens. The overall goal of this proposal is to identify optimized helper molecules capable of rescuing antibiotics from resistance in animal models of infection against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens and to understand their mode of actions.

column36: Regulation of cerebral blood flow in obstructive sleep apnea
column37: In healthy humans, brain blood flow is influenced by changes in the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the circulating blood. However, the brain's important ability to regulate its blood flow is impaired in disease processes such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). People who have OSA stop breathing intermittently throughout the night, resulting in repeated episodes of low oxygen and high carbon dioxide in the blood. Because of these repeated episodes, the ability of the brain vessels to regulate blood flow becomes impaired. This impairment can lead to hypertension and stroke. The mechanisms that regulate brain blood flow in health, and how these mechanisms become impaired with disease, is poorly understood. It is thought that nitric oxide (NO) plays a major role in regulating blood flow in several vascular beds, including the brain. In a first study, we will determine, in an experimental human model of intermittent hypoxia during sleep, the effects of intermittent hypoxia on the regulation of brain blood flow and the role of changes in brain blood flow on the stability of breathing. In a second study, we will determine the extent to which the brain blood flow response to low oxygen is altered in a broad range of patients with moderate to severe OSA. Finally, our research will determine if the brain blood flow impairments observed in untreated OSA patients can be corrected after treatment with night-time continuous positive airway pressure. This work may help us better understand conditions such as hypertension, OSA, stroke and aging, in which endothelium-dependent relaxation (i.e., relaxation of cells that line brain blood vessels) by NO is impaired. Our research will provide useful information about how well treatment for OSA reverses brain blood flow impairments that may lead to stroke. Ultimately, this will translate into improved health and disease prevention for Canadians.

column37: IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis (GN), a major cause of kidney failure. Using samples from patients with known outcome from multiple clinical centres, urine peptides associated with response to specific treatment will be identified. An algorithm to predict response based on the urinary peptides and relevant variables, will be developed and tested in an independent sample. If the algorithm enabling personalized intervention shows benefit, a well-powered exploratory trial will support implementation in routine care. The Canadian arm includes expansion of a web-based data collection tool, designed for multi-centre translational research in GN. Scales will be refined through cognitive patient interviews and expert input. In Phase 2, preliminary scales will be administered to a large international sample of transgender people. Phase 3 involves studies to examine responsiveness to change for a range of gender-affirming treatments. Phase 4 involves implementing the GENDER-Q into clinical practice for use in patient care. column36: Development of a therapeutic modality to treat GM2 gangliosidoses
column37: Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff Disease (also knows as the GM2 gangliosidoses) are inherited neurodegenerative diseases that result from genetic mutations that inactivate an enzyme known as HexA. HexA is a protein in our cells that degrades GM2-ganglioside (GM2), a molecule found primarily on neurons of the central and peripheral nervous system. HexA degrades GM2, and if it is not active, GM2 rapidly accumulates and causes severe neurological disease. The rate of GM2 accumulation depends on how severely the genetic mutations impact HexA activity. Totally inactive HexA leads to rapid GM2 accumulation and death by 1-4 years of age; whereas, mutations that allow for some residual HexA activity (1-10% of normal), GM2 accumulation is slowed and disease progression is delayed. While still neurologically debilitating, these late-onset forms of the disease may not significantly impact lifespan. Importantly, HexA activity as low as 10% can prevent, and possibly reverse, GM2 accumulation and the associated neurodegeneration. We hypothesize that a therapy for infantile and late-onset forms of GM2 gangliosidosis is achievable by supplementing patients with active Hex enzyme (i.e. enzyme replacement therapy), and in late-onset cases, combing enzyme replacement with drugs known to boost residual Hex activity to bring the total Hex activity above the critical 10% activity threshold. We have recently engineered HexA to markedly improve its stability and function for enzyme replacement therapy. We now propose to use the engineered enzyme, known as HexM, to develop an enzyme replacement therapy that will be evaluated in mouse models of GM2 gangliosidosis in combination with a drug known to rescue residual HexA activity in cells. Our approach holds promise to reduce GM2 accumulation and reverse the progression of this debilitating family of neurological diseases.

column36: Regulation of chaperone-mediated proteostasis by STI1
column37: Proteins need help to attain their three dimensional structure and their abnormal folding is linked to many neurodegenerative diseases. To help nerve cells deal with abnormally folded proteins and other types of cellular stresses during aging, organisms evolved a set of chaperone and co-chaperone proteins that are present from yeast to humans. Chaperones such as Hsp70 and Hsp90 bind to proteins to help them to stabilize a given conformation; these proteins are known as "clients" of chaperones. A protein named Stress-inducible phosphoprotein I or STI1 interacts with Hsp70 and Hsp90 and it is critical to regulate the activity of the chaperone network. We find that decreased levels of STI1 in mice affects proteins that are stabilized by Hsp70/Hsp90 and causes age-dependent degeneration of neurons. Our experiments also show that certain proteins involved in neurodegenerative diseases are stabilized by STI1, and that STI1 can protect against toxic effects of these proteins by moonlighting outside cells. Our proposed research will investigate whether increasing STI1 levels may protect against age-dependent neurodegeneration and the abnormal folding of alpha-synuclein, a protein that is critical in Parkinson's disease. This work may provide new ways to help neurons to become resilient to stress and to deal with misfolded proteins that can cause neurodegeneration.

column36: The role of chronic stress and sleep reactivity in the persistence of insomnia over time.
column37: While many individuals experience transient sleep disturbances, about 9% of the Canadian population suffers from chronic insomnia. Although stress is recognized as a common cause for the onset of insomnia, the role of chronic stress in the maintenance of insomnia over time is less well understood. One reason is that there are individual differences in stress reactivity; that is, some people experience stronger bodily responses to stress than others. This means that some individuals are more vulnerable to experience insomnia in response to stress than others. Furthermore, most of the past studies have not examined the types of stressors that are chronic in nature. Moreover, some studies suggest that not only can stress lead to poor sleep, but poor sleep is also associated with increased stress. To better understand the role of chronic stress in insomnia, we will follow a group of insomniacs who will receive a psychological treatment for insomnia. At the beginning of the study, insomniacs will complete assessments of chronic stress, stress reactivity, and current insomnia symptoms. Then, the participants will be assigned to either a cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia or to a waiting period. Changes in insomnia and chronic stress will be assessed after treatment as well as 12 months later. This study will allow us to examine whether chronic stress is related to changes in insomnia over time, whether insomnia treatment reduces chronic stress, and whether individuals with high stress reactivity are more susceptible to the impact of chronic stress on sleep. Our overall goal is to identify a subgroup of insomniacs more susceptible to the impact of chronic stress on insomnia that may benefit from treatment targeting stress reactivity.

column37: As we move about in our environment during regular everyday activities (e.g., walking to work), we constantly rely on signals sent from our inner ear to our brain. Their signals are then processed by the brain, which gives us our sense of balance and perception of our body's orientation in space. Unfortunately, patients suffering from vestibular disorders experience dizziness, imbalance, and an increased risk of falls - all symptoms that profoundly impair quality of life, which imposes a substantial burden on the economy in the form of increased medical costs, work-related absenteeism, and reduced productivity. Unfortunately, almost all previous studies of vestibular processing have used low amplitude sinusoidal head movements that have nothing to do with the signals experience during our everyday lives (e.g., when walking). Here we will instead investigate how single and multiple vestibular neurons encode self-motion signals experienced naturally. Our results will yield new knowledge that will revolutionize our understanding of how the brain processes vestibular input that is experienced during natural everyday activities (e.g., walking), which will yield better treatment options for patients suffering from vestibular disorders.

column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects more than 16% of Canadian adults and results in more than $27.5 billion in annual economic burden. The knee is the most commonly affected joint, and people with knee OA report chronic pain, physical dysfunction, and reduced quality of life. Maintaining an active lifestyle is advocated for all patients with knee OA. Recreational running (jogging) is enjoyed by millions of Canadians as an inexpensive and effective means to remain physically active. However, many former runners have stopped running upon receiving a diagnosis of knee OA, and many current runners would stop running if they were to receive a similar diagnosis. Further, many people choose not to take up running in order to protect their knees. These beliefs are based on a fear of causing joint damage and/or speeding up disease progression. This information can be used to refine strategies such as running modification that can help to prevent the onset of knee OA for many physically-active individuals.

column36: Determining The Architecture Of Genetic Disease: Statistical Methods and Applications
column37: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) affects children and is caused by the gene CFTR. Many different changes (i.e. mutations) in CFTR can cause disease, and an effective medicine for 4% of individuals with one type of CFTR mutation is now available. However, recent efforts to identify drugs for other mutations have resulted in more modest improvements; and the majority of individuals with CF have no approved CFTR-targeting medicine. Alternative drugs that could lead to better outcomes are needed. CF affects the normal functioning of several organs resulting in co-morbidities and progressive lung disease which ultimately leads to premature death. Not every individual with CF has an equally severe course of disease. For example, only 15% are born with intestinal obstruction and there is significant variability in lung disease across patients. These differences are due to other genes, called modifier genes. Designing modifier-targeting medicines could be an effective strategy to treat CF, independent of the CFTR mutation. We are leaders in modifier gene research, and we have identified several that influence CF disease severity. For one modifier, we have learned how it influences different CF-affected organs and how it works in concert with CFTR; we have recently partnered with industry to develop a therapy targeting this modifier. The other modifiers have been much more difficult to study because, until now, we have not had the genetic information necessary. In this foundation grant we are proposing to identify the changes in the modifier genes that could impact CF disease severity using new genome sequencing technologies. We are developing statistical models that can combine the genetic changes we identify with experimental data, paving the way towards more modifier-targeting medicines. We are ensuring broad impact by developing computer software for other researchers to use and we are applying the methods ourselves to studies in epilepsy.

column37: Our bodies have systems in the blood that co-ordinately respond to injuries: the blood clotting system controls bleeding, and the immune system removes damaged cells and infection. If these systems are out of balance due to genetic or environmental factors, bleeding may persist or too much clotting may occur; infections may spread or too much inflammation may cause organ damage. Such imbalances are manifest as disease (e.g. heart disease, stroke, venous thrombosis, atherosclerosis, haemophilia). A major trigger of these systems is a protein called Tissue Factor (TF). Indeed, such information will help in designing treatments to correct imbalances that may cause disease. The mice will be challenged by inducing blood clots and inflammation to replicate what happens in humans. We expect that reducing CD248 in one or the other cell, will be protective. In other experiments, we will figure out how CD248 participates with TF and its partners in controlling blood clotting and inflammation. We hope our results will yield new information for the design of better therapies for patients who otherwise suffer from immune and/or clotting & bleeding disorders.

column37: During aging, the human mortality rate rises exponentially as a result of a loss of normal organ functions. column36: Manipulating the neuroimmune response to promote spinal cord repair
column37: Over four million individuals are afflicted by different types of spinal cord injury (SCI). One of the consequences of SCI is the loss of neural tissue at the site of injury. This results in an inflammatory response characterized by the entry of immune cells that are essential for the clearance of cellular debris. It has been assumed that during this process the inflammatory response may also contribute to secondary bystander damage in the spinal cord, causing the death of neighbouring neurons and myelin-producing cells called oligodendrocytes. As a consequence of this, both lesion volume and demyelination increase with time. Because of the inability of the human spinal cord to repair itself, damages sustained after injury often lead to permanent functional deficits for which no cure is currently available. Among the factors that mediate neuroinflammation are molecules normally found within cells that get released upon cell lysis. These intracellular host molecules, called danger signals or alarmins, include the inflammatory protein interleukin (IL)-1 alpha and nucleotides. IL-1 alpha and nucleotides are normally sequestrated inside cells, where they participate in gene expression regulation. However, when released after cell damage and death, they become powerful activators of neuroinflammation. We recently discovered that in addition to its role in inflammation, IL-1 alpha can act on oligodendrocytes to reduce their expression of genes coding for cell survival. Our results also revealed that nucleotides, as well as possibly other alarmins, stimulate microglia to form a rim between infiltrating immune cells and reactive astrocytes, a response that we called the 'microglial scar' and which we believe plays a key role in regulating axon regeneration and plasticity. The main goal of this research proposal is to identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in these responses and to utilize this knowledge to promote spinal cord repair after injury.

column36: Molecular basis of PPM1A controlled macrophage apoptosis in tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB), a contagious respiratory disease of the lung caused by inhaling the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is responsible for over 2 million deaths each year, establishing it as one of the leading causes of infectious disease-related deaths worldwide. Inhaled Mtb are engulfed by special cells in the lung called macrophages, which normally kill invading bacteria. However, Mtb reprograms host macrophages to deprive their killing ability, allowing the bacteria to remain hidden from the immune response and protected from drug therapy while inside these cells. Host-directed therapy, which targets host cell proteins rather than the bacteria itself offers a promising alternative treatment for TB as this strategy will circumvent development of antibiotic resistance and the need for drugs to penetrate the impermeable Mtb cell wall. We have identified PPM1A as critical host protein produced by macrophages that is exploited by Mtb to shut down the killing function of these immune cells. In this proposal, we will (1) elucidate the mechanisms regulating PPM1A expression during Mtb infection, and (2) characterize PPM1A associated signaling proteins that allow the bacteria to survive inside the cell. These approaches will identify and characterize key host proteins involved in the PPM1A signaling pathway that could be targeted for host-directed TB therapy. Finally, we will (3) examine the feasibility of targeting PPM1A to restore and improve the ability of macrophages to kill Mtb in vivo. This research will advance host-directed therapies aimed at eliminating TB.

Despite improvements in short-term outcome, long-term patient and graft survival remain suboptimal due to the toxic side effects associated with long-term use of these immune suppression drugs. Our preliminary study show that this circular RNA was over-expressed in long term survival recipients and immune suppressive cells. This study aims to understand the role of this circular RNA in heart transplantation. We will investigate the effect of this circular RNA on immune cells in vitro using cell culture system. We will then investigate the effect of this circular RNA in vivo on preventing immune rejection in heart transplantation using a mouse transplantation model. Finally we will investigate how this circular RNA functions. The proposed study will provide better understanding of this RNA and its role in heart transplantation. It will also help in the development of new treatments for prevent allograft rejection.

column36: Brain oscillations in the dynamic pain connectome
column37: Pain is a major public health issue and societal problem that affects millions of Canadians (more than those with heart disease, cancer, and diabetes combined), costs >$43B annually and is difficult to treat when chronic because it is not well understood. We developed a concept called the Dynamic Pain Connectome (DPC) that emphasizes the flexibility of connections between brain networks that are involved in the processing and modulation of pain, attention and salience. The DPC has only been studied with functional MRI, whose signals arise from slow blood flow changes that indirectly relate to activity in neurons. To understand the timing of communication in the DPC, an approach like magnetoencephalograhy (MEG) is needed because it measures fast brain signals every millisecond and directly reflects neuronal activity. The brain uses temporal codes to represent perception. Neurons in the brain have spontaneous (ongoing) activity that provides a baseline from which responses to a given situation can arise and so contributes to behavioural responsivity and sensitivity. Neuronal firing pattern signatures on millisecond timescales characterize brain regions, and aberrant firing patterns can reflect pathology in disease states. Temporal dynamics in the DPC may code for chronic pain and for sensing, processing, modulation, and response to pain. Thus, the goal of this project is to measure DPC regional activity on a fine temporal scale with MEG to characterize the DPC in health and chronic pain conditions. Characterizing MEG activity in the DPC will provide 1) fundamental knowledge of regional activity and how it reflects individual pain sensitivity, 2) a framework to characterize communication between brain regions in the DPC, and 3) insight into aberrant activity that characterizes chronic pain. In the future, methods that stimulate the brain could be developed to normalize aberrant activity in the DPC as a strategy to manage chronic pain.

column36: Does residential proximity to natural environments impact the mental health and well-being of participants of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging?
column37: Over 80% of Canadians live in urban areas, where they may be exposed regularly to traffic congestion, heat islands, and air and noise pollution. Natural features within built environments, including green spaces and views of open water, have the potential to mitigate the adverse effects of these stresses of urban living. For example, measures of green vegetation have been associated with reductions in: negative perceptions of noise, temperatures from urban heat islands, concentrations of air pollution, stress, and mortality rates. Although previous studies have suggested that exposures to natural environments can benefit levels of well-being, there remains a lack of strong evidence. The goal of this study is to describe the association among Canadian adults between residential exposure to natural environments and indicators of positive well-being (i.e., satisfaction with life, absence of depression and sleep disorders). For this, we will use data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA), which is a national-level study of approximately 51,000 Canadians who were aged 45 to 85 years old at baseline. The CLSA includes information on sociodemographic, biological, medical, psychological, social, and economic characteristics. We will use data describing the presence of green vegetation from both an aerial view and from the street view, along with a dataset of water features, around each participant's residential postal code, as estimates of exposure to natural environments. Our results will identify whether older Canadians living in areas with more green and natural spaces around their homes also have better levels of well-being. Our analyses will also take into consideration factors such as age, sex, income, and evidence of clinical depression, season of sampling, retirement status, and social support.

column36: Exploring New Graduate Nurses' Transition into Critical Care Nursing Practice
column37: It can be difficult for a new graduate nurse to transition into the role of registered nurse. New graduates report feelings of uncertainty, insecurity and generally feeling overwhelmed. These nurses are the most at risk for leaving the nursing profession because they may feel like they are not adequately prepared to work independently and may not feel supported in their new roles or job settings. New graduate nurses who work in critical care practice areas like the emergency department and the intensive care unit, are even more vulnerable and at risk for leaving jobs than graduate nurses working elsewhere. Critical care practice areas are very fast paced and unpredictable; the patients these nurses care for are extremely ill and are often experiencing life threatening situations. In an effort to better understand the experiences of these new graduate nurses, this project will explore what it is like for them to transition into their roles as registered nurses practicing in the critical care areas of the emergency department and the intensive care unit. Our research team will thoroughly review the literature currently published on this topic and the team will survey and interview new graduate nurses working in emergency and intensive care across Canada in order to gain an in-depth understanding of their experiences. The new knowledge that we gain from this study will be used to create a national guideline, in collaboration with the Canadian Association of Critical Care Nurses and the National Emergency Nurses Association, with the aim of better supporting new graduate nurses who become employed in these critical care practice areas.

column36: Exploring and Exploiting Reduced USP22 Expression in Colorectal Cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada, and although advances in treatment options have improved the overall survival for early stage CRCs, ~50% of individuals are still diagnosed with late stage disease that is often incurable. The development of highly specific, anti-cancer treatments is a significant research challenge; however, recent efforts suggest that exploiting the mutated genes and abnormal pathways that drive cancer development may hold tremendous clinical potential. Accordingly, greater insight into the mutated genes and abnormal pathways driving CRC formation is needed so that new treatment strategies and drug options can be developed that exploit them. Mutations in specific genes cause genome instability, which is an early step in the development of most CRCs. Genome instability often leads to abnormal numbers of chromosomes (structural elements that contain the DNA or genes) that further promote cancer development. We believe that to create new, effective chemotherapeutic options requires a deeper understanding of the abnormal genes and pathways driving CRC formation. In this regard, emerging data have identified a gene (USP22) that we suspect is a driver of CRC. Data from patient samples shows that USP22 is altered in ~50% of CRCs, while our pilot studies show that reduced expression causes genome instability and is associated with changes in chromosome numbers, which collectively suggest that abnormal expression may play a key role in CRC. To explore this possibility, we will employ newly generated and disease relevant models along with leading-edge genetic and cell biology techniques to gain unprecedented insight into USP22 and its role in CRC development. We will exploit this information to identify novel drug targets and lead chemotherapeutics that we will test in pre-clinical studies to ideally and ultimately deliver new therapeutic options to individuals diagnosed with CRC.

column36: Genomics of antimicrobial resistance and drug/target discovery
column37: Pathogens and their human hosts are locked in an evolutionary arms race. Humans are fighting back with better drugs, but the pathogens adapt to evolve drug resistance. As a result, the medicines become ineffective and infections persist in the body, increasing the risk of spread to others. We have entered in an era of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a phenomenon of serious public health concern. If nothing is done by 2050 it will have cost $100 trillion and 10M people/yr are expected to die. Our research program will address this issue. We propose to investigate at the whole genome level how a microorganism becomes resistant. In order to achieve this we will conduct high throughput sequencing of resistant microorganisms. We will complement these data with a series of powerful chemogenomic screens developed in the laboratory. These screens are niched and complementary, offering a holistic view of AMR. The output data will be integrated using bioinformatics pipeline to generate a complete map of genes/mutations necessary to achieve resistance. The role of these mutations will each be evaluated experimentally. This knowledge will be used to implement new diagnostics approaches using machine learning. It will also lead to novel drug targets against new promising drug candidates and to novel more effective treatments of infectious diseases.

column36: Reshaping the cancer clinic: Genomics-driven clinical trials and the evanescent boundary between research and treatment
column37: The nature and scope of genomic initiatives in the cancer domain has expanded dramatically in recent years. A shift from the initial focus on diagnosis to the development of targeted drugs and novel immunotherapies has given renewed meaning to notions such as personalized or precision medicine. The exploration, validation and testing of these therapies in clinical trials, their approval by regulators, and the necessary articulation of novel approaches with established clinical practices raise, however, a number of major organizational, regulatory, and sociotechnical issues, which in turn call for innovative solutions. These often-controversial solutions include the redesign of clinical trials in connection with the deployment of novel analytical platforms, new organizational infrastructures, and revised conceptual perspectives. The purpose of our project is to provide an analytical understanding of this intricate process, based on a detailed empirical investigation of the aforementioned initiatives. In particular, we seek to analyze how fundamental changes in the social, organizational, and conceptual configuration of clinical trials, the gold standard of modern medicine, are expressed in new collective modes of practice and interaction. A number of observers have expressed concerns about the premature adoption of genomic techniques or the dire consequences of delaying it. Our analysis of clinical research will provide the grounds for exploring these issues and thus offer both oncologists and healthcare analysts implements with which to better frame genomic medicine initiatives.

column37: Self-harm among youth is a major public health concern. This information is essential in order to design better services and supports for this population. Youth with a history of engaging in self-harming behaviours and their families will be interviewed. Healthcare and social service providers and school counsellors will also be interviewed. This study will engage youth who self-harm, their families and service providers and provide them an opportunity to more fully articulate their experiences and develop a shared vision of care for those affected, whose voices are virtually absent in healthcare research and practice. This study is a necessary initial step of a first of its kind research program aimed at advancing patient-oriented service delivery and outcomes for youth who self-harm.

column36: Taking the "idiopathic" out of scoliosis: from biology and genetics to non-invasive therapies
column37: Idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a poorly understood disorder characterized by rotational spine deformity that typically arises during adolescence in otherwise healthy individuals. AIS afflicts 4% of children worldwide and in severe cases (predominantly females) can produce chronic back pain, disfigurement and functional disability. First described by Hippocrates, scoliosis is the oldest birth defect known to humankind. Historically, AIS was thought to result from defects in bone or cartilage development. However, despite decades of intense research, the causes of AIS remain unknown and, as a result, treatment options are limited to archaic measures like prolonged bracing and/or invasive corrective surgery. Our poor understanding of AIS stems largely from a lack of appropriate animal models. Human upright posture, with head-to-toe spine compression, contributes greatly to scoliosis progression. However, most lab animals walk on four legs and the structure, center of gravity, and biomechanical loading of their spines differ radically from humans. Fish, however, experience head-to-tail spinal loads generated by swimming forward through water. The zebrafish, in particular, has emerged as a powerful animal for studying human birth defects and disease, and my lab has pioneered the use of zebrafish for modeling human AIS. Remarkably, we discovered an "inside-out" cause of AIS - where defects in the movement of fluid through ventricles of the brain and spinal cord ultimately cause spine curvature. We have even identified non-invasive pharmaceutical therapies that might block scoliosis. Here, we apply our unique zebrafish models to define the full range of mechanisms driving scoliosis, and to identify genetic causes of human disease. We screen for more powerful drugs that block scoliosis, and translate our findings towards clinical applications. Proposed studies thus hold tremendous potential to improve the lives of Canadians diagnosed with AIS and related spine deformities.

column36: Towards a patient-centered system: Integrating preferences of patients with osteoarthritis into evaluation of health services interventions to improve patient outcomes and health system efficiency
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic disease affecting 10-15% of Canada's population. It causes severe pain and disability, and is the leading cause of joint replacement surgery. Healthcare service planning does not currently consider patient preferences and its impact on health interventions. This could lead to the introduction of programs that patients do not use, which is a waste of system resources. The explicit consideration of evidence from patient-preferences in assessing uptake of health services and the impact on wait times, patient outcomes and costs is essential to inform the design of effective patient-centered health services delivery. In previous work by our team, we built a simulation model that captures OA patient flows, healthcare resource use and costs. We will measure individual patient preferences, and incorporate these into the simulation model. Then, we will use it evaluate how patient outcomes and system performance will be altered when new health interventions are implemented, taking into account how many patients would choose those interventions. We will look at two different policies aimed at addressing wait times for surgery. The first is a referral management policy which would give patients information about wait times for different surgeons, and allows them to choose their preferred surgeon or the surgeon with the shortest wait time. The second policy offers patients the choice of an evidence-based conservative medical management program. Our study will look at whether patients would take up this alternative program and how this varies by characteristics of the program such as its cost. Depending on patient choices, both policies may shorten overall wait times, improve outcomes and reduce costs. Our team of OA clinicians, decision makers, researchers, patients and analysts has the expertise and engagement to ensure our research is clinically meaningful and is translated into patient-centred policy and practice.

column36: Perineuronal nets-mediated regulation of spinal nociceptive circuits
column37: In the nervous system, neurons and glial cells are embedded within a network of molecules called the extracellular matrix (ECM). The ECM components provide structural support, regulate synapse formation and function, and modulate neuronal excitability. In the brain, the ECM restricts neuroplasticity; thus, enzymatic digestion of the ECM enhances acquisition of memories and promotes cognitive flexibility and extinction. In the pain pathway, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), the major ECM-digesting enzymes, are activated in neuropathic pain conditions to promote mechanical hypersensitivity. However, it remains unknown whether this remodelling of the spinal cord ECM contributes to pathological changes in dorsal horn nociceptive circuits and pain hypersensitivity. We hypothesize that, similar to cognitive functions, the ECM restrains spinal plasticity and its remodelling facilitates the sensitization of nociceptive circuits. One of the major forms of the ECM found in the nervous system is perineuronal nets (PNNs). PNNs are densely packed network of the ECM located around cell bodies and proximal dendrites, predominantly enwrapping a subset of inhibitory interneurons. Inhibitory neurons have been shown to suppress nociceptive circuits' activation in the dorsal horn. Interestingly, digestion of PNNs around inhibitory neurons decreases their inhibitory activity. This raises the hypothesis that the digestion of PNNs in neuropathic pain sensitizes spinal cord central circuits by decreasing the activity of the inhibitory neurons. We will study the remodeling of spinal PNNs in neuropathic and inflammatory pain, and examine whether the degradation of PNNs surrounding inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord contributes to hyperexcitability. In summary, we will test the intriguing hypothesis that the ECM in the spinal cord restricts neuroplasticity, and that the remodeling of the ECM in neuropathic pain conditions contributes to the hypersensitivity.

column36: Dysregulation of eIF2a-dependent translational control in Fragile X syndrome and autism spectrum disorders
column37: Despite the prevalence of neuropsychiatric disorders, the progress in understanding the pathophysiology and the development of effective therapies is very slow. Thus, the development of new therapies for Fragile-X Syndrome (FXS) and Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) is imperative. Dysregulation of translation has been documented in several mouse models of autism and FXS. Previous studies have focused on the mTOR and ERK pathways in mediating the aberrant translation in these disorders. An additional key signaling pathway controlling translation is the integrated stress response (ISR) pathway regulated via phosphorylation of the a subunit of eIF2. The function of ISR in the pathophysiology of autism has not been investigated. Our preliminary data indicate that eIF2a phosphorylation is reduced in the brain of Fmr1 KO mice and in other mouse models of autism. In the proposed project, we will examine the hypothesis that dysregulation of eIF2a-dependent translational control leads to an altered repertoire of proteins in the mouse model of Fragile X syndrome and conceivable other models of ASD, underlying abnormal synaptic function and behavioural deficits. A better understanding of the eIF2a phosphorylation-dependent translational control in autism might lead to the development of more targeted and efficient therapeutics for several forms of autism, where this pathway is dysregulated.

column36: Optimizing hospital-to-home transitional care to promote functioning in older persons with dementia in rural communities
column37: During and after a hospital stay, older people with dementia are at risk of losing the ability to function independently in everyday activities like getting up and dressing themselves. If they do not get back to functioning independently within one month of coming home, they are unlikely to ever do so. Transitional care refers to the healthcare services people receive to ensure their needs continue to be met as they move from hospital to home. Most transitional care studies excluded older people with dementia and their families and did not focus on helping people get back to functioning in everyday activities. In addition, the few studies that focused on functioning excluded rural communities. These exclusions have resulted in gaps in knowledge to guide practice and policy for this population. This study will address these gaps. We reviewed the research literature and found six practical care strategies that are likely to be helpful. In this study, we will invite older people with dementia who were discharged from hospital and their families in rural areas in Ontario and Nova Scotia to tell us what they think about the care strategies. We will ask them if the care strategies fit their needs and how to improve the care strategies so that they better fit their needs. Then, we will bring these care strategies forward to healthcare providers who give transitional care in rural Ontario and Nova Scotia. We will invite the healthcare providers to tell us what they think about the care strategies, what they would need to provide them, and how to adjust their delivery so that healthcare providers can help older people with dementia and their families learn about the care strategies and participate in them. We will use the results to refine the care strategies so that they become part of transitional care in rural areas and help older people with dementia and their families learn how to promote functioning at home after a hospital stay.

column36: Designing a Responsive and Integrative Model of Respite Care for Families of Children with Complex Care Needs and Conditions (CCNC) through Patient-Oriented Research
column37: Children with complex care needs and conditions (CCNC) are those with chronic physical and developmental disabilities who require multiple services. Caring for children with CCNC is an immense undertaking for families that involves constantly coordinating multiple needs and services in a complex system with limited supports. As such, family well-being can be greatly impacted. Grounded on the premise of providing families periodic relief from ongoing extraordinary caregiving responsibilities, respite care has been shown to have many benefits, including reduced fatigue and stress for parents as well as increased independence, functioning and social participation for children. However, demand for respite care continues to exceed supply. Families experience issues with availability, affordability and accessibility. Current models of respite care need to be reshaped to become more accessible and effective for families of children with CCNC. The goal of this study is to provide evidence to inform the design of a new model of respite care that can respond to the diverse and changing needs of families of children with CCNC in Manitoba (MB). Multiple data collection methods are planned, including a review of existing models of respite care, interviews with families of children with CCNC as well as service providers and other stakeholders in MB and an analysis of population-based data sets. Families of children with CCNC will also take part in the photovoice process, which will involve them taking photos to document their experiences. Short-term, a new model of respite care for families of children with CCNC in MB will emerge so that respite care may be responsive and integrative. This work is foundational for future studies to test the effectiveness of a new respite model in MB. Long-term, what is learned from the implementation and testing of the MB model may be used to inform respite care policy nationally and internationally to improve outcomes for children with CCNC.

column36: Cellular Drivers of Skeletal Muscle Aging
column37: Global gains in life expectancy allow current generations to enjoy many extra healthy and active years. However, aging is also associated with a higher incidence of disease, which severely affects the quality of life and increases pressure on healthcare systems. Declining skeletal muscle (SkM) mass and function coupled with a reduced tissue healing capacity is one of the main drivers of loss of independence in the elderly. SkM tissue is highly complex and composed of a wide range of different cell types. Up to date, it remains unclear which cell types in SkM are most susceptible to aging and how age-induced dysfunction in these cellular compartments affects the maintenance and healing capacity of the tissue. Here we propose to model the impact of aging on the different cell populations in SkM using a range of novel and innovative mouse models. These models allow us to induce accelerated aging restricted to certain cell populations in SkM so that we can interrogate effects on tissue composition, function and regeneration. For the first time, this approach will allow us to identify the cell populations that represent the main "drivers" of SkM aging. We also propose to investigate a novel cell-therapy based approach that can restore the youthful function of cellular compartments involved in muscle aging. Lastly, we will evaluate the systemic application of growth factors controlling driver cell function for therapeutic efficiency in rejuvenating SkM tissue in aged mice. Our work will not only provide fundamental insights into the biology of SkM tissue but will also lay the foundation for the development of much needed therapeutic interventions for SkM aging and its associated pathologies.

column36: Molecular imaging of autotaxin: Targeting the crossroad of cancer and inflammation
column37: The proposed health research project aims at the development of a medical imaging assay using a novel class of drugs exerting combined anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer effects. The novel drug molecules are decorated with a radioactive atom to detect chronic inflammatory diseases like fibrosis and cancer in patients at an early disease stage with high accuracy. The novel medical imaging assay will allow physicians to look into the patient's body from the outside to find inflamed and cancerous tissue. The technology will enable physicians to select patients for the most optimal treatment option using innovative hybrid anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer drugs. This concept is in alignment with the prominent principle "to select the right treatment-for the right patient-at the right time". The treatment success and response can also be monitored with the novel medical imaging assay. A task of this magnitude is only achievable with a strong team of cancer research experts and strong partners from the health service and industrial community. Such a team has been assembled for the project to ultimately enhance patient care, especially with difficult to treat diseases like chronic inflammation and cancer.

column36: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 for Detecting Major Depression: An Updated Systematic Review and Independent Participant Data Meta-analysis
column37: Major depression is common among Canadians. Effective interventions are available, but most depressed Canadians do not receive adequate care. Depression screening, which involves using questionnaires to identify people who may have unrecognized depression is a way to improve the condition. However, it is not recommended in Canada's main healthcare guidelines due to concerns that screening tools are not accurate enough. Often, primary studies only publish results for cutoff scores that work well in a particular group of people. Also, existing screening methods do not consider patient risk factors such as age, sex, care setting, and medical diagnoses, which may be associated with depression. In this project, we will combine original patient data from published studies that used PHQ-9 as a screening tool to create a very large database that can be used to determine more accurate ways to identify patients with depression. The proposed research will provide accurate, unbiased estimates of diagnostic accuracy for PHQ-9, incorporating individual patient characteristics, which has not been done previously. Results will be used to develop and test improved depression screening and management programs and to make better decisions for individual patients.

column36: Host and viral determinants of ZIKV fitness and the immune response to infection
column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) is an emerging mosquito-borne pathogen that is a significant global health concern. Although historically a mild infection characterized by flu-like symptoms that was limited to Africa and Asia, the recents outbreaks in South and Latin America, as well as the Southern USA, has been associated with more severe neurological complications including Guillain-Barre syndrome and fetal microcephaly. Since outbreaks were relatively rare until recently, no vaccine or specific treatment exists for ZIKV. In addition, research on the virus has been limited, meaning that few molecular tools and animal models exist to study the virus. Furthermore, we currently have a poor understanding of the factors that have led to the rapid spread and increased severity of the currently circulating ZIKV strains. In the current proposal, we will study ZIKV infection, pathogenesis, and the immune response to infection. We will compare several historical ZIKV isolates in order to better understand the factors underlying the rapid dissemination and increased severity of ZIKV in recent outbreaks. This comparative analysis of historical ZIKV isolates will allow us to gain a broader understanding of viral replication, pathogenesis and the immune response to ZIKV infection. In turn, this will help inform the design and screening of antivirals and the development of effective vaccine strategies.

column36: Longitudinal Monitoring for Quality of Care at the End of Life in Nursing Homes
column37: Nursing homes are important sites of care for people who can no longer live safely in their own homes. The majority of people who enter a nursing home will die there, meaning that nursing homes should be experts in providing quality end of life care; yet, nursing home residents at the end of life often receive aggressive treatments that provide little benefit (such as use of certain medications or physical restraints) and they frequently suffer from distressing yet treatable symptoms (such as pain or shortness of breath). Accurately measuring and monitoring such care practices and distressing symptoms is important to reduce their occurrence and improve quality end of life care in nursing homes. Most provinces mandate the use of a clinical assessment tool called the Resident Assessment Instrument - Minimum Data Set 2.0 (RAI-MDS 2.0), which is regularly used to monitor overall quality; however, the tool is not regularly used to monitor quality of care at the end of life, specifically. In this research project, we will partner with care staff, decision makers, and nursing home residents and their families to study the modifiable symptoms and inappropriate care practices experienced by residents in Canadian nursing homes during the last year of life. Together with our partners, we will identify priority symptoms and practices for quality monitoring and will use RAI-MDS 2.0 data to develop quality measures for these priorities. The goal is to develop a new set of quality measures that can be used by different groups (including residents and their families, nursing home administrators and staff, and decision makers) to understand the quality of care at end of life provided in nursing homes and identify opportunities for improvement.

column36: Mechanisms and targets of intron dependent regulation of cell growth and adaptation to starvation
column37: The secret to cure human disease is to understand how the cell, the fundamental building block of the human body, functions. We simply cannot fix what we do not understand and the key to understanding cellular behavior is determining how the static information stored within genes is converted into visible effects. Recently my lab has shown that by and large, the amount and type of gene-output, i.e. the amount and type of proteins made, depend on the nature of a certain part of the coding tape dedicated to this synthesis. The coding tape is called RNA and it contains in fact non-coding fragments, or introns, that interrupt the code of protein synthesis. These non-coding fragments need to be removed in order for the tape to work, a process called splicing. Dysregulation of splicing is the hallmark of many human diseases including cancer. Indeed, our work indicates that introns play an important role in improving cell fitness under stress and that variation in splicing patterns promotes the survival of cancer cells. However, we know very little about why introns were first inserted in the coding tape nor do we understand the signaling pathways leading to the removal of a specific intron at a given time. Understanding the function of introns and the mechanisms of normal and alternative splicing represents a key challenge for future biomedical research, the discovery of biomarkers and therapy development. We will draw on our world-leading expertise in RNA biology and yeast genetics to generate the first global assessment of intron function on an organismal scale and annotate factors that modify splicing in human diseases.

column36: Quantitative analysis of calcium arrhythmogenicity in the Purkinje fibers of ischemic heart: a search for the molecular origins of Sudden Cardiac Death.
column37: Heart diseases remain the first cause of mortality in the world. In Canada, it affects 1.4 million people, taking more than 50,000 lives per year in the country. Half of this mortality is due to heart failure, a progressive deterioration of cardiac contraction. The other half occurs suddenly (Sudden Cardiac Death, SCD) owing to ventricular tachycardias (VTs), abrupt accelerations of heart rate which precede cardiac arrest and death. Most victims of SCD were not identified as high risk individuals and could not be protected by specific drug treatments or implantable medical device (defibrillator). This unacceptable situation is the direct consequence of our poor understanding of what exactly triggers VTs. Our research addresses this issue. A majority of VTs is associated with structural heart disease (virtually any disease of the heart), and about 40% of VTs arise as complications of heart attack (myocardial infarction; MI). The origin of VTs is attributed to abnormal electric signals from the cells (Pcells) that compose the "electric wires" of the heart. Experimental animal models showed that electric properties of these "wires" are affected after MI due to an abnormal elevations of calcium (Ca2+) in Pcells. The first goal of the project is to identify abnormal proteins responsible for these Ca2+ elevations in Pcells after MI. The second goal is to understand how cell death in the cardiac wall during MI affects these proteins in Pcells. Experiments will be conducted on Pcells of pig heart. Advanced technical approaches including predicting abnormal Ca2+ activity in Pcells by a computer program will be implemented to identify the "triggers" of the process leading to SCD. The project is anticipated to provide clinically measurable indicators of the risk of VT and to identify new avenues for (so far nonexistent) specific treatments of patients at risk of SCD. The impact of MI will be investigated in males and females to evaluate the sex-differences in the risk of SCD.

column36: Cellular dynamics at the maternal-placental interface
column37: Excess body weight is a serious concern for many women of reproductive age. Being overweight or obese has several potential effects on the health of mother and baby, especially because of higher rates of complications like gestational diabetes, high blood pressure and spontaneous pregnancy loss. These effects may be related to an effect of excess body weight on the very earliest developmental events, such as the development of the placenta. The placenta is the essential link between the mother and developing baby, so if it does not form properly, there can be severe consequences. My proposal aims to examine the effects of obesity in altering the cell make-up of the fetal-maternal environment in early human pregnancy. We hypothesize that the state of obesity alters the local makeup and function of maternal and fetal cells leading to impaired placenta function. To achieve these aims, we will directly compare placenta and uterine tissues obtained from obese and non- obese women in the first trimester of pregnancy, and findings from human clinical specimens will be mechanistically examined using an obesity mouse model. I will compare cellular, molecular and genetic characteristics of the two groups by measuring blood chemistry, cellular composition (maternal and fetal), cell function and gene expression. The proposed studies will establish if there are inherent differences in the cell biology of placentas from obese women compared to non-obese women. I anticipate that there will be differences in fetal-maternal cellular composition between these groups of women. These changes in the local placental-uterine environment are predicted to modify placental function, in part by altering gene expression. Results from these experiments will lay the groundwork for future studies aiming to define the role of obesity in the development of pregnancy-related disorders.

column36: Asthma exacerbations, exercise and vascular function
column37: Even though asthma is a disease of the lungs, people with asthma have an increased risk for cardiovascular disease such as heart attack and stroke. During asthma attacks, the risk for cardiovascular problems is especially high. The cardiovascular risk is also higher in older people and in women with asthma. It is not known why asthmatics have a higher cardiovascular risk and we aim to investigate this. Inflammation and poor function of the blood vessels are two risk factors for cardiovascular disease. We will study how an asthma attack affects inflammation in the lungs, the spill-over to the rest of the body and the blood vessel function. We think that the attack will increase inflammation and impair the function of the blood vessels. We will also test whether an 8 week rehabilitation program involving exercise is effective at decreasing the inflammation and preventing impaired blood vessel function after an induced asthma attack. This will be done in older asthmatics as they appear to be at the highest cardiovascular risk, and more often have difficulties in controlling their asthma. With this research we will understand more about how asthma and cardiovascular disease are linked and find out whether exercise is an effective way to improve cardiovascular risk and asthma control.

column37: The right ventricle is one of four chambers in the heart. It is responsible for pumping blood from the heart to the lungs, where the blood is replenished with oxygen. If the muscle of the right ventricle by changing either its structure or its functioning is not pumping as efficiently as it should be, right ventricular failure and premature death occur. This can be caused by a number of conditions, including high blood pressure in the lungs. Indeed, due to high blood pressure, the right ventricle has to work harder, that means over time that the right ventricle thickens and weakens because of the extra work it does. Although right ventricular failure is a common, costly and fatal condition, its diagnosis is suboptimal and no cure exists. In the present research proposal, we hypothesize that a molecule called H19 is specifically increased in the right ventricle of human patients with high blood pressure and animal models causing failure of the latter and that its detection in blood can serve as a tool in diagnosis and monitoring the disease. In addition, we propose that inhibition of H19 could be a new and promising avenue to improve the function of diseased right ventricle and thus help patients to live longer. We expect that the knowledge gained from the proposed project will provide new ways to treat the disease.

column37: Provision of pediatric palliative care to alleviate suffering and enhance quality of life for children with life-threatening conditions is considered a basic human right. Little is known about which children access which types of services, the impact of the different services on outcomes linked to increased suffering and reduced quality of life, or the cost of these types of services. column37: Spinal cord injury is devastating due to the physical, societal, and economical harms incurred on individuals as well as on our society. Although the spinal cord contains all the circuitry necessary to locomotion, in the absence of commands from the brain, people with spinal cord injuries are unable to walk. Motor recovery can be partially achieved by strategies or therapies intended to regenerate axons from the brain to the spinal cord. column36: Revisiting the Mitochondria-Associated Membrane: Redox Controls Tethers
column37: The control of cellular energy production is an area of intense investigation. The reason for this interest is that many devastating diseases, such as cancer, diabetes or various brain dysfunctions are now recognized as "metabolic diseases". This designation means that these diseases result from defects in the metabolic, chemical reactions that generate energy from "respiration" or breakdown of sugar within the cells of our organs. Because of this insight, cell biologists today investigate the mechanisms that control cellular me-tabolism with the aim to tweak or rescue the balance of cellular energy production in disease. Our laboratory works on an intracellular membrane structure that controls cellular metabolism. This struc-ture is called the mitochondria-associated membrane (MAM). The MAM is a very small site inside our cells where multiple "biomembranes" attach to each other. At the MAM, calcium- and chemical-based signals turn on respiration when energy becomes scarce. If this crosstalk is disrupted, energy production is shifted towards the breakdown of sugar, and this is a known signature of cancer. We have discovered a mechanism that allows the MAM to control cellular energy production. The MAM activates this mechanism when cells are stressed. Under this condition, a protein assembly forms that chemically modifies the MAM structure. We will investigate what is needed to form this assembly and how the proteins that make up the MAM react to these chemical modifications. We will then determine what our discoveries mean for metabolism in cancer tissue. Using cell culture models and tumor growth in animals, we will explore pharmacological strategies to control the MAM structure. The new insight we gain will explain how metabolic changes allow tumors to speed up growth and how this property may be eventually harnessed to control cancer.
