column36: Cardiac Metabolism and Signaling in Heart Failure Pathogenesis and Treatment
column37: Although advancements in therapies to treat cardiovascular disease have reduced the number of deaths of patients with heart disease, these treatments/interventions have ultimately increased the number of people who eventually go on to develop another clinical condition called heart failure. Simply stated, clinical heart failure is a condition that is defined by poor heart function that prevents the heart from pumping enough blood to the rest of the body for proper organ function. As a result, heart failure patients have a very poor quality of life. Although heart failure is often a "chronic" condition, the chances of dying at one year following diagnosis are between 20-30%, even with our most state-of-the-art treatments. Due to the short life expectancy and poor quality of life of the heart failure patient, the increasing amount of people developing heart failure is a major medical concern. A long-standing concept in heart failure is that the failing heart has defects in specific processes that allow the heart to generate enough energy to function normally. Since scientists already know that the failing heart is starved for energy, a new approach to treating heart failure may reside in improving the ability of the heart to use fuels appropriately and thus restore the amount of energy being produced by the heart. The proposed research will investigate what processes involved in energy production are decreased in the failing heart, and will determine if normalizing these processes can improve the function of the heart. We will use this information to develop novel approaches to treating heart failure. Given the accumulating information regarding the occurrence and poor health outcomes associated with heart failure, there is need to identify additional treatment options for this condition in a large and growing population of Canadians.

column37: In Canada, there is a growing number of people who develop a condition called heart failure. Simply stated, clinical heart failure is a condition that is defined by poor heart function that prevents the heart from pumping enough blood to the rest of the body for proper organ function. As a result, heart failure patients have a very poor quality of life. Although heart failure is often a "chronic" condition, the chances of dying at one year following diagnosis are between 20-30%, even with our most state-of-the-art treatments. Due to the short life expectancy and poor quality of life of the heart failure patient, the increasing amount of people developing heart failure is a major medical concern. In fact, the lifetime risk of developing heart failure for North American adults who have reached 45 years of age is 20%. As such, there is the need for new strategies to treat this debilitating condition and improve the health of these heart failure patients. My lab has been investigating the non-conventional mechanisms that contribute to heart failure (i.e. the contribution of other organs to poor health outcomes in heart failure patients). Recently, we have generated exciting data that indicates that heart failure induces abnormal cellular processes in fat cells that then causes cardiac insulin resistance (essentially the heart becomes resistant to the effects of insulin and cannot extract sugar from the blood to subsequently use as a fuel for energy). This implicates communication between organs (i.e. heart and fat) that can lead to the worsening health of people with heart failure. As such, the objective of this project is to test whether or not heart failure-induced changes in fat cells contribute to worsening heart failure and understand the mechanisms by which this occurs. We will use mice with heart failure as our model in order to better understand how abnormal cellular processes in fat cells communicate with the heart to cause worsening heart function.

column36: Regulation of microglial pannexin-1 channels in arthritis pain
column37: Pain is a key feature of arthritis, a disease of the joint and a leading cause of disability in both young and old. Despite recent advances in treating joint inflammation, and the widespread use of pain medications by arthritis patients, adequate pain control is an ongoing and challenging health care problem. Joint pain is poorly understood: some individuals with severe joint damage report little pain, while paradoxically others with seemingly minor joint damage, complain of debilitating pain. This disconnect suggests joint damage somehow influences arthritis pain, possibly by "filtering" the sensation of pain at some level in our body before reaching our brain. This proposal examines how arthritis pain impacts immune cells (microglia) in the spinal cord to mediate pain sensations between the joint and the brain. Although microglia reside within the confines of the blood brain barrier (a protective barrier that normally shields the brain), the injured joint can somehow communicate with these cells. In preliminary studies, we discovered that joint injury activates a specific molecule (the pannexin-1 channel) in microglia located in the region of the spinal cord associated with joint pain sensation. We also discovered that blocking pannexin-1 substantially reduces pain in this experimental arthritis model. Microglia, working as an amplifier at the level of the spinal cord, may influence how joint damage signals chronic pain to the brain. Understanding why and how arthritis pain occurs will enable us to develop new health care strategies to prevent or treat pain in patients with chronic joint disease.

column36: Controlling Glucose Metabolism to Develop Superior Tissue Engineered Cartilage
column37: Damage to articular cartilage by arthritis or injury is a significant healthcare problem as this tissue cannot repair itself. One potential approach to repair damaged cartilage is to use tissue-engineered cartilage implants. However, despite its great potential, several technical hurdles remain which hinder the efficacy of tissue repair. Recently, we have discovered a novel pathway to improve the growth of engineered cartilage by controlling the way the cells metabolize glucose. Thus, the objective of the proposed study is to harness this effect to create functional engineered cartilage implants suitable for joint repair. In this project, the underlying mechanisms responsible will first be determined and engineered cartilage implants will be created to possess the appropriate structure and properties suitable for implantation. Developed tissue implants will then be assessed in clinically relevant animal models of cartilage repair. Currently, there is no optimal treatment for damaged or diseased cartilage. This research will improve patient quality of life while also reducing healthcare costs associated with conventional therapies. Thus, this project represents a critical step to translate important scientific discoveries to the clinic where, one day it can benefit a significant portion of Canadians. This proposed research also represents a novel, paradigm shifting approach to develop functional engineered cartilage that can be easily produced without the need of sophisticated methods and can be readily adapted to any such approach currently under investigation.

column36: Elucidating a role for Rho-kinase-thrombospondin signaling in experimental and human bronchopulmonary dysplasia: Novel targets for prevention and treatment of chronic lung disease in premature newborns.
column37: About 1,500 babies are born extremely premature in Canada each year. Advances in medical care over the last 20 years have improved the survival of these babies, but in about half at the cost of a severe injury to the lung called bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Babies with BPD suffer from a permanent interruption of normal lung development; therefore, they carry their lung disease with them their entire lives and in the most severe cases die before school age. Medical costs related to BPD are among the highest for all childhood diseases, being second only to asthma. Preventing disease due to prematurity is therefore of critical importance to the health of Canadians. The proposed experiments will use animals with experimental BPD and lung tissues from human newborn infants to define and confirm the involvement of specific pathways leading to lung injury: Rho-kinase (ROCK) and thrombospondin (TSP)-1. We will give a promising class of drug by inhalation, known as a ROCK inhibitor, to determine safety and efficacy in rats with BPD. Another molecule regulated by ROCK is TSP-1, which our work suggests is critical to interruption of normal lung development. Importantly, we will allow rats to grow into adults to see whether benefits of targeting ROCK and TSP-1 are long-lasting. Our group is uniquely equipped with the facilities and expertise to perform the experiments that are proposed. In particular, ours is the only group possessing the ability to perform precise measurements of lung structure using a technique called "unbiased stereology". Collectively, these experiments represent a critical step toward the translation of novel drugs targeting molecules implicated in BPD, which could represent a breakthrough in our ability to improve health outcomes among Canadians who were born premature.

column36: Amelioration of Pulmonary Fibrosis Using Induced Progenitor-Like Cells via Rejuvenation of Stem Cells
column37: Lung disease is an important clinical problem and our group has a proven track record of translating laboratory advances into clinical use. Acute and chronic lung diseases remain major healthcare burdens, and are expected to increase with an aging population. For patients with end-stage lung disease, lung transplantation is often the only life-saving option, despite significant associated risks of mortality and morbidity due to graft rejection and infection. Regenerative medicine approaches, while exciting in their potential, remain limited by an inadequate supply of appropriate cell types required for therapeutic benefit. For both autologous and allogeneic cell-based therapeutic applications, the potential benefit of the therapy is critically dependent on the efficacy of donor cells which declines with age. This is particularly important an elderly population as many of the most challenging lung diseases affect older individuals. To avoid all the issues of rejection, it will be required to utilize 'rejuvenated' cells derived from the patient's own aged cells. We have been working to develop a conceptual approach called transient reprogramming. We have shown that initiating the reprogramming process but NOT ALLOWING it to continue to the full pluripotent state (which would result in induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells), leads to a cell type we have called an induced Progenitor-Like (iPL) cell, whose proliferation and differentiation can be controlled. These iPL cells are powerful therapeutic products and we have been investigating their potential in the lung. Herein we propose to test the hypothesis that (1) transient expression of reprogramming factors generates 'rejuvenated' iPL cells from aged lung alveolar epithelial cells. And (2) these 'rejuvenated' iPL cells can be used in cell-based regenerative medicine applications, specifically for the amelioration of Pulmonary Fibrosis.

column36: Gender inequalities in adolescent mental health in Canada
column37: During early childhood, boys and girls have similar mental health experiences. By adolescence, gaps start to appear for mental health outcomes. Anxiety and depression are diagnosed more commonly among girls, while for boys risk-taking behaviours and fatal outcomes such as suicide pose greater risks. These are examples of "gender-based mental health inequalities", and we want to focus here on the deep reasons why they exist. Using survey data and young people's own stories, we want to understand: (1) how individual behaviours and social processes (such as use of social media, available peer and adult supports, and risk-taking) contribute to mental health inequalities between adolescent boys and girls; (2) how differences in mental health between boys and girls are shaped by gendered differences in their social backgrounds. We will bring together new analyses of health survey data with information from a series of interviews with young Canadians. Integration of all study findings will provide new evidence about factors that effect mental health among groups of adolescents, inform interventions, and enrich the evidence base for health policy. This project is especially timely because the mental health of Canadian adolescents, as well as gender-based inequalities, have emerged as two very pressing social challenges in our country.

column36: How much movement do workers need to be healthy? Understanding work-related and non-work contributions to the movement patterns of Canadian workers and their cardiometabolic consequences.
column37: Physical inactivity and excessive sedentary behaviour (SB) are two current public health concerns. Current activity recommendations have focused on promoting total levels of PA and reducing total or bouts of SB (e.g., accumulating 30 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity on most days and minimizing total SB). However, the movements of adults are usually variable and can be accumulated in numerous bouts and breaks of PA and SB. Furthermore, the relationship between the variation in these patterns and their health effects are not well understood. Adults spend the majority of their wakeful hours at work; therefore, the workplace provides an important setting to explore movement behaviours. A worker's movement patterns including PA and SB can be influenced by work demands, as well as the social and environmental context at work. A detailed exploration of typical movement patterns of workers is needed to inform practical recommendations that can be implemented in actual working situations. This project will leverage objectively measured Canadian population-level data to provide a novel exploration of the typical movement patterns of workers at work and outside of work and their effects on cardiometabolic health. We will analyse data from the five cycles of the Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS; 2007 to 2017). Movement patterns include different movement behaviours (light-, moderate-, vigorous-intensity physical activity, and sedentary behaviour) at work and outside of work. Associations between movement patterns and cardiometabolic risk markers will also be explored. Our project fills an unexplored gap in our understanding of how movements are accumulated by Canadians in free-living conditions at their jobs and how they influence overall movements, and in turn cardiometabolic health. The project is also novel in its use of cluster analysis to identify groups of work and non-work patterns through similar and dissimilar movements and durations.

column36: Mechanisms of neuronal and vascular impairments in ischemic retinopathies
column37: Ischemic retinopathies are a group of ocular diseases, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), responsible for major vision deficits. According to the International Diabetes Federation, 382 millions of people suffer of diabetes in the world. DR is a severe complication of diabetes that can lead to blindness. One estimates that DR is one of the most prevalent ocular diseases impairing vision in the working population. The number of DR patients is expected to dramatically increase in the next decades by the World Health Organization. Current therapies are not sufficient to stop the disease or can cause severe side-effects. The search for new therapeutic approaches to fight ischemic retinopathies such as DR is therefore a public health priority. Clinical signs of DR retinae consist of abnormal blood vessel morphologies and bleeding in the eyes. Moreover, aberrant proliferation of blood vessels and retinal edema dramatically worsen vision in 50% of type 1 patients and in 10% of type 2 patients after 15 years. Retinal neuron dysfunction is a direct consequence of ensuing ischemic damage. Indeed, the ability of retinal neurons to repair after injury is very poor. In this project, the potential implication of a new molecule will be investigated in neuronal and blood vessel dysfunctions using retinal ischemia animal models, in vivo. In the current research proposal, it is suggested that this molecule disturbs blood supply of the eye and alters the neurological processing of the visual information by the eye. Developing a new treatment targeting this molecule may stabilize blood supply of the eye and may restore the visual function of the eye in DR patients.

column36: Advanced multi-modal imaging to monitor progressive joint adaptation in the knee following an acute ligament injury
column37: The role of subchondral bone in the knee following an acute injury is not well understood, yet there are significant changes in all the joint tissues that lead to a high likelihood of developing post-traumatic osteoarthritis (OA) in the long-term. While much of the focus has been on the degeneration of cartilage, largely because in knee OA cartilage wear is associated with disease severity, it is well known that other tissues in the joint are also affected. Bone, which has been associated with knee pain, is a particularly dynamic tissue in terms of adaptation due to physiological and mechanical stimuli, both of which are present in an acutely injured knee. However, the ability to monitor bone changes has been hampered by a lack of sensitive technology to assess 3D changes, in particular the microarchitectural features that lead to functional changes of the tissue. Our lab has developed a new technique that allows longitudinal assessment of knee bone microarchitecture following an acute knee injury, and this allows unprecedented insight into the adaptive processes. Preliminary work has shown significant changes to subchondral bone microarchitecture that are associated with concurrent cartilage adaptation following a rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament of the knee. Our goal in this study is to establish the time course of bone, ligament and cartilage changes following an acute ligament injury of the knee, both before and after reconstructive surgery. These novel longitudinal data, based on multi-modal imaging techniques, will provide insight into the early tissue changes of a knee injury that are likely associated with the long-term debilitating development of knee OA. This information will form a basis to develop future interventions and improved surgical practices that can lead to better long-term outcomes. Key to our approach is the advanced imaging technologies we have developed to simultaneously measure bone and cartilage in injured patients over time.

column36: GAL-7-specific nanobodies for treatment of triple-negative breast cancer
column37: The immune system plays a key role in fighting cancer. Unfortunately, cancer cells release a number of factors that neutralize the activity of cancer-killing immune cells. Galectin-7 is a small protein that is produced and released at abnormally high levels by breast cancer cells. Binding of galectin-7 on the surface of immune T cells induce cell death, favoring the development of an immunosuppressive environment within the tumor. In this work, we propose to validate the commercial potential of the first galectin-7-specific drug for the treatment of patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Among all subtypes of breast cancer, TNBC has the fewest therapeutic options due to the lack of well-defined molecular target(s). TNBCs account for 10-20% of all cases of breast carcinoma and have a 5-year mortality rate of 30%. Because they do not express significant levels of progesterone receptor (PR), estrogen receptor (ER), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), they are not responsive to hormonal intervention or to HER2-targeted therapy. TNBC is thus a biologically aggressive disease that is particularly difficult to treat.

column36: Irnisursiriartutuq nunaringngitamini (birthing outside the community): Childbirth evacuation, perinatal mental health, and postnatal health outcomes of Nunavimmiut mothers and their infants
column37: In Nunavik, Inuit women with medically high-risk pregnancies are sent to Montreal for childbirth. Childbirth evacuation may affect maternal-infant health through maternal mental health pathways. The study will 1) explore whether and how childbirth evacuation affects prenatal stress and antepartum depression; 2) examine the associations among antepartum depression, postpartum depression, and infant growth/development; 3) validate the EPDS-Inuktitut, a cross-culturally adapted questionnaire that screens for perinatal depression; and 4) implement a knowledge transfer plan with community members and organizations to raise awareness of perinatal depression, promote healthy pregnancies, and increase support for childbirth evacuees and their families. In this mixed method, longitudinal observational study. Eligible women will be enrolled in the study upon their arrival in Montreal and will be followed through childbirth and up to 12 months postpartum in Nunavik. Our target sample size is 334 women over 5 years. Using a participatory framework, a Steering Committee consisting of representatives of key Inuit health and social service organizations, an Inuk Elder, and an Inuk spiritual leader is involved in all stages of the study. Community engagement activities include annual community open houses in four Nunavik villages and quarterly meetings of a women's advisory group (Inuit midwife trainees and mothers). The researchers are experts in maternal-infant health, maternal-fetal medicine, Inuit health services, and Indigenous mental health. Expected products include a validated perinatal depression screening tool specifically for Inuit; Elder-led videos and community radio programming on traditional Inuit childbirth practices and healthy pregnancy; annual community open houses in Nunavik; journal articles; conference presentations; infographics; and a report for community organizations and government agencies.

column36: Epithelial-specific role of SOCS1 in prevention of intestinal inflammation
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a common inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) typified by recurring episodes of inflammation and tissue injury in the mucosal layers of the colon. The SOCS1 protein is an inhibitor of cytokine signaling affecting intestinal inflammation in a cell-specific manner, but its role in the intestinal epithelial cells (IEC) is unknown. This research team previously showed that mice with Socs1 gene deletion in IECs (Socs1dIEC) develop fatal UC at about seven months of age. Comparison of Socs1dIEC mice who displayed UC with those younger having no clinical sign of intestinal disease support a model whereby SOCS1 deficit in IECs may trigger UC by causing IEC secretory defects. This would lead to aberrant mucosal immune response to commensal bacterial invasion, where IEC hypersensitivity to death-inducing molecules produced by pathogenic immune cells may account for erosion of the colon epithelium. To tackle these postulates, we will define IEC-microbial-immune dynamic changes in the intestine of Socs1dIEC mouse cohorts (paired with WT littermates) featuring discrete disease evolution by performing functional, histologic and biochemical analyses. We will test whether disruption of the intestinal barrier integrity, bacterial invasion or mucosal infiltration of specific immune cell subsets cause UC or affect its evolution in Socs1dIEC mice. We will define IEC-intrinsic SOCS1 molecular pathways by global profiling changes in protein and gene abundance in IECs driven by SOCS1-deficiency, while SOCS1-regulated biological processes in mouse intestinal organoid culture systems. The cause of IBD is unknown but their pathogenesis is linked with aberrant immune response to the commensal microbiota. Insights of the mechanisms by which SOCS1 in IECs limits colitis may shed light on novel causes of IBD and identify cell targets for designing tailored new therapies to fight these diseases. Thus, our work would impact future diagnosis or treatments for IBD patients.

column36: Improving Health Economic Evaluation: Better Measures of Work Productivity Losses due to Illness in Canada
column37: Societal and health care resources are limited. Stakeholders such as policy makers, insurers, and employers need to make decisions on how to best allocate funding to different health care interventions such as new drugs. Health economic evaluation is a tool commonly used to inform these funding decisions. In economic evaluations, the costs of an intervention are compared to its benefits. Productivity losses for some diseases are substantial and even greater than their direct healthcare costs (e.g., physician, hospital and drug costs). Therefore, productivity loss due to illness is an important cost component that should be considered in economic evaluations from a societal perspective. The impact of illness on work productivity is usually measured in terms of three components: job loss, absenteeism (absence from work) and presenteeism (reduced performance and productivity while working). Currently, only a few population-based studies in other countries, and none in Canada, have comprehensively measured work productivity losses due to illness. Consequently, economic evaluations largely do not incorporate appropriately estimated productivity losses. The goal of our research is to improve the quality of economic evaluations by providing better productivity loss estimates. Specifically, using a population-based survey conducted by Statistics Canada, we will measure and value productivity losses among different chronic diseases, compare two different methods of measuring presenteeism, and identify the factors other than health (e.g., lifestyle and work-related characteristics) that may affect productivity. This study will enhance our understanding of the burden of specific diseases in terms of work productivity losses. The information generated can be used in other economic evaluation studies to improve the accuracy of their productivity loss estimates. When funding for health care interventions is based on better economic evaluations, society will directly benefit.

column36: BRCA1-induced pro-inflammatory signaling associated with ovarian cancer predisposition
column37: Ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in Canadian women and is the most lethal cancer of the female reproductive tract. Unfortunately, there are no reliable tests for early detection of the disease, and symptoms that might alert a woman to seek medical treatment at an early disease stage are easily dismissed as being due to minor ailments. Women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer are at very high risk of developing ovarian cancer, with much of this risk being due to a mutation within the breast cancer susceptibility gene BRCA1. Studies indicate that the most common and lethal form of ovarian cancer arises from cells lining the fallopian tube, and women with BRCA1 mutations often have their ovaries and fallopian tubes removed to reduce their risk of the disease. The fallopian tube is a structure that carries the egg cell to the uterus following its release from the ovary. We have identified molecular differences in the cells lining fallopian tubes from women with BRCA1 mutations relative to those from control patients, that could contribute to cancer development. Besides genetic risks, other risk factors for ovarian cancer suggest that factors associated with a lifetime of ovulatory events may contribute to predisposition to ovarian/fallopian tube cancer. Our studies are targeted at providing an understanding of how ovulation and BRCA1 mutations can predispose to ovarian cancer. It is hoped that this work will identify potential molecules that are likely to participate in turning cells within the fallopian tube to cancer cells, and ultimately lead to non-surgical ways to prevent ovarian cancer in women who are at an elevated risk.

column36: Control of B cell metabolism by the PI3K pathway: applications for autoimmunity
column37: The immune system is critical to human health. In order to develop vaccines and treatments for diseases where the immune system malfunctions (such as autoimmunity, inflammatory diseases or immunodeficiency), we need to better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing immune responses. Our research deals with the arm of the immune system responsible for producing antibodies, which are specialized proteins that bind to microorganisms and target them for destruction by the immune system. Antibodies are secreted into the blood and mucosal surfaces by cells called B lymphocytes. B lymphocytes express receptor proteins on their cell surface which allow them to sense the presence of foreign invaders, damaged cells and tissues, and other activated immune cells. Signals from these receptors trigger activation of individual B lymphocytes to divide, producing more copies of themselves, and mature into antibody secreting factories. Cell surface receptors deliver signals to the interior of the cell through signal transduction proteins which in turn activate enzymes that reprogram cellular metabolism to carry out either protective or damaging activities of these cells. Our research aims to define the molecular signaling pathways that regulate the activities of B lymphocytes during normal immune responses or abnormal autoimmune responses. Our work is identifying new molecular pathways that can be targeted to shut down B cells and treat autoimmune disease.

column36: Disentangling the intricate functions of the RNA polymerase II CTD
column37: Transcription is the very first step in gene expression. It consists in producing a messenger molecule (the messenger RNA) that provides instructions for the synthesis of the protein encoded by a given gene. Transcription is tightly regulated as it is in large part dictating which proteins are produced by a given cell. Regulating transcription is therefore key for processes such as cellular differentiation and homeostasis. Inappropriate transcription can have catastrophic consequences such as emergence of cancer cells. Transcription of protein-encoding genes is executed by an enzyme called RNA polymerase II. This enzyme contains a unique domain called CTD. The CTD acts as a connector that allows coherent organization of the different enzymatic reactions required to produce a functional messenger RNA, and hence a functional protein. This application aims at understanding the molecular mechanisms allowing the CTD to achieve its connecting function.

column36: White adipose tissue LDL receptors and omega-3 as modulators of the risk for type 2 diabetes
column37: Every 3 minutes a new case of diabetes is diagnosed in Canada, mostly type 2 diabetes (T2D). Diabetes increases the risk of having many other disease, such as heart disease, and about 65-80% of diabetic patients die from heart disease and stroke. T2D and heart disease develop because many risk factors such as aging, obesity and unhealthy lifestyle accumulate over years leading to their onset. Lowering blood LDL, commonly known as "bad cholesterol", is protective against heart disease. However human studies over the past 10 years have shown that the lower is blood LDL, the higher is the chance of developing T2D. This phenomena is happening whether blood LDL is lowered by widely used drugs against heart disease (statins), or by being born with certain genes, some of which are very common (~80% of people have them). The reason why lowering blood LDL is associated with higher risk for diabetes and how to naturally treat them with nutrients is unknown. We believe that blood LDL is low in some people because more LDL is entering into their tissues. We were the first to show that when LDL enters into human fat tissue it induces multiple defects that lead to its dysfunction. Fat tissue dysfunction induces the accumulation of risk factors for T2D. On the other hand, omega-3 is a unique type of fat that is found mostly in fish oil. We also were the first to show that omega-3 can directly treat the same defects that are induced by LDL entry into fat tissue. Thus the aim from this study is to establish in 48 overweight and obese subjects with normal plasma LDL; 1) if people with higher LDL entry into fat tissue have higher risk for T2D, and 2) if 6-month supplementation of omega-3 from fish oil can treat these people reducing their risk for T2D. This study is original and important as it aims to understand and treat a new risk factor for T2D using an inexpensive and widely accessible nutraceutical. It will help prevent T2D in large proportion of Canadians.

column36: Defining the mechanism of ALDH1A3 in breast cancer for the identification of novel therapeutic targets
column37: To treat breast cancer patients more effectively, we need to better understand why cancer spreads and comes back years later after treatment. Breast tumors are made up of different cancer cells. Among them, cancer stem cells (CSCs) have the greatest potential to form new tumors, are very hard to kill and can cause cancer to come back. My lab is investigating these CSCs and the mechanisms that cause cancer to spread. Our long-term goal is to identify new targets for drugs that kill CSCs and stop the spread of cancer. This should decrease the chance the cancer will return. Previously, we found that breast CSCs make an enzyme called aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A3 (ALDH1A3) that promotes tumor growth and the spread of cancer. Patients with higher levels of this enzyme in their tumors are less likely to survive in the long term. We have new data showing that ALDH1A3 promotes breast cancer growth and spread by producing other factors. First, we found a new ALDH1A3-induced molecule (a long non-coding RNA) that is linked to breast cancer growth and CSCs, with potential as a drug target to treat breast cancer. Second, we found that ALDH1A3 increases the production of plasmin; a cell component that helps cancer cells spread by breaking down surrounding structures. Last, by producing retinoic acid, a molecule that controls the expression of many genes in cells, ALDH1A3 causes cancer to spread. We propose to investigate the consequences of these ALDH1A3-induced factors on breast cancer growth and spread, and CSCs. We will use many breast cancer models, from cultured cells to sophisticated mouse models that mimic the patient and act as patient avatars. Our research will give fundamental insight into the mechanisms of how ALDH1A3 promotes cancer growth and spread as well as identifying new ways to treat cancer by killing CSCs. Our findings will make a major impact in understanding cancer and identifying novel drug targets. This will eventually lead to improved outcomes for patients.

column36: The Endocannabinoid System in Borderline Personality Disorder: Relationships to Fluctuations in Anger and Comorbid Psychiatric Conditions
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a common and serious psychiatric illness that places a heavy burden on affected individuals, their families, and healthcare systems. Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), or the intentional destruction of bodily tissue, is a hallmark of BPD. High levels of anger often precede NSSI and are a potent risk factor for continued self-harm. We previously discovered that fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), a component of the brain endocannabinoid system that dampens neural signaling, is elevated in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) of BPD assessed using positron emission tomography, a state-of-the-art brain imaging technique. We also found that PFC FAAH levels were correlated with a measure of anger in BPD. The present proposal seeks to understand whether high levels of FAAH in BPD can change in response to psychosocial interventions that treat anger and other clinical symptoms of BPD, such as NSSI. We are also interested in pursuing whether FAAH levels are increased in clinical disorders related to BPD, such as major depressive episodes (MDEs). Thus, we will also test FAAH binding in MDEs. We predict that we will find higher levels of FAAH in MDEs, because there are clinical similarities between BPD and MDEs. Finally, we will measure whether FAAH levels are increased in BPD+MDE compared with MDE alone to discover whether FAAH is elevated even further in comorbid conditions. These series of experiments will help discern whether FAAH is malleable to change, especially in relation to core features of BPD. They will also uncover whether similar disorders have the same pathology; if so, results would provide an impetus for developing new treatments that could ameliorate multiple psychiatric conditions. Ultimately, we hope to decrease the clinical burden associated with BPD, including anger, and reduce NSSI that contributes to the exceedingly high morbidity and mortality associated with BPD.

column36: A genome-wide association study of dysanapsis
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airflow limitation (inability to empty the lungs), and is a major public health problem in Canada and globally. Smoking is the best known COPD risk factor, and reducing smoking is essential to public health. There are, however, some inconvenient truths about COPD that we must confront if we want to meaningfully lower the public health burden of COPD. First, smoking rates in several countries have declined by 50% over the past 5 decades (including Canada), but the corresponding COPD mortality is not declining. Second, one-quarter of COPD occurs in never-smokers (27% in Canada). Third, only a minority of lifetime smokers develop COPD. As COPD mortality continues to increase, understanding major determinants of COPD susceptibility and progression beyond smoking is critical. A growing body of evidence suggests that dysanapsis is a major contributor to COPD. Dysanapsis refers to the disproportionate scaling of airway-to-lung dimensions. Since airway dimensions determine airflow resistance, disproportionate scaling of airway-to-lung dimensions (dysanapsis) may contribute to airflow limitation. We recently developed and validated a computed tomography (CT) measure of dysanapsis. This dysanapsis measure explains more airflow limitation than all traditional COPD risk factors including smoking. Furthermore, our dysanapsis measure was strongly associated with the COPD Genetic Risk Score - a composite genetic score based on 97 known COPD genes, suggesting that genetic pathways contribute to dysanapsis. Unraveling the mechanisms of dysanapsis - a major contributor to COPD on par with smoking - is essential in order to develop early life interventions to promote healthy lungs for life. We propose a genome-wide association study of CT-measured dysanapsis among older adults, and testing whether these polymorphisms predict airflow limitation and respiratory events in children.

column36: Stopping Syphilis Transmission in Arctic communities through Rapid Diagnostic Testing (STAR study)
column37: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with serious health consequences if left untreated, including transmission to unborn children. This may result in death or serious complications. In several parts of the Arctic, syphilis has emerged in the last few years and continues unabated. Identifying and treating cases promptly is critical to preventing transmission. The remoteness of most villages and lack of specialized diagnostic labs however, makes timely access to diagnostics difficult. Reliance on testing in distant labs leads to delays of typically 6-19 days between screening and treatment. This delay may contribute to continued transmission within sexual networks and between communities. Reducing this delay is therefore a key priority in Arctic communities. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) intended to screen for syphilis, have been developed and used successfully in several counties. To stop disease transmission and overcome obstacles to timely treatment, we will evaluate the use of RDTs in parallel with current standard lab-based testing. Unlike traditional testing, the RDTs will be used directly in affected communities and provide results in minutes, allowing for immediate initiation of treatment to help stop transmission. We will estimate the number of cases averted by early treatment of infectious syphilis, and model the impact of rapid testing on syphilis transmission. Our research aims to provide robust evidence for both the benefit and lack-of-harm from much needed interventions to control of syphilis transmission in remote Arctic communities. column36: Chemokine-mediated control of anti-tumor immunity in DNA-repair deficient colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer afflicting Canadians. Cancer cells arise when the body's own cells become mutated to the point that they develop independence from the body's normal growth control mechanisms. In many cases, mutations in a gene mean that it cannot function normally. Mutations in many different types of genes can lead to colorectal cancer and some of the most common mutations change the ability of a cell to keep its DNA healthy. When this happens, cancer cells cannot repair damage to their genes and so even more faulty and abnormal-looking proteins build up inside of them. The body possesses a natural defense (the immune system) that detects and attacks foreign looking cells such as bacteria and viruses. While this system expertly recognizes and destroys infecting microbes, it consistently fails to recognize mutated cancer cells as dangerous despite their high content of abnormal proteins. Scientists are still trying to understand why this is the case and how we can help the immune system "see" cancer cells as foreign. In the proposed project, we will investigate whether there is any association between the failure of a cancer cell to maintain healthy DNA and how easily it can be detected by the immune system. We are interested in doing this because it is relatively easy with current technology to look at a colon cancer sample and determine if it has mutations that disable DNA monitoring but it is difficult to find out how visible a particular cancer is to the immune system. If we do find such an association, it would be possible for doctors to screen a patient's tumor sample for such mutations in DNA monitoring genes and use this information to better determine a patient's prognosis and optimal treatment strategy. This research will also help us develop a better understanding of why the immune system is blind to most colorectal cancer cells and help us develop new treatments that can boost natural cancer detection.

column36: The impact of the in utero environment on the developing human brain: Longitudinal investigations of epigenetic mechanisms in monozygotic twins from birth to adolescence
column37: Many studies have shown that what happens to a fetus in the womb (so-called in utero environment) influences the way the brain develops. Studies in animals have shown that undesirable factors during a mother's pregnancy (e.g. malnutrition, stress exposure) can influence the way her baby's genes are expressed through "DNA methylation", a process in which genes are marked with a chemical coating. This alters the development of certain brain regions and may have later consequences for the way the child will develop emotionally, socially and cognitively. In the proposed project, we will study whether this is also the case in humans. To accomplish this, we have followed the behaviour and family environment of genetically identical twins since birth. We have also collected DNA regularly in the first 2 years of life. They will now undergo a brain scan (called MRI) at 4 years old in order to measure the size of certain brain regions and the connections between them. While these twins have the same genes, their prenatal environment can be different, leading to differences in birth weight, which are related to health differences later in life. We expect that differences in birth weight will be related to differences in the size of certain brain regions and the connections between them. We will assess DNA methylation across the genome and in specific genes that affect serotonin, a brain chemical important for early brain development, as well as for regulation of emotions and cognition. We will determine whether DNA methylation in the first years of life is a process through which the in utero environment can influence a child's brain development. We hope that this study will improve our understanding of the specific role of stressors during pregnancy on brain development and psychological problems later in life. Results should eventually lead to a better understanding of possible early ways to foster optimal brain development and prevent health problems.

column36: Muscarinic receptor antagonism as a novel mechanism for sensory nerve repair
column37: Objective Diabetic sensory neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by loss of nerve fibers in the skin. Both diseases cause significant pain and eventually lead to sensory loss. The impact of these diseases on human health is enormously damaging and there are no therapies. Our recent work has uncovered an endogenous signaling pathway in neurons that negatively modulates nerve fiber growth of sensory neurons. The neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, is produced by sensory neurons and skin cells and activates the muscarinic receptor. Inhibiting the function of the receptor in sensory neurons using selective drugs or by genetically removing the gene significantly increases nerve fiber growth. We propose a "cholinergic constraint hypothesis" describing a role for acetylcholine in restricting growth of nerves within the skin. The general objectives are: a) To suppress the muscarinic receptor pathway to repair nerve endings damaged by diabetes or anti-cancer agents. b) To determine the mechanism whereby receptor blockade enhances nerve growth with a focus on a role in control of calcium signaling and mitochondrial function. Impact statement The proposed studies have a strong translational potential if successful. Our work with topical delivery of muscarinic blocking drugs (already FDA-approved for another indication) has progressed to a point where one small phase 2 clinical trial is complete and additional studies are envisaged for early 2019 for treatment of diabetic neuropathy. A company, WinSanTor, Inc., has been set up and will oversee delivery of this plan. This proposal, if funded, will enable the work to broaden in scope and permit this therapeutic approach to be performed in a wide range of distal dying back neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Regulation of bone remodeling by transglutaminases
column37: Osteoporosis is a disease that is characterized by low bone mass, bone fragility and increased prevalence of fractures. Osteoporosis hinders the life of over to 2 million Canadians and fractures cause loss of mobility, increased pain and dramatically compromised quality of life. The cost of treating osteoporosis related fractures and immobility is over 2 billion dollars each year and it is predicted that these numbers will keep increasing as Canadian population ages. The causes for osteoporosis can be linked to genetics, nutrition, medication, and it can occur at any time during life of both men and women. Bone mass is maintained by bone cells that renew bone in cycles of bone tissue removal and new bone formation. In osteoporosis, this cycle does not function properly and is tilted towards bone removal which leads to total decrease in bone mass and weakened bones. We have discovered that transglutaminase-enzymes are important regulators of bone tissue removal. Mice lacking transglutaminases develop osteoporosis, because bone cells do not function properly and produce biochemical that increase bone removal. In this proposal, we further explore how transglutaminases can cause the loss of bone mass and we will test if they can be targeted in osteoporosis in mice to correct the bone removal-formation balance. Our aims are to examine mechanisms how transglutaminases work inside bone cells and to test chemical inhibitors of transglutaminases as therapeutics in osteoporotic mice. From this work, we hope to understand how human bone tissue is formed and removed and how bone cell activity could be modulated in osteoporosis to maintain optimal bone formation activity and bone mass throughout life.

column37: Mobility impairment is the third most common disability; nearly 300,000 Canadians use a wheelchair or scooter because their disability makes walking difficult. Many Canadians receive their wheelchair while in hospital and must learn to contend with the social and environmental challenges of use when they return home. Because of shorter hospital stays and reduced access to outpatient rehabilitation services, wheelchair users often receive little training in how to operate and manage their mobility device. Without the appropriate skills, wheelchair users can experience health declines, diminished physical activity, and restricted participation in activities of life. The impact of reduced independence can have social and financial costs for the individual, their caregivers, and the health care system. Training to Enhance Adaptation and Management for Wheelchair users (TEAM Wheel) is a novel intervention designed to address this important transition to wheelchair use. The program features two innovative elements. First, it is delivered by a peer trainer (an experienced wheelchair user) who can relate to wheelchair mobility issues and offer insight into wheelchair management. Second, a computer tablet is provided to participants with a custom wheelchair skills training program to learn and practice at home. With over 150 video demonstrations and training activities, participants can practice at their own convenience in any location they choose. The peer trainer monitors the home training program and provides input when required. The aim of this project is to translate the TEAM Wheel program from English into French and then evaluate the benefits of the program with individuals in three provinces transitioning to wheelchair use. We will compare the TEAM Wheel program to services currently provided and evaluate its impact on participation in activities of life; confidence and skill with wheelchair use; mobility in the community; and quality of life.

column37: Herpesviruses include the common human pathogens, herpes simplex virus (HSV) types 1 and 2, and varicella zoster virus. HSV-2, the focus of this proposal, is the main cause of HSV genital infections, devastating neonatal infections, and is fueling the epidemic transmission of HIV in Africa. The initial stages of herpesvirus assembly take place in the cell nucleus where virus DNA is replicated and packaged into a protein shell called a capsid. DNA-containing capsids must exit the nucleus into the cell cytoplasm where final steps in virus assembly take place. This process is referred to as nuclear egress. During the past funding period we identified two new viral molecules, pUL16 and pUL21, that are required for nuclear egress and discovered that a third viral molecule previously known to be involved in nuclear egress, pUs3, has a unique and unexpected activity. We hypothesize that pUL16, pUL21 and pUs3 act sequentially in the nuclear egress of HSV-2 capsids. The goals of the experiments described in this proposal are to understand the mechanisms by which pUL21 and pUs3 function to promote HSV-2 assembly. These studies are expected to reveal vulnerabilities that may be exploited for the treatment of HSV-2 disease.

column36: Improving diagnosis and prognosis in acute brain injury: a multimodal imaging approach
column37: Advances in life-saving medical technology have dramatically increased survival rates for patients after severe brain injury. The recovery and continued care of these individuals often require extensive stays in intensive care units (ICUs), where critical treatment decisions are made to maximize the likelihood of recovering consciousness and cognitive function. This program of work will have significant direct impact on the assessment and clinical care of patients in the ICU, inform medical ethics and legal discussions (in terms of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies), and drive efforts to develop interventions to facilitate recovery and quality of life after serious brain injury.

column37: As all cells contain the same genes, the ability to shut off genes is essential if an organism is to have different cell types. Understanding how genes are shut off is challenging, but silencing of one of the X chromosomes in females is an excellent model with which to study this fundamental process. Males only have one X chromosome (and a sex-determining Y chromosome), while females have two. To avoid a double dose of the almost one thousand genes on the X chromosome, mechanisms have evolved to silence one of the female X chromosomes. The initial silencing event, which occurs very early in development, is random but once an X is silenced, that status is maintained in all progeny cells. Silencing is not always complete, about 20 percent of the genes on the 'silent' X chromosome still show expression - we call them escapees. Because silencing takes place very early in development, much research is done using mouse embryonic stem cells. column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are diseases of the immune system that affect many parts of the body (e.g., joints, heart, eyes, skin), dramatically altering quality of life, and can result in other medical complications and untimely death. A drug called hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is commonly used to treat SLE and RA. Many studies have highlighted benefits of HCQ, including less severe disease, fewer complications (e.g., blood clots, problems with pregnancy or kidneys), and longer life. Stopping HCQ can lead to episodes of more severe disease. Also, because HCQ is safe and inexpensive, this drug is now also being studied as a method to prevent RA in people who are at risk. Although HCQ is typically safe and easy to take, a serious long-term side-effect is eye damage that could cause blindness. Although it was previously thought that there was a very small risk of vision damage, a recent study showed that the risk may be greater. However, the way that study was designed may have overestimated the risk. Therefore, it is important to now determine the 'real risk' using state-of-the-art eye testing equipment. Given the benefits and common use of HCQ, it is critical that the real risk be determined and findings shared with doctors and patients so that patients receive the best and safest care, and the health care system can use its dollars wisely.

column36: The role of dedifferentiated Schwann cells in non-healing skin wounds
column37: The incidence of chronic (non-healing) wounds is rising in Canada, yet there is no effective therapeutic approach to treat chronic wounds. To this end, we identified a novel mechanism that regulates both skin and nerve repair which relies on a particular cell type that is associated with small nerves in the skin (cutaneous nerves): Schwann cells. We uncovered that skin damage "activates" cutaneous Schwann cells, inducing them to transform into a stem cell-like state (termed dedifferentiated Schwann cells, or DSCs). It is these DSCs that function to promote skin wound healing, and do so by encouraging other skin cells (dermal cells) to divide. Additionally, these DSCs also promote the repair of skin nerves following injury. These findings suggest that DSCs are imperative to multiple facets of skin/nerve biology and represent a novel experimental therapy target, potentially useful in the treatment of both chronic wounds and peripheral neuropathy. We will test if DSCs or the factors they produce have therapeutic potential for chronic wounds. Using a pre-diabetic rodent model which displays poor wound healing, we will either transplant DSCs or known factors they produce into the wounds of these mice and assess if they are able to rescue the defects in wound healing capacity. This work will define a novel linkage between peripheral neuropathy and impaired wound healing, which are hallmarks of many chronic conditions including diabetes. Therefore, these experiments have broad therapeutic potential and represent the first steps in developing novel therapeutic strategies for many chronic skin conditions.

column36: Untangling tau contribution to cognitive impairments in Huntington's disease.
column37: Tau is a protein present mainly in brain cells. Tau helps maintain cell structure due to its presence in the cellular internal skeleton, however, in many disorders of the central nervous system, tau forms into clumps and impairs neuronal function. This is particularly well described in Alzheimer's disease, but other disorders, such as Huntington's disease (HD) - a genetic disorder of the brain - were only recently found to have detrimental changes in tau. The presence of tau clumps in multiple nervous system disorders presenting with cognitive decline suggests that the abnormal tau may contribute to this aspect of disease. Further evidence of this relationship, at least in HD, comes from studies demonstrating that different forms of the gene leading to the production of tau, correlate with cognitive decline and its severity in patients. By further investigating tau pathology in HD patients and by decreasing tau levels in HD mice, we aim to gain a more complete understanding of the contribution of tau to cognitive decline in patients. We anticipate that this information can lead to the design of a tau-targeted therapy to improve cognition for HD patients.

column36: Interventions research in homelessness, housing, and health
column37: Homelessness is a serious problem, with more than 235,000 Canadians experiencing homelessness each year. People who are homeless suffer from high rates of physical and mental illness, and they often need specialized services and supports to obtain stable housing and improve their life situation. column36: Characterizing Dopamine D2 and D3 Receptor Binding in Treatment Resistant Depression
column37: It is estimated that 30% of individuals with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) do not significantly improve with antidepressant medication, accounting for over 1 million Canadians in their lifetime. Treatment resistant depression (TRD), defined as a failure of at least two antidepressant trials for the current episode, results in almost double the health-associated costs and a greater likelihood of occupational disability, causing significant economic and personal burden. Importantly, there are few treatment strategies to target TRD and we do not have a comprehensive understanding of what processes in the brain cause it. Preliminary evidence from our group suggests there is an impairment in the dopamine system that plays an important role in processing rewarding stimuli. Deficits in this system are associated with loss of pleasure, one of the core symptoms of depression that is more prevalent in those with TRD. How the dopamine system functions in TRD compared to non-resistant patients and the full extent of the impairment is unclear. Consequently, more comprehensive evaluation of the dopamine system is necessary to determine if it is a relevant avenue for the development of new therapeutics. The goal of this study is to characterize the dopamine system in the brain within patients with TRD, non-resistant MDD and healthy controls. Three groups of participants aged 25-55 will be recruited: 15 unmedicated MDD, 15 unmedicated TRD, and 15 healthy controls. The TRD and MDD groups will have depression of moderate severity with no presence of bipolarity, psychosis or substance abuse. Healthy controls will have no lifetime psychiatric history. Imaging of the dopamine system will be done using two positron emission tomography (PET) scans to determine impairment across the whole brain. Results of this study will represent the first comprehensive assessment of dopamine in the brain among resistant and non-resistant MDD patients.

column36: Mono-ADP-ribosylation by TIPARP regulates AHR biology and dioxin toxicity
column37: Dioxins and related chemicals are a class of persistent environmental pollutants that, despite their tight regulation, still contaminate the global environment. Laboratory animals exposed to dioxins show a range of toxic responses including fatty liver, reproductive problems and weight loss leading to a lethal wasting syndrome. Although the toxic effects of dioxins in humans seem to be less severe, dioxin exposure has been linked to reproductive disorders, metabolic syndrome and increased cancer risk. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) is the signalling protein that is responsible for mediating the toxic effects of dioxins. More recently, however, the importance of AHR signalling in inflammation, intestinal immunity and overall gut health has led to the development of therapeutic agents that target AHR for the treatment of a variety of human diseases, including colitis, multiple sclerosis, arthritis and cancer. Despite extensive research efforts, our understanding of the normal biological roles of AHR and of how dioxins cause their wide variety of toxic effects remain poorly understood. We have found that another protein called TCDD-inducible poly-ADP-ribose polymerase (TIPARP) turns off AHR signalling, and it may therefore represent another key regulator of both the toxic and beneficial actions of the activated AHR. Our laboratory uses molecular and cell biology techniques combined with unique animal models to determine the role of the AHR-TIPARP signaling axis in either the toxicity or the beneficial effects of dioxin-like and other food-derived chemicals. By better understanding the function of TIPARP and its role in AHR action our research may lead to the development of new strategies to treat human disease, and allow for better prediction of both the health risks and the benefits associated with exposure to various chemicals that activate AHR.

column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death and nearly 1 in 2 Canadians is expected to develop cancer in its lifetime. This pathway could be targeted to prevent/delay progression and restore drug sensitivity. By this mean we want to identify cancer cell weaknesses that could be exploited by novel therapies. Our research program offers high translational potential. We anticipate that it will provide new tools to help decision-making process, offer mechanistic insights and relevant drug targets. This knowledge will lead to the development of more effective strategies to identify and treat high-risk CLL and PCa patients and ultimately improve their survival.

column36: Improving palliative care in the home and community: Building CAPACITI (Community Access to PAlliative Care via Interprofessional primary care Teams Intervention)
column37: Palliative care is care that emphasizes quality-of-life rather than curative treatment for patients with advanced illness. Particularly home-based palliative care is important because 80% of patients want to die at home, yet 65% die in hospital. Strong evidence shows home-based palliative care-delivered by physicians working in primary care teams-reduces pain and symptoms, improves quality-of-life, and reduces health care costs. Yet <10% of patients get access to home-based palliative care by family physicians in the last year of life. Improving access to home-based palliative care can improve patient and system outcomes. However, we lack interventions that build capacity among primary care teams to deliver home-base palliative care. To address this, we propose an intervention called CAPACITI (Community Access to PAlliative Care via Interprofessional Teams Intervention). CAPACITI is a 1-year palliative care training and coaching program for primary care teams. Over monthly sessions and bi-weekly calls, it integrates 4 components: clinical education for early identification and communication; evidence-based tools for symptom management and care pathways; practice supports for team collaboration and system coordination; and high-facilitation and expert coaching for adaptation to local context. Our study will evaluate outcomes in 53 primary care teams in Ontario before vs. after implementation of CAPACITI, using a phased approach that compares intervention teams to control teams who have yet to start CAPACITI. The outcomes are access to home-based palliative care, team knowledge and collaboration, and patient-caregiver satisfaction. Our team has tested, evaluated and refined elements of CAPACITI, demonstrating its effectiveness on small numbers of primary care teams. We are ready to test CAPACITI on a provincial scale. Ultimately this study's results will strengthen the primary care system and increase access to home-based palliative care for patients across Canada.

column37: Given the continued high HIV prevalence rates among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in North American cities, there is a critical need for HIV prevention programs that meet the needs of this population. Social anxiety - anxiety about being evaluated in interpersonal and performance situations - is a risk factor for condomless anal sex (CAS), the main HIV transmission route among MSM. Social anxiety may increase substance use in sexual situations, which is also linked to increased CAS. Following this logic, treating social anxiety using cognitive behavioural therapy, an evidence-based social anxiety treatment, may also reduce HIV risk behaviour. This study will evaluate a new HIV prevention intervention designed to reduce HIV risk, social anxiety, and problematic substance use among MSM. We will randomly assign 176 participants to receive either this new intervention ("Sexual Confidence") or applied relaxation, which is an empirically-supported behavior therapy for social anxiety disorder that does not address substance use problems or risks for contracting HIV or sexually transmitted infections. Participants will be eligible for the trial if they self-identify as a man aged 18-65, and report HIV-negative status, symptoms of social anxiety disorder, substance use within 2 hours before or during sexual activity, and CAS with a man who was not known to be HIV-negative. This study will be the first in Canada to evaluate a combined cognitive behavioural therapy and HIV prevention program for HIV-negative MSM using a randomized controlled trial. This therapy, if found to be efficacious, will allow mental health clinicians to not only treat social anxiety and substance use problems but also to reduce the risk of contracting HIV in their higher-risk clients. The potential contribution of this research to advancing effective HIV prevention programming for gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men is therefore substantial.

The first brain changes in humans appear quite early as production of abnormal tau protein by these cells. The abnormal tau spreads from locus coeruleus along memory pathways until reaching the cortex and becoming tangles. Abnormal tau in locus coeruleus cells occurs early in our lives and is seen in most by age 30, but its effects are not noticeable and spread occurs over decades. We need to detect and prevent these early events. Our evidence suggests distinguishing between very similar patterns is helped by the locus coeruleus. We will test this idea by producing abnormal human tau in rat locus coeruleus cells and testing similar odor discrimination ability. We know the locus coeruleus is activated by new, and by stressful, experiences. Importantly, it is activated differently by these two experiences. We think novel experience activation will slow abnormal brain changes, while stress will increase their rate and extent. We will activate rat locus coeruleus cells containing abnormal tau to mimic either novel and enriched or stressful experience. We predict the spread of abnormal tau along memory pathways will be fast with stress patterns and slow, or prevented by, novelty patterns that can promote learning and memory. Locus coeruleus may be a two-edged sword in Alzheimer's Disease acting either to diminish or accelerate the later likelihood of Alzheimer's Disease appearing. We will identify activity patterns that decrease, or increase, the spread of the earliest brain changes and we will relate their occurrence to pattern discrimination ability to provide new ideas for detecting early locus coeruleus changes and for designing lifestyles to prevent the spread and expression of abnormality, thus stopping later Alzheimer's Disease.

column36: Understanding cancer burden and outcomes for Canadians living with intellectual and developmental disabilities
column37: Not all Canadians have the same cancer risk, receive the same quality of healthcare after a cancer diagnosis, or have the same prognosis. This may be the result of many things including how much money someone has, their education, where they live, or discrimination within the healthcare system that causes people to be treated differently, regardless of how sick they are. Although cancer is a leading cause of death for Canadians living with intellectual disabilities and developmental disabilities (IDD), they may be less likely to receive high quality cancer treatment compared to other Canadians. Because people living with IDD are more likely to live in vulnerable circumstances (such as those described above), this may impact how quickly their cancer is diagnosed, their access to life-saving treatment and result in worse outcomes. The goal of this project is to determine whether or not Canadians living with IDD are more likely than Canadians who do not have IDD to be 1) diagnosed with cancer; 2) diagnosed with incurable cancer; 3) not receive the right cancer treatment; and 4) to die of their cancer. To achieve our goal, our team of cancer and IDD researchers and clinicians will perform simultaneous research studies of breast, colorectal, and cancer patients living in Manitoba and Ontario. This will be done by using data routinely collected during encounters with provincial health, social, and education systems. Analyses will be conducted within each respective province. This study will provide the first Canadian research describing cancer outcomes for people with IDD. Without this information, people with IDD may not receive the best care for their cancer, causing unnecessary harm. This study will highlight ways to improve the quality of care provided. We will work with our policy partners to ensure this information is usable and informative to the care of underserved cancer populations.

column36: Alpha particle-labeled antibody-drug radioconjugates for radiotherapy of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC)
column37: Metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is the second leading cause of death from cancer. At initial diagnosis almost half of patients have advanced disease and fewer than 10% live for more than five years. Surgery is the most effective treatment for controlling further spread, although local recurrence rates can range from 36-88%. A protein called epidermal growth factor receptor I (EGFR) has been shown to be increased in up to 80% of mCRC. Available drugs that target this protein are not effective. Another problem with treating patients with EGFR positive mCRC is that the current method for patient selection is less than optimal. Our goal is to develop more effective therapeutic and imaging agents that will improve the care of mCRC Radioimmunotherapy (i.e.radiolabeled antibodies ) have shown some promise in treating mCRC. However, current strategies have often given suboptimal results since all studies have focused on beta emitting radiation, which is less potent and tends to be toxic to adjacent healthy cells. In contrast, radioimmunotherapy strategies based on alpha particles, such as 225Ac, are up to 1000-fold more effective. Firstly, we propose to develop a set of novel therapeutic compounds which will be based on an antibody nimotuzumab (an antibody that specifically binds to EGFR protein on the cancer cell), linked to two other anticancer agents namely a drug and an alpha particle (actinium-225: 225Ac). The approach will be tested in cells and in mice bearing colorectal cancers. Secondly, we will develop an antibody imaging agent 89Zr-FABH that can be used together with PET/CT to more accurately diagnose and evaluate response to the new treatments against colorectal cancer. We anticipate that these strategies will be more effective than current treatment approaches for colorectal cancer and can be beneficial to other cancer types that express this protein - annually about 1 million new cases of EGFR-positive cancers are reported in North America.

column36: Regulation of human memory B cell responses by Fc-Receptor like molecules
column37: Memory B cells are pivotal to the establishment and maintenance of protection from re-encountered pathogens, both in the context of natural infection and vaccination. Following activation memory B cells divide and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells more rapidly than naive B cells. The importance of pathogen-specific antibodies is emphasized by observations illustrating that neutralizing antibody responses are an important component of most successful vaccines. It is therefore of critical importance to identify mechanisms regulating memory B cell responses. The Fc Receptor-Like (FCRL) family of cell surface receptors is preferentially expressed on B lineage cells. Among these, FCRL4 family member is expressed only on a subpopulation of memory B cells that are functionally impaired in chronic infectious diseases like HIV. In previous work, we could demonstrate the strong regulatory activity of FCRL4 on memory B cells. Furthermore, we determined that antibodies encoded by FCRL4+ memory B cells preferentially detect commensal microbiota. In this research proposal we will investigate the antibodies to known antigens from vaccinations that are encoded by FCRL4+ and FCRL4- memory B cells. We will determine the factors that lead to the generation of FCRL4-bearing memory B cells and we will investigate the characteristics antibody secreting plasma cells derived from FCRL4+ and FCRL4- memory B cells. The results from this study will provide deeper understanding of functionally distinct memory B cell populations and their plasma cell progeny. Ultimately, this information will be important in vaccine design efforts aiming to elicit long lasting protective antibody titres to pathogens to which presently no effective vaccines are available.

column36: Myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF) and serum response factor (SRF) are constituents and key regulators of the primary cilium
column37: The primary cilium is an important chemical and mechanical antenna of practically every cell in the body. This organelle, once thought to be vestigial, is a major organizer of differentiation, cell growth and proliferation. The paramount importance of the cilium became obvious with the recognition that errors in the genes that encode cilium proteins cause serious and ultimately often lethal hereditary diseases, so called ciliopathies. The most common of these is polycystic kidney disease, but mutation in ciliary proteins lead to a set of other syndromes too, with wide-ranging symptoms including impaired mental function due to malformation of the nervous system, blindness, left-right side inversion, bone deformities, obesity as well as liver, heart and other kidney diseases. Moreover, acquired (non-inherited) abnormalities in the cilium contribute to cancer and chronic scarring of tissues (fibrosis). While complex machineries control both the assembly and the disassembly of the cilium and coordinate these evens with cell division, the underlying molecular mechanisms are not well understood. Our proposal stems from our discovery that two proteins, myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF) and serum response factor (SRF) regulate cilium assembly and disassembly. These factors, controlled by the cell's skeleton, can drive genes, some of which are necessary for cilium maintenance. However, in addition to their gene-regulating (transcriptional) effect, we found that MRTF and SRF are also part of the cilium itself. These recognitions open a new way to affect the cilium. Using a variety of cell and molecular biology techniques, we propose to uncover how these proteins contribute to the normal structure and function of the primary cilium, and how they might be involved in serious ciliopathies and cancer-related cilium defects. Understanding these processes will lead to fundamental insights necessary for correcting cilium errors.

column36: Indigenous Knowledge Development Centres with a focus on Wellness - miyo-pimatisiwin
column37: In Canada, most health research is focused on a disease or deficit end-point, whether designing, testing or implementing interventions, treatments or preventive measures. The focus of this Indigenous knowledge development project is on wellness - promoting, maintaining and re-gaining wellness, by itself, or in the context of a variety of conditions or life circumstances that First Nations, Inuit and Metis peoples may find themselves. There is much Indigenous health and wellness knowledge/wisdom that has yet to be re-awakened, and in fact, cannot be well-supported in our current colonized structures and conceptualizations. To do so will take the development and re-development of roles and processes within community. It is within this context that we see Indigenous community as being the primary research leader, with the academy and the health system as being knowledge users. We propose a network of Indigenous health knowledge development centres. These centres will be grounded in the land and in culture, with land-based Indigenous research methodologies a critical component of the network. Using a health determinants approach and working with communities of Indigenous people including Elders, Knowledge Holders, youth, researchers and health workers, we will explore what makes Indigenous people well, what keeps them well, and how Indigenous wellness can be achieved or re-gained and maintained through practices and interventions based on traditional and western knowledge. Through meaningful engagement between academic centres and Indigenous communities, our network of knowledge development centres will increase and build on our understanding of wellness. In the words of the Elder: "Let's research ourselves back to life."
