column36: Creating a Living Knowledge Translation Agenda to Improve the Delivery of Evidence-based Care in Adult Critical Care Medicine
column37: Healthcare systems need to more consistently incorporate findings from research into patient care. With the amount of research in the current medical literature, and limited resources available to apply this research, some research findings should be given higher priority over others. This is especially important for patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) where multiple expensive, potentially risky tests, and treatments are used to save lives. In a review of ICU research, we identified 14 medical practices that high-quality research suggests are beneficial among ICU patients, and 21 practices that are of no benefit. Decision-makers for ICUs in Alberta have asked us to use this list of 35 ICU practices to develop a method that can both determine from within a list of current research which ICU care practices should be given greater priority for use or removal from patient care, and allows for annual updating of the list by being responsive to new research. We plan to do this in 4 connected steps, guided by a governing group consisting of patients, researchers, and healthcare providers. First, we will develop a method that enables our review of ICU research to be continuously updated in response to new research. Second, using electronic health data, we will determine predicted outcomes and costs associated with changes in use of each practice. Third, we will survey a national group of healthcare providers and former ICU patients and their family members to rank priorities for practice change. Fourth, we will present the results of steps 1-3 to decision-makers in Alberta to determine which patient care practices will be targets for practice change in Alberta ICUs. This work is important because it will help improve care in ICUs, and potentially contribute to future improvements in other areas of healthcare through development of a strong, widely applicable, sustainable approach for incorporating high-quality science into the care of patients admitted to ICUs.

column36: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) for intestinal decolonization of multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogens
column37: Antimicrobial resistance is a global threat to public health. The Canadian government recently made antimicrobial resistance a nationwide health priority (Antimicrobial Resistance and Use in Canada: A Federal Framework for Action). Kidney transplant patients are at especially high-risk of developing infections caused by multidrug-resistant bacteria, so-called 'super-bugs'. These drug-resistant infections are hard to treat, result in longer hospital stays, and lead to more deaths and higher medical costs. The source of these 'super-bugs' is often the patient's own gut, where they can remain until escaping to cause infection. Current approaches to eliminating resistant bacteria from the gut do not work very well and can sometimes lead to an increase in resistant bacteria. Emerging evidence suggests that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), otherwise known as a 'poop' transplant, may be an effective and innovative approach to eradicating multidrug-resistant bacteria from the gut before they can cause infection. FMT involves the infusion of fully screened, healthy donor stool into a patient. FMT is already known to be a safe and effective way to remove Clostridium difficile, a cause of hospital-associated diarrhea, from infected patients. In this randomized controlled trial, we will test the efficacy of FMT via enema to eliminate highly resistant bacteria from the intestinal tract of kidney transplant patients. We will also examine (1) FMT safety; (2) how long patients remain decolonized; (3) if there are fewer infections after FMT; and (4) how FMT might work. Our research team has obtained all the necessary ethics and Health Canada approvals and started study recruitment. Ideally, FMT donor feces will be replaced by a well-defined community of bacteria that is just as effective as FMT. Vedanta Biosciences, our industry partner, will work with us to develop a transformative microbial therapy to prevent carriage and infection by highly drug-resistant 'super-bugs'.

column36: Discovery of non-coding driver mutations and pathways in thousands of whole cancer genomes using gene regulatory and long-range chromatin interactions
column37: Cancer is a genetic disease however most cancers are not inherited but are instead caused by random mutations in individuals' DNA over time. While most such mutations are harmless, a minority called cancer driver mutations (drivers) affect critical genes and cause unlimited cell growth and other cancerous properties. To understand cancer biology and develop therapies, we need to deeply characterize drivers. As drivers are known to affect the same DNA region more frequently than expected by chance alone, we can find drivers statistically by analysing many cancer genomes and millions of mutations. While earlier studies only mapped the small fraction (<2%) of the human genome that produces proteins, recent DNA sequencing tools map entire genomes. As such whole-genome sequencing datasets are only becoming available recently, little is known about drivers in the entire genome. We will build the largest dataset of whole cancer genomes by combining all available studies of this kind, using statistical and machine-learning tools we and others developed. We will study different cancer types and also combine all data to find drivers that are rare but important in many cancer types. We will focus on the least-studied part of the genome outside of protein-coding genes. As genes often act together in cancer, we will find additional drivers by grouping biologically related genes. We will conduct modern genetic experiments using CRISPR with cancer cell lines and confirm top-ranking candidates as true drivers of cancer by measuring cell growth, motility and other oncogenic properties. We will produce a reliable catalogue of cancer drivers supported by validation experiments of our best findings at project completion. The catalogue will increase understanding of cancer biology and ultimately improve therapies. Some drivers may be applicable as biomarkers to diagnose cancer and predict response to chemotherapies.

column36: Role of miR-299a in regulating diabetic kidney disease
column37: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure, leading to scarring of the filtering units of the kidneys. Patients with diabetes have high glucose levels in their blood. High glucose causes kidney cells called mesangial cells to make scar proteins. These scar proteins accumulate in the filtering units of the kidneys and prevent them from functioning properly. It is not yet known how high glucose levels cause kidney cells to produce these scar proteins. Our previous studies showed that absence of the protein caveolin-1 from kidney cells and from kidneys protected against scarring due to diabetes. Since caveolin-1 is difficult to change with treatment, we looked to see the differences in micro RNA levels between kidney cells with and without caveolin-1. Here we found micro RNA 299a-5p levels to be decreased in kidney cells without caveolin-1. In diabetic kidneys and kidney cells exposed to high glucose, micro RNA 299a-5p is increased, and blocking it prevents cells from making scar proteins. In our studies, we would like to understand how micro RNA-299a-5p allows high glucose to direct kidney cells to make scar proteins, and whether blocking the function of miRNA-299a-5p will prevent kidney scarring and help to prevent kidney function from getting worse in mice with diabetes. Drugs which block other molecules like micro RNA-299a-5p have already been successfully used in patients. If our studies show that blocking micro RNA-299a-5p prevents or improves diabetic kidney disease, this will give us a new treatment to test in patients with kidney disease due to diabetes.

column36: A Novel Genetic Subtype of Human Atrial Fibrillation: Physiologic Characterization and Therapeutic Drug Targeting
column37: Our research focuses on the most common arrhythmia affecting humans. This arrhythmia is known as atrial fibrillation (AF). The lifetime risk of developing this arrhythmia is 25%, and the risk increases with age. This arrhythmia causes blood to stagnate in the top chambers, where blood clots can form, and consequently this arrhythmia is the most common cause of stroke in older individuals. The cost of managing this arrhythmia and the consequences are significant and pose a large burden on health care costs. Unfortunately, treatment of this arrhythmia is challenging and for many patients this arrhythmia becomes chronic with an ongoing risk of stroke. We recently studied a large family where 9 individuals were suffering from AF, highlighting that this is a genetic condition in this family (and in many individuals). Using cutting edge genetic technology (whole exome sequencing), we identified the genetic cause for AF in this family. Affected family members had a mutation in the gene known as CACNA1H. This gene makes a protein in the heart that regulates calcium flow. Our preliminary work in cell models indicates that the mutant protein functions abnormally and that a novel class of drugs in development that specifically targets this gene/protein can return function to normal. These observations are promising and could lead to potential development of a new class of drugs for more effective treatment of AF. In this study, we have created a mouse that specifically expressed the mutant protein found in the large family studied. We wish to study these mice to gain a better understanding of the disease physiology, and importantly, to study the effect of a novel drug that may prevent AF from developing in these mice. This goal of this work is to translate the observations from this research to human patients.

column36: Respiratory management of extremely preterm neonates: Evidence generation and implementation by comparative effectiveness research (CER) using real world data (RWD) from a practice-based research network (PBRN)
column37: Infants born extremely preterm before 29 weeks' gestational age face a myriad of potential challenges, many of which result from immature brain and lungs at birth. For example, extremely preterm infants have a 10% risk of mortality, 15% risk of severe brain injury, and 45% risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (chronic lung disease). In the first week of life, survival is the primary goal for an extremely preterm infant and often treatment results in a tube in the airway and mechanical ventilation to assist or replace spontaneous breathing. The transition of an infant from respiratory support to breathing on his or her own is difficult because there are multiple respiratory management strategies without evidence indicating which is optimal. Our proposal addresses two questions about respiratory management of extremely premature infants. First, we know that 90% of brain hemorrhages happen in the first 3 days following birth; therefore, if an infant born at less than 26 weeks' gestational age needs a tube placed in his or her airway in the first 3 days following birth, is there less brain injury and lung disease if the tube is left in the airway until the infant is at least 3 days old or if the tube is taken out as soon as possible? Second, in infants born at less than 29 weeks' gestational age who required mechanical breathing assistance does intermittent pressure that gives the infant a breath (nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation) or continuous pressure that opens up the lungs (nasal continuous positive airway pressure) lead to similar risk of either re-placing a tube in the airway or bronchopulmonary dysplasia? Our studies will identify the best respiratory management practice for reducing the risk of severe brain injury and bronchopulmonary dysplasia in extremely preterm infants. The evidence we generate will be used to inform future practice guidelines for the respiratory management of extremely preterm infants across Canada.

column36: Role of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase Lyn in the regulation of pancreatic beta-cell mass and function
column37: Pancreatic beta-cells are specialized cells residing in the pancreas. Their biological role is unique: they secrete insulin in order to maintain blood glucose concentrations in a narrow physiological range. When this mechanism fails, blood glucose increases and diabetes arises. Thus, type 2 diabetes is characterized by a progressive deterioration of beta-cells. However, the molecular mechanisms governing beta-cell life and death are not completely understood. It is important that we elucidate these mechanisms to identify new therapeutic targets for diabetes treatment. We previously published that a family of proteins called "Src" could regulate beta-cell "life and death". However, we did not precisely identify the Src member that is involved in this process. Altogether, very little is known about Src family members in beta-cells. In this project, we are going to study the role of one member in particular called Lyn. First, we will understand the regulation of Lyn in pancreatic beta-cells. Then, we will investigate its role in the regulation of beta-cells, using both in vivo and in vitro models. Finally, we will elucidate the targets of Lyn to understand its downstream signals and mode of action. Our study will characterize for the first time the role of Lyn in pancreatic beta-cells, thereby identifying Lyn (and perhaps some of its downstream effectors) as a potential therapeutic target for diabetes treatment.

column36: Mechanisms Regulating Chronic Skeletal Muscle Atrophy and Weakness in the Critical Illness Survivor
column37: Intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICUAW) describes muscle weakness that develops in some people who have been admitted to an ICU with a serious illness. It is associated with problems such as prolonged ICU length of stay, and increased ICU, hospital, and 1-year rates of death. In up to 50% of critical illness survivors, muscle wasting and weakness lasts a lifetime and cause permanent physical disability, reduced quality of life, inability to work, and increased number of return trips to hospital. This also negatively impacts the individual's caregivers, who demonstrate increased incidence of depression. We have no therapy that is capable of preventing, or treating, ICUAW sustained months after ICU discharge because we do not understand the mechanisms that cause persistent wasting and weakness in the critical illness survivor. Our group has shown that the ability of muscle to re-grow following wasting in the ICU is permanently impaired in patients who have sustained ICUAW. We found that muscle stem (satellite) cells are lost, implying the muscle is unable to regenerate. We have identified some molecular regulators, known as microRNAs (miRs), are likely to play a causative role. In this study we propose to determine the mechanism by which our candidate factors impair muscle regeneration and growth and determine if we can in turn, impact muscle regeneration and growth by modulating our candidate factors in cell culture models and patients with ICUAW. The significance and strength of this proposal lies in its potential translatability to the clinical setting. By generating totally novel insights into sustained muscle wasting and potential therapeutic target identification, this will allow us to develop various approaches aimed at limiting loss of, and/or enhancing growth of muscle in individuals with sustained ICUAW.

column36: The BCC3 cohort: Cellular aging in women living with HIV
column37: People living with HIV show accelerated aging meaning they experience age-related illnesses earlier in life. This is clearly related to their HIV infection, but it could also be exacerbated by the treatment they receive, as well as by other viral infections of the type that stay with people for life (i.e. herpes virus and chicken pox virus)., or even bad habits such as smoking. Smoking rates are high among people living with HIV in Canada. This research will try to elucidate the contribution of each of these factors to the aging of immune cells, and how this may relate to age-associated illnesses and conditions such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and cancer. We will study women living with HIV or not whom we have already been following for a long time. We will measure markers of aging, and consider other factors such as life habits, psychosocial stressors such as stigma or raciism, to understand what drives the acceleration of natural aging.

column36: Non-canonical role of initiator caspases in colorectal cancer
column37: The body relies on a particular cell death program called apoptosis to eliminate defective cells. This program involves the sequential activation of a distinct set of caspases, which are enzymes that cleave and thereby inactivate hundreds of proteins necessary for cell survival. A fundamental trait of cancer cells is their inherent or acquired resistance to apoptosis. This cancer feature often accounts for chemotherapeutic failure and is associated with enhanced tumorigenesis and metastasis. At the molecular level, resistance to apoptosis usually involves a block of death signal transmission from the initiator to the executioner caspases, the latter of which is responsible for killing the cell. As such, a direct consequence of resistance to apoptosis is that tumor cells can uniquely sustain the activity of initiator caspases by avoiding the killing effects of the others. Results from our recent study support the hypothesis that substrate products of initiator caspases contribute to enhancing tumorigenic and metastatic features of apoptosis-resistant cancer cells. The proposed project seeks to validate this postulate by designing a method for detecting the activity of initiator caspases and their cleaved substrates as biomarkers of colorectal cancer progression, by identifying proteins cleaved by initiator caspases in apoptosis-resistant cancer cells, and by verifying the tumorigenic and metastatic properties of these identified substrates in colorectal cancer cell models. Experimental validation of our hypothesis would offer a ground-breaking paradigm shift in the current understanding of the roles of caspases in cell death and when tumor cells become resistant to apoptosis. Notably, our work could lead to the development of new biomarkers and innovative therapies to overcome clinical resistance to several types of current clinically used cancer-death-based chemotherapies.

column36: Pre-clinical evaluation of micro-tissue injection and self-assembly in vivo for cardiac repairs.
column37: The field of tissue engineering aims to create functional tissues from human cells and scaffolds that can replace damaged tissues in patients. However, to perform therapeutic repairs, lab-grown tissues often need to be delivered deep into the interior of a damaged organ in a patient while preserving a high-level of tissue structural organization, which makes the implantation surgery not only invasive but in many cases impossible to achieve. This project seeks to address the way we implement tissue engineered products by developing smart scaffolds and functional tissues that can be delivered minimally invasively and then self-assemble in the human body with external guidance. Specifically, we will develop a new therapeutic solution to deliver functional tissues for heart repairs in a minimally invasive manner. Building on our prior success in cardiovascular tissue engineering, our lab is taking a leap forward to introduce a new strategy in tissue repairs with smart functional materials. We envision that incorporating magnetic particles inside a biodegradable scaffold will result in a biodegradable, magnetic-responsive scaffold-based carrier that can be used to support the culture of engineered heart muscles. Then a collection of these magnetic-scaffolds will serve as carriers to deliver and assemble the engineered heart tissues directly into the interior of the damaged heart muscle wall in a patient with minimally invasive injections. The magnetic-scaffolds will induce cellular alignment as well as tissue alignment with remotely controlled magnetic guidance. Finally, our scaffold materials will degrade as the heart heals. Collectively, these smart micro-scaffolds will guide tissue assembly in the body in a step-by-step fashion. This delivery method will allow us to reverse heart failure by delivering engineered heart tissues with a minimally invasive surgical procedure and by re-growing new muscles inside the heart.

column36: Targeting AMPK to treat muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) are the most prevalent muscular dystrophies in children and adults in Canada and worldwide. There are no cures, thus the health- and life-limiting nature of these disorders is, at present, inevitable. Therefore, a critical, unmet clinical need exists for the identification and evaluation of new, effective therapies. We know that when a protein in our muscles called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is turned on, it has some benefit in reducing the severity of DMD and DM1 in animals engineered to have these disorders. However, AMPK-activating drugs that have been used to date in muscular dystrophy studies are neither safe for long-term human use, nor particularly potent. The use of better compounds to activate AMPK, those that are safe, effective, and able to be taken orally, would greatly increase their clinical impact and translation into human DMD and DM1 patients. Here we will employ new approaches to examine the effectiveness of targeting AMPK for the treatment of muscular dystrophy. Specifically, the purpose of this project is to investigate whether stimulation of AMPK with practical, next-generation compounds improves the health of mice with DMD and DM1, which would provide a better outlook for applicability in human muscular dystrophy patients. We will focus on the ability of the AMPK-activating drugs to restore the proper structure and function of dystrophic skeletal muscles, as well as explore the underlying molecular mechanisms of their action. There is no better time than the present to perform these studies since these drugs are also currently in clinical trials for treating epidemics such as diabetes and metabolic disease. This proposal is designed to reveal critical information about the therapeutic potential of a new class of AMPK-stimulating compounds, which may ultimately improve the quality and quantity of life of Canadians.

column36: Towards the micro-elimination of hepatitis C virus among Canadian provincial prison inmates: The effectiveness of patient navigation on treatment uptake
column37: The prevalence of chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is approximately 40-fold higher among provincial prison inmates compared to the Canadian population. Left untreated, there is ongoing risk of transmission within prisons and to the community at large upon release. Treatment of prisoners for HCV could substantially reduce prevalent and incident infections. However, due to short sentences in provincial prisons, inmates are often released prior to treatment completion, making linkage to HCV care upon release essential. Currently, less than 1% of inmates link to care following release. Patient navigation, whereby a peer typically assists patients in completing a health care goal, may have a role in linking inmates to HCV care following release. However, no research has yet to be done on different models of patient navigation for inmates. While linkage to care is the rate-limiting step in the HCV cascade of care for released inmates, linkage in the absence of treatment uptake will fail to achieve the goal of HCV micro-elimination, underscoring treatment uptake as the most meaningful clinical outcome. This study will assess two models of patient navigation, a transitional and a tailored model, on HCV treatment uptake. The tailored model will be designed following one-to-one qualitative interviews with inmates and an expert review of providers and inmates. Both models will be implemented and evaluated on treatment uptake, the primary outcome measure, as well as linkage to care, the secondary outcome measure. The goal will be to capitalize on the existing infrastructure and partnerships that are currently in place at Bordeaux prison to conduct this study. The findings of this study will be critical in developing optimal models of patient navigation for scale up in other provincial prisons, ensuring that we are one step closer towards to the "micro-elimination" of HCV among one of the most important sub-populations fueling the current epidemic in Canada.

column36: Understanding the allosteric and functional selectivity regulation of the Prostaglandin F2 receptor.
column37: Our research focuses on a class of membrane receptor for hormones know as prostaglandins that are involved in normal delivery, but that also play a role in premature birth. Pharmacological therapies targeting these receptors to prevent premature birth would greatly reduce the personal and socio-economical burden associated with this problem, for which no safe drugs exist. Our research has unveiled the properties of a new class of drugs that act in an unconventional way on these receptors to selectively affect the response of the natural hormone prostaglandin and regulate uterine contraction. We propose to characterize the functional domains of these receptors, known as "allosteric" sites, which are targeted by our newly discovered compounds, to iteratively generate more selective and efficacious drugs. Complications related to preterm birth contribute to 40% of all neonatal deaths and have continued increasing in the last 30 years. Our research should thus have great impact on managing preterm delivery in Canadian women, which is the primary cause of neonatal mortality.

This project will determine the mechanisms of action and functional consequences of these EBV protein activities, including how they impact EBV infection and cancer-associated pathways. The novel activities of these EBV proteins provide new therapeutic opportunities to inhibit EBV infection.

column36: Unveiling the role of alpha-synuclein clustering and Lewy body formation in Parkinson's disease pathogenesis using an optogenetic-mediated protein aggregation system
column37: More than a century ago, the neurologist Friedrich Lewy described for the first time, in the brain of patients suffering from Parkinson's disease (PD), the presence of abnormal protein inclusions, called Lewy bodies (LBs). These inclusions have been suggested to play a deleterious role in the brain and to induce neuronal loss. However, the exact mechanisms by which these inclusions precipitate the cell death and PD progression remain unknown. In our laboratory, we took advantage of recent technologies, allowing the manipulation of protein clustering under light (optogenetic), to create a new cellular and animal model of PD based on the formation of intra-neuronal inclusions mimicking PD-derived authentic LBs. Using this unique model, we will seek to address the question on how LBs disrupt the neuronal functions leading to neuronal degeneration in the brain and progression of PD. The expected results will help us identify new pharmacological targets for the development of effective therapies for PD and related disorders.

column36: Nanoplexes for Targeted Anti-Inflammatory Gene Therapy in Atherosclerosis
column37: Despite enormous advances in prevention, diagnosis and management over the past few decades, heart disease remains the leading cause of death and disability in western societies. This disease burden translates into a huge cost to healthcare systems, which could be curbed if better approaches for treatment were developed. This proposal aims to develop a multifunctional gene delivery vehicle that can be administered non-locally for treatment of atherosclerosis. Current treatments involve revascularization procedures or the use of drugs, which require frequent dosing and are associated with untoward side effects such as toxicity, development of resistance, and off-target effects. Conversely, gene therapy has always had high potential but its translation to the clinic has been slow, mainly due to unpredictable and unsafe viruses as gene carriers. To date, there is no report involving non-viral nanotechnology to provide gene-based therapies for atherosclerosis. We propose a synthetic polymer-based nanocarrier to deliver anti-inflammatory genes directly to the disease site to slow atherosclerotic progression and stabilize fatty plaques. The main features of the proposed delivery vehicle include a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer and bioconjugated targeting peptides capable of localizing preferentially to the disease site. Our preliminary results showed that the multifunctional nanoplex is non-toxic, able to deliver anti-inflammatory genes with high efficiency, and able to attenuate inflammation in vitro. As such, the proposed non-viral and anti-inflammatory gene therapy strategy would be the first of its kind to address the underlying driver of atherosclerotic plaque formation, non-resolving inflammation. The project would contribute to advancing the knowledge of cardiovascular disease progression and could also be envisioned for other chronic inflammatory diseases such as Crohn's, arthritis, and multiple sclerosis.

column36: GRADE: GRAded challenge for Drug allergy Evaluation
column37: Adverse reactions to antibiotics, principally different types of skin rashes, are often reported in children and complicate future management. The majority are diagnosed, without further evaluation, as allergic to the implicated antibiotic. They avoid it into adulthood, replacing it with antibiotics that may be less effective, more toxic, and more expensive. It is currently unknown how many of the reported antibiotic allergies represent "true" allergies. Furthermore, there is no accepted method to diagnose allergic versus non-allergic reactions. We aim to evaluate the risk of true antibiotic allergies in children with suspected antibiotic allergy and to develop simple evaluation approach to help diagnose correctly "true" allergies. In 2012, our team initiated a study collecting data from children with suspected antibiotic allergy to characterize immediate and non-immediate allergic reactions associated with antibiotics. All participants are evaluated through direct supervised ingestion (oral challenge) of the suspected antibiotic in our clinic. All participants who tolerate the antibiotic are followed for 5 years to ensure safe future use of this antibiotic. We now aim to expand our registry to evaluate the major antibiotics used to treat infections, and identify factors associated with positive challenges. Our study will provide valuable data on the safe use of antibiotics in children and the strategies to diagnose and predict allergic reactions.

column36: A randomized controlled trial of cognitive behaviour therapy for insomnia and perceived cognitive impairment in cancer survivors
column37: For cancer survivors, one of the biggest barriers to getting back to "normal" is perceived cognitive impairment (PCI). Approximately 75% of cancer patients have difficulty remembering things, concentrating, and paying attention after completing cancer treatments. No one agrees on the best way of treating PCI. Insomnia is also an extremely common side effect of cancer and can increase cognitive impairments. Cognitive Behaviour Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended treatment for insomnia in cancer survivors. Our research suggests that CBT-I may also improve PCI but we need to investigate this question with better measures of cognitive abilities and sleep. We will recruit 135 people with insomnia and cognitive complaints who have completed cancer treatment at least 12 months prior to the study. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive immediate treatment with CBT-I or treatment after an 8-week waiting period. We want to determine whether treating insomnia with CBT-I can also improve PCI. For this, we will measure changes in cognitive abilities and sleep in a few ways. Patients will report on their own perception of their cognitive abilities. We will also ask participants to remember lists of words and follow instructions. Sleep will be assessed using sleep diaries and actigraphy, a type of "wristwatch" that can detect sleep based on whether or not a person is moving. We will also measure fatigue, anxiety, and depression, as we know these can also impact sleep and cognition. This study will take place in Newfoundland which has the highest incidence rate for cancer in Canada. The relative survival rate for cancer is better than ever before, meaning that more people will be living as cancer survivors and managing the long term side effects of the disease and its treatment. This research will expand currently available treatment options in order to address two of the most problematic consequences of cancer.

column36: Molecular mechanisms underlying T cell/oligodendrocyte interactions as target for neuroprotective strategies in MS
column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory disease of brain and spinal cord affecting up to 1/500 people in Canada. It causes substantial disability in young adults and results in considerable emotional, physical, social and economic burden on the patients and their relatives. While the exact cause of MS is still unknown, we know that there is an aberrant response of immune cells against cells of the brain and spinal cord in MS. Oligodendrocytes are myelin-producing cells which support and insulate neurons. In MS they are injured by the inflammatory immune cells, leaving neurons vulnerable. This leads to neurological deficits that can be reversible if the oligodendrocytes can recover sufficiently, but this is often not the case. Immune cells called pro-inflammatory T cells are considered to orchestrate neuroinflammation in MS and its animal model experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), but whether they can directly injure oligodendrocytes remains undefined. Using live imaging, we have recently shown that T cells can directly contact oligodendrocytes in the brain/spinal cord of EAE animals, and we also found T cells juxtaposed with oligodendrocytes in human MS brain tissue. We now want to characterize which molecules are implicated and what are the consequences of these direct T cell-oligodendrocytes interactions. As preventing immune-mediated oligodendrocyte damage could decrease the accumulation of neurological disability in MS, we will moreover test if targeting the contact molecules identified could represent a future treatment avenue to protect the cells of the brain and spinal cord in MS.

column36: Role of Human Oviductin in Enhancement of Sperm Fertilizing Competence
column37: Infertility affects around 15% of couples of reproductive age, and about half of the infertility is associated with male partner. To date, intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is a common clinical practice as an assisted reproductive technology (ART) procedure to achieve fertilization in vitro. Despite the relatively high fertilization rate of ICSI, the latter is a more expensive and invasive treatment compared to the standard in vitro fertilization (IVF) and the intrauterine insemination (IUI) procedures. There has been increasing reports on the association of increased genetic anomalies and birth defects in ICSI concepti. This may be due partly to damages to gamete chromosomes caused by the invasive ICSI procedure. To encourage the use of the less invasive standard IVF and IUI for male infertility treatment, there is need to improve the fertilization rate of standard IVF and IUI. One possible approach is to treat sperm with oviductin, a secreted oviductal glycoprotein which has been shown to enhance sperm functions and fertilization. In subfertile men, sperm motility is highly correlated with fertilizing ability. It is generally recognized that sperm with severe motility aberrations are incapable of fertilization without extensive ART interventions. Despite its clinical importance, little is known about the molecular mechanisms that regulate human sperm motility. Underlying the present investigation are two fundamental questions that need to be addressed before oviductin can be applied to standard IVF and IUI in fertility centers. Functionally, does oviductin enhance sperm fertilizing ability and what is the mechanism that regulates the functional property of oviductin? Clinically, will supplementation of culture medium with oviductin enhance fertilization as measured by in vitro functional assays? The ultimate goal is to improve the health service use of IVF and IUI procedures involving couples with male infertility indications in Canada and worldwide.

column36: The SafeCare(R) Program for Child Neglect: Examining Differential Outcomes and Change Mechanisms
column37: Child abuse and neglect is a serious public health concern not only in North America but worldwide. In Ontario, child neglect is the second most common form of substantiated maltreatment among cases investigated by child welfare, with an incidence rate of 24%. SafeCare(R) is an evidence-based, in-home parenting program that specifically addresses child neglect for young families (newborn-5 years) involved in child welfare. Following a previous CIHR grant in which we successfully implemented SafeCare across 6 Ontario child welfare agencies, we are now seeking funds to evaluate the program in greater detail across child welfare agencies that are diverse in terms of size (urban, rural), location (northern, southern Ontario), and culture (Indigenous families). For the evaluation, we will gather information from both children and caregivers prior to the SafeCare program and at various time points following program completion. We will use various data collection methods (questionnaires, testing, child welfare data) to examine three research questions: 1) Does the program work differently for families and if so, what factors are associated with better outcomes over time? 2) How does SafeCare work in terms of mechanisms of change (parental improvements in emotion regulation)? and 3) Does participation in SafeCare decrease rates of re-entry into child welfare? The current project not only has the potential to impact the health of individual children and families but it also has population health implications. Specifically, child neglect is expensive from a community point of view (medical care, out-of-home placement, poor educational outcomes) and once established, it tends to remain persistent. By evaluating SafeCare outcomes over a long-term basis and better understanding the ways in which it works, child welfare may continue to invest in this evidence-based program and make refinements to improve its effectiveness

column36: PGC-1alpha: pivotal role in the protection of the brain in chronic liver disease
column37: Liver disease has a significant impact on the Canadian population affecting more than 8 million Canadians. Muscle wasting and hepatic encephalopathy (HE; complex neuropsychiatric disorder) are serious complications of chronic liver disease (CLD; cirrhosis) affecting 80% of patients. These complications increase hospital admissions and mortality, hence adding to the already significant economic burden on health care systems. Liver transplantation, the only curative treatment for CLD, is a limiting therapeutic option due to a shortage of available livers. Therefore, development of alternative therapeutic strategies to prevent complications and prolong survival until a liver becomes available for transplantation is crucial. Inflammation and ammonia are major factors implicated in the development of HE. We hypothesize that ammonia and inflammation-induced PGC-1alpha downregulation in cirrhosis adversely leads to muscle mass loss (through decreased BDNF) and, consequently, to HE, which are attenuated with exercise training and omega-3 fatty acids supplementation. We will use in vitro, in vivo model systems and cirrhotic patients to verify our hypothesis. Results of this study will clarify the role of PGC-1alpha/BNDF in the pathogenesis of cirrhosis-related muscle mass loss and HE. Finally, as the pathophysiological mechanisms are identified, insights for efficient therapeutic strategies will be uncovered, not only to improve the quality of life of cirrhotic patients while waiting for a healthy liver, but also to lead to a better outcome following liver transplantation.

column36: Development of novel risk prediction scores for emergency department patients with suspected coronary artery disease
column37: Canadian emergency rooms (ERs) see over 600,000 patients per year with symptoms of a possible heart attack. 85% or more of these patients do not have a heart-related cause for their symptoms, and are at low risk of adverse heart events like death, a later heart attack or an emergency cardiac procedure after their ER visit. Many patients who have a heart attack ruled out in the ER get additional testing to diagnose coronary artery disease, even though their risk of a short-term heart event is low. Data from Alberta and Ontario research suggests that doctors over-test low-risk patients while sometimes under-testing high-risk patients, leading to unnecessary procedures, complications and health system costs. This research project will develop better ways for doctors to predict ER patients' risk of coronary disease. This will help doctors more accurately identify which patients need additional testing and when after their ER visit. The objective of this research project is to use existing Canadian data, collected from emergency department patients experiencing chest pain, to adapt and refine existing risk prediction tools to more accurately identify patients who are-or are not-at risk of an adverse event after a heart attack has been ruled out in the emergency department. Better risk prediction tools will help emergency doctors and patients make better, personalized decisions about whether a patient should undergo additional testing after a heart attack has been ruled out, and whether that testing needs to happen immediately or at a more convenient time as an outpatient. The refined risk prediction tools that we will develop will ensure that the right patients get the right test at the right time, to improve patient outcomes and ensure that health system resources are used wisely.

column36: Characterizing a Process of Stress-Inducible Protein Aggregation
column37: Proteins are the building blocks of life and are essential to all basic cellular and organismal pathways (e.g. survival, growth and replication). Once made, a protein is carefully folded to generate a functional molecule, which "floats" around the cell and associates with DNA, RNA or other molecules to accomplish important tasks. Under harsh or stressful environmental conditions (e.g., high fever and oxygen-deprivation) proteins can change shape and clump together, inactivating themselves and turning off certain cellular pathways. This natural process is similar to hibernation, as it allows the cell to save energy and ensure survival. Once favourable conditions are restored, the cell can wake up by dissolving the aggregates, re-fold the proteins and re-activate the important machinery. In this study we will investigate the mechanisms controlling protein aggregation. Here, we plan to: 1) identify the sensing and control molecules that regulate protein clumping and 2) examine the cellular pathways that are shutdown under distinct environmental settings, thereby creating a basic understanding of how cells recognize and tailor their responses to different harmful stressors. It is also interesting to note that abnormal protein clumping is seen in many neurodegenerative disorders (i.e., Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases). Therefore, we suspect that dysregulation of this natural pathway may be associated with these debilitating conditions.

column36: Reverse engineering working memory circuits in the primate brain: Implications for the study of memory deficits.
column37: Working memory (WM), the ability to maintain and manipulate information for short time periods, is one of the main pillars of human and animal cognition. WM is deeply impaired in mental diseases such as Alzheimer and Schizophrenia. There is no effective treatment for WM deficits in humans, partly because we have a poor understanding of the mechanisms underlying WM function in the human brain. Studies in non-human primates have revealed that the persistent activity of neurons in the lateral prefrontal cortex encodes the features and location of remembered objects. Thus, it has been proposed that persistent activity in this area supports WM coding in the brain. The mechanisms by which persistent activity encoding WM arises remain a matter of debate. In this proposal, we will conduct a series of experiments in behaving non-human primates using behavioral, electrophysiological and anatomical/histological techniques in order to clarify these and other related issues. We will: first, contrast two main mechanisms by which persistent activity may arise, network dynamics vs intrinsic cell properties, second, identify the features of cortical microcircuits that allow persistent activity to emerge in association areas of the primate neocortex; third, investigate whether and how persistent activity encodes the content of WM in naturalistic environments simulated via virtual reality; and finally, we will test predictions of how Ketamine, a recreational drug that block NMDA receptors and interfere with synaptic transmission, produces specific changes in neural activity and WM deficits. Our results will provide a mechanistic understanding of the mechanisms underlying WM function in the primate brain. They will pave the road to our understanding of WM impairments during mental disease and the search for effective treatment solutions.

column36: A Sensitive Biomarker for Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy
column37: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is a disorder of heart muscle and heart rhythm that is passed on in families. ARVC occurs in 1 in 2500 persons, but is responsible for 11% of sudden cardiac deaths (SCD) in adults (under 65), 22% of athletes and up to 25% of children. The average age at death is 40 years, and so it contributes even more to SCD when measured in years of potential life lost. SCD is exceeded only by all cancer in this measure. ARVC is hard to detect, and many tests are needed to identify people with the disease. These tests still miss disease in almost 1/3 of people assessed. Genetic testing also missed most people with disease. There are some similarities between ARVC and blistering diseases of the skin, which can bee caused by either gene changes or antibodies. We therefore looked for antibodies in ARVC, and found one antibody that detects 98% of people with disease. The objectives of our study are: 1.) identify whether anti-DSG2 antibody will be accurate in a large study of patients, and identify persons even before disease can be detected through other tests. 2.) evaluate whether antibody level predicts severity and risk of disease. 3.) Use this test to help find new ARVC genes. To study these objectives, we are collecting information and blood samples from many subjects with ARVC, by working with other large expert groups including the Toronto General Hospital, the Canadian ARVC Registry, Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, Zurich, Poland and China. These will provide us with 2600 samples and data including groups patients with definite disease, 'pre-clinical' disease and high-risk disease. These groups will let us address each of our objectives above. We will measure antibody using standard research and clinical methods. For comparison, we have access to blood samples from large groups of normal individuals over a broad range of ages and both sexes. Our study is unique in studying a novel sensitive and specific marker of ARVC.

column36: PCSK9, a novel contributor to the development of castration resistant prostate cancer
column37: Prostate cancer is the most common male malignancy in Canada. The disease affects one in six men and is the second leading cause of cancer-associated deaths in Canadian men. Mortality is mainly caused by disease progression on the standard of care: androgen deprivation therapy. Since the 1940s, androgen deprivation is the first line therapy used in patients with advanced prostate cancer. This treatment temporarily stops prostate cancer growth. However, resistant tumors in the form of castration resistant prostate cancers (CRPCs) always arise, and are lethal. CRPC is the dominant cause of prostate cancer death. Understanding what causes CRPC development is critical to offer patients the best medical care. Our group has recently found a protein that promotes CRPC development. The expression of this protein is increased in prostate cancers metastasized to the bone. Bone is the major site of prostate cancer metastasis; prostate cancers metastatic to bone are the dominant source of CRPC. Furthermore, we found that prostate cancers with higher levels of this protein are likely to progress to CRPC. Importantly, using mouse models for human CRPC, we have shown that by increasing the level of this protein expression alone is sufficient to convert castration-sensitive prostate cancer cells to cells resistant to castration. Collectively, our research suggests this protein being an important contributor to CRPC development in human prostate cancer. In this project, we will thoroughly examine this protein's contributions to the progression of castration resistant prostate cancers using human prostate cancer cell lines, mouse models for CRPC, and patients' tumor tissues. We will also determine whether by reducing this protein expression will prevent or reduce CRPC development. This research will reveal a new factor that enhances CRPC development. This knowledge will pave the way to develop new means of diagnosis and new treatments in patients with advanced prostate cancer.

column36: Efficacy of a novel idiotypic antibody to inhibit cholesterol retention in atherosclerotic vascular disease during insulin resistance and diabetes.
column37: Excess fat (cholesterol) deposits in our blood vessels can lead to heart disease. The blood vessel wall is made up of special proteins that contain sugar molecules with sticky regions that specifically attach and trap the cholesterol-carrying particles circulating in our blood. Current treatments aim to reduce the amount of cholesterol (e.g LDL or bad cholesterol) in the blood stream. There is currently no drug (available or under research) that can specifically target the blood vessels to reduce the accumulation of cholesterol. We have collaborated with the Centre for Molecular Immunology in Cuba, that are experts in developing vaccine like drugs. They have recently developed a compound (antibody) called 'chP3R99' that has two fold action: (i) It specifically binds to the sugar chains which prevents the cholesterol from attaching to blood vessels (ii) This antibody has vaccine-like properties, which means it does not have to be injected repeatedly to maintain its effect. Once injected it can continue to produce similar antibodies and reduce the overall cost of the therapy. Diabetes increases the risk for heart disease. There are two types of bad forms of cholesterol in our blood (i) Traditional bad cholesterol (LDL) produced from the liver and (ii) 'Remnant' cholesterol, derived from diet and secreted by the intestine. During diabetes, remnant cholesterol is often increased while the LDL cholesterol can remain normal. Therefore the aim of this project is to determine if the novel antibody 'chP3R99' can reduce the accumulation of remnant cholesterol as well as LDL cholesterol in blood vessels of animal models that have diabetes. We also have a collaboration with a cardiologist who can provide us with donor (discarded) human blood vessels and other tissues. We propose to use donor blood vessels to circulate remnant cholesterol with/without the antibody chP3R99 to assess the extent that we can reduce cholesterol build up in human tissue.

column37: Diabetes and pre-diabetes are metabolic disorders affecting more than 15% of the world's population. The prevalence of these disorders is currently increasing mainly due to the increasingly sedentary lifestyles associated with rising obesity rates and aging of the population. Because diabetes and pre-diabetes are so closely associated with major health problems such as high blood pressure, high blood lipids and cardiovascular disease (CVD), they have a tremendous impact on the health-care costs of our society. Significant efforts should therefore be dedicated to tackling this problem from a societal perspective. Although elevated blood lipid levels observed in diabetes and pre-diabetes have largely been attributed to overproduction by the liver, recent studies by our group have indicated that the small intestine also contributes significantly to elevated blood lipid levels. Recent studies provide strong support for the beneficial role of dietary monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) for primary cardiovascular prevention. New data also suggest that MUFAs from olive oil may exert beneficial effects on CVD risk by reducing intestinal lipid production, but no studies have examined this issue in patients with diabetes or pre-diabetes. This study will allow us to investigate whether substitution of canola oil rich in MUFAs for saturated fats could reduce intestinal lipid production in patients with pre-diabetes. We will also examine the impact of MUFAs on the expression of the major genes involved in the regulation of intestinal lipid metabolism. The identification of therapeutic strategies using non-pharmacologic agents such as MUFAs is likely to lead to significant advances in our attempts to reduce CVD risk in this vulnerable population.

column37: As Canadians get older, more people will die in long-term care (LTC) homes, but research has shown that palliative care is poor in LTC. Most LTC homes do not have a formal way to approach palliative care and have barriers to delivering palliative care. As a result, clinical decision-making is challenging for LTC. LTC residents often have many medical conditions that happen at the same time. This makes anticipating how the patient will do difficult and can cause stress for family and staff. We will build on our Canadian research program and use our existing networks to make sure that our work is sustainable. So far, we have 8 study sites in 4 provinces (ON, MB, SK, AB). We will also develop an online tool to help families and residents with advanced care planning, create training modules and bereavement pamphlets. Our research involves residents, family and staff in all research activities. We make sure that their voices are heard to learn from them. Together, we build our tools to help improve resident and family experience with living and dying in LTC. We evaluate how our work is developing and let the residents, families and staff know what is happening through LTC visits and meetings. Our research team regularly meets with national leaders across organizations, communities, and disciplines to exchange ideas. By exploring what happens within each LTC site, we will make accessible online tools that meet the needs of diverse groups across Canada. Our research has the potential for widespread use across sectors. As a result, we will support improvements in health-related knowledge and health system and health care.

column36: Identifying the regulatory functions of nuclear lipid synthesis and storage pathways
column37: The nucleus contains the chromosomes necessary to transmit genetic information from one generation to the next. Similar to most cellular compartments, the nucleus is surrounded by a membrane that is composed of lipids. The membrane surrounding the nucleus keeps it separated from other compartments in the cells but also allows connections to these other compartments. It was thought that this membrane connection allowed the nucleus to receive lipids from other compartments instead of making them. However, we have shown that the nucleus contains enzymes that make lipids, and these lipids are stored within the nucleus. Furthermore, these stored lipids interact with a protein complex in the nucleus called PML that controls the ability of the cell to respond to stress, such as DNA damage. We hypothesize that the interaction between lipids and PML regulates the cell's response to fat-induced stress. Here we propose to identify the enzymes that are responsible for making and storing lipids in the nucleus, and how the activities of these enzymes are controlled. Importantly we will identify how making lipids in the nucleus affects the function of PML. These studies will identify how the production of lipids in the nucleus potentially affects the ability of liver cells to respond to excess fat and prevent its accumulation, which is a cause of disease in the liver and other organs and tissues.

column36: Targeting scleraxis to combat cardiac fibrosis
column37: Heart disease is the primary cause of death in the western world. Cardiac fibrosis is a stiffening of the heart caused by many forms of heart disease. Fibrosis dramatically increases the risk of death and disability independently of other risk factors (up to 17 times), yet no treatments for cardiac fibrosis are available to patients. Our laboratory has identified a protein (scleraxis) as a powerful cause of fibrosis, and our initial data has indicated that interfering with scleraxis can reduce fibrosis. We hypothesize that blocking scleraxis in the heart is beneficial for heart disease patients. To control scleraxis in the heart, we propose to study the cell signals that regulate scleraxis production to identify new drug targets. We will also test existing drugs that have shown beneficial effects on fibrosis, as well as novel scleraxis-directed treatments, for their ability to block scleraxis and fibrosis. Extending our preliminary data, we will test four aims: Aim 1: we will define the mechanism by which angiotensin II, a hormone driver of high blood pressure and fibrosis, increases fibrosis by activating the scleraxis gene. Aim 2: we will test existing drugs (angiotensin II inhibitors - ACEi/ARB) that have shown beneficial effects on fibrosis for their ability to reduce scleraxis levels, and show that these drugs lose their efficacy when excessive scleraxis is made. Aim 3: using mouse models, we will demonstrate that deleting the scleraxis gene reverses heart fibrosis even when the disease is well-established. Aim 4: we will test the ability of a novel scleraxis mutant, developed in our lab, to interfere with normal scleraxis in the heart in order to reduce fibrosis. These results will reveal new details of how scleraxis causes cardiac fibrosis, will provide crucial supporting evidence for the eventual adoption of ACEi/ARB as treatments for this condition, and will demonstrate the efficacy of our scleraxis mutant as a potential new treatment for fibrosis.

column36: Comprehensive mapping and evolutionary dynamics of the mutational landscape of antimicrobial resistance
column37: We are surrounded by bacteria that could potentially cause harmful infections. However, we have been able to keep them at bay because of antibiotics. Indeed, advances in medicine, such as chemotherapy, surgery, and treatment of chronic diseases, crucially depend on our ability to control infections with antibiotics. But this has been compromised by the evolution of bacterial strains with mutations that make them resistant to antibiotics. The classic approach to antibiotic resistance is to discover new drugs. But this may not be enough. We also need to conserve the efficacy and maximize the duration of the usefulness of both current and future antibiotics. Antibiotic resistance will always arise, but if we are able to predict how they evolve, we could potentially delay their emergence. To predict bacterial evolution, we need to know what types of mutations can arise in the bacteria and how much resistance level they confer. Moreover, since multiple co-existing mutations can compete amongst themselves for evolutionary dominance, we also need to track the history of the bacterial population. This project proposes an interdisciplinary approach that brings together concepts from biochemistry, microbiology, and evolutionary biology. We will use state-of-the-art experimental techniques in protein engineering to determine the fitness effects of several thousands of mutations in 3 proteins that are crucial antibiotic targets. Then, by performing lab evolution using robotics and microfluidics, we will determine the survival probability of these mutations. We also developed a novel genetic tool that uniquely barcodes each cell in an evolving bacterial community. This enables us to track at high resolution the lineage and history of the bacterial population as resistance emerges. Ultimately, uncovering how bacteria evolve resistance could lead to novel regimens for optimal drug use that may delay antibiotic resistance and thus help preserve our ability to fight infections.

column36: Metabolic disorders of pregnancy and early-onset disease risk in the offspring: role of adipose tissue expandability
column37: Babies born to mothers who were obese or diabetic during pregnancy are more likely to develop risk factors for cardiovascular disease before they reach adulthood. Given that these metabolic disorders have become the most common complications of pregnancy, they have likely contributed significantly to the current epidemic of early-onset cardiovascular risk among Canadian youth. We have developed novel mouse models of maternal metabolic dysfunction that allow us to identify the developmental perturbations underlying later-life risk and understand how these perturbations impact health at the level of the cell, organ and organ system. Our data suggest that early-onset cardiovascular risk results from a perturbation in the development of fat tissue during fetal life that impairs its ability to expand after birth. Expansion of fat tissue to buffer excess energy plays a critical role in maintaining cardiovascular health under conditions of high caloric intake. Fat tissue has a defined limit of expansion, which is eventually reached as an individual gains weight. Recent studies in obese humans reveal that a failure in fat tissue expansion precipitates the onset of obesity-associated cardiovascular disease. Therefore, we will test the hypothesis that early-onset cardiovascular risk in offspring born to mothers with metabolic dysfunction during pregnancy results from accelerated fat cell maturation leading to a premature limitation in fat expansion. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) promote cardiovascular health by regulating fat cell expansion. Several clinical trials have demonstrated PUFA supplementation to be safe in human infants; however, their utility in optimizing long-term cardiovascular health in infants born to obese or diabetic mothers is currently unknown. Thus, we will determine if early-life PUFA supplementation prevents the development of cardiovascular risk factors in babies born to pregnancies complicated by maternal metabolic dysfunction.

column36: The role of the Inhibitors of Apoptosis (IAPs) in health and disease
column37: Twenty-three years ago, my research group discovered a novel family of mammalian genes, which we called the inhibitors of apoptosis (or IAPs) due to their similarity with viral genes that regulate a process of cell death known as apoptosis. The IAPs not only control how cells die under stress but also have critical roles in cell division and in cell signalling. Moreover, they are especially important for the function of the immune system. The dysregulation of the IAPs are associated with a range of diseases, from cancer to neurodegeneration to infection. Indeed, drugs that target key IAPs, known as Smac mimetics (SMCs) are in clinical trials for the treatment of various cancers and infectious diseases. The inactivation of the IAPs by SMCs renders cancer cells quite sensitive to death triggers produced by the immune system. Remarkably, normal cells do not die when treated with SMCs. We have recently shown that SMCs can complement a new class of revolutionary anti-cancer drugs, called cancer immunotherapy. The combination of SMCs and cancer immunotherapy cures mice of cancer and this research has now led to the initiation of human clinical trials for cancer in 2017-18. My research program studies how the IAPs control life and death decisions at the cellular level and how the IAPs modulate immunity to enhance the activity of immunotherapies. In the span of two decades, we have gone from gene discovery and the creation of a whole new field of study, to the clinical investigation of novel drug classes and approaches that are expected to yield insights into disease and therapy.

column36: Economic impact of falls prevention interventions: We know the "value", but what about the "value for money"?
column37: RATIONALE: Falls have a substantial impact on the quality of life, morbidity, and mortality of older adults, and are costly for our healthcare system. Many falls prevention interventions have proven to be effective. With constrained healthcare resources, the most effective intervention is not always cost-effective, and we are often faced with determining whether an intervention is truly worth the resources it requires. Therefore, in addition to answering the question "does the intervention work?", decision- and policy-makers must also answer the 'value for money' question, "is it cost-effective?". OBJECTIVE: Members of our team previously conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis on falls prevention interventions. This project will examine the cost-effectiveness of effective falls prevention interventions identified through our previous work. Our findings will help identify falls prevention interventions that are not only effective but also cost-effective. METHODS: We will develop a health economics model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of each falls prevention intervention from the perspective of public healthcare payers, using data from our previous work and published literature. We will explore factors that influence the interventions' cost-effectiveness and conduct subgroup analyses by factors such as history of falls. IMPACT: Information on the cost-effectiveness of falls prevention interventions will assist policy-makers to make informed decisions on which intervention they should fund and implement. Our findings will provide evidence on both the value for money and budget impact of falls prevention interventions to decision-makers who fund these interventions and to those who are considering their implementation, namely our colleagues from Department of Medicine at the University of Toronto, Alberta Health Services, the Regional Geriatrics Program of Toronto, Osteoporosis Canada, and the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care.

column36: Improving the specificity of CRISPR/Cas9 using chemically-modified guide RNAs
column37: Thousands of human genetic diseases ranging from cystic fibrosis to muscular dystrophy are caused by a mutation in a single known gene. Yet, despite extensive effort, we have been unable to identify conventional pharmaceuticals to treat many of them. However, modern-day gene editing technology could revolutionize the treatment of these diseases by allowing researchers to permanently correct the underlying genetic mutations causing these diseases. For example, a recently described system called CRISPR/Cas9 can be used to precisely delete, insert, or edit genetic information (DNA) in cell and animal models. In the future, this system could also be applied to the treatment of many of the human diseases listed above by replacing the defective copy of a gene with a correct copy. However, there still remains several hurdles that must be overcome to translate this technology to the clinic. The greatest of these challenges is imperfect specificity. While these tools alter the sequence at the correct target location the majority of the time, they also occasionally alter the genetic information at off-target locations. Unintended DNA cleavage or editing could have detrimental consequences in humans and could give rise to diseases such as cancer. This project proposes to dramatically improve the precision of CRISPR/Cas9, making it safer for eventual human applications. My lab has recently uncovered a way to decrease off-target DNA cutting by CRISPR/Cas9 by over 10,000-fold. This project will broaden and extend our findings to enable precise cleavage of any gene using CRISPR/Cas9. In addition, we will apply our findings to not only Cas9 DNA cutting, but also to optimizing the precision of safer gene editing technology that has recently been invented. Ultimately, we hope to partner with a biotechnology company to advance the development of safer, next-generation gene editing technology for humans.

column36: Developing radioimmunotherapy of osteosarcoma using comparative oncology approach
column37: Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common primary malignant bone tumor and the fifth most common primary malignancy among adolescents and young adults. Unfortunately, overall survival is approximately 70%, with no meaningful improvement realized in over 20 years. Patients with metastatic disease to the lungs and to the bone generally have poor outcomes, with an overall survival of less than 40% and 20%, respectively. In addition, OS demonstrates sweeping genetic variability from one tumor to the next which makes it challenging to pursue conventional targeting approaches. In our previous studies we have found out that a protein called Insulin Growth Factor Receptor Type 2 (IGF2R) is consistently expressed on all OS cell lines, including the ones derived from patients. When targeting the experimental OS tumors in mice with the mouse antibodies to the IGF2R protein, which were carrying the radioactive "payload" capable of destroying tumor cells, we observed considerable slowing down of tumor growth without side effects. However, to move this encouraging approach into the clinical trials, we need two things: make human antibodies to IGF2R which would allow to treat patients multiple times without side effects from the immune system, and to test these antibodies in the animals with the tumors comparable to human ones. It turns to be that OS is one of the most widespread cancers in companion dogs, it very closely resembles human OS, and treatments for dogs are very limited. Thus, our hypothesis is that we will be able to create highly IGF2R-specific human antibodies which would effectively target OS tumor cells in companion dogs with OS and deliver curative tumoricidal doses of radioactivity to the tumors without toxicity to normal organs. If successful, this project will generate the antibodies and the data needed to move this approach into the clinical trials in patients with OS, and, as added benefit, will create the treatment for companion dogs with OS.

column36: HIV-1's hold on host cell vesicular trafficking and metabolism and the impact on pathogenesis, latency and treatment
column37: Over 40 million people worldwide are infected by HIV-1 and it still represents a major health and economic problem worldwide. HIV-1 infection has devastating effects on the immune system resulting in diminishing levels of T cells, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and death. As of mid-2016, there is still no cure or vaccine. Nevertheless, over forty anti-HIV- 1 drugs are available to infected individuals and make HIV-1 infection a chronic and manageable disease since these drugs suppress circulating virus to undetectable levels, allaying many of the pathological effects on the immune system. The pathologies are largely due to the impact of the virus' ability to hijack the host cell. In this work, we uncover HIV-1's ability to commandeer a central regulator of the host cell metabolism (the mammalian target of rapamycin, mTOR) and the host's vesicular trafficking machinery. These two machineries impact on the host at several points including how proteins are synthesized, and how the cell clears cellular debris and derives energy sources, especially when nutrients are lacking or when cells are submitted to stress or pathogen insult. The latter process, called autophagy, represents an important degradative process that maintains cell homeostasis. It recycles cellular components under nutrient deprivation in order to decrease the cell's energy needs. Interestingly, autophagy is also a key component in the defense against pathogens and consequently, viruses, including HIV-1, have evolved to manipulate autophagy to their advantage. In this grant request, we propose to examine the consequences of HIV-1- mediated modulation of mTOR, lysosomal trafficking and autophagy. Biochemistry, the latest gene editing and quantitative microscopy techniques will be used to measure the metabolic consequences of HIV-1 infection in clinically relevant HIV-1 infected CD4+ T cells and macrophages and during latent infection. Targeting these processes may effectively suppress HIV-1.

column36: Structural biology of innate immune proteins
column37: Innate immunity is an ancient system of host defense that predates the adaptive immune system and is conserved in almost all multicellular organisms from insects to mammals. Innate immunity relies on a set of protein receptors that are strategically expressed in cells that are likely to encounter pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, early on in an infection. The interaction of these receptors with components from the pathogen, propagates a signal into the cell that leads to changes in gene expression and accompanying responses by the host that work to eliminate the pathogen. Pathogens try to counteract immunity to gain an advantage by for example injecting toxic proteins into the host. It is necessary to understand the molecular of both of these processes to help develop better therapeutics against infection. This research proposal aims to elucidate the atomic level details for host-pathogen interactions on both sides of interface: 1) IFIT host defence proteins that fend of viral infection and 2) Bacterial effector proteins called YopJ acetyltransferases, which are enzymes that bacteria deliver into the host to subvert the immune response. Understanding the molecular details of how these proteins engage their respective target molecules to enhance or undermine the immune response is an important step towards the development of therapeutic drugs in diseases like cancer and autoimmune disorders, as well as several infectious and inflammatory diseases.

column36: The McMaster Cohort of Extremely Low Birth Weight Survivors in the Fifth Decade of Life: Physical, Neuropsychiatric, and Socioeconomic Outcomes
column37: With advances in neonatal care, more of the 21,000 babies born in Canada each year at extremely low birth weight (ELBW; less than 1000 g at birth) are surviving. These problems do not appear to resolve in adulthood. ELBW survivors are also at greater risk than adults born at normal birth weight (NBW; more than 2500 g at birth) for health-threatening chronic diseases such as hypertension and diabetes at a relatively young age. The McMaster University Cohort is the oldest-known cohort of ELBW survivors in the world. They are now entering their 40s, a life stage that requires active management to maintain physical and psychological health. However, the long-term physical and psychological consequences of being born extremely preterm are unknown and of critical importance. The first goal of the proposed study is to assess the physical, mental, economic, and social challenges faced by ELBW survivors at middle age. This will determine the current health status of ELBW survivors, and also establish valuable benchmarks against which to compare future age-related risks for disease and cognitive decline. Some factors (e.g., differences in brain structure and metabolic regulation) are likely to continue to impact preterm health as the cohort ages, but others may be modifiable. Therefore, the second goal of this study is to identify resilience factors that will modify ELBW outcomes beyond middle age. These factors will provide potential targets for interventions to promote long-term good health and optimal aging in ELBW survivors.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) including heart failure (HF) are leading causes of death & disability worldwide, and are particular problematic for patients with diabetes. column36: Understanding the burden and health system impact of loneliness and social isolation in older adults in Canada
column37: Feeling lonely or being socially isolated puts older adults at risk of dying sooner, and may lead to increased use of health system resources. Many older adults report loneliness and social isolation, especially women, due to major life transitions that accompany aging including declining health and/or losing a spouse, relatives and friends. As countries like Canada move towards "super-aged" status, tackling loneliness and social isolation has become an important priority. Whether strategies to address loneliness and social isolation could also alleviate demands on the health system is unclear, but an important question. Prior studies of the relationship between loneliness, social isolation and health use have found mixed results, which may be due to important limitations. We can overcome these problems in Canada with the availability of unique population-level data. Our goals are to measure the burden of loneliness and social isolation in older adults and their impact on the health system, and to see whether there are important differences between women and men. We will use Canada's most comprehensive health survey data (Canadian Community Health Survey) linked with health encounters captured by our universal health care system. These data will allow us to identify vulnerable groups of older adults who are more likely to be lonely or isolated. We will measure the impact of isolation on the health system by comparing patterns of health system use (e.g. medication dispensing, home care, primary care and emergency department visits, hospitalization, long-term care, and death) in older adults who are lonely or socially isolated to their socially engaged peers. We will engage a diverse group of stakeholders across sectors so that our findings are useful to those who can action them, and to form a partnership that can propose community-based solutions. Our research will help communities and the health system improve the health of our aging population.
