column37: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a blood clot that forms in a vein. VTE is a common, lethal, costly, yet treatable condition. There are effective drugs to prevent VTE but they increase the risk of bleeding. Our team has long-term interest in understanding what causes VTE, and how to prevent and treat VTE. We argue that we need to understand how DNA and the way it is packaged and 'read' (i.e. the epigenetic 'code') leads to disease in order to better prevent and manage VTE. The epigenetic code is the intermediate player linking a person's environment and his/her genetic make up. An individual's sex is an important variable on how the genetic and epigenetic codes impact a person's risk to VTE, and how he or she responds to treatment. In particular, we are intrigued by the fact that men and women have a similar risk of developing a first VTE, but men have more than twice the risk of a subsequent VTE after a 'blood thinner' drug treatment is stopped. We propose that sex-specific epigenetic marks underlie the protective effects against subsequent VTE observed in women after treatment with a 'blood thinner'. We will analyze patients' blood samples, biological and clinical data, and perform lab experiments, to understand the biology behind sex differences in the response to VTE treatment. This will be the basis of new tests that will ultimately improve the standard of care received by men and women after a first VTE event. Given the importance and the risk of using 'blood thinners' to manage patients following a VTE, being able to predict who will benefit the most from such drugs and who can safely discontinue their use after initial treatment are of major importance in caring for these patients. This will also inform on novel intervention targets that could reverse the risk of VTE.

column37: The incidence of the severe pneumonia that Legionella causes (Legionnaires' disease) is inexplicably on the rise - and deadly outbreaks have occurred in Toronto, Quebec City, and Calgary. Legionella can be isolated from the water systems of approximately 1 in 8 homes - and our aging population and aging infrastructure are only increasing the risk to health. Legionella pneumophila is the leading cause of waterborne outbreaks in the US, where it is estimated to cost over $400 million in direct hospitalization costs per year. Given worldwide incidence and trends, a similar relative impact on Canadian health is likely, if not as well quantified. Defining the molecular mechanisms by which Legionella replicates in our water and causes disease is essential to understanding and responding to these alarming trends. A central pillar of molecular pathogenesis is that bacteria inject proteins (effectors) into the host cell in order to modulate host proteins. We have recently uncovered a functionally novel class of effectors in Legionella pneumophila: "metaeffectors" (or "effectors of effectors") that target other effectors rather than host proteins. Metaeffectors are a gamechanger in the study of effector biology - they fundamentally change the way in which we study these important proteins and provide powerful connections to known biology from which we can build outwards from. In this proposal, we will leverage our discovery of metaeffectors to learn how effectors are regulated once inside the host cell. We will build outward from experimental beachheads of known biology to discover new aspects of the host-pathogen interface. Emerging data suggest that metaeffectors are a common feature of bacterial pathogens - meaning that we can no longer afford to overlook this biology. In addition to understanding Legionella metaeffectors, one key deliverable from this work is the establishment of a set of tools and approaches that will be broadly applicable to these other pathogens.

We will identify the exact conditions of activity that enable the destabilization of the memory trace and use these findings to reverse pathological sensory processing in animal models of pain. column36: Genetic drivers of medulloblastoma metastasis
column37: Medulloblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer that most often affects children and adolescents. Current multimodal treatment comprising chemotherapy, surgery and radiation cures about ~70% of the patients. Neurosurgeons remove the tumor in the brain - the so called 'primary tumor' - very easily, however in some patients the tumor can spread (metastasize) to form cancer in other areas of the brain different from the original location. Very often these metastases present in the form of a layer of tumor cells that covers regions of the brain hardly accessible by surgery. As a consequence, medulloblastoma metastases are usually inoperable and patients that have metastases have a very low chance of survival. The therapies that work on the primary tumors are ineffective on the metastases for unknown reasons. In fact, despite metastases represent a major clinical challenge, almost no effort has been directed toward understanding the mechanisms of metastatic spread of medulloblastoma tumor cells. In this proposal we will use a new model of medulloblastoma metastasis based on human cells grown in mice. This approach will allow us to reproduce the life cycle of medulloblastoma in a mouse model, by the way of treating the tumor bearing mice with surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy with the same protocols used in paediatric medulloblastoma patients. Some medulloblastomas will metastasize, just like human cancers do, and then we will be able to directly compare the genetic mutations of the primary tumors and the metastases by using next-generation sequencing techniques. By direct comparison of pre-therapy and post-therapy metastases we will gain key knowledge into the mechanism of metastatic dissemination of medulloblastoma, and identify new potential targets for treatment.

column37: On October 17, 2018, cannabis use for non-medical purposes will be legalized in Canada. Canadian researchers have recommended a number of indicators that need to be monitored in order to understand the impact of this major policy change on public health and safety. The results justify the need to monitor these patterns following legalization. Through this study, we will continue to collect information from this group of workers to determine whether legalization is associated with changes in workplace use and related perceptions and norms. We will survey 4,000 workers at one, two, and three years after legalization and explore whether differences in trends exist across segments of the labour market. We will also examine how perceptions and norms may influence future cannabis use and vice versa. This project will provide information to understand the short-term effects of legalization on the workplace and help to inform development of policies, practices, and prevention initiatives to ensure lower risk use among Canadian workers.

Since 1936, the prevailing view of seizures has been "The harmony of the symphony orchestra has become a single note (William Lennox, 1936)". However, given that neurons in the brain are known to be heterogeneous, these neurons may show very different activities during early life seizures. Thus, for precise understanding early life epilepsy at the cellular level, it is crucial to selectively label neurons with different activities during seizures and analyze their specific nature in detail. c-fos, an immediate early gene, has been extensively used as a marker for neuronal activation induced by numerous kinds of stimulations, including seizures. We have bred c-Fos-GFP/c-Fos-tTA mice that express green fluorescent protein in activated neurons. Identification of live hippocampal neurons that were active during early life seizures has never been done before. We have found unique physiological alterations that occur only in selectively activated neurons in early life seizures. Here, we hypothesize that the selectively activated neurons have crucial roles in early life epilepsy. We will determine whether these selectively activated neurons appear to be the key cellular targets mediating seizure-induced neural network alterations and long-term cognitive consequences. We will also probe the potential to reverse early-life epilepsy and associated long-term cognitive deficits by precisely suppressing the activity of these neurons. If successful, our study will identify novel cellular and molecular mechanisms and reveal new potential therapeutic strategies for controlling early life epilepsy.

column36: Development and evaluation of a toolkit to support low- and middle-income country implementers' through the steps of effective implementation planning to improve uptake of evidence into practice and maternal health outcomes.
column37: Despite progress in recent years, maternal mortality rates remain unacceptably high with the majority of maternal deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and resulting from causes for which proven interventions exist but are not optimally implemented. Effective implementation requires that barriers and facilitators to implementation are identified and addressed using theory-informed, evidence-based implementation strategies adapted to the relevant political and cultural context. However, optimizing implementation involves a complex series of steps that are resource intensive and dependent on expertise often not readily available in LMICs where improved implementation could achieve the greatest benefit. Our goal is to develop and evaluate an inexpensive tool-kit designed for use by non-experts to support effective implementation planning and execution. Our group includes implementation scientists, maternal health content experts, and stakeholders including front line clinicians, researchers, and policy makers based in participating LMICs. Prior work conducted by our group found a high degree of commonality among barriers and facilitators to implementation across a range of LMICs and clinical areas, as well as unique barriers and facilitators requiring specific attention. Based on a comprehensive literature review, our prior research and our experience in conducting implementation planning workshops with LMIC stakeholders, we will develop and usability test a novel tool-kit, designed to facilitate assessment of barriers and facilitators to implementation and mapping of barriers and facilitators to theory-informed evidence-based implementation strategies. The tool-kit will be pilot tested in 2 LMICs with varying levels of in-country implementation experience and barrier/facilitator distributions within a locally identified maternal health implementation priority with the ultimate goal of improving maternal health outcomes.

column36: Parallel Radiofrequency Transmission MRI Applied to Deep Brain Stimulation
column37: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is increasingly used to treat the symptoms of many brain conditions. Neurosurgery is performed to implant metal electrodes into targets deep within the brain; then, a small device is also implanted underneath the skin, in the upper chest, to send electrical signals to the brain to achieve the DBS treatment effect. DBS patients need short-term and long-term follow-up to make sure that the electrodes are implanted correctly, to check for side effects, and to make sure that the electrodes continue to work well. Also, DBS patients develop other health problems throughout life. For their ongoing healthcare management, it is highly desirable for DBS patients to be able to have magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) exams. MRI is the main medical imaging method for examining diseases of the brain and spinal cord, and of other soft tissues in the body. MRI is also a very flexible, non-invasive way to measure both brain anatomy and function, and so it is highly desirable to use MRI as a tool in research studies of DBS patients. Such research will help to unravel how DBS actually works, towards improving DBS devices for even better treatments. Presently, however, extremely few DBS patients are receiving MRI exams after their devices are implanted, and MRI research studies of DBS patients are at a very early stage. This is because of a major safety concern: brain tissue near the DBS implant can be permanently damaged from heating during MRI. This grant proposal investigates a promising MRI method called "parallel radiofrequency transmission (PTX)" for its ability to suppress these heating effects. The optimal PTX conditions that minimize heating will be determined, and practical methods will be developed so that safe and comprehensive PTX MRI becomes viable for DBS patients. Ultimately this work will lay the groundwork for improved healthcare for DBS patients, and for safe research MRI studies to improve understanding of DBS mechanisms.

column36: Neuropathic pain through misregulated excitability and abnormal neural coding
column37: The nervous system encodes information using pulses of electricity known as spikes. Our perception of sensory input relies on spike-based neural codes. If neurons generate too many or too few spikes, our sensory experience can be profoundly altered. This is what occurs in neuropathic pain. Neuropathic pain is a form of chronic pain that results from damage to the nervous system. When damaged, neurons often become hyperexcitable, which is to say that they generate too many spikes in response to a given input, or start responding to weaker inputs. The primary sensory neurons responsible for sensing stimuli applied to the skin and relaying that information to the central nervous system are especially prone to becoming hyperexcitable. But precisely how that hyperexcitability develops, and how it disrupts sensation, remain poorly understood. Neuron excitability is controlled by ion channels. Changes in specific ion channels have been linked to neuropathic pain. But any one type of ion channel rarely changes in isolation; in fact, a pathological change in one ion channel may trigger other types of ion channels to undergo compensatory changes that offset effects of the primary change on excitability. I predict that hyperexcitability occurs when compensation fails. My proposed research will explore changes in gene regulation to decipher exactly how and why compensation fails. This will help identify new ways in which drugs can be used to restore regulation and reverse hyperexcitability. We will also explore how changes in the excitability of different types of sensory neurons affect the pattern of neurons activated by different types of stimuli, and how changes in neuron activation patterns ultimately impact perception. With this information, we hope to use a patient's sensory symptoms to identify the underlying pattern of sensory neuron hyperexcitability, and that information will, in turn, be used to choose the best therapy.

column36: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction using Bone Patellar Bone or Quad Tendon Autograft with or without Lateral Extra Articular Tenodesis in Individuals who are at High Risk of Graft Failure (STABILITY II)
column37: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is complicated by high failure rates in young active individuals, which is associated with worse outcomes and higher rates of osteoarthritis (OA). Therefore, strategies to reduce ACLR failure are imperative. Traditionally, surgeons believed that the different tendons used to rebuild the torn ACL, did not impact failure. Specifically, a bone patella tendon bone (BPTB) graft was thought to be just as good as a hamstring tendon (HT) graft. Recent reviews, however, suggest BPTB provides better stability albeit with greater complications at the site of the donor tendon. Moreover, the quadriceps tendon (QT) is now being used to build ACL grafts, with claims of similar stability as the BPTB graft without the same complications. In addition, rebuilding the ligaments associated with rotational stability of the knee such as lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) at the same time as the ACLR may provide even greater overall stability; however, LET may contribute to increased knee OA. Despite its importance, there has not been a good study to prove whether one graft is better at reducing failure and minimizing donor site complications. Furthermore, no study has determined whether the addition of a LET helps to reduce failure. Research Questions: Is there a graft type +/- LET that offers a greater reduction in rate of failure, better functional performance, and rate of return-to-sport at two years following ACLR? Which graft type +/- LET offers the lowest complication rates? Do females do better with a particular graft type? Methods: Adding to our recent study comparing 624 patients who underwent ACLR using HT (+/- LET), this is an international, multi-centre, RCT that will assign 1200 patients to ACLR using QT (+/- LET) or BPTB (+/- LET) (n=1800). Expected Results: This study will determine the best graft choice for young patients at-risk of ACLR failure which will ultimately lead to positive effects on activity and QOL.

column36: Promoting Just and Inclusive End-of-life Decision-making for Long-term Care Home Residents with Dementia and their Care Partners
column37: By 2031, the number of people in Canada with Alzheimer's disease will nearly double. People with dementia experience progressive physical and mental decline and often require extensive care, with many spending the remainder of their lives in long-term care homes(LTCHs). Yet, many residents with dementia do not receive palliative care, an approach focused on comfort and quality of life. Because of stigmatizing attitudes and a system that focuses on mental functioning, residents with dementia and their care partners are often excluded from making decisions. As a result, many people with dementia have fewer opportunities for choice and may not die in the way they wish. The purpose of this study is to include residents with dementia and their care partners (paid care workers and unpaid family members) when making decisions about dying. We will use methods of interview, observation and review of documents to understand how care decisions are made for residents with dementia. We will employ two theories. First, we use a relational model of citizenship to understand the meaning of actions and intentions of people with dementia and include them in decision-making. Second, we use a critical feminist lens to highlight the influence of gender and other social relations in end-of-life decision-making. We will partner with LTCH care partners and people with dementia in the community to create a video that sheds light on fair practices and policies. This study is important to point to new ways of including residents with dementia and the people who care for them in making decisions towards palliative care. This study is essential for residents with dementia to have a fair chance to receive quality palliative care and die in the way they wish.

column36: Cognitive assays of hippocampal dysfunction in Parkinson's Disease
column37: In addition to physical symptoms, people with Parkinson's disease often experience cognitive decline with the progression of their illness and as a side-effect of therapies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS). There is marked heterogeneity in the rate and degree of cognitive decline across individuals, and therefore identifying predictors of poor cognitive outcome is a key research priority. Recent data suggest that alterations in brain regions such as the hippocampus are potentially strong predictors of cognitive decline in PD and DBS. This has not been corroborated using cognitive tasks that are sensitive and specific indicators of hippocampal function. Tests such as word list recall, used in standard clinical practice, lack specificity because they are impacted strongly by the type of executive deficits that are common in PD. Standardized clinical recognition memory tasks have lower executive demands, but they lack sensitivity as they do not tap core hippocampal operations that have been identified in experimental research. Our research aims to overcome these limitations by applying the latest cognitive neuroscience methods to the study of memory in PD. We will identify novel memory tasks that are minimally influenced by executive abilities, are sensitive to hippocampal integrity, and are accurate predictors of cognitive decline with disease progression and after DBS. Importantly, we expect to identify and validate memory assays of hippocampal integrity in PD that can be readily integrated into clinical practice. Our results will greatly improve understanding of memory deficits in PD and of cognitive side-effects of DBS. Critically, we believe our research will enhance our ability to predict cognitive decline in individual patients, and will contribute to future cognitive intervention research in PD.

column36: OSMR Regulation of Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
column37: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adult with a median survival rate of only 16 months after the disease diagnosis. The present standard of care includes maximal surgical removal of the tumors followed by standard treatment with radiation and chemotherapy. Unfortunately, these current treatments are ineffective in prolonging life and alleviating patient suffering. There is an urgent need to develop new and more effective treatment modalities for glioblastoma patients. Although multiple genetic mutations have been implicated as oncogenic (tumor-causing) genes in glioblastoma, the EGFRvIII gene is one of the major drivers of the GBM oncogenesis. Therefore, strategies to block the activities of EGFRvIII is a promising area in glioblastoma research. Problematically, despite intense research, therapies against EGFRvIII alone have not led to clinically significant outcome or improved prognosis. Our recent discoveries that EGFRvIII acts in tandem with another gene called OSMR to drive glioblastoma tumorigenesis, suggests that inhibition of OSMR either alone or as a combination therapy suppresses these tumors. Here, we will first define the mechanisms through which OSMR promotes tumor growth. Second, we will use patient derived models of glioblastoma to establish that OSMR is a viable drug target for these patients. We predict that inhibition of OSMR in combination with EGFRvIII will be an effective therapeutic strategy to treat these deadly tumors.

column36: Synchrony and reset of fast brain oscillations for perception and speech encoding
column37: When we interact with our environment, we interpret what we see, hear, and feel effortless. We can separate the image of a person from the background, although colours and textures may be very similar. We can listen to the voice of a speaker when concurrently other people are talking. How the brain combines sensory details into a meaningful object is still unknown. One concept is that neurons that are rhythmically active, we say they oscillate at a certain frequency, help to solve the problem of binding. Neurons, representing sensory information, oscillate in synchrony and communicate with each other. Thus the sensory information is combined into an object. Such fast synchronous oscillations last for about 200 ms, which is time enough for conscious perception of an object and forming a memory. In this project, we are using MEG for recording brain oscillations while participants listen to speech sounds. In recent years, we developed experimental techniques and data analysis methods to study how neural oscillations change their state of synchrony, which we term a phase reset. We will study how the phase resets of neural oscillations relate to the syllable structure of speech. The results will give us new insights into the brain function of perception and how speech is encoded in the brain. Knowing the details about the brain mechanism of perceptual binding will help us to explain what is going wrong when people cannot understand what they hear or misinterpret what they see. Varies disorders and deterioration of brain function can be explained with reduced ability of binding information in the correct way. The underlying cause seems to be disruptions of rhythmic brain activity.

column36: Targeting Relapsed Metastatic Neuroblastoma
column37: Neuroblastoma (NB) is the 3rd most common pediatric cancer, but the most frequent cause of death in children with cancer with a survival rate < 40%. Localized tumors (usually in the abdomen) are curable. However, for children with NB that has spread, over 50% relapse, usually with metastases to bone, bone marrow, and/or brain. When NB recurs it often initially responds to chemotherapy, but over time and with multiple recurrences NB becomes increasingly resistant and ultimately most patients die. Most NB cells and animal models do not get metastases like our patients, and there are no effective drugs for metastases. Thus, to identify novel therapies, we have (1) amassed a collection of NB cells isolated from patients' metastatic tumors and (2) developed a new mouse model for NB that spreads to the bone, bone marrow, and the brain. We have used a technique called 'in vivo selection' to select increasingly more aggressive "hypermetastatic" NB cells. When injected into our mice these "hypermetastatic" cells give the mice metastases in their bones and brains much earlier than the original cells. Using this model, we have identified genes, pathways, and drug targets for metastatic NB. We will generate additional models with different mutations commonly found in patients with the most aggressive relapses. We propose to use state of the art techniques to identify small groups of difficult to detect cells (clones) that spread from the primary tumor to form metastases. We will also use a technique called phosphoproteomics to identify "protein fingerprints" of the metastatic cells to give us clues to better treatments that can reverse this fingerprint to that of a primary tumor that cannot spread. We have a track record for translating drug discoveries from the lab to NB clinical trials. Our multi-faceted approach will lead to identification of new drugs to use in clinical trials for patients with NB metastatic recurrences in the bone, bone marrow brain.

column36: Mechanism and function of mitochondrial derived vesicle transport to peroxisomes.
column37: The cell is a highly ordered and compartmentalized place with intracellular organelles carrying protein, lipid and signals throughout the cell. In addition to these carriers, there are two important compartments in the cell that perform a host of essential biochemical reactions, mitochondria and peroxisomes. Mitochondria are primarily known as the "energy powerhouse" of the cell, recycling sugar, protein and fat into cellular energy. However, there are many other reactions that occur in mitochondria and a host of these reactions rely on a second, smaller organelle called the peroxisomes to complete the chain reaction and build, or degrade, the final product. For example, the breakdown of very long chain fatty acids occurs first in peroxisomes, and the resulting shorter chain lipids are then transferred to mitochondria to be burned as energy. Without peroxisomes this cannot occur and the very long chain fatty acids are highly toxic, causing cell death and disease. In other cases enzymes in each organelle work sequentially to build new molecules, like bile acids in liver, or unique protective lipids called plasmalogen in the brain. The extent of the relationship between mitochondria and peroxisomes is so high that they share a number of common proteins, and we have shown that there is a direct, vesicle based delivery of protein and lipid from mitochondria to peroxisomes both in steady state, and for the formation of newly born peroxisomes. This proposal aims to understand how and why this type of vesicle transport exists in health and disease. There are many devastating diseases, both rare and more common, where peroxisomes or mitochondria are dysfunctional and we are currently without any therapy to treat them. By understanding the molecular basis of the integration between these two organelles we can contribute to the strategic design of new therapies to target disease.

column36: Regulating the dynamic cycling of palmitate on proteins
column37: Proteins are essential for all processes in our cells. Some proteins can be modified by the repeated addition and removal of a fatty molecule called palmitate. This process, termed the "palmitoylation cycle", helps direct these proteins to parts of the cell where they are needed to carry out their roles. One target of palmitoylation is NRAS, which is a protein that can promote the development of cancers such as leukemia and melanoma. By interrupting the NRAS palmitoylation cycle, we may be able to block the growth of cancer cells. We understand quite a lot about how palmitate is added to proteins, but much less about how it is removed. Until recently, researchers had identified only two enzymes - known as APT1 and APT2 - that can remove palmitate from proteins. My lab showed that APT1 and APT2 are not needed to remove palmitate from NRAS or from a brain protein called PSD95. Instead we discovered another enzyme called ABHD17 that does remove palmitate from NRAS. A drug against ABHD17 might stop the cancer-causing activity of NRAS by blocking its palmitoylation cycle. Before we try to develop such a drug, we first need to find out if ABHD17 acts on other proteins in cells and, if so, which ones. We also want to understand what makes ABHD17 specific for some proteins but not others, and how its action on NRAS is controlled. Cells have three different types of ABHD17 enzymes, so it will also be important to know if we can target just one form of the enzyme, or if we need to inhibit all three. This project will help establish if ABHD17 is a good target for future drug development. If so, the longer-term challenge will be to develop specific chemicals that inhibit ABHD17 activity and test if they can treat cancers such as leukemia and melanoma.

column36: Accuracy of general paediatrician diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder compared to multi-disciplinary team assessment
column37: Background: Increasing rates of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have contributed to lengthy waits for expert diagnostic assessment that negatively impact ASD outcomes. Many ASD diagnostic guidelines state that an expert team is needed to make the diagnosis; although some children currently receive their diagnosis from a community-based clinician, e.g. a general paediatrician (GP). There are no studies of the accuracy of GPs in diagnosing ASD. Project aims: The aims of this project are to: 1) determine accuracy of GP ASD diagnosis compared to an expert team assessment; 2) to determine child features associated with accurate diagnosis by GPs. Possible features include: child's age; sex; cultural background; ASD severity; developmental delays; and having a sibling with ASD. Methods: We will recruit 30 GPs from across Ontario, as well as 300 of their patients (10 per GP) who have been referred with possible ASD. The GP will complete their assessment and decide on a diagnosis, but will not tell the family. The ASD expert team, consisting of a developmental paediatrician and a psychologist, will also perform a diagnostic assessment without knowing the GP's opinion. The ASD expert team will inform the family of their diagnostic opinion. We will determine the diagnostic agreement between the two assessments. We will then determine which of the child's characteristics (age, sex, cultural background, ASD severity, developmental delays, having a sibling with ASD) predict agreement in diagnosis. Expected Results: Results from this study will determine whether GPs can independently and accurately diagnose ASD. Future activities include refinement of educational workshops for GPs on ASD diagnosis and development of pathways to identify which children can be diagnosed in a community setting.

column36: Brain development and internalizing symptoms in youth with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder
column37: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is caused by prenatal exposure to alcohol, and affects 4% of individuals in Canada. Key features of FASD are learning, growth and behaviour problems, and most people with FASD (>90%) also have mental health problems. Depression and anxiety are among the most common. However, treatments for depression and anxiety are much less likely to be effective in individuals with FASD. This is, in part, because we do not understand the brain differences in youth FASD, and how these underlie symptoms of anxiety and depression. A better knowledge of brain development in children and youth with FASD, and how the brain is related to mental health symptoms, would enable us to target treatments to the right time, place, and individual. We will recruit youth with FASD and unexposed controls aged 7-15 years in Calgary and Edmonton. Using longitudinal neuroimaging and mental health assessments, we will (1) measure patterns of brain development in children and youth with FASD, (2) test whether brain abnormalities underlie the increased risk of depression and anxiety in youth with FASD, and (3) evaluate baseline brain factors that predict mental health outcomes in these children and youth. We will use structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine brain connectivity, and caregiver and child reports of mental health symptoms to measure anxiety and depression. Measurements will be done at baseline, and again two years later. This study will provide new knowledge of brain alterations that underlie anxiety and depression in children and youth with FASD, and identify predictors of mental health outcomes. Ultimately, this will help improve the lives of children and youth with FASD and their families, as well as reduce the negative consequences and costs for society.

column36: STAT6-dependent control of innate immunity as a target for therapeutic intervention in asthma
column37: Both the incidence and severity of asthma have been increasing steadily over the last 2-3 decades. Although asthma in childhood is more prominent in boys, this sex difference changes around the time of puberty, when asthma prevalence declines in men and rises in women. We have developed a model of allergic lung inflammation where we deliver (directly to the lungs) a cytokine called IL-33, which is implicated in asthma onset. Our data show that adult mice treated with this cytokine develop 'acute' inflammation in the lung within days that is similar in many aspects to the inflammation found in asthmatics with established disease. We have found that females have much greater responses than males. We have also developed a combined viral infection-asthma model that mimics studies showing that, in children, there is an association between some viral infections, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and asthma development. RSV infection increases IL-33 levels in the lung, particularly in young mice, and thus we believe responses in the lung driven by RSV infection are similar to those caused by IL-33. As part of our ongoing studies, we are characterizing an inhibitor we developed called STAT6-IP. Our data show that STAT6-IP reduces some of the inflammatory responses in the lung caused by IL-33 delivery in adults or RSV infection in young mice. Our goals are now to define which responses promote asthma onset, including disease that develops as a consequence of prior RSV infection. We will define how these responses differ in males and females and we will define how they are modulated by STAT6-IP, recognizing that STAT6-IP may provide protection by targeting different responses in males and females. We believe these preclinical studies may provide a foundation to reduce the induction of asthma in both men and women.

column36: Microvascular Blood Flow Regulation and Insulin Resistance in an Animal Model of Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a growing public health concern affecting over 3 million Canadians. The risk of cardiovascular disease is substantially higher in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), including increased risk of heart attack, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease. T2D causes the loss of the ability of pancreatic cells to produce sufficient insulin and the development of persistent high blood sugar. Excess glucose in the blood can damage blood vessels, further exacerbating factors that impair the body's ability to respond to insulin and clear glucose. These factors include vascular surface area, distance between capillaries and skeletal muscle, and the distribution of blood flow. We aim to examine how changes in capillary network structure, and defects in microvascular blood flow regulation contribute to impaired glucose uptake in T2D. Our approach uses an animal model that recreates the insulin resistance of T2D, combined with obesity, to replicate the conditions observed in human disease. Using microscopy we can then to look at capillaries, the smallest blood vessels in the body, and specialized software to measure blood flow in living muscle tissue. The predictable progression of T2D in our animal model makes it ideal to study microvascular changes similar to that which would be observed in humans. The data collected will also be integrated into a mathematical model of glucose and insulin transport to further our understanding of insulin resistance. Quantifying how T2D impacts microvascular function and structure in our animal model furthers our understanding of the progression of T2D in humans due to the similar physiology and physical properties of our vascular systems. This study will be the first to study oxygen mediated blood flow regulation and the impact of insulin on blood flow distribution in capillaries which informs our understanding of exercise intolerance in T2D as well as how insulin resistance is linked to microvascular factors.

column36: Network Meta-Analysis of Opioid Agonist Treatments for street opioid users
column37: Opioids (e.g. heroin, fentanyl, etc.) acquired in the street and injected in unsafe conditions remain a significant public health challenge. While oral medications such as methadone work well, only approximately 40% of people with opioid use disorder are retained in methadone treatment in their first year. Discontinuing treatment and continuing to inject street opioids leaves people at high risk of HIV, hepatitis C and overdose death. Other opioid agonist treatments exist that can be used instead of methadone, including buprenorphine, morphine, diacetylmorphine, the active ingredient in heroin, and hydromorphone, also known as Dilaudid (TM). Currently, it is difficult to make an informed decision between treatments, as evidence comparing these treatments to one another is limited. Most trials have compared methadone against alternative opioid treatments. As a result, evidence of the effectiveness of different treatments to one another, for example, buprenorphine compared to morphine or compared to hydromorphone is unknown. While a new trial could answer this question, it would be expensive, complicated to conduct, and take too long to complete to address the current crisis. Instead we propose to use network meta-analysis, a methodology that enables us to synthesize trials to make indirect comparisons of effectiveness between different treatments. Network meta-analysis is routinely used by federal policy makers in Canada to address drugs and technologies, but so far has not been applied to opioid agonist treatments. We will identify all relevant trials to form the 'network', extract their data, and then apply statistical meta-analysis techniques to calculate the results. In addition to publishing the results, in partnership with our study's Knowledge Users and Collaborator, we will produce a simple results info-graphic and an online tool that will provide users with individualized estimates of their risk of outcomes on each of the compared treatments.

column36: Role of inflammation during the genesis of intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasia associated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
column37: Pancreatic cancer is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related deaths, primarily because the majority of patients have late stage disease when diagnosed. Three major types of precancerous lesions are associated with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and increased detection of the large cystic versions of these precursor lesions in non-symptomatic patients via medical imaging modalities creates an opportunity to treat these patients and limit their disease progression. In order to provide targeted treatment to patients with these cystic lesions, we must better understand the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the initiation and progression of these lesions. We recently created a novel mouse model that spontaneously develops pancreatic cystic precursor lesions and recapitulates many aspects of human disease. Here, we propose to use this animal model to begin to understand how the immune response contributes to initiation and progression of intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasia, a subtype of cystic precancerous lesion associated with pancreatic cancer. These studies will shed light on the etiology of this subtype of lesion, identify a potential method to halt the progression of cystic precursors into invasive pancreatic cancer, and determine whether cancers associated with these lesions could be more responsive to immune modulatory therapies.

column36: Understanding organizational culture to improve admission-discharge processes: A systems approach to healthcare performance, evaluation and education
column37: Emergency departments (ED) are very important places for the whole health system to sort out patients not only when they need to come to hospital but also when they get what they need and return home, or go to other places in the community. The ED's busyness also promises lessons for other health services on what makes health services work well together or not. When ED patient sorting is not done well, patients can die or be harmed, and it costs the health system a lot of money. The sorting out role is happening more poorly in Canada than other similar countries. Attempts to fix the problem over 30 years have looked mainly at technology, and in only one place. But these problems also happen because of how people work together in different places. So, patients are waiting longer and longer. This research looks to find out how people can work together better and how patient sorting can be improved. Our observers will spend a lot of time with a small number of carefully selected doctors, in two EDs in two Canadian cities. We will listen, observe and write notes of what they say and do with others. We will then ask doctors, nurses, community professionals and patients for their views on sorting patients to go to different places. Different researchers will read and summarize many times typed documents of what we see and hear. We will see what is similar and different in behaviours and views, to say how staff can work together better. We will share the lessons from this study by writing papers for other researchers, and also making presentations. We will give specific advice on how health staff can be better taught to arrange care, and how the places in which they work can help this. The findings of the study will help researchers, and people who teach and make health decisions, to improve the way health care organizations in general can help future health workers to care for patients properly, by sending them to the right people, in the right place at the right time.

column36: Genomics-based radiosensitization for HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the aerodigestive tract
column37: Squamous cell carcinomas of the aerodigestive tract that are not associated with the human papillomavirus (HPV-negative SCC) are locally aggressive and treatment resistant cancers with only ~50% local control despite aggressive management. A backbone of definitive treatment includes high-dose radiotherapy (RT) in combination platinum-based chemotherapy (i.e., chemoradiotherapy); this regimen only cures a subset of patients and causes significant toxicities, highlighting the dire need for improved treatment approaches. Despite known differences in radiosensitivity between individual tumours, molecular biomarkers of treatment sensitivity are not available, so clinicians continue to employ a one-size-fits-all approach. Aside from platinum-based chemotherapy, alternative systemic agents have not been systematically profiled for their radiosensitization potential due to the lack of robust and pragmatic preclinical pipelines needed to assess the large number of candidate drugs. We hypothesize that the efficacy of RT could be substantially improved by a more personalized medicine approach, in which the delivery of radiosensitizing drugs is tailored to each patient based on molecular features of their tumour in order to maximize the curative potential while limiting side effects. Our objective is to enable genomics-based precision medicine for HPV-negative SCCs of the aerodigestive tract. To achieve this, will evaluate promising drug-RT combinations that have the potential to specifically benefit subsets of patients based on molecular features of their tumours. We will also explore novel biomarkers that can be tested in future studies. By the end of this project, we will have a set of drugs and biomarker tests that can be further evaluated in prospective early phase clinical trials. Thus, our project will lead to new frontiers in personalized treatment of HPV-negative SCC and will usher the Precision Medicine era into the field of radiation oncology.

column36: Pilot Optimizing Transfusion Thresholds in Critically-ill Children with Anaemia (P-OpTTICCA): a pilot trial for a large pragmatic international parallel open-label non-inferiority randomised controlled trial.
column37: Une transfusion peut s'averer benefique chez les enfants les plus malades, comme ceux traites en soins intensifs, mais les complications sont aussi plus frequentes dans cette population. On sait deja avec certitude qu'il faut transfuser un enfant anemique hospitalise si sa concentration sanguine d'hemoglobine est inferieure a 50 g/L (la norme est de 120 g/L ou plus). On sait aussi qu'il est inutile de transfuser les enfants traites aux soins intensifs dont le taux d'hemoglobine se situe au-dessus de 95 g/L, a la condition que leur etat de sante se soit stabilise. La necessite de transfuser un enfant dont la concentration sanguine d'hemoglobine se situe entre 50 et 95 g/L n'est pas demontree, mais certaines donnees suggerent que la majorite des patients devraient pouvoir tolerer une telle anemie. Si tel est le cas, on pourrait eviter une transfusion et les risques de complications liees a une transfusion, comme une insuffisance respiratoire (exemple: syndrome de detresse respiratoire aigue) ou une insuffisance cardiaque (exemple: surcharge cardiovasculaire). Il est imperatif de mieux connaitre quand les benefices d'une transfusion de globules rouges depassent les risques a craindre chez les enfants traites aux soins intensifs. Cela s'applique a tous les enfants dont la concentration sanguine d'hemoglobine se situe entre 50 et 95 g/L. Toute etude qui permettrait de mieux reconnaitre les situations ou il faut transfuser et celles ou il faut s'en abstenir serait la bienvenue. Le projet de recherche que nous allons entreprendre permettra de mieux personnaliser la prescription de transfusions de globules rouges aux enfants traites en soins intensifs dont la concentration d'hemoglobine se chiffre au-dessus de 50 et en bas de 95 g/L. Le meilleur usage des produits sanguins qui devrait en resulter sera benefique non seulement pour les enfants anemiques, mais aussi pour les institutions qui fournissent les produits sanguins et pour le systeme de sante.

column36: Mechanisms and implications of fast turnover in the DNA replication machinery of bacteria
column37: Cells originate from other cells. A crucial part of this process requires them to inherit their DNA to the next generation. This task is accomplished by an elegant multicomponent protein machine, called the replisome. Even though the basic underlying chemical reactions are understood, the question of how this machine works remains unanswered. Since the initial description of the replisome in bacteria, it was thought that a tight physical association among its components allowed them to act as a single unit. As such, the replisome could function uninterrupted from the time it starts copying the long chromosomal DNA, to the point it finishes it, one hour later! Making an analogy, it would be like typing at a rate of 1,000 letters per second for an hour-period without making any mistakes. Not to mention that mistakes, prolonged pauses, or the permanent inability of the writer to continue, can cause complete loss of the text - and for the cell, its death. Recent data from my lab shows instead that most replisome components participate in the process in pulses that last for few seconds - in the analogy, a new writer would seat in front of the keyboard every few hundreds of words. As this discovery was unexpected in the field, its molecular causes and consequences for the cell are yet unknown. Understanding these aspects is the aim of this proposal. As DNA replication in bacteria is a factor in the spread of antibiotic resistance and a potential target for antibiotics, the outcome of our work may help in the development of new strategies to counter the current antibiotic resistance crisis.

column36: Preimplantation et implantation d'un programme de prevention de l'agression sexuelle pour les etudiantes en milieu universitaire : Les milieux sont-ils prets et le programme est-il efficace lorsque plusieurs facteurs de risque sont presents?
column37: L'agression sexuelle des femmes adultes au Canada en 2009 a entraine des couts de plus de 4,8 milliards en frais medicaux et autres couts associes. Si rien ne change, 1 femme sur 4 sera agressee sexuellement, ou vivra une tentative d'agression, durant ses etudes universitaires. Ces experiences ont des consequences negatives immediates et a long terme sur la sante mentale et physique. Une equipe de chercheurs canadiens a mis au point un programme visant a diminuer le risque de subir une agression sexuelle pour les etudiantes universitaires, que l'on nomme EAAA. Le programme a demontre son efficacite et permet de reduire l'agression sexuelle de 46% et les tentatives d'agression sexuelle de 63% pour les femmes l'ayant recu en comparaison a celles ne l'ayant pas recu. La recherche proposee constitue la prochaine etape logique qui permettra de determiner si les milieux universitaires sont prets a l'offrir et a verifier s'il est efficace lorsqu'offert en milieu naturel et aupres de toutes les etudiantes, meme celles presentant des niveaux de risque de subir de la violence sexuelle qui sont plus eleves que la moyenne. La formation et la supervision sera transferee aux professionnels des campus universitaires, qui offriront ensuite le programme EAAA a leurs etudiantes. Les professionnels et les etudiantes participeront a la recherche visant a identifier les conditions necessaires a son implantation et a examiner l'efficacite du programme dans ce contexte, notamment s'il demeure efficace en presence de plusieurs facteurs de risque de violence sexuelle (handicap, maltraitance durant l'enfance, minorite de genre et sexuelle, etc.). En plus d'etre diffuses a d'autres chercheurs par des conferences et publications, les resultats seront partages avec divers intervenants en prevention de la violence sexuelle, etudiants et decideurs des milieux impliques dans un atelier deliberatif qui permettra de determiner les conditions d'implantation du programme dans d'autres universites.

column36: Analyse economique de la prevention et controle des infections nosocomiales au Quebec: AnePCI
column37: Les infections nosocomiales (INs) constituent l'un des principaux accidents de soins de sante evitables. A l'instar de tous les pays du monde, le Quebec est particulierement affecte par les INs. Pour faire face a ce probleme persistant, le ministere de la sante et des services sociaux du Quebec (MSSS) de l'epoque avait mis en place en 2004, un programme obligatoire de prevention et controle des INs (programme PCI) dans les etablissements hospitaliers du Quebec. Dans son plan d'action 2015-2020 sur la prevention et le controle des INs pour une prestation securitaire des soins de sante au Quebec, le MSSS indique dans sa cible 22 vouloir evaluer l'implantation, les couts, les effets et le retour sur investissement du programme PCI dans les etablissements de sante de soins de courte duree. Le present projet s'inscrit dans la meme perspective et se presente comme la premiere recherche d'envergure dans la province du Quebec au Canada en matiere d'evaluation de l'efficience du programme PCI. Il a pour objectif principal d'evaluer l'efficience d'un programme de prevention et controle des INs a travers l'analyse economique des pratiques cliniques exemplaires associees. Trois objectifs specifiques seront poursuivis : i) Evaluer le cout des pratiques cliniques associees a la prevention et controle des INs au Quebec; ii) Evaluer le fardeau economique attribuable aux INs ; iii) Examiner la rentabilite de la prevention et controle des INs en comparant le cout d'implantation et les couts des infections. Cette recherche produira des evidences empiriques sur l'efficience du programme PCI au Quebec, et au Canada. Il permettrait a tous les acteurs du systeme de soins de sante de prendre conscience des gains economiques potentiels attribuables a la PCI. Il contribuera au renforcement de son implantation, a l'amelioration de son suivi et surtout a la sensibilisation de tous les acteurs de la sante sur l'importance de la prevention des infections.

column37: More than 200,000 older Canadians have major surgery each year; 40% live with frailty. This is important for a number of reasons. First, older people represent well over half of all people having major surgery in Canada. Second, older people with frailty face a greater than two times higher risk of having a major complication, developing a new disability, or dying after surgery than older people without frailty. Strategies and treatments to decrease the risks faced by older people with frailty having surgery are urgently needed but have not been widely developed or studied. The strongest findings suggest that exercise before surgery may improve older people's ability to walk and stand after surgery and lower rates of complications. Unfortunately, these findings are limited by a number of factors: 1) studies have been small and conducted in single hospitals, which means that we don't know if these findings are widely applicable; 2) existing studies have many flaws which could invalidate their findings; 3) outcomes measured in these studies have not been patient-reported or patient-centered, whereas we know that patient-reported outcomes are key to ensuring that research directly influences care in a way that matters to patients; and 4) most exercise interventions have been very resource-intensive, which can limit people's access to exercise, especially if they have trouble getting around or don't live near the hospital. Therefore, to help improve outcomes after surgery in a meaningful way for the growing number of older Canadians with frailty, we propose to study a home-based exercise program compared to the type of care that people usually receive. Using a randomized trial design performed across eleven different hospitals we will evaluate whether participating in this home-based exercise program, which we already know can be performed by older people with frailty, leads to lower levels of patient-reported disability and complication rates after surgery.

column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder affecting almost 1.5% of youth (children and adolescents) in North America. Youth with ASD present with social difficulties and repetitive behavior, but also with a variety of other conditions including anxiety, ADHD, intellectual disability, neurological, immune and gastrointestinal differences. Data suggest that untreated childhood anxiety often leads to long-term mental health disability. In typically developing youth with anxiety, evidence supports the use of cognitive behavioral therapies, medications, and more recently, their combination. The goal of this research is to collect pilot data on the effects of sertraline, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, in reducing anxiety in youth with ASD, in order to inform the design of a follow-up pivotal clinical trial. We will recruit youth with ASD who experience clinically significant symptoms of anxiety. Participants will be randomized to sertraline or placebo for 16 weeks. We will measure the effect of the medication on anxiety severity and quality of life. The role of biological markers such as autonomic nervous system function an d blood serotonin levels will also be explored. Given the frequency of debilitating levels of anxiety in youth with ASD, and how little is known about treatment response to medication in these youth, this research is critical for its potential to inform clinical practice across Canada and beyond.

column37: Voluntary movement of muscles in humans requires electric signalling down the nerves: beginning at the spinal cord and ending at muscles that help us speak, eat, breathe and move. This process is impaired in neuromuscular diseases (NMDs), which are associated with progressive muscle weakness, disability and early death. Until recently, most NMDs were very difficult to diagnose and considered untreatable. Fortunately, genomics (deciphering a person's genetic code to understand the mutation responsible for a particular disease) has transformed our ability to diagnose and treat these devastating disorders. My research program studies gene mutations responsible for NMDs to provide a diagnosis, understand disease progression, and test new therapies. My program focuses on two types of NMDs: congenital myasthenia syndromes (CMS) and myotonic dystrophy (DM1). I will use a combination of genomics, molecular biology, animal models, and clinical trials to improve their diagnosis and treatment. Specifically, I will: 1.Use genomics to identify the genetic causes of CMS while discovering new disease genes. I will provide a genetic diagnosis for at least 300 families with CMS while discovering at least 20 novel genes. 2.Use genomics, molecular biology, and animal models to understand how genetic mutations cause NMD in order to guide treatment and identify new therapies. I will reveal the genetic mechanisms of 20 new NMD genes, discover 5 new therapies, and study 7 therapies (4 re-purposed, 3 new) in animal models. 3.Build an 'Ottawa River' cohort of 250 families with DM1 and use patient samples to study biomarkers. I will identify 10 biomarkers to indicate which patients will be most responsive to therapy and another 5 to measure treatment response in clinical trials. 4.Conduct clinical trials to test new NMD therapies for CMS and DM1 using novel and repurposed drugs. This research will improve the diagnosis and treatment of NMDs and grow Canada's international leadership.

column37: The efficiency and safety of radiotherapy, in which ionizing radiation is used to kill cancer cells, rests largely on our ability to determine the amount of radiation (or radiation dose) delivered to a tumor and nearby healthy tissue. Well-established methods exist to do this when the source of radiation lies outside the patient. However, if the radiation source is inside the patient, for example as a radioactive atom delivered into a cancer cell, then the situation is more complex. In such cases, we require information on where radioactive atoms are found in the cell and of how and where their radiation travels once it is emitted. This latter can be achieved through computer simulations that follow step-by-step the slowing down of the emitted radiation. This basic quantitative information will be included in new computer models of radiation damage to more accurately calculate radiation dose delivered to patients in such novel types of radiotherapy.

column36: Obesity exacerbates ammonia-induced neurological dysfunction in cirrhosis
column37: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE), characterized by cognitive, psychiatric and motor disturbances, is a devastating complication of liver disease. With as much as 80% of patients with cirrhosis suffering from HE, the burden of HE is immense considering its wide-ranging effects on the patients, family and society. Ammonia is believed to be the major factor involved in the pathogenesis of HE. Cirrhosis causes an increase in blood ammonia (hyperammonemia) which leads to increased neurotoxic levels of ammonia in the brain. Obesity has become a major worldwide health problem. As a result, the number of patients with liver disease due to fatty-liver is rising and is becoming the leading cause of cirrhosis. Obesity has been demonstrated to induce cognitive changes but it is not clear how obesity impact HE. Our project proposes to study the effect of ammonia and obesity alone as well as together on neurological dysfunction. This will be studied using complimentary rat models of cirrhosis and obesity and closely looking at the impact of fatty acids, adipokines and ammonia on the blood-brain barrier. In addition, lipids can infiltrate into muscle (myosteatosis) which can impact the muscle's capacity to remove ammonia. Therefore, obesity can directly (via the blood brain barrier) or indirectly (by inhibiting ammonia clearance in the muscle) affect the brain, leading to a higher risk of developing HE. Cognitive impairment due to obese cirrhosis will be a challenging population of patients to treat as neurological dysfunction may develop due to either hyperammonemia and/or obesity. To date, treatment strategies remain an unmet clinical need in this population of patients. Therefore, the results from this project will provide valuable insights on the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment in patients with obesity-induced cirrhosis and lead to new management strategies for these patients.

column37: Sexual arousal, desire, and pleasure are integral parts of the human condition, hardwired within our brains and bodies, yet molded by our experiences. column37: Increasing the function and number of insulin-secreting cells is critical to the treatment of type 2 diabetes. This wide span of models is necessary to develop our technology, and confirm the uniformity of our results across species. column36: Transcriptional memory and plasticity in embryonic stem cells
column37: A kidney cell functions differently from a skin cell despite the fact that all the cells in one organism share the same DNA. This is because not all of the genes encoded within the DNA are active in the cells. Instead, cells can turn on just those genes that are specific to how that cell type works. One way that cells can regulate their genes is by using proteins called transcription factors and chromatin modifiers that can bind to DNA to turn nearby genes on and off. We study these processes using embryonic stem cells, a specialized cell type that can maintain its identity indefinitely while having the capacity to differentiate into all cell types of the body. When embryonic stem cells divide to form new embryonic stem cells to maintain its identity, the DNA is condensed and gene activity is turned off. However, each dividing cell also has to 'remember' the program of genes that specifies its identity. After division, how do the new embryonic stem cells know which genes to turn on and which ones to keep off? On the other hand, when embryonic stem cells differentiate into a new cell type, this transcriptional memory needs to be wiped clean, and a new transcription program needs to be established. How do differentiating embryonic stem cells achieve this complex process? These questions will be addressed in my proposed research project.

column37: Drug addiction is a chronic and debilitating disorder that has an immense social and financial impact on individuals and society. Substance abuse accounts for the highest number of preventable illnesses and deaths each year in Canada and places a significant social and financial toll on individuals, families and society. Drugs of abuse are believed to elicit changes in neural circuits that ultimately manifest themselves in a variety of self-destructive behaviors. Emerging evidence indicates that changes of glutamatergic synapses in key reward structures is critical for functional changes of neurons in addiction; however, the various molecular mechanisms involved are only partly understood. Inflammation is an observed part of the response to drugs of abuse, but its role in addiction is not defined. The pro-inflammatory cytokine Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF) is a key player in the inflammatory response, and can directly regulate synaptic function. Here we investigate how TNF modifies circuit properties in reward relevant parts of the brain in a model of drug self-administration. We then investigate how engaging TNF signaling from microglia can alter the motivation to acquire drug in animals trained to chronically administration cocaine.

column36: Using C.elegans to understand how the GAR-3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor modulates other signaling pathways
column37: The human nervous system is bewilderingly complex. There are over 100 billion nerve cells, but this is just the start of the complexity. The key properties of the nervous system - eg how we respond to stimuli or coordinate our movement - come not from single nerve cells but from the ways they connect with eachother and there are over a trillion such connections in the brain. This raises key challenges. We can understand how cells divide or make energy by studying single cells in a dish, but we cannot understand how the nervous system works by studying a single nerve cell - we need to know how they are connected and how they talk to each other. Rather than study the complex human nervous system, we turn to a simpler nervous system. The nematode worm C.elegans has just over 300 nerve cells - crucially, every connection between them is known and it is the best characterised nervous system of any animal. We study how perturbing the nervous system either with drugs or with genetic mutations affects worm movement. To do this, we built a system for measuring worm movement in a very rapid way - this system is unique to our group. This lets us examine many thousands of mutant worms to look for changes in movement. Crucially, we can use combinations of drugs, or combinations of mutants to look for examples where one pathway appears to affect another, showing cross-talk. We used this system to discover a new crosstalk between nerve signaling pathways. One signal rapidly affects movement, while a second signal slowly shut this down again. Now we want to understand exactly how this cross talk works. Do these pathways affect eachother in the same nerve cells or does one nerve cell talk to another? What are the genes involved? If we understand how these pathways interact in worms, we may be able to regulate them in humans, where they play key roles in multiple disorders of the nervous system.

column37: Voluntary movement of muscles in humans requires electric signalling from the nerve cells in the spinal cord to the muscles that help us speak, eat, breathe and walk. This process, called neuromuscular transmission, can be impaired by poisoning, autoimmunity, ageing, and genetic disease. In this research project, I propose to study gene mutations that lead to impaired neuromuscular transmission, so-called congenital myasthenic syndromes (CMS). CMS usually start at birth or early childhood, cause severe muscle weakness, and are often fatal because of respiratory complications. Effective drugs are available to treat CMS, but to select the best drug we need to understand the underlying genetic mutation and its effect on neuromuscular transmission. We currently know about 35 different genes that can cause CMS, many of which were discovered by my research team. However, around 40% of all patients with CMS do not have a genetic diagnosis and available drug therapy is not effective for 50% of patients. The goal of my project is to improve the diagnosis and treatment of CMS; specifically I will: 1. Provide a genetic diagnosis for patients with CMS and discover new CMS genes. I will use genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) to identify gene mutations that cause CMS in a group of 1000 patients with CMS. 2. Understand how gene mutations cause CMS to identify the most appropriate drug or new targets for drugs. I will study the underlying defects in cell and animal models using a variety of scientific techniques. 3. Develop new drug therapies for CMS by testing them in cell and animal models. I will test a variety of drugs in cell and animal models. This research will lead to better diagnosis and therapies for Canadians affected by CMS. Knowledge gained through my research will improve our understanding of neuromuscular transmission disorders.

column36: Regulation of skeletal muscle function by PINK-1-Parkin mitophagy pathway
column37: Sepsis is a leading cause of death in the intensive care units and is responsible for ten thousand deaths in Canada each year. Skeletal muscle dysfunction manifested as fiber atrophy and weakness is a primary clinical observation in critically ill septic patients during the acute phase of sepsis . Long-term ramifications of limb muscle weakness include functional impairment and poor quality of life. Sepsis-induced skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness are associated with accumulation of damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria (the main source of cellular energy). In normal skeletal muscles, dysfunctional mitochondria are selectively recycled through the autophagy pathway, a process known as mitophagy. In this process, autophagosomes recognize dysfunctional mitochondria primarily through the PINK1-Parkin pathway. This process is inhibited by a protein called P53 which retains Parkin in the cytosol. The main aim of this proposal is to evaluate the therapeutic potentials of enhancing mitophagy by overexpressing Parkin and PINK1 selectively in skeletal muscles or by inhibiting p53 on mitochondrial function, atrophy and depressed contractility in two models of sepsis in mice. To achieve this aim, we have assembled an experienced team of leading investigators in the field of muscle research, Hussain, and Gouspillou, who have extensive expertise in skeletal muscle disease, mitochondrial function, proteolysis, and autophagy and have produced many papers linking mitochondrial injury to skeletal muscle dysfunction in catabolic conditions. Overexpression of Parkin and PINK1 will be achieved by injection of adeno-associated viruses in limb muscles and these muscles will be examined under control and septic conditions. P53 inhibition will be achieved by using mice defective in muscle p53 or by using a pharmacological p53 inhibitor. Mitochondrial function and morphology as well as muscle fiber size and contractile performance will be evaluated in both control and septic mice.

column36: PRMT6 as a novel therapeutic target for breast cancer
column37: Although therapies for breast cancer have been improving, it remains a very common problem that patients develop a resistance to their therapy. When this happens there are unfortunately very few alternatives available to clinicians to help those patients and this usually means that the chances of surviving the cancer are greatly reduced. We are working on a new strategy that could help to make a drug that is currently used in the clinic (so we know it is safe) work for breast cancer. Specifically, we are focusing on a cancer drug named Velcade, which works really well for cancers of blood origin, but has proven significantly less efficient at killing other cancers, including breast cancer tumours. Our lab is working towards gaining a better understanding of the role(s) of a protein modification, called 'arginine methylation'. This modification of proteins is a 'flag' that is added to certain proteins in our cells. This mark in turn can change how the protein will work, and can even confer new functions to it. This work has led to the discovery that arginine methylation is somehow involved in the way that Velcade works to kill cancer cells, and in turn, that tinkering with this modification in breast cancer cells using various strategies can in fact make them more sensitive to this drug. We thus propose in the current project to assess the feasibility of a novel strategy to sensitize breast cancer cells to the chemotherapeutic drug Velcade. The proposed research will first aim to assess the relative whether our strategy works in all types of breast cancer or just in a specific subtype. We will also pursue experiments to gain a better understanding of how blocking arginine methylation can make Velcade work better in breast cancer cells. Finally, we will use mouse models of breast cancer to determine whether our strategy can also work in the context of a whole animal. This project could enable the development of alternative therapies for patients developing resistance.

column36: Reducing HIV-related Stigma in School Children in Northern Uganda: A Multi-level Arts-based Population Health Intervention
column37: Over 2.6 million children aged 0-15 years are living with HIV globally, with the majority living in low and middle income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa (1). Stigma associated with HIV is recognized as a key global problem due to its harmful health and social impacts which are particularly pronounced for children. Children living with HIV experience stigma among their peers at school. Previous research with this population in Uganda showed that stigma comes in the form of verbal and physical abuse from teachers and peers (bullying), leading to social isolation, school drop-out, depression and feelings of suicide. Little information is known about how to reduce this HIV-related stigma. Efforts to help these stigmatized children to live a healthy and vibrant life are of tremendous importance. Our proposed study addresses the need to reduce stigma in school-going (10-18 years) children by utilizing an arts-based program in twelve rural schools in the Omoro District of Northern Uganda (Acholi people). Traditional Northern Ugandan storytelling, proverbs, and songs whose messages and moral teachings demonstrate what society expects of children and transfer these teachings from Elder to child, form the foundation of the arts-based intervention. These traditional activities will help to instill the Acholi's long-held values and beliefs that promote peace and conflict resolution. Additionally, this intervention will create an opportunity to revitalize and sustain intergenerational knowledge transfer that has been diminished due to the impact of the civil war. Utilizing traditional knowledge as an arts-based program could provide an effective context-specific intervention to improve knowledge, attitudes, and behaviour of these children as well as a strategy to change policy at the school level and impact the broader community.

column36: Physical regulation of chromatin during development
column37: Appropriate control over gene activation is essential to many biological processes including embryonic development. Current models of gene control invoke biochemical molecules that unfold DNA/protein strands called chromatin to allow for the activation of genes contained therein. One largely unexplored possibility is that physical force can directly unravel chromatin to control gene activation. Our laboratories developed tools that allow us to test for this possibility in the mouse embyo. We will first use our transgenic force sensors to measure how much force (in pico-Newtons) is normally applied to chromatin that contains a group of Hox genes that control limb development. We will then manipulate how much force is transmitted to chromatin in the developing limb using a nano-scale magnetic bead system that we developed to test the degree to which force directly influences Hox gene activation. By using these biophysical methods in mutant embryos, we will determine whether known molecular regulators of chromatin folding act in part by modulating force transmission to chromatin. This project bridges biochemical and physical mechanisms of genetic control and will be useful to understand numerous biological and disease processes in greater depth.

column37: Rhabdoid brain tumours, also celled ATRTs, are the most common malignant brain tumours in children less than 3 years old. column36: Evaluating eye-movement and brain imaging indicators that predict dementia in healthy older adults
column37: Early detection of dementia is important for effective treatment of the disease. However, no test is sufficiently reliable in the detection of dementia prior to symptom onset. These brain and eye-tracking measures may indicate the earliest markers of cognitive decline, which may predict dementia in otherwise healthy older adults. Funding of the current grant application will allow for the expansion of this study, including follow-up testing of these individuals three years later. We expect that the brain and cognitive measures associated with cognitive decline will be impacted by genetic risk factors. This research will allow scientists and clinicians to make better predictions about who will go on to develop dementia and allow for more effective treatment. Moreover, the brain and eye-tracking tools developed by this research can be used to evaluate treatment efficacy in clinical trials of dementia interventions.
