column36: Active surveillance or surgery for primary management of very low risk papillary thyroid cancer: How often are the long-term disease management goals achieved?
column37: Treatment of low risk cancers that are detected early must be balanced with the possible risks of negative effects of therapy. Low risk cancers are those that cause no symptoms and are highly unlikely to become life-threatening. A traditional approach in managing low risk solid tumors is surgery with the intent to cure the cancer. An alternative approach to reduce potential overtreatment of low risk cancers that may never cause harm, is to consider close monitoring, with the intent to perform curative surgery if there is evidence of disease progression; this approach is referred to as active surveillance (AS). AS may reduce the risk of treatment-related complications and associated potential quality of life impairment, in individuals whose disease is unlikely to progress. Very low risk papillary thyroid cancer (VL-PTC) is defined as papillary thyroid cancer that is smaller than 2 cm in maximum diameter, which has not spread outside the gland. In this prospective multi-centre long-term follow-up study, we will determine how often disease management goals are met in patients with VL-PTC who choose AS or surgery, respectively. The disease management of goals will be defined as follows for respective groups: active surveillance group - survival without thyroid surgery (in absence of significant growth of the primary tumor or development of metastatic disease), and for the surgical arm - an excellent response to therapy (analogous to cure), as defined by current clinical practice guidelines. Our study will also compare the following outcomes in AS and surgical groups: quality of life, psychological distress, quality of life, rate of requirement for long-term thyroid hormone treatment, and healthcare resource utilization. We will also conduct an in-depth qualitative analysis of the experiences of a subgroup of study participants in the AS and surgical groups. This study will inform disease management options for future VL-PTC patients.

column36: Preserving synaptic function following gene-silencing therapy in Huntington disease: mechanisms and specificity requirements
column37: Huntington disease (HD) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by debilitating motor, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms. HD has been described as having symptoms of ALS, Alzheimer's disease and Schizophrenia at the same time. There is no cure for HD; however, great excitement lies ahead in the potential of so-called "gene-silencing drugs." Unlike the majority of brain disorders, HD has a known cause. A protein known as the huntingtin protein is found in everybody's brain, and appears to be important for the health of our brain cells. The huntingtin protein exists in two forms; one good, one bad. In individuals without HD, there is no bad huntingtin and plenty of good huntingtin. In HD, the good huntingtin is reduced and the bad huntingtin is present, resulting in the slow death of brain cells. As a result of this known cause, drugs can be developed that decrease the brain's production of huntingtin. Gene-silencing drugs do just this. However, one potential roadblock to successful HD treatment is the fact that many gene-silencing drugs are not specific for bad or good huntingtin, and will therefore reduce both the good and the bad. Reducing bad huntingtin will likely help delay or even prevent HD symptoms; however, we have no idea how the long-term reduction of good huntingtin affects the brain. Clinical trials with gene-silencing drugs are already underway, making it extremely important to prioritize basic research into studying the consequences of reducing good huntingtin. In the proposed research, we will use a variety of strategies to understand how good huntingtin reductions can alter the way our brain cells communicate with each other, and whether gene-silencing drugs that are specific for the bad protein should be used exclusively for the treatment of HD. Our research will help to make more informed decisions on which drugs should be administered to those suffering from this devastating disease.

This diagnostic tool will be extremely useful for younger individuals with a cam deformity who have not yet developed symptoms. In the future we could use this to detect early degeneration in adolescents to prevent and mitigate development of OA later on. This will also help us develop activity guidelines for people with smaller cam deformities in order to avoid surgery and prevent degeneration.

column36: The Prevention of Group B Streptococcal (GBS) disease in infants
column37: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease is a life-threatening bacterial infection that is the leading cause of blood and brain infections in newborns. Despite advances in treatment, many infants with GBS disease die from the infection. Of the babies who survive, up to half suffer long-term effects, including deafness, mild to severe delays in mental function, or paralysis of all four limbs. The highest risk of GBS disease occurs in the first week of life when the infection is acquired from the baby's mother during birth. In order to prevent these early cases, women are screened when they are 35-37 weeks pregnant to see if GBS bacteria are present. Antibiotics are given to all women who are found to have the bacteria, plus women who go into labour prematurely. This reduces cases in the first week of life, but misses some cases and does not prevent cases in older babies. Treating the mother with antibiotics is risky if she has allergies, and might harm the baby by killing beneficial bacteria. The solution may be a vaccine that would be given to women during pregnancy to prevent GBS in the baby. Although vaccines are quite advanced in development, we need to know more about the impact of GBS on babies and the effectiveness of the current screen-and-treat strategy to understand whether a vaccine will be better at preventing cases and reducing healthcare costs. Our study aims to fill the evidence gap by linking information about all pregnant women who give birth in Ontario with health care information about their baby to understand how many babies get sick with GBS disease. Our results will show how well our current strategy is working, how much it costs and how this compares with the potential benefits and costs of a vaccine. In this way we can find out the best way to protect Canadian children from this devastating infection.

column36: Novel insights into TGFbeta superfamily regulation of follicle-stimulating hormone synthesis
column37: Reproduction is controlled by a hormonal feedback system called the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The hypothalamus of the brain produces and secretes gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which reaches the pituitary gland. The pituitary sits at the base of the brain and, in response to GnRH, produces two additional hormones called luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). LH and FSH travel via the bloodstream to the ovaries in women and testicles in men where they stimulate fundamental aspects of reproductive physiology. In women, the two hormones stimulate growth and ovulation of egg-containing structures called follicles. They also stimulate production of hormones such estrogen and inhibin. In men, LH stimulates testosterone production. Together with FSH, this testosterone controls sperm production. FSH also stimulates inhibin production. Steroid hormones, like estrogen and testosterone, travel back to the brain, where they suppress GnRH secretion. This leads to decreases in LH and FSH secretion. In contrast, inhibins travel to the pituitary where they suppress FSH without affecting LH. Inhibins are thought to produce their actions by blocking the activity of yet another hormone called activin. Activins are thought to be made by the pituitary and stimulate FSH production. In contrast, research from our lab suggests that hormones like activins, but not activins themselves, stimulate FSH and are blocked by inhibins. Moreover, our work shows that our current conceptions of how inhibins suppress FSH are either incorrect or incomplete. In this application, we propose to identify the activin-like hormone that stimulates FSH as well as the mechanisms through which inhibins block this hormone. The result of this work will redefine our understanding of basic mechanisms of reproductive hormone control. Moreover, we may identify a new approach to treat human infertility.

column36: Centrosome-cilium biogenesis and function in human cells.
column37: Centrosomes are cellular structures composed of a centriole pair surrounded by an ordered matrix of proteins, collectively referred to as pericentriolar material. Centrosomes play a key role in mitotic spindle assembly and therefore need to duplicate once and only once per cell cycle so that two centrosomes are present during mitosis, each centrosome organizing one of the two spindle poles. Without a normal complement of centrosomes, chromosomes would not segregate properly to each daughter cell, giving rise to aneuploidy, a condition that can cause cancer. Centrioles also template the formation of cilia and flagella, cellular "antennas" that play a prominent role during human development. When cilia or flagella are defective, this can lead to polycystic kidney disease and infertility. The work proposed in this application will use protein identification tools to discover novel proteins that localize to centrosome and cilia. To study these proteins, our laboratory will use cutting-edge microscopy in both live and fixed cells in combination with genome-editing tools like CRISPR and biochemical approaches to pinpoint the exact role of these proteins in cilia and/or centrosome assembly and function. More specifically, our research program will investigate the cellular mechanisms that ensure cells have the correct number of centrosomes, through the tight control of centriole duplication and decipher how cilia assemble, disassemble and receive signal from outside the cell. Moreover, we will investigate non-conventional functions for centrosome proteins in the regulation of cell motility and proteostasis, a process by which cells control the level of proteins they contain which can go awry in cancer and Huntington's disease. Ultimately, our goal is to determine if the novel proteins identified contribute to the establishment of centrosome-related diseases, including neurological disorders and cancer.

column36: Integrative genomics and functional analyses to uncover the molecular mechanisms involved in bicuspid aortic valve disease
column37: The aortic valve is one of the four valves present in a human heart that ensure that blood flows only in one direction. A normal aortic valve is composed of three leaflets. A problem during heart development can lead to a valve with only two leaflets, a condition called bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). It is the most common congenital heart defect in adults. It has a prevalence as high as 2% in the general population. It is associated with a significant increase in the risk of obstruction and calcification of the aortic valve, a condition that can lead to severe cardiac disease and death. There is currently no medical treatment for this condition, only surgical treatment is available. BAV is present in as much as 50% of cases of patients requiring surgery for obstruction of the aortic valve. It is therefore a serious medical condition with an important societal and economic burden. BAV can be found in many individuals from the same family, suggesting that is has a strong genetic component. The genetic mechanisms responsible for this condition are however largely unknown, with only a few genes identified so far. This project proposes to integrate genomic data from different sources to identify the mechanisms involved in BAV and obstruction of the aortic valve. We will use blood and heart tissue samples from patients who had cardiac surgery to obtain genomic data in cases of BAV. We will compare this data to individuals with a normally formed but obstructed aortic valve and individuals with a normal aortic valve. We will use recent bioinformatics tools to integrate this large amount of data. We will also make experiments directly on cardiac cells and tissue to confirm the findings. We plan to identify the genetic mechanisms involved in BAV and how they differ from obstruction of normally formed aortic valve. This could lead to the development of new treatments for obstruction of the aortic valve.

column36: Redefining Human Liver Disease Using Single Cell RNA Transcriptomics
column37: The human liver is critical to our health, but we do not really understand how it responds to disease. As a result, many diseases of the liver lead to terminal scarring and liver failure that can only be treated by transplanting a new liver into the patient. Liver transplantation is effective, but the liver grafts can be rejected by the recipient immune system and the drugs used to prevent rejection have serious side effects. We want to identify new drugs that can prevent liver graft rejection and liver disease, but up until now it has been very hard to study the cells that make up the human liver. This is because it is difficult to get samples of human livers and because it is hard to isolate the cells that form its structure. Five years ago we modified our liver transplant procedure so that we now routinely obtain samples from liver donors; using this source of liver tissue we have developed ways to isolate and study the cells that make up the organ. In this grant we are proposing to use an exciting new technology, single cell RNA sequencing, to study each cell from the liver and generate a map of the genes expressed in each individual cell. This powerful technology will allow us to describe exactly what cells are in the human liver and how they react to disease. We will use this information to identify drugs that can target and treat the cells that are important for disease. We will use this technology to describe the human liver in both health and disease: we will focus first on describing the cellular composition of transplanted livers that are undergoing rejection. In this way, we can identify new drugs to treat liver graft rejection which will improve post-transplantation outcomes and patient quality of life.

column36: The 'Cholesteryl ester transfer protein' in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia. We now understand that the first changes in the brain occur as early as 15-30 years before symptoms of Alzheimer's disease become evident. Therefore, new strategies are needed to both prevent and treat Alzheimer's disease. At the molecular level, protein fragments called amyloid-beta are produced in the brain and form the characteristic pathology that defines Alzheimer's disease. They thus constitute a specific marker of Alzheimer's disease. The goal of our research program is to identify molecular processes that have not been investigated before to stop Alzheimer's disease at early stages. Alzheimer's disease patients often suffer from hardening of blood vessels (atherosclerosis). Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis share the same risk factors, including high cholesterol levels in the blood, high blood pressure, and type II diabetes. There is a blood protein contributing to high levels of "bad" cholesterol called CETP. Blockers of CETP activity have been developed for the treatment of cardiovascular disease including atherosclerosis and myocardial infarct and have been tested in clinical trials. Interestingly, several genetic studies showed an association of CETP variants with maintenance of good brain functioning during aging. Some studies even implied that CETP variants may protect from Alzheimer's disease. However, CETP has never been investigated in relation to Alzheimer's disease on a molecular level. Results from our laboratory indicate that CETP has a strong impact on amyloid-beta formation. With the data generated in this project, we aim to able to initiate clinical trials to investigate if CETP blockers may be effective in preventing or treating Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Antiretroviral-based HIV prevention and its impact on sexual risk behaviours and HIV/STIs among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men: Engage Cohort Study
column37: In Canada, half of new HIV cases continue to be among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM). GbMSM are also more affected by sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as syphilis. Antiretroviral (ARV)-based HIV prevention, such as Treatment as Prevention (TasP; screening, ARV treatment and care retention) for HIV-positive individuals and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV-negative individuals, is changing how we think about preventing HIV and other STIs among gbMSM. The use of these new prevention strategies is expected to vary greatly across Canada because of differing provincial policies affecting availability and access. Also, ARV-based HIV prevention may lead to unforeseen effects such as less condom use and more STIs. The Engage Cohort Study will investigate trends in the use of ARV-based HIV prevention by following 1489 HIV-positive and high-risk HIV-negative gbMSM in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal. Participants will do study visits (questionnaire and HIV/STI screening) every 6 months for three years. The study aims to 1) measure trends in the use of ARV-based HIV prevention, psychosocial-behavioural factors (e.g., experiences of discrimination, substance use, etc.), condom-use, STIs, and HIV and 2) examine relationships between ARV-based HIV prevention and various sexual health outcomes (e.g., occurrence of STIs). Also, because some groups of gbMSM (e.g., transmen) may have unique experiences of ARV-based HIV prevention, interviews will be done in each city to better understand their realities. The experienced study team will work with community engagement committees and knowledge users in each city to ensure the study is conducted appropriately and that study results are communicated properly. Doing the Engage Cohort Study now, as ARV-based HIV prevention becomes more available, is an important opportunity to learn how best to use these new prevention strategies in controlling HIV and STI epidemics among gbMSM in Canada.

column36: Using deep learning to estimate breast cancer recurrence scores from histopathology images
column37: Breast cancer is not a single disease and there are many different sub-types. It is important to understand what kind of cancer an individual patient has before deciding on treatment. Some breast cancers are not very aggressive and are unlikely to recur after the primary tumour is removed; for women with this kind of cancer it could be possible to avoid toxic chemotherapy drugs without affecting survival. Some subtypes of cancer can be identified by staining tissue sections from surgery with a special marker, but more recently, there have been many advances in personalized medicine based on the genetic makeup of the cancer cells. There are several genetic tests available that can help to differentiate between high risk and low-risk cancer, but these are very expensive and are therefore only made available to certain groups of women. They are also not 100% accurate and many patients end up with an intermediate risk score which is not helpful. More recently, advances in deep learning have led to some very encouraging work in digital pathology. A group from Google have shown that a computer can detect cancer cells more accurately than a pathologist and another group has shown that it is possible to predict the results from an expansive genomic test using a simple tissue slide image. Other work has demonstrated that using information from images can improve the accuracy of genetic tests. We have a large database of image data, pathologist's reports and genetic tests carried out on patients enrolled in a clinical trial. We also know which patients went on to have a recurrence of cancer. We propose to train deep learning algorithms to use the lower cost, more readily available image data to predict whether a particular cancer will lead to recurrence. We will compare the accuracy of these algorithms with the genetic tests. Our aim is to develop a tool for identifying high and low-risk cancers so that an individual patient can be offered the best course of therapy for them.

column36: Mitotic regulation of the Condensin complex
column37: Any mistake in the transmission of our genetic material is sufficient to generate genome instability, one of the most potent stimulator of cancer development. The overall objective of this proposal is to understand how living organisms promote effective separation of chromosomes during cell division. To achieve this objective, our team takes advantage of yeast as a simple model organism to study the regulation of chromosomes behavior during cell proliferation. This organism allows scientists to study chromosomes very efficiently because it is possible to remove genes involved in chromosome separation in yeast in ways that are not possible in other organisms. Using this approach, we have identified in our previous research key mechanisms responsible for changes in chromosome structure during cell division. The new mechanisms we identified rely on conserved enzymes that are key to normal cell division and that are also frequently misregulated in human cancers, the polo-like kinase, casein kinase and cyclin-dependent kinase. We have found that each of these players acts by adding a tag of negative charge -a simple phosphate molecule- onto an important chromosome regulator, the "condensin" factor. The next step for us is to find out how these tags of negative charge control condensin. In particular, we propose to remove the negative tags on condensin and determine how this affects the ability of cells to maintain chromosome structure and to allow effective separation of chromosomes during cell multiplication. We also want to understand how different types of tags added on condensin affect its functions at the molecular level. Ultimately, our work will have a major positive impact on human health by revealing new cellular mechanisms critical for cancer development and by identifying new genetic vulnerabilities that could be used for cancer treatment.

column36: Architecture and chemical modulation of genetic networks
column37: Complex networks of interacting genes and proteins control all aspects of human biology and are perturbed in genetic disorders, cancer, diabetes, infection, autoimmunity, neurological dysfunction and literally every other disease state. The overarching challenge in biomedical research is thus to understand how these interconnected networks govern cellular behaviour in both health and disease. This research program will exploit leading edge genome-scale technologies to systematically map biological networks in human cells. In particular, we will use genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic screens and sensitive protein mass spectrometry techniques to probe the cellular networks that control the growth and division of normal and cancer cells. The complexity of these measurements will require the development of databases, software tools and computational models to track and predict network responses. To exploit this knowledge for therapeutic benefit, chemicals that alter cellular networks will be identified and combined to specifically control network outputs and thereby provide a more precise means of treating disease. In parallel, the effects of thousands of different drugs, toxins and industrial chemicals will be investigated using CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic screens to understand how these compounds act on human cells. To address a serious shortfall in the drug discovery pipeline, an innovative synthetic biology strategy will be used to create massive collections of natural product-like compounds that will be screened in ultra-high throughput and low-cost formats. These novel screening technologies will allow us to identify novel modulators of network activity and will be focused on targets in infectious disease and cancer. The combined systems biology, chemical biology and synthetic biology approaches we propose will help underpin a long-term framework that will transform our understanding and treatment of disease.

column36: The Role of Active Deresuscitation After Resuscitation (RADAR): A pilot randomized clinical trial
column37: Life support measures provided to critically ill patients in an intensive care unit (ICU) include the infusion of fluids directly into a vein (intravenously - IV). IV fluids support the circulation when a patient is unable to drink, and provide a means of delivering medications, and many liters may be given over the first few days. However the accumulation of salt and water in the tissues can contribute to impaired organ function. Out work and that of others suggests that fluid retention results in an increased risk of death and prolonged ICU stay, raising the possibility that actively intervening to remove excess fluid by increasing urine output may improve patient outcomes. Since the administration of fluids is called resuscitation, we have termed this approach "deresuscitation". We know from our observational study that ICU physicians use such an approach in some, but not all patients suffering from fluid overload. But we do not know how best to deresuscitate patients, or even whether it is possible in most patients. Moreover we do not know the risks and benefits of such an approach. Consequently the RADAR (Role of Active Deresuscitation After Resuscitation) pilot trial will be conducted to determine how best to design and run a larger study to evaluate the risks and benefits to patients. This pilot study will: 1.) Determine whether a deresuscitation protocol is more effective than usual care in hastening fluid removal 2.) Determine whether clinicians will be willing to enroll patients and to keep them in the arm to which they have been randomized 3). Estimate the number of eligible patients who can be recruited to determine the size and duration of a definitive trial 4). column36: Electrical stimulation prior to nerve transection and surgical repair promotes nerve regeneration and functional recovery in a manner exceeding a conditioning lesion
column37: Peripheral nerve injury is common, especially among young, working individuals. Unfortunately, with current treatments, nerve regeneration following severe injury is often poor. A major reason is the very slow rate of regrowth, at 0.5-1 mm/day. Through animal studies, there is strong evidence that a conditioning lesion (CL), in which a nerve is deliberately damaged before the actual nerve injury, increases the speed of axon regeneration up to 3 mm/day. Faster regeneration increases the likelihood of functional motor and sensory recovery, therefore this accelerated nerve regeneration is extremely important. CL, however, cannot be applied to patients because it is not ethically acceptable or clinically feasible to subject patients to an additional surgery to crush a nerve. As such, another method of conditioning that does not require injuring the nerve is needed. A recent study showed brief electrical stimulation (ES) administered prior to injury increased the speed of regeneration of sensory neurons grown in culture. This opens the possibility that conditioning ES may be an clinically feasible alternative to CL. This treatment would be particularly applicable to nerve transfer surgeries in which a healthy nerve is cut and rerouted to a damaged nerve in order to reinnervate a muscle. These increasingly common elective procedures are pre-planned so they are ideally suited for conditioning ES. Our goal is to systemically evaluate the effects and mechanisms of conditioning ES on nerve regeneration and functional recovery in a rat model. We will concurrently perform a pilot clinical trial to ensure a seamless bidirectional translation between the bench and the bedside.

column36: Measuring cardiovascular Outcomes of Depression in reFerred Youth (MODIFY)
column37: Depression is a serious and recurrent chronic disorder that affects 5-8% of children. Individuals with depression are at increased risk of experiencing heart disease (heart attack and stroke). Heart disease is the leading cause of death for people suffering from depression. Research has shown that early manifestations of heart disease can be detected years, even decades, before a person with depression experiences symptoms. Population-based studies have shown that depressed adolescents are at increased risk of heart disease compared with non-depressed youth, and demonstrate early signs of heart disease in research studies. Studies have also found sex differences in the association between depression and heart disease, in that the relationship is stronger, and the role of obesity is more central, for depressed women compared with depressed men. How depression is related to heart disease biologically, and whether markers of increased heart disease risk vary with an individual's mood, however, is not known. This is important because prevention interventions are more likely to be effective when they are targeted to key factors, early in the course of illness, and directed at those most likely to benefit. This study will determine the relationship between depressive symptoms and early markers of heart disease over a 12 month period. We will study 300 adolescents with depression who are referred to a clinical research program in Toronto. We will investigate indicators of early heart disease, eating behaviours, (for example, eating when feeling upset) and their relationship to depressive symptom burden among depressed youth. This will help physicians determine which young people are at risk of heart disease, identify critical periods for identification, and allow physicians to make early suggestions in order to prevent heart disease among this high-risk group of adolescents.

column36: Improving the Outcomes of Peritoneal Dialysis Catheter Insertion
column37: Individuals with kidney failure are responsible for up to 7% of health care expenditures in developed countries. PD is felt to be equivalent to hemodialysis with respect to important clinical outcomes, is associated with significant cost savings, and is actively promoted. column37: Background: Indigenous peoples have negative experiences with health care services. The study will provide a comparative case analysis of London and Thunder Bay, Ontario, examining processes of transforming current health system norms, guided by Indigenous concepts of wholism and relationship, combined with systematic measurement tools from complexity theory on documenting the impact of multiple and contextually specific factors. This will be done through a mixed-methods comparative design that includes participant observation, interviews, focus groups and survey data. column37: Hardening of the arteries leads to heart disease and stroke, and therefore, is a major health burden for Canadians. Blood cholesterol has an important role in the development of this disease and is an important target for therapies aimed at reducing heart attacks and stroke. Cholesterol is a fat and does not, by itself, dissolve in the watery environment of the blood. Instead, it is carried in the blood packaged in specialized structures called lipoproteins. Two types of lipoproteins that have the most influence on hardening of the arteries, and therefore heart disease and stroke, are LDL (the bad cholesterol) and HDL (the good cholesterol). High levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood support the development of hardening of the arteries and treatment efforts have been aimed at reducing LDL cholesterol. On the other hand, high levels of HDL cholesterol counteract hardening of the arteries because HDL both prevents and reverses cholesterol build up in the arteries. Treatments centered on HDL have so far been aimed at increasing HDL levels, without regarding HDL function. This application is aimed at understanding the role of a novel cellular factor, PDZK1, in mediating beneficial functions of HDL in cells within atherosclerotic plaques, which can both halt the development and even reverse the growth of the plaques. We will carry out our studies using laboratory mice engineered to develop atherosclerosis when fed a fatty diet. Moreover, these mice are engineered to lack or express PDZK1 in specific tissues which will allow us to tease apart how it protects against atherosclerosis and its role in protection brought about by HDL. Understanding how HDL brings about reversal or "regression" of atherosclerosis will pave the way to identifying new pathways that can be potential targets for treatment.

column37: Objective: The goal of this research project is to identify clinically-relevant circulating protein biomarkers for osteoporosis using a genetics-based approach. The use of circulating protein biomarkers has improved clinical care since they can identify individuals at risk, providing opportunities for prevention and diagnosis. When causal, biomarkers also point to disease mechanisms and provide targets for prevention. Despite this promise, many diseases, such as osteoporosis still lack clinically-relevant disease susceptibility biomarkers. We propose to use cutting-edge genomic and proteomic techniques to identify circulating proteins that influence risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic fracture. Building on experience that we have developed through the use of similar methods on other diseases, we will identify whether the genetic determinants of circulating protein biomarkers are also associated with risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic fracture. This method helps to solve a major limitation in traditional biomarker studies because it uses genetic determinants of the biomarkers, which are not influenced by other factors that are not in the causal pathway between the biomarker and disease. The resultant evidence thus provides insights as to whether the biomarker causes the disease. The outcome of our experiments will be evidence testing the causal role for circulating protein biomarkers in the risk of osteoporosis and osteoporotic fracture. This information will be helpful to patients and their clinicians because it can help to identify people at risk of fractures. It can also be helpful to identify critical control points in osteoporosis development, which can be targeted through pharmacotherapies.

column36: Immunological consequences of inhaled cannabis and selected cannabinoids
column37: Cannabis is a plant that is commonly referred to as marijuana. Cannabis has been used for medicinal purposes for thousands of years. Canada will be one of the first countries in the world to legalize cannabis. Reports estimate that between 9-14% of Canadians use cannabis- a number that has doubled in the past 2 decades. With impending legalization, regular use is predicted to increase even more. Most people still use cannabis by inhalation of cannabis smoke. Other ways to now use cannabis is vaporizing the cannabis plant. This means the plant is heated but not burned like for smoke. Both ways in which cannabis is used releases chemicals called cannabinoids, which are only found in cannabis. One is called THC. THC causes the psychoactive effects of cannabis; in other words, THC causes the "high" from smoking cannabis. Pure THC oil is now available for purchase and can also be vaporized for inhalation directly into the lungs. This is very much like an e-cigarette- except THC replaces nicotine. Cannabinoids are believed to be why cannabis has therapeutic properties for many diseases- including autoimmune and chronic inflammatory conditions (asthma), pain and lung infections. These chemicals may work by affecting how the immune system functions. For example, THC and CBD can cause an immune cell in the body- called a T cell- to switch its armour. THC and CBD make a T cell become regulatory (as in regulates the disease to help make it better) and not pathogenic (disease-causing). In this research project, we will test whether cannabis alters the immune response to protect against infection. We will also provide answers as to whether there are long term health consequences of inhaling cannabis on a regular basis. Given the paucity of information on the long term consequences of cannabis smoke, together with the increasing use of pure cannabinoids for medical purposes, we are in a unique position to provide novel mechanistic evidence on the health impact of cannabis.

column36: Visceral obesity and ectopic fat: the missing links between lifestyle and chronic societal cardiometabolic diseases?
column37: My team is one of the world's leading multidisciplinary health research group in the field of obesity. Over 30 years ago, with the use of computed tomography (CT), I began measuring the inner fat located in the abdomen (commonly called visceral fat). My team was the first to report that an excessive amount of visceral fat is related to major health problems such as diabetes and heart disease. We also found that fat underneath the skin (subcutaneous fat) was much less dangerous to health. Since then, the notion that visceral fat (visceral obesity) is dangerous to health has been widely accepted by scientists worldwide. Recently, we found that visceral obesity was also associated with too much fat stored in normally lean tissues such as the liver, the heart, and muscles. For instance, although excess liver fat is a major cause of liver failure and transplantation, its link with visceral obesity and lifestyle habits is not considered by clinicians and patients. The central theme of my program grant application is that when we are exposed to a "toxic lifestyle" (sedentary habits and poor diet), those who put on a certain amount of subcutaneous fat remain relatively healthy, while individuals who store fat in their inner organs become viscerally obese and develop chronic diseases. This notion has major clinical and public health consequences and represents a conceptual shift as the risk of overweight/obesity is largely estimated by the assessment of excess body weight without distinguishing where the fat is stored. Globally, the research program that I propose aims at a better understanding of how we store fat in various regions of the body, how genetic factors play a role (visceral obesity runs in families) and how this can be affected by our lifestyle habits. I will also remain committed to medical and lay public education as my research program is relevant to the health of millions of Canadians.

column36: The DECIPHER Study: DEterminants of Function and Clinically Important outcomes in Proximal Humerus Fractures in the Elder Population: A National CohoRt
column37: Shoulder fractures are increasingly common in older adults, and result in considerable limitations in function and quality of life. Unfortunately, the best way to treat shoulder fractures is currently one of the most debated areas of orthopaedics. Existing clinical studies comparing various methods of surgical and non-surgical management have reported conflicting results. These studies have had limited numbers of patients, involved single centres, and used inconsistent treatment methods and inclusion/exclusion criteria. Therefore, there is insufficient evidence supporting any one treatment type, and a poor understanding of what factors influence the outcomes that are important to patients, making decisions regarding treatment difficult. We propose to establish DECIPHER, the first nation-wide, multi-centre observational study with 744 fully characterized patients with the ultimate goal of determining what specific factors influence patient important outcomes. Additionally, we will answer important research questions concerning treatment and rehabilitation strategies. Patients 50 and older with shoulder fractures will be recruited from 17 centres across Canada. Patients will be followed for two years, during which time patient function and quality of life measures will be collected at regular intervals. An economic analysis will be conducted to determine the impact of treatment type on patient and healthcare system costs. The information collected through DECIPHER will not only help improve patient care, but provide critical data for future studies to determine the best strategies for managing these difficult and prevalent injuries.

column36: Significance of S100A10 (p11) in breast cancer tumor progression
column37: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. The high incidence of deaths linked to this cancer is due to spreading (metastasis) of the cancer to organs such as lungs and bones. Cancer cell spreading is assisted by a protein called plasmin which chews other proteins surrounding the tumor cells thereby making the way for the cancer cells to move from the tumor site to distant organs. Plasmin is produced from a blood protein called, plasminogen, by the action of proteins located on the surface of the cancer cells. One such protein, S100A10 (p11), binds plasminogen on the cell surface and speeds up plasmin formation. In our initial studies, we observed that breast tumors and metastasis to the lung are dramatically reduced in mice engineered not to make p11 (p11- null). Moreover, we have shown, by analyzing breast cancer patient tumor samples, that patients with low p11 levels in their breast tissue have a better rate of survival than patients with high p11 levels. In the current project, we will investigate how p11 affects tumor growth and metastasis in breast cancer using a well-established breast cancer mouse model that is known to mimic human breast cancer, the PyMT mouse model. We will determine if the plasmin generated by p11 is important for the ability of the cancer cells to develop tumors, leave the tumor site and/or grow in other tissues. We will determine if the reduction in tumor growth seen when cancer cells cannot produce p11 is due to decreased cancer cell growth or increased cancer cell death. We will also determine if p11 produced by the other cells in the tumor that support cancer cell development and growth are important or necessary for tumor growth and metastasis. Identifying the mechanisms by which p11 contributes to tumor growth and metastasis will facilitate the development of new therapies to block tumor growth and metastasis by specifically targeting p11.

column36: A universal self-calibrating in vivo real-time optical radiation dosimeter for quality assurance and quality control of radiotherapy treatment.
column37: A new prototype technology that measures absorbed radiation dose on a patient (dosimeter) in real-time has been recently created by combining 10-20-micron layer of radiation sensitive material with an optical fibre and reflector. This approach will significantly reduce the workload associated with patient dosimetry, enabling uptake of this technology and driving improved quality control of all radiotherapy treatments. column36: A randomized controlled trial of individualized yoga to reduce fatigue in hospitalized children receiving intensive chemotherapy
column37: Fatigue or tiredness is a major problem in children and adolescents receiving intensive treatment for cancer and undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). While exercise is good for reducing fatigue, these patients are often too sick to participate in regular exercise sessions. A unique intervention that combines exercise and relaxation is yoga. Yoga is particularly good since it can be tailored to be more or less intensive depending on how the child is feeling. We previously performed 2 feasibility studies of yoga in children admitted to the hospital receiving very intensive chemotherapy or HSCT and found that our program of yoga is doable. We also found children and their parents like the program. This is a randomized controlled trial which will determine if a 3 week program of yoga is associated with less fatigue, better quality of life and less pain mediation use compared to the control intervention of iPad games, music, movies or books. Yoga sessions will be conducted once a day during the regular work week and will be led by a trained yoga teacher. In the control arm, the yoga teacher will visit once a day and will offer children games, music, movies or books on an iPad. Fatigue and quality of life will be measured by the parent at baseline, on day 10 and on day 21. We plan to enroll 210 subjects total at 4 centers in Canada and the United States over 4 years. Yoga has the potential to improve the health of children who are at the highest risk of poor quality of life. This trial is an important step in a program of research designed to improve quality of life for children with cancer and HSCT.

column36: Development of allosteric inhibitors for HECT E3 ligases
column37: In the past decade, we have witnessed a burst of knowledge about cellular processes that are deregulated in human cancer cells. One such biological process is the regulation of protein stability by ubiquitin, a small protein that is assembled to other proteins (so-called "ubiquitination") and signals for their destruction or functional changes. Among several protein families involved in this process, ubiquitin ligases (~600 in human) have attracted increasing attention as anti-cancer targets, as they catalyze the attachment of ubiquitin and therefore determine the specificity of ubiquitination. In particular, the HECT family members (28 in human) are deemed as promising targets due to the availability of an active site and other biochemical properties. However, existing inhibitory molecules of HECT ligases fall short in terms of potency, selectivity, and generally have had limited utility in probing unknown HECT mechanisms. To tackle this problem, we have used protein design and engineering approaches to systematically develop protein modulators for HECT ligases. We showed that the synthetic molecules could bind HECT ligases tightly on places other than the active site and were able to compromise or enhance their biological function. In this proposal, we will generate potent and specific non-active site inhibitors of selected oncogenic HECT ligases and validate their function in human cells. Additional biochemical and cellular analyses will provide information on molecular mechanisms by which HECT ligases function and further aid the design of chemical inhibitors as drug leads. In summary, this work will generate unique probes to understand and manipulate HECT ligases in normal and cancerous cells and will provide novel routes for cancer therapy.

column36: Development and Application of a Patient-Defined Outcome in Patients with Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
column37: Coronary artery disease is the number one killer globally and will remain so for the next 20 years. Revascularization by bypass surgery or stents relieves blockages in coronary arteries and improves survival, but we do not completely understand which of these treatments is preferable over the long-term, especially from the perspective of patients. Research has shown that bypass surgery leads to better survival at 10 years, but surgery comes with considerable upfront risks. These risks are important because patients with weak hearts are often older, medically complex and are concerned with their ability to lead an independent life outside of a chronic care institution. One may consider coronary stents as an attractive alternative to bypass, but the long-term results of stenting has not been studied in this patient population. Traditional cardiovascular research has focused on "tombstone" outcomes such as death and cardiac events, but a prior survey led by our group indicated that important outcomes identified by patients were very different from those used in traditional studies. We believe that the incorporation of patient preferences and values is key to increase the relevance of research to patients and to empower patients to make more informed decisions. We will seek input from a panel of patients, caregivers and clinicians, to reach a consensus definition of a patient-oriented outcome after bypass surgery or stenting. We will then use high quality, population-level data to develop mathematical formulas to calculate a patient's risk of developing this outcome, using the characteristics of the patient as input variables. These formulas will be made freely available to patients, families, caregivers and clinicians over a web-based app to provide personalized risk estimates, to enhance the shared decision-making process and to place patients back at the center of the care they receive.

column36: Development of a novel mesothelin CAR-T immunotherapy and pharmacologic combinations for triple negative breast cancer
column37: Triple negative breast cancer is an aggressive form of the disease, for which current treatment options are limited, and survival outcomes are poor. More effective options are needed, and successful development of the next generation of treatments demands new approaches. In this project, we combine the complementary expertise of our investigators to develop a new engineered immune cell treatment, building upon recent discoveries in our laboratory. Cellular immune therapies (also called adoptive cell therapies), which involve administering living immune cells to hunt and kill a persons cancer cells, have shown remarkable effectiveness in the treatment of resistant blood cancers, but to date have had limited success in other tumor types. We have developed a boosted version of this type of therapy, and shown that our approach has potential to overcome several of the limitations observed to date with existing versions. We propose to harness these technical advances for the specific development of a cellular immune therapy that can target treatment resistant triple negative breast cancer. Using a platform of breast cancer models derived from real patient tumors, we will optimize and characterize the effectiveness of this adoptive cell therapy strategy in the laboratory setting. We will identity features which predict whether this treatment will work for a given tumor, and test strategies to combine this new treatment with other drugs that can boost the immune response. If successful, we will be prepared and well-positioned to develop clinical trials of these new therapeutic approaches, towards the ultimate goal of transforming the outcome of this deadly disease, by harnessing the immune system to control triple negative breast cancer growth.

column36: The Canadian Study of Arterial Inflammation in Patients with Diabetes and Recent Vascular Events: EvaluatioN of Canakinumab Effectiveness (CADENCE)
column37: Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death in the developed world. Atherosclerosis causes plaques in the blood vessels and is a common form of CVD. Inflammation is now recognized as a major cause of atherosclerosis. New effective therapies (biologics) that target inflammation are on the horizon, but it is unclear if they have a direct effect on the atherosclerotic plaque itself. They are also costly and have increased risks. Imaging to detect inflammation may be a solution to understand mechanisms and to optimize patient selection and outcomes for these drugs. Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET imaging can detect inflammation in the plaque and identify patients vulnerable to plaque rupture which cause events such as heart attacks and strokes. The primary objective of this proposal (CADENCE) is to determine if the biologic drug canakinumab has an effect on plaque inflammation in patients at high risk for events (patients with diabetes or pre-diabetes and recent heart attack, stroke or transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)). This mechanistic and proof-of-concept study will set the stage for future studies that will determine if inflammation imaging can be integrated into clinical practice to personalize decisions for anti-inflammation therapies.

column36: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Study III (LAAOS III)
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rhythm disorder that causes one out of six strokes. Prevention of strokes in AF is achieved through the use of blood thinners such as coumadin. Although blood thinners are effective, they are limited by the risk of serious bleeding, by physician and patient unwillingness to use, and by noncompliance and discontinuation. The left atrial appendage is a structure on the upper chamber of the heart that is the most common source of stroke in patients with AF. This structure is easily accessible for removal during open heart surgery, and has been a target of interest for stroke prevention. However, there is currently no definitive evidence that removing it prevents strokes. The LAAOS III trial randomly (like the flip of a coin) assigned patients with AF undergoing heart surgery for other reasons to have their left atrial appendage closed or not closed. These patients are treated in the usual manner except for this small procedure which has been shown to be quite safe. Having successfully recruited 4700 participants into the trial supported by multiple grants, we now seek funding to complete long-term follow-up of the 4,700 participants required to know if left atrial appendage closure works. The LAAOS III trial will determine if closing the left atrial appendage can reduce stroke and other complications in addition to usual therapy. A positive study will change the way heart surgery is performed on patients with AF and result in a large reduction in the number of strokes in Canada. Further, it will promote further research into this approach that could be applied beyond AF patients undergoing heart surgery.

column36: Repair and Regeneration of the Injured Cervical Spinal Cord
column37: Traumatic spinal cord injuries (SCIs) have devastating long-term physical, social, and financial impacts on patients and their families. Currently, there are no effective regenerative therapies available for nearly one million North Americans living with SCI. Damage to the spinal cord results in the loss of cells critical for sending signals from the brain to the rest of the body. Without these signals, the ability to perform everyday activities such as walking, grasping and controlling bowel/bladder function is lost resulting in debilitating impairments such as para/quadriplegia, reduced breathing capacity, immune system dysfunction and death. My application focuses on a novel mechanistic human cell-based strategy that addresses key deficiencies in current cell-based therapies for SCI. Neural Precursor Cells (NPCs) show exciting promise for regenerating lost cells in SCI patients due to their ability to replace any cell type within the human body, however, key barriers exist in the application of NPCs for SCI, these include 1) the low level of cell survival following transplantation into the spinal cord, 2) generation of the correct cell type to repair the spinal cord and 3) the presence of scar tissue refractory to therapy. To overcome these issues, I have developed novel human NPCs that have been specifically engineered to repair the spinal cord. This proposal focuses on mechanistically understanding how these novel engineered cells replace those lost through injury and how they promote recovery. Additionally, this proposal aims to determine how these cells can be further optimized to maximise recovery. I believe these novel engineered human cells will result in the restoration of function following SCI by promoting the formation of new spinal cord cells whilst repairing other cells damaged by the injury. I expect that by the end of the grant my research will result in the generation of a viable living cell therapy for SCI.

column36: Genomic, proteomic and microbiomic approaches to understanding the biology and pathogenesis of anaerobic protozoa
column37: Protozoan parasites infect ~2 billion people worldwide and are responsible for the sickness of hundreds of millions. A number of these parasites colonize oxygen-poor (anaerobic) environments in the human body such as the gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts. Most of these organisms are understudied and their genomes, cell structures, and roles in human microbiomes remain poorly understood, despite their high prevalence in both affluent and developing-world populations. Using powerful high-throughput genome sequencing, high-resolution mapping of whole cellular 'proteomes' and sophisticated computational analyses, we are addressing how these anaerobic protozoa: (i) live without oxygen, (ii) parasitize humans, and (iii) influence human gastrointestinal health. We will generate 'parts lists' for prevalent protozoan parasite cells and identify the genes that allowed them to live without oxygen, parasitize their hosts and cause disease. The roles of these organisms in the human gut and disease will be investigated using novel computational methods applied to genomic data obtained from faecal samples from hundreds of individuals from four distinct populations worldwide. There are several of potential practical benefits of the proposed research. The species examined include common human gut parasites and close relatives of serious human pathogens; revealing unique aspects of their biology will help identify new drug targets and other interventions. By understanding the mechanisms by which free-living organisms become disease-causing parasites we may better evaluate risks associated with the emergence of new pathogens. Our genomic data can also be used to detect and monitor parasites in DNA samples extracted from human feces; we will use this approach to investigate the roles these parasites in diseases.

column36: Understanding Cellular Response to Stress: Role of DEAD Box 1
column37: The cells in our body are routinely exposed to different types of stress, such as agents that damage DNA, and 'environmental' stressors that affect the function of cells. Environmental stressors include agents that induce reactive oxygen species which can damage cells. Importantly, the presence of excessive reactive oxygen species in brain neurons has been associated with a number of neurodegenerative diseases. DEAD box proteins are RNA unwinding proteins whose main role is to alter the structure of RNA, thereby affecting the amount and types of proteins expressed in cells. We are working on a DEAD box gene called DEAD Box 1, or DDX1, originally identified in my lab. Over the last few years, we have shown that DDX1 helps to repair a type of DNA damage called 'double strand breaks'. We have also shown that DDX1 is important for the resolution of stress caused by agents that induce reactive oxygen species. Intriguingly, we have recently discovered that DDX1 interacts with DNA repair proteins (such as ATM) associated with neurodegeneration. Mutations in the ATM gene are the underlying cause of ataxia telangiectasia, an inherited neurodegenerative disease that affects children and adults. Our combined research findings have led us to hypothesize that DDX1 helps to resolve stress in neurons. Thus, we propose that inability of DDX1 to carry out its normal function keeps cells in a state of stress, a condition that leads to premature cell death in neurons. The goal of this proposal is to determine how DDX1 resolves stress with a focus on understanding DDX1's mechanism of action in cells that are defective in ATM, as well as in neuronal cells. Thus, we will use cells from patients with ataxia telangiectasia and neuronal cells to examine the molecules that DDX1 interacts with under normal versus stress conditions. Our long term goal is to determine whether DDX1 and its partners could be used to either prevent or slow down neuronal cell death in susceptible individuals.

column36: Defining mechanisms of PI4P-dependent transport during secretory granule biogenesis
column37: Each of our cells is like a busy city, with fleets of trucks that pick up and deliver cargo to specific destinations. Instead of street signs, the drivers of these vehicles find the correct address by reading signals provided by lipids, which are fatty molecules present in cellular membranes. Different membranous structures (organelles) within each cell contain different lipids. If the correct lipid signals are not present, cellular materials can be delivered to the wrong destination or wind up in the trash. We are studying an enzyme, PI4KII, that makes an important lipid called PI4P. PI4P is found at the Golgi, which is an organelle devoted to transport of cargo (proteins) to many destinations in the cell. PI4P is also found at membrane contact sites, where it helps transfer other lipids such as cholesterol between organelles. A small amount of PI4P is found on endosomal tubules, which retrieve proteins and send them back to the Golgi. Our experiments ask how PI4KII and PI4P act at these organelles to help form the storage depots (secretory granules) that house hormones, digest enzymes and other biologically active molecules in the cell. To understand how secretory granules form, we developed the fruit fly salivary gland as a model system. This allows us to take advantage of powerful genetics and microscopy techniques available in the fly to study the role of PI4P in this process. So far, we discovered that endosomal tubules and cholesterol help drive secretory granule maturation. The proposed experiments will enable us to understand how PI4KII and PI4P control these transport pathways. Our findings will have application to human diseases that result from defects in secretory granule formation.

column36: Improving Indigenous cultural safety in Ontario's cancer screening programs
column37: While historically uncommon, today, cancer is common and has a greater impact on Ontario Indigenous populations. Cancer Care Ontario (CCO), Ontario's provincial cancer agency, runs the screening programs for breast, colorectal and cervical cancer. Screening catches cancers early, at a stage when they are more likely to be treatable. Indigenous persons in Ontario are screened less often in Ontario than the general population. In prior work, we learned that a generally poor Indigenous experience of cancer screening (racism during health care encounters, problems with CCO's mailed invitations to be screened (did not receive or difficulties understanding) and poor support for screening participants) might lead to lower participation. To address these gaps, we will do 3 linked projects with the overall objective of improving Indigenous peoples' experience of cancer screening in Ontario. First, we will examine Indigenous cultural safety (CS) at CCO. CS is defined as quality care for people of diverse ethnicities. CS emphasizes respecting cultural differences, demands empathy and self-reflection, and is attentive to empowering the care recipient. We will develop a CS Assessment tool then use it to interview CCO leaders and employees about their values, beliefs, and experiences of Indigenous CS and their opinion of CCO's commitment to these issues. Second, we will work with First Nations, Inuit and Metis partners separately to develop CS and implementable communication strategies and materials using established health communication principles. Third, we will collaboratively develop a CS shared decision making (SDM) strategy with Indigenous partners. SDM is a process where patients work with clinicians or peers to make health care decisions based on science as well as their values and preferences. Findings from these 3 projects will inform recommendations for change in Ontario's cancer screening programs so as to improve Indigenous persons' experiences with cancer screening.

column36: Community-driven Helicobacter pylori genomics investigation of the disproportionate H. pylori-associated disease burden among northern Indigenous Canadians
column37: Northern Indigenous communities view H. pylori infection as a health research priority because of its link to stomach cancer, which occurs more frequently in northern Canada than on average across the nation. Compared to southern Canadians, this infection is diagnosed more often in northern Indigenous Canadians, in whom it also causes more severe disease and is more difficult to cure. This proposal was developed in partnership with Northwest Territories (NT) and Yukon (YT) communities that seek research aimed at explaining why this common infection causes a disproportionate health burden in their region. The Canadian North Helicobacter pylori (CANHelp) Working Group conducts community-driven research on H. pylori infection, with projects in 4 NT and 5 YT communities. We propose to conduct a genomic analysis of H. pylori bacteria cultured from stomach biopsies of 274 community project participants. Genomic studies examine an organism's genome (its full set of genes). We will describe features of genomes of the H. pylori strains that infect residents of participating communities and investigate whether these genomic features determine how H. pylori infection impacts stomach health among participants. Our proposed research aims to: describe genomic features of H. pylori strains and how they are distributed across NT and YT communities; examine the relatedness of H. pylori strains within household, families, and communities; and estimate associations of genomic features with disease severity. The CANHelp Working Group has a unique collection of H. pylori isolated from northern Indigenous communities, along with clinical outcome data. It is one of few population-based collections of H. pylori in the world. Thus, the proposed research has the potential to advance knowledge of H. pylori genomics in human populations while furthering community-driven biomedical research that addresses priorities of Indigenous Canadian communities.

column36: Determining the etiologies of age-related clonal hematopoiesis (ARCH), a new biomarker of cancer and cardiovascular disease development: focus on the roles of inflammation and genetic predisposition.
column37: Aging is associated with the acquisition of small changes (mutations) in the genes of blood cells called Age-Related Clonal Hematopoiesis (ARCH). It seems benign as people have no abnormalities in their blood counts. However, ARCH is associated with a 10-fold increased risk of developing a blood cancer, and it also doubles the risk of having a heart disease. In this application, we seek to clarify the cause of ARCH and to find a way to prevent its deleterious impact on health. Our previous work suggests that there are two major factors influencing ARCH: inflammation and genetic predisposition. The Hopital Maisonneuve-Rosemont (HMR) group, led by Dr. Busque, has 20 years' experience in the field of ARCH. To undertake the proposed study, it will be joined by world leaders in the field of cardiology (Dr. Tardif) and epidemiogenetics (Dr. Dube) from the Montreal Heart Institute (MHI). We will first evaluate the role of inflammation in ARCH by using a previously established cohort of over 5000 subjects. We will correlate deep sequencing data (determining ARCH) and blood levels of the C-reactive protein (a reliable biomarker of inflammation). Secondly, we will investigate if inflammation is related to bacterial translocation coming from the gut's microbiota (germs), as we have previously shown in mice. Thirdly, we will evaluate if an anti-inflammatory treatment (colchicine) impacts ARCH development and patient outcome in the context of an ongoing randomized clinical trial called COLCOT. Fourthly, we will search for a genetic predisposition to ARCH using an already recruited cohort comprised of 311 families. If our study hypotheses hold true, we will be in positon to identify subjects at risk of ARCH early in life and hopefully curb the emergence and/or clinical impacts of cardiovascular disease and cancer through anti-inflammatory intervention. Our work is ultimately intended to promote healthy aging, one of the most important societal objectives of the present time

column37: An estimated 35,000 people die from bone metastases each year in Canada, and skeletal complications before death cause considerable suffering and morbidity. Bone metastases are currently treated with anti-resorptive agents such as the potent bisphosphonate zoledronate or Denosumab (Xgeva). Unfortunately, this is not a cure and the number of patients experiencing skeletal complications is reduced by only 40% with no survival benefit, which exemplifies the need for improving the efficacy of such therapy. A lack of vitamin D has been linked to several types of cancer including breast cancer and the majority of breast cancer patients who have a recurrence will develop cancer spread to the skeleton. Active forms of vitamin D have anti-cancer properties but have not been effective when administered in humans. Significant side effects limit their use at high doses that can lead to hypercalcemia (elevation of blood calcium) with severe consequences such as tissue calcification and heart arrhythmias. Our goals are to understand how vitamin D may be beneficial to patients with bone metastasis, and to develop improved vitamin D therapies with minimal side effects by enhancing the local activity of vitamin D in the bone microenvironment to prevent its systemic effects and hypercalcemia-related complications. These novel therapies will be combined with currently approved anti-resorptive therapies such as bisphosphonates and Denosumab to treat/prevent bone metastasis in breast cancer patients. Overall, we propose to develop pre-clinical models that will serve as proofs of principle for therapeutic intervention in breast cancer spreading to the skeleton.

column37: Blood vessels in the brain form a barrier that protects the brain from toxic components of the blood. We identified a protein from the liver that is involved in the maintenance of the blood brain barrier and can prevent barrier opening following stroke. The liver is known to affect brain health however, to our knowledge no liver-secreted protein was shown to protect the maintenance of the blood barrier. Thus, this application will contribute to our understanding of how the liver can influence brain health, which is important in many conditions (e.g. Stroke, MS). We will examine the impact of early DAA treatment on HCV-specific immune cell frequency, transcriptional profile and functionality and will examine whether immunological changes might have an impact on enhancing HCV clearance upon reinfection.

column36: Evaluating the renoprotective effect of acetaminophen in pediatric severe falciparum malaria: A randomized controlled trial.
column37: Acute kidney injury (AKI) complicating critical illness is an important problem, contributing to an estimated 1.7 million deaths annually. The burden of AKI care is estimated to cost US1.72 billion per year. Treatment is limited to dialysis which is resource intensive and frequently unavailable in resource-limited settings. Therefore, preventing AKI is a critical step in reducing mortality. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) has the potential to reduce AKI caused by hemoglobin (released from red blood cells) and myoglobin (released from muscle cells). Hemoglobin and myoglobin cause oxidative damage and this is a common mechanism of AKI seen in various conditions including sepsis, malaria and crush injuries. Acetaminophen has been shown to inhibit oxidative stress and reduce kidney dysfunction in pre-clinical models and to reduce hemoglobin-mediated oxidative stress in patients post-cardiac surgery and in patients with sepsis. Our recent randomized controlled trial in adults with severe malaria showed that acetaminophen improved kidney function and reduced the odds of developing AKI. Since children bear the major burden of malaria, it is now crucial to test this protective effect in African children where AKI affects up to 45% of patients. The ultimate goal is to assess the role of acetaminophen as a renoprotective adjunctive therapy in severe malaria. The hypothesis is that acetaminophen will reduce kidney dysfunction by inhibiting hemoglobin-mediated oxidative damage. We propose a randomized controlled trial of adjunctive acetaminophen in African children with severe malaria. If the trial is positive, our results would change management of severe malaria globally. It could be rapidly scalable as acetaminophen is inexpensive, safe and widely used. Our findings will also have broad implications for other major causes of hemoprotein-mediated AKI including crush injury and sepsis, which directly impact thousands of Canadians.

column36: Studies on the safety of prescription opioids
column37: With more than 30,000 deaths over the past 20 years, the opioid crisis is one of the greatest public health crises in Canadian history. It consists of two distinct but overlapping elements: opioid addiction and its consequences, and harms arising from the treatment of pain with opioids such as codeine, morphine, oxycodone and others. Unfortunately, despite two decades of liberal opioid prescribing, important questions remain about the safety of opioids as currently prescribed. In this grant, we will conduct 5 studies to generate new insights about the safety of opioid pain medicines. To do this, we will link several large healthcare databases (pharmacy prescription claims, emergency department visits, hospital admissions, doctor visits, opioid fatalities from coroner's data, and others) for the entire population of Ontario over many years to explore the following questions: 1. Does the treatment of pain with opioids increase the risk of infection? 2. After spine surgery, what are the risks of fatal and nonfatal opioid overdose? 3. In women prescribed opioids following childbirth: a) has codeine (a weak opioid) been progressively replaced by oxycodone (a much stronger and more dangerous opioid)? b) is new, ongoing opioid use more likely among new mothers started on oxycodone after delivery, as compared to codeine? c) do opioids prescribed to women after childbirth pose any risk to the newborn, via passage through breast milk? Our team has extensive experience in the conduct of this sort of research, collectively publishing hundreds of studies over the past 15 years. Over the past 10 years our group has been at the forefront of opioid safety research, informing policy nationally and internationally. The studies proposed in this application are novel, feasible in few research institutes worldwide, and relevant to the health of millions of people in Canada and elsewhere.

column37: Any mistake in the repair or transmission of our genetic material is sufficient to generate genome instability, one of the most potent stimulator of cancer development. The overall objective of this proposal is to understand how living organisms promote effective maintenance and repair of their chromosomal DNA during cell division. Ultimately, our work will have a major positive impact on human health by revealing new cellular mechanisms critical for cancer development and by identifying new genetic vulnerabilities that could be used for cancer treatment.

column36: Apo(a):apoB100 interactions as key determinants of Lp(a) biosynthesis
column37: Lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) is a fat/protein complex that circulates in blood. High concentrations of Lp(a) in the blood place individuals at a higher risk of having a heart attack or stroke. Lp(a) consists of a lipoprotein particle identical to low density lipoprotein (LDL) as well as an additional protein called apolipoprotein(a) (apo(a)). It is apo(a) that is thought to be responsible for the unique effects of Lp(a) in the body. Lp(a) can promote a process called atherosclerosis, which involves deposition of fatty material and overactive inflammation in the artery wall and which is ultimately the cause of the blood clots that form in arteries to cause heart attacks and strokes. Although concentrations of Lp(a) are thought to be determined mainly by genetic factors (i.e. are largely inherited), this does not explain all the variability that is observed. Furthermore, very little is known about how apo(a) production by the liver and assembly of Lp(a) from its component parts are controlled. Interestingly, some drugs have been shown to lower Lp(a) levels, although how they work in this context is unknown. In this project, we will demonstrate the importance of two factors that we believe are key regulators of Lp(a) production by the liver. The first is interactions between the two proteins that make up Lp(a) - apo(a) and apoB100 - within the cell itself. The second is a series of proteins and drugs that may regulate apo(a) and/or apoB100 production and therefore Lp(a) secretion from liver cells. We will study the molecular mechanisms by which these two factors regulate Lp(a) synthesis in the liver, and will look for evidence of their action in human subjects. Our findings will indicate new targets for drug development to lower Lp(a) concentrations.

column36: Therapeutic potential of bloodless oxygenated perfusion of donor kidneys for prolonged storage and protection for transplantation
column37: Kidney failure among Canadians has tripled over the past 20 years. Transplantation improves the quality of life and survival of patients at a much lower cost than dialysis. However, only 40% of patients receive functional kidneys due to a lack of living organ donors. To increase the number of kidneys available for transplantation, surgeons are accepting organs from deceased donors. These kidneys are commonly stored at 4C without oxygen. While this method can increase storage times, it does not properly preserve kidneys as the organs can suffer injuries from a lack of oxygen as well as cold temperature. Moreover, these conditions are not conducive to apply any drugs to prevent damage even when they are available. Therefore, we need to develop a new method to preserve donated kidneys that address these issues. To this end, we used pig kidneys to resemble human kidneys donated from dead donors. We showed that perfusing pig kidneys with oxygenated blood at 22C (near room temperature) instead of storing them in static cold conditions improved their preservation. However, the lack of availability of type-matched blood and the potential presence of infectious agents can limit the use of blood in the clinic. Thus, our objective is to study the effects of a bloodless oxygen carrying perfusion liquid on storing human donor kidneys for long periods of time (16 hours) at room temperature. We will also evaluate if certain drugs can maximize the preservation of these organs. Our main goal is to properly preserve kidneys coming from dead donors, to extend their lifetime after transplantation and to improve the quality of life of patients while reducing the cost of transplantation worldwide.
