column36: The INITIATE Study: Initiating nicotine dependence treatment for smokers admitted to emergency departments
column37: Tobacco-related illnesses cost the healthcare system millions each year. Quitting smoking improves smoking-related outcomes, like the onset or management of heart disease, stroke, lung diseases, and several cancers. There are ~16 million visits to Canadian emergency departments (ED) each year; an estimated 3-4 million involve smokers. Effective quit smoking interventions exist, but are underutilized. Given the realities of the ED environment, interventions need to be simple. Considering that stopping smoking improves health outcomes, that tobacco-use is an important cause of preventable ED-use, and the volume of smokers, Canadian EDs are a missed opportunity in the initiation of quit smoking support. The INITIATE study aims to test the effect of a tobacco treatment intervention initiated in hospital EDs that includes a behavioural incentive and proactive follow-up support, on long-term smoking abstinence, health and healthcare utilization. This will be a 6-site, prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial. Individuals will be randomly allocated to either the Quit Card intervention (QCI, n=604) or usual care (UC) condition (n=604). The CCI group will receive: a "Quit Card" (a gift card worth $600 that can be used to buy nicotine replacement therapies at any pharmacy); a self-help booklet; and, enrolment in tailored telephone follow-up support. The UC will receive a brochure for a local smoking cessation program. The primary outcome will be 26-week prolonged smoking abstinence, bio-chemically validated through expired carbon monoxide measurement. Secondary outcomes will include 4, 52, and 104 week smoking status and all-cause and smoking-related health and health services outcomes. We hypothesize that intervention participants will have higher abstinence rates, improved health outcomes, and decreased healthcare utilization.

column36: Extracellular matrix mediated regulation of microRNAs in health and disease
column37: Fibrillin-1 is a protein in the connective tissue of many organs, including blood vessels and bone. Abnormalities in the fibrillin-1 gene cause various disorders which lead to severe and continuously developing clinical complications. Examples of this include various forms of Marfan syndrome, stiff skin syndrome, dominant Weill-Marchesani syndrome, acromicric and geleophysic dysplasias, familial tall stature, ectopia lentis, among others. It is estimated that about 1 in 3,000-5,000 individuals suffer from one of these disorders, resulting in high levels of physical and mental distress for patients and families, in addition to immense costs for the health care system. Marfan syndrome is the most frequent disorder in this group. We have recently found that the molecular interaction of fibrillin-1 with connective tissue cells controls a group of important regulatory molecules, the so-called microRNAs. These are molecules within cells that determine which proteins are produced. We also found that some of these microRNAs are dysregulated in a Marfan syndrome mouse model. The current proposal aims to determine how fibrillin-1 regulates different microRNAs under physiological conditions, and to identify some that can be exploited therapeutically in the long term in Marfan syndrome. We will use cell culture and genetically modified mice affected with Marfan syndrome as model systems. We will identify microRNAs and the genes they control in normal and in the disease situation, and define their function in relation to fibrillin-1. Since microRNAs are very small molecules, they can be potentially used for therapeutic approaches. In this context, we will explore whether inhibition or elevation of some microRNAs in mice leads to an improvement of the typical disease symptoms in blood vessels and bone. The identification of microRNAs in the pathogenesis of Marfan syndrome has the potential to open new avenues for novel treatment strategies for the affected patients.

column36: Evaluation, optimization and validation of structural and functional MRI-based parcellation of the cerebral cortex
column37: The human brain can be modeled as a network of brain areas (network nodes) with anatomical connections (links between the nodes) that transfer information between brain areas. In order to understand the function of the healthy human brain and the development of neurological diseases, it is essential to correctly delineate distinct brain areas. Structural and functional MRI are non-invasive imaging methods that hold the potential to identify relevant brain areas. However, MRI and functional MRI-based delineation of brain areas have neither been thoroughly validated nor optimized. We propose to apply non-invasive structural and functional MRI methods in an animal model, followed by the evaluation and optimization of methods for delineating brain areas. Specifically, we will optimize the non-invasive MRI and functional MRI methods for delineation of areas based on the variation of neuron density and size, as well as myelin content - all of which will be quantified using tissue processing. Our study will optimize and validate non-invasive MRI and functional MRI methods for parcellating the healthy human brain in order to set the stage for understanding changes in this parcellation in neurological diseases.

column36: Paving the Way for ICD-11 Adoption to Advance Health Information
column37: The World Health Organization (WHO) routinely collects global information on causes of death and diseases/conditions using a system called the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Since its original release in 1893, ICD has evolved to become the standard by which global, national, and local health information systems and databases support population health and healthcare performance monitoring. These, in turn, facilitate surveillance, healthcare planning and research. To support advancement of medical science in disease specification and new conditions, the WHO regularly updates the ICD. It is currently preparing the 11th version (ICD-11; released June 2018, implementation planned for 2023/24), which will track 40,000 additional clinical concepts over ICD-10 (1989) and integrate new features such as richer descriptions of diseases/conditions, the tracking of disease severity and progression, and disease clustering. This new version is poised to catalyze the advancement of health and medical sciences, the identification of optimal clinical care pathways, and evidence-based decision-making. Research is required to explore and understand the extensive ICD-11 adoption challenges faced by healthcare systems worldwide, and to develop the methods, technologies and approaches needed to overcome these challenges. This is the goal of the proposed research program. Dr. Hude Quan is the Director of the WHO Collaborating Centre in Classification, Terminology and Standards at the University of Calgary and a world leader in ICD health data science and methodology. CIHR funding will enable global ICD-11 preparedness and adoption, and advance Canadian and global health information research and practice. Thomson Reuters has identified him as one of the world's most highly cited researchers. Collaborators include the WHO, Health Canada, the Public Health Agency of Canada, Statistics Canada and the Canadian Institute for Health Information.

column36: Developing a Computer-Assisted Coding Program to Facilitate Hospital Discharge Abstract Administrative Data Generation.
column37: High-quality data is the driver for accelerating innovation and improving value of health care in Canada. Administrative health data are routinely collected through every patients' encounter with the health system (e.g. hospitals, emergency departments, and primary cares). Hospital discharge abstract database (DAD) is one of the most important administrative health databases. To create the DAD, coders are trained to manually review charts and translate medical information into medical diagnosis and intervention codes. These codes enable comparisons of health outcomes within and between hospitals to determine reimbursements, funding, and resource planning. The current abstraction practices are costly and unsustainable due to the growing and aging population. Meanwhile, there is persistent issue of underreporting or misreporting of conditions in DAD. In turn, poor data quality poses a significant threat to the efforts in conducting meaningful health system evaluation and health services research. Innovation on DAD data collection is urgently needed. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has been quickly adopted into many industries, health care industry has lagged behind, partly due to the lack of digital data. However, with the continuous investment of electronic medical records (EMR) to digitally collect health information throughout Canada and advancement of computing power, we are ideally now positioned to leverage AI technologies to improve the healthcare. This project will develop a computer-assisted coding system to facilitate DAD collection. We will develop the system using state-of-the-art natural language processing tool in combination with machine learning and deep learning techniques. column36: Hematopoietic stem cell aging
column37: Blood stem cells create all the cells in the circulating blood system, and are also able to generate new stem cells. As an individual gets older, their blood stem cells do not replenish themselves as well. The stem cells also tend to become more of one type of white blood cell while not producing as many immune cells. This combination leads to more inflammation and inflammation-related diseases and less ability to fight infections. microRNAs are small molecules that regulate the function of genes. A single microRNA can regulate the function of many genes. We have found that one of these microRNAs, called miR-146a, decreases with age. Loss of miR-146a results in blood stem cells that do not function as well and resemble the aging stem cell. In part this is because miR-146a regulates genes that drive inflammation. Loss of this microRNA results in continued low level inflammation that we predict results in aging. In this grant, we will examine how miR-146a affects blood stem cell aging with a focus on the inflammatory molecules that it regulates in both mouse and human models. We will also determine whether we can reverse the poor function of old blood stem cells by replenishing miR-146a or blocking inflammation. Because the blood system produces many inflammation-related cells and molecules, and because blood travels all over the body, it is likely that by reversing the aging of blood stem cells that we might also help to reduce the impact of aging on other systems such as the heart and brain.

column37: Over the past 50 years, care for children born with heart defects or congenital heart disease (CHD) has focused on surgical repair with unquestionable success. Although heart surgery enables >95% of children to survive to adulthood, many will experience a slow decline in heart function. Heart failure is now the leading cause of death in the CHD population affecting patients at a much younger age than their counterparts with acquired heart disease. Failure of the right heart pumping chamber (the right ventricle or RV) is a recurring theme in long-term outcome studies in CHD and is an important driver of HF. In contrast to the left heart pumping chamber (the left ventricle or [LV]), contemporary management guidelines highlight the absence of evidence to support medical therapy for right heart failure. In the absence of recognized treatments to address right heart failure, there is a desperate need to answer the following: (1) What causes scarring of the right heart muscle? (2) Can we identify new drugs to treat scarring of the right heart muscle? (3) Can we improve our prediction tools (serum and imaging biomarkers) to identify those at risk of deterioration secondary to right heart muscle scarring? (4) Do novel therapies for CHD apply to other forms of acquired RV failure? In this study, we address each of these critical questions through focused study of right heart failure in adults with extreme heart dilation due to a leaking pulmonary valve in the setting of a CHD defect called "tetralogy of Fallot". We anticipate that early detection of heart muscle scarring and early treatment may transform care through prevention of late right heart failure. Finally, new insights into the diagnosis and therapy of right heart failure to emerge from this study may inform care for other populations with non-congenital forms of right or left heart dysfunction.

column36: Elucidating the role of CD33 in regulating microglia
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative disease. Despite the enormous efforts, we still do not understand the origins of AD. This lack of knowledge translates to the inability to effectively treat patients suffering from the plethora of pathologies associated with the disease, let alone a preventative. Keys to better understanding AD and developing new treatment strategies may lie in genetic factors that correlate with AD-susceptibility, which have much to teach us about brain homeostasis. Of particular interest are genetic factors related to genes expressed in immune cells of the brain called microglia. Microglia play many roles in the brain with the most well characterized being the removal of unwanted matter. This removal is an orchestrated event with specific receptors on microglia that guide this process known as phagocytosis. Curiously, several of the recently-emerging genetic factors correlating with AD-susceptibility are receptors in microglia that regulate phagocytosis. Accordingly, it has been proposed that an altered phagocytic ability by microglia could be a key element in AD-susceptibility. However, due to the complex role(s) played by microglia in AD, there are still many unanswered questions. One of the aforementioned genetic factors is CD33, a receptor on microglia that is a sugar-binding lectin. Two different versions (alleles) of CD33 are present in the human population with the rare allele correlating with protection from AD. It is of great interest to discover precisely how this protective controls microglia compared to the common risk allele of CD33. This project aims to elucidates the roles for these CD33 alleles by studying them in the context of a mouse model of AD and their divergent abilities to regulate microglia.

column36: Benzodiazepine-free cardiac anesthesia for reduction of postoperative delirium in the intensive care unit (B-Free): A multi-centre, randomized, cluster crossover trial
column37: Delirium, an acute state of confusion, occurs in approximately 1 in 5 adults after open heart surgery. Even though it is a temporary state, patients who experience delirium are at increased risk of serious problems that last after the delirium has resolved. These problems include decreases in thinking, mobility, self-care, and the ability to live independently in a community setting. Patients who experience delirium have longer stays in hospital, are more likely to be discharged to a nursing home, and are more likely to die. Benzodiazepines are a sedative and amnestic medication that may be associated with delirium. As such, benzodiazepines are rarely used for sedation in the intensive care unit after cardiac surgery. However, benzodiazepines continue to be used frequently in the operating room by anesthesiologists during open heart surgery because of their amnestic effects and limited impact on blood pressure. Nevertheless, practice is divided among cardiac anesthesiologists, with some never using benzodiazepines and others using them for nearly all patients. Because the best approach (routine benzodiazepines or restricted benzodiazepines) remains uncertain, we will compare the effect of a hospital policy of intraoperative medication use that includes benzodiazepines to a policy that uses alternative medications and no benzodiazepines on the incidence of delirium after open heart surgery. The study will include 16 centres around the world that will test the two policies in alternating sequence during 12 periods of 4 weeks. The feasibility of this trial design has been demonstrated in a pilot study that included 800 patients, and is being endorsed by the Canadian Perioperative Anesthesia Clinical Trials group (PACT). The findings of the study have the potential to improve the outcomes of tens of thousands of patients around the world and will provide the basis for cardiac anesthesiology practice guidelines.

column36: Effects of Cannabidiol on Cellular and Mitochondrial Metabolism: Implications for the Epileptic Brain
column37: Public and scientific interest in marijuana (or cannabis)-derived products for treatment resistant epilepsy has increased exponentially in recent years. Specifically, cannabidiol (CBD) has been used by a growing number of patients in mostly unregulated ways due to immediate accessibility of commercial artisanal forms. Recent clinical studies indicate that pharmaceutical grade CBD is effective in pediatric patients with treatment-resistant epilepsy (i.e., those with Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes), but how this compound works remains a mystery. Given the mounting use of CBD and other cannabinoids, it is vitally important to understand the mechanisms of action, as this knowledge is necessary for uncovering new medications with greater clinical efficacy and improved tolerability. Recently, we have identified a novel target inside brain mitochondria (the specialized structures that generate energy molecules) that is affected directly by CBD. Specifically, we found that CBD blocks a chloride channel on the inner membrane of mitochondria, and that this action affects the metabolic function of mitochondria as well as the neuron itself. The overall goal of our research project is to study the effects of CBD on the mitochondrial chloride channel, and to determine whether this action contributes to seizure control in two animal models of epilepsy (one that models Dravet syndrome). Further, we will examine the effects of CBD on various aspects of cellular metabolism and mitochondrial function, and in validated tests of cognition (learning/memory) and behavior. Importantly, these experiments are designed to establish safe and effective dose and concentration ranges for CBD. Our team possesses the necessary expertise in molecular neuropharmacology to successfully implement the proposed studies. With the explosive growth of cannabis and cannabinoid use, especially in Canada, the research described herein is both timely and clinically relevant.

column36: Role of CD109 in regulating cellular signaling and responses in skin and oral squamous cell carcinoma cells
column37: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is one of the most prevalent types of malignancy and its incidence continues to increase globally. The fatal consequences of cancer are due to the spreading (metastasis) of cancer cells from the original tumor site to other organs of the body. Despite intensive research efforts, there has been limited success in blocking recurrence and metastasis that occurs in a significant proportion of these patients. Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) is a growth factor that is important for normal development and maintenance of healthy tissues. TGF-beta normally acts as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting the growth of cells but switches to a tumor promoter during cancer progression by making cells more invasive and metastatic. We have identified a cell surface protein named CD109 and found that it acts as a strong inhibitor of TGF-beta actions. Emerging evidence indicates that CD109 levels are increased in skin and oral SCC, and premalignant lesions in the oral cavity that highly express CD109 show a greater risk to progress to SCC. In addition, studies indicate that CD109 not only inhibits TGF-beta but may also activate other tumor promoting (oncogenic) pathways including those initiated by proteins known as EGFR and Jak/Stat3. The proposed research will determine whether CD109 promotes skin and oral SCC progression and metastasis in experimental models and establish the mechanisms that mediate the CD109's actions. The findings from the proposed studies is anticipated to lead to the development of novel CD109-based molecules for the treatment of skin and oral SCC.

column36: Short, medium, and long term effectiveness of interdisciplinary teams and other primary care reforms in Ontario
column37: Better access to primary care results in better patient health, fewer visits to emergency departments, and fewer hospital stays leading to lower health system costs. Therefore, health care policy makers across the country and internationally have focused on improving quality and increasing patient access to primary care in order to achieve these outcomes. In Canada, Ontario has implemented the greatest number of changes to primary care delivery but the models they introduced were focused on two key areas: how physicians are paid and the introduction of multidisciplinary teams. Despite more than doubling spending on primary care between 2006 and 2009 to accommodate these changes, there is only very limited evidence telling us whether they have translated into better health or cost savings. The goal of this project is to study the short, medium, and long term effectiveness of the models that were introduced in Ontario over the last 15 years. We are looking to determine which models resulted in changes to the cost of delivering primary care and the total cost of caring for each patient. Multi-disciplinary teams were introduced in part to offload some of the work done by physicians and give that work to other practitioners, so we will also determine whether family physicians were able to care for more patients because of this. Finally, we will also compare the different models of primary care for health outcomes (mortality) and health service utilization (emergency department visits and hospitalizations). Many other provinces are now considering or piloting reforms similar to the ones introduced in Ontario. The results of this study will help Ontario to plan the future of their primary care, and will help other provinces choose the most cost effective changes to introduce.

column37: Background: Our Sohki Teyhew Group consists of community members and Elders, community partners and researchers. column36: Extracellular vesicle-based therapy for atrial fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent and persistent heart rhythm disorder worldwide. AF occurs when electrical coordination of the top two chambers of the heart (the atria) becomes disorganized and chaotic. AF afflicts almost 350,000 Canadians and accounts for over 200,000 hospitalizations every year. In 80% of patients, AF significantly impacts daily quality of life causing dizziness, palpitations and syncope. Although not life threatening itself, AF increases the risk of blood clots and the risk of debilitating stroke by five fold. Treatment strategies for AF are limited. Drug therapy is non-specific, often ineffective with significant side effects. While catheter ablation has received much attention, success rates varies and this invasive approach has the potential for rare, but serious, complications. These realities rationalize a new focus on developing novel biological therapies to prevent AF and reverse the biological causes of AF. In this study, we explore the ability of cardioprotective extracellular vesicles to reduce atrial fibrosis causative for AF. Extracelullar vesicles are small membrane-bound signaling "packets" secreted by all cells. Extracelullar vesicles from blood and heart stem cells reduce scar sizes after heart attacks. Our preliminary data has shown extracelullar vesicles also reduce scar formation in the atria of the heart by re-programming connective tissue cells (fibroblasts) to a pro-healing, non-scar, fate. The ability of extracelullar vesicles to reduce atrial fibrillation will be investigated using our rat model of atrial fibrillation to see if injecting extracelullar vesicles can prevent the development of AF. If successful, this study will provide a new way to reduce AF beyond simply destroying tissue (ablation) or imperfect suppression using potentially toxic drugs.

column36: Preventing the progression of Alzheimer's disease pathology by targeting the effects of lifestyle factors and personality traits.
column37: There are over half a million Canadians living with dementia, the leading cause being Alzheimer's disease (AD). Amyloid and tau are the pathological hallmarks of AD. They start to accumulate between one and two decades before memory impairment. We know that the apolipoprotein (APOE) 4 allele, the main genetic risk factor for AD, influences amyloid and tau accumulation. It is unclear if other factors, such as lifestyle factors (e.g. education and cognitive activity) or personality traits (e.g. optimism and neuroticism), can also modify amyloid and tau accumulation and/or if these factors can buffer the deleterious effect of APOE4 on AD pathology accumulation. Lifestyle and personality traits are of interest because they are modifiable (particularly lifestyle) and, therefore, could be prime targets for prevention efforts. The first objective of this proposal is to determine the lifestyle factors and personality traits that are associated with amyloid and tau burden in cognitively normal older adults at risk of developing AD dementia. The second objective is to determine if some lifestyle/personality factors can counteract the negative effects of APOE4 on AD pathology accumulation. Finally, we want to test if the lifestyle/personality factors can delay the clinical onset of the disease by buffering the negative impact of AD pathology on cognition. Finally, we will test if the factors influencing AD pathology differ between men and women, since we know that women are at increased risk of developing AD dementia. This work will be done in collaboration with the PREVENT-AD, a cohort of almost 400 cognitively normal or very mildly impaired older adults who have a parental history of AD-like dementia. It will focus on 120 individuals that did a brain scan to quantify amyloid and tau in vivo. This multidisciplinary study will give insights about new, sex-specific prevention strategies.

column36: Reversal of Adipose Fibrosis by Intermittent Fasting and VEGF
column37: White fat plays an important role in energy balance and metabolic health. In response to diet and temperature, white fat undergoes rapid remodelling, such as "browning" in order to consume more energy. This remodeling is critical to adapt to different nutritional and environmental conditions. In obese and aged fat, unhealthy remodeling results in inflammation, low oxygen supply, and tissue stiffness (fibrosis). This process, called fat fibrosis, is directly linked with age-associated metabolic disorders, such as fatty liver disease and type 2 diabetes. Unfortunately, there are no promising therapies available for this crucial condition. Thus, understanding the fundamentals of fat fibrotic process is very important to develop proper therapeutic and preventive measures. Our research previously reported that intermittent fasting - a periodic diet restriction regimen - improves metabolism by promoting healthy fat remodelling, such as browning of white fat, via production of fat-derived vascular endothelial growth factor (fat-VEGF). Recently, our group discovered that aged fat contains unhealthy fat stem cells, which could be the source of fat fibrosis. Interestingly, our preliminary study found that intermittent fasting can prevent and even reverse this unhealthy remodelling of the fat tissue, generating a good and healthy fat, likely through the action of fat-VEGF. In this research proposal, we will study the pathway of how intermittent fasting can halt unhealthy fat remodelling, and whether these effects are mediated through fat-VEGF's action on fat stem cells. We will use genetically modified mouse models, advanced molecular visualization techniques, gene expression assays and single cell analysis systems. Our study will shed light on the potential implication of dietary intervention and fat-VEGF for the treatment and prevention of abnormal fat remodelling associated with age-related obesity and metabolic diseases.

column36: Utilization of a DNA aptamer to impede the in vitro and in vivo aggregation properties of alpha-synuclein.
column37: A hallmark of Parkinson's disease is the aggregation of the neuronal protein alpha-synuclein. One hypothesis states that as the protein aggregates, toxic oligomers are formed on the way to forming insoluble protein inclusions that may be responsible for neuronal death. With this premise, the proposed research program asks the question: Can a DNA aptamer targeted to bind to alpha-synuclein monomers inhibit protein aggregation and reduce Parkinson's-related neurodegeneration? Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that bind to targets with high affinity and specificity. Aptamers can be chemically synthesized at low cost with no batch-to-batch variability, are chemically stable, and have long shelf lives. These properties make aptamers attractive in the development of novel therapeutics and diagnostic tools. We have recently discovered aptamer sequences that can bind to alpha synuclein and limit its aggregation in vitro. In pilot studies, we have packaged one of these aptamers into a targeting delivery vehicle (liposome) that can cross the blood-brain barrier. We have preliminary data to support that the aptamer binds to alpha synuclein in vivo and reduces the prevalence of alpha synuclein. With the long-term goal of developing DNA-based aptamer therapeutics as novel treatment strategies to stave off neurodegenerative processes associated with protein aggregation, the three specific aims of this research project are: 1) Optimize aptamer sequences for optimal binding affinity and selectivity to prevent alpha-synuclein protein aggregation in vitro. 2) Explore these aptamers in a cell culture model whereby neurons are infected with mutated alpha-synuclein to investigate optimal dose and to confirm neuroprotective properties. 3) Investigate the pharmokinetics of the aptamer packaged in the delivery vectors and assess both the ability of this aptamer to bind alpha-synuclein in vivo and its ability to inhibit aggregation.

column36: Randomized comparison of the Outcome of single versus Multiple Arterial grafts: ROMA Trial - The Definitive Phase
column37: Coronary artery bypass surgery is an operation to improve the circulation of the heart where healthy blood vessels from the patients are used to go around blockages caused by hardening of the arteries, like a detour (bypass). Leg veins (saphenous veins) are used for most of the bypasses. Survival, prevention of further heart attacks and relief of angina are improved following coronary surgery when a chest wall artery (left internal thoracic artery) is used for one of the bypasses rather than using leg veins for all the bypasses. This is the most commonly performed coronary bypass operation. It has also been assumed that patients with an otherwise long anticipated life expectancy who receive a second chest wall artery (right internal thoracic artery) or an artery from the arm (radial artery) have better cardiac outcomes than following the standard operation. Yet this viewpoint is largely based on scientifically weak evidence, rather than randomized clinical trials. ROMA is an international, multicentre randomized clinical trial of 4300 patients with extended follow-up designed to address whether the use of two or more bypass grafts using arteries from the chest wall or the arm improves outcomes compared to the standard operation late after coronary surgery. The pilot phase of the study of 430 patients is currently underway with CIHR funding to determine the viability of the project prior to commitment to the full study. As of July 31, 2018, 380 patients have been enrolled - we predict that the pilot phase will be completed in October 2018. The pilot phase is on target in terms of the timelines and the stated pilot phase objectives and strongly supports the viability of the project. This submission is to fund the definitive phase of the study, i.e. complete the total study enrollment and extend the patient follow-up (up to 7 years) to determine with confidence if the multiple arterial grafting approach is better for patients.

column36: Proportional Assist Ventilation for Minimizing the Duration of Mechanical Ventilation: The PROMIZING Study
column37: Mechanical ventilation is the most common form of life support and is required by most patients who receive treatment in intensive care units. Although mechanical ventilation is essential in such situations, it can induce weakness of the respiratory muscles which may lead to prolonged dependence on the ventilator. Prolonged dependence on mechanical ventilation is associated with worse patient outcomes and high cost to the healthcare system. Pressure support ventilation (PSV) is the most frequently used mode of ventilation for assisting breathing of patients during the recovery phase of acute respiratory failure. Proportional assist ventilation (PAV) is a newer method of mechanical ventilation which delivers assistance to breathe in proportion to the patient's effort. This method may preserve respiratory muscle function while supporting the patient's need for respiratory assistance. Several studies have shown short term advantages of PAV over PSV, including improved patient-ventilator synchronization, improved adaptability to changes in patient effort, and improved sleep quality. There are no studies showing superiority of either method for clinically important outcomes. In our study, we will compare PAV to PSV using a randomized controlled trial. column36: Pathophysiology and treatment of adult somnambulism
column37: Despite almost 5 decades of clinical and laboratory investigations of sleep disorders, relatively little is known about the mechanisms which give rise to sleepwalking (somnambulism) and even less about how to effectively treat the disorder. Sleepwalking occurs in 4% to 17% of children and is far more common in adults (approximately 4%) than commonly acknowledged. Patients suffering from this sleep disorder often consult due to a history of aggressive and/or injurious behaviour during sleep. In a significant number of cases, patients report having suffered serious injuries (e.g., contusions, fractures to limbs, rib cage, multiple lacerations) and/or having attacked a bed partner during an episode. Establishing a correct diagnosis and adequately treating sleepwalking is vital for the patient's health as well as in light of the growing number of medico-legal cases of sleep-related violence. In most centers, the benzodiazepinic drug clonazepam is used for treatment. A significant proportion of clinicians, however, are reluctant to prescribe daily doses of benzodiazepines over long periods of time due to concerns about drug habituation and potentially harmful consequences of long-term usage. Moreover, many sleepwalkers do not respond to this medication or present side effects. Numerous descriptive studies suggest that hypnosis can be effective in the long-term management of sleepwalking. The first aim of the proposed research is to evaluate the treatment effects of hypnosis on sleepwalking frequency and intensity. A second aim of the proposed research is to elucidate our understanding of sleepwalking by recording sleepwalkers' brain activity during sleep both before and after a period sleep deprivation. Taken together, these studies should a) lead us to a better understanding of why some people suffer from sleepwalking, b) help identify neurobiological markers of the disorder, and c) guide future clinical treatments.

column36: Indigenous women from the sixties scoop healing through the full moon ceremony and storytelling
column37: This project idea focuses on working with Indigenous women living at the YWCA Toronto's Winona's Place at the Elm Centre which provides a safe, affordable, culturally appropriate, and empowering place for Indigenous women and their children to live. The objectives are for Indigenous women who are sixties scoop survivors to begin their healing journey by: 1) increasing their cultural knowledge through teachings and engagement with a Knowledge Keeper, 2) having other supports and resources they require identified, and 3) participating in a Full Moon Ceremony. Healing circles will be facilitated on a weekly basis for 8 weeks. Two 8-week cycles will be held with circles lasting at least 2 hours plus additional time to share in a meal. The circles will include 6 to 10 women. The participants of the circles will receive specific gifts at each circle to build their medicine bundles such that those who may not be ready for ceremony possess gifts that they can use for their healing journey. One of the desired outcomes of the project is to create a "guideline" for incoming clients and service providers to prepare for a Full Moon Ceremony. A necessary resource to ensure consistency with regards to ceremonial practices and meeting client expectations. Another outcome is to assess wellness and cultural knowledge through group discussions with the women completing a cycle. They also hope to identify other resources desired by the women beyond the Full Moon Ceremony which may involve other ceremonies or more mainstream health and support services. Finally, they would like to increase the understanding of clients and staff around the practice of ceremony and harm reduction.

column36: Our Counts, Our Future: Building Applied and Self-Determined First Nations, Inuit and Metis Health and Well-Being Information Systems in Urban Homelands
column37: First Nations, Inuit, and Metis (FNIM) peoples living in Canadian cities are not being "counted in". The systems that collect information about population size, health, illness, healthcare use, and living conditions either exclude or don't correctly recognize Indigenous peoples living in cities. This is a big problem since the majority of Indigenous peoples now live in cities and Indigenous peoples experience a high burden health and social challenges that doesn't improve with urban residence. A new approach to gathering FNIM health information in cities is needed. The goal of this research program is to develop, share, test and apply new models and methods to gather this information. We will do this by working together with FNIM and allied health and health information organizations at the national, regional, and city levels. We will also work to train more people who have advanced skills to do this work. Working together at a national level we will develop and share new models and standards for urban FNIM health information. At the regional level we will design and test training workshops. At the city level we will continue to build better urban FNIM datasets using some specialized methods we have developed over the past 10 years. These methods use social networks to find FNIM peoples living in cities who are otherwise hidden in the regular information systems. In this research program we will test out these methods in Winnipeg, which will be the first time that we have tested them outside of Ontario. To do this work we have gathered together a team of over 50 FNIM organizational partners and researchers from across Canada and around the world. This research program has the potential to change the way that FNIM living in cities are counted, ensuring that in the future every FNIM person is counted in, regardless of where they live. This new information will in turn improve health services for FNIM in cities, making them more effective and efficient.

column36: Application of Nutrigenomics and Multi-User Virtual Environments for Health Education and Promotion in Emerging Adults
column37: Chronic disease is creating an ever-increasing global burden. Dietary intake is a significant modifiable risk factor in the development of chronic diseases, however, current nutrition strategies are not adequately addressing the issue of chronic diseases. Health practitioners and researchers suggest that by targeting eating behaviours of emerging adults (18 to 25 years) that are known to continue into later adulthood, the burden of chronic disease may be reduced. It has been suggested that to generate interest among emerging adults to adopt lifelong healthy eating habits, that technologies such as nutrigenomics and interactive virtual environments be applied. In addition, using peer support approaches to nutrition education may also be beneficial. This investigation proposes to examine how effective a peer supported personalized nutrition approach, which is based on nutrigenomics (i.e., the study of how nutrients and active food compounds affect human health through environment and gene interactions) and that is provided in an interactive online virtual environment, is at fostering positive eating behaviour changes in emerging adults. The project will be conducted by an interdisciplinary team with expertise in nutrigenomics, health education, and the use of multi-user virtual environments for adolescents and young adults. The results of this study will provide guidance for different health stakeholders in terms of developing program and policy initiatives aimed at emerging adults and that could reduce the burden of chronic disease.

column36: Fostering a healthy food system for vulnerable families.
column37: Canada's food system is focused on producing inexpensive, high volume commodities that, although adequate in calories, provide poor nutrition. Combined with systemic challenges such as food insecurity, and food access issues, the burden of lifestyle diseases hits vulnerable populations, such as First Nations communities, hardest. Despite Canadians being among the healthiest people in the world, a closer look reveals the grave reality of the health disparities between specific populations with First Nations being the most vulnerable. Although the solution seems simple - consumption of a healthy diet, systemic challenges are overlooked in this prescriptive, oversimplified approach. Furthermore, at an individual level, the biggest problem is that such a dietary change entails a complete shift in how time and money is spent. With this understanding we propose an innovative approach that will address these systemic and individual level challenges specifically in low-income populations in BC and across Canada. Through this project, in partner First Nations' communities, we will enable vulnerable families dealing with food-related health challenges to receive a weekly produce box throughout a growing season (approximately 24 weeks). The boxes will be sourced from local, new entrant small-scale farmers that we will provide business management and technical support to. Educational tools, recipes as well as support groups will accompany the weekly produce boxes. We will track outcomes such as dietary change, weight and waist circumference, as well as health data. Project outcomes will provide a framework to understand how food system conditions interplay with community health and development, establish pathways to utilize these as social innovation avenues to reduce health disparities, and develop/refine a food provision model. Program outcomes will also inform the training of a new generation of community-focused farmers, and creating meaningful linkages between local food producers and consumers, restoring community connections to land, food and health.

column36: Eating up the plaque: Investigating the metabolism of foam cell lipid droplets
column37: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of heart disease and death worldwide. While the prevalence of this disease is high, there is no cure. In atherosclerosis, lipid-rich plaque builds up within artery walls. Moreover, plaques rupture, can cause a stroke or a heart attack, and may result in death. Current therapies include cholesterol-lowering drugs such as statins, which reduce plaque progression, but they are not effective at reversing plaque buildup. Therapies that could reverse pre-existing plaque would prove to be a breakthrough in atherosclerosis treatment as it could potentially cure heart disease. Cells of our body possess a natural ability to degrade cell components, through a recycling system called autophagy. It has been shown that autophagy is involved in the degradation of lipids within atherosclerotic plaques. This allows for the removal of cholesterol, a type of lipid highly abundant within the plaque environment, from plaques. Little is known on how the cells are able to utilize this excess lipid found in the plaque through autophagy. Our study aims at understanding mechanisms of lipid metabolism, or more specifically cholesterol metabolism, in lipid-rich foam cells. By selectively inhibiting proteins thought to be key players in autophagy and lipid metabolism, we hope to discover how lipids are degraded through autophagy. Ultimately, our understanding of the specific autophagy of lipids may lead to the discovery of new drug targets to enhance lipid degradation within the atherosclerotic plaque.

column36: Differences in Nef-mediated SERINC3/5 antagonism across viral subtypes modulates HIV-1 infectivity and pathogenesis
column37: With ~37 million people infected globally, HIV-1 remains a priority public health concern. With approximately 26.6 million cases, sub-Saharan Africa is the most affected region of the world. However, among the circulating HIV-1 subtypes in sub-Saharan Africa, multiple reports have consistently shown that subtype D infection is associated with a more rapid disease progression (faster rates of CD4 T-cell decline & higher mortality rates) when compared to subtypes A & C. To understand the virological mechanisms behind the contrasting pathogenicity observed between these subtypes, I hypothesized that HIV Nef, an accessory protein crucial for viral pathogenesis, may be a key modulator. Recently, it was discovered that Nef enhances the infectivity of progeny virions by downregulating two cell-surface host restriction factors, SERINC3 and 5. Incorporation of SERINC3/5 into budding virions diminishes the ability of the virus to infect a new cell, & therefore Nef antagonizes these antiviral proteins by removing it from the cell membrane. Given the importance of this "long-lost" Nef function, I characterized SERINC3/5 downregulation by 248 patient-derived Nef clones representing subtypes A, C or D to assess the population-level functional diversity of this activity. I observed that subtype D Nef clones were modestly better at downregulating SERINC3 (median 88% activity) vs. subtype A (83%) & subtype C (82%). However, for Nef-mediated SERINC5 downregulation, subtype D Nef clones were significantly more efficient (98%) vs. subtype C (88%) and subtype A (83%). Moreover, the ability of Nef to downregulate SERINC3/5 correlated strongly with the infectivity of HIV-1 viruses produced in vitro (p=0.02 & p<0.001, respectively). Lastly, both SERINC3/5 downregulation activity correlated with plasma viral load (p<0.01 & p<0.05, respectively). Altogether, my results demonstrate that differences in this Nef function could partly contribute to distinct virulence between HIV-1 subtypes.

column36: BRD4 Inhibition in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: a Phase 2 Clinical Trial
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive condition characterized by the chronic elevation of pulmonary artery (PA) pressure leading to failure of the heart. In spite of recent advances in approved therapies, PAH remains a serious disease with significant mortality. In contrast to the earlier belief that contraction of pulmonary vessels played a key role in PAH, it is now established that excessive proliferation of the cells within the pulmonary artery wall is a pivotal component of pulmonary vascular obliteration, a currently irreversible feature of PAH for which available pharmacotherapies have no/limited efficacy. In recent years, it has become increasingly appreciated that, in addition to rare mutations in genes, changes in their expression in the absence of changes in their structure (i.e. epigenetics) largely contributes to this phenomenon in PAH. Changes in gene expression influence numerous functions of the cells. We recently documented that by regulating genes known to be deregulated in PAH, Bromodomain-containing Protein-4 (BRD4) largely contributes to excessive cell proliferation and pulmonary vascular obliteration in PAH. More importantly, we observed that the pharmacological inhibition of BRD4, reverses PAH in human cells and animal models of PAH. Very recently, apabetalone, an orally available BRD4inhibitor, was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in treating cancers vascular cell proliferation leading to other types of vascular obliteration such as coronary artery disease. The time is thus right to translate our findings in human PAH. This proposal addresses a very novel and promising therapeutic avenue to treat and is one of the first steps of personalized medicine in PAH. We propose an early phase clinical trial to determine whether: BRD4 inhibition with apabetalone is safe and effective and; patients' characteristics can predict response to therapy in adult patients with symptomatic PAH.

column36: DNA Methylation and Mediation of Risk Factors for Chronic Facial Pain
column37: About 5 to 10% of Canadians live with chronic pain in their mouth, jaws and face (called orofacial pain) caused by temporomandibular disorder (or TMD, meaning issues with your jaw or the muscles that control it). TMD's cause is unknown and there are no specific molecular markers for TMD to help diagnose, predict or treat it. While TMD has some inherited genetic components that are passed on through families, how are genes work can be modulated by environmental factors such as exposure to stress, inflammation, diet, and medication. One way that environmental factors alter how our genes work is by adding 'marks' to the DNA through a process called methylation. We will study blood and tissue samples provided by healthy people and people with TMD, as well as people with other chronic pain conditions. All samples will be examined for genome-wide methylation patterns. These studies will allow us to identify how methylation patterns affect TMD, who will get TMD and who will not, and whose TMD will persist over time. In addition, by comparing to samples from other types of chronic pain, we will identify methylation patterns in people that are common to TMD and other chronic pain conditions. Ultimately this will help us understand more about how the environment affects a person's genetics in terms of their risk of TMD and how better to predict, diagnose, and ultimately treat or prevent painful TMD.

column36: Targeting the epigenetic state of refractory and relapsing acute myeloid leukemia
column37: In 2013, according to the Canadian Cancer Society, 1315 patients in Canada were diagnosed with the blood cancer acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and 1047 died of the disease. AML is the most common adult blood cancer and one of the most deadly forms of cancer. Unfortunately, these numbers have not changed much in the last 30 plus years. This is due primarily because only minor changes to therapy have occurred over this time period. About 40 year ago, an innovative chemotherapy known as induction therapy was introduced as the frontline treatment for AML patients. While some modest improvements have been made to induction therapy, new innovative therapeutic approaches are necessary to make substantive improvements to the survival of AML patients. In contrast to the "one size fits all" induction therapy, we propose to implement a "precision medicine" strategy to treat AML patients. To implement precision medicine in AML, we need to identify different sub-classes of AML, identify which patients fit a particular subclass, develop targeted therapies for these sub-classes of AML and treat the patients accordingly. In this proposal, we will focus on the "epigenetic state" of AML because these states can be reversed. Recently, we demonstrated in mice that we can reverse the epigenetic state of a group of AML patients who are resistant to induction therapy. This group of patients are known as "refractory" AML patients. In this proposal, we aim to determine how different drugs reverse the epigenetic state of this group of refractory AML patients and perform additional experiments to enable us to file for a precision medicine clinical trial in this group of AML patients. We will also develop the tools to treat other groups of refractory and relapse AML patients. These tools include methods to identify these patients at diagnosis and novel drugs to treat these normally drug resistant AML cells.

column37: Indigenous peoples' health is deeply impacted by social determinants including those related to the effects of colonization and its resultant intergenerational traumas. During the CIHR Component 2 funded young adult suicide research project with this team in Northern BC, First Nation Elders, together with community members noted unmet mental wellness needs among their older adults. Those aged 45+ are exposed to specific risk factors including isolation, addictions, poverty, elder abuse, and a cultural gap between Elders and younger generations. column37: Type 2 diabetes and obesity disproportionately affect Indigenous children in Canada. The inequities in diabetes and obesity can be traced back to several forms of transgenerational trauma, stress and adversity that accompanies settler-led cultural genocide and on-going institutional racism that Indigenous children face. Strengths-based, resilience, centred programs are therefore needed to overcome these inequities. With the support of Indigenous youth in Manitoba, we developed a peer-based mentoring program, centred on an Indigenous model of resilience; Dr.Martin Brokenleg's Circle of Courage, called the Indigenous Youth Mentorship Program (IYMP). During the last 2 years as a Pathways 2 Implementation Research Team we expanded from 5 communities in Manitoba and to 13 communities across 4 provinces in Canada. Using a participatory action model, guided by the teachings of elders, knowledge keepers and youth on our team, we will build on the successes of the past 2 years to (1) explore a novel pathway through which IYMP can reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes in youth, through the Indigenous concept of Mino-pimatisiwin/bimaadiziwin "living in a god way", (2) deepen the reach of IYMP within existing communities, (3) explore relational models of rippling IYMP to new communities, and (4) study the process of moving IYMP from a university-based program to a sustainable community-led organization. This information will provide information and infrastructure to support rippling of other wellness promoting community-based programs across Canada.

The CTN proposes a renewed scientific vision for 2019-2024 through a National and Strategic Research Agenda for HIV research in Canada. column36: Understanding glycan transport across the outer-membrane of Bacteroides species, prominent members of the human gut microbiota, using a structural and functional approach.
column37: The human gut plays host to an incredibly complex microbial community. Beneficial gut microbes are shown alleviate inflammatory bowel and metabolic disease symptoms and protect against gut infections. The ability to degrade and utilize carbohydrates is essential to survival in the human gut and is reflected in the over representation of carbohydrate active enzymes and glycan binding proteins expressed by gut bacteria. Gut microbes utilize dietary glycans, primarily from plant sources. A prominent genus in the human gut microbiota, Bacteroides, possess well developed glycan utilization systems. Astoundingly, the Bacteroides ovatus genome encodes over 100 individual polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs). PULs are equipped with integral outer-membrane SusC-like TonB-dependent Transporters (TBDTs) paired with an outer-membrane lipid anchored glycan binding protein, SusD-homologue. Alongside the TBDTs are carbohydrate active enzymes in the periplasm or on the cell surface. Given the ubiquity of this class of TBDT in Bacteroides PULs and the great strides made recently in our understanding of glycan binding and degradation by gut microbes astonishingly little is known about this class of transporter. TBDTs are essential to Bacteroides glycan utilization in the gut and by extension, human health. In this research proposal I outline methodology to structurally and functionally characterize TBDTs targeting xyloglucan, ubiquitous a dietary glycan. I will explore cross-feeding, where keystone species like Bacteroides increase accessibility to complex glycans for other microbes, which can increase species diversity in the human gut. I will use in vivo growth studies to understand how glycan transport during utilization impact carbohydrate cross-feeding. A greater understanding of Bacteroides TBDTs and how they impact other gut bacteria will inform prebiotic strategies for use in inflammatory bowel diseases and the maintenance of a healthy gut flora.

column36: A Clinical Prediction Rule for Pediatric Acute Gastroenteritis Etiology
column37: Diarrhea and vomiting are common and distressing illnesses in children. It is often difficult to identify the disease agent causing the illness, such as a specific bacteria or virus, without testing a child's stool. Testing is not recommended for all cases, because frequently it will not change how the child is treated and historically testing was challenging to perform. However, identification of the disease agent is important for some infections that require specific treatment or have public health implications. Several guidelines recommend which cases to test, but they are inconsistent and either miss important cases or recommend testing for many children who do not need it, wasting healthcare resources. A smartphone app or automated tool in electronic medical records could be developed to identify the most likely disease agent and whether testing should be done. This tool would help clinicians decide whether to test a child with diarrhea or vomiting and provide an early idea of what treatments should be either used or avoided. Using data from Alberta, I will develop the algorithm for such a tool, identifying the most likely disease agent and whether it is of high clinical or public health importance. To make sure that the algorithm I develop will work in children from different regions, I will assess its performance in data collected for three other research studies from across North America. If the algorithm works, follow-up research will test whether using the tool helps clinicians better treat children with diarrhea and vomiting.

column36: Psychotropic Medication Use and Ectopic Pregnancy
column37: In up to 2% of pregnancies, the embryo implants and begins to develop outside of the uterus - this is referred to as an ectopic pregnancy (EP). These pregnancies are extremely painful, can result in serious complications, and are responsible up to 13% of all pregnancy-related deaths. EPs occur when the fallopian tube environment changes, preventing the embryo from moving to the uterus. Since the embryo moves through the fallopian tube by muscle contraction and ciliary beating, exposures that affect either of these mechanisms could potentially result in EP. This study is the first to look at whether the risk of EP is higher for women who use SSRIs, a common type of antidepressant that can affect ciliary beating in the fallopian tube, or benzodiazepines, a common type of anti-anxiety drug that can affect muscle contractions in the fallopian tube. The rate of SSRI and benzodiazepine prescriptions are rising, but virtually nothing is known about the impact of these medications on early pregnancy outcomes such as EP. This study will use large administrative claims databases of over 2 million pregnancies and advanced methods to make considerable strides toward understanding, and potentially reducing the incidence of, EP. The findings from this research are important contributions to the fields of perinatal epidemiology and pharmacoepidemiology. Since EPs never progress past the first trimester, they are largely neglected in both fields. Given the serious outcomes associated with EPs (complications and death), this topic deserves a lot more attention. The rate of EP is high in Canada, ranging from less than 1% of reported pregnancies in Prince Edward Island, to more than 3% of reported pregnancies in the Northwest Territories. The findings from this research can contribute towards guidelines for the prescription of SSRIs and benzodiazepines for women of reproductive age in Canada.

column36: Investigating lipid homeostasis using haploid genetics in lysosomal storage disease and cancer
column37: Cells are divided into different compartments, each with a specialized function, by lipid membranes composed of fat and cholesterol molecules. These molecules, which can be thought of as membrane "building blocks", can either be made by the cell itself or taken up from the bloodstream. This, however, presents a logistical challenge: how do cells get the right amount of building blocks to the right place? Indeed, pathways that transport these molecules become defective or altered with aging, in cancer, and in inheritable genetic diseases. Often, a particular molecule will end up in the wrong place, causing serious problems. For example, in the case of Niemann-Pick disease type C1 (NPC1), an inherited and devastating disorder caused by mutations in the NPC1 gene, cholesterol abnormally builds up in a part of the cell called the lysosome - where it's not normally supposed to be - and, at the patient level, results in a wide variety of progressive symptoms. Here, I propose to understand how fats and cholesterol are transported between different parts of the cell using genome-wide screening; an analytical process that asks how each of our ~20,000 genes singularly affects processes in the cell. I will do this in normal cells, in order to understand how building blocks are normally transported, and then in cells modeling inherited diseases (such as cells lacking the NPC1 gene), so that we can understand how other genes affect unhealthy accumulations of these molecules. This work seeks to understand which building blocks are going where on a fundamental level, and has the potential to identify new pathways that, in an inherited disease or in cancer, could be targeted by a drug in order to alleviate symptoms and help patients.

column36: Harnessing spinal electrical stimulation to modulate autonomic function after spinal cord injury
column37: Autonomic dysfunction (i.e., the unconscious control of many of the body's systems) is a top health priority after spinal cord injury (SCI), and cardiovascular issues (i.e., a major autonomic function) are the #1 cause of death. Brief, but severe, decreases and increases in blood pressure are some of the most common effects of autonomic dysfunction after SCI and these issues are well-established risk factors for stroke and heart attack (both of which those with SCI suffer from at an alarming rate). The clinical options for managing swings in blood pressure are limited. Drugs are designed to either increase or decrease blood pressure, and most last hours to a full day, meaning that clinically managing blood pressure in those with SCI is extremely difficult. New technology capable of electrically stimulating the spinal cord, or "neuroprosthetics", has become a promising therapy for recovering voluntary motor function after SCI. Our pilot data shows that this same intervention may be able to restore autonomic control of blood pressure. Our study aims to: a) utilize targeted spinal electrical stimulation to acutely improve autonomic/cardiovascular function after SCI; b) employ chronic spinal electrical stimulation to neurorehabilitate autonomic control of blood pressure after SCI; and c) understand the mechanisms underlying neuroprosthetic-mediated improvements of autonomic function after SCI. This technology would provide a novel, rapid, non-pharmacologic therapy to improve the care and management of blood pressure instability after SCI, and improve the quality and quantity of life with people living with this condition.

column36: Informing Policy Through Evidence: Applying Health Technology Assessment in Cardiac Electrophysiology to Disseminate High-Value Care
column37: The past several decades have witnessed the emergence of disruptive technologies in the field of cardiac electrophysiology. New technologies have afforded clinicians exciting new opportunities to improve the quality and cardiac health of Canadians. Yet, these therapies attract scrutiny from health administrators and provincial policy-makers due to their associated upfront costs in the context of a healthcare system with finite resources. Health technology assessment is becoming ever more important in the field of electrophysiology as the rate of technologic innovation exceeds our fiscal ability to provide and deliver equitable care. In this research program, we endeavor to evaluate the economic impact of new technology within two important clinical domains in electrophysiology: (a) reduction of sudden cardiac death and (b) enhancing the detection of atrial fibrillation (AF). Project A is the economic substudy of the REFINE ICD ("Risk Estimation Following Infarction Noninvasive Evaluation-ICD efficacy") randomized trial. This substudy will assess the cost-effectiveness of extending primary prevention implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) therapy to patients with lesser degrees of left ventricular dysfunction. Project B is a proposed economic evaluation of extended (>30 day) and long-term (>1 year) electrocardiographic (ECG) monitors for AF detection compared to the traditional short-term (<48 hr) monitor in patients stroke of unknown cause. Barriers to adoption of new technologies include the possible impact on health care budgets. This portfolio of projects will formally assess the economic impact of expanding the indication for ICDs (Project A) and the impact of newer ECG monitoring technology to reveal occult atrial fibrillation to treat and prevent recurrent stroke (Project B). Results from this program will be used to inform health care professionals, administrators, and government policy-makers to advocate for implementation of high value care.

column36: CRISPR-GWAS: Leveraging genome-editing to identify disease-causing genes
column37: The discovery of disease-causing genes is crucial to understand how diseases function and to design new drug targets. Over the past decade, researchers have performed large genetic studies, looking at DNA base pair differences that commonly occur in the population-single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Researchers ask whether a SNP occurs more than expected by chance in individuals with a specific disease, and then inspect the DNA near the SNP for which genes may be under its influence. This powerful approach, known as a genome-wide association study (GWAS), has uncovered several possible disease-causing genes, but exactly which gene is influenced by a GWAS-identified SNP, and how this results in disease, remains unknown. We urgently need new methods to study these SNPs and definitively uncover human disease-causing genes. To this end, I propose to develop and apply the CRISPR-GWAS method for functional dissection of multiple GWAS findings for any disease in a massively parallel fashion. My goal is to harness pooled genome editing screens with the CRISPR technology (e.g. 100s or 1000s of DNA edits in a single experiment) to introduce GWAS-identified SNPs in a cell sample, analyze edited cells, and identify causal genes. We are currently developing computational methods for identifying which SNPs to target, and a novel CRISPR editing protein variant to use, xCas9. The outcome of this work, the systematic identification of disease-causing genes, will be important across many fields. This work will benefit genetic epidemiology by realizing the promise of GWAS to identify human disease-causing genes. This work will also benefit genome engineering, because we will develop and optimize novel CRISPR methods for precise DNA editing. Finally, this work will benefit Canadians by uncovering new drug targets for diseases, allowing researchers, clinicians, and pharmaceutical companies to develop and administer preventative care or treatment options.

column36: The Caloric Restriction and Exercise protection from Anthracycline Toxic Effects (CREATE) study
column37: Anthracyclines are chemotherapy agents that are commonly used to treat breast cancer. Although these treatments work well against the tumor, they are known to cause damage to the heart muscle cells and may also damage the blood vessels and skeletal muscles. These anthracycline side effects likely contribute to the increased risk of cardiovascular disease in women who have had breast cancer, as well as the reduced exercise capacity, quality of life and cancer-related fatigue reported in this population. In animal studies, both exercise and a reduction in calorie intake can reduce the detrimental effects of anthracyclines on the heart, and may also reduce cancer progression. Maintaining regular exercise training and a strict diet during chemotherapy treatment is challenging for many women with breast cancer due to treatment symptoms. This study will determine whether short-term application of these interventions shortly prior to the receipt of each treatment can prevent the negative effects of anthracycline treatment on the heart, aorta, and skeletal muscle, improve treatment symptoms and quality of life and reduce tumor size. Fifty-six early women with stage breast cancer who will receive anthracycline treatment will be randomly assigned to 1 of 3 groups who will: 1) perform a single 30-minute aerobic exercise session 24 hours prior to each treatment; 2) eat a diet consisting of 50% less calories for 48 hours prior to each treatment; or 3) receive usual cancer care. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) will be used to precisely measure the function of the heart, aorta, and the lower leg skeletal muscle at rest, and again during exercise to allow detection of more subtle signs of damage. These low-cost and accessible interventions may be a drug-free way to protect the heart, aorta, and skeletal muscle from anthracycline treatment, and thereby result in short and long-term improvements in cardiovascular health in women diagnosed with breast cancer.

column36: Mapping the determinants of immunotherapy response
column37: Cancer immunotherapy is an approach where the immune system is marshalled to destroy tumours like they were an infection. This involves either vaccination , or putting in large numbers of immune cells that can recognise and destroy a tumour, or the use of drugs that metaphorically lift the foot off the brakes on immune cells that are kept at bay from destroying the cancer. These approaches, collectively, have produced some remarkable advances and have had hugely significant clinical impact in previously incurable late-stage cancers such as melanoma and some of the other forms of late-stage cancer. However, only a subset of patients actually benefit from these drugs and while we know some factors that are linked to response, the picture is largely incomplete and multiple possibilities remain to be investigated. For instance, the immune cells within a tumour can either be the wrong sort, making them unable to respond, or alternatively the cancer may not contain mutations that evoke a vigorous immune response, or immune cells may only target a small proportion of cells in the tumour rather than all the cells in a tumour, or finally some cancers may have genetic changes that make them resistant. My proposal aims to investigate each of these possibilities and whether these factors can inform how we select patients for immunotherapy, or develop novel combinations that then permit a significantly larger fraction of late-stage cancer patients to derive benefit from these cutting-edge therapies.

column37: Ancestry is a risk factor and predictor of poor outcomes for cancers. In Canada, there are more than 1.3 million people identified as being of Native American heritage. This proposal will answer a critical question: why people with Native American ancestry, particularly non-smokers, tend to have higher risk of lung cancer with genetic change (mutation) in a gene called EGFR, than other populations? The approach I will use is to study patients' genome - genome inherited from the ancestors - and tumor genome - genome with mutations causing cancer - in a systematic manner. I will use advanced sequencing technologies to decipher the genetic code in the Latin American lung cancer patients who have EGFR mutations in their tumors. My mentor and I will bring together international researchers to achieve the common goal. The completion of the proposed work will discover the molecular mechanism contributing to the increased EGFR mutation risk. The findings will be highly transformative in lung cancer prevention, screening and early detection for non-smokers in Canada. My work will open a new field of studying host and tumor genome together, and inspire future cancer studies for the indigenous populations.

column36: Non-invasive mapping of pulmonary vein to left atrium electrical conduction in patients with atrial fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained abnormal heart rhythm (cardiac arrhythmia) and is characterized by a loss of coordinated electrical activity and therefore loss of coordinated contraction in the atria (the top chambers of the heart). It is estimated that one's lifetime risk of AF is 1 in 4, with projected increases in prevalence in the coming decades and therefore substantial public health implications given its associated morbidity and mortality. For patients in whom attempts to restore and maintain a normal (sinus) heart rhythm are pursued, two main options exist: antiarrhythmic medications and catheter ablation, the latter of which is more effective. Catheter ablation is generally a safe procedure, but it requires advancing catheters from peripheral blood vessels into the atria and delivering ablation lesions to specific areas to electrically disconnect the left atrium from the pulmonary veins (the latter have been shown to be important sources of triggers of this arrhythmia). When successful, the arrhythmia is no longer able to start and be sustained in the atria. However, recurrences of the arrhythmia are unfortunately not uncommon after ablation procedures. In cases when the arrhythmia recurs, physicians are currently unable to determine whether it is because the left atrium and pulmonary veins have reconnected (which is usually easily treated with high success rates) or if new triggers for the arrhythmia have arisen elsewhere in the heart (which is more difficult to treat with lower success rates). The only way to know currently is to repeat the procedure. We believe that a non-invasive alternative exists that relies on recently developed technology that merges complex analysis of cardiac electrical signals detected from the body's surface with cardiac imaging. If shown to be feasible and accurate, our proposed study could substantially impact how we counsel patients with this arrhythmia and how we perform repeat ablation procedures.

column36: Non-Invasive Epigenetic Profiling of Cell Free Fetal DNA: Markers of Common Prenatal Exposures that Shape the Risk for Neurodevelopmental Disorders and Autism Spectrum Disorders
column37: This research impacts Indigenous Peoples. Exposures to negative environmental conditions during pregnancy increase the risk for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), which include Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs). These exposures represent a public health crisis in Canada, as 1 in 10 children are diagnosed with an NDD and 1 in 66 are diagnosed with an ASD. In this research, two common exposures will be investigated using established mouse and non-human primate models with 'ASD-like' behaviours. First, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent organic pollutants (POPs). Although banned from manufacturing over 40 years ago, PCBs have accumulated in the Artic and are present at unsafe levels in the marine food chain that is critical to the Indigenous Peoples in Canada. Second, maternal obesity doubles the risk for ASDs and potentially affects the 50% of pregnant women who are obese or overweight in Canada. By using state-of-the-art genomic technologies, it will be possible to examine the unique profiles of these exposures. Specifically, DNA methylation, an epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression during development, contains a footprint of disruptions to past events that can also shape future events. The placenta is an available birth byproduct that contains a large amount of information about early brain development due to the presence of unique DNA methylation profiles that function as storage boxes for genes critical to brain development. During pregnancy, placental DNA, which is of fetal origin, is released into the maternal bloodstream as cell free fetal DNA and the placental DNA methylation profiles can consequently be examined non-invasively from maternal blood samples. This work will generate the first non-invasively obtained placental epigenetic profiles of prenatal exposures that can be translated not only to identify the risk for NDDs and ASDs but to also guide behavioural and therapeutic interventions to mitigate the negative impact.
