column37: Chronic joint and muscle pain are among the most common reasons for visiting a primary care physician. However, often patients are sent for several imaging tests, out of place specialist appointments or inappropriate surgery, and are given only pills for their pain with no rehabilitation to improve their mobility and long-term quality of life. Patients are rarely involved in deciding the best choices from among all the possible options when they receive care for joint and muscle pain, and their values and preferences are rarely considered. Shared decision making between clinician and patient is known to improve patients' knowledge about their health problems and their confidence in the treatment chosen. Exercise therapy and pain education offered by rehabilitation professionals have proven useful for short- and long-term management of joint and muscle pain, but not all physicians and patients discuss this option or are even aware of it. A better conversation about options could reduce possibly harmful treatments. We will develop PRISM, an education program for physicians, nurses, physiotherapists and occupational therapists to help them share decisions with patients about the best choices for diagnosing and treating joint and muscle pain. We will test the program on a small group of clinicians and patients to see if a larger study is feasible. We will assess clinicians' and patients' level of satisfaction with the program. We will assess patients' confidence that the options offered respect their preferences and that the chosen options improve their well-being. This project has great potential to improve communication among physicians, rehabilitation professionals and patients and increase patients' knowledge, satisfaction and confidence about high-quality alternatives to advanced imaging, pills and surgery for their joint and muscle pain. This will contribute to a better experience with our public healthcare system and improved quality of care for Canadians.

column36: Developing a nonhuman primate model of social dysfunction
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) affect 1 in 66 children in Canada, with boys four times more likely to be diagnosed than girls. There is currently no medical treatment for autism, and the cost of services provided to autistic children and adults has reached $268 billion annually in the U.S. alone. Autism, as well as other psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia and depression, is hard to study and to model in small laboratory animals. In particular, some social dysfunctions characteristic of these conditions are part of a behavioural repertoire that is uniquely shared between humans and other nonhuman primates. Unfortunately, the scientific community currently lacks a nonhuman primate model of social dysfunction, which seriously impedes our research efforts to understand the neuronal basis of autism and other disorders. In this research program, I will tackle this challenge head-on by generating a new model of social dysfunction in nonhuman primates. To do so, I will combine three existing methods for the first time in monkeys: optogenetics, wireless light delivery, and behavioural testing in naturalistic conditions. With collaborators from molecular biology, neuro-engineering, and primatology, I will combine these techniques to allow the selective, reversible deactivation of brain areas in unrestrained monkeys that are interacting socially during a variety of behavioural tasks. More specifically, I will test the necessity of a putative social brain area, the temporal-parietal junction, in generating normal social behaviour. By reversibly deactivating this brain area, I aim to reproduce some of the social deficits observed in various psychiatric conditions, generating a first primate model of social dysfunction. With this program, my goal is to provide causal evidence about the role of certain brain areas in normal and abnormal social cognition and orient efforts to develop evidence-based therapies for social dysfunction in human patient populations.

column36: Identification and characterization of a novel checkpoint regulating T cell activity
column37: The immune system plays an essential role in the elimination of disease-causing microbes and in protection from cancers. To achieve this, it uses a variety of potent defense mechanisms that effectively neutralize potential threats. However, if an immune response is dysregulated, it can cause severe damage to the body's own cells and tissues, causing autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes. One critical mechanism that regulates immune responses and prevents autoimmunity is the upregulation of inhibitory receptors on the surface of activated immune cells. These receptors act as internal 'brakes' to slow down the immune response after clearing an infection. While a few of these so-called 'checkpoints' have been extensively studied, several others may still need to be identified and characterized. We have identified one novel checkpoint molecule expressed by T lymphocytes. This molecule is highly upregulated on activated cytotoxic T cells, which is the T cell type directly responsible for eliminating virally-infected cells and killing cancerous cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this novel molecule impairs the proliferation of cells that express it, indicating that it can act as an inhibitory receptor. We propose here to further investigate this checkpoint in order to determine the molecular mechanisms through which it regulates T cell activity, and to develop therapeutic tools to modulate its activity in various diseases. The proposed studies will expand our understanding of immune regulation and will provide valuable targets for the modulation of immune responses in multiple diseases. Specifically, this same checkpoint molecule may be differently targeted to either suppress inflammation in autoimmune patients, or to boost inflammation in cancer patients in order to enhance immune-mediated killing of tumor cells.

column36: The role of 14-3-3zeta-mediated RNA splicing during the development of obesity
column37: Obesity is a well-known risk factor for chronic diseases, including type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Despite intensive research, there are no treatments that effectively promote weight loss for long periods of time. At the center of obesity is the fat cell. Surprisingly, no treatments specifically target fat cells, which need a complicated roadmap of signals to grow. One protein that provides direction for these signals is 14-3-3zeta, which we previously found to have important roles in the growth of fat cells. Depending on conditions, proteins that interact with 14-3-3zeta can change. For example, during fat cell growth, a large number of proteins that interact with 14-3-3zeta are those that influence RNA splicing. When RNA splicing is inhibited, fat cells do not develop properly. Recently, high-fat diet-induced obesity has been found to alter RNA splicing in fat cells. This raises the question of whether obesity causes the aberrant recruitment of 14-3-3zeta-associated RNA splicing factors, thereby promoting the development of obesity. Therefore, in my post-doctoral fellowship, I wish to undertake new studies aimed at testing whether altered RNA splicing promotes the development of obesity and understand in great detail how 14-3-3zeta controls this process in a fat cell. Results from these studies will determine whether 14-3-3zeta can influence the development of obesity, and they may lead to new ways to prevent or treat obesity, a disease that affects people of all ages and throughout the world.

column36: A new ultra-high resolution 3D digital atlas of the human brain connectome derived from the 3D-PLI dataset and its application to the validation of diffusion MRI fiber tracking
column37: Research on human brain connections use three dimensional (3D) images of the brain obtained through magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A brain connections atlas is an essential tool in that research field. It is composed of a set of digital maps which describe brain anatomy and identify the connections between functional regions of the brain. We propose to build an ultra-high resolution atlas of the human brain connections. Recently, the 3D-PLI dataset as been produced in Germany. It is a 3D digital image of the human brain fibers with unparalleled 3D resolution. It reveals 3D details that are 2.5 million times smaller than a regular MRI volume. However, at present it is only an image, not an atlas. For it to be an atlas, we have to identify in 3D every fiber connection and group them into family of fibers towards a functional region of the brain (such as "visual cortex" or "memory area"). This will allow the 3D-PLI dataset to be used in a variety of brain research and clinical applications and also to be used for teaching purposes such as training medical students in the 3D brain connectivity. For research, the ultra-high resolution of the atlas will be used as a template to interpret and validate the lower-resolution MRI images that we use to identify the fiber connections in the brain. This will help to understand brain development in children and the neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease. We will also use the atlas as a guide to the study of normal brain functions, such as sensation (vision, hearing), memory and language. For clinical applications, the new atlas will be most useful as a guide to neurosurgeons who always make use of brain atlases to plan their surgery. This is typically done using 2D atlas pages in a book, thus restricting the angle of view. The 3D-PLI digital atlas will allow them to view from any angle the relevant brain connections between areas, making it much easier to get the information they need for surgical planning.

column36: Identifying co-operating genetic mutations within large chromosomal deletions associated with triple negative breast cancer
column37: Cancer is associated with an accumulation of alterations in genes that confer the ability of cancer cells to grow uncontrollably. These alterations can contribute to increased deleterious function or loss of function of genes that normally regulate cell growth. Genes in our cells are organized on chromosomes which duplicate every time a cell divides. We have 23 pairs of chromosomes in every cell and genes are highly organized along their length. In addition to alterations in single genes, it is now recognized that large deletions on chromosomes comprising multiple genes are also important events in cancer. Since these changes are repeatedly found in certain cancers it is now considered that multiple genes in these deleted regions may collaborate to promote cancer. Until recently this remained poorly understood because of limitations in technology. My project will focus on a common deletion on chromosome 4, which contains 211 genes that are frequently lost in a subset of breast cancer called triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). This subset has no targeted therapies and has the worst survival. The aim of my project is to use recently developed technology to study which combinations of genes in large chromosomal deletions are important in cancer. Such a systematic identification of genetic interactions within large chromosomal deletions is expected to reveal genetic events that modulate TNBC, enhance our understanding of the disease and offer possible avenues for personalized interventions to individuals diagnosed with TNBC.

column36: Uncovering the role of a core Foxp3+ Regulatory T cell gene in establishing peripheral tolerance and preventing autoimmunity
column37: Our bodies rely on a network of cells and tissues, collectively termed the immune system, to protect us from disease. The process by which the immune system attacks one's own healthy cells and tissues is known as autoimmunity. Regulatory T cells are a subset of immune cells whose primary function is preventing the development of autoimmune diseases through maintaining a balanced immune response (thus "regulating" the immune system). However, regulatory T cells themselves can become the villain if they inappropriately subdue the immune response against diseases such as cancer. Hence, effective treatment for autoimmune diseases and cancer requires a fundamental understanding of the elements that are important for regulatory T cell development and function. Here, I propose to investigate Izumo1r, a gene which is highly expressed in regulatory T cells but for which a function in the immune system has not yet been defined. Studies so far show Izumo1r to be vital for fertilization as its absence results in female infertility. Our preliminary work suggests that Izumo1r may also play an essential but underappreciated role in regulating the immune system. I will use a multidisciplinary approach to build on these findings and illuminate the function of Izumor1 in regulatory T cells during health and disease. In particular, I will translate the findings about the basic functions of the receptor using state of the art models of autoimmune disease. I believe our findings will be pertinent to the development of better therapeutic options for cancer and autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatic arthritis, which will in combination burden more than 50% of Canadians at some point during their life.

column36: Architecture and Regulation of the PI3KC2B Lipid Kinase Complex for Nutrient Signaling at the Lysosome
column37: Cells must coordinate many messages from outside and within the cell to determine their actions. When the cell environment has abundant nutrients, the cell receives messages that lead to cell growth. If the cell detects low nutrients, the messages will lead to a survival state that relies upon the recycling of large molecules into their building blocks. The detection of low nutrients and the breaking down of molecules is coordinated by the cell "trash bin", the lysosome. Scientists at the proposed host institution recently identified that a protein called PI3KC2B moves to the lysosome when nutrients are low and produces a lipid molecule [PI(3,4)P2] that switches off a multi-protein complex, mTORC1. How PI3KC2B function and localisation is controlled is currently not well understood. Previous data, along with unpublished data from the proposed host, have revealed that PI3KC2B interacts with mTORC1 and the lysosome resident protein Rab7. To better understand how PI3KC2B and mTORC1 or Rab7 work in concert to control lysosome function, the proposed research will map the interfaces of the complexes formed between these proteins using the 2017 Nobel Prize winning technique cryo electron microscopy in combination with cellular imaging to investigate how interrupting these relationships in cells affects lysosome function. Overall, the knowledge we gain from this research will provide novel insight into lysosome function in the cell and how the relationships between PI3KC2B and other proteins control this function. Improper function of the lysosome leads to many human diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and neurological dysfunction, so understanding how the lysosome coordinates these functions is crucial to identifying new therapies for these diseases.

column36: Fishing for Food Security: Weathering Climate Change Impacts on Health in Coastal Indigenous Communities
column37: This research involves Indigenous Peoples. Traditional foods (TFs) confer significant, dietary/nutritional, health, cultural, and economic benefits to Indigenous Peoples across Canada. In recent decades, however, TFs have been increasingly replaced by store bought foods of high energy density but low nutritional quality - including ultra-processed foods, high in sodium, refined carbohydrates, and trans-fatty acids. A major driver of this transition, is the decreased availability and safety of TF related to environmental and ecological factors. Already, climate change is altering the abundance of marine species, while depleted fish stocks and current fishery policies are concomitantly constraining Indigenous Peoples' access to TF seafood, thereby elevating the risk of food insecurity, poor nutrition and chronic diet-related diseases in coastal seafood-dependent communities. While direct links between environmental change, ecosystem status, food security, and human nutrition remain elusive (and particularly little is known about the dynamics of these relationships under climate change) there is a strong scientific rationale and public policy imperative to further knowledge in this area. This project comprises two participatory case studies involving coastal Indigenous Peoples in geographically, culturally, and socio-politically, distinct contexts across Canada (Coastal First Nations in British Columbia and Qikiqtani Inuit) to examine the human health implication of marine ecosystem change. Trough the development of a participatory EcoHealth modelling approach, the study will link marine ecosystem models with local knowledge, as well as human diet and nutrition information to increase understanding of current and future community vulnerabilities to climate change and co-develop culturally-favoured intersectional solutions to support food security, subsistence fisheries, public health and cultural wellness.

column36: IMPACTT: A Microbiome Research Core based on Integrated Microbiome Platforms for Advancing Causation Testing and Translation
column37: Our body surfaces, including the gut, mouth, skin, and lung are colonized by trillions of microbes. This colonization is a dynamic process that begins primarily at birth and is heavily influenced by environmental factors, including mode of birth, diet, antibiotic use, hygiene and health status. Alterations in microbial communities are associated with a number of diseases, such as allergy, autoimmunity, autism, and obesity. However, association is not the same as causation. Changes in the microbiome could lead to disease, occur as a result of disease, or both. Therefore, researchers must now clearly define microbial function and identify the molecular mechanisms by which the microbiome interacts with the human host to influence health. Such functional studies will facilitate the design of new approaches for disease treatment and prevention. We will establish a Microbiome Research Core based on Integrated Microbiome Platforms for Advancing Causation Testing and Translation (IMPACTT). IMPACTT is a multi-centre collaboration to provide expertise and sharing of resources to foster and standardize microbiome research across Canada. The new gnotobiotic facility at the University of Calgary will form the basis for the study of complex functional interactions between the microbiome and the host. It will allow for precise control of all colonizing microbes to identify mechanistic links between the microbiome and the host. IMPACTT will also facilitate microbiome studies in human cohorts by providing expertise for study design, sample collection, and computational analysis. IMPACTT will establish and maintain a large repository of microbes, with genetic and metabolic information, available to microbiome researchers across Canada to enable functional microbiome studies. Finally, we will also develop a platform to discover links between microbial genes, proteins, and metabolism with microbial function, and then further link this to human health and disease.

column37: Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is among the most common life-limiting genetic disorders in Canada, with more than 4000 people living with this disease. The primary cause of death in CF is respiratory failure from chronic infection of the lung. In CF care, it is routine practice to monitor the sputum for bacterial infection. The most common bacterium isolated in the airways of children with CF is methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Antibiotics are a mainstay of treatment in CF, and are of clear benefit when people with CF have increased pulmonary symptoms (cough, increased sputum etc). However, there is controversy in the CF community over whether we should treat people who are clinically well, but have bacteria in their airways. Part of this uncertainty has arisen from the fact that traditional pulmonary function measures are often not sensitive enough to detect subtle improvements in lung function following treatment in mild CF lung disease. The forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) is the most commonly used pulmonary function test in CF but is a poor marker of early lung disease. The lung clearance index (LCI) is a new marker that has been shown to be a more sensitive measure of early CF lung disease. In this study, we will use LCI and other outcomes measures to assess the effect of antibiotic treatment in clinically stable children with CF who have MSSA growing in their sputum. Question: Does treatment with three weeks of oral cephalexin (a common antibiotic used in CF care) result in an improvement in the lung function of children with CF who are symptomatically stable, but have MSSA growing in their sputum? Study Design: This is a randomised trial, comparing placebo to cephalexin. Children will receive a blinded medication for 3 weeks. We will use LCI, FEV1 and clinical symptoms to measure response. Hypothesis: Compared to placebo, a 3 week course of cepahalexin will result in an improvement in lung function in this population.

column37: Heart attack (blockage of heart blood vessels) is a major health issue in Canada. Irregular heartbeats (cardiac arrhythmias) are common in patients who have survived a heart attack and are often the reason for sudden death in these patients. Available therapies for treating or preventing lethal irregular heartbeats in these patients are not satisfactory, because we do not know exactly how these irregular heartbeats happen after the heart attack. The objective of this project is to study the mechanisms underlying irregular heartbeats after heart attack, and develop new strategies for better treatment of patients. Recent work in my laboratory has demonstrated, for the first time, that Tbx3, a factor that is normally only expressed in the pacemaker tissues of the heart, is also expressed in the heart chambers (which pump blood) after a heart attack. We will test the idea that expression of Tbx3 in chamber muscle cells will bring pacemaker properties and cause irregular heartbeats in patients that had heart attacks before. We will use laboratory animals (rats and mice) and ligate a major blood vessel in their hearts to mimic the blockage of heart blood vessels and heart attack in patients. We will then examine if Tbx3 level is increased in the chamber muscles in these animal hearts at different timepoints after the artery ligation. Next, we will isolate single muscle cells from these animal hearts, and use a special technique (patch-clamp technique) to examine these cells for any evidence of pacemaker activity (i.e. cells beat by themselves). Finally, we will use approaches to inhibit the expression of Tbx3 in animal heart after artery ligation, and we expect to see protection of the hearts from developing irregular heartbeats. This project is expected to elucidate novel mechanisms underlying irregular heartbeats and guide the designing of new therapies to improve quality of life and reduce premature deaths, as well as reduce healthcare cost.

column37: Every year in Canada, over 100,000 patients develop severe breathing difficulties and require life support from a breathing machine ('mechanical ventilator'). By pumping oxygen into the lungs, the ventilator can save their life. However, the ventilator can cause damage by overstretching the lungs. Also, if the ventilator does the full work of breathing and patients are not using their diaphragm (the main breathing muscle), the diaphragm rapidly becomes thin and weak. Diaphragm weakness makes it harder for patients to breathe without ventilator support and significantly delays their recovery. This delay increases the chances of complications, death, and long-term disability. Certain methods of ventilation can protect the lungs from damage during ventilation, but no methods of ventilation have ever been developed to protect the diaphragm from damage during ventilation. We are developing a new strategy for setting the ventilator to protect both the lungs and the diaphragm by ensuring that patients are actively breathing at the right effort level (not too high and not too low). We will test this new strategy in patients who are on a mechanical ventilator. First, we will determine whether it is possible to protect the lung and the diaphragm at the same time during ventilation. Second, we will test whether applying higher pressures with the ventilator protects the lungs and the diaphragm more effectively than applying lower pressures. Third, we will determine whether we can predict the effect of changing ventilator settings on the lung and the diaphragm. This is the first-ever attempt to protect the diaphragm during ventilation. Our goal is to enable patients to recover faster and more easily after severe breathing difficulties so that they avoid long-term disability due to their illness and enjoy an improved quality of life. We aim to develop a computerized artificial intelligence system to improve ventilation and deliver safe ventilation automatically.

column36: Characterization of Tumor Proteases that Reduce Reovirus Oncolysis
column37: Reovirus is an oncolytic (cancer-killing) virus undergoing clinical trials against various cancers. However, to be an effective treatment, reovirus must overcome unique factors found in the tumor microenvironment (TME). The TME is enriched in a class of enzymes known as metalloproteases (MPs). We found that treating reovirus with MPs extracted from mouse tumors (tumor extract; TE) resulted in a loss of infectivity, suggesting that the TME contains factors which inactivate reovirus. We hypothesize that protease levels in specific cancer patients will alter the efficacy of reovirus therapy. If we can determine the precise proteases that inactivate reovirus, and develop protease resistant reovirus variants, we hope we can advance personalized treatments with reovirus. To better understand and overcome TME proteases which inactivate reovirus, we propose the following objectives: (1) The MPs will be purified from the TE, and analyzed by mass spectrometry, allowing us to determine the likely identity of the MP. Purified proteases of the best candidates will be purchased and assessed for their effect on reovirus. (2) We've found that human cancer cell lines also secrete proteases that inactivate reovirus. We will assess the prevalence of the MP identified in aim 1 in a variety of cancer cell lines to determine if the MP is cancer type specific. (3) The specific site on reovirus which MPs target will be determined using N-terminal sequencing. This will allow us to generate viruses with mutations in the target site, which I predict will be resistant to MP inactivation. (4) These mutant viruses from aim 3 will be tested for oncolytic activity relative to wild-type reovirus. I hope my findings help improve the potency of reovirus as an oncolytic therapy.

column37: This research involves Indigenous Peoples. Emerging infectious diseases represent an increasing threat to wildlife and to the people who depend on wildlife for food security, economic opportunity, and cultural practices. However, the role of disease in wildlife declines can be difficult to identify because health surveillance of wildlife populations is challenging and the impact of disease can be overshadowed by the cumulative effects of multiple stressors. In the Arctic, climate change is facilitating the emergence and spread of novel parasites while putting stress on wildlife that are adapted to a cold climate. Wildlife health surveillance in such a vast and remote area is a huge challenge, making timely detection of disease and population impacts an impossibility for scientists. However, a wealth of knowledge exists in local communities that are intimately connected to the land through a long and continuous history of subsistence use of natural resources. Connecting with local and Indigenous knowledge on wildlife health can address data gaps, while simultaneously increasing local relevance of scientific research and promoting co-management of natural resources. This project will elucidate how disease may act synergistically with other stressors to contribute to wildlife declines by developing and integrating ecological models with scientific, local, and Indigenous knowledge on wildlife health and abundance. I will focus on caribou, which are a highly valued species in Canada, particularly for Indigenous cultures, but have experienced widespread declines in recent decades. The outcomes will provide new theory in wildlife disease ecology, address the knowledge gap around how health interacts with other stressors to influence caribou population dynamics, and guide effective conservation and co-management efforts for caribou.

Since waiting this long to treat infections poses a serious health risk, clinicians must prescribe drugs using their best guess as to which pathogen is causing an infection. This circumstance encourages the overuse of antibiotics-up to half of all antibiotic prescriptions have no benefit. Fortunately, we have found a promising solution. Our MicroUDxTM system can detect bacteria in urine and find the best antibiotic in under 4 hours. This is fast enough that clinicians can wait for laboratory test results to help guide their prescriptions. The best antibiotic therapy can then be called in to the patient's pharmacy the same day. This solution will significantly reduce the inappropriate use of antibiotics and will extend the service life of our existing drugs. In addition, the MicroUDxTM will save thousands of people who are currently being given the wrong drug. These patients are at a much higher risk of developing urosepsis, a life-threatening condition that can occur if infections are not treated quickly. Thus, the MicroUDxTM is an exciting step forward because it fights antibiotic resistant organisms and prevents people from dying as a result of slow diagnostics. This grant provides the critical support for transitioning this diagnostic technology into the real world.

column37: The emerging problem of the resistance of microorganisms to drugs formerly effective in treating various human diseases is spreading globally and threatens many of the gains of modern medicine. In humans, this occurs most often when individuals suffering from viral infections with similar symptoms to those of analogous bacterial illnesses are mis-prescribed antibiotics. column36: How do human cells regulate their death? Uncovering the molecular basis of apoptotic regulation
column37: Human cells grow and proliferate under conditions of limited space and resources, and therefore must control their population to preserve balance. This is achieved through 'apoptosis', or programmed cell death. Such a powerful process requires exquisite control to prevent too much or too little cell death, as the dysregulation of apoptosis contributes to many human diseases. For instance, cancerous cells often proliferate uncontrollably and evade death by preventing apoptosis, rendering themselves resistant to chemotherapy. In neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's or dementia, the massive and uncontrollable loss of neurons through apoptosis eventually leads to death. Canadian health care costs associated with cancer and Alzheimer's sum to nearly $30 billion, but the complex molecular origins of these diseases remain unclear, hindering the development of new therapies. Apoptosis is carried out by proteins, nanometer-sized molecules that perform essential biological roles, often by interacting with other proteins. To understand apoptosis and its role in disease, proteins' three-dimensional structures and their dynamic web of interactions must be studied at the molecular level. Here, I aim to determine the molecular events that regulate apoptosis in humans. I will use cutting-edge biophysical methods to address two questions: how does the protein caspase-9 become activated to promote apoptosis, and how do the Hsp70 and Hsp90 proteins inhibit caspase-9 activation to prevent apoptosis? Both processes occur through presently unknown mechanisms, and yet significantly impact human health. For instance, caspase-9 activity has been used in immunotherapy, a promising new treatment for cancer, and many cancers exploit Hsp70 and Hsp90 to shut down apoptosis and evade death. Results from my research will provide critical insight that can be used to design drugs to disrupt or activate apoptosis as potential therapies for human diseases.

column36: Imaging the behavior of peritoneal macrophages under homeostasis and in liver metastasis.
column37: It is well known that an immune cell called the monocyte in blood can enter into the tumor become a macrophage and help the tumor grow. We also think that to target these cells we may either need novel drugs or at the very least different delivery of existing drugs. We will test whether placing immunotherapies into the blood versus into the cavity versus into both sites will derive different results. With huge attention being placed on immunotherapy and on preventing macrophages from entering into tumors from the blood stream, it would be a shame if poor outcomes were simply due to not delivering the drug in an optimal way. We believe that our research has the potential to improve success rates for immunotherapy by considering the peritoneal cavity as a portal of entry into tumors.

column36: Clocks for a healthy brain: dissecting the role of the pluripotency factor SOX2 in biological timekeeping
column37: We live in a 24-hour world where our daily activities are organized around the day-night cycle. Many of us wake up, eat our meals, go to work, and sleep at approximately the same time every day. Our internal organs behave in a similar fashion, changing their activities over the course of 24 hours. These bodily rhythms, or so-called "circadian" rhythms, are the result of an internal clock in the brain, called the SCN (short for suprachiasmatic nucleus), that keeps track of the time of day and communicates that information to the rest of the body. However, many aspects of modern life are at odds with the workings of this internal timekeeping system. Rotating shift work, traveling across time zones and even "sleeping in" on weekends can lead to misalignment between our internal clock and the outside world. A misaligned or perturbed clock can have serious health consequences, such as increasing the risk of becoming overweight or developing diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, breast and prostate cancer, major depression, and Alzheimer's disease. Another major risk factor for many of these pathologies is aging, which is associated with a worsening in the performance of the SCN. By restoring or bolstering its performance and improving circadian rhythms, we may be able to treat or ameliorate various diseases, promote healthy aging, and enhance physical and mental health. The objective of this proposal is to identify and understand the genes responsible for the optimal performance of the SCN. We have found a gene called SOX2 that appears to be necessary for maintaining normal circadian rhythms. We will use various approaches, including mouse models where the Sox2 gene is "knocked out" in the SCN, to determine its roles in circadian timekeeping. Through our work, we will acquire new insights into how the SCN is regulated, knowledge that may be leveraged for the development of therapeutic and health-promoting strategies that target our internal clock.

column36: Defining the immune dysfunction in childhood nephrotic syndrome: Toward therapeutic reversal without glucocorticoids
column37: Nephrotic syndrome is the most common kidney disease among children. Affected children have massive leakage of protein into the urine and as a consequence, develop body swelling (edema). Most children respond to treatment with steroids, however many of them require repeated courses for frequent relapses of the disease. Long-term use of steroids causes many side effects including obesity, growth retardation, hypertension, cataracts, poor bone health, and cosmetic effects. Minimizing the use of steroids has been identified as the number one priority of the patients and families. A non-steroid drug, rituximab, is now known to be effective in the treatment of nephrotic syndrome, but it is entirely unclear how it works. In this study, we will investigate the mechanisms by which rituximab alleviates the symptoms associated with nephrotic syndrome, allowing patients to go into remission. Blood collected from affected patients when their disease is active, and after successfully treated with steroid or rituximab, will be analyzed using the state-of-the-art technique called immunophenotyping. One of the investigators in the research team, Dr. Piccirillo, is the leading researcher of this technology in Canada. The analyses will inform us which cells in the blood are active before treatment, and become inactive after treatment. We will also find out if steroids and rituximab have different effects on blood cells. With this approach, we are likely to uncover how this common pediatric disease occurs - it has been a mystery for over five decades. Furthermore, understanding how rituximab works in nephrotic syndrome will enable us to identify patients who are most likely to respond to rituximab thus avoiding steroids. Finally, if the culprit cells are known, we can develop new drugs specifically targeting these cells. The hope is that we will not need to use steroids at all in the future.

column36: Social Ecological Approaches to Research on Care for HIV (S.E.A.R.C.H.): A pilot study of an ecological momentary intervention to improve antiretroviral therapy adherence with gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men in Jamaica
column37: THE ISSUE: Globally gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) are overrepresented in new HIV infections. HIV prevalence among gbMSM in Jamaica is 33%-the Caribbean's highest. Our 2013-16 CIHR-funded research identified social and health disparities associated with HIV infection among gbMSM in Jamaica. Although 95% of people living with HIV live in low and middle-income countries (LMIC), we know little about strategies to increase antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence with HIV-positive gbMSM in LMIC. Suboptimal ART adherence may contribute to virological failure and death. OUR IDEA: Ecological Momentary Assessments (EMA) capture human experiences and health practices in 'normal routines' and contexts using texts on mobile phones. Participants respond in real time. Ecological momentary interventions combine EMA's real-time assessment of contextual factors with care provision in one's natural environment. We will develop and pilot-test the 'Social Ecological Approaches to Research on Care for HIV' (SEARCH) EMI to improve ART adherence. SEARCH has 2 components: daily EMA+ peer navigation. While used to manage various health conditions (e.g. diabetes), EMI's utility for ART adherence is understudied. OUR APPROACH: Our project involves: Phase 1: qualitative work with HIV-positive gbMSM in Jamaica to develop SEARCH components; Phase 2: randomized pilot study with 150 HIV-positive gbMSM in Kingston, Ocho Rios and Montego Bay, Jamaica. Arm 1: SEARCH (EMA+peer navigation), Arm 2: standard of care. Phase 3: Qualitative interviews, workshops, and mixed-methods analyses to assess SEARCH's feasibility and acceptability to inform scale-up. IMPACT: We build on our successful CIHR-funded research that highlighted social/health disparities with HIV-positive gbMSM in Jamaica to develop and pilot test SEARCH, an innovative EMI to improve ART adherence. Findings will highlight the feasibility and promise of EMI for ART adherence with gbMSM in Jamaica and LMIC contexts.

column36: Substance Use and Addiction Services Engagement among Vulnerable Youth: An Ethno-Epidemiological Study
column37: Canadian youth who use drugs are vulnerable to severe health and social harms. Recently, the emergence of fentanyl and other opioid analogues in the illicit drug market has led to dramatic increases in overdoses across Canada. In British Columbia, young people ages 20 to 29 comprise approximately one quarter of overdose fatalities, while youth ages 15 to 24 represent the fastest growing age demographic for hospitalizations due to opioid poisoning in Canada. Street-involved youth (defined as those temporarily or absolutely without housing or accessing street youth services) are particularly vulnerable to overdose and other drug-related harms. The overdose crisis underscores the urgent need to intervene early to address substance use among vulnerable youth ages 14 to 18. As a setting that has been badly affected by the opioid overdose crisis, efforts are currently underway in Greater Vancouver to improve youth's engagement with addiction services, including harm reduction services, residential detoxification and treatment, psychosocial programs, and opioid agonist treatment. However, given the well documented systemic gaps and barriers to addiction services experienced by Canadian youth, and in particular street-involved youth, many important questions remain regarding how to effectively implement, adapt, and scale up services in this and other affected settings. In particular, we lack an understanding of how to best integrate services across the multiple systems that vulnerable youth interface with, including pediatric care, mental health care, foster care, criminal justice and frontline service (e.g., shelter) systems. The proposed ethno-epidemiological study will integrate qualitative methods, including longitudinal interviewing and ethnographic fieldwork, with quantitative behavioral and clinical data to delineate the individual, social, structural and environmental contexts that influence the effectiveness of different youth-focused addiction services, and to identify how they can best be adapted to meet the unique needs of youth as they move across multiple systems of care and supervision.

column36: The Montreal Immune-Related Adverse Events (MIRAE) Study
column37: The pillars of cancer treatment have traditionally consisted of surgery, chemotherapy and radiation therapy. A new generation of treatments, immune checkpoint inhibitors, or more commonly known as immunotherapy, are revolutionizing the treatment of cancer. Humans all have tumor cells in their bodies. However, the reason we do not develop cancer is because of the ongoing work of our immune system to seek and destroy tumor cells. Over time, some tumor cells develop new tools to escape destruction and send signals to our immune system declaring themselves as normal. Immunotherapy works by modulating these signals and stimulates the immune system to look for and destroy cancer cells. These treatments are quickly becoming the standard of care for many cancers, and many terminally ill cancer patients, once considered incurable, have achieved long-term remission with these treatments. The major side effect of an immune system boosted with immunotherapy is an attack on healthy organs. At any time, during or after treatment, critical organs such as the heart, lungs, colon, liver, and skin may be affected when activated immune cells mistakenly seek them as targets. Many patients need to stop treatment due to these toxicities, and up to 1 patient out of 50 will die of the toxicity of these life-saving treatments. The purpose of our research project is to study why some patients develop these reactions while others don't. Using cutting-edge research technologies, we are looking at developing tools to predict which patients will have these toxicities and to understand what biological factors driving these reactions. Our research will result in a better understanding of our immune systems and will also result in a safer and more targeted delivery of immunotherapies that represent the future of cancer care.

column36: Co-developing innovative approaches with Indigenous partners to foster coastal resilience, food security and sustainable marine harvests
column37: Country food significant, dietary/nutritional, health, cultural, and economic benefits to the Inuit in the Canadian Arctic. The availability of country food is important for their food security. Climate change is the most significant health equity challenges of the century and is already impacting access to country foods and contributing hazards and risks on ice. While the potential impacts of climate change on northern food security has been highlighted for several years, limited research has sought to explicitly link environmental change with nutrition implications for Inuit. Working with the community of Qikiqtarjuaq, this project aims to co-construct innovative methodologies and adaptation strategies to address the impact of climate change on food security in the Canadian North. The main research questions are: O1. How can local oceanographic and marine ecosystem and diet/health data be integrated to address key questions regarding climate change and food security? O2. What strategies can be used to proactively respond to climate change to support food security at different levels? This two-year project will deliver feasibility adaptation plans for the community of Qikiqtarjuaq and models and frameworks that can be used by a follow-up Research Team to translate the knowledge to other Inuit regions and communities.

column36: Food Security and Resiliency in the Face of Climate Change: From Assessment to Improvement in the Sahtu Region, NWT.
column37: In response to communities' concerns about the health risks from contaminants in country foods, a human biomonitoring project was implemented in the Sahtu Region, NWT (2016-2018). In addition to the potentially elevated contaminant exposure, Northern Indigenous groups face higher rates of food insecurity and inadequate nutrient intakes. The aim of the proposed project is to assess food security and to increase resilience to climate change in the region. To do so, the project will be divided in two components. First, nutrients will be measured in blood samples already collected from participants and then compared to deficiency thresholds. These results will be used to identify the most vulnerable groups in the region and investigate the role of country foods in preventing food insecurity. Each participant will receive his or her individual results. In parallel, the knowledge users will document the food security issue in the community using a semi-quantitative survey. Secondly, the conclusions will be shared with the community delegates during a five-day workshop at University of Waterloo with the involvement of community and academic researchers and knowledge users in food security, food systems and nutrition. A two-way knowledge exchange will be conducted to strengthen academic and indigenous capacity building for the benefit of all. The community researchers/knowledge users will then have the resources to share these findings with the communities and engage community members in brainstorming on food security challenges and opportunities. An approach of de-stigmatisation and openness will be adopted, while collecting key ideas on potential local and regional mitigation strategies related to climate change. This project will support discussions within the community about the challenges to food security, climate change, and possibilities to increase resilience in the region.

column36: Brain Development and Reading Acquisition in Preschool Children
column37: Brain development supports numerous cognitive and behavioural functions, including language and reading. Early childhood (2-7 years) is a critical period for the acquisition of language and reading skills, yet we currently have a limited understanding of brain development in this age range due to practical difficulties associated with MRI scanning. Research that has been undertaken in children just beginning to read (~6-7 years) suggests that structural brain abnormalities may precede, rather than result from, reading difficulties. It has not yet been explored whether these abnormalities exist before reading begins. The main aim of the proposed research project is to explore brain development during the preschool years, and how it is related to pre-reading skills and early reading abilities. This project will be using one of the largest longitudinal neuroimaging dataset in this age range, which will allow us to explore grey and white matter brain development, and the relationship between brain development and pre-reading performance. A better understanding of healthy brain development, and the relationship with pre-reading, will assist research into reading disorders to enable the development of targeted early interventions.

column36: Understanding the impacts of climate change on Nunavik Inuit Food security: An Inuit-led initiative to ensure that the influences of climate change on traditional foods are considered in efforts to address the food security of Nunavik Inuit.
column37: Nunavik is situated in the southernmost portions of Inuit Nunangat and is therefore at the forefront of climate induced impacts on food security. The harvest of wildlife for subsistence purposes (i.e. country food) remains a significant contributor to food security in the region. Yet, although significant effort has been deployed to better understand food security in Nunavik, the influences of climate change on traditional foods have been understudied and even less work has been done towards determining how these can be considered when developing a comprehensive approach to addressing food security. Moreover, the recent peak in research and policy related to climate change, food security, or both, has left Nunavik Inuit struggling to remain abreast of the various research programs, policy initiatives and other actions that are taking place within their own communities. With an aim of building healthy and resilient communities, the Makivik Corporation will work closely with Inuit, other regional organizations and with the scientific community to build an overall picture of the influences that climate change exerts on Inuit food security in Nunavik. This approach will ensure that research is aligned with, and complimentary to, ongoing regional initiatives aimed at developing a comprehensive and practical approach to address food security within Nunavik Inuit communities.

column36: Caribou Decline and Food Security for the Tlicho People of the Northwest Territories
column37: Climate change and industrial development has disrupted the migratory and reproductive habits of the barren-ground caribou of the Northwest Territories. In an effort to protect the remaining caribou, a ban on caribou hunting was instituted in 2010 which had a myriad of consequences beyond its well-intentioned goal of protecting the species. The Tlicho people, who have long depended on the caribou as a primary and culturally-significant food source, have been deeply impacted by this shift. This project seeks to characterize the impact that the loss of caribou has had on Tlicho food security, mental wellness, and community resiliency in the face of major climatic and legislative changes. Within the community-based research framework, a combination of conversational qualitative methods and other indigenous research paradigms will be employed throughout the course of this work, and guidance from Tlicho Elders will be sought at all phases of research, from initial conception, through to execution and eventual data dissemination. We anticipate that this work will build capacity among Tlicho youth and scholars, and will form the foundation for future evidence-based policy recommendations.

column36: Shifting the Paradigm in Home Physiotherapy: Implementation and Implications of Adherence Monitoring with Artificial Intelligence
column37: Physical therapy is essential for the successful rehabilitation of common shoulder injuries and following shoulder surgery. Patients may receive some training and supervision for shoulder physiotherapy through private pay or private insurance, but they are typically responsible for performing most of their physiotherapy independently at home. It is unknown how often patients perform their home exercises and if these exercises are done correctly without supervision. There are no established tools for measuring this. It is therefore unclear if the full benefit of shoulder physiotherapy treatments are being realized. Our team has recently developed a Smart Physiotherapy Activity Recognition System (SPARS) for tracking home shoulder physiotherapy exercises using sensors in a commercial smart watch and artificial intelligence (AI). SPARS was successful in identifying shoulder exercises in healthy adults in the laboratory setting. Further inquiry is required to establish the clinical effectiveness of this technology and investigate the potential individual and societal impacts of its use. The proposed research will 1) Further develop and validate the SPARS technology for evaluating adherence to shoulder exercise participation and technique in a clinical patient population with rotator cuff pathology, advancing the state-of-the-art in rehabilitation engineering AI. 2) Use SPARS to quantify the rate of home physiotherapy adherence, determine the effects of adherence on recovery, and identify barriers to successful adherence; leading to novel actionable insights on current treatment protocols. 3) Develop and pilot test an ethically conscious SPARS-powered rehabilitation program that individualizes patient-care based on their adherence. A careful examination of the ethical and policy challenges related to surveillance for self-managed medical treatments will help ensure SPARS and related technologies be deployed conscientiously and to a benefit of patients and society.

column36: Refining processes to maximize the provision of donor human milk rich in nutrients and bioactive components: An integrated multidisciplinary approach at a human milk bank serving critically-ill neonates.
column37: Infant formulas attempt to mimic the nutrient composition of human breastmilk, but cannot provide its bioactive factors. These factors enhance immune function, and optimum growth and development of the newborn. Human milk is also the best health promoter for preterm babies (approximately 10 % of the 350,000 children born annually in Canada), who are often ill and may require extended hospitalization. However, preterm babies may be separated from their mothers while hospitalized, or mothers may not be able to produce an adequate milk supply due to their own illness and/or stress associated with preterm delivery. The Rogers Hixon Ontario Human Milk Bank (OMB) dispenses, by prescription, milk from approved donor mothers to these ill newborns. At the OMB, donated milk undergoes thermal pasteurization (heating at 62.5C for 30 min). This heat treatment has two fundamental problems: 1) nutrient composition is affected and human milk bioactive molecules may be inactivated, and 2) Bacillus cereus, a spore-forming bacterium, can resist pasteurization. Because current methods cannot differentiate between pathogenic and non-pathogenic B. cereus, the OMB must discard 15-30% of their milk supply. We have formed a multidisciplinary team that will tackle these two problems simultaneously. Firstly, by adopting a non-thermal pasteurization method known as high hydrostatic pressure pasteurization (HHPP), we hypothesize that we will be able to preserve milk nutrients and biologically active molecules. Consequently, the OMB will be able to dispense donor milk that can fully exert its multiple beneficial biological/immunological functions, improving health outcomes for vulnerable infants. Secondly, we will leverage HHPP to further reduce B. cereus contamination, and create and deploy genome-based bioinformatics means to differentiate between non-pathogenic and pathogenic B. cereus. As a result, our research will help reduce milk losses, and permit the OMB to serve more preterm newborns.

column36: Using "enhanced ultrasound" to help select the best kidneys for transplantation
column37: Transplantation has revolutionized the lives of patients with kidney failure, being the only therapy that prolongs life span and improves quality of life. Donor kidneys, however, are in very short supply, such that patients must wait up to 8 years for a transplant, and in many cases never receive a kidney. With this shortage in mind, doctors are often accepting kidneys for transplant from sicker donors. While many of these kidneys are suitable for transplant, some unfortunately are already chronically injured when they are transplanted. Ultimately, the end result is that some patients who wait years for a transplant receive kidneys that work less well, and which fail prematurely. Scarring and blood vessel injury are the most common and important types of chronic injury seen in donor kidneys. Unfortunately, doctors have very limited ways to assess this chronic damage, relying instead on non-specific and insensitive measures that do not reliably reflect these processes. There is a desperate need for accurate tools to assess the degree of chronic injury in potential transplant kidneys, and that predict how well these kidneys will function in the long term. We are working to develop new cutting edge ultrasound-based techniques to measure scarring and blood vessel damage in transplant kidneys. Our ultimate goal is to help doctors better select kidneys for transplantation, and thus improve kidney transplant outcomes. Our multidisciplinary team, composed of kidney doctors, radiologists, pathologists, and physicists, is uniquely suited to conduct these studies. Most importantly, working with a world leading industry partner with key connections to transplant centres across Canada (VisualSonics), we are ideally positioned to translate our research findings into clinical practice.

column36: Microcircuitry of performance monitoring and executive control
column37: I propose to investigate the mechanisms for cognitive functions that are severely compromised in mental illnesses such as schizophrenia to rationalize effective treatment and diagnosis strategies. One of the hallmarks of many neuropsychiatric conditions is their inability to evaluate aversive and rewarding outcomes, attribute causes to them, and develop strategies to improve future outcomes. Previous research has pinpointed specific parts of the frontal lobe supporting these cognitive functions. However, we do not know enough about how neurons within these areas communicate to understand how these functions arise and why they are compromised in neuropsychiatric conditions. My research aims to elucidate how ensembles of neurons in these areas communicate to achieve specific functions. I will collect neural activity of non-human primates while they perform a cognitive task that has been extensively tested in psychological experiments and used in diagnosis of schizophrenia. I will determine the flow of information between neurons related to error detection, feedback and reward processing, and the resulting adjustments in behaviour. Information from the proposed studies will provide a solid understanding of the underlying processes for these cognitive functions and rationalize more effective non-invasive and pharmacological treatment strategies. Furthermore, by relating the information flow between neurons to the electrical currents that drive EEG voltage fluctuations recorded over the scalp, results from this study will render this non-invasive method a more powerful tool for diagnosing neuropsychiatric conditions.

column36: Understanding the Leadership Experience of African Nova Scotian Nurses and the Implications for the Health of the African Nova Scotian Community Using a Black Feminist Lens
column37: The purpose of this project is to understand leadership experiences from the perspective of Black nurses in Nova Scotia and how this affects the health of the Black community. This research is timely and necessary as the Black community in Nova Scotia continues to experience tremendous oppression in the form of racism and discrimination. As a result of significant discrimination and racism, Black communities, specifically within Nova Scotia, have much poorer health compared to the rest of Nova Scotia and Canada. Research shows that Black communities in Nova Scotia experience higher rates of high blood pressure, diabetes and mental illness, among other chronic health conditions. Moreover, across Canada, there is a substantial absence of information that shows how diseases and illness affect people based on their race. Nurse leaders are nurses who have skills and knowledge that allow them to influence teams, initiate change and improve our health system. Nurse leaders use their experience and training to inform their actions. However, within the Canadian healthcare system, there is an underrepresentation of Black nurse leaders, which has led to major issues within the Black community being ignored. In order to determine the issues that are present for Black nurses and the community, it is necessary to interview these nurses and learn what issues they view as important. This will inform and direct our approach for improving the health of the Black community. There is very little research that has been done with Black communities in Nova Scotia and as a result, there is not a lot of information available about the community. Therefore, this research will show how race, class and gender impact the leadership of Black nurses and how the underrepresentation of Black nurse leaders is detrimental to the health of the Black community. The information from this research will inform decision-makers, healthcare providers and researchers in their work with the Black community.

column36: Trajectoires longitudinales de bien-etre psychologique et leur impact sur la sante cardiometabolique
column37: Les maladies cardiometaboliques (MCM), qui regroupent les maladies cardiovasculaires, l'hypertension, le diabete de type 2 et les accidents vasculaires cerebraux, sont l'une des principales causes de deces et d'incapacite chez les adultes ages de 50 ans et plus. Des recherches recentes suggerent que le bien-etre psychologique, c'est-a-dire le fait d'avoir des sentiments positifs envers la vie, joue un role protecteur dans le developpement et la progression des MCM. Cependant, les etudes existantes se sont principalement concentrees sur le bien-etre psychologique mesure a un seul moment dans le temps: les relations entre l'evolution longitudinale du bien-etre psychologique et le developpement des MCM n'ont pas ete etudiees pour l'instant. Ce projet investiguera les relations entre les trajectoires d'evolution du bien-etre psychologique et le risque d'incidence de MCM chez des adultes ages de 50 ans et plus. Premierement, cette recherche examinera les differentes trajectoires d'evolution du bien-etre psychologique chez 11,391 hommes et femmes sur une periode de 14 ans. Deuxiemement, cette etude verifiera si les trajectoires d'evolution du bien-etre psychologique predisent la survenue de MCM. Par exemple, un bien-etre continuellement eleve pourrait etre associe a un risque reduit de MCM comparativement a un bien-etre continuellement faible ou qui decline dans le temps. Troisiemement, cette recherche examinera le role mediateur de marqueurs biologiques, a savoir si la relation entre le bien-etre psychologique et le risque de MCM s'explique par des alterations de marqueurs biologiques associes a la fois a la sante mentale et aux MCM comme la proteine C-reactive, le cholesterol HDL et la composition du microbiome intestinal. Une meilleure comprehension du role du bien-etre psychologique dans le developpement des MCM permettra de developper de nouvelles interventions psychosociales visant a augmenter et a soutenir le bien-etre pour proteger la sante cardiometabolique.

column36: The association between immigration status and ethnicity, and stroke incidence, care and outcomes
column37: Stroke is one of the leading causes of death and disability in Canada with over 60,000 strokes in Canada every year. Previous studies have found that immigrants to Canada have a lower incidence of stroke compared to long-term residents. This has been attributed to the "healthy immigrant effect" whereby only those who are healthy choose to or are able to immigrate, and therefore these individuals have a lower risk of developing disease than long-term residents of a country. However, upon immigration competing risk factors such as poor socioeconomic class, western life-style, differences in access to healthcare, and work-related risk factors among immigrants may lead to dilution of the protective healthy immigrant effect with more time spent in the host country ("acculturation" effect). The impact of immigration on stroke care and outcomes and its interplay with ethnicity and acculturation have not been studied in Canada. In this study, I will use information that is already being collected on patients with stroke from hospitals across Ontario, through a project called the Ontario Stroke Registry. I will also use data available at our research institution (the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences) through a project called the CANHEART study, which has health information, including immigration status and ethnicity, on approximately 9 million people, and 80,000 with previous stroke. I will compare lifetime risk of stroke, acute stroke care, and stroke outcomes in immigrants compared to long-term residents of Ontario, and in people from different ethnic groups. I hypothesize that stroke care and outcomes will be similar in immigrants and long-term residents of Ontario. This study is important because if variations in care or outcomes among immigrant groups are identified, then work can be done to develop targeted interventions to address potential gaps in care, with the goal of decreasing the risk of death and disability from stroke in all Canadians.

column36: Economic Inequalities and Associated Health Impacts Among LGBTQ2S+ People in Canada
column37: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, queer, two-spirit and other sexual and gender minority (LGBTQ2S+) people are at elevated risk of poor health outcomes. Limited research indicates that these individuals are also at heightened risk for poverty. To date, there are no studies assessing the extent to which poverty may contribute to health problems among LGBTQ2S+ individuals. This research aims to compare poverty and health outcomes between sexual and gender minority and non-minority Canadians. We will also study how other social positions (e.g., race) can affect the extent of poverty and health inequalities in these populations. Finally, we will assess how poverty may contribute to health inequalities; alone and combined with other social positions. We will address these objectives by examining Statistics Canada surveys (e.g., Canadian Community Health Survey) through the lens of intersectionality. This approach allows exploration of inequalities across groups of individuals who experience multiple forms of oppression (e.g., among bisexual women of color). The outcomes of this research will provide evidence for development of promising interventions to reduce poverty and health inequalities that continue to affect sexual and gender minority Canadians.

column36: Magnetic Seizure Therapy for the Treatment of Treatment-Resistant Depression and Suicidality in Borderline Personality Disorder
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a severe mental health disorder with one of the highest rates of suicide among all psychiatric illnesses. About 1 in 10 persons with BPD dies by suicide, which is 50 times greater than the rate of suicide in the general population. A new brain stimulation therapy called magnetic seizure therapy (MST) is a safe and effective treatment for people with treatment-resistant depression, and produces substantial reductions in suicidal thinking in about 75% patients. Given the high rates of suicidal thinking and depression-related symptoms in individuals with BPD, MST could also be an effective treatment for these individuals, but has never been studied in this population. Our research group is conducting an ongoing Health Canada-approved pilot study investigating the effectiveness of conjoint MST plus psychotherapy, compared to psychotherapy alone, for treatment-resistant depression and suicidal thinking in patients with BPD. Brain imaging scans are acquired before and after treatment to examine brain changes in each treatment group. In the proposed study, I continue to recruit an additional 10 patients in order to complete the pilot study, and I analyze pre- and post-treatment brain scans. I hypothesize that the MST treatment group will show greater reductions in suicidal thinking and depression, and that these changes will correspond with an increase in brain functional connectivity between brain areas involved in the control of emotion (i.e., the prefrontal cortex and limbic system). This is the first ever study to investigate the feasibility of brain stimulation therapy for suicidal patients with treatment-resistant depression and BPD. This research could identify a safe and effective treatment for patients with BPD that require more intensive intervention, ultimately helping to prevent loss of life in patients who do not respond to first-line treatments.

column36: Deciphering the molecular mechanism of RAF family kinase dimerization and regulation.
column37: In our body, the proper functioning of cells is under the control of small machines called proteins. When proteins lose their proper function (by mutations for example) they can cause cells to grow uncontrollable and cause diseases such as cancer. Among all the proteins in the cell, the RAF proteins family, composed of five members, are some of the most crucial to control cell growth and proliferation. Thus, not unexpectedly this family of proteins is commonly mutated in human cancers (8% of all human cancers) and more specifically melanoma (50% of human melanomas). Previous work in Dr Sicheri's lab has shown that the RAF proteins need to interact with themselves in a process called dimerization to function properly. Importantly, RAF proteins dimerization is responsible for the resistance of cancer cells to RAF-targeting clinical treatments resulting in many patients relapsing within a year. How RAF proteins dimerize is still not well understood and a better understanding of the process may lead to better cancer treatments. To this aim, my research project is to determine how two crucial RAF family members BRAF and KSR1 dimerize. In collaboration with Dr. Marc Therrien's lab at the university of Montreal, I recently identified and characterized the minimal regions of BRAF and KSR1 that are essential for their dimerization using X-Ray crystallography and NMR technologies. These findings published in Nature help to understand how BRAF and KSR1 dimerize and how they function in normal and cancer cells. Going forward, I intend to solve the structure of the entire BRAF and KSR1 proteins bound together using a cutting-edge technology called cryo-electron microscopy. This will reveal the big picture of how the dimerization of BRAF and KSR1 works to keep these proteins under control. This research program will improve our understanding of how RAF proteins family regulate cell growth and eventually may translate into improved anti-cancer therapies.

column36: Evaluating the impact of a province-wide capacity building intervention on nutrition policies and practices in early years providers
column37: The early years of life are critical for lifelong health. Sadly, many Canadian preschoolers do not meet national dietary recommendations for vegetables and fruit while frequently consuming foods of little nutritional value. In 2016, the BC government and partners developed a capacity-building intervention to support the implementation of recommended practices encouraging physical activity and healthy eating in childcare settings. Research is underway to evaluate whether this intervention has improved childcare's policies and practices around children's physical activity. My research will expand the focus to healthy eating and add indicators to the assessments already underway and proposed. My specific aims are to: 1) define the factors (individual, childcare settings and regional) that facilitate or hinder full implementation of these new recommendations ; 2) assess whether the provincial intervention changed childcare providers' nutrition policies and practices; and 3) evaluate whether children aged 3-5 years attending childcare centres that adhere to these recommendations have healthier dietary behaviours and lower nutritional risk scores compared to children attending childcare centres that do not adhere to these recommendations. These aims will be met by: 1) conducting 60 min interviews with childcare providers to gain an in-depth understanding of the factors that influence the implementation of these new recommended practices; 2) analyzing data from province-wide surveys to examine longitudinal change in childcare providers' healthy eating policies and practices; 3) collecting child-level dietary data using the Nutrition Screening Tool for Every Preschooler (NutriSTEP(R)). My findings will provide invaluable information about the food environments and dietary behaviours children in childcare settings and help decision makers tailor approaches in the early years.

column36: Adipocyte AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) as a cellular target to treat obesity-related diseases in vivo: From mechanism to treatment
column37: The rising rates of obesity-related diseases including cardiovascular disease, type II diabetes, and some cancers, pose an immense threat to society. Individuals affected by these diseases have a higher risk of premature death and a decreased quality of life. Finding a new class of therapeutics to manage and treat the symptoms associated with these diseases is of utmost importance. One potential way to prevent or treat these diseases is by increasing the metabolism of adipose tissue. Specifically, increasing the metabolism of brown and beige adipose tissues (BAT) could "suck up" sugars and fats from the system and burn them away as heat as opposed to storing them. The applicant's lab has discovered a crucial molecule, the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), for the function of these adipose tissues and is proposing to develop a new drug using Nano-particles that specifically activate it in BAT to reduce weight gain, blood sugar, and liver fat. Understanding how this molecule works could provide a basis for future therapies specifically targeted to obesity-related diseases. This project has the potential to impact the quality of life of over 7 million Canadians and could address a shortcoming in effective therapies that prevent or treat obesity-related diseases.

column36: Recovery from Postpartum Depression in Indigenous and Non-Indigenous Women and Offspring Risk
column37: THIS RESEARCH INVOLVES INDIGENOUS PEOPLES Postpartum depression (PPD) affects 1 in 5 women and can have widespread adverse effects on her children and family. The children of depressed mothers are more likely to have school problems and struggle with emotional and behavioural problems. Importantly, if mothers are successfully treated and recover, their children can benefit. However, only 1/3 of all women fully recover. It is not known whether the children of women who only partially recover experience similar improvements. Furthermore, the mechanisms by which risk for future problems is transmitted from mother to child are not well understood. If these were known, they could be targeted to improve outcomes. One of the experiences that has been most closely linked to poor PPD recovery and offspring risk is childhood trauma, which Indigenous Peoples have directly and indirectly experienced due to barriers impacting their language, culture, and family structure. Despite these experiences, Indigenous women's perinatal mental health and its impact on infants remains completely unknown. To fully ascertain the impact of maternal PPD on offspring risk, it is important to examine recovery in these women, and to understand the potential mechanisms by which it operates so that we can improve conditions for children and reduce their risk across the lifespan in Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations. We hypothesize that the extent of recovery from PPD experienced by 114 mothers will correlate directly with their offspring's ability to regulate their own emotions at 1 and 2 years of age. We will use a range of measures (neurophysiological, observed tasks, parent-reports) to assess infants and toddlers. To our knowledge, this will be the first study to examine associations between PPD recovery and offspring emotion regulation (a potent predictor of later psychiatric risk), and to examine differences in these outcomes in Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations.

column36: Explaining Self-Reported Health Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults with Depressive Symptoms and Multimorbidity: A Mixed Methods Study
column37: There is a growing number of older adults in Canada. In the year 2031 it is predicted that 25% of the total population will be made up of adults over the age of 65 years. These older adults often live with multiple chronic health conditions as well as depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms, together with other health conditions, can cause a decreased health related quality of life, increase the chance of developing other health conditions, and increase the use of expensive health services. This represents a significant public health issue. Despite these challenges, many older adults with multiple chronic health conditions and depressive symptoms self-report their health as positive ("good", "very good", or "excellent") when asked in a survey. Self-reported health status is a strong predictor of future health status among older adults. This includes predicting the development of other health problems or death because of these problems. However, the reasons that older adults with multiple chronic health conditions and depressive symptoms report positive health over reporting negative health is unknown. This research will focus on understanding the factors that explain self-reported health in older adults with depressive symptoms and multiple chronic health conditions. It is important to understand the reasons that older adults report positive health (although they experience challenges from depressive symptoms and multiple chronic health conditions) as this understanding will inform effective programs and policies that can help to promote health and support healthy aging at home.
