column36: Developing and enhancing novel cancer immunotherapies by harnessing the anti-cancer abilities of patients' own Natural Killer immune cells
column37: Ovarian and lung cancer are among the most deadly cancers; the majority of patients with these diseases do not survive 5 years. For such poor prognosis cancers, there is a critical need for new effective treatments. The body's immune system is its primary protection mechanism against cancer: immune cells constantly survey the body and eliminate cancerous cells. However, cancer develops when malignant cells overwhelm this system. Therefore, reinforcing the body's natural immune defenses against cancer in the form of immunotherapy is emerging as a promising treatment modality for cancers that are resistant to current therapies. Natural Killer (NK) cells are immune cells that play a critical role in the body's defense against cancer due to their capacity to kill cancer cells without harming healthy cells. Given this ability, they have attracted attention as a promising cancer immunotherapy and have proven effective in treating blood cancers. Despite the therapeutic potential, immune therapies including NK cells have had limited success against solid tumours, such as ovarian and lung cancer, due to the hostile environment produced by tumours which impairs immune cell function. This impairment also limits efficacy of current therapies, such as antibody therapies which function largely through NK cells. Thus, understanding how the tumour environment alters NK cells is paramount to developing strategies to block inhibition and extend their therapeutic ability to solid tumours. The current project will uncover key changes in NK cells that impair their function after exposure to the tumour environment. Once identified, we will assess if blocking these changes can overcome NK cell inhibition and improve their therapeutic ability to reduce tumour burden. This project will uncover feasible targets to enhance NK cell function against ovarian and lung cancer in order to provide new effective therapies and improve outcomes of current therapies for cancers with poor prognosis.

column36: Deformability based Cell Sorting Enabling Quality Control of Stored Red Blood Cells
column37: Red blood cells circulate in the bloodstream for approximately 120 days, delivering oxygen to all tissues in the body. A key property of red blood cells is their ability to squeeze into capillary blood vessels that are many times smaller than their own diameter. Donated red blood cells, collected by the Canadian Blood Service for use in blood transfusions, can be stored for up to 42 days. During this time, the deformability of these cells is degraded, impairing their ability to circulate in capillary blood vessels. As a result, the viability of these cells in transfusion recipients is reduced from 120 days to, in some cases, hours or minutes. Currently, there are no simple methods to measure the quality of donated blood units, as defined by how long they will circulate in transfusion recipients. Additionally, there appears to be significant differences between donors, where some donors could provide blood that circulate longer in recipients than other donors. Our research team recently developed a method to analyze red blood cell deformability by sorting these cells based on their deformability in order to determine if the more deformable red blood cells circulate for longer in recipients than less deformable cells. We plan to use this approach to analyze donated red blood cells in order to estimate the expected circulation time of donated blood units. This capability would enable physicians to identify high-quality blood units in order to treat patients where a longer circulation time is critical, which would reduce the number of blood transfusions for these patients, and thus increase the overall blood supply. Additionally, the ability to estimate circulation time of individual donated blood units would allow Canadian Blood Service to improve their production and storage practices in order to improve the quality of blood provided to transfusion recipients.

column36: Adipocyte adhesion molecule (ACAM) as a new therapeutic target for MS.
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) affects more than 2 million people worldwide and has a severe impact on their quality of life. MS involves an abnormal response of the body's immune system which is directed against the brain. In MS patients, an abnormal immune cell infiltration across blood vessels occurs, enabling harmful cells to enter the brain where they start attacking myelin, the protective sheath surrounding nerve cells. To enter the brain, immune cells use so-called "adhesion molecules". In this project, I aim to restrict this immune cell infiltration by blocking a novel adhesion molecule called "adipocyte adhesion molecule" (or ACAM). ACAM was originally characterized in fat cells and was found to be critically involved in the development of obesity. To date, the possible implication of ACAM in inflammatory processes or MS has not yet been studied. Nevertheless, my own preliminary findings show that ACAM is expressed on both immune cells and on blood vessels of the brain, both in humans and in mice, especially during inflammatory processes. Indeed, I showed that there is an abnormal increase of the quantity of ACAM on vessels and immune cells in active MS lesions. Furthermore, ACAM expression is also increased in animal models of MS. Therefore, my hypothesis is that ACAM plays a critical role in MS by promoting the migration of disease-causing immune cells across blood vessels of the brain. I aim to unravel how ACAM plays a role in immune cell entry into the brain and establish the therapeutic potential of blocking ACAM in preventing MS development and/or progression.

column36: Super-resolution microscopy network analysis: Drug target validation for cystic fibrosis
column37: The goal of genome-based precision medicine is to selectively target drugs to responsive patients. This is particularly important in cystic fibrosis (CF), where ~75% of eligible patients, carrying the F508del-CFTR mutation, do not show demonstrable improvement in lung function with the clinically-available drug Orkambi. Orkambi treatment costs >$250,000/yr and is not formally covered by publically funded health-care in Canada at this time. New drugs in phase 2 clinical trials may be more effective than others for individual patients. To identify which patients are most likely to benefit from CF modulator drugs, it is important to study CFTR at the protein level as patient-patient variation is not only dependent on genomic differences (e.g. specific CFTR mutations). We will apply machine learning based network analysis of single molecule localization super-resolution microscopy (SMLM) to develop an imaging-based assay to identify patients likely to benefit from a particular therapeutic. Optimization of therapies for individual patients will increase drug efficacy and substantially reduce cost of treatment for Canadian CF patients. SMLM generates resolution ten-fold beyond the diffraction limit. However, quantitative approaches to analyze the large data sets of 3D point localizations generated are limited. We developed a novel and powerful approach to model SMLM particle localization data sets, transforming 3D localizations into a network by virtual connections between the points. This approach allows us to determine molecular architecture, i.e. how proteins within a protein complex interact. We now propose to refine and apply the technology to CFTR and thereby validate our analysis pipeline for personalized medicine applications in CF and other diseases with a known drug target. We will partner with Quorum Technologies, a Canadian microscopy company, to commercialize the software for use by super-resolution microscopy users and pharmaceutical companies worldwide.

column36: Role of FGFRs in modulating fibrogenicity of perivascular cells in cerebrovascular diseases
column37: Improper blood flow within the brain impairs neural activity, physical movement and cognitive ability, and these negative effects can occur at any age. Important cellular events within the wall of brain arteries control blood flow throughout the brain by changing the diameter of these vessels. When this control is impaired, the long-term consequence may be insufficient blood flow and ischemia, or the rupture of small vessels and bleeding within the brain. Recently, we have identified a novel genetic defect in a protein, the type 1 IP3 receptor (IP3R1), that disrupts this control, similar to what is observed in patients. I believe that this dysfunction is a direct result of the important role played by IP3R1 in regulating Ca2+ movement within small arteries of the brain. I hypothesize that genetically modified IP3R1s negatively affect Ca2+ movement in cells of the vessel wall, the control of vessel diameter and blood flow throughout the brain. Thus, my research will utilize microscopic imaging techniques to investigate how this type of protein defect observed in patients impairs Ca2+ movement in small arteries within the brain, and identify new strategies that minimize its negative impact on cerebral blood flow. To do so, we have created genetically modified mice that exhibit defects in this key protein similar to those found in patients, allowing us to study its impact on Ca2+ movement in arterial smooth muscle and endothelial cells. These studies will thus provide new information on blood vessel function and possibly how to manipulate these vessels in patients to maintain normal blood flow and brain activity.

column36: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial of the "PEP" (Personal Energy Planning) Program for Adults on Chronic Dialysis with Fatigue
column37: People who have kidney failure (ESRD) often feel unusually tired, which interferes with their ability to live life normally. We have created a program (the "PEP" Program) that teaches people with ESRD how they can save energy during their everyday life, using strategies like being organized, prioritizing, and using good body postures. A large study is needed to test whether the PEP program is helpful for people with ESRD, but first, we need to do a smaller-scale "practice" study to help us plan this large study. The purpose of this "practice" study is to see whether people with ESRD are able to do the PEP program, to see what they think of the program, and to see how many people we need to include in the large study. We plan to invite 50 people with ESRD from dialysis units across Calgary, Alberta to participate. People with ESRD who report feeling unusually tired a lot of the time will be asked to take part in the study. People who agree will either do the "PEP" program, or another program that gives them general information about kidney disease. We will measure whether the PEP program helps people feel less tired, by asking them to complete questionnaires before and after the study. We will also interview people after they participate in the study, to learn what they think. This "practice" study will help us plan next steps for the PEP program, with an aim to improve the lives of people with ESRD.

column36: Long-term trends in acute stroke care and outcomes: A population-based study using administrative data from 2003-2018
column37: Stroke is a common and potentially devastating condition caused by lack of blood flow or bleeding in the brain. Invasive measures are often taken to prevent death in the days to weeks following a stroke. However, people who survive stroke can commonly be left with severe disabilities in motor, speech, and cognitive domains, which may significantly reduce their quality of life. Many interventions for stroke, such as feeding tubes, can prolong life successfully, but people surviving often have full dependence on others and require long-term care. Although stroke mortality is decreasing over time, studies have been limited to short time periods after stroke. In addition, we do not know whether disability is also decreasing, or if more people are surviving with higher levels of dependence. We plan to use Alberta and Ontario administrative data to study how mortality, disability, home-time and chronic care after stroke have changed over a 15-year period between 2003-2018. Our findings will demonstrate whether the there have been reductions in long-term mortality over time. Furthermore, our results will add insight to our use of aggressive and life-sustaining care after stroke, and how this affects specific groups of people based on age, sex, and stroke type. Lastly, the findings will identify important trends in post-stroke dependence and help plan for providing services to people with disability after stroke in Canada, including rehabilitation, home care, and chronic care facilities.

column36: Confidential Automatic Monitoring, Examination, and Recognition of disease Activity (CAMERA): Application to Parkinson and Alzheimer Diseases
column37: Current in-home monitoring of aging populations includes the use of patient-worn sensors and alarms and traditional camera systems. However, patients may forget to wear the sensor or be unable to trigger an alarm in case of a fall, while cameras intervenes with a person's privacy. Our innovative monitoring project uses smart cameras to generate video recordings of people with Parkinson's or Alzheimer's. These cameras immediately anonymize the patient identification to preserve privacy. The uniqueness of our project is that the processing of these data is done within the camera, so the images do not need to be stored or transmitted. We will use the cameras developed by AltumView Systems Inc, our knowledge user company, to process and analyze such video recordings to facilitate clinical assessments of body movement and emotional status, such as depression. The camera could also trigger assistance alerts to family members or health services and inform physicians about a patient's health status. Monitoring of aging populations with smart cameras has economic benefits and can improve patient outcomes. Balancing our ethical duties of protecting patients' privacy, respecting their freedom, promoting their well-being, and using health resources responsibly, smart cameras will help maintain patients' independence longer, which in turn can reduce the costs of hospitalization and long-term care facilities. The camera-derived information can help physicians make better decisions on treatment and consequently may reduce the number of additional visits to physicians, hospitals, and emergency rooms. This project will have significant commercialization potential as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's affect roughly 600,000 Canadians, and - with suitable modifications - could be adapted to monitoring the healthy elderly. Training of HQP will be greatly facilitated by this inherently multidisciplinary project that combines engineering, medical, and ethical skills.

column36: Decision making capacity and triage acuity among emergency department users.
column37: Overloaded emergency departments are a serious and chronic problem in most health care settings. Patients visit the emergency department hoping for immediate treatment for their medical complaint, regardless of its severity. However, 25% to 40% of patients could be treated more efficiently elsewhere. While we know some of the sociodemographic and clinical reasons that lead to the overuse of emergency departments, we still do not understand how behavioural and social determinants of health could help to explain patients' decision-making. I will examine the factors influencing patient motivation as it relates to emergency department use. My main aim is to explain how health literacy, health-related personal beliefs, emotional intelligence, and severity of presenting complaint combine to influence emergency department use. I will recruit adult patients presenting to an emergency department in London, Ontario between September 2019 and August 2020. I will ask them to complete validated surveys assessing their health literacy, health-related personal beliefs, and emotional intelligence. Separately, I will also collect sociodemographic and clinical acuity data from their medical records. I will explore these data to find relationships between the variables to uncover trends in emergency department use. My study will be the first to link clinical data with primary data on health behaviour. An evaluation of reasons for emergency department use will demonstrate how improvements to health literacy, personal-health beliefs, and increased patient control could enhance and inform patient's decision-making capacity. As a result, some patients may be less likely to attend, thereby relieving pressure and directly improving patient access and flow in the system.

column36: Molecular factors that mediate antibiotic resistance by membrane protein efflux pumps.
column37: Proteins carry out nearly all cellular functions. Some proteins are anchored in cell membranes and control the exchange of molecules into and out of cells. Antibiotic resistant bacteria have developed ways to efficiently drive antibiotics out of the cell interior using membrane protein pumps. Understanding and combatting antibiotic resistance is a frontier problem in scientific research as worldwide demand for antibiotics has increased and progress developing new antibiotics has slowed. The proposed research programme develops new mass spectrometry tools to directly measure the molecular interactions between membrane protein pumps, lipid molecules in the surrounding membrane, and antibiotics. MacAB-TolC is a membrane protein pump in E. coli that confers resistance to macrolide antibiotics. The pump is an intricate molecular machine, assembled from six copies of MacA, two copies of MacB, and three copies of TolC, that bridges the inner and outer cell membranes. The proposed studies aim to determine the effects of the surrounding membrane lipids on antibiotic recognition and are anticipated to reveal trends in how antibiotics are recognized and pumped out of cells. Furthermore, the research programme aims to determine the molecular details involved in the step-by-step mechanisms for pump assembly, to devise new strategies to completely abrogate pump formation.

column36: Characterizing the inflammatory phenotype of human and mouse models of depression
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) represents the leading cause of disability, affecting over 300 million people worldwide. Largely characterized by behavioural symptoms, there is a need to identify biological changes, or 'biomarkers', associated with MDD for effective diagnosis and treatment, as 30-50% of patients with MDD do not respond to current antidepressant therapies. Recent findings suggest that MDD or chronic stress may be associated with inflammation - a response of the immune system to danger - and that this inflammation triggers depressive behaviour. However, the link between inflammation and depression has not been widely characterized. Moreover, it is not known how stress initiates inflammation or how this inflammation acts on the brain to influence mood and behaviour. The goal of this project is to generate a comprehensive profile of inflammation during MDD. Using blood from human patients with MDD or a mouse model of depression, we will analyze cells of the immune system to determine if they more readily migrate towards, or are more prone to attacking, the brain. To further expand this profile, we will measure levels of 'cytokines', inflammatory messengers produced by immune cells, in these blood samples. Once we have identified potential inflammatory mediators of depression, we genetically deplete these candidate factors in mice to test their role in susceptibility to stress-induced depression. To elucidate the mechanisms of how inflammation alters behaviour, we will focus on the effects on brain cells that regulate mood and motivation, along with cells that comprise the blood-brain barrier, which normally protects the brain from danger. Understanding an inflammatory basis of MDD will be critical in developing diagnostic criteria and novel antidepressant drugs.

column37: Heart disease and stroke are the second and third most common cause of death in Canadians. Currently, doctors use a tool based on a patient's medical history and cholesterol levels to predict if they will have a heart attack or stroke in the next 5-10 years. Patients in whom heart attack or stroke are likely, can be offered medications to prevent this from happening. Unfortunately, these tools are difficult to use in every-day clinical practice. This tool can be automated into laboratory reports so that a prediction for future heart attack or stroke is reported to the physician alongside bloodwork results. This tool has the potential to streamline physician's workflow during patient encounters and ensure high quality care is delivered efficiently without lost opportunities to offer live-saving treatments.

column36: Dendritic Cells during Radiotherapy: revealing DC subset dynamics for the rational design of complementary immunotherapies
column37: Radiotherapy (RT), the use of ionizing radiation to treat tumors, represents a routine standard-of-care treatment option for Canadians diagnosed with cancer. Recent studies have illustrated that RT acts similar to a "vaccine"; promoting the recognition of cancer cells as dangerous targets for the immune system (i.e., anti-tumor T cell immunity). Such RT-induced anti-tumor immunity could eliminate cancer and prevent future relapse. Unfortunately, RT can also lead to suppressive effects, which both promote tumor progression and limit T cell immunity. Thus, it is crucial to understand the underlying mechanisms that dictate the "unwanted" suppressive effects and "desired" anti-tumor T cell immunity. This understanding would allow for the development of rationally designed combination therapies that enhance the success of RT. Dendritic cells (DCs) are pivotal immune cells in the regulation of both immune stimulation and suppression. For instance, tumors tend to favor the accumulation of suppressive DCs and other suppressive myeloid cells; whereas infections promote immunogenic DCs that have a unique ability to activate T cell immunity. Importantly, immunogenic DCs also reliably correlate with increased anti-tumor T cell immunity and cancer therapeutic efficacy. I hypothesize that modulation of immunogenic and suppressive DCs and other myeloid cells would significant impact the outcome RT. Thus, this research project aims to use cutting-edge technology, such as image-guided radiation technology and high parametric single-cell analysis (CyTOF), to mimic clinical RT practices and characterize the nature and function of DCs localized in the tumor, respectively. By exploiting such findings, I will implement rational combination therapies that promote immunogenic DCs or block the function of suppressive DCs. I am convinced that this project will uncover novel biological principles and positively impact the design of cancer treatment strategies.

column37: Cent cinquante a deux cents millions de personnes dans le monde sont touchees par le virus de l'hepatite C (VHC), et 0.6-0.7% de Canadiens presenteraient une forme chronique de la maladie. Son evolution naturelle est majoritairement asymptomatique et se caracterise par une fibrose progressive du foie. La strategie therapeutique actuelle s'interesse a la determination du stade de fibrose du foie, evaluee de maniere optimale par l'histologie obtenue a l'aide de biopsies hepatiques. Cependant, en raison du caractere particulierement invasif et parfois risque de ces biopsies, des approches alternatives ont ete developpees, comme le fibroscan et le fibrotest. Bien que ces approches soient moins intrusives et moins risquees, elles demeurent toutefois nettement moins efficaces que les biopsies hepatiques. Le defi actuel consiste donc a decouvrir une approche qui soit aussi efficace que la biopsie hepatique sur le plan de la determination du stade de fibrose du foie et aussi securitaire et respectueuse de l'integrite physique des patients. Au cours des dernieres annees, certaines equipes ont developpe des algorithmes visant a predire l'evolution de la fibrose et determiner l'indication de traitement. Bien que securitaires et respectueux de l'integrite des patients, les outils developpes ne sont pas aussi efficaces que la biopsie hepatique. Il convient de souligner que ces algorithmes ne furent generalement nourris que de donnees biologiques simples; l'integration des genotypes du virus est assez recente, et celle des antecedents et de l'historique medical demeure exceptionnelle. Des techniques propres a l'intelligence artificielle (IA) permettent aujourd'hui d'analyser ces donnees heterogenes et potentiellement de mettre en lumiere des patrons qui passent inapercus dans une approche statistique classique. Nous croyons que l'IA, jumelee a des ensembles de donnees plus exhaustifs, permettra de mieux predire l'evolution de la maladie et mieux cibler les interventions.

column36: Cell specific functions of Lysyl oxidases in the heart.
column37: Significance evidence from clinical studies and animal models, indicated that excessive deposition of collagens (Fibrosis) is an important contributor for heart failure. Lysyl oxidase (LOX) protein family members play a critical role in the cross linking of the collagen fibrils that determines the tensile strength of collagens in various organs during pathological conditions. LOX enzymes family members consist of 5 members: Canonical LOX & 4 LOX-like isoforms (LOXL-1, -2, -3, -4). We have identified in a clinical relevant dog cardiac fibrosis model that LOX & LOXL1 are extensively dysregulated in two cardiac cell types, myocytes & fibroblast. As such our research proposal will determine whether LOX/LOXL1 has a direct cell specific role in the heart. We will study their role in mediating cardiac fibrosis using transgenic mouse strains that prevents it from responding to the actions of LOX/LOXL1 in specifically in cardiac cell types. We will examine the heart function & structure in transgenic & normal mice. In addition, we will subject these transgenic & control mice to number of stresses such as heart attack (by blocking a major blood vessel supplying the heart) & pressure overload (by generating a constriction around largest blood vessel to increase a load on the heart). We anticipate that cell specific LOX/LOXL1 transgenic mice could be less susceptible for cardiac stress, develop less cardiac fibrosis, compared to normal mice, thereby suggesting direct actions of LOX proteins in cardiac cell types. We will further study detailed mechanism for cell specificity of LOX & LOXL1 proteins using advanced cell physiology and molecular biology approaches. These results could have significant clinical importance as cardiac fibrosis is important clinical feature for development and progression of heart failure, burden which on rise at an alarming rate in our population & have limited therapeutic approach.

column37: More than 14 million severe skin wounds (resulting from burns, trauma, ulcers) are treated each year in North America. The result is intractable chronic pain, immobility, disfigurement and in many cases infection leading to further medical complication or death. The annual societal cost of wound care in Canada alone is estimated at $4 billion. One of the primary reasons that wounds do not heal is an inability to regenerate functional dermis. The dermis provides essential trophic and mechanical support to the overlying epidermis and skin appendages (hair follicles, glands, vessels) embedded within it. Strategies to regenerate functional dermis and its appendages are desperately needed to restore quality of life and reduce the economic burden of wound care. An attractive approach is to stimulate stem cells that reside in adult skin. Our preliminary studies have identified a pool of dermal stem cells that are activated in response to injury and are recruited into healing wounds where they typically form scar. However, under some circumstances, these same cells can become regenerative (rather than scar-forming) and initiate formation of new hair follicles and healthy fat cells within the wound. Thus, understanding the molecular signals that bias dermal stem cell response towards regeneration can mitigate scarring and improve skin healing. To realize this clinical potential, we will: 1) Characterize the signals within the wound that drive regenerative versus scar-forming stem cell responses 2) Identify mechanisms through which these signals are integrated within the stem cells and 3) Develop therapeutics that activate regenerative programs within stem cells to promote skin regeneration. Our long-term goal is to develop a comprehensive genomic Wound Atlas that guides development of novel interventions to modulate dermal stem cell response after injury to improve the quality of wound healing, thereby improving outcomes for Canadians suffering severe skin injury or disease.

column36: Enhancing Person-Centred Care Practice in Primary Care: Implementation & Evaluation of Quality Indicators Informed by the Patient Perspective
column37: Person-centred care (PCC) is a way of providing care that incorporates the perspectives of patients and family members, and is responsive to their preferences, needs, and values. Research shows that PCC improves patient health outcomes and experiences, healthcare provider satisfaction, and promotes cost savings for the healthcare system. The College of Family Physicians of Canada identifies PCC as a priority for primary healthcare. Despite such efforts to make healthcare person-centred, PCC is not being measured routinely. If PCC is not evaluated, how can it be improved? With funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, our research team at the University of Calgary has developed Person-Centred Quality Indicators (PC-QIs). These indicators will be used by healthcare systems to measure PCC and ensure that primary care services address patient needs. For example, PC-QIs can measure patient involvement in decisions about their care. To get this information, we will engage patients and ask them to complete surveys about their experiences with the care received at their clinic. This data will tell clinic staff and patients about how well the clinic is providing PCC and help identify areas for improvement. Partnering with Alberta primary care clinics, researchers, policy-makers, and patients, my proposed doctoral research will support the implementation of PC-QIs and evaluate their use in an urban primary care clinic in Calgary, serving a diverse population of 8,000 patients. Using a theory-informed approach, I will use the best available evidence to identify effective strategies to implement the PC-QIs and determine what factors ensure successful implementation (e.g. clinic characteristics, resources needed). The findings from this study will inform future implementation of the PC-QIs in primary care across Alberta. Importantly, this research will help foster a person-centred healthcare system and provide patients with the care they value and need.

column36: Effects of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) and High Definition-tDCS (HD-tDCS) on motor learning in children: Robotic Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) motor maps, current modelling, and resting state functional connectivity
column37: Many of the 50000 Canadians had brain injuries near the time of birth, such as perinatal stroke. Perinatal stroke is the leading cause of cerebral palsy, a lifelong movement disability affecting the quality of life for both the individual and the family. Though treatment options are limited, we have shown that non-invasive brain stimulation may enhance motor function in such children. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), painlessly delivers very weak electric currents to change the excitability of the brain. A newer form, High-Definition tDCS may be more effective but was untested in children. A major limitation to advancing such treatments is that we have little understanding of how they work. Many new technologies can map the brain and explore how it changes with stimulation and learning. This project aims to understand how non-invasive brain stimulation can enhance motor learning in children. First, we are completing a trial to prove that both forms can help children learn motor tasks faster. Within this study, we are completing measurements of each child's brain before and after the intervention. A special robot will compare how a child's "motor map" changes with learning and stimulation. Specialized pictures from MRI scans will explore how the motor network changes and how non-invasive brain stimulation current moves through a child's brain. Finally, we will extrapolate this approach to understand how non-invasive brain stimulation works within the largest cross Canada clinical trial of 100 children with perinatal stroke. With cutting edge technologies including the only Pediatric Neurostimulation lab in Canada and the first Pediatric TMS Robot in the world, we are uniquely positioned to accomplish this work to lead definitive trials. This work will immediately improve our ability to design personalized rehabilitation approaches for the youngest stroke patients to ultimately reduce the morbidities of their strokes that last an entire lifetime.

column36: Perinatal stroke connectomics: Non-invasive neuromodulation target discovery in children with hemiparetic cerebral palsy
column37: When you think of a stroke patient, how old are they? A stroke is a brain injury due to interruption of blood supply. Strokes often lead to impairments in physical function. While most strokes occur in adults, a very high period of risk is the first week of life. Such perinatal stroke affects over 10,000 Canadian children. Most survivors suffer lifelong disabilities that affect quality of life for the child and entire family. The most common complication is a permanent weakness to one side of the body and the diagnosis of cerebral palsy. With no way of stopping perinatal stroke from happening, we focus on improving these physical disabilities. We do this through two main strategies. First, modern technology allows us to take pictures of patient's brains. Using a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we can see different connections within the brain. We can use the MRI to see how these connections change following stroke and how they relate to the child's impairments. Second, another technology called non-invasive brain stimulation may be able to improve physical function in children disabled by stroke. By sending a weak electrical current over the head, small amounts of electricity can reach specific areas on the surface of the brain and possibly help them learn better during therapy. We have used MRI pictures to understand the brains of children with perinatal stroke. We have used brain stimulation to enhance their function. However, most children remain significantly disabled. We therefore need a deeper understanding of how the brain recovers and how stimulation can work better to improve the lives of these children. The current research project will achieve this, getting detailed pictures of how the entire brain changes after injury and learn how to develop new brain stimulation therapies. Our proven ability to deliver such advances means this work could directly improve the lives of thousands of children with cerebral palsy in Canada.

column36: Contributions of household income on the longitudinal associations between the built environment and walking
column37: Background: The design of modern cities may be leading to decreases in population levels of physical activity. Cross-sectional studies suggest that neighbourhood built environment characteristics, including street design patterns, types of destinations nearby, and overall walkability are associated with physical activity. However, these studies may be biased by self-selection (individuals choosing a neighbourhood matched to their physical activity preferences). One way to address this limitation is to use residential relocation studies, which measure people's physical activity before and after they move neighbourhoods. Most of this research has examined people from high income backgrounds; therefore, very little is known about the effects for lower income people. Research aim: To examine whether changes in neighbourhood walkability impact walking and whether this relationship differs according to household income. Method: Study 1 will be a literature review of built environment and physical activity residential relocation studies that consider income. Study 2 will be a residential relocation study of people with diverse incomes from a longitudinal study. Study 3 will focus on a low income population by following people as they move into affordable housing. Both Study 2 & 3 will have questionnaire items measuring walking, demographic, and health characteristics. Using spatial data, we will create walkability scores for participants' postal codes to group participants by relocation status (i.e., increased walkability, decreased walkability, no change, or no relocation). Statistical models will test if changes in walkability resulted in changes in walking and how income affects this relationship. Implications: These studies will provide novel and rigorous evidence regarding the role of income in the relationship between built characteristics and physical activity. These results could influence urban design policy to positively impact population health.

column37: Emerging cultured cell therapies have the potential to treat or cure multiple degenerative and fatal diseases, and hundreds of cell immunotherapy clinical trials are currently underway. The first two immune cell (T-cell) therapies approved in 2017 are highly effective, and can treat blood-cell cancers for which no treatment options remained. In contrast to using chemotherapy to kill cancer cells, these T-cell immunotherapies are based on amplifying natural human defences to kill cancer cells. This proposal is focussed on producing T cells that suppress other immune cells going after the wrong target, such as in transplant rejection or autoimmune disorders. These cell therapies could replace the use of immunosuppressive drugs that are often ineffective and have many negative side effects. Although cell immunotherapy is poised to revolutionize medical treatments, many challenges must be overcome to make these therapies a reality for the many patients needing them. As the culture of T cells coming from human donors is very complex, we must increase our understanding and control of the processes used to produce these therapeutic cells. This is the focus of our project. We will improve the production of therapeutic cells so that hundreds of patients can be treated with each cell donor. We also seek to enable networked Canadian skills and resources to facilitate clinical trials. Through reducing the cell production costs and increasing the number of cells produced for treatment, we will contribute toward reducing overall costs, to make these treatments economically feasible for our healthcare system and widely available to save lives. Our development of T-cell manufacturing technology will be systematically networked with Canadian cell therapy manufacturing facilities to broadly inform this and other promising clinical treatments that depend on cell manufacturing.

column37: BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE: Obesity is a leading cause of preventable diseases in Canada. Behavioral weight loss programs like the NIH-developed Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) are successful in achieving clinically relevant weight reductions that translate into substantial prevention and/or delay of diabetes even after 10 years. These programs however involve year-long frequent in-person sessions, are costly to both patients and providers, require extensively trained staff, and are not widely available outside of research studies. As a result, their reach, impact, and application in real-world settings has been severely limited. The Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care has recommended that physicians provide obese patients with intensive behavioral interventions for weight loss. Physicians are however not formally trained in behavioral weight management and have little time to take on the burden of implementing a full-length (e.g. 12 session) program to treat their obese patients. To address these barriers, I have developed a standardized physician/web delivered behavioral weight loss program for obesity treatment that combines 4 DPP-derived sessions delivered by physicians with an evidence-based DPP web program to maximize effectiveness and minimize costs. column36: Targeting distinct therapeutic vulnerabilities in homologous repair-deficient pancreatic adenocarcinoma
column37: Pancreatic cancer (PAC) will become the second-leading cause of cancer death in North America by 2030. The 5-year survival is a dismal 8%, and responses to chemotherapy are poor. Pancreatic cancer continues to be treated as a single disease, with patients generally receiving one-size-fits-all chemotherapy regimens. Recent advances have shown that there are, in fact, many distinct subtypes of pancreatic cancer. An important subtype is homologous repair-deficient PAC (HRD-PAC), which arises from genetic mutations that impair the tumour's ability to repair genetic errors. This subtype may be sensitive to targeted therapies that specifically exploit the tumour's unique vulnerabilities. A major challenge in developing targeted therapies for HRD-PAC is the lack of robust animal models and patient tissue samples. To address this need, we have built a research program nested within a high-volume pancreatic cancer centre, allowing fluid access to patient samples. To generate patient-derived mouse models of HRD-PAC, pancreatic tumours are collected directly from the operating room, and transplanted into immune-deficient mice. Using these mouse models, I am conducting a preclinical trial to evaluate the efficacy of various targeted therapies. I will also use these mouse models to study how tumours develop resistance to targeted therapies, and strategies to overcome this resistance. Finally, I will use human tissue samples to study the interaction between the tumour and the immune system, to identify potential immune therapies which may be effective in HRD-PAC. Altogether, this work will better our understanding of targeted treatment strategies for HRD-PAC, and have important, real-time clinical implications for patients suffering from this deadly disease.

column36: Identifying and targeting functional mediators of leptomeningeal metastasis
column37: With recent improvements in the treatment of cancer, patients are living longer than ever before. However, with this comes an increased incidence of spread, or metastasis, to the brain. Brain metastasis is a particularly devastating complication of cancer that results in the death of many patients, especially those with primary cancers of the breast, lung, and skin. A major problem facing the research community is that there are no patient-derived animal models of brain metastasis, rendering it difficult to study brain metastasis and develop new treatments. For this reason, I have established a research program whereby I transplant human brain metastasis specimens from the operating room directly into the brains of mice. In the mouse hosts, the human cancer cells grow and proliferate infinitely, as they would in the patient they came from. Establishing a large number of these human tumour models allows us to better understand brain metastases. With these models, I am working towards understanding how cancer spreads from the primary site, such as the breast, to colonize the brain and spinal cord. Preliminary results from these unique and novel model systems suggests that they can be instrumental in improving our understanding of the molecular processes that allow cancer cells to reach the brain and spinal cord. This knowledge can them be exploited in the form of new therapeutic approaches to prevent or treat brain metastasis.

column36: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and bladder cancer - a causal association or detection bias? An international multicenter cohort study.
column37: Type 2 diabetes is one of the fastest growing diseases in Canada, with approximately 60,000 new patients diagnosed each year. In recent years, there have been major advancements in the treatment of type 2 diabetes with the discovery of new drug classes, such as the sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. SGLT2 inhibitors have become increasingly popular, as they effectively lower blood sugar levels without the side effects of other antidiabetic drugs. However, these drugs have been associated with frequent urinary tract infections, and there are signals from trials that they may be associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer. To date, however, no study has been conducted in the real-world setting to assess this association. Thus, to address this gap in knowledge, I will conduct a multicenter cohort study among patients with type 2 diabetes using data sources from Canada, Europe and the Middle East. As a possible association may be explained by increased screening of the urinary tract, this international study will be specifically designed to differentiate between a possible biological effect and detection bias. Thus, this study will provide much needed information on the safety of SGLT2 inhibitors, and will be of value to regulatory agencies, physicians, and patients.

column37: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) constitutes a major health issue in Canada and worldwide. Nearly 3 million Canadians are living with CKD and its incidence is predicted to continue rising coincident with rates of obesity, diabetes and hypertension, all which greatly increase the likelihood of disease. Currently, there is no cure for CKD and existing treatments focus instead on limiting its progression. Unfortunately, however, the early stages of disease are often asymptomatic and nearly 3/10 newly diagnosed individuals in Canada each year are already in renal failure. Dialysis and transplantation remain the only forms of treatment for advanced kidney disease, and these approaches are associated with considerable morbidity, mortality and healthcare costs. Despite the burden of disease, the molecular and cellular basis of CKD is poorly understood, limiting opportunities for the diagnosis of disease at early stages or the development of targeted therapies. My research project aims to identify previously indiscernible molecular pathways that are integral for the maintenance of the kidney's blood filtration function, pathways that can now be revealed thanks to recent advancements in the fields of proteomics and cell and animal modelling. Leveraging cutting-edge developments in viral delivery systems and proximity mass spectrometry, and integrating them with cell and animal-based strategies, I will generate a molecular 'map' of the kidney's blood filter. These investigations are likely to reveal the involvement of previously undetectable molecules in regulating kidney function. The knowledge gained from these studies is poised to have major implications in our understanding of how the kidney functions, representing a new frontier in research towards the treatment and potentially prevention of kidney disease.

column36: Azithromycin as add-on therapy in patients failing medical and surgical treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
column37: Background Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is estimated to currently affect three million people in Canada alone, with most showing adequate response to standard medical and/or surgical therapy. Unfortunately, one in three patients with CRS will have disease persistence and require additional medical and surgical interventions. This not only affects the quality of life of patients but also represents an immense socioeconomic burden. Finding more effective alternatives is primordial. The first step is to identify patients that are at risk of failing standard therapy, and then targeting them for alternative therapy. The former was already completed by our team, allowing us to now focus on this high-risk population for additional therapy. Primary Objective Evaluate whether adding a macrolide, azithromycin, three times weekly is effective in not only controlling, but curing signs and symptoms of CRS in high-risk patients unresponsive to standard management after sinus surgery and nasal irrigations with corticosteroid respules (budesonide). Study design Patients meeting inclusion and exclusion criteria operated for CRS will receive budesonide nasal irrigations postoperatively. Patients with signs and symptoms of disease recurrence despite surgical and medical treatment will enter the randomized clinical trial. All patients included in the study will undergo thorough evaluations at every visit, looking at the symptom and surgical outcome, while also evaluating the genetic and bacterial evolution of the sinuses. Long-term significance Identifying a more personalized approach to the disease can lead to significant symptom alleviation, decreased need for additional medical and surgical interventions and an important socioeconomic gain. Furthermore, properly identifying and characterizing this population, as well as the immunomodulatory aspects of azithromycin in CRS can open future therapeutic avenues not only in rhinology but in respiratory diseases as a whole.

column36: Investigation, development and validation of software tools for the diagnosis of perinatal asphyxia based on the infant cry
column37: Birth asphyxia is a condition that results when a newborn is unable to establish spontaneous respiration after birth. It causes shortage of oxygen supply to the brain, and could result to multiple disabilities (such as deafness, brain damage, paralysis) or death of the newborn. Presently, diagnosis of birth asphyxia requires blood gas analysis to be conducted by trained personnel. In Canada and many developed countries, such analysis is part of routine clinical practice immediately after birth, ensuring that newborns with or at risk of birth asphyxia are referred for advanced care. In many low- and middle-income countries, the cost of acquiring and maintaining a blood gas analyser is prohibitively high. As such, many babies do not get early screening and birth asphyxia is usually only discovered when significant damage may have already occurred. Birth asphyxia causes over 2 million newborn deaths and disabilities, and is ranked by the WHO as one of the top 3 causes of newborn mortality. The aim of this research project is to develop a set of algorithms for diagnosing asphyxia using only the cry as input. The infant cry is one of the first signs of life, and clinical research has gone further to indicate that because speech and breathing are coordinated by the same regions of the brain, a newborn with asphyxia with have altered cry patterns. The algorithms we develop will be based on techniques of automatic speech recognition and integrated into a mobile app. Data for development and validation of the app will be acquired during a clinical study in Montreal. The app will be significantly cheaper, faster and easier to use in resource-limited settings than blood gas analysers. This would empower birth attendants to detect asphyxia early enough for the application of life-saving treatment. Furthermore, the algorithms that will be developed as part of this work could be extended for use in the diagnosis of other conditions affecting newborns.

column36: The clinical significance of Wingless signaling in atherosclerosis: a new player in an old disease
column37: The world has been burdened by atherosclerosis for centuries and it still remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. It is characterized by the accumulation of fat and cholesterol in the vessels of the neck or heart and if left untreated, can lead to severe cardiovascular events such as a stroke or heart attack. Despite some therapeutic advances, patients with atherosclerosis have limited treatment options and are usually forced to undergo invasive surgeries to remove the diseased vessel. A better understanding of how atherosclerosis develops is critical to the identification of novel therapies to battle this perilous disease. The Wingless (Wnt) signaling pathway is a complex molecular mechanism implicated in organ development, while also being involved in several diseases such as cancer, metabolic and cardiovascular diseases. There are 19 Wnt proteins, which aid in the regulation of cell movement, growth and expansion. Recently, Wnt-signaling has been implicated in the development of atherosclerosis, however the mechanism by which this occurs is not well understood. The goal of this research project is to unravel the contributions of Wnt-signaling to development of atherosclerosis in the vessels of the neck and heart. In the first part of the project, we will assess the presence of Wnt proteins in the blood and vessels of atherosclerosis patients undergoing cardiovascular surgery. The second part of the project will focus on the mechanisms by which Wnt-signaling promotes the development of atherosclerosis by using several cell types found in the vessel wall. Completion of this project will provide important insights into the mechanisms through which atherosclerosis develops, in hopes of identifying novel diagnostic markers and unique therapies for patients.

column36: The role of VGLUT1 expressing proprioceptive afferents on exercise-induced pain and motor recovery following peripheral nerve injuries
column37: Neuropathic pain is a debilitating chronic pain condition, caused by injuries to the nervous system and impacts 7 to 8% of the global population. Individual differences in pain tolerance, and the diverse cause of nerve injuries including trauma, sport injuries, inflammation, and chemotherapy, makes neuropathic pain particularly difficult to treat. My proposal aims to investigate new therapeutic targets. It is known that exercise benefits both pain and motor recovery after injuries, but a key question is how exercise changes the activity of the nervous system, and contributes to relief of pain and motor disability. To address this gap, I will empirically quantify the effects of exercise on pain and motor functions in a rodent model of peripheral nerve injury. Rodents will exercise voluntarily on a running wheel placed inside their cages, I will examine the cellular and molecular changes in the spinal cord - a key hub of sensory and motor processing. Next, I will then target these changes, and test their ability on reducing pain and motor disabilities. Specifically, peripheral nerve injuries cause a loss of VGLUT1 (vesicular glutamate transporter 1) expressing neurons in the spinal circuit, I will investigate whether the pain and motor disability are linked to a reduction in VGLUT1, and whether exercise can rescue this loss. Finally, I will manipulate the activity of VGLUT1 using pharmacological approaches, and test whether this can improve pain and motor disability following peripheral nerve injuries. Elucidating these mechanisms will help realise an evidence-based therapeutic solution for neuropathic pain and motor recovery, aid translational implementation of rehabilitation based treatments, and relieve the huge economic burden on the health care system.

column36: The role of developing group 2 innate lymphoid cell perivascular niches in early life lung immunity
column37: Allergic asthma is the leading chronic disease in children, defined by recurrent episodes of shortness of breath, wheezing, and in some cases catastrophic respiratory failure. Although medications can treat asthma symptoms, it remains an incurable and debilitating disease. Early-life exposure to allergens or respiratory viruses are common triggers, and childhood asthma frequently persists into adulthood, indicating that early-life 'immune education' can shape adult immunity and asthma susceptibility. A new type of immune cell called group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) have been recently identified as critical drivers of allergic inflammation, including allergic asthma. Interestingly, ILC2s are abundant in healthy neonatal mouse lungs, and the majority of lung ILC2s in adults are derived from this neonatal period. Preliminary results show that ILC2s remain in conserved lung "niches" throughout life and are regulated by surrounding stromal cells. How these niches develop after birth, and whether this contributes to age-specific sensitivity to allergens and viruses, has yet to be elucidated. This project aims to determine what signals are required for the development of these ILC2 niches, how exposure to allergens and common respiratory viruses alter the niche development and function, and whether this may contribute to the initiation of asthma in children. The obtained results will contribute to our understanding of early immune education and may lead to potential therapeutics for the prevention of asthma.

column36: A Wearable Technology Approach to Determine Exercise Fidelity during a Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Program and its Effect on Injury Rates in Youth Basketball
column37: In North America, there is a high level of participation in youth basketball, and youth basketball players are frequently injured. Injury in youth sport has been linked to chronic health problems and obesity, thus injury prevention in youth sport is vital for maintaining an active and healthy population. It has been shown that a warm-up routine can reduce the risk of injury in youth basketball players. Previous analyses of the effect of the warm-up routine on injury rates have focused simply on whether the routine was completed or not. Evaluating whether the warm-up routine exercises are being done correctly or incorrectly may further help to reduce the risk of injury. However, effective monitoring of warm-up performance in real-world settings is challenging due to lack of qualified personnel, time, or access to specialized equipment. Alternatively, recent advancements in wearable devices have made this technology portable and affordable, providing the means to measure movement quality in real-world settings. This proposed study has two parts. First, a wearable device will be worn by youth basketball players as they perform the warm-up routine. Their movement will be recorded by video, and a physiotherapist-trained observer will evaluate the videos to determine if the warm-up routine was done correctly or incorrectly. The signal from the wearable device will then be used to differentiate between correct and incorrect execution of the warm-up routine. In the second part of the study, the wearable device will be worn all season during the warm-up routine, and all injuries sustained during the season will be recorded. Using the methods established in the first part of the study, the effect of correct or incorrect execution of the warm-up routine on injury rates will be determined. Future studies may also use these methods to provide feedback to athletes during the warm-up routine to determine if correcting their movement patterns contributes to a lower risk of injury.

column37: Neurodevelopmental disabilities (NDD) are a group of conditions including learning difficulty, intellectual disability and autism. NDD affects 16% of Canadian and is frequently associated with disabling challenging behaviours such as aggression toward others, self-injury and not following requests. In a 2017 survey, individuals with NDD, their families and health professionals reported a lack of information about the best interventions. Indeed, it is still challenging to identify relevant and trusted information online for NDD and to keep updated. New advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have led to the development of computer programs able to reproduce the way humans interact to ask questions and provide answers; these programs are known as chatbots. We therefore assembled a large multidisciplinary team including experts on NDD, parents and AI experts to build a chatbot that will allow families, health professionals and teachers to identify interventions and resources to help individuals with NDD experiencing challenging behaviours. We have developed a prototype chatbot named CAMI (Chatbot Assistant for Medical Information), which we will improve with information from families, educators and health professionals. The chatbot will also provide coaching to families and health professionals to allow them to be more independent in accessing and navigating the healthcare system. Using AI will allow the chatbot to take advantage of comments from users with similar profiles to make personalized recommendations based on what other users facing similar situations thought was useful to them. Together, our project will reduce the time spent online by parents and healthcare professionals, make quality information currently buried online more accessible and improve the proper utilization of the resources of the healthcare system using technologies already shown to be effective in the commercial sector.

column37: Problems and Solution: Chronic pressure ulcer (PU) is among the top five leading causes of re-hospitalization in patients with spinal cord injury (SCI) which frequently leads to infections, low quality of life, depression, and even a risk of death. To solve these difficulties, we have recently addressed the 1st problem by developing and using liquid nutritional scaffold called MeshFill in our ongoing pilot clinical trial. Thus, in this study, a new product, referred as to MeshFill-Plus consists of: 1) liquid nutritional scaffold (MeshFill), 2) Spongy and flexible nano-fiberous skeleton and 3) Antibacterial nano-silver particles will be generated and tested for its functionally in infected and control wounds initially in the lab and then in a pre-clinical pig wound model which has a similar skin to human. Finally, evidence related to the safety and capability of the tested and optimized MeshFill-Plus will be submitted to University of British Columbia / Vancouver General Hospital Ethic Board for approval of small clinical feasibility study for treating 12 patients with PUs. column36: Azacyclopeptide Modulators of Immuno-metabolism to Treat Age-Related Macular Degeneration
column37: Peptides are important molecules for drug discovery, but inherent properties such as poor bioavailability and rapid disposal handicap their clinical use. These drawbacks have however been surmounted using approaches such as cyclization and azapeptides. Combing the latter two methods, we have conceived an effective protocol for making cyclic azapeptides (azacyclopeptides) that demonstrate remarkable attributes for drug development. Macrophages are an important class of white blood cells that recognize damaged and foreign substances (e.g., cellular debris, microbes and cancer cells) which they engulf and digest in a process called phagocytosis, that triggers signaling pathways leading to inflammation. Macrophage response to oxidized lipids, lipoproteins and their degradation products is central for maintaining healthy tissue. During disease states, such as macular degeneration, however, pronounced macrophage function can aggravate inflamed tissue by creating reactive oxygen species and amplifying inflammation thus causing further tissue damage. Molecules that can modulate macrophage activity are pertinent targets due to their potential to enhance clearance of cellular debris without generating reactive oxygen species and accrued inflammatory factors. Targeting the CD36 scavenger receptor, which is commonly found on the surface of macrophages and integrally engaged in the absorption of oxidized lipid and lipoprotein debris, we have conceived cyclic azapeptides that can modulate the inflammatory response to favor clearance without production of reactive oxygen species. Central to the proposed research will be the further optimization and use of the cyclic azapeptides to mitigate the causes of age-related macular degeneration, the leading cause of adult vision loss by modulating macrophage-mediated inflammation.

column36: Intraoperative Surgical Tools for Advanced Reconstruction Workflow to Optimize Outcomes of Head and Neck Cancer Treatment
column37: Advanced head and neck cancers involving the jaw often require aggressive removal of the diseased parts of the jaw. Reconstruction of the resulting defect is typically done with patient donor bone from the fibula. The singular, typically linear, piece of donor bone is cut into pieces and shaped to best recreate occlusion with a curvilinear shape. This process involves multiple complex osteotomies, since the accuracy of the reconstruction significantly impacts cosmetic and functional outcomes. Traditional intraoperative execution of this procedure is challenging, time consuming and may not provide effective eating and speaking outcomes. Recently, some healthcare centers, including our own, have adopted a pre-planning approach. Patient CT scans are used to create a digital 3D model, which can be manipulated to a target reconstruction. Then surgical cutting guides are 3D printed to replicate the plan intraoperatively. This process has been demonstrated to save OR time and lead to higher quality reconstructions. We have developed our own in-house version of this program has been in use for over a year at VGH. However, this approach still has flaws: current planning techniques only seek to optimize occlusion, and do not consider functional outcomes such as chewing, speaking and swallowing. Additionally, these surgeries rely on the optimal resection planes not changing between the day of planning and the day of surgery. We seek to create an Intraoperative Surgical Tools for Advanced Reconstruction Workflow (ISTAR) that solves both of these problems. Rather than planning the case days or even weeks prior to surgery and leaving time for the tumour to grow, ISTAR will enable planning based on intraoperatively defined cutting planes. We will create image guided tools that will facilitate interfacing between the digital and physical space. The planning will be based on advanced functional modeling that can simulate functional outcomes, leading to better reconstructions.

column36: An integrated spectroscopy-ultrasound surgical navigation system for residual cancer detection in breast surgery.
column37: Breast cancer affects 1 in 8 women during their lives and is the second-leading cause of female cancer related deaths. The ideal treatment is breast-conservation surgery , during its early stage, to remove cancer while conserving healthy tissue. Unfortunately, the current resection methods have high positive margin rates (when cancer cells are found on the edge of the resected specimen) of up to nearly 40%. Positive margins are linked to high probability of recurrence and thus require repeat surgery. On average, one out of every three women undergoing breast-conservation surgery needs at least one additional surgery due to positive margins. Repeat surgery leads to increased risk of postoperative complications, impaired cosmetics, delayed radiation therapy, increased psychological distress, and increased costs and risks of a second general anesthesia. Repeat surgery often leads to full mastectomy, which is a traumatic experience for a patient who expected a curative treatment with breast-conservation. Through development of a unique surgical navigation system that integrates intra-operative ultrasound imaging with an acoustic spectroscopy technique, we intend to ensure that the resection cavity is clear of cancer before releasing the patient from the operating table. We take advantage of conventional ultrasound scanners, while building a unique spectroscopic-ultrasound probe, and thus the resulting system will be affordable and accessible to all care facilities in Canada. The proposed system should enable significant reduction in positive margin rates, thereby reducing the number of repeat surgeries, and yielding significant quality of life benefits to patients and a significant reduction in health care costs.

column36: The Virtual Music Teacher: Children of all abilities banding together in early childhood music education
column37: Children with disabilities are less likely to take part in music learning than their typically developing peers. Learning to play a musical instrument can have positive social and health benefits for children with and without disabilities, especially in the preschool years. Many young children with disabilities are unable to benefit from music lessons because of scheduling, resource, and accessibility barriers. A "virtual music teacher" that can engage young children with disabilities in early music learning at home may overcome some of these barriers. We will develop a music application (AI-MiRMA) that intelligently responds to children's play with real-life musical instruments (e.g. maracas) and guides them in music learning. AI-MiRMA will be co-created with the community of clients, families, therapists, music therapists, engineers, games developers, and researchers at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital and music educators at the University of Toronto and Humber College. New ways to track a child's music play, encourage learning and group play, and adapt musical tasks to diverse physical abilities will be created. We will test AI-MiRMA with 15 children with Cerebral Palsy (aged 3-6 years) and their families to understand: (i) if young children using AI-MiRMA at home can achieve the minimum "dose" of music-making training expected to impact outcomes (i.e. 6 hours over 10 weeks), (ii) if it contributes to family-led goals in music learning and participation, and (iii) what families' think about the risks and opportunities of using artificial intelligence to support young children's music learning. AI-MiRMA will put music learning and its benefits within reach of thousands of young children with and without disabilities. Sharing AI-MiRMA will happen first at Holland Bloorview, then through our partnering organizations, the Ontario Association of Children's Rehabilitation Services, Humber, Toronto Symphony Orchestra, and TVOKids.

column36: Development of Machine Learning to Assess Lung Function Using Airway Oscillometry
column37: Pulmonary function (PF) tests are useful tools to diagnose and monitor lung disease. The gold standard test uses spirometry to measure FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 sec). However, FEV1 only measures the large airways although many lung diseases begin in the small airways (SAw). If we could measure SAw function accurately, we could detect and treat lung diseases earlier. Airway oscillometry (OSc) measures SAw function accurately but OSc outputs are complex and difficult to interpret. For these reasons, OSc is not commonly used. To improve the clinical utility of OSc, we will develop machine learning (ML) to classify OSc outputs as normal or SAw obstruction. ML will 'learn' from spirometry and OSc data of bone marrow and lung transplant patients who undergo frequent PF testing because SAw obstruction develops often post-transplant. A large dataset with a wide range of normal/abnormal lung function values are important features that will allow ML to develop with high predictive accuracy. We will then validate the ML algorithm in patients with confirmed SAw obstruction. We will also assess the wider applicability of OSc and ML in the general population in 2 community PF laboratories with diverse lung diseases, and a community cohort in Fort McMurray. The project is led by a Lung Specialist (Chow) and Engineer with expertise in ML (Valaee). Our partners are appropriate: University Health Network is a world leading centre in lung diseases. Thorasys, a Canadian company, developed the only Health Canada approved OSc device. Earlier diagnosis of lung disease using ML with OSc will improve the health of Canadians and decrease the overall health burden. The project contributes to human resource development by providing rich learning experiences for graduate students and cardiopulmonary function technologists in Medicine and Engineering. The project adds to the Canadian economy by contributing to the medical device development and manufacturing in Canada.

column36: Neonatal Stem Cell Secretomes as a Novel Regenerative Therapy for Heart Failure
column37: Heart failure has a universally poor outcome, with only 50% of patients surviving a further five years after diagnosis. The medications that are available for heart failure have little impact on patient survival, mostly targeting the control of disease symptoms. Regenerative medicine, where the heart is promoted to repair itself, is a new, potentially disruptive, treatment paradigm that could provide lasting change to organ function. In determining how this concept could be harnessed for benefit, we and others have described how the hearts of very young patients (neonates) have a higher intrinsic ability to repair and regenerative themselves. Using tissue samples from pediatric patients undergoing open heart surgery, we have found that cells with regenerative potential (stem cells) isolated from neonatal hearts secrete different molecules than cells isolated from older patients. We now propose to harness this capacity into a novel biologic therapy for heart failure patients. We have collected and preliminarily characterized an initial set of samples from pediatric heart surgery patients. In this project, we will expand our analysis to include a broader range of patient age and cardiac diagnosis. The secreted mixtures will be tested for regenerative potential in established assays, and their composition determined, illuminating the components with the highest therapeutic potential. Using a novel biocompatible scaffold invented by a member of our collaborative group, we will create an optimal delivery vehicle for injection into the failing hearts of patients, allowing for sustained release of the reparative molecules. Finally, we will test the utility of the new therapies in a large animal model of heart failure. We will work in close collaboration with our industry partner, Bluerock Therapeutics, whose sole mandate is to bring regenerative therapies to market, allowing for immediate commercial application and translation into patient care.

column36: Development and clinical assessment of novel biomarker drugs targeting SSAT1 for detection and therapeutic monitoring of glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common brain tumor in adults and is a death sentence for patients. The strikingly poor survival for patients with GBM (average survival 14-16 months following diagnosis) is due in part to limited early detection methods and an absence of effective therapeutic options. The studies proposed would establish important evidence for the use of Health Canada approved drugs such as amantadine and rimantadine as a safe, effective and affordable way to monitor GBM. The method is based on the over-production of a key enzyme in GBM cells called spermine/ spermadine n-acetyl transferase (SSAT1). The increased SSAT1 expression in GBM results in increased metabolism of the drug which is detected in the blood or urine of patients with GBM. Studies will provide evidence for the effectiveness of the drug amantadine, in detecting GBM in both cell culture and accepted rodent brain tumor models. Other drugs with similar chemical structure to amantadine will be examined in the cell culture and animal models to optimize the drug biomarker for brain penetration and tumor cell activity. The studies will conclude with an initial assessment of the selected drug biomarker in patients with GBM to determine feasibility for clinical brain tumor applications. These bench to bedside studies will be utilized by our industrial partner, BioMark Diagnostics, to help improve identification and care for patients with GB.

column36: Using artificial intelligence to identify and predict delirium among hospitalized medical patients
column37: Delirium is an acute neurocognitive disorder which affects up to half of older hospitalized medical patients. It can cause confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, and agitation, leading to significant distress for patients and their caregivers. It can lead to dementia, longer hospital stays, increased health costs, and death. While delirium can be prevented and treated, it is difficult to identify and predict. Current methods require either ongoing clinical assessment or use of complicated screening tools. This is expensive and often impractical for most hospitals. Given these challenges, delirium reporting relies on administrative data, which significantly underestimate true rates of delirium. From a quality of care perspective, this inaccuracy makes it difficult to compare rates of delirium across hospitals and evaluate the impact of interventions to improve delirium care. In this project, we will utilize artificial intelligence to develop two automated tools, which will use routine data extracted from electronic medical records to identify delirium cases and predict patient delirium risk. As there is concern that AI applications may worsen health inequity because they do not take into consideration social and economic variables, we will test whether there is bias in the detection and prediction of delirium with our tools. Our approach is novel in delirium care and healthcare quality improvement more generally, and could change how quality indicators are measured. Moreover, it has the potential to improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare costs. With has assembled a multidisciplinary research team from computer, health, and social sciences, and are partnering with Health Quality Ontario (HQO), a provincial advisor on quality in health care. HQO are an active participant in the planning the methods and outcomes for the project to ensure that they can be used to improve health care at both a systems and individual patient level.
