column36: Studying the single-neuronal representation of higher-order cognitive processes in the human brain
column37: Despite ongoing progress in our understanding of brain areas involved in human cognition, the underlying single cellular mechanisms remain almost completely unknown. Here, I aim to use unique access to acute neuronal recordings in subjects undergoing planned intra-operative neurophysiology to evaluate human cognitive processes that cannot be evaluated by other study modalities or animal models. A core foundation of human social behavior is "theory of mind", or the capacity to infer another's beliefs, thoughts or desires and recognize that others may have different beliefs than one's own. This ability is a fundamental milestone in human development and is broadly disrupted in psychiatric conditions such as autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. Its single neuronal and population based underpinnings, however, are not known. Building upon extensive experience in the Dr. Williams lab, I aim to record from individual neurons in the dorsal prefrontal cortex as participants perform a structured task that presents them with short narratives about real-world scenarios. The task requires them to formulate an idea about the hidden state-of-mind of individuals in the narratives and demonstrate understanding of another's beliefs even when they differ from one's own. This project will allow me to test, for the first time, a number of core hypotheses about how individual neurons in the human prefrontal cortex processes information about basic events, their relation to other social agents and internal beliefs. It will also allow me to construct an explicit neuron-based model of how beliefs are represented within the human brain and determine the degree to which the semantic features describing the information is encoded in the prefrontal cortex. This proposal will provide insight on a foundational human cognitive process at the single cellular level and will dramatically advance our understanding of pathologic conditions such as autism spectrum disorder.

column36: Mapping the Human Apoptosis Genetic Interaction Network
column37: Despite great advances in genetic research, we cannot fully explain how traits and diseases are inherited. Studies in organisms with simple genomes have indicated that genetic interactions, i.e cooperating genes, play a role in how genetic information encodes appearance and function of cells. With the new precise and efficient CRISPR genome editing technology, such interaction studies can now be carried out for human genes. We will utilize CRISPR to map genetic interactions in human cells. Due to the large number of human genes, it is not possible to test all of them for their pairwise interactions. We will thus focus on genes that regulate programmed cell death (apoptosis) and map their interactions with all other genes. Apoptosis is a tightly regulated process that is essential for the balance of cell growth and death. If it is misregulated, cancer and other diseases can arise. The crosstalk between different apoptosis components is not fully understood, and not all genes involved in this process are known. Our preliminary experiments have identified interesting candidates for novel apoptosis genes, confirming the feasibility of our approach. We will determine the genetic interactions for other apoptosis genes, enabling us to assemble a network, because genes with similar functions are expected to have similar interactions. We can then classify genes into functional groups and predict the functions of uncharacterized genes when they are found connected to well-studied genes in the network. Our approach will also identify interaction partners of genes that are involved in diseases, which could allow indirect treatment through targeting of their interaction partners. In summary, this project will generate a genome-wide map of how apoptosis genes work together with their interaction partners in health and disease, which will benefit fundamental biology as well as medical research aimed at identifying the vulnerabilities of cancer and other apoptosis-related diseases.

column36: Comparaison des effets a court et moyen termes d'un entrainement par intervalles vs. en puissance sur la fonction musculaire et les capacites fonctionnelles d'hommes ages dynapeniques-obeses
column37: Le vieillissement est associe a une perte de masse musculaire et de force musculaire (dynapenie [DYN]) ainsi qu'a une augmentation de masse grasse (obesite [Ob]), ce qui entraine une deterioration des capacites fonctionnelles (CF). Les personnes DYN-Ob (~ 20% de la population) presentent des CF inferieures a celles ayant une seule de ces deux conditions. En relatif, les hommes sont plus touches par ce phenomene. L'activite physique et plus specifiquement l'entrainement en puissance (EP) est une solution efficace pour contrer ces effets deleteres. Malheureusement, plus de 50% des aines sont sedentaires et une des raisons est le manque de temps. De ce fait, l'entrainement par intervalle (EI) plus court a emerge comme une alternative. Neanmoins, les effets de EI et EP sur les consequences de la DYN-OB restent meconnus. L'objectif de ce projet post-doctoral est de comparer via un essai randomise et controle mene en double aveugle, les effets d'un EP vs. un EI sur la CF d'hommes ages DYN-Ob a court (post-intervention) et moyen (6 mois apres) terme. Pour ce faire, 90 hommes DYN-Ob (65 ans et +) seront repartis aleatoirement en 3 groupes d'intervention (12 semaines) soit : 1) EP (type resistance - explosif: 1 heure/seance, 3fois/sem) vs 2) EI (type cardiovasculaire - intense : 30 min/seance, 3fois/sem) vs. 3) controle (sans intervention). La composition corporelle, les capacites fonctionnelles, la force et la puissance musculaire, le volume et l'infiltration du gras dans le muscle, les habitudes de vie et les depenses energetiques, seront mesurees avant, a la fin et 6 mois apres l'intervention. Considerant l'evolution demographique de notre population et sa trajectoire en terme de prevalence de l'obesite, definir si une de ces modalites d'AP s'avere plus benefique pour les personnes DYN-Ob est une priorite pour notre systeme de sante pour maintenir la qualite de vie des aines.

column37: Almost 37 millions of people are living with HIV (PLWH) worldwide, including 75,000 in Canada. HIV infection is characterized by a progressive destruction of the overall immune defenses. Actual HIV treatments help PLWH to live almost as long as people who are not infected by HIV. However, the virus persists and hides within their body and exhausts their immune system. Recently, a population of human immune cells, called "regulatory T-cells" (Treg) has been identified to contribute in cancer and chronic viral illnesses progression. It has also been demonstrated that the levels of Tregs are higher in PLWH than general population in line with disease progression as these cells are able to inhibit anti-HIV immune responses. Besides Tregs, another type of immune cells, Th17 cells, plays a pivotal role in the maintenance of mucosal immunity and imbalance between Th17 and Tregs results in HIV disease progression. We hypothesize that changes in cellular metabolism contribute in Tregs increased frequencies, which in turn, help HIV to hide in viral reservoirs of PLWH. Specifically, we aim to understand (1) what is the status of Th17/Treg balance in PLWH with different clinical outcomes; (2) what are the metabolic mechanisms involved in Th17/Treg balance during HIV infection; and, (3) how Tregs contribute in HIV persistence and the immuno-deficiency. In this regard, our laboratories will use different well-established experiments on biological specimens from PLWH with different clinical and therapeutic outcomes. This research will help to develop new therapeutic approaches aimed at modulating deleterious functions of Tregs. Targeting of Tregs with appropriate immuno-therapeutic interventions in PLWH, could lead to a better immune recovery and might help to find an HIV cure.

column36: A systems biology approach to understand the determinants of protein robustness to mutation
column37: All humans carry mutations, both inherited and acquired during their life, making every genome unique. Some of these changes can significantly impact human health, for example causing genetic diseases or increasing the risk of cancer in those who carry them. Since it is impossible to perform laboratory experiments to test the impact of all known and possible mutations, scientists have worked to develop tools that help predict their effect. These methods are not perfect and could be improved by the integration of more experimental data. Many of these mutations alter proteins, the molecular machines responsible for the survival of the cell. Organisms from bacteria to human have developed specialized proteins called chaperones to help them ensure proteins remain functional in periods of stress, but their ability to protect the cell from harmful mutations remains misunderstood. The objective of this project is to generate new reference information to better predict the health impact of mutations, as well as understand the influence of cell mechanisms such as chaperones in buffering or aggravating their effects. By integrating this data, we will gain a better understanding of how a person's heritage influences disease risk and make significant progress towards personalized therapies adapted to the individual.

column37: Current treatments for metastatic breast cancer are ineffective for disease that has spread (metastasized) to other organs. We have also shown that these drugs can unleash immune responses suppressed by tumor cells, potentially stimulating the immune system to attack metastatic breast cancer. In this project, we will test these drugs in sophisticated models of metastatic breast cancer and bring them to the clinic for phase I trials in breast cancer patients. Our team unites world-leading Canadian fundamental and translational scientists with breast cancer clinical trials experts. We will carry out a pan-Canadian clinical trial testing our new therapeutic strategy and use unique resources, including extensive banks of tumour tissue and specialized animal models, to determine how these drugs work and how future treatments can be improved. We will identify all proteins whose production is altered by these drugs, identify responsive breast cancer subtypes and therapeutic combinations that allow us to maximize their effects, and determine whether their immunity-enhancing actions can be harnessed to further increase their effectiveness. column37: Mental illness accounts for a large and growing share of the total burden of disease in Canada. The objectives of the proposed research are: (i) to measure the prevalence of psychosocial work factors in the Canadian population; (ii) to examine how these psychosocial work factors cluster together across the labour market; (iii) to examine the association between different clusters of psychosocial work factors and mental health outcomes; and (iv) to investigate whether clusters of psychosocial work factors contribute to inequalities in mental health outcomes across age, gender, and occupational groups. To meet these objectives, the proposed research will use data from a 2016 population-based survey administered to a sample of 5,697 Canadian workers. This unique survey provides the most comprehensive portrait of the psychosocial work environment currently available in Canada. The knowledge gained through this research will aid in the development of effective workplace intervention strategies to promote the mental health of the Canadian workforce.

column37: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy diagnosed and the second leading cause of cancer related deaths in women both in Canada and worldwide. This classification of breast cancer was established based on molecular research that identified the biological changes in cell function that leads to the development of breast cancer, by measuring RNA expression. As a result, RNA profiling methods are now used to identify breast cancer types, significantly improving the diagnosis and management of breast cancer overall. However, these molecular tests can currently guide effective treatment only for two of the four main types, and there are still improvements needed, particularly in the type known as basal-like breast cancer. This is the most aggressive form of the disease, with a propensity to afflict younger women, and still lacks successful treatments beyond partial benefits from cytotoxic chemotherapy. Thus, new treatments are highly needed for young women with this aggressive group of breast cancers. We plan to address this problem using a new technology that can measure the expression of thousands of proteins in the same routine surgical tissues that are used for patient diagnosis. We propose to analyze 300 tumor samples from breast cancer patients, many with the basal-like RNA type, and link the expression of proteins with patient treatment and outcome. We expect that this study will identify basal-like breast cancers that may prove treatable with new targeted therapies. If successful, this study will guide more specific and effective treatment options for early stage breast cancer patients with the most aggressive type of the disease.

column36: Neuroprotective Effect of Sigma-1 Receptor and Activin A on Synaptic Function and Calcium Handling in Huntington's Disease
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a devastating inherited disease that can be detected before symptoms arise, but which is incurable. In HD patients, neurons involved in motor functions deteriorate, causing motor and cognitive problems. Neurons transmit signals in our brains, relying heavily on calcium for their function. The function impairment of the connections between neurons, known as synaptic function, as well as their ability to control calcium levels, form a common trait of many neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and HD. One level of calcium control is at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a cell organelle playing a significant part in protein production. This calcium regulation is abnormal in HD, leading to a change in protein production and a decrease in synaptic function. Interestingly, activating Sigma-1 receptors (S1Rs) - proteins located on the ER that play an important role in calcium regulation and therefore protein production - has been shown to normalize this calcium handling and restore synaptic function. The purpose of this project is to determine the relationship between S1Rs, protein production, calcium handling, and synaptic function, in order to better understand the disease mechanisms of HD and other neurodegenerative diseases, and to find new potential treatments. To conduct this project, I will utilize electrophysiological, pharmacological, imaging, and behavioral techniques. As there are currently no effective treatments for HD, the results from this study may revolutionize our approach to patients with this debilitating disease.

column37: This research involves Indigenous peoples. Canada is in the midst of a growing overdose crisis which accounted for at least 3,980 deaths in 2017. Overdose deaths have been particularly devastating in British Columbia (BC), where approximately four people die each day from an overdose. The crisis highlights the urgent need for life-saving overdose prevention interventions, including the expansion of supervised drug consumption services where people may use illicit drugs in the presence of health care professionals and other staff trained to intervene during an overdose. Diverse new models of supervised drug consumption services are being rapidly scaled-up across the province, including peer-run 'overdose prevention sites', in-hospital sites, mobile vans, housing-based services, and those integrated within community health centers. The diversity of supervised drug consumption models currently being implemented in BC represents an unprecedented opportunity to examine how supervised drug consumption services may be designed and delivered across different contexts to maximize their reach and public health benefit. As services are implemented in new settings, research is also urgently required to examine how features of the social and structural environment-including drug laws, regulatory environments, policing practices, and local drug use cultures-influence the implementation and impact of supervised consumption services. This study addresses this gap by using ethnographic approaches to examine how emerging models of supervised drug consumption services (e.g. peer-run, in-hospital, housing-based) interact with social and structural features of the implementation context to shape the social practices of people who use drugs and their onward risk of overdose. Findings from this study will contribute to the overdose response by identifying policy and programmatic changes to optimize the reach and public health benefits of supervised drug consumption services.

column36: Evaluation of pertussis immunization in pregnancy
column37: Pertussis, also called whooping cough, is a lung infection caused by the bacteria Bordetella pertussis. It is a major public health concern. Despite high vaccination coverage, we have seen a resurgence of the disease, both globally and in Canada. In Canada, 60-74% of pertussis cases are among infants younger than 2 months, who are too young to be vaccinated. Among infants younger than 2 months and admitted to the hospital with pertussis, 38% are admitted to intensive care and 2.3% die. To protect infants too young to be vaccinated, a number of countries (e.g. the US, UK, Australia) including Canada recommend vaccinating pregnant women against whooping cough. This approach to vaccination relies, at least in part, on the transfer of anti-pertussis antibodies from the mother to the newborn via the placenta. However, there are critical questions that must be addressed before this strategy is widely implemented: (1) we must determine the best time during pregnancy to give whooping cough vaccine; (2) we must show how efficiently anti-pertussis antibodies transferred from the mother to the newborn protect babies; and (3) we must determine whether vaccination against whooping cough in pregnancy suppresses the infant's immune response to the routine vaccines administered during infancy. This project aims to answer these gaps in knowledge. I will assess the function of anti-pertussis antibodies in newborns born to women immunized against whooping cough in different times in pregnancy. I will establish new laboratory tests that will further assess the function of anti-pertussis antibodies produced after vaccination in pregnancy. Lastly, I will analyze antibody levels of all published studies to date that addressed whether vaccination against whooping cough in pregnancy affects the antibody levels in the infants after their own vaccination. Altogether, this project will ensure we use the best strategy possible to prevent whooping cough in young infants.

column36: Profiling sex differences in neuronal network activity and drug responsiveness in an animal model of depression
column37: Depression is a devastating disorder with incidence in women two times higher than in men, however little is known about the mechanisms that contribute to this increased vulnerability. Normal brain function requires coordinated electrical activity of networks for the communication within and between brain regions. Not only has the dysregulation of electrical activity been shown to play an important role in depression, the normalization of aberrant activity relates directly to treatment success. In these studies, sex differences in innate and stress-induced changes in the functionality of brain electrical output will first be evaluated using a rat model of depression. The goal is to assess the capacity of these electrical alterations to associate with and predict subsequent depression behaviours. In a second study, we will evaluate sex differences in antidepressant responsiveness using a specific diagnostic measure: the normalization of brain electrical patterns. In the final study we will evaluate whether sex differences in the activity of the protein GSK-3 influences brain electrical activity and depression behaviours, and whether suppressing GSK-3 activation can be protective for the development of depression. In all studies, female cycling will be monitored to determine the relationship between the reproductive cycle and changes in brain patterns and behaviour. The goal of these studies is to take a novel approach to evaluate how brain regions are functionally linked in depression, and to identify critical sex differences in brain electrical patterns that may contribute to, or predict, depression susceptibility and drug responsiveness. This research will identify a potential mechanism by which brain activity may be regulated in a sex-dependent manner, via GSK-3. The results will identify electrical patterns that may serve as biomarkers for depression and will lead to more personalized therapies to offer significantly improved health outcomes for this disorder.

column36: Characterizing the roles of synapse organizers in mediating synaptic function and brain-based diseases
column37: The human brain is made up of neural circuits that are thought to underlie all brain function. These circuits are made up of contact points called synapses where individual nerve cells communicate with each other. For many years, scientists have been working to shed light on how nerve cells transmit information to each other, as well as the molecules involved in this process. In order for information to be delivered efficiently, or at all, proper synapse development has to take place. Synapse development is a process mediated by the binding of cell surface molecules located on the outer borders of both the nerve cell transmitting signals, and the nerve cell receiving them. The binding of these cell surface molecules, which have been coined 'synapse organizing molecules', acts as an anchor that physically glues the synapse together. In addition, depending on which synapse organizers are partnered up, certain properties will be conferred to that synapse. For example, certain binding configurations will give rise to synapses that release excitatory signals, whereas other ones will lead to the development of synapses that release inhibitory signals. This is especially important given that aberrant synaptic development has been emerging as a significant factor that underlies altered neuronal function in complex neuropsychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder. Moreover, little was known about mechanisms regulating the functions of these synapse organizers until recently. Our lab has discovered a process essential to the binding between many of these synaptic molecules and in turn, proper synapse development. Thus, my research is geared towards further functional characterization of synapse organizing molecules to develop a therapy to alleviate the brain-based defects in those suffering from mental disorders.

column36: Survival of the fittest: cell competition in cancer progression
column37: Despite decades of research and development of diagnostic technology, cancer is still often diagnosed based on relatively large abnormalities in the tissue - growths, lumps, or bumps visible to the naked eye. The size of the smallest detectable tumor is still approximately a billion cells. Furthermore, it is often only possible to detect cancer cells that have spread from the initial tumor site to distant organs at late stages, when the cancer has progressed past the point of being curable. Thus, being able to identify cancer cells at very early stages and low numbers could enable identification of molecules to mark cancerous and pre-cancerous cells, and lead to development of therapies to kill cancer cells before the cancer spreads. One potential way to identify cancer cells at early stages is by discovering novel mechanisms cancer cells use to promote their own growth and survival. Cell competition is a process by which faster growing ("winner") cells kill the slower growing ("loser") cells around them, in order to enable their own growth. Although cell competition is known to be important for animal development and for maintaining tissue health, it has not been extensively studied in cancer in animals. I will use a zebrafish model of melanoma to investigate if cancer cells use cell competition to promote their own growth by killing the cells around them. I will transplant melanoma cells into transparent fish and use cutting-edge live, whole-animal microscopy to investigate if tumors cause the death of the surrounding normal cells. In parallel, I will induce cell competition in tumors by upregulating the cancer-promoting gene Myc, and perform a drug screen to identify molecules that inhibit competition and tumor growth, to provide insight into signaling pathways that could be driving cell competition in cancer. These studies will detail molecules that promote cancer progression, and describe potential targets for development of drugs to block cancer spreading.

column36: Predicting response to cognitive behavioural therapy for major depressive disorder
column37: While a variety of antidepressant medications and psychological ("talk") therapies have been shown to effectively treat depression, fewer than half of depressed individuals will reach remission following initial treatment. This is due, in part, to a trial-and-error approach often used in the treatment of depression, and a lack of tools for determining which treatment will be most effective for an individual. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which consists of skill-building techniques for helping individuals think and act in ways that will help alleviate and prevent depressive symptoms, has been shown to be as effective as antidepressant medication in treating acute depression and preventing future depressive episodes. However, we do not currently have a method for predicting what specific CBT techniques will be helpful for a person, and which can be omitted to save time and costs associated with psychological interventions. Therefore, the current research will investigate whether cost-effective, easy-to-administer computer-based tasks measuring core features of depression, namely negative emotional bias and motivational insensitivity, can predict what specific CBT techniques will be most effective for treating an individual's depressive symptoms. If shown to selectively predict response to cognitive and behavioural strategies for improving depressed mood, these computer-based tools may be useful for streamlining depression treatment decisions in a range of clinical and geographical contexts.

column37: Congenital heart diseases (CHD) are caused by structural abnormalities of the heart that are present at birth. CHD occurs in 1% of all births worldwide and are the leading cause of death from birth defects. 257,000 Canadians have CHD, most of them adults who require multiple surgeries and interventions. Surprisingly, the cause of the majority of CHD cases is unknown due to the large number of genes that can be affected or mutated in this disease. The regulation of these messenger RNAs (mRNAs) by other small non-protein coding RNAs (miRNAs) is essential for the production of heart structures, such as the valves, which are often found to be abnormal in CHD. I will use powerful next-generation sequencing techniques and generate mutants of candidate genes to study their role in heart development and ultimately use these candidates in human genetic analyses to further the study of congenital heart disease.

column36: Air Pollution Induces Glucocorticoid Resistance in Humans
column37: Asthma is a chronic disease that affects over 2.5 million Canadians, placing a significant burden on families and the Canadian health care system. Asthma attacks or exacerbations are periods of progressively worsening symptoms due to swelling and closure of the airways, leading to frightening feelings of suffocation, hospitalization, and even death. Inhaling allergens and/or air pollution from various sources such as forest fires or automobile exhaust often provokes these attacks. Asthmatics cope with their symptoms using medications broadly called inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). These medications act on cells lining the lungs by turning on and off sets of genes that suppress airway inflammation and asthma symptoms. Recent studies have suggested that increased air pollution may lead to increased ICS use, and our lab's research has shown that air pollution interrupts ICS's actions on human lung cells grown on petri dishes. To further examine this complex interaction, we need to investigate the relationship between air pollution and ICS in a rigorous controlled human clinical study. In our study, research volunteers will be exposed for two hours to filtered air or air pollution at a level experienced in major cities such as Beijing before taking a placebo or ICS. Every volunteer will experience each combination in a random order. Cells collected directly from the volunteers' airways will be examined using state of the art gene sequencing techniques to determine which genes have turned on and off. This will enable me to investigate how increased air pollution influences ICS effectiveness in asthmatic patients. This is significant because it can immediately be used to improve treatment guidelines and inform educational policies aimed at preventing asthma attacks. Considering that 92% of the world's population live in areas exceeding WHO air pollution guidelines, findings from our research have the potential to impact millions of lives in Canada and abroad.

column36: Development of a Concussion Management Platform for Children and Youth: Bridging the Gap Between Research and Practice
column37: Concussion is a major public health concern. Despite increased recognition of the serious health impacts of concussion, the number of injuries is rising. The presentation of symptoms after a concussion can have a significant impact on a child/youth's participation in daily life, including at school and in sport. While child/youth specific guidelines exist to help navigate return to activity (RTA) and return to school (RTS), they are poorly understood and adhered to in general practice. Most existing concussion management Apps, of which there are only a few, aim to provide education and some method for recording and tracking symptoms. These Apps are information dense, lack user interaction and fail to integrate child/youth patterns of activity with symptom exacerbation to provide guidance about RTA- and RTS based on evidence-based guidelines. The proposed project aims to create a concussion management platform that incorporates and streamlines all aspects of concussion management and monitoring. The platform will be interactive and provide children and their families with more autonomy, knowledge and control of their recovery trajectories, increasing overall adherence. Features of the platform include symptom monitoring, cognitive testing, and real-time activity monitoring and feedback. Feedback will allow the child/youth to immediately adjust activity level to prevent symptom exacerbation and longer recovery time.

column36: Regulation of NLRP3 inflammasome activation
column37: NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex, plays a critical role in innate immunity, which enables us to fight against pathogens. NLRP3 inflammasome is activated by various stimuli that directly or indirectly related to pathogen invasion. K+ efflux is a common cellular event associated with these stimuli. A protein called Nek7 is required for the inflammasome activation through interacting with NLRP3, a central component of NLRP3 inflammasome. Importantly the interaction is promoted by K+ efflux. Here I propose to study at molecular level how K+ efflux leads to Nek7-mediated NLRP3 activation. Since only activated NLRP3 triggers key inflammatory responses to defend invaded pathogens, it is vital to understand how NLRP3 is activated. The proposed study will yield essential information regarding NLRP3 activation and advance the field of innate immunity. NLRP3 inflammasome links to the pathogenesis of a wide array of inflammatory disorders, such as silicosis, gouty arthritis, atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Understanding the mechanism of NLRP3 activation will also provide basis for designing drugs to target NLRP3 activation process, benefiting human health.

column36: Investigating the Neural Basis of Social Cognition in Autism Spectrum Disorders
column37: Impaired social functioning is a central feature of Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs); however, few treatments are available. There is evidence that two networks in the brain are important for social functioning: one for understanding the actions and basic emotions of others (mirror neuron system), and another for understanding that others can have thoughts and feelings that differ from one's own (theory of mind). Social functioning deficits are also central to schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs), and healthy controls (HCs) exhibit a wide range of social functioning. These two networks have been shown to exist along a continuum in ASDs, SSDs and HCs; thus, studying these populations together has the potential to reveal patterns of brain-behaviour relationships that cut across these diagnoses and that underlie social functioning. In the proposed study, we will evaluate how brain structure is related to brain function, and how both are related to social functioning. To achieve this, we will use two types of brain imaging: one to examine structural connections between these networks, and another to examine brain activity in these networks (while performing a task that activates them). We will relate both these brain measures to behavioural and clinical assessments of social functioning. We hypothesize that altered brain structure will result in impaired brain function, and consequently poor social functioning. We also expect that greater usage of the theory of mind network will be associated with better social functioning, whereas greater usage of the mirror neuron network will be associated with worse social functioning. By characterizing brain structure-function-behaviour relations in and between each network, we are taking a critical step towards identifying targets for novel treatments to improve social functioning. Improvements in social functioning will ameliorate the quality of life of individuals with ASD and their families, and benefit Canada economically.

column36: In search of neuroimaging markers for neurodegeneration in presymptomatic frontotemporal dementia: A longitudinal study of genetically at-risk cohort
column37: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) affects up to 37,000 Canadians. Many people develop FTD during their 40's and 50's, accompanied by a broad range of behavioral and personality changes as well as speech and language difficulties. Looking from outside, it is difficult to distinguish FTD from other types of dementias such as Alzheimer's disease; what's more, FTD might be mistakenly perceived as psychiatric diseases with detrimental delay in diagnosis. FTD is marked by progressive nerve cell death in the frontal and temporal regions of the brain, which influence personality, behavior, emotion and speech. Once the symptoms set in, it is impossible to reverse FTD. This means it is crucial to treat patients at risk of developing FTD as early as possible before their brains suffer irreversible damage. But how do we know if someone is at risk if one is not yet showing any symptoms? People with mutations in specific genes are at risk of developing FTD in the future. In these people, abnormal changes in brain structures can be found years before the full symptoms appear. If we can follow how the abnormal changes propagate during this early period, we may be able to predict who may develop the disease before the deficits set in. We will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI brain scans) and other tools to understand the sites and kinds of brain injury and define their relationships to behavioral and cognitive abnormalities. This will be done in a unique group of subjects recruited at our clinic at UBC who are potential carriers of genetic mutations that cause FTD due to their family history. Our findings will help clinicians and patients to recognize the changes in brain structures that may occur before FTD symptoms develop. This information will be necessary to make informed decisions in determining the timing and type of therapies that can best suit the needs of the patients, with the ultimate goal of facilitating testing of new treatments for people at risk of developing FTD.

column37: Autism Spectrum Disorders affect hundreds of thousands of individuals, their families and community. More than 80% of parents and caregivers of children with ASD complain about sleep problems, which lead to parental stress and decrease in family well-being. This protocol will allow us to establish a sleep profile, verify the presence of physiological causes associated with poor sleep, and determine whether sleep has an impact on cognitive functioning (learning and memory). The results will help developing specific interventions, according to their clinical status, to improve sleep in these children, therefore increase their quality of life, the well-being of families and reduce the pressure on health and social systems.

column36: Role of placental serotonin and estrogens in the fetal programming of depression and cardiovascular alterations following in utero exposure to pre-eclampsia
column37: Pre-eclampsia is a placental disease that affects maternal and fetal health. Alteration of placental estrogen and serotonin levels are notably associated with alteration of placental cell function in this disease. Both serotonin and estrogens are crucial regulators of fetal development and placental function. Intrauterine exposition to pre-eclampsia has been associated with increased risk of depression and cardiac defect in the offspring. Fetal programming is a concept that stipulates that the intrauterine environment affects permanently the development of structure and function of tissues in the offspring, which can lead to diseases in the later adult life when the offspring is maladapted to the actual environment. In this project, we want to assess if this phenomenon explains the known association between pre-eclampsia and development of depression and cardiovascular diseases in the offspring. Using animal models and cells isolated from human placentas, we will test the hypothesis that placental estrogen and serotonin disruption contribute to this association. Depression and cardiac defects both have important societal impacts as depression has a high lifetime prevalence (10-20%), early age onset and persistence, which contribute to important costs, while cardiovascular diseases are leading causes of overall infant and adult mortality. Understanding the development of these diseases and eventually preventing them is of great interest for the population. Moreover, the placenta is often considered as a medical waste, but our study will contribute to giving more attention to this organ, which could predict health and diseases in later life. Pre-eclampsia is relatively well monitored during pregnancy, but considering the impact on the fetus at the level of organ development, not only at the survival level, could bring new insights in the research for treatments of the maternal-feto-placental unit.

column36: Evidence-informed implementation of low-barrier interventions to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with Canada's opioid overdose crisis
column37: Opioid overdose has caused more deaths in Canada than seen at the peak of the HIV epidemic in the 1990s. Overdose prevention sites (OPS) and injectable opioid agonist treatment (iOAT) are two new approaches to this issue. Community-based OPS monitor people at risk of overdose and provide rapid overdose response. They also offer access to education, addiction treatment and social services. iOAT is an addiction treatment for people who have not had success on oral medications. Both of these services save lives and reduce harm to people with severe opioid use disorders. Implementation of these services has begun, primarily in British Columbia. Yet, implementing evidence-based interventions broadly in health care usually takes 10-20 years. Greater urgency is needed. Implementation science (IS) is a research field focused on finding the best ways to shorten this gap. No IS research currently exists to guide the implementation and spread of these services in Canada's healthcare system. National planning requires evidence about which implementation strategies are effective in different settings. This study is the first of its kind in North America. We will engage policy makers, health care providers, people who use drugs and the recovery community. Together, we will identify factors supporting or hindering implementation in British Columbia and Canada. We will then test the effectiveness of different implementation strategies in different settings. Some of these strategies will include education, changing policy and improving communication networks. Effective implementation will mean better access to these life-saving interventions. Access will help keep more people in addiction treatment and decrease the risk of overdose and other health issues. These benefits will reduce burden on families and on the Canadian health and justice systems.

column36: Cognitive function in a sleep clinic cohort of patients with obstructive sleep apnea
column37: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic medical condition where patients stop breathing during sleep due to recurrent collapse of their upper airway, causing low oxygen levels (called "hypoxemia") and disturbed sleep. OSA can lead to trouble with memory, concentration and decision making (termed "cognitive impairment") in some, but not all, patients. Similarly, treatment of OSA improves cognitive functioning in some, but not all, patients. Though hypoxemia and sleep disruption are the most likely mechanisms whereby OSA leads to cognitive impairment, the size of this effect may be modified by co-existing factors such as age, gender, sleepiness, cognitive reserve (the brain's ability to resist damage), genetics, other health conditions and medications. Also, how much these factors impact the benefits of treating OSA is not known. Thus, the objectives of this study are to 1) determine the prevalence and severity of cognitive impairment in OSA before, and after, treatment, and 2) identify patient traits (termed "biomarkers") that can help predict which patients are at the greatest risk for cognitive impairment and who may benefit the most from OSA treatment. Adults with suspected OSA will be recruited from 5 academic sleep centres in Calgary, Saskatoon, Vancouver, Montreal and Quebec City. Patients will complete sleep and medical questionnaires and undergo cognitive testing (tests of memory and decision making) at study entry and 3 years later. All patients diagnosed with OSA will be offered the gold-standard treatment of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and their adherence to this therapy will be monitored. Blood samples will be taken at study entry for genetic analyses. The prevalence of cognitive impairment and its link to hypoxemia and disturbed sleep will be determined at study entry and 3 years later, while controlling for age, gender, sleepiness, cognitive reserve, genetics, other health conditions and medications, and adherence to CPAP treatment.

column36: Prenatal programming of child neurodevelopment and mental health problems
column37: More than 1 in 4 children in Canada show delays in at least one area of development by school entry. Current research indicates that prenatal stress is a significant risk factor for child mental health and neurocognitive problems. It is estimated that close to two-thirds of women experience a significant stressor in the year prior to an infant's birth. Thus, at birth, many infants may have already been exposed to risk factors that can affect their health and well-being. As a result, provincial health campaigns (e.g., Alberta's Ready or Not campaign) highlight maternal mental health and stress as one of the key areas to improve before and during pregnancy. However, it is still unclear why and how prenatal stress affects child mental health and cognitive development (e.g., language skills). In addition, the association between prenatal stress and child health outcomes vary between studies. This suggests that some individuals or populations of individuals may be at greater or lesser risk than others. Accordingly, this study will use a large, longitudinal pregnancy cohort based in Alberta, Canada to examine two main aims. First, will we examine a cascade of events between pregnancy and child age 5 to examine how prenatal stress impacts the parent, child, and family over time. Our second aim will be to examine whether certain genetic markers increase or decrease the risks associated with prenatal stress. The results of this study will inform preventative intervention efforts aimed at promoting both maternal mental health and child well-being. Identifying how prenatal stress impacts maternal, child, and family well-being across early childhood can help intervention programs determine which areas to target during specific time periods (e.g., prenatal, infancy, toddlerhood). Identifying genes that promote risk will allow us to classify individuals who are most susceptible to the negative effects of prenatal stress, an important goal of precision medicine.

column36: Modifying brain connectivity to optimize motor learning and recovery of function after stroke
column37: Stroke is the leading cause of adult disability in Canada. Impaired arm and hand function after stroke is linked to changes in the way different parts of our brain work together. These changes in brain activity impair processes that help with recovery of arm and hand function. Restoring brain activity to the pattern seen before the stroke can maximize recovery. We can alter patterns of brain activity using brain stimulation. This non-invasive, painless approach temporarily turns down the activity in overactive parts of the brain before we practice a task, allowing other regions to have greater involvement. This approach has shown benefit - pairing brain stimulation with practice of movements using the arm and hand after stroke can result in improvements in function. However, the response has been varied. We think the reason for variable responses to brain stimulation is because patterns of brain activity after stroke are highly individualized. To improve effectiveness, we will use individual data to determine the target (i.e., brain area) for brain stimulation, an approach that has yet to be taken. The proposed research will 1) determine targets for brain stimulation after stroke by examining patterns of brain activity on an individual basis, and 2) investigative individualized brain stimulation paired with practice of movements using the arm and hand to aid recovery after stroke. By using this novel approach to identify targets for brain stimulation paired with movement practice on an individual basis after stroke, this work represents a critical step in improving interventions that pair brain stimulation with motor practice for stroke recovery. Further, this work will show that improvements in hand and arm function are maximized when targets are tailored to the individual. Ultimately, this research will advance rehabilitation and recovery after stroke, leading to improved daily function and better quality of life for Canadians living with stroke.

column36: Targeting Post-Translational Modifications of Huntingtin to treat Huntington disease
column37: Huntington disease is an inherited degenerative brain disorder that affects 1 in 7,500 individuals in the Western world. It is characterised by involuntary movements, cognitive deficits, and dementia leading ultimately to death. The cause of Huntington disease is a mutation in the HTT gene, which then produces the toxic mutant huntingtin protein. This mutant protein disrupts many vital cellular functions, and is ultimately responsible for the brain cell death. There is no cure for this disorder. Targeting the cause of Huntington disease by reducing mutant huntingtin in the brain should prevent or delay disease onset. One approach to reducing mutant huntingtin is to promote its degradation in cells. I will target mechanisms that should increase clearance of mutant huntingtin from the cells, and reduce its toxicity. The huntingtin protein is normally subjected to a variety of modifications (addition of small molecules) that allow it to be functional and properly degraded in cells. However, these modifications are altered in the mutant protein, which decreases the brain's ability to eliminate the toxic protein. Our lab has previously identified specific modifications of huntingtin that play key roles in Huntington disease when altered: restoring their levels in transgenic mice can improve, and even suppress, Huntington disease symptoms. My research now suggests that key modifications of huntingtin regulate each other and regulate the elimination of the protein through autophagy, a degradation process abnormally reduced in Huntington disease. The objectives of my project are to investigate modifications of huntingtin in vitro and in vivo in Huntington disease mouse models to characterise the interrelationships between these modifications, and evaluate how they regulate mutant huntingtin degradation. My ultimate goal is to identify relevant modifications to target in order to elaborate therapeutic strategies to enhance mutant huntingtin degradation through autophagy.

column36: Do bias signaling of the apelinergic receptor can improve the treatment of acute cardiovascular dysfunction and injury related to septic shock?
column37: Urgent stabilization of hemodynamics and organ/tissue perfusion is a cornerstone in septic shock treatment, which seriously affects the myocardial function and the vascular tree. Catecholamines treatment, in concert with fluid resuscitation, has long been recommended. However, not all patients respond positively and current controversy questions the efficacy-to-safety profile of this drug family. Considering that current therapeutic approaches are less than optimal, it is time to identify new safer and life-saving alternative therapies. Our group and others recently demonstrated that the endogenous apelinergic system is a compelling target to sustain cardiovascular function in septic shock. The apelin receptor stimulation through infusion of either Apelin-13 or ELABELA improves hemodynamics, limits cardiovascular dysfunction as well as mortality in experimental septic shock. Considering this proven potential therapeutic impact of the apelin receptor stimulation, the purpose of the current project is to study the cellular processes involved in this cardioprotection in order to ultimately identify novel analogs with improved therapeutic capabilities. By generating novel bias agonists of the apelinergic system, we propose a two years project to study how the apelin receptor regulates myocardial cells function to increase their performance in face of great hemodynamic stress in the context of septic shock. Furthermore, this project could be the first pre-clinical proof of concept for the therapeutic efficiency of GPCR biased ligand in the research field of critical care illness.

column36: Restoring Supraspinal Cardiovascular Control to Mitigate Vascular-Cognitive Impairment after Spinal Cord Injury
column37: While paralysis is commonly viewed as the most devastating consequence of spinal cord injury (SCI), a major under-appreciated issue is cognitive impairment which occurs due to dysfunction of brain blood vessels. Impaired cognition drastically impacts the rehabilitation process, social integration and overall quality of life. My recently published study shows that up to 60% of individuals with SCI have impaired cognition and thus highlights the seriousness of this issue. Long term high blood pressure, in otherwise healthy individuals is known to damage blood vessels in the brain and cause cognitive impairment. Strikingly, majority of people with a high-level SCI suffer from a life-threatening condition called autonomic dysreflexia, where daily activities such as a bowel routine trigger extreme uncontrolled spikes in blood pressure up to 40 times per day. These spikes in blood pressures go up to 300mmHg- well above brain's maximum tolerable limit of 150mmHg, To study this, we have developed a rat model of SCI that shows blood pressure dysfunction similar to humans and also significant cognitive decline post injury. First, we will use this model to thoroughly understand how extreme blood pressure fluctuations cause brain damage resulting in cognitive decline. Second, the main reason behind blood pressure dysregulation is loss of crucial regulatory pathways brainstem after SCI. We will reconnect those lost pathways using a nerve bridge and enzymatic treatment of injury scar. Our preliminary studies show that the nerve bridge significantly improves blood pressure control. We predict that this treatment approach will improve brain health and cognitive function following SCI. Therapies based on nerve transplantation are already in safety trials in humans with SCI. Understanding its implications in blood pressure control and cognitive function can help address these issues, which are of higher patient priority that walking but are unfortunately, understudied.

column36: Structural Valve Degeneration in Bioprosthetic Heart Valves
column37: Bioprosthetic heart valves (BPHVs) have revolutionized the treatment of disease of valves in the heart that control blood flow within the heart. Such heart valve disease constitutes a significant health and economic burden in Canada and around the world. BPHVs serve as an alternative to mechanical valves that require lifelong treatment to prevent clotting and thereby cause increase risk of bleeding for patients. Notably, use of BPHVs has continued to evolve with the advent of transcatheter technologies wherein a minimally invasive technique has expanded the benefit of BPHVs to include patients that are unable to have surgery to replace a dysfunctional valve. Despite these successes, the long-term durability of BPHVs continues to be of great concern. Thus, our proposed work aims to compare how BPHVs degenerate and potential ways to assess this in patients. This will be addressed using a combination of analysis of dysfunctional valves and novel imaging approaches using computed tomography (CT) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. Overall, this research will provide key new information on the BPHV dysfunction which will help guide innovation of new valve design, patient selection, and treatment that will ultimately serve to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Genetic Characterization of the Latent HIV Reservoir Towards its Immune-mediated Elimination
column37: HIV infection, while manageable with antiretroviral drugs, cannot be cured, leaving 37 million persons globally vulnerable to the long-term health effects and stigma associated with this condition. Current antiretroviral drugs cannot cure HIV because of the presence of a subset of immune cells that, after infection, enter a state of "hibernation" or latency. Latently HIV-infected cells are invisible to the immune system and can persist in the body for years or even decades. Furthermore, a subset of these cells is capable of reactivating at a future date to produce infectious HIV. We refer to the total pool of hibernating viruses as "the latent HIV reservoir", and to the latter subset as the "inducible, replication competent" fraction. Curing HIV will require us to eliminate the latter, but multiple challenges remain. First, since HIV continually mutates during untreated infection, an individual's pool of hibernating viruses is likely to be genetically diverse. In addition, some hibernating viral strains would harbor mutations that, upon reactivation, would render them resistant to host immune responses. Achieving a better understanding of latent HIV reservoir genetic composition and responsiveness to immune-mediated elimination, and the extent to which these features vary between individuals, is critical for designing HIV cure strategies. Using a unique cohort for whom longitudinal historic bio-specimens are available, we will investigate the genetic characteristics of both the total and inducible, replication competent pool of hibernating viruses in each individual. In doing so, we will identify viral targets that remain susceptible to recognition by the immune system in a "personalized" manner. Finally, we will test whether these "personalized" targets can better stimulate an individual's immune cells to kill latently infected cells in vitro, compared to standard targets. Results will help scientists design therapeutic strategies towards achieving an HIV cure.

column36: Identification of IL1RAP as an oncoprotein and candidate immunotherapeutic target in Ewing sarcoma
column37: Ewing Sarcoma (EWS) is an aggressive form of childhood cancer that occurs on bone and soft tissue. Although conventional cancer therapeutic strategies, such as chemotherapy, radiation and surgery, have improved survival in patients with localized EWS tumors, they are ineffective for patients with metastatic disease. In addition, conventional chemotherapy is often toxic and carcinogenic, which carries short- and long-term toxicities. In the past few years, immunotherapy has been promoted as an effective means to prolong survival or even eliminate tumor cells in patients with specific cancers. However, effective immunotherapeutic strategies for EWS have not yet been described. Identification of highly specific cell surface markers of tumor cells is critical for developing targeted immunotherapy strategies. We have identified IL1RAP (Interleukin 1 receptor accessory protein) as a cell surface protein that is highly expressed in EWS in comparison to normal tissues/organs, and that is important for tumorigenesis in this disease. In this project, we aim to develop immunotherapeutic strategies by targeting IL1RAP in human EWS, while also delineating the key mechanisms mediating the tumor-promoting function of this protein.

column36: Characterizing the response of the gut microbiota and the host to attaching and effacing pathogens
column37: Diarrheal disease affects 1.7 billion people every year, killing more than 760,000 children worldwide. A leading cause of diarrhea are the attaching and effacing (A/E) pathogens, which include both bacteria that infect humans (such as enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli or EHEC, the cause of "hamburger disease") and bacteria that infect mice (Citrobacter rodentium or CR). The first major hurdle that A/E pathogens must overcome to infect their hosts is the gut microbiota, which is a microbial community of trillions of bacteria present in the mammalian digestive tract. Next, A/E pathogens face the intestinal mucosal surface, which represents another tightly regulated barrier against pathogens. To overcome these barriers, A/E pathogens have evolved to secrete toxins directly into target cells using complex machines called secretion systems, such as the type 6 secretion system (T6SS). My research will examine how A/E pathogens use this sophisticated mechanism to successfully colonize the gut. I propose to show how A/E pathogens use the T6SS to shape the gut microbial community by killing specific microbiota members. I will first use an animal model of infection to identify whether the T6SS is crucial for the success of CR infection, and to measure how this secretion system affects the abundance of other bacteria in the gut. I also aim to reveal for the first time how EHEC manipulates not only the gut microbiota, but also the host cell, thus creating a suitable niche for bacterial survival. I will achieve this using proteomic techniques to explore the interactions between secreted bacterial toxins and host proteins. Finally, I will investigate whether interfering with this toxin-host interaction blocks EHEC infection. Together, these experiments will improve our understanding of the interactions between the gut microbiota, the host and A/E pathogens. Importantly, this research may lead to new therapeutic approaches for treating infectious diseases.

column36: Psychiatric phenotypes in chronic traumatic encephalopathy
column37: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive, psychiatric, and motor symptoms, and is caused by repetitive head impacts such as those seen in athletes of contact sports and military veterans. However, the exact causes of the disease progression, as well as its particular symptoms, is largely unknown, particularly for its psychiatric symptoms, which include depression and suicidality. As the foremost research group into CTE with the world's largest collection of pathologically-verified postmortem samples, we are examining prevalence, causes, and treatments for this disorder. My particular focus is on the psychiatric symptoms in these patients, and I am distinguishing between cases with and without depression or suicidality to determine whether and where particular brain pathology distinguishes between these groups. I am also investigating whether the causes of depressive symptoms in these cases might differ from non-CTE depressed individuals. Finally, I am attempting to determine the prevalence of suicide in a group at high risk for developing CTE. Together, these studies will inform how CTE can induce psychiatric symptoms, potentially leading to a better understanding of causes and treatments of this disorder, and may also inform regarding potential causes for psychiatric symptoms such as these in the general non-CTE population.

column36: Investigating how ribosome heterogeneity guides cell fate specification of human embryonic stem cells into cardiac cell lineages
column37: The regulation of protein production is critical to maintain cellular homeostasis. When disrupted, this can result in devastating human disease. The cellular machinery used to produce proteins, termed ribosomes, has traditionally been viewed as a universal machine that is similar between organisms and cell types. Interestingly, mutations in core ribosome proteins lead to devastating congenital birth defects (e.g. neural crest defects) and stem cell defects (e.g. Diamond Blackfan Anemia), suggesting that specific proteins are required for proper development and cellular maintenance. Indeed, specialized ribosomes have been found to drive synthesis of specific proteins in key pathways of tissue development. As well, this level of specialization has recently been found to be augmented by auxiliary proteins that bind to the ribosome to effect its function; however, the role of these ribosome-associated proteins in human health and disease remains largely unknown. Here, we aim to fill this gap in knowledge by characterizing ribosome-associated proteins and their functions during stem cell differentiation. Specifically, we hypothesize that proteins bound to the ribosome are crucial in directing cell fate decisions of human embryonic stem cells down cardiac cell lineages. To study this, we will combine state-of-the-art methodologies including high-throughput ribosome profiling and mass spectrometry to fully understand the repertoire of ribosome-associated proteins during cardiac cell development and their cognate regulatory targets. Moreover, we will use gene editing technology to further understand their specific functional roles in cellular protein synthesis and eventually use animal models to assess their impacts on disease.

column36: Frontal-hippocampal interactions in temporal memory formation
column37: Our daily lives consist of a continuous stream of information and experiences. Although our memories of such experiences tend to be parsed into separate events (e.g., "what happened at the library"), we are still capable of linking those events together and remembering their chronology, thus preserving our subjective sense of continuity of time. The aim of the proposed research is to identify the brain mechanisms involved in deploying attention internally in order to link together disparate events into a seamless experience. In doing so, this work will offer key insights into the relationship between internally guided attention and memory, and how these processes change with both healthy and pathological aging. Given that both attention and memory for the order of events is often impaired with age, the proposed research will help move us closer to interventions designed to improve memory in healthy older adults and those with early Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Inhibition of neutrophil extracellular trap formation for the prevention of breast cancer metastasis.
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in females worldwide. Metastasis is the occurrence of tumors at distant sites in the body and is a major predictor of cancer outcome. Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells in the blood and play a significant role in shaping the immune response. Paradoxically, neutrophil infiltration of tumors is correlated with poor prognosis and decreased survival in breast cancer and several malignancies. Recently, it was shown that neutrophils can release their cellular contents in a mesh of DNA (similar to a spider's web) in what has been described as neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. Importantly, breast cancer cells have been shown to induce NET formation and NETs provide anchorage for circulating tumor cells and thereby serve as hot spots for metastasis. Additionally, several proteins released during NETs formation damage blood vessels and contribute to mortality in breast cancer patients. Hence, inhibiting NET formation is beneficial in breast cancer therapy. The role of immune signaling pathways in the formation of NETs is unknown. In particular, SYK is a protein that functions as an "on or off" switch in neutrophils but its role in NET formation is unknown. My goal is to decipher the role of SYK in NET formation. Our current models suggest that inhibition of SYK prevents NET formation which leads to decrease in growth and invasion of breast cancer cells. We will engineer a tumor microenvironment of metastasis involving endothelial cells, neutrophils and breast cancer cells and investigate the effect of SYK inhibition on NET formation and metastasis using laboratory and animal models. We will use nanoparticles to deliver SYK inhibitor to neutrophils as a strategy to inhibit NET formation and metastasis in breast cancer. These studies will create new knowledge on the role of SYK in NET formation and develop new therapy targeting SYK pathway for the prevention of metastasis in breast cancer patients.

column36: Evaluating gender-sensitive interventions for people who use drugs in the context of British Columbia's opioid overdose crisis
column37: Overdose death rates have increased dramatically in Canada in recent years, largely driven by contamination of the drug supply with illicitly manufactured synthetic opioids such as fentanyl. The overdose crisis has been hardest felt in British Columbia (BC), which declared a public health emergency in 2016. Strategies to address the overdose crisis have therefore become an urgent public health priority. Previous research and evidence have shown that gender plays a key role in shaping contexts of drug use (e.g., within sex work or intimate partnerships) and access to treatment and harm reduction services. Women access treatment with more severe substance-related profiles relative to men (e.g., physical/sexual violence and trauma), yet few services are women-specific. New Vancouver Coastal Health guidelines highlight grave gaps in supports and prevention for marginalized women, and several new models of care are being rolled out (e.g., women-only supervised consumption rooms). Clinical interventions to address the overdose crisis and expand access to evidence-based treatments in BC include randomized clinical trials (RCTs) on the efficacy of opioid agonist therapies (OAT), slow-release oral morphine (SROM), and psychedelic-assisted therapy. However, the gender-related impacts of these interventions remain poorly understood and under investigated. The proposed research will evaluate the impacts of 'naturally occurring' and clinical interventions (i.e., through prospective methods and RCTs) to address the overdose crisis using a gendered lens, to identify gender differences in treatment outcomes and barriers to accessing services. This project also aims to widely disseminate findings to support scale-up of gender-sensitive substance use programs and policies, and inform directions for future research. It is hoped that this research will make important contributions to optimizing gender-specific treatment and care for people who use drugs in Canada and internationally.

column36: Regulation of axonal damage signaling by the dileucine zipper kinase, DLK
column37: A fundamental feature of nervous system function is communication between neurons, which is carried out via communication cables, called axons. Damage to axons in the central nervous system (CNS) often leads to debilitating paralysis, and defects in axons are associated with neuropathology and death in neurodegenerative diseases. In contrast, axon injury in the mammalian peripheral nervous system (PNS) is usually not debilitating, since mechanisms exist to stimulate regrowth of damaged axons and to repair damaged circuits. My work studies the mechanisms of an enzyme that detects defects in axons, and regulates dual responses of new axonal growth in the PNS, and death of neurons in the CNS. Understanding the activation mechanisms of this enzyme will help in strategies to stimulate repair after spinal cord injury and stroke, and to inhibit pathology in neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's Disease. My goal is to understand how this enzyme, a dileucine zipper kinase named DLK, becomes activated in damaged axons. I have developed a new injury paradigm in the model organism Drosophila for introducing axonal damage to specific locations in branched axons while monitoring DLK activation. My data indicate that injury location is important for DLK activation mechanism: injuries to synaptic branches that leave at least one synaptic connection intact fail to activate DLK signaling. In the proposed project, I will use my new injury assay to: (Aim 1) test the hypothesis that functional synaptic communication at spared presynaptic terminals restrains DLK signaling, and (Aim 2) test whether the E3 ubiquitin ligase Hiw, which promotes the destruction of DLK protein, regulates DLK at intact synaptic terminals. This work will shed light on how neurons detect axonal damage which is important for understanding the mechanisms of repair and degeneration in the nervous system.

column36: Evaluation of a pediatric shared decision making implementation program: a feasibility stepped wedge cluster randomized controlled trial
column37: Shared decision making (SDM) is considered the best approach for making health decisions. In pediatrics, SDM occurs when the healthcare team, parents, and children exchange information and work together as partners to decide the best treatment plan for the child. SDM helps parents and children participate in decision making, feel more confident about the decision that was made, and can improve the child's health. Unfortunately, SDM is rarely used in pediatric clinical settings. The goal of my research is to improve the use of SDM in pediatric clinical practice. To do this, I am developing a SDM program that will include education, training, clinical tools, and expert support for healthcare teams, parents, and children. To ensure the SDM program works, we must test it using advanced research methods. Although very informative, these methods are resource and time intensive. To avoid waste, it is often necessary to 'pilot' the methods using a smaller-scale experiment that will identify and provide an opportunity to fix problems before doing the larger experiment. Therefore, I am proposing to pilot advanced research methods for evaluating how well the SDM program works in pediatric clinical practice. We will ask healthcare teams, parents and children to participate in the study. The results will provide valuable information about recruiting people to our study, collecting data, and whether the program is likely to improve child and parent decision making experiences. We will use this information to run a larger experiment that will provide a definitive answer about whether our program improves the use of shared decision making in pediatric clinical practice.

column36: Caracterisation longitudinale de la neuropathologie sous-jacente aux changements cerebraux anormaux chez les athletes retraitees presentant un historique de commotions cerebrales / Longitudinal characterization of the neuropathology underlying abnormal brain changes in retired male and female athletes presenting with a history of sports-related concussions
column37: En raison de la prevalence alarmante, l'interet scientifique et celui du public a l'egard des effets des commotions ne cesse de grandir, ce qui en fait l'une des questions de sante publique les plus actuelles et debattues. La commotion cerebrale est un traumatisme cranien subi dans le sport dont les symptomes se resorbent en general de facon spontanee lors du mois subsequent. Toute discussion des effets a long terme mene inevitablement a l'encephalopathie traumatique chronique (ETC), une maladie neurodegenerative qui ne peut etre diagnostiquee qu'a l'autopsie et pour laquelle les medias etablissent un lien de cause a effet entre l'exposition aux coups repetes a la tete et le developpement de cette maladie. Cependant, il est trop precoce d'affirmer un lien de causalite en raison de lacunes scientifiques importantes. Il a ete demontre que les patients atteints d'ETC partagent des symptomes similaires avec d'autres maladies neurodegeneratives, telle la maladie d'Alzheimer, ce qui complexifie l'etablissement d'un diagnostic clinique et la comprehension des mecanismes pathologiques. Le present projet propose une etude longitudinale des changements anormaux du cerveau qui pourraient etre impliques dans le declin cognitif anormal chez les athletes commotionnes. Grace a l'avancement fulgurant de la qualite des examens de neuroimagerie, il sera possible de deceler des particularites biologiques du cerveau commotionne nous permettant de predire le declin cognitif d'anciennes athletes commotionnees. Les connaissances qui seront acquises en definissant la signature biologique des effets a long terme des commotions faciliteront l'identification des athletes a risque de souffrir de neurodegenerescence. De plus, les resultats permettront d'identifier des pistes de traitement precoce pour retarder la progression de la maladie avant que ne s'installent des changements irreversibles au cerveau tout en ameliorant la qualite de vie d'athletes commotionnes qui souffrent en silence.

column36: Les facteurs influencant le pronostic medical lors de grossesses avec malformations congenitales ou a risque d'accouchement premature.
column37: Ce projet etudie les facteurs qui font que les medecins font des predictions erronees sur le devenir du nouveau-ne chez les femmes avec grossesse a risque. En effet, certaines grossesses peuvent etre compliquees par des decouvertes de malformations congenitales chez le foetus ou un risque d'accouchement premature. Les parents dans de telles situations font face a des choix difficiles tels que poursuivre ou non la grossesse ou quels soins apporter a la naissance de leur nouveau-ne. Ils doivent faire ces choix en considerant le bien-etre futur du nouveau-ne et de leur famille. Les medecins accompagnent les parents dans ces decisions critiques de vie et de mort en leur faisant part de leurs predictions quant aux chances de survie, handicap et de qualite de vie future pour leur enfant. Or, ces predictions futures, appelees pronostics, peuvent etre tres variables d'un medecin a l'autre, et sont souvent plus pessimistes que la realite. Cette variation peut s'expliquer par la presence de nombreux facteurs agissant comme des biais. Il est important de comprendre l'influence de ces facteurs sur le pronostic du medecin, car ils peuvent mener a des choix irreversibles par les parents. Ce projet s'interesse particulierement aux facteurs relies au medecin, soit sa personnalite, son attitude face au handicap et s'il fait le suivi a long terme des patients nes de grossesse a risque. Aussi, ce projet de recherche propose la creation de strategies pour reduire l'impact de ces facteurs sur leurs predictions pour l'enfant a venir. Ce projet permettra de donner l'heure juste aux parents quant a la prediction du bien-etre futur possible de l'enfant. Il pourra etre integre dans l'education des futurs medecins. De plus, cette recherche unique et pionniere pourrait s'etendre a d'autres situations ou les medecins se prononcent sur le futur de leur patient pouvant parfois mener a des decisions de soins importantes.
