column36: Suicidalite chez les jeunes atteints d'un premier episode psychotique : trajectoires d'evolution et facteurs associes.
column37: Le suicide est un grave probleme de sante publique representant une cause importante de mortalite. Plus de 5 % des individus atteints d'un trouble psychotique meurent par suicide (Melle & Barrett, 2014). Au cours des premiers stades de la psychose, le risque suicidaire est 60 % plus eleve qu'au cours des stades subsequents (Bornheimer, 2018). La psychose est caracterisee par une alteration du contact avec la realite, des hallucinations et des idees delirantes (Abdel-Baki, Lalonde, & Gingras, 2016). Peu d'etudes ont evalue de facon approfondie les facteurs de risque de la suicidalite. De plus, aucune etude quebecoise ou canadienne n'a etudie ce phenomene chez les jeunes atteints d'un premier episode psychotique (PEP). Objectifs : Les objectifs sont de decrire la frequence des differents types de suicidalite (idees suicidaires, tentatives de suicide et suicide complete), d'identifier les facteurs de risque de la suicidalite, de determiner les trajectoires d'augmentation, de maintien ou de diminution de la suicidalite sur une periode de cinq ans chez les jeunes atteints d'un PEP et d'explorer les predicteurs de ces trajectoires. Methode : Cette etude a lieu dans deux services d'intervention precoce en psychose en milieu urbain a Montreal (Quebec). L'echantillon est compose de 567 Jeunes souffrants d'un PEP ayant ete suivis par ces services pendant une periode de cinq ans. Les donnees sociodemographiques, les symptomes, la suicidalite, le fonctionnement global, la consommation d'alcool et de drogues, les traumatismes vecus pendant l'enfance et le diagnostic des participants sont consideres pour mieux comprendre les facteurs associes aux trajectoires de la suicidalite. Retombees : Le projet permettra de mieux soutenir les jeunes atteints d'un PEP qui sont a risque de passage a l'acte suicidaire en developpant de meilleurs outils pour predire le suicide et en mettant en place des strategies preventives specifiques a cette population.

column36: Targeting M3R's internalization to treat Asthma and COPD
column37: Asthma and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) are obstructive lung disorders affecting about 435 million individuals worldwide in which the symptoms of difficulty of breathing derived from the obstruction of the airways. In both respiratory disorders, this obstruction of the airways involves the activation of the muscarinic receptor M3 (M3R) leading to the contraction of the airway smooth muscle that compress the airways. Nevertheless, the current drugs blocking the M3R upregulate, paradoxically, their expression over time leading to negative side effects, such as an aggravation of airway hyperresponsiveness, a characteristic feature of asthma correlating with the symptoms. This project evaluates a new avenue to target M3R which avoids these side effects by inducing the receptor downregulation. M3R is a member of the large family of transmembrane proteins called G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). In a situation of over-activation, GPCRs downregulate their activity, a phenomenon called desensitization. Previously, we demonstrated, in vivo, that desensitization of the M3R has potential clinical benefits such as reversing the airway hyperresponsiveness in a murine model of asthma. This project aims to develop a compound that inducing exclusively the molecular pathways leading to the M3R's desensitization to treat asthma and COPD. For this purpose, firstly, the molecular pathways of contraction and desensitization will be characterized in tissue and cell-based models with molecular biology methods. Secondly, the actual compounds known to interact with the M3R will be screens to find some with a capacity to induce the desensitization of the receptor. Thirdly, these compounds will be chemically optimized, and their potential clinical benefits will be confirmed in murine models of asthma.

column36: Can aerobic exercise to improve brain health and cognition in youths with obesity? A randomized intervention assessing the feasibility, tolerability, and efficacy of a 12-week moderate intensity exercise intervention in improving cognitive functioning, dietary self-regulation, and the structure and function of the brain in adolescents with obesity.
column37: Canada is in the midst of an obesity epidemic that is disproportionally affecting children and youth; one third of children and adolescents are classified as overweight and obese. This is of central concern, as not only is obesity associated with poor physical and mental health, but also brain health and cognitive functioning. Adolescents with obesity show widespread impairments in brain structure and function, which manifest as poor cognitive functioning and heightened impulsivity. Such, impairments can have profound and enduring effects on physical, mental, and psychosocial health into and throughout adulthood. Indeed, poor cognitive control has been linked to a variety of adverse health and interpersonal problems, such as substance abuse and addiction and poor academic performance. It is evident that there is a clear need to develop effective clinical strategies that can be used to mitigate obesity-induced alternations in brain health and cognitive control, particularly during the critical developmental period of adolescence. A growing number of randomized trials have linked aerobic exercise to brain health and cognitive functioning, however, no prior interventions have conducted in adolescent populations. Therefore, the feasibility of an aerobic exercise intervention within this population remains unclear. The primary aims of this study is (1) conduct a comprehensive assessment of the feasibility, tolerability and acceptability of the intervention within this population, and (2) assess the preliminary efficacy of aerobic exercise in improving cognitive functioning and brain health. These findings could have wide-ranging applications, not only in establishing transformative and causal evidence demonstrating that aerobic exercise can significantly reduce the impact of obesity-related cognitive dysfunction, but also in the formulation of strategic public policies and priorities aimed at improving neurocognitive functioning in adolescent populations

column36: In silico elucidation and functional characterization of human intestinal microbiota enzymes targeting host-derived carbohydrates
column37: Within the human intestinal tract reside an enormous consortium of bacterial species. Although a full picture of human-bacteria interactions is still emerging, it is clear that these microbes play important roles in human health, as patients suffering from gastrointestinal diseases typically posses fewer species than healthy individuals. One critical responsibility of intestinal bacteria is digestion of the elaborate array of complex carbohydrates from dietary sources, which largely remain untouched by human enzymes. Bacterial carbohydrate digestion ultimately yields short-chain fatty acid end products which collectively benefit their human host. Short-chain fatty acids serve as a main energy source for epithelial cells in the colon, have anti-tumorigenic and anti-inflammatory properties and reduce the incidence of type II diabetes and obesity. In addition to dietary polysaccharides, some bacteria digest polysaccharides produced by human cells. These processes are important for in how bacteria colonize the gut and regulate the immune system throughout life. Recent advancements have allowed us to grow the complete human intestinal microbiome within mixed communities in the lab. This has resulted in increased bacterial DNA yields and richer DNA sequence datasets. The goal of this research is to use computational approaches to search through DNA sequences and identify novel genes involved in degradation of human-derived polysaccharides. From there, we will identify which organism it is derived from, and purify the enzyme it encodes. Biochemical experiments on these enzymes will elucidate their precise substrates. Insights from this research may be important for the development of therapeutic strategies and preventative measures favouring the proliferation of beneficial bacterial species important for intestinal wellbeing.

column36: Incorporating human brain connectome in planning deep brain stimulation to treat Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic and progressive neurological disorder that primarily impairs movement, sometimes accompanied by psychiatric symptoms and cognitive impairment. It affects 100,000 Canadians and costs Canada 558 million dollars each year. Complementing medication, deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an effective surgical therapy, where an electrode is implanted in the brain to electrically stimulate the designated nucleus (a cluster of neurons) to relieve motor dysfunctions. However, in current DBS therapy, variations in individual surgical outcomes and certain inherent side effects are still not well understood, and non-motor symptoms are rarely addressed, thus complicating the care and management of the disease. New advancements in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including diffusion and functional MRI, can be used to extract the map of brain circuitry as a complex network to help reveal the mechanisms of neurological diseases. This proposal employs brain network information obtained from large public databases and from the latest 7T MRI technology at Western University to understand the interplay of disease progression, brain connectivity, and the true influence of DBS. The research will use artificial intelligence to transform these insights into software that offers DBS plans tailored to the patient's personal situations with predicted and enhanced surgical outcomes. Finally, we will explore new stimulation targets that can treat both motor and non-motor symptoms of the disease. With the promise to yield new diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, this project has the potential to greatly improve the patients' quality of life and to reduce the burden on the healthcare system. Furthermore, the proposed framework is expected to open doors to the DBS treatment of other devastating brain disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease and depression, and help Canada gain a competitive edge in the research and treatment of neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Modifying Aspergillomarasmine A to Improve Metallo-Beta-Lactamase Inhibition and the Efficacy of Carbapenem Antibiotics
column37: The global spread of antibiotic resistance continues to challenge clinicians and threaten the lives of infected patients. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaciae (CRE), which include the pathogenic bacteria Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are a major public health concern. This is because of the high mortality rates associated with these bacterial infections and their ability to rapidly spread from person to person. CRE are resistant to last-resort antibiotics known as carbapenems, because they produce metallo-beta-lactamases (MBL) which break these drugs down. Therefore, the development of new countermeasures are sorely needed to mitigate the threat of CRE. A promising solution to this problem is the identification of antibiotic adjuvants, which are non-antibiotic compounds that block antibiotic resistance. An example of one such compound is aspergillomarasmine A (AMA), as it inhibits the activity of MBLs and rescues carbapenems from degradation. The purpose of this study is to better understand the inhibitory activity of AMA so that more potent AMA-related adjuvants can be made. At the Michael G. DeGroote Institute for Infectious Disease Research (IIDR), Dr. Gerry Wright and his group have access to state-of-the art facilities that will facilitate completion of this research. The overall findings of this work will add significant knowledge to the growing body of research on AMA, and the new adjuvants developed will help to overcome this major public health threat in Canada and the rest of the World.

column36: Systematic assessment of event-related potentials analyses for detecting consciousness and predicting recovery in disorders of consciousness
column37: Each year, over 20% of unresponsive patients in intensive care units (ICU) are not fully assessed to determine their neurofunctional state. Additionally, over 40% of unresponsive patients in neurological stepdown units (SDU) are actually misdiagnosed as unconscious because of their inability to behaviorally communicate with the outside world. This can be a source of profound distress for patients, their families, and health-care professionals, and has grave consequences with respect to patient care and end-of-life decision-making. Recently, brain responses to external auditory stimuli (event-related potentials; ERPs) and brain network properties have been used to show a patient's conscious awareness, even if the patient is only passively paying attention. Current methods of assessing consciousness, however, are limited in their potential clinical application. The work done to-date does not involve the use of ERP/EEG measures for true clinical purposes of assessment, prediction of recovery (i.e. prognosis), and therapeutic treatment. Our objective for this research is to develop an electroencephalography (EEG)-based toolbox for detecting consciousness and predicting recovery on a case-by-case basis in patients with disorders of consciousness (DOC). Our hypothesis is that a systematic assessment of the injured brain using both stimulus-response and brain network analyses will enable accurate detection of levels of consciousness on a patient-by-patient basis at bedside, and will be able to accurately predict outcomes of DOC. The successful completion of this research will provide a standardized and individualized approach to detecting neural signals of consciousness in patients with DOC. This will have a profound impact on increasing diagnostic accuracy, reducing feelings of stress for both patients and families, and ultimately improving patient outcomes.

column36: Identifying host-specific adaptations of Crohn's-associated Escherichia coli
column37: Canada has one of the highest worldwide rates of Crohn's disease. The relapsing nature of this disease threatens the quality of life for many people inside and outside Canada. Moreover, the disease represents a burden on the health care system with an estimate of 3 billion dollars annually. The exact cause of Crohn's disease remains to be determined. However, it is believed to be mediated by multiple factors. This includes genetic, environmental and microbial factors. Our gut hosts trillions of bacteria that are beneficial to our health. During Crohn's disease, there is a decline in the numbers of beneficial bacteria and an enrichment of harmful microbes. The latter group include certain strains of Escherichia coli that are known to mediate inflammation, and were commonly isolated from Crohn's disease patients. One of the major challenges in the clinic is the detection of Crohn's-associated Escherichia coli. In the work proposed here, I will use animal models and state of the art genomics to understand how Crohn's-associated Escherichia coli adapt to the host environment, and cause disease. This research will allow us to discriminate the harmful bacteria from the good ones in the gut. Accordingly, we can design new drugs that can specifically target the harmful bacteria in the gut of Crohn's patients.

column37: At approximately the fifth decade of life humans start losing muscle mass and strength (i.e., sarcopenia). Importantly, sarcopenia is associated with a number of negative health outcomes including fracture risk, cardiovascular disease, and all-cause mortality. Thus, understanding, preventing, and reversing sarcopenia would substantially improve public health. Accordingly, the present research project proposal is designed to identify the biological and behavioural causes of sarcopenia. Using large datasets generated from the Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology Study and the UK Biobank, we will explore the behavioural (e.g., diet and physical activity) and biological (e.g., proteins measured in the blood) factors that may mediate sarcopenia. Our findings will establish behavioural factors that mediate sarcopenia, which will encourage healthcare professionals to advocate for them as preventative medicine. In addition, by identifying a biomarker for sarcopenia we will provide healthcare professionals and researchers with a feasible assessment tool and an outcome to target for intervention. We hypothesize this project will considerably improve our understanding of sarcopenia and will be a strong contribution towards the goal of preventing, reversing, and eliminating sarcopenia altogether.

column36: Investigating the validity and reliability of measuring physical activity, sedentary time and cardiovascular health outcomes in toddlers and preschoolers with cerebral palsy
column37: There is a growing population of people with cerebral palsy (CP) in Canada from 75000 now to 95000 in 2030 due to an increase in life expectancy and improved health care at birth. As CP is a permanent, childhood physical disability that results in reduced motor function, overall this population participates in less physical activity than the general population. People with CP are at greater risk for long-term diseases, such as obesity, high blood pressure (i.e. hypertension), and stroke, than the general population. There is a need to increase physical activity in this population, and from an early age, to minimize early motor function loss and decrease long-term disease risk. However, our understanding of physical activity in toddlers and preschoolers with CP is poorly understood due to a lack of proper measurement technique. In order to provide health care recommendations for this population, a better understanding of physical activity and its relationship with health risk outcomes are needed. The key aims of this project are to: 1) measure physical activity using activity monitors in toddlers and preschoolers with CP; 2) measure the thickness of the artery wall in the artery of the neck using ultrasound; and 3) measure the relationship between physical activity and health risk outcomes (e.g. thickness of carotid artery wall) in this population. The findings from this project can help health professionals who work with toddlers and preschoolers with CP understand physical activity and its relationship with health risk outcomes at an early age, and to help develop interventions to care for this population. These findings also have the potential to extend to other populations with childhood-onset physical disabilities.

column36: Investigating the effect of physical activity on executive functions and health in adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: Executive functions (EF) are brain-based processes that are necessary for controlling goal-directed behaviours, and are related to several physical and mental health outcomes. Adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) experience significant deficits in their EF, along with low levels of physical activity, poor health, and an increased risk of mental health concerns. My postdoctoral research will seek to improve EF, and by extension mental and physical health, in adolescents with NDD through increased participation in physical activity. This work will include a series of studies to test both the immediate and long-term effects of physical activity on EF and health in this population. Results from initial lab-based studies will inform modifications to existing clinical and community physical activity programs, and the effectiveness of these modified programs will also be evaluated. Specifically, I will examine the immediate effect of different types of physical activity on changes in EF in adolescents with NDD. These results will inform a study exploring the long-term effect of physical activity on EF and health outcomes. Finally, in collaboration with existing clinical and community partners, modifications will be made to inclusive physical activity programs in order to target improvements in EF and health outcomes for adolescents with NDD, and the effect of these modifications will be tested in comparison to unmodified programs. These will be among the first studies to systematically test the effect of physical activity on EF and health outcomes in adolescents with NDD through a series of efficacy and effectiveness trials. It is anticipated that the results will contribute to the development of evidence-based physical activity programming for this at-risk population, which will have numerous implications across the sectors of health, education, and recreation.

column36: Elucidating the microstructural and genetic risk architecture of major adolescent-onset psychiatric disorders in early life
column37: One in five Canadians are affected by mental illness, with a high proportion of these individuals experiencing their first symptoms in adolescence. This dynamic and critical time period in the lifespan of an individual holds key milestones in the development of white matter "highways" in the brain, and offers a unique and informative target to study alongside genetic information. Genome-wide association studies have rapidly increased our knowledge of the genetic risk architecture that underlies individual psychiatric disorders, but there is a need to look beyond current symptom-based definitions, which do not map onto biological findings. This project will harness the rich genotypic, imaging and phenotypic data from nearly 12,000 children recruited for the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and findings from multiple genome-wide association studies to build a multivariate model of polygenic risk for schizophrenia, bipolar, major depressive, anxiety, and eating disorders. I aim to capture the unique and shared contributions of psychiatric polygenic risk in one score using cutting-edge genomic data science methods. This score will then be related to measures of white matter in the brain that can be assessed non-invasively with magnetic resonance imaging. I will then integrate findings of microstructural features most related to polygenic risk for psychiatric disorders to maladaptive behaviours in childhood that could be predictive of the onset of future psychiatric symptoms. This project will provide an important neurobiological framework to assess psychiatric risk in early life that represents a significant departure from the classical definitions of psychiatric disorders, with the hope of re-routing current treatment plans to better meet the needs of patients and their families.

column36: Targeting brain inflammation in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most frequent cause of dementia worldwide and its incidence increases with the aging of the population. Several factors are involved in the development of the disease, including a toxic protein called amyloid beta. This protein accumulates in the brain and in the blood vessels and can trigger inflammation. Because AD is a disease that develops before the onset of symptoms, it is crucial to develop preventive strategies that could slow down the progression of the disease or stop it. Lifestyle is one of the risk factors that could contribute to the development of AD and the nutrients we introduce through our diet could help to prevent AD. Nutritional and dietary approaches are powerful and promising tools that need to be further explored. There is evidence supporting that the anti-inflammatory properties of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (omega3 PUFA) might prevent AD progression. Considering that omega3 PUFA levels are low in the brains of AD patients, boosting the consumption of omega3 PUFA enriched food might be beneficial. With this project, I aim to study the effect an omega3 PUFA enriched diet in mice prior to the development of the disease. The mice will consume a diet enriched or deprived of omega3 PUFA and at 12 weeks of age, I will induce a disease-like phenotype by injecting the toxic protein amyloid beta in the brain of these mice. I will then observe whether omega3 PUFA enriched diet will have a positive impact on the cerebral inflammatory response and on the accumulation of the toxic protein. This project could lead to the development of nutritional guidelines for the prevention of AD, which could be extended to the entire population and not only to people at risk.

column36: Understanding the preconception health of women with disabilities in Ontario: Service user and provider perspectives
column37: Being healthy before pregnancy is vital, as preconception health (PCH) impacts maternal and infant outcomes. However, half of pregnancies are unplanned and improving health at the first prenatal visit is too late to prevent poor outcomes. Women with disabilities (WWD) represent about 10% of women of reproductive age and are becoming pregnant at similar rates to women without disabilities; yet, there is little research on the PCH of WWD in Canada. Attending to the PCH of WWD is important, as WWD experience physical and psychological health disparities that put them at increased risk for poor PCH. Further, compared to women without disability, WWD have lower rates of contraception use and experience higher rates of unplanned pregnancy, short spacing between pregnancies, and sexual violence. Using qualitative methods, this study aims to (1) understand the PCH of WWD in Ontario, (2) explore how social, health, and health care factors may impact the PCH of WWD, and (3) identify how knowledge of barriers to care and risks for poor PCH outcomes can be used to improve care for WWD. Women from three disability subgroups (physical, sensory, intellectual and developmental) and health care providers will be interviewed. Analysis will explore similarities and differences across disability subgroups, as well as compare WWD and health care providers' responses, to identify key PCH health needs of WWD, what might be contributing to PCH disparities among WWD, and which interventions may be most effective. This study will be one of the first to explore similarities and differences across disability groups from the perspective of both WWD and care providers. This study will have important implications for reducing health disparities among WWD; it will inform the development of interventions to improve the PCH of WWD, which may in turn contribute to better outcomes for WWD and their infants.

column36: What comes next? Uptake of cancer risk reduction strategies by women who receive inconclusive results from BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing
column37: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the 2nd leading cause of cancer death for women in Canada. 20% of familial forms of breast cancer are due to genetic mutations, most commonly in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. When a risk-increasing mutation is identified in these genes, women are eligible for risk reduction strategies such as yearly breast cancer screening with MRI and mammography and/or preventive surgery. However, many women who are tested do not receive a definitive result as to whether they carry a genetic predisposition to cancer; instead, many receive inconclusive results (a mutation with uncertain cancer risk is identified or no BRCA mutation is identified but a mutation may exist in an untested gene). For these women, cancer risk is harder to predict. Although no previous studies have shown a benefit to risk-reduction strategies for women with inconclusive results, current guidelines are vague about the need for further treatment. It is, therefore, likely that recommendations made to these women vary by treating physician. The goal of this study is to examine how frequently women who receive inconclusive results from BRCA testing undertake risk reducing strategies. Specifically, we will use a unique data platform that brings together genetic testing and health care utilization information for close to 17,000 women who underwent BRCA testing in Ontario from 2007 to 2016. We will determine factors that influence the use of screening and preventive surgery, including the role of an inconclusive test result. In examining how often these strategies are used, we will identify targets for patients and healthcare provider education around genetic test interpretation and risk reduction. As direct-to-consumer genetic testing becomes more readily available, accurate genetic test interpretation will be increasingly important as both patients and physicians will be faced with the challenge of how to manage an inconclusive genetic test result.

column36: Brain connectivity and cognitive control in children with Tourette syndrome: the impact of comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
column37: Tourette syndrome (TS) is a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one phonic tic. TS patients often faces various comorbid disorders, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). For a child with TS, having comorbid ADHD comes with a lot of complications, such as more inhibitory deficits and increased impulsivity. Our project aims to assess the brain function of children with TS and/or ADHD. We want to identify markers that would facilitate an earlier diagnosis of these conditions. An earlier diagnosis would enable treatment strategies to be put in place more quickly. For instance, earlier treatment of ADHD symptoms could prevent the development of several behavioral problems in adulthood. To evaluate the brain function of these children, we will use electroencephalography, which records the electrical activity of the brain. We will evaluate the connections between some regions of the brain during different conditions. We will first use a cognitive control task. Cognitive control is very important in TS patients because it allows them to control their tics in certain situations and for short periods. In addition, we will evaluate brain function directly while children with TS are voluntarily attempting to suppress their tics. We expect that having both TS and ADHD will have a negative impact on cognitive control. This should also be reflected in brain function, which should differ between children with TS, those with ADHD, and those with both TS and ADHD.

column36: Population-Level Effects of Pregnancy Complications on Maternal and Offspring Mortality
column37: Pregnancy complications, including hypertension and diabetes during pregnancy, occur in 1-8% of pregnancies and are associated with serious outcomes in mothers and infants. Previous studies have shown that women with more than 2 complications and/or consecutive pregnancies affected by pregnancy complications are at higher risk of a negative outcome. Additionally, women with pregnancy complications have been found to have a higher risk of heart disease. New research suggests that these complications may also impact the long-term health of children. There is therefore a need to understand how pregnancy complications effect the risk of death in women and their children and how the risk of death differs within and between pregnancies. There is also a need to find new risk factors that will identify women and children at increased risk of death. This project will use 46,474 women enrolled in the Collaborative Perinatal Project from 1959-1965 across the United States. Children of women enrolled in this study will also be used. We will examine the effect of pregnancy complications on the risk of all-cause and cause-specific death among women and children and how this effect differs within and between pregnancies. A predictive model will be subsequently developed to identify factors prior to or during pregnancy that predict future risk of death in women and children. This study will provide a better understanding of the impact of pregnancy complications on the risk of death in women and children. The findings of this work will also help to isolate risk factors that can identify women and children at highest risk. This work has the potential to improve the long-term health outcomes of mothers and children through the early detection and management of risk factors.

column36: Eukaryotic Elongation Factor-2 Kinase (eEF2K) as a new therapeutic target in pediatric brain cancer
column37: More than 600,000 people in North America die from cancer each year. Within the scope of people affected by this disease, brain cancer is the most common pediatric solid cancer, devastating the lives of more than 4,600 children and their families every year. Aggressive brain surgery and radiation are the treatments currently available for children. However, these therapies are often ineffective and cause serious side effects on the developing brain, such as permanent seizures and learning disabilities. Thus, more specific and less damaging therapies are urgently needed. Cancers grow very quickly and need high quantities of nutrients. However, increased nutrient supply to the cancer is not always possible for the human body. When cancer cells do not have enough nutrients to grow, they find ways to compensate for this. Our laboratory team at the BC Cancer Agency recently made a significant discovery: a small protein called eEF2K helps cancer to survive when it has no nutrients. Pediatric brain tumors produce a very high amount of this protein. In addition, children with tumors that produce excessive eEF2K protein usually die earlier than children with tumors that do not produce the protein. We are convinced that by blocking the function of the eEF2K protein, we can starve tumors to death. To test our idea, we will work with cells derived from childhood brain tumors such as medulloblastoma. We will first study if cells lacking the eEF2K protein grow slower under starvation conditions, compared to cells that have the protein. We will then grow these cells in mice and look at the same effect. If our assumption is confirmed, we will try a drug that blocks eEF2K to determine if it can kill tumor cells. No specific and effective therapy for children with brain tumors is currently available. Our study is crucial not only in understanding how eEF2K affects pediatric brain tumors, but also in finding new possible therapies for children affected by this destructing disease.

column36: Maternal prenatal depression and past trauma: Intergenerational effects on fetal neurobehavior and early childhood mental health
column37: There is ample evidence that when a mother is distressed during pregnancy (e.g., depression, anxiety, stressful life events), this can lead to greater risk that her child will develop mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, ADHD, and conduct problems. What remains unclear are the mechanisms or pathways through which maternal distress can transcend to the fetus to influence child development; a potential pathway is through the methylation of genes in the placenta. What also remains unclear is whether past maternal trauma can also influence child mental health outcomes, beyond exposure to maternal prenatal distress. The group that I will study are women and their children followed throughout pregnancy and childhood who are part of the Environmental Influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) consortium, a multi-site study of 62 cohorts across the United States under the auspices of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). My research will be part of the Boricua Youth Study, which includes a high-adversity sample of Puerto Rican women - these women have been followed from childhood to adulthood to the second generation of children, allowing for the study of how the mother's exposure to Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs, a well known measure of trauma) may affect the next generation. During my Fellowship under the supervision of Dr. Monk at Columbia University Medical Center in New York, my aim is to expand my training in perinatal development to include skills such as: the assessment of fetal neurobehavior in utero, the extraction DNA from biospecimens, procedural knowledge to conduct observational studies, the development of treatment interventions, and proficiency in translational research. Overall, I aim to gain new knowledge to underscore the need for preventative healthcare and to inform specific, time-sensitive interventions to improve the mental health of women and their children in the first years of life.

column36: Elucidating the role of prefrontal cortex GABAergic interneuron subtypes in the enduring effects of adolescent cannabis exposure using electrophysiological and behavioral approaches
column37: Adolescence is a dynamic period characterized by maturation of higher-order cognitive functions, including decision-making and working memory, to their adult levels. It can also be a period of increased risk-taking, during which some individuals commence use of drugs such as cannabis. Several of the biological changes that support adolescent maturation of complex behavior occur within a brain region called the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Given the extended development of PFC, it is particularly vulnerable to the deleterious effects of drug-taking during adolescence, which may have lasting consequences on cognition and increase risk for psychiatric disorders including schizophrenia. Indeed, past research has shown that cannabis exposure, particularly during the early adolescent period, leads to enduring changes in cognitive and emotional processes that stem from PFC functional changes. In particular, certain PFC cells that release the inhibitory neurochemical GABA undergo physiological maturation during adolescence that is disrupted by drug exposure. PFC GABA cells are also impacted in schizophrenia, and may represent the cellular mechanism by which cannabis exposure increases the risk of developing the disorder. This proposal is aimed at identifying the cellular players that underlie the long-lasting effects of cannabis use during adolescence within PFC. It uses electrophysiological approaches to examine how cannabis exposure affects the function of particular types of PFC GABA cells, including how they process input from other brain regions, coupled with behavioral approaches probing how these alterations may be implicated in cognitive changes relevant to psychiatric disorders. These insights into impacts of cannabis may be particularly valuable given its recent legalization and possible increased accessibility for adolescents. Furthermore, the work has the potential to identify new intervention targets for schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders.

column36: Elucidating the mechanisms driving formation and maintenance of healthy heart valves
column37: Heart valves are important structures that promote optimal circulation within the body. Heart valve disease affects about 2.5% of the Canadian population, and can cause debilitating health issues or mortality. Identifying the genes involved in heart valve formation or valve dysfunction will give insight into the underlying cause of heart valve disease. My proposed work uses zebrafish as a model to study valve development and disease, with the aim of potentially applying our findings in a clinical setting and identifying genetic targets for diagnosis and therapeutic treatments. My first aim is to characterize the development of valve interstitial cells (VICs), which are crucial specialized cells that maintain valve strength and flexibility. I am particularly interested in studying the roles of three molecules - Nfatc1, Notch and Wnt - all of which have been linked to heart valve defects. By genetically altering their expression, I can examine the effects on VIC development and valve function. Furthermore, I propose to identify targets of Nfatc1, a molecule whose function is to regulate genes that control cellular behaviours. In patients, drugs inhibiting Nfatc1 alleviate heart problems, but have strong off-target effects. Finding Nfatc1 targets has the potential to yield more specialized therapies for treating valve dysfunction. My second aim is to study the molecular anomalies that manifest in valve disease progression. A molecular aberration found in diseased valves is abnormal overactivation of the Wnt pathway. I propose to examine the effects of increasing Wnt in normal VICs, and perform a large scale screen to identify the misregulated molecules. In particular, I am interested in whether Wnt overactivation induces pro-inflammation effects that cause excessive immune response and valve pathogenesis. In the long term, I aim to establish an assay for compounds that can alleviate inflammatory response causing symptoms of valve disease.

column36: Development of a framework for assistive technology policy development (TemplAT) and evaluative tool (EvaluAT) to enhance global capacity for assistive technology provision
column37: Only one in ten people with disabilities who need assistive technologies to complete day to day tasks currently have access to those technologies. Assistive technologies are devices, services, and systems which allow people with disabilities to maintain or enhance their independence. To reach the anticipated needs of 2 billion individuals by the year 2050, a global coordinated effort is needed. Most importantly, national governments have the responsibility to address the needs of their citizens by providing these devices at an affordable cost with the right services in place to ensure safe and effective use. Currently, very few governments have policies which support timely, effective, and affordable distribution of assistive technologies. Over the next two years, we will develop and test a framework that can be used by national governments to assess their current policies, or craft new ones which meet the specific needs of their citizens, in their countries. Critically, this framework will provide guidance on the criteria necessary to craft effective policy, while maintaining flexibility necessary to accommodate local customs and cultures. We will do this in partnership with the World Health Organization's Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology, by incorporating current research, and the opinions of experts from around the world. Ultimately, this project will provide a structure for countries to provide safe and effective access to assistive technologies and promote independence and inclusion for all individuals with disabilities.

column36: Investigation of FcRn-FcgammaR3a cooperation: implications for rheumatoid arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, incurable disease with painful symptoms including joint stiffness and swelling affecting more than 300 000 Canadians. We know that this disease is caused by the antibodies of the immune system attacking the lining of the joints, but we do not know why some people develop the disease and others do not. White blood cells, called antigen presenting cells, have proteins, called the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) and Fcgamma receptors, which are responsible for responding to antibodies that are produced during an immune response. The FcRn and Fcgamma receptors were once thought to play separate roles, but our research indicates that these proteins co-operate to orchestrate an effective immune response. We are studying how these proteins interact, and how the FcRn could predispose people to develop RA, when they possess a variation in a gene that encodes for a specific Fcgamma receptor, the FcgammaR3a. We will test whether a new medication that blocks the FcRn can be beneficial in mice which have been genetically engineered to have the FcgammaR3a variation and predisposed to RA. These studies will help us understand basic biological mechanisms involving the FcRn and FcgammaR3a, which will help us understand why people with the FcgammaR3a variation develop rheumatoid arthritis or other autoimmune diseases. Our research may lead to personalized medical treatments for rheumatoid arthritis, which will depend on a person's genetics.

column36: Ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion: the evolution of treatment, outcomes, and the health system in response to the availability of highly efficacious treatment options.
column37: Stroke is one of the leading causes of disability and death in Canada. However, stroke affects men and women differently. Women experience greater disability compared to men after stroke. The reasons for these differences are unknown and are difficult to study in large populations. A new stroke outcome measure, 90-day home-time (the number of days a patient is living at home - and not in a hospital - in the first 90 days after their stroke), may make measuring stroke outcomes in large populations easier. However, 90-day home-time has properties which make it difficult to analyze and the optimal method for analyzing 90-day home-time is unknown. This research will use several methods from the machine learning literature to determine which is most appropriate for use with 90-day home-time. Once the most appropriate method is determined it will be used to help identify risk factors for poor outcome after stroke and if these are different between men and women. For example, perhaps smoking men compared to non-smoking men spend an average of 3 fewer days at home in the first 90 after their stroke while smoking women compared to non-smoking women spend an average of 6 fewer days at home in the first 90 after their stroke. This type of information will help inform the public on specific risk factors for poor outcome after stroke and which of these risk factors are different in men and women. For physicians and health care administrators, predicting the amount days a patient is at home in the first 90 days after their stroke helps plan for the amount of days a patient is in hospital in the first 90 days after their stroke. Knowing when 90-day home-time may be different among men and women will help plan for future hospital lengths of stay and how these lengths of stay may change if certain risk factors could be eliminated from the population.

column36: Using eHealth Technology to Drive Shared Decision-Making in Asthma Care
column37: Asthma affects 7.8% of Canadians, leads to serious respiratory symptoms, and could cost our health system $4.2 billion per year by 2030. Health-related smartphone apps can provide patients with personalized health information anytime and anywhere, allowing them to better manage diseases like asthma. Health providers can also benefit from electronic tools to improve the efficiency and quality of asthma care. Together, patients and health care providers could use a smartphone app to engage in discussions about asthma medication choices. We previously built the Electronic Asthma Management System (eAMS). The system required patients to complete a questionnaire about their asthma on a tablet device in the waiting room and this information was processed and transmitted to their doctor's computer. Our pilot study of this tool showed that it does improve care, however less than one third of patients completed the tablet questionnaire. We are now improving the system by developing and testing an asthma care app that will: 1) allow patients to complete the questionnaire on their own devices; and 2) provide a tool that will help patients and doctors to make shared decisions about medication choices. We will integrate this app with the eAMS such that both systems share all data. This study aims to test the updated system to see if and how patients and doctors actually use it, if they are satisfied with it, and how it affects the care that they receive. If successful, our unique approach may be a model for the design of similar technologies for the care of other chronic diseases. Ultimately, we will seek to implement our app and asthma care system across Canada to improve not only the way that healthcare is delivered, but also the everyday health of Canada's 2.4 million asthma sufferers.

column36: Investigating the Contextual Effects Associated with Intimate Partner Violence and its Negative Health and Economic Consequences in Toronto: Longitudinal Analyses of the Neighbourhood Effects on Health and Wellbeing (NEHW) Study
column37: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) is a major health concern in Canada, with more than 20% of women experiencing physical, sexual, or emotional violence from a male partner. Indigenous Canadians, those in same-sex partnerships, and transgender people often experience IPV at much higher rates. IPV is associated with negative health outcomes such as anxiety, depression, sexually-transmitted infections, and suicide. Considering IPV is a social problem, it stands to reason that some of the risk of experiencing IPV stems from the characteristics of where a person lives. However, research into which aspects are associated with IPV and how best to mitigate them is still relatively new. Known as contextual effects, these factors consist of neighbourhood characteristics (i.e. community wealth, neighbourhood safety, access to healthcare, greenspace) and the social norms prevalent in each community (i.e. gender and cultural norms). We propose to use individual- and neighbourhood-level data from a 2011 survey of 2,412 Toronto residents to examine the aspects of a person's environment that are associated with IPV. By combining this data with respondents' Ontario Health Insurance Program number, we also follow respondents' health outcomes and expenditures from 2011-2018. This allows us to investigate which contextual effects are associated with patterns of reporting IPV to healthcare providers since 2011, as well as how IPV is associated with long-term health outcomes and costs in different environments. A novel analysis will be able to examine not just whether IPV is associated with health outcomes and increased costs, but the rate of the increase- something never done in the Canadian context. A better understanding of the contextual effects pertinent to IPV, as well as how these are associated with health outcomes and healthcare costs, can focus policies and interventions aimed at reducing the toll IPV places on individuals, neighbourhoods, and the healthcare system in Canada.

column36: Assessing the effectiveness of a structured exercise program on exercise- and disease-related outcomes in a long-term lifestyle intervention study for the secondary prevention of heart disease.
column37: Cardiovascular disease affects the heart and major blood vessels and is the second leading cause of death in Canada. Lifestyle behaviours account for the majority of cardiovascular disease risk. Consuming a diet rich in plant-based foods decreases disease risk factors, namely cholesterol and inflammation. Regular exercise also mitigates disease risk; however, some evidence suggests that women may not respond to exercise the same way as men. Moreover, whether the long-term combination of an established diet for cholesterol reduction, called the Portfolio Diet, and exercise training enhances health improvements in adults with cardiovascular disease is unknown. The purpose of our ongoing, multi-centre, three year, randomized clinical trial is to investigate the combined effects of the Portfolio Diet and structured exercise training on health markers in adults with cardiovascular disease. We hypothesize that consuming a Portfolio Diet will enhance improvements in body composition (reduced fat and increased muscle mass), disease risk biomarkers (lower cholesterol and inflammation) and fitness following regular exercise training. To investigate this, we will recruit a large sample of 200 adults with cardiovascular disease. Participants will be randomized to receive either i) food from the Portfolio Diet and a monitored exercise program; ii) food from the Portfolio Diet and advice on healthy exercise habits; iii) advice on healthy eating and a monitored exercise program; and iv) advice on both healthy eating and exercise habits. We will compare health changes across the four groups and between men and women. The major goal of this project is to provide evidence-based recommendations for long-term, feasible, lifestyle modification strategies for improving cardiovascular disease risk. Importantly, this research will also increase our knowledge about the influence of sex on lifestyle behaviour-induced improvements on the secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

column36: WNT signaling in the postnatal brain: roles for Interferon Regulatory Factor 2 Binding Protein-Like in development and neuronal maintenance.
column37: We have recently identified IRF2BPL as a novel human disease gene causing a progressive and severe neurodegenerative disorder. Patients are born normal, but at age ~3-5 years, begin falling, develop seizures and eventually become immobile before the age of 10. Brain imaging in older patients shows progressive brain atrophy. Neuronal loss of IRF2BPL in fruit flies results in gradual neurodegeneration and behavioral defects reminiscent of the human condition. The function of IRF2BPL is very poorly understood across species. My preliminary data indicates that IRF2BPL can inhibit WNT signaling in vivo, a critical biological pathway conserved in animals with well-established roles in development including the brain. However, a role for WNT signaling in the mature brain and neurodegenerative disorders is currently ill defined. A cell based study suggested that IRF2BPL reduces WNT signaling activity by ubiquitinating beta-catenin, a core WNT activator. I hypothesize that IRF2BPL inhibits WNT signaling and that loss of IRF2BPL should result in excess WNT signaling in the postnatal brain. In this proposal, I will: 1) Determine the functional consequences of increased WNT signaling in mature brains and determine if IRF2BPL loss of function ectopically activates WNT signaling in vivo. 2) Determine if IRF2BPL targets beta-catenin or other proteins implicated in WNT signaling in flies, mice and human cells. 3) Generate and characterize Irf2bpl knockout mice and assess if WNT signaling is affected. I will also use these mice to model the human disease as they may serve as a therapeutic testing platform. Mechanistic insight into a role for WNT, which is highly therapeutically targetable as drugs have been developed to reduce WNT signaling, and IRF2BPL in the postnatal brain will deepen our understanding of both neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.

column36: Sustained engagement in HIV care: Novel approaches to identify and evaluate the impact of socioeconomic disparities
column37: HIV remains a global public health threat, with 37 million people living with HIV (PLWH). Advancements in HIV therapy have transformed the clinical landscape increasing life expectancies and reducing new HIV infections. But benefits rest on the lifetime commitment of PLWH to adhere to treatments. Over the last 20 years, the proportion of patients virally suppressed- and therefore those with controlled infections- has risen from 25% to over 80% in the United States (US). Although encouraging, progress is uneven and falls short of global targets. Race continues to play a differentiating role in the inequality of HIV infections. African Americans make up more than half of new cases while only representing 14% of the US population. Moreover, even in cities with universal health care coverage such as San Francisco, where overall ~85% of PLWH are virally suppressed, that number plummets to 30% among those marginally housed and homeless. Worldwide, people who fare poorly in HIV care have little or no access to care, face stigma and encounter socio-structural barriers. Socioeconomic status and race have been shown to predict health outcomes. But research on this topic has not optimally captured the multi-dimensional ways in which disparities interact and how this leads to adverse health outcomes for PLWH. For example, low income is often the consequence of mental illness, substance abuse, limited education. Even though each of these factors has been shown to be associated with poor health outcomes, the extent to which these factors intersect to create underlying expressions of socioeconomic deprivation remains to be explored. Identifying and understanding the consequences of disparities is the first step in addressing inequalities through targeted interventions and health policies. Results from this research will characterize and evaluate the role of socioeconomic drivers of HIV care engagement, which will ultimately play a critical role in ending the HIV epidemic.

column36: Investigating host susceptibility factors and a pathobiont in Crohn's disease-like intestinal inflammation
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of Crohn's disease (CD) in the world. This chronic inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract significantly reduces the quality of life for the 130 000 Canadians living with CD as they experience symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and fatigue. While the composition of bacteria in the gut is severely altered in CD patients, it is unclear whether this is secondary to intestinal inflammation or plays a causal role in the disease. Moreover, it is unclear whether a specific bacterium can trigger disease in genetically susceptible individuals. A major limitation in understanding the causes of CD is the lack of experimental models that address these factors. Intriguingly, we found that the deficiency of genes involved in bacteria detection and killing triggers spontaneous intestinal inflammation in mice that resembles CD pathology. Furthermore, development of disease in the genetically susceptible host required the presence of Mucispirillum schaedleri (Mucispirillum), a bacterium that inhabits the colon of normal mice. The current proposal focuses on identifying the processes by which bacteria sensing and Mucispirillum accumulation causes CD-like pathology. This work provides important insights into the causes of CD and offers the possibility of targeting specific-disease causing bacterium as an innovative strategy to treat the CD.

column36: Prospective study of psychosocial predictors and outcomes of breast cancer surgery among women with unilateral breast cancer.
column37: When a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer, the standard of care for surgery is to remove any evidence of disease on the affected breast. However, more and more women are choosing to remove both breasts. This overtreatment has placed increased financial and resource burden on the Canadian healthcare system. In addition, women treated with bilateral mastectomies have an increased risk of post-surgical complications. There is significant interest in finding out why this phenomenon is occurring but research has so far focused on administrative and clinical reasons behind why more women are choosing to remove both breasts. It seems intuitive that psychosocial reasons are playing a major role behind this decision process but this has not been adequately studied. The goal of our studies is to understand why women choose the surgery that they do for their breast cancer, including those who choose to remove both breasts. We will also determine satisfaction and health-related quality of life after such surgeries and compare by surgical procedure (lumpectomy versus removing one breast versus removing both breasts). Women with breast cancer will be recruited at three major hospital centers in Toronto, Ontario (Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, Toronto General Hospital and Women's College Hospital). Baseline information regarding patients and their breast cancer will be collected. We will use validated psychosocial questionnaires and instruments to measure our outcomes of interest, including cancer worry, cancer-related distress, body image, quality of life, decision satisfaction and decision regret. By performing these studies, we hope to understand the psychosocial reasons behind why more women are choosing to remove both breasts when they are diagnosed with breast cancer. In doing so, we may be better able to counsel women with newly-diagnosed breast cancer, with the hopes of not having to overtreat them and lessen the burden on the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Lowering dietary omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid intake as a novel strategy to preserve brain function in a mouse model of neuroinflammation
column37: Both omega-3 and omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 and n-6 PUFA) are considered nutritionally essential as the human body does not have the required enzyme to synthesise their precursors. In the diet, it is recommended to consume a balanced ratio of n-3 PUFA:n-6 PUFA. However, the North-American diet is very low in n-3 PUFA and high in n-6 PUFA with the ratio estimated to be approximately 1:30. Eating too much n-6 PUFA is associated with elevated inflammation and this could increase the risk of developing a plethora of diseases, including neurological diseases. To reduce inflammation, it is recommended to consume fish-derived n-3 PUFA in the diet, but fish stocks are declining worldwide. One alternative dietary strategy could be to lower the consumption of n-6 PUFA as they compete for the same enzymes as n-3 PUFA. Our hypothesis is that compared to high dietary consumption of n-6 PUFA, low consumption will be associated with lower neuroinflammation which will contribute to preserve brain function. By using mice that are fed one of three westernized diets differing in PUFA composition, we will induce neuroinflammation by injecting a pro inflammatory protein into the brain of mice. Neuroinflammation and its resolution will be monitored by quantifying proinflammatory markers, gene expression, and PUFA derived metabolites. In a parallel project involving the same diets and interventions, the cognition of mice will be evaluated to assess whether dietary PUFA modification play a role in the prevention of cognitive deficits related to inflammation. Considering that dietary factors are important in the prevention of neurological diseases, understanding the contribution of dietary fats in particular is especially important. If lowering dietary n-6 PUFA prevents inflammation and cognitive abnormalities in this mouse model of neuroinflammation, this could represent a feasible strategy to prevent neurological diseases associated with this condition in humans.

column36: Cellular and Molecular Basis for Impaired Autonomic Nervous System Regulation of the Sinoatrial Node in Diabetes Mellitus
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a growing epidemic health issue that is associated with many severe cardiovascular complications that ultimately result in death in as many as 65% of diabetic patients. Included amongst these are cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, which results in an inability to properly regulate heart rate. My objective is to determine how and why abnormal heart rate regulation occurs in diabetic patients. Heart rate is determined by specialized 'pacemaker cells' in a region of the heart called the sinoatrial node (the natural pacemaker present in everyone's heart). Although often attributed to damage to the nerves innervating the sinoatrial node, our work demonstrates that improper regulation of heart rate in diabetes is also associated with abnormal sinoatrial node function, independently of the nerves. This represents an important new way of looking at cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy. My proposed studies will greatly advance our understanding of abnormal heart rate regulation in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. This will be accomplished using a range of powerful experimental approaches in intact diabetic mice, as well as in isolated hearts and isolated cells from the sinoatrial node. Our laboratory is one of only a handful worldwide that can study the sinoatrial node in mice, which uniquely positions us carry out these highly important studies. The ultimate goal of our work is to identify new therapeutic targets for cardiovascular disease in diabetics.

column36: The role of the gut microbiota in host defense against infection during critical illness
column37: Our gut is home to trillions of microbes, called the microbiota, that engage in a symbiotic relationship with our body's immune system to maintain health. Disruption of the gut microbiota, or "dysbiosis," is linked to the development of immune system dysfunction and diseases, including susceptibility to infections. Nowhere is this more relevant than in the intensive care unit (ICU), where critically ill patients battle life-threatening infections as a result of impaired immune defenses. Recent research has discovered that critically ill patients in the ICU develop severe dysbiosis of their gut microbiota, but how this impacts immune defenses and the development of hospital-acquired infections is poorly understood. Therefore, we propose a comprehensive study of how gut microbiota dysbiosis impacts immune defenses against infections during critical illness. Our study will investigate this important clinical question in both critically-ill patients, as well as cutting-edge animal models with "designer microbiota." We will systematically identify microbiota species that control the balance between immune defense and infection, characterize the mechanisms of microbiota-immune interactions, and test the therapeutic potential of rationally-designed microbiota reconstitution to augment protection against infection in models of critical illness. Overall, this research will advance our understanding of how changes to the microbiota impact host defense, and will create new knowledge to drive therapeutic innovations that harness the microbiota for the treatment of critically ill patients in the ICU.

column36: Investigating the developmental origins of childhood asthma and allergies: Maternal prenatal social stress, infant immune cell epigenetic patterns, and risk for early childhood asthma and allergies at 3- and 5-years of age
column37: Asthma and respiratory allergies are common chronic diseases, affecting >10% of Albertan children, and costing $2.1 billion annually in Canada. Asthma and allergies are leading causes of school absenteeism, emergency room visits, and reduced quality of life. Understanding the risk factors for childhood asthma and allergies has important implications for reducing occurrence and burden of these diseases. Experiences in early life, i.e. prenatally or perinatally, "get under the skin" and program long-term immune activity in a way that can increase risk for immune-related diseases. One biological mechanism through which this occurs is epigenetic modification of immune cells, which determines whether and by how much immune cells are activated when challenged, e.g. by allergens. The social environment is a potent predictor of health. Although the mother's prenatal social environment has been linked to immune activity in offspring, no studies have tested whether the mother's prenatal social environment serves as a "cue" that gets embedded in offspring's immune system via epigenetic modifications, and whether epigenetic modifications affect risk for allergies and asthma. The purpose of this project is to test this developmental pathway using the Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition Study (APrON) data. Maternal social environment data was collected over pregnancy, and offspring were followed-up at 3-months postpartum (blood samples for epigenetic analysis), and at 3- and 5-years of age (allergies and asthma diagnosis). This project will contribute to our understanding of the developmental origins of childhood asthma and allergies, and examine maternal social environment factors that could be intervention targets.

column36: The role of RNA granules in atherosclerosis
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality has declined over the past 50 years due to improvements in drug therapy and disease management, most notably in lipid-lowering therapy. Despite patients meeting lipid-lowering goals, CVD remains a leading cause of death. Therefore, identifying molecular mechanisms that regulate CVD progression may provide insight into how to further mitigate disease risk. Cells within the fatty plaques on artery walls are under conditions of stress. Cells respond to changes in conditions and stress by forming complexes called RNA granules, comprised of RNA and protein, that coordinate the cells response. Although these complexes have been observed in cells within fatty plaques, there exact role and which molecular events they coordinate in CVD is uncharacterized. The proposed project will investigate the role of two RNA granules, stress granules and processing bodies, in two different cell types in CVD, the smooth muscle cell and macrophage. In my first aim, I plan to establish the techniques required to study these granules in macrophages and smooth muscle cells. In my final aim, I plan to take these findings and extend them to a mouse model of CVD. Understanding the role of RNA granule formation in the context of CVD could provide novel molecular insight into CVD development and could identify potential therapeutic targets.

column36: Measuring and Valuing Health Benefits for Economic Evaluations in Breast Cancer: Development and Validation of a Scoring Algorithm for the BREAST-Q Utility Scale (BREAST-QU)
column37: Explicit rationing attempts to battle fiscal debt and increasing demand for healthcare were the focus of 2018 Ontario provincial elections. While rationing is one of the options to curb health care costs, it slowly disinherits us from the core principles of the Canada Health Act. An alternative solution is to base budget allocation decisions on "value" of healthcare interventions (cost vs. outcome). Quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) is the preferred metric for valuing health outcomes in terms of quality of life (QOL). Once cost per QALY is determined, service with the lowest cost per QALY is chosen. Traditionally, generic preference-based measures (PBM) have been used to calculate QALYs. However, they do not include concerns unique to breast cancer patients (body image, appearance, sexual) and hence lack sensitivity. The BREAST-Q is a widely used and validated breast cancer-specific QOL instrument, but it cannot be used to calculate QALYs. Hence, a descriptive classification system, the BREAST-Q Utility (BREAST-QU), was developed from BREAST-Q using patient interviews and input from an international team of experts. My postdoctoral research will advance this work by generating a scoring algorithm (i.e., preference weights for health states defined by BREAST-QU). A representative sample of the general population and women with breast cancer will be asked to participate in choice-based tasks (discrete choice experiment and best-worst scaling) to identify their preferences for various breast cancer health states. The responses will be analyzed using advanced statistical techniques, resulting in scoring algorithm for the BREAST-QU. The reliability, validity, and responsiveness of BREAST-QU will be assessed. The use of BREAST-QU in clinical practice, economic evaluation and policy-making will be promoted through publications, presentations, and professional networks; ultimately resulting in "biggest bang for the buck" in breast cancer and improved population health.

column36: Identifying clinically-relevant circulating protein biomarkers for osteoporosis
column37: Osteoporosis is an aging-related skeletal disease and a major cause of morbidity and mortality. While therapies currently exist to prevent fractures, current risk stratification algorithms fail to identify the majority of people who fracture. Thus, a major clinical goal in osteoporosis is to identify individuals at risk. Our objective is to improve fracture screening programs by identifying clinically relevant circulating biomarkers for osteoporosis and incorporate them in the risk stratification algorithms. We will first use Mendelian randomization (MR) to high-throughput screen circulating proteins using available proteomic GWAS studies in our large cohort of individuals with osteoporosis phenotypes from UK Biobank and the international GEFOS consortium. We will then validate our prioritized biomarkers in well-characterized cohorts (CaMos and Rotterdam) with rich phenotypic information, by measuring protein levels using validated ELISA based assays. Eventually, we will combine the biomarkers with the strongest prediction power with traditional fracture prediction algorithm (FRAX) and our newly developed polygenic risk score via machine learning, in order to provide clinically-relevant fracture risk stratification. We have already generated preliminary data from 83 candidate biomarkers that associate with fracture and bone mineral density, a major risk factor for osteoporosis, which were identified from 922 proteins. We have prioritized RSPO3 as a novel, functionally relevant biomarker for osteoporosis and the validation process is currently underway. We plan to increase the number of proteins tested to identify additional circulating biomarkers that strongly associated with the risk of fracture, in order to provide targets for clinical interventions and to effectively identify high-risk individuals for more effectively tailored preventive therapy.

column36: Role of circulating dipeptidyl peptidase 4 in insulin resistance and cardiovascular disease
column37: Patients with Diabetes have an increased risk of heart disease compared with patients who do not. It is also known that when patients have diabetes, communication between the liver, pancreas, immune system and cardiovascular system becomes disturbed. The current project will evaluate one specific messenger from the liver, Dipeptidyl Peptidase 4 (DPP4). Through communications with other organs, DPP4 causes inflammation and contributes to diabetes. DPP4 has two roles - cutting other proteins and stopping their function, and talking to the immune system and increasing their inflammatory potential. Stopping the cutting activity of DPP4 has proved to be an effective way to treat diabetes. Now we want to evaluate if stopping both cutting and communicating actions of DPP4 can improve therapy for patients with diabetes and prevent cardiovascular disease. It is well accepted today that diabetes and heart disease are ailments that involve inflammation. We will use cell and animal models to define the mechanisms of DPP4 release into the blood and its regulation at the cell and gene level. We will also examine data that are collected from patients suffering from liver and heart disease to inspect connections between DPP4 and the level of their disease. At the end of this project, our results will better define the role of DPP4 and will guide development of new drugs, lessening the burden on our health care system and helping people who suffer from heart disease and/or diabetes.

column36: CryoEM analysis of the structural dynamics of mitochondrial Complex I during catalysis
column37: Complex I is a large protein found in the energy producing compartments of cells. Complex I is essential for life, performing the first step in a series of chemical reactions that eventually lead to the production of ATP, the chemical energy currency of living cells and is a potential drug target for a number of diseases, including diabetes and cancer. In addition, it is a significant producer of reactive oxygen species, molecules that cause damage to components of the cell and can lead to cell death. The production of reactive oxygen species by Complex I is particularly problematic after tissues are resupplied with oxygenated blood following a period when the supply of oxygenated blood was blocked, such as during a heart attack, stroke, or surgery. During this sort of injury, Complex I transitions between an operative and inoperative state and its structure changes. Importantly, these states are thought to be related to how Complex I carries out its function and its roll in tissue damage through the production of reactive oxygen species. The relationship between structural changes in Complex I and its function remains unknown. In this project, I will use state-of-the-art electron microscopy techniques available at SickKids to determine the structure of mammalian Complex I as it performs its chemical reactions. These experiments will allow me to determine how changes in its structure relate to its function, and will reveal how Complex I operates on a molecular level. This knowledge will help provide a framework for the design of therapeutics to protect against the injury to tissues that occur in heart attack and stroke, and to treat diabetes and cancer. Thus, this project has the potential to improve human health, in particular in relation to cardiovascular disease.

column36: Functional characterization of regulatory mutations in mantle cell lymphoma
column37: This research will identify new strategies for treating non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs). Lymphomas are a diverse group of cancers that will afflict roughly one in 50 Canadians in their lifetime. These cancers that develop in cells of the immune system and arise from errors, known as mutations, in the DNA of the cell. These errors provide cells with incorrect or incomplete instructions, which can cause changes in cells that may vary their behaviour and ultimately lead to cancer. My research aims to look at a rare and aggressive variety of NHL known as mantle cell lymphoma. By using genetic information from a number of patient samples, I will first identify significant patterns of mutations that appear in the DNA of their cancer. Once identified, I will then investigate how these mutations affect the behaviour of mantle cell lymphoma and other types of NHL. Specifically, I will focus on how cancers respond to treatment. The identification of mutations that affect the response of lymphomas to available treatments can aid doctors in tailoring therapies they choose in the future. This project will provide new insight into the complicated genetic changes that occur in cancer cells and positively affect patient outcomes.
