column36: Modeling the long-term contribution of incarceration and of prison-based prevention strategies to drug-related harms among people who inject drugs
column37: Drug use is criminalized at various degrees globally. Incarceration and the period post-release can increase risk for HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections and overdose among people who inject drugs (PWID). Thus, over time, incarceration is likely to be "responsible" for a significant proportion of the total new cases of these health-harms among PWID. Yet, no study has attempted to estimate its potential contribution over time. In addition, access to prison-based strategies such as opioid agonist treatment, needle and syringe provision and naloxone kits, with continuation upon release, can prevent the occurrence of these health harms but no study has yet estimated their potential long-term prevention benefit. This study seeks to address these gaps using mathematical modeling. This technique enables the forecasting of the future burden of an epidemic and of the potential impact of introducing an intervention on its course. Such modelling outputs are widely used by policy-makers to inform their decisions regarding the control of diseases. Given that different global settings have distinct incarceration levels and distinct realistic scenarios of future scale-up of prevention strategies within prisons, these simulations must be tailored to specific settings. In this study, we will carry out the simulations in two distinct settings, Montreal, Canada and Nairobi and Mombasa, Kenya. For each setting, the model parameters will be informed by data collected through two studies (HEPCO, Montreal and TLC-IDU, Nairobi and Mombasa, Kenya). Altogether, this study has the potential to provide estimates on the extent to which incarceration may be fueling HIV and HCV transmission and overdose among PWID, and the necessary scale-up levels of prison-based prevention interventions to achieve meaningful reductions in these health harms over time. In the long-run, findings could inform appropriate public health and policy changes to reduce the burden of HIV, HCV and overdose.

column36: Informing high-resolution functional MRI through modeling microvascular dynamics
column37: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is the most widely used technique for measuring dynamic neuronal activity across the whole brain with no harmful effects, making it an invaluable tool for human neuroscience. FMRI measurements are based on tracking focal changes in blood flow and oxygenation that occur during brain activity to meet energetic demand. Because fMRI is, therefore, an indirect measure of neuronal activity, the confidence with which changes in neuronal activity can be inferred is limited. The hypothesis of this study is that a more complete picture of the blood vessels in the brain, and how they react to brain activity, will help us to better interpret the fMRI signals. New evidence from microscopy studies in rodents indicates that the control of blood flow in response to neuronal activity is far more precise than previously believed, suggesting that fMRI has the potential to be a reliable marker of neuronal activity if measured and interpreted correctly. However, it is challenging to translate these findings to humans since the organization of rodent blood vessels is markedly different from ours. This project will create a 3D reconstruction of the blood vessel network-down to the smallest capillaries-from human brain specimens, from which a model of how the vessels react to neuronal firing to control blood delivery will be generated-and from this, how the fMRI signals change in response to brain activity. To ensure accuracy, the model will be validated against high-resolution human fMRI data acquired on an ultra-high magnetic field strength MRI scanner. This bottom-up approach will provide a crucial missing link between measured fMRI signals and the detailed underlying physiology, helping to better understand fMRI signals and improve our ability to accurately measure brain function.

column36: Growth trajectories of children with autism spectrum disorder: Latent class growth model analysis using two sources of primary care data
column37: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may be at high risk of obesity because of restricted diet with a preference for processed foods, low levels of physical activity participation, excessive screen time, and use of medications that may contribute to weight gain. Previous scientific work has suggested that obesity risk in children with ASD might be seen early, with unhealthy weight gain between 2 to 5 years of age. However, we do not truly understand how patterns of weight gain over time (weight trajectories) are different in ASD than in typically-developing children. As ASD now affects about 1 in 68 individuals, results will be important to a large group of Canadian children. I will explore weight trajectories in ASD, using two sources of data: (1) the Applied Research Group for Kids (TARGet Kids!), which collects rich early childhood data from paediatricians' and family doctors' offices, and (2) the Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database (EMRALD(R)), which contains electronic medical record data from family doctors in Ontario. Using statistical methods, I will see how weight trajectories in children with ASD compare to weight trajectories in children without ASD. If the ASD group shows unhealthy weight trajectories (for example, early development of obesity), the time when growth becomes abnormal will be explored. In addition, I will identify what nutritional, behavioural and medical factors are linked with abnormal weight trajectories in ASD. We know that addressing obesity is important, because unhealthy weight is associated with negative impacts on health, quality of life, and use of health services. We also know that children with ASD likely need different types of intervention for obesity than typically developing children. Results of my work will help in preventing and treating obesity specifically in children with ASD, thereby making an important contribution to improving the health of Canadian children.

column36: Dissecting tissue-resident memory T cell heterogeneity in human tissues
column37: Despite the extraordinary advances in medicine over the last few decades, infectious disease remains among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Our understanding of how protective immune responses can be generated and augmented by vaccines or immunotherapies are therefore of prime importance for improving human health. Recent studies have identified a heterogeneous population of non-circulating memory T cells, known as tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), that are distributed in mucosal/barrier sites and are essential in mediating protective immunity during infection and after vaccination. However, due to the difficulty of studying immune cells directly in human tissues, basic questions of how TRM function and how they differ across multiple tissues within the same individual remain unanswered. My research will utilize a unique human tissue resource in which multiple mucosal and lymphoid organs are obtained from research-consented organ donors in order to dissect the similarities and differences between TRM subsets across tissue sites. I will use a combination of cutting-edge techniques including high-dimensional immune profiling, multi-parameter imaging, and single cell transcriptomic approaches to generate a "human atlas" of TRM phenotype and function throughout the human body. With this investigation, my objective is to define and characterize TRM identity and function using a one-of-a-kind tissue resource that allows unprecedented access to study human tissue immunity. Understanding how TRM function in humans is central to the design of new vaccines and immunotherapies aimed at boosting tissue immunity, with the ultimate goal reducing deaths from infectious disease.

column36: The role of mesenchymal tissues in the establishment of the blastema and their contribution to mammalian digit tip regeneration
column37: Some animals, such as newts and lizards display a remarkable ability to regenerate parts of their body. In mammals, however, this ability has been lost, with one exception; in both mice and humans, true multi-tissue regeneration occurs when you injure your fingertip. The process of regeneration in the mouse fingertip following injury involves first, a wound-healing response, followed by the formation of a specialized mass of cells called the blastema. These cells are then responsible for regenerating the missing portion of the digit tip including the bone and the nail. In amphibians, the origin of the regenerative blastema has been widely studied. It has been shown that mature cells revert back to an earlier cell state (dedifferentiate) to serve as one of the sources of cells that build this transient cell mass, the blastema, ultimately resulting in tissue regeneration. By comparison, the mechanisms by which the mammalian digit tip blastema forms is much less well understood. Therefore the primary objective of this project is to identify the specific cells that make up your fingertip, and to understand how they work together to regenerate this structure following injury. If we are able to understand how this process of regeneration occurs in the fingertip, we can then take this knowledge and potentially regenerate other parts of the body.

column36: Spatial molecular profiling at single-cell level during hPSCs to HSCs differentiation in both in vitro and teratoma models using tFISSEQ
column37: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are specialized stem cells (SCs) that give rise to the blood and immune cells. First HSCs emerge during the embryogenesis. These new HSCs have a higher ability for proliferation and differentiation into different cell types than the adult HSCs, suggesting that their environment influences their fate. Previous studies showed that SCs reside in small niche environment. Such environments provide a special setting for cell-cell communication, extracellular matrix construction, and control of signalling between the cells. Yet, genes/pathways and expression profile of individual cells within the human embryonic HSCs niches remain poorly understood. Our current inability to generate bona fide human HSCs from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) suggests that these HSCs derived in vitro may have different gene expression profile than the ones developed in embryos due to different stem cell niche environments. Studying these niche environments was difficult until the recent development of the Fluorescent In Situ Sequencing (FISSEQ) by the Church lab. FISSEQ enables single-cell transcriptome sequencing of fixed, intact tissue samples. Subsequent development of a modified version of FISSEQ called targeted FISSEQ (tFISSEQ) allows detection of small RNAs and even proteins by FISSEQ. These technologies, for the very first time, enable us to evaluate the gene expression landscape of SCs and all other cells in the SCs niche, in the context of their native spatial environment. Human PSCs-derived teratoma engrafted in immunodeficient mice, develops HSCs that possess good repopulation ability in secondary recipient mice. This could be a faithful model that represents at least in part the heamogenic emergence process in the embryo. Using tFISSEQ to obtain spatial expression landscape of proteins and miRNAs in the teratoma and PSC-to-HSCs in vitro models will finally shed light on the key effectors and pathways in heamogenic development in human embryos.

column36: Structural characterization of candidate anti-mycobacterial antibiotics bound to the CIII2CIV2 respiratory supercomplex
column37: Just like humans, mycobacteria, such as the species that cause tuberculosis (TB) and leprosy, need oxygen to live. However, the cellular systems that allow mycobacteria to use oxygen differ dramatically from the equivalent systems in humans. This combination of essentiality and uniqueness make these systems vulnerable to drugs designed to treat mycobacterial infections. Indeed, the breakthrough drug bedaquiline (also known as Sirturo, produced by Janssen Pharmaceutica), which was the first new TB therapeutic in 40 years when it was approved in 2012, targets the process of using oxygen to burn fuel and provide cells with energy. We will use the technique of electron cryomicroscopy (cryoEM) to reveal, at near-atomic resolution, how candidate drugs target an essential component of the cellular respiration system in mycobacteria, known as the respiratory supercomplex. These structures will provide information on how drugs can be improved, through a process known as structure-based drug design. We will also perform high-throughput experiments, known as screens, to find new candidate drugs and use our structural studies to guide the improvement of these molecules into useful therapeutics. Together, these studies will help us and our collaborators to lay the foundation for a new generation of drugs to combat the constant threat of mycobacterial drug resistance.

column36: Key stakeholder engagement to define the core components and presentation for a collaborative Longitudinal Care Plan e-Tool prototype
column37: Health professionals often work in silos. If any health information is communicated, the most common formats are paper or fax. This fragmentation has been shown to compromise patient safety by leading to inefficient, low-quality and low-value care. The ideal would be to use a longitudinal care plan, which is intended to be a single, reconciled source of health information shared between health professionals and patients to address a unified set of treatment and care goals. It should be patient-centered, dynamic and integrated with local electronic health records to facilitate real-time updates and bi-directional communication. The purpose of this research project is to inform the design and development of a collaborative Longitudinal Care Plan e-Tool (eLCP). Objectives: 1) To describe the current state of information exchange during care transitions for patients managed by multiple health professionals and services 2) To define key information needs, core components and desired presentation to inform the design of an eLCP prototype Methods: In-depth, unstructured interviews with patients and family members, workflow observations of health professionals, and medical document review will be used to develop comprehensive patient journey maps to understand the current state of care coordination and information exchange during care transitions to identify gaps for improvement. Focus groups will be conducted using semi-structured interview guides with patients, family members, and various health professionals to identify key information needs, core components and desired presentation of an eLCP. Separate Delphi processes will be conducted to refine the lists of information needs and components, and to prioritize by value added to the eLCP for 'patient and family' and 'health professional' views. Final rank-ordered lists will be created to inform the design and development of an eLCP prototype.

column36: Amelioration des soins offerts par les cliniciens de premiere ligne aux personnes atteintes de la maladie d'Alzheimer: quel impact sur leurs trajectoires de soin ?
column37: L'Organisation Mondiale de la Sante a reconnu la maladie d'Alzheimer comme une priorite du 21e siecle. Toutefois les systemes de sante Canadiens peinent a offrir un diagnostic precoce et des soins de qualite a ces patients dont la population est en croissance exponentielle. Cela affecte leur qualite de vie et induit de nombreuses visites a l'urgence, et hospitalisations evitables et des couts majeurs pour la societe. Le renforcement des capacites des cliniciens en Groupes de Medecine de Famille (GMF) (infirmieres et medecins de famille) est propose comme la solution pour ameliorer les soins offerts aux personnes atteintes de la maladie d'Alzheimer. Depuis 2014, 38 GMF au Quebec participant au Plan Alzheimer, ont ete formes et ont recu des ressources supplementaires, notamment des infirmieres cliniciennes dediees a la prise en charge des personnes atteintes de la maladie d'Alzheimer. Ce renforcement des capacites a pour objectif de permettre aux GMF de prendre rapidement en charge les personnes atteintes de cas typiques de maladie d'Alzheimer, du diagnostic au traitement et d'assurer un suivi de qualite; les cas complexes etant referes aux specialistes. Cependant, l'impact du Plan Alzheimer n'a pas encore ete mesure et est l'objet de mon doctorat. J'etudie si les patients pris en charge par les GMF du Plan Alzheimer obtiennent plus rapidement un diagnostic, sont plus regulierement suivis et ont moins souvent besoin d'aller a l'hopital. Pour cela, j'analyse la base de donnees de la Regie d'Assurance Maladie du Quebec. Mes resultats sont attendus par le Ministere de la Sante et des Services sociaux pour ameliorer le Plan Alzheimer. Cette recherche, une des premieres dans le monde, sera partagee au sein d'un reseau international de chercheurs qui souhaitent alleger le fardeau des patients et de leurs familles et offrir les meilleurs soins au plus grand nombre.

column36: Antidepressant effect of d-lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) microdoses
column37: Mood disorder is a mental disease with an incidence of 5% in Canada, and for which antidepressants currently available are efficacious only in 50% of patients. Depression involves a dysfunction of serotoninergic system in dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), as well as an hypofunction of the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC). D-lysergic diethylamide acid (LSD) is a hallucinogen that has gained popularity as a recreational drug and recent clinical evidences suggest that it exerts an effect on mood, although this pharmacological and physiological mechanism has not been well explored in animal models. Our hypothesis is that a short-term treatment of LSD could have an antidepressant effect in a model of chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) in mice through the modulation of serotonin and glutamatergic neurotransmissions. Our objectives are : 1)perform behavioral test to evaluate the effect of a short-treatment (7days) of systemic injection of LSD on mice after 6 weeks of CUS, compared with their controls; 2) carry out in vivo electrophysiological recordings to characterize the activity of serotonin and pyramidal neurons in the DRN and in the PFC, respectively, in both stressed and control mice and to test the effect of LSD on these neurons; 3)employ western blotting analysis to investigate whether LSD modulates cortical intracellular signaling proteins which are involved in depression and mood disorders. Adult male and female mice C57BL/6J will be used. We expect that LSD will revert the depressive-like behavior, restore the altered 5-HT and glutamatergic neurotransmissions and normalize the protein levels in the PFC of stressed mice. This study will be useful to understand the pharmacological and molecular mechanism of LSD that could lead to its beneficial use.

column36: Investigating the role of APJ heterodimers in pain modulation
column37: A large number of currently prescribed drugs target G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). These transmembrane proteins form the most important protein family present at the cell surface. GPCRs are involved in transducing a signal from the surrounding cellular environment into intracellular activity. Drugs targeting the same binding pocket as the endogenous ligand may have an activity similar to that of the ligand (agonist), or may block its effect (antagonists). Prescribed drugs often have side effects that could be due to a lack of specificity of these molecules. Traditionally, GPCR signaling was conceptualized with monomeric receptors, however, it is now accepted that some GPCRs are able to associate with others to form heteromeric complexes. The close relationship maintained by two GPCRs in a dimeric complex could influence the intracellular signaling events triggered by each. In this study, we propose to evaluate the activity of dimers formed by the apelin receptor and the neurotensin NTS1 receptor, or the apelin receptor and the kappa-opioid receptor. These three GPCRs are known to have powerful analgesic properties, thus we would like to evaluate the role played by these heterodimeric complexes in pain modulation. A better understanding of the role of heterodimeric complexes involving the apelin receptor would allow the development of new molecules specifically targeting these GPCR dimers. Such drugs would be more efficient, more specific, and therefore, have fewer side effects.

column37: As a result of medical advancement, the population lifespan has increased significantly in the past century. However, this increase in lifespan has introduced new challenges. Brain aging related disorders such as neurodegenerative disorders are on the rise and there is an urgent need for further mechanistic understanding and immediate interventions to enable effective treatments. Our goal is to study the process of healthy brain aging using multimodal neuroimging data from several publicly available datasets (N~18,000) and model the trajectories of healthy aging brain as a 4-D reference template. We will also investigate age related alterations in brain functional and structural network organization and how they are affected by genetic and environmental risk factors. Finally, we will use the healthy brain aging model to study the deviations caused by neurodegenerative disorders and how they contribute to dementia: Genetic/environmental risk factors ---> Aging brain ---> Neurodegeneration ---> Dementia This project will improve our understanding of brain aging as well as age-related disorders and will provide potential novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for neurodegeneration to identify individuals at high risk of cognitive impairment. The study will also provide a scientific basis for healthy brain aging trajectories as a reference point to design and evaluate interventions to prevent, control, or mitigate the deviations that will lead to neurodegeneration and dementia.

column36: Identifying the neuronal activity of adult born neurons in the dentate gyrus that support behavioural pattern separation.
column37: Until as recently as the 1990s it was assumed that in the adult brain cells die, but are never born. This was shown to be incorrect: in some regions of the brain - and of interest to us, the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus - new cells are born. Evidence increasingly suggests that these adult born neurons (ABNs) are essential for hippocampal function; specifically, in the formation of distinct representations of similar inputs, a mechanism known as pattern separation (PS). Abnormalities in adult neurogenesis, and consequent PS impairments, were then linked to several neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases, such as Parkinsons, Alzheimer's, Huntingtons disease and schizophrenia. Although we know about ABNs involvement in PS, we know almost nothing about how ABNs operate at the network level to support it. This is in part because determining the answer to this question is difficult: it requires recording from multiple, sparsely-organized neurons along with precise and well-controlled assessment of a subtle aspect of cognition. To do so, we proposed to use Miniscopes, that allow us to visualize the activity of large populations of neurons during behavior, in combination with genetically targeted expression of a calcium indicator to ABNs in the DG. By combining cutting-edge technology in calcium imaging with precise assessment of behavioral PS we are confident that we can determine how ABNs supports PS hippocampal processing at the network and behavioral levels. Because of the paucity of information on the role of ABNs in cognition, using precise molecular and behavioural tools to discover clear evidence of this relationship along with underlying mechanism will be high-impact and transformative; understanding the basis of this process will help us to develop new tools for an early diagnosis of different disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease or dementias, and will unveil new targets for intervention in neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases.

column36: Investigating the role of cellular metabolism in effector T cell responses and T cell exhaustion
column37: T cells play a crucial role in the immune response against infections and cancer. Over the course of an immune response, T cells engage various metabolic pathways to meet the energetic demands of expansion and development of their effector functions. The proposed research aims to characterize the metabolic pathways used by T cells during both functional and dysregulated immune responses. The different strains of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus are ideal to study T cell metabolism. The Armstrong strain induces a normal T cell response in mice. In contrast, infection of mice with the Clone-13 strain leads to T cell "exhaustion", a term used to describe T cells that are dysfunctional. Exhausted T cells, which are often associated with chronic infections as well as cancer, are characterized by their reduced proliferation and poor effector functions. Taken together, these infection models serve as great tools to study cellular metabolism in T cells during both normal and dysregulated immune responses. Recent studies suggest that exhausted T cells have altered cellular metabolism. The unique immune and metabolic environment linked with chronic infections and cancer triggers metabolic adaptation in exhausted T cells to promote survival in these stressful conditions. Our research therefore aims to characterize and compare the metabolic demands of functional and exhausted T cells. In addition, our work will determine the impact of immune checkpoint therapy, which is used to reverse T cell exhaustion to treat cancer, on T cell metabolism. Finally, by performing a large-scale screen of metabolic genes in T cells, our research seeks to identify novel metabolic pathways that regulate T cell function and exhaustion. Overall, the findings of this study will lead to a better understanding of how metabolism regulates T cell function and may potentially uncover novel strategies to increase the effectiveness of T cell-based therapies by modulating cellular metabolism.

column36: Comprehensive analysis of neuronal RNA-binding protein function in a multicellular organism
column37: To create the many different organs in our bodies, and allow their proper function, different genes encoded by our DNA are switched on or off in specific tissues at particular times. In the human brain and the nervous system, defects in these genetic switches lead to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, as well as neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's. Our research asks how genes are turned on and off in the brain, using a small ~1mm long round worm, called C. elegans, which is very simple to study, yet has been found through decades of research to share many aspects of its cellular and molecular functioning with humans. We are particularly interested in how one particular group of molecules, called RNA-binding proteins, helps to turn genes on or off in the brain cells of these animals. We expect that this research will lead to a better understanding of how nervous systems are built, and shed light on how improper control of these mechanisms can lead to neurological diseases.

column36: Reducing patient boarding practices and impact on patient mortality by using optimization and machine learning methodologies that account for the heterogeneity of individual patients
column37: Critically ill patients, requiring timely and specialized treatment, are subject to substantial delays before admission into intensive care units (ICUs) due to patient overcrowding and the lack of staffed ICU beds. Patient "boarding" has become a common strategy for hospitals to provide care for patients despite bed allocation problems in the ICU and involves caring for patients in alternative locations, such as emergency departments, until an ICU bed is available. However, these alternative locations are generally neither trained for, nor designed to treat critically ill patients, compromising the quality of care provided. As such, patient boarding and delays in ICU admission significantly increases increase patient mortality The development of optimization and simulation tools have been promising towards reducing the number of boarded patients and delays to admission but rarely account for differences between each individual patient. By assessing patients at an individual level, hospitals may more accurately measure the impact of delays to ICU admission on patient survival. The goal of my proposed research is to develop a novel optimization model, integrated with machine learning algorithms, that accounts for the heterogeneity of individual patients to reduce boarding practices and patient mortality. To do this, I will estimate the difference in survival between boarded and nonboarded patients based on individual patient demographics and disease characteristics, and operating information from hospitals. I will then develop an optimization model to optimize decisions regarding patient boarding, bed capacity, and staffing to maximize the predicted survival of each patient. The novel combination of predictive and optimization methodologies will allow hospitals to minimize the effects of patient boarding, reduce and eliminate boarding practices, and ultimately increase patient survival.

column36: Revealing the contribution of medial septal glutamatergic neurons in spatial navigation and memory using combination of calcium imaging, electrophysiological recordings and optogenetic in freely behaving mice.
column37: Memory functions decline during aging is a major health issue. Inefficient spatial navigation and the accompanying feeling of being lost often came as among the first source of incapacitation during the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. So far, attempts to reverse those symptoms have failed. The lack of basic knowledge about how the brain proceeds to generate spatial memory represent a major gap precluding more sophisticated therapies to be developed. Despite accumulating evidence about how neurons code the current spatial location of the body in the environment, the way the brain uses that information to plan and monitor navigation toward specific destinations remains enigmatic. We propose that glutamatergic neurons from a brain region named the medial septum, play a crucial and unexpected role in those processes. We propose to use wearable miniature microscope to record task-elicited glutamate neurons of the medial septum in freely behaving mice. Then, to refine our understanding of the function of those neurons, we propose to manipulate their activity during navigation tasks. We have already demonstrated that the activity of medial septum glutamatergic neurons correlates with the destination of spatial trajectories in a maze. Now we want to understand how that signal interact with the neuronal representation of the current position of the individual to allow for an efficient navigation. The contribution of glutamatergic neurons to spatial navigation is particularly important to study as the function of these neurons first discovered by our laboratory has just begun. Also, since the medial septum is known to be severely affected in both normal aging and Alzheimer's disease, understanding how this structure contributes to spatial navigation should help us to better to reverse age-related memory dysfunctions.

column36: Transboundary environmental contamination in the Upper Saint John River Basin (New Brunswick - Maine): an ecosystem approach to health study
column37: The Saint John River acts as a border between the Madawaska County (NB, Canada) and the Arrostook County (Maine, USA). The economy of the Upper Saint John River Basin (USJRB) is based mostly on forest and transportation industries. While these economic activities bring benefits to the region, they can contribute to the emission of environmental contaminants, which can easily cross national borders and affect the health of the population on both sides. The World Health Organization estimates that 20% of cancer cases worldwide are attributable to environmental exposures. A recent survey showed that cancer rates are a concern for the Madawaska County citizens. Both sides of the River have high incidence of colorectal and lung cancers. However, there are no studies that provide the potential effects of the environmental contamination on the USJRB population health. The objective of this postdoctoral research is to develop a participatory and interdisciplinary project based on health and environmental concerns of the USJRB population. The research will document these concerns and identify influential regional stakeholders in environmental health in four phases: (1) A web-based survey to describe the social network of stakeholders in the USJRB; (2) Workshops with USJRB's communities (Madawaska County, Aroostook County and Madawaska Maliseet First Nation) to collect citizen's concerns about health and the environment; (3) Meetings with local stakeholders in order to co-construct an environmental health study in the USJRB, based on citizen's priorities, that will be submitted to the CIHR Project Grant competition in Spring 2020 and (4) the implementation of the study by collecting evidence based on selected priorities (research survey, environmental and biological material sampling, etc.). This postdoctoral fellowship will contribute to a healthier population by promoting prosperity, resilience and environmental protection while considering transboundary contamination.

column36: Digital Bridge: Using technology to support patient-centered care transitions from hospital to home
column37: Background: Falls in people with spinal cord injury (SCI) are common, but we know little about why falls occur and how they can be prevented. Falls can cause fractures, hospital admissions, decreased ability to move and depression. In this project, we would like to find out: 1) what causes falls and how falls impact the lives of those with SCI, and 2) how we can improve fall prevention practices in Canadian SCI rehabilitation hospitals. Methods: This research will happen at Canada's largest SCI rehabilitation hospital in Toronto. We will track the number of falls in 64 people with SCI over six months. Twenty-four of those that have one or more falls will move on to part two, where they will be asked to take photographs of: what increases and decreases their chances of falling, and how the risk of falling affects their day-to-day activities. This will help us learn about how falls impact their lives. Interviews will also be conducted with 10 hospital administrators and 15 therapists working in SCI hospitals to understand what does and does not work well in current fall prevention policies and determine how policies can be improved. Implications: Our research will shine light on prevalence and causes of falls in people with SCI. The information from our study will help develop effective fall prevention initiatives that can reduce the risk of falls and improve life satisfaction for people with SCI. People with SCI often have low education and income. By lowering the risk of falls, people with SCI may participate more in their community, school and workplace. As our research targets people with SCI as well as hospital administrators and therapists, the research findings can be applied in hospitals, rehabilitation centers and in homes.

column36: Generation of Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Left Ventricular Cardiomyocytes for the Treatment of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
column37: The normal human heart has two pumping chambers: the right ventricle and left ventricle. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs (low-pressure system), whereas the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body (high-pressure system). Some children are born without a left ventricle, a malformation called hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). To survive, these children must undergo surgery to connect the right ventricle to the rest of the body. However, the right ventricle, which is designed to pump blood into a low-pressure system, is often unable to sustain the high pressure of the rest of the body, and gradually starts failing, leading to heart failure and death. Unfortunately, we currently have no drugs to treat this type of heart failure. The goal of our project is to develop a novel therapy for HLHS using human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). These cells are unique in that they can give rise to all the cell types in the body. Our lab has previously designed a protocol to generate heart muscle cells - called cardiomyocytes - from hPSCs. However, all cardiomyocytes are not identical, and there are significant differences between cardiomyocytes in the right versus left ventricle. We hypothesize that cardiomyocytes from the left ventricle are better suited to sustain high pressure and that transplanting left ventricular cardiomyocytes into a pressure-overloaded right ventricle could prevent heart failure. The aims of our proposal are to 1) understand the molecular differences between right and left ventricle cardiomyocytes; 2) elaborate a protocol to make left ventricle cardiomyocytes from hPSCs; 3) transplant left ventricle cardiomyocytes into pigs with a pressure-overloaded right ventricle to see if these cells can prevent failure. If successful, this project could transform the care of children with HLHS. This would have a profound impact on our healthcare system, as HLHS has become the largest driver of cost in pediatric cardiovascular care.

column36: Uncovering how cortical and subcortical inhibitory brain structures contribute to uncontrollable freezing of movement in Parkinson's disease.
column37: Freezing of gait (FOG) is a devastating symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) affecting more than half of the people in the advanced stages. FOG is characterized as sudden, uncontrollable moments of freezing in place and inability to move. FOG is considered one of the most significant symptoms influencing quality of life, yet notably has a poor and variable response to antiparkinsonian medications. Despite a great deal of empirical research, the cause underlying FOG in PD patients remains unclear. It's hypothesized that the brain areas activated in healthy humans to inhibit or stop movements, may also be responsible for FOG in PD. Overactivity of these inhibitory brain areas due to PD dysfunction may cause the stopping of movement resulting in FOG. This research program will investigate the role of cortical (pre-supplementary motor area & right inferior frontal) and subcortical (subthalamic nucleus & internal globus pallidus) brain structures in the inhibitory network and how modulation of their activity contributes to the uncontrollable freezing of movement. To answer several specific questions regarding the role of cortical and subcortical structures in the inhibitory network we will integrate several state-of-the-art research tools including Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS). DBS will allow in vivo recording of human subcortical brain activity via implanted electrodes to determine whether overactivation of subcortical brain areas that supress movement contributes to FOG. TMS will allow us to manipulate brain activity to determine whether decreasing brain activity in inhibitory cortical structures reduces inhibition and FOG. This knowledge will yield an understanding of the dysfunctional brain areas in PD and define the next generation of therapeutic procedures. Results may guide the targeted modulation of brain activity as an effective treatment option to improve the lives of Canadians impacted by this debilitating PD symptom.

column36: Peripheral and central chemoreceptor reflex regulation of sympathetic activity in heart failure patients
column37: When the heart fails to pump normally, the brain releases into the bloodstream increased amounts of a chemical called noradrenaline. Noradrenaline increases heart rate, causes the kidneys to pass less salt and water and constricts blood vessels. At first, more noradrenaline improves heart function but over time this muscle weakens and can no longer pump enough blood to the bodies organs. This condition is called "heart failure". For older Canadians, heart failure is the most common cause of hospital visits and a major cause of early death. Our long term research goal has been to identify what it is about heart failure that causes more noradrenaline to be released from noradrenaline-releasing (sympathetic) nerves that can be countered with new treatments. In about 50% of heart failure patients, the specialized blood oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors in the blood vessels and brain become very sensitive to changes in these gases. These patients breathe more vigorously if blood O2 is low or blood and brain CO2 is high. This hyperventilation then brings O2 or CO2 back to normal. Importantly, these sensors also connect to brain areas controlling noradrenaline release. We think that: i) if these O2/CO2 sensors are more sensitive they will tell the sympathetic nerves to release more noradrenaline and ii) heart failure patients with the most overactive O2/CO2 sensors will have the most frequent nerve firing. My study will determine: i) if O2 or CO2 sensors are more active in heart failure patients; ii) if this causes more sympathetic firing during blood O2 or CO2 changes; and iii) if more active O2/CO2 sensors contribute to high nerve firing even when patients are at rest and blood O2 or CO2 are within normal ranges. We are confident that these experiments will discover one or more causes of high noradrenaline in heart failure and that this will promote new ways of identifying and treating this important cause of suffering and death.

column36: Study of the mechanisms underlying seizures and epilepsy after traumatic brain injury in a zebrafish model.
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) occurs in 160,000 Canadians yearly, more than the combined number of patients with breast cancer, HIV/AIDS, spinal cord injury, and multiple sclerosis. One of the effects of TBI is seizures or epilepsy, and TBI is the most common cause of symptomatic epilepsy in people ages 15 to 24. There is no treatment to prevent epilepsy after TBI. Animal studies in rodents are expensive and time-consuming. Most of the conducted studies had a small sample size and there is a need to move toward larger and more randomized animal studies. Studies in zebrafish would allow for more rapid screening of potential targets before moving to rodent studies. Zebrafish are widely used in other disease studies because their genomes are 70% similar to humans, they spawn hundreds of eggs per week, they are cheap to breed, and are readily genetically modifiable. The overall aim of this project is to establish a zebrafish model of severe TBI to understand how this leads to seizures or epilepsy. We will confirm that the spontaneous seizures we have seen in this model are due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain and will also determine whether inflammation and abnormal proteins are involved in the development of epilepsy by using genetic studies. This project will apply modern engineering techniques in neuroscience to enhance our understanding of why some TBI patients develop seizures while others do not. Findings from this project are expected to help in developing treatment options to prevent post-traumatic epilepsy.

column36: Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) as a Crucial Regulatory Cytokine and Therapeutic Target in Ankylosing Spondylitis
column37: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common form of spine arthritis which causes bones in the spine to fuse together, making the spine rigid and leading to severe low back pain (LBP). The main characteristics in AS are inflammation and abnormal new bone formation. Despite biomedical advancements in suppressing joint inflammation, there is no effective treatment to slow down the bone formation. The exact mechanism that links inflammation and spinal bone fusion remains unknown. Therefore, finding the key regulators that control both inflammation and bone formation is critical in AS. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a molecule plays pivotal roles in inflammation which is also reported as a potential regulator for bone formation. However, the roles of MIF in AS have never been explored. We recently discovered that the expression of MIF is remarkably higher in blood obtained from AS patients compared to healthy individuals. We also determined that MIF has a great potential as a disease progression marker in the prediction of spinal bone fusion. In my preliminary data using a well-established mouse model of AS, I found that the expression of MIF in the both serum and tissue are remarkably higher in mice with AS compared to healthy mice. Mice with enhanced MIF expression clearly showed AS clinical features including severe arthritis and new bone formation in spine and ankle joints. In contrast, MIF deficient mice or MIF suppression with specific blockers dramatically prevented the AS clinical features. I also determined the cell groups that substantially produce MIF in AS disease conditions. Interestingly, injection of these cells into a MIF deficient healthy mouse led to AS clinical features, whereas blocking the function of these cells also blocked the AS clinical features. This proposal aims to comprehensively confirm my pilot studies on the role of MIF in AS disease-onset and progression, and establish MIF as a new therapeutic target in AS.

column36: Identification of novel vulnerabilities and therapeutic strategies for breast cancers with acquired resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors
column37: Improvements in the early detection and drug treatments for breast cancer have led to increased rates of survival and cure. However, metastatic breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body remain incurable and represent a major challenge. The recent development of a new targeted treatments called CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) have substantially improved the ability to control disease in the most common form of metastatic breast cancer. Unfortunately, this therapy does not provide a cure. Despite the initial response to the treatment, resistance to CDK4/6i eventually develops and tumors continue to grow. Since the tumors evolve during this process, finding new strategies for breast cancers that acquire resistance to CDK4/6i is an imperative for improving survival rates. To address this health challenge, I will use cutting edge laboratory tools identify the factors which the drug-resistant breast tumors rely on to survive and grow. Then, blocking the function of these genes by using specific targeted drugs will allow us to tackle the tumor cell vulnerabilities, and develop new approaches to improve the survival of these patients. My discoveries could be tested through clinical trials, and linked to specific markers to permit "personalized" treatment in this setting. The findings from this project have the potential to be rapidly integrated into the clinical management of patients and to ultimately improve breast cancer survival.

column36: Delineation of the molecular heterogeneity underlying patient outcomes in follicular lymphoma
column37: Follicular lymphoma (FL) represents the second most common lymphoma overall. Despite recent advances, FL remains largely incurable and the vast majority of patients experience progression over the course of their disease. The disease outcomes are highly variable, with some patients remaining free of disease for ten years or longer following initial treatment, while others experience early progression followed by death. Although an increasing number of treatment options is becoming available, we are currently unable to tailor treatment to each individual patient's lymphoma due to two main reasons. First, we are unable to accurately predict risk of progression before starting treatment. Second, we do not understand what patients would benefit more from one treatment compared to another. In our research work, we aim to overcome these challenges that currently impede personalized treatment. We plan to accrue 300 samples from FL patients across Canada and perform analyses at molecular, cellular, tumour, and patient levels. Our goal is to identify patterns that are currently hidden, but that can be uncovered by leveraging statistical computational tools. These patterns will reveal that not all follicular lymphoma patients have the exact same disease, but that they can be grouped based on similar molecular and cellular trends. Such subtypes of follicular lymphoma are expected to be associated with distinct risk of progression and susceptibility to specific treatments. We will validate our findings using independent lymphoma datasets. Our project has key implications for the treatment of lymphoma in Canada and beyond. The identification of novel subtypes will allow to adjust our treatment approach for each individual patient. By identification of the mechanisms underlying poor outcome we can propose novel therapies for patients who were previously thought to be at high risk, thereby circumventing adverse outcome.

column36: Molecular Regulation of Dendritic Cell Homeostasis
column37: The immune system consists of a variety of different cell types working together to actively maintain a delicate balance between responsiveness to foreign pathogens while maintaining tolerance to self-tissue, and avoiding autoimmunity. T cells are a specialized cell type of the immune system important for protection from infections, as well as from tumor growth. Dendritic cells are another type of immune cell and play a vital role directing T cell immune responses. Dendritic cells actively survey the periphery, searching for pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, as well as neoplastic tissue. They can then direct the recruitment and activation of other immune effector cells, such as T and B cells to the site of insult, propagating the inflammatory response. Current understanding suggests that dendritic cells exist at a resting, or immature state, and require activation signals before they can initiate an immune response. Immature dendritic cell interactions with T cells results in programmed cell death or anergy, resulting in a regulatory or anti-inflammatory response. Once stimulated with activating or 'danger' signals, such as those produced by bacteria, dendritic cells can mature and lead to activation of T cells and a robust inflammatory response. Our lab has recently discovered a family of molecules that act as the 'brakes' of dendritic cells, and actively maintain them in an immature state. Dendritic cells that lack these molecules are constitutively active and lead to continuous T cell activation without requiring additional activation signals. Our proposal aims to explore this novel concept and further investigate how these molecules keep dendritic cells in an immature state. Understanding the mechanisms that regulate dendritic cell activity could prove invaluable in boosting T cell mediated anti-tumor immune response, as well as help limit inappropriate inflammatory responses.

column36: The Impact of Exposure to Dolutegravir and other HIV Antiretrovirals during Pregnancy: Risks Associated with Neural Tube Defects and Impaired Metabolism
column37: The majority of people living with HIV are women of childbearing age. Dolutegravir (DTG) and other integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTI) are commonly used antiretrovirals (ARVs) in people living with HIV, including pregnant women. While these ARVs are very good at preventing transmission of HIV from mother to child, the secondary effects of ARVs, which include maternal metabolic perturbations and negative effects on early fetal development remain a concern. Higher incidence of neural tube defects (NTD) in women living with HIV receiving DTG from conception was reported by an ongoing NIH-funded observational study in Botswana. These findings highlight the urgent need to improve our understanding of the underlying pathophysiology associated with DTG exposure in pregnancy. Maternal obesity and diabetes are recognised risk factors for NTD. DTG has been associated with hyperglycemia and metabolic complications are common side-effects of ARVs. In this study we will investigate the impact of exposure to DTG and other INSTIs during pregnancy on maternal metabolic health and fetal development - focusing on NTD - using a mouse model. We will examine whether DTG exposure affects maternal liver function and glucose metabolism. We will study the effect of DTG exposure on insulin-responsive tissues and examine the effects on insulin production and activity. Our study will help to determine if DTG exposure increases the risk for NTD and if this risk extends to other INSTIs. We will identify potential biomarkers of NTD in DTG exposed pregnancies, and mechanistically assess biological pathways contributing to NTD, specifically metabolic dysregulation. Our study will address critical knowledge gaps in our understanding of the pathobiology of NTD in the context of ARV use in pregnancy, establish a rational basis for further evaluation of effective interventions, and help inform regimen selection in pregnancy.

column36: Delineating molecular signatures mediating osteoarthritis progression in the synovium by using single-cell RNA sequencing
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a disabling condition targeting joints affecting mobility and quality of life. There are no effective treatments for OA due to the lack of understanding of molecular mechanisms which drive the disease. OA affects all joint tissues but changes to the synovium are integral to disease progression. The synovium can strongly predict cartilage breakdown, as well as perpetuate a vicious feedback cycle between the two tissues fuelling further joint damage. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), is a new robust technique examining which genes are actively expressed on a single cell level. It accounts for individual differences between cells, and gives us a better understanding of the cell in its own environment. Currently, there are no scRNAseq studies profiling molecular changes in the OA synovium, leading to a weak foundation for therapeutic studies and a lack of effective targets. We hypothesize that scRNAseq on synovium from early and late stage OA patients will identify molecular signatures underlying OA progression that can be used to determine effective therapeutic targets. We will accomplish this by performing scRNAseq on synovium from patients (50 per group) with early or late stage OA as determined by x-ray. We will then perform comprehensive computational analysis to identify molecular mechanisms responsible for regulating disease progression. Our comparisons will give us insight into early vs late disease, sex differences, BMI and more. Promising targets will be evaluated in an animal model of surgically induced osteoarthritis to test therapeutic potential. Our approach stems from building a foundation for comparison between early and late stage OA, using this foundation to identify promising, clinically relevant targets, and determining whether these targets are capable of disease modification. If these approaches prove successful in modifying animal disease, we will be able to apply these treatments to impact clinical prognosis.

column36: Interaction of exercise, gut microbiome, and gut nutrient sensing
column37: Obesity and type II diabetes are two of the most prevalent chronic health conditions in Canada and lead to impaired control of blood sugar. Exercise is an effective treatment option, but more information is required to understand how exercise leads to beneficial effects. Previous research has focused on muscle, heart, and fat as important contributors to the beneficial effects of exercise, but little is known about how exercise influences the bacteria inside the gut which are collectively known as the gut microbiome. As the first-line type II diabetic drug metformin improves control of blood sugar alongside changes in the composition of the gut microbiome, we believe that exercise may lead to similar results. Therefore, the purpose of this work is to identify whether exercise changes the composition of the gut microbiome and if this is necessary for the beneficial effects of exercise in the treatment of obesity and type II diabetes. Using rodent models of obesity and type II diabetes recently developed in our lab, we will characterize the impact of exercise on the composition of the gut microbiome, and determine whether this occurs alongside known beneficial effects of exercise on control of blood sugar. Additionally, we will identify specific bacteria species increased and decreased by exercise, and will determine whether these bacteria are necessary for the beneficial effects of exercise on control of blood sugar through transplantation, probiotic, or chemical approaches. As exercise is already known as an effective treatment against obesity and type II diabetes, our work will determine whether the gut microbiome is involved in these beneficial effects. As early evidence suggests that microbiome transfer may become a viable therapeutic option in the treatment of obesity and type II diabetes, our results may help to identify novel bacteria that can be used to maximize the therapeutic potential.

column36: Overcoming epigenetic therapy resistance to augment immunotherapy in ovarian cancer
column37: High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the most common and lethal gynaecological malignancy, accounting for nearly 80% of all ovarian cancer deaths globally. Of the nearly 2,800 Canadian diagnosed with HGSOC annually, only 30% survive beyond 5 years. Standard first line therapy consists of debulking surgery combined with carboplatin/paxitaxel-based chemotherapy. While most patients initially respond to this regimen, ~80% relapse within months. Relapse has remained incurable for over 50 years, emphasizing an urgent need to expand treatment options. Treatment of ovarian cancer with immunotherapies known as 'immune checkpoint inhibitors' (ICI) achieves modest response rates of ~15%. ICI resistance in ovarian cancer is characterized by an 'immunosuppressive' tumor micro-environment. A landmark discovery at UHN reveals that epigenetic therapies can promote an inflamed tumor microenvironment that primes tumors to ICI therapy. Unfortunately, emerging clinical trials demonstrate that many ovarian tumors exhibit resistance to epigenetic therapies. The goal of this project is to conduct the first comprehensive investigation into epigenetic therapy resistance to uncover alternate means to circumvent resistance and re-sensitize ovarian tumors to immunotherapy. This project characterizes tumors and tumor-infiltrating immune cells from preclinical models and ovarian cancer patients treated with ICI and epigenetic therapies in several clinical trials at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre. In addition, this project uses CRISPR technology to screen for yet-unidentified therapeutic vulnerabilities in ICI-resistant ovarian cancers. This work will uncover how ovarian cancers evade the immune system and resist epigenetic therapies. The expected impact of this work will establish 'biomarkers' to match patients to the appropriate epigenetic therapy or immunotherapy, and to develop new drugs that target vulnerabilities in ICI and epigenetic therapy-resistant ovarian cancer cells.

column36: An IFN-iron axis reprograms hematopoietic stem cells to generate trained immunity
column37: It has been recently shown that memory capacity of immune response is not limited to only adaptive immunity as innate immune cells present memory-like capacity termed "trained immunity". However, many aspects of this new paradigm in immunity as well as its relevance for vaccine design remain to be determined. One of the major limitation of exploring the concept of trained immunity in vaccines was how we achieve a long lasting memory in innate immune cells, which have hours to days life span. We have recently demonstrated that Bacillus Calmette Guerin (BCG), the only available vaccine against tuberculosis is able to educate the hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) in the bone marrow (BM) to generate long-term protective innate immune memory responses. However, the key regulatory mechanisms that coordinate HSC self-renewal, proliferation and differentiation in this context as well as the mechanisms involved in durability of trained immunity have not been defined. In the current study, we aim to address these fundamental questions by comparing the impact of BCG on imprinting of HSCs to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), which also get access into the bone marrow and reprograms HSCs. The current study is focused to dissect the mechanism acquired by BCG and Mtb in reprogramming of HSCs to generate trained immunity. However, we envision while BCG imprinting of HSCs generates a protective trained immunity, Mtb imprinting of HSCs leads to detrimental immunity. Thus identifying the cellular and molecular signatures of protective versus detrimental trained immunity will allow us to design an effective vaccines against tuberculosis and potentially many other infectious diseases.

column36: Effets d'un blogue base sur les donnees probantes sur la saine alimentation sur les habitudes alimentaires, les comportements alimentaires et le poids des meres et leurs enfants.
column37: L'adoption d'une saine alimentation, integrant notamment une grande consommation de legumes et fruits et de lait et substituts, est reconnue comme une pierre angulaire dans la prevention de nombreux problemes de sante chroniques et est associee a une saine gestion du poids. Or, la majorite des Canadiens n'atteint pas les recommandations quotidiennes minimales pour ces deux groupes alimentaires malgre des actions soutenues du systeme de sante a promouvoir leur consommation. Un nombre grandissant d'evidences suggere la faisabilite et l'efficacite d'interventions transmises par l'intermediaire des nouvelles technologies de communication, tels que les medias sociaux, pour promouvoir l'adoption de comportements sains en sante comme une meilleure adhesion aux recommandations nutritionnelles. De plus en plus utilises par les dietetistes, les recentes etudes sur les blogues en nutrition montrent que ces outils sont des influences emergentes sur les pratiques alimentaires des meres qui les consultent pour trouver des idees de recettes et des strategies pour guider l'alimentation de leurs enfants. L'impact de l'exposition a ces blogues sur l'alimentation des lecteurs est toutefois encore meconnu. L'objectif de cette etude est d'examiner, a l'aide d'un devis experimental randomise et controle, l'effet d'un blogue base sur les donnees probantes sur la saine alimentation, redige par un dietetiste, sur la consommation de legumes et fruits et de lait et substituts de meres. Un objectif secondaire de cette etude qui aura un impact important dans une perspective de sante publique est d'examiner si l'exposition au blogue se traduira en ameliorations de l'environnement familial permettant d'augmenter la qualite de l'alimentation des enfants et les competences culinaires des meres. Cette etude fournira les premieres donnees empiriques sur l'utilisation des blogues comme strategie de prevention ayant un vaste potentiel de diffusion pour aider les Canadiens a mieux manger.

column36: Randomized pilot trial of a parental Guided Participation intervention in their preterm infant's Positioning (GP_Posit)
column37: In the context of prematurity, parents of preterm infants experience difficulties in developing their parental sensitivity. The four main competencies associated with parental sensitivity that parents learn to develop from the birth of their infant are: 1) to be able to recognize and 2) to interpret their infant's cues as well as to 3) select, and 4) quickly apply an appropriate response. Parental sensitivity is essential to consolidate the long-term attachment between parents and their child as well as to promote the neurodevelopment of infants. Considering the fact that parents of preterm infants may have difficulty developing their sensitivity, it is essential to implement interventions promoting its development from hospitalization in the neonatal unit. As part of this research project, the feasibility and acceptability as well as the preliminary effects of an innovative intervention will be measured to promote parental sensitivity and neurodevelopment of preterm infants. As part of this intervention, parents will develop the four core competencies of parental sensitivity through a nurse-led, participatory intervention in the positioning of their preterm infant.

column36: Applying a molecular understanding of the aging process to develop novel treatments for neurodegenerative disease
column37: While aging is the greatest risk factor for the development of neurodegenerative disease, the role of aging in these diseases is poorly understood. In the inherited forms of disease, the disease-causing mutation is present from birth and yet disease onset occurs multiple decades later. This indicates that these mutations are well-tolerated in younger individuals. Based on this observation, we hypothesized that changes that take place during normal aging make the cells in the brain (and elsewhere) susceptible to the disease-causing mutations. If so, then delaying some of these age-related changes may be beneficial in disease treatment. To test this idea, we used a simple model organism, the worm C. elegans, which has been used extensively to identify genes that modulate aging. We found that targeting molecular pathways that have been shown to modulate aging is neuroprotective in C. elegans models of Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease. These experiments provide support for our idea that delaying changes that take place during aging will be beneficial in treating neurodegenerative disease. The current proposal will build upon these exciting preliminary studies by (1) identifying common downstream factors that contribute to longevity in different long-lived genetic mutants, (2) exploring the mechanisms by which these mutations extend longevity, and (3) examining the effect of modulating these aging pathways in animal models of neurodegenerative disease. Overall this work will advance our understanding of the aging process and apply that knowledge to the development of novel treatments for neurodegenerative disease.

column36: Investigating single cell biophysical properties and the basis for the loss of functional diversity in epileptic networks
column37: Epilepsy is a neurological disease where the brain experiences seizures repeatedly over a life-time. Seizures are debilitating states of abnormal and widespread firing of neurons in the brain. Their impact on an individual's life is significant. Given their largely unpredictable nature, epilepsy patients may lose their ability to drive and work in certain jobs, thus suffering from a loss of independence. Furthermore, about half of all epilepsy cases cannot be managed by medication alone. Currently, the only solution for these 'medication-resistant' patients is invasive surgery to excise the region of the brain causing the seizures. I am interested in seizures because they appear to be the result of a "final common pathway" that develops across a myriad of neurological disorders including genetic disorders, stroke, brain tumors, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's. This begs the question, what is this mechanistic "final common pathway", that allows the brain to transition unpredictably to the abnormal neuronal firing seen during seizures? Our hypothesis is that epilepsy develops in the brain when populations of neurons lose their ability to efficiently parse incoming inputs into their various parts, known as de-correlation. When these neurons are not able to sufficiently de-correlate incoming inputs from other brain regions, they begin to fire in a hyper-synchronous manner that defines seizure activity. Our lab's vision is to develop a neuro-electronics platform, precisely analogous to a computer chip, that can be implanted into the brain. This computer chip will have the ability to detect the transition of the brain into the abnormal seizure state and provide electrical stimulation to prevent the seizure from fully taking form. Such a device would routinely stop seizures in a patient's brain without them even knowing it. My doctoral studies will contribute to the development of this device by providing mechanistic insights into seizures and epilepsy.

column36: Overcoming Obstacles in Cancer Nanomedicine Delivery using a Versatile In Situ Ultrasound-Triggered Microbubble-to-Nanoparticle Conversion
column37: Difficult-to-treat solid tumours have long been a problem for the cancer research community. While modern advances in nanomedicine have created smart drugs that are designed to specifically target different cancers, the improvement they provide is limited by the amount of drug that can infiltrate the complex tumour environment relative to normal, healthy tissue. The development of a delivery system that could load drugs and be selectively triggered to release them into the tumour would revolutionize drug design for some of the deadliest cancers. In 2015, researchers discovered that specially designed contrast agents called microbubbles could be converted into stable nanostructures using a particular type of ultrasound. While microbubbles themselves must remain in the blood vessels, these smaller structures have the potential to leave the circulation and enter their surrounding environment. This opens up the possibility of loading a microbubble with therapeutic nanoparticles and initiating the conversion at a tumour boundary, enhancing local delivery at the tumour site. Because the delivery platform would not depend on the drug itself, it could be used to deliver all types of nanoagents in a versatile and consistent manner. This would open new doors for those designing cancer drugs, allowing for researchers to use more specialized nanomedicines at lower doses and with fewer systemic side-effects. This tool and its accompanying shift in the mindset of drug development is necessary in order to produce the next wave of therapies that will help us fight the most lethal cancers.

column36: Picket-fences in the plasma membrane: functions of endothelial diffusion barriers in health and disease
column37: Despite the availability of multiple therapeutic approaches, diabetes, cancer and atherosclerosis continue to incur significant health risks to many Canadians. In these diseases, endothelial cells, which form the innermost lining of all blood vessels, interact improperly with cells and soluble factors that circulate in the blood, leading to adverse effects. I hypothesize that the arrangement and mobility of their surface proteins directly impacts how well endothelial cells can make specific interactions their environment, particularly during disease. I am therefore studying the mechanisms that govern cell-surface architecture and molecular mobility in endothelial cells. Presumably, targeting these mechanisms will allow us to modify endothelial responses to external factors. The aim is to uncover novel targets for disease-specific treatments that will outperform current therapies. New technology allows us to accurately track the motions of single particles on the surfaces of live cells. I will use this technology in combination with other imaging techniques to describe how important endothelial receptors move in response to different stimuli. The networks that give cells their shape interact closely with the cell membrane and are likely to be important regulators of molecular mobility. For this reason, I will investigate the effects of disrupting these networks on molecular movements, as well as the consequences of these interventions on endothelial responsiveness. My studies will establish important connections between receptor movements and endothelial cell functions. The impact of this study will be to improve our understanding of the biophysical mechanisms by which endothelial cells regulate their functions, especially during disease. By studying these mechanisms, we will accelerate the path to discovery of disease-specific treatments.

column36: The impact of chronic/latent viral infections on aging
column37: Some viruses give us a nasty cold then go away but other viruses stay with us our whole life. Some of these viruses can make us sick, for example HIV or hepatitis C, but others come back intermittently and are very annoying, for example herpes simplex virus (HSV) which recurrently give us cold sores or genital wards. Several of these chronic or persistent viruses (Epstein-Barr virus responsible for "mono" or cytomegalovirus) are quite common in the population. Whether they lead to sickness or not, they keep our immune system busy fighting the virus each time they come back. As we age, we are less and less able to fight against infections, such as the influenza virus, that we could easily beat when younger. A weaker immune system also increase the risk of several cancers linked to these viruses. We hypothesize that these persistent viruses damage our immune system over time, change the type of immune cells we have, and reduce our immune cells' ability to activate in order to fight new infections. Furthermore, we contend that the recurrent on and off activation of the immune system because of these viruses leads to the accumulation of mutations within immune cells, eventually rendering them less functional. We propose to study a group of people of all ages (1-80 years old), half of them living with HIV, the other half not. We will test for 8 chronic/persistent viruses and determine how many each person carries, how these relate to the health of their immune cells, and to their risk of disease. Understanding the effect of these viruses on immune cells and ultimately cellular aging will inform on the potential benefits of treating or vaccinating against these viruses in the future.

column36: Using models of early life stress to identify prognostic biomarkers of unhealthy aging
column37: Despite our concerted efforts and aspirations to live healthy, active lives, there is significant variability in the aging process, where some individuals age well and live long, but those on an unhealthy aging trajectory, age earlier and develop chronic diseases earlier than their healthy counterparts. Our project will uncover markers that we believe are present very early in life, long before visible signs of aging begin. column36: Age-dependent development of a primary Tauopathy: the gut/brain axis and biogenesis of Tau strains
column37: Diverse diseases appear during aging and some of the more important ones affect the brain. Specifically, chronological age is the most potent risk factor for the common form of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). This form of AD is not caused by inherited mutations and comprises an enormous challenge for the patients, their families and for public health services. One way to meet this challenge is to test a variety of candidate therapies in animal models but the utility of this approach is thwarted by the availability of suitable models. Inherited forms of AD account for only 10% of cases but are heavily represented in research labs by animal models that overproduce mutant protein molecules involved in the disease. Conversely, models with lower protein production that might better mimic the common form of these diseases are underrepresented. We have created such a "low production" model based on the brain protein called Tau, and, of note, we have observed intriguing animal-to-animal diversity in the disease process. This not only offers a parallel to diversity seen in the human disease but also suggests the action of environmental influences as disease evolves late in the lifespan of these mice. In this work we plan to study how the types of natural bacteria in the gut affect disease, how misshapen forms of Tau protein kill cells and how age-accelerating mutations might affect Tau protein in petri-dish models and in a special area of the mouse brain. As bacterial populations in the gut are more accessible physically and easier to manipulate than protein molecules inside the brain, we believe they comprise a novel and potentially important route towards stopping these brain diseases. intervention.

column36: Linking Inflammation and Metabolism with Frailty in Chronic Cancer
column37: Is 70 the new 60? One of the greatest risks to developing cancer is age. As the average age of Canadians continues to increase, we anticipate a doubling of newly diagnosed cancer patients. Oncologist decision-making currently includes age as a factor when determining a cancer patient's treatment plan as a reflection of risk of being frail. This assumption that age and frailty are directly linked potentially leads to over- or under-treatment which impacts patient quality and length of life. A more precise treatment approach would use biomarkers with other measures of health to inform patients and clinicians to tailor their options accordingly. Building on work we have previously published measuring inflammation, cellular energetics, and telomere length, we will use banked and fresh blood from a cohort of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), a type of blood cancer, to investigate biomarkers associated with aging and measures of frailty. This will help to understand the complex interconnected relationship between aging, cancer, frailty, and patient outcomes. Recognized as a national centre for excellence in CLL research, Manitoba is uniquely suited to conduct this work through our centralized CLL Clinic to recruit patients for research, the Manitoba Tumour Bank to collect biospecimens from CLL patients, the CLL CAISIS database to collect clinical data and research results on patients, and the CLLuster, a funded multi-disciplinary research team dedicated improving CLL patient outcomes. We will leverage these resources to improve the understanding of the biological mechanisms of aging, the development and evaluation of frailty, and improving clinical practice.
