column36: Establishing a new class of senolytics to treat age-related pathologies and extending lifespan
column37: Gradual decline of physical functions during aging increases susceptibility to chronic diseases and inevitably lead to increased health expenditures, morbidity and mortality. During the lifespan, cells within the organism undergo numerous stresses that can lead to irreversible damage. Damaged cells, also called senescent cells, lose their ability to properly function within the tissue leading to disruption of tissue integrity due to their secretion of numerous factors promoting inflammation. Recent evidences suggested that targeted elimination of damaged cells delays the onset of numerous age-related pathologies, such as cataracts, muscular degeneration, atherosclerosis, cardiac hypertrophy, kidney dysfunction, and cancer, and significantly extended the longevity of the animals. We recently identified a new drug displaying senolytic activity (the ability to kill damaged cells while sparing normal healthy cells). Here we propose to study the molecular mechanisms leading to the death of damaged cells, and to validate the use of our newly identified senolytic agent in vivo to improve both healthspan and lifespan. The proposed research program will not only define the molecular pathways allowing clearance of damaged cells, but also provide the proof-of-concept of targeting the viability of senescent cells can ameliorate both healthspan and lifespan. Our research in the area of geroscience will directly benefit to all Canadians by identifying therapeutic avenues decreasing morbidity within the population, but also decreasing the economical burden of age-related diseases on the Canadian health system by alleviating physical dysfunction in the elderly population.

column36: Genetic and chemical ablation of senescent cells that result from age-dependent telomere erosion
column37: The question: Major questions remain unanswered as to how and why we age, and whether we can intervene in the aging process. Recent technological advances in molecular biology and genetics have opened new avenues to investigate how genes function to influence aging at the cellular, tissue and whole body level. Remarkably, in certain cases these gene functions can now be manipulated, either genetically or chemically, to induce aged cells within tissues to be selectively removed to improve the function of tissues, and even improve health outcomes in mammals. This emerging new field of research is called geroscience. The approach: In this proposal, we will take advantage of CRISPR-based gene editing technology to understand how individual genes in the human genome contribute to cellular aging. We will focus on a central mechanism by which human cells age, namely through erosion of their chromosome protective caps, called telomeres. The research we propose will address the important question of whether removal of telomere-eroded "old" or senescent cells could also improve health outcomes. Our preliminary result have identified candidate gene functions whose absence appears to selectively impede the growth of cells with eroded telomeres. We have also identified chemicals that mimic this genetic sensitivity. We will extend these exciting preliminary results to comprehensively identify gene functions and chemicals that permit the removal of old cells that arise due to telomere erosion, and to test how the removal of these cells may improve the health of a mouse model engineered to possess human-like telomeres. Significance of the study: Since cellular senescence due to telomere erosion is already known to be critically important in age-associated human disease, our results may provide new clinical approaches to ameliorate the manifold effects of aging on human health.

column36: Investigating the contributions of mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired neuromuscular junction integrity to the aging-related loss of muscle mass and function in humans
column37: One of the most significant changes associated with normal aging is a progressive loss of muscle mass and strength, a biological process called sarcopenia. Sarcopenia can lead to mobility impairment, falls, and physical frailty in the elderly, dramatically impairing the quality of life of afflicted individuals. With the rapid demographic change of the aging population, sarcopenia will soon rank as one of the major financial burdens that our health care system will have to face. There is currently a lack of effective therapies to either prevent or treat sarcopenia, due in large part to the fact that its molecular and cellular bases are poorly understood. In the present research, we will test, directly in humans, the hypothesis that mitochondria, tiny structures essential for the muscle cell functioning, become dysfunctional with aging and that this accumulation of mitochondrial dysfunction results in a deterioration of the integrity of neuromuscular junction (the interface between neurones and muscle cells) and a decline in muscle mass and performance. We will also assess how physical activity protects against these aging-related changes affecting mitochondria and the NMJ. Finally, we will assess the robustness of recently identified biomarkers of sarcopenia. To ensure success, we have assembled a team of experts in mitochondrial biology (G Gouspillou), neurophysiology and the NMJ (R Robitaille & M Belanger) as well as in Geriatrics and Gerontology (JA Morais, M Aubertin-Leheudre, & P Gaudreau). The results of the present research will provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying the aging-related deterioration of muscle function. In addition, they will enable us to better understand how physical activity exerts its protective impact against sarcopenia. This knowledge will be critical in developing novel strategies to prevent or even reverse sarcopenia and might provide medical professionals with robust biomarkers to identify patients at risk.

column36: From orbit to bedside: using space-based bed-rest techniques to study cardiovascular and skeletal muscle-pump orthostatic reflexes with and without a strength and HIIT exercise intervention to prevent falls in older patients after hospitalization.
column37: Many of the changes that occur to astronauts during a six-month time in space appear to mimic an accelerated aging process of a few decades. These include bone and muscle loss, difficulty with balance and walking properly, and an inability to stand without feeling dizzy and about to fall. Scientists have found that bed rest can have the same negative effects on health. CIHR and the Canadian Space Agency are combining resources to use bed rest to examine these effects as they may relate to older persons who are hospitalized or otherwise confined to bed. It is expected that bed rest will have more severe consequences on old compared to young patients. In older persons, falls often result in a fractured hip, and for the frail, the changes caused by bed rest may be irreversible. The impact of these is decreased quality of life and increased occurrence of illness and mortality. The study design will include in-bed strength and high intensity interval training (HIIT) exercises to see if they are effective in preventing bed rest deconditioning. The research team led by Dr. Blaber at Simon Fraser University will be looking at the relationship between posture control and blood pressure regulation. His group has studied the effect of 60-days bed rest on middle-aged participants and found a large reduction of the ability of the muscles in the leg to pump blood back to the heart. This is an important part of the blood pressure control system and could result in increased incidence of fainting and falls. His team will now study the same system in the older participants to see if they are similarly affected after 15 days. The exercise group will be used to examine the effectiveness of in-bed strength and HIIT exercises to stop these changes. The team will also look at reflexes related to skeletal muscle activity and for specific biomarkers related to declines in nerve myelination as well as self-reports of the bed-rest experience and exercise intervention.

column36: Unraveling the mechanisms underlying of bed rest-induced muscle atrophy and of an exercise countermeasure
column37: Inactivity is associated with muscle loss and decreased bone mineral density, conditions seen with aging and during spaceflights. A model of inactivity of musculoskeletal unloading mimicking lack of gravity is bed rest with head-down tilt. Our reasoning is that bed rest leads to reduced fat oxidation and increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) from the mitochondria, the power house of the cell, which stimulates intracellular mechanisms responsible for developing insulin resistance and to decrease muscle and bone masses. These mechanisms involve the activity- and energy-sensing AMPK and the food-sensing mTOR, under which there are many key factors involved in muscle protein synthesis and breakdown. At the bone level, there is decreased production of osteocalcin, a protein shown to promote insulin sensitivity and to be associated with muscle atrophy in rats. We propose to study 24 men and women of 55-65 years of age engaged in moderate-vigorous exercise. Participants will be randomized into two groups for a two-week bed rest with half of them performing one hour of daily exercise while in bed as a countermeasure. At baseline and at 3, 7 and 14 days of bed rest, we will obtain venous blood and perform muscle biopsies of the thigh to measure muscle protein synthesis and breakdown using the deuterated water method. We will also measure mitochondrial respiration and ROS production in fresh permeabilized fibers, and in frozen muscle tissue, fiber type and size and several regulating factors by western blots. We will measure osteocalcin and many hormones regulating muscle and bone mass in blood samples. Participants will undergo an oral glucose tolerance test, assessment of their body compartments and physical performance before and at the end of bed rest. We wish to uncover the mechanisms related to muscle mass loss with inactivity and in response to exercise, which should open the door to future interventions to prevent the consequences of inactivity

column36: Bed rest in older adults accelerates "aging-like" changes
column37: Older adults confined in bed rest with the head tilted down slightly experience unloading of the heart, muscles and bones that cause rapid deconditioning. The changes they experience will be similar to the responses of astronauts during spaceflight. Our research group has measured "aging-like" increases in arterial stiffness and insulin resistance in astronauts who have reduced aerobic fitness because of their extended periods of inactivity while floating in space. In this research, we will monitor changes in physical function and in blood indicators of cardiovascular, muscular, skeletal, and metabolic and nutritional health. We will monitor the effect of bed rest on changes in cognitive function and spiritual well-being. In this study, we will introduce a new concept for bed rest studies by determining the biological age in addition to the chronological age of each participant. We anticipate that persons with an older biological age will have larger decreases in their body health during the bed rest. We anticipate as well that half of the older adults in the study who are asked to complete a specific exercise regime while in bed rest will have fewer changes in their health indicators. The results from our study will provide unique information for astronauts to maintain health while in space. Importantly for us on Earth, our results will inform older adults and health care providers about causes of physical deterioration with bed rest and of the benefits of daily exercise even if confined to bed.

column36: Sniffing around the Issue: investigating the relationship between solvent use and HIV risk
column37: HIV disproportionally affects the indigenous peoples of Canada with an incident rate 3.5 times higher than the national average and is associated with social-health factors such as poverty. Solvent use, the inhaling of substances to get a psychoactive effect, among street-involved individuals in Winnipeg is considerably higher than the population average. As HIV risk and solvent use are both associated with poverty, understanding how they interact with each other is an important question. Inflammation is a major biological risk factor for contracting HIV. Since solvent use is believed to cause inflammation, it may contribute to HIV acquisition risk and disease progression. However, there is a little information about the effect of solvent use on the immune system generally or HIV susceptibility specifically. Following consultations with the community, and in conjunction with our community partner Sunshine House, I conducted a pilot study of 14 HIV- solvent users and 13 community matched controls. When I analyzed their blood, I found that solvent users exhibited higher levels of immune activation. To confirm and extend this observation, we will enroll 100 Individuals with and without HIV who are or are not solvent users. We will perform studies to determine if solvent users have more inflammation than matched non-solvent users and if HIV positive individuals are at greater risk for faster HIV-disease progression. We will assess the impact of solvent use on: bacteria access to the blood, markers of inflammation and the functioning of the immune system. Understanding the effects of solvent use on the immune system and the potential impact on HIV risk and diseases progression is an important step in improving the health of this underserved community.

column36: So Far From Denendeh
column37: I am a Dene woman who was removed from Denendeh before I was born. I am a member of the Deninu Kue First Nation in Northwest Territories. I am an image-based storyteller. I come from generations of translators but I do not speak my language. My translation takes place in a different capacity. I am a translator of images. I situate Dene concepts of wellness in digital images I paint and I extract story from them. In my thesis, I will use Dene land-based systems of knowledge and image-based storytelling as my methodology). Specifically, I will use the arts-based approach of digital painting whereby I will paint images and extract stories to draw out Indigenous experience and perspectives about disability. Paintings give me the ability to confront the colonial indignities my family have suffered while simultaneously illuminating our resilience as Indigenous people. It is important to be truthful about the brutality of colonialism, yet I must honor our strength, spirit and resilience in my thesis. My objective in this thesis is to explore the disabling effects of colonialism by reflecting on and contrasting: (1) my journey as an Indigenous person who has been diagnosed with a disability (i.e., a learning disability) and (2) the journey of my father as an Indigenous person who was diagnosed with a disability (i.e. a mobility impairment caused by polio). I will use arts-based Indigenous research methods to compare our journeys in terms of our educational/academic and healthcare/clinical experiences as 'disabled' individuals. I will also explore the role of healing and 'rehabilitation' in addressing our disabilities and the disabling effects of the academic and healthcare structures. Both were extremely harmful; there was no healing to take place in the academy or through clinical methods of rehabilitation. We rejected colonial constructed identities. Rather, I will explore how rehabilitation took place through reclamation of culture.

column36: Integrating Indigenous Ways of Knowing into overdose responses for urban Indigenous people who use drugs
column37: The overdose epidemic remains one of the most pressing public health issues in Canada. In British Columba (BC), Indigenous people who use drugs (IPWUD) have been disproportionally affected by the overdose crisis. Further, it has become clear that overdose epidemic patterns are different among IPWUD. For example, while non-Indigenous men are overdosing at greater rates than non-Indigenous women, Indigenous women remain disproportionately impacted by the overdose crisis, and are experiencing non-fatal overdoses and overdose deaths at rates similar to Indigenous men. Diverse models of overdose-focused interventions are now being implemented in jurisdictions such as Vancouver's Downtown Eastside neighbourhood. However, research to date has failed to examine the overdose risk environment surrounding IPWUD living off reserve in inner cities. Given the ongoing harms experienced by off-reserve IPWUD, research is urgently needed to improve overdose-focused harm reduction and substance use programs for this population. This study addresses this gap by using ethnographic approaches that center Indigenous knowledges and ways of knowing to examine how social-structural and environmental conditions shape access to and outcomes from overdose-focused harm reduction and substance use treatment programs among IPWUD. Findings from this study will contribute to the overdose response for IPWUD by identifying policy and programmatic changes to improve the public health benefits of overdose response services.

column36: Interplay of diet, bile acid-metabolizing bacteria and bile acid receptors as a gut microbiota-driven immunomodulatory pathway in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) encompasses ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. These are chronic inflammatory conditions involving the intestinal tract. Symptoms include bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and loss of weight. IBD can result in serious medical complications, significant impairment of quality of life, and huge economic burden. Canada has among the highest reported prevalence and incidence of IBD in the world. The cause of IBD has not been elucidated which has prevented development of curative therapies; however, alteration of the composition of bacteria in the gut plays a key role in intestinal inflammation. Bile acids are molecules present in the intestinal tract which have many functions, including absorption of dietary fat. Since the discovery of bile acid receptors about 20 years ago, functions ascribed to these molecules have increased, and currently include modulation of intestinal barrier function and inflammation. Gut bacteria and bile acids have reciprocal effects; while bile acids exert an antibacterial role, bacteria are capable of transforming bile acids, changing their structure and ability to bind to their receptors. These bile acid receptors in turn, could modulate inflammation in the gut. In addition, specific diet compounds can modify the gut bacteria and activate bile acid receptors, adding another element to this axis. The complex interplay of environment, gut microbiota, bile acids, and intestinal inflammation in the process causing IBD has not been explored. We hypothesize that bile acid-dependent interaction between diet, gut bacteria, and the human gut represents an important pathway leading to IBD. Thus, capacity to modify bile acid-metabolizing bacteria, bile acids, or bile acid receptors might prove to be a successful therapeutic strategy for this chronic, incurable, and disabling disease.

column36: Identification of novel single gene variants in the IL-17 pathway leading to early onset Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
column37: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a condition where someone's immune system attacks their gut and results in damage. Although, in most people, IBD is caused by a mixture of genetics and the environment, there are a subset of patients who get the condition very early on in life and in this subset a damaging change in a single gene is the cause of the disease. We have gathered a cohort of patients with very early onset Inflammatory Bowel Disease (VEOIBD) and used a technology called ' whole exome sequencing' to read the genetic code of all the genes that code for proteins. We looked in this data to see if there were any changes in genes we thought may be linked to IBD. It has been well documented from previous studies that genes involved in a particular immune pathway that involves a messenger molecule called 'interleukin-17' (IL-17) are associated with the risk of developing IBD. We therefore searched for changes in genes involved in this pathway in the gene code data from the VEOIBD patients. We found very rare changes that are not seen at all in the general population in the codes from three candidate genes in multiple families. A gene is made up of DNA and codes for another molecule called RNA, which then forms a particular protein in a cell. This project will use techniques to determine if these rare changes in the gene code of these families are causing problems in the amount of RNA and protein that is produced in the patient's cells. This work will potentially identify new extremely rare single gene causes for IBD happening in young children. This could provide a rationale to try personalized treatments for these children that might help treat their underlying disease.

column36: Prognostic Value of a Prospective, Longitudinal Evaluation of Body Composition in Patients with Cirrhosis Evaluated for Liver Transplantation
column37: Two main body compartments, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (fat), exhibit independent functions. Patients with liver cirrhosis frequently experience body composition abnormalities including loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat but not visceral fat (around internal organs). Liver cirrhosis, characterized by liver failure and replacement of normal tissue by scarring is the main indication for liver transplantation. These body composition abnormalities are associated with higher risk of complications such as infections, longer recovery after surgeries, and higher probability of death. The aim of this study is to evaluate muscle and subcutaneous fat abnormalities in relation to adverse outcomes both before and after liver transplantation. Muscle and fat amount and condition will be assessed using high resolution image-based techniques (computed tomography) at 6-month intervals in cirrhotic patients being evaluated for liver transplantation. During liver transplantation surgery, a small biopsy of muscle and fat will be obtained for analysis of cell types and signals. This information will establish the real burden of body composition abnormalities and their behavior in patients with cirrhosis over time to improve the prediction of outcomes, identify potential targets for treatment, and facilitate development of clinical trials for these conditions.

column36: Intrahepatic immune response to discontinuation of antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B patients
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infects the liver, causing chronic Hepatitis B in 250 million people and killing more than 800,000 people every year. There is no cure for chronic hepatitis B. Antiviral treatment can suppress HBV but treatment can be indefinite because the drugs do not eliminate the virus. However, 40-50% of patients can stop taking their drugs. In some patients, increased viral replication after stopping treatment can spark an immune response that clears the virus, effectively curing them of HBV. A majority of patients will maintain a state of chronic infection that does not require treatment. However, some patients that stop their drugs will develop life-threatening liver inflammation. Currently, there is no predictor for who will clear HBV, who will not clear HBV but also not require further treatment or those who will develop severe liver inflammation. The goal of our project is to define the immunological characteristics of patients who can safely stop treatment and control HBV. We will use state-of-the-art techniques to study the immune response in liver biopsies, at the individual cell level, in patients who stop taking their drugs as part of a structured clinical trial. Successful implementation of this project will lead to a test that can predict patients that can and cannot safely stop their antiviral treatment for chronic HBV infection.

column36: Examining housing-based overdose response interventions in Vancouver
column37: British Columbia is amidst an overdose epidemic with over 1400 overdose deaths in 2017. The majority of these preventable deaths (89%) have occurred in housing environments such as single room occupancy hotels and emergency shelters. In Vancouver, there has been an increase in overdose response interventions such as overdose prevention sites and naloxone distribution; however, the public health response within housing environments specifically has been challenging due to a range of contextual factors that have impeded the effective implementation of overdose response interventions. Through a qualitative and ethnographic approach, this study will examine the influence of physical (e.g., building conditions, geographical distribution of services), social (e.g., stigma, discrimination), and structural (e.g., policies, programs) factors that impact overdose risk, as well as the use and outcomes of overdose response interventions within housing environments by people who use drugs (PWUD). This work will also seek to identify policy and programmatic priorities to improve the health outcomes of PWUD, including the reduction of overdose risk and mortality. A range of knowledge translation activities will be included in this study, such as facilitating exchange of knowledge and best practices in collaboration with an established housing and overdose working group; disseminating research summaries to PWUD and other community stakeholders; presenting at conferences; and publishing articles in peer-reviewed journals.

column36: Can Blending Together Traditional and Western Knowledge Improve Diabetes and Obesity Health Outcomes in Urban Indigenous Communities?
column37: Indigenous peoples in Canada suffer from significantly higher rates of diabetes and obesity, resulting in reduced quality of life. Health, government and community organizations often lack Traditional Knowledge and community ownership, required to decrease healthcare gaps and burden of disease. The limited impact of Western health services on improving health in Indigenous peoples needs to be addressed. In our previous study, three urban Indigenous Friendship Centre (FC) sites identified and prioritized healthcare gaps and community needs into a collective vision for action towards diabetes and obesity-related interventions. The FCs unanimously agreed that there was an urgent need to act on these priorities, resulting in the current study. Our current newly funded CIHR study includes three additional FC/Metis Centre (MC) sites. The overall aim is to offer both Traditional and Western approaches to diabetes and obesity health services. Site-specific, culturally safe, and locally-informed interventions will be co-developed/implemented/evaluated within the six FC/MC partner sites. Indigenous methodologies will be used to acknowledge and honour Indigenous knowledge, traditions, and protocols. Two sites will be offered to join a sub-study exploring the effects/outcomes of the community interventions on diabetes and obesity clinical variables (blood glucose, HbA1c, blood pressure, and waist circumference). One to two community interventions will be implemented at each site per year over three years. Diabetes and obesity clinical variables will be measured before, after, and one month following each intervention in the sub-study sites. The goal of the overall project is to reduce diabetes and obesity health inequities in Indigenous communities. Ultimately, the knowledge gained from this project will support change in diabetes and obesity policy, research, and practice in urban Indigenous communities and health systems, and to ultimately improve wellness.

column36: Cell populations regulating opioid-induced respiratory depression in sleep-wake states
column37: Opioids are used extensively for their analgesic properties but they have a variety of unwanted side effects, including tolerance, dependence, and most signicantly, respiratory depression. According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, there were more than 8,000 apparent opioid-related deaths in Canada between January 2016 and March 2018, an epidemic responsible for thousands of emergency visits every year, therefore causing a severe social, health and financial burden. The analgesic effects of opioids result from activation of classical opioid receptors (MORs) in the central nervous system and no treatments are currently available to prevent respiratory depression without reducing their analgesic proprieties. MORs are expressed in various brain structures regulating breathing including the preBotzinger Complex (preBotC). The preBotC is composed of neuronal subpopulations expressing neurokinin-1 receptors (NK1-R) and the peptide somatostatin (SST). We propose that genetic deletion of MORs in NK1-R and SST cells, pharmacological activation of NK1-R and antagonism of SST as well as optogenetic stimulation of said cells will reduce opioids-induced respiratory depression. My project aims to determine whether NK1-R and SST cells are sensitive to MOR ligands and whether they regulate opioid-induced respiratory depression and sedation To do so, we will use a variety of physiological (electrocortical and respiratory recordings), pharmacological (MORs agonist injection) and genetic (MORs deletion) approaches. My research hypothesis will open a new path towards the understanding of respiratory depression with opioids abuse, an essential step to develop new therapeutic targets to reduce the risk of opioids overdose, hypoxemia, critical care, and mortality. The benefits will be significant both from a fundamental and clinical point of view.

column36: The Process of Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation - A Combined EEG-fMRI study.
column37: Although we all need to sleep, its function is not yet fully understood. A growing domain in sleep research focuses on sleep's link to memory consolidation, which is to say the strengthening of newly formed memories as they become enduring long-term memories. A form of memory known as "cognitive procedural memory" (i.e., learning a new logical strategy to acquire a new skill) undergoes memory consolidation during sleep. Consequently, the proposed study will use simultaneous EEG-fMRI to identify the hemodynamic cerebral correlates of spindle activity in the post-training night, and their association with cognitive procedural memory consolidation in young participants. Immediately following the evening training session (i.e., at 23h00), post-training simultaneous EEG-fMRI will be recorded while subjects are required to sleep in the scanner where their sleep spindles will be subsequently identified for the main analysis of interest. Spindles have been found to be involved in memory consolidation for declarative memory and simple procedural memory, via the reactivation of the same brain structures recruited during learning. We hypothesize that spindles will be involved in reactivation of the same brain regions recruited during learning (e.g., prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and striatum) for cognitive procedural memory. In addition, greater spindle-related activation in these structures will be associated with greater overnight improvements in performance. This will reveal whether spindle-related reactivation supports memory consolidation for cognitive procedural memory.

column36: Development of a user-centred and evidence-based novel eHealth online sleep program for infant sleep problems
column37: About 25% of families have sleep problems with their baby during the first year, which can impact parental health and the baby's development and behaviour. While researchers know what works to improve sleep, families do not have universal access to baby sleep programs that are based on best clinical practices and up-to-date research. Families often turn to unregulated sleep products or sleep-coaching services, which can be expensive and not research-based. Offering research-based sleep programs online (eHealth) could help parents access high-quality service options. To take advantage of eHealth options, we need to know more about the 'active ingredients' to include in a parent-centered online program that helps parents learn how to help their baby sleep better. My fellowship goal is to develop and test an online sleep program to improve parents' access to best available information about how to help their baby sleep better. I will lead three studies to do this. First, I will systematically review existing research to determine what makes baby sleep programs and parent-centered eHealth programs effective. Next, I will gather information from parents, as well as parenting and sleep experts, about factors that may influence the use of an online baby sleep program. Finally, after developing an online baby sleep program prototype, I will test its usability with an online pilot test and survey with parents. These research studies will result in a final version of an online baby sleep program (Better Nights, Better Days for Babies). Following my fellowship, I will test this final version in a multi-centre trial to assess its short- and long-term effects on family sleep and child development. If effects are positive, I will test how well the program scales up for use across Canada and other countries. This program could increase access to research-based advice for families who are struggling with their baby's sleep and support overall child development and family wellbeing.

column36: Correlation between Odds Ratio Product (ORP), a novel, automatic measure of sleep-wakefulness continuum and patient-ventilator asynchronies - a step towards improvement of sleep in critically ill patients under mechanical ventilation
column37: Very sick patients connected to breathing machines have a high mortality and those who survive experience psychological and functional disabilities. These problems might be related to modifiable factors such as sleep disruption and uncomfortable interactions between the patients and breathing machines ("asynchronies"). Previous research proved that "asynchronies" are related to sleep problems in these patients, but what is the exact relation between these factors remains unknown. Adequately evaluating sleep in patients connected to breathing machines was not possible until the recent invention of a new scoring system named Odds Ratio Product (ORP), a numerical scale that ranges from 0 to 2.5. We used ORP in a previous study for the first time in this type of patients and showed that is a useful tool to measure sleep problems in patients connected to breathing machines. I hypothesize that sleep problems measured with ORP will be intimately related with the presence of "asynchronies" and sleep problems measured with ORP will be more frequent in patients with "asynchronies". I will enroll patients with breathing failure connected to breathing machines and measure sleep using ORP and "asynchronies". I will then correlate the two variables trying to understand the relationship between the two. This project will prove what the exact relationship between sleep problems and "asyncrhonies" is and help to design a strategy to modify the settings of the breathing machines to avoid "asynchronies" and improve sleep in very sick patients preventing future psychological and functional disabilities.

column36: Colchicine for the prevention of perioperative atrial fibrillation (COP-AF)
column37: The development of atrial fibrillation (AF) during or shortly after major thoracic surgery is one of the most common serious complications in this patient population. The occurrence of AF leads to adverse changes in blood pressure, problems with the management of blood thinners required in many of these patients, prolonged hospital stays and an increased risk of death and stroke. Prior studies suggest that inflammation is the primary mechanism for AF developing during or after surgery. Colchicine is a potent drug that strongly inhibits inflammation. In patients undergoing cardiac surgery colchicine has been effective in preventing inflammatory complications and AF. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that colchicine effectively prevents the occurrence of AF in patients undergoing major thoracic surgery. In this population, colchicine may also reduce the time to chest tube extraction, an important patient-centered outcome, as it may shorten hospital stay, reduce the incidence of postoperative infections and improve patient's well-being. Colchicine administration may even reduce the occurrence of death or stroke. To test these hypotheses, we will conduct a large double-blind randomized placebo controlled trial of 2,800 patients who are at least 55 years old and undergoing thoracic surgery. The trial will be conducted in thoracic centres in Canada and internationally. Oral colchicine or matching placebo will be given twice daily for 10 days. Study personnel will follow patients throughout the trial. This large trial will determine whether colchicine lowers the risk of AF and other inflammatory complications in patients undergoing thoracic surgery. Finding a safe, effective and low-cost intervention to prevent AF in this setting addresses a major unmet clinical need as it may decrease length of hospital stay, improve the quality of perioperative care, lower costs and reduce the risk of stroke or death.

column36: Role of BRCT proteins in DNA damage signaling
column37: Damage to our DNA is a major cause of ageing, cancer, and neurodevelopmental disorders. To defend against DNA damage, our cells have evolved systems that scan the more than 1 metre of DNA that is in each of our cells to look for and repair microscopic forms of damage before problems can occur. The importance of these systems has been underlined by the fact that defects in these systems are related to major forms of hereditary cancers. In this proposal, we have set out a plan to develop tools to allow us to control the activities of BRCT proteins, and to image these proteins as they interact with the damaged DNA. column36: The small GTPase Rab4 as a target for breast cancer metastasis

Les approaches traditionnelles pour cibler la proteine Rab4 n'ont pas reussi a fournir des bloqueurs de Rab4 efficaces cliniquement. Les proteines Rab ont besoin d'etre activee par une autre proteine nommee "guanine nucleotide exchange factor" (ou GEF) pour pouvoir accomplir leur role nefaste. En etudiant les regions d'interactions entre les proteines Rab4 et LPGDS, nous avons identifie une petite region de 8 acides amines (les blocs qui constituent les proteines) qui peut activer la Rab4 a elle seule. En faisant une etude detaillee, nous avons reussie a developper des petits peptides (petites molecules) qui bloquent l'activite de Rab4. Nous utiliserons ces petites molecules pour developper des bloqueurs d'activite de Rab4 qui pourront etre utilises pour prevenir de le developpement de metastases dans le cancer du sein, et possiblement dans d'autre types de cancers.

column36: Impact of age, sex and frailty on the heart: HF risk & interventions
column37: Heart failure is a serious disease that happens when the heart cannot pump blood very well. It occurs most often in older men and women. But how many years someone has lived is not the whole story. People age at different rates. Those who are aging quickly are said to be frail. Frailty is important because, compared to fit people, frail people are much more likely to develop heart failure regardless of their age. They also develop a type of heart failure in which the heart has trouble relaxing. This is especially true in frail older women. Even though heart failure is most likely to happen in frail older men and women, most research uses young animals, mostly males. We can do better. Our research group has discovered how to measure frailty in aging mice, using methods developed in people. We measured many different health problems in individual mice and used this information to estimate a frailty score. We found that even though the heart becomes very large in frail male animals, the ability of the heart to contract weakens. We even saw these changes not just in whole hearts but in individual heart cells. We also discovered that the effects of age on the heart are quite different between the sexes. The goal of this research project is to find out how age and frailty affect the heart and whether this differs between the sexes. We will see if these changes make hearts more susceptible to diseases like heart failure. We also will treat mice with a drug that lowers frailty in both sexes and see if this prevents adverse effects of age and frailty on the heart. This research project is important because it will help us understand the links between age, sex, frailty and heart failure and will help us understand if treatment of frailty can improve heart function in older people.

column36: Neural repair in glaucoma: the role of insulin signaling
column37: Sight is essential for humans to gather critical information about their surroundings. The fear of going blind has been reported to be more powerful than that of having cancer or heart disease. Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, affecting >60 million people worldwide. There is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the death of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the neurons that convey visual information from the retina to the brain. High intraocular pressure is the most significant risk factor for developing the disease. A challenge in the management of glaucoma is that pathological changes in these patients occur years, possibly decades, before symptoms appear. Thus, there is an unmet need for novel therapies that stimulate RGC regeneration and restore vision. One of the earliest signs of damage in glaucoma is the retraction of RGC dendrites, the fine processes that connect neurons within the retina. In an exciting recent study, we discovered that insulin promoted remarkable dendrite regeneration, restored circuit function, and extended neuronal survival in mouse glaucoma models. In this application, we will: 1) determine whether deficits in insulin signaling trigger early dendritic pathology in glaucoma, 2) elucidate molecular mechanisms that promote insulin-mediated dendrite regeneration, and 3) establish the efficacy of insulin for RGC repair and vision restoration in nonhuman primates. The proposed project is unique because it will provide critical knowledge on whether insulin signaling deficits contribute to early dendrite retraction and synapse loss, and it will elucidate molecular mechanisms driving arbor regeneration and circuit repair. Furthermore, this work is timely and important because it will provide pre-clinical validation of the efficacy of insulin in glaucomatous monkeys, which will inform the design of future human clinical trials for this indication.

We will further expand our studies to examine tissue removed from patients and examine whether the abnormalities identified in the cells and in the animals occur in humans. This proposal represents a comprehensive set of studies to investigate a specific process, i.e, the heart damage in diabetes. Understanding such mechanisms will help to develop preventive treatment for such conditions.

In response, post-secondary institutions across the country have launched programs to encourage Indigenous youth to pursue careers in health professions. Since 2008, Memorial University's Faculty of Medicine has offered the Aboriginal Health Initiative; one of its goals is to recruit more Indigenous students into Memorial's medical program. How successful are program like the Aboriginal Health Initiative? While the number of Indigenous trainees may appear to be the most relevant outcome, the program may have important impacts on participants, including on those who choose or are not able to become physicians. The purpose of this project is to develop an evaluation framework that includes community and participant-relevant outcomes. Using a two-eyed seeing approach we will create an evaluation framework by reviewing existing evaluations of programs in Canadian medical schools, reviewing of the literature, and consulting stakeholders including Indigenous community partners, program participants, medical trainees, and program organizers. We will then use the framework to evaluate Memorial University's Aboriginal Health Initiative program. The project addresses priorities identified in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and other recent national inquiries into the wellbeing of Indigenous people in Canada. The project will create a framework that can guide evaluations of programs designed to increase Indigenous participation in the physician workforce and other health professions. Finally, it responds to the call for social accountability from Canada's medical schools.

column36: Indigenous Health Counts: Advancing Meta-analysis Methods for Respondent-Driven Sampling and Urban Indigenous Children's Health
column37: The Our Health Counts studies are six urban Indigenous community-based research partnerships in the cities of Hamilton, Ottawa, Toronto, London, Thunder Bay and Kenora, Ontario. Each of these studies was done using an advanced statistical method, called respondent-driven sampling. Meta-analysis is a commonly used statistical technique that combines results from different studies to produce one single, overall summary of the available information. Traditionally used in the area of clinical trials, meta-analysis is often considered the 'gold-standard' technique as it provides a complete picture of all available information across studies and increases the reliability of our information. Unfortunately, due to its statistical complexities, appropriate meta-analysis methods are not developed for studies using respondent-driven sampling. Using advanced statistical methods, we will develop an appropriate meta-analysis approach to combine data across all six Our Health Counts study sites. Of pressing interest, early evidence from the Toronto children's health data shows a potentially higher rate of many health concerns, including emergency room and neonatal intensive care unit usage, depression and anxiety relative to the general Canadian youth population, but each single study site lacks the precision to make strong conclusions. In partnership with our six Indigenous community partners, our research team will develop these advanced statistical methods and provide a more complete and accurate picture of urban Indigenous children's health.

column36: The Water-Food-Health Nexus: A Nunavut-led Assessment
column37: Water plays an important role in sustaining ecosystems that support food production and other activities that are key for food security and human health. For many Inuit, marine and freshwater ecosystems provide critical transportation routes to harvesting grounds (e.g. boating and snowmobiling); habitat for many country foods (e.g. whales, seals, bears, fish, shellfish); opportunities for business and employment that promote cultural continuity (e.g. fisheries, fur trade); craft materials; and food. The Water-Food-Health Nexus research project is led by Inuit organizations and Northern governments, and addresses a significant gap in understanding how water and food intersect to impact Inuit health in Nunavut. We will examine the interconnections among sewage effluent and water-related foodborne disease (i.e. shellfish), and their cumulative impact on health in the context of climate change. The project is guided by 3 interconnected research themes. (1) The water-food-health nexus in Nunavut: We will use a systems approach to characterize the water-food-health nexus in Nunavut, based on Inuit knowledge, and the health, social, and natural sciences. (2) Climate change and the water-food-health nexus: We will use mixed qualitative and quantitative methods to conduct participatory quantitative microbial risk assessments, that connect Inuit knowledge and quantitative methods to model future climate change impacts at the water-food-health nexus. (3) Water-food-health adaptation pathways: We will use integrated analytic approaches to co-develop climate-health-intervention scenarios with communities and partners, and co-produce adaptation options that promote, value, and reflect Inuit knowledge systems. Our participatory, community-based approach will offer best practice guidance for other initiatives, will create community and scientific leaders with expertise in Inuit water-food-health nexus, and demonstrate the importance of Inuit knowledge for adaptation.

Our CIHR-funded research demonstrated the potential of Fostering Open eXpression among Youth (FOXY) and Strengths, Masculinities & Sexual Health (SMASH). FOXY and SMASH are arts-based, culturally-grounded, strengths-focused and Indigenous-led sexual health programs to improve sexual health outcomes among Northern and Indigenous youth. OUR IDEA: We will conduct a longitudinal cohort study with Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT to explore trajectories of health and resilience. We will conduct mixed-methods research to explore social contexts that shape health and wellbeing, and illuminate the ways in which youth navigate these contexts. 1) We will conduct intervention adaptation using realist evaluation with qualitative and quantitative methods to explore how to better meet the needs of youth. 2) We will conduct FOXY and SMASH school-based workshops, with a pre-and post test, 6-month, 12-month and 18-month follow-up surveys. 3) We will conduct longitudinal qualitative interviews with youth to explore social ecological factors associated with health and resilience trajectories. 4) Interconnected knowledge mobilization. IMPACT: We will gather and integrate multiple knowledge sources to refine sexual health programs to better meet the needs of Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT, and evaluate the long term effects of participating in arts-based sexual health programs. We fill knowledge gaps of resilience and wellbeing among Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT.

column36: Assessing vitamin D intake and status among peoples with different skin pigmentation in Yellowknife
column37: Vitamin D is important for bone health and many other aspects of human health. Deficiency in vitamin D is attributed to long dark periods of winter and the lack of consuming vitamin D rich foods. Vitamin D deficiency is associated with a number of chronic diseases including cancer, diabetes, heart disease, osteoporosis, arthritis, asthma, and pelvic floor disorders. Older adults are at increased risk of developing vitamin D deficiency in part because aged skin cannot synthesize vitamin D as efficiently and seniors are likely to spend more time indoors. Vitamin D status varies among people of different social and ethnic/racial backgrounds. It also differs in people from different geographic locations. The main source of vitamin D intake is through the skin's absorption of the sun. Factors such as high latitude, dark skin color, sunscreen use, not enough time in the sun, air pollution, and clothing coverage are known to decrease vitamin D production in the skin. Obtaining enough vitamin D from dietary sources is difficult for many Canadians, especially for people living in the Northwest Territories (NT) with low sun exposure for half of the year. This study will document the differences in vitamin D intake and status among multi-ethnic populations in Yellowknife, NT. This research will also gather evidence in order to support further vitamin D research and a possible program for improving vitamin D status among populations living in the North.

column36: Regathering the Strengths of First Nations Women to Promote Youth Wellness
column37: The goal of the proposed research is to facilitate the co-creation of a social safety net for First Nations youth, enabling them to cope with the challenges they face and promoting wellness. In many First Nations communities, the disempowerment of girls and women as a result of colonialist patriarchal policies has been profound, placing them at risk physically, socially, and emotionally. It has also resulted in the devaluation of the inter and intragenerational relational behaviors that colonialism deemed feminine, and thus inferior. In the proposed research, we will work together with female and two-spirit First Nations youth to established culturally-grounded and gender affirming peer mentoring programs for youth across the gender spectrum, as such supports are expected to be integral to youths' sense of belonging and positive mental health. In addition, together with First Nations communities, we are proposing to enable youth to create digital stories of strong female role models, thereby providing inspiration and fostering respect. Finally, we will encourage First Nations youth who are about to become mothers to bring together their trusted social supports to co-create their collective story of strength to be gifted to her newborn later in life, and in so doing, consolidate the supports surrounding young mothers (and infants), and affirming these mothers' value and purpose. Ongoing multi-method (qualitative, quantitative, and behavioral) measurements will form the basis of formative and outcome evaluations of the program effects on youth wellness. Qualitative analyses of the program outputs (co-created training curriculum, stories) will be conducted to understand the processes by which empowered gender and cultural identities are expressed and consolidated. It is expected that by affirming the strengths of First Nations women, gender relations, social support behaviors, coping skills, and the health and wellness of First Nations youth will be enhanced.

column36: Stopping the crisis in its tracks: Community driven, cultural evidence-based Indigenous mental health interventions with urban Indigenous homeless peoples
column37: All homeless people face health care challenges, including limited access to mental health care. The Indigenous homeless face additional barriers due to racism, oppression, and intergenerational trauma of residential school and child welfare systems. Indigenous homelessness is complex; recent research shows that challenges related to cultural identity, food insecurity, cultural career development, culture clash between biomedicine and Indigenous healing, and failure of Canada's health policy are mediating factors. Toronto has Canada's largest Indigenous population, with thousands of Indigenous youth and families searching for jobs, education, and homes, often ending up stuck in cycles of couch surfing, staying in emergency shelters, or sleeping on the streets. Current homeless services focus on crisis mental health programs; this project will move the focus to interventions that prevent homelessness and strengthen individuals' chances of successfully exiting the streets. There is a lack of evaluation data in homeless services generally and specifically in Indigenous mental health programs. In partnership with Toronto's Indigenous providers of mental health to the Indigenous homeless, Dr. Stewart and her team will develop and evaluate culturally based evidence-based programs to improve the mental health by preventing homelessness and at the same time creating better outcomes for those trying to exit the cycle. The project will document the use and experiences of cultural mental health care for the Indigenous homeless through research that uses surveys and individual interviews with mental health providers and their patients; focus groups with Indigenous Elders and Healers will also be conducted to identify culturally based solutions. An Indigenous knowledges evaluation framework will be developed. Based on findings, toolkits for policymakers, texts on evidence-based Indigenous mental health models, and curriculum for training health care workers will be published.

column36: A BC wide program for Indigenous patients to Gain Equitable access to kidney transplantation: The BRIDGE to Transplantation Initiative.
column37: Indigenous populations in Canada have a higher risk of developing kidney failure, but are much less likely to get access to the best treatment for kidney failure - a living donor kidney transplant. We recently partnered with Indigenous people who have kidney disease and those that have previously donated their kidney to a loved one to better understand the barriers to transplantation and develop a new program which aims to support Indigenous patients better. The BRIDGE to Transplantation Initiative is a program that will be implemented by the Provincial Health Services Authority (PHSA) in kidney care clinics across BC where Indigenous Patient Liaisons (IPLs) will provide targeted and culturally tailored education about transplantation and living donation to Indigenous people with kidney failure. The education will occur outside of hospitals (usually at Aboriginal Friendship Centres) and will include Indigenous patients and prior living donors. The Initiative also will help patients and potential donors to navigate the medical evaluation for transplantation and donation and coordinate any followup needed after donation. As part of the evaluation of this program, we anticipate that the rates of Indigenous people that are referred for transplantation will double and that the entire process around transplantation will become more culturally safe.

column36: A framework to describe risks associated with dementia-related wandering
column37: Introduction: Three in five Canadians with dementia will wander and become lost raising concern as to how it can be managed effectively. Hundreds of interventions, such as GPS devices have been developed to manage this issue, however no guideline exists to allow for the successful adoption of these strategies. Objectives: To develop a practice framework that will help stakeholders choose strategies to manage challenging behaviours associated with dementia-related wandering. Methods: Semi-structured individual phone interviews containing 12 questions were conducted with family and formal caregivers, persons with mild dementia, occupational therapists, police, social workers, and staff from community organizations concerned about dementia-related wandering. The purpose of the interviews was to determine what factors influenced successful adoption of wander-management strategies and to identify if any differences across stakeholders exist. Responses from these interviews were used to develop a practice framework for adoption of wander-management strategies. Results: Thirty-five participants from four Canadian provinces were recruited. Responses from the interviews highlighted 3 contextual factors that influence the successful adoption of wander-management strategies: (1) Risk associated with wandering; (2) Culture; (3) Geography. Perceived risk was conveyed as the most influential factor of strategy adoption across all stakeholder groups. The relationships of these three factors were further reflected in the framework. Conclusion: This is the first study to identify and describe factors that influence strategy adoption for dementia-related wandering. This framework can be used by caregivers, health and community service providers to enhance the safety and well-being of older adults at risk of getting lost.

column36: Epidemiological Correlates of HIV Phylogenetic Diversification Rate in British Columbia
column37: Identifying HIV transmission risk factors can inform the prioritization of treatment and prevention services. The analysis of patients' HIV sequences can illuminate transmission activity beyond what is visible by traditional epidemiology methods alone. Although identifying clusters of similar HIV sequences is routinely performed to evaluate patient characteristics associated with high transmission activity, using cluster membership alone over-simplifies the range of transmission activity across a population. We introduce an alternative method to investigate HIV transmission risk factors in British Columbia (BC), Canada, based on patients' viral diversification rates. For 8,103 people living with HIV (PLHIV) in BC in March 2018, we recovered the oldest available HIV protease and RT sequences from the BC Drug Treatment Program database. We applied phylogenetics to infer the family history of viral sequences across the population of PLHIV, and then for each viral tip in the tree, we calculated its diversification rate as an estimate of its transmission rate. Patient attributes significantly associated with high viral transmission were evaluated using a generalized linear model. High HIV transmission activity was positively associated with being younger, using injection drugs, having hepatitis C virus, having a high recent viral load, and residing within the Northern BC Health authority. In contrast, having ever had AIDS and identifying as black were both significantly associated with lower transmission activity. By identifying risk factors associated with HIV transmission using the viral diversification rate among PLHIV, we can confidently recommend prioritized provision of treatment and prevention services for key groups. Additionally, these analyses highlight that HIV diversification rates can illuminate differences in individuals' transmission activity, regardless of phylogenetic cluster membership.

column36: Evaluating the effects of British Columbia's Supervised Consumption and Overdose PrEvention Sites (SCOPES) Study
column37: In April 2016, British Columbia's Provincial Medical Officer declared the opioid crisis a public health emergency. This enabled the quick adoption of new harm reduction services to meet the needs of people who use illicit drugs (PWUD). Beginning in December 2016, overdose prevention (OPSs) and supervised consumption (SCSs) sites opened across the province, including mobile units in Kelowna and Kamloops. Multiple studies have demonstrated the local effects of Vancouver's InSite program in reducing mortality and the transmission of infectious diseases. To date however, there have been no evaluations of the population-level health and health system effects of OPSs and SCSs. This includes a dearth of information on the effectiveness of SCSs/OPSs on mitigating severe overdose events and overdose-related sequelae, and the consumption of acute care services. The objective of the project is to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the effects (including intended and unintended positive and negative consequences) of the newly implemented OPSs and SCSs on opioid overdose related events, health outcomes, and health services used. We will use the BC Overdose Cohort and modern epidemiologic and econometric methods to: a) conduct an exploratory analysis of the disease and health system burdens of severe opioid overdoses in BC; b) estimate the risk of overdose-related sequelae by overdose exposure, and the hazards of repeat overdose events on developing a sequela; and c) evaluate the population-level effects of the new SCSs and OPSs on overdose-related hospitalization, sequelae, and mortality events, and health services used. A timely evaluation of this set of interventions is critical to ensure we are responding appropriately to the opioid epidemic, and will fill in gaps in our collective knowledge to a growing international problem.

column36: Cholinergic receptor nicotinic alpha 5 expression in the airways of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a progressively worsening lung disease commonly caused by cigarette smoking. It affects 1 in 20 people in Canada and has been predicted to be the third leading cause of death by 2030. COPD is the 4th leading cause of death in North America and costs the Canadian health care system billions of dollars. Current drug treatments have been unsuccessful in slowing the progression of COPD, which prompted us to discover new drug classes from genes identified from large genome wide association studies (GWAS) to target COPD. A protein called Cholinergic Receptor Nicotinic Alpha 5 Subunit (CHRNA5) has been strongly involved in the risk for heavy smoking and nicotine dependence (ND). ND is directly related to the number of cigarettes smokes per days as well as the risk for COPD. Nicotine can activate this protein and increase the growth and movement of cells that line the airway tubes. When this happens, the tissue scarring may occur and reduce the flow of air moving through the lung, leading to difficulty in breathing. We will show if this protein is increased or decreased in the airway tissues in human lung tissues, and then test how this protein responses to cigarette smoke treatment in cells that line the airway tube. Effective treatment for COPD is currently limited, leading to high rates of hospitalization and mortality for COPD patients. By understanding the relationship between the biology of CHRNA5 and nicotine activation from cigarette smoke, we will be able to identify a unique way to target this disease process. This is fundamentally important in controlling the increased risks of smoking, morbidity and mortality in patients with COPD in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Does socioeconomic status of older adults affect their level of mobility? A State-of-the-art review.
column37: Background & Aims: Research shows that people who went to school and worked in a job that paid well are healthier than those who did not. We decided to find out if older adults who went to school and worked in a job that paid well have better mobility than those who did not. We also give information that healthcare workers can use to decide how older adults move inside and outside of their homes and around their communities Methods: We looked at five different records of literature. We reviewed English language research papers that were online between the year 2000-2018. Two of us looked at the studies and agreed to include any paper that talked about older adults' income, education level, and occupation (job) and how it affects how they move around either by walking, using transportation or any assistive device (e.g. wheelchair). Results: We included 36 studies from eleven countries. Thirty-four of the 36 studies are good quality studies. We found 68 statistical summaries of how better education and working in a well-paying job affected how older adults move around. Out of the 68 summaries, 55 (81%) stated better educated and wealthier older adults move around their home and communities better. We also found that assessing older adults walking over long distances ( e.g. 400m or 800m) considers many things that support mobility (e.g. endurance, power, speed). Conclusion: Better educated older adults who worked in well-paying jobs move better than those did not. Healthcare worker that want to look at how an older adult walks about in their home or community, should ask the older adult to walk a longer distance (e.g. 400m or 800m) during testing.

column36: Cost-effectiveness of palivizumab prophylaxis for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV): A systematic review
column37: Introduction: Palivizumab (PMB) is a preventative therapeutic (prophylaxis) given to infants for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). However, due to its high drug costs, the value of this intervention is unclear. The objective of this study was to conduct a systematic review on the value of providing PMB prophylaxis compared to no prophylaxis in infants under 24 months of age. Methods: We searched three databases: Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library and included economic evaluations conducted from Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries, published between 2000 and 2018. Quality appraisal was completed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Costs were adjusted and inflated to 2017 United States (US) dollars. We categorized and reported the value of PMB based on study characteristics, and RSV risk factors (e.g. premature birth, lung disease, and heart disease). Results: We identified 28 economic studies that met our eligibility criteria. Most studies were conducted in the US (n=6), and Canada (n=5). Studies were considered high quality based on the checklist criteria used. PMB prophylaxis ranged from being a program that was cost saving and provided health benefits, to costing an additional $2,526,203 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), depending on the study setting, target population and risk factors. From the healthcare payer's perspective, PMB for infants born prematurely at 29 to 35 weeks gestational age cost an additional $5,188 to $791,265/QALY, with 90% of cost-effectiveness estimates below a $50,000/QALY threshold. Influential parameters to the value of PMB reported were: reduction in RSV hospitalization rates, PMB cost, and the discounting rate. Conclusions: Palivizumab as a RSV prophylaxis was considered to have good value in specific subgroups: infants with lung disease or heart disease, infants from specific remote communities, and preterm infants with and without lung complications.

column36: Examining psychosocial, behavioural and biological factors related to mental health and diabetes
column37: Approximately 10% Canadian adults have been diagnosed with diabetes and approximately 20% of Canadian adults experience a mental health problem annually. Moreover, mental health problems, particularly elevated depressive symptoms, and diabetes often co-occur; individuals with diabetes are approximately twice as likely to have elevated depressive symptoms compared to the general population. My research explores the complex associations between mental health and diabetes by considering psychosocial, behavioural, and biological factors. For example, my work has examined if coping strategies predict mental health outcomes in adults with diabetes and has demonstrated the cyclical associations between depressive symptoms and social support in adults with diabetes. Some of my other work has examined the role of biological factors in the context of diabetes and mental health. One of my current research projects examines if patterns of depressive symptoms predict the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. Another series of projects that I am working on examines spousal influences in the context of diabetes. For example, I am examining if spousal depressive symptoms are associated with glycemic control and physical activity among adults with diabetes. I have also recently received funding to examine associations between positive mental health (e.g., satisfaction with life, purpose in life) and physical activity in adults with diabetes.

column36: Benefit of Aortic Valve Replacement in Aortic Stenosis With Very Low Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction
column37: Having a severe yet treatable disease while doctors are reluctant to prescribe the treatment is an undesirable situation. This is happening for patients who suffer from aortic stenosis (AS) and severe heart failure (HF). They are perceived to be in such an advanced disease that therapeutic benefit (from surgical or trans-catheter aortic valve replacement (AVR)) is not likely. AS consists in progressive stiffening of the aortic valve, which narrows the aortic orifice. This leads to compensatory left ventricular hypertrophy, which mantains a normal cardiac performance. In advanced AS, left ventricular hypertophy becomes ineffective and cardiac performances are no longer sufficient to supply the body needs, defining the HF state. HF increases the risk associated with the AVR procedure. Thus, in clinical practice doctors are reluctant to prescribe AVR in the presence of HF and AS. However, the degree of HF that renders AVR futile is unknown. In clinical practice, heart failure severity is graded by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) i.e. the proportion of blood pumped to the circulation during each heart beat. Normal LVEF is > 55%. Very low LVEF <25% dcreases the likelihood for a patient to be prescribed AVR. A failing heart is more vulnerable to AS than a normally functioning one. Hence, AS patients with severe HF are facing a double whammy.Therefore, the need for AVR is even more urgent than in AS patients with preserved hearts. In this conference paper, we demonstrate that patients with LVEF <25% i) derive similar survival benefit from AVR as patients with LVEF>25% and ii) have a markedly improved survival after AVR as compared to untreated patients. We found that more than 50% of the patients die within 2 years if left without treatment, a rate that could be reduced to 20% with AVR. We believe that our study delivers an important and convincing message to physicians and might lead to a favourable change in clinical practice.

column36: Canadian Sepsis Research Network: Improving CareBefore, During and After Sepsis
column37: Sepsis, the life-threatening response to infection, costs the Canadians more than $1.5 billon each year, leads to more than 1 in 18 deaths each year, and leaves many survivors with significant disability. In 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared sepsis a global emergency. To meet the WHO strategic plan in Canada, team members are committed to identifying at risk populations, develop novel strategies to prevent and reduce the economic and health burden by 30% in 2025. This sepsis team will bring together Critical Care Medicine, Emergency Medicine, Paramedic and Diabetes experts. We will partner with patients who have survived sepsis and family members who have lost loved-ones. We have identified stakeholders within the professional organizations and government. Our network has identified the following projects: 1. Develop and construct a Pan-Canadian framework to identify and interpret the the complex nature of human sepsis. 2. Develop a structure to study the mechanisms associated with variations of sepsis presentation and outcomes. 3. Develop innovative animal and human sepsis studies that address complexity and are targeted toward sepsis prevention, identification, treatment and recovery. 4. Improve the pre-hospital recognition of sepsis amongst the Canadian public and health professionals. 5. Identify what helps to improve sepsis care in Canadian Emergency Departments. 6. Develop a structure to identify and catalogue sepsis from current information. 7. Describe where and in who sepsis occurs 8. Describe the cost of sepsis To support these projects we there is a core that supports the teams. We will train our patient partners in research methods to lead their own qualitative program. Our proposed research will improve sepsis recognition and prevention, develop innovative treatment strategies, improve the sepsis knowledge of the public and health professionals and improve the outcomes of those who develop sepsis.

column37: There is a growing body of evidence indicating that the healthcare needs of people living with substance use disorders (SUD) are not being fully met by the existing health system. Optimistically, there is growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI), which presents a unique opportunity to redefine how data is used in health, with potential for significant impact on patient care and the health of populations. Aligned with CIHR-Institute of Population and Public Health's mandate and the 'Equitable AI' strategic research priority, my program of research utilizes linked administrative data to answer key questions related to optimizing healthcare for people living with SUD. As part of this work, my research also seeks to understand the ethical and societal implications of applying these data-driven and technologically advanced approaches to population and public health, particularly as it pertains to marginalized populations. Alongside key stakeholders, I also aim to apply the knowledge gained to ethically and appropriately design and implement AI interventions to optimize health systems, and by extension, treatment and care for this population.

Through a combination of interventional and observational research approaches I will address two related objectives: (1) to advance the implementation of evidence-base treatments for opioid use disorder (OUD) by developing a clinical research program evaluating innovative and promising treatment strategies; and (2) to assess the impact of innovative and evolving addiction medicine programs and policies (e.g., new clinical guidelines, emergent pharmacotherapies, integrated models of care) on engagement in the OUD care cascade and related comorbidities (e.g., hepatitis C [HCV], HIV) among people who use drugs (PWUD). I believe my proposed program of research has high potential to generate strong evidence to inform the implementation of evidence-based and patient-centered interventions along the continuum of opioid addiction care, and thereby reduce health inequities faced by people who use drugs in BC and elsewhere. And as such, is directly relevant to CIHR-IPPH's mandate.

column36: The role of fat-free mass in metabolic health: An opposing perspective
column37: The metabolic syndrome (MetS) increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes. Since fat-free mass (FFM) is a metabolically active tissue, it is generally recognized that a greater FFM has a protective effect on the risk of developing MetS. This assumption is often based on studies reporting FFM as a percentage of body weight (BW). However, recent work from our group suggests that greater absolute FFM could be deleterious to metabolic health. The objectives were thus to investigate if the conflicting results are explained by the various indices of FFM (absolute, relative to BW or relative to height). Secondly, we sought to assess the impact of FFM per se on the relative risk (RR) of MetS. A total of 5401 individuals (46.4 16.2 y; 27.5 5.0 kg/m2) were included in the analyses. Absolute FFM (kg), FFM index [FFMi; (kg/m2)] and FFM% [FFM/BW *100] were determined using DXA. Quartiles were determined in a sex and age-specific fashion. The ATP III definition was used to identify individuals with MetS. The RR of having the MetS was estimated with FFMi, corrected for FM index (FMi) and physical activity (PA). The reference group for RRs was the first quartiles (Q1) of FFMi in each subgroup. The prevalence of MetS was greater with increasing quartiles of FFM or FFMi, yet decreased with higher quartiles of FFM% (all p<0.001). Additionally, the RR of having MetS was greater compared to the reference group in all subgroups (all p<0.05), except for Q2 and Q3 in young men (p=0.347 and 0.095 respectively). These results first suggest that the indices of FFM greatly impacts the association with MetS. Secondly, the present study suggests a greater RR of having MetS with increasing FFMi, even when corrected for FMi and PA levels. Hence, the largely purported idea that a large FFM has a protective effect against metabolic abnormalities might stem from flawed conclusions. It would, therefore, be critical to re-examine the contribution of FFM to metabolic health.
