column36: Preconception health characteristics of women with physical, sensory, and intellectual and developmental disabilities in Ontario
column37: There is a growing recognition that preconception health, that is, the health of women of reproductive age, impacts perinatal and infant outcomes. Although about 10% women of reproductive age has a disability, we know little about their preconception health. In the presentation, I will describe the preconception health characteristics of women with physical, sensory, and intellectual and developmental disabilities in Ontario. We conducted a population-based, cross-sectional study using Ontario health administrative data (2015-2016). We identified 15-44-year-old women with physical (n=254,844), sensory (n=87,639), intellectual and developmental (n=7,900), and multiple disabilities (n=27,920) and women without disabilities (n=2,303,066). Preconception health variables were social (poverty), health (chronic disease, teratogenic medication use, mental illness, history of assault), and health care factors (continuity of care). We described these characteristics using frequencies and percentages and compared women in each disability group to those without disabilities using standardized differences, wherein differences >0.10 were clinically meaningful. We found that, compared to women without disabilities, women with intellectual and developmental disabilities were more likely to live in poverty. All four disability groups were more likely to have diabetes, hypertension, and asthma and to be using teratogenic medications. They were also more likely to have a mood or anxiety disorder, and women with physical, intellectual and developmental, and multiple disabilities were more likely to have a substance use disorder and to have experienced assault. However, all four groups were more likely to routinely access the same primary care provider, indicating high continuity of care. My presentation will conclude with a discussion of future research directions and what obstetricians and gynecologists might do to help improve the preconception health of women with disabilities.

column36: Multi-center validation of non-invasive biomarkers of renal allograft outcomes
column37: End-stage kidney failure (ESKF) is common (38,833 Canadians in 2017), increasing (by 35% since 2008) and costly (more than $1.8 billion/year). Transplantation is the therapy of choice for many patients with better survival and quality of life, and provides healthcare savings of $33,000-$84,000 per patient each year after the first year compared to staying on dialysis. When a patient loses their transplant and returns to dialysis, there is a 3-fold higher risk of dying. Therefore, developing new strategies to keep kidney transplants healthy is a key priority for patients and caregivers. We have identified non-invasive urine tests that can predict late kidney transplant results. We showed that two urine proteins (CCL2 and CXCL10) are elevated 6-months after transplant in patients most likely to lose their transplant. The primary goal of these two large multi-center studies is to independently confirm that these new urine tests predict kidney transplant results, as this is the next critical step to bring these new urine tests into clinical practice. These new urine tests could be used to help personalize transplant care based on individual risk profile. For example, identifying low risk individuals can help doctors decide who may be safe to reduce the amount of anti-rejection medications they are taking. Conversely, high risk patients could be enrolled into clinical trials aimed at improving their long-term transplant health. If these new tests are confirmed as strong predictors of transplant outcome (or "surrogate markers") they could make clinical trials more feasible to conduct. Ultimately, the results from these studies may be used to help inform the design and conduct of the next generation of kidney transplant trials, with the goal of improving kidney transplant results.

column36: Elastolytic activity of cysteine cathepsins K, S and V promotes vascular calcification
column37: Cardiovascular diseases remain the main causes of death in industrialized countries and especially in North America. A common complication of vascular diseases is the calcification of blood vessels, i.e. the formation of bone-like minerals in the circulatory system. Calcification makes blood vessels brittle and affects blood flow. Arterial calcification is a strong marker of cardiovascular mortality and is tightly associated with aging and arterial remodeling. Calcification occurs in particular in the extracellular matrix of blood vessels, especially in damaged area. The main extracellular matrix components, elastin and collagen, are both heavily degraded by cathepsins during the hardening of arteries (atherosclerosis). However little is known about the mechanism of calcification and whether the degradation of the matrix leads to mineralization or whether the calcification constitutes a protective but out of control response to the vessel destruction. Human cysteine protease cathepsins (Cat) K, S and V are of particular interest as we and others have demonstrated that these enzymes are critically involved in the weakening of arteries associated with the formation of the atheroma plaque. Our objectives are to understand the role of cathepsins in arterial calcification and to device strategies to treat cardiovascular diseases. In our latest study we demonstrated that the degradation of elastin by catK, S and V increases its calcification and conversely, calcified elastin was more resistant to degradation. Moreover, the cleavage of elastin by these three enzymes releases fragments that can act on the cells constituting the vessels wall. These elastin fragments stimulate the production of mineral matrix by vascular cells.

column36: Decreased Baseline Diaphragm Thickness Independently Predicts Increased Risk of Morbidity and Mortality in Mechanically Ventilated Patients
column37: Every year in Ontario approximately 40,000 patients develop severe breathing difficulties and require the support from a breathing machine ('mechanical ventilator') to safe their life. Outcomes of patients who need mechanical ventilation however can negatively impact the strength of their own breathing muscles, at or before the onset of their illness. The biggest and most important breathing muscle is the diaphragm. A strong diaphragm helps patients to recover from breathing difficulties more quickly and easily, with a shorter stay in hospital, fewer complications such as pneumonia, and therefore a higher chance of being alive at the end of their illness compared to those patients with thinner diaphragms. Therefore, if patients have a stronger diaphragm when they get sick it is more likely that they will have enough strength to breath on their own once they recover from critical illness. In other words, a strong diaphragm increases their "reserve" to tolerate the acute illness. We performed ultrasound measurements of the diaphragms of 200 patients who needed a machine to support their breathing on every day of their ICU stay. We found that patients with thicker diaphragms at baseline recovered more quickly and were more likely to survive to hospital discharge compared to those patients with thinner diaphragms at baseline. Specifically, patients with thicker diaphragms had lower in-hospital death rates, more days off of the breathing machine, and fewer patients needed a breathing machine for more than 14 days. Our results suggest that identifying patients with thin diaphragms and implementing strategies to thicken and strengthen the diaphragm before major surgery or unplanned, but high-risk patient groups for requiring a breathing machine, such as those with advanced heart or lung disease who require advanced rehabilitation - muscle strengthening strategies can help accelerate their recovery.

column36: Beyond meaning and connectedness: Family caregiver's spiritual experiences in a hospice setting
column37: Family caregivers play a vital role during the time of illness of a family member. While caring for a dying family member in a hospice setting, family caregivers experience multiple transitions, make new resolutions, adjust to changing roles and expectations, and experience grief and other complex caregiving situations where their search for meaning becomes evident. The study aimed to describe the experiences of spirituality among family caregivers caring for a dying family member in a hospice setting. The study used interpretive description, a qualitative approach to guide the study. Individual in-depth interviews and follow up interviews were conducted among18 family caregivers. Ethical approval was obtained from the Human Research Ethics Board of the University of Alberta. Findings revealed that spirituality was a major coping resource for family caregivers. Family caregivers uncovered meaningful engagement, sense of belonging, and a sense of attachment while serving their dying family member. They highly valued the love, respect, and honour of the family, showed compassion, believed in God's blessings and grace and experienced constant spiritual growth and self-transcendence. For most participants, all these spiritual experiences and spiritual values helped them to cope with their uncertainties, grief and loss, and sufferings faced while caregiving actions and practices in a hospice setting. Some family caregivers expressed spiritual distress and therefore needed additional spiritual support and care. The study findings inform healthcare professionals to acknowledge and integrate spirituality as an important dimension of palliative care and develop supportive care interventions to enhance family caregivers' spirituality, prevent spiritual distress and promote spiritual wellbeing at the end of life in the hospice setting.

column37: Friedreich Ataxia (FRDA) is the most common form of hereditary ataxia. This is a recessive disease, i.e., both parents have to be carriers of the mutated gene. However, they are not symptomatic. Only the child who inherits two copies of the mutated gene will develop the disease. It is important to note that in the province of Quebec because of the low number of initial colons from France, ONE QUEBECKER OUT OF 50 IS A CARRIER OF THAT DISEASE! It is thus important to pursue in Canada research on the development of a therapy for this disease. The mutation responsible for Friedreich is an unusual expansion of the GAA trinucleotide in the frataxin gene leading to a reduced expression of frataxin resulting in cell death. Neuron death leads to coordination problems (confining patient to wheel chair) and cardiomyocytes death to cardiac insufficiency (main cause of premature death). Our long-term goal is to develop a gene therapy treatment for FRDA based on a single injection of an Adeno Associated Virus (AAV) coding for the correcting agents. We have already showed that our approach using the CRISPR technology, where an enzyme named SpCas9 permits to cut DNA before and after GAA repeat to induce a permanent deletion. This restores the frataxin protein level. The present project aims to optimize the AAV to improve the treatment while avoiding mutations of other genes. We will also investigate a new method (named Hara-Kiri) to avoid a sustained expression of a smaller Cas9 (CjCas9) to reduce off-target effect mutations and prevent a possible immune response. We will conduct in vivo experiments in a mouse model to accumulate data for an eventual Phase I clinical study. Developing an in vivo gene editing therapy approach for monogenic diseases is highly significant and medically relevant. The impact of a single gene therapy treatment for these patients will greatly enhance their quality of life and reduce the cost associated with long-term health care management.

column36: Evaluating Comparative Effectiveness of Psychosocial Interventions for Persons Receiving Opioid Agonist Therapy for Opioid Use Disorder: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
column37: The opioid crisis has involved rapid rise in drug overdose and death involving prescription and illegal opioids. Part of the Government of Canada's approach to drug policy aims to focus on a strong foundation of evidence and treatment. Guidelines for treating individuals with opioid use disorder recommends individuals receive treatment that involves medication (i.e., opioid agonist therapy) and psychosocial treatment (e.g., counselling). Previous reviews, however, have found inconsistent results about the effectiveness of psychosocial treatments and no previous reviews have analyzed findings numerically (quantitatively). Our study is the first to compile evidence to determine if psychosocial therapies used in combination with medication is more effective than medication alone. This work also compares different types of psychosocial treatments to determine the benefit and harms of each and we present an understanding of what approach may be most effective. Due to a large number of studies included, our study also aimed to look at specific subgroups of people such as those using opioids for chronic pain, pregnant females with opioid use disorder, and individuals with comorbid mental health concerns. A second goal of our work was to determine the aspects that are most important to measure in future studies of treating people with opioid use disorder. To do this, we have been conducting interviews, focus groups, and surveys in collaboration with patient partners, policy makers, clinicians, and researchers to ensure that future research defines effectiveness of treatment in line with how those most impact by opioid use disorder understand successful treatment. The results of this work are being distributed widely in order to facilitate an improved understanding of the role that psychosocial therapy can have in treating opioid use disorder.

column36: S'engager avec des partenaires de la communaute pour identifier des leviers d'action au soutien a domicile: vers des retombees inattendues d'une recherche participative axee sur la participation sociale des aines
column37: Les personnes ayant une vie sociale active sont en meilleure sante et vivent plus longtemps. En vieillissant, une personne sur trois est a risque d'etre isolee socialement. Heureusement, il est possible d'agir pour aider les aines a s'integrer plus facilement dans la communaute. En effet, les cliniciens, dont les ergotherapeutes, peuvent offrir un eventail d'interventions rentables pour ameliorer la vie sociale des aines. Par exemple, les ergotherapeutes peuvent batir des liens avec des ressources de la communaute ou offrir aux aines des interventions en groupe, en plus de les accompagner pour avoir une vie sociale saine et pleine de sens. Or, ces interventions sont peu offertes aux aines dans les services d'ergotherapie a domicile, notamment en raison d'un manque de partenariat. Cette etude visait donc a repenser les services d'ergotherapie a domicile en vue de favoriser la participation sociale des aines. Des chercheurs, des decideurs, des cliniciens et des membres de la communaute se sont d'abord reunis afin d'initier un partenariat de recherche participative. Lors d'entretiens individuels et de groupe suivis d'un atelier collaboratif, les chercheurs et un facilitateur en innovation sociale ont rencontre 28 partenaires pour co-construire les pratiques souhaitees et identifier les leviers d'action a deployer pour les integrer. Les partenaires ont elabore une serie d'interventions innovantes (individuelles, de groupe et communautaires). Selon les participants, les principaux leviers d'action consistent a changer la culture institutionnelle et les indicateurs de performance du systeme. Les partenaires ont identifie des retombees inattendues, dont la possibilite de marquer un renouveau et d'influencer sa communaute, ce qui leur a donne un espoir de changement. Ces recommandations guideront les decideurs, les cliniciens et les membres de la communaute dans l'implantation de services et de politiques de sante mieux adaptes a la population vieillissante canadienne.

column36: Clustering COPD Patient Trajectories via Dirichlet Process Mixture Models with Fixed Effects Continuous-Time Hidden Markov Models
column37: Understanding the progression of chronic diseases, such as COPD, is important to inform early diagnosis, personalize care and healthcare system management. Data from clinical and administrative systems have the potential to advance this understanding, but traditional methods for modeling disease progression are not well suited to analyzing data collected at irregular intervals, such as when a patient chooses to interact with the healthcare system. Many cases of severe illness can be traced back to a lack of appropriate and ongoing followup health care. To help understand the long-term causes of severe and preventable illness, we need to understand not only how many patients have severe illness, but also what their "care path" or "trajectory" was before they ended up with severe illness. Until recently, it was very difficult and costly to collect the patient data from paper-based records, making it impossible to efficiently track patient trajectories. With the advent of electronic health records, we can now collect patient data automatically. The patient data is still, however, very complex; to identify patient trajectories automatically, we need new statistical methods. From my previous work, I have developed a new statistical method via continuous-time processes to identify meaningful disease progression and transition patterns according to individual characteristics, which are interpretable by healthcare system managers and can be used to measure the performance of the healthcare system over time. Based on this work, I extended the model to cluster the patient trajectories to explain population-level variations in trajectories and to optimize clinical care strategies by using health care trajectories for dynamic treatment decisions. Unlike most clustering techniques, the approach I proposed allows the number of clusters to be learned as a function of the sample size.

For individuals struggling to clear this mucous, airway suctioning is one technique that can be used by health care professionals, such as physical therapists, to make breathing easier. Suctioning uses a system similar to a small vacuum to remove mucous and clear the airways. Unfortunately, this technique can be dangerous when done incorrectly. In order to ensure this technique is done safely and effectively, it is important that health care professionals are tested on their ability to perform this technique properly. Thus, the objective of this project was to develop a new tool to assess physical therapists' competency related to the performance of airway suctioning. This project is important because the proper application of airway suctioning can help a wide variety of individuals with serious lung related illnesses to experience higher quality health care and to breathe easier.

column36: Sympathetic nervous system activity in women with gestational diabetes
column37: Background: Gestational diabetes is the most common pregnancy complication and it is associated with acute and long-term cardiovascular dysfunction putting these women at higher risk of developing cardiovascular disease later in life. Evidence suggests that complicated pregnancies are associated with an elevated fight or flight response. This result in negative changes in the function of blood vessels. The mechanisms that control these changes, however, are not fully understood. The chemoreflex, an organ that senses oxygen and sugars in the blood, is a potent regulator of the fight or flight response. High sugar levels are associated with an increase of the activity of the chemoreflex and the fight or flight response in non-pregnant population, thus, we hypothesize that chemoreflex hyperactivity may be an important mechanism associated with the development of gestational diabetes. Methodology: We recruited 18 women with gestational diabetes and compared them with 18 healthy pregnant women. Blood pressure and direct measures of the fight or flight response were determined 1) at rest; 2) while the participant is breathing elevated oxygen; 3) during a stress test (while the participant put her hand in an ice bath). Results: Women with gestational diabetes do not display a basal increased flight or fight activity, however, our data suggests that during stress their flight or fight response is indeed increased. Moreover, we found that women with gestational diabetes are more responsive to high levels of oxygen than healthy pregnant women; suggesting that chemoreflex hyperactivity can be one of the mechanisms associated with the pathophysiology of this disease. Conclusion: Chemoreflex hyperactivity can be one of the mechanisms associated with the pathophysiology of gestational diabetes.

column36: Assessing the economic value of CAR T-cell therapy using short-term single-arm clinical trial data: A multi-state simulation modelling approach
column37: Novel therapies in oncology bring a promise for disrupting current medical practice and potential for cure. They also carry an eagerness for timely integration into clinical practice. Evaluation of the clinical and economic value of these therapies is however hindered by limited access to individual-level data, evidence on comparative and long-term effectiveness, and potential reporting bias in available data sources. Novel methods in economic evaluation are necessary to assess the clinical and economic value of such strategies. We illustrate the use of multi-state simulation modelling to estimate the long-term comparative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy for Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. To build a CAR T-cell arm, we pool digitized survival data from published single-arm clinical trial results. We then construct a broad standard care arm using individual-level data from a pediatric cancer registry. We matched this data to clinical trial inclusion/exclusion criteria and baseline patient characteristics - both treatment arms forecast movement to sequential health or treatment states and death using predicted transitions. We assumed a range of cure rates in the treatment arm given limited information on long-term effectiveness. The simulation model includes 100,000 individuals. We test uncertainty around published clinical trial results in robustness analysis. We also consider scenario analysis of novel therapy costing schemes. We estimate that CAR T-cell therapy has an incremental cost over standard care on a range of $85,478 to $347,348 per QALY gain, based on the assumed cure rates of 10% to 40%. These results indicate that the cost-effectiveness of CAR T-cell is highly dependent on a number of uncertain factors. The combined use of survival curve digitization, comparator cohort matching and MSM provides improved precision in assessing cost-effectiveness for novel therapies, however.

column37: Cellular signaling, including that of immune cells, starts at the plasma membrane. Conventional understanding is that a receptor engaging a suitable ligand sends a signal across the membrane. This notion is increasingly regarded as being too simplistic. In this project, we aim to study how lipids can transduce the signal across the membrane, and how the lipid domains are used by protein receptor to organize and fine-tune the downstream effectors. column37: Motivation, a non-profit organization that provides mobility and associated services in developing countries, has been providing a peer-support for 25 years. The Motivation peer program consists of 16 sessions that cover various topics (e.g., advocacy, peer, self-care, wheelchair training, vocation and sport). Anecdotally, the program seems to work, but there is little evidence to support the underlying mechanisms that may influence behaviour change among individuals with disabilities. The purpose of this study was to classify behaviour change techniques that exist in Motivation's peer-program using an evidence-based taxonomy of behaviour change. Individual sessions apply between 8 - 26 BCTs to target behaviour change, with the most commonly used BCTs including vicarious experience, social support, natural consequences, social comparison, and verbal persuasion. Significance: Although the Motivation Peer Training program was not initially developed within a theoretical framework, the is evidence of BCTs that fall within 14 behaviour clusters suggests that the program contains important theoretical precursors to behaviour change. Future research will align existing BCTs to within existing behavior change theory, which may inform future programming decisions for individuals with disabilities.

column36: Effectiveness of a Home-Based Exercise Program for Lung Transplant Candidates- A Retrospective Chart Review
column37: In Canada, most lung transplant programs offer mandatory hospital-based pre-transplant exercise programs to optimize fitness and prevent deconditioning in transplant candidates. Home-based programs can give access to rehabilitation to a larger number of patients at lower healthcare costs. Objectives: To describe the changes in functional exercise capacity (6-minute walk distance (6MWD)) in lung transplant candidates who participated in a home-based exercise program and determine the relationship between changes in 6MWD pre and post-transplant variables. Methods: a retrospective cohort study of 119 individuals who received a lung transplant between 2011-2015, participated in a home-based exercise program while waiting list. 6MWD was assessed at 3-time points: time of assessment for transplant, last test prior to transplant and one-month post-transplant. Other variables included: age, sex, primary diagnosis, date of transplantation, body mass index (BMI), total hospital length of stay (LOS), intensive care unit (ICU) LOS and time on mechanical ventilation. Results: LOS on the waiting list=1.8 yrs (median). There was a mean decrease of 17.993.9m between the 6MWD at the time of assessment and the last 6MWD prior to surgery (p<0.001; whole sample). Thirty-two patients (26%) increased their 6MWD (mean change 9042.8m); 50 patients (42%) decreased 6MWD (10071.2m); and 37 patients (32%) had no change in 6MWD (115.7m). There was a weak negative correlation between change in 6MWD prior to transplant and time on mechanical ventilation (r= -0.232; p<0.05). Conclusion: Most patients (58%) were able to either increase or maintain their 6MWD using a home exercise program while on the waiting list. Home-based semi-supervised exercise programs may be an effective approach prior to transplantation.

column37: Kidney transplant is the only effective treatment for end-stage renal diseases, however, survival of a transplanted kidney is usually affected by acute kidney injury(AKI), which often happens in recipients post-transplant. column36: Parkinson's disease and aging affect neural activation during continuous gait alterations to the split-belt treadmill: An [18F] FDG PET Study.
column37: As we age, we may experience a feeling of having to "think" about how we walk. This impedes our ability to make quick changes from one step to the next, like we may have to do to navigate around a puddle in our path. This is especially true for older adults with Parkinson's Disease (PD). Interestingly, both healthy older adults and adults with PD can change their gait pattern to walk on a split-belt treadmill- a treadmill with a separate belt under each leg. This treadmill can drive each foot at a different speed, quickly creating a bizarre asymmetric gait pattern. While we know older adults and adults with PD can change their walking pattern quickly, we are still not sure of how the brain is able to control these step-to-step alterations. In this project, we use brain imaging to compare the brain activity of young adults, older adults and adults with PD during typical treadmill walking (both belts at a comfortable walking speed) to split-belt treadmill walking (belts at different speeds). To quickly modify their walking pattern, all participants increased activity in brain regions responsible for movement planning, consolidating their movements with sensations from their feet and updating their plan for their walking pattern. With age, however, their brain widened this activity to include regions for memory and cognition. Finally, the presence of PD required even further activation from areas responsible for information of sensation from their body and legs. This widespread and increased use of brain resources may help to explain why more complex walking tasks, such as walking and talking or turning, show detriments with aging and the progression of PD. By better understanding how the brain controls the way we walk, we may be able to help those who find these changes to their walking pattern difficult.

column37: The degradation of proteins in muscle is of high importance and is the process underlying muscle atrophy and sarcopenia. The autophagy-lysosomal and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways are the two main proteolytic systems in skeletal muscle. column37: The elegance of 'helminth (worm) therapy' is it requires only that the host mount a natural response to a helminth (one that has been fine-tuned over millennia), and consequently concomitant disease can be suppressed. Thus, helminth therapy is presented as a novel approach to inflammatory disease that can be used to individualize therapy to a patient. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects ~270,000 Canadians; Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are devastating diseases, physiologically and psychologically, for which there is no cure and current treatments, while improving, are far from perfect. Using mouse model systems, we have shown that infection with a tapeworm parasite reduces the severity of inflammation in the colon. Our preliminary data show that the protective effect of infection with the worm is lost if mice are co-treated with antibiotics. The antibiotics do not affect the parasite, clearly indicating that disruption of the normal composition of the bacteria in the colon negates the protective effect of infection with the worm. Using cutting-edge methods and model systems established in my laboratory, a series of experiments are proposed to assess the worm-bacteria-host relationship. The goal is to define the precise requirements for the mechanism of action of helminth therapy in the suppression of colitis that can ultimately be applied to patients. The proposed research advances a personalized-medicine paradigm for IBD where a therapeutic helminth may be prescribed that is matched to the genetic, immunological and gut-bacteria characteristics of the patient.

column36: Scale-up: Adapting an effective older adult physical activity intervention to achieve impact at the population level
column37: By 2050, 30% of Canadians will be older adults. Thus healthy aging is a public health priority. Health promoting physical activity programs contribute to healthy aging by decreasing prevalence of chronic disease and preserving mobility and independence. Still, older adults are among the most sedentary Canadians; 85% fail to meet physical activity guidelines. To improve population health, programs need to be scaled-up to reach more people and adapted across diverse settings to meet the needs of diverse populations. In 2015 the British Columbia (BC) Ministry of Health released a physical activity strategy; older adults were identified as a priority. Thus, we engaged government and community stakeholders to co-design and deliver a physical activity program (Choose to Move, CTM) for older adults. CTM increased physical activity and mobility among older adults at small scale (2016-17; 56 programs). It will be scaled-up across BC in 2018-20, providing an opportunity to study how best to adapt CTM for scale-up. The purpose of my research is to describe the adaptation process and resultant adaptations to CTM prior to its scale-up across BC. We adopted a 9-step adaptation process: 1) identify stakeholders; 2) conduct needs assessment; 3) develop prototype of recommended adaptations; 4) validate prototype with stakeholders, 5) create adapted program; 6) pilot test adaptations, 7) modify adapted program, 8) implement adapted program; and 9) evaluate effectiveness of adapted program. Here we describe steps 1-6 and organize the data with an adaptation coding tool. The adapted program includes content, context and training adaptations. To address the need for more 'opportunities to socially connect' among CTM participants we: added more group meetings, reduced phone check-ins and adapted provider training to integrate social connections for older adults. Flexible, adaptable programs are more likely to be successfully delivered at scale and have equal impact as smaller trials.

column36: Efficacy of serious games and influence of design elements in healthcare education.
column37: Les jeux electroniques pedagogiques (JEP) sont des outils interactifs et divertissants visant prioritairement l'apprentissage. Des revues des ecrits scientifiques ont rapporte que l'efficacite des JEP a ameliorer l'apprentissage des professionnels et des etudiants en sante etait grandement variable. La qualite methodologique des etudes realisees et la diversite des composantes dans les JEP (p. ex., un niveau de difficulte pouvant etre module, l'integration d'une trame narrative) pourraient expliquer cette efficacite variable. Le but de cette revue des ecrits etait 1) d'identifier les etudes realisees aupres de professionnels ou d'etudiants en sante et ayant evalue l'efficacite d'un JEP versus une autre intervention educative, et 2) d'analyser et de synthetiser les donnees provenant de ces etudes par rapport a la qualite methodologique de celles-ci, l'efficacite des JEP, et les composantes integrees au JEP. Nous avons recherche sur des bases de donnees les etudes pertinentes, publiees en anglais ou francais, et ce, jusqu'en decembre 2017. Deux chercheurs ont identifie les ecrits, extrait les donnees de ces ecrits et analyses celles-ci. La synthese des donnees a ete realisee a l'aide de methodes statistiques et en produisant un resume ecrit des resultats obtenus. Nous avons inclus 29 etudes realisees aupres de divers professionnels et etudiants en sante. Les JEP sont plus efficaces que d'autres interventions educatives pour ameliorer les connaissances, la confiance et l'execution de procedures. Toutefois, la qualite methodologique des etudes incluses est pauvre, ce qui limite la validite des resultats obtenus. L'integration d'une composante multijoueur ou d'un compte a rebours dans les JEP est associe a l'acquisition de connaissances. Les futures etudes devraient porter attention aux elements methodologiques pouvant biaiser les resultats et evaluer l'efficacite des JEP a modifier la pratique clinique et leur impact sur des indicateurs cliniques chez les patients.

column36: Impact of Missing Data and Auxiliary Information on Bias and Precision when Estimating Longitudinal Change in Patient- Reported Outcomes from Clinical Registries
column37: Our main research objective was to test the effect of missing data and supplementary variables on the precision of longitudinal change in patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in clinical registries. Clinical registry is an electronic database that contains information about the health and healthcare use of patients defined by a particular disease, condition or treatment. PROs are information provided by patients on aspects of their health status that are relevant to their health-related quality of life, including physical and mental health functioning. The secondary objective was to test association of multiple chronic diseases on estimates of change in health-related quality of life over time, in the presence of missing data, amongst older people undergoing knee replacement surgery. Study data were from a population-based joint replacement registry for Manitoba, Canada. PRO information was collected using the 12-item Short Form Survey (SF-12) one month before surgery at a patient pre-assessment clinic and one-year after surgery via a mailed questionnaire. We used a statistical model to estimate the average change in PRO scores, after adjusting for confounding demographic and comorbid chronic condition covariates. Methods suitable to address missing data problems was adopted. The study cohort was comprised of 5631 patients that underwent joint replacement surgery, 58.7% were females and the average age of patients was 66.7 years. Our results revealed that chronic conditions such as back pain, diabetes and heart disease reduced the amount of improvement on physical health summary scores and depression had a negative impact on mental health summary scores in patients undergoing joint replacement. The choice of methods to address missing data had a substantial impact on the precision of these estimates. In anticipation of unavoidable missing data in clinical registries, collection of supplemental information is beneficial to increase precision in estimates of change.

column36: First Characterization Of Extracellular Vesicles Derived From Human Amniotic Stromal Stem Cells And Their Applications For Cardiac Repair And Rejuvenation
column37: The buildup of fatty deposits in the coronary arteries can lead to a myocardial infarction, one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Even if these patients are lucky enough to undergo surgery to repair the damage blood vessels, a large part of the heart tissue dies and is unable to regenerate itself. Over the past 20 years, stem cells have been used a means to regenerate the dead heart tissue. However, when these cells are injected into patients, the fail to integrate into the damaged tissue, resulting in very limited improvement in heart function. More recently, research has found the the stem cells themselves are not neccesary regenerate the damaged tissue, but rather its substances that they produce, called extracellular vesicles, that have a larger therapeutic potential. Thus, the focus of this study was to assess how extracellular vesicles from stem cells can be utilized to repair the diseased cardiac tissue. We isolated vesicles from stem cells derived from the amniotic membrane of the post-term placenta and treated cells of the heart (cardiomyocytes) and blood vessels (endothelial cells) with the vesicles after we depleted them of oxygen to mimic a heart attack. We found that the vesicles contain molecules that are involved in biological pathways that form new blood vessels and regenerate heart muscle tissue. We also found that vesicles were able to protect the cells from injury due to lack of oxygen, while also promoting cell division. Together, these results show that the use of vesicles repairing damaged heart tissue is a promising and novel therapeutic option for patients who have had a heart attack. In the near future, we hope to be able to test the efficacy of these vesicles in an animal model.

column37: There is now substantial evidence that sleep consolidates (i.e., strengthens and stabilizes) memory. More recent research is now extending this knowledge to observe which aspects of memory sleep might benefit the most. Memory can be divided into declarative (e.g., remembering facts and past events) and procedural (e.g., learning and carrying out the ideal moves to win a game of chess). Procedural memory can be further differentiated into its motor components, and its strategy components. Our recent research found that sleep benefited the strategy of learning a procedural memory task more so than it benefited the simple motor movements when performing that same task. We are now expanding on these findings to identify which sleep stages are responsible for the strategy learning component, and how these sleep stages might relate to the brain regions that are activated while performing the task prior to sleep.

column36: The role of GABA releasing neurons in the SLD in regulating rapid eye movement sleep
column37: INTRODUCTION: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is characterized by cortical activation, muscle atonia and rapid eye movements. The neuronal circuitry that regulates REM sleep remains speculative; however, the sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (SLD) located in the brainstem is hypothesized to be important for controlling REM sleep. Previous findings suggest that gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) releasing cells in the SLD (SLD-GABA) are active during REM sleep, and lesions of these neurons impair REM sleep expression suggesting its link to REM sleep regulation. Here, we used optogenetic to inhibit the activity of SLD-GABA neurons in order to identify their potential role in REM sleep control in mice. METHOD: Optogenetic is a technique used to manipulate the activity of neurons using light stimulation. This technique requires the expression of light sensitive membrane bound protein called opsins. In our study, we drove expression of inhibitory opsins (eArch3.0) in the SLD-GABA neurons using a viral vector driven genetic manipulation. Optic fibers were implanted above SLD for focal light delivery and electrodes were implanted to record brain and muscle activity for sleep-wake identification. RESULTS: Compared to the sham controls, we found that inhibition of SLD-GABA neurons during REM or non-REM (NREM) sleep promotes transition into wakefulness (n=5; unpaired t-test, p<0.001*** and p<0.001***, respectively.) Moreover, we demonstrated that 20s inhibition of SLD-GABA neurons promote longer period of wakefulness than 10s (two-way ANOVA RM, p<0.01*) suggesting that inhibition of SLD-GABA neurons also maintains wakefulness. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings show that inhibition of SLD-GABA neurons terminates sleep and promotes wakefulness. Our study will provide a deeper understanding of the REM sleep circuit and potentially make contributions in improving the therapeutic treatment for disorders linked to REM sleep dysregulation like REM sleep behavior disorder and narcolepsy.

column36: Financial risk protection for informal caregivers of community-dwelling dependent seniors: a comparative analysis of three welfare states (France, England and Ontario)
column37: In Canada, dependent seniors are choosing to age at home instead of in long-term care. Ontario evidence suggests this has shifted the responsibility of care and monetary care costs to informal caregivers. This study explores how Ontario compares to France and England in terms of financial risk protection for informal caregivers of community-dwelling dependent seniors, and what policy lessons Ontario can learn from, or share with, these jurisdictions. This study utilizes descriptive comparative methodology using publicly available policy documents to compare and contrast financial risk protection policies for informal caregivers in the three jurisdictions. I draw on Esping-Andersen's welfare state typology to select jurisdictions that provide variation in state type, and to examine the connection between broader notions of social protection for citizens and the system of financial protection of informal caregivers. I applied an institutional approach to examine how design features of financial protection mechanisms may contribute to coverage inequities. Results reveal two financial protection mechanisms: cash allowances and tax credits. Coverage inequities can be linked to mechanism design, e.g, eligibility and means-testing criteria for cash allowances (France), and restrictions on receiving additional financial protections for those who qualify for cash allowances (France) and tax credits (Ontario/England). Overall, France's financial protection system is congruent with its conservative notions of social welfare; however, less congruency exists in liberal England and Ontario. A liberal state accepts an active role in the social welfare of its citizens, yet, in Ontario, provincial and federal tax credits appear insufficient at protecting informal caregivers from financial risk. Findings suggest that Ontario may want to consider a non-means-tested cash allowance alongside existing tax credits to facilitate choice among caregivers and improve equity in coverage.

column36: Acute control of fibroblast contraction by macrophage contact formation
column37: Body implants are used in reconstructive surgery and orthopedics to support lost tissue function. All body implants are causing inflammatory reactions that often lead to formation of dense scar tissue. Implants then must be operatively removed due to loss of function, deformities, and pain caused by the scar. The culprit cells for scarring are called myofibroblasts because they secrete collagen ("fibro") that is contracted ("myo") into scar tissue. Excessive myofibroblast activities are also responsible for loss of function of vital organs after injury, such as the heart after an infarct - this life-threatening condition is called fibrosis. Fibrosis ensues from normal repair partly because unresolved inflammation promotes continued activation of myofibroblasts. Our lab found that this pulling activity generates far-reaching movements in the matrix that mechanically attract inflammatory macrophages. Once touched by attracted macrophage, fibroblasts undergo bursts of contraction that further enhance matrix deformation. The receptors involved in fibroblast-macrophage recognition and the macrophage signals inducing fibroblast contraction are not known. It is our aim to identify the molecular players mediating macrophage-induced fibroblast activation. We propose that preventing these cells to touch or blocking the interaction signaling molecules will ultimately reduce tissue scarring. We will study macrophages and fibroblasts derived from mouse tissue in unique skin tissue-soft or scar-stiff co-culture environments. We will delete and inhibit already identified receptors on the macrophage and/or fibroblast surface to test how they can promote contact-induced signaling. We will likewise target components of known signaling pathways associated with these receptors. Key to the success of these inhibition strategies is targeting only the macrophage-fibroblast couple whereas other cells with beneficial functions in tissues under repair remain - literally - untouched.

column36: New and Expanding Ventricular Hemorrhage Predicts Poor Outcome in Acute Hemorrhagic Stroke
column37: Hemorrhagic stroke, also known as "bleeding stroke", is caused by the rupture of blood vessels within the brain. It is the second most common form of stroke and is arguably the most devastating. When they first present to hospital, patients with hemorrhagic stroke are often still bleeding into the brain, and the bleed can expand and enlarge. This phenomenon, termed hematoma expansion, is responsible for the poor outcomes seen in patients with hemorrhagic stroke. In most cases, blood expands and pushes onto adjacent brain tissue. But in at least a quarter of patients, blood can also expand into the ventricles of the brain. The presence of blood in the ventricles is particularly devastating and often impairs recovery. However, we know very little about the full effects that new or expanding ventricular blood can have on survival and recovery after hemorrhagic stroke. In this study, we sought to better understand the relationship between new or expanding ventricular blood and long-term recovery. Through an international hemorrhagic stroke collaboration, we used the data of hundreds of patients with hemorrhagic stroke to build a predictive model looking at expanding ventricular blood and outcome at 90 days post-stroke occurrence. We found that even small amounts of ventricular blood expansion, less than a teaspoon, was strongly predictive of disability and death. Individuals who had blood develop in their ventricles were at three times increased odds of dying by 90 days. We validated our findings in a separate hemorrhage database, courtesy of our colleagues at Harvard University, and found similar findings. Our study shows the importance that ventricular blood has on the outcomes of patients with hemorrhagic stroke. Our findings suggest that stopping ventricular blood expansion could be a novel target for future therapies. Our findings can also help researchers refine their clinical trials to help discover future treatments for this disease.

column36: Influence of Dietary Protein Intake on Skeletal Muscle Protein Turnover and Proteomic Profile in Healthy and Sarcopenic Older Men and Women
column37: Protein requirements for everyone over the age of 19 have been set at the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) level of 0.8 g/kg/d, despite evidence that older persons require more. Sarcopenia is only one of the potential consequences of inadequate protein intake, and since sarcopenia is associated with many chronic conditions, such as diabetes and osteoporosis, it is important to limit the prevalence of this disease in the older population in order to improve their quality of life and to alleviate the costs on the healthcare system. There is also evidence that there are sex-based differences in muscle tissue production. Prior to embarking on a costly trial, we need to understand how muscle protein turnover is regulated in older persons (65-75y) who are healthy and those that are sarcopenic. We propose a few hypotheses: 1) There are important sex-based differences in muscle tissue production and breakdown; 2) The RDA for protein is insufficient to support the highest rates of muscle tissue production in older adults; 3) The amino acid leucine will increase net muscle tissue production in both men and women when added to a protein intake at the RDA level; and 4) Sarcopenic older adults will show a lower net muscle tissue production at all protein intakes compared to the healthy group. We will be the first to show responses on a protein-by-protein basis at protein intakes above and below the current protein RDA in older adults. Our findings will also be the first to show that at a muscle-level, the current protein RDA is insufficient for older persons. Our data will yield important information to provide rationale for longer term trials, which will help us in developing better dietary guidelines to improve the health and daily life of older persons, as well as reduce the healthcare costs associated with sarcopenia.

column36: The impact of motherhood and APOE genotype on the aging brain
column37: Women are more likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and show greater AD neuropathology and cognitive decline compared to men. Pregnancy and motherhood (parity) play important roles in the aging brain; increased parity is associated with a greater risk of dementia, AD, neuropathology, and an earlier age of AD onset. Research in our laboratory has shown that parity influences hippocampal neuroplasticity and cognition in middle-age rats. APOE4, a major genetic risk factor for AD, has been shown to interact with parity to influence AD pathology, age of AD onset, and cognition. The objective of this project is to determine how previous parity interacts with APOE genotype to influence cognitive decline in older female rats. We used a rat model of AD that expresses the human form of APOE4. Age-matched APOE4 and wild-type female rats were either nulliparous (never mothered and with no sexual experience) or primiparous (first time mothers). The primiparous (WT and APOE4) female rats were bred at 5 months old in our animal facility. Pups were culled and the sex ratio of the litters were recorded. Maternal observations were completed twice a day, on days 2 to 6 postpartum. All rats were aged and then trained and tested during middle-age (9 months postpartum; equivalent to 13-14 months old) on the delayed win-shift Radial Arm Maze (RAM), a spatial working memory task mediated by the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. I am currently analyzing the data for this study. It is hypothesized that APOE4 primiparous rats will perform worse than APOE4 nulliparous rats, and APOE4 rats will perform worse than wild-type rats, in the RAM. It is further hypothesized that APOE4 genotype interacts with parity to contribute to cognitive decline.These results will offer insight into how parity and genotype are linked to cognition. This has implications for the importance of tailored treatments based on the genotype and reproductive history of women with AD.

column36: Vieillissement cerebral et perception de la parole dans le bruit : effet protecteur du chant choral
column37: La difficulte a percevoir la parole en presence de bruit est un declin cognitif frequent lors du vieillissement normal. Malheureusement, les causes de ce declin ne sont pas encore connues, mais des donnees suggerent que le vieillissement du cerveau pourrait etre en partie responsable. Plus specifiquement, le vieillissement de la voie dorsale du langage pourrait expliquer en partie ces difficultes. Des evidences suggerent que la pratique d'activites musicales peut modifier la structure de cette voie et ameliorer la perception auditive. Le chant choral est une activite musicale sensorimotrice qui pourrait constituer une avenue interessante pour ralentir les declins cerebraux lies au vieillissement. Bien que des evidences suggerent que le chant modifie la structure et le fonctionnement de cette voie, les avantages potentiels du chant choral sur la perception de la parole sont peu connus. Les objectifs de cette etude sont d'investiguer la relation entre la structure du cerveau et le vieillissement de la perception de la parole dans le bruit, et d'investiguer comment cette relation est moderee par la pratique du chant choral a l'aide de l'imagerie par resonance magnetique (IRM). Notre hypothese est que le vieillissement cerebral sera ralenti chez les chanteurs, ce qui sera associe a une meilleure perception de la parole dans le bruit. Les participants completeront une seance d'IRM, une evaluation cognitive et auditive, et une tache de discrimination de syllabes dans le bruit. Ce projet fournira de nouvelles informations sur les effets protecteurs du chant choral, une activite ayant le potentiel de favoriser un vieillissement positif.

column36: Multimorbidity and Polypharmacy in Canada: Examining Prevalence and Patterns in Primary Health Care Using a National Electronic Medical Record Database
column37: The accumulation of multiple chronic diseases (multimorbidity) and multiple prescribed medications (polypharmacy) over time may influence the extent to which an individual maintains health and well-being in later life. The sequence and timing of multimorbidity and polypharmacy could be important predictors of increasing treatment burden and decreasing quality of life for an aging population. In fact, reducing the burden of prescribed medications and the harms of polypharmacy are key tasks within the context of multimorbidity. The findings from this research can be used strategically to inform health care delivery and to build a more nuanced understanding of multimorbidity and polypharmacy in the international literature. This research aims to describe the patterns of multimorbidity and polypharmacy that accumulate over time in Canada. Further research is needed to establish the international evidence-base for multimorbidity and polypharmacy, in order to help inform the development of higher quality and more sustainable primary and community-based health care in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Assessing the effects of an arts-based HIV/AIDS education workshop for Indigenous youth
column37: Arts-based strategies have become increasingly popular for HIV prevention and education with Indigenous youth; however, there is a dearth of research on their implementation and effectiveness. The aim of this study was to evaluate Indigenous youths' HIV/AIDS knowledge and attitude change after participation in an arts-based HIV/AIDS education workshop. Eleven self-identifying Indigenous youth, ages eleven to seventeen, attended a 3.5-day participatory filmmaking workshop hosted as part of a community-based study examining the use of the arts in HIV prevention with Indigenous youth in Labrador. Participatory filmmaking was used to engage participants and facilitate dialogue about HIV/AIDS, sexual health, and health in general. A mixed methods design was used to assess knowledge and attitude change. Participants completed pre and post-test survey before and after the workshop. Approximately two weeks later, youth participated in in-depth interviews about their experiences. Using content analysis, interview transcripts were analyzed for themes related to HIV/AIDS knowledge and attitude change. Participants' knowledge and attitudes about HIV/AIDS improved after the workshop. HIV/AIDS knowledge and attitudes scores improved by 21.7% (Mean difference (M) = 3.9; 95% CI 2.8- 5.0) and by 18% (M = 1.8; CI 95% 0.7-2.9) respectively. Analysis of the interview transcripts revealed that participants: 1) learned what HIV is; 2) learned how HIV is transmitted; 3) learned about stigma; 4) operationalized new knowledge; 5) learned about boundaries/healthy relationships; and 6) attributed their knowledge and attitude change to the environment created through participatory filmmaking. These findings suggest participatory filmmaking is a promising strategy for HIV/AIDS education with Indigenous youth. Improving HIV/AIDS knowledge and attitudes among Indigenous youth is an essential component of addressing the overrepresentation of Indigenous youth in the HIV/AIDS pandemic in Canada.

column36: Identification of key factors mediating the tumor suppressor properties of the RAS/MAPK pathway during the commitment of cells towards cellular senescence
column37: Cellular senescence is a powerful intrinsic anti-cancer mechanism characterized by a stable cell proliferation arrest. As a result, several pharmaceutical companies and laboratories are working on anti-cancer therapies following this idea. Therefore, elucidation of the processes regulating the onset and maintenance of senescence will help to identify pro-senescence therapies for cancer. In the Ferbeyre laboratory, we aim to identify key factors specifically regulated by the RAS/MAPK pathway, that mediate the commitment of cells towards cellular senescence. Importantly, it is well known that 30% of all human cancers have an activating mutation in the RAS oncogene, which leads to an increased proliferation rate. However, it is also known that, through an unknown mechanism, a sustained hyper-activation of this same pathway leads to an antagonistic phenotype, which is, cellular senescence. This cellular fate characterizes benign lesions, and progression into a malignant tumor is associated to the bypass of this intrinsic anti-cancer program. Recent results obtained in our lab allowed us to define a time window of activation of the RAS/MAPK pathway leading to a "pre-senescence" state where cells are negative for classic senescence markers at this moment, but committed towards cellular senescence within seven days. Our working hypothesis is that hyperactivation of RAS/MAPK pathway leads to important transcriptional changes occurring during this precise short time window, and that it is these changes that are crucial to compromise cells towards cellular senescence. We are confident that our research will not only lead to identification of novel senescence biomarkers, but also to identification of senescence drivers. This will ultimately allow the design of novel therapeutic strategies aiming to promote and maintain the senescent state and inhibit progression of RAS-mutated cancers, in order to eliminate these senescent cells afterwards via the use of senolytic drugs.

column36: Chronic postsurgical pain in children: A prospective observational study to examine the transition from acute to chronic pain after major surgery
column37: Chronic Postsurgical Pain (CPSP) is an adverse effect of surgery defined as pain that persists for at least three months after surgery. CPSP is associated with longer recovery, disruptions in normal childhood development, and increased health care costs. Chronic pain disproportionately affects more females than males. While there is extensive literature on the transition from acute to chronic post-surgical pain in adults, the transition in children is far less studied. The aims of this study were to follow a group of 265 children undergoing major surgery at four time points (pre-surgical, in-hospital, 6- and 12-months after surgery) in order to: (1) examine the incidence of CPSP in children 6- and 12- months after surgery; (2) identify pain intensity and pain unpleasantness trajectories beginning before and through to 12 months after surgery; (3) identify pre-operative factors that predict group trajectory membership; and (4) identify factors that predict disability at 12-months. To accomplish these aims, children and parents completed questionnaires at each time point. The results of this study showed that 35% and 38% of children reported moderate-to-severe CPSP at 6- and 12-months, respectively. Analyses revealed that a two-class trajectory model with a quadratic slope best fitting the data for both pain intensity and pain unpleasantness over the course of 12-months. Significant predictors of pain intensity trajectories included functional disability and sex. Significant predictors of pain unpleasantness trajectories included functional disability. Preoperative functional disability and pain unpleasantness trajectories predicted 12-month moderate-to-severe functional disability. In conclusion, the results from this study raise the possibility that "prehabilitation" interventions administered in advance of surgery, which address functional disability and pain-related psychological factors, may minimize functional disability in the long-term.

column36: Assessing gaps in comprehensive HIV and women's health care across a typology of care for women living with HIV in Canada.
column37: Despite universal healthcare, women living with HIV in Canada experience barriers to comprehensive care. Strengthening clinical management beyond antiretroviral treatment requires an understanding of care gaps and care delivery. This study sought to answer the questions: 1) what care gaps occur for women living with HIV; and 2) do care gaps vary depending on where (clinics) and from whom (specialist of family doctors) women access care. We analysed data from the Canadian HIV Women's Sexual and Reproductive Health Cohort Study (n=1422). Women with HIV aged >=16 years, and residing in British Columbia, Ontario or Quebec participated from 2013-2015. Women currently accessing HIV-care (n=1242) were asked about components of women's care (pap test, pap test discussions, mammography, and reproductive discussions) and HIV-care (antiretroviral use, adherence, viral load, and viral load discussions). We defined comprehensive care as pap test, mammography, reproductive discussion, and HIV viral load. Overall, 62.3% women experienced at least one gap in care, the most common being reproductive discussions 65.3%, followed by mammography 38.7%, pap test 29.3%, and detectable viral loads 19.0%. Across the typology of care women accessed care from HIV-clinicians in HIV-clinics (70.9%), specialists in non-HIV clinics (17.6%), and family doctors in non-HIV clinics (11.4%). Women accessing care from family doctors in non-HIV clinics had nearly double the odds of not being currently on ART. Women accessing care from specialist in non-HIV clinics had 1.6 times higher odds of not having discussed the importance of regular Pap Tests, while having lower odds of having a detectable viral load. There were no observed differences in comprehensive care gaps across the typology of care. The majority of women in our study continue to experience gaps in care, irrespective of care type, indicating the need for models of care that address both HIV and women's health in a chronic disease era.

column36: Arterial Compliance is Improved Following a Community-led 12-week Indigenous Wholistic Health and Wellness Program
column37: PURPOSE: Indigenous peoples are at a higher risk for many chronic diseases compared to the general population. Colonization and forced assimilation have led to marked changes in traditional roles and healthy lifestyle behaviors. The purpose of this study was to examine vascular health (arterial compliance) prior to and following an Indigenous-led, and community-based 12-week lifestyle program representing Indigenous views of wholistic health and wellness. METHODS: Indigenous adults were recruited to participate in a healthy lifestyle program through a community walk on National Indigenous Peoples Day (21/06/2018) in an Indigenous community. The program was a once weekly education session on healthy lifestyle behaviours (e.g., traditional diet), including sharing circles and a physical activity component (e.g., walk). Vascular health was measured before and following the program. RESULTS: A total of 11 participants (1 male; Age = 47.310.7 yr, Height = 161.16.4 cm, and Weight = 82.318.3 kg) completed vascular health assessments. Vascular health (artery stiffness) was improved over the program duration. There were no significant changes in blood pressure or vascular resistance following the program. CONCLUSIONS: Artery stiffness, an important predictor of vascular health, is improved in Indigenous adults living in rural British Columbia following a 12-week program based on Indigenous worldviews. This data demonstrates health-related benefit of culturally appropriate programs.

column36: Brain activation during real-time walking post-stroke: systematic review
column37: With the advance of technology, the ability to record brain activity while an individual completes large movements, such as walking, has become increasingly achievable. Recent systematic reviews on this topic (Hamacher et al 2015; Vitorio et al 2017) non-specifically grouped neurological populations together. As neurostimulation and individualized interventions are receiving increasing attention to improve walking in the post-stroke population, it is important to identify areas of activation during walking specific to the post-stroke brain. METHODS: Two independent reviewers assessed search results from 6 databases and relevant references. Search categories included terms for stroke, ambulation/stepping, brain activation, and specific techniques to record brain activity. Studies that did not measure or report activation during actual upright walking or stepping (e.g. simulated walking or seated stepping) were excluded. RESULTS: From the 937 papers identified, 12 studies were included for review. Real-time walking tasks varied: initiation of walking or stepping, overground walking, treadmill walking, body weight-supported walking, or robotic-assisted walking. The majority of fNIRS studies did not utilize techniques for precise localization of probes, nor account for individualized brain anatomy, or task-related systemic changes. Further, recordings were often over a limited area, and were not compared to an age-matched healthy group. Significant heterogeneity in task and analysis techniques also resulted in varied findings showing increases, decreases, or no difference between activation areas, tasks, or groups. CONCLUSIONS: While the ability to record brain activity during walking has become increasingly feasible, numerous limitations hinder the interpretation of current results. Although some patterns are beginning to emerge, future work would benefit from more rigorous methods suggested within this presentation.

column36: Investigating the impact of aging dermal stem/progenitor cells on tissue regeneration and wound healing
column37: Each year, 14 million people suffer severe skin injuries including burns, trauma, or chronic wounds in North America - resulting in permanent disfigurement, chronic disability, intractable pain, and fatal infections. The estimated annual cost of wound care in Canada is $3.9 billion and is expected to rise due to our aging population, as the elderly have a significantly higher prevalence of skin disease. It is estimated that one-third of individuals over the age of 65 are afflicted with a skin disorder worthy of medical attention. Hence, innovative treatments designed to prevent age-related skin dysfunction and enhance dermal regeneration is of utmost importance. Fittingly, our lab has identified two stem cell populations residing within the dermis - which hold natural abilities to regenerate components of the hair follicle and generate new cells in the dermis after injury. These stem cells hold immense potential to be employed for skin regeneration and improving dermal function in aged tissue. My project takes three unique approaches to investigate how the dermal stem cell populations are impacted by advanced age. 1) Utilize high-resolution imaging techniques on the skin from young and old transgenic mice to determine how aging affects stem cell function and identify drug-targetable signaling pathways to reverse these dysfunctions. 2) Employ cutting-edge single-cell gene expression analysis to understand how advanced age impacts dermal progenitor response to injury. 3) Study a mouse model of premature aging to understand how DNA damage contributes to stem cell dysfunction. My goal is to understand how dermal stem cell populations are affected by advanced age, to devise strategies for activating or rejuvenating these cells to promote tissue regeneration and improved skin wound healing in the elderly.

column36: Research Overview: Social Determinants of Women's Health
column37: My research examines the social issues that influence women's health globally and contributes to evidence-based policy making by quantitatively evaluating the effectiveness of policies aimed at improving women's health. My current work focuses primarily on two issues: child marriage and female genital cutting. Child marriage, defined by the United Nations as marriage before the age of 18, is associated with poor reproductive and mental health. Most research on child marriage has been conducted in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, but my work examines the health consequences of child marriage in wealthy countries, including Canada. My work also examines the effectiveness of laws that prohibit child marriage and the unintended consequences such policies may have for the health of girls who marry and their children. Female genital cutting (FGC) refers to a wide range of procedures that involve injury to the genitalia for non-medical reasons. Severe forms of cutting are associated with increased risks during childbirth and may have lifelong implications for sexual wellbeing. Global efforts to curb this practice have resulted in laws that make it a crime to perform FGC in many countries. However, these laws appear to have had little impact on the number of women who experience it. I am conducting research to better understand why some communities persist in this practice and whether driving the practice underground increases the health risks for girls. A common theme of my research is to include policies that affect women's and girls' health in wealthy countries, including Canada, under the umbrella of global health. Wealthy countries are often not considered in global health research but failure to critically examine how their policies align with international development goals may lead to the perpetuation of harms. Throughout my research, I stress that an inclusive definition of global health is a necessary component of Canada's strong leadership in this realm.

column36: Neurological Outcome of Glycemia in Neonatal Encephalopathy
column37: Newborn brain injury is one of the most significant causes of neurological and developmental problems in Canadian children. Inadequate blood and oxygen delivery are the most common causes for newborn brain injury. Although cooling therapy helps some babies, there continues to be high rates of death and major disabilities in many of these children. Using continuous monitoring of sugar levels, we have made the shocking new discovery that more than half of newborns who have suffered from brain injury from lack of blood or oxygen will have excessively high blood sugar levels in the first few days of life. While we were expecting to find low sugars associated with brain injury, we were surprised to find that high sugars, and not low sugars, corresponded with worse brain function and worse brain injury in the nursery, with concerning outcomes in movement, cognition, language, and behavior when the children were 18 months old. To properly target sugar management in these newborns, we need to better understand how high blood sugars may impact long-term outcomes. The objective of this proposed study is to correlate high blood sugar levels with bad long-term vision, cognitive, language, social, and behavioural outcomes in newborns who have suffered from brain injury from lack of oxygen. Our first aim will be to correlate high blood sugar levels in the early newborn period with brain-related vision processing outcomes by early school age. The second aim will be to correlate high blood sugar in the early newborn period with cognitive, language, social, and behavioural outcomes by early school age. Clarifying the relationships between specific levels of high and low blood sugar on long-term outcomes will help to guide targeted blood sugar management in these acutely ill newborns, as well as to identify which babies are in urgent need for additional treatment strategies to decrease brain injury and improve long-term outcomes after newborn brain injury.

column36: Gait Instability, Fall History, Sex, and Neuropsychiatric Symptoms are associated with Falls in People with Dementia
column37: Dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with cognitive and motor symptoms. Among the activities of daily living of people with dementia, gait is of high concern as gait impairments are associated with increased risk of falls. Previous studies have mainly quantified spatiotemporal gait variables in people with dementia. However, impairment in spatiotemporal measures could reflect cautious gait arising from a fear of falling in this population and not the cause of falls. Many of these studies assess gait in a laboratory environment or at a single time point and may not reflect gait in a natural environment. The aim of the present study was therefore to investigate the relationship between gait features extracted from naturalistic vision-based gait assessments to future falls in older people with dementia. 52 people with dementia admitted to this study. The following information and tests were gathered upon enrollment to the study: demographic data, admission neuropsychiatric inventory score (NPI), history of falls, severe impairment battery-short version (SIBS), Tinetti performance oriented mobility assessment (POMA) for balance and gait, and the Katz index of independence in activities of daily living (KATZ). Fall incidents during the inpatient admission were recorded from the medical chart. Thirty measures of gait in five categories were calculated namely, spatiotemporal, variability, symmetry, stability and frequency domain measures. column36: Anti-Inflammatory Effects of Long-Acting Beta Agonists on Bronchial Epithelium
column37: Chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) is a respiratory illness and one of the leading causes of death worldwide. It is heavily correlated with smoking and other inhaled irritants. Patients who suffer from COPD experience a variety of symptoms including breathlessness, increased mucus production, chronic airway inflammation and emphysema. There is no cure for COPD, and current treatments focus on controlling symptoms and improving patients' quality of life. One such treatment is the use of long-acting beta agonists (LABA), a type of bronchodilator. LABAs can be taken once or twice daily and function by relaxing the airway smooth muscle in order to increase airflow to the lungs. These medications may also decrease inflammation by lowering mucus production and neutrophil (a type of white blood cell) count in the lungs, but this effect has not been well-studied. However, this is notable as a large portion of the irreversible damage seen in COPD patient lungs occurs due to chronic inflammation mediated by the immune system in response to inhaled irritants. Investigation of the anti-inflammatory effect of LABAs may therefore be a promising direction leading to new treatments to combat airway destruction. The goal of my project is therefore to characterize the pathway by which LABAs decrease inflammation using human tissue culture as my model system. Rather than cigarette smoke, I will use respiratory syncytial virus and lipopolysaccharide as the irritant to produce an inflammatory effect. Through this project, I aim to better understand how the inflammatory pathway is affected by the use of LABAs and furthermore, to pinpoint specific proteins as potential new drug targets for more targeted treatment of inflammation in COPD patients.

column36: Sex-independent and sex-dependent effects of older age on motor input variability during preferred-speed gait
column37: Introduction: The variability of movements during walking is linked to fall risk in aging males and females. Currently, the source of this variability is unclear. One potential source is the variability of the muscle patterns, as these muscle patterns produce the movements involved in walking. However, the influences of older age and sex on the variability of muscle patterns during walking is unknown; this information could help understand how falls occur in aging males and females. Methods: Males and females aged 20 to 82 years walked over a platform at their preferred speed. These participants wore electrical sensors over several lower limb muscles to measure their muscle patterns. The variabilities of these patterns, from stride-to-stride, were calculated; these muscle pattern variabilities were then analyzed using statistical models to test how they were influenced by older age and sex. Results: Older age was generally associated with higher muscle pattern variability in males and females, except for the single leg support phase of walking. During this phase, older age was associated with lower muscle pattern variability in females only. Conclusions: There were both sex-independent and sex-dependent influences of older age on the variability of muscle patterns. The sex-dependent influence points towards less flexibility in how aging females, when compared to males, stabilize their ankle during the single leg support phase of walking. This may help explain the sex difference in fall risk of aging adults.
