column36: "Weaving Our Wisdoms": Using a Land-Based Approach to Optimize Whole-istic Health Among Indigenous People Living with HIV
column37: Background: Indigenous land-based approaches to wellness are gaining attention and are increasingly used as wellness interventions with Indigenous People living with HIV/AIDS (IPHAs). The role of IPHAs in developing these wellness interventions, however, has received little attention. The Weaving Our Wisdoms (WoW) project, designed by IPHAs, Indigenous and allied researchers, is developing land-based interventions rooted in Indigenous perspectives of wellness and guided by the wisdom of Indigenous knowledge holders who have been living long-term with HIV. In this presentation, we introduce the concept of HIV Olders, a phrase coined by WoW project IPHAs to refer to IPHA leaders, and outline the characteristics of an HIV Older. Study Design and Objectives: The WoW project engages four complementary research approaches: community-based research, Indigenous knowledge, decolonizing methods, and two-eyed seeing. Our objective is to develop land-based HIV interventions that are "woven" from Indigenous perspectives of wholistic wellness and the wisdom of HIV Olders. The team's goal is to develop these interventions to support IPHAs in building their leadership and self-care. Preliminary Results: A land-based team meeting in Bella Bella, BC explored the concept of HIV Olders and land-based healing. Discussions were recorded and combined with field notes to identify key themes including the qualities of an HIV Older, the value of peer-to-peer engagement in the IPHA context and ways that traditional knowledge and ceremony can optimize HIV wellness. This presentation will share these findings and introduce our next phase of research; a Gathering of IPHAs to co-develop a strategy to integrate land-based healing with HIV wellness. Conclusion: HIV Olders is a living concept; one that will grow alongside our understanding of HIV, the resources available to support wellness living with HIV, and the reconnection to teachings about wellness through the land and through culture.

column36: Exposure to fast food vs other restaurant types in relation to the development of diabetes and hypertension: a population-based retrospective cohort study
column37: BACKGROUND: The types and density of different stores and restaurants located near where people live can shape residents' food choices and subsequent risk of obesity and other chronic diseases, like diabetes and hypertension. OBJECTIVE: We investigated whether residents living in areas with a high proportion of fast-food restaurants relative to total restaurants are more likely to develop diabetes or hypertension, and whether this risk varies by volume (i.e. number) of fast-food restaurants. METHODS: We performed a population-based, retrospective cohort study in 2,940,804 adults aged 20+ who lived within walking distance (800 m) of at least one restaurant in one of five urban regions of southern Ontario. Administrative health databases were used to follow individuals from 2003 to 2013 for the development of diabetes and hypertension. RESULTS: Among younger adults (aged 20-49, 1,939,825 people in the diabetes sample and 1,830,873 people in the hypertension sample), living near more restaurants of any type was associated with slightly lower risk of developing diabetes and hypertension. However, living near a greater proportion of fast-food outlets relative to all restaurants increased the risk of both outcomes, particularly in areas with high volumes (5+) of fast-food restaurants. For both the development of diabetes and hypertension, weaker associations with fast-food exposures were observed for adults aged 50-64, and few significant associations were seen for adults aged 65+. CONCLUSIONS: Areas with the double burden of high volume of fast-food outlets and few restaurant alternatives may represent an adverse environment for the development of diabetes and hypertension, particularly among younger adults. Health promoting policies that merely target the volume of fast-food restaurants may be ineffective without also considering the overall balance of more and less healthful food retailers.

column36: How nurses respond to social iniquities in health through health equity nursing practices
column37: In Canada like elsewhere, social inequalities in health are threatening population health. Given this situation, what are the practices of nurses working in community health to ensure greater health equity? My doctoral research project combined oral history (12 interviews) and collaborative ethnography (420 hours in the field) with the nurses of the Pointe-Saint-Charles Community Clinic. 21 nurses and 11 ex-nurses from the Clinic participated in this research, from 2016 to 2018. Results highlight the contribution of personal (reciprocal relationship and therapeutic use of the self) and aesthetics (intuitions induced by experience) knowledge to the development of health equity practices. When confronted to people's living conditions and through exchanges with citizens, nurses open their scope of evaluation to include problems in the social and physical environment, as well as a consideration for people's life paths. They also shift the paradigm of intervention, from a controlled and predictable process of care to one that deals with unpredictability, while making themselves available in time, place and approach. Nurses then craft generic nursing interventions learned in school to adapt people's reality. Because the bureaucratic health care system fails to answer urgent needs of people living at disadvantage, nurses will often take immediate actions to alleviate scarcity of material resources and advocate for access to healthcare. At a collective level, nurses also initiate actions on social determinants of health. Through this presentation, I intend to restore the place of nursing knowledge historically undervalued within the nursing profession. Submerge in a liberal system of care, acting according to values of equity, inclusion, non-judgement and respect for the right to self-determination represents a political stance of nurses in favor of social justice.

column36: Rapid activation of cell signaling cascades by 17beta-estradiol in the dentate gyrus of adult rats
column37: Estrogens typically act on cells through interactions with genes, a process which takes hours to days. However, more rapid actions have been identified and occur through activation of chemical signals (cell signaling cascades) within cells. The dentate gyrus, a region within the hippocampus, experiences a increase in cell proliferation (the creation of new cells) within 30 minutes of giving the estrogen 17beta-estradiol (E2) to female rats. Whether this is a result of cell signaling cascade activation and, if so, which cascades are involved remains unknown. In this experiment, we gave E2 to male and female rats and female rats with their ovaries removed. Thirty minutes later, these rats were sacrificed and their brains collected for protein analysis. Using a multiplex electrochemiluminescent reader, we measured levels of phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated protein kinase (ERK), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), p38, Akt, glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK-3beta), and ribosomal protein S6 kinase (p70S6K) cell signaling proteins in the dentate gyrus. In this way, we can determine what pathways are rapidly activated by E2 and may be involved in the rapid effects of E2 on cell proliferation.

column36: Comparative Assessment of Central and Peripheral Chemoreceptor Reflex Regulation of Muscle Sympathetic Nerve Activity and Ventilation
column37: In humans, blood oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) levels are maintained at normal biological levels by specialized O2 and CO2 sensors in the blood vessels and brain. These sensors cause people to breathe more if blood O2 is low or blood and brain carbon dioxide is high. This hyperventilation (known as the ventilatory "chemoreflex") then brings O2 or CO2 back to normal. These sensors also connect to brain areas controlling the release into the bloodstream of noradrenaline; a chemical that increases heart rate and constricts blood vessels. It has been assumed, without clear evidence, that humans who breathe more vigorously if blood O2 is low or blood and brain CO2 is high also release larger amounts of noradrenaline from noradrenaline-releasing (sympathetic) nerves. This assumption is important to test because high ventilatory chemoreflex responses are now recognized as key to chronic conditions where low blood O2, high blood and brain CO2 and high activity of noradrenaline releasing nerves are common; such as heart and lung disease and breathing disorders that occur during sleep. In fact, in some parts of the world, patients may be recommended for procedures that target these O2 and CO2 sensors with the specific intent of reducing noradrenaline release based completely on breathing responsiveness! We believe therapies of this nature are premature. My study measured at the same time, the breathing and sympathetic nerve firing rates of healthy men in response low blood O2 and high blood and brain CO2. We found that vigorous breathing responses to low blood O2 or high blood and brain CO2 did not predict elevated sympathetic nerve firing responsiveness. Having established this "normal healthy response", we now are investigating whether this finding occurs also in individuals with heart failure or sleep breathing disorders. Our results should temper enthusiasm of studies and clinical trials targeting chemoreflex sensors based on breathing responses alone.

column36: Exploring how pathoadaptations commonly observed in chronic Pseudomonas isolates modulate host-microbe interactions in the Cystic Fibrosis airway epithelium
column37: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an inherited life-limiting disease affecting approximately 4,000 Canadians. The mortality observed in CF patients is predominantly due to recurrent bacterial infections and chronic inflammation, which eventually cause respiratory failure. Our lab's research is focused on the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA), an opportunistic pathogen that responds poorly to antibiotic treatments and has been linked to accelerated disease progression in CF. While PA is traditionally considered to be an extracellular pathogen, our lab has found evidence of intracellular PA in CF patient lung samples, indicating that PA might persist intracellularly. An intracellular reservoir might offer a growth advantage to bacteria, as they would be less succeptible to antibiotic treatments and clearance through the host immune system. In this project, we examine which bacterial factors promote an intracellular PA lifestyle by infecting immortalized airway cells with PA strains deficient in certain bacterial factors and identifying which strains are particularly persistant intracellularly. Preliminary results suggest that strains that are deficient in factors that are commonly lost in chronic PA isolates increase internalization of PA into airway cells as well as PA persistence. In conclusion, our findings suggest that typically "chronic" PA adaptations promote an intracellular lifestyle. This might be a possible explanation for why some PA strains are particularly persistent and eventually develop chronic infections. Targeting these "chronic" PA factors might decrease PA persistence and increase antibiotic eradication therapy efficacy, potentially leading to decreased mortality in CF patients.

column36: Prediction de cibles canoniques et non-canoniques de snoRNA par apprentissage automatise
column37: Les petits ARN nucleolaires (snoRNA) sont de petites molecules qui interagissent avec des proteines specifiques afin d'accomplir une fonction bien caracterisee, appelee canonique, qui est de guider la modification chimique de l'ARN ribosomique. Pour ce faire, une region bien precise du snoRNA reconnait la cible d'ARN, la rapproche des proteines, leur permettant d'executer leur fonction. Dernierement, de nouvelles fonctions ont ete decouvertes pour les snoRNA, impliquant d'autres proteines, et d'autres regions du snoRNA servent de guide. Celles-ci sont importantes a caracteriser puisque bien des evidences indiquent qu'elles sont impliquees dans le syndrome de Prader-Willi, le cancer et le diabete. Nous nous interessons a leur implication dans le cancer de l'ovaire. Nos resultats preliminaires indiquent un changement important d'abondance pour plusieurs snoRNA dans ce cancer. Mon projet consiste a recueillir toutes les cibles connues de snoRNA, canoniques et non-canoniques, afin de creer un predicteur de cibles de snoRNA par apprentissage automatise, ce qui permettra de mieux comprendre les consequences du changement d'abondance des snoRNA dans le cancer de l'ovaire. Un ordinateur sera entraine a reconnaitre les cibles validees et a discrediter les controles negatifs qui lui seront presentes. Le modele utilise sera un reseau de neurones artificiels qui apprend de la meme maniere que nous, c'est-a-dire en reconnaissant certaines caracteristiques qui discriminent entre deux categories et en leur accordant un poids different. Une fois cet outil complete, de nouvelles sequences lui seront fournies afin qu'il puisse identifier de nouvelles cibles, semblables a celles avec lesquelles il a ete entraine. Ainsi, nous pourrons predire les cibles les plus probables des snoRNA deregules dans le cancer de l'ovaire, ce qui permettra de les valider et de les caracteriser avec des outils de biologie moleculaire, et ultimement de mieux comprendre leur implication dans cette maladie.

column36: Hypogammaglobulinemia as a predictor of hospitalizations in COPD: a meta-analysis
column37: Patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) are prone to developing acute exacerbations (AECOPD), defined as periods of severe shortness of breath. AECOPDs often lead to hospitalizations and the economic burden of these hospitalizations on the Canadian healthcare system is approximately $1 billion per year. AECOPD are mostly driven by lung infections and preventing these infections can reduce the frequency of these events. Immunoglobulins (Ig), also known as antibodies, are an important part of the immune system. The main class of immunoglobulins in the human body is IgG, making up 75% of all antibodies in the blood. We hypothesized that COPD patients with lower levels of IgG in their bodies cannot fight off infections properly, leading to increased risk of AECOPDs and COPD hospitalizations. To test this hypothesis, we measured blood IgG levels in 2,267 COPD subjects who were previously enrolled in four studies. We observed that low IgG levels are relatively common among COPD subjects, affecting approximately 1 in 4 patients. Importantly, we found that the risk of COPD hospitalizations was 41% higher in those with decreased IgG levels compared to those with normal IgG levels. Our data support that COPD subjects with lower IgG levels are at increased risk of hospitalizations. By examining blood IgG levels, which can be measured in a quick and cheap laboratory test, clinicians may be able to identify high-risk COPD patients for escalation of treatment and closer clinical monitoring. These measures may prevent AECOPDs and hospitalizations, thereby alleviating an enormous health burden to patients as well as considerable health care costs.

column36: Effects of syncytiotrophoblast extracellular vesicles on angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction in uterine arteries from lectin-like oxidized LDL receptor-1 overexpressing mice
column37: Preeclampsia (PE) is a vascular complication of pregnancy that is a leading cause of maternal disease and death worldwide. It is one of the most common reasons for induced preterm delivery. PE is diagnosed by the development of high blood pressure and kidney damage after the 20th week of gestation. Both the cause and course of the disease remain poorly understood and delivery of the placenta and fetus is currently the only known cure for PE. Nonetheless, there is substantial evidence that reduced blood vessel function contributes to the development of high blood pressure in the disease. It is believed that this might be due to small (toxic) particles that are released from the placenta into the mother's bloodstream. This could affect the function of the mother's blood vessels and contribute to the development of high blood pressure later in her pregnancy. However, the specific cause(s) and process(es) are not completely understood. The research in this abstract focuses on how the placental particles released from the placenta can affect the function of blood vessels. Our lab recently made the exciting discovery of a new pathway involving a receptor called LOX-1 that disrupts the normal function of blood vessels in women with PE. We used uterine arteries from mice and incubated them with the placental particles to measure the blood vessel function afterwards. We observed that the placental particles can help with the adaptations that blood vessels normally make during pregnancy to support normal development of the fetus. We also showed that the specific pathway via LOX-1 indeed appeared to be activated by the placental particles. This study further determined the role of the LOX-1 pathway and the role the placental particles play in this in the development of reduced blood vessel function in PE. This increased our understanding of the development of PE during pregnancy in order to develop new therapeutic strategies to treat this disorder in the future.

column36: The effect of a novel presenilin 1 mutation on Alzheimer's Disease pathogenesis
column37: Amyloid plaque is a hallmark of Alzheimer's Disease (AD) neuropathology and the amyloid beta protein (Abeta) is the central component of the plaques. Abeta is derived from APP protein through sequential cleavages by beta-secretase and gamma-secretase. The pathogenic mutations in the presenilin-1 (PS1) gene are the major cause of familial AD (FAD). PS1 is the core component of gamma-secretase to cleave APP and Notch. Notch plays a fundamental role in neurodevelopment. One of the major reasons of the failed AD clinical trials on gamma-secretase inhibitors is that those inhibitors cause abnormalities in gastrointestinal tract, thymus, spleen and skin due to their inhibition of Notch cleavage. We identified a novel FAD-causing PS1 mutation that has differential effects on APP and Notch cleavage. This proposal seeks to investigate how this PS1 mutation selectively regulates APP without affecting Notch cleavage, and to define the mechanism underlying the PS1's role in AD pathogenesis. The study highlights a possibility of developing novel specific gamma-secretase modulators as drugs that inhibit Abeta generation but may maintain normal Notch signaling for AD treatment.

column36: Sex and gender differences in polypharmacy in persons with dementia: a scoping review
column37: Purpose: To date, research studies in most disciplines have not made sex-based analysis a priority despite increasing evidence of its importance. We now understand that both sex and gender impact medication prescribing, use, and effect. This is particularly true for older adults with dementia who have alterations in; drug metabolism, drug response, and the permeability of the blood brain barrier. To better understand the influence of sex and gender on drug use in older adults with dementia we conducted a scoping review. Methods: This scoping review systematically searched the Medline, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL and Proquest databases to find published reports on polypharmacy in populations of older adults with dementia that included a sex- or gender-based analysis. Results: Twelve published reports were identified. Findings were predominantly cohort studies and case control trials that commented on sex-related differences in medication use as a secondary analysis to the studies' primary objective. These studies showed that community dwelling women received more potentially inappropriate medications (PIM) and more psychotropic medications, while nursing home dwelling men received more PIM, cholinesterase inhibitors and antipsychotics. None of the identified studies explicitly examined gender-related differences in medication use. Conclusions: This scoping review supports that there is inadequate understanding of both sex and gender differences in drug use in older men and women with dementia. To tailor medication specific interventions to improve drug therapy for older adults with dementia it is important that future work includes sex- or gender-based analysis of drug use.

column36: Effect of treatment of the placenta with a mitochondrial targeted antioxidant (nMitoQ) on later-life cardiac function in adult offspring exposed to prenatal hypoxia
column37: Low oxygen delivery from the mother to the fetus due to placental dysfunction is a common consequence of complicated pregnancies. It leads to abnormal fetal heart development and heart dysfunction in the offspring born from complicated pregnancies. Our laboratory demonstrated that hearts from offspring of complicated pregnancies, using a rat model of prenatal low oxygen, are unable to work properly due to changes in heart structure. We showed that those hearts experience lower recovery after an insult. Many interventions have been studied to improve oxygen delivery to the fetus, but the main problem when treating pregnant women is the ability of therapeutic agents to cross the placental barrier and directly affect the fetus, with potential toxic side-effects. Our laboratory has been testing early interventions based on treating the mother during her complicated pregnancy by treating the placenta. We have developed a therapeutic drug attached to specific nanoparticles (nMitoQ). By being attached to the nanoparticles the drug does not cross the placental barrier and treats the placenta without any exposure of the fetus. Recent studies from our laboratory showed a positive effect of nMitoQ treatment on blood vessel function in offspring from complicated pregnancies. However, the effect of nMitoQ treatment on offspring`s heart function is unknown. In this study we used hearts from adult offspring born from control pregnancies and pregnancies complicated with low oxygen delivery to the fetus and performed molecular analyses to test the heart structure. The heart function was evaluated via accessing the recovery rate after subjecting the hearts to an insult. We found that nMitoQ treatment did not affect the structure of the heart of offspring born from complicated pregnancies, but improved the heart function. This study demonstrates that nMitoQ provides a potential therapeutic strategy to improve heart function later in life of offspring born from complicated pregnancies.

column36: Will that work here? Advancing evidence-informed decision-making in work disability prevention policy, practice and research efforts.
column37: Physical and mental health conditions dominate as the leading causes of work disability worldwide. Over the last decade, systematic reviews have synthesized the best research evidence across more than 150 studies to learn what we can do to support return-to-work (RTW), improve recovery and reduce productivity losses. Despite this evidence, workplaces face challenges in implementing these strategies. Canadian workplaces face many challenges, including: distinct industry sectors, a high prevalence of remote and small workplaces, and an aging and increasingly precariously-employed workforce. Many provinces also have high rates of disability and unemployment and declining labour forces. Successful RTW is critical to minimizing unemployment while maximizing the capacities of the dwindling labour force across these jurisdictions. Using an illustrative example on supporting workers with physical and mental health conditions in RTW, this project outlines a novel synthesis approach that links evidence to practice. Applying a model for evidence-informed decision support, we draw on the best research evidence and integrate it with contextual evidence from practitioner expertise and stakeholder experiences to answer the questions: what works?, will it work here? and, can we implement it in practice? Findings from three projects will document our experience applying this decision support model to help workers with physical and mental health conditions in RTW. Results highlight the effectiveness of this model in bridging research-to-practice knowledge gaps. This synthesis approach demonstrates a practical way to enhance the use of current knowledge tailored to the context of specific industries and workplaces. The model's primary strength lies in the use of three sources of evidence: research findings, practitioner expertise and stakeholder experience. The full integration of these sources of evidence enhances the opportunity for optimal work disability prevention efforts.

column36: Clinical Impact of Oncomine Myeloid Targeted DNA Sequencing Assay for Patients with Hematological Disorders
column37: In recent years, the significance of genetic information in the diagnosis, screening, and treatment of myeloid (blood) cancers has become highly evident. The increasing impact of identifying genes associated with these cancers necessitates more comprehensive screening techniques. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a tool that permits the identification of many genes in one efficient test that can be applied for patients using blood or bone marrow. NGS works by assessing a patient's DNA (obtained from these blood or bone marrow samples) to determine whether there are any variations in the sequence (mutations) that may be contributing to their disease. Targeted NGS refers specifically to the assessment of a group of genes known to play a role in blood cancers. NGS allows the simultaneous assessment of many genes in a single, efficient, comprehensive test. The results of this test (showing whether there is variation in a patients' DNA) can inform clinicians about this patients' disease based on current research surrounding affected genes. This tool will not only complement current techniques but may in fact replace them. We performed sequencing of DNA from patient samples using the Thermo Fisher Ion Chef and Ion S5 sequencer. We analyzed the sequencing results and classified variants (changes in genes/DNA) into 1 of 3 tiers to determine their potential impact on patient care. To date, we have performed sequencing of 101 samples from 94 unique patients with a variety of myeloid cancers. Of the variants (abnormalities) detected, 63% were potentially actionable (impacted patient care). In the majority of patients, we were able to identify variants that may aid clinicians in achieving/clarifying diagnoses, inform follow-up/prognosis, and guide treatment decisions. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating NGS into clinical testing for patients with myeloid cancers.

column36: Effect of the selective MT1 receptor partial agonist UCM871 in the activity of noraphineprine neurons of the locus coeruleus during the sleep/wake cycle
column37: Melatonin is a neurohormone produced in the pineal gland which is involved in numerous physiological functions, including sleep regulation, via its receptors MT1 and MT2. The Locus Coeruleus (LC) nucleus contain critical wakefulness-promoting neurons which discharge at highest rates during wakefulness (W), and lower rates during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. However, the activity of melatonin MT1 receptor in the LC is poorly understood due to the lack of receptor-selective compounds. Here we investigate the role of the first selective MT1 receptor partial agonist UCM871 in the sleep-wake cycle, and the activity of the noradrenergic (NE) neurons in the LC over a 24-hour period. To assess the effects of UCM871 on the sleep-wake cycle, electroencephalograms (EEG) were recorded in free-moving rats for a period of 24 h, within which a subcutaneous injection of vehicle (veh) or UCM871 (7, 14 and 21 mg/kg) was administrated every 4 hours. To assess the localization and the distribution of MT1 receptors in LC-NE neurons, we used immunolabeling with receptor-specific antibodies. In-vivo single unit extracellular recordings of NE neurons were performed following the administration of veh or UCM871 (3.5, 7, 10 and 14 mg/kg, i.v.) to investigate role of the NE neurons of LC in sleep activity. Rats treated with UCM871 at 14 mg/kg s.c. exhibited an increase in the duration (min) of REM sleep (veh: 96.6; UCM871: 119.7, p<0.05) in light phase. Furthermore, immunolabeling showed a higher co-expression of MT1 receptors with NE neurons in dark and light phase. Finally, electrophysiology showed that LC-NE neurons' activity decreased in both phases with the administration of UCM871 at 10 and 14 mg/kg. Conclusion: MT1 receptors play an important role in REM sleep and in adrenergic function, but in a distinct manner. While MT1 activation in LC by UCM871 is pronounced in the dark phase, the effect in the REM sleep is higher during the light phase.

column36: Discovery of Novel Suppressors of HIV Transcription from African Natural Products
column37: Infection with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a global epidemic affecting thousands of Canadians and millions of people worldwide. Although current anti-retroviral therapies (ART) control HIV replication and prevent progression to AIDS, they do not eradicate the virus. Instead, HIV persists in latent reservoirs by integrating into the DNA of infected cells and "hiding" from treatment. If ART is suspended, the virus is free to re-emerge. One proposed strategy to treat latent virus, termed "Block-and-Lock", involves the use of pro-latency agents (PLAs) to durably suppress viral re-emergence from latency and provide drug-free remission. Recently, PLAs have been identified that can induce "Block-and-Lock" in human cells by interfering with viral proteins necessary for re-emergence. While encouraging, few PLAs have been described and none have advanced to human trials, indicating a likely need to find and characterize additional agents. Natural product compound libraries are rich sources of unique bioactive compounds. Recently, the Tietjen Lab screened the pan-African Natural Product Library in search of novel PLA candidates and identified a series of flavonoid compounds with antiviral activity. Flavonoids are a class of plant-derived compounds with thousands of structural derivatives, many of which exhibit anti-oxidant and anti-cancer properties. Some are known to feature anti-HIV activity as well; however, their ability to cause "Block-and-Lock" has not been investigated and their exact mechanisms are unclear. The flavonoids identified in this screen appear to act by interfering with Tat and/or Rev, key viral proteins necessary for the reactivation process. By using latently infected cell lines and primary cells from HIV+ donors, my research explores the PLA mechanisms of these natural compounds and their potential to safely induce "Block-and-Lock", with the aim of determining their suitability for future HIV cure and remission studies.

column36: Healthcare Utilization Associated with Chronic Opioid Use among Medical and Surgical Patients in the One-Year Hospital Post-Discharge Period: A Retrospective Cohort Study
column37: Prescription opioid use and overdose has steadily increased over the past two decades, resulting in a dramatic increase in opioid poisoning-related emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. The purpose of this study is to assess post-discharge opioid prescriptions and dispensations in medical and surgical patients, and to identify potential patterns of planned and unplanned health service use. Patients admitted to a tertiary care teaching hospital in Montreal (2014 - 2016) were part of a cohort randomized to the RightRx study which evaluated the impact of electronically enabled medication reconciliation software on adverse drug events. Patients were included if there were =>18 years at admission, not transferred from another hospital, having a continuous health insurance coverage (RAMQ), and discharged alive to the community. RAMQ health administrative claims were used to measure opioid dispensations in the 1-year prior to and post discharge, as well as hospital re-admissions and ED visits. Patient characteristics and discharge prescriptions were obtained from the hospital chart. Time-varying use of opioids after discharge will be modeled as: 1) current use, 2) continuous duration of use, and 3) cumulative duration of use. For the main analyses, marginal structural models will be used to model the association between use of opioids and risk of emergency department visits and hospitalizations. Inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights will be constructed to properly adjust for the time-fixed and time-varying confounders that may be unbalanced between the opioid and non-opioid users as well as to account for competing risk due to mortality. Reasons for the re-admissions will also be presented as part of the analyses. All analyses will be adjusted for a number of important covariates including patient comorbidities, medication history and healthcare system characteristics such as nurse-to-patient and attending physician-to-patient ratios.

column36: The effects of exercise and inflammation on musculoskeletal pain in individuals with a spinal cord injury.
column37: Musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is self-reported as the most common type of pain following a traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI). MSK pain places a substantial burden on both the individuals who suffer from it and the Canadian healthcare system as the current first line of treatment is pharmaceuticals which are an issue as they address the symptoms rather than the causes of MSK pain. Promising research has shown that exercise can reduce pain although the mechanism by which this occurs is not yet fully known. One proposed explanation is that exercise reduces inflammation which in turn reduces pain. Under normal circumstances, the inflammatory response is a healthy way for the body to be made aware of acute injurious stimuli and respond accordingly. However, in individuals with SCI, evidence suggests that nervous system impairments can lead to the dysregulation of both endocrine and immune function which can lead to chronic low-grade inflammation. This chronic low-grade inflammation has been linked to a variety of negative health problems. This study attempts to use exercise to reduce inflammation in people with SCI to reduce MSK pain. Participants will complete a single bout of exercise consisting of 30-minutes of upper body exercise in accordance with SCI-specific exercise guidelines. Blood samples will be taken to monitor the levels of inflammation in the blood and MSK will be assessed using a validated subjective measure. This study will allow us to better understand how exercise can reduce MSK in people with SCI and more specifically what role exercise plays in inflammation. Understanding this connection will allow clinicians, rehabilitation specialists, and other healthcare professionals to create better nonpharmaceutical interventions aimed to reduce inflammation and MSK in people with SCI.

column36: Association transversale entre la dose d'activite physique quotidienne et le niveau de PCR chez des adultes en sante et touches par l'arthrite ou la fibromyalgie: donnees de l'Enquete canadienne sur les mesures de la sante
column37: Les bienfaits de l'activite physique (AP) sur la diminution de l'inflammation est une thematique de recherche qui attire de plus en plus les professionnels de la sante. Le PCR, un biomarqueur de l'inflammation, est souvent utilise par les cliniciens afin de valider la presence d'inflammation chez des patients atteints d'arthrite et de fibromyalgie, des maladies chroniques. Parmi les comportements de sante qui peuvent diminuer la concentration plasmatique du PCR, l'AP et la sedentarite jouent un role respectivement positif et negatif. Malgre les benefices associes a l'AP sur la diminution du taux de PCR, elles ne permettent pas de savoir si cet effet est independant ou non de la sedentarite. Nous proposons d'examiner l'association entre la dose d'activite physique quotidienne mesuree par accelerometrie et le niveau PCR chez les adultes canadiens en sante et touches par l'arthrite et la fibromyalgie, deux maladies de type inflammatoire. Il s'agira de la premiere etude qui examine l'association entre activite physique mesuree objectivement et le taux de PCR chez des adultes sains et presentant des symptomes d'arthrite et de fibromyalgie dans la population canadienne. Au niveau clinique, nos resultats pourront offrir une aide aux cliniciens en rhumatologie a recommander une dose d'activite physique precise comme etant un <<traitement>> anti-inflammatoire accessible aux patients et savoir si la promotion de l'activite physique doit etre couplee avec la lutte contre la sedentarite.

column36: Circulating sex-specific markers of plaque instability in women and men with severe carotid atherosclerosis
column37: Every 10 minutes a Canadian has a stroke, killing more women than men. Strokes are caused by a build-up of fatty deposits (plaques) in the neck arteries that can break-off and travel to the brain. We only know if a plaque is dangerous when it is removed by surgery and examined under the microscope. Often this is too late as the person may have already had a stroke. Men have more dangerous plaques than women. Thus, it is important that research focuses on identifying molecules that contribute to making a plaque dangerous and understanding the sex differences that exist. Current knowledge: 1) Cells in plaques, called macrophages (Mfs), can make the plaque more dangerous. Monocytes in the blood will enter the plaque and transform into Mfs. 2) Adiponectin is a protein in the body that may protect our arteries from developing dangerous plaques. Adiponectin works like a key that must attach to its lock (receptors). Research goals: To 1) examine sex differences in adiponectin receptors and sex hormone receptors on blood monocytes from men and women with dangerous and harmless plaques, 2) measure circulating adiponectin and sex hormones in the blood to determine whether they can act as sex-specific markers to predict dangerous plaques. Methods: Women and men who underwent surgery to remove the dangerous or harmless plaques from their neck arteries were recruited for participation in the study. Advanced lab methods were used to a) measure adiponectin/ sex hormone receptors on blood monocytes of men and women, c) measure adiponectin and sex hormones in the blood. Impact: We identified sex differences in circulating adiponectin and adiponectin/ sex hormone receptors, which may contribute to the development of dangerous plaques in women and men. These findings can help identify: 1) markers that predict dangerous plaques, and 2) new targets of therapy, that may result in patient care that is specific to women and to men. Ultimately, this could prevent strokes and save lives!

column36: Integration of a palliative approach in the care of older adults with dementia in primary care settings: a scoping review
column37: Background: People with dementia often receive harmful medical treatments in the last year of their life. This could be because a palliative approach is not included in caring for them throughout their disease. There is no recent exploration of scientific research to find out if the inclusion of a palliative approach is effective in the care of older adults with dementia who live in the community. Objectives: - Assess nurses' and doctors' viewpoints and experiences regarding the inclusion of a palliative approach in the care of older adults with dementia in primary care settings. - Explore the effectiveness of a palliative approach in the care of older adults with dementia in community settings. Method: We used a 6-step framework for developing the protocol of this review. We included original research in the English language related to primary care settings, that addressed the topic of a palliative approach in the care of older adults with dementia and included nurses or doctors. We searched five research databases. Results: Our search retrieved 1657 articles. They were scanned and reviewed by two reviewers independently for eligibility. Thirteen studies were included to extract details from each one of them to answer the two questions above. Viewpoints and experiences of nurses and doctors were summarized using the characteristics of a palliative approach in dementia care, that we had identified for this literature review, they include advance care planning, pain and symptom management; and psychosocial and spiritual support with shared decision-making as a core approach. Three themes of effectiveness include the impact on patient-related outcomes, caregiver related outcomes and healthcare utilization. Conclusion: The results of this review confirm that there is a lack of research on this topic. More research needs to be carried out that explores the feasibility of including a palliative approach in the care of older adults with dementia in the community.

column36: Platelet signaling in juvenile arthritis
column37: Juvenile arthritis is a very serious disease that affects over 300,000 children and teenagers in North America and causes severe pain, physical deformities and confers a risk of long-term disability. While it is known that juvenile arthritis is characterized by chronic inflammation of the joints, it is currently impossible to accurately identify those children who may be at highest risk for future disease. In chronic diseases such as arthritis, signaling molecules called cytokines are largely responsible for tissue inflammation and destruction. Platelets are tiny cells in the blood that control blood clotting but also release cytokines that can promote inflammation during arthritis. The purpose of this grant application is to study whether platelet-derived cytokines contribute to juvenile arthritis. An improved understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying juvenile arthritis will eventually lead to improved clinical tools for diagnosing, prognosticating and treating this debilitating disease.

column36: Evaluation of Appropriate Use of COPD Pharmacotherapy Over Time
column37: Rationale Chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) is a common and manageable respiratory disease responsible for significant mortality and morbidity worldwide. Evidence suggests COPD pharmacotherapy reduces exacerbations, decreases hospitalizations and improves patient's functional status. However, while great strides have been made towards pharmacotherapy options, it remains unclear if the proportion of patients receiving recommended maintenance pharmacotherapies has improved. Methods We conducted a large, population-based retrospective cohort study using health administrative data from Ontario, the largest province in Canada. Patients aged 66 years or older with physician-diagnosed COPD from 2004-2015 were stratified by severity using the 2018 GOLD COPD criteria. Crude and age-sex direct standardized rates of patients receiving COPD medications appropriate to each severity of COPD were calculated in accordance with GOLD recommendations. Confidence limits were calculated using a gamma distribution function. Results A total of 144,035 people were identified with physician diagnosed COPD. A stable proportion of people with COPD received appropriate short-acting bronchodilators over time with standardized rates ranging from 44% to 49%. Proportions of people with both low severity (Group B) COPD who received appropriate pharmacotherapy increased to 51.3%, in 2015, an absolute increase of 21.5% since 2004. Similarly, the proportion of people with high-risk COPD who received appropriate long-term maintenance therapy increased to more than 85% of individuals, representing an absolute increase of 20.7%. Conclusion Despite significant improvements in the use of long-term maintenance pharmacotherapy, recommended COPD therapy continues to be underused, especially in patients with Group B COPD. Future strategies should be aimed at optimizing prescription practices with the goal of improving patient's health and reducing the financial burden toward health care systems.

column36: Clinical and genetic factors in response to treatment of bipolar disorder
column37: Most people with bipolar disorder require ongoing treatment to prevent further recurrences of mania or depression. Several medications have been found effective in this indication, but each works only in a proportion of patients. The treatment in individual patients is commonly chosen by trial-and-error; each such trial takes a number of months and, as a result, most people achieve stability after considerable amount of time. We propose to test three groups of factors that could differentiate people who do and do not respond to one of the most effective treatments, lithium. First, we will study detailed clinical characteristics of lithium responders and non-responders from four cohorts totaling more than 1800 individuals and followed prospectively for several decades. Second, we will analyze genetic data from a cohort of over 3000 patients studied in collaboration with international consortium, ConLiGen. To understand better whether people respond better specifically to lithium or whether they would improve with other treatments as well, we will compare results in the lithium group with patients treated with other commonly used medications, valproate and lamotrigine. Finally, the lack of adequate response could be related to factors that modify activity of certain genes; we will study this by examining so called epigenetic marks on these patients' DNA. Together, these studies will help in selecting optimal long-term treatment in a timely fashion.

column36: The challenge of dementia in the era of increasing longevity and changing care organizations
column37: The study focuses on the changing impact of increasing longevity, dementia and other memory disorders on the use of and need for informal and formal care in the era of reorganized health and social service structures and ageing in place ideology. The aims are 1) to reveal the effect of dementia and increasing longevity on care use, 2) to explore the possibilities of people with and without dementia to live at home with the help from informal caregivers and formal homecare, and 3) to explore the effect of changes in different health and social care systems on the use of care. The study starts from retrospective investigation of the association of dementia and age at the time of death with health and social care use. The time period studied represents the time during which longevity has increased and long-term care coverage decreased in several countries. I will use Finnish and Swedish national health and social care registers. Next, focus is on how the changes in cognitive ability affect care use and satisfaction with life in the course of ageing, and on the interdependency between them. For this part, I will use data from LASA (the Netherlands) and explore my options to use CLSA data in collaboration with researchers from the University of British Columbia. A six-month visit to UBC in the spring of 2019 is part of this collaboration. Third, an in-depth investigation focus on how people with cognitive problems and/or dementia and their informal caregivers describe their experiences on the adequacy of care and support they receive in the community. I will use longitudinal interview data, collected in Finland in 2018-2020. The study will offer novel information for ageing research and health and social care policymakers. The Project started in 2018 and is funded by the Academy of Finland until July 2021. The project is conducted as part of the studies in Centre of Excellence in Research on Ageing and Care (2018-2025) (CoEAgeCare).

column36: Effects of NK cell adaptation to cytomegalovirus and engagement of TIGIT on HIV-specific antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity
column37: Over the course of our lifetime, we are exposed to many different types of virus infections. Though many viruses linger briefly, some viruses, including human cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis, cause lifelong infection. Our natural killer (NK) cells are immune cells that fight virus infections and become specialized killers after prolonged exposure to the common herpesvirus, CMV. This work explores how the pressures of CMV and HIV co-infection affect the formation of these specialized NK cells, whether they are better able to target virus-infected cells and whether we can harness their potential against HIV-infected cells. One way in which NK cells recognize and kill infected cells is by recognizing the stem of antibodies that specifically attach to virus-infected cells. Unfortunately, in many instances of viral infection, our immune cells become exhausted and are less capable of controlling viral infection. We hope to not only guide specialized NK cells toward HIV-infected targets using specific antibody therapy, but also ameliorate exhaustion by blocking the NK cell receptors conveying messages that mute this important response. These specialized NK cells could provide a novel platform for broad immune protection and could set the stage for a new iteration of immunotherapy for HIV, other chronic viral infections and cancer.

column36: Kinematic analysis of videos of real-life falls in older adults using Kinovea software
column37: My Ph.D. research focuses on the mechanics of falls and fall-related injuries in older adults. I am specifically interested in examining the movement strategies that are used during falls to avoid injury. My efforts combine laboratory experiments with young adults with video analysis of real-life falls in older adults in long term care. My application for the CIHR ICS travel award is to support travel to present my research at the International Society of Posture and Gait Research (ISPGR) World Congress in Edinburgh, Scotland, from June 30 - July 4, 2019. My ISPGR abstract describes a new approach (using Kinovea open-source digitization software) for quantifying body segment movements during real-life falls captured on video, including the impact velocities of the head, pelvis and hand. My results provide the first in-depth kinematic analysis of impact severity during real-life falls, to inform improved approaches to fall injury prevention.

column36: Hypoxia contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis by regulating CNTNAP2 gene
column37: Azheimer's Disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder, causing 2/3 of dementia. 11% of the population over 65 years old suffer from the AD, and AD is the 4th leading cause to death in the aging population. However, the cause and mechanisms leading to AD remain elusive. The world is facing a dementia epidemic without effective prevention and treatment. Intensive researches have suggested the brain accumulation of the amyloid-beta protein (Abeta) as the initial event and deposition of Abeta to form neuritic plaques in the brain is the pathological hallmark of AD process. Over the past 15 years, several drugs that targeting Abeta have been tested in AD patients but with no satisfactory results. These disappointing efforts encourage us to think from a broader perspective, perhaps from the "seeds" during development. We focus on the role of a new gene CNTNAP2 in AD development. CNTNAP2 has been shown to play important roles in brain development. Abnormal CNTNAP2 expression and its genetic variations have been found in the brains of AD patients. These evidences encourage us to investigate how abnormal CNTNAP2 during development contributes to AD pathogenesis in the aging stage. Previously we demonstrated that hypoxia, primarily caused by vascular events in aging population, facilitates AD pathogenesis. Our study showed that CNTNAP2 gene expression is tightly regulated by hypoxia condition. Our study indicates that CNTNAP2 may serve as a new key molecule mediating stroke-induced dementia. The study provides novel insights into AD pathogenesis.

column36: Evaluating the impact of a media literacy and food marketing intervention for children
column37: In light of children's exposure to high levels of food marketing, media literacy skills are needed to navigate advertising appeals promoting the consumption of unhealthy (e.g., high fat, salt and sugar) foods. Health-promoting media literacy education encourages children to use analytical skills to critically examine media messages, and recognize their influence on perceptions, in order to make more informed health choices. However, there is limited research on media literacy intervention efficacy where nutrition promotion is concerned, including how to measure the acquisition of analytical skills needed to navigate food marketing appeals. This study addresses those gaps through the evaluation of evidence-based health-promoting media literacy lesson plans for children focusing on critical knowledge of food marketing and packaging. Two evidence-based "Media Literacy & Food Marketing" lesson plans developed for grades 3-6, and grades 6-9, were used by teachers in the classroom. A measurement tool (four question assignment) was created to assess children's pre and post-lesson levels of critical knowledge about packaged food and marketing messages, in relation to specific core constructs contained within the lesson plans (e.g., analysis and evaluation skills). A total of 71 students participated from grades five, seven, eight, and nine, from two Alberta schools (one urban, one rural). Qualitative analysis (using Nvivo 12) of the participant responses showed small relative increases in analysis and evaluation skills in post-lesson responses, in comparison with pre-lesson answers. Students were better able to understand food marketing appeals, and to assess the nutritional content of packaged foods. This study provides researchers, educators and practitioners with an approach to evaluating the acquisition of critical analytical skills around food, nutrition and health which have the potential to support informed food choices.

column36: "We're raped and defiled cause they think we're into witchcraft": Examining the Health Impacts of Witchcraft Accusations Among Elderly Women in Uganda
column37: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) has the fastest aging population in the world. Women are a larger share of this population and face a lifetime of inequality and discrimination. These inequalities mean that they have no access to social protection and are vulnerable to psychological and emotional abuse. On top of this, they face the disturbing but neglected issue of witchcraft accusations. Thousands of older women in SSA are targets of witchcraft accusations which have negative impacts on their health and wellbeing. We use feminist political to examine why witchcraft accusations occur and how accusations impact older women's health and wellbeing in Uganda SSA. Results from elderly women (n=23) and key informants (n=20) indicate that witchcraft accusations are due to spiritual beliefs but are increasing due to poverty, sociocultural and environmental change. Older women highlight that witchcraft accusations severely impact their physical, psychosocial and sexual health. Due to their age and gender, they were stigmatized, isolated, physical attacked and raped. Key informants underscore that witchcraft accusations are a growing problem for older women in communities but recognized that no policy framework exists to respond to the violations. Overall, policy attention is needed to address the health and human rights violations caused by witchcraft accusations so older women can remain active society members.

column36: La sante en fin de vie : Theoriser les pratiques par l'approche des capabilites
column37: Objectif: Les soins dans le contexte de fin de vie sont critiques pour offrir une approche technicisee, normee et orientee vers une finalite individuelle. Ces soins nuisent a l'expression de l'autonomie des personnes mourantes par le manque de reconnaissance des libertes individuelles. Dans une visee salutogenique, un changement s'impose pour redefinir la place de l'autonomie des personnes en fin de vie dans les soins. En postulant la pertinence de l'approche des capabilites (AC) pour soutenir cette reflexion, cette presentation vise a proposer une conception renouvelee de la pratique professionnelle en fin de vie. Methodologie: Au travers d'une histoire de cas inspiree d'une pratique infirmiere, une proposition de pratique de sante, theorisee par l'AC sera effectuee. L'AC, developpee par Sen a comme objectif de centraliser l'action autour du developpement des possibilites et les libertes individuelles pour permettre a la personne de vivre la vie souhaitee. L'AC permet de reflechir la pratique professionnelle autour de la mobilisation des ressources de l'individu et de l'environnement. Resultats: Cette histoire de cas proposera, au travers de l'AC, une perspective salutogenique de la pratique professionnelle en fin de vie en reflechissant le soin en soutien a ce que les individus sont capable de faire et d'etre. Cette proposition theorique, par la mise en relation des dimensions individuelles, sociales et environnementales qui constituent la pratique, met de l'avant un agir intersubjectif dans une finalite de promotion de la sante. Ainsi, la pratique actuelle de soins de fin de vie sera critiquee par une proposition theorique reflechissant l'AC comme un repere pour promouvoir l'autonomie et mobiliser la sante des individus. Par les croisements des aspects individuels et sociaux que l'AC, cette proposition offre une avenue nouvelle pour concevoir et orienter le soin autour du << droit a la sante >> de tous les individus, meme dans les derniers moments de vie.

column36: Risk factors contributing to the risk of young-onset colorectal cancer: A systematic review
column37: Increasing numbers of adults under the age of 50 years are diagnosed with young-onset colorectal cancer (yCRC). Our research team has searched for research articles on this topic and has concluded more younger adults are diagnosed with and living with yCRC. However, the reasons why younger adults are being diagnosed is not clear. Our team is systematically searching for published research articles that investigate the reasons why yCRC diagnoses are increasing, including whether certain risk factors place certain groups of younger adults at greater risk of being diagnosed with yCRC. Some risk factors (i.e. ethnicity, gender/sex, medical history) can be reduced by promoting colorectal cancer screening, while others (i.e. alcohol and tobacco use, diet, physical activity) can be reduced through lifestyle changes. The aim of our review is to determine which risk factors in younger adults are contributing to the increase in yCRC diagnoses, with the aim of developing interventions to help reduce this risk. These interventions could include expanding screening programs to include those under 50 years of age (current guidelines only recommend screening for those over 50 years of age) or developing educational programs to encourage younger adults to modify their lifestyle characteristics and thus reduce their risk.

column36: V-ATPase "a" subunit/phospholipid interactions: a novel therapeutic target for preventing bone-loss in inflammatory arthritis
column37: Current therapies to prevent pathological bone loss resulting from arthritis and osteoporosis lack effectiveness and have serious side effects. Osteoclasts normally dissolve bone by pumping acid onto the bone surface as part of a continuous renewal process, but this is accelerated in pathological bone loss. V-ATPase molecules are the acid pumps of osteoclasts, and inhibiting V-ATPase activity prevents bone loss in the laboratory, but compounds that reduce V-ATPase function also interfere with their essential activity in other parts of the body and are toxic. V-ATPases consist of many subunits, some having different isoforms. The distribution of isoforms varies, depending on the V-ATPase's final destination. One such isoform, a3, is found primarily in the osteoclast plasma membrane where it is responsible for pumping the acid onto bone. We have preliminary evidence that the N-terminal half of a3 targets the rest of the acid pump to the plasma membrane. Our goal is to understand exactly how a3 brings the pump to the osteoclast plasma membrane then use this protein/lipid interaction to screen for compounds that disrupt this interaction and thereby potentially 'knock down' the osteoclast VATPase without affecting other essential V-ATPases. Here we propose that Brooke Aspen assess the phosphoinositides (PIP) specificity of the a3 N-terminus in vitro using a protein-lipid overlay assay with a lipid array containing concentration gradients of common PIPs, towards the development of antiresorptive drugs that would only affect the osteoclast V-ATPase involved in pathological bone loss in inflammatory arthritis and osteoporosis

column36: Attentional Biases in Pediatric Chronic Pain: Preliminary Evidence from a Longitudinal Eye Tracking Study on Pain and Mental Health in Youth
column37: Pediatric chronic pain is a highly prevalent condition and is associated with significant distress, functional impairment, and high psychiatric comorbidity. Theoretical models of chronic pain and anxiety suggest attention bias as one modifiable mechanism underlying the development and maintenance of both conditions. To date, the results of research examining attentional biases in pain have yielded mixed results. Novel eye-tracking technology offers advantages in measuring sustained attention over time. This is the first study to use eye-tracking to examine attention biases to pain-related information in a sample of youth with chronic pain. Youth with chronic pain were recruited from the Vi Riddell Pain Outpatient Clinics at the Alberta Children's Hospital. Participants attended a lab visit at the Alberta Children's Pain Research Laboratory and completed an eye-tracking task as part of a larger study on pain and mental health. Participants were asked to view images of other children depicting pain expressions of varying severity (low, moderate, high) and neutral facial expressions while their eye gaze was recorded. Total gaze duration assessed sustained attention over time and time to first fixation assessed early attentional capture. Results revealed that youth with chronic pain exhibited significantly higher gaze duration for pain faces as compared to neutral faces, indicative of an attentional bias towards pain-related information. Moreover, youth demonstrated the strongest attentional bias towards the high pain faces. In addition, participants' time to first fixation was significantly shorter for pain faces, indicative of hypervigilance. These preliminary results indicate a significant attentional bias towards pain-related information (as compared to neutral information). Future longitudinal research will examine whether the attention biases underlie the co-occurrence of anxiety and pain over time.

column36: Quantitative Sensory Testing in Pediatric Pain: Methods, Perspectives and Applications
column37: Pain is a significant health issue for children across age groups and medical conditions. In fact, one in five Canadian children experience chronic pain, and two-thirds of these children will go on to experience chronic pain as adults. Unfortunately, the reasons why pain persists is unclear for many children. A better understanding of these reasons will help with the development of new treatments for children with pain. Quantitative Sensory Testing (QST) is an experimental method that is used to assess how individuals process different stimuli, such as pain. QST has been a helpful method in understanding the mechanisms behind chronic pain in adults. QST also holds promise as a tool in pediatric pain research to better understand the mechanisms behind persistent pain for children with various medical conditions. My presentation will provide an overview of QST methods and how they can be applied to pain research with children. In my presentation, I will also share new data on the mechanisms of pain processing in children with cancer. Finally, I will cover practical advice on the use of QST in children including ethical and safety considerations.

column36: Interventions to Treat Frailty: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
column37: Frailty is an important clinical state that contributes to falls, hospitalization, institutionalization and death. When an individual simultaneously has many health problems, a frailty "tipping point" may be triggered by even a minor stressful event such as adding a new drug or urinary tract infection. Research suggests that approximately 23% of Canadians over age 65 are frail, and by age 85 this estimate increases to over 40%. As we learn more about frailty and its consequences, there is an urgent need to determine the most effective interventions that improve physical performance of frail older adults. Our study aimed to determine the effect of frailty interventions on physical performance of older adults. We searched electronic databases to find and screen relevant studies. After extracting the required information from these relevant studies, we tested the quality of the included studies and conducted our analysis. A total of 180 RCTs were included. The average age of included studies ranged between 75 and 85 years, and 62.5% of participants were female. Our results suggested that medication management interventions, when compared to standard care, were associated with the greatest improvement of physical performance followed by physical activity with nutritional supplementation. Given the low quality of the included studies, more high quality studies that examine the effect of frailty treatments on physical performance are required.

column36: Investigating the role of Six family transcription factors in skeletal muscle
column37: The differentiation of muscle stem cells into skeletal muscles or myogenesis, is essential to muscle formation in embryonic development, tissue growth and the regeneration of muscle after injury. Despite its importance in establishing musculoskeletal health, the molecular basis of myogenesis is not fully understood. Research has shown that MyoD, a transcription factor, is a "master regulator" of myogenesis, and that its overexpression is able to induce differentiation of many different cell types, such as fibroblasts, into muscle. However, certain cell types such as HepG2 are refractory to myogenic conversion by overexpression of MyoD. We hypothesize that the lack of the putative pioneer factor Six1 and its cofactors of the Eya family in HepG2 cells obstructs the binding of MyoD at muscle identity genes, impeding the expression of muscle genes. To test the role of Six family transcription factors in muscle differentiation, we will evaluate myogenic conversion in HepG2 cells overexpressing Six and Eya proteins. Furthermore, changes in chromatin accessibility will be assessed in fibroblasts and muscle stem cells where Six and Eya expression is silenced by short-interfering RNA, and in HepG2 cells where Six and Eya are overexpressed. Our research has direct implications in understanding human musculo-skeletal health, and has the long-term potential to provide information that may help to devise novel or improved therapeutic approaches for patients affected by musculo-skeletal diseases.

column36: Exercise as supportive care has selective benefits for chemotherapy tolerance and weight gain
column37: Chemotherapy is commonly used to treat breast cancer. While it causes cancer cells to die, it also causes death of healthy cells, resulting in many unpleasant symptoms. When symptoms get severe, the patient's doctor may choose to reduce the amount of chemotherapy in order to continue with treatment. However, reducing the amount of chemotherapy also reduces how well it works to reduce the risk of cancer returning, so it is best for the patient to receive the full amount of treatment. Research has shown that exercise can improve fitness, strength, well-being, prevent weight gain and reduce certain side effects when performed during chemotherapy. However, the ability of exercise to help patients to receive greater doses of chemotherapy and potentially greater benefits for reducing risk of cancer recurrence and overall survival is poorly understood. In this study, women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer were compared to another group of similar women who received a supervised exercise program during their chemotherapy treatment. Exercise was offered three times per week and included both aerobic and strength training. The medical records of both groups of patients were compared. Women in the exercise group were 60% less likely to have the amount of doxorubicin chemotherapy reduced. Women receiving another type of chemotherapy called docetaxel were 39% less likely to gain weight if they were in the exercise group. Exercise did not change the amount of other types of chemotherapy received or the risk of gaining weight on other types of chemotherapy. These results suggest that the benefits of exercise during chemotherapy treatment may differ by the type of chemotherapy agent received. Grouping all chemotherapy treatment types together may hide potential selective benefits.

column36: What to bundle next? Building a case for bundled care
column37: Episode-based payments holds potential for improving quality and efficiency in care. Bundled care is a service delivery and funding model that defines a basket of services for a targeted condition and pays for these services in a single payment for multiple providers and across multiple settings. Bundled care is an approach used to reduce unnecessary variation and shift the system towards best practice care. Better planning and coordination of care between acute and post-acute care, across multiple healthcare providers has been one of the most relevant and common approaches to achieve these improvements. The Ontario government has piloted six bundled care projects with positive interim results creating a motivation to expand bundled care, however, it is unclear what to bundle next. The overall objective of the project is to identify which clinical area holds the most promise for bundled care. To achieve this goal, we developed a cross-disciplinary approach to engage stakeholders, decision-makers, clinical and administrative leaders to identify important patient, hospital and health system outcomes. Five clinical areas requiring surgical procedures that have been shown to have positive results in other countries will be assessed using standard definitions for episodes of care. The outcome of the project will be the identification of the most promising clinical area to bundle and an approach that is applicable to other clinical areas, and to other jurisdictions locally, nationally and internationally.

column36: Expression of the pan-neurotrophic receptor p75NTR in platelets
column37: BACKGROUND: Platelets are small cells that circulate in blood. They form a plug to prevent bleeding in case of injury in the blood vessel. Platelets then take on a role in wound healing. Platelets can discharge many proteins around the wound, including growth factors that help the vessel grow new cells to close the wound. Surprisingly, platelets also contain brain growth factors, which they also discharge when they respond to injury. There is 100 times more brain growth factors released by platelets than from brain cells. However, what brain growth factors do in the blood vessels remains unknown. WHAT WE HAVE DONE: We have isolated platelets from the blood of healthy volunteers to study their ability to release a specific brain growth factor named the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). We have found that platelets release large amounts of BDNF. We have also found that BDNF can stimulate platelets to stick together, form a clot and release more of their cargo. If we think of BDNF as a key, we do not know which lock (receptor) on platelets it turns. We have looked at a receptor called p75NTR, because in the brain, it unlocks the effects of BDNF. Through a number of different experiments, we have found platelets to express this same receptor. We do not yet know what is the role of this receptor on platelets and in vessel walls. POTENTIAL BENEFITS: By better understanding how platelets respond to brain growth factors, we will be able to encourage platelet to release of their useful cargoes and help vessels heal. This might be particularly important in the vessels that nourish the brain, where damaged blood vessels could lead to stroke and dementia. Platelets may be a new avenue of treatment for these crippling diseases.

column36: Influence des facteurs psychologiques sur l'excitabilite corticomotrice suite a l'induction d'une douleur experimentale
column37: L'interaction entre la douleur et le systeme moteur est un champ d'interet grandissant aupres des cliniciens et des chercheurs. Des etudes anterieures ont notamment montre que des stimulations douloureuses modulent l'excitabilite des cellules du cerveau. Toutefois, il n'y a pas de conclusion claire quant a la direction de cette modulation. Ainsi, l'objectif de cette etude etait de determiner si des facteurs psychologiques comme la kinesiophobie et la dramatisation face a la douleur pouvaient influencer le patron de modulation des cellules du cerveau en presence de douleur. La stimulation magnetique transcranienne, une technique non invasive permettant d'induire de legeres contractions musculaires, a ete utilisee afin d'evaluer l'excitabilite des cellules du cerveau. Ces mesures ont ete prises avant et apres l'application d'une creme a base de capsaicine (utilisee pour induire une douleur experimentale). Au cours de l'experimentation, les participants devaient evaluer l'intensite de la douleur provoquee, la kinesiophobie et la dramatisation face a la douleur. L'analyse des resultats a permis de reveler une correlation positive entre la variation de l'excitabilite des cellules (avant vs pendant la douleur) et les scores de kinesiophobie. De plus, alors que les participants ayant de faibles scores de kinesiophobie ont montre une reduction de l'excitabilite des cellules apres l'application de capsaicine, les participants ayant des scores eleves de kinesiophobie ont montre une augmentation de l'excitabilite des cellules. Les resultats actuels suggerent que la peur du mouvement (kinesiophobie) peut influencer de maniere importante l'effet modulatoire qu'a la douleur sur l'excitabilite des cellules du cerveau. Ces observations offrent des pistes d'explications interessantes pour comprendre comment les facteurs psychologiques comme la kinesiophobie, connus pour jouer un role cle dans la chronicisation de la douleur, peuvent interferer avec la readaptation des patients.

column36: Providing prehab education to family caregivers of patients with total hip replacement: Development and assessment of an eHealth tool
column37: The number of hip replacements is increasing by about 20% every 5 years. In 2017, about 7K of these surgeries were performed in British Columbia. In most cases, patients are discharged from the hospital in less than 2 days, leaving a majority of aftercare responsibilities to family caregivers who often receive little medical education. Education before surgery (prehab) aims to improve a patient's experiences and outcomes after surgery and reduce healthcare costs. However, prehab focuses on educating patients and not their family caregivers. Family caregivers are often unable to attend these educational classes due to barriers such as lack of time and travel costs. Since family caregivers are the main care providers after the surgery, it is essential to address their educational needs and provide prehab in an accessible online format. This study will investigate the educational needs of family caregivers and will develop and assess the usability of an eHealth tool that provide prehab to family caregivers.

column36: Education After Lower Limb Amputation: A Qualitative Study on Clients' Perspectives to Develop an Online Self-Management Program
column37: On average, 7,300 Canadians have a Lower Limb Amputation (LLA) each year, with 86% of those being adults aged >50 years. Extensive rehabilitation is required to assist these clients in addressing decreased confidence, mobility, depression and pain. However, in a climate of reduced health care investment (e.g., shorter lengths of stay for inpatients, move to outpatient services), self-management programs are required. Self-management programs teach people important coping skills, build their confidence, and motivate them to manage disease-related physical and psychological challenges. These programs can be provided to clients through mobile health (mHealth) technologies, which-as they are smartphone- or tablet-based-can provide accessible, low-cost, and ongoing continuous rehabilitation after discharge in both urban and rural areas. Therefore, to improve rehabilitation outcomes in adults post-LLA, we have explored clients' perspectives on education and training program post LLA to develop an online self-management program called Self-Management for Amputees Rehabilitation using Technology (SMART). We have conducted qualitative interviews with clients with a unilateral LLA aged 50 years and over to explore their needs and preferences in regard to education contents and format of delivery. Our analyses will disclose the contents of self-management program based on LLA population health needs. The results of this study will lead to the design and development of SMART, which has the potential to allow for greater clients' choice with regards to pace and style of learning to deal with health needs and prosthetic training after LLA.
