column36: Harnessing the power of assistive technology to enable ageing in place: Future directions for policy development and advocacy efforts.
column37: Background: Assistive technology (e.g. walkers, hearing aids) has been proposed as a strategy to support Canada's ageing population. Assistive technology (AT) maximizes the functional ability of older adults and therefore enables healthy, independent and in-place ageing. However, without appropriate and equitable access to AT, its benefits for ageing adults are futile. Purpose: The aim of this paper is two-fold: 1) to examine access to AT among older adults within Canada; 2) inform advocacy strategy directed at changes within the AT healthcare system to better support older adults in the home environment of their choice. Methodology: This paper draws on the accessibility principle of the United Nation's Human Rights-Based Approach (HRBA) to healthcare and current literature on AT to examine access to AT and associated programs. Results: Access to AT is inconsistent throughout Canada resulting in unmet needs. Indirect inequities in access are evident through inconsistencies in federal provisions. Federal provisions apply to only specific subset of Canadians and are unavailable to the rest of the population with similar needs. Economic accessibility (affordability) is a key barrier to AT access. With high cost of AT and inadequate levels of funding, many older adults are forced to go without AT or choose less appropriate but more affordable options, potentially decreasing functionality and safety. Limited selection of AT and AT suppliers restrict older adults' choices, resulting in compromises that do not adequately meet users' needs. AT programs are highly disintegrated, leading to the lack of information accessibility and difficulty in navigation for users. Conclusion: Access to the AT is highly variable, complex and restricted. To maximize the promise of innovation and technology to support the older adults preference of ageing in their environment of choice, there is an urgent need to facilitate development of policies that enhance equitable access to AT.

column36: Epidemiology of Mental Health Complications in Pregnant and Postpartum Women With Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Systematic Review
column37: Many women are diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) during childbearing years. Evidence shows substantial prevalence and incidence of mental health complications, namely anxiety and depression among individuals with RA. However, there are currently very little data and no systematic reviews on the prevalence and incidence of depression and anxiety in women living with RA during pregnancy or postpartum, despite this population being at risk for developing depression. Considering the increased risk of depression in the RA population and the lack of pooled information for antepartum and postpartum depression in RA patients, we decided to address this knowledge gap and conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to look at mental health in RA pregnancies. The overall objective of this project is to address the understudied issue of mental health among pregnant and postpartum women with RA. The specific objectives of this project are to: 1) determine the prevalence of anxiety and depression in women with RA during pregnancy; and 2) determine the incidence of postpartum depression among women with RA.

column36: Designing and Evaluating the Impacts of Different Bundled Payment Options to Incentivize Community-based Integrated Care for Patients with Heart failure
column37: There is tremendous pressure on healthcare systems to meet the demands of chronic diseases care, while containing costs. Various financial incentives have been recently introduced to promote interprofessional and organizational collaboration across the health system. In Ontario, Canada, bundled payment models were piloted in three health centres for the management of patients hospitalized for congestive heart failure (CHF). These models offered prospective payments covering disease-specific management and coordination in acute and home care settings for 30 days but do not include primary or specialist care in their coverage. There are two main challenges with designing bundled payments for chronic disease such as CHF, which our study will aim to address: 1) selecting the appropriate services to include in the bundle after hospitalization; 2) determining whether the integration of these services in the episode of care improves patient outcomes such as readmission and mortality rates. This study will follow a prospective cohort of patients hospitalized for CHF in Ontario, Canada, from April 1st, 2012 to March 31st, 2016. The index event will be the first hospital discharge experienced by a patient, which will trigger the bundled care services. Patients will be followed for up to 2 years after the conclusion of their first bundled episode. The main exposures will be whether patients received a bundled care episode with different service components including: 1) primary care follow up within 7 days of discharge; 2) home care services within 21 days; 3) access to an outpatient cardiologist within 30 days of discharge. Categorized by different combination of service components, our analysis will examine the risk adjusted 30-day and 1-year mortality rates and all-cause hospitalization in patients. The results of this study will help support future discussions on the feasibility of extending existing bundled payments for individuals living with CHF, in Ontario, Canada.

column36: Prendre soin d'un animal de compagnie: comprendre l'equilibre entre les bienfaits et les contraintes de cette occupation pour soutenir l'autonomie et la securite des aines fragiles vivant dans la communaute
column37: Au Canada, les aines de 65 ans et plus constituent 16,9 % de la population, et cette proportion devrait atteindre 25 % en 2036. Ce vieillissement de la population s'accompagne d'une augmentation importante du nombre d'aines fragiles. La majorite de ces aines souhaitant vieillir chez soi le plus longtemps possible, plusieurs services communautaires sont mis en place pour favoriser leur maintien a domicile. Des etudes suggerent toutefois que pres d'un aine sur cinq vit un isolement social et de l'ennui, ce qui est associe a une diminution de leur etat fonctionnel, de leur sante et une augmentation de la mortalite. Pour repondre a ces besoins non combles, les animaux de compagnie s'averent une avenue prometteuse a explorer. En effet, de nombreuses etudes suggerent que les interactions avec un animal peuvent etre benefiques pour la sante et que la participation dans des activites signifiantes ameliore le bien-etre des aines. Toutefois, s'occuper d'un animal de compagnie s'accompagne de certaines contraintes et peut comporter un risque pour l'aine et l'animal de compagnie, surtout si les exigences liees a cette activite excedent les capacites du proprietaire vieillissant. Ce projet de recherche a donc pour but de mieux comprendre l'importance et l'influence des animaux de compagnie dans le quotidien des aines fragiles vivant dans la communaute (p.ex. : structure et routine), en plus de l'exploration de l'equilibre entre bienfaits et les risques associes a cette activite. Des entrevues seront realisees aupres d'aines fragiles proprietaires d'animaux de compagnie et vivant dans la communaute ainsi que des ergotherapeutes travaillant en soutien a domicile. Ces nouvelles connaissances aideront a identifier des interventions susceptibles de maximiser les bienfaits associes aux animaux de compagnie, tout en diminuant les risques pour les aines fragiles en vue de favoriser leur autonomie, leur maintien a domicile et leur qualite de vie.

column36: Supporting older adults with health and social care needs in the community-a case study of case management in Ontario's home and community care system
column37: Seniors tend to experience more chronic health conditions and disability and require a spectrum of supports to live independently in the community. A widely adopted strategy to facilitate the coordination of both health care and social care services employs professionals, known as case managers, who help individuals access care. As case managers continue to be key in the care of seniors, it is important to understand how case managers help seniors, including how they coordinate across different services to address health care needs and social care needs. This study explores the policies and the practices of case management for seniors in two sub-sectors of home and community care in Ontario, Canada: i) home care (HC) case management, that coordinates publicly funded services (personal supports, nursing, professional therapists) and ii) community support services (CSS) case management, that deliver a range of subsidized and fee-for-service supports (housing with supports, meal delivery, socialization programs). Policy documents suggest that HC and CSS should be complementary in their case management roles with HC case managers responsible for 'higher' needs seniors and CSS case managers responsible for 'lower' needs seniors. However, case managers from both sub-sectors describe challenges in this arrangement because 'high' needs clients are entitled to medically-orientated services but lack the same entitlements for socially-orientated services; thus, there are gaps in care to help seniors live independently in the community despite a 'complementary' policy intention for care.

column36: Fourier decomposition free-breathing 1H MRI perfusion maps in asthma
column37: Objective: We aimed to develop a software tool to convert conventional magnetic resonance images of lung structure into maps representing the strength of bloodflow and breathing across the lung. Methods: Conventional proton magnetic resonance image (MRI) sequences were transformed to change moving images into a stable image with changing brightness. Brightness changes over time in the image should therefore be a combination of changes due to breathing and blood pulse. The Fourier transform, a mathematical technique for separating patterns or rhythms in data, was used to separate out the contributions of breathing and pulse to image brightness. This technique was repeated for each image element until two maps were generated representing how effectively blood and air flowed in the lung. The maps were categorized into five levels of breathing or bloodflow effectiveness, and an algorithm was used to best assign image elements one of the five levels. Measurements were performed in 15 asthma patients who consented to participate in lung function tests and MRI. Results: The software tool we proposed was used to create maps of breathing and bloodflow effectiveness in 15 patients. Our results were compared against hyperpolarized helium MRI - a technique to generate breathing effectiveness maps by imaging magnetic gas briefly inhaled into the lung. Measurements of overall bloodflow defects significantly correlated with overall breathing defects measured using both the Fourier transform method and the helium method. Conclusion: We generated bloodflow and breathing maps from conventional MRI scans that demonstrated clinically acceptable accuracy. The software developed to create these maps was heavily automated, making the software very efficient for busy clinical settings.

column36: Lewy pathology in REM sleep circuits triggers REM sleep behavior disorder symptoms in mice
column37: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a neurological condition characterized by lack of motor suprression during REM sleep, which subseqeuently results in dream enactment behaviors. Although the exact cause of RBD remains unclear, previous basic science studies suggest that brainstem contains neuronal populations that are involved in REM sleep motor suppression, and conversely that their dysfunction could be involved in RBD. Despite much clinical evidence supporting a close link between REM sleep behavior disorder and synucleopathies such as Parkinson's disease, there is no direct experimental evidence that shows that they are caused by the same neurodegenerative disease mechanism. In this study, we use disease-causing vectors to induce Parkinson's disease-like pathology in brainstem REM sleep circuits. If neurodegenerative processes are involved in the pathogenesis of RBD, we hypothesize that targeted degeneration of brainstem structures will induce RBD symptoms in mice. Our preliminary results shows that Parkinson's disease-like pathology in the mouse brainstem results in abnormal muscle activity during REM sleep, which is observed in RBD patients. Next, we will investigate whether neurodegnerative processes can spread from the spinal cord to REM sleep circuits to cause RBD-like symptoms. Altogether, the these experiments aim to address the association between RBD and the synucleopathies and represent the most comprehensive dissection of RBD mechanisms to date.

column36: Oscillometry Detects Different Airway Abnormalities that Manifest as MRI Ventilation Heterogeneity in Asthma and COPD
column37: Oscillometry is a new lung function test used to measure lung function in patients with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) that is performed while a patient breathes normally in and out. However, the cutoffs that define abnormal lung function are not standardized yet. This means that it is difficult to determine just how abnormal a patient's lung function is and this is important to understand for oscillometry to be used more widely for patients with lung disease. Once effective cutoffs are determined, oscillometry measurements can be more easily understood and applied. Here we have used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lung as a way to determine cutoffs for abnormal lung function in patients with asthma and COPD. We used MRI measurements of the lung because MRI provides a way to directly see and measure the problems that are caused by abnormal lung function. We showed that the cutoffs for abnormal oscillometry measurements were different in patients with asthma than patients with COPD, and this means that there may not be a one-size-fits-all cutoff for patients with different lung diseases. Overall, oscillometry provides a way to measure lung function that is easy to perform for both the patient and the technologist performing the test. Now with a better understanding of these cutoffs, oscillometry may be applied more widely for lung function testing in patients with lung disease.

column37: Contexte: L'implantation des innovations dans le systeme de sante et de services sociaux au Canada necessite souvent le changement des pratiques infirmieres. A ce titre, le processus de developpement theorique est un aspect essentiel de la recherche associee aux interventions de changement des pratiques infirmieres. Celui-ci permet de comprendre les mecanismes d'action theoriques de l'intervention et de selectionner les techniques de changement de comportement qui meneront au changement des pratiques infirmieres. Objectif: Cette etude visait a realiser le processus de developpement theorique de l'intervention numerique de changement des pratiques infirmieres E_MOTIV visant a augmenter la mise en oeuvre de counseling par les infirmieres en milieu hospitalier. Methode: Le processus de developpement theorique de l'intervention, mene selon l'approche de Sidani et Braden, comptait cinq etapes: 1) developper une comprehension de la problematique; 2) identifier les objectifs et les mecanismes d'action theoriques de l'intervention; 3) selectionner les techniques de changement de comportement appropriees; 4) selectionner le mode et le dosage de l'intervention; 5) selectionner les resultats anticipes. Resultats: Le processus de developpement theorique a permis d'identifier 10 mecanismes d'action theoriques cibles par l'intervention numerique E_MOTIV (p. ex. norme subjective) et 16 techniques de changement de comportement visant a modifier ces MAT (p. ex. comparaison sociale). Conclusion: L'approche de Sidani et Braden a fourni une methode systematique pour le developpement theorique de l'intervention. La prochaine etape consiste a evaluer l'efficacite de l'intervention numerique E_MOTIV.

column36: Identification of endogenous retroelements-derived MHC I-associated peptides in ovarian cancer using proteogenomics
column37: The cells of our body express, on their surface, MHC I molecules. These MHC I molecules present small protein fragments, that we call peptides, to the immune system. Altogether, all the peptides presented by a cell represent its "ID card" that is scanned by our immune cells, which elicit immune responses to destroy any cell presenting abnormal peptides that are recognized as foreign. These foreign peptides are presented by cells infected by viruses or by cancer cells. It is however known that tumours are able to hide from the immune system: the goal of immunotherapy is does to stimulate immune cells in order to increase cancer cell recognition and destruction of the tumour. The goal of this project is thus to identify peptides presented on cancer cells that could be recognized by immune cells and could thus be used as targets for immunotherapies. We decided to focus on endogenous retroelements, which are viruses that integrated our DNA millions of years ago. These sequences are not dangerous, since normal cells inhibit their expression, but it is known that they are aberrantly expressed by cancer cells. Since they have a viral origin, they could be easily recognized as foreign by immune cells, which makes them promising targets for immunotherapies.

column36: The impact of park access on physical activity among residents in Southern Ontario, Canada
column37: We aimed to determine whether access to parks and greenspace influences physical activity of residents in Southern Ontario, and whether these patterns vary by age group and neighbourhood walkability. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis using data from four consecutive cycles of the Canadian Community Health Survey from 2007 and 2008 to 2013 and 2014, including participants aged 20-74 in Southern Ontario. We used geographic information system tools to create neighbourhood level park exposures based on size of parks (small or medium-0.5-4.9 hectares, large- greater than 5 hectares) and number of parks within 800m of participants' postal code of residence. Our cohort was comprised of 41,945 individuals, with both age groups being equally represented. Overall access to parks was also associated with greater levels of physical activity; however, effects were greatest among younger adults. In this age group, living closer to large-sized parks was strongly associated with physical activity, respectively. Similar associations were seen in those over age 50. Access to small or medium sized parks demonstrated lesser associations overall with physical activity, except in highly walkable areas. For instance, residents in highly walkable areas had substantially higher levels of physical activity than those in areas of low walkability, particularly in the presence of greater than 1 small or medium park.

column36: Examining caregiver distress among seniors with care needs: a population-based study
column37: By 2031, 2.2 million older Canadians will need someone to care for them. Most (about 80%) of this care will be provided by informal caregivers such as family and friends. The burden of caregiving can make caregivers distressed, affecting the health of both patients and caregivers. Currently, we do not have a good understanding of factors that make caregivers distressed, nor how distress impacts the care-recipients in the long term. In my research, I aim to 1) Describe the proportion of distressed caregivers in Ontario and identify characteristics of care-recipients/caregivers associated to caregivers being distressed. 2) Determine if older adults cared by distressed versus non-distressed caregivers differ in their health and resource use. 3) Describe how caregivers' distress status change over time, and identify factors associated with initially non-distressed caregivers becoming distressed. 4) Evaluate if older adults cared by distressed caregivers will have poorer health outcomes and more resource use over time than those with non-distressed caregiver To achieve these, I will use population-based data collected by the interRAI Home Care Assessment (RAI-HC). RAI-HC is routinely given to all Ontarians seeking or receiving home care. It is linked to other healthcare data, including hospital records and physician claims, at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Science. This allows us to comprehensively and longitudinally analyze the long-term health and resource use of older adults according to their caregivers' distress status. As supporting older Canadians becomes a policy priority, research on caregiver distress and its effect on patient outcomes will inform policy decisions on home care reform, including the $2.3 additional funding for home care recently announced through the Federal Health Accord. It will also help healthcare providers identify caregivers who are likely to become distressed and enable development of better resources to support caregivers.

column36: Relationship between Schwann cells, diabetic neuropathy and wound healing defects
column37: Following an injury to the skin, the ability to quickly heal is something many of us take for granted. Within one week, there is often little evidence of the original cut or scrape. Without the ability to heal efficiently, wounds can persist and may develop into more serious outcomes such as wound bed infection, which could lead to serious tissue damage requiring amputation. These non-healing wounds are costly for the healthcare system of Canada. Many of the chronic wounds requiring treatment under the Canadian healthcare system are those in conjunction with diabetes. Current statistics suggest that 415 million people across the world suffer from either type-I or type-II diabetes, with this number being expected to rise to 642 million by 2040. Individuals with diabetes are very likely to be affected by a chronic wound at some point throughout their life, with estimates ranging from 8-25%. An array of processes contribute to the inefficient wound healing viewed in diabetics, and recent therapeutics have had moderate clinical success, but demonstrate that our understanding of chronic wound healing is incomplete. There is an evident gap in our knowledge as to which processes limit healing in diabetes, specifically, one crucial element that has yet to be alluded to within scientific research, is the requirement for functional neural connections within the wounded tissue for proper healing. A common complication of diabetes is neuropathy, which affects as much as 50% of the diabetic population. It is known that proper innervation is required for wound repair, and that the amount of functional axons is reduced in the skin of diabetics, with further decline in axonal number occurring following a skin injury. While cutaneous innervation may play an important role, we believe that the Schwann cells associated with the cutaneous axons may be the most critical factor in wound repair, as these cells appear to be very sensitive to the diabetic environment.

column36: Characteristics of women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and future cardiovascular diseases risk
column37: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancies (HDPs) affect up to 10% of pregnancies and are associated with serious outcomes for the mother and her baby such as kidney disease and stillbirth. HDPs also increase the risk of developing future cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) i.e. diseases of the heart and blood vessels. Therefore, we sought to describe the characteristics of women with a history of HDP and present demographic factors of those that developed future CVD versus those who did not, in order to identify factors that may contribute to the increased risks of CVD in these women. The MED-ECHO dataset, consisting of all women who delivered in hospitals in the Quebec province of Canada between 1989 and 2016, was used for this study. Outcomes were CVDs such as heart diseases e.g. heart failure, cerebrovascular diseases e.g. stroke pulmonary heart diseases, procedures involving the heart and blood vessels, and coronary care unit admission. The demographics and characteristics of women with and without CVD were presented. Of 2,197,124 pregnancies admitted for hospital delivery, HDP occurred in 5.2%, with the majority (69.7%) occurring in first births. Among women with HDP, the rate of CVD was 9.8%. Women who developed CVDs were more likely to be older, have had substance abuse during pregnancy, pre-existing diabetes, and socio-economic disadvantage compared with women without CVD. Women with CVD were also more likely to have have poor obstetric history such as a history of gestational diabetes and adverse perinatal outcomes such as preterm delivery and stillbirth. These results present important factors that may be used to identify women at higher risk of CVDs and potentially predict CVDs in women with a history of HDPs. Such findings could lead to earlier identification of high-risk women, and effective management strategies such as follow-up after delivery and healthy lifestyle promotion; thus prevent CVDs in women and improving the health of women in Canada and globally.

column36: Instrument Development to Measure the Designs of and the Exposures to the Natural Environments in Long-Term Care Homes Among Residents and their Care Staff
column37: The research in healthcare settings reports that natural environments are beneficial for people's health and staff's work. The research on the natural environment in Canadian nursing homes is relatively new and growing. So far, there are no surveys tested for their dependability to collect information on the natural environments' designs and uses (among seniors and caregiving staff) in nursing homes. These types of surveys are critical to producing scientific evidence that is precise. Therefore, this presentation will describe the results of creating two new surveys with dependable topics, questions, and language. The researcher prepared multiple rounds of questionnaires based on research to ask the opinions of twenty-four experts. Their opinions helped determine the most important topics and questions for the new surveys. The experts also helped with the wording, which will be finalized (before the conference dates) by 30 research participants who work in the nursing homes. The results show that sunlight and nature are the most important focus for the new surveys. Experts highlighted considerations, such as distinguishing sunlight from daylight, having control, specifying weather, and wording. One survey will collect information on design in shared spaces and residents' activities. This first survey covers 20 topics, such as "view out of the main windows" and asks questions like "When I look out of the main window what do I see?". Another survey will collect information on caregiving staff's activities and perceptions. This second survey covers ten topics, such as "Daylight and me" and asks how frequently they encounter scenarios like "I walk by windows while I am working." The creation of these surveys is timely because Ontario is redeveloping nursing homes. As a licensed landscape architect and health services researcher, I believe that dependable surveys will help produce precise scientific evidence, which can be used to build health-promoting environments.

column36: Preimplantation du Lifestyle Redesign(R) : qu'en pensent les partenaires-experts?
column37: Le present projet de recherche vise a : 1) traduire et valider la formation du Lifestyle Redesign(R) aupres d'ergotherapeutes oeuvrant en milieu communautaire quebecois, 2) documenter la preimplantation de cette intervention en identifiant les facilitateurs et les obstacles et 3) identifier des actions a deployer afin d'integrer cette intervention dans les milieux communautaires quebecois. Developpe et experimente en Californie, le Lifestyle Redesign(R) est une intervention innovante et efficace qui a pour objectif de soutenir, a travers l'elaboration de routines occupationnelles saines et signifiantes, la sante, le fonctionnement et la qualite de vie des aines. Cette intervention recoit un appui favorable et un interet grandissant de la part des chercheurs, des ergotherapeutes et des gestionnaires quebecois, et ce, en raison des evidences scientifiques indiquant un bon rapport cout-efficacite et une amelioration significative de la qualite des interactions sociales des aines, de leur fonctionnement, leur vitalite, leur sante mentale et leur satisfaction envers la vie. Au Quebec, le Lifestyle Redesign(R) est toutefois uniquement disponible en recherche et n'a jamais ete implante en clinique. Ce projet contribuera donc au renforcement des pratiques de pointe des ergotherapeutes en matiere de promotion de la sante. Il propose egalement un partenariat exceptionnel entre la clinique, la communaute et la recherche afin de repondre aux defis engendres par le vieillissement de la population. Ultimement, l'integration du Lifestyle Redesign(R) a la pratique pourrait contribuer au maintien ou a l'amelioration de la sante et du mieux-etre des aines quebecois et canadiens.

column36: Combining Secreted and Lung Tissue Proteome Reveals Unique Pathobiological Pathways Associated with House Dust Mite Challenge in Mice
column37: To develop new drug therapies for asthma, you need to have a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms of the disease. To do this, animal models are needed. Currently the most appropriate model for allergic asthma involves mice who are exposed to house dust mite (HDM) extract. However, despite this model being used all over the world for numerous studies, we still do not fully understand the big picture of how the thousands of proteins within the lung integrate with one another to create this "allergic mouse model". To answer this question, we used two groups of mice. One group was exposed to HDM and the other was our control (naive group). For each mouse we collected both lung lavage fluid (BALF) and lung tissue. Using these samples we performed proteomics using mass spectroscopy in order to measure all the proteins within both the lavage fluid and lung tissue. Once we obtained all the information on the abundance and diversity of the proteins we used bioinformatics to assess how HDM exposure alters the lung. Through our work we discovered that the protiens from both BALF and lung tissue are significantly different from one another. Additionally when you merge the balf and lung tissue together to create a "Combined" view of the lung we show that its also significantly different from both BALF and lung tissue. We further showed that this "Combined Lung" contains molecular and biological information which is often overlooked when you examine either the BALF or lung tissue seperately. This result is important as many studies involving HDM exposed mice only look at either the BALF or lung tissue, not both. Our results suggest that these studies could be missing key biological mechanisms which are hidden when you look at the BALF or lung tissue seperately and we suggest that future studies examine both the BALF and tissue together in order to get a fully picture of the biology of the lung.

column36: Analyse epigenomique integrative pour identifier les biomarqueurs potentiels de la leucemie aigue causee par la fusion MLL-AF9
column37: Les leucemies sont des cancers du sang et de la moelle osseuse. Elles se caracterisent par des mutations genetiques pouvant dereguler l'activite de certains genes intervenant dans la production des cellules sanguines et etant responsables de la maladie. L'une de ces mutations correspond a la fusion de 2 genes: MLL et AF9. Le diagnostic des patients porteurs de cette mutation est defavorable ce qui pousse les chercheurs a caracteriser les facteurs intervenant dans ce sous-type de leucemies. Cependant, etudier les patients se revele etre complexe de par la forte diversite genetique entre eux. C'est la raison pour laquelle le laboratoire a cree un modele de leucemie humaine chez la souris dans l'espoir d'investiguer les effets specifiques de la fusion MLL-AF9 a chacun des stades de developpement de la maladie. Dans la litterature, il est connu que le rapprochement MLL-AF9 a pour consequence de bouleverser le paysage << epigenetique >> ce qui interfere dans l'activite de genes cibles dont l'identite reste a definir. Le principal objectif de mon projet de doctorat est d'utiliser la bioinformatique pour trouver ces genes, les caracteriser et comprendre en quoi la perturbation de ceux-ci joue un role primordial dans le developpement de la maladie. Pour atteindre mon objectif, des outils de sequencage dits de << nouvelle generation >> me permettront de passer en revue chacune des activites des genes du modele et de les comparer avec les donnees des patients. Chacun d'entre eux ayant un fonctionnement anormal sera alors teste en utilisant des ciseaux genetiques pour voir l'impact d'une interruption artificielle de l'activite des genes dans les cellules leucemiques. Une meilleure comprehension de la maladie facilitera la recherche de nouveaux traitements adaptes et plus cibles.

column36: Best approaches for identifying, incorporating and reporting patient preferences in clinical guidelines
column37: It is imperative to improve quality of care. Guidelines are produced to provide recommendations on how to optimize care delivery and patient outcomes. Guideline developers gather, evaluate and synthesize evidence to form recommendations that inform health care planning, delivery, policy and quality improvement. However, past research has shown that guidelines are underused due to multiple determinants (facilitators and barriers) including patient-, clinician-, institutional, organizational, and system- level factors. Efforts to overcome challenges and more broadly implementing facilitators to improve guideline use, including educational material and meetings, opinion leaders, audit and feedback, and pay-for-performance, have had inconsistent and limited impact. Past research has shown that guidelines that are based on or identify patient preferences are more likely to be used by patients and clinicians. However, research has shown that many guideline developers have not been informed by patient preferences when developing guidelines. Therefore, primary research is needed to generate insight on best practices for developing patient informed guidelines. Improving the development of patient-relevant guidelines is widely advocated; yet, little guidance exists on how to do so. This thesis will synthesize published evidence on approaches for identifying, incorporating and reporting patient preferences in guidelines (scoping review) and explore best practices for doing so among national and international guideline developers (qualitative interviews).

column36: N-terminomics identifies protease substrates between heterogeneous macrophage populations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) is a lung condition characterized by prolonged inflammation due to unregulated inflammatory signalling in immune cells such as macrophages. Proteases, Cathepsin S (CatS) and Cathepsin L (CatL), whose function is to cut other proteins, are found to be highly expressed in patients with COPD and their degradative activity within macrophages has been correlated with the development of COPD. Different macrophage populations in the lung, including alveolar and interstitial macrophages, have unique roles in COPD inflammatory networks however the action of CatS and CatL in each corresponding macrophage population has not yet been fully characterized. We hypothesize that cathepsins have widely different repertoires of proteins they cut within macrophages. Macrophages from mice lacking cathepsins were first compared to obtain a baseline protease cleavage profile for CatS and CatL. Using terminal amine isotopic labelling of substrates (TAILS), a technique to study what proteases cut, we identified unique candidates cut by different cathepsins. These include vimentin, and tumor-necrosis factor receptor II (TNF-RII). Furthermore, these results suggest that CatL primarily performs limited degradation (processing) while CatS performs multiple cuts (digest) on its substrates. In conclusion, our large scale analysis data have shown that some macrophage populations subjected to inflammation had different profiles with high similarity of candidates including vimentin and TNF-RII. We aim to establish a signatures of candidates to be validated in a COPD model and extend our findings to investigate human COPD patient's sputum at exacerbation and recovery.

column36: Exploring the Link Between Retail Food Environments and Teen Purchasing in London, Ontario
column37: The retail food environments in many London neighbourhoods do not support teenagers' nutritional needs. These areas, which are defined by their degree of spatial access to food within a neighbourhood, contain an overabundance of convenience stores and fast food vendors, rather than easily-accessible, affordable, healthy food outlets. Since these food environments often tend to be concentrated around schools, it is essential that these settings are further examined to answer the following research question: what is the relationship between food exposure and teen purchasing? This research will examine the retail food environments around high schools in London, Ontario, focusing on the food/beverage advertisements found on billboards, transit shelters, and storefronts that are located within 2000 meters of these schools. This research will also explore what these food retailers sell, their advertising techniques, and how this exposure influences teens' purchasing and consumption behaviours. A mixed-methods approach, including food environment audits and consultations with a local Youth Advisory Council (YAC), will be used to explore this dietary issue. Overall, evaluating students' exposure to food marketing techniques and teens' associated dietary behaviours will produce relevant, geographic knowledge through understanding this complex relationship within the context of London, Ontario. On a broader scale, my findings will contribute to the creation of a teen-informed, validated photo analysis tool that can be used by other researchers to comprehensively assess food environments across diverse research contexts. It will particularly shed light on the importance of measuring the 'information environment' within communities, which includes the food advertising and food marketing strategies that are exposed to teenagers. This research will ultimately inform land use planning, nutrition policy, and improve the health of adolescents worldwide.

column36: Examining the use of Inuit knowledge within community-based HIV prevention research
column37: Inuit hold great knowledge, skills, and strength, all of which have sustained their people through some of the most rapid social, economic, and political changes ever experienced by Indigenous Peoples across the world. For Inuit this way of knowing is known as Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (IQ). Within health research, a shift has occurred and research with Indigenous communities is now expected to recognize (and include) Indigenous knowledge. An approach to research that claims to create space for upholding Indigenous ways of knowing is community-based participatory research (CBPR). Much of the literature surrounding CBPR strongly promotes this approach as a successful process for collaborative research between University-based researchers and Indigenous communities. However, missing from the literature is research examining CBPR processes and Indigenous knowledge, their alignment, and if and how they work together. To address this gap, using a case study approach and the conceptual framework of Two Eyed Seeing, this case study examined an HIV prevention CBPR project that took place with three Inuit communities across Nunavut. Aiming to examine the congruency of IQ and CBPR principles, this case study sought to answer questions to determine in what ways these two sets of principles were reflected throughout the research process; what may be some challenges and opportunities of a CBPR project that follows IQ, and what the strengths of IQ as a guide for knowledge creation are. This case study produced knowledge for Inuit-specific research frameworks that has utility across disciplines. The findings from this research project can help ensure Inuit ways of knowing are explicitly incorporated into research processes and contribute to knowledge for both Inuit communities and university-based researchers to conduct culturally affirming research following Wise Practices for community-driven research.

column36: Investigating the Effects of Interpersonal Feedback on Relation-inferred Self-efficacy, Self-efficacy and Exercise Performance in Young Children with Developmental Coordination Disorder
column37: Children with Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) struggle to perform everyday tasks due to coordination difficulties. A recent study found that 5-7 year old children with DCD have poorer performance on exercise tests compared to typically developing (TD) children due to lower confidence in their motor skills. Children's motivation also affects fitness performance. Yet, no research has looked at possible ways to increase confidence and motivation, which in turn could increase their performance on exercise tests. This study will investigate whether positive feedback ("I believe in you", "I know you are going to do a lot better than last time") from a research assistant posed as an athletic trainer can increase children's confidence, motivation, and exercise performance. 5 participants have completed the study to date (2 TD; 3 DCD). Participants completed questionnaires asking about their confidence and motivation for performing the upcoming exercise tests. About two weeks later they returned to the lab to complete the same questionnaires and exercise tests. However, before completing these measures, some participants received positive feedback from a researcher pretending to be an athletic trainer. Children with DCD did worse on all exercise tests than TD children. There were no differences between groups for confidence and motivation scores; however, DCD children who received positive feedback improved their performance on some exercise tests while DCD children who did not receive feedback did worse at the second appointment. We aim to recruit 50 children with DCD and 50 TD children for this study. Initial findings suggest exercise performance in children with DCD may be manipulated to improve performance. Findings from this study will help us find ways to build their confidence for difficult tasks requiring motor coordination and physical effort. Hopefully, this will encourage them to continue playing sports and other physical activities.

column36: Injection initiation assistance as harm reduction during a fentanyl-driven overdose crisis: Injection drug users' experiences and implications for structural interventions
column37: Despite the proliferation of fentanyl in North America, the impact of this drug market change on injection initiation processes has not been examined. An understanding of the dynamic between drug supply and injection initiation norms will help inform interventions to prevent injection initiation, which are imperative for preventing HIV. We explore how people who inject drugs (PWID) in Vancouver, BC, understand and navigate social norms of initiating others into injecting within the context of an opioid overdose crisis. In-depth interviews were conducted with 19 PWID who reported helping someone inject for the first time. Participants expressed moral dilemmas about assisting others with injecting. While participants described a 'moral code' prohibiting assisting injection-naive individuals, this code was not the sole consideration shaping social action around injection initiation. Rather, PWID made decisions about whether and how to assist novice injectors with consideration for social norms around 'inter-personal responsibility'. Some PWID were reluctant to assist novice injectors due to uncertainties around drug potency and concerns about being criminally liable for the overdose deaths of those who they assisted. However, PWID also sought to protect novice injectors from harms associated with an increasingly potent drug supply by providing them with injection assistance, education, and supervision. Assisting novice injectors was seen as a form of harm reduction to prevent novice injectors from using alone or engaging in riskier injection practices. Our findings suggest that efforts to prevent injection drug use must be balanced with ensuring novice injectors have access to safer injecting environments. Structural interventions reducing the vulnerability of novice injectors should be prioritized, including the implementation of supervised injection sites allowing for assisted injection, Good Samaritan laws, and policy changes conducive to safer drug supply.

column36: Understanding how and why audit and feedback works: The role of process evaluations
column37: Health service interventions are inherently complex, involving a range of individuals and components. In order to inform policy and practice, it is essential to understand not only whether interventions work, but how or why they work. Process evaluations embedded within trials of health services interventions provide this valuable insight. This insight is critical for both understanding success (or failure) in the context of the trial, but also to support 1) adoption across trial sites and 2) spread and scale within the system. Identifying core components within complex interventions is necessary to produce definitive results of patient-oriented research and effectiveness studies and ensure interventions are adapted in a way that maintains previously demonstrated levels of effectiveness. In the absence of this insight, complex interventions cannot adapt without the risk of compromising their core function(s) or mechanism(s) of action, which is likely to render the intervention ineffective in new contexts. This work outlines the approaches to process evaluation of performance feedback interventions, using two case examples to illustrate their application. The first example demonstrates how to assess the factors that influence engagement with an intervention, and how this influences intervention design. The second example demonstrates how the contextual factors can influence the success (or failure) of evidence-based performance feedback interventions.

column36: Knockdown of the Mixed Lineage Kinase Domain-Like Protein (MLKL) Enhances Extramedullary Hematopoiesis to Increase Atherosclerosis
column37: Atherosclerosis is the greatest contributor to death and is characterized by increased blood cholesterol, as well as inflammation in the heart, and is typically recognized as a narrowing of vessels in the heart by a build up of cholesterol-rich plaques. During atherosclerosis, these plaques become unstable and break apart, leading to stroke or heart attack. This in part occurs as the cells of the plaque die, including a mode of cell death known as necroptosis. During necroptosis, through activation of the mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL), the cells release their contents and promote inflammation in the heart. We thus hypothesized that inhibiting MLKL would decrease the progression of plaque development during heart disease, however, we found that decreasing MLKL expression in fact increased plaque development. Plaque buildup begins as circulating immune cells home to the heart. These immune cells originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, however during heart disease, these stem cells migrate to the spleen and produce mature immune cells that are released into circulation. This process of stem cell production of mature immune populations in the spleen, however, is incompletely understood. In line with this we found that inhibition of MLKL increased the size of the spleens, as well as the number of the immune stem cells within the spleen but not the bone marrow. Furthermore, decreased MLKL expression in stem cells from the spleen increased their ability to form mature pro-inflammatory immune cells known to contribute to heart disease. These data therefore indicate that MLKL plays a critical role in repressing immune stem cells in the spleen, which therefore limit the production of the mature immune cells that to contribute to heart disease. Further study of MLKL function in controlling immune cells will in turn expand our knowledge of how immune cells are produced with the goal of developing methods to target this in humans to reduce heart disease.

column36: Bayesian modelling as an unsupervised approach to infer biological patterns in cancers and normal tissues
column37: Genes encode information to form proteins. Expression of genes as proteins results in observable biological properties. Studying how all the genes in our genome are expressed in different tissues and diseases can help us find better treatments and to understand our own biology. However, we have over 19,000 protein-coding genes in our genome, and understanding the behaviour of all of these genes at the same time is a challenging task. This makes it particularly difficult to study rare cancers and to understand the biology of aggressive cancers that have not been studied rigorously through molecular methods. The encoded information in every gene is translated into protein via multiple readouts called transcripts. These transcripts can be used to quantify the amount that each gene is expressed. We taught a neural network to take the expression values for all the genes (as the transcriptome) in various cancers and healthy tissues, and compress them into a smaller set of values. We then decoded the whole transcriptome back from this compressed set, and tested which genes were de-compressed accurately and which ones were not. We found that genes that are known to be essential for cells to survive, are learnt well, whereas obsolete genes and genes with minimal value in cellular development are learnt poorly. This suggests that our method is able to automatically learn which genes are relevant to the biology of individual cancers and healthy tissues, and discards the genes that do not play any important role in this dataset. Our results show potential in studying rare, advanced cancers and dissecting their biology using machine learning. This will eventually help us find better, targeted cures for the same in a short span of time.

column36: Dynamic influence of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition on circulating tumour cell generation, phenotype, and progression to metastasis in prostate cancer.
column37: Prostate cancer occurs as cells in the prostate gland accumulate mutations and become cancerous. Occasionally, these cells may enter the blood and migrate from the prostate to other parts of the body through a process known as metastasis. The process of metastasis is poorly understood and thus more research is required to fully comprehend the mechanisms involved in achieving metastasis. The CellSearch system is a test available to collect these circulating tumor cells (CTCs) from the blood and can be an indicator of metastasis of prostate cancer cells. However, this test may be unable to accurately detect the most aggressive CTCs. The purpose of this proposal is to use innovative technology and mouse models of metastasis to determine the key identifying characteristics of aggressive prostate cancer CTCs; to investigate how they contribute to prostate cancer metastasis; and to determine the best technology to analyze these important CTCs. CTCs hold enormous promise as biomarkers for prostate cancer progression. However, several scientific and technical issues remain to be resolved before the full potential of CTC analysis can be realized. This study aims to provide an important basis for development of improved CTC blood tests for minimally-invasive "real- time" tracking of CTCs and cell phenotype analysis throughout disease progression. These findings will improve the understanding of the mechanisms that underlie the metastatic process and will identify key characteristics of the most aggressive CTCs. This will lay the groundwork for improvement of technologies which may be used to investigate metastasis in mouse prostate cancer models and in human patient samples.

column36: Immune cell infiltration and tumour location predicts prognosis in colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer among the most commonly diagnosed cancers in Canada. The overall survival for metastatic colorectal cancer is 13%. There are several factors that limit our ability to accurately predict prognosis of individuals with colorectal cancer. Therefore, studies are warranted to discover more reliable prognostic factors, to better improve patient outcome. Additionally, there is an urgent need to develop more effective therapeutics, specifically to target advanced disease. Our study focuses on characterizing the influences of the immune system on colorectal cancer and identifying markers that will better predict patient outcomes. We therefore looked at the composition of immune cells within colorectal cancer and normal colon and examined differences in between the two. We also identified types of immune cells that are important for determining patient outcomes and used this in combination with genetic analysis to develop an algorithm that predicts patient prognosis for colorectal cancer. It is our hope that this algorithm will be a powerful tool to effectively assess prognosis of colorectal cancer patients.

column36: The Elapsed Time between Simulated Deep Inspirations on the Mechanics of Airway Smooth Muscle in Ovine Tracheal Strips
column37: We take deep inspirations unconsciously at a rate of about 1 every 6 minutes. The deep inspiration stretches the lungs, which also tends to elongate and dilate the airways embedded within the lungs. Oppositely, one special lung tissue, called the airway smooth muscle, is encircling the airways and sometimes contracts to constrict the airway lumen. This is especially concerning in patients with asthma, where respiratory symptoms occur due to excessive airway constriction caused by exaggerated contraction of the airway smooth muscle. It was previously demonstrated that the stretch inflicted by a deep inspiration relaxes the airway smooth muscle and thus accounts for the respiratory relief afforded by a deep inspiration. Obviously, the depth of the deep inspiration determines the magnitude of the stretch and the extent by which it is relaxing the airway smooth muscle. Interestingly, this relaxing response to a stretch is lost in asthma. The mechanisms liable for this aberrant response may contribute to excessive airway narrowing in asthma. Beyond the magnitude of the stretch, the frequency with which the deep inspirations are taken may also influence the contraction of airway smooth muscle. In this study, we have stretched the airway smooth muscle from sheep after different time intervals in order to determine whether the time elapsed without stretches influences the relaxing effect of a subsequent stretch. The preliminary results show that changing the time elapsed between stretches greatly influences its relaxing effect on the airway smooth muscle. These results are relevant to asthma as they may link the excessive airway constriction seen in asthma to a naturally abnormal frequency of deep inspirations.

column36: Constant Rate Shuttle Walking and Stair Stepping Tests to Assess Exertional Dyspnea in COPD: Responsiveness to Pulmonary Rehabilitation and Minimal Clinically Important Difference
column37: Breathlessness is the most common and troublesome symptom experienced by people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The 3-minute constant-rate stair stepping (3MST) & shuttle walking tests (3MWT) were recently developed and validated as standardized tests to evaluate breathlessness on exertion in the clinical care setting of COPD. While research suggests that these tests can detect acute changes in breathlessness after the use of common respiratory medications, it is not yet known whether they can detect changes in breathlessness following pulmonary rehabilitation (PR). In addition, the change in breathlessness that would be considered clinically important for a COPD patient during these tests is not yet known. Therefore, we evaluated the responsiveness of the 3MST & 3MWT to identify changes in breathlessness on exertion in 37 adults living with COPD after an 8 to 12-week PR program. Patients were asked to rate their levels of breathlessness on a 10-unit scale at the end of the 3MST & 3MWT before and after PR. Results of all pooled participants showed no statistically significant change in levels of breathlessness after the 3MST or 3MWT following PR. However, when the analyses were limited to patients whose level breathlessness was rated as moderately severe (3 or higher on the 10-point scale) at the end of these tests prior to the start of PR, the changes in breathlessness were statistically significant. We also estimated that the minimal clinically important change in breathlessness ratings was 0.9 out of 10 units for the 3MST and 1.0 units for the 3MWT. The preliminary results of this project suggest that the 3MST and the 3MWT are responsive to identify changes in breathlessness on exertion following PR in COPD patients, but only if their baseline levels of breathlessness are at least moderately severe. In addition, a change in self-reported breathlessness of 0.9 units or more during the 3MST and 3MWT are clinically meaningful to people with COPD.

column36: Adaptation and implementation of a decision support tool for patient prioritization following mild traumatic brain injury: a study protocol
column37: Mild traumatic brain injuries (mTBI) represent 70% to 90% of all TBI cases and their incidence has more than doubled in the past years. Patients who suffered a mTBI can experience persistent symptoms for a few weeks up to over a year post-injury, which could result in functional disabilities. In Quebec, three months post-injury, patients at risk of chronic symptoms are referred to rehabilitation centers so they can receive specialized services by a multidisciplinary team. However, long waiting lists are common and often make timely access to rehabilitation services impossible. Waiting lists management and patient prioritization are not standardized practice and are often based on opinion of one person. Optimizing waiting list management for rehabilitation services is crucial for mTBI patients and an adapted decision support tool (DST) for patient prioritization could be an interesting solution to help waiting lists management for those patients. The aim of this project is to implement a prioritization DST for mTBI patients in three Quebec trauma rehabilitation programs. To achieve this goal, a survey of stakeholders (patients, clinicians, decision-makers, researchers) will be conducted using the Delphi method until a consensual list of prioritization criteria is obtained. These criteria will be included in the DST-mTBI to facilitate and standardize the assessment of patients' needs. Based on this evaluation, patients will be assigned to a dynamic list according to the consensus-based criteria. DST-mTBI will then be implemented in three rehabilitation settings in the province of Quebec. Changes induced by this DST-mTBI will be measured on patients (TBI symptoms, anxiety, depression, satisfaction with services) and clinicians (attitudes and sense of clinical utility) using a pre/post design. This project proposes a significant paradigm shift in waiting list management from a time-focused approach to a standardized approach based on potential impacts on individuals.

column36: Cellular Photoprotective and Antioxidant Properties of Lipids in an Oral Skincare Supplement
column37: Ultraviolet (UV) light is associated with multiple health risks, such as sunburn, premature skin-aging, and skin cancers, which are in part the result of damaging UV-induced oxidative stress. The ingestion of certain natural products, known as "photoprotectors", can increase skin's UV-resistance. Our research focuses on the cellular effects of Bend Beauty, Inc.'s oral supplement called "Bend Skincare Anti-Aging Formula" (AAF), which contains daily doses of a combination of active ingredients: the omega-3 fatty acids (1) eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA; 1050 mg) and (2) docosahexaenoic acid (DHA; 350 mg) from fish oil, an anti-inflammatory omega-6 fatty acid called (3) gamma-linolenic acid (GLA; 120 mg), plant pigment compounds called (4) zeaxanthin (2.5 mg) and (5) lutein (5 mg), and (6) vitamin D3 (1,000 IU). A clinical trial completed using AAF found that the skin of volunteers who took the supplement daily for 8 weeks required an average of 84% more UV radiation to induce skin redness. I am testing the ability of AAF to protect human skin cells from UVA and UVB light, the two forms of UV light that reach the Earth's surface and cause harm to our skin. Through a variety of cell-based experiments, I have shown that cells treated with AAF for 2 weeks require over 3x as much UV light to induce the same amount of cell death as seen in untreated cells. In addition, skin cells treated with AAF become 2.5-fold more resistant to hydrogen peroxide; a compound commonly used in laboratories to mimic cellular oxidative stress and which is known to be induced in skin by UV-radiation. The data we have collected so far provides evidence that Bend Beauty's Anti-Aging Formula can increase skin cell resistance to UV-light and oxidative stress, which are associated with premature skin-aging and the development of skin cancers. We are therefore excited to continue our research into this product and to share our results with the scientific community.

column36: Effect of holding and grasping objects on risk for head impact during falls in older adults
column37: Falls account for nearly 80% of traumatic brain injuries in older adults, and head impact occurs in one-third of falls in long-term care (LTC) residents. Grasping objects while falling may affect upper limb fall arrest strategies and risk for head impact during falls. We analyzed videos of 1238 real-life falls from standing-height in LTC residents, to determine whether falling with the hands free versus grasping objects affects the odds of head impact. Holding weight-bearing objects (e.g., chairs; walkers) at the onset of a fall, or successfully reaching to grasp weight-bearing objects after balance loss, both reduced the odds of head impact. Conversely, holding non-weight-bearing objects (e.g., cups, purses, clothing) increased odds of head impact. Our results can inform strategies to reduce the consequence of falls, by showing that risk for head impact during falls in LTC residents was strongly influenced by holding objects, and the nature of the object.

column36: Promotion of cognitive health in older people from the perspective of the theory of salutogenesis: a review of literature
column37: To promote healthy cognitive aging, public health could shift efforts from a model that emphasizes frailty and "gaps" to one that reinforces "assets". The theory of salutogenesis (SalT) is a promising framework for the reinforcement of assets; however, it has not become a working instrument for policymakers or public health professionals. Possible reasons include the fact that (a) the principal concept of the SalT, sense of coherence (SOC, the perception of the world as meaningful, manageable and comprehensive), was not shown to predict health status in empirical studies; (b) resources about SOC (wealth/status, ego identity, spirituality, protective health orientation, coping, social support, skills/knowledge and commitment) have not been systematically studied in the SalT frameworks. In this work, we assessed the usefulness of the SalT to explain cognitive health in elderly populations. We conducted a Pubmed search. Further, we examined pertinent results of empirical studies with key concepts of the SalT (SOC and resources about SOC), namely: the concept of the SalT as an independent variable, and cognitive health outcomes (cognitive functions, and incidence and prevalence of dementia) as a dependent variable. We found consistent positive associations between all the key concepts of the SalT and cognitive health outcomes in the elderly. Also, we found that (1) some of these associations were more studied than others; (2) some of the key concepts are indistinguishable (e.g.: coping and skills/knowledge) in real-life empirical studies and (3) that the recent development of the theory in public health would permit the rearrangement of the SalT to make the theory more suitable for the practical implementation.. Further discussion between researchers, health professionals and community members is needed to create a workable SalT.2.0 framework to promote cognitive health among older adults.

column37: My current research examines health worker dilemmas and decision-making in humanitarian emergencies. In particular, my research focuses on the multifaceted set of clinical, social and operational challenges that arise in these complex settings and almost immediately become daily and significant dilemmas for local health workers on the frontlines of service delivery. Unlike their expatriate counterparts, local health workers have minimal training on emergency preparedness and response, yet they face overwhelming circumstances when emergencies strike including limited supplies and equipment, increased workload and long working days, lack of pay, dangerous transportation and working conditions, and disconnection from social and professional support systems. How health workers navigate these everyday challenges has been demonstrated as critical to the provision of quality care which ultimately affects health outcomes, but has received inadequate attention. If left unaddressed, these challenges can erode the skills, motivation and retention of local health workers leading to ineffective health care services and exacerbating the already poor health outcomes characteristic of these settings. Working in South Sudan and Rwanda, my research aims to produce evidence of local health workers' dilemmas and decision-making experiences in humanitarian emergencies to inform the design and evaluation of locally-responsive interventions that support the provision of quality essential health care during difficult times and in marginalized areas. Taking an interdisciplinary and participatory approach, I am employing a mix of anthropological and epidemiological methods to incorporate and feature the complexity of the context and health workers' dilemmas into the design and evaluation of the intervention. This research will contribute to the increasing emphasis for evidence to inform policymaking on human resource development and health systems strengthening in humanitarian emergencies.

column36: Care Pathway on "Promoting Physical Activity and Reducing Sedentary Behaviour in Individuals with Cerebral Palsy over the Life Course"
column37: Many children with cerebral palsy (CP) aged 2-3 with limited walking and physical activity (PA) ability showed marked improvement by adolescence after intensive rehabilitation, demonstrating the impact of PA in improving functioning in persons with CP. In fact, individuals with CP need more PA compared to the typically developed population to offset their more rapid decline in physical fitness as they age. However, up to 50% of adults experience a decline in physical functioning from adolescence, suggesting that individuals do not continue to engage in PA in order to maintain the effects of rehabilitation. Therefore, clinicians and policy-makers need a set of guidelines to help recommend PA interventions and community-based resources, respectively, that will promote sustained and long-term PA so individuals with CP can continue to experience the benefits of PA as they age; Interventions with a behavioural component and those that consider contextual factors such as community resources show promise. The Care Pathway on "promoting PA and reducing sedentary behaviour in individuals with CP over the life course", which will be published on the American Academy for CP and Developmental Medicine (AACPDM) website, aims to address the need for sustained PA through a set of guidelines informed by best evidence which helps clinicians and policy-makers make judgements in increasing PA in children and adults with CP. The aim of the Care Pathway is to integrate research and clinical opinion to accomplish the following goals: (1) Help clinicians make more individualized recommendations for interventions to increase PA for persons with CP by considering factors such as level of pain and ambulation (2) inform individuals with CP, their families and caregivers on the best PA intervention for their specific symptoms (3) Motivate and guide policy-makers in establishing community-based projects to make PA resources widely available.

column36: Impact of pathogenic DNMT3A mutations on cell lineage specification and programming in Tatton-Brown-Rahman Syndrome
column37: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by tall stature, intellectual disability, heart defects and dysmorphic facial features. With this approach, we will be able to analyse how newly brain, muscle, bone and heart cells are affected. Overall, this project will uncover the functional impact of DNMT3A mutations, and provide a functional model to test new therapeutic avenues to treat TBRS.

column36: The Dynamic Relationships of Physical Activity and Sleep Quality with Cognitive Health
column37: Maintaining sleep quality and cognitive health are critical for healthy ageing. Specifically, poor sleep quality is linked to impaired cognitive performance across the lifespan and with dementia in late life. Thus, effective lifestyle strategies which can positively impact both are greatly needed. One potential strategy is promoting physical activity (PA). Strong empirical evidence suggests PA promotes cognitive health, and there is increasing evidence PA may maintain cognitive health by promoting better sleep. In addition, preliminary evidence suggests PA may help maintain circadian rhythm alignment, which weakens with age leading to declines in sleep quality and cognitive function. Thus, this symposium will provide a summary of the current evidence for 1) the implications of poor sleep on cognitive health; 2) how PA and sleep are linked to cognitive function and each other; and 3) how PA may be useful in circadian re-alignment (i.e., chronotherapy) to promote sleep and cognitive health.

column36: Stakeholder recommendations to increase access of marginalized young women to government support programs in Botswana: evidence-based group discussions
column37: Young women in southern Africa are at high risk of contracting HIV due to structural factors like poverty, poor education and gender-based violence. The INSTRUCT intervention aims to provide young women with better access to government support programs to reduce their reliance on transactional sex and prevent the spread of HIV. Recruiting young women to participate in this intervention proved challenging, and so we explored novel methods to engage this population. In discussions with young women, community leaders, and government service providers, we presented findings from our previous survey on the support networks of young women, and discussed strategies for how to reach young women with information about support programs. Short-term suggestions for sharing information about available programs included forming local committees of young women, using existing village committees, and using social media. Longer-term suggestions included creating a database of phone numbers for mass SMS notifications, and changing the requirements for program applications. Although community leaders felt program information should be shared via social media, young women were not interested in this strategy since they had limited access to phones, internet, and, at times, electricity. Trust was an important factor in determining who young women sought information from and it was often associated with people that had similar lived experiences. They preferred going to friends and family, rather than going to government service providers to learn about available support programs. These findings provide an opportunity to better include young women in support programs and prevent HIV in Botswana. Using existing committees within communities and building new connections to government service providers could help spread information. The participatory process of sharing findings with stakeholders and discussing local solutions is generalizable to others working with hard-to-reach populations.

column36: Investigation of the role of progerin-induced aging in tauopathies
column37: Tauopathies are a diverse group of age-related dementia characterized by filamentous tau lesions in brain. Alzheimer's disease and Pick's disease are examples of tauopathies that have presented a tremendous challenge to health care systems worldwide. Genetically, tauopathies often do not run in families and are therefore described as 'sporadic', which is typically encountered in late adulthood. Although chronological age has been reported to be the greatest risk factor of sporadic tauopathies, very little is known about how aging gives rise to the pathology at a molecular level. The overarching goal of my research is to visualize the initial aging-related molecular events that result in sporadic tauopathies, in models that can mimic the physiology of normally aged human central nervous system. To achieve this, we can take advantage of the mutation of Hutchinson Gilford progeria syndrome (mutant protein termed 'progerin'), a lethal condition associated with accelerated aging. By artificially introducing the progeric mutations into cell models of tauopathies, we can construct a molecular environment that, to a large extent, mimics natural aging. Then by assessing initial aging-induced pathology, we may tease apart the complexity in its sporadic nature of tauopathies, which may provide insights into the development of new disease models and early disease intervention.

column36: Evaluating the relationship between circulating osteoprotegerin levels and bone mineral density in BRCA mutation carriers
column37: Women who inherit a deleterious mutation in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes face a high lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. column37: Latent virus integrated into the host's genome in CD4+ T-cells remains the main barrier to HIV cure. Here we characterized these distributions in four subsets of CD4+ T-cell: naive, central memory, transitional memory and effector memory. We sorted CD4+ T-cells collected from 5 participants into the four subsets and then sequenced HIV DNA integrated into these cells. We then assessed the subsets for compartmentalization of HIV; in other words we asked if viruses in the same subset were more similar to each other than viruses found in other subsets. Finally we applied a phylogenetic approach to estimate the ages of the integrated virus in each cell type using previously extracted virus from 4 of the participants' plasma. Two of the five participants showed evidence of compartmentalization. The age distributions between were comparable in two of the participants; however in one participant, viruses in effector memory cells were youngest and in a different participant, viruses in naive cells were youngest. HIV cure researchers should consider the varying composition of latent HIV sequences between hosts and between CD4+ T-cell subsets when developing cure strategies.

column36: Cerebrovascular regulation in breath-hold divers with chronic exposure to long-duration apneas
column37: Breath-hold divers complete long duration breath-holds repeatedly in training and competition with the current world record sitting over 11 minutes for a stationary breath-hold. With long duration breath-holds, divers experience simultaneous decreases in arterial oxygen content and increases in arterial carbon dioxide levels. The changes in arterial blood gases generates a severe physiological stress for the human body. Understanding the impact of this repeated stress on brain function is of interest and has not been studied to date. This study investigates the regulatory mechanisms of the blood vessels in the brain in breath-hold divers and healthy controls. Specifically, rate of regulation was calculated to assess cerebral autoregulation, a fundamental control mechanism in the brain. Participants completed a sit-to-stand task to perturb blood pressure and brain blood flow. Upon standing arterial blood pressure drops. The resulting reflex response is a drop in vascular resistance to allow an increase in flow to ultimately maintain cerebral blood flow at a relatively stable level. The rate of regulation assess the percent change in vascular resistance per second for a given change in arterial blood pressure. With standing the breath-hold divers and healthy controls experienced a similar drop in arterial blood pressure. However, the breath-hold divers demonstrated reduced rate of regulation, by 50%, compared with the controls. Underlying the reduced rate of regulation in the divers was a longer time to achieve the required change in vascular resistance. Therefore, the divers demonstrated a slower recovery of brain blood flow to baseline levels. The data suggest impaired cerebral autoregulatory mechanisms in divers exposed to repeated long-duration breath-holds, demonstrating the chronic adaptations in brain blood flow control that may accompany repeated exposure to stress.
