column36: Platelets express a truncated form of TrkB involved in BDNF signalling
column37: BACKGROUND: The brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a naturally occurring substance that has been discovered in the brain. It is responsible for neurons growth, healing of brain vessels and has a role in depression, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. BDNF has also been found in platelets with much higher amounts than the brain. Platelets are small cells that circulate in blood and help form a plug to prevent bleeding in case of injury. This fact raises the question about what role can a brain growth factor have in platelets and how it is involved in clot formation. WHAT WE HAVE DONE: We have isolated platelets from the blood of healthy volunteers to study their response to BDNF. We have found that BDNF is able to stimulate platelets, so they can form clots. Since we don't know how BDNF is able to stimulate platelets, we blocked different pathways (like locking doors) in order to determine which pathway (door) BDNF uses. We were able to identify few players in the pathway. WHAT WE WILL DO: We will continue the work and identify the whole pathway activated by BDNF. As mentioned earlier, platelets contain very large amounts of BDNF and surprisingly, they are unable to produce it since they don't have the necessary machinery. We will investigate where all the BDNF in platelets comes from and what role it can have in platelets and blood vessels. POTENTIAL BENEFITS: By better understanding how platelets respond to brain growth factors, we will be able to encourage platelet to release of their useful cargoes and help vessels heal. This might be particularly important in the vessels that nourish the brain, where damaged blood vessels could lead to stroke and dementia. Platelets may be a new avenue of treatment for these crippling diseases.

column36: Informant's distress caused by neuropsychiatric symptoms is correlated with tau deposition in the Alzheimer's disease spectrum
column37: Introduction: Neuropsychiatric Inventory-Questionnaire (NPI-Q) is a survey addressed to informants to assess the participant's neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) and their impact on the participant (global severity) and their informant (global distress). Although NPS has been closely related to the clinical progression to dementia in carriers of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology, the relationship between NPS and brain amyloid and tau pathologies is still unclear. Here we hypothesize that tau and amyloid deposition associate with different subscales of the NPI-Q, across the AD clinical spectrum. Methods: 94 individuals (AD, MCI, CN) underwent scans observing deposition of AD pathophysiologies and their informants filled in the NPI-Q. A model evaluated the relationship between the accumulation of each biomarker and the NPI-Q global scores, and the 12 subscales. Results: We did not find association between global NPI-Q scores (distress and severity) and brain amyloid deposition. Tau deposition was however correlated with global NPI-Q distress, but not with global severity score. The most impacted regions were the frontal lobe and precuneus. Additionally, 9/12 subscales correlated with tau accumulation. The strongest correlations were with depression, correlated with frontal lobe/precuneus tau deposition, and hallucinations and delusions both showing high tau pathology in the cuneus. Conclusion: These preliminary results showed a strong association between the distress caused by the patients' NPS in their caregivers and tau aggregation in regions of brain recognized as being associated with NPS and AD. The findings align with the idea that tau is more closely related with cognitive and behavioral symptoms than amyloid. This study demonstrates NPS correlate with tau and it is thus important to assess them in the AD clinical spectrum. Moreover, it emphasizes the importance of the informant's perspective in the management of diseases, which is often overlooked.

column36: The Case Management Challenge: A systematic review and thematic synthesis of barriers and facilitators to case management in primary care
column37: As baby boomers grow older and levels of chronic illness rise in our society, the current healthcare system has become increasingly ill-equipped to meet the needs of these patients. In response to this increased burden of chronic illness, a new model of healthcare delivery - case management - has emerged as a way for healthcare professionals to better care for patients with complex needs. Case management is defined as the collaborative process of assessment, planning, facilitation, care coordination, evaluation and advocacy for options and services to meet an individual's and family's comprehensive health needs (Case Management Society of America). While case management works well, healthcare teams have notoriously struggled to implement this new model into daily practice. Accordingly, we sought to understands the factors that affect the ability of healthcare professionals and teams to do - or not do - case management in primary care. To do so, we searched for every study around the world that examined this topic. We found 19 research studies, originating from six countries. Overall, nine common "factors" (aspects that help or hinder case management) were identified from the studies. We spend the majority of our analysis describing these factors, mapping them out, and explaining potential relationships between individual factors. Overall, this review identifies important factors that influence the ability of healthcare professionals to do case management in primary care. Such findings may allow for the development of interventions of policy- or clinic-level interventions to improve case management function and, by extension, to provide better care for patients with complex needs.

column36: Prevalence of pretreatment low frequency drug resistance mutations and its implication on treatment outcome in Uganda
column37: HIV is a virus that impairs the immune system by destroying white blood cells. If left untreated, HIV can cause Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) and have deadly consequences. Today, there are more than 85,000 Canadians living with HIV and more than 36 million individuals globally infected. HIV can be treated using a combination of drugs, a treatment method known as "Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy". This combinational form of treatment prevents AIDS and HIV transmission to others. Unfortunately, HIV can become resistant to one or more of the drugs within combinational treatment. Drug resistance occurs by random changes (mutations) in the genetic material of HIV. Some mutations can lead to drug resistance resulting in treatment failure and progression of HIV disease in patients. Drug resistant HIV can also be transmitted to other individuals. Individuals who start HIV treatment with drug resistant HIV have fewer treatment options in their lifetime. In certain low- and middle-income countries in the world, such as Uganda, pretreatment drug resistance to widely used drugs called nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors are found in >10% of adults and children starting HIV treatment for the first time. Current drug resistance tests detect resistance mutations present in the majority of the HIV population found in an individual. However, low frequency drug resistance mutations not commonly detected using standard resistance tests have been suspected to affect how individuals respond to HIV treatment. Our study uses a deep-sequencing methodology to detect pretreatment low frequency drug resistance mutations in Uganda. We will investigate the prevalence of pretreatment low frequency drug resistance mutations and determine whether their presence has an impact on how individuals respond treatment. Treating HIV has both individual and public health benefits, and low frequency drug resistance may be a key factor in a patient's response to treatment.

column36: Pursuing change in illicit stimulant use in the context of daily injectable opioid agonist treatment: a grounded theory study with patients at Vancouver's Crosstown Clinic
column37: For people with severe opioid use disorder (i.e. heroin addiction) not responding to first-line treatments, evidence supports the effectiveness of injectable opioid agonist treatment (iOAT), where patients inject pharmaceutical-grade opioids daily under the supervision of nurses. Outcomes include significant reductions in opioid use, crime, health improvements, and modest declines in illicit stimulant use (i.e. cocaine and amphetamines). This study was the first to investigate the experiences of iOAT patients that use illicit stimulants. The study aimed to investigate from the perspective of patients, the processes by which their use of illicit stimulants changed in context of daily iOAT care. Qualitative interviews were done with 31 patients at the first iOAT clinic in North America. Using a grounded theory approach sampling, data collection, and data analysis were conducted in a back and forth process. Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The process of changing stimulant use in iOAT care was found to have four stages: 1) building capacity: where daily iOAT medication offered a sense of "freedom", and contact with care providers offered "connection"; 2) realizing potential: where participants described "identifying evolving goals" (e.g. relationships, health, employment) and "finding hope", seeing these goals as realistic; 3) taking action: where participants described "gaining control" over their stimulant use (e.g. practicing financial responsibility) and engaging in meaningful alternative activities (e.g. hobbies); 4) sustaining change: where participants described "recognizing progress" and "becoming experts" in their own health and service needs. When integrated, these four stages form the process of "pursuing change". Findings can support clinicians in understanding patients' evolving needs relating to their pursuit of stimulant use recovery in the context of iOAT care as treatment with injectable opioids expands across Canada.

column36: Hospice Use Among Long-Term Care Facility Residents in Canada
column37: It is estimated that between 16% and 30% of Canadians who die annually have access to or receive end-of-life care services, many of whom are referred to hospice programs in their last days of life. This study aims to describe and compare the characteristics of residents who received hospice care versus those who did not receive hospice care in their last year of life in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) in Canada. This retrospective cohort study used linked health administrative data from the Canadian Continuing Reporting System (CCRS) and the Discharge Abstract Database. Data in CCRS is routinely collected via the interRAI MDS 2.0. All persons residing in LTCFs between Jan. 1st, 2015 and Dec 31st, 2015 were included in this study. Death records were linked up to Dec 31th, 2016. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to describe and compare the characteristic of residents who received hospice care versus those who did not receive hospice care in their last year of life. Among the 185,715 residents resided in LTCFs in Canada in 2015, 30.9% died within one year of assessment, and 7.7% of them received hospice care in their last days of life. Residents more likely to receive hospice care in their last year of life were: younger; male; had a do not resuscitate order; lived in urban LTCFs; had diagnosis of cancer, anemia, or gastrointestinal disease; had a diagnosis of dementia, depression, stroke, or congestive heart failure; had less severe aggressive behaviors, lower level of social engagement, more severe physical impairment, more severe pain, higher pressure ulcer risk, and exhibited severe health instability. Expanding awareness of characteristics of residents who may benefit from hospice care compared to those who actually received hospice care may help LTCFs administrators, hospice care providers, and policy makers to identify ways to implement services and interventions that can improve access, utilization, and quality of hospice care in LTCFs.

column36: Thyroid hormone supplementation dampens GABAergic inhibition of the brainstem respiratory network in newborn rat
column37: Les hormones thyroidiennes (TH) sont essentielles au developpement du foetus et du nouveau-ne. Au cours de la grossesse, la mere sera la principale source de TH et ce n'est qu'en fin de gestation que la TH sera produite par le foetus. Par consequent, un deficit en TH compromet le developpement neurologique du foetus et du nouveau-ne et constitue un facteur de risque important pour plusieurs maladies. Les desordres respiratoires tels que l'apnee du premature et l'instabilite respiratoire sont une importante cause d'hospitalisation et de mortalite chez les prematures. Bien que ces desordres soient lies a l'immaturite ou une dysfonction de la commande respiratoire, l'influence de TH sur les circuits nerveux qui generent et regulent la respiration reste meconnus. Nous avons precedemment montre que le deficit en hormones thyroidiennes augmente l'inhibition GABAergique dans les elements centraux du circuit de controle respiratoire. Pour comprendre les mecanismes sous-jacents, nous avons teste les hypotheses selon lesquelles 1) les mecanismes cellulaires, y compris, mais sans s'y limiter, les co-transporteurs K + / Cl-, contribuent au retard du developpement du systeme GABAergique chez les rats nouveau-nes deficients en TH et 2) la supplementation en TH apres la naissance peut inverser cette inhibition renforcee. Grace aux techniques de Western blot et d'enregistrement electrophysiologique sur tronc cerebral isole, nous avons demontre que plusieurs mecanismes cellulaires sont en cause dans l'inhibition respiratoire par le systeme GABAergique chez les nouveau-nes deficient en TH et que la supplementation en TH agit precisement sur le developpement du systeme GABAergique pour contrer cet effet inhibiteur. Ces resultats fournissent de nouvelles hypotheses sur les origines des troubles respiratoires du nouveau-ne impliquant une reduction du rythme respiratoire telle que l'apnee du prematurite.

column37: Despite the health benefits, individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) do not accrue adequate amounts of physical activity (PA). Using peers and smartphone technology to deliver a PA intervention integrates important psychological precursors to behaviour change. The secondary objectives are to evaluate the influence of ALLWheel on psychosocial determinants of behaviour change. Participants will complete 14, 30-minute sessions of PA counselling that will be facilitate by a peer using a smartphone. Objective PA will be assessed using actigraphy. Theoretical psychosocial precursors to PA (ie, autonomy, motivation, self-efficacy) will be evaluated using self-report questionnaires. The ALLWheel program, available in English and French, presents a novel approach to PA promotion for individuals with SCI that may provide sustainable health benefits to many Canadians. An RCT is a important evaluation step before pursuing implementation trials with community partners. If effective, ALLWheel may be implemented across various age and diagnostic groups to have a broad geographic reach across Canada.

column36: Role of extracellular ATP in bone adaptation to mechanical environment
column37: Physical forces are critical for successful function of many organs including bone; however, they also have a destructive potential. Many cell types, including bone cells, such as bone forming osteoblasts, sense and actively adapt to physical perturbations to prevent critical damage. ATP release is one of the earliest cellular responses to mechanical stimulation. ATP and related molecules act through receptors of P2 family, which includes seven P2X ligand gated ion channels and eight P2Y G-protein-coupled receptors. Even though abnormal ATP release and signaling have been implicated in mechanoadaptation, the coordination between this fast signaling and long-term changes in bone mass is poorly understood. In this project, we combine expertise in cellular and tissue mechanobiology of bone to: 1) To determine how mechanically-induced cell membrane injury, repair and ATP release change with ageing; 2) To resolve the roles of multiple P2 receptors in generating cellular responses that are adaptive to the force of mechanical forces; 3) To understand the contribution of mechanically-induced cell injury, repair and ATP release to age-related decrease in bone capacity for mechanoadaptation. Thus, we will determine the causative links between the i) exposure to mechanical force, ii) early cellular events, including micro-injury and repair, and ATP release and signaling, and iii) a mechanoadaptive response of bone tissue as an organ. Importantly, understanding molecular mechanisms of age-related decline in bone capacity for adaptation to mechanical stimuli will allow to personalize exercise regimes for people of different ages, in particular for elderly, in order to improve their effectiveness.

column36: Cardiovascular Risk Moderates Aerobic Training Efficacy on Executive Function in Older Adults
column37: PURPOSE: To examine whether the Framingham Cardiovascular Risk Profile Score (FCRP) moderates the effect of a 6-month progressive aerobic training program (AT) on executive function in older adults with vascular cognitive impairment. METHODS: This is a secondary analysis of a proof-of-concept RCT in 71 older adults, who were randomized to either a 6-month, thrice-weekly, AT program, or usual care (CON). At baseline and completion, three executive processes were measured: 1) response inhibition by Stroop Colour Word Test; 2) working memory by digit span backward test (DSB), and 3) set shifting by the Trail Making Test (B-A; TMT). Baseline cardiovascular risk (CVR) was calculated using the FCRP, and participants were classified as low risk (<20% FCRP score; LCVR) or high risk (>20% FCRP score; HCVR). A complete case analysis (n=57) was conducted by an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to evaluate between-group differences. Age, baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment score, education, and baseline score for the outcome variable were entered as covariates. RESULTS: A significant interaction was found between FCRP and group (AT or CON) for the DSB (F(1,49)=4.67, p=0.03) and the TMT (F(1,50)=4.09, p=0.04). There was no significant interaction for the Stroop Test (F(1,48)=.802 p=.38). On the DSB test, AT improved performance compared to CON (3.74 vs. 2.75) in those with LCVR, while in those with HCVR, AT did not provide improvements compared to CON (2.97vs. 3.76). Similarly, for the TMT (B-A), AT improved performance compared to CON (52.66 vs. 80.12 in those with LCVR, while AT was not beneficial compared to CON in those with HCVR (98.80vs. 59.92). CONCLUSION: We found that CVR significantly moderates the efficacy of aerobic exercise on working memory and set shifting in older adults with vascular cognitive impairment. Our findings highlight the importance of intervening early in the disease course, when CVR may be lower, to reap maximum benefits of aerobic exercise.

column36: Identification of blood-based biomarkers to distinguish subtypes of interstitial lung disease
column37: Interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) are a group of disorders in which the lungs progressively get stiffer due to defective tissue repair mechanisms. This leads to decreased oxygen uptake into the blood and breathing difficulties, which can escalate into a series of life-threatening complications including respiratory or heart failure. Within the older Canadian population, ILDs have a comparable incidence (39.5-156.4 per 100,000) to breast and prostate cancer (68.1 and 110.4 per 100,000). Because there are several subtypes of ILDs, one of the major hurdles in effectively treating ILDs is accurately classifying the ILD subtype; many of the subtypes look similar on standard medical tests, but require vastly different treatments. As a result, establishing an accurate diagnosis can take several years and often requires invasive diagnostic tests such as a lung biopsy that have potential for significant complications. Importantly, misdiagnosis of ILD subtypes and inappropriate treatment can worsen patient outcomes. To date, there is no diagnostic tool that can accurately identify a single ILD subtype, which is a problem given the frequently inconclusive findings from traditional tests. Our project aims to be the first to develop a simple blood test that can provide clarity in the diagnosis of ILD cases.

column36: Development and Evaluation of Pulmonary Imaging Multi-Parametric Response Maps for Deep Phenotyping of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a lung disease caused by smoke inhalation leading to the inflammation and closure of airways as well as the destruction of lung tissue. X-ray computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lungs have provided unique characteristics of COPD. Although they both provide insight into COPD, CT and MRI look at completely different aspects of the lungs. CT measures lung structure while MRI measures lung function, and using only one of these measures limits what we can assess about COPD. Here we have developed a method to combine the measurements from both CT and MRI to provide a complete assessment of COPD in the lungs. This combined measurement is called a multi-parametric response map (mPRM) which provides a regional map of healthy and disease lung tissue. These mPRM may help characterise the diversity of COPD within patients and provide new insight into treatment choice for specific patients. In the future, we will apply this method to a larger study of patients to determine the clinical relevance of this technique and how these mPRM change with time and increasing disease severity.

column36: Sex and gender considerations in the evaluation of mobile health apps
column37: Sex and gender are often not considered in the development lifecycle of mobile health apps, including the evaluation phases; however, many diseases are experienced differently according to one's sex and gender. For example, previous research highlighted how chronic disease characteristics, such as those of Multiple Sclerosis (MS), which have known sex and gender differences, are not represented in the mobile health app space. The purpose of this research is to develop an evaluation framework tool for assessing the inclusion of sex and gender considerations into mobile health apps. This research outlines how sex and gender can be considered in the evaluation of apps through an evaluation framework tool. The tool guides evaluators to question whether the features of or information on the app reinforce sex or gender stereotypes, the assumptions the app is making about the user, and implied values. The evaluation tool was created by consulting the literature and identifying gaps in current health app evaluation frameworks. The tool offers a guide for app developers to critique their work through a sex and gender lens and determine if the app could be improved to promote inclusivity. This research also offers an example of how health information systems can curb gendered discourses. As no other health app evaluation tool exists that explicitly assesses sex and gender considerations, this tool contributes to incorporating equity lenses into health innovations. This tool is currently being tested through use by two health informaticians with expertise in evaluation frameworks for mobile health apps. Feedback from the evaluation will be used to refine the tool. Further evaluation will be done with experts in sex and gender research through consultation and simulation testing. More experts will be involved to provide insight into making the tool more inclusive and to add more comprehensive social justice lenses to this work.

column36: Assessment of Facilitators, Barriers and Preferences for Safe Exercise Routines in Firefighters: An Injury Prevention Investigation
column37: Firefighters have one of the highest rates of muscle, bone and joint injury of any profession. Firefighters train at very high levels to be prepared for the physically demanding tasks that they are required to do on the job. Surprisingly, almost half of their injuries occur during exercise/training, rather than on the fireground, and are due to overexertion, as well as unsafe practices and techniques. Firefighters may be aware of the risks of injury on the fireground, but unaware of the exercise/training risks. The costs of these injuries are high and can lead to early retirement. This study will accomplish three things. First, we will gain an understanding of why firefighters, despite being relatively healthy, have such high injury rates during training. We will conduct interviews with firefighters to understand their current training practices, techniques and habits. Using qualitative methods, we will identify key areas to address in order to improve the safety of firefighter training. We will also conduct a national survey with our firefighter partners to describe how these themes can be applied to the larger population of firefighters. This will allow us to determine if age, gender, location and the type of firefighting work influence training practices and perceived injury risk. This information will then be integrated with findings from our previous firefighter studies on musculoskeletal injury patterns to create three brief videos addressing injury risk, principles of safe exercise, and best practices in avoiding accidents during training. The videos will be created in consultation with firefighters. This research should lead to new applicable knowledge that can be shared to increase firefighter injury awareness. Direct benefits to firefighters should include a reduction in injury rates. Indirect effects of this work would reduce the costs of firefighter injury to municipalities and the healthcare system.

column36: Front-of-package nutrition labels: experimental evidence to guide national and global policy development
column37: As part of the Healthy Eating Strategy, the Canadian government is developing a range of new food policies to promote healthy diets, including the introduction of mandatory front-of-package (FOP) nutrition labels that will label foods high in sugars, sodium and saturated fats. There is also growing interest in FOP labelling policies globally: several FOP labels are in place in other countries (e.g., traffic light labels in the UK, Health Star Ratings in Australia, 'high in' nutrient warnings in Chile, 5-colour Nutri-Score labels in France), and many other countries are working to introduce their own FOP labelling strategies. There is an urgent need for evidence to guide the successful development of these labelling policies, including evidence to compare the relative efficacy of different labelling formats. This symposium will provide an overview of FOP labelling and summarize findings from three studies investigating the impact of FOP nutrition labelling systems. The studies presented in this symposium use innovative research designs (both Canadian and international) to assess consumer understanding and purchasing behaviours in response to different FOP labelling systems. All studies compared different FOP label designs to explore differences between Canada's proposed 'high in' system and other common FOP label formats used internationally. Delegates attending this symposium will gain an understanding of the status of FOP regulations in Canada and internationally, and will become familiar with different experimental methods that can be used to assess FOP labels and other nutrition policies. The session will also provide a context for discussion of the potential benefits, weaknesses and policy implications of the many different FOP nutrition labelling formats.

column36: Targeted epigenetic downregulation of osteopontin as a potential therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common fatal genetic disorder diagnosed in childhood, affecting 1 in 3,500 live male births. There is currently no curative treatment, with management of symptoms, including progressive muscle wasting and cardiovascular decline, being the only option. DMD is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene resulting in the lack of dystrophin protein which is required for muscle structure and function. Utilizing the rapidly advancing CRISPR/Cas9 technology, potential gene regulation of DMD modifiers is a promising strategy to reduce the disease progression in patients. We hypothesize that downregulation of proinflammatory disease enabling genes can be achieved using a modified CRISR/Cas9 system delivered by clinically relevant AAV vectors. In preliminary in vitro studies we developed a system to downregulate expression of osteopontin, a multifunctional protein regulating inflammation and fibrosis in dystrophic muscle. In the current proposal, we will test the efficacy of osteopontin downregulation using a re-engineered version of Cas9 coupled with a histone modifier HDAC3, through intramuscular administration in a mouse model of DMD. Successful results of this project will provide crucial data regarding therapeutic utility of this novel AAV compatible genome engineering vector for patients with DMD and establish a method for targeted epigenetic repression of osteopontin expression.

column36: Patient-Researcher Partnerships: Evaluating the Impact of an Online Module Featuring Video Narratives of Partnership Experiences
column37: Background: The conduct of patient-oriented research requires pragmatic support for successful partnerships amongst providers, researchers, and patients. A multidisciplinary team funded by the Ontario SPOR Support Unit is co-designing an online module featuring video narratives from patients' and researchers' stories of partnership so that others can learn from their experiences. This presentation will focus on the evaluation plan to better understand the value and impact of learning from this kind of resource from users' perspectives. Methods: The evaluation will employ a mixed methods approach. We will hold 3 focus groups of 4-6 patients and researchers with experience of research partnerships to: assess attitudes and experience with online learning; identify learning needs and interests; and review the content and navigation of the online training module. Participants will explore the module at home for 2 weeks; a follow-up survey will capture the perceived value of the resource, impact on partnership expectations and behavior, and suggestions for improvement. Web access and utilization data will be collected for 3 months following the public launch of the module. Conclusion: Given the limited evaluation evidence to date regarding the perceived value and impact of training and resource materials that aim to support patient-researcher engagement in research, we anticipate that the results will provide insights in several areas: 1) identification of learning needs of patients and researchers related to the creation and sustainability of patient-researcher partnerships across the different phases of the research life cycle; 2) patients' and researchers' perceptions of the value and impact of learning from a diverse sample of others' lived experiences of partnership in their own voices; 3) users' perspectives on the content, design and navigation of an evidence-based online resource that was co-designed with patient and researcher engagement.

column36: Calcium channel blockers and diuretics: A retrospective cohort study exploring a common prescribing cascade in older adults
column37: A prescribing cascades occurs when a drug-related side effect is interpreted by a health care provider as a new condition and a second, potentially unnecessary, drug is prescribed to "treat" the side effect. Prescribing cascades can lead to adverse events among older adults and avoidable costs to the health care system. It is important to identify when these cascades occur and to take steps to prevent or mitigate them. There have been reports documenting a prescribing cascade with calcium channel blockers (CCBs). CCBs are one of the most commonly prescribed drugs and are used to treat hypertension. Unfortunately, a common side effect is lower leg swelling, which may lead to a prescription for a diuretic to manage the swelling. Because we do not know how commonly this prescribing cascade occurs and who is at greatest risk, we analyzed health care databases for a population of older adults with hypertension in Ontario. Using drug claims databases, we identified all individuals who were newly prescribed a CCB and followed them over time to see if they were prescribed a diuretic. We compared how commonly this group was prescribed a diuretic to controls who were not on a CCB. From this analysis, we found that the rate of prescription of a diuretic was more than two-fold higher in those newly prescribed a CCB. We also found that the rates were similar in men and women. Our findings confirm the occurrence of this potentially inappropriate prescribing cascade in clinical practice. Interventions are needed to raise clinicians' awareness of the role of CCBs in lower leg swelling.

column36: Circulating Extracellular Vesicle-Associated MicroRNAs as Predictive Biomarkers of Cardiovascular Complications in End-Stage Renal Disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects roughly three million Canadians and is accompanied by considerable human suffering, premature death, and costly medical care. The incidence of ESRD and its associated cardiovascular (CV) complications continues to rise despite improved treatments for many of it's risk factors such as diabetes and high blood pressure. Recently, small circulating molecules in the blood, known as "Extracellular Vesicles" (EVs), have been though to be better biomarkers than the ones currently used to diagnose and predict these complications. We are therefore using multiple approaches to better understand the organ-level effects of extracellular vesicles and their cargo to gather the detailed mechanistic insight necessary for the development of an integrative cardiovascular risk prediction model for diabetic ESRD patients. The foundation of this study is the Predictors of Arrhythmic and Cardiovascular Risk in End Stage Renal Disease (PACE) cohort (n=571); a cohort of ESRD patients followed over four years, with a repository of clinical data with matched biological samples. We isolated these extracellular vesicles from plasma, characterized their properties using advanced molecular biology techniques and genetic sequencing. EV analysis revealed diabetic ESRD patients have increased circulating vesicle concentrations; in addition to having vesicles of a larger size. Data from our clinically translatable methologies identified numerous potential cargo biomarkers for cardiovascular complications of ESRD. We utilized statistical models to generate a panel of biomarkers which may serve as cardiovascular risk predictors for diabetic ESRD patients. This data will be weighted with the novel biomarker data and fully integrated to build a clinical risk prediction model for the development of CV complications in ESRD and re-assessed in a new cohort to replicate the findings and validate the risk prediction model.

column36: Dried-Blood Spot HIV and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Testing Uptake in Community-Based Bio-Behavioural Research
column37: Dried-blood spot (DBS) sampling is a way of easily collecting blood samples that can be carried out by any trained individual, with no professional designation required. DBS samples can be tested for the presence of HIV and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), thereby giving an estimate of the level of each virus that is present in the population that is sampled. Knowing the burden of these viruses can help identify priorities for prevention and treatment programs and for areas of research. DBS sampling hasn't been used widely in HIV or HCV testing settings, so this research project evaluates what the impact of DBS was in a community-based Canadian health survey survey of gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) called Sex Now 2018. GBMSM were recruited at 16 LGBTQ Pride festivals across Canada from June to September 2018. Participants had the option to provide DBS samples for HIV/HCV testing and could opt-in to receiving the results of these tests. Among 3634 total participants in Sex Now 2018, 85% (3106 participants) provided DBS samples for HIV and HCV testing. HIV was detected in 7% of all DBS samples and HCV infection was found in 0.3% of all DBS samples. 2% of the DBS samples did not have a sufficient sample that could be tested for HIV and 4% were insufficient for HCV testing. Most of the participants opted into receiving the results of the HIV and HCV tests. Sex Now 2018 represents the largest cross-sectional survey using DBS as a way of collecting biological samples for testing. DBS sampling had a reasonably high uptake, and the majority of DBS samples were sufficient for laboratory testing. Public health organizations and health survey researchers could benefit from using DBS sampling, with the option of returning participants' test results, as a relatively easy way of measuring HIV and HCV in specific populations that are affected by these viruses.

column36: A gendered perspective on healthy equity: Protective health practices and equitable access to local built environments
column37: The prevalence of chronic disease in Canada is a growing concern. Individual engagement in healthy behaviours (e.g., physical activity, healthy eating, medical screenings, etc.) can help to prevent the onset of chronic diseases. Adult engagement in healthy behaviours, however, is relatively low in Canada and may be moderated by factors outside of individuals' control, such as the built environment. Further, normalized behaviour patterns have created environments that disproportionately limit women's opportunities to fully participate in a range of healthy behaviours. Women, particularly, can experience avoidable and unfair barriers to engaging in healthy behaviours due to socialized gender norms such as household and care-taking responsibilities. From a critical feminist perspective, this proposed doctoral research aims to understand gendered experiences in the built environment related to health behaviours. A multi-method approach will be utilized to gather data on the perceptions and lived experience of adult women, as well as an assessment of the economic, physical, political, and social aspects of their local environment. This presentation will provide an outline of the proposed research including a hypothesis, timeline, and budget. This research intends to contribute to the limited literature that focuses on gendered experiences that impact health behaviours in the built environment. Specifically, it is anticipated that the findings will be used to draw attention to women's opportunities to engage in health behaviours that protect against chronic diseases and highlight aspects of the built environment that dictate these experiences. Recommendations will be made to both research and practice communities to assist in remediating barriers women face due to the features or characteristics of the built environments in which they live.

column36: Place and home among people living with HIV who use drugs: A qualitative study
column37: Research shows that sense-of-home can influence health of people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, impacts of home-making on HIV treatment among marginally-housed PLHIV who use drugs are poorly understood. We examined this relationship in Vancouver, Canada. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 31 PLHIV who use drugs, focusing on housing conditions, drug use, and HIV management. Interviews were analyzed thematically and interpreted by drawing on concepts of home. Findings indicate that sense of place may enable ability to manage HIV care, and is promoted through feelings of security within, and control over, housing environments.

column36: Do women with cardiovascular disease respond differently to aerobic interval training? Exploring the interaction between sex and exercise modality on psychological and cardiomtabolic health
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death and serious consequences in women. Following cardiovascular events, women suffer from worse mental and physical health when compared to men, leading to poorer recovery. While cardiac rehabilitation (CR) improves mental and physical health, fewer women than men participate in CR programs due to greater time constraints and less interest in a conventional moderate-intensity continuous exercise (MICE) program. High-intensity aerobic interval training (AIT) has emerged as an alternative time-efficient, effective exercise program. However, it was unknown if women and men benefit similarly from AIT and MICE. We investigated if the effects of AIT and MICE on mental and physical health were influenced by sex. We analyzed the records of 120 patients with CVD who attended an 8-week, twice weekly outpatient CR program. Depression and anxiety were assessed using a questionnaire. Physical heath (i.e., body mass, waist circumference and resting blood pressure) was assessed using standardized procedures at baseline and following CR. Sixty (30 women and 30 men) patients completed AIT and another 60 patients (30 women and 30 men) completed MICE. There were no differences in exercise sessions attended between women and men or between AIT and MICE. Both women and men improved anxiety, depression, body mass and waist circumference. In women, however, AIT lowered anxiety severity more than MICE (-1.7 2.7 vs. -0.4 2.8 points). In men, MICE lowered anxiety severity more than AIT (-3.2 2.9 vs. -2.3 2.9 points). AIT is an alternative exercise modality in CR settings to improve mental and physical health of women and men. However, the improvement in anxiety severity was clinically meaningful (i.e., more than 1.7 points decrease) only following AIT in women. These findings underscore that CR interventions tailored to sex have the potential to augment the effectiveness of CR.

column36: Structured exercise as a potential treatment option for prenatal depression
column37: Up to 20% of women experience depression during pregnancy and approximately 19% will continue to have feelings of depression after delivery. Most women will choose not to have prescribed medication for depression during pregnancy. Untreated prenatal depression significantly increases the risk for postpartum depression. Previous research supports exercise during pregnancy as a way to prevent prenatal depression, however exercise as a potential treatment for women who enter pregnancy at risk for depression has not been studied. Therefore the purpose of this study was to determine if exercise during pregnancy is an effective option to treat depression during pregnancy. This study took place in Madrid, Spain. Women <16 weeks pregnant were randomly placed in an exercise group (EG) or standard prenatal care (no exercise intervention) control group (CG). The EG participated in group fitness classes three times per week. All participants completed the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression scale (CES-D) at the beginning and at the end of the program (36-38 weeks gestation). A score greater than or equal to 16 on the CES-D indicates risk for depression. Thirty-six women in the EG and 25 women in the CG scored above 16 on the CES-D at the beginning of the program. At the end of the program, the EG had a significantly lower CES-D score (14.48.6) than the CG (19.411.1; p<0.05). Furthermore, the EG average CES-D score was below 16 at the end of the intervention, meaning they are out of the at risk category, whereas the score remained above 16 for the CG. More women in the EG had a score that decreased (n=30, 83.3%) than the CG (n=14, 56%; p<0.05). The results of this study show that a structured exercise program offered during pregnancy may be a treatment option among women who begin pregnancy already at risk for prenatal depression. Exercise may be better received by women than medication for reducing symptoms of depression during pregnancy.

column36: Distributed Leadership Enactment in the Implementation of Inter-Organizational Networks
column37: Providing care for populations that are increasing in medical and social complexity is a well-recognized challenge that necessitates coordinating services across multiple sectors and organizations. There is a need to re-organize how care is delivered to align with coordination efforts, in the form of inter-organizational networks. Drawing on distributed leadership theory, we examine how leadership is enacted in Health Links networks, a care coordination initiative in Ontario, Canada. We conducted a qualitative multiple case study of three Health Links. 30 participants participated in hour-long, semi-structured interviews. In all cases, the lead organization's influence was critical to the network's perceived successful implementation. When effectively leveraging their role, the lead organization empowered partners to enact distributed leadership across their network. However, strong variability was seen in the capacity of each lead organization to harness their power and position, resulting in mixed experiences of implementation.

column36: Characterizing regulatory pathways of ING1a-induced cellular senescence
column37: As our cells age and undergo multiple rounds of cell division, they enter a state called replicative senescence where they are still viable and metabolically active but no longer able to proliferate. The accumulation of senescent cells in aged tissues impairs the regenerative capacity of human systems and contributes to many age-related chronic diseases such as arthritis, type II diabetes, and cancer. Despite the growing interest in developing therapies that target senescent cells, the molecular mechanisms which underlie cellular senescence are not fully understood. We have previously identified INhibitor of Growth 1 (ING1), the first member of the ING family of type II tumor suppressor proteins, which regulate critical cellular processes such as senescence, apoptosis, proliferation, and cell migration. ING1a, one of the isoforms of the ING1 gene, increases in both RNA and protein levels during replicative senescence. Overexpression of ING1a in primary fibroblasts itself causes a replicative senescence-like arrest with associated phenotypes, including senescence-associated beta-galactosidase staining. In order to understand the mechanisms by which ING1a functions during replicative senescence and cellular aging, I am using a mass spectrometry-based approach to identify binding partners which are specific to this gene isoform. Such genes will help us identify mechanisms of ING1a and replicative senescence and can be considered potential targets of intervention for age and senescence-associated disorders.

column36: Composition of the Gut Microbiota and Its Metabolites Regulate Neutrophil Responses Towards Vascular Allografts
column37: Our immune system develops a close relationship with our gut bacteria. Early in life, the relative proportions of different bacteria are important for preventing the development of allergy and asthma and can regulate our immune system throughout the body. This is in part done by short chain fatty acids that bacteria produce when they break down fiber in the colon. This is an attractive field of research in the context of organ transplants since nearly all organ transplants fail due to damage caused by the recipient's immune system. This occurs even with anti-rejection drugs, so understanding how gut bacteria influence transplant rejection may forestall or prevent rejection with new therapies. Our studies looked at how the immune system attacks the blood vessels of an organ transplant. A section of aorta, was taken from donor mice and transplanted into the same position in recipient mice. Recipient mice who were given antibiotics at a very young age, equivalent to infancy and childhood in humans, had increased rejection of their transplants. We found a dramatically higher amount of neutrophils, a type of immune cell, in transplants. Antibiotic treated mice have an altered composition of bacteria in their gut, so we housed some of them in the same cage as untreated mice. Since mice derive some energy in their diet by eating stool, the gut bacteria was normalized between both groups of mice. This reversed the antibiotic-caused increase in rejection. We also provided acetate, a short chain fatty acid, in the drinking water and this had the same effect. Our results suggest that the specific composition of the gut microbiota can exacerbate transplant rejection.

column36: Examining Telegeriatrics in Northern British Columbia
column37: Canada's population is aging at a rapid rate and it is imperative that the health care system is able to meet the challenges associated with an increased older population. column36: Les proprietes neuroprotectrices de l'erythropoietine comme nouvel outil therapeutique contre l'apnee du premature
column37: L'apnee du premature est une complication qui touche plus de 85% des enfants nees prematures (moins de 34 semaines d'age gestationnelle) principalement due a l'immaturite du cerveau. L'apnee du premature est associee a des desaturations arterielles qui aboutissent a une augmentation du stress oxydatif conduisant a des morbidites systemiques dont un probleme de maturation et de developpement du cerveau qui est deja immature. De plus, L'apnee du premature est systematiquement traitee par la cafeine. La cafeine est un stimulant respiratoire capable de reduire la frequence des apnees. Cependant la cafeine n'est pas completement efficace, a peu pres 1 enfant sur 2 traite avec de la cafeine continue a faire des apnees elevees. La ventilation mecanique doit souvent etre associe a la cafeine pour avoir 100 % de reussite, mais ce traitement est tres agressif et aboutit souvent a des consequences nefastes surtout au niveau des poumons. Il est donc important de developper une nouvelle approche capable de d'etre combine a la cafeine. L'erythropoietine (EPO) est un puissant stimulant respiratoire mais egalement un antioxydant. C'est dans ce cadre-la que nous avons teste l'hypothese que dans un modele d'apnees du premature (hypoxie intermittente HI), L'EPO combine a la cafeine pourrait lutter contre les consequences respiratoires et le stress oxydatif cerebral chez les males et les femelles. Nos resultats montrent que L'EPO comme la cafeine diminue les instabilites respiratoires chez les males induites par l'HI sans changement chez les femelles. L'augmentation du stress oxydatif induite par l'HI est diminue par le traitement a l'EPO et a la cafeine chez les males et les femelles. L'administration des deux drogues ne montre pas d'effets benefiques cumulatifs

column36: Poly-substance use trends among COMPASS secondary school students from 2013-2017
column37: Poly-substance use refers to the current use of two or more substances and is a behaviour with uniquely adverse consequences. While current estimates are unavailable, 2008 data found that 12% of Canadian students in grades 7-12 were current poly-substance users. Since this time, e-cigarette vaping has seen a rise in popularity and recreational cannabis use has been legalized, potentially influencing youth poly-substance trends. The objective of this research was to examine poly-substance use trends among Canadian high school students in the COMPASS study over the past five years. The COMPASS study is a large prospective cohort study that collects behavioural health data from 60,000 students per year attending secondary schools (grades 9-12) in Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, British Columbia, and Nunavut. Five years of data were used, starting in 2013. Students reported current (i.e., past 30-day) cigarette, e-cigarette, alcohol, and cannabis use. Poly-substance users were defined as students reporting current use of more than one substance and rates of substance use and poly-substance use were determined each year. Poly-substance use is on the rise among Canadian high school students and this trend appears to be driven by increases in e-cigarette use. 23% of students reported current use of two or more substances in 2017 compared to 19% in 2013. E-cigarette use has risen from 8% in 2013 to 18% by 2017. Male and Indiegnous students were significantly more likely to report poly-substance use than female and white students respectively. Future policy, practice, and research should acknowledge this growing health behaviour among secondary school students.

column36: Defining and Evaluating Overdiagnosis in Mental Health: A Cross-sectional Study
column37: There is concern that some mental health disorders are overdiagnosed because of expanded definitions of disorders that medicalize ordinary life experiences and because many people diagnosed with some psychiatric disorders recover quickly without treatment. The term overdiagnosis is used to describe the application of diagnoses in a way that is consistent with agreed upon standards but does not result in net benefit for patients. It is not known, however, how the concept of overdiagnosis has been applied in the academic mental health literature and if it is being used in a way that is consistent with its intended meaning or if it is being used to describe other phenomena, such as misdiagnosis or false-positive tests. Additionally, it is not known if there are studies that have empirically evaluated whether overdiagnosis is present in mental health disorders or attempted to estimate its magnitude. The objectives of this study were describe how the term 'overdiagnosis' has been defined explicitly or implicitly in published articles on mental health disorders and to identify examples where attempts have been made to quantify overdiagnosis in a way consistent with its intended meaning. Articles were included if overdiagnosis was a dominant theme. We found that there are very few examples of the term overdiagnosis being used consistent with the intended meaning in the mental health literature. Most articles that used the term used it incorrectly, most commonly to refer to individuals who have been incorrectly diagnosed with one disorder instead of another or who do not meet diagnostic criteria for any disorder. Analyses are needed that attempt to quantify overdiagnosis and that identify classes of patients unlikely to benefit from diagnosis.

column36: Deep Learning Approach to Localization of Skeletal Landmarks in Ultrasound for Scoliosis Measurement
column37: Scoliosis, which is an excessive curvature of the spine, affects approximately 1 in 1,000 individuals in early adolescence, progressing until the spine is fully developed. Bracing is a common treatment method, which decreases the progression of curves and significantly reduces the probability of needing surgery. For bracing to be effective, early referral is critical, but often difficult due to the lack of a safe and widely usable spinal curvature measurement method. One possible spinal measurement method is ultrasound; spinal curvatures can accurately be computed from skeletal landmarks, typically the transverse processes, localized in the ultrasound images. But obtaining ultrasound images of the spine that contain transverse processes with the necessary clarity is a technically difficult skill which requires considerable training and practice. In order to aid the sonographer and make spinal ultrasound scanning a more straightforward practice, we propose the use of deep learning to help with the detection and localization of transverse processes in the image. Deep learning using convolutional neural networks is very powerful for image classification and computer vision and it can be applied to the spinal ultrasound images. Use of deep learning may open the way for ultrasound to be deployed as a wide-scale safe, affordable and accurate scoliosis screening tool.

column36: Neurocognitive Aging and the Frontal Lobe: A Diffusion Tensor Imaging Study
column37: Our population is growing older. By 2030 1 in 5 Canadians will be aged 65 or over; this rise results in heavy costs to the health care system and to caretakers. While this is partly due to an increase in the prevalence of dementia with age, healthy aging is also known to cause cognitive declines in working memory, processing speed, and attention, which impact the health and quality of life of the elderly. At the center of these declines is the frontal lobe. Studies have found that of all brain regions the frontal lobe is most affected by the aging process; frontal lobe white matter, which contains the axons necessary for neuronal communication, experiences a disproportionately greater loss of integrity compared to white matter in other lobes. Despite these findings, no study has examined how discrete changes in frontal lobe connectivity correspond to changes in cognitive ability. Our group was the first to develop imaging methods to study frontal lobe white matter in more detail by measuring structural changes in frontal white matter subregions related to cognitive performance. The proposed study will use diffusion tensor imaging to measure various white matter tracts of the frontal lobe in participants across the lifespan (18-85). Age related changes will be compared to cognitive test scores for tasks that correspond to that frontal lobe area. This study will help us better understand the effects of healthy aging on the human brain, both in terms of structural and cognitive changes. By characterizing healthy brain changes and the corresponding cognitive declines with age, scientists will better understand how the functions of the frontal lobes change with age, and better diagnose and treat age-related brain disorders.

column36: Pro-resolving lipid mediator Resolvin D1 reduces inflammation and promotes lesion regression by targeting cell death pathways in atherosclerosis
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) are the leading cause of illness and death in the world. Atherosclerosis is one them and is responsible of one fifth of death in Canada. Atherosclerosis affect blood vessel (arteries) that carry fresh oxygen rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body. In this disease, fatty plaques are developing in arteries leading to reduced and blocked the blood flow. The formation of plaques is asymptomatic but the complete obstruction lead to heart attack or stroke in brain. Targeting risk factors for atherosclerosis has reduced mortality. But current therapies are not preventive and remain partially effective. Further understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms and regulatory pathways active in atherosclerotic plaques promises to yield more effective treatment for patients afflicted with this disease. Recently, the role of anti-inflammatory lipids could be a player in artery inflammation stability. This breakthrough discovery prompted us to evaluate the role of this anti-inflammatory lipids with particular attention to its interaction with other process in this disease. We believe our work is unique as it implicates the unexplored pro-resolving mediators in atherosclerosis and studies novel targets in this context of inflammation. Therefore, the benefits that will stream from our research are likely to be complementary and not redundant to current medications for atherosclerosis.

column36: Addressing Equity Considerations in the Canadian Rheumatology Association (CRA) Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) Guidelines Update
column37: In 2012, the Canadian Rheumatology Association (CRA) published a 2-part guideline focussed on the treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). In the upcoming update of these recommendations, a new section will be included: health equity. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is known to manifest differently in subgroup populations, such as by ethnicity and biological sex, with worse treatment outcomes seen. Treatment goals and patient preferences for treatment may also vary by population group. To fully address health equity in the guidelines, we need to understand which differences exist, and also how implementation of the treatment recommendations may differ by population group. In this project, the student will assist in finalizing which populations from the PROGRESS-Plus categories are of priority for Canadian rheumatology practice and will be specifically discussed in the CRA RA Guidelines update. From there, clinical trial data will be analyzed for population-specific treatment effect. Enough data needs to be present in order to draw comprehensive and true conclusions. Differences in patient preferences (for either therapy, or outcome) of selected population groups will be examined from existing data sources. Collaboration with experts in the field and identified subgroup population patients will identify how treatment recommendations should be implemented in order to minimize differential outcome effects.

column36: How is gestational weight gain between clinical visits best estimated in twin and singleton pregnancies?
column37: Maternal weight gain is a potentially modifiable characteristic of pregnancy that has been associated with the health of both mothers and children. Traditional studies often explore the total or rate of maternal weight gain in pregnancy; however, these measures are imprecise, and their cumulative nature may bias results in studies of some health outcomes. Emerging research aims to leverage serial maternal weight measurements to more reliably investigate this association. However, research is often constrained by limited availability of information obtained at discrete gestational ages. Therefore, this research aimed to investigate and compare methods for estimating maternal weight between clinical visits. Two large clinical chart abstractions studies in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania were leveraged to address this objective, although results are likely similarly applicable to pregnancies in Canada. Among the wealth of longitudinal data collected, we retained select maternal weight measurements (i.e. pre-pregnancy/delivery weight, as well as weight measured at first prenatal and glucose screening visits) in models to predict measurements at all other visits. We then calculated the difference between measured and predicted maternal weight, and summarized these differences (i.e. median, range, and mean squared error) to determine the relative performance of each model. Overall, 16 models were explored; 4 individual models that considered each mother's data separately, and 12 pooled models that borrowed information from all mothers to estimate each mother's pattern of weight change throughout pregnancy. We found that individual and pooled models that incorporated considerable variation in both pre-pregnancy weight and pattern of weight gain performed best. It is anticipated that these results will inform both ongoing and future studies investigating the relationship between maternal weight gain and pregnancy outcomes in North America and internationally.

column36: Foodservice manager perspectives on the feasibility of sustainable menu practices in Quebec healthcare institutions
column37: Food sustainability is a concept that is emerging in many countries around the world, including Canada. Sustainable food explores many dimensions related to food, namely its nutritional value, its quality, its social value, its environmental impact, and its economic and governing influences. The goal of food sustainability is to achieve better human and environmental health through these dimensions. Foodservices in institutions may take actions, termed sustainable menu practices (SMPs), to align themselves with these dimensions. The purpose of this research is to describe if including SMPs in healthcare institutions menus is acceptable and/or suitable, in the province of Quebec, Canada. In partnership with Nourish, a national initiative on the future of food in healthcare, this study is conducted out to allow the development of a practical tool for foodservice managers, helping them achieve SMPs in their menus. To carry out the research, 17 foodservice managers participated in the study, where they were interviewed about their perceptions on sustainable food in their foodservice. Results show many barriers and facilitators in including SMPs in foodservice menus, as well as different motivations set by managers. Knowing this information can help better adapt a tool meant to help foodservice managers, based on what they find most difficult to overcome when including SMPs. This knowledge can then guide Canadian institutions in adopting SMPs, providing all the health benefits of sustainability at the human and at the environmental levels.

column36: Grey Tsunami: A narrative ethics argument against the trend of existing ageist word choices
column37: The Grey Tsunami metaphor is gaining momentum and a Google search returned with 70 million hits with projections to rise even higher in the next couple of years. This increasingly popular metaphor, and its many variations, is being used to describe the predicted "apocalyptic" effects of the aging baby boomer generation. In addition to popular media, professional registers and organizations have used such metaphors to title their reports. I argue that extensive use of such word choices not only propagate ageist sentiments but also cannot be ethically justified. By invoking - the aging population as a threat to healthcare, economy, and a continued future it deprives the concepts of personhood and citizenship from this highly variable and vulnerable population. Furthermore, it discourages more holistic and positivistic methods of investing in research for improving palliative care. The method I will use is the narrative ethics approach. I will use three different approaches; 1) narrative ethics as identifying voice, 2) word choice implications for elderly personhood, 3) mimetic content as re-defining citizenship. I believe this will be most appropriate because it disrupts the stifling of elderly individuals' narratives and individuality. Framing the elderly as a literal Grey Tsunami compounds more problems than would exist if this population was approached with an optimistic framework. Metaphors shape the way we think and thinking shapes the way we behave. There is a practical need for more hopeful metaphors to describe aging processes and with it new aging metaphors.

column36: DNA nanoscience for the design of anti-cariogenic dental resins
column37: Dental caries (or tooth decay) is a highly prevalent disease affecting over 95% of the Canadian population. The cause of caries is multifactorial, mainly involving the production of acidic by-products by bacteria in the oral cavity, which activate the degradation of tooth structure and form 'cavities.' The bulk of a tooth's structure is made up of dentin, and decayed dentin can be restored by its replacement with composite resin filling materials. However, because currently marketed resin composites lack antimicrobial properties, recurrent caries near the margins of these restorations remain the most significant cause of their failure. Consequently, replacement of restorations accounts for 75% of general practice procedures, 60% of which are due to such recurrent caries. Epigallocatechin-gallate (EGCG) is a natural, biocompatible extract of green tea that exhibits activity against caries-causing bacteria and inhibits enzymes that degrade dentin. Clinical studies have therefore investigated the passive (i.e. unattached) incorporation of EGCG into composite resin filling materials, in which its antimicrobial properties have been retained. Unfortunately, passively incorporated EGCG contributes to incomplete curing, and will additionally leach from the filling, compromising biocompatibility and long-term material stability. The objective of this proposal is to design new resins that are structurally attached to EGCG using DNA as a building block, which is chosen for its ease of modification, precision and biocompatibility. These proposed materials would benefit from the properties of EGCG, while maintaining material strength and stability, to prevent recurrent decay.

column36: Maternal Sleep-Disordered Breathing in Pregnancy Increases Nocturnal Glucose Levels In Women with Gestational Diabetes
column37: Rationale: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) increases in prevalence over the course of pregnancy and occurs in ~30% of women by the third trimester. Maternal SDB is associated with an increased risk of developing gestational diabetes (GDM). However, the relationship between maternal SDB and glucose levels is unknown. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is an emerging technique for continuous glucose data collection over several days. Our objective was to determine if there are time-dependent changes in glucose levels from CGM data in relation to severity of maternal SDB. Methods: Women with GDM underwent at-home level 2 sleep recordings for assessment of SDB and continuous 72-hour glucose level measurements using CGM (iPro2, MedTronic). After subcutaneous insertion, interstitial glucose measurements occurred every five minutes across 72-hours consecutively. Accuracy validation occurred daily with 3-4 capillary blood glucose measurements. Glucose results were blinded from participants. Results: Sixty-eight pregnant participants with GDM underwent sleep recordings with the following characteristics (mean SD): 354.1 years of age, BMI of 327 kg/m2, 293.6 weeks gestational age at enrolment, and 33% on insulin/metformin. The mean AHI was 17.110.9 while the mean oxygen desaturation index (ODI) was 3.35.1. Increasing AHI was significantly associated with elevated nocturnal glucose levels between 11pm-3am (p=0.02) and 3am-6am (p=0.01), but not mean 24-hour glucose (p=0.1), even after adjustment for age, BMI and use of insulin/metformin. Conclusion: Increasing AHI is associated with nocturnal glucose levels (11pm-6am), even after adjustment for all confounders. Without treatment, SDB may be a risk factor for the development of GDM and/or poor glucose control in pregnancy. Interventional studies aimed at treating SDB in pregnancy are needed to further determine the causal relationship between maternal SDB and glucose control in GDM.

column36: Investigating the role of System xC(-) in statin-induced muscle pain
column37: Statins are a class of drugs that are used to manage high-cholesterol and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. It is estimated that approximately 10% of Canadians have been prescribed statins, and even more should be on them. While these drugs have proven to be highly effective and generally have a favourable safety profile, one of the most commonly reported side effects is muscle pain (myalgia). Statin-induced myalgia is leading cause of non-compliance and discontinuation of statin treatment; however, the cause of these symptoms remains largely unknown. In this proposed study, we aim to understand the biological mechanism underlying muscle pain in statin therapy. This fundamental knowledge will provide the basis for novel drug development that can treat high cholesterol and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, while minimizing the incidence of adverse events. This research will also help to identify people at risk of more serious muscle complications in statin therapy.

column36: Mechanisms Underlying Corticosteroid Insensitivity Induction by Interleukin-17A in Bronchial Epithelial Cells
column37: Asthma is a heterogeneous chronic obstructive lung disorder that is characterized by an invasion of inflammatory cells in the lung. Inhaled corticosteroids are typically used for the treatment of asthma. However, up to 10% of patients can be insensitive to high dose corticosteroids, rendering treatment options ineffective. Among these corticosteroid-insensitive patients, also known as severe asthmatics, a subset has a specific type of lung inflammation caused by inflammatory cells known as neutrophils. Neutrophils are attracted to the lung by Interleukin (IL)-8, a chemokine that is mainly produced by airway epithelial cells. The inflammatory cytokine IL-17A enhances recruitment of neutrophils by inducing the production of IL-8 in bronchial epithelial cells. The implication of IL-17A in provoking corticosteroid insensitivity in severe neutrophilic asthma requires clarification. We hypothesize that IL-17A may decrease the effect of corticosteroids at the transcriptional level. This work will examine the effects of corticosteroids and IL-17A on the regulation of IL-8 in respiratory epithelial cells. First, the primary mechanism underlying IL-17A's ability to decrease corticosteroid sensitivity will be assessed in both cell lines and primary airway epithelial cells from healthy donors and patients with severe neutrophilic asthma. Next, potential therapeutic targets will be identified with the goal to develop targeted therapies that have fewer and less severe side effects. A better understanding of the role of IL-17A on airway epithelial cells in severe neutrophilic asthma will help us develop new personalized therapies.

column36: Latent TGF-beta-1 presentation by macrophages to fibroblasts
column37: Body implants are used in reconstructive surgery and orthopedics to support lost tissue function. All body implants are causing inflammatory reactions that often culminate in formation of dense scar tissue around the implant. Substantial numbers of implants have to be operatively removed due to loss of function, severe deformities, and pain caused by the scar. The culprit cells for scarring are called myofibroblasts because they secrete fibrous collagen matrix ("fibro") that is contracted ("myo") into scar tissue. Excessive myofibroblast activities not only occur in skin scarring but are also responsible for loss of function of vital organs after injury, such as the heart after an infarct - this life-threatening condition is called fibrosis. Fibrosis ensues from normal repair partly because unresolved inflammation promotes continued activation of myofibroblasts to make and pull fibrous collagen matrix into stiff scar tissue. Our lab found that inflammatory macrophages carry an inactive fibrosis-inducing factor on their surface. We propose that myofibroblast can grab onto and activate this factor by pulling it our of a 'straight-jacket'. The receptors involved in the grabbing process will need to be identified. It is our aim to identify the molecular players mediating macrophage-induced fibroblast activation. We propose that preventing these cells to touch or blocking the interaction signaling molecules will ultimately reduce tissue scarring. We will study macrophages and fibroblasts derived from mouse tissue in unique co-culture environments. We will delete and inhibit already identified receptors on the macrophage and/or myofibroblast surface to test their involvement in promoting contact-induced signaling. Key to the success of these inhibition strategies is targeting only the macrophage-fibroblast couple whereas other cells with beneficial functions in tissues under repair remain - literally - untouched.

column36: A novel approach to predicting adverse cardiovascular events in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease using respiratory biomarkers
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the fourth leading cause of death and cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in the world. COPD patients are at higher risk for CVD, yet cardiovascular (CV) risk is not routinely assessed in COPD care. Identifying which COPD patients that will progress to CVD is the first step in development a new CV risk model for COPD patients. We collected data from CanCOLD, a longitudinal population-based study of adults over 40 years. Subjects were assessed at baseline with clinical questionnaires and lung function tests and followed for 3 years. A total of 1115 subjects (533 with COPD and 582 without COPD) finished follow up. Cardiac events were defined as new heart disease, stroke, heart failure or arrhythmia. Statistical analysis was done to determine association of COPD with cardiac events, adjusting for age, sex and smoking. The odds of having cardiac disease was increased for those with moderate COPD by over 60% compared to those without COPD. Severe COPD subjects had over twice the likelihood of having cardiac disease compared to non-COPD. As lung function and exercise capacity increase, the odds of having a cardiac event are reduced. Increased exercise capacity in COPD reduces the likelihood of a new cardiac event by almost two-thirds, and could be a good indicator of decreased CV risk. Our findings suggest that lung physiology is important as CV risk factor COPD.

column36: Impact of drug insurance type (private/public) on the cost of drugs of Quebecers.
column37: Background: Drug cost in Quebec can vary between publicly and privately insured patients because the pharmacist's fee is determined freely by the pharmacy owner for the privately insured patients and fixed for the publicly insured patients. Therefore, some studies showed that drug cost is higher for privately insured patients versus publicly insured patients due to higher pharmacist's fee. Objective: This study aimed to assess the difference in drug cost between persons covered with private and public drug insurance. Methods: To compare the difference in drug cost of Quebecers when insured by the RPAM and a private drug insurance, we used prescriptions from reMed (an administrative database of Quebecers insured by the RPAM and private insurances). We matched 3766 pairs of prescriptions bought by 1386 patients between January 1st 2015 and September 14th 2017. Each pair of filled prescriptions had the same drug, DIN, quantity, pharmacy and had to be bought twice within three months: once while the patient was insured by the RPAM and once while she/he was insured by a private drug insurance. Results: More than 65% of the patients in our sample were between 40 and 65 years old. More than 59 % of the patients were covered by a private drug insurance before changing to the RPAM and more than 59 % of the patients contributed 2 prescriptions or more to the analysis. We observed that privately insured patients had to pay CAD$7.54 (25.7%); (95% CI 7.03-8.05) more for their medication than did publicly insured patients. This study estimated that this mean CAD$7.54 excess paid by privately insured patients represent an excess of approximately 973 million CAD in one year at the province level. Conclusion: This study showed that on average drug cost is higher for privately insured Quebecers. Knowing that adherence is affected by drug cost, these results will be useful to help public health authorities to make informed decisions about drug insurance policies.
