column36: Children's Perceptions of the Ontario Student Nutrition Program's Farm-to-School Initiative in Southwestern Ontario
column37: Poor nutrition is a principle contributor to the rising rates of obesity, type-2 diabetes, and other diet-related diseases among Canadian children. Identifying effective strategies for promoting healthy eating can aid in reversing declining nutrition levels and ultimately improve the overall health of children. The Ontario Student Nutrition Program's (OSNP) Farm-to-School initiative delivers locally-sourced fruit, vegetable, and supplementary food group snacks to elementary schools. This approach offers consistent, high-nutrient-quality snacks that follow Ministry nutrition guidelines, a change from traditional school food models, where nutritional quality and sources of food vary greatly by school. With increased access to healthy food, the program aims to support children's nutrition and prevent diet-related diseases. The purpose of my research is to assess children's perceptions of OSNP's Farm-to-School program through focus groups. Group discussions with child participants will assess influences of the program on their dietary behaviours, preferences, intake, willingness to try, and nutritional knowledge. A total of 37 child focus groups were conducted at 21 elementary schools in Southwestern Ontario. Preliminary results suggest that the program was positively received by the students. Some students indicated that the snacks helped them to feel full. Most of the children liked the foods offered, with few items that were disliked. The program also influenced many of the children to eat healthier at school and home. It was recommended by some of the students that they receive more and a greater variety of foods. The farm-to-school program had a positive impact on children's diets. Using the findings from this study, the program can be further improved and streamlined across all 480+ schools involved with OSNP. It is anticipated that this initiative will have a considerable influence on children's nutrition in Southwestern Ontario.

column36: Exploring the role of the KDM4A Jumonji-C demethylase in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia
column37: Leukemic stem cells are endowed with unlimited self-renewal potential, locked in an undifferentiated state, and are a major cause of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) therapy failure and relapse. The goal of treatment of leukemia is to kill the malignant cells without damaging the residual normal bone marrow, which contains the normal stem cells required for production of blood cells. Research has revealed that multiple events at the genome level are required for progression of leukemic cancer that enable the cells to develop their malignant properties. This process includes genetic events (DNA mutations, for example), as well as epigenetic events, which can occur on proteins bound to the DNA molecule and lead to modulation of gene expression. Recent research has found that genes coding for epigenetic regulators are frequently mutated, deleted or amplified in leukemia. We have determined that the depletion of a specific epigenetic modifier, KDM4A, results in a dramatic decrease in the proliferation rate of leukemic cells. Furthermore, these cells exhibit features of differentiation and loss of pluripotency. Importantly, these effects are specific to leukemic cells and not observed in normal stem and progenitor cells. The goal of this research is to decipher the precise molecular mechanisms by which this epigenetic regulator promotes progression of blood cancers and pediatric AML. Our methods will include current and innovative cellular, molecular, and pharmacological tools. Using these approaches, we will generate new insights into epigenetic dynamics of leukemogenesis and characterize targets for novel and specific treatments of AML, a disease still plagued with dismal survival rates.

column36: Research 101: Empowering community members in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside to develop local guidelines for ethical research with people who use drugs
column37: The Downtown Eastside (DTES) of Vancouver is one of the poorest neighborhoods in Canada and has been the site of several public health crises, including multiple epidemics of HIV/AIDS in the 1980s (primarily affecting Men Who Have Sex With Men) and 1990s (primarily affecting injection drug users) as well as the more recent opioid overdose crisis. This background of intersecting social and health issues has made the DTES one of the most heavily-researched communities in the world. Too often, however, this research has benefitted researchers disproportionately, and left community members feeling exploited, misrepresented, and exhausted. Mistrust of researchers and their projects may reduce the willingness of community organizations and individuals to work with researchers, either as participants or community-based collaborators, ultimately decreasing the potential reach and robustness of community-based health research. Our project utilized a partnership between academic researchers and community members to begin to address the longstanding mismatch between university ethics boards and community concerns with research. Together, we developed "Research 101", a series of workshops that brought together approximately 13 representatives from peer-based, research-involved organizations in the DTES to discuss the pitfalls and potential of research in their neighborhood and to express community expectations for more ethical and respectful research. This led to the development of a co-authored "Manifesto for ethical research in the Downtown Eastside" that serves as a resource to empower community organizations to develop more equitable partnerships with researchers and instruct researchers in community expectations for better research relationships, ultimately leading to better partnerships and better research. Local guidelines for ethical research could be elicited from community members in other heavily-researched communities using a similar approach to ours.

column36: No causality in - no causality out: utility and limits of machine learning in HIV research using EMR data
column37: Machine Learning (ML) is a current buzzword in many public, commercial and scientific domains. This approach has given rise to advancements in speech recognition, medical imaging, precision medicine, and drug development due to the rapid developments in computing power and increasing availability of data. Current ML applications in clinical epidemiology include identification of risk factors for health outcomes, classification of patients into risk strata to optimize individual treatment recommendations, and surveillance over the course of treatment. This is a promising avenue in modern HIV research as >36.9M people are living with HIV worldwide. The popularity of ML coincides with the implementation of electronic medical records (EMR) in healthcare systems globally. However, EMRs containing HIV patient data vary highly in content, scope, and quality across different health jurisdictions and institutions. Yet they are being used to develop ML algorithms to inform clinical decision making or to gain evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of HIV treatments at the population level. The enthusiasm of automated learning from big data brings up risks of disregarding fundamental principals of proper study design and data collection, rendering findings invalid due to confounding bias: association does not imply causation! Over the last 30 years, there has been tremendous success in identifying the conditions necessary for causal claims based on observational data. The ML research community is starting to recognize the fundamental importance of these developments, which is igniting a major paradigm shift from associational to causal ML approaches. Applying the causal inference framework, we evaluate current structures of HIV EMR data in the literature and from a large HIV cohort based in Montreal to assess threats to the validity of inferences and outcome predictions (e.g. treatment adherence) using machine learning methods (random forests, neural networks).

column36: Indigenous Women's Health in the Mining Sector
column37: In Canada, a dearth of research exists on Indigenous women's health and their participation in the natural resource development sector's decision-making processes leading to the question: What barriers do Indigenous women face in negotiating their health concerns in the mining sector's impact benefit agreement (IBA)? When a mining company enters a community, Indigenous women's experience of declining health is well documented by scholars, non-profit organizations, and Indigenous activists. Water contamination, drug use, violence against women and their children increases in the community resulting in women being disproportionality and affected differently by the negative impacts of mining. In short, the health impacts of mining are not gender neutral. However, scant research exists on whether these health impacts and women's health concerns are taken into account in an IBA. In the Canadian mining sector and globally, the IBA is the dominant instrument that structures the relationship between the company and the Indigenous community. The purpose of this private contract is to take into account the impacts and benefits of the development project upon the community, and to obtain consent from the First Nation to gain access to the resources. However, the confidential nature of the IBA and the dominance of the agreement in the sector highlights the pressing need to understand how Indigenous women and their health concerns are taken into account in an IBA negotiation, and the final agreement. This interdisciplinary research project builds on my doctoral research on the governance of drinking water in Canadian provinces, and expands into the area of Indigenous women's health. A finding from my doctoral research is that Indigenous women were absent in the governance process resulting in Indigenous women's health underreported. This current research expands upon the collaborative research completed during my doctoral studies on women's health with the NNEWH.

column36: Healthcare services use before COPD diagnosis: A registry-based longitudinal cohort study
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a progressive lung disease that causes decreasing lung function over time and affects over 2.6 million Canadians. There is no cure for COPD, and modifying risk factors such as smoking in the early stages of disease offers the best chance to improve patient outcomes. Unfortunately, because 70% of patients with COPD are not diagnosed, this opportunity is largely being missed. Several authorities have suggested systematic programs to diagnose COPD during the routine healthcare visits of high-risk individuals. However, these programs rely on sufficient points of contact between undiagnosed COPD patients and the healthcare system. We used health databases to examine the healthcare encounters of patients before they received a diagnosis of COPD. We found that COPD patients frequently visit their pharmacist, family doctor, and specialist doctors for other diseases in the five years before diagnosis. 87% of patients visited a family doctor for reasons related to their lungs in the five years before they were diagnosed with COPD. These types of visits may present ideal opportunities for detecting undiagnosed COPD. Improving the early diagnosis of COPD can increase patient quality of life, reduce mortality, and decrease the burden on healthcare systems.

column36: Proteinase-activated Receptor 2 Signalling in Psoriatic Arthritis Synovial Fluid Macrophages
column37: Psoriasis is a common inflammatory skin disease affecting more than 9 million people in N. America. Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a specific form of arthritis that occurs in up to 30% of patients with psoriasis. Inflammation within the psoriatic joint leads to joint destruction, limitation of function and poor quality of life. Amongst the inflammatory components of joint, immune cells called macrophages have the capacity to regulate tissue degradation, regeneration and release of other inflammatory components that affect progression of arthritis in the joint. This study aims to identify whether a group of protein-digesting enzymes called proteinases and their receptors act to increase release of inflammatory components from macrophages in psoriatic arthritis joints. This project is part of an extended investigation that will provide insights on potential mechanisms that facilitate inflammation and joint damage in PsA patients. This investigation will ultimately allow for the identification of cells or molecules that can be targeted in the clinic to treat inflammation and prevent joint damage in PsA.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling T follicular helper (TFH) cell biology
column37: The Germinal center (GC) is a small lymphoid structure and its function is to generate high affinity antibodies against various invading pathogens. However, abnormal regulation of the GC reaction has been linked not only to the immune deficiency but also to the production of antibodies against self, the latter may lead to the development of autoimmune diseases. GC responses involve B lymphocytes, the cells that produce antibodies after the GC reaction. While it is known that activation and differentiation of B lymphocytes into antibody secreting cells require the help from a special subset of helper T lymphocytes, called Tfh cells, the control over the development and number of Tfh cells at steady state remains not fully understood. Our preliminary studies have made significant progresses in this direction. We have found recently that Cbl proteins, a group of similar protein modifiers, play a critical role in the GC reaction. We show that genetic disruption of Cbl proteins in Tfh cells markedly increases the total number of Tfh cells. The mutation also leads to recruitment of more B cells into the GC reaction. Interestingly, the Cbl mutant mice produce more autoantibodies and die at early age, suggesting that they have developed severe autoimmune diseases. We have also conducted preliminary studies to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which Cbls regulate Tfh biology, and found that Cbls may regulate a key cell surface receptor, called Icos, and a transcription factor, termed Bcl6, through novel protein dumping processes. These findings thus warrant further studies to understand how Cbl proteins exert their function in Tfh cell biology and antibody mediated autoimmune diseases. Completion of this project will not only bring new insight in our understanding of GC reaction but also provide clues in the prevention and treatment of various immune system disorders and promote vaccination.

column36: Design, Synthesis and Testing of Proteolytically Stable Analogs of Apelin-13 and Apelin-17 for Treatment of Cardiovascular Disease
column37: Approximately 17.7 million deaths worldwide were attributed to diseases of the cardiovascular system by the World Health Organization. About 80% are due to heart attack or stroke. It is predicted that by 2030, almost 23.6 million people will die from heart disease and stroke. Furthermore, these problems are increasing in prevalence in both women and the developing world, making cardiovascular health an increasing significant target to improve the health and well-being of society. In the late 1990s, a small protein hormone, named apelin, was discovered in the human body which has a wide variety of physiological functions; including regulation of blood pressure. Apelin has been shown to have potent vasodilator activity, which effectively widens blood vessels and lowers blood pressure. More critical for our study, recent work on apelin has shown that it plays a significant role in the recovery of damaged heart and arterial tissues after heart attacks, leading to improved chances of survival in mouse models. Despite all these beneficial cardiovascular effects, this molecule only has a short lifespan of a few minutes in the bloodstream before other proteins in the blood cut it into smaller fragments. These apelin fragments have limited effects on the regulation of blood pressure and also the recovery of heart tissue from trauma. We propose to use chemical synthesis to make analogues of apelin that retain similar shape (conformation) of this natural hormone, while altering the specific sites that are cut by proteins in the bloodstream. The slight variations in structure introduced will allow the apelin analogs to become more resistant to being cut, thereby prolonging the beneficial physiological effects. This will provide stable long-lasting drug candidates for further development and testing as therapeutic agents. We also propose to make them orally active. Such drugs may be useful for other problems, including loss of muscle mass due to aging (sarcopenia).

column36: Electron cryomicroscopy studies of eukaryotic rotary ATPases
column37: The molecule ATP is the universal energy currency of cells. In humans, ATP is made in a part of the cell called the mitochondrion. During respiration, cells establish a concentration gradient of hydrogen ions (also known as protons) across the inner membranes of mitochondria. A molecular machine called ATP synthase, consisting of a large assembly of protein molecules, uses energy from the proton gradient to drive the production of ATP. ATP synthases not only make ATP, but also control the structure of the mitochondrion, which is essential for respiration and can change during aging and in regulated cell death. In contrast, V-ATPases use ATP to pump protons across other membranes in the cell. This proton pumping controls the pH of compartments within cells for numerous fundamental cellular processes and also for specialized roles. In particular, V-ATPases play a central role in signal transmission between the cells known as neurons that make up the brain. Understanding how these essential cellular machines work requires seeing their structures at high resolution. However, both ATP synthases and V-ATPases are large and fragile, with many moving parts, and they have resisted structure determination by conventional methods. We have helped to develop methods to study the structure and dynamics of these molecular machines using electron microscopy at cryogenic temperatures (cryoEM). We previously resolved the first high-resolution structures of the membrane-embedded parts of both ATP synthases and V-ATPases from yeast. We will use this expertise to understand how the proteins operate. We will also provide the first insight into the structure and function of these machines in mammals. Understanding the fundamental processes that ATP synthases and V-ATPases control in cells will allow us to understand how the processes are altered in disease, providing opportunities to develop new therapeutics that target them.

column36: The impact of mild behavioral impairment on cognitive decline and associated patterns of anatomical and functional neuroimaging in Parkinson's disease.
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is primarily recognized for its motor symptoms. However, deficits in cognition such as learning, memory and problem solving are noted in the early stages of PD. In some patients, these can evolve rapidly, and eventually resulting in dementia. The ability to identify patients who are predisposed to develop dementia at early stages of PD can allow for better management strategy and early intervention, and help improve quality of life. However, the current clinical tools used to detect cognitive deficits are time-consuming, and often available to a minority of PD patients. Furthermore, diagnosis often occurs too late when these deficits are well established. A new approach to detect dementia risk earlier involves identifying behavioral or personality changes in later life as potential early indicators of brain dysfunction that can lead to dementia. A neurobehavioral syndrome called Mild Behavioral Impairment (MBI), identifies later life onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS- i.e. changes in behavior or personality) as a high-risk group for developing dementia. For some, NPS may be the earliest manifestation of dementia, and can be first noticed by family members or caregivers using the MBI checklist (MBI-C). Outside the context of PD, previous studies have established a connection between high MBI-C scores at baseline and later occurrence of dementia. However it is not known whether MBI can also predict cognitive decline in PD. We will recruit patients with PD, perform cognitive and neuropsychiatric testing, as well as brain imaging at baseline, and again two and a half years later. We will evaluate how the MBI-C scores relate to cognitive decline and potential conversion to dementia in PD, and determine its relationship with brain anatomical and functional changes in PD. If successful, this study will demonstrate that the MBI-C is a sensitive, easy to apply and clinically relevant tool for the early prediction of cognitive decline in PD.

column36: Sustained Improvement of Adolescents' Sleep and Mental Health by Rapid Dissemination of Evidence Based Interventions For Insomnia Through School-Board Partnership
column37: Insomnia is found in 23.8% of adolescents. Mounting evidence indicates that insomnia compromises mental health and is an independent risk factor for suicidality and substance use. Cognitive-behavioral intervention for insomnia (CBT-I) represents an efficacious and safe evidence-based treatment modality, and is recommended as the first-line treatment for insomnia. Despite the high prevalence of insomnia in youth and the evidence showing that it has significant negative impacts on functioning and quality of life, only 1% of Canadian youth has access to evidence-based for insomnia, such as CBT-I. This is a critical problem, because the lack of access to evidence-based behavioral intervention for insomnia leaves adolescents with insomnia vulnerable to psychiatric diseases and puts them at significant risk for academic, emotional, and physical problems. The goal of the proposed study is to fill this gap by providing access to evidence-based interventions for insomnia through school mental health services. To attain this goal, our team of clinicians, decision makers, and knowledge users will develop and evaluate a school-based program to diagnose and treat insomnia among high school students. The proposed work is expected to have an important positive impact because it will create unparalleled access to evidence-based non-pharmacological care for a insomnia in adolescents, which will be expected to improve the sleep and mental health of Canadian youth.

column36: Biology of S100A8 and S100A9 proteins in Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia
column37: Acute leukemia are still the leading cause of death by cancer before the age of 40. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) have only a 50% cure rate in children and less than 10% in > 65 year old patients. Improvements at all levels, from basic science to patient care, are needed to improve these bad numbers. AML is a genetically heterogeneous disease with recurrent translocations and mutations that arise in stem/progenitors cells leading to the clinical disease. A better understanding of the biology of the different AML can lead to better therapy and outcome. This approach has been successful for acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) which had a very poor outcome before the development of ATRA and arsenic trioxide, two molecules that induce the differentiation of APL cells. Their combination now cures more than 90% of this subtype of AML. Our team has recently studied the role of S100A8 and S100A9 proteins in AML. We found that S100A8 maintains the undifferentiated state of leukemic cells while S100A9 can induce their differentiation through the cell surface receptor TLR4. We showed that a small population of leukemic cells expresses the S100A8/A9 proteins and we suspect these cells are responsible for the maintenance of the leukemia which can also be called leukemic stem cells. Using murine models of leukemia, we showed that treatment with the S100A9 protein or an anti-S100A8 antibody prolonged the survival of the mice through differentiation of leukemic cells. In the current proposal, we aim to better characterize the cells expressing S100A8/A9 proteins and determine if they are leukemic stem cells. We will also better understand the effects of the proteins, their receptors and their cellular pathways. Finally, we will test our proteins and antibodies in vivo on both human AML models and on patient samples in mice. These studies are essential to move towards the clinical application of differentiation therapy in AML using our new tools.

column36: Resensitizing bacteria to itaconate as a new approach for the treatment of infections
column37: Although bacteria can cause disease in humans (bad bacteria), most do not and can even be beneficial (e.g. microbiome). When harmful bacteria find their way in our body, the immune system is activated and clears the bad bacteria without affecting our microbiome. Occasionally, bacteria overcome our immune defenses which leads to a bacterial infection and requires medical treatment. Antibiotics are at the basis of modern medicine; they are used not only to cure bacterial infections but also to protect pre-term babies, AIDS patients, patients undergoing chemotherapy, hemodialysis or any surgery (e.g. C-section, biopsies, hip replacement, introducing a stent etc.). Antibiotics save millions of lives every year. Unlike our immune system, however, antibiotics kill not only the bad bacteria but also those that make up our microbiome, leading to side effects such as diarrhea. Since the discovery of antibiotics and their use in the clinic, humans and bacteria have become locked in an arms race: as we develop new antibiotics the bacteria evolve resistance to them. Therefore antibiotics have a finite useful lifespan and most do not work well anymore. We definitely need new antibiotics, however, to end the arms race we must learn to treat infections without antibiotics. We propose to replace antibiotics with bacterio-modulators, which we define as molecules that make bacteria more susceptible to our immune system. This results in our immune defenses selectively killing the bad bacteria without causing harm to our microbiome. We have reported a proof-of-principle study demonstrating the efficacy of some bacterio-modulators towards Salmonella. We propose here not only to expand on this study but also to adapt it to other pathogens such as tuberculosis, a disease which kills >1.5 million people annually in the world. Once this concept is demonstrated with tuberculosis, we believe that it will rapidly be adapted to other infectious diseases and will revolutionize modern medicine.

column36: Neural mechanisms of embodied decision-making
column37: Deficits in decision-making are a major aspect of many brain disorders. For example, in addition to its motor symptoms, Parkinson's disease often also affects decision-making. Worse still, treatments for the motor symptoms often have side effects leading to decision-making problems including impulsivity and addiction. Understanding the neural bases of decisions is therefore critical to developing more effective therapies that act at the sources of the deficit without disturbing other brain functions. Traditionally, research on decision-making treated it as a purely cognitive process based on abstract representations of costs and benefits. However, growing neurophysiological data suggests that many decisions involve a distributed network of brain regions including those implicated in controlling actions. This makes sense because during the brain's evolution, animal behavior was dominated by decisions about actions in an unpredictable and constantly changing world, such as selecting what to do when searching for food or when faced with a threat. In such natural scenarios, the options themselves as well as their payoffs and risks are constantly changing, and decisions must be made even during ongoing behavior. To understand a brain whose evolution was dominated by the demands of such natural scenarios, we need to study how it deals with real-time, dynamic decision-making. This project will investigate, through a combined experimental and computational approach, how the brain combines sensory information to influence a competition between different potential reaching actions, how it arrives at a commitment to a specific movement, and how it learns from the outcomes of performing that action. The results will lead to a computational framework that can provide a mechanistic link between fundamental mechanisms of adaptive behavior, inter-individual differences in decision-making policies, and the kinds of deficits seen in a variety of brain disorders.

column36: Multiphoton Photothermolysis Based Laser Therapy for Precision Treatment of Neovascular Eye Diseases
column37: In this project, a novel laser therapy will be developed for vascular eye disease treatment. It utilizes ultrafast laser pulses that are tightly focused to a micron-size volume inside vessels in eye diseases. Because of the locally very high instantaneous laser power density, multiple photons will be simultaneously absorbed at the focal point (and only there) to generate heat to destroy the vessel. Outside of the focal point, multiphoton absorption does not occur because the optical power density is below the threshold value. Compared to conventional method for laser therapy of vascular diseases, our new method will be able to destroy selected vessels much precisely, while leave surrounding tissues intact. Conventional laser therapy is based on one photon absorption, which could occur along the light pathway beyond the focal point although the absorption is the highest at the focal point. This could cause collateral damage to normal eye tissues and affect vision. If successfully developed, our new laser treatment technology could bring immediate benefits to Canadians with corneal neovasularization (NV) disease and other vascular diseases e.g. diabetic retinopathy/macular degeneration. It is estimated that 1.4 milllion people develop corneal NV worldwide per year, 12% of whom suffer the subsequent loss of vision.

column36: Role of the gut microbiota and physiological systems underlying internalizing problems during the transition from childhood to adolescence
column37: The human gut is colonized by trillions of bacteria that play a role in human health and disease. Recent animal and human evidence shows that communication between the gut microbiota and the brain has the ability to influence behavior and mood. Although it isn't entirely clear how this happens, there is strong evidence that the stress-response systems are involved. Many of the findings differ by sex. In the current study, we will investigate the role of gut microbiota in mental health outcomes in youth. We will study this relationship during the transition from childhood to youth because this is a period during which 70% of mental health concerns first appear and because there are significant changes in the stress response systems that could be influenced by the gut microbiota. column36: Omics, Histopathology and AI: An Integrative Approach for Biomarker Discovery in Ovarian Cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer ranks fifth in cancer deaths among women, accounting for more deaths than any other cancer of the female reproductive system. The revolution in our understanding of genetic and molecular drivers of other cancers has resulted in major improvements in how such cancers are routinely managed. However, standard clinical management of ovarian cancer and patient outcomes have not seen any improvements. Recent findings, including ours, in the classification of ovarian cancer based on genetic markers have important clinical implications, including the potential for identifying new treatments. However, until the discovery of surrogate biomarkers, these sub-classifications are based on labor-intensive assays with long turn around times, limiting their routine use. Visual microscopic study of diseased tissue (referred to as histology) by pathologists has been a cornerstone in cancer diagnosis and prognostication for more than a century. The information present in histology reflects the aggregate effect of genetic alterations on cancer cells and provides a convenient visual readout of disease biology. We will build a platform for characterizing ovarian cancer, based on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, by combining genetic and histology markers. More specifically, we will build automated differential diagnostic tool for major ovarian cancer subtypes, investigate the relationship between genetic markers, histology and disease outcome, and combine these data for a comprehensive profile of each tumor. New knowledge generated from this project will shed light on the link between histology and genetic markers and identify potential biomarkers that can be rapidly and accurately tested to stratify ovarian cancer for accurate treatment selection.

column36: Receptor binding and Kinase Signalling regulate Respiratory Syncytial Virus Replication and Provide New Therapeutic Opportunities
column37: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the leading cause of hospitalisation of infants in North America and the second leading cause of death of children worldwide. RSV causes infection of the lungs leading to flu-like symptoms and pneumonia. Despite the severity of this particular infection there is no vaccine available and the only medication against RSV is a very expensive drug called palivizumab, that can only be used to prevent infection. This means that when a patient is suffering from RSV infection there aren't any specific treatments available to treat the infection itself. In summary, we need to learn more about RSV infection so that we can develop new drugs to treat it. We are researching the steps that RSV takes to enter and infect lung cells. In order for infection to happen the virus must first cross the outer membrane that surrounds the cell, which is called virus entry. We are studying the entry stage of the virus replication cycle so that we can develop the basis of new drugs that block RSV infection from happening. The biggest hurdle with developing drugs against RSV entry into cells is that very little is known about this phase of the RSV replication cycle. Firstly, viruses must bind receptors. Virus receptors are molecules made by the cell to which a virus binds in order to enter the cell. Our group shed new light on RSV entry by discovering a cellular entry receptor for RSV (2011) and we have just recently discovered a new receptor for RSV. The purpose of our studies is to understand the RSV-receptor interaction so that we can develop drugs that block these interactions. In summary, we are discovering the cellular factors that RSV uses to infect cells as the basis of new drugs to block RSV infection.

column36: Reducing Homeostatic Synaptic Plasticity: A New Antiepileptogenic Approach to Cure Focal Epilepsy
column37: Our goal is to control the biological processes that occur in the brain after an initial insult (e.g., status epilepticus, SE) and lead to focal epileptic disorders such as mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), the most common type of adult refractory epilepsy. To this end, we will use a rodent model that recapitulates many of the features of the human condition, including an initial brain insult (i.e., a pilocarpine-induced SE) followed by a seizure-free, latent period before the recurrence of spontaneous focal seizures. Established experimental evidence along with preliminary data obtained in our laboratories have led us to hypothesize that the transient decrease in neuronal excitability that follows the initial SE, induces homeostatic synaptic plasticity (HSP). HSP, which allows neurons to normalize their firing without changing synaptic input strength, may, under pathological conditions such as those following SE, cause adaptive processes leading to spontaneous seizures once the post-SE depression is over. HSP is modulated by the glia-released pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF). Therefore, we will: (i) identify the dynamic changes in excitability occurring in mice shortly after a pilocarpine-induced SE; (ii) establish whether the changes in excitability occurring during this latent period are modulated by TNF as HSP does; (iii) prove that augmenting or decreasing TNF function during the latent period modifies the establishment of the epileptic condition; (iv) control the establishment of the epileptic condition by rescuing post-SE hypoexcitability (and thus reducing HSP) with optogenetic activation of CA3, CamKII-positive, principal cells. We believe our studies to be fundamental for identifying new pharmacological strategies for preventing the development of MTLE and, potentially, of other focal epileptic disorder such as post-traumatic epilepsy.

column36: Optimizing nurse staffing practices in acute care hospitals for safer patient care
column37: Adverse events (AEs) are a leading cause of death in acute care hospitals. Recent cross-sectional studies have suggested that several nurse staffing practices (e.g., understaffing, the use of less qualified nursing staff and of high volumes of overtime hours) may be important contributors to the incidence of AEs in these settings. There is also emerging evidence that nurses' levels of education and experience might also be related to AE occurrence. The next step in investigation is to determine the optimal number and composition of the nursing staff, and the optimal volumes of overtime hours that are needed to minimize the risk of AEs. To this end, the temporal associations between these nurse staffing practices and the incidence of AEs, and the thresholds for safe staffing levels need to be determined by conducting longitudinal studies. Until recently, detailed daily patient and staffing data were not readily available to conduct such an investigation. With the advent of electronic health records and the digital capture of payroll and staffing data, an exciting opportunity has emerged to address these important questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals. The objectives of this multisite study are to determine: a) if and which nurse staffing practices are associated with an increased risk of AEs and, b) if thresholds for 'safe' nurse staffing can be established. The results of this study will likely produce evidence-based information that will assist hospital managers in making the most effective use of the scare nursing resources, and in identifying optimal nurse staffing practices that minimize the incidence of AEs. Such evidence is urgently needed given that the international shortage of registered nurses is expected to worsen in the coming years, and because hospitals are increasingly turning to overtime hours and to hiring less experienced or less qualified nursing workers to maintain the accessibility to health care services.

column36: The small GTPase Rab4 as a target for breast cancer metastasis
column37: Les progres se font attendre dans le traitement des metastases, la cause principale de mortalite associee au cancer, particulierement pour le cancer du sein triple negatif recurrent (TNBC). Les approaches traditionnelles pour cibler la proteine Rab4 n'ont pas reussi a fournir des bloqueurs de Rab4 efficaces cliniquement. En faisant une etude detaillee, nous avons reussie a developper des petits peptides (petites molecules) qui bloquent l'activite de Rab4. Nous utiliserons ces petites molecules pour developper des bloqueurs d'activite de Rab4 qui pourront etre utilises pour prevenir de le developpement de metastases dans le cancer du sein, et possiblement dans d'autre types de cancers.

column36: Elimination of senescent endothelial cells to prevent vascular dementia in aging atherosclerotic mice
column37: Aging alone or in combination with risk factors for cardiovascular diseases such as high blood pressure, high levels of fat and sugar in the blood, is associated with a decline in memory that can lead to dementia in some of us. The mechanisms underlying dementia are not clear and so far, no drug treatment has been successful. In this project, we propose that the inner layer of cells in the brain arteries, the endothelium, becomes senescent with age; this could cause damage to our neurons (brain cells) and promote memory loss. Indeed, although senescent cells do no divide anymore, they produce factors responsible for inflammation, destruction of the structures that maintain the architecture of the vessels and lead to lower cerebral perfusion. This deleterious inflammatory environment could also affect the neurons, promote neuronal death and therefore loss of memory and cognitive decline. We have discovered in old patients with cardiovascular diseases a protein produced by these senescent endothelial cells. We now have preliminary data showing that if we inactivate this protein in mice, it improves the function of the cerebral arteries, reduces the amount of senescent endothelial cells in the aorta, decreases the level of inflammation in the aorta, reduces atheroma plaque formation in the aorta, and increases healthspan, that is, increases median mouse lifespan. Nothing is known about the impact of senescence of the endothelial cells specifically in the brain. Our aim is to demonstrate that by eliminating these senescent vascular cells, brain structure, perfusion and function will be preserved, slowing the loss of memory and delay the onset of age-related dementia.

column36: The CUP Study: Comparative analysis of centralized waitlist effectiveness, policies, and innovations for Connecting Unattached Patients to primary care providers
column37: Background: People who have access to a regular primary care provider (family doctor or nurse practitioner) receive better and more appropriate care and have better health outcomes than those who do not. Across Canada, 15% of people do not have a regular provider (i.e. are "unattached patients"). Seven Canadian provinces have centralized waitlists that coordinate matching unattached patients to a primary care provider. These centralized waitlists work differently, and we conducted a previous study that compared how they work (e.g. How do unattached patients get on the waitlist? Are there any rules about who is allowed on the waitlist? What is the process for connecting patients on the list?). Some of the waitlists prioritize certain kinds of patients (e.g. people with chronic conditions or a mental illness) first. However, no one has studied yet how well centralized waitlists work. Goal: This study will compare centralized waitlists in NS, QC, and ON to see how effective they are at connecting unattached patients to primary care providers. Methods: We will use waitlist and administrative data to compare the effectiveness of the waitlists. We will also analyze policies in each province that might impact the waitlists' effectiveness. We will also gather information on other programs, besides centralized waitlists, that connect unattached patients to primary healthcare services. Finally, we will interview patients who have been attached to a provider through a centralized waitlist and providers who take patients from centralized waitlists. By using a variety of methods, we will be able to compare the three centralized waitlists and understand why they have different effectiveness. We will bring the findings to meetings with stakeholders (e.g. policymakers who oversee the waitlists, unattached patients, primary care providers) in each of the three provinces for their feedback. At the end of the study, we will share the findings with stakeholders from all provinces.

column36: Neural repair in glaucoma: the role of insulin signaling
column37: Sight is essential for humans to gather critical information about their surroundings. The fear of going blind has been reported to be more powerful than that of having cancer or heart disease. Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, affecting >60 million people worldwide. There is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the death of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the neurons that convey visual information from the retina to the brain. High intraocular pressure is the most significant risk factor for developing the disease. A challenge in the management of glaucoma is that pathological changes in these patients occur years, possibly decades, before symptoms appear. Thus, there is an unmet need for novel therapies that stimulate RGC regeneration and restore vision. One of the earliest signs of damage in glaucoma is the retraction of RGC dendrites, the fine processes that connect neurons within the retina. In an exciting recent study, we discovered that insulin promoted remarkable dendrite regeneration, restored circuit function, and extended neuronal survival in mouse glaucoma models. In this application, we will: 1) determine whether deficits in insulin signaling trigger early dendritic pathology in glaucoma, 2) elucidate molecular mechanisms that promote insulin-mediated dendrite regeneration, and 3) establish the efficacy of insulin for RGC repair and vision restoration in nonhuman primates. The proposed project is unique because it will provide critical knowledge on whether insulin signaling deficits contribute to early dendrite retraction and synapse loss, and it will elucidate molecular mechanisms driving arbor regeneration and circuit repair. Furthermore, this work is timely and important because it will provide pre-clinical validation of the efficacy of insulin in non-human primate glaucoma, which will inform the design of future human clinical trials for this indication.

column37: Nephrotic syndrome is the most common kidney disease among children. Affected children have massive leakage of protein into the urine and as a consequence, develop body swelling (edema). Most children respond to treatment with steroids, however many of them require repeated courses for frequent relapses of the disease. Long-term use of steroids causes many side effects including obesity, growth retardation, hypertension, cataracts, poor bone health, and cosmetic effects. Minimizing the use of steroids has been identified as the number one priority of the patients and families. A non-steroid drug, rituximab, is now known to be effective in the treatment of nephrotic syndrome, but it is entirely unclear how it works. In this study, we will investigate the mechanisms by which rituximab alleviates the symptoms associated with nephrotic syndrome, allowing patients to stay in remission. Blood collected from affected patients when their disease is active, and after successfully treated with steroid or rituximab, will be analyzed using the state-of-the-art technique called immunophenotyping. One of the investigators in the research team, Dr. Piccirillo, is the leading researcher of this technology in Canada. The analyses will inform us which cells in the blood are active before treatment, and become inactive after treatment. We will also find out if steroids and rituximab have different effects on blood cells. With this approach, we are likely to uncover how this common pediatric disease occurs - it has been a mystery for over five decades. Furthermore, understanding how rituximab works in nephrotic syndrome will enable us to identify patients who are most likely to respond to rituximab thus avoiding steroids. Finally, if the culprit cells are known, we can develop new drugs specifically targeting these cells. The hope is that we will not need to use steroids at all in the future.

column37: Congenital toxoplasmosis is an infectious disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii (T. gondii), an obligate intracellular parasite commonly transmitted to humans by ingestion of contaminated raw meat, water, or soil. During pregnancy, T. gondii infection can lead to miscarriage, premature births, or serious birth defects (e.g. blindness, hydrocephalus, and mental retardation). Hence, it has become critical to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the interactions between T. gondii and the infected patient, particularly at the mother/fetus interface. In light of this problem, we investigate the strategies employed by T. gondii to dysregulate molecular signaling and to disrupt normal functions of trophoblasts, specialized placental cells vital in the support of the developing fetus within the womb, in order to promote its intracellular survival. Our study also relies on the use of clinical samples from infected pregnant women and cultures generated from placental explants to address these questions. These valuable resources help validate our results and directly assess the implications of our findings in a clinical setting. Our long-term goal is to advance our understanding of the biological underpinnings implicated during congenital toxoplasmosis and to devise ways to thwart T. gondii replication and transmission. Ultimately, we wish to provide insight into the pathogenesis of clinically relevant infectious organisms and to pave the way to safer therapies to prevent illnesses and promote healthy pregnancies.

column37: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a condition of the hip where there is a mis-fit between the femoral head (ball) and hip acetabulum (socket). Typically, patients with this condition are young adults who present with hip pain, loss of hip function, and in many cases, osteoarthritis later in life. In the past 20 years, sport injuries among children have dramatically increased, where close to 45 million young athletes participate in organized sports annually in Canada and the US alone. There is a current trend among coaches and parents to have children focus on one sport with the thought that this dedication will allow them to reach an elite level. We are proposing the first international, longitudinal cohort study to determine the effect of sport specialization on the development of FAI during the critical phase of hip development (i.e. between the ages of 12-14 years). Volunteer participants will be recruited across Canada and internationally and will be evaluated clinically and radiographically (i.e. using MRI) over 2 years. This study will not only prospectively evaluate the role of sport activity the development of FAI, but also inform preventative training protocols to potentially reduce its incidence among adolescents, and later as adults, as well as identify parameters to detect hips that are at risk for developing FAI.

column37: Mechanical ventilation (MV) is indispensable for the survival of critically ill patients, such as those with respiratory failure. However, improperly delivered, can aggravate or cause acute lung injury (ALI) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a universal source of energy (fuel) in all living cells. ATP can be also released outside the cell, where it serves as a signaling molecule for cell-to-cell communication. However, high levels of extracellular ATP act as danger-associated signal leading to lung inflammation, edema and tissue damage. Such detrimental effects of ATP are implicated in a number of respiratory diseases including ventilator induced lung injury (VILI), ALI and ARDS and involve binding of ATP to specific proteins (called receptors) on the surface of neighboring cells. One of such ATP receptor, designated as P2X7, is specifically implicated in pathogenesis of VILI. However, the mechanisms of massive ATP release that activate P2X7 during lung mechanical ventilation remain unknown. Interventions that would reduce excessive release of ATP would benefit patients with ALI/ARDS. We hypothesize that massive ATP release results from rupture of cell membranes (cell lysis) due to excessive mechanical stress during MV. In this project we will study the impact of MV on lung injury using in vivo and ex vivo mice lungs. We will also use recently developed by our team a novel bioluminescence microscopy to visualize in real-time injury-induced ATP release in ex vivo lungs. We will test pharmacological interventions (ATP metabolizing enzymes and inhibitors of ATP receptor P2X7) to reduce excessive ATP release and its downstream detrimental effects. This project will help to understand pathogenesis of ALI/ARDS - major critical care pulmonary complications. It will facilitate design of novel strategies to mitigate or prevent these pathologies.

column37: Digestive diseases represent an important financial burden for Canadians with an expense of $5,7 billion annually (2008) in health care cost and lost productivity. One in 150 people in Canada suffer from inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) making Canadians suffering from the disease the highest than anywhere in the world. Moreover, digestive cancers represent one out of every five new cancer cases diagnosed in the country (2009) with colorectal cancer having the 2nd highest death rate of all cancers in Canada. The seed and soil hypothesis suggests that the successful function of a complex organ, such as the one found in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, depends on the interactions and properties of the epithelial cells (seeds) and their sub-epithelial microenvironment and mesenchymal cells (soil). Until recently, mesenchymal cells have been recognized mainly for their role in sustaining the GI epithelium rather than for their potential contribution to GI pathologies. It is now well established that genetic changes in troubled epithelium or disturbance in immune cells regulation are insufficient to recapitulate entirely GI disease initiation and progression. Thus far, it is beginning to be accepted that the mesenchymal cells and the sub-epithelial microenvironment may play a critical role in many GI disorders. The main hypothesis for this project is that mesenchymal cells are central for the preservation of the microenvironment mechanical and biochemical cues regulating the epithelial homeostasis with consequences on gut pathophysiology. This project will unravel the precise contribution of mesenchymal cells in the establishment of this chemically and mechanically dynamic environment and the molecular cascade of events emerging from this interaction. Improving our knowledge on the microenvironment instructing the epithelial responses during gut diseases opens possibilities for new therapeutic intervention targeting relevant molecules in the sub-epithelial milieu.

column36: Poly(ADP-ribose) writers, readers, and erasers: Functions in DNA double-strand break repair and synthetic lethality.
column37: Inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) proteins, which cells use in a variety of DNA damage repair mechanisms, is a promising therapy for cancers. Because cancer cells often have preexisting defects in DNA damage repair pathways, the inhibition of PARP can result in preferential death of cancer cells when another mechanism for repairing DNA is defective. This is called synthetic lethality. The concept of synthetic lethality is that cell death occurs when two separate mechanisms for repair of defective DNA are present in a cell and both are incapacitated. Our project aims to discover and characterize previously unknown proteins that can affect synthetic lethality, notably through modulation of the DNA repair machinery. All organisms have evolved mechanisms that allow the maintenance of genomic integrity. The consequences of damaged DNA, and especially double-strand breaks, may be disastrous and lead to cancer if left unrepaired. All organisms can suffer DNA damage, during normal cellular processes or as a consequence of DNA damaging agents such as UV and ionizing radiation. Conversely, treatment of cancer cells with chemotherapy and radiotherapy aims at damaging the DNA of cancer cells to kill them specifically. The present project aims at understanding how cells detect and repair DNA double-strand breaks. Particularly, we want to understand how poly(ADP-ribose), a molecule which is synthesized at sites of damaged DNA, orchestrates the detection and repair of broken DNA. Specifically, we will analyze how PARPs affect the pathways by which double-strand breaks are repaired. Because studies have shown the usefulness of inhibiting poly(ADP-ribose) synthesis in killing breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer cells, understanding the interplay between poly(ADP-ribose) and proteins involved in DNA damage repair is critical to design better cancer therapies and to improve clinical outcome.

column36: Individualized pathways to recovery after stroke
column37: Today over 80% of Canadians who have a stroke will survive. Recent advances in immediate medical care have made stroke into a chronic disease. However, rehabilitation approaches have fallen short of the goal of restoring function after stroke. The net result is more people living with disability after stroke. As a result there is a critical need for new rehabilitation interventions, treatments that can restore function and return people to their daily lives and families. Pairing brain stimulation with rehabilitation after stroke is a promising approach. However, early studies of this intervention responses proved to be highly variable. Some people showed a strong benefit while others did not. Biomarkers are measurements of brain function that can be taken in humans and are useful in making predictions about which therapy may best help a patient after stroke. The main aim of the proposed program of research is to identify biomarkers that can be used to predict response to brain stimulation interventions. We will use this information to predict how individual patients will respond and how much recovery we can expect. This research is urgently needed to rapidly advance recovery of function after stroke. In sum this work will define a new therapy for stroke patients and identify who it is most likely to benefit.

column37: Now more than ever, human genome sequencing is providing unparalleled insights into the causes of undiagnosed genetic diseases. The next step is to investigate how identified mutations affect development of cells, tissues or organs. Through these studies we will also learn more about the normal roles of the gene. However, there are often dozens of human gene mutations affecting a single gene and it is a daunting task to study all of them. We need to use cost-effective animal models to study multiple gene variants. Our team is using the chicken embryo which has many of the same genes as human plus follows similar developmental steps. We are also using the fruit fly as a way to test the function of human genes that are incorporated into the fly genome. Our disease of interest is Robinow Syndrome, which is characterized by abnormal development of the limbs and face. Robinow Syndrome affects one of the major control checkpoints in developing embryos, the WNT or Wingless-related pathway. WNTs are secreted proteins that can act at all stages of development from the earliest embryo to differentiating cells in bone or brain. Through the proposed studies, we will gain insights into the syndrome and more broadly into the general functions of WNT signalling. The principal investigator has extensive experience studying the chicken embryo and can deliver human genes to chickens inside the egg. The co-applicant Esther Verheyen of SFU is an expert in WNT signalling in the Drosophila model. Our team is uniquely prepared to make many exciting new discoveries about how WNT signalling regulates cells and tissues that will one day be used to treat a variety of human diseases with abnormal WNT signalling.

column36: Outcomes following salpingectomy in BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers
column37: Women who inherit a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation face the highest known risk of developing ovarian cancer, a disease with a very poor prognosis. There are currently no effective methods to detect ovarian cancer at an early stage, and thus, these women are strongly advised to undergo preventive removal of their fallopian tubes and ovaries ('oophorectomy') at a young age (prior to age 45). There is evidence to suggest that some ovarian tumours actually begin in the fallopian tube rather than the ovary and that removing the fallopian tubes but not the ovaries ('salpingectomy') may prevent a subset of ovarian cancers. This has resulted in a dramatic change in clinical practice among women in the general population, where only fallopian tubes (not ovaries) are now removed at the time of hysterectomy or instead of tubal ligation. Since early surgical menopause in BRCA mutation carriers may be associated with unwanted side-effects such as the onset of menopausal symptoms and a decline in bone or brain health, there has also been increasing interest in salpingectomy in these women to simultaneously prevent disease but prevent menopause. This is of concern given that there is no evidence to support that salpingectomy will prevent ovarian cancer to the extent that we see with oophorectomy. Thus, we propose to use data from the largest cohort of BRCA mutation carriers that we have assembled to compare the risk of developing and dying of ovarian cancer among those with salpingectomy vs. oophorectomy. We will also evaluate what factors (personal, health care provider) influence the decision of women with a BRCA mutation. Our team is well-positioned to address these important scientific and clinical questions. Given the high fatality associated with ovarian cancer along with the extremely high lifetime risks in BRCA mutation carriers, it is imperative and timely that we evaluate whether 'salpingectomy' is equally effective as 'oophorectomy' before widespread uptake by these women.

column36: Investigating the mechanisms of iron delivery to mitochondria.
column37: Iron is an essential metal for life. However, it is also very reactive and just as it can rust in your car, it can also be oxidized in the cell, causing chain reactions that damage cells, tissues, and cause disease. In fact there are many diseases where iron handling in the body is disrupted, sometimes with too little iron and sometimes with too much. Therefore it is essential that we understand how elemental iron is released from its protective carrier within the bloodstream to move deep into the cells to it's final destination. That destination is the mitochondria, most famous as the "energy powerhouse of the cell". However, a second essential function of mitochondria is to act as an "iron forge" in assembling elemental iron into a more stable complex called an iron-sulfur cluster. This cluster is used as a type of co-factor in assembling numerous essential proteins both inside mitochondria and throughout the cell. Even in some single cell organisms whose mitochondria do not make energy, the only function remaining is the assembly of iron sulfur clusters. This proposal stems from some unexpected data we obtained that identifies a new kind of circuitry that tightly regulates how and when iron may leave the membrane bound endosome that carries it into the cell, and be delivered directly to mitochondria through sites of direct contact. The circuitry mechanisms we have identified so far have led us to a number of testable ideas that make up the bulk of this proposal. However, we will also immediately survey how this new circuitry may be altered in different models of iron-related diseases, from Freidrich's ataxia to anemia, Parkinsons' disease and others. We hope our work may identify new ways of treating these diseases if we can "trick" the cells to stop taking in iron, or the reverse, opening the possibility for targeted therapies for these devastating diseases.

column36: Correcting monogenic skin diseases in situ: Assessing the potential of topically applicable gene therapy.
column37: Monogenic skin diseases such as autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) are caused by mutations in a single gene. If these mutations could be corrected, the disease should be mitigated. Indeed, for recessively inherited conditions such as ARCI, correction in even a small percentage of disease affected cells should be therapeutic. Recent advances, particularly the rise of CRISPR/Cas9 technology, have greatly improved the efficacy, fidelity and cost of gene editing. The overall goal of this project is to evaluate the feasibility of topically applied CRISPR/Cas9 mediated strategy to correct monogenic mutations in human skin. Whilst the components of the CRISPR/Cas9 system are not themselves capable of overcoming the skin barrier, a major focus will be to develop and evaluate smart delivery strategies for these biomacromolecules. Firstly, the ability of different delivery systems such as nanocarriers for gene-delivery, microneedles and skin-penetrating peptides to deliver CRISPR/Cas9 systems into human skin will be explored. In parallel, CRISPR/Cas9 based gene editing strategies will be developed and optimised in keratinocytes - the primary cell type of the epidermis of the skin - derived from healthy subjects and ARCI patients. Once strategies capable of correcting ARCI causing mutations have been established, the proportion of gene correction in the epidermis required to produce therapeutic effects will be determined. The overall intent of this project is to demonstrate the feasibility of CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing for the treatment of monogenic diseases, and to lay the ground work for future optimisations to improve on its therapeutic potential.

column36: EXURCISe for improving URinary Continence in people with Spinal cord injury
column37: Up to 80% of people with spinal cord injury (SCI) are unable to control their bladder. Lack of bladder control (urinary incontinence) and changes in bladder function following SCI have dramatic impacts on quality of life and can lead to serious side effects, even death. Regaining bladder control is a top priority for those with SCI. There are treatments (mainly medications) for bladder problems for people with SCI, but these are associated with side effects and high failure rates. Some reports estimate that up to 70% of people taking medications for bladder problems stop taking them within the first year due to their negative side effects. New strategies for managing bladder problems are therefore necessary. In this research project, we will explore how different types of exercises targeting the 'core' may help improve bladder function in people with SCI. This research could ultimately benefit most people with SCI who suffer from bladder problems. We are building upon well-established physiotherapy strategies that have been developed for other populations that aim to strengthen the muscles of the abdomen and the pelvic floor (the muscles used to hold in or stop the flow of urine). People with SCI are generally assumed to have trouble activating their core muscles, which might be why exercise-based therapies have not been tried before to treat them. However, we have found that many individuals with SCI are able to recruit the muscles of the core and are able to activate their pelvic floor muscles indirectly, even if they are considered to be completely paralyzed. We have also found that when they walk with the help of a robotic exoskeleton, their abdominal and pelvic floor muscles are active. We already know that exercise is good for bone, muscle, and heart health in people with SCI; we hope to show that exercise can also help improve bladder health.

column36: Signal integration and action potential coding in hippocampal microcircuits
column37: Many animals, from insects to mammals exhibit complex collections of spatial behaviours for survival, including foraging for food, remembering where the home is, remembering safe routes back home after explanatory outbound path to a previously unvisited location, learning maps of new environments, and setting goal locations. To be successful, these spatial behaviors must be robust and able to deal with obstacles that hamper straight paths and occlude views, with novel environments, and with dynamically changing cues with familiar environments. Spatial navigation is dependent upon the formation, storage and retrieval of spatial memories, which permit repeated visits to fixed points in the environment. Our work is focused on understanding how the brain codes this information. Toward this aim we will unveil the interactions between neurones participating in spatial information coding. We will investigate how neurotransmitter release from single axon terminals is shaped by incoming input signals and how neurons in a small network cooperate to transmit this information to other brain areas. We will investigate these questions in rodents. In addition, we will use hippocampi resected during epilepsy surgery from patients to study the functional properties of these synapses in order to determine how similar or different they are compared to rodents.

column36: Modulation of spontaneous and rehabilitation-induced recovery after stroke by pleiotrophin
column37: Stroke refers to brain damage due to blocked blood flow in the brain. The spinal cord can "rewire" itself to help stroke survivors recover movement. Sadly, recovery is not complete. Incomplete recovery may be because the spinal cord rewires only for a short period of time after stroke. A protein called pleiotrophin (PTN) is a growth factor naturally produced by the body. PTN is known to increase the growth of new connections between brain cells. We have recently shown in rats that injecting PTN into the spinal cord after stroke significantly improves recovery. More data in animal models of stroke such as this are needed to confirm PTN therapy can improve recovery. Additionally, the role of PTN in the recovery that occurs naturally after stroke or recovery due to physical therapy needs to be defined. Here, we will use animal models of stroke to determine how the levels of PTN in the brain and spinal cord change in the weeks that follow a stroke. Additionally, we will block PTN in the spinal cord to show its role in the rewiring and recovery that follows stroke. Finally, we will increase PTN signaling in the spinal cord and determine if this can improve recovery make physical therapy more effective after stroke. We predict that: (1) PTN levels in the spinal cord will be highest early after stroke, and return to normal levels at the same time that recovery stops. (2) Blocking PTN levels in the spinal cord will make recovery worse. (3) Increasing PTN signaling will improve recovery even long after the stroke has occurred. We believe PTN is an exciting new stroke therapy. By defining how PTN contributes to recovery from stroke, we hope to find new ways to reduce disability in stroke survivors. Most stroke survivors have some degree of disability, and this research may lead to methods to reduce disability even years after the stroke.

column36: EPCAT III - Extended Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis Comparing Rivaroxaban and Aspirin to Aspirin Alone Following Total Hip and Knee Arthroplasty
column37: Background: Blood clots in the legs and lungs are common complications following hip and knee replacement surgery. Blood thinners are given after these surgeries to prevent blood clots, but are expensive and can lead to bleeding. Aspirin has been shown to work just as well and may be cheaper and safer. In this study, we plan to prove that aspirin works as well as blood thinners to prevent blood clots after hip and knee replacement surgery. Study design: Patients are randomized (like a flip of a coin) to either receive a blood thinner, rivaroxaban, for five days and then aspirin for a few weeks, or just aspirin alone, after these surgeries. Outcomes: We will look at the rates of blood clots, bleeding and death in these patients over 90 days after surgery. Summary: This study has the potential to show that a cheap, commonly used medication like aspirin is just as good and safe as an expensive blood thinner after hip and knee replacement surgeries, which would result in huge cost savings to the health care system.

column36: A multi-method study of self-expansion in couples coping with Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder
column37: Sexual health is a fundamental aspect of quality of life; a satisfying sexual relationship is associated with better physical, psychological, and relationship health and well-being. In fact, people who maintain a satisfying, active sex life over time live longer than those who report lower sexual frequency and satisfaction. Yet problems with sexual function are extremely common, especially for women: a persistent difficulty with sexual desire and/or arousal that is personally upsetting-Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder (FSIAD)-affects 7% to 23% of the general population. FSIAD is linked to more healthcare costs, depressive symptoms and anxiety, and lower relationship satisfaction. Prior research has mainly focused on medical interventions that are costly and ineffective, while etiological factors that could inform more effective treatment have been ignored. Current clinical models suggest that interpersonal processes play a critical role in FSIAD, yet existing studies have not examined their daily or long-term impacts, and almost none have involved romantic partners. One highly relevant interpersonal factor that has been associated with greater sexual desire and satisfaction in community couples is self-expansion (i.e., novelty and broadening in a relationship). The goal of this two-centre study is to examine how self-expansion influences sexual desire and associated impairments in couples coping with FSIAD. We expect that women with FSIAD and their partners' (same-sex, mixed-sex, and gender diverse relationships) higher self-expansion will lead to a reduction in FSIAD symptoms (e.g., higher sexual desire) and better relational and psychological adjustment for both partners in daily life and over time. We also expect that greater feelings of both intimacy and autonomy within the relationship will explain these associations. Results have the potential to improve the health of couples coping with FSIAD by providing novel targets for couple interventions.

column36: Prioritization and functional characterization of regulatory mutations in non-Hodgkin lymphoma
column37: The genetic material in cancer cells contains many errors, known as mutations, which can be identified using DNA sequencing. The entire genome can now be sequenced in individual tumours to identify the full suite of such mutations in individual cancer patients. We will analyze whole genome sequence data alongside measurements of the abundance of individual functional units of the genome ("genes") using sophisticated techniques. This analysis will determine which of the many mutations might cause changes to the regulation of gene abundance ("expression") in the cell. These so-called regulatory changes have been largely elusive in cancer genomes due to the challenges involved in inferring the function of mutations that do not directly alter the sequence of proteins. We have preliminary examples of regulatory mutations that affect genes important in a common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma known as DLBCL. In one of the examples identified thus far, the NFKBIZ gene contains many mutations in a region termed the UTR, a portion of the gene that is transcribed into RNA but does not directly dictate the protein sequence. Mutations such as these, which may lead to increased levels of a protein needed by cancer cells (oncogenes), can represent a new target for drug development. Our project will continue to identify and prioritize such events and extend our analysis to additional lymphoma types. Using a combination of molecular techniques, we will directly study the impact of individual mutations on normal cellular processes.

column36: Reshaping the epigenetic landscape to improve outcomes after acute kidney injury
column37: One in five people admitted to hospital develop acute kidney injury (AKI) and AKI is responsible for some 2 million deaths each year. Even if a person recovers from a bout of AKI, they are at increased risk of developing long-term damage to their kidneys. We urgently need new treatments. Our research team has discovered that a particular group of processes that goes on within cells plays an important role in the development of kidney disease. This group of processes is called "epigenetics". The term epigenetics refers to changes in the way genes carry the genetic code to make proteins that do not involve changes in the typical DNA code. For example, in order for each DNA strand to be packed inside of a cell, it has to be wrapped around spools of proteins called histones. If these spools are modified by chemical reactions this can affect how genes nearby make the proteins that they code for. Building on work we recently published, we have discovered that a particular chemical modification to histones (that normally happens in cells) is lost after AKI and that this loss predisposes to the development of AKI. In the present application, we will expand on our recent discoveries to explore the role of this histone modification in AKI and in the development of long-term kidney damage after AKI. We will perform experiments to maintain the histone modification in kidney cells grown in Petri dishes and in mice that develop AKI using both a pharmacological approach (a new drug) and a genetic approach (called cell-specific knockout mice). We will look to see whether this strategy improves outcomes after AKI caused by a reduced blood flow to the kidneys, a blockage to the outflow of the kidneys or a toxin (the three most common causes of AKI) and we will relate our findings to changes we see in human kidney samples. If the project is successful, it could lead to the development of a new treatment that could benefit the millions of people who develop AKI each year.
