column36: Intra-arterial chilled saline and external cooling to treat severe ischemic stroke
column37: Stroke affects over 62,000 Canadians each year. Most cases result from a blood clot that impairs blood flow to part of the brain. Brain damage occurs when this ischemia is severe or prolonged, and that leads to behavioral and cognitive deficits or even death. There are clinically approved pharmacological and mechanical therapies to remove clots, which when done quickly can rescue brain tissue and improve outcome. Sadly, some do not benefit from clot removal. Those patients are left with life-long disability. We will use rats to model those patients with severe stroke who receive modest to no benefit from clot removal, as these patients desperately need additional treatments. We will test a combination of hypothermia therapies that should reduce brain injury and improve behavioral outcome. The first involves infusing intra-arterial cold saline (20C) into the ischemic brain for 20 min at the time blood flow is restored (clot removal time in patients). This should improve blood flow and attenuate injury. Second, we will test whether adding external head cooling (e.g., brain temperature at 35C for up to a day) will further lessen brain damage. These therapies have many beneficial effects, such as reducing brain swelling, and we expect that they will improve outcome after this severe stroke. However, while these cooling therapies work in certain animal models and settings, existing studies were quite limited in scope, and there was little done to evaluate combination treatments against severe stroke. Thus, we will test these therapies using translationally rigorous, clinically relevant endpoints and experimental design features (e.g., high statistical power, use of hypertensive animals, and comparisons of aged male and female animals). Our goals are to identify the best hypothermia therapy to inform upcoming clinical trials on therapeutic cooling, and to further improve our mechanistic knowledge of these treatments.

column36: Bipolar Bridges: A Digital Health Innovation Targeting Quality of Life in Bipolar Disorder
column37: More than half a million Canadians live with bipolar disorder (BD), a long-term and potentially disabling mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings from depression to mania. Suicide rates are disturbingly high - up to 15% of people with BD will end their own lives. This evidence paints a bleak picture. Yet, with optimal support, care and empowerment, people with BD can flourish, and make important and creative contributions to society. Our research network - the Collaborative RESearch Team to study psychosocial issues in BD (CREST.BD) - uses a pioneering participatory approach in which researchers, healthcare providers and, critically, people who live with BD work collectively to conduct BD research, and to move research results into action. CREST.BD has recently produced two flagship websites designed for people with BD and their healthcare providers: a 'Quality of Life Tool' and a state-of-the-art 'Bipolar Wellness Centre.' In this project, we will build on our prior work to develop a new mobile app called Bipolar Bridges. The app will addresses some of the most pressing real-world problems that people with BD currently face when using online technologies. First, it will take advantage of advances in online technologies to provide a secure and safe interface where the user is in control of their own health data. Second, it will empower the user to combine and learn from different forms of online self-management or self-care data (for example, medication use, sleep quality, mood variability, activity levels) in one place. Third, it will be co-designed with diverse (for example, people with different gender identities, or of different ethnic or cultural backgrounds) people with bipolar disorder. At the same time, Bipolar Bridges will provide a new way for researchers to assess the relationship between self-management and quality of life outcomes in diverse people with BD.

column36: Cryobiology and Cryopreservation of Corneal Endothelial Monolayers
column37: Cryobiology is the study of the effects of extremely low temperatures on living systems. A major application is the low-temperature storage (cryopreservation, for example in liquid nitrogen at -196 C) of cells and tissues to be distributed for transplantation to treat injury and disease. While many cell types have been successfully cryopreserved and used clinically for decades, some cells and the vast majority of tissues present significant hurdles for cryopreservation. For example, a widely transplanted tissue is the cornea, the clear tissue of the eye through which people see. The endothelial monolayer is the delicate layer of cells on the inner surface of the cornea that is critical to its transparency, and is the functional element that needs to be replaced in the majority of corneal transplants. Corneal endothelial monolayers cannot be adequately cryopreserved using current techniques without considerable cell loss. For this reason, currently corneal endothelial monolayer transplants (85% of all cornea transplants) must use fresh tissue, leading to tissue wastage and inequities in distribution. In addition, lab-grown corneal endothelial monolayers are poised to meet transplant needs despite donor shortage, but will require cryopreservation for widespread distribution. We are developing procedures to cryopreserve both lab-grown and natural corneal endothelial monolayers. As cellular therapies and transplant of both natural and engineered tissue are increasingly used in modern medicine, there is an urgent need for effective cryopreservation strategies. The objective of the proposed research is to combine advanced engineering modeling, cryobiological expertise, and biological experimentation to develop key understanding of identified issues in cell and tissue cryopreservation with immediate application to corneal endothelial monolayers. Proposed experiments will use cultured cells, discarded pig eyeballs, and non-transplantable donated human corneas.

column37: Depressive disorders are common and debilitating conditions affecting about 20% of people in North America within their lifetime. Despite some effective treatments, roughly one third of depressive patients are treatment-resistant. It is well known that responses to life-stressful events are extremely different from one individual to another. Our research proposal will focus on the identification of the mechanisms that are implicated in these differential responses, what makes us resilient or vulnerable facing stressful events. Very recently, we identified that the noradrenergic transmission in our brain has a bi-directional control in animal models of depression. All together, this research should allow identifying vulnerability or resistant factors in human facing depression, but also the development of original antidepressant therapies.

column37: Preventing the transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) during unprotected heterosexual intercourse is an international concern. Women face unique challenges in preventing transmission. Women are biologically two times more likely than men to become infected because after sexual intercourse, semen remains within the female genital tract for prolonged periods of time, increasing exposure to HIV. The scaffolds are designed to be simple to use without the assistance of a healthcare professional, and scaffold replacement is infrequent (once every 30 days as opposed to daily applications using vaginal gels). From a sociocultural perspective, this technology is designed to increase user adherence - a major factor that can hinder the effectiveness of HIV prevention strategies. This novel technology may provide a significant breakthrough for addressing the challenges associated with HIV transmission and infection for women.

column37: Chronic pain is one of the most prevalent and debilitating conditions worldwide. It afflicts as many as 1 in 5 Canadians and remains poorly managed. We plan to apply techniques from molecular biology and behavioural/cellular/electrophysiological neuroscience to deduce the neurobiological relationship between learning and changes in pain response. column36: The role of fractalkine signalling during remyelination
column37: Myelin is a fatty substance that coats nerve projections for efficient signal propagation. When myelin is damaged, demyelination disorders occur leading to neurological impairments in vision, movement and/or cognition. Demyelination occurs in Multiple Sclerosis (MS), which is known as "Canada's disease" because the country has one of the highest rates in the world with an estimated 100,000 patients. MS is caused by abnormal activity of the immune system whereby the body's own immune cells damage myelin and myelin-producing cells, oligodendrocytes, in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). Current MS treatments are disease-modifying drugs that target inflammation and aid patients with relapse-remitting MS, in which episodes of neurological dysfunction are followed by remission. Yet, they are ineffective for progressive MS, which usually evolves from the relapsing stage and involves a continual worsening of the disease with no improvement. Effective treatments for this type of MS would require central nervous system regeneration and remyelination (restoration of myelin). Remyelination can be achieved by forming oligodendrocytes from oligodendrocyte precursor cells in the human central nervous system. However, this process is highly inefficient in MS patients. I discovered that a specific type of neurons (inhibitory neurons) secrete an immunological molecule, called fractalkine, that acts directly on the oligodendrocyte precursor cells in the developing mouse brain and promotes oligodendrocyte formation. This effect could form the basis of much needed future MS therapies. This proposal will determine whether fractalkine regulates remyelination and regeneration in the adult central nervous system using mouse demyelination models. We will determine if fractalkine a) enhances oligodendrocyte formation from precursor cells and subsequent remyelination; and b) modulates interactions between precursors and neighbouring brain immune cells called microglia.

We will measure several different forms of folate in the blood, hemoglobin, vitamins B12 and B6, and other clinical outcomes (anemia and pain crises) in children. Our study will be the first-step towards determining if the recommendation for high-dose folic acid supplementation in children with sickle cell disease requires re-evaluation. Most T-lymphocytes in the blood of a patient perform normally their task, which is to attack and destroy bacteria, viruses and other non-self substances. column36: Transitioning to Adulthood: Risk and Protective Factors for Mental Health Problems (MHPs) between Adolescence and Adulthood in a Representative Population Sample.
column37: Mental health problems (MHPs) affect 1 in 5 young people in Canada. Youth with mental disorders such as cannabis abuse and depression are less likely to attain adult life milestones. Our goal is to generate knowledge to improve the prevention of the social, personal and economic burdens of MHPs. Research on MHPs indicates that many MHPs have their roots in childhood and persist across the lifespan. The strongest environmental risk factor for MHPs in childhood is victimization (CV). The most common types of CV come from parents (eg, neglect, abuse and exposure to domestic violence) and from peers (eg, bullying-victimization). While CV increases risk for MHPs, not all individuals exposed to CV will develop MHPs. Indeed, many victimized individuals may not develop MHPs or may initially develop symptoms and recover as adults. Conversely, MHPs may increase in severity for others. These differences might emerge during the transition into adulthood, because this period coincides with major changes in social roles and responsibilities. To better inform preventive interventions, we need to understand the reasons for the wide variations in MHPs responses to CV. Our goals are (1) to characterize the trajectories of 5 MHPs including depression, anxiety, suicidality, cannabis use and mental health services use from ages 15 to 22 years among children exposed to different levels of CV and (2) to identify familial, social and lifestyle factors that can modify these trajectories. In order to do so, we will assess MHPs at age 22 years and collect complementary information on CV in a well-documented Canadian birth cohort assessed repeatedly since birth. Importance. This research will provide useful information on factors that can modify the course of MHPs in a critical period of life such as transitioning from adolescence into adulthood. Given this project will collect reliable data on MHPs in a Canadian cohort studied extensively since birth, the return on investment will be high.

column36: Understanding the impact of smoking cessation treatment on health and healthcare service use among smokers in Ontario
column37: Healthcare service use and costs of current of smokers are higher than those of non-smokers. This fact highlights the healthcare burden that results from smoking and suggests benefits of interventions that decrease smoking prevalence. There are evidence-based treatments that can help smokers quit. Studies of such treatments are usually judged only on how effective they are in helping smokers achieve full abstinence at a particular time point. This narrow focus does not reflect the variation in cessation trajectories of smokers who lapse and relapse during a quit attempt, employ a reduce-to-quit strategy, or seek to reduce, but not quit, smoking. Nor does it speak to the ultimate reason for funding large-scale interventions: improving the health of smokers and avoiding the healthcare burden associated with treating continuing smokers. The Smoking Treatment for Ontario Patients program is a publicly-funded smoking cessation treatment program accessed by 25,000 smokers per year in over 300 health care organizations. Treatment is individually tailored, and within a one year episode of care, there is no set number or frequency of clinical care visits. Evaluation is currently limited to survey questions answered by a portion of patients, which, in the context of a relapsing remitting condition, provide a slim understanding of the effects of receiving smoking cessation treatment. Healthcare use data provide an objective means by which to determine effects. We will use a database of patients who received STOP smoking cessation treatments, a population-based comparison group of smokers who did not receive STOP smoking cessation treatments, and population-based healthcare databases (e.g. physician billings, emergency room and hospital visits) to compare health and healthcare use between groups of smokers. This information can be used to help inform debates concerning how to best implement smoking cessation services within the publicly funded healthcare system in Ontario.

column36: Defining the role of DEPTOR in the regulation of brown adipose tissue development/function and evaluation of its impact on systemic metabolism.
column37: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) serves as a key heat-producing organ required to maintain body temperature and homeothermy. In response to cold, activation of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) rapidly turns on oxidative metabolism and heat production in BAT. Until recently, BAT was thought to be present and active only in small mammals and human newborns. Over the last years, several groups confirmed the existence of BAT in adult humans. Interestingly, BAT activation is reduced in obese and type 2 diabetic individuals. Moreover, studies show inverse relationships between BAT activity, diabetes and glycemia. These results suggest that BAT may be exploited to dissipate energy excess and improve metabolic homeostasis. Unfortunately, the precise mechanisms regulating BAT development, recruitment and function are still incompletely characterized. Over the last years, we and other have discovered that the mTOR signaling pathway plays key roles in BAT. The loss of mTOR signaling severely impairs BAT development/function and impairs systemic glucose and lipid metabolism. Here we propose a research project whose objective is to define whether modulating the action of mTOR through one of its well-established modulator (DEPTOR) could represent a viable approach to promote BAT development and function and improve systemic metabolism. We believe that our work has the potential to provide additional knowledge to generate new options to improve metabolism and enhance human health.

column36: Role of the deubiquitylating enzyme USP17 in colorectal cancer
column37: A protein called beta-catenin is often dysregulated human diseases, most notably in a variety of solid tumors, including colorectal cancer. It was indeed found to be highly express and hyperactive in tissue specimens and cells derived from colorectal cancer and it is viewed as a very promising target for future therapies. Drug discovery efforts have focused so far on the identification of small molecule inhibitors of the interaction between beta-catenin and other proteins with oncogenic properties, with marginal success. An alternative therapeutic approach would be to promote the degradation of beta-catenin in cancer cells. With this in mind, we have identified an enzyme called USP17, which act as a major regulator of beta-catenin protein levels and growth in colorectal cancer cells. The objective of this research proposal is to define the role of USP17 in the formation and malignant progression of colorectal cancer using in vitro cell culture systems and mouse models.

column36: Situating Suicide Risk: An inquiry into the production of the lives and afterlives of neurobiological vulnerability
column37: With at least 3900 Canadians lost to suicide each year, identifying the factors thought to lead to suicide risk is a top priority of scientific researchers and clinicians. Recently, neuroscience researchers identified biomarkers that they believe reflect suicide risk acquired over the life course as a result of specific negative experiences. These experiences include child abuse, which is thought to lead to measurable neurobiological changes that have durable and tangible effects. Researchers argue that these "embodied" forms of vulnerability are associated with the development of personality traits directly related to increased risk of suicidal behaviour. In this project we ask: what understandings of suicide risk are emerging in specific forms of scientific and psychiatric research? How do emerging notions of vulnerability overlap or not? We will examine the extent to which studies of biomarkers for suicide risk might change people's understandings of choice, risk, and volition as well as beliefs about appropriate management of suicide risk if it comes to be understood as "in the brain". Drawing on a unique, long-term engagement with a team of clinical and molecular researchers, this project traces intersecting notions of psychiatric vulnerability within the fields of developmental research, neuroscience, and environmental epigenetics. Based on qualitative interviews and ethnographic research, this empirically grounded study focuses on three intersections: (1) of the lab and the clinic, (2) of epigenetics and neuroanatomical studies, and (3) of prospective cohort studies and retrospectively produced models of neuropsychiatric risk. This project will offer a clarifying role of the specific nature of risk emerging at each of these intersections along with the implications of these risk models for addressing psychiatric conditions and suffering in the 21st century, at the crossroads of different sciences, experiences of suffering, and health care.

column36: Role of cortical CCK-GABA cells in cognition and cognitive impairments of schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental illness affecting approximately 1% of the world population. It is one of the leading causes of long-term disability, costing the Canadian health care system approximately $7 billion per year in medical care and lost productivity. One of the major obstacles in developing new therapeutics for schizophrenia is a lack of understanding of the cellular basis of the disease. Studies with schizophrenia brains consistently show deficits in inhibitory neurons in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Despite this important link, little is known about how such dysfunctional inhibitory neurons contribute to schizophrenia and whether one can rescue behavioural impairments by restoring the neuron dysfunction. The proposed experiments are aimed at addressing this knowledge gap. We will first study the changes in the important characteristics of inhibitory neurons (known as CCK-GABA cells) in well-established mouse models of schizophrenia. Next, using light-mediated neuron silencing and imaging, we will demonstrate its causal contribution to cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia and determine how their activity dynamically change during working memory task. Lastly, we will explore the therapeutic benefit of activating inhibitory neurons as a treatment of behavioural impairments. To this end, we have established a highly selective genetic method called the intersectional approach. This innovative tool allows us to examine systemically the core features of specific inhibitory neuron subtypes and manipulate their activity in freely behaving animals. The proposed research is an essential step for identifying pathophysiologically-based targets for novel therapeutic interventions for schizophrenia. If successful, it will lead to a better understanding of how distinct cortical interneuron subtypes contribute to schizophrenia and reveal novel treatment strategies that aim at correcting the underlying neural circuit deficits.

column36: A novel approach for personalized metabolomics profiling using DIA mass spectrometry
column37: Over the last decades, we have learned to use information about small molecules to predict disease risk, help in diagnosis, select the right drug and monitor the effectiveness of a given therapy. However, doctors and researchers currently have to order specific lab tests one at a time, which drives up costs and carries the risk of missing something important that was not explicitly tested for. We propose to combine recent advances in measurement technologies and new algorithms to implement a method that can measure thousands of small molecules in the blood of a patient, creating a comprehensive molecular profile. Our method can store this profile in a "digital biobank" for later analysis and comparison, essentially allowing us to convert a biological sample (blood, urine, tissue) into a digital representation of the sample containing all the information needed for scientific and diagnostic analysis. Our approach uses a novel acquisition method available in high resolution mass spectrometry called "DIA", which has not yet been systematically applied to small molecule analysis. The method will be capable of performing the equivalent of thousands of blood tests all at once on a single patient sample, thus allowing researchers and doctors to gain a much more detailed view of patient samples on a molecular level. If successful, we will demonstrate the capability of the DIA method by optimizing it for two important patient samples: blood samples and patient-derived stem cells. We will study blood samples of pre-diabetic patients and follow these patients over several years. By comparing the molecular profile of the same patient over time, we will be able to tell which molecules change when the patients get better or worse. Secondly, we will use DIA to profile patient-derived stem cells from the same patients, trying to understand how their cells react to stimulation with various factors.

column36: Using real-world data to simulate the effects of efficient referral strategies on wait times for elective surgery in Canada
column37: Surgical care in Canada is in crisis. Wait times for elective surgery can be long. Lack of hospital beds frequently causes cancellations or delays in surgery. We still rely on old systems to coordinate care for people having surgery. The way we provide surgical care must be reimagined so that we can continue to provide high-quality health care for Canadians in the future. Transforming surgical care for the future requires a number of innovations. We need better ways of getting people to surgery with shorter wait times, and we need sensible policies to guide how we organize surgery within the health system. This research project will use information routinely collected by the provincial government to describe wait times for surgery. We will create simulation models using this real-world information to create a computerized model of elective surgery. We will then be able to test different ways to improve surgical wait times (eg. single-entry models) to see what the effect will be. Finally, we will use Canada-wide information to see if there are any differences across the country. Data for all persons having elective surgery for which wait times are collected will be included. We will link this information with other health information databases such as physician billing data. This will allow us to develop simulations to test which referral systems have the potential to reduce wait times. We will then use national data from other provinces to estimate improvements in wait times that could be achieved in Canada. This study will provide guidance to improve access to elective surgery in Canada, and will demonstrate the potential benefits of efficient referral strategies and other innovative methods of organizing surgical care.

column36: RNA splicing and epigenetics in tuning the fate of neurons
column37: The birth of new neurons, a process called neurogenesis, occurs throughout our entire life. Every day, new neurons are derived from neural stem cells which have the capacity to renew themselves endlessly. Indeed, even people in their eighties still grow new neurons! However, aging, stress or poor diet all can reduce the natural rate of neurogenesis. The challenge is to make the most of our brain, prevent our neurons from dying in old age and keep growing new ones in order to stave off neurodegenerative diseases. Therefore, we need to understand the mechanisms promoting the generation of neurons. Each cell contains about 20,000 genes on its DNA. Those genes spell out instructions for making proteins. Each gene may instruct different yet similar proteins through a process called alternative splicing. The genome is like an enormous cookbook of 20,000 recipes. It's as if a "recipe-reader" omits or replaces ingredients; the resulting dish from one recipe may be similar but taste differently! Now, the DNA molecule that carries all genes (the enormous cookbook) is about 2 meters long and needs to be condensed to fit into the nucleus. The DNA packaging renders access to the genes harder to make proteins. The writing in the book is difficult to read! Transcription factors (the "recipe-readers") help to recognize some specific genes, modify the condensation on them and allow the production of a variety of proteins essential for the birth of neurons. If "recipe-readers" are faulty, neurogenesis suffers. This project will focus on a transcription factor called GATA3. GATA3 is expressed in multiple areas of the brain and is important for the birth of different types of neurons. We wish to determine how GATA3 regulates DNA condensation of its target genes and how it controls the production of proteins. The findings will provide novel insights into mechanisms regulating the birth of neurons, and will help to develop new therapeutic strategies against neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Long-term effects of mild traumatic brain injury through premature cellular senescence
column37: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) or concussions are very common, and tend to occur frequently in contact sports. They are also very common in situations of domestic abuse, in the military and can be a concern in certain work-places such as factories and construction sites. Recurrent mTBI has been linked to serious disabilities and some people, mainly those who sustain multiple trauma and women, suffer from persistent symptoms such as behavioural changes, memory problems, attention deficits, depression, increased suicidality and aggression. As concussion and its complications are not only limited and exclusive to elite athletes, the long-term effects of mTBI are a public health issue and require further clarification. Currently, there is no effective clinical and therapeutic approaches to help patients who deal with lingering and long-term effects of concussions. Many are left feeling desperate and helpless. Numerous sufferers are disabled for life, several fall into the grips of questionable and costly alternative therapeutic approaches or potent street drugs, and others opt to end prematurely their lives because of the severity of their mental despair and the lack of effective treatments. Unraveling the molecular changes initiated by mTBI and leading to long-term complications, will open the door to more suitable diagnostic and prognostic tools as well as proper effective treatments that are presently absent. Combining postmortem Human brains and animal models, we will look for evidence in support of this hypothesis and this will drive the design of biomarkers and effective treatments in the future.

column36: Finding the Optimal Resistance Training Intensity For Your Bones: A randomized controlled trial (FORTIFY Bones)
column37: Osteoporosis is a bone disease that can result in fractures, disability and an increased risk of premature death. Exercise is recommended for fall and fracture prevention, but health care professionals often recommend walking or lower intensity community exercise classes, which may not be effective for building bone. Further, individuals with osteoporosis are often told to avoid lifting or moving in certain ways, which creates fear and activity avoidance. Conversely, research suggests that to stimulate bone, you need higher loads on bone, with either higher intensity resistance training or impact exercise - the types of things people with low bone mass are told to avoid. In fact, not many studies have tested whether you can still build bone with exercise when you have osteoporosis, or whether moderate or high intensity strength training is safe in people with low bone mass. Our study will examine whether strength training can increase bone strength in people with osteoporosis, and what exercise intensities are effective. We will examine the effects of moderate or high intensity strength training, when compared to a typical community exercise class, on bone strength outcomes, muscle strength, physical function and quality of life. We will carefully measure injuries, and assess if strength training causes spine fractures (even ones without symptoms) by taking X-rays. We will then use our findings to design an exercise class that can be taught as part of Osteoporosis Canada's BoneFit training workshops to exercise professionals across Canada.

column36: Immunosuppressive pathways and HIV reservoirs in tissues
column37: HIV is a lifelong infection, which causes immunosuppression, decreasing body defense. The current antiretroviral therapy used to fight HIV infection has improved the lives of people living with HIV. However, these medications are unable to cure HIV due to the persistence of hidden virus inside certain cells called HIV reservoirs. Strategies to reduce HIV reservoir size is thought to be important to achieve HIV remission or cure. Most studies focusing on HIV reservoirs have been conducted in blood as opposed to tissues where HIV is hidden. Therefore, we will study HIV reservoirs in gut and lymph nodes which bear the vast majority of HIV reservoirs. The size of the HIV reservoir is larger with delayed treatment, heightened inflammation and leaky gut. We hypothesize that immunosuppressive pathways differ between gut and lymph nodes due to different local environment. Therefore, we will study how immunosuppressive pathways affect differently the size of HIV reservoirs in gut, lymph nodes and blood from participants receiving antiretroviral therapy. To access gut tissues and lymph nodes, we will perform colonoscopy and/or a small incision to remove lymph nodes. We will use state of the art techniques to assess immune changes which may contribute to HIV reservoirs in blood and tissues. In addition, we will conduct experiments on cells to test new drugs that reactivate the immune system to decrease HIV reservoir size. Our team of gastroenterologists, surgeons, physicians, immunologists and participant advocates will contribute to HIV cure research.

column36: Staphylococcus aureus at the commensal-pathogen interface: the superantigen paradox
column37: Staphylococcus aureus is a bacterium known to cause very serious disease in humans, but much of the time it can live harmlessly as a colonizing organism on the skin or in other sites such as the nose. This current research proposal is designed to understand how S. aureus can move from being a harmless colonizer to a serious pathogen by focusing on a group of important toxins called 'superantigens' which are found in all strains of S. aureus. These toxins can inappropriately activate a large number of white blood cells (called T lymphocytes) which in turn disrupts the ability of the immune system to respond properly to S. aureus. This proposal aims to answer the question of what role superantigens play in colonization and the progression to disease. To investigate this, we will use both colonization and infection models in mice, as well as analysis of the immune system and how it is manipulated by the bacteria during human blood stream infections. These studies are designed to provide a better understanding as to how this prominent bacterial pathogen can overcome our immune defenses with a goal of helping to devise rational therapeutic strategies including vaccines.

column36: Molecular Mechanisms of Non-homologous DNA End-joining
column37: Maintaining the integrity of genetic information is central to all aspects of life. DNA, the molecule in which this information is stored, is continually under attack from exposure to many types of harmful agents. Estimates put the frequency of DNA damage at up to 1,000,000 events each day in every cell. Although DNA is damaged in many ways, the most severe form of occurs when the long thread-like DNA molecule is broken in two or more pieces. If not repaired, a cell harboring this kind of damage will die. If repaired improperly, genetic information will be lost rendering such a cell susceptible to misregulation that can ultimately manifest itself in the onset of cancer. Fortunately, cells harbor a number of proteins which collectively act as guardians of the genome. Several such guardian proteins have now been identified in humans, however the way in which they come together to form a functional DNA repair machine is not yet understood. Using a technique (X-ray crystallography) that permits the detailed 3-dimensional visualization of proteins, it is possible to approach the understanding of DNA repair machinery from the perspective of a molecular mechanic. Specific parts or proteins can be studied both individually and in context of other parts of the machine. By first achieving a better understanding of how the DNA repair machinery functions normally, it may then be possible to evaluate why an individual's DNA repair machinery malfunctions and ultimately take measures to fix the repair machinery before harmful mutations are acquired.

column36: Is Ontario prepared for the return of measles?
column37: Measles is one of the most infectious diseases, causing severe illness and nearly 110,000 deaths every year worldwide, mostly in young children. Although a vaccine has been available for over 50 years, measles is not controlled in many countries, and there is a resurgence of outbreaks worldwide. Despite no longer circulating in Canada, measles continues to be imported from abroad, increasing our risk of outbreaks. In addition, an insufficient vaccination rate in some communities, and the possibility that protection from measles vaccine will decrease over time, may limit our ability to control measles. Our risk of outbreaks depends on the number of people in our population who are protected from measles, who can then protect others around them who are not immune. Our study aims to evaluate whether enough Ontarians are immune to measles to avoid large outbreaks, and to predict when declining immunity may become a risk to measles control. Our results will also assess whether vaccine immunity varies based on age, sex, vaccine program eligibility, and where an individual is born. This study will provide important evidence needed to inform policy advisers and decision-makers to improve practices related to measles immunization programs to ensure measles remains eliminated in Canada. It will also provide important evidence to help other countries optimize measles control strategies.

column36: The Political Economy of Tobacco Production and Control in Mozambique and Zimbabwe
column37: Tobacco use remains a leading cause of non-communicable diseases, creates an enormous burden on health care systems, and imperils the quality of life of users and their families. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) growing tobacco often pursue tobacco production as an economic development strategy, creating challenges to the tobacco control efforts of health ministries'. This development strategy assumes that tobacco production is beneficial to farmers' livelihoods and to the country's overall economy. There is little empirical research supporting this assumption and, to the contrary, our research demonstrates that tobacco farmers generally experience precarious economic livelihoods. Policy makers are often unaware of the economic circumstances of tobacco farmers, the costs of tobacco growing, and experience numerous pressures from industry and other actors to support tobacco growing. We seek to extend our current research in four countries (Kenya, Zambia, Malawi and Indonesia) to Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Mozambique and Zimbabwe are experiencing steady increases in tobacco consumption and production. Though the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) compels parties to find alternative livelihoods for smallholder tobacco growers, both countries have experienced substantial increases in smallholder tobacco production. In tandem with our other (already funded) studies, we will examine the factors that led to this increase in tobacco production, while inquiring into the livelihood conditions of tobacco farmers. We will also analyze the barriers and opportunities to stronger tobacco control policy in the two countries (both demand- and supply-side). Our results will better inform policy, programs and strategies to strengthen the control of tobacco supply and demand. Our research will inform tobacco control measures that are compatible with both health and economic development including economically viable alternatives to tobacco growing.

column36: Investigating the role of glycogen synthase kinase (GSK)-3 in atherosclerosis
column37: Heart attacks and strokes are a major cause of death and disability in Canada and around the world. It is known that a condition called atherosclerosis (the thickening of the blood vessel walls) is the underlying cause of most heart attacks and strokes. It is also known that certain risk factors, including smoking, obesity, high blood cholesterol, diabetes, and high blood pressure, promote the development of atherosclerosis. However, it is not known how or why this occurs. If we know how risk factors cause atherosclerosis, we can design ways to slow, stop or reverse disease progression. We have found a new pathway that might be an important link between cardiovascular risk factors and atherosclerosis. The objective of this study is to determine the role of this pathway in disease development and progression. The pathway that we have found involves a particular kind of stress (called ER stress). We believe that, when this stress is present, a factor (a protein) called GSK3 is activated. We have evidence that activated GSK3 can turn on other factors that can lead to the development of atherosclerosis. We have established a unique collection of cells and animal model systems that will allow us to investigate the links between risk factors - like diabetes - and the development of atherosclerosis. We are working in a step by step fashion to determine how risk factors cause ER stress, how ER stress activates GSK3 and how GSK3 is involved in atherosclerosis. In the course of these studies we hope to find ways in which this whole process can be blocked and perhaps reversed. In this way, our research could lead to the development of new effective treatments for cardiovascular disease.

column36: Etude longitudinale prospective du developpement des troubles de la personnalite au debut de l'age adulte chez des garcons et des filles qui presentaient des troubles de comportement perturbateur des l'enfance : le role des facteurs de risque specifiques en fonction du sexe et du genre
column37: Les filles et les garcons qui ont des troubles de comportements a l'enfance sont exposes a de nombreux facteurs de risque pouvant entrainer plusieurs problemes d'adaptation a l'age adulte, dont des troubles de la personnalite. A leur tour, ces troubles affectent severement la qualite de vie et generent des couts eleves en soins de sante mentale et physique. Alors qu'il est clair que la presence de troubles de comportement chez les enfants est un risque pour le developpement de tous les troubles de la personnalite, les etudes abordant la question des facteurs de risque qui pourraient expliquer que ces filles et garcons developpent un trouble plutot qu'un autre a l'age adulte sont peu nombreuses. Les resultats de quelques etudes ainsi que les donnees sur la prevalence des troubles selon le sexe suggerent que les filles pourraient etre plus a risque de developper un trouble de la personnalite borderline et les garcons un trouble de la personnalite antisociale. On ignore toutefois quels sont les facteurs qui conduisent ces filles et ces garcons a developper des troubles de la personnalite similaires ou differents. Ces connaissances sont importantes dans le contexte ou les interventions offertes sont surtout issues d'etudes sur des garcons et s'averent souvent moins efficaces chez les filles. Ce projet de recherche s'inscrit dans la suite d'une etude longitudinale debutee en 2007 aupres d'enfants presentant des troubles graves de comportement des le debut de l'ecole primaire. Maintenant que ces enfants sont rendus des adultes emergents, le projet permettra d'identifier, en tenant compte du sexe et du genre, les facteurs impliques, et leur role, dans le developpement des troubles de la personnalite au debut de l'age adulte. L'identification des facteurs de risques specifiques a chaque trouble de la personnalite et propres au sexe et au genre est primordiale pour la definition et l'adaptation des services de sante et des services sociaux offerts aux filles et aux garcons.

column36: Developing a platform for "off-the-shelf" CAR-T cell therapies for cancer using double negative T cells
column37: Immunotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses the immune system to find and attack cancer. One type of immunotherapy uses T cells, genetically-modified to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), which helps T cells to seek and kill cancers. CAR-modified T cells (CAR-T) have been very successful for the treatment of certain types of leukemia and lymphoma, but unfortunately are restricted to certain forms of B cell malignancies and are not available to all patients with those cancers due to the complicated manufacturing procedures to make and store this therapeutic product. Our proposal seeks to develop an alternative platform for CAR-technology using immune cells called double negative T cells (DNTs) which we hope will provide an easier, safer, and more reliable way to obtain CAR-modified cells. In laboratory settings, we have shown that DNTs can be easily obtained from healthy donors and are effective at killing leukemia and lung cancers and have found that DNTs are safe and do not cause damage to healthy tissue. We are currently testing DNTs in a clinical trial to treat high-risk AML patients. Due to the ability of DNTs to kill cancers without harming healthy tissue and the fact that they can be easily manufactured at lower costs and stored for later use, this proposal will test whether CAR-modified DNTs (CAR-DNTs) will be as effective and more accessible than conventional CAR-T cells for cancer patients. We will test this using animal models of human cancers in which mice will receive CAR-DNTs or conventional CAR-T cells and their safety and effectiveness to reduce cancer will be monitored. We will also test whether CAR-DNTs can be generated and stored in settings more adaptable for patient use, and study if CAR-DNTs can be used to treat cancers beyond B-cell malignancies. By providing a cost-effective, safe, and reliable method to utilize CAR-technology using DNTs, we hope that these CAR-DNTs will increase patient access to this very powerful treatment option.

column36: Combating Stigma and Social Isolation Among People Living with Lymphatic Filariasis in Ghana through Culturally Appropriate Interventions
column37: Lymphatic Filariasis (LF) is a neglected and stigmatized mosquito-borne illness that damages the lymphatic system leading to disfiguring swelling of the limbs, breasts and genitals. Widespread in 72 countries affecting some 120 million worldwide, LF is one of the world's leading causes of permanent and long-term disability. People living with LF typically experience a triple burden: (1) the direct impact of the disease, (2) social stigma (such as shame, harassment, exclusion) and isolation, and (3) mental health impacts resulting from both the disease and consequent stigma. Current literature is treatment-focused and largely neglects the cultural and social context of the illness, with limited attention paid to stigma and few stigma-oriented interventions. Drawing together an interdisciplinary team of researchers from Canada and Ghana, our project addresses five aims focused on health, wellbeing, social inclusion and cultural understandings of LF with a geographic focus on areas of Ghana particularly hard hit by the disease. We aim to: (1) understand community perceptions, interpretations and cultural perspectives of LF, (2) determine the causes underpinning social stigmatization of people with LF, (3) develop an intervention to assist in alleviating stigma and isolation related to LF, (4) implement and assess the intervention (5) design a framework for the development of culturally appropriate and effective interventions that can be applied in other African countries where LF is endemic. We aim to improve the health and wellbeing of people living with LF through: (1) an increased understanding of the underlying causes of stigma and isolation, (2) the development, implementation and evaluation of a culturally-sensitive intervention to prevent and alleviate these experiences and (3) the creation of a framework to help adapt this intervention to other contexts.

column36: Vaping e-cigarettes: Prospective Outcome Study

Public health organizations fear that young people who otherwise would not have smoked cigarettes will become established long-term vapers with associated negative health outcomes. Participants will be followed-up annually for 2 years, with brief assessments every 3-months. In-depth interviews with up to 20 vapers and non-vapers will inform reasons for use/non-use and trajectories over time.

column36: Alteplase Compared to Tenecteplase in patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke: QuICR & OPTIMISE Registry based Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: When a clot blocks blood supply to a blood vessel supplying the brain, it causes a stroke. Patients who suffer from stroke can lose important brain functions like speech, motor power and vision can even die from the stroke. Modern acute stroke treatment is based on removing the clot from the blocked artery either by dissolving the clot using a clot busting drug (alteplase) or by removing the clot mechanically. The clot busting drug (alteplase) that is currently being used does not always succeed in dissolving the clot. Small recent studies show that newer drugs like tenecteplase may have better ability to dissolve clots blocking brain arteries while also being safer than alteplase when used in patients with acute stroke. Moreover, tenecteplase is a single injection unlike alteplase which is given using an infusion pump over a period of an hour. This means tenecteplase could be given more easily, thus saving time. Time saved is brain saved. Tenecteplase may also result in less need for expensive stroke therapies such as mechanical removal of clots, thus saving costs. We therefore propose a randomized trial that compares intravenous tenecteplase to intravenous alteplase in patients who are currently being treated with intravenous alteplase. The trial will enroll 1600 patients from 25 emergency departments across Canada. The trial will use a pragmatic design so as to not affect patient care in any way. Patients and caregivers will be engaged to inform study design and conduct. All data for the trial will be collected from ongoing patient registries, thereby reducing the costs of running such a trial significantly. The results of this trial are likely to change clinical practice, improve delivery of care to acute stroke patients, result in better patient outcomes and save the health system costs.

column36: Developing a Pan-Canadian Risk-Assessment Tool to Proactively Assess Hospital Opioid Safeguards
column37: As the opioid crisis escalates, so too does the rate of opioid loss and theft from Canadian hospitals, otherwise known as diversion. Freedom of information requests to Health Canada reveal that 800 to 1000 self-reported hospital losses of controlled drugs are captured each year, with some reports showing losses of several drugs at a time. Between 2010 and 2016, hospital losses of controlled drugs increased over 200%, with true numbers likely higher due to under-reporting and the difficulty of detecting diversion. In turn, these challenges impede awareness of, and research on, this stigmatized issue. Diversion is associated with serious safety concerns, affecting health care workers (HCWs) (e.g., those with substance use disorder often overdose), patients (e.g., impaired staff have committed errors on the job), population health (e.g., a single HCW infected over 40 patients with hepatitis C), and costs (e.g., hospitals have paid million dollar lawsuits). The main goal of this study is to improve opioid guidance for Canadian hospitals. First, we will review, appraise, and consolidate recommendations to prevent or detect diversion. We will then design and evaluate an online risk-assessment tool for hospitals to assess their opioid safeguards against the consolidated recommendations, and a quick reference guide (QRG) to help them decide what to do with their results. Finally, we will disseminate the risk-assessment tool and QRG to Canadian hospitals which will have the double knowledge translation benefit of (1) delivering best available guidance to hospitals (e.g., assess their individual vulnerabilities) and (2) aggregating information from hospitals to highlight systemic issues that require further focus (e.g., innovation, research, future diversion prevention efforts). Consequently, the outputs of this study will help improve hospital opioid safety in the short- and long-term, minimizing opioid-related harm to patients, staff, hospitals and the larger community.

column37: Collectively, traumatic and degenerative brain injuries afflict millions of Canadians, and burden society at both the human and financial levels. Since the human brain has very little regenerative capacity, injury typically leads to permanent deficits. Harnessing the regenerative potential of neural stem cells represents one of the only approaches with the promise of restoring function to treat these conditions. However, the complexity of the brain represents a formidable barrier to the fulfilment of this goal. In order to develop effective cell replacement therapies, we need to greatly improve our understanding of how brain circuits are generated during development, so that we can generate the appropriate types of cells. During brain development, stem cells must give rise to a multitude of different cell types in order to generate a fully functional nervous system. Stem cells must tightly regulate the expression of thousands of genes in order to generate the diversity of neurons and glia found in the brain. This process is very poorly understood. We have recently identified a gene called Casz1 that appears to play an important role in this process. We hypothesize that Casz1 coordinates gene expression to limit and control the types of cells that a neural stem cell can produce. We propose to study the precise biological pathway that Casz1 uses to do this, using the developing retina as a model system. We anticipate that this work will shed light on the mechanism through which neural stem cells regulate their potential, which should allow us to control and tailor their output for regenerative medicine. By improving our knowledge of how neural stem cells behave during brain development, we also anticipate that this study may provide insights into congenital neurodevelopmental disorders.

column36: The Epidemiology and Economic Burden of Hepatitis C Viral infection in the First Nations Population in Ontario
column37: Hepatitis C viral (HCV) infection has the highest health burden among infectious diseases in Ontario. No research has fully addressed the burden of HCV among First Nations people in Ontario. Research that helps us understand the burden of HCV among the First Nations population can help communities influence policy and/or community action, and improve health and well-being. This study will bring together researchers and the Ontario First Nations communities to evaluate the burden of HCV infection. This study has 4 parts: 1) we will use healthcare administrative data governed by the First Nations in Ontario and HCV testing records from Public Health Ontario Laboratories data to examine the extent of HCV infection within the First Nations population in Ontario. These results will be interpreted with members of the Ontario First Nations communities to understand the contextual roots underlying HCV infection; 2) we will describe patterns of health care for HCV, based on records of patient interactions with the healthcare system. This will identify any potential barriers to access and/or gaps in service delivery; 3) we will measure the cost to the Ontario health care system for HCV infection and determine the effects of clinical and demographic variables on health care costs. This will help make decisions regarding community treatment and prevention programs; 4) we will use community-based participatory research approaches to engage, collaborate and understand the needs of First Nations communities and organizations, and to make sure that the results of our research go back to the community and are interpreted appropriately for the First Nations context. column36: Vascular normalization improves immunotherapy in advanced stage ovarian cancer.
column37: Most women are diagnosed with ovarian cancer at late stages, where current treatment protocols have limited effectiveness. In this proposal we describe a novel treatment approach that could significantly improve our ability to treat women with advanced stage ovarian cancer. We propose to target the abnormal tumor blood vessels that form, to reestablish a healthy blood supply to the tumor. In doing this, we will facilitate delivery of therapeutic compounds to the tumor. Currently, a significant impediment to cancer treatment is the inability to efficiently deliver therapies to the tumor. Normalization of the tumor vasculature will inhibit the intratumoral immune suppression that is commonly seen in ovarian cancer. Another anticipated outcome of vascular normalization is a reduction in interstitial fluid pressure, which creates an impediment for therapy uptake in the tumor. By reducing pressure within the tumor, we will also improve lymphatic vascular function to enhance tumor blood flow and migration of immune cells to lymph nodes to maximize activation of tumoral immunity. With this combined treatment approach, we anticipate that we will be able to induce significant regression of advanced stage disease and dramatically improve health and survival in our preclinical model of ovarian cancer. This therapeutic approach may lead to a dramatic improvement in our ability to treat women with advanced stage ovarian cancer.

column36: Older adults' trajectories of health and social care in two Canadian provinces
column37: Navigating the health and social care system can be difficult, in particular for older adults and their caregivers who may interact with different providers of care over time. This study seeks to create evidence that will support improved integration of care services across the system. We have 4 objectives. First, we will prioritize relevant patient-centred outcomes based on previous international work and in collaboration with our diverse stakeholders. Second, we will explore care trajectories (the sequence of interactions with the health and social care system) and identify factors that may lead to certain types of trajectories, as well as how the trajectories are related to the prioritized outcomes. Third, we will explore how to classify the observed types as trajectories as either preferred or less preferred (still in consultation with our stakeholders). Finally, we will identify innovative programs or policies from Quebec and Ontario and examine their potential to improve trajectories of care. We will achieve these objectives using both qualitative and quantitative methods. We will conduct a deliberative prioritization and validation of the outcome measures with our stakeholders. Then, using a dataset that links responses to the Canadian Community Health Survey to the respondents' health administrative data, we will explore and group trajectories and relate them to the relevant outcomes. We will use an existing registry of innovative programs that was developed with previous CIHR funding support, to identify programs that are beneficial for preferred trajectories. We will conduct a comparative study between Quebec and Ontario. Finally, we will interview patients and practitioners to gain their ideas about how to improve trajectories for everyone. This work is expected to support efforts to better integrate care services with the goal of improving care trajectories, ultimately improving the experience and outcomes of the health and social care system.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling photoreceptor genome organization and neurodegeneration
column37: The nucleus of each human cell contains approximately 2 metres of DNA. Cells must confine this enormous amount of genetic information within a microscopic space, while simultaneously maintaining the ability to access and utilize genes. To do this, cells must partition the genome into different compartments of the nucleus. Some regions of the genome remain accessible, while other regions are compacted. This very basic process is vital for cells to function and survive, but it remains very challenging to study, and is therefore poorly understood. We have uncovered several proteins that influence this process in retinal photoreceptors. When these proteins are removed, the retina degenerates, and the genome becomes disorganized. This proposal will study these proteins in detail, in order to untangle their role in genome organization, retinal function, and neurodegeneration. Our work will shed light on the role of this poorly understood process, and determine its contribution to retinal degeneration, which is an increasingly prevalent problem due to Canada's aging demographics.

column36: Risk of infections with tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) in pregnant women and their offspring
column37: Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) are important drugs in the treatment of pregnant women with chronic inflammatory diseases. Despite existing concerns that these potent drugs may cause immunosuppression, there are limited data on the risk of infections in exposed pregnant women and their offspring. The goal of our research project is to assess the risk of serious infections associated with TNFi in pregnant women and their offspring. We will use data from a large United States administrative database to identify pregnant women with chronic inflammatory diseases for which TNFi are indicated (i.e. rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel diseases). We will assess the risk of serious infections during pregnancy and the postpartum period (i.e. the period after delivery) in mothers exposed to TNFi compared to unexposed mothers with chronic inflammatory diseases. We will link mothers exposed to TNFi with their offspring. In these children, we will assess the risk of serious infections occurring during the first year of life, as well as the risk of hospitalizations and/or outpatient visits for diarrhea according to rotavirus vaccine exposure. Our study results will help guide counselling, monitoring, and management of pregnant women requiring TNFi during pregnancy to minimize infectious complications. Our research project will provide much-needed data to help inform best practice guidelines. Ultimately, our findings will help optimize reproductive outcomes in chronic inflammatory diseases and improve the health of offspring, while reducing the burden of infections in this susceptible population.

column36: Understanding and enhancing anti-inflammatory stromal cell functions to treat osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common cause of disability in people over the age of 50. OA involves loss of cushioning cartilage in the joint, changes in bone and inflammation. OA is becoming more prevalent as our population ages with 1 in 4 Canadians predicted to have OA by 2040. There are direct and indirect healthcare and socio-economic costs, over 2% of our GDP. Although many drugs have been developed, there is no treatment. Patients typically get steroid or other biologics to help manage their pain and symptoms; ultimately patients have to resort to joint-replacement surgery. Stromal cell therapy has recently emerged as a promising therapy, with evidence that it improves patients' pain and function. My own lab has conducted Canada's first stromal cell therapy trial in 12 patients with knee OA, and we reported improvements in pain, symptoms and joint stiffness. We also saw that stromal cells were reducing inflammation. Our working hypothesis is that stromal cells are reducing inflammation in the joint through their interactions with immune cells known as macrophages. We want to better understand how stromal cells work in the context of OA. This is important to understand before we undertake a larger, more expensive clinical trial, because if we know how the stromal cells work, we can design more effective clinical trials. This includes screening stromal cells from different donors to pick the ones that are going to be most effective in treating OA; choosing patients who will best respond to stromal cell therapy, and modifying the stromal cells using genetic engineering tools such that they are really good at treating OA (likely by reducing joint inflammation, and therefore pain). Our study results will help make stromal cell therapy for OA effective, which is needed if this treatment is to receive approval by the regulators. Only then can stromal cell therapy become a routine clinical treatment available to Canadian patients.

column37: The majority of solid cancers in adults originate from cells known as epithelial cells. Normally, these epithelial cells are confined to specific places in the body. For example, breast epithelial cells migrate great distances during puberty to eventually form a glandular organ in the adult. column36: Neuroplastic mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology of tinnitus
column37: Tinnitus is a bothersome noise or ringing in the ears occurring in the absence of external auditory stimulation. It is a common problem affecting approximately 1 person in 4 in Canada and is most often linked to age-related hearing loss. In around 6% of these cases, tinnitus is so distracting that it interferes with several central aspects of their lives including sleeping and working, and in the worse cases can lead to even depression and suicide. There is currently no effective treatment for tinnitus in large part because the mechanisms causing it are mostly unknown. Aberrant rewiring of the sound processing areas of the brain is thought to play an important role in the emergence of tinnitus, but the very nature of this reorganization remains very controversial. The primary goal of this project is to understand precisely if and how the brain is reorganized in tinnitus sufferers and to relate identified brain changes to individual tinnitus parameters and measures of tinnitus severity. We propose experiments that will make use of novel neurophysiological techniques we have developed to map the auditory cortex's functional organization using in high-resolution magnetoencephalography (MEG). MEG is the ideal neuroimaging technique to achieve this as it operates in silence, as opposed to fMRI, and has a higher spatial resolution than EEG. We will, among other objectives, test the hypothesis that tinnitus in humans is associated with an over-representation of the dominant tinnitus frequency within the auditory cortex, and determine which neurophysiological measures are the best correlates of tinnitus severity. We expect that our findings will significantly enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the emergence of tinnitus and will also hopefully provide new therapeutic targets for future research.

column37: HPVs are widespread in all populations. While certain HPV types infect our skin, others infect the mucosa of our oral cavity or anal and genital regions. Many HPV types that are sexually transmitted can lead, several years after the initial infection, to development of cervical cancer, the second most common cancer in women worldwide These same viruses also cause the majority of anal cancers and a growing proportion of head-and-neck cancers, in particular those affecting the base of the tongue and the tonsils. E1 must use several components (i.e. proteins) from the infected cell to make copies of the HPV genetic material. In this project, we will use a microscopy assays to study the process used by E1 to make copies of the HPV genome. We will test if specific cellular components that are used to make copies of our own DNA are also used by the virus. We will also identify cellular components that E1 attaches to and test if they are used to make new copies of the viral DNA. As such, our proposed studies will identify cellular components that are necessary for HPV to copy its genetic material and, thus, to cause disease. Identification of these cellular components will suggest new ways of interfering with the virus that could be used to develop antiviral drugs against HPVs.

Indeed, vascular stiffness has become synonymous with vascular aging. Stiffness of blood vessels is a major cause of arterial high blood pressure and increased incidence of heart failure and stroke. However, the way that arterial stiffness is measured, it is blood pressure dependent, and this makes it difficult to distinguish the cause and effect relationship between blood pressure and vascular stiffness. While stiffness of large arteries has been studied over the past two decades, our progress has shown that we are better with a model that integrates large, medium and small sized vessels. The integrated and novel vision may be a paradigm shifting concept that is need to approach the problem of hypertension in the elderly subjects, with diabetes or kidney disease. Supported by Heart and Stroke foundation, we have discovered that stiffness of the arteries behave differently in response to accelerated aging. Therefore, we proposed a new index of vascular aging that is shown to be better and it has the added advantage of being blood pressure independent. This new index is based on the theory of arterial stiffness gradient. In this study, our objectives are to determine how we can modulate arterial stiffness gradient, and how this modulation can affect blood circulation in the smaller blood vessels. In this proposal we will conduct studies in two groups of patients with or without kidney disease. This novel index of vascular aging is key concept in risk stratification and development of novel therapeutic strategies.

column36: Better understanding vulnerability to the consequences of discrimination: Externalizing behaviours and social support as moderators between racism, sexism and homophobia and depressive and substance use outcomes
column37: In Canada, the three most common stigmatized identities for adolescents are those based on gender, race/ethnicity and sexuality. Discrimination based on these stigmatized identities (i.e., sexism, racism, and homophobia) increases individual level risk for depressive symptoms and problematic substance use. Not all youth who experience these kinds of discrimination, however, are at risk for depressive symptoms and substance use. This project focuses on externalizing behaviour and social support as two key risk and resilience processes to better understand variation in the consequences of discrimination. This project has two objectives. The first is to use quantitative methods to explore if the links between sexism, racism, and homophobia and depressive symptoms and substance use are mitigated or exacerbated by social support and externalizing behaviour, respectively. This objective will be tested using secondary data analyses with four existing datasets. The second objective employs a mixed-methods approach to examine how sex and gender shape the link between externalizing behaviours and social support and depressive symptom and substance use outcomes. Quantitative analyses with a longitudinal dataset will be complimented with qualitative interviews of 48 youth who will speak to how their gender and sexual identities shape how they are treated by others, and the consequences of this discrimination for their health and wellbeing. The findings have clinical implications for (1) identifying pockets of vulnerability among youth experiencing discrimination, (2) understanding how social support can be used to protect youth against the consequences of discrimination, and (3) focusing intervention efforts on addressing discrimination among youth with externalizing problems. This project provides a practical framework for addressing the impact of discrimination by identifying factors that serve to augment or mitigate its consequences.

column36: Public Health Risk Assessment Tools for Emerging Vector-borne Diseases 2.0
column37: Lyme disease is rapidly emerging in Canada due to recent climate and environmental changes. Despite the existence of transmission 'hotspots' for Lyme disease and other tick-borne pathogens, the link between environmental risk (where infected ticks are found) and epidemiological risk (the incidence of human disease) is poorly understood at a practical scale. This project aims to identify the socioecological determinants and distribution of Lyme disease risk in a Canadian urban centre using spatial analytic and epidemiological methods. Risk maps will be developed as practical tools for local public health officer application, and population knowledge and behaviours will be characterized to inform targeted interventions. Ultimately these results will help to improve the prevention of vector-borne diseases among Canadians. It is intended that this methodology for public health risk assessment can be applied in other Canadian cities and to other emerging disease systems, in order to predict the impact of vector-borne diseases and develop appropriate response plans.

column36: Mechanisms of Sensory Dysfunction in Christianson Syndrome
column37: The ability to perceive pain is an evolutionary advantage aimed at protecting the host against potential injury. Defects in sensing pain as well as other types of external stimuli have been frequently observed in children with Christianson Syndrome (CS), and can lead to frequent injuries, self-mutilation, and shortened life expectancy. This syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC9A6 gene encoding the pH-regulating alkali cation (sodium or potassium)/proton exchanger NHE6 isoform. How changes in the function of this protein lead to an elevated pain threshold, as well as other distortions in sensory perception, in CS patients is currently unknown. We hypothesize that these defects impair the proper pH and functioning of intracellular vesicles that carry neurotransmitter receptors and other ion channels to synapses of neurons, which in turn affects nervous system electrical activity and function, including the ability to sense pain. In the current project, we propose to combine clinical and basic science approaches, including a range of molecular, cellular, and electrophysiological techniques in cultured cells and genetically-engineered mouse models of this disorder, to understand the mechanisms underlying sensory dysfunction in CS patients. We also propose genetic mouse models and viral approaches to rescue NHE6 gene expression and determine whether complementation strategies can be a therapeutic option for these patients.

column36: Transcriptional Regulation of Human Trophoblast Development
column37: In the course of human development, a single fertilized egg has to give rise to an entire person. In order for this to happen correctly, some cells have to become the placenta that nourishes the embryo and some have to become the tissues that form the future baby. Correct formation of the placenta is critical for the health of the mother and baby. Certain proteins called "transcription factors" determine which other proteins are produced in each cell type, and by extension, the identity of the cell. Our goal is to figure out which transcription factors are critical for making the different types of cells that form the placenta and how they act in development. This will help us understand why sometimes there are abnormalities of placenta function that lead to miscarriage and pregnancy complications and provide new opportunities to address diseases of the placenta.

column36: Magnetic Resonance-guided Focused Ultrasound for Incisionless Musculotendinous Contracture Release
column37: Shortening of muscles and tendons occur in many diseases, such as cerebral palsy, stroke, dementia, and spinal cord injury to name a few. Depending on where the shortenings occur, they are painful and disabling, making it difficult for a patient to walk, sit, or use their hands. It causes emotional and financial stress to the patients, their families, and the health care system. Current treatments include splinting and surgery. Splinting is a long-term and often ineffective intervention. Open surgery has significant morbidity, costs, and often requires extensive rehabilitation. Magnetic Resonance-guided Focused Ultrasound (MRgFUS) has emerged as a tool for minimally-invasive and incisionless treatment. By using many ultrasound beams and focusing them onto a point in our bodies, MRgFUS can heat up or cut through tissue at that point without cutting through skin, nerves or blood vessels. Our research will explore MRgFUS as a safe, and accurate way to cut shortened tendons without cutting through skin. When tendons are released, the patient will regain some functionality. We successfully completed a study using MRgFUS to cut tendons in an animal model. The future direction of our research will be to optimize the parameters used, and to deliver the best treatment with the least amount of harm. Extensive studies in animal models will evaluate each parameter and their effects on different types of tendons. Once completed, these studies will be repeated in live animals, and subsequently in humans. This is a collaboration between Biomedical Engineering, Neurosurgery, Orthopedic Surgery, and Radiology at SickKids. In all, MRgFUS is a noninvasive treatment for tendon shortening. Patients will have a better quality of life with less scars, less infection, less pain, less anesthetics and less opioids. The health care system will have more resources available due to the shortened hospital stay. Our research sets the foundation for future studies in non-invasive treatments.

column36: Elucidating the role of lipoprotein(a) in calcific aortic valve stenosis using novel proteomic and imaging approaches
column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is the most common form of heart valve diseases, affecting almost 3% of the population older than 65. CAVS is caused by the calcification of cells in the aortic valve. In patients with CAVS, if the valve is not surgically removed and replaced, 4 out of 5 patients will die within 5 years. Unfortunately, no pharmacological agents have been proven effective in the treatment of CAVS. The identification of CAVS risk factors might give us insights about new treatment opportunities for these high-risk patients. Our team has contributed to the identification of a particle carried in the blood called lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) as one of the strongest genetic risk factor for CAVS. Between one in four and one in three patients with CAVS might have elevated Lp(a) levels. Lp(a) is also associated with the risk of developing a broad range of cardiovascular diseases such as coronary artery disease (CAD), peripheral artery disease, heart failure and stroke. Whether the measurement of blood Lp(a) levels in patients with CAVS would be clinically useful is unsure. Additionally, why Lp(a) causes aortic valve calcification and CAVS is still a mystery. The objective of this research project aims are twofold: First, we will determine whether Lp(a) is associated with CAVS risk independently of the presence or absence of CAD and test whether siblings of patients with CAVS and high Lp(a) levels are at increased risk of future CAVS using state-of-the-art cardiac imaging techniques. Second, we will perform experimental using blood and explanted aortic valves of patients who have had their aortic valve removed because of CAVS to determine specifically how Lp(a) increases aortic valve calcification and CAVS. On top of generating new knowledge on Lp(a) and CAVS biology, this study will contribute to identifying the key patients in whom Lp(a) should be assessed and targeted.
