column36: Adapting transitions-in-care (TiC) strategies for cancer to be culturally relevant with First Nations communities
column37: Cancer mortality in Canada is higher among First Nations people than the general population. Historical trauma from colonization and residential schools has negatively influenced First Nations people's trust in western health care, and these post-colonial relations continues to disadvantage First Nations people from engaging in transitions-in-care (TiC) services for cancer. From diagnosis onwards, cancer care TiC strategies do not reflect First Nations people's cultural values and practices or build upon communities' strengths. Building on our existing partnership with Pikwakanagan First Nations, an Algonquin community in Ontario, the overall purpose of this study is to implement and evaluate a TiC strategy that has been adapted to be culturally relevant for First Nations people who have experienced cancer. We will first collaboratively determine a TiC strategy for system navigation with a community Advisory Group, and adapt it to be culturally relevant to First Nations people who have experienced cancer. Working in full partnership with First Nations partners will ensure the adapted TiC strategy is culturally relevant. We will then co-design an evaluation framework and implement the strategy with Pikwakanagan First Nations Health Services and Family Health Team for 6 months. We will evaluate outcomes that include: feasibility and costs of integrating the strategy into health services; acceptability, use and influence of the strategy on system navigation; and the process of adapting the TiC strategy to be culturally relevant. Data will be collected through a process log, administrative health services databases, focus groups and interviews. This research is urgently required given the high cancer rates among First Nations people and the lack of culturally responsive healthcare services that build on First Nations peoples' strengths to meaningfully address TiC cancer care needs.

column36: Addressing variation in practice in red blood cells transfusion for patients undergoing gastrointestinal cancer surgery.
column37: Red blood cell transfusions are common in patients receiving gastrointestinal surgery, however, they often cause significant harm, including increased risk of death, cancer recurrence and longer hospital stays. There exists significant evidence that shows restricting transfusions improves patient outcomes, but still every second transfusion administered to gastrointestinal surgery patients is unnecessary and potentially avoidable. We propose to fill these gaps analyze transfusion practices with a focus on avoidable red blood cell transfusions, and develop quality indicators to identify institutional performance and quality assessment. This project has four objectives performed in a population of gastrointestinal cancer surgery patients. First we will examine variation in the use of all red blood cell transfusions between institutions, and identify factors associated with use of transfusions. Second, we will examine variation in the use of avoidable red blood cell transfusions between institutions, and identify factors associated with use of unnecessary transfusions. Third, we will examine variation in post-operative outcomes (30-day mortality, 90-day readmission, and overall survival) between institutions, and assess their association with red blood cell transfusions. Finally, in collaboration with patients, heath care providers, and policy-makers, we will identify consensus-based quality indicators for use of red blood cell transfusions that can be used to assess institutional quality of care and performance in gastrointestinal surgery. This project has the potential to minimize already scarce blood resources. Information on avoidable red blood cell transfusions and quality indicators for perioperative use of transfusions is needed to design interventions aimed at reducing variation via increased uptake of best practices.

column36: Tendon impairment in people with familal hypercholesterolemia: clinical and laboratory studies
column37: Some people are born without the ability to clear cholesterol from their blood stream. This condition is known as FH (familial hypercholsterolemia), and in particular blood levels of LDL (low density lipoprotein, sometimes called "bad cholesterol") are often very high. FH can cause heart attacks or strokes. FH affects around 1/250 people. A warning sign that someone may have FH is when they develop Achilles tendon pain and thickening. Tendons are usually tough connective tissues, made of collagen. Many people have a long history of Achilles tendon pain and do not tolerate tendon loading (walking, jogging) very well, only to find out years later that they have FH. It is not fully known why the Achilles tendons of people with high cholesterol become painful and thickened and lose their load tolerance. In this research, we want to find out more about what causes Achilles tendon problems in people with FH. We want to learn how FH affects the function of tendons. We think that LDL can become harmful to tendon cells, reducing the ability to make collagen and resulting in softer tendons. If our hypothesis is true, then we could start to develop therapies to help rebuild the collagen and regain the tendon's ability to tolerate exercise. This would make it easier to engage in healthy exercise, which is really important in lowering cholesterol levels.

column36: Psychotropic drug use and safety among children and youth
column37: Use of medications for treating mental health illness is increasing in Canadian children and youth, with nearly 1 out of every 12 being prescribed one of these drugs. However, little is known about the long-term safety of medications for mental health illness in children and youth, and very few of these drugs are approved by Health Canada for use in young people. As a result, most of these drugs are being used 'off-label' in children, meaning that they are being used in a manner that is different from that for which they were approved. Because use of these drugs is increasing, it is important to understand how these drugs are being prescribed and the chances of long-term side effects. In Ontario, which is home to close to 40% of Canadian children and youth, researchers now have access to the information needed to conduct such studies. That is, by combining different sources of data, we can use Ontario's health care databases to answer questions about drugs for mental health illness in children and youth. Our research proposal will answer these specific questions: 1) Did prescribing of medications for mental health illness to children and youth change in the period before and after the Ontario government started covering the cost of all medications?; 2) How does use of these drugs differ across the province?; 3) Do drugs for attention deficit disorder cause serious eye problems with long-term use? and 4) Does the combination of drugs for attention deficit disorder and schizophrenia cause serious heart problems? For each question, we will also see whether differences exist between girls and boys. Our research team is well qualified to answer these questions, with pharmacists, doctors, psychologists and researchers working together over a planned 4 year period. We will also work closely with parents and policy makers to ensure that our research is used to improve the health of Ontario's children and youth who require these medications.

column36: Translational Control by the La and La-Related Proteins
column37: Healthy cells have evolved a number of ways to respond to their environment and adapt to stresses. One critical way that cells respond to such cues is by controlling the cohort of proteins they synthesize, which allows the cell to adapt to new situations. However, dysregulation of of these responses can lead to diseases like cancer and neurodegeneration. One class of factors known to have an important function in the control of protein synthesis is the La and La-related proteins. Dysregulation of function of the La and La-related proteins has been linked extensively to cancer and infection by viruses, but we do not understand how. In this proposal, we will identify the genes that rely on these factors as well the ways in which they control protein synthesis. Our work will therefore lead to a substantial new understanding for many challenges to human health.

column36: Mechanisms regulating telomerase and telomeres
column37: Cancers are often characterized by genetic instability. Telomerase is an enzyme that plays a role in stabilizing the genetic material and protecting cells from death. To understand the role that this enzyme plays in the development and maintenance of cancer cells, and its potential cell survival properties, it is essential to understand how the enzyme works biochemically. Telomerase is generally present in cancer cells and absent from most normal cells making it a specific target for anticancer therapy. A knowledge of how this enzyme works is necessary to design and test drugs that specifically target and inactivate this enzyme. A knowledge of how the enzyme works is also necessary to design strategies to activate this enzyme, and protect essential cells from death, for instance in premature aging syndromes characterized by telomerase deficiencies. I propose to dissect the function of telomerase at the molecular and cellular level. The analysis of telomerase which is altered compared to the normal enzyme will allow the identification of regions of the enzyme which are important to its function. Having this information and thus a better understanding of how telomerase works will provide us with tools to address the role of telomerase in cancer and cell survival.

column36: Zebrafish fin regeneration: Cellilar mechanisms.
column37: Fish fins and limbs of mammals evolved from similar structures. Fish have kept the ability to regenerate their fins after injury and to re-develop bony rays that were lost. Regeneration depends on the formation of a group of proliferative and undifferentiated cells which will progressively differentiate as the regenerate is growing. One important question to address mechanisms of regeneration is to determine how interactions between cells allow the regeneration process. Fin rays are made of a series of bone segments separated by joints. We are interested in understanding how these bone segments and joints are regularly added at the tip of the ray as the fin regenerates. We showed that bone cells (osteoblasts) and joint cells come from the same precursor cells. Our first hypothesis is that changes in the level of gene expression or activation of others is informing the precursor to form a joint cell or an osteoblast. Osteoblast maturation follows a step by step program. We recently identified osteoblasts expressing a combination of genes indicating that this osteoblast population represents a new ''step'' in the maturation program. Our second hypothesis is that the presence of this new osteoblast population depends on interactions with adjacent cells. We propose to test our hypotheses by using techniques that allow 1) to perturb gene activity or 2) to eliminate specific cells (e.g. joint cells) to examine the impact on bone and joint formation and on the regeneration process in general. This work will allow to better understand how cells communicate to assure the formation of new bone and of joints between these bones. The relative simplicity of the fin regenerate make it an excellent model to study regeneration mechanisms, a fundamental knowledge that will be important in establishing strategies to develop methods, drugs or tools to induce a regeneration response to injury, trauma or degenerative event in species that do not regenerate, including humans.

column36: Lentivirus persistence in the brain: viral, host and therapeutic determinants
column37: Soon after a person is infected with HIV-1, the virus enters the brain. It stores itself in specific types of brain cells. About one in four people with HIV/AIDS develops a dementia-like brain disorder even when they get antiretroviral therapy (ART). ART does not remove all virus from the brain, even when ART eliminates virus from blood. We do not yet know what allows HIV-1 to persist in the brain even when ART removes it from a person's blood and other parts of their body. This may depend on the specific variety of HIV-1 virus, a person's sex, age and natural immunity, or how effective the ART drugs are. Not all current ART drugs work efficiently in the types of brain cells that HIV-1 infects. These drugs also may not penetrate brain tissue easily. We have a major gap in what we know about how different types of ART affect virus that persists in the brain. This gap is an obstacle to improving health care of people with HIV-1 infection, especially those with HIV-related brain disease. It is also an obstacle to fully curing HIV/AIDS. In our research, we will first investigate how virus persists in a person's brain even when ART drugs have removed virus from their blood. How does the virus affect the brain so that the virus can persist? With that information, we can develop ways to reduce virus in the brain. We have unique resources to meet these goals: 1) Archived brain samples from people with HIV/AIDS who received ART 2) Laboratory models of brain infection with HIV-1 From our studies, we expect to learn about how the virus reproduces and persists in specific types of brain cells. We will also learn about how it causes brain disease. We will better understand which ART drugs are efficient in infected brain cells. We will model how the virus stores itself in brain and examine how those stores respond to ART drugs. These new insights into the mechanisms of HIV-1 disease may lead to new therapies and new approaches to fully removing HIV-1 from a person's body.

column36: Facilitating Effective Mental Health Care Transitions for Youth: Evaluation of the Transition Support Worker Model
column37: Transitions out of hospital child and adolescent acute mental health services (CAMHS) to the community or adult mental health services (AMHS) remain a serious health system issue in Canada. We know that about half of youth drop out of care during this critical developmental and service transition. Lack of care as well as poorly planned discharges lead to worse mental health, unnecessary health costs, and increased use of correctional and social services. Given the unmet need and long wait times for mental health care among this population, ensuring more effective transitions is a priority. While transition support worker programs exist across Ontario and Canada to facilitate the complex transitions out of hospital-based CAMHS care, there is no evidence to support their use or determine which aspects of the program are most effective for supporting transition success. Despite this being a National priority by the current Federal and Provincial ministers of health, the lack of evidence is not surprising, as noted in the 2016 Auditor General of Ontario Report, we lack evidence-based interventions to ensure continuity of care between CAMHS, community and/or AMHS. Our team's research project will fill this critical health system gap. Using the Triple Aim Framework for evaluation of transition interventions, we will evaluate the TSW model in three hospitals, focusing on youth, caregivers, and clinician outcomes and experiences. This evaluation will be useful to numerous stakeholders, informing clinical practice, system integration, policy directions, and providing the groundwork for scalability and evaluation of the TSW model across Canada. This project should also inform investments that target improved transitions thereby enabling the Canadian healthcare system to provide continuity of mental health care for youth.

column36: An evaluation of the use of Community Transition Teams to improve health outcomes for individuals with an opioid use disorder following release from British Columbia Corrections
column37: The period following release from jail is one of increased vulnerability for individuals with an opioid use disorder, as they re-immerse into their communities, search for housing and employment and attempt to access health care services. Without proper support, this population is at high risk for a relapse to opioid use, overdose and death. To help improve health outcomes associated this critical time of transition from a correctional facility to community, Correctional Health Services (CHS) has implemented Community Transition Teams (CTTs) in BC. CTTs adopt a client-centred approach to care, where a case manager works closely with an individual to help them identify their priorities and takes an active role in supporting them to achieve their treatment goals following release from provincial corrections. While the implementation of CTTs in correctional settings in BC is confirmed to proceed, no formal evaluation of the impact such an evidence-based treatment approach may have on resulting health or social outcomes for this high-risk population has yet been proposed. To address this, the proposed research will evaluate the impact of CTT participation on health and social outcomes among incarcerated individuals with opioid addiction, as well as identify relevant barriers impeding successful scale-up of CTTs within BC. Participants will complete a one-time questionnaire and provide consent to the use of their personal identifiers for linkage to a variety of healthcare databases for ongoing community follow-up over a 5-year period. A sample of participants will also be invited to participate in a cross-sectional qualitative interview to identify existing barriers or challenges associated with the successful implementation or scale-up of CTTs, and to identify feasible solutions. Knowledge gained through this research will identify health outcomes associated with the use of CTTs and inform successful implementation and scale-up of the program.

column36: Evaluating Subacute Care Hospital Transitions for Older Adults: Understanding How, Why and for Whom a Planned Intervention is Working
column37: Community-dwelling frail older adults are frequently hospitalized. Most are poorly prepared to return to the community which often results in emergency department visits, hospital re-admission, and transfer to a nursing home. 'Subacute care' is a type of hospital care designed to reduce these poor outcomes. Once a patient no longer needs regular hospital care, they are transferred from an acute to a subacute hospital bed, and provided with rehab care (e.g., to improve their strength and coping skills) until they are ready to return home. While several groups have implemented this process, subacute care has never been properly evaluated. As a result, we don't really know if it works, what providers and patients think of it, and how it could be improved. In 2018, Winnipeg Health Region planners converted 90 acute care hospital beds to subacute beds. A team of expert researchers has partnered with planners in charge in this process and with patients who have been through it, to study how it is working. We will first use large healthcare datasets to measure how subacute beds were used (e.g., how long patients had to wait to get into them), if they were cared for safely while in these beds, and if this process reduced later healthcare use (fewer hospital re-admissions, etc.). We will then review patient medical charts to see what kind of subacute care they got and if this could have been better. Lastly, we will interview hospital providers and past patients to get their perspective on how well subacute care works. Providers will be asked about the benefits and challenges of subacute care, and what they need to make it work better. Patients will be asked similar questions to see if the care they received met their needs. Our team will assess all of this information to evaluate subacute care, to see if some patients benefit more than others, and to determine how it could be improved. Our unique methods can also be used to assess how other areas of healthcare are working.

column36: A pilot study assessing the feasibility of a randomized controlled trial evaluating aspirin in postpartum women at risk of developing venous thromboembolism (pilot PARTUM trial: Postpartum Aspirin to Reduce Thromboembolism Undue Morbidity)
column37: Women are at an increased risk of developing blood clots (venous thrombosis, including deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) during pregnancy and in the postpartum period. For postpartum women who have additional risk factors for venous thrombosis, it is still unknown whether preventative blood thinners are needed after delivery. Previous studies have evaluated whether daily low-molecular-weight heparin injections after delivery prevents blood clots, however, one major barrier to study recruitment has been patients' lack of comfort with doing the injections at home. Recently, low-dose aspirin has been shown to be effective at preventing blood clots after orthopedic surgery. Low doses of aspirin is considered safe while breastfeeding. We plan to conduct a study where postpartum women at risk of blood clots are randomized to 6 weeks of low-dose aspirin versus placebo. The main purpose of this pilot study is to see if we can recruit enough women to make a larger trial feasible. Over a 6 week time period we will complete a D-dimer blood test and leg ultrasounds to screen for deep vein thrombosis, as well as track symptoms of blood clots, bleeding and side effects of aspirin. We will also call subjects at 90 days to see if there are any symptoms of blood clots, bleeding or side effects. If this pilot study is feasible, then the clinical information we collect will be used in the larger trial to determine if aspirin prevents more blood clots in postpartum women compared to placebo. By competing this pilot study we will be able to better prepare for a larger trial to definitively answer the question of whether women at risk of blood clots may benefit from taking aspirin after delivery to prevent blood clots.

column36: Liver fibrosis and CD8 T cell dysfunction in hepatitis C virus infection
column37: Despite the spectacular results for hepatitis C virus (HCV) clearance with new antiviral therapies, significant challenges remain for those with advanced liver fibrosis/cirrhosis. Progressive fibrosis results in symptomatic liver disease, predisposing to end-stage liver disease with a high mortality. Although antiviral therapy reduces the risk of liver cancer, cirrhotic patients remain at risk, and data suggests an atypically aggressive form can occur. Weakened responses to routine vaccinations and co-infections and chronicity with HCV re-exposure demonstrate the consequences of an immune system weakened by cirrhosis. Given that the majority of the 175 million HCV cases worldwide become chronic infections, with most remaining undiagnosed and only a fraction of known infections being treated annually, studies estimate the number of HCV+ individuals with cirrhosis will remain high for decades. An immune cell profoundly affected by chronic HCV infection is the CD8 T cell. Effective CD8 T cell responses are not only vital for viral clearance but are central to cancer surveillance and responses to other viral infections and increasingly important for vaccines in development against chronic viral infections requiring robust T cell immunity. We have found significant CD8 T cell dysfunction in cirrhotic HCV-infected individuals that persists long after cure, and suspect similar dysfunction in non-infectious liver disease. We are using gene sequencing methods to identify the underlying mechanism and are already following up on promising candidates. We are also using a mouse model emulating liver disease and CD8 T cell dysfunction, performing elegant mechanistic studies to complement our human research. These mice are clinically relevant with impaired responses to both cancer and immunotherapy, as is seen in humans. Our research will identify new immunorestorative therapeutic targets to improve clinical outcomes for cirrhotic HCV+ individuals and other liver diseases.

column36: The Evaluation of the Connected Care Program for Children with Medical Complexity: A Prospective Cohort Study with Embedded Health Economic and Qualitative Analysis
column37: In Canada, there are a growing number of children who are living longer than before due to new medical technologies that allow them to survive such as a feeding tube or a breathing machine. These new supports are used in the home setting, which allows these families to be at home with their child rather than in hospital but also increases the challenges of the care that needs to be provided. These children are often back and forth from the hospital to home especially after the initiation of new technology. This is one of the most risky times because of not enough training or education to families and homecare providers on the use of the new medical technologies as well as a lack of supportive systems in place to help families succeed. Often the care received during this transition period isn't well coordinated which results in frequent visits to the hospital and stress on the patient and family. The Connected Care Program is the largest Canadian transition to home program for children with medical complexity to date funded by the Ministry of Health in Ontario in 2018. This study will evaluate the Connected Care Program for children with medical complexity transitioning home with new medical technology in Ontario, Canada. We are studying the effect on the following: visits to the Emergency Department, patient and families' experience, the costs on the healthcare system and the experience of healthcare providers with the intervention. Our study will increase the understanding of the benefits of the Connected Care Program on the patient and family as well as the healthcare system. Our results will help to improve the quality of life for children going home with new medical technology by making their healthcare and overall lives better.

column36: Elimination of cervical cancer through vaccination and screening in high HIV prevalence settings: a mathematical modeling and cost effectiveness study
column37: Cervical cancer is the number one cancer killing women in South Africa, a country at the epicenter of the HIV epidemic. Cervical cancer is caused by human papillomaviruses (HPV), which are vaccine-preventable infections. The World Health Organization has now set goals to eliminate cervical cancer. What might complicate elimination efforts in high HIV prevalence settings, however, is that people living with HIV are more susceptible to HPV and vice versa. These biological interactions affect the transmission dynamics of both viruses with important public health implications. When used at sufficient coverage, vaccines are powerful prevention tools because they protect those immunized and the wider population by limiting HPV spread and, eventually, cervical cancer. South Africa's HPV vaccination program currently only immunizes 4th grade schoolgirls. Though South Africa wishes to improve the program, they lack the necessary evidence and policy guidance about the benefits of different vaccination and screening strategies in a context of high HIV prevalence. Our overall objective is to fill this knowledge gap by investigating how to achieve cervical cancer elimination through HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening in South Africa. Our proposed study combines state-of-the-art data and computer simulations of HIV/HPV transmission, to identify vaccination and screening strategies that can lead to cervical cancer elimination in South Africa (who to vaccinate? with which vaccine? how many doses?). We will also identify the strategies that would lead to faster cervical cancer elimination, determine which ones are most cost-effective, and investigate the specific impact of HIV transmission on elimination efforts. By drawing on the expertise of a multidisciplinary team of researchers in epidemiology, economics, and mathematical modeling, our results will help mitigate the double threat of HIV and HPV to one of sub-Saharan Africa's most vulnerable groups, women.

column36: Protecting children from unhealthy food and brand marketing in the digital age: A novel artificial intelligence system to assess food and brand marketing on digital media
column37: Background: Unhealthy food/brand marketing has a negative impact on what children eat and on their health. Canada will soon ban marketing unhealthy foods/brands to children <13 years old on television, the internet and other media. However, very little is known about the amount and types of unhealthy food/brand ads that children see online and the government does not have a way to monitor whether companies are obeying the new law. The problem is that public health has fallen behind technologically. Marketers are using artificial intelligence (AI), but public health is still relying on humans to try to find out what marketers are doing. Goals: We will develop and test the first AI system that can assess the amounts and types of food/brand marketing that is online. We will use the system to assess differences in the amount and type of food/brand marketing that is online from before to after Canada's new marketing ban comes into effect. We will also study whether companies are obeying the new law. Methods: We will use AI to identify food/brand marketing on Canadian websites, gaming applications and YouTube videos. AI will also be used to: 1) rate the healthfulness of the foods/brands that are being marketed; 2) assess the types of marketing strategies that are being used; and 3) determine whether marketing targets children. AI and marketing experts will test our system to make sure it is accurate. We will conduct statistical testing to understand how the amount and type of marketing changes from 12 months before to 12 months after Canada's marketing ban is implemented, and whether companies are obeying the new law. Significance: This AI system will provide the first scientific evidence about the amount and type of unhealthy food/brand marketing that Canadian children may see online. It will also provide a way to study whether companies are obeying the Canadian government's marketing ban. This information can help to understand how to improve child nutrition and health.

column36: Examining the Psychometric Properties of an Open-Access Diagnostic Interview for Researchers and Clinicians: The Diagnostic Assessment Research Tool (DART) for DSM-5
column37: One in five Canadians experiences a mental illness in their lifetime. In addition to the detrimental personal costs, mental illness results in an economic burden of $50 billion due to health costs and lost employment opportunities (Smetanin et al., 2011). To ensure Canadians are directed to appropriate treatment, it is critical that they receive a thorough assessment that accurately identifies their mental problems (or conditions). Current available interview tools are costly and too time consuming to administer. To overcome these significant limitations, we developed the Diagnostic Assessment Research Tool (DART; McCabe et al., 2017). The DART is a diagnostic interview to be used by clinicians, learners and researchers to assist with accurately identifying mental disorders in any setting. The goal of this study is to test if diagnoses that are determined when a clinician uses the DART are accurate and reliable. The DART was developed to offer interviewers with a diagnostic tool that is free to use, easy to administer, and designed to minimize patient burden and inconvenience. Given the limitations of existing diagnostic tools, a new diagnostic tool that is valid and reliable will directly impact the health of Canadians suffering with mental illness by guiding them to appropriate treatment and resources and by advancing research. It will also significantly reduce costs to Canadian clinicians and researchers who currently must pay for the use of most existing diagnostic tools.

column36: FoxO3a acts as a key checkpoint that regulates inflammation in the gut
column37: Crohn's disease (CD) is a subset of IBD that affects 1 in 150 Canadians and requires hospitalization and surgical intervention in extreme cases. CD, unlike ulcerative colitis (UC), may affect any part of the GI tract with a predilection for the distal ileum, and causes a patchy pattern of inflammation extending through the thickness of the bowel wall. Mutations in various genes have been shown to correlate with IBD. However, these do not always seem to result in disease progression. Recently, genome-wide association studies have identified that additional mutations in four distinct genes correlate to Crohn's disease progression. Mutation in FoxO3a gene has been identified as one of those disease progression genes. It is not known how a mutation in FoxO3a correlates to aggressive disease. We have developed an experimental model wherein inactivation of both the disease susceptibility gene (IL-10) and the disease progression gene (FoxO3a) results in aggressive, spontaneous Crohn's disease. Preliminary results indicate that there are potent changes in the gut microbiome and the inflammatory response in the gut of FoxO3a-IL-10 double-deficient mice. In this proposal, we aim to identify how inactivation of FoxO3a influences Crohn's disease progression. We believe that by understanding the role of FoxO3a in the gut, our studies will open up new avenues for therapy.

column36: Transformation of the Tumor Microenvironment with Genetically-modifed Dendritic Cells for T cell-mediated Immunotherapy
column37: Immune checkpoint blockade and adoptive cytotoxic T cell (CTL) therapy exemplify the major breakthroughs in cancer immunotherapy over the past decade. Although subsets of cancer patients have experienced spectacular and durable remissions, clinical responses are heterogeneous, with most patients deriving little benefit. The urgent demand to improve these therapies has driven over a thousand clinical trials that target one or few of the many individual molecules that inhibit anti-tumor immunity. Here we propose a novel approach by genetically-modifying an activation pathway in dendritic cells (DCs) to fundamentally change the immune landscape in cancer. Our preliminary data provides the first clear evidence that targeting DCs in this manner augments anti-tumor immunity in the absence of any other therapy. This project aims to test whether DC-restricted genetic targeting can serve as a new strategy for the development of next generation cancer immunotherapy. The strategy overcomes the inherent problems of current therapies with respect to efficacy, duration of response, and off-target related side-effects that limit clinical success.

column36: Role of Smooth Muscle Autophagy in Aging-Associated Vascular Stiffness
column37: As people age, their arteries stiffen, leading to various cardiovascular diseases. Arterial stiffening, as the primary feature of aging, involves mechanisms present both inside (active) and outside (passive) of the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) that make up the arterial walls. Currently, what regulates these mechanisms remains largely unclear. We recently developed a novel mouse model in which we deleted a gene, called Atg7, in the SMCs of 5-month old mice. Atg7 is responsible for the recycling process of cellular materials (autophagy, or "self-eating"). We found these mice had arterial stiffening, hypertension and several disease changes in arteries like those in naturally aged animals (>18 months old). These results are novel because the previous mouse models with the Atg7 gene deleted in embryos did not show these changes. Therefore, we will use this mouse model to explore how Atg7 elimination - i.e. the disruption of autophagy - impacts the active and passive mechanisms of arterial stiffening. We will also study whether these vascular changes are present in naturally aged mice. We also observed an increase in YAP (Yes-associated protein 1) in SMCs from our Atg7 mouse model. YAP is known to be involved in arterial stiffness; therefore, we will examine the role of YAP in arterial stiffening by deleting the YAP gene in SMCs in our Atg7 mouse model. In our Atg7 mouse model, we also found an increase in DNA content in the nuclei of arterial SMCs, called polyploidization. Given that SMC polyploidization is also present in naturally aged arteries, we will examine whether SMC polyploidization contributes to arterial stiffening induced by Atg7 deletion in SMCs. In sum, our proposed studies using a unique mouse model will reveal the mechanisms of arterial stiffness and associated cardiovascular diseases. Our research outcome will help develop new drugs and treatments for aging-associated cardiovascular diseases.

column36: Investigating the role of non-coding variations in epilepsy
column37: Epilepsy affects ~3% of individuals, with half of the cases starting during childhood. Despite the fact that more than 20 anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) are available, a significant portion of patients with epilepsy will continue to have seizures. This by itself justifies the need to continue to search for the genetic mechanism underlying epilepsies in order to better treat patients. Epilepsy is characterized by great genetic heterogeneity, with the involvement of hundreds of genes. Since the coding variations in genes have been extensively studied in the last few years and cannot explain the genetic cause for a vast majority of epileptic patients, we aim here to study the non-coding portion of the genome of epileptic patients using already available whole-genome sequences and genotyping and genealogical data. Specific aims consist in 1) Prioritization of non-coding genomic regions using genealogies. In this aim we will use the genealogies of patients as well as the identity-by-descent (IBD) genomic segments to identify patients with more or longer shared IBD regions than expected given the genealogical kinship and prioritize within these regions the ones that could be associated to the disease. 2) Investigation of genomic segments prioritized in aim 1 for non-coding causal single nucleotide variants (SNVs), structural variants (SVs) and short tandem repeats (STRs) associated with epilepsy using different bioinformatic tools. With this proposal we expect to increase the number of epileptic patients for whom we can find a genetic cause for their disease. This will allow us to better understand the genetic mechanisms underlying the disease. Moreover, these findings could also give us insights towards better epilepsy management and treatment.

column36: Ensuring a Successful Transition from Pap to HPV DNA Testing in Primary Cervical Cancer Screening: Exploring and Listening to Canadian Women's Needs is Critical for Effective Public Policy Change
column37: In their lifetime, 75% of sexually active women will be infected with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) which is the proven cause of cervical cancer. In Canada, the Pap test (smear) is used to monitor changes in the cervix, usually every 2-3 years. Too many women do not participate regularly in screening (defined as underscreened), especially vulnerable groups (e.g., recent immigrants, low household income). A new cervical screening test detects the HPV virus in cervical cells (HPV test), offers greater protection than the Pap test against cervical cancer and permits extending the testing interval to 5 years or more. Provinces are planning to replace the Pap test with the HPV test, but public health authorities are concerned that women are not yet prepared. In 2017, Australia postponed replacing the Pap test with the HPV test because women did not know that HPV causes cervical cancer, were worried that a cancer could be missed due to longer testing intervals and believed that the government only wanted to save money by extending the screening interval. In Canada, we know little about women's information needs and their perceived barriers (fears and worries) regarding the HPV test. As a result, they might hesitate or refuse the HPV test and miss the opportunity of early detection and prevention of cervical cancer. In this study, we will carry out an internet-based survey of women age 21 to 70 across Canada and ask about their knowledge, attitudes and beliefs, and their willingness and intentions to accept the HPV test. We will use scientifically valid questions to understand perceived benefits and barriers to the HPV test. Our international research team has many years of experience in studying HPV vaccination and HPV testing decision-making. This study is critical for informing public health authorities about how to educate and encourage women to participate in HPV testing in the most sensitive and timely manner with the goal of improving cervical cancer prevention.

column36: Metabolomics for prediction of cisplatin mediated acute kidney injury: a Canadian multi-centre adult and pediatric study
column37: Cisplatin is a widely used drug to treat cancer in both children and adults. Although effective in treating cancer, cisplatin causes kidney damage in approximately one third of patients that take the drug. The objective of this project is to determine why one third (33%) of patients have kidney damage when they take cisplatin yet the other two thirds (66%) of patients do not have kidney injury. Precision medicine is a new field that uses information about individual patients to predict their response to drug therapy. We propose using a precision medicine based approach for predicting cisplatin toxicity. We will recruit pediatric and adult patients undergoing treatment with cisplatin from oncology centres across Canada. Patients will provide blood and urine samples before they receive their dose of cisplatin, 24 hours and 3-5 days after they receive their first dose. Patients will be followed over time to see if they develop kidney damage. Specimens will be immediately frozen and shipped to a central facility where they will be subjected to a sophisticated "metabolomics" analysis. In metabolomics, hundreds of metabolites are identified and quantified in each sample. We will then use this information to determine metabolites that predispose patients to developing kidney injury. The ultimate goal is to be able to do a simple test (blood and/or urine) prior to patients taking cisplatin, in order to predict which patients are susceptible to kidney injury. This precision medicine approach will allow treating doctors to alter the treatment regimen and conduct more thorough monitoring in high-risk patients, which is expected to significantly improve their long-term quality of life.

column37: Many clinical trials have demonstrated the benefits of statins (cholesterol-lowering drugs) for preventing a first cardiovascular event in people at risk of such events. From an economic perspective, statin treatment for preventing a first cardiovascular event in people at high risk of a cardiovascular event would be advantageous. Unfortunately, few studies have investigated the benefits and risks of statins for preventing a first cardiovascular events in the elderly. Although these studies indicate there are benefits for these people as well, much remains to be known about the full range of benefits and risks. Data are particularly scarce for very old people, elderly that already have many diseases or those that are already taking multiple drugs. Finally, it is unclear if the benefits that have been observed in clinical trials fully translate in real life, because medical monitoring is often better in clinical trials than it is in real life. For instance, it is known that people do not take their statin medication as well in real life as they do in clinical trials. The primary goal of this project is to provide additional evidence regarding the real-life benefits and risks of statins medication in the elderly for preventing a first cardiovascular event. To do this, we will use data from anonymized population-wide administrative databases. We will examine the patterns of how the elderly get statin medication over time and see how these different patterns are associated with the occurrence of cardiovascular events, mortality or possible major side effects. We will also perform an economic evaluation of statin treatment. To be able to do this, we will first need to develop new data analysis methods. These methods will not only be essential to answer the important questions of the current project, but many other research questions regarding treatment patterns over time using administrative databases.

column37: The health and wellness of Indigenous peoples today continue to be impacted by the harmful colonization practices enforced by the Government of Canada. While we have shown the long-term impacts of the Residential School system in relation to health and wellness, there remains a large gap in understanding the health impacts of other collective traumas such as the Sixties Scoop and the continued inequities within the child welfare system. During the Sixties Scoop, large numbers of children and youth were removed from their families and the practice of taking Indigenous children and youth from their families and communities continues today. As a result, family units and connections to Indigenous culture have and continue to be impacted, however, the empirical evidence on health and wellness are largely unavailable. The current proposal addresses this gap by taking a mixed methods approach to understand the risk factors of child welfare involvement within communities and the effects of the Sixties Scoop and child welfare system on Indigenous health and wellness. In the current project we will work with large national survey data to examine the individual-level and community-level factors associated with child welfare system involvement and the impacts on health. We will also work together with the 60's Scoop Legacy of Canada, a non-profit organization focused on healing and wellness for Sixties Scoop Survivors to conduct a quantitative survey across Manitoba. Broadly we will examine experiences within the child welfare system, and the direct and intergenerational impacts of the loss of culture and community on Indigenous health and wellness. It is expected that this work will help promote an understanding of the long-term outcomes and healing opportunities required for Indigenous peoples who have been affected by the child welfare system. This work will also help provide evidence informed policy changes related to child welfare practices for Indigenous children.

column36: Sustainable Healthy Cities: The Interplay between Urban Interventions, Gentrification, and Population Health
column37: The way our cities are designed influences population-level physical activity, social participation, well-being and health inequalities. Although massive investments are made in urban infrastructure, even well-intentioned change may adversely affect vulnerable populations through gentrification processes. The goal of this research is to analyse how urban interventions, gentrification, and population health and health inequalities relate. Specifically, we aim to: 1) document if urban interventions (e.g., new bike lanes) aiming to improve quality of life tend to be located primarily in more deprived areas. 2) assess whether urban interventions lead to gentrification or vice versa, or if both processes are at play 3) measure the impact of urban interventions, neighbourhood gentrification, and experienced residential gentrification on physical activity, social participation and well-being, and 4) analyse differences in health outcome trajectories between low SES individuals who were displaced from gentrified neighbourhoods and those who could stay, and lastly 5) build a pilot simulation tool to help decision makers choose the best urban intervention scenario for health and equity. This study will build on an existing CIHR-funded team (INTERACT, 2016-2021), adding study participants to an existing cohort to specifically analyse effects of urban change on health and health inequalities while accounting for gentrification processes in Montreal. GIS and spatial analysis tools will be used to analyse retrospective and prospective dynamics of urban change, gentrification, and health. A battery of tools including online questionnaires, smartphone apps and dedicated sensors will provide detailed data about daily mobility, physical activity, and well-being. Results will provide insights on how urban form changes impact population health outcomes and health inequalities, and support local and regional decision makers in designing and creating healthier communities.

column36: Lung cancer early detection and classification using methylome analysis of plasma cell free DNA
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in Canada. Early diagnosis can have a dramatic influence on lung cancer survival, but the tests that are currently available for early detection of lung cancer presents many challenges that lessen their impact. Therefore, new kinds of tests will be needed to fully realize the potential of early detection of lung cancer on reducing cancer-related deaths in Canada. We have developed a new kind of test that uses cell-free DNA from a simple blood draw. This 'liquid biopsy' approach has generated intense interest from researchers but so far has failed to perform well enough for early detection of lung cancer. Our recent breakthrough discovery now opens the door to new diagnostic tests for many cancer types including for the early diagnosis of lung cancer. This project will develop our promising new liquid biopsy technology into a bona fide lung cancer early detection diagnostic test. Since lung cancer consists of several distinct subtypes, we will first need to attain a significantly deeper understanding of the biology of different subtypes of lung cancer. Each of these subtypes will require different features to be included in a lung cancer early detection liquid biopsy test. To identify these important new features, we will undertake comprehensive and complementary approaches to profiling blood and tumour samples from hundreds of lung cancer patients and controls. By the completion of this project, we expect to turn our current lung cancer liquid biopsy test into a robust diagnostic tool for early detection of lung cancer. In the future, this new liquid biopsy test could be validated in lung cancer screening studies in order to prove how useful it can be for preventing lung cancer deaths. This project will also produce a valuable body of new knowledge regarding the biology of lung cancer subtypes that could someday lead to new therapies for the prevention or treatment of lung cancer.

column36: Causes of muscle spindle afferents excitability changes associated to chronic myalgia
column37: We have all experienced muscle pain in our life, whether after strenuous or eccentric exercise or just repetition of unaccustomed movements. The pain following these movements is caused by minor damage or inflammation to the muscle and is usually not felt at rest. The soreness or tenderness perceived upon palpation of the exercised muscle or an attempt to move is usually considered as a subclinical situation since it is short lasting and recess by itself without need for treatment. However, in some people it leads to a debilitating chronic condition where the pain eventually spreads to several muscles rendering movements very difficult and sometimes even just contact with objects like a chair or a bed become painful. Normally, painful stimuli activate the nerve endings of specialized sensory neurons that inform the brain of their presence. Every type of sensory neuron is specialized for the type of stimuli it is designed to detect. Sensory neurons in the eye detect light but not sound, for instance. In a previous study, we made small injections (2 injections, 2 days apart) of an acidic solution into muscles to mimic, in an animal model, the changes that occur in muscles that are slightly damaged or inflamed, and found that a type of sensory neuron, which is not normally associated to pain perception, becomes abnormally hyperactive. These sensory neurons should detect muscle stretch and not painful stimuli, but because the period of their hyperactivity lasted for as long as the muscle pain lasted in the animals, we asked if the two are related. The aim of this project is to understand the sequence of cellular events that leads to this abnormal activity and to understand how abnormal activity in these cells ends up causing the brain to feel pain instead of muscle stretch.

column36: Unravelling the complex roles of TDP-43 and FUS ALS variants in the vertebrate nervous system
column37: Amid the great diversity of neurodegenerative disorders, there is a growing body of evidence suggesting that synapses are preferentially altered early in the disease process. Though there is compelling evidence that de-innervation of neuromuscular junctions (NMJ) occurs early and throughout the clinical progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the cellular mechanisms that result in loss of NMJ connectivity remain poorly understood. To investigate these defects, my laboratory uses zebrafish ALS models. This animal is uniquely suited for investigations pertaining to the fundamental nature of NMJ defects in ALS as it permits investigations of in vivo physiological function resulting from the expression of mutant ALS-causing genes. We study two ALS genes: TARDBP and FUS, these encode the RNA-binding proteins TDP-43 and FUS respectively, and in ALS mutations in these two genes are believed to interfere with the normal processing of transcripts involved with synaptic function. We have developed genetic animal models of ALS in which analogous disease-causing mutations have been CRISPR-edited into tardbp (encoding zebrafish tdp-43) and fus (encoding zebrafish fus). These models develop an ALS-like motor phenotype and die prematurely. We propose to investigate the synaptic transcripts processed by tdp-43 and fus specifically in the spinal cords and motor neuron cell population and examine how these transcripts are processed differently in our ALS models. In parallel, we will use an array of physiological approaches to explore physiological defects that arise in synaptic function at the NMJ. We propose that furthering our understanding of synaptic defects arising in ALS will provide the necessary foundation for a more complete understanding of the disease, which we believe is needed for therapeutic development.

column37: Cilia function a bit like a satellite antenna, protruding from most cells and relaying information from the surroundings back to the cell. An increasing number of conditions are being identified where cilia function abnormally, and these disorders (termed ciliopathies), represent important causes of pediatric and adult-onset disease. Unfortunately, such conditions are largely untreatable at present. In experiments undertaken in cell lines, as well as in two animal models, we have discovered that one member (FOXC1) of a larger transcription factor family has roles in controlling the structure and function of cilia. This grant proposes to investigate the precise mechanisms involved. Specific aims study the mechanistic basis of hydrocephalus, examine the Hedgehog signaling pathway which depends on the primary cilium for function, and investigate the contribution of vesicular shedding to this area of cell biology. The overarching goal is to define the underlying mechanisms so as to facilitate future development of novel therapeutic approaches.

Attempts to harness the properties of high density lipoproteins (HDL- the "good" cholesterol) to reduce the risk of ASCVD have failed in large clinical trials. HDL removes cholesterol from the arterial wall but this pathway remains untapped. We have found a protein, desmocollin 1 (DSC1) that prevents the removal of cholesterol from cells and is found in large quantities in human atherosclerosis lesions. Our laboratory work indicates that blocking this pathway is feasible and may provide benefit to prevent fatty buildup in arteries. We have found an inhibitor of DSC1 by virtual screening of over 10 million pharmacological compounds. Our top candidate, Docetaxel is an FDA approved drug for cancer treatment. We found that Docetaxel inhibits DSC1 in minute quantities (0.7 nonomolar), a concentration much lower that used in cancer treatment. We will first study Docetaxel in the laboratory using cholesterol-laden cells (similar to the ones found in the atherosclerotic plaque) and determine optimal conditions. Then, we will study the effects of Docetaxel in preventing atherosclerosis in an early-stage mouse model, but also to treat atherosclerosis in a late-stage model of atherosclerosis. In a separate objective, we will measure DSC1 levels in the blood of patients with heart attacks and healthy individuals to determine whether DSC1 levels can be a biomarker of atherosclerosis. These studies will pave the way for first-in-man trials of very low dose Docetaxel to prevent and treat atherosclerosis.

Our automated artificial pancreas system is composed of: (i) Dexcom G5 glucose sensor, (ii) Tandem t:slim pumps (to deliver insulin and pramlintide), (iii) an LG Google Nexus Smartphone controller with our dosing algorithms. The primary aim of the study is to assess whether our insulin-and-pramlintide artificial pancreas increases the time spent in target range (3.9-10.0 mmol/L) compared to insulin-plus-placebo artificial pancreas in outpatient, unsupervised, free-living settings. .

column36: Which exercise for chronic low back pain? Predicting response to exercise treatments for patients with low back pain.
column37: Exercise therapy is the most recommended treatment for chronic low back pain. There is a wide range of exercises available and research studies have shown that no exercise is superior to another. The problem is that the effects of exercise in reducing pain and disability are small to moderate. Researchers and clinicians believe that different patients may best respond to different types of exercises. This means that if patients could be better matched to specific exercises, then the effects of exercise would be greater. A study conducted by the investigators of this proposal tested whether patient's characteristics could predict outcomes to two of the most common exercises for low back pain: motor control exercises or graded activity. The results showed that a simple questionnaire (Lumbar Spine Instability Questionnaire) could identify patients who responded best to either exercise. Patients with low clinical instability (measured by the questionnaire) responded best to graded activity. Patients with high clinical instability responded best to motor control exercises. These results were the first to show that better matching patients to specific exercises improves outcomes. Although these results have the potential to significantly improve the delivery of exercises for low back pain, validation of the results in a high-quality study with a large group of patients is a prerequisite to clinical implementation. The aim of this study is to conduct a randomized controlled trial comparing the effects of graded activity to motor control exercises and identify groups of respondents to these exercises. We will also evaluate the costs and benefits of these interventions and the potential impact of matched treatment to patients and the health care system. The results of this study has the potential to increase the effects of exercise in low back pain and consequently lead to better patient outcomes and decreased health related costs.

column36: Rates, Mechanisms, and Indicators of Youth Suicide Contagion in the Digital Age: A 20-year Population Study in British Columbia
column37: Despite rising public awareness, suicide remains a leading cause of death among youth aged 10-29 worldwide. Youth are especially vulnerable to suicide contagion, where their risk is elevated through direct or indirect exposure to suicidal peers, and to suicide clusters. Suicide clusters can have devastating impacts on peers, families, and communities. Although we know that suicide-related content is often shared and discussed on online and social media, we don't yet know how this has affected patterns of suicidal behaviour in youth. The aims of this study are to: (1) examine whether rates or mechanisms of suicide clustering have changed with rising use of online and social media by youth; and (2) identify early indicators of clustering to improve monitoring and intervention. We predict that use of online media will produce more diffuse exposures to suicide among youth, which will result in suicidal behaviours that are clustered in time but not space. It is expected that population-level healthcare utilization and online behaviour may indicate when and where suicide clusters are about to occur. This study uses population-level health and administrative records to gather a comprehensive picture of suicidal behaviours in over one million youth, aged 10-29, living in BC between 1998-2017. Analyses will use spatial statistics to detect clustering in space (geographic) and time (temporal). Analyses will also examine how rates and patterns of suicide clusters have changed over the past two decades, with special attention to how patterns may have shifted since online and social media became prominent methods of communication among youth. This study addresses several important gaps in knowledge regarding whether, when, and why suicide clustering occurs in youth. Findings will inform monitoring, prevention, intervention and public policy efforts that can reduce the global health burden associated with youth suicide.

column36: Evaluating the Impact of Primary Care Patient-Provider Relationships on Emergency Department Utilization by Adolescents with Chronic Conditions
column37: Traditionally, primary care has focused on establishing long-standing patient-physician relationships as a means to providing coordinated, continuous, patient-centered, and comprehensive care. Yet, it is unknown whether adolescents and young adults with chronic conditions maintain relationships with primary care providers when they transfer from specialized pediatric to adult-oriented care. Our project will evaluate patient-provider relationships in primary care before and after transfer from specialized pediatric services. We will profile patterns of primary care use by young Albertans (ages 12-25) who receive specialist care as an adolescent (12-18 years old). We will focus on those who have received care in specialist clinics at pediatric hospitals in Alberta (i.e., diabetes, endocrinology, gastroenterology, neurology, nephrology, rheumatology, cardiology, mental health). We will achieve 3 aims: (1) we will describe patterns of primary care use by adolescents and young adults during the transition from adolescence to adulthood; (2) we will determine if continuity of primary care changes after transfer (age 18) and assess the relationship between continuity of primary care and rate of Emergency Department (ED) use; and (3) we will gain deeper insights into our quantitative findings through interviews with key stakeholders (e.g., adolescents, caregivers, physicians). The new knowledge generated by this project will be used to facilitate stronger linkages between specialty pediatric care, mental health care, and primary care, and inform transition policies and practices for the growing population of young adults with chronic conditions in Alberta, and in Canada.

column36: The influence of Cytomegalovirus infection on cystic fibrosis disease progression
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common lethal genetic disease of Canadians. In CF, a vicious cycle of infection and inflammation leads to lung destruction. Understanding how this process contributes to disease progression is key for those with CF to live longer, healthier lives. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes a chronic viral infection in humans. The immune system acts to control CMV but it is never cleared from the body. Its prevalence increases over time and >50% of adults have evidence of CMV infection. CMV reactivation and invasion in to various organ systems causes tremendous disease specifically in immune-suppressed individuals. However, an increasing body of literature has demonstrated that CMV may have negative consequences even in general populations. CMV positive individuals have increased rates of chronic inflammatory diseases including cancers, dementia and heart disease. Indeed, CMV positive individuals live shorter lives. How this occurs is unknown - but it is suspected that CMV replicates in already inflamed tissues - exaggerating resultant tissue damage. CF, a disease of chronic infection and inflammation, is a perfect candidate for exploitation by CMV. Provocative preliminary data from the University of Calgary has confirmed the presence of CMV in the lungs of individuals with CF and that CMV positive individuals progress to end-stage lung disease ten years earlier then CMV negative. We propose a multi-centre observational study in several leading Canadian CF centres to determine the role of CMV in CF disease progression. In this study we will determine; the rates and risk factors for CMV infection, correlate disease burden and progression rates with CMV status, and identify how CMV reactivation associates with this process. As potent therapies and vaccines to treat and prevent CMV infections exist - our study has the potential to provide immediately actionable information and improve the quality of life of those living with CF.

column36: Glycan-galectin interactions in the regulation of B cell responses
column37: B cells are important cells of the immune system that produce molecules called antibodies, which help protect the body from infection and disease. Equally important, however, is that the activation of these cells is tightly controlled so that B cells do not aberrantly produce antibodies which target our own tissues, as happens in autoimmune diseases. Lastly, we will examine the role of this sugar-binding protein in a subset of B cells called B1 B cells, which produce protective antibodies within mucosal tissues such as the lung and gut, but which are also implicated in the development of autoimmune disease. These studies are likely to yield fundamental advances in our understanding of the immune response, how it is regulated, and how it can most effectively be modulated for therapeutic purposes.

column36: Role of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 1 (PDK1) in triglyceride metabolism and heart health
column37: The continuous beating of our hearts requires a large amount of energy. Heart muscle metabolism is essential to maintain this function. It is well known that in many forms of heart disease, heart metabolism is abnormal. But, we don't know whether these differences caused the disease, or are a result of it. Many have proposed that altering metabolism in the heart may be a way to improve the function of failing hearts. New treatments for this debilitating condition, which affects 2-3% of Canadians and results in fatality in half the cases are urgently needed. Through genetic studies, we have found a protein, called PDK1, and have shown that when this protein is inactive, fat levels in our blood are lower (good) but fat builds up in the heart (potentially bad). PDK1 is found at high levels in the heart and regulates the metabolism of fat and sugar. Manipulation of PDK1 may be useful to improve metabolism in failing hearts but first we need to know how exactly blocking PDK1 affects heart metabolism and the resulting effects on heart function. In these studies we will: 1) test how reduced PDK1 affects metabolism in the heart and the resulting effects on heart function, and how drugs that are currently being made that block PDK1 affect metabolism and heart function; 2) test what effects are specifically due to the action of PDK1 in the heart, as opposed to changes in metabolism occurring elsewhere in the body; 3) test how the amount of fat and sugar in the diet influences the effects of changing PDK1. Together, these studies will determine how PDK1 affects metabolism and heart function and provide key information about the potential role(s) of PDK1 in heart health. Ultimately it is expected the knowledge created will inform the development of new treatment strategies to improve the health of Canadians with heart disease.

column36: Individualized prognosis and prediction of cognitive decline in cognitively normal individuals at risk of AD and in individuals with mild cognitive impairment
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology may be present in the brain as many as 10-15 years before symptoms occur. As in most diseases, early treatment, before too much brain damage has been done, is likely to be more effective. However, accurately identifying people at risk of dementia due to AD early, before symptoms appear, is extremely difficult. We propose to study people with subjective cognitive decline - they have issues with memory or cognition, but not enough to be captured by standard cognitive tests. We will also study people with mild cognitive impairment - their memory issues can be measured with standard tests. Both groups have significantly increased risk of later dementia, making them very interesting to study for early AD. We have built a database of magnetic resonance images (MRI), cognitive and clinical data, with extensive follow up information from 7000+ subjects. We will use this data to develop and validate our DaMoCLES (Decline prediction using MRI, Cognition and LifEStyle) score. DaMoCLES will combine (1) results from sophisticated MRI analysis to detect patterns of brain atrophy typical of AD, (2) tests of cognition that can be completed quickly in the clinic, and (3) clinically available cardiovascular risk lifestyle factors known to be associated with cognitive decline. DaMoCLES is formulated to be a clinically useful tool to help determine which patients will develop cognitive decline. It will help clinicians to develop optimal patient-specific preventive treatment. In addition, the DaMoCLES score will enable enrichment of study populations in clinical trials, so that only people that are likely to decline are included in the trials, and any benefit of the drug will be easier to see. This makes clinical trials more powerful, allowing drugs to be properly tested with fewer participants over shorter durations, bringing new treatments to patients sooner.

column36: Exploring the Existence of Gender Inequity with an Intersectionality Lens in Academic Health Care, Health Sciences and Health Policy and Interventions to Optimise Gender Equity
column37: For gender equity to be present among the health research community, we expect fairness in the distribution of benefits and responsibilities between women and men. Findings from gender equity studies, however, are often derived from a single organisation or only focus on a few issues. To fully understand whether gender inequity is present for researchers, we require a full review of all variables that may influence the career development and success of a researcher. We must also uncover and understand what strategies have already been tested to promote gender equity in the research setting. First, we will conduct a large scoping review to synthesise evidence about gender inequity in the academic health sector. We will supplement this with a national environmental scan and survey to determine the proportion of women and their intersections with Indigenous peoples, persons with disabilities and members of visible minorities in health faculty leadership for Canada's research-intensive universities versus the student body and Canadian population. Our second scoping review will synthesise evidence on interventions to optimise gender equity and inform knowledge users about existing strategies targeted to individuals, organisations or systems used to promote gender equity. These reviews will be updated every 6 months so our knowledge users are always provided with the latest research findings available. Results will be particularly important for members of funding agencies, professional associations, academic institutions, gender and equity committees and researchers. Next, we will discuss the findings from the reviews with knowledge users and work with them to determine what area(s) require further exploration using an agreement-building approach. This exercise will inform future research projects on gender equity.

column36: Inflammation and autoimmunity as triggers of axonal dying-back in PD
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative brain disorder that causes a range of motor and non-motor symptoms. Some of the major symptoms of PD are caused by the loss of a class of neurons using the chemical messenger dopamine (DA). There is also a large reduction in the density of DA-containing axon terminals. It has been proposed that loss of terminals may precede the loss of cell bodies, a hypothesis called "dying-back". The specific trigger of the early degeneration of DA-containing axonal terminals is unclear. In a recent publication, we discovered that two genes associated with familial forms of PD, Parkin and Pink1, also negatively regulate the presentation of mitochondrial proteins to the immune system, suggesting that forms of PD associated with mutations in these genes may implicate auto-immune mechanisms. Based on exciting recent data obtained by our team showing that gut infection of mice in which the Pink1 gene has been inactivated (KO), leads to the production of cytotoxic immune cells and to loss of DA-containing axon terminals, but not to loss of cell bodies, we propose here that auto-immune mechanisms and inflammatory signals may cause a selective attack on DA-containing axon terminals, perhaps providing a first insight into a mechanism triggering the dying back of terminals in PD. In the present application, we propose here three series of experiments to better document the model and test the hypothesis that following an infection in Pink1 KO mice, inflammatory signals and cytotoxic immune cells recognizing mitochondrial proteins directly affect the integrity of DA-containing axon terminals. This project, performed by a team of complementary investigators has the potential to shed light on a key, early mechanism of PD pathophysiology, paving the way to new potential strategies to slow down or halt the progression of PD.

column36: Islet macrophages: regulators of beta cell function in health and diabetes
column37: The hormone insulin, which is critical for control of blood glucose levels, is produced by islets - clusters of hundreds of insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. When beta cells are lost or are impaired in function, diabetes occurs. A type of white blood cell called macrophages - the garbage eaters of the body- are now recognized as important regulators of the function of many organs, including insulin-producing beta cells. Although macrophages comprise only a few cells out of hundreds of cells in each islet, they can produce powerful chemical modulators including proteins called cytokines which strongly affect how beta cells work. It is now becoming appreciated that macrophages in islets in the pancreas can play important supportive roles, producing growth factors for beta cells, or during disease states can produce proteins that contribute to inflammation in the pancreas, leading to loss insulin production and contributing to the development of diabetes. We have found that one important trigger of the activation of macrophages in the pancreas, leading to inflammation, is a protein accumulation called amyloid. Here we propose to study islet macrophages in the pancreas in health and in disease, using mouse models and pancreas tissue obtained from human organ donors. We aim to understand how certain protein aggregates can activate islet macrophages and trigger inflammation, and to learn what signals stimulate them to produce factors that help islets function better. We will test drugs that target pathways in islet macrophages to turn down inflammation, to try to slow diabetes. We will try to identify factors made by islet macrophages that might be used as drugs in the treatment of diabetes. The overall goal is to understand how these garbage eating cells in the pancreas regulate the life and death of insulin-producing cells, and to exploit this knowledge towards the creation and testing of drugs for the treatment of diabetes.

column37: Un grand nombre d'etudes soutiennent que le sejour au Departement d'urgence et meme l'hospitalisation peuvent etre dommageables pour les personnes agees. En 2017, les gestionnaires de l'Unite de soins de courte duree geriatrique (UCDG) du CHU de Quebec-Universite Laval - l'Hopital Saint-Francois d'Assise (HSFA) ont mesure l'impact du vieillissement de la population locale et les besoins en ressources hospitalieres de leur UCDG, et le constat etait inquietant : on anticipe, en 2031, une augmentation de 175% du nombre de consultations a l'urgence et de 165% le nombre d'hospitalisation. Il serait donc impossible de repondre a ces demandes avec l'infrastructure actuelle. Il fallait penser autrement ! Les gestionnaires et representants medicaux ont decide d'innover en creant la Clinique des aines (CDA) avec le but de diminuer le nombre et la duree des hospitalisations et faire de << l'hospitalisation a domicile >> avec des ressources specifiques. La CDA offre des services de clinique externe de soins aux personnes agees, une clinique medicale mobile ainsi qu'une unite d'hospitalisation. Notre projet a donc pour objectif d'evaluer les effets de la transition a la CDA et l'acceptabilite de cette derniere sur les patients aines, leurs proches aidants et sur les professionnels de la sante. A la fin, les conclusions pourront permettre aux decideurs d'orienter les soins aux aines pour les prochaines annees.
