column36: Using Antibiotics Wisely - Development of National Neonatal Intensive Care Unit-specific Antimicrobial Stewardship Plan
column37: Infections are one of the most prevalent threats to infants who are born prematurely. Antibiotics have been developed to kill germs or stop their growth and are the most commonly prescribed drugs in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). However, antibiotics are not always prescribed optimally, and their overuse can result in drug resistance (reduced effectiveness), which can lead to serious problems in infants. We know little about how often broad-spectrum antibiotics (i.e. antibiotic that acts against a wide range of disease-causing bacteria) are used and about how many infants have multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria (i.e. resistant to multiple antibiotics) presented in their body across Canadian NICUs. Unlike in adults, there is lack of consensus on the optimal interventions used to improve and measure the appropriate use of antimicrobials in infants. In this study, we wish to determine how frequently broad-spectrum antibiotics are used in daily care and how often MDR bacteria are encountered among premature infants, with a birth weight <1.5 kg. A national surveillance program, called the Canadian Neonatal Network (CNN), has been conducted in the past two decades to study the outcomes of all infants admitted to NICUs across Canada. Our study will gather data from the CNN regarding antibiotic use in each infant and the presence of drug resistance if infection exists. We can also study whether particular attributes (risk factors) predispose an infant to resistant infections. The information that will be obtained from this study will help each centre compare their own treatment standards with those of other centres ('benchmarking'), and can allow us to develop specific national strategies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use ('antimicrobial stewardship') in the future.

column36: Understanding how the maternal microbiota, metabolites and maternal antibodies interact to shape development of the neonatal immune system.
column37: Our bodies are home to trillions of microbes that constantly stimulate the immune system and impact our health. Colonization of our intestines and all other mucosal surfaces is a dynamic process that begins at birth and takes several years to reach a stable but diverse mixture of different bacterial species. Importantly, development of the immune system also occurs during these critical early years, and we now know that the presence of our intestinal bacteria heavily influences development of a regulated and balanced immune system. Studies have shown that changes in the developing microbiota in early life are associated with increased susceptibility to multiple diseases later in life, including allergic disease and autoimmunity. Since the environment in utero is thought to be sterile, microbial stimulation of the developing immune system was thought to begin at birth, when the newborn is exposed to the outside environment. However, we have recently shown that the maternal microbiota can already start to influence development of the fetal immune system before birth. This early stimulation is required to train the baby's immune system to cope with the onslaught of microbes it is faced with at birth. In this study, we aim to identify the precise mechanisms and pathways by which the microbiota of the mother before birth educates and shapes the developing immune system. This project will help to establish novel strategies to promote a healthy microbiome during pregnancy to ensure each new baby is born with a trained immune system and will provide information for the rational design of microbial therapies designed to protect from development of diseases later in life.

column36: From cells to tissues: molecular mechanisms mediating coordination of RhoGTPase signaling between cells during collective endothelial cell migration and vascular morphogenesis
column37: Tissues in multicellular organisms are formed by large numbers of cells that are physically and functionally connected with each other. While surrounded by neighbors, individual cells remain the basic units of life and are responsible for a range of autonomous cellular decisions, such as whether to secrete hormones, to change shape, to divide, or to die. To ensure tissue function, many cells must act together as one functional unit, and this requires coordination of individual cells' behavior with the behavior of their neighbors, through communication between them. Despite their fundamental importance for multicellular biology, the molecular mechanisms enabling such communication, and ultimately resulting in collective behavior of cells, have remained incompletely understood. Capitalizing on established and experimentally tractable models of collective movement of cultured endothelial cells and the formation of vascular tubes, the proposed research aims to identify novel mechanisms of intercellular communication. We will use genetic manipulations of cells, automated cell tracking, and advanced imaging technologies for visualizing and manipulating cellular activities in real time. Endothelial cells form a lining at the inner surface of blood vessels and represent a highly functional barrier between the bloodstream and surrounding tissues. This selective barrier enables distribution of nutrients and oxygen to tissues and, when necessary, the passage of immune cells to sites of infection or injury for clearance. Endothelial cells are also involved in the development of a range of vasculature-related diseases and therefore are of central importance for human health. The anticipated results will not only unveil fundamental principles of how cells are organized into tissues, but also identify new targets of future therapies to treat vasculature-related diseases, a major cause of mortality in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Improving Transitions in Care from ICU: Evaluation of an Electronic Communication Tool
column37: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are very sick. When a patient leaves the ICU it is important that doctors and other healthcare providers have an effective way to communicate between themselves to share important information, like new medical problems or new medications. Often, the doctor taking charge of the patient's care, or the 'receiving' doctor, will not have met or been involved in the patient's care up to that point. Because of this, it is crucial that ICU doctors and nurses have an effective way to share important information about the patient with the 'receiving' doctor. It is also important that this method be easy to share with other ICUs in other regions to streamline communication and information about the patient after they leave the ICU. The goal of this study is to evaluate and improve an electronic tool that enables ICU doctors and nurses to create and share electronic transfer documents when patients leave the ICU. The tool was recently implemented in four (4) ICUs in Calgary, AB. This study will explore the capacity of the tool to improve the quality of communication between ICU and 'receiving' doctors and nurses. It will also investigate whether using the tool improves the quality of care patients receive as they move between healthcare teams and locations. Once evaluated, the tool will be updated to create the best version possible. The final step will be creating a plan to share the new, updated tool with ICUS across the province of Alberta, and eventually the rest of Canada. Overall, we expect that this tool will improve the outcomes of patients who leave the ICU by facilitating the quality and exchange of information between ICU and 'receiving' doctors and establishing a standardized process for patients leaving the ICU.

column36: Evaluating the Impact of a Navigation Service for Transitional-Aged Youth with Mental Health and/or Addictions Concerns and their Families
column37: Transitional-aged youth (TAY) with mental health and/or addictions (MHA) concerns often fall through gaps between care settings and systems, which can negatively impact their long-term outcomes. Many TAY may also have family members involved in their care, yet their families might not know where to turn for support in finding the best resources for the TAY and for themselves, when needed. There needs to be more support for TAY with MHA concerns and their families leading up to, during, and after care transitions. Navigation is one such model of support. The Family Navigation Project (FNP) is a service in which Navigators work one-on-one with TAY between the ages of 13-26 with MHA concerns and their families to help them find their way through the MHA system and get connected to the right care. Evaluation of this program is important to help understand if it is leading to benefits for TAY, families, and the health care system. This project will involve three studies. First, we will look at the literature, both academic and non-academic, to understand what the needs, barriers, and facilitators to MHA care are for TAY and families. Secondly, we will conduct focus groups with TAY, family members, Navigators, service providers, and system decision-makers to understand their ideas about the needs of TAY and families, how families can be involved in the care of the TAY, and the role of Navigation. Finally, we will conduct a program evaluation of the FNP, to better understand if and how Navigation leads to changes in youth, caregiver, and family functioning, quality of life, satisfaction with services, and use of appropriate health services for their needs. These findings will all be merged to present a picture of how Navigation can lead to system transformation for TAY and their families. We will share our findings through webinars for various audiences and a toolkit that will provide resources for TAY, family members, service providers, and system decision-makers.

column36: Sex-based differences in cardiac function and cardiovascular disease risk in spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating condition that causes significant changes to the cardiovascular system. Our group has recently identified that SCI leads to reductions in heart size, and reduced ejection and filling. Remarkably, of the data available, only 5% represented females with SCI. In Canada, females represent over 25% of the SCI population, thus females are majorly underrepresented in SCI research to date. Heart disease is a leading cause of death for individuals with SCI yet no work to date has examined whether differences exist in the heart's structure and function in males and females with SCI. We believe that such differences could play a major role in determining differential heart disease risk profiles between males and females with SCI. If we find sex-differences in heart function and/or heart disease risk then these findings are expected to influence treatment options. This research aims to 1) determine if sex-differences exist in cardiac structure and function at rest and in response to moving from a supine to upright position, and 2) investigate sex differences in heart disease risk and acute heart events (i.e., heart attack) in SCI, by analyzing data from existing large health survey databases. This research is important because heart disease is the leading cause of death for individuals with SCI yet no efforts have sought to determine either the sex-specific differences in heart disease risk after SCI, or whether the excess risks of heart disease in SCI are comparable between males and females. Our preliminary analysis of one of the databases found that the odds for heart disease are more than 2-fold higher in males vs. females with SCI. By examining the impacts of sex on cardiac function and heart risk in SCI, this work will help us determine potential sex-based differences in treatment options/targets in SCI and may improve our ability to appropriately manage males and females with SCI.

column36: High-throughput in vivo functional characterization of Autism Spectrum Disorder associated genes using Caenorhabditis elegans
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a diverse group of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by social impairment, repetitive behaviour, and sensory processing abnormalities. This disorder affects ~1% of the population, and is often severely debilitating with no broadly successful treatments available. Although a very large number of mutations in many, many genes have been implicated in ASD it is not clear what all of these genes do, how these genes interact, and how the mutations contribute to ASD. I propose using a microscopic round worm, Caenorhabditis elegans to characterize the function ASD-associated genes. C. elegans is cheap and easy to genetically engineer, and our automated behavioural scoring system allows us to rapidly and systematically study neurodevelopmental and behavioural effects of mutations in each of the hundreds of genes associated with ASD. This research will help us understand what these genes do and how they might contribute to ASD. Thus understanding how these genes function in the nervous systems of living animals may shed light on what causes ASD. We will also be able to use the genome-editing tool CRISPR-Cas9 to determine if behavioural abnormalities caused by mutations in a large number of ASD-associated genes are reversible by reintroducing the gene in adulthood. This has been shown for a few ASD-associated genes before, and has offered tremendous hope for families with ASD and is critical for designing treatments. These studies will also allow grouping genes into network that contributing to specific behavioural phenotypes which may allow a greater understanding of the heterogeneous nature of ASD, and identify novel therapeutic targets for treating ASD.

column36: Platelet Transfusions in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation - The PATH Phase III Trial
column37: Platelet transfusions have been part of routine supportive care for patients with hematologic malignancies since the 1960s. Current standard of practice is to transfuse platelets prophylactically to prevent bleeding when the platelet count is very low (less than 10 x 10^9/L). However, recent studies suggest that this practice may not reduce bleeding in patients undergoing autologous stem cell transplantion. We have successfully undertaken a pilot study to evaluate a trial comparing prophylactic tranexamic acid (a drug that reduces bleeding by preventing the break down of blood clots) to prophylactic platelet transfusions in patients undergoing an autologous stem cell transplantation. We will now undertake a large study to determine if prophylactic tranexamic acid as compared to prophylactic platelet transfusions will reduce the amount of serious bleeding in patients undergoing an autologous stem cell transplant. A total of 662 patients will be enrolled at 9 Canadian transplant centres over the next 5 years. Patients will be randomly assigned to either prophylactic tranexamic acid or prophylactic platelet transfusions during the period immediately following the stem cell transplant. All patients can receive additional platelet transfusions to treat bleeding episodes. All patients will be followed daily for 6 months following their stem cell transplant. They will be monitored daily for bleeding daily using a standardized bleeding assessment until their platelet counts recover. They will also be followed for quality of life measureents (4 weeks) and any adverse events (6 months).

column36: Prebiotics to modify the gut microbiome and enhance immune checkpoint blockers
column37: The immune system of patients living with cancer is often altered and weakened. Immune checkpoint blockers (ICB) are a new class of drugs that re-awaken the immune system to kill cancer cells that have revolutionized the management of various cancers. Unfortunately, despite unprecedented results, 70% of patients' diseases will progress. Therefore, predictors of response (biomarkers) and ways to safely enhance ICB efficacy are urgently needed. The immune system itself is now known to be influenced by the gut microbiome, which is made up of trillions of bacteria in our intestines that are in constant communication with our immune cells. We pioneered the concept that the gut microbiome influences the clinical response to treatments in both experimental models as well as cancer patients treated with ICB. We demonstrated that antibiotics, by killing pathogens but also beneficial bacteria, negatively impacted clinical outcomes. We also found that lung cancer patients with favorable microbiomes (high bacterial diversity and an abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila bacteria) had a stronger immune response translating into a better clinical outcome. More recently, our unpublished results revealed that in experimental models, a natural prebiotic, Camu Camu, can enhance ICB response. The goal of this project is to demonstrate that Camu Camu can favorably transform the microbiome composition, promoting a stronger ICB anticancer response. To demonstrate our hypothesis, we will sequence feces (gut microbiome) from lung cancer patients treated with ICB. We will then transplant the fecal microbiota of patients into mice who will also receive Camu Camu in order to better understand how prebiotics can improve the microbiome composition and systemic anticancer response. Our ultimate goal is to launch clinical trials based on our results that will use new therapeutic strategies to modify patients' microbiomes, thereby safely increasing ICB effectiveness and improving overall survival.

column36: Studying prenatal exposure to maternal immune activation as risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders: from the fetus to adulthood
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia are complex and debilitating neurodevelopmental disorder that affect ~1-3% of the population worldwide. Symptoms usually develop in childhood, adolescence, or early adulthood (sensitive maturational periods), and include impaired communication, social abilities, and motor and cognitive function. Although the cause of these disorders are still unclear, it is thought that adverse environmental factors during development and adolescence are fundamental to the onset of symptoms. Multiple studies have shown a link between maternal infection as increasing risk for developing ASD and schizophrenia. To further investigate this risk factor, rodent models have been created whereby a pregnant mother is injected with a virus that elicits an immune response. These offspring exhibit similar impairments in behaviour, immune function, and brain structure to what is observed in patients with ASD and schizophrenia. It is still unclear when these deficits arise during development and how they change throughout the lifespan. Therefore, this study aims to investigate development brain anatomy and behaviour in offspring exposed to maternal infection and stress and if it can be rescued by administering and anti-inflammatory agent to the pregnancy mother. This research is critical in defining how the brain responds to well known risk factors for ASD and schizophrenia, and for the refinement of therapeutic interventions.

column36: Can Exercise Prescribed According to the International Scientific Spinal Cord Injury Exercise Guidelines Alleviate Chronic Pain in Adults Living with Spinal Cord Injury? A Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Most people living with a spinal cord injury (SCI) experience pain every day. This chronic pain is often more physically, psychologically, and socially debilitating than the injury itself. Currently, drugs are the most frequently prescribed treatment for SCI pain, but drugs have many negative side-effects. The primary purpose of this project is to determine whether a regular program of exercise, performed in a person's home or in a local fitness facility, can significantly reduce chronic pain in adults with SCI. As secondary purposes, this study will test whether exercise has different effects on different types of pain, if exercise reduces pain by reducing inflammation in the body and reducing a person's sensitivity to pain, and if reductions in pain lead to improvements in how people feel about themselves and their lives. We will also test whether the exercise intervention has the potential to reduce health care costs. Our team includes people with expertise in exercise psychology, exercise physiology, pain, physical medicine, immunology, biostatistics, health economics, and trial design and management. Our team also includes a community-researcher with lived experience of SCI, and groups and individuals who will use the knowledge generated by this study. These knowledge users represent local, provincial and national SCI organizations. Our novel idea is that exercise performed according to a prescription specifically tailored to people with SCI, performed in one's community (rather than in a laboratory or a clinic) can be an effective behavioural strategy for reducing chronic pain. This study may also help to explain how exercise alleviates pain. By working with key stakeholders throughout the project, we will ensure the results are appropriately shared with Canadian and international end-users including clinicians, fitness programmers, people living with SCI and the community organizations that support them.

column36: A 15 months, double-Blind, randomized controlled trial comparing 18 weeks of two doses of Omalizumab to placebo to accelerate a symptom-driven Oral immunotherapy schedule in subjects aged 6 to 25 years with Multiple food allergies (BOOM).
column37: Oral immunotherapy (OIT) is a new treatment for food allergy, where allergists administer patients precisely measured amounts of their allergen to progressively deplete antibodies on allergy cells and build their tolerance over time up to a full portion of the food. While creating hopes for tens of thousands of families across the country, universal access to OIT in its current form it not realistic because the updosing phase, which can last up to 2 years in moderate to severe cases, associates with frequent reactions and anaphylaxis and requires unrealistic amounts of ressources to be delivered safely. Omalizumab is a medication that blocks allergy antibodies which is currently approved for moderate to severe allergic asthma. When used in patients with food allergy, it increases the amount of food tolerated by 30 to 100-folds. When combined with OIT, phase 1 and phase 2a trials have shown that a short transient treatment with omalizumab enables a very fast desensitization, requiring minimal amounts of clinical resources while protecting against potential allergic reactions. Before it can be used in clinic for this indication, larger clinical trials designed to quantify the efficacy at modulating OIT treatment speed and safety must be conducted and optimal dosage must be determined. The proposed trial will enrol 90 subjects with at least 3 food allergies to receive either of 2 dosages of omalizumab or placebo for 18 weeks as adjunct therapy to a multi-food OIT. After 8 weeks of pre-treatment, subjects will start an OIT to three food allergens. The OIT updosing schedule will be continuously adapted to the subject's tolerance, withtout knowledge of dosage (or placebo) received. All subjects will be followed for a minimum of 12 months after beginning OIT. The main objective is to determine the dose-related efficacy of omalizumab at decraseing the time required to reach final protective maintenance food doses (i.e. desenstization).

column36: Electronic Patient Reported Outcome Measures to Improve Patient Centered Solid Organ Transplant Care
column37: Solid-organ transplantation is a life-saving treatment. Many recipients, however, still have symptoms, such as fatigue, pain, anxiety or depression after their transplant, and these patients with symptoms may end up in hospitals more often or even die sooner. Current post-transplant treatment does not include screening for these symptoms, which often go undiagnosed and untreated. Some doctors use questionnaires called Patient Reported Outcome Measures to detect emotional and physical symptoms. These questionnaires are better at recognizing symptoms than clinical assessments by healthcare providers. Using Patient Reported Outcome Measures can improve doctor-patient communication, patient satisfaction by giving them a greater say in their care, and survival rates. Using these tools for transplant recipients would likely deliver similar benefits, so this should be a high priority. To do so, we need tools that are accurate, and don't take too long to complete. The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System - Computer Adaptive Testing (PROMIS CAT) tools, developed by the National Institutes of Health may be such tools. PROMIS CATs are able to detect physical and emotional symptoms in healthy individuals and also in patients with chronic diseases. Based on the answer to the questions, the computer determines what the next best question will be for that particular patient. In our study, we will: 1. Compare PROMIS CATs to current questionnaires to see if they are precise enough; 2. Develop an electronic Patient Reported Outcome Measure toolkit to guide transplant clinicians in using the PROMIS CATs in clinics; 3. Test if a subsequent study with the PROMIS CATs is doable and acceptable for patients and clinicians. We hope that our electronic Patient Reported Outcome Measure toolkit will become an important tool in helping transplant clinicians to provide more effective, patient-oriented care.

column36: Brain connectivity-based optimization of non-invasive brain stimulation to improve cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness that affects around 250,000 Canadians. Beyond positive symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions, and negative symptoms such as blunted affect or social withdrawal, cognitive impairments (for instance, deficits in short- term memory and sustained attention) are a cardinal feature of schizophrenia. Cognitive deficits are particularly disabling for patients trying to lead a normal life and are unfortunately poorly treated with current medications. A non-invasive brain stimulation technique known as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation holds great promise to improve cognitive symptoms. Stimulating the prefrontal lobe of the brain is thought to regulate its abnormal interaction with distant brain regions, which may reduce cognitive symptoms. Unfortunately, the research conducted up to now has omitted to consider a critical factor to optimize treatment success using this neuromodulatory approach. The one-size-fits-all approach typically employed, where all patients are repetitively stimulated at an identical scalp location, has indeed been shown to have small benefits only. Yet, functional brain organization varies considerably from one individual to another as well as from one mental state to another. Our research program therefore aims to determine optimal characteristics of stimulation on an individual basis in order to best modulate abnormal brain connectivity in schizophrenia. We will use neuroimaging mapping techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography along with state-of-the-art statistical approaches to better describe how functional brain organization varies both between individuals and within an individual over time. Findings will pave the way for increasing the success rate of non-invasive brain stimulation in treating medication-resistant cognitive symptoms in persons suffering from schizophrenia.

column36: Modelling Mitochondrial Disease
column37: Mitochondria are the power plants of our cells, converting the food that we eat into energy needed to survive. Thus, it should come as no surprise that mitochondrial dysfunction can have adverse effects on human health. Mitochondrial disease is a rare, though not uncommon, difficult to diagnose genetic disorder, caused by mitochondrial dysfunction. At present there are no cures, and treatment is mostly to manage symptoms. As such, fewer than 50% of diagnosed children survive to adulthood. However, a genetic diagnosis of disease is of immense value to both clinicians as well as patients and their families. While recent advances in genetic analyses have accelerated mitochondrial disease diagnosis, by helping to identify mutations in genes causing mitochondrial dysfunction, a definitive answer is found less than half of the time. When novel candidate disease genes and mutations are identified, they require additional functional validation. Such work can take significant time and effort, and has created a bottleneck in diagnosing mitochondrial disease patients. Thus, it is imperative to evaluate these candidate mutations. In addition to providing a genetic diagnosis, characterizing these novel disease-causing mutations helps to identify the underlying cause of mitochondrial dysfunction, which provides fundamental insight and understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating mitochondria. This insight is essential groundwork prior to developing a cure for mitochondrial disease. By employing methods and approaches that allow us to characterize mitochondrial dysfunction, our research will help provide clinical diagnoses for patients with mitochondrial disease, and deliver a better understanding of the mechanisms regulating mitochondrial function. Given the growing appreciation for the role mitochondria play in human health and disease, our research has both short and long-term benefits to Canadians and the Canadian health care system.

column36: Gaia Project: Intervention Program for Adolescents who have Engaged in Sexual Abuse and their Families
column37: According to a national survey, one third of Canadians aged 15 and older were victims of childhood maltreatment. It is noteworthy that 60% of victims experienced abuse at the hands of a family member, suggesting intergenerational transmission of abuse. In 2014, in the province of Quebec, 95.5% of the 605 adolescents adjudicated as having engaged in sexual abuse (AESA) perpetrated these offences against minors. Nevertheless, AESA represent a vulnerable population given their own experiences of past victimization (e.g., 50% physical; 30% sexual), as well as their risk for sexual (6 to 20%) and violent recidivism (21 to 40%). Furthermore, with 50% of mothers and 30% of fathers of AESA reporting a history of victimization, manifestations associated with sexual and non-sexual interpersonal violence in these families is undeniable. A systemic approach to research and intervention is thus necessary to address the cumulative forms of victimization in these families. The Gaia Project seeks to implement and assess the effectiveness of the clinical Gaia program to promote targeted changes in improving mental and relational health in AESA and their families at the end of the treatment and at the 6-month follow-up. The Gaia program will be implemented in 3 organizations, the Centre integre universitaire de sante et services sociaux de l'Estrie (CIUSSSE) and de la Mauricie-et-du-Centre-du-Quebec (CIUSSSMCQ), as well as the Institut Philippe-Pinel de Montreal. Program implementation and effectiveness will be based on a quasi-experimental design with comparison group and 3 assessment time points. Given referral rates of partnering organizations, a sample of 200 families is expected. The Gaia program is innovative in that 1) AESA and their families are targeted for treatment; 2) symptomatic repercussions of victimization and interpersonal violence in families are treated; and 3) the program is designed with modules that are implemented while AESA complete their treatment as usual.

column37: A neurotransmitter receptor is a receptor protein that is activated by a neurotransmitter. Chemicals on the outside of the cell, such as a neurotransmitter, can bump into the cell's membrane and along the membrane we can find receptors. Therefore, a membrane receptor is part of the molecular machinery that allows cells to communicate with one another. It has become clear that the amount of neurotransmitter receptors present on the surface of nerve cells changes based on experience or environment. This change allows the brain to adjust to the experience and environment. Our study proposes to investigate the mechanism how neurotransmitter receptors are transported to the surface of nerve cells. Our preliminary investigation has led us to the development of new models for disorders affecting brain cell communication. This work will lay the groundwork for developing novel therapies for neurological disorders.

column36: Poor muscle-bone quality and its downstream impact on knee osteoarthritis disease development in postmenopausal women: the Appendicular Muscle and Bone Extension Research Study (AMBERS)
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is 4 times as prevalent as stroke and heart disease. While obesity has often been coined the culprit, and cartilage named the victim of knee OA, there are other important causes and tissues involved within subgroups of knee OA patients, which have yet to be fully explored. We recently determined that over 40% of OA patients receiving knee surgeries are neither overweight nor obese. Many of these patients are postmenopausal women and in a recent study we published, 15% of knee OA patients showed evidence of bone loss. Bone and muscle abnormalities at the joint have been associated with OA, but few investigators have explored how they may be the causes rather than the consequences of the disease. Even fewer studies have examined this relationship over time to establish evidence for cause. For the last 5 years, the lead investigator has directed a study measuring leg bone and muscle properties using CT scans in women 60-85 years old to predict falls and fractures over 4 years. For the proposed study, the team will use the same cohort, inviting participants back to complete follow-up imaging of their leg bones and muscles, also administering knee OA symptom questionnaires and acquiring MRI and CT scans of the knee. Bone and muscle differences will be used to predict more painful and worsening knee symptoms 5 years later. Within a subset of participants, the study will also address how changes in these bone and muscle features can impact what happens in the tissues of the knee joint. Finally, the study will examine the pathway that leads from bone and muscle loss to knee tissue damage and subsequently greater knee symptoms. By studying bone-muscle and joint interactions over time in the context of knee OA, we can pinpoint earlier stages in the disease process that can be targeted for disease prevention. This study will address postmenopausal OA patients, a group that has so far, been underserved with few treatment options available.

column36: Prenatal diagnosis of congenital heart diseases in Canada: The FREQUENCY study
column37: Heart malformations are the most frequent malformations at birth. Serious heart malformations require immediate care at birth and many affected children will need open-heart surgery. It is important to diagnose heart malformations before birth as it increases the likelihood of survival and decreases healthcare costs and hospitalization duration. Obstetricians and radiologists perform an ultrasound at the second trimester of pregnancy. Most malformations will be identified during that ultrasound, but unfortunately, some go unnoticed. There are various strategies to improve the detection of heart malformations on small fetuses. Some of them involve referring pregnant women for a specialized exam called a fetal echocardiogram. However, we do not know yet if and when this is truly beneficial. There are many unanswered questions: How good are we at diagnosing heart malformations before birth? Who should undergo a fetal echocardiogram? Are there heart malformations that are more difficult to diagnose? The FREQUENCY study aims to find answers to these questions on a large group of women who were pregnant between 2007 and 2015. We will investigate who had a correct prenatal diagnosis and who did not, who underwent a fetal echocardiogram and why, and what the impacts were on healthcare costs. Getting answers to these questions will enable us to design and test new strategies to detect heart malformations before birth with the hope of improving diagnosis accuracy without increasing healthcare costs.

column36: Surveillance of Complex Renal Cysts: The SOCRATIC study
column37: Background: One in three patients over 60 years old will be diagnosed with a renal cyst following abdominal imaging. Traditionally, experts have recommended that complex cystic lesions (also known as Bosniak III - IV cysts) should be surgically removed, but recent evidences suggest that many are benign and that if malignant, most have low-metastatic risk. Given that many patients may not require surgery due to the excellent prognosis, alternative management should be studied. Thus, active surveillance which involves close follow-up of a patient's condition without treatment unless its condition changes, was proposed as a tradeoff option to surgery. Objectives: The goal of this multicenter project is to conduct a prospective study with a 5-year follow-up to confirm the oncologic outcomes of active surveillance in the management of complex cysts. The main objectives are: 1) to compare the 5-year cancer specific survival between cysts managed by surgery and active surveillance; 2) evaluate disease progression; and 3) evaluate patient's well-being according to each management strategy. Description: Participants (220 under active surveillance and 110 undergoing surgery) will be selected on the basis of age (over 18y), life expectancy (over 5y), diagnosis (Bosniak III and IV) and treatment choice. They will be followed with semi-annual and annual visits. Visits will serve to evaluate vital status and quality of life scores. Patients on active surveillance will also be assessed for cyst progression and will be offered surgery if progression is observed. This study, conducted in 6 large-volume Canadian centers, will be led by medical/scientific experts and patient advocates. Relevance: Validating the safety of active surveillance of complex renal cysts will be determinant in reducing overtreatment, sparing thousands of patients from unnecessary treatment, reducing the risk associated to surgery and potentially saving costs to the healthcare system.

column36: EpiGen Marks for Human Sepsis
column37: Sepsis, systemic organ dysfunction triggered by a dysregulated host response to infection, incurs enormous human and health care burden. Globally it is estimated to affect more than 30 million people each year, ~40% of whom die. The sequelae include physical, cognitive, and psychological disability; profoundly impacting quality of life of survivors. The biggest problem is that we have no specific treatments. Patients receive fluid resuscitation, antibiotics and supportive care, but an under appreciation for patient heterogeneity and inadequate characterization of the complexity of the host response to infection has made it difficult to design clinical trials that show benefit. The issue is that, despite development of robust therapeutic candidates, we lack the tools to accurately categorize sepsis (prognostic enrichment) and identify those patients that are more likely to respond to therapy (predictive enrichment). In the cancer literature, personalizing treatment on the basis of the molecular characteristics of a tumor is simply 'good practice'- there is an urgent need to do the same for septic patients. Here we propose to use an approach that has never been used for sepsis before; to identify DNA methylation changes that classify septic vs non-septic critically ill patients (often it is very difficult to differentiate these patients on the basis of clinical tools alone) and determine the association between methylation changes with time-to-death and/or response to therapy. We will capitalize on banked DNA samples collected in the context of RCTs where patient heterogeneity was minimized through randomization and bias was reduced by blinding. We will use predictive modeling to integrate clinical and molecular data to identify a set of informative methylation marks - and validate their ability to risk stratify patients using independent cohorts. Successful completion of this project is expected to significantly advance care.

column36: K+ channels as key targets to favor alveolar epithelial integrity and function during the resolution of acute respiratory distress syndrome
column37: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a devastating form of respiratory failure in adults and children. Although ARDS causes may be multiple (infection, trauma, transplantation...), this syndrome initially commonly features severe injury of the epithelial cell layer lining alveoli, accumulation of liquid in the lungs (edema) and massive inflammation. Rapid resolution is pivotal for ARDS. If not, a fibrotic process rapidly arises, ultimately leading to respiratory failure. No specific treatment exists for ARDS and mortality rates remain unacceptably high. Improvement in survival relies on the development of novel therapies favoring the restoration of alveolar integrity, before establishment of fibrosis. Importantly, we discovered that a specific class of proteins transporting potassium (K+ channels) through alveolar epithelial cells plays key role in alveolar repair. In addition, our data from animal models strongly support that these channels are not only crucial to favor alveolar integrity but are also implicated in resorption of lung edema and inflammation. Therefore, we propose that targeting K+ channels will promote alveolar integrity and lung function, favoring ARDS resolution. Our main goal is to address key questions regarding the mode of action of alveolar K+ channels in the resolution of ARDS parameters. At the cellular level, we will dissect the mechanisms on how K+ channels regulate alveolar epithelial repair and we will study the relationship between K+ channel function and inflammation. Using complementary genetic and pharmacological strategies in animal models of ARDS, our aim is then to demonstrate the role of K+ channels in the resolution of ARDS parameters, through improvement of alveolar epithelial integrity and function. In summary, our project will provide a comprehensive knowledge of the action mechanisms of K+ channels for the resolution of ARDS and important insights into the development of innovative therapeutic strategies.

column36: Restorative System for Cervical Lesions with Enhanced Biostability, Antidegradative and Antimicrobial Properties
column37: Root and recurrent dental caries are prevalent among adults and the elderly, especially amid disadvantaged groups of the Canadian population. This approach to material design is comprehensive to address the needs of the dental health care community and Canadian society and will introduce new formulations of materials to the field of dentistry.

Ces jeux mobiles, connectes et multiplateformes integrent les aspects ludiques du gaming et les aspects monetaires du gambling et presentent de nouveaux parametres propices a la perte de controle dans la consommation de ces jeux. Leur popularite et leur omnipresence soulevent des questions quant aux facteurs individuels et structurels qui influencent la regulation de leurs modes d'usage. Ce projet vise a 1) produire un premier portrait des habitudes de participation aux jeux hybrides dans la population canadienne, 2) examiner les facteurs qui influencent leurs modes de consommation, 3) comprendre les dimensions experientielles des joueurs, 4) documenter les perceptions des acteurs cles concernant les jeux hybrides. Une analyse des caracteristiques du jeu, du joueur et des contextes de jeu permettra de degager les parametres associes a un usage excessif et envahissant de ces jeux dans la vie des individus. En s'integrant au sein d'une initiative internationale d'envergure, nos donnees permettront de contraster la situation au Canada a celle observee dans d'autres contextes socioculturels. Le projet produira des donnees qui seront utiles pour orienter l'action de sante publique en permettant d'identifier les parametres associes a une integration harmonieuse de ces jeux dans le quotidien des individus et les points de flexions vers une perte de controle. Le projet regroupera des chercheurs et des intervenants et assurera un dialogue continu avec les acteurs cles.

column36: Long-Term Outcomes of Hip Interventions for Children with Cerebral Palsy - An International Multi-Centre Prospective Comparative Cohort Study (CHOP-II)
column37: Children with cerebral palsy are at high risk for dislocating their hips. Hip dislocations occur over months or years, during which time these children can experience muscle tightness (contractures) and pain. These symptoms interfere with care-giving (dressing, toileting, hygiene, positioning, sitting and mobility) and affect quality of life. There are many ways to prevent or treat these hips. Some are treated early before any symptoms start, while others are treated at the earliest signs of any symptoms. Earlier treatments are less invasive, but often have to be repeated because the hips can begin to dislocate again as the child grows. Later treatments are usually more invasive but might have the advantage of lasting longer. Currently there is little evidence from high quality research to suggest which strategies work best. Previous research has relied on x-rays of the hips to make judgments about the success of any treatment. While x-rays are an important way to record the results of different treatments, they do not tell us whether a child has really benefited from treatment in terms of the child's comfort, ease of care, health or quality of life. Our research team has developed a way to measure the effect of treatments more meaningfully for children with severe cerebral palsy. In 2014, CIHR funded a 5 year project, involving a large group of surgeons and pediatricians from 28 centres in Canada, the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Europe and Asia to study the impact of hip displacement on the lives of children with severe cerebral palsy, and to compare which treatment strategy would be most beneficial for these children using the outcome measure developed for this purpose. This study has enrolled 678 patients who are being followed for at least 2 years after initiation of treatment. This new project proposes to follow the same children over the next 6 years or until end of growth to study the longer term outcomes of these children.

column36: Pathways to neurodegeneration from natural human tRNA variation
column37: The ability of cells to properly manage the synthesis, folding, and degradation of their constituent proteins is essential for all aspects of cellular function and life. Many diseases, particularly age-related and neurodegenerative diseases, are characterized by increased levels of misfolded proteins. Correct reading of the genetic code is essential for accurate protein synthesis and protein folding. An often-overlooked step in the synthesis of proteins involves the correct attachment of amino acids to specific tRNAs by enzymes called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Lack of specificity at this step can result in the incorrect reading of the genetic code or mistranslation, which may lead to protein mis-folding, aggregation, and disease. The 1000 Genomes Project revealed a higher than anticipated degree of variation in the ~600 human tRNA genes, indicating more than half of individuals contain at least one mutant tRNA. We developed a novel targeted capture array and deep sequenced 610 tRNA loci in a group of 84 individuals. Our data show that individuals carry significantly more tRNA variants than previously anticipated. We identified many human tRNA variants some with obvious potential to mistranslate. We predict that mistranslating tRNA variants contribute to human disease. We will, for the first time, elucidate to what extent naturally occurring tRNA mutations in humans cause mistranslation, and whether mistranslation exacerbates the toxicity of mis-folded proteins that are associated with neurodegenerative disease. Our proposed project has great potential to identify genetic mutations that cause mistranslation as an important contributor to neurodegeneration. Our data will also be relevant to other age-related diseases characterized by compromised cellular protein quality control, such as cancer and cardio-vascular diseases.

column37: Need for project Once cancer is established, it becomes complex and resistant to standard therapies. column36: Determining the mechanisms underlying disease pathology and the genetic reversibility of the ATR-X syndrome.
column37: Our genes are arranged on large pieces of DNA called chromosomes. Chromosomes are huge molecules that must undergo multiple levels of compaction to fit into the cell. At the same time, the genes characteristic of that cell type must remain accessible for activation. In a stem cell the chromosomes are loosely packaged and many genes are poised for activation. When the stem cell commits to becoming a specific cell type (eg. neuron) it must tightly package and silence those genes that are not required and fully activate those genes that will be turned on. To do this cells have developed a complex series of proteins to control the structure of chromosomes and the regulation of genes. When this process is defective, cells cannot divide, differentiate or initiate gene expression effectively. Recent work has shown that mutations in chromosome regulating proteins cause a variety of human diseases, including developmental disorders with severe intellectual disability and numerous types of cancer. This project studies the ATRX gene that, when mutated, causes a severe intellectual disability syndrome. Despite our success in identifying these genes, our understanding of how these chromosome regulatory proteins coordinate which genes to turn on or off, when to turn them on or off, and in what order remains poorly defined. This project aims to define the function of ATRX during brain development, learning, and memory formation by studying a mouse model in which the ATRX gene has been inactivated. Since many of these changes to our chromosomes are dynamic and reversible we will also explore whether we can rescue the phenotypic features of the disease by adding back a normal copy of the gene. With our current ability to use viruses to re-introduce genes to kill cancer cells and clinical trials underway to use them to treat neuromuscular disease, the possibility that they could be used to treat a devastating intellectual disability is promising and provides immense hope.

column36: Development of an AAV gene therapy approach for the treatment of surfactant protein B deficiency
column37: Surfactant protein B (SP-B) deficiency is a rare genetic disease that causes lethal respiratory distress in infants due to the absence of an essential surfactant protein that allows the lung to inflate. The disease results from mutations in the SP-B gene (SFTPB). Infants with SP-B deficiency exhibit early onset severe respiratory distress followed by progressive respiratory failure and death within the first year of life. The only effective treatment is lung transplantation. Due to the rapidly fatal nature of this disease and the lack of available treatment options, novel therapies for neonates suffering from SP-B deficiency are needed. Since SP-B deficiency is caused by mutations in a single gene, and the only organ affected by these mutations is the lung, targeted delivery of gene therapies to the respiratory tract is an attractive treatment option. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is a highly effective gene therapy vector that infects both dividing and non-dividing cells and promotes long-term transgene expression, making it one of the most promising vectors in the field of gene therapy. We have developed a novel lung tropic AAV vector expressing the murine SFTPB gene (AAV-SPB) that when delivered to the respiratory tract of SP-B null mice significantly improves respiratory function and extends survival. Here we aim to investigate whether repeat administration of AAV-SPB will lead to longer-term expression of therapeutic levels of SPB, potentially even curing mice. In an effort to move this therapy toward human clinical trials, we have engineered an AAV vector expressing human SPB and aim to test it first in the mouse model of SP-B deficiency, followed by human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived lung cells from SP-B null patients and finally in human lung slices. If successful, this technology would have profound therapeutic implications for neonates suffering from SP-B deficiency and could impact how we treat other life-threatening monogenic lung diseases.

column36: Facilitating interpretation of cognitive impairment: The development of reliable changes scores for the cognitive measures in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: The first objective is to develop reliable change methods, which are critical for measurement of change over time on the cognitive measures collected in the CLSA. Interpretation of cognitive assessment data requires some comparison standard, such as a cut-off score for screening tests, or, for neuropsychological tests, comparison of an individual's performance with that of cognitively healthy persons of the same age. Similarly, interpretation of change in cognitive performance over time requires an appropriate comparison standard, but the study of change over time is more complicated; for example, measurement error is unavoidable and is present at each assessment point. Change is assessed by comparing baseline performance versus performance on the same cognitive tests at a follow-up assessment. Reliable change methods detail whether any change was beyond expected fluctuations in cognitive performance resulting from measurement error or other factors, such as practice effects, maturation effects, and/or regression to the mean. Reliable change methods can be compared with external criteria, such as change in self-reported diagnosis, to create minimum clinically important difference scores. Our secondary objective is to create robust norms, which leverage longitudinal assessment to refine cross-sectional normative comparisons that can be used for clinical practice. Development of appropriate comparison standards for individual participant's change in cognitive performance over time will provide a powerful basis for measuring health, aging, and cognition in the CLSA. Reliable change scores for cognitive variables will be a foundation for future work for determining incident dementia at the individual participant level in the CLSA, and will serve as a methodological model for other longitudinal aging studies.

column36: Hormonal Contraceptives and Risk of Pseudotumor Cerebri Syndrome in Women of Child Bearing Age
column37: Hormonal contraceptives (HCs) are one of the most popular classes of medications. It is estimated that approximately 750 million women around the world uses HCs. A number of studies have looked at serious adverse events with HCs including risk of blood clots, heart attacks and breast cancer. One serious adverse event that has not received as much attention is the risk of pseudotumor cerebri syndrome (PTCS) with HC use. PTCS is a serious neurological condition that leads to an increase in pressure within the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). If untreated, PTCS can lead to visual disturbances and even vision loss. A number of studies have attempted to examine the risk of PTCs in women who use HCs. However, these studies have been limited by small sample sizes and lack of control for strong confounding variables such as boy mass index. PTCs is a rare condition that affects between 4-19/ 100,000 women. However, since close to 750 million women around the world take HCs and increase in the risk off PTCS may translate to thousands of women who may experience a potentially life changing adverse event every year. Thus, we seek to study the association between PTCS and HC using a large database in the United States that captures data on approximately 9 million women of child bearing age including data on body mass index. Using this data, we will undertake a case-control study and examine the risk of different types of HCs with respect to PTCS adjusting for potential confounding variables. Results from our study can inform physician and women around the world with respect to the potential risk of PTCS with different type, duration and dose of HCs.

column36: Low INR to Minimize bleeding with mechanical valves Trial - Vanguard (LIMIT)
column37: Heart valves control blood flow through the heart. If they are damaged, patients may need heart surgery to replace the diseased valve with a mechanical valve. Mechanical heart valves require life-long blood thinners to prevent blood clots from forming. These clots can cause strokes or valve failure. The only approved blood thinner for mechanical valves is called warfarin (Coumadin). The amount of warfarin that a patient takes is adjusted to achieve a degree of blood thinness called the International Normalized Ratio (INR). If the INR is too high, there is higher risk of bleeding, while an INR that is too low increases the risk of blood clots. The recommended INR targets for patients with mechanical heart valves aim to prevent blood clots while keeping the risk of bleeding low, but these recommended targets are based on low quality evidence. Newer designs of mechanical valves are thought to be a lower risk of clot formation and may not require the INR targets to be as high as once believed. A recent summary of studies on higher versus lower INR targets suggests that lower INR targets may prevent blood clots just as well as higher INR target with less risk of bleeding. A large study comparing a lower INR target to the standard INR target in patients with a mechanical heart valve is needed to determine the optimal target. In the Low INR to Minimize bleeding with mechanical valves Trial (LIMIT trial), patients will be randomized (like the flip of a coin) to either a low INR target or to the current recommended INR target. Adult patients who have had their aortic heart valve replaced with a mechanical valve for at least 3 months will be eligible. In this early study phase, we will enroll 400 patients from 5 centres in Canada to assess if a large, international study is feasible with the current study design. The LIMIT trial has the potential to increase the safety of using blood thinners in patients with mechanical heart valves.

column37: MicroRNAs are short nucleic acid polymers that guide gene regulation activities. Using the latest in genomic edition, proteomics and molecular interaction analyzes, this grant will test the idea that the structures and interactions of the miRNA polycistronic precursors control their functions, and exert an influence over each other through coordinated and competitive functional interactions. This project will shine an entirely new light on a newly identified layer of gene control, and potentially reveal new genomic bases for diseases.

column37: A third of young Canadians now reach adulthood overweight or obese, a condition that puts them at higher risk for premature death from chronic diseases. Study participants are young adults taking part in the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development (QLSCD), under the direction of the Institut de la Statistique du Quebec (ISQ). This birth cohort comprises a representative sample of children born in Quebec 20 years ago; 1,750 young adults still actively participate in the study. Over the years, ISQ staff have met with these children and their families to collect data on multiple aspects of child development since birth. We also conducted an extensive nutrition study when the children were aged 4.5 years. We propose this project to assess dietary habits and weight status at age 22. The data collected from birth to early adulthood will enable us to analyze how dietary factors and other determinants active in early childhood are associated with the dietary habits of young adults according to weight status. Findings of this research will reinforce and add to current knowledge about early-life influences on later-life diet and excess weight; allow identifying the ages at which influences are first detectable; identify protective factors that could reduce risks over time; and assess the cumulative effects of a variety of influences prevalent from birth to early adulthood.

column36: Maskwiomin (Birch Bark-Oil): Re-discovery of an L'nu skin ointment, working collaboratively with Indigenous communities through stories and awakening of knowledge, study of the processing of the oil and identification of active ingredients, and determination of its medical indications
column37: Birch bark-oil (maskwiomin) is an almost forgotten traditional L'nu medicine for the topical treatment of skin conditions such as rashes, eczema and psoriasis. Only two Elders of Membertou First Nation, Sydney, Nova Scotia held the knowledge of which one has since passed away. Funded by a 2017/18 CIHR Catalyst grant, Young and Bierenstiel successfully worked with the indigenous community in an equal partnership and based on a 2-Eyed Seeing approach. The team worked with Elders and community members through stories and recreation to re-discover maskwiomin. Maskwiomin is made in a torrefaction process in a campfire and compounded as creme or mixed into soap bars -now made regularly by community members for individual use. There is excellent anecdotal evidence of over 70 persons that daily washing of skin with maskwiomin soap reduces skin outbreaks, eczema and psoriasis within days. Preliminary scientific chemistry and microbiology studies showed that maskwiomin is a complex organic mixture composed likely of derivatives of betulin, a secondary metabolite and main component in birch bark. Betulin is known to have antibacterial, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer and anti-viral properties. The research demonstrated for the first time that maskwiomin is a broadspectrum antibiotic against Gram+ and Gram- strains with the same efficacy as commercially available antibiotics. This also shows that the Mi'kmak people had a topical antibiotic centuries, if not longer, prior to Fleming's penicillin discovery in 1928! This proposed CIHR Project Grant expands the work on the community level (social science and indigenous knowledge) and in pharmaceutical science (processing and identification of active ingredients and medicinal studies beyond antibiotics). It also contains a medical component with a team of nursing researchers and clinician for pilot studies and preliminary human trials to study the extent and wide range of clinical indications of maskwiomin.

column36: The role of FK506 binding protein 51 in the regulation of glucocorticoid receptor signaling
column37: PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) occurs in some people after severe traumatic events such as sexual assault or military combat. Patients suffer nightmares, flashbacks, and can be very anxious, avoiding reminders of the traumatic event. In severe cases, PTSD can be completely disabling and current treatments are often ineffective. The main treatment for PTSD consists of repeatedly exposing the patient to cues related to the trauma with the hope that they will become less sensitive to these triggers. Some antidepressant medications can also be helpful, but better treatments based on the causes and disease mechanisms for PTSD are needed. We have recently discovered that two proteins involved in the stress response system can bind together and form a complex, and that this protein complex is elevated in patients with PTSD (but not in healthy controls or people exposed to trauma but who don't develop PTSD). We have also created a tiny protein molecule called a peptide that can block this interaction and separate the complex. We have used a mouse model of PTSD that involves exposing the animals to fearful stimuli, after which they develop anxious behaviours similar to human PTSD. Our peptide can block the emergence of PTSD-like behaviours in mice after exposure to fearful situations, suggesting that our peptide could actually prevent PTSD if given after a traumatic event. This grant application proposes a series of experiments to investigate the detailed mechanism underlying these preliminary results. We will investigate if other proteins are involved in this complex, how downstream signaling pathways are affected, and how stress hormones like cortisol affect the proteins in the complex. We will also take the first steps towards testing our peptide as a treatment for PTSD by determining the optimal timing and delivery of the peptide. If successful, our work may lead to the first preventative treatment for PTSD that is based on new knowledge of disease mechanisms

column36: Healing from Intimate Partner Violence: An Evaluation of an Intervention for Indigenous Mothers and Children Affected by Intimate Partner Violence
column37: Intimate partner violence (IPV) and the exposure of children to IPV are serious societal concerns. Notably, Indigenous women in Canada are four times more likely to experience IPV than non-Indigenous women. These inequities among Indigenous women and children need to be understood within a broad context of Canadian colonization and the intergenerational effects of the collective traumas experienced by previous generations of families and communities. The negative impacts of IPV for women and their children have been well documented. Women survivors of IPV are at elevated risk for a variety of physical and psychological problems which may also impact their parenting. Children exposed to IPV are 5 to 7 times more likely to experience a wide variety of emotional and behavioral problems in the short term and over their lifetime, compared to unexposed children. They are also at greater risk of continuing the cycle of violence later in adulthood than children who have not been exposed. Effective interventions are urgently needed; unfortunately, many existing programs were not designed to meet the needs of Indigenous mothers and their children. When used without the proper cultural contexts and adaptations, interventions can inadvertently exacerbate existing traumas and continue the histories of Canadian colonialism and health inequity among Indigenous populations. Our team combines the necessary expertise of Indigenous knowledge keepers and experienced researchers to address this problem. Our goal is to conduct a feasibility study of an evidence-based intervention designed specifically to meet the needs of Indigenous mothers and their children who have experienced IPV using a two-eyed seeing approach. To our knowledge, we will be the first team to do so in Canada. Our findings will significantly improve the lives of Indigenous mothers and children by providing counsellors and social workers with more effective tools specifically designed to help Indigenous families.

column36: Electrophysiology and Neurostimulation in Treatment-Resistant Youth Depression (ENTRY-D)
column37: Depression affects more than 350 million people worldwide. Prevalence of depression peaks in youth 16 to 24 years of age. However up to 50% of youth do not respond to existing treatment approaches or develop serious side effects. An ideal treatment in youth should precisely target the underlying biological impairments to have maximum therapeutic efficacy and minimized side effects. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a noninvasive neurostimulation therapy that is FDA approved for patients who fail responding to antidepressant medications. While efficacy of rTMS has been studied in several clinical trials in adult depression, these trials have not been extended to benefit youth. When applied to the prefrontal cortex, rTMS is shown to target biological mechanisms that are closely linked with youth depression. We have preliminary data that shows the safety and feasibility of a brief and novel rTMS protocol, named theta burst stimulation (TBS), in youth depression. Our goal is to extend these early studies and for the first time examine the efficacy and biological targets of TBS treatment for youth depression. We will assess the efficacy of TBS in a placebo controlled clinical trial. We will examine targets and predictors of response to TBS using novel brain mapping technologies to monitor changes in prefrontal cortex throughout the clinical trial. If our results are positive, we will have identified a novel treatment that may be a more efficacious and acceptable treatment for youth depression. Finally, identifying the biological targets of TBS in youth will lead to optimizing the dosage and efficacy of rTMS therapy for youth and moving toward more personalized treatments for youth depression. This will also be groundbreaking in predicting which patients will benefit from this treatment to minimize time wasted in ineffective trials and reduce burden on patients and the health system.

column36: Re-examining Maintenance Antipsychotic Treatment in Schizophrenia: "Extended" Antipsychotic Dosing
column37: Background and Importance Continuous antipsychotic treatment represents our current standard of care in the long-term management of schizophrenia. This is a concern because of the significant side effects associated with these drugs. Unfortunately, though, many individuals need to stay on antipsychotic treatment to prevent relapses. Goals/Research Aims Our group has evidence that "extended" antipsychotic dosing represents a possible alternative to continuous antipsychotic exposure. This strategy allows for individuals to take their medications every other day, thereby decreasing their exposure by 50% - a very sizable reduction. This strategy seems to work, but we need to study more individuals to ensure our initial findings are correct. We also need to confirm that this strategy comes with advantages in terms of decreased side effects. Methods/Approach/Expertise The proposed study constitutes a 5-year, randomized controlled trial (i.e. both patients and doctors don't know which treatment an individual is receiving so as not to bias results), comparing continuous vs. extended (i.e. alternate day dosing) antipsychotic treatment over a period of 1 year. Participants will be monitored on a regular basis using a variety of measures to assess clinical and functional outcome, as well as side effects. Expected Outcomes Based on our work to date, we predict comparable clinical efficacy between the 2 study populations. At the same time, we predict benefits in terms of certain clinical measures as well as side effects (e.g. weight gain, risk of diabetes). Further, there will be automatic cost savings in that individuals in the extended dosing receive only 50% of the antipsychotic medication administered to those in the continuous group. This work has the potential to revolutionize maintenance antipsychotic treatment through support of an alternative strategy that decreases antipsychotic exposure by 50%.

column36: Integrating Prenatal Environmental Health Education into Clinical Care in Canada: The PEHE Study
column37: There is robust evidence linking prenatal exposures to common environmental toxicants such as lead, pesticides, Bisphenol A and second-hand smoke to a variety of negative reproductive and developmental health outcomes. Prenatal healthcare providers (PHPs) have shown considerable success in educating prospective parents about the importance of reducing fetal exposures to some toxicants, namely tobacco smoke and alcohol. Problematically, PHPs rarely counsel patients about other toxicants despite evidence of risks, patient demand and the proliferation of potentially harmful advice. Given the importance of reducing exposures and the crucial role PHPs play in counselling patients, the goal of this project is to understand the factors that promote and inhibit uptake of prenatal environmental health preventive care activities across diverse prenatal care, community, occupational and environmental health contexts in Canada. To address this we will first conduct a national survey of reproductive-aged women to assess environmental health knowledge, attitudes, protective practices and educational preferences. This will be followed by a national survey of PHPs to examine their environmental health knowledge, attitudes, clinical practices, experiences and patient education opportunities and barriers. Finally, we will carry out focus groups with a) patients and b) PHPs to identify and examine the suitability of education strategies for diverse clinical, community, occupational and environmental contexts. Our multidisciplinary team is comprised of experts in reproductive health and clinical care, environmental health and health education and we are partnered with key prenatal care and environmental health organizations. This project will directly influence Canadian policy and practice and it represents a critical step toward ensuring that PHPs are equipped to effectively counsel patients, and that patients have the information they need to make informed choices during pregnancy.

column36: Development of a novel universal (cross-protective) vaccine technology for influenza viruses
column37: Influenza viruses represent a public health threat worldwide, infecting 5-20% of the population each year, causing annual epidemics leading to ~500,000 deaths every year. Besides seasonal influenza, intermittent pandemic influenza poses the real threat of increased mortality and morbidity. The emergence of highly pathogenic influenza strains with pandemic-potential H5N1 (2003) and H1N1 (2009), have infected millions with thousands of fatalities in the last decade alone. The recent, highly fatal H7N9 strain (2013-2017) represents an ominous trend. In the 2018 flu season, a number of children died due to influenza infections in Canada. Worldwide, influenza infections can be prevented by prophylactic vaccines. An effective vaccine can control the spread and limit the devastating consequences of influenza infection. However, current influenza vaccines suffer from limited efficacy, require annual updates and provide short-term protection. In addition, it takes ~6 months after detection of a new strain to produce a vaccine, and another 2-6 weeks to be effective. World Health Organization (WHO) has estimated that an outbreak of 1918-like pandemic influenza could claim the lives of >100 million people before a matching vaccine could be prepared. Therefore, there is a high unmet need to discover a universal influenza vaccine to prevent deadly infections. We have discovered a novel vaccine technology, which has huge potential to be developed as a universal influenza vaccine. In this project, we will conduct preclinical efficacy (against different subtypes of influenza virus), dose and schedule optimization and toxicity studies of the novel vaccine candidates in animal models. These studies will facilitate the clinical development of the vaccine candidate and strengthen the value of the IP. Development of a universal cross-protective vaccine providing protection against multiple influenza virus strains will have a major impact on health of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: CVT in BC: Incidence, Diagnosis, Treatment Strategies and Prognosis of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis in British Columbia, Canada
column37: Cerebral venous thrombosis describes blood clots that form in veins that drain blood from the brain. It is most common in younger adults and around pregnancy. It can cause headaches, vision loss, weakness, seizures and coma. Fifteen percent of patients are left dead or disabled and 25% cannot return to work. CVT is also a difficult condition to diagnose, and patients may visit a doctor multiple times before the CVT is found. We want to study how frequently CVT occurs in British Columbia and what types of patients (in terms of age, sex, use of hormone containing medications and past medical history) have a higher risk of dying, spending longer in the hospital or having to come back to hospital for complications with this condition. We also want to see how many times a CVT patient will visit a doctor before she/he is diagnosed. We will do this by looking at hospital records and linking them to other data sources from the government. CVT is a rare condition so it is hard to study its treatment with large trials. Most experts agree that strong blood thinners should be used but which one, and how long people should be treated, is unclear. We want to link hospital records to prescription records to see how doctors have been treating CVT in British Columbia since 2000. We will see what factors may determine the type of blood thinner the patient gets and how long they get the treatment for. It is important to see if certain types of doctors (different specialist or doctors in different geographic areas) treat the condition differently. One of the long-term serious complications of CVT is seizures. Using prescription records, we can see how many people with CVT need treatment for seizures, what types of drugs are used and for how long. This will allow us to better understand the total cost and disability of CVT. Through this project, we hope to understand how CVT has been treated by physicians when there is no high-quality Canadian data for this condition.
