column36: Age-dependent sex differences in graft and patient outcomes among solid organ transplant recipients
column37: In many areas of medicine, identification of sex differences in the outcome of a condition has sparked innovative research to understand why these differences exist, leading to new insights into the biology of the condition and how to treat it. Surprisingly, little is known about sex differences in the outcome of organ transplants. Sex differences are of particular interest in organ transplant since the sex of the donor, the sex of the recipient, and the interaction between donor and recipient sex may each play a role. Successful transplantation requires medication to suppress the immune system. There is evidence that females have a stronger immune system than males. Sex differences in the immune system are likely largest among adolescents and young adults, whose immune systems are fully developed but have not started to weaken due to age. Despite this evidence, sex is usually ignored in transplant care and research. This may put females at higher risk of graft loss due to rejection and males at higher risk of infections and cancers. Ignoring the role of sex may also limit our ability to design studies to improve transplant outcomes. We will use large, international transplant databases to compare survival of the graft between male and female kidney, heart, and liver transplant recipients of different ages. We will also compare the survival of grafts based on the sex of the donor. In addition, we will compare the overall excess risk of death and the excess risk of death with a functioning graft in male transplant recipients with those in female transplant recipients. Excess risk is how much more likely transplant recipients are to die than people of the same age and sex in the general population. This will help determine if males are over-immunosuppressed and females under-immunosuppressed. These studies will be the first to determine the roles of recipient and donor sex in graft outcomes, and will lead to fundamental work to figure out why differences exist.

column36: Whole Genome Sequencing Defines Leiomyosarcoma Evolution and Identifies Therapeutic Opportunities in the DNA Damage Pathway
column37: Leiomyosarcoma (LMS) is a common adult sarcoma that is only cured by surgery. However, the majority of patients do not survive LMS as they develop metastasis or spread of the cancer from the original site of disease. Current drug therapy to treat this cancer is largely ineffective and thus survival rates are low in many LMS patient groups (30%). Thus, researchers need to find more effective drugs. Our research team has taken the approach of performing comprehensive testing of LMS using state of the art genetics. One of the benefits of using the latest technology or whole genome sequencing is that very detailed analysis of the tumor is performed. Although this can lead to almost too much information, our team has the means to analyze the data so we can try to determine why these cancers develop. If we can better understand what is leading to cancer formation, this helps us try to identify and test new drugs. Recent studies in our program found a signature of fingerprint in LMS that is associated with cancer cells not being able to undergo proper repair of broken DNA. DNA is the material that carries all the information about how a living thing will look and function. It has been long understood that cancers can arise from DNA not getting fixed properly. We will test if a type of DNA repair called homologous recombination is abnormal in LMS, as drugs already have been developed that will selectively kill cancer cells off with this problem. We have three study goals: 1. To determine how similar mutational profiles are between the main tumor and metastatic disease. This will allow us to better understand if drugs should be developed in a similar way for both sites or if in fact they are quite different. 2. column36: Impact of Infertility and its Treatment on Women's Mental Health
column37: Mental illness, especially perinatal depression affects about 10% of women during and around pregnancy. However, while about 15% of reproductive-aged women suffer from infertility, and many turn to infertility treatment to achieve pregnancy, we do not know as much about the mental health needs of these women. In this study, we will describe the relationship between infertility, infertility treatment, and mental illness in a Canadian population. We will measure how often infertile women who received infertility treatment experienced mental illness. We will compare the development of mental illnesses among women who became pregnant with infertility treatment with women who became pregnant without infertility treatment, and also to women who attempted pregnancy with infertility treatment but were not successful. In addition to looking at newly arising mental illness, we will also measure which women had previously existing mental illnesses before they received infertility treatment. We will use information gathered from health-related databases for women in Ontario from 2006 until 2017. To determine which women were infertile, we will look in records for either an infertility-related diagnosis or use of infertility treatment. To measure mental illness, we will look in records for visits to a physician, hospital, or emergency department for mental illness, self-harm, or a record of suicide. Infertility and its treatment are both rising in Canada, and it is unclear how these trends are affecting women's mental health. Results from our study can help guide and customize fertility treatment and can also help in planning mental health support for women who have fertility problems.

column36: Development of dynamic 1H MRSI for the assessment of impaired brain glucose metabolism in patients with early Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease whose prevalence and impact on society are steadily on the rise. AD is characterized by marked cognitive decline and memory loss, as well as insidious brain pathology that accumulates long before the appearance of clinical symptoms. Thus, early detection and intervention are of great importance. One of the early hallmarks of AD progression is an impairment in the main pathway for energy production in the brain: glucose metabolism. As such, measures of brain glucose metabolism have been used for many years as a biomarker for identifying pathology associated with AD. However, mapping glucose metabolism in the brain is difficult, and the current gold-standard method - positron emission tomography with 18F fludeoxyglucose (FDG-PET) - has several drawbacks such as exposing patients to ionizing radiation. In this work, we aim to develop a new method for mapping brain glucose metabolism that involves proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) scans acquired during an infusion of carbon-13 labelled glucose. The aims of this proposed work are: 1) To develop and optimize imaging methods for rapid proton MRSI detection of glucose metabolism in the human brain; 2) to validate MRSI measures of glucose metabolism by comparison against gold-standard PET images; and 3) To apply these new techniques towards detection of impaired brain glucose metabolism in patients with AD and mild cognitive impairment. The result of this work will be a new MRI-based method for assessing impaired glucose metabolism in patients with AD. Importantly, since these measures can be obtained in a standard clinical MRI scanner, they can easily be combined with complimentary MR imaging measures such as structural, functional or diffusion imaging, to provide a multiparametric assessment of disease status. Finally, this method will avoid the need for a separate PET scan, thus minimizing radiation exposure to patients.

column36: Multi-pathway cholesterol depletion on top of FOLFIRINOX in newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma: a feasibility and proof-of-concept study
column37: According to the Canadian Cancer Statistics, out of 100 patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, only 8 will still be alive 5 years later. Most patients will die within the first year after diagnosis. Given this very poor survival, there is an urgent need for new treatments that will prolong survival and hopefully cure pancreatic cancer. Recent studies have shown that pancreatic cancer needs cholesterol to progress. Cutting cholesterol supplies could slow or even stop pancreatic cancer progression while sensitizing the tumor to chemotherapy. Given that powerful, well tolerated and affordable cholesterol-lowering drugs are now available and routinely used in patients with heart diseases, it is indicated to verify if these safe drugs can also treat patients with pancreatic cancer. The current project is to verify whether adding cholesterol-lowering drugs on top of current cancer therapies is feasible. To answer this question, a small number of patients newly diagnosed with pancreatic cancers will be given a combination of cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy. Many data will be collected, including acceptability of the treatment, observed adverse effects and more. These preliminary data are needed to proceed to future tolerability, safety and efficacy studies. Pancreatic cancer is not the only cancer that requires cholesterol to thrive. There are indications that cancers such as breast, prostate, colon, kidney, melanoma and many others rewire their metabolism in order to secure abundant cholesterol supplies. There is a possibility that besieging tumors with a sustained cholesterol blockade combined with chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy could translate into increased survival in many cancers and bring us closer to a cure.

column36: Automated analysis of natural speech in personalized treatment for major depressive disorder

column36: Colchicine for the prevention of perioperative atrial fibrillation (COP-AF)
column37: The development of atrial fibrillation (AF) during or shortly after major thoracic surgery is one of the most common serious complications in this patient population. The occurrence of AF leads to adverse changes in blood pressure, problems with the management of blood thinners required in many of these patients, prolonged hospital stays and an increased risk of death and stroke. Prior studies suggest that inflammation is the primary mechanism for AF developing during or after surgery. Colchicine is a potent drug that strongly inhibits inflammation. In patients undergoing cardiac surgery colchicine has been effective in preventing inflammatory complications and AF. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that colchicine effectively prevents the occurrence of AF in patients undergoing major thoracic surgery. In this population, colchicine may also reduce the time to chest tube extraction, an important patient-centered outcome, as it may shorten hospital stay, reduce the incidence of postoperative infections and improve patient's well-being. Colchicine administration may even reduce the occurrence of death or stroke. To test these hypotheses, we will conduct a large double-blind randomized placebo controlled trial of 2,800 patients who are at least 55 years old and undergoing thoracic surgery. The trial will be conducted in thoracic centres in Canada and internationally. Oral colchicine or matching placebo will be given twice daily for 10 days. Study personnel will follow patients throughout the trial. This large trial will determine whether colchicine lowers the risk of AF and other inflammatory complications in patients undergoing thoracic surgery. Finding a safe, effective and low-cost intervention to prevent AF in this setting addresses a major unmet clinical need as it may decrease length of hospital stay, improve the quality of perioperative care, lower costs and reduce the risk of stroke or death.

column36: Pilot study of a community pharmacy-based program to enhance adherence to adjuvant endocrine therapy among breast cancer survivors
column37: Context: Adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) is an oral medication prescribed to women with hormone-sensitive breast cancer (75% of cases) to reduce recurrence and mortality risks. To optimize AET adherence, we have designed a community pharmacy-based program, the PAcHA program (programme en Pharmacie pour l'ACcompagnement des femmes ayant de l'Hormonotherapie Adjuvante). Pharmacists working in pharmacies assigned to the PAcHA group (33 pharmacies) will receive a web-based training and manuals to use during their counselling with women having an AET. Those in pharmacies assigned to the control group (n=33) will provide usual care. Preliminary effects of the program and the experience of pharmacists and women with the program will be evaluated using questionnaires, interviews and pharmacy records. Contributions: Pilot study results will provide crucial information on the potential of this first community pharmacy-based program designed to enhance AET adherence. Results will be used to optimize the program and plan a study to assess its effects on adherence. If effective, this program has the potential to fill a gap in breast cancer support care and optimize the benefits of a drug largely prescribed.

column36: Translation of Highly Promising Basic Science Research into Clinical Applications: A Systematic Review
column37: Drugs and other treatments are often shown to be very effective in animal studies performed in laboratories. However, these promising findings rarely translate to the human population. In 2003, a landmark review of laboratory studies demonstrated only 5% of highly promising animal experiments led to successful treatments in humans. This statistic is frequently quoted however it is unclear if the rate of 'bench-to-beside' translation has changed in the fifteen years since the study was published. In the interim, many initiatives have been implemented to address underlying reasons for this failure, including poor experimental design, suboptimal laboratory models, and poor reporting. Given the vast amount of resources consumed by basic biomedical research meant to inform human health, an update of this landmark study is needed to understand if the rate of successful 'bench-to-bedside' translation has changed. Through this updated review we will also identify the trajectory of therapies that have been translated from the lab to patients. By studying these success stories we hope to be understand the characteristics of successful translation.

column36: Is mechanical bowel preparation necessary to reduce surgical site infection following colon surgery? A randomized controlled trial
column37: Background: Following colon surgery, surgical site infection (SSI) is the most common complication and leads to longer recovery time for patients as well as increased health care costs. Currently, there is high quality evidence to show that the combination of intravenous antibiotics (IVA), mechanical bowel preparation (MBP) and antibiotics (OA) is the most effective bowel preparation to reduce SSI. However, there are no studies comparing IVA+MBP+OA and IVA+OA. This is an important question because if IVA+OA works the same as IVA+MBP+OA, then MBP may be safely omitted as part of the bowel preparation to reduce SSI and patients would avoid the side effects of MBP prior to their surgery. Objectives: Therefore, the objective of this study is to perform a trial to determine if IVA+OA works the same as IVA+MBP+OA to reduce SSI following colon surgery. Methods: This study will be performed in 4 hospitals across Canada. Patients are eligible to participate in the study if they are (i) undergoing elective colon surgery, (ii) are 18 years of age or older and (3) provide informed consent. Eligible patients will be randomly assigned (i.e. flip of a coin) to one of two groups, either IVA+MBP+OA or IVA+OA. The primary outcome for the study is the number of patients that develop a SSI within 30 days after surgery. At the end of the study, the number of SSI between the two groups will be compared to determine if IVA+OA works the same as IVA+MBP+OA. Relevance: This study is important because we expect that IVA+OA will work similarly to IVA+MBP+OA and will show that MBP is not necessary to reduce SSI. This will be important to both patients and physicians as it will improve both patient experience and outcomes following colon surgery. Given the high volume of colon surgeries done annually, as well the impact SSI has on patient outcomes, our results have potential to change practice in Canada and worldwide.

column37: The airways of asthma patients are sensitive to inhaled allergens, like pollen. Long term allergen exposure increases lung inflammation and sensitization; once sensitized, exposure can trigger acute asthmatic attacks involving intense anxiety, airway narrowing, impaired breathing and, in severe cases, death. In recent rodents studies, we showed that during an allergen-induced asthmatic attack, the asthmatic lung releases chemicals into the general circulation that trigger a powerful neuronal reflex pathway causing airway narrowing. This pathway involves activation of the carotid bodies (nerve clusters in the neck) via specific receptors called TRPV1. Importantly, pharmacological disruption of this pathway with a single drug dose dramatically reduces airway narrowing and the breathing pattern associated with respiratory distress. These effects were long lived (days). Moreover, our preliminary data suggest that when carotid bodies are removed entirely, the lung inflammation and sensitivity to allergens associated with asthma is reduced. These observations lead to three important questions: 1/ How do chemicals from the lung activate the nerves associated with the carotid body; 2/ Does blocking the mechanisms involved have long-term beneficial effects on asthmatic lung health; 3/ Can blocking this reflex pathway reduce asthmatic symptoms in humans? This proposal addresses these questions with the aim of identifying novel targets to improve asthma treatment and prevent asthma-related morbidity and death. Specifically, we will determine how chemicals from the lung activate the carotid body using state-of-the-art experimental preparations and functional cellular imaging techniques, and test the consequences of blocking this signaling using surgical isolation, pharmacological and modern gene manipulation techniques. Finally, we will test whether blocking carotid body signalling using a best-in-class drug developed in Canada can reduce symptoms in human asthma sufferers.

column36: Translating to the Community (T2C): A Social Epigenetic Study of FASD
column37: Social epigenomics involves the study of how social experiences affect genes and our biology. For instance, living in disadvantaged circumstances, exposure to discrimination, residential segregation, violence, trauma (historical, contemporary, intergenerational), psychosocial stress, food insecurity, and health risk behaviours can affect a person's ability to be healthy, stay healthy, and have healthy children. Translating to the Community (T2C) is a university, Indigenous community and FASD clinic led social epigenetic biobank developed to investigate the way such social experiences affect genes and our biology leading to Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) and its associated behaviours and co-morbidities (herein called FASD). The aims of this research are to: 1) Investigate the association between social experiences and PAE and FASD; 2) Investigate the association between epigenetic changes and PAE and FASD; 3) Advance community pre-assessment of PAE and FASD and improve PAE and FASD diagnostic tools and interventions. To elucidate the social-epigenetic link, our team represented by Indigenous science, social science, clinical science and basic science developed Translating to the Community (T2C), a social epigenetic biobank that has University and Indigenous community ethical approval, and is governed with our partner Cree Nation Tribal Health Centre. The social biobank is designed to accrue data via partners/communities in Manitoba and from anywhere in the world. Its governance structure includes Indigenous families and communities, community health and social programs, and FASD clinics. The research informs the potential for social-epigenetic informed diagnostic and assessment tools, demonstrates the merit of community-assessments and shows new pathways for an early diagnosis and early clinical, health, education and cultural preventions/interventions.

column37: Acute leukemia (AL) is a cancer of the blood cells. Patients assigned to receive EASE will receive psychological support from a trained mental health clinician for 8 weeks and will be assessed for physical symptoms weekly for the initial 4 weeks. When physical symptoms are reported by patients in the intervention group, the patients will be referred to a symptom-control team for symptom management. The symptom-control team consists of a physician and a nurse and other professionals as needed. All participants will complete questionnaires at the start of the study and again at 4, 8, and 12 weeks. This study will provide essential information about the effectiveness of EASE, which will inform policy and practice in the treatment of patients with AL nationally and internationally.

column36: Behavioural and brain network adaptations associated with chronic amygdala hyperactivation
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a devastating disorder affecting over 3.2 million Canadians and current antidepressants are effective in only half of the treated patients. Anxiety is one of the most common MDD's comorbidities. Patients with anxiety disorders in early life are more likely to develop MDD and be treatment-resistant. Understanding how chronic stress and chronic anxiety can lead to depression is of utmost importance for the field. A common feature of anxiety, depression and stress-related disorders is hyperactivity of the amygdala, a key brain region involved in emotion processing. A lot is known about amygdala activity and its role in acute stress response, fear and anxiety; however the effects of sustained amygdala hyperactivity and its role in chronic stress at the behavioral or functional level are unclear. Taking advantage of growing advances in small animal brain imaging, we recently showed that chronic stress in mice increases amygdala structural connectivity at the detriment of overall brain structural synchrony. A similar shift is found in people with history of childhood trauma. In mice and humans increased amygdala connectivity correlated with depressive behaviors. Here we aim to determine: 1) if chronic stress-induced amygdala structural changes appear first and induce brain-wide changes, following a trajectory that maps onto the development of specific behavioral deficits, 2) if artificial (via transgenic tools) chronic amygdala hyperactivation causes depressive-like behavioral and structural changes, 3) if anxiolytic or antidepressant treatment can reverse the behavioral and structural deficits induced by chronic stress or hyperactivated amygdala. Considering the central role of amygdala in stress-related illnesses, this work will shed light on the direct contribution of chronic amygdala dysfunction to stress-induced behavioral and brain connectivity deficits, while determining which deficits are not targeted by current pharmacotherapy.

column36: Evaluating Impacts of Structural and Community-Led Interventions on STBBI Risk Environments for Street and Off-Street Sex Workers
column37: Three decades into the HIV epidemic, sex workers continue to face a disproportionate burden of HIV and other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs), alongside and driven by high rates of violence and other rights violations. Whereas most STBBI prevention, treatment, and care interventions continue to focus on individual and behavioural factors, evidence suggests a critical need for interventions that also address broader structural factors such as law/policy, stigma, and labour conditions. In Metro Vancouver, BC, several innovative structural and community-led interventions are currently being rolled out, including peer-based HIV/STI testing; community empowerment initiatives (eg, anti-stigma, sensitivity trainings, peer outreach); and changes in policing practices and policies in some policing jurisdictions. column36: Endothelial colony forming cell-derived exosomes and cardiac repair after myocardial infarction
column37: Myocardial infarction (MI), also commonly known as a heart attack, occurs when there is a blockage of a blood vessel supplying oxygen and nutrients to the heart muscles. Current therapy aims at re-establishing the blood flow to protect the heart muscles from further damage. This strategy is effective in the recovery from a heart attack. However, the death of a significant portion of heart cells leads to progressive and substantial loss of heart function resulting in heart failure. Our research focuses on endothelial colony forming cells (ECFCs) that are present in the human blood. These are believed to be the precursor of endothelial cells, which create inner-lining of blood vessels. We recently isolated these cells and injected them into the mice with the heart attack caused by permanent blockage of blood flow to a significant portion of the heart. While the cells reduced damage to heart muscles, the effects were identified to be mediated by nanoparticles released from ECFCs, termed as "exosomes". Exosomes are nanometer-sized vesicles, which are secreted by many cell types in the human body. These vesicles transport genetic material from the cells of their source to the receiver cells. Our current primary research question is: "Can the exosomes repair the heart after myocardial infarction?" To address this question, we first have to decode the genetic message present in the exosomes released from ECFCs. We will carry out a series of animal experiments to understand the exosome cargo, an ideal dose and route of administration, and effects on the heart attack on both sexes. Our research goal is to identify a novel therapeutic intervention for patients with heart attack, which will not only limit the heart damage but will also improve the tissue repair.

column36: Modelling the impact and cost-effectiveness of novel approaches for TB control in Nunavut
column37: Rates of Tuberculosis (TB) among the Inuit are up to 296 times higher than the Canadian, leading to significantly higher number of cases of disease and morbidity. TB is curable, but providing specialized health care in remote northern communities poses many challenges. In 2018 the Federal government and Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (National Inuit organization) pledged to eliminate TB in Inuit Nunangat by 2030. A federal investment of $27.5 million over five years to develop plans support this goal was also announced. Presently, Inuit led region specific plans are being developed by the four regions in Inuit Nunangat. The largest of the four regions is Nunavut. We are working working our partners in the government of Nunavut and Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated to model the potential epidemiological impact and cost-effectiveness of novel community wide TB screening programs. These programs have health professionals go into the communities, providing education around TB, offering TB screening and diagnostic tests to proactively diagnose TB among people who are not yet showing symptoms. By diagnosing patients before they become very sick and present to the health care system we can improve treatment outcomes and hopefully reduce further ongoing transmission in the community. These programs are very expensive and not all approaches can be employed or studied. This modelling study will allow us to answer key questions on the affordability and cost-effectiveness of scaling up and optimizing community wide screening programs that incorporate new tests and treatment approaches. It will help inform evidence-based policy development, allowing decision makers in Nunavut to assess under what conditions community wide screening programs may be scaled up, based on a value for money analysis that reflects local experience and needs.

column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the first cause of death in Canadian adults, accounting for 34% of deaths, and it is estimated that over 3 million Canadians have diabetes. These conditions often occur together and are both related to chronic inflammation. While infrequent in children and adolescents, we know that atherosclerosis - the formation of plaque in arterial blood vessels - begins in childhood. Similarly, prediabetes is increasingly common, particularly among obese youth who have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes as young adults. In recent years, growing attention has been given to the microbes that are naturally present in the digestive track. Evidence suggests a link between the types and diversity of microbes in the mouth and intestine, chronic inflammation, as well as obesity, CVD and diabetes. Our study will help us better understand how lifestyle behaviors (including physical activity, diet, sedentary behaviors and sleep), microbes from the digestive track, obesity, CVD, and diabetes are linked. It will also address critical issues related to early prevention, from childhood to adolescence to early adulthood, of CVD and diabetes. Our investigation will be conducted within a well-established study, the Quebec Adipose and Lifestyle InvesTigation in Youth (QUALITY) Cohort, allowing us to study 630 participants over 4 waves of data collection, from childhood to early adulthood.

column36: Cannabis and Impaired Driving: A Knowledge Synthesis
column37: Following the recent legalization of recreational cannabis use in Canada, there is a critical need to conduct knowledge syntheses regarding how best to reduce harms and ensure public safety. We will conduct systematic and scoping reviews of the literature concerning cannabis and impaired driving. This includes the detection and prevention of cannabis-impaired driving, identification of gaps in knowledge, and the provision of recommendations for harm reduction in Canada. Literature reviews are the first step in establishing what evidence exists, the quality of this evidence, and what gaps in knowledge require future research to address. Our reviews will include searching databases as well as governmental and organizational publications. If collected data are similar, it may be possible to perform meta-analyses to pool and compare our findings. The project will require 18 months to complete. Our proposal addresses the needs of knowledge users at Health Canada and the Canadian Task Force for Preventive Health Care for literature reviews concerning cannabis-impaired driving. The full development of this proposal included a librarian, epidemiologist, ethicist, statistician, diagnostic test accuracy and knowledge translation experts, as well as knowledge users. Based on our findings, we will make recommendations, suggest avenues for future research, and inform the debate for appropriate health policy and practice in Canada. Our findings will ultimately contribute to the larger goal of reducing harms associated with recreational cannabis legalization.

column36: Molecular control of apoptotic cell death in the C. elegans germline
column37: Reproductive tissue called the germline produces gametes that give rise to the next generation. The genomes of these gametes need to be protected to ensure fitness of progeny. Similarly, stem cells in tissues of adult organisms must be protected from internal and external stresses that threaten the stability of their genomes. For example, mutations in the DNA of these cells can inactivate genes necessary for survival, which can lead to tumours that ultimately kill the organism. Cells have acquired mechanisms that detect damage to their genomes, which determines whether to repair this damage or activate a suicide program called "apoptosis". While much has been learned about the nuts and bolts of apoptosis very little is known about how an organism controls these life or death decisions. Cells reside within neighbourhoods (tissues), and there is a great deal of communication between different tissues that determines if they live or die after encountering stresses that attack their genomes. We have taken advantage of the powerful genetic tools of a simple organism called Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode worm, to discover new genes and signalling events that communicate survival and death signals across tissue boundaries. In this grant application I propose to determine how specific proteins communicate these survival and death signals from the somatic (body) tissues to the germline (reproductive stem cells). We will focus our investigation on a gene we found to be a central component of this cascade called kri-1, which is homologous to the human CCM1/Krit1 gene that is frequently mutated in the neurovascular disease cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM). Understanding these fundamental cross-tissue signalling mechanisms will help us develop new ways to treat diseases in which these signalling cascades have been disrupted, such as cancer and CCM.

column36: Developing and validating NAFLD advanced fibrosis diagnostic prediction model in primary care
column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), commonly called fatty liver, has become the leading cause of chronic liver disease in North America. It is estimated that up to 24% of Canadian population has NAFLD. NAFLD will become the main cause of end stage liver disease, liver cancer, liver transplantation, and death related to liver disease. Individuals with diabetes, lipid disorders, or who are overweight / obese are at high risk of having NAFLD. The severity of NAFLD depends on the stage of liver scarring, known as fibrosis. To confirm that a patient has advanced fibrosis a liver biopsy, a complicated and intrusive procedure, is needed. Recently, multiple techniques to avoid liver biopsy have been developed, including an ultrasound-based approach called shear wave elastography which can accurately rule out advanced liver fibrosis. In Calgary, our team has established the first program in North America to make it easy for family doctors to assess people with NAFLD by shearwave elastography to rule out advanced fibrosis. Patients with suspected advanced fibrosis, will be referred to a liver specialist for further testing to confirm their liver fibrosis stage. In our proposed project, we aim to develop a clinical decision support tool to help primary care physicians identifying NAFLD patients with advanced liver fibrosis. This tool will be developed from our large NAFLD cohort. We will present our clinical decision support tools as a webpage risk calculator, smart phone application, and paper-based risk tabulation. This project is novel and essential to meet the urgent and growing need to accurately identify NAFLD patients with advanced liver fibrosis to provide them with accessible and timely health care.

column37: Insulin is an amazing Canadian discovery and insulin has saved the lives of millions of diabetics. Insulin is a very important hormone that is required to regulate blood glucose levels. My lab will provide a valuable resource for students who want to pursue graduate work in molecular genetics. Currently, my research on C. elegans presents one of the few genetic models for understanding how the Insulin-like hormones function in a living animal.

column36: Assessing the impact of Canadian food policies and nutritional composition of packaged foods on food price and purchases
column37: Food policies to help Canadians limit their intakes of "less healthy" nutrients, like the Sodium Reduction Strategy, will soon be joined by a set of policies, the Healthy Eating Strategy, that aim to improve overall diets of Canadians. It is possible, however, that introducing these policies may lead to higher food prices, which is especially important for consumers with lower incomes. The goal of this research is to determine how food price relates to food healthfulness, the introduction of food policies, and consumer purchases. Four studies will be conducted. Study 1 will examine the relationship between food price and healthfulness (i.e. the level of "less healthy" nutrients and overall "healthfulness"). This study will use food price and nutrient information from our database of food and beverage labels (FLIP) collected in 2017. Study 2 will compare the price of foods that have lower sodium levels and meet the Sodium Reduction Strategy targets with those that have higher sodium levels. Study 3 will evaluate the price of foods before, in-between, and after the Healthy Eating Strategy is in force. Study 2 and 3 will use FLIP collections from 2017, 2020, and 2023. Study 4 will determine how consumer food purchases differ over time for the foods found to be more expensive in Studies 3, especially by low income households. This will be done using a representative database of Canadian household food purchases. We think the relationship between food price and healthfulness will be different for each food category, but in general, healthier foods will be more expensive. Also, foods with nutrient levels that changed in response to food policies will be more expensive and purchased less often than foods that stayed the same. This research will help us better understand how food price and healthfulness are related. It will also provide information to help improve food policies to ensure that regardless of income, all Canadians can benefit.

column36: Magnetic Seizure Therapy for Schizophrenia (MAST) - Trial
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe psychiatric disorder that causes a substantial burden to patients, their families, and society as a whole. Unfortunately, an estimated 40% of patients attain only a partial response and 10% show no response with conventional antipsychotic treatment. Patients that fail to respond to conventional antipsychotic medication are said to have treatment resistant schizophrenia (TRS). Neuromodulation therapies involve the use of technologies that act directly on the nervous system to alter or modulate nerve activity by applying electrical or magnetic stimulation to the brain. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is one of the oldest neuromodulation therapies and continues to serve as a useful management option in resistant mental illnesses. For TRS, ECT is safe and effective in combination with standard antipsychotic therapy. However, ECT is a very limited treatment option due to the feared complication of memory side effects amongst patients. Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) is a newer neuromodulation treatment that induces therapeutic seizures through the use of high frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. MST may have a favorable clinical benefit in terms of the risks of cognitive side-effects and is also free of the heavy burden of stigma that accompanies ECT. Thus, MST could potentially offer a cognition-sparing and clinically useful alternative to ECT for treatment-resistant illnesses. The overall aim of this project is to compare the efficacy of MST to ECT with regards to psychotic symptoms and adverse cognitive side-effects in patients with TRS. If our results indicate that MST is as effective as ECT in reducing psychotic symptoms while sparing cognitive function; our proposed work will lead to MST as the new treatment for TRS. This is particularly important as no new treatments have been made available for TRS since the release of clozapine in the late 1960s.

column36: Which Test is Best? Advancing Evidence-Based Practice for Fall Prevention in Older Canadians
column37: It is estimated that one in three older Canadians falls each year. This can result in injury, hospitalization and even death. Falls also decrease quality of life and cause a high fear of falling. Balance and walking problems increase with age and are one of the most important risk factors for falling. International best practice guidelines for the prevention of falls recommend testing balance and physical function to identify older adults who are most likely to fall and who need preventative treatment. But there is no agreement on which test to use and we still do not know which tests best predict falls. The goal of this research is to identify the best physical test for fall risk screening in older Canadians. To achieve this goal, we will administer 5 short tests of balance and function to 520 older adults who live in the community. We will then monitor participants for 1 year to track the occurrence of falls. By looking at the physical performance scores of people who fall we will be able to compare the predictive ability of the 5 screening tests. We will also be able to determine the most suitable cut-off scores to identify those most likely to fall. This information will allow health care providers to accurately identify older adults who are most likely to fall and who need preventative treatment. Our results will be important for informing both clinical care and health policy to prevent falls in older Canadians.

column36: Novel Catheter Based Therapeutic Ultrasound Approach for the Treatment of Coronary Artery Occlusions
column37: Blockages of the coronary or femoral arteries begin as soft blood clots but over time they can harden becoming what are called chronic total occlusions (CTOs). In the heart, patients can often survive the formation of CTOs but have degraded lifestyles and reduced life expectancy due to poor cardiac performance. To fix this problem, clinicians often try to open the vessels up again using a catheter that is put in through an artery in the leg and worked up into the coronary artery until it reaches the blockage. A thin wire then goes into the CTO and is used to guide balloon catheter that re-opens the vessel. However, because of the stiffness of the CTOs this is often unsuccessful and this remains one of the most challenging problems facing cardiologists. To address this problem, we developed an approach that involves the injection of a drug (enzyme) that softens the CTO so that it is easier to slide a wire through it to re-open it. This new approach is now in clinical trials and evidence is showing that it improves the success rates for unblocking difficult CTOs. For this procedure, the drug injection occurs on one day and then the unblocking procedure is attempted the following day to allow enough time for the drug to work. In other parallel work we have investigated using a specialized form of ultrasound to help improve the drug effects. We have shown in bench-top experiments as well as in animal models of CTOs that when ultrasound is used to 'pop' small injected bubbles nearby the clot, it is damaged in a way that makes the drug work better and faster. Here we propose to build on this work to develop a new catheter based ultrasound device that can be used to enhance the performance of this emerging CTO drug therapy. It will use a new approach to generating ultrasound waves at the tip of a catheter, which will be used to vibrate bubbles and accelerate drug effects. This work will further improve CTO treatment success rates and have them done in a single day.

column36: Age-related patterns in the experience of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
column37: Although cancer can occur at any age, most newly diagnosed people are aged 60 and older. As treatments are getting better, many people are living longer after their first cancer treatment. With CIPN, people may experience pain, numbness, sensitivity, tingling, burning, or weakness in their hands, arms, feet, and legs. These symptoms may last long after the end of treatment and may cause balance problems, falls, and other serious injuries, and impact on quality of life. Older people may be especially at risk for CIPN and its negative impacts. Unfortunately, very little is known about CIPN, including the number of people who experience symptoms during and after treatment. In this research study, we will evaluate the experiences of CIPN in younger and older people undergoing certain common chemotherapy treatments for breast, ovarian, colorectal, and lung cancers, during treatment, and up to 1 year after treatment. This study will help us describe when CIPN occurs, how long it lasts, and the factors that influence CIPN and that may be changed. We will also study the impacts of CIPN on important daily activities. This research study will contribute to better symptom monitoring and care during and after cancer treatment and to the development of treatments for CIPN that are able to best help people depending on their unique needs.

column36: Neural control of locomotion : Supraspinal mechanisms
column37: Locomotion allows individuals to move within their environment and the loss of this important motor function has dire consequences on the quality of life. Research carried out in my lab focuses on the neural mechanisms responsible for initiating, maintaining, and terminating locomotion, using a basal vertebrate animal model, the lamprey. The brain structures controlling locomotion in the lamprey have a very similar organisation to that of mammals, but they are relatively simpler (much fewer cells) and more accessible for studying the cellular mechanisms underlying locomotion. One brain area known to play a crucial role in the control of locomotion is the Mesencephalic Locomotor Region (MLR). There has recently been a resurgence of interest in the MLR, because Deep Brain Stimulation of this region is now used as a clinical tool to improve walking in patients with gait disorders associated with neurodegenerative disorders. In addition, clinical trials have recently begun using MLR stimulation to improve locomotion in patients with partial spinal cord injury. Because the MLR is now a target for stimulation in humans, it becomes essential to understand how this brain region operates. Using an array of neuroscience techniques, we will define the neural mechanisms by which the MLR activates specific populations of cells that start, maintain, and stop locomotion. In addition, we will determine how the neural activity in the MLR is controlled by incoming inputs from higher brain structures. By providing a better knowledge of the cellular mechanisms involved in MLR function, our work will complement the research on genetically defined populations of neurons in mammals and the findings should collectively translate into better strategies for restoring locomotor function in patients.

column36: Testing a mixed reality video game for home-based practice of arm-hand skills for children with cerebral palsy: A pilot randomized controlled trial
column37: Rationale. Cerebral palsy (CP) is a lifelong condition that affects movement and function. Movement therapies benefit children with CP but can be unexciting, costly and hard to access. Children, parents, and clinicians want video games that motivate home practice for hand and arm therapy. Yet, few home-based video games for therapy have proven effective. Our interdisciplinary team worked with children to co-create BootleBlast. BootleBlast is a motivating, adaptable video game that tracks movement and interaction with real-life objects. Early findings show that children with CP can improve in function by playing BootleBlast at home. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is needed to establish the effectiveness of BootleBlast. Large-scale RCTs are costly. Pilot RCTs are used to increase the chances that large-scale RCTs lead to clinically meaningful results. Objective. We will answer the question: Is it feasible and acceptable to carry out a RCT to determine if 15 weeks of home practice with BootleBlast improves upper limb function, activity, and participation? Approach. A 30-week pilot RCT with 46 children with CP, aged 6-17 years who have difficulty handling objects. The intervention group will play BootleBlast at home for 15 weeks. The control group will receive usual care for the first 15 weeks and then will play BootleBlast. Feasibility will be measured by rates of recruitment and adherence. Children/caregivers will be asked about the positive and negative parts of BootleBlast. We will report how many children make clinically important gains. We will also look at factors influencing outcomes (e.g. age, dose) and engagement. Impact. Study results will inform future work to establish BootleBlast as an effective, motivating option for home-based hand/arm therapy. We will create new knowledge that will be shared widely.

column36: Interplay of AMPK and mTOR pathways at the lysosome: starvation, nutrient availability and metabolic disease.
column37: Humans, like all other animals, evolved to be able to survive periods of starvation, in part by creating stores in periods of plenty. However in these days of easy food availability, periods of starvation are near to non-existent and the trend is to store much more that is used. These constant over-feeding can lead to obesity and health problems, including diabetes, and metabolic syndrome and cancer. At the level of the cell, two major proteins are involved in the fine regulation between responses to nutrient availability and starvation. These proteins are called AMPK and mTOR and have opposite responses. When one is activated the other is inhibited and vice versa. There needs to be a fine delicate control of their activities for the proper responses to nutrients or their absences. This happens in part through the actions of other proteins called FLCN and FNIPs. In this proposal, we want to study how exactly FLCN and FNIPs regulate the switch from a state of nutrient excess to a state of starvation and vice versa by understanding their interactions with AMPK and mTOR. We propose to do this in both conditions of using cells grown in petri dishes and in a mouse model system for a metabolic disease. The major goal is to better understand what happens in normal condition to then be better able to understand detect the specific problems in cases of metabolic disease so that eventually new approaches to treatment can be found.

column36: Novel role of exercise timing to improve obesity prevention and treatment
column37: Energy balance is under the influence of energy intake and expenditure but, in addition to their independent impact on energy balance, they interact together for an indirect effect on body weight regulation. To optimize this effect, strategic exercise timing appears to be important. Preliminary findings support that the closer exercise is before a meal, the greater the reduction in energy and lipid intake will be. Those findings, seen in normal weight males need to be further explored using more exercise timing scenarios, with more populations of interest, and should study potential mechanisms involved and monitoring of complementary lifestyle behaviours important for energy balance. This project is extremely well balanced, with researchers in the field of exercise, nutrition and medicine, and will measure short-term responses in laboratory and real-life settings. Lifestyle (physical activity, nutrition, sedentariness and sleep) and mechanistic (hormones, brain response to smell and taste) outcomes following three different exercise timing scenarios and one control condition will be studied in strategic populations (individuals without and with obesity; both sexes). Outcomes of this project are essential for the development of more efficient lifestyle interventions for obesity prevention and treatment using strategic exercise timing. Professionals in the medical field and in schools will be able to use the findings to improve lifestyle interventions in youth. The fact that exercise timing requires the same amount of effort but yields better results is important for health and motivation of individuals aiming at regulating their body weight.

column36: SAFE PNB -Safe Analgesia For Elders receiving Peripheral Nerve Blocks for hip fracture
column37: Over 20,000 older Canadians break their hips yearly, a painful occurrence that usually requires surgery. Older people who have a hip fracture are also at high risk of bad health outcomes. Over 20% of older people with a hip fracture have a serious complication, many do not regain the full ability to walk after surgery, and 25% die within six months. This means that we need to develop ways to make hip fracture care safer. Because hip fractures cause a lot of pain, strong painkillers (like morphine and other opioid drugs) are often needed. But these drugs can have serious side effects, like breathing problems, memory loss and delirium. Unfortunately, if hip fracture pain isn't treated, patients can also suffer issues with their ability to walk and move, their memory function, and other serious complications. So, finding ways to effectively manage hip fracture pain without strong opioid medications could lead to less pain and lower rates of bad health outcomes. Research suggests that using nerve blocks, where local anesthetic (aka freezing) medication is injected near the pain nerves that supply the fracture, can improve pain and decrease complications. While these improvements sound promising, recent reports also tell of a person dying after a nerve block because the health system wasn't properly set up to care for the nerve block in a high-risk hip fracture patient. This means that before nerve blocks are widely used for hip fracture pain, we should do research to understand their safety profile and how the health system can best-support safely giving these nerve blocks. To help to understand the safety profile of nerve blocks, we propose a study to: (1) define how often complications arise directly related to nerve blocks, (2) to determine how the health system could be best prepared to safely provide nerve blocks, and (3) to see if using nerve blocks leads to an overall increase or decrease in complications during hip fracture hospital stays.

column36: Management of Bleeding Emergencies in Patients with Immune Thrombocytopenia
column37: Blood platelets are needed to prevent bleeding in the body. One of the main causes of low blood platelets is the disease called immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Children and adults with ITP are at high risk of bleeding and when serious bleeds occur, they need to go to the Emergency Department immediately. The problem is that there is no standard way for emergency doctors to treat these ITP bleeding emergencies, and they are often unprepared to deal with them. This can cause delays in treatment and people can end up bleeding more, or even dying. For this research project, we will develop a standard guideline for treating ITP bleeding emergencies using the best available information. We will bring together a group of ITP doctors, emergency doctors and nurses, researchers and patients who will work together to create a guideline for ITP bleeding emergencies. Right now, guidelines for rare diseases can be hard to develop because sometimes there is not enough information to help create them. We will overcome this challenge by collecting new information from experts in the field where necessary. As we design our guideline, we will build in features that will make it easy to implement in the future across most Emergency Departments in Canada. Our project will fill an important gap for emergency treatment in a particularly vulnerable group of people. This will be an important first step towards improving the health of people with low blood platelets, by making sure bleeding emergencies are handled quickly and properly, and restricting expensive treatments to those who need it most.

column36: Understanding the translational mechanisms of neuronal subtype specification in the mammalian cortex
column37: The cerebral cortex is the most complex structure within the mammalian brain and plays a key role in consciousness, perception, learning, and memory. These higher-order functions rely on hundreds of different types of nerve cells (neurons) that have distinct molecular and functional characteristics. Interestingly, distinct neuron subtypes are all made from a relatively homogeneous group of neural stem cells. However, what controls neural stem cells to specifically produce one type of neuron over another and how specific identity is ultimately determined is still largely a mystery. It is generally thought that the process is initiated by the activation of specific identity genes in the cell's nucleus, which involves making an RNA copy of the gene. Nevertheless, evidence from our recent studies has revised this simplified view by showing that a critical decision point is the "translation" of that RNA into the corresponding protein. We have recently identified a novel gene that regulates the decision of where and when translation occurs. In this proposed study, we will further explore the mechanisms that underlie the translational regulation of neuronal subtype specification. Our work will be relevant to neurological diseases, such as autism spectrum disorder, and will have other important implications for human health.

column36: Wildfire Smoke and Emergency Planning for First Nations People Living with Lung Disease in Remote and Rural British Columbia
column37: In the summers of 2017 and 2018, many First Nations communities in the north central BC were affected by wildfires. For many First Nations communities, the emergency response for all members, but especially those with chronic conditions, was reactive, not proactive, due to a reliance on external agencies for information about fire and air quality, and the lack of a coordinated response. The objective of this project is to develop and evaluate an emergency preparedness and response strategy for First Nations people living with chronic lung disease, their community, and the local health care services in the Carrier Sekani territory in north central BC. This project is a partnership between Carrier Sekani Family Services (CSFS) and UBC. Our project will address 3 aims: Aim 1: LEARN how wildfires impacted community members with chronic lung disease, community services, and CSFS as the primary health care provider by conducting an analysis of wildfire seasons. We will collect information data on the extent and impact of the fires, air quality data, and the experiences of the community members and agencies. Aim 2: PLAN for upcoming wildfire seasons by developing an emergency preparedness and response strategy. This strategy will include a "citizen's science" approach by using local deployment of air quality sensors, an evaluation of the emergency preparedness of First Nations people with chronic lung disease, and a plan for how CSFS and the community will respond to local wildfires and worsening air quality. Aim 3: ACT by deploying the strategy during the wildfire seasons and assessing the impact of the strategy on: 1) individual and community emergency preparedness; 2) communication about risks; and 3) satisfaction with the emergency response. Our project will be the first to create and evaluate a novel emergency preparedness and response strategy that is designed for people with chronic lung disease living in remote and rural First Nations communities.

column36: Inhibitory control of hippocampal inhibitory circuits: cell types, neuromodulation and function
column37: Every important event and every significant life episode is encoded in our brain through a concerted dialogue between several cortical structures, including the hippocampus. The hippocampal circuitry takes a central place in the brain cognitive map, making up the memory orchestra. It is composed of two major neuron types: excitatory principal cells and inhibitory neurons. The inhibitory neurons make local and long-range connections with principal cells but also with each other. Intriguingly, a distinct population of inhibitory cells exists in the hippocampus that innervates specifically other inhibitory neurons and, therefore, via selective control over entire hippocampal circuitry, may mediate executive cognitive functions important for learning. These disinhibitory cells are highly heterogeneous, comprising morphologically and molecularly distinct cell types. And it is still unknown how many cell types are positioned at different hippocampal crossroads and what can be their function. This project aims to shed light on the diversity of the disinhbibitory neurons, their modulation via subcortical projections and their cellular function. Given that imbalanced circuit inhibition is reported in numerous disorders, such as epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia and autism, this research may open up new therapeutic avenues towards prevention and treatment of several devastating pathologies.

column36: PrEP-RN: A Literature Review and Qualitative Exploration of HIV PrEP
column37: Giving HIV-negative persons antiretroviral medications before a potential HIV exposure to reduce their risk of becoming HIV-positive is a newer prevention strategy. It is known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). While most PrEP programs rely on persons' deciding they wish to initiate this interventions, this approach leads to a self-selection bias, in which persons who use PrEP are those who feel they are at-risk for HIV, not necessarily those who are at-risk. While it is important that anyone who wants to start PrEP should be able to, it is also important to know why persons who are at high-risk for HIV do not use this intervention. In Ottawa, we operate an active-offer nurse-led PrEP service (PrEP-RN), in which public health nurses automatically offer a PrEP referral to anyone who is identified as an HIV contact, and anyone who is diagnosed with infectious syphilis or >1 rectal bacterial sexually transmitted infection (specifically gonorrhea or chlamydia). These criteria were selected because they have published 100-person-year HIV incidence rates ranging from 5.0 to 17.3. In the first 6 months of PrEP-RN operations, we have offered over over 120 of such referrals, with an uptake rate that is less than half. We now wish to update the literature on PrEP and PrEP delivery, and engage in interviews with persons who declined PrEP-RN to better understand how and why they did so. Specifically, we will perform a state-of-the-art literature review to update what is known about PrEP. We will then engage in an exploratory qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews. We will interview approximately 30 participants. We will perform thematic analysis of the interview data. Our goals are to better understand these persons' understandings of HIV risk, transmission, and prevention, so as to inform future PrEP initiatives.

column36: Occupational health, safety and labour rights among street and indoor sex workers in the context of evolving laws and policing: Ethnographic and qualitative participatory-action research
column37: Prohibitive sex work legislation and restrictive policing strategies have consistently been shown to endanger the health and safety of sex workers both in Canada and globally. Despite this, in December 2014 the former Canadian government implemented new legislation to regulate sex work, termed the Protection of Communities and Exploited Persons Act (PCEPA). The PCEPA criminalizes the purchase of sex and anyone who commercially profits from the proceeds of sex work (e.g., receptionists, security personnel, drivers etc.). Emerging research from Canada now suggests that end-demand approaches such as the PCEPA may recreate the harms of previous punitive approaches, while introducing new restrictions that put sex workers and sex industry actors such third parties (e.g. receptionists, security personnel etc.) in precarious legal positions. The proposed 5-year participatory-action research project aims to evaluate how evolving laws and policies regulating sex work (PCEPA, municipal licensing, policing appoarches, venue-based regulations) shape occupational health (e.g. experiences of physical and sexual violence, negotiation of safer sex practices) and safety (e.g. working conditions, access to workplace protections and labour rights) in the sex industry in Metro Vancouver. This new longitudinal research project will be well positioned to inform sex work law reform efforts, strategic litigation and the development, evaluation and implementation of sex work environment interventions at the municipal-level (e.g. enforcement policies, safe workplace standards for the sex industry, licensing regimes) and community-level (e.g. sex worker tools for safer workplace standards, potential for labour organization, collectivization of workers).

column36: Transformer les modeles actuels pour favoriser la securisation culturelle des soins offerts aux patients autochtones: Co-developpement d'un nouveau modele d'intervenant avec trois communautes atikamekw
column37: Les systemes de sante sont penses et organises par les groupes majoritaires et dominants des societes. Pour cette raison, le systeme de sante ne repond pas toujours aux besoins des groupes culturellement minoritaires, tels que les populations autochtones (Premieres Nations, Inuits, Metis). Des soins mal adaptes culturellement peuvent augmenter les inegalites de sante que ces groupes experimentent. La securisation culturelle est une approche qui vise a transformer les soins pour mieux repondre aux besoins et respecter la culture des patients issus de groupes culturels minoritaires comme les Autochtones. Ce projet de recherche est mene en partenariat respectueux avec la Nation Atikamekw, repartie au sein de trois communautes (Manawan, d'Opitciwan et de Wemotaci) au Quebec. Il vise a repenser la facon de donner des soins aux patients autochtones a l'exterieur de leur communaute, en creant un nouveau type d'intervenant pour la securisation culturelle qui puisse integrer les savoirs, les valeurs et les traditions de la culture atikamekw a l'interieur de notre systeme de sante occidental. D'abord, nous co-developperons un nouveau modele d'intervenant en nous basant a la fois sur les connaissances de la litterature scientifique mais aussi sur les valeurs, les pratiques de guerison et les perspectives de la sante atikamekw. Ensuite, nous organiserons un forum avec plusieurs acteurs des trois communautes pour leur presenter ce modele et evaluer s'il est acceptable pour tous. Puis, nous co-developperons un cadre de competences et une formation pour les futurs intervenants, ainsi que des ententes de collaboration avec des organisations de sante. Enfin, nous co-developperons, avec un groupe de patients atikamekws, une echelle pour evaluer la securisation culturelle, qui puisse servir a mesurer les effets de l'intervention. Ce projet participatif reconnait le role central des populations autochtones dans le developpement de solutions pertinentes pour ameliorer leur sante.

column36: Spit for Science 2 Autism Spectrum Project: Harnessing the Power of Population-Based Samples for Gene x Environment Studies
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can have devastating effects throughout life. Genetic factors play an important role in ASD but the specific genes are still unclear. Spit for Science 2 - Autism Spectrum Project continues the work of the original Spit for Science by using alternative approaches to identify risk genes for ASD. Most studies focus on clinical diagnoses, which are complex and vary considerably from person to person. We are studying behavioural (e.g., social communication) and cognitive traits (executive functions - how you control behaviour to reach your goals) strongly linked to the disorders and that cut across disorders. Patients are considered to be at the extreme of these traits but these traits vary widely in the population (excellent to poor social communication). We also can leverage leading Canadian expertise in using Postal Codes to map environmental factors like air pollution and psychosocial disadvantage so we can examine how genetic factors might interact with environmental factors to impact risk for ASD. To understand the genetics of mental illness in youth, we will recruit a large sample of children and adolescents (30,000) from the Ontario Science Centre. These children will provide DNA via spit, Postal Codes and trait information related ASD and other related disorders, and complete cognitive task (Stop-Signal Task) that measures different aspects of executive function. We will use a range of cutting-edge gene by environment and genetic methods to identify genetic risk variants for these traits, validate them in clinical samples and understand which genetic risk are unique and shared across traits and disorders. We hope to identify novel genes involved in childhood mental illness which could potentially lead to early detection, better treatments and improved treatment-outcomes for Canadian youth.

column36: Integrating community-based recruitment with data linkage to inform and enhance scale-up of hepatitis C treatment among people who inject drugs: A pan-Canadian 'virtual' cohort study
column37: Roughly 250,000 Canadians live with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, a major cause of liver cirrhosis, cancer, and transplantation that places a significant burden on infected individuals and the health system. People who inject drugs (PWID) are the principal group at risk of this blood-borne infection. Recent advances in curative treatment present an opportunity to drastically reduce HCV transmission in the absence of a vaccine. However, even a universally effective treatment cannot cure people who remain undiagnosed and untreated, and the public health impact of new medications will rely on linking and retaining infected individuals in appropriate healthcare. For PWID, a range of conditions (discrimination, stigma, a lack of insurance or stable housing, and difficulty navigating the health system) can hinder access to necessary services, and many individuals are lost along the 'cascade of care' connecting HCV testing, treatment, and cure. This study seeks to improve our understanding of the accessibility of HCV care and treatment for diverse groups of people with a history of injecting drug use, including Indigenous people and women who inject drugs. In partnership with community-based organisations across Canada, we will recruit current or former PWID and provide on-the-spot hepatitis C testing, with counselling and clinical referral for those testing positive. Participants will complete a short questionnaire to collect information on their background, medical history, and perspectives on barriers to healthcare. We will then request permission to follow their healthcare utilisation and medical outcomes "virtually" through records routinely collected and stored in administrative databases during clinic, hospital, laboratory, and pharmacy visits for the next five years. Altogether, the study aims to identify modifiable barriers and facilitators to care and guide evidence-based public health interventions and policy in the new landscape of HCV therapy.

To look at possible sex differences and the impact of past alcohol use, these studies will be done in non-dependent as well as alcohol-dependent male and female animals. Secondly, we will examine underlying mechanisms mediating effects of pimavanserin and lorcaserin on alcohol use. This will be done by measuring changes in brain activity following exposure to alcohol with and without pimavanserin and lorcaserin. We will also assess how lorcaserin and pimavanserin alter alcohol-induced changes in dopamine release, since this neurotransmitter is the one most closely linked to reward-related behaviours. The significance of this work is that it may lead to the testing of clinically used drugs, pimavanserin and lorcaserin, for treating alcohol abuse and addiction.

column36: Prevention of preterm birth (PTB) and fetal inflammation (FI): the pharmacology and toxicology of targeting interleukin (IL)6 with HSJ633, a small peptide allosteric IL6 receptor antagonist
column37: Preterm birth (PTB) and fetal inflammation (FI) are the major perinatal causes of mortality in children <5 years and of life-long morbidity. These are caused by maternal inflammation or infection and can lead to the arrest of fetal organ development and death. A key mediator for these events is interleukin (IL)6. We have synthesized a very specific allosteric peptide antagonist to the IL6 receptor, HSJ633 (sequence: VRKFQNSPA), that is highly effective in preliminary experiments in blocking PTB and FI due to infectious stimulants. We hypothesize that HSJ633 is a safe and efficacious therapeutic for preventing PTB and FI. Our objective is to understand better the pharmacology and toxicology of HSJ633. We will use sophisticated methodology to discern how HSJ633 selectively blocks molecular and cellular mechanisms of the IL6 receptor and specifically the STAT3 intracellular signaling pathway. Next, we will test whether HSJ633 antagonizes IL6 actions in human fetal membranes to prove that it works in humans. Then, we will continue testing various doses HSJ633 in mouse models to determine its optimal dosage. To demonstrate it is pharmacologically superior, we will compare it to the established monoclonal antibody antagonist to IL6, Tocilizumab (TOC), which is FDA approved for rheumatoid arthritis. To demonstrate its safety, we will test the toxicology of HSJ633 in two generations of mice to show that fetal exposure does not impair offspring growth and reproduction. An exhaustive examination of fetal organs will be made. Last, we will test the efficacy of HSJ633 in a chronically inflamed pregnant mouse model using low dose LPS to ascertain whether it blocks FI. Together these tests will confirm that IL6 is a key target for blocking PTB and FI, that HSJ633 is effective and safe, and is a therapeutic that should undergo more rigorous testing for its clinical and commercial potential.

column36: Anticoagulation for stroke prevention in patients with recent episodes of perioperative atrial fibrillation after noncardiac surgery - The ASPIRE-AF pilot study
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) during or after surgery (i.e. perioperative AF) is very common after surgery. Approximately 3% of patients are diagnosed with perioperative AF within 30 days of a surgical procedure not including open heart surgery (i.e. noncardiac surgery. Patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery have a high risk of stroke. For patients who develop AF outside of the surgical setting, there is strong evidence that blood thinners ('anticoagulants') are beneficial in lowering the risk of stroke. This suggests that patients with perioperative AF may benefit from an anticoagulant. However, whether these medications are also effective and safe in patients with perioperative AF is currently unclear. The aim of this proposal is to assess the feasibility of a randomized clinical trial of an anticoagulant versus usual clinical care in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. We will perform a randomized clinical pilot study of an anticoagulant versus usual care in patients with perioperative AF after noncardiac surgery. Patients will be assigned by chance (randomized) to a blood thinner (oral anticoagulant) or usual care. For this pilot study, we will include 100 patients to test the feasibility of our trial. Patient have at least 1 confirmed episode of perioperative AF, be in normal sinus rhythm at the time of randomization, and have some additional risk factors for stroke. Patients will be followed at 1 month, 6 months and then every 6 months up to a maximum of 24 months. We will consider this pilot study to be successful if we can recruit 100 patients at an average recruitment rate of 1 patient per centre per month. In summary, this research proposal will inform the feasibility of a large clinical trial to determine the ability of blood thinners to prevent stroke in patients with perioperative AF.

column36: Mechanisms of Leishmania dissemination and transit in the mammalian host following vector transmission
column37: Many infectious diseases are initiated following pathogen deposition into the skin by an insect vector but subsequently cause systemic disease. These diseases include Malaria, Lyme's Disease, Zika and West Nile virus disease and Leishmaniasis. These infections represent a current and growing global health problem, accounting for 17% of the human global infectious disease burden. Increasing or altered geographical distribution of insect vectors due to climate change and increased migration, travel and urbanization of human populations is exposing larger numbers of people to vector transmitted infections. In Canada, the spread of West Nile virus disease and Lyme's disease emphasizes the need for institutions to meet the challenge of vector-transmitted infections in a changing world. A major factor contributing to the manner in which these infections cause disease is their ability to move around the body after deposition into the skin by an insect bite. Understanding how vector transmitted infections disseminate out of the skin and subsequently move around the body is understudied, and how various treatment options influence this dissemination is almost completely unknown. This new knowledge is especially relevant to prophylactic vaccination against disseminating vector transmitted pathogens, where, despite old assumptions that the skin stage of infection is transient and somehow less important than subsequent systemic stages, the early expression of immunity at the dermal site of vector inoculation may be essential for vaccine efficacy. We aim to define and understand how pathogens leave the skin and move around the body in order to develop therapies or strategies to prevent this from happening, thereby reducing the burden of disease caused by vector transmitted disseminating infections.
