column36: Facilitating access across the pregnancy continuum of care - A health system intervention to improve care transitions and health outcomes for Indigenous women in northern Manitoba
column37: Pregnancy is a time of transition for women and families. Throughout pregnancy women receive care in a variety of health settings including office medical care, ultrasound departments, hospitals for birth, and at home after discharge from hospital. Each of these transition requires a connection to various health care providers. The federal government provides health care in most First Nations communities however, in order to receive obstetrical consultations, ultrasound services, and to deliver their babies, women need to transition to the provincial health care system adding yet another layer of complexity. Many barriers including, travel, transportation issues, financial constraints, poor communication, different providers, and weak referral links are encountered through those transitions. For many, relocating for care and birth away from home is characterized by insecurity, strange surroundings, and isolation from family. Women often experience a lack of choice, control and power in these transitions. Effective transitions with improved linkages between programs and services is needed with opportunities for women to participate in shared decision making with their health care providers is a culturally safe manner. A northern pregnancy network is proposed to improve access to care, assist with navigation of complex system transitions, and improve linkages between service providers across systems. The network will be made up of system navigators linked to a core team of service providers, community members and guided by Elders. Culturally safe care and shared-decision making are foundational. It is not enough to facilitate access and navigation, services need to be inclusive and respectful of Indigenous health beliefs. These strategies are expected to increase use of care, decrease low birth weight and premature birth, increase breastfeeding, increase use of well-child care and vaccination rates, and improve patient experiences.

column36: Concomitant use of sulfonylureas with warfarin and the risk of severe hypoglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes
column37: Sulfonylureas are oral antidiabetic drugs commonly used in the management of type 2 diabetes. While they are highly efficacious in controlling blood glucose levels, sulfonylureas can increase the risk of hypoglycemia, a potentially fatal adverse event. Importantly, drug-drug interactions occurring during the concomitant use of sulfonylureas with other medications could modify this risk. Our study will provide much needed insight on the safety of the concomitant use of sulfonylureas and warfarin.

column36: Getting to the heart of hard-to-treat cancers: Anti-CD133 theranostics for molecular imaging and treatment of GBM
column37: A fundamental reason why many cancer treatments fail to provide long-term patient survival is the presence of specialized cancer cells that resist standard radiation and drug therapies. These resilient cells, often referred to as cancer stem cells or tumour initiating cells, can cause the regrowth of a tumour or result in the spread of cancer throughout the body after treatments have been completed. It is possible for antibodies to be created that target surface molecules that are unique to tumour initiating cells, and to use those antibodies to deliver radioactive compounds directly to those cells. One type of radioactive compound can mark the cells so they can be seen on imaging scanners, creating a non-invasive means of detecting highly resistant cancers. A different but complementary radioactive compound can also be used to kill the cancer stem cells with exquisite potency and selectivity. For the latter, a specific type of radiation will be used, which is highly effective at killing cancer cells but will only penetrate a distance of 1 or 2 cells, reducing damage to nearby normal tissue. There is no known resistance mechanism by cancer cells to this type of radiation, and this radiotherapy has the added benefit that it can enhance the ability of the patient's own immune system to attack tumour cells. Consequently, this antibody-targeted radiotherapy against tumour initiating cells represents a viable and new approach for treating highly-resistant tumours. Thus, a novel antibody-targeted radiotherapy will be developed and evaluated for its ability to treat glioblastoma: a form of brain cancer, where the prognosis is poor and there are no effective therapies. The proposed research involves a multidisciplinary team that will develop and validate the new therapy, and in doing so will advance both new diagnostic and treatment options for brain cancer, for early use in clinical trials.

column36: A novel approach to studying the function of the Batten disease protein CLN5
column37: Mutations in CLN5 cause neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) commonly known as Batten disease. This devastating neurological disorder is linked to mutations in 13 genetically distinct genes. NCL affects all ages and ethnicities, is the most common form of childhood neurodegeneration, and is particularly prevalent in certain regions of Canada. Unfortunately, the precise functions of many of the NCL proteins are not known. Understanding a protein's function is central to being able to devise ways to target it therapeutically. Since mutations in NCL proteins result in nearly identical clinical phenotypes, they are thought to participate in the same biological pathway. Thus, studying the function of any one NCL protein is highly likely to enhance our knowledge of the neurodegenerative process, knowledge that can then be applied to all subtypes of the disease. The proposed research will study the localization and function of the CLN5 protein in the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, which has emerged as an excellent model system for studying a variety of human neurological disorders, and is one of the only model organisms that contains the CLN5 gene. We will then perform a small molecule drug screen to identify compounds that suppress the effects of CLN5-deficiency in Dictyostelium and human cells to advance targeted therapy development for this currently untreatable disease. Finally, we will translate CLN5-deficiency phenotypes revealed in Dictyostelium to human cell models to enhance our understanding of NCL pathology. Recent genetic advances show a strong overlap of NCL with later onset forms of neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and frontotemporal dementia. Thus, this work has the potential to provide fresh new insight into the mechanisms underlying other forms of neurodegeneration, which is of paramount importance considering the aging Canadian population.

column37: Blood clots in the veins (called venous thromboembolism or VTE) are common and affect up to 70,000 Canadians per year. Wearable, mobile phone sensor and assessment, speech, face, rating scale and EMR text data will be integrated. We will use the computer programs to develop new insights and support better understanding of the course of MDD over time. column37: Progression-Free survival (PFS) time is a common outcome in cancer clinical trials. PFS indicates how long treatment keeps a cancer under control (e.g., before x-rays show worsening). New therapies are often approved on the basis of offering longer PFS, often without information about whether patients live any longer (overall survival, OS) or their quality of life (QOL). Since many treatments have side effects, their value is unclear if only PFS is prolonged. The goals are to 1) gather patient's attitudes and preferences for cancer treatments under certain combinations of treatment attributes (e.g. length of PFS and amount of side-effects) using both established trade-off methods and interview (qualitative) methods; 2) to identify which elements of the treatment attributes are most relevant to patients; 3) to use these findings to inform multi-stakeholder driven research designed to generate next-step research on a larger scale. Patients with advanced cancer will participate in a 1:1 interview in Kingston or Ottawa. The interviewer will explain a new hypothetical scenario, related outcomes, and treatment attributes. Patients will weigh preferences for treatments with different attributes (e.g., side effects and impact on PFS) and respond to open-ended questions about their preferences. The findings will inform a multi-stakeholder process for designing additional research on a larger scale that will be useful from the knowledge-user and patient perspectives. The project could impact health services in many ways, including: understanding how patients value undesirable treatment impact vs its impact on duration of PFS, and informing health-economic assessment of value of therapies that have isolated PFS benefits. Understanding the cancer outcome endpoints that are most meaningful to patients is crucial for decision-making around which new treatments are priorities to offer, and in the design of new trials aimed at improving outcomes.

column36: Suicide-Related Behaviours of Lesbians, Gay, and Bisexual individuals in Ontario: Investigating the Socio-Environmental Determinants of Risk and Care using Linked Longitudinal Population-Based Data
column37: There is growing evidence that lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) individuals suffer from significantly greater risk of suicide-related behaviours (SRB) compared to the general population. However, LGB suicidal risk and quality of care is under-researched in Canada and worldwide. Current studies typically use convenience samples and solely rely on self-reported data, which leads to limited generalizability and survival bias (i.e. only survivors can participate in surveys). As a result, we currently lack population-based estimates of the SRB disparity by sexual orientation based on clinical & mortality data. Our project will fill this evidentiary gap using a large population-based retrospective cohort study with validated clinical and mortality measures (through linked health administrative datasets), providing the strong evidence that are vitally important for prioritising the funding of programs to reduce LGB suicidal behaviours. Our project will also address the lack of research on the quality of care of LGB people who suffer from SRB, which is an important factor in preventing further suicidal behaviours. The LGB population suffers from unique mental health challenges due to discrimination and uneven distribution of LGB-specific stressors/resources, which the dominant biomedical research paradigm does not adequately address. Our proposed study addresses these gaps by generating and testing hypotheses on the socio-environmental determinants of LGB SRB risk and care. Using longitudinal clinical, mortality, and geospatial data, our project will answer the following research questions: 1) Are there differences in the prevalence of SRB by sexual orientation in the Canadian context? And if so, do socio-environmental factors influence the SRB disparity by sexual orientation? 2)Does the quality of care for those at risk of SRB differ by sexual orientation? And if so, are there geographical variations in the disparities?

column36: An intervention study of prenatal air pollution exposure and its impacts on cardiometabolic and respiratory health in children
column37: Globally over 380 million individuals under the age of 19 are overweight or obese, including 41 million children under age five. Among other effects, excess weight in childhood is linked with reduced lung function and chronic disease in adulthood. Most previous research on children has focused on diet and physical activity, but given the rising prevalence and potential for lifelong impacts it is important to identify other risk factors. Moreover, most interventions have targeted school-aged children, but the risk of overweight/obesity may be "programmed" early in life so there is a need for prevention at earlier stages of development. There is evidence that air pollution exposure during pregnancy may cause the fetus to undergo changes that affect health later in life. Air pollution is the most widespread environmental risk factor - nearly 90% of the world's population breathes air that is considered unhealthy - so developmental effects from prenatal exposure could have major public health implications for generations to come. Unfortunately, the few studies conducted to date have had important limitations and have not evaluated the potential for exposure interventions during pregnancy to reduce the risks of overweight/obesity or impaired lung function in childhood. Portable indoor air cleaners represent a promising intervention because they are relatively inexpensive and reduce concentrations indoors, where individuals spend the majority of time. In our ongoing CIHR-funded birth cohort study in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia - one of the world's most polluted cities - we randomly allocated pregnant participants to an intervention or control group, with participants in the intervention group operating air cleaners in their homes during pregnancy. We propose to extend follow-up of children in this cohort to assess the impacts of prenatal air pollution on growth and development and to evaluate the potential for a simple intervention to reduce those impacts.

column36: Treating advanced retinal degeneration - rebuilding multiple co-dependent retinal layers with stem cells
column37: Despite dozens of clinical trials, and countless animal trials, to regenerate the retina with stem cell transplants, none have solved the challenge successfully. This is because the retina has many layers, and all layers are necessary in order to permanently restore vision in patients with advanced retinal degeneration - ~1 million patients in Canada and >50 million worldwide. This results in a staggering amount of suffering and considerable global economic burden of 1/3rd of a trillion dollars (USD) annually for age-related macular degeneration alone. The millions of patients that suffer from advanced, diabetes-related or inherited, retinal degeneration add to these costs. Current stem-cell suspension transplants can only replace a single retinal layer. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplants can delay further degeneration, but they cannot replace dead photoreceptors. Photoreceptor transplants can restore vision, but only briefly since the diseased RPE cannot maintain the new photoreceptor graft. Current scaffold- or sheet-based transplants can be multi-layered. However, they provide limited retinal coverage, result in higher levels of surgical trauma than suspension injection, can form inappropriate graft structure, and can cause additional cell death - in many cases, scaffolds harm the layer they were designed to regenerate. Given this, there is considerable need for simple and safe replacement of multiple retinal layers. Here, we propose to develop a new technology that organizes subretinal graft (including RPE and photoreceptors) into correct orientation and layering with wide coverage. In the future, this therapeutic will be administered using standard surgical techniques and infrastructure and will offer tangible hope for those suffering from vision loss due to retinal degeneration.

column37: Within the healthcare community, there have been growing concerns about the time it takes for research to be applied to practice. Recent initiatives, such as the Strategy for Patient-Oriented Research (SPOR), have stressed the need for researchers to work with patients and other stakeholders to develop research that reflects patient values and improves health. While there has been a sharp increase in research that explores how patients are engaged in research, little is known about the organizational factors that support patient engagement. Our research attempts to address this gap by: 1) examining the organizational factors that support patient engagement in six Canadian and two British health research networks; and 2) developing markers (or indicators) of engagement-capacity for patient engagement in health research networks. To learn more about the organizational supports for patient engagement, we will undertake: 1) A systematic review of the literature to examine current knowledge; 2) Case studies with networks to understand how organizational factors influence patient engagement; and 3) Structured meetings with network members and patients to develop indicators of engagement. The findings of this work can help health research networks to assess and improve the conditions needed for patient engagement. Our team brings together experienced researchers, stakeholders, and patient partners and our findings will be of interest to researchers, networks, research funders and patient groups.

column36: Role of extrasynaptic GABA in the recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury.
column37: This proposal explores a fundamentally new mechanism for regulating nerve conduction in the spinal cord, with far reaching implications to understanding normal sensorimotor control and opening new therapeutic opportunities for restoring locomotion after spinal cord injury (SCI). While the primary inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord is GABA, we have discovered that GABA seems to have a paradoxical excitatory action on conduction in sensory axons, which likely generalizes to other types of axons. That is, our recent finding that extrasynaptic GABA receptors are adjacent to the sodium channels in sensory axons has led us to the idea that sodium spike transmission in sensory axons is facilitated by these GABA receptors, by virtue of their long-lasting depolarizing excitatory actions (termed PAD). To test this idea we will record from inside fine branches of sensory axons in the spinal cord of mice while activating the neuronal circuits that provide GABA to the axons, using genetically modified mice that allow light activation and visualization of specific GABA neurons, and also traditional nerve stimulation protocols known to evoke PAD. We will also make recordings from motoneurons in mice and single motor units in humans to further confirm that activating these GABA neurons (and PAD, indirectly with nerve stimulation in humans) increases sensory transmission to motoneurons, and also to demonstrate the relevance of the animal studies to humans. Finally, we will repeat these studies in mice and humans with SCI, and explore whether excess extrasynaptic GABA contributes to motor disorders. Our preliminary results suggest that drugs that selectively block extrasynaptic GABA receptors inhibit spasms and markedly improve walking after SCI. These drugs lack the negative sedative side effects of other drugs used in SCI, and are already being tested by other laboratories in human stroke patients, and thus now hold considerable promise for treating SCI.

column37: The cornea is the transparent protective layer in front of the colored (blue or brown) iris. Our work focusses on a disease of the cornea called Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD). column36: Examining the impact of a self-compassion intervention on physical activity behaviour among people with prediabetes: A pilot and feasibility study
column37: Six million Canadians are at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D). Without lifestyle changes, one-third of these Canadians will develop T2D within 3-5 years. Although engaging in regular physical activity (PA) is one of the most effective ways to reduce T2D risk, increasing PA is challenging and requires ongoing self-management (e.g., planning, goal-setting). Further, people at risk for T2D often experience negative emotions (e.g., guilt, distress) that can make it even more challenging for them to engage in PA because these emotions interfere with self-management. People who are self-compassionate, that is, kind to themselves in difficult times, are good at self-managing; they prioritize their health, respond to challenges with less distress, and engage in helpful processes such as planning and goal-setting. Therefore, self-compassion (SC) would be an asset for people at risk for T2D who face the challenge of increasing their PA in the midst of a health threat. No research has examined whether teaching people at risk for T2D to use SC helps them self-manage and increase their PA. We plan to examine this in our study. People at risk for T2D will learn about their T2D risk and strategies to increase their PA, which represents the recommended information that people at risk for T2D should receive. In addition to this, some participants, but not all, will be taught to be self-compassionate in relation to their T2D risk and their efforts to increase their PA. We expect that people who receive the additional training about how to be self-compassionate will engage in more PA than people who do not and they will do so because of SC's positive effect on aspects of self-management - adaptive reactions and a tendency to use strong self-management skills. This study is important for health promotion because it allows us to determine if we can improve how we currently help people prevent T2D through engaging in PA.

column36: Drivers of oligodendrocyte precursor cell dysfunction in the origin and maintenance of oligodendroglioma
column37: Oligodendrocytes are cells in the brain that make myelin to help nerve cells send signals to each another. Oligodendrogliomas are malignant brain tumours composed of cells resembling early immature oligodendrocytes. Recently, the gene CIC has been found to be mutated in most oligodendrogliomas, and this change is suspected to be important in how oligodendrogliomas arise and how they behave. But what CIC does, and why oligodendrogliomas may arise when this gene is altered remain unknown. Recently, using a mouse model in which we genetically deleted CIC, we showed that CIC loss increases the proliferation of the very earliest and most primitive of cells in the brain, the neural stem cells. Loss of CIC also biases the stem cells to start to become early oligodendrocytes. Interestingly, however, these increased early oligodendrocytes appear to be trapped in a proliferative immature state and do not progress to form non-dividing myelin-generating cells. These as-yet-undescribed functions for CIC are important to understand, as cancer is not only a problem of overproduction of stem-like cells but also a problem of their survival and failed maturation. We hypothesize that CIC functions as a key tumour suppressor in oligodendrogliomas through its regulation of neural stem cell and oligodendrocyte precursor proliferation, and its requirement for progression to mature oligodendrocytes - thus leading to an excess of cells that form a tumour when CIC is lost. Our project aims to: 1) Gain a comprehensive view of OPC differentiation and population dynamics regulated by CIC 2) Determine the contribution of CIC-ETV5 to cell cycle control in OPCs and ODG 3) Identify molecular mechanisms by which the CIC-ETV5 axis maintains malignancy in ODG Our work will shed light on the biology of a poorly understood brain tumour, has the potential to reveal new functions of for this recently identified gene, and may point to new therapeutic strategies for brain tumours.

column36: Dissecting the role of hemodynamics in ascending aorta aneurysm development
column37: About 2% of the population is born with a biscupid aortic valve, which has only two cusps rather than the normal three. The aortas of these patients commonly balloon due to breakdown of the blood vessel wall. This can cause the aorta to split, which is usually fatal. Why patients with biscupid valves are particularly prone to aortic ballooning is unknown. It may be due to their underlying genetics or it may be due to disrupted blood flow patterns through their bicuspid valve, which cause the blood to drag on the wall of the aorta in ways it shouldn't. Most likely, both factors are at play, but it is important to dissect the contributions of each so that medical and surgical plans can take them into account. We discovered in a mouse model that a protein called C-type natriuretic peptide or CNP protects against aortic ballooning. Some mice without the protective effects of CNP had bicuspid aortic valves and worse aortic ballooning than mice with tricuspid valves, just as in humans. The advantage of our mice is that they all have the same genetics and therefore the differences in ballooning are due only to the "bad" blood flow that occurs with a bicuspid valve. Using this mouse and a new imaging method we developed, we will determine which proteins and molecular pathways are disrupted by abnormal blood flow to lead to ballooning. Based on our mouse model, we will also specifically test the role of CNP in protecting against aortic ballooning. First we will test in the lab whether patterns of blood flow that are associated with aortic ballooning reduce the amount of CNP in the aorta, leading to ballooning. Second, we will examine normal and ballooned aortas removed from patients at surgery to determine whether there is less CNP in ballooned aortas and in women, which is something we have seen in heart valves. Together, these studies may lead to new targets for the treatment and diagnosis of aortic ballooning in patients with bicuspid valves.

Patients on BP medications will be also randomly assigned to a 'hypotension avoidance strategy', or to a strategy aiming more at avoiding relatively higher BP ('hypertension avoidance strategy', which is often the current practice). Upon consent, patients will be assessed for the occurrence of POD while in hospital, and followed up to evaluate their cognitive performance at 1 year. column36: Characterizing Canada's Refugee Healthcare Delivery System
column37: The world is facing the highest numbers of forcibly displaced people and refugees ever seen. The United Nations High Commission for Refugees says that about 69 million people have been forced to flee from their homes because of war, famine, persecution, natural disasters and other crises. Canada has been a global leader in accepting refugees and asylum seekers for over 60 years, especially in the face of humanitarian crises. In keeping with this tradition Canada accepted almost 41,000 refugees fleeing the Syrian civil war from November 2015 to January 2017 in a program called the Syrian Refugee Initiative. Also, 116,990 people claimed asylum in Canada from 2016 to 2018. Combined, this increase in refugees and asylum seekers can put stress on Canada's refugee healthcare and public health systems. Once in Canada, refugees often have complicated medical issues and social needs that are often caused by previous lack of access to food, housing, medical care, or because of traumatic experiences during their migration to Canada. For the Syrian Refugee Initiative, many cities and towns across Canada accepted refugees, many of which use different care models. Despite Canada's experience caring for refugees, the best way to deliver healthcare to newly arrived refugees is not clear, nor is where and what different care models exist. We aim to complete a study to better understand and describe how different cities and regions in Canada care for new refugees and asylum seekers. To do this, we will survey refugee healthcare, public health, and resettlement workers in cities that received 10 or more refugees during the Syrian Refugee Initiative and catalogue the different models of care. Our findings will be grouped together online into an interactive map to create an "atlas" of the Canadian refugee health system. This study will give us information that can be used to improve healthcare for refugees and asylum seekers and better prepare Canada for future humanitarian crises.

column36: A unique model to assess the oral transfer of dietary microRNAs
column37: MicroRNAs modulate ~60% of our genes and are important to our health, as deregulation of microRNA levels has been associated with a panoply of major human diseases, including cancer. Intriguingly, all the plant and animal species composing our diet contain "dietary" microRNAs that we ingest on a daily basis. A long-standing belief is that microRNAs contained in foods do not resist the chemical and biochemical conditions of digestion, and are readily degraded. This dogma, however, was shaken by a provocative study suggesting that a plant microRNA could be absorbed orally and detected in the circulation and organs of mice. Subsequent studies and analyses failed to appease this controversy, due mainly to intrinsic limitations related to the conservation of microRNA sequences between species. Seven years later, whether microRNAs can be transferred orally remains highly debated and controversial. To address most of these limitations, we established a partnership with a major biotechnology firm to set up a unique experimental approach based on the use of milk produced by transgenic (TG) cows. This milk contains endogenously expressed, TG microRNA sequences inexistent in the species under study. Its comparison to the milk of wild-type (WT) cows of the same lineage will allow us to fully assess cow's milk microRNA bioavailability with little to no bias. Preliminary analyses of TG cow's milk revealed the abundance of TG microRNAs and their association with extracellular vesicles formed of a lipid bilayer, coated with proteins and containing the microRNA effector protein Argonaute 2. This unique packaging, offering "triple" protection, may explain that 7-14% of TG microRNAs resisted simulated human digestion and could reach the colon of mice fed by gavage. Our proposal is expected to settle the controversy surrounding the oral transfer of dietary microRNAs and establish the basis for the formulation of a safe and reliable vehicle for the delivery of therapeutic RNAs.

column36: Perioperative Targeting of Myeloid Derived Suppressor Cells to Alleviate Postoperative Immunosuppression and Metastases
column37: With few exceptions, surgery remains the most effective treatment for patients with solid tumors. However, the trauma of undergoing surgery invariably leads to a weakened immune system which contributes to the likelihood of the tumour reappearing and spreading throughout the patient's body. Natural killer (NK) cells, as their name suggests, are proficient at surveying the body and destroying any cancer cells that appear before they can develop into solid tumours. Although the importance of NK cells in controlling tumour growth is well recognized, my research has shown that surgery dramatically impairs their ability to recognize and respond to tumour cells. Unfortunately, there is no current strategy for addressing the suppression in NK cell activity which occurs following surgery and new approaches targeting this critical stage may hold the potential for improving patient outcomes. We have recently shown that following surgery a large number highly immune suppressive cells are released from the bone marrow and that strategies that prevent their interaction with NK cells can have beneficial effects in animal models. Therefore, we believe that targeting these myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in patients may provide an effective approach for reversing the immune suppressive effects of surgery. To accomplish this goal we have attempted to identify ways of targeting the MDSC population that arises following surgery. These efforts have revealed a distinct identifier present only on MDSCs which we propose can be used to deliver a drug to inhibit their suppressive activity ultimately restoring normal NK cell activity. The current proposal seeks to answer whether this strategy would be safe and effective prior to use in cancer surgery patients. Considering that over 65,000 Canadians undergo tumour removal surgery each year, we believe this research has the potential to benefit a significant number of Canadians and cancer patients throughout the world.

column36: Functional dissection of the role of the Anaphase Promoting Complex in cellular longevity
column37: Humans are living longer than ever before, but it is often with age-related illnesses. Almost 100 years of research indicates that aging and age-related disease can be delayed, for example, through caloric restriction. While a great deal has been learned about why and how we age at the cellular and whole-body level, much remains unknown. Over time aging impairs the cell's ability to respond to environmental stimuli, and it is this impairment that likely leads to cell death, and eventual organ malfunction. Because the aging process is similar in yeast and humans at the cellular level, we use the brewing yeast as a model to discover molecular networks that can be tweaked in order to increase a cell's response to its environment, resulting in enhanced cell health and longevity. We have discovered a protein complex in yeast that links extracellular stimuli with intracellular signaling. When this complex is inactive the cell does not respond appropriately to external stimuli and shows signs of aging, but when it is active, the cell responds appropriately and cell health and lifespan are improved. We will use small peptides that we have identified that activate this complex to glean insight into molecular mechanisms that increase lifespan. We will also test if aging can be reversed in a novel yeast model of a human premature aging disease called Progeria. Progeria causes children to age normally, but at an 8-fold accelerated rate. We will also use the Progeria model to discover novel conserved pathways that reverse the effects of aging. Our team, composed of researchers with broad expertise in aging at the molecular, cellular and organismal levels, will identify ways to improve health during aging, such that the quality of life humans live will benefit.

column36: TRICS IV - Restrictive versus Liberal Transfusion in Younger Patients Undergoing Cardiac Surgery
column37: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, both red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and anemia are associated with an increased risk for morbidity and mortality; and the point at which the risks associated with anemia and transfusion are balanced remains undefined. We recently published the results of our TRICS III trial in the New England Journal of Medicine, where we demonstrated non-inferiority of a restrictive RBC transfusion strategy compared to a liberal strategy with respect to a composite outcome of death, heart attack, stroke, or new-onset renal failure with dialysis in adults undergoing cardiac surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass. The interaction was robust in a series of sensitivity analyses, with the age at which the differences become manifest around 65. However, in the absence of other randomized controlled trial evidence, it remains unknown which transfusion strategy is preferable in these patients. To address this, we will conduct the TRICS IV study, which is a multi-center open-label randomized controlled trial of a restrictive versus liberal transfusion strategy in high risk patients under 65 years of age having cardiac surgery, using a superiority trial design. The study will incorporate an innovative pragmatic and adaptive design. The results from TRICS IV will provide definitive evidence to determine whether a liberal strategy is better than a restrictive one in younger patients. Irrespective of the results, such information is likely to be of high impact for transfusion practice in cardiac surgery around the world, with significant potential implications for all patients undergoing surgical procedures.

We believe the proposed research holds great promise to provide practical tools to aid public health decision-making to support rabies elimination.

column37: All cells contain two main compartments, the inner nucleus, which contains all of our genetic material, and the cytoplasm where much of this material is converted into proteins. This work is being conducted in the fruit fly, as it has proven to be the ideal model organism for the study of these highly conserved genes and processes.

column36: Can-SHARE Connect (2019-2020): Supporting the Regulatory and Ethics Work Stream of the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health
column37: The Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) is an international consortium that frames policy and establishes standards for the international exchange of genomic and health related data. Data sharing between institutions, sectors and countries is essential for accelerating research, ensuring databases are ethnically diverse, and improving health care. To guide effective and responsible data sharing, the GA4GH formed a foundational Regulatory and Ethics Work Stream (REWS). "CanSHARE Connect" will support continued Canadian leadership and coordination of the REWS. A central responsibility of the REWS is to develop a forward-looking policy "tool-kit" addressing ethical and legal issues. This tool-kit addresses consent, privacy & security, accountability, and coordinated ethics review of international collaborative research. The tool-kit must continue to expand and evolve in order to address the changing needs of open science as well as shifting legal and ethical requirements. The goal is to promote harmonization of policies and protections across countries and settings, to improve certainty and foster the trust that data sharing protects the rights and interests of participants, researchers, and society. The REWS also supports the implementation of the tool-kit by 15 real world genomic data sharing "Driver Projects". In addition to developing and supporting the implementation of policy, the REWS also collaborates with the Technical Work Streams of the GA4GH who develop essential search, cloud computing, networking, authentication and encryption standards for genomics. The REWS helps to assess if these technical standards have any unintended ethical and legal impacts, and if so, how they can be addressed. International collaboration to develop and harmonize legal and ethical policies offers valuable opportunities to pool resources and accelerate research, but requires extensive communication. REWS coordination makes an important contribution to the connective tissue of the GA4GH. The REWS alone connects 200 ethical and legal professionals and researchers around the world to collaboratively identify and address emerging issues. The REWS also maintains extensive coordination between these regulatory experts and an international community of technologists, scientists, medical professionals, and patient advocates who are collectively defining the future of the "internet of genomics".

column37: Les hommes gais, bisexuels et autres hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec des hommes (GBHRSH) demeurent la population la plus touchee par le VIH. Offrir plus de possibilites de depistage permettrait de diminuer les barrieres dans l'acces aux services. Les intervenants communautaires qui administrent la trousse de depistage rapide (TDR) du VIH representent une initiative prometteuse pour y contribuer. Ce projet de recherche communautaire d'une duree de 3 ans vise a evaluer la mise en oeuvre d'une intervention de depistage rapide du VIH offerte par des pairs intervenants communautaires aupres des GBHRSH a Montreal. L'intervention de depistage prevoit : l'utilisation de la TDR du VIH administre par un pair intervenant communautaire forme, offert en depistage de proximite et en site fixe, accompagne d'un counseling pre et post-test incluant le referencement vers d'autres services de sante. Afin de mettre en place le service, des entretiens avec des informateurs-cles seront necessaires afin d'elaborer une intervention qui respectera les meilleures pratiques en depistage du VIH. Plusieurs collectes de donnees seront deployees : des questionnaires pour les usagers serviront a les decrire et evaluer leur satisfaction, des journaux de bord, un questionnaire et des entretiens individuels pour les intervenants permettront d'evaluer comment l'intervention s'est deroulee et les facteurs qui ont influence son implantation et de mesurer comment la participation au projet permettra le renforcement des capacites des communautes. column36: Mapping the journey: Developing culturally appropriate, geographically-responsive HIV care for northern Manitoba First Nations People.
column37: There is a critical need to understand the journey that northern Manitoba First Nations people living with HIV are navigating. The rates of HIV infection and disease are increasing in the Indigenous population in Canada and Manitoba. In discussions and meetings with First Nations in northern Manitoba we recognized that we know and understand very little about the experiences of First Nation people who are living with HIV and are navigating the HIV care cascade. Engaging individuals living with HIV into early antiretroviral treatment will delay progression to AIDS and importantly reduces the risk of HIV transmission in heterosexual and homosexual couples. First Nations in northern Manitoba experience barriers to HIV testing, treating and care which include stigma, access to services, geographic isolation and barriers derived from historical racism and trauma, colonialism, poverty and personal and community circumstances. There is limited understanding of culturally appropriate best practices for HIV testing and care for northern Manitoban First Nations people and a perceived lack of integration of First Nation cultural ways of knowing and healing practices with western medicine practices. We propose to build on existing relationships between northern First Nations knowledge keepers (people and organizations), academia, Provincial and Federal health organizations and the Manitoba HIV Collective Impact Network to establish ethical spaces and use a two-eyed seeing approach to investigate the complexities of how First Nations and northern residents come to be tested, linked to care, and supported to live with HIV. We will work collectively to develop culturally appropriate interventions, tools, programs and polices that can be used by communities, northern First Nation health organizations, and provincial and federal HIV related programs to better support northern First Nations people living with HIV.

column36: Matching and regression to the mean in difference-in-differences analysis.
column37: Difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis is one of the most popular approaches for measuring the impact of health policies and programs. This method involves comparing the change in a treatment group exposed to a policy to a control group not exposed to the policy, before and after the policy change. DiD assumes certain similarities between the treatment and control groups before the policy change. Researchers often try to further improve the comparability of the two groups by matching individuals from each group with similar observable characteristics and then evaluating the effects of the policy. We performed a simulation experiment to demonstrate that matching in DiD can lead to incorrect estimates of policy impacts. We generated many datasets for a hypothetical outcome for treatment and control units under different assumptions about how similar or different the units were prior to a hypothetical policy intervention. We then used DiD to estimate the impact of the intervention with and without matching the treatment and control units. We found that under a specific set of circumstances, which are likely common in health services and policy analysis, matching led to incorrect estimates of the policy effect. Based on our findings, we provide guidance on how and when to appropriately incorporate matching into the DiD study design. This study will directly inform the use and application of an increasingly common method to measure the impact of health policies and programs.

column36: Death and readmissions after hospital discharge during the December holiday period: cohort study
column37: Background: Reduced healthcare staffing around major holidays may affect patient outcomes after hospital discharge. The objective of this study was to determine whether patients discharged from hospital during the December holiday period have fewer outpatient follow-ups and higher rates of death or readmission than patients discharged at other times. Methods: We examined the outcomes of patients discharged home after an urgent hospitalisation in Ontario, Canada, between 1 April 2002 and 31 January 2016. We compared children and adults discharged during the two week December holiday period to those discharged during two control periods in late November and January. Results: Patients discharged during the holiday period and those discharged during control periods had similar baseline characteristics and previous healthcare utilisation. Patients who were discharged during the holiday period were less likely to have follow-up with a physician within 7 and 14 days after discharge, and were at higher risk of 30 day death or readmission. Per 100,000 patients, there were 2,999 fewer follow-up appointments with 14 days, 26 excess deaths, 188 excess hospital admissions and 483 excess emergency department visits attributable to hospital discharge during the holiday period. Conclusions: Patients discharged from hospital during the December holiday period are less likely to have prompt outpatient follow-up and are at higher risk of death or readmission within 30 days.

column36: Comparative risk of harm associated with trazodone or atypical antipsychotic use in older adults with dementia: a retrospective cohort study
column37: Background: Trazodone is increasingly prescribed for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia, but little is known about its risk of harm. Our objective was to describe the comparative risk of falls and fractures among older adults with dementia dispensed trazodone or atypical antipsychotics. Methods: We obtained data on long-term care dwelling adults with dementia (excluding patients with chronic psychotic illnesses) aged 66 years and older from routinely-collected, linked health administrative databases in Ontario, Canada. We compared new users of trazodone with new users of atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine) between December 1, 2009 and December 31, 2015. The primary outcome was a composite of fall or major osteoporotic fracture within 90 days of first prescription. Secondary outcomes were falls, major osteoporotic fractures, hip fractures, and all-cause mortality. Results: We included 6,588 older adults dispensed trazodone and 2,875 dispensed an atypical antipsychotic, of whom 95.2% received a low dose of these medications. Compared to atypical antipsychotics, trazodone was associated with similar rates of falls or major osteoporotic fractures (weighted hazard ratio (HR) 0.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.07), major osteoporotic fracture (weighted HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.47), falls (weighted HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.11), or hip fractures (weighted HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.43). Trazodone was associated with a lower rate of mortality (weighted HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.85). Conclusion: Trazodone is not a uniformly safer alternative to atypical antipsychotics given their similar risk of falls and fractures among older adults with dementia.

column36: Developing biomaterials-based portable stem cell niches to enhance stem cell survival and engraftment for regenerative medicine therapies
column37: Heart and blood diseases are leading causes of disability and death in Canada. Damage to blood vessels can reduce the function of vital organs leading to heart and lung failure. Stem cell therapies hold great promise for the repair and regeneration of these organs. Over the last two decades there has been substantial interest in the use of cell therapies for these serious diseases. However, a major limitation for most cell therapies is that the transplanted cells do not stay in the target organ where they are delivered. Transplanted cells are either lost or end up in other areas such as the spleen of bone marrow. This greatly limits the ability of stem cells to repair the damage and improve function. Since the stem cells do not stay where they are needed, any therapeutic benefit they may have is dependent on their ability to secrete proteins or other factors that can promote repair indirectly, rather than directly contributing to blood vessel repair by embedding into the damaged tissue. Micro-encapsulation, or "cocooning", of therapeutic cells within a supportive biomaterial provides a protective environment, similar to a natural stem cell niche, in which the cells can thrive. These cocoons will also increase the retention of the cells within a target organ, such as the lung, by enhancing cell survival and promoting their emergence from the cocoons, so that they can better repair and regenerate the damaged tissue. Thus, cell cocooning could be a major advance by potentially overcoming some of the greatest challenges in this field, namely poor transplanted cell survival and retention. By developing better methods and materials for the production of cocooned cells, this project will create new technologies that could greatly improve our ability to maximize the potential benefit of stem cell therapies and ultimately turn them into truly effective treatments for patients with life-threatening lung and heart diseases.

column36: Examining the effects of low back pain and mental health symptoms on health care utilization and costs
column37: Background: Low back pain is the leading cause of years lived with disability globally, and associated with high health care use and costs. High health care use and costs are likely driven by high risk subgroups with low back pain, but these priority groups have not yet been defined. Previous research strongly links mental health symptoms with poor recovery in people with low back pain. However, the joint effects of low back pain and mental health symptoms on health care utilization are unknown. Objectives: 1) To synthesize the literature on the association between mental health symptoms and health care utilization and costs in individuals with low back pain; 2) To determine whether adults with low back pain have greater health care utilization and costs compared to those without low back pain; and 3) To examine the joint effects of low back pain and mental health symptoms on health care utilization rates and costs. Methods: A systematic review will be conducted using database searches, and paired reviewers for relevance and quality appraisal. We will conduct a population-based cohort study using data at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, including linked population-based surveys (Canadian Community Health Survey) with health administrative data. We will conduct Poisson and log-linear regression models to quantify the association between low back pain and health care use and costs, respectively, controlling for confounders. We will calculate measures of effect modification (with mental health symptoms) on additive and multiplicative scales. Significance: Linked population-based surveys offer a unique opportunity to build a cohort of individuals with low back pain, which has never been used for this purpose. This study will identify groups at risk of high health care use and costs, and tailor strategies for low back pain. Identifying high risk groups informs decisions to improve population health and health care sustainability in Canada and abroad.

column36: La dependance alimentaire comme une adaptation a un historique traumatique et un obstacle au traitement
column37: L'obesite, estimee a 25,4% au Canada, est associee a plusieurs complications physiques et psychologiques. Parmi les individus souffrant d'obesite, plusieurs rapportent une relation dysfonctionnelle avec la nourriture recemment conceptualisee comme une dependance alimentaire (DA). Les resultats d'etudes recentes font ressortir que la DA est associee a un portrait clinique severe observable par un indice ponderal plus eleve, une forte comorbidite avec d'autres troubles alimentaires et une detresse psychologique marquee. Ces associations amenent plusieurs a penser que la DA est une strategie afin de gerer des experiences traumatiques et eviter la detresse ressentie et ainsi, pourrait expliquer pourquoi certains individus n'adherent pas aux traitements psychologiques et comportementaux conventionnels de perte de poids. Le premier objectif est d'examiner l'historique traumatique des individus avec de la DA. Le deuxieme objectif est de verifier le role moderateur de la DA sur l'efficacite d'une intervention de groupe visant l'adhesion a de saines habitudes de vie. 200 adultes en surpoids (IMC > 25 kg/m2) qui consultent pour des comportements alimentaires dysfonctionnels seront recrutes sur 3 ans. Une intervention de groupe de 12 rencontres sur 6 mois visant une diminution du poids et des comportements alimentaires dysfonctionnels sera offerte aux participants. Ils seront peses et mesures, passeront une entrevue et repondront a une batterie de questionnaires a trois reprises, avant l'intervention (T1), a la fin (T2) et 6 mois plus tard (T3). Un nombre incalculable d'etudes se sont interessees au traitement de l'obesite sans succes significatif. La DA est un concept nouveau et prometteur qui cible specifiquement une clientele plus severe et qui pourrait enfin apporter des resultats interessants. Les retombes escomptes de ce projet sont de mieux comprendre l'etiologie de la DA et d'emettre des recommandations afin d'offrir un traitement mieux adapte a cette clientele.

column36: Social Learning as an Underlying Mechanism in the Co-development of Problem Gambling, Substance Use, and Delinquent Behaviour among Adolescents.
column37: Problem gambling, substance use, and delinquent behaviour co-occur among many adolescents. To understand the reason for this association, it is necessary to explore what underlying mechanisms contribute to the co-development of these problem issues. The research literature indicates that a primary factor is the influence of peers and family members. Adolescents who have peers and family involved in problem gambling, substance use, and crime are more likely to engage in the behaviours themselves. However, current research does not provide insights into the social context in which this learning process occurs and how it differs for boys and girls. As such, it is difficult to design an intervention for adolescents experiencing these multiple concerns. Through qualitative interviews with 18 male and 18 female adolescents, I will explore if and how interpersonal experiences with peers and family can influence early life development of multiple problem behaviours. My analysis will describe how participants' thought processes (cognitive factors), their perception of their social experiences with peers and family (environmental factors), and their development of problem behaviours (behavioural factors) relate to each other. I will also compare how these processes might differ if the participant is male versus if they are female. This research is important because adolescent prevention and treatment services for problem gambling, substance abuse, and criminal behaviour are scarce and those available are delivered in silos. With a better understanding of how these behaviours develop together, we can design programs and interventions that treat these problems holistically. In addition, findings on gender from this study may inform the creation of interventions tailored to the unique needs of male and female adolescents experiencing problem behaviour.

column36: Characterizing naive CD4 T cell transcriptional heterogeneity and its effect on T cell function
column37: The military exists in order to protect a country from all kinds of dangers including foreign threats and civil unrest. The immune system is similar in that it must protect the body from invading pathogens and prevent the body from attacking itself. T lymphocytes are crucial in this respect and are often called the soldiers of the immune system. Like in the military, there are different kinds of soldier T lymphocytes that all have different specialized skills. While the factors that help train these T lymphocytes after they encounter an enemy are well understood, whether there are pre-existing untapped skills prior to deployment that impact their future responses remains unclear. The goal of this research is to identify whether we can predict what kind of soldier a T lymphocyte will become prior to encountering the enemy. To do this I will use new genomics tools, computational biology, and a novel approach that we have developed in the lab to shed new light on heterogeneity within the T lymphocyte population. Being able to predict what kind of soldier a T lymphocyte will become, even while it is still on reserve, could allow us to create an improved battle plan for an immune response against a particular pathogen. In addition, we may be able to modify our T lymphocyte soldiers to be better prepared for an attack. In the long-term, this knowledge can contribute to the design of superior therapies for diseases like cancer, allergy, and autoimmunity and also allow us to harness T lymphocyte functions to improve treatment or prevent infections, from HIV to the flu, and beyond.

column36: Low-intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation of Human Cortical Activity
column37: INTRODUCTION: There is a pressing need to develop safer and more effective methods of treating movement disorders of the brain, such as Parkinson's Disease. Low-intensity Focused Ultrasound (US) is a new technique that has been studied for its ability to safely affect brain activity, but how exactly ultrasound interacts with the brain is unknown. Our study combines US with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a brain stimulation tool with a well-described electrical response on healthy subjects. By pairing different US parameters with TMS and comparing the response to TMS alone, we aim to discover a dose-response relationship between US settings and brain activity. HYPOTHESIS: We predict that that shorter (<0.5 s) and faster US (>1 kHz) ultrasound pulses will be more effective at suppressing motor activity, compared to sham. METHODS: A custom TMS/US wand will be held over the subject's left scalp. TMS will be delivered with US (active), or without US (sham). An electrode taped over the subject's right thumb muscle will measure the resulting electrical activity and muscle twitches. The mean size of MEPs elicited from each condition will be analyzed. Statistical analysis will be performed to determine how certain US parameters affect the subject's motor brain circuit. To test the safety of US, all subjects receive a neurological examination before and after the experiment and are asked about any side effects. PRELIMINARY RESULTS: We report that low-intensity focused US is safe, as it only causes mild tingling at the scalp when applied. Preliminary analysis shows a trend, with shorter US pulses and faster pulsing, decreases MEP amplitude, whereas longer durations have no effect. In summary, our research is discovering the optimal settings of US stimulation to safely affect brain circuits. We hope to translate our findings into a future pilot study in Parkinson's Disease patients, where US stimulation of deeper brain regions could yield therapeutic benefit.

column36: Cerebral blood flow and pain: An arterial spin labeling study of children after traumatic brain injury compared to orthopedic injury
column37: Concussion affects millions of children in North America each year. Headache is the most common symptom after concussion, the most likely symptom to persist, and the most common reason families seek medical attention for their child after a concussion. My study aims to better understand headache after concussion by examining blood flow to the brain. Past research has already found that children after concussion demonstrate changes in brain blood flow, and those who have more symptoms tend to also have increased brain blood flow weeks after their injury. However, many kinds of symptoms are possible after a concussion (e.g., difficulty concentrating, fatigue, dizziness), so we do not know whether changes in blood flow are related to headache specifically. My study will be the first to investigate whether pain, and especially headache pain, is related to changes in brain blood flow in children after concussion. We will examine brain blood flow and pain in 700 children with concussion compared to 300 children with orthopedic injury. Participants are children and youth recruited from five children's hospitals across Canada. One week after injury, children complete neuroimaging and rate their pain intensity and location, and how much the pain interferes with their daily lives. This will be the largest brain imaging dataset on children with concussion in the world, and my study will help determine why headaches may be so common after concussion. The results will not only contribute important new scientific insights, but also suggest potential treatments for headaches in children after concussion.

column37: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is a hereditary disease that affects 1 in 3,500 individuals and results in the development of multiple tumours outside the skull that are called peripheral nerve sheath tumours (PNSTs). Preliminary data from our laboratory has uncovered specific modifications in the DNA of majority of ANNUBPs, which is a finding not observed in other benign neurofibroma types. We hypothesize that ANNUBPs have specific genomic features that increase the risk of malignant transformation. The goal of our research proposal is to characterize the molecular alterations in both malignant and benign PNSTs and identify potential therapeutic methods. This will allow future research to target the critical mutated genes with specific drugs that may be already available for other tumor types. Ultimately, any new findings will be tested in cells and mice with PNSTs to confirm their functional role in tumor development and malignancy. The genomic analysis proposed in this study would establish distinct signatures in PNSTs that would potentially predict malignant transformation and enable identification of patient-specific therapies.

column36: Testing the causality of hyperinsulinemia in pancreatic cancer
column37: Pancreatic cancer is the 4th leading cause of cancer death in Canada. Pancreatic cancer is known as a silent killer as there are no recognizable symptoms or effective treatments. Being overweight and having type 2 diabetes are risk factors for pancreatic cancer, and both conditions are increasing in the general population. However, it is not clear how obesity and diabetes are connected to pancreatic cancer. Insulin is the hormone that the body uses to control blood sugar levels and people who don't make enough develop diabetes. However, insulin can also be too high, and it has been shown that excess insulin between meals could be a factor linking obesity and diabetes to pancreatic cancer. Many studies showed a high level of insulin is associated with higher cancer incidence and death, especially from pancreatic cancer. Even for healthy weight people, the chances of dying from cancer is higher in those with high insulin levels. Whether the high levels of insulin are causing the cancer is an important but unanswered question. The goal of my Ph.D. project is to directly test the cause and effect relationship between insulin and pancreatic cancer. This may help us understand the root causes of pancreatic cancer better and provide new insight into possible ways to prevent and treat it. The Johnson lab has developed special strains of mice that have controlled insulin secretion. Through comparing cancer development in mice having different insulin levels, we can test if high insulin itself can promote pancreatic cancer. Similarly, we have designed mice that are engineered not to respond to insulin in the potential cancer cells, so we can also test if insulin is acting directly on pancreatic cancer. This study may not only provide new targets in anticancer therapy but also may have implications to prevent and treat pancreatic cancer since there are diets and available drugs that can reduce circulating insulin in people.

column36: Survivors of Childhood Cancer: Risk Factors and Health Outcomes Associated with Fear of Cancer Recurrence
column37: Survivors of adult cancers often experience fear of cancer recurrence (FoCR) - the worry that one's cancer will return. FoCR negatively impacts mental health, and may lead to increased financial burden on our healthcare system due to unnecessary medical visits and testing. Almost no research has studied FoCR in survivors of childhood cancer. Importantly, FoCR experienced by children may be different from FoCR experienced by adults. It is unclear if FoCR experienced by children leads to negative health outcomes (e.g. poor mental health), or increased health system use. It is also unknown if specific risk factors (e.g. type of cancer) effect FoCR experienced by children. No tool exists to measure FoCR experienced by survivors of childhood cancer. The purpose of this project is to 1) develop a tool to measure FoCR for survivors of childhood cancer, and 2) identify risk factors and negative health outcomes related to FoCR in this group. We will invite survivors of childhood cancer between ages 8-18, and >2 years off of treatment to participate. First, we will conduct 10 small focus groups to develop questions for the FoCR tool. Second, we will administer each of these questions to a new group of 50 participants and remove unclear or confusing questions. Third, we will administer the remaining questions to a new group of 100 participants and use statistical analyses to determine which questions to use in the final FoCR measurement tool. Finally, we will administer the FoCR tool to survivors of childhood cancer at the Alberta Children's Hospital during regular clinic visits. This information will be compared to medical records to identify risk factors and negative health outcomes related to higher FoCR. This research is the first step to better understanding the impact of FoCR on survivors of childhood cancer. These results will help to inform future interventions aimed at improving health outcomes and reducing burden on our healthcare system.

column36: Investigation of Gastrointestinal Adverse Events of Brand Versus Generic Osteoporosis Medications: Merits and Limitations of Different Non-Experimental Research Methods
column37: Osteoporosis is a condition of brittle bone which makes patients susceptible to fractures. Over 2 million Canadians are affected by osteoporosis. The bisphosphonate (BP) class of medications is widely used today for osteoporosis treatment and prevention. Medication adherence is imperative for patients taking BP, as every osteoporosis fracture is estimated to cost the Canadian healthcare system 17,000 dollars. Upper gastrointestinal (GI) complaints, such as heartburn and ulcers, are the most common reason for BP discontinuation. Generic formulations of BP, which are preferred by most insurances due to lower costs, do not have identical disintegration properties as their brand counterparts because of differences in inactive ingredients; these differences have led to inquiries about the GI safety of generic BP. Previous studies have shown that patients taking generic BP had higher rates of drug discontinuation and GI endoscopies than patients taking brand BP. However, previous studies included too few patients to obtain precise results, examined outcomes which are not reliably recorded in databases, or compared groups which had different baseline risks for GI conditions. The proposed research will describe characteristics of over 500,000 new BP users over time in Ontario; compare the rates of GI side effects between brand versus generic BP using three different non-experimental study designs; and compare results, strengths, and limitations of the designs for educational purposes. In addition to informing whether public drug formularies should include brand BP or enforce better evidence of safety of generic oral BP prior to market entry, findings will help to educate a variety of stakeholders (e.g., clinicians, policy-makers) on the implementation and interpretation of these designs.

column37: One of the largest issues currently facing biomedical research is that many published results cannot be replicated by other research groups. An important reason for this is that many of the assays and models we use have substantial intrinsic variability, and small differences in the testing conditions can lead to large differences in results. This is especially true when testing the behaviour of animals that are used as models of disease, where factors such as stress caused by experimenter handling can strongly affect the outcome of experiments. To address many of these issues, we have developed an automated behavioural testing system which can assess motor skills in several mice at a time within their own home-cage in a standardized and low-stress manner. Specifically, we plan to use this to investigate the behaviour of mice that carry the genetic mutation that causes Huntington's disease (HD), a disorder that results in loss of motor control and affects approximately 1 in 10,000 Canadians. Testing of motor skills in these mice is an important part of determining both whether the animals are a good model for the human disease, and if a potential treatment is effective or not. In this proposed research, I will test two distinct mouse models of HD at early and late stages in order to determine when these motor deficits first appear and how they progress over time. I will also validate the usefulness of this system for drug discovery by assessing the effectiveness of a novel therapeutic in improving the motor performance of these mice. This proposed research will contribute to the further development and automation of behavioural testing methods, increasing our ability to translate findings from basic research to the clinic.

column36: Investigating the role of the complement cascade in NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic plasticity during hippocampus development.
column37: Synapses are the primary sites of communication between neurons within the brain, and are capable of undergoing a process known as synaptic plasticity, in which synaptic connections are added or remove to mediate learning and memory. It has become evident from numerous studies that the dysfunction and aberrant elimination of synapses is a critical process underlying the etiology of a number of neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and schizophrenia. The immune cells of the brain, known as microglia, engulf excess 'weak' synapses to refine the connectivity patterns of the brain during development. In mouse models of AD and schizophrenia, it has been found that microglia become abnormally active and that gene mutations found to be risk factors for AD and schizophrenia are microglia-specific. This evidence suggests that microglia play an important role in the pathological synaptic loss seen in multiple neurological disorders. Therefore, a better understanding of how this process occurs normally during development provides the basis for knowing how it goes wrong in a number of disorders. Though it is known that brain activity plays a role in this process of synapse removal during development, the exact activity patterns and molecules involved are unexplored. Therefore, my project aims to elucidate the types of neuronal activity and molecules involved by examining the types of synaptic plasticity during development that can recruit microglia to synapses to eat them. The knowledge gained from my project will contribute to a better understanding of the role of microglia in synaptic plasticity in the healthy brain and how this process can go awry in disease.

column36: Brain circuitry underlying social buffering after stress
column37: Although an appropriate response to a stress is essential for survival, its dysregulation is implicated in the emergence of numerous neuropsychiatric diseases. These diseases affect 1 in 5 Canadians, exacting an enormous personal, societal and economic cost, with the latter estimated $51 billion per year. Many psychopathologies show sex-specific differences, yet our understanding of how sex shapes neural circuits and behaviour remains poor. There are many underlying reasons for these differences, but one intriguing possibility is that increased social isolation has a more profound effect on female brains. Our lab has made two recent observations in a preclinical mouse model that provide the substrate for a foundation to examine social interactions, neural circuits and stress coping in females. First, we have shown that female mice separated from others for short periods of time exhibit changes in neuronal biophysical properties that are observed following an acute stress. Second, we have shown that the consequences of stress on synapses are buffered in females, but not males, by the presence of another individual. Neither the neural circuits responsible for sex-specific stress buffering, nor the cellular mechanisms through which this phenomenon occurs, are known. My proposed research aims to answer these questions. Preliminary experiments have suggested a potential role for vasopressin, a peptide hormone that may act in the brain's stress command centre to reduce the neuronal consequences of stress. I will investigate the mechanisms by which vasopressin is released and acts to buffer stress in female mice. My research will also focus on an olfactory subsystem that has been implicated in stress buffering as part of the circuitry involved. This research has implications for therapeutic strategies for stress-related disorders, such as post-traumatic stress disorder and depression.

column36: Hemiarthroplasty versus total hip arthroplasty for femoral neck fracture: propensity-score matched cohort study and census of Orthopaedic Surgeons in Ontario
column37: Approximately 30,000 Canadians suffer a hip fracture per year, and this number is expected to increase with an aging population. Patients aged 60 years and older with a displaced femoral neck fracture (representing >30% of all hip fractures) are typically treated with one of two prosthetic implants: a total hip replacement or a partial hip replacement. Several trials suggest that total hip replacement is superior to partial hip replacement, since it is associated with less pain and fewer complications; however, there are important differences between patients recruited in these trials and the average patient who has a hip fracture. The latter tends to be older, frailer, and have multiple health conditions that puts him/her at higher risk of complications. Population-level research suggests that patients treated with total hip replacement are having more complications than expected from trial data. Also, there is significant variation in treatment type based on surgeon training and geographic location. This project has two parts. The first set of objectives involves the use of healthcare administrative data to look at the outcomes (death, complications, pain, functional status, and ministry healthcare costs) of all Ontario patients aged 60 years and older treated with each type of prosthetic implant for hip fracture. For the second part, we will explore reasons for the existing variation in care by conducting a census of Orthopaedic Surgeons across Ontario. This research will allow us to understand why there are individual-level and system-level differences in the care of older patients with hip fractures. This is the first step to changing medical practice and improving the care we provide to patients with hip fractures. This work will help clinicians decide which surgical treatment is most effective for patients with displaced femoral neck fractures outside the trial setting.

column36: Methacrylic Acid Based Hydrogels for Enhanced Muscle Regeneration
column37: Skeletal muscles make up the largest organ system in the human body and are used in most daily activities. While muscles have a remarkable ability to regenerate following injury, massive loss of muscle tissue from trauma or surgery results in injuries that do not heal on their own. In these instances, patients suffer from a decline in muscle function and quality of life. The current standard of care for muscle loss, tissue grafts, is limited by graft availability and scar tissue formation, which impedes the growth of healthy muscle. In this project, a biomaterial that has been shown to improve skin wounds is investigated for its use in muscle repair. Preliminary studies have shown that this material reduces inflammation and enhances blood vessel growth in muscles compared to other materials. Next testing will examine how this material affects the strength of regenerated muscle after large injuries compared to that of native muscle. This material will be a unique treatment for patients who currently take months to recover or do not recover muscle function without intervention. As this biomaterial would not require hormones, growth factors or cells from donors, we expect it to be safe and easy to manufacture on a large scale. Thus, this project will address an unmet clinical need to restore tissue integrity and strength following muscle trauma.
