column36: In-solution targeted capture for sequencing of antibiotic resistance genes
column37: Antibiotic resistance mechanisms are rapidly spreading amongst bacteria globally, limiting current antibiotic treatment options. An accurate and rapid method to profile antibiotic resistance genes in various environments including the human gastrointestinal tract is needed to increase our understanding of antibiotic resistance, the changes that affect resistance, and ultimately improve targeting antibiotic use. Current methods for detecting resistance are not time- nor cost-effective. In a bacterial genome, antibiotic resistance determinants represent a small proportion of all the genetic content; therefore a method that is targeted and specifically captures resistance-conferring genes will revolutionize the study of antibiotic resistance. This project aims to develop and optimize an enrichment approach by designing capture probes that are specific to a set of resistance gene sequences. DNA isolated from multi-drug resistant clinical pathogens was investigated through this approach and sequenced. Across various bacteria, more than 80% of the sequencing data was determined to belong to antibiotic resistance genes. A method will be optimized to identify antibiotic resistance sequences from bacteria in the human gastrointestinal tract and applied to samples from patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy. The goal of this project is to provide a cost-effective and timely approach to understand the factors that select for antibiotic resistance. As a potential method for surveillance in environments where resistance determinants are likely to spread, this technique can help to prepare physicians for impending antibiotic-resistant outbreaks, improve the prudent use of antibiotics, and prevent further selection for antibiotic resistance. Along with a better understanding of the connection between the presence of individual genes and antibiotic susceptibility, this method can be developed into a diagnostic to improve human health and ultimately prevent a post-antibiotic era.

column36: Defining the consequences associated with early embryonic alcohol exposure and investigate the impact of a nutritional preventive intervention.
column37: In Canada, about 2-3% of children are born with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD) because of prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE). FASD are the most common cause of brain damage before birth and the leading cause of nonhereditary neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). About 40% of pregnancies are unplanned, consequently many women inadvertently subject their embryos to PAE during early pregnancy. With this project, we aim to investigate the adverse effect of a PAE during the first week of pregnancy on the future baby and get a better comprehension of the epigenetic mechanisms underlying those adverse consequences. Epigenetic modifications are chemical modifications associated to genes that provide the means by which genes can be turned on or off at specific times. These modifications provide a link between the environment and gene function. Early embryonic development is critical for the rest of the pregnancy. During that period, cells divide and grow under a specific program, dictated by major changes of epigenetic modifications. We hypothesis that irregularities occurring during the organisation of this program may increase the vulnerability of the central nervous system to NDDs development later in life. Since alcohol can alter the epigenetic landscape, which is heavily reworked in the early embryo, we believe that embryonic epigenetic disruption caused by alcohol could alter the normal developmental program of the central nervous system and lead to FASD. We aim also to determine the therapeutic potential of a preventive diet enrich in methyl donor groups to counteract the adverse effect of early PAE on the embryo development. Altogether, our finding will deepen understanding on the epigenetics mechanisms underlying the adverse consequences of an early PAE on embryo and nervous system development. Moreover, this project could lead to novel information and tools to promote earlier diagnosis, better treatment, and optimal outcomes for children affected of FASD.

column36: Assessment of products with child-appealing packaging in the Canadian food supply: Evidence to inform and monitor the impact of public health nutrition policy
column37: Child-appealing food marketing has been shown to influence food preferences in children, subsequently impacting their diets and contributing to the growing burden of obesity and diet-related disease in Canadian children. column36: Marqueurs inflammatoires, telomeres, fonction cognitive et contraintes psychosociales au travail : une etude de cohorte de 22 ans.
column37: La demence et la dysfonction cognitive se manifestent par des troubles affectant la memoire. Avec le vieillissement de la population, ces troubles cognitifs auront de serieuses repercussions pour les personnes atteintes, les familles qui s'en occupent et le systeme des soins de sante. L'inflammation et l'oxydation sont des reactions dans l'organisme associees au vieillissement et au developpement de la demence. Ainsi, des concentrations sanguines elevees de facteurs d'inflammation comme la proteine C-reactive (CRP) et l'interleukine-6 (IL-6) de meme que le raccourcissement des telomeres, des structures qui protegent nos cellules de l'oxydation et de l'inflammation, pourraient etre relies a un risque plus eleve de demence. Par ailleurs, certains stresseurs au travail ont ete associes a des concentrations elevees de CRP et d'IL-6 et a un raccourcissement des telomeres. Il serait alors possible que ces stresseurs au travail jouent un role dans le developpement de la demence via l'effet intermediaire des facteurs d'inflammation et d'oxydation. Le present projet de recherche vise a evaluer : 1) l'association entre trois facteurs d'inflammation et d'oxydation (CRP, IL-6 et telomeres) et la dysfonction cognitive; et 2) le role intermediaire de ces facteurs sanguins dans la relation entre les stresseurs au travail et la dysfonction cognitive. Ces objectifs seront realises a partir d'une etude importante constituee de plus de 9 000 Canadiens suivis depuis 22 ans. Les resultats de ce projet de recherche contribueront a identifier des facteurs qui precedent le diagnostic de troubles cognitifs comme la dysfonction cognitive. Les stresseurs au travail etant frequents, il serait possible d'intervenir eventuellement dans les milieux de travail pour ralentir le developpement de troubles cognitifs plus severes comme la demence. Cette etude permettra d'obtenir des informations qui serviront aux connaissances pour un vieillissement actif et satisfaisant.

column36: The Role of Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase (iNOS) in Promoting Cytokine-Induced Cachexia
column37: Historically overlooked, cachexia is a debilitating illness that currently has no available treatments. Cachexia develops in patients suffering from inflammatory diseases such as cancer and is marked by uncontrolled and involuntary muscle and fat loss. The muscle loss within cachectic patients is believed to be the predominant cause of its pathology leading to dramatic decreases in patient quality of life. Cancer patients suffering from cachexia are also significantly less responsive to their treatments and have much higher mortality rates. As a result, this draining disease that almost doubles the durations of hospitalization for patients, not only places a serious financial burden on patients' families, but also on the health care system. Due to its significant impacts on patient wellbeing and its economic burden, there is a strong need to develop treatments for cachexia. Currently it is believed that cachexia is caused by the elevation of several inflammatory factors that are made during our body's response to overlying diseases. The fundamental mechanisms induced by these factors, which drive the negative symptoms of cachexia are poorly understood. Due to the complex nature of the disease, all previous attempts to treat it have failed; therefore, further investigations into the main drivers of its pathology may uncover more efficacious treatment strategies. An accumulating body of evidence suggests that the enzyme inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is a primary promoter of cachexia. iNOS has been observed to target and disrupt factors involved in metabolism within muscle cells, and the programs required for muscle formation, integrity, and activity. We believe that revealing the targets of iNOS could unveil potential drug targets to help alleviate this disease.

column36: Pain sensitivities in patients with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
column37: Patient H.M. revolutionized our understanding of how memory is processed in the brain, but could he also be the key to our future understanding of pain? In 1957, both of his medial temporal lobes (MTL) were removed to cure his epilepsy. Following his surgery, Patient H.M. developed dementia, and unexpected high levels of pain tolerance. Second, we predict that the degree of sensory abnormalities will be related to the degree of hippocampal structural and functional abnormalities. If patients with mTLE have abnormal pain thresholds, this provides new evidence that the hippocampus is implicated in pain mechanism and of its potential as a new therapeutic marker for pain.

column36: Identification of blood-based biomarkers to distinguish subtypes of interstitial lung disease
column37: Interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) are a group of disorders in which the lungs progressively get harder due to faulty tissue repair mechanisms. Ultimately this leads to decreased oxygen uptake into the blood and difficulty breathing, which can escalate into a series of life-threatening complications including respiratory or heart failure. Within the older Canadian population, ILDs have a comparable incidence and prevalence to breast and prostate cancer. Unfortunately, there are several subtypes of these diseases, and one of the major hurdles in effectively treating ILDs is distinguishing one subtype from another: many of the subtypes look similar on standard medical tests, but require vastly different treatments. As a result, diagnosis can take up to 5 years. Importantly, misdiagnosis of ILD subtypes and inappropriate treatment can actually worsen patient outcomes. The objective of my doctoral research project, therefore, is to improve ILD diagnosis by identifying key molecular differences between different ILD subtypes. I will use a 'big data' approach to compare the relative amounts of genes, proteins, and metabolites in blood samples from patients with different ILD subtypes. My goal is to use these findings to develop a simple blood-based test that can improve the diagnostic accuracy for ILD and potentially improve patient outcomes. An added benefit of this research will be the discovery of new biological targets against which we can develop new ILD treatments.

column37: Heart diseases such as congestive heart failure become more common as we age. These diseases happen at the same time as when levels of sex hormones fall in males and females. column36: Predictors of primary care provider confidence and perceived skill in treating adults with developmental disabilities: Are Community Health Centres the answer?
column37: Background: Adults with developmental disabilities (DD) are a vulnerable population with complex health needs and poor health outcomes. Primary care is often the front door to the health care system, and plays an important role in health promotion, prevention and treatment. Improving the quality of primary care for this population can support better health outcomes. There are many different types of primary care practices in Ontario and it is possible that some delivery models promote higher quality care than others. The aim of this study is to investigate whether providers working in one primary care model, Community Health Centres (CHCs), are more likely to report they have the skills needed to provide high quality care to adults with DD. Additionally, this study will explore why some delivery models are more effective than others in supporting quality care for adults with DD. Approach: First, primary care providers across Ontario will be surveyed to assess their confidence and skills related to caring for adults with DD. The survey will also collect information about the provider (e.g., age, gender, years of experience, provider type) and the primary care practice where they work (e.g., delivery model, funding model, location, size). Second, interviews will be conducted with providers in CHCs and other models to better understand what aspects of the practice they work in has helped or hindered them in caring for adults with DD. Discussion: Since the release of the Ontario Ombudsman report "Nowhere to Turn", increasing focus has been given to the challenges faced by adults with DD. With the current transformation of the primary care system, and the recent release of the updated 2018 primary care guidelines for adults with DD, there is an opportunity to improve the quality of care for this population. Understanding which primary care delivery models are associated with better care can help inform primary care reform and system planning for adults with DD.

The aim of this study is to field test the WHO tool internationally to assess how useful, reliable, and accurate the new tool is compared to standard tests. This is a cross-cultural study led and coordinated in Canada. A total of 60 children and youth (aged 0 months to 17 years) with a suspected or established diagnosis of ASD will be recruited in five countries (India, Sri Lanka, Brazil, United Kingdom, and Italy). At the first appointment, a clinician will assess participants using the novel WHO tool, collect information to make a diagnosis, and complete an assessment of the tool's clinical usefulness. A second clinician will test the same person within two weeks to see if the test produces the same result over time. A third clinician will administer standard tests (Leiter-3, Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II) of intellectual and every-day abilities. The development of a valid and accessible diagnostic tool may reduce health differences and substantially improve the accurate identification and proper description of individuals with ASD. This project is useful for all Canadians in that it has the potential to improve identification of people with Autism in areas where special services are not available. This data will also be provided to the WHO Secretariat for ongoing ICD development.

column36: Understanding and improving the quality of melanoma diagnosis in Ontario: A population-based study
column37: The incidence rate of melanoma is rising in Canada and other economically developed countries. There is a wide range of survival expectancies depending on the thickness at which the melanoma is diagnosed, with thick melanomas having 5-year survival rates of only 56% (compared to ~100% for thin lesions). Since melanoma thickness is highly related to survival, discovering factors related to an increased risk of a diagnosis of thick melanoma is critical to the development of public health strategies that target high-risk populations. Our previous research showed that living in certain healthcare regions in Ontario, being elderly, male, or living in more deprived neighbourhoods were all independently associated with a diagnosis of thick melanoma. However, further research is needed to determine the fundamental causes of advanced melanoma in universal health care settings. This will be the topic of our proposed research. One explanation is that differences in healthcare availability, utilization, and quality that result in diagnostic delay are leading to differences in tumour thickness, and thus melanoma survival. We plan to assess whether differences exist between advanced and non-advanced patients according to factors such as the diagnostic process and its length, patients' usual use of healthcare, patient characteristics and health status, and the melanoma-related resources in their community (e.g. dermatologist supply). This study will be conducted using electronic health data for the province of Ontario linked to our clinical population database containing detailed information on patient's melanoma characteristics. This work is important to Ontario and Canada as it will deliver knowledge on modifiable health system factors associated with a prolonged diagnostic interval, and provide benchmarks on optimal diagnostic intervals for melanoma, which are informed by real world data from Ontario, including information on the link between survival and diagnostic delay.

column36: Intergenerational Risk for Pediatric Chronic Pain
column37: Chronic pain is prevalent in adolescence, is associated with high societal and economic costs and higher risk of mental health disorders into adulthood. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), including childhood abuse, neglect, and household challenges, are linked to physical and mental health problems (e.g., PTSD). High rates of ACEs and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms have been found among parents of youth with chronic pain and are linked to worse child pain outcomes (e.g., pain intensity and disability). Mothers' sleep quality and responses to their child when they have pain may be ways through which maternal trauma influences child chronic pain. Parent protective responses (e.g. letting the child stay home from school, bringing them special treats) to child chronic pain are linked to worse pain outcomes. These types of parent responses often restrict children's activity and reinforce children's pain complaints. Parents who are more distressed are more likely to engage in these types of parenting behaviours. Maternal trauma may lead to sleep disturbances and increased distress, which lead parents to overprotective responding to their child's pain, and thus, worse child pain outcomes. The proposed research aims to understand whether maternal trauma influences child chronic pain through sleep disturbances and overprotective responding. The study findings will contribute to a growing body of research regarding how and why child chronic pain develops and persists. It is critical to understand the influence of parent mental health on children's pain, in order to identify children who are most at risk for poor pain outcomes and response to treatment. Given that parent trauma symptoms, sleep, and parenting responses are modifiable, findings from this study may lead to new interventions for child chronic pain.

column36: Understanding the timing, mechanism and recovery of brain injury in complex congenital heart disease (CHD)
column37: Structural heart defects in newborn babies, termed congenital heart disease (CHD), are the most common birth defect. Babies with CHD often go on to develop neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), which limit their quality of life. Unsurprisingly, MRI of CHD babies show brain abnormalities, with white matter (tracts of the brain which allow brain regions to communicate) often implicated. The link between an abnormal heart, its action on the developing brain, and the subsequent abnormalities seen on MRI are poorly understood. Current consensus is that CHD results in the developing brain receiving less oxygen than normal. How this results in brain injuries remains to be seen. To address the link between CHD and subsequent brain injuries, and to determine whether increased oxygen protects the newborn brain, I will examine CHD-related laboratory mice using advanced imaging techniques developed at our lab. Mice share common developmental features with humans, all while allowing for short studies due to their rapid development and for invasive procedures not possible in humans. I will first establish a mouse model of CHD by creating a heart specific defect through surgical manipulation. Next, I will image the brain and label its cells to identify the underlying cellular events responsible for brain injury in CHD. I predict that the lack of oxygen will affect brain regions containing cell types that are vulnerable to oxygen deficits. Additionally, I will investigate whether these abnormalities can be reduced by increasing oxygen delivery to the mother. I hypothesize that increased oxygen will have a protective effect on the brain, and that both brain MRI and cellular imaging will show a recovery back to normal. NDDs cost Ontario approximately $2 million / person over their lifetime. A successful outcome of this study promises a reduction in the prevalence of NDDs due to CHD, lower healthcare costs, and more importantly, a better quality of life for individuals with CHD.

column36: Investigating the underlying mechanisms of TBI-induced hyponatremia
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a serious public health concern and a major cause of disability. It is increasingly being recognized that patients with a TBI have a propensity to develop hyponatremia, also known as a low sodium concentration in the blood. Since sodium is the major ion in the blood, a drop in sodium often equates to a decrease in blood plasma solute concentration (hypo-osmolality). This is a serious condition because as plasma osmolality drops, the osmotic gradient between the blood and the brain is shifted to promote the passage of water into the cells of the brain. This causes swelling of the brain and further exacerbates the initial trauma. However, it is unclear how TBI induces hyponatremia. An important homeostatic mechanism that maintains plasma osmolality in a stable range is the regulation of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secretion by the central nervous system (CNS). The neurons in the supraoptic nucleus (SON) of the hypothalamus are specialized to sense changes in plasma osmolality and consequently regulate the release of ADH into the circulation. We hypothesize that TBI induces a failure in this mechanism to promote inappropriate ADH secretion and water retention. The ADH SON neurons are inherently mechanosensitive and mechanical perturbations can increase their ADH secretion. Therefore, we hypothesize that the force of the TBI activates these neurons to induce ADH secretion independent of the plasma osmolality. Indeed, our preliminary data suggest that these neurons are strongly activated following TBI. I will investigate the cellular, molecular, and neural circuit mechanisms underlying the mechanical activation of ADH SON neurons following TBI. Furthermore, I will investigate whether inhibition of these neurons prevents TBI-induced hyponatremia. Understanding the mechanisms by which TBI can cause hyponatremia will aid in the development of therapeutic treatments for this condition.

column36: Valve Choice in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease
column37: Heart disease is the most common cause of death in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Affecting three million Canadians, CKD can progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) when patients require dialysis. Valvular heart disease is found in over 30% of patients with ESRD and diagnosed at a rate four to five times higher than the general population. As a result, a large proportion of patients with ESRD need valve replacement surgery to relieve symptoms and prevent permanent heart damage. Native valves can be replaced with a mechanical or bioprosthetic valve, each with their own advantages and disadvantages. Mechanical valves are more durable, but require life-long blood thinning medication (i.e. warfarin) to prevent clot formation on the valve and other parts of the body. In addition to challenges of medication adherence, blood thinning medication is associated with increased risk of bleeding. Bioprosthetic valves, made with tissue, avoid life-long blood thinning medication and its complications, but are less durable and require a complex reoperation long-term. Currently, there is a lack of research to support choosing either valve in patients with ESRD, contributing to variable clinical practice amongst physicians. Using various types of studies, we will 1) Describe the quality of current research. 2) Describe the preferences of patients and physicians for different prosthetic valves. 3) Evaluate outcomes of patients with ESRD who previously received either valve, using advanced statistics. 4) Evaluate outcomes of valve surgery in patients in earlier stages of CKD. These studies will evaluate the best valve given current body of scientific evidence, and contribute new evidence that improves on the shortcomings of past research. The evidence gained from these studies will inform a randomized control trial in this patient population. Ultimately, we hope to improve the decision making and outcomes of patients with CKD who require valve replacement surgery.

column36: Effect of T regulatory cell transplant in demyelinating disease; using the visual system as a model to study potential remyelinating and neuroprotective therapies for multiple sclerosis.
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease where the normal immunological function is disrupted, and immune cells attack the central nervous system. Myelin - the insulation around the nerve crucial for electrical conduction - is targeted and destroyed by a dysregulated immune response. Any part of the central nervous system can be affected, and lesions may cause unpredictable neurological deficits. The most common form of MS is called "relapsing-remitting" because it manifests with episodes of neurological dysfunction followed by slow recovery, which can be incomplete and leave the patient with severe disabilities. Decades of research in the field has given rise to a number of anti-inflammatory therapies, which reduce immune-mediated injury and curb relapsing events. However, no treatment has been developed that can repair myelin and unambiguously save axons. In this research project, we set out to evaluate whether an innovative treatment with transplantation of regulatory T (Treg) cells may enhance repair in addition to reducing inflammatory injury. Treg depletion has been linked to the development of autoimmune diseases and was recently associated with the inability to remyelinate. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that the injection of Treg cells may have a remyelinating effect and induce functional repair. This project will be carried out in three steps: 1) Evaluating the remyelinating potential of Treg cells transplant in the optic nerve and its neuroprotective effect on the retina; 2) Elucidate the processes involved by comparing two models of MS: inflammation-induced and inflammation-independent; 3) Carry out longitudinal studies to assess long-term effect of Treg cells transplantation on the integrity of the nervous system. This project may aid us in the development of a novel treatment for patients with MS by reducing inflammation and enhancing recovery at the same time - a unique opportunity and the first step towards a treatment breakthrough.

column36: Modelling the regulatory networks that govern mRNA stability and their implication in cancer
column37: Gene expression is the process by which deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)'s genetic instructions are used to synthesize gene products. Genes are read by the cell to produce ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules, which carry their genetic information. Gene expression is often de-regulated in diseases such as cancer, as many genes have either increased or decreased expression compared to normal cells, leading to their abnormal behavior. However, the specific mechanisms that lead to these changes are mostly unknown. Identifying these processes would allow us to better understand the underlying mechanisms of cancer progression and to develop potential therapeutic approaches to reverse it. The goal of my research project is to investigate the regulation of RNA stability, one of the least characterized aspects of gene expression regulation in cancer. The stability of individual RNAs determines their lifespan, which in turn determines the amount of gene products they will be able to generate. However, the genes that have altered stability in cancer and the factors responsible for these changes are still unknown. I am developing new computational tools to systematically analyze genomics data, with the aim of identifying the specific factors responsible for the changes in RNA stability observed in cancer. Identifying these mechanisms will improve our understanding of gene expression regulation and provide new insights into the causes of gene expression changes in cancer, pointing to new therapeutic approaches.

column36: Biomarkers in breast cancer survivors: The search for biological, physical, psychosocial, and behavioral predictors
column37: With continued advances in detection and treatments along with the aging and growth of the population, there is an ever-increasing number of breast cancer (BC) survivors in Canada who are experiencing long-term physiological sequelae. Investigating the extend to which biomarker patterns and biopsychosocial (BPS) variables are affected by BC is important for several reasons, but most notably because these physiological post-treatment outcomes are related to survival and quality of life (QOL). To this end, the overall purpose of this research program is to examine the secretion patterns of four key biomarkers (i.e., cortisol, salivary alpha-amylase, secretory immunoglobulin A, and C-reactive protein) in BC survivors and generate novel knowledge on their BPS predictors and outcomes. Three inter-related studies will be conducted. Study 1 aims to describe secretion profiles of biomarkers in BC survivors and to compare these to women with no history of BC. Studies 2 seeks to determine whether a modifiable life factor such as physical activity can be used to counterbalance the negative physiological effects of a cancer experience. Finally, Study 3 uses a longitudinal design to assess the bi-directional associations between the physiological sequelae of BC and multiple BPS variables during the first five years post-treatment. Collectively, these studies will allow us to expand current knowledge on the late and long-term physiological impact of BC and to identify factors that can be targeted in interventions to treat and ameliorate health outcomes in the thousands of women diagnosed with BC yearly. This research is the first to compare the profiles of several biomarkers in tandem in the same BC survivors. With the number of cancer survivors climbing each year, cancer survivorship needs to be a priority in research in order to keep up with the needs of the population and efforts to better understand, monitor, and mitigate the consequences of a cancer experience is critical.

column36: CRISPR-mediated engineering of autophagy-deficient human T lymphocytes for CAR-T cell immunotherapy
column37: Fighting cancer is no easy task. Our immune system has the ability to detect and eradicate cancer cells, but these cells use a wide variety of mechanisms to evade or impair our immune surveillance. Hence restoring and strengthening our immune system is a promising approach to fight back diverse tumours. CAR-T cell immunotherapy, a promising treatment, consists of collecting patient's immune T cells and genetically reprogramming them to specifically target and destroy cancer cells. The engineered T cells are then administered to cancer patients to eradicate the malignant cells. This new treatment showed impressive results against blood cancers. However, treating solid tumours remains a difficult challenge for the scientific community and many hurdles need to be overcome before this therapy is accessible to all. During immune cells reprogramming, a new gene coding for a receptor called CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) is incorporated in the patient's immune cells. This CAR receptor will recognize cancer cells and trigger the immune response. Even if these CAR-T cells are effective against cancer cells in the bloodstream, they don't persist in solid tumours. This lack of activity is attributed to the low amount of nutrients and oxygen near the tumour, which activates a pathway called autophagy. Preliminary results showed that autophagy-deficient mice had a significantly enhanced anti-tumour activity against prostate and breast cancer cells. We hypothesize that autophagy-deficient CAR-T cells will have an increased lifespan and anti-tumour activity in solid tumours. This project aims at using a molecular scissor called CRISPR-Cas9 to simultaneously target and inactivate a gene essential for autophagy and insert the CAR receptor. By modifying the CAR specificity, it will be possible to generate CAR-T cells targeting a wide array of cancer. I will develop a safe, rapid and efficient method to generate powerful CAR-T cells against a variety of cancer cells.

column36: Language Conectome and Aphasia Therapy: A Comparative Study of the Behavioural and Neurofunctional Effects of Two Approaches for the Treatment of Anomia in Chronic Aphasia.
column37: Around 30,000 Canadians are diagnosed with post-stroke aphasia each year. Aphasia is an acquired language disorder that occurs after brain injury and leads to significant consequences, such as social isolation and depression. The principal symptom is a difficulty finding words, called anomia. Anomia is present in the majority of persons with aphasia (PWA). Recovery from aphasia is dependent on brain plasticity (BP) mechanisms; the brain's ability to adapt and remodel throughout life, especially after an injury such as stroke leading to aphasia. This project proposes to study the recovery of the capacity to find words, and the brain's changes that support this recovery. To do so, we study the effects of two therapies, one based on the sounds of the words and the other based on the meaning of the words. We will recruit PWA who suffer from anomia, and assign them randomly to each therapy. It is expected that both of these therapies will lead to improvements in the ability to find words, but that the strategies used will differ. Also, by using functional magnetic resonance imaging, we aim to identify the areas in the brain where activity is essential to achieve recovery. The identification of these mechanisms of recovery following language therapy will allow optimizing the chances of recovery of people with aphasia by predicting the most effective therapy to trigger BP and recovery. The final purpose of this work is to deliver aphasia therapy guidelines that will maximize each person's recovery according to their stroke recovery and symptoms. The impact of this research on the health and quality of life of PWA lies in its potential to maximize recovery from aphasia, thus preventing depression and isolation that occurs when PWA do not improve their communication abilities.

column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a debilitating disease affecting one in 4200 boys which leads to death within the second decade of life. It is characterized by progressive muscle weakness and respiratory failure due to the absence of a protein called dystrophin in the muscle fibers. Currently, there is no cure for DMD, and steroid treatments only serve to modestly increase lifespan. Therefore, research is needed to better understand the disease. Recent studies from our lab have shown that muscle stem cells in mice suffering from DMD (mdx mice) do not divide properly and are less efficient at regenerating muscle following injury. A more recent study has linked DMD to the mis-regulation of a protein called CARM1. We know from previous work that CARM1 normally methylates PAX7, a gene that is absolutely required for normal muscle stem cell function. Methylated Pax7 then binds a protein complex that modifies chromatin to properly program the expression of genes, Therefore, we believe PAX7 exists in an unmethylated form in muscle stem cells from mdx mice. Consequently, we sought to study the effect of this modification in the context of DMD. To this end, we used CRISPR-Cas9, a new and exciting gene editing technology, to mutate PAX7 directly in mice, preventing its methylation by CARM1, and hopefully mimicking its state in DMD. We will use this mouse to study the effects the mutation will have on muscle regeneration and muscle stem cell divisions, as well as comparing the effect to mdx mice. Lastly, drug treatments to increase PAX7 methylation levels will be looked at as a potential treatment to ameliorate muscle stem cell function in mdx mice.

column36: Examining the nutritional quality of the Canadian product portfolios of major packaged food and beverage companies
column37: The nutritional quality of the products available in the national food supply has a direct influence on nutritional status and diet quality, with downstream effects on health and disease risk. Canada's current food supply fosters unhealthy food choices and overconsumption, contributing to the development of obesity and non-communicable diseases. There is, however, limited data on food company policies and practices regarding the nutritional composition and pricing of food and beverage products in Canada. My research will evaluate the nutritional quality of the product portfolios of major Canadian packaged food and beverage companies. Specifically, this study will assess the nutritional quality of companies' portfolios at two points in time and in relation to the strength of voluntary commitments made by companies to improve the formulation of their products. This work will also investigate the relationship between the nutritional quality and prices of products in several key food categories, and examine if improvement in product healthfulness is associated with an increase in price. The nutritional composition and prices of products will be determined from a large, highly-representative database of Canadian packaged foods. Overall, this study will provide the first comprehensive evaluation of the nutritional quality of the national food supply, and the relationship between the nutritional composition and prices of foods in Canada. My research will also offer insight into the effectiveness of voluntary company policies, commitments and actions in improving the nutritional quality of foods in Canada. Comparing company practices in the areas of product nutrition and pricing may prompt initiatives to improve the healthfulness and affordability of their products. Lastly, this work will provide a baseline to monitor the effectiveness of policies recently proposed by Health Canada, and inform future government policies to improve the nutritional quality of foods in Canada.

column36: Engaging Families as Advisors in Child Health Organizations in Ontario, Canada
column37: There is growing momentum for involving patients and families in treatment decisions, health research, health service delivery, and health policy development across the world. While various policy frameworks have defined broad principles and approaches for engaging patients, they have been unable to address thorny ethical challenges arising from value conflicts and power asymmetries that are prevalent in engagement-led decision-making. Without a foundation for the ethics of patient engagement, engagement processes vary widely across health care organizations, making token involvement difficult to prevent. My research seeks to understand how ethical issues that are rooted in value differences affect the engagement of family members serving as advisors in child health organizations in Ontario, Canada. Using a mixed methods design consisting of (1) a theoretical review of patient engagement frameworks, (2) a multiple-case study of three family advisory councils using key informant interviews, (3) surveys to characterize family advisory council membership, and (4) content analysis of family member interactions on social media, this research will identify the values held by key stakeholders and policy frameworks regarding patient engagement, and assess the gaps and barriers to implementing these values into practice. The study results will contribute to the development of an ethics framework to guide the engagement of patients and families as advisors in diverse areas of health care policy and practice.

column36: Creation and Evaluation of a Natural History-Informed Complications Screening Program in Type 1 Diabetes Clinical Care
column37: People with type 1 diabetes are at high risk of developing retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy. These complications are difficult to treat and they create a significant burden on patients and on our healthcare system. Recent advances in highly-sensitive clinical tools can help us detect the earliest stages of these complications and will improve patient care if deployed correctly. Clinical practice guidelines currently recommend routine screening of retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy in type 1 diabetes; however, screening for these three complications occurs independently of one another. Therefore, it would be more efficient if screening for one complication could rule out the need for screening of others. As such, we will determine if a sequence of complications exists using these clinical tools in a one stop complications screening unit. Specifically, 200 people with type 1 diabetes will undergo a 40-minute clinical evaluation to determine the presence of the three complications. Evaluations will take place at the Leadership Sinai Centre for Diabetes, and will occur during regularly-scheduled endocrinologist visits in an existing dedicated clinical exam room. The highly-sensitive clinical tools include high quality retinal imaging, novel measurement of corneal nerves, urine testing for albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and blood testing to determine estimated glomerular filtration rate. Advanced statistical methods will be used to infer the sequence of incidence of complications.

column36: Characterizing social-structural factors in the implementation of a treatment continuum for opioid use disorder: An ethnographic study of patient trajectories
column37: Canada is in the midst of a public health crisis of opiod-related overdoses that resulted in approximatley 7000 overdose deaths from 2016 to 2017. This crisis highlights a growing trend of opioid use disorder, and urgent need to scale up and effectively implement medication-based treatments (e.g. Methadone, Suboxone, slow releasese oral morphine and injectible opioid agonist treatments) to improve the health outcomes of this population. Recently, a number of best practice guidelines have been developed, and policy changes implemented, that make it easier for health care providers to deliver these treatments in response to persistent gaps in treatment enrollment and retention. To date, there is a poor understanding of the social-structural factors that influence how patients initiate treatment; adhere to treatment, and transition between treatment options, as well as subsequent impacts on overdose-related outcomes. This study will use an ethnographic approach in order to characterize these social-structural factors and identify further gaps in the implementation of treatment for people with opioid use disorder. Patient interviews, ethnographic observations, and a patient chart reviews will be conducted in order to develop an in-depth understanding of treatment implementation. This study will contribute to the overdose response by indicating ways that the provision of treatment for opioid use disorder can be optimized and in turn contribute to a concerted public health response to the ongoing crisis.

column36: Systems Level Analysis of Hepatitis B Care in Canada: A mixed methods approach to identifying optimal integrated care services and informing strategies for implementation at the policy level.
column37: Hepatitis B (HBV) is one of the top five most burdensome infectious diseases in Ontario. HBV can lead to serious chronic complications such as liver cancer placing a substantial burden on patients and the health care system. Individuals infected with HBV often do not know they have the disease because a high proportion remain without symptoms or present with mild or non-specific symptoms. Cost-effective interventions for prevention, vaccination, screening, and treatment have been identified, however, they are typically assessed in isolation. There is a need for methods, processes, and policies to allow for a coordinated approach to the delivery of HBV interventions in Canada. The first aim of my research is to identify the group of patients in Ontario with HBV using laboratory and health administrative databases in order to map the number of patients who are screened, monitored and managed appropriately by health care services in Canada. The second aim of my research is to conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis of an integrated set of HBV interventions (e.g., vaccination, screening, treatment, patient management and monitoring) compared to the current standard of care in Ontario. Lastly, the third aim of my research is to conduct interviews with individuals from key organizations making funding recommendations for HBV interventions (e.g., vaccination, screening, and therapy recommendations) to identify the barriers and facilitators of considering the entire continuum of patient care in their discussion processes. My research will offer substantial value to the health of Canadians by informing a framework for strengthening the coordination of health care services in Canada, and by providing critical evidence on gaps along the HBV care continuum, allow for the tracking progress of HBV elimination in Canada, and identifying integrated cost-effective interventions in an effort to help Canada meet its Global commitment to the WHO for Hepatitis B elimination by 2030.

column36: Predicting the Impact of Somatic Structural Variation in Cancer Whole Genomes
column37: Cancer is driven by mutations in the genome that accumulate over the course of lifetime. Some of these mutations are harmful and drive the progression of cancer while others are tolerated without damage to cells and tissues. To distinguish between these mutations, we look for patterns of mutational recurrence across a population, determine whether they are present in the healthy population and design strategies to predict their impact on biological function based on established knowledge. Small mutations involving changes to several bases of DNA are becoming easier to characterize using enhanced sequencing technology and computer algorithms but large rearrangements of the genome still present a problem in every step of the pipeline. Yet, genomic rearrangements are the predominant mutation type in almost half of all cancers, leaving the resolution of these challenges both poignant and pressing. Currently, several technologies are improving the cost and accuracy of the detection of genomic rearrangements while the recent assemblies of the 3-dimensional genome are improving our knowledge of their functional impact. Our lab is part of the largest collaboratory to date for the analysis of cancer genomes and have contributed several algorithms for the purpose of identifying recurrent small mutations which drive cancer. We propose to take this opportune time to develop a new method for the prioritization of genomic rearrangements. Using some of the largest collections of cancer genomes, we will examine both molecular and clinical correlates of genomic rearrangements, identifying associated changes in cell biology and clinical presentation. We aim to present a logical progression of how these molecular features lead to better or worse outcomes. The ultimate purpose of our research is to improve clinical practice based on molecular features of tumours.

column36: Genome-wide discovery and analysis of copy number variation in metastatic cancer
column37: Cancer is a genetic disease. One notable characteristic of cancer is its high rate of DNA mutation. Mutations can range from small changes in the genetic sequence to duplications and deletions of large segments of DNA, known as copy number alterations. Recently, there have been a large number of studies published outlining the many different types of mutations, including copy number changes present in various types of cancer. However, these studies have focused on cancer which has not spread beyond its initial location, known as the primary site. While these studies are informative, they fail to describe the landscape of mutations that may be present in cancer which has spread beyond its primary site and become metastatic. While primary cancer represents the initial development of the disease, metastatic cancer represents the vast majority of cancer that causes death. We propose to investigate the types of copy number variations that occur in metastatic cancer. We hope to identify mutations that might help to explain why a patient's cancer has spread beyond the primary site. We will also investigate the ways in which metastatic tumours differ from primary tumours from the perspective of copy number changes. We will also investigate ways in which we might be able to target a patient's specific cancer with personalised medicine. This project will provide valuable insights into the genetic landscape of metastatic cancer and identify treatment strategies to better combat this disease.

column36: The role of RNA granules on the regulation of cellular senescence
column37: Aging has been one of the fundamentally least understood physiological processes. Moreover, methods of increasing human longevity and quality of life would decrease our burden on healthcare systems. Therefore, my project consists of studying the relationship between the formation of a unique class of protein aggregates, essential for the regulation of RNA expression known as RNA granules, and the development of age-related diseases and symptoms associated with chronic inflammation . It has been established that with age, a certain number of cells stop dividing (through a process known as "senescence") as a potent tumour suppressive mechanism leading to their accumulation in various tissues. However, this accumulation leads to the secretion of senescence associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors, which are capable of transforming of neighbouring cells and promoting metastasis of various cancers. Preliminary results indicate that formation of RNA granules is capable of decreasing the presence of senescent cells and the secretion of the SASPs. This suggests that RNA granules play a key role in senescence progression and may provide a means of promoting the beneficial effects of senescence and reducing age-related pathologies. My project is to determine how RNA granules regulate these factors and the role of this regulation on the development of age-related diseases, symptoms, and accumulation of senescent cells in elderly patients.

column36: The role of Sdk1 in the assembly and function of feature-detecting retinal circuits
column37: The wiring pattern that neurons create during early development give rise to all the functions of our brain and lead to disease when gone awry. Understanding the factors governing this process and linking early wiring events to mature brain function is critical for developing new tools to address neurological disorders. One of the key factors that governs the development of neural circuits is wiring genes, which lay the foundations for a mature brain by defining the eventual synaptic partners of its neurons. My goal is to use the mouse retina as a model to assess the role of one of these wiring genes called Sidekick 1 (Sdk1) in the assembly of retinal circuits. We hypothesize that Sdk1 is necessary for establishing a distinct retinal circuit and endowing it with a unique function. To test this hypothesis, I will use immunological, electrophysiological and behavioral techniques to characterize Sdk1-expressing cells in the retina, verify how they connect to one another, observe how these connections change in the absence of Sdk1 and address the functional and ethological deficits arising from this absence. As our understanding grows, we will misexpress this gene in non-expressing neurons to assess whether we can change their circuitry. Our goal is to understand the principles governing circuit assembly and offer a tangible starting point to address the miswiring that occurs during neurological diseases.

column36: Reprogramming the immune response to peanut in established peanut allergy.
column37: Some food allergies, like those to peanuts, are maintained for a lifetime in up to 80% of individuals. Currently, no curative interventions exist, only drugs that mitigate symptoms or are given post-anaphylaxis. Immune responses to food allergens are mediated by antibodies, namely IgE. However, IgE and IgE-producing cells vanish shortly after allergen exposure, thus other allergen-specific cells must persist. Recently it has been demonstrated that allergen-specific memory B cells are maintained for a lifetime and, under specific stimuli, these cells can transition into IgE-producing cells. One such stimuli is IL-4, a small protein secreted by numerous immune cells with critical involvement in allergic disease and IgE production. We hypothesize that blockade of the IL-4 receptor will not only suppress the production of IgE but will also promote a shift from a deleterious response to a protective immune response. To investigate this, we will first identify the cell type(s) that contribute to IL-4 production in a recall response in a mouse model. Subsequently, two novel platforms will be used to assess the effect of IL-4 receptor blockade. One platform involves mice that uniquely model peanut allergy with human immune cells. Here we will measure the production of peanut-specific IgE following treatment with an IL-4 receptor block. Next, human immune cells from the blood of peanut-allergic individuals will be cultured in the presence or absence of IL-4 receptor block. The production of other non-allergy, allegedly protective, antibodies and changes in gene expression and protein secretion will be investigated. There has been little advancement in the treatment of food allergy, despite a relatively well-characterized understanding of underlying immunological mechanisms. IL-4 is positioned as a key molecule in the maintenance of lifelong food allergy. Therefore, this research is critical for the identification of therapeutic targets with disease-transforming potential.

column36: Understanding Childhood Apraxia of Speech through Systematic Disruptions of the Auditory and Somatosensory Systems
column37: Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) disrupts a child's ability to send signals to the mouth (e.g., lips, tongue) to speak. In typical development, information about "how a word sounds", "how a word feels" (i.e., the lips in a rounded position when saying "boo"), and the actual movements of the mouth all work together to produce speech. In CAS, it is not known whether one of the pieces (i.e., "how it sounds", "how it feels" or the mouth movement) is damaged or whether the pieces are not working together. This then makes it very challenging to determine what CAS looks like (e.g., speech, language and/or literacy difficulties), or what tools should be used for diagnosis. As such, the purpose of this project is to investigate the role that "how it sounds" and "how it feels" play in speech and reading in children with CAS. Children with and without CAS will complete tasks that test their ability to use "how it sounds", "how it feels" and the movements of the mouth in normal conditions, as well as in disrupted conditions, namely presenting noise to cover up information about "how it sounds" and using an oral numbing mouthwash to cover up information about "how it feels". Together, these studies will move us closer to an understanding of the core deficit in CAS, and help to inform the development of high-quality procedures for identifying children with CAS (i.e., diagnosis) and tools/protocols for evaluating their strengths and weaknesses (i.e., assessment). In addition, it will inform clinicians who treat children with CAS by ensuring they provide the best possible care and treatment. Finally, the results will also inform teachers and specialists who guide reading development.

column36: Discovering the effects of DRD2 genotype-based variants on D2 receptor distribution in patients with Parkinson's disease: a [11C]-(+)-PHNO PET study
column37: The underlying impairment of mental functioning and motor planning in Parkinson's disease (PD) stems from the dopaminergic signal loss within the striatum and prefrontal cortex. Neurons within these brain regions contain two dopamine D2 receptor isoforms-D2 long (D2L) and D2 short (D2S). The degree of expression for these receptor isoforms are affected by the genotype within two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), rs2283265 and rs1076560 (both are in high linkage disequilibrium; C>A), found in the DRD2 gene. The importance of these SNPs are heightened clinically as PD patients with the CC genotype showed the most clinical improvement in motor and mental functioning to an anti-parkinsonian medication known as rasagiline compared to minor A allele carriers (AC/AA) (Masellis et al., 2016). However, it is fundamentally unclear how these SNPs affect the distribution of D2 receptors in vivo within the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system and its relevance to behavioral and movement impairment in patients with PD. Therefore, we propose to image PD patients and age-matching controls grouped by their genotype using a high-affinity PET radiotracer biomarker-[11C]-(+)-PHNO (PHNO). This agonist probe has properties allowing high sensitivity and specificity in detecting D2 receptors in certain regions of the brain. Through PHNO PET imaging of PD patients and controls, our objectives are: (1) examine genotype group effects on D2 receptor distribution and correlate it with behaviour and movement functioning; and (2) elucidate how the genotype modulates the dopaminergic system in PD patients. Achieving these objectives will (1) reveal a deeper understanding of the genetic impact on the dopaminergic pathophysiology of PD in vivo and its role in mental and movement impairment; and (2) help pave a path towards the improvement and advancement of personalized medicine for PD patients.

Disruption to white matter integrity (i.e., how healthy the white matter is) has been observed as an early component of pediatric-onset MS. The cerebellum is a structure involved in motor coordination, but more recently implicated in cognitive processes, such as memory and attention. This region is particularly vulnerable due to a high propensity for lesions in this area in pediatric-onset patients compared to adults who have had MS for the same amount of time. This highlights the need to gain a better understanding of how MS affects the developing brain. While recent studies have noted disrupted cerebellum development in pediatric-onset MS, none have examined white matter integrity of the cerebellum and its impact on cognition. This study will examine whether white matter of the cerebellum is associated with cognitive functioning in pediatric-onset MS, and if changes in cerebellar white matter can predict cognitive outcomes over time. This research may provide evidence for the utility of examining white matter to detect early degenerative processes in MS, prior to the development of cognitive decline.

column36: Investigating the risk of tic disorder and associated comorbidities with antipsychotic use
column37: Antipsychotic medications are used to treat various psychiatric illnesses, such as schizophrenia and Tourette syndrome. However, these drugs are often associated with serious adverse events. One adverse event that is of concern to date is movement disorders. It is particularly interesting that there have been case reports on antipsychotic-induced symptoms of Tourette syndrome, which are sudden, repetitive, nonrhythmic muscle movements or vocalizations known as tics. This adverse event is not well characterized and is paradoxical because antipsychotics are used to treat Tourette syndrome. Our group has already performed and published a systematic literature review on this topic to better understand the complex relationship. Because most studies were case reports and had many methodological limitations, there is a need to investigate this relationship using a larger population database. column36: Comparing Attention Interventions in Individuals with Generalized Anxiety Disorder
column37: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a chronic illness characterized by excessive and uncontrollable worry. GAD affects roughly 5% of Canadians, and is associated with elevated use of health services, decreased work productivity, and coronary heart disease. Individuals with GAD experience their worry as overwhelming and often report that it makes concentration extremely difficult. It has been proposed that excessive worry is maintained by two attention processes. One is a heightened bias or sensitivity to threatening information. The other is a decreased ability to control attention, or to shift attention away from a worry spiral and back to the task at hand. Attention Bias Modification (ABM) was designed to help people train their attention away from threat and towards neutral information instead. The Attention Training Technique (ATT) aims to train attentional control in worriers. Preliminary evidence suggests that ABM and the ATT are successful in reducing anxiety and worry in people who worry excessively; however, the two interventions have never been compared in such a population. This next step is important so that clinicians can determine which interventions to recommend to clients. This study will be the first to compare the effects of ABM and ATT to a control condition in people with GAD, on worry and attention. It is predicted that relative to control, ABM and ATT will both be associated with a reduction in worry, attention bias, and attention control, with the ATT being more effective. It is also predicted that attention control improvement will be responsible for improvement in worry. These hypotheses will be tested by randomly assigning participants to engage in 12-minutes of ABM, ATT, or listening to a recording of sounds (control condition), once at the lab and then for six consecutive days at home, and monitoring changes before, during, and after the interventions.

column36: Investigating the Mechanisms of Immune Evasion by a Brazilian Zika Virus Isolate
column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) has recently emerged as a major global health burden, causing numerous outbreaks across South America since early 2015. The most concerning characteristic of these outbreaks is that ZIKV has become associated with more severe disease. This includes neurological symptoms like Guillain-Barre Syndrome, which causes paralysis, and fetal microcephaly, a condition that leads to children being born with poorly formed brains and heads. To understand this sudden change, our laboratory has established a mouse model of ZIKV infection, which we will use to study the immune response to various ZIKV strains that have or have not been associated with these complications. Our data indicate that recent strains are able to suppress important aspects of the anti-viral immune response in order to establish longer-lasting infections. We anticipate that recent strains are able to actively suppress the immune response by disrupting the production of a key anti-viral molecule, type I interferon, by the "first responders" of the immune system, innate immune cells. In addition, it has been shown that pregnancy temporarily weakens the mother's immune system to protect the developing fetus. Using our mouse model, we will explore the impact this has on the immune response to ZIKV during pregnancy, and how this relates to the fetal microcephaly seen during recent ZIKV outbreaks. Together, these studies will tell us how the virus has changed over time to evade the host immune response and establish more severe infections. We can use this information to develop vaccines and identify targets for anti-viral therapies to protect against and treat ZIKV infection.

column36: Titrating Mood on the Basis of Functional Networks: fMRI-guided Programming of Deep Brain Stimulation for Depression
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a widespread and debilitating condition that does not respond to medication or psychotherapy in up to 1/3rd of patients. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a surgical treatment for neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders in which electrical stimulation is delivered via implanted electrodes to specific brain circuits. In order to achieve good clinical responses to DBS, physicians must carefully select (i.e., 'program') several electrical stimulation settings, such as contact (which part of the electrode the electricity is delivered through) and voltage. DBS targeting the subgenual cingulate (SGC - a brain structure involved in mood regulation) has shown promising early results for treatment-resistant MDD. However, SGC DBS has been less successful in larger, controlled studies, likely due to suboptimal DBS programming. Compared to DBS for disorders like Parkinson's disease, DBS for MDD is particularly difficult to program because there is no immediate clinical feedback to help indicate which settings are 'optimal'. DBS programming is instead a trial-and-error process that usually requires multiple clinic visits and imposes substantial financial and time burdens on patients. Given the limitations of this current approach, there is a need for more objective, physiological markers of good response to DBS settings that could help guide DBS programming. Building upon extensive experience at my institution using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in DBS patients, I intend to use functional MRI (fMRI) to better understand and individualize DBS for MDD. Specifically, I aim to 1) use fMRI to investigate how DBS interacts with brain networks in MDD; 2) identify a brain connectivity pattern or 'signature' that is associated with good responses to DBS; 3) use this connectivity signature to guide the adjustment of contact settings in MDD patients who respond poorly to DBS in order to hopefully improve their clinical outcomes.

column36: Optimized manufacturing of thymus-derived regulatory T cells for immune cell-based therapy
column37: Blood and bone marrow transplants can be used to treat blood cancers such as leukemia. The transplant can provide a cure when the donor immune cells attack and kill leukemia cells. Unfortunately, the donor cells often also attack the patient's own tissue, causing serious short- and long-term consequences. To prevent these negative immune responses without inhibiting the anti-cancer effect of the transplant, our strategy is to also give patients a dose of the type of immune cell that suppress the negative immune responses. These are called regulatory T cells, or Tregs. Initial studies with Tregs have been promising, but there are many challenges to using Tregs as a therapy. One major issue is that Tregs are very rare - less than 1% of white blood cells - so to obtain enough cells to use in a patient, we must develop methods to isolate and grow Tregs. Rather than obtaining rare Tregs from blood, my goal is to isolate these cells from Treg-rich tissue and increase their numbers in the lab. For this study, the tissue source is the thymus gland, an immune organ located above the heart that is routinely removed during pediatric cardiac surgery. The thymus is a plentiful source of Tregs that are more uniform in their characteristics than Tregs in the blood. I am developing a protocol to grow thymus-derived Tregs that is compatible with clinical standards and will also identify new conditions that can further enhance Treg growth in culture. Ultimately, this work will result in methods to efficiently produce Tregs for cell therapy applications, a crucial step towards the clinical use of thymus-derived Tregs as a therapy to improve transplantation outcomes.

column36: The effect of a viral mimetic on the expression of nutrient transporters: Exploring the link between maternal immune activation and Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects 1.5% of Canadians. Characteristics of ASD include difficulties in behaviour, social interaction, and communication. Being a spectrum disorder, these symptoms can range from mild to severe, depending on the individual. Recent research has shown that women who are infected with a virus during pregnancy are at an increased risk of having a child with ASD. However, the underlying reason for this association is unknown. To help understand this association, we are investigating whether viral infection alters the transport of nutrients from the mother to the fetus. Many of the nutrients transferred from the mother to the fetus are required for the fetal brain to form properly. If viral infection causes physiological changes that alter the ability of nutrients to be transported to the fetus while the brain is developing, typical brain development could be impacted which could possibly result in ASD. To detect these physiological changes, we will use a pregnant rat model; we will mimic a viral infection in pregnant rats and then examine the placenta and fetal brain to identify changes that may alter nutrient transport. We will then identify the molecular pathways involved in these changes to understand how they occur. Identifying these changes and their causes will provide new treatment targets for early intervention in the development of ASD.

La litterature scientifique presente actuellement les parents comme obstacle critique a ce type de jeu en vertu de normes sociales liees a l'education des enfants. Des craintes croissantes pour la securite des enfants, des pratiques de surprotection, et des preferences envers d'autres activites academiques ou culturelles restreignent ainsi la place du jeu exterieur dans le quotidien des enfants. En milieu urbain, le declin du jeu exterieur serait aussi attribuable aux amenagements de moins en moins concus pour les besoins des enfants, releguant ces derniers a des espaces de plus en plus confines. Malgre ces constats, les facons de raviver le jeu exterieur sont peu connues. Depuis 2015, la Ville de Montreal implante son programme de rues pietonnes et partagees, creant de nouveaux espaces publics de proximite. En reprenant une partie de la voie publique existante pour y amenager des espaces actifs, ludiques et securitaires, ce programme a le potentiel de favoriser le jeu libre en milieu urbain. Ce projet vise a mieux comprendre comment une strategie de promotion du jeu libre axee sur le reamenagement d'un espace public, telles que les rues pietonnes et partagees, pourrait contribuer a optimiser les opportunites de jouer a l'exterieur pour les enfants et reduire les pratiques dites "intensives" des parents. Pour atteindre cet objectif, des peres et des meres seront mis a contribution au moyen d'entrevues et de questionnaires en ligne. S'inscrivant dans le secteur prioritaire de la "promotion des villes en sante" de l'Institut de la sante publique et des populations des IRSC, ce projet contribuera a comprendre comment l'amenagement des municipalites contribue a promouvoir la sante, tant pour les enfants que pour leurs parents.

column37: Chronic pain is one of the most underestimated health care problems in the world today, causing a major burden to the patient and society. In Canada, one in five adults experience chronic pain, with associated costs estimated at $40 billion a year and rising. On top of this, Canada is currently facing an opioid crisis, affecting many chronic pain patients who use opioid medications to manage their pain. Despite overwhelming evidence of the prevalence and impact of chronic pain on our society, research for pain is greatly underfunded. This results in a lack of understanding and treatment of the disease, with only a small percentage of patients achieving full recovery. Chronic facial pain can be especially debilitating, being described as one of the most excruciating pains one can experience. Therefore, technologies and advances that can help improve the care of patients with chronic facial pain is necessary. Towards this goal, neuroimaging and machine learning have the capacity to assess treatment response and help physicians with their clinical decision-making for an individual chronic facial pain patient. Neuroimaging uses various techniques to measure the structure and function of the brain. Machine learning provides a computer with the ability to learn from data, identify patterns, and make predictions on new, unseen data. My research combines neuroimaging techniques and machine learning to elucidate the brain features that distinguishes treatment responders from non-responders. Using this novel approach, physicians can draw on additional information to better evaluate the selection of optimal treatment and assessment of long-term outcome for patients with chronic facial pain. My research will ultimately advance our fundamental understanding of brain mechanisms in chronic facial pain and improve the quality of life for these patients.

column37: Despite evidence that criminalization promotes stigma, violence, HIV/STI burden and labour rights violations among sex workers, in 2014 Canada enacted end-demand sex work legislation (Protection of Exploited Communities and Persons Act, PCEPA) which upholds the criminalization of clients and third party activities while leaving the sale of sex legal. Qualitative research suggests im/migrant sex workers may fear jeopardizing their legal status (i.e., work permit) as a result of police interactions, which has been shown to impede reporting violence to authorities and limit health access through fear of disclosing sex work to health providers. Authorities' broad discretion in enforcing sex work and immigration laws, and the conflation of sex work (consensual exchange of sex services) and sex trafficking (forced sexual labour) among racialized women may exacerbate barriers to healthcare and legal protections. Given that punitive PCEPA and immigration enforcement may disproportionately impact im/migrant sex workers, there is an urgent need to assess how such criminalization impacts their health and human rights. As policy shifts impacting im/migrant sex workers in Canada have occurred despite a dearth of evidence on their experiences, and given the PCEPA's stated goal of protecting vulnerable communities, I will evaluate how shifts in criminalized interactions post-PCEPA relate to im/migrant sex workers' health access and human rights to inform national and global policy discussions on end-demand legislation.

column36: Exploring End of Life Nutrition Care Practices for Residents of Ontario Long-Term Care Homes: A Mixed Methods Approach
column37: Eating and nutrition care for residents at the end of life can be challenging in long-term care (LTC). As residents approach death, they will often lose their interest in food and may stop eating altogether. Conditions such as dementia can pose further challenges. The uncertainty of the dying process can be a great source of stress for family and care staff. Current recommendations for nutrition care at the end of life emphasize comfort and meeting personal care goals. However, it is unclear whether these recommendations are applied consistently in LTC homes. Further, the role of several factors (e.g., resources, policies, family wishes) that likely influence nutrition care decisions at the end of life are not well understood. The goal of this research is to explore the current state of nutrition care for LTC residents at the end of life, and to understand the influential factors behind these care decisions. Mixed methods will be used to gather data from residents, families, and care staff to gain an understanding of end of life nutrition care. Data from resident medical charts will be collected in 12 LTC homes from Ontario. The type of nutrition care practices provided will be identified and compared to resident characteristics (e.g., weight loss, swallowing problems). Interviews will also be conducted with residents, families, and staff who will be recruited on a voluntary basis from the same homes. These interviews will explore various perspectives of nutrition care and the associated decision-making processes among LTC staff, family, and residents at the end of life. Working together with residents, families and LTC staff, this research will help to describe current practices around nutrition care for residents at the end of life. Findings will improve the understanding of the current approaches to end-of-life nutrition care in Ontario LTC homes and is a key step towards improving personalized comfort care for residents up to the moment of death.

column36: The role of uncoupling proteins in post-burn wound healing and keloid formation
column37: Burns are responsible for an estimated 300,000 deaths per year worldwide, with approximately 11 million cases requiring medical attention. One of the negative consequences of thermal injuries is aberrant wound healing, such as keloids. Treatment and prevention of keloids is one of the greatest unmet challenges in burns, with no curative strategies at this time. Recent studies link local glucose and glucose transporter levels with wound healing. Specifically, lack of glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) impairs healing of wounds or UV-damaged skin. Conversely, lack of GLUT1 decreases inflammation and excessive tissue production in psoriasis. Therefore, local glucose levels and GLUT1 expression have an integral role in the balance between impaired and excessive healing in conditions like keloids. Elevated generalized glucose levels and inflammation are consequences of increased metabolism seen in burns. One of mediators involved in this increased metabolism are mitochondrial uncoupling proteins. Uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2), which is at many sites including skin, increases GLUT1 expression and facilitates glucose uptake. UCP2 also activates a mediator of inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome, which is elevated in burns. We propose that UCP2 expression is increased in burn skin and has role in normal and aberrant wound healing, likely through NLRP3 and GLUT1 expression. Ultimately, persistent alterations in inflammation and local glucose levels could detrimentally affect wound healing, predisposing patients to keloids.
