column36: Identifying early white matter changes within the brain that predict cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease using novel blood-based microparticle screening.
column37: With the aging population and rise of dementia, there is a need for an improved understanding of early markers of cognitive decline. Current treatment strategies have been largely ineffective at treating later disease states. The need to identify and halt early disease progression is being increasingly recognized. White matter inflammation is one of the earliest changes that predicts future dementia and occurs years before significant memory impairment. My work will focus on understanding how white matter inflammation contributes to cognitive decline, and how this can be detected in early stages of Alzheimer's disease. I will study profiles of proteins within the blood that are released by cells in the brain. They are released into the blood within microparticles called exosomes. I will study microparticles from the blood of healthy subjects and those with Alzheimer's disease to identify proteins that indicate white matter inflammation and dysfunction. This blood analysis will be combined with neuroimaging of white matter inflammation to assess the affected locations within the brain. I will then use drugs that reduce inflammation in the brain to test whether this can prevent cognitive impairment in a preclinical model. White matter inflammation is an ideal target because it precedes memory impairments and occurs in potentially treatable stages of the Alzheimer's disease. The outcome of this work will allow for the detection of microparticles that indicate damage to the white matter, representing novel blood-based screening for early Alzheimer's disease and a potential therapeutic target.

column36: Understanding the processes that dictate excitatory versus inhibitory neuronal cell fate specification from cortically derived neural stem cells
column37: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are brain cells that have the potential to make all neural cell types in the brain such as neurons or glial cells. The recruitment of endogenous NSCs for neurological repair is a promising area of biomedicine that is currently being investigated as a therapeutic strategy to regenerate damaged tissue following brain injury. The rationale of this strategy is to manipulate NSCs following brain injury and instruct them to produce new neurons to replace any particular neural tissue that would have been damaged from a brain injury such as stroke. One of the main challenges of this strategy is to ensure that the recruited NSCs produce the correct type of neurons to replace the cells that had died following the brain injury. This is challenging because NSCs are known to make different types of neurons in different contexts. For example, NSCs that come from the cerebral cortex have been shown to make two different types of neurons (excitatory neurons which trigger electric impulses and inhibitory neurons which inhibit electric impulses) at different periods of life: excitatory neurons are made prenatally whereas inhibitory neurons are made during adulthood. Our lab has previously shown that the extracellular environment or niche of a NSC plays a critical role in dictating NSC behaviour. The hypothesis of my research project states that the niche of a NSC plays an important role in instructing the NSC to make one type of neuron over another: the prenatal environment of cortical NSCs favours excitatory neuron production and the adult environment favours inhibitory neuron production. I hope to identify candidate factors within the niche that are essential in promoting either excitatory or inhibitory neuronal specification. The elucidation of these novel factors will lead to new insights regarding the mechanisms by which a NSC can be recruited to make the correct type of neuron in the context of endogenous repair following brain injury.

column36: Developpement et mecanismes cerebraux du raisonnement fluide chez les enfants sur le spectre de l'autisme
column37: Le raisonnement fluide est la capacite d'inferer des solutions a des problemes nouveaux en integrant et en manipulant les relations entre les items d'un probleme. Chez les individus au developpement typique, cette capacite se base sur l'activite d'un large reseau neuronal, impliquant le cortex parietal posterieur et le cortex prefrontal. Les personnes ayant un trouble du spectre de l'autisme (TSA) presentent des particularites sur le plan perceptif, avec un traitement preferentiel pour le contenu visuospatial. Ces particularites donnent lieu a des activations cerebrales distinctes pendant le raisonnement, qui se manifestent par une suractivation des aires occipitales et une sous-activation des aires frontales. Il est bien connu que la capacite de raisonner en se basant sur des liens semantiques plutot que perceptifs emergerait vers l'age de 5 ans chez les enfants au developpement typique. Comment la capacite de raisonnement se developpe-t-elle chez les enfants TSA, plus precisement sur les plans comportemental et cerebral? L'objectif du projet est de documenter la trajectoire developpementale des mecanismes cerebraux du raisonnement fluide d'enfants TSA. 30 enfants TSA et 30 enfants typiques, ages entre 6-14 ans, apparies en genre, age et quotient intellectuel (QI), completeront une tache de raisonnement informatisee, presentant un contenu (semantique vs visuospatial) et un niveau de complexite (simple vs complexe) varies, dans un appareil d'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle (IRMf). Une evaluation neuropsychologique sera effectuee (QI, memoire, raisonnement fluide) et deux collectes de donnees en IRMf seront realisees avec un intervalle de 2 ans. Les connaissances qui decouleront de ce projet auront des retombees sur 1) la comprehension du developpement cerebral des enfants TSA, 2) le developpement de methodes d'intervention adaptees a leurs particularites et 3) l'optimisation des methodes d'enseignement pour favoriser leurs apprentissages.

column36: Impaired Autonomic Signalling in the Sinoatrial Node During Angiotensin II Mediated Hypertensive Heart Disease
column37: The prevalence of hypertension (high blood pressure) in Canada has increased nearly 2-fold over the past 2 decades. Around 40% of adults suffer from hypertension which substantially increases the risk of life threatening cardiac arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms). A small area of specialized cells located in the upper right chamber of the heart are responsible for controlling the normal heart beat. This area, called the sinoatrial node, is commonly referred to as the heart's pacemaker. However, in diseases such as hypertension, the heart's pacemaker cells can become dysfunctional leading to abnormally low and dysregulated heart rates that can be life-threatening; this is known as "sinoatrial node disease" or "sick sinus syndrome". The autonomic nervous system (ANS) acts largely unconsciously and helps to regulate heart rate and pacemaker function. In individuals with sick sinus syndrome, the diseased pacemaker cells also begin to fail to respond to ANS signals causing a progressive worsening of heart function. Currently, artificial pacemaker implantation is the major treatment approach for sick sinus syndrome. However, this comes with substantial costs and a number of attendant risks including infections and lead dislodgment. This has serious implications as failure to appropriately regulate heart rate has been shown to increase the risk of long term morbidity and mortality. This indicates a clear need for improved treatment options for patients with sick sinus syndrome. Accordingly, my project aims to assess the mechanisms responsible for sick sinus syndrome and reduced ability for the ANS to regulate heart rate in the setting of hypertension. This study will provide critical new insight into why the heart's pacemaker fails to respond to ANS stimulation and may help facilitate the development of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of sick sinus syndrome.

column36: Effect of Gut Microbial Perturbations on Parkinson's Disease Progression
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease worldwide, characterized the death of certain nerve cells within the brain that produce the chemical dopamine. The loss of dopamine leads to movement symptoms such as tremors, problems with balance, and slowed muscle movement. In Canada, PD affects 1 in every 500 people. Genetic and environmental factors play a role, but in many cases the cause is unknown. PD is currently incurable and there is a desperate need for new and better treatment methods. Recently, the bacteria that live in the healthy human gut, or gut microbiota, have also been found to play a role in PD. Studies have found that PD patients have different amounts of certain bacteria present in their guts when compared to people of the same age without PD. Also, many patients report problems with their gut, such as constipation, that start many years before movement symptoms and official diagnosis with PD. This shows that we need to look more closely at what could be causing the early symptoms of PD, and that the gut microbiota might be a good place to start. In my study, I propose to use a mouse model of early PD. Mice are an excellent model for many human diseases because they are similar to humans in many ways, such as the fact that they have a gut microbiota. The model I propose to use has a genetic mutation that produces gut and movement symptoms similar to those in human PD patients. I plan to investigate how changing the gut microbiota influences these symptoms. The gut microbiota will be changed through treatment with antibiotics to wipe out bacteria or through the addition of certain bacterial species that are thought to influence PD. This study will reveal specific changes in gut bacteria that can influence PD and will increase our understanding of how this disease works. This is an important step towards understanding the early causes of PD, and developing better non-invasive treatments and preventative strategies.

column36: Physiological roles of the dark microglia in normal postnatal brain development
column37: One of the cells involved in brain development and maturation, as well as the normal function of adult brain is microglia, the brain-resident immune cells. Microglia can help the brain remain healthy by surveying the environment and clearing any harmful elements (i.e. dying neurons, cellular debris). A new subtype of these cells, named dark microglia, has been discovered by our laboratory led by Dr. Marie-Eve Tremblay. Dark microglia are particularly active around synapses, the structures that mediate the exchanges between neurons. Their interactions with these elements suggest that they could strongly influence the transmission of neuronal messages which could affect the brain's development. Despite their characterization in various conditions, including development, chronic social stress, aging, as well as neuropathologies (Alzheimer's disease), very little is known about the genes and proteins expressed by dark microglia. To this end, we have identified a specific protein to label dark microglia. This protein will allow us to identify and analyze their characteristics using imagery techniques to further deepen our knowledge of the dark microglia and their relevance during development. These cells will be isolated using a state-of-the-art technique known as single-cell RNA sequencing that will allow us to identify in an individual cells the unique set of genes that can become proteins. This study will help us understand the role of this new subtype in brain development. Since the elimination of superfluous synapses is particularly seen in postnatal brain development, we are confident that dark microglia could play a crucial role in this essential process. This knowledge could be essential to target these cells for eventual therapeutic avenues by modulating their interaction with synapses to prevent or limit the extent of pathological neurodevelopment.

column36: What works for whom, how and why? A Realist Evaluation of a Telehealth Heart Failure Disease Management (HFDM) Program
column37: Heart failure (HF) is the most common and costly disease for seniors in Canada. It weakens the heart and has deteriorating effects on patients' breathing, sleep, ability to work, and mental health. It requires frequent hospitalization, which increases suffering and expense. Heart Failure Disease Management Interventions (HFDMIs) are health services that help patients in taking better care of themselves in order to prevent from worsening of symptoms, leading to less frequent hospital admissions , reduced suffering and cost. These services consist of different components such as educating and following up with patients around medicines, diet, exercise, and symptoms; providing support; and improving access to care. HFDMIs are sometimes provided face-to-face during hospital stay, while sometimes these are provided via tele-health (through web, email and smart phone Apps) at home. At times, these are delivered by individual health professionals such as nurses or doctors or physiotherapists, or sometimes by combined teams of various health professionals. As HFDMIs are diverse in the way these are performed; therefore, it requires a sophisticated statistical analysis to compare the various HFDMIs. We will search for, and analyze data from the randomized trials of HFDMIs, published after 1994. This would be the largest and the most specific literature synthesis, which will identify the fine details around HFDMIs and the context in which these are more or less effective. Such as the HFDMIs that are more effective, using a specific mode of communication (in-person or tele-health), in a specific setting (home, hospital, general practice clinic), delivered by a specific or diverse group of health professionals. This will also be the first ever synthesis to identify the effect of patients' sex on the effectiveness of various parts of the HFDMIs. The findings will guide health professionals and policy makers to design and implement the specifically useful HFDMI components.

column36: Distress regulation during toddlerhood: Discerning parental influences.
column37: The term "Terrible Twos" is used to describe the intense and often unpredictable tantrums that many toddlers experience during the second year of life. This period of difficulty may be explained by the fact that toddlers are still developing distress regulation skills, the skills that we use to manage our emotions in stressful situations, such as when we experience a painful procedure, become frustrated, or receive bad news. While difficulties with distress regulation can be challenging for parents and caregivers to manage in the short term, these difficulties are associated with many types of mental health problems for the developing child later in life. Because of this, it's important to understand what factors contribute to children's distress regulation skills early in life so that at-risk children can be identified and supported. Social influences, and in particular, a child's parents and caregivers, are known to be an important factor contributing to the child's distress regulation skills. When a parent experiences stress, their ability to support their child may be negatively impacted. My project aims to understand how parent characteristics and behaviours predict more optimal or less optimal patterns in the child's distress regulation skills. To do this, the study will follow caregiver-toddler dyads at 12, 18, and 24 months, and record the child's physiology (heart rate) and behaviour during low-, moderate-, and high-distress situations. Characteristics of the parent (e.g., soothing behaviours, mental health, sociodemographic background, culture) will also be measured, in order to identify which characteristics might put children at risk of or protect them from less adaptive outcomes. This is the first step toward developing strategies to support parents in need, so that parents can in turn support their child in learning distress regulation skills that will prepare them to deal with stress in a healthy way.

column36: Physical activity and mental health: Does inflammation explain the relationship?
column37: Mental illness costs our health care system $51 billion per year. To address this burden, it is vital that treatments other than medication and therapy are explored. It is concerning that recent research has found that individuals with serious mental illness (SMI) may have higher levels of inflammation, the reactive process of the body's immune system when a threat is sensed (i.e. injury, infection), even if a threat is not present. In addition, in recent years there has been support for the use of physical activity as a treatment and prevention strategy for mental illness. Interestingly, it has been found that physical activity can decrease inflammation, among healthy individuals. Specifically, I will be looking at 4 different groups (i.e. individuals with depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and anxiety), and the effects that physical activity has on the inflammation levels of each group, and subsequent changes in mental health outcomes. If it is found that physical activity does exert positive changes in mental health and anti-inflammatory effects on those with SMI, this can provide support for its use as an additional treatment in psychiatric care. This would result in improved health of these individuals, and decreased health care spending. This study would be the first of its kind to assess levels of mental health and of inflammation following a physical activity intervention among individuals with SMI, and the first to assess these immune responses to physical activity by illness, the findings of which may inform the development of future condition-specific physical activity treatment.

column37: Opioid use during pregnancy is a growing public health concern. While poor health outcomes in infants have been documented, the developmental and long-term health outcomes associated with prenatal opioid exposure are poorly understood. We will compare the health of children with prenatal opioid exposure to children who were not exposed to estimate the effect of prenatal opioid exposure on child health and development. The opioid crisis and increase in Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome incidence make prenatal opioid exposure a major public health concern. Through rigorous and well-powered analyses this project will address a critical knowledge gap by identifying specific health risks and developmental deficits associated with prenatal opioid exposure. Findings can be used to inform perinatal and maternal care and to develop targeted health interventions to support healthy child development.

column36: A population health economics approach to assessing tuberculosis interventions in Ontario
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) recently surpassed HIV as the world's leading infectious disease. In Canada, TB rates declined between 1940 and 1980; however, annual rates have remained steady since then, with an estimated 1,600 TB cases diagnosed per year. Canada has endorsed the World Health Organization's EndTB Strategy, aiming to eliminate TB worldwide by 2050. To meet the elimination targets, Canada's TB rates must decline by 10% annually. Moving forward, it is essential to address the social determinants that impact TB infection rates, given that TB affects primarily Aboriginal and foreign-born populations. The economic evaluation of interventions is important in priority setting. However, the majority of economic evaluations focus on single biomedical interventions. For TB, where social determinants of health are important intervention targets in conjunction with biomedical interventions such as screening programs and novel vaccines, well-established methods for economic evaluations face several challenges: equity considerations, complexity of interventions, and the measurement of costs and benefits across multiple sectors. My research will expand established methods for economic evaluation by considering health and non-health outcomes in an equity informed economic evaluation approach. My research aims to (1) elicit societal values for non-health outcomes that may result from interventions aimed at social determinants of health using a discrete choice experiment (DCE); (2) estimate healthcare costs attributable to TB; and (3) assess the equity-informed cost-effectiveness of TB interventions considering health and non-health outcomes. My research will culminate in the development of a data-driven decision-analytic model that relies on real-world data and current literature to inform policy priorities for TB. This research will contribute to the understanding of TB in Ontario, and methods development for conducting economic evaluations on population health interventions.

column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) and Type 2 Diabetes are leading causes of health-related disability in Canada and cause more than sixty percent of global chronic disease-related deaths annually. While lifestyle factors contribute to the development of these conditions, recent evidence has shown that adversity during fetal life can increase the risk of developing these metabolic diseases in adulthood. Maternal obesity during pregnancy is one such adverse condition and a strong predictor of childhood obesity, insulin resistance, and hypertension, which precedes diabetes and CVD. Current estimates place nearly half of women as being overweight or obese during pregnancy. While efforts have been made to intervene during pregnancy to reduce offspring disease risk induced by maternal obesity, diet and lifestyle interventions in the second half of pregnancy do little to improve these outcomes. Attention has now shifted towards the period surrounding conception and early embryonic development as a window of intervention. This research aims to understand how obesity alters the earliest stages of development and how this predisposes to chronic diseases later in life. The embryonic period consists of rapid development of the placenta, an organ which principally supports fetal development. Placental dysfunction is a leading cause of pregnancy-related complications and is believed to underlie the connection between maternal obesity and childhood metabolic disease. Obesity has been described as an inflammatory condition, and this elevated inflammation may disturb early placental development with consequences for fetal growth and postnatal health, however this area has remained largely unstudied. Understanding how early placental development is altered in the context of obesity will help to inform strategies to intervene during the periconceptional window and prevent both complications during pregnancy as well as the metabolic disease burden in the next generation.

column37: Cigarette smoking (CS) remains a major contributor to the rising incidence of many pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases, most importantly chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The contents of CS induce damage in the lung tissue, which in turn causes an inflammatory response marked by the activation and recruitment of white blood cells to help initiate repair mechanisms. However, repeated injury caused by years of smoking leads to chronic inflammation and improper remodelling of the lung. Previous research has shown that the response to CS exposure involves mostly macrophages, responsible for the clearance of damaged tissue and debris, and neutrophils, normally involved in the response to bacterial infection. Although the cell types and the mediators involved in the response to CS have largely been identified, the extent to which each element of this network contributes to the healthy and/or pathological response is not well understood. The proposed project involves elucidating the specific and collective contributions of alveolar macrophages and neutrophils in the response to CS in acute and chronic conditions. Firstly, depletion or enrichment of individual cell populations will be assessed in mouse models to assess their impact on the response to short- and long-term CS exposure. Secondly, the effect of blocking specific inflammatory molecules on the development of lung damage and inflammation will be assessed in mice exposed to CS. Thirdly, collaboration with clinicians will allow for the collection of lung inflammatory cells from COPD and healthy patients to determine whether the activity of these cell types correlates with lung function. Elucidating which cell populations and which signaling molecules are involved in the development of lung damage and inflammation in response to CS will help us to better understand how the lung defends itself, how lung diseases like COPD develop and how best to tackle their treatment.

column36: Estradiol and cognitive functioning in the menopause transition.
column37: It is widely recognized that many women experience cognitive difficulties such as forgetfulness and poor concentration when they reach menopause, which begins one year after a woman's final menstrual period. However, it is much less recognized that as many as 50% of women report cognitive problems in the years leading up to menopause, otherwise known as the menopause transition (or 'perimenopause'). Although it has been proposed that the hormonal changes associated with the menopause transition may contribute, very little research has been devoted to studying cognitive deficits during this transition period. The goal of this study is therefore to improve our understanding of both the nature and hormonal causes of perimenopausal cognitive deficits. The proposed study will enroll 50 women aged 45-55 years who are complaining of cognitive difficulties and currently in the menopause transition (defined according to menstrual bleeding patterns). Once every three weeks across a 12-week period, the participants will provide a urine sample for hormone measurements and undergo cognitive testing, including assessments of immediate and delayed memory, attention, language and executive function. We anticipate that weeks characterized by low estrogen levels will also be characterized by deficits in cognitive ability. The results of this study will not only serve to validate and legitimize perimenopausal women's cognitive complaints but will also point to potential treatment options, including estrogen therapy, for women suffering from bothersome cognitive difficulties.

column37: Myelin basic protein (MBP) is a major protein constituent of the myelin sheath expressed by oligodendrocytes of the central nervous system (CNS). Its canonical function is to enable the adhesion of multilayered compact myelin throughout the CNS for improved saltatory conduction. We have recently demonstrated that MBP inhibits proliferation of two distinct populations of spinal cord derived neural stem cells (NSCs), in a dose dependent fashion without affecting their survival. Interestingly, this inhibitory effect of MBP is regionally distinct along the neuroaxis as revealed by the finding that primary cultures of forebrain-derived NSCs are not inhibited by exogenous MBP unless it is presented in the context of the spinal cord niche. The regionally distinct responsiveness is lost when pure populations of NSCs (i.e. cells derived from passaged neurospheres - cultured in the absence of niche cells) are not inhibited by exogenous MBP, irrespective of where they were derived (i.e. spinal cord or forebrain). The finding that MBP's effect on NSCs is regionally distinct along the neuraxis is consistent with MBP being classified as an intrinsically unstructured protein whereby its structure and function are both dependent on the microenvironment it is presented in, further supporting the finding that the stem cell niche is the key regulator of MBP's inhibitory actions on NSCs. We are currently in pursuit of analyzing possible regionally distinct structural differences in MBP using patented spectroscopic technology. We are also taking advantage of recombinant forms of MBP to try and elucidate the mechanism by which MBP inhibits NPC proliferation. Our current research has implications for understanding the role of the stem cell niche in regulating NPC behaviour and finding potential therapeutic targets for stem cell based regenerative strategies for brain and spinal cord repair following injury.

column37: Brain surgery is among the most effective treatment options to cure childhood diseases such as drug-resistant epilepsy, brain tumors, and stroke. column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a degenerative brain disorder that affects over six million individuals worldwide. However, certain lifestyle factors such as stress, diet, pesticide exposure, and exercise have been associated with increased or decreased rates of PD. These factors can alter how genes are regulated, and might help explain why PD develops in some individuals but not others. My project will investigate how pesticides, high fat diet, and stress affect gene regulation in healthy individuals and whether each environment may increase risk of PD. To understand how these environments affect the brain, I will use human neurons and brains of mice, that are either healthy or have PD genetic risk. To discover whether we can detect markers of PD before diagnosis, I will also look at blood samples from early-stage PD patients. With information on which patients were exposed to pesticides and how much each person smoked and drank alcohol, I will explore whether indicators of PD are specific to certain lifestyles. This work will enhance our understanding of how disease develops and why it affects some individuals more than others, ultimately leading to identification of early indicators of PD, novel therapeutic targets, and lifestyle prevention strategies.

column37: Ovarian cancer remains one of the deadliest cancers in spite of growing knowledge on its underlying mechanisms. Changes in their expression patterns can be used to distinguish types of tumour, reflect the underlying gene defects, and point to sensitivity or resistance to drug treatment. With this project, we will use miRNA profiles to guide our understanding of the genetic defects underlying HGSOC, and determine the interplay of TP53, BRCA1 and miRNAs in response to drug treatments. Towards this, we will develop a panel of HGSOC cell lines bearing very specific genetic lesions in TP53 and BRCA1, using genome edition methods (CRISPR). We will define the impact of these gene defects on miRNA expression with and without treatment with anticancer drugs, and determine their functional importance for treatment sensitivity in HGSOC. This project will provide insight on the synergistic actions of P53 and BRCA1 through miRNAs, and potentially new mechanisms of drug resistance in HGSOC.

column37: Le vieillissement actif et en sante est une importante cible des societes vieillissantes necessitant davantage d'interventions a visee preventive. Developpe et experimente en Californie, le Lifestyle Redesign(R) (LR) est une intervention d'ergotherapie preventive realisee principalement en groupe et qui a pour objectif de soutenir le developpement de modes de vie sains et signifiants. En raison des evidences scientifiques indiquant une amelioration du fonctionnement, de la vitalite, de la sante mentale globale, de la qualite des interactions sociales de meme que de la satisfaction envers la vie chez ses participants, cette intervention est hautement pertinente pour les aines quebecois et canadiens. Recemment traduite et adaptee au Quebec, la version francophone du LR n'a cependant pas ete implantee en milieu clinique quebecois et aucune etude n'a documente son efficacite et sa rentabilite dans ce contexte. Ce projet de recherche vise donc a evaluer les effets a court terme du LR sur la sante, la participation sociale et les loisirs des aines ainsi qu'a documenter sa rentabilite, tel qu'implante pour une premiere fois en milieu clinique quebecois. Pour ce faire, un essai clinique a repartition aleatoire sera realise dans huit milieux (6 prives et 2 publics). Ces milieux recruteront 19 a 20 participants pour un total de 154 aines (77 par groupe) autonomes ou a risque de perte d'autonomie et habitant dans la communaute. Ces personnes seront reparties au hasard en deux groupes : l'un recevant le LR et l'autre les services sociaux et de sante usuels. Au terme de six mois d'intervention, une analyse des questionnaires, des journaux de bord et des entrevues individuelles aupres des ergotherapeutes sera realisee. Issu d'un partenariat exceptionnel entre la clinique, la communaute et la recherche, ce projet contribuera a soutenir l'integration d'approches preventives innovantes susceptibles d'ameliorer la sante et le mieux-etre des Canadiens vieillissants.

column36: Improving transferability of clinical decision support systems: estimating bounds for dataset-specific generalization error and rescuing performance with transfer learning
column37: Clinical decision support tools are currently revolutionizing the field of medicine. These tools help clinicians stay on top of their patients' risk for things like sepsis, cardiac arrest, and cancer so when these tools don't work as expected, the results can be devastating. My PhD research will tackle one reason these tools may misbehave known as "dataset shift". Dataset shift occurs when the data you develop your tool in is so different from the data it's being applied to that errors occur more frequently than one would expect. To combat this problem, I will first develop a set of statistics that will let users know if there is the potential for increased errors when using a given tool in their institution (with their own data). I will then test and develop methods to improve tools for specific patient populations, once users identify that a tool will not work in their institution. These methods will be developed and tested on different types of predictive systems using imaging, genomic, streaming, and patient record data to compare their efficacy across these settings. They will also be directly incorporated into predictive systems that are currently being developed so these statistics describing predictive accuracy and methods to improve transferability will be rapidly translated to clinical use. It is important that clinical decision support tools behave as expected since the information they provide can result in life or death. Moreover, having a way to avert large errors that occur when transferring these tools to different institutions will allow more remote populations to safely enjoy the same benefits from clinical decision support tools that major research hospitals are able to.

column36: How do adult cancer patients and their healthcare providers perceive, respond to, and manage uncertainty related to incidental results from genome sequencing?
column37: Genome sequencing is a new type of genetic test that can help diagnosis and manage patients' risk for hereditary cancers. A challenge with using this test is that risks for thousands of other diseases can also be found, called "incidental results." There is a lot of uncertainty associated with these incidental results. It is uncertain if or when the diseases associated with them will occur, and what the impacts of the disease will be on patients' lives. Patients may feel uncertain about what their incidental results mean for their health, or how to act on them. Uncertainty may cause over-diagnosis, over-treatment, and misuse of health services. The impacts of uncertainty related to incidental results on adult cancer patients and their healthcare providers are not known. This study will address the question, how do adult cancer patients and their healthcare providers (primary care and genetics specialists) perceive, respond to and manage uncertainty related to incidental results from genome sequencing? Patients will be participants in a trial (n=260) where they will receive genome sequencing, and half will have the option to learn incidental results. Using survey scales, I will measure perceived uncertainty, psychological distress, and health service use at baseline, 2 weeks, 1 month, 6 months and 1 year after return of results. I will compare perceived uncertainty between patients who receive incidental results and those who do not. Among patients who receive incidental results, I will evaluate the relationship between perceived uncertainty and distress, and between perceived uncertainty and health service use. I will also conduct interviews with up to 30 patients to explore their experiences with uncertainty in more depth. I will interview up to 30 healthcare providers who care for these patients, to explore their experiences with managing their patients' incidental genome sequencing results. This research could inform how genome sequencing is offered clinically.

column36: Indigenous Data Sovereignty in Canada and Beyond
column37: Prior to settler contact, Indigenous peoples practiced traditional healing methods that were embedded in ceremony and other culturally appropriate means. Today, in the wake of colonization, there is an unequal distribution of mental health services for individuals who reside in Ontario's rural, remote, and air access communities. These individuals also face increased mental health challenges for a variety of reasons including; geographic isolation, cross-generational impacts from colonization, discrimination, marginalization, and economic and social conditions that can negatively influence individuals and whole communities. Many First Nations communities across Canada are taking innovative and effective measures to address the mental wellness of members within their communities through community and family-based programs that offer local and culturally relevant approaches to wellness and resilience. Through the use of an Indigenous research paradigm, this project aims to shed light on the Weeneebayko Area Health Authority's (WAHA) mental health system's response to MHA needs within the James and Hudson Bay regions for young adults aged 18 to 29. This project will incorporate a mixed-methods design. The three objectives of this work include: 1) Describing WAHA physician perspectives on the MHA care of patients who have been given a Form 1; 2) Determining the rates of Emergency Department (ED) visits for young adults in WAHA who have experienced a Form 1; and 3) Documenting the experiencing of providing MHA care to young adults from the perspectives of front-line workers who offer in-community MHA care and services.

column36: Les associations entre les caracteristiques et la disponibilite des ressources infirmieres, le rationnement des soins et la survenue de la mortalite et d'evenements indesirables aux soins intensifs.
column37: Introduction : Plusieurs etudes ont mis en evidence des associations ecologiques entre les caracteristiques des ressources infirmieres aux soins intensifs (SI) et l'incidence de la mortalite et d'evenements indesirables (EI). Pour expliquer ces associations, on suppose qu'en situation de manque de ressources, les infirmieres rationnent certains soins importants requis par l'etat de sante des patients. Or, cette hypothese n'a jamais pu etre verifiee empiriquement, faute d'un instrument valide mesurant le rationnement des soins. L'etude doctorale proposee vise a: 1) developper et valider un instrument de mesure du rationnement des soins infirmiers aux SI; 2) decrire la prevalence et les caracteristiques du rationnement aux SI, et; 3) examiner ses associations avec les caracteristiques des ressources infirmieres et l'incidence de la mortalite et d'EI. Methodes : Un devis de recherche mixte en trois phases est propose. Phase 1 : Une analyse conceptuelle permettra de generer une liste preliminaire d'enonces et d'echelles mesurant le concept de rationnement aux SI. L'approche iterative par sondage Delphi sera ensuite employee aupres d'un comite d'experts afin d'en etablir la validite de contenu. Phase 2 : Une enquete provinciale sera realisee aupres des infirmieres des SI afin de decrire la prevalence et les caracteristiques du rationnement dans ce milieu. Phase 3 : Une cohorte de patients admis aux SI de deux centres hospitaliers universitaires quebecois permettra d'examiner les associations entre les caracteristiques des ressources infirmieres, le rationnement des soins et l'incidence de la mortalite et d'EI. Resultats attendus: Cette etude produira un instrument valide du rationnement des soins infirmiers aux SI. Il pourra permettre : 1) decrire l'impact du rationnement des soins aux SI sur la securite de services offerts; 2) aux gestionnaires d'evaluer l'efficacite d'interventions visant a reduire son incidence et ses effets indesirables pour les patients.

column36: Decrypting Cryptogenic Strokes using an Integrated Molecular Approach
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, most often caused by a blockage of an artery leading to reduced blood flow to the brain. One in every four stroke patients have no identifiable cause of disease and are considered "cryptogenic". Beyond the frustration of being unable to pinpoint the cause of disease, cryptogenic stroke patients are at greater risk of having additional strokes. No effective treatments to prevent these secondary strokes are currently available, and this is largely due to the fact that so little is known about the biology of cryptogenic stroke. Therefore, there is an urgent need to study the biology of cryptogenic stroke in order to develop effective and safe treatments. We propose to study the genes and proteins that may predispose and help diagnose cryptogenic stroke patients using a systematic and comprehensive approach. More specifically, we will examine millions of genetic variants and thousands of proteins to find those that are most strongly associated with risk of cryptogenic stroke. We hypothesize that some genes and proteins will be highly predictive of cryptogenic stroke. Learning about the specific molecular markers that have a strong role in cryptogenic stroke will hopefully bring clarity to this subgroup of stroke patients and their caregivers who are desperately in need of answers and effective treatments.

column36: Investigating the Regulation of Muscle Stem Cell Polarity during Muscle Regeneration
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating childhood disorder marked by severely debilitating muscle weakness that worsens with age. DMD arises as a consequence of muscular degeneration caused by a genetic mutation that primarily affects boys, with a worldwide incidence of 1 in every 3500 male births. Defects caused by the mutant gene create abnormalities in muscle fibers and muscle stem cells. Because of these abnormalities, the muscles of people with DMD are highly prone to damage. Normally, muscle stem cells are able to easily heal injured muscle; however, the muscle stem cells residing in people with DMD are defective and can't keep up with the muscle damage. Even with current treatments, boys with the disease are wheelchair bound between the ages of 9-12, paralysed below the neck by 21, and usually die in their 20's or 30's due to heart or breathing failure. Previous studies in our lab have shown that treatment with a specific protein (Wnt7a) improves the symptoms of DMD. Wnt7a improves DMD symptoms by stimulating the defective muscle stem cells to multiply and heal damaged muscle more effectively. However, the cellular mechanism behind Wnt7a's ability to improve muscle stem cell function remains unknown. My project aims to identify precisely how Wnt7a improves muscle regeneration by studying the molecular events responsible for making a muscle stem cell divide and multiply. Studying the molecular events within muscle stem cells will allow us to use Wnt7a more effectively for improving muscle regeneration, and potentially reveal new therapeutic targets for treating people suffering from DMD. The ultimate goal of this research is to set the stage for Wnt7a's use as a clinical therapeutic that improves the quality of life and lifespan of people suffering from DMD. Furthermore, it is predicted that this treatment will be used to regenerate muscle in combination with future gene therapies that attempt to fix the underlying genetic mutation that causes DMD.

column36: A novel mechanism of reactive oxygen species-induced synthetic lethality in lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, mainly due to the lack of effective drugs available. This project studies a new way to inhibit lung cancer cells that focuses on exploiting cancer's inability to balance a chemical process called redox. A large-scale screen of ~200,000 chemical compounds revealed a new drug that selectively kills lung cancer cells but not normal cells. We discovered that in lung cancer cells, this drug disrupts redox balance, and that normal cells are resistant to its effects. This project aims to find the molecular target for this new drug and to understand how, in detail, it kills cancer cells. By using a new drug to prove that redox balance is a weakness of lung cancer cells, we can bring forward a new strategy for cancer therapeutics. This approach may also yield applications for other cancer types and therefore has significant potential to move drug development forward and impact a large subset of cancer patients.

column36: Investigating the molecular basis of the Nedd4-FGFR1 interaction and its role in cancer
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada, accounting for 30% of deaths nationwide in 2017. Oftentimes, cancer is associated with detrimental mutations in many proteins, causing them to have altered structures and functions. My project focuses on Nedd4 and FGFR1, two proteins that are often mutated in cancer. FGFR1 is a receptor involved in processes such as cell growth and differentiation, while Nedd4 is an enzyme that regulates FGFR1 degradation. Mutations in either protein may result in uncontrolled cell growth and differentiation, phenomena often seen in cancer. The goal of my project is to determine why a subset of Nedd4 mutations, specifically those located at the FGFR1 binding interface, are associated with cancer. To do so, I will create these Nedd4 mutants and introduce them into cells to study if they can bind FGFR1 and induce its degradation. Moreover, I will introduce these mutants into cancer cells to see how they affect various parameters such as cell proliferation. Finally, I will utilize a technique called nuclear magnetic resonance to solve the structure of the Nedd4:FGFR1 complex. Understanding how these proteins interact at a microscopic level would allow for strategic drug design for future cancer therapy.

column36: Determining Vertebral Stability on Metastatically Involved Vertebrae using Deep Learning
column37: The spine is the most common site of secondary tumour growth for patients with breast, prostate, lung and renal cancers. These tumours can cause osteolytic and/or osteoblastic diseases and in severe cases lead to vertebral compression fracture (VCF). An effective way to treat these tumours is with Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT). However, a complication with SBRT is induced VCF ranging from 10% to 40% occurrence rate. Current evaluation of the risk of SBRT induced VCF is done based on a scoring of six criteria, but this score only provides a qualitative metric to determine risk of fracture. Previous work has shown that the size of the osteolytic tumour compared to overall size of the vertebral body is highly linked to VCF occurring. However, that work did not provide a quantifiable probability of fracture, only a threshold for when it is more likely to occur. The proposed work here is to use deep learning to evaluate both Computed Tomography (CT) images and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to provide a quantitative probability of fracture occurring. This will be done by developing a network that can first isolate a vertebral body from the different images and extract information of the vertebral body including size of the tumour and vertebral body and shape of the spine. This information will then be used to determine the probability of the vertebra fracturing.

column36: Process-specific Cortical Contributions of Olfaction and Memory: A Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Study of Cognitive Decline
column37: Dementia currently affects more than 700,000 people in Canada, impacting both their life expectancy and quality of life. Effects are widespread, with ramifications extending beyond their own life and into the lives of their family, friends, and the larger society they live in. The incidence of dementia is projected to rise over the coming decades, but no system is currently in place to quickly and cheaply screen large populations for risk of dementia. The earliest symptom of Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia, is traditionally considered to be the progressive loss of memory and cognitive ability that individuals suffer as a result of the disease. Unfortunately, cognitive decline occurs well into disease progression and is a symptom of significant neurodegeneration. However, an emerging body of evidence strongly indicates that olfactory declines precede the onset of cognitive impairment and dementia by 5-15 years and, significantly, that with early detection, interventions may be more effective in preventing or treating cognitive decline and AD dementia. The olfactory system has rich cortical representation in the brain. To capture this, we will use Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy to examine brain activation patterns in olfactory and memory tests in individuals with and without dementia. We expect that those with a high risk of dementia can be differentiated from normal controls, providing additional information on how to detect and monitor early-stage neurodegenerative disease using inexpensive tests that can scale up to screen populations. Early detection and monitoring could maximize targeted interventions, leading to more preventative measures, personalized care, and better patient outcomes. This study will lay the groundwork for olfactory interventions and aims to take a proactive approach to understanding and addressing cognitive decline via targeting the improvement of health outcomes in the areas of prevention and diagnosis.

column37: Many infectious bacteria surround themselves in capsules, which are surface layers of long- chain polymers formed from complex sugars. column36: Imagining the glass half-full: An intervention to improve negative interpretation bias in GAD
column37: In 2012, 2.4 million Canadians reported suffering from generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in their lifetime. GAD is a chronic condition characterized by excessive and uncontrollable worry, associated with high medical utilization (e.g., high risk of heart attacks, peptic ulcer disease) and considerable societal and economic burden (e.g., high unemployment). Over 50% of Canadians with GAD report their mental health needs go unmet, which necessitates research on novel interventions for GAD that are effective and easy to disseminate. Cognitive bias modification (CBM) is a computerized intervention that directly targets a process that maintains worry and GAD: the tendency to appraise ambiguous information in a negative or catastrophic way. CBM training repeatedly guides favorable appraisals of ambiguous information. Research in depression has found that the effects of CBM are augmented through the use of mental imagery. The present study is a novel investigation of the therapeutic potential of imagery enhanced CBM (IE-CBM) for GAD. Individuals with GAD will be assigned to one of three conditions: 1) IE-CBM where they will practice generating positive resolutions of ambiguous information using mental imagery; 2) CBM, in which participants will complete the CBM training without instruction to use imagery; and 3) a neutral condition that will determine whether it is the act of reading scenarios alone that improves GAD related processes. All conditions will complete 30 minutes of their respective practice at home every day for 7 days. It is hypothesized that IE-CBM will lead to the greatest improvements in GAD processes, relative to the other conditions, pre- to post-training and at a 2-week follow-up. IE-CBM has considerable promise as an intervention to improve the tendency to assume the worst in GAD, a tendency that maintains chronic worry. PI-CBM is inexpensive, easy to disseminate, and could help meet the high mental health care needs of Canadians with GAD.

column36: Connectivite cerebrale fonctionnelle au repos dans l'apnee obstructive du sommeil chez les personnes d'age moyen et agees
column37: L'apnee obstructive du sommeil (AOS) est un probleme de sante majeur qui se caracterise par des arrets respiratoires repetees au cours du sommeil. Bien que les consequences specifiques de l'AOS sur un cerveau vieillissant ne soient pas entierement connues, l'evaluation du fonctionnement cerebral a l'aide de la neuroimagerie pourrait etre un marqueur precoce d'atteintes cerebrales et de risque de neurodegenerescence chez les personnes agees presentant de l'AOS. Or, l'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle (IRMf) mesuree au repos permet d'evaluer comment les regions du cerveau sont connectees ensemble et fonctionnent entre elles. En effet, la connectivite cerebrale fonctionnelle est modifiee lors d'atteintes cerebrales et de maladie neurodegenerative comme la maladie d'Alzheimer. Le premier objectif de mon projet est d'evaluer la relation entre la severite de l'AOS chez des individus ages et la connectivite cerebrale fonctionnelle. Ensuite, notre second objectif est de determiner si ces changements de connectivite cerebrale fonctionnelle chez les individus atteints d'AOS predit un declin cognitif accelere apres un delai de 18 mois. Pour atteindre ces objectifs, 80 sujets ages de 55 a 85 ans ont ete recrutes dans les dernieres annees. Parmi les participants, des sujets en sante sans AOS et des sujets de toutes les severites d'AOS seront representes. Les participants ont ete enregistres pour une nuit de polysomnographie afin d'evaluer la severite de l'AOS. Une evaluation neuropsychologique et une evaluation en neuroimagerie IRMf ont ete completees. Les sujets ont par la suite ete evalues en neuropsychologie avec des versions alternatives des tests 18 mois apres la premiere evaluation.

column36: Spatial variation in PM2.5 oxidative potential and its relationship with neurodegenerative disease
column37: Exposure to ambient air pollution particles is associated with a wide range of negative health outcomes, ranging from short-term respiratory issues to chronic diseases including cardiovascular disease and cancer. However, assessing a population's exposure to particulate air pollution remains a major challenge in epidemiologic studies of the health effects of air pollution. Individuals are exposed to a complex mixture of particles which vary in size, shape, surface area, chemical composition, and origin and may have differing impacts on health outcomes. The ability of particles to cause oxidative stress in the human body has been identified as a possible mechanism for the health effects associated with air pollution exposure. A new metric, oxidative potential, has been developed as a means to assess exposure to air pollution that reflects the ability of particulate matter to cause oxidative stress. Despite increasing evidence of an association between air pollution exposure and neurological disease, the relationship between oxidative potential and chronic neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia has not been evaluated. In the proposed project, I will characterize the spatial variability in oxidative potential that exists in two Canadian cities, develop models for oxidative potential, and apply these models in cohort studies based on existing databases of administrative data to estimate the association between oxidative potential of particulate air pollution and dementia incidence. By identifying new disease-exposure relationships, this research will inform policy on air pollution regulation in Canada. Ultimately, I hope to enable the development of more efficient risk reduction strategies to improve the health of Canadian urban populations.

column36: The liabilities associated with repurposing apramycin for the clinic: a genomic enzymology study of the unprecedented apramycin-resistance enzyme ApmA
column37: The global threat of antibiotic resistance has created an urgent need for new antibiotics. With a considerable lack of new drugs in the pipeline, older classes of antibiotics are being reconsidered for their effectiveness in the clinic. The aminoglycoside apramycin has been traditionally used in veterinary medicine, however, it has now become an attractive candidate as a repurposed therapeutic. Due to its unique structure, apramycin has the potential to be the saving grace against priority pathogens when all other clinically relevant aminoglycosides, including the next-generation aminoglycoside plazomicin, are ineffective. Prior to its introduction into the clinic it is important to understand any resistance mechanisms that may become a liability or threaten apramycin's success as a drug. As such, the goal of this project is to understand the recently discovered resistance element apmA. This work aims to provide an understanding of the mechanism of resistance for the encoded enzyme and how it has evolved to modify apramycin along with other aminoglycosides. Originally found in bacterial isolates from farm animals, this gene will render apramycin ineffective in the clinic against pathogens deemed a priority by the World Health Organization. Results gathered thus far show the encoded protein to be a from a family of enzymes that have not yet been encountered in hospitals with respect to aminoglycoside resistance. Researchers will be able to use the knowledge obtained through this work to better guide the development of apramycin analogues that can circumvent this unforeseen form of resistance.

column36: Determining the role of peroxisome contact in maintaining mitochondrial health
column37: All cells contain membrane bound compartments, called organelles. There are many different types of organelles in the cell, each with a specific function, that must work together for cells to function properly. One organelle of particular interest is the mitochondria, as they are consistently seen to be dysfunctional in neurological diseases (and thus may be what is causing disease). Scientists are therefore interested in learning more about the mechanisms cells normally use to keep mitochondria healthy, and how these mechanisms may break down and cause disease. The peroxisome, another organelle in the cell, may be one of these mechanisms. Peroxisomes appear to be very important for mitochondrial health as cells that are unable to form peroxisomes have severely dysfunctional mitochondria. While peroxisomes and mitochondria are known to work together in several cellular functions, such as lipid metabolism and oxidative species maintenance, we don't know specifically how peroxisomes keep mitochondria healthy. One mechanism that peroxisomes may use to affect mitochondria health is through membrane contact sites. Membrane contact sites are small areas where organelles come into physical contact with each other. This contact is facilitated by interactions between tether proteins on adjacent organelle membranes, somewhat like an "organelle handshake". Membrane contact sites act as a means of quickly and directly exchanging metabolites and communication signals between organelles, and are very important for organelle function. We hypothesise that peroxisomes and mitochondria connect through a membrane contact site and that this contact is important to maintain normal mitochondria functioning. We aim to identify the tether proteins between mitochondria and peroxisomes, what signals are being exchanged at the peroxisome mitochondria contact site, and how the breakdown of this contact site might be involved in the mitochondrial dysfunction observed in neurological disease.

column36: Identification des reservoirs du VIH competents pour la replication au cours des traitements antiretroviraux.
column37: Le virus responsable du SIDA, le VIH, cause une infection dont il n'est pas possible de guerir a ce jour. Les traitements antiretroviraux, mieux connus sous l'appellation tritherapie, permettent de controler la replication du virus, ce qui freine la progression de la maladie chez les gens vivant avec le VIH en plus d'empecher l'infection de nouvelles personnes. En revanche, cette medication doit etre prise a vie, puisqu'une interruption de traitement provoque inevitablement un retour de la replication virale. Au cours de ce << rebond viral >>, certains virus endormis, dits en latence, se reactivent pour produire de nouvelles particules virales infectieuses. Le virus est alors a nouveau detectable dans le sang du patient. La population de cellules infectees avec des virus inactifs constitue le reservoir viral. La guerison du VIH passe donc par leur elimination. Mais ceci n'est pas simple pour plusieurs raisons. En effet, on retrouve principalement le reservoir latent parmi des cellules appelees lymphocytes T memoires, des cellules de la defense immunitaire qui persistent dans le corps pour toute la duree de la vie. De plus, au sein de ce reservoir cellulaire, il n'y a qu'une tres petite proportion de virus latents qui ont le pouvoir de retablir une infection active, ce qui represente moins d'une cellule par million. Finalement, aucun marqueur connu ne permet de discerner specifiquement ces cellules reservoirs. Mon projet de doctorat vise donc a identifier des marqueurs caracteristiques de ces tres rares cellules infectees pour pouvoir les eliminer sans endommager le reste du systeme immunitaire. Ainsi nous pourrons developper des traitements curatifs contre le VIH qui elimineront specifiquement ces cellules infectees sans toucher les autres cellules necessaires au bon fonctionnement du systeme immunitaire. Les personnes infectees par le VIH seront ainsi gueries et pourront vivre sans prendre de traitement.

column36: Novel Radiotracers Targeting Proteases Overexpressed in Invasive Cancers
column37: Approximately 1 in 2 Canadians will be diagnosed with a type of cancer during their lifetimes, with a mortality rate of 1 in 4. One key contributor to the higher mortality rate is the spread of cancerous cells throughout the patient's body, called metastasis. Therefore, diagnosing and treating the cancer prior to metastasis would greatly improve the odds of successful treatment. One key player in metastasis are proteases, which are proteins that speed up the normal recycling of other proteins. However, in cancers, they can destroy the tissue around the tumour site, enabling their spread, and participate in other processes that enable tumour tissue growth. There is a significant focus on developing methods to monitor protease activity in tumours to ascertain the degree of aggressiveness and potential for metastasis. One method doctors use to diagnose cancers is called positron emission tomography (PET), where the patient receives a small dose of a radioactive drug, which enters the tumour and sends a signal to a camera, localizing the tumour. Furthermore, these radioactive drugs can be used to detect cancers based on specific traits. Our goal is to develop specific radioactive drugs that target select species of proteases overexpressed in cancers by putting a radioactive tag on chemical structures that bind to the proteases. These radioactive drugs will be investigated in animals carrying different types of cancers. This strategy has shown promise in targeting a family of proteases called matrix metalloproteinases and a protease called matriptase, both of which are highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic cancers. This research will enable the development of the next generation of imaging agents, enabling the diagnosis and differentiation of aggressive types of cancers, improving the prognosis of cancer patients in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Epidemiology of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae infection in hospitals: bridging within-host, between-host and between-hospital scales using mathematical modelling, statistical inference and computer simulation to predict dynamic transmission pathways and inform infection control
column37: A growing number of bacterial pathogens have evolved antimicrobial resistance (AMR), limiting options to treat and contain infections that were once easily managed. Evidence is required to inform investment in the prevention of these infections, particularly in hospitals where the burden of AMR is most dire. Yet understanding AMR control is complicated by the multiple scales at which it operates: within patients, AMR arises through genetic mutation and the sharing of resistance genes between bacteria; between patients, bacterial transmission depends on types and levels of inter-human contact; and across health systems, AMR outbreaks depend on the movement of patients within and between wards and hospitals. These scales have traditionally been studied in isolation, precluding a holistic view of AMR dynamics. The goal of my PhD is to use epidemiological and biostatistical methods to unify these scales into one framework, and to use this multi-scale structure to predict optimal means of AMR control. First, I will develop mathematical models of bacterial evolution and transmission to describe theoretical dynamics of AMR emergence across scales. Second, I will use this model to analyze AMR transmission in a real hospital setting, as informed by analysis of an existing hospital dataset that includes longitudinal samples of patient microbiota to capture within-host dynamics, and inter-human contact patterns to capture between-patient transmission. Third, I will build this within-hospital transmission network into a regional model of patient transfer between multiple hospitals. Lastly, I will use the resulting multi-scale model to conduct simulation studies of hospital outbreaks and potential interventions. This novel bridging of within-host, between-host and between-hospital scales will facilitate improved estimation of optimal AMR control, and resulting estimates of the clinical and cost efficacy of interventions should ultimately inform clinical practice and policy.

column36: Characterization and Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA in Liquid Biopsy for Cancer
column37: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death in Canada and technologies to detect and monitor the disease are sorely needed. Currently, this is done through frequent tissue biopsy, but this is unpractical and challenging if the tumor is too small. Alternatively, cancer mutational targets can be found in the blood and saliva of cancer patients in a concept called liquid biopsy. Recently, the fragment lengths of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has been shown to differ amongst cancer and healthy patients which can explain why current DNA detection technologies such as digital droplet PCR have difficulty finding tumor DNA in biofluids. Electric field-induced release and measurement (EFIRM) technology, however, can detect these tumor fragments accurately in plasma and saliva samples from lung cancer patients. We hypothesize that a combination of shorter circulating tumor DNA and EFIRM's mechanics may explain the detection performance in biofluids. This proposal has three fundamental goals to scientifically underpin the performance of EFIRM liquid biopsy. Firstly, we will isolate DNA from plasma and saliva samples from lung cancer patients to study various characteristics, one being length. Secondly, we will examine and describe how DNA capturing probe design and density impact EFIRM's ability to locate tumor DNA in biofluids. Thirdly, we will use EFIRM to demonstrate a proof of concept of liquid biopsy by measuring the changes of tumor DNA in the saliva and blood samples of lung cancer patients throughout their cancer treatment. The impact of this study is multi-factorial. Learning about tumor DNA characteristic will provide new biological information about these tumor biomarker targets. Understanding EFIRM fundamental mechanics will reveal the scientific rationale of its performance. Third, we will introduce a tool which can reliably monitor and adjust drug selection in patients undergoing cancer therapy.

column36: Identifying Immunological Basis for Bladder Cancer Sex Bias
column37: Bladder cancer incidence shows an enigmatic male bias, as it is the 4th most common cancer in men but only the 12th most common cancer in women in Canada. The bias cannot be fully accounted for by lifestyle factors such as smoking, suggesting that it is likely a consequence of more fundamental biological differences between two sexes. To this end, we analyzed human primary bladder cancers and discovered that immune pathways are more enriched in women than in men, which hinted that sex bias may be driven by sex-specific differences in immune function. To address this possibility, we utilized the preclinical murine bladder cancer models that recapitulate the male bias seen in human bladder cancer. Remarkably, we observed that hormonally mediated differences in T cell immunity are responsible for sexual dimorphism in tumor growth. Our Research Proposal seeks to determine exact mechanisms by which sex hormones regulate T cell immunity. Male-based studies predominate in immunology research despite clear evidence that sex discrepancy exists in the outcome from many infectious and autoimmune diseases, vaccines and malignancies. Erroneous assumption that such results can be generalized to both sexes not only damages the scientific rigor and reproducibility but is also a major barrier to the long-term goal of personalizing treatments for immune-related diseases. Specific study design in our Proposal, explicitly aiming to highlight the immune mechanisms underlying unique protection against bladder cancer in females, presents an innovative approach to identify novel therapeutic targets. Also, completion of proposed research will establish an important insight that anti-tumor immunity may be largely different between men and women, thereby emphasizing sex as a critical biological variable to consider in designing future pre-clinical/clinical immunotherapy studies.

column37: The formation of skeletal muscle during development and following muscle injury requires muscle cells to fuse with each other and with existing muscle to form mature muscle fibers. column36: Implementing effective community health worker programs to address health disparities among the urban poor in low- and middle-income countries
column37: By 2050, 80% of the world's urban population will live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with the urban poor experiencing stark health inequities. Innovative strategies are needed to meet the health needs of the growing urban poor. In light of health worker shortages and resource constraints in LMICs, this research seeks to understand how community health worker (CHW) programs - which have been predominantly implemented in rural contexts - can be effectively applied in urban settings. CHWs are lay persons who are briefly trained in specific health tasks, but do not hold formal professional medical certificates. Past experience demonstrates that 'proven' primary health care innovations designed for rural communities are not always well-suited to urban contexts. In urban contexts where community cohesion, safety, employment, and other factors differ significantly from rural settings, CHW program features require adaptation. This research will explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when adapting the CHW model to the urban context, with the intention of providing practical recommendations for the design and implementation of urban-specific programs. A scoping review of urban, LMIC-based, CHW programs will be conducted to synthesize the little evidence available. Interviews with LMIC-based program managers will document lessons on how CHW program design and implementation can respond to urban contexts and challenges. Finally, a case study in Colombia will investigate whether a newly piloted role for CHWs (conducting follow-up home visits for patients with chronic diseases) improves CHW job satisfaction and accountability - two important elements for effective and sustainable urban programming. This study is the first to synthesize evidence from urban CHW programs and generate cross-cutting implementation lessons. The findings will contribute to theory-building and serve as a resource for developing future research and guidelines.

column36: The Effect of Developmental Odour Exposure on the Development of the Olfactory System, Eating Habits, and Metabolic Health
column37: The World Health Organization estimates that 340 million people under 19 are overweight or obese. This is troubling as childhood obesity is the strongest predictor of lifelong obesity, a major health burden worldwide. Strong evidence from the past decade indicates that a strong predictor for childhood obesity is nutritional quality during pregnancy. Maternal diets high in fats and calories correlate strongly with overeating in children, predisposing them to a lifetime of obesity. Separately, the olfactory system has been increasingly shown to influence the metabolic health of individuals. Enhancement or elimination of the olfactory system within mice alters their metabolic health and weight, without changing eating habits. Within humans, the olfactory system has been shown to be sensitive to metabolic hormones, including insulin. As well, a decline in olfactory ability is associated with many metabolic diseases. Currently, there is very little information on how maternal diet alters the development of the olfactory system, and its subsequent effects on metabolic health. Therefore, my project will aim to understand how fat-related odors in the maternal diet alter the olfactory system of the developing child, and if that has lifelong consequences on metabolic health. Pregnant mice will be fed specially designed food enriched in odours common to high-fat foods, but containing identical nutrition. I will then measure the olfactory development, eating habits, and metabolic health of the offspring mice. I will use analytical chemistry, molecular biology, and systems neuroscience approaches to determine possible mechanisms contributing to any changes found. Information from this project will help determine whether the olfactory system may contribute to the modern prevalence of overeating, obesity, and metabolic disease. Additionally, the project aims to begin studying more nuanced aspects of maternal nutrition and its effects on childhood and lifelong metabolic health.

column36: Endogenous retroelements as novel immune escape mechanisms in human cancers
column37: Immunotherapy has drastically changed the landscape of cancer treatment. By retargeting the body's own immune system towards a tumour, immunotherapy has proved effective where more traditional therapies have failed. However, tumours have developed sophisticated mechanisms to evade the anti-tumour immune response, thus rendering such immunotherapies ineffective. The advent of next-generation sequencing technologies has highlighted the importance of the non-coding genome in health and disease. A significant proportion of these non-coding genes comprise endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), remnants of ancient viral infections that have since become a part of human DNA. Given their viral origins, these genes have retained their capacity to modulate immune responses. As ERVs and other retroelements are globally deregulated in cancer cells, we propose that they may promote the immune evasive capacity of tumours. Our preliminary analysis of gene expression patterns from 964 cancer patients comprising 31 tumour types has uncovered a novel subset of immune genes that may be regulated by ERVs and other retroelements. My preliminary findings show a novel mechanism by which a retroelement drives expression of alternative soluble form of PD-L1, a molecule that inhibits antitumour immune responses and is thus a key immunotherapeutic target. We propose that this retroelement-derived PD-L1 may affect patient response to immunotherapy, which we will test using in vitro and in vivo models as well as screening patient samples. We aim to uncover diverse mechanisms by which ERVs can contribute to resistance to immunotherapy as well as potential novel therapeutic targets.

column36: Studies of the structure, function and regulation of the ATR-ATRIP complex
column37: The complete and accurate replication of the genetic information in our DNA prior to each cycle of cell division is critical to our health and survival. Changes to the integrity of our genome can result from ongoing intracellular and environmental sources of DNA damage that, if left unrepaired, could disrupt key cellular processes. Importantly, such damage is often a barrier to the completion of DNA replication, a phenomenon known as replication stress. Human cells have mechanisms of preserving genomic integrity during replication that are controlled by a protein called ATR (short for 'ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related'). ATR sits atop a signaling network known as the DNA damage response that detects, signals and resolves DNA damage and replication stress. Upon recognition of aberrant DNA structures, ATR binds to DNA near affected sites where it gets "turned on" by interaction with other signaling molecules. ATR proceeds to coordinate a number of processes required for repairing the damage and restarting the replication process. This study will address two important aspects of ATR function at the molecular level: its ability to bind to damaged DNA, and how it becomes activated in response to damage. In recent years, ATR has been proposed as a potential anti-cancer drug target for a number of reasons. Cancer cells are prone to replication stress and thus highly reliant on ATR for their survival. The DNA repair capacity of ATR signaling mediates resistance to chemotherapy, a mainstay of cancer treatment whose efficacy is dependent on the ability to cause lethal amounts of DNA damage. Taken together, pharmacological inhibition of ATR can be effective on two fronts: by targeting an essential process on which cancer cells depend, and sensitizing the cells to existing chemotherapeutic agents. A better mechanistic understanding of ATR will allow for the rational design of new drugs and open up new cancer treatment options.
