column36: A longitudinal evaluation of food insufficiency, cardiovascular disease risk, and obesity among adults living in the United States
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of mortality in high-income countries, with 30% of all deaths in the United States (U.S.) and 25% of all deaths in Canada attributable to heart disease and stroke. Similarly, the global prevalence of obesity has more than doubled since the 1980s, increasing related morbidity and mortality, as well as placing a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems. One potential risk factor for CVD and obesity is food insufficiency. Households lacking financial resources to purchase food may compensate by increasing reliance on cheap, energy-dense, and nutrient-poor foods, a diet which can lead to fat accumulation and metabolic disturbances. Food insufficiency may also affect CVD and obesity risk in other ways, such as by increasing stress, triggering harmful coping behaviors (e.g., smoking), or reducing the ability to effectively manage chronic disease conditions (e.g., diabetes). The aim of this project is to examine longitudinal relationships of food insufficiency with CVD risk and obesity, as well as to identify which factors explain these relationships. To answer this research question, we will analyze 10-years of data from the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study of black and white adults (n=5155, ages 18-30y at baseline in 1985-6). We will examine several CVD risk factors (blood pressure, fasting cholesterol (total, HDL, LDL), and fasting glucose), summary CVD risk using the Pooled Cohort Equations for estimation of 10-year risk for atherosclerotic CVD, and measures of adiposity (measured BMI, waist circumference). column36: Unlocking HIV-1 Env Towards a Cure
column37: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected more than 77 million people since the beginning of the epidemic. In the absence of treatment, HIV causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 35.4 million people worldwide. Available treatments control viral replication in infected individuals but are unable to eradicate the virus. This is because the virus "hides" in some immune cells and establishes a reservoir from which it can replicate again as soon as the treatment is interrupted. The goal of this proposal is to evaluate the potential of an innovative strategy to decrease the size of the viral reservoir and ultimately eliminate it. We found that the majority of HIV-infected individuals have all the elements required to kill infected cells but fail to do so due to the ability of the virus to cover one of its most vulnerable parts (Env). By using certain small molecules we were able to uncover parts of Env and showed that infected cells can be easily eliminated. In this proposal we will test if this strategy is able to eliminate HIV-infected cells isolated from patients (ex-vivo) and in an animal model (in-vivo). Altogether, this strategy will put us a step closer towards HIV eradication.

column36: Testing, Reaching the Undiagnosed and Linkages to Care: "REACHing" for Impact
column37: Rates of sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections (STBBI) are on the rise in Canada. Hepatitis C virus and syphilis are curable, and HIV is treatable. Most concerning, 44% of those with HCV and 16% with HIV infection are not diagnosed. This represents 9,090 individuals with HIV who are unaware, whom account for over half of new HIV infections. Testing is the entry point to care and treatment, and a required element of any elimination strategy. Current testing options have failed to reach many marginalized Canadians. The major aim of this CIHR Team in "REACHing" for Impact will be to bring together national leadership network of interdisciplinary experts. This includes biomedical scientists and clinical investigators, public health practitioners, policy-makers, industry partners, and community-based organizations. Our innovative research will address major "knowledge to action" gaps in testing, reaching the undiagnosed, and linkages to care. We propose five complementary biomedical and clinical/public health implementation and evaluation research projects: 1) accuracy, usability and acceptance of INSTI and OraQuick HIV self-tests, and validation for HCV and other tests; 2) HIV self-testing strategies in clinic and community-based settings using innovative App technology; 3) dried blood spot testing with Indigenous communities and gbMSM through targeted scale-out, peer linkage to biomedical prevention, and self-testing at home; 4) community-based intervention with peers to diversify HIV testing for gbMSM and ACB; and 5) pharmacy-based STBBI testing through integration with existing infrastructure. Our team is focused on new STBBI testing being available, accessible and implemented, specifically for hard-to-reach priority populations. We will formalize linkage to care to improve biomedical and clinical prevention/public health impacts. Through this team grant, we can significantly reduce, and eventually eliminate, the burden and impact of STBBIs on Canadians.

column36: Combination HIV Prevention: Using anti-retroviral and anti-inflammatory medications to prevent new HIV infections
column37: The number of new HIV infections each year continues to remain unacceptably high. Just as cancer therapy attacks with multiple drugs, we will employ a combination of biomedical approaches that blocks HIV infections in different ways. Firstly, will be to use anti-HIV drugs that work by blocking the ability of the virus to replicate. Secondly, will be to block the inflammatory process that brings the cells that HIV primarily infects into the genital tract using anti-inflammatory drugs. Based on research pioneered by our team members, we have shown that inflammation greatly increases the risk of HIV transmission and can actually nullify the effects of anti-HIV drugs to prevent infections. A pilot study we performed shows that using the anti-inflammatory drug acetylsalicylic acid (ASA or aspirin) reduces by 35% the number of HIV target cells in the genital tract. We will conduct studies with immediate, mid-term and long-term goals. For the immediate impact studies, we will work with a cohort of female sex workers in Nairobi, Kenya who are highly exposed to HIV and are using anti-HIV drugs for prevention. We will place women with high levels of genital inflammation on the anti-inflammatory drug ASA to assess if the number of HIV target cells in the genital tract is reduced. Our mid-term studies will use a laboratory mouse with a human immune system to determine the mechanism of how ASA affects the migration of HIV target cells and we perform HIV infection studies to directly test is ASA can reduce HIV infection. Finally, because taking drug daily can be challenging for some people, we will assess in the humanized mouse model, the long-term goal of using an intravaginal ring that would deliver a contraceptive, an anti-HIV drug and an anti-inflammatory drug. This proposal will determine if our "Combination HIV Prevention" approach is more effective thereby providing women with more options for protecting themselves.

column36: Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise 2.0: Targeting the interplay between myeloid cells and CD4+ T-cells for HIV cure
column37: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in decreasing mortality for HIV-infected individuals, ART has not cured HIV/AIDS. The failure to eradicate HIV infection during ART stems from the virus' ability to persist in the body in multiple cell types and tissues. Without lifetime therapy, the virus quickly rebounds resulting in accelerated morbidity and mortality. The most commonly studied form of persistence is in memory CD4+ T-cells (CD4+ Tm-cells) that are harboring virus out of view of drugs or from the immune system. However, evidence indicates that other long-lived cells, known as myeloid cells, might contribute to HIV persistence. Cells that allow virus persistence are called viral reservoirs (VRs) and represent the main barrier to an HIV cure. While much is known about HIV persistence, many puzzles remain about the source of persistent HIV, the mechanisms underlying the establishment and persistence of VRs, particularly in CD4+ Tm-cells, and the ways to eliminate VRs. The Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise 2.0 (CanCURE 2.0), a team of leading Canadian HIV researchers, proposes an integrated and innovative research program informed by new knowledge in the field and new findings generated under CanCURE 1.0 (2014-2019) to: 1) Define the role and impact of long-lived self-renewing tissue-resident myeloid cells called macrophages in HIV persistence during ART; 2) Conduct detailed mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the critical role played by myeloid cells in the establishment and persistence of VR in CD4+ Tm-cells; 3) Identify new therapeutic strategies to tackle HIV persistence that capitalize on these discoveries and pursue the preclinical and clinical development of therapeutic interventions aimed at targeting VRs initiated under CanCURE 1.0. These studies are all aimed at finding new effective approaches to curing HIV infection in humans by eliminating persistent HIV infection from VRs in ART-treated patients.

column36: CD8 T cell based eradication of HIV reservoirs: toward a personalized approach to HIV cure therapy
column37: The war against HIV/AIDS is not yet over. Although anti-viral drug cocktails have changed HIV/AIDS to a chronic manageable disease, people living with HIV infection still have an increased risk of drug side effects, heart, kidney, and brain diseases, as well as cancer. In addition, living with HIV infection is associated with stigma. Thus, a cure for HIV infection is needed. A main obstacle to cure is the presence of a persistent reservoir of HIV infected cells in the body, where our current drugs cannot reach. Our project proposes harnessing the immune system, in particular, a cell called a 'killer T cell' to eradicate the remaining reservoir in order to cure the infection. In order to do this, we will first extensively characterize the genetic signatures of the remaining virus hiding in the reservoir from blood samples from persons living with HIV. We will then design a number of strategies, where we can mobilize a person's killer cells to be able to eliminate their remaining viruses. We will use a 'personalized' approach by studying each person's own viruses and their own immune systems. We will also borrow from a recent revolution in the cancer field, to improve the killer cells to kill HIV infected cells better and more efficiently, by using new genetic engineering techniques. All of our work will be done in the test tube or in pre-clinical models as a preparation to design clinical trials to cure HIV infection.follow

column36: The role of platelets in rheumatoid arthritis- an animated journey in the arthritic joint
column37: Inflammation plays a role in a wide variety of diseases, from rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, to cardiovascular disease. While there are many laboratories exploring how traditional immune cells, such as white blood cells, contribute to inflammation, our group is one of the very few in the world looking at the role of platelets, tiny blood cells normally implicated in the prevention of bleedings, in inflammation. Our findings could be hugely beneficial in terms of developing new treatments for inflammatory arthritis. In 2010, we made a seminal observation: We found that during arthritis, platelets could liberate very small platelet blebs, we called microparticles. Our findings were recognized as the most important findings of the year in arthritis research and among the top-5 findings in medical research. Thereafter, we have endeavored to decipher how platelets, and their microparticles amplify inflammation in arthritis. Our research was supported by the CIHR, and has culminated with the publication of several other breakthrough findings concerning platelets and arthritis. "'The essential is invisible to the eye' - that is the message of the tale Le Petit Prince by Saint-Exupery. In line with this reasoning, our research explores the role of platelets and their minuscule particles in disease. We now wish to communicate our vision to the community using a movie. Our movie will permit to better explain our findings to arthritis patients as well to the scientific community.

column36: Creation of a TOR-BSST(C) eLearning Platform for Dysphagia Screeners
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of death globally, and abnormal swallowing (dysphagia) is a common consequence of stroke. Patients with stroke and dysphagia have an increased risk of developing pneumonia. They also have longer hospital stays, higher health care associated costs, and increased rates of mortality and disability compared to those without dysphagia. There is growing evidence that being able to identify dysphagia early reduces these risks. Currently, Canadian and American stroke guidelines recommend early identification of dysphagia by bedside screening of all patients admitted to hospital with acute stroke. As a result, many hospitals include dysphagia screening as a required component of stroke care protocols. The Toronto Bedside Swallowing Screening Test (TOR-BSST(C)) is one of the only properly tested dysphagia screening tools for stroke patients and one of the most commonly used within Ontario hospitals. The current training model for the TOR-BSST(C) involves 4 hours of live education by a Speech-Language Pathologist, followed by one-on-one certification. The proposed project will create a TOR-BSST(C) eLearning platform that will replace in-class training for dysphagia screeners who care for stroke patients. By creating this platform, we will significantly reduce the required training time and associated costs of implementing and maintaining a dysphagia screening program for stroke patients. This will, in turn, increase the feasibility of implementing the TOR-BSST(C) and ensure its continued use among both teaching and community hospitals. Ultimately, this project will strengthen care for stroke patients by supporting the implementation of a proven dysphagia screening tool and reduce dysphagia-related complications.

column37: Deliberate self-harm (DSH), which includes suicide, suicide attempts, and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a substantial public health problem. NSSI, defined as deliberate damage caused to one's own body tissue in the absence of suicidal intent, has a lifetime prevalence ranging from 13 to 23%, with rates over 17% among adolescents. NSSI is a significant health concern due to its association with negative health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, personality disorders, and suicidality. Although by definition, NSSI does not involve suicidal intent, people who engage in NSSI are at increased risk of suicide. In fact, suicide rates are seven times higher among individuals who engage in NSSI. Suicide is the second leading cause of death among young Canadians, accounting for one quarter of all deaths at ages 15 to 24. Besides the human cost on individuals, families, and society, the economic burden of DSH to Canadians is estimated at $3 billion yearly, making it a major health concern. Therefore, devising and validating treatments to reduce DSH is imperative. Mindfulness-Based Interventions (MBIs), which are based on accepting negative thoughts and sensations and attending to present moment experience without judgement or avoidance have been tested in clinical trials for reducing DSH among different clinical populations. However, no systematic review quantitatively evaluated their effectiveness. Therefore, our objective is to evaluate the effectiveness of MBIs for reducing DSH in order to provide clear recommendations for researchers, clinicians, and the public. Using the synthesis of knowledge and in consultation with researchers, clinicians, and individuals who self-harm, we also aim at developing a new tailored intervention for DSH. Results from this project will provide accurate information to health care users, policy makers, and the public regarding effective treatments for DSH, contributing therefore, to the reduction of this serious mental health problem.

column37: Our overall goal is to determine research priorities related to Aging in Place (AIP) initiatives and to prepare a grant application to seek the funding required to address the research priorities. Nursing home (NH) care has become increasingly expensive in the past decades, and costs will increase further. Also, older adults prefer to receive care at home over NH care. Therefore, many Canadian health authorities have developed AIP initiatives that aim to support older adults to stay at home or in the community for as long as possible. However, we lack research that evaluates whether AIP initiatives are effective in delaying NH admissions, and whether they have any unintended consequences on clients (e.g. more pain), family/friend caregivers (e.g. increased caregiver burden) and paid care staff (e.g. increased burnout). To determine research priorities and to prepare the grant application, we will bring together and partner researchers, policy/decision makers, continuing care operators, older adults (including those with dementia) and their family/friend caregivers. From each of the mentioned groups, we will invite representatives from various Canadian provinces, including Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario and Atlantic Canada (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador). This integrated approach will ensure that the priorities we set and the knowledge we produce will be relevant and meaningful to all key stakeholder groups involved in or affected by AIP initiatives, maximizing the impact of our research. Specifically, we will compare differences and similarities in AIP initiatives across Canadian health authorities and we will determine which approaches are most effective in preventing or delaying NH admissions and maximizing health and well-being of older adults and their caregivers. We will also determine how to improve AIP initiatives.

column36: Feasibility of engaging IMGs (International Medical Graduate) in the community-based health literacy initiatives among immigrant communities.
column37: Canadian immigrant populations come from a number of ethno-geographical backgrounds. Through our community-engaged initiatives to identify community-prioritized issues to work on, health literacy is an issue that the community members identified as a priority to work further on. Focusing on health literacy of immigrants in Canada is particularly important, as many immigrants are from countries with languages and/or cultures which are different from Canada. During our informal stakeholder consultations, we identified the possibility of engaging the International Medical Graduates (IMG) from the immigrant communities in the work around health literacy. IMGs are immigrants who have completed their medical education and/or training outside of Canada. Majority of the immigrant communities in Canada includes IMGs and they can provide tremendous value through the possible roles they can play towards improved community health literacy. We are proposing to build further on our budding collaboration and develop capacity by undertaking a project focusing on community based health literacy improvement initiatives through IMGs.

column36: An Early-Stage Planning Strategy for Applying Artificial Intelligence to Investigate Opioid-Related Health Inequities
column37: This proposal outlines a strategy to help Canada understand much more about our opioid crisis, so that we can put an end to it. We are starting to learn that people with lower incomes are experiencing more opioid issues than people with higher incomes. This means that not only is there an opioid crisis, but that disadvantaged Canadians are unfairly bearing the largest burden of it. At the same time, we are also learning that new technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), can help us to do a better job of understanding why this is happening. It can provide high-quality answers to the following types of questions. Who are the Canadians most likely to be affected by the crisis? Where in Canada is the crisis the worst? Why are some people and places experiencing more of the crisis than others? It is important to get good quality answers to these questions so that we can develop the best possible solutions to the opioid crisis. But, in order to do this research well, we have to be systematic about it. We have to understand what 'data' (information) is available to help us answer these questions. We have to understand what the logistical considerations are for applying AI to this data. This proposal provides these understandings. It includes reviewing the scientific literature, to see how other health researchers have applied AI. It also includes an assessment of the data we have in Canada, and the possibilities and constraints of applying AI techniques to this data. Finally, it involves locating the best scientific collaborators and other partners with whom we can enter into long-term relationships to accomplish this research and to make sure it is communicated to people who can use the information to help Canadians overcome this tremendous problem.

column36: Championing Health Professional Dementia Care Education
column37: Worldwide, the prevalence of dementia is a growing public health challenge. Dementia is a syndrome, usually of chronic or progressive nature, the primary symptom is impaired cognitive function. Increasing numbers of people with dementia are living longer and with an increased risk for other physical conditions including falls, infections and stroke. Those living with dementia over the age of 65 years have on average four comorbidities, twice as many as those over 65 years without a dementia. This means that increasing numbers of people living with dementia require acute care services. Unfortunately, the literature is abound with descriptions of poor care experiences in acute care settings. Although poor care is unacceptable, it is unsurprising given the lack of dementia care education for professionals who work outside of mental health. The Scottish Government responded to this in 2011 by commissioning the National Dementia Champions Programme. The key aim of the programme is to enable health and social care professionals working in acute care settings to support and lead change in the workplace so they can improve the experience, care, treatment and outcomes for people living with dementia and their families. The programme has been shown to have a measurable impact on participant's knowledge and attitudes. The purpose of this planning grant is to adapt this successful Scottish programme to the Canadian context. We will create a plan for future research to trial the adapted program to lay the groundwork in acute care settings for a positive impact on older people's health and wellness across Canada.

column36: TRUSTY: A Knowledge Dissemination Tool to Strengthen Practice Guideline Literacy and Promote their Use in Child and Youth Mental Health Care Decision-making.
column37: High-quality practice guidelines (PGs) about child and youth mental health (CYMH) problems summarize the best available research evidence into recommendations about how to assess, prevent and treat them. If clinicians, health service planners and policy makers, caregivers and youth used PGs more often to guide decisions this might help increase the use of evidence-based practices, and reduce the burden of illness caused by CYMH problems. However, unfortunately many people who could utilize rigorous PGs may be unaware they are available to guide the decisions they need to make. Even if they are aware of CYMH PGs, potential users may lack the time and skills needed to track down PGs and identify which ones are trustworthy - that is, which PGs among the large number available were developed using strong methods that minimize the potential for flawed recommendations, and therefore harm and wasted resources. Finally, potential CYMH PG users may not use PGs simply because they don't understand what a PG is and how it can help them. Hence, there is an urgent need to strengthen CYMH PG 'literacy' and promote PG use using appropriately designed knowledge dissemination tools. We have completed the foundational work needed to achieve this goal -- we identified all PGs relevant to common CYMH problems and determined which ones are trustworthy. Now we want to make our findings widely available by creating a knowledge dissemination tool. Therefore, we will create a user-informed website and facilitate its dissemination using a companion webinar and targeted Twitter messaging. TRUSTY will: i) communicate our findings regarding which existing PGs relevant to common CYMH disorders are trustworthy; ii) provide information and learning tools designed to help users increase their PG literacy skills; iii) invite user feedback regarding relevance and gaps in the list of currently available trustworthy PGs.

column36: RiboWest Conference 2019
column37: The 15th annual RiboWest Conference is a meeting of over 100 researchers sharing a general interest into the universal biomolecule ribonucleic acid (RNA). The last decade has unambiguously revealed RNA as a major regulator of all cellular processes leading to the implication of RNA in numerous diseases such as cancer, viral and bacterial infections and inherited diseases. Moreover, RNA has become a major tool in biomedical research as exemplified by gene silencing by RNA interference (RNAi) and genome editing by the CRISPR-Cas system. RNA and its derivatives are also emerging as highly promising new therapeutics. All these aspects of RNA research will be explored at the RiboWest Conference 2019. This event encourages exchange of scientific findings among participants, fosters the formation of inter-disciplinary research networks from biochemistry to medical biology including development of joint grant applications. In 2019, advances in RNA Health and Disease will be excellently represented by the keynote speaker, Dr. Susan Baserga (Yale University) and a special invited speaker Dr. Sherif Abou Elala (Universite de Sherbrooke). The New RNA Technologies theme will be presented by our second keynote speaker, Dr. Rodolphe Barrangou (North Carolina State University) and supported by a special invited speaker Dr. Ren-Jang Lin (Beckman Research Institute, City of Hope). To further facilitate scientific exchange and to inspire participants, the conference will include two panel discussions on recent RNA innovations and funding/collaboration strategies. It is the specific aim of the RiboWest Conference to facilitate student participation to support their training in RNA research. Therefore, students have reduced registration fees, give oral presentations and win awards for presentations or posters. Ultimately, the RiboWest Conference will catalyze new research into the molecular causes of diseases that lays the foundation for development new treatments in the next 10 years.

column36: mRNA Turnover: Mechanisms, Regulation and their Implication in Infectious and Age-Related Diseases
column37: Since its inception in 2003, the mRNA Turnover meeting on mechanisms of mRNA decay and stability has developed into a unique conference that brings together the leading experts in the field. This meeting focuses on the mechanisms of mRNA degradation and stability, and how these mechanisms are regulated to contribute to proper gene expression in normal physiology as well as during disease progression such as cancer and other age-related diseases. The understanding that mRNA degradation is critical for gene expression traces back to 1959 when Pardee, Jacob and Monod demonstrated in a historical paper that there had to be an unstable intermediate directing protein synthesis (Pardee et al., 1959). The importance of undertaking studies aimed at understanding mRNA degradation is underscored by the fact that defects in the mechanisms mediating this process leads to the aberrant production of protooncogenes, resulting in the development, progression and/or metastasis of cancer. Thus, mRNA degradation is clearly of fundamental importance to gene expression, and a complete understanding of mRNA degradation mechanisms and their regulation has clear applications for understanding biomedical and health problems and for generating new tools for biomedical research and clinical applications. As Canadian scientists, we are fortunate to have been involved in the inception of the mRNA stability and decay conference, that has now become a sought-after event by all scientists world-wide. This conference offers the unique opportunity for Canadian students and trainees to learn about the recent advances in the field, and to present their work in front leaders in the field. In addition, the conference offers venues for trainees and scientists to establish novel collaboration to solve health-related questions that are directly relevant to Canada and the world.

column36: Optimizing strategies to identify patient risks of prescription opioid addiction when initiating opioids for pain
column37: Opioids are often prescribed to treat pain, but are increasingly being prescribed injudiciously, which has led to high rates of prescription opioid addiction and fatal overdose in BC and Canada. Some people who are prescribed opioids for pain will have addiction while others will not. Little is known about why some people who are prescribed opioids for pain relief develop opioid addiction or opioid use disorder (OUD), but these conditions have become major drivers of the opioid epidemic as the opioid prescribing continues to increase. Better identification of persons at risk of OUD requires a better understanding of the neurobiological and social influences of increased risk for OUD. Despite the costs to society of both chronic pain and OUD, knowledge on the identification of persons at risk of OUD has not been disseminated. More awareness is needed to better provide pain care with opioids and use science to avoid unnecessary OUD. We want to disseminate knowledge for and educate prescribers on the tools mis-predicting who is at risk of developing addiction to prescribed opioids. We will do this in three steps. First, we will create a Newsletter that looks at all scientific literature on the risk of developing addiction to prescription opioids. Second, we will share our Newsletter with health professionals and experts in the field via a facilitated workshop. Third, we will use our workshop and expert feedback to create recommendations and educational package for emergency rooms and family physicians who prescribe opioids. We want to do this project as an invited special issue for the Therapeutics Letter. Our centre has done numerous educational packages and is part of CIHR's national substance use network (Canadian Research Initiative on Substance Misuse - CRISM). This project will help prevent iatrogenic opioid addiction, and the overall prescription opioid epidemic, by disseminating knowledge for opioid prescribers so they have better evidence to prescribe safely.

column36: National Workshop on Radon and Alpha Particle Induced Disease (RAPID) Prevention
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death globally. It is overwhelmingly caused by chronic inhalation of tobacco smoke and/or radioactive radon gas. Radon is the primary cause of lung cancer in never smokers, encompassing 10,000-40,000 Canadians per decade. Radon emits alpha particle radiation, a profound source of DNA damage leading to genetic mutations. Unlike tobacco, radon inhalation is not addictive and effective testing and mitigation techniques exist; thus, radon exposure represents a readily preventable cause of the most lethal and common cancer. Knowledge to meaningfully reduce alpha particle from radon exposure (or intervene at the earliest stages before lung cancer manifestation) is unacceptably low. It is our goal to be impactful by increasing the radon 'literacy' of the Canadian population, systematically determine human radon (alpha particle radiation) dosimetry across the nation, isolate new biomarkers of historic radon exposure, and encourage radon exposure reduction by understanding both environmental and (modifiable) human behavioural radon risk factors. We also aim to develop the knowledge needed to identify those at risk of radon-induced malignancy, and the essential tools needed to refer them for future screening based on novel, next-generation methods fuelled by expert knowledge of DNA damage repair biology. The purpose of this summit workshop is to bring together the Canadian research leaders and major funding partners in the areas of radon gas exposure, radon-induced lung cancer and alpha particle radiation protection. The summit aims at advancing two major and national interdisciplinary team projects, networking key stakeholders, developing future funding strategies and showcasing current research. If successful, this will consolidate the leadership role for Canadian investigators within worldwide radon research and dramatically accelerate the pace of research in this area to protect Canadians from a potent source of lung cancer.

column36: Smart cities, Healthy citizens? Optimizing health and equity in city policy making
column37: Urban planning, investment and innovation is driven by policies outside the health sector, such as sustainability, housing, or transportation. However, there is rarely explicit consideration of health. The smart cities movement-fueled by great financial investment, and political and public interest-is a driving force of urban transformation with immense potential to impact population health. A smart city aspires to improve city life using better (and often bigger) data and technology. But will smart cities actually lead to healthier citizens? The paradox of 'smart' solutions is the potential for unintended consequences that may instead damage health. Using Infrastructure Canada's $75M Smart Cities Challenge competition as a testing ground, the overall goal of this planning grant is to convene Canadian researchers and citizen- and city-partners to move forward in optimizing health and equity in city policy making. Through case studies and a planning symposium, our objectives are: 1. to uncover how health and equity are considered in smart city policies, map pathways to health outcomes, and craft plausible policy implementation scenarios; and 2. to formalize an interdisciplinary, intersectoral team interested in modelling health impacts and creating a decision support platform for healthy city policy making. The proposed activities were envisioned and will be executed together with researchers (spanning population health, geography, urban planning, and policy) and diverse stakeholders, including primary partners Evergreen and CityInclusive, practitioners (Smart Cities teams, city staff), public health actors, and research organizations. Ultimately, our vision is a resource that invites stakeholders at all levels to reflect upon, review, and (where needed) adapt policies to more effectively translate investments into health benefits for those who live in cities today or tomorrow.

column36: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Sport Group Mobilization Event - A Planning Meeting to Collaborate, Identify Barriers, and Establish the Foundations for a National Cardiovascular Screening and Care of Athletes Program
column37: There is at present no consistent, organized, evidence-based approach to the screening of athletes in Canadian post-secondary institutions. In 2019, the Canadian Cardiovascular Society and the Canadian Heart Rhythm Society jointly published a Position Statement on the cardiovascular screening of competitive athletes. Fundamental to their recommendations was that institutions develop a 'tiered approach' to the development and introduction of programs designed to protect and maintain the cardiovascular health of athletes. In this respect, the application of a screening history questionnaire, the performance of a physical exam, and the acquisition of an electrocardiogram were seen as sequential steps that were built on a pre-existing commitment to ensure the presence of emergency protocols, equipment and training appropriate for the physical environments in which sport activities occur. Following the publication of these recommendations, there is now a substantial need to ensure the development of consistent protocols and programs to permit the introduction of the tiered program, in a uniform manner, across Canadian post-secondary institutions. To this end, this proposal seeks support for an organizational meeting to ensure the development of a high quality protocol for the introduction of a uniform, consistently applied screening program in Canada's colleges and universities. Participants will have demonstrated expertise in the care of athletes, an understanding of the advantages and limitations of cardiac screening programs and recognize the opportunities to enhance clinical care and facilitate ongoing research as a consequence of introducing such a national program. Of particular interest will be the identification of those conditions that might predispose to cardiac complications including 'sudden cardiac death'. As a consequence of this meeting it is anticipated that the introduction of a high-quality screening program can be initiated and accelerated.

column36: Celebrating Ten Years: APrON Achievements and Evolution
column37: Understanding influences on health across the life span, from pregnancy to adulthood, and how health risks are passed from generation-to-generation, is an important health research priority. Intergenerational cohorts, or studies that begin in pregnancy/gestation and follow infants until they become parents, at which time the second generation of infants is added to the cohort, are needed to address those questions. Human intergenerational cohorts, however, take a lot of time, energy and money to maintain, and because of this they are also rare. Existing long-term studies, such as the Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) study, have already successfully followed large groups of people over more than ten years, from pregnancy to childhood, and so are already half-way to becoming an intergenerational cohort. The APrON Study is also unique in that a diverse range of academics and clinicians are involved, with extensive biological, social, psychological, medical, environmental, developmental and nutrition information collected from mothers, fathers and children. To the best of our knowledge, there are currently no Canadian intergenerational cohorts, and certainly not one with such diverse, in-depth and far-reaching data. The goal of the "Celebrating Ten Years: APrON Achievements and Evolution" meeting is to share with the public all that APrON has discovered and accomplished over the last ten years, and to bring together experts that can help APrON plan to become an intergenerational cohort over the next ten years and beyond, including how to attract early career investigators and additional funding. By doing this, we will be in a position to gain valuable and rare information on how the early life experiences of Canadians affects their health from infancy to adulthood, and how health is passed from generation-to-generation - which will be invaluable in guiding creation of health care policy that will help to protect Canadian health for generations to come.

column36: The Social Exposome in Child Health and Development: Building Partnerships and Collaborations to Reduce Inequalities in Canada
column37: Despite being the 5th most prosperous country in the world, when compared to other developed countries, Canada's rankings are alarmingly low on key measures of children's health and safety, as well as child poverty (17% of all children). These conditions have resulted in large and growing inequalities in the development and health of Canadian children. For example, using standard measures, children from low income neighbourhoods are more vulnerable on key areas of development than those from high income neighbourhoods. In addition, children with chronic diseases, like asthma, who are from low income neighbourhoods or families are admitted to the hospital more frequently. This impact of living conditions on health and well-being is referred to as the social determinants of health, and when experienced during development, has life-long implications for the risk of developing chronic diseases and mental illnesses. It is crucial that we understand the specific factors leading to these inequalities in order to devise policies and interventions to reduce them. We are proposing to host a workshop that will bring together researchers, health care practitioners, experts in policy, and relevant community and government groups to understand the social and environmental factors that lead to these disparities, the biological processes in the body by which they do so, and to explore potential policies and interventions to reduce them. We anticipate this leading to new collaborations and partnerships and identifying the next steps required to optimize child health and development for all children in Canada.

column36: Exploring the intersections of HIV treatment interventions and the ongoing criminalization of HIV in Canada: Setting a new research and practice agenda
column37: Canada has been a leader in advancing TasP which is characterized by a shift in the use of HIV treatment from improving individual health outcomes to also reducing transmission. Disappointingly, Canada also has high rates of criminalizing people living with HIV for transmission, non-disclosure and exposure. The overarching goal of this event is to explore intersections between the criminalization of HIV and the use of new HIV treatment and prevention technologies and interventions in the Canadian context (e.g., the use of HIV treatment with the goal of obtaining an undetectable viral load to reduce transmission). In keeping with the objectives of the CIHR planning and dissemination grant opportunity, we will undertake a series of related activities. First, we will host a one-day symposium to disseminate findings from CIHR funded research and to facilitate a structured dialogue between interdisciplinary and inter-professional stakeholders working at the intersection of research, clinical care, service delivery, public health and criminal justice with the aim of planning future directions for research and practice. The objectives of the symposium are as follows: 1. To disseminate findings from an innovative CIHR-funded research study that explores the health and social impacts of criminalization in relation to HIV non-disclosure in Canada; 2. To promote dialogue about the health and social impacts of HIV criminalization facing different populations in Canada (e.g. people who use drugs, people who sell sex, migrants) from the perspective of those most affected and those in research and practice roles, and plan next steps; 3. To promote dialogue about ethical and methodological issues in conducting health and social research with criminalized people and identify best-practices and plan future research; 4. To provide content for a report and fact sheets to disseminate findings from the symposium for academic, provider, policy and community audiences.

column36: Dissemination of a National Set of Family Practice Nursing Competencies to Support the Integration of Family Practice Nurses within Primary Care
column37: Family practice nursing offers a feasible and affordable solution to improve access to primary care, reduce costs, and promote high-quality of care. Family practice nurses are Registered Nurses who practice in primary care. Across many jurisdictions in Canada, family practice nurses form the core of interprofessional primary care teams. Currently, a national research/stakeholder team are developing the first set of national family practice nursing competencies to support the integration and optimization of Registered Nurses in primary care. Competencies are the integrated knowledge, skills, judgement and attributes required of a family practice nurse to practice safely and ethically. Therefore, the objectives of this project are: (1) To support knowledge translation and dissemination of family practice nursing competencies to patients/public citizens, primary care providers, health administrators, educators, decision-makers, and relevant associations nationally and internationally, and (2) To facilitate the use of family practice nursing competencies by key stakeholders in activities focused on the integration of family practice nurses in primary care. Family practice nursing competencies will have tremendous value to relevant stakeholders and sectors nationally and internationally. The dissemination of these competencies is key to strengthening the family practice nursing workforce in Canada and shaping the development of family practice nursing competencies internationally. These competencies will clarify roles of family practice nurses, serve as a valuable tool to support inter-professional team functioning, inform undergraduate nursing education, and reassure the public that nurses are delivering a high-standard of care. Sharing these competencies at an international-level has the potential to catalyze similar initiatives across the globe that will facilitate the integration of family practice nurses in primary care.

column36: Identifying research priorities to improve understanding of the role of cognition for power mobility device use: In pursuit of better screening, assessment and training tools.
column37: Cognition is the primary concern among clinicians for the provision of power mobility devices (PMD), yet existing assessment and training tools for PMD primarily consider motor skills and performance. Although it is suspected that cognitive functions are important to operate a PMD, we do not fully understand the relationship between cognitive function and PMD use. Cognition is modifiable, but before effective interventions can be developed, we need to better understand the role of cognition in mobility to ensure valid assessment tools. The goal of this planning grant is to explore the role of cognition for PMD use to develop specific research objectives related to assessment and training of cognitive functions required for PMD use. The proposed planning initiative will facilitate discussions among an interdisciplinary and international team of experts consisting of kinesiologists, occupational therapists, physical therapists, and clinicians to support attainment of grant initiatives. Study team members are experts in the area of cognition and PMD use and share common goals to explore the role of cognition in PMD driving and to develop novel methods for assessment and training. Active involvement of interdisciplinary researchers and clinicians will allow us to identify new research priorities that may facilitate independent mobility and participation among older adults who have cognitive impairments. In this way, the proposed planning activities fit within the mandate of the Institute of Aging. The outcomes of this grant can potentially revolutionize current assessment and training tools for PMD use and may provide clinicians with more support for clinical decision-making.

column36: Weinstein Cardiovascular Development Conference 2020
column37: The Weinstein Cardiovascular Development and Regeneration Meeting is the largest meeting in the field of heart development, and the premier opportunity for researchers in the field to meet and share data and ideas. During this 3-day meeting, basic scientists, clinicians and physician-scientists interact and discuss many diverse aspects related to cardiovascular embryology and its impact on congenital heart disease and adult cardiac dysfunction. Our understanding of how the cardiovascular system develops has grown is in direct relationship to expansion of the Weinstein Meeting, and thus its key objectives are to continue to promote a collegiate environment for dissemination and discussion of innovative scientific findings, and encourage interactions and collaborations. Innovative objectives for the 2020 meeting include a focus on cardiovascular single cell biology and translational aspects towards paediatric and adult congenital heart disease. The conference will be held at the Hotel Bonaventure in Montreal, a location that is convenient for an international attendance of approximately 350 participants, from May 14-16, 2020. It will feature 9 platform sessions with a total of 36 platform speakers, two keynote presentations, four breakout sessions and two poster sessions. A strong emphasis is put on young investigators to present their work in both oral and poster form, and on the willingness of all to share new and unpublished information. This will provide opportunities to devise new experiments and to develop new hypotheses in a collaborative manner. The Weinstein Conference has never before been hosted in Canada, thus increasing greatly the exposure of the Canadian cardiovascular community internationally. The single venue setting at the recently renovated Hotel Bonaventure will facilitate informal networking and exchange and help stimulate the development of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for these devastating disorders.

column36: Promoting Access to Culturally Safe Health Services for Indigenous Mothers and Their Infants
column37: Access to health care is important to promote health, but some Indigenous people in Canada, have trouble accessing health care for many reasons, including experiences of racism and a lack of understanding about traditional medicines. Because of colonization and racist policies like the Indian Act, some Indigenous people face difficult social conditions that lead to poor health. Indigenous women and infants are especially impacted. To promote their health, Indigenous mothers and infants should be able to easily access health care that meets their unique needs. A research study by Dr. Wright asked Indigenous mothers living in Hamilton, Ontario about their experiences of using health care for their infants. Mothers suggested ways that health providers could improve their access to health care. These included: (a) having trusting relationships with their health provider; (b) when needed, involving child protection services in sensitive and supportive ways; (c) removing fees linked to using health care services; (d) allowing flexibility in booking appointments; (e) having welcoming and friendly clinics; and (f) providing holistic care that meets not only physical health needs, but emotional, mental and spiritual health needs as well. This project will create three videos to share the mothers' suggestions with health providers in Canada. The videos will be created by a group of Indigenous mothers, Elders, staff from the Hamilton Indigenous Friendship Centre, Dr. Wright and other health providers. The videos will be shared with health providers and leaders from universities and colleges as well as placed online so people can continue to view them from across Canada. Our goal is to share mothers' suggestions with health providers so they can provide better care for Indigenous mothers and infants and make health care easier to access. If health providers can make these changes to their care, they may also help to improve the health of Indigenous mothers and infants.

column36: MITO2019 | The Power of Mitochondria to Transform Human Health
column37: Mitochondria have long been recognized as the powerhouses of the cell. These tiny organelles are responsible for providing 90% of the energy required by our body and as a consequence mitochondrial function is central to health. Patients, families, healthcare providers and policymakers need a solid foundation of science and knowledge of mitochondrial function and dysfunction to develop strategies to prevent, protect and mitigate the impact of mitochondrial mutations on the health of the population. Timely research is informing improved disease outcomes and supporting responsible health system resource management.

column36: Developing a Research Agenda on Exercise and Physical Activity for People with Lower Limb Amputations
column37: Lower limb amputations (LLAs) have multiple causes but the majority are the result of diabetes or peripheral vascular disease. LLAs can impact an individual's walking ability, balance, functional ability, mental health and quality of life. Half of people with LLAs are limited in their ability to walk in the community. Studies show people tend to be sedentary, participating in low levels of physical activity. This may lead to further cardiorespiratory deconditioning and impede independence. Exercise is recommended as a key component of early rehabilitation to improve function and mobility. Exercise and physical activity are also important for management of common comorbid conditions associated with LLAs (e.g. diabetes) and the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular risk factors. However, there is a lack of high quality evidence about exercise or physical activity interventions for community-dwelling adults after initial rehabilitation/prosthetic training. There is an urgent need for more research on exercise and physical activity to improve the health and wellbeing of people living with LLA in the community. As a first step, a one-day research planning meeting will be held to identify key research priorities related to exercise and physical activity for people with LLAs. The meeting will help form research partnerships and collaborations among a range of stakeholders including researchers from various fields (amputation rehabilitation, exercise and physical activity, cardiac rehabilitation), clinicians, people living with LLAs, and community organizations. Participants will share their views on key issues and gaps in the field, research priorities and methodological approaches to address research questions related to exercise and physical activity for people with LLA. The outcomes of the planning event will be a strategy to move forward with the identified research priorities, including plans for submission of a research grant(s).

column36: Artificial intelligence approaches to precision mental health: Convening experts and stakeholders to ensure the acceptability and feasibility of motion-sensing data-capture technology in older adult populations
column37: Feeling down or worried happens to everyone, but for some people these feelings are very strong, long-lasting, and can be damaging to them and their families. Mental illnesses, such as depression or anxiety, may include feelings of hopelessness, helplessness, guilt, or even suicide. Worldwide, mental illness affects one in five people aged 60+. However, problems faced by older adults impacting their mental health are often overlooked, such as loneliness, loss of a spouse, or ill-health. We need to change the way we treat mental health, with services that consider older adults' specific needs and situations. "Precision medicine" means using information we learn about someone, such their diet or lifestyle, to provide treatment/care specific to them as an individual. This has been successful with physical illnesses, such as early-diagnosis and treatment for cancer. We want to apply these ideas to help improve older adults' mental health. Motion sensing technologies are being developed that are able to able to collect information about older adults' movements that can be used in the identification of mental illnesses. However, we do not yet know what older adults think about these technologies and if they are willing to these sensors into their homes. To ensure our system and services/technologies meet older adults' needs and are easy-to-use, older adults will be involved at all stages of the project from early ideas, to building/testing the services/technologies. To do this, we will host a workshop that will bring together experts who design these sensors and older adults who will be using them. By the end of this workshop we hope to have identified technologies that the engineers can design, the older adults are happy with, and that are able to collect the data required to use a precision medicine approach to mental health.

column36: Exploring opportunities for AI and a primary care patient engagement platform to advance health equity across Canadian communities
column37: A recent report from the Public Health Agency of Canada called for better information to inform government policy-makers, health care providers, patients, members of the public, and community organizations, about inequalities in health in our communities and how to improve them. There are new opportunities to use increasing amounts of data from primary care to identify and reduce health inequalities among Canadians. Artificial intelligence applied to primary care data, especially patient reported information, may offer greater understanding of health and how it evolves differently across subpopulations. Guided by the Strategy for Patient Oriented Research (SPOR) patient engagement framework, we will bring together public health and primary care leaders, clinicians and patients, information technology and artificial intelligence leaders with researchers to identify the most important research questions to answer with the application of artificial intelligence to the Canadian Practice Information Network (CPIN) to promote health equity across Canadian communities. Through a consensus building approach we will draw on the diverse individual expertise, lived experiences, and perspectives of participants to identify priority research opportunities arising from advancing AI capabilities and this primary care practice-based patient engagement platform. column36: How to cook? What to cook? A video series for those living with advanced liver disease
column37: All diseases of the liver eventually progress to a common end stage called cirrhosis. At this point, the liver has deteriorated to such a state that the only option remaining is liver transplantation. Some patients are on the liver transplant wait list for many years. As symptoms worsen and overall health fails, patients are at increasing risk for not meeting daily nutritional needs. In turn, this exacerbates symptoms placing them at risk for infections, hospitalizations, and poor health outcomes. In response to patients' needs, we previously developed the award-winning "Nutrition in Cirrhosis Guide" for patients to use at home. The Guide helps patients to understand some of roles the liver has in digestion and why it is important for them to follow a low sodium, high protein diet with frequent eating. At the request of our patients, they want to knwo HOW they can achieve this in their kitchens. For this dissemintation project, we have created a team consisting of a hepatologist specializing in cirrhosis, nutritionists, and a culinary expert. Together with patient volunteers, they will develop a 6-part video series demonstrating basic cooking and baking techniques using basic kitchen items. Patients will learn how to cook tasty, liver-friendly meals so that they can take better care of themselves at home. This video series will also be helpful for other patients prescribed a low sodium diet, such as those with heart failure or high blood pressure. Our well-established dissemination network and partners will host the freely available videos on their websites targeting patients and care givers, health care professionals, and the public. This dissemination project will equip patients with the skills they need to empower them to actively participate in self-care and retain their independence.

column36: Towards Improving Screening of Retinal Toxicity of Hydroxychloroquine in patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA).
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are diseases of the immune system that affect many parts of the body (e.g., joints, heart, eyes, skin), dramatically altering quality of life, and can result in other medical complications and untimely death. A drug called hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is commonly used to treat SLE and RA. Many studies have highlighted benefits of HCQ, including less severe disease, fewer complications (e.g., blood clots, problems with pregnancy or kidneys), and longer life. Stopping HCQ can lead to episodes of more severe disease and premature death. Although HCQ is typically safe and easy to take, a serious long-term side-effect is eye damage that could cause vision loss. The risk of vision loss in HCQ users can be prevented by routine screening, however, a recent study by our team found that only a small percentage (40%) of people using HCQ had received annual screening as per current guidelines. Therefore, it is important to identify the barriers to guideline-recommended screening and develop strategies to improve screening for HCQ retinal toxicity that lead to vision loss.

column36: Economic modeling to inform the public health response to opioid use disorder
column37: Opioid-related morbidity and mortality is among the most urgent public health priorities in North America. The co-chairs of Canada's Special Advisory Committee on the Epidemic of Opioid Overdoses have estimated that over 4,000 Canadians died of opioid overdoses in 2017, with drastic increases in opioid overdoses and overdose deaths being documented across North America following the introduction of illicit fentanyl into the drug supply. The opioid overdose epidemic is thus exacting an enormous toll on North Americans, and posing significant challenges for local health systems charged with responding to it. Health economic modeling is ideally suited to inform the challenging decisions policy makers face in combating the North American opioid crisis, and can clarify, within a causal framework, the relationships between program inputs and effects, thus providing credible evidence of the value of programs and interventions and guide their roll out and improvement as they are implemented. The overarching goal of this application is to re-convene a collaborative of experts working in the area of simulation modeling and economic analysis to improve the quality, timeliness, relevance, and impact of modeling in opioid use disorder (OUD). Specific deliverables include the development of a policy manuscript to the International Journal of Drug Policy and the submission of a grant to secure ongoing funding to support the collaboration. This Planning Grant is an essential next step in forming partnerships and collaborations between leading researchers studying OUD throughout North America to address the urgent public health crisis.

column37: This proposal requests funds to support activities that facilitate the exchange of ideas about a novel area of ageing and health research: how exposure to war and related traumatic wartime events, in a developing country setting, influences biological ageing. Further, it requires individuals with a deep appreciation of the social context of Vietnam. Moreover, putting the results to best use, or translating knowledge from this type of project into practice, requires input and engagement from local investigators, in this case being the Vietnamese academic community. This workshop puts together such a team for the purpose of long-term collaboration.

column36: Optimizing the city decision-making process through AI and big data for better population health and social equity
column37: Urban planning has a significant impact on population health, equity, environment, sustainable development, etc. Thus, there is an urgency in the development of reliable decision-making supporting tools to help plan future cities. Mathematical optimization models can properly mirror decision making processes and, in addition, there is a vast literature on methods to tackle and thus, determine, an optimal decision. Consequently, mathematical optimization provides the perfect framework to assist urban planning. Another factor to take into account is associated with the population's reaction to the policies in the context of urban planning. In this way, mathematical models must integrate the interaction of policy makers and citizens. Thereafter, a game theoretical framework would be suitable to determine the best policy, i.e., the policy that provides the best outcome in terms of the population health and equity. In order to achieve these goals, data associated with urban mobility will be used to determine the parameters of the decision process model. This proposal aims to build a multidisciplinary steering committee with representatives from the City of Montreal, practitioners from Montreal Public Health Office, experts in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and population health researchers. Furthermore, it aims to devise a project using AI techniques to develop tools able to support the complex process of decision making in megalopolises, as mentioned above. The objectives are to learn population utilities associated with urban mobility through big data, model their interaction with policy maker decisions, and develop optimization tools that can support their decisions by providing a clear view of population health and equity impact.

column36: Development of a Website for a Living Systematic Review and Meta-analysis on the Diagnostic Accuracy of Novel Rapid Tests for Influenza Infection
column37: Influenza is a major public health concern, resulting in 180,000 emergency room visits and 12,200 hospitalizations per year in Canada. The use of diagnostic tests and proper interpretation of results is important to accurately identify patients with influenza. Timely and correct diagnosis reduces unnecessary antibiotic prescribing and increases prompt antiviral use to improve patient care and outcomes. Although lab-based tests are the gold standard for influenza diagnosis, there are inherent delays in result reporting. Rapid influenza diagnostic tests (RIDTs) are simple enough to use outside the lab and provide results in 10-30 minutes. First generation RIDTs have poor sensitivity (ability to detect true cases). Recently, two new classes of RIDTs, digital immunoassays (DIAs) and rapid nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), were commercialized. In 2017, we published a landmark systematic review demonstrating significantly higher sensitivities for DIAs (77-80%) and NAATs (92-95%) than for first-generation RIDTs (53-55%). However, the number of DIA and NAAT studies available at the time limited our ability to perform important subgroup analyses. New technologies have since been approved and 20 additional DIA/NAAT studies were published last year, highlighting that as technologies evolve, evidence emerges at a rapid pace. Thus, we propose to develop and pilot a website for a Living Systematic Review (LSR) with continual, active monitoring of the evidence to update our review as new data become available. An LSR is an efficient, cost-effective, and pragmatic solution to the challenge of rapid research output. LSRs capitalize on existing reviews to ensure their continued usefulness for end-users. This LSR will continuously integrate the latest RIDT evidence into actionable summaries on a website that we will develop. With our knowledge users, our work will inform national influenza clinical and laboratory practice guidelines and public health surveillance strategies.

column36: Planning research priorities to support the role of nurses in providing optimal medical abortion care
column37: Abortion practices are changing rapidly in Canada. Despite being widely available and widely used for three decades around the world, it was only in 2017 that mifepristone (medical abortion) became available in Canada, to be provided by a physician. The same year, regulatory changes allowed nurse practitioners to prescribe mifepristone. The availability of medical abortion and the authorization of nurse practitioners as prescribers offer the potential for significant expansion in access and options for women seeking abortion services. Registered nurses are also affected by these changes because, while not authorized to prescribe mifepristone, they care for and counsel women seeking abortion services. Nurses play a role in counselling women and pregnant people as they consider the benefits and risks of medical versus surgical abortion procedures; facilitating complementary interventions such as serology, ultrasonography, and pain relief; providing in-person and telephone support during the medical abortion; and caring for patients during follow up appointments. Nurses are highly trusted health care providers who provide holistic, patient-centred care and are optimally suited to support patients in medical abortion care. Since medical abortion is so new in Canada, little is known about the characteristics of nurses involved and the extent of their involvement or practice patterns. There is also little information on implementation barriers of medical abortion and nurses' experiences with the provision of mifepristone. We propose a one-day meeting to bring together key clinical, research and government stakeholders to identify research priorities relevant to nurses in medical abortion care and discuss how their role within the current scope of practice can be better supported and optimized to improve access to and ensure the quality of medical abortion care.

column36: International Burkholderia Cepacia Working Group (IBCWG) 22nd Meeting
column37: Burkholderia is a group of bacteria that live in many environments and in association with plants and invertebrate animals. A subset of this group, known as Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) has emerged as human pathogens infecting individuals with an immunocompromised system and those with the genetic disease cystic fibrosis. Unfortunately, once people are infected with Bcc there are very few options for treatment as Bcc bacteria are naturally resistant to antibiotics. Moreover, Bcc can survive in medical devices and disinfectants meaning that they occasionally cause outbreaks in hospitals, affecting the most vulnerable patients, such as newborns and the elderly. The understanding of how to control a superbug able to thrive in diverse environments and colonize different hosts necessitates a multidisciplinary approach. The International Burkholderia cepacia Working Group (IBCWG) is a community of scientists, physicians, and health workers from Canada, USA, Europe, and Latin America working together to understand the biology of Bcc, to prevent the spread of Bcc in hospital settings and to cure infections with Bcc. They gather every two years which the common goal of exchanging knowledge, fostering international collaborations and establishing the next research priorities. The next IBCG conference will be held at the University of Toronto on April 22-25, 2020 and will be promoted by mailing lists, social media, and through the IBCWG website. Event activities include opening and keynote lectures, short presentation sessions and research workshops. These activities will be moderated by senior IBCWG members and organized around the central concept of One Health. Proposed themes are: Bcc in the environment, Bcc in human-made products, Bcc interactions with the host, and Curing infections with Bcc. A final section will highlight current progress and define strategic research actions on areas where knowledge gaps are identified.

column36: Promouvoir l'alimentation durable dans les organisations de sante : Projet de mobilisation et de planification d'une initiative quebecoise
column37: La notion d'alimentation durable a ete elaboree afin de repondre aux defis environnementaux planetaires majeurs comme le rechauffement climatique, l'epuisement des ressources naturelles, la perte de biodiversite, la deforestation et la degradation des sols. L'alimentation durable designe des regimes alimentaires qui protegent et respectent les ecosystemes, sont culturellement acceptables, economiquement abordables et nutritionnellement sains. Le Canada fait partie des pays qui tiennent compte de l'alimentation durable dans leurs recommandations alimentaires. La nouvelle version du guide alimentaire canadien recommande de << choisir plus souvent des proteines vegetales >>. En plus de ses benefices pour la sante, la consommation de proteines vegetales a une incidence ecologique nettement inferieure a la consommation de proteines d'origine animale. Le present projet consiste en la planification d'une initiative quebecoise visant a promouvoir l'alimentation durable dans les organisations de sante. Considerant que les habitudes alimentaires ont un tres grand impact sur l'environnement, ce projet permettra d'identifier les strategies et les outils les plus prometteurs afin de soutenir les differents acteurs des organisations de sante dans la promotion de l'alimentation durable. Plus specifiquement, les objectifs sont: 1) synthetiser la litterature sur l'alimentation durable et ses implications pour les organisations de sante; 2) reunir des acteurs oeuvrant dans des organisations de sante et etablir des liens de collaboration; 3) susciter des echanges et 4) identifier les strategies et les outils a developper afin de promouvoir l'alimentation durable dans les organisations de sante. Au terme des activites, les principales orientations d'une initiative quebecoise de promotion de l'alimentation durable dans les organisations de sante seront formulees et s'inscriront intimement dans les preoccupations des differentes parties prenantes consultees dans le cadre du projet.

column36: Workshop to CAPTURE ALS
column37: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is the most common adult-onset motor neuron disease, characterized by a degeneration of the brain and spinal cord leading to progressive muscular weakness. Despite an increasing understanding of the complex biology of ALS, an important barrier to development of effective tests and treatments is the lack of sensitive and objective human biomarkers. To address this issue, the Canadian ALS Neuroimaging Consortium (CALSNIC) was established. CALSNIC is a multidisciplinary group of scientists funded by CIHR, ALS Canada and Brain Canada. It provides a platform for clinical and translational studies on a national scale. Its strength is the ability to collect disease information over multiple clinical visits, with clinical, cognitive and MRI metrics in a standardized fashion across 7 sites. We propose to create the Comprehensive Analysis Platform To Understand, Remedy and Eliminate (CAPTURE) ALS initiative, which builds on the CALSNIC clinical and imaging program by adding pan-Canadian procurement of biological samples. This will form a national biorepository network that facilitates rapid sharing of invaluable data and samples with Canadian and international scientists, and contribute to large discovery projects aimed at understanding ALS further. CAPTURE ALS will drive more impactful research, accelerate our understanding of the heterogeneity of ALS, accelerate highly needed biomarker discoveries and lead to novel treatments for ALS. Most importantly, it will reinforce Canada's standing as an international leader in ALS research. As a necessary step to establishing CAPTURE ALS, we propose to hold a 1-day workshop in Montreal to bring together the various ALS research and clinical groups in Canada to establish the foundation for a pan-Canadian ALS research network with harmonized tools (consent forms, SOPs, protocols, etc.) and shared resources (biosamples, datasets, etc.).

column36: Neighbours saving Neighbours: Planning a community volunteer resuscitation program for victims of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Canada
column37: "Sudden cardiac arrest" occurs when the heart stops beating unexpectedly. Each year, 45,000 Canadians suffer a cardiac arrest and less than 12% percent survive. CPR and defibrillation can improve survival but need to be done as soon as possible to be effective. Defibrillation involves the use of an automated external defibrillator or "AED" to deliver an electrical shock and restart the heart. Unfortunately, it can take 10 minutes or longer for an ambulance to arrive after calling 9-1-1, so bystanders must act to optimize chances of survival. Witnesses to cardiac arrest provide CPR in only half of cases and use an AED in less than 3%. Increasing the number of people who receive early CPR and defibrillation before paramedics arrive will save more lives. Some countries, like the United Kingdom, have developed a new approach to this problem. They have developed programs that involve community volunteers. Volunteers are recruited, trained in CPR and equipped with an AED. Then, when on duty, these community volunteers are dispatched to nearby cardiac arrest emergencies along with paramedics. Because these volunteers are embedded in communities, they tend to be closer to the patients than paramedics on many occasions. Volunteers arrive with the patient before paramedics can begin CPR and use the AED until paramedics arrive. Very little research has been done on this new idea. We are planning a Canadian version of this approach called "Neighbours saving Neighbours". Because this has never been done in Canada before, we need to consult with experts in cardiac arrest, paramedics, emergency medical dispatchers, decision-makers in government, patients, and other community members to determine the best approach. This grant will support a one-day meeting in Kingston where stakeholders and researchers will design the Neighbours saving Neighbours program, identify important research questions, plan for future research and begin work on future grant applications.
