column36: Digitizing Stepped Mental Health Care: A Pragmatic Trial
column37: Access to mental health care in Canada is considerably delayed compared to other countries; a finding which is due, in part, to an under supply of services and long wait lists.This study will evaluate a new mental health care service model called Stepped Care 2.0 at 15 sites in Newfoundland and 15 sites in Nova Scotia. This new approach to organizing and delivering care will be compared to standard approaches to care. A software system will be designed and used to help manage the new approach. We expect the new approach, along with the new technology, will have the potential to improve the quality of care, reduce wait times and increase access to care, especially for people living in remote areas and those whose changing life circumstances require a more flexible kind of care tailored to their unique challenges. This new approach to care includes a wider range of treatment options, including psychiatric care, individual and group counselling, online treatment programs with built in professional support, self-help resources and peer support. The management system will make it easy to tell quickly when treatment is working well or when a transition in care is required. The program will also allow patients to be more involved in care planning and decision making. Training will be provided to care providers to use the new system. Changes will be made to the program as we learn what does and does not work. This attention to continuous improvement is expected to empower patients to be more resourceful and to encourage providers to be more innovative and flexible. We also expect that programming will be available to more people without increasing costs. In other words, we expect this approach to care to be more efficient, effective and sustainable. Finally, with a team of researchers, patients, providers and other stakeholders representing every province, it will be possible to implement across the country any of the new programming that proves effective.

column36: The Impact of an Innovative eHealth Transition Intervention on Self-Management Skills Among Young Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
column37: There have been major advances in the care of children born with heart defects ("congenital heart disease"- CHD) over the past 3 decades. Now over 90% of children with CHD reach adulthood. However, adolescent and young adult "survivors" are at risk of further heart problems. Unfortunately, most have very little understanding of their CHD and they lack confidence communicating with doctors and nurses about their heart. Over half do not attend specialized adult CHD clinics after graduating from their children's hospital, despite being advised to do so. This increases the risk that new heart problems, which may develop in early adulthood, will be discovered too late. Transition is the planned movement of adolescents with lifelong health conditions from child to adult healthcare. The Canadian Pediatric Society and other organizations have published guidelines about how children's hospitals should help adolescents prepare for the move to adult healthcare. Nurse-led programs to help with transition are effective but time-consuming, expensive, and not easily accessible to adolescents living in rural communities. However, smartphone apps are widely accessible and may be helpful in providing important transition information and coping strategies to adolescents as they enter adult health care. The objective of this research is to determine whether a transition app is better than a nurse-led transition intervention in preparing adolescents (age 16-17) with CHD to take on responsibility for their healthcare (self-management). We will enroll 188 participants across 5 children's hospitals. Each participant will randomly (like the flip of a coin) be assigned to either receive the transition app or the nurse-led transition intervention. We will also determine if the transition app results in better knowledge of their heart condition, greater self-efficacy, timelier first appointments in the adult health care system, and cost savings relative to the nurse-led transition program.

column36: U-Flourish student mental health research: Transitions to mental health care
column37: The demand for student mental health care is increasing and threatening to overwhelm resources across university campuses. However, there is limited data to inform universities about how best to support the mental health of an increasingly diverse student population, identify those at highest risk, and facilitate the timely transition to appropriate mental health care. This proposal builds on a funded CIHR study of first year students transitioning to Queen's and Oxford universities. The study will follow these students through the next two years of university life. Objectives include to: (i) evaluate transitions to mental health care, (ii) identify barriers and gaps, and (iii) assess the impact of access to mental health care on the association between risk factors, mental health and academic success. To address these objectives, the study will use mixed methods including electronic surveys each fall and spring term, linkage to administrative, academic and electronic medical record data, as well as an optional remote capture study using a free App downloaded to student smartphones. To ensure full representation of the undergraduate student population, an abbreviated electronic survey study addressing the same objectives will be offered to all undergraduate students at each university. This study addresses a major knowledge gap about transitions to mental health care in the undergraduate student population, as well as providing data on transitions for key subgroups (transgender, international students, history of a mental illness). Study findings will produce a model to inform the organization of student mental health care addressing identified barriers and gaps. The study will also importantly build capacity for study mental health research in Canada and internationally.

column36: Neurotropic human pegivirus-associated encephalitis
column37: Encephalitis is a disease characterized by brain swelling and inflammation and is commonly caused by viral infection leading to serious physical and mental disabilities as well as death. The cause of encephalitis is unknown for over 50% of patients affected with it. Viruses from the Flaviviridae family (e.g., West Nile Virus, Zika virus) are well known to cause encephalitis. In my research project, I will characterize human pegivirus (HPgV), a single-stranded RNA virus from the Flaviviridae family, which I identified in the brains of patients with encephalitis (Annals of Neurology, 2018). HPgV is present in blood from 1-5% of the general population in developed countries. I discovered that HPgV infection of the brain was associated with intense inflammation with accompanying damage to brain cells that are typical of encephalitis. Furthermore, I identified HPgV virus in three different cell types within the brain that are involved in normal brain functioning: T-cells, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. I also found unique genetic mutations within HPgV that might control brain infection.Based on these findings, I hypothesize that HPgV infection of the brain causes encephalitis and that an 87-nucleotide deletion within HPgV contributes to the severity of infection. To test my hypothesis, I will define the mechanisms by which HPgV produces encephalitis using cultured human neural cells and animal models. I will also determine the prevalence of the deletion in brain tissue and blood serum from over 100 patients with and without encephalitis. This project will provide new knowledge regarding the cause and disease mechanisms underlying encephalitis in humans. These results will be significant because in many patients with encephalitis, the cause is unknown.

column36: Hypoxia in the Tumour Microenvironment and the Interplay between the Hypoxia Inducible Factor and Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor Pathways
column37: The 5-year survival rates for pancreatic cancer are among the lowest of any cancer type and patients are resistant to most therapies. Interestingly, pancreatic cancer is characterized by a significant amount of immune cells infiltrating the tumour. This is encouraging since immune cells play a crucial role in fighting many cancers. However, certain immune cells can also suppress the immune response to cancer. In pancreatic cancer, macrophages, a type of immune cell, are important suppressors of the immune system. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) cell-signalling pathway plays a crucial role in determining whether macrophages will suppress the immune system, or lead to an inflammatory state that is favourable for clearing tumours. Our lab has shown that AhR is essential for desirable, suppressive macrophage function in autoimmune disease. Thus, eliminating AhR may relieve suppression of the immune system and lead to a better anti-tumour response in a cancer setting. Preliminary data supports this line of thinking, but macrophage signalling is complex; the AhR pathway is closely intertwined with the hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) pathway. HIF is also of interest because tumours are characterized by a lack of oxygen (hypoxia), which triggers HIF. There is evidence that the HIF and AhR pathways play opposing roles in macrophages. We aim to reveal the different roles hypoxia, HIF, and AhR play in polarizing macrophages towards either an inflammatory or suppressive subtype. Being able to control the immune suppressive vs. inflammatory function of macrophages by drugging HIF and AhR will be useful not only in the treatment of cancer, but other diseases characterized by hypoxia, such as irritable bowel disease.

column36: Therapeutic Outcomes Following Intensive Voice and Speech Treatment in Children with Dysarthria Secondary to Cerebral Palsy
column37: Cerebral Palsy (CP) is a non-progressive neurogenic movement disorder that requires lifelong rehabilitation and is the most common motor disorder in children. While it affects individuals differently, up to 80% have motor speech disorders that result in impaired intelligibility due to poor control and coordination of the systems required for speech. These children often have difficulties with vocal loudness and intelligibility. Moreover, difficulties may be apparent as differences in prosody, which includes speech rate, loudness changes, and the normal, meaningful pitch changes that are part of typical speech. Prosody is critical to overall intelligibility and for signalling the communication intention. This study involves the use of an intensive voice and speech intervention (LSVT LOUD (R)) with children who have speech difficulties secondary to CP. We want to know if LSVT LOUD has a clinically meaningful effect on prosody and related features of speech intelligibility. In addition, we will examine adherence to a 12-week post-treatment maintenance program and its relation to preservation or further improvements of prosodic and articulatory features of speech. The results will be used to inform motor speech intervention for children with motor speech disorders secondary to CP.

column36: Professional regulation and medicolegal actions in pharmacy practice: Exploring trends, predictors, and the disciplinary action process for pharmacists in Canada
column37: Little is known about how and why Canadian pharmacists are disciplined by their regulatory body or "college" when they act in a way that is inconsistent with pharmacy practice guidelines and laws. During my pharmacy degree, I reviewed reports of college disciplinary investigations from 2010 to 2017 find out what actions caused disciplinary action for pharmacists and what penalties were applied. This research was the first of its kind in North America, and the first review that studied only pharmacists, not other healthcare professionals, since 2003. My research found that disciplinary action is uncommon, permanent loss of a license to practice is rare, and that most disciplinary cases resulted from charges of professionalism or dishonest business practices rather than from clinical errors. The proposed research will explore the discipline process for pharmacists and health professionals in Canada through three objectives: 1) determine the differences in disciplinary action processes among health professions and jurisdictions; 2) investigate pharmacy malpractice cases that are taken to civil court (which is separate from discipline by a college); and 3) examine the impact of the disciplinary process on pharmacists who have been disciplined. This novel research will provide new information to enable regulatory bodies, professional associations, and universities to prepare pharmacists and healthcare providers for professionals practice and to support those undergoing disciplinary action. This research will provide important information to help pharmacists determine the risks of liability from providing clinical services at a time when there is pressure to increase access to clinical services and streamline the delivery of healthcare services.

column36: Structural Determinants of Family Planning Access for Im/migrant Women
column37: One in five Canadian women is an immigrant or refugee (i.e., an im/migrant) and the number of im/migrants around the world and in Canada is steadily growing. Women need to be able to access family planning services (e.g., contraception, abortion, pregnancy planning) where and when they need them for their own health, the health of their babies, and as a basic sexual and reproductive health right. We do not know much about access to family planning services for im/migrant women in Canada. Limited research has found that refugees may face poor access to needed contraception services, and im/migrant women may be more likely to experience unplanned pregnancy. Work by our team to date with im/migrant women and service providers in Metro Vancouver has shown that this community faces serious concerns regarding barriers to care related to language barriers, racism and discrimination, worries about legal immigration status, and difficulty navigating British Columbia's (BC) health care system. The goal of this study is to understand the experiences of im/migrant women and their service providers with barriers to family planning services for women who recently arrived as im/migrants in Metro Vancouver. Through close collaboration with im/migrant women and community-based organizations, this MSc project will be based on interviews with im/migrant women who came to Canada in different ways (as refugees, for economic opportunity, without legal documentation), as well as their service providers (health, legal, settlement), to learn about their experiences with family planning services. We will use our results to make direct recommendations for policies and programmes that will improve access to family planning services for im/migrant women in BC and beyond.

column36: Evaluation of Treatment Modalities for Female Fetal Abdominal Cysts: A Multicenter Retrospective Review
column37: One of the most common reasons for referral to a pediatric surgeon for a fetal consultation is a diagnosis of an abdominal cystic mass in a female fetus, with an estimated occurrence rate of about 1 in 2600 pregnancies. With the broader application of routine prenatal ultrasound screening, the detection of fetal abdominal cysts has increased considerably. Most of these cysts arise from the fetal ovaries late in gestation as a result of maternal hormonal stimulation. However, these cysts can also originate from a variety of other organs including the intestine, liver, spleen, or kidney. Traditionally, surgeons managed these cysts based on the nature of the cyst or its size as measured on ultrasound. Most cysts that were simple, or smaller than 5 cm, were managed simply by observation and repeated ultrasounds. Larger and more complex cysts were usually removed surgically since they were thought to have little potential to regress, and could lead to more serious problems such as bowel obstruction. Currently, there are no evidence-based guidelines for prenatal or postnatal management and treatment of these cysts. Significant variability of care exists between institutions and even among surgeons in the same institution. Recently, some studies have shown that not only do small simple cysts have the potential to regress, but so do large and complex cysts. Our study aims to examine the management and outcomes of female fetuses in the last 10 years across 15 pediatric hospitals in Canada who were prenatally diagnosed with an abdominal cyst. The goal is to generate the first evidence-based Canadian recommendations to guide management and treatment of these patients.

column36: Analysis of metabolic and immune consequences of host-microbe interactions in diabetic mouse models
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) results from self-destruction of insulin-secreting pancreatic cells, and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) results from insulin resistance and its impaired secretion. The frequency of both diseases has increased significantly over the last 50 years, leading us to believe that they may be influenced by similar environmental factors. One hypothesis to explain these changes is that widespread antibiotic use has changed the composition of human gut bacteria (termed 'microbiome'; Mb) that reside in our intestines and play a significant role in our metabolism. The Mb is highly sensitive to diet and antibiotics, and its disruption (termed 'dysbiosis') is implicated in T1D and T2D risk. We believe that the Mb influences the development of diabetes, and that identifying bacteria that impact insulin-secreting cells and insulin-sensitive tissue can transform approaches to prevent both diseases. We hypothesize that children at risk for T1D and T2D exhibit dysbiosis that impair insulin secretion and action. Our goal is to identify intestinal microbes associated with diabetes and the consequences of their metabolic output. We will isolate and identify gut microbes from children at high risk for T1D or T2D in two prospective studies. We will isolate and cultivate the microbial communities of these pre-diabetic subjects, analyze their metabolic output, and determine whether they cause metabolic and immune disturbances by transfer into and analysis of specialized mouse models. Results from this study seek to fill a major knowledge gap in defining the cause-effect relationships involved in Mb contributions to disease. The identification of these mechanisms will help to identify human and microbial therapeutic targets for diabetes' prevention and treatment.

column36: Investigating Stat3 dependent and independent mechanisms of immune evasion
column37: The immune system has the ability to recognize and eliminate cancer cells before a tumor arises. But as time passes by, cancer cells develop mechanisms to evade or suppress the immune system, allowing them to proliferate, grow out of control and spread to other organs. There is significant evidence that the Stat3 gene plays a role in suppressing the immune system and promoting cancer progression. When we deleted Stat3 in one of our mouse models, we observed an enhanced immune response that completely eliminated the initial breast tumor. However, some cancer cells escape the immune system and are able to re-establish the cancerous growth. The details and exact mechanism that promote immune evasion are still unclear. Using advanced single cell sequencing technology available at our disposal, we aim to identify target genes required for these tumors to escape the immune system, and utilize that knowledge in order to develop more effective immunotherapies against breast cancers.

column36: Employing Adaptive Interventions and SMART Designs for the Creation of Optimal Post-Stroke Rehabilitation Programs
column37: Background: Stroke is a leading cause of disability in Canada. The probability of stroke reoccurring is high among survivors, and recurrent strokes are associated with increased mortality and disability severity. Although physical activity (PA) is effective in preventing recurrent strokes, adherence to PA programs is inadequate in this patient population. Adaptive interventions (AIs) are a way to increase adherence among patients by adapting treatments regimens based on their characteristics and treatment response (adherence). To create an AI, a Sequential Multiple Randomized Trial (SMART) design can be used where participants undergo multiple stages of treatment, with randomizations at the beginning of each stage. Interventions: Combinations of telephone consultations(TC), group exercise sessions(GS), and personal coaching(PC) will be used due to their demonstrated efficacy in improving PA adherence. Objectives: 1) Is there a difference in the proportion of chronic(>6months) post-stroke patients responding to PA when undergoing 6 vs 12 weeks of TC? 2) For non-adhering participants, is GS+TC+PC more effective than GS+PC for eliciting higher proportion of PA adherence when evaluated at 12 and 18 weeks? Methods: Forty participants from an outpatient rehabilitation program will be recruited. 1st stage: Participants will be randomized to either a 6 or 12 week TC group and proportion of responders will be identified. 2nd stage: Responders will continue with TC for 12 weeks. Non-responders will be re-randomized to either GS+TC+PC group or a GS+PC group for 12 weeks. Proportion of responders will be identified at 12 and 18 weeks. Data analysts will be blinded to groups. Significance: This is the first ever AI intervention and SMART trial created for post-stroke recovery.

column36: Restoring ion concentrations to improve outcome after hemorrhagic stroke
column37: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), a bleed in the brain, is a devastating disease. This bleed damages tissue and dramatically disrupts brain function, leading to death or disability. For those who survive, there is no treatment to improve recovery, which is often limited. One factor that limits the brain's ability to recover is the brain environment itself. Even weeks after ICH, important ions such as sodium and chloride are not present in the correct concentrations. There are many factors that lead to ion imbalances, including increased ion channel expression. Neurons communicate using these ions, and not having them in proper concentrations affects the ability to function properly. Restoring these ions to the right amounts may improve the brain's repair processes. Previous research has shown that rehabilitation, a common treatment after ICH, restores chloride levels and reduces damage. I will use a rat model of ICH to investigate a pharmacological approach to restoring ion levels. This will further characterize the relationship between ion levels and outcome and to test a potential therapy for ICH patients. Glibenclamide, a drug that blocks sodium movement into cells, will be used to restore sodium concentrations. This drug acts on a sodium channel that is only expressed after brain injury, including ICH. By blocking this channel, I hope to limit sodium increases and restore the brain environment to improve recovery processes. After inducing an ICH in rats, we will give glibenclamide at safe doses during the period of injury. We will assess the impact of glibenclamide on brain injury, behavioural outcome, and ion concentrations. This will allow us to determine if fixing the ion imbalances improves recovery after ICH. If it does, this is a promising target for patients.

column36: Role of gangliosides in the secretion of extracellular vesicles in neurodegenerative disease
column37: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids enriched in the brain with important roles in cell signaling, cell-cell communication and immune-modulation. Their levels are decreased in several neurodegenerative conditions, including Huntington's disease (HD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Therapeutic administration of ganglioside GM1 in animal models of both diseases results in significant attenuation of neurodegeneration and improvement of symptoms. In HD mice, these beneficial effects are associated with decreased brain accumulation of mutant huntingtin (mHTT), the toxic protein that causes HD. The underlying mechanisms are unknown, but preliminary data in our laboratory suggest that GM1 increases neuronal secretion of mHTT within extracellular vesicles (EVs), membrane-bound cell-derived particles with roles in cell-cell communication and immune modulation. I will test the hypothesis that cellular levels of gangliosides regulate the secretion of EVs containing toxic misfolded proteins, and that increased ganglioside levels and/or altered ganglioside profile on the surface of EVs facilitate their uptake and clearance by microglia and modulate microglia function towards neuroprotection. My studies will uncover a novel role for gangliosides in EV secretion under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, and will provide mechanistic insights on the neuroprotective role of GM1 in HD and in PD. This knowledge may accelerate translation of ganglioside-based therapies to clinical trials.

column36: Semantic False Memories in Parkinson's Disease
column37: The aim of this project is to explore the impact of Parkinson’s disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disorder that produces motor and cognitive deficits, on semantic false memory. After reading a list of semantically associated words, we often recall reading an associated non-presented word. This semantic false memory occurs because we naturally make associations between concepts. PD has been shown to inhibit semantic false memory due to the impact of PD on the ability to make associations. However, we cannot conclude that association impairment is responsible due to the many processes involved. To isolate association impairment, some authors proposing having participants read a list of words and then recall both presented words and any associated words they might have thought. A lower number of associated words compared with healthy controls would indicate association impairments. In this study, healthy older adults and adults with PD will complete a false memory task. Six lists of twelve words will be presented on a computer screen with one second intervals between words and no breaks between lists. In one condition, participants will be instructed to write down the words they studied. In the other condition, participants will be instructed to write down the words they studied and that came to mind in the study or test phase. In a separate session, participants will fill out various cognitive assessments, including the Mini Mental State Examination, the Stroop Task, and the Verbal Fluency task. Because PD is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, with cognitive impairments exerting significant influences on mortality and quality of life, this line of research is vital for improving the lives of older adults with PD.

column36: The Longitudinal Impact of Social Media Use: Disordered Eating and Body Image Disturbance in Adolescents
column37: A new and important factor to study in relation to disordered eating (DE) and body image issues in adolescents is the impact of social media use, which is associated with the development of risk factors for eating disorders. One factor that may act as a buffer against the effects of social media is self-compassion (SC). The objective of this research is to examine the relationship between eating disorder symptoms and SC in adolescents and to explore the role of SC as a buffer against the negative effects of social media use. The proposed longitudinal study will be conducted with a sample of approximately 475 adolescents of all genders from several local high schools over two time points. Adolescents aged 13-18 will complete questionnaires related to social media use, DE, body dissatisfaction, appearance comparison, and SC. I expect that greater use of social media will be associated with higher levels of appearance comparison, body dissatisfaction, and DE, especially among adolescents who present with low levels of SC. This study has several important strengths: (1) it investigates the extent to which SC attenuates the negative impact of social media use on body image and DE, (2) it includes males, who are underrepresented in eating disorder research, and (3) it incorporates a qualitative component which will provide information about how adolescents are using social media, rather than just the amount. This research will help us to better understand the factors that contribute to the onset and maintenance of eating disorders in adolescents.

column36: Role of dopamine and reward in the selective allocation of cognitive resources: Implications for Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease is a relatively well known neurological condition that has been classically understood in terms the motor difficulties it produces. In the past few decades, however, our view of the disease's complexity has evolved and we now know that it causes considerable cognitive impairment as well. Despite continues research, the identifiable cognitive deficits remain poorly characterized. Our research uses cognitive tasks and pharmacological manipulation to better understand such cognitive issues and connect them to the degeneration of brain cells seen in Parkinson's disease. The specific aim of this project is to identify the specific mechanism underlying the attention and working memory (the ability to temporarily hold information in your mind) deficits that the disease is known to cause. Recent investigations have shown healthy individuals have the ability to prioritize what information they pay attention to and what information they choose to store in memory. Evidence suggests that the ability to prioritize information in this way is linked with dopamine signals in the brain. These dopamine signals are reduced in Parkinson's patients. In this research project, we will test whether Parkinson's patients lose the ability to prioritize information for entry into the brain's processing, and whether this can be corrected with dopamine-replacement medications. Should this be the case, we will have provided an important step in our mechanistic understanding of cognitive deficits in Parkinson's disease. This exiting work allows us to both further our understanding of human cognition and develop a more specific view of the clinical non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease.

column36: Characterizing the role of the SWI/SNF Complex in Oncolytic Virotherapy.
column37: Despite extensive research and efforts, cancer remains the leading cause of death among Canadians. Therapeutic advances have led to the development of immunotherapies; treatments that utilize the patient's immune system to help target and eliminate tumors. One such treatment is oncolytic virotherapy, which uses engineered oncolytic or "cancer-killing" viruses (OVs) to specifically infect and kill cancer cells. These OVs subsequently activate the immune system to stimulate durable anti-tumor responses. Despite strong and promising anti-tumor responses by OV in certain cancer patients, tumor diversity presents as a significant hurdle to the development of widespread cures. The SWItch/Sucrose Non-Fermentable (SWI/SWF) complex is a complex that regulates gene transcription thereby controlling numerous biological processes. Previous work in our lab has shown that functional loss of various subunits of the SWI/SNF complex leads to increased viral sensitivity and cancer cell killing of multiple OV platforms in otherwise resistant cancer cell lines. The goal of this project is to engineer an OV that is specifically equipped to target and inactivate components of the SWI/SNF complex. This should improve the infectability and killing of cancer cells, sensitizing tumors to immunotherapy and leading to durable cures. The project will also elucidate the mechanisms by which complex disruption increases tumor sensitivity to virus and assess the SWI/SNF complex status as a potential predictive marker for OV treatment response. This work will generate a novel OV candidate and has the potential to identify a biomarker predictive of tumor response to OV therapy.

column36: Impacts de l'offre de services en physiotherapie au sein d'une urgence quebecoise - Essai clinique randomise
column37: Les delais d'attente a l'urgence sont un probleme preoccupant dans les centres hospitaliers canadiens et quebecois. En reaction a ce probleme, plusieurs pays ont integre une offre de services en physiotherapie dans les urgences, principalement pour des patients se presentant avec une condition neuro-musculosquelettique. Une telle offre a permis de diminuer les temps d'attente et de traitement et reduire le nombre de consultations et de prescriptions de tests diagnostiques non indiques. Au Quebec, l'offre de services de physiotherapie a l'urgence est marginale et son impact n'a pas ete documente. L'objectif de ce projet est d'evaluer les effets de la prise en charge de patients par un physiotherapeute a l'urgence sur leur evolution, l'utilisation des services et des ressources et le temps d'attente. La collecte de donnees est actuellement en cours au Centre hospitalier de l'Universite Laval. Des analyses statistiques seront effectuees en comparant les resultats de patients ayant ete pris en charge par un physiotherapeute a ceux n'ayant ete vus que par le medecin de l'urgence. En evaluant les effets d'une prise en charge par un physiotherapeute a l'urgence, ce projet contribuera a ameliorer l'acces aux soins et l'efficience des services en sante et a reduire les longs delais d'attente et de prise en charge a l'urgence. column36: The Development and Validation of Patient Satisfaction Tools for Adult and Pediatric Surgical Patients
column37: Patient satisfaction has become a growing area of study within the health care field. We will then administer both the paediatric and adult satisfaction questionnaires to a pilot group of paediatric and adult surgical patients. The pilot testing will help to establish the validity of the Patient Experience and Satisfaction Tools by determining whether they are reliable at generating an accurate impression of patient satisfaction.

column36: The Impact of Culture on Parent-Targeted Interventions in Pediatric Pain Care
column37: Children and families identify pain as a primary concern during hospitalization, but there is a continued lack of effective pain treatment in the pediatric population. column36: Structural and Functional Characterization of an Enterobactin-Producing Megaenzyme
column37: Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) are microbial megaenzymes that produce antibacterials, antitumours, immunosuppressants, toxins, and virulence factors. They use complex synthetic cycles, requiring many different reactions to occur with high fidelity and processivity. NRPSs are organized into modules ~3 domains with each module adding one specific amino acid monomer to the peptide as it grows. The very last domain in the final module is responsible for releasing the product in its final form. This domain is usually a thioesterase (TE) domain. TE domains are especially impressive because they can either hydrolyze, cyclize, or oligomerize the reaction intermediate presented to them. The decision is very important for the biological activity of the product because a product that is meant to be cyclic will not have the same activity if it is hydrolyzed to the linear form, for example. In this project, I will study the TE domain from the NRPS that makes enterobactin, a siderophore compound that allows E. coli to grow in low iron conditions. This TE domain takes an intermediate, oligomerizes it three times and then cyclizes it to produce mature enterobactin. I will use molecular biology, biochemistry, crystallography, genetic code expansion, mutagenesis, and enterobactin synthesis assays to visualize and interrogate how exactly three intermediates are assembled, and how then the TE domain switches to cyclization activity. Together, these experiments will provide increased understanding of how NRPSs produce virulence factors and therapeutics. This understanding could be important in future experiments aimed at inhibiting virulence factor production, or modifying NRPSs to produce novel therapeutics.

column36: The rate of recurrent tuberculosis attributable to relapse or reinfection after successful treatment among the Inuit

People previously treated for TB are expected to have an increased risk of re-developing TB.Methods: This study will use previously collected culture-positive TB cases from 14 Inuit communities in Nunavik. 10 culture-positive samples will be analyzed with whole-genome sequencing, which can distinguish relapse from re-infection with superior accuracy compared to classical genotyping methods. column36: Brain nicotinic receptor function assessed in vivo during chronic nicotine exposure and withdrawal
column37: The common consensus is that tobacco smokers smoke to obtain the stimulating effects of nicotine upon nicotinic receptors in the reward pathway of the brain; conversely, withdrawal symptoms are thought to be due to underactivation of these receptors. Therefore, nicotine replacement therapy is based around intending to stimulate these same receptors. However, there is considerable evidence that while nicotine acts to stimulate the reward pathway in the short term, chronic nicotine use actually leads to desensitization of this pathway. Further research has shown evidence that nicotine withdrawal syndrome is linked to overactivation of receptors in the reward pathway, not underactivation as commonly thought. The evidence for supersensitive receptors in withdrawal has almost exclusively been studied in cell culture or electrophysiology experiments. While these studies are helpful, it is also necessary to study nicotine withdrawal syndrome in the complex biology of behaving organisms. This project will therefore investigate the effects of chronic nicotine administration and nicotine withdrawal on the reward pathway in rats using a recently-developed method called fiber photometry. This method allows one to image the activity of selected neuronal populations in real-time, in freely behaving rats. We hypothesize that during chronic nicotine administration the brain's reward pathway loses its ability to respond to nicotine and during withdrawal the receptors in this pathway are supersensitive. The findings from this study will potentially provide the first evidence of a supersensitive response to nicotine in the reward pathway during withdrawal in living organisms. Our results will potentially force a reconsideration of nicotine replacement therapy.

column36: Determining the predominant autophagic forms and genetic determinants of macrophage lipophagy
column37: High fat diets lead to an increased risk of a disease known as atherosclerosis, which is a major cause of heart disease. Atherosclerosis is characterized by the accumulation of fat particles within specialized cells of the immune system known as macrophages. Once laden with fat particles these cells aggregate within blood vessels and block circulation, which can ultimately lead to heart attacks. The recent discovery of a novel biological process within macrophages has the potential to reduce the fat particle accumulation within macrophages. This process, known as lipophagy, is a specialized means for the macrophage cell to break down fat particles and excrete the byproducts out of the cell. With a decreased fat level, the macrophages will have a lower risk of obstructing blood flow and causing heart attacks. However, little is known about how lipophagy works. Before a drug can be developed to upregulate it within macrophage cells, a better understanding of how lipophagy functions must be achieved. This proposal is aimed at filling in the lipophagy knowledge gap. Specifically, we are interested in identifying all of the genes that play a role in this process. We will perform this analysis using single-cellular yeast. Yeast are an excellent organism for genetic studies because the technology already exists to efficiently remove any of their genes, one at a time, and monitor the effect. Additionally, macrophage lipophagy is believed to operate in a certain conventional form, similar to other related processes. There is some evidence, though, that it may also operate in another way. We would like to address which form of lipophagy is the most common one in macrophages. To do this we will use microscopy to look at the specific patterns of each possible lipophagy form.

column36: Functional and cellular benefits of aerobic exercise in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patients
column37: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is the most common adult-onset muscular dystrophy and second most common muscular dystrophy. DM1 is an autosomal dominant neuromuscular disease that is caused by a trinucleotide repeat mutation in the 3' untranslated region of the Dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene. This results in a multisystemic disease that is primarily characterized by skeletal muscle wasting, weakness and myotonia. Disease manifestation begins when 50+ CTG repeats are transcribed to form nuclear foci resulting in a toxic gain of function such as sequestration of important RNA-binding proteins leading to defects in RNA metabolism. Studies in murine models of DM1 have shown that exercise training can induce beneficial molecular and physiological effects that ameliorate the disease pathology. Studies in DM1 patients have demonstrated that exercise training increased exercise capacity; however, it is unclear if there were molecular and/or clinically meaningful benefits. This is due to limitations in the previous studies that lacked direct histological, electrophysiologic and molecular outcomes. Thus, the purpose of this study is to examine the functional and cellular benefits of 12-weeks of moderate intensity endurance exercise training in DM1 patients. This study aims to test the hypothesis that aerobic exercise training will induce functional and molecular benefits in DM1 patients, deeming it an easy lifestyle intervention that mitigates the DM1 pathology. Furthermore, through understanding exercise-induced cellular adaptation, it could provide information for future discovery of pharmaceutical, nutritional or exercise interventions. This is the first study to comprehensively understand both the functional and cellular effects of exercise in DM1 patients.

column36: Neural mechanisms underlying negative cognitive bias in at-risk females of depressed mothers
column37: Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. Women are twice as likely to develop depression compared to men and the daughters of depressed mothers have a particularly high risk. Nevertheless, sex bias in the occurrence of depression is rarely addressed in interventions. Understanding why the daughters of depressed mothers are more vulnerable to exhibit depression is essential to develop appropriate and sex-specific treatments, which are presently lacking. Recent research has identified that negative cognitive bias, the negative interpretation of neutral contexts, occurs more often in females and predicts the onset of depressive episodes in daughters at risk for depression. However, the underlying mechanisms of this risk factor remain largely unknown. This research will investigate if negative cognitive bias is associated with neural markers of depression, such as dysregulated stress hormones, increased neuroinflammation, and decreased neurogenesis. We will employ extensive behavioural and neuroscientific techniques to assess the mechanisms underlying negative cognitive bias in a robust rat model. Thus, it will determine whether daughters of 'depressed' mothers show greater HPA dysregulation, aberrant neurogenesis, and increased pro-inflammatory signaling compared with the daughters of control dams. Elucidating if such alterations correlate with negative cognitive bias, may serve as an important step towards the discovery of interventions for cognitive dysfunctions that predict the onset and maintenance of depressive episodes in at-risk females. Thus, this study targets prevention and health promotion, and importantly, serves as the groundwork for improving the development of sex-specific treatments for depression.

column36: The Psychometric Properties and Normative Values of the Life-Space Assessment in Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Canada
column37: Background: Life-space mobility is a construct that reflects the ability of an individual to safely maneuver oneself within their immediate and surrounding life-spaces (places one visits in daily life). The Life-Space Assessment (LSA) is a self-reported questionnaire that quantifies this construct. It asks questions regarding the different areas one visited in the past 4 weeks (bedroom to beyond their town), the frequency of that movement, and if assistance was required. Many studies have summarized the ability of this questionnaire to accurately and precisely quantify (called measurement properties) life-space mobility, however, no systematic reviews have been conducted. Additionally, no age and sex based population values have been developed for healthy older adults in Canada. Objectives: 1) conduct a systematic review summarizing the measurement properties of the LSA in community dwelling older adults; 2) confirm the measurement properties that emerged from the systematic review through analysis of a population-based dataset and; 3) establish sex and age stratified normative values for the LSA in older Canadians. Methods: 1) multiple databases will be searched, in consultation with a librarian, to identify studies that have evaluated the psychometric properties of the LSA. 2) A secondary analysis of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) will be conducted to evaluate measurement properties of the LSA. 3) The distribution of values from the LSA in the CLSA will be produced which will define typical Canadian values for senior men and women. Significance: To our knowledge, this will be the first study to summarize the measurement properties of the LSA in community-dwelling older adults, and establish age and sex stratified norms for the LSA in older Canadians.

column36: The efficacy of oxygen therapy in reducing grey matter hypoxia and degeneration in an animal model of multiple sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological disease that causes significant disability. This is due to an upregulated immune response involving inflammation that attacks the brain and spinal cord (central nervous system; CNS). An unrelenting loss of brain leads to a reduction in physical and mental abilities, greatly affecting the quality of life of people with MS. When brain oxygen levels are low (hypoxia), the upregulated immune response could worsen, leading to further impairment. Animal model and clinical patient data show that CNS hypoxia may contribute to MS disease progression. Therefore, treating hypoxia by administering oxygen therapy may reduce damage in the CNS. Although clinical trials of oxygen therapy were deemed unsuccessful, we believe that this was because levels of brain hypoxia could not be controlled for, and oxygen was given with no regard to current disease status. We believe that oxygen administered at the onset of an inflammatory event could reduce inflammation. We have preliminary data supporting this idea, which we want to investigate further before testing in patients. We will test the hypothesis that oxygen therapy can reduce brain hypoxia and injury in a mouse model of MS when therapy is started at the onset of inflammation. We will measure brain hypoxia, cell damage, and brain size in oxygen-treated groups and untreated groups using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and histology. We will compare behavioral test scores between groups to assess whether oxygen therapy can slow disease progression. This study will provide new data on the potential for oxygen to be used as a therapy in MS. If successful, we will re-open the door to this accessible therapy that could be combined with other current MS medications to improve outcome.

column36: Community-led action to improve wellness within BC First Nations communities: Process evaluation of an engagement process addressing commercial tobacco wellness strategies.
column37: Indigenous populations in Canada smoke commercial tobacco (CT) at a rate three times higher than other Canadians (Elton-Marshall, Leatherdale, and Burkhalter 2011; de Finney et al. 2013). Yet, little is known regarding the relationship between Indigenous peoples of Canada and their uses and consumption of CT. Under Canada's Tobacco Strategy, there is a call for "distinct approaches" to support tobacco control for Indigenous peoples, yet there are no clear guidelines regarding how to effectively address this public health issue in a culturally respectful way; one which fully engages the community. This study will conduct a process evaluation of an Indigenous-led, health engagement strategy for respecting tobacco, namely, A context-specific and comprehensive menu of commercial tobacco control measures for First Nation communities. As part of a larger study, this process evaluation will be informed and supported by a team of Indigenous and non-Indigenous health researchers and a rich data source. A mixed-methods approach will use data from community engagement meetings, key informant interviews, survey data, research logs, and observations of the author. This study, through engagement with 5 BC Indigenous communities will develop an evaluation tool to assess levels of research partnership (consult, collaborate, engage) and will identify strengths and weaknesses in each. This study will describe the process of respectful community engagement and offer future guidance in the form of lessons learned. The purpose of this study is twofold; 1) create a tool researchers can use when engaging in culturally respectful research partnerships with Indigenous communities and 2) Create a tool communities can use when engaging in research partnerships with non-Indigenous researchers.

column36: Cardiac Energy Metabolism in Barth Syndrome
column37: Heart failure presents as the leading cause of infant death in patients with Barth Syndrome, a rare genetic disorder first described by Peter Barth and colleagues in 1983. Fortunately, with current medical strategies, individuals with Barth Syndrome now have a greater likelihood of surviving past infancy, however heart disease remains a constant clinical concern throughout their lifespan. Recently, it has been discovered that the heart of an individual with Barth Syndrome may not be able to produce energy as efficiently as a healthy heart. Because of this malfunction in energy production, the heart is compromised in its ability to effectively pump blood through the rest of the body, thus leading to heart failure. The goal of our research is to determine whether correcting the heart's ability to produce energy may be an effective therapy to prevent the development of heart disease in Barth Syndrome. Our early data has suggested that the Barth Syndrome heart may be impaired in its ability to effectively burn sugar for energy, and that an energy source made by the liver, the ketone body, may be a better substrate for the Barth Syndrome heart to metabolize. Recently, a genetically modified mouse model has been developed with the same genetic mutation that causes Barth syndrome, and these mice also develop heart failure mimicking the human condition. We will treat these mice with drugs that increase sugar (dichloroacetate) or ketone body (empagliflozin) metabolism in the heart, and assess whether these drugs improve heart function and prevent heart failure. If our hypothesis is correct, our research will suggest that increasing the heart's ability to burn sugar and/or ketone bodies for energy, may be an exciting approach to prevent heart failure in Barth Syndrome children.

column36: Metabolic function of the hepatic GLP-1-Wnt-FGF-21 axis
column37: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF-21) is an endocrine hormone mainly produced in the liver and released during fasting, functioning as an insulin signaling sensitizer. FGF-21 and its homologues are intensively studied in pre-clinical studies and in clinical trials. These homologues may become a novel category of pharmacological agents for patients with impaired glucose and lipid metabolism. Recently, we found that in LTCFDN, a Wnt signaling deficient mouse model generated in our lab, hepatic FGF-21 mRNA and protein levels were reduced, associated with impaired glucose and lipid homeostasis. As the incretin hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and its based drugs (i.e. exenatides and liraglutide) were shown to exert metabolic beneficial effects via up-regulating Wnt pathway effector ?-catenin, we propose the existence of the hepatic GLP-1-Wnt-FGF-21 axis in mediating the function of GLP-1 and its based drugs. Our lab is now aiming to examine the role of this signaling axis in health and diseases. My research project will focus mainly on exploring mechanisms underlying hepatic FGF-21 transcription. I hypothesize that FGF-21 is positively regulated by the Wnt signaling pathway effector ?-catenin/TCF, and that GLP-1 can exert its hepatic metabolic beneficial effects by activating FGF-21 production. This is achieved by stimulating both ?-catenin Ser675 phosphorylation and expression of the TCF family members. We are studying a novel signaling axis, which will deepen our knowledge on the two key metabolic hormones in the liver. We link the starvation hormone FGF-21 with the postprandial active hormone GLP-1 in this axis together, which may lead to novel therapeutic possibilities in treating impaired glucose and lipid metabolism.

column36: Metabolic Inflexibility during Sprint Interval Training: The iFLEX Study
column37: The prevalence of physical inactivity and obesity increased worldwide, and New Brunswick is no exception. It is now well established that exercise is a cornerstone to managing obesity and obesity-related comorbidities. However, it is crucial that we gain a better understanding of how exercise improves health outcomes in individuals carrying extra body weight in order to offer them long-lasting exercise interventions. Recently, the concept of metabolic flexibility has been of interest in the scientific community. Metabolic flexibility is the body's ability to respond to changes in exercise. For example, as the intensity of exercise changes, the body typically would change the type of fuel it used (fat or sugars). Healthy weight individuals have typically shown to have better metabolic flexibility than individual living with extra body weight. In addition, it has been shown that both healthy weight individuals and individuals living with extra body weight can enhance metabolic flexibility with exercise. However, very limited information is available on the effects of sprint-interval training has on metabolic flexibility in both healthy weight individuals and individuals living with extra body weight. This study is being conducted to investigate whether sprint interval training produces a larger improvement in metabolic flexibility for both healthy weight individuals and individuals living with extra body weight. The purpose of this study is to find out whether 1) your body has a greater metabolic flexibility following a 4-week sprint interval intervention and 2) to determine whether this change in metabolic flexibility is associated with better insulin sensitivity (which is a common risk factor for Type 2 Diabetes).

column36: Dietary and Microbial Metabolites in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), including Crohn disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis, affect 1 in 150 Canadians; 25% of cases are diagnosed in children. IBD manifests with chronic gastrointestinal inflammation and altered microbial composition. Dietary changes impact IBD, including the pediatric CD therapy exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN), which entails exclusive intake of liquid meal-replacement, making adherence challenging. Predicting patient outcomes to EEN requires improved understanding of pathogenesis. Our study examines how intestinal microorganisms are involved in IBD development. We hypothesize that an altered intestinal microbiome in response to dietary or bacterial-secreted metabolites mediates patient response to dietary therapy. I will investigate whether previous diet is a valid predictor of EEN success, using metabolomics to develop biomarkers that will identify candidates for EEN success. Pilot analysis of pre-diagnosis food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) data shows that simple carbohydrates and processed meat are predictors of EEN failure and success, respectively. I will expand the analysis to a nation-wide FFQ database, and correlate results with stool microbiome analysis and metabolomics to identify potential mediators. Significantly altered metabolites will be assessed in vitro: gentamicin protection assays and immunofluorescent microscopy will identify effects on bacterial invasion, transepithelial electrical resistance will indicate epithelial barrier integrity changes, and qPCR with Western blotting and ELISA will determine human cell line inflammatory responses. Understanding diet and microbial interactions in pediatric IBD can guide novel therapies and facilitate identification of patients likely to respond to dietary therapies.

column36: Quantification et modelisation de l'effet des variants genetiques sur la cognition, le comportement et la neuroconnectivite
column37: Les troubles neurodeveloppementaux (TNDs), tels que les troubles du spectre de l'autisme (TSA) sont caracterises par une heterogeneite clinique et genetique importante. Parmi les variants genetiques contribuant a ces TNDs, les variants de nombre de copies (CNVs)(deletion ou duplication) sont identifies dans 10-15% des patients referes en clinique. Cependant, la tres grande majorite de ces CNVs sont extremement rares donc leur etude est tres difficile. Vu l'absence de methodologie pour les etudier, nous avons peu de connaissance sur les mecanismes qui sous-tendent leurs effets sur differents traits phenotypiques tels que la cognition, le comportement et la neuroanatomie. Hypothese: Les effets des CNVs peuvent etre estimes en utilisant des modeles integrant des variables qui caracterisent la nature et la fonction des genes alteres. Objectif : Developper des modeles en se basant sur les scores genetiques et les annotations fonctionnelles pour estimer l'effet des CNVs dans la population generale ainsi que dans des populations cliniques avec un diagnostic de TNDs. Methodes: Des probands avec TNDs et porteurs de CNVs sont recrutes avec leurs parents (porteurs et non-porteurs) dans notre etude. Des evaluations cognitives, comportementales et d'imagerie cerebrale sont collectees et combinees a des donnees de cohortes cliniques et de la population generale. Analyses : Les CNVs seront caracterises par des scores d'intolerance a la mutation. Ces scores sont par la suite inclus dans des modeles lineaires et non-parametriques dans le but d'expliquer l'effet des CNVs sur differents traits phenotypiques. Conclusion : Cette approche permettra de developper un outil qui assiste les cliniciens pour l'interpretation de l'effet de CNVs rares sur l'apparition de phenotypes cliniques.

column36: How does bedaquiline kill drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis? A structural investigation with electron cryomicroscopy
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the top ten causes of death worldwide, in Canada largely affecting foreign-born individuals and Canadian-born Indigenous peoples. TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and, like many bacterial infections, can become resistant to antibiotics. A drug approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2012 called bedaquiline (also known as Sirturo), although still requiring long treatment regimens with major side effects, has been shown to be part of an effective treatment strategy for extensively drug-resistant TB. While it is known that the drug affects M. tuberculosis' ATP synthase, the enzyme that makes ATP (the cell's energy source), it is unclear how the drug affects this enzyme. It is also unknown why bedaquiline inhibits other bacterial ATP synthases, but kills M. tuberculosis and its close relatives specifically. Electron cryomicroscopy (cryoEM) can permit us to determine the structure of the bacterium's ATP synthase with bedaquline bound to it with atomic-level resolution. Knowledge of the structure will enable us to understand how the drug works, and how it is able to sterilize a M. tuberculosis infection. This information can be used to develop more effective and faster treatments for TB with fewer side effects.

column36: Role of the tumour microenvironment in medulloblastoma progression
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common childhood brain cancer. Treatment involves surgery, followed by radiation and chemotherapy. These treatments often fail and result in significant loss of brain function. In some cancers, a specific population of stem cells located around blood vessels can become activated, migrate towards the tumour and create a favourable environment for tumour growth. This project will characterize how these cells aid in medulloblastoma development by assessing their activity and ability to increase tumour severity and growth rate. Understanding how non-cancer cells can promote tumour growth can lead to the development of more effective, targeted treatments for medulloblastoma.

column36: Identifying intratumoral transcriptional heterogeneity in BCR-ABL1 lymphoblastic leukemia
column37: BCR-ABL1 acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common form of ALL in adults, contributing to 25-40% of cases. The development of drugs that inhibit BCR-ABL1, such as imatinib, has improved clinical outcomes for BCR-ABL1 ALL patients, yet many patients still relapse for reasons not entirely known. One contributor to relapse in the disease is the persistence of treatment-resistant leukemic subpopulations that are sufficient to restart the disease. Recent research in the Notta lab has demonstrated that BCR-ABL1 ALL patients can be separated into two subgroups, 'core-B' and 'mixed-B', with different molecular profiles and treatment outcomes. To better understand the subgroups and why they feature differences in relapse rates, I will identify the extent of intratumoral heterogeneity in samples from the 'core-B' and 'mixed-B' subgroups and characterize the resulting cell subpopulations using single-cell RNA sequencing. I plan to analyze the single-cell data by applying novel machine learning approaches to cluster cells. I will identify the cell populations we find from this clustering by comparing to known transcriptional profiles of leukemic and normal cells. Finally, I will compare the composition of cell populations between samples from the 'core-B' and 'mixed-B' groups. Identifying the common and unique subpopulations of blast among the two molecularly and clinically different subgroups will help with developing therapies that target all cancerous populations and prevent relapse.

column36: Correlations Between Thalamocortical White Matter Fiber Tracts and Non-Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Electroencephalogram Oscillations
column37: Based on the neural oscillation, muscle activity and movement of eyes, sleep is divided into two major components: rapid eye movement sleep (REM) and non-rapid eye movement (NREM). NREM is further divided into three distinct stages based on the frequency and amplitude of neural oscillation. In addition, there exist micro-events specific to each stage, which facilitates the detection of each stage. One of these micro-events is spindles. Two of the prominent features of NREM sleep are spindles and slow wave activity. A growing number of human neuroscience studies demonstrate that sleep spindles and slow wave activity play an essential role in different cognitive processes. On the other hand, it has been shown that the neural oscillation and electroencephalography (EEG) features of sleep remain unchanged within an individual from one night to the next. However, there is evidence that the amount of sleep spindle and slow wave activity differ between individuals. It is unclear what exactly causes these inter-individual differences. One recent study attempted to discover if macroscopic differences of the volume of grey matter in humans contribute to these inter-individual differences. However, the relationship of these EEG phasic traits of NREM sleep and other anatomical metrics of the brain, such as the volume of white matter fiber tracts projecting from the thalamus to the neocortex is yet to be investigated. Our study's aim is to utilize neuroimaging and EEG technique to investigate the relation of the volume of white matter fiber tracts projected from thalamus to the neocortex in human and examine whether it can explain the inter-individual differences of spindles and slow wave activity in NREM sleep.

column36: Role of Glucagon-Like Peptide 2 in the Treatment of Celiac Disease
column37: Celiac disease is a common condition in Canadians, and occurs as an immune response of sensitive individuals to ingestion of gluten, a molecule found in wheat. Exposure to gluten in these individuals results in damage to the intestines, resulting in pain and an inability to absorb food that, then, causes diarrhea and (in children), failure to grow normally. Over the past 20 years, we have studied a natural hormone that is produced by the intestines, glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), which not only causes the intestines to grow but, also, promotes intestinal repair after injury. The aim of the proposed study is to develop a mouse model of celiac disease and to determine whether treatment of these mice with GLP-2 can help prevent intestinal damage and/or promote intestinal repair after damage has been caused by adding gluten to the diet. The long-term goal of these studies is to develop GLP-2 as a novel treatment for patients with severe celiac disease that cannot be prevented by gluten avoidance alone.

column36: Investigating the safety and efficacy of intra-arterial chilled saline following ischemic stroke
column37: Ischemic stroke impacts over 50,000 Canadians each year, costing billions of dollars. Despite recent treatment advances, not all patients benefit. My goal is to benefit all patients - especially those that do not respond to current stroke treatments. To this end, I will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a novel therapy, known as intra-arterial chilled saline that is hypothesized to work in synergy with current treatment methods. Frankly, animal research findings do not tend to translate to patients. This is often due to unrealistic experimental design. For example, it is not uncommon to see small sample sizes, inappropriate stroke models, and impossibly high treatment dosages used in animal research. These design flaws lead to a paradoxical overestimate of treatment effectiveness in animals, and underwhelming results in patient trials. My research will bridge the gap between treating stroke models, and real strokes. This research has been crafted in collaboration with clinicians that are interested in future use of this method. As such, this data will guide future clinical research and trials. Our approach involves the use of a rat model that mimics our target population, and a more realistic treatment protocol than previous studies, with attention to both risks and potential benefits. I have three aims, which will address the safety and efficacy of the proposed treatment through relevant biological and behavioural endpoints. I hypothesize that intra-arterial chilled saline will improve neurological outcomes, with low risk. Multimodal assessment will confer more confidence in our findings. Although early studies using this therapy in rodents and a few patients are promising, more studies are needed to understand this approach before more humans are tested.

column36: The Effect of Antioxidant Supplementation in Intravenous Nutrition on Gastrointestinal Health in a Neonatal Piglet Model
column37: Intravenous (IV) nutrition is a lifesaving tool used by clinicians to treat premature infants. However, the use of IV nutrition presents with adverse consequences including changes to the structure and function of the intestinal tract. This subsequently reduces the infant's ability to absorb nutrients from the diet once normal feeding into the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is resumed. The loss of GI function is due in part to a decrease in blood flow to the intestinal tract during IV nutrition. Blood flow is regulated by a compound called nitric oxide (NO), so greater availability of NO may help sustain blood flow during IV feeding. However, IV feeding introduces pro-oxidant compounds that contribute to tissue damage and cell death. NO is known to react with pro-oxidant compounds and the resultant compound, peroxynitrite, can also cause tissue damage. These negative effects must be mitigated by the infant's own antioxidant system. Glutathione is the compound within the antioxidant system that reacts with the pro-oxidant compounds. In premature infants, this glutathione system is under-developed and unable to overcome the production and presence of these pro-oxidant compounds. In this study, we will be using newborn piglets that are supported with IV nutrition supplemented with glutathione (versus un-supplemented). We predict that the addition of glutathione will enhance antioxidant capabilities which in turn, will protect NO so it can function as a blood flow regulator rather than contributing to oxidative tissue damage. Glutathione supplementation is potentially an innovative method of reducing intestinal injury caused by oxidative damage and poor intestinal blood flow, and could be applied clinically to aid in the survival and growth of premature infants.

column36: L'effet d'un entrainement metacognitif sur les deficits en theorie de l'esprit en schizophrenie
column37: La schizophrenie (SZ) est une psychopathologie qui affecte les cognitions, les perceptions et les comportements. Les individus atteints de SZ presentent souvent des difficultes dans leur fonctionnement quotidien. La medication contribue a diminuer les symptomes positifs de la maladie (idees delirantes, hallucinations), mais n'elimine pas les difficultes fonctionnelles. Un obstacle important au bon fonctionnement en SZ est la presence de difficultes de cognition sociale. Jusqu'ici, les traitements developpes pour cibler la cognition sociale sont principalement des traitements de remediation cognitive visant l'amelioration des processus cognitifs, la durabilite et la generalisation des acquis au quotidien. La Theorie de l'esprit (TdE) soit la capacite a inferer les etats mentaux des autres, est particulierement alteree en SZ. En outre, la performance de TdE est un des meilleurs predicteurs de fonctionnement quotidien. Le Metacognitive training (MCT) est un traitement psychologique ayant pour but principal d'informer les patients sur les difficultes cognitives susceptibles de sous-tendre leurs symptomes et leurs difficultes fonctionnelles. Ce programme cible notamment les difficultes de cognition sociale, mais son effet sur les habiletes de cognition sociale n'a pas ete demontre. L'objectif 1 est de mener une etude pilote afin de documenter si l'effet du MCT est observe sur la performance de cognition sociale en SZ et en particulier sur les deficits de TdE presents chez les patients atteints de SZ. Ensuite, les objectifs 2 et 3 sont respectivement de repliquer les effets du MCT sur les symptomes psychiatriques et sur le fonctionnement social des patients atteints de SZ et d'etudier les liens entre ces ameliorations et celles observees au niveau de la cognition sociale.

column36: Megakaryocyte Engineering to Create Designer Platelets
column37: Platelets are small circulating cells that act as natural delivery vehicles for numerous small molecules and regulate many physiological processes such as blood clotting, immune function, and cancers. Platelets are often transfused to help stop bleeding, but their application in other diseases is limited by challenges to modify and enhance platelet function for therapeutic purposes. For example, there are currently no methods to modify the protein content of transfusable platelets. This project therefore aims to develop novel approaches to engineer platelets by modifying their precursor cells, megakaryocytes (MKs). This will be achieved by using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)-a recently FDA-approved drug delivery vehicle-targeted to MKs, delivering nucleic acids to alter the protein composition of platelets. Successful implementation of this strategy will therefore create a platform technology to produce platelets with new and modified functions that current transfused platelets do not possess. The technology will enable platelets to locally deliver therapeutics to injured tissues, such as sites of trauma, or potentially to treat diseased tissues and organs where platelets accumulate, such as tumours or the brain for treating Alzheimer's disease.

column36: A Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating an Information Decision Aid for Late-Life Depression
column37: As Canada's population ages, it is important to protect, maintain, and promote older adults' mental health. The ability to live meaningful and enjoyable lives may be reduced when older adults experience a diagnosis of depression. Older adults face many barriers when accessing mental health services, one of which is decreased knowledge about mental health problems. Information decision-aids (IDAs) are a type of tool that can increase and individual's knowledge about mental health problems by presenting unbiased and research based information on health problems and treatment options in clear and concise language. IDAs help patients to be engaged in the treatment decision making process and improve communication between patients and health care providers. The purpose of this study is to (1) evaluate the effectiveness of a web-based IDA for late-life depression that was developed by our research team, and (2) compare its effectiveness to an existing online IDA. Older adults will be randomly selected to be in an intervention group (IDA developed by our research team) or comparison group (existing online IDA), and will be given an assessment measuring general depression knowledge, conflict about treatment decisions and attitudes about seeking mental health treatment. This study will provide new evidence on the effectiveness of web-based IDAs for late-life depression. Highly effective IDAs have the potential to reduce barriers that older adults face in accessing mental health services by improving mental health knowledge and enhancing their ability to participate in the treatment decision-making process.

column36: The role of 2-hydroxyglutarate as a contributor to immune system evasion in cancer
column37: Our body's immune system is responsible for protecting us from infectious organisms and other invaders. The immune system is made up of cells, tissues and organs that work together to fight infection to keep us healthy. Importantly, the immune system must also detect cancerous cells in the body. As tumors grow, they develop different ways to turn off the immune system, allowing the cancer to grow and spread throughout the body. Many types of cancer have alterations in metabolic pathways - the ways by which the cancer cells produce energy. One of these alterations results in the production of a compound called 2-hydroxyglutarate. We are interested in the ways by which 2-hydroxyglutarate suppresses a specific type of immune cell called Natural Killer cells. Natural Killer cells have a critical function in detecting tumors. We hypothesize that 2-hydroxyglutarate produced by tumor cells is secreted in to the surrounding environment and reduces the capacity of the Natural Killer cells to detect the presence of the cancer cells, which allows the tumor to progress. This project will focus on the mechanisms 2-hydroxyglutarate alters Natural Killer cells' efficiency to kill cancer cells.

column36: Neoantigens in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
column37: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is a type of skin cancer that presents with red patches on the skin. These patches can develop into tumours, marking advanced disease. The disease can then spread to other organs. MF is considered incurable and once patients develop tumours, they have only a 56% chance of surviving 5 years. There is an urgent need for advances in therapies. Immunotherapies work by using the patient's immune system to fight tumour cells. These therapies can be non-specific, such as exposure to ultraviolet light in photopheresis, however MF tumours show no response to this. Immunotherapies can also be designed specifically to recognize tumour cells. Neoantigens are new, unique proteins produced only due to mutations in tumors and not by healthy cells. Hence targeting neoantigens with immunotherapy, whether specific or non-specific, has been highly effective in other cancers. Neoantigens have never been investigated in mycosis fungoides, and my project will aim to do this for the first time. My hypothesis is that MF has only a small number of neoantigens that stimulate the immune system, explaining its poor response to non-specific immunotherapies. To characterize neoantigens, I will use DNA sequences of MF samples compiled by our lab. I will then apply computer algorithms to detect mutations and predict what neoantigens will result and cause an immune response. Such a discovery could provide the foundation for new immunotherapies to be designed specifically to target neoantigens. I will also compare the MF neoantigen profile to another skin cancer in the same family, Sezary Syndrome. This will provide insight into whether a higher number of neoantigens are responsible for Sezary Syndrome's superior response to non-specific immunotherapies such as photopheresis.
