column36: An Investigation into Arresting the Support of Cancer Associated Fibroblasts on Cancer Metastasis
column37: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is one of the most common types of cancers, with a high relapse rate and poor survival. Its growth and spread is heavily supported by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which when activated, provide tumour cells with a continual stream of nutrients and structural resources. Previous work has shown the importance of CAFs to tumour invasive potential and so the goal of my project is to better understand CAF biology and find ways of inhibiting its activity to reduce the rate of cancer metastasis. There are two main components of my project. The first is to make sense of CAF diversity by using machine-learning techniques to categorize CAFs into functional subgroups. I will then analyse the gene expression and methylation profiles of each category to determine 1) from what cells those CAFs were derived, 2) how they became activated, and 3) why they have remained activated in the presence of cancer cells. This work will improve our understanding of CAF lineages and find potential mechanisms by which to prevent CAF formation. The second component is to inhibit CAF activity to reduce HNSCC metastasis. To do this, I will screen a library of small molecule inhibitors for compounds capable of inactivating CAFs. The inhibitors' performance will be assessed via three functional tests: the ability to 1) limit CAF proliferation and change its shape, 2) reduce CAFs' contractibility of collagen, and 3) decrease cancer cell invasion when exposed to treated CAFs. These experiments together will serve as the first step in developing a drug capable of controlling cancer metastasis. Overall, my project will not only further our understanding of tumour biology but also has the potential to improve HNSCC prognosis for all patients.

column36: Investigating the mechanism of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome development.
column37: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS) is a genetic disorder caused by deficiencies in the Liver Kinase B1 (LKB1) protein. Patients experience chronic inflammation and benign tumor growth along their gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and have a 90% chance of developing cancer by age 65. T cells are part of the adaptive immune system, and either promote or dampen inflammation. We previously discovered that T cell-specific LKB1 deficiencies (LT) are sufficient to induce PJS in mice; however, a subset of these LT mice develop no disease and appear normal. This suggests that inflammation and tumor growth are not intrinsic results of an LKB1-deficient genotype, but require an environmental trigger. The proposed research will investigate whether pro-inflammatory gut-microbiome interactions may trigger an immune response that cannot be adequately dampened, leading to a pro-cancerous, chronic inflammatory state. There are 3 proposed study objectives. Firstly, it is well established that changes in gut microbiome composition are strongly associated with intestinal disease. The microbiome compositions of LT mice will thus be determined and compared to elucidate any differences between a diseased and a non-diseased state. Secondly, Th17 (pro-inflammatory T) cells will be over- and under-expressed in LT mice to determine whether their expression drives PJS development. Lastly, if objective 1 shows observable differences in the microbiomes, young LT mice will be inoculated with diseased and non-diseased microbiomes to determine whether their composition directly modulates disease severity. Current therapies for PJS focus on symptomatic treatment, but understanding the disease mechanism would allow the development of preventative therapies that reduce inflammation and improve prognosis.

column36: Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Cerebral Autoregulation: a BOLD Approach to Fetal Monitoring
column37: When a fetus's oxygen supply is restricted, oxygenated blood is preferentially redirected towards the brain and heart in a process known as cerebral autoregulation. This process is reversed when the oxygen supply increases above normal levels. Assessing the fetal response to a systematic increase in maternal blood oxygenation could help clinicians detect and prognose fetal distress, but a non-invasive method to reliably quantify fetal tissue oxygenation must first be developed. Blood-oxygen-level-dependent magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD MRI), a technique to measure local changes in blood oxygenation, has potential as a modality to monitor the autoregulatory response. I aim to develop a BOLD MRI method to quantify tissue oxygenation in fetal mice as a step towards clinical BOLD MRI monitoring of high-risk pregnancies, for which existing methods lack sensitivity in predicting adverse outcomes. The blood volume fraction and 3D microvascular geometry of fetal and placental mouse tissues will be microscopically characterized to construct a model relating changes in tissue oxygenation to the BOLD MRI signal. The model predictions will be compared against in-utero BOLD MRI measurements obtained in fetal mice under varying maternal oxygenation conditions. After validation against optical measurements of local blood oxygen saturation, the model predictions and measurements will be used to characterize the autoregulatory response in fetal mice and the corresponding variation in tissue oxygenation. A mouse model of intrauterine growth restriction will be used to evaluate the BOLD MRI method for identifying fetal distress, with the expectation that distressed fetuses will differ from controls with respect to tissue oxygenation and the blood flow redistribution response.

column36: Engaging neonatal intensive care staff in the development of interventions to enhance breastfeeding support in Medellin, Colombia
column37: The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, and continued breastfeeding for up to two years and beyond to support optimal infant growth and development. In 2010, Colombia's Ministry of Health released a ten-year public health strategy to improve breastfeeding rates. Breastfeeding support initiatives are crucial for preterm or ill infants in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), for whom the health benefits of human milk can be life-saving. However, there is scant information on breastfeeding practices and outcomes in Colombian NICUs. McGill University and the Hospital Universitario San Vicente Fundacion (HUSVF) in Medellin, Colombia developed a multi-phase study to identify, implement, and evaluate evidence-based practices to support breastfeeding in the NICU. Phase 1 involved the collection of baseline data on current breastfeeding support practices, completed in May 2018. This proposal is for Phase 2 of the project, a multi-method study using a participatory framework to engage NICU staff in the planning of interventions to enhance breastfeeding support practices. Participatory Action Research (PAR) is a form of inquiry in which investigator and participants collaborate in the process of studying problems and developing plans to deal with them. The objectives of the project are to 1) determine staff priorities for practice improvements related to breastfeeding support, 2) identify local barriers and facilitators for addressing the identified priorities, and 3) collaboratively design strategies for improving breastfeeding support practices in the NICU. The co-designed practice improvement strategies will be implemented and evaluated in future studies (Phase 3).

column36: Vieillissement cerebral et perception de la parole dans le bruit : effet protecteur du chant choral
column37: La difficulte a percevoir la parole en presence de bruit est un declin cognitif frequent lors du vieillissement normal. Malheureusement, les causes de ce declin ne sont pas encore connues, mais des donnees suggerent que le vieillissement du cerveau pourrait etre en partie responsable. Plus specifiquement, le vieillissement de la voie dorsale du langage pourrait expliquer en partie ces difficultes. Des evidences suggerent que la pratique d'activites musicales peut modifier la structure de cette voie et ameliorer la perception auditive. Le chant choral est une activite musicale sensorimotrice qui pourrait constituer une avenue interessante pour ralentir les declins cerebraux lies au vieillissement. Bien que des evidences suggerent que le chant modifie la structure et le fonctionnement de cette voie, les avantages potentiels du chant choral sur la perception de la parole sont peu connus. Les objectifs de cette etude sont d'investiguer la relation entre la structure du cerveau et le vieillissement de la perception de la parole dans le bruit, et d'investiguer comment cette relation est moderee par la pratique du chant choral a l'aide de l'imagerie par resonance magnetique (IRM). Notre hypothese est que le vieillissement cerebral sera ralenti chez les chanteurs, ce qui sera associe a une meilleure perception de la parole dans le bruit. Les participants completeront une seance d'IRM, une evaluation cognitive et auditive, et une tache de discrimination de syllabes dans le bruit. Ce projet fournira de nouvelles informations sur les effets protecteurs du chant choral, une activite ayant le potentiel de favoriser un vieillissement positif.

column36: Improving outcomes of partial wrist fusion for wrist arthritis
column37: Patients with scapholunate advanced collapse or scaphoid non-union advanced collapse are often offered salvage procedures which attempt to preserve wrist motion. Most commonly, a four-corner fusion is performed. This operation involves fusion of 4 carpal bones (capitate, lunate, hamate, triquetrum) with or without scaphoidectomy. This procedure aims to provide pain relief and preserve wrist motion and stability. Presently, there is controversy regarding the optimal position of fusion of the four carpal bones. The goal of this project is to delineate optimal positioning of carpal bone fusion during a four-corner fusion to maximize wrist range of motion. This will improve patient quality of life by maximizing function and providing symptom relief. Additionally, this study will address whether scaphoidectomy should routinely be combined with a four-corner fusion surgery and determine how scaphoid excision affects intercarpal kinematics. Clinically, this will have significant impact since four-corner fusions are the most common form of partial wrist fusion for wrist arthritis. A cadaveric model (n=8, standard for biomechanics studies to allow for sufficient power) will be used. CT scans will exclude any specimens with pre-existing arthritis. Optical trackers will be inserted and wrist range of motion will be measured. A custom jig will then simulate predetermined positions of carpal fusion and range of motion measurements will be taken. Simulations will then be repeated after scaphoid excision. We will repeat CT scans to identify changes in joint contact. We hypothesize that this study will identify whether the scaphoid should be preserved or excised, and how carpal bone positioning in a four-corner fusion affects carpal bone biomechanics and joint contact.

column36: Etude prospective observationnelle de cohortes visant a caracteriser la trajectoire postoperatoire des patients admis pour une fracture de la hanche
column37: ETUDE PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONNELLE DE COHORTES VISANT A CARACTERISER LA TRAJECTOIRE POSTOPERATOIRE DES PATIENTS ADMIS POUR UNE FRACTURE DE LA HANCHE La fracture de la hanche chez la personne agee est un enjeu de sante majeur. Au Canada, il y a eu 23 621 hospitalisations pour des fractures de la hanche chez les 60 ans et plus en 2003. En raison du vieillissement de la population, leur nombre augmentera de 12 % par annee d'ici 2030. Pres d'une personne sur 3 decede en moins d'un an suite a une fracture de la hanche. La plupart des patients qui subissent une telle blessure ne retrouveront jamais leur mobilite d'origine. A notre connaissance, la litterature medicale actuelle ne fournit pas assez d'information sur l'evolution des patients ayant subi une chirurgie pour une fracture de la hanche, notamment en ce qui a trait aux milieux de vie frequentes apres leur hospitalisation. C'est dans cette problematique que notre projet vient s'inscrire. L'objectif de ce projet est de caracteriser, en termes de milieux de vie, le devenir des patients hospitalises pour une fracture de la hanche dans les 12 mois qui suivent leur admission. L'etude est actuellement en cours dans un hopital de la region de Quebec. Plusieurs donnees sont comptabilisees durant l'hospitalisation. Tous les milieux de vie que les patients vont frequenter apres leur passage a l'hopital (trajectoire) sont notes. Les analyses permettront d'identifier les facteurs ayant une influence sur la trajectoire de sortie de ces patients. Ce projet a pour but de dresser le portrait actuel

column36: Defining the Role of Primary Cilia in Axon Development
column37: During brain development, neurons each extend a long and thin projection called an axon to reach their targets and form neuronal circuits. Disruptions in axon growth and pathfinding can lead to faulty assembly of neural circuits and results in neurodevelopmental disorders. Thus, knowing how axonal development is regulated is essential for not only understanding the functional wiring of the brain but also for a better comprehension of brain disorders. Joubert syndrome related disorders (JSRD) are among the handful of human genetic disorders that are mainly characterized by axonal defects and are diagnosed with intellectual disabilities. JSRD are caused by dysfunction of primary cilia, tiny signalling antennae of cells that are essential for coordinating major cell functions in response to environmental signals. However, little is known about how primary cilia regulate axonal development. Using a mouse disease model of JSRD, this proposal aims to rectify this gap by defining the role of primary cilia, tiny and largely mysterious organelles, in axonal development. We will first characterize the disrupted axonal development in JSRD mutant mice. This information will provide valuable insights into how JSRD gene mutations in humans might affect the brain development and circuit formation. We will then examine the effects of cilia-receptor signaling modulation on axonal development. With the expertise from Dr. Jiami Guo on neuronal primary cilia and brain development, and the support from her international collaborator who invented the innovative microfluidic axon guidance devices, these studies will not only uncover an unappreciated cellular mechanism that underlies brain development and brain disorders, but may also reveal a novel therapeutic approach.

column36: Improving multisensory integration as a remediation for individuals with schizophrenia
column37: The ability of our brains to integrate what we see and hear into coherent, unitary perceptions is foundational to how we experience the world. This process, called multisensory integration, is guided by how close together in time sensory inputs occur. The ability to use temporal information to properly integrate inputs from multiple senses is impaired in individuals with schizophrenia. As a result, individuals with schizophrenia are faced with many perceptual abnormalities, including hallucinations. In healthy individuals, multisensory integration can be improved with perceptual-learning paradigms, in which the brain learns when multisensory information should be perceived as simultaneous or not. These well-established paradigms lead to lasting changes in the brain, and improved perception. I will adapt these learning paradigms as a novel remediation in individuals with schizophrenia with the goal of reducing perceptual abnormalities. Adults with schizophrenia and non-clinical controls will be recruited; half will receive five daily learning sessions, and half will receive five control sessions. Baseline measures of multisensory integration and clinical symptomatology will be compared to measures immediately, one week, and one month after learning. I hypothesize that the learning sessions will improve multisensory integration in individuals with schizophrenia, leading to improvements in abnormal perceptual symptomatology. The perceptual symptoms that frequently accompany schizophrenia can be extremely impairing, and are often not treated effectively by medications, which can have severe side effects. With such a strong need for treatment options for individuals with schizophrenia, this learning paradigm has the potential to greatly improve their health and well-being.

column36: LSM7: a novel genetic variant in ultra-rare cases of leukodystrophy
column37: Leukodystrophies (LD) are a diverse group of genetically-determined neurodegenerative disorders that affect the central nervous system. We recently uncovered a novel gene, LSM7 which has been implicated in ultra-rare cases of non-hypomyelinating leukodystrophy (non-HLD). We propose in depth functional studies to determine the role and pathophysiological mechanisms of LSM7 in disease. LSM7 functions in two complexes: Lsm1-7 and Lsm2-8. Our goal is to investigate how our two variants alter the gene's functional role in the cells. As such, the next steps in this project include proteomic studies looking at the stability of the human mutated LSM7 RNA, its localization in the cell, as well as its ability to interact with its binding partners to form complexes and carry out its functions. These experiments will be conducted with the help of our collaborators, using techniques such as affinity purification, mass spectroscopy and fluorescent labelling. Additionally, we will perform studies in yeast analyzing the effects of the LSM7 variants on the formation of the two complexes, as well as complex interactions with other proteins/RNAs such as Pat1 and U6 snRNA. Specifically, we will focus on mRNA degradation, the principal function of Lsm1-7 complex as well as splicing, the primary function of the Lsm2-8 complex. We predict that the LSM7 variants do indeed influence LSM complex formation and/or activity and hence lead to disrupted mRNA decay and spliceosomal function. We are confident that the results of this study will set the ground for directed research on therapeutic strategies to rescue these important cellular processes and give hope to the present and future patients affected by LSM7-related leukodystrophy.

column36: Investigating the role DNAJC Chaperones in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder causing impaired movement, in addition to autonomous and cognitive dysfunction. It is a progressive condition for which there is no known cure. Dopamine neurons in the Substantia Nigra pars compacta are slowly lost during progression of PD, the reason for this remains enigmatic. Genetic studies have revealed mutations in multiple genes which are causative of PD. With this, converging pathways have emerged, allowing researchers to focus on specific cellular activities likely related to PD onset and progression. Recently, mutations in two chaperone proteins, DNAJC12 and DNAJC13, were discovered as causes of PD. Importantly, these discoveries highlight a potential mechanism in PD, as all 5 DNAJC chaperone proteins now implicated in PD are expressed in the brain (including DNAJC5, CSP?; DNAJC6, Auxilin; and DNAJC26, GAK).We have recently made and begun characterizing a DNAJC13 knock-in mouse expressing the human p.N855S mutation and a DNAJC12 knock-out mouse. Research into these models will provide novel insight into: 1) the role of DNAJC chaperone proteins in PD pathogenesis; 2) the coordinated regulation of DNAJC proteins on dopamine cell homeostasis, and; 3) molecular targets for therapeutic drug development. Insights gained will be relevant not only to PD research, but also to many dopamine dis-regulation disorders including addiction, depression, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.

column36: Supporting research use among oncology nurses through knowledge translation interventions
column37: Health research loses its value without effective strategies to translate the findings from research into everyday practice and policy. The process of getting research into practice is known as knowledge translation (KT). Nurses have a unique opportunity to use research evidence to support better patient outcomes and experiences because of their front-line role in the healthcare system. Current evidence suggests that the most effective way to get research findings to nurses is likely through educational interventions; however, more studies must be done to explore what KT strategies work best in improving research use among nurses. There are a number of evidence-based guidelines available to oncology nurses to help identify and manage common symptoms associated with cancer treatment (e.g. Cancer Care Ontario symptom management algorithms). Unfortunately, even though they are available, nurses do not always use these guidelines in their practice. This study will collaborate with oncology nurses to create an educational intervention to increase the use of these evidence-based practice guidelines in their daily patient care. Interviews with nurses will be done to explore what works and what is challenging when using research in practice, and to determine if the educational activity improves nurses' research use. This study will also investigate whether patients undergoing cancer treatment experience better symptom management when nurses apply evidence-based guidelines by monitoring their symptoms before and after the knowledge translation intervention. Conducting research about knowledge translation in nursing has the potential to improve the way healthcare is delivered, possibly leading to better care and improved symptom management for patients with cancer.

column36: Exploring the Effect of Nutrition on Mortality and Cardiovascular Disease using Linked Population-based Dietary Data
column37: Diet is a major determinant of health and is considered to be largely responsible for the reduction in cardiovascular disease (CVD) in industrialized countries since the 1960s. Dietary recommendations focus on elimination of trans-fat, reduction of saturated fatty acids (SAFAs), and increases in vegetable and fruit consumption. However, recently it has been highlighted that the evidence-base may not be very strong for these recommendations. For example, systematic reviews fail to demonstrate consistent relationships between SAFAs, CVD, and mortality. The most recently published large nutritional cohort study has identified carbohydrates as detrimental, while fats were protective against death and CVD. Then, a meta-analysis published this summer suggested a u-shaped relationship between carbohydrate and mortality, and that fats are only protective if they're plant-based. Given the inconsistencies, a reliance on predetermined nutrient categories may be problematic. I propose applying novel machine learning techniques to both identify the dietary components truly related to health, and to better characterize the complex relationship. I plan to use the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), which contains the only detailed Canadian population-based dietary data available and has been linked to participants' later healthcare utilization. This will allow development of a model to both predict CVD and mortality and determine their dietary risk factors, applying both traditional and ML techniques. This would be the first time that such a study has been performed in Canada, and could help identify whether ML may be useful. Ultimately, the project aims to better inform decision-makers, clinicians, and individuals about diet-related policy and behaviour impacts on health.

column36: Validating Three-Dimensional Ultrasound Measurements of Synovial Tissues for Diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common autoimmune disease that is associated with disability, pain, inflammation, and even early death. Characteristic of patients with RA is inflamed synovial tissue - the tissue lining the joints in the body. Unfortunately, there is no definitive test to confirm the diagnosis of RA, and the exact cause of the disease is unknown. The current standard for diagnosis involves receiving an X-ray or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan and comparing the image results with patient's symptoms confirm the presence of the disease. However, three-dimensional ultrasound (3DUS) may provide a faster, more efficient method for diagnosing RA and possibly provide insight in to the causes of the disease. 3DUS acquires images at a higher frame rate and a greater flexibility of image orientation compared to X-ray and MRI. 3DUS operates by taking a series of 2D images while translating the transducer linearly to sweep out a 3D space. This project will develop and validate a handheld 3DUS device that will be used to scan patients and measure the volume of their synovial tissue with high precision. Comparing healthy and inflamed synovial tissue volumes may provide physicians with a definitive metric for diagnosing RA. The system will be used to scan simulated tissue phantoms to validate its volumetric tissue measurement capabilities. The system will then be used to scan RA patients in conjunction with MRI. The images from each modality will be registered to each other and the volumetric measurements of the synovial tissue from each system will be directly compared. Providing physicians with a tool that will enable a definitive diagnosis of RA while requiring less scan time and operating costs will increase the quality of care patients will receive.

column36: Do microorganisms have a role in 'aseptic' total knee and total hip replacement implant failure? A prospective molecular and implant retrieval study
column37: Arthritis is the leading cause of physical disability in Canada and the demand for total knee (TKR) and total hip replacement (THR) is rapidly increasing. TKR and THR offer patients with end-stage arthritis pain relief and improved function. However, approximately 2% of these patients suffer a deep joint bacterial infection (PJI), a dreaded complication often requiring multiple surgeries to treat, resulting in poor patient outcomes and high healthcare costs. TKR and THR implants can wear out, loosen, or fail over time and require revision surgery to replace. It is now suspected that a large number of TKR and THR revision surgeries for 'non-infected' loose or failed implants are actually undiagnosed PJI because modern molecular methods have identified bacterial microorganisms (MO) on some of these implants. However, the frequency and consequences of this remain unclear. In this study, we will use modern molecular gene sequencing techniques to identify how often and what type of MO are on TKR and THR implants that required revision surgery for 'non-infection' causes. We will also study the removed joint implants to determine where on the implants MO are found and whether MO are associated with implant damage and failure. The impact of MO and PJI on TKR and THR implant failure may have been greatly underestimated for patients requiring 'non-infection' revision surgery. We expect this study to show that joint implants are frequently contaminated with MO, certain locations on implants are susceptible to MO colonization, and MO are associated with implant damage. These results will provide an important stepping stone to guide future studies with the potential to improve the diagnosis and prevention of PJI.

column36: Le soins de plaies en debut de pratique: comprendre ce defi de taille pour les infirmieres.
column37: Les plaies representent une problematique de sante preoccupante qui a d'importantes consequences sur la qualite de vie des personnes qui en souffrent. Les plaies sont courantes en milieu hospitalier et le fardeau financier qu'elles imposent est considerable. Dans le present contexte du vieillissement de la population et de l'augmentation des maladies chroniques comme le diabete, une hausse du nombre de plaies est a prevoir. Heureusement, les infirmieres peuvent jouer un role primordial pour reduire ce fleau ou en limiter les consequences. En effet, la determination du plan de traitement relie aux plaies et aux alterations de la peau releve d'une activite reservee a l'infirmiere. La formation initiale transmet l'enseignement necessaire pour assumer cette responsabilite professionnelle. Par contre, il en demeure un defi de taille pour les infirmieres novices d'appliquer ces connaissances en debut de pratique. Un ecart est souvent observe entre la theorie apprise sur les bancs d'ecole et la realite du terrain. Ce projet de recherche explore les moyens que les hopitaux utilisent pour faciliter le transfert des connaissances en soins de plaies ainsi que leurs effets sur les infirmieres nouvellement diplomees. Une analyse de terrain permettra de decrire et de comparer la place qu'occupent les soins de plaies dans les programmes d'orientation et d'explorer les perceptions des nouvelles infirmieres en regard de leur responsabilite professionnelle en soins de plaies. Il est attendu que les resultats de la recherche permettront d'ameliorer les programmes d'orientation et d'augmenter les competences des infirmieres en soins de plaie. Ultimement, cela contribuera a eviter ou reduire les consequences des plaies aupres de la clientele soignee, du nouveau-ne a la personne ainee.

column36: Design of a gradient-generating bioreactor for zonal cartilage growth
column37: Arthritis leads to the progressive degradation of articular cartilage of the joints, resulting in pain and loss of mobility. Affecting 6M Canadians, it is the most prevalent incurable chronic health condition. Current treatments are often surgical, and range from joint replacement to cell-based therapies that produce repair tissue. None of these approaches, however, regenerate the native structural and mechanical properties; the resulting tissue is structurally and chemically isotropic. However, native cartilage is anisotropic, zonally organized along its depth, with each zone comprising a distinct cell phenotype. This affects the composition and organization of the tissue, and thus its structural and functional properties. Biomolecular gradients, such as those arising from avascular cartilage tissue, are known to affect cell responses. It is hypothesized that these gradients, specifically of glucose, drive the zonal organization of cartilage. This work aims to: (I) test the hypothesis that glucose gradients drive zonal specification of cartilage; (II) develop a mathematical model of a continuous flow bioreactor capable of generating nutrient gradients; and (III) design and construct said reactor. To test (I), chondrocytes will be grown in 2D and 3D conditions, with varying glucose concentrations, and the resulting tissues tested for zone-linked markers. The model of (II) will be developed by combining biochemical, reaction engineering, and mass transfer principles, then used to design and 3D print a reactor (III). The resulting cartilage will be subject to similar analyses as in (I). This has the potential to solve a major problem in the field and improve current practices in the regeneration of anisotropic tissues, including but not limited to articular cartilage.

column36: Mechanism of cell-free nucleic acid release and its utility as a cancer biomarker
column37: Cancer diagnosis often requires invasive tissue biopsy procedures that can be risky, painful, and costly. Non-invasive detection methods would make cancer diagnosis safer and more convenient and would allow for monitoring cancer during and after treatment. Since all cancer cells harbor alterations in their genetic material (DNA), detection of these alternations has clinical potential as a diagnostic tool. Free-floating DNA fragments in the bloodstream that is not associated with cells (cell-free DNA, cfDNA) can be used to detect cancer-specific alterations and could potentially be used to replace invasive biopsies. Since blood collection is relatively easy and can be done regularly, researchers aim to use cfDNA as a biomarker for cancer detection and treatment response monitoring. However, it is poorly understood how cfDNA is released into the bloodstream, limiting its clinical potential. Studies have identified multiple mechanisms of cfDNA release, and the relative contribution of each mechanism has been hotly debated. One such mechanism is via exosomes, which are small lipid structures released by cells that can also be found in the bloodstream. Due to the mounting interest in the use of exosomes as a source of cfDNA, there is an urgent need for rigorous study of the cfDNA content of exosomes and their potential as a cancer diagnostic tool. The objective of this proposed study is to investigate how much cfDNA is contained within exosomes in both cancer patients and healthy individuals. This work will resolve controversies in the field and reveal insights that can advance the use of cfDNA as a non-invasive biomarker to replace traditional biopsy.

column36: Education prenatale et l'anxiete liee a la grossesse et a l'accouchement des futurs meres et peres
column37: Une premiere grossesse est un evenement marquant dans la vie d'un couple, qui peut causer de l'anxiete autant chez la mere que le pere. Differentes formations prenatales se sont montrees efficaces pour reduire cette anxiete. Cependant, selon la disponibilite des services dans leur region, les futurs parents peuvent faire appel a diverses ressources d'education prenatale, autant en ligne qu'en groupe. Ce projet doctoral, qui s'inscrit dans une etude plus large sur les services d'education prenatales, propose de verifier 1) si l'anxiete des peres et des meres predit leur recherche d'education prenatale, et 2) si la quantite et la nature des sources consultees predisent le niveau d'anxiete ressenti au troisieme trimestre et a l'accouchement, en considerant que les conjoints peuvent influencer mutuellement leurs choix et experience. L'etude, menee dans les regions de la Capitale-Nationale et Chaudiere-Appalaches fait appel a 795 femmes enceintes de leur premier enfant et leurs conjoints. Tous sont invites a remplir des questionnaires a trois reprises : entre 10 et 20 semaines de grossesse (T1), apres 33 semaines de grossesse (T2) et 6 a 8 semaines apres l'accouchement (T3). Les resultats serviront a clarifier comment l'education prenatale peut aider a attenuer l'anxiete des futurs parents a l'egard de la grossesse et l'accouchement. Ils informeront egalement les intervenants sur les facteurs pouvant motiver la recherche d'education prenatale, de meme que l'influence possible que les futurs peres et meres peuvent avoir l'un sur l'autre.

column36: Changes in gut microbiota and risk of colitis associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors
column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are a class of drugs which relieve suppression of the immune system to induce an anti-tumour immune response in cancer patients. Despite the rise in usage and efficacy of ICI in mainstream cancer therapy, many patients still fail to achieve an adequate response towards the drug, and toxicities associated with ICI, such as colitis, remain common in treated patients. Recently, interactions between regular gut bacteria and tumor response have been well studied largely due to the gut microbiome being implicated as a modulator of systemic immune responses. Thus, this project seeks to identify gut bacteria which may be contributing towards the therapeutic efficacy and toxicities associated with ICIs. My hypothesis is that tumor response and risk of colitis can be predicted by baseline differences between gut bacteria in cancer patients, and that changes in bacteria caused by ICI can improve tumor response and/or induce the development of colitis. Using fecal samples obtained from metastatic melanoma patients, we plan on identifying gut bacteria at baseline before ICI treatment. We will compare this to post-treatment bacterial profiles to identify any changes. Additionally, harmful bacteria causing colitis will be identified post-treatment to determine which specific bacteria induced by ICIs contribute to colitis development. This study is important as there are currently inconclusive findings over which bacteria are predictive of tumor responses after ICI treatment. The involvement of patients from separate institutions may provide clarity on which bacteria contribute towards tumor responses. Determining bacteria associated with post-ICI colitis will also help with the identification of patients at high risk of colitis.

column36: Comparing the cognitive effects of outdoor versus indoor walking among healthy older adults
column37: With a growing elderly population, dementia is a critical global health challenge. Lifestyle factors are promising as accessible, low-cost approaches to prevent or mitigate cognitive decline. In particular, physical activity, such as aerobic exercise, can improve cognitive function in older adults, but more research is needed to determine optimal exercise strategies. Recent evidence shows that time spent in nature can also provide a range of physical and cognitive health benefits. In fact, the benefits of exercise appear to be enhanced when performed in outdoor, natural settings, such as parks and forests, as compared to indoor or built settings, such as gyms or urban environments. However, the role of a green exercise environment in promoting cognitive health in older adults requires further investigation. The goal of my research is to compare the effects of outdoor versus indoor walking programs on cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults. Participants will be randomly assigned into two groups for a 12-week walking program: one group will walk on forest trails, while the other group will walk indoors on a treadmill. The main outcome will be a subset of cognitive skills called executive functions, such as self-control and working memory, which are important for maintaining independence while aging. This research will help better understand the potential of outdoor exercise as a lifestyle strategy to support cognitive health throughout the aging process.

column36: Isolation and Characterization of the Active Algogenic Toxin(s) in Lionfish Venom
column37: The red lionfish (Pterois volitans) is a venomous invasive species endemic to the Indo-Pacific, but now found in the Caribbean and Northwestern Atlantic. In addition to the ecological stress it poses due to its invasiveness, the lionfish delivers and incredibly painful sting for which there exists no anti-venom and no knowledge of the venom's algogenic (pain-causing) mechanism of action. The immediate and intense pain caused by the sting extends radially from the wound, reaching its peak about 1 hour after envenomation and maintaining this level for up to 24 hours. In my previous work, I have shown that the algogenic component in the venom is a heat-labile peptide, which seems to act on a subset of pain-sensing neurons, called nociceptors, known to express the P2X3 ion channel. Based on preliminary studies, I have found that blocking this channel with pharmacological drugs can abolish the venom-elicited calcium response in mouse nociceptors. Yet, the identity of the algogenic peptide(s) and how it interacts with its receptor remain unknown. In this project, I will examine the molecular basis of lionfish venom sensitivity and identify its algogenic toxin. To do this, I will first confirm that the venom's receptor on nociceptors is P2X3 by reducing P2X3 expression and verifying that this reduces the cellular response to the venom. I will then see if reducing P2X3 expression in vivo in mice reduces their pain behaviour in response to venom injection. Finally, I will identify the venom's algogenic toxin using a combination of separation techniques to identify active fractions. These active fractions will then be analyzed to identify the toxin's DNA and amino acid sequences, allowing me to draw between the evolution of the venom's toxin and toxins from other species.

column36: Modification of Protein-Nanoparticle Complexes for Delivery of Nucleic Acid Therapeutics
column37: Improved nucleic acid therapy targeting towards cancer cells in vivo would improve efficacy of treatment, reduce off-target effects and subsequently, reduce toxicity. One technique that may improve targeting is the use of nanoparticles as carriers for therapeutics. Studies have shown that nanoparticles can have positive effects on circulation and biodistribution, however few are currently employed as clinical treatments. By developing a nanoparticle that binds to human serum albumin (HSA) we hope to develop a novel therapeutic technique for treatment of different diseases via the implementation of siRNA based gene silencing. Previous work in the Sleiman lab has shown that rigid nanocube scaffolds can be made with control over the spatial orientation of ligands around the structure. One such ligand that has been conjugated to nanostructures is D1, a molecule made of monomeric alkane chains shown to bind HSA and may hold promise as a method to increase viability of nucleic acid therapeutics in vivo. A D1-fluorophore-siRNA strand will be made via solid phase phosphoramidite chemistry with the siRNA strand silencing luciferase. This molecule will be bound to nanostructures through Watson-Crick base pairing and purified using gel electrophoresis and reverse phase chromatography. The binding of the nanoparticle to HSA will be analyzed using gel electrophoresis and surface plasmon resonance. The tumour penetration, internalization and silencing of luciferase will be tested in cell models to probe the efficacy of this method for potential therapeutic delivery. Future studies may look at other factors such as biodistribution and tumor accumulation or the differences caused by changes in geometry via addition of D1 to other DNA nanostructures made in the Sleiman lab.

column36: Fecal microbial transplantation and fiber supplementation in patients with obesity and metabolic syndrome
column37: This study is looking at the safety and effectiveness of stool transplant, also known as Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT), and prebiotic supplementation in the management of metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is a common chronic progressive medical condition that is linked to obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. Obesity and metabolic syndrome are associated with abnormalities in gut flora which lead to a state of chronic inflammation. This chronic inflammation is thought to worsen the insulin resistance and heart disease seen with metabolic syndrome. Current treatment strategies have shown limited effect, are expensive, and have significant side effects with long-term use. FMT is a one-time treatment that has been shown to replace abnormal gut flora and improve metabolic disease by increasing anti-inflammatory short chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. However, the effects from FMT are not permanent because of the eventual depletion of SCFAs. Prebiotic supplementation has been demonstrated to sustain high SCFA levels, and is thus one strategy that may help to extend the benefits of FMT. At this point, we don't know how FMT and prebiotics work together to affect SCFA levels in participants with metabolic syndrome. Our study will look at this interaction and help to answer if prebiotic therapy is effective in prolonging the benefits of FMT in participants with metabolic syndrome.

column36: The impact of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV-infected children on antimicrobial resistance gene carriage in the fecal microbiome.
column37: The immune system is the body's defence against invading pathogens. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) interferes with the normal functioning of the immune system, thereby increasing the chances of infection. Antibiotics have primarily been used to treat and prevent bacterial infections; but with continued usage these organisms have developed antibiotic resistance, rendering some infections untreatable. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that the antibiotic cotrimoxazole (CTX) be given, along with antiretroviral therapy, to any child born with or exposed to HIV, to help prevent serious infections and death. Antiretroviral Research for Watoto (ARROW) is a clinical trial of Ugandan and Zimbabwean HIV-infected children, aged 3 months to 17 years, designed in part to investigate whether stopping versus continuing CTX would benefit the child health over the long term. ARROW found that continuing CTX did further reduce infections and hospitalizations. However, long term use of CTX might lead to big increases in carriage of or infection with highly drug resistant bacteria (so-called 'superbugs'). My research project is to understand the extent of CTX resistance in these children by analyzing fecal microbes using DNA sequencing methods to determine if stopping CTX prophylaxis reduced the quantity and diversity of resistance genes carried by the gut bacteria of these HIV-infected children. Results of this research will inform future WHO decisions regarding the trade-off between the use of CTX to prevent infections and further increases in multi-drug-resistant bacteria.

column36: Explicit and Implicit Cannabis-Related Cognitions in People with Social Anxiety
column37: Social anxiety and cannabis use are both prevalent and often co-occur. Moreover, researchers have found that undergraduates with high social anxiety report greater endorsement of using cannabis to cope with negative emotions (i.e., expectancies). Participants will complete two computerized tasks measuring their automatic associations related to cannabis, in addition to completing online self-report questionnaires. This study will help improve cognitive behavioural models and evidence-based treatments of social anxiety disorder. column36: The association between benzodiazepine use and healthcare utilization in patients with dementia
column37: Background: Canada's aging population poses challenges to healthcare systems, partly due to a rising incidence of dementia. These persons have twice the acute hospital use of elders without dementia. Benzodiazepines (BZDs) are widely prescribed to patients with dementia, despite guidelines recommending against their use due to adverse side effects, risks and little evidence for their effectiveness. Adverse BZD-linked events may prompt consultations with the healthcare system, which can be distressing for the patient and costly to the system. It is thus essential to understand the implications of BZD use for dementia patients' interactions with healthcare systems.Objective: The objective of this research is to evaluate the association between BZD use and healthcare utilization in persons with dementia.Proposed Methods: Data for this cross-sectional study will be collected from the INSPQ database (exhaustive repository of health information for Quebecois population aged 65+). Those with dementia will be identified and divided into exposure groups based on their prescription status March 31, 2018: 1) chronic BZD users, 2) acute BZD users and 3) non-users. Healthcare utilization data (number of emergency visits, number and length of hospitalizations, transfer to long-term care) and mortality in the following three months will then be collected. We will conduct linear regression analyses to compare each utilization component and mortality between groups. Multivariate analyses will account for confounders (previous utilization, comorbidities, chronic pain, S.E.S., sex and age).Significance: This research is expected to inform policy, guidelines and physician decision-making for BZD prescriptions for patients with dementia to minimize unnecessary healthcare utilization.

column36: Body Compression in Postural Tachycardia Syndrome: Effects on Orthostatic Tolerance
column37: When a person stands up, about half a litre of blood shifts down to the lower abdomen, pelvis and legs. In a healthy individual, the body is able to adjust for this change. When someone with Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) stands up, this adjustment mechanism does not work. Their heart rate goes too high and they may experience symptoms such as lightheadedness, dizziness, shortness of breath, nausea and mental confusion. As well, individuals with POTS may experience chronic symptoms including fatigue and impaired sleep. There are no approved medications for use in POTS and no single treatment that works for all individuals with POTS. One commonly prescribed treatment is compression garments. Compression garments squeeze veins to help return blood back to the heart. However, there is little research about the effectiveness of compression in adults with POTS. In this study, we are using the Lifewrap garment, which compresses the abdomen, pelvis and lower extremities, to evaluate the effectiveness of compression in POTS. We use a tilt table which simulates standing. The study participant completes 4x 10 minute tilt tests wearing 4 different compression configurations: full lower body, partial (abdomen only, leg only) and no compression. We hypothesize that with full compression, the participant's heart rate increase from laying down to upright will be lower than when they are not wearing any compression. We will also ask the participant about their symptoms when they are upright. After the study, participants will complete an online survey. The results of this study could demonstrate the potential benefits of compression and what configuration is most effective. These findings could rapidly translate to the clinical setting, providing improved care.

column36: Measuring the Clinical Impact of Participating in Pediatric Oncology Trials
column37: My current Master's research project will aim to examine various methodological and ethical questions in pediatric cancer clinical trials. The ethical pursuit of pediatric cancer trials depends on the ability to convey accurate information about risks and the clinical impact associated with study participation. This is of particular concern because children cannot legally consent to participate in clinical research studies and there is an underlying hesitancy to expose vulnerable children to unproven drugs. It also requires selecting treatments for testing that have the greatest prospect of impacting care. However, both of these are greatly challenged by limited systematic evidence about the clinical impact associated with trial participation in pediatric populations. In particular, there is presently no way of telling a guardian and/or prospective child how likely their participation in a trial will lead to major advances in pediatric cancer care. Thus, this project will address this evidence gap. In this study, we will use clinical trial registration records to estimate the proportion of pediatric patients who participate in trials that lead to clinical care. Secondarily, we will probe these type of trials where impact is the greatest and where it is the weakest. This study will serve many implications, especially relating to informed consent, to better estimate the likelihood of a patient's participation meaningfully advancing the care of future patients, and to help clarify what types of pediatric cancer trials are most likely to result in major advances in care.

column36: Targeting a subtype of GABA-A receptors to treat perioperative neurocognitive disorders
column37: Millions of surgeries occur around the world each year where patients are exposed to general anesthetics. A proportion of these patients will experience deficits in learning and memory after their operation that can persist for months to years. These cognitive deficits have significant effects on a person's life as they are associated with early retirement and increased mortality. There is a need to develop effective treatments as the current therapeutic tools are inadequate. Although the causes of these deficits are multifactorial, research has illustrated that general anesthetics are a key player. It has been determined that these cognitive deficits are triggered by an anesthetic-induced increase in a specific receptor function in the brain. Upregulation of this receptor can lead to the disruption of learning and memory. However, the exact mechanisms underlying the upregulation of this receptor remain unknown. The identification of this receptor was crucial for the development of pharmacological interventions. Therapeutic drugs are now being developed to selectively block the function of this receptor, thus preventing deficits. However, these drugs are limited by the strength of their effects and their selectivity. Therefore, it would be beneficial to develop alternative therapeutic strategies to attenuate the receptor function. To do so, the mechanism driving the increase of this receptor must be investigated. As a result, the goals of my project will be to 1) screen for the best available drug and 2) to investigate the mechanisms driving the upregulation of this receptor, in order to identify novel therapeutic targets.

column36: Biomarker expression and treatment response following neoadjuvant chemotherapy in western gastric cancer
column37: Stomach cancer is one of the most common cancers worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer related death. Stomach cancer is treated with a combination of surgery and medicine such as chemotherapy. Despite treatment, patients often pass away from cancer spread or from cancer returning after treatment. Using laboratory tests certain molecules have been found to be involved in the growth and spread of stomach cancer. Much in the way that every individual has a unique signature to identify themselves, stomach cancers also have a signature of molecules that may differ from one to the other. Some cancers may be more aggressive than others and are less responsive to chemotherapy treatment whereas other cancers diminish significantly by the exact same treatment. We believe that each cancer's unique signature of molecules may be related to treatment effectiveness. Furthermore, we plan to identify new effective drugs for stomach cancer based on their ability to attack certain molecules. In our study, western Canadian human gastric cancer samples will be tested in the laboratory for a variety of molecules. We will then correlate these molecules to the severity of cancer and a variety of chemotherapy drugs will be administered to the cancer cells in order to determine if certain molecules can predict treatment response. We hope to connect each unique stomach cancer's molecular signature to the effectiveness of different chemotherapy treatments in order to one day provide personalized medicine. For example one patient's cancer may respond to one drug whereas another patient's cancer responds to another. If we can predict which drugs will be most beneficial then we can provide better treatment, potentially with fewer medications and less side effects.

column37: Concussions are increasingly prevalent among children and youth in Ontario and the rest of Canada, demonstrating the need for effective treatment methods. One potentially effective treatment being put forward is to encourage children to resume light, non-strenuous physical activity soon after being diagnosed with a pediatric concussion. The proposed research will be investigating the impact of early resumption of physical activity and brain functioning on quality of life following a concussion in children and youth aged 10-18. column36: Identification of new drugs to treat triple negative breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the 2nd leading cause of death from cancer in Canadian women, affecting approximately 1 in 8. The four major subtypes of breast cancer are: luminal A, luminal B, HER2+ and triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). TNBCs do not have the clinical characteristics present in the other major subtypes of breast cancer, making them difficult to treat. In addition, breast cancers of this subtype are typically aggressive and highly metastatic (meaning they have the ability to spread throughout the body). Chemotherapy is currently the only treatment option for TNBC. Our lab has been studying a protein, cAMP-responsive element-binding protein 3-like protein 1 (CREB3L1) which inhibits metastasis in breast cancer. Approximately 30% of breast cancers have deficient amounts of CREB3L1 (including ~90% of TNBCs) and these patients usually have a poor prognosis. This project aims to identify new, FDA-approved drugs that effectively target CREB3L1-deficient TNBC. An "Approved Drug Library" of 1818 drugs currently used to treat other diseases will be evaluated for the ability to selectively kill CREB3L1-deficient TNBC cells. This global approach will swiftly and effectively identify the most promising approved drugs to target this specific type of breast cancer. These initial experiments would lay the foundation for pre-clinical evaluations in mice harbouring human TNBCs. Promising results would warrant pursuit of clinical trials to quickly implement the use of these drugs to benefit 90% of the TNBC patients whose cancers are CREB3L1-deficient.

column36: Decisions surrounding prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy: Experiences of BRCA-positive patients within a Hereditary Gynecology Clinic
column37: Women with mutations in genes called BRCA1 and BRCA2 are considered to be "BRCA-positive" and have a higher risk of getting both breast and ovarian cancer (OC). There are good tests to find breast cancer early in these at-risk women before it spreads to other parts of the body. However, similar tests do not exist for detecting OC, which if untreated will cause death. Since OC can go undetected, doctors recommend that women with mutations in BRCA genes consider preventative surgery to remove their ovaries and fallopian tubes in order to dramatically reduce their risk of developing OC. Deciding to remove their ovaries and fallopian tubes is a difficult decision for many women because it may have consequences for their health, family planning, and quality of life. In Manitoba, patients with a high risk for OC are seen by healthcare providers at a clinic especially for BRCA-positive women called the Hereditary Gynecology Clinic. In my research, I hope to learn more about how and why these women make decisions for or against preventative surgery. I will also evaluate patients' experiences and satisfaction within this innovative clinic model. This will be the first study within Canada to investigate the efficacy and value of having a follow-up clinic specifically for helping BRCA-positive women make decisions about their health based on their increased OC risk. The results of my research will provide insight into how specialty healthcare clinics across Canada can be best modeled to support the unique needs of BRCA-positive women who are considering preventive surgery for OC and ultimately improve the overall health of Canadians.

column36: Determining biomarkers of response to docetaxel for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer using circulating cell-free tumour DNA
column37: The primary chemotherapy for late-stage prostate cancer is only effective in 45% of patients. However, there is currently no way of knowing in advance which patients will benefit from treatment, and which patients could avoid the side-effects of chemotherapy and receive a different therapy instead. Herein lies an urgent clinical need for tests that can predict patient response to chemotherapy, thereby helping clinicians select the best cancer treatment for an individual patient. My aim is to identify molecular markers capable of predicting whether a patient will respond to the chemotherapy docetaxel. My approach relies on the fact that cancerous tissues shed a small amount of their DNA into the bloodstream, creating an opportunity to examine the tumour by analyzing DNA isolated from a patient's blood sample. This DNA, termed 'circulating tumour DNA' (ctDNA), provides a molecular snapshot of the tumor. CtDNA profiling is a novel technique that enables capture of information about a cancer via a blood test. This means that breakthroughs can be quickly translated to the clinic to inform treatment decisions. To identify biomarkers predictive of docetaxel response, I have identified 74 eligible patients from a provincial biobank (established by my supervisors) of ctDNA samples from hundreds of metastatic patients. I will profile DNA from these patients using a custom bioinformatics approach, and will subsequently correlate findings to patient clinical history and treatment outcomes. Success with this project will help optimize treatment selection for patients with late-stage prostate cancer, resulting in improved quality and length of life for men with this aggressive disease.

column36: Manipulation of Impulsivity through Optogenetic Stimulation of Serotonergic Neurons in the Dorsal and Median Raphe Nuclei
column37: Impulsivity is a trait defined by a lack of self-control, often as a result of acting before all information has been acquired. Impulsivity can become pathological and contribute to substance abuse disorders. Neurologically, impulsivity has been linked to the neurotransmitter serotonin (5-HT), which is supplied by two distinct brain pathways originating in the median (MRN) and dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN). It is unclear as to which pathway is more important in mediating impulsivity. Accordingly, my main objective is to discover the relative importance of MRN and DRN 5-HT pathways to impulsivity. To achieve this, I will use an animal model of impulsivity. In this model, mice are first trained on a touch-screen task where they must respond to a visual stimulus for food reward while showing low impulsivity. Once mice have learned the task, they are surgically implanted with optical fibres, which allow the use of a laser to selectively activate the MRN and DRN pathways. Mice will then be tested on two varieties of the task where impulsivity is at a higher level. While completing this task, the mice will have their DRN or MRN pathways activated by the laser. This will allow me to measure the effect of selective stimulation of the DRN or MRN pathways on impulsivity. Accordingly, my main hypothesis is that stimulation of either pathway will reduce mice's impulsive behavior on the task. Furthermore, I hypothesize that the selective stimulation of the DRN or MRN will reveal which pathway is more important for the expression of impulsivity. The results of this study may help delineate the neurobiological basis of impulsivity and provide insight into how impulsivity contributes to the maladaptive drug-seeking behaviors symptomatic of substance abuse.

column36: Investigating Facial Mimicry in Parkinson's Disease and its Relationship to Emotion Recognition
column37: Emotions are a vital part of human social interaction yet are often taken for granted. Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) unfortunately show decreased facial expression production and difficulties recognizing the emotional expressions of others. Interestingly, these two symptoms might be linked by facial mimicry (FM), which is the tendency to imitate the facial expressions of others. Research shows that in healthy people, blocking FM hampers emotion recognition. Consequently, if PD patients have reduced FM, due to decreased expressivity, this might contribute to problems with emotion recognition. The neural mechanisms of FM and emotion recognition are not fully elaborated but areas of the brain that are affected by PD have been associated with FM. This study will investigate whether PD patients indeed show lower FM and if this translates to reduced emotion recognition, emphasizing the neural basis behind these deficits. We will use functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure brain activity in PD patients and healthy controls during an emotion recognition task, while simultaneously measuring facial muscle activity with electromyography. We predict that PD patients will have reduced FM correlated with worse emotion recognition and that this will be accompanied by altered patterns of brain activity in areas important for FM, such as the mirror neuron network. Overall, this will contribute to our understanding of emotional dysfunction in PD and could inform future treatment approaches.

column36: Computational modelling of interplay between histone tail modifications and its effects on chromatin dynamics in human development and cancer
column37: The causes of cancer have long been an important area of research, and recent studies have indicated an under-appreciation of "epigenetic" changes' contribution to the development of cancer, which concern the chemical modifications to DNA or to the proteins around which DNA is wrapped in the cell nucleus. To study such changes, high-throughput technologies are used to generate a profusion of data comprehensively profiling genetic materials. Although very educational, previous models derived from these observations have oftentimes been rather hand-wavy and commonly suffer from a lack of strong quantitative foundation. With recent reports emphasizing the importance of epigenetics in cancer research, grasping the mechanisms underlying these events are ever more crucial. As we have improved our understanding of these reversible epigenetic changes, we have also noticed potential interplays between them in human cancer cell lines. For instance, based on previous reports and our own data, certain epigenetic marks appear to participate in a tug-of-war of sorts, establishing a delicate equilibrium. Consequently, we would like to model and comprehend these types of phenomenon by applying established statistical tools and algorithms to a variety of tumour, normal, and engineered cell lines. We have already been able to recapitulate the behaviour of a set of marks which builds upon one another in a specific manner using a preliminary model. Although studies directly describing tumour cells can be incredibly informative, they often lack information on earlier, casual events. Given the targetable nature of proteins effecting epigenetic changes, the predictive capabilities of our models could allow us to identify and possibly counteract disease-causing changes at an earlier stage.

column37: Chronic neuropathic pain is a debilitating condition that affects around 20% of Canadians but effective treatments are lacking. To develop treatments, we must understand the mechanisms underlying chronic pain at the central pain processing site - the spinal cord. Recent studies have identified that autophagy, a cellular degradation process, is impaired in spinal cord neurons during chronic pain. However, little is known about the upstream mechanisms that inhibit autophagy or the function of autophagy in pain processing, which is the focus of my proposal. Aim 1 is to identify the receptors responsible for suppressing autophagy during pain and test whether reversing their action can reduce pain. Three of the candidate receptors I will test are TrkB, mGluR1, and mGluR5 because they have been linked to autophagy inhibition in different nervous system diseases, though their involvement in autophagy regulation has yet to be studied in the spinal cord or in the context of pain. The results of these experiments may identify specific molecular pathways to target for treating chronic pain. Aim 2 is to elucidate how impaired autophagy leads to pain sensitization by studying the biophysical properties of spinal cord neurons. Pain is associated with increased excitability of spinal cord neurons by increasing current flow through the NMDAR ion channels. Thus, I will test whether inhibiting autophagy increases the excitability of these neurons by measuring NMDAR currents. My studies will provide a greater understanding of the mechanisms by which the autophagy pathway regulates pain signalling. Since autophagy-modulating drugs are already used clinically to treat a variety of conditions, my findings could lead to the repurposing of such drugs as potential treatment for chronic pain.

column36: Identifying the Ig domain of titin interacting with filamin and analyzing its mutation
column37: Identifying the Ig domain of titin interacting with filamin and analyzing its mutation Titin is a giant elastic protein holding the sarcomere together by connecting myosin thick filaments in the A-band to the Z-disc. Titin fulfills crucial structural functions and is mutated in many myopathies. We have previously shown both genetically and biochemically that titin interacts with filamin in the Z-disc, where both together contribute to stabilizing Z-discs longitudinally and perpendicularly. In Drosophila indirect flight muscles the distance from the A-band to the Z-disc is much shorter than in other muscles, and therefore the Drosophila titin isoform kettin of IFM is much smaller than regular titin with just over 14000 amino acids. Kettin has 35 immunoglobulin domains and we will first identify the Ig domain responsible for filamin binding. We will start by overexpressing and purifying 5 His-tagged kettin constructs ranging from 828-1084 amino acids and 6-8 Ig domains. Pull-down assays with GST-tagged C-terminal filamin will identify the interacting subdomain of kettin. Smaller constructs with just one Ig domain will then be generated, expressed and purified to determine the interacting Ig domain. Site-directed mutagenesis may identify individual amino acids crucial for the interaction. We will then attempt to generate a CRISPR mutation in the titin locus deleting only the interacting Ig domain or just several amino acids. This will identify the precise role of filamin binding to titin in sarcomere and Z-disc structure and its potential role in human disease.

column36: The effects of exercise therapy on the cognitive functions of patients with chronic low back pain
column37: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is the most prevalent and problematic of all chronic pain syndromes. In addition to enduring persistent excruciating pain, they also experience a constellation of symptoms that further contribute to their disability, including a reduction of cognitive abilities. This is because patients with CLBP have more difficulty summoning the cognitive resources necessary to meet professional and personal responsibilities, often providing them with a major obstacle in every day functioning. Despite this, these cognitive deficits are rarely the focus of therapeutic interventions for CLBP since they are widely viewed as a secondary side effect of chronic pain. Thus, an effective treatment for them is still unknown. Fortunately, research shows that physical exercise is beneficial throughout the lifespan by optimizing overall physical and cognitive health and is one of few interventions that reliably improves pain management in CLBP. The proposed study aims to test the impact of a physical exercise intervention on CLBP and its associated cognitive deficits. It is hypothesized that the physical exercise intervention will affect the cognitive deficits seen in CLBP by either having a direct impact on those cognitive symptoms or having an indirect impact through a reduction in pain experience. To prove this, we will assign CLBP patients to a 14-week physical exercise program of high intensity aerobic and muscular exercise and examine pre- and post-levels of pain intensity and disability, and cognitive performance on a series of neuropsychological tasks. This study will provide insight into a feasible intervention that can enhance the cognitive health as well as the functionality and quality of life of chronic pain sufferers.

column36: Effect of Parental Support on Child Cognitive Reappraisal: A Transition into Adolescence Study
column37: Cognitive reappraisal is an emotion regulation (ER) strategy which involves cognitively altering one's emotional response to an event through reinterpretation (Gross, 1998; Giuliani & Gross, 2009). Findings suggest that adolescents use less adaptive ER strategies and as such may be more at risk of development of mental illness as a relationship has been found between poor ER strategies and depressive and anxiety symptoms in adolescents (Schafer, Naumann, Holmes, Tuschen-Caffier, & Samson, 2017). Thus, it is important to identify factors in the development of adaptive ER. Two factors that influence ER development in children are parent's ER strategies and how they support their children's use of adaptive ER strategies (Lunkenheimer, Shields, & Cortina, 2007; Thompson, 1994). What remains unknown is how the relationship between cognitive reappraisal and parental support unfolds for children transitioning into adolescence and when using experimental methods and objective measures of ER. The current study seeks to rely on brain imaging to measure emotional arousal in children, in an effort to determine how parent's support might affect the relationship between parent ER and child ER through the child's ability to make use of cognitive reappraisal strategies. This research contributes to the goals of the CIHR by directly identifying how parental support influences ER strategies in those transitioning into adolescence through the utilization of experimental methods and imaging technology in support of pen-paper questionnaires/measures. Further, this research has the potential to inform the development of interventions that seek to teach adaptive ER strategies to children and adolescents in an effort to reduce poor ER use, and thereby the risk of development of mental illness.

column37: The microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) is a master regulator of melanocytes one of the three many cell types of the skin. Suppression of MITF and inhibition of CBP/p300 has previously been shown to cause cell senescence in various melanoma cell lines. Despite the therapeutic potential of controlling MITF function by modulating its interaction with CBP/p300, the mechanistic details of this interaction remain unknown. This study will use a multi-disciplinary approach of biophysical and functional techniques to better understand how MITF interacts with CBP/p300 to control target gene expression. column36: The Effect of Supervised Consumption Services on Overdose Rates, Infectious Disease Complications, and Opioid Agonist Therapy in Ontario
column37: The opioid overdose crisis has resulted in the death of thousands of Canadians and has been declared a public health emergency by the Government of Canada. As part of Canada's public health response to the crisis, several new Supervised Consumption Services (SCSs) have been approved and are operating across the country. At minimum, SCSs provide people who use drugs with sterile injection supplies, observation after injection, and, as needed, administration of an overdose reversal agent. Prior studies have shown that SCSs reduce overdoses and infectious disease risk behaviour while remaining cost effective. Much of this evidence comes from British Columbia prior to the current epidemic, however little is known this may differ in Ontario and in the current context. Given the important geographical, social, and political differences across provinces, this thesis study aims to evaluate the impact of the implementation of SCSs in Ontario on three primary outcomes: rates of (1) overdose, (2) infectious disease complications, and (3) prescribed opioid agonist therapy. Data will be obtained using Ontario-wide administrative health data. Analyses will be performed to determine the rates of the primary outcomes within defined neighbourhoods surrounding an SCS in the year before and after its implementation. The results of this study will contribute significantly to our understanding of the impact of SCSs on important morbidity and mortality outcomes. It also represents one of the first studies to examine the effect of SCSs on the treatment of opioid use disorder. Overall, an accurate understanding of the role of SCSs in different geographical settings is critical in guiding ongoing harm reduction health policy in Ontario, nationally, and internationally amidst this crisis.

column37: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) vasculitis is a rare inflammatory disease which affects small blood vessels. column36: A NOVEL COMBINATION TREATMENT FOR CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA
column37: The body is made up of organs, which are made up of tissues, and tissues are made up of even smaller parts called cells. Cells in the body can divide to make more cells - like healing after an injury, and cells can also die. Cancer is a disease that occurs when cells divide without control and lose the ability to die; these cells can become a threat to other cells, tissues and organs and can lead to death. Thus, the aim of cancer research is to find treatments that kill cancer cells without hurting normal cells. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a cancer of the blood that usually affects the elderly. There is currently no cure for most CLL patients and CLL cells can become resistant to treatment, making patients' condition worse. One of the medications used to treat CLL is called ibrutinib; over time, side effects like infections, hypertension and bleeding prevent patients from continuing on ibrutinib. Previous work in our laboratory showed that a medication/drug called KU55933, when combined with ibrutinib, can kill more cancer cells than ibrutinib alone. We are currently testing whether the combination of AZD0156 with ibrutinib can improve CLL cell killing. We are also working on understanding why AZD0156 and KU55933 help kill more CLL cells when combined with ibrutinib. This research is important because ibrutinib and AZD0156 are already being used in the clinic; therefore, when we show that this new combination is more effective in killing CLL cells than ibrutinib alone, the combination could be implemented quickly to immediately benefit CLL patients.
