column36: Trial of thiamine supplementation in Cambodia: thiamine diphosphate dose in human milk
column37: In Cambodia and throughout Southeast Asia, babies are still dying from beriberi, a disease caused by a deficiency in thiamine (vitamin B1). Infantile beriberi rates peak at 3 months of age, when breast milk is the only source of infant nutrition. In Cambodia, a heavy reliance on white rice means that women consume a thiamine-poor diet, so women produce breast milk low in thiamine, putting their breastfed infants at risk of deficiency and infantile beriberi. We need to focus efforts to improve women's thiamine intake during the perinatal period to optimize health outcomes of their infants. Research has shown maternal thiamine supplementation is effective in raising thiamine status and reducing the incidence of infantile beriberi in regions where thiamine deficiency is prevalent, but trial data is limited and the lowest effective dose of supplementation has never been established. Therefore, my proposed research is a 22-week double-blind, four-parallel arm, placebo-controlled randomized trial of thiamine supplementation to assess human milk total thiamine concentration at 24 weeks postpartum. The objective of this study is to estimate the dose on the dose response curve where additional maternal intake of thiamine (oral dose) no longer meaningfully increases human milk total thiamine concentration at 24 weeks postpartum. Women will be randomized to one of four treatment arms, and will be asked to consume one oral capsule daily. We will collect breast milk at 2, 4, 12, and 24 weeks postnatal, to assess thiamine concentrations. Results from this study may inform future public health fortification interventions, that may be implemented in Cambodia and other at-risk countries to increase maternal thiamine intake, and prevent infantile beriberi and related mortality.

column36: Determining the effects of reduced cerebral oxygenation on delirium and long-term neurological outcomes in critically ill patients
column37: Delirium is an abnormal state of consciousness that often occurs when a patient is critically ill. Significant behavioural changes can be seen when a patient is delirious, including the inability to focus, confusion, emotional changes, and hallucinations. What is surprising is that delirium frequently affects those who aren't admitted for neurological issues, with up to 80% of patients developing this disorder in the intensive care unit (ICU). These patients experience longer ICU stays, depression and higher mortality rates. It was recently discovered that delirium's consequences can be long-term, lasting even after a patient leaves the hospital, with cognitive disturbances as severe as moderate traumatic brain injury. There is currently no cure for delirium and the underlying cause is unknown, but new research suggests that it is caused by the lack of oxygenated blood delivered to the brain. Without the critical oxygen that it needs, patients may develop delirium and long-term cognitive impairments. To validate this model 500 ICU patients from across Canada will be recruited, measuring the amount of oxygenated blood that is delivered to the brain. Statistical modelling will be used to determine whether low brain oxygenation can be used to predict delirium and cognitive impairments. Overall, the primary goal of this work is aimed towards discovering the underlying cause of delirium. With this knowledge, we will be able to provide effective treatment, not only in the ICU but to all patients affected by delirium. This is especially important as treating delirium can significantly improve outcomes and ensure a full recovery to resume a healthy life.

column36: PHASE-SPECIFIC EVALUATION OF COST-EFFECTIVENESS FOR LUNG TRANSPLANT AND EX-VIVO LUNG PERFUSION
column37: Patients with lung disease not responsive to medical therapy may undergo lung transplant as a definitive surgical therapy. Lung transplants have been shown to improve quality of life for patients with severe lung disease, and has been shown to extend length of life. However, the frequency with which donor lungs are determined to be of inadequate quality for transplant and the increasing enlistment of patients on the transplant wait-list means that the demand for lung transplant exceeds the available organ supply. Close to 20% of patients die while waiting for donor lungs. Ex-vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) is a promising new technology which allows for rehabilitation of donor lungs prior to transplant in a recipient. This technology has been shown to be safe and effective. However, the effect that EVLP may have on rates of lung transplant are yet to be determined. Lung transplant and EVLP may offer improved survival and quality of life for patients with severe lung disease, but these technologies come at significant cost to the healthcare system. Few studies have investigated the cost-effectiveness of lung transplant programs, and none has done so in the Canadian context. It remains unclear how cost-effective lung transplant programs are, and what impact, if any, EVLP may have on program efficiency. Further implementation of EVLP in transplant programs must be supported by data that reflects a value-added to patients as well as to the healthcare system. We propose to use health technology assessment principles to study cost-effectiveness of lung transplant and EVLP at one of the world's largest lung transplant centers. This project aims to demonstrate that EVLP may increase the number of potential organs for transplant and improve patient outcomes following transplant.

column37: La presence d'inegalites sociales de sante (ISS) entre les individus d'une communaute est reconnue pour expliquer les ecarts de leur etat de sante physique et psychologique et de la prevalence de maladies chroniques. Les ISS, notamment les inegalites alimentaires, peuvent se traduire par la disparite dans l'acces physique et economique aux fruits et aux legumes (FL) frais. Le developpement de systemes alimentaires alternatifs, dont font partie les kiosques de FL locaux, serait une strategie d'intervention prometteuse pour en ameliorer l'acces et la consommation au sein des quartiers defavorises. Toutefois, peu de donnees reconnues comme fiables ont ete produites a ce jour. Dans l'est de Montreal, l'organisme Y'a Quelqu'un l'aut'bord du mur a opere le Marche solidaire Cadillac (MSC), un kiosque maraicher situe a la station de metro Cadillac dans l'arrondissement de Mercier-Hochelaga-Maisonneuve lors des saisons estivales 2016 et 2017. Un projet collaboratif a ete elabore avec differentes instances, dont l'organisme responsable du MSC, et a permis la realisation d'une etude s'interessant aux deux premieres annees d'operation du MSC. L'objectif de cette etude est d'analyser la progression des ventes du MSC, son utilisation par les citoyens du secteur et les benefices percus par ses utilisateurs. Les donnees de ventes du MSC et celles obtenues par un questionnaire administre aux utilisateurs des deux saisons seront analysees. Il s'agira d'une des rares etudes concernant trois dimensions d'un nouveau kiosque de FL. Ce projet de recherche contribuera a mieux documenter cette strategie d'intervention, qui suscite un vif interet aupres des praticiens et des decideurs de politiques publiques locales. Il vise a repondre a des enjeux importants de nutrition en sante publique.

column36: To assess the feasibility of 3D printed polycaprolactone scaffolds for the reconstruction of rabbit tracheas
column37: The trachea is a vital organ that is responsible for the passage of air to the lungs. As with all organs, the trachea can be affected by various medical conditions which can cause significant symptoms and sometimes even death. Some children may be born with these conditions or they may develop later on in life. For example, they can include tracheal narrowing from birth or from trauma, autoimmune conditions and even cancers that arise from or invade the trachea. Surgical options to repair the trachea can be very challenging and subject patients to high operative risks, especially in cases where long segments of diseased trachea need to be resected. With the advancements of 3D-printing in medicine, we foresee a possible solution to the issues of reconstructing long segment tracheal defects. 3D-printing offers a customizable solution that can possibly allow for the gap of resected trachea to be bridged with a 3D-printed polymer. This study aims to evaluate the use of a 3D-printed Polycaprolactone (PCL) implant to reconstruct tracheas in rabbits. 10 rabbits will undergo surgery to resect approximately 50% of their trachea, we will then use 3D-printed implants that will replace these segments that have been removed. Following the operation, the rabbits will be monitored for any discomfort and breathing issues. Half of the rabbits will be sacrificed at 4 weeks and the other half at 8 weeks in order for us to evaluate the patency of the tracheal implants and to assess if there would be any integration of native rabbit cells within the implant. The findings of this study would further our knowledge on the use of 3D-printed implants as an option to reconstruct tracheas in rabbits with the intent of one day using this as a surgical option in humans.

column36: Investigating the role of Gly482Ser single nucleotide polymorphism in hepatocyte function through induced pluripotent stem cells and human samples
column37: Diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) are growing metabolic problems in our society today. PGC-1a is a protein expressed in liver cells, and is involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation and increased gluconeogenesis. It is found to be upregulated in mouse models as well as patients with diabetes. The single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) Gly482Ser is known to exist on PGC-1a, and we wish to investigate its effect on hepatocyte mitochondrial function. The glycine SNP is "normal" in humans, and the variant serine SNP is found in about 10% of people. I wish to investigate the role of this SNP in hepatocyte metabolic function. I will be genotyping induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), and using CRISPR technology to create lines of all three genotypes (gly/gly, ser/gly, ser/ser). Then we will differentiate the cells into hepatocyte-like cells, and validate that the cells function like hepatocytes. I will need to optimize this process to ensure the cells have the proper characteristics. Once I have shown the cells have been correctly differentiated, i will test their mitochondrial function using a Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit. This test detects basal mitochondrial respiration, ATP production-coupled respiration and other respiration. By stratifying these results by genotype, I will see if the genotype of a hepatocyte has an effect on the mitochondrial function in these cell types. Additionally, I will be genotyping patients who are receiving an MRI for NAFLD. I will analyze their biochemical data, as well as MRI results for liver fat content and stiffness, stratified by genotype. Overall I hope to find the phenotypic significance of this SNP, as it could provide a genetic marker for these prevalent diseases.

column36: Les immigrants et l'insecurite alimentaire au Canada: les effets a long terme des programmes de depannage alimentaire chez les nouveaux utilisateurs
column37: Ne pas avoir ou craindre de ne pas avoir suffisamment de nourriture pour repondre a ses besoins est une situation a laquelle 3,2 millions de Canadiens ont ete confrontes en 2014. Ce probleme, l'insecurite alimentaire, nuit a la sante physique et psychologique. Certains Canadiens sont plus a risque d'en souffrir. C'est le cas des personnes issues de l'immigration, particulierement dans les 5 annees suivant leur arrivee au pays. Traditionnellement, le don d'aliments constituait le principal programme d'intervention de depannage alimentaire. Maintenant, des programmes alternatifs (p. ex. cuisine collective) sont aussi offerts dans le but de developper les competences culinaires et d'ameliorer les conditions de vie des utilisateurs. Jusqu'a present, les strategies adoptees par la population immigrante pour faire face a l'insecurite alimentaire ont ete peu decrites. Des etudes avancent que les caracteristiques des immigrants ayant recours aux programmes et leurs utilisations different des utilisateurs nes au Canada. Or, on en connait peu sur les programmes arrivant le mieux a repondre aux besoins de cette population a risque. Ce projet a donc pour objectif d'evaluer les effets a long terme du depannage alimentaire (avec et sans programmes alternatifs) sur l'insecurite alimentaire, les competences culinaires et la qualite de l'alimentation chez les nouveaux utilisateurs issus de l'immigration. Le profil de Montrealais issus de l'immigration nouvellement utilisateurs de depannage alimentaire sera dresse selon leur utilisation des programmes. Les effets de leur utilisation seront mesures sur an. Ce projet de recherche contribuera a eclairer la question controversee sur la facon d'intervenir aupres de la population immigrante pour favoriser la securite alimentaire au Canada.

column37: Environ 3 enfants sur 1000 naissent avec une malformation cardiaque (MCC) severe. Ces enfants doivent etre pris en charge immediatement a la naissance et subir une chirurgie cardiaque des leurs premiers mois de vie. Heureusement, si la MCC est diagnostiquee avant la naissance, les chances de survie augmentent et le sejour a l'hopital et les couts d'hospitalisation diminuent. La majorite des enfants avec une MCC severe sont identifies lors de l'echographie obstetricale du 2e trimestre de grossesse, mais une minorite ne l'est malheureusement pas. Afin d'aider a identifier ces enfants, chaque mere enceinte a risque augmente d'avoir un enfant avec une MCC passe un examen specialise nomme l'echocardiographie foetale, meme si l'echographie obstetricale n'a revele aucune MCC. Cependant, l'efficacite de cette strategie n'a jamais ete prouvee et nous ne savons pas si elle est avantageuse dans le contexte canadien, d'autant plus que l'echocardiographie foetale est un examen long et couteux. Ce projet de recherche vise donc a determiner le nombre de MCC severes qui sont identifiees par l'echocardiographie foetale lorsque l'echographie obstetricale est normale. Il vise egalement a determiner la capacite de l'echographie obstetricale et de l'echocardiographie foetale a identifier une MCC. Pour ce faire, nous allons obtenir des donnees des quatre centres de cardiologie pediatrique au Quebec ainsi que du systeme de sante pour identifier tous les enfants nes en sante ou avec une MCC au Quebec et de determiner s'ils proviennent d'une grossesse a risque ou non, ainsi que le resultat de leur echographie obstetricale et de leur echocardiographie foetale. column36: The Evolution of Robotic Surgery in Ontario: A Population-Based Retrospective Cohort Study Examining Costs and Outcomes Compared with Laparoscopic and Open Surgery
column37: Surgery of the abdomen and chest can be approached through either open or minimally invasive techniques. Open techniques are associated with longer patient recovery and reater post-operative pain due to the length of the incision. Conversely, minimally invasive techniques use smaller incision and are therefore associated with less pain and faster recovery. Minimally invasive approaches include laparoscopy and robotic surgery. Laparoscopy is more affordable but uses straight instruments which at times can be ergonomically challenging. Robotic surgery is more expensive but uses articulating instruments that allow more degrees of freedom. Advocates of robotic surgery report improved range of motion and visibility with less surgeon fatigue and physiologic tremor. However, the benefits in patient-important outcomes after robotic surgery compared with laparoscopic or open procedures remain unclear and controversial. Preliminary analysis demonstrated that 1606 robotic procedures were performed in Ontario between 2016-2017; most frequently for management of prostate, uterus, kidney, rectum and lung conditions. Recently the Ontario Health Technology Advisory Committee recommended against publicly funding robotic prostate surgery due to minimal patient benefits and high cost. The goal of my project is to examine patient outcomes and costs after robotic surgery compared to laparoscopic and open surgery. This project will provide important information that would be critical in guiding funding decisions of robotic procedures in the future.

column36: Comparison of costimulatory domains in combined GD2 chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy and oncolytic vaccine therapy for neuroblastoma
column37: Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer with a poor prognosis in advanced or relapsed disease. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells is a promising new treatment for neuroblastoma. In this treatment, immune cells called T cells are engineered to selectively recognize and kill cancer cells. In the case of neuroblastoma, these CAR T cells recognize a molecule on the surface of the tumour cell called GD2. One important component of the CAR T cell is the costimulatory domain, which consists of either the molecule CD28, 41BB, or both in combination. It has been found that 41BB leads to a longer duration of CAR T cells in the body (persistence), which is associated with a better outcome for the patient. However, CD28 leads to improved killing initially. The combination of CD28 and 41BB appears to lead to enhanced function of the CAR T cell. Initial studies of CAR T cells in solid tumors have encountered some challenges, including insufficient numbers of T cells and poor trafficking of the CAR T cells to the tumor. Our laboratory is interested in using viruses that specifically target tumor cells (oncolytic viruses) to overcome these challenges. We have found that by delivering the oncolytic virus after transfer of CAR T cells, the CAR T cell product is expanded, known as a viral boost. What remains unknown is which costimulatory domain leads to persistence and better function of the CAR T cell product after viral boost. I propose to study GD2-CAR T cells with different costimulatory domains (CD28, 41BB or combined CD28/41BB). I hypothesize that 41BB will lead to improved persistence and function of the CAR T cell against GD2-expressing tumour cells.

column36: Access to Post-Discharge Care for Transgender and Gender-Expansive Individuals After Psychiatric Hospitalization in Ontario
column37: Transgender (trans) individuals, estimated to be 0.5% of the population, are people whose gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth. Gender-expansive (GE) refers to gender identities not necessarily male or female, such as genderqueer and non-binary. Trans people carry a very high mental health burden, with estimates of five times the rates of depression and ten times the suicide attempts compared to the general population. The time after discharge from a psychiatric hospitalization is known to be high risk for suicide and re-hospitalization. Follow up with a physician after discharge has been shown to reduce those risks. The high mental health burden in the trans population suggests an even greater need for post-discharge care in this population. We will study post-discharge care for trans and GE (TGE) individuals using health administrative data. We will collect data for every adult Ontario patient with a discharge after psychiatric hospitalization between 2012 and 2016 to form the discharge group. From within this discharge group, we will identify all individuals identified as TGE by four clinics in three Ontario cities to create the TGE group. We will select non-TGE individuals from the discharge group to form the comparison group, matching individuals to the TGE group on age and where they live. We will study how many in the TGE group versus the comparison group had a post-discharge visit with a family doctor, a psychiatrist, neither, or both within 7 days of discharge. We suspect TGE individuals have reduced access to post-discharge care due to transphobic health providers and systems not meeting their needs. Findings from this study can guide how to improve mental health policy for TGE individuals post-discharge.

column36: The Role of Microvascular Function in Bed Rest Induced Insulin Resistance and the Countermeasure Potential of High Intensity Interval Training
column37: Physical inactivity and muscle disuse, particularly bed rest, induces insulin resistance from which recovery is prolonged and often incomplete in persons of middle age. As such, along with change in glucose concentrations, the impact of vascular changes on insulin signaling should be considered in characterizing bed-rest induced insulin resistance. Insulin is a peptide hormone critical in the regulation of energy availability. Delivery of insulin to muscle tissue requires dense networks of blood vessels and movement from circulation to tissues via transcytosis, or movement, across the endothelium lining blood vessels. This research addresses the hypothesis that bed rest induced alterations in microvascular function are attenuated by the countermeasure of high intensity interval training (HIIT). I hypothesize muscle disuse will reduce microvascular flow responses to an insulin stimulating challenge involving meal tolerance testing, and that the exercise countermeasure will mitigate these reductions. I also hypothesize an increase in circulating microvesicles with bed rest, and that this increase will depress insulin transcytosis suggesting microvesicle involvement in insulin resistance resulting from bed rest. To assess the skeletal muscle microvascular function, contrast enhanced ultrasound imaging will be used. Subsequently, extracellular vesicles in the blood stream will be assessed using several instruments. The effect of microvesicles on insulin transcytosis by endothelial cells will be assessed using fluorescently labelled insulin. This research will aid in the characterization of bed rest induced changes to microvascular function and role of microvesicles. Additionally, the efficacy of the countermeasure HIIT to mitigate insulin resistance will be determined.

column36: Investigation of breast cancer cell dormancy
column37: The majority of cancer-related deaths are caused by the spread of cancer cells to secondary sites in the body. These cells are difficult to kill using current cancer therapies due to their ability to stop dividing, allowing them to hide from chemotherapy. Months or years later, dormant cells may start growing again and cause cancer to return; therefore, dormancy is an important area of study. DREAM (DP, RB-family, E2F4/5, and MuvB) is a complex of proteins known to induce dormancy and allow ovarian cancer cells to survive as they spread. My proposed work aims to determine if DREAM behaves similarly in breast cancer and if it could be used as a drug target to reduce breast cancer spread. I have already identified conditions that stop breast cancer cells from growing and used gene-editing technology to create cells that no longer form DREAM, which will allow me to identify processes normally controlled by this complex in breast cancer. I will also observe how these cells spread in mice to investigate whether DREAM loss improves cancer prognosis. Overall, this project may identify mechanisms that contribute to breast cancer relapse and lead to development of new therapeutic tools to prevent cancer spread and reduce mortality rates.

column36: Mutual Antibody T cell Engagers (MATEs): A safe, flexible alternative to Chimeric Antigen Receptor T cell therapy for leukemia and lymphoma
column37: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is a revolutionary treatment delivering complete response rates up to 90% for CD19+ B cell leukemias and lymphomas, yet problems with response durability and toxicity remain. CARs are engineered receptors expressed in T cells that contain an extracellular Antibody Domain (AD), targeting a known antigen, and an intracellular Signaling Domain (SD), which initiates proliferation, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity. Despite impressive efficacy, CAR T cells exhibit unpredictable expansion, ranging from inadequate, which allows tumor escape, to excessive, resulting in life-threatening side effects including cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity. To resolve this, our lab is developing a novel strategy called Mutual Antibody T cell Engagers (MATEs). The MATE strategy splits the CAR AD and SD into two separate proteins, utilizing a leucine zipper to connect them in a non-covalent fashion. In this way, the MATE behaves like a CAR only when the AD is present, providing physicians with exquisite control over T cell activity. My research aims to test the activation, proliferation, and target cell cytotoxicity of T cells transduced to express the MATE SD (MATE T cells) in the presence of varying doses of the MATE AD. We expect these activities to increase with escalating doses of the AD, defining the dose-dependent relationship between it and MATE T cells. In summary, the MATE strategy offers control not previously afforded by CAR T cell therapy, improving safety and flexibility. In future, this strategy could also be used to target several antigens simultaneously using multiple ADs and a single SD, thereby reducing the risk of tumor escape as seen with about one-third of patients after they receive CD19+ CAR T cell therapy.

column36: Towards Optimizing Value-Based Systemic Therapy in Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Cost-Utility Analysis Using Decision Analytic Modeling of First-Line Systemic Therapy
column37: Given a better understanding of how kidney cancers behave, there have been several new drugs developed over the last decade that are effective against this disease. While this is exciting for patients, it creates a decision-making problem for clinicians to identify the most effective treatment for individuals. Clinical trials have typically provided the necessary data to inform these decisions. Unfortunately, given the significant cost of clinical trials and the growing number of new drug treatments, it is impractical to conduct clinical trials to test all potential comparator treatments with one another. As such there is great need to develop new methods to systematically compare all drugs for kidney cancer to help decide the most effective treatment. Further, although it would be ideal to fund all new drugs, given the significant costs associated with these new treatments, our publicly funded health care system is unable to sustain this. Therefore, to inform health care policy makers on the most effective treatment for public funding, we require a method to compare both the cost and effectiveness of treatments, particularly when there is an absence of clinical trial data. The current research project aims to evaluate and compare the cost and effectiveness of all currently available first-line drug treatments for kidney cancer. This will be done through the use of decision-analytic modeling. This technique allows for the simulation of "mock" clinical trials to compare drug treatments that have not been compared directly, under different conditions. Overall, we anticipate the results of this study will provide the necessary information to help clinicians and policy-makers to choose the best first-line drug treatments for our patients with kidney cancer.

column36: Updating the Evidence on the Use of Age Adjustment in the Assessment of Preterm Infants' Growth
column37: Preterm birth is defined as an infant born alive before 37 weeks of gestation. The Canadian rate of preterm birth was 8% is 2012 and has shown to be increasing, accounting for over 50% of neonatal mortality and for the majority of all infant deaths. Optimal growth assessment strategies are necessary to support the growth and wellbeing of preterm infants. Clinicians have previously used either the infant's chronological age or the adjusted age in the assessment of preterm infant growth. The adjusted age is the age that corrects for the infant's prematurity by subtracting the number of weeks of prematurity from the infant's chronological age. The chronological age neglects the fact the infant was born early, which can lead to misclassification of infant growth as the infant is expected to grow similar to term infants of the same chronological age. Age adjustment can ensure the accurate assessment of preterm infant growth. Nonetheless, the limited use of age adjustment may be due to the fact that the available evidence is over 20 years old. Also, there remain critical gaps in the literature on the appropriate period for age adjustment, specifically with regards to the various degrees of prematurity: early (< 28 weeks of gestation) moderate (28-32 weeks) and late preterm infants (33-36 weeks). In this retrospective cohort study, preterm infant growth will be assessed using both the chronological and adjusted age. Potential differences in growth assessment will be explored using recent preterm growth reference charts and the World Health Organisation Growth Standard. This study may alter or reinforce the 20-year-old advice about age adjustment for prematurity, providing evidence-based guidance on the optimal strategies for the assessment of preterm infants' growth.

column36: Calibrating CLEFT-Q as a Disease-Specific, Patient-Reported Utility Score in Ethiopia: A Pilot Study - in Honour of Nelson Mandela
column37: Children with cleft lip and palate (CLP) in Ethiopia face poor access to care, leading to delays in treatment until adolescence or adulthood. Social stigma leads to drop-out from school, difficulty forming healthy relationships, and decreased productivity. CLEFT-Q is a patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) used to evaluate health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in CLP patients, and validated in low-middle income countries for children eight years and older. CLP has a significant and unique burden for Ethiopian children, thus patient-based utilities will provide critical data for economic evaluations of CLP interventions to inform health policy in a context with scarce resources. We will work with our Ethiopian partners in Yekatit Hospital, through Addis Ababa University (AAU) and Cure Hospital to conduct a multi-center prospective cohort study to evaluate CLEFT-Q HRQoL and patient preferences pre- and post- surgery using standard gamble (SG), time-trade-off, and the visual analogue scale (VAS) in patients with unilateral cleft lip and/or palate aged eight and older. We will map CLEFT-Q scores to utility scores using the 2017 ISPOR Task Force guidelines. A formal regression-based mapping model approach will be used. This work builds on pre-existing sustainable networks between AAU and the University of Toronto to inform health policy for stigmatized CLP children aged eight and older. This study provides critical information for economic evaluations of CLP interventions in Ethiopia and advances HRQoL research mapping PROMs to utility scores.

column36: Injury mechanism and social support as moderators of the effects of pediatric concussion on post-concussive symptoms
column37: Concussions can result in physical, cognitive, and emotional problems, known as post-concussive symptoms (PCS). Although most children recover from concussion without complication, a subset will be hindered by persistent PCS that reduce their quality of life. Social support, the perceived or actual support a person receives from their community and social networks, is known to protect against detrimental consequences of health problems. However, little research has examined the effect of social support on PCS after concussion. Social support may foster recovery, particularly for children with sport-related concussions, who are often isolated from their teams, resulting in feelings of loneliness and isolation. This study aims to identify the effects of social support on PCS in children after sport-related versus non-sport-related concussion (i.e., concussions caused by falls, motor vehicle collisions, etc.). The central hypothesis is that greater social support will predict fewer PCS for children with concussion, especially when sport-related. Participants will be part of a parent study that recruits children/adolescents aged 8-17 years with concussions or orthopaedic injuries during emergency department (ED) visits at five sites from the Pediatric Emergency Research Canada network. Injury information is collected in the ED, and social support and PCS are measured at 10 days, 3 months, and 6 months post-injury. In addition, weekly PCS ratings are obtained electronically. The study findings will clarify the role of social support in recovery from PCS after concussion in children and youth. If greater social support predicts fewer PCS, then efforts to enhance children's social support would be warranted, perhaps especially after sport-related concussion.

column36: Novel delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide to the brain for Huntington Disease
column37: Huntington Disease (HD) is fatal genetic brain disorder whose symptoms include cognitive decline and uncontrollable movement. In mouse models of HD, it is possible to reverse these symptoms by lowering levels of the disease-causing mutant protein, huntingtin. Currently, a clinical trial is testing a treatment called HTTRX in HD patients, but to reach the brain, this drug must be injected into the fluid surrounding the spinal cord. This delivery method is invasive and risky. When the drug is delivered this way, it does not distribute across the entire brain or reach the rest of the body. Some brain regions that are poorly reached are known to be damaged in HD and the source of debilitating symptoms. Delivering the drug by injecting it into the bloodstream would allow it to reach other parts of the body. The challenge to this approach is that the brain is protected by a structure called the blood-brain barrier (BBB) which does not allow foreign compounds to reach the brain. There are several proteins known to cross the BBB as part of their normal function. These proteins can be used as a "Trojan Horse" to shuttle other molecules into the brain. In this project, I will attach a drug similar to HTTRX to one of these proteins, and test in mice whether this hybrid molecule can reach the brain when injected into the blood. Then, I will test whether it can lower the levels of the mutant protein that causes HD. Delivering drugs like HTTRX to the brain through the blood could improve treatments for HD patients, because the drug delivery would be less invasive, and would reach target regions of the brain, as well as the rest of the body. If successful, this approach could be modified for use with other similar drugs and thus could be used to treat many genetic brain diseases.

column36: Fast characterization of multiple prion strains in cultured murine neuronal organotypic slices
column37: Prion diseases are a group of fatal diseases that affect both humans and animals. They result in death of brain cells and a decline in the mental capacity of affected individuals. The disease causing agent is called a prion, which is a misfolded form of a normal protein found in the brain of all mammals. Prions convert additional normal protein into the misfolded shape. Prions can sometimes spread from animals to humans, as was the case for mad cow disease, and so pose a public health concern. Human prion diseases vary widely in terms of the symptoms, age of onset, and patterns of damage seen within the brain. These differences are thought to be related to the shape of each prion version. Different prion shapes are referred to as strains and each has distinct properties that can be studied in laboratory assays. Very little is known about the stains that cause human prion diseases for a number of reasons. Human diseases are rare and so the amount of infected tissue available for research is limited. Also, human prions cannot be grown in the laboratory. Characterizing them would help us understand more about the ways in which prions cause disease as well as the origin of infectious prions. I aim to develop a model system that could be used to grow human prions in the laboratory for the first time, and to rapidly characterize many different prion strains. This will be achieved by exposing thin slices of genetically engineered mouse brain tissue to different prion strains, resulting in infection of the brain tissue with the corresponding prion strain. A model system such as this will allow for the comparison of a multitude of different prion strains and provide a new tool to further our understanding of how different prion strains cause disease in both humans and animals.

column36: The long-term sex-specific effects of TrkB receptor antagonism on neurochemical signalling in the hippocampus of rats exposed to repeated stress during adolescence
column37: Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis during adolescence is reported to trigger the onset of mood disorders later in life. Upon a perceived psychological or physiological threat, the axis releases glucocorticoids (GCs). The hippocampus is a GC sensitive brain region where stress exposure is known to affect glucocorticoid receptors (GR) expression, leading to altered hippocampal function and cognitive impairments. Chronic stress also reduces levels of the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) at this sensitive region. The main objective of this study is to observe the long-term effects of blocking BDNF-tyrosine-related kinase B (TrkB) receptors, using ANA-12, on neurochemical signalling within the CA1 and CA3 layers of the hippocampus of adult rats that were exposed to repeated stress during adolescence. ANA-12 has shown its efficacy in reducing anxiety and depression related behaviours by selectively binding to TrkB and preventing downstream signalling effects of BDNF. This study will examine the modulatory effects of ANA-12 on BDNF and GR expression, and possible sex differences in stress-related expression. Adolescent male and female Wistar rats will be subjected to a 10-day heterotypic stress/ no stress paradigm from PND 26 to PND 35. The rat sample will be randomly divided into 4 groups per sex: ANA-12 + stress (AS), ANA-12 + no stress (ANS), vehicle + stress (VS) and vehicle + no stress (VNS). Immunohistochemistry and Western blotting will be conducted to assess the levels of BDNF and GR in the CA1 and CA3 layers of the hippocampus. Discrete changes in GR and BDNF expression in the CA1 and CA3 layers of the hippocampus across groups, as well as sex differences in response to stress and ANA-12 treatment are expected.

column36: Born Into a Life Sentence
column37: Pedophilia is the sexual attraction of a man or woman to a minor child. It differs from other sexual orientations as the object of the attraction is determined by age not by gender and, if acted upon in Canada, invokes criminality. The term "non-offending pedophile" describes a person who has not committed offences. Examining pedophilia from the interdisciplinary perspective of Women and Gender Studies allows for new questions by foregrounding issues of social justice. In Canada, treatment and support are almost exclusively offered in prisons, to offenders. For non-offenders, resources are scarce, and support is difficult to access. This study will consider the legitimacy of arguments used to restrict treatment for non-offenders to identify the systemic barriers, employing, where available, non-offenders' first-hand accounts on treatment and support. Employing textual data and interviews, a Canadian case study, the ongoing trial of Kenneth Harrison, will be used to analyze arguments for and against non-offenders' use of child sex dolls to manage their attractions, and the legal and social repercussions of doing so. Drawing on labelling, panic, and social construction theories, the proposed work will develop a new framework, preliminarily called a support-based treatment framework, for the study of pedophilic interest to bring forth a nuanced intersectional framework including critical feminist discourse. The intended purpose of this theoretical framework is the rethinking of the treatment of non-offenders, and the expansion of legal, criminology, and women and gender studies, as well as, recommendations to the Canadian Psychological Association on improved training.

column36: Perinatal obesity and allergic disease development in offspring: a population-based cohort study in Ontario, Canada
column37: Mothers are now more likely than ever to be overweight or obese during pregnancy. Obesity is known to cause changes in metabolism and inflammation that can pose a serious threat to the baby's development and long-term health. As such, some experts have questioned whether there could be a connection between the rising trends in obesity during pregnancy and common childhood allergic diseases such as asthma, eczema, and rhinitis. These allergic diseases often lead to increased psychological, social, and financial burden for affected children and their families. Only a few studies have evaluated the possible link between obesity during pregnancy and childhood allergic disease, and none were performed in Canada. In our study, we propose to describe the relationship between maternal obesity during pregnancy and childhood allergic disease in Ontario. Using clinical and health administrative databases and statistical modelling techniques, this study will follow approximately 280,000 babies from birth to the age of 6 years to determine if children born to overweight or obese mothers have a higher risk for allergic disease. Additionally, we will determine whether other risk factors in the mothers and children may also play a role in this relationship. Our hope is that our study results will help inform public health initiatives and increase early identification, treatment, and prevention of childhood allergic disease.

column36: Advanced Trial Design in Critical Care Medicine
column37: I am an academic critical care physician proposing a program of research focused on evolving clinical trial design. Randomized trials yield the highest level of evidence for therapies, however many clinical questions are unsuitable for classical trials due to costs, sample size, and patient heterogeneity. This is apparent in critical care medicine where patient populations are small and heterogeneous. One mechanism to address these limitations is to explore innovative designs such as adaptive trials. Adaptive trials may answer clinical questions with more efficiency and patient-level resolution but uptake has been limited by the unfamiliarity and complexity of the design and its strengths and limitations are not well known. My graduate work will use a Bayesian analytic framework to evolve adaptive trial designs and facilitate their application to critical care medicine. During the CGS-M award we will conduct reanalyses of prominent critical care medicine trials with simulation to demonstrate principles of adaptive trial design. My supervisor will be George Tomlinson (Professor, Faculty of Medicine, Bayesian statistics expertise) and my mentor Rob Fowler (Faculty of Medicine, Director of Clinical Epidemiology and Health Care Research, critical care physician) will be closely involved. Potential committee members include Peter Juni (Professor, Faculty of Medicine, clinical trials expertise) or Marzyeh Ghassemi (Professor, Faculties of Medicine and Computer Science). Our research in adaptive trial designs for critical care medicine will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and limitations of adaptive trials with corresponding improvements in efficiency and applicability of research that will benefit patients, clinicians and health systems.

column36: The role of embryonic-derived macrophages in cardiac inflammation and disease caused by viral infections
column37: Cardiac disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Although recent advances in cardiac care have greatly improved treatment outcomes, the prevalence of chronic disease is still significant, and is a major contributor to morbidity. Previous studies have demonstrated that viral infections of the heart are linked to chronic inflammation. Fortunately, immune cells, including macrophages (MFs), have roles in the clearance of virus from the body. In the past, cardiac MFs were believed to originate from a single cell type, like what is observed in other tissues. With the recent use of innovative experimental approaches, the Epelman lab has defined two distinct lineages that exist in adults, known as embryonic-derived and adult monocyte-derived MFs, whose roles differ greatly in response to injury. Embryonic MFs form from early development and tend to promote cardiac recovery (and regeneration) in the heart. On the other hand, adult derived MFs are recruited to tissues in adulthood and tend to promote inflammation. The role of these cells in the heart has never been investigated. In order to assess the role of embryonic MFs, we will use a mice strain that lacks embryonic-derived MFs and determine the effects after viral infection of heart tissue. We predict to see that the absence of embryonic-derived MFs will lead to greater disease due to its expected protective role. Then, we will look at the gene expression profile of these cells as well as their ability in cardiac regenerative processes, in order to assess their functional role after viral injury. The ability to determine the exact cell types responsible for reparative processes provide the potential for new treatment options that target such cells in order to promote better health outcomes.

column36: Characterization of Filovirus cell tropism in isolated primary cells and in a 3D blood-testis barrier co-culture model
column37: Ebola virus (EBOV), the causative agent of Ebola virus disease (EVD), garnered international attention with the West Africa epidemic becoming a global health threat, and demonstrating potential for large scale filoviral epidemics. Studies of EVD survivors have shown potential for persistence in immune privileged sites following recovery, including the testes and semen. Further, sexual transmission from EVD survivors up to 16 months after infection has resulted in re-emergence of EBOV. Computer models of persistent survivor data have predicted that EBOV will persist in the testes of 50% of male EVD survivors 115 days post infection. Taken together, wide spread EBOV testicular persistence is of great concern for future outbreaks. In a recently published review, I compiled historical data regarding filovirus persistence and sexual transmission demonstrating that these were first observed following the 1967 Marburg virus outbreak and subsequently in Ebolavirus outbreaks. Collectively, this demonstrates filoviruses have the potential to persist and re-emerge via sexual transmission. There has been limited work towards understanding the molecular mechanisms of filovirus persistence. Given this public health threat, research is desperately needed to understand the underlying mechanisms of viral transmission to the testis, persistence within this niche and the potential risks for persistence and transmission across different filoviruses. Ultimately, these mechanistic studies will allow the characterization of filovirus persistence and lead to targeted therapies to combat filovirus testicular persistence. The knowledge gained from these investigations is critical for preventing filovirus re-emergence and transmission to new geographic locations during future outbreaks.

column36: The role of inhibitory and immunoregulatory signalling pathways in CD8 T cell memory generation
column37: Most current vaccines cause the immune system to produce antibodies, which are proteins that specifically target invading bacteria or viruses. These antibodies decrease the ability of invading pathogens to attach to cells, and additionally can neutralize their excreted toxins, both of which are ways that these invaders can make us sick. The protection offered by antibodies is incomplete and a vaccine that also produces memory CD8 T cells would offer better protection against intracellular pathogens as well as against pathogens that rapidly mutate, such as the influenza virus (the flu). We know that the selection of CD8 T cells that become memory cells is not random, but the factors involved are not fully understood. It has been suggested that T cells that are protected from activating signals are more likely to become memory cells. Since the main role of inhibitory signalling pathways is to dampen or counteract the effects of activating signals received by cells, we will look at the role of inhibitory signalling in CD8 T cell memory development. Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) is a well-studied immunoregulatory pathway that plays an important role in exhausting CD8 T cells during chronic infections and cancer, and recent studies have shown that it may also play important roles during the CD8 T cell response to regular acute infections. This project aims to further the understanding of the role that inhibitory pathways such as PD-1 play in CD8 T cell memory generation and will help inform the development of T-cell vaccines for rapidly mutating pathogens such as influenza by defining the pathways that can increase the number and functionality of memory CD8 T cells.

column36: Determination of the initial aging-associated molecular events in the development of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD), as the most common form of senile dementia, is a heavy burden to the health care systems worldwide. AD is frequently attributed to protein misfolding and aggregation; one such trouble-prone protein is Tau. AD often does not run in families and is described as 'sporadic' (sAD), which is typically encountered in late adulthood. Although chronological age has been reported to be the greatest risk factor of sAD, little is known about how aging gives rise to sAD pathology at a molecular level. In the experimental realm, the lack of plausible sAD animal model adds another layer of complexity to sporadic Alzheimer's disease research. The overarching goal of my research is to visualize the initial aging-related molecular events that result in sAD pathology, such as Tau misfolding, in sAD models expressing low levels of the human Tau protein (low-expresser). The mutated gene causing the Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) proves to be a powerful tool to construct a molecular environment that mimics natural aging. I will first express the HGPS gene in both a low-expresser sAD cell culture model via transfection and in a transgenic mouse model via stereotaxic injection. Once the HGPS phenotype and sAD pathology are both observed, misfolded Tau proteins will be purified and analysed using biochemical techniques that help determine their folding state. By assessing initial aging-related protein misfolding events in the development of sAD, we may tease apart the complexity in AD's sporadic nature, which may provide insights into the development of new AD models and early disease intervention.

column36: L'impact des calcifications aortiques sur le risque de rupture d'anevrisme de l'aorte abdominale
column37: Les anevrismes de l'aorte abdominale (AAA) sont un probleme de sante publique vu que 20 000 Canadiens en sont diagnostiques chaque annee. Bien qu'ils constituent souvent une atteinte asymptomatique, les patients dont l'AAA rompt ont une mortalite de 90%. Au jour d'aujourd'hui, les deux principaux facteurs pouvant stratifier le risque de rupture d'un AAA sont le diametre dudit AAA ainsi que la vitesse a laquelle son diametre croit. Le probleme est que ce modele a une sensitivite d'environ 60%, ce qui laisse place a un nombre de faux negatifs tres important. En d'autres mots, il est encore trop difficile d'exclure le risque de rupture chez les patients atteints d'AAA. Recemment, un projet de recherche a demontre l'existence de trois formes de calcifications aortiques : << strip, stone et flake. >> Nous voulons donc savoir si la forme des calcifications aortiques pourrait devenir un parametre de prediction de la rupture d'AAA. Nous voulons savoir si la quantite, la forme et la location des calcifications aortiques pourraient etre des facteurs de risque independants de la rupture d'AAA. Nous voulons egalement savoir si ces memes variables sont liees a la mortalite causee par rupture d'AAA. Nous pensons que les AAA contenant de grandes proportions de calcifications de type << stone >> pourraient etre plus a risque de rupturer. A l'inverse, nous pensons que les AAA contant de grandes proportions de calcifications <<flake >> pourraient etre moins a risque de rupture. Il s'agira d'une etude cas-temoin retrospective, multicentrique (CHUM et CUSUM) et realisee a partir des dossiers cliniques des patients.

column36: BRCA1 regulation of Osteoprotegerin: A Novel Biomarker for BRCA1-Associated Breast Cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in women, affecting approximately 1 in 8 women in Canada. A subset of the female population faces an even greater risk of developing breast cancer due to a mutation in the BRCA1 gene. This mutation drastically increases their risk of developing breast cancer to about 70%. It is the women with this mutation that I am focusing on for my Master's research. Currently, the most effective prevention strategy for mutation carriers is a bilateral mastectomy, however, the invasive nature of the surgery means many women instead choose to undergo more frequent screening to identify possible breast cancers at an earlier and more treatable stage. Despite having known about the risks associated with BRCA1 gene mutations for over two decades, there have been few advancements in our breast cancer prevention strategies. Thus, new avenues for preventing BRCA1-associated breast cancers must be explored. Recently, the protein Osteoprotegerin (OPG) has been implicated in the biological pathway contributing to the development of breast cancer in BRCA1-mutation carriers. Clinical studies reported low blood levels of OPG in BRCA1-mutation carriers, whereas women with higher levels of OPG were reported to be at a much lower risk of developing BRCA-associated breast cancer. This suggests that OPG may be protective against breast cancer. What remains unknown is how BRCA1 is regulating circulating OPG, and it is this question that I hope to answer through my Master's research. Our research aims to understand OPG regulation in BRCA1 mutation carriers in the hopes of identifying new targets for drug interventions that increase or mimic the anti-cancer activity of OPG and therefore reduce the incidence of breast cancer in these high-risk women.

column36: Stress, Parenting Behaviors, and Cortisol's Impact on Maternal Mental Illness and Child Psychopathology
column37: Children who grow up with mothers with mental illness (MI) are more likely to develop their own mental health and behavioural problems. Similar to other difficulties such as neglect or being separated from a parent, exposure to maternal MI is a 'toxic stressor' for children, with preliminary research in infants linking this experience to the excess secretion of stress hormones (i.e. cortisol). Despite established links between maternal MI and higher levels of cortisol secretion in children, there are gaps in understanding how mothers' parenting behaviours underlie this link. I will explore how parenting skills of mother's with MI, toxic stress, and cortisol levels all relate to the early-life mental health and behaviour problems of children. It is hypothesized that mothers with MI will have poor parenting behaviours (i.e. low empathy, low positive emotion, or low sensitivity) that are associated with excessive stress hormone secretion in children and mental health difficulties. The study will include 120 mothers (60 who have MI) and their children (ages 36-48 months). They will be recruited from flyers, community postings and local agencies such as the Seven Oaks School Division and The Manitoba Crisis Response Centre. I will collect information on parenting behaviours using questionnaires and standardized observations of parents interacting with their children. Children's stress levels will be measured through cortisol that is built up in their hair. This research will help to understand the parenting mechanisms that place children of mothers with MI at elevated risk for intergenerational psychopathology. This research may facilitate the development of specific interventions to support well-being in children at-risk for early mental health and behavioural problems.

column36: The Role of Notch Signaling in the Pathogenesis of Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that is characterized by the destruction of myelin in the central nervous system (CNS) by immune cells recognizing self-antigen. The main driver of the demyelination activity are subtypes of T helper (Th) cell, particularly Th1 and Th17 cells, which recruit other immune cells to cause damage to the CNS. There is some evidence that Notch signaling regulates the differentiation and proliferation of Th1 and Th17 cells during multiple sclerosis. However, the exact role that Th1 and Th17 cells play and the disease progression stage at which Notch signaling is critical for Th1 and Th17 cells development are still unclear. Thus, the aims of my project are to identify the role that Th1 and Th17 cells play in multiple sclerosis, what other populations of immune cells also cause damages to the CNS, and when does Notch signaling play a critical role in disease establishment and relapse. My hypothesis is stage-specific modulation of Notch signaling in T cells will lead to different disease severities or amelioration in combination with the local immune microenvironment. To address my hypothesis, I will analyze the impact of Notch signaling in Th1 and Th17 cell responses in the development of multiple sclerosis. I will also determine the role Notch signaling plays in the activation of other immune cell populations during disease development. By answering these questions, my project aims to provide a better understanding of disease development and immune cell functions in the establishment of the disease, which will ultimately provide further insights for more selective and effective therapies for multiple sclerosis.

column36: Does implementation of a comprehensive school health program improve self-esteem among students in Indigenous and northern communities?
column37: Mental health concerns affect at least 20% of youth in Canada, making it a major public health challenge. Poor self-esteem and lack of optimism are early signs for depression and poor mental health in children. There is an opportunity to improve self-esteem and optimism in children and youth by teaching them about good mental health habits along with promoting healthy eating and physical activity. Schools are an ideal place to do this by using the Comprehensive School Health (CSH) model. CSH programs give children the chance to see and learn good health habits. A Project Promoting healthy Living for Everyone in schools (APPLE Schools) is an evidence-based CSH program that promotes healthy eating and physical activity in school communities across Alberta. This program recently expanded to also promote good mental well-being. It also grew to include northern rural and remote communities and Indigenous populations in northern Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Manitoba. There is nothing known about whether such school programs can improve self-esteem and optimism in these populations. This is why this research is urgently needed. This study will use survey data collected at baseline line in 2016, and follow up surveys from 2018 and 2020. Students in grades 4-8 in 16 northern APPLE Schools completed these surveys. We think findings will show that students in APPLE Schools will benefit from the program and are more likely to develop good self-esteem and optimism. column36: Metabolic engineering of chimeric antigen receptor T cells for cancer immunotherapy
column37: Immunotherapy, a biological therapy that utilizes the immune system to fight disease, has emerged in the last few years as a major player in the field of cancer treatment. The effect of immunotherapy depends largely on the action of white blood cells with powerful tumour-killing capabilities, called T cells. Novel approaches are currently being explored to enhance T cell function and improve responses to immunotherapy in hard-to-treat cancers. One such approach is the engineering of chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells, wherein patient T cells are extracted, modified with a receptor that enables them to better recognize tumour cells, and then re-infused in large numbers. CAR-T cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable success in blood-based cancers, but in solid tumours, physical and functional barriers pose a unique challenge. In particular, rapidly growing tumour cells produce toxic metabolites and consume large amounts of glucose and oxygen, creating a hostile environment that inhibits immune cells. It is the goal of my research to find a new way to overcome this suppression and improve CAR-T cell therapy for solid tumours. To achieve this goal, I am designing the world's first metabolic engineering platform for cancer immunotherapy. Working within the context of ovarian cancer, I will use sophisticated gene-editing techniques to produce supercharged CAR-T cells with enhanced metabolic and tumour-killing capabilities. Rigorous testing and optimization in the laboratory and in mouse models will enable me to deliver a successful metabolic engineering platform with the potential to finally advance CAR-T cell therapy in solid cancers.

column36: Cerebral Organoids as a Model for Endogenous Retrovirus-K Reactivation in Neurodegenerative Disease
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that affect the motor neurons of the central nervous system. This motor neuron death leads to progressive loss of muscle function resulting in death within 2-5 years of diagnosis. Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) are viral elements that make up 8% of the human genome. These ERVs have been associated with ALS neuropathology, along with other inflammatory and neurological diseases. Endogenous Retrovirus-K (ERVK) is a viral parasite that is known to produce a functionally active enzyme integrase (IN). The Douville lab has found high levels of ERVK IN expression in ALS brain and spinal cord tissue. Along with this IN expression, there is also an increase in expression of DNA damage markers ?H2AX and the disruption of DNA repair protein BRCA1. This DNA damage can lead to a form of inflammatory programmed cell death known as necroptosis. Our research will involve the generation of human cerebral organoids with a cumate-inducible ERVK IN vector. These organoids will be treated with cumate to induce ERVK IN expression and DNA damage, inflammation, and necroptosis patterns will be assessed. We will also test known integrase inhibitors on these IN-expressing organoids to test the ability of these drugs in preventing this damage and cell death. If successful, these anti-retroviral drugs may be used in future ALS clinical trials, and provide a basis for desperately needed therapies.

column36: Melatonin, sleep and circadian gene methylation, with implications for breast cancer risk among female shift workers
column37: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer in Canadian women. Strong evidence has linked long-term shiftwork to breast cancer, but there remains uncertainty regarding the underlying mechanisms. In the healthcare industry, where shiftwork is necessary and the prevalence of this type of work is high, over 80% of workers are female. As such, female hospital workers represent an at-risk population for circadian-induced breast cancer. Many studies have examined melatonin patterns as a biomarker for circadian disruption, although few have considered exactly how circadian disruption is linked to breast cancer. A potential pathway between circadian disruption and breast cancer is circadian gene methylation. The scant research on this pathway has neglected specific aspects of shiftwork such as intensity, duration, and frequency, leading to exposure misclassification. Despite the evidence that both shiftwork and breast cancer risk are associated with melatonin disruption, there has been no study that considers the interaction between melatonin and circadian gene methylation. Using data collected in a new cross-sectional study (funded by the Cancer Research Society) at the Kingston Health Sciences Center, this study aims to examine two relationships: 1) sleep patterns and melatonin levels; and 2) melatonin levels and circadian gene methylation. Data collected from pre-menopausal female hospital employees will also consider current shiftwork status, detailed lifetime shiftwork parameters, and shift intensity. This study will provide epigenetic insight into early breast cancer development in hopes of informing future large-scale studies and providing evidence for workplace policy decisions including considerations of breast cancer prevention.

column36: Validity and Reliability of a Food Frequency Questionnaire for the Characterization of Toddlers' Diets and their Determinants
column37: During the early years of life, the brain develops rapidly and is particularly sensitive to the nutrition provided. The intake of specific nutrients including zinc, vitamin B-12, choline and omega-3 fatty acids have been associated with cognition and brain development in toddlers. In addition, there is growing literature indicating that the nutrition provided during the first two years of life has a lasting effect on long-term health outcomes. Despite the impact of the early life diet, there is a lack of information on what a toddler's diet is comprised of in Canada. Reliable and validated dietary assessment tools are essential for accurately describing the dietary intake in the early years. As toddlers' diets are dynamic, food frequency questionnaires (FFQs) may represent the most accurate dietary assessment tool as they provide information about nutrient intake over a longer period. The goals of this study are to evaluate the validity and reliability of a toddler FFQ and to characterize the dietary intake and patterns in healthy toddlers at 18 months of age. Gender differences and sociodemographic determinants of dietary intake in toddlers will also be explored. Diet records, FFQs and biochemical data will be used from a cohort of healthy toddlers enrolled in a study on nutrient intake and cognitive development at the British Columbia Children's Hospital Research Institute. The validated novel tool will allow the characterization of the dietary intake of Canadian toddlers and the identification of nutrients associated with cognitive outcomes, with the overall goal of optimizing child development and reducing the risk of adverse long-term health outcomes.

column36: Fast I(n)Dentification of PATHogens in Neonates (FINDPATH-N): A prospective pilot study of next generation sequencing for pathogen identification in neonates with suspected sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition caused by the body's reaction to a serious infection. Sepsis is common in neonates (babies under one month of age) and is a major cause of death and disability. The current gold-standard test for sepsis in neonates is a blood culture, which incubates the blood followed by microscopy to identify which bacteria have grown. However, blood culture does not detect bacteria in many cases where doctors think that neonates actually do have sepsis. There is a need for an accurate and fast test for sepsis. Next generation sequencing (NGS) is a technique used to quickly sequence DNA. NGS can detect very small amounts of bacterial or viral DNA in a blood sample and can also provide information on which antibiotics might work through sequencing resistance genes. The bacteria do not have to be alive still, unlike blood culture. To investigate the feasibility of using NGS in neonates, we will perform a study at McMaster Children's Hospital Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. Neonates with suspected sepsis will have both a blood culture and a 0.7 mL blood sample for NGS drawn. Neonates who are already on IV antibiotics, already recently enrolled in the study or are palliative will be excluded. Medical chart review of participating neonates will record culture results, physical symptoms, lab results and antibiotic treatment. Our primary outcome is the ability to enroll neonates and successfully collect and process their blood using NGS. Additionally, the ability of NGS to detect bacteria will be compared to the gold-standard blood culture taken at the same time. This study would be an important step to investigate the potential of NGS to improve the diagnosis and treatment of sepsis in neonates.

column36: Effets de l'entrainement par intervalle a haute intensite sur les facteurs de risque de complications vasculaires du diabete de type 2
column37: Les femmes agees ayant un diabete de type 2 (DT2) sont a risque de developper des complications vasculaires (CV) telles que les maladies coronarienne et arterielle peripherique. De ces femmes agees, tres peu reussissent a realiser la quantite optimale d'exercice aerobie par semaine tel que recommande par Diabete Canada. L'entrainement par intervalle a haute intensite (HIIT) represente une strategie interessante pour cette population puisqu'il necessite peu de temps. Toutefois, comme on dispose pour l'instant que de tres peu de donnees quant aux effets de cette modalite d'entrainement sur la sante cardiovasculaire de populations a risque, le premier objectif de ce projet est d'etudier l'impact du HIIT, jumele a une diete a faible indice glycemique (DFIG), sur de multiples mecanismes moleculaires associes aux facteurs de risque de CV chez des femmes agees atteintes du DT2. Le deuxieme objectif du projet est de comparer l'impact du HIIT a celui d'un entrainement en continu a intensite moderee (EIM) sur les memes parametres. Trente-deux femmes ayant un diabete de type 2 seront divisees en deux groupes egaux : 1) DFIG combinee au HIIT; 2) DFIG combinee a l'EIM. Leur participation est d'une duree de 12 semaines et comprend 3 seances d'entrainement par semaine sur tapis roulant. Des mesures de composition corporelle, de pression arterielle sur 24h et des prelevements sanguins a jeun seront effectues avant et apres les 12 semaines d'intervention. A partir du sang preleve, divers mecanismes inflammatoires et genomiques decoulant de la fonction vasculaire seront etudies. Ce projet permettra d'explorer les bases fondamentales favorisant la comprehension de l'effet de l'entrainement par intervalle a haute intensite sur des facteurs de risque de CV liees au DT2.

column36: Are eyes more than just windows to the soul? Exploring the link between age-related macular degeneration and Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and Alzheimer's disease are both degenerative conditions primarily affecting the elderly population. One type of AMD, "wet" AMD, is characterized by an increased number of leaky blood vessels within the retina, similar to what has been reported in the brains of Alzheimer's animal models and patients. We propose that these two diseases may have similar underlying pathologies via the development of leaky vessels that result in the disruption of the tight barriers protecting the eye/brain. We will further investigate this possible link by using the Tg2576 mouse model and human retinal cell cultures to determine whether leaky vessels and inflammation link these two conditions. The purpose of these experiments is to understand the cause and progression of both conditions and whether the detection of AMD can lead to an early prognosis of Alzheimer's disease. There are currently no cures or even treatments to slow down the progression of Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's disease medications have one of the highest failure rates in clinical trials: 99.6% of drugs tested between 2000-2015 failed. It is believed that the primary reason so many drugs fail is because the medication needs to be administered before cognitive symptoms arise. If a link is discovered between AMD and Alzheimer's disease, this can lead to a new, painless and non-invasive way of diagnosing or detecting early signs of Alzheimer's by simply examining the eyes. Furthermore, it may be possible to test current AMD medications, that are already FDA-approved, as potential therapeutics for delaying the progression or preventing Alzheimer's disease. Ultimately, through our research we plan to demonstrate that the eyes are more than just windows to the soul.

column36: Relation des comportements alimentaires sur l'axe microbiome intestinal - endocannabinoidome
column37: Les bacteries constituant le microbiome intestinal contribuent a la digestion des nutriments et a la production de derives qui interagiront avec l'humain pour reguler plusieurs fonctions biologiques. Le systeme endocannabinoide est un acteur determinant du controle du metabolisme energetique, de l'appetit et de l'humeur. Ce systeme est associe a plusieurs mediateurs lipidiques qui forment l'endocannabinoidome. Le dereglement de ces systemes est implique dans des maladies metaboliques et mentales. De recentes evidences supportent l'existence d'une relation bidirectionnelle entre ces deux systemes dans l'axe microbiome intestinal-endocannabinoidome. Par ailleurs, les apports alimentaires influencent la composition, la diversite et la fonction de certaines bacteries du microbiome intestinal ainsi que le type et la quantite d'endocannabinoides produits pouvant par la suite moduler les comportements alimentaires. Cependant, les evidences scientifiques liant l'axe microbiome-endocannabinoidome aux comportements alimentaires sont tres limitees. L'objectif de ce projet est d'etablir les relations entre les comportements alimentaires et certains parametres de l'axe microbiome-endocannabinoidome. Les habitudes et comportements alimentaires ainsi que le bien-etre psychologique ont ete evalues a l'aide de questionnaires. Ce projet permettra d'obtenir une meilleure comprehension de la relation entre l'axe et les comportements alimentaires. Les resultats pourraient ouvrir la porte au developpement de recommandations alimentaires pour les individus vivant avec un trouble du comportement alimentaire.

column36: Facilitating engagement in cervical cancer screening for Indigenous women in Northern British Columbia: A qualitative analysis of community based self-collected HPV

column36: Progression of Aortic Stenosis Following Acute Myocardial Infarction
column37: Progression of Aortic Stenosis Following Acute Myocardial Infarction Aortic stenosis (AS) is a frequent degenerative disease of the valve through which blood exits the heart. In AS, the valve becomes calcified and causes obstruction to the blood flow. It is a major health burden and can lead to heart failure and death if replacement of the aortic valve is not performed timely. The factors influencing the deterioration of the stenosis are poorly known. Myocardial infarction (MI) is the death of cardiac tissue following occlusion of one of the arteries feeding the heart. MI has been shown to also cause thickening and remodeling of another cardiac valve, the mitral valve, process that can lead to valve dysfunction. It is not known if MI also affects all of the other cardiac valves. We hypothesize that MI produces similar changes in the aortic valve, which could fasten the progression of AS in the early period following the MI. To do so, we will review serial cardiac echography exams of adult patients with acute MI, compared with patients with past MI and with patients without MI. We will compare the rate of progression of the aortic valve disease in these three groups with echocardiographic markers of AS severity. We will also study the aortic valves of animal models in which an MI is induced and compare them to animals without the procedure. We will compare results of imaging studies and perform microscopic and molecular analysis of the harvested aortic valves. The protocol of our study has been approved by the research ethics committee of our institute. To our knowledge, the influence of MI in the evolution of AS has not been demonstrated. Our study could provide new prognostic and therapeutic avenues in the field of AS.

column36: The Effect of Clonal Hematopoiesis on Neutrophil Function
column37: Bone marrow stem cells work together to produce the body's red and white blood cells. In a condition called Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP), a mutant stem cell dominates blood production, generating large numbers of mutant cells. CHIP is common among older adults and one study estimated that 10% of people over 65 have CHIP. Previous studies found that CHIP increases the risk of developing leukemia or heart disease, but the mechanism through which CHIP causes these diseases is poorly understood. Studies suggest that CHIP causes macrophages, a type of white blood cell, to become highly inflammatory and this inflammation drives heart disease. However, studies have not considered the involvement of other white blood cells such as neutrophils. Neutrophils may be more important because they outnumber macrophages 6 to 1. A recent RNA-sequencing study found that CHIP may alter neutrophil function and these mutant cells may contribute to disease. This study investigates differences in the expression of neutrophil genes between individuals with and without CHIP. Blood samples were collected from healthy adults over 65 and 20 samples (15 CHIP and 5 non-CHIP) are analyzed. Differences in the amount of neutrophil gene RNA between CHIP and non-CHIP samples is compared using Quantitative Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction. The amount of neutrophil protein in CHIP and non-CHIP samples is quantified using Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays. Our study is the first to investigate the effects of CHIP on neutrophils. While current research has focused on macrophages, this study sheds light on the role of neutrophils in the disease process. The research contributes to a clearer understanding of how CHIP causes heart disease and leukemia.
