column36: Identification and Characterization of Host Proteins Hijacked by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) currently affects 37 million people worldwide and has led to over 35 million deaths. Although antiretroviral treatments (ART) can control viral replication, they cannot cure infection. As nascent virions bud through the cellular membranes of the CD4+ T cells that they infect, they can acquire cellular host proteins which become embedded in the viral envelope. Key host proteins are selectively incorporated by virions that can alter viral homing and infectivity. Integrin ?4?7 is an adhesion protein on CD4+ T cells that facilitates homing to the gut through interactions with gut-resident mucosal adhesion molecules. Virions that incorporate ?4?7 effectively hijack the homing mechanism used by T cells to migrate to the gut. This allows HIV virions to rapidly infect and deplete CD4+ T cells, as the gut is the largest reservoir for CD4+ T cells, likely leading to accelerated disease progression in HIV-infected individuals. Primate studies highlight the importance of the integrin during infection by showing that blocking ?4?7 homing with an anti-?4?7 antibody can delay disease progression and provide persistent control of viral infection, even in the absence of ART. The mechanism(s) behind these findings is unknown and is the topic of my proposal. My research aims to investigate how ?4?7 integrin becomes selectively enriched in HIV virions, with a goal of characterizing the viral determinants underpinning ?4?7 incorporation. I also plan to characterize new unidentified host proteins in the viral envelope that may also impact HIV infectivity and homing. Collectively, these findings may help identify new targets on virions that can be used for novel drug and vaccine designs, which may help reduce the burden of HIV in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Protective Effects of Akkermansia muciniphila on Intestinal Barrier Function and Inflammation
column37: The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is inhabited by trillions of microorganisms that play a crucial role in digesting food, protecting the gut from harmful bacteria and developing the immune system. These microorganisms are also implicated in various GI disorders including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). According to the Crohn's and Colitis Foundation of Canada, the prevalence of IBD in Canada is one of the highest in the world and over 270,000 Canadians deal with these lifelong conditions for which there is currently no cure. Akkermansia muciniphila is a bacterium that accounts for approximately 3% of fecal microbes and has been shown to stimulate intestinal mucus production and strengthen the GI barrier. Studies have illustrated that lower levels of A. muciniphila are associated with higher levels of inflammation suggesting that A. muciniphila may have anti-inflammatory effects. Though several studies have linked IBD to decreased levels of A. muciniphila, the precise role and mechanism of A. muciniphila in the initiation and progression of IBD is yet to be determined. Based on recent findings, we believe A. muciniphila provides protective effects on intestinal inflammation by strengthening the epithelial barrier of the gut. Thus, the aim of this research study is to investigate the role and mechanism of A. muciniphila in intestinal inflammation and its protective effects on the gut barrier. This research has the potential to enhance the understanding of the development of IBD and the role that microbes play in intestinal inflammation. In addition, this research has the potential to lead to the development of new treatments by utilizing A. muciniphila to alleviate the symptoms experienced with IBD.

column36: The Role of Streptolysin O and Streptolysin S in Streptococcus pyogenes Nasopharyngeal Infection
column37: Streptococcus pyogenes is a human-specific bacterial pathogen that contributes to the global burden of disease. Although S. pyogenes acts primarily as an asymptomatic colonizer of the upper respiratory tract and skin, it may cause mild infections such as strep throat, or more serious diseases such as flesh-eating disease and toxic shock syndrome. S. pyogenes has two toxins, streptolysin O (SLO) and streptolysin S (SLS), which promote disease progression by initiating cell death. The streptolysins have been extensively studied in mouse models of soft tissue infection; however, their role in acute nasopharyngeal infection is unknown. Preliminary data has demonstrated that SLS is a key toxin during acute nasopharyngeal infection. An SLS-deficient strain exhibited a significant reduction in nasopharyngeal colonization in mice, while an SLO-deficient strain did not exhibit reduced colonization. We hypothesize that SLS contributes to disease progression through the destruction of the mucosal membrane and by causing inflammation during nasopharyngeal infection. We will evaluate the role of SLO and SLS on tissue damage and cell death, and tissue analyses of mouse nasal passages will be done to evaluate the role of these toxins in membrane damage and inflammation. We will also assess the immune response to the bacteria, including inflammatory responses and determining the immune cell populations. Pharyngeal carriage represents the predominant state of S. pyogenes colonization, yet initial molecular strategies used by the bacteria are not well defined. Understanding the mechanism of streptolysin activity during acute nasopharyngeal infection is essential to thoroughly understand how S. pyogenes establishes infection and causes disease.

column36: Circulating and dietary saturated fatty acids and risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality in low-, middle-, and high-income countries
column37: Diet is considered a major risk factor for non-communicable disease and death. Nutritional guidelines generally encourage low consumption of saturated fats for cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention (1-2). These guidelines are based on a possible adverse effect of saturated fat on LDL cholesterol which presumably would increase risk of CVD (2-5). However, recent observational studies have challenged this framework, with saturated fat shown to have a neutral association with CVD and an inverse association with stroke and total mortality (6). Previous work was conducted mostly in high income countries, while limited information is available from low- and middle-income countries, resulting in evidence that may not be applicable to most parts of the world. A major challenge in large epidemiological studies is measurement error in estimating fatty acid intake from dietary assessment. Blood biomarkers may be more sensitive and informative to shed light on specific fatty acids that may play an important role in CVD. To address these gaps, using data from a cohort study of 225,000 individuals aged 35 to 70 years old in 25 low-, middle- and high-income countries, the PURE study, the association between circulating and dietary saturated fatty acids and CVD and mortality will be examined. By capturing broad patterns of diet globally, the PURE study is ideal for characterizing shapes of association between dietary exposures and clinical outcomes across a broad range of dietary intakes. Since PURE covers multiple world regions, the findings would be widely applicable to populations of varying levels of fat intake. This work is expected to have immediate impact and help to influence policy and public health strategies for cardiovascular prevention in Canada and around the world.

column36: The role of ICOS signalling in germinal centre T cell generation and function
column37: The immune system should be kept in balance in order to destroy bacteria and viruses without harming our own body's cells. A group of immune cells known as T follicular helper (Tfh) cells act like firefighters that extinguish "fires" (bacteria and viruses) by facilitating the generation of antibodies which work as flame retardants. However, once the threat has been eradicated, the Tfh cells need to be stopped to prevent the production of autoantibodies that are known to cause autoimmune diseases such as lupus. Therefore, the immune system is also equipped with another group of cells called T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cells, which can stop the Tfh cells' activity after an optimal number of antibodies are produced. A protein called inducible costimulator (ICOS), found on the surface of both Tfh and Tfr cells, appear to play a critical role in controlling the delicate balance between Tfh and Tfr cells. My research goal is to understand how ICOS regulates the generation and function of Tfh versus Tfr cells using genetically engineered mouse models. A better understanding of how the two kinds of cells are controlled by ICOS will help us find better ways to prevent or treat autoimmune diseases and improve vaccination strategies.

column36: Precise Pancreatic Tumour Targeting with Natural Killer Cell Mediated Immunotherapy
column37: Cancer is difficult to treat because no two cancers are the same. Current treatments are often painful and do not meet the needs of individual patients. Pancreatic cancer is hard to treat because, often, it is not detected before it has migrated to another organ. We, and others, are finding that the immune system can be recruited to fight cancer and we are trying to figure out how best to use one type of cell, called the natural killer (NK) cell, to fight pancreatic cancer. NK cells can identify and kill cancer cells by measuring markers that label cells as healthy or not. However, because cancer cells are damaged versions of our own cells they can trick the NK cells into seeing them as healthy. The markers that cells use to communicate with NK cells are decided by a person's genes and not everyone's NK cells recognize all of the same markers. An NK cell will not kill another cell if it displays a marker that signals stop, but we can use NK cells from healthy people with different signs for stop to treat patients with cancer. In my studies, we will test pancreatic cancer cells to see which markers they are using to trick the NK cells. We can then identify the NK cells that with likely fail to recognize a specific stop marker, but still recognize a cancer's go signals, and use them to kill cancer cells. To understand if this may work in patients, we will test our system using a mouse model that we designed to mimic the human immune system. By showing that NK cells can be used to precisely target individual patient's tumours, future work can focus on creating treatment plans that meet the needs of each patient and can target that patient's specific tumour profile.

column36: The Role of Lysosomal Acid Lipase in Atherosclerotic Lesion Smooth Muscle Cells
column37: BACKGROUND: Heart attack and stroke together are the leading cause of death in Canada and the world. They result from atherosclerosis, or hardening of the arteries, a disease in which cholesterol builds up in artery walls. This causes arteries to become inflamed and blocked. Our team discovered that smooth muscle cells (SMCs), a type of cell in the artery wall, have low levels of a protein called Lysosomal Acid Lipase (LAL) that is important for processing and expelling excess cholesterol. We therefore believe that SMCs are resistant to expelling cholesterol, and that this contributes to atherosclerosis even when blood cholesterol is lowered by diet and medications. Because more than half the cells in hardened artery walls are SMCs, developing strategies to release their cholesterol may be very effective in treating atherosclerosis. GOAL: Previously, we showed that giving LAL to human SMCs in a dish increases their cholesterol export. The goal of my project is to test if increasing the amount of LAL in mouse SMCs in a dish will also increase cholesterol export. APPROACH: First, I will confirm that mouse SMCs, like human SMCs, have low LAL, by measuring LAL levels in aortic arches (a common site of artery hardening) from mice that have atherosclerosis. Second, I will increase the amount of LAL in mouse SMCs in a dish using a gene manipulation technique. Third, I will determine if this increase in LAL causes an increase in cholesterol export from the SMCs. OUTCOMES: I expect that mouse SMCs in the aortic arch will have low levels of LAL, and that mouse SMCs, like human SMCs, will release more cholesterol when LAL levels are increased. These results would support studying the effect of increasing LAL in SMCs in live mice on treating and preventing atherosclerosis.

column36: Validation of a new measure of abdominal pain severity in irritable bowel syndrome
column37: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is characterized by abdominal pain and alterations in bowel habit. Chronic recurrent abdominal pain is required to make the diagnosis and is often the driver of symptom severity and functional impairment in patients. Due to this, improvement in abdominal pain is required by regulatory bodies when assessing new medications to treat IBS. However, the optimal method to measure abdominal pain in IBS is unclear. Currently, a scale from one to eleven is used to describe the intensity of abdominal pain. This, however, only measures one aspect of chronic pain (intensity) and excludes other pain dimensions such as frequency, constancy, predictability and the effect on a patient's daily function or quality of life. Other tools that have been designed to measure symptom severity in IBS measure global IBS symptom severity including alterations in bowel habit, bloating and distension in addition to abdominal pain and, thus, are limited in their assessment of abdominal pain specifically. Given that improvement in abdominal pain is an important outcome in patients with IBS, a tool that focuses specifically on abdominal pain and its impact on daily function is necessary. The Brief Pain Inventory is a questionnaire that was designed to assess cancer pain. It measures both pain intensity as well the effect of pain on daily function. It is short and simple to complete. It has been tested in various populations since its development but has not been adapted or tested in the IBS patient population. This thesis project will adapt and test the Brief Pain Inventory to measure abdominal pain in patients with IBS. This will likely have implications for both the evaluation of new treatments in IBS and clinical practice.

column36: Effectiveness of Peer Support Groups for Adults with Medical Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
column37: Peer support services are services that bring non-professionals with similar health problems together for the purpose of providing mutual support or to establish a relationship in which a more experienced peer can deliver support to a newly diagnosed or novice peer. Peer support groups for people with medical illness provide individuals the opportunity to reduce feelings of isolation, share practical health information related to their disease, and to give and receive emotional support. Although it has been hypothesized that peer support interventions may improve health outcomes, the effectiveness of peer support interventions is not well-established. Published reviews are outdated, focus on a single disease, include various forms of peer support, or are of poor methodological quality. The proposed study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effectiveness of peer support groups among adults with medical illness. Specifically, the review will determine if peer support groups are effective for improving physical and psychological health outcomes, including self-efficacy and perceived ability to cope (1) compared to inactive controls (e.g., usual care) and (2) compared to standard psychological interventions (e.g., psychotherapy groups). If found to be effective, the conclusions drawn from this systematic review, once disseminated to healthcare providers and researchers, have the potential to positively impact individuals with medical illness who do not have regular access to affordable support services and, if found to be an effective adjunct intervention, to improve care among those who do.

column36: Novel therapeutic approaches targeting the development of medulloblastoma
column37: TThe most frequent solid pediatric cancer is medulloblastoma, a brain tumour. The prognostic of this cancer is very variable depending on its specific subtype. Approximately 30% of medulloblastomas are of the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) subtype, which leads to a limited prognosis. The actual treatment available to these children includes surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. They offer a limited efficacy, and cause serious adverse effects including permanent cognitive decline caused by radiotherapy. In the last years, researchers began to better understand the molecular underpinnings of this disease. Our research project objective is to better characterize specific molecular mechanisms of SHH medulloblastoma, and develop a targeted treatment designed to increase patients' survival while decreasing the adverse effects of the currently available treatments. Our project will specifically target the mechanisms by which the activation of the SHH pathway leads to DNA damage. This research will be done using in vitro assays and in vivo animal experimentation on mice. If the efficacy of the tested treatment is confirmed, it may lead to its testing in a clinical research protocol.

column36: Prostate Specific Antigen Dynamics and Prostate Cancer Risk: A Population-Based Study
column37: Prostate cancer will affect one in seven Canadian men. Prostate cancer can be detected early using a screening blood test, called prostate specific antigen (PSA). While PSA is almost always increased in men with prostate cancer, other conditions can also increase the PSA. This can lead to unnecessary biopsies and has caused debate about the usefulness of PSA as a screening tool. Newer tools, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are beginning to be used with the PSA blood test to determine when the risk of cancer is highest and when a prostate biopsy is needed. However, the benefits of these tests are still undetermined, and their high cost limits their use. Given the debate around PSA screening, it is important to find a new way to interpret the PSA that will better identify men at the highest risk of having prostate cancer. The Ontario Laboratory Information System contains more than one million PSA results for tens of thousands of men in Ontario. This system has been recently linked to large cancer-specific population datasets. This linkage provides the unique opportunity to study PSA change and prostate cancer risk among men in a real-world setting. I will develop a model to determine when to complete a prostate biopsy based on patient characteristics, PSA level, number of prior PSA tests and PSA change over time. This can be achieved at no additional cost to the health care system and at no additional cost or inconvenience to the patient. This project will result in better identification of high-risk patients and has the potential to transform prostate cancer screening.

column36: Role of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2) in group 2 innate lymphoid cell (ILC2) function
column37: The immune system is complex and multi-layered but can be divided into two major types of host responses: innate and adaptive. The innate response is rapid but non-specific; for example, it quickly and non-specifically clears bacteria from wounds. The adaptive response develops more slowly, but mounts a much stronger, pathogen-specific response that develops into immunological memory. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2) serve as messengers between these two major arms of the immune system, responding to innate signals and activating the adaptive response. ILC2 are an essential part of type 2 immunity, which evolved as a tissue restorative response to infections at mucosal barrier sites, such as the lung and the gut. However, when this response is dysregulated, it can lead to immunopathologies such as allergies and asthma. Thus, studying its regulation is critical to discover novel therapies to treat these diseases, and ILC2 are promising therapeutic targets. Nevertheless, many mechanisms governing their regulation remain largely unknown. Unpublished research in our laboratory has revealed that activation of ILC2 leads to a strong induction of an enzyme involved lipid metabolism, diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2 (Dgat2). This enzyme catalyzes the formation of fat within a cell, which is then stored in lipid droplets as an energy reservoir, preventing toxic accumulation of free fatty acids. Therefore, we hypothesize that higher levels of Dgat2 allow activated ILC2 to take up high levels of fatty acids for storage without any toxic effects. Elucidating the role of Dgat2 and lipid metabolism in ILC2 will contribute to understanding their poorly characterized metabolic requirements and will lead to novel drug targets to alter ILC2 functions in type 2 immunopathologies.

column36: La relation entre le microbiote intestinal, la fuite anastomotique en chirurgie colorectale et le comportement du cancer du colon et du rectum.
column37: Le role du microbiote semble bien etabli dans plusieurs pathologies tels le diabete et l'obesite. Des etudes recentes suggerent que le microbiote est implique dans la guerison tissulaire et la carcinogenese. La fuite anastomotique est une complication majeure en chirurgie digestive. Elle augmente la morbidite et affecte negativement le pronostic du cancer colorectal. Elle est imprevisible et survient chez 5 a 15% des patients en chirurgie colorectale. Les antibiotiques oraux preoperatoires semble d'apres quelques etudes cliniques recentes diminuer la fuite anastomotique, et un effet potentiel sur le microbiome est souleve comme mecanisme d'action. Une question se pose ainsi sur la potentielle relation entre la signature microbienne chez un individu et le risque de developper une fuite anastomotique apres une resection intestinale. L'identification d'une dysbiose pouvant mener a cette complication ouvrirait la voie a des approches ciblees permettant de corriger ce desequilibre, du moins transitoirement, avant une intervention chirurgicale afin de prevenir la fuite et ameliorer le pronostic du cancer colorectal opere. L'etude vise a evaluer la correlation entre le microbiote pre-/per-/post-operatoire et le risque de fuite anastomotique. De plus, on evaluera la correlation entre le microbiote et l'evolution du cancer colorectal apres une resection, ou apres un traitement neoadjuvant de chimioradiotherapie avec reponse pathologique complete. Un volet d'experimentation animale avec interventions ciblees (probiotiques et antibiotiques) suivra. L'effet de telles interventions sur le microbiote et sur les issues cliniques sera evalue chez un modele de rongeur apres une anastomose colorectale et une transplantation fecale de selles provenant de patients du volet clinique.

column36: Prenatal and Postnatal Care for Refugees in Ontario
column37: As the world responds to a global refugee crisis, countries face the challenge of providing effective health care to displaced populations. Canada has a unique refugee program which has been the subject of international interest and ranks in the top five countries for resettling refugees. In Canada, Government Assisted Refugees (GARs) receive supportive resettlement services from professional case workers whereas private citizens are responsible for the settlement needs of Private Sponsored Refugees (PSRs). Non-sponsored refugees such as asylum seekers have no pre-organized sponsor support or resettlement services. Most refugees resettle in Ontario, where certain types of primary care models target the needs of newcomers. The objective of our study is to determine the effect of resettlement category on the provision of adequate prenatal and early postnatal care to pregnant refugees in Ontario. We will include all refugee women who arrived in Ontario from 2008-2017, and were pregnant within 3 years of resettlement. Our analysis will use Ontario administrative databases that link health (hospital and primary care), demographic, and refugee data. Our findings will be contextualized by comparing results for refugees with non-refugee immigrants, and urban long-term residents. We will also adjust for primary care affiliation and demographic characteristics. Through this well-powered analysis, we will determine whether resettlement category influences the provision of adequate prenatal and postnatal care. We will also be able to determine if women affiliated with certain models of primary care are more likely to receive adequate care. Our findings are timely and generalizable, and therefore can be used to improve the health for women at the national and international level.

column36: Generating a comprehensive human miRNA expression atlas to advance miRNA-guided diagnostics
column37: Diagnosis of diseases, including cancers and rare diseases, is a medical challenge. Small molecules in the blood or within tissues can be indicators, or biomarkers, of disease and can improve diagnosis. In my proposal, I focus on a class of genetic control molecules termed microRNAs. These molecules are excellent markers of health and disease because they have distinct patterns in all normal and diseased cells. These molecules are also useful to study because they are present in all tissues, cells, and body fluids. The goal of my research is to create a large database of miRNAs to identify possible biomarkers. I will first increase our knowledge of microRNA expression in healthy and diseased tissues and cells. Then, I will apply computational approaches to identify miRNA biomarkers of normal tissue, cancers and rare diseases. Through this research, I expect to improve resources available for diagnostic research, identify new biomarkers, and ultimately improve the accuracy of diagnostic methods.

column37: CRISPR-Cas9 targeting of secretory pathway furin in human cells: Insights into the biological roles of furin in the flaviviral lifecycle. There is currently a lack of therapeutic options to treat neurotropic viral diseases caused by flaviviruses like Dengue (DENV) and Zika (ZIKV) viruses. These human envelope viruses are known to exploit host-cell pathways and use host factors in cellular events vital to the viral life cycle. To develop new therapeutic methods to combat these neurotropic flaviviruses, we aim to validate novel host factors, such as intracellular enzyme furin, that are critical elements involved in the viral lifecycle and could be potential drug targets. To accomplish our objective, CRISPR-mediated gene editing has been successfully performed to knock out selected host factors in human glioma cell lines, creating 2D cell cultures and human pluripotent stem cell-derived 3D brain organoid systems that can used to model viral infection. The resultant cell toxicity and antiviral effects associated with the knockout will be analyzed with colorimetric MTT and virological assays to determine common host factors that could potentially be targeted by indirect-acting antiviral agents (IAAs) as viral infection treatment. This project would provide significant molecular and mechanistic insight into viral manipulation of host-cell pathways, which would further the development of new IAA strategies to combat neurotropic viral diseases.

column36: Canadian Study of Arterial Inflammation in Diabetes and the Evaluation of Canakinumab Effectiveness (CADENCE)
column37: Diabetic patients are at very high risk of suffering premature atherosclerotic disease related events (eg acute coronary syndromes (ACS), stroke, transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)) and have a higher recurrence rate than the general population. Inflammation has been extensively investigated as a promoter of atherosclerosis development and destabilization. Very recently the CANTOS trial demonstrated that therapy focused at blocking the inflammatory cascade reduced recurrent events in patients with prior acute coronary syndromes. Canakinumab treatment was particularly effective in patients who achieved a significant hsCRP reduction, but was associated with a significant increase in fatal sepsis, with no impact on de-novo diabetes mellitus or worsening of diabetes control. This is important since approximately 40% of the patients enrolled in the CANTOS trial were patients with diabetes. The results from CANTOS raise an intriguing question of how to identify the patients who will benefit the most from this innovative therapy. Investigators in the field of imaging have been investigating means to identify patients at greater risk of suffering events who would benefit from specific therapeutic interventions. Simultaneous blood biomarker analysis can provide potential screening candidates calibrated to the response on the 18FDG scan to facilitate future screening of patients suitable for evaluation.

column36: At-home dog therapy for community-dwelling individuals with dementia
column37: It is estimated that over half a million Canadians currently live with dementia and this number is expected to increase by 66 percent by 2031 (Chambers, Bancej, & McDowell, 2016). Individuals with dementia and their caregivers need access to effective interventions that improve their well-being and quality of life. People with dementia often feel socially isolated and lonely (Poey, Burr, & Roberts, 2017). Increasing their socialization has been found to decrease stress and improve mood (Cheung et al., 2018; Gongora et al., 2018). Our research lab held a patient-advisory meeting for individuals with dementia and their caregivers from Saskatchewan. This advisory committee expressed a need for more accessible socialization support such as a dog-therapy intervention that occurs in their own home. Care homes and community centres have provided pet therapy for people with dementia and found that it has a positive impact on mood, social behaviour, motivation and quality of life (Filan & Llewellyn-Jones, 2006; Mossello et al., 2011; Peluso et al., 2018; Wood et al., 2017). However, a pet-therapy intervention has not been developed for at-home delivery. This study aims to determine whether an at-home dog therapy intervention is practical, achievable and sustainable for people living with dementia in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Improving support and quality of life for community-dwelling individuals with dementia is essential if Canada wants to shift away from acute service delivery care and promote home or community-based care for this population.

column36: The Role of Personal Responsibility in Mental Contamination in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
column37: Mental contamination (MC) refers to feelings of dirtiness or contamination that are experienced in the absence of any physical contaminant. This feeling is often brought on by thoughts or memories of immoral acts, betrayal, and/or shame, and is common in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Researchers have found that when people are told to think about immoral situations (either hypothetical, or real events from their past), they tend to experience feelings of dirtiness, and are more likely to wash themselves to alleviate such feelings. Victims of sexual assault have also been found to experience MC, and it has been induced in experimental studies in which people listened to a recording of a non-consensual kiss and imagined being the victim or the perpetrator. While past studies have found certain factors to be associated with the severity of MC that people experience (i.e. participants' perception of personal responsibility, violation, and immorality), we still do not know the mechanisms through which this relationship functions. In the present study, we aim to understand the role that perception of personal responsibility plays on the degree of MC a person feels after being told to imagine that they are the protagonist in a sexual harassment recording. A better understanding of the mechanisms underlying MC will help to inform therapeutic interventions aimed at reducing MC in individuals with OCD or post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from sexual trauma.

column37: La preeclampsie et la restriction de croissance intra-uterine (RCIU) sont des complications de la grossesse qui surviennent chez 5% et 10% des femmes enceintes respectivement. Elles constituent, avec le travail premature, les Grands Syndromes Obstetricaux qui sont les principales causes de morbidite et mortalite perinatales. Au cours des dernieres annees, de nombreux marqueurs sanguins et echographiques ont ete developpes pour identifier precocement ces Syndromes, et plus particulierement la preeclampsie et la RCIU. De plus, il existe maintenant des mesures preventives pour prevenir ces complications, dont l'aspirine, et pour limiter leurs impacts sur la sante des nouveaux-nes. Mon projet de maitrise evalue nombreux marqueurs dans une population quebecoise de femmes enceintes et permettra de mieux cibler les marqueurs a privilegier dans notre population. Ultimement, mon projet pourrait permettre d'offrir des outils aux cliniciens et aux femmes enceintes afin de prevenir les consequences de la preeclampsie et de la RCIU sur la sante des enfants a naitre.

column36: Targeting Spliced X-Box Binding Protein 1 in Alternatively Activated Macrophages to prevent progression of lung fibrosis
column37: Fibroproliferative diseases, or diseases involving organ scarring and hardening, are associated with approximately 45% of deaths worldwide. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a lung disease of unknown cause that leads to excessive scarring of the lungs. This causes compromised uptake of oxygen and decreased lung function. The median survival of patients with IPF after diagnosis is 2.5 to 3.5 years. Despite this short amount of time, this disease is poorly understood and there are limited treatment options. Therefore, it is important to better understand what causes this disease, and what can be done to investigate additional therapies. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress has been shown to play a role in fibrotic disease. The ER is a part of the cell where proteins are made and folded, and is also the quality control centre to ensure that proteins are folded correctly. When ER stress occurs, causing a build-up of unfolded or misfolded proteins, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated, which aims to help fix or destroy the faulty proteins. There are three main pathways of the UPR, and the one being investigated here is called the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1) pathway. When IRE1 is activated, a protein called spliced x-box protein 1 (XBP1) is present. The IRE1 pathway and spliced XBP1 will be explored to determine if they play a key role in IPF, and if blocking this pathway can help to prevent the worsening of the disease. Inhibitors, or blockers, of the IRE1 pathway will be given to mouse models of pulmonary fibrosis, and the levels of spliced XBP1 as well as effects on fibrosis will then be studied through various techniques. The results of this study will help to determine if targeting this pathway could be a potential route of treatment for IPF.

column36: Role of Calmodulin in KCNQ1-KCNE1 Channel Gating
column37: In this study we will examine a channel protein that conducts potassium called KCNQ1. This channel protein is known to combine with other subunit proteins that greatly affect the behavior of the channel protein. Together the channel and subunit protein complex has been shown to play a vital role in restoring resting activity in cardiac cells. Mutations in both the channel and subunit proteins have all been linked to life-threatening cardiovascular rhythm diseases however, we still do not fully understand how the different proteins function together to cause disease. Our overarching objective is thus to gain a better understanding of the relationship between KCNQ1 and its subunit proteins. The work will entail using different mutant versions of the human subunit protein, calmodulin, and studying the functional effects each mutant has on the behavior of the channel protein in a cell-based system using whole-cell patch clamp. Whole-cell patch clamp involves using a small glass electrode to stimulate and record the resulting electrical activity of a cell. In 2017, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to three scientists for developing cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Cryo-EM involves firing an electron beam onto a frozen protein sample. The subsequent scattering of these electrons after they come into contact with the frozen protein is detected and used to determine the structure of proteins. Using this novel method, we aim to examine on a near atomic level specifically where and how subunit proteins interact with the channel protein. From this work we expect to obtain completely new information about the interactive relationships between these proteins, which will help us to understand how they contribute to cardiovascular diseases.

column36: The Relation Between Narrative Coherence and Repetitive Negative Thinking
column37: Telling a coherent story about a life event reflects individuals' abilities to understand and organize their experiences, as well as the thoughts and feelings they have come to connect with them. Several benefits are associated with possessing this ability, including mental well-being. It is possible that having difficulty telling a coherent story about a past event is related to experiencing the repetitive negative thoughts that characterize many psychological disorders. The proposed study aims to determine whether this relation indeed exists, and, if so, to identify the mechanisms that underlie it. Participants will be asked to tell two different stories, one about a positive event in their lives and one about a negative event, which will be analyzed for structure, content, and the inclusion of interpretations about thoughts and feelings. Questionnaires will also be completed to indicate participants' tendencies to experience repetitive negative thoughts. Understanding the relation between the ability to tell coherent life stories and the experience of repetitive negative thoughts has implications for the prevention and treatment of various psychological disorders. Research in this area could also inform therapies that focus on changing negative thought patterns in affected populations.

column36: Seeing Clearly: A Decision Analysis of MRI and Biomarkers in Prostate Cancer
column37: Seeing Clearly: A Decision Analysis of MRI and Biomarkers in Prostate Cancer Prostate cancer is the most common cancer amongst men in Canada affecting 1 in 7 individuals. MRI and biomarkers have revolutionized the approach to early stage prostate cancer detection, identifying prostate pathology in a clinically useful and reliable manner. Given the prevalence of prostate cancer, these findings are remarkably impactful to early stage and active surveillance patients. In particular, when MRI and biomarkers are used in combination, studies have reported an excellent ability to discriminate patients who do not harbour clinically significant disease from those who do. This avoids potential overtreatment in low risk individuals while properly risk stratifying high risk patients. However, choosing wisely is necessary in a resource limited setting like Canada. Both biomarker testing and MRI are expensive and not widely available. Their relation to and unintended consequences on other services will require infrastructure investment, funding reprioritization, and wait time assessments prior to widespread adoption. To date, no decision analyses have evaluated the effect of MRI and biomarkers on our healthcare system. Methods: We will create a decision analysis model to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of incorporating MRI and biomarker testing in primary prostate cancer detection, compared to standard of care, for the detection of clinically significant PCa, avoidance of clinically insignificant PCa, and biopsies saved. Our model will stratify clinically effective and cost effective approaches across a wide variety of patient, physician, and societal scenarios to inform broad-based policy decisions as well as individualized patient-level decisions.

column36: The interneuron AVG modulates the activity of downstream circuit components underlying forward movement in Caenorhabditis elegans
column37: Humans and many other multicellular organisms rely on nervous systems to enact complex behaviours in response to their environment, including locomotion. The functional units of the nervous system are neurons and they are arranged into networks known as neural circuits. Use of the model system Caenorhabditis elegans, a transparent worm that grows to about 1 mm in length, affords an excellent approach to understanding such neural circuits involved in locomotion due, in part, to its well-characterized biology. Furthermore, the adult worm possesses only about 300 neurons, contrasted with the billions of neurons constituting the human nervous system. C. elegans is thus amenable as a model for study. Many of the neurons involved in locomotion in C. elegans have been previously well-established but our present understanding of this behaviour remains incomplete. The current study will employ genetic, analytical and sophisticated imaging tools to understand one such uncharacterized neuron, AVG, its role in forward body movement, the biological mechanisms by which it acts and its connectivity to other neurons with well-established locomotive roles. Ultimately, this study will bring us closer to a holistic understanding of the C. elegans nervous system and locomotion. Despite its numerically small nervous system, the density of connections among neurons and their associated multifunctionalities in C. elegans presents analogies with the nervous systems of higher organisms, including humans. Finally, the conservation of key biological mechanisms implies that the fundamental biological insights gleaned from the current study of C. elegans locomotion will ultimately prove invaluable in deconvoluting the human nervous system and its associated neurological diseases.

column36: Effect of length of storage of transfused red blood cell units on the risk for hospital-acquired infections in the critical care setting
column37: Infections acquired during a hospital stay are an important health problem. This is especially true for severely ill patients admitted to intensive care units, who are at a higher risk of dying from such infections. It is thought that blood transfusions could increase the risk for hospital-acquired infections. This might be especially true if the blood transfused is fresh, i.e., had been recently donated, because fresh blood has a higher number of live and functional cells that modulate our capacity to fight infections. These cells can interact with the transfusion recipient’s immunologic system and lead to the suppression of his/her defences, thereby increasing the risk for hospital-acquired infections. However, this hypothesis still needs to be proved. To do so, we will use mathematical models to pool the data from studies that investigated the effect of age of transfused blood on severely ill patients to determine if the transfusion of fresh blood actually leads to more hospital-acquired infections. We have built a team of experts in blood transfusions, infection control, and statistics to ensure the success of this study. Answering this question is essential because, if we show that transfusion of fresh blood leads to more hospital-acquired infections, we can modify blood transfusion protocols for severely ill patients to transfuse blood that has not been freshly donated. This will lead to a decrease in these patients’ risk of acquiring infections during their hospital stay and improve their chances of survival.

column36: The Built Environment and Bicycling Safety in Children
column37: Traffic is one of the leading causes of injury and death in Canadian children. Collisions involving vehicles and child bicyclists contribute significantly to these injuries and are a cause for concern for the safety of children. While bicycling and other forms of active transportation improve the physical and mental health of children, there is a decline in participation in part due to the safety concerns of traffic related injury. Child bicyclists experience and interact with traffic and traffic infrastructure differently than adults, which can increase risk of injury. Strategies to prevent these injuries must continue to be explored by both government and non-government organizations across municipalities. By examining the traffic infrastructure/built environment and its link to injury risk in child bicyclists throughout Canada, we can make built environment changes to increase child bicycling safety. This study uses a case-crossover design were participants are their own comparisons by looking at the location they were injured at, to two other locations on their route where they were not injured (i.e., control locations). We will examine child bicyclist injuries and the built environment through child interviews and site observations. Using this approach will allow us to identify the built environment features that influence child bicyclist safety.

column36: Interactions Between Human ADAR1 and PACT and their Pro-viral Role in the Pathology of Human Immunodeficiency Virus
column37: Upon its entry in the cell, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is restricted through innate immunity, mediated in part by cytokines, including interferons (IFN). Contrary to the antiviral roles of most human IFN Stimulated Genes (ISGs), a discrete number of ISGs have been shown to have net proviral effects in cells affected by HIV. Dr. Gatignol's lab has spent years elucidating the mechanisms by which a number of these paradoxically proviral ISGs help in viral replication or in dampening the host immune response. In this project, we are looking to better understand how adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1 - an RNA-editing ISG) interacts with binding partners Protein Kinase R (PKR) and PKR activator (PACT) during HIV infection to reverse their antiviral roles. We will pursue the elucidation of ADAR1's function by studying its interaction with PACT and by functional assays in HIV infected lymphocytic cells.

column36: Continuity of Care for Seniors
column37: Many seniors experience a lack of continuity of care due to difficulties with memory, reliance on informal caregivers, frailty, and difficulties scheduling appointments, for example. As health challenges increase, seniors may be relocated to long-term care; however, in this setting they still experience fragmented care as they rely on multiple providers who face strict time constraints and a stressful work environment. Innovative research emphasizes the importance of 'patient-centred care' in a long-term care setting. Goal-oriented care, an approach that focuses on a patient's individual health goals, is a potential solution to achieving patient-centered care. However, its effects on care continuity have yet to be explored. The objective of this mixed methods research study is to describe continuity of care within a centre which uses a goal-oriented care approach and to determine factors (such as age, sex and health status) influencing continuity of care in this setting. The research setting is a 450-bed community health long-term care centre in Ottawa, Ontario. The quantitative component will use a validated questionnaire to assess the continuity of care in 200 randomly sampled participants. The qualitative component will use semi-structured interviews to investigate factors influencing perceived continuity of care. Goal-oriented care may positively impact the continuity of care experienced by seniors, supporting better patient outcomes in long-term care settings. This new knowledge will impact the development and improvement of continuity of care for Canadian seniors within long-term care facilities.

column36: Outcomes following surgical management of endometriosis: A prospective cohort
column37: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory process where endometrial tissue is found outside the uterus. Associated with pelvic pain and infertility, the condition has significant impacts on quality of life, productivity, and healthcare costs. Though endometriosis is diagnosed by laparoscopy, surgery is reserved for those who have failed first line treatment. Surgical options include conservative management with destruction or cutting of endometriosis lesions and definitive surgery with removal of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and/or ovaries. There is a lack of studies examining surgical outcomes at an interdisciplinary centre. Our research aims to address these deficits in a two part-study. The first part will evaluate the impact on surgery on pelvic pain at the interdisciplinary BC Women's Centre for Pelvic Pain and Endometriosis. Specifically, we will examine the influence of the following factors: (1) stage of endometriosis, (2) definitive vs. conservative surgery, (3) diagnosis of endometriosis vs. no endometriosis, and (4) definitive surgery in those under age 35 vs. over age 35. In the second part, we will examine the literature for the impact of removing the ovaries on pelvic pain in the context of both conservative and definitive surgery. For the first part, we will evaluate a prospective cohort of patients undergoing surgery at our interdisciplinary centre in British Columbia, Canada from December 2013 to December 2017. Data collected will be entered into an online Research Electronic Data Capture database. We will analyze our variables of interest and its influence on pelvic pain using SPSS software. For the second part, we will complete a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the impact of removing the ovaries on pelvic pain and recurrence rates.

column36: Characterizing selective pressures shaping stem cell evolution and health outcomes
column37: The hematopoietic system is a highly regenerative system derived from a population of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Owing to their ability to self-renew and maintain the mature blood cell pool, HSC populations have to be highly regulated. A common mechanisms of dysregulation is the accumulation of somatic mutations as a function of aging that results in a subset of HSCs contributing disproportionately more to the mature blood cell pool; a process termed Age-Related Clonal Hematopoiesis (ARCH). ARCH has largely been studied in populations of European descent where it has been found to exist as a latent, pre-disease state for some cancers and cardiovascular disease but little is known about ARCH and disease outcomes in other population groups. Further, the evolutionary parameters driving stem cell populations towards ARCH and disease states remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we draw from classic evolutionary theory to develop population genetic models to characterize the impact of mutation on somatic and stem cell evolution in three population groups. We will use genomic datasets from Europe, Africa and Canada to estimate parameters impacting mutation accumulation such as mutation rate and strength of selection. These will be used to develop statistical models of stem cell evolution to study the interaction effects of different mutation classes in clonal mitotic systems. These models will enable a robust assessment of the net selective environment contribution to stem cell evolution through capturing the interaction of beneficial and deleterious selection and resultant disease outcomes. An improved understanding of the evolutionary context underscoring stem cell dynamics will establish a framework for understanding aging and the early stages of disease development.

column36: Spatial Navigation Intervention for patients with moderate-severe TBI
column37: Memory impairments associated with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (m-sTBI) can be persistent and life-altering, particularly for individuals living in rural and remote areas of Northern Ontario. The hippocampus is a critical brain structure for memory and is negatively affected in m-sTBI. Unfortunately, not only does the hippocampus sustain damage at the time of injury, but it has been found to continue to atrophy in the months and years after injury. Encouragingly, there is a promising opportunity to help patients prevent this shrinkage and improve memory function. It entails continuously and intensively navigating around cities, creating mental maps of novel routes and key landmarks through an allocentric or bird's eye view approach. Based on past research, we have developed an intervention in which people engage in these activities using an online Google Street View interface for an hour, 5 days a week, for 4 months, with various rewards along the way to make it more fun. The intervention requires minimal therapist involvement and is accessible from the comfort of one's home computer. In the proposed study, I am to evaluate the benefits of this intervention for improving memory and brain function, and determine the shortest optimal length of the intervention. Fifty m-sTBI patients from Northern Ontario will complete either the spatial navigation intervention (treatment group) or watch TedTalk videos (control group) for the same duration. Groups will be compared in their memory improvements before, part-way through (12 weeks) or after the intervention. Ultimately, if effective, our treatment will be the first of its kind to help m-sTBI patients across Ontario regardless of where they live, their physical mobility restrictions or financial status.

column36: Caracterisation des petites molecules anti-inflammatoires pour l'etude de l'inflammation intra-uterine
column37: Les macrophages uterins sont exceptionnels dans leur capacite a proteger la muqueuse uterine des infections tout en supportant l'implantation d'un embryon. Il est propose que la fonction des macrophages au site d'implantation est adaptee a chaque stade de la grossesse pour etablir des environnements inflammatoires distincts. En consequence, les periodes de peri-implantation et d'accouchement sont associees a une reponse pro-inflammatoire alors qu'un environnement anti-inflammatoire est requis pour le maintien de la grossesse. Toutefois, une activation indument prolongee ou prematuree des macrophages serait associee avec un dommage tissulaire intra-uterin causant une mort embryonnaire precoce. Cette perte de regulation des macrophages serait attribuee a une surproduction des facteurs de stress inflammatoire. L'objectif general du projet est de mieux documenter les mecanismes de regulation de la reponse inflammatoire a l'interface des systemes immun et reproducteur afin d'ameliorer la sante reproductive chez les mammiferes en general et les humains en particulier. La caracterisation et l'utilisation des molecules anti-inflammatoires est donc actuellement proposee pour prevenir l'inflammation intra-uterine au cours de la gestation. Nos laboratoires ont recemment caracterise plusieurs petites molecules capables d'inhiber efficacement les principales voies de signalisation pro-inflammatoires. Ainsi, le projet du candidat visera tout d'abord a etudier l'activite anti-inflammatoire de ces petites molecules dans un modele animal d'inflammation aigue. Ensuite, le potentiel regulateur de ces molecules sera evalue lors du processus de desactivation des macrophages pro-inflammatoires a l'aide d'analyses biochimiques, immunologiques et genetiques.

column36: Gender Differences in the Association between Dementia with Lewy Bodies and Attention-deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
column37: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), a neurodevelopmental disorder, and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), a neurodegenerative disorder, have been often associated with one another in previous literature. Both disorders are primarily diagnosed in males, with previous literature demonstrating that both disorders separately may have a gendered presentation. However, there is a gap in the research literature investigating the effects of gender on the association between the two disorders. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the effects of gender on adults diagnosed with DLB who also have a characteristically high level of ADHD traits. Both male and female participants will be recruited from the Movement Disorders Clinic and the Cognitive Neurosciences Clinic. The presentation of ADHD traits will be determined using the Connor's Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS). Memory, language and executive function will be measured through the utilization of a full neuropsychological test library. column36: Capturing Murine Gut Microbes to Improve Mouse Models of Disease
column37: The gut microbiota is the community of microorganisms found within the gastrointestinal tract and harbours the largest number of bacteria in the human body. These microbes influence a number of diseases, ranging from gastrointestinal to neurodevelopmental disorders. In order to study these diseases many scientists use mice. Recently, inconsistencies in these mouse models has been attributed to differences in the microbiota due to differences in providers, facilities, and housing conditions (e.g. bedding and diet). Moreover, due to the complexity and variability of the gut microbiota many causative links between microbes and disease remain to be identified. Thus, future mouse studies should use mice with known and defined gut microbial communities. However, this approach is limited by the current lack of isolated and characterized mouse-associated microbes. Current attempts at isolating gut microbes are focused on obtaining monoisolates, which are populations of bacteria consisting of a single species. Despite these efforts, many microbes continue to resist attempts at isolation, several of which appear to play important roles in health and disease. I hypothesize that some bacteria from the mouse gut are functionally codependent on other microbes and therefore cannot be obtained in monoisolation. Thus, I propose to isolate the missing microbes in communities with other bacteria, rather than independently, and through this process I will identify codependent bacterial relationships. My contributions to the gut microbial collection will enable the establishment of defined microbial communities. This approach will ultimately allow the standardization of murine gut microbiota and consequently, will improve accuracy of mouse models of human disease.

column36: Characterization of the EchA20 catalyzed ring cleavage during Cholesterol Catabolism in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
column37: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the bacterium responsible for the fatal lung disease tuberculosis, infects one third of the world's population and causes over 1.5 million deaths annually. The increasing prevalence of drug-resistant strains intensifies the need for novel and more effective treatments. Targeting physiological traits specific to Mtb are ideal for developing therapies, as it minimizes the possibility of harming beneficial bacteria or human cells. One such trait is the complete degradation of cholesterol into small molecular building-blocks to be utilized in growth and virulence. This is a characteristic unique to only a select few bacterial species. As cholesterol is found in significant quantities within human cells walls, it is crucial for Mtb survival. Interestingly, upon of elimination of EchA20, a protein involved in this degradation pathway, cholesterol becomes toxic to Mtb. The goal of this research will be to elucidate the requirements and mechanics of the reaction performed by this protein. I will use structural and biochemical techniques to determine the speed of reaction, structure, and specifics of target molecule recognition. Specifically, the involved techniques include: purification of EchA20, identification of the kinetic parameters, directed mutagenesis, and X-ray crystallography. This will establish foundational information for further investigation into how this protein can be used as a drug target against Mtb. Overall, this research will provide insight into this enzyme's mechanism of action, contribute to determining EchA20's role in the pathogenicity of Mtb, and provide a basis for designing novel therapeutics.

column36: Systematic Validation of Novel Lung Cancer Drivers
column37: Lung cancer is the number one cause of cancer-related deaths. Targeted therapy ("personalized medicine") fights specific genetic changes that allow a given cancer to exist. This has improved life expectancy for some of those affected. Still, problems remain. Many cancer-causing genetic changes haven't been discovered, and even target-treatable cancers will eventually become drug-resistant through further changes. Discovery of new drug targets is therefore important to help improve outcomes. Targets can be found by examining the differences in healthy and tumor lung DNA. However, thousands of changes exist in any given tumor. Separating cancer-causing from irrelevant is complex and can dismiss important genes. We used a genetic technology termed Sleeping Beauty (SB) to discover new cancer-causing genes. In our mouse model, SB randomly inserts itself into various locations in lung DNA, changing nearby genes. Some of these changes promote cancer. Once tumors formed, we could determine genes SB had frequently changed. This provided powerful causal evidence that these genes are important in lung cancer. Many of these genes are known, showing SB's success. Other genes are new, and their roles in cancer have yet to be determined. My project will aim to confirm the importance of these genes in lung cancer. I will validate about 150 genes found with SB that are consistent with changes in human lung cancer using a gene disruption screen. I will further confirm and characterize overlapping results from these screens in mice and in human cell lines. The results from this study will aid in the development of new therapies and in improving outcomes for people who suffer from this devastating disease.

column36: SUNRISE Pilot Study: Canadian Surveillance study of Movement Behaviours in the Early Years
column37: The early years of life (5yrs) are arguably the most critical period for healthy physical, social, motor, and cognitive development. column36: Improving word sense disambiguation in clinical narratives using deep learning
column37: My proposal is focused on using deep learning to disambiguate abbreviations in clinical notes so that they are more comprehensive. Abbreviation disambiguation (AD) is challenging since abbreviations can have many senses. For example, ra can mean right atrium, rheumatoid arthritis or room air depending on its context. Correctly expanding medical terms is important to build accurate patient profiles, link notes to ontological concepts, and allow for easier interpretation by fellow healthcare professionals. Current methods for AD are often based on feature engineering, require large amounts training data, and have poor generalizability to novel settings. Secondly, supervised learning techniques generally require training data which can be expensive to obtain since health-care professionals must manually label it. This is not practical when building a model that needs to disambiguate many abbreviations. The goal of my research project is to develop a model that is trained to disambiguate over 80,000 medical abbreviations in a semi-supervised manner without the need for any manual labelling. I will generate a training set using a method that finds long forms in a corpus of clinical notes and replaces them with their corresponding abbreviation. To ensure all long forms are well represented, I will generate additional training samples by gathering sentences of words that are close to a given long form in vector space. Once I generate my training set, I will train a feed-forward neural network and test generalizability on a novel dataset. The outcomes of this project can be used in existing electronic medical records for abbreviation disambiguation tasks or in real-time by clinicians for on-the-spot abbreviation expansion to reduce note ambiguity.

column36: Evaluating the neuroprotective potential of exosome delivered catalase-SKL in a pre-clinical model of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with inflammation in the brain; this phenomenon is also seen in mice that carry genes known to cause AD in humans. A core pathological feature of AD is the over-expression of reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to a form of microscopic injury in the brain known as oxidative stress. This is in part caused by the progressive dysfunction of peroxisomes, which are a crucial component of the cell that reduce oxidative stress. A genetically optimized version of catalase (CAT-SKL), an enzyme that is naturally found in nearly all living organisms, specifically targets these peroxisomes and provides antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-aging effects. This project will investigate the use of a new biological method to deliver the powerful anti-oxidant, CAT-SKL, to the brain where it can reduce oxidative stress. To test the protective and therapeutic potential of CAT-SKL, it will be evaluated in mice that carry genetic risk factors known to cause AD. In addition, we will assess a new biological method of therapeutic molecule delivery known as exosomes. Exosomes are nanosized vesicles that can be prepared from the mouse's own cells. If delivery of CAT-SKL is effective, exosomes could also be prepared from a human patient's own cells to treat antioxidant stress in their brain. Intranasal administration of CAT-SKL loaded exosomes can penetrate the brain, potentially preventing and/or ameliorating pathological, biochemical, and behavioural outcomes. This project will also provide further validation for the use of nanoparticles to deliver therapeutics to the brain.

column36: Investigation of antibody-mediated immune mechanisms in pregnancy-associated malaria
column37: Malaria, one of the top 10 causes of death in low-income countries, targets the most vulnerable populations - pregnant women and children. Despite some acquired immunity to malaria that develops throughout an individual's lifetime, pregnancy offers a new site of attack for the parasite; the placenta. Pregnancy-associated malaria (PAM) greatly increases the risk of pregnancy complications and maternal mortality, especially in communities with limited access to healthcare. Antibodies against the parasite's variant surface antigens seen in PAM (VSAPAM) have been previously shown to have protective effects, including reduced parasite sequestration in the placenta. Yet, the specific mechanisms of protection are still unknown. I hypothesize that in addition to blocking sequestration, VSAPAM antibodies triggers other mechanisms that sit at the interface of innate and adaptive immunity. Using well-established techniques and new methods currently being optimized, I will investigate the extent of activation of the complement system and macrophage recruitment throughout the stages of pregnancy. Our laboratory has previously collected samples from pregnant women from enrolment to delivery, as well as non-pregnant populations (men and children), which will be used to determine if protection is pregnancy-specific. I will also use non-exposed samples as controls. Relationships between antibody-mediated mechanisms and protective effects will provide novel insight into the host's natural defence against pregnancy-associated malaria. These findings can be used to develop more effective therapies for individuals in the greatest danger.

column37: Tendons connect muscle to bone. They are a strong connective tissue, similar to ligament. When they get injured, they take a long time to heal. Tendons often cause chronic pain in people who engage in repetitive activities, because the injured tendon is continually irritated by the movement, causing tendinopathy. Physiotherapists and doctors often advise their tendinopathy patients to reduce, and then gradually increase, their tendon-loading activities, but currently we don't know the best way to provide this advice or ensure that people can accurately monitor their own activity level. We will also begin to explore the potential relationships between patellar tendinopathy symptom severity, with jump count and peak landing force, as groundwork for a larger study. The results of the study will contribute to developing a better understanding of how we can help people recover from patellar tendinopathy.

column36: Innovative Immunotherapy Approach in Chimeric Antigen Receptor based therapy for acute leukemia using transplantation of genetically modified hematopoietic stem cells.
column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common pediatric cancer and, despite an 80% remission rate, it remains the most lethal pediatric cancer. A promising new therapeutic tool for resistant leukemias uses engineered T cells to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that allows specific recognition and killing of cancer cells. Despite the efficacy of this treatment in chemotherapy-refractory patients, 50% of patients do not respond or relapse because CAR T-cells get exhausted and/or do not persist in the patient. Also, it is associated with a life-threatening side effect, called cytokine release syndrome, which results from the simultaneous activation of the injected CAR-T cells. Hence, there is a need for improving this technology. We thus propose an alternative strategy consisting of inserting the CAR gene into the patient's own hematopoietic stem cells (instead of T cells) and re-engraft them to ensure a continuous and progressive replenishment of CAR-T cells. With this method, the anti-leukemic effect would be prolonged and relapses could be tackled from the very first day. However, modifying stem cell would generate CAR bearing cells that should not express it. Hence, to limit the expression of the CAR only to the effector cells, we have developed a genetic tool that controls the expression of the receptor on T cells exclusively. In this project, we will test the effectiveness and safety of our new approach. We will use sophisticated humanized mouse models that are engrafted with the patient's immune system and leukemia cell. This improved therapy would: 1) increase efficacy; 2) reduce side-effects; and 3) eliminate graft-vs-host disease risks associated with classic bone-marrow transplant. This research project could result in a rapid translation to clinic.

column36: A New Perspective on Amyloid Precursor Protein Processing: Rhomboid Protease-4 and Cholesterol in the Alzheimer Pathology
column37: Alzheimer disease (AD) currently affects over 24 million people worldwide, and is defined by the presence of plaques in the brain comprised of protein fragments called amyloid beta (A?). It is well established that A? is formed through the consecutive cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) by two proteins in the cell membrane: ?- and ?-secretase. Recently, it has been shown that another protein called rhomboid intramembrane protease 4 (RHBDL4) is also able to cleave APP, and this RHBDL4-mediated cleavage prevents APP from reaching the cell membrane. Interestingly, it was just shown that this cleavage is likely regulated by the cholesterol content of the cell. When cholesterol levels are high, RHBDL4 activity is reduced, and vice versa. In cell models of AD, less A? has already been observed in conditions of low cholesterol, but it remains unclear why that is. This RHBDL4-mediated cleavage could provide insight into the mechanism behind this observation. It is hypothesized that the RHBDL4 cleavage of APP offsets the pathogenic ?-/?-secretase cleavage, and that this offset is influenced by cholesterol levels. This project aims to generate more robust results surrounding RHBDL4 cleavage of APP, and how cholesterol is involved. A new method will be developed to directly measure the activity of RHBDL4, and previous experiments will be repeated in a better cell model of AD. It is expected that when cholesterol levels are high, ?-/?-secretase cleavage will dominate, as a result of decreased RHBDL4 activity, ultimately resulting in more A?. Considering the high levels of cholesterol shown in brains of those affected by AD and the myriad of AD risk factors related to cholesterol, this research is vital in further connecting cholesterol to the AD pathology.

column36: Characterization of M. catarrhalis iron uptake proteins and their application in vaccine design
column37: Moraxella catarrhalis is a bacterium that normally colonizes the human respiratory and urinary tracts, causing no disease. However, it can be an opportunistic pathogen in individuals with weakened or naive immune systems. M. catarrhalis causes otitis media and in severe cases, sepsis. The emergence of antimicrobial resistance in M. catarrhalis signify the need for a vaccine against the bacterium as a preventative treatment method. Bacterial iron acquisition proteins are potential targets as vaccine antigens, due to their importance in obtaining iron from host iron carriers, such as transferrin (Tf) and lactoferrin (Lf), to allow for bacterial survival inside the human host. M. catarrhalis iron acquisition proteins include Tf-binding proteins (Tbps) and Lfbinding proteins (Lbps). Lbps are known to contribute to bacterial defense against host antimicrobial peptides. A vaccine designed against M. catarrhalis based on Tbps and Lbps can prevent the bacteria from colonizing and causing disease. In this study, various M. catarrhalis proteins that are essential for iron uptake will be studied through structural genomics, proteomics, and genetic approaches. A thorough understanding of these proteins is important for designing a protective vaccine that is crossprotective against all M. catarrhalis strains and prevent vaccine escape. Furthermore, putative TbpB-based vaccine antigens will be engineered and evaluated for its suitability in a pan-M. catarrhalis vaccine.

column36: Bacterial metabolites produced by the intestinal microbiota modulate maternal metabolic adaptations to pregnancy in the context of maternal obesity
column37: Overweight and obesity affects 39% of the adult population, a proportion that continues to grow. While this can be attributed to poor nutrition and sedentary lifestyles, it is also important to note the role of early life exposure to parental obesity. A child born to an obese mother is at higher risk for obesity, regardless of their own diet as an adult, as well as a host of other metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease. Thus, it is important to understand how we can intervene in these pregnancies to prevent this increased risk of metabolic dysfunction. A healthy pregnancy involves many important changes in the mother that allow more energy to be directed to the growing fetus. There are many factors that contribute to this change, recent research has suggested that bacterial communities that reside in the gut, known as the gut microbiota, influence these maternal changes. These bacteria are known to help break down digested food, as well as help the human body regulate energy storage and usage. Furthermore, the composition of the gut microbiota is altered in obesity as well as during pregnancy, this might also change how bacteria regulate energy in obesity and pregnancy. We believe that understanding how these bacteria change during pregnancy and in obesity can help us identify a potential intervention to reduce the risk of metabolic diseases in future generations.

column36: Structure-Based Design of Ubiquitin-Specific Protease 18 Inhibitors
column37: During a viral infection such as the flu, viruses invade the host organism's cells and hijack their resources to generate new viral particles, which go on to infect other cells within the host. However, if a cellular protein known as interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15) interacts with a piece of the novel viral particle before it is assembled, it blocks the proper formation of these new viruses; thus, preventing further spread of the virus throughout the body. In contrast, another protein in the cell known as ubiquitin-specific protease 18 (USP18) can bind ISG15 and inhibit its ability to interact with the components of novel viral particles. My goal is to determine precisely how USP18 binds ISG15 on a molecular level. I plan to do this using a high-resolution technique known as x-ray crystallography, which will allow me to look at the structure of proteins on an atomic scale. Ultimately, by understanding exactly how USP18 interacts with ISG15, I will be able to design new antiviral drugs that will block these interactions, and therefore, stop USP18 from binding ISG15. In doing so, if taken at the time of a viral infection, this drug will lead to greater inhibition of viral particle assembly by ISG15, slowing the spread of the virus throughout the host's body and making it easier for the individual's immune system to fight off the disease.

column36: Connaissances et stigmatisation des aines a l'egard des troubles anxieux et depressifs en lien avec la recherche d'aide.

column36: The effects of non-invasive neuromodulation on tinnitus
column37: Tinnitus affects approximately 42% of Canadians. Patients with this condition suffer from high anxiety and depressive symptoms that severely impact their quality of life. Efficacy of current pharmacological and behavioural interventions is limited. Therefore, the need to develop new treatment approaches is critical. Our main goal is to evaluate the effectiveness of non-invasive neuromodulation on tinnitus symptoms. This technique can modulate the activity of brain areas that have been associated with tinnitus. It is delivered by applying a low electric current or electromagnetic field directly to the skull. Some studies found that non-invasive neuromodulation can suppress tinnitus in patients. However, neuromodulation parameters, such as the intensity and the targeted brain regions, vary across studies. Thus, it is difficult to know which neuromodulation parameters are optimal to treat tinnitus. We will use two methods to identify effective neuromodulation parameters: 1) We will conduct a meta-analysis to identify the approaches that suppress the most tinnitus distress and intensity; and we will: 2) use computer modeling to simulate and evaluate the processes by which specific brain regions can decrease tinnitus intensity and/or distress. Ultimately, we aim to find the best neuromodulation technique that could help these patients. This research project seeks to enhance the therapeutic potential of existing non-invasive neuromodulation in order to better treat patients. We hope to understand more clearly how non-invasive neuromodulation works and how it can eradicate tinnitus. Finally, we hope to elucidate the mechanism of action underlying tinnitus to ultimately bring important knowledge to the scientific community and patients.
