column36: Le role du soutien social dans l'abandon et l'efficacite de la therapie cognitive comportementale sur Internet chez les adultes atteints de symptomes de stress post-traumatique
column37: Il est bien etabli que l'absence de soutien social contribue au developpement et au maintien des symptomes du trouble de stress post-traumatique (TSPT). Toutefois, l'influence qu'a le soutien social sur l'efficacite de la therapie cognitive comportementale sur Internet (TCCI) n'a pas encore ete definie. De plus, le taux d'abandon de traitement du TSPS est de 25 a 40% et peu d'etudes ont examine les causes de cet abandon. Il serait ainsi pertinent de s'attaquer au probleme d'abandon en examinant l'influence de divers facteurs, tels que le soutien social. Cette etude longitudinale a donc comme premier objectif de mettre en evidence la relation entre le soutien social et l'abandon de la TCCI chez 145 residents de Fort McMurray souffrant de symptomes de stress post-traumatique (SPT) suite aux feux de foret de 2016. Il est postule qu'un faible soutien social sera associe a l'abandon de traitement tandis qu'un soutien social eleve favorisera l'achevement de la TCCI. Le second objectif cherche a demontrer le lien entre le soutien social pre et post-traitement et l'efficacite de la TCCI. Il est postule que le soutien social sera associe negativement au niveau de symptomes post-traitement de SPT. Les symptomes d'insomnie et de depression seront egalement examines puisqu'ils sont souvent comorbides aux symptomes de SPT. Les participants completent presentement une TCCI de 12 sessions ciblant le TSPT, les symptomes depressifs et l'insomnie. L'implication du soutien social dans l'abandon de traitement sera etudiee a l'aide d'une regression logistique. Des regressions lineaires multivariees seront egalement effectuees afin d'observer l'influence du soutien social pre et post-traitement sur l'efficacite de la TCCI.

column36: Role of micro ribonucleic acids in progesterone resistance in endometriosis
column37: Endometriosis is a disorder in which endometrial tissue grows outside of the uterus; this tissue is known as ectopic endometrium. It is highly prevalent and causes pain and subfertility. It is known that ectopic endometrium is resistant to progesterone, one of the major female sex hormones, due to suppression of progesterone receptor (PR) expression. However, the mechanisms by which this suppression occurs have not been completely elucidated. Improved understanding of these mechanisms may lead to novel therapies based on the reversal of receptor suppression. MicroRNAs are short RNA molecules that regulate protein expression by binding to complementary mRNA molecules. mRNA molecules are read by cellular machinery to produce proteins, and the binding of microRNA prevents this reading. Previous research on progesterone resistance caused by microRNA-26a and microRNA-181a in breast cancer and endometrial cancer hint towards their possible involvement in endometriosis-associated progesterone resistance. I hypothesize that microRNA-26a and microRNA-181a are upregulated in ectopic endometrium and act to suppress PR expression. In this proposed research, endometrial samples will be collected from women without endometriosis and from the ectopic sites of women with endometriosis. microRNA-26a, microRNA-181a, and PR mRNA will be quantified in order to compare the differences in expression between healthy and ectopic endometrium. Cells taken from the ectopic samples will be cultured and treated with microRNA mimics and inhibitors. The protein content of the treated cells will be quantified to assess PR levels in relation to microRNA-26a or microRNA-181a concentrations.

column36: Sensitizing quiescent medulloblastoma stem cells to anti-mitotic chemotherapy
column37: Pediatric medulloblastoma (MB) is a brain cancer that arises in the cerebellum. Its treatment can damage developing brain tissue, leaving survivors with long-term health complications. It has been shown using a mouse model that MB tumours are driven by a rare population of quiescent cancer stem cells (CSCs) that differentiate to form the rapidly proliferating cells of the tumour bulk. Current chemotherapy drugs used to treat MB eradicate the tumour bulk, but CSCs are resistant to such treatment partially because of their quiescence. One mechanism that contributes to quiescence is regulation of resting membrane potential (RMP): the difference in ionic concentrations across a cell membrane at rest. Quiescent cells tend to be hyperpolarized relative to proliferating cells. Accordingly, MB CSCs have been observed to have a more negative RMP than the rapidly proliferating cells of the tumour bulk. I hypothesize that RMP hyperpolarization contributes to CSC quiescence and that perturbing the pathways that maintain this quiescent state will sensitize them to chemotherapy. Using a chemogenetics approach, I will depolarize and hyperpolarize CSCs in vitro and in vivo. I will test how changing RMP alters proliferation and differentiation. Next, to identify the molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying CSC quiescence and proliferation, I will perform transcriptomic and epigenetic analyses. Data from these experiments will allow me to uncover druggable pathways unique to CSCs that can disrupt their quiescence. The work proposed here aims to explore the unknown ways in which RMP contributes to CSC quiescence and develop a novel approach to selectively target the CSCs that potentiate MB tumours to treat and cure this cancer while minimizing collateral damage to the developing brain.

column36: Modeling Latent Gene Cooperativity in Viral Tumourigenesis
column37: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the etiological agent of the most common malignancy in untreated AIDS patients: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). The cancer is characterized by large purple skin lesions composed mainly of infected endothelial cells (ECs) that rapidly proliferate, elongate (spindle), and release inflammatory factors. While KSHV has both a latent (minimal gene expression) and a lytic (full genome replication with infectious virion production) phase, KS lesions are composed predominantly of latently infected cells. During latency only six protein products are expressed, underscoring their significance to both tumourigenesis and the EC reprogramming phenotypes described above. Previous work has shown that two of these proteins, KapB (kaposin B) and vFLIP (Fas-associated death domain-like interleukin-1?-converting enzyme-inhibitory protein), are critical to the spindling and inflammatory gene expression phenotypes in virus infected ECs. However, previous studies linking KapB and vFLIP to these phenotypes were heavily reliant on ectopic expression models and the mechanism behind vFLIP induced EC remodeling remains mostly obscure. Therefore, the role of these proteins in tumourigenesis remains largely unexplored. Due to their redundancy, I hypothesize that KapB and vFLIP may be acting cooperatively to maintain the KSHV tumour environment. To investigate this, I will generate KSHV recombinants lacking KapB, vFLIP or the combination and test how these mutant viruses behave with respect to KSHV tumourigenesis phenotypes such as EC reprogramming, viral episome maintenance, processing body loss, and angiogenesis. This work is critical to our understanding of viral oncogenesis and will provide new targets for KS therapy.

column36: Inpatient Rehabilitation Exergames in Children with Cerebral Palsy after Lower Extremity Orthopedic Surgery
column37: Cycling is often incorporated into rehabilitation programs for adults after hip replacement surgery to reduce pain, however, studies have yet to look at the role of cycling post-orthopedic surgery in children with cerebral palsy (CP). Children with CP often require lower extremity orthopedic surgery, and pain is commonly experienced during the post-surgical recovery period. Our team has developed a recumbent bicycling-based exercise video game, or 'exergame' station, called "Liberi Exergames". These multi-player exercise video games are powered by pedaling on a stationary bicycle and using game controllers to control what the characters do in the game. Since cycling has been shown to relieve pain in post-orthopedic rehabilitation for adults, I hypothesize that the use of exergames for children with CP after orthopedic surgery will be feasible, will reduce pain, and will enhance psychosocial wellbeing. This will be a case-comparison study with consecutive recruitment. 10 children will be recruited from the inpatient unit at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital. The first 5 enrolled will receive standard physiotherapy ('comparison group') and the last 5 enrolled will participate in the exergames in addition to standard physiotherapy ('case group'.) The case group will engage in 30 minutes of exergames play 5 times a week for 3 weeks (15 exergame sessions). Questionnaires and surveys, based on pain and psychosocial health, will be administered at baseline and the end of each week during the 3 week intervention phase. This study will serve as a crucial platform for future projects to expand exergames in reducing pain for patient populations in both clinical and non-healthcare settings.

column36: A Collaborative Approach to Explore Ways to Promote Infant Mental Health
column37: My project is rooted in the idea that the experiences and environments we are exposed to in the first three years of life can determine health outcomes in adulthood. The experiences and environments shape future results because of the rapid brain development during the first three years of life. To ensure proper brain development, infants need positive interactions with their caregivers. The absence of positive interactions results in a stress pathway overdeveloping and leading to toxic stress. Toxic stress damages brain development of infants. Research firmly supports that IMH promotion is needed for healthy development, but IMH promotion has been slow to be integrated into professional practice. There is a gap in preventative services for mental illness. My project seeks to fill in this gap by studying ways to integrate IMH into training for health professionals and allied health professionals for future use. This project is relevant to future health professionals and allied health professionals who are interested in the field of IMH promotion. The list professionals that are interested in this research, but not limited to, are family doctors, pediatricians, psychologists, early childhood educators, nurse practitioners, and social workers. This project will add knowledge to the growing field of promoting IMH. My project will help guide the development of IMH promotion policies and practices at multiple levels, such as the community, organizational, and government. This project aligns with the Government of Newfoundland's action plan to tackle addiction and mental illness. Outside this area of research, the creation of IMH promotion will likely reduce the need for treating mental illness if it can be prevented in the first place.

column36: Predictive Models for Carboplatin with or without Hyperthermia Treatment Response in Epithelial Ovarian Cancer: Comparison of 2D, 3D, and in-vivo Models
column37: Despite many advances in surgical techniques and chemotherapies, ovarian cancer (OC) remains a deadly disease with only half of patients surviving 5 years after diagnosis. To address this issue, research has shifted to develop a more personalized medicine approach, which dictates that each cancer patient be paired to her most appropriate treatment. Direct testing of treatments on biopsied tumor mass (or derivative) may enable to predict patient response. Our laboratory has been a leader in developing new model systems to evaluate drug response, including using microtumors in devices that allow treatment testing. Our recent unpublished data has shown that the sensitivity of our patient-derived samples to carboplatin, the most used chemotherapy in OC, does not perfectly correlate when tested in 2D and 3D models. This is concerning since the accuracy of a pre-clinical model is essential for predicting patient response. We believe that the precision of treatment testing is related to the tissue spatial composition, in which the closer a model is to the initial tumor sample, the better the prediction power it will have. To this end, we will categorize and compare the sensitivities of OC tumor samples to 2 different treatments across 2D, 3D and mouse models to determine the most accurate pre-clinical model. The 2 treatments to be tested are carboplatin and/or hyperthermic treatment (HT), which involves heating a solution above 37C and has been shown to increase survival in OC patients. This study will enlighten researchers on determining the pre-clinical model with the highest translational potential for predicting patient outcomes in the new era of precision medicine.

column36: Granzyme K in the Pathogenesis of Psoriasis
column37: Psoriasis is a common skin disease characterized by thick, itchy, red patches with a silvery white build-up of dead skin called 'plaques'. Around one million Canadians are currently living with psoriasis. Although psoriasis is not usually deadly, this chronic condition can seriously impact a person's overall quality of life, as it is linked with social stigmatization, physical disability, pain, psychological distress and increased health risks. Unfortunately there is no cure, and current therapies often have negative side-effects and fail to provide long term relief. There is therefore a crucial need to further understand how psoriasis arises so that we can develop more effective and better targeted drugs. A family of proteins called granzymes are drastically elevated in a number of inflammatory skin diseases including psoriasis. One granzyme, called granzyme K (GzmK), has recently been shown to promote inflammation in the skin. As our preliminary data suggest that GzmK is elevated in psoriasis, I believe that this inflammation-promoting enzyme could play a key role in the cause of this condition. To understand the role of GzmK in psoriasis, I will use a combination of skin cell, mouse and human models of disease. I will look at the direct effects of GzmK on skin cells and will study the role of GzmK in the causation of psoriasis using a mouse model in which GzmK is genetically removed. Based on our preliminary data, I predict that these studies will show that GzmK plays a key role in psoriasis and will provide a strong rationale for developing new drugs targeting GzmK to treat this disease.

column36: Association between Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Age at Natural Menopause: Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: Although menopause is a natural part of aging in women, the timing of the onset of menopause can reveal a lot about one's future health risks. The average age of menopause in women is between 45 and 55 years, however, as many as 9.6% of the women can enter menopause earlier than the age of 45. Various cardiovascular outcomes such as total cholesterol, blood pressure and body weight have been shown to be associated with an earlier menopause. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), on the other hand, is characterized by the onset of glucose intolerance during pregnancy. Worldwide, the incidence of GDM has increased by more than 30%, making it one of the most common pregnancy complications. Along with increasing the risks of childbirth, GDM can have long-term effects on the mother's health, including high blood pressure, reduction in good cholesterol levels and greater triglyceride levels post gestation as compared to women with normal pregnancies. Therefore, given that gestational diabetes can predispose women to worse cardiovascular health, which in turn is associated with premature menopause, we hypothesize that a direct association between GDM and the age at natural menopause might exist. This project will utilize data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging (CLSA)- a CIHR funded, national study on aging in Canada and will investigate the relationship between the incidence of GDM and the age at natural menopause. This will be the first study to look at this association and can help clinicians in Canada and around the world direct early and focussed care towards at-risk patients.

column36: Effects of Interruptions in HIV Therapy on Cellular Aging
column37: People living with HIV experience accelerated aging. HIV+ individuals die a decade earlier and develop age related diseases earlier than the general population. Such diseases include heart, liver, bone, kidney, and Alzheimer's disease, as well as some cancers. It is unclear if this is due to the HIV virus (which can cause chronic inflammation) or because of the side effects of the HIV drugs taken to treat the disease. Many HIV drugs are known to negatively affect mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). The mitochondria are the power houses of the cell. As we grow older, we accumulate mutations in the mtDNA, which contains the instructions to build proteins needed for energy production. The more mutations we accumulate, the less energy we can produce, and the less able we are to maintain the health of our tissues. People living with HIV may age faster in part because they experience an accelerated accumulation of mtDNA mutations. Previous studies suggested that uncontrolled HIV replication, as might occur during interruption(s) in HIV therapy, may accelerate aging and promote disease in people living with HIV. In fact, a clinical trial showed that taking scheduled breaks from HIV therapy increased the chance of heart, kidney, and liver disease, as well as death. These diseases are linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and/or older age. We hypothesize that periodically stopping and re-starting HIV therapy promotes the duplication of mutated copies of mtDNA and accelerates aging. I will measure mtDNA mutations among people living with HIV who either never stopped therapy or interrupted it many times, as well as HIV-negative controls. My study will inform health care providers and people living with HIV about the potential effects associated with therapy interruptions.

column36: The Role of Exercise and Obesity in Radiation-Induced Leukemia and Survival in Mice
column37: The number of long-term cancer survivors in Canada who have been exposed to radiation therapy as part of their treatment is increasing. As such, the late effects of radiation therapy, including secondary cancers like leukemias, are becoming a major clinical concern. In addition, obesity and physical inactivity are two physiological host factors that are prevalent in cancer survivors and have been linked to increased cancer risk. It remains unclear, however, how obesity and increasing physical activity impact the incidence of radiation-induced leukemia in cancer survivors long-term. As such, a critical need exists to develop (1) a better understanding of host factors that affect the risk of radiation-induced malignancies, and (2) strategies such as exercise training, to minimize their effects. Thus, the primary research question of this project is: how do host factors, such as obesity and exercise, influence radiation-induced leukemia risk? Our objective is to quantify leukemia incidence and overall survival in the following groups: obese/sedentary, obese/exercise-trained, lean/sedentary, and lean/exercise-trained mice exposed to a high dose of radiation. We hypothesize that mortality and the incidence of radiation-induced leukemia will be greatest in obese/sedentary mice but will be attenuated by exercise. We expect results from this work to identify modifiable risk factors that are related to radiation-induced leukemia and in turn, we aim to advance health-related knowledge by providing novel information to oncologists and patients on everyday diet and exercise decisions that could improve overall human health and also protect against cancer.

column36: Examining the impact of bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II (BMPR-II) loss on the expression of the splicing factor 3B complex
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a fatal disease that causes blockage and tightening of arteries in the lungs. This increases blood pressure in the lungs. If individuals with PAH do not receive treatment, they will die from right heart failure in 2-3 years. Unfortunately, current treatments only treat the symptoms of PAH, and have little impact on disease progression and death. Many individuals with PAH have a mutation in the gene BMPR2, which encodes a protein receptor. This mutation is found in 70% of patients who inherit PAH and 20% of individuals who develop PAH for unknown reasons. An individual with a BMPR2 mutation has a 20,000 times greater risk of developing PAH than someone who does not; however, how BMPR2 mutations cause PAH is still not fully understood.BMPR2 mutations cause increased cell growth in pulmonary arteries, which gives PAH characteristics that are similar to cancer. In addition, these mutations may also influence the type of genes expressed by a cell, through a process known as mRNA splicing. Splicing is regulated by many proteins, including proteins of the SF3B complex. Preliminary studies have suggested a link between SF3B proteins and BMPR2, as well as to certain cancers. Our work will test if BMPR2 loss influences the expression or interactions of two specific SF3B proteins, SF3B3 and SF3B4. The goal of this project is to identify whether these two SF3B subunits are involved in PAH development when BMPR2 is mutated. This will broaden the current understanding of BMPR2 effects in PAH, and could lead to the development of improved treatments for this disease.

column36: Mindfulness as a Predictor of Alcohol and Cannabis Use Among First Year Undergraduates
column37: Alcohol and drug use are common among first year undergraduate students. The first year of university is associated with the highest rates of alcohol and cannabis use, and misuse can lead to a wide range of negative consequences. Therefore, it is critical to determine what protective factors may buffer against risky alcohol and cannabis use during this stage. One factor that may be useful is mindfulness. Mindfulness is commonly conceptualized into five facets: observing, describing, acting with awareness, nonjudgment of inner experience, and nonreactivity to inner experience. Prior research has demonstrated that certain facets of mindfulness combat risky drinking behaviour, but comparatively fewer studies have examined how these facets relate to cannabis use among first year undergraduates. A longitudinal design will examine the impact of mindfulness facets on alcohol and cannabis use during the first year of university. Participants will be assessed at three time-points throughout the academic year. Various measures will assess mindfulness, alcohol and cannabis use patterns, alcohol and cannabis use motives, and alcohol and cannabis use related problems. If certain facets of mindfulness are predictive of alcohol and cannabis use, prevention programs that target high-school students before they transition into university could utilize mindfulness techniques. Additionally, it is essential to understand factors that relate to low-risk cannabis use during young adulthood, as the negative effects of cannabis use are strongest during this time. Results of this study could help mitigate negative outcomes associated with the utilization of this substance, especially given the recent legalization of cannabis in Canada.

column36: Royal Alexandra Hospital Supervised Consumption Services: Evaluation of Patient Uptake and Access
column37: In April 2018, the Royal Alexandra Hospital (RAH) and its Addiction Recovery and Community Health (ARCH) team in Edmonton implemented North America's first safe consumption site (SCS) in primary care. To date, there are no peer-reviewed research reports on the provision of SCS for hospital patients, and the RAH SCS has not yet been evaluated. Assessing patient uptake and identifying potential access barriers is a critical first step to refining the RAH SCS service model, supporting further evaluation of its effectiveness, and informing the medical and academic communities regarding this innovation in acute care for patients who use drugs. As such, this project will used mixed methods to examine 1) the rate of uptake of the SCS amongst eligible ARCH patients, 2) analyze whether any sociodemographic or clinical differences exist between those eligible patients who access the SCS and those who do not, and 3) describe patient motivations for using the SCS, and extant barriers or facilitators to access. Findings from this research will help ARCH and RAH identify and eliminate barriers to accessing the SCS, and contribute to better optimization of the intervention. As such, the study may contribute to better care for some of the hospital's most vulnerable patients.

column36: Epilepsy and Dementia in the Elderly: Prevalence, Associated Risk Factors, and Frailty
column37: BACKGROUND: Dementia, seizures and epilepsy are conditions that are common in older adults, and that are expected to become even more common with the aging of the population. A known complication of epilepsy is cognitive impairment and dementia. Here we propose to study how common these conditions co-exist in older adults and what the needs of these persons living with both of these conditions are. We suspect that dementia will be more likely to occur in individuals who have epilepsy than individuals in the general population, and vice versa. METHODS: Data will be collected from a large database (~12 million records) in the United Kingdom. We will examine how common is epilepsy in persons with dementia, and vice versa. Statistical software will be used to analyze risk factors, comorbidities, and frailty in this population. The frailty indexes of those with epilepsy and dementia will be compared to populations of individuals with only epilepsy, and only dementia to see how this particular population affected by both condition (epilepsy and dementia) is unique. We will then do focus groups to understand the needs and concerns of people affected by these two conditions simultaneously. This is a group that has been overlooked in the past, and whereby resources to support them are limited. EXPECTED OUTCOME: We hope to make public health policy recommendations that could eventually become implemented and allow for better care and prevention strategies for people living with dementia and epilepsy. This project will provide information that will guide future public health policy, prevention and intervention strategies by examining factors associated with dementia in epilepsy (and vice versa) and will help us understand potential health resource needs for this population.

column36: James Saville Canada Graduate Scholarships-Master's Program Application
column37: Cells are encased by membranes that separate their contents from the environment and allows cells to exist as a stand-alone units. Embedded in these membranes are proteins that play crucial roles in transport of materials and transduction of signals across the membrane. ?60% of current drugs target membrane proteins (MP) to elicit their therapeutic effects. Despite their importance, the study of MPs lags behind the study of soluble proteins (proteins dissolved within the cell). The main barrier to MP study is their hydrophobic (water-hating) nature. Practically all of the methods biochemists have developed to investigate proteins require the protein to first be dissolved in aqueous (water-based) solutions. This proves difficult for MPs, as they tend to unfold and crash out of solution in these water-based solutions. Enter membrane mimetics, technologies that strive to replicate the native membrane environment, while allowing for MPs to be dissolved in aqueous solution. Through my research, I seek to apply the Peptidisc, an in-house developed membrane mimetic, to discover nanobodies (NBs) against MPs to facilitate their study. NBs are a type of antibody that can bind MPs, freezing them in different functional states - such as halfway through transporting a molecule across the membrane, or just as the MP binds a signalling molecule. Locking these MPs into key states and determining their structure, will provide insights into how these MPs function, or dysfunction. A secondary application of NBs, is as therapeutic drugs that label invading pathogens or mutant cells for immune system response. Whether it be through determining MP structure, developing therapeutics or a combination therein, this research strives to broaden fundamental knowledge on MP structure and function.

column36: Utility of Cognitive Dispersion in a Heterogenous Memory Clinic Population
column37: It is important to understand differences between healthy and unhealthy aging to help in early detection of conditions such as dementia due to Alzheimer Disease (AD). Past research in this area focused on decreases of scores on single tests of ability. A single-task approach was incomplete because it looked at average scores; it ignored variability, leading to the assumption that everybody experiences age-related cognitive decline in the same way. More recently, it was shown that variability can tell us about the less stable ways we decline and develop dementia. Variability within a person can be described over many time points or at a single time and it has been linked to the brain and its systems. Dispersion is defined as variability of one person across many tasks at a single time; its increase has been linked with faster mental decline, but it has only been tried in groups of people that have the same conditions causing unhealthy aging. This study will see whether dispersion is useful for organizing people into groups who have dementia caused by several conditions. People attending the Rural and Remote Memory Clinic were put into 1 of 4 groups: no cognitive impairment, Mild Cognitive Impairment, dementia due to AD, or non-AD dementia. Each participant did a series of tasks to test their functioning. To predict the risk of a person being put in a given group we will create a dispersion score for each person, a single score to reflect each person's variability across the tasks. By doing this study we will be adding to our tools for looking at unhealthy aging and laying the foundation for examining variability's use as a predictor of daily functioning. This research is necessary because Canadians will be developing dementia in large numbers in the coming years.

column36: The Effect of 8 Weeks of Sprint Interval Training or Moderate Intensity Continuous Training on Resting Blood Pressure and Heart Rate
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of disability and is the leading risk factor in the world for mortality. Both elevated heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP) are risk factors for CVD. Recently new data has been released on the classification of hypertension, stating that BP >130/80 (systolic/diastolic) is considered hypertensive. This significantly increases the amount of individuals classified as hypertensive. Acute bouts of endurance exercise have a lowering effect on blood pressure in the hours following exercise, termed post exercise hypotension (PEH). This is important as the magnitude of PEH may predict the magnitude of BP lowering after chronic training. The onset of hypertension can be reduced or prevented with the use of an endurance exercise training program, however, lack of time is usually a barrier to beginning or undergoing this type of program. Sprint interval training (SIT) has emerged as a time-efficient protocol that typically includes 4 repeated 30 second efforts, interspersed by 4 minutes of recovery. The aerobic adaptions to SIT are similar to those observed in endurance training even though training volume and time is reduced. Modified SIT protocols that included the same total amount of work and rest, just a different work and rest times have been shown to be just as effective, and even more enjoyable than traditional SIT protocols. The use of SIT is a potentially promising avenue for pre-hypertensive and hypertensive individuals to lower and/or stabilize their blood pressure in a time efficient, effective manner. The proposed study looks to identify if a modified SIT protocol would be effective in reducing resting BP and HR, both acutely and with chronic training in middle aged adults.

column36: Modelling Serous Cancers of the Mullerian Tract using Organoids
column37: Ovarian cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death in women. Our study focuses on two subtypes of ovarian cancer: high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) of the ovary and low-grade serous carcinoma (LGSC) of the ovary. HGSC is an aggressive type and accounts for up to 70% of all ovarian cancer cases. LGSC is less aggressive, but also much less common (5% of all ovarian cancer cases). Because LGSC is so rare, it is poorly understood. HGSC is often not diagnosed until the cancer is widespread. Treatment for ovarian cancer has not been updated for over 30 years, despite the fact that many women fail therapy to or develop resistance of the drugs. In spite of their differences, HGSC and LGSC are thought to both come from the same type of cells in the Fallopian tube. As a result, we hypothesize that different detrimental changes (mutations) in DNA lead to the initiation and progression of the two distinct subtypes. To model the initiation process, we adopt the novel organoid system wherein we take normal fallopian tube cells and grow them in specialized conditions so that they form 3D structures resembling small organs. We will introduce different mutations specific to HGSC and LGSC into healthy Fallopian tube-organoids and study changes in cells. Cutting-edge sequencing technologies will be utilized to study the changes on a single-cell level. The combination of organoid and single-cell technology well-position us to address the question of how HGSC and LGSC of the ovary occur in the first place. Understanding why and how cancer occur could considerably open up venues for developing early detection and prevention strategies, as well as more targeted therapies for different patients.

column36: Dual-Task Gait Assessment May Predict Future Cognitive Decline in a Memory Clinic Setting
column37: My research project explores the usefulness a dual-task test, or "walking and talking" test, to predict which patients in memory clinics are at higher risk of progressing to dementia. Physical symptoms, such as a slowed walking speed, may be some of the earliest indicators of Alzheimer's disease, and may be detectable even before memory impairments. Recently, it has been shown that patients with a more pronounced slow down when walking and talking (when compared to just walking) may be more likely to progress to dementia, but this test has not been thoroughly studied in a clinic setting. Based on previous research, we expect that patients who slow down a large amount during the dual-task test will be more likely to be diagnosed with dementia in the future. We will be collecting retrospective data from patient charts at the Aging Brain and Memory Clinic (Parkwood Institute) to see if this test is helpful in better evaluating risk of dementia. We will also be able to compare patients original test performance with performance at their next clinic visit, which is 2-3 years later. The dual-task test is performed in a hallway outside the clinic, where there is a measured distance marked on the floor. Patients are timed as they walk down the hallway to calculate their walking speed. First, patients walk at their usual speed, and then they are asked to walk while doing cognitive tasks, such as listing animal names and counting backwards. This research will potentially improve our ability to diagnose cognitive impairments and to identify patients who are at high risk for developing dementia. This earlier detection could lead to further research on early risk factors for cognitive impairments and also improve the efficacy of both pharmaceutical and lifestyle interventions.

column36: Spinal Cord Repair and Regeneration
column37: Effect of Glial-derived Neurotrophic Factor and Tetanus Toxin Light Chain Expression in Neural Progenitor Cells After Spinal Cord Injury Spinal cord injuries (SCI) have devastating physical impacts due to loss of motor function, especially of hands, and lack of restorative treatments. In search of therapeutic strategies, our lab has shown that in a rat model of cervical SCI (cSCI), forelimb function can improve by neural progenitor cell (NPC) transplants which replace lost neural cells and promote tissue sparing. Additionally, glial derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) has shown promising results in increasing graft survival and number of stem cells that can differentiate into neurons. However, molecular mechanisms behind NPC and GDNF-mediated neural circuit formation and functional recovery remain unclear. To address this gap, a protein that blocks transmission between neurons, tetanus toxin light chain (TeTxLC), will be expressed in GDNF expressing NPCs. Blocking transmission with TeTxLC, thus inhibiting proper integration of the stem cells into the host, will highlight the importance of synaptic integration on NPC differentiation, neuronal connectivity, and functional recovery compared to other potential mechanisms of stem-cell mediated recovery. The experiments will take place both in vitro and in vivo in rats injured at C6/7 level of the spinal cord. I hypothesize that GDNF will promote integration of NPCs into host circuits and enhance motor recovery; effects which will be diminished by TeTxLC. The understanding of mechanisms behind how NPCs and GDNF promote formation of neural circuits and functional recovery will allow for taking further steps closer to incorporating treatment strategies involving stem cells into the clinic for people suffering from SCI.

column36: A Novel Mouse Model of Endometriosis with Epithelial-Restricted Cancer-Drivers
column37: Endometriosis is a condition where uterine endometrial tissue is found outside of the uterus, and it affects approximately 10-15% of reproductive-aged women and causes a variety of debilitating symptoms, such as painful periods, discomfort during intercourse, and infertility. Therapeutic technologies are available to help relieve patients of some of their symptoms; however, more research needs to be done in order to improve the available therapies and to develop new technologies for patients who desire to conceive. The development of a novel mouse model is vital for future studies on endometriosis that will allow for the evolution of our knowledge on the disease and of potential treatments. The most common mutation found in endometriosis typically results in the cell growth seen in cancer; however, the role of this mutation in endometriosis is currently unknown. This animal model will express the mutation in the uterine tissue layer of the mouse, comparable to where it is typically found in human endometriosis. This project will involve a donor-recipient model system for endometriosis. Recipient mice will be injected with endometrial tissue from donor mice that exhibit the mutation in the outer lining of the inside of the uterus. The implants will be injected into the abdominal cavity, outside of the uterus in recipient mice, in order to mimic true endometriosis in humans. The lesions will then be collected and various biomarkers associated with endometriosis and pelvic pain will be monitored and compared to what is seen in true endometriosis. The development of an accurate model will allow us to better understand the role of cancer-driver mutations in endometriosis, and it will be used in future studies for therapeutic symptom relieve in women with endometriosis.

column36: CGS/OGS Application for Masters of Medical Sciences Fall 2019 (Jae Hyun Byun)
column37: The discovery of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type-9 (PCSK9) has provided a novel therapeutic to combat against cardiovascular disease (CVD). Secreted by the liver, PCSK9 binds to cell-surface low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor to enhance its degradation, thereby reducing the capacity of the liver to clear LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) from circulation. Monoclonal antibodies targeted against PCSK9 have demonstrated to significantly reduce circulating LDL-C of approximately 50-60% in patients deemed high risk of cardiovascular events. Despite its initial success, the high cost in the manufacturing of these monoclonal antibodies provides context in the need for novel therapeutics and alternative modalities in the reduction of circulating PCSK9. Genetic screens reveal that gain-of-function (GOF) mutations in the PCSK9 gene represent the third locus associated with autosomal-dominant hypercholesterolemia. Accordingly, individuals with the loss-of-function (LOF) variant exhibit increased expression of the hepatic LDL receptor (LDLR) and a concomitant reduction in circulating LDL-C levels. In particular, LOF variants including PCSK9 Q152H were identified and extensively studied due to the inability of endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident PCSK9 to undergo autocatalytic cleavage, an essential step for its maturation and secretion out of the ER. Thus, the retention of PCSK9 in the ER accounts for the increased LDLR expression and reduced circulating LDL-C levels attributed to the LOF variants. As such, the focus of this study is to assess ER stress and liver toxicity as a potential consequence of retaining PCSK9 in the ER. Our findings will determine if this approach will represent a safe novel strategy to provide a cost-effective solution in combatting against CVD.

column36: Equity in health care utilization among Indigenous populations in Canada
column37: Equity in health care utilization is one of the primary objectives legislated in the Canada Health Act (1984). The Canadian government has also brought inequities in health faced by Indigenous peoples to the forefront with documents like the Truth and Reconciliation Committee's "Calls to Action". Notwithstanding such concern about equity in health care (access to health care based on individual's need), there have been few studies that assess inequities in health care utilization in Canada, especially within Indigenous peoples. This research will, for the first time, aim to quantify trends in income-related inequities in four measures of health care utilization, GP visits, dental care visits, specialist visits and mental health-related visits within the four distinct Indigenous groups living off-reserve in Canada: registered First-Nations, non-registered First-Nations, Metis and Inuit. This study will use data from the Aboriginal Peoples Surveys (APS) conducted by Statistics Canada in 2001, 2006, 2012 and 2017. This research will fill a gap in the literature surrounding the issues related to equity in health care within Indigenous peoples in Canada. The findings may help in creating strategies to reduce inequities in health care in the future.

column36: The influence of genetically variable CYP2A13 on lung cancer risk in smokers
column37: Smoking-related lung cancer represents one of the most preventable health burdens worldwide and one of the leading causes of premature death in Canada. A major contributor to lung cancer risk is genetic variation between individual smokers. One genetic risk factor that may contribute to these variations is a cytochrome P450 enzyme, CYP2A13. CYP2A13 plays a major role in the activation of tobacco-derived nitrosamines into carcinogens. My research will focus on understanding how genetic changes in the CYP2A13 gene may influence lung cancer risk. Past research on CYP2A13 genetic variation has highlighted reduced smoking-derived lung cancer risk in an East Asian population. However, these findings could only conclude that East Asian smokers with reduced CYP2A13 activity have lower lung cancer risk-which may or may not be the same in other racial populations like African Americans or Caucasians. The reason behind this suspicion is due to major genetic differences seen between different races. For example, despite lower cigarette consumption, African American smokers experience a higher risk of lung cancer compared to other smokers. My research will focus on understanding how genetic changes in the CYP2A13 gene may affect lung cancer risk in other racial groups of African American and Caucasian smokers. Ultimately, my research on CYP2A13 genetic variation may highlight an understudied genetic risk factor for smoking-derived lung cancer and may potentially be included in future genetic screenings to optimize lung cancer prevention programs for smokers.

column36: Combating genome instability with the SMX tri-nuclease complex
column37: The human genome encodes for critical biological information that ensure survival. Should the genome be damaged, the information encoded within would be altered, thereby leading to mutations. In turn, these mutations can promote a wide range of diseases, from cancer to neurodegeneration. Most prominent sources of DNA damage are environmental, such as ultraviolet radiation. Strikingly, the innate properties of the genome, such as the sequence of the DNA itself, can promote large aberrant structures that impede crucial processes that maintain the stability of the genome. In turn, these structures induce gross rearrangement of the genome and thereby introduce harmful mutations. Therefore, DNA repair pathways are vital to the health of the genome and of the individual. Humans employ a wide assortment of proteins called the SMX tri-nuclease complex, which consist of SLX4-SLX1, MUS81-EME1, and XPF-ERCC1, that is essential for repairing damage-inducing structures. Moreover, mutations in SMX have been associated with an array of diseases, including Xeroderma pigmentosa, Cockayne syndrome and Fanconi anemia. The SMX complex has been shown to repair sites in the genome that are known to produce deleterious structures; however, the human genome likely contains many more unidentified regions. In this proposal, I present my aims to identify precise genomic targets of SMX and to study the variation in target range in various genetic disorders. My research will elucidate the substrate repertoire of SMX and progress our understanding of the role of the SMX complex in genome maintenance and genetic disorders.

column36: Somatostatin antagonism in Type 2 Diabetes: a novel strategy for optimizing glycemic control
column37: For individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D), glucose-lowering medications are often necessary to regain control over blood glucose (BG) regulation in order to avoid disease-related complications, such as heart and kidney disease, blindness, and nerve damage. Though strict maintenance of BG within a tight range confers the greatest protect against these complications, it is often unattainable due to the risk of hypoglycemia, or low BG. If untreated, symptoms of hypoglycemia can progress from hunger and lightheadedness, to seizure, coma, and even death. Unlike insulin-producing beta cells, these medications incapable of detecting and responding to fluctuations in blood glucose levels, and as a result, they will continually lower BG, even as it approaches and enter the hypoglycemic range. To make matters worse, each exposure to hypoglycemia progressively impair's the body's defences against future episodes, which includes physiological warning signs, like hunger. Patients often raise their BG targets due to fear of hypoglycemia, forcing them to accept a greater risk of long-term complications. This highlights the urgency for better preventative strategies. My laboratory has recently tested a drug, called SSTR2a, that was successful in preventing hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetic rats. It works by blocking the effects of somatostatin, which is a hormone that reduces glucagon activity. As a result, glucagon, the hormone responsible for raising BG levels, was able to maintain stable BG, even in response to an excessive dose of insulin. The goal of my research is to test SSTR2a in rats with T2D. This drug has the potential to change the future of T2D management by relieving the barrier to optimal BG control, while offering more lifestyle freedom and piece of mind.

column36: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing to predict post-surgical complications in patients with colorectal cancer separated by sex
column37: Cancer surgery places great physiological stress on a patient, even if it is intended to ultimately improve their condition. If a patient is not in adequate physical condition to cope with this stress, surgery can cause serious complications, longer hospital stays, higher readmission rates, reduced patient quality of life and physical function, as well as increased morbidity and mortality. Recent studies indicate that cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is an objective evaluation of fitness which may provide surgeons with the ability to better assess the risk in these patients. The goals of this project are 1) to test whether pre-surgical CPET can predict post-surgical outcomes in our colorectal cancer patient population; 2) to explore whether CPET can predict risk equally in men and women or whether there are sex-based differences in the information provided by CPET testing in the pre-operative time frame, and 3) to investigate whether CPET is feasible for colorectal cancer patients awaiting cancer resection. By conducting CPET on 250 colorectal cancer patients (equal males and females represented) at baseline and immediately prior to surgery and collecting data on various post-surgical complications, this project will provide important information for risk assessment, identification of patients who would benefit from pre-surgical intervention, tailoring of healthcare needs, medical cost value and, ultimately, for improving quality of life.

column36: Implementation of predictive analytics in primary care
column37: Acute care utilization rates in Canada are among the highest for developed countries with universal health care;1 this is in part driven by Canadians visiting emergency departments (EDs) or who are hospitalized for conditions that could be ameliorated by timely primary care intervention.2 The increased penetration of EMRs in primary care settings presents an opportunity to use predictive analytics to help clinicians reduce preventable hospital use.9 However, the successful uptake of any health information tool is predicated upon its designed ability to integrate within existing clinical workflows, while improving the clinician's user experience. As part of an ongoing effort to develop and implement a real-time EMR-integrated predictive risk model within the workflow of routine primary care, the proposed research 1) identifies the critical features of a predictive model required for its adoption by primary care physicians, and 2) pilots this novel predictive model in a primary care setting. I will use multiple qualitative methods to analyze primary care clinical workflows and characterize how primary care providers interact with patient data in the EMR, including time-motion studies and focus groups. Results will inform model development and user-computer interface design. I will act as project coordinator in the piloting of this model, developing the study protocol and research ethics board applications, as well as liaising between biostatisticians and the primary care providers involved in the study. We plan to publish the results of this work as a guiding framework for the implementation of other predictive analytic tools in Canadian primary care settings.

column36: Screening for toxicity of emerging chemicals
column37: In recent years, import, production and use of chemicals that have been shown to be endocrine disruptor compounds (EDCs) have been regulated. These compounds include bisphenol A (BPA), bis (2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) and 2,2'4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (BDE-47) which belong to the families of bisphenols, phthalates and brominated flame retardants respectively. They are found in plastics and food packaging products. These compounds are being replaced by emerging products whose ECDs potential are still unknown. We propose to screen their toxicity in vitro and to compare it with the products they replace by using an organ culture model of rat fetal testes, an organ sensitive to variations of steroid hormones. Disruption of androgen levels during fetal life is associated with abnormalities of testicular development. Our culture model allows to reproduce ex vivo the normal development of the testis while preserving intercellular communications. This method has already been used to evaluate the effects of BPA and MEHP, the main active metabolite of DEHP. Rat testes, sampled at 15 days of gestation, are deposited on filters floating on a culture medium without serum. One testis is deposited on a control medium and the contralateral on a culture medium supplemented with a compound of interest. Replacements known to be already present in consumer products will be tested and compared with the original compounds. Basal and LH-stimulated testosterone secretions will be measured by ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay). Morphology, number and proliferation rate of the main cell types of the testis will be analyzed by immunofluorescence. The obtained results will help the risk assessment of emerging chemicals and establish if these require further toxicological studies and regulations.

column36: Melanoma Specific Codon Optimization in Oncolytic Virotherapy
column37: A cancer cell results from a healthy cell that becomes mutated in specific genes which cause it to divide out of control and resist regular cell death. Around half of all melanoma cases arise from a mutation in a gene called BRAF, with the most common mutation being called BRAFV600E. Tumours which have this mutation often become resistant to chemotherapy and the cancer relapses. Recently, scientists found that the melanoma cells with this BRAFV600E mutation change the way they make proteins from DNA. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is essentially an instruction manual to produce proteins, which are components of the cell. One can think of an Ikea manual used to assemble wardrobes. Hypothetically, the Ikea manual could be rewritten in a way that helps the builder assemble the wardrobe more efficiently. Similarly, scientists are able to make small changes in DNA so that the proteins made from it are assembled faster. This proposal outlines a strategy in which we can rewrite the DNA manual so that only the BRAFV600E melanoma can efficiently assemble proteins from it, whereas healthy cells will take much longer. We are interested in this is because our cancer therapy uses viruses to deliver DNA into cancer cells. The DNA that we deliver contains instructions to make toxic proteins that kill the cancer. By redesigning the DNA to make it easy for the melanoma to read, the toxins will be be made efficiently inside the tumour, but poorly in healthy tissues. I predict this effect will be even more powerful against BRAFV600E tumours that have acquired resistance to chemotherapy, which could make our viruses a beneficial addition to treatment regimens. This idea of "optimizing" DNA for easy-reading in cancer will open doors for improving DNA-based cancer therapies like ours.

column36: Using a smartphone based application to improve diet quality among high school students in London Ontario.
column37: Among Canadian teens, diet quality tends to decrease around the age of 14 years old and remain low into adulthood. For example, less than half of Canadians aged 12 and older eat the recommended daily servings of fruit and vegetables. Adolescence is a crucial time for interventions promoting positive dietary behaviors due to their increased independence in decision-making involving eating habits and food purchasing. One method to influence diet quality is to increase food literacy. Food literacy is defined as "a collection of inter-related knowledge, skills, and behaviors required to plan, manage, select, prepare, and eat food to meet needs and determine intake." Accordingly, creative and research-driven food literacy programming would help youth better understand the context of their choices. Therefore, as part of the Human Environments Analysis Laboratory at Western University, we are developing a novel smartphone intervention called SmartAPPetite. The overarching goals of SmartAPPetite is to improve food literacy, food quality, and gently nudge youth to choose smarter food options. SmartAPPetite features food facts, tips and tricks, teenager appropriate recipes, and external links that contain additional resources such as Dietitian approved videos and engaging food articles. The messaging presented in the app is also developed and/or approved by Registered Dietitians, who are nutrition experts. The primary objective of my thesis will be to assess the effectiveness of SmartAPPetite to improve the diet quality of teen users. I will determine what aspects of the application were most engaging to the teen users and which aspects had the greatest influence on diet quality improvement, providing insight into the effectiveness of SmartAPPetite to engage with youth and improve diet quality.

column36: Exploring and Evaluating the Effectiveness of Cultural Safety Training for Point of Care Registered Nurses
column37: Historical and ongoing colonialism continues to be a main cause of poor health outcomes for Indigenous peoples. The effects of colonialism often manifest through systemic and interpersonal racism towards Indigenous people. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) of Canada (2015) has called on health care systems to address the health inequities Indigenous people face through changes in policy and practice. One intervention with significant promise is the implementation of Indigenous cultural safety training. Cultural safety is defined as a practice that enables health care providers to reflect on the ways they provide equitable care by considering the effects of power inequities, social justice, self-determination, and the decolonization of systems and structures. Cultural safety training has been implemented to different degrees and in different ways within the health sector however, there remains a significant gap in evaluating and assessing the effectiveness of cultural safety programming. Measuring the effectiveness of cultural safety programming ensures that these interventions are working to promote health equity for Indigenous people. The proposed study will explore and evaluate the effectiveness of cultural safety training for point of care registered nurses (RNs). The indicators of effective cultural safety learning and uptake will be measured using the following: 1) how nurses acknowledge their complicities in harm, 2) understand what needs to change, and 3) how they have taken action on their practice settings to disrupt everyday racism. Results and recommendations will support health care institutions, professional nursing organizations, and government with the development and evaluation of cultural safety programming.

column36: Non-Nutritive Sweetened Beverages and Risk of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
column37: Worldwide rates of diabetes are increasing making them an important challenge in healthcare. Excess intakes of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), such as pop, may lead to diabetes. One way to limit SSB intake is by replacing them with water or non-nutritive sweetened beverages (NSBs), such as diet pop, which contain non-nutritive sweeteners (NNSs). Health authorities recommend water instead of NSBs as the best replacement for SSBs, however, SSB consumers may not accept water as it lacks a sweet taste. Health Canada has determined that NNSs are safe for human consumption, yet, recent reports suggest that NNSs may increase the risk of diabetes. One study suggested that NSBs may raise blood sugars in humans by changing gut bacteria. While this study had various limitations including testing only one type of NNS and having no control group, it led to a lot of media attention which labelled all NNSs as harmful. Whether NNSs in NSBs raise future risk of diabetes is unclear. My research will be done in two parts. Part 1 will be a summary and analysis of all published studies that compared NSBs to water on risk factors for diabetes. Part 2 will be a clinical trial consisting of three interventions (SSB, NSB and water). Eligible participants will be daily SSB consumers who are overweight and healthy. Blood sugar levels will be measured from an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at the beginning and end of each intervention. This will be the first trial done in humans looking into how NSBs compare to water as SSB replacements on future diabetes risk. Together, these projects will update current practice guidelines providing healthcare professionals with evidence on how NSBs compare to water as replacements for SSBs for the prevention of diabetes.

column36: Pilot Randomized Control Trial Investigating Tai-chi/Qigong for Older Adults with Bipolar Disorder
column37: It is expected that by 2030, the percentage of patients with bipolar disorder (BD) over 60 years of age will exceed 50% of all patients with BD. Despite this, there is a lack of research specific to older adults (age 60+) with bipolar disorder (OABD). In this population, poor cognition and persistent sub-syndromal depressive symptoms are particularly common, difficult to treat, associated with mood relapse, and poor daily functioning. As there are no current evidence-based treatments for cognition in OABD and current pharmacotherapies are limited, not effective in cognition, and often poorly-tolerated, there an urgent need to find alternative interventions for OABD. Mind-body interventions has increasingly been found to be effective in treating several psychiatric condition including BD. A few pilot studies examining mindfulness-based intervention in younger adult BD have been promising for depressive symptoms, but some pilot research by our team suggest that patients with OABD may benefit more from moving mindfulness, which is more accessible, requires less baseline cognitive abilities and allow easier engagement with mindfulness. Our study is a 12-week pilot randomized control trial (RCT) comparing 1h/week sessions of Tai-chi/Qigong (treatment) vs. light exercise (active control) in 30 OABD patients (age ? 50) to assess whether Tai-chi-Qigong, a form of moving mindfulness, is effective in 1) improving depressive symptoms, 2) preventing mood relapse, and 3) improving cognition in OABD. Pariticipants will be measured for depression and cognition at 0 weeks (baseline), 12 weeks (primary endpoint), and 24 weeks (long-term assessment), and results will be compared between the treatment and active control groups.

column36: Using Structural and Functional Neuroimaging to Investigate the Relationship Between Memory and Hearing Loss
column37: This study aims to investigate how hearing loss can alter the brain's functions and structures related to memory. Event-related potentials, electrical measurements of the brain's responses to a stimulus, will be used to look at a pattern called the late-positive component (LPC), which occurs when people recognize a word. 3 groups will be included: people with significant (50 dB) hearing loss with hearing aids, people with significant hearing loss with no treatment, and a control group. Including a group with and without hearing aids is important because the effect of hearing aids on cognition is unclear. In the first phase of the experiment, participants will be shown 50 nouns, and asked to remember them. Then they will do mental math for 12 minutes as a distraction from rehearsing the words. In the testing phase participants will be shown 100 nouns and asked to indicate if the words are old (from the first phase) or new (not yet presented). During the testing phase, participant's electrical brain patterns will be recorded to measure the LPC differences between the 3 groups. Participants will also being doing an experiment which uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to look at the structures and functions of the brain. These results will be used to investigate structures of the brain that may be related to hearing loss and memory. The hippocampus, a brain structure related to memory, has been found to be significantly different in mice with hearing loss compared to mice with typical hearing. This structure has also been associated with the LPC response in humans. Hearing loss is the biggest potentially modifiable risk factor for dementia, and by adding to our understanding of how hearing loss is related to memory may help prevent dementia.

column36: Dissecting the Injured Spinal Cord Microenvironment to Optimize Neural Stem Cell Transplantation
column37: Over 1 million North Americans live with spinal cord injury (SCI), yet there is no effective treatment for patients in the chronic stage. In SCI, the neurons of the spinal cord become damaged which leads to the loss of motor skills and sensory abilities. With the development of regenerative medicine, stem cells have become an exciting treatment option to repair and replace dead neurons. While transplanting neural stem cells into the spinal cord is a promising approach, studies testing stem cells in chronic SCI have only shown modest effects due to the post-injury scar tissue that blocks regeneration. My strategy will be to break down the major component of the scar tissue, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs), to improve the regenerative effect of neural stem cells. However, CSPGs are also important in the uninjured spinal cord. In fact, lower levels of CSPGs play a role in normal development and maintenance of the healthy regions in the spinal cord. Therefore, it is important to only target the excess CSPGs in the injured regions while preserving the normal levels. In my project, I will create human neural stem cells that respond to the CSPG levels in their environment by breaking down only the excess amounts while preserving the low levels of CSPGs. To do this, I will use state-of-the-art genetic sequencing to better understand how CSPGs interact with neural stem cells. Then, I will use new gene editing technology to genetically engineer more effective neural stem cells for regeneration. Ultimately, the results of my project will present a new regenerative therapy that may improve the lives of millions of patients who live with SCI.

column36: Impact of the tegument proteins VP16 and VP22 on the replication of herpes simplex virus type 1
column37: Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) is a ubiquitous human pathogen that causes common ailments such as cold sores and genital herpes but can also cause serious diseases like encephalitis. In conversations surrounding viral fitness and spread, the DNA elements of HSV-1 are normally discussed, however the number and amount of proteins present in a single virion likely play a role in infection. My project focuses on adjusting the amount of certain proteins, VP22 and VP16, found in infectious viral particles to determine their role in HSV-1 infection. Previous work in our lab has shown that high VP22- and VP16-expressing viruses are better at infecting human cell lines, but the biological relevance has not been confirmed. I will be using a bacterial recombination system to insert an inducible gene promoter in front of our genes of interest. This will allow me to adjust protein expression by adding different levels of activating drug, which will be more precise than the classic knockout/overexpression system. Once my two viruses are made, I will be testing them in cell culture to confirm our previous findings, before exploring the biological role in a mouse model. By determining if changes in expression of key virion proteins effect infectivity, we can explore how exactly the virus modulates its expression which may lead us to a mechanism that can be exploited to stop infection.

column36: Morphine: A Novel Adjunct to Maximize the Benefits of Exercise Training in Adults with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease?
column37: Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) is a proven intervention for alleviating symptom burden and improving functional capacity in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Supervised exercise training (ExT) is the cornerstone of PR. ExT performed at high compared with low intensities has more positive effects on exercise capacity, symptom burden and quality of life in COPD patients. However, many COPD patients become too short of breath to exercise at high intensities for a long enough time to obtain associated benefits. Thus, research is needed to identify new ways to help increase the intensity of exercise that adults with COPD can perform so that the positive effects of ExT can be maximized. This study will test the hypothesis that 5-weeks of three times weekly ExT with morphine (ExT+MOR) versus placebo (ExT+PLA) will yield greater improvements in exercise tolerance and exertional breathlessness during constant-load cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) at 75% peak power output, in 34 adults with advanced COPD. Participants will be randomized to receive MOR (0.1 mg/kg body mass) or PLA 30-min prior to each ExT session. Furthermore, they will rate the intensity of their breathlessness at rest and at regular intervals during CPET using Borg's 0-10 scale, while cardiac, metabolic, gas exchange and ventilatory parameters will be measured via metabolic cart. The primary outcome will be the ExT-induced change in exercise endurance time (min) during constant-load CPET and the co-primary outcome will be the ExT-induced change in Borg scale intensity ratings of breathlessness during exercise at isotime. The results of this study have the potential to help maximize the positive physiologic and clinical effects of ExT in symptomatic adults with advanced COPD.

column36: One Health Clinics to Improve Public Health and Promote Access to Primary Healthcare for Vulnerable Populations
column37: One Health clinics are interdisciplinary outreach clinics coordinated by veterinary and human healthcare teams with the primary objective to improve public health by providing free health services to vulnerable individuals and their pets. One Health clinics improve public health by increasing access to primary care services and leveraging the benefits of human-animal bond to promote uptake of human health services. The proposed project will examine the results of this outreach model in Kelowna and Vancouver, two communities highly impacted by homelessness and substance use. Since December 2016, ten One Health clinics have taken place, connecting over 400 marginalized people and their pets to healthcare services that may otherwise not have been accessed. Preliminary data from the clinics suggest that over half of the clients served reported no connection to primary health care separate from their attendance at the One Health clinics. This data not only demonstrates the benefits for individuals accessing services at these clinics, but also highlights the potential value that this developing program has on public health and an overburdened healthcare system. I will be evaluating this program as part of my academic studies in the Masters of Nursing Science Program at the University of British Columbia. The plan for my research is to perform a mixed method study examining existing quantitative data from the One Health clinics and conduct semi-structured interviews with clinic participants to enhance understanding of the factors that limit this population from engaging in healthcare services. This clinical research demonstrates significant potential in its application to increase access to the healthcare system and improve the health of our most vulnerable Canadians.

column36: Characterizing the protein-protein interactions associated with Ataxin-1
column37: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive loss of coordination and balance, difficulties with speech and swallowing, muscle stiffness, and weakness in the muscles that control eye movement. Currently, there is no treatment for SCA1. Patients typically survive 10-30 years after diagnosis. This disease is caused by a mutation in the ataxin-1 protein, specifically the expansion of glutamine repeats in the coding region of the protein. Despite our understanding that the mutated protein causes toxicity primarily in the cerebellum, the function of ataxin-1 is unknown. Ataxin-1 has been shown to interact with several proteins involved in gene expression, and these interactions are dysregulated in mice with SCA1. To our knowledge, the interaction of ataxin-1 with these proteins has not been studied in the context of humans. In several other disease models, mice do not recapitulate human disease, emphasizing the importance of human model systems in disease research. We hypothesize that the protein interactions associated with ataxin-1 will be dysregulated in cells taken from SCA1 patients. In this study, we aim to develop a SCA1 patient cell line with fluorescently tagged ataxin-1, which allows for the visualization of ataxin-1 protein interactions. The protein interactions in SCA1 patient cell lines can be compared to that in unaffected cells, in order to identify differences in ataxin-1 protein interactions. This could provide valuable insight into the normal function of ataxin-1, as well as potential mechanisms for SCA1 development.

column36: Exploring challenges, motivators and community engagement strategies relating to researchers' experiences of conducting biological health research involving biospecimen in Indigenous contexts
column37: Trauma from Indian Residential Schools has shown to influence gene expression, increase the risk of disorders including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and cardiovascular disease. As such, there is a need to identify disease markers within Indigenous populations specifically, as the shared negative effects of colonization have influenced the expression of genetic material and changed disease risk It will be necessary for Indigenous communities to participate in biological research if they are to benefit from it, as the presence of various biomarkers can vary both across and within ethno-racial groups, as can biomarkers' influence on health and wellness. Historically, Indigenous persons' participation in biological health research projects has been complicated by mistrust, lack of cultural familiarity of the research, and a lack of community understanding of the benefit of participation. The unwillingness of Indigenous communities to participate is thus likely a reflection of historical inequities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians, which are perpetuated today. The purpose of this research is thus to explore the experiences of Canadian researchers who have conducted biological health research involving biospecimen collection in Indigenous contexts to identify common concerns, perceived benefits, and reasons for communities' willingness to participate. Similar research has been conducted exploring the experiences of researchers conduction biological health research that did not involve biospecimens collection. Consequently, this project will provide unique insight for future policy development for respectful biospecimen collection with Indigenous populations.

column36: Investigating the Host-Pathogen Interactions of the Human Fungal Pathogen Candida albicans
column37: Investigating the Interactions of the Fungal Pathogen Candida albicans with Human Immune Cells Candida albicans is the leading cause of human fungal infections, which collectively result in more than 1.5 million deaths per year, as many as the pathogens causing tuberculosis and malaria. There are a limited number of antifungal drugs available and even those are troubled by issues of both patient toxicity and the emergence of drug-resistant fungi. Developing a deeper understanding of the interactions of C. albicans with human immune cells could lead to new avenues for antifungal drug discovery. The first line of defence against fungal infections are cells of the human immune system called macrophages that engulf C. albicans but are ineffective at killing them. Engulfment triggers a physical change in C. albicans from yeast to filaments - a transition important for the fungi's ability to cause disease. Identifying the genetic circuitry underlying C. albicans filamentation could uncover therapeutic targets, but the mechanism of filamentation in macrophages remains largely unknown. The goal of my research is to identify the macrophage component that triggers C. albicans filamentation and to determine the circuitry that C. albicans uses to respond to this cue. Our lab recently identified a group of small modified proteins as potential triggers and I will conduct biochemical analyses to determine which of these proteins induce C. albicans filamentation. Additionally, I will perform experiments to determine the fungal genes required for turning on filamentation in response to the macrophage trigger. My project will identify key genetic circuitry for interactions between C. albicans and macrophages, which could reveal new therapeutic strategies for life-threatening disease.

column36: Genetic Modifiers of Eukaryotic Translation Termination
column37: Genes function as instruction manuals for making proteins, encoding transcripts that are ultimately decoded to make proteins that perform a vast array of functions in our cells. During the translation of these transcripts, certain sequences (termed stop or termination codons) signal to the cell machinery that the full-length protein has been synthesized and it is time to stop. Sometimes, however, this process can be disrupted by mutations that introduce premature termination codons (PTCs), resulting in the synthesis of truncated proteins. These mutations have been linked to many genetic diseases, such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, and a plethora of cancer syndromes. Therefore, developing strategies to "mask" stop codon recognition and re-initiate production of full-length proteins in order to restore, at the very least, partial protein function could have significant therapeutic applications. In fact, certain drugs (eg. aminoglycosides) already do this and have been shown to reduce disease severity in cancer cells, but they only do so at very high concentrations that are eventually toxic. Another drug (Ataluren) that promotes readthrough of PTCs is already being used in Europe to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients, demonstrating the feasibility of suppressing stop codons as a form of therapy. In this project, we hope to better understand the mechanisms behind translation termination and how fidelity is maintained. To achieve this, we will design genetic screens using CRISPR technology to find suppressors of translation termination. Should we be successful, we would elucidate a process that is currently poorly understood while potentially uncovering novel therapeutic avenues for the treatment of many genetic diseases and cancers.
