column36: A pharmacological approach to inhibiting tumor growth and improving radiation response
column37: Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men. In solid tumors, the oxygen levels fluctuate due to abnormal tumor vasculature. The fluctuation in oxygen levels includes periods of low oxygen (hypoxia) followed by normal oxygen levels, known as reoxygenation. Hypoxia in prostate cancer causes treatment failure and poorer prognosis. Therefore, hypoxia is an attractive target to improving response to chemo- and radiotherapy. Our group has conducted a large-scale drug screen of 600 compounds to identify novel drugs that decrease proliferation of reoxygenated prostate cancer cells. The top hits of this screen were compounds called SB203580 and PI-828. The targets of these drugs are activated under hypoxic conditions, suggesting their importance in adaptation to hypoxia. My first aim is to identify whether these compounds better inhibit proliferation in reoxygenated prostate cancer cells. In my graduate training thus far, I have shown that SB203580 and PI-828 are more effective in decreasing proliferation in reoxygenated cells compared to cells in normal and low oxygen conditions. I will be conducting basic mechanistic studies of these drugs in hypoxia, normal oxygen, and reoxygenated cells to understand how these compounds exert their effects under different oxygenation conditions. My second aim is to test if SB203580 inhibits tumor growth and improves response to radiation treatment using a mouse model with tumors derived from patients. This is the first study to study SB203580 in a mouse model of cancer. This study has the potential to identify novel therapeutic agents for the treatment of hypoxic prostate cancer. Importantly, these mechanistic studies allow us to identify important pathways for adaptation to hypoxia that can be targeted for treatment.

column36: Effets des iniquites socio-economiques sur les problemes de sante a la naissance : le cas de l'Ile de Montreal
column37: Des iniquites socioeconomiques ont ete correlees avec certains problemes de sante chez les nouveau-nes aux Etats-Unis et au Royaume Uni. Or, il n'existe pas d'analyse specifique a l'Ile de Montreal quant aux effets des composantes socioeconomiques sur la sante infantile. La proximite geographique des iniquites socioeconomiques et l'acces a des centres de sante specialises en font un territoire pertinent a etudier pour des raisons d'equite sociale et de sante publique. Mon projet de recherche, sous reserve de l'approbation de la commission d'acces a l'information et du comite d'ethique, vise a utiliser les donnees des centres de naissances montrealais pour identifier l'effet du milieu socio-economique des parents sur la sante neonatale. Les donnees ont ete collectees de 2010 a 2015. Elles incluent des indicateurs de sante infantile intra-hospitalieres (mortalite, duree de sejour et acquisition d'infections nosocomiales), de meme que des variables prehospitalieres (poids a la naissance, prematurite et score Apgar). Etant donne le caractere quasi universel de la naissance en milieu hospitalier au Quebec, il est permis d'ecarter tout biais de selection des participants. A l'aide du code postal de l'enfant, il est possible de modeliser son milieu socio-economique. Je m'interesse egalement aux donnees economiques des quartiers voisins a celui de l'enfant, sous hypothese qu'il existe un effet du quartier sur la sante. Suivant ces donnees, je realiserai une analyse de regression pour detailler l'effet des iniquites socioeconomiques et spatiales sur l'etat de sante a la naissance. L'identification plus precise des facteurs socio-economiques et geographiques qui influencent la sante infantile permettra d'orienter les politiques publiques dans une optique de sante durable.

column36: Effectiveness of reconsolidation therapy with propranolol to treat adjustment disorder (AD) stemming from romantic betrayal: A 2-year follow-up
column37: Considering that romantic betrayal events can result in the development of an adjustment disorder (AD) in the betrayed partner, effective therapies with long-lasting benefits are needed for this population. The aim of the current study is to provide a follow-up assessment of romantically betrayed participants from a previous clinical trial, who received a trauma-focused intervention known as reconsolidation therapy to treat an AD. Research demonstrates that propranolol, a beta-blocker commonly used to treat hypertension, can dampen the emotional intensity of a memory when taken before memory recall. Propranolol does so by effectively disrupting memory reconsolidation, a process by which memories are reinforced. The previous study found that compared to participants on the wait-list, 4-6 sessions of reconsolidation therapy reduced stressor-related symptoms, and symptoms of depression and anxiety. Still, little is known of the long-term effectiveness of reconsolidation therapy. The current study will therefore examine whether reconsolidation therapy shows long-term benefits for romantically betrayed individuals with an AD. Compared to participants who did not complete the treatment, those who completed the treatment are expected to show a continued reduction in stressor-related, depression, and anxiety symptoms, 2-years following treatment. These findings may have important implications for understanding romantic betrayal as a stressful event leading to the development of AD and may further our understanding of effective treatments for this population.

column36: The Type I Interferon Response in Cancer Progression
column37: Type I interferon (IFN-I) signalling plays a role in both immunosuppressive and inflammation during chronic infections such as chronic viral infections and cancer, however IFN-I signalling is poorly understood in the context of cancer. IFN-I signalling contributes to T cell exhaustion and the expression of immunosuppressive ligands such as PD-L1, while IFN-I signalling blockades increases the population of TCF1+ T cells that are essential to maintaining the immune response during a chronic viral infection. It is likely that IFN-I signalling plays a similar role in cancer. Improved understanding of IFN-I signalling on immunosuppression in the context of cancer is crucial to the development of therapeutics to counter this process in the tumour microenvironment, and allow the immune system to act against cancer cells. I propose using a cancer mouse model to study the effects of an IFN-I blockade of immune cell populations and the expression of immunoregulatory ligands and receptors in the tumour microenvironment through flow cytometry. Using this data, studies on IFN-I blockades as a combinatory immunotherapy with other immunotherapies such as PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors can be conducted to investigate if there are any synergistic effects on tumour shrinkage. Combinatory therapy with IFN-I blockades could improve prognosis for cancers such as pancreatic cancers that are particularly resistant to current immunotherapies due to their high tumour burden leading to high immunosuppression.

column36: The Picture of Health? Eating Disorders and Weight Bias in Canadian Fitness Professionals
column37: Eating disorders (ED) are serious illnesses, and those suffering from them often use fitness centres to exercise. Research indicates ED symptoms are also elevated in gym attendees (McCabe & James, 2009), and most fitness professionals (FP) report having encountered clients with severe EDs (Manley, O'Brien, & Samuels, 2008; Wojtowicz, Alberga, Parsons, & von Ranson, 2015). In addition, studies indicate that FPs tend to harbour weight bias (Panza et al., 2018), suggesting they side with the dominant cultural values of appearance over health. Fitness centres and FPs therefore represent an untapped opportunity for ED prevention efforts. This study aims to provide a base-rate for ED symptomatology in Canadian FPs and to assess if these base-rates, along with ED history and weight bias, will predict a) FPs' ability to identify an ED in a client, and b) the likelihood of endorsing extreme diet and exercise for that client. Higher levels of ED symptoms and weight bias are hypothesized to predict a) lower accuracy in ED identification and b) more support for extreme diet and fitness goals. ED history is expected to moderate these relationships. FPs will be recruited in partnership with Canadian fitness centres and regulatory bodies. In addition to completing measures assessing ED symptoms and weight bias, participants will read a vignette featuring a client with an ED. They will also be asked to classify the client's exercise behaviour and to select the type of fitness program they would recommend. Hypotheses will be evaluated using logistical regression. column36: Therapie cognitivo-comportementale de l'insomnie chez des personnes atteintes de depression; Integration de l'actigraphie avec une application mobile
column37: On estime que 80 a 90% des personnes atteintes de depression rapportent des perturbations significatives du sommeil. L'insomnie est liee a des symptomes depressifs plus severes et a un taux plus eleve de rechute de depression. La therapie cognitivo-comportementale pour l'insomnie (TCC-i) est un traitement bien etabli qui a egalement des effets benefiques pour les symptomes lies a la depression. Alors que le nombre limite de cliniciens specialises en TCC-i limite l'accessibilite au traitement, les applications pour telephones intelligents representent une piste de solution prometteuse. Developpe par des chercheurs en psychiatrie du sommeil, iREST est une nouvelle application mobile pour administrer la TCC-i tout en permettant l'integration de mesures objectives de sommeil collectees par actigraphie. Cette application comprend une plateforme interactive qui permet au clinicien traitant d'adapter la therapie de maniere dynamique et d'interagir avec l'usager pour offrir des conseils personnalises. Cette etude vise a evaluer l'efficacite de l'application iREST chez des personnes souffrant de depression qui presentent aussi des symptomes d'insomnie. De plus, cette etude examinera si l'integration de donnees objectives de sommeil (mesures ambulatoires) transmises en temps reel a l'application pour ajuster les parametres de la TCC-i augmente l'efficacite du traitement. Ces mesures objectives visent notamment a minimiser le biais des evaluations subjectives du sommeil, un phenomene souvent relie a la depression, et par consequent d'ameliorer la precision des manipulations de sommeil qui font partie de la TCC-i. Ce type de ressource est particulierement important pour les personnes vivant en milieu rural, incapable de se deplacer, ou en attente d'un clinicien.

column36: Pharmacokinetic evaluation of novel bone-targeting Parathyroid Hormone conjugates to treat Osteoporosis
column37: Currently, there are several classes of compounds used for the treatment and prevention of osteoporosis (OP). Due to patent expirations, lack of potency and selectivity, adverse events and toxicity concerns, companies are searching for novel drug classes to treat OP. To address these concerns, our lab has developed, synthesized and patented a bone-targeting variant of parathyroid hormone (PTH), by conjugation to bisphosphonate (BP) drug bone-seeking functional groups. The bisphosphonate-tethered PTH molecules are thereby able to be guided to the surfaces of bone where they interact with their specific receptors on the surface of bone cells. The objectives of this project are to refine the separation strategies for our BP-tethered PTH compound and determine the effective therapeutic index, toxicology and efficacy in comparison to unmodified parathyroid hormone using rat as an "in-vivo" animal model, in order to evaluate and prepare this novel bone-targeting compound for clinical trial. Our general hypothesis is that: Bisphosphonate-targeted delivery of parathyroid hormone to bone will increase its concentration to bone cell receptors at the site of its desired antiresorptive or anabolic actions, relative to its presentation to competing receptors in other organs and cells. The bone-targeting formulation of BP-tethered PTH represents a novel drug compound offers enormous promise in the reduction of serious side-effects experienced with current bone drugs and improved treatments for bone disease. This research will advance our understanding of how the body treats conjugated bone seeking peptide hormones and define new methodology capable of determining pharmacokinetic parameters of drug conjugates.

column36: Self-efficacy in Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Enrolled in Community-based Intervention and its Relation to Family Quality of Life
column37: Being a parent of a child with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can be challenging, given their deficits in social communication and their restrictive and repetitive behaviours and interests. Parents of children with ASD are shown to value their parenting role less, have less knowledge in parenting skills, and exhibit more stress than parents of typically developing children. Less well-studied in autism research is family quality of life, which encompasses how the family functions as a unit, the impact of the disorder on siblings, and the family's ability to engage in mutually important activities. We are interested in investigating whether self-efficacy in parents of preschoolers with ASD enrolled in a publicly-funded intervention program is related to family quality of life. Parental self-efficacy refers to the extent to which parents believe in their parenting skills and ability to influence their children's behaviour and development. Given Nova Scotia's innovative Early Intensive Behavioural Intervention program coaches parents in intervention strategies in their first week, we are particularly interested in exploring whether this coaching indirectly increases parents' self-efficacy and in turn, influences family quality of life. Further, we are interested in whether parents' accurate implementation of intervention strategies after coaching and at end-of-program together with their self-efficacy levels at end-of-program predict greater family quality of life. Given the accessibility of this program and the integral parent coaching component, we believe we are well-positioned to investigate these important constructs within this population.

column36: Engineering functionalized nanoparticles for HIV prevention
column37: It has been more than 30 years since the discovery of HIV-1 as the cause of AIDS and so far, there are no vaccines that exists to prevent HIV-1 infection. The challenge in developing an HIV-1 vaccine is that the virus is immensely diverse and can evade our immune system's responses. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) were recently discovered and individually, bNAbs can neutralize >90% of circulating HIV-1 isolates. Nevertheless, combining different bNAbs together in a single molecule, called bi-specific and tri-specific antibodies, can achieve near 100% neutralization with high potency. This breakthrough discovery has attracted considerable attention as bNAbs hold the promise of helping guide vaccine development, which can be used as a prophylactic against HIV-1. The Julien lab has developed and patented a novel protein-based nanoparticle platform to multimerize antibody fragments that bind to antigens (Fabs). Using the Fab-nanaoparticle technology, I will genetically engineer a functionalized nanoparticle that combines up to 24 different Fab regions of bNAbs in a single antibody prophylactic. The nanoparticle will increase breadth of coverage with high potency to surpass the activity of bi-specific and even tri-specific antibodies. To effectively translate the technology as an injectable prophylactic for HIV-1 prevention pre-clinically, I must assess its half-life, biodistribution, toxicity and immunogenicity. The study involves designing, expressing and purifying a fully mouse-derived functionalized nanoparticle to test in mice. The results of this study will guide the development of a fully human-derived functionalized nanoparticle and this novel approach will transform the field of HIV-1 antibody vaccine development and help end the HIV/AIDS pandemic.

column36: Exploring the quality and quantity of food provided to children outside of parental supervision.
column37: The high prevalence of childhood obesity in Canada is an important public health issue, requiring multiple difference treatment and prevention approaches. Research has shown that the food environment - in particular, readily available, cheap, and convenient foods high in calories and served in large portion sizes - is one important area of focus in addressing this issue. Much research has been conducted around consumption of food away from home (FAFH) in children and adults. This refers to food from fast food outlets, restaurants, and school lunch programs. However, little is known about the extent to which children receive foods away from home from non-parental sources (i.e., birthday parties, visits to family members, school events, doctors' offices, sporting events, etc.). This study will explore the quality and quantity of food that children in London, Ontario (ages 6-11) receive away from the home and outside of parental supervision. Parents and children will work together to fill out a daily self-report food log for food of this nature over a 2-week period. Following data collection, parents will be asked to participate in a focus group exploring attitudes towards and awareness of food provided to children outside the home. The proposed study will fill an important gap in the literature, potentially providing insight into childhood obesity prevention through regulation of foods and beverages provided to children in school and community settings. In addition, the results from this study will shed light on the prevalence of children's consumption of food outside of parental supervision. As well, it will set the stage for future research examining the impact of the food environment on children's overall health and wellbeing.

column36: Transcriptional Differences Between Males and Females in Childhood Group 4 Medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common childhood brain tumour and can be divided into four subgroups based on distinct clinical and molecular characteristics: Wingless, Sonic Hedgehog, Group 3 and Group 4. Group 4 MB is the most commonly diagnosed subgroup (35% of all MB cases) and cases are three times higher in boys than in girls. Furthermore, boys tend to have worse outcomes following standardized treatments than girls. While the higher incidence among males has been well documented, the biological underpinnings of these differences remain unknown. Due to the early age of onset and male bias in incidence, we suspect that there are inherent differences in gene expression by specific cell types during the development of the cerebellum, where these tumours are often diagnosed. Furthermore, we hypothesize that differences in these expressed genes predispose males to developing Group 4 MB. To investigate our hypothesis, we will compare gene expression in developing male and female mouse embryonic hindbrain using a powerful, new technique called single cell RNA sequencing. This gene expression will be matched to tumour gene expression profiles from male and female patients to identify genes that predispose males to developing Group 4 MB. Our research will bring us closer to understanding why Group 4 MB is more prevalent in males than in females, and what predisposes males to developing these tumors. Furthermore, this information will allow us to improve the standardized therapies and clinical outcomes of male patients diagnosed with these aggressive, childhood malignancies.

column36: Is a vegetarian diet in childhood associated with growth and micronutrient status?
column37: Vegetarian diets are becoming increasingly common among young adults and their children. In adults, vegetarian diets have been associated with positive health outcomes including lower risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and various cancers. However, the rapid growth of infants and children may place them at higher risk of nutritional inadequacy in the setting of dietary restriction when following a vegetarian diet. While vegetarian diets are presumed to be healthy due to increased intake of fruit, vegetables, fibre, whole grains, and reduced saturated fat, few studies have evaluated the impact of vegetarian diets on childhood growth and nutritional status. Outdated and conflicting evidence has formed uncertainty about the benefits or harms of vegetarian diets in childhood. This has led to conflicting international health professional recommendations and guidelines. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the association between vegetarian diet among healthy children 6 months to 10 years of age and adiposity. Secondary objectives include exploring the relationship between diet, height and iron and vitamin D stores. This study will use already collected data from Canada's largest children's cohort study - TARGet Kids!. TARGet Kids! is a collaboration between primary care physicians and researchers at the Hospital for Sick Children and St. Michael's Hospital, in Toronto, Canada. This will be the first Canadian study to evaluate the relationship between vegetarian diets in childhood and growth and nutrition. Results from this study will inform international child nutrition guidelines and provide important evidence to healthcare providers and policy makers about the potential benefits or risks of vegetarian diets for healthy Canadian children.

column36: The Role of Metacognition as a Mediating Variable Between Social Cognition and Functional Outcome in Chronic Schizophrenia
column37: Patients with Schizophrenia (SZ) demonstrate impairments associated with psychological processes necessary to encode and regulate information related to the intentions and behaviours of others; broadly referred to as social cognition (SC). Current antipsychotics fail to alleviate SC deficits despite the fact they show a stronger correlation with functioning than nonsocial cognitive deficits or clinical symptoms. This relationship highlights SC as a promising treatment target and has prompted the development of SC remediation programs. However, some reviews have suggested that this relationship may not be direct, prompting the identification of mediating variables. Metacognition (MC), a higher-order cognitive process facilitating an individual's ability to scrutinize mental states and cognitive products to support their integration and application into real world scenarios, has been proposed as a candidate variable. However, additional research is needed to elucidate the possible role of MC in the relationship between SC and functional outcome. The primary objectives of this study are to analyze the mediating role of MC in the relationships between four domains of SC (i.e. Theory of Mind, Emotional Processing, Social Perception, and Attributional Style) and measures of community functioning (e.g. capacity, social, & occupational) in a sample of chronic SZ patients. Results from this study will contribute to our understanding of the relationship between SC, MC, and functional outcome in SZ. From a clinical perspective, if MC is shown to mediate the relationship between SC performance and functional outcome then incorporating MC training into cognitive remediation programs could improve treatment effectiveness.

column36: Improving Immunotherapy for Lung Cancer Using Double-Negative T-Cells in Combination with Hypoxia-Reducing Manganese Dioxide Nanoparticles
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of all cancer-related deaths, with current therapies often ineffective. Recently, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising approach that utilizes the host immune system to fight cancer, but only a subset of patients are responsive. As a result, better treatments are urgently required. Discovered by our lab, double-negative T-cells (DNTs) are a distinct subset of mature T-cells that express CD3 in the absence of CD4 and CD8. They possess advantages such as the ability to inhibit the growth of established lung cancer tumors and acute myeloid leukemia without attacking normal cells. They also have the potential to be a safe and feasible off-the-shelf immunotherapy. Nonetheless, like other T-cell immunotherapies, DNTs are limited by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of solid tumors such as lung cancer. A key TME feature and barrier to treating solid tumors is hypoxia, a deficiency of oxygen in the tumor. It is a negative prognostic marker predicting poor survival and outcome in patients. Hypoxia inhibits T-cell function and tumor infiltration, while inducing T-cell death and exhaustion to suppress antitumor responses. Consequently, the purpose of my project is to investigate a novel combination therapy between DNTs and biocompatible hybrid manganese dioxide nanoparticles (LMD NPs) that reduce hypoxia. The effects of LMD NPs on the hypoxic TME, the mechanism by which TME modulations by NPs may improve DNT aspects such as function and infiltration, and the efficacy of the combination therapy in murine lung cancer models will be examined. In combining LMD NPs with DNTs, typical barriers prevalent in immunotherapy and the hostile TME of solid tumors may be overcome to further enhance the unique cellular therapy provided by DNTs.

column36: Temporary Employment and the Health of Canadian Workers
column37: Temporary employment is growing rapidly in Canada's labour market. It is typically characterized by part-time, subcontracted, and on call work, and is marked by precarity. In Canada, workers tend to find such jobs from temporary agencies. Those who occupy temporary work are often women, racialized people, and immigrants. As our job market becomes filled with precarious, unstable, and insecure jobs, it is more important than ever to understand the health impact of the changing nature of work. The aim of this research is to quantify the prevalence and distribution of temporary work exposure in the Canadian population, and more importantly, the association of temporary work with adverse health outcomes. Research from the US and Europe has demonstrated that temporary work exposures (eg. poor labour conditions, wage uncertainty) are major factors contributing to the development of health problems. This research would assess health outcomes such as occupational injuries, chronic health conditions, and self-rated mental health. Using population-based data sources such as the Canadian Community Health Survey and the Labour Force Survey, epidemiological methods (eg. descriptive statistics and multiple regression models) will be used to understand the relationship between temporary work and health. Particular attention will be given to how this association varies based on gender, ethnicity/race, and occupational groups. Understanding the association between temporary work and health outcomes would not only inform policy interventions to improve the well-being of Canadian workers, but can also shed light on health inequities in the labour market.

column36: Skeletal Muscle Repair in Healthy Young Men and Women With and Without Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
column37: Skeletal muscle is the largest organ system in the human body, and in addition to allowing us to move, plays a vital role in regulating our metabolic health. Maintaining healthy skeletal muscle is especially important in conditions like Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1D), where individuals are unable to control their blood sugar levels due to an inability to make insulin. Unfortunately, T1D has been shown to weaken skeletal muscle (even in young, newly diagnosed adults), which in turn, worsens a number of serious diabetes-related complications. To date, no one has studied the ability of the skeletal muscle to recover following exercise in those with T1D. Given the proven benefit of exercise in the long-term health of persons with T1D, my goal is to understand if muscle repair is similar in those with T1D (versus those without diabetes). This work will uncover for the first time, whether the capacity for skeletal muscle recovery is reduced in people with T1D, and will provide the knowledge necessary to develop safe exercise guidelines targeted towards improving diabetics' muscle health, and ultimately, their quality of life.

column36: The hippocampus in pain: Gray matter and diffusion tensor imaging microstructural studies in trigeminal neuralgia
column37: Trigeminal Neuralgia (TN), a disorder historically known as the "suicide disease", is the most prevalent chronic neuropathic facial pain. It is characterized by episodes of intense electric-like pain and has a tremendous impact on patients' quality of life. While common surgical interventions, such as microvascular decompression and Gamma knife radiosurgery, result in complete resolution of pain in some TN patients, a proportion of the patients remain non-responsive to these interventions. Recent studies have suggested that the limbic system, specifically the hippocampus, may be involved in pain processing and is associated with pain modulation, learning, and emotions. Furthermore, volumetric abnormalities in the hippocampus have been readily observed in chronic pain patients. For instance, our lab has recently shown that different segments of the hippocampus, including CA1, CA4, and hippocampus-amygdala transition area, exhibit ipsilaterally reduced volume in TN patients. Therefore, the aim of the current study is to further our understanding and investigate the impact of surgical interventions on the hippocampus in TN. To achieve this goal, 100 TN patients will be recruited, and T1 anatomical and diffusion tensor images (DTI) will be obtained before and 6 months after surgery for these patients. Thereafter hippocampal subfield volumes will be contrasted between responders and non-responders. As the first study to focus on the understanding of hippocampal changes in chronic neuropathic facial pain patients, we expect to uncover the links between memory and long-term pain and delineate pain processing modules in the limbic system. Furthermore, this study will bring us closer to unraveling the CNS substrate of neuropathic pain and can be a cornerstone for new treatments.

Descriptive analysis will be used to analyze sociodemographic information and study data will be analyzed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis. Knowledge gained from this study can be used in the development of a cutting-edge app, with the goal of improving health outcomes in heart failure patients.

column36: Les troubles de la reconnaissance des visages dans la maladie d'Alzheimer : developpement d'un nouvel outil clinique et caracterisation des deficits aupres de personnes atteintes de la maladie d'Alzheimer
column37: La maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) est de loin la forme de demence la plus frequente a travers le monde, et est estimee a toucher de plus en plus d'individus. Parmi les pertes cognitives dans la maladie d'Alzheimer, les troubles de la memoire sont au premier plan. Les difficultes a reconnaitre des visages sont aussi tres presentes dans la maladie, bien qu'elles demeurent sous-etudiees et documentees. Celles-ci ont un impact important sur les interactions sociales et elles affectent autant les patients que leurs proches-aidants. Cependant, peu de tests cliniques permettent d'evaluer les differents aspects de la reconnaissance des visages. De plus, la nature precise des atteintes liees a la reconnaissance des visages dans la MA demeure encore mal comprise et peu etudiee. Le premier but du projet est de developper et valider une nouvelle batterie clinique d'evaluation des processus lies a la reconnaissance des visages et d'obtenir des normes de references en administrant la batterie a une population saine. Le second but du projet est d'administrer cette batterie a un groupe de participants atteints de la MA, afin de mieux documenter les atteintes de la perception des visages dans cette maladie, en comparant la performance a celle d'un groupe d'agees sains. L'hypothese est que les patients MA presenteront des atteintes a differents niveaux du traitement des visages, tels que la perception des emotions faciales, l'estimation de l'age, l'appariement de visages presentes sous des angles differents, ou encore lors du traitement holistique des visages. Le developpement de cette batterie est pertinent d'abord dans un contexte clinique d'evaluation de la demence, puis dans un contexte de recherche visant a mieux comprendre et documenter les atteintes perceptivo-visuelles liees a la MA.

column36: Use of the Nominal Group Technique and a Cohort-based Survey to Identify Important Barriers and Facilitators to Physical Activity for People with Scleroderma
column37: Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis, SSc) is a debilitating, chronic autoimmune disease that affects the skin and internal organs. Physical activity is often recommended, but the complex symptoms of SSc are a barrier for many patients. To develop a program to support people with SSc to engage in physical activity, information on (1) specific barriers or problems and (2) facilitators or solutions is needed. The purpose of the proposed study is to (1) identify important barriers and facilitators to physical activity experienced by people with SSc, and (2) use this information to create survey items to be completed by people with SSc. To obtain an initial list, guided discussions will be conducted with 6-8 groups of 4-8 SSc participants per group at patient conferences. Participants will share a personal list of barriers to physical activity and corresponding facilitators. Guided by a moderator, each group will revise or merge individual items and agree upon a final list. Then, participants will independently rate each barrier and facilitator in the list on a scale of 0 to 10 based on importance and will indicate whether they have tried each facilitator. Lists of barriers and facilitators will be merged across groups with the input of a patient advisory team and health care providers to create a condensed list of survey items to be administered to over 1,800 people with SSc from an ongoing cohort. Survey results will provide information on how often barriers are experienced, how important they are, and the likelihood that different facilitators would be used, which will subsequently inform the development of a guided online program to support physical activity in SSc. The program will be tested and, if effective, distributed free-of-charge to people with SSc.

column36: Does pre-gestational type 1 or type 2 diabetes lower omega-3 fatty acids in the cord blood of new borns and thus interfere with neurodevelopment?
column37: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid that is essential for healthy brain and nervous system development during pregnancy. During the third trimester, maternal lipolytic activity is increased in order to meet the fetus's increased need for DHA. A deficiency in DHA at this time could be detrimental to the neurodevelopment of the fetus. Previous studies have shown that pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes (T1D or T2D), also known as pre-gestational diabetes (PGD), have lower levels of DHA in their red blood cells. It has also been observed that in diabetic pregnancies, less DHA is present in the umbilical cord blood compared to non-diabetic pregnancies and that DHA may be accumulated in the placenta instead of being released into the cord blood. In this project, we will explore the link between fatty acids in newborns and T1D and T2D mothers and neurological measurements in the babies. We hypothesize that PGD mothers have a placental defect that alters the transfer of DHA to the cord blood and this will result in lower neurodevelopment of the occipital brain region. We also hypothesize that the neurodevelopment of the newborn is positively correlated with DHA concentrations in the cord blood. We will evaluate the fatty acid profile of maternal plasma, cord blood, and the placenta using gas chromatography. Moreover, we will assess the expression of various placental fatty acid transporters using Western Blot and mass spectrometry. Finally, we will evaluate the neurodevelopment of the newborns using electroencephalography (EEG) 24-48 hours after birth and at 2 months of age. The results of this project will help us to better understand the impact that PGD may have on the fatty acid status and the neurodevelopment of newborns.

column36: Application for the Canada Graduate Scholarships _master's Program
column37: Cannabis is a commonly used psychotropic agent in Canada. With the legalization of cannabis in 2018, there is greater need to study and understand the effect of cannabis in the workplace. The effects of impairment of cannabis have been well studied in automobile safety, with established standards for impairment, and differ based on route of administration and chronicity of use. The main compound responsible for psychotropic effects is tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and when inhaled rapidly uptakes through the blood brain barrier to produce effects of euphoria, altered mood or perception, slowed reaction time and impaired attention, concentration and memory. Less studied is the impact of cannabis use in the workplace. Work-related injuries lead to loss of economic productivities, and can lead to long-term disability and loss of income. Recreational cannabis use and its decriminalization has raised additional concerns for workers in safety sensitive industries. Currently there is a paucity of literature on the effect of cannabis use and work-related injuries. column36: Combination treatment of Indapamide and Hydroxychloroquine to attenuate neurodegeneration in an animal model of MS
column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS), affecting roughly 2.5% of Canadians, is a chronic inflammatory disease where immune cells attack the central nervous system leading to damaged areas called lesions. These lesions are partly caused by the release of toxic molecules called free-radicals (FRs) that cause nerve cell death and neurological impairments. There are multiple forms of the disease, however a progressive form called primary progressive MS (PPMS) is more likely to occur in older individuals. PPMS currently lacks effective treatment options and any drugs available are insufficient and are at a high cost. Therefore, the present study seeks to unveil an effective and affordable treatment for the aging PPMS population. We will investigate two inexpensive generic drugs: Indapamide, a high blood pressure medication and neutralizer of FRs, and Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), an anti-malarial drug known to inhibit microglia, an immune cell of which increased activation is a hallmark of PPMS. Over-activation of microglia results in the degradation of myelin, an insulator surrounding nerve cells, along with myelin-producing cells. This breakdown releases molecules contributing to FR formation, thus enhancing the risk of disease progression, especially in older patients. Using an animal model of MS, called EAE, we will observe the effects that the combination of these drugs has on symptom severity, neurodegeneration and inflammation. With HCQ currently in a Phase 2 clinical trial for PPMS and indapamide showing promising effects on FRs in animals, there is optimism that in combination, the drugs will have strong therapeutic potential targeting multiple aspects of the disease. This will give rise to a new treatment plan to fill the void that currently exists for PPMS.

column36: Examining the Individual and Combined Effects of Exercise and Neurofeedback in Major Depressive Disorder
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a national public health concern and will be the leading cause of disability by 2030. The most widespread interventions for MDD have poor outcomes: anti-depressants have serious side effects and poor patient adherence and cognitive behavioural therapy is expensive and 36% of patients are in remission following treatment. Therefore, alternative treatments are necessary for reducing MDD. Aerobic exercise is among the most effective methods for reducing stress, improving mood, decision making and promoting synaptic plasticity in the dentate gyrus. It also increases the neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus, however, a significant number of newborn neurons die a few weeks after being born. Apoptosis can be reduced by engaging in mindfulness training (MT). MT increases sustained attention and working memory, and reduce feelings of distress in MDD. While aerobic exercise and MT are effective methods in reducing depressive symptoms, limited research has been conducted to examine their synergistic effects. I propose to provide a novel intervention in treating MDD through combining aerobic exercise and MT. Both healthy controls and patients with MDD will be assigned into one of four conditions a (1) wait-list control, (2) running, (3) MT, or (4) combined running and MT program. I will use a series of neuropsychological assessments, maximal aerobic fitness and EEG testing to examine the efficacy of an 8-week program pre- and post-intervention, and after a 3-month follow-up. I hypothesize that a combined running and MT program will reduce depressive symptoms and neurocognitive functioning.

column36: Contributions of Tissue Resident and Bone-Marrow Derived Macrophages in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms
column37: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are the most common form of aortic aneurysms. They occur in 5% to 10% of men aged 65 to 79 years and are five times more prevalent in men, resulting in death in 50-85% of patients if left untreated. The lack of understanding of mechanisms contributing to AAA pathogenesis hinders the development of pharmacological interventions and necessitates emergency surgical intervention, showcasing an unmet clinical need. Macrophages (M?) play a key role in the inflammation-mediated breakdown of the aortic wall, however the molecular processes that drive chronic inflammation in AAA remain incompletely understood. We hypothesize that tissue-resident (TR) M? are reparative and maintain tissue homeostasis, while infiltrating bone-marrow (BM) M? produce inflammatory mediators and degradative enzymes that promote AAA. To determine the relative composition of TR vs. BM M? during AAA formation, profiling of M? by multi parameter flow cytometry and immunofluorescence microscopy will be performed in aneurysmal tissue. To determine the relative contribution of M? proliferation vs. monocyte recruitment to M? accumulation in AAA, AAA-induced C57BL/6J mice will be joined by parabiosis to investigate the relative proportion of host and partner-derived M? over time. To determine the in vivo functions of TR and BM M? in AAA, Transcriptional profiling will be performed for TR and BM M? in AAA using gene array analysis. To assess the effects of depleting TR vs. BM M? on AAA progression, CX3CR1-/- and Ccr2-/- mice will be used, respectively. Aneurysm size, histological features of developing lesions, and functional M? profiling will be assessed. The proposal seeks to understand the functional contributions of TR and BM M? in AAA for development of new therapies.

column36: Using the Hearing in Noise Test to Screen for Hidden Hearing Loss
column37: The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety regulates occupational noise exposure limits for Canadian workers through federal legislation. These limits are based on the idea that a temporary hearing threshold shift does not cause permanent damage to the inner hair cells. However, recent rodent studies show that such noise exposure may first have an effect on the hair cell synapses. There is emerging evidence of similar synapse damage in humans. This type of damage is known in the literature as "cochlear synaptopathy" or "hidden hearing loss" (HHL). HHL is the likely cause for difficulties recognizing speech in noise. Electrophysiological studies demonstrate that damage to hair cell synapses lead to impaired processing of interaural time difference cues (ITDs), used for sound localization and recognizing speech in noise. This research project will investigate whether the Hearing in Noise Test (HINT) can be used in a clinical setting to screen individuals at risk of HHL due to noise exposure. This test employs ITDs to manipulate the perceived location of noise, relative to speech. Thus, my research question is the following: can the HINT test be an effective tool to screen individuals at risk of HHL due to noise exposure? The at-risk group will consist of 15 adult musicians recruited through the UBC School of Music. Musicians are often exposed to sounds that exceed the national permitted levels through performances, rehearsals and individual practice. I expect that musicians will not benefit as much as control listeners from the spatial separation of speech and noise provided by ITDs. If successful, this project will have a large impact on future clinical practice for the diagnosis and the prevention of HHL.

column36: Factors Associated with Length of Stay Following Elective Spine Surgery
column37: Background:Elective (i.e. pre-planned) spine surgeries are common procedures that utilize significant hospital resources. Length of stay (LOS) in hospital following surgery is an important measure of health resource use and contributes to hospital costs. A limited number of previous studies have identified factors associated with LOS following elective spine surgery, and findings are variable. Identifying the average LOS for each surgical procedure and the factors that are associated with prolonged LOS is an important first step to better understand the local patient population and inform care delivery. Objectives:This research will be conducted in two phases: 1) Conduct a systematic review of the literature to identify factors that have been consistently associated with LOS following elective spine surgery. 2) Evaluate pre-, intra-, and post-operative characteristics that are associated with prolonged LOS in a Nova Scotian elective spine surgical setting. Methods and Procedures: All elective procedures performed by two orthopaedic spine surgeons that occurred between October 2014 and October 2018 (~1,600) will be included. Factors identified in the systematic review will be collected from a review of patients' electronic medical records. It is hypothesized that these factors will be associated with LOS. Significance:The identification of factors associated with LOS will provide evidence for the development of a model to predict LOS and inform individual care. These findings may also identify modifiable factors that can be targeted with interventions to improve patient outcomes and reduce LOS. This research will also allow for a better understanding of the patient population and provide a foundation for future research to build upon.

column36: Weight Status and Lower Academic Acheivement for Canadian Adolescents with Obesity
column37: My research will examine the relationship between weight status and academic achievement in Canadian youth with obesity. My interest in weight bias, or the prejudice and discrimination that people with obesity encounter in health care and employment settings led me to question what impact, if any, does weight bias have on students with obesity in the school environment; and whether it can explain lower grades? Few studies examined the relationship between weight status and academic performance for youth with obesity and they show a connection between increased weight and lower academic performance. The reasons for this correlation are not yet clear. We know from weight bias literature that some physical education teacher hold biased beliefs about students with obesity. My thesis will focus on examining if low self-concept, potentially because of the negative impact of weight bias, can explain why youth with obesity perform lower than their average weight peers. I plan on doing this using quantitative statistics from a large sample of Canadian secondary school students using the COMPASS study data. This is an important relationship to examine because lower academic achievement can set a lifelong trajectory into adulthood for young people. Lower grades are associated with less pursuit of post-secondary education and higher chances of unemployment, poverty and poor health. The findings can impact millions of Canadian children and youth since an estimated third or more of Canadian children/youth are at risk of obesity. Findings can also be used to inform public health programing in an attempt to implement early intervention programs in primary school settings and foster non-biased environments in school for students and staff.

column36: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) for Breast Cancer Patients undergoing Autologous Microvascular Breast Reconstruction
column37: Breast cancer affects 1 in 8 Canadian women. While treatments for breast cancer have improved survival to 87%, studies show that women who undergo mastectomy often experience a negative impact to their quality of life. Breast reconstruction benefits patients by improving their physical, psychosocial and sexual well-being. Patients who undergo breast reconstruction have the choice between alloplastic (implant-based) or autologous (tissue-based). Although implant-based reconstruction is the most common form of breast reconstruction in North America, autologous reconstruction using the patient's own skin, fat and muscle has superior long-term patient satisfaction. The current standard for autologous reconstruction is the DIEP (deep inferior epigastric perforator) flap, using the patient's abdominal tissue to reconstruct the breast using microsurgical techniques. However, DIEP reconstruction is a longer and more complex operation involving surgery at the breasts and abdominal donor-site. This results in longer hospital stays and increased opioid use for pain control compared to implant-based reconstruction. Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) is a multidisciplinary approach to patient care before, during, and after surgery that has improved recovery for patients that undergo colorectal surgery. Patients who are in the ERAS pathway are able to return home earlier following surgery, with better pain control and less opioid use. The principles of ERAS can be transferred for patients undergoing autologous breast reconstruction. The proposed research is to implement ERAS for breast cancer patients undergoing DIEP breast reconstruction and understand its impact on patient recovery. The results have the potential to improve patient care and reduce healthcare costs.

column36: Identification of a novel compound that reduces mortality from severe influenza and elucidation of its molecular mechanisms
column37: The influenza virus causes hundreds of thousands of deaths annually worldwide. There is a constant threat of a novel strain developing, leading to an influenza pandemic. While antivirals exist for the treatment of infections, the virus changes quickly and cases of resistance to these drugs have already occurred. As such, novel therapeutics for the treatment of influenza are urgently needed. Recent findings have shown that the host body's response to infection can be damaging and cause death. Consequently, drugs that alter the body's response to the virus, instead of directly targeting the virus, may be useful for the treatment of influenza. We have identified a drug that protects both zebrafish and mice from death due to influenza infection. So far, our studies show that the drug does not seem to repress the virus itself, which means it should not lead to viral resistance. Rather, it seems that the drug is improving how the body responds to the virus. This project is designed to figure out specifically how the drug works at the level of cells and molecules, so it can be developed to use for the treatment of influenza patients. To do this, we will use sophisticated molecular biology techniques and computer-aided analysis to identify the target of the drug.

column36: Core Outcome Set for Studies Addressing Perinatally-Encountered Venous Thromboembolism
column37: Women are at an increased risk for developing blood clots during and soon after pregnancy. These blood clots could travel to organs such as the lungs and brain resulting in death or long-term disability. Although research is being conducted to determine how best to prevent, diagnose and treat blood clots in pregnancy, this has not been translated into clinical practice or health policy for two reasons. First, every study reports and defines outcomes differently, making it difficult to compare outcomes across studies. Second, there is no research to support whether the outcomes reported in medical literature are important to women. My thesis project aims to standardize how outcomes are reported and defined so that all future studies use one standard set of outcomes, making it possible to compare studies and draw conclusions that inform clinical practice and health policy, and improve the health of women and their babies. This will be done by developing a core outcome set (COS), a five-step process. The first involves systematically reviewing published literature to identify how outcomes have been reported and defined by researchers. The second is to conduct interviews with women that have experienced blood clots during or after pregnancy, to determine what outcomes they consider important. The third is to conduct an international survey involving women and those involved in their care (stakeholders), to narrow down the list of outcomes obtained from earlier steps. The fourth is a face-to-face consensus meeting to finalize the components of the COS. The final step is to determine how the core outcomes should be measured. This COS will become the reference standard for all future studies aimed at preventing, diagnosing and treating blood clots around the time of pregnancy.

column36: The liver-x-receptor/endothelial progenitor cell secretome: a new source of anti-atherogenic proteins
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide, representing 31% of annual mortalities. A major contributing factor to heart disease is atherosclerosis, the hardening of arteries due to plaque buildup. Atherosclerosis begins when endothelial cells lining the artery become physically or chemically damaged. This induces endothelial dysfunction, which allows the accumulation of cholesterol and inflammatory cells within the arteries, leading to plaque formation. Cholesterol-rich plaques can rupture, creating blood clots that can cause a heart attack or stroke. Currently, the prevention of atherosclerosis is managed by statin drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels. However, since cholesterol reduction does not fully prevent vascular complications, novel therapies targeting early atherosclerosis are urgently needed. The proposed project will study bone-marrow derived endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) and investigate how enhancing EPC function can repair and protect endothelial cells during early atherosclerosis. Previous studies have shown that the activation of a nuclear protein, liver X receptor (LXR), reduces intracellular cholesterol levels in macrophages, a primary atherosclerotic inflammatory cell type. Interestingly, our lab recently found that LXR activation in murine EPCs causes these stem-like cells to secrete protective factors to decrease early plaque formation. We aim to reveal how LXRs interact with EPCs to elicit their protective role, identify which secreted factors contribute to the observed effects and determine its reproducibility in human EPCs. This project will enhance our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms by which EPCs support damaged endothelial cells during early atherogenesis, and identify potential new therapeutic targets.

column36: A prospective randomized controlled trial comparing operative versus non-operative management of patella fractures in the elderly
column37: Operative management is indicated for all displaced patellar fractures in young and active patients. While this is widely agreed upon, surgical indications for elderly patients with displaced fractures remains controversial. Elderly patients often have an intact extensor mechanism due to the low-energy mechanism of their injury. Treatment indications are further complicated by the frequent presence of other health problems, poor bone quality for repair, and lower functional demands. There is a lack of high level scientific demonstrating that the benefits of surgery significantly outweigh the risks in this patient population. Non-operative management may result in equivalent outcomes, while avoiding the risks associated with surgery, such as infection or the need for further surgery. In fact, previous studies of other injuries in orthopaedics have demonstrated precisely this. Given an increasing elderly Canadian population, the incidence of low-energy patellar fractures is expected to rise substantially in the future. Therefore, defining the optimal treatment of these injuries is of significant importance. Minimizing complications while ensuring a rapid return of function and independence in this vulnerable population is critical. Our study is a multi-centered, prospective, randomized controlled trial across North America. Elderly (>65 years), low-demand patients will be randomized into operative or non-operative management with a standardized post-treatment protocol. Our hypothesis is that non-operative treatment will lead to equivalent functional outcomes as compared to surgery, while resulting in a lower rate of complications.

column36: Temporal processing in autism spectrum disorder and dyslexia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and developmental dyslexia (DD) are neurodevelopmental disorders associated with sensory processing deficits. ASD is a disorder characterized by social and communication impairments and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior. DD is a learning disorder characterized by deficits in reading and writing abilities in individuals with normal intelligence. Individuals with ASD or DD show deficits in processing rapidly timed information, as well as temporally integrating sensory information from different sensory modalities. Failure to temporally integrate sensory cues can lead to deficits in higher-order communicative skills like reading and writing, as well as in social and communication skills in these disorders. For example, everyday social interactions involve the integration of visual and auditory social information (e.g., facial gestures, voice prosody) to create a holistic and dynamic percept. The current project will compare temporal integration in ASD and DD to determine whether impaired sensory integration is a core feature of these disorders, and to understand its relation with clinical symptom severity and age. Specifically, a quantitative meta-analysis will be performed on systematically reviewed research on temporal processing in ASD and DD. The ultimate aim of this research is to better refine these clinical phenotypes and to set a theoretical groundwork for future interventions that could potentially ameliorate atypical temporal processing and lead to improved outcomes in core symptoms. Namely, future music interventions in ASD and DD aimed at developing temporal processing through musical training could lead to reduced social and communication deficits in these disorders.

column36: The Neurochemical Niche of Glioblastoma Stem Cells
column37: Brain cancer is a nasty disease, and virtually all patients die within two years of developing its most aggressive tumour called glioblastoma. Though decades of research have helped us better understand the biology of these tumours, we have surprisingly overlooked their home. Here, I propose to investigate what makes the brain the only home in which glioblastoma can grow. I suspect it has to do with one of the brain's unique chemicals: dopamine. We know that new treatments will only work if they target the cells in the tumour that act like stem cells. Early evidence suggests that these cells may exploit dopamine to grow the tumour in the brain. I intend to figure out if this is the case. I will first add dopamine to these cells (isolated from human glioblastoma tumours) and study if/how it makes them change. Then, adhering to Canada's animal care guidelines, I will work with genetically-altered mice that accept human cells and enable controlled release of dopamine from neurons. Following injection of human glioblastoma stem cells into the brains of these mice, I will either shine light to stimulate the release of dopamine or add a drug to inhibit dopamine release into the human cells' surrounding environment. Then, I will see if/how altered dopamine levels affected tumour growth. Dopamine helps us think, feel pleasure, and move our limbs. So it makes sense that unusual levels of dopamine in the brain is linked to disorders like schizophrenia, drug addiction, and Parkinson's. Today, many dopamine-modifying drugs are approved to treat those disorders. If my theory is supported by my findings, drugs that decrease the brain's dopamine levels may weaken the growth of glioblastoma, thus enabling us to provide patients with new treatments to tackle this deadly brain cancer.

column37: Antipsychotics (AP)s are the cornerstone of treatment for many severe mental illnesses. column36: Evaluating the impact of public policies on responses to drug overdoses among people who use illicit drugs (PWUD) in Vancouver, Canada
column37: Canada has been experiencing an opioid overdose crisis in the past few years. The first and most critical response to an overdose event is to call 911 for help. Despite this, many people who use illicit drugs (PWUD) do not call 911 at the scene of an overdose because of fear towards the police. In response, two key policies have emerged in hopes to encourage PWUD to call for emergency help. In 2005, the Vancouver Police Department (VPD) adopted a non-attendance policy, which means that the police will not attend overdose events unless a death has occurred or if the BC Emergency Health Services request for their attendance. Similarly, in 2017, a federal law known as the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act (GSA) was introduced. This law provides legal protection from simple drug possession charges to any person who calls for help at the scene of an overdose. However, for various reasons, it is unclear whether the GSA or VPD's non-attendance policy have been successful in increasing the amount of calls to 911 at the event of an overdose. The effectiveness of these policies may determine whether PWUD call for emergency help, which reduces the chance an overdose becomes fatal. This proposal will evaluate the effectiveness and the impact of both policies using a large study that consists of over 3,000 PWUD. Information regarding police attendance and overdose response have been collected since 2004. Currently, no research has evaluated the effectiveness of these policies and little is known about PWUD's responses to overdose events in Canada. Therefore, this study will fill an important knowledge gap in the scientific community that will help inform the current policies, as well as future policies, aimed to encourage PWUD to call for emergency help at the scene of an overdose.

column36: Early-Life Emotional Expressivity and Cognitive Resilience
column37: This study takes an epidemiological approach to the investigation of early-life factors and their association with cognitive resilience (CR). CR is the ability for the brain to buffer against neuropathology using pre-existing processing approaches that have been developed over the life course through experience. Individuals who have developed higher CR should remain cognitively normal longer, despite aversive pathology. CR has been effective in delaying or preventing the detrimental effects of AD, as seen in the Nun Study and other populations where individuals who exhibit significant AD pathology remain cognitively intact. Though factors in adulthood can contribute to the development of CR, they can only partially predict the risk of AD development in late-life. Thus, early-life factors are important to understanding and advancing our knowledge of resilience and how it develops. Evidence supports emotional expressivity and personal positivity as risk factors and predictors of AD. We will consider how these predictors of AD, are associated with later-life CR development. The Nun Study, a longitudinal study of aging and AD, involving 678 nuns from the School Sisters of Notre Dame, will be used as the population. This data set offers a unique advantage for the investigation of CR, as it not only provides access to early-life information through archives and records, but the participants have agreed to donate their brains after death, allowing for neuropathological assessments of AD and related pathology necessary for investigations concerning CR. With the rising tide of AD on the horizon, public policy and health interventions will benefit greatly from the results of this study as prevention is key since there is no cure for AD.

column37: Toutes maladies de l'oeil causent des pertes de vision et peuvent meme mener a la cecite. C'est le cas d'une maladie de l'oeil qui affecte la cornee (la partie transparente a l'avant de l'oeil) appelee << Dystrophie endotheliale corneenne de Fuchs >>. Cette maladie touche 4% de la population et est responsable de 17 000 greffes de cornee annuellement en Amerique du nord. Le premier signe clinique de cette maladie est l'epaississement d'une membrane, causee par l'accumulation de proteines matricielles. Or, le corps humain possede des enzymes qui sont responsables de la regulation des proteines matricielles, soit des proteases. Nous suggerons qu'une deregulation de ces proteases dans l'oeil serait responsable de l'epaississement de la membrane retrouvee dans la Dystrophie endotheliale corneenne de Fuchs. L'objectif de ce projet est donc d'analyser le profil de proteases produites par les cellules de la cornee. Pour ce faire, notre laboratoire utilise les cellules de la cornee qui ont ete isolees et mises en culture pour permettre leur etude dans des conditions controlees. Nous allons ensuite valider l'importance de cette deregulation de proteases dans le developpement de la maladie. Ce projet permettra une meilleure comprehension de l'etape charniere de la Dystrophie endotheliale corneenne de Fuchs, soit de l'accumulation excessive de proteines matricielles. De plus, l'identification d'une diminution des proteases pourrait mener au developpement de nouvelles avenues therapeutiques specifiques, visant par exemple la degradation partielle de la membrane, ce qui eviterait la perte de vision et le recours aux greffes.

column36: Contribution of glucagon-expressing alpha-cells and cytokeratin-19-expressing ductal cells in multipotent stromal cell-induced pancreatic islet regeneration
column37: Diabetes results from the destruction of insulin-producing ?-cells in pancreatic islets of Langerhans, leaving patients unable to control blood glucose. Regeneration of lost ?-cells represents a promising treatment strategy. Our lab pioneered the use of transplanted human bone-marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) to stimulate islet regeneration in mice with ?-cell deletion. We used secreted protein analyses to determine that activation of the Wnt-signaling pathway was a characteristic of regenerative MSC. Pharmacological activation of the Wnt-pathway in MSC cultures generated a concentrated protein mixture (CM) that consistently improved human islet cell survival and replication, and reliably reduced blood glucose levels in mice with diabetes. However, the regenerative cascade induced in signal-receiving cells within the pancreas remains unknown. Initial results after MSC CM injection revealed glucagon and insulin co-expressing cells, suggesting ?-to-?-cell conversion, and the emergence of mature insulin-expressing cells associated with pancreatic ducts, two islet regenerative mechanisms supported by mouse model studies following cell fates. We hypothesize that MSC CM will stimulate ?-to-?-cell conversion and mediate new islet formation from duct-derived precursor cells after injection into hyperglycemic mouse models. The objectives of this study include: (1) to stimulate isolated duct cells and islets with MSC CM to measure survival and ?-cell phenotype acquisition in culture, and (2) to characterize islet regenerative mechanisms and phenotype transitions after CM injection into specialized mouse models designed to follow the fates of duct and ?-cells. This study will contribute to the development of 'cell-free' regenerative medicine therapies for diabetes.

column36: Technology for promoting exercise adherence and physical function in older adults
column37: Older adults with health issues have a hard time moving around safely, which can lead to negative events like injury and death. Exercising can help improve physical ability and decrease disability in older adults with different health issues, but getting people to continue exercising is very difficult, especially when exercising at home. In the past 10 years, there has been an increase in the use of technology to try to encourage exercise and improve physical ability in older adults. Technology can range from simple or "low tech" digital/hard copy approaches to complex "smart" technologies such as iPads or smartphones. However, it is not known whether these technologies actually increase the maintenance of exercise and physical ability in older adults. The proposed study will ask older adults who have completed a home-based exercise program using DVDs what their experiences were, and what they did and did not like about the program. We will also be looking at other studies that have looked at technology, exercise, and older adults to understand whether "low tech" or "smart" technologies work better in maintaining exercise and physical ability in older adults. The findings of this project can be used to improve exercise-based rehabilitation for older adults with health issues.

column36: Impact d'une therapie cognitivo comportementale par Internet pour reduire les listes d'attentes de centres de sante mentale communautaires: etude de faisabilite aupres de jeunes canadiens
column37: Les jeunes adultes de 18 a 25 ans ont le plus haut taux de prevalence de depression et d'anxiete comparativement a d'autres groupes d'age (Marcus et Westra, 2012). Ces problemes entrainent des couts societaux et personnels importants chez cette population. Toutefois, peu recoivent ou recherchent de l'aide (Harrar, Affspring et Long, 2010). Ceux qui font la demande sont souvent en attente de services pendant des mois, en raison d'un manque de professionnels en sante mentale (Pin et Martin, 2012). La therapie cognitivo comportementale via Internet (TCCi) offre une solution. Les TCCi pour l'anxiete et la depression mettent l'accent sur des techniques tels que la modification des pensees et des comportements non aidants. Elles ont recu un appui empirique important (Andrews et al., 2018; Hedman et al., 2013). Le programme propose pour cette recherche est le Mood Mechanic Course et sa traduction canadienne-francaise, Mecanique de l'humeur. Il prend la forme de cinq lecons a lire sur une periode de huit semaines et peut etre offert de facon securitaire et efficace avec ou sans assistance clinique (Johnston et al., 2014). Un echantillon de 100 participants sera recrute dans deux centres communautaires de sante mentale. Un protocole a un groupe avec pretest, post-test et suivi de trois mois sera utilise. Il inclut un entretien telephonique au debut et a la fin de la TCCi et des courriels ou messages automatiques hebdomadaires. Peu d'etudes ont evalue le role de la TCCi pour reduire le temps d'attente pour acceder a des services de sante mentale. La recherche proposee vise a evaluer l'impact d'une TCCi pour la gestion du stress, de l'anxiete et de la depression chez des jeunes en attente de services de sante mentale dans le systeme de sante public.

column36: Virtual Reality-based Spatial Memory Intervention to Improve hippocampus-dependent memory in patients with Traumatic Brain Injury
column37: The proposed study seeks to use the automated spatial memory improvement program (auto-SMIP) to alleviate memory deficits associated with dysfunction of the hippocampus (HPC) in patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI). Both healthy and TBI patients will undergo 16 hours of auto-SMIP intervention over 8 weeks. Both groups are expected to show cognitive improvements related to the HPC and MRI differences at post-test and at the 6-month follow-up. Differences between these groups will also demonstrate auto-SMIP to be an effective intervention in protecting against hippocampal atrophy, thereby preserving associated cognitive functions. The micro-vascularization of the HPC, which shares networks with many other key brain areas, makes it particularly susceptible to TBI-related atrophy. Further to HPC-related memory deficits, secondary damage resulting from neuronal hyperexcitation have lead to functional disturbances related to mood disorders and prolonged decrease in quality of life for TBI patients. Nevertheless, previous research suggest that interventions promoting cognitive activity may significantly moderate recovery outcomes. Specifically, HPC-dependent spatial memory strategies have been associated with improved cognition and greater HPC activity compared to non-HPC dependent compensatory strategies. In a recent study, the 8-week auto-SMIP intervention was found to induce HPC growth in older adults with reduced HPC, maintained over 6 months, which the current study proposes to demonstrate in TBI patients. To date, auto-SMIP is the only cognitive intervention that has demonstrated targeted improvements specific to the HPC. As such the current study will demonstrate auto-SMIP training effects such as enhanced spatial memory and improved quality of life.

column36: Exploring shade as a tool to promote physical activity and prevent skin cancer
column37: Chronic diseases contribute to a large proportion of disease, death, and health care costs in Canada. Many risk factors for chronic diseases are modifiable, hence the importance of prevention. Shade has recently been indicated as an effective tool to both prevent skin cancer and promote physical activity. Given skin cancer is the most common type of cancer in Canada, and with obesity rates continuing to rise, it is important to explore shade further, especially as little research has been conducted in Canada. The goal of this research project is to explore the availability of shade and how it influences the use of public parks and outdoor recreation areas. First, shade audits of local parks and outdoor recreation areas in Guelph, Ontario will be conducted to evaluate the amount of existing shade in the area, along with if and how that shade is being used. Second, the impact of increasing shade in parks and outdoor recreation areas will be examined by setting up shade sails - built structures made of tensile fabric that create shade - and observing how these structures influence park use. We will conduct intercept interviews of park-goers to determine their thoughts and opinions of the shade sails, and reasons why they used them, if applicable. The results will be useful to public health professionals, urban planners, and policy makers. With a push towards healthy cities, this research will provide timely evidence about the impact of increasing shade availability in outdoor public areas.

column36: Function of CD36 mediated albumin transcytosis across microvascular endothelial cells
column37: Albumin is the most abundant protein in the blood and it circulates fat and other molecules to target tissues. Molecules need to leave the blood vessel in order to reach the target cells. The main route of transport for albumin is to pass through cells lining the vessels, known as endothelial cells. Recently, our lab has shown that a molecule known as the cluster of differentiation 36 (CD36) is able to bind albumin and transport it through endothelial cells of the skin but not lung endothelial cells. It is unknown why albumin is transported through this process only in the skin. Therefore, I plan to determine the function of albumin transport mediated by CD36 in the skin by studying mice that don't express CD36 on endothelial cells. I will characterize the layer of fat beneath the skin in addition to study the growth and development of hair in these mice. The importance of this study is with regards to a condition known as edema, which is swelling of tissue. It often occurs as a secondary effect to injury, infection, and diseases. The proposed research will identify whether the transport of albumin through CD36 contributes to edema in the skin and what physical characteristics may be associated with absence of CD36 expression in skin endothelial cells.

column36: Inhibition of hypoxia-inducible metastasis promoting gene transcription
column37: Despite the improvement of therapeutics for cancer, it is still the leading cause of death in North America. Cancers become more fatal once they spread to organs which are essential for survival. Undoubtedly, a better strategy which will selectively target and prevent the spreading of cancers is needed. It has been shown that cancers which form solid tumours outgrow their oxygen-rich blood supply and develop a response to survive under a low oxygen environment (hypoxia). This low oxygen driven response not only allows tumour cells to survive under hypoxia but also transforms the cells to become more invasive (metastatic) and aggressive. This survival response is only activated in the tumour cells and not healthy cells. Thus, targeting the mechanism of the survival response is a novel strategy to prevent cancer metastasis which can lead to more effective therapeutics. Our hypothesis is that if the mechanism of the survival response is disrupted, this will stop tumour cells from spreading. I will first characterize this mechanism using highly sensitive biochemical techniques. I will then screen for small molecules that disrupt this survival response. As metastatic cancer accounts for the majority of cancer-related deaths, and the currently available treatments, such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy, cannot effectively target metastatic cancers and instead affect healthy cells, this research will provide helpful information for better therapeutics. The insight I may gain from this research will be useful to all cancer types which form solid tumours such as prostate and breast cancers, the most commonly diagnosed cancers in Canadian males and females, respectively.
