column36: Gold-Lipid Hybrid Nanoparticles for Synergistic Treatment Using Radiation for Spatially and Temporally Specific Cancer Therapy
column37: Many attempts have been made to modify the distribution of chemotherapy drugs within the body in order to concentrate their activity within the tumour. An effective strategy has been to sequester the drug in a non-reactive carrier which then selectively accumulates in the tumour, degrades, and releases the drug. Liposomes, a non-reactive carrier, have found success in this regard; they have been shown to change the drug's distribution, reduce systemic toxicities, and increase drug concentrations at the tumour. Attempts have been made to further improve the drug accumulation at the tumour site or to increase the rate of liposome release relative to normal tissue, but limited success has been achieved. Recently, liposomes have been designed with the possibility for triggered release. In this case, an external source of energy is applied to the disease site to degrade liposomes designed with a vulnerability that is susceptible to exposure by external energy. The degraded liposomes subsequently release their drug only at the disease site. We hypothesize that by focusing the trigger (X-rays) on the disease site, only hybrid liposomes (such as, liposomes attached to gold nanoparticles, which are known to enhance X-rays) present in the energy field will release their drug contents and, thus, drug release will be controlled in a temporal and spatial manner. The following specific aims will be used to test this hypothesis: 1) Optimize and purify hybrids, 2) Using a panel of chemotherapies loaded into hybrids, evaluate the characteristics of the system, and 3) Determine the level of synergy between the formulations and radiation in the presence of cells with successful formulations being further tested in mice. The overall therapeutic implication is that the spatially and temporally specific delivery platform would allow for a synergistic therapy combining both radiation and chemotherapy to lower systemic toxicities and improve the efficacy and quality-of-life for patients.

column36: Beneficial and harmful effects of early-life environmental exposures on childhood development - a cohort study.
column37: Approximately one in four Canadian children are considered to have deficiencies in early development prior to entering primary education. Vulnerabilities in early development are of great concern, as early childhood development is an important predictor for physical, mental, and social health through the life course. While the impact of socioeconomic status (SES) is well-researched, the potential influence of environmental exposures on children's early development is poorly understood. The primary aim of this project is to study the associations between various environmental exposures on children's early development in Metro Vancouver, Canada. The project will focus on environmental exposures during early life - prenatally up to the age of five. The project will specifically investigate the impacts of beneficial (natural environments) and harmful (air pollution and noise) environmental exposures on childhood development, including whether the beneficial effects of natural environments have a moderating effect on harmful exposures. A secondary aim of this project is to evaluate if exposure to natural environments can contribute to mitigating the adverse effects of children living in poor socioeconomic conditions. This project is of high significance as it addresses rising Canadian concerns, including children's early development, disparities in public health, and the environmental effects of an urbanizing society. Knowledge from this project may contribute to preventative strategies aimed towards improving health outcomes across the life course.

column36: Modelisation des atteintes neurologiques dans la dystrophie myotonique de type 1 de forme congenitale a l'aide d'organoides de cerveau
column37: La dystrophie myotonique de type 1 (DM1) est une maladie genetique provoquant entre autres une faiblesse musculaire et une difficulte a relacher le muscle apres une contraction. Alors que la DM1 apparait generalement au debut de la vingtaine, il existe une forme congenitale de la maladie qui entraine des symptomes plus graves et donne lieu a des bebes mous a la naissance. Ceux-ci developpent egalement un retard mental severe dont la cause n'est pas encore connue. Recemment, de nouvelles methodes ont permis de produire en laboratoire des organoides de cerveau. Ces ebauches d'organe reproduisent en partie la composition cellulaire et la structure du cerveau. Nous pensons que ce modele permettra de comprendre l'effet de la DM1 sur le developpement embryonnaire du cerveau. Notre objectif est de comparer des organoides de cerveau derives d'individus normaux et de patients ayant la forme congenitale ou adulte de la DM1. Pour ce faire, nous allons prelever des biopsies de peau afin d'obtenir des cellules dans lesquelles nous injecterons a l'aide de virus inactives des genes associes au stade embryonnaire. Cela aura pour effet de << reprogrammer >> genetiquement ces cellules afin qu'elles redeviennent souches et qu'elles aient la capacite de de se differencier en n'importe quelle cellule des trois feuillets embryonnaires. Lorsque ces cellules reprogrammees seront placees dans un cocktail induisant la differenciation en neurone et qu'elles seront enrobees dans un gel leur permettant de se developper dans l'espace 3-D, elles formeront un organoide de cerveau. Nous regarderons s'il y a une difference au niveau de la proliferation et de la migration des cellules souches neuronales dans les organoides avec la forme congenitale de la DM1. Enfin, nous verifierons s'il est possible de corriger le gene mute dans la DM1 avec une technologie d'edition de genome appelee CRISPR-Cas9. Ce projet pourrait permettre de developper de nouvelles therapies pour la DM1 de forme congenitale.

column36: Investigating FGL2 as an Immunotherapeutic Target in High-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is a debilitating disease affecting thousands of women every year in Canada. In 2018, 2800 women will be diagnosed with Ovarian Cancer and 1800 women will die from the disease. Ovarian Cancer is the 5th leading cause of cancer related death among women and the leaded cause of death from a gynaecological cancer. Symptoms may not appear until late stages of the disease and there is currently no screening methods for early detection of the disease. Ovarian cancer is therefore typically diagnosed at later stages, where the five-year survival rate is around 40%. Research is vital to developing new methods for early detection and developing new treatments to combat late stages of the disease and increase survival for Canadian women and women around the world. We have recent evidence that suggests that the FGL2 gene may be an important target in Ovarian Cancer. FGL2 is a gene involved in suppression of the immune system, which means the body is less able to recognize a tumour as a foreign invader and eliminate the cancer. This gene is found at higher than normal levels in other cancers as well; such as lung, liver, brain, renal and colorectal. We believe that this highlights the importance of targeting this gene to reduce the suppression of the immune system which would help the body fight off the cancer from within and increase survival of ovarian cancer patients. This project will investigate the potential of targeting FGL2 as a new treatment for ovarian cancer.

column36: Investigating the Role of Vitamin A Signals in Dendritic Cell and Stromal Cell Interactions
column37: Dendritic cells (DC) are specialized cells that react to environmental cues to shape the immune response. An appropriate immune response relies on coordinated exchanges between white blood cells and DC, with stromal cells providing a foundation for these interactions. Surrounding stromal cells direct the entry and produce survival factors for white blood cells to sample DC that had been surveying the blood and tissues for harmful microbes. The precise positioning of DC by stromal cells in tissues such as the spleen and gut is necessary for mounting an optimal immune response. However, relatively little is known about the molecular mechanisms that govern DC and stromal cell interactions in intact tissues. Recent work from our lab has revealed a requirement for Retinoic Acid (RA), a metabolic product of dietary Vitamin A, in maintaining DC numbers and function in a mouse model of inflammation. RA plays a key role in both protective and regulatory immune responses, and Vitamin A supplementation improves immunological health in malnourished children. Curiously, I have found that RA-deficient mice also exhibit some defects in stromal cell function - in particular, the production of collagen-rich fibres. Such fibres have been shown to be critical for the proper positioning and migration of immune cell subsets. We hypothesize that inputs from RA exert effects on both DC and stromal cells to maintain DC numbers, position, and function. Additionally, I will be assessing the role of RA in models of rotavirus infection since RA has been proposed to improve the efficacy of rotavirus vaccines in resource-poor countries where vaccine responses are sub-optimal. These experiments will ultimately provide a framework for testing how RA may improve responses to oral vaccines and has important implications in the design of other therapies that activate or inhibit pathways downstream of RA signals in humans.

column36: High-Throughput Discovery of Enzymes for Engineering of Glycoprotein Therapeutics
column37: In nature, proteins are commonly modified by the attachment of sugars in a process known as glycosylation. Glycosylation of proteins is important and different sugar structures can have different effects. One of the most well-known sets of sugar structures are the blood-type determining ABO antigens. O blood is often called the universal donor because it can be transfused into any individual. Thus, it is often used in emergencies and is in the highest demand. The supply of O blood would be improved if A- or B-type blood could be converted to O-type. While there exist enzymes that can convert A or B blood to O blood, they are too inefficient to work at the needed scale. Besides blood groups, glycosylation can dictate many aspects of a protein's function including the activities it carries out, how long the protein survives, as well as how its recognized within the body. Because many drugs are glycosylated proteins, the ability to manipulate their glycosylation (both taking sugars off and putting new sugars on) using enzymes would allow for improved study of the roles of specific sugar structures as well as open the door towards "optimal" protein glycosylation. The focus of my research is then to identify enzymes which can cleave sugars from proteins. I will identify such enzymes from the 10-100 trillion microbes which reside within the human gut. Many of these microbes provide a benefit to humans through digestion of carbohydrates that we cannot digest ourselves. Nevertheless, the mucous membranes of the gut carry a high density of glycosylated proteins. Some gut bacteria then digest these mucosal sugars for energy in order to gain a competitive advantage. My research will aim to identify some of these bacterial enzymes involved in the cleavage of mucosal sugars. Once identified I will harness their abilities for the improvement of drug glycosylation as well as the production of O-blood.

column37: Dopamine transmission in the brain is a tightly regulated process, and alterations in dopamine signaling result in several disease with enormous human and economic burden, including schizophrenia, ADHD, Bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease and dyskinesias. One of the key regulators of dopamine transmission is the plasma membrane dopamine transporter, DAT, which transports released dopamine back into the neuron. In addition to the above prevalent diseases, there is also a rare, fatal disease caused by mutations in the dopamine transporter, called dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. We have developed several models to study dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome and in this study we will be assessing the effects of various drug treatments on these models to see if they can have beneficial effects. We hypothesize that manipulating neurotransmitters in the brain could improve some of the sympotms associated with dopamine transporter deficiency syndrome. Positive results from our studies could be quickly translated into the clinic, since the drugs that we will be testing are already an approved and used in humans.

column36: PROSPAX: an integrated multimodal progression chart in spastic ataxias
column37: Spastic ataxias (SPAX) present an expanding group of >100 rare degenerative diseases with joined damage of cerebellum and corticospinal tract (CST). While rapid genetic stratification facilitates current development of molecular therapies, effective trial-planning for SPAX is hampered by a lack of valid outcome measures and natural history studies. Uniting all major European ataxia and spastic paraplegia networks, PROSPAX will establish a paradigmatic IRDiRC-guided integrated trial-ready model of disease progression and mechanistic evolution in SPAX, which will allow to track and understand selective as well as overlapping dysfunction of the cerebellum and CST. In a 2-year transatlantic natural history study we will validate clinician- and patient-reported, digital and molecular outcomes. In addition, PROSPAX will improve on existing and develop new outcome parameters that show superior sensitivity to change. These include a clinical SPAX composite score, a smartphone mHealth toolbox combining wearable sensors with app-based patient-entered outcomes, and multimodal MRI radiomics with an innovative machine learning approach for multisite MRI analysis. Single-cell multi-omic studies in mouse will identify shared pathways and vulnerabilities between cerebellar and corticospinal neurons and will unravel new molecular biomarkers. By example of the two most common recessive SPAX (SPG7, ARSACS) PROSPAX will create a paradigmatic trial-readiness pathway for charting disease progression and multimodal outcome measures that will be applicable to many of the >100 SPAX diseases alike.

column37: Genetic defects may cause congenital disfigurements of the face which may have profound effects on the appearance of the person leading to psychological complications. column36: A K-mer Based Approach for Institutional AMR Surveillance, Transmission Monitoring, and Rapid Diagnostics
column37: Antibiotic resistant organisms (AROs) have become increasingly difficult to treat, with rising morbidity and mortality worldwide. Healthcare institutions are often the epicenter for outbreaks of these antibiotic resistant organisms, and are also windows into their circulation within the broader community. Transmission of antibiotic resistant organisms within hospitals is under appreciated. Moreover, identification of linked strains that may be causing occult outbreaks is often not systematically performed. Genomic approaches can provide a better understanding of within-hospital transmission of AROs, which can be used to guide infection control practices. Some institutions have augmented their ARO surveillance with whole genome sequencing, but this is both expensive and time consuming, making it unsuitable for routine use. However, new approaches that use k-mer based algorithms along with genomic reference databases can provide rapid evaluation of pathogen lineage and potential for linked transmission. These same approaches can also be used to provide important rapid diagnostic information about the likelihood of resistance to a given antibiotic. While there is much potential in these approaches, they need to be formally evaluated across care settings and geography before they can be trialled in the clinical setting. Here we propose a multi-continental prospective evaluation of the performance of a k-mer based approach for institutional surveillance of common multidrug resistant Gram-negative pathogens as well rapid prediction of antibiotic resistance patterns.

column36: Multi-level integrative 'omics to identify biomarkers in a Schizophrenia and other major psychoses. Jeremie Poschmann. Muliobio
column37: We will leverage a unique, large patient cohort selected based on molecular and clinical characteristics, combined with advanced molecular profiling and computational analysis to identify and then validate clinically useful biomarkers predictive of major psychosis. Our goal is to leverage a multi-level, interdisciplinary approach and simultaneously monitor serum protein levels, promising molecular phenotypes including gene expression and epigenetics, cellular immune phenotypes known to be altered during major psychosis while precisely controlling for immune cell population variation. We will use integrative computational analyses and machine learning methods to define a novel and unique set of BM predictive of major psychosis. This will enable us to compare for the first time: (i) longitudinal patient information reaching until childhood trauma, (ii) polygenic risk scores, (iii) cellular phenotypes including the variation in immune cell populations and their response to stimuli, (iii) molecular phenotypes such miRNA expression, whole transcriptome analysis and epigenomic analysis, together (iv) with serum protein investigation based on BM candidates from psychosis literature. The project is organized into four objectives. This project unites clinical neuroscientists, genomics scientists, cell biologists and immunologists each employing cutting edge methods in their own respective field. This collaboration highlights the different layers of investigations. Notably, it integrates patient phenotypic time courses assessed by our clinical scientists, immune cell phenotypes as determined by our immunologist, molecular phenotype information investigated by genomics scientists combined with machine learning approaches and integrative analysis by computational scientists.

column37: The discovery of antimicrobial agents was one of the great triumphs of the 20th century. The sobering news is that antibiotic resistance was part of the process as well. If nothing is done by 2050, AMR will cost $100 trillion with 10M people/year expected to die (https://amr-review.org). Factors driving AMR extend beyond human healthcare with implications in agriculture and the environment (the One Health approach). New and improved approaches for tackling AMR include better surveillance; rational drug use, different business model for generating antibiotics, innovation at all levels and most importantly a global approach. This transnational team grant proposal is tasked to apply new machine learning approaches for modeling AMR for faster diagnosis, better surveillance and prediction of resistance emergence. Specifically, we will develop machine learning implementation that can orient the selection of treatments by assessing the level of resistance, provide rational for the generation of novel antibiotics, and assist in the surveillance of human and livestock AMR around the globe. To achieve this, we have assembled a transnational team (Canada, China, Finland, France) with complementary skills with demonstrated expertise in machine learning applied to both genomics and metabolomics and AMR domain experts. Our transnational team has all the elements to be highly impactful and to continue collaborating well past the JPIAMR funding. Our complementarity of expertise will help us tackle the challenges ahead and ensure our continued success.

column36: Develop a multi-disciplinary approach for the personalized prenatal diagnostic and antepartum feto-maternal risk evaluation for twin pregnancies.
column37: The frequency of twin pregnancies has risen globally due to increased use of assisted conception and increasing maternal age. Twin pregnancies have 5-9 times higher frequencies of fetal chromosomal and structural abnormalities, often deliver preterm, and have high prevalence of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), preeclampsia (PE), and intrauterine growth restriction compared to singletons. Twins have unique complications such as the twin-to twin transfusion syndrome in monochorionic (MC) twins. Consequently, more twins are born prematurely, suffer from low birth weight, require admission to newborn intensive care units, and are at greater risk of developing motor and cognitive disorders and cerebral palsy in later life. These impose a huge burden on individuals, families, and societies. We aim to develop a multi-marker, personalized, prenatal diagnostic model to predict feto-maternal complications in twin pregnancies. A multi-national network will recruit a statistically powered cohort of 1,200 twins and follow them through pregnancy until delivery using biochemical, endocrine, imaging, immunologic and cell free DNA (cfDNA) parameters to modify a priori risks. Initial cohorts (Prof Maymon, Israel), demonstrated good prediction of Down syndrome, PE, and GDM using ultrasound and serum markers. We will use these markers and evaluate structural and chromosomal abnormalities [developed by Prof Kagan (Tubingen, Germany)], standardised imaging for MC twins [Prof's Brown and Miron (McGill, Canada)], and endocrine, sonographic, and biophysical markers [Prof Borrell (Barcelona, Spain), and Dr Geipel (Bonn, Germany)]. Prof Nicolaides (London, UK) will contribute his twin cohort data. Prof. Cuckle (Israel) will perform modelling using this large dataset to identify risk stratification algorithms for twins, offering personalized, preventive clinical care pathways for feto-maternal disorders. This would enable a paradigm shift in prenatal personalized care for twin pregnancy.

column36: IDx: An exploration of regulatory, corporate, relational, and technical barriers to uptake of diagnostics in the fight against AMR
column37: Greater availability of fast and accurate diagnostics for infections would greatly reduce the over-prescription of antibiotics and slow the growth of antibiotic resistance which limits treatment options. It would also help prescribe the right drug at the right time, thus reducing suffering and increasing survival. However, despite advances in technology, few useful diagnostics for bacterial infections have come to market and we are seeing a downward trend in innovation. This study proposes to identify the key barriers that remain once a new diagnostic has been developed, looking at recent technological advances that ultimately failed to be authorized, adopted, or able to change prescribing. It will also look at technologies that have helped in the fight against antimicrobial resistance. Are there any features or particularities that seem to have improved their chance of success? Lessons from the failures and few successes will be used to assess chances for products in the pipeline, examining how regulation, reimbursement, technology transfer, and organizational characteristics might be improved to make them succeed within the clinical setting. The work will focus on each of these themes in developed world settings but also use them as a lens (in addition to diagnostic technical characteristics) to examine determinants of uptake in rural parts of South Africa, which are to some extent a proxy for LMIC.

column37: This trial is comparing medical approaches for stroke prevention in people who have atrial fibrillation (AF) but have undergone a successful procedure called ablation to eliminate or substantially reduce the arrhythmia. If it does reduce the stroke risk, then patients who have a successful ablation may not need to continue on lifelong oral anticoagulant therapy. This trial will compare a strategy of oral anticoagulant therapy to an aspirin per day after successful AF ablation. The results of this trial will help improve the health of thousands of Canadians who suffer from AF and receive ablations, but are unsure of the best approach for stroke prevention.

column36: Innate immune activity, the normal aging brain, Alzheimer's disease pathology and symptoms: new answers, new questions?
column37: Immune activation is a key feature of both normal brain aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD). But until now we haven't had assays that are sensitive enough to measure the key actors in this sort of brain "inflammation." And we don't know whether these molecular changes cause -- or are a response to -- the destructive brain changes that are occurring at the same time. Application of new, ultra-sensitive methods to 5 - 9 years of longitudinal clinical and imaging data and ~675 serial samples of cerebrospinal fluid from 170 members of an aging high-risk population will tell us: 1) what's going on over time in these "inflammatory" changes at the molecular level; 2) in what sequence these changes occur; 3) whether the "inflammatory"changes cause or result from the ongoing damage to the brain that are characteristic of both normal aging and the development of Alzheimer's disease; 4) whether this immune activity can alter the severity of symptoms that result from the damage; and 5) if so, whether the immune changes make things worse or, possibly, better. The ultimate aim is to learn enough about "inflammatory" or immune brain changes in aging and Alzheimer's disease that we can find target pathways for the development of new treatments to either reduce or prevent the symptoms -- and therefore the morbidity -- of brain aging or evolution of Alzheimer's pathology.

column36: Land-based Approaches to Health and Wellness in Isolated Indigenous Communities: Agroforestry Stewardship Practices and Traditional Pursuits
column37: Recently, governments and researchers have recognized the importance of land (which includes water and air) to Indigenous people - and more specifically - the importance of land-based activities to health and wellness. In a previous CIHR-funded project, we successfully pioneered agroforestry practices in subarctic Indigenous communities; our on-the-land program viewed global warming as an opportunity to grow vegetables in subarctic Canada under ambient conditions, by extending the historical distributional range of produce. Agroforestry is a more sustainable agricultural stewardship practice that combines woody perennials (trees, shrubs) with crops in arrangements that optimizes yields of vegetables and fruit. Being more diverse, and thus more resilient to environmental disturbance than conventional agriculture, agroforestry stewardship has the potential to act as a more reliable local-food system. Further, we harmonized agroforestry activities with traditional harvesting activities - utilizing the by-products of goose harvesting (e.g. offal, bones) to make a locally-sourced, nutrient-rich fertilizer - to form a more sustainable import-substitution strategy. In the present project, we propose to test the potential scalability/transferability, nationally (Miawpukek First Nation, Newfoundland, Canada) and internationally (Widjabul Nation, New South Wales, Australia) of our climate-change adaptation (food system) protocol in communities experiencing disparate climate change challenges and opportunities. Expected benefits include: the harvesting and sharing of traditional meats, fruits and vegetables; social and cultural benefits from interacting with fellow harvesters; empowerment through community capacity enhancement; and novel information on health and wellness with respect to land-based initiatives, will be provided to Indigenous communities, health care professionals, and policy makers.

column36: Indigenous People and Diabetes - Indigenous Knowledge and Wellness Practices disrupting Biomedical Colonization: Research Governed by Decolonizing and Two-Eyed Seeing Methods
column37: "Everyone is struggling with this same problem, diabetes, it's a huge problem and we are trying to get people to start the conversation to see how to fix it ... it's not a simple pill or injection ... It involves the cost of food, the housing, the social structures, the traditional teachings, the animals on the land." Paul Linton, Eeyou Istchee James Bay Cree Community member Before the 1950s, type 2 diabetes (TTD) was unheard of in most Indigenous populations. However, since the number of Indigenous peoples with TTD has increased and age of diagnosis is younger than in the general population. Current treatments for TTD are based on a biomedical worldview, or western science, such as increased physical activity and dietary changes. Health from this worldview focuses on the physical body. Most Indigenous people, however, look at the whole body (emotional, spiritual, physical and mental) in relational to the land. Since Europeans, the colonizers, came to North America or Turtle Island, Indigenous people have lost their relationship to the land, gathering and hunting less traditional foods while rates of TTD continue to rise. To address this, a diverse group of settler and Indigenous peoples developed a 4-year multiple-methods study that will use Indigenous methodologies, such as ceremonies, stories and oral history, which will be guided by 4 Elders. The study aims to value and respect Indigenous, biomedical, and historical perspectives of health and TTD using decolonizing and two-eyed seeing approaches. Research objectives to address are to: 1) Create spaces to elevate Indigenous knowledge relevant to TTD, relation to the land and traditional foods; and 2) Collaboratively build bridges between Indigenous knowledge and places where Indigenous people access TTD healthcare services. The hope is that new pathways to address TTD will be realized through Indigenous peoples' awakening to original teachings of the importance of the sacred relationship to the land.

column36: Metis Youth Health Issues and Research Training Needs
column37: Metis peoples are significantly under-represented in Indigenous health research in Canada. Metis health research needs to be designed to recognize their distinctive collective identities, historical contexts, ways of knowing and unique health challenges. Based on our previous successful research with Indigenous youth, we recognize the power of giving youth a 'voice' in the health issues they see in their communities, and the value of building research capacity amongst those who are the future agents of change. We are thereby proposing a gathering of Metis youth/young adults from across western Canada to explore concepts of health, health issues, and health research training needs. This proposal reflects a partnership involving academic researchers (Metis and those with significant Indigenous lived experience), Metis partner organizations and Metis Elders. The focus on Indigenous research and research training responds to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) Call to Action #65 on building Indigenous research capacity. The focus on youth is also consistent with the TRC report, which prioritized recommendations relating to ensuring this generation of Indigenous children can grow up safely at home, get a good education, be healthy and be proud of their culture. The gathering will occur over three days at the Batoche National Historic Site in Saskatchewan, as a site of significance to Metis peoples. Metis Elders and knowledge guardians will be present to provide knowledge, context and grounding for the discussions, and to ensure that Metis knowledge-specific protocols are observed and followed. Metis undergraduate and graduate student research assistants will be responsible for leading the small-group discussions and information capture. Outcomes of the gathering will include a plain language booklet outlining the results and recommendations and a video of the event. Knowledge translation will include youth-led presentations back to their communities.

column36: Decolonizing and Reorienting Health Systems Towards Health Equity: The xaqana itkini (Many Ways of Working Together) Research Project
column37: Research and health services tend to exclude the voices and cultures of Indigenous peoples or fail to represent them in a respectful way. The goal of this project is to do research in a better way and improve relationships between health care systems and Indigenous peoples to help improve health and wellness in Indigenous communities. Over the last year, our team has worked with Ktunaxa First Nation in the Kootenay region of British Columbia to develop and test a new approach to research that is led by Ktunaxa peoples and reflects Ktunaxa culture. Ktunaxa Elders named this approach xaqana itkini (Many Ways of Working Together). Important features of this approach include: coming together during community gatherings and ceremonies, starting with a shared meal, using traditional approaches for sharing information and solving problems, including everyone's voices, and getting feedback often. We tested the xaqana itkini (Many Ways of Working Together) approach in Ktunaxa communities by working together to create a Ktunaxa Model of Wellness. During this process, community members shared their ideas about what a healthy community looks like. Community members liked this approach and said that the process was "really meaningful, really powerful." Testing the xaqana itkini (Many Ways of Working Together) approach was the first step along the pathway toward a long-term working relationship between Ktunaxa Nation and Interior Health Authority. The goal of the next step is to use the xaqana itkini (Many Ways of Working Together) approach to look at how the health care system can learn from Ktunaxa understandings of wellness to improve health services in Ktunaxa communities.

column37: Rural and remote residents of Canada (including Indigenous peoples) must overcome barriers to access high quality medical care. They receive low quality care, incur high out-of-pocket health-related expenses and have difficulty scheduling timely appointments with specialists, a contributing factor why they are more likely to suffer from long-term diseases and worse health outcomes than urban residents. To improve health outcomes for rural and remote Albertans, we will study four new health care innovations (called SMART-CARE) and identify how they may be optimally combined: (a) a community-based screening tool shown to be an effective way to diagnose chronic diseases (e.g., kidney disease) earlier; (b) the Kidney Failure Risk Equation, which effectively identifies which patients need to be seen by specialists; (c) care pathways to help family doctors or nurse practitioners (NPs) ensure that patients get appropriate treatment for kidney disease, diabetes and high blood pressure; and (d) a computer system called eConsult which enables patients to obtain advice from specialists through their primary care providers, thereby eliminating the need to travel to a city. We will study the effects of these tools on patients' health, satisfaction with health care, access to care and health care costs. In four remote communities across Alberta, local health care workers will be trained on these tools and will offer screening services to adult residents to assess who is likely to develop kidney disease or conditions that may lead to it. People showing no signs of chronic disease will be encouraged to maintain a healthy lifestyle. People at low risk for poor health outcomes will be linked to local family doctors or NPs; those at medium and some at high risk will be treated by local doctors or NPs with specialist support via eConsult. If SMART-CARE works well, we will scale up implementation and provide policy makers with evidence to justify funding a nationwide rollout.

column36: To determine the impact of breastfeeding, maternal food intake and infant gut microbiota on the risk of obesity and diabetes in First Nations women and children in rural communities
column37: First Nations (FN) people in rural Canada have high risk for obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). The prevalence of youth-onset T2D in Manitoba is the highest among the provinces in Canada. The majority of youth-onset T2D in Manitoba lives in rural or remote FN communities. Breastfeeding initiation reduced the risk of diabetes in mothers and their children. Breastfeeding is the traditional method of FN people for feeding babies, but the rate of breastfeeding is low in FN communities. FN women in rural or remote communities have less access to prenatal and breastfeeding education compared to urban women due to geographic, socioeconomic and historical factors. Gut bacteria in infants play important roles in growth and the development of obesity, T2D and the beneficial effects of breastfeeding. The disorders of gut bacteria may be implicated in the high prevalence of T2D in rural-living FN children. The proposed study will partner with community Elders to educate FN pregnant women and their family members with traditional and modern knowledge on the importance of a healthy diet, breast milk, and the role of gut bacteria in the development of obesity and diabetes. We will examine the impact of breastfeeding on infant gut bacteria and the relationship with breastfeeding and infant growth with supports from Elders and community assistants. The results will help to guide breastfeeding and mother's food intake. We have invited FN Elders, healthcare workers and researchers to join the research team. FN people and their traditions will be respected. The privacy of participants will be protected. The FN communities and participants will have the ownership and the control of the data. The project will reduce the inequity of perinatal care for rural-living FN women and help to rationalize an evidence-based and scalable breastfeeding program to reduce the risk of obesity and T2D in other rural and remote Indigenous communities in Canada.

column36: Decolonizing childbirth with Nunavik Inuit women transferred to high-risk hospitals for childbirth: a co-designed pilot intervention
column37: BACKGROUND Inuit women in Canada carry a disproportionate burden of poor health, with higher rates of maternal mortality and negative birth outcomes. Some 14% of Inuit women in Nunavik (Inuit territory in Quebec) travel to tertiary southern hospitals for specialized obstetric care. Fly-out births are linked to adverse health outcomes for Inuit women, their families and communities. This participatory research supports culturally safe Inuit childbirth, and will co-design pilot interventions with Inuit stakeholders and their care providers, to inform the decolonization of obstetric care in Quebec tertiary hospitals. METHODS The study engages three stakeholder groups: (i) Montreal-based Inuit women, their families and community members; (ii) Inuit residing in Nunavik and (iii) care providers and policy makers in Nunavik and Montreal. With each group, a series of group fuzzy cognitive mapping sessions will explore experiences with fly-out childbirth and perspectives of decolonization in obstetric care. Individual and household questionnaires will document the frequency of these findings. Stakeholders will co-design an intervention through deliberative dialogue and community meetings. Recommendations will be shared with obstetrical staff of a Montreal tertiary hospital. A follow-up survey will measure quantitative changes in birth outcomes, patient satisfaction, and decolonizing care practices. An integrated knowledge translation and exchange strategy engages stakeholders in cognitive mapping sessions, and co-design interventions in deliberative dialogue. DISCUSSION Evacuation for childbirth aims to reduce health disparities faced by Inuit women, yet it is inadvertently associated with adverse health outcomes. Affirming Inuit values of childbirth and engaging Inuit voices in service delivery improvement can support culturally safe care. The protocol and instruments developed may have wider relevance for rural Inuit across Canada.

column36: Moving Engagement Beyond the Beside: Family-Partnered Delirium Prevention, Detection and Management in the Critically Ill
column37: Almost half of the patients in an intensive care unit (ICU) have delirium during their stay. Patients who have delirium cannot pay attention, are often confused, and may seem sleepier than usual. Research has shown that patients with delirium are more likely to die or have long-term mental health issues. Family members find it upsetting to see their loved one with delirium. This means that family members are also more likely to have long-term mental health issues. We think family members of ICU patients can see delirium before doctors and nurses. We also think family members can stop delirium from happening or shorten how long it lasts. Helping with delirium may protect family members and their loved ones from long-term mental health issues. Family members new to an ICU may not know about delirium. This study will tell family members how to use a questionnaire to identify delirium and how they can help stop delirium from happening or shorten how long it lasts. The goal of our study is to see if family members like helping with delirium in the ICU. If we show that family members like helping, we will do a larger study that will see if their help can reduce the amount of delirium in the ICU or reduce the long-term mental health issues. The results from this study may lead to a change in policy that would partner with family members to improve delirium in the ICU. In turn, this would improve patient and family care and outcomes in the ICU.

column36: Diagnostic and prognostic precision medicine for behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia
column37: The behavioral variant of frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) is a common cause of early-onset dementia (before age 65) with a lot of different variations in underlying pathology, genetics, and natural course. It therefore demands a customized approach to predict individual prognosis and develop personalized treatments. BvFTD is often mistaken for a primary psychiatric disorder (PPD), causing substantial diagnostic delay up to 6 years in average. Therefore, the most time critical clinical challenge is how to differentiate early bvFTD (in majority non-genetic) from late-onset psychiatric disorders that may mimic FTD, in order to deliver relevant interventions and treatments. All members of our multidisciplinary consortium have a strong track record in bvFTD research. We selected the most promising results of our ongoing research, including neuropsychological and social cognitive markers; neuroimaging- based classifiers; cerebrospinal fluid and serum biomarkers; and genetic makers. In this project, we will combined cohorts from all sites to examine and validate the above-mentioned markers (discovery cohort). This includes a large number of autopsy confirmed cases. We will then validate these markers in a deeply phenotyped prospective multi-national cohort that we will collect over the next 3 years. We will use advanced statistics to create the best diagnostic and prognostic models for bvFTD and PPD. Our project will contribute towards an early and accurate bvFTD identification, that is crucial for trial enrollment, whereas on the other hand early PPD identification will lead to the appropriate psychiatric treatments.

column36: Extending the safety net: How can interprofessional primary care teams facilitate successful hospital discharges?
column37: Coordinating care between providers in the hospital and the community is challenging. This challenge hampers the continuity of care for older adults who have complex health and social needs. There is limited evidence on how to best coordinate care for older adults transitioning from the hospital back to the community. Recently, several provinces have introduced two types of interprofessional teams that have potential to improve post-hospital care. One is community-based transitional care teams that provide rehabilitation and support services to promote post-hospital recovery. The second is networks of health and social care professionals that support family physicians. Hospital, community, and primary care teams need to work well together to address transitions in care. Otherwise, the addition of more teams to the health care system can further hamper coordination. Increasing the ability of health care teams to support transitions from hospital to home is a complex issue that requires the input of multiple stakeholders. Important stakeholders include patients and their families, health and social care professionals in hospital and community, and policymakers. Patients in particular, have not had their values and needs attended to in care transitions research. This project will engage all necessary stakeholders to collaboratively design a research study that will develop solutions for improving continuity between interprofessional teams. We will pilot the methods and evaluate the process we used to engage patients in the research process. The result will be a tested study protocol and participatory research process to support a successful national grant application. In the long-term, our work will propel practice change in how teams work across settings to support care transitions from hospital to home. Using the experiential knowledge of patients, families and care providers will make the research relevant to the people it will impact the most.

column36: Improving the quality of life for long-term care residents living with frailty: A mixed methods exploration of factors affecting healthcare provision and outcomes.
column37: Residents of long term care (LTC) are typically female, over the age of 85 with low income and multiple complex health conditions. Access to primary care, which is an essential component of quality of life (QoL), is limited by resident physical or psychosocial factors and the expertise of providers to manage care. The resultant problem is residents becoming unwell or being transferred to the emergency department (ED), further impacting QoL. Evidence supports the role of nurse practitioners in reducing health service utilization, decreasing rates of transfer and admission to hospital, and decreasing length of stay post-transfer. This research team mobilizes knowledge gained through the foundation study (Compton et al., 2019) which was a partnership with residents of LTC, family members, staff and content experts, and explored resident QoL, staff skills-mix, and care processes, including the decision to transfer residents to the ED, within six LTC homes in Saskatchewan. The aim of this catalyst study is to identify innovative models of care that will improve the QoL and outcomes for residents living in LTC. The research strategy uses a patient-oriented research approach. Phase 1 of the grant is to build capacity of all team members through sharing lived experiences in LTC, as family caregivers and as researchers by developing infographics on the data from the foundation study. In phase 2 the research team co-produces and engages with residents, families and stakeholders in a World Cafe at each of the six LTC sites. The data generated from the World Cafes will be analyzed in phase 3 to propose innovative models of care to trial in LTC homes. The findings will be compiled for all LTC homes for deliberation and use by decision makers and collaborators. Both the research process and results are significant in empowering LTC residents and stakeholders to advocate for resident-centred care and enhance models of care to improve outcomes for older adults.

column37: In response to the Catalyst Grant- Patient Oriented Research, this application proposes to apply innovative big-data and community-based methodologies to support research that is aligned with Canada's Strategy for Patient Oriented Research (SPOR) Framework, which advocates for collaboration amongst patients, researchers and healthcare providers. We want to know which recovery-oriented outcomes matter most to patients/students of the RCs. Most evaluations developed in healthcare settings tend to measure the outcomes that are important to staff or the organization rather than those of the patient. Partnering with patients/students to shape how RCs are evaluated will ensure that the identified outcomes are relevant and important to the users of the program. The aim of this research is to do this pilot work together so we can apply for a larger grant. Our next grant can focus on taking what we found and co-creating an actual evaluation for RCs that can be conducted across our three sites.

column36: Addressing Loneliness and Social Isolation: Building Bridges in Seniors' Housing
column37: Because of the increase in one-person households and the geographic dispersion of families, loneliness and social isolation (LSI) may be more common for older adults now than in the past. Loneliness refers to having fewer or less close relationships than a person would like, whereas social isolation means not having many relationships with other people. LSI have been linked to the development of physical illnesses, mental health problems, impaired cognitive functioning and a higher risk of death. Low-income older adults in social housing have many important risk factors for LSI. The majority are women who live alone with inadequate income, may have personal health challenges and have often lost a spouse or partner. In the spring of 2019, our team ran a successful 14-week program (Building Bridges) to enhance social interaction with 53 older adults in seniors' social housing. A major research priority for participants was the development of strategies to address LSI. Our team includes four patient advisors who participated in the program and two older adults from the Saskatoon Council on Aging. This proposal reflects the guidance and direction from these key team members. Our aim is to co-design, implement and evaluate patient-oriented strategies to address LSI in two seniors' social housing units. Using a variety of research methods and guided by Age-Friendly and Positive Aging approaches, we will: 1) determine the patterns of LSI in the units; 2) elicit the perspectives, priorities and preferences for strategies to address LSI through meaningful and cooperative dialogue with tenants; 3) assess the ways in which Life Story Work might address LSI; 4) co-create and evaluate an eight week group program; and 5) build community capacity to create a sustainable approach to addressing LSI. World Cafes, surveys, interviews, Life Story Work and focus groups will provide us with rich, patient-oriented data to meet our objectives and guide future research.

column36: Activity-based Therapy after Spinal Cord Injury or Disease: Development of a Tracking Tool Using the Delphi Method
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a costly condition that has life-long, negative effects on mobility, function, and independence. People with SCI may recover some function by engaging in activities that strengthen and re-organize connections in the nervous system. These activities, called activity-based therapies (ABT), involve repeatedly practicing a specific movement or task. ABT result in many benefits, such improved mobility and quality of life, as well as reducing the likelihood of developing other chronic conditions, such as heart disease. Despite these benefits, ABT is infrequently used in the rehabilitation of Canadians with SCI. The intensity of ABT (i.e. thousands of movement repetitions) is difficult to achieve in hospital and community settings. In March 2019, people with SCI, clinicians, hospital administrators, researchers and policy-makers met to identify priorities for ABT research and practice. One priority is the development of a tool that people with SCI and health care workers can use to track participation in ABT. As a first step, we will determine the content of the ABT tracking tool. For example, which activity details (e.g. duration, number of repetitions, assistance required, etc.) would be the most useful to record? First, we will complete a literature review and group meetings with people with SCI, physical and occupational therapists, hospital administrators, community exercise trainers and policy makers to identify all types of ABT. Second, we will complete a Delphi process with the above-mentioned groups to finalize the content of the ABT tracking tool. The Delphi process is a means of reaching consensus among a group of experts. About 60 experts will identify the important content to include in the ABT tracking tool through 2-3 rounds of online surveys. This project will ideally position the research team to develop and evaluate a tool in future research. The ABT tracking tool will provide valuable data to inform health care decisions.

column36: Elevating the Uses of Storytelling Approaches within Indigenous Health Research: A Patient-engaged Scoping Review Study Involving Indigenous People and Settlers
column37: There are calls to integrate Indigenous knowledges and wellness practices into healthcare systems. However, Western research approaches are often used in an attempt to understand Indigenous perspectives, resulting in findings and policies which fail to address the priorities and health needs of Indigenous peoples. Storytelling, long used by Indigenous communities to share knowledge, is increasingly being used as a research approach by Indigenous people and settlers to privilege Indigenous perspectives. However, this work has not been critically reviewed. Our study purpose is to better understand and elevate the use of storytelling as an approach in Indigenous health research. In this collaborative research project, a team of Indigenous patients, Elders, healthcare providers, and administrators will join Indigenous and non-Indigenous researchers to bring multiple perspectives and experiences to the research. Our multidisciplinary team will find and critically review research using storytelling to determine how this approach has been used in Indigenous health research. Team members will co-create the research objectives, and continue to work together throughout the research project to ensure that Indigenous patient voices and perspectives are prioritized. We will also develop a framework to guide the respectful use of storytelling approaches in health research that involves Indigenous and non-Indigenous people. Although we understand some of the reasons behind why the health of Indigenous peoples is worse than the health of other Canadians, there are still many unknowns. Research that prioritizes Indigenous voices and knowledges using storytelling is crucial for filling the gaps in our understanding. column36: Understanding how vulnerable older adults (are new immigrants, Indigenous, have mild-to-moderate dementia or identify as LGBTQ) experience social isolation and loneliness
column37: In Canada, the frailty in seniors is almost twice that of mid-age adults. Frailty has traditionally been conceptualized as a clinical phenomenon, but a person's social activities, social supports, social networks, loneliness and whether they are living alone contributes substantially to social frailty. Frailty is a public health concern as it has been shown to lead to mortality and disability and decreased quality of life. In Canada, seniors who are new immigrants, are Indigenous, have language barriers and/or identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, or queer (LGBTQ) are at even greater risk to become socially isolated or lonely. However, we don't really understand the health risks and challenges of older adults who are socially frail. One reason for this may be that we don't always involve seniors in research, particularly those who are truly representative of the health condition being studied. Patients in general don't tend to drive research initiatives or not involved at all stages of research. However, their insights are the most valuable to understand their lived experience. Our research will address these challenges through a qualitative study of interviews to help us to understand what seniors need to be able to engage in research. We will also investigate how to engage them in research by evaluating how they experience participation in patient-oriented research training as well as in our integrated KT team.

column36: Actively waiting for interdisciplinary chronic pain care: A multi-site feasibility study investigating levels of clinical support and the cost-effectiveness of an internet-delivered psychotherapy treatment for individuals on wait-lists for chronic pain clinics
column37: The impact of chronic pain on Canadians is well known. Wait times for care for chronic pain patients can range from six months to two and a half years. Wait-times provide an opportunity to use accessible interventions that improve psychosocial function and patients' readiness and ability to actively manage their condition. Self-management is recognized as key to improving self-efficacy and functional outcomes and reducing healthcare costs although engagement of patients depends on their readiness to make change. Patient's self-report of readiness to engage has been reported to be less than 50%, potentially contributing to the frequent drop-out typically seen in prescribed pain rehabilitation programs. There is interest in using virtual methods to improve access to care in a manner that is useful across regions with different resource availability. No online programs have evaluated the effect of Motivational interviewing (MI) on uptake of chronic pain self-management. MI is an intervention that focuses on motivation and commitment for change by exploring and resolving ambivalence. Our aim is to examine the feasibility of an online program designed to enhance readiness for change and self-management of patients waiting for care at the KHSC chronic pain clinic. This program will follow a MI approach and will be comprised of self-directed modules and exercises with coaching support. The study will build the foundation to enable future large-scale, multicenter trials testing the effectiveness of this intervention. Fifty patients will be recruited from the waitlists of 2 CPN clinics (n=25 Kingston, n=25 Toronto). Patients will participate in either the educational control or motivationally enhanced arms. The online education has been previously established and contains 10 weeks of content. Outcomes will be assessed pre and post intervention. Knowledge translation activities are built into our approach and will be led by patient partner and knowledge user team members.

column36: Seamless Transitions for Adolescent Trajectories In Care (STATIC)
column37: Half of mental health conditions emerge by the age of 16 years and 75% by the age of 24. However, this increased incidence in youth corresponds to a weak point in mental health care service delivery. The transition from Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) to Adult Mental Health Services (AMHS) is a vulnerable period where youth disengage from utilizing mental health services at higher rates than other age groups. Gaps and suboptimal care carry a risk of illness extension and chronicity, which have multiple adverse effects. The Mental Health Commission of Canada has identified improving the experience of transitions as one of the primary policy objectives for the 2017 - 2022 framework for action. Modern e-health technologies could be used to personalize and tailor transition supports yet there have been very few adequately powered or controlled studies evaluating their effectiveness. In line with CIHR's priority agenda, Knowledge Users are specifically interested in e-health services that democratize access geographically, reduce costly 'middlemen' administration in face to face services and can leverage digital functionality to become more patient-oriented and data driven. Our interdisciplinary team views this as a priority knowledge-to-action opportunity for policy, innovation and research. We propose a 3 part catalyst project: 1. consensus analysis around healthy behaviours and information needs during this transition period; 2. theory-driven co-design process to create a Short-Messaging Service (text-messaging) based intervention; and 3. usability study with a cohort of youth and parents to inform trial planning. Combined, these activities will catalyze a new partnership between multiple research labs, health authorities and youth advocacy groups in Atlantic Canada. The proposed activities will build much needed evidence-based policy capacity for using e-health for mental health service transitions for youth and their families.

column36: An Electronic System for Individualized Monitoring of Patient Reported Outcomes for Value and Effectiveness in Cardiovascular Care (IMPROVE CV Care)
column37: Person-centered care is fundamental to high-quality health systems because it improves experiences people have with care, better aligns health services delivery with individual needs, reduces inappropriate use of services influencing the cost of care, improves health outcomes, and fosters greater satisfaction of the professionals who provide care. This is achieved by integrating clinical data with both objectively collected patient reported outcomes (PROMs) and patient reported experiences (PREMs), which quantify the subjective aspects of a person's health status and their experience with processes of care. Unfortunately, PROMs and PREMs are still generally collected through telephone and paper-based surveys and as outcomes in research studies, with results only made available in aggregate after considerable delay. Recent advances in PROMs and PREMs collection have focused on electronic formats for administration because of the ease of implementation into routine clinical care. Although there are well developed and validated PROMs and PREMs for cardiovascular disease, there is a lack of electronic tools for collecting and reporting these measures back to care providers and patients so that they can use them to improve quality and outcomes of care. Given that cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditures, this represents a missed opportunity for patients and care providers. This study aims to develop a user-tested and acceptable automated electronic PROMs and PREMS (ePROM/PREM) platform that can be deployed for collection of PROMs and PREMS in routine clinical care for use by patients and their care providers

column36: When Problematic Substance Use, Parenting, and Child Welfare Collide: Giving Voice to Women on Processes that Promote Family Health and Well-being
column37: Motherhood can open a window of opportunity to engage women in substance use treatment. However, fear of intervention by child welfare can hinder this engagement. This fear is well substantiated and carries with it a host of negative health consequences for women (e.g., increased symptoms of depression, anxiety, problematic substance use, risk of mortality). These health needs often go unrecognized and unsupported as the focus is placed on the child. This fear and the stigma experienced being a mother who has experienced substance use problems can also impact on engagement of women in the research process. This experience is crucial to health as it silences the voice of women, potentially reducing the representativeness of our research findings and hindering our ability to improve service quality and equity. We propose to undertake a fully patient-engaged research process to meet the following objectives: We will (1) explore, develop, employ, and evaluate guidelines for creating safe spaces for women with problematic substance use to as participate at community co-researchers; (2) create guidelines for culturally safe research with women with problematic substance use as research participants; (3) apply research guidelines to practice by summarizing key themes across discussions and developing a proposal for future research; and (4) co-create a strategy to mobilize the knowledge learned and guidelines to varied stakeholder audiences, including community members, service providers, academic researchers, and policy makers across health and social services fields. This may improve the validity and representativeness of our research and ultimately improve our ability to promote health and positive parenting outcomes in mothers who experience problematic substance use.

column36: Answering questions that matter to people living with diabetes using the Canadian National Diabetes Registry
column37: Canada has a new database of carefully-collected and securely-protected medical data about people living with diabetes across multiple provinces. These kinds of databases are used in medical research to answer questions; for example, "Do people taking a specific type of pill for type 2 diabetes have better or worse medical results than people who don't take those pills?" or, "Out of all children and adults with type 1 diabetes in the database who would be eligible for a provincially-funded insulin pump, how many are actually using insulin pumps?" or, "If a man and a woman with type 1 diabetes have the same hemoglobin A1c results, are they likely to have the same chances of complications of diabetes?" Normally, these kinds of questions are chosen by researchers and doctors. We believe that people living with diabetes are likely to have new ideas of questions that need answering, and may choose questions that matter more to people with diabetes. This project will assemble people living with type 1 and type 2 diabetes to come up with research questions (a) for which there isn't yet enough medical evidence and (b) that could potentially be answered with this kind of database, prioritize which ones most urgently need to be answered, and start answering the questions that matter most to people living with diabetes. Our team includes researchers (including a lead researcher who has lived with type 1 diabetes since 1983), doctors (including the doctor who is in charge of managing the database), people who can help make sure this work is used to make life and medical care better for people with diabetes, and patient partners who want to help other people living with diabetes get their questions answered.

column36: Setting a new research agenda in pediatric cancer: a priority-setting partnership with patient-, survivor-, family-, and clinician-knowledge users
column37: Cancer is the most common life-limiting disease in Canadian children and adolescents and its burden on the quality of life of young patients, survivors, and families is large. Pediatric cancer care and survivor research can improve outcomes for these key stakeholders. To date, however, the priorities for research have mainly been determined by researchers and industry, whose goals may differ from those of patients, families, and clinicians. To increase the benefit and sustain the impact of pediatric cancer research the needs and priorities of the people with lived experience of the disease must drive the scientific agenda. This approach will involve equally engaging patient-, survivor-, family- and clinician-knowledge users in all study phases to identify unanswered questions in pediatric cancer and survivorship. column36: Partnering For Pain: Mobilizing Stakeholders to Co-Design Healthcare Services to Prevent Pediatric Chronic Pain
column37: One to three million Canadian children and teens often deal with pain lasting months to years. Our Partnering For Pain team recently asked hundreds of youth, families, and healthcare providers across Canada to identify their top priorities for treating chronic pain during childhood. We learned that preventing chronic pain was their #1 concern. About 1 in 5 children and teens will develop chronic pain after surgery, and many will continue to use opioids months later. This means that improving how we treat pain from surgery is an ideal and critical time to stop chronic pain before it starts. The goal of this project is to design a new hospital care team that helps to prevent the development of chronic pain in children and teens after surgery. We know that children's hospitals in Canada want a hospital care team like this, but they don't yet know how to do it well. We will talk to and partner with all groups of people who would be impacted by this new hospital care team, including youth with pain, family members, healthcare providers, and hospital leaders. We will engage them through interviews, surveys, and in-person planning meetings. This group of people will work together to decide when, where, and how the new hospital care team should be available. The group will also decide what healthcare providers are needed for the new care team, and what questions we should ask to know whether the new care team is helpful, acceptable, and ready to be adopted by other children's hospitals. What we learn will help us to plan future projects to keep improving care for youth with pain. We will also evaluate whether our partnership was successful, and share how we worked together as an example for others who want to address top priorities identified by children, teens, and their families.

column36: Patient-oriented scale up and spread for enhanced patient-centred care
column37: Despite major public investment and a favourable climate for creating healthcare improvement projects in Canada, few new initiatives that are successful on a local scale are scaled up to reach more people. In fact a former health minister described Canada as "a country of perpetual pilot projects." Spread or scale-up is a process that aims to increase the number of users of a successful healthcare initiative so as to benefit more health services users. By including patients in designing, planning and carrying out new health initiatives, researchers make sure that their projects meet patients' needs and reflect their priorities. Research shows that patient involvement also improves health outcomes, reduces costs, and results in a better healthcare experience. However, efforts to scale up new healthcare initiatives rarely include patients or the public, either in their design, planning or execution. Those who carry out scaling up should involve patients and indeed all stakeholders (including policy makers, clinicians, and researchers) to make sure their results are relevant in the real world, and especially for those whom they are meant to benefit-the patient. Often, scaling up is top-down process initiated by governments, and the perspective of the patient is forgotten. In this study, we aim to produce information and guidance on how to engage patients and other stakeholders in scaling up. We will start by finding out what strategies, if any, already exist for this purpose, by searching the scientific literature (including unpublished works). Then we will ask a diverse group of people around the world, including patients, to come to a consensus on which are the best strategies we found for engaging patients and other stakeholders in scaling up. This diverse group will evolve into an international expert network for carrying out and advising others on future patient-oriented research and practice in scaling up.

column36: Pressure injury in people with lived experience of Spinal Cord Injury
column37: 86,000 Canadians live with spinal cord injury (SCI), a complex condition that leads to serious and costly healthcare challenges. Around 44,000 of SCIs occur as a result of a traumatic injury, leaving the individual to cope with a range of physical health challenges, including paralysis, as well as other complications and costs. Pressure injury (PI) is one of the most serious complications of SCI and over 90% of sufferers will experience at least one PI in their lifetime. Persons with PI and SCI require ongoing access to healthcare, including frequent dressing changes. While the costs to the healthcare system are enormous, the burden to the individual is even greater as PIs contribute to further mobility challenges, social isolation, and potentially death. While there is growing evidence to support the management of PIs, little is known about how persons with SCI experience PI and how they interact with the healthcare system. This research is patient-driven and explores the perspectives and priorities of PI in persons with SCI in British Columbia (BC). Guiding research questions are: 1) What are the experiences of preventing and managing pressure injury in adults with traumatic SCI in BC? 2) What are the major patient-identified factors that impact individuals' interaction with healthcare services? And 3) What are the patient-oriented research priorities for pressure injury prevention and management in people with SCI? To address these, we will first undertake mapping and focus group/individual interviews to explore the experiences of persons with PI and SCI and their interactions with the health system. We will then conduct a workshop with patients to share our findings and to develop patient-oriented research priorities for PI and SCI. Exploring the experiences and priorities of PI in persons with SCI will address an important knowledge gap and will inform future healthcare practices and research initiatives that respond to issues of importance to patients.

It is further supported by proactive and committed community partners (the Greater Victoria Coalition to End Homelessness, Community Social Planning Council, BC Housing, BC SUPPORT Unit Vancouver Island Centre, Island Health, and the BC Office of the Seniors Advocate). The purpose of this project is to undertake 'patient-oriented research' to build evidence and knowledge regarding understanding the pathways into homelessness, and the impacts of homelessness on health and QoL for older women; and to share the insights gained with wider stakeholder audiences and knowledge users to catalyze positive health-related system-level changes. A related goal is to use the evidence from this project to catalyse a larger, more comprehensive research grant that considers other diverse geographic areas and populations with vulnerability to homelessness.

column36: Assessing the physiological and behavioural effects of orally ingested cannabidiol (CBD) in older adults with dementia living at home
column37: Background & Aim: The legalization of cannabis products has allowed access to cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive cannabinoid. According to our patient partners and the national organizations they represent, CBD oil is commonly being orally administered by caregivers to reduce the agitation and anxiety in older adults (OAs) with dementia - despite the many unknowns about CBD's health and safety effects. There is an urgent need for evidence to inform therapeutic practice. The aim of this pilot feasibility study is to explore the physiological, functional, and behavioural effects of orally ingested CBD by OAs with dementia living at home using an in-home sensor system. Design: We apply SPOR-PEF and Integrated Knowledge Translation principles. An Advisory Stakeholder Panel of knowledge users and experts will be formed. This pilot feasibility study targets OAs with dementia living at home with a caregiver. An in-home sensor system will collect continuous data with high sensitivity and objectivity to detect physiological data (e.g. heart rate, mobility data, motion or sedentary activity, sleep quality) and subtle changes in function and behaviour. Participants will be monitored for 2-weeks to establish control data, followed by a 6-week CBD oil period according to a protocol with gradually escalating doses. Caregivers will record observed changes in a digital diary and an RA will conduct bi-weekly visits. Caregiver interviews will be conducted to understand their perspectives about CBD. Statistical analysis will identify dose-related changes to outcomes, and the sample will be stratified to explore sex-related differences. Significance: This interdisciplinary project uses state-of-the-art technology to objectively assess physiological, functional, and behavioural changes related to CBD use. Results of this project will provide critical preliminary data and expand our understanding of the potential harms and benefits of CBD in OAs with dementia living at home.

column36: Artificial Intelligence in Systematic Reviews: Evaluation of Emerging Electronic Tools for Researchers in Knowledge Synthesis
column37: Systematic reviews in healthcare are a longstanding cornerstone of evidence based medicine. These reviews are commonly used to inform many vital initiatives including the development of clinical practice guidelines, generation of reimbursement decisions, evaluation of clinical equipoise for clinical trials and other applications. The range of knowledge users is broad, and includes physicians, decision makers, researchers and patients alike. While systematic reviews are of tremendous importance in progressing patient healthcare, users of these studies often express interest in finding ways to complete them faster and at lower costs. Reviews may often take as long as a year to complete, and often cost $100,000 or more to cover all resources and staffing. Recently, experts in systematic reviews and computer science have developed artificial intelligence methods which offer a way in which to have computers assist with the systematic review process to enhance speed and lower staff needs. While appealing, there is great need to establish the dependability of these tools in this role to ensure the scientific quality of systematic reviews are not compromised. The current study proposes a plan to perform primary research studies to evaluate the performance of artificial intelligence tools in the context of systematic reviews. We will share our findings with key organizations in Canada and abroad whose objectives are to use systematic reviews to optimize healthcare for Canada and elsewhere.

column36: Inhibitory synaptic pruning as a substrate of neuropathic pain
column37: Chronic pain does not serve any useful purpose and is now considered a disease by itself. Unfortunately, it is often poorly managed in the clinic as we still have a limited knowledge of what causes it. Neuropathic pain is a form of chronic pain that sometimes appears after lesions to nerves and is particularly difficult to treat. Understanding the changes in neuronal connections (synapses) that process sensory information in the spinal cord is essential for developing better treatments. Here we propose that after nerve damage, there is a loss of a specific type of synapse that control pain transmission by inhibiting the hyperactivity of neuronal networks in the spinal cord, and that such loss is mediated by resident immune cells of the nervous system. The detailed mechanisms of this will be investigated in mouse models of neuropathic pain. The information obtained with this research will provide important clues for the development of new approaches to treat chronic pain after nerve lesions. A multidisciplinary approach will be used for these investigations.
