column36: Control of B cell receptor (BCR) spatial organization, BCR signaling, and B cell activation by proteins that regulate actin remodeling
column37: Activated B cells make antibodies that protect against infection. Impaired B cell activation can cause immunodeficiency diseases with chronic infections. Conversely, in some autoimmune diseases, abnormal B cells make antibodies that attack one's own cells and tissues. Each B cell in the body has B cell receptor (BCR) proteins on its surface that determine what molecule (antigen) it responds to. Binding of antigen to the BCR triggers intracellular signals that cause B cell activation. Other cell types in the body can capture antigens and display them on their surface. These antigen-presenting cells (APCs) effectively activate B cells. Our work focuses on how the spatial organization of the BCR at the B cell-APC contact site impacts the magnitude of BCR signaling and whether a B cell becomes activated. When B cells contact an APC with a relevant antigen on its surface, the B cell forms an immune synapse (IS). At the IS, BCRs are organized into a spatial pattern that increase their signaling output. Antigen-bound BCRs initially form microclusters, which then coalesce into one large cluster. The movement and coalescence of BCR microclusters depend on the cell's actin cytoskeleton that lies just beneath the cell surface. The actin cytoskeleton is composed of actin protein units that can be rapidly disassembled and then reassembled in different ways. The movement of BCR microclusters towards the center of the B cell-APC contact site requires rapid actin remodeling. Using sophisticated microscopy, we have visualized actin reorganization at the IS and shown how this drives BCR microcluster movement, enhances BCR signaling, and promotes B cell activation. We now aim to identify specific proteins that control actin remodeling and determine how they regulate B cell activation. Because actin-regulatory proteins are mutated in multiple immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases, elucidating their mechanisms of action may suggest new approaches for treating these diseases.

column36: Deafness Induced Brain Reorganization: Impacts on Rehabilitation with Cochlear Implants
column37: It is well established that auditory deprivation results in brain reorganization at the anatomical and functional levels. For deaf individuals (DI), the cochlear implant (CI) is the most effective rehabilitation method to reestablish audition. However, following CI implantation, cortices undergo reverse neuroplasticity to acquire their normal functions. The effect these processes have on rehabilitation is yet to be fully understood. Therefore, we want to extensively study the neuroplasticity induced by deafness and how we can predict CI efficacy. We have shown that cross-modal plasticity between visual and auditory cortices in DIs often leads to supraperformances in visual tasks but a reduced one in auditory tasks. We thus want to study this phenomenon in DIs by comparing their performance to normal-hearing individuals (NH). We want to examine if the type of reorganization of auditory areas of DI will influence performance for sounds following implantation in general and for voice and word recognition in particular. To answer these questions, we will apply a paradigm combining behavioral, electrophysiological (Evoked Potentials) and imaging (MRI/fMRI) tasks. We have shown in past studies anatomical cortical differences between DI and NH. Using Voxel Based Morphometry and Cortical Thickness imaging, we want to determine whether these differences influence future rehabilitation in CI. Using resting state fMRI and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), we want to examine the connectivity using activated structures as seed regions of interest (ROI). While individual factors such as deafness duration and hearing aid use will be taken into account, the proposed project will allow a better understanding of the cortical modifications underlying CI performance variability. A better understanding of the neuroplasticity occurring in auditory deprivation will be beneficial to CI users and will allow professionals to offer better rehabilitation strategies adapted to each CI user.

column36: Aging and the injured peripheral nervous system
column37: Damage to nerves in limbs often results in motor and sensory problems because the fibers (axons) that form the nerves do not regrow in large numbers back to their targets. Some of the ensuing problems that occur, such as motor incoordination and neuropathic pain, disrupt the quality of life for millions of humans worldwide and create significant personal and economic burden. Because surgical interventions are limited in their efficacy, new and specific therapies are urgently needed. Schwann cells are the glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. They wrap axons with myelin, a fatty substance that acts like an insulator that allows electrical signals to pass rapidly from one nerve cell to another. After peripheral nerve damage, Schwann cells play a critical role in creating a favourable environment for damaged peripheral fibers to regrow. They accomplish this by secreting growth promoting factors, remyelinating regrowing axons and removing inhibitory molecules. However, the functions of Schwann cells decline with age and this contributes to impaired regeneration of damaged nerve fibers and thus poor functional recovery in older individuals. This deficit has become a pressing clinical issue with the growing maturing population and humans living longer because older individuals experience more peripheral injuries because of muscle weakness and slower reflexes. My lab is interested in understanding why regeneration of damaged peripheral nerves and functional recovery are worse with age. We will specifically investigate whether a small heat shock protein called alphaB-crystallin (alphaBC) that is expressed by Schwann cells, and whose expression in peripheral nerves reduces as an animal ages, is responsible for the deficit in Schwann cell function and thus poorer regeneration in older injured animals. This grant will also inform us whether alphaBC is a possible therapeutic agent for improving functional recovery in older animals.

column36: Are day-to-day changes in air pollution and weather associated with suicide? Exploring the relationships among adults in the population-based Canadian Census Health and Environment Cohorts
column37: Suicides are a leading cause of premature death, and about 4,000 Canadians die by suicide each year. Emerging evidence suggests that daily changes in outdoor air pollution impacts mental health, and is a risk factor for suicide. These studies have found positive associations between suicide and outdoor air pollution levels. The possible association between air pollution and suicide is controversial because past studies have important limitations. These include inaccuracies in coding suicide as a cause of death, differences in the reporting of suicides by urban ural areas (which differ in pollution levels), and unaccounted day of week effects that are related to both pollution levels and number of suicides. In addition, previous research has also reported links between suicide and weather characteristics such as temperature and number of daylight hours. These findings are also controversial as they were found to diminish after adjusting for seasonal trends in suicide. Our study proposes to investigate associations between air pollution, weather, and suicide using a study design that overcomes common limitations of previous work. We would analyze associations between day to day changes in air pollution and death from suicide among those who completed the Canadian long form census. Combined, this includes about 13 million adults followed between 1991 and 2017. Among those in the cohort who died from suicide, we will compare daily weather and air pollution concentrations at the time of suicide death to suitable control times. Daily concentrations of air pollution and weather data will be obtained, and linked to the place of death of those who died from suicide. We will also study whether associations between air pollution, weather and suicide vary: by age-group, sex, ethnicity, and socio-demographic status. Finally, we will apply our risk estimates to forecasted changes in extreme heat event to estimate impacts from climate change on suicide risk through to 2100.

column36: Investigating the Role of Lipoxin Signaling in Neurodegeneration

In particular, LXB4 treatment was effective in protecting neurons in a chronic model of retinal degeneration related to glaucoma. Based on these data we hypothesize that the lipoxins are an important signaling mechanism to maintain nerve function and survival. We propose a research program to characterize this novel neuroprotective network, define its mechanism of action, and explore the potential of lipoxin signals as a therapeutic target for neuroprotection.

column36: Uptake, determinants, and gaps of HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use among HIV-negative gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) in Metro Vancouver, Canada
column37: Antiretroviral medication taken prior to HIV exposure to prevent infection is known as pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. Men who have sex with men (MSM) are the most affected HIV risk-group in Canada and among high-risk MSM. In randomized trials, PrEP has been shown to be about 90% effective in preventing HIV infection when taken regularly (at least 4 pills/week). On January 1, 2018, the BC Ministry of Health, through the BC Centre for Excellence (BC-CfE) in HIV/AIDS, began full public funding for PrEP for individuals at high risk of getting HIV. The initial uptake of PrEP thorugh this program has been very high -- more than 2000 individuals have accessed PrEP through the program as of June 2018. Nearly all (99%) PrEP users through this program are male and most (70%) live in Greater Vancouver. However, the impact of PrEP on the HIV epidemic among MSM will depend on uptake by those most at-risk. Further, behavioural risk compensation (e.g., decreased condom use) may result in higher incidence of other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This study aims to: 1) evaluate determinants and trends of initiation of PrEP among of HIV-negative MSM over a four-year period from February 2017-December 2021, 2) compare new STIs, including syphilis, chlamydia, and gonorrhea, prior to and after PrEP initiation, and 3) determine factors associated with individuals who meet clinical eligibility criteria for PrEP but who have never initiated its use. This study will provide important evidence as to the success and/or challenges faced by scaling up a publicly funded program. Through our study team's position within the BC-CfE and existing collaborations with government and community agencies, these results will directly influence provincial and national policies regarding PrEP. Further, our results will inform health promotion and clinical interventions to support PrEP uptake and adherence among Canadian MSM.

column36: Gene Therapy for Alzheimer's Disease
column37: In the brain of people with Alzheimer's disease, toxic molecules are produced, leading to cellular and functional deficits, compromising the ability to learn and remember. Gradually, new memories can no longer be formed, and old memories are lost, causing devastating consequences on daily living. The efficacy of many promising therapeutics for Alzheimer's patients is limited by their poor ability to travel from the blood, where they are administered, to the brain, where they are needed. We propose to deliver genes which will integrate into brain cells and make them capable of producing molecules neutralizing toxic products related to the pathology of Alzheimer's disease. Genetic engineering of brain cells can provide self-defence mechanisms to fight Alzheimer's disease. Briefly, genes encoding for therapeutic antibodies are placed in gene carriers. Then, these gene carriers are injected in the blood and they enter the brain to modify cells affected by the disease, namely neuronal and vascular cells. Genetically modified cells gain the capability to produce therapeutics for years to come to alter the course of the disease. This approach is refined with a technology pioneered by researchers at Sunnybrook, coupling magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and focused ultrasound. MRI-guided focused ultrasound does not require surgical procedure. Using MRI, parts of the brain that are burdened with the disease are localized and targeted with the ultrasound to facilitate the entry of gene carriers. This research will be done in animal models of Alzheimer's disease. We aim to provide a proof-of-concept at a preclinical stage, with the long-term goal to treat and improve the quality of life for people living with Alzheimer's disease. In 2018, the first MRI-guided focused ultrasound clinical trial in Alzheimer's patients was completed at Sunnybrook. Combined with ultrasound, gene therapy bodes well to provide brain cells the therapeutics they need to fight Alzheimer's disease.

column36: Patient experiences of health care access challenges for back pain care across the rural-urban continuum
column37: Back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. One in five Canadian adults experience chronic back pain. The health care costs of back pain in Canada are estimated to be up to $12 billion annually, with high rates of family physician and specialist visits, diagnostic procedures, and prescription drugs. Improving access to non-medical treatment options is an especially important public health issue in Canada in the midst of the current opioid crisis. People with back pain may encounter barriers to accessing non-medical services, such as physiotherapy, which may not be publicly funded. Potential barriers include location of available services, costs, and wait times. People living in rural and remote areas and Indigenous people are more likely to experience back pain. Little is known about barriers and facilitators to health care access among rural, remote and Indigenous people with back pain compared to urban and/or non-Indigenous people. With approximately 30% of Saskatchewan's population living in rural and remote settings and 16% of the province's population being Indigenous, this is a critical gap to address. This project will explore and apply the experiences of rural, remote and urban Indigenous and non-Indigenous people with chronic back pain to develop a deeper understanding of health care access barriers and facilitators across rural, remote, and urban communities. This project will also investigate which indicators of access and effectiveness of health care for back pain are most meaningful to rural, remote and urban patients. This information will inform the development of comprehensive measures that will be sensitive to geographical location and relevant to culturally diverse patients with chronic back pain. These measures can be used in future studies to evaluate community-based chronic back pain interventions and cross provincial/ national comparisons, ultimately leading to enhanced access to more patient-centred care for chronic back pain.

column36: Partnering with patients at the earliest stages of the research continuum: building a framework to involve patients in preclinical laboratory work
column37: Patient engagement can have many benefits, such as making sure that research results are useful to patients. While this practice is becoming more common in clinical (human) research, it is less often used in "preclinical research" (animal/cell laboratory research). Our patient partner recently participated in a preclinical research - patient engagement initiative. This experience demonstrated the need for guidance on how preclinical researchers who study sepsis (organ dysfunction caused by severe infection) and patients can work together at this very early stage of research. We think that patient engagement is important for preclinical research, and we want to develop guidance for preclinical scientists and patient partners to work together. The main objective of our project is to better understand how researchers and patient partners have worked together in laboratory studies to date and, using this information, provide suggestions on how to improve this process. To do this, our research team is completing a search to identify all preclinical papers that include patient engagement (a 'scoping review'). This will give us a general idea of what has been done so far, and how other researchers have included patients as partners in their projects. From here, we want to interview the identified researchers and patients who have experience with patient engagement in preclinical research. This will help us learn how they did it. Using this information, our team (which includes patient partners) will develop guidance for preclinical researchers and patients on how to engage each other. Finally, we will conduct focus groups to ask patients and preclinical sepsis researchers what they think of our framework, to ensure both groups agree with our guidance and to confirm that nothing is missing. This research project will create a tool to facilitate patient engagement in preclinical research, and we believe it may impact downstream clinical research.

column36: Harm Reduction and Residential Supportive Care for High-risk Pregnant Women living with HIV: A Realist Evaluation
column37: The proposed research is an evaluation of a program, Sanctum 1.5, that offers residential and specialized health care services to pregnant women living with HIV in Saskatoon, SK. For this research, clients of Sanctum 1.5 will be full partners throughout the research process. Other team members include university-based multidisciplinary researchers, Sanctum's executive director and staff, and Sanctum board members. During initial meetings for this project, research questions that clients generated led to the adoption of our methodology: a Realist Evaluation. This approach to evaluation establishes what works (and does not work) in a program, for whom, in what contexts, through identification of the how (mechanisms), and why. The goal of a Realist Evaluation is to develop and refine a program theory that identifies how program activities cause or contribute to outcomes and impacts. Our research aims to determine how and why Sanctum works (or does not work), for which clients, and under what circumstances. Both quantitative data (e.g. hospital admission records) and qualitative data (e.g. interviews with various stakeholders) will be collected to inform outcomes and outline context and mechanisms for theory development. Our analysis will consider the pattern of context, mechanisms, and outcomes that make Sanctum work (or not work); clients will play a central role in this process and validating these results. The development and refinement of a program theory will help us understand how Sanctum 1.5 enhances health outcomes for both mother and child, which will inform how to facilitate improvements and replication of the program.

column36: Trauma Informed Narrative Exposure Therapy Study: Using the Multiphase Optimization Strategy (MOST) to develop a framework for a complex intervention to treat PTSD among homeless and vulnerably housed populations in Ottawa.
column37: This proposal aims to develop and mobilize partnerships between people with lived experience of vulnerable housing , healthcare professionals and health system administrators to develop a trauma-informed care intervention for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the vulnerably housed. We propose to mobilize these partnerships to develop a theoretical model of trauma informed care for this population as part of the preparation phase of a multiphase optimization strategy (MOST). To do this, we will collaborate with people with lived experience of PTSD and vulnerable house, health professional and health care system administrators to develop a theoretical model that forms the basis of the intervention. This will be informed by the existing literature, clinical experience, secondary analysis of any existing data and any other relevant information. Second, we will mobilize our partnerships with people with lived experience of vulnerable housing and PTSD, healthcare professionals and health-care system administrators to identify the important components of the intervention that they will develop and evaluate through a one-day event. Patient partners will also help the research team decide on the "optimization criteria"; that is, what constraints the intervention is going to operate under. What we are doing that is novel is explicitly incorporating patients lived experience into a MOST strategy. That is, through this proposal, we plan to extend the benefits of the MOST framework by pairing it with the patient-oriented research principles of inclusiveness, support, mutual respect, and co-building. Trauma-informed care is suited to patient-oriented research projects as it emphasizes the importance of understanding a patient's lived experience as the foundation of providing effective care.

column36: Creating a National Aftercare Strategy for Survivors of Pediatric Cancer
column37: Rationale: Today, most children diagnosed with cancer will survive thanks to amazing advances in the medicines needed to treat childhood cancer. The treatments needed to cure childhood cancer, however, are toxic and can lead to serious medical conditions later in life. Unfortunately, most survivors of childhood cancer are not aware that they are at risk for serious medical conditions later in life. Without this knowledge, survivors can't advocate for themselves in the health care system. As our population of survivors grows, if we do not help survivors of childhood cancer understand their health care needs, survivors, the health care system and our communities as a whole are at risk of the burden of these medical conditions. Interventions to improve the care of survivors are not well developed. Importantly, those with lived experience to help inform the nature of such highly needed programs are missing. The overall goal of this project will be to identify which set of program components, as prioritized by survivors and health care stakeholders, should be included in an mHealth intervention to increase adherence to aftercare for survivors of childhood cancer. Design: Together with survivors, health care professionals and health care system administrators we will conduct focus groups across the country to gather ideas for a survivor platform. Survivors and health care professionals will also answer questions about their cancer experience, health beliefs. Expected Outcomes: The outcomes of this study will enable development of a Canada-wide mHealth platform to educate and engage, and connect survivors and health care professionals on all aspects of their late effects. Our ultimate goal is to partner with survivors to advocate for their health care needs, to reduce the potential burden on the health care system, and improve QOL for survivors.

column36: Creating patient-centred pathology reports (PAPRs) to empower patients with prostate cancer
column37: Clinical decisions that patients face in cancer care often rely on results seen in biopsy pathology reports, however, these use complex medical language and are formatted for physicians, not patients. How can patients be expected to make decisions under these circumstances? To improve this situation, in this study, patient-centred pathology reports (PAPRs) will be designed. This study focuses on prostate biopsy pathology reports because this is a common procedure, but the methods can be used for other patients with other diseases. In part 1, with guidance from patients, family members, patient education specialists, and clinical and human-centered design experts, the prostate PAPR prototype will be created by including only the most important pieces of information that patients need to make treatment decisions. Particular attention will be made to use diagrams, keep the design clean and the language easily understood. In phase 2, the process of automatically generating PAPRs from standard reports will begin. With patient portals, progress is being made and patients are gaining control of their medical records. But, it does not make sense to release medical records to patients in a format that is not suitable to their level of medical expertise. Of course, medical experts are still needed to review standard reports with patients and their families, but if there were access to personalized patient-friendly reports for pathology reports, it could empower patients, alleviate stress and make their clinical encounters more valuable. Our research team has wide range of expertise and experience creating patient-friendly reports with prior work on patient-centred MRI reports. In the proposal we are setting the stage for a multicentre study where the PAPRs will be created and their clinical usefulness will be studied. Our goal is to redefine how patients interact with their medical records and health care professional teams.

column36: Co-design of a patient/caregiver discharge communication tool for emergency practice settings
column37: Most people who visit an emergency department will be discharged home at the end of their visit with information on how to manage their care at home. Good communication between healthcare providers and patients or their caregivers is critical to ensure important information is shared and understood throughout the emergency department stay. However, patients and/or caregivers often leave the emergency department without receiving or understanding all of the information required to achieve optimal health. To date, strategies to improve discharge communication in emergency departments have primarily targeted patients and/or caregivers with minimal consideration of the environment in which the communication occurs. Further, patients and/or caregivers have rarely, if ever, been involved in the design or evaluation of discharge communication tools prior to implementation. According to the Institute of Medicine, health literate organizations assess barriers to information exchange and enable people to access and use health information and services. Our service partners are committed to the involvement of patients and families in the design, implementation and evaluation of health services. Our team of patients, caregivers, clinicians and researchers have used a theory-based co-design approach to develop a patient managed communication tool to improve recall and comprehension of important discharge information shared during an emergency department visit. The aim of our project is to evaluate our communication tool to determine its usability and acceptability by patients, caregivers and emergency department healthcare providers. We will use our findings to refine the communication tool and develop an implementation plan for a future multi-site trial with emergency departments across Canada.

column36: Establishing best practices in online cancer support groups: A realist review
column37: One in two Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime. At least one in four cancer patients will turn to online support groups (OSGs) for information and support. OSGs may be discussion forums and social media like Facebook and Twitter. Some of them are moderated by community managers or health professionals; others are not. Many studies suggest the information and support shared in OSGs helps cancer patients and families. They can reduce feelings of isolation, depression and anxiety, enhance coping and self-management of health issues, and lead to better informed patients who use fewer health care resources. But some OSGs may cause harm, such as distress. OSGs are complex; what works for one group or setting, may not work for another. Overall, reviews of the research on the effects of OSGs are mixed. They seem to benefit some patients some of the time, but research does not tell us why. Our project aims to increase our understanding of how OSGs can be made to work most effectively for Canadians affected by cancer. We will: 1) conduct a realist review of OSGs for cancer patients; 2) develop a theoretical framework explaining how OSGs work, for whom and why; and 3) make best practice recommendations. We are an international, multidisciplinary team of researchers, clinicians, patient partners, and healthcare administrators. OSG providers include the Canadian Cancer Society, de Souza Institute, and Mayo Clinic. This project forms a starting point for explaining outcomes found with participation in OSGs, and suggests ways to improve their design and delivery to maximize benefits for Canadians. We will use the knowledge from this review to inform a future team grant to evaluate the best practice recommendations in partnership OSG providers to improve what they offer. This is a novel and important project that will lead to the spread of more effective online support interventions for cancer patients in Canada and beyond.

column36: Using Priority-Based Patient Reported Outcome Measures to Facilitate Shared Decision Making in Cerebral Palsy
column37: Patient and parent reported outcome measures (PROMs) are used in clinical research to decide which treatments are most suitable for individual patients. For example, children with cerebral palsy (CP) are recommended major surgery, decisions about which are difficult for patients and parents. Whether these treatments are worthwhile should be judged by whether they achieve patients' or parents' goals. The outcome measures used to make these judgments must incorporate the goals and priorities of children with CP and their parents so that treatments are being evaluated on the basis of what is relevant and important to them. The CPCHILD and the GOAL are two such PROMs that were developed for children with CP. These measures were developed using the patient priority framework (https://lab.research.sickkids.ca/pscoreprogram/) and are unique in that patients (when able) and parents, have the opportunity to indicate which items in the questionnaire are important to them and wish to improve. The ability to identify patient and parent specific goals while completing these PROMs might provide patients and parents useful information for them to share with their doctors. This information can be used to focus clinical visits to areas that matter most to patients and parents, and to guide decision making about the choice of treatments that will best address the patient's and parents' goals. In this project, the CPCHILD and GOAL questionnaires will be adapted to develop electronic versions (ePROMs) that will produce summary reports for children and their parents, that includes their scores as well as the items they have identified as important goals to address. These ePROMs will be pilot tested to determine if patients, parents and doctors find them useful for decision-making. These measures might serve the dual purpose of improving the decision-making process while also allowing us to record the outcomes of whether treatments have the achieved the goals for which they were chosen.

column36: A Patient-Oriented Approach to Evaluate the Clinical Effectiveness of the Levitation Tri-Compartment Unloader Knee Brace for Multicompartment Knee Osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a debilitating disease affecting 1/3 of Canadians over age 25. Loss of cartilage in OA affected joints causes pain, disability, and reduced quality of life. Conservative treatments include knee braces to manage symptoms and improve joint function. Most knee OA (KOA) braces are designed to offload one knee compartment, but are not usually indicated for multicompartment KOA. The Levitation "Tri-Compartment Unloader" (TCU) knee brace was designed to reduce KOA pain by decreasing compressive forces in all three knee compartments with a "liquid spring" providing knee extension assist. While there is strong anecdotal evidence that the TCU brace can provide pain relief and improved knee function to KOA patients, the generalizability of these benefits to a larger group needs to be investigated through a controlled clinical study. Participation from patients and other key stakeholders is critical to ensure research priorities and outcomes are relevant and meaningful. Therefore, the overall research goal is to conduct a clinical evaluation of the TCU brace for treating multicompartment KOA while incorporating patient and knowledge-user participation to optimize study design, implementation and analysis of key outcome measures. This goal will be accomplished with 5 objectives: (1) Assemble a committee of patient partners; (2) Review and improve clinical trial objectives, design and methodology; (3) Perform a pilot trial on a subset of study participants; (4) Interpret study results and create a knowledge translation plan; and (5) Evaluate the impact of patient and researcher engagement in the study. Generating scientific evidence on the effectiveness of the TCU brace will allow patients and healthcare providers to make informed decisions regarding their treatment options for KOA. Involving patients as partners will ensure that the research outputs are useful and meaningful for KOA patients, resulting in wider impact and application of the findings.

column36: Strengthening and validation of a new 360-degree tool to evaluate patient and public engagement in health research
column37: Patient and Public collaboration in health research is strongly promoted across Canada. Although many researchers recognize the value of collaborating with patients and the public as partners in the research, tokenistic patient and public collaborations continues to be a major concern. Current understanding of patient collaboration in research does not address issues around trauma and safety. Thus, it is important to evaluate patient and public collaborations in health research by using a validated, evaluation tool, which incorporates the voices of diverse patient partners, decision-makers, and researchers. The main objective of our project is to strengthen and validate a newly developed evaluation tool that incorporates issues around trauma and safety, to assess the quality of patient and public collaboration in health research. We will strengthen our tool by identifying the missing components using the following methods: by conducting a review to identify key components and by conducting discussion groups and interviews in multiple provinces across Canada to get expert feedback on the tool. As a next step, using appropriate methods, we will check if the tool measures what it is supposed to measure and check if it is reliable. A large team of researchers, patient partners, and decision-makers will be involved in conducting this project. This evaluative tool will play an important role in strengthening meaningful patient and public collaborations in health research and thus strengthen the health of Canadians.

column36: The EMBOLDEN study: Enhancing physical and community MoBility in OLDEr adults with health inequities using commuNity co-design, implementation and evaluation of a complex intervention incorporating exercise, nutrition, social participation, and system navigation
column37: Reduced physical activity and ability to carry out daily activities are common with aging and can lead to frailty3, increased use of hospital and long-term care services, and death4. Despite known benefits of physical activity and diet change interventions for older adults7,9-11, optimal design features of such interventions to support real-world implementation and address health inequities are poorly understood. The EMBOLDEN study aims to promote physical and community mobility (moving around in the community), among people 55 years of age and older living in Hamilton, ON. We will co-design a program to foster positive changes in health, quality of life, and social participation. The City of Hamilton has partnered with the Hamilton Council on Aging (HCoA) and Seniors Advisory Committee (SAC) to establish Hamilton as an Age-Friendly City. The EMBOLDEN study capitalizes on the momentum of these initiatives and brings together researchers, the HCoA, SAC, and other key stakeholders including older adult citizens. A key feature of the EMBOLDEN study is the collaborative approach to co-designing the program and its implementation and evaluation. In a number of Hamilton neighborhoods, there are striking connections between social health determinants and both the health status and access to health resources of residents. Our study will build on existing best practices and local supports to promote health and mobility through physical activity, nutrition support, social support, and strengthening connections with existing service supports. The co-design process will identify strategies to address needs not met by existing services and accessibility barriers older adults face, as well as select one neighbourhood in which to pilot test the EMBOLDEN intervention. This co-design will also result in a protocol for the pilot study. The EMBOLDEN program will be developed such that it can be implemented throughout the City of Hamilton and adapted to other Canadian communities.

column36: Canadian Network for Youth-Friendly Mental Health Services: developing a standard for implementing, evaluating, and improving youth-friendly mental health services
column37: MAYNet (Mental health and Addictions Youth Network) will connect organizations and champions across Canada to explore what youth-friendliness looks like in a Canadian, mental health and addictions context. The goal is to conduct a mixed-methods approach to scan the environment and lay the groundwork for a youth-friendly mental health and addiction services research protocol. The World Health Organization (WHO) released its Adolescent-Friendly Health Services Framework in 2002, which officially highlighted the different needs of adolescents to the attention of healthcare providers around the world. In response to this framework, Ambresin and colleagues completed a systematic review in 2013 which revisited the WHO AFHS with an emphasis on youth perspective and expanded the definition of youth to include youth 12-25 years. Despite the availability of AFHS resources, youth-friendliness remains a poorly defined concept in Canada's youth mental health and addictions services. Many initiatives have included youth-friendliness as a core principle of quality services, but do not specifically define or measure youth-friendliness. MAYNet will leverage existing networks in each process to explore the need for a Canadian framework for youth-friendliness in mental health and addictions services by building on the work already done by WHO and Ambresin. MAYNet will engage and empower the youth lived-experience voice and strengthen youth-partnerships in mental health and addictions research using Youth Participatory Action Research methods. Our network will be guided by a national youth council with a dedicated strategy for maintaining engagement with youth with lived-experience accessing mental health and addictions services. column36: Engaging with youth with mental health and/or addiction issues and their families in health care navigation and research (NAV-RES)
column37: Youth with mental health and/or addictions (MHA) concerns often fall through gaps between care settings and systems, which can negatively impact their long-term outcomes. Many youth may also have family members involved in their care, yet their families might not know where to turn for support in finding the best resources for the youth and for themselves, when needed. Navigation is one model of support for youth and families trying to access MHA care. The Family Navigation Project (FNP) is a service in which Navigators work one-on-one with youth between the ages of 13-26 with MHA concerns and their families to help them find their way through the MHA system and get connected to the right care. Understanding how to best engage youth in navigation services will help ensure that these services are most helpful for youth and families. This project will involve two phases. First, we will conduct interviews and focus groups with youth, family members, Navigators, and other service providers who have successful youth engagement strategies, to understand the elements that may lead to effective youth engagement in navigation services. Then, we will use what we learned to implement a youth engagement strategy at the FNP, to test whether this leads to any changes in youth involvement in navigation, youth and family members' satisfaction with navigation services and the other services they are connected to, and how involved and in control they feel in the care process. We will also check if this results in more youth accessing services as a result of Navigation. Youth with MHA concerns and family caregivers will be involved every step of the way, so that we know we are asking the right questions, understanding what we are learning, and using the findings in a way that can best support youth with MHA concerns and their families in need of navigation services.

column36: Overdose Response in Fraser East
column37: In the context of the current public health crisis, the Fraser East region has experienced some of the highest rates of overdose deaths in BC, with the number of deaths increasing more than 700% since 2007. Semi-urban and rural communities such as Fraser East are struggling to identify and implement effective strategies to reduce and prevent overdose-related deaths because most of the interventions in Canada are based on research that has been conducted in urban communities. To address this gap in research and practice, the Overdose Response in Fraser East project is working with peers, families, community members, and organizations in Fraser East to identify practical and supportive interventions to reduce overdose death and increase connectivity to existing services in rural communities. Based on community engagement activities to date, peer researchers from the Overdose Response team have developed and pilot-tested a demographic survey and detailed interview guide to investigate the perspectives and experiences of people who are currently at highest risk of overdose death in the Fraser East region: those using drugs alone in a private residence. The CIHR Catalyst Grant will be used to extend these peer-led interviews to other more rural and remote communities in the region (n=60), which will then be contextualized, validated, and refined with administrative health data from BC's Provincial Overdose Cohort. These research and community engagement activities represent the first steps needed to develop a practical, evidence-informed, scalable plan (including specific interventions) to reduce fentanyl-related overdose deaths in Fraser East, with significant potential for transferability to other semi-urban and rural communities in Canada.

column37: "Despite recent advances, certain types of breast cancer remain difficult to treat. New effective therapies are urgently needed. Many breast cancer cells differ from healthy cells in their metabolism - their ability to make and use sugars, lipids and amino acids. We propose to study a new cancer cell signaling system that we have recently discovered, by which breast cancer cells sense their own metabolic state, and thus adapt to promote their own survival and growth. Understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms of this new metabolism sensing and adaptive signaling system of cancer cells will allow identification of new drug targets that may be effective in preventing chemotherapy resistance in breast cancer, and thus improve patient outcomes."

column36: Establishing the impact of deregulated oncogenic kinase signaling on the translational machinery during breast cancer metastasis
column37: One of the defining feature of all breast cancer cells is their ability to increase the synthesis of new proteins, through a process called mRNA translation. In particular, proteins that increase the ability of cancer cells to divide and spread throughout the body (a process called metastasis) are preferentially upregulated in cancer cells. This selective synthesis of growth- and metastasis-promoting proteins is regulated by the ratio of two proteins, called eIF4E and 4E-BP. eIF4E increases protein synthesis, whereas 4E-BP sequesters away eIF4E to prevent protein synthesis. Thus breast cancer cells must maintain an optimal eIF4E/4E-BP ratio to increase their ability to grow and metastasize. We have discovered that perturbations in this ratio profoundly impairs breast cancer lung metastasis. We will elucidate how breast cancer cells maintain an optimal eIF4E/4E-BP ratio to increase their metastatic potential. This may pave the way to identification of novel strategies to prevent metastasis by targeting the eIF4E/4E-BP ratio.

column36: Investigating how the differences in ribosomes can alter the expression of genes in cancer.
column37: The ribosome is a large and complex molecular machine that is central to all life as it is the molecular decoding center where the genetic sequence information contained in the genes in our DNA are translated in proteins. These proteins made by the ribosome are the functional molecules of the cell and are essential for the diverse functions of a cell, including movement, metabolism and cell growth. Recent discoveries are revealing a new level of complexity to the ribosomal machinery, it now appears that many of the 80+ components of the ribosome may be variable and if a component is absent, the ribosome may not translate a specific set of genes associated with the absent component. Our data indicates that in breast tissue many of the ribosomal components are absent, but upon spontaneous tumor development many have reappeared. This suggests there may be high selective pressure for tumors to utilize the ribosomal components so they can translate the proteins they need for uncontrolled growth, and as such made be a point of intervention.

column36: Establishing patient priorities for a prospective Canadian pulmonary hypertension registry
column37: Pulmonary hypertension is a life-threatening lung disease that affect thousands of Canadians and causes severe disability in people of all ages, genders, and ethnicity. Pulmonary hypertension also results in significant burden and reduced quality of life for caregivers and families. Our team has recently launched a national registry to study gaps in care, treatment and outcomes for pulmonary hypertension in Canada. The objective of the current project is to set the research agenda for the Canadian registry, and globally, for years to come. This is the first initiative to establish priorities for future research in pulmonary hypertension by engaging patients, their caregivers, and other stakeholders. Our proposed approach has been validated & used in other diseases and medical conditions, but never for pulmonary hypertension. We will develop a patient engagement strategy in partnership with patients, representatives from the Pulmonary Hypertension Association of Canada and a national network of researchers. We will survey patients, caregivers and clinicians (e.g. physicians, nurses, pharmacists) across Canada to identify their questions or perceived uncertainties. The initial survey will be narrowed to a short list of 20-30 questions about pulmonary hypertension that have not yet been answered and could be addressed in future research. Next, we will conduct a workshop with patients, caregivers, clinicians and researchers to identify a "Top 10" list of uncertainties for future pulmonary hypertension research. We expect our results to have important implications for the Canadian Pulmonary Hypertension Registry and elsewhere around the world. Furthermore, this project catalyzes a new, sustainable partnership between patients and the Canadian Pulmonary Hypertension Registry network. Our findings will promote new research on the most important problems in the eyes of pulmonary hypertension patients, their caregivers, families, and health care providers.

column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Charcot's disease, is a severe neurodegenerative disease occurring between the ages of 50 and 70 years. It causes progressive paralysis of the limbs as well as muscles of speech and swallowing. There is no effective treatment and death occurs by respiratory failure after 3 to 5 years. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop new treatments, a limit being the extreme variability of the disease in its causes (there are hereditary and non-familial forms) and its clinical presentations. It is thus essential to characterize these different forms, in order to propose a personalized treatment. Importantly, a pre-symptomatic period is now well characterized in individuals who carry a mutation responsible for familial forms of ALS, and who have not yet developed the disease. Recent developments in gene therapy, which are currently evaluated in symptomatic patients, open for the first time the possibility to prevent the disease. To achieve this goal, we need to develop new tools that will allow us to characterize this pre-symptomatic phase and to monitor the effect of these new therapies as well. For example, new imaging methods with magnetic resonance imaging now offers the possibility of knowing when the first lesions begin and how they evolve over time. In this study, we plan to develop new imaging tools and outcome metrics that will allow even finer analysis of the changes occurring in the nervous system, especially in the spinal cord, which is the main site of abnormalities. We will apply these methods to individuals carrying a mutation causing ALS, whether they are pre-symptomatic or symptomatic, and will monitor their evolution over time. Thanks to this project we will be able to better predict the evolution of this devastating disease, and to design the clinical trials with drugs under development for future therapies

column36: Implementation of a maternal pertussis immunization program: Improving coverage among Inuit women
column37: Whooping cough is a respiratory infection that is especially common in children. Infants get vaccines to protect them from pertussis as early as 2 months of age, but those under 6 months are too young to get all the doses required to fully protect them. Whooping cough disproportionately affects Canadian Inuit infants and families compared to the rest of the country. One way to protect these infants is by giving their mothers the whooping cough vaccine (Tdap) while they are pregnant. A maternal Tdap vaccination program was initiated in Nunavut in 2016, in response to an outbreak of 154 confirmed cases of whooping cough. At that time, the National Advisory Committee on Immunization (NACI) had a recommendation that pregnant women be offered a Tdap vaccine when there was an outbreak in the area that they live. In February 2018 that recommendation was revised and now all pregnant women are encouraged to receive a Tdap vaccination during every pregnancy. The established program in Nunavut and a nascent program in the self-governing Inuit region of Nunatsiavut in Labrador provides us with an excellent opportunity to compare the two programs. In collaboration with local public health authorities and researchers, we aim to determine what community members think, feel, believe, and plan to do about giving vaccines to pregnant women in Nunavut and Nunatsiavut. This will be done through individual narrative collection with community experts, sharing circles with pregnant women and healthcare providers, and surveys of pregnant women. We aim to broaden understanding of facilitators and barriers to this and future maternal immunization program (e.g. group B streptococcus, respiratory syncytial virus) to protect infants in the future.

column36: Improving the evaluation of health inequities through advanced geographic methods across urban, rural and remote Canada
column37: The Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) is committed to reducing health inequities. Health equity is the absence of unjust, avoidable differences in health and health care access, quality or outcomes across the population. Health inequities are often reported for large areas such as health regions. This approach reports measurements for an entire region, with no distinction between urban, rural and remote communities. This approach masks inequities in rural and remote communities. CIHI has developed a Rural Health System Model, which includes geospatial measures such as drive time, availability of services and social determinants of health. The current gap exists in establishing geospatial analysis methods to implement this system model. My objectives are to (1) identify successes and challenges among geodemographic sensitivity analysis literature to establish best practices; (2) evaluate health inequities across Western Canada by integrating CIHI's Rural Health System Model; and (3) to translate the analysis plan from #2 to standardized geodemographic sensitivity analysis methods to be tested for other CIHI projects. This analysis will be achieved by establishing best practice methods for aggregating geographies, particularly for rural and remote areas, that are specific to three priority hospitalization indicators (alcohol harm, opioid poisoning, and child day-surgeries), already established by CIHI, stratified by income and sex. The analytical plan used will be translated into general geospatial analysis methods that will be shared with internal stakeholders, who will test these methods for ongoing health system measurement. This project directly aligns with my expertise in quantitative health geography and long-standing dedication to reducing health inequities for rural and remote Canada. This program of work will provide the opportunity to develop my knowledge translation, leadership, and project management skills.

column36: Illuminating Innovation in Canadian Hospitals - An Economic Evaluation of Ultra-Violet Germicidal Irradiation (UVGI) Devices
column37: When patients stay in hospital, they face risk of infection that can cause them to become even more sick leading to a longer stays in hospital and possibly death. In Canada, approximately 10% of adults that visit the hospital become infected. Since this is a very serious risk for patients, hospitals are always looking for new technologies to help them prevent infections. Ultra Violet Germicidal Irradiation (UVGI) devices are robots that use ultra violet light to kill the pathogens that cause infection. In past studies these devices have been successful in killing pathogens, but researchers and hospital managers still aren't sure whether they reduce the risk of a patient being infected or if the benefit they provide is worth their significant costs. In fact, no studies in a Canadian context have been published on these devices. Fraser Health Authority - a health region in British Columbia - has implemented these devices in several of their hospitals, and now has the data to be able to examine the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the devices. In this project, we will use the administrative data they have collected to analyze both the clinical impact of these devices and their economic impact. Our analysis will help managers in Fraser Health Authority decide if they want to invest in this new technology, and by sharing our results in journals and at conferences we hope to help hospitals across Canada who are faced with this same decision.

column36: Health Workforce Planning to Promote Equitable Access to the Full Range of Maternity Care Providers Across the Champlain Region
column37: Background: In Ontario, women can theoretically choose to seek maternity care from a midwife, a family physician, or an obstetrician. Evidence of unmet demand for midwifery services within the Champlain Region has raised local concerns regarding women's access to their maternity care provider of choice. Therefore, the Champlain Maternal Newborn Regional Program has identified workforce planning as an important next step to inform targeted midwifery expansion in areas of moderate to high unaccommodated demand. Objectives: In response to this locally-identified critical health system challenge, this project aims to engage local stakeholders in Ontario's Champlain Region in a collaborative health workforce planning process to elicit the structural conditions that would be necessary to equitably support women's access to the full range of maternity care providers. Approach: This project adopts a community-based participatory research approach using a mixed methods design, and encompasses two major components: 1) a quantitative geospatial mapping exercise to assess women's access to the full range of maternity care providers across the Champlain Region and identify any persistent inequities in women's access on the basis of geography and, or, socioeconomic marginalization; and 2) a qualitative participatory system dynamics modelling exercise employing individual and focus groups interviews to explore the factors that are enabling or restricting choice of maternity care provider at the local level, and identify locally-relevant policy solutions to address barriers of access and support the development of innovative and integrated models of maternity care. Impact: Together, these complementary exercises will provide the CMNRP with evidence to support better alignment of health workforce supply, distribution, and mix with women's choices and needs. This initial planning exercise could generate opportunities for scale-up of this approach to other regions across Ontario.

column36: Achieving health systems integration through policy development and implementation
column37: Integrated health systems where services and supports are well linked to each other, continue to evolve. A lack of integrated services can result in poor coordination of care, increased health care costs, and dissatisfied patients and caregivers. The Health Standards Organization (HSO) has been developing an integration standard to help health care organizations to provide better integrated care for patients. This fellowship project will work in partnership with HSO and include the following: 1) assist with final development of the standard, putting it into practice, and dissemination of the standard; 2) develop strategies to integrate knowledge-users for the implementation and spread of the standard; 3) outline the process for standard development and publish this process; and 4) develop a research proposal to test the implementation and outcomes of the standard. The impact of the project occurs at many levels. For patients, health services delivery will be more integrated and improve health outcomes; for healthcare providers, there will be information to recognize what are barriers to the delivery of integrated care, as well as enablers to improve integration; and for healthcare managers, the standard will provide a roadmap for health services integration to deliver quality health and social care for all putting people's needs at the center of the planning and design processes. Finally, for the Health Systems Impact Fellow, this project will provide a great opportunity to learn new knowledge and skills in health systems and integration, policy development and implementation, and health services research.

column36: BC's prisons & the overdose emergency: understanding the impact of policy on continuity of care and healthcare utilization for people who experience incarceration
column37: British Columbia (BC) is experiencing a public health emergency related to the increasing rate of overdose and overdose-related deaths. In 2018 there were 1,489 overdose deaths in British Columbia (BC). A recent report revealed that two thirds of persons who died of an overdose in BC had experienced involvement with the BC criminal justice system. Addressing the complexities of this disparity requires evidence-based, multi-faceted approaches to health systems and policies. In October of 2017, BC became the third Canadian province to make the Ministry of Health responsible for healthcare services in provincial correctional facilities. In partnership with the Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions (MMHA) and the BC Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC), the aim of this study is to use data from the BCCDC's Provincial Overdose Cohort to assess whether and to what degree the change in governance of prison health services has succeeded in addressing continuity of Opioid Agonist Therapy during transitions between prison and community. Additionally, I aim to examine change in patterns of healthcare utilization after release from prison in order to identify opportunities and gaps in the cascade of care for mental health and substance use services. The Provincial Overdose Cohort is a set of linked administrative datasets which combines information related to an individual's overdose event(s) with patient-level health information from multiple sources of administrative data including Medial Services Plan (MSP), Pharmanet, National Ambulatory Care Reporting System (NACRS), Discharge Abstract Database (DAD), BC Coroners Service and BC Corrections Data. At the index overdose event, a five-year health history is appended, and individuals are followed forward in time. This project will contribute understanding of prison health policy as a component of healthcare systems and services, which is essential to addressing the overdose public health emergency.

column36: Co-developing a Novel System to Detect and Act on Harmful Drug-Drug Interactions (DAHDDI) using Administrative Health Databases in Quebec
column37: Prescription medications help us live healthy lives and reach an old age. The number of medications taken by patients in Canada is higher now than ever before. In rare cases, medications can hurt the people taking them, even if they take them as prescribed by their doctor. Dangerous drug combinations can cause serious harm to some people. These are very difficult to study and recognize, as the effect of a medication may be completely different when taken in combination with another medication. These dangerous combinations may include medications used to treat very common diseases and conditions among relatively healthy, young people. Those with multiple chronic health conditions are at greatest risk. We are developing a new method to identify the dangerous drug combinations which are harming Quebecers, by using data from the administration of health care in Quebec. For this method to be useful, it needs to be used regularly by decision-makers working within the health system, and a course of action needs to be proposed for preventing harm to patients. In this proposed fellowship I will explore whether the institute in charge of guiding clinical care in Quebec (INESSS) can use my method to detect dangerous drug combinations which are harming the population. To do this I will work in close collaboration with INESSS staff to learn how the institute works, and I will conduct interviews with professional staff working in drug evaluation. I expect that doing this will enhance the usefulness of my previous work for the benefit of Canadian society.

column36: Learning from Gwich'in Patient Journeys and Other Established Evidence to Identify Gwich'in Tribal Council Priorities and Actions on Medical Travel
column37: In the four Gwich'in First Nation communities in Northwest Territories, medical travel is a way of life. Patients must travel great distances for healthcare services unavailable in their communities. This comes with many unnecessary burdens and bureaucratic challenges that are major community concerns. The Gwich'in Tribal Council (GTC), the Indigenous organization responsible for the Gwich'in people, would like to find ways to provide more support to Gwich'in patients in their medical travel journeys. Working within the GTC and in collaboration with Hotii ts'eeda, a research support unit in Northwest Territories, my project will achieve three objectives: (1) Understand the gaps, successes and challenges experienced by Gwich'in medical travel patients; (2) Identify priorities for the GTC to act on; and (3) Propose a scope of work for a Health System Navigator position with the GTC. In alignment with Gwich'in principles, this collaborative, community-based project will occur in three parts. First, I will review the literature and synthesize evidence related to medical travel problems and solutions in rural, remote or Indigenous communities. I will compare my findings with the experiences of Gwich'in communities and their healthcare providers. Second, I will use talking circles and interviews with Gwich'in community members to develop a visual illustration of the Gwich'in medical travel journey and better understand the challenges they face as well as potential solutions. Third, I will use all this information to develop recommendations, including a job description for a Health System Navigator position in the GTC. The results of my project will be shared in person, in writing and through other media with Gwich'in communities as well as with influential stakeholders such as the Northwest Territories and Canadian governments. My project will support the GTC in its responsibilities to listen and respond to community needs in a way that informs policy and programs.

column36: Using machine learning for prediction of cardiac arrest in the intensive care unit
column37: The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is one of the units in the hospital that provide care to critically ill patients in risk of sudden changes in their health state. These patients require constant and active monitoring to identify signs of deterioration. Therefore, monitoring devices are utilized to keep track of patient vital signs during their stay at the ICU. Machine learning models can take advantage of this large and complex data in order to assimilate and track patterns and trends that exist in patient's physiological signals prior to events such as a cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest is one of the main causes of mortality in pediatric ICU with the survival to discharge rate of on average 33 percent of patients. Limited treatments are available when cardiac arrest occurs that are mostly high-risk and also contribute to the injury associated with cardiac arrest. In fact the most effective way of improving outcomes for pediatric patients in risk of cardiac arrest is early identification of those individuals and prevention of cardiac arrest with the need for resuscitation. The goal of this project is to apply machine learning to the analysis of continuously collected physiological signals generated by critically ill children in order to develop a tool for prediction of cardiac arrest for pediatric patients in the ICU. Effective prediction models would improve the identification of pediatric patients at risk of cardiac arrest and enable medical and surgical interventions to prevent the arrest from happening.

column36: Evaluating a culturally-safe, strengths-based case management approach to facilitate hepatitis C treatment among Indigenous people who use drugs in BC
column37: Colonization and colonial systems have led to the overrepresentation of Indigenous people impacted by substance use and hepatitis C (HCV) infection in Canada. Ensuring access to highly-effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapies among this key population is critical. However, systemic and structural barriers to health care will likely hinder access to this life saving treatment. To achieve the equitable scale-up of DAA delivery at the population-level, the BC Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC) has identified the following impact goals: 1) understanding factors related to gaps across HCV cascade of care among Indigenous people who use drugs; and 2) working in collaboration with Indigenous communities to develop a culturally-safe implementation strategy for HCV treatment. The Cedar Project, an Indigenous community-governed cohort study, is actively piloting a culturally-safe intervention to facilitate HCV treatment among Indigenous people who use drugs in BC. To support BCCDC impact goals, the proposed study will use an integrated knowledge translation (IKT) approach to examine the application of Cedar Project findings to BCCDC's work in HCV. This collaborative research model will bring together BCCDC and Indigenous Knowledge Keepers and scholars to address the following objectives: 1) interpret and translate findings from a culturally-safe HCV pilot intervention to develop a culturally-safe HCV model of care and policies to promote its sustainability ; 2) integrate intervention findings into BC-Hepatitis Testers Cohort to improve the evaluation of HCV programming at a population-level; 3) identify recommendations that will facilitate implementation processes to promote the scale-up of culturally-safe models of care; and 4) integrate ceremony to honor the voices of Cedar participants and Indigenous partners. This proposed program of work provides a unique opportunity to bridge findings from an Indigenous-led HCV intervention into action at a provincial level.

column36: Developing a visual analytic, artificial intelligence-based framework for analyzing unstructured electronic medical record data
column37: Data from Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) are stored in text-based form, much like emails and letters, which makes them extremely difficult to analyze using traditional statistical techniques. The opportunity for the use of EMRs for analysis comes from innovative and modern computer based tools and techniques. These include artificial intelligence, which is based in coding to look for patterns and iterative learning from emerging patterns, and visual analytics, which is visual exploration of data. column36: Evaluation of a strategy to optimize the implementation and sustainability of Choosing Wisely interventions at Ontario community hospitals and Family Health Teams: An exploratory, multi-centre evaluation study
column37: The reduction of low-value health care practices is necessary to ensure patient safety and satisfaction, reduce costs and develop a sustainable healthcare system. The objectives of this study are to evaluate the influence of an implementation guide (ISG) and facilitation support on the implementation and sustainability of Choosing Wisely (CW) interventions at Ontario hospitals and affiliated family health teams (FHTs). Three propositions will be tested through this project: -Greater fidelity to the guide during implementation will afford better outcomes than CW interventions implemented with less fidelity to the guide. -Facilitation support of the guide's application during the implementation of CW interventions will further enhance the outcomes of CW interventions. -Sustainment of CW interventions will be greater in the two intervention arms than in the control arm. Employing a 3-arm exploratory, evaluation design we will test two versions of implementation and sustainability support. Intervention teams will receive the ISG (n=3) or the ISG plus facilitation (n=3). The control teams (n=3) will receive no intervention. This study will involve 9 CW implementation teams at 6 community hospitals and 3 affiliated FHTs. We will collect data on the CW intervention objectives and target outcomes, process and our intervention process and impact through document analysis, focus groups and interviews at prior to implementation of the CW intervention, the conclusion of the intervention's implementation and 3- and 6-months post implementation. We will use the i-PARIHS framework and Outcome Evaluation Framework for evaluation. The study will evaluate the relationship amongst 1) adherence and fidelity to the guide, 2) facilitation and 3) outcomes regarding the reduction in the target practice. This research aligns with numerous strategic health system priorities and will contribute evidence on implementation, sustainment support and facilitation for de-implementation efforts.

column36: Improving the Canadian drug approval framework: Evaluation of effectiveness; safety and economic uncertainty associated with new cancer medicines using real world evidence
column37: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) are necessary to show that a drug works in ideal patients and circumstances, and to obtain a licence for new drugs. However, not all questions can be answered by randomized trials because patients treated in the real world differ in many important ways from RCTs. Thus there is an increasing trend to use real world evidence (RWE) to supplement data from RCTs. As the Canadian population is growing and aging, efficient use of limited healthcare resources is crucial. In this respect, one of the goals of both Cancer Care Ontario (CCO) and the Canadian Centre for Applied Research in Cancer Control (ARCC) is to increase value for money. CCO is working with ARCC and cancer organizations in other provinces to develop a framework that incorporates RWE to evaluate publicly funded cancer drugs in Canada. In theory, RWE data give insights into how drugs work in the real world, which may differ from RCTs in terms of efficacy, safety, or costs. The objective of this study is to compare RWE for efficacy, safety, and costs of approved drugs to results of RCTs for all new cancer medicines approved by CCO between 2013-2017. This study consists of two phases. In the first phase, to shed light on the clinical risks and value of all new cancer drugs. This phase will look at drug appraisals using a scoping review approach to health technology assessment (HTA) reports submitted for drug approvals and published studies for all new cancer medicines approved by CCO. We will compare real-world effectiveness, safety, and cost data with those of the RCTs and HTAs to understand where, how often, and how much they differ. In the second phase, using RWE, we will build a cost-effectiveness model of one high priority new cancer medicine lacking RWE. This study will help refine the drug approval framework and support clinical practice by taking RWE into account in the regulatory and drug approval process to enrich sound value-based decision-making.

column36: Traffic calming implementation around Calgary elementary schools
column37: Across Canada, collisions with motor-vehicles are a leading cause of child bicyclist and pedestrian injuries. Each year in Alberta, over 300 children are admitted to hospital due to a severe pedestrian or bicyclist injury. Injury rates and severity can be associated with higher vehicle speeds and traffic volume, and specific traffic calming features. Active transportation can provide significant health benefits to children that last into adult-hood. However, concerns regarding injury risk can influence decisions to participate in active transportation. Given that a third of child pedestrian and bicyclist injuries occur within 300m of a school, it is important to ensure vehicles travel in a safe manner at these locations. Installing specific traffic calming features designed to reduce vehicle speed around schools can lead to a reduction in injury risk for child pedestrians and bicyclists, and increase active transportation, if traffic calming measures are appropriately aligned to the current built environment. This project will therefore seek to install specific traffic calming features around various Calgary elementary schools, and evaluate their impact on traffic behavior. This project will use a stepped wedge cluster randomized trial design to sequentially evaluate implementation of a specific traffic safety feature at all public Calgary elementary schools. Schools will be randomly ordered for traffic calming installation. Vehicle traffic volume and speed in front of the school will be monitored one month prior to installation, one week prior to installation, and one week following installation. School administration and parents will be contacted before and after the intervention to determine changes in perceived traffic safety. Schools will be clustered by traffic calming installation date and stratified by traffic calming feature. Traffic behavior and perceived safety will be compared between baseline, pre-intervention, and post-intervention.

column36: Development and implementation of a patient-oriented evaluation framework for the province-wide Continuous Improvement Program in the Saskatchewan health sector
column37: Healthcare system inefficiencies result in decreased life expectancy and up to 24,500 premature deaths annually in Canada. In order to improve efficiency and ongoing system improvements, the Saskatchewan Ministry of Health implemented the Continuous Improvement Program (CIP) in 2008. Over 2200 continuous improvement projects have been completed in the past decade, however a comprehensive evaluation of CIP's impacts on patient outcomes has not been conducted. Using Emergency Medicine (EM) as a model, this project aims to develop an evaluation framework that could be replicated across all other areas of healthcare delivery in Saskatchewan. A collaborative process and outcome evaluation of CIP's impact on EM will be conducted. Patient and Evaluation Advisory Committees will be formed, including representatives from clinical (i.e., nurses, clinicians) and non-clinical (i.e., improvement specialists) stakeholder groups across Saskatchewan. A logic model will drive the evaluation framework by focusing on five key outcome categories: patient experience and satisfaction, patient barriers to healthcare access, staff empowerment and engagement, system defects and errors, and system costs related to waste. Mixed-methods data would be used to answer key evaluation questions, and would include review of administrative records, improvement activities (currently tracked in the CIP database, KAIZEN Tracker), and conducting surveys and interviews with relevant stakeholders to receive feedback on program delivery, satisfaction, and health outcomes. In collaboration with the Advisory Committees, reports will be developed summarizing key findings and recommendations from the EM-focused process and outcome evaluation of CIP. The evaluation framework will serve as a foundation for ongoing evaluation of other sectors of the healthcare system.
