column36: What to bundle next? The case for bundled care.
column37: Bundled care is an emerging service delivery and funding model that defines a basket of services for a targeted condition and pays for these services in a single payment for multiple providers and across multiple settings. Bundled care promotes better planning and coordination of care between acute and post-acute care, and across multiple health care providers. This form of value-based payment has demonstrated improved care quality and efficiency by integrating care across previously separate providers. The Ontario government has piloted six bundled care projects with positive interim results. There is an opportunity to expand bundled care, however, it is unclear what to bundle next. The overall objective of the project is to identify which bundled care model holds the most promise. To achieve this goal, we will use a participatory and co-design process to model care pathways of care and identify strategic and financial impacts for evidence-based and sustainable bundles care models at Trillium Health Partners. We will engage stakeholders, clinical and administrative leaders, and health system payers to identify important patient, hospital and health system outcomes, and to design communication strategies and products for the implementation of bundled care across different units. The outcome of the project will inform the design of bundled care models and which clinical area has the most potential for the next bundled care implementation.

column36: Improving the identification of and integration of care for patients experiencing intimate partner violence in Toronto
column37: Intimate partner violence (IPV) has severe health consequences, especially among women, for whom IPV is the most common form of violence experienced. Healthcare providers thus serve as an important point of contact for identifying cases of IPV. In line with the goals of the host partner organization, St. Michael's Hospital, this program of work aims to strengthen the hospital's IPV screening and integrated response strategies in three ways. Second, using routine hospital data I will identify departments where patients are most commonly presenting with IPV experiences and characteristics of these patients to inform intervention priorities. Finally, I will work with partner organizations and stakeholders to develop and pilot strategies for integrated care between hospital and community services to better address the needs of high-risk patients experiencing IPV. This work is relevant to CIHR-IHSPR, in that it aims to strengthen evidence- and patient-informed health services and integrated care, and CIHR-IGH, given its sex and gender approach. In particular, analyses will explore the intersections between IPV and gender and sex variables and intervention strategies will be developed and evaluated accounting for differences in IPV experiences and related needs across gender and sexual identities. column36: Preparing the Canadian health care system to meet the needs of older adults with combined vision and hearing impairments and their caregivers
column37: Dual Sensory Impairment (DSI), also referred to as age-related deafblindness, is the combined loss of vision and hearing that results in a condition that is more complex and disabling than hearing or vision loss alone. Older adults with DSI often present with severe communication challenges and experience barriers in access to healthcare. Invariably, healthcare professionals also face challenges while screening, clinical assessments and delivering interventions due to associated communication difficulties and possible age-related cognitive decline. Two percent of the world population is estimated to have DSI. With the rapid increase in our ageing trends, over 500,000 to 1 million Canadians are expected to experience DSI by 2036. To address the problem in time, we need to prepare our healthcare system to provide optimal care for those aging with DSI in Canada. Using an appreciative inquiry approach, I aim to understand the challenges associated while accessing or providing care to older adults with DSI, in a phase-wise manner wherein each study will inform the next. In study 1, I plan to conduct a systematic review to synthesize evidence on existing and emergent strategies to provide optimal care to older adults with DSI. I will collect data from older adults with DSI and their caregivers (study 2), healthcare professionals (study 3), and policymakers or healthcare administrators (study 4) to develop a holistic understanding of what can be done to provide optimal care to older adults with DSI. The study will be guided by the World Report on Ageing and Health (2015), the Institut Nazareth et Louis-Braille (research priorities) and the Universite de Montreal Action Plan for Research, Discovery, Creation, and Innovation (2017-2021) on Aging. Findings will inform future service design, healthcare workforce development, and policy changes by providing recommendations and an action plan required to meet the needs of the rising population of older adults with DSI.

column36: Evaluating the response to British Columbia's overdose crisis within Vancouver Coastal Health: Moving research into practice
column37: The opioid crisis has been hardest felt in British Columbia (BC), which declared a public health emergency in 2016. Last year, there were 1510 drug overdose deaths recorded in BC, which represented 4.5 times the deaths from motor vehicle accidents. The overdose crisis has been largely driven by increasing contamination of the illicit drug supply with powerful synthetic opioids (e.g., fentanyl). Despite efforts to expand harm reduction services and treatments for opioid use disorder, these have had limited success in curbing the current crisis. Innovative strategies to mitigate the crisis have become an urgent public health priority. This includes a critical need to evaluate the response to the overdose crisis to help develop and implement a comprehensive addiction treatment program across BC and ultimately prevent future drug-related fatalities. Vancouver Coastal Health (VCH) provides services to more than 1.25 million residents in BC (nearly 25% of the population), and has been a primary player at the heart of the overdose crisis response. As such, alongside the newly implemented VCH Regional Addiction Program, VCH has identified key policy-related challenges that the proposed work will seek to address: prevent fatal overdoses, reduce drug-related harms, increase access to low barrier services, and improve integration of harm reduction and treatment. The proposed work will consist of several overlapping components to achieve the overarching goal to establish comprehensive and integrated addiction care programs across the region. This will include evaluating the impacts of 'naturally occurring' interventions (e.g., supervised consumption sites) and efficacy of novel clinical therapies, conducting health system and program evaluation to identify gaps in care and healthcare provider capacity, and engaging in integrated knowledge translation to mobilize research into evidence-based policies and practices across the health system.

column36: Ensuring screening quality in a complex governance system: A vision for Prenatal Screening Ontario
column37: Prenatal screening is offered to all pregnant women to determine if a pregnancy is at risk for specific health problems. To maintain a high quality program that is up to date with new technology, health care providers, laboratories and policymakers must work collaboratively. Prenatal Screening Ontario (PSO) is responsible for overseeing and coordinating health care providers (e.g. sonographers, physicians, midwives, radiologists, genetic counsellors etc.) laboratories, and policymakers, in an effort to ensure care is of high-quality and accessible to all women across the province. This is a challenging task because the relationships among the stakeholders are complex, and decision-making authority is not always clear. Motivated by this challenge, the proposed project seeks to understand how program organization impacts quality of care, within the context of a population screening system. Through fieldwork and a range of qualitative data collection strategies, this project will explore and define the specific quality challenges Ontario is facing (e.g. inaccurate tests, inappropriate spending/testing, poor access to care). This work involves describing where and how various stakeholders are interacting, and whether and how that impacts quality. Building from the Ontario case, a scoping review will identify approaches to ensuring prenatal screening quality in other jurisdictions and settings. Three cases will be selected for comparison to Ontario. The purpose of this research is to identify barriers and facilitators to achieving a high-quality prenatal screening system. Finally, in consultation with screening system experts, the findings will be developed into a quality improvement framework that PSO can implement and use to enhance care delivery.

column36: Predicting treatment response with machine learning from clinical notes: Informing clinical decisions and improving the representation of clients with depression at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health
column37: The Major Depressive Disorder Care Pathway (MDD-ICP) is a standardized pathway of care for clients with depression at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH). In the MDD-ICP, psychiatrists write detailed notes about their meetings with clients. Analyzing these notes can help improve our understanding of clients with depression and inform decisions about their care. However, these notes are challenging to analyze because they are unstructured. Advancements in language modelling and machine learning offer solutions to this issue. In the first stage of the Health Systems Impact Fellowship (HSIF), we will use these methods to analyze the MDD-ICP clinical notes. Specifically, we will predict clients' responses to treatment using machine learning models. We will train our models based on clinical notes from intake assessments, as well as questionnaire data available in CAMH health records. According to previous research, the ability of our models to predict treatment responses may depend on client demographics (like sex or income), as well as the writing style of psychiatrists. We will also assess for these biases in our models, by stratifying our analyses according to these characteristics. In the second stage of the HSIF, we will use our findings to develop support tools and workshops that help psychiatrists make clinical decisions and improve the quality of their notes. We will implement these interventions in small groups of MDD-ICP psychiatrists. To evaluate whether the interventions are useful, we will compare outcomes from these psychiatrists to groups of control psychiatrists. This HSIF advances a goal of CAMH's Krembil Centre for Neuroinformatics to gain insights into mental health using innovative technologies. By using these insights to inform clinical decisions, it addresses the MDD-ICP's aim to optimize treatments for clients with depression.

column36: Patient Engagement Toolkit for Health Information Technology Initiatives
column37: Health information technology have a tremendous potential to improve the quality and efficiency of our healthcare system. Despite the potential benefits, there are many policy and practical challenges to implementing health information technology. Several experts and research studies suggest that engaging patients throughout the development and implementation of health information technology is critical in ensuring its success. The purpose of this project is to develop a toolkit to guide healthcare organizations in developing and integrating patient engagement activities in their health information technology implementations. This project will be conducted in three stages. The first stage will focus on understanding the the dynamics of engaging patients through a survey and interviews with patients and healthcare providers. Based on the findings of the first stage, a prototype toolkit will be developed in the second phase. The content of the toolkit will be validated by patient engagement experts. The toolkit will also be tested with patients and healthcare providers to determine its usability and ease of use. The prototype toolkit will applied to a patient portal implementation to understand how the toolkit will work and ways to improve it. The final product of this project is a finished toolkit for healthcare organizations to use in supporting their patient engagement plans when implementing health information technology.

column36: Evaluation of the Neighbourhood Care Team Model: Providing a rigorous evidence base to inform integrated health care policy
column37: The Neighbourhood Care Team Model (NCTM) is a model of integrated care that builds on the strengths of local services and coordinates health care provided in the community to meet local population health needs in densely populated urban neighbourhoods in Toronto, Ontario. Integrated care is an approach to the organization and delivery of health services that is intended to improve continuity of care across services. Continuity of care means better consistency of information sharing between health care providers, relationships between people and their specific health care teams, and the overall approach to managing peoples' health and illness over time. It is widely considered to be ideally suited to serve people with complex health and social needs, which can lead to downstream challenges in the health system, including inappropriate emergency room visits and growing system costs. The NCTM is meant to address these challenges by combining efforts across primary care, home and community care, social support services, and community housing. The objective of this project is to evaluate the program effectiveness of the Neighbourhood Care Team Model (NCTM) being implemented in Toronto. The NCTM will be evaluated according to the Triple Aim framework of improved patient outcomes, steady/reduced health system costs, and improved patient/provider experience to provide evidence to inform policy decisions. If evidence is found in support of NCTM achieving its goals and alleviating downstream challenges in the health care system, it could be considered for implementation more widely across the province and country.

column36: Using Evidence to Inform Health Policy: Supportive Housing as a Case Study
column37: Government health policies rooted in evidence and collaboration are essential for safe and effective health care delivery. While the steps in policy development and the use of evidence to guide this process are well documented, the ways in which policy cycles work in 'real-world' and complex government settings are less well defined. This is especially the case for supportive housing (SH) services in Canada, where current policies inadequately describe the program purpose and recipients of care. Using SH as a case study, the purpose of my fellowship is to (i) understand how policy cycles 'work' in a complex government setting, (ii) explore how evidence can be used more effectively to ensure that policies achieve their intended goals, and (iii) investigate ways in which other stakeholders (e.g., regional planners, SH clients and their families) can contribute meaningfully to policy development. From these activities I will establish an enriched understanding of government context and the ways in which policies are developed, create synergistic partnerships with key government personnel and health service researchers, develop additional core competencies to help ensure my short- and long-term career success, and produce several publications and related knowledge translation activities (e.g., showing how evidence and intersectoral collaborations can be used to improve policy cycles). My fellowship will occur at Manitoba Health, Seniors and Active Living (MHSAL; Brie DeMone as primary supervisor) and the University of Manitoba (Dr. Malcolm Doupe as academic supervisor). These organizations and preceptors have a rich collaborative history through previous grants and government initiatives designed to train graduate students in applied health services research. Building on their experiences, my preceptors will meaningfully combine the research and policy aspects of the fellowship in ways that help to enrich my training experience and foster a learning health system.

column36: Can primary care and community-based child & youth mental health services work together? An evaluation of a proposed model that improves integration and care for children and their families.
column37: The Ontario Centre for excellence in Child and Youth Mental Health is conducting a project to improve clinical and service pathways for mental health services within the community. Specifically, this 2-year mixed methods project aims to use the knowledge gained from the pilot project conducted in 2018 to work along with six regions in Ontario to implement and evaluate a 'Primary Care Provider Mental Health' clinical pathways model. The project aims to address three of the key recommendations from the Centre's policy-ready paper on strengthening the interface between primary care and community-based child and youth mental health services, including: (1) Organizational structures and practices that support inter-provider communication, (2) Development of guidelines and standardized clinical pathways, and (3) Integrating standardized tools in primary care practices. Our team will work alongside primary care and community-based mental health provider partners to support the implementation of new pathways; tailoring pathways to the unique needs of each region and their population and building them into their existing workflow. The project includes 3 phases: (1) Developing tailored clinical pathways through strategic planning and stakeholder engagement; (2) Implementing the pathways through the use of standardized tools adapted to local contexts; and (3) Sustainability, feedback and maintenance of pathways. We will assess the usefulness of standardized tools to improve care, and providers' and families' views on the acceptability, utility and impact of the pathways. This is the first project to facilitate a seamless and timely transition for children and youth identified with a mental health need by their primary care providers to appropriate community-based supports in Ontario. This will lead to reduced wait times and an increase in services provided to youth. Our study will rigorously address requirements for success and inform scalability to other Canadian settings.

column36: Building Capacity for Surveillance and Policy Development: Health Impact Assessments of Air Quality in Northern British Columbia
column37: In Northern British Columbia, a region rich in natural resources, there has been a rapid expansion of resource extraction projects across the region in recent years. While generating economic growth for local communities, this has also led to concerns among health practitioners and community members about the potential health risks associated with declining air quality due to increased industrial emissions. In the BC Northwest, in particular, projections indicate that sulphur dioxide emissions will likely increase in the Kitimat airshed due to multiple new industrial projects and expansion of existing projects.Timely information about air quality and associated health risks is important for developing public health policies, to prevent potential negative health impacts, and for planning at both local and regional levels. The objectives of this project are to 1) conduct a health impact assessment of impacts of SO2 emissions on human health in the Kitimat region; 2) make recommendations for development of effective surveillance tools to assess air quality health impacts in the region; and 3) review how local and regional policy makers use environmental health impact information for decision-making.This project will directly support Northern Health's organizational impact goal of healthy people in healthy communities, through promoting and protecting healthy environments, and through helping to build regional capacity for conducting health impact assessments and surveillance.

column36: Combining behavioural sciences and user centred design methodology to improve the surveillance of childhood cancer survivors at high-risk of late effects
column37: There are over 14,000 survivors of childhood and adolescent cancer in Ontario. Unfortunately, the treatments used to cure their cancer in childhood leads to a high risk for severe health conditions during adulthood, including the development of new cancers and heart problems. These are called "late effects" of cancer treatment. My main fellowship project will involve developing a health-system-wide, evidence-based program to identify adult survivors of childhood cancer at highest risk of these late effects and provide them (and their primary care providers) with the information they need to prevent or mitigate their impact. Presently, most adult survivors of childhood cancer do not complete recommended tests to screen for late effects. This leads to missed opportunities to take early action to stay healthy. Working with survivors, clinicians, and health-system partners, we will design a province-wide intervention to deliver personalized reminders and supports. We will engage survivors and their doctors to ensure the planned strategy is user-centred while incorporating the science of behaviour change. By the end of this project, we will be prepared to work with our provincial partners on implementing and evaluating a province-wide scale-up of the intervention. This fellowship will enhance my academic training, and expand my skills using patient engagement and patient-centred methods in the design and delivery of health care, as well as my capacity to conduct applied research in partnership with health system organizations. The training from the fellowship project, in combination with network building and leadership skills, will give me a strong foundation to begin a career of developing innovative solutions to challenges facing the health care system.

column36: Share. Learn. Optimize. Disseminating Knowledge Within Ontario Regarding Spinal Cord Injury Rehabilitation Services And Health Systems
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes paralysis which affects the person's ability to feed, bathe, or dress themselves and affects their ability to move about their home/community. The complexity of SCI care in the health system is reflected in the number of health care professionals involved in the rehabilitation process (doctors, nurses, physical and occupational therapists, social workers, and psychologists). Although delivery of rehabilitation is interprofessional, clinicians tend to work alone, and often do not know have time for continuing education and do not understand the impact of their practice on health system efficiency. Thus, strategies to integrate clinical expertise and improve the quality of rehabilitation services across the health system are needed. This application aims to support the development of a continuing education model for SCI rehabilitation for clinicians. The first phase of this fellowship will identify and synthesize current successful models of continuing education used in other health conditions. The second phase will use the products of phase one to inform the creation of a continuing education model specific to SCI rehabilitation providers. This project is the result of a partnership between the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation (ONF) and the University Health Network allowing knowledge produced in an academic setting to be incorporated into the partner organization's processes. We envision creating a platform for interprofessional groups of clinicians to share their expertise and identify the best pathway of care for SCI rehabilitation. This fellowship will support the creation of a continuing education model. The model will enable the initiatives of ONF related to advancing the SCI Quality Consortium (i.e. measuring and improving quality of SCI rehabilitation care in Ontario) and the Care Pathways (i.e. appropriate care for people with motor vehicle injuries), to achieve ONF's mandate of improved access to quality care across Ontario.

column36: Investing wisely: using economic modelling to optimize public health strategies to reduce harm from alcohol, tobacco and cannabis and optimize benefits in British Columbia
column37: Substance use costs British Columbia $4.9 billion in 2014, of which 70% was due to alcohol and tobacco. These estimates include costs related to the use of health care resources, productivity losses, criminal justice, and other direct costs such as accidents, research and prevention. Broader societal costs not included in these estimates relate to inequities, marginalization and hindered social development. This project aims to develop a model to evaluate the economic and social impact of legal substance use harm prevention in British Columbia. Evidence on economic consequences and how public health programs can minimize costs and harms from substance use is important for policy makers, who need to consider the health system priorities against efficiency, scalability and sustainability of interventions. The challenges to developing comprehensive economic evaluations in public health are well known. In the area of substance use, these pertain to the multitude of the socioeconomic determinants that influence use - such as employment, income, social exclusion, and hopelessness - and the difficulty of measuring broader benefits including family wellbeing, community development and equity gains. This fellowship will facilitate collaboration between knowledge users and academics with the aim of optimizing investment in the area of alcohol, tobacco and cannabis harm prevention in BC. It will provide the Ministry of Health with tools to implement efficient priority setting that aligns with the institution's values and development goals. This will be achieved through important methodological advances to allow evaluations to account for the broader societal impact of preventing harm from legal substance use in BC. As a result, this fellowship will sustain future research in health economics with an increased ability to respond to policy makers' needs when it comes to priority setting.

Les travaux realises dans ce projet pourront ensuite etre etendus a toutes les thematiques couvertes par les APRs en capitalisant sur les donnees provenant de PARS3 et de l'INESSS. column36: Enhancing collaborative care planning with older adults receiving home-care services
column37: Older adults and their family caregivers and receive home-care services to support living at home with complex and chronic conditions. Setting goals, developing a care plan for home care, and measuring to ensure those goals are being met is an important process. However, current home-care planning processes do not do a good job of learning the goals and needs of older adults and their caregivers and providing care to meet those needs. Also, service providers of home-care and older adults' primary-care physicians do not always work together with home-care clients to develop the care plan or measure if the plan is actually working. Working together with older adults, caregivers, service providers, and primary-care physicians, a model of care- planning will be developed and tested. The anticipated benefits of the project for older adults and their caregivers receiving home-care services will be an improved care planning experience where they feel heard, respected and satisfied with the plan and care. In turn, home-care service providers will gain skill in taking a person- and family-centred approach to care-planning and work together with all providers including primary-care physicians.

column36: Fairness: An institutional ethnography to identify risks, benefits and mediation strategies for AI/machine learning in mental healthcare delivery
column37: A strategic priority for the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), the host organization, is evidence based care. The heart of this initiative is the Krembil Centre for Neuroinfomatics (KCNI), which employs state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) techniques to identify, manage and treat mental illnesses, while shaping policy at national and global levels. KCNI manages and curates patient data to create algorithms capable of modelling disease pathways, predicting adverse effects, and facilitating personalized treatment interventions. Concerns about AI applications systematically discriminating against specific populations have spearheaded an urgent conversation about notions of fairness. Namely, who will/should benefit the most from these techniques and why? Thus, the primary objective of this project is to examine how fairness is defined, managed and produced along an Integrated Care Pathway (ICP) for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). We ask: what makes training datasets "fair" and how are principles of "fairness" incorporated into decision-making by human (patients, clinicians, data curators) and non-human (AI) care teams? We anticipate that the concept of fairness is not fully developed, thus a key health system impact objective is to develop guiding principles for incorporating fairness into hospital-wide efforts to engage with AI/ML techniques for health equity. To achieve these objectives the fellow will conduct an institutional ethnography to analyze how concepts of fairness are used to inform the ICP for MDD. Patients, clinicians, and data curators who use and interpret data for recovery will be interviewed and observed. This project will foster the responsible interpretation of knowledge derived from AI/ML and is essential to ensure that policy uptake is relevant and beneficial for all.

column36: Supporting health system stakeholders to sustain their effective innovations
column37: The Women's College Hospital Institute for Health System Solutions and Virtual Care (WIHV) works in partnership with leading decision makers and organizations to influence health system policy across the province. As an embedded researcher on this team, I will have the unique opportunity to apply my scientific skills to real-world policy initiatives that aim to improve health care and patient outcomes at scale. I will be supervised by the Director of the Institute, Dr. Sacha Bhatia (health system supervisor) and Dr. Noah Ivers, Chair in Implementation Science at Women's College Research Institute and the University of Toronto (academic supervisor). The overarching goal of this fellowship is to help WIHV systematically assess program sustainability across the initiatives they evaluate. Specifically, my role at WIHV will be: 1) To understand if and how sustainability is considered by provincial partners such as Health Quality Ontario, the Ontario Telemedicine Network, and Public Health Ontario, who have implemented interventions with potential for large-scale impact; 2) To create a toolkit for WIHV to use to support their partners in achieving sustainable change; and 3) To disseminate findings regarding how to consider sustainability when developing and implementing new models of care. My supervisors have a strong and productive history of collaboration and a broad network of experts capable of supporting my development. For instance, my academic supervisor and I will visit quarterly to the Center for Implementation Research, led by Dr. Jeremy Grimshaw of the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (OHRI). Working with the team at OHRI will increase my skills in applying an integrated knowledge translation approach. Overall, I will conduct methodologically robust and highly collaborative projects that aim to improve health outcomes for patients while furthering my career interests in understanding sustainability of health system interventions.

column36: Applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and supervised Machine Learning (ML) for immunization programmes in Ontario
column37: Vaccine hesitancy is the phenomena of the delay or refusal of receiving vaccinations. For public health professionals and immunization experts, vaccine hesitancy poses significant challenges to immunization delivery because a successful immunization program is reliant on public's confidence in vaccines. One of the ways vaccine hesitancy spread is through social media platforms. These social media platforms allow user-generated content, with the inclusion of vaccine misinformation, to be passed on. The spread of vaccine misinformation on social media results in observable decreases in the public's confidence in vaccines, as well as an increase in vaccine-preventable outbreaks in Canada and abroad. Three complementary studies will be conducted at the Ontario Agency of Public Health Protection and Promotion (also known as Public Health Ontario, PHO), a Crown corporation dedicated to protecting and promoting the health of all Ontarians. The three studies are: (1) Interviewing stakeholders and decision-makers in key organizations to identify areas in immunization delivery where AI can be applied to address vaccine hesitancy, (2) using AI to explore the linguistic differences among the vaccine-hesitant, the anti-vaccine, and the vaccine supporters, and based on these findings, deploying a surveillance dashboard to monitor the surges of misinformation on social media in real-time, and (3) classifying vaccine information/misinformation using AI to improve the function of the dashboard and explore novel methods to deploy accurate vaccine information that will spread wider, deeper, and farther on social media. The studies address issues of distributive justice pertaining to immunization information on social media. The findings will strengthen PHO's capacity to foster a sustainable and collaborative project-oriented platform for future researchers to conduct AI research for public health.

column36: Leveraging implementation and behavioural science to support laboratory stewardship
column37: Blood samples taken in hospitals are sent to a laboratory, analyzed, and results used to diagnose and treat patients. However, many tests ordered are not needed. This leads to wasted healthcare spending and negative effects on patients, such as false positives (test results which incorrectly indicate that a person has a condition). Researchers have designed strategies to support hospital staff to reduce unnecessary testing. However, these strategies don't work all the time, which prevents widespread uptake. We need to know more about what influences hospital staff to order these tests, and what they think about these strategies, so that we can develop strategies that best suit their needs. The Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association (EORLA), a group of 18 laboratories connected to 16 hospitals in Eastern Ontario, have been testing various different strategies to support hospital staff to reduce their orders of these tests. In study 1, we will assess the extent to which these strategies are working, by comparing the number of tests ordered before and after the strategies were put in place. We will also review the strategy documentation to pinpoint the specific techniques which may be supporting staff to change their behaviour. Finally, we will interview those who set up the strategies to explore the process and challenges, and hospital staff to explore how they think the strategies affected their test ordering. In study 2, we will interview hospital staff to help with the design of new strategies. Finally, we will develop a list of all the data EORLA have and investigate how it could be better linked so that EORLA can compare test-ordering practices across all their hospital sites.

column36: Building an Integrated Health Delivery System in Burlington, Ontario
column37: In Canada and internationally, the demographic is aging and increasingly faces challenges with leading a strong quality of life while managing chronic conditions. While technological advancements have made it possible to care for many of these conditions outside of hospitals, the fragmentation of traditional models of care delivery does not meet patient needs or expectations and often leads to suboptimal outcomes. The Burlington sub-region, co-facilitated by Joseph Brant Hospital, seeks to establish an Integrated Health Delivery System (IHDS) that will provide comprehensive, integrated 24/7 care to a defined population of approximately 250,000 residents in the City of Burlington and surrounding communities. In the first year, the IHDS will focus on integrating primary care, acute care, and home care for patients affiliated with two family health teams and two family health groups (approximately 60,000 patients). In the second year, there will be a plan to expand the patient population and to phase in the full continuum of care, with a focus on community mental health, palliative care, and COPD care. As a member of the IHDS steering committee, the Fellow will contribute to the planning and implementation of the care pathways (including the development of a shared dashboard), and lead the program's evaluation. Recently, the Government of Ontario released its vision for the creation of local health teams that will advance population health and access to care, improve outcomes, and enhance the patient experience. With established relationships and commitments from partner organisations already in place, learnings from the IHDS will provide emerging insights that are relevant for informing the development, sustainability, and spread and scale of future integrated care models.

column36: Interpreting and addressing barriers impeding effective care transitions for women diagnosed with breast cancer in British Columbia
column37: The number of Canadians diagnosed with cancer is rising with a growing and aging population and we need to ensure our healthcare system is equipped to meet this growing demand. As the most common female cancer worldwide, breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in Canadian women. In recent decades, advancements in breast cancer screening and treatments have resulted in approximately 87% of Canadian women diagnosed with breast cancer surviving 5 years after diagnosis. Increased survival rates are due in part to adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) (e.g., tamoxifen), which is used to treat early-stage, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, representing the large majority of breast cancer diagnoses. Women prescribed AET are recommended to take this medication everyday for 5-10 years depending on their diagnosis, which results in the need for increased follow-up care over a long period of time. Previous research, however, has shown there are many issues associated with transitions in care, particularly as breast cancer survivors move from receiving care from their oncologist back to seeing their family physician or nurse practitioner in the community. The objective of this project is to improve transitions in care to better support women diagnosed with breast cancer and also the healthcare providers that deliver care to these women. The goal is to meet the supportive care needs of breast cancer survivors as they transition through the healthcare system to support them in living well beyond their breast cancer diagnosis.

column36: Better Serving People with Multiple, Complex Needs in BC through Health System Impact.
column37: The aim of this research project is to better understand and address the health needs and service requirements of people with multiple, complex needs under the purview of Community Living British Columbia (CLBC). The proposed research project will build on existing research and fill important gaps in knowledge regarding the health of people with a multiple complex needs designation and effective service delivery mechanisms at points of intersection with the healthcare system. This research project will advance CLBC's research efforts through two key objectives. The first is to better understand the health-related needs of this population, which includes an analysis of health-related contacts (type and frequency), outcomes, and costs associated with this population. In BC, much is not known about the health-related needs of this group. The second objective is to identify and learn from promising practices in BC - specifically, what is being done that works for this population and why, with particular attention to issues of sustainability and scalability. Although findings from CLBC's qualitative research highlight the need for significant systemic change in the delivery of services for people with multiple complex needs, it also identified "pockets of excellence" in BC where local or regional solutions have emerged as examples of practice excellence. Through this objective, I will focus on services that directly intersect with the healthcare system (e.g., acute care, residential detox/treatment, etc.) and address underlying social determinants of health, including, for example: homelessness, poverty, and issues of gender and race (indigenous people). The research will include an evaluation of selected services. In addition, an inventory of services for the multiple, complex needs people in BC will be developed.

column36: Early Mechanistic Biomarkers for late Epilepsy and long-term Brain Injury Outcome Jens P. Dreier EBio2
column37: Stroke and traumatic brain injuries (TBI) in humans are common causes of mortality and impose a poor quality of life on the affected individuals and their families. Life-saving treatments after brain injuries improved patients' survival but long-term severe complications, such as motor and cognitive disabilities and epilepsy, still lack preventive treatments. Our studies indicate that specific structural and functional alterations involving neurons, glia and brain vessels underlie the progressive evolution of brain injuries and contribute to the late onset of epilepsy. The unmet need for early identification of these pathologic events in injured patients with clinically applicable approaches is the basis for the current project. Our ultimate goal is to improve current treatment interventions in brain-injured patients by discovering mechanism-driven biomarkers that will permit early preventive treatments for neurological complications. Through a combination approach based on improved and novel analyses of electrophysiological signals, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and selected blood molecules, we will search for common fingerprints of brain network dysfunctions reflecting disease progression using (1) our existing database of brain-injured patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage who underwent intensive neuromonitoring, serial MRI scans, blood collection, and were evaluated for epilepsy after 3 years, and (2) clinically relevant animal models of brain injury that are associated with late epilepsy development and allow neuromonitoring in a similar manner as in the ICU. We envision that monitoring of post-injury brain dynamics will allow us to develop biomarkers that identify patients at high-risk for developing a disease progressive course and epilepsy, thus permitting novel treatments to be applied timely following the concept of Personalized Medicine.

column36: Biomarkers of ANTidepressant RESponse : early indicators and novel targets
column37: Antidepressants (AD) are for now, the best treatment we have for major depression (MDD) a severe mental disorder. AD are one of the most commonly prescribed drugs in the western hemisphere, however their trial-and error nature combined with unwanted side-effects, leave a lot to be desired. More than 60% of patients suffering from MDD fail to respond to the first AD they are prescribed. For those that respond, full response is only observed after several weeks of treatment, and, in case of failure it can take too long a time before alternative options are explored. To be able to predict clinical response at an early-stage of AD treatment is an important aim for the clinician and the potential impact for patients suffering from MDD and for the health system is very high. However, up to date there are no early biomarkers that could help therapeutic decision while this is already true in cancer and other fields of medicine. We recently described the involvement of ELK1 in depression, particularly how ELK1 gene expression in blood may help follow treatment response and will further characterize ELK1 and related genes, and other regulators of cell machinery associated with early clinical improvement. First we aim to identify peripheral "early post-treatment biomarkers" in a novel multicentre human cohort of patients with MDE. Then, we want to validate "early post-treatment biomarkers" in animal models of depression, in the blood. Last, we want to explore the plausibility of our blood biomarkers by studying our biomarkers in the brain. We will focus our analysis on both long and small RNA, by using cutting-edge approaches. These results will constitute the necessary first step to develop new biomarkers predictive of AD response. Such biomarkers, would reduce time to change medication and help avoid unnecessary side effects for patients, inform therapeutic decisions and reduce stress for clinicians, and reduce personal and public health costs.

column36: Defining the cellular origin of colorectal cancer.
column37: The gut lining is replaced every 3 to 5 days by rapidly dividing cells. Specialized cells known as stem cells have the longevity and capacity to continually renew all the other cell types. Unfortunately, this unique longevity of stem cells is also what predisposes them to acquire mutations that lead to cancer. Hence, the recent identification of intestinal stem cells has created excitement for both regenerative medicine and the discovery of the cellular origin of colon cancer. More recently, we have identified a radioresistant stem cell population present in the normal (non-mutated) colon and demonstrated that they can contribute to the cellular origin of cancer. The goal of this research is to determine whether a secretory (non-stem) cell can also give rise to colon cancer. My lab has considerable expertise in intestinal stem cells and colon cancer, and we have developed innovative models to help determine the cell of origin for these tumors. These studies will inform us about the origin of colon cancer and how this can predict tumor phenotypes and response.

column36: Investigation of Mechanisms Leading to Synthetic Lethality of BRCA-associated Cancers
column37: Inheriting defects in the tumor suppressor genes BRCA1 and BRCA2 significantly increases risk of developing breast and ovarian cancers. Tumors that arise as a result of these defects tend to be aggressive. Currently, healthy women carriers of BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations can opt for prophylactic mastectomy and oophorectomy to reduce their cancer risk. There is an urgent need to identify novel optimal therapeutic options for the majority of breast and ovarian cancer patients carrying defects in BRCA1 or BRCA2. We have performed a large analysis for hits that kill BRCA1 breast tumor cells and identified a protein (MePCE) as a candidate essential for the survival of BRCA1 defective breast tumors. We have extended our finding to BRCA1 defective ovarian tumors. Our overarching goal is to perform several studies to validate MePCE as a target to kill breast and ovarian tumors defective for BRCA1 or BRCA2. These studies have a great potential to help patients with poor prognosis breast and ovarian cancers.

column36: Radio-selective effects of a natural occurring muscle-derived dipeptide in an orthotopic lung cancer rat model
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of the death for women and men in Canada and worldwide. Radiotherapy is one of the most commonly used treatments for lung cancer and even though it increases the survival of lung cancer patients, it can also cause radiation induced lung damage. Our proposal aims to improve the efficiency of radiotherapy and reduce the damaging effects of radiotherapy to normal lung tissue, which is known as radiation induced lung damage. We have tested the effects of a naturally occurring compound, L-carnosine (CAR), and we found that in cell culture experiments CAR reduced the capacity of lung cancer to multiply, CAR also made lung cancer cells more susceptible and improved the way radiotherapy kills cancer cells. We also tested CAR effects on normal cells, we exposed them to radiotherapy, and CAR did not affect normal cells or even reduced the damage caused by radiotherapy to normal cells.

column36: Supporting public health applications of artificial intelligence to improve health equity and prevent chronic diseases in the population
column37: Predictive risk algorithms for chronic disease are used by organizations like Public Health Ontario (PHO) for population health surveillance, examining the contribution of risk factors to disease, and assessing the impact of prevention strategies. Vast amounts of population health data are now available and able to support a wide range of "big data" approaches for chronic disease risk prediction. Population health has traditionally used simple risk prediction methods, however, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are ideally suited to enhancing population risk prediction tools. To date, however, evidence on risk prediction using these methods for population health applications is limited and it is unclear how AI approaches could be used to benefit health protection, promotion, prevention and health equity. The objectives of the proposed program of work are to: 1) develop an AI strategy for PHO, the host organization; 2) develop two new risk prediction models for dementia and multiple chronic disease using AI methods; and 3) support public health units in building AI capacity. It is important for Canada to build capacity for AI, as there is significant potential for these methods to support population health surveillance and disease prevention.

column36: Enhancing population health monitoring and evaluation using text analytics on clinical data
column37: With the emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases and rising burden of chronic diseases, it is critical to improve prevention, control and management of disease by using innovative and cost-effective solutions. Given the large amount of digital data generated as part of patient interactions with the healthcare system, most of which is in the form of notes, text analytics and natural language processing (NLP) techniques can support detection, management, and long term follow-up of patients, thus allowing health systems to improve upon patient wellness. The BCCDC and UBC Data Science Institute have partnered with the goal of applying text analytics and NLP techniques to identify useful information for informing health policy and the design of health services. This proposed HSIF program of work will examine big text data including laboratory results, medical notes, and discussion forum data with objectives of: a) text classification to mine disease-related information and main concerns of patients, and; b) topic modeling to identify the major issues of public health. This proposal supports the BCCDC impact goals which include informing health policy and design of health services to improve health of British Columbians by enhancing population health monitoring and evaluation.

column37: As people age, the benefits of previously safe medications can be outweighed by potential harms. Deprescribing is the planned and supervised process of reducing or stopping medications that may be causing harm, or may no longer be of benefit. Since 2013, Dr. Barbara Farrell has the led the development of the first evidence-based deprescribing guidelines for priority drug classes to help clinicians make decisions about when and how to stop medications safely. Because guidelines alone do not result in clinical practice change, Dr. Farrell's team created tools for clinicians and the public that help them navigate the process of deprescribing using the guidelines. This includes decision-support algorithms for guidelines, patient pamphlets and infographics, whiteboard training videos, and a mobile app. These tools, as well as webinars, video and written testimonials, regular e-newsletters, resources, publications and media reports are freely available on https://deprescribing.org/. Dr. Farrell's team has also: -Hosted a 3-day symposium (March 2018) for guideline developers, healthcare providers, educators, researchers, decision-makers, and members of the public attended by 130 people from 10 countries; and, -Delivered approximately 140 presentations and workshops for clinicians, policymakers and the public, reaching more than 5500 people locally, nationally, and internationally. Dr. Farrell's team is now studying best practices for tailoring interventions to support deprescribing in primary care, long-term care, and community pharmacies. The team is also partnering with the public to help people have deprescribing conversations with their clinicians. The clinical and economic impacts of deprescribing using the guidelines are being evaluated in ongoing studies. Most importantly, the deprescribing guidelines are being used in practice settings around the world, improving medication experiences and optimizing health for Canadians and beyond.

column36: In the shadows of the opioid crisis: the epidemiology and impact of methamphetamine use in Canada
column37: Methamphetamines are potent stimulants with significant health and societal consequences. In the United States, amphetamine-related hospitalizations have recently tripled following a brief period of decline. In Canada, anecdotal reports have noted similar trends, but surprisingly little research has been conducted to assess the purported increase in the use of the drug. Of special importance is the lack of nationwide epidemiological data. Given this growing concern and the paucity of research on the topic, our work will investigate trends in methamphetamine use in Canada. Specifically, we will examine geographic, sociodemographic, and temporal trends of methamphetamine use, as well as trends in polysubstance abuse. We will also quantify corresponding health care utilization and hospital costs to understand the national economic impact. Our study will use a nationally representative Canadian cohort, which will provide the most comprehensive and up to date figures of epidemiological trends on methamphetamine use in Canada. In order to lay the groundwork for successful interventions at all levels (including treatment, harm reduction, and at the levels of health service systems), epidemiological studies using large, current, and representative samples are urgently needed.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling photoreceptor genome organization and neurodegeneration - ICS IG Maud Menten New Investigator Prize
column37: The nucleus of each human cell contains approximately 2 metres of DNA. Cells must confine this enormous amount of genetic information within a microscopic space, while simultaneously maintaining the ability to access and utilize genes. To do this, cells must partition the genome into different compartments of the nucleus. Some regions of the genome remain accessible, while other regions are compacted. This very basic process is vital for cells to function and survive, but it remains very challenging to study, and is therefore poorly understood. We have uncovered several proteins that influence this process in retinal photoreceptors. When these proteins are removed, the retina degenerates, and the genome becomes disorganized. This proposal will study these proteins in detail, in order to untangle their role in genome organization, retinal function, and neurodegeneration. Our work will shed light on the role of this poorly understood process, and determine its contribution to retinal degeneration, which is an increasingly prevalent problem due to Canada's aging demographics.

column36: AI for public health (AI4PH): A focus on equity and prevention
column37: The vision of the Artificial Intelligence for Public Health (AI4PH) Summer Institute is to enable participants to apply AI innovations in public health research with a health equity focus. Our goal is to develop, deliver, and disseminate a comprehensive set of resources for teaching how artificial intelligence (AI), including the subfield of machine learning (ML), can be applied to address important public health problems while explicitly prioritizing health equity. Trainees and early-career researchers in public health and computer science disciplines will benefit from these resources delivered online and in-person, initially in Canada and subsequently around the world. This training will produce a highly qualified and equity-informed global network of peers and mentors from multiple disciplines relevant to public health and AI. Participants in the AI4PH Summer Institute will understand the most important problems facing public health agencies and organizations and have the expertise and collaborative network to apply AI methods in concert with established techniques to invent novel and equitable solutions for the prevention and control of critical public health problems with a high level of ethical rigour. Upon successful completion of the institute, we expect AI4PH Summer Institute participants will have the knowledge and skills to: 1) Understand the conceptual underpinnings of AI and related sub-disciplines so that they can articulate why and when these methods should be used; 2) Apply AI methods and interpret results in the context of real-life public health issues; 3) Advance Equity by i) Understanding the concept of 'equity', and ii) applying this understanding of equity throughout the AI research process (problem definition, research design and methods, knowledge translation); and 4) Understand the contributions of different disciplines (e.g., social science, ethics, computational science, public health policy) and methods in public health AI research.

column36: Les fuseaux de sommeil dans l'apnee obstructive du sommeil chez les hommes et les femmes ages
column37: Le syndrome d'apnees obstructives du sommeil (SAOS) est un trouble de sante qui affecte 50% de la population de plus de 65 ans. Le SAOS est caracterise par des obstructions partielles (hypopnees) ou completes (apnees) des voies respiratoires qui se repetent plus d'une centaine de fois pendant le sommeil. Ces pauses respiratoires peuvent entrainer des consequences telles que des problemes de fonctionnement cerebral, des deficits cognitifs et de la somnolence diurne. Le SAOS a recemment ete lie a un risque accru de trouble cognitif leger et de demence dans plusieurs cohortes suivies longitudinalement et les differentes equipes de recherche tentent maintenant de comprendre les mecanismes physiologiques liant le SAOS a la demence. De plus, certaines etudes ont montre que les femmes seraient plus vulnerables aux effets du SAOS sur leur sante cerebrale. Les fuseaux de sommeil sont des oscillations qui se produisent lors d'une des phases du sommeil profond. Une plus grande densite de ces oscillations a ete associee a une meilleure consolidation des apprentissages et au maintien du sommeil. Des etudes ont demontre qu'une diminution des fuseaux est associee au trouble cognitif leger et a la demence. A ce jour, aucune etude n'a mesure les caracteristiques des fuseaux chez les apneiques de plus de 55 ans. Puisque le SAOS est associe a un plus grand risque de declin cognitif anormal, nous faisons l'hypothese que la severite du SAOS sera associee a une plus petite densite de fuseaux de sommeil. Nous predisons qu'une densite plus faible de fuseaux sera associee a plus de deficits cognitifs. Enfin, en fonction des connaissances actuelles, nous allons verifier que l'association entre la densite des fuseaux et la severite du SAOS est plus grande chez les femmes que chez les hommes.

column36: The effects of cognitive training on neurobiological mechanisms: an intervention study to promote cognitive health in the elderly
column37: Background: Cognitive stimulation throughout life, such as intellectual activities and a high level of education, has been shown to protect against age-related diseases and dementia. Thus, cognitive training programs for the elderly may help promote cognitive health as we age. Two working memory components, inhibition and updating, are of particular interest because they are recruited throughout complex daily tasks and are susceptible to markers of cognitive vulnerability. While we know that training programs can be effective in improving certain targeted abilities, little is known about the brain mechanisms underlying their efficacy. Objectives: Older adults will complete cognitive training aiming to improve inhibition or updating. Our objective is to examine the differential effects of these interventions on the structure and functioning of the brain through magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We will also examine whether individual variables, such as gene polymorphisms, level of education, and cerebrovascular health, predict a change in activational patterns associated with the training. Methods: Ninety older adults, between the ages of 60 and 85, will be randomized into one of three intervention groups: updating training, inhibition training, and a control condition. Subjects will complete 12 sessions of training and an MRI examination three times throughout the study: before the start of training (PRE), after the sixth session of training (MID), and after the twelfth session (POST). Our analyses will compare task-related neural activity at the three time points, according to intervention type. We will pay particular attention in examining whether new regions are recruited or if the interventions enhance or lessen activity in the initially-activated regions.

column36: Impact of Bio-Feedback on Activity-Dependent Neural Plasticity after Spinal Cord Injury
column37: Spinal Cord Injuries (SCIs) impact over 85,000 individuals in Canada, notably affecting ones ability to independently perform activities of daily living due to reduced functional outcomes. In incomplete SCIs, sensory and motor function are partially preserved offering a neural interface for assistive devices, or even the possibility of rehabilitation. Despite advancements in rehabilitative technology, the lack of adequate sensory feedback and functional precision from assistive devices interferes with individuals' motivation, which remains fundamental to the rehabilitation process. Furthermore, research suggests that neuroplasticity is driven in part by the uptake of sensory feedback. This process suggests that humans are able to adapt and reorganize their neural networks following an obstruction of the brain or spinal cord. In fact, repetitive training of the impaired limb has been shown to promote activity-dependent plasticity (ADP) and improve motor function following incomplete SCIs in humans. ADP has been extensively studied; however, the effects of bio-sensory feedback on ADP during movement intent require further investigation. We hypothesize that a subject's perception of their intended movement, provided through sensory feedback, will reinforce the accurate neural pathway and promote self-correction through neural-plastic changes. In this experiment we will investigate the significance of performance-associated feedback and which types of sensory feedback best support subjects' understanding of the relationship between their efforts, actions, and consequences. These findings could have the potential to give patients hope in their rehabilitation by showing them that their intention to move is effectively being conveyed, and that improvement could be possible.

column36: The Effects of BMP-9 on Tumour Angiogenesis With and Without the Loss of Endothelial BMPR2
column37: The Effects of BMP-9 on Tumour Angiogenesis With and Without the Loss of Endothelial BMPR2 One ligand whose involvement in cancer requires more study is bone morphogenetic protein 9 (BMP-9). BMP-9 is involved in both normal and pathogenic angiogenesis, normally acting as a quiescence factor to suppress vascular growth. BMP-9 signals through binding Bone Morphogenetic Protein Receptor II (gene: BMPR2), however it is promiscuous, which may lead to bidirectional effects on angiogenesis. Although previous research on the role of BMP-9 in cancer has been conducted, the results have been contradictory. To fill in the gaps in current knowledge, the overarching question being explored in this proposed research is, "Does the loss of BMPR2 influence the contribution of BMP-9 to the vascularization of solid tumours?" The current proposal is based on the hypothesis that BMP-9 suppresses angiogenesis under normal conditions but promotes endothelial cell proliferation when BMPR2 is down-regulated or lost. The main challenges with previous studies addressing this question are associated with the fact that many tumour models are also responsive to BMP-9. This makes it impossible to determine if responses to treatment are due to the influence of BMP-9 on tumour vascularization or a direct action of the ligand on tumour growth. The current proposal will address this question through the targeted deletion of BMPR2 in either the vasculature or the tumour of an in vivo metastatic breast cancer model. This project will give insight into the effects of BMP-9 on pathogenic angiogenesis and whether its effects are modified with the loss of endothelial BMPR2. A new role of BMP-9 may be identified which could lead to the discovery of potential new pathways to target during cancer treatment.

column36: Aliphatic polycarbonates for effective local and sustained peptide delivery
column37: Peptides are a quickly growing drug class, which continue to garner attention in pharmaceutical research due to their applications in the treatment of a variety of diseases. The major challenge when working with these drugs is that they degrade quickly in vivo and have poor membrane permeability. This makes simple administration methods such as oral consumption infeasible and necessitates the use of a localized drug delivery system. One example of such a system is to load the peptide into biodegradable polymer microspheres which can then be injected close to the intended delivery site of the drug. These microspheres provide a sustained release of the peptide, before eventually degrading and being removed by the body. This is done commercially by a polymer called poly(lactide-co-glycolide), or PLGA. However, PLGA breaks down in the body to form highly acidic byproducts, which can react with the peptide drug and alter the drug's chemistry. Depending on the peptide, this can lead to reduced effectiveness or inactivation. Recent work in the Amsden Group has found that polymer microspheres based on poly(trimethylene carbonate) (PTMC) show great promise for this application, as the degradation byproducts are far less acidic. The proposed research focuses on developing innovative new polymer microspheres based on PTMC for the sustained delivery of peptide drugs.

column36: Integrative Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Cutaneous Melanoma
column37: Cutaneous melanoma (CM) is the deadliest form of skin cancer. Understanding the molecular features of this disease is essential to the development of more effective treatments. This study aims to dissect the heterogeneity of melanoma tumor gene expression between patients, because (1) pre-treatment gene expression has been shown to predict efficacy of treatments currently in use, and (2) gene expression changes in response to treatment may cause a cancer to become resistant to treatment. What makes this study unique is its attempt to examine the gene expression of individual cells that comprise a tumor, rather than the average gene expression of all cells in a tumor. The increased resolution will better our understanding of melanoma tumor gene expression and will inform us how well the constituents of pre-treatment gene expression predict response. The results will potentially allow (after further study) better tailored patient treatments and promote the development of novel treatments for patients who do not respond well to current treatments.

column36: Characterizing the human mitochondrial processing peptidase in neurodegenerative disease
column37: Neurodegenerative disorders have become one of the most critical health issues, as the world's aging population increases and treatments remain scarce. For most of these disorders, current treatments serve solely as "symptomatic band-aids" given too late in the disease progression. As such, there exists a desperate need to study these disorders from unique avenues to reveal novel points of regulation and other potential drug targets. In our bodies, mitochondria have been typically labelled as the "energy generators" of our cells, however, their importance in the brain and their implications in neurodegenerative disorders have become increasingly apparent over the last 10 years. Today, biologists acknowledge the existence of an intimate link between mitochondrial dysfunction and neurodegeneration. This project will investigate this link through the lens of one specific, overlooked molecular player: the mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP). Recently, mutations in both MPP and its interactors have been implicated in Parkinson's disease and certain ataxias, yet their underlying mechanisms and neuronal consequences remain uncharacterized. Our work will serve to answer a few key questions: how does MPP contribute to these disorders? Can we study these interactions to design neuroprotective drugs? Our work will lay the foundation for a drug design platform targeting MPP whose effect will be two-fold: first, it will allow us to design research tools for studying basic mitochondrial mechanisms, and second, it will propel the development of therapeutics against MPP-linked neurodegenerative disorders. Our results will also provide new biochemical models to reveal how key mitochondrial functions exert such a unique effect in our brains. Globally, this project will foster collaboration with scientists across the world, and will be directly impactful to researchers, clinicians, and those suffering from neurodegenerative disease alike.

column36: Examining biomarkers of frailty and cardiovascular health in older women
column37: Current methods of assessing cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in women underestimate their risk. A suggested method of improving CVD risk management is the addition of frailty assessments as vital signs, as frailty, and its intermediary stage pre-frailty, both increase risk for CVD. Thus, this observational, cohort study aims to examine the interactions of frailty status and biomarkers of cardiovascular health and frailty in the prediction of CVD in 1000 women. Personal Health Information Numbers will be used to access health usage data over the course of the cohort study to determine if participants experienced adverse CVD-related health outcomes. This information will allow for the identification of frailty biomarkers that are associated with CVD risk and adverse CVD outcomes.

column36: Children with Medical Complexity in the Canadian Maritimes: A Mixed Methods Study
column37: Children with medical complexity refer to those who experience a variety of complex chronic health conditions which impact their daily life. While we expect this population of children to be small in numbers, they require a large amount of health care resources to manage their medical conditions. Many of these children are discharged from hospital to be cared for in their home communities by their families and a range of interdisciplinary care providers. This transfer of responsibility highlights the need to adequately support the complex medical, social, and financial needs of these families. Unfortunately, there is a disconnect between our current health care system and the needs of these children and their families. Thus, this proposed research will focus on examining and describing the population of children with medical complexity who live in the Canadian Maritimes to develop practice and policy recommendations. A multi-phase mixed methods research approach to will be used to examine this issue. I will begin by using existing health data to identify these children and their characteristics over a 10-year period (2005-2015). Findings from this first phase will guide the development of in-depth case studies in phase 2 to deepen our understanding of the experiences of this vulnerable population in their home communities. Developing a greater understanding of the population of children with medical complexity in Canada is urgently needed as the first step in designing patient-oriented health policies and programs to improve the health care experiences, health system use, and health outcomes of children with medical complexity and their families.

column36: Studies of the PRL/CNNM pathway in metastatic cancer
column37: PRL phosphatases have been known to promote cancer metastasis for over 15 years but how they do so was unknown until very recently. New studies have shown that PRL phosphatases inhibit CNNM proteins that transport magnesium across the cell membrane. Magnesium is an essential element and involved in a wide variety of biological activities. Increase in magnesium levels stimulate cell growth and migration, which are characteristic of metastatic cancer. We propose to study how PRLs inhibit CNNM proteins by imaging the three-dimensional shapes of the proteins alone and in a complex together. We will use X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy to determine the proteins' structure. These studies of the PRL/CNNM pathway will provide the structural and chemical basis for developing novel drugs to block metastatic cancer.

column36: Investigating the role of approach-avoidance conflict and the hippocampus in anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder
column37: Approach-avoidance (AA) conflict, elicited by the simultaneous occurrence of both positive and negative stimuli, could be a potential transdiagnostic construct to consider integrating into the NIMH Research Domain Criteria. Three disorders that are likely to have dysfunctional AA conflict processing are anxiety, obsessive-compulsive (OCD), and post-traumatic stress (PTSD) disorder. Importantly, a brain region critical to successful AA conflict resolution, the anterior hippocampus, is structurally compromised in these disorders. To elucidate whether the link between disordered AA conflict processing and the anterior hippocampus are implicated in anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD the current study will test patients from each of these groups and compare their performance on an AA conflict task to that of healthy controls while they undergo functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). More specifically, participants will first learn to approach or avoid a series of face-scene pairs that will either be rewarding or punishing, respectively. During fMRI, participants will be asked to approach or avoid recombined face-scene pairs that will be either no-conflict positive, no-conflict negative, or conflict mixed. Statistical analyses will include behavioral measures of the proportion of approach and reaction time responses to each conflict category. Neuroimaging analyses will include univariate and multivariate methods to determine whether the groups differ from each other in their behavioral and neural response to conflict. The findings from this research will help understand factors underlying anxiety, OCD, and PTSD which in turn may inform improved assessment and intervention techniques for Canadians.

column36: Revealing processes that confer immunity against nasal colonization by Neisseria meningitidis
column37: Neisseria meningitidis (the meningococcus) is a bacterial pathogen that regularly colonizes the human nasopharynx, with no negative impact on its host, that is also capable of causing lethal invasive infections. The most effective way to protect individuals against invasive meningococcal infections is through immunization. Vaccine programs that target both invasive infections and nasal colonization have been most effective at reducing prevalence of infection, because prevention of nasal colonization limits the spread of the bacteria within a population. Unfortunately, there is no universal vaccine available to prevent all forms of meningococcal infections, and not all vaccines that have been developed are capable of preventing nasal colonization. The immune processes that confer protection from colonization are not characterized, making it difficult to target nasal colonization during vaccine development. My project makes use of a mouse model of nasal colonization by Neisseria meningitidis and attempts to characterize immune processes that govern nasal colonization. Using a combination of immunodeficient mice and antibody mediated depletion of target cells, I aim to establish what immune cells are needed to prevent nasal colonization. My studies thus far have identified an essential role for neutrophils in mucosal protection against Neisseria meningitidis, suggesting that a vaccine capable of eliciting neutrophil recruitment to the site of infection may be advantageous. Moving forward, my studies aim to characterize the role of B cells and T cells in mucosal immunity against Neisseria meninigitidis, as well as characterize the mechanism through which neutrophils are clearing the bacterial infection.
