column36: Longitudinal implications of adverse childhood experiences on cardiovascular health and function, inflammation, and cardiovascular reactivity to postural stress
column37: Childhood cardiovascular (CV) health is a key factor that influences risk of adult CV disease. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), a term encompassing abuse, severe household dysfunction, and other toxic childhood events, are shown to contribute towards increased health risks such as adult CV disease. Once perceived as rare occurrences and their overall effect minimal, recent studies have reported Canadian prevalence estimates of childhood abuse at 32%. As CV disease is a leading cause of death in Canada, the potential implications of ACEs are more significant than initially believed, yet how ACEs amplify the risk for CV disease later in life remains unclear. Researchers hypothesize ACEs "get under the skin" and alter neuro-immune pathways which further stress the CV system and contribute towards adverse responses to stress. In fact, there is evidence of altered acute stress responses in individuals with ACEs for both psychosocial and mild postural stress although the latter is unexplored in young adults. The link between postural stress and ACEs is also evident in late life and older adults with greater early life stress reported fainting more often, suggesting a link between CV regulatory processes and ACEs. I propose to conduct a longitudinal study investigating the effects of ACEs on changes in CV health in a sample of ~550 young adults whom completed CV testing in our lab 10 years prior as children. Additionally, I will implement a postural challenge designed to detect altered CV response in these young adults. I anticipate ACEs will be associated with increased inflammation, arterial stiffening, and decreases in cardiac function over time. Moreover, that individuals with ACEs will demonstrate a blunted CV response to postural stress. Results of my studies will help explain why ACEs amplify CV disease risk and the pathways involved.

column36: Etude de la contribution de la kinase WNK1 a la guerison des plaies corneennes in vitro et in vivo
column37: La cornee est une structure transparente qui forme la couche externe de l'oeil. Sa localisation anatomique superficielle la rend particulierement vulnerable aux forces abrasives et aux traumatismes. Ces dommages peuvent mener a des deficiences visuelles importantes, telles que la perte de la vision. A la suite d'une lesion, differents mecanismes sont enclenches afin de permettre aux cellules de restaurer la surface corneenne lesee et de reorganiser les cellules des couches sous-jacentes. Une meilleure comprehension de ces mecanismes pourrait permettre d'ameliorer les traitements existants, qui, pour la plupart, ne permettent pas une guerison rapide et adequate de la cornee et ne previennent pas contre les recidives. Au laboratoire, nous utilisons un modele de cornees humaines reconstruites par genie tissulaire (hCRs) afin d'etudier les mecanismes impliques dans la guerison des plaies corneennes. Des travaux anterieurs realises en utilisant ce modele ont demontre que l'expression de certains genes et l'activite de certaines proteines etaient differentiellement regulees durant la guerison des plaies corneennes. C'est le cas de WNK1, qui est en fait la proteine la plus fortement activee durant la guerison des plaies corneennes. En raison de son statut d'activation particulierement eleve, nous soulevons l'hypothese que WNK1 joue un role important durant le processus de guerison des plaies corneennes. Nos objectifs de recherche sont donc d'etudier la contribution de WNK1 a la guerison des plaies corneennes en utilisant des modeles in vitro (hCRs et modele en culture monocouche) et in vivo chez le lapin. Les resultats de ce projet permettront d'ameliorer nos connaissances sur les mecanismes cellulaires et moleculaires impliques dans la guerison des plaies corneennes et pourraient aussi mener a des progres cliniques dans le domaine des lesions corneennes grace a l'identification de nouvelles cibles therapeutiques.

column36: B-cells regulate blood pressure through vasopressin receptor 2.
column37: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a very common risk factor for cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of mortality worldwide. As such, studies into regulators of blood pressure are of the utmost importance. Multiple complex systems (cardiovascular, neuroendocrine, kidney, and immune) are known to regulate blood pressure; however, the role of a specific immune cell, the B-cell, is poorly understood. We have recently found that genetically-engineered mice that have either zero or a small number of B-cells have lower blood pressure. After investigations into the other systems, we examined the kidney and vasopressin receptor 2, which is a receptor required for normal salt- and water handling by the kidney. Both mice had reductions in vasopressin receptor 2, and consequently, increased salt- and water-loss by the kidney. Importantly, increased salt- and water-loss accounts for the low blood pressure of these mice. Together, these data suggest that B-cells can regulate vasopressin receptor 2, which affects determinants of blood pressure (i.e. salt and water). We now propose experiments to confirm the importance of B-cells in blood pressure regulation, to show the importance of vasopressin receptor 2 in blood pressure regulation, and to determine how B-cells directly (or indirectly) affect vasopressin receptor 2. The proposed studies are logical extensions of our work to-date, have important implications for cardiovascular health and disease, and could lead to an 'immunotherapy' approach for hypertension.

column37: L'enzyme "mitogen-activated protein kinase " (MAPK) p38 est connue depuis plus de 15 ans comme etant necessaire au maintien des fonctions normales du coeur tout en contribuant paradoxalement au developpement de pathologies cardiaques. En debut d'etudes graduees, j'ai identifie par une approche novatrice la "serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3 " (SRSF3) parmi les proteines interagissant avec la MAPK p38 active. column37: Antibiotics and other antimicrobial agents are central for the treatment of microbial infections. However, the indiscriminate use of these agents has led to the development of high rates of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in various microorganisms, rendering many drugs useless. Recently, 'metagenomics', or techniques that can profile microbes as a community, rather than as a single species, are emerging as a powerful tool for AMR surveillance and public health risk assessment that dramatically increases the speed of diagnosis and epidemiological investigations. Although advances have been made in AMR research, current methods are still limited and cannot be used by public health due to the lack of understanding of AMR genes that have the ability to spread between pathogens and harmless bacteria. Furthermore, better tools are needed for rapid AMR predictions from metagenomics data. To address this, I will conduct a comprehensive analysis of AMR gene mobility in the context of different antimicrobial properties, e.g. drug classes. I will also contribute to the development of an AMR metagenomics predictor, as part of a nationwide effort, and apply it to study temporal and spatial AMR gene prevalence in freshwater microbiomes impacted by agriculture/urbanization. Taken together, my research aims to significantly strengthen the effectiveness of public health AMR risk assessment, improving the ability of the public health system to monitor and respond to AMR and infectious disease outbreak threats.

column37: The vast expansion of DNA data now enables large-scale comparisons of thousands of bacterial genomes to elucidate the distinction in gene/protein composition between pathogens (disease-causing microbes) and non-pathogens. The remaining majority are hypothetical proteins, with no validated existence or function, of which some are present in multiple bacterial genera/families. The subset of uncharacterized proteins found only in disease-causing bacteria in multiple families, but not in bacteria thought not to cause disease in these same families, are of particular interest and provide an underexplored avenue to study the mechanism of infections of important pathogens, leading to potential new anti-virulence therapies. I will develop a more sophisticated computational approach to identify and then functionally characterize hypothetical proteins found exclusively in pathogens that are not found in closely related non-pathogens. I will characterize them in datasets of microbes associated with disease outbreaks data and evaluate their mutation rates to identify those that are being selected for. Finally, I will validate the functional predictions of the proteins through laboratory testing in an infection model. The outcome of my work will provide insight into the functional importance of previously undefined proteins, potentially identifying their potential roles in the mechanisms of infection. The research output will potentially generate novel anti-infective drug target candidates and protein markers for tracking infectious disease transmission, offering novel insights into disease pathogenesis.

column36: Evaluation of Dynamic Axis Optimization for Ablative Radiotherapy
column37: Radiation dose reduction to healthy tissue is a primary objective when treating cancerous disease. Conventional radiotherapy is delivered using a medical linear accelerator (LINAC) that rotates 360 degrees around a patient laying stationary on a treatment couch. The couch can translate and rotate for initial alignment, however literature has shown that rotating it dynamically during treatment offered geometries where greater sparing of healthy brain tissue was possible. The goal of this research is to build on the dynamic algorithm that currently exists for brain treatments, to make it applicable to any site in the body. The main limitation when treating other anatomies with this technique is due to changing "collision zones". A collision zone is defined as a location in the treatment room where the LINAC gantry and couch would physically collide, halting treatment. Treatments to patient extremities (head, feet, or hands) have less collision zones, compared to centralized anatomies. To decrease the collision zones in a centralized treatment (e.g. - breast), the couch could also be dynamically translated laterally and vertically. If this movement is accounted for in the current algorithm, better sparing of healthy tissues (e.g. - heart, for breast treatments) could be realized. These new patient specific collision zones will be tested using human-like phantoms. Phantoms will have radiation sensitive detectors embedded within so new treatments can be delivered in a research setting to compare with the current standard. Successful implementation of this research will allow for widespread adoption of dynamic techniques, by addressing critical needs in the field to reduce dose to healthy tissues and improve long-term patient quality of life. Furthermore, this technique aims to promote dose reductions without requiring completely new radiotherapy infrastructures, and could serve as a foundation for fully automated treatment planning.

column36: Investigating the effect of subclinical stroke in the TgF344-AD rat model of Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Stroke and dementia are two of the leading causes of death in Canada, affecting more than 1.5 million people and costing over 13 billion dollars annually. As the prevalence, for both diseases, increases with age and with more elderly versus younger Canadians, the percentage of the population effected is expected to increase. Although two distinctly different diseases, stroke affects blood vessels and dementia is degeneration of neurons, stroke survivors are twice as likely to develop dementia compared to healthy individuals. Studies suggests that after stroke, changes to brain blood vessels play a crucial role in initiating and/or contributing to dementia, and in particular Alzheimer's disease. As silent strokes do not exhibit recognizable symptoms, patients are usually unaware of the occurrence. It is estimated that 31% of adults over the age of 65 have had at least 1 silent stroke. Moreover, as the age of prominence for silent strokes overlaps with the 10-15 year presymptomatic period where Alzheimer's disease develops, there lies a significant importance for investigating the interaction between these two diseases. The first objective of my study is to examine behavioral changes in rats that have received a stroke and subsequently exhibit Alzheimer's disease. Behavioral tests conducted before stroke, after stroke recovery, and after Alzheimer's disease development will allow for analysis of severity and time-dependent memory, locomotion and activities of daily living deficits. The second objective is to examine common pathways involved in the progression of dementia in the brain. By examining plaque levels, the activation of protective brain cells and vessel-related changes from the rat brain tissue, this will allow me to determine the effective impact of silent strokes on dementia progression. Overall, the results of this study will help to provide conclusive evidence on the effects and impact of silent strokes on the development of Alzheimer's disease.

column36: A Randomized Pilot Trial of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) and Multi-Modal Aphasia Treatment (M-MAT) to Improve Post-Stroke Non-Fluent Aphasia
column37: A stroke harms the brain by a disruption in blood flow, either by a clot blocking an artery or a bleed because of a broken blood vessel. When a stroke occurs on the left side of the brain, it can cause something called aphasia. Aphasia is the inability to communicate and happens in about one third of all cases of stroke. Speech Therapists work with persons with aphasia to improve communication after stroke. Unfortunately, the therapy is often unsuccessful, and the patient is left with lifelong problems with communication. The left side of the brain contains the center for language production - Broca's area. When someone suffers a stroke in the left side of the brain, the brain attempts to recruit areas of the brain on the right side to produce speech. However, this does not work very well. Therefore, it is believed that recovery of speech after stroke is requires restoration of function in and around Broca's area. The primary objective of this project is to help people with aphasia after stroke. We want to understand whether a new treatment that uses a magnet placed over the head to alter electrical activity in the brain will help the brain to rewire itself and thus improve aphasia. This technique is called repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS). We also want to understand factors in the brain that may predict improvements in language following therapy. This will help us to understand why rTMS works and predict who will and who will not respond to this therapy.

column36: Maladaptive Network Remodeling Underlying Motor Compensation Following a Focal Cortical Stroke
column37: Stroke is a cerebrovascular disease in which perturbed blood flow to the brain results in the death of brain tissue. Although stroke is often lethal, survivors are usually left with some form of residual disability. Despite concerted efforts to optimize rehabilitation programs, stroke remains the primary cause of adult long-term disability. To cope with deficits, patients develop compensatory strategies to complete daily motor tasks. For instance, patients with one-sided injuries become reliant on the unimpaired side and cease using their impaired side for daily activities. Strikingly, reliance on the unimpaired limb triggers neuronal remodeling processes in associated cortical regions of the brain, and evidence suggests that this hinders recovery of the impaired limb. Because of its clear implication in determining recovery outcomes, a more complete understanding of post-stroke neural network remodeling is necessary. Here, we propose to use a rodent model of stroke to study network remodeling in the cerebral cortex associated with the unimpaired limb. We will monitor stroke-induced changes in activity of cortical neurons during a complex motor task (i.e. reaching for food). We will then characterize, at the cellular level, how stroke alters neuronal excitability and long-range connectivity with other brain regions. We hypothesize that stroke will alter activity levels of networks associated with the unimpaired limb. We believe that neurons will then respond by tuning their excitability levels, which will alter the dynamic properties of their networks, and that this will contribute to a compensatory reliance on the unimpaired limb. Beyond current efforts to improve stroke survival rates and optimize rehabilitation protocols, a better understanding of neural network remodeling after stroke will enable development of novel, innovative strategies to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Reducing Type 2 Diabetes Through a Youth-Led Vision of Community Wellness
column37: Background The project I am proposing is ancillary to a community-controlled health promotion recognized best practice called the Kahnawake Schools Diabetes Prevention Project (KSDPP) Community Mobilization Training (CMT). Through the CMT process, community members collaborate with one another and/or people from outside the community to move the community toward positive change. To date, few youth have been involved in the CMT, yet it has been widely documented that youth are essential partners in community mobilization, and that community mobilization can provide developmental opportunities for the youth. Purpose My doctoral research aims to 1) gain a better understanding of Indigenous youth's conceptualization of health and wellness in their community, 2) to facilitate positive youth development opportunities through youth-led participatory evaluation and advocacy, and 3) to increase uptake of the larger KSDPP CMT project within the community of Tyendinaga by involving the youth in the process of community mobilization. Methods The three studies done within this project will follow a rubric for participatory practice outlined by (Ledwith & Springett, 2010) which includes three interlinked components of storytelling, respectful dialogue, and reflexivity. Research design, methods, analysis and dissemination of the storytelling, and dialogue components will rely heavily on consultation with the youth at Quinte Mohawk School. Data Analysis In order to ensure positive and accurate representation of the youth's stories, the youth will be engaged as full partners in the research process, including data analysis.

column36: A persisting presence: Using natural language processing methods to identify previously uncaptured and mild cases of pertussis in the Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database (EMRALD) to assess how waning immunity from the acellular vaccine contributes to the existence of mild cases in Ontario and to understand the role of these cases in sustaining community disease transmission
column37: Pertussis (whooping cough) is a serious health concern that can lead to death, particularly in infants. Pertussis is preventable through vaccination, but in recent years the number of cases has been increasing. The estimated number of pertussis cases worldwide in 2014 was 24.1 million with 160, 700 deaths. In Canada, a large-scale outbreak of pertussis last occurred in 2015, with 700 cases reported in Ontario alone. However, the number of actual cases is suspected to be much higher than the reported number. A recent study estimated that up to 98% of pertussis cases go unreported in Ontario. It is essential to have correct counts of pertussis cases to guide vaccination policy and programmes. Of particular concern are mild cases of pertussis which do not have typical symptoms and as a result are difficult to correctly diagnose. It is believed that these cases may be sustaining the spread of disease in communities as they remain undetected and able to transmit infection to other people. The existence of milder cases could be due to using the acellular pertussis vaccine, which has been demonstrated to become ineffective faster than the whole-cell vaccine. It is of great importance to public health to correctly estimate the number of pertussis cases in Ontario, including mild cases. This study aims to apply artificial intelligence methods to electronic medical record and health administrative data to accomplish this goal. Additionally, statistical analyses will be used to identify reasons for the existence of mild cases, such as acellular vaccine use, and determine their role in transmitting disease. Such information will support public health agencies in making necessary changes to vaccination programmes by identifying key populations to target with boosters or whole-cell vaccines. This would greatly assist in reducing the number of pertussis cases and deaths in Ontario and could be used more broadly to set an example for vaccination policy elsewhere in Canada.

column36: Are cognitive deficits in Parkinson's disease associated with dopaminergic dysfunction
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is typically known for its motor symptoms, however progressive cognitive decline is a common complication of the disease, with over 60% of PD patients impaired in one or more cognitive domains. Cognitive decline contributes to significant impairments, resulting in a poorer quality of life and higher levels of care dependency. Despite its significance, the neural basis cognitive decline in PD is poorly understood. PD motor progression has been well characterized by the loss of the neurotransmitter dopamine in the brain due to the death of dopamine-producing cells in the brain. New research suggests the loss of dopamine may also play a role in the cognitive decline of PD as well. A better understanding of the neural mechanisms involved in PD cognitive decline is an important prerequisite for improved therapeutic strategies. The proposed study will look at how dopamine regulation is affected in PD patients both with and without cognitive decline. Using a neuroimaging technique called positron emission tomography (PET), we will visualize the dopamine receptors in the brains of PD patients in vivo using a radiotracer that binds preferentially to one common type of dopamine receptor called the D2 receptor. Whole-brain network dysfunction of this dopamine receptor may have a role in cognitive decline and we will use graph theory analysis to investigate in vivo D2 communication patterns in the brains of PD patients. Uncovering the pathological mechanisms involved in PD cognitive decline can have many benefits, such as 1) finding an early indicator of cognitive decline 2) discovering new treatment options for present PD patients and 3) possible new development of future preventative measures to slow the progression into PD dementia. Additionally, validation of this approach will allow for the use of network analysis tools for a wider range of neurotransmitters to measure dysfunctional brain activation patterns in other neurotransmitter systems.

column36: Molecular control of genome architecture
column37: Genome organization within the nucleus is crucial for cell viability and gene expression. Proteins that control nuclear organization have been identified, but this process has not been well characterized so far. Importantly, nuclear organization has been shown to be disrupted in diseases classified as laminopathies, as well as in some neurodegenerative diseases. We hypothesize that Lamin A is one of the key players responsible for maintaining nuclear organization and normal cell function. Our goal is to characterize the molecular mechanism through which Lamin A interacts with DNA, by defining the domains within Lamin A that are sufficient for this effect. We also want to use next generation sequencing methods to determine the effects of Lamin A on genome organization, as well the changes in gene expression. For these purposes, we have developed an assay for specifically isolating the effects of Lamin A on the genome. We propose to take advantage of the unique architecture of mouse rod photoreceptor nuclei. Rods are devoid of any other tethering proteins, allowing a very clean read-out of Lamin A activity. We expect to characterize new determinants of chromatin organization and disentangle their roles in higher order chromatin organization and gene expression, which is vital for finding a solution for the treatment of some of the most deadly neurodegenerative disorders and syndromes, as well as ageing. We expect to find a critical region of Lamin A that is important in reorganizing the genome and with this knowledge we will contribute to finding a cure for laminopathic and neurodegenerative diseases connected with chromatin disorganization.

column36: Support services To Empower Parenting Skills (Baby STEPS): An innovative rehabilitation approach to respond the needs of parents with disabilities and their babies
column37: Infant parenting is an important role that encompasses pressing physical and cognitive demands to ensure constant safety and care. When a parent has physical and cognitive disabilities following traumatic injuries, congenital or degenerative disorders, the challenges associated with parenting are even more important. Despite the increasing number of parents with disabilities, the needs regarding infant parenting have to date received scarce attention in research. A comprehensive understanding of those families' needs is crucial to offer prompt and personalized support aiming to foster their social participation along with their baby's safety and optimal development. In collaboration with a pioneer Canadian clinic offering parenting rehabilitation services, this novel clinical-research project aims to explore the unmet needs of these individuals. To do so, the state of knowledge regarding infant parenting with disabilities will be examined using a scoping review, along with a grey literature review to examine the current resources and rehabilitation services available for this clientele. At the core of this project, interviews with parents with physical and cognitive disabilities and in-home assessments of their everyday parenting tasks will be conducted to fully grasp their needs. Additional interviews with significant family members and expert health care professionals will complete the identification of priority needs for safe parenting. Finally, focus groups will be held with parents with disabilities, clinicians, national and international researchers, community organizations and policy makers to collectively problem solve how to best respond to the reported family needs. Such work will provide needed knowledge to better understand the needs for autonomous, meaningful and safe parenting.

column36: Mechanisms of dysfunctional labour associated with steroid and prostanoid signalling
column37: Labour is the process leading to childbirth, and its initiation, progression, and completion are not fully understood in humans. There are a number of molecules that have been implicated in initiating and maintaining labour, and the proper levels of these molecules are necessary for labour to proceed correctly. Additionally, certain drugs such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including ibuprofen, can disrupt these important signalling molecules. As labour is a very complex process, several problems can occur and require the need for medical interventions. In addition to the use of NSAIDs, there are certain situations in which pregnancy and labour complications are known to be higher. The use of assisted reproduction technologies (ART) and pregnancies in which an enzyme involved in hormone elimination is lacking have a higher risk of labour complications. We aim to use these models to investigate and increase our understanding of the process of labour in humans. My research will be carried out using human tissues which come from pregnancies that used ART to conceive and those that conceived naturally. First, we plan to screen these tissues for NSAIDs, and compare this to the levels of signalling molecules involved in labour and the outcomes experienced by these women. Next, we aim to measure the levels of hormones and signalling molecules present in these tissues and determine the differences between pregnancies which utilized ART and those who did not. Because we have access to medical information documenting complications in pregnancy and labour, we can combine this with our results to determine any associations with pregnancy outcome. Overall, these studies will deepen our understanding of the labour process, including how assisted reproduction and hormone imbalance, as well as external factors such as drugs can contribute to labour complications, potentially revealing insight on how these complications can be avoided.

column36: Neural and Psychological Markers of Dysregulated Emotion and Treatment Response in Children with Disruptive Behaviours
column37: Childhood Disruptive Behaviour Disorders (DBD) have onset early in development and are a robust predictor of chronic and severe mental illness in adolescence and adulthood. Although high prevalence, referral-rates, and negative outcomes signal great need, current treatment approaches are inadequate, with recent data estimating that approximately 25 - 40% of children continue to experience clinically significant symptoms and behavioral and emotional dysregulation following treatment completion. Emerging research suggests that heterogeneity (i.e., diversity) in the factors that contribute to a child's DBD, including their neurobiology and clinical dimensions such as emotion dysregulation, are important factors that may influence treatment effectiveness. Novel approaches that distill heterogeneity are necessary to improve treatment precision and outcomes. My proposed doctoral dissertation consists of three studies with the overall objective of identifying biomarkers of emotion dysregulation in children with DBD to inform novel targets for intervention. These studies include, 1) a systematic review to identify and classify neural correlates of emotion dysregulation in children with DBD. 2) Analysing existing data from an ongoing neuroimaging study to identify biomarkers (i.e., brain structure) of emotion dysregulation in children with DBD. 3) A randomized and controlled micro-trial (RCT) to test whether treatment non-responders benefit from a brief intervention that targets their emotion regulation and distress tolerance skills. These studies will pave the way for novel assessment practices and treatment innovation by bridging and integrating biological, psychological, and clinical perspectives.

column36: Caracterisation des variables nutritionnelles et hormonales durant la grossesse: associations avec le profil metabolique.
column37: Problematique : La grossesse est caracterisee par des variations hormonales qui entrainent, des le 1er trimestre, de nombreux changements chez la mere. La litterature demeure cependant pauvre et incoherente quant aux variations dans les facteurs alimentaires et hormonaux tout au long de la grossesse et quant a leur impact sur la sante de la mere et celle de son enfant. Objectifs : Caracteriser et etudier les liens, a chaque trimestre, entre les variables alimentaires, hormonales et metaboliques durant la grossesse. Methodologie : A chaque trimestre, les apports alimentaires de 106 femmes enceintes seront evalues via 3 rappels de 24h Web. L'epaisseur des tissus adipeux sera mesuree par echographie au 1er trimestre, tandis que les hormones de regulation de la prise alimentaire seront mesures, a chaque trimestre, a la suite d'un repas-test effectue chez 20 des 106 participantes. Des marqueurs metaboliques tels que le gain de poids, la glycemie a jeun, le marqueur inflammatoire interleukine-6 et le statut en vitamine D seront aussi mesures et mis en association avec les variables alimentaires et hormonales. Impact potentiel : Les femmes enceintes representent une sous population vulnerable pour qui l'alimentation a un impact considerable. De plus, un nombre grandissant de femmes debutent aujourd'hui leur grossesse avec un surpoids, suggerant des habitudes alimentaires inadequates et augmentant leur risque de complications perinatales, tel que la preeclampsie et le diabete gestationnel. L'analyse des spheres nutritionnelle, hormonale et metabolique entrainera une meilleure comprehension des determinants de la sante durant la periode perinatale, ce qui contribuera a l'amelioration de la prise en charge des femmes a risque de complications. L'avancement des connaissances dans ce domaine precis servira egalement de base pour des etudes d'intervention visant a optimiser la sante des femmes enceintes et des generations futures.

column36: Self-Compassion among people undergoing cardiac surgery: associations with physical activity, other health behaviors and health outcomes.
column37: Heart surgeries are being performed on people who are not engaging in enough health behaviours (HBs; physical activity); low engagement increases the risk of poor health outcomes after surgery. People with cardiovascular disease (CVD) may not engage in enough HBs because they face barriers (e.g., fear of exercise). Self-regulation, a form of behavioral control, is important for behavior change because it helps find solutions to barriers. Self-regulation of HBs is hard for people who have had heart surgery because they must self-regulate while dealing with the barriers of living with CVD. These negative emotional experiences can negatively affect an individuals' ability to self-regulate HBs. Self-compassion (SC), extending support to oneself in difficult times, may help people self-regulate their HBs after heart surgery. No research has examined SC in the context of CVD. I will determine whether SC relates to HB engagement and health outcomes after surgery, negatively relates to negative emotions, and if people are open to SC while recovering from heart surgery. This information may help researchers develop interventions to reduce the number of complications that occur after surgery. I plan to take a two-study approach; the first study will follow participants before heart surgery to a year after surgery and the second study will involve interviewing a sub-sample of participants through the recovery period. Participants will be asked to provide information on HB participation, health outcomes, negative emotions, and their ability to manage their health goals. Twenty participants will be asked to participate in the interview process to explore their openness to SC. This will be the first study to look at SC in the context of CVD. column36: The Clinical Utility of Genomic Sequencing in Hereditary Cancer Syndrome Care: A Prospective, Mixed-Methods Cohort Study
column37: Genetic tests are used to identify patients who have inherited diseases. For patients who are diagnosed with cancer, genetic testing can be used to see if they have an inherited genetic mutation that caused their cancer. Patients with inherited cancer mutations have a hereditary cancer syndrome and have a high risk to develop more cancers over their lifetime. Once they are found to have a hereditary cancer syndrome from genetic testing, doctors will place patients in advanced cancer screening programs and refer to them to specialists to help reduce their risk to develop cancer or detect it earlier. Although genetic testing for cancer patients has advanced in recent years, it is still only able to look at a few genes at a time. Because of this, most patients who have testing to determine if they have a hereditary cancer syndrome receive a negative result, meaning that no genetic mutation was found. These patients are not eligible for advanced screening programs and do not benefit from genetic testing. However, a new genetic test called genomic sequencing may help to change this. Unlike other genetic tests, genomic sequencing can analyze all of the genes in the human body . Therefore, it is more likely than current genetic tests to find a mutation in patients who have a hereditary cancer syndrome. This means that more patients will become eligible for cancer screening and other procedures to reduce their risk. However, genomic sequencing is a new test, and so information on its benefits for patients is limited. This study will aim to evaluate the benefits of genomic sequencing for cancer patients by determining the number of patients who are found to have a cancer mutation and the number of patients who have changes in their cancer screening and management. Our study will give important information to doctors who may wish to use this test if it is shown to improve patient care.

column36: Interpretable Deep Learning to Unlock the Potential of Clinical RNA Sequencing for Precision Oncology Research
column37: When a patient fails standard cancer therapy, the oncologist is faced with the conundrum of selecting one of dozens of treatments. Present clinical trials are investigating whether DNA sequencing of tumors can inform the choice of treatment, but for 50+% of patients, none of the mutations found provide information predictive of treatment response. What could supply greater predictive value is gene expression profiling, which gives insights into which processes are active inside a given cell type. For cancer cells grown in a petri dish, the additional information of gene expression has been shown to be more informative than only DNA sequencing for predicting drug response. We want to translate these positive results into the clinic, to help patients for which DNA sequencing cannot inform the optimal treatment. In this project, we will use advances in Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence to build a computer system helping oncologists interpret this gene expression data. Using 50,000 human expression profiles, we will teach the system to map gene expression onto measures of biological pathways and processes activity. we will then focus on 13 drugs tested in a pan-Canadian clinical trial, building human-interpretable models to predict response to these drugs from my pathway measures. Looking retrospectively at patient data, we will validate the prediction accuracy of our models. Finally, for validated models, we will automate the system to make predictions for future patients. Outcomes of this study include: 1) buildings models that select patients who will respond to these 13 drugs, 2) strengthening the rationale for transcriptomic profiling to help guide cancer treatment, and 3) proof-of-concept for intelligent computer systems that can guide cancer care.

column36: A Preoperative Virtual Reality Simulation of Surgery to Reduce Perioperative Psychiatric Sequelae
column37: Mental health difficulties such as anxiety and distress are commonly experienced before and after surgery. For some, surgery may be traumatic and can cause symptoms of posttraumatic stress. Given that elective surgeries are scheduled in advanced, this provides a unique opportunity for preventative interventions to target poor mental health outcomes. The primary objective of this research is to scientifically evaluate the effectiveness of a virtual reality (VR) simulation prior to surgery on mental health outcomes. This simulation is informed by the military literature on pre-deployment interventions, and will mirror the pre-surgical experience for patients, from arrival at the hospital up until anesthetic induction in the operating room. A series of two study methodologies will evaluate the primary objective of this research: (1) a randomized controlled trial will assess whether a novel VR pre-surgical simulation of surgery, compared to treatment as usual, can help reduce mental health difficulties throughout the surgical period and (2) qualitative interviews will examine a subset of participants' perceptions of this intervention and the impact it had on their experience throughout the surgical period. I hypothesize that individuals who participate in the VR simulation of surgery will experience fewer mental health difficulties before and after surgery compared to individuals who do not participate in the intervention. This research will help health providers understand whether and how a pre-surgical VR simulation of surgery is effective in reducing mental health difficulties throughout the surgical period. If results support the effectiveness of this intervention, this research will inform future larger replication studies and studies evaluating whether this intervention can also improve physical health outcomes throughout the surgical period. Ultimately, results of this research may inform changes to standard of care throughout the surgical period.

column37: Since the initiation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, there has been increasing demand for culturally-rooted interventions to support the wellness of Indigenous people. The context of colonialism in Canada has serious implications for the well-being of Indigenous people. To address the source of illness, including social determinants of health such as colonization, this study will use a decolonizing, community-based approach in both the implementation of a decolonizing arts-based intervention for Indigenous families and the study of that intervention. An Indigenous approach will be considered throughout the research process to support the centring of Indigenous voices in research. The intervention will be facilitated by Indigenous leaders in the community deemed suitable by community Elders. The intervention will incorporate traditional cultural engagement such as artistic expression and the process of creating, as this has shown to be a positive determinant of health that improves wellness for many Indigenous people. In this study, the purpose is to gain an understanding of Indigenous families, Elders, and community artists' experiences and impressions of the intervention as it relates to physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual well-being. For this purpose, an Indigenous storywork method will be used to analyze research conversations and talking circles facilitated with the Elders, artists, and families who take part in the intervention. The findings of this study have practical implications for the integration of art in illness prevention and intervention to improve Indigenous peoples' health and wellness.

column36: Vulnerability of GLUT4 Translocation During Insulin Resistance: A Focus on Rab GTPases
column37: Glucose (sugar) is the main source of fuel for most tissues in the body. After a meal, dietary glucose enters the blood stream and causes glucose levels to rise. The pancreas senses this increase in blood glucose and dispatches insulin into the circulation to instruct the skeletal muscle to extract glucose from the blood. In healthy muscle cells, insulin binds to the insulin receptor and tells the muscle to put more glucose transporters (GLUT4) on the surface of each cell. This increase in glucose transporters allows more glucose to enter the muscle, where it is stored and eventually used for energy. This process of increasing surface GLUT4 transporters is called GLUT4 translocation and involves a complex network of signalling events. During Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), the skeletal muscle does not respond to insulin (called insulin resistance) and fails to increase surface GLUT4 levels, causing chronic hyperglycemia (high blood sugar). Yet, our knowledge of how and why GLUT4 translocation fails during insulin resistance is unknown. The major goal of this research is to identify and study, at the molecular level, which elements of GLUT4 translocation dysfunction during insulin resistance and thereby contribute to impaired skeletal muscle glucose disposal. Identifying these mechanisms could generate unique avenues for therapeutic intervention targeting the muscle in T2D.

column37: Le cancer de la prostate touche environ 21 300 hommes au Canada par annee, il est le troisieme plus mortel des cancers. Ce serait une precieuse aide pour predire quels patients sont predisposes a recidiver. column36: Discovering novel antimicrobials against intracellular pathogens
column37: There is an urgent need to identify new treatments for multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. The continuous evolution of resistance has rendered many of our frequently prescribed and last-resort antibiotics ineffective, yet very little progress has been made to identify suitable alternatives. Overcoming this global health crisis will require remarkable innovation in antibiotic discovery, to search for drugs that kill bacteria in unique ways. To meet this demand, I propose to screen for small molecules that selectively target and inhibit intracellular bacteria such as Salmonella Typhimurium. Traditional antibiotic discovery efforts have not focused on intracellular pathogens, which reside within host cells during infection and are therefore difficult to eradicate. Our lab has previously established a platform in which to measure antimicrobial activity in the intracellular environment. We now aim to apply this technique to identify new leads for antibiotics that target a highly invasive, multidrug-resistant strain of Salmonella (ST313). ST313 is a distinct, human-adapted lineage of Salmonella, and is capable of causing life-threatening systemic disease. In my proposed research project, I aim to (1) characterize the genetic requirements for intracellular growth of ST313 using RNA-sequencing, (2) identify novel compounds with antibacterial activity against ST313 grown in human macrophages, and (3) determine the mechanism of action of any lead antimicrobial compounds and test for their activity in an animal model of Salmonella infection. This proposed research will help us to unravel the genetic basis of bacterial survival within host cells, while also identifying new treatment alternatives for complicated and recurrent intracellular infections.

column36: Targeting the DNA Replication Stress Response in Pancreatic Cancer
column37: Pancreatic cancer is among the highest mortality cancers in Canada, with a prognosis that has remained unchanged for many decades. This is in part due to the inadequacy of reliable methods for early detection of the cancer, but more notably due to the lack of effective treatment against advanced stage disease. Gemcitabine is currently the leading treatment for patients with pancreatic cancer and functions by targeting the critical process of DNA replication in cancer cells, resulting in cell death. However, resistance to gemcitabine treatments is either naturally present within cells or rapidly acquired in cells that were initially sensitive, with little improvement found in current gemcitabine combination therapies. Hence, to develop effective combination treatments, it is critical to identify which cellular factors are responsible for modulating gemcitabine sensitivity in pancreatic cancer cells. With recent advances in genetic screening technology, we are now able to see the individual effects of deleting each gene from the human genome, a task that was unachievable before. In my project, I have taken advantage of this technology to identify the full complement of genes that, when deleted, increase sensitivity or resistance to gemcitabine in different pancreatic cancer cell lines. I am now focusing on determining the cellular mechanisms by which some of these genes modulate gemcitabine sensitivity. My work will provide the first exhaustive list of genes that modulate gemcitabine response in pancreatic cancer cells, as well as great insight into the molecular basis of the sensitivity and resistance of pancreatic cancers to therapy, both of which are essential for the development of new pancreatic cancer treatments.

column36: HEARTSMAP-U: A psychosocial screening and management tool for youth pursuing post-secondary education
column37: In Canada, 74% of youth pursue higher education after high school; this is often the first time young people move away from home and assume adult responsibilities. This experience can cause great financial, academic, and social stress, and can give rise to severe mental health concerns. Post-secondary students are particularly susceptible to persistent mental health issues, such as anxiety, depression, and eating disorders. However, few tools exist to identify these concerns early and connect students with care. As a result, students may not receive support until a crisis situation, when treatment may not be as effective. To address these issues, this research aims to: 1) Engage young people, post-secondary healthcare providers, and mental health experts in developing a screening tool (HEARTSMAP-U) that students can use to determine their mental health needs and seek out appropriate and accessible support. 2) Assess how reliably and accurately students score their mental health status using HEARTSMAP-U compared to healthcare provider assessments. 3) Explore how acceptable the screening tool and its digital format are for students (e.g., is it easy to use and navigate), and how feasible screening is for students and whether it reduces unnecessary health care visits (e.g., are students less likely to go to the emergency department?). Finally, this work will examine whether screening affects students' likelihood of accessing mental health resources and whether it changes how they view their own mental health. In summary, this work will contribute to the development of a reliable and accurate mental health self-assessment tool to identify youth who could benefit from early intervention in post-secondary settings, while improving coordination and access to appropriate mental health care for an under-served population.

column36: The role of NLRP6 in intestinal anti-parasitic responses and colorectal cancer
column37: Every week, dozens of Canadians die from colorectal cancer. While treatments have improved, therapies are limited by an incomplete understanding of cancer development. For example, doctors have long noted a link between parasitic infections and exacerbated colorectal cancer, yet how these infections aggravate cancer is unknown. A key step in the immune response against parasites is their detection by our cells. The protein NLRP6 belongs to a family of proteins whose role is to detect infection. However, what NLRP6 recognizes is unknown. As NRLP6 is abundant in intestinal cells, we asked whether it may play a role in intestinal parasite detection and cancer development. We gave an intestinal parasite to NLRP6 deficient mice predisposed to develop colon cancer. We found that infected NLRP6 deficient animals had worse cancer than infected, normal mice. Moreover, in non-cancerous infected mice, NLRP6 deficient animals had higher levels of a pro-cancerous cell, called tuft cells, that are also involved in immune responses against parasites. We are now trying to understand how NLRP6 acts on tuft cells. Collectively, this work could help explain a decades old parasite-cancer link, while also uncovering novel therapies.

column36: Dissecting the Interaction between AHI-1 SH3 Domain and Dynamin-2 Proline Rich Domain for Potential Therapeutic Strategies
column37: In 2017, there was an average of 17 patients diagnosed with leukemia (blood cancer) every day in Canada. The National Cancer Institute (US) calculated an overall 5-year survival rate of 56% for various blood cancers. This is because most current therapies are short-lived; drug resistance and relapse pose significant clinical problems. Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) can be treated with the Imatinib Mesylate (IM) drug; however, this is not a widespread cure. Life-long treatment is required, with potential long-term side-effects and a high cost. At first, CML cells respond well to the drug, but the treatment loses its effect over a short period. Our lab and others have discovered that this is due to the drug's inability to kill the blood cancer stem cells, which can replenish the pool of blood cancer cells. Therefore, new therapies targeting other critical cancer-causing genes are required to eliminate blood cancer stem cells. IM is used to stop the activity of an unusually active fusion protein in CML called BCR-ABL. Prolonged IM treatment eventually leads to drug resistance and we must find alternative treatment strategies to overcome drug resistance. AHI-1, a key cancer-causing protein that interacts and enhances the effects of BCR-ABL could be a potential target. AHI-1 is abnormally expressed in blood cancer stem cells and is a major player in abnormal blood cancer stem cell activities and resistance in IM treatment. Another protein, Dynamin-2 (DNM2), also contributes to the characteristics of CML. BCR-ABL in the presence of AHI-1 can better activate DNM2 to give blood cancer cells a growth advantage. Experiments will be performed to understand the effects of the interaction between these proteins to uncover a potential therapeutic strategy to overcome drug resistance. Studying the interactions and its effect can help better understand how to overcome the consequences of the interaction, thus improving the success rate of treating drug-resistant leukemia patients.

column36: Microbiota-immune interactions and host defense in sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by an uncontrolled immune reaction against infectious agents spread in the patient's bloodstream and organs. It can emerge from the body's response against very distinct microorganisms, such as bacteria, fungi, viruses and even protozoan parasites. Bacterial sepsis is a major cause of death worldwide, with mortality rates ranging from 30% up to 50%. In the United States of America, severe sepsis most often arises from infections in the respiratory tract (pneumonia), being considered the leading cause of death in non-coronary intensive care units (ICU). In sepsis, many complications arise from the interplay between immune cells, including platelets, which are commonly associated with blood clotting. For instance, the activation of the coagulation system leads to formation of thrombi, which obstruct microvasculature, contributing to organ failure. Paradoxically, patients may also present bleeding due to depletion of coagulation factors. The mechanisms underlying coagulation disorders in the microvasculature are not fully understood. In order to investigate such mechanisms, we intend to use animal models of abdominal sepsis. By taking advantage of groundbreaking research tools, we will be able to investigate the role of specific targets present in platelets during experimental sepsis. In doing so, we hope to shed a light on further development of therapeutic strategies that address the characteristic uncontrolled immune seen in sepsis.

column36: Emotion regulation and treatment-based change in children with neurodevelopmental disorders: A diffusion spectrum imaging tractography study
column37: Between 40 - 70% of children with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) such as autism, ADHD and specific learning disorder experience complex emotional problems. Few accessible treatment options are available and current approaches are limited by their focus on one diagnostic category despite frequent overlap of symptoms across disorders; currently over a third of children with NDDs are non-responsive to cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Emotion regulation - a child's ability to appropriately adapt the intensity of their behaviour - may play a critical role as a moderator of treatment efficacy, modulating symptom expression across a range of emotional difficulties and diagnoses. Additionally, research has identified shared brain-based impairments between groups of children with autism and ADHD, but not OCD, suggesting that these impairments may be common across only the first two disorders. Currently, no research exists using advanced neuroimaging techniques to investigate common neural targets for emotion regulation and treatment-based change in children with NDDs. Further, females are severely underrepresented in clinical pediatric neuroimaging research, limiting the generalizability of current findings. column36: The Initial Development and Validation of the neuroCognitive Bias Scale for Depression
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide. While many factors may contribute to disability, the extant literature suggests that impairments in thinking abilities (e.g., attention, memory, concentration, decision-making, etc.) that are the primary factors leading to impairment in the day to day functioning. Our research has suggested that it is the perception of these impairments that a patient experiences that lead to disability; not the organic, neurological deficit, per se. As such, I have developed a theory that extends Beck's (1979) seminal research in cognition and depression. I posit that patients with depression have a unique perception (i.e., biased thinking) related to their neurocognitive symptoms. As such, my dissertation will seek to validate a novel construct in the depression literature - 'neurocognitive bias'. Neurocognitive bias is defined as the flawed, or distorted thinking style unique to depressed patients that leads to the perception that one has organic, actual neurocognitive deficits. These deficits can, therefore, lead to disability and impairment in the day to day functioning. It is, therefore, necessary to develop a valid and reliable test to measure neurocognitive bias to accurately diagnose these challenges and to identify treatment targets. My dissertation will 1) develop this tool - the neuroCognitive Impairment Bias Scale (CIBS); 2) validate the CIBS in a patient and control sample; and 3) examine how neurocognitive bias can be targeting in a psychological treatment (i.e., cognitive restructuring), and examine how targeting this bias can improve real-world functioning. Validating this construct, and creating an instrument to measure it will equip clinicians and researchers with an empirically derived method to better understand functional impairments related to depression. Further, treatment targets can be identified to plan and promote the successful return to premorbid levels of social and occupational functioning.

column36: Testing the Efficacy of an Online Self-Help Treatment for Alcohol Misuse and Emotional Problems in Young Adult Manitobans: A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
column37: Nearly half of individuals who struggle with alcohol use also experience emotional problems (i.e., depression and anxiety), especially in Manitoba. The combination of these challenges can have devastating consequences such as more severe symptoms of each disorder, disease, and early death. These combined difficulties also place a financial burden on the healthcare system. The highest rates of these problems are seen among young adults, especially those living in Northern and remote communities. This is concerning as there are often barriers to accessing health services in these areas (e.g., stigma, lack of resources, distance). Considering the high co-occurrence between alcohol use and emotional problems, there is a critical need to develop accessible, cost-effective, self-guided treatments in order to reach the thousands of struggling Manitobans. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to examine the benefits of an online, integrated (i.e., treatment for alcohol use and emotional problems together), self-guided program. Currently, for young adults, no intervention like this exists in Canada that targets the full spectrum of negative emotions (i.e., depression and anxiety). A total of 214 young adults experiencing issues with alcohol use and depression and/or anxiety will be recruited through the treatment website. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either an 8-week online intervention (i.e., integrated cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing) or to the control group (i.e., education about mental health). This research stands to provide a user-friendly, cost-effective, and feasible option in order to improve the mental health of young adults struggling in the community.

column36: Monitoring food security with Indigenous Batwa in a changing climate

Climate change is further threatening Indigenous food security by reducing access to traditional foods. As the impacts of climate change are projected to intensify over the coming decades, adaptation efforts that reduce vulnerability of Indigenous food systems to climate change are urgently needed. Community-based monitoring is considered a promising strategy to improve monitoring of, and local adaptation, to environmental change. Yet, its application towards food security, particularly Indigenous food security, is limited. The goal of my research is to better understand the process of community-based monitoring as well as enhance existing monitoring systems for Indigenous Batwa food security under a changing climate. The project builds on expertise and partnerships of a larger food security and climate change research project in Uganda. Overall, my research aims to improve the capacity of Batwa and other community partners in Uganda to adapt food systems to climate change, along with advance tools to monitor Indigenous food security under a changing climate.

column36: Healthy Aging: The effects of Parenthood and APOE Genotype on Cognitive Decline
column37: Parenthood is a dramatic life transformation that has profound effects on the brain however this has mostly been studied in the short term (during pregnancy and postpartum) and in females. In the long term, multiple pregnancies increase risk for conditions like Alzheimer's disease, stroke, cardiovascular disease, and obesity. Females who have had multiple pregnancies are a higher risk of developing dementia, show worse brain pathological symptoms and an earlier onset of Alzheimer's disease. This suggests that fundamental aspects of female physiology and life experiences contribute to the disease. Females that have not had any children show better memory in middle age compared to females that have had children but not all studies agree. Factors such as genes (APOE, a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease) and female specific factors such as age of menopause, sex of the fetus, and hormone therapies can affect cognition. On the other hand, in the short-term, males show changes in hormones and brain structure in response to fatherhood, but long-term changes on brain, disease and cognition have received very little attention. To better understand the effects of parenthood on cognition later in life, it is important to study large populations and take genes and female-specific factors into account. This study will investigate how parenthood and genes (APOE) along with sociological factors (age and education) affect cognition in older females and males using a large Canadian database (The Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging). These findings will advance our understanding of how parenthood influences brain aging and cognitive decline in older females and males. Isolating specific risk factors and incidence trends could have significant impact on future treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. This work will also address important and understudied physiological aspects of aging in females. We expect our findings will eventually lead to improved outcomes for all patients.

column36: An epigenetic "inflammaging" score (EIS) as a tool to quantify healthy aging and predict adverse health outcomes in older adults
column37: As we age, levels of cells and molecules commonly associated with inflammation increase in the body. This phenomenon, coined "inflammaging", is a natural process that occurs in everyone, although for those that are less healthy as they age, inflammaging can be much greater. When inflammaging is greater, so is the likelihood of developing chronic conditions, being hospitalized for an infectious disease, or dying at a relatively young age. Frailty, a complex syndrome that represents one's overall health status, is also associated with inflammaging, and is a major determinant of longevity and well-being. We have developed an innovative measure based on the molecular "hard-wiring" of immune cells called the "epigenetic inflammaging score (EIS)", which not only increases with age, but is associated with one's current and future health. Using the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, we propose to validate the EIS and explore its relationship with important sociodemographic, health and lifestyle factors, as well as the change in frailty over time.

column36: The role of guaranteed income in healthy aging: Canadian public pensions and their association with physical health, mental health, and health risks.
column37: The idea of government-sponsored guaranteed annual income, giving people money with little or no conditions, is popular among health and poverty advocates. We know that health and income are related, with the lowest income individuals experiencing the worst average level of health. However, there is little evidence in Canada that giving people money on a large scale improves their health. One underexplored source of evidence for this relationship is Canadian public pensions. These pensions give a guaranteed annual income of about $18,000 to individuals who satisfy eligibility criteria upon reaching age 65. Using the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging baseline and follow-up data, we will follow individuals over time as they transition onto public pensions. We will apply statistical models to this data to describe how guaranteed income influences physical and mental health outcomes across the income spectrum. We will have a special focus on individuals who can experience a real benefit from a guaranteed annual income, like people who are on social assistance or otherwise at risk of low income prior to age 65. These estimates will be broken out for different identifiable groups and, when appropriate, we will model the change in the distribution of variables rather than changes in the average. This work will provide information to policymakers on the expected benefit of changing the age of eligibility for public pensions, or more broadly, the health impact on different groups in Canada of providing a guaranteed minimum income.

column36: Exploring the obesity paradox - The association between body fat distribution and muscle mass on health in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: In older adults, there is an "obesity paradox" in which people with obesity measured as body mass index (BMI) are more likely to have diseases such as diabetes and heart disease, but less likely to die from the disease compared to individuals with normal BMI values. BMI is known to be a poor measure of obesity, and may be particularly problematic in older adults due to the body composition changes that occur with aging. When obesity is measured using waist circumference, the obesity paradox is no longer observed. Waist circumference measures central obesity which estimates the amount of visceral adipose tissue (VAT). Greater volumes of VAT are associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and mortality. Technology such as dual energy x-ray absorptiometry can provide accurate measures of VAT, as well as subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) and muscle mass. Greater amounts of SAT and muscle mass have been hypothesized to be protective against the harmful effects of VAT, however there is a paucity of research addressing this hypothesis. The objective of this project is to determine, using data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA), the association between VAT, SAT, and muscle mass with health outcomes including incident incidence of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, impaired lung function (normal versus obstructive or restrictive), and all-cause mortality. The potential protective effect of greater amounts of SAT and muscle mass in individuals with varying levels of VAT will be explored. All analyses will be stratified by sex and age to determine if the relationships between these variables and health are different for males and females or with age.

column36: Impact of frailty biomarkers on the accumulation of age-related health deficits
column37: As people grow old, they are more likely to develop health problems. However, not everyone ages in the same way. Some people will be healthier in their later years, while others will develop many health issues. One way to determine a person's overall health is to measure their frailty level. Frailer people are more likely to have worse health outcomes. This means that finding ways to manage or even prevent frailty will be important for the health and well-being of aging Canadians. The problems of frailty begin before noticeable health issues occur. We can learn about frailty by using tests which show how well the body is functioning, known as biomarkers. Biomarkers are commonly used to diagnose health problems. Some single biomarkers work well in this way but may not increase our understanding of frailty. We have developed a method to measure a person's level of frailty by combining individual tests into one biomarker by counting the number of abnormal test results. People with more abnormalities measured with our frailty biomarker are at a greater risk of dying prematurely. However, it is unknown if our frailty biomarker can identify an individual's risk for developing health problems related to older age such as chronic diseases. We want to address this knowledge gap by using information collected from a large study of middle-aged to older Canadians called the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, or CLSA. The CLSA collects people's health, biological, lifestyle, social, and psychological information at multiple times which allow us to follow people's change in frailty. Previous research shows that a person's level of frailty can depend on many reasons, such as social factors and lifestyle behaviors. Therefore, we will identify if these factors relate to a person's risk of developing health problems based on their frailty biomarkers. This study could help delay health problems of old age and to deliver timely care to individuals.

column36: Sleep behaviours and multimorbidity risk in middle-aged and older adults: prospective analyses from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA)
column37: Sleep problems, including short sleep duration and poor sleep quality, represent a significant and neglected public health issue, affecting large numbers of older adults in Canada and worldwide. Poor sleep can negatively impact health. Poor sleep behaviours are associated with problems with daily functioning, poor mental health and quality of life, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. Sleep problems are particularly problematic among middle-aged and older adults, since aging affects how sleep. Sleep problems do not occur randomly across the population-certain subgroups of people may experience more problems than others, including socioeconomically disadvantaged people (for example, people with low incomes), and ethnic minority groups. Sleep problems may also differ depending on where you live. People living in neighbourhoods with high levels of nighttime light, noise, and air pollution may have more problems with sleep, whereas people living in neighbourhoods with more greenspace (for example, living closer to a park) may have better sleep. This study will use national data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging and the Canadian Urban Health Research Consortium to examine socioeconomic and environmental determinants of inequities in sleep behaviours among middle-aged and older adults in Canada. This project will help to identify groups of people who do not sleep well in Canada, and who are at risk of poorer health outcomes as a result. Information from our study can be used to inform public health interventions to improve sleep for people in these groups.

column37: Adversity and trauma experienced during childhood such as physical, sexual, or emotional abuse, neglect, witnessing intimate partner violence, and parental separation or divorce is known to increase the risk of various physical and mental health conditions. However, it is unclear how childhood adversity leads to not only development of a single disease, but multiple diseases in an individual. It is proposed that exposure to severe or long-term stress during childhood may alter the function of the biological systems, thereby leading to poor health outcomes. Our project will examine the potential biological pathways through which childhood adversity leads to development of several chronic diseases within the same individual. Assessing the biomarkers across different biological systems will help us understand the burden that childhood adversity places on our body and allow us to assess the risk for development of multiple diseases. Understanding whether childhood adversity is associated with increased risk for development of more than one chronic disease will also allow us to identify at risk individuals earlier so that appropriate interventions, which could be treatments and/or lifestyle changes can be implemented to decrease the risk of disease and untimely death.

column36: Do genetic and social factors modify associations between sensory impairment and cognitive decline? An analysis of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: Sensory loss and cognitive problems are very common in older adults. Importantly, vision and hearing loss are correlated with cognitive decline, above and beyond what is expected due to aging alone. The reason(s) remain uncertain, and not everyone is affected equally. On average, people with higher levels of sensory loss have a greater likelihood of experiencing cognitive decline, but there are exceptions to the rule. Our research aims to understand if genetic and/or social factors affect the degree to which hearing and vision are associated with cognitive decline. The results may help clarify underlying mechanism(s), and identify individuals with sensory loss who are most at risk, who might be targeted for interventions that aim to slow cognitive declines. First, we will determine if genes that cause both sensory loss and cognitive decline explain the associations. We will investigate the apolipoprotein E gene, since having the epsilon-4 version of the gene is a major risk factor for cognitive decline, and may also increase the risk of hearing and vision loss. Second, we will assess if social isolation affects the association. Social interaction is thought to stimulate the brain and protect it from cognitive decline. Hearing and vision loss, however, may disrupt communication and social participation and lead to isolation and loneliness. If our hypothesis is correct, the association between sensory loss and cognitive decline would be mediated by social isolation. The study will use data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, which includes 30,000 participants from across the country who have health measures collected every 3 years. We will have access two sets of data for every participant: Their baseline data (collected in 2012-2015) and their 3-year follow-up data (collected in 2015-2018). Sensory, social and genetic information will be ascertained from the baseline data, and change in cognition will be assessed using data from both time points.

column36: Prediabetes in Canadians 45-85 years of age and predictors of 3-year progression to diabetes: a longitudinal examination using data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: Diabetes is a life-long disease in which the body cannot make enough insulin or does not properly use the insulin it makes. Insulin is a hormone that helps the body change sugar from food into energy. Low insulin production or impaired insulin function results in glucose (sugar) building up in the blood, which over time, can cause major complications such as heart disease, kidney disease and blindness. Most individuals with diabetes go through a prediabetes state during which time blood glucose levels are higher than normal, but lower than established thresholds for diabetes itself. Physical exercise and a healthy diet may help revert prediabetes to normal glucose level and prevent progression to diabetes. Because the number of individuals with prediabetes is high and not all will develop diabetes, offering lifestyle interventions and close monitoring to all of them would waste valuable resources. Identifying those who would benefit the most from such interventions is important to inform prevention efforts. The Canadian Diabetes Risk (CANRISK) is a questionnaire based on age, sex, weight, height, waist circumference, physical activity, fruits and vegetables intake, hypertension, prior high blood sugar, given birth to a large baby, diabetes in the family, ethnicity and education to determine the risk of having diabetes. CANRISK performance to predict progression from prediabetes to diabetes is not known. We will use data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging to determine among the Canadian population 45-85 years old 1) the proportion of those with prediabetes who will develop diabetes over three years; and 2) the ability of CANRISK, either alone or combined with other genetic, environmental and personal factors to predict progression from prediabetes to diabetes over three years in men and in women from different Canadian regions.
