column36: Explaining Self-Reported Health Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults with Multimorbidity and Depressive Symptoms using a Resilience Framework: An Analysis of CLSA Data
column37: There is a growing number of older adults in Canada. These older adults often live with multiple chronic health conditions as well as depressive symptoms. Together with other health conditions, depressive symptoms can cause decreased health-related quality of life, increase the chance of developing other health conditions, and increase the use of expensive health services. Despite these challenges, when asked "In general, how would you rate your health?" some older adults still report their health positively. These reports of positive health in the face of illness may point to an ability to bounce back from health-related challenges. Self-reported health status is a strong predictor of future health status including the development of other health problems or death because of these problems. Previous studies have shown that this measure is related to many factors, but it is not understood how these factors effect self-reported health. This research will focus on understanding the ways in which this ability to bounce-back explains self-reported health among older adults with multiple chronic conditions and depressive symptoms. Using data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, three research questions will be answered in order to understand: 1) the relationship between the number of chronic health conditions and self-reported health; 2) the factors that shape self-reported health, and; 3) the unique influence of depressive symptoms on self-reported health. It is important to understand the reasons that older adults report positive health (although they experience challenges from multiple chronic health conditions and depressive symptoms) as this understanding will inform effective programs and policies that can help to promote health and support healthy aging.

column36: How to Handle Missing Spirometry Data in Population-Based Studies?
column37: Spirometry has increasingly been utilized in population-based studies including the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA), to assess the presence of lung disease at the population level. According to the literature, about 10 to 30% of participants in population-based studies do not have valid spirometry data due to either contraindication from spirometry tests or poor quality spirometry. Of the 30,097 participants within the CLSA comprehensive cohort, 29.1% have no spirometry data available at baseline due to low quality spirometry or contraindication for spirometry and are considered as "missing" in the statistical analysis. The substantial amount of missing spirometry data may lead to efficiency reduction and serious bias, which undermine the validity of research findings. Two measures are commonly collected from the spirometry for evaluation of lung function: forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC), which measure flow rate and lung volume in one maximal breath. The ratio of FEV1 to FVC together with FEV1 and FVC are used to identify obstructive and restrictive lung defects. The FEV1 and FVC are found to have a very strong, age-independent linear relationship in healthy individuals; however, this relationship does not hold among those with lung impairment. Traditional imputation techniques are inappropriate to handle the missing spirometry data since (1) FEV1 and FVC are paired measures from one spirometry test and they are observed or missing simultaneously; and (2) the relationship between FEV1 and FVC depends on whether an individual has lung impairment. This investigation will help researchers appreciate the complexity of missing spirometry data and adopt appropriate imputation methods to handle them. Moreover, methods developed in this investigation can be generalized to handle the missingness of any paired data, such as systolic and diastolic blood pressure, a common phenomenon in health research.

column36: Oral Health, Nutrition, and Frailty: A mediation analysis from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging.
column37: Oral health is a critical component of overall health, and poor oral health has been shown to be a risk factor for incident frailty. Frailty is a clinical state in which there is an increase in an individual's vulnerability for developing increased dependency and/or mortality when exposed to a stressor. There is a hypothesis that the link between poor oral health and frailty is through poor nutrition. Poor oral health (such as loss of teeth, dental pain, and/or chewing problems) could cause an individual to choose foods that are easier to chew and eat (generally less healthy and less nutrient dense foods), and this then contributes frailty. However, studies where this is tested over time to be able to take into account the effects of poor oral health and poor nutrition on worsening frailty have not yet been done. We propose to test for the effects of age, gender, and potentially changeable risk factors such as smoking, poor social support, and low physical activity, on the worsening over time of oral health, nutrition, and frailty. We will also describe the influence of being poor on these changes. Finally, we propose a longitudinal analyses to better explain how to delay or lessen frailly by improving oral health or by improving nutrition, and therefore to promote healthy aging.

column36: Using retinal images of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging to elucidate the causal mechanisms linking cardiometabolic risk factors with microvascular health and to predict cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases
column37: More than two hundred thousand people suffer from myocardial infarction or stroke every year in Canada. This number continues to grow despite drug developments to treat diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol and obesity. Vascular diseases that affect arteries in the heart and brain are, in fact, the end-stage of a progressive vessel alteration that begins by silently affecting the very small vessels of the body. Thus, a better understanding of the causal mechanisms linking cardiometabolic risk factors, including smoking, small vessel alteration, and artery diseases would provide earlier and improved risk prediction for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. Retinal images can be used to assess an individual's overall small vessel condition for three reasons: (1) retinal vessel images are an easily-observable part of an individual's small vessel health using ocular fundus photographs; (2) retinal vessel architecture is affected by diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, obesity, and smoking; and (3) retinal vessel changes can predict the occurrence of heart attack and stroke. By combining high-throughput genetic methods with artificial intelligence algorithms to automate the analysis of retinal images from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging and the UK Biobank, we will identify genes that determine retinal vessel architecture. Those findings will then be used as inputs to estimate the causal effects of cardiometabolic risk factors on the retinal vessel changes. We will finally test whether retinal images can be used to improve the prediction of myocardial infarction and stroke. By providing a better understanding of the causal and modifiable risk factors involved in small vessel health, our project will guide prevention strategies, and help properly direct clinical trials. This study will also provide targets for effective lifestyle and pharmacological interventions for small vessel changes, and in fine, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases.

column36: Health service use and unmet care needs among lonely and/or socially isolated older adults
column37: Loneliness and isolation are increasingly recognized as affecting older adults' health, including the risk for death. Some research has shown that loneliness and social isolation increase the risk of hospital readmission and prolonged stays. Beyond this, though, there is little research on the relationship between loneliness and/or social isolation and health service use. Hospitals and emergency departments, while crucial sites of care, can have negative consequences for older adults. Among older adults, emergency department visits can result in pressure ulcers, delirium, and prolonged hospital admissions. To date, the research that has looked at emergency department and health practitioner visits in relation to loneliness and social isolation has shown mixed results; further, because there have been few population-based studies, it is difficult to know the effects on the larger population of older adults. The purpose of this project is to examine the association between loneliness and social isolation on health service use and unmet needs. Our project will also specifically examine if there are sex and gender-related differences in these associations. We will use Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) telephone survey data to identify if poor social connection affects health service use and unmet needs. This work is critical to help determine if social disconnection is a barrier to accessing health services. Given the growth in the older adult population, it is essential that we understand the impact of social connection so we can optimize the available services and reduce potentially inappropriate service use.

column36: The association between loneliness and cognitive decline and the roles personality traits may play
column37: Loneliness has been linked to negative physical and mental health and the impact has been compared to that of obesity and smoking. Loneliness may also be associated with dementia, although it's still not clear why. For example, loneliness may increase our risk of dementia but the early symptoms of dementia may also make people feel lonely. Personality traits are also tied to loneliness and heath. In fact, certain personality traits have been found to predict both loneliness and dementia. Despite the apparent link, very few studies have simultaneously considered the health impacts of personality traits and loneliness. The purpose of our study is to test the association between loneliness and cognitive change, while exploring the roles personality traits may play. For example, certain personality traits may predispose people to being lonely and this could impact their cognitive function. On the other hand, being lonely may impact cognitive function more or less, depending on a person's personality traits. For this study, we will use data from the comprehensive cohort of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA), a randomly selected sample of just over 30,000 Canadians aged 45 years and older. Detailed data on CLSA study participants includes demographic and clinical information, as well as measures of loneliness, personality and cognition. We will use data that was collected at baseline and follow-up (roughly three years later) to analyze the relationship between loneliness and cognitive change, as well as the roles personality traits may play. In our analyses, we will account for a person's social support and participation, as well as demographic and health factors. We will also test whether these relationships are different for men and women. Ultimately, understanding the relationship between loneliness and cognitive change would help to identify strategies to maintain cognitive health.

column36: Development of Machine Learning Models to Characterize Homebound Status in Older Adults in Canada.
column37: Homebound status is defined as never or rarely leaving the house, or only being able to leave the house with assistance. In the U.S., 6.6% of Medicare recipients are mostly or completely homebound and 15% meet criteria for semi-home bound status. Homebound older adults (OAs) are high users of healthcare services, and are typically frail, sedentary and socially isolated, with significant adverse effects on their physical and mental health. Most previous studies of homebound OAs have used small cross-sectional or longitudinal datasets to examine correlates of homebound status, including variables such as medication use, comorbidity profile, functional limitations, gender, and BMI. We hypothesize that the development of homebound status in OAs is a complex process and simple combination of manually chosen variables may not be sufficient to build accurate machine learning classifiers to detect it. No studies have attempted a machine learning approach to detect the outcome of homebound status based on a variety of social, physical and psychological variables, including those related to mental and mobility. In this project, we propose to use the baseline wave of the Comprehensive cohort in the CLSA dataset to develop and validate a homebound definition, and then to use it to 1) determine the prevalence of homebound OAs at baseline, and 2) determine the incidence of homebound OAs after the first three-year follow-up. We will then select important features from the CLSA database using both experts in the care of homebound seniors and automatic feature selection methods aimed at improving the performance of the classification models. Using these two feature sets, we will use machine learning methods to develop classification models to predict the likelihood of homebound status at baseline and follow-up. The outcomes of this project will help develop models that identify those who are currently homebound and which can be used to identify people at risk of being homebound.

column36: Depression and Cognitive Function in Mid- to Late-life: Longitudinal Associations and Vulnerable Subgroups in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: Cognitive function is critical to healthy aging. Even mild cognitive impairment may limit independence (e.g., loss of ability to drive) and reduce quality of life. More severe cognitive decline leads to further losses of independence and increased morbidity, mortality and institutionalization. Understanding factors that put people at risk of developing cognitive impairment is thus important to maintain the quality of life of older adults and reduce health care costs. One such key factor is depression. Depression is a common mood disorder and the leading cause of disability world-wide. We will examine the association between depression and cognition within vulnerable subgroups defined by sex, gender, age and social support in Canadians aged 45 to 85 years using longitudinal data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA). Our team will build upon its previous work with the baseline CLSA data. Longitudinal data will allow us to address issues that could not be addressed previously with the baseline data: 1) temporality (i.e., whether depression precedes cognitive function or vice versa); 2) whether types of social support act as a mechanism through which depression affects cognition (i.e., mediation); and 3) whether factors such as age, sex, and gender influence the strength of the association between depression and cognition, and the mediation of this association by social support. Longitudinally examining different types of social support as mediators within age, sex and gender subgroups will provide new information about the mechanisms linking depression and cognition, and whether social support can exert a protective effect over time in vulnerable subgroups. By contributing to our understanding of the impact of middle and late-life depression on cognition and identifying vulnerable subgroups that may most benefit from intervention, our study will help to improve the health of middle-aged and older Canadians

column36: Wrist fracture: Does it identify a healthy cohort or at-risk population?
column37: A broken wrist is the most common broken bone seen in the emergency department and causes great pain and disability. Between the age of 50 and 65 there is a dramatic increase in the incidence of broken wrists, especially in women. Despite this common occurrence, we do not fully understand the reasons for this rapid increase. Some research suggests that women are particularly at risk because of their smaller bones and changing hormonal status which weakens their bones. Other studies suggest that people start to lose their balance and visual acuity in this age range and it is an increased rate of falling that is the problem. These reasons would suggest that a wrist fracture is a sign of compromised health and an important precursor of future health problems, including more serious osteoporosis related fractures. Other studies suggest that overly active and "extra healthy" people have broken wrists, but that a broken shoulder indicates a major health concern. We suspect that both positive and negative risk-profiles exist in people who break their wrists. The problem is we do not know how to identify which risk group someone is in at the time of injury. This information is needed to target prevention of future health problems. This study will compare the risk profiles of 50 to 65-year-old people who have had a broken wrist or shoulder to other similarly aged people within the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging (CLSA) cohort to identify factors that might be associated with different health profiles and how they change over time. We will consider factors like physical activity, gender, hormonal status, and co-morbid health problems and see which predict negative health status. The outcomes we will examine will include bone health using measures of bone density, overall health, and frailty. This information will be used to identify the subgroup of people who should be targeted in the future for more intensive preventive health services to optimize healthy aging.

column36: Falls and fragmentation: the impact of a personalized information sharing intervention on primary care provision for patients in home care
column37: Health care in Canada has been criticized as being siloed, provider-centred, and inefficient. Information sharing in our health care system is poor and communication is inadequate. Ineffective information sharing can lead to adverse consequences such as falling, the second leading cause of death by accidental injury worldwide. This is particularly important for home care patients, who have a higher risk of health problems and admission to a hospital or long-term care home. The aim of the proposed study is to determine the importance of personalized information surrounding falls risk to primary care practitioners (such as family doctors) and their home care patients. The intervention will involve sharing personalized pamphlets surrounding falls risk and falls prevention to primary care practitioners and patients. With supervision from geriatrician and Schlegel Research Chair Dr. George Heckman, and collaboration from the Waterloo Wellington Local Health Integration Network, this study is expected to take place over 6 months and will (1) measure the impact of sharing these pamphlets on quality of follow-up visits with primary care and (2) improve understanding on how and why changes should occur with information sharing. I anticipate that sharing personalized information on falls will facilitate discussion between primary care practitioners and patients, enable patient engagement, and reduce fall occurrences. I firmly believe that this research has the potential to show researchers, health care practitioners, and policymakers that effective information sharing is a critical instrument for health care.

column36: Predicting future primary psychotic disorders in youth with methamphetamine-psychosis disorder.
column37: People who abuse stimulant-type drugs like methamphetamines can develop various problems, including temporary or even longterm psychotic symptoms (e.g. paranoia, hearing voices). Many will develop these symptoms but only for a brief period of time, whereas others can develop more severe symptoms that become a psychotic disorder. To date, we have not been able to determine who will need longer treatment from who will not. Our team has developed an expertise in methamphetamine-psychosis and proposes to verify three hypotheses based on our past studies: 1) those who will develop a psychotic disorder will have more severe and specific symptoms at first hospitalisation; 2) those who will develop a psychotic disorder will have different cognitive deficits (e.g. memory or attention deficits), 3) those who will develop a psychotic disorder will have different beliefs about their symptoms compared to those with temporary methamphetamine-related psychotic symptoms. Participants with psychotic symptoms and stimulant or methamphetmaine abuse will be recruited from hospitals with psychiatric units. They will be asked to answer interviews, tests and questionnaires and will be assessed monthly for three months. The results from this study will allow us to develop a new screening tool for clinicians that will help determine who who is more likely to need more intensive treatment.

column36: Establishing Next Steps for SPIN-SHARE: An International Collaboration to Disseminate eHealth Disease-Management Tools for People Living with Scleroderma
column37: Scleroderma is a rare autoimmune disease characterized by thickening and hardening of the skin and internal organs. The burden of scleroderma on quality of life is high. Psychosocial, educational, and rehabilitation interventions could help improve functioning and reduce distress in individuals with scleroderma. Although these kinds of programs are a key part of patient-centered care in more common chronic diseases, they are not typically available for people with rare diseases, including scleroderma. The Scleroderma Patient-centered Intervention Network (SPIN) was created to address this issue. SPIN is an international collaboration of patient organizations, clinicians, and researchers, who have developed an infrastructure to test accessible, low-cost programs to reduce disability and improve the quality of life in scleroderma. SPIN has developed online programs to help address areas such as hand function, symptom self-management, appearance anxiety, emotional distress, and physical activity. The goal of SPIN-SHARE is to make all of its programs available to patients with scleroderma, free of charge, starting with SPIN's first two programs (SPIN-HAND for hand rehabilitation and SPIN-SELF for self-management), which are currently being tested via clinical trials and will be publicly released in 2020. The proposed SPIN-SHARE meeting will be held during the 2020 Systemic Sclerosis World Congress, taking advantage of the fact that representatives from many of SPIN's 18+ international patient organization partners will be in attendance. This meeting will update SPIN's partners on the status of SPIN programs and establish a plan to provide scleroderma patients with free access to the programs. The present funding would cover travel costs for six representatives from Canadian patient organizations who would otherwise not be able to attend the meeting and who are integral to SPIN's goal of disseminating its online programs free of charge to people with scleroderma.

column36: Scoping Review of Evidence Regarding Psychosocial and Pharmacologic Interventions for Methamphetamine Use Disorder and Problematic Methamphetamine Use: Planning and Prioritizing Future Research
column37: Methamphetamine use and harms are rising at a concerning rate in Canada, resulting in a rapidly emerging public health crisis. While psychosocial treatments as well as drug treatments have been studied, treating individuals with problematic methamphetamine use is a challenge for clinicians, with no clear best approach. Additionally, we do not currently know whether certain treatments work better for certain individuals with problematic methamphetamine use, such as: adolescents; those with other existing mental health problems (e.g., depression); gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men; individuals in the corrections system; and pregnant women. The planned study will use a 'scoping review' approach to identify, assess and summarize existing studies of psychosocial and drug treatments for methamphetamine use problems. This research method uses a structured approach to mapping the characteristics and findings of available research on a focused question. We will review all research that has previously studied the use of psychosocial and drug treatments for methamphetamine use problems. This work will allow for the planning of future research to inform comparisons between treatment strategies using the available information, while also identifying gaps in the current evidence (including treatments requiring study, as well as population subgroups that have thus far been ignored by research). We will work with our partners from the Canadian Center on Substance Use and Addiction, the Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine, Public Health Ontario, the Community Addictions Peer Support Association, the Mental Health Commission of Canada, Corrections Services Canada, the University of Western Ontario, the Lawson Health Research Institute, Max Ottawa and the Drug Users Advocacy League to ensure this work has an impact on future policies, clinical practice, the design of future research and efforts to curtail this threat before greater impacts on public health.

column36: Concurrent Use and Transition to Methamphetamine among persons at risk of OverDose (CUT Meth OD)
column37: While illicit opioids and the current overdose crisis continue to claim thousands of Canadian lives, a new drug use epidemic is emerging. Use of methamphetamine has been rapidly increasing globally. Availability and use of methamphetamine has increased in Canada, particularly in British Columbia (BC) where self-reported methamphetamine use tripled among harm reduction site clients between 2012 and 2018, and the presence of methamphetamine among illicit drug-related deaths increased almost 10 times between 2012 and 2017. Methamphetamine use is associated with a range of health and social harms including serious mental health conditions such as psychosis, brain damage, heart disease, and increased risk of disease transmission through higher-risk sexual behaviour and unsafe injection practices. Many people who use drugs use both methamphetamine and opioids which can be particularly risky, increasing the chance of overdose death, and non-fatal overdose and its long-term consequences. The nature of the rise in methamphetamine use in Canada is poorly understood. Through this BC wide study, we seek to: 1) describe the characteristics of increased methamphetamine use; 2) explore factors related to use of methamphetamine, including how people use the drug and if by itself or in combination with other drugs; and 3) better understand the reasons for use of methamphetamine. We will also look at how these factors differ across the province. To answer our questions, we will interview about 60 people who use drugs from around BC. The focus will be on methamphetamine use and co-use with other drugs such as opioids. An annual survey administered to about 1000 people at harm reduction sites across BC will ask about recent substances used including route and order of use; reported substances used will be confirmed by urine testing. Understanding factors that drive increasing methamphetamine use and its use with other drugs are essential to guide effective harm reduction efforts.

column36: Supporting the trajectories of our spirit: Living Cree Pimatisiwin and Blackfoot Kiipaataapiisiinii (Our spiritual way of life)
column37: Indigenous knowledge states that we originate from the stars and that our life begins before conception (Buck, 2009). All Indigenous peoples have a creation story which details the instructions on how to live our spiritual way of life. This project will support the trajectory of our spirits by ensuring our children have access to their spiritual way of life from birth. The spiritual way of life includes speaking the language, connection to land and water and participating in ceremonies that support wellness across the lifespan. The long history of colonial practices in this country has disrupted the traditional lifeways of nations, including the transmission of birth knowledge and practices. The project will seek to answer the question, How do cultural, spiritual, land-based and community connections from the time of birth impact the health and wellness of our children as defined by our nations? The all Indigenous research team will work with three Cree communities in Manitoba and three Blackfoot communities in Alberta. The project will be governed by the Collaboration Circle and the Knowledge Keeper Circle. In addition each community will have a community-based research associate and an advisory circle that will oversee the implementation of the project activities in their community. The focus will be on examining what is working to promote wellness rather than measuring contributors to chronic illness. At the end of the two years the project will have (1) developed and refined nation based indicators of well-being, (2) have documented the existing culturally based activities that support living the good life, (3) will have a cohort of children that were born with the support of a culturally trained birth helper, (4) will have preliminary data on the impacts of culture as a foundation of wellness starting at birth for the Cree and Blackfoot nations and (5) key recommendations for biological sampling in research for the Cree and Blackfoot nations.

column36: Hishuk-ish tsawalk (everything is one, everything is connected): Using two-eyed seeing to optimize healthy early life trajectories for Indigenous Peoples
column37: The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council (NTC), BC's First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) and academic partners are collaborating on a long-term study to learn how to improve health and wellness for Indigenous children. We will specifically look at how to reduce mental health problems (anxiety, depression, substance use and suicide) and cardio-metabolic problems (obesity, type-2 diabetes and heart disease) - starting early in childhood, yet with potential benefits across the lifespan. To achieve these aims we will: 1.Gather and consolidate traditional Indigenous knowledge on raising healthy children, recovering and respecting our ancestral traditions, values and culture 2.Use both Indigenous Knowledge and scientific methods to evaluate existing early child health and parenting programs, and to inform the development and evaluation of new programs 3.Investigate early developmental origins of mental and cardio-metabolic health, starting at conception 4.Build new opportunities for Indigenous students and community researchers to obtain training and participate in public health research and policy development, preparing for future leadership 5.Share our findings with our own and other Indigenous communities, and join with other Indigenous groups to improve health and wellness for our children across Canada. Mi'kmaq Elder Albert Marshall described "two-eyed seeing" as an approach that uses the best strengths of both Indigenous and Western scientific ways of knowing for the benefit of all. Two-eyed seeing will inform all of our work. We are also guided by the FNHA's strengths-based perspective on health and wellness - encouraging the acknowledgment of challenges such as the ongoing legacy of colonialism, while also building the conditions for building resilience. We hope that our findings will benefit all children and families within our NTC communities, as well as Indigenous and other children and families more broadly.

column36: Restoring the Healthy Family System in Indigenous Communities: A Collaborative Research Partnership in Alberta to Address the Gap in Indigenous Health Outcomes
column37: Healthy families are the building blocks of Indigenous communities, and are pivotal to the well-being and survival of communities. They are the cornerstone through which infants and children develop, learn, grow, and flourish, and the basis for well-being for people across the lifespan. Our team brings together partners from across research disciplines and Indigenous communities with the overall goal of supporting optimal health during preconception, pregnancy and postpartum for diverse Indigenous populations through community-led and community-specific strategies that promote the best possible healthy life for families and children. The Indigenous Healthy Life Trajectory Initiative (I-HeLTI) is an important and timely opportunity for Indigenous communities to identify strategies that are considered critical for optimizing health, beginning in early life (i.e. in pre-conception, pregnancy, infancy, and early childhood). The three I-HeLTI Development Grant Teams funded in Alberta that were led by Maskwacis Health Services, McMurray Metis Local 1935, and the Alberta First Nations Information Governance Centre (AFNIGC) have come together on this application.

column36: A Meta-Ethnography of Methamphetamine Use: Mobilizing qualitative synthesis and the lived experiences of People Who Use Drugs to inform harm reduction and public health interventions in Alberta
column37: Aims & Objectives: The aim of project is to ensure that harm reduction and public health interventions for mitigating the negative outcomes of use among structurally vulnerable populations are responsive to the lived experiences of people who use drugs (PWUD). We plan to hold at minimum of three consultations with PWUD in Calgary, Edmonton and Lethbridge in collaboration with AAWEAR. Partnerships & Significance: Alberta Addicts Who Educate and Advocate Responsibly (AAWEAR) will be the Principal Knowledge User for this project. AAWEAR is a Provincial group of people in Alberta with a history of drug use. AAWEAR members will be closely involved in the development of the review protocol and will be engaged throughout the project as embedded partners. column36: A participatory approach to implementing peer-run inhalation overdose prevention services
column37: While safe injection site services have expanded in the ongoing overdose crisis, there are very few overdose prevention services for people who use non-injection drugs. There is an innovative peer-run outdoor smoking tent that has been established and operating for over 2 years in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. To respond to the increase in methamphetamine users, the Overdose Prevention Society (OPS) in partnership with the British Columbia Centre for Substance Use proposes a collaborative examination of the smoking tent program model to so that this effective model can be expanded and adapted for new places. The purpose of the project is to understand what it is about the program that makes it work and how to modify it when moving to new contexts. This one-year project will involve people who use the tent services in the research and will take a mixed-methods approach including quantitative and qualitative analyses. Quantitative data for this study will come from short surveys with n=200 current tent users administered by peer research assistants. Qualitative data come from interviews conducted with 15 current tent users and 5 service providers at OPS in Vancouver. This project will help with decision-making for people working at OPS about how to proceed with expanding their services. It will additionally support other overdose prevention sites and service providers interested in starting up new overdose prevention smoking tents in their areas through the toolkit that will be created. This has the potential to reduce harm and overdose for methamphetamine users, who are underserved in the overdose crisis.

column36: Measures of Aortic Stiffness, Central Blood Pressure and Pulsatile Arterial Load Predict Future Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Expansion
column37: Background: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is a disease associated with high morbidity and mortality. As such, clinically useful strategies for risk assessment and medical management of TAA are critically needed. We sought to determine the predictive role of aortic stiffness and pulsatile arterial load on future TAA expansion. Methods and Results: One hundred and six consecutive, unoperated subjects with TAA were recruited. By combining arterial tonometry with echocardiography, we estimated measures of aortic stiffness, central blood pressure, steady and pulsatile arterial load at baseline. Aneurysm size was measured at baseline and follow-up with imaging and indexed to height; growth was calculated in (mm/m)/year. Stepwise multivariable linear regression assessed associations of arterial stiffness and load measures with aneurysm growth after adjusting for potential confounders. MeanSD age, baseline aneurysm size and follow-up time were 62.811.4 years, 46.53.9 mm and 2.20.9 years, respectively. Aneurysm growth rate was 0.40.5 mm. column36: Gender/Sex Across the Lifespan: Embracing Complexity in Biomedical Research
column37: Over the last 3 decades, it has become increasingly apparent that health research needs to account for gender and sex in order to apply research findings appropriately, develop technologies and policies, and make well-informed clinical decisions for people of all genders. Similarly, research has shown clearly that many types of biological processes occur differently at different points in the lifespan, and in order to do research that promotes healthy development and aging, our research must account for these trajectories. Addressing these considerations in laboratory-based experimental research has particular complexities and opportunities, and requires attention to the realities and context of research done using cells, experimental animals, and tissues. In this application, our team proposes to develop a suite of resources for biomedical researchers to use that will enhance their ability to incorporate gender, sex, and aging considerations into experimental laboratory-based research. We will build a comprehensive tissue bank and database to allow researchers to benchmark and validate their findings with respect to important signifiers of gender, sex, and aging, and use that information to identify 'molecular signatures' that can provide insight into function, and aim to validate these against large human databases. We will develop conceptual models of gender, sex, and aging that are specifically tailored for biomedical researchers, along with statistical and data presentation approaches. In terms of Education & Training, we will develop courses for university students across the country to build capacity in these areas, and pilot a consultant position to assist established researchers in applying these insights to their specific research contexts. Our Knowledge Translation activities will aim to put tailored resources into the hands of biomedical researchers, and evaluate the impact of these efforts as we proceed.

column36: The Impact of Nursing Home Medical Staff Organization on Quality of Care and Outcomes for Long Term Care Residents
column37: The relationship between Long Term Care (LTC) Medical Staff Organization (MSO) and the quality of care received by LTC residents is largely unknown. It has been suggested that quality of care provided to these individuals remains inconsistent and has not kept pace with the growing needs of the population. The objective of this study is to understand the existing LTC MSO and culture from two different informants, medical directors and attending physicians. Specifically, to investigate whether MSO impacts quality of care and unplanned emergency department visits. The validated Nursing Home Medical Staff Organization Survey (NHMSOS) will be emailed to medical directors and attending physicians from 18 Schlegel Villages (in Ontario) and 8 Senior Quality Leap Initiative (Canada and United States) associated LTC homes. The aggregate results will be analyzed to describe the impact on quality of care outcomes such as unplanned emergency department visits and practice sensitive quality care indicators in the RAI-MDS 2.0 nursing home data. The results of this study will be used to understand the implications of current MSO models and the impact on the quality of care received by LTC residents. Specifically, the findings will be used to guide policy development and derive an MSO model which optimize MSO culture and resident quality of care.

column36: A sex-difference evaluation of an aerobic interval training cardiac rehabilitation program in adults with heart disease
column37: Heart disease affects women and men differently. Women develop the disease at an older age and experience more health complications. Following a cardiac event, patients are encouraged to attend cardiac rehabilitation to improve cardiovascular risk factors (e.g. blood pressure, obesity, diabetes), quality of life and exercise capacity. Unfortunately, cardiac rehabilitation remains underutilized, with women reporting a 20% lower enrolment and being more likely to withdraw from a program than men. Aerobic interval training is emerging as an alternative type of exercise that extends beyond the traditional continuous aerobic exercise to address frequently cited barriers of women to participate in the program such as lack of motivation/enjoyment and time, perceive exercise regime as tiring/boring. We conducted a sex-specific evaluation of the effects of an aerobic interval training cardiac rehabilitation program in physical and mental health outcomes in women and men with heart disease. Patients (n=147) engaged in an outpatient aerobic interval training cardiac rehabilitation program twice a week for 12 weeks. Anthropometric and cardiometabolic health indicators, exercise capacity, depression, and anxiety were measured at baseline and at follow up. At baseline, women compared to men had significantly lower waist circumference, exercise capacity; higher total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein. Changes in the measured variables were similar between sexes. A similar proportion of women and men completed the aerobic interval training program. On average, men attended one more week of cardiac rehabilitation than women (176 vs. 157 exercise sessions) Performing aerobic interval training led to low dropout rates (16.6%) and similar improvements in physical and mental health for women and men. As sex-differences were present at baseline, women may need alternative and more aggressive programs to reach a similar level of health as men.

column36: Listening to Children's Voices - Promoting Indigenous Mental Wellness (I aM Well)
column37: Indigenous children face serious health inequities in Canada. Suicide rates among youth, a marker of the devastating impact of intergenerational trauma, are higher in rural and remote communities where access to treatment is limited, and children are reluctant to seek help. There is currently an urgent need to address these inequities, a culturally-relevant screening tool to identify children-at-risk, and promising programs to support their healing (e.g., Journey to Wellness). This proposal focuses on the scale-up and national spread of the Aboriginal Children's Health and Well-being Measure (ACHWM); a tablet-based wellness measure, co-created with Indigenous children. It is remarkably efficient in screening for mental health challenges, connects children-at-risk to local supports, and provides locally relevant data to inform program planning and policy. Two factors are restricting the reach of the ACHWM: the structure of the existing sharing strategy has reached maximum capacity with 50 partners and is unable to meet the growing demand; and the children most in need of assessment and support are often not able to obtain parental consent. We propose to: (1) leverage technology to recreate our digital processes to redesign scale-up, spread nationally and create sustainability; and (2) study alternative consent options to respect the rights of parents and the needs of children, to develop culturally appropriate wise practices that extend the tool's reach and promote equitable access. Our team is strong, with years of respectful collaborative research with Indigenous communities across Canada. Our program will impact children by identifying needs and connecting them to healing services. It will reduce barriers to participation in community-based screening to enhance equitable access, and deliver a sustainable strategy to share the ACHWM. Together we will explore integration within local health systems, and develop community-to-community sharing of the approach.

column36: Understanding the transport of pathogenic proteins into the central nervous system for the Huntington's disease
column37: Recent work conducted in Dr. Cicchetti's laboratory has demonstrated that healthy tissue transplants implanted into the brains of patients with Huntington's disease expressed, after several years, pathological signs of the disease, such as the mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) - the genetic product of the disease. Her research team also demonstrated that the permeability of the blood-brain barrier - a barrier that allows blood vessels to filter toxins from the periphery to prevent contaminating the brain - presented certain anomalies in these patients. Taken together, these observations suggest that mHtt is capable of being transported from a diseased to a healthy cell and/or possibly via blood vessels that were made more permeable by the disease. A better understanding of the transmission mechanisms of mHtt to the central nervous system could radically change how we treat Huntington's disease. My master's thesis focuses on studying the impacts of certain transporters of the blood-brain barrier, such as LRP-1, and its effect in facilitating or inhibiting the transport of mHtt into the central nervous system. We will use a pharmacological approach to influence the transport of mHtt by LRP-1 in mice models of the disease and evaluate behaviour to determine if the treatment results in beneficial effects; both the improvement of behavioural abnormalities as well as pathological features.

column36: Discovering the connection between the feature space of Generative Adversarial Networks and human psychological processes
column37: Humans have the ability to perform fine tuned discrimination between different natural images. Previous studies exploring visual discrimination often used low-level grating stimuli due to their ease of manipulation. However gratings are often quite different from real world images, that contain complex and nonlinear structure. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have given rise to generative image models based on deep neural networks, known as Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs). GANs provide an avenue for the parametric manipulation of naturalistic images, allowing for the parametric study of higher level human perception. My previous study focused on how algebraic properties of the GANs latent space are related to objective human discrimination performance. The proposed study will further this by examining the topological properties of the simulated images and understanding how the aspects learned by a GAN are related to subjective qualities of human experience. During the relatively short time GANs have been present, one of the main questions in the field has been how these parameterization can be evaluated against human perception. The proposed study is a novel attempt to draw a connection between GAN parameters and underlying human processes using a multidimensional psychophysical scaling method.

column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating illness that affects millions of people worldwide. Characterized by clinical symptoms, (e.g. loss of pleasure, feelings of worthlessness) and cognitive impairments (e.g. memory, attention), individuals suffering from MDD often experience significant difficulty in their day-to-day activities. While approximately half of MDD sufferers seek out treatment, less than half report their treatment as satisfactory. One demographic for whom treatment is particularly difficult is individuals in their late teens to early 20s, referred to as transitional aged youth (TAY). Although this group represents a crucial developmental stage for the onset of MDD, many TAY with depression do not respond well to antidepressants. Further, many may not have regular access to therapy, demonstrating an urgent need for alternative strategies suitable specifically to their needs. Aerobic exercise (AE, or "cardio") is known to have numerous physiological benefits, however, its role in the treatment and prevention of mental illness is still largely not understood. Despite a growing body of research reporting a reduction in MDD symptoms in adults, few studies have focused on the benefits of AE for TAY, or what intensity of AE may offer the most benefit. Furthermore, even less is known about the brain changes that occur in depressed TAY as a result of AE. The goal of this study is to determine the effects of moderate and high intensity AE on the clinical and cognitive symptoms of TAY with MDD. Additionally, this study will investigate the brain changes linked to AE, as measured by brain imaging. Such insight is critical for guide further development of AE as a potential treatment for TAY suffering from MDD.

column36: Inhibitory control as a mediator of the association between emotion dysregulation and disruptive behaviors in childhood
column37: Approximately 5-15% of children are diagnosed with a Disruptive Behavior Disorder (DBD) that is associated with tremendous impairment in social, academic and family functioning. Determining the emotional and cognitive factors that contribute to DBD is of pressing concern to refine prevention, assessment and treatment approaches. Children with DBD show elevated difficulties with regulating their emotion (i.e., emotion dysregulation) and are quick to react to mild provocation, show sustained negative emotionality (i.e., anger) and appear irritable. Much research has also demonstrated cognitive deficits in inhibitory control, or the ability to stop ongoing thoughts and behavior, in children with DBD. Emerging research suggests that these emotional and cognitive processes may be linked, such that deficits in inhibitory control may partially account for the association between children's emotion dysregulation and severity of DBD. The proposed study will investigate the associations between emotion regulation, inhibitory control and severity of behavior in children with DBD. Understanding how emotion regulation and inhibitory control are associated with the severity of behavior problems in children with DBD could potentially ignite possibilities for enhanced assessment and treatment approaches. For example, confirmation of hypotheses may suggest a need to include a core component to enhance inhibitory control in psychosocial skills building programs for children with DBD.

column36: The effect of displacing sugar-sweetened beverages with non-nutritive sweetened beverages or water on the human gut microbiome: Strategies To OPpose SUGARS with Non-nutritive sweeteners Or Water (STOP SUGARS NOW) Trial The effect of displacing sugar-sweetened beverages with non-nutritive sweetened beverages or water on the human gut microbiome: Strategies To OPpose SUGARS with Non-nutritive sweeteners Or Water (STOP SUGARS NOW) Trial
column37: High intake of sugar-sweetened pop has been linked with excess weight gain and an increased risk for type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Because of this, health experts have recommended that people replace their pop with water. As a replacement, non-nutritive sweetened beverages, or "diet" pop, are a sweeter alternative to water. However, the role of "diet" pop to replace pop have not been addressed in dietary guidelines. Health Canada has said that non-nutritive sweeteners are safe for use, but new research suggests that through the gut microbiome, non-nutritive sweeteners may actually increase the risk of the above-mentioned diseases. Not all research agrees on this topic; only one human study looked at the relationship between a very high amount of a single non-nutritive sweetener and the gut microbiome. This study did not look at the role of non-nutritive sweetened beverages in replacing pop, compared to water, on the gut microbiome. Considering we consume whole foods, and not individual non-nutritive sweeteners on their own, looking at whole beverages is more applicable as a "real world" replacement. To find out what are the health effects of "diet" pop to replace pop, we will be doing a CIHR-funded, randomized controlled crossover study on the effect of replacing regular pop with "diet" pop or water on the gut microbiome: the STOP Sugars NOW Trial. This means participants will be asked to participate in all treatments in an order determined by chance. This study will be useful to see what is the best replacement for pop, and it will shed light on the effects of "diet" pop on the gut microbiome, and how these compare to just water.

column36: Effets d'un programme d'entrainement locomoteur avec un exosquelette robotise de marche au sol chez des personnes ayant une lesion medullaire chronique : Une etude prospective longitudinale avec mesures repetees
column37: Plusieurs personnes ayant une lesion de la moelle epiniere (LME) utilisent un fauteuil roulant (FR) comme principal mode de locomotion. La position assise prolongee et la reduction de l'activite physique liee a ce mode de locomotion contribuent a l'aggravation de problemes secondaires de sante. Pour contrer ce cercle vicieux, il est suggere de s'engager dans la pratique reguliere d'activite physique. Dans cette perspective, la marche au sol avec un exosquelette robotise (EXO) est une intervention prometteuse : elle augmente la mise en charge et la mobilite aux jambes, necessite des efforts musculaires aux bras et au tronc et sollicite le systeme cardiorespiratoire. Nos travaux preliminaires demontrent qu'un tel programme pourrait amener plusieurs bienfaits physiques et psychologiques. Cependant, davantage d'etudes sont necessaires pour renforcer le faible niveau de preuve actuel. Ce projet vise a mesurer les effets immediats d'un programme de marche avec un EXO sur la sante cardiorespiratoire, la sante musculosquelettique et la composition corporelle. Vingt utilisateurs de FR ayant une LME chronique completeront un programme de 34 seances de marche sur 16 semaines avec un EXO, soit 1 a 3 sessions d'entrainement par semaine sous la supervision d'un physiotherapeute. Des mesures seront recueillies 1 mois et immediatement avant le debut du programme ainsi qu'immediatement apres sa fin. Des evaluations cliniques et de laboratoire seront completees et des questionnaires seront remplis. Des entrevues seront menees pour mesurer la satisfaction et capter les perspectives des participants a la fin du programme. Les nouvelles connaissances meneront au developpement de futurs programmes d'activite physique offerts aux utilisateurs de FR ayant une LME chronique dans la communaute.

column36: Organic Mitral Regurgitation: Controversy, Predictors and Impact on Cardiac Function
column37: Organic mitral regurgitation (OMR) is one of the most common degenerative valve diseases. Asymptomatic patients with OMR do not undergo early mitral valve repair or replacement due to a controversy over the choice of treatment: early surgery or medical follow-up. This controversy exists mainly because there are limited demographic, clinical, metabolic or hemodynamic factors currently available about the progression of the OMR and the prognosis of these patients. The main objective of this study is to identify the determinants of progression of OMR severity and clinical events in these patients. Our hypotheses are that: 1) mitral regurgitation (MR) severity varies significantly during exercise, so an evaluation of the MR by stress echocardiography makes it possible to determine the real severity, to observe the occurrence of symptoms and thus, to optimize the timing of the surgery; 2) biomarkers of cardiac function impairment would be useful for the assessment of patient prognosis and for stratifying long-term risk. To achieve these objectives, patients with an OMR over mild of severity are currently being recruited or in the recruitment process in the prospective PROGRAM study. These patients are followed over a period of 10 years where a short physical examination, a blood test, and a resting echocardiography are performed each year. Upon entry, other tests such as a stress echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance are performed. This project will help to better represent the real impact of OMR on the patient's functional ability in their daily activities. This study could also contribute to a better risk stratification in these patients, to early detect the negative impacts of OMR on cardiac function, and thus to establish better patient care and management.

column37: Providing proper care and offering therapeutic possibilities for patients with autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) is the end goal. The highest worldwide incidence of ARSACS is in Saguenay-Charlevoix, Quebec, home to our research center the GRIMN. With two potential therapeutic compounds, recently shown to significantly reduce symptoms in knockout mice with ARSACS, ensuring clinical trial readiness is key. The most common neurological scale used to evaluate ataxia is the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA). The SARA has yet to be validated in the ARSACS population, limiting potential outcome measures needed to track patient progress, for upcoming clinical trials. This Master's project, as a first objective, will document the validity of the SARA using a cross-sectional design with data from 75 patients with ARSACS. The second objective is to detect change of the SARA over a 5-year period, using a longitudinal design of 50 patients with ARSACS in their fifth year of follow-up. Finally, the results of this project will advance clinical trial readiness by documenting the validity of the SARA for the ARSACS population.

column36: The Effects of Estrogen on Associative Memory in Spontaneous Menopause and Surgically-Induced Menopause: An fMRI Analysis
column37: Estrogen loss from ovarian removal via bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) prior to spontaneous/natural menopause (SM) has been linked to increased incidence of Alzheimer's disease (AD). The present research considers the differential impact of estrogen loss from SM and BSO on functional brain activity during associative memory encoding in spontaneously menopausal women, women who have undergone BSO, and age-matched premenopausal control women (AMCs). Endogenous estrogen levels are measured in all groups, and women perform a face-name associative memory task during functional image acquisition. This task has shown previous sensitivity to the subclinical state of AD. The aim of this study is to clarify the distinct roles of estrogen and age on functional brain activity in the anterior hippocampus and frontoparietal network during associative encoding. Understanding functional activity variations between SM and BSO women compared to AMCs during association learning will be critically necessary for differentiating memory effects that result from normal aging versus those related to AD pathology in women. Further understanding the relationship between estrogens, functional brain activity, and cognition will help to clarify estrogen's impact on the AD trajectory, greatly benefiting women's brain health and cognitive neuroscience more broadly.

column36: Prediction of differential treatment response for depression using personality facets: A machine learning approach
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a debilitating mental disorder characterized by negative mood and thinking, with a Canadian prevalence estimated to be 4.7%. Current recommended treatments for MDD include various forms of psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy. Unfortunately, many individuals with MDD do not readily respond to these treatments, and it may be the case that a certain treatments work better for people with certain characteristics - an approach to treatment called 'personalized medicine'. To date, research within a personalized medicine approach to treating MDD has examined whether demographic and biological characteristics can determine whether one treatment is better for a given individual than another treatment. For example, research has suggested that married individuals may benefit from psychotherapy over pharmacotherapy for MDD treatment. Less research has been devoted to examining whether personality traits (relatively consistent patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaviours) can also determine whether an individual would benefit in one form of MDD treatment over another, despite personality traits being predictive of other life outcomes. Studies to date have demonstrated mixed/inconsistent results, which may be due to differing study designs and characteristics. Using a big data approach, the goal of the present study is to aggregate multiple MDD treatment studies, that have used similar methodology, in order to derive an 'algorithm' that can potentially predict whether an individual would benefit from being either in psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy, using self-reported personality traits. Results have the potential to further aid clinicians in selecting a beneficial MDD treatment for a given client based on their personality traits.

column36: Food Insecurity and Common Mental Disorders in Los Robles, Nicaragua
column37: Food insecurity is a pressing global health issue as rates of food insecurity are rising despite the fact that ending world hunger is one of the United Nation's Sustainable Development Goals. Rates of common mental disorders (CMDs) are also increasing globally, particularly in low and middle-income countries. The goal of this research project is to determine whether a correlation exists between food insecurity and CMDs for mothers living in Los Robles, Nicaragua. Nicaragua is one of the poorest countries in Latin America and Los Robles is in one of the poorest regions in Nicaragua. Consequently, citizens of Los Robles face high levels of food insecurity and lack healthcare for CMDs. Currently, there is a lack of diachronic data on the relationship between food insecurity and CMDs, making causality between the variables uncertain. This research project addresses this gap by conducting a longitudinal study of food insecurity and CMDs experienced by mothers in Los Robles. column36: Development of a computer-aided algorithm using artificial intelligence for the segmentation of ultrasonographic features of lymph nodes during endobronchial ultrasound.
column37: Lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, warranting the need for accurate lymph node (LN) staging to determine treatment plans. However, as ultrasound is operator dependent, agreement between operators was only achieved 22.54% of the time using this tool. If researchers are able to train artificial intelligence (AI) to perform segmentation on images of LNs, it is believed that a computer algorithm will be able to generate an accurate and reliable score for these LNs. In order for AI to predict cancer, it must be proven that AI can segment accurately. We hypothesize that AI will be segment the ultrasonographic criteria more accurately and reliably than a clinician. A sample of 300 retrospectively collected LNs will be used for the training set for AI learning. A clinician will segment the LN images using a computer software, and NeuralSeg, an artificial intelligence program will use this derivation set to develop an algorithm. The algorithm output will be compared against the reference standard as determined by the spatial overlap of the target segmentations to determine reliability and accuracy using SORNSEN-DICE scores. Continuous measures will also be created from the segmentation images and compared against the binary score.

column36: Physiological benefits of high-intensity interval training for individuals with Parkinson's disease
column37: Currently, Parkinson Canada recommends aerobic exercise based on the Adult Canadian Physical Activity Guidelines of =150 min of moderate-to-vigorous exercise per week, conventionally, taking form as continuous moderate intensity training (CMIT) (e.g. 20 min of cycling). We will study the effects of HIIT and CMIT on cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with PD. We propose a 1:1 randomized controlled trial of 40 participants (50-85 years) to 10 weeks (3 times per week) of CMIT or HIIT cycling. Our specific research aims are to compare, in PD, the effects of HIIT and CMIT on: - Resting hemodynamics (Blood pressure, and heart rate), arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity), muscle sympathetic nerve activity - Hemodynamic and sympathetic responses to isometric hand grip contractions (30% MVC for 2 min) and post exercise circulatory occlusion (3 min after hand grip contractions) We expect that HIIT will produce greater improvements in hemodynamic, autonomic, and clinical markers than CMIT in individuals with PD. The outcome measures in this study are known to relate importantly to functional daily living and quality of life. Demonstration of superior outcomes with HIIT would represent a new paradigm for prescribing exercise in PD.

column36: Doxorubicin and Microtubules: Mechanisms of Chemotherapy-Induced Cognitive Impairment
column37: The study will focus on identifying microtubule (MT) destabilization as a component factor of chemotherapy-induced cognitive dysfunction (CICI). With increasing numbers of cancer survivorship, symptoms of chemotherapy are becoming more of a concern. Deficits in memory are a common complaint of chemo patients, lasting months to years, and are correlated with reductions in quality of life and well-being. The molecular mechanisms underlying CICI have remained largely unknown. Evidence suggests oxidative damage of biomolecules as a key factor to CICI. This study focuses on the impact of doxorubicin (DOX) on MT stabilization and subsequent changes in spatial memory, and aims to demonstrate that stabilization of MT protects against DOX-induced hippocampal neuron damage, neuron death, and impairments in spatial memory. Mice will be administered DOX and will be compared on measures of MT-density, axon integrity, neuron survival, and spatial memory with mice administered both DOX and caltubin, via analysis of electron-microscopy, immunohistochemical analysis, and the Morris water maze. Caltubin is a protein that is known to stabilize MT polymers and induce axon growth and regeneration after injury in mammalian cells. It is expected that stabilization of MT with caltubin will significantly rectify loss of neuronal MT density, axon degeneration, and neuron degeneration within the hippocampus after DOX administration and consequently will improve spatial memory. This will provide sound evidence of microtubule destabilization as one of the mechanisms underlying CICI. This research could provide insight into mechanisms of other neurocognitive disorders that have an oxidative component (eg. Alzheimer's Disease), and be taken into consideration of future chemotherapy developments.

column36: Upregulated H/ACA snoRNA in high grade ovarian cancer promote cell survival and proliferation ?
column37: SnoRNAs are small RNAs functioning in the nucleolus of eukaryotic cells. They are separated in two groups (H/ACA box and C/D box) which guide different modifications on the ribosomal RNA. Several previous studies have identified snoRNAs as being dysregulated in cancers. They are promising biomarkers because they are stable and are detectable in blood. Ovarian cancer is one of the deadliest cancers in the female reproductive system, lack of particular symptoms and late diagnosis, results in lower success of conventional treatments. There is a need to identify biomarkers that would permit earlier detection of high grade ovarian cancers, which are very aggressive as compared to borderline tumors which have a higher treatment efficiency. Previous experiments carried out in our laboratory confirmed that the expression of snoRNA H/ACA box is upregulated and the expression of snoRNA C/D box is downregulated in high grade ovarian cancers as compared to serous borderline tumors. Two snoRNAs (SNORA19 & SNORA81) were therefore selected as being able to differentiate between high grade and borderline ovarian cancer. In order to understand if the cancer cells phenotype is affected by these snoRNAs, their expression was knockdown in a high grade ovarian cancer cell line. Reducing the expression of SNORA19 and SNORA81 led to a decreased cell survival and proliferation in ovarian cancer cells. More experiments are necessary to specifically understand the role of these snoRNAs and why their expression is increased in high grade ovarian cancer as compared to borderline tumors. More importantly understanding how these snoRNAs are providing cancer cells a resistance to cell death could offer new strategies for early diagnosis of this cancer.

column36: Novel Transglutaminase Inhibitors as an Anti-Cancer Therapeutic in High Grade Serous Ovarian Carcinoma
column37: Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecological cancer worldwide and has a 5-year survival rate of less than 40%. Women are usually diagnosed after their cancer has grown large and/or metastasized throughout the body. Many of these women's tumours will develop resistance to their chemotherapy medication and stop responding to treatment. Cancer biologists believe that chemotherapy often fails to completely rid patients of their cancer because of the presence of there exists cancer stem-like cells. Cancer stem cells can divide and repopulate a tumour. Currently used chemotherapies successfully kill quickly growing cancer cells, however, it will not affect slow-growing cancer cells, like cancer stem cells, as much. If as few as 100 cancer stem cells remain after surgery or chemotherapy treatments, a tumour can reform and metastasize. To improve treatment option for patients diagnosed with chemo-resistant forms of ovarian cancer, new drugs that target these cancer stem cells must be developed. We propose that a new drug called NC9 that inhibits the protein Transglutaminase (TG2), will do just that. This protein, when at higher levels than normal in a cell, have been shown to help tumour cells divide, spread, invade and develop resistance to chemotherapy. Inhibiting this protein has also been shown to make chemo-resistant cancer cells sensitive to common anti-cancer drugs again. We will be examining whether a new TG2 inhibitor will improve carboplatin treatment effectiveness of ovarian cancer cell lines and whether it will reduce the ability of these cells to divide, invade, metastasize and to make new cancer stem cells. The NC9 inhibitor has the potential to improve chemo-resistant ovarian cancer treatment, reduce rates of cancer recurrence, and increase patient survival.

column36: Drug discovery guided by artificial intelligence
column37: The increasing prevalence of antibiotic resistant pathogens demands the discovery of biologically active compounds. Nature has provided molecules with chemical structures that have evolved to provide microbes with competitive advantages. Currently, new compounds are found through bioactivity-guided screening. Mixtures of organic compounds are extracted from microbial cultures and screened for biological activities of interest. However, this method progressively meets with failure due to high rediscovery rates. The objective of my research is to propose an alternative approach by using machine learning algorithms to analyze genomic and chemical information of microbes. Machine learning algorithms learn patterns in data to produce reliable and repeatable predictions. Since the genome encodes the blueprints for natural products, algorithms can analyze DNA sequences to make predictions of the chemical structures. Next, the algorithm uses these predictions to survey compounds produced by microbes, identifying the target of interest. By creating technologies connecting genomic and chemical information, my research hopes to lower rediscovery rates and accelerate the discovery of new therapeutics.

column36: Investigating the role of pro-inflammatory galectin-3 protein and sialic acid sugar deficiency in renal thrombosis
column37: Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare kidney disease caused by abnormal blood clots (thrombosis) in small blood vessels. About 1% of patients with respiratory infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae develop aHUS, known as pneumococcal-associated aHUS (P-HUS). There is currently no specific therapy for P-HUS due to our poor understanding of its pathobiology. The only clue we have is that these patients have high blood levels of pneumococcal sialidase, an enzyme that cleaves terminal sialic acid from glycoproteins. We previously identified loss-of-function mutations in the gene ST3Gal1 in 3 patients with aHUS. ST3Gal1 is a sialyltransferase that adds terminal sialic acid sugar to galactose residues on glycoproteins. St3gal1-null mice and rats had increased asialoglycoproteins (absence of terminal sialic acid) in the glomeruli of the kidney. The same results were observed with addition of exogenous sialidase. We recently found that glomeruli of St3gal1-null rats had high levels of galectin-3 and control animals did not. Galectin-3 is a pro-inflammatory protein that binds terminal galactose: it would therefore be expected to bind to asialoglycoproteins. We do not know if galectin-3 interacts with asialoglycoproteins or whether it plays a role in the pro-thrombotic process experienced by patients. We hypothesize that the interaction between galectin-3 and glomerular asialoglycoproteins is critical to promote renal thrombosis in ST3Gal1 deficiency and P-HUS. We will investigate by first determining where galectin-3 is expressed in glomeruli, using various glomerular endothelial and immune cell markers. Our work will contribute to the understanding of P-HUS pathobiology for development of treatments of this rare, detrimental disease.

column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide, and of the different types of heart disease, coronary artery disease (CAD) is the most common. There is currently no cure for CAD as current treatments only temporarily alleviate symptoms. This suggests that IL-B may contribute to early disease progression. Thus, we aim to determine the specific mechanism by which IL-1B increases movement of cholesterol through the cells that line the blood vessels. column36: Quadriceps Muscle Layer Thickness and Hospital Length of Stay (LOS) in Kidney Pancreas [KP] and Kidney Transplants: A Cohort Study
column37: Kidney-pancreas (KP) and kidney transplantation (KTx) improves quality of life and life expectancy. However, decreasing benefits from surgery such as transplant can sometimes be seen as age increases. It has become important to appreciate that some people are "frail" while others are not, despite their age. The term frailty was developed to better describe one's ability to withstand stress, such as major surgery. The impact of one's frailty on transplant outcomes is an emerging concept: it's been shown to increase hospital admissions and mortality risk after KTx. Frail patients receiving a KTx can also have problems with their kidneys working early after surgery. To assess frailty, one can measure things like strength, walking ability, and energy levels. A major part of the body's ability to respond to stress is lean muscle mass (LMM), which repairs injury and produces immune responses. If illness is prolonged, LMM can be lost. Recently, ultrasound imaging (US) has emerged as a convenient bedside tool to assess LMM by using ultrasonic waves to visualize tissue. Our study will be using US to measure thigh muscle thickness. We will compare this to other measures of frailty. After measuring the frailty and LMM of people about to undergo a KTx or KP transplant, we will follow them to find out how long they stay in hospital and see if there are issues with organ rejection or infection. They will be re-assessed at 3 months as well. We hope to find a strong association of US measured LMM and outcomes after transplant, so that US can be used in the future to identify patients at risk of complications, and be used to monitor improvements in frailty with interventions such as exercise, diet, or others, to make potential organ recipients healthier for surgery.

column36: The association between growth trajectories and cardiometabolic risk in young children
column37: Background: The number of overweight and obese Canadian children has been rising over the past decades. It is concerning because when obesity combines with high blood pressure, high blood sugar and abnormal amounts of lipids, it can result in a number of diseases such as diabetes and heart diseases. The risk of having those diseases is called cardiometabolic risk (CMR). Children who grow rapidly in early childhood might be associated with later CMR. Objective: We will use a score called CMR score to assess the cardiometabolic risk. The CMR score consists of measurements of blood sugar, blood pressure, lipids and excess fat around the waist. A lower CMR score means lower cardiometabolic risk. The primary objective of this study is to determine whether growth trajectories in early childhood are associated with the CMR score. The secondary objectives include examining the association between growth trajectories and the individual CMR measurements. Method: This study will use data from a large group of healthy children called TARGet Kids!. The data of children 1 to 5 years old will be used to generate 4 or 5 different types of growth trajectories. Then we will determine if there are associations between different types of growth trajectories and CMR scores. Hypothesis: We believe that children who grow rapidly in early childhood will have a higher CMR score. Significance: Identifying how and when growth trajectories are associated with CMR in early childhood is important. The findings will have implications for doctors and parents of Canadian children, and may lead to the development of interventions for children who grow rapidly in early childhood, therefore improving Canadian children's cardiometabolic health.
