column36: Combinative Effect of Inflammatory Bowel Disease Risk Factors on Pathogenesis
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a disease that mainly affects parts of the intestines. Long-term inflammation arises due to an immune response against the bacteria that live in the gut. Incidence of IBD is very high in the western world, but the cause remains unclear. Both genetic and environmental factors have been shown to play a role in the development of IBD. Of note, mutations in a gene called NOD2 is the strongest genetic risk factor for Crohn's disease, and early life antibiotic exposure and consumption of a 'Western' diet have been shown to increase the risk of developing IBD. In this project, we will be investigating the combinative effect of these three factors on the development of IBD in mice. Mice with and without NOD2 will either be given food representative of a 'Western' diet or not. In addition, some mice within each treatment group will be given antibiotics from birth to weaning. Throughout the experiment, mice stool will be collected to observe differences in the intestinal bacteria populations, and later in their lives, a chemical will be used to induce inflammation in the intestines to observe differences in IBD susceptibility. Results from this study will provide insight into the combinative effect of IBD risk factors.

column36: Management of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) among an inner-city population with psychosocial barriers to treatment
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health threat. TB is the biological expression of social inequality and poverty. Wealthy nations, such as Canada experience relatively low rates overall, but certain sub-populations experience disproportionate burdens of disease. In Canada, the vast majority of cases occur in two minority groups, Indigenous peoples and the foreign-born. A major contributor to active TB disease is the large reservoir of latent TB infection (LTBI), from which active TB develops with its potential to replenish the reservoir. Since LTBI is a necessary precursor to active TB disease, removal of this reservoir is critical to achieving TB elimination goals in Canada. This is achieved through screening and administration of preventative therapy. Long treatment duration and frequent dosing (9 months of twice weekly or daily isoniazid) characterizes the current first choice treatment regimen in Canada. Poor adherence and completion rates among high-risk groups result. In response, an approved shortened treatment regimen with much less frequent dosing has recently been made available in Alberta and Canada. This new regimen is now available to hard-to-reach persons at greatest risk of progressing from LTBI to active TB disease; in particular to individuals with psychosocial barriers to otherwise long treatments. My study will employ a mixed methods design to explore knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions of LTBI and treatment experience. Understanding the patient perspective is critical to reforming preventive TB therapy administration, and promoting adherence. Findings from this study will be applicable to other settings of high TB burden in Canada, and support advocacy efforts related to shorter treatment regimens for underserved populations.

column36: Pourquoi les exercices fonctionnent ? Comprendre l'influence des exercices sur les mecanismes du traitement de la douleur chez les individus souffrant de differents types de lombalgie.
column37: La lombalgie chronique (LC) constitue un probleme multidimensionnel dont la prise en charge represente un enjeu important. Des exercices des muscles du dos sont souvent prescrits, mais les effets sont modestes, ce qui signifie que certaines personnes ne repondent pas a ce type d'intervention. Pour optimiser la prise en charge, il est devenu essentiel de (i) mieux stratifier la LC pour en diminuer l'heterogeneite et (ii) mieux comprendre comment les exercices fonctionnent. La LC pourrait etre nociceptive (LCN) ou centrale (LCC). Une douleur nociceptive est caracterisee par une douleur generee principalement par l'activation de nocicepteurs dans un systeme nerveux central (SNC) qui fonctionne normalement alors qu'une douleur centrale implique une douleur generee principalement par des differences dans le fonctionnement du SNC entrainant une alteration dans le controle de la douleur. La reponse a l'exercice peut varier d'une etiologie a l'autre. Les exercices entrainent une diminution de la sensibilite a la douleur (hypoalgesie induite par l'exercice (HIE)) produite par les regions du SNC impliquees dans le controle de la douleur. L'objectif de cette etude est de determiner si les differents sous-groupes de LC (LCC et LCN) repondent differemment a un exercice des muscles du dos. Les sujets participeront a deux rencontres. A la premiere, une evaluation clinique et de la sensibilite a la douleur seront realisees afin de proceder a la classification (LCN ou LCC). A la seconde visite, les participants realiseront un exercice des muscles du dos pendant 4 minutes. La sensibilite a la douleur sera evaluee avant et apres l'exercice. Il s'agit de la premiere etape d'une serie d'etudes sur la comprehension des exercices pouvant avoir un impact important sur le traitement de la LC.

column36: The functional role of the rs2603751 polymorphism on the expression of Nur77 and its effects related to antipsychotic treatment
column37: The side effects induced by antipsychotics (AP) are numerous. Currently, no validated biomarker exists that would allow us to identify if an individual is at risk of developing side effects related to the use of AP. Nur77 is a gene that was recently associated with a reduction in the development of tardive dyskinesia (a type of involuntary movement) caused by AP. It is also expressed in the regions of the brain involved with the therapeutic effects of AP and could therefore play a role in the effectiveness of AP in the treatment of schizophrenia. In addition, a polymorphism located on the mRNA of Nur77 is associated with an increase in the risk of developing tardive dyskinesia. This research project therefore aims to study this specific polymorphism in order to observe how it modulates the expression of Nur77 and consequently, how it affects the development of side effects secondary to the use of AP. We will observe the effect of the polymorphism on the expression of Nur77 in cells as well as in mice brains. These results could eventually allow the identification and the validation of a biomarker (the polymorphism of Nur77) in the response to treatment with AP as well as in the vulnerability of developing side effects with the use of AP. To conclude, the knowledge acquired with this study could eventually allow the development of a targeted and individualized pharmacotherapy with less side effects in the treatment of schizophrenia.

column36: Understanding Neurobiological Mechanisms of Autism: Investigating the Effects of Sex/Gender on the Structural Connectivity of the Brain
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that has been reported to affect males four to five times more than females; however, research over the last two decades suggest potential diagnostic biases leading to many under-recognized female cases. Past studies investigating ASD primarily focused on males, which explains the significant gap in our knowledge about females with this condition. As females are screened based on what is known about ASD in males, many cases may be undiagnosed until later in their development. With an increased understanding of the complexity of ASD, we acknowledge differences between males and females in their risk for ASD and behavioural characteristics. A question that remains is whether there are factors associated with biological sex that would explain these differences and provide insight for mechanisms that lead to ASD. More recent studies have shown abnormal changes in the brain related to ASD symptoms but the effect of sex/gender on these brain abnormalities have yet to be investigated. Thus, this study will investigate the effect of sex/gender on structural connectivity of the brain in ASD. Using neuroimaging data from the POND Network, an integrated discovery program across Ontario, the goal is to generate a sex-balanced, well-powered dataset for analysis in comparison to controls. We aim to investigate two models that may coexist: males and females with ASD differ by 1) regions of the brain that are affected and 2) extent of the brain that is affected. Findings from this study will give direction for future investigations of how changes in the brain are related to differences in behaviour between males and females with ASD and help determine possible sex-specific targets for intervention and support.

column36: ICD-11 Guidelines for Depressive Episode Severity: An Examination of Concurrent Validity
column37: Depression, one of the most common mental disorders in Canada, is associated with substantial burden on the individual and society. Current treatment decisions rely on an accurate assessment of depression severity without a universal definition of severity. The World Health Organization is working on the 11th revision of the International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Conditions (ICD-11), with the goal of improving its clinical practicality. The ICD-11 outlines a definition for depressive severity, and as such, it is important to examine how well the new guidelines measure depressive severity compared to a well-established depression tool. The present study aims to examine how well clinicians' depressive episode severity ratings proposed in ICD-11 compare to the severity levels on the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II), a gold standard self-report questionnaire. Data from participants assessed for mood disorders at the Royal Ottawa Mental Health Centre as part of a larger ICD-11 clinical field trial, who were given a diagnosis of a depressive episode and completed the BDI-II, will be included. Both the ICD-11 and the BDI-II define depressive severity using three levels: mild, moderate and severe, and the relationship between the two scales will be analyzed. For instance, do most of the participants assigned a 'severe' rating on the ICD-11 also receive a 'severe' rating on the BDI-II for depressive episode? Determining the relationship between the two severity rating scales will provide useful information on how helpful the ICD-11 guidelines will be for clinicians in defining depressive severity among Canadian patients. This is especially relevant to public health, given Canada currently uses the ICD for health statistics.

column36: Maternal consumption of freeze-dried grape powder in pregnancy to mitigate the deleterious effects of perinatal iron deficiency on fetal development.
column37: Studies on the developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) have shown that susceptibility to non-communicable diseases may be traced to stressors during pregnancy. Pregnant women are most at risk for iron-deficiency (ID), due to blood volume expansion and increased demands from the fetus and placenta. In spite of oral iron supplementation, an estimated 23% of Canadian women become iron-deficient during pregnancy; this number is a staggering 50% in developing countries. Our group has shown that ID during pregnancy leads to abnormal development of the fetus, which results in long-term health complications including high blood pressure (which is evident in early childhood) and kidney and blood vessel dysfunction. Our laboratory has identified key mechanisms by which prenatal ID causes abnormal growth and development of the fetus; these mechanisms include, increased free radical production, and dysfunction of the mitochondria. On the basis of these studies, we hypothesize that using a novel freeze-dried whole grape powder containing a number of polyphenols and antioxidants, could reduce free radical production, enhancing mitochondrial function, and hence improve fetal growth and development. The use of freeze-dried grape powder during pregnancy could be a simple and easily implemented strategy to reduce the risk of long-term health complications such as cardiovascular and renal disease.

column36: Indel evolution in the surface glycoprotein of Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1
column37: In 2017 alone, human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) killed over 900,000 people and spread to roughly 1.7 million new individuals.The rapid spread of HIV-1 places an enormous burden on global health and shows the importance of researching new methods to block its transmission. To infect a new human host, HIV-1 must attach itself to immune cells using its surface protein: gp120. This gp120 protein contains five loop structures on its surface that rapidly change their amino acid sequences and are heavily covered in sugars, thereby acting as a protective shield from the human immune system. Changes to the length, composition, and sugar content of these protective loop structures can influence the success of HIV-1 at evading the immune system and spreading between people. The insertion of new amino acids and the deletion of existing ones within these loop structures are two common sources of these influential changes, and therefore, these insertion and deletion events (indels) can influence HIV-1 infection and spread. However, little research has been conducted on indels within the gp120 protein. By performing computational analysis of thousands of HIV-1 sequences from infected patients around the world, I contributed to this understudied topic by estimating the rates, lengths, and compositions of indels in the five loop structures of gp120. As my past study analyzed indels among infected people, my next goal is to apply my computational methods to HIV-1 sequence data collected from the same infected individual over time. Analyzing within-host data promises to reveal additional, more accurate information about indels due to shorter sampling time intervals, thereby increasing understanding of this powerful mechanism which HIV-1 uses to adapt to the human population.

column36: The effect of gene knockdown in anthracycline induced cardiotoxicity in human induced pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes
column37: Anthracyclines, a chemotherapeutic agent, play an important role in improving the survival rates of a wide range of childhood cancers. Despite the importance of anthracyclines in cancer treatments, their use is complicated by the development of heart-related toxicities (known as cardiotoxicities) that have the potential of resulting in heart failure. While there are a variety of known risk factors (e.g. age of diagnosis and dose of drug) implicated in anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity, it is difficult to accurately determine who is most at risk. Therefore there is a major need to better predict and identify the patients at the highest risk for cardiotoxicity. Recently, variations in genes have been explored as more accurate predictors of a susceptibility to cardiotoxicity. However, there is a limited understanding of how these genetic variations affect cardiomyocytes, primary cells of the heart. In order to address this, I will model cardiotoxicity using human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes in order to study the effect of anthracyclines at a functional, structural, and molecular level. I will also use gene silencing and genetic sequencing methods to identify the genetic involvement of cardiotoxicity and the molecular mechanisms of cardiac injury and death. This research will help to provide physicians with the knowledge to personalize chemotherapeutic treatments and better manage cancer survivors who are at an increased risk of cardiotoxicity and cardiovascular mortality. Additionally, the identification of the mechanisms of cardiotoxicity will help basic scientists gain insight into the disease and develop targeted therapies, which will allow for an improvement in patient outcomes and the potential for reducing the global health burden of heart failure.

column36: Understanding the Links between Personality and Depression: The Impact of Life Stress
column37: Depression is a prevalent and debilitating mental disorder in Canada. Despite years of research, only recently we have begun to consider how patient vulnerabilities can interact with their environment to lead to depression. One patient vulnerability factor that shows repeated links with depression is personality. The predominant model of personality in the literature is the Five Factor Model, which includes five broad personality traits: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness and contentiousness. Of these, neuroticism and extraversion have shown the strongest links with depression. Environmental factors such as life events (i.e. desirable events like new relationships, or undesirable events like natural disasters) are also closely tied to depression. Despite their importance, how specific personality traits and life events are linked to depression is unknown. As such, the purpose of this study is to test how personality traits differ in people who have and have not recently experienced a life event, and people who are and are not currently suffering from depression. We hypothesize that people who have experienced a life event and are suffering from depression will score highest on neuroticism and lowest on extraversion. We also hypothesize that different traits and life event types will be linked to depression, anxiety, and other important clinical outcomes. Data will be extracted from two previous studies of youth and young adults, including 241 with depression and 191 without. The results of this study will provide clarity on the links between personality traits, life events, and depression. Ultimately, it is hoped that these results and subsequent studies will help inform holistic treatment approaches to provide relief from this debilitating illness.

column36: Does preservation of the nerve to the mylohyoid improve hyoid excursion in surgically treated oral cavity cancer patients?
column37: Swallowing dysfunction is a common consequence among surgically treated oral cavity cancer patients, which can adversely impact risks of aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, social isolation, and decrease quality of life in patients. The nerve to the mylohyoid is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, which is a branch of the mandibular nerve. This nerve assists in the upward movement of the hyoid bone, which facilitates swallowing by aiding in laryngeal movement, cricopharyngeus muscle relaxation, and upper esophageal sphincter opening. Level IA neck dissections put the nerve to the mylohyoid at risk of being damaged during the removal of cancerous tissue. This study will examine if preserving the nerve to the mylohyoid during surgery influences hyoid excursion in oral cavity cancer patients. This study is a retrospective chart review of a prospectively collected database of head and neck cancer patients. Patient charts of 40 adults who have been surgically treated for oral cavity cancer will be identified by chart review. Patient charts will be placed into an experimental group if the nerve to the mylohyoid was preserved during surgery, and a control group if the nerve to the mylohyoid was not preserved. Using videofluroscopy swallowing study (VFSS), the changes in hyoid excursion from pre- to post-surgery will be examined between the two groups to assess the horizontal, vertical, and vector displacement of the hyoid. Pre- and post-surgical VFSS hyoid excursion will be examined using an independent sample t-test if data are normally distributed, and a Mann-Whitney U test if data are not. Study findings can help refine surgical management strategies, which can significantly impact the long-term functional outcomes of oral cavity cancer patient's quality of life.

column36: The Effects of Early Life Stress on Prefrontal Cortex-Amygdala Maturation
column37: Early life stress (ELS) is a significant risk factor for mental health disorders and cognitive impairments. Although past research suggests that ELS preys on immature brain circuits, which undergo rapid growth and maturation in early life, there is a major gap in knowledge about how ELS manipulates functional circuits to result in its deleterious effects to mental health. In particular, the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and amygdala are brain regions that are subjected to dynamic changes in early life and are sensitive to stress. The proposed study will investigate the effects of ELS on the PFC-amygdala circuit in mice, since this circuit is critical for fear extinction - a process by which rodents extinguish tone-shock fear memories. Importantly, the immature extinction system is permanent, while the adult extinction system is ineffective, since the fear memory returns after the passage of time. We hypothesize that ELS accelerates the maturation of the PFC-amygdala circuit to promote an early switch to the adult-type extinction system. To investigate the effects of ELS, we will utilize the maternal separation paradigm, which parallels parental deprivation or neglect in humans. Using a combination of optogenetic and electrophysiological tools, this study will be the first to elucidate the mechanism by which ELS impairs circuit function to exert its adverse effects. The current study has important implications for understanding the mechanisms by which ELS impairs mental health and will provide novel insights for the development of more targeted interventions to counter the effects of ELS.

column36: Incompleteness as a Predictor of Treatment Response in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive thoughts that lead to repetitive behaviours. Traditionally, cognitive theories of OCD emphasized that compulsions occur to prevent perceived harm. It is now recognized that some people with OCD engage in compulsions due to feeling like something is incomplete or "not just right". Therefore, research suggests that harm avoidance (HA) and incompleteness (INC) are the motivational core dimensions of OCD. Despite this recognition, most of the research and cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) protocols for OCD have focused on the HA motivation. Therefore, current protocols may not meet the needs of individuals with OCD driven by INC. Treatment that is not tailored to the correct underlying motivation (i.e., INC versus HA), may be a significant factor in accounting for poor treatment response and attrition in trials using CBT for OCD based on a HA conceptualization. There are few studies investigating INC in clinical samples, especially focusing on treatment response. This proposed study will address this gap by investigating the relationship between INC and HA motivations and CBT treatment outcome in individuals with OCD. Specifically, it will examine whether increased INC motivation at pre-treatment predicts poorer treatment response post CBT and whether individuals with high INC have a significantly poorer treatment response compared to individuals with high HA. Participants will complete a battery of questionnaires before and after completing a 12 session CBT program. The results of this study could have significant implications for improving treatment outcomes and the efficacy of CBT interventions for OCD.

column36: Predictors of Arsenic and Breast Cancer Risk
column37: Arsenic is a bona fide carcinogen; however, data linking arsenic exposure and breast cancer is inconclusive. Human exposure to this metallic element can originate from many sources, such as specific occupations (e.g., working within a mine), consumption of contaminated food (e.g., rice), or ingestion of contaminated water (e.g., well water). In a large prospective study of 1,702 Polish women, our team recently reported a significant 12- fold increased risk of breast cancer among women with the highest quartile of total circulating blood arsenic (HR Q4 vs. ref.= 12.72; 95%CI 3.89-41.57, P trend < 0.0001). This strong, dose-dependent finding suggests that blood arsenic status is a strong predictor for breast cancer, underscoring the importance of identifying potential sources of arsenic exposure. Thus, the overall study goal is to (1) identify predictors of circulating blood arsenic and (2) determine any trends in the variation of arsenic levels (and its intermediates) between people. To fulfill these objectives, a cross-sectional, prospective investigation will be conducted with the 1,702 women in the pre-existing Polish cohort. Each will be asked to complete a study-specific questionnaire, identifying common sources of arsenic, and provide a venous blood sample. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy will determine total blood arsenic levels and high-performance liquid chromatography will indicate levels of metabolic intermediates. Multivariate regression will be used to evaluate the predictors of arsenic in the blood and breast cancer risk. These results will identify the predictors of circulating total blood arsenic, indicating an important time point for intervention and potential population health strategies to reduce the risk of breast cancer incidence.

column36: Assessing the association between laboratory-confirmed seasonal influenza during pregnancy and health outcomes in early childhood
column37: Pregnant women and young infants are considered to be a high-risk groups for severe influenza disease. For these reasons, influenza immunization during pregnancy is recommended to prevent influenza in the mothers as well as the newborns, who are protected for several months after birth. The developing fetal immune and neurological systems may be sensitive to in-utero exposures such as maternal infection which later affects function and ongoing development. The World Health Organization examined the consequences of maternal influenza infection on fetal and birth outcomes. They found evidence that severe maternal 2009 pandemic H1N1 influenza disease increased the risk of preterm birth and fetal death; however, there were few studies that assessed the risks from seasonal influenza. Therefore our study will investigate if infants born to women who have seasonal influenza during pregnancy are at higher risk for adverse immune-mediated (i.e. infectious and atopic diseases) and neurological (i.e. autism spectrum disorder) health outcomes in early childhood. This retrospective cohort study will be done using the BORN Ontario birth registry database and provincial health administrative databases from 2010-2015. The developmental origin of health and disease (DOHaD) hypothesis states that exposures during gestation can positively or negatively influence health during childhood and beyond. Little is known about pediatric health outcomes that may be associated with confirmed seasonal influenza during pregnancy, and this lack of evidence may be a barrier to achieving higher influenza vaccine uptake among pregnant women. The goal is that these findings will help strengthen the evidence base underlying the potential impacts of influenza immunization during pregnancy.

column36: An efficient CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in system to restore full-length dystrophin
column37: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is a neuromuscular disease causing progressive muscle loss. At 10 years old, patients lose independent movement, with fatal respiratory or cardiac complications in their mid to late teens. Mutations in the gene for dystrophin, a protein essential to muscle integrity, cause DMD. There is no cure, with current and proposed treatments lacking effectiveness or feasibility. CRISPR/Cas9 is a gene editing protein that could fix dystrophin, as it can be programmed to cut DNA at a specific spot, opening an editing window during DNA repair. 70% of DMD patients have lost critical DNA in their dystrophin gene. Therefore, this project aims to reinsert the DNA precisely where it was lost. However, insertion efficiency is low, and worse in non-dividing cells like muscle. Recent work shows a DNA repair system called homologous-mediated end joining (HMEJ) is highly efficient for insertions in non-dividing cells, reaching rates of 58% in the neurons of live mice. HMEJ works by attaching additional DNA to the lost dystrophin DNA that will be inserted. This newly added DNA is identical to the area in the genome where the insertion will occur. Insertion efficiency is significantly increased because of the matching sequences. After CRISPR/Cas9 cuts the genome at the desired spot, the insertion process takes place to repair the dystrophin gene. Muscles should then produce fully functional dystrophin, preventing degradation. The threshold to cure DMD is surprisingly low, requiring only 15% of normal dystrophin levels. Today, human gene editing is prohibited. But should that change, and this gene therapy can restore dystrophin, most DMD patients would have a future to look toward.

Recent studies are suggesting that nutritional strategies are related to differences in the GI microbiota of VLBW infants; however, these studies excluded infants with the major morbidities such as necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and late-onset sepsis (LOS), and are limited by small sample sizes and cross-sectional study designs. Therefore, it is unclear whether in-hospital nutrition practices and the GI microbiota of infants born <1250 g with major morbidities across initial hospitalization. It is hypothesized that the relationship between nutritional practices and the GI microbiota of VLBW infants will differ depending on a morbidity diagnosis.

column36: The Impact of Self Awareness of Injury Intervention on Depression in a Traumatic Brain Injury Population
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of disability in Canada. Self awareness of injury (SAI), which is the ability of the patient to identify deficits in their own brain function, can be impaired in individuals with TBI. This impairment can create a reluctance to participate in post-injury therapy which can hinder an individual's treatment and recovery from injury. Therefore, it is imperative to treat impaired SAI in rehabilitation programs in order to improve patient outcome. Limited research has been done on the influence that changing level of awareness of injury through intervention has on other outcomes such as mood. Depression, a condition that is already highly comorbid with TBI, has been shown to occur more frequently in individuals with higher levels of SAI. Therefore, an issue arises in the treatment of impaired SAI. Could intervention to treat SAI inadvertently increase depressive symptomology in patients? The proposed research will investigate if an intervention for impaired SAI can lead to higher depressive symptomology by assessing individuals before and after SAI intervention. The SAI intervention will be based on a previous treatment that significantly increased SAI levels in a brain injury population. Outcome variables of SAI level, depressive symptoms, executive functioning, and illness perception will be analyzed. If SAI intervention does lead to an increase in depression levels, further investigation into treatment and shaping new intervention strategies would be warranted. There is great significance to the proposed research as determining a link between SAI intervention and depressive symptoms could provide a new target of treatment for individuals in neurorehabilitation settings.

column36: Improving extraneural electrode recording selectivity through application of adaptive algorithms
column37: Signal recordings obtained from the nervous system can be used to create commands for electronic prosthetic devices and to regulate the activity of the nervous system. These signals can be applied to treat amputees and spinal cord injury patients. One method of collecting these signals is using electrodes that surround the outside of the nerve (non-nerve penetrating or extraneural). Signals may also be collected using electrodes which penetrate the nerve (nerve penetrating or intraneural) and while this method provides more distinct recordings, nerve penetrating electrodes are not suitable for long-term use and often cause adverse events. Two major factors that make recordings from extraneural electrodes less reliable over time are shifts in the position of the electrodes and a buildup of tissue around the nerve fibers. We believe that we can significantly improve recording from extraneural electrodes by developing a set of rules or procedures (i.e., an algorithm) that take these factors into consideration. Using a computer model of a rat nerve, we will identify signal changes resulting from these two major factors and create algorithms that compensate for these changes through machine learning techniques. Applying these new algorithms will result in improved control signals and more effective assistive technologies for a variety of clinical populations, including amputees and those living with spinal cord injuries.

column36: The genetic and environmental determinants of weight gain in undergraduate students
column37: Obesity has reached epidemic proportions globally and is a major risk factor for diseases like type II diabetes, and several cardiovascular diseases. The high prevalence of obesity presents a serious public health concern and economic burden on society. Literature suggests that obesity development may have age-sensitive periods. In Canada, the prevalence of obesity increases till the age of 65. Previous studies suggest that young adulthood may be a critical period of obesity development. When comparing the prevalence of obesity/overweight in Canadian adults from 2010 to 2014, the largest increase was observed among individuals aged 18-19. The common perception of Freshman 15 suggests that undergraduate students in university gain 15 pounds during their first year of study. However, previous studies estimate a more modest weight gain at 3-5 pounds. The etiology of obesity is complex and multi-factorial involving an interplay between genetic, biological, lifestyle, and social factors. The factors influencing weight in young adults have yet to be described. The GENEiUS study aims to investigate the genetic and environmental determinants of weight evolution in undergraduate students at McMaster University. The study aims to recruit 2000 students for assessment every 6 months over 4 years. A saliva sample is collected for DNA analysis of each participant and hair samples for analysis of stress levels (cortisol). Four anthropometric measures are taken: height, weight, waist circumference, and hip circumference. Self-reported nutritional information is collected with a validated food frequency questionnaire. Information regarding lifestyle and medical history is collected via self-reported questionnaire. Weight evolution will be assessed in first set of cumulative 4-year data.

column36: The Feasibility of Remotely-Delivered Physical Environmental Engagement Training in Moderate-Severe Brain Injury
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading causes of global death and disability. Recently, TBI has begun to be reconceptualised as a chronic condition causing cognitive decline over time. Progressive loss of brain volume among TBI patients leads to impaired function in areas such as attention, memory and balance. Environmental enrichment (EE), referring to exposure of the brain to novel stimuli, is a method for reducing this loss of brain structure and function. Previous research has shown that EE improves behavioural, cognitive and physical outcomes in TBI patients. Although most studies focus on cognitive EE, such as brain games, there is evidence to suggest that physical EE, such as light exercise or motor skill training may provide similar benefits. Following discharge, significant barriers often prevent access to EE in chronic stage TBI patients living at home, such as lack of community resources or transportation, especially for those in remote communities. Online self-administered cognitive training has been identified as a possible solution to EE inaccessibility. While remotely-delivered cognitive EE appears promising, the feasibility of similar online resources providing remote delivery physical EE is currently unknown. The proposed study will explore the feasibility of online physical EE training for moderate-severe TBI patients. The online resource will be designed based on previous remotely-delivered physical rehab programs that have shown positive outcomes in TBI patients. Feasibility will be assessed via the level of engagement of participants with the resource. Ultimately, the development of online training resources for both cognitive and physical EE provides an accessible therapeutic intervention to reduce cognitive deterioration in TBI patients.

column37: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) is a very rare disease (referred to as "orphan disease") characterized by extremely high levels of plasma levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and severe atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (heart attacks, sudden cardiac death) in youth. We have established a national registry for FH in Canada at 19 academic centers across Canada with more than 200 physicians and health care participants (www.FHCanada.net). The registry uses a centralized, secure web-based database. From the onset, we created smaller registries for orphan lipoprotein disorders under an initiative entitled: Systems and Molecular Approaches to Severe Hyperlipidemias which includes HoFH and other orphan diseases of lipids. We have previously published several systematic reviews and meta-analysis on heterozygous FH. Collectively these activities demonstrate the productivity of the FH Canada network, and the ability to leverage the significant national expertise that exists in this topic into both new health-related knowledge about this condition, and the translation of this knowledge into practice. The track record to-date establishes the ability of this team of national investigators to collaborate productively and efficiently. The current proposal builds on the existing infrastructure of the FH Canada National Registry, and the network of engaged experts, to develop a world-class national research effort in HoFH.

column36: Best Practices During the First 72 Hours of Geriatric Trauma Care
column37: The population of those aged 65 and older is increasing and therefore, the number of patients requiring care for life-threatening injuries is also rising. Guidelines recommend consultation with a geriatrics medicine team within the first 72 hours of a patient's admission for older adults with traumatic injuries. The goal of our project is to introduce a program to address the needs of older adults with severe injuries within the first 72 hours of hospital admission. We believe that by taking these actions to improve older adult trauma patient care within the first 72 hours of admission, we will reduce complications and length of stay in hospital in these patients.

column36: The Canada lymph node sonographic score as an evaluation of mediastinal lymph node malignancy for lung cancer: a feasibility study
column37: For clinical stage I Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, surgical resection is usually the preferred method of treatment. However, to confirm patients are eligible for surgery, current guidelines mandate preoperative mediastinal lymph node (LN) staging through Endobronchial Ultrasound (EBUS). Unfortunately, up to 42% of biopsies conducted during EBUS provide inconclusive pathology results. This is especially true in patients with benign appearing LNs on preoperative CT or PET/CT scans. To improve the accuracy of mediastinal staging for those with negative PET/CT scans, researchers have created the Canada Lymph Node Score (CLNS). The CLNS is a four-point score based on the presence of four ultrasonographic features observed during EBUS. Together these features form a criteria of malignancy for the LN. Scores from 0 to 2 out of 4 imply low chance of malignancy in LN, while scores of 3 to 4 out of 4 describe high chance of malignancy. If a LN appears benign on PET/CT and its CLNS is less or equal to 2, then it is considered "triple negative". For "triple negative" LNs, we hypothesize that they do not need to be biopsied because there is a very low probability of malignancy (less than 5% chance). To test the proposed hypothesis, a randomized control trial (RCT) is required. However, prior to warranting such a large scale trial, a feasibility study is needed to determine the adaptability of the CLNS within clinical setting. This study aims to evaluate the recruitment rate and differences in frequency of biopsies, procedure length, amount of sedation given, number of samples obtained, costs and diagnostic results between systematic sampling and targeted sampling of LNs. With these outcomes a better understanding of the practicability of this novel score will be achieved.

column36: Exploring the Determinants of Diabetes Control among Canadians with Pregestational Diabetes
column37: In Canada, diabetes occurs in 5.6% of pregnancies, a rate that doubled in 10 years. Globally, diabetes occurs in 16.9% of pregnancies, representing 21.4 million births. Diabetes in pregnancy is associated with morbidity and mortality, such as miscarriage, stillbirth, and congenital malformations. Its costs to the healthcare system are also on the rise, with estimates of yearly medical costs increasing by $636 million. When optimal glucose levels are achieved complications are reduced, yet only a small percentage of women meet appropriate glucose targets. There is a lack of evidence that explores the impact of maternal factors on glycemic control, and predictors of optimal control remain unknown. This project aims to answer: What maternal factors are associated with optimal diabetes control in pregnancy? Can diabetes control in pregnancy be predicted by maternal factors?Can specific factors be modified to achieve optimal diabetes control in pregnancy? We hypothesize that an interaction of maternal factors such as social support and self-care behaviours influence whether or not a woman achieves optimal diabetes control, measured by hemoglobin A1C. To answer the research questions, a prospective cohort study has been undertaken. A cohort of over 100 women with pregestational diabetes, have been identified and self-reported data were obtained, including demographic characteristics, diabetes self-care behaviours, patient reported outcomes, and hemoglobin A1C during the first, second, and third trimesters. As there is little evidence that exists about what factors are important in achieving optimal diabetes control in pregnancy, we hope to provide insight into the complexities of diabetes control in pregnancy and support clinicians in improving perinatal outcomes in Canada.

column36: Engineering probes and cancer therapeutics from epigenetic reader libraries Engineering probes and cancer therapeutics from epigenetic reader libraries
column37: Epigenetics is an emerging field in science that focuses on the regulation of DNA through modifications of DNA binding proteins. These modifications, or epigenetic markers, are added to DNA binding proteins by proteins called "epigenetic writers". Depending on the marker added, different changes to local DNA accessibility can result causing alterations to gene expression via gene silencing or gene activation. "Epigenetic readers" also play an important role in gene expression. They act like interpreters and translate specific epigenetic modifications into changes in cellular processes such as DNA repair and replication. The study of epigenetic modifications is important because a wide range of cancers (e.g. lymphoma and pancreatic cancer) can be caused by misregulation of epigenetic writers and readers. Although links between epigenetics and cancer are becoming more evident, the specific mechanisms behind these processes remain largely undiscovered. And thus, the rationale to study the role of epigenetic modifications in cancers has only grown. Unfortunately, the scarcity of molecular probes has become a roadblock for those studying epigenetics and the specific mechanisms that cause epigenetically-linked cancers. Through my research, I aim to create libraries containing billions of protein variants engineered from epigenetic readers that are already known to bind to specific epigenetic markers involved in lymphoma and pancreatic cancer. These libraries will be subsequently screened for protein variants that bind both more tightly and precisely to their target epigenetic markers. Finally, these proteins will be tested as novel probes to compare epigenetic markers between healthy and cancer cells and further engineered into novel cancer therapeutics.

column36: Examining oxidative stress and white matter hyperintensities in mild vascular cognitive impairment
column37: Mild vascular cognitive impairment (mVCI) is the precursor stage to vascular cognitive impairment and is associated with a higher risk of the most common forms of dementia: Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia. mVCI is marked by early cognitive deficits arising from cerebrovascular burden and is linked to brain white matter damage that is distinguished on neuroimaging scans as white matter hyperintensities. This condition is more prevalent in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD). Research has also shown that patients with CAD exhibit elevated levels of oxidative stress, which occurs when the body's antioxidant defenses are overcome by reactive oxygen species produced by metabolic reactions. Oxidative stress has been linked to the progressive loss of neurons and cognitive decline in aging populations. In the brain, glutathione (GSH) works to clear up excess reactive oxygen species. Patients in early stages of Alzheimer's disease exhibited lower levels of GSH in the blood. However, few studies have explored the relationship between oxidative stress and white matter hyperintensities. The proposed study will explore the relationship between GSH levels and damage to brain white matter in patients with CAD. Older adults entering a cardiac rehabilitation program will be administered cognitive tests to determine their level of cognitive deficits. They will then have a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of their brain to quantify white matter hyperintensities and a blood draw to analyze GSH levels. A novel approach of magnetic resonance spectroscopy will be used to quantify brain GSH levels in vivo. Understanding how oxidative stress relates to early brain changes can influence discovery of new therapies to mitigate the development of dementia in older adults.

column37: L'epidemie du virus de l'immunodefience humaine (VIH), virus responsable du syndrome d'immunodeficience acquise (SIDA), est un probleme majeur de sante publique mondiale. La therapie antiretrovirale (ART) est actuellement le traitement le plus utilise contre le VIH et bien qu'elle ait permis d'ameliorer grandement la qualite de vie des personnes infectees, elle ne permet pas d'eliminer le virus. En effet, le VIH est tres ruse; sous therapie, il reste en << dormance >> dans ce qu'on appelle des reservoirs viraux. Ainsi, meme si les personnes traitees peuvent sembler gueries, c'est-a-dire qu'elles ont peu de virus dans leur sang et n'ont aucun symptome, le virus reapparait rapidement si la personne infectee arrete son traitement. Les reservoirs viraux sont donc le principal obstacle a l'elimination du virus. Plus le reservoir viral est grand et plus le virus sera difficile a eliminer. Il est connu que le delai entre l'infection et l'initiation de la therapie ainsi que divers facteurs genetiques sont determinants pour la taille du reservoir viral chez une personne infectee. Recemment, nous avons mis en evidence un nouveau facteur associe a la taille de ce reservoir : l'age du patient . Notre objectif principal est donc d'identifier les mecanismes responsables de la difference de taille des reservoirs entre les personnes jeunes et plus agees. Une comprehension approfondie de ces mecanismes permettrait de developper de nouvelles approches therapeutiques visant a reduire suffisamment la taille des reservoirs viraux pour que le virus soit controle par le systeme immunitaire lors de l'arret de la therapie et ainsi permettre aux personnes infectees de vivre sans traitement. Il s'agit donc d'un des plus grands defis de la medecine moderne.

column36: Developing a novel allogeneic chimeric antigen receptor-modified double-negative T cell (CAR-DNT) therapy for the treatment of chemotherapy-resistant CD4+ T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL)
column37: Lasting remissions from induction chemotherapy for T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) are rare and long-term survival for relapsed patients is below 7%. There is an unmet need for a safer and more effective treatment for chemotherapy-resistant T-ALL. Chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cell (CAR-T) therapies are effective but current CAR-carrier cells still face issues with fratricide, graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), in vivo tumorigenesis and short persistence. Our group initially characterized double negative T cells (DNTs), a subset of mature CD3+CD4-CD8- T cells, and developed a protocol to expand them ex vivo from the peripheral blood of healthy donors. We have extensively characterized the safety and efficacy of allogeneic DNTs as an adoptive cellular therapy (ACT) for leukemia. Also, DNTs fulfill the requirements of an off-the-shelf (OtS) ACT including donor-independent function, no GvHD, cryo-preservability, resistance to host-versus-graft (HvG) rejection and no observed off-tumor toxicity. The objective of this project is to develop a safer and more effective ACT against T-ALL by combining the potency of CAR technology with the OtS properties of DNTs. In particular, we aim to take advantage of using DNTs as a cell vehicle by targeting the CD4 T-lineage molecule found on T-ALL. In addition to fratricide-free manufacturing of CAR4-DNTs, we hypothesize they will not cause GvHD and will have a tolerable degree of on-target, off-tumor toxicity. This project will determine the safety and efficacy of CAR4-DNTs against CD4+ T-ALL, a potential novel therapeutic option for chemotherapy-resistant T-ALL. Also, these studies will provide insight into the generalized application of DNTs as an OtS CAR-vehicle beyond ALL.

column37: Participer a des activites cognitivement stimulantes protege contre le declin cognitif associe au vieillissement et contribue a retarder les symptomes de la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) (Stern, 2009). Les entrainements cognitifs sont donc interessants dans le developpement d'outils preventifs, non pharmacologiques, contre le declin cognitif associe a cette maladie. Ceux-ci provoqueraient des effets durables sur les performances cognitives ciblees 5 ans apres l'intervention (Willis & al., 2006) et contribueraient a creer une protection cognitive a un age avance (Belleville & al., 2018). Toutefois, ils sont tres varies et des etudes montrent qu'ils pourraient avoir un impact tres different sur le cerveau en fonction de leur contenu (Belleville & al., 2014) et des caracteristiques des patients. L'objectif de ce projet est de decortiquer les effets cerebraux qu'engendre un entrainement de la memoire associative reposant sur l'apprentissage strategique ou la pratique repetee. Evaluer si les caracteristiques individuelles (genotype, education, age, statut clinique) modifient l'impact des interventions sur le cerveau est aussi une visee de l'etude. 50 aines atteints d'un trouble cognitif leger et 50 aines avec une plainte subjective de memoire seront assignes au hasard a deux types d'entrainement cognitif (strategique et non strategique). L'effet de ces 2 entrainements sera evalue a plusieurs reprises par des seances impliquant des tests cognitifs et par l'imagerie cerebrale. L'identification des caracteristiques favorisant l'efficacite des entrainements permettra d'intervenir de maniere precoce sur les personnes les plus a risque de developper vers la maladie d'Alzheimer avec l'espoir d'en ralentir cette progression.

column36: Developing a mouse model of CTE: Time Course of GSK3B and Tau Phosphorylation
column37: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease that develops from repetitive impacts sustained to the head causing concussions. This has been observed in both athletes, especially those involved in contact sports, and military personnel. CTE is characterized as a tauopathy due to the involvement of hyperphosphorylated tau that leads to aggregates, fibrils, and tangles within the brain. It has been proposed that a known tau kinase, glycogen synthase kinase 3-beta (GSK3B), is involved with the abnormal phosphorylation of tau. These mechanisms lead to the degeneration of brain tissue which in turn causes the development of cognitive deficits. The purpose of this study is to explore the time course of the activation of GSK3 and tau phosphorylation, as well as to determine if the administration of a GSK3 inhibitor will deter the development of these cognitive deficits. Mice will be subject to multiple mild traumatic brain injuries using a controlled cortical impact device to mimic concussions seen in humans. Afterwards selected brain structures will be extracted in order to conduct protein assays and western blots to determine the time course of activation of GSK3B. It is of the utmost importance that an animal model for CTE be developed in order to better understand and observe the mechanisms involved.

column37: High grade prostate cancer (PCa) patients are at risk of developing metastases despite radiotherapy. A study found that patients treated with brachytherapy (BT) and EBRT (external beam radiotherapy) had a lower rate of metastases compared to EBRT alone1. It is hypothesized that the high radiation of BT results in significant tumour death, priming the immune system to recognize tumour cells. High risk patients (BT+EBRT (n=25) and EBRT (n=25)) will have blood drawn before, during, and after treatment. Changes in peripheral immune cell composition will be assessed and correlated with patient response. This will provide evidence that BT induces a distinct immunological response compared to EBRT alone. High grade PCa patients are also at risk of recurrence following radiotherapy. A study discovered that tumours made resistant to cisplatin were more responsive to PDL1 checkpoint inhibitor than parental tumours2. The enhanced PDL1 blockade sensitivity was a result of greater mutational load, generating neoantigens which triggered an immune response. A mouse PCa cell line will be treated with radiation to generate radiorecurrent cells. Mice will be transplanted with parental or radiorecurrent cells, administered PDL1 inhibitor or control, and mock irradiated or irradiated. Blood will be drawn from mice before, during, and after radiation and lymphocyte composition will be measured. Whole exome sequencing will allow comparison of mutational load between in radiorecurrent cells and parentals. The proposed research can potentially identify new therapeutic biomarkers and allow usage of immune checkpoint therapy as a novel approach to salvage radiorecurrent tumours. 1Kishan et al., Eur Urol 2017 71(5):766-773 2Kuczynski et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2018 17(4):869-882

column36: Effects of Maxillomandibular Advancement Surgery for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea on Oropharynx Volume & Tissue Displacement
column37: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is a chronic and increasingly common sleep-related breathing disorder in which the airway is either partially or completely closed, resulting in hypopneic (low respiratory rate) or apneic (cessation of breathing) episodes. In the last 8 years, OSA diagnosis has jumped from 3%-7% of the Canadian population, and 25% of Canadians are at high risk of developing the disorder. OSA is associated with long-term health effects, such as cardiovascular disease, neurocognitive changes, diabetes, and even early death. Initial treatment of OSA is typically non-invasive treatment devices. However, if such treatments are ineffective or the patient is non-compliant, surgical treatment may be considered. Maxillomandibular Advancement (MMA) surgery, in which the mandible and maxilla are moved forward, is one of the most effective, safe, and long-term treatments from OSA. This treatment has a success rate of 96-100%, however a true mechanistic understanding of the procedure remains unclear. The proposed projects explores the relationship between the distance of the maxilla & mandible are advanced and the subsequent change in the airway. More specifically, this project aims to 1) determine the volumetric changes that occur incrementally during MMA and 2) to determine the movement of underlying tissues during the incremental MMA. This will be accomplished by marking the airway of cadavers with microbeads, performing the MMA surgery, obtaining CT images at 2mm incremental advancements, and analyzing both the volumetric change and tissue movement in the airway. This work will inform surgeons performing MMA produced by identifying the optimal distance for advancement with minimal alterations to the patient's anatomy.

column36: Mechanistic analysis of the mycobacterial CIII2CIV2 respiratory supercomplex by cryoEM
column37: Tuberculosis (TB), which was responsible for 1.6 million deaths in 2017 including 230 000 children, is caused by infection with the mycobacterial pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Antibiotics traditionally used to treat TB have given rise to drug-resistant forms of the disease, presenting an urgent need to produce new therapies. There are a number of proteins found in both human and mycobacterial cells that act as molecular machines to generate usable energy for cell growth and survival. A new generation of TB drugs works by exploiting structural differences between human and mycobacterial versions of these proteins. They specifically target the mycobacterial proteins to deplete the energy supply of the pathogen while minimizing damage to human cells. I will study the structure and mechanism of a key energy-generating protein in mycobacteria, the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex. CIII2CIV2 converts oxygen to water, using the energy released to pump protons across a membrane, thereby driving the production of chemical energy in the cell. This mycobacterial protein has different features from its human counterparts, making it vulnerable to drugs. I will isolate the supercomplex from a non-pathogenic species of mycobacteria and use high-resolution electron cryomicroscopy to image it at high resolution (~0.3 nm). I will then image the purified supercomplex at each step in its mechanism by controlling its access to oxygen and by adding chemicals that block the transfer of electrons. Finally, I will piece these structures together to create a movie that shows how the supercomplex couples the transfer of electrons to oxygen with proton pumping. This study will provide insight into fundamental principles of bioenergetics and accelerate the development of new TB drugs.

column36: Loneliness and social isolation in supportive living settings: A meeting to develop priorities and a grant
column37: As people age, a spectrum of care is required. This can include home care, assisted/supportive living (SL), and nursing home (NH) placement. Historically, when advanced levels of care were required, support was provided in NHs. Recently, SL has emerged as a more community-based and less costly alternative. Introduced to restrict or delay entry to NHs, SL is the fastest growing sector of continuing care in Canada and the United States. Provinces such as Alberta and British Columbia have been at the forefront of the SL expansion. Alberta has made major public investments in SL and consequently, has restricted investment in NHs. While this policy decision is meant to align with older adults' preferences and to reduce costs, there is little evidence to suggest the SL sector can meet older adults' needs or reduce costs. SL facilities have less staff, fewer skilled staff, and less recreation services than NHs. There is an expectation in SL facilities that residents have family or friends who can provide support (shopping, transportation, social). Little is known about SL residents who have insufficient quantity (social isolation) or quality (loneliness) relationships. Fewer staff, limited recreation services and an expectation for family involvement raises concerns about the quality of care and quality of life for socially isolated and/or lonely SL residents. The purpose of this proposed meeting is to bring together experts in SL and loneliness and social isolation. It will be the first step in establishing a program of research specifically targeted to studying these issues in continuing care settings. We plan to advance the science of loneliness and social isolation by bringing attention to the needs of individuals living in SL and similar continuing care settings. During this meeting we will establish priorities for the research program and prepare for the first grant proposal to be submitted to the fall CIHR project grant competition in 2020.

column37: Indigenous peoples do not have the same level of health and wellness as non-Indigenous peoples. They have higher rates of chronic diseases, infection, suicide, poverty, and mental health issues. This is not surprising given the history of colonization in Canada- the epidemics, residential school, and the 60s scoop. The roots for these health inequalities is related to the historical and current relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. The Truth and Reconciliation Calls to Action recognizes and acknowledges the necessity of improving relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples as the foundation for reconciliation. The goal of this Research Program is to create the opportunity for personal, community, and collective healing, ultimately transform relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. This action oriented Program will be guided by an Indigenous Advisory Committee and Indigenous worldviews - The Seven Sacred Teachings and the Medicine Wheel. These Indigenous values and teachings will ensure a holistic approach throughout this Program. This Indigenous philosophy will guide the mentoring of nursing students and the foundation to address reconciliation in the College of Nursing, USask. By introducing and teaching Indigenous values, all Canadians will have the opportunity to learn how to live in harmony with each other and with Mother Earth. The Program will use both Indigenous and Western ways to address and evaluate the impact of mentorship with Indigenous students and will formalize an important first step towards collaborative reconciliation in the College of Nursing and on campus at the USask.

column36: Promoting Indigenous health equity and culturally safe health care through decolonizing nursing education and practice
column37: Health inequities still persist for Indigenous Peoples in Canada. One of the root causes of these inequities is systemic racism, resulting from ongoing effects of Canada's long history of colonialism. Ongoing colonial beliefs about and attitudes towards Indigenous people influence the ways in which they are treated in the health care system today. Consequently, many Indigenous people do not trust mainstream healthcare services and do not feel safe using them. Indigenous patients are more likely to be diagnosed at a later stage of disease, to discontinue or avoid treatment. Understanding how to create structural change through actively counteracting racism and racialized ways of interacting with Indigenous peoples at individual and organizational level within health care systems is essential for creating a more inclusive, equitable, and healthier society. This Indigenous Research Chair in Nursing will promote Indigenous health equity and culturally safe health care through decolonizing nursing education and practice. The objectives of the Chair are to, 1) advance knowledge on the development and evaluation of interventions aiming at decolonizing nursing education and practice, 2) mobilize knowledge on approaches and interventions to foster health equity and culturally safe health care for Indigenous Peoples, 3) build Indigenous research capacity of students, mentees, and researchers in culturally safe health care and Indigenous health equity. This Chair will enable Indigenous and non-Indigenous researchers, stakeholders and practitioners to co-construct knowledge on the best approaches for promoting Indigenous health equity and culturally safe nursing education and practice. It will contribute to building local capacity of Faculties, Schools, and Universities to decolonize their education programs, and will provide tools to decision makers and policy-makers working in regional health authorities to integrate a cultural safety approach to nursing and health care.

column37: Exercise is an evidence-based self-management strategy that benefits all cancer survivors (CS). However, the majority of research, and the limited development of evidence-based clinical or community programs in exercise and cancer, has been conducted almost exclusively in urban academic and clinical settings. Very limited implementation in "hard to reach" CS, such as those in rural or non-urban environments, has occurred. There are unique features of the rural environment that are significant barriers to cancer care in general, and to supportive cancer care resources in particular, such as: geographic diversity, isolation, limited access/travel distances to resources and facilities, and lack of trained personnel to implement survivorship services,. Rural CS (RCS), or those living in non-urban settings (defined as <100,000 in population), report higher cancer burden from diagnosis through treatment and into survivorship (i.e., greater symptom burden). This burden is associated with inequitable access to supportive cancer care resources, including exercise programs, resulting in RCS experiencing more negative effects after treatment than their urban counterparts and being overall less healthy. Objectives: To disseminate, implement, and assess the effectiveness of our Exercise Oncology Survivorship (EOS) partnership model to increase the reach and delivery of exercise programs to RCS. Reaching more RCS with an exercise program will enhance cancer survivorship, providing fitness, health, and psychosocial benefits. Significance: Given our previous implementation success, we will extend the reach of our EOS partnership model across rural Canada and change the exercise levels of RCS. Our impact will include a sustainable environment to support exercise as a supportive cancer care for RCS towards greater quality of life.

column37: Because of advances in treatment, survival rates for pediatric brain tumours have improved dramatically in the last 25 years: currently there are at least 30,000 survivors in North America. Currently, there are no effective medical therapies to help brain recovery and reduce disability in paediatric cancer. We hope to change this. The drug metformin can promote rescue of cognition and brain growth in animal models by activating stem cells in the brain: we have found that it is safe and feasible to use in children treated for a brain tumor and may improve cognition. We seek to ask if this is indeed true by using a multi-site clinical trial to test the efficacy of metformin treatment for cognitive recovery in children and adolescents treated for medulloblastoma which requires aggressive therapy leaving survivors with significant cognitive impairment. If we find that metformin promotes cognitive improvement and brain growth in pediatric survivors of medulloblastoma, then this may offer a viable therapeutic approach that may significantly improve the quality of life of these vulnerable patients - and provide a model for treatment of late effects in other pediatric cancers.

column36: Deciphering recurrence of glioblastoma for precision medicine using multi-omics data integration
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most lethal form of brain tumor. On average, patients survive only 15 months after diagnosis because most tumors inevitably recur after surgery. Intra-tumor heterogeneity is believed to cause this dismal outcome: GBMs are complex tumors that are made up of many different types of cells. Some of these cells likely escape surgery and chemotherapy and evolve into secondary tumors that ultimately kill patients. However, the mechanisms of recurrence remain unknown. In this project, we build genetic maps of primary and recurrent GBMs to understand tumor recurrence and to find novel target genes for further study. We will first perform genome sequencing of primary and recurrent GBMs from the same patients. We will build the largest dataset of this kind by also collecting and analyzing data from existing studies. We will then map distinct cell populations in the tumors and statistically predict which mutations in these cells likely caused tumor recurrence. column36: Preparing to survive: improving outcomes for young women with breast cancer
column37: Women aged 40 and under with breast cancer experience poorer outcomes, havea wide spectrum of supportive needs and face unique survivorship issues compared to their older counterparts. Comprising approximately 5.4% of all women diagnosed with breast cancer, research and supports are lacking for this population. To address this, we created RUBY (Reducing the bUrden of Breast cancer in Young women), one of the world's largest prospective cohorts of women with young-onset breast cancer. To date, we have enrolled over 1000 women from 32 sites across Canada at the time of cancer diagnosis following them through treatment and into the survivorship period. Through RUBY, we have identified a number of unique survivorship gaps, including high levels of anxiety at diagnosis and beyond especially given extended hormonal therapies, marital and motherhood challenges, and social isolation. Specific, accessible interventions are required, but are currently lacking. ICAN Survive, is a promising self-management, on-line intervention for patients with cancer designed to address global survivorship issues at diagnosis and beyond. Key areas of need include regaining balance/dealing with diagnosis, coping with treatment and side-effects, management of anxiety and depression, fatigue management, sexuality and relationships. The ICAN intervention aims to build self management skills through guided training and education, however does not focus on the specific needs of young women. Thus, we propose to modify the ICAN intervention in collaboration with young onset survivors and evaluate the modified tool (ICAN-RUBY) for effectiveness. We are uniquely positioned to develop this young women specific intervention given the direct knowledge of gaps identified to date from existing RUBY cohort. We will leverage established RUBY study infrastructure with a proven track record of recruitment, to evaluate the effectiveness of the ICAN-RUBY tool in an embedded randomized trial.

column36: Access to precision therapies for young people with cancer: Developing a policy framework to guide technology assessment and public funding in Canada
column37: Cancer remains the leading cause of disease-related death in Canadian children, adolescents and young adults (CAYA). Advances in understanding the genetic causes of cancer have opened up new treatment possibilities tailored to individual patients. Canada is a leader in precision medicine for childhood cancer: PRecision Oncology For Young peopLE (PROFYLE), a unique national precision oncology initiative, will determine the entire genomic sequence of tumours in CAYA with hard-to-treat cancers in order to identify alterations that are potential targets for new drugs. All CAYA with high-risk cancers in Canada, regardless of where they live, are eligible to take part in this project. However, the potential health system impacts of PROFYLE, and precision oncology more broadly, are not well understood. Many countries are grappling with how best to incorporate precision medicine innovations, including new expensive cancer drugs, into existing health care budgets. If precision medicine initiatives are to achieve lasting impact in Canada's publicly funded health care system, sound knowledge to guide their implementation is required. The overall objective of this project is to understand the policy and regulatory challenges of access to precision cancer therapies for CAYA in Canada. We will achieve this objective through a rigorous program of qualitative research that: analyzes and compares policies, regulations and funding of precision therapies for CAYA in different international contexts, and generates a policy framework and options to guide access to precision therapies for Canadian CAYA with cancer. These data will provide policymakers with evidence-informed considerations for the design and implementation of policies to govern fair and sustainable access to precision cancer therapies for young people.

column36: Innate and adaptive immune regulation in human type 1 diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease caused by the immune system mistakenly killing the cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone, insulin. Without insulin, the body cannot regulate blood sugar and this can be life threatening. Insulin can be taken by injection (by syringe or insulin pump), but this cannot replace the natural ability of the pancreas to make insulin only when it is needed, and at the exact level needed. Hence, people with T1D face a lifetime of fluctuating blood sugar and run the risk of life-threatening highs and lows. A true cure for T1D requires the immune system to be re-set so it no longer attacks the pancreas, combined with regeneration of the insulin-producing cells. In this project we aim to assemble a unique cross-Canada team of experts in immune cell biology and diabetes, in order to study specific aspects of how the immune system kills insulin-producing cells (called beta cells) to cause T1D. First, we will collect blood samples from individuals with T1D, another autoimmune disease, or healthy controls. We will then use these blood samples to study how different aspects of the immune system change over time in T1D vs non-T1D subjects, to learn how immune changes correlate with beta cell changes. Results will also be analyzed to determine whether any observed changes are different in males versus females. Second, we will study how three promising types of immune cell therapies might be applied in T1D. We will study how these immune cell therapies might affect beta cell function/regeneration and develop new ways to apply such therapies as a treatment for T1D. Overall, this research will explore several never-before-investigated aspects of T1D biology and take existing therapeutic concepts a step closer to use in the clinic. We will also create synergy with other on-going international studies in T1D and further strengthen our research capacity in this domain.

column36: Prediction and prevention of rheumatoid arthritis in First Nations People
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common autoimmune disease that causes progressive damage to the joints. It is known that individuals destined to develop future RA have autoantibodies (Ab) in their blood that are detectable months to years before the disease actually starts. Our studies have shown that RA is very common in some First Nations families, and that this is based on complex and unique interactions between genetic and environmental factors. Since 2005, we have worked in partnership with several First Nations communities and followed more than 750 unaffected family members of RA patients to determine their risk of developing future RA. To date, 20 individuals have developed RA, indicating a rate of ~1% new cases per year in the family members. We found that the detection of RA Abs in the blood does increase the risk of future RA, but we also show that most individuals with these Abs do NOT develop RA. This compelled us to find ways of predicting future RA that are based on a better understanding the immune system abnormalities that occur during this preclinical stage, and how these changes advance over time in some individuals but not others. With this knowledge, our ultimate aim is to find effective and safe ways to reduce RA risk in these predisposed individuals. Based on existing human and animal model data, we think that a dietary supplement of the spice turmeric, which contains the active ingredient curcumin, has the potential to safely reduce RA risk by modifying the immune changes that lead to RA. Omega-3 fish oils and adequate vitamin D blood levels seem to help the curcumin even further to achieve this. We therefore propose a clinical study to test this in individuals who have RA Abs but have not developed RA. We will use state-of-the-art immune tests to let us know whether there has been some correction of the abnormalities in treated individuals. We also hope to understand how First Nations People view clinical trials that aim to prevent disease

column36: Deciphering the therapy-driven molecular evolution of glioblastoma stem cells
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive form of brain cancer with an expected survival of only 15 months. Traditional models of cancer that considered GBM to be comprised of identical tumour cells have not led to improved therapies. New research, however, now shows that cancer is instead comprised of a mixture of biologically distinct cell types. Importantly, one subpopulation of cancer cells shares many of the biological properties of "stem cells", primitive cells that facilitate the growth and cell diversity of our body during early life. These "cancer stem cells" have now shown to be the driving force in GBM growth and highly resistant to traditional therapy. This may explain why drugs developed to target the overall cancer biology eventually lead to recurrence and failure. To overcome this, Dr. Diamandis' team wants to better understand the biology of these rare cells and apply it to design cancer stem cell-specific therapies. Dr. Diamandis' team will first study the biology of cancer stem cells directly in GBM patient tissue before and after therapy. To achieve this, Dr. Diamandis' team will carefully cut out clusters of cells from the rest of the tumour using a laser and analyze them with a technology known as mass spectrometry. This has major therapeutic implications as this tool quantifies proteins, the same molecules that drugs are designed to target. To complement this, they will bioengineer artificial human-like brain tissue structures called "organoids" to model important aspects of how GBM interacts with normal brain tissue elements to evade therapy. Finally, will take advantage of a technology called "artificial intelligence" to study vast amounts of patient data to uncover subtle but critical interactions between the various cells found in cancer. Together, these activities hope to help develop cancer stem cell-specific therapies that debilitate cancer growth in its roots and holds promise to provide effective therapies for GBM patients.
