column36: Advancing equitable access to diagnostics
column37: Accurate and timely diagnostic tests are essential for appropriate healthcare treatment. Laboratory tests, pathology tests (using microscopes) and medical imaging (using ultrasound, X-ray or more advanced technologies) are essential for accurate diagnosis. Without accurate diagnostic tests, there can be overuse of antibiotics leading to antimicrobial resistance, inappropriate treatment, wasted healthcare resources, worse health outcomes and, in the extreme, preventable patient deaths. Access to diagnostic tests is highly inequitable. Low- and middle-income countries do not yet have broad national health insurance coverage, and households have to pay out of pocket for diagnostic tests. Given resource constraints, patients often accept "presumptive treatment" i.e. without a proper diagnosis, in order to reserve their limited funds for treatment. Availability of diagnostic tests is also poorer in more remote and rural locations, leading to geographic inequities in access in all countries. There are solutions which can help make access to diagnostics more equitable. Point-of-care tests can improve access - as long as they are provided as part of a networked system to ensure tests used are appropriate and of good quality. Increased awareness and advocacy are vital. The World Health Organization's newly-developed Essential Diagnostics List can help to prioritize resources for key tests rather than allowing market forces to dictate availability. Teleradiology and telepathology can help improve access for more remote communities. International markets can be "shaped" to ensure a pipeline of affordable tests for low-resource environments The Lancet Commission on Diagnostics aims to bring together experts and stakeholders to identify solutions and to increase awareness of the importance of diagnostics as a key component of Universal Health Coverage, one of the Sustainable Development Goals. Grant support from CIHR will assist with a planning meeting in January 2020.

column36: Minimal clinically important difference using one-repetition maximum in COPD
column37: People with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) often have reduced muscle strength in their legs and chest compared to healthy people of the same age and sex. Weak muscles affect people's ability to carry-out activities of daily living, such as climbing stairs and washing dishes. Pulmonary rehabilitation is one of the most effective treatments to improve the muscle strength of people with COPD. However, it is difficult to interpret changes achieved in pulmonary rehabilitation due to lack of cut-off values to define a person's clinical improvement. We have estimated this cut-off value for leg extension and chest press muscle strength exercises in 51 people with COPD (44 men) with a mean age of 69 years old and moderate-to-severe disease. Participants performed 1 maximum repetition in a multigym, walked for 6 minutes in a 30-meter corridor and filled a scale about their shortness of breath, before and after a 12-week pulmonary rehabilitation program. We found that people who increased their leg muscle strength walked further on the 6 minutes test, but no relationships occurred between changes in leg strength and shortness of breath. Likewise, no relationships were found between changes in chest strength and changes on the 6 minutes test and shortness of breath. We concluded that improvements of 5.14kg for leg extension and of 6.25kg for chest press strength exercises might be clinical meaningful for patients after pulmonary rehabilitation. Studies enrolling more people are needed to consolidate these results.

column36: Asthma medication use during pregnancy: Does timing of asthma diagnosis matter?
column37: Asthma is the most frequent chronic disease that can complicate pregnancy, with a prevalence of approximately 13% worldwide. The use of asthma medications during pregnancy is recommended by international guidelines to achieve disease control. Women newly diagnosed with asthma prior to pregnancy might be able to incorporate medication use into their routine and persist after becoming pregnant. Women newly diagnosed with asthma during pregnancy may be less likely to use asthma medications due to fear of adverse effects or may be prescribed sub-optimal treatments due to physicians' fear of starting a new therapy during pregnancy. To date, no studies have evaluated the association between the timing of 'new-onset' asthma and asthma medication use during pregnancy. To address this knowledge gap, my study aimed to assess whether asthma medication use during pregnancy differs in women newly diagnosed with asthma during pregnancy compared to women newly diagnosed with asthma prior to pregnancy. We analyzed a large sample of pregnant women aged 15 to 45 years with new-onset asthma at any point in time 2 years prior to pregnancy or in the first 19 weeks of pregnancy. Asthma medication use during pregnancy was defined as filling at least 1 prescription starting 20 weeks of pregnancy (Cohort entry) until delivery considering the last filled prescription during 3 months prior to cohort entry. Newly diagnosed asthma during pregnancy is associated with more use of asthma medications compared to newly diagnosed asthma prior to pregnancy. Asthma diagnosed during pregnancy might be of a different phenotype and more likely to be severe in nature requiring more use of asthma medications. Women with asthma diagnosed prior to pregnancy might step-down in therapy during pregnancy once asthma control is sustained. This study can be used as an impetus for the development of an educational intervention to screen for asthma and initiate the appropriate therapy to reduce perinatal outcomes.

column36: Pathogenic Antibodies in Heparin-induced Thrombocytopenia Specifically Target an Immunodominant Region on Platelet Factor 4
column37: At least 30% of patients admitted into the hospital will be exposed to heparin. However, up to 5% of patients can have an adverse drug reaction against heparin where the body mounts an immune response and subsequently activates platelets. This disorder has been named heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Prompt diagnosis and treatments mitigate the life-threatening complications of HIT. There are numerous challenges to quick and reliable diagnosis of HIT. The golden standard for testing HIT can be done in only six laboratories across Canada. The test available in most hospitals have high false-positive rate due to recognize specifically the class of antibodies that cause HIT. To improve HIT diagnosis, we will identify the molecular differences between the antibodies that cause HIT and those that do not. This will be done through developing mutants of the HIT antibody target. Each mutant target will be tested for its ability to incite HIT in the presence of known HIT antibodies. This will allow us to identify a specific binding site for pathogenic HIT antibodies. From this, we can develop a new diagnostic assay that will be able to dictate whether the antibodies found in patients are specific in causing HIT. HIT can lead to the loss of limbs, strokes, or death if not diagnosed and treated in a timely manner. Therefore, the development of a rapid and accurate diagnostic test will improve the management of HIT patients. In addition to a robust application for diagnosing HIT, the binding site of pathogenic HIT antibodies identified by this research may also improve HIT therapeutics, as blocking of these targets may inhibit pathogenic antibodies in the circulation of HIT patients.

column36: The feasibility of implementing aerobic interval training in a cardiac rehabilitation setting
column37: Heart disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada. Despite the well-known benefits of cardiac rehabilitation (CR), adherence to CR remains low, particularly among women. Aerobic interval training (AIT) has received specific attention for the greater heart health benefits after completing the exercise program and may address the frequently cited barriers to participating in CR. Yet, health professionals have been reluctant to prescribe AIT for patients with heart disease due to safety and feasibility concerns. Over 10-weeks CR patients performed AIT which involved 4 minutes at high-intensity exercise, followed by 3 minutes of low intensity active recovery. Heart rate responses,number of sessions attended, number of patients who discontinued AIT, adverse events and patient-reported satisfaction and safety were collected to assess the feasibility of this style of training program. column36: Pleiotropic activation of endothelial function by angiotensin II receptor blockers is crucial to their protective anti-vascular remodeling effects
column37: The endothelium describes the layer of cells that line the inside of our blood vessels. The overall state of these cells, referred to as endothelial function, is regulated by the diffusible gas nitric oxide, a molecule that controls blood pressure and other functions. Therefore, the endothelium plays an important role in blood vessel health where a dysfunctional endothelium is associated with numerous cardiovascular diseases. Unfortunately, no drugs exist on the market today designed to improve endothelial function. We have recently discovered that a group of related blood pressure lowering medication are able to greatly increase endothelial function in a manner that is unrelated to their blood pressure lowering effects. In this study, we have shown that these drugs can also prevent the progression of aortic aneurysm, which is the dilation of the blood vessel that supplies blood from the heart to the rest of the body. Using a well established mouse model of aortic aneurysm, we have also shown that these blood pressure lowering drugs can prevent blood vessel remodeling by increasing the level of nitric oxide within the aortic wall, and not by lowering blood pressure. This study opens a new direction for the use of selected blood pressure lowering drugs at a much lower dose as a preventive therapy in many forms of vascular diseases where a dysfunctional endothelium is present.

column36: Let's Start Counting (and make it count)! A scoping review of the socioeconomic burden of rare genetic diseases
column37: There are more than 5600 single-gene disorders (diseases primary caused by one gene), and while they are individually rare, when considered as a group these diseases contribute significantly to illness, death, quality of life and healthcare costs. Rare genetic diseases affect both children and adults. They can impact schooling, job possibilities, and family life. In addition to the emotional burden, the cost of obtaining a diagnosis for a rare genetic disease may reach more than US$10,000 per person. Treatments may not be available, and when they are they can be very expensive. Previous estimates of the cost of caring for individuals with rare genetic diseases vary and do not capture the full socioeconomic burden (SEB) of these diseases. SEB can include four key cost areas: costs to the health care system (for example, specialist visits, tests and procedures); costs to other government sectors (for example, home care); costs to patients and families (for example, travel, mobility aids); and costs to individuals and society associated with work impacts (for example, time off work due to poor health or inability to work at all). We aim to identify the specific elements that should be measured within each cost area. We will review the studies in the literature on SEB of rare genetic diseases to see how well they capture the elements we identified. We will then describe what is missing, and provide suggestions for ways to do better studies in the future. This will allow future studies to produce clear and comparable estimates of the costs of individual diseases. In turn, this will mean we can add them together to understand the burden of these rare genetic diseases as a whole. This will help governments to make sure that fair decisions are being made about how to use Canada's scarce health care funds.

column36: Consensus meeting for dental guidelines development to optimize oral health in head and neck cancer survivors
column37: Head and neck cancer (HNC) is a curable cancer often treated with radiation therapy (RT). Unfortunately, RT can cause permanent oral problems that substantially impact quality of life (QOL) and increase cost on cancer survivors. Even with advanced technologies, normal tissues can receive high radiation doses which can damage salivary glands, skin, muscle bone and other tissues. The damage causes mouth sores, dry mouth, gum diseases, mouth infections, tooth decay, limitation in mouth opening, and even damage of the jaw bones also known as osteoradionecrosis (ORN). In Canada, current practice among dentists to reduce this damage involves a wide disparity in dental care offered HNC patients before RT. This means an HNC patient will most likely undergo different treatment depending on the choice of the dentist without clear data supporting these choices. Hypothesis: The oral health of head and neck cancer survivors can be maintained by evidence-based guidelines for dental interventions. This will be evaluated by creating evidence-based HNC dental guidelines and disseminate these guidelines throughout Canada. Summary guidelines will be created using a modified Delphi approach and a consensus meeting. These guidelines will be implemented across Canada starting with our network of Canadian dental clinics. Participants at the meeting will include dental oncologists from 9 Canadian oncology treatment centres. The team has over 250 years' cumulative clinical and research experience in the management of HNC survivors. Cancer survivors who have experienced life-threatening oral problems will be at the meeting. This research will generate guidelines that will reduce oral problems in HNC survivors, reduce oral care disparity, maximize their QOL and reduce financial burden. It may also highlight the significant need for a change in health policy, where optimal dental treatment in HNC should be funded by provincial health plans, in order to improve QOL in HNC survivors.

column36: Identification of polysialylated proteins in breast cancer and correlation with patient prognosis
column37: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in women worldwide. Metastasis, which is the spread of cancer cells from a primary tumor to other areas in the body, remains the main cause of patient related death, due to organ damage caused by the growing metastases.The 5-year survival of patients with localized, organ confined, breast cancer ranges from 98-72% dependent on stage, but this drops significantly to 27% once the tumor has metastasized. Awareness of the clinical importance of metastasis and our basic scientific understanding of the metastatic process has improved substantially over the past few decades. However, many aspects of metastasis are still not well defined and our ability to identify and treat patients at high risk for cancer recurrence is limited. This highlights the need for better prognostic markers to identify patients at high risk for developing metastatic disease. We have identified a novel sugar, or glycan, based prognostic marker in breast cancer and propose a project that will investigate expression on breast cancer patient tissue and in blood-plasma for use as a prognostic indicator. We also propose to identify the proteins carrying the glycan chains and determine if they have prognostic significance or correlate with any of the well-established clinical biomarkers of ER (estrogen receptor), PR (progesterone receptor) or HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2). Our work has potential to develop a breast cancer test that would provide evidence-based information capable of directing patient treatment to support important decisions about breast cancer treatment reducing the overtreatment of low-risk patients while providing aggressive treatments to high-risk patients.

column36: Measuring and understanding symptom burden among adolescents and young adults with cancer: A population-based study using routinely collected patient reported outcomes
column37: Adolescents and young adults (AYA) with cancer are neglected in cancer research, and often see doctors that do not have expertise in their unique issues. Cancer patients say it is important to control the symptoms that result from cancer or cancer treatment. Good symptom control is linked to better outcomes. Despite this, very few studies have looked at symptoms in AYA with cancer. Early evidence suggests that symptoms in AYA differ than in older patients. Our study will thus study cancer symptoms in Ontario AYA with cancer. We will study what kinds of symptoms are experienced and which AYA are at highest risk of the most severe symptoms. Across Ontario, symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and depression are routinely measured in cancer patients using the Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS). The resulting symptom scores are collected electronically and centrally, and can be tracked over time. We will identify all AYA aged 15-29 diagnosed with cancer between 2010-2017 in Ontario (8,700 patients) and collect all their ESAS symptom scores in the year after their diagnosis. By linking these scores to other population-based health care databases (hospitalizations, emergency visits, chemotherapy records), we will provide a detailed picture of symptom burden in AYA with cancer and what determines how severe this burden is. For example, we will determine whether AYA treated by doctors with more AYA expertise experience fewer symptoms. We will do this for the entire AYA group, and for AYA with specific cancers (e.g. lymphomas, testicular cancer). Our results will be communicated to doctors, nurses, and AYA patients so that they know which symptoms are most relevant to AYA. Our results will help design interventions aimed at controlling the worst symptoms. Our results will show which AYA should be the target of interventions because they are at high risk. Our study will therefore help improve quality of life in AYA treated for cancer.

column36: Role of PKM2/oxidative DNA damage axis in the pathogenesis of Right Ventricular Failure associated with Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
column37: Background: Right ventricular failure (RVF) is an independent prognostic factor for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) patients. Recent studies have demonstrated that a metabolic shift toward increased glycolysis over glucose oxidation (Warburg effect) in compensated RV hypertrophy (cRVH). While the pyruvate kinase muscle isozyme M2 (PKM2) regulates metabolism, it also promotes DNA damage repair which triggers inflammation. However, its role has never been studied in RVF. We hypothesized that, in addition to promoting the Warburg effect in cRVH, PKM2 accounts for sustained DNA damage repair activation, contributing to enhanced cardiac inflammation and decompensated RV hypertrophy (dRVH). Methods and Results: We found in human RV biopsies that PKM2/PKM1 ratio was upregulated in cRVH patients (Cardiac index >2.2, n=14) and dRVH patients (died of RVF, n=9), compared to control donors (n=14), and correlated with RV hypertrophy. Similar findings were found in three PH rat models (monocrotaline, PA banding and sugen-hypoxia). Interestingly, inflammation (CD68) and oxidative DNA damage (8-OxoDG, MTH1) were significantly increased in dRVH compared to cRVH despite similar PKM2/PKM1 ratios. Specifically, MTH1 (protein level) inversely correlated with cardiac output and positively correlated with RVEDP, ANP, BNP, hypertrophy and fibrosis (Masson trichrome staining); suggesting that MTH1 is a predictive factor of dRVH. Using rat neonate RV cardiomyocytes, we confirmed that endothelin 1 promotes PKM2 upregulation, ultimately leading to increased inflammation (NF-kB), oxidative DNA damage (8-OxoDG) and apoptosis (TUNEL) (All p<0.05). Conclusions: We demonstrated for the first time that PKM2 is critical for RVF and PKM2/inflammation/oxidative DNA damage signaling is implicated in the transition from cRVH to dRVH in RVF by impacting RV functions.

column37: Arthritis is the most common chronic health condition in Canada, affecting about 6 million Canadians. Its impact on lives can be devastating, and its prevalence is rising. Given the significant burden that arthritis places on patients, the healthcare system, and society at large, a strategic focus on arthritis research is critical to ensuring that people living with arthritis receive the best possible care, while also working towards changing the future of arthritis. Since the sunsetting of the Canadian Arthritis Network in 2014, there is no longer a national meeting to bring together Canadian researchers and clinicians across all arthritis disciplines. This has created major knowledge translation, training and mentorship gaps across the arthritis ecosystem. To fill this gap, the Arthritis Society recently entered into a partnership with the Canadian Rheumatology Association and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research Institute of Musculoskeletal Health and Arthritis (CIHR-IMHA) to pilot an inaugural Canadian Arthritis Research Conference in February 2020 to promote knowledge dissemination and exchange among Canadian arthritis researchers and research trainees across all disciplines and pillars, along with the patients/consumer perspective. In doing so, this conference will spark new initiatives, support trainee development, inform ongoing and future research, and bring together the Canadian arthritis community. A CIHR Planning and Dissemination Grant would allow the Arthritis Society to ensure that all Society-funded research trainees have the opportunity to attend in order to access the latest research evidence and integrate themselves into the Canadian arthritis research landscape.

column36: Premature Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: Cardiovascular Risk and Primary Prevention Eligibility.
column37: Rates of cardiovascular disease (CVD) such as heart attack, coronary heart disease or stroke in young adults (younger than 50 years old) have not decreased over the past two decades. Primary prevention, which is aimed to reduce risk factors and avoid CVD completely, is the best way to change this situation. Current screening algorithms that assess risk of CVD are sufficiently effective in finding individuals in older populations who are at high risk of the disease and who are candidates for preventive therapy. However, because all current risk calculators are highly dependent on age, they often underperform in young people. Consequently, many young adults remain undiagnosed and unaware of their high risk of CVD, do not receive further screening procedures, and do not receive preventive treatment. In this study we: 1) assessed the prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors, such as high blood cholesterol, diabetes, high blood pressure in the population of young adults with CVD in British Columbia and evaluated how many of these patients had their risk estimated and received preventive treatment before developing CVD; 2) Using medical history of these patients and other data available I estimated how many of these patients would not have been identified by current risk calculators and screening guidelines as being at high risk and good candidates for preventive treatment before developing the disease. We found, that the prevalence of all risk factors was high and 81.5% of patients had multiple risk factors, but only 61.6% would be recognised as patients at high risk and eligible for preventive treatment according to the current Canadian guidelines and only 15.7% of these patients had received primary prevention before developing the disease. The study provided important knowledge about the determinants of premature CVD in a contemporary Canadian population. It will inform the development of better screening and treatment approaches.

column36: Ministernotomy Aortic valve replacement provides equivalent short and long terms survival rate in BC patients in comparison with the standard approach.
column37: What was the aim of this study? We wanted to see if using a smaller cut to replace the diseased aortic valve has similar outcomes to valve replacement by the traditional approach. What was the question? The aortic valve prevents blood from flowing backwards into the heart. A diseased aortic valve needs to be surgically replaced to avoid fatal consequences such as heart failure and sudden death. The standard surgery is done by completely cutting the breastbone open to gain access to the heart and replace the valve. However, this results in a large and painful incision. The proposed surgical technique uses only a small cut to replace the damaged valve and prevents the complete cutting of the breastbone. While this approach makes the operation more challenging to perform, it could have several advantages such as decreased bleeding and faster recovery. What was done in this study? We evaluated the Cardiac Service BC database to compare all isolated aortic valve replacements performed in our institution from Jan 2007 to Dec 2016. Nine hundred ten patients were identified (776 undergoing standard surgery and 134 undergoing surgery with the small cut) with a median follow-up of 6.2 years. What did we find? We found no difference in the number of deaths between the two groups both during 30 days post-surgery and in the long term. Patients undergoing surgery using the small cut were put on a heart-lung machine for a shorter duration during the surgery compared to the standard group. Similarly, the amount of time that the aortic artery needed to be closed was shorter with the small-cut surgery. Small-cut surgery patients were discharged home earlier after the operation. There was no difference between the two groups in the prevalence of irregular heart rhythms or kidney problems after surgery. What do we conclude? The smaller incision surgery is a safe and effective alternative to standard surgery and provides similar survival outcomes.

We also aim to identify key knowledge and research needs within the GBM community as well as local or provincial HIV/STBBI prevention projects that can be supported by Engage Study outcomes. column36: Establishing an international research collaboration to improve health outcomes associated with cannabis use among 2SLGBTQ+ youth
column37: The proposed planning activities aim to establish a set of new international interdisciplinary research collaborations, including with partners from Canada, United States, United Kingdom and Australia. Together, we will build a new program of research focusing on health outcomes associated with cannabis use among Two-Spirit, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and other sexual and gender minority (2SLGBTQ+) youth (<30 years). By establishing an international collaboration, we will bring into sharper focus on how features of implementation context (e.g., legal and regulatory status for non-medical cannabis use), health care delivery systems and individual behaviour impact the outcomes of cannabis use interventions to improve health outcomes associated with cannabis use where they have been implemented at different stages and with differential effects.

column37: Team-based approaches to primary care are becoming more common across Canada. Although physiotherapists are increasingly being integrated within primary care teams, there is a lack of research on physiotherapy practice in this setting. The purpose of this survey is to: (1) describe physiotherapy practice among primary care teams and (2) explore barriers and facilitators of integrating physiotherapy among primary care teams in Ontario. An improved understanding of the physiotherapist role in primary care teams will help to appreciate current challenges and provide opportunities to improve physiotherapy service delivery in Ontario, Canada.

column36: High throughput small molecule screening with 3D lung-mimetic hydrogels in the rare lung disease Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
column37: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare lung disease that predominantly strikes women during reproductive years. In patients, aggressive LAM cells invade the lungs, causing destruction of essential tissue and leading to respiratory failure. LAM is driven by genetic mutations which alter molecular pathways and allow the LAM cells to grow and cause severe damage. Unfortunately, the current treatment regime for LAM has limited efficacy and is unable to rid patients of disease. The goal of this project is to develop an improved therapeutic option. To do so, we have simulated human lungs in the lab using novel chemical techniques. In parallel, we have established new cellular models of LAM which accurately reflect the human disease. By combining our synthetic lungs and LAM cellular models, we have been able to recapitulate the invasive nature of this lung disease. We have now harnessed this system to screen hundreds of Health Canada-approved therapeutics, looking for drugs that selectively eliminate LAM cells. From this drug screen, we have identified a subset of candidates which show promising therapeutic potential. We are now attempting to better understand how these drugs eliminate LAM cells, and importantly, if they continue to demonstrate efficacy when tested in an animal model of the disease. We will then nominate our most promising therapeutic for clinical trials. Considering all these drugs have already received Health Canada approval, we anticipate rapid clinical translation. Importantly, this works seeks to advance essential, life saving therapeutic options for LAM patients.

column36: Disseminating drug checking results in response to the overdose crisis
column37: Drug checking is an emerging response to the escalating illicit drug overdose crisis in Canada which allows people to identify the contents of a substance and receive real-time drug information, made possible through innovations in portable spectroscopy instruments. Over the last year, the Vancouver Island Drug Checking Project has been providing free and confidential drug checking at Victoria BC harm reduction sites. Our team can determine a sample's main active ingredients, fillers or cutting agents, any unexpected adulterants, and the presence of fentanyl. The project is guided by Canada's Strategy for Patient-Oriented Research (SPOR) and our project team includes people who use drugs, healthcare providers, health system decision makers and researchers. Now that we are fully operational, these stakeholders have requested drug checking dissemination strategies that are effective, accessible and appropriate for multiple audiences. Specifically, patient partners identified the need to disseminate written, rather than verbal, drug checking results to service users while healthcare providers identified the dissemination of community-level (aggregate) drug checking reports as a priority. The proposed project will therefore create knowledge dissemination products for this drug-checking project responding to the illicit drug overdose emergency. Specifically, we will: (1) Create and implement user-informed written drug checking reports for service users using text and visualizations to communicate data in a format that is understandable, usable, and respectful, while conveying uncertainty and risks. (2) Develop and launch web-based community drug checking reports using text and visualizations to disseminate aggregate drug checking data to the general population, healthcare providers and policy makers. (3) Continue engaging with collaborators and service users to inform ongoing and potentially broader dissemination efforts.

column36: DNA deamination in adaptive and innate immunity: 20 years after the discovery of Activation induced deaminase
column37: This meeting attracts scientists studying of a unique type of enzymes that edit the genome of cells and viruses. In 2020 we mark the 20th anniversary of the landmark discovery that the enzyme Activation induced deaminase (AID) underpins antibody-mediated immunity. AID remodels the antibody genes to improve the quality of the antibodies to fight pathogens. This finding illuminated the nature of a class of antibodies that can neutralize a wide range of viruses, paving the way for the rational design of vaccines. We then learned that AID-related enzymes named APOBECs use a similar mutagenic activity to defend cells from viruses. Moreover, collateral damage from the mutagenic activity of AID/APOBECs can cause cancer. Thus, AID hatched several health and immunity research fields, which often advance in parallel. This anniversary prompted us to organize a forum to bring those fields together and exchange the latest advances and identify areas of potential collaboration, seeking to "strengthen and coordinate infection and immunity research", a strategic research priority of the Institute of Infection and Immunity. This will be the 5th of a series of meetings started in 2008, organized by AID/APOBEC scientists and attracting most of the ~50 laboratories working on these enzymes. Donations from the participating institutions, vendors and government agencies, cover the conference and hospitality costs to enable the participation of research groups regardless of their funding situation. The meeting has a workshop format of oral presentations to encourage discussion. Held in Quebec, this meeting will showcase Canadian research to immunologists of the highest caliber, including the 2018 Nobel Laureate in in Medicine or Physiology, and provide a cost-free learning experience for local trainees, thus "supporting research and helping to build research capacity in the areas of infectious disease and the body's immune system", as mandated to the Institute of Infection and Immunity.

column36: Circulating long non-coding RNA H19 as a novel biomarker for right ventricular failure associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension
column37: Background: Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a major adverse prognostic factor in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Recent Omics analyses demonstrated the deregulation of long non-coding RNAs (LncRNAs) in cardiovascular disease. Moreover, circulating LncRNAs have been considered as promising novel biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases. The LncRNA H19 has been implicated in cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis but its role in PAH-related RVF remains unknown. Methods and Results: In human RV from control donors, patients with compensated RV hypertrophy (cRV, cardiac index (CI) >2.2) and decompensated RV (dRV, PAH patients that died from RVF), H19 was specifically up-regulated in dRV and correlated with RVF severity. Similar findings were noted in monocrotaline and pulmonary artery banding models of RVF. In patients with idiopathic PAH (IPAH) from Canada and UK H19 plasma levels, measured by qRT-PCR, were significantly elevated and correlated with RVF severity (CI and NT-proBNP). Contrary to NT-proBNP, H19 circulating levels were not significantly influenced by estimated glomerular filtration rate. H19 levels were also associated with increased risk of all-cause death or lung transplant (HR 1.61; 95% CI 1.23-2.11, p<0.0001). Event-free survival estimates at 1, 3 and 5 years were 98%, 92% and 84% for patients with H19 levels below 37.2 units versus 85%, 54% and 46% for those with H19 levels above 37.2 units (HR 5.7, 95% CI:3.0-10.7, P<0.001). column36: Analysing secondary data to identify and disseminate sustainable improvements in the quality and safety practices of medication delivery in Canadian community pharmacies
column37: This Forum will bring together stakeholders international and domestic stakeholders to discuss new practices, systems, and technologies in a key area of patient safety: the systematic and comprehensive reporting of medication errors in primary health care. Medication errors are unintended failures in the drug treatment process that lead to actual or potential harm to patients. These errors are a major public health burden. The WHO notes the cost associated with medication errors has been estimated at $42 billion USD annually or almost 1% of total global health expenditure, and that these harms "can be prevented through comprehensive systematic approaches to patient safety." In the EU alone, states the WHO, strategies to reduce such events could lead to "the prevention of more than 750 000 harm-inflicting medical errors per year, leading in turn to over 3.2 million fewer days of hospitalization, 260 000 fewer incidents of permanent disability, and 95 000 fewer deaths per year." The objective of this project is to bring together key stakeholders in Canada, the EU, and US in order to share best practices in the area of patient safety/medication errors in community pharmacies, and to facilitate connections between stakeholder for future development of patient safety strategies. The main activity will consist of a stakeholder forum to compare and contrast processes, institutions, regulations, and technologies that have emerged within the relevant jurisdictions in this area. Participants from academia, government, the private sector, and civil society will be invited in order to share best practices, and to establish constructive collaborative endeavours. The main outputs of this project will be the sharing of cutting-edge regulatory, technological, and training developments in the field of medication error reporting; and the establishment of international learning networks among pharmacists, researchers, and regulators dedicated to quality improvement processes.

column36: Type 2 diabetes duration and risk of incident cardiovascular disease
column37: People with type 2 diabetes are at increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease (CVD), such as heart attacks and strokes. Through improved treatments, people are living longer with type 2 diabetes. However we do not know how living longer with diabetes influences risk of CVD. Using data for all people with type 2 diabetes in Scotland, we examined the influence of diabetes duration on risk of CVD. Our study included 214,298 people who were diagnosed with diabetes between 1998 and 2016 in Scotland, of which 27,697 developed CVD during the study period. We found that risk of CVD increased by 3% each year of living with diabetes. This finding suggests that CVD may become more common as people live longer with diabetes.

column36: Learning to Address and Understand New Challenges by young Persons using Assistive Devices: Project LAUNCH-PAD
column37: Assistive technology (AT) are set of tools, strategies, and services that play a pivotal role in everyday participation, social inclusion, and societal contribution for people with disabilities. Canada is a signatory on the United Nations Convention of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, where assistive technology access has been identified as a human right. Therefore, it is imperative that individuals have access to AT resources needed at all stages of life and that service provision be designed to meet the often increasing AT needs of individuals as they age. However, there are gaps in access to AT devices and services as children with disabilities age out of pediatric services in Canadian provinces such as Manitoba. Young adult users of AT, their family members, and service providers have highlighted the marked contrast in the differing mandates of the pediatric and adult services, discrepancies in the availability of customized devices and funding, and the change in expectations for self-management of care upon aging out of pediatric service. In this planning grant we will work with stakeholders to develop a feasible and effective assistive technology transition service model for young Manitobans that can be tested in future research. We will begin by conducting an environmental scan of similar existing programs or models in Canada and abroad. Using an appreciative inquiry approach, we will engage stakeholders in a meeting designed to explore what is needed for successful transition, envision a direction for the future, and determine research priorities. Through the project, we will connect pediatric and adult AT service providers, researchers, and individuals who use AT in a Community of Practice to enhance communication, collaboration and knowledge exchange. These initiatives that will lead to the establishment of a research proposal with the overall aim of developing an evidence-informed AT transition service model for young adults with disabilities.

column36: Creating Synergy in Women's Maternal and Reproductive Health: Building Global Research Capacity to Eradicate Obstetric Fistula.
column37: Obstetric fistula (OF) is a tragic maternal health condition affecting between two to three million women worldwide. OF is a hole between the vagina and bladder and/or rectum which is usually the result of prolonged obstructed labor, where a woman does not have access to adequate obstetric care. When left untreated, the continuous and uncontrollable stream of urine and/or feces from the vagina becomes physically, psychologically and socially insufferable. The circumstances surrounding OF are deeply rooted in gender imparity, inaccessibility of health care services, lack of health education, and harmful cultural practices experienced by women and girls in marginalized communities globally. Failure to acknowledge and address OF as an international health concern violates women's human right to reproductive health care. Canada has already stated its commitment to advancing the rights and health of women and girls around the world at the 2019 Women Deliver Conference. Following on from previous research completed in Ghana where the incidence of OF is high, this proposed project seeks to use a participatory approach to engage stakeholders in composing comprehensive strategies to support global and country-specific needs and policy development for the eradication of OF. Grounded in the work of Habermas (1974), a participatory approach relies on equitable sharing of knowledge and power to enable communities to exercise greater control over their lives and health. The proposal outlines a three-day knowledge exchange workshop bringing together Ghanaian women affected by OF and their families, policy makers, service providers, nongovernmental organizations, women's advocates, and researchers with the goal of creating an action plan or framework towards the prevention and care of OF. An outline of the workshop is included as well as plans for evaluation.

column36: Exercise as a primer for excitatory stimulation study (EXPRESS): A combined exercise and transcranial direct current stimulation intervention for cognition
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a type of dementia that causes problems with memory, thinking, function and behaviour. Currently, a group of drugs called cholinesterase inhibitors are used to improve memory, but are frequented by side-effects. Moreover, benefits from these drugs are modest and AD patients eventually worsen even with continued use. There remains a critical need for treatments focused on early stages of the disease, when quality of life is still potentially excellent. While transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; neurostimulation with a non-painful current to the brain) has been shown to improve memory in some people with mild AD with minimal side-effects, recent evidence suggests that tDCS works better when brain circuits are active. As exercise increases brain activity using mechanisms that may support tDCS response, it may be an effective primer given before tDCS. This study assesses whether exercise priming with tDCS can help improve memory in mild AD, and whether this combination improves memory better than exercise or tDCS alone. Patients are randomly assigned to receive either 1) combined exercise and tDCS, 2) exercise and nonactive tDCS or 3) exercise education only and tDCS. Blinded preliminary findings will be presented (N=10, mean age=746 years, 50% female, mean years of education=16.22.5 years, mean Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score= 21.52.9). There was a significant effect of treatment over time on Word Recall scores (F(2,7)=5.5, p=0.036). While not statistically significant, there were differences between treatment groups over time on MoCA scores (F(2,7)=3.6, p=0.085) and on Word Recognition scores (F(2,7)=4.5, p=0.054). Overall adherence to study interventions was 98%. Recruitment is ongoing (N=10/30). Updated results will be presented. This study may identify a new, feasible, non-invasive therapy that preserves memory in early stages of AD, therefore having major health implications

column36: Examining HIV and HCV risk and prevalence during the conflict in Eastern Ukraine: a planning meeting to design and implement a bio-behavioural survey among military personnel
column37: Political conflict erupted in Ukraine in 2014, aggravating Ukraine's growing HIV/HCV epidemic, resulting in contraction in economy and cuts to many health and social support programs. Prevention programs need timely and rigorous evidence on how conflict and its consequences impact HIV and HCV risk and prevalence to adapt and deliver effective services that address unmet needs and mitigate HIV and HCV epidemics. Yet, little data exists to inform the response in conflict settings. In order to better understand how conflict affects the organization of sex work and HIV and HCV risk, we received CIHR funding to undertake a study entitled "The impact of political conflict on the dynamics of sex work and the HIV/STI and HCV epidemic in Ukraine" (Dynamics Study). The ongoing study (2016-2021) is exploring HIV/STI and HCV risk and prevalence among sex workers and their clients in Dnipro, Eastern Ukraine. Building on our work on the Dynamics Study, we have been approached by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine to conduct a study among their personnel to understand how the conflict has impacted HIV/HCV rates, as they are observing increases in HIV notification rates since the beginning of the conflict. HIV and HCV risk behaviours and prevalence remain generally unknown and underreported due to a lack of routine HIV screening and a lack of epidemiological investigation. We propose to hold a 3-day planning meeting in Kiev, Ukraine to bring together our multi-disciplinary team along with local Ukraine government officials to collaboratively develop a CIHR Project Grant proposal and a plan for moving forward with this important research project.

column36: Association entre la duree de l'allaitement maternel et la trajectoire du poids de la naissance a 5 ans chez des enfants exposes et non exposes au diabete gestationnel in utero
column37: Les enfants nes de meres ayant eu un diabete de grossesse (DG) presentent un risque eleve de developper de l'obesite plus tard dans la vie. A ce jour, aucune strategie efficace de prevention de cette complication n'a ete etablie. Plusieurs etudes ont permis de demontrer que l'alimentation dans les deux premieres annees de vie pourrait influencer la programmation de la sante d'un individu a long terme. Entre autres, l'allaitement maternel serait susceptible d'affecter la croissance des enfants, influencant leur risque d'obesite plus tard dans la vie. Certaines etudes ont demontre que le lait maternel de femmes ayant eu un DG ou un diabete serait altere en certaines composantes, ce qui pourrait expliquer les resultats de quelques etudes demontrant un lien entre l'allaitement maternel et un poids plus eleve chez des enfants nes de meres avec un diabete. Cependant, a notre connaissance, tres peu d'etudes ont evalue l'association entre l'allaitement maternel et la courbe de croissance de ces enfants, et aucune n'a ete realisee dans une population quebecoise. En ce sens, l'objectif de ce projet est d'evaluer l'association entre la duree de l'allaitement maternel et la courbe de poids, de la naissance a 5 ans, chez des enfants exposes et non expose au DG pendant la periode intra-uterine. Considerant le risque eleve d'obesite de ces enfants, l'etude du role de l'alimentation en debut de vie sur la croissance de ceux-ci est essentielle afin d'etablir de nouvelles strategies de prevention et assurer une meilleure qualite de vie pour ces enfants.

column36: Planning for home birth knowledge mobilization: a scoping review and stakeholder consultation.
column37: Good quality health care should include opportunities for personal choice and be focused on individual needs. Decisions about health care made by clients, their support people, and by health professionals and policy makers can be supported by the use of research evidence. Where to give birth is one such decision. Research on different people's experiences and perspectives of home birth could usefully inform individual decisions about where to give birth, and policy decisions about the type of birthplace services that are supported. However, the research exploring different people's perspectives and experiences of home birth is fragmented, spans multiple countries and contexts, and has not been thoroughly examined. Health care service provision and use could be improved by bringing this research together to make its key findings available. To support the use of evidence about different people's perspectives on home birth when making personal and policy decisions, we propose using systematic review methods to conduct a scoping review of this research. This will be informed by, and contribute to, two planning meetings working with key experts in home birth, including members of the public. These stakeholders will consider the usefulness of this evidence for personal and policy decision making and how well it fits with Canadian (and possibly international) settings. Findings will then be presented at and explored in an upcoming international conference on global maternity care. This work will build relationships between researchers and knowledge users. It will form the basis of future collaborative funding applications that will focus on important priorities surrounding home birth issues among different groups of stakeholders. These will inform personal decision aids or evidence briefings. The results will also show were gaps exist in the current evidence focused on people's perspectives and experiences of home birth, suggesting where new research should focus.

column36: Advancing Equity through Health Professions Education: Collaborative Development of a Research Program based on the 'Coin Model of Privilege and Allyship'
column37: THE PROBLEM: Health inequities result from systems of inequality that give unearned advantage to some and disadvantage to others. Reducing inequities is a priority for many working in health (e.g., clinicians, health professions educators, policy makers), but there is a major obstacle that prevents lasting change. People commonly do not understand their own positions of unearned advantage (i.e., privilege), and how these are directly related to systems of inequality. For example, white people understanding structural racism; settlers recognizing their ongoing role in colonialism; able-bodied people resisting ableist norms; males dismantling patriarchy; or straight people resisting heteronormativity. This lack of understanding not only reduces the effectiveness of efforts to mitigate health inequities, but unwittingly reinforces the status quo. A SOLUTION: We have developed a framework to help clinicians, educators, researchers, policy-makers and others in health understand their personal connections to systems of inequality and, importantly, how to use their unearned advantage to challenge these unfair structures. We call it the "Coin Model of Privilege and Allyship". So far, the Coin Model has been used to educate physicians, nurses, physiotherapists, bioethicists, global health workers, hospital administrators, and public health leaders across Canada to more meaningfully address the root causes of health inequities. However, the focus thus far has been education without a research component. THE NEXT STEP: Our team of 32 diverse health leaders - led by people who are Black, Indigenous and/or disabled - proposes to collaboratively develop a multi-faceted research program that investigates how the Coin Model of Privilege and Allyship can be used to build the capacity of people working in health, in order to reduce health inequities. We will then identify initial research priorities and create teams across disciplines and sectors to drive these projects forward.

column36: Development of a RT Bot on Radiotherapy using IBM Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
column37: We will develop a RT Bot on radiotherapy for patients, families, practitioners and the general public, using IBM Watson Assistant artificial intelligence and machine learning. The bot will be a bot character that can be personalized according to the user's temperament, through using sets of dialogues powered by natural language understanding, entities, slots and customizations on the IBM Cloud. The research team will leverage our existing partnership with IBM. Through multiple sets of dialogues with the RT Bot, the users will be provided with knowledge specially personalized for them. In Canada, over 60% of cancer treatment requires radiotherapy, and a radiotherapy chain includes the patient consultancy to radiation dose delivery. As this process is complicated, it is often challenging to explain it comprehensively to the patient and general public. Also, most cancer patients are seniors who may not be familiar with recent web-based technologies such as YouTube and Twitter. Although their treatment concerns can be explained by the radiation staff, the transient contact time cannot be compared to the round-the-clock company provided by the RT Bot. The proposed RT Bot is a bot character having its role customized to interact with different users, providing personalized radiotherapy information using artificial intelligence interfacing technology provided by the IBM. The short term objective is to develop a RT Bot which can (1) provide general educational information regarding radiotherapy such as concept/science of radiotherapy, patient care and roles of different radiation staff; (2) answer questions on radiotherapy and interact with the patient using artificial intelligence; and (3) impart knowledge about radiotherapy for the general public . The long term objective is to expand the RT Bot from radiotherapy to other cancer treatment modulates such as surgery, chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

column36: Defining and measuring the commercial determinants of health as risk factors for non-communicable diseases: Advancing a new framework for addressing the global epidemiological transition
column37: The steady and continuing rise in the prevalence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), notably since the 1990s, is profoundly challenging "the very foundations of public health" according to the World Health Organization. NCDs now cause 71% of deaths worldwide, affecting populations at every income level in every country. Given the prohibitive costs of treating NCDs, this trend is also worsening health inequities. There is thus an urgent need for more effective prevention strategies focused on reducing the risk factors associated with NCDs. Traditional approaches have focused on metabolic and modifiable behavioural risk factors, such as reducing tobacco use and increasing physical activity, but the need to also change the social conditions shaping these risk factors is now widely accepted. The concept of the commercial determinants of health (CDH) has been put forth in this context. One commonly used definition is "factors that influence health which stem from the profit motive." Current definitions, however, remain difficult to measure and operationalize to inform public health action. The purpose of this project is to develop a clear definition and set of indicators to measure CDH as risk factors for NCDs. Following the completion of a scoping review, we will bring together leading experts, from both the research and policy communities, to develop a composite CDH Risk Factor Index and preliminary methodology for its application to selected populations. The index will seek to measure risk of NCDs in a given population associated with CDHs. The outputs produced by this project will include a CIHR project grant application to pilot this definition, index and methodology as a novel approach for understanding the relationship among three types of NCD risk factors (metabolic, modifiable behavioural and CDHs), how CDH risk factors contribute to patterns of NCDs in a selected population over time, and how these metrics can inform public health action to reduce NCDs.

column36: Developing a national Real-World Evidence decision making framework
column37: Background: The Canadian Real-World Evidence for Value of Cancer Drugs (CanREValue) collaboration is a pan-Canadian team of researchers, clinicians, decision-makers, and others committed to establishing a framework for the use of real-world evidence (RWE) in cancer drug funding decisions. With a view to build capacity within the collaboration and widen our stakeholder reach, we have been holding in-person meetings in satellite to the Canadian Centre for Applied Research in Cancer Control (ARCC) annual conference. The prairie region of Canada, including Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, is a region where CanREValue has identified a need to build further capacity and broaden engagement regarding the potential use of RWE in Canadian cancer drug funding decisions. In support of this goal, we will be hosting a "Developing a national Real-World Evidence decision making framework" interactive workshop in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, which will be held as a satellite meeting to the 2020 ARCC Conference (May 25-26, 2020). Objective: The goal of the "Developing a national Real-World Evidence decision making framework" workshop is to engage national and local stakeholders to provide feedback regarding the CanREValue draft framework for the use of RWE in Canadian cancer drug funding decisions, focusing especially on stakeholders without previous involvement with CanREValue. Approach: The established core CanREValue team will lead the workshop, and the format will consist of presentations, group deliberations, and breakout sessions. Outcomes: Following the workshop CanREValue will have stakeholder feedback to inform and refine the draft framework to a version more ready for system implementation. We further anticipate an increase in CanREValue collaboration within the prairies, as well as the direct development of new collaborations between existing CanREValue members and invited participants.

column36: Contribution of the microbiome to asthma risk in premature infants
column37: Premature infants are at increased risk of life-long diseases and treatments. Among the most compromised organs of premature infants are the lungs. In Canada and globally, very premature infants (between 28-32 weeks of gestation) and extremely premature infants (less than 28 weeks of gestation) are up to three and four times respectively, more likely to develop recurrent wheeze than term infants. Until now, lung compromise has been an accepted result of developmental delay and lung structural damage caused by medical practices needed to support respiration. However, epidemiological evidence shows that infants who do not develop lung structural damage are nevertheless at increased risk of asthma, indicating that other variables impact this risk. Exciting recent findings from infant studies and animal models implicate the large community of microbes (microbiome) in the human gut as a factor that contributes to asthma. However, despite their heightened risk of asthma and the pronounced microbiome alterations linked to prematurity, no clinical study of the microbiome and asthma has studied premature infants. Leveraging a world class team of microbiome experts and an established cohort specifically designed to capture clinical and environmental exposures unique to the NICU, this team grant will be the first to unravel microbiome-asthma linkages in the highly vulnerable premature infant population. We will apply powerful statistical tools to detect independent associations between microbiome features and asthma risk, and to interrogate the capacity of these species to mediate asthma risk. We will then use animal models to define the mechanisms by which specific microbes contribute to immune and neuroimmune pathways that lead to allergic airway inflammation. Our work will culminate in the identification of pre-clinical microbiome-based therapeutics aimed at decreasing the risk of asthma in thousands of Canadian children born prematurely every year.

column36: Planning for a needs-based programme to support the psychosocial health of children and youth living with food allergy
column37: As many as 8% of children - approximately 2 children in a typical-sized classroom - live with food allergy. Food allergy affects every activity where food is involved: at school, socially and at home. When children are told they have food allergy, they are also told that they must never eat the food to which they are allergic. But, always avoiding these foods can be hard. Children are often bullied simply because they have food allergy. Both they and their families have poor psychosocial health. Yet, there are few psychosocial supports for these families. Our team will hold 2 activities that will help us create a program to support these families. Activity 1 is a two-day scientific workshop at the University of Manitoba. The aim of this activity is to create meaningful dialogue that would set the foundation for our second activity, the public forum. At the workshop, we will identify questions to guide the public forum. Activity 2 is a public forum. The forum will be open to different groups: patient advocacy organisations, families of children with and without food allergy, and teachers. As we want as many people as possible to attend, we will cover parking and bus costs, provide allergy-safe foods, and offer childcare. We will start by talking about the psychosocial impact of food allergy. Then, we will give groups time to talk about, and provide feedback on what they think the key issues are. Groups will then report back to us what they think. We will record all of this information. Within one week of the public forum, our team will look at all of the recorded information to identify common ideas. We will use these ideas to create a program to support the psychosocial needs of families with food allergy. We will first create this program in Winnipeg. After we get feedback on the program, and make necessary changes, we will roll this program out across Canada.

column36: Identification of Mammaglobin-A breast derived EVs in breast cancer patient plasma using nanoscale flow cytometry
column37: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women in Canada with an estimated 27,000 new cases being diagnosed in 2019 (Canadian Cancer Society). Currently, mammograms and needle biopsies are used to diagnose breast cancer, both of these techniques are invasive and uncomfortable. Therefore, there is a need for improved methods for diagnosis and monitoring of the disease. Fragments of healthy and breast cancer cells are constantly released into the blood stream and the fragments reflect the health or disease status of the cells that released them. Detection of cancer cell fragments in the blood of patients after a simple blood draw, would provide a non-invasive method to diagnose breast cancer. We aimed to use nanoscale flow cytometry to rapidly detect cancer cell derived fragments in small volumes of patient blood. We successfully identified breast-derived cell fragments in just a drop of blood from healthy and breast cancer patients. Next, we will use breast cancer specific markers to differentiate between healthy and cancerous breast derived cell fragments. This research will further advance a new technology that could be used in the clinic to screen for, diagnose and monitor breast cancer.

column36: Staying Strong, Balance and FAST: Together, Let's Prevent Fall Injuries
column37: Fall-related injuries can have a serious impact on the quality of life of Canadian older adults and their families. Our patient-oriented research team found that a simple exercise program focusing on improving strength, balance, response time and confidence (Fall Arrest Strategy Training or FAST) is effective in decreasing fall risk and improving capacity to prevent fall-related injury. A tailored Yoga intervention called Balance-Flow also shows potential to improve fall risk and injury prevention. The purpose of this project is to enrich fall prevention programming and thereby decrease the number of serious fall-related injuries in older adults. We will do this by leveraging our team's experience of engaging with patients and community partners in order to move knowledge into health and community practices. Our proposed plans have been guided by input from our patient/family advisors, other research participants, and approximately 100 attendees at a recent public forum we convened. The activities planned include: 1) engaging public and professional audiences in knowledge sharing through the production of a series of videos, 2) Establishing a process of implementation for fall prevention programming in community settings through a series of meetings with our community collaborators, 3) Engaging participants in discussion to inform future ideas and collaborations through a public cafe style forum, 4) Providing a continuing education event to inform health care providers, exercise trainers and yoga instructors of best evidence approaches and 5) Presenting findings at a national conference. This knowledge exchange project spans results from four studies including adults aged 50 to 95 years, men and women, with and without signs of frailty. The impact and relevance is applicable to a wide range of knowledge users including older adults, community organizations, recreational facilities, the health care system, exercise/yoga instructors and rehabilitation professionals.

column36: A mechanistic understanding of the impact of pathogen-microbiome dynamics on maternal nutrition during pregnancy in young women
column37: Maternal and child undernutrition are global problems with important consequences for survival, incidence of acute and chronic diseases, healthy development, and economic productivity. Aside from dietary deficiencies, the gut microbiome (i.e. an assemblage of diverse microorganisms occupying the human gastro-intestinal tract) is increasingly viewed as playing a critical role in nutritional status. While much is known concerning the dramatic impact of maternal nutritional status during pregnancy on birth outcomes, little is known concerning how dynamic changes in the microbiome can modulate maternal and fetal health during pregnancy. To understand the links between maternal nutrition, birth outcomes and the gut microbiome, we will study changes in microbiome communities in two groups of young women over the course of their pregnancy. The first group, from Pakistan, will be recruited from the recently established Matiari Preconception and Pregnancy Supplementation Trial. The second group, from Canada, will be recruited from clinics in Toronto serving refugee communities. Both groups will provide direct access to samples that will reveal the composition and functions of the maternal microbiome over the course of their pregnancy. Computational analyses allied with unique mouse and swine models will allow us to associate microbial communities with pregnancy outcomes. Of particular interest are the abundance and diversity of gut parasites that we expect will influence other microbes in the gut to negatively impact nutritional status during pregnancy. Understanding these complex relationships and their impact on malnutrition and birth outcomes, will improve diagnoses and inform the development of novel targeted interventions that can significantly improve maternal health and child development. This project directly relates to CIHR's mandate to improve global child health.

column36: Causational Roles of the Gut Microbiome in Childhood Asthma: Leveraging the CHILD Cohort Study
column37: Asthma is a lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. It is the most common reason why children miss school or end up in hospital. The CHILD Cohort Study was set up to research why some children develop asthma, and find out how we can prevent it from starting. Nearly 3500 babies and their families have joined this study. They have been answering questions and coming to clinic visits for over 8 years. Scientists working on the CHILD data have already made some exciting discoveries about who gets asthma and why this happens. One of these discoveries was about the importance of our gut bacteria in helping our immune systems to develop properly so that we don't get asthma. Other important discoveries showed that how babies are born, what they eat, and what medicines they take can affect their gut bacteria. But we need a lot more information to move from these discoveries to making treatments or policies to prevent asthma. In this project, we will use new technologies to find out how gut bacteria are causing or preventing asthma. Information from the CHILD study will guide us to do experiments in cells and mice to better understand how gut bacteria affect asthma. This research will help us develop new ways to prevent and treat asthma in the future by using or targeting gut bacteria.

column36: Dissecting host-microbiome modifiers of type 2 diabetes risk
column37: The global epidemic of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) reduces lifespan and quality of life, and exerts enormous pressure on Canadian health systems. It is now well documented that changes in the composition of the gut microbiota (bacteria living in the intestine) accompany obesity and factors that increase risk of T2D. Most of the evidence for the microbiome's role in T2D is from bacteria in the feces. We have exciting evidence that bacteria and/or bacterial fragments are altered in the upper gut and selectively accumulate in the circulation, liver and various fat depots of obese women and men. Critically, T2D status dictates the body site-specific bacterial signatures in these obese subjects. The long-term objective of our team research program is to define the identity and function of the specific bacterial strains compartmentalized in specific gut segments versus body tissues in the progression of insulin resistance and T2D. We aim to use this knowledge to develop novel diagnostic, preventive and therapeutic approaches for diabetes to reduce disease burden. The overarching goal of this team grant application is to build synergies among Canadian microbiome and diabetes experts to advance knowledge by integrating new concepts and state-of-the-art technologies.

column36: Factors Associated with Self-Reported Health in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Scoping Review
column37: Background Self-reported health status is a strong predictor of future health status including the development of other health problems or death because of these problems. Previous studies have shown that this measure is related to many factors, but it is not understood how these factors influence self-reported health ratings. The purpose of this review was to describe what factors international research has described as influencing self-reported health. Methods A scoping review was completed. Four hundred and thirty-one articles were identified from four databases. Eighteen additional articles were identified through hand searching reference lists. Articles and information was reviewed by two independent reviewers. Results Thirty studies were included in the review. Forty-two individual factors were identified. These forty-two factors were found to influence self-reported health among older adults living in the community. Most of the studies included in this review identified that the presence of multiple chronic conditions and the presence of depressive symptoms decreased self-reported health. These findings suggest that the presence of multiple chronic conditions and the presence of depressive symptoms have an important influence on self-reported health and that there is a need to further explore how these factors influence this measure. Conclusion and Next Steps Factors that influence self-reported health are broad. Further research is needed to understand how the presence of multiple chronic conditions and depressive symptoms influences self-reported health. It is important to understand the ways that self-reported health is influenced as this understanding may inform the design of new interventions that can help promote health in a growing population.

column37: INTRODUCTION: Le Performance Assessment of Self-Care Skills (PASS) est un outil d'evaluation standardise fonde sur l'observation disponible en 2 versions (hopital et domicile). Les ergotherapeutes s'appuient sur ce type d'outil pour evaluer la capacite de leurs clients ages hospitalises a accomplir leurs activites quotidiennes. Ces evaluations visent a emettre des recommandations appropriees pour reduire les risques d'evenements indesirables (blessures, readmission, relogement) apres le conge. OBJECTIFS: Explorer la capacite du PASS a predire les evenements indesirables chez les aines durant les 3 mois suivant leur conge de l'hopital et la comparer a celles d'evaluations deja utilisees a l'hopital. METHODOLOGIE: Pour cette etude pilote a devis predictif prospectif, 24 aines hospitalises seront recrutes. Le PASS et 3 autres evaluations (Systeme de mesure de l'autonomie fonctionnelle, Mesure canadienne du rendement occupationnel et jugement clinique concernant la securite du conge) sont administres a l'hopital, puis une semaine apres le conge, a domicile. La survenue d'evenements indesirables est documentee durant 3 mois suivant le conge par questionnaires telephoniques. Des analyses statistiques de sensibilite et specificite seront effectuees. CONCLUSION: Les resultats informeront les ergotherapeutes sur le lieu et la maniere d'evaluer les aines lors du conge afin d'offrir des recommandations centrees sur leurs besoins. column36: Open the window! An administrative-data exploration of observation windows to capture chronic comorbidities among people living with HIV
column37: Administrative databases depicting healthcare utilization have become an important data source in HIV epidemiological research, providing a unique opportunity to implement rapid, inexpensive measurements crucial to public health. With people living with HIV (PLWH) living longer than ever before, large-scale administrative data are often used to estimate the prevalence and incidence of chronic age-associated comorbidities, which further inform intervention investment and prioritization that best addresses the healthcare needs of PLWH. However, to date, only a handful of methodological studies on administrative data have evaluated the influence of study design choices, such as the number of years of data examined, in the estimates of prevalence and incidence. As such, we conducted a data-driven exploration to determine optimal look-back windows (LBWs) for measuring prevalence and incidence of nine chronic comorbidities in PLWH, compared to HIV-negative controls, using administrative data. To do so, we applied multiple LBWs, from zero to 16 years, to estimate the prevalence and incidence of cardiovascular, kidney, lung, liver, and neurocognitive diseases, cancers, diabetes, hypertension, and osteoarthritis in 2012. The presence of these diseases in both populations was ascertained using BC-wide hospitalization, physician billing and drug dispensation databases. We found that a shorter LBW underestimated prevalence and overestimated incidence. On the contrary, extending LBWs resulted in a higher estimated prevalence, but had a relatively small effect on the incidence rates. The patterns of LBW greatly varied across comorbidities and between PLWH and HIV-negative controls. Overall, this study highlights the underacknowledged concern for widely varying incidence and prevalence estimates, with implications for treatment planning and intervention development in aging PLWH and beyond.

column36: Dynamic PET Image Reconstruction Using the Wavelet Kernel Method
column37: Dynamic PET imaging is used to monitor the spatio-temporal distribution of a tracer in a tissue region. Dynamic PET can suffer from high noise; to address this problem, the kernel method has been developed for efficient dynamic PET image reconstruction. Previous kernel approaches used a Gaussian kernel to exploit nonlocal spatial correlations from image priors. The Gaussian kernel, has an undesired effect of smoothing high frequencies. In this work, we propose using a wavelet kernel with good energy compaction to further enhance kernel-based dynamic PET image reconstruction. The oscillation in the wavelet kernel can result in better representation of details in the final reconstructed images. We evaluated the wavelet kernel approach using patient data acquired from dynamic C-11 hydroxyephedrine (HED) PET imaging. Reconstruction results demonstrate that this wavelet kernel approach achieves better image quality than standard reconstruction and the Gaussian kernel approaches.

column36: Lipid loading of macrophages suppresses LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression by negatively regulating HIF1a-dependent glycolysis
column37: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by the progressive buildup of plaques on the inner surface of the artery wall. Atherosclerosis significantly impacts the health of Canadians by being the underlying cause of heart attack, stroke and peripheral vascular disease. A key risk factor of atherosclerosis is elevated blood cholesterol in low-density lipoproteins (LDL). This is because native and oxidized LDL (oxLDL) are constantly taken up by macrophages in the artery wall, leading to the formation of foam cells that constitute the major component of lipid-rich plaques. Although it is well established that foam cell formation accompanies inflammation in the artery wall, the link between lipid loading of macrophages and their response to inflammatory stimuli remains elusive. Our research group has previously showed that the loading of macrophages with oxLDL suppresses inflammatory responses upon activation with bacterial products. Why this occurs remains to be determined. Recent research has shown that the breakdown of glucose (glycolysis) in immune cells is required for an optimal inflammatory responses to bacterial products. Given this relationship between glycolysis and inflammation, we will test the possibility that lipid loading of macrophages suppresses their inflammatory response by modulating glycolysis. The proposed research may lead to new future therapies that improve the health of Canadians. Molecular pathways that reduce the inflammatory response in lipid-loaded macrophages will be identified. Targeted these pathways by therapeutics may further suppress inflammation in atherosclerosis and potentially abrogate its progression.
