column36: Exploring the use of emergency medical services by stroke survivors in British Columbia
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability in Canada. Scientists have observed that people who suffer a stroke and are transported to the hospital by ambulance have lower rates of death and better outcomes. Because of this campaigns, like the Face Arms Speech Time (F.A.S.T) program, have been created to increase public awareness of stroke symptoms and what to do in the event of a stroke. Still we know many people have a stroke and do not use an ambulance to get to hospital. Instead they choose to wait for symptoms to go away, drive themselves, or get others to drive them. It is unclear how mode of arrival, especially outside a large metropolitan city, affects one's hospital medical care. This represents an important gap in current knowledge because we do not fully understand factors or effects associated with calling an ambulance in the event of a stroke, specifically in smaller urban or rural areas. The purpose of this study is to understand why (or why not) people call an ambulance when they or someone in their care is having a stroke and how calling an ambulance affects medical care they receive in hospital. To answer these questions, we are quantitatively examining a dataset of stroke patients (19,000 cases) to determine differences in ambulance usage across British Columbia. In a smaller subset of the sample (784 cases), we are looking at if mode of arrival affects time to seeing a healthcare professional and treatment including brain scan. To understand the decision-making process, we are qualitatively study stroke patients by interviewing a sample of 10 persons who called an ambulance and 10 who did not. The results of this study will be important for people at risk for stroke, their caregivers, and the general public to understand why it is important to call an ambulance when a stroke is happening. This research is also important for health organizations who can use information from this work to refine services and public awareness campaigns.

column36: Manipulating IL-15 and TGFb signaling augments Natural Killer cell homeostasis and protects from experimental pulmonary arterial hypertension
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes narrowing and loss of blood vessels in the lungs, leading to increased stress on the heart and death by heart failure. Treatments for PAH are expensive and provide little benefit to the patient in terms of symptoms and survival. For many years, PAH has been associated with dysfunction in the immune system. Recently we have discovered that Natural Killer (NK) immune cells are reduced in number and impaired in function in PAH. We hypothesized that this may be caused by changes in the two main regulators of NK cells, called interleukin-15 (IL-15) and transforming growth factor beta (TGFb). To test this hypothesis, we bred mice with NK cells that either can or cannot produce the main receptor for TGFb, called TGFbRII. These mice were then exposed to low oxygen levels, which causes symptoms of PAH in normal mice. Some of these mice were also treated with IL-15. We then tested our mice for lung and heart function, as well as measured number and function of NK cells. We found that exposure to low oxygen levels caused NK cell numbers to drop, and IL-15 treatment prevented this from happening. Mice that could not produce TGFbRII had similar numbers of NK cells as normal mice, and also had a drop in NK cells when exposed to low oxygen levels. However, the mice that could not produce TGFbRII did not develop symptoms of PAH when exposed to low oxygen levels, unlike normal mice. These studies have helped to better understand how NK cells contribute to PAH. We can now focus our work on changing IL-15 and TGFb signaling in order to restore NK cells, and hopefully treat PAH. Future work will aim to develop a new treatment based on this idea.

column36: Obtaining data directly from children with severe motor and communication impairments for pediatric disability wellbeing-health-learning-systems in Canada.
column37: Children with severe motor and communication impairment (SMCI) form less than 1% of Canadian children but account for approximately 10% of pediatric health care expenditures. Their low speech or language and motor capacity make them more vulnerable to social isolation, often resulting in 47% greater wellbeing concerns compared to other children. Yet they are unable to complete self-report assessments (patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs)) that would allow systems to capture this disparity. We aim to identify/appraise options for obtaining wellbeing directly from children with SMCI. A systematic scoping review will be conducted via grey and peer-reviewed databases. Searches will be based on: 1) (non-verbal/non-written) methods for capturing self-expression; 2) wellbeing; and 3) severe impairment. Articles will be excluded if focused on >25 years of age, autism, or typically developing children. Preliminary results from MEDLINE, INSPEC, and Compendex (5353 non-duplicate studies screened) identified 24 potentially suitable options. Three options found accessed wellbeing information directly from the child (observation, microswitch, and a facial expression detection system (FacEx-Comm)). Twelve high technology options were found: switch device, joystick, sensor, physiological measure, chorded keyboard, eye-tracking, FacEx-comm, and a communication jacket. Four low-technology options were found: Picture Exchange Communication System, non-speech-based qualitative methods, interviews, and observations. High-technology options appear too individualized to obtain information from children with SMCI who vary greatly across specific impairments. Utilizing low-technology options may bridge the gap between sender and receiver communication for a greater range of children with SMCI to express their wellbeing. Appropriate options found can be tested and implemented within learning health systems to enhance wellbeing health services for children with disabilities in Canada.

column36: International Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy Conference
column37: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a brain blood vessel disease caused by deposition of a protein, beta-amyloid, in the walls of blood vessels of the brain. CAA is a common finding at autospy in older persons (ore than 10% of persons age >80 have evidence of moderate or severe CAA) but we have trouble diagnosing it during life. There are no highly sensitive and specific diagnostic tests. The most severely affected patients suffer hemorrhages in the brain or on the brain's surface. Once hemorrhages begin, we can recognize the disease. The prognosis is poor, because the hemorrhages often recur (average 9% risk per year) and are frequently fatal. More insidiously, CAA causes more subtle damage to the brain that increases the risk for dementia. Statistical models indicate that if there were a cure for CAA, 7% of dementia cases would be prevented. We are applying for support to host the 7th International CAA Conference in Banff, Alberta, Canada on October 1-3, 2020. The Conference Chair is Dr. Eric Smith (University of Calgary), a world-leading expert on CAA. The conference will be attended by 180-200 leading CAA scientists, physicians, graduate students and post-doctoral fellows, staff from organizations such as the International CAA Association (Leiden, Netherlands), Alzheimer Society of Alberta and the Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging, and persons with lived experience with CAA and their care partners. This is the 7th international conference but the first one located in Canada. The objective of the conference will be to disseminate the latest research on CAA (including basic science and human-based research), share best practices for clinical care and management of persons with CAA, and advance a research agenda to translate basic science discoveries into clinical trials of new treatments.

This reality poses significant challenges for local clinicians and threatens continuity of care. Our current planning activities will assist with understanding why this is the case and explore opportunities for better transnational health care access and continuity of care for the many Canadians managing diabetes who winter abroad. The planning activities we propose here and the previous meetings we held in Yuma will inform our development of a CIHR Project Grant focused on this particular transnational health care mobility that will work towards developing interventions to facilitate better continuity of care.

column37: For decades, researchers have studied sex differences and gender as health determinants. A new field of Sex and Gender Science is emerging out of the intersection between these paradigms and it is catapulting our understanding of how biology and society interact to affect health and disease. Much like the development of the field of Neuroscience (c. 1969), Sex and Gender Science is emerging from individual research disciplines. It incorporates sex and gender into existing experimental paradigms and is engaged in developing methods to investigate how sex and gender influence health and the etiology, progress, and treatment of diseases in men, women, boys, girls, and gender-diverse people. Canada leads the world in Sex and Gender research. Yet, we have no Canadian organization for sex and gender researchers across disciplines and communities to meet to discuss the field or form partnerships to support and grow the field in Canada. The purpose of this Planning and Dissemination Grant is to have the Inaugural meeting of the Canadian Organization for Gender and Sex (COGS) Research. The meeting will be held in Vancouver in January 8-9, 2020 at the University of British Columbia. This meeting will include multiple invited stakeholders-academics from across disciplines, charitable organizations, funders, and community members-all invited to provide the nexus of the Organization going forward. The question of the meeting will be, "How do you incorporate sex and gender in your research." The meeting will provide an opportunity to share perspectives, build community, and make plans for the Organization going forward. Ultimately, the goal of COGS is to advance and apply sex and gender science to improve the health, wellness, and equity of all.

column36: Minding the Brain Gap: A National Meeting on Advancing Women's Brain Health
column37: The meeting aims to explore women's brain health research through a multidisciplinary lens with a lens to clear up common misunderstandings in the literature. For example, did you know that hormone therapy during menopause substantially improves cognitive, cardiovascular and bone health but only increases the risk for breast cancer by 2%? Did you know that the pregnancy and motherhood is associated with an increased risk for mental health disorders but also can be a barometer for conditions in later life that lead to dementia? This grant will support the organization of a 1.5-day conference focused on women's brain health. The purpose of this conference is to bring together a group of researchers, clinicians, community partners, trainees, funders and policymakers engaging in women's health research to share research and develop strategies to catalyze new research to advance women's brain health. Understanding women's brain health from multiple perspectives is critical because research has shown that women are more likely to be diagnosed with brain disorders such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD), depression and anxiety. Women also experience different stress-related symptoms, particularly in relation to emotional outcomes and cognitive disruption. There are still gaps in addressing, diagnosing, and treating women's brain health conditions. Thus, building capacity for collaborations between diverse disciplines to bridge the knowledge gaps in women's health research is vital in contributing to the understanding and response to women's health issues. During this meeting, the diverse stakeholders will discuss the current research on women's brain health and develop approaches to inform research, policy decisions, and clinical care. It is anticipated this meeting will not only engage various stakeholders involved in women's health research but will also offer a supportive and interactive environment to engage trainees and the next generation of women's health researcher.

column36: Sexually Transmitted Infections among Canadian International Retirement Migrants in the United States
column37: Every year tens of thousands of older Canadians spend the winter months abroad in warmer climates. We popularly refer to them as 'snowbirds.' Many experience divorce, widowhood, re-entry to the dating scene, new social contexts, and other factors that can cause them to adopt new sexual practices and even become exposed to sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The southern United States serves as a popular destination for Canadian snowbirds, including the city of Yuma, Arizona. Here we propose to undertake research planning activities in Yuma specific to STI transmission and sexual health care access among retired Canadians who winter there. We will explore how sexual health is promoted within the local healthcare system through touring hospitals and clinics and holding consultative meetings with health workers. We will also meet with leaders in the Canadian snowbird community to understand the sexual health risks and access to testing and treatment for these older Canadians while abroad. These proposed planning activities build the our team's joint interests in mobilities and STIs and deepen our emerging collaboration with the main hospital in Yuma. These planning activities will also assist with understanding how the social, epidemiological, and health service contexts of retirement communities abroad can contribute to STI transmission, late diagnoses, and onward implications for care among older Canadians. The planning activities we propose here will inform our development of a CIHR Project Grant focused on STI risks in international retirement communities and strategies for sexual health promotion among older Canadians travelling to and living in these contexts. The information gleaned from these activities will help to develop a project with strong potential to reduce STIs and improve quality of life in a relatively under-researched Canadian population.

column36: Modernizing Sex and Gender Information Practices in Electronic Health Records
column37: The LGBTQIA2 communities are among the most neglected populations with respect to their health needs. column36: Establishing a Relationship Between Philosophy and Epidemiological Research and Practice: Modelling Ethical Standards of Health Equity (MESHE)
column37: Health inequities are differences in health that are 'unjust'. As such, it follows that the concept of 'health inequity' involves both a descriptive and a normative, philosophical component: the descriptive component tells us what differences in health count as health inequities (e.g., 'differences in rates of breast cancer between Canadians of South Asian descent and the general population'), and the normative, philosophical component tells us why those differences in health should be viewed as ethically wrong or bad, i.e., 'unjust', such that they should count as 'inequities'. Two groups of scholars have worked in parallel on health equity-one on the descriptive component (those in public health sciences, e.g., epidemiologists) and one on the normative component (those in the humanities and social sciences, e.g., philosophers and ethicists)-yet a significant gulf exists between their respective research. This is problematic, because by failing to explicitly ground public health interventions in specific philosophical criteria of health equity, such interventions may fail to target the most appropriate populations or the most ethically important differences in health, thereby failing to achieve the most 'equitable' health outcomes. Conversely, without empirically testing different ethical criteria of health equity, philosophers may end up producing guidance for public health interventions that ultimately have undesirable outcomes in practice. Thus, we plan to host a full-day meeting which will bring together scholars from the humanities and social sciences (i.e., philosophy and ethics) with scholars and knowledge users from public health sciences to discuss the establishment of a program of research that would seek to better integrate the fields of philosophy and epidemiology via a project that aims to empirically model public health interventions, and, namely, their capacity to reduce 'health inequities', according to key philosophical criteria of health equity.

column36: 'Self' after Traumatic Brain Injury and its Impact on Health
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) significantly changes a person's sense of who they are, or their 'self'-their self-identity, self-perception, and self-awareness can all change after injury, which can lead to reduced long-term health. Although research has given us some understanding of how these changes happen, there is still a need to identify the top research priorities and, in the long term, to develop methods for an individual with a TBI and their family/carers to positively manage self after injury. The goal of this Planning Grant is to bring together key stakeholders, including junior and senior researchers, clinicians, individuals with TBI, and their families, using an approach that will both generate and implement new knowledge, to develop international research priorities on changes to one's self after traumatic brain injury. The proposed Planning Meeting will enable discussions among experts from various areas including researchers, clinicians, people who have experienced brain injury, and their carers. The following goals will be addressed in the meeting: 1) develop an international research network 2) develop an international research agenda with specific priorities on topics related to self after brain injury and the impact on overall health, with plans for obtaining grants to pursue this research 3) communicate the results of the meetings to the public and researchers, outlining the proposed research priorities In summary, this Planning Grant will develop an international collaborative research network, in partnership with key stakeholders, to develop a research agenda on topics of the altered self after brain injury. Ultimately, the outcomes from the research will enable development of novel therapeutic approaches to positively approach changes to one's self after brain injury.

column36: Establishing Research Priorities in Adult Congenital Heart Disease Interventions in Canada
column37: Congenital heart diseases are the most common congenital defects. Over the last 20 years the major shift from surgical to less invasive transcatheter interventions resulted in improved patient outcomes such as faster recovery, earlier return to work and study, less time in hospital, and less discomfort. Most congenital heart diseases however are rare diseases with inherent difficulties to conduct research to generate sound evidence on the relative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of different interventions. Currently, there are significant knowledge gaps in the field that can be addressed only via strong national and international collaborative efforts. This is a proposal to organize a research prioritization activity for adult congenital heart disease interventions (ACHDi). In April-July 2019 we led an international effort to elicit the most important research priorities in five most common ACHDi. We received over 500 questions that were grouped into 20-25 research priorities per intervention category. The final stage of international priority ranking will be held in May 2020. We recognize that considering differences in health care systems, and patient and provider preferences, national research priorities should reflect the Canadian context. In April 2019 we created a Canadian Network of stakeholders for Adult Congenital Heart Disease Interventions (ACHDi) that brought together patients (Canadian Congenital Heart Alliance), healthcare providers, researchers and policy makers from four provinces and seven largest centres in Canada. We are proposing to organize a research prioritization activity for ACHDi in Canada, under the umbrella of our Network to create the groundwork for several future national (and potentially international) studies in the coming decade. The meeting is planned be held in Toronto and engage 17 participants who will go through a structured process to rank and select top 10 most important research questions in ACHDi.

column36: Youth Vaping Assessment, Prevention and Early intervention (Y-VAPE): A combined policy and intervention approach to curb youth vaping.
column37: Vaping among school-aged youth is a major public health problem, with the last few years marking a concerning surge in youth vaping. Tobacco control advocates, provincial leaders, and federal leaders are therefore urgently calling for efforts to curb youth vaping. Schools are ideally suited to address the issue; however, a lack of school policies and upstream interventions has left schools empty-handed. This project will address this gap through the development of a community-driven, interdisciplinary research initiative called the Youth Vaping Assessment, Prevention and Early Intervention (Y-VAPE) project, a school-based vaping prevention program that will integrate policy and intervention research into the school environment. Through a collaborative, interdisciplinary and engaged stakeholder approach, this project will lend to an increased understanding of vaping among youth, and how to meaningfully respond to it through policy and intervention. The ultimate aim of this project is to inform the development of school policy and peer-led, youth-driven interventions. This will be accomplished through the following four activities: 1) an environmental scan of existing literature on youth vaping and interventions to date; 2) a policy scan of national, policy, and school-level policies related to vaping; 3) foster collaborative relationships with multiple stakeholders, including youth; and 4) develop a CIHR operating project grant. Outcomes of this project will include the establishment of a multi-stakeholder team, evidence syntheses, directions for next steps in project development, early knowledge translation outputs, and proposal development. Between the expertise of the research team and the underpinning collaborative, integrated knowledge translation approach, this project will position Canada as a leader in efforts to curb youth vaping.

column36: L'acces aux services sociaux et de sante pour la population estrienne ainee anglophone: etat de la situation
column37: Introduction. Bien que les droits des anglophones du Quebec d'obtenir des services sociaux et de sante (SSS) en anglais soient proteges par des lois, cet acces est inegal. Par exemple, vivre dans une municipalite avec de nombreux anglophones et etre bilingue favoriseraient l'acces aux SSS. Or, les autres elements influencant l'acces aux SSS dans sa langue sont peu connus, tout comme leurs besoins en matiere de SSS. Comme les aines anglophones quebecois sont generalement peu bilingues, en savoir plus sur leur acces aux SSS en anglais s'avere ainsi primordial. C'est pourquoi cette recherche visait a connaitre les elements influencant la capacite a obtenir ces SSS et comparer ces elements selon la taille de la communaute anglophone ou vit l'aine. Methodes. Des entretiens individuels semi-diriges aupres de 12 aines unilingues anglophones estriens ainsi qu'une collecte de documents ont ete effectues. Les donnees ont ete analysees thematiquement. Resultats preliminaires. 15 elements influencent l'obtention de SSS, dont les plus importants sont presentes ici. Ont une influence negative de grandes distances a parcourir pour obtenir des services, la presence de listes d'attente, des couts a debourser et le manque de proches aidants. Par contre, ont une influence positive des organismes dedies aux aines anglophones quebecois, un medecin de famille parlant anglais, la proactivite de l'aine (p. ex. prendre un rendez-vous medical directement a la clinique plutot que par telephone) et des taux de bilinguismes plus eleves chez les professionnels des SSS plus jeunes. Enfin, les aines anglophones quebecois de milieux fortement anglophones rencontrent tres peu d'elements negatifs contrairement a ceux de milieu faiblement anglophone. Conclusion. Reduire les obstacles rencontres par les aines anglophones quebecois en milieu faiblement anglophone s'avere necessaire afin d'identifier les leviers pour favoriser leur acces aux SSS, et donc leur sante.

column36: Scaling up Principles for Equity-Centred Global Health Research
column37: The health and wellness someone experiences - even how long they live - differs dramatically depending on how they are positioned in society-both within and between countries. People with more money and resources enjoy better jobs and access to schools, parks, and other health-promoting places while people with less are systematically excluded. column36: Assessing parents' uptake of evidence-based vaccination pain management strategies and confidence using an electronic knowledge translation tool
column37: Parent-directed knowledge translation (KT) resources for children's vaccination pain management may increase the use of research-based strategies to reduce pain. An electronic, research-based KT resource to inform parents about vaccination pain management was created in partnership with a parenting magazine. While the resource had a wide reach, its effect on parents' use of research-based strategy is unknown. The goals of this research study were to explore the relationship between parents' plans to use strategies from the electronic KT resource and their actual use at their child's vaccination, as well as their confidence in using the strategies. Parents of children aged 0 to 17 years took part in the survey and learned about the study through social media and e-newsletters. Parents read the electronic KT resource and completed an online survey, including the Information Assessment Method for Parents questionnaire to evaluate their opinions on the KT resource. Parents also answered questions about their attitudes towards pain management, use of strategies to manage pain, and their confidence in doing so before their child's vaccination and again after. 128 parents completed both surveys. Most parents planned to use the KT resource and felt confident using the information. When parents felt confident in their ability to use the strategies after reading about them, they were more likely to use the strategies during their child's vaccination and planned to continue using them. These findings show the importance of providing parents with strategies which they can access electronically so that they can feel confident in managing their children's vaccination pain and use strategies regularly to reduce pain and increase adherence to vaccine schedules.

column36: Investigating the role of the HNF-1aG319S gene variant in experimental models reflective of early-onset type 2 diabetes in Anishininiiwuk youth
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by high blood sugar due to the reduced ability of the body to respond to insulin and the inadequate release of insulin from pancreatic islets. Youth-onset T2D is the fastest growing disease among Indigenous children of Central Canada, the majority being of Anishininiiwuk (Oji-Cree) heritage. This is a serious concern because 50% of youth living with T2D will develop complications such as kidney failure within 15 years of diagnosis. In the last two generations, dramatic changes in diet likely contribute to T2D. Moreover, a change in the DNA of the HNF-1a gene (HNF-1aG319S) strongly predicts T2D development. As a result, we need to decipher how these environmental and genetic factors interact to affect the development of T2D. HNF-1a is a transcription factor, meaning it works to control the expression of other genes within a cell. We have created the first mouse model carrying this gene variant using state-of-the-art gene editing technology. Male and female mice that carry zero, one or two copies of the gene variant will be fed one of three experimental diets: a standard mouse diet, a diet similar to a traditional Anishininiiwuk diet, or a diet similar to an average modern diet. We will assess markers of diabetes development including whole-body glucose responses and insulin sensitivity from birth to old age. The pancreatic islets that secrete insulin will be isolated to define the cellular pathways through which this gene variant influences T2D development. This will be the first detailed investigation into the relationship between genetics, diet, and diabetes in the Anishininiiwuk population. By situating our science within the legacy of colonization and present-day food insecurity, we hope to inform nutritional interventions and support community-led efforts to access traditional foods. This model will also serve as a foundation to develop culturally-appropriate therapeutic strategies in the future.

column36: Using patient-reported outcomes to improve the quality of palliative care: Establishing priorities and actions for data collection and reporting in Canada
column37: Patients' perspectives on their health and well-being, captured through patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), are vital to guide and evaluate palliative care delivery. The aim of our proposal is to host a one-day meeting of key stakeholders from across Canada, with patient and family partners forming core members of the team, to establish a framework for a national palliative care data collection platform. The objectives of our meeting are to: 1. Review existing literature on the importance of collecting patient-reported and patient-centred outcomes in palliative care. 2. Establish agreed-upon goals for a Canadian palliative care data collection platform. 3. Identify what patient-reported and patient-centred palliative care data and outcomes should be collected. 4. Identify options for standardizing data collection, including the use of common tools and measurement approaches. 5. Determine best practices for developing a national data resource that adds value to palliative care delivery and research while maintaining data privacy and patient confidentiality. 6. Establish next steps in our efforts to develop a national palliative care data collection platform, including the identification of care providers and future funding sources to facilitate our work. Our proposed one-day planning meeting is the necessary first step towards the development of a national palliative care data collection platform. We anticipate that the results of this meeting will provide direction into future activities that will be required to develop such a data platform, including further consultations with providers, patients and families, and collaborations with policy and data experts.

column36: Inhibition of Metalloproteinase Activity Promotes PMVEC Barrier Function Under Septic Conditions
column37: Sepsis, is one of the major causes of death in the elderly. The lungs are one of the major organs that fail during sepsis. The endothelial cells, the cells that covered the smallest blood vessels in the lung, become injured leading fluid leak into the lungs during sepsis. A special protein called metalloproteinases are capable of cleaving cell surface proteins, such as cell-cell junctional proteins, causing the fluid leak. Recent work in our lab found that endothelial cells that lacking a special protein called tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase (TIMP), a critical regulator of metalloproteinase activity, had cause increased leakiness in endothelial cells. We hypothesize that metalloproteinase activity will be increased under septic conditions and that vascular leak will be reduced with the application of synthetic metalloproteinase inhibitors. To test this, mice endothelial cells with and without inhibitors(TIMP) stimulated with septic condition to assessed the Metalloproteinase activity, leakiness and junctional protein distribution in endothelial cells. To confirm the role of metalloproteinases, endothelial cells were treated with synthetic metalloproteinase inhibitors. Analysis of metalloproteinase activity revealed that increased of metalloproteinase activity in septic endothelial cells lead to increase the leakiness of endothelial cells. The application of synthetic metalloproteinase inhibitors reduced the leakiness. Thus, these studies suggest that inhibition of metalloproteinase activity may promote endothelial cell barrier function by reducing inter-junctional protein degradation during sepsis and thereby reducing septic vascular permeability.

column36: The Role of TIMP3 in Microvascular Endothelial Cell-Extracellular Matrix Interaction and Regulation of Barrier Function
column37: Endothelial cells (EC) of small blood vessels in the lungs play a crucial role in forming a barrier to regulate proper tissue functioning. In pro-inflammatory conditions, like sepsis, loss of this barrier causes fluid to leak into the surrounding tissue, leading to organ failure and death. Many mechanisms help promote EC barrier function, including EC binding to the underlying extracellular matrix (ECM). Decreased EC-ECM interactions under inflammatory conditions, shown through changes in adhesion proteins like the focal adhesion kinases (FAK), is associated with compromised barrier function. A special protein in the lungs called the tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 3 (TIMP3) may regulate EC barrier function, since EC from mice lacking TIMP3 have increased leak; however, the underlying mechanism is unknown. Previous studies in the developing lung found that TIMP3 can promote EC-ECM interactions. As such, I hypothesized that TIMP3 maintains EC barrier function by promoting lung EC-ECM interactions. To test this, EC were isolated from wild type (WT) and Timp3-/- mice, cultured on various matrices, and stimulated with either PBS or inflammatory cytokines. EC-ECM interactions were assessed using adhesion assays, immunocytochemistry, and the XPERT-permeability assay. The former two methods showed that Timp3-/- EC had impaired EC-ECM adhesion and altered pFAK, compared to WT EC. The XPERT assay showed that localized leak was paracellular and associated with disruption of EC junction proteins. Additionally, total fluorescence was greater in cytomix-stimulated WT EC, and augmented in the Timp3-/- EC. Timp3-/- EC also had greater leak between the cells and ECM vs. WT cells under cytomix-stimulation. These results suggest that there is altered EC-ECM interaction under pro-inflammatory conditions, which may be regulated by TIMP3. This study may be crucial in uncovering therapeutic targets to decrease EC permeability and maintain or rescue barrier integrity in sepsis.

column36: Transplacental delivery of medicine across the placenta with IgG-modified nanoparticles for prenatal therapy
column37: Options are limited to treat a fetus developing abnormally. Surgery can remove or repair damaged tissue, but it does not fix poorly formed organs or tissue. This is a problem without a proper solution. A challenge for delivering life-changing medicine to the unborn baby is the placenta. The placenta provides nutrition to the baby from the mother. It can also block medicine from reaching the baby or can allow dangerous chemicals to reach the baby. To overcome this, we have developed nanoparticles as a new therapy option. They are 1000 times thinner than a human hair and smaller than the eye can see. Nanoparticles are safe drug 'chauffeurs' for a variety of medicine. Once the medicine is loaded into the nanoparticles, it can be injected into the mother. The nanoparticle is then chauffeured across the placenta to the fetus. We have added antibodies onto the surface of our nanoparticle. This can trick the placenta into transporting the medicine-loaded nanoparticles to the baby. The antibodies also act as a 'GPS' to guide the nanoparticles to where it is needed most. This method is so far the safest method to deliver drugs during pregnancy. We demonstrated the delivery of the GPS-enabled nanoparticles across the placenta is possible. They were neither toxic nor harmful to the placenta. This design has great potential to be adapted to deliver other medicine. Many babies will benefit from this method of treatment. Nanoparticles are a safe way to deliver life-changing medicine for pregnant mothers and their unborn baby. As medicine advances, new medications will be available. The nanoparticle is an excellent drug chauffeur to treat the unborn child safely and limit dangerous outcomes.

Research in the area has focused on accessible public transportation and the use of artificial intelligence or crowd-sourced information. With the funding from the grant we will build a research team that includes the City of Edmonton, local dis/ability advocacy organizations, and people with lived experience of dis/ability. Together, we will create a research project on equitable urban accessibility that highlights the diverse experiences and priorities of disabled persons. Having individuals with lived experiences of dis/ability on the team and part of the research planning will provide vital insight and guidance to ensure the process and resulting project align with their needs. The support we receive through this grant will help us to build strong research partnerships and a project that has the potential to advance urban accessibility in Edmonton and beyond. We would share lessons learned and provide an example of how to improve accessibility in cities, which could have an impact across Canada and internationally.

In addition, we will seek to understand which patient-reported outcome and experience measures will be important to measure as Island Health moves forward with HIT implementation. column36: A Meta-analysis of Children's Activity During Physical Education Lessons Taught by Generalist and Specialist Teachers
column37: Physical education (PE) class allows for regular and structured opportunities to be active during the school day, while providing time for children to develop the skills, knowledge, and attitudes needed to lead a healthy active lifestyle. However, quality of instruction and physical activity opportunities vary as specialists do not exclusively teach PE at the elementary school level. Therefore, it becomes the responsibility of the classroom teacher (i.e., generalist teacher) to teach this subject, despite possessing, in some cases, little or no PE knowledge or qualifications. The purpose of this review was to explore the extent to which teacher specialization contributes to physical activity accumulation and sedentary time in this environment. Seven databases were searched for peer-reviewed, English-language, original research. Percentage of PE lesson spent in moderate-to vigorous-intensity physical activity (MVPA) and sedentary time was synthesized across two types of teachers: generalists and specialists. Of the 42 articles included in this review, 32 assessed physical activity/sedentary time during PE offered by specialist teachers, nine assessed PE offered by generalist teachers, and one presented results for both types of teachers. Subgroup analyses found that children spent an average of 33.8% of their PE class time in MVPA when taught by a specialist, and 29.9% of their PE class time in MVPA when a generalist was responsible for instruction. Similarly, children spent 34.2% of PE class time in sedentary pursuits under the instruction of a specialist, and 40.9% of PE class time when taught by a generalist teacher. Overall, this review highlights that regardless of teacher specialization, physical activity levels during PE class at the elementary school level are much lower than the recommendation of 50% of lesson time spent in MVPA.

Afin de comprendre comment intervenir pour controler la resistance aux antibiotiques, il est necessaire de mesurer l'utilisation d'antibiotiques dans la communaute, puis de verifier si ces antibiotiques sont utilises de facon appropriee. La repetition reguliere de ces mesures permet d'evaluer l'impact de differentes interventions, comme la publication de guide cliniques, sur l'utilisation d'antibiotiques et sur la resistance. Des interventions plus adaptees a la situation auront un impact plus grand, preservant l'efficacite et la securite des soins de sante. Il n'existe pas encore de repertoire exhaustif decrivant l'usage d'antibiotiques au Quebec. Toutefois, une source d'information sur l'utilisation d'antibiotiques pourrait etre developpee en jumelant des donnees medico-administratives. Le Systeme integre de surveillance des maladies chroniques du Quebec (SISMACQ) contient l'information sur les ordonnances d'antibiotiques et les consultations medicales remboursees par le gouvernement, ce qui lui donne un point de vue unique sur les maladies chroniques et leur impact sur l'utilisation des soins de sante, dont l'utilisation d'antibiotiques. Ce projet decrira les quantites d'antibiotiques utilisees dans la communaute, puis de la qualite de ces ordonnances, en utilisant les donnees du SISMACQ et en tirant avantage de leur information sur les maladies chroniques. Les resultats seront compares a ceux de l'Agence de sante publique du Canada et de trois compagnies d'assurance. Etant donne la rarete de telles donnees au Canada, un effort particulier doit etre consacre a diffuser les resultats de ce projet.

column36: Towards Equitable Universal Health Coverage in a Globalized Era: a research agenda setting workshop
column37: Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 calls on all member countries to "Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages, which includes the provision of financial risk protection, access to quality essential health-care services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all". Meaningful progress towards SDG3 hinges, however, on the availability and access to Universal Health Coverage (UHC) - while ensuring no one is left behind. UHC is grounded in several principles including: equity, quality and financial protection. While there is growing evidence linking UHC to different health, economic and social outcomes, recent estimates suggest that about 800 Million people globally still do not have access to full financial coverage of essential health services. There are many pathways to scaling and achieving UHC requiring the generation of evidence-based, cost-effective and context-specific policies, programs, and practices. Equity (including gender equity), quality and financial protection are particularly challenging to tackle on the road to achieving UHC in the face of complex political, structural, fiscal, and other implementation bottlenecks across regions/countries. To this end, this project aims to: 1.Characterize the equity (including gender equity), financial protection and quality dimensions of universal health coverage globally 2.Prepare a background paper that synthesizes current policy trends and existing knowledge related to UHC and priority sub-themes (equity, financial protection, quality), and identifies priority knowledge gaps across sub-themes and regions 3.Facilitate interdisciplinary engagement on UHC through a one-day research agenda-setting workshop with local and international researchers, knowledge users, global institutions, research funders and journal editors 4.Contribute to advancements in research and policy related to UHC globally

column36: Listening and Learning: A Case for Indigenous Conceptualizations of a Learning Health System
column37: If you go to the doctor with a problem and the doctor tells you there is nothing wrong, you might feel rejected and misunderstood. Maybe in your community there is no other doctor to go to, so next time you are ill you decide not to go to the doctor at all, making things worse. Unfortunately, this situation is common in many parts of Canada. Our health care systems assume disease is the cause of illness. However, there is more than one way to understand health and health care. My research will help to build a health care system that learns from our different understandings, and constantly improves to provide better care. Many Indigenous peoples do not see health as an absence of disease, but as the result of good relationships with their family, community, environment, and spirit. The differences between these beliefs and the beliefs of our health care system mean that Indigenous patients often receive unhelpful, and even harmful, care. One idea is to build "learning health systems" that continuously improve care by learning from a variety of information sources, including patients. To improve care for Indigenous patients, learning health systems must know what to learn, how, and from whom. My analysis braids together Indigenous and non-Indigenous knowledges and ways of knowing to build a better understanding of what a learning health system is. My results suggest that meaningful engagement with Indigenous knowledge holders is necessary for health systems to learn. Built on respectful relationships, the learning health system could be developed as a system to improve healthcare for Indigenous patients and all Canadians.

column36: Exploring the effects of sedentary behaviour and physical activity on healthy ageing through an individual patient data meta-analysis: Harmonization of international longitudinal studies
column37: Recent demographic estimates showed that global population is ageing. Individuals over 60 years of age have more than doubled in numbers from 1980 to 2017, and these figures are expected to double again by 2050, reaching a staggering figure of 2.1 billion older persons. Even though there is emerging evidence that high levels of sedentary behaviour (SB) are detrimental, older populations spend around 9.4 hours per day in a sedentary state, and many of them do not engage in recommended physical activity (PA) levels. There is an on-going debate whether current guidelines on PA are appropriate for the aging population. In that sense, it would be extremely important to provide citizens with appropriate advice on the necessary amounts and modalities of PA and SB that would lead to meaningful health benefits. Disability-free life expectancy incorporates mortality and disability together, and has been considered as a crucial population health indicator for exploring whether the extra years lived have been spent in good or poor health. We will perform an Individual Patient Data (IPD) meta-analysis and use existing international longitudinal studies in order to identify minimal levels and patterns of SB and PA elderly individuals will need to engage in to increase DFLE by 2 years. IPD meta-analysis uses actual data from multiple cohort studies, rather than using data information taken from published articles alone. Before performing the IPD meta-analysis, complex retrospective data harmonization needs to be performed in order to integrate multiple datasets together, making provided information comparable to each other. Moreover, we will explore how the effects of these behaviours vary across populations of different age, sex, gender, ethnic background, and social status.

column36: Implementation and scale-up science: Tackling challenges in prevention and health promotion research
column37: Health promotion through physical activity can effectively enhance older adults' social connections and physical and mental health. Despite this, only 11% of Canadian older adults are active enough to enjoy health benefits. To positively affect the health of populations, physical activity programs that demonstrate effectiveness on a small scale must be scaled-up and sustained. In our recent (unpublished) systematic review of older adult physical activity interventions, of 1364 studies less than 1% were scaled up and only 8% assessed implementation. Of these, only four studies assessed implementation at scale-up. Scale-up is often relegated to the 'too hard' basket, which may reflect the many partnerships that must be in place for scale-up to succeed, and the substantial cost. Therefore, we aim to identify strategies that can be used to adapt, implement and evaluate scale-up of effective health promotion interventions. Our global goal is to enhance the mobility, health, and independence of older adults through enhanced physical activity. Thus, we propose to invite national and international experts in scale-up science and healthy aging, as well as key knowledge users, to Vancouver, BC. Our objectives for the meeting are threefold. First, we will develop an action plan to acknowledge and fill gaps in implementation and scale-up science research in healthy aging. Second, we will focus our action plan toward developing a CIHR Implementation Science Team Grant in Healthy Aging. Third, we will lay the groundwork for an opinion piece for the new Implementation Science Communications journal to highlight; i) the state of implementation and scale-up science in healthy aging (guided by our systematic review); ii) issues in implementation and scale-up science (e.g. inconsistent language, lack of standardized tools and measures); and iii) suggested ways forward. What we learn in BC can be applied to scale-up of physical activity interventions across Canada and the world.

column36: Developing a Doorway to Accessible Supportive Care Resources for Parents of Seriously Ill Children: An Innovative Pediatric Palliative Care ePortal
column37: Serious childhood illness disrupts family life and wellbeing. In Canada, over 1400 children with complex treatment needs receive specialized pediatric palliative care every year. To support development of improved pediatric palliative care, our team will bring together families, community organizations, knowledge users, researchers, graduate students, digital health specialists, and decision-makers from five Canadian provinces to come to agreement about important priorities for an electronic pediatric palliative care portal (ePortal). The results of our meeting and work will be shared with our team and others through presentations and publications, and we will involve all participants in determining the next steps towards a new grant application aimed at developing a pediatric palliative care ePortal and evaluating its feasibility and effectiveness. We firmly believe that an ePortal will improve families' healthcare experiences and wellbeing during a very difficult and often traumatic time.

column36: Knowledge Translation, Patient Safety, and Peri-operative Care Research and the Quality of Rectal Cancer Surgery - a pan-Canadian Workshop
column37: Our group has done large projects with surgeons that are meant to make the quality of surgery received by patients diagnosed with rectal cancer almost perfect. While we are learning a great deal, we are still seeing gaps or problems with what surgeons are doing. We would like to bring together for a one-day workshop patient representatives, surgeons who are experts in rectal cancer surgery, and, researchers from different areas to think about ways to fix these gaps or problems. The researchers we would like to invite are all interested in improving clinical care, but they work in somewhat different areas and ways. These areas include Knowledge Translation (e.g., getting surgeons to use guidelines that suggest things a surgeon should do), Patient Safety (e.g., getting surgeons to use checklists that force surgeons to do certain things), and Peri-operative Care (e.g., making sure surgeons order things before surgery for their patients). A workshop facilitator will make sure the meeting keeps moving, and that these different people and groups all have a chance to share their knowledge and viewpoints. There would be three goals. First, we would want people to decide what they mean by high-quality rectal cancer surgery. Second, we would want people to think about ways to measure high-quality surgery. Third, we would want the group to decide on the best ways to help surgeons always do high-quality rectal cancer surgery. We think this kind of workshop will help get new thinking and approaches to our ultimate goal of perfect surgery for every patient having a rectal cancer operation. After the workshop we will take any new ideas and solutions, and put them into larger projects with surgeons to test if they truly help surgeons provide perfect care. A diagnosis of rectal cancer causes much suffering and even death for many Canadians, and treatments like surgery are not always given in the best way possible.

Sex and gender issues, indigenous affairs and youth will all be addressed within the symposium. Importantly, the science presented at this symposia will be made openly accessible as video presentations on the online educational platform we developed with the previous CIHR knowledge and dissemination grant we received last year, which will ensure that this knowledge is accessible to those unable to attend in person, as well as the general public.

column36: Non-pharmacological interventions for caregivers with depression and care recipients with co-occurring depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis
column37: Family members or friends, known as caregivers, provide more and more of the care needed by older people and people with chronic conditions like dementia, cancer, or diabetes. In North America, in the past year more than 25% of people provided care to a chronically ill, disabled, or aging family member or friend. Caregivers provide valuable and often time-consuming or challenging care, but rarely receive training or much support. As a result, caregivers experience more physical and mental health challenges than the general population. Research has shown that caregivers often experience more anxiety and depression than the people for whom they provide care (care recipient). More than half of caregivers experience significant symptoms of depression. Notably, research also shows that the caregiver's health and well-being affects that of the care recipient, and vice versa. For example, a caregiver who is depressed provides lower-quality care and caring for someone who is depressed can result in the caregiver feeling distressed. To address this cycle, more support is needed for caregivers with depression and caregivers providing care to someone with depression. We conducted a review of published studies of interventions (other than prescribing medication) to help caregivers and care recipients with their depression. After searching and reviewing, we found that 15 studies matched our criteria. Overall, we found that interventions, like meditation, counselling, or learning to problem-solve, can improve the symptoms of depression of caregivers for up to a year. The biggest improvements were from a cognitive behaviour therapy intervention. We also found that there is very little information on what interventions can help for a year or more. We are looking into what factors, such as who gave the intervention or how long it was, that might be important in why certain interventions worked better than others at improving symptoms of depression.

column36: The impacts of digital food environments on health and nutrition: Setting research priorities
column37: The internet and mobile apps are transforming our way of life-even daily practices like eating. Digital food environments are making it possible for people to select and purchase food online, reducing barriers to both healthy and unhealthy food access. Social media networks influence food-, nutrition-, and diet-related knowledge through the rapid spread of (mis)information. Nutrition policies designed to inform and protect the public, such as front-of-package labeling, may have limited impact when food shopping online. The impacts of these emerging and rapidly changing digital food environments on health and nutrition are completely unknown and difficult to anticipate. Adopting a proactive approach to monitor and evaluate their impact, and identify opportunities for change will be critical to support healthy food choices within the realities of our modern digital environment. We propose to host a planning meeting to: 1) identify research priorities for digital food environments, 2) promote collaborations to develop research programs and projects on digital food environments, and 3) build capacity to conduct digital food environment research in Canada. This process will be documented and the outcomes of the meeting and evaluation will be synthesized into a consensus paper that will be published. A group of multi-disciplinary researchers and stakeholders will be formed to develop a future research project. The priorities identified will be ranked according to potential for feasibility and impact, and top priorities will be incorporated into a CIHR project grant proposal.

column36: Multiple imputation to address confounding bias due to missing data in large primary care databases
column37: Background: Missing data on important variables in large clinical databases is a challenge for primary care researchers. Including only complete cases (with no missing data) in an analysis may decrease the accuracy of results. Different statistical approaches were suggested to deal with this problem. There is, however, no general rule on how to evaluate which of them provides more accurate results. A so-called "plasmode simulation" technique is a promising modern method to deal with this problem. Objective: Using a "plasmode simulation" approach, we compare the accuracy and precision of results between the two statistical techniques. The first technique includes only complete cases in the analysis (CC). The second replaces missing data with data obtained by another statistical method called "multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE)". We will apply these techniques to a large real-life primary care dataset. Methods: This study uses population-based data, the national Primary Care Practice-based Electronic Medical Records Database, for 2011-2016. We will measure weight, antidepressants (AD) prescribing, age, sex, comorbidities, smoking. A statistical method called logistic regression will be used to analyze the "plasmode" (part real, part generated) data in order to estimate whether obese patients are more likely to be prescribed AD than normal weight patients. Results: Of 120381 patients, 46.8% lacked data on weight, 0.02% on sex, and 64.2% on smoking. Patients with obesity were 1.16 to 1.26 times more likely to have AD prescription than patients with normal weight when using the CC analysis. With the MICE technique, obese patients were 1.10 to 1.21 times more likely to receive AD. Use of a "plasmode simulation" will show which of these methods is more accurate and precise. Conclusion: In the original data, results differed between CC and MICE analyses. Plasmode simulations will help to choose the best way to handle missing data in primary care databases.

column36: Sustaining the gains of NTD elimination programs through focused support of community drug distributors
column37: Neglected tropical diseases are a group of 20 infectious diseases that have been historically overlooked by donors and researchers. NTDs are debilitating diseases that disproportionately burden the world's poorest and most vulnerable communities, trapping millions in inescapable cycles of poverty. Volunteer community drug distributors (CDDs) are the cornerstone upon which ongoing international efforts to eliminate or control NTDs rests. Through mass drug administration (MDA), CDDs have successfully delivered millions of donated treatments to individuals living in endemic communities. However, NTD program managers from the Ministries of Health in endemic countries have recently faced implementation challenges regarding the use of volunteers in MDA. Forums that foster interdisciplinary collaboration between researchers and NTD program managers, such as the meeting outlined in this proposal, are urgently needed to develop operational strategies that will better support CDDs in their essential work. The research upon which the proposed meeting is based has investigated the challenges faced by CDDs conducting MDA in Cote d'Ivoire and Uganda and has led to the development of several supportive interventions. We intend to use this meeting to share the findings of this work with NTD program managers, develop plans for disseminating this information, plan for the scale-up of the interventions and identify areas for future investigation. The success of this research project is a testament to the ongoing collaboration of researchers, medical professionals, government workers, program managers, and front line health staff, who are working together from countries around the world. It is the intention of this team to use this meeting to help nations across sub-Saharan Africa in their mission to eliminate these NTDs as a global public health problem.

column36: Planning to create partnerships and advance research to understand system-level opportunities to expand midwives' contributions to improve access to sexual and reproductive health care
column37: Sexual and reproductive health are essential to gender equality. In 2019, Canada hosted the international Women Deliver conference which highlighted the need to ensure access to sexual and reproductive health care in order to realize the full potential of girls and women. However, in Canada, not all girls and women have adequate access to sexual and reproductive health care. Registered midwives in Canada are highly-trained health care providers who specialize in women's reproductive health. Currently the role of most midwives in Canada is limited to care during pregnancy, birth, and the first six weeks following birth, but midwives have the knowledge and skills to play a bigger role in sexual and reproductive health care. Globally, midwives provide safe and effective contraception and abortion services. Expanding the role of midwives in Canada could improve access to sexual and reproductive health care, particularly in rural and remote areas and for people in urban areas who have poor access to care. Decision makers need high quality evidence to help them to create policies that will expand the role that midwives play in order to make access to key sexual and reproductive health services more equitable in Canada. This project will involve one-day meeting in Toronto on April 3, 2020 of national leaders in sexual and reproductive health, and in midwifery. This will include physicians and midwives, researchers, leaders from professional and regulator organizations, and policy-makers. The meeting will be used to a) share what is already known about expanding the role and scope of midwives in sexual and reproductive health care in Canada, and b) to develop strong partnerships and plan research to address the evidence needs of key stakeholders. The team will then use the discussions at the meeting to develop a research plan and submit a grant application to support that research.

column36: A plan for establishing a sustainable, practical, and effective multi-sectoral working platform for the prevention and control of NCDs in a middle-income country: Thailand
column37: Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and their burdens are prevalent worldwide, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Thailand. Countries need to establish robust multi-sectoral actions (MSA) to implement effective policies to prevent and control NCDs successfully. The reason is that the nature of influencing factors contributing to NCDs is usually beyond the scope of the health sector. Nevertheless, true multi-sectoral collaboration is not easy to implement. The main barriers to creating a successful MSA are a lack of awareness by various other sectors about their potential contribution, weak political will, coordination complexity, and inadequate resources. The research team plans to introduce innovative approaches to establish a sustainable, practical, and effective multi-sectoral working platform for the prevention and control of NCDs in Thailand. These include (1) the outside-in approach to complement the conventional inside-out approach which is usually initiated by the Ministry of Health, (2) the approach using the informal, knowledge-based learning initiative to complement the conventional official routine meeting, and (3) the approach to enhance public support to complement the political will enhancement approach. With this planning grant, we will conduct three consultative meetings with key stakeholders in developing an implementation research proposal (IRP) to establish an effective MSA in Thailand. We will hold a one-day introductory meeting in Step I. Then, we will conduct a one-day informal, knowledge-based learning initiative to share and learn information regarding international best practices of ministerial policy intervention in NCDs prevention and control in Step II. After that, in Step III, a two-day meeting will be operated to do knowledge exchange and translation, and to design for an IRP for establishing the effective MSA in Thailand. Lastly, we will write up the IRP and ask for its approval from stakeholders.

The benefits of this exploratory study are to help illuminate how girls in SLFN experience various influences that shape their daily lives, and how they characterize these influences as empowering or disempowering to inform health promoting strategies.

column36: The Stronger at Home Study: Planning for a Trial to Evaluate a New Home-based Rehabilitation Program for Hip Fracture Patients Using an Integrated Knowledge Translation Approach
column37: With increasing life expectancy and the corresponding increasing number of ageing adults, hip fractures are expected to become a worldwide health problem in the near future. With the current trend of reducing length of hospital stays, some responsibility for care of patients who have had hip fractures is being shifted from hospitals to communities, frequently without adequate resources in place to support patients when they return home. Evidence indicates that extended rehabilitation programs in the community and at patients' homes could improve health outcomes for older adults who have had hip fracture by helping them recover at home. Thus, the time is right to invest in creating evidence-informed treatment programs that provide seniors who have had a hip fracture with better care, better health and greater opportunity to continue to live independently at home. We are requesting support to organize a meeting to continue building a varied team of stakeholders, which will focus on integrating care related to recovery after hip fracture. At this planning meeting, we will aim to establish a collaborative research relationship among a group of experts, clinicians, policymakers, patients and caregivers with interest in the care of seniors with hip fractures after they are discharged from hospital to their home. By forming this multidisciplinary team, we hope to create a long-term multidisciplinary collaboration to enhance research in recovery after hip fracture. The results of this research will be reflected in improved clinical health practices over the continuum of recovery, which will help both patients and their caregivers and reduce the burden on the healthcare system. Ultimately, this research aims to improve senior patients' health and reduce the burden on the healthcare system.

column36: 5th Cancer Cachexia Conference: Bridging Molecular Advances to Clinical Care
column37: Cachexia is a debilitating syndrome of cancer, characterized by severe weight loss resulting from the depletion of mainly skeletal muscle and adipose. Muscle atrophy in particular is associated with weakness and fatigue, a lower tolerance to chemotherapy, and increased risk for adverse outcomes following surgery. Estimates indicate that the prevalence of cachexia in cancer is 50-80%, and 20% of all cancer deaths are linked to cachexia rather than directly to the tumor burden. Although Phase III clinical studies have been performed in cancer cachexia, they have failed to reach their primary endpoint. Thus, there remains an urgent need to better understand the underlying mechanisms by which tumor factors drive muscle and fat loss, so as to identify viable therapeutic targets that can be translated to an effective treatment. In 2012, a committee was formed to organize the first, cancer cachexia focused international conference, which was held in Boston. Based on the success of that first meeting, subsequent biennial conferences took place in Montreal (2014), Washington DC (2016), and Philadelphia (2018). The results from those meetings contributed a growing number of new laboratories entering the field and provided new knowledge. Still, much remains to be answered in the areas of clinical trial design, prognostic and diagnostic biomarkers, and choice of animal models. We propose to tackle these gaps through the organization of this meeting. As Canadian scientists, we are fortunate to have been involved in the inception of the Cancer Cachexia conference. This conference offers the unique opportunity for Canadian students and trainees to learn about the recent advances in the field, and to present their work in front leaders in the field. In addition, the conference offers venues for trainees and scientists to establish novel collaboration to solve health-related questions that are directly relevant to Canada and the world.

column37: Siblings of people with developmental disabilities have the longest lasting relationship with their brothers and sisters but have been quite ignored when it comes to health research, as well as patient engagement efforts. Non-disabled adult siblings have an important role to play as caregivers, particularly as their disabled sibling ages but they struggle in terms of navigating the health care system with their sibling, as well as maintaining their own physical and mental health. There is much to be done, to bring the sibling voice to health care research and clinical efforts and a great deal which can be learned from more established National sibling efforts from the UK and the US, as well as from listening to and working collaboratively with Canadian siblings. The purpose of this project is to bring Canadian siblings together, for the first time, to learn from one another and to develop priority areas of focus. In turn, siblings will share that information with a group of policy makers, health administrators, and researchers, in order to collectively establish a national research, policy and practice agenda. Building off of a two year successful partnership between researchers and adult siblings, we will work together to establish and begin to address sibling research priorities to better address their health, and the health and health care needs of their brothers and sisters.

column36: Transforming the development and dissemination of expertise, knowledge and technologies in neuroscience through scientific platforms.
column37: Fundamental research in health sciences, disease diagnosis and treatment rely heavily on new technologies. The growing complexity and capabilities they offer for development and applications have made it difficult for individual research labs and single organizations to master and apply them rigorously. To address this situation, many research efforts have turned to multidisciplinarity. Scientific platforms (SP), which are centralized and shared laboratories that offer highly specialized instrumentation and services are at the heart of this new reality. They provide unique expertise so researchers can exploit the incredible benefits of technologies. The importance of shared knowledge, resources and equipment is uniquely exemplified in the field of neuroscience where multidisciplinary teams of brain researchers must come together to tackle the challenge of unraveling the functional connectome of the human brain. The 2020 meeting organized by the Canadian Network of Scientific Platforms (CNSP) will focus on Canadian initiatives in brain research. Almost 20% of the 140 platform members of the CNSP are directly involved in neuroscience research and many more are being used by that community. The Canadian Brain Research Strategy, which promotes strong and successful collaborative efforts in neuroscience will be featured at the meeting. The 2020 meeting will connect expert platform scientists from various fields, university administrators, industrial collaborators and funding agencies. It is a unique and much needed opportunity for networking and discussing important issues such as SP funding, best practices in research and career paths for platform scientists. International guests will also be invited to share their experience. The CIHR funding will largely be used to support travel and merit awards to recognize the contribution of world-class platform scientists.The event is scheduled for June 9-11 2020 in Toronto and is expected to gather 200 people.

column37: In 2012, the F-words in Childhood Disability (Function, Family, Fitness, Fun, Friends, Future) began to capture the attention of families, service providers and organizations worldwide. column36: Development of International Partnership to Identify and Examine Priority Research Questions on Tuberculosis in Africa's Most Populous Nation, Nigeria
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of death from infectious disease globally and is among the top 10 causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. It is also the main cause of death among people living with HIV. Nigeria, which is Africa's most populous nation with an estimated 197 million people, has the highest burden of TB, multi-drug resistant TB, and TB/HIV co-infection in the continent, and the sixth highest burden of TB globally. According to the World Health Organization's recent report on the 'End TB Strategy', "the Sustainable Development Goals and the End TB Strategy targets set for 2030 cannot be met without intensified research and development". Without question, research to address this health challenge will require international collaborative efforts; and will need to happen in settings with the greatest burden of TB disease. Clearly, there is a need for a meeting to share knowledge and discuss gaps and opportunities for further research in a setting like Nigeria with such enormous TB problems. The objective of this proposal is to plan a meeting between Canadian investigators and multi-stakeholder teams (including researchers) from Nigeria to exchange knowledge on TB disease and co-develop priority and emerging research questions, that could form the basis of a future grant application to CIHR. If funded, we are poised to hold a series of face-to-face meetings in Nigeria, the epicentre of the TB epidemic in Africa. These meetings will represent a significant step in our efforts to facilitate knowledge transfer, co-develop and identify pressing research questions on TB; initiate new research collaborations; and move towards the development of a CIHR grant application to plan future research. Ultimately, an effort like this could evolve in the long-term into a research program that will place Canada and Nigeria at the cutting-edge of TB research internationally, by potentially demonstrating new approaches and strategies to address complex epidemics.

column36: University of Toronto Summer Institute in Pain
column37: Pain is a public health issue that has reached crisis proportions with social, ethical, legal and economic consequences. Unfortunately, a wide gap exists between pain research and clinical practice. While scientists constantly produce new knowledge relevant to pain prevention and clinical care, much of their work is never incorporated into practice. Similarly, clinical problems are rarely translated into research questions and projects. We must work together to effectively integrate research of pain mechanisms and its neural underpinnings with pain management using knowledge translation strategies, and ensure optimal outcomes for individuals who suffer from pain. Accordingly, we have created the University of Toronto Summer Institute in Pain (Pain Institute); an annual educational summit that brings 30 of the best and brightest graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and clinical trainees to learn from Canadian research experts in a range of disciplines in basic science and clinical fields. Trainees come from the University of Toronto and other leading international universities. The goal of this institute is to foster interdisciplinary collaboration and creative new methods for pain research and innovation, and biologically-informed treatment practices integrating recent neuroscience advances. For the past 4 years, the Pain Institute has been organized as a 4-day, high-intensity summer workshop that culminates in a 1-day international scientific meeting hosted by interfaculty leaders in the University of Toronto Centre for the Study of Pain (UTCSP) along with trainees and other national and international scholars. The theme of our 2020 school will be "The brain behind the pain: from neural encoding to the patient experience". The CIHR Planning and Dissemination Grant will allow us to continue to attract and recruit top students from across Canada to participate in this unique and highly-acclaimed opportunity.

column36: 27th International Symposium on Hepatitis C Virus and Related Viruses
column37: The International Symposium on Hepatitis C Virus and Related Viruses has been a recurring annual conference since 1994. It has become the main forum for basic science investigators working on hepatitis C virus (HCV) and related viruses. Over the past 26 years, this conference has been instrumental in developing and advancing major discoveries in the HCV field including the understanding of the virus life cycle and development of in vitro replication systems and animal models. This meeting has fostered the discovery and development of direct acting antivirals (DAA) that have revolutionized the treatment of HCV infection. Understanding the immune response and pathogenesis of chronic HCV infection presented at this meeting are now the basis for ongoing vaccine development and preclinical trials. Despite this progress, basic research on HCV infection remains at the forefront to drive HCV elimination efforts and reduce the morbidity and mortality of the disease. Research into vaccine development, HCV pathogenesis and liver cancer following DAA treatment, novel diagnostics and sequencing approaches to track the evolution and transmission of HCV in at-risk populations are only some of the key remaining research questions. The HCV2020 meeting will focus on the main objective of HCV elimination by bringing together Basic and Clinical investigators to discuss the remaining challenges in the HCV field and novel approaches to tackle them towards this aim. The symposium will bring together keynote lectures from outstanding senior investigators and rising stars in virology, immunology and liver disease. In addition, high quality oral and poster presentations will be selected from submitted abstracts.
