column36: 9th Canadian Symposium on HCV - Advances in HCV Research and Treatment Towards Elimination
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) affects at least 270,000 Canadians and causes more years of life lost than any infectious disease in the country. The Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) and the Public Health Agency of Canada have identified liver disease due to HCV as a major public health problem. Providing better care for HCV-infected individuals requires interactions between researchers and policy makers across the four CIHR pillars (Biomedical, Clinical, Health Services and Social, Cultural, Environmental, and Population Health). Over the past 9 years, the National Canadian Research Training Program in Hepatitis C, now The Canadian Network on Hepatitis C Virus (CanHepC), have organized the Canadian Symposium on Hepatitis C Virus (CSHCV), using funds from CIHR, industry sponsors and our sister event immediately thereafter (The Canadian Liver Meeting). The CSHCV has been highly successful and has promoted the exchange of ideas and expertise between social scientists, public health experts, economists, basic scientists, clinicians and community members all working towards the elimination of HCV in Canada. The goal of this CIHR Meetings, Planning and Dissemination Grant is to seek support for the 9th symposium, to be held on February 28th, 2019 in Montreal. The theme of this year's symposium will be "Advances in HCV Research and Treatment Towards Elimination" and will focus on vaccine research, HCV in pregnancy and childhood, and achieving elimination targets by improving diagnosis, linkage to care and access to HCV medications. We will highlight Canadian treatment successes during an interactive, community lead lunchtime symposium. We aim to encourage collaboration and exchange among researchers, policy makers and community members to improve health and achieve elimination of HCV in Canada.

column36: Evaluating protocols for treating moderate acute malnutrition in the Philippines: Knowledge synthesis and agenda setting
column37: Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) among children under five is a serious public health concern in the Philippines. Recently, the Philippines Department of Health and the World Food Programme have promoted a new protocol for the identification and treatment of cases of MAM. This new protocol recommends treating children with MAM with one of three possible supplementary foods: ready-to-use supplementary food (RUSF); locally prepared foods with added micronutrient powder; or blended cereals. While the Department of Health primarily promotes RUSF, civil society organizations that fill service gaps may have their own internal protocols. However, no research has investigated the relative effectiveness of these treatment options in the Philippines. Our overall objective is to work with the health-oriented civil society organization International Care Ministries to synthesize current knowledge on supplementary foods for treating MAM and establish a new research project to evaluate the effectiveness and acceptability of RUSF versus other treatment protocols for MAM. Specific objectives are: (1) to conduct an updated systematic review of the effectiveness of supplementary food interventions for treating childhood MAM; (2) to conduct a scoping review to synthesize literature available on factors that affect the effectiveness of supplementary food interventions, including cultural congruity, allergy concerns, marketing, and stigma; and (3) to strengthen international and local collaborations, refine research priorities, and co-develop a research proposal through stakeholder consultations and a collaborative agenda-setting meeting.

column36: Mitochondrial dynamics directs macrophage polarization during atherosclerosis: implications for disease regression
column37: Heart attacks and strokes are caused primarily by atherosclerosis- cholesterol driven inflammatory disease of the vessel wall. A hallmark of worsening disease is the accumulation of pro-inflammatory (M1) macrophages (white blood cells) within the vessel wall, which sustain the pro-inflammatory environment of the atherosclerotic plaque. In contrast, during plaque repair, macrophages adopt a pro-resolving, anti-inflammatory phenotype (M2). Macrophage subtypes also exhibit different preferences in how they produce cell energy within their mitochondria. M1 macrophages primarily use glucose and don't require oxygen, while M2 macrophages mainly use oxygen. Mitochondria within the macrophages adapt to these different sources of energy by allowing their mitochondria to undergo constant physical changes. Mitochondria undergo cycles of fragmentation & elongation, which have been demonstrated to direct cell phenotype and function in other cell types. We found that M1 macrophages have a very elongated mitochondrial network whereas M2 mitochondria are more fragmented. Based on these observed differences and known metabolic preferences, we hypothesize that the balance of mitochondrial elongation and fragmentation directs macrophage type leading to repair or worsening of the inflammation in the plaque. By exploring the role, mitochondria may play in macrophage cell type decisions this opens up a new target to promote repair within the vessel wall.

column36: Disseminating findings from the 'Bridging the Gap' Study: A study examining a digital tool to transform mental health and wellness help-seeking in transition-aged youth
column37: About 70% of all lifetime mental health problems arise by the age of 251, with many cases persisting into adulthood. While 1 in 4 transition-aged youth (16-25 years old) are currently affected by mental illness, less than 20% of these individuals received the appropriate care and support. Digital mental health innovations have been identified as a promising means to bridge many of the aforementioned gaps in the delivery of mental health care for transition-aged youth. However, despite the development of many rigorous solutions, there is currently a lack of widespread adoption of these solutions. As a result, there is a strong need to disseminate the current findings from a mobile health (mHealth) app evaluation locally conducted in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) and closely examine how evidence-based mental health technologies can be mobilized to make an impact on mental health help-seeking needs and experiences. The current project aims to disseminate the findings from the 'Bridging the Gap' study, a mixed-methods randomized controlled trial that examines the impact of 'Thought Spot', a mental health help-seeking app designed for the needs of transition-aged youth, and identify next steps in the development of an optimization plan to ensure operational readiness of Thought Spot. Additionally, relevant stakeholders are engaged for the planning of an appropriate dissemination strategy to effectively scale and enable usage of Thought Spot across universities and colleges in Canada

column36: "CAN LhIVE WELL": The Canadian HIV Wellness Research Initiative
column37: In the early 1980s, HIV was found to be the virus that causes AIDS. At that time, people with AIDS would fall ill and often die early. Now we have anti-HIV drugs that are life-saving and can allow people living with HIV (PLWH) to live long and healthy lives. HIV care providers now need to ensure that PLWH have good quality of life and can do the activities they wish to do. The meeting we are proposing will bring together a group of HIV researchers, program staff, and PLWH (community members) that are interested in the wellness of PLWH to brainstorm future "wellness in HIV" projects. We will bring together a team that does research or provides programs that address many areas of wellness in PLWH as well as community members that represent the diverse groups of PLWH in Canada. This includes: men who have sex with men; people who inject drugs; sex workers; people in prisons; Indigenous Peoples; African, Caribbean and Black communities; youth born with HIV; and others. How people view wellness and identify priorities for wellness research, may differ for the different groups of PLWH. Having a discussion between researchers, community agency staff, and community members about wellness will be very important to advance this area of research and improve wellness among PLWH in Canada. This proposal is to have a 2-day meeting to work towards the following goals: 1) To understand the meaning of wellness among PLWH in Canada; 2) To identify the wellness research and activities currently happening for PLWH in Canada and which aspects of wellness need support; 3) To create goals and teams to work on future "wellness in HIV" projects; 4) To come up with research questions and plans for future grant applications; 5) To create a meeting report with recommendations; and 6) To develop a story or article about the meeting to share with the greater community.

column36: Montreal International DNA Tumour Virus Meeting 2020
column37: In the current proposal we are seeking CIHR support towards the organization of the Montreal DNA Tumour Virus (DNATV) Meeting, which will take place from July 21-25, 2020 at the Centre Mont Royal in downtown Montreal. This meeting brings together a diverse group of researchers with common research interests in the study of DNA tumor viruses. These viruses include the polyomaviruses, the adenoviruses, certain herpesviruses and the papillomaviruses. These viruses have served as invaluable models towards understanding the process of cancer progression. In some cases the DNA tumour viruses are also clinically important pathogens that cause cancer in humans. The most notable examples are the human papillomavirus that are the cause of essentially all cervical cancers. The significance of this finding was recognized in 2008 with the awarding of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Harold zur Hausen, the discoverer of the relationship between HPV and cervical cancer. Research of HPV and other DNA tumour viruses continues to progress rapidly and the current meeting is a major forum for the dissemination of these findings. The DNATV meeting has occurred yearly for over 5 decades and over the years has included some major breakthroughs in cancer biology research. This will be the third time that this meeting is held in Canada. Attendance at the meeting is expected to be from 200-250 based upon previous years. During the last DNATV meeting in 2016 in Montreal, 200 scientists from 19 different countries attended and the meeting was a great success in part due to the support of the CIHR. This yearly meeting brings together the DNA tumour virus research community from across the globe, highlights the year's most outstanding research, accomplishments in the field, and fosters international collaboration. The DNATV meeting continues to be an outstanding opportunity to showcase Canadian science on an international stage.

Winnipeg has committed $13M to improving active transportation infrastructure in poor neighbourhoods but need a plan for how to spend this budget. column36: 11th Meeting of the Canadian Oxidative Stress Consortium
column37: The Canadian Oxidative Stress Consortium (COSC) aims to advance research and education on the role of oxidative stress in health and disease. The 11th COSC meeting will be held in Montreal (13-15 May 2020) at the Jewish General Hospital. This is the largest Canadian conference about oxidative stress and health. Created in 1999 through CIHR funds by Dr Ashok Grover (McMaster Univ.), COSC consists of researchers from over 50 laboratories and 15 universities in Canada. COSC creates an environment that initiates and strengthens research collaborations between researchers, promotes opportunities for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, and facilitates ties with industry and non-profit agencies. Oxidative stress is an imbalance between levels of antioxidants and reactive oxidants, leading to cell and tissue damage. Conference symposia will address the role of oxidative stress in diseases such as cancer, aging-related diseases, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, antibiotic resistance, lung and cardiac diseases, arthritis, inflammation, stroke, spinal cord injury, as well health and nutrition. COSC attracts over 150 attendees from across Canada and internationally, and will feature three leading international plenary speakers, Helmut Sies and Marcus Conrad (Germany) and Sharon Campbell (USA). COSC aims to develop the next generation of world-class scientists. COSC 2020 will feature two Symposia for trainees to hone their skills at delivering effective oral presentations and discussing their research through poster presentations. Awards will be bestowed for the best oral and poster presentations plus travel awards. The biennial COSC meeting provides outstanding networking opportunities for trainees to discuss their research with top experts in the field. The Jewish General Hospital, a world class McGill University-affiliated Teaching Hospital, is uniquely positioned to host this meeting and represents an eminent institution of health research through the Lady Davis Institute.

column36: BEFORE: Education and dissemination of an oncofertility decision aid
column37: Young adults diagnosed with cancer may be at an increased risk of infertility as a result of their cancer treatment. Fertility in survivorship is of great importance to many cancer patients and infertility can lead to lower quality of life. While fertility risks should be discussed with all patients, clinicians report having low levels of knowledge on the available fertility options and resources available for patients. Clinicians require more education on fertility and resources to help them feel comfortable raising this topic with their patients. To help fertility discussions, our team created a decision aid for young adults with breast cancer, called the Begin Exploring Fertility Options, Risks and Expectations (BEFORE) decision aid. This decision aid is being disseminated to 21 sites across Canada. To assist with the dissemination of the aid, we host a webinar for nurses and support staff on fertility in young adults with breast cancer and provide an introduction to the BEFORE decision aid. Due to the positive response from the webinar and BEFORE DA, we recognize the need to broaden the content and provide this education to more clinicians. We aim to revise the webinar to include the fertility options, risks and available resources for all young adults with any cancer type and disseminate it more widely to clinicians. The webinar will be hosted through the Canadian Association of Nurses in Oncology national webinar platform allowing nurses and other interested clinicians from across Canada to attend. A post-webinar survey will assess webinar attendees intended behaviour changes, current fertility care practices and needs when discussing fertility, enabling our team to identify new initiatives that are required to enhance the fertility care provided to YA with cancer in Canada.

column36: Turning Oral Narratives of British Columbia's HIV/AIDS Epidemic in Action: Expansive Knowledge Translation to Address Present & Persistent Challenges
column37: Within communities most impacted by the epidemic in Canada (gay men, Indigenous peoples, people of colour, etc.), HIV/AIDS is both a historical experience of loss and community resilience, and an ongoing public health concern. Oral history offers a way of addressing persistent health challenges, not just by preserving the past, but by providing insight into how current prevention and treatment interventions can be reinvigorated. This proposal aims to build on an ongoing CIHR Catalyst Grant-funded project collecting oral history of the early years of British Columbia's HIV/AIDS epidemic, with the end goal of sharing our findings with diverse community audiences. Thus far, we have conducted over 110 interviews with a diverse group of long-term survivors and caregivers across British Columbia. This knowledge translation and exchange with affected communities will help to preserve cultural memory of the early AIDS epidemic, promote much-needed cross-generational and cross-sector dialogue in the present, and contribute a more nuanced temporal lens to future health research, promotion, and care. If secured, funding would be used to produce community-oriented dissemination events, programming, and tools to maximize the impacts of our oral histories on key stakeholders in the community and health sector. Specifically, we will: 1) Hold two community forums in Vancouver and Victoria to share the main results of our research with affected communities. 2) Generate intergenerational community dialogue by integrating our findings within existing programming run by our community-based partners at YouthCO and the Community-Based Research Centre. 3) Adapt our archival collection into a multi-media exhibit (including interview clips and quotations, and archival materials) and present it in Vancouver, Victoria, and elsewhere. And 4) Produce at least one community-oriented, arts-based output from the project, likely a short film, to share our findings with a wider audience.

column36: Mutation co-operativity in early tumorigenesis events of low-grade serous ovarian carcinoma: Lesson from an organoid model system and single-cell RNA-sequencing
column37: Ovarian cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death in women. Such poor outcome is due to lack of reliable early detection strategies and suboptimal response to chemotherapies. Our study focuses on a rare subtype of ovarian cancer: low-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (LGSOC). Since LGSOC is rarer than other subtypes, accounting for 5% of all ovarian cancer cases, it is relatively understudied. But there is an urgent clinical need to understand this disease as it typically presents in young women and is usually resistant to conventional chemotherapy. LGSOC is thought to come from the Fallopian tube, with 2 frequent mutations occurring together. We are interested in how these different mutations work together to drive the initiation of LGSOC. To model the initiation process, we adopt the novel organoid system wherein we take normal fallopian tube cells and grow them in specialized conditions so that they form 3D structures resembling small organs. We will introduce different mutations specific to LGSOC into healthy human Fallopian tube organoids and study changes in cells. Cutting-edge sequencing technologies will be utilized to study the changes that occur as a result of added mutations at single-cell levels. The combination of organoid and single-cell technology has positioned us to address the question of how LGSOC occur in the first place. Understanding why and how cancer occur could considerably open up venues for developing early detection and prevention strategies, as well as more targeted therapies for different individuals.

column37: Individuals experiencing mental health and addictions concerns face many physical, emotional, and social strains as a result of their illnesses, all the while trying to navigate unfamiliar territory in the healthcare system. Navigation is a strategy that can help people facing complex care needs and barriers to care in finding and accessing needed supports in the health care system. Navigators provide patient-centered service, guiding individuals through their care plans and overcoming barriers to care. Navigation for individuals experiencing mental health and addictions concerns has shown significant promise and has been gaining traction across Canada. The Canadian Healthcare Navigation Conference will be the first event of its kind in Canada to bring together navigation researchers, service providers, students, decision makers, and individuals with lived experience to share lessons learned, promising practices, and research findings. This event will be co-hosted by the Family Navigation Project at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre and NaviCare/SoinsNavi at the University of New Brunswick, and will take place on April 30th to May 1st 2020 in Toronto. This event will begin with an evening networking reception, where attendees will connect before the full day of presentations. The next day, there will be two keynote presentations; one from a research or practice leader in navigation in the morning, and another from an individual with lived experience involved in advocacy in Canadian healthcare in the afternoon. Concurrent presentations will also be held following each keynote presentation. A poster session will be held at the end of the day for participants to engage with each other and discuss their work. This conference is an important first step to creating a shared national conversation about navigation services so that we can continue to develop, implement, and share best evidence and practices in the field.

column36: The Monarch Collaboration: Improving the Health of Migrants and Refugees through Immunization
column37: Recent outbreaks of vaccine preventable diseases, such as measles, are of concern to both the public and health agencies. These events have emphasized the need to improve immunization to reduce adverse health effects and provide protection for everyone. Migrants and refugees may be at increased risk of getting vaccine preventable diseases because they may not be immunized and may be more vulnerable to disease. However, our knowledge of actual immunization rates and factors affecting immunization decision-making for these populations remains limited. A group of experienced and concerned international researchers, representing Canada, Europe (Germany and the United Kingdom) and Australasia (New Zealand and Australia) have formed The Monarch Collaboration. Our goal is to protect and improve the health of migrant and refugee populations through producing research evidence on immunization access and uptake. A planning workshop for The Monarch Collaboration will be held to update research needs and priorities (in light of significant new information), and develop and submit one or more multinational grant proposals to further our research goals and objectives. The workshop will also allow us to strengthen our collaborative relationships. These anticipated workshop outcomes will further our efforts to promote health and health equity in these globally vulnerable population groups. Conducting research across countries using a common approach will allow us to explain issues related to migrant and refugee immunization within a global context, including how these are impacted by factors such as migrant intake policies and access to health care. Finally, our collaborative research efforts may help prevent the transmission of vaccine preventable diseases through migration, thus protecting both migrants/refugees and the residents of their host countries.

column36: Healthy Mom, Healthy Heart: National Planning for the Evaluation of Knowledge & Cardiac Risk Assessment in Women with a History of Cardiovascular Complications During Pregnancy
column37: Women with a history of a high blood pressure and diabetes during pregnancy have a much higher risk of developing cardiac risk factors and future heart disease, including chronic high blood pressure, stroke, and death from heart disease. Despite the significant impact pregnancy complications have on a woman's future heart health risk, there are limited education resources or community programs to improve lifelong heart health in these young women. Promoting public awareness, education and early screening after delivery are critical initiatives that could improve lifelong heart health as well as improve future pregnancy outcomes. We will bring together key stakeholders, patients and experts in maternal-postpartum health, community health and cardiac rehabilitation for a 1 day in-person meeting in order to identify key gaps in knowledge, barriers regarding women's education needs and lifelong heart health. Using a group decision-making technique, specific strategies to address barriers and gaps will be formulated in addition to action plans. This work is a first step that will inform the team of women's education needs following delivery and lifelong heart health risk. The results of this planning meeting will guide the future development of an online survey targeting the learning needs and preferences of women of childbearing age across Canada.

column36: Towards National Recommendations for Perioperative Corticosteroids Stress Dose Administration
column37: Steroids are medications that can be given to treat many diseases to reduce inflammation. If steroids are taken for a long period of time, this can lead to the suppression of glands called adrenal glands (those glands produce cortisone/steroid in our body). If these adrenal glands don't work well and patient undergo surgery, this can lead to low blood pressure and even death. These complications can be prevented by giving steroids intravenously before the surgery. However, there are side effects associated to giving steroids before surgery such as higher risk of infection after surgery. This project consists of gathering a group of Canadian experts to discuss which patients would benefit from receiving steroids around the surgery. At the end our discussions, we will write and publish recommendations to help other physicians around the country to treat those patients.

column36: Food Literacy: Shaping the health of children and youth
column37: Unhealthy eating continues to be a major risk factor for chronic disease in Ontario. It is well understood that healthy eating, including avoiding foods higher in sodium, sugars, and saturated fat and eating plenty of vegetables and fruits, helps mitigate the risk of chronic disease. Promoting food literacy is an essential strategy to support healthy eating behaviours and food preferences, especially in children and youth. To bring attention to the need to support children and youth in becoming food literate, the Nutrition Connections team at the Ontario Public Health Association (OPHA) has been examining the state of food literacy in Ontario. The OPHA has undertaken several projects in recent years to identify the key players, policies, and programs that make up the food literacy landscape in Ontario. Although there are many groups and individuals involved in activities that support children and youth to become food literate across the province, a facilitated connection among these players is lacking and this has created gaps in food literacy research, policy, and programming. We are proposing to host a two-day workshop in June 2020 in Toronto, Ontario to bring together key players to discuss, identify, and reach consensus on priorities for food literacy research, policy, and programming. The workshop will include presentations by invited food literacy and child health experts across sectors (e.g., researchers, policy makers, and practitioners). Break-out sessions with guided discussions and activities to encourage networking, knowledge sharing, problem solving, and priority setting will make up the majority of the workshop. To date, there have been limited opportunities for experts, researchers, practitioners, government, and funders to convene and discuss priorities related to food literacy research, policy, and programming. The proposed workshop will create such an opportunity and is expected to ignite ongoing relationships and collaborations.

column36: Developing a Patient Partnership to Decrease Age and Stage of Retinoblastoma at Diagnosis
column37: The most common presenting signs of retinoblastoma, an aggressive childhood eye cancer, are a white reflex in the eye or crossed eyes. The sooner these initial signs are noticed and the affected child seen by a knowledgeable doctor, the better the child's survival and vision outcome will be. The Canadian Retinoblastoma Research Advisory Board (CRRAB) is a group of patients, clinicians and researchers who work together to identify retinoblastoma research priorities and inspire action to solve them. The top identified research priority is to improve early detection of retinoblastoma. We propose to develop a multidisciplinary working group that will develop a research proposal to solve the top priority. Participants will include members of CRRAB, interested patients identified through the CRRAB electronic patient registry, researchers with an interest or expertise in early detection, clinicians who diagnose and treat retinoblastoma, and advocacy groups that raise awareness about presenting signs of retinoblastoma. Together, all aspects of early detection will be considered (i.e. awareness of the public, knowledge of clinical teams, technological approaches to detection and diagnosis) to devise a research protocol to address the priority. Through a series of in-person and online working meetings, the working group will develop a research proposal and grant application to fund the actualization of the priority.

column36: Improving the monitoring of alcohol consumption and alcohol-related harms in Ecuador
column37: Alcohol consumption constitutes a serious public health issue in Ecuador, with per capita consumption of alcohol increasing in the last three decades from 3.3 liters of ethanol per adult in 1990 to 5.0 liters per adult in 2017 and is predicted to increase to 11.4 liters by 2030. However, there is considerable variation as well as gaps in the data related to alcohol consumption and harms in Ecuador. These factors limit the ability to accurately assess the magnitude of Ecuador's alcohol use. Accordingly, consultations with key stakeholders concerning alcohol consumption, harms measurement, and policy formulation and adoption of such policies which can reduce the harmful consumption of alcohol can help address research gaps and are crucial for guiding the development and implementation of alcohol policy initiatives. This planning grant will support meetings with stakeholders representing community members, healthcare providers, and government officials, with the goal achieving the following aims: 1)to make an inventory and discuss data sources used to measure the patterns of alcohol and data sources used to measure the health harms due to alcohol consumption in Ecuador, 2)to discuss current Ecuadorian alcohol policies and to create a report of synthesized findings for dissemination to stakeholders, and 3)to develop a full-scale grant proposal. The proposed project aligns with the roadmap of CIHR, specifically with research priority C, by focusing on prevention of the harms caused by alcohol through improved monitoring and surveillance. This work will bring to the forefront alcohol consumption and alcohol-attributable health harms, and will create a network of researchers, policy stakeholders, and policy makers to identify knowledge gaps and research priorities in alcohol research and to determine how best to address these gaps and priorities in a resource-limited setting.

column36: 10th Canadian Developmental Biology Conference
column37: The 2020 meeting is officially the 10th Canadian Developmental Biology Conference and the 4th Canadian Regional meeting of the Society of Developmental Biology (SDB), an international organization established in 1939. Since 2002, this outstanding scientific event has run every other year, alternating between Banff and Mont-Tremblant. Embryonic development is controlled by both environmental and genetic factors, which together determine whether a child will be born healthy and follow a normal developmental trajectory. Advances made in model system research are helping to decipher how embryonic growth is controlled, allowing us to better understand how development may go awry. This has become even more critical with whole genome sequencing and discovery of novel disease genes with no previous known functions. Developmental biology is able to assist in understanding the origins of the disease, and to potentially make models to identify therapeutics. Regenerative approaches aimed at correcting developmental defects depend upon the basic discoveries made over the years by basic scientists. Towards this goal, we are requesting funds to assist in running the 10th Biennial Canadian Developmental Biology Conference. Our goals are to attract the entire Canadian developmental biology community. This meeting is strategic as we have invited several key stakeholders in the international and Canadian science communities so that we can discuss our visions for further strengthening Canadian research in this important area.

column36: Canadian Collaboration for Patients with Complexity: Innovation to promote optimal and appropriate care for all.
column37: Nearly 10 million Canadians live with multiple chronic conditions like diabetes, heart disease, depression, arthritis or lung disease. These conditions can make daily life challenging, and having several conditions can increase the risk of poor health and low quality of life. Having chronic conditions often means that people need to do a lot of health care work (take specialized medications, attend appointments, do the necessary tests that their doctors need to make decisions about their care, monitor their conditions at home and watch their diet and exercise) and the more work that people need to do, sometimes the worse they feel about their health. The work does not make them feel well; it just reminds them they are sick. When doctors talk to patients to better understand the effects of chronic conditions on the patient, and to identify what matters most to the patient in terms of working toward health- patients do better. These conversations help doctors and patients understand and trust each other and they work together to make a treatment plan that make sense. Patients are more likely to be successful in treatment because they helped decide on the treatment. Unfortunately, these conversations and shared decision-making on treatment plans does not happen as often as they should because these conversations can be complicated and time consuming, and because the science on patients with many chronic conditions is limited. This meeting will bring together patients, family physicians and specialists to create tools and resources that help doctors and patients have these important conversations and promote shared decision-making. These tools will be easy to use and provide the information needed by patients and doctors to make care decisions that are right and customized for each patient.

column36: Global CALM Leadership Summit - A Dissemination of Global CALM Research
column37: Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully, (CALM) is a brief, evidence-based psychotherapy developed by Drs. Rodin and Hales at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (PM). CALM was designed to reduce distress and promote the psychological well-being of patients with advanced cancer. CALM provides the opportunity for advanced cancer patients and their caregivers to reflect on the disease and facilitates the resolution of practical and existential questions that face dying patients and their families. CALM addresses four domains that have been identified as important to advanced cancer patients and their caregivers, including: i) symptom management and communication with healthcare providers; ii) changes in self and relationships with close others; iii) spiritual well-being, sense of meaning and purpose; iv) future-oriented concerns, sustaining hope and facing mortality. The growing and sustained interest in CALM has led to the establishment of the Global CALM Program. It is devoted to promoting and developing interdisciplinary research related to psychosocial and palliative care of individuals with advanced cancer and terminal disease. The goal of the Global CALM Program is to make CALM available as a standard of clinical care for advanced cancer patients internationally. The objectives of the program are to: build capacity fo CALM, develop CALM education, and to generate an evidence base internationally. In spring 2020, two years following the launch of the program, GIPPEC will host a Leadership Summit to evaluate progress and to enhance sustainability and success. The summit will follow a CALM training workshop. The workshop will focus on the clinical training of the intervention. The Leadership Summit will focus on CALM research to ensure the ongoing critical evaluation of CALM in diverse settings. This planning and dissemination grant will support the Leadership Summit.

column36: Using ctDNA analysis from liquid biopsy to inform clinical management of metastatic renal cell carcinoma
column37: Over 30% of kidney cancer patients are diagnosed at the advanced stages of their disease. Despite the advent of new, more effective treatment options, a late-stage diagnosis of kidney cancer generally remains fatal. Improving patient survival will require the development of new methods for better predicting a patient's response to therapy. In other cancers, researchers have developed blood-based tests that are capable of isolating DNA fragments shed by dying tumour cells. These DNA fragments, called circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), can be used to non-invasively explore the genetic makeup of a tumour, allowing doctors to more precisely administer treatments using the tumour's genetic vulnerabilities. To explore the utility of this technology in advanced kidney cancer, I collected blood samples from 55 patients and performed ctDNA sequencing across 964 cancer-related genes. I also obtained matched tumour specimens, where possible, to assess the similarity between our ctDNA findings and DNA sampled from the original tumour. In this study, we determined that ctDNA was present in only a minority of patients with advanced kidney cancer (33%). Among ctDNA-positive patients, levels of ctDNA were much lower than our findings in other common cancer types - such as prostate and bladder cancer. We were also unable to predict which patients would be ctDNA-positive using their clinical characteristics. However, when ctDNA was detected, there were clear similarities between the genetic changes in both the ctDNA and matched tissue specimen. We also observed that patients with the highest levels of ctDNA got sicker faster and died earlier than patients without ctDNA. Further studies using greater numbers will be required to confirm whether ctDNA can be used to inform clinical management and predict a patient's response to treatment.

column36: Timing is Everything: Comorbid Conditions Diagnosed after Multiple Sclerosis have Greater Effect on Disability, Participation and Quality of Life Among Older People with Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Introduction: People with multiple sclerosis (MS) have higher rates of comorbid conditions than people their own age without MS. It is also known that the prevalence of comorbid conditions increases as people grow older. With the advent of disease-modifying therapies, people with MS are now aging longer, requiring longer-term maintenance of function and quality of life. However, we do not know the prevalence or impact of comorbid conditions in this demographic, as the first cohort of people with MS who were treated with disease-modifying therapies are only now reaching elderly age. Objective: To determine the prevalence and impact of comorbid conditions on disability, participation and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in older individuals living with MS. Methods: Participants were 743 Canadians older than 55 years who had MS symptoms >20 years. They completed a national postal survey. They answered questions about their health conditions, function at home (disability), participation in various activities and HRQoL. Results: 85.2% of the sample reported at least one comorbid condition, with 2.54 average conditions per person. The most common conditions were hypertension (35.7%), dyslipidemia (26.6%) and depression (25.7%). Conditions such as thyroid disease (16.4%), skin/breast cancer (8.3/4.0), hip/knee replacements (4.2/2.8%), and eye conditions (cataracts 18.8%, glaucoma 4.4%) were more common in this older sample than previously reported in younger groups with MS. Having depression or anxiety had a negative effect on HRQoL, but only if diagnosed after MS diagnosis. Similarly, diabetes predicted greater disability when diagnosed after MS. Lastly, arthritis or fibromyalgia comorbidity was associated with less disability and greater participation. Conclusion: Cardiovascular conditions and depression were the most common comorbidities. The impact of comorbid conditions were greater when diagnosed after MS diagnosis.

column36: Cultural considerations in early intervention rehabilitation services: Lessons from Canada and India
column37: Rationale: The mainstream approach to early intervention rehabilitation services for children with developmental delay in the Western world assumes that children who do not achieve age-linked skill norms require therapy to help them catch up. However, this doesn't resonate in the cultural views of every population around the world. Further, therapy is most effective when it matches the cultural values and socioeconomic situations of the people it is provided to. Acting with humility and thinking critically about practice approaches have been proposed as ways to improve rehabilitation practices in non-Western contexts. Objectives: By examining research projects exploring experiences with early intervention in India and Nunavut, this paper will identify assumptions in Western rehabilitation norms that do not work in all contexts. Approach: By using critical theory and critical reflections, this presentation examines mainstream rehabilitation norms in terms of their application in two culturally contexts: India and Nunavut, Canada. This is done through examination of research results from projects interviewing parents of children receiving rehabilitation services in each of the two locations. Results: Interviews with parents in Nunavut and India show very different experiences with developmental rehabilitation services. However, they share a theme of Western rehabilitation norms not always being a good fit. This lack of fit is attributed to assumptions that rehabilitation norms make with regards to culture, values and economic class. Social norms and understandings of how people are integrated into society differed between the two contexts, as did thoughts about the power inherent in the services they had been exposed to. Conclusions: Therapists should think critically before integrating Western research evidence or practice guidelines in non-Western contexts. Practicing with humility shows potential to improve practice.

column36: Functional Relationship of CARS2 locus to Coronary Artery Disease
column37: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. It typically results from atherosclerosis, an inflammatory process characterised by the build up of plaque specifically in the coronary arteries. Genetics plays a large role in the cause of CAD. There is a 50% proportion of risk for CAD from genetic differences, also known as variants. Large genetic association studies have revealed many inherited genetic variants linked to CAD risk. One genetic variant was shown to affect the expression of the CARS2 gene. This gene encodes a protein that has a role in how other proteins are made. We found high CARS2 gene expression in monocytes using gene expression profiles. Monocytes are a sub-population of white blood cells and can be transformed into macrophages. Macrophages are important in the atherosclerotic process and affects inflammation. We found CARS2 gene expression to be lower in pro-inflammatory macrophages, which releases inflammatory cytokines, and higher in anti-inflammatory macrophages, which promotes resolving inflammation. We blocked CARS2 production in macrophages using small interfering RNAs and then measured the gene expression of a panel of inflammatory cytokines. There was increased expression of many pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNFa and CSF-1. Using the panel of inflammatory cytokines, we identified the anti-inflammatory IL-10 signaling pathway as the most affected pathway when blocking CARS2. In this pathway, the protein STAT3 is activated to repress expression of inflammatory cytokines. When CARS2 production was blocked in macrophages, there was less activation of STAT3. These results help us understand how CARS2 may play a role in inflammation and may be able to provide protection against CAD. We will examine how CARS2 affects the IL-10 signaling pathway by looking at other players. We plan to further define the role of CARS2 in inflammation and identify new mechanisms leading to increased inflammation.

column36: La continuite des soins aupres du medecin generaliste peut elle prevenir les hospitalisations evitables chez les personnes agees dementes? Perspectives Quebecoises
column37: Les personnes vivant avec une demence vont deux fois plus a l'hopital (urgences ou hospitalisation) que les personnes agees sans demence. Une partie de ces hospitalisations serait evitable avec de meilleurs soins en premiere ligne. Ces hospitalisations retentissent dramatiquement sur l'etat de sante des personnes, et leur qualite de vie. Reduire ces hospitalisations evitables et ameliorer les soins offerts aux personnes ayant une demence sont des priorites mondiales de sante publique et une des priorites de la strategie Canadienne 2019 sur la demence. Cependant, les moyens de les prevenir sont encore controverses. L'objectif de mon projet de recherche est d'explorer les moyens de prevention de ces hospitalisations evitables. J'ai mesure l'impact de la continuite des soins aupres du medecin de famille sur les utilisations evitables de l'hopital chez les personnes vivant avec une demence au Quebec (Canada). J'ai analyse les donnees de l'assurance maladie, a l'aide de methodes statistiques avancees permettant de reduire les biais dans l'analyse des donnees observationnelles. Au sein des 22060 personnes inclues, une continuite elevee des soins etait associee a une reduction du risque d'utilisation evitable de l'hopital de 20% environ. Mes resultats me permettent d'informer les politiques de sante visant a reduire les utilisations evitables de l'hopital et ameliorer les soins et services pour cette population vulnerable. Cette conference me permettra de poursuivre le partage de ces resultats aupres d'un reseau international de chercheurs, cliniciens et decideurs qui souhaitent alleger le fardeau des patients et de leurs familles et offrir les meilleurs soins au plus grand nombre.

A planning committee engaging people living with obesity, health professionals and researchers will oversee the development and implementation of the public engagement workshops. A participatory process will be implemented to plan and host these public education workshops. The primary audiences of these workshops will be persons living with obesity and the general public. In line with our objectives to engage, educate and empower persons living with obesity, our approach will apply a mixed model of evidence syntheses, inclusion of knowledge users and experts, and build on existing obesity science and clinical practice expertise. column36: Bringing together the ACCESS TO REHAB TEAM to improve access to rehabilitation services for persons experiencing musculoskeletal pain
column37: Pain is the primary reason people seek care from a healthcare professional. It is a major source of disability all over the world. Approximately one in five Canadians experience chronic pain, over 75% reporting musculoskeletal pain associated with conditions such as back pain, osteoarthritis or inflammatory arthritis. In light of its significant human and societal costs, pain is now viewed as a crisis and a major public health problem. Still, every day, people experience pain, many without receiving appropriate care. Access to quality health services in a timely manner is essential to ensure adequate pain management. Poor access to such services may contribute to the presence of chronic pain and disability. In this context, our proposal aims to bring together researchers from a variety of backgrounds across Canada and internationally and actors from outside the conventional scientific community to consolidate a collaborative network that will lead the study and improvement of access to rehabilitation services for persons of all ages experiencing musculoskeletal pain in Canada. This goal will be met by conducting two activities. First, we will perform a preliminary literature review to appraise and summarise current evidence on the use of strategies to improve access to rehabilitation services for persons experiencing musculoskeletal pain. This review will help team members identify main issues and potential courses of action. Secondly, a knowledge exchange day will be organized. During this event, participants (e.g. researchers, health professionals, patients, decision-makers, unions) will discuss their work, share their needs and experiences, and explore specific project ideas that could be conducted through new research collaborations. This proposal is directly aligned with the Institute of Musculoskeletal Health and Arthritis' research priorities, especially in the areas of chronic pain and fatigue, as well as disability, mobility and health.

column36: The co-development of a patient-prioritized liver cirrhosis educational toolkit
column37: All diseases of the liver eventually progress to a common end stage called cirrhosis. At this point, the liver has deteriorated making liver transplantation the only curable option. Some patients are on the liver transplant wait list for many years while and others are never eligible. Those with cirrhosis and their caregivers have a poor quality of life and constantly struggle with the disease. Care for patients with cirrhosis involves many things, such as medication management, diet changes, appointments and medical procedures, lab tests, and counselling for addiction management as needed. A lot of research has been done about cirrhosis yet most of this information is written by medical specialists intended for other specialists. The information is very detailed, technical, and usually available in medical journals or at health conferences. For patients to effectively care for themselves, they need information that they can understand. These resources should not just be about treatments for cirrhosis, but should include practical tips, "how to's", and relevant, reputable information that are needed to manage their day-to-day routines. This collaborative project is a direct response to patient needs and engages patients at every step. The project will create cirrhosis-specific educational materials that will be accessible to individuals regardless of their education, socioeconomic status, or prior healthcare knowledge. Illustrations will enhance meaning and comprehension. We will work with our well-established dissemination network and partners to share the materials in different formats with patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers across Canada and internationally. This dissemination project will provide educational resources that will empower, enable, and equip patients to practice better self-care and participate in their cirrhosis care journey.

column36: Snack Chat: A Low Barrier, Community-based Knowledge Exchange Initiative
column37: People living with HIV are often asked to participate as subjects in research studies but rarely get opportunities to hear about new discoveries in research themselves later on. We want to support community-based knowledge exchange events that bring science back to community members in accessible ways. We have proposed a series of monthly "Snack Chat" events around the Vancouver area within community-based organizations in order to share new research with diverse communities of people living with and/or impacted by HIV. The research areas and topics at the Snack Chat sessions will reflect the identified needs of community but will primarily focus on HIV, Hepatitis C, substance use, mental health, and/or health care utilization. Peers (community members living with HIV) will be involved in the "Snack Chat" events as leaders and facilitators along with researchers who will volunteer to share their research in accessible, engaging ways. Finding inclusive and informal ways to encourage ongoing dialogue between researchers and community members is an important part of community-based research. Our team's has a long history of community-based research and we have established strong partnerships with scientists and researchers as well as local community organizations serving PLHIV, including the Dr. Peter Centre (DPC) and Positive Living BC (PLBC). The activities proposed in this grant will expand the reach of HIV health research findings by making them relevant and accessible for PLHIV through low barrier, community-based events. This is a model for knowledge dissemination that could be adapted to fit various settings across Canada in order to better support responsible and reciprocal research processes.

column36: Private Parts? Finding the Balance of Public and Private in Health Care
column37: The UBC Centre for Health Services and Policy Research (CHSPR) is holding its 32nd annual health policy conference, March 5 and 6, 2020, at the Pinnacle Hotel Vancouver Harbourfront. This long-standing conference promotes discussion between policy-makers, academics, providers, patients and national organizations on timely issues shaping health systems in Canada. What role the private sector plays in financing health care has been the subject of longstanding and intense debate in Canada. This debate has been the subject of major court battles, from Chaoulli in Quebec, to Allen in Alberta, and the Cambie trial in British Columbia. It has also been present in the ongoing discussions about the future of coverage for prescription drugs as National Pharmacare has again reappeared in the national discussion. The 2020 CHSPR Conference will delve into the evidence under these debates. What evidence do we have on private financing? What remains to be known? What balance do other countries strike in these decisions? Our conference will feature two days of distinguished speakers, informed debates, and networking opportunities on this critically important aspect of Canadian health care.

column36: Implementing Active Transportation Initiatives for a Healthier Region of Waterloo
column37: Transportation is the fastest-growing source of greenhouse gases in Canada and a priority concern for all levels of government. Indeed, the rise of private automobile use in North America is associated with a wide range of negative health, environmental and social outcomes i. Accordingly, governments are actively promoting and incentivizing active (i.e., walking/cycling) transportation in an attempt to reduce the negative impacts of widespread automobile use. Despite the well-known health benefits of walking and cycling, their uptake in many North American cities lags well behind their European counterparts. The science in support of building active transportation infrastructure to facilitate healthier and more sustainable communities is ubiquitous, but implementing that evidence-base has proved more challenging for many communities. The broad aim of this grant is to help the Region reach its goal of achieving 12% active mode share before 2031. More specifically, we would like to leverage our recent light rail transit investments to increase the number of persons who are commuting to school or work using active modes of transport for part of their trip. Through this urban health policy opportunity, we will focus on improving high-risk intersections where collisions between automobiles and active road users are highest. Our mobilization plan includes three objectives: 1) to disseminate knowledge from the workshop to key staff members and councillors in the Region and municipalities; 2) to mobilize knowledge from community members, advocacy groups, staff and experts on a specific active transportation issue (high-risk intersections); and, 3) to foster new collaborative relationships between various stakeholders in the Region for future research and policy-making. In meeting these objectives, we will host a five-part Regional Tour and host a day-long immersive workshop to mobilize knowledge to improve high-risk intersections for increased AT in the Region.

column36: Establishing a Canadian evidence base for addressing sexual orientation and gender identity change efforts
column37: "Conversion therapies" are pseudo-scientific practices intended to change or deny unwanted feelings or expressions of attraction to members of the same gender (e.g., gay, lesbian, bisexual, queer sexual orientation) or unwanted feelings or expressions of gender that differ from one's sex assigned at birth (e.g., transgender experiences). Conversion therapies continue in Canada today, despite that doctors and psychologists have said these practices are unethical and harmful. Conversion therapy survivors have begun to speak out and demand government action at all levels (federal, provincial, municipal) to stop these harmful practices. In 2019, the Canadian federal government, BC provincial government, and numerous municipal governments have introduced legislation to ban conversion therapy. We do not have current Canadian research to help us understand whether these bans will work, or what else is needed to support conversion therapy survivors. This research project will allow for a team of researchers, healthcare providers, conversion therapy survivors, and community leaders to plan and share urgently needed national research on conversion therapy, in order to identify policy options for ending conversion therapy and improving supports for survivors. Specifically, we will: 1) gather international data to describe how many people are exposed to conversion therapy and what are the health effects of being exposed; 2) meet as a team-including conversion therapy survivors of diverse genders and sexual orientations; and 3) prepare research grants to conduct interviews and surveys with conversion therapy survivors across Canada. Our goal is to create current, local, and detailed information about where, when, by whom, and to whom conversion therapies are practiced.

column36: Supporting Clinician Behaviour Change to lead to Mental Health System Transformation
column37: Improving mental health services for youth and families is a priority in many countries, including Canada. The Choice and Partnership Approach (CAPA) is a model for child and adolescent mental health services that helps to guide the development of a better system of care. CAPA is different from traditional models in which clinicians are seen as experts and lead the planning of a treatment path for a client to follow. CAPA is youth and family focused. It engages youth and families at the right time, with the right service, at the right level of care necessary to meet their mental health needs and goals. Youth and families share in decision making and work together with clinicians to understand and address problems, and to develop skills in advocating for their needs. Progress toward goals is measured along the way to make sure things that are important to youth and families are on track and if they're not, to support moving forward together in a way that makes sense. The CAPA model requires clinicians to change the way they think about and deliver care. We have learned, with time and with mistakes, that we need to support clinicians during this time of major changes in the health system. We are hosting a conference to bring together experts in youth mental health and CAPA (clinicians, clients and families, researchers, health system decision makers) to learn about the key components of the CAPA model, to identify gaps in what we know about the model, and to develop ways to support clinician behaviour change to change the way we organize and deliver mental health services. We aim to build upon the conference to support our working together in research and education going forward, with a focus on making sure we are doing it right and making a difference for youth and families in ways that are important to them.

column36: The International Forum for Acute Care Trialists (InFACT): Shaping the next decade of global acute care research collaboration
column37: Canada has led the world in research to improve the care of seriously ill patients in an intensive care unit (ICU). We formed the first investigator-led clinical research group - the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group (CCCTG) - in 1989. InFACT now has more than 3 dozen member groups, from every continent. It has helped build international collaboration, has launched research programs to combat global challenges such as antibiotic resistance and pandemic research preparedness, and has provided education and mentorship to emerging groups in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. InFACT is an unfunded organization, sustained largely through the volunteer activities of its members. Our initial successes have underlined the need to evolve our operating model so that it is more transparent and accountable to its members and our external stakeholders, and so that we can support our activities and ensure long term sustainability. Earlier this year we launched a strategic planning process to accomplish this goal. We have completed a membership survey, and are currently conducting one on one interviews with member groups and other key partners. We seek support to complete this process by developing a draft plan, distributing it widely for discussion, and hosting a meeting in June 2020 to finalize the plan and to adopt the new structural changes.

column36: Making Harm Reduction Work for Communities
column37: Mainstream harm reduction practices such as needle exchange programs, naloxone distribution and opioid substitution therapies have been established as a main approach in the prevention of HIV, hepatitis C, and overdoses. While these approaches are lifesaving, they are not enough to make a meaningful difference within Indigenous communities. Mainstream harm reduction models focus too narrowly on substance using behaviours, neglecting the broader social and system-wide issues that contribute to and intersect with substance use for Indigenous peoples in the first place. For Indigenous communities, harm reduction = reducing the harms of colonization. It is inclusive of, but much broader than, a focus on using substances or safer sex. Indigenous harm reduction is a way of life, rooted in Indigenous Knowledges and worldviews, combined with the best of what the Western world can offer, and focused on mitigating the living legacy of colonization. Among Indigenous communities however, harm reduction can be contentious and contested. If Indigenous approaches to harm reduction are to be successful, communities and community leaders must find ways to engage in conversations informed by evidence and understanding to facilitate inclusion of all Indigenous people in ceremony, programs and community life. In 2018, we received PHAC funding to develop an Indigenous Harm Reduction policy brief and 4 accompanying case studies that highlight wise practices in Indigenous Harm Reduction. In this proposal, we seek funds to create a culturally-relevant and community-friendly online package to disseminate the concepts and messaging to make this more accessible to the individuals and communities who need them. Specifically, we will develop: 1) an implementation guide to assist communities in putting the principles into practice; 2) a social media package; 3) a series of videos; 4) a website/portal to host our materials; and 5) two webinars to assist communities in how to use our resources.

column36: Measuring What Matters to Patients and Families and Acting on it to Improve Health Care
column37: Health care systems are trying to improve how they deliver care for patients and their families. When people use health care, information is collected from them (and sometimes their family) to better understand their needs and experiences. Sometimes the information that is collected from patients and families exclude things that are important to them. It is also unclear how this information is used to improve care. In order to improve the value of the health care system, it is important to focus on things that matter to patients and families, and understand how the information can be used to make the health system work better. Our project has two key goals: 1) to share findings from a large, multi-country study on patient and caregiver values, and, 2) to explore how such data can best be collected to inform care improvements. For our project, we will start with a site visit to Kaiser Permanente Colorado who are leaders in the collection and use of patient reported data. Our research on patient values will be shared following by meetings with clinical and quality improvement staff to understand how they collect and use patient experience data to inform better care. Our team will then take these insights back to Ontario to share our findings and lessons learned with other patients, caregivers, providers, managers and decision makers at Trillium Health Partners (THP) and others across Canada who are looking to improve how they collect patient experiences to improve care. THP, is a large hospital network in Ontario that is in the process of implementing a new health information system. This project will help us determine how patient experience data can be included within (or alongside) this new system. Our findings will then be presented to others across Canada so that they can learn how to optimize similar efforts in their health system organizations. This fills an important gap because it is unclear how patient data are currently used to improve care.

column36: Development of best practice recommendations regarding the assessment and prevention of long term opioid use, opioid misuse, and opioid related harms in patients prescribed opioids for the management of acute pain following surgery.
column37: In 2018, 4460 people lost their lives to opioid related deaths. In addition, there was a 27% increase in hospitalizations related to opioid withdrawal, overdose, intoxication, and psychosis between 2013 and 2017. Although many opioid related hospitalizations are due to opioids obtained outside of the health care system, people report that their first exposure to an opioid was through a personal prescription. The challenge associated with prescription drug misuse is that opioids can be helpful in the management of pain. Opioids are used to manage pain after surgery, and they are often combined with acetaminophen or an anti-inflammatory drugs. Therefore, physicians, dentists and nurse practitioners who prescribe opioids need to balance the treatment of acute pain with the risk of harm associated with long term opioid use and opioid misuse. Some patients who undergo surgery may be at a higher risk than others to have behaviors associated with opioid misuse. Misuse behaviors may include taking opioids for longer than intended, taking opioids more frequently or in ways that were not prescribed, or obtaining opioids from someone other than their health care provider. It is important that members of the health care team conduct an appropriate assessment to determine if a surgical patient is at risk for behaviors associated with opioid misuse. However, there is a lack of standardized tools to guide this assessment. The aim of this proposed planning and dissemination grant is to develop a best practice recommendation document that will provide health care teams with information regarding which factors to assess to help identify the risk of long term opoid use, opioid misuse, and opioid related harms in opioid naive surgical patients. Recommendations regarding follow-up of patients' who are using opioids to manage pain following discharge from hospital after surgery will also be developed.

column36: Parent-Offspring Record Linkage for Population-Based Chronic Disease Research: Planning for an International Consortium Meeting
column37: Rates of chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and depression, are on the rise worldwide. Predicting who is likely to get a chronic disease is important for preventing disease and promoting healthy behaviors. Just a handful of research groups worldwide have the rich data and analytic expertise to conduct intergenerational chronic disease studies, which link together objective and detailed health histories from offspring with health histories from their mothers and fathers. There is a lot to learn about physical and mental chronic diseases over the entire life course of offspring and their parents from these studies, such as: "What is the impact of early-onset dementia in mothers and fathers on the risk of early-onset dementia in their adult children?" Intergenerational chronic disease studies can help to improve the lives of all Canadians, but particularly those of women and girls, because they can lead to targeted treatments and health promotion activities. We propose to host a planning workshop at the 2020 conference of the International Population Data Linkage Network (IPDLN) in Australia to build an international network of established and new intergenerational chronic disease researchers. The IPDLN connects data linkage centres in more than 30 countries; the conference hosts events to stimulate discussions in emerging areas of population health improvement. Our workshop will bring together speakers from data linkage centres in six countries to share their research, and discuss the challenges that they face. The workshop will also explore approaches and methods to effectively address sex-specific research questions and encourage advanced analytic techniques to extract new knowledge from linked health history data. The workshop will identify research priorities to guide future intergenerational studies of chronic diseases in multiple countries.

column36: Early Targeted Interventions for Vulnerable and Marginalized Youth: Planning the Future Directions of Implementing Personality-targeted Interventions for Building Resilience against Substance Use and Mental Health Problems
column37: Early substance use prevention and mental health programs are essential to reducing disparities in health promotion practices for children and youth. Several school-based prevention programs have been developed and used to prevent, delay, or reduce substance use and related problems among adolescents. Most of these programs have been evaluated at the community-level impact. However, the effect of contextual factors, such as childhood victimisation, socioeconomic status, and cultural values have rarely been considered in the development and evaluation of these programs. The Well-Venture project aimed to examine the feasibility and proof-of-concept of implementing an evidence-based substance use prevention program (i.e., Preventure programme) for reducing the risk of substance use and related outcomes in (1) adolescents receiving services from the Youth Protection System, and (2) Indigenous youth. To guide future research and practice with these groups of youth, and to extend the outcomes of current project to other vulnerable and marginalised groups of adolescents, we are proposing a one-day meeting to disseminate the findings from the Well-Venture project and bring together the research team, program experts, and knowledge users, including both youth and their healthcare providers, to plan future directions of the Preventure programme with vulnerable and marginalised youth in April 2020. The meeting objectives and activities include:1) to discuss opportunities, success and challenges of using the Preventure programme with adolescents in Youth Protection Services, and Indigenous youth; 2) to incorporate the perspectives of program experts, stakeholders, and knowledge users (both youth and their healthcare providers) in the development of the plan for future implementation of the Preventure programme with vulnerable and marginalised groups of youth; and 3) to provide better communication and dissemination of research findings to the public and knowledge users.

column36: Personal, clinical and functional characteristics of patients with multimorbidity receiving home care referrals in Ontario, Canada
column37: Individuals that experience more than one chronic condition (multimorbidity) tend to access the healthcare system more often. These people are at a higher risk for hospital use because their treatment is more complex due to the impact of disease and disability on their day-to-day activities. Functional decline increases health service utilization. Rehabilitation therapies (occupational therapy and physical therapy), are well positioned within the health care system to address the functional needs of individuals with multiple chronic conditions. Occupational therapists and physical therapists have expertise in assessing and treating both physical and functional complications that are experienced by these individuals. There is a lack of research about who receives rehabilitation therapy services among this population within the home care setting. It is also unclear whether rehabilitation therapy can impact health utilization. Understanding the characteristics of those who receive or do not receive rehabilitation services can assist in understanding who would most benefit from these services. This study involves using linked provincial-level data in Ontario to describe and compare the characteristics of patients with multimorbidity who have been discharged from an acute or inpatient rehabilitation unit in Ontario across three groups: 1) patients referred to home care rehabilitation therapy; 2) patients who do not receive rehabilitation therapy upon referral to home care; and 3) patients who do not receive home care. Understanding the characteristics of people referred to rehabilitation therapy services can shed light on health system utilization patterns and the system-level impact of rehabilitation therapy services.

column36: Physiological Changes in Infants Following Maternal Participation in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Postpartum Depression
column37: While the birth of a new baby can be one of the most joyous times in a woman's life, for many, this can also be a time of significant suffering. Indeed, postpartum depression (PPD) affects 20% of women in the first year after delivery. PPD is associated with suffering for women and their families however its long-term impact on the children of these woman may be the most costly of all. Fortunately, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for PPD and one that is preferred over medications by many women. However, while CBT can lead to improvements in mothers, it is unclear if CBT for mothers can produce similar improvements in their infants. The purpose of this study is to determine if group CBT treatment for women with PPD improves her baby's brain function over a 9-week period. We recruited 80 mother and their infants (40 mothers with PPD, and 40 mothers free of PPD and matched on infant age and family SES). Mothers with PPD received 9-weeks of group CBT. Brain activity was assessed in infants at two-time points a) baseline for healthy controls/pre-CBT for infants of women with PPD and b) 9-weeks post baseline/post-CBT. Before CBT, infants of mothers with PPD exhibited brain activity that has been linked to an increased risk for mental disorders and was significantly different from the activity in healthy control babies. However, following maternal treatment, we observed adaptive changes in brain activity such that infants of women treated for PPD were no different than infants of health control women. No changes over time were noted in healthy control infants. These findings suggest that following maternal receipt of CBT, the infant brain appears to 'catch up' to the infants never exposed to maternal depression. Therefore, treating mothers with CBT for PPD may represent a powerful opportunity to prevent mental illness from being transmitted from mother to child and boost the mental health of the population.

column36: Audit and feedback to address prescribing of high-risk medications in long-term care: theory-based process evaluation alongside a pragmatic, factorial, cluster-randomized trial
column37: One approach to improving quality of healthcare is known as Audit and Feedback: this involves providing healthcare professionals with data on how often they follow best practices. We are conducting a study to investigate whether presenting the same feedback in different ways has differing effects on practice change. Part of this study involves investigating how feedback changes what physicians working in long-term care think about their own prescribing of high-risk medications, and the factors shaping how physicians use this feedback. Thirty-three physicians completed a questionnaire assessing their intention to adjust their prescribing; their confidence in adjusting their prescribing; their expectations that adjusting prescribing is beneficial for patient health; whether adjusting prescribing is a priority; and whether they thought other physicians were adjusting prescribing. We compared the responses of those who received different versions of the feedback. Five of these physicians also took part in an interview about their use of the feedback. We found that physicians whose feedback was compared to provincial average prescribing rates were more likely to agree that other physicians are adjusting antipsychotic prescribing, compared to physicians whose feedback was compared to the top performers. There were no other differences. All physicians interviewed reported aiming to achieve similar prescribing rates to their comparator. Also, physicians whose feedback was positively framed (reporting the number of patients for whom high-risk medications were not prescribed) reported not perceiving such feedback to be immediately actionable. In conclusion, the feedback did not greatly alter what physicians thought about their practice, and there were few differences across different versions of the feedback. Further work is needed to identify features of feedback which may have differing effects.
