column36: The THRIVE collaborative: an initiative to improve our understanding of the factors that determine resiliency and risk using a DOHaD framework
column37: THRIVE: Tracking Human Resiliency In Varying Environments is a novel research approach that attempts to identify factors that provide children resilience against adversities. Currently, our understanding of the role that early life exposures have on poor health outcomes remains severely limited by approaches which are not complex, multidimensional or multifactorial. In turn these shortcomings impinge our ability to develop interventions that identify, prevent, intervene early and build resiliency. The proposed initiative will overcome the limitations by assembling an interdisciplinary team of health scientists, clinicians and researchers who will investigate, identify and understand how early biological, psychological and social life risk factors, affect development, health and well-being across the life course. Moreover, we aim to uncover environmental factors that can increase resiliency by examining individual variation in susceptibility to adverse exposures experienced in early life. This collaboration will consider how technology and new tools, such as machine learning, can facilitate data sharing and dissemination of knowledge to help individuals and other stakeholders make informed decisions, about health, and intervene in a timely manner. Our research team is a national working group drawn from the Canadian chapter of the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD), a chapter created to reflect the growing base of transdisciplinary expertise in this field in Canada. Our workshop will ensure cross-disciplinary exposure and training of scientists, clinicians, and trainees. A multi-tiered research structure for all co-applicants across the continuum of research to clinical application and policy implication will help to foster the next generation of interdisciplinary DOHaD researchers.

column36: Inhibiting lung cancer by targeting disulfide reductase enzymes with a novel small molecule that induces reactive oxygen species
column37: Lung cancer (LC) is the leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide, mainly due to the lack of effective drugs available. Most current therapies are focused on targeting genes mutated in lung cancer; however, tumours may require other, non-mutated genes for survival. The difficult part is identifying these non-mutated genes, especially those that are "druggable". A large-scale screen of ~200,000 compounds revealed a new drug that selectively kills lung cancer but not normal cells. Our research has characterized the effects of this drug and used a new, cutting-edge technology to discover that the drug targets enzymes involved in chemical reactions called redox. By proving how these reactions are essential for cancer survival but not normal lung cells, we can bring this new strategy for therapeutic intervention one step closer to clinical testing. Thus, this project has tremendous potential to shift the current status of lung cancer drug development that may impact a large subset of lung cancer patients, for whom treatment is urgently needed.

column36: Prepared to live with the unknown: Adult cancer patients' experiences with uncertainty when deciding to learn incidental genomic sequencing results
column37: Genomic sequencing is a relatively new type of genetic test that looks broadly at most of an individual's genetic code. This test can be used to identify whether people are at risk for hereditary conditions, such as hereditary cancer syndromes. This can be useful for making decisions about how patients and their family members are managed clinically. However, genomic sequencing can also identify genetic predisposition for many other types of diseases, called "incidental results." Incidental results are very uncertain. It is uncertain if or even when the diseases associated with them will occur. Patients deciding if they would like to learn these types of results, and what types of incidental results they would like to learn, may feel uncertain. This study used qualitative interviews to explore how adults who had a history of cancer experienced uncertainty when making decisions about learning incidental genomic sequencing results. Fifteen participants were interviewed. From interviews, it was found that experiences with cancer uncertainty helped participants accept uncertainty related to incidental results. Participants viewed incidental results as valuable information, even though the information could be uncertain. Participants felt prepared to manage uncertainty in a variety of ways, such as through information seeking, support from healthcare providers, or trying not to focus on uncertainty. In conclusion, cancer experiences fostered participants' tolerance of uncertainty related to incidental results, and heightened the perceived value of incidental results.These findings provide insight into how patients experience uncertainty when considering learning incidental results from genomic sequencing, which could inform genetic counseling for incidental results.

column36: Implementing an Artificial Intelligence-based decision support system in emergency care: A qualitative study of physician technology adoption
column37: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to support diagnostic decision making is rapidly expanding in healthcare. Yet, several challenges exist to execute algorithmic systems at the frontlines of clinical practice, where, most often, they have not been trained to fit local patterns of care. This research analyses the implementation of an AI-based decision support system (DSS) in the emergency department of a large Academic Health Center. The DSS presents as a mobile application that questions patients prior to their encounter with physicians. Using Natural Language Processing, the DSS first identifies the patient chief complaint; then, it adapts the questionnaire according to patient answers. The DSS finally outputs a medical history that is given to physicians to streamline patient questioning and medical note-taking, and help them determine the more accurate diagnostic. This research focuses on the DSS implementation with the aim to identify the main barriers to physician adoption of the AI-generated medical history. To achieve this objective, this research relies on complementary qualitative methods: 20 semi-directed interviews with managers, developers, physicians and nurses; informal conversations; non-participant observation; and document analysis. Data were collected from January to September 2019 and analyzed using thematic analysis methodology with NVIVO 12 software. This research evidences several interrelated technical, social and organizational factors that, according to research participants, limited physician adoption of the AI-based DSS. In particular, the research shows how the DSS was perceived by physicians as introducing additional risk in clinical practice, which led to resistance to adoption. For healthcare managers, these results point out to the importance of considering the unique challenges associated with the implementation of AI-based systems, such as physicians' distrust in the effectivity of automated decision making.

column36: The Role of Invadopodia in Tumor Cell Dissemination through the Lymphatic System
column37: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related death with metastasis accounting around 90% of the total deaths. Metastasis is the successful colonization of tumor cells from one organ of the body to a secondary site. Small feet-like structures termed invadopodia play key role in this process, aiding tumor cell invasion by providing mechanical force and protein-degrading enzymes. Invadopodia have documented roles in helping tumor cells move through blood vessels but we do not know if they also help cancer cells move through the lymphatics. Movement through the lymphatics could be an important route of cancer cell movement and metastasis. Therefore, our work aims to understand the role of invadopodia during tumor cells invasion through the lymphatics system. In order to understand the role of these feet-like protrusions, loss of function assay approach was adopted in our experiments. To impair invadopodia formation, we removed part of a gene in breast cancer cells so that these cells cannot make a protein needed for invadopodia formation. We then looked to see if these cells could invade through a layer of lymphatic cells. We found that if cells could not form invadopodia it compromised their ability to invade through the lymphatics suggesting that invadopodia aid tumor cells invasion through the lymphatic system. Current studies are expanding on this work to better understand the role of invadopodia in lymphatic invasion using live-cell imaging in cells and lymphatic invasion in mice. Results from our studies will increase our understanding of tumor cell metastasis and will highlight the pathways cancer cells can take to form metastatic lesions.

column36: Whole-body motion correction in 13N-ammonia myocardial perfusion imaging using positron emission tracking.
column37: Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) imaging is clinical imaging test that can evaluate heart health and function. It requires injections of radioactive materials that mimic the behaviours of chemicals used naturally by the heart to beat normally. Radioactive materials are used becuase the radiation can be measured outside the body which lets clinicians "look inside" a patient without the need for surgical procedures. When people move during these scans image quality can be negatively affected. Motion can hide heart disease or, alternatively, make a healthy heart look like those with disease. In this study we examined the benefits of a new approach of correcting patient motion during cardiac PET scans. We did this by tracking the motion of small radioactive markers, placed on the patients, throughout the PET scan. Our method, called PeTrack, provided information about how the patients moved which was used to correct the motion after the scan was done. Approaches like this have the potential to improve the accuracy of cardiac PET scans when patient motion is relatively severe. Previous studies have shown that 2 out of 3 patients that undergo these types of scans could benefit from motion correction. We performed a pilot test of our method in a group of three patients. To test our approach we measured the thickness of the walls and volume of heart chamber responsible for pumping blood to the body, the left ventricle. We also looked at the uniformity of image brightness throughout the left ventricle, an indication of healthy function, before and after motion correction. While modest improvement in image quality was observed with motion correction, motion was not severe enough in this small group to see signficant impacts of motion correction. This pilot study allowed us to refine our approach but in the end our study must be extended to include more cases with more severe motion.

column36: Items for reporting scaling studies of health interventions: a systematic review
column37: Health research generates evidence-based knowledge that need to be reported adequately to be translated effectively in decision making. Moreover, health interventions proven to be effective need to be scaled up to help improve health outcomes for the entire population in order to promote health equity. However, gap in the quality of reporting of health research are well documented in the literature, particularly for scaling studies, as documented in a systematic review. In addition, although the importance of sex and gender in the manifestation and management of health conditions and in health outcomes is well established, their considerations are rarely integrated into research design and reporting guidelines. To address this gap, the aim of this research project is to develop the standards for a reporting guideline for studies assessing the impact of scaling up of health interventions. The project will be guided by the steps recommended for developing health research reporting guidelines by EQUATOR, an international network that promotes transparent and accurate reporting of health research. As successful scaling up of health innovations is highly context-dependent, sex and gender considerations will be integrated into the development process. The whole process will involve national and international collaborators. As a result, the guidelines developed will be useful both in Canada and around the world to improving the quality of reporting of scaling studies and facilitate the replication and spread of the health innovations studied. An initial step in the development of this reporting guideline is to systematically compile a list of potential items through literature review.

column36: Frequency and etiology of ctDNA-positive metastatic prostate cancer with BRCA2, ATM, or CDK12 mutations
column37: Despite decades of intensive clinical research, advanced prostate cancer remains a lethal disease. Research has shown that some prostate tumours are unable to properly repair changes (mutations) to their DNA; these cases are often particularly aggressive, and can rapidly develop resistance to most treatments. However, the inability to repair DNA damage also creates vulnerabilities to specific therapies, as seen by the dramatic response these tumours can have to platinum-based chemotherapy. Moreover, recent findings have shown the efficacy of a new therapy, poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, in treating tumours that have non-functional DNA repair. Unfortunately, the disruption of DNA repair in prostate cancer is still poorly understood, and patients that could benefit from specific anticancer medications are often missed, instead managed with conventional, but ultimately ineffective, therapy. My project aims to better characterize DNA repair-deficient prostate tumours; in understanding the molecular and genetic characteristics unique to these aggressive cases, we can better determine which patients might benefit from platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibition. My preliminary research has identified three genes (BRCA2, ATM, and CDK12) that contribute to DNA repair, but are non-functional in ~15% of patients with advanced prostate cancer. Initial findings suggest that tumours with disruption of these three genes are unique, possessing specific mutations that set them apart from other prostate tumours. In this project, I will use DNA sequencing to determine the frequency of BRCA2, ATM, and CDK12 disruption in a cohort of ~1800 prostate cancer patients. I will then employ computational tools to identify specific combinations of mutations unique to DNA repair-deficient prostate tumours. Findings from my research will readily translate to the clinic, facilitating a more personalized approach for treating men with advanced prostate cancer.

column36: Smoking and its association with changes in cardiorespiratory fitness among men enrolled in cardiac rehabilitation
column37: In Canada, 2.4 million people are living with heart disease. After a diagnosis, cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is often prescribed to individuals with heart disease. It typically involves exercise and education to help improve their health, and has been proven to reduce the risk for another cardiovascular event and death by improving fitness. Because of the differences in activity levels, eating and other healthy habits of people in CR, it isn't clear whether improvements in fitness can be seen in everyone. Recent studies found that people who smoke or have previously smoked had less fitness improvements in short-term CR, lasting less than 3 months. Still, the effects haven't been studied in the long-term. This study explains how smoking habits relate to long-term changes in fitness. The results of this study found that past and current smokers have lower fitness in long-term CR compared to people who have never smoked. But, even though their fitness was lower, the way their fitness changed was not different. In short, while smoking consistently lowered fitness levels, people might still benefit from long-term CR, regardless of their smoking habits. This study highlights the need for CR in Canada beyond short-term programs and shows that everyone may still benefit from long-term rehabilitation, regardless of their past habits.

column36: The Impact of Cultural Connectedness on Mental Wellness in Indigenous Children and Youth
column37: Indigenous peoples face significant health inequities when compared with the rest of Canadians, which is evident even among children and youth. First Nations children and youth have higher rates of acute and chronic pain, mental illness, substance use disorders, and suicidal thoughts. A recent study found that First Nations youth had an elevated risk of suicidal ideation and attempts if they had a parent or grandparent who attended residential school. One avenue that shows promise for addressing mental health concerns among Indigenous children and youth is cultural connectedness. In Indigenous communities, culture is foundational to healing and is nurtured through participation in cultural activities. The proposed project is based on a community-identified need for research surrounding how cultural connection promotes positive mental health for children and youth. This study uses multiple research methods to understand the impact of cultural connectedness and cultural identity on the mental health of Indigenous children and youth in present-day Nova Scotia. A comprehensive review of the literature will be conducted to identify definitions of cultural identity and current strategies that use cultural connectedness in the context of mental health care. The second phase is a secondary analysis of national survey data, which will use statistical tests to determine the relationship between cultural connectedness and mental health outcomes. The third phase is a community-based project that will use arts-based qualitative methods to explore how Indigenous youth conceptualize cultural identity and its connection with mental health.

column36: The Role of Sphingosine-1-Phosphate in the Reverse Transendothelial Migration of Intimal Myeloid Cells
column37: Immune cells play a critical role in atherosclerosis, a disease in which fat accumulates in the artery wall and results in heart attacks and strokes. A group of immune cells known as myeloid cells are found within the inner wall of the aortic arch, the main artery that exits the heart. The role of these cells in healthy individuals is mostly unknown, but they have been found to migrate out of the artery wall upon exposure to infection. This migration is coordinated by several signalling events between different cell types in the aorta, including myeloid cells and the endothelial cells that line the artery wall. Our goal is to determine how sphingosine-1-phosphate, a lipid molecule, directs the migration of these myeloid cells out of the artery wall. We will investigate which cell types in the artery wall are responsible for the production and sensing of the molecule to cue myeloid cell movement. We will also study how this signal interacts with other signalling events in the aorta that are known to direct cell migration. We hope to use this information to induce the exit of these cells when they become loaded with fat in the early stages of atherosclerosis. When myeloid cells in the aorta accumulate fat, they are no longer able to migrate out of the artery wall, and this causes fat to build-up and eventually block arteries. Therefore, by discovering mechanisms that promote cell movement and prevent fatty arteries, we can develop new therapies that reduce the number of heart attacks and strokes.

column37: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive type of breast cancer, which can invade other vital organs of the patients, and as a result causes death. column36: Effect of sex on acute changes in blood pressure following sequences of sympathetic bursts and non-bursts.
column37: The sympathetic (i.e. fight or flight) nervous system (SNS) plays an important role in regulating blood pressure by altering blood flow through large blood vessels. It has been suggested that the sympathetic-blood pressure relationship, termed neurovascular transduction (NVT) differs between the sexes. However, this evidence comes from time-averaged data, whereas NVT functions on a short-term basis in which changes in blood pressure can be observed during each individual heart beat. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to examine the effect of sex on changes in blood pressure during consecutive heart beats following activation and inactivation of the SNS. In line with previous research, we predicted that women would demonstrate reduced blood pressure responses following activation of the SNS. We used gold standard measures of neural control (microneurography to directly measure activity of the sympathetic nervous system), blood pressure (per heart beat), and a custom analysis tool which allows us to examine the time-sensitive relationships between nerves and blood pressure outcomes. In contrast to our prediction, we saw that women demonstrated a greater blood pressure response following activation of the SNS when compared to men. In conclusion, our findings suggest that the short-term changes in the sympathetic-blood pressure relationship may be enhanced in women relative to men.

column36: Immunomodulatory exosomes derived from human mesenchymal stem cells for treatment of acute and chronic pulmonary vascular conditions
column37: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) are acute and chronic respiratory illnesses which share inflammation as an essential part of their development. ARDS is characterized by severe inflammation which can impair gas exchange and result in respiratory failure. In PAH, inflammation changes the structure of blood vessels in the lungs which increases back pressure to the right heart, potentially causing heart failure. Despite decades of research, there are no curative therapies for either condition. Animal studies have shown a potential for mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to reduce inflammation, promote tissue regeneration and improve survival. We believe that small particles released by MSCs, known as exosomes, may have similar beneficial effects without the risks of whole cell injections. The aims of this project are to evaluate the ability of exosomes to treat cell and animal models of ARDS and PAH, to identify the biologically active factors that may be mediating this protective property and, given this insight, explore ways to genetically modify the cargo in exosomes to enhance their effects. In cell experiments, labelled exosomes were taken up by cells and improved their migration. In animal studies, a mouse model of ARDS showed an improved barrier function in lungs and reduced markers of inflammation after exosome treatment. In the chronic model of PAH, rats showed a significant reduction in lung pressure from a single dose of exosomes after three weeks. These promising results suggest that exosomes may be a viable therapy for both ARDS and PAH. Future studies will identify and increase expression of packaged molecules that facilitate the protective effects of exosomes to enhance efficacy. If this cell-free therapy is proven beneficial, our research group is ideally positioned to move this potentially life-saving treatment into clinical trials with hopes of improving management for these devastating lung conditions.

column36: 17th TPRM Regenerative Medicine Symposium
column37: The 17th Annual Symposium on Regenerative Medicine is the premier event hosted by the Training Program in Regenerative Medicine (TPRM) in collaboration with the Stem Cell Network, Ontario Institute for Regenerative Medicine and the Sprott Centre for Regenerative Medicine (Ottawa). This symposium showcases the work of 2 world-renowned keynote lecturers as well as graduate students involved in research related to regenerative medicine. Their work in regenerative medicine, which is broadly defined as the practice of repairing, regenerating, or replacing failing organs, addresses shortcomings in the current treatment of many of the most devastating diseases. This includes common diseases that put a strain on current health care resources including diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and liver failure. It also includes more rare diseases whose treatment is astronomically expensive such as muscular dystrophies, spinal cord injuries, and certain genetic conditions. column36: Identifying potential cancer disparities for individuals living with HIV using population-based data in Manitoba and Ontario
column37: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a virus which attacks your immune system, making it easier to get sick. Cancer stage at diagnosis tells you how bad the disease is. When a cancer is diagnosed at a late stage, it has had more time to grow, making it harder to treat. People who are more likely to get HIV are also more likely be diagnosed with late stage cancer and die from cancer. I am interested in Manitobans and Ontarians living with cancer. I want to find out whether having cancer and HIV makes you more likely to have worse cancer outcomes compared to having cancer without HIV. I will use information from cancer and death records in Manitoba (1983-2018) and Ontario (1992-2018) to determine cancer stage at diagnosis and who died of their cancer. In Manitoba, before 2007, blood tests for HIV did not include any information that would identify the individual. This means, it is not possible to find out who had HIV, using blood test data, before that time. I will use doctor visits, hospital visits, and prescriptions to find out if someone had HIV before 2007, which will allow for more research on HIV to be performed, in Manitoba. I will use cancer stage at diagnosis as a way to determine whether someone had access to cancer screening. If people who have cancer and HIV have different cancer stages at diagnosis than people who have cancer without HIV this means they have different access to cancer screening. I will use who died of their cancer as a way to determine whether someone had access to cancer screening, diagnostic services, and the right medicine. If people who have cancer and HIV die of cancer more often than people who have cancer without HIV this means they have different access to cancer screening, diagnostic services, and the right medicine. Finding these differences would mean that cancer care programs for people who have HIV need to be looked at to make sure they provide the same level of care as cancer programs for people who do not have HIV.

column37: Edmonton is one of the fastest-growing cities in Canada, with a population set to double in 30 years. As such, the City has developed a municipal vision to support growing 'up' (higher density), 'in' (infill development) and 'out' (new neighborhoods). As Edmonton grows, novel ways to promote active transportation and engagement with public spaces are needed. Active School Travel (AST), or walking and wheeling to/from school, is an innovative way to support healthy cities and aligns with Canada's Common Vision. AST improves mental and physical health and provides social, economic, and environmental benefits. However, current AST initiatives focus on getting from 'A' to 'B' (home/school). To create a healthy cities culture, active transportation, including AST, must prioritize the journey and the destination - engaging youth with public spaces. We propose a new model of AST: Active School Travel ABC's: Just getting from 'A' to 'B' misses what you could 'C'. This work will build on our existing knowledge, experience, and momentum for active transportation and public spaces in Edmonton and directly aligns with the City's Vision 2050. Edmonton has the necessary infrastructure to support AST. Our River Valley has over 160km of maintained multi-use pathways, all protected by Edmonton's Open Space policy. Cyclists are supported by Edmonton's Bike Plan with a growing system of bike lanes, shared roadways, and paths. Collectively, these assets support a connected, accessible city - one that is ripe for AST. Our strong team represents a diverse group of city leaders, researchers, developers, architects, health services, government, education, and the arts who have the capacity to implement our plan. We will: 1) co-develop an AST/public space strategy for Edmonton informed through youth engagement, 2) design implementation research projects to operationalize our plan, and 3) use our networks to ensure pan-Canadian impact and inform the scale-up of healthy cities initiatives.

column36: Cancer patients' preferences for incidental genomic sequencing results
column37: Genomic sequencing is a new type of genetic test that has the potential to provide patients with a wide range of information about their risks for many different diseases. Currently, guidelines recommend that patients undergoing genomic sequencing should be offered the option to receive incidental results that are medically actionable, that is, risks for diseases that can be prevented or cured. However, early research suggests that patients and the public are interested in receiving all types of results, including those not considered to be 'medically actionable'. However, to our knowledge the preferences of cancer patients , who represent a large population of patients who will receive genomic sequencing has not been explored in the Canadian setting. Furthermore, there are no effective platforms to provide patients with education and counselling about the array of possible findings. We explored the preferences of cancer patients for incidental findings from genomics sequencing, using a patient-centred decision-aid tool, the Genomics Adviser. Patients had the option to select results from 5 possible categories (medically actionable results, common disease risks, rare genetic disorders, brain diseases and carrier results). Overall, patients were enthusiastic about receiving incidental findings, with 97% of participants choosing to receive medically actionable results and over one third (35%) of patients selecting to receive all 5 categories. Our results suggest that cancer patients are interested in receiving results beyond those that are medically actionable. Given that patients will need a considerable amount of pre-test education and counselling to make an informed decision on the possible array of results, tools such as the Genomics Adviser can play an important role in the delivery of genetic health services.

column36: Targeting the NO-sGC axis for the treatment of organ hypoperfusion in sepsis and septic shock
column37: Background: Sepsis (blood poisoning) is a medical condition in which overwhelming infection in the body can no longer be contained by the body's natural defenses. This infection can start in almost any organ and can spread throughout the body. If untreated, sepsis leads to low blood pressure and decreased blood flow to organs, which can result in injury and death. Sepsis is a common cause of Intensive Care admission and is the primary cause of death of hospitalized patients in Canada and abroad. The mortality rate in sepsis is very high at 30% overall; if sepsis progresses to septic shock, the mortality increases to over 50%. Treatment of septic patients is difficult, and medications used to prevent dangerously low blood pressure do so by constricting blood vessels, which can make things worse for septic patients because they also reduce blood flow to organs. Therefore, new treatments to prevent blood vessel dysfunction and improve organ blood flow without causing dangerously low blood pressure are needed. Objectives of the project: There are two objectives of this work. The first objective is to thoroughly examine how blood pressure and organ blood flow patterns change with sepsis. These experiments will help us to identify the organs that are the most susceptible to reduced blood flow and damage in sepsis. In addition, we can decipher what causes blood vessels to become dysfunctional in sepsis, so we can devise better diagnostic tests. The second objective is to test a new therapeutic given after the onset of sepsis and study whether it can prevent blood vessel dysfunction, improve organ blood flow and function, and finally improve survival in septic mice. Significance: This study will equip physicians with a better understanding of the patient's response to sepsis with the goal of developing new treatments to improve the care of critically ill patients.

column36: Role of gestational hypercholesterolemia in maternal vascular dysfunction in a mouse model of preeclampsia
column37: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive syndrome that occurs during pregnancy and is the leading cause of maternal disease and death worldwide. Even though the causes of preeclampsia are unknown, this syndrome negatively impacts the function of the mother's (maternal) blood vessels. In preeclampsia, the amount of oxidized-LDL (bad) cholesterol (oxLDL) increases, which binds to its receptor (LOX-1) on the blood vessels, thereby damaging the function of the blood vessels. In this study, we evaluated the mechanisms by which oxLDL can result in a detrimental effect on the maternal blood vessel function during pregnancy. To evaluate our research question, we designed an experimental model of preeclampsia by feeding pregnant mice a diet high in cholesterol (HC) between mid-gestation to the end of pregnancy. The mice on our preeclampsia model (HC-diet) had a lower weight, and the fetuses and placenta weights were also decreased compared to the controls. Moreover, we evaluated the maternal blood vessel function and observed impaired blood vessel function via LOX-1 in the mice on the HC-diet compared to controls. Because the placenta plays a vital role in the development of preeclampsia and can also impact blood vessel function, we evaluated if the placentas were affected by the HC-diet. We found that HC-diet increased the production of harmful molecules in the placenta, which could affect the function of the placenta. Overall, the high cholesterol diet during pregnancy compromised pregnancy outcomes, potentially by negatively affecting the function of the placenta and blood vessels, as seen in preeclampsia. We will continue to investigate the specific mechanisms for this dysfunction in order to identify the vascular mechanisms that could potentially lead to novel therapeutic strategies for preeclampsia.

column36: Effects of nanoparticle-encapsulated MitoQ (nMitoQ) delivery to the placenta on fetal cardiomyocyte development in a rat model of prenatal hypoxia
column37: We are now aware that pregnancy complications leading to low oxygen delivery (hypoxia) to the fetus increases susceptibility to later-life cardiovascular disease in the offspring. A hypoxic environment within a mother's womb is thought to lead to placental dysfunction (placental oxidative stress) and abnormal cardiac development. This could be due to the release of factors by the placenta into the fetal circulation. Moreover, our laboratory previously showed that treating the placenta against oxidative stress with antioxidants (which reduce production of harmful molecules) improved cardiac function later in life in offspring born from hypoxic pregnancies. The advantage of this placenta-targeted treatment strategy is that it prevents passage across the placenta and avoids direct drug exposure to the fetus in order to avoid off-target effects during development. We recently showed that placental circulating factors from the hypoxic placenta impaired fetal neuronal development, which was prevented by placental antioxidant treatment. The research in the current study focuses on how placental treatment with antioxidants can affect fetal cardiac development. We cultured fetal cardiac cells from rats and incubated them with placental media containing circulating factors to understand effects of these factors on cardiac cell development. We found that factors released from the hypoxic placentae negatively altered normal cardiac development to a different extent in male versus female offspring. We also showed that our placental treatment may contribute to preventing abnormal increases in cardiac cell size but only in male offspring. Our findings indicate that factors released from hypoxic placenta impair fetal cardiac cell growth, which was improved by our placental antioxidant treatment. Most importantly, sex differences need to be taken into account to develop therapeutic strategies for offspring from hypoxic pregnancies.

column36: Identifying the genomic and clinical features of AKT1 / PIK3CA mutant metastatic prostate cancer using circulating tumour DNA
column37: Late-stage prostate cancer (PCa) is invariably lethal. Despite many available treatment options, there are few biomarkers to assist with pairing drugs to individual patients who are most likely to receive benefit. This means that many patients are ultimately treated with drugs that are ineffective for their individual cancer, leading to unnecessary toxicity and wasted time as their disease worsens. Herein lies an urgent clinical need for tests that can identify patients most likely to respond to therapy, thereby helping clinicians select the best cancer treatment for an individual patient. A minority of PCas harbour rare mutations (in genes AKT1 or PIK3CA) that may predict favourable response to the drug Ipatisertib. Our aim was to develop a test to identify these patients who may benefit, and furthermore understand the molecular and clinical features of this rare subtype. Our assay relies on the fact that cancerous tissues shed a small amount of their DNA into the bloodstream, creating an opportunity to examine the tumor by analyzing DNA isolated from a patient's blood sample. This DNA, termed 'circulating tumor DNA' (ctDNA), provides a molecular snapshot of the tumor. CtDNA profiling is a novel technique that enables us to extract information about a cancer via a routine blood test, where it can be quickly translated to the clinic to inform treatment decisions, eliminating the need for invasive tissue biopsies. We have obtained blood samples from 774 patients with advanced PCa. The DNA extracted from these blood samples was profiled to identify patients whose cancer harboured AKT1 or PIK3CA mutations. These mutations were identified in 5.8% of patients and were associated with aggressive molecular features. My work suggests that ctDNA profiling can identify patients with AKT1 / PIK3CA mutations who may respond to novel targeted therapy. Work is ongoing to understand the clinical features of these patients, including their response to standard-of-care drugs.

column36: Examining the Effect of Virtual Reality Therapy on Cognition Post-Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
column37: Stroke can lead to changes in thinking and memory, which can in turn affect mobility, independence, and quality of life. For these reasons, it is important to establish effective interventions to improve thinking and memory after stroke. Virtual reality (VR) therapy is a form of technology that allows for real-time simulation of an activity or environment, and can be tailored to the user's abilities or interests. VR has been used successfully in individuals with stroke to improve balance abilities and indeed, participants have reported that VR therapy is more satisfactory and enjoyable than standard therapy. VR therapy can improve thinking and memory in people with Parkinson's disease, but whether these benefits translate to the stroke population has not been studied extensively. The purpose of this study was to summarize the literature surrounding the effectiveness of VR therapy on thinking and memory in individuals with stroke. Eight studies were identified, summarized and described. These studies varied in terms of type of VR therapy used (combination of VR therapy with standard therapy, combination of VR therapy and computer-based thinking and memory training, or VR therapy alone), length of sessions (20-180 minutes), duration of the studies (4-8 weeks), and tests used to assess thinking and memory. We were able to combine results of 4 of the 8 studies to examine the overall effect of VR therapy on thinking and memory. We found that there were no differences in thinking and memory after VR therapy compared to regular therapy in people living with stroke. As new technologies continue to develop, more research is needed to establish the best way that VR can be incorporated into rehabilitation to enhance thinking and memory after stroke.

column36: Outcome Reporting in Studies on Perinatal Venous Thromboembolism: A Systematic Review
column37: Introduction: Pregnancy puts women at a risk for developing blood clots. Over the past few years, many studies have been conducted with a view to preventing and treating blood clots in pregnant women. It should have been possible to combine the results of all these studies to draft guidelines on preventing and treating blood clots in pregnant women. However, this has not occurred as published studies do not report on the same outcomes, and when they do, they do not define these outcomes in the same way. This results in 'research wastage'. To stop this, it has been suggested that pregnant women and their care providers work together to develop a core set of outcomes, which can be used in all future research. This study is the first step in developing this core outcome set. We have explored published literature to identify what outcomes have been reported and how they have been defined. Methods: We conducted a systematic review in which we searched three databases for studies that looked into preventing and/or treating blood clots in pregnancy. We grouped outcomes under recommended domains: death, clinical outcomes, functioning, resource-use and side-effects of treatment. We reported on proportions of studies reporting each outcome as well as how they were defined or measured. Results: We identified 69 eligible studies, which reported on 165 outcomes. Most outcomes were related to the mother's health as follows: clinical outcomes (96), side-effects (31), resource-use (7), mortality (3) and functioning (3). Only 25 outcomes were related to the baby's health. There was little consistency in how outcomes were defined or measured. Conclusion: We conclude that published studies do not report on important domains such as death, side-effects, functioning, resource-use and the health of the baby. We will be interviewing pregnant women and care providers to determine what outcomes they consider important in order to develop the core outcome set.

column36: Medications and Pregnancy - 1st Canadian Mother-Child Cohort Active Surveillance Initiative Symposium.
column37: Evidence suggests that over 75% of women take at least one medication during pregnancy. Yet, data on the safety and efficacy of medications used during pregnancy is lacking due to the routine exclusion of pregnant women from clinical trials because of concerns about potential harm to the developing fetus. Hence, data on the safety, and effectiveness of drug exposure during pregnancy before marketing of new medications, or medications with new indications, is scarce. In May 2019, the Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) and Health Canada have provided seed funding to the Canadian Mother-Child Cohort Active Surveillance Initiative (CAMCCO) to put in place provincial mother-child cohorts using real-world evidence (www.motherchildcohort.ca). Digitization of health care provides new opportunities to close the divide between research and clinical care for medications used during pregnancy. This allowed Canadian perinatal pharmacoepidemiology researchers to join forces to start developing standardized and harmonized cohorts, based on the Quebec Pregnancy/Child Cohort and US Sentinel program models. Including data from multiple provinces will also result in access to more diverse populations. The aim of CAMCCO is to quantify the benefits/risks of medication use during pregnancy for mothers/children in a timely and valid manner in order to have significant impacts on how medications are used and prescribed during pregnancy and childhood, and how health policies are implemented. CAMCCO is actively working on the implementation of this initiative by training within-province programmers, and has established a working environment among team members and stakeholders. Given that in-person meetings allow more brainstorming and increased efficiency as well as an opportunity for knowledge-transfer and training, we are planning the 1st CAMCCO Symposium in Montreal on February 20th, 2020. This team-building event is essential for future planning, and to establish priorities.

column36: Identifying the genetic determinants of lipophagy using Saccharomyces cerevisiae
column37: Macrophages are specialized cells of the immune system that play a key role in the progression of atherosclerosis, a disease that is a major cause of heart attacks - a significant killer of Canadians each year. Atherosclerosis is characterized by cholesterol rich particles in the bloodstream that become stuck within the artery wall and induce macrophages to follow them and 'eat up' the cholesterol. These hungry macrophages become full of cholesterol, and unable to leave the artery. These complex accumulations of macrophages, known as plaques, continue to grow as we age. Eventually, they can rupture, block circulation and lead to heart attacks. Recently, macrophage lipophagy was discovered which has the potential to reverse the growth of plaques. In lipophagy, lipid droplets (cholesterol storage sites) are broken apart in the lysosome (a degradative site) and the free cholesterol is excreted from the cell. Put simply, lipophagy can reverse the accumulation of cholesterol in macrophages and thus the severity of plaques. However, little is currently known about the genes involved in lipophagy, which is what we seek to address. We aim to conduct a comprehensive genetic analysis of lipophagy using baker's yeast. The genetic functions of yeast are remarkably similar to their mammalian counterparts and technology is available for efficient and large-scale genetic manipulation. For these reasons, it is viable to use yeast to answer basic questions about lipophagy. Presently, we have developed a library of several thousand single-gene deletion yeast and are now assessing intact or defective lipophagy in these yeast strains, which will indicate if a deleted gene is required for lipophagy or not. To do this, we are using microscopy and flow cytometry to detect interactions between fluorescent markers attached to yeast lipid droplets and lysosomes. We expect this analysis will identify novel lipophagy genes that can be used as targets of future atherosclerosis therapies.

column37: An alarming 20% of adults in the United States and 6% of youth are taking one or more psychiatric drugs, including antidepressants, benzodiazepine sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics,, all of which can lead to physical dependency as well as prolonged and potentially debilitating withdrawal symptoms upon cessation. Among adults, 85% -- more than 40 million Americans -- have been taking psychiatric drugs for more than three years, even though the long-term efficacy and risks have not been well-studied.3,4Despite these numbers, there is essentially no research on harm-reduction methods of psychiatric drug tapering, and it is nearly impossible for patients to find adequate help for tapering safely. Official recommendations are poor and doctors have limited knowledge and skill in managing medication cessation and are often not understanding of patients' concerns. While recognizing the positive health implications for tapering off their medications, many patients are very apprehensive to do so, especially when they may have been taking these drugs for many years and have built aspects of their identity around being "compliant" with their treatment. This proposal seeks funding for a two-day workshop to establish a working group and collaborations that will advance and help disseminate person-centred psychiatric drug de-prescription through inverse knowledge-translation. column36: Arts-based Indigenous resurgence: Queering connections between sovereignty, sexuality and gender
column37: This research project traces the connections between the theoretical concepts of Indigenous sovereignty, gender, and sexuality by asking: within the colonial borders of Canada, in what ways do Indigenous peoples - especially, Indigenous women, Two Spirit and queer people - disengage from colonial policies, practices, and structures of heteropatriarchy in favour of the promotion of Indigenous sovereignty? I argue that the literary works of Indigenous writers can be read (and listened to) as decolonial acts that promote the revitalization and resurgence of our communities and distinct expressions of Indigenous sovereignty. Utilizing my own interpretation of Indigenous feminisms and an intersectional analytical lens to guide the theoretical approach, this project engages critical discourse analysis to find the connections between queering, governance and resurgence exemplified in case studies of poetry and podcasts of Indigenous women, Two Spirit and queer people. This research has two distinct purposes; one, to prioritize Indigenous ways of knowing, examining artistic and scholarly works of Indigenous gender and sexuality through individual and community expressions of sovereignty that place Indigenous peoples firmly in the present to (re)imagine Indigenous futurities. Secondly, this research interrogates settler colonial structures of and the foundational role that heteropatriarchy and heteronormativity play in perpetuating such colonial power formations. Overall, this research work seeks to engage in a healing process for Indigenous peoples and communities that prioritizes a queering of resurgence as a promising avenue towards Indigenous wellbeing.

column36: Targeting metabolic adaptation in MYC driven medulloblastoma
column37: Every day, 43 children are diagnosed with cancer in North America. Aggressive brain cancer, such as medulloblastoma, is the most common pediatric solid tumor and the number one cause of death by disease for children in the Western world. Cancers grow very quickly and need high quantities of nutrients. However, increased nutrient supply to the cancer is not always possible for the human body. When cancer cells do not have enough nutrients to grow, they need to find ways to compensate for this. Our laboratory team at the BC Cancer Agency recently made a significant discovery: a small protein called eEF2K helps cancer to survive when it has no nutrients. Pediatric brain tumors produce a very high amount of this protein. In addition, children with tumors that produce excessive eEF2K protein usually die earlier than children with tumors that do not produce the protein. We are convinced that by blocking the function of the eEF2K protein, we can starve tumors to death. To test our idea, we first checked if cells lacking the eEF2K protein grew slower or died more often under starvation conditions, compared to cells that have the protein. We then grew these cells in mice and looked at the same effects, noticing that tumors lacking the eEF2K protein grew slower. No specific and effective therapies for children with brain tumors are currently available. Our study is crucial not only in understanding how eEF2K affects pediatric brain tumors, but also in finding new possible therapies for children afflicted by this destructing disease.

column36: The zebrafish, an emerging animal model to identify safe opioid pain therapies
column37: Opioid drugs are powerful pain-relieving drugs which present the risk of respiratory depression, which can be lethal with overdose. Naloxone, sold under the trade name Narcan, is a life-saving drug when administered during overdose but it is not a preventive treatment as it blocks the pain relief provided by opioids. To identify safe opioid pain therapies, we propose to screen and identify drug compounds that can block the respiratory side-effects of opioids, while preserving their pain-relieving properties. Drug screening using rodent models, the primary animal used in opioid research, is impractical as they have long reproductive and developmental rates. Zebrafish, however, develop quickly, have cost-effective maintenance and produce many offspring. This makes them ideal for drug screening of a safe opioid pain therapy. My research focuses on developing a zebrafish model for measuring opioid-induced respiratory depression to test drugs in combination with existing opioids, so to find a safe opioid pain therapy. These models will accelerate drug discovery, identify safe options for patients taking opioid drugs for pain management and greatly reduce the risk of lethal overdose.

column36: Decomposition Analysis of Spending and Price Trends for Biologic Anti-Rheumatic Drugs in Medicare and Medicaid
column37: More than 1 in 100 Canadians are living with forms of inflammatory arthritis (i.e. rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, lupus, systemic vasculitis), chronic disabling diseases which tend to affect more females than males. Biologic DMARD medications (biologics), which have transformed the lives of many patients, are a special, very expensive class of drugs (~$20,000-$40,000 per-person/year). Biologics DMARD spending is on the rise in many countries, including Canada, but the drivers are not well understood. Are more people receiving biologics, or have doses or prices increased? To learn more, we looked at recent trends in biologic spending and prices (cost per dose) within the US Medicare and Medicaid programs. Yearly spending doubled from $3.8 billion USD in 2012 to $8.6 billion in 2016. 57% of the Medicare spending increase was from price increases, and 37% was from increases in the number of people receiving biologics. Surprisingly, while prices usually decrease when there's more competition, it was the oldest biologics whose prices increased the most. This is important because when the prices of biologics go up, Medicare patients' out-of-pocket costs go up as well. These findings should help policymakers in the US, Canada, and beyond who together are looking for ways to contain the costs of these drugs for governments, employers, and patients, while ensuring they'll remain available for the patients who rely on these treatments.

column36: Glucose Lowering Drugs or Strategies, Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events and Heart Failure Outcomes, and Association with Weight Loss - A Meta-analysis of Large Cardiovascular Outcome Trials
column37: The consistency of diabetes therapies to reduce or increase cardiovascular (CV) risk such as heart failure (HF) or major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) - stroke, heart attack, or CV death - remains unclear. We searched online research databases and meeting abstracts up to 2019 for large (at least 1000 individuals enrolled) CV outcome trials of diabetes therapies for at least 12 months in patients with or at risk for type 2 diabetes. The primary outcomes were MACE and HF. Additionally, we evaluated the risk of HF by changes in weight between therapies. We further analyzed these outcomes by patient subgroups including sex and history of CV disease, HF, and chronic kidney disease. Data from 30 CV outcome trials were included. Among a total 225,305 patients, after a mean 4.0 years of follow-up, 23,016 (10.2%) experienced a MACE and 8,169 (3.6%) an HF event. Diabetes therapies lowered the risk of MACE by 8% compared to standard care with no overall effect on HF. However, the risk of HF varied significantly between different diabetes therapies where there was a 5.7% change in HF risk for every 1.0 kg difference in weight achieved. Among 12 trials that evaluated therapies with effective weight loss (intensive lifestyle changes, glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists or sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors), a 12-16% risk reduction for MACE was observed in both male and female patients with and without CV disease, Overall, diabetes therapies reduced fatal and non-fatal MACE events and may impact HF outcomes via effects on weight. Newer diabetes therapies that lower weight reduce both MACE and HF. These findings may reassure clinicians that they can select among either class of these therapies in patients with type 2 diabetes and CV disease, and CV benefits may extend to patients without a history of CV disease.

column36: Patients' journey toward healing: A grounded theory study of engagement in self-management of diabetic foot ulcer
column37: Background: Worldwide, diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is the main cause of emergency room admission, long hospital stays, and high mortality rates for patients with diabetes. Until recently, efforts to manage DFU have focused primarily on biomedical aspects of healthcare, including pharmacological and technical approaches rather than on patient engagement in self-management. The purpose of this doctoral study was to develop the first theory that explains the processes of engagement in self-management for individuals with DFUs and to identify the factors that facilitate or limit such engagement. Methods: A constructivist grounded theory, informed by Charmaz, was used to guide the study design. Theoretical sampling and intensive semi-structured interviews were conducted with thirty individuals with active DFU attending a wound care clinic in southeastern Ontario, Canada, between May and August 2017. Results: The study results draw attention to the complexity that exists for individuals with DFU to balance life and manage their chronic condition. The processes of engagement in SM of DFU involved five phases: 1) perceiving illness, 2) noticing foot changes, 3) realizing seriousness, 4) beginning to learn about SM, and 5) engaging in SM. Engagement is a complex and multifactorial process. Study participants describe factors such as aging and/or living with multiple chronic conditions, motivation, self-efficacy, self-management knowledge, self-management support, and access to services and resources. Conclusion: The results of my study showed the pathway participants used to learn about self-management practices and how engagement in day-to-day management of DFU occurred. The study has also helped to uncover inequities in accessing formal SM education and specialized services and resources for this population, inequities that in turn contribute to inform practice, education, and health policy.

column36: Treating pulmonary hypertension in miR-200b null mice as a model for pulmonary hypertension in Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia
column37: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia patients are born with underdeveloped lungs and pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary hypertension is a condition where the blood vessels in the lung become thickened, stiff, and constricted, which impairs breathing. Bosentan is a drug currently used to treat pulmonary hypertension in these patients, but unfortunately the effectiveness of this treatment is unknown. In order to determine how effective bosentan is we created a mouse model that has pulmonary hypertension like that of congenital diaphragmatic hernia patients. Next we evaluated the severity of the mouses pulmonary hypertension using a treadmill exercise test and echocardiographs. We then treated the mice with bosentan for three weeks. After three weeks of treatment we then reevaluated the pulmonary hypertension in the mice. We found that after three weeks of treatment the mice had improved exercise capacity and decreased pulmonary hypertension. This shows that bosentan is an effective drug in treating pulmonary hypertension. Our hope is that understanding how effective this drug is can lead to more informed use in congenital diaphragmatic hernia patients and help these patients live better healthier lives.

column36: Do Naps in Young Children Affect Night-Time Sleep Outcomes? If so, When? An Application of Multilevel Modelling
column37: Naps among preschool and early-school-age children decline with age. The association between naps and night-time sleep is largely unknown. Others report longer naps predict shorter night-time sleep duration, but the relation between naps and other sleep outcomes are unclear. Further, others have not investigated day-to-day changes in the relation between naps and nigh-time sleep, nor interactions between other factors (i.e., child age and sex, other sleep problems and behavioral problems, and parent emotional problems), naps, and night-time sleep. We predict: (1) longer nap times and naps taken later in the day predict worse night-time sleep; and (2) this relation is stronger among (a) school-age children (vs. preschoolers), (b) those with more sleep problems, (c) those with more behavioral problems, (d) and those with parents with greater emotional problems. Parents (N = 279) of 1-10-year-old children from Canada, the United States, and Australia completed questionnaires (child sleep and behavioral problems, parent emotional problems) and 1-week of sleep diaries on naps and night-time sleep. Night-to-night changes were accounted with a statistical approach. Naps varied: 41% did not nap, 9% napped only once, 19% napped frequently, and 31% napped daily. Children who napped only once slept less at night and took longer to fall asleep on napping (vs. non-napping) nights. Children who napped frequently also took longer to fall asleep on napping (vs. non-napping) nights. While accounting for night-to-night variations within children, longer naps, but not later naps, and more child sleep problems predicted shorter night-time sleep and a longer time to fall asleep. This effect was greater among school-aged children (vs. preschoolers) but was not different if children had more sleep or behavioral problems, or if parents had emotional problems. These findings suggest longer naps can impact night-time sleep, especially among older children and those who did not nap always.

column36: Exposure to air pollution is associated with lower sleep duration and higher odds of snoring and suspected OSA in China
column37: Air pollution is a mixture of chemicals that negatively impacts human health, but we know little about its influence on sleep health. Some of the chemicals found in air pollution crosses into the brain, changing the brain chemistry that affects sleep. Among air pollution components, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and black carbon can irritate the lungs and increase sleep-related breathing problems. We studied the effect of PM2.5 and black carbon air pollution on sleep duration, snoring and sleep apnea in 741 adults in China. We measured personal exposure to air pollution over 2 consecutive days and collected detailed information on participants' socio-economic and demographics, medical history, and behaviours, including sleep duration, snoring and sleep apnea in 2015-2016. We then evaluated the link between air pollution and sleep controlling for common confounders, such as age, gender, waist circumference, tobacco smoke exposure, physical activity, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, outdoor temperature and province of residence. We also assessed the link in selected vulnerable subpopulations, such as older adults, men/women, current tobacco smoke exposure, and the presence of co-morbid diseases. We found that 62% of our participants slept 7-9 hours per day, 60% reported snoring, and 13% had sleep apnea. For an average participant in our study, exposure to air pollution lowered sleep duration by 10 minutes, increased snoring by 20-30%, and increased sleep apnea by 350-450% compared to participants without any exposure to air pollution. Higher exposure to air pollution also linked with more significant sleep loss, 40 minutes at 300 mu g/m for PM2.5. The link was stronger in older adults and in those living with co-morbid diseases. In summary, we found that exposure to air pollution lowered sleep duration, and increased the odds of snoring and sleep apnea. These links are dose-dependent and are higher in some groups.

column36: Biobanks in a Primary Care Setting: What is missing?
column37: Biobanks have expanded to multiple areas of medical research. Population-based biobanks (PBB) are designed to link biomarkers with medical history and lifestyle information. Biobanks in primary care (PC) will support a better understanding from its users and service providers as well as the complexities associated with chronic diseases including multiple co-morbidities, spectrum of disease from symptom to mortality and the human life cycle. In this study, we evaluate the gap that PC based biobanks might fill by completing a narrative review to provide a comprehensive, critical and objective analysis of the current knowledge around PBB. The search returned 2067 articles cited in PubMed Central. A total of 630 articles were included in our study where we identified 136 biobanks in which 41 PBBs were identified. Three major biobanks identified with the most articles published in our series. The most comprehensive type of PPB, represented by these three biobanks, is designed to link biomarkers with medical history without any collection of prospective data at the PC level. All three biobanks have a follow-up that is based on electronic medical records (EMR) and national mortality registries. The collection of data and biospecimens are performed during specific routine visits with the participants. PBBs do not solve the challenge of cata and sample collection in a PC setting. Fundamental and usually complex questions should be the hallmark of PC research. We cannot rely on PBBs to cover the 99% gap between the general healthy population and the university teaching hospitals in the provision of healthcare services. Also, the misuse of biobanking terms can misrepresent PBBs and mislead researchers who seek population- based data from biobanks and not registries or prospective cohort studies. The biobanking community needs to scrutinize biobanks on the type of labels they associate their structures as the need of a PC biobank is now more evident.

column37: International cooperation is instrumental in fighting the global HIV/AIDS epidemics. column36: A Canadian preclinical multicenter collaborative to improve acute and chronic lung disease research
column37: Canadian researchers are recognized internationally as leaders in two separate lung diseases: 'acute respiratory distress syndrome' (ARDS) and 'pulmonary arterial hypertension' (PAH). ARDS is a deadly disease that occurs in intensive care unit patients, usually during life-threatening infections. PAH is a chronic disease that strikes young Canadians and causes death. Neither disease has curative treatments and new therapies are desperately needed. In order to develop new therapies, preclinical (laboratory) animal research is often used. Preclinical research is a complex process and only about five percent of promising findings result in treatments for patients. This represents a large waste of both research funds and animal lives. Any methods aimed at increasing the success rate of developing therapies should be explored. In human research, studies are often carried out at multiple centers at once, termed 'multicenter studies.' By doing this, we increase the efficiency of a trial and confidence in its results. However, despite numerous known benefits, multicenter research approaches have not been adopted by preclinical scientists. Here we propose a meeting to help build a network of researchers with the intent of conducting Canada's first multicenter preclinical studies. This network will consist of researchers, doctors, laboratory animal veterinarians, and other ARDS and PAH experts who will combine their efforts to create well designed, impactful multicenter preclinical studies. Importantly, non-ARDS/PAH scientists will also be invited to ensure other research areas consider using this approach. This meeting grant will support our first in-person investigator meeting with 34 participants. Multiple issues need to be discussed to ensure that Canada's first multicenter preclinical studies are successful. By the conclusion of this meeting, our network of experts will have outlined a blueprint to create a new paradigm of multicenter preclinical research in Canada.

column36: Planning for the development of new Canadian multidimensional deprivation indices
column37: Deprivation is a widely used measure to assess health equity. Traditionally, deprivation indices integrate various socioeconomic variables into one value. They support research in equity, diversity and inclusion. Canadian researchers have been creating first-generation deprivation indices from aggregated Census data for the past 20 years. Second-generation deprivation indices, first developed in the UK, add information about barriers to housing (overcrowding, affordability), services (distance in meters and minutes), living environment (cancer incidence, preventable death ratio), physical environment (air quality, flood risk, distance to industrial sites, road traffic collisions) and community safety (crime, theft, burglary, fires). These domains can be viewed as an environmental dimension. They require the inclusion of supplementary data sources from provincial or municipal institutions (eg. addresses). Developing such multidimensional deprivation indices for Canada requires the collaboration of representatives from all provinces in the sourcing, access, transformation and sharing of the data. Augmenting the datasets used in the making of these indices with routinely collected administrative data will result in a more up-to-date and relevant tool for health equity analysis in urban and rural areas. To scope interests for new Canadian deprivation indices, we have invited researchers from across the country with expertise in the application and creation of such tools, to take part in a meeting in Montreal in April 2020. Discussions around feasibility, data availability, and sustainability will be key components of the meeting. Presentation of Quebec's prototype of multidimensional deprivation indices will initiate discussions and planning. The meeting provides a platform to create a working group to collaborate in drafting a joint grant proposal in support of Canadian second-generation deprivation indices, to be submitted to the next CIHR project grants competition.

column36: A national platform to study inflammatory acute lung injury
column37: The acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a devastating inflammatory clinical condition in the intensive care unit. Serious infection often causes ARDS and it results in death of up to 60% of people who develop it. There are currently limited treatments for this disease, and ongoing research is the only way to discover new treatments for ARDS. Using animals to perform research on ARDS is currently the best way to represent the complex processes that underlie it. Many researchers across Canada use 'animal models' of this disease in order to study it. One aspect which makes this research difficult is the lack of standardized procedures to run these studies and analyze the results. We propose a meeting to help standardize some of the ways we study this disease. This will establish a Canadian group of researchers that can test therapies in a number of labs at the same time. We believe this will test the "reproducibility" of findings, and increase confidence in the results of these studies. This type of collaborative approach is very common in clinical trials with patients, but it has not been established in laboratory research. In fact, the study we will begin to plan at this meeting will be Canada's first multicenter preclinical study. Our meeting will bring together a diverse group of scientists, trainees, and veterinarians needed to make this type of collaborative work possible. Ultimately, we believe this will lead to results from animal research being 'translated' more readily to clinical therapies for patients with ARDS.

column36: Disseminating a scoping review of hospital-based psychosocial response to disaster
column37: Disaster survivors are vulnerable to physical and psychological injuries. Hospitals must triage victims for distress, to ensure that those who are traumatized or at risk benefit from early psychological intervention. Hospitals also need to manage the influx of walking wounded and distressed family and friends searching for missing loved ones. Hospitals must help to reunite or identify deceased family members in a timely and organized fashion to reduce distress and prevent hospital skipping. The scoping review will summarize recent literature on psychosocial response to disaster to inform future planning. A database search was conducted and abstracts were screened independently by 2 reviewers for inclusion. The search yielded 5,294 articles; 338 were included after abstract review and 138 after full manuscript review. Data extraction is underway. Key themes to be analyzed include: 1) Triage and risk assessment, 2) Response to psychological casualties, 3) Influx of walking wounded and searching loved ones, 4) Family reunification, 5) Phases of disaster response, and 6) Staff wellness. The proposed project includes disseminating the findings of this review, targeting knowledge users to inform hospital-based psychosocial disaster response planning. We will share results with our hospital's Code Orange (Disaster) Steering Committee, other trauma centers and stakeholders in the Greater Toronto Area, in addition to presenting at 3 conferences/meetings, conducting 1 webinar, and preparing 2 manuscripts for open-access submission to peer-reviewed journals. Although existing literature notes the need for effective psychosocial disaster response planning, no prior research has reviewed vital aspects of psychosocial planning for, and response to, disasters. By sharing the results of this review, we will enable local and international institutions to adjust their disaster protocols, which could provide real-world benefit to disaster responders and survivors.

column36: Understanding Pathways to Mental Health Care During and After the Psychotic Prodrome: A mixed methods study
column37: BACKGROUND: Multicomponent early intervention services have undoubtedly improved care for adolescents and young adults experiencing a first threshold-level episode of psychosis (FEP). However, access to such care remains challenging for many-especially since distress, symptoms and impairment begin long before the FEP, during a psychotic 'prodrome' consisting of non-specific and sub-threshold symptoms. Access can be operationalized by measuring 'pathways to care' (PTC) in the form of (a) treatment delays following onset of symptoms, and (b) subsequent attempts at help-seeking. PTC are well known in FEP, yet unstudied in the prodrome-even though most patients appear to seek help for mental health reasons prior to their FEP. METHODS/OBJECTIVES: Through mixed (qualitative and quantitative) methods, we will undertake the first direct examination of PTC during the psychotic prodrome in a well-established, catchment-based service for FEP based in Montreal, Quebec. We will utilize the Circumstances of Onset and Relapse Schedule in 148 consecutive patients, along with a series of smaller focus groups to better understand: 1) Treatment delays and help-seeking during the prodrome versus the FEP 2) When and why individuals, their families, and others delay decisions to seek help during the prodrome; 3) By whom, how, when and why help is eventually sought during the prodrome; 4) Reasons for and experiences of treatment delays and help-seeking before (versus after) the age of 18. SIGNIFICANCE: This study will be the first to fill the important knowledge gap of PTC during the psychotic prodrome; its KT strategy is designed to obtain multi-stakeholder input on how our findings are relevant to future research and service delivery. Finally, applying a mixed-methods lens to PTC during the prodrome permits us to identify which actors or agencies should be targeted in the next phase of our research: future early identification campaigns aimed at reducing treatment delays or simplifying help-seeking.

column36: Canadian Sepsis Research Network: Improving Care Before, During and After Sepsis.
column37: Sepsis is the life-threatening response to infection. It affects everybody, especially children, seniors and those with other health issues. Sepsis costs the Canadian healthcare system over $1.5 billion every year, and causes more deaths than breast, bowel and lung cancer put together. Survivors may end up with weak muscles and memory problems. They may lose an arm or leg, have to go on dialysis, and still be at risk for more infections. Yet most Canadians have never heard of sepsis. In 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared sepsis to be a world emergency. It asked countries to count their numbers of septic patients, educate the public and healthcare workers on how recognize and treat sepsis, and to develop new treatments. To meet the WHO's strategic plan, Sepsis Canada scientists, patients and families promise to do exactly that. By 2025, our goal is to ensure that every septic patient in Canada is identified and treated. Our slogan is: Suspect sepsis, save lives, support recovery! We will learn which Canadians are at greatest risk of sepsis and the impact on their families. We will create a bank of evidence-based tools to teach the public and health workers and we will study new sepsis treatments. As a result, more Canadians will be alive and well after sepsis, thanks to better and timely access to care. The healthcare system will save money (about $380 million dollars every year within the next 5 years). We will share our knowledge around the world so that every citizen of the planet will benefit.

column36: Investigating autoimmune responses for tailoring biologic therapies in severe asthma
column37: Asthma can be very sever for approximately 10% of patients who suffer from significant symptoms, frequent hospitalizations, loss of productivity/income, and impose a significant economic burden. Severity is driven by a type of white blood cells (eosinophils) that gets recurited to the lungs as a result of allergy and other triggers and plugs the airways. This is treated with glucocorticosteroids (prednisone) which causes serious side effects. Antiobodies (biologicals) have been developed that blocks the specific proteins which mediates allergy and further recruits these eosinphils to the lungs. However, for a number of reasons, they are not equally effective for all patients. Our research shows that antibodies in the airways of some patients may interfere with the action of the biologicals. This project will investigate how antibodies might mediate these effects and develop strategies to identify patients in whom these biologicals may not work.
