column36: Metaphors of Youth Living with Anxiety: The Monster and Fighting to Stay on the Path
column37: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health problem in youth. Although there is a growing amount of research focusing on anxiety in children and adolescents, this research often fails to include the experiences of youth living with anxiety, including their thoughts, perceptions and feelings, and perspectives. With that in mind, Dr. Roberta Woodgate and her team at the College of Nursing, University of Manitoba, undertook a Canadian Institutes of Health Research-funded project entitled "Youth Voices: Their Lives and Experiences of Living with an Anxiety Disorder." The project involved 58 youth (10-22 years) and their parents sharing their experiences through in-depth interviews. Youth also took part in photovoice, a process that involved youth taking photographs to document their experiences. Photovoice was a powerful tool for amplifying the voices of youth in the study and helped bring creative insights to the research. Woodgate and her team reviewed the interviews and the photographs created by the youth and identified key metaphors that youth used to represent what it is like to live anxiety. Working with Wookey Films, she created a 5-part video series that is based entirely on the metaphors used by youth to describe their experiences of anxiety. Each video features the unedited words of youth from the research interviews and animations inspired by their ideas and photographs. The video featured for this video competition includes the 'monster' metaphor reinforcing the frightening nature of anxiety and the 'fighting to stay on the path' metaphor showing how youth fight to deal with their anxiety. This video series is not only compelling and thought-provoking, but is a powerful way to establish a connection between youth and the audience. Using a creative approach to share the metaphors promotes an understanding of what it is like to be a youth living with anxiety and help others see the very real impact that anxiety can have on the lives of young people.

column36: Systematic preclinical evaluation of cannabinoid influences on sleep and breathing
column37: Although a multitude of undocumented evidence suggests that marihuana (cannabis) promotes relaxation and sleep, there is a lack of systematic scientific studies showing this to be the case. Medically, cannabis may provide fundamental health benefits if it can promote the full spectrum of sleep and also if it has beneficial effects on breathing during sleep (unlike opioids). The purpose of this team grant is to systematically explore the effects of cannabis principal components on sleep dynamics and breathing in order to evaluate its potential therapeutic benefits and/or harms. In this way, we can explore how acute and chronic cannabis (or its components) use may impact both sleep and respiratory functions through development and in adulthood. We will use animal models of both sexes to strengthen the evidence base for this targeted approach and build pre-clinical scientific and health related knowledge for future development of a much needed treatment for both sleep and sleep disordered breathing.

column36: Is iron supplementation harmful in populations where iron deficiency is not the cause of anemia? A 12 week RCT in Cambodia
column37: The World Health Organization (WHO) set a Global Nutrition Target to reduce anemia in women of reproductive age by 50% by 2025. In 2016, the WHO implemented a global policy recommending oral iron supplementation (60 mg daily for 12 weeks) for all women where anemia prevalence is more than 40%, such as in Cambodia. However, recent studies have shown the prevalence of iron deficiency to be low in Cambodian women. If iron deficiency is not the cause of anemia, then iron supplementation will not be effective at treating it. Further, iron supplementation may be harmful in some individuals, especially those with anemia caused by genetic blood disorders (which are common in Cambodia), as these individuals are already at an increased risk of iron overload. The risks are made greater by the fact that the type of iron that is commonly used in supplements (ferrous sulfate) is poorly absorbed. Typically, less than 20% is absorbed in the gut; the remaining 80% is unabsorbed in the colon where it can increase the risk of pathogen growth and gut inflammation. To investigate the safety of untargeted iron supplementation, we will undertake a new study in Cambodia, where we will evaluate a newer type of iron supplement that may be absorbed better, and thus, safer than the conventional type. We will recruit non-pregnant women (18-45 years) and ask them to take one of the two forms of iron (ferrous sulfate or ferrous bisglycinate) or a placebo for 12 weeks (in line with the WHO global policy). We will measure hemoglobin and ferritin levels, which are markers of anemia and iron status, and markers of gut inflammation and gut pathogen abundance, before and after the intervention. This study will contribute to the evidence for safe and effective iron supplementation for women worldwide.

column36: How & When to Call 911
column37: Although mobile devices are increasingly common in children's lives, our research indicates that most primary school-age children lack the knowledge and skills necessary to call 9-1-1 using a smartphone. Emergency education is regularly offered in elementary schools through regional police school visits. However, school-based emergency education largely focuses on the use of landline phones and does not adequately reflect today's digital technology. Our research took children through a simulated emergency scenario to evaluate whether children know how to use a smartphone to call 9-1-1 in an emergency. The results of our research showed that only 17% of children in junior kindergarten to grade three who recognized the situation as an emergency were able to call 9-1-1 on a smartphone. Additionally, we identified the specific tasks that prevented children from successfully calling 9-1-1. These included pushing the 'emergency' button to bypass a locked screen and pushing the 'call' button after dialing 9-1-1 to initiate the call, both of which are unique features of dialing 9-1-1 on a smartphone and are vital steps to making an emergency call. This study highlighted the need to develop emergency skills education aimed at enhancing children's emergency preparedness in today's digital era. As an immediate and widely accessible solution to this problem, we developed the child-friendly video, "When & How to Call 911" (available in both English and French). This video reviews how to call 9-1-1 on a smartphone, as well as the various other types of phones children are exposed to today, and specifically teaches the steps that many children in our study had difficulty with, in order to address this knowledge gap. We hope this video is a valuable resource for emergency education that can be used widely by schools, police agencies, community organizations, and parents and caregivers to prepare children to effectively respond to emergencies in today's digital era.

column36: Pregnancy and Depression: How exercise can help!
column37: Depression affects approximately 13% of pregnant women and is established to have immediate and persisting adverse impacts on both mother and child. Standard treatments for depression include pharmacological and psychological intervention but the long term impact of some medications on the fetus have not been established and psychotherapy can be costly and difficult to access. Alternative therapies and preventative measures are needed in the perinatal period. Our team reviewed the impact of randomized controlled trials comparing an exercise intervention plus standard care to standard care alone. We found that prenatal exercise reduced the odds of developing depression during pregnancy by 67%, and reduced the severity of prenatal depressive symptoms. In a second review, we found that exercise in the postpartum period also improved the severity of depressive symptoms and reduced the risk of postpartum depression. It is our hope that this video will raise awareness and provide pregnant/postpartum women and their health-care providers with an informative overview of the importance of exercise for mental health. We believe that this video is an important step in promoting the health and development of mothers and their growing babies in Canada and throughout the world.

column36: Partnering For Pain: Partnering with patients and families to identify the Top 10 priorities for childhood chronic pain in Canada
column37: Chronic pain affects 1 in 5 children and teens. This means that 1-3 million Canadian youth often deal with pain lasting months to years. This pain can get in the way of being active, sleeping, going to school, and getting along with friends and family. Teens with chronic pain and their families are experts on what it's like to live with pain, but until now, research has not asked what issues they care about most. The goal of the Partnering For Pain project is to develop a list of the top 10 most important things we still need to learn about chronic pain during childhood according to people who have lived with chronic pain as a child or teen, their families, and healthcare providers. We did this in four steps: (1) a survey with 215 people who shared 540 concerns they have about chronic pain in childhood; (2) turning those concerns into questions that can be answered by research; (3) a survey with 57 people who ranked how important each research question was; and (4) an in-person discussion with 20 people who chose the top 10 research priorities. Each step included Canadians who have had chronic pain during childhood, their families, and healthcare providers. Our video presents the Partnering For Pain priority setting partnership through the voice of patient and parent partners. The final top 10 list has questions about how to better prevent and care for children and teens with chronic pain. These priorities are a call to action make sure that future research focuses on what is most important to people who need it in their everyday lives.

column36: Spread and Scale of Integrated Models of Team-Based Care for Chronic Disease Management: A Multi-site Case Study
column37: The prevalence of chronic disease represents a significant burden for the Canadian health care system. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a chronic condition that affects lung function and reduces the quality of life for nearly 5% Canadians. Care for patients living with COPD can be improved through the use of integrated models of team-based care. These models involve coordination of services across providers to provide better care for patients, caregivers and families. Integrated models of team-based care involve multiple healthcare professionals working together to provide appropriate care for patients. The aim of this research is to gain a better understanding of how integrated models team-based care are spread to new contexts, to allow more patients to benefit. The objective of this research is to explore the spread of an integrated model of team-based care for COPD. This one-year study will use a mixed methods approach (surveys, observations, and focus groups). The expected outcomes of this study will be a description of how integrated models of team-based care are spread in different contexts along with an in-depth understanding of the barriers and facilitators to this process. Our research will provide guidance of policymakers wanting to improve in chronic disease management. We will also offer a common language for research and practice, and support best care for patients and caregivers.

column36: Spreading the Alongside Midwifery-led Unit to Strengthen Midwifery Care in Hamilton Ontario
column37: Our aim is to spread the innovative and successful model of the Alongside Midwifery Unit (AMU) from Markham to Hamilton, Ontario. AMUs provide 'home-like' care that supports normal birth for low-risk women but in the hospital setting with close proximity to obstetric-led care if needed. The model improves maternal birth outcomes, lowers costs and improves satisfaction. The Markham AMU, the first of its kind in Canada, was created with the intention of spreading to other sites. The Hamilton AMU will include core features of the Markham model like the hospitalist midwife, a built environment that supports physiologic birth and midwifery leadership and autonomy, but will be scaled-up to include new and innovative in-unit clinics for newborn assessment and early pregnancy loss. The anticipated improvements of spreading this model to Hamilton include: better health outcomes such as a reduction in Cesarean section, cost savings through early hospital discharge, and effective use of health services through a reduction in unnecessary transfers of care from midwifery to obstetric services. Our spread plan, based on existing community relationships with underserved and marginalized populations, will ensure equitable access to this model of care. The consolidation of services at the AMU and the role of hospitalist midwife will allow midwives in Hamilton to increase their caseloads and grow midwifery capacity, thereby improving outcomes for a greater number of women. Our spread plan activities examine our readiness, identify community needs, build a team of leaders and champions, map a strategic plan, and secure funds for implementation. Our team is comprised of midwifery faculty and researchers from McMaster University, midwives and healthcare leaders in the city of Hamilton, as well as the current director and innovator behind the Markham AMU. This team will facilitate synergy between researchers and decision-makers that will aid in implementation.

column36: There may be a time and a place, but is pregnancy one? Weeding out the myths from the facts to help make informed choices about cannabis use in pregnancy.
column37: Use of cannabis, also known as "weed" or "pot," is increasing among Canadians, including new and expectant parents. Research led by our team has shown that more individuals in Ontario are reporting cannabis use in pregnancy to their healthcare providers. We are seeing similar trends in other provinces. New and expectant parents may choose to use cannabis for therapeutic or recreational purposes. Some women may use cannabis to treat pregnancy-related symptoms, like nausea. Unfortunately, there is still a lot we do not know about how exposure to cannabis during fetal and early life can affect the short- and long-term health of children. Early research findings from our group and others suggest that cannabis exposure in pregnancy may lead to poor birth outcomes and behavioural challenges in later life. However, new, high-quality data are needed to help us better understand the potential risks and benefits to mothers and babies. The goal of our research program is to provide timely and accurate data to support evidence-based decision-making about cannabis use in pregnancy. The goal of our video submission is to stimulate questions about cannabis use among new and expectant parents to help them have healthy, balanced conversations with their healthcare providers. Our team is working with new and expectant parents, their maternity care providers, paediatricians, and policymakers to help answer the most relevant questions related to cannabis use in pregnancy for Canadians. These questions include: Is it safe? Does the timing of use in pregnancy matter? How much is too much? Are there important differences between smoking, vaping, and eating cannabis?. Using modern Canadian data, the perspectives of Canadians, and their healthcare providers, our goal is to develop evidence-based resources and recommendations for improved, shared decision-making and patient care.

column36: CPIN-REACH: Spreading and scaling the CPIN automated patient survey system for primary care practices to support regional health system evaluation
column37: Health systems across Canada are trying to better integrate care across sectors to improve patients' experiences. Patient reported experience measures ( PREMs) of navigating the health system and their reported outcome measures (PROMs) such as functional health status, are critical to shaping and evaluating efforts for better integration. A logical place to collect PREMs and PROMs is in primary care. A strong primary care system is the foundation of a high functioning health system. It plays an important role in meeting most of the medical needs of patients longitudinally and across conditions while also ensuring access to and coordination with the rest of the system. Our team developed and tested an automated patient survey system, the Canadian Practice Information Network (CPIN), as a primary care practice tool that addresses the pressing need for infrastructure and mechanisms to engage patients across the small independent primary care practices where they receive most of their care and care coordination. This proposal is to implement the CPIN system to embed early in our scale up model the capacity for practice-based patient experience measurement to align with and inform regional efforts to improve patient experiences across Canada. We will implement CPIN in ten practices across Eastern Ontario and Kootenay BC, to collect PREMs and PROMs and deploy and evaluate a regional data aggregation approach for PREMs and PROMs to contribute to evaluating health system integration. CPIN allows primary care providers to share short messages, such as flu shot availability, by email or text messaging and collect data on patient experience through an embedded survey. Patient data, is anonymized and reported back to the provider. For CPIN to be scaled up to serve as a foundation for learning about how the health system impacts patients' experiences, we need to build it in partnership with regional decision makers and providers.

column36: The Monitoring Activities of Teenagers to Comprehend their Habits (MATCH) study - Results video
column37: The intricate nature of sport and physical activity behaviour, especially amongst children and adolescents, is an area that many Canadian policy makers, administrators and other sport system stakeholders are trying to better understand, whether to influence health outcomes or bolster club registration. Longitudinal research plays an important role in understanding the factors that influence these changes to inform policy and practice and provoke behavioural change. The Monitoring Activities of Teenagers to Comprehend their Habits (MATCH) study is unique in the world. It followed nearly 1,000 children for 8 years, from ages 10 to 17. Participants completed questionnaires administered 3 times per year about their level of participation in specific sports and physical activities, associated motives, and key influences including screen time, sleep, barriers to participation, and life events. Longitudinal studies such as MATCH are uniquely designed to document long-term patterns of sport and physical activity participation. Understanding the correlations between childhood participation patterns and those in adolescence, and the impact of life transitions and stressors on participation, can inform policies and programs aimed at increasing and maintaining participation in sport. These range from promotion of a multisport approach in childhood sport programming, to promoting unorganized sport and physical activity as a way for adolescents to manage stress, to program design based on skill development in fun, social environments. Government departments, education institutions, parent groups, sport and physical activity organizations, and communities can all be potential users of the findings. Since 2011, MATCH has provided a foundation for insight into the determinants of sport and physical activity behaviours. To date, its results were the subject of ten graduate student theses, 21 published or under review manuscripts, and 60 presentations at academic conferences.

column36: Exercise Messengers
column37: Exercise Messengers is an animated research video that describes the effects of exercise on bone health in children. This video is intended for elementary school-aged children and is designed to promote physical activity by describing the physiological effects of exercise on bone health in an age-appropriate manner. The setting of the video takes place in a classroom during science period, where three children named Mai, Arjun, and PJ engage in a thought-provoking conversation about bones with their science teacher, Ms. Z. They begin by asking how exercise makes them grow, after which Ms. Z explains the role that exercise plays in bone growth. The children also learn about the importance of exercise-induced molecules, which Ms. Z refers to as exercise messengers, in relaying messages from different organs in the body to cells that are found in bone tissue. These cells, called osteoblasts and osteoclasts, respond to these messages by breaking down and forming new bone tissue, all of which contributes to the growth of bone. Ms. Z also emphasizes to the children the importance of engaging in an active life style so that exercise messengers and bone cells continue to work together to build healthier and stronger bones. By the end of the lesson, the children are motivated to move and suggest to play a game of tag, inviting Ms. Z to play along with them. Exercise Messengers was created as an end-of-grant knowledge translation chapter of a doctoral thesis project, which investigates the effects of exercise on physiological regulators of bone in children and adults. The development of this video at a graduate level exemplifies the prioritization of knowledge translation initiatives at the early stage of knowledge generation. Furthermore, it builds a generation of researchers who prioritize public interest throughout all stages of their work, which leads to improved child and family health outcomes across the country.

column36: 24-hour movement behaviors and impulsivity among children
column37: The 24-hour movement behavior guidelines recommend that children ages 5 to 17 years accumulate a minimum of 60 minutes per day in moderate to vigorous physical activity, spend no more than 2 hours per day in recreational screen time, and obtain 9 to 11 hours (5-13 years) and 8 to 10 hours (14-17 years) of sleep per night. The purpose of this study was to determine whether meeting the 24-hour movement behaviors were associated with dimensions of impulsivity. Data from this cross-sectional observational study were part of the first annual curated release of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Participants included 4524 children between the ages of 8 and 11 years. Children were assessed on eight different dimensions of impulsivity, such as their tendency to seek out thrilling experiences, to set desired goals, to respond sensitively to rewarding or unpleasant stimuli, and to act rashly in negative and positive moods. Results showed that adherence to individual movement behavior recommendations as well as combinations of adherence to movement behavior recommendations were associated with each dimension of impulsivity. Specifically, the results showed that children who met all three movement behaviors scored more favorably on 5 of the 8 dimensions of impulsivity, and that children who met the screen time and sleep recommendations scored more favorably on all 8 dimensions of impulsivity. These findings have important implications for pediatricians, psychiatrists, educators, parents, and policy makers as they suggest that strategies to limit recreational screen time while simultaneously promoting early, routine bedtimes and more sleep may enhance the treatment and prevention of impulsivity-related psychiatric disorders.

column36: ADHD In a Nutshell
column37: Media can be a powerful tool for educational information. Our video aims to present evidence-based information about Attentional-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, also known as ADHD, in a format that will be easily accessible to the public. Between 5 to 11% of children and adolescents will suffer from ADHD. Disseminating more information about this disorder it is a powerful educational tool. If a child/adolescent, or even their parents, are able to understand and explain their symptoms, it may be easier to deal with the day-to-day challenges that arise when living with ADHD. The goal of this video is to demonstrate that ADHD is not just related to inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity but it is also related to additional deficits including problems with emotional regulation, organization skills, and attention regulation. Moreover, we would like to clarify what ADHD is not. Once parents and teachers understand that it is not an intentional behavior issue, they may manage better the ADHD symptoms. ADHD symptoms can cause difficulties at school, at home, and with friends. There is also an increased risk of developing depression and anxiety during life. Parent's and teachers' comprehension can be very important for the child or adolescent that has ADHD, making their ambient healthier. A higher understanding of ADHD may not only increase awareness about this disorder, but may help with earlier diagnosis and treatment, and more rapid improvement in symptoms. Also, earlier treatments can prevent escalation of problems and negative consequences, which can have a positive effect not only for the children and youth life but also in their families' life. In summary, knowing more about ADHD can be helpful for children, youth and families.

column36: French translation of the iGeriCare web-based dementia caregiver educational program, with dissemination to organizations and francophone caregivers in the Champlain region of Ontario.
column37: Over 419,000 Canadians aged 65 years and older are living with diagnosed dementia and, with our aging population, the numbers are expected to at least double by the year 2031. The vast majority of people living with dementia rely on family caregivers to provide support, most often without any formal education or training. Canada's new National Dementia Strategy and other guidelines all highlight the importance of education and training that helps care partners develop knowledge and skills to support themselves and a person with dementia in living well. Web-based caregiver interventions have been shown to improve knowledge, self-efficacy, and self-esteem of caregivers; and reduce caregiver depression, stress and distress. We have created an award-winning, web-based educational program for informal family caregivers of dementia. The iGeriCare online education platform consists of 10 multimedia lessons on a variety of topics such as 'What is Dementia?', 'How to Promote Brain Health', 'Caregiver Wellness', and lessons related to responsive behaviours and psychiatric symptoms. It is currently available in English only. The Champlain Dementia Network consists of 16 partner organizations, such as the Alzheimer Society and the Dementia Society of Ottawa & Renfrew County, that provide education, support, and other programs to people living with dementia and their caregivers/families. 30% of Ontario's francophone population lives in the Champlain region, and a large number of dementia caregivers and their service providers would prefer to have educational materials in French. In this proposal, we plan to work with decision makers/knowledge users in the Champlain Dementia Network to translate, disseminate, and evaluate a French-language version of the iGeriCare program to benefit francophone caregivers. In particular, we will evaluate the Reach (uptake by francophone caregivers) and Adoption (by organizations), looking at a range of different web analytics and other metrics.

Compte tenu des impacts favorables de cette approche sur les aines, les proches et les professionnels de la sante, le CIUSSS de la Capitale-Nationale a mobilise une equipe pour implanter cette approche dans l'ensemble de son organisation. Ainsi, tous les intervenants des soins a domicile seront formes pour utiliser cette approche avec les usagers. Notre equipe a pour objectif de documenter et evaluer ce processus afin de comprendre comment une organisation de soins peut implanter une innovation a large echelle. Nous proposons de faire des entrevues avec diverses categories de participants : professionnels de la sante, gestionnaires des equipes de soins a domicile, aines et proches aidants. Cette etude nous permettra d'identifier les facteurs qui influencent l'implantation de l'innovation et de recueillir des suggestions d'amelioration. Ultimement, l'implantation de cette approche a le potentiel d'ameliorer la qualite des soins offerts a un plus grand nombre d'aines et leurs proches et de guider les futurs projets qui visent a implanter une innovation dans des organisations de sante dans les pays industrialises.

column36: Outcomes Associated with Direct Rapid Genetic Testing at Time of Breast Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Approximately 11% of all breast cancers are due to a mutation in a cancer predisposition gene, most frequently BRCA1 or BRCA2. These breast cancers should receive different treatments to increase the chance that a woman will survive, including bilateral mastectomy. However, women must know if they have a genetic mutation in a cancer causing gene at the time of diagnosis when treatment decisions are being made (rapid genetic testing). A new model of genetic testing at time of cancer diagnosis is needed to ensure equitable access to genetic testing for Canadian patients. Direct genetic testing offers patients limited to no pre-test discussion with a genetic counsellor, and written documents or other resources are provided. Our overall objective is to evaluate the impact of Direct Rapid Genetic Testing (DRGT) for breast cancer susceptibility genes in newly-diagnosed breast cancer patients on treatment and psychosocial outcomes, compared to women who received rapid genetic testing (RGT) with standard pre and post-test genetic counselling. We will recruit from 1000 women from hospitals throughout Canada, including those which do not have genetic counselling programs. Sequencing will be done on BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, PALB2, PTEN, STK11, TP53, ATM, and CHEK2 genes. We will have one central genetic counsellor (Women's College Hospital) who will provide post-test counselling. Genetic test results will available in 7 days. Outcomes will be compared between those who received RGT with standard genetic counselling to those who received Direct Rapid Genetic Testing. The traditional cancer genetics model is not sustainable with the current volumes of genetic testing. This proposed delivery of RGT at the time of breast cancer diagnosis is responsive to the need for new models. This research has the potential to lead to the development of a sustainable and accessible model of genetic testing at the time of cancer diagnosis, which has a very high potential to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Design and evaluation of a system-wide surveillance system for late effects of treatment in childhood cancer survivors
column37: There are over 14,000 survivors of childhood cancer in Ontario. Unfortunately, the therapy needed to cure their cancer puts them at high risk of developing new cancers and/or heart problems. Most adult survivors of childhood cancer do not complete the recommended tests to check for these problems. There are many reasons for this. One important reason is that once these survivors become young adults, most of them are 'lost' to the cancer system. There is a need to build a system that can ensure that childhood cancer survivors continue to get the follow-up care they need when they transition from the intensive childhood cancer care system to the routine health care system in adulthood. We will develop a sustainable, centralized solution that builds upon our experience conducting similar work. We will use existing data sources to build a provincial registry of survivors that can benefit from early detection of the health problems that are at high risk of developing. We will send these survivors personalized information about the surveillance tests they are due for, based on their cancer treatment history. Before launching this solution, we will work with stakeholders and survivors, to ensure the intervention is user-centred. We will test the solution in a province-wide experiment to determine whether the reminder system leads to an increase in adult survivor screening test completion. If the reminder system is effective, it will be implemented as a program for all Ontario childhood cancer survivors. It will be applicable to other age groups (e.g. young adults) and high-risk groups (e.g. patients with genetic risks for cancer) who can benefit from routine surveillance for new cancers and other long-term side effects of therapy. Furthermore, our national partners have expressed interest in sharing it with pediatric cancer centres across Canada. Let's not save the lives of children with cancer only to have them die from heart disease or a new cancer as young adults.

column36: Variation in G protein expression in bone cells determines bone quality and skeletal responses to catabolic and anabolic stimuli
column37: Poor bone health is a major issue in the aging Canadian population, in which 2 million people (1 in 3 postmenopausal women and 1 in 6 older men)1 have osteoporosis and half will have a fragility fracture. Hip fractures in people over 65 years of age significantly increase mortality and therefore it is important that we understand the factors that contribute to bone fragility. Lack of exercise, insufficient calcium and vitamin D intake, and loss of estrogen and testosterone with age all negatively impact bone health, but there are also genetic differences that make some people more vulnerable to these skeletal stresses. In our previous studies on bone health we have shown a large variability in expression of two proteins, called G proteins, in human cells. These G proteins are important for cell responses to messages from the hormone and nervous systems. To simulate differences in levels of expression of the two major G proteins, Gs and G11, we created two mouse types with high levels of each of these proteins in bone cells. Our two mouse lines look normal but both have weaker bone that fractures more easily. In our proposed research we will now test if these mice respond differently after they eat a diet low in calcium or vitamin D and when we remove their estrogen and testosterone. We will also assess how their bones repair after fracture, and look at the molecular pathways controlled by these G proteins to understand how they cause bone to be weaker. Our studies will help us decide if people with high G protein levels are more likely to get osteoporosis or have bone fractures or have slow healing after a fracture and what we can do to help keep their bones healthy into old age.

column37: As diabetes reaches epidemic magnitude worldwide, more diabetics face the problems of morbidity and mortality due to chronic complications. Diabetes causes scarring and damage to heart and is one of the leading causes heart disease in Canada. We plan to investigate the mechanisms leading to development of heart damage in diabetes. If this processes continues the cells ultimately fails to function. The signal sent out by the nucleus contains some special type of molecules called lncRNA. They are also known as 'dark matter of the genome'. These molecules have been recently discovered and have a major role in regulating protein production. We plan to examine how lncRNA can interact with other RNA molecules and other mechanisms and change the production of abnormal molecules and whether by manipulating these mechanisms, we can prevent damage to the heart in diabetes. The proposed research is based on several aims, each of which will be investigated at multiple levels of complexities. Our experiments will include examinations of various types of cells from the heart and the cells of the blood vessels. We will also use animal with diabetes. We will also use several compounds to block these mechanisms to understand how this can be prevented. Some of our experiment will focus on specific lncRNAs that we have identified in our laboratory. We will further expand our studies to examine tissue removed from patients and examine whether the abnormalities identified in the cells and in the animals occur in humans. This proposal represents a comprehensive set of studies to investigate a specific process, i.e, the heart damage in diabetes. Understanding such mechanisms will help to develop preventive treatment for such conditions.

column36: Molecular Imaging biomarkers of cognition in Parkinson's disease
column37: Cognitive decline in Parkinson's Disease (PD) may occur, anywhere from 20-60%, with an impairment in one or more cognitive domains. Different subtypes of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) have been identified in PD. Single-domain non-amnestic impairments are most commonly frontal-executive in nature, while multi-domain impairments include any combination of deficits in various cognitive domains. Recent studies found that multi-domain MCI is highly associated with conversion to dementia. Today, the lack of information on the biological bases of these cognitive complications in PD has prevented the development of optimal treatments to alleviate these non-motor aspects. While the role of dopaminergic degeneration in cognitive dysfunction in PD may appear obvious, it has become clear that this alone cannot explain the severity of cognitive decline in those patients with multi-domain MCI and dementia. Other factors have to play an important role as well. In support of this, while there is large preclinical data suggesting a potential role of activated microglia, beta-amyloid and tau deposition in neurodegenerative processes, to date the in-vivo evidence of these pathologies in PD manifesting with multi-domain MCI and dementia remains unclear. This grant proposal shifts the focus from neurotransmitter changes to study the relationship between neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau deposition, using a set of new PET radiotracers. This data set will offer a unique multi-modal integrated approach to investigate and correlate clinical and pathophysiological mechanisms associated with more severe cognitive decline in PD.

column36: Using bioengineered human vessels to understand how brain and peripheral apoE affect cerebrovascular functions relevant to Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Genetic variants in apolipoprotein E (apoE) account for most of the risk of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Humans have three genetic types of apoE, called apoE2 (the protective form), apoE3 (the neutral form), and apoE4 (the risky form). Exactly how apoE affects AD is not known. ApoE is made by multiple cell types in the brain, including astrocytes. Although apoE is also made by the liver, peripheral apoE has largely been ignored in AD as apoE does cross the blood brain barrier. As most AD patients have cerebrovascular pathologies including cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), we hypothesize that brain and peripheral apoE may interact at the cerebral vessel. We recently pioneered a novel experimental platform to investigate vascular contributions to AD, where we engineered three-dimensional human blood vessels with both a "brain" side and a "blood side". We showed that addition of Abeta to the "brain side" increased CAA, especially in the presence of apoE4. We also showed that addition of high-density lipoprotein (HDL; good cholesterol) to the "blood side" prevented CAA, even in the presence of "brain" apoE4. Further, we recently found that HDL particles enriched in apoE (HDL-E) are best at preventing CAA. We now propose to use our innovative model to determine the relative contributions of astrocyte apoE and HDL-E on CAA, Abeta transport and monocyte binding in bioengineered vessels. We will first engineer vessels with astrocytes that express apoE2, apoE3 or apoE4 to study how astrocyte apoE genotype affects CAA from the "brain" side. We will then isolate HDL-E from healthy people of different apoE genotypes to study how circulating HDL-E affects CAA from the "blood" side. We will then combine these approaches to test whether HDL-E from apoE3 donors can counteract astrocyte apoE4. If so, this could open up new ways to treat or prevent vascular AD risk factors, as therapies that can work from the inside of the vessel may not need to enter the brain to be effective.

column36: Prediction of multiple sclerosis disability worsening scores using multi-stream deep learning
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a complex neurological disease that disables mostly young Canadians. While therapies are available for many who have a relapsing remitting clinical form (RRMS), >50% of them worsen to a secondary progressive form (SPMS) within 10-15 years of disease onset despite treatment, from which point the disease is hardly manageable. A major current limitation is our inability to identify who worsens rapidly that needs immediate aggressive therapies, and when, as disease course is never the same between RRMS patients. In this project, we will establish a novel deep machine learning method to predict the 5-year risk of disability score worsening in RRMS individuals. This will take a unique approach that simultaneously evaluate patient outcomes from brain pathology, clinical measures, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Deep learning algorithms have shown enormous fascinating data recently in image analysis and paralleled human ability in disease prediction. Based on standard brain MRI, we have now achieved an ~85% accuracy using deep learning to separate RRMS from SPMS. Yet deep learning is better using pathology-directed image feature maps than standard MRI, and far superior using both. We have done pioneering work in assessing the pattern (texture) of MRI scans and are the first to show that MRI texture features detect specific elements of brain MS pathology. Now we have made new advancement in deep learning that integrates image texture, brain MRI, and clinical variables including sex and age that are known to impact MS patient outcomes, and built cutting-edge technologies to uncover how deep learning works. Built on these exciting results, this project will provide a novel objective method to identify the high and low risks of sustained worsening or SPMS onset for RRMS individual so that each will receive the best personalized care. This will be crucial for people with RRMS, their families, the health care system, and the Society.

column36: Harnessing exercise epigenomics to protect the brain from neurodegeneration
column37: Can exercise help heal the brain and protect it from degeneration? This is a critical question that not only applies to people who have a neurodegenerative condition like multiple sclerosis (MS) but anyone who wishes to maintain a healthy brain as they age. We think that participation in aerobic exercise can alter the immune system and shift the balance from a state of inflammation towards one that fosters brain repair. We can measure levels of inflammation and markers of brain repair, such as neurotrophins, in the blood. We detect changes to brain networks using a special device called transcranial magnetic stimulation, which provides a window on brain function and integrity. The chemical switch that makes the link between inflammation and restoration is likely a special molecule called a 'microRNA'. MicroRNAs help cross talk between the brain and the immune system. This field of 'exercise epigenomics' is new and could have important implications for MS as well as other diseases that involve neurodegeneration. Beginning in 2016, we created a unique longitudinal MS patient registry and biorepository which includes detailed demographic, clinical, immune, and exercise/rehabilitation profiles. Of the 220+ people recruited, we have complete data on 84 that are eligible for this project (have mild MS). We intend to gather three years of data on at least 100 people. In this project we will investigate potential links between aerobic fitness/physical activity and the balance of inflammation and brain repair on preservation of brain function, and sensorimotor and cognitive deficits in people with mild MS. People with MS, like anyone else, want to live long and productive lives. Using this unique and powerful dataset we will be able to probe the links between lifestyle and brain health like never before.

column36: Could mitotic exhaustion of NG2-glia explain the remyelination deficit in MS?
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the fatty sheaths that are wrapped around neuronal processes and that aid communication between brain cells become damaged. During the initial phase of the disease, the brain is able to repair those damages but this ability is frequently lost as MS progresses. So far the exact cause of this failure has not been pinpointed. Much of the sheath repair is reliant on new sheath-forming cells (called oligodendrocytes) produced by brain cells known as NG2-glia. We propose that the status of these NG2-glia is key to effective repair. Evidence suggest that these cells need to divide to ensure effective remyelination. We aim to determine whether the need of continuous brain repair as in case of progressive MS, eventually wears out the NG2-glia, rendering them successively less effective at restoring brain function after each period of damage. The proposed research may critically contribute to our understanding of the exact causes that lead to the transition to progressive MS disease stages. Based on our findings, future treatment strategies may focus on preventing or slowing down the decline of the repair capacity of NG2-glia thereby helping to prevent or delay disease progression.

column36: Role and therapeutic potential of MicroRNA-34a-5p in knee osteoarthritis
column37: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and among the leading cause of disability worldwide. Ways to detect or treat knee OA at the onset of disease are not available. Current treatments only target pain while early detection methods are absent. By the time of diagnosis, knee OA has usually progressed to a point leading to severe joint damage. Thus, it's critical to identify early detection methods that can allow early intervention and potential therapies to stop knee joint destruction during OA. Our studies have identified a particular molecule called microRNA-34a that is highly present in the blood, synovial (joint) fluid as well as joints tissues of patients with advanced-stage knee OA patients compared to early-stage and healthy subjects. These elevated levels are not only present in humans with knee OA but also in joint tissues of mouse with knee OA. We anticipate that the levels of this molecule can help us detect or predict the extent of joint damage in the patients with knee OA. To do this, we have created a large-scale biobank of patient biospecimens (blood and tissues) with early to advanced stages of knee OA to help us identify the reliability and specificity of this molecule to detect or measure the degree of joint degeneration in patients with knee OA. Our studies further show that this molecule is not only elevated during OA but also promotes joint destructive activities in the knee joint by degenerating cartilage and promoting inflammation. We anticipate that blocking the activity of this molecule will help us stop the degeneration of knee joints. We have now created a blocker of this molecule and we will test if injecting this blocker in animal models can help stop knee OA. This project will help us comprehensively understand: (1) If this molecule can be used a biomarker to detect or measure the presence or extent of joint damage in patient with knee OA. (2) if the molecule blocker can be used as a drug to stop knee OA.

column36: Improving Care for Knee Osteoarthritis by Predicting Who Will Get Worse: Exploring the Interactions of Joint Biomechanics, Inflammation and Immunity
column37: IMPORTANCE By 2041, over 10 million Canadians will have osteoarthritis (OA), with the knee most often affected. Knee OA causes long-term pain and immobility. It damages all tissues in and around a joint. About half of people with knee OA will decline toward disability, some very rapidly. At diagnosis, we cannot predict who will experience steady disease, versus those on a fast path to disability. Our goal is to predict knee OA worsening so that we target treatment to those who need it the most. In-depth movement analysis shows that the torque rotating the lower leg into a bow-legged position at the knee (called the knee adduction moment (KAM)) predicts worsening knee OA - but only people who are obese. The reason why obesity heightened the effect of KAM is unknown. We believe obesity creates inflammation and changes the way our immune system fights off disease. OBJECTIVES To figure out how KAM and obesity work together to worsen knee OA, we will determine if: 1) Obesity-related alterations in tissue quality, inflammation and immunity relate to tissue function for cartilage and muscle. 2) The combination of KAM with poor cartilage function predicts cartilage loss over 3 y. 3) Pain, mobility and function are related with obesity-related inflammation and immune responses. METHOD In 94 people with knee OA, at baseline and 3 y we will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure the quantity and quality of cartilage and muscle. We will use MRI to assess cartilage function (changes in cartilage thickness after walking) and a strength-testing machine to assess muscle function. Every 6 months for 3 y, we will collect blood to measure inflammation and immune function; analyze walking; and measure pain, mobility and function. OUTCOMES By examining how KAM and obesity work together to worsen knee OA, we will understand why some with knee OA remain stable, while others get worse. This work is essential to targeting treatment for those facing rapid decline.

column36: Apprentissage de la sante apres le cancer : place aux savoirs experientiels
column37: Apres la fin des traitements, les personnes touchees par le cancer (PTC) doivent apprendre a vivre avec une sante differente. Elles ont besoin d'un accompagnement pendant cette periode. Par contre, les ecrits disponibles expliquent que les professionnels de la sante se sentent peu outilles pour accompagner les PTC apres la fin des traitements. Notre projet propose d'aborder cet accompagnement en explorant l'utilisation des savoirs issus de l'experience des PTC ainsi que des professionnels. Les savoirs experientiels sont utilises, de maniere inconsciente, par la personne lors de situations rencontrees (ex., gestion de la fatigue) et elle les utilise en fonctions du contexte (ex., travail, prendre soin des enfants). Le but de cette etude est de documenter et comprendre l'accompagnement de l'apprentissage de la sante apres les traitements du cancer. Les objectifs sont : 1.Explorer quelles connaissances utilisent les PTC ainsi que les professionnels de la sante et comment elles sont utilisees lors de la gestion de leur sante ou l'accompagnement d'une PTC 2.Documenter comment les PTC ainsi que les professionnels de la sante construisent et contextualisent leurs connaissances 3.Produire des parcours d'apprentissage de la sante afin que les professionnels de la sante puissent soutenir les PTC Des approches de recherches qualitatives seront employees soit l'entretien narratif et l'instruction aux sosies. Des PTC survivant a un cancer hematologique seront recrutes ainsi que des professionnels de la sante. Cette etude permettra de comprendre de quelles manieres les PTC apprennent a gerer leur sante suite aux traitements du cancer. Ultimement, ce projet produira des recommandations pour que les professionnels de la sante puissent soutenir cet apprentissage chez les PTC.

column36: CardiacDOC: Prospective multi-centre feasibility and validation of a unified screening tool for Depression, Obstructive sleep apnea and Cognition (DOC) in heart failure patients
column37: Heart Failure (HF) is very common. Many people die or are disabled by it and it worsens their quality of life. Depression, sleep apnea (problems breathing at night referred to as OSA) and cognitive impairment (memory, thinking problems) are very common in people with HF. We call these "DOC" conditions for short. Finding out if people with HF have DOC conditions may help them improve their quality of life. It can also help them better control their HF symptoms. For example, someone with cognitive difficulties might need different instructions about when to take or change their HF medicines to make it easier for them to manage their HF. Regular testing for these conditions is complicated and time-consuming, so doctors can't test all HF patients for them. A fast way to know if people have any DOC conditions is needed. This study will test how well a short screening test, that's been studied in stroke patients (and shown to work well), can work to screen for DOC conditions in people with HF. The first goal is to see if screening can be done quickly and easily in HF clinics. The second is to see if the screen scores reliably predict the actual conditions. To do this, we are going to screen people in HF clinics and ask them to volunteer for more detailed testing. We'll compare the screening to the detailed testing to see how well it predicts them. If the screening works well, it can help people with HF improve their quality of life by treating DOC conditions. It may also allow us to study new ways of improving HF treatment; for example, by giving more personalized treatment instructions to those with depression or memory problems. The heart and the brain are very closely connected - each affects the other. We hope we can use this approach to improve both the hearts and minds of many of the 600,000 people living with HF in Canada and in doing so, help them to live longer, healthier lives.

column36: Xi-Care: eXplainable intelligent system for Cardiovascular disease management among women in primary Care
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remain the leading cause of death in Canadian women, and recent data suggest mortality is increasing. In Canada, 206 people (60% of them women) die of CVD every day. It cost Canada $20.9 billion per year. Most of these CVD can be prevented/managed. Identification of high-risk patients is not well done in particular in women, and prevention options are not often timely provided to them. Artificial Intelligent (AI) can play an important role in supporting clinicians and patients, yet rarely used. We aim to develop and test an explainable intelligent system, Xi-Care, which will help clinicians to accurately and timely predict risk of CVD (at point of care) and equip women with a system that gives personalized recommendations for lowering their risk of CVD. First, we will assess users (i.e. clinicians and women) needs and preferences regarding different aspects of CVD prediction and prevention in primary care. Then, along with users, we will develop an explainable AI solution that can predict the likelihood of having CVD in the future years based on different features among women, and recommend personalized preventive strategies to them-facilitating making informed value based decisions. Lastly, we will pilot test Xi-Care among clinicians and women, and improve it iteratively. Xi-Care is expected to improve CVD risk stratification and increase prediction accuracy and give personalized recommendations for CVD prevention. It will not only have high accuracy but will also allow users to understand why the system predicted risk/recommended a particular strategy. Xi-Care will be delivered in primary care-where women make their first and most frequent contact with the health care system-thus, it can play an important role in early detection of CVD and timely treatment. Xi-Care will be a first step toward saving millions of lives by advancing traditional female CVD prediction and prevention using explainable AI technologies.

column36: Psychological Profile and Intervention Needs of Patients with Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection
column37: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a serious medical condition that occurs when the lining of an artery in the heart separates or tears. This may cause a heart attack. The exact cause of SCAD is unknown but almost half of these patients report an emotional trigger. Patients with SCAD are at higher risk for experiencing future cardiac events and developing psychiatric illness post-event. Tailored psychosocial counselling for these patients in cardiac rehabilitation is sorely needed. As a first step to develop an intervention supporting patients as they cope with the challenges of SCAD, the overall aim of this research is to measure the psychological health and intervention needs of patients with SCAD. This research will include two studies. Study 1 will include interviews with 45-60 patients with SCAD asking about their psychological health and intervention needs. Study 2 will include a survey on these topics with a larger number of patients with SCAD (N=323). We will compare their psychological health to 323 patients that have had an acute coronary event due to atherosclerosis. Patients will be recruited from three sites within Canada: Vancouver General Hospital, the University of Ottawa Heart Institute, and QEII Health Sciences Centre (Halifax). To investigate the relationship between psychological health and cardiac outcomes, we will link our data with Canadian medical data measuring future cardiovascular events. Although clearly an important factor pre- and post-SCAD, the psychological health of patients with SCAD has been neglected to date. Preliminary work indicates that patients with SCAD are distressed. This distress deserves treatment. If this distress is associated with worse cardiac outcomes, there is an even greater reason to intervene. The information obtained in these studies will be used to design a targeted, patient-approved intervention with the potential to impact SCAD patients' mental health, quality of life, and heart health.

column36: Early diagnosis of mortality using Admission CT perfusion in severe Traumatic Brain Injury patients (ACT-TBI study)
column37: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a principal cause of post-injury hospitalization, disability, and death throughout the world primarily afflicting a young, healthy population with a previously excellent quality of life. In addition to being the leading cause of death and disability among people under 45 years of age, TBI represents the bulk of financial expenditure incurred by the different medical insurance companies for rehabilitation in Canada. TBI is predicted to be the most prevalent and costliest neurological condition in Canada through the year 2031. Outcome assessment after TBI is complex. Clinical examination of these patients are almost impossible as they are on life support and sedated at the time of their hospital admission. Roughly half of these patients who die, die in the first 48 hrs of hospital admission, despite receiving the most resource intensive treatment. These patients receive treatment despite lack of a clear understanding of their prognoses. We believe that some patients with severe TBI have a fatal brain injury at hospital admission, which is not recognized because of inadequate clinical examination. An advanced type of CT scan of brain called Computed Tomographic Perfusion (CTP) can establish brain death, when present. In a small pilot study, CTP done at the time of hospital admission, accurately diagnosed brain death in patients with severe TBI. The proposed research is to confirm these findings in a larger, powerful, well designed and a robust multi-center study. This study will directly address the existing lack of a routine robust neuroimaging test to improve diagnosis and prognosis of patients with severe TBI. This will provide a confident prognosis for the patients with severe TBI and optimize the use of health care resources by preventing the use of expensive intense care for potentially dead patients in the emergency room. Thereby this may improve trust and investment in organ donation in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Neuro-immune control of postoperative pain via CCL22:CCR4 signalling
column37: Pain is one of the major complaints of patients suffering from various neurological and non-neurological conditions, such as autoimmune diseases, tissue infection, and injury. Current therapies for pain caused by inflammation, such as after surgical wound or bacterial infection, include NSAIDs and acetaminophen. These drugs often provide inadequate pain relief and are accompanied by serious gastrointestinal and cardiovascular side effects. Opioids are more effective pain-killers but carry a heavy burden to both the patient and society. While treatments targeting the spinal cord or brain can be challenging and carry risks of unwanted side effects, modulating the inflammation that occurs at the site of injury may be more amenable to treatment. Recent work from our lab has found that dendritic cells in the skin, which act as sentinels to injury and infection, secrete specific immune mediators after injury that can directly activate sensory neurons to cause pain. In preliminary studies, we discovered that tissue injury activates a specific molecule (the chemokine CCL22) in dendritic cells located at the site of tissue injury. We also discovered that blocking its receptor, CCR4, substantially reduces pain. Our work also suggests that pain-sensing neurons control the activation state of dendritic cells in response to injury, and may function in a feedback loop. This proposal will examine how these immune cells communicate with pain-sensing neurons to mediate pain, and whether the neurons themselves can alter the dendritic cell response. Understanding why and how pain occurs during inflammation will enable us to develop new health care strategies to prevent or treat pain in patients with bacterial infection and tissue injury.

column36: Social adjustment in survivors of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
column37: Background: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a cancer that affects the white blood cells and is the most common cancer affecting children. Thanks to many advances in treatment, most children diagnosed with ALL will survive. The treatments needed to cure ALL, however, are toxic because they are directed at the brain and therefore negatively impact survivor's health and psychological well-being. Survivors of ALL experience social difficulties. As children, these survivors do not have as many friends because they are more withdrawn. As adults, these survivors are less likely to go as far in school, have a job or be married compared to others who have not had ALL. Social difficulties are a serious health risk that may be comparable to the health risks associated with drinking and smoking. Yet, we do not understand why these survivors may have social difficulties. We need to understand this in order to find the best way to treat these problems. The goal of the current study is to identify some of the risk and protective factors that might be contributing to social difficulties in survivors of pediatric ALL. Methods: One hundred survivors of pediatric ALL and 100 survivors of solid tumours who have not received brain-directed therapy will be invited to participate and complete tests that will assess aspects of their social function. Their parents, teachers and classroom peers will also complete measures designed to assess the social function of survivors of pediatric ALL compared to survivors who have not received brain-directed therapy. Expected Results: This study will identify some of the factors related to the social function in survivors of pediatric ALL. This will help us learn to better identify which survivors may be at greatest risk of social difficulties and to design better treatments to help these survivors.

column36: Elucidation of bromodomain functions within SWI/SNF complexes
column37: The effective structural regulation and utilization of a cell's genetic material is essential to its fitness. Unsurprisingly, it is now clear that epigenetic regulators, proteins that organize and regulate the accessibility of the genetic material, are commonly altered in human diseases, including cancer. Notably, the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes are among the most commonly mutated protein complexes in human cancers, with ~20% of patients possessing at least one affected subunit. Intriguingly, SWI/SNF complexes contain a high density of bromodomains, conserved protein domains responsible for binding acetylated lysine residues, suggesting that they may have important functions in these complexes. In recent years, bromodomains have become actionable therapeutic targets, with the development of numerous small molecule inhibitors that effectively and specifically block their function. Clinical trials investigating these innovative inhibitors are ongoing in Canada and elsewhere. Unfortunately, fundamental understanding of the functions of the ten bromodomains incorporated in SWI/SNF complex components is still lacking. This project aims to provide this knowledge by employing state-of-the-art tools to identify the cellular targets of SWI/SNF bromodomains, examine how they engage these targets, and determine the functions of these interactions. This will aid in predicting the molecular consequences of specific mutations within SWI/SNF complex components, support the ongoing development of novel bromodomain inhibitors, and further our understanding of the regulatory processes controlling a cell's genomic material.

column36: Antibody-functionalized nanoparticles for HIV prevention
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cause of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS), affects 37 million of individuals. Development of HIV prevention strategies is a global health priority to help end the HIV/AIDS pandemic. One of the major challenges is that the virus mutates rapidly but maintains its power to cause AIDS. It changes configuration on its surface and escapes detection by the immune system that would have blocked it otherwise. Earlier test vaccines failed to overcome this problem and did not confer protection against HIV. Molecules of the immune system called antibodies have been discovered in some individuals who have been infected with HIV for several years that are unique compared to other antibodies people usually make. These special antibodies are needed before first exposure to HIV to confer protection. These antibodies are produced by cells of the immune system called B cells, and block most of the HIV types around the world that uninfected people could encounter because they block surface portions of the virus that don't mutate. They also recruit other protective immune functions. These special antibodies can confer protection against infection when directly administered into a patient. Also, the unchanged surface areas are ideal targets for vaccines that can quickly teach the body to block correctly. This proposal combines innovations in molecular engineering, nanotechnology and modulation of the immune system. Specifically, we will investigate how to develop nanoparticles into two HIV prevention products: 1) the special antibodies themselves as stable and long-lasting nanoparticles that can be administered to directly protect against HIV, and 2) a mimic of the natural virus surface that can activate B cells to produce these special antibodies by vaccination. Our studies will provide evidence to advance our HIV nanoparticles into future prevention studies in animals and in human clinical trials.

column36: Investigating Use of Prescription Opioids and Multiple Psychotropic Medications During Pregnancy: Impact on the Mother and Developing Child
column37: Canada is in the midst of an opioid crisis. With more women taking prescription opioids during pregnancy now than at any time in the past, it is important to understand how these drugs are used during pregnancy and how they affect the development of children. This information is critical to policymakers working to reduce negative effects related to prescription opioids, and to women faced with the decision of whether to take these medications during pregnancy or not. Increasing the complexity of the issue is the fact that prescription opioids are often taken together with other psychotropic medications, such as anti-depressants. The risks to mothers who use these drugs and to their infants are largely unknown. We will use powerful, comprehensive administrative data from two Canadian provinces and sophisticated statistical analysis techniques to investigate the effect of prescription opioid and psychotropic medication use during pregnancy. We will include women from the full spectrum of income, generating insight into how these medications affect mothers and their developing children over time. The project will: 1) describe patterns of prescription opioid use during pregnancy, including the specific opioid (e.g., codeine, hydromorphone), the intensity of use (total days supply and morphine equivalent), the demographics of users (age, socioeconomic status, morbidity), and information about the prescribers (e.g. specialty, location of training); and compare women who use prescription opioids to non-users to examine 2) short term outcomes (e.g., neonatal abstinence syndrome), and 3) long term outcomes (e.g., ADHD, autism) for children exposed in the womb. 4) We will also use education data to assess impacts on school readiness and test performance.

column36: Harnessing mast cell responses to viral infections
column37: Mast cells are cells of the immune system that are found in areas of the body that are prone to infection, such as the skin, and airways and also found in increased numbers around areas of cancer growth. In the current study we will examine the importance of mast cells to effective immunity against a common viral infection known as Respiratory Syncytial Virus or RSV and their response to viruses known as "oncolytic viruses" which are used in cancer treatment. In particular we will look at the mechanisms that mast cells use to drive the activities of immune cells which can limit viral infection and identify ways to reduce harmful activities of these cells during infection of the airways while promoting their positive activities in promoting effective immunity. Investigating a new approach to therapy, we will also use mast cells that have been modified to produce chemicals that will boost their ability to limit damage associated with viral infection or to inhibit tumor growth and spread. Through these studies we will find out more about the immune system's response to viruses and cancer and also aim to develop new approaches to the treatment of RSV infection and more effective use of oncolytic viruses to treat cancer.

column36: Intra-articular Delivery of PPAR-delta Inhibitors for the Treatment of Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis
column37: Musculosketetal diseases, led by back pain and osteoarthritis (OA) are among the most common causes of lifetime disability worldwide, affecting more than 1.7 billion people. OA currently affects one in six Canadians, and its prevalence is predicted to increase to one in four Canadians by 2035. It is a progressive disease, involving the breakdown of joint cartilage and underlying bone, resulting in joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and dysfunction. There is currently no cure for OA, and while medications such as anti-inflammatory drugs can be taken to manage pain and improve joint function, these drugs suffer from significant side effects and do not alter the disease progression. Millions of people suffer for years or decades until joint replacement, which provides relief, but suffers from significant shortcomings including lack of efficacy in some patients, risk of infections during or after surgery, high cost, and limited lifespan of implants, especially when implanted in mid life. Research in our laboratories has shown that blocking a receptor called peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPAR-delta inhibitors) may provide protective and therapeutic effects for OA. Molecules capable of interacting with this receptor are known, but cannot be administered as conventional oral drugs due to their potential for side effects. The aim of our project is to develop a delivery system that will allow PPAR-delta inhibitors to be delivered to joints, where they are needed, by an injection and then released over a period of 3 months. Our project will involve the development of the delivery system for PPAR-delta inhibitors that is specifically designed for application in joints. We will then evaluate this system in small and large animals. Through this work, we will determine the potential of PPAR-delta inhibitors to serve as the first OA treatment capable of halting the progression of the disease.

column36: Establishing an International Core Outcome Set in SAH - What and When to Measure in SAH Research
column37: What is the problem?: In research studies, clinicians and researchers measure specific signs of injury or recovery called 'outcomes' to measure success. In bleeds in the brain from a burst artery (called subarachnoid hemorrhage or 'SAH' for short), there is little consistency in reporting outcomes, literally hundreds exist. We use tools that were not informed by SAH patients and made for use in other diseases. No set of agreed upon measures of outcome in SAH research has been established. As a result, we cannot learn from combining study results and research looking at SAH may be misinformed by not looking at the outcomes that make the biggest difference in the lives of those affected by SAH. Who are we and what will we do?: Our team is made up of patients, families, researchers and clinicians from around the world. Our goal is to create a list of outcomes that all three groups value, agree on, and think should be included in all future research in SAH, called a Core Outcome Set (or "COS"). To create a COS for SAH, we will focus on 'what' outcomes, and 'when', are important to patients/families, clinicians and researchers. How will we do it?: We will achieve this by following a standard and established model with three main steps. First, we will generate full lists of outcomes that each group values by reviewing articles, interviewing people from each group, conducting focus groups, and sending out surveys. Next, each group will rank the outcomes that they think are the most important. We will pool these responses together in the third step and host an in-person meeting with equal representation from the groups. In the end, we will have one prioritized list to be used in and guide future SAH research. Why is this important?: Having a core set of outcomes in SAH that is created by these key groups will help ensure consistency and allow comparisons across studies that are planned with the goal of improving outcomes that matter most to those affected by SAH.

column36: Reducing the activity of the phosphatase STEP to improve memory performance during aging
column37: The majority of older adults will experience some deterioration in cognitive function as they age. Unfortunately, the cellular and molecular changes that lead to memory decline during aging are still poorly understood. The striatal-enriched phosphatase (STEP) is a brain-specific protein highly expressed in regions involved in learning and memory, such as the hippocampus. The physiological role of STEP is to oppose strengthening of connections (synapses) existing between cells (neurons) in the brain. It was shown that STEP acts as a tonic brake on the induction of memory formation and needs to be degraded to enable the activation of cellular and molecular pathways important for learning and memory. Recently, we reported an elevation in the level of active STEP in aged memory-impaired mice and rats, aged rhesus monkeys, and individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. However, we still ignore if lowering the level of active STEP represents a promising strategy to enhance cognitive performance during aging. The main goal of this project is to determine if reducing the level of active STEP ameliorates memory performance during aging and to determine which proteins are altered after STEP-inhibiting treatment used to improve memory capacities of aged mice. To achieve our goal, we will use genetic and pharmacological approaches to reduce and inhibit STEP function in aged mouse model. These animals will be evaluated in various behavioural memory tasks, and molecular mechanisms underpinning the effects of STEP will be investigated using molecular biology techniques. Currently there is no medication to enhance memory abilities of elderly. This research has the potential to uncover the beneficial effects of decreasing STEP function to improve age-related memory deficits. This project could pave the way to human clinical trials targeting STEP or its substrates to enhance memory capacities of elderly.

column36: Towards eliminating viral hepatitis - Addressing hepatitis B using a multidisciplinary approach
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is one of the most burdensome infectious disease and one of the most expensive infectious disease to prevent and treat. In Canada, 0.4% of the population are infected with HBV. HBV infection can cause chronic infection of the liver (i.e. chronic hepatitis B), that is silent for 20-30 years before about one in five infected people develop liver failure or liver cancer. The Government of Canada has endorsed and committed to the World Health Organization (WHO)'s strategy on viral hepatitis, who has called for a 90% reduction in new HBV cases, a 65% reduction in HBV-related deaths, and treatment of 80% of eligible patients by 2030. To achieve these targets, the government has to consider strategies that include vaccination, screening and treatment, which are expensive for Canada's health care system. As a result, research that assesses how to provide the best quality care with limited health care resources is essential for government agencies who make HBV policies and funding decisions. This study will determine the burden of HBV to patients and the healthcare payer, and will assess the value of integrated HBV interventions to inform policy decision-making. We propose to 1) measure the patients' burden of HBV by surveying patients about their quality of life, the effect of HBV on their workplace productivity and out-of-pocket costs at three liver clinics in Toronto, Calgary and Montreal; 2) develop a computer simulation model that can predict future health outcomes and cost of different integrated HBV intervention strategies (vaccination, screening, treatment); and 3) to identify a set of effective integrated HBV intervention strategies and assess the cost-effectiveness and health equity impact of the most effective strategies. Our research will develop method to better assess the burden of HBV and predict the benefit of interventions, and provide needed evidence to help decision makers to improve HBV care and help Canada achieve the WHO targets.
