column36: Sexual Health and STI Prevention For Sexual Minority Men In Suburban Cities
column37: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are at an all-time high in Canada. The Greater Toronto Area (GTA) has an active syphilis epidemic and emerging gonorrhea epidemic among men who have sex with men (MSM). They ways we usually stop STI epidemics are not working; maybe because we have been focusing interventions on MSM in Toronto's urban downtown, where infection rates are highest, and have largely ignored MSM living in suburban and rural areas as part of the epidemic. Our goal is to stop these STI epidemics by improving sexual health care services for MSM in suburbs and rural areas. This requires exploring how MSM from these places manage their sexual lives and sexual health. Our objectives are to: 1.Explore how MSM connect with their social, cultural, racial, ethnic, religious, sexual, and health service communities, and protect themselves from discrimination. 2.Explore how MSM in the suburbs take care (or not) of their sexual health, where they access sexual health services, and how to improve local access and services. 3.Expand STI transmission theory beyond urban cities to include suburban and rural areas. 4.Suggest ways to improve sexual health care for suburban and rural MSM, especially in Peel Region. This qualitative study is a partnership between Region of Peel - Public Health and the University of Toronto. We will interview 60 MSM living in Peel Region (Mississauga, Brampton, or Caledon). We will ask these men about their sex lives, their sexual health, and what it is like getting tested for STIs in Peel. We will suggest ways to improve sexual health services that respect the different identities, communities, and relationships MSM in suburbs and rural areas have to manage. We will host workshops online and in-person with community and health care providers to share results, check our interpretations, get feedback, and maximize uptake of results.

column36: Predicting and Evaluating Anal Cancer in HIV with novel biomarkers: The PEACH Study
column37: Though there have been many improvements in the health of those living with HIV since the mid 1990s when effective therapies first emerged including reductions in AIDS-associated cancers, there have been increases in other types of cancer since that time. One category of these is cancers caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is the main cause of anal cancer, and gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) have rates of anal cancer up to 100 times higher than the general population. Despite this, there are currently no clear guidelines for anal cancer screening in gbMSM living with HIV, the currently available screening tools do not perform particularly well, and there are very few clinics and health care providers trained in providing these services. As such, there is an urgent need to investigate ways to better provide anal cancer screening to this at-risk population. One of the ways to do this is to develop and examine different tests that can predict the presence of lesions in the anal canal that may lead to cancer (called high-grade dysplasia, or anal precancers). These are called biomarkers, and there are several that have not been adequately examined as possible predictors of anal cancers and pre-cancers in gbMSM living with HIV. The proposed study will recruit participants from an existing set of Canadian studies to examine how well these novel biomarkers perform as predictors of anal pre-cancers.

column36: A novel multimodal intervention for surgical prehabilitation of patients with lung cancer
column37: Many persons with lung cancer lose muscle, are fatigued and have more difficulties performing their normal activities. Those who undergo surgery in these conditions suffer from more complications, take more time to recover and have more risk of mortality. Our research group has shown that a moderate exercise and nutrition intervention can improve functional status, not only during recovery but even before surgery. We will take advantage of the 4-week waiting period to engage patients in this intervention that also includes consultation to reduce anxiety and to improve diet, and which will last for 8 weeks after surgery. Patients scheduled for lung cancer surgery will be assigned by change to one of three groups: 1) receiving the usual care including education on a healthy lifestyle, 2) receiving a novel nutritional supplement that combines important nutrients involved in muscle health, or 3) taking the supplement and following an exercise program (with one supervised session per week). All groups will attend anxiety management sessions and counseling with the dietitian. Tests will include walking endurance, muscle strength, scans for body composition, heart-lung-muscle capacity, and questionnaires for the quality of life before and after surgery. Their length of stay in the hospital and complications due to surgery will be recorded. Small muscle samples will be collected during surgery in a subset of participants to study how the supplement influences the muscle quality and its capacity to build new proteins and store lipids. This work has the potential to help persons with lung cancer regain their normal functions and quality of life faster and with lesser complications after surgery. This would benefit the health care system as well.

column36: HEAL-ME ACE: An Interactive eHealth Network Delivering Personalized Exercise, Physiotherapy and Nutrition Programming and Support to Rural and Remote Breast Cancer Survivors
column37: Breast cancer survivors (BCS) living in rural and remote communities do not have access to services to meet their unique exercise, physiotherapy, and nutrition needs. In 2017, we implemented the Alberta Cancer Exercise (ACE) program that has been successful in improving fitness and reducing cancer-related symptoms in urban centres. HEAL-ME is an innovative e-Health program that has features designed for ease of clinical implementation and adoption by a wider chronic disease population. HEAL-ME offers a virtual solution to improve accessibility to multidisciplinary supportive care for individuals living in rural and remote communities. The goal of the study is to adapt HEAL-ME for use with BCS and test its effectiveness. We will combine exercise, physiotherapy and nutrition elements from the breast cancer survivor rehabilitation program into the existing HEAL-ME app. HEAL-ME "ACE" will then be assessed for its effectiveness and acceptability for use in rural and remote communities where ACE is not offered. We hypothesize that this supported home-based program will offer state of the art multidisciplinary rehabilitation programming. In Phase I we will develop the specific content of HEAL-ME ACE for use with BCS. We will conduct a survey and two focus group sessions with rural and remote BCS residents to collect information on needs and preferences for content and delivery of HEAL-ME ACE. We will then pilot test components of the program with rural and remote BCS. For Phase II, we will conduct a roll-out implementation study across Alberta to test the feasibility and effectiveness of the full HEAL-ME ACE program on exercise, physiotherapy, and nutritional outcomes in BCS living in rural and remote communities. If proven feasible and effective, HEAL-ME ACE will allow for scheduled one-to-one and group video conferences between a healthcare professional and BCS to facilitate semi-supervised, home-based wellness programming accessible by all regardless of location.

column36: Rescuing beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations from resistance against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens
column37: According to the United Nations and the World Health Organization antimicrobial resistance is the largest threat to public health and economic growth. Currently, the greatest threat to human health derives from three multidrug-resistant Gram-negative priority pathogens that include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii and Enterobacteriaceae. These pathogens have become resistant to all or almost all of our antibiotics. Beta-lactam antibiotics are the most widely used class of antibacterial agents to combat bacterial infections. Beta-lactam antibiotics account for 65% of all prescriptions for injectable antibiotics in the United States. Current strategies to cope with beta-lactam antibiotic resistance are limited to inhibit beta-lactamase enzymes that hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring, thereby inactivating the drug. This can be achieved by combination therapy using a combination of beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor. However, this approach does not address other resistance mechanisms that are prevalent in Gram-negative priority pathogens including outer membrane impermeability and efflux. To overcome these limitations we have developed beta-lactam antibiotic potentiators that restore efficacy of beta-lactam antibiotic/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens. The overall goal of this project is (i) to develop optimized and safe beta-lactam antibiotic potentiators that overcome resistance and extend the life of clinically approved beta-lactam antibiotics/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens and (ii) to demonstrate efficacy by protecting mice infected with beta-lactam antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Successful demonstration of efficacy and safety of the triple component combination in animal models will serve as a proof of principle to attract an industrial partner with the goal to commercialize novel anti-infective therapies.

column36: Identifying a novel neuromuscular biomarker signature of chronic temporomandibular disorders
column37: Pain poses the most significant health-related burden on society and is the primary cause of long-term disability. Temporomandibular disorders (TMD), a set of conditions affecting the muscles of mastication and the temporomandibular joint (the jaw joint), is the most common cause of chronic (persistent) pain relating to the mouth and face. Mechanisms of chronic muscular TMD (mTMD), the most common TMD, are still poorly understood, and a definite cause of this condition has yet to be identified. Of importance, the lack of clear biological correlates of disease severity, which could be used by health care providers to complement patient pain self-report, makes treatment of chronic mTMD challenging. More than 30% of patients with TMD have recurrent or persistent pain after 5 years regardless of the treatment they had received. This project aims to identify and characterize the muscular and neural abnormalities associated with chronic muscular TMD and determine whether the biological severity of these abnormalities predicts patient disability. We will use multiple imaging methods to characterize the structure and function of the muscles of mastication, and the structure of the nerves and the brain in patients with chronic mTMD. In the long term, our project will allow to classifying the extent of spread of TMD, thereby informing about its biological severity and develop more personalized and cost-effective treatments, which will reduce the burden to patients and the healthcare system.

column36: Perinatal Anxiety Disorder Screening Study
column37: At present, little if any routine screening for perinatal anxiety and related disorders is carried out. This is despite the fact that the anxiety and their related disorders affect 20% of pregnant and postpartum women, and are significantly more common than is depression. They are significantly more common among women compared with men, and are associated with significant distress and life interference for sufferers, as well as negative consequences for fetal/infant development. Despite the above, perinatal anxiety and related disorders remains a relatively neglected area of research compared with other mental health conditions. Although screening is a critical step in the pathway to effective care, an accurate and effective screening tool for perinatal anxiety and related disorders has yet to be identified. The majority of studies in this area have used inadequate methodology, or have assessed measures which appear to perform too poorly to recommend for wide-spread use. The primary objective of this research is to identify an effective self-report measure to screen for perinatal anxiety and related disorders. To do this, we are proposing to conduct a large scale study using a representative sample of pregnant and postpartum women in which a broad range of self-report measures are assessed and compared with gold standard diagnostic interviews. Ours will be the first comprehensive study of perinatal anxiety and related disorder screening tools in which gold standard methodology is used. This research responds to an urgent public health need. Specifically, women who suffer from anxiety and related disorders during pregnancy and the postpartum currently remain unidentified and therefore suffer without adequate treatment. This research will provide important information that will inform health care providers, policy makers and scientists about the most effective approach to screening for anxiety and related disorders in pregnancy and the postpartum.

column36: Roles for mitochondrial adaptation in fatty liver disease and associated liver cancer
column37: Fatty liver disease affects one third of people in North America. The disease has few symptoms, but over time causes irreversible damage to the liver. Fatty liver disease involves both an accumulation of fat and increased inflammation in liver, which combine to cause permanent damage. Having fatty liver disease increases the chance of liver failure and of developing other diseases such as diabetes, heart problems, and cancer since damaged livers release harmful substances (fats, hormones, and inflammatory signals) into the blood. Diets high in fat and/or sugar and low physical activity contribute to the rising number of people afflicted. There is no cure for the disease and diagnosis is difficult, mainly because we do not understand the triggers. We have shown that low levels of a protein called PGC-1alpha in liver may cause or worsen fatty liver disease and our new studies will help to understand how this happens. We will investigate how low levels of PGC-1alpha decrease the ability of liver to repair damage and whether we can improve this by increasing the levels of this protein in liver cells. We are also investigating whether a common gene variant in PGC-1alpha is associated with the incidence or severity of the disease in humans. Identifying the cause of fatty liver disease will help to discover ways to diagnosis patients early and to design more effective treatments.

column36: WeChoose: a mixed-methods study for developing a personalized risk communication tool in pediatric surgery
column37: Making decisions for surgery is difficult for children and their parents, and each family is unique in how they approach this decision and what information they need for it. Unfortunately, surgeons counsel regarding surgery using scientific data from their, rather than patients', perspective. Moreover, patient and family priorities essential to making personalized decisions for surgery are often ignored by the surgeons, and rarely expressly asked. We plan to turn the tables on this process by placing the patient and the family in the center of the surgical decision-making process. We will use scientific approaches from psychology and medical ethics to identify patient and family priorities and values regarding their information needs in the surgical decision-making process. The resulting personalized communication tool will empower patients to help make ultimately satisfactory surgical decisions. For our study, parents of children consulting a surgeon for groin or tonsils problems and their parents will be asked to participate in a focus group discussion and complete a survey. This will allow us to identify the information needs, preferences and priorities that patients have when facing surgery and determine how patients and their families rate outcomes after surgery. We will then use the results to create a personalized interactive risk communication tool for surgeons to use with their patients, which we will test in a clinic setting. The study will identify the real communication and decision-making needs of families facing pediatric surgery. The proposed tool is expected to change the way surgeons discuss treatment with their patients, improve patient-related experience and satisfaction with the surgical process, and potentially reduce the number of unnecessary surgeries.

column36: Filling Knowledge Gaps for the Success of Ontario Renal Plan 3
column37: One in 10 Canadians suffer from kidney disease. Many have expressed difficulties related to their mental health, the safety of their prescription drugs, and their access to life-improving kidney transplants. For members of First Nations communities, who are disproportionately burdened by the disease, these challenges are made more difficult due to the health and socioeconomic inequities they face. However, most concerning is the lack of meaningful research evidence to guide their health care needs. Improving the health of people with kidney disease requires effective partnerships between patients, researchers, doctors, and policy makers. Our Ontario-wide research program (ICES KDT) has been building these partnerships for seven years. Together, we conduct research to improve the health and experiences of people living with kidney disease. We are partnering with the Ontario Renal Network to conduct research that will focus on the issues that matter most to people living day-to-day with kidney disease. We will begin by conducting timely and effective research that will inform the effective use of health care resources in four areas: Mental health for kidney disease patients, prescription drug safety, kidney disease in First Nations communities, and kidney transplantation. We will work with our patient partners as well as provincial and national organizations to directly inform how Canadian health care should be strengthened to meet the needs of patients and their families.

column37: Deficient blood supply to the central nervous system (CNS) leads to several debilitating diseases. Examples of such diseases include stroke which is a leading cause of brain injury affecting 800,000 individuals per year in the United States alone and causing upwards of 150,000 deaths. To study the molecular mechanisms of stroke, an easily accessible model system in which to investigate how blood vessels interact with nerve cells is the retina, the membrane of nerve cells at the back of the eye that relays visual information to the brain. The retina is biochemically analogous to the brain and its anatomical location allows for thorough investigation. In addition, findings that are obtained from studying stroke in the retina can be translated to better understand ischemic retinopathies, such as diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity which are the leading causes of blindness in the industrial world. These blinding diseases happen to also stem from compromised blood supply to the neurons of the retina. This proposal seeks to understand how blood vessels degenerate in ischemic diseases of the CNS by using the retina as a model. Furthermore, we propose to investigate the role of cholesterol metabolism in modulating inflammation upon ischemia. Ultimately, we hope to interfere with the disease process and promote regeneration of functional blood vessels.

column36: Ectopic reactivation of normally silenced germ cell programs contributes to genomic instability, carcinogenesis and cancer progression in Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas (CTCL).
column37: Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (CTCL) is the most common lymphoma of the skin. Despite recent advances, this lymphoma remains difficult to diagnose (time to diagnosis ~6 years) because it mimics other common skin rashes such as eczema and psoriasis. It is also not possible to predict which patients with early stage CTCL will progress to advanced stages. Furthermore, advanced CTCL remains difficult to treat with a median survival of only 2-4 years. Hence, new diagnostic/prognostic markers and novel therapeutic targets are urgently needed to aid the medical management of this cancer. We showed that a number of programs that are usually only present in germline tissues (testis/ovaries) are abnormally re-expressed in CTCL. We are proposing to study how reactivation of these genes/programs (e.g., LINE-1 retrotransposition, cancer testis/meiosis regulatory genes) arises contributing to genomic instability, CTCL cancer development and progression. Since these programs are usually not expressed in healthy somatic tissues, their upregulation could be used as a diagnostic marker. Also, since these genes likely promote cancer progression, their expression in early stages may serve as a harbinger for an aggressive disease requiring systemic therapy. Finally, activity of several of these genes is likely central to cancer cell division/survival and, hence, targeting them may lead to novel therapies for CTCL patients. In the proposed grant we will study expression/activation patterns for these genes, their regulation and molecular function in CTCL, determine how they could be used as novel diagnostic/prognostic markers and exploited as therapeutic targets. This project will produce a reliable set of markers that will help shorten the time to diagnosis and help distinguish CTCL from other benign skin rashes; select prognostic markers that will identify early stage patients requiring aggressive therapies and define how these important genes/proteins could be targeted to treat CTCL.

column36: Mapping cellular and extracellular white-matter changes in aging using MRI: Towards clinical translation
column37: The white matter is the information highway for the brain. Microstructural degeneration in the white matter has been known to occur in normal aging, and has been associated with cognitive decline and the potential development of dementia. Scientists have mostly been monitor these changes using diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). However, DWI currently does not provide enough details about what type(s) of changes the white matter undergoes, which limits our understanding of the brain-aging process. Specifically, most researchers are still unable to quantify the amount of extracelluar water in the white matter, which can be a useful indicator of early changes in the brain. In this work, we will validate and optimize a new technique for mapping extracellular water noninvasively in humans. In addition, we will apply this technique to the study of aging, made possible by collaborations with large international studies of aging (the US and UK). The proposed work may drive a paradigm shift in clinical assessment of white-matter health and open the possibility for new clinical questions regarding brain health. These questions will be critical for understanding the neuroinflammation process, enabling clinicians to push the limits for early intervention to delay or even prevent neurodegeneration in dementia.

column36: Modeling Cognitive Impairment in Patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Clinical Phenotyping, Predictive Trajectory, and Associated Risk Factors.
column37: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem chronic autoimmune disease, which is highly variable in patterns of organ involvement and prognosis. Cognitive Impairment (CI) is one of the most common manifestations of brain disorders in SLE with a prevalence of 33-43%. CI includes decline in memory, thinking speed, attention, and planning abilities and can be associated with significant reduction of patient's quality of life and employment potential. There is an unmet need to establish clinical subtypes of CI in SLE and a necessity to identify patients with a high risk for developing CI. The objective of our study is to enhance the clinical assessment of CI among SLE patients, by establishing subtypes of CI. Through the use of novel data analyses techniques such as machine learning analyses and data modeling, the study aims to: 1) identify clinical subtypes of CI among SLE patients; and 2) predict which patients are at risk for CI, identify what factors increase risk persistent CI, and predict the trajectory of cognitive function over time. We further aim to shed light on the progression of CI over time, in an effort to establish evidence informed personalized medicine and to improve quality of life among SLE patients. This work will build upon previous work of this multi-disciplinary research study team at our clinic which is composed of lupologists, psychologists, psychometrists, neurologists, outcome measure scientists, experts in basic and translational research, biostatisticians, experts in machine-learning analyses, and patient research partners. Impact: Given the high prevalence of CI in SLE, our research initiative will impact a large number of patients. Identifying patients with a high risk of CI and those who are likely to have severe CI overtime will enhance the management of the disease and its progression. Ultimately, our project can help alleviate the burden of disease due to CI and improve the overall quality of life among patients.

column36: Pathogenic roles of platelets in sepsis.
column37: Billions of platelets patrol blood vessels on the ready to prevent the loos of blood when a vessel is injured. The prevention of bleedings is the primarily recognized role of platelets, known since their first description in the late 19th century. When microbes such as bacteria enter the blood circulation, it generates multiple reactions such as fever, loss of blood pressure, alteration of heart rate and respiration. With their abundance in blood, platelets are chiefly positioned to interact with bacteria in blood. During blood invasion by bacteria, called sepsis, it is recognized that the platelet number diminishes dramatically. Moreover, platelets form aggregates in blood vessels during sepsis. However, how exactly platelets contribute to the pathogenesis in sepsis is not fully understood. We recently developed a novel mouse model of sepsis. In this model, we observed the formation of platelet aggregates in lungs and brain, and we noticed a dramatic reduction of platelet number in circulation. Herein in this application, we wish to utilize our model to determine how platelets may contribute to sepsis pathogenesis and we wish to interfere in the process. For this, we will use compelling mouse models of blood infections (sepsis) and we will administer drugs that target platelets. Using genetic and pharmacological approaches, we wish to improve the success of the therapies to combat infections. At the end of this project, we will have identified how platelets modify responses in blood-borne infections and how manipulating platelets can improve success in clinic.

column36: The physiological, molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying lateralization of motor control
column37: Lateralization of motor control refers to the ability to perform asymmetric and unilateral movements, and is essential for activities such as coordinated hand movements and walking. The right and left sides of the nervous system communicate through crossing fibers. Defective lateralized motor control can result in mirror movements (MM), involuntary movements that mirror voluntary ones on the opposite side of the body. In 2010, we reported that MM can result from mutations in DCC, a gene critical in guiding developing axons to the nervous system midline. We have assembled the world's largest cohort of MM individuals (n=90). 60% carry mutations in DCC and 40% are genetically unexplained, suggesting that many more MM genes remain to be discovered. Furthermore, though DCC deficits in animals result in locomotion deficits, the role of DCC in human gait circuitry and motor control of legs has not yet been explored. Our unique MM cohort provides an exceptional opportunity to study the physiological, molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying lateralization of motor control. We will: 1-Identify novel genes important for lateralization of motor control by genetically studying our MM cohort. 2-Functionally assess the role of novel MM gene mutations using in vitro and mouse experiments. We hypothesize that the majority of novel genes will have a role in midline axon guidance and DCC signaling. 3-Investigate the role of DCC in human gait patterning. We will use biomechanical and electrophysiologic approaches to investigate left-right coordination and motor tract lateralization abnormalities in DCC individuals. This study will (1) expand understanding of the physiological and molecular basis of lateralization of motor control, axon guidance and circuit formation, (2) decipher the effects DCC deficits on human gait circuitry, and (3) identify novel MM genes.

column36: Role of neutrophils in liver fibrosis
column37: Chronic inflammation and fibrosis or scarring are the first triggers of cancer in the liver. Liver fibrosis occurs in response to injury like inflammation due to infection or fatty liver disease where high levels of collagen deposits in the liver leading to stiffness or fibrosis and gradual loss of liver function. The immune system, specifically different subsets of white blood cells produce immune mediators (cytokines) that may increase or decrease the inflammation in the liver and the progression of liver fibrosis. We and other groups have identified a cytokine known as IL-17 as a key accelerator of liver fibrosis. We have also identified a subset of white blood cells known as "neutrophils" that produce IL-17 and that are increased in advanced fibrosis. In this proposal we are interested in understanding how these neutrophils go to the liver during different types of injury and whether different subsets or types of neutrophils can have different functions or play different roles during early versus late stages of liver injury and fibrosis. We would also like to know where these neutrophils are located in the injured liver and how they interact with the different liver cells. Finally, we would like to see if blocking the activity of these neutrophils can stop or delay liver fibrosis. To achieve these goals, we will use a combination of imaging techniques and assays to examine these cells in liver tissues from patients at different fibrosis stages as well as mice. We will also use genetically modified mice lacking the capacity to produce IL-17 and to examine whether they will develop fibrosis at the same rate as normal mice or not and what are the other cells implicated. The results obtained will guide the development of new treatments to stop liver fibrosis and prevent cancer.

column36: Targeting 14-3-3zeta to promote human pancreatic beta-cell proliferation
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a devastating disease caused by the death of insulin-producing pancreatic beta-cells by our own immune system. There is no cure for T1D, and current treatment involves daily injections of insulin to keep blood glucose levels with a healthy range. It is generally thought that patients with long-standing T1D do not have any beta-cells, but numerous studies have now identified the presence of residual beta-cells. This raises the question of whether it is possible to coax these remaining beta-cells to expand in number, which would remove the need for daily insulin injections. Ultimately, this could represent an effective treatment for T1D. The pathways that control human beta-cells proliferation are very complex, and they require precise and accurate actions of numerous proteins at specific times and places within the cell. Currently, the identity of factors that coordinate these proteins in the human beta-cell is not known, but specialized proteins called molecular scaffolds are logical candidates, as they coordinate the actions of proteins within cells and have the ability to control cell growth. Previously, we reported that molecular scaffolds belonging to the 14-3-3 protein family are essential for the regulation of metabolism, and they are important in regulating the survival and growth of mouse beta-cells. Mice lacking 14-3-3zeta in all cells have significantly higher numbers of beta-cells, in addition to better glucose control. This raises the question of whether one can specifically target 14-3-3zeta in human beta-cells to increase proliferation and treat diabetes. This will be tested by first determining the precise roles of 14-3-3 proteins in human beta-cells, followed by developing gene-targeting approaches to reduce 14-3-3zeta function in human beta-cells to stimulate their proliferation. Ultimately, it is the over-arching goal of this proposal to see whether it is possible to stimulate the growth of human beta-cells to cure T1D.

column36: Delineation of the epigenomic principles underlying microglial transcriptional and cellular activity in chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
column37: Microglia are the immune cells residing in the brain and play key roles in its development maintenance of proper functioning, and immune response against infections and injuries. To date, most pathological conditions affecting the brain, ranging from neurodevelopment disorders like schizophrenia to neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's, appear to involve an accompanying inflammatory response that is driven by microglia. However, the mechanisms involved in triggering this microglial-driven inflammatory response, or in sustaining it, are not well understood to this day. To large extent, the cellular functions of microglia stem from the genes that these cells express. Work by us and others recently demonstrated that discrete regions of the genome called enhancers are critical to ensure that genes are correctly expressed in microglia. However, how enhancers, in the number of 40,000 in microglia, are regulated in the brain under both under healthy and pathological conditions remains largely unknown. To investigate how these genomic regions contribute to gene regulation, we will characterize the interactions between proteins involved in gene regulation and enhancers. To do so, we will isolate microglia from the mouse brain and perform assays with next-generation sequencing technologies to reveal how enhancers are involved in specifying microglia gene expression in a given context. Collectively, this research program will enable a much greater understanding of the signaling and epigenetic mechanisms that are responsible for gene regulation microglia, and by extension, the mechanisms that underlie the cellular functions of microglia. Thus, precisely defining the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate microglia gene expression in mice as proposed by this research program represents a critical step towards the development of more efficient therapies to treat neuropsychiatric disorders and neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Diagnostic and predictive biomarkers for Frontotemporal Dementia with TDP-43 pathology
column37: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a devastating disease, characterized by profound changes in behavior, personality, language and movement. It is the second most common cause of dementia under the age of 70 years, affecting approximately 50,000 North Americans. Almost half of FTD patients have a positive family history, often with a very strong inheritance pattern. Recent advances in our understanding of the genetic abnormalities and pathology that underlie FTD provide a basis for the development of the first disease-modifying therapies. Unfortunately, clinical testing and implementation of FTD treatments are severely hampered by a lack of useful biomarkers and understanding of the natural history of the disease. Over the past decade, we have established the largest, well-characterized cohort of familial FTD subjects in Canada and one of the most extensive collections of FTD genetic and neuropathological material, worldwide. This unique cohort of participants with genetic mutations are at risk of developing the disease, and provide us the opportunity to examine changes in brain scans and body fluid chemistry at the earliest stages of disease when treatment is likely to have the greatest impact. This valuable resource, together with our team of experts in clinical, imaging, and biochemical research, will allow us to develop new diagnostic tests and provide rational therapeutic approaches for this currently untreatable disease.

column36: Criminalization, Public Health and Incarceration - A participatory qualitative and digital storytelling investigation of the experiences of cis and trans women living with HIV
column37: Cis and transgender women living with HIV women living with HIV are over criminalized and overrepresented in Canadian prisons. The ultimate goal is to inform HIV law reform, best practice guidelines for public health authorities and women-specific interventions to reduce the negative effects of criminalization and incarceration among women living with HIV. column36: A mixed methods study of stakeholders' perspectives on ethical and logistical issues related to advanced living donation in kidney transplantation in Canada, and a proposal for guidelines in a Canadian context.
column37: Living kidney transplantation offers the best medical outcomes for end stage renal disease (ESRD) patients. Prior to the launch of kidney paired donation programs (KPDs), the living kidney donor had to be compatible with his intended recipient. KPD provides the ability to circumvent this incompatibility obstacle by matching a donor who is incompatible with his intended recipient with a different recipient who is also incompatible with his donor and vice versa. Since its beginning, the Canadian KPD program has facilitated 682 living donor kidney transplantations which would not have been possible before. Recently, advanced donation programs with vouchers have been developed in the US. This program allows the living donor to donate at the most appropriate moment for him and provides a voucher for named persons (up to five) who are not currently ready to receive or could potentially receive a kidney transplant, to receive a living donor kidney transplant at the end of KPD chain in the future. Advanced donation raises numerous ethical and logistical issues such informed consent, fairness and justice, gift-exchange, etc. The objective of this exploratory study is to gather key stakeholders' perspectives, with qualitative interviews and surveys, on the ethical and logistical issues related to advanced donation and to develop preliminary ethical guidelines adapted for the Canadian transplant context. The results of this study will provide important topical information to the transplant community and may inform future discussions on any advanced donation programs developed for the Canadian KPD program.

These MSM attend the community-run sexual health program known as Health Options for Young Men Against STIs (HOYMAS). According to program data we collected with HOYMAS between 2016 and 2018, anal warts-the most common STIs observed in sexually active populations-persist among program participants at high rates. Yet HOYMAS participants rarely request anal exams and those who do often present with anal warts at very late stages. Within the context of high HIV prevalence (26% in Nairobi) and homophobia, which inhibits and delays health services utilization, the growing frequency and late presentation of HPV-related anal warts among Kenyan MSM often appear as large, obstructive masses that require invasive surgical intervention-procedures which are accompanied by intense pain and suffering during the recovery and major losses of income for those who earn a living through sex work. Anal cancer is also being diagnosed and treated at a late stage. We currently lack the evidence base necessary to inform an effective HPV prevention or early detection and treatment program. By nesting our study within a mature and dynamic HIV program following >5000 MSM in Nairobi, we will build a multidisciplinary evidence base that feeds out from and into a community-driven intervention with the aim of drastically reducing the frequency of future severe HPV-related disease. Our project responds to the global health alarm over emerging cancer epidemics in African contexts hardest hit by the HIV epidemic.

column36: Defining the role of ER stress in glomerular disease: identification of new therapeutic and diagnostic targets
column37: Glomerular podocytes are vital in maintaining the structure and function of the glomerulus, the filtering unit of the kidney. Intact function of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is important for protein homeostasis in the podocyte, including production of components of the slit diaphragm, adhesion complexes and glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Disorders of ER function can contribute to disease. Diseases of the renal glomerulus, especially those initiated by immunological processes ("glomerulonephritis"), account for approximately half of the causes of chronic kidney disease in Canada. Treatment of patients with kidney disease with dialysis and kidney transplantation has resulted in a dramatic improvement in the survival of patients, but at a large cost to the Canadian economy. Fundamental research into the disordered mechanisms that lead to glomerulonephritis is essential to the understanding of these diseases, an understanding that will ultimately lead to therapy and prevention. column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a severe, progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing dementia and ultimately death. This type of small RNA (like DNA) has a strong impact on protein networks important for brain health. As of yet, however, it remains uncertain if and how micro-RNAs can be used to treat neurodegenerative disorders such as AD. For more than a decade, my research team and others have gathered substantial evidence pointing to one particular micro-RNA, namely miR-132, as a prime candidate to treat, delay, or prevent AD. This is based on multiple studies in cells and mice where the delivery of miR-132 can, for instance, restore disease symptoms, including memory. Our goal now is to perform the necessary pre-clinical tests to advance miR-132 to clinical trials in humans. For this, we have already developed specialized tools and methods to deliver miR-132 molecules directly into the brain of mice and non-human primates (monkeys). The next steps involve the biological characterization of these molecules following treatment (e.g., bioavailability, degradation, target engagement). Of course, we will also perform extensive biosafety (toxicology) tests in both animal models. Overall, these cutting-edge studies will provide an essential basis for the development of micro-RNA therapies for AD and related neurodegenerative disorders.

column37: A promising class of drugs has recently emerged that recruits the patient's own immune system to fight cancer, fulfilling a long-held belief that 'immunotherapy' can help in the treatment of cancer. column36: Central mechanisms of opioid withdrawal
column37: Opioid medications provide potent pain relief in the short-term, but their long-term use can cause serious adverse effects. A major problem is that chronic opioid users experience debilitating withdrawal symptoms when attempting to stop or reduce their opioid medications. In an attempt to curb withdrawal, these individuals continue to use opioid drugs. A misconception is that only illicit opioid use or "opioid addicts" are susceptible to withdrawal. The careful use of prescription opioids can also lead to significant withdrawal symptoms. Optimal therapies for opioid withdrawal are unavailable. Our team recently discovered that immune cells (microglia) residing within the brain and spinal cord play an important role in opioid withdrawal. These immune cells communicate with other cells through specialized channels (pannexin-1), which are like gates that open and close to allow passage of chemical signals. Blocking these channels in the spinal cord alleviates withdrawal without diminishing the pain-relieving benefits of opioid medications. We have new data that pannexin-1 channels gate activity within the locus coeruleus, an area of the brain that communicates with the spinal cord by sending specialized projections containing a chemical (norepinephrine). This proposal addresses exciting new questions about how pannexin-1 channels modulate specific circuitry in the brain and spinal cord that are important for opioid withdrawal. Using advanced cellular imaging, biochemical, and behavioural approaches, experiments will also deconstruct the machinery by which norepinephrine enhances pannexin-1 activity and its impact on microglia signaling. Finally, we will translate this detailed mechanistic understanding into the development of next generation, more potent pannexin-1 targeted drugs for treating opioid withdrawal.

column36: Role of the cytoskeletal adaptor protein leupaxin in immune response regulation
column37: Killer cells of the immune system are important for eliminating most virus infections and serve as a natural defense against tumor cells. We want to understand how killer cells crawl through the body to seek and destroy infected cells and cancer cells. We predicted that a particular protein called leupaxin would be important for controlling either the migration or function of killer cells. We showed that leupaxin localizes to the front end of migrating cells and to the contact zone where killer cells bind to their target cell, consistent with a role for leupaxin in these processes. To directly test its role, we generated a model system where the leupaxin was genetically deleted so that we could study immune responses to viruses and to cancer in its absence. Our preliminary data show that deleting leupaxin causes less severe symptoms in response to influenza virus infection. This was surprising as we predicted the response would be worse. Many of the symptoms of influenza infection are related to damage caused by immune cells responding to the virus and not due to the virus itself. While killer cells contribute to the clearance of influenza virus, too many of these cells could cause some of the symptoms associated with influenza infection. Our hypothesis is that leupaxin contributes to the entry or retention of killer cells and other cells that promote damage in the lungs. By having fewer cells, virus may still be eliminated efficiently, but with less severe disease. To test our hypothesis, we will examine numbers of killer cells and relevant cells in the lungs before and after infection. We will also use genetic mechanisms to pinpoint the function that is responsible for the improved recovery from influenza infection. We want to understand how this improved response occurs to potentially translate the results into therapeutics to improve the outcome after influenza infection, and perhaps other inflammatory diseases.

We will observe whether these treatments improve symptoms of depression as well as brain structure/function and memory/cognition. Currently there is a lack of affordable non-medication treatments for LLD that can be scaled to reach many people. If successful, MBCT may be a potential solution to this gap in treatment options, as it is easily given in groups and is well-tolerated by older adults with LLD.

column36: Tumour microenvironment mediated cell surface shedding creates unique targets and markers
column37: Traditional chemo- and radiation-therapy, though often effective, has serious side and long-term effects, particularly for children, who face significant life-long health problems and increased risk for secondary cancers. We need to develop new "targeted therapies" that selectively attack cancer cells and leave healthy organs untouched. Targeted therapies are drugs that interfere with a specific molecule, the 'target', in the cancer cell to block its growth or kill it. The most specific targets are 'abnormal' proteins created by mutation or fusion between two genes. These abnormal proteins are found only in cancer cells, and are distinguishable from normal proteins. But they are also rare. Therefore, most targeted therapies are directed at proteins that occur in both healthy and cancer cells, and so they cause side effects. When they are uncoiled, proteins are a long chain of amino acids that have a start and an end, called the termini. The process called proteolysis cuts the protein apart, creating fragments that have different termini. We have shown that we can identify and quantify these termini in healthy and unhealthy cells, and we could show that in cancer proteolysis creates new termini not found in healthy cells. We found that there are more differences between termini than between the proteins. We now propose to study bone marrow biopsies from children with leukemia to identify cancer specific termini that have the potential to work as drug target. In addition, we will test blood and spinal fluid from these children. If we can find the other part of the protein, that has been cleaved off and released from the cancer cell, we may be able to use this fragment as very specific marker, not only for leukemia in general, but for the presence of the specific drug target. We will also investigate the mechanisms leading to the cleavage that generates the terminus and fragment. Our work will help to develop therapies that target only cancer cells.

column37: Vitamin K is an essential micronutrient known to regulate the activity of proteins implicated in blood coagulation and mineralized tissues. Diabetes is caused by a reduction in the number of beta cells or by a decrease in their capacity to secrete insulin. This research project aims at understanding the function of vitamin K-dependent proteins in pancreatic beta cells and its potential link with the development of diabetes. Our approach includes the use of genetically modified mice lacking the components of the vitamin K cycle in pancreatic beta cells. We will analyze these animals to determine the role of vitamin K in protecting beta cells from cell death, and in promoting their proliferation and function. We will also study the interaction between vitamin K and the endoplasmic reticulum stress in human and mouse beta cells. Finally, we will test if vitamin K can improve or prevent diabetes in pre-clinical mouse models. Altogether, these studies will allow us to understand how vitamin K is implicated in the biology of beta cell and how partial vitamin K deficiency contributes to the development of diabetes.

column37: Stigma is widely considered a barrier to service seeking among individuals with mental health problems. Negative, stigmatizing attitudes are found throughout society - in the general public, within the families and social circles of people with mental illness, among healthcare professionals, and among youth. Since most mental health problems begin in adolescence and persist into adulthood, early access to services has the potential of long-term benefits for vulnerable youth. However, only 25-30% of youth in need access specialized treatment, and stigma is one of the key reasons youth choose not to seek services. There have been calls for increased research to understand aspects of youth mental health stigma, ideally through qualitative and quantitative research with stakeholder engagement. This project is a direct response to such calls. Working with youth as full partners in the project, this study will identify the aspects and sources of stigma that are considered to be the greatest barriers to service seeking among youth with mental health and/or substance use challenges. By doing so, this project will guide researchers, anti-stigma interventionists, investors, and policymakers interested in working toward a stigma-free Canada in which youth and their caregivers are empowered to reach out for services that could benefit the youth. Analyses will identify anti-stigma priorities for youth with diverse levels of mental health service need, across genders, and for Anglophone and Francophone communities. The results will lead not only to clear research agendas to advance stigma reduction, but also direct implementation guidance ensuring that investments are being channeled into the aspects of stigma with the most potential to break down the barriers preventing youth from seeking the services they need.

column36: Deciphering Neisseria pathogens cell envelope evolution: optimisation for virulence or Achilles' heel of N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae?.
column37: The Neisseria genus is composed of bacteria that all evolved to colonize the mucosa of many mammals and that are all obligate symbionts of their respective hosts. In humans, the majority of species reside in the oral cavity or the nasopharynx but evolution has also permitted the adaptation of a few species from this oral ecosystem to the urogenital tract mucosae. If the majority of species have strictly developed a commensal type of symbiosis with humans and are rarely implicated in human diseases, two species named Neisseria meningitidis (causing meningitidis resulting in 0.15 million of death/year) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (causing gonorrheae and infecting around 88 millions persons/year), constitute major human threats. Several invasive strains of N. meningitidis (serogroups A, C, W, Y and nowadays B) are the target of vaccination. However, there is no vaccination available for N. gonorrhoeae. In both cases, a limited number of antibiotics are available which help reduce death rates and other complications. Unfortunately, N. gonorrhoeae is evolving rapidly and is generating resistance with a high risk of worldwide emergence of untreatable infections. This serious situation makes research of novel molecules against N. gonorrhoeae one of the twelve priorities of the WHO. It is therefore crucial to understand the factors that led to the emergence of pathogenic strains from a non-pathogenic commensal ancestors but also develop new avenues of treatments to fight these bacteria. In this proposal, we will focus our research on the cell envelope of these two pathogens. We will try to describe the evolutionary events that led to a specialization of this structure for the symbiosis and pathogenesis, dissect the forces that naturally selected these cell-envelope changes in different infectious contexts which will subsequently help the exploration of how we can target this structure to fight these pathogens.

column36: Genetic Determinants of Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a heterogeneous group of disorders that result in irreversible scarring over time. CKD affects more than 750 million people globally, and results in more than 1 million deaths. Large, granular datasets have now been gathered from world leading cohorts in Canada and the United States, with growing expertise to apply novel biomarker combinations collected at different disease time points with clinical traits. In this proposal, we will focus on a leading cause of CKD called Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and genomics, which is emerging as one tool to identify disease subtypes according to mechanism and treatment outcomes. We have recently reported that a series of rare genetic variations account for ~11% of adults with FSGS, leaving the remaining cases unexplained. We also find that within these genetic cases, different gene categories influence disease progression. However, the cumulative effects of common, subtle changes (called single nucleotide polymorphisms or SNPs) in many genes that are important for normal kidney function have not been explored in FSGS. We will address this critical knowledge gap. By bringing together leading investigators in Canada and the US, we aim to uncover the effects of common genetic determinants, in isolation and cumulatively, important for disease progression and study their effects on gene expression in a large cohort of FSGS patients (n=6500). There is a large unmet clinical need for mechanism-based therapy and to achieve this goal, precise definitions of FSGS subtypes are required. Genomics has emerged as one tool to successfully stratify patients with heterogeneous diseases like major depressive disorder, coronary artery disease and cancers such as breast cancer that have, like FSGS, been historically heavily reliant on pathology. We intend to apply these same genomic approaches to identify clinically meaningful FSGS subtypes to inform management.

column36: Exercise as a primer for excitatory stimulation study (EXPRESS): A combined exercise and transcranial direct current stimulation intervention for cognition
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a type of dementia that causes problems with memory, thinking, function and behaviour. Currently, a group of drugs called cholinesterase inhibitors are used to improve memory, but have important side-effects such as loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea and sometimes slow heart rates and fainting. Moreover, benefits from these drugs are modest and AD patients eventually worsen even with continued use. There remains a critical need for treatments focused on early stages of the disease, when quality of life is still potentially excellent. While transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; neurostimulation with a non-painful current to the brain) has been shown to improve memory in some people with mild AD with minimal side-effects, recent evidence suggests that tDCS works better when brain circuits are active. As exercise increases brain activity using mechanisms that may support tDCS response, it may be an effective primer given before tDCS. This study will assess whether combining exercise and tDCS can help improve memory in mild AD, and whether this combination improves memory better than exercise alone, tDCS alone, or neither (exercise education only with non-active tDCS). Patients will be randomly assigned to receive either 1) combined exercise and tDCS, 2) exercise and non-active tDCS, 3) exercise education only and tDCS, or 4) exercise education only with non-active tDCS for two weeks. Memory, mood and behaviour, as well as measures of brain activity, and brain and blood vessel health will be assessed before, during, and after treatment. This study may identify a new, non-invasive therapy that preserves memory in early stages of AD, therefore having major health implications.

column36: Scaling up eVisits (Home Video Visits) for ambulatory care in Kingston Health Sciences Center, A mixed-methods implementation study
column37: The Canadian healthcare system faces many challenges. Some of these are rising healthcare costs, barriers to accessing outpatient care, and long wait times. Providing health care consultation between two hospitals by video conferencing is called telemedicine. This needs special equipment and needs the patient to travel to the local hospital. It addresses some of the above challenges but does not go far enough. Nowadays, personal devices like smartphones, tablets and computers with high-speed internet are widely available. They are capable of high-quality video conferencing. The use of these devices to provide telemedicine through a secure connection is called Home Video Visit (eVisit). This allows the patient to stay at home and receive medical consultation. eVisits are ideal for routine outpatient health care. We did a 6 month pilot of the eVisits in the Stroke Clinic in 2018. The experience from the pilot was very positive. Patients find them convenient, easy to use, comfortable, and economical. They are very helpful for people with driving issues or physical disabilities. They are also quicker to do and can be more efficient for physicians and hospitals. Following the successful pilot, eVisits are routinely available in the stroke clinic and some other neurology clinics at Kingston. We plan to further expand this service to all 14 specialties (125 physicians) within the Department of Medicine at Kingston Health Sciences Center. We aim to convert 20% of out-patient visits to eVisits in the next 2 years. We will measure the patient and physician experience using surveys, semi structured interviews and focus groups. We will also measure the economic impact on the healthcare system, patient out of pocket costs and impact on hospital resources. With the experience gained, we will expand this to other departments in the hospital. The data and experience from this degree of expansion will help inform digital health policy in Ontario and Canada.

column36: Accelerating the Spread of Integrated Community-Based Primary Health Care in Ontario
column37: As health systems across the globe continue to engage in primary care transformation, spreading and scaling up effective models of Integrated Community-Based Primary Health Care (ICBPHC) remains a significant challenge. Addressing this challenge requires a shift in how we think about, and address, the questions of why, how, for whom and in what context, an innovation, such as a model of care, can be effective. Over the past six years, our team has taken a rigorous approach to addressing these questions and generating new evidence to support spread and scale up of ICBPHC. Our work identified key elements that enable implementation of high-performing models of ICBPHC and supports evidence from large-scale primary/integrated care transformation initiatives, which show that effective spread and scale up require greater attention to two critical elements: the interplay between innovations and the contexts into which they spread, and how to promote change readiness in individuals doing change work. Our current work builds on and extends prior findings in a 'pre-spread, comparative testing' of a model of ICBPHC, which advances access to team-based care for individuals with complex care needs. Comparative 'testing and revision' of the model has enabled us: i) to learn from variations in performance across sites and contexts, ii) to build capacity for reciprocal learning, and iii) to generate new knowledge about factors enabling successful adoption and potential spread. We are prepared to proceed to the next phase of our research: designing and testing a program to spread this model to new sites and identifying the supports required for successful spread of ICBPHC innovations. Since 2017, Ontario has invested $248.4 million to expand access to primary care across the province. This study will provide new evidence to capitalize on these investments and support effective primary care transformation across Ontario and other Canadian jurisdictions.

column36: IMPACT 2.0: Leveraging promising community-health-system partnerships to improve access to appropriate care for vulnerable populations
column37: Innovative Models Promoting Access-to-Care Transformation (IMPACT) was a five-year research program to improve access to community-based primary health care for vulnerable populations. Members of the research team worked with local healthcare providers, health policy makers and community members to develop programs specifically designed for the community. Two of the programs, a volunteer guide from the community who was trained to call patients to support them before their first appointment with their new family doctor and pop-up health events that were organized at locations in the community where anyone could receive services such as vaccinations, dental care, mental health services and physician care free-of-charge, were successful enough that groups in new regions have requested that the programs be spread to their area. Over the next year, the research team will build on tools developed for the original program to support partnerships between healthcare providers and health policy makers in the new regions that will adapt the two programs to their needs. Specifically, two guides, a Partnership Development Guide and Intervention Implementation Guide, will be updated based on literature, advice from experts and lessons learned from the original IMPACT program. Those who were involved in the original program will help tailor the programs to the needs of the communities in the new regions. We will also develop a plan to evaluate the success of the adapted programs. In addition to helping spread the programs to specific communities, the tools and plan that will be developed will help others create similar partnerships and design programs that will improve access to primary health care.

column37: EQIPactiv est un programme de prevention et de gestion integre en maladies chroniques qui modifie la prestation de services en premiere ligne par le biais de trois composantes : 1) la formation de l'equipe interdisciplinaire en GMF (infirmiere, nutritionniste, kinesiologue, etc); 2) une demarche structuree sur quelques visites (4 a 6) avec des membres de l'equipe interdisciplinaire en reponse aux besoins exprimes du patient; 3) la creation d'une communaute de pratique reunissant les equipes interdisciplinaires des Groupes de medecine de famille (GMF) d'une region ou sous-region. EQIPactiv s'appuie sur l'apprentissage des experiences anterieures ayant genere des resultats positifs. Apres avoir ete prouve efficace dans le cadre de projets innovants au Saguenay Lac-St-Jean, EQIPactiv est en voie d'implantation dans les groupes de medecine de famille (GMF) d'une autre region du Quebec soit le Bas St-Laurent. Les roles du facilitateur clinique incluent : la formation des professionnels, l'assistance au deploiement de la demarche et l'animation de la communaute de pratique. La formation que recevront les professionnels porte sur : l'approche centree sur le patient avec maladies chroniques multiples, le soutien a l'autogestion, la collaboration interprofessionnelle et l'approche motivationnelle. La presente demande vise a soutenir l'introduction de l'EQIPactiv au Bas St-Laurent par la poursuite de deux objectifs : 1) identifier les facteurs contextuels pouvant faciliter ou entraver l'implantation; et 2) developper et mettre en place des strategies pour reduire les barrieres potentielles a l'implantation. column36: National Pediatric Drug Resource
column37: Canada lacks a national approach to the establishment of medication guidelines for use in children, and lags significantly behind others countries like the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and New Zealand - all of whom have established and invested in online, national infrastructures to provide evidence-based drug information for children. National resources provide evidence-based, unbiased, up-to-date, transparent, peer-reviewed information including age- and weight-based dosing for children alongside potential formulation considerations (e.g., compounding) and links to formulation recipes. Previous work by an international group of formulary leaders identified an extremely comprehensive list of 116 items to be included in a paediatric drug monograph (drug information sheet). This exhaustive list highlights the need for a standard approach to evidence curation. Currently, this technology-based health innovation has been successfully implemented is the Netherlands, where a group of pharmacists, paediatricians, clinical pharmacologists, general practitioners and community pharmacists developed the Kinderformularium in 2006. The Kinderformularium is a well-established, freely available and publicly accessible online paediatric drug resource. It contains evidence-based drug specific information developed from a review of product labels, clinical findings, daily practice and cultural differences and curated by a pharmacist. It is also the only national resource that is transparent in the evidence used to develop the information, by including the full reference list for each listed drug. This operating grant will evaluate the feasibility of spreading and scaling an existing e-health innovation (Kinderformularium) to Canada in the form of a National Paediatric Drug Resource (NPDR) though the development of a Stakeholder Advisory Board and an in-person workshop.

column36: Adapting an effective health promotion intervention for scale-up: a focus on older adults in receipt of home and community care services
column37: Health promotion through physical activity can effectively enhance older adults' social connections, physical and mental health. Despite this, only 11% of Canadian older adults are active enough to enjoy health benefits. To positively affect the health of populations, physical activity programs that demonstrate effectiveness on a small scale must be scaled-up to reach diverse populations across a variety of settings. With BC Ministry of Health, we designed and implemented a community-, choice-based, 6-month health promoting intervention for older adults called Choose to Move (CTM). We called upon the science of implementation as a guide to effectively implement CTM at larger scale-- in 26 communities across BC. CTM improved physical activity, mobility, social connectedness and decreased loneliness in community-dwelling older adults (n=458). As a next step, we aim to scale-up CTM to target older adults at greater risk - those in receipt of home and community care services. Home and community care services are a lifeline for older adults in BC (and across Canada), many of whom are unable to perform activities of daily living. Thus, we propose to 'reimagine' home and community care services to integrate strategies that support the physical and social well-being of older adults who wish to stay at home. To do so we will convene established and new partners to adapt CTM and co-create an action plan to reach older adults in receipt of home and community care services. Our objectives for this operating grant are threefold. First, we will adapt the CTM intervention and implementation strategies to 'fit' the home and community care context. Second, we will adapt the current CTM implementation/scale-up action and evaluation plans for the home and community care context. Third, we will describe the CTM adaptation process. What we learn in BC can be applied to scale-up of health promoting interventions across Canada and the world.

column36: Examining Patient-Healthcare Practitioner Relationships with Deaf Patients who use Healthcare Sign Language Interpreters
column37: Deaf British Columbians whose first language is American Sign Language often interact with their primary healthcare practitioner through the services of a healthcare sign language interpreter. The introduction of an interpreter adds complexity to the navigation of patient-healthcare practitioner relationships. Yet, little research exists to guide both healthcare practitioners and healthcare sign language interpreters through this complexity. Without a foundation of evidence, each of these practitioners may be unintentionally hindering effective relationship development with deaf patients. My research aims to add a foundation of evidence to support the development of best practices for healthcare practitioners and healthcare sign language interpreters. Specifically, it will examine how the behaviours of each of these practitioners supports or hinders the development of high-quality relationships between an healthcare practitioner and their deaf patients. Each stakeholder perspective (deaf patient, healthcare practitioner and healthcare interpreter) will be compared and contrasted, to build a complex understanding of the behaviours each group perceives to be supportive or hindering. This research has the potential to significantly add to our understanding of the effective care of deaf patients who use healthcare interpreters in primary care appointments. As a Registered Sign Language Interpreter and healthcare sign language interpreter, I am in a unique position to conduct and disseminate this research in meaningful and culturally safe ways in both American Sign Language and English. Through this and future research, I hope to make healthcare in Canada more inclusive for deaf patients and minority language users.

column36: The role of stress and the microbiome on glucocorticoid synthesis in the intestine
column37: The purpose of this research is to examine the mechanisms by which stress and the intestinal microbiome regulate the synthesis of glucocorticoids (e.g. cortisol, corticosterone) in the intestine. Glucocorticoids are primarily synthesized in the adrenal glands, however they can also be synthesized locally in various tissues including the intestines. In the intestines, glucocorticoids play a role in regulating the immune system and inflammation. Stress and the microbiome have both been implicated as factors that regulate the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis, which regulates the adrenal glands, however it is not known how these factors might influence local synthesis of glucocorticoids. To better understand how glucocorticoids are synthesized in the gut, this project will utilize a mouse model to test how psychosocial stress and the gut microbiome influence the expression of enzymes used in glucocorticoid synthesis in the intestine. I am also interested in whether oral probiotics have a protective role against deregulation of synthesis in stressed mice. I expect that stress will decrease the amount of "healthy" bacteria, leading to increased glucocorticoid enzymes and therefore increased synthesis, and stressed mice given probiotics will not exhibit the same increase in enzymes as mice not given the probiotic. The goal of the study is to understand the mechanisms by which stress influences physiology and to identify bacteria involved in glucocorticoid synthesis, ultimately leading to improved knowledge of the brain-gut axis and the functions of the microbiome in the context of gut health. This can lead to better treatments for stress related disorders and intestinal diseases such as Crohn's disease.

column36: Deliberative Public Engagement informing Canadian Cancer Care Priority Setting-A Focus on Facilitation
column37: Expenditure in cancer care has risen faster in recent years compared to other areas of health care. This is due to expensive drugs, new therapies, improved access in rural areas and increased cases in the population. There is a concern that the economic burden of cancer spending is not proportional to patient benefits such as increased survival rates or quality of life. Policy makers are turning to public input to guide and distribute scarce resources. Deliberative public engagement is well suited for this ethical and fiscal challenge and has been used successfully as a democratic approach to other health care challenges. In a process of facilitated small and large group discussions, stakeholders share views and values and work collaboratively towards decision making. Despite the obvious importance of facilitation of such events, little is known about the role, techniques and strategies facilitators use to support participants. The public are often asked to make decisions in contentious areas where lived experiences collide. In charged environments, conversations can be unstructured without a skilled facilitator. This proposal seeks to further understand the role, techniques and strategies used by facilitators within the context of deliberative public engagement informing cancer control priority setting processes across Canada. Using a mixed method approach, a specific focus on facilitation will ensure the quality of group exchange is consistent with the principles of deliberation. It will ensure policy recommendations for decision makers are meaningful and representative of participants and ultimately contribute to a sustainable model of deliberation that can continue to guide priorities in Canadian cancer care.

column36: Carcinogenic Transcriptional Aberrations caused by Epigenomic Misregulation
column37: While the genetic information encoded in our DNA is stable, there is a layer of chemical modifications acting on the DNA's organization that can control transcription, or how genetic information is expressed, called the epigenome. The epigenome can be compared to a series of dimmer switches acting on the genome, "turning up", or "increasing transcription" of certain genes, or "turning down", or "repressing transcription" of genes, through different chemical modifications performed by epigenetic regulators either on the DNA itself or on histones, which are DNA-organizational units that package the DNA into structures called chromatin. Epigenetic malfunctions are often seen in certain cancers, and notably in multiple childhood cancers like pediatric glioblastoma or chondroblastoma. For this reason, understanding the effects of epigenetic dysregulation, like how it affects transcription and triggers aberrant transcription events, is key to understanding how these cancers begin and how to improve the efficacy of the treatment of these cancers. However, very little is known about how epigenetic dysregulation affects transcription, and whatever is known was based on unreliable experimental models. This project aims to improve this situation by using a bioinformatics-based approach to identify aberrant transcription initiation events occurring across the genome and understand the mechanism driving these events using a series of datasets obtained from appropriate models that better reflect what occurs in these cancers.

column36: Optimized Bombesin Analogues for the Imaging and Treatment of Cancer
column37: Cancer imaging and therapy with radioactive drugs are powerful emerging methods to diagnose and treat cancer. These radiopharmaceuticals deliver radiation to cancer cells throughout the body by targeting traits that distinguish cancer cells from our healthy ones. Depending on the type of radiation, it either can destroy cancer cells or be detected by an instrument to form a precise image of the cancer in the body. One distinguishing marker in many cancer subtypes, such as prostate, breast, lung, ovarian, and colon cancers, is the abundance of gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR). Previous research has shown that bombesin (BBN) selectively binds to GRPR, and several radiopharmaceuticals based on BBN are being used clinically. However, current BBN analogues have relatively low tumour uptake, which results in poor image contrast, and they do not bind tightly enough to GRPR when carrying radiation for therapy. Our goal is to make and test new GRPR binding molecules based on BBN that bind more tightly to GRPR, thereby improving image quality and enabling use as a radiotherapeutic. I have already identified a key structural modification to include in this candidate drug that has shown to drastically improve its binding to GRPR. Furthermore, I will modify the linker, the part of the radiopharmaceutical that links the radioactivity to the targeting component, to improve tumour uptake and image contrast using established methods. These candidate drugs will be labelled with radioactivity and tested in cancer mouse models to gauge their potential as clinical imaging and therapy agents. This research will allow us to pre-clinically evaluate new potential radiopharmaceuticals that can provide earlier diagnoses and more effective therapy for multiple types of cancers.
