column36: Can aggressive Forms of Ductal Carcinoma In Situ Be Identified with Molecular Markers?
column37: Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer in women. 1 in 5 women diagnosed with breast cancer will have a preinvasive type of cancer called ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). We know that roughly 20-30% of DCIS will progress to become invasive cancers. They do this by crossing what is known as the basement membrane, a layer forming a protective barrier preventing cancers from spreading in the body. However, it is not currently known which DCIS will become invasive or why. We therefore treat all DCIS the same way, with surgery followed by radiation therapy to the chest to prevent recurrence and transformation into invasive cancer. Our hypothesis is that, by determining what causes DCIS to cross the basement membrane, we could determine which DCIS are more likely to become invasive cancers. Our objective is therefore to study DCIS samples from real patients in animal models and to examine what characterizes a DCIS with invasive potential, and how they differ from more indolent DCIS. Eventually, it is our hope that this would allow us to predict, from a patient's biopsy, whether the patient's DCIS requires aggressive treatment, or if it can rather be observed, thus preventing the patient from needing surgery and radiation therapy.

column36: Can Slow Breathing Reduce Hypertension in Women With Polycystic Ovary Syndrome?
column37: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) affects ~10% of premenopausal women in Canada. Most commonly associated with infertility, PCOS is diagnosed in women who meet two of the following criteria: high testosterone levels, irregular menstrual cycles, and polycystic ovaries. Women with this disorder may also be at risk for high blood pressure (BP). This is a concern given that even moderately high BP can predict poor cardiovascular outcomes including heart disease and stroke. Unfortunately, anti-hypertensive medications are not effective in all patients due to problems with compliance and drug resistance. As such, alternative treatments are needed to reduce BP in hypertensive individuals. Most notably, device-guided slow breathing has been recommended by the American Heart Association (AHA) as an alternative therapy to lower BP. Specifically, the AHA recommends the FDA-approved RESPeRATE device, which has been shown to decrease BP in men and postmenopausal women. However, no previous study has examined whether this intervention can decrease BP in women with PCOS. Therefore, this project will examine whether 8 weeks of device-guided slow breathing using the RESPeRATE device is effective in improving BP and other markers of cardiovascular health in women with PCOS. Participants will complete a 15-minute slow breathing session once per day. We hypothesize that after the 8 week intervention, participants will have lower resting BP and reduced breathing frequency. This study will provide preliminary evidence as to whether device-guided breathing can effectively reduce BP in women with PCOS.

column36: Frailty Assessment in Heart Failure: a Multi-Domain Approach
column37: Frailty is a geriatric syndrome of physiological decline, characterized by vulnerability to stressors. Frailty has been shown to be associated with greater risk of incident heart failure (HF) and hospitalizations and mortality at 1 year. Prevalence of frailty among HF patients ranges from 15% to 74% depending on frailty tool used. Current literature shows HF in older adults is associated with disproportionate loss of lean mass specifically among men and that severe fatigue presentation over 1 year is a predictor of increased mortality. However, it is also reported that worsening fatigue is associated with higher risk of HF hospital stay, but not mortality in this patient population. Knowledge gaps in the field of HF are as follows: i) there is no gold standard for evaluating frailty, ii) body composition profile via measurement of psoas muscle is not well established, and iii) causes of fatigue are not consistently identified. This study aims to determine the prevalence of frailty, develop a body composition profile, and investigate determinants of fatigue in HF patients. The multi-domain assessment will include evaluation of the following parameters: body composition, frailty, fatigue, disability, vision, polypharmacy, quality of life, hearing, social environment, sleep, cognition, nutrition, mood and clinical markers. Physical frailty evaluation will involve measurement of gait speed, chair rise, balance test, grip strength and a 6-minute walk test. A multi-domain assessment which accounts for changes in body composition and determinants of fatigue and attempts to compare frailty tools is needed to more accurately assess the risk of adverse outcomes in HF patients. The proposed study will enable development of a robust geriatric assessment for better HF management.

column36: Characterizing the functional relevance of neuronal PAS domain-containing protein 4 (NPAS4) to inflammatory and neurodegenerative processes in models of multiple sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the leading neurological disease in young adults in Canada, and it is second only to trauma as the most disabling. MS is a neurodegenerative disease where immune cells attacks myelin that protects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. This damages their ability to send information and results in nerve cell loss. MS causes disabling symptoms including vision loss, muscle weakness or paralysis, and problems with thinking and memory. Current MS drugs help people with relapsing MS where disease changes between attacks and recovery, but they do not treat progressive MS where disability worsens significantly. This drives the need to identify pathways that not only limit immune attack but also protect against neurodegeneration. Our laboratory found that levels of neuronal PAS domain-containing protein 4 (NPAS4), a key protein in nerve cell health and signaling, changes over time in a mouse model of MS. Importantly, deleting Npas4 protects against disability. Npas4 also directs other genes, many of which remain to be identified. Our project will study the role of Npas4 in disease development and nerve cell protection. Npas4 will be measured in MS mouse models at each disease stage - onset, progression, and recovery. We will identify immune cells and their products that regulate Npas4 and test how deleting or over producing Npas4 impacts nerve cell survival in a culture dish. We will also delete Npas4 during disease development in the MS mouse model to see when it is most important. Overall, this project will give valuable insight into the role of Npas4 as a regulator of neurodegeneration and disability. The goal is to use these findings to identify Npas4-mediated neuroprotective factors that may be targeted to limit disability for people with MS.

column36: Functional characterization of SMG1 variants associated with pancreatic cancer susceptibility

Overall, my work will help to validate SMG1 as a cancer predisposing gene, which could be implemented into screening programs to identify individuals at risk for pancreatic cancer.

column36: Understanding the role of progranulin in neurodevelopment and neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: There is a clear and pressing need to provide support for Canadians living with neurodevelopmental disorders like Fragile X Syndrome (FXS). FXS is the most common cause of heritable intellectual disability, affecting 1 in 4000 males and 1 in 6000 females in Canada. Beyond symptom management, there is currently no approved treatment for FXS. This is partly due to gaps in our understanding of the root causes of this syndrome. A clue was identified recently when it was demonstrated that mouse models of FXS have elevated levels of a protein called progranulin (GRN). Moreover, by reducing progranulin levels in these mice, some of the FXS symptoms were alleviated. To further investigate the link between high levels of progranulin and FXS, we in the Leavitt lab have developed mice that express an excess of progranulin (GRN+ mice). We are characterizing the behaviour of these mice to see if they exhibit the same FXS-like symptoms as mouse models of FXS. Indeed, both GRN+ mice and FXS-like mice show hyperactivity, reduced social dominance, and abnormal repetitive behaviour engagement. To explore how increased progranulin has come to affect the behaviour of GRN+ mice, we will perform an in-depth characterization of their brains. In comparing the brains of GRN+ mice to those from FXS-like mice we will also gain insights into the extent of progranulin's involvement in FXS. Should increased progranulin expression be involved in causing FXS symptoms, this research will facilitate the development of therapeutics that treat FXS by reducing the levels of progranulin in the brain. Independent of determining the extent of progranulin's role in FXS, this research is expected to improve the current understanding of how this enigmatic gene shapes the mammalian brain during development.

As such, genetic mutations in palmitoylating enzymes are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, including schizophrenia, autism, and intellectual disability. column36: Incidence and healthcare utilization patterns of undiagnosed subrachnoid hemorrhage: a population-based study
column37: Strokes remain a leading cause of death in Canada, with a reported incidence of 400-500 new cases per 100000 person-years. Non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhages (SAH) due to ruptured intracranial aneurysms represent 5-10% of all strokes. SAH remains a devastating condition as the case fatality is still around 50%. This study design will allow the inclusion of patients who passed away, and as the data is collected prospectively, will avoid recall bias. Furthermore, our data would provide an estimate of the incidence of cases that a healthcare professional could have potentially altered by early confirmation of the diagnosis ((LP/CT/history taking) and treatment.

column36: Defining the Interplay Between Fetal Sex, Inflammation, and Immune Cell Function in Pregnancy
column37: The placenta is an organ necessary for healthy pregnancy. Important in forming the placenta are specialized trophoblast cells created by the fetus. These cells perform many functions to maintain pregnancy health. Importantly, trophoblasts regulate the mother's uterine immune system throughout pregnancy. Because the fetus is a genetic mix of mother and father, there should be a maternal immune response against the fetus. However, through unknown mechanisms trophoblasts are able to modulate this response and keep the fetus healthy. Without this trophoblast regulation, maternal immune responses against the fetus may result in pregnancy miscarriage and pregnancy conditions such as preterm birth and preeclampsia. Biological differences may be present in pregnancy as a result of the baby's sex, creating different risks for specific pregnancy conditions. For example, male fetuses exposed to infection and/or inflammation have a higher risk for spontaneous miscarriage or pre-term delivery. Because trophoblasts regulate the mother's uterine immune system, male and female trophoblasts may respond differently to processes initiated by infection and/or inflammation. My research will use trophoblasts and uterine immune cells isolated from male/female placental (fetal) and decidual (maternal) tissue for analysis of genetic differences in male and female trophoblasts. As well, my research will test the uterine immune response to male/female trophoblasts infected by a common bacterial stimulus. My research aims to establish new insight into why pregnancies of male or female babies have greater risk for developing specific pregnancy disorders and set the groundwork for future experimental design aimed at deciphering how biological sex of the fetus influences pregnancy health and outcome.

column36: IgA opsonized viruses stimulate NETosis using a pathway distinct from that of IgG
column37: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells in the body, and the first innate immune cells to respond to sites of infection and inflammation. Neutrophils can perform a variety of effector functions but most recently characterized is the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) through the process of NETosis, a unique form of programmed cell death. NETs are extracellular chromatin structures that play a role in trapping and killing a variety of pathogens, such as bacteria, fungi and viruses. These extracellular structures become coated with anti-bacterial enzymes and have been shown to be beneficial in the clearance of infections, but may have detrimental effects during sterile inflammation, as often occurs in the context of autoimmune conditions. In diseases such as Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) NETs act as a source of auto-antigen and can worsen disease prognosis. Neutrophils express a variety of Fc receptors on their surface, which allow them to undergo several unique effector functions in response to antibodies, including NETosis. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype and interacts, via its Fc region, with the FcaRI receptor on the surface of neutrophils. IgA has been shown to increase NET release and phagocytosis in the context of bacterial infections. Additionally, our recent work suggests that various antibody isotypes, IgA or IgG, may induce NETosis through distinct mechanisms. Phagocytosis, another effector function of neutrophils, does not appear to be required in the context of IgA, but is required in the context of IgG-induced Fc-effector functions. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that IgA opsonized viruses stimulate NETosis using a pathway distinct from that of IgG.

column36: Cardiovascular Risk and Primary Prevention Eligibility of Patients with Premature Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in British Columbia
column37: Rates of cardiovascular (CV) events such as myocardial infarctions or stroke in young adults (younger than 55 years old) has not decreased over the last 20 years. column36: Sick day protocols for inherited metabolic diseases: current practice and evaluation design
column37: Children with certain rare metabolic diseases identified by newborn screening, particularly fatty acid oxidation disorders, are at risk of experiencing sudden and potentially life-threatening periods of illness. Appropriately responding to this risk can prevent death and severe side effects. There is uncertainty about the effectiveness of specific clinical approaches to managing 'sick days' among children with rare metabolic disease. We need to better understand the association between more or less aggressive approaches to sick day care and meaningful outcomes such as clinical symptoms, adherence to care, patient and family experiences, and use of health services. As a first step toward informing long-term management of these risks, we aim to characterize current practice, describe the care experiences of parents and providers, and develop a protocol for an evaluative study. This study will describe the content of sick day protocols for children with fatty acid oxidation disorders enrolled in an existing Canadian study across 13 participating metabolic clinics. Children, parents and providers at Canadian metabolic centres will be invited to complete a survey to highlight their experiences with sick day plans, their perspectives regarding implementation of sick day plans, and their perceptions about key outcomes. We will design a study protocol to evaluate sick day plans from the results of the clinical data analysis and surveys, and relying on the outcomes derived from the surveys. By identifying the most important questions, key outcomes, and study designs, this work will help to inform future research toward preventive management approaches that best meet children's clinical needs during intercurrent illness while also optimizing patient and family experiences.

column36: Therapy induced hypermutation to stimulate immune responses in recurrent cancer
column37: In the battle against cancer, massive amounts of time and resources have gone towards the development of chemotherapeutic agents that act to kill cancer cells, while leaving healthy cells relatively unaffected. Unfortunately, when these drugs are unable to fully eradicate all cancer populations, recurrence can occur which leads to prolonged treatment, increased costs, and further stress on the patient. Due to this risk, it is vital that initial treatment plans take into account the widely varying characteristics of each cancer and give the best chance for complete remission. One way this can be accomplished is through the process of "synthetic hypermutation", which is a gene-drug interaction that gives rise to an unexpected number of mutations in surviving cells. When hypermutation occurs naturally, it is often indicative of positive clinical outcomes due to the increased response of the host's immune system against the cancer cells. The elevated immune response is due to the presence of neoantigens, which are mutated proteins found in tumour cells but not in normal cells. Considering this, the Stirling Lab (BC Cancer Research Centre) hypothesizes that cells can be hypermutated in response to certain genotoxic chemotherapies, creating more of these neoantigens and thereby stimulating the host immune response. My research will involve screening a multitude of drugs and chemicals to determine which will result in the highest mutation rate and consistent generation of mutant proteins in these cells. Ideally, these results will allow clinicians to make informed decisions when deciding between chemotherapies and ultimately lead to improved treatment outcomes.

column36: Developing Recommendations for Tailoring Smoking Cessation Interventions for People with Spinal Cord Injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a life-changing condition impairing sensory, motor, and autonomic function. This function can be further impaired by secondary health conditions such as cardiovascular disease and respiratory problems. Smoking can increase the likelihood of developing these health conditions. The SCI populations smoking rates are double those of the general population. To date no theory-informed interventions have been developed to support smoking cessation among people with SCI. Therefore, this study aims to understand smoking cessation behaviours of people with SCI and develop recommendations to tailor interventions for people with SCI. This study will use the theory-informed Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) to systematically develop recommendations. The BCW outlines understanding the behaviour as the key first stage of intervention design, and recommends conducting interviews to comprehensively understand the theoretical factors influencing behaviour. Interviews will be recorded and transcribed verbatim. An inductive narrative analysis will provide a narrative of the lived experiences of people with SCI quitting smoking. In addition, transcripts will be deductively coded using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) to identify barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation. Using both analyses provides in-depth understanding of the theoretical factors influencing smoking cessation behaviours and provides a systematic method to use these factors to inform intervention design using the BCW and TDF. This study will be the first to make theory-based recommendations to develop and tailor smoking cessation interventions for people with SCI. This research will contribute to reducing health disparities between people with SCI and their able-bodied counterparts.

column36: The impact of different learning styles on the performance of physician assistants in Canada
column37: The physician assistant (PA) profession has been established in many countries, including Canada. Canada has four PA programs: three civilian programs and one military program. Each institute approaches its delivery of education differently. The University of Toronto approaches its program through a distant learning style, McMaster University through a problem-based learning style, the University of Manitoba through a didactic learning style and Canadian Forces through an extension of prior knowledge in combination with didactic learning style. Each program has a unique approach in educating and training their students where in the end, all students share the same competency and equivalence. It is important to assess the differences in transfer-of-learning that results from the varying PA educational platforms in Canada. The purpose of this study is to determine how the delivery of education and different teaching styles in Canada influence the performance of PAs in the first two of their practice. The significance of this study lies in its ability to inform PA educators, those involved in helping develop the PA profession, and those involved in developing PAs as clinicians about the influence that learning styles have on the novice PAs transfer-of-learning when transitioning from formal training into a clinical setting. Ultimately, this will help with the development of the PA profession in Canada.

column36: Peer Coaching for Practising Surgeons - Modernization of Continuous Professional Development in Surgery
column37: Deliberate practice and intensive structured curriculums are the cornerstones of surgical residency and training. Once training ends however, there is very little structured learning and feedback provided to practicing surgeons to improve their skills. Current methods rely on written literature, presentations at conferences and sporadic courses, which are poorly-geared towards the needs of adult learners. The aim of this project is to introduce peer coaching as a way to tackle this deficit in long-term professional development. It will also assess the need for different methods of continued professional development and the barriers to the implementation of peer coaching in surgery. The first part of the project will be a qualitative study, inviting surgeons from multiple disciplines to individual interviews. These interviews will focus on their attitudes towards existing methods of professional development, as well as the need and potential barriers for the implementation of a structured peer coaching program. Using the same topics and information obtained from the first part, the second part of the project is to develop a survey to gauge opinions of surgeons from all surgeons across North America. The survey will be created and electronically distributed through professional surgical associations, with the hope of reaching up to 15,000 surgeons. Ultimately, this is a first step in a complete paradigm shift in continuing professional development. By acquiring data on attitudes, perceived needs and barriers to peer coaching, we can establish the basis of structured program that can greatly improve the continuing education of surgeons across North America.

column36: Exploring Predictors of Quitting Smoking in an Exercise-based Smoking Cessation Program
column37: Smoking has long been associated with negative health outcomes, leading to a wealth of programs that aim to help people quit smoking. In contrast, physical activity is related to positive physical and mental health and there is some evidence that exercise-based smoking cessation programs can be effective at helping people quit smoking. One of the challenges of smoking cessation programs is the amount of participants who do not complete them. Previous research on smoking cessation has largely focused on individual factors affecting program drop outs, while physical activity literature on group programs has found factors such as leadership and group cohesion to also play a role. This research will investigate predictors of successfully quitting smoking in a nation-wide program, Walk or Run to Quit, that combines a smoking cessation program from the Canadian Cancer Society with a 10-week learn to run 5km program at the Running Room. Results from year 1 of the program show promising results for quitting smoking, with 90% of participants who completed the program reporting a reduction in smoking. Additionally, interviewed participants have reported that group support and their coaches played a large role in encouraging them to succeed. Using the combined data from three years of evaluation and over 700 participants, predictors of quitting smoking such as individual factors, group cohesion, and leadership will be investigated. Findings from this project include adding to research findings on multiple health behaviour programs that target both smoking and running, and could impact future program designs by identifying potentially modifiable individual- and group-level determinants of behaviour change.

column36: Achieving health equity for individuals living with HIV in Manitoba: Identifying potential cancer disparities using population-based data
column37: As Canadians diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) live longer due to effective antiretrovirals, there is an emerging focus on the control of chronic illnesses, such as cancer. Individuals living with HIV, in particular sexual minorities, those with low income, newcomers, indigenous Canadians, and injection drug users, may be more vulnerable to cancer disparities as these populations already have a greater risk of delayed cancer diagnoses, advanced stage cancer, and poor survival. Equity is a key priority for provincial, national, and international cancer and HIV organizations but, there is currently little research investigating potential cancer stage and survival inequities for Canadians living with HIV. In a cohort of Manitobans living with cancer I will: 1) investigate the association between HIV status and cancer stage at cancer diagnosis, and 2) investigate the association between HIV status and cancer-specific survival. This study will use population-based, linked, and routinely collected health and social data held at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy. HIV cases will be identified using a combination of laboratory, medication, physician visit, and hospitalization data and then linked to cancer cases identified using the Manitoba Cancer Registry. This will be the first Canadian study linking HIV laboratory tests, prescription data, and cancer registry data to investigate cancer outcomes for this potentially vulnerable population. Examining cancer outcomes for individuals with HIV is an important step to advance equity agendas and reduce barriers to achieving optimal health and wellbeing for Canadians with HIV. The methods from this study could be used as a framework for examining other chronic disease outcomes for individuals living with HIV.

column36: Etude de faisabilite du dosage de medicaments dans le lait maternel par chromatographie liquide couplee a la spectrometrie de masse (LC-MS/MS)
column37: De nombreuses femmes sont confrontees a la prise de medicaments durant l'allaitement. Or, peu d'informations sont disponibles sur le passage du medicament dans le lait maternel. Ainsi, les professionnels de la sante preferent deconseiller l'allaitement privant, malheureusement, le nouveau-ne de tous les avantages que procurent le lait maternel. Au CHU Sainte-Justine, le centre IMAGe recoit des appels de professionnels de la sante qui ont des questions concernant la compatibilite entre l'allaitement ou la grossesse et les medicaments. Les pharmaciennes de ce centre ont identifie 19 medicaments pour lesquels elles recevaient de nombreux appels et pour lesquels elles n'avaient pas d'information sur leur innocuite et devaient se fier aux donnees pharmacocinetiques et cliniques pour guider les professionnels de la sante. Ainsi, nous nous demandons s'il est possible de doser ces medicaments par chromatographie liquide couplee a la spectrometrie de masse (LC-MS/MS) a partir de lait maternel recolte directement de femmes allaitantes. Pour cela, nous allons effectuer une etude clinique de faisabilite de dosage des medicaments dans le lait maternel par LC-MS/MS. Cette etude consistera a recruter des femmes qui prennent ces medicaments et qui allaitent via le centre IMAGe et le CHU Sainte-Justine, a recolter des echantillons de leur lait et a analyser ces echantillons. Avant de commencer l'etude, il sera necessaire de valider la methode de dosage de medicament par differentes etudes de linearite, de limite de detection (LOD) et de quantification (LOQ), de precision, d'exactitude, de selectivite, d'effet de matrice, de carryover, de recouvrement et de stabilite.

column36: Identification of Lipophagy Cargo Receptors
column37: Heart disease is a leading cause of death worldwide. Atherosclerosis underlies many of the complications of cardiovascular disease and arises as lipid-rich plaque builds up within the artery wall. Atherosclerosis occurs over a lifetime and progressively narrows the blood vessels and consequently impedes blood flow in the heart. As the plaque progresses, it becomes unstable and prone to rupture. Plaque rupture can cause a stroke or a heart attack and may result in death. Statins, a class of cholesterol-lowering drugs, are commonly prescribed to patients suffering from atherosclerosis. While statins have the capacity to halt plaque progression, they have little effect on reducing plaque size. As such, the discovery of drugs able to promote lipid removal from cells in the plaque would allow for not only a stop in the progression but reversal of this disease. Cells in our body have a natural ability to degrade cellular components through a recycling system called autophagy. Autophagy allows for the disassembly of large cellular components, such as organelles containing lipids and proteins, into smaller components like fatty acids and amino acids to be reused by the cells. Lipid droplets are small circular organelles used by our cells to store excess lipids and cholesterol which are abundant within the plaque. However, the process of how lipid droplets are recycled through autophagy is poorly understood. Our study will determine which components are involved during autophagy of lipids droplets. Our data will present exciting new opportunities to exploit these components for the development of new therapies that can lead to plaque regression, eliminating the need for invasive surgical procedures to treat heart disease.

column36: The effect of alternative visceral osteopathic treatment on pain and quality of life in patients with non-specific low back pain: A study protocol
column37: Les lombalgies chroniques sont une cause d'incapacite majeure du point de vue psychologique et social et de pertes economiques considerables. Bon nombre de ces lombalgies ne presentent aucunes anomalies pathologiques reconnues leur conferent un caractere non-specifiques. A l'heure actuelle, il n'existe aucun traitement curatif pour ces patients qui utilisent beaucoup de ressources du systeme de sante. Les manipulations osteopathiques viscerales representent une avenue complementaire interessante, mais aucune etude n'a demontre leur efficacite. Ce projet permettra d'evaluer l'efficacite des manipulations osteopathiques viscerales aupres de personnes atteintes de lombalgies chroniques non-specifiques sur les aspects qualitatifs et quantitatifs percu de leur douleur et leur anxiete. l'objectif secondaire sera d'evaluer l'effet de l'empathie du therapeute, telle que percue par les patients, sur ces meme variables. Un essai randomise controle multicentrique sera utilise pour mener a terme ce projet au sein de cliniques osteopathiques de la region de Montreal. Deux groupes de patients atteints de lombalgies chroniques non-specifiques seront recrutes: 1) groupe temoin avec traitements visceraux non-osteopathiques ; 2) groupe avec manipulations osteopathiques viscerales. La selection des participants remplira des questionnaires sur la qualite de vie, la caracterisation de la douleur, l'anxiete et leur perception de l'empathie de leur osteopathe assigne. Les caracteristiques seront analysees au moyen de statistiques descriptives, puis par des analyses de covariances. Cette etude permettra, dans un contexte de professionnalisation de l'osteopathie au Quebec, de soutenir l'integration des osteopathes dans la prise en charge multidisciplinaire des lombalgies chroniques.

column36: Elucidate the relationship between maltreatment, attachment, and substance use in youth
column37: Maltreatment leads to poor health outcomes in adolescence and adulthood (Stoltenborgh et al., 2015). Most research has been done on the impact of child maltreatment and less is understood about adolescent maltreatment. This is important because adolescence is a period that can be accompanied by many challenges due to rapid changes in development (Spear, 2013), and can lead youth to risky behaviours such as substance use (Tonmyr et al., 2010). Maltreatment also impacts the caregiver-child attachment relationship which often leads to maladaptive attachment bonds. The mechanism for these relationships isn't well understood in adolescence. Therefore, this study aims to expand on current understandings of the impact of psychological and physical maltreatment on substance use by focusing on adolescent development, through insecure parent-youth attachment. There are 4 hypotheses: 1) Psychological and physical maltreatment will be related to higher rates of substance use. 2) Insecure attachment will be related to higher rates of substance use. 3) Exposure to both forms of maltreatment will increase risk for substance use. 4) Insecure attachment will affect the relationship between maltreatment and substance use. Data from youth self-reports will be collected from an on-going study based on the Connect program. Connect is an attachment-based parenting intervention program that promotes adolescent health through the parent-child relationship (Moretti et al., 2009). The proposed study will help elucidate the relationship between maltreatment, attachment, and substance use in youth and therefore help inform interventions aimed at reducing risk behaviours by providing support for factors that buffer youth against substance use.

column36: Neural underpinnings of pain and cognition
column37: Pain poses the largest health-related burden on society, costing Canadians billions of dollars each year. Chronic pain patients report forgetfulness and impairments in problem-solving and mental flexibility. The cognitive burden of pain could be due to pain acting as its own task with an inherent value, or by simply distracting from a task. If the former is true, the impact of pain can determine its value. If a task has a high reward, pain will not hinder task performance. In a standard cognitive branching task, two competing tasks are presented, one with a high monetary reward for each correct response, and one with a low monetary reward. The introduction of a third task adversely affects the performance in the low reward task. Our lab has shown that moderate pain reduces task performance on the low reward task but not the high reward task, and that pain acts as its own task with an inherent value. The frontopolar cortex (FPC) is a brain region active during the cognitive branching task that selects the concurrent task of highest reward to complete. The FPC also demonstrates abnormal structure and function in chronic pain, which co-localizes pain and cognitive branching. I plan to elucidate the neural mechanisms behind pain-cognition interactions to identify how pain imposes a burden on cognitive resources. I will recruit subjects to complete the branching task during functional magnetic resonance imaging under a 1) Baseline condition 2) Heat pain condition and 3) salience-matched non-painful electric condition. I hypothesize that 1) pain will adversely affect low reward task performance, 2) the FPC will show greater activity during the painful condition than the baseline and electric conditions, and 3) that activity in the FPC will be related to pain intensity.

column36: Epigenetic regulation of neurogenesis in response to early experience
column37: The brain consists of billions of neurons that are crucial for lifelong function. The birth and maturation of new neurons is referred to as neurogenesis. Generally, neurogenesis is highly active in early stages of development of an organism. An impressive feature of the brain is that it is plastic, defined as the ability of neurons to change both in number and function in response to the environment. This phenomenon is referred to as neuroplasticity and is highly sensitive to experience during early development. Previous research has indicated that sensorimotor experience (sensation and movement) can act as an environment capable of regulating the rate or neurogenesis. It has been proposed that the mechanism by which this occurs involves the alteration of fundamental genetic instructions which regulate neuronal populations - epigenetic modification of DNA. Specifically, it is thought that this modification has the ability to increase mobilization of a type of "jumping gene" known as retrotransposons (RTs), which translocate from one location in the genome to another. The proposed project aims to study whether a specific type of epigenetic alteration, DNA methylation, plays a role in regulating neurogenic levels in response to sensorimotor experience during early development in the zebrafish model. This will be done by first determining if there is an observed difference in DNA methylation at known locations of RTs in the genome in response to restrained movement (sensorimotor deprivation), then testing whether the number of RTs increases as a result of this restraint. Lastly, we will investigate the effects of elevated levels of DNA methylation on neurogenesis. This work will provide novel insight towards the epigenetic regulation of neuroplasticity in vertebrates.

column37: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a neurological disorder that is associated with a wide range of symptoms, including diminished cognitive function, emotional dysregulation, and fatigue. Unfortunately, there is no cure for MS to date. Nonetheless, recent evidence shows that exercise may have positive effects on symptoms and disease progression. The problem is that there is a lack of research investigating the effects of exercise in a detrimental, sub-population of MS- Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)- using neuroimaging and clinical measures together. The goal of the proposed research is to examine symptom presentations and microstructural features of neuronal connections in a group of patients with PPMS before and after a weekly exercise intervention. This study could have significant implications for the management of MS symptoms and overall improved quality of life. Given that pharmaceutical treatments to delay progressive neurodegeneration in PPMS have been unsuccessful, the proposed study has the potential to change the first-line intervention for individuals with PPMS. If there is evidence that exercise leads to changes in brain structure, paralleled by symptom changes, the knowledge translation to physicians and other health care professionals could ensure that patients with PPMS are encouraged to implement exercise as part of rehabilitation (thereby providing a no-cost, evidence-based intervention). The ultimate goal is to help individuals with MS to build a better quality of life, for instance with reduced fatigue and depression, and increased cognitive function by protecting the brain from the degenerative effects of MS through exercise. This research has the ability to change lives of individuals with MS across Canada and globally.

column36: Reduction of Pftk1 as a novel therapeutic target for Parkinson's Disease
column37: A New Target for Parkinson's Disease Over 100,000 Canadians suffer from Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disease that causes a number of clinical presentations including rigidity and tremors. There are currently medications to help with symptom management, but a cure has yet to be found. One of the hallmarks of PD are aggregates called Lewy bodies, which are found in the brain, and we've recently learned that Lewy bodies are mostly made up of a protein called a-Synuclein (a-Syn). The levels of a-Syn are directly related to disease severity; with higher levels we see increased severity in both humans and model organisms. Based on these findings, lowering a-Syn levels will likely enable us to treat PD patients much better by stopping or slowing disease progression. It is difficult to suppress a-Syn directly, so we're focusing on a protein that controls a-Syn levels, PFTAIRE protein kinase 1 (Pftk1), which can be targeted with traditional pharmaceuticals. When Pftk1 is inhibited a-Syn levels are reduced. A recently produced mouse model, completely lacking the gene to produce Pftk1, shows no sign of abnormalities which may indicate that chronic loss of Pftk1 would be safe for humans. Our first goal is to study these mice to confirm that chronic loss is safe and effective at lowering a-Syn levels. Our second goal is to determine whether partial loss of Pftk1 is sufficient to improve PD presentation by using a PD mouse model that contains half of the genes that produce Pftk1. This partial loss will be a better representation of what a pharmaceutical inhibition would look like. If these results are promising our next step will be to identify and test pharmaceutical Pftk1 inhibitors, with the ultimate goal of finding a medication for PD patients.

column36: Evaluation of Electrocochleography for the Diagnosis of Hidden Hearing Loss
column37: Hidden hearing loss, as the name implies, is a type of hearing loss undetectable by current conventional audiometry. Some individuals present with seemingly normal hearing despite reporting symptoms such as a phantom ringing in the ears (i.e. tinnitus) or difficulty understanding speech in noise. Consequently, clinicians will deem these individuals as healthy, leaving the debilitating symptoms untreated and ignored. I am proposing a project to investigate the efficacy of electrocochleography (ECochG), an electrophysiological measure for cochlear activity, as an objective diagnostic measure for hidden hearing loss. The proposed mechanism underlying this condition is poor neural activity between the hearing receptors (i.e. inner hair cells) and auditory neurons. My project will use ECochG to record the electrical signals from activated hair cells in response to auditory stimuli (i.e. cochlear microphonic; CM), which has yet to be investigated in the case of hidden hearing loss. I will collect and compare electrophysiological data from musicians with high noise exposure and non-musicians with low noise exposure to assess if ECochG will reliably differ between groups. My hypothesis is that the CM will be enlarged and prolonged in the high noise exposure group compared to the low exposure group.

column37: While access to HIV-related healthcare - including HIV medications - is critical to prevent virologic failure and death, trans women living with HIV (WLWH) experience differences in their access to HIV-related and other forms of healthcare. Classism, racism, and HIV, trans, sex work, and substance use stigma may all negatively contribute to the experiences of trans WLWH in accessing care. Recognizing the complicated factors that create barriers for WLWH in accessing healthcare, we developed a Women-centred HIV Care (WCHC) Model using data from the Canadian HIV Women's Sexual and Reproductive Health Cohort Study (CHIWOS). Although CHIWOS included trans women and nonbinary and two-spirit participants, the WCHC Model requires further consideration to address the needs of trans WLWH and make healthcare better for them. Therefore, we aim to conduct focus groups (FGs) with 48 trans WLWH in British Columbia and Ontario to explore how the WCHC model can be adapted to address the needs and barriers they experience. FGs will be recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using thematic analysis. The themes will be used to inform the development of a Trans WCHC Model and make recommendations for toolkits to prepare healthcare providers, community service workers, and trans WLWH themselves to use this model of care. The results from this study will be shared with all relevant stakeholders, including trans WLWH, healthcare providers, policy makers, and researchers through the use of community-based research strategies and networks that will support our knowledge translation activities. Our study has the potential to positively impact the health and wellbeing of trans WLWH by adapting and defining the WCHC Model using feedback from trans WLWH themselves. By working together in a group of diverse genders including trans women, we may collectively design a Trans WCHC Model that can be used to facilitate integrated, comprehensive, competent, and affirming care for trans WLWH.

column37: In the Canadian health care system, just under 60% of medical learners report experiencing mistreatment, including physical abuse, verbal abuse, humiliation, gender discrimination, and racism. Despite what is known about health professional mistreatment, little research exists on how this environment of mistreatment may affect patients who occupy the same clinical spaces. To investigate this link, the proposed study will explore the experience of patient mistreatment in the Canadian health care system, the environmental factors that may facilitate this mistreatment, and the alignment of these factors with the factors that engender health professional mistreatment. These questions will be investigated through reviewing the academic literature to determine the factors contributing to both health professional and patient mistreatment. This will be followed by interviews with patients with lived experience of mistreatment, and with relevant health system leaders including Directors of Patient Safety and Patient Complaints and lawyers who have dealt with cases of medical negligence; these interviews will serve to refine what was found in the review of the literature. Finally, past patient complaints will be reviewed to assess the utility of the suspected factors in the identification of contexts in which mistreatment is most likely to occur. If utility is demonstrated, these factors could be used to predict settings with high risk for mistreatment, providing the opportunity for preventative action.

column36: Getting to Zero: Catalyzing Community-based Research capacity in sexual and reproductive health among men living with HIV in rural Uganda
column37: Millions of men and women living with HIV around the world want to have children and an estimated half have HIV-uninfected sexual partners. For the majority, achieving pregnancy involves condomless sex, presenting risks of HIV transmission to uninfected partners and infants. A range of available safer conception strategies can support individuals and couples to meet reproductive goals with minimal HIV risk. These strategies include sustained use of antiretroviral therapy with viral suppression by the partner living with HIV and/or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) by the HIV-uninfected partner, which can eliminate HIV transmission risk during condomless sex. While increasing attention has focused on improving access to safer conception care for women, much less is known about the needs of men. In 2018, we launched a pilot safer conception clinical program in a rural district of Uganda and recruited men living with HIV who reported wanting to have a child in the next year with an HIV-serodifferent pregnancy partner. Our preliminary findings revealed a strong demand, need, and retention in safer conception care. After sharing preliminary findings, community and government leaders in Uganda emphasized three critical next steps: (1) support and enhance engagement of people living with HIV in the research, consistent with the GIPA and MIPA principles; (2) assess 18-month outcomes of men who enrolled in the safer conception program; and (3) pursue future applications in the area of HIV and STBBI research, grounded in community-based research principles. Thus, the overall goal of this proposal is to foster a collaboration between Canadian and Ugandan research and community stakeholders to catalyze community-based research capacity in male-inclusive safer conception research in rural Uganda. With a commitment to reciprocal learning, we will leverage Canadian expertise and experience in community-based research to inform safer conception research and clinical care in Uganda.

column36: An Exploratory Qualitative Study of Migration, Sexual Health, and HIV/STBBI in Manitoba
column37: Racialized migrant communities (including newcomers, immigrants, refugees, and people without resident status from Black/African/Caribbean, Latin American, East and Southeast Asian communities) remain one of the most commonly reported categories among new human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and sexually transmitted and blood-borne infection (STBBI) cases in Manitoba. Yet, very limited community-based research (CBR) on sexual health, HIV/STBBI, and health care access is available for this population. Little is known also about how migration experiences shape HIV/STBBI risks for racialized migrant communities in Manitoba. A focus on the relationship between migration and sexual health is critical in order to reduce the impact of HIV/STBBI on these communities. Besides an enormous gap in knowledge in this area, there are also limited CBR capacity building opportunities available for racialized migrant communities in Manitoba. To address these issues, we will: 1) conduct CBR on racialized migrants' sexual health, HIV/STBBI risks, and their access to HIV and health services in Manitoba, 2) build capacity among community scholars, and catalyze CBR collaborations in migrants' sexual health in Manitoba. To accomplish the first goal, we will use in-depth interviews to gather data on migration experiences, HIV/STBBI sexual risk practices, and the use of HIV/STBBI services and health care among a sample of racialized migrants (n = 85) who will be recruited in Winnipeg, Brandon, Steinbach, and Thompson. In addition, key informant interviews (n=10) will be also conducted with advocates and providers in health and social services. To accomplish the second goal we will initiate CBR collaborations in migrant sexual health, and build capacity among community members/scholars in migrant health. This CBR will inform culturally relevant sexual health promotion, service delivery, HIV/STBBI interventions, and build capacity among racialized migrant community members in Manitoba.

column36: Evaluating the Risk of Cardiovascular Disease in Women with Endometriosis
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD), a class of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels in the body, remains the leading cause of premature death for women in Canada. Unfortunately, women with CVD are underdiagnosed and experience worse prognosis compared to men. This is likely due to the fact that much of many of the diagnostic and treatment strategies are based on research performed preferentially in men. There is an urgent need to reduce CVD in women, which requires recognition of CVD risk factors specific to women. In 2016, the Nurses' Health Study II became the first study to suggest an association between endometriosis, a female specific disease, and CVD. Endometriosis is a chronic condition of pelvic pain affecting up to 10% of the female population. Although it is known as a gynecologic condition, it is becoming clear that endometriosis leads to chronic inflammation and oxidative stress in multiple organ systems. Furthermore, women with endometriosis are more likely to receive surgical and medical management which lead to early menopause - an independent risk factor for CVD. We hypothesize that women with endometriosis are at an increased risk of developing CVD. To investigate these hypothesis, we will use a population-based approach to determine the association between a diagnosis of endometriosis and subsequent risk of CVD. We plan to conduct a retrospective cohort study using data sets from the Institute of Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) in Ontario. Secondly, we will use a biometric approach, including blood tests and other investigations, to assess CVD risk in women with a surgical diagnosis of endometriosis and age matched controls. It is important to investigate if patients with endometriosis are at increased risk of CVD. Identifying such patients can allow for implementation of effective prevention strategies to reduce the risk of CVD diagnosis as well as the negative impact of this condition.

column36: CRISPR/Cas9 Mediated Knockout of PGC1a to Propose the Zebrafish as a Biomedical Model for Treating Metabolic Diseases
column37: All biological life is dependent on energy acquisition and expenditure in order to survive, reproduce and thrive. Most of our energy is derived from the mitochondria, an organelle responsible for converting nutrients into energy with the use of oxygen and accessory proteins. The energy produced by the mitochondria is controlled by 'Peroxisome-Proliferator Activated Receptor Gamma Coactivator 1-Alpha' (PGC1-a), a protein that has been recently established as a mitochondrial 'Master Regulator'. Increased levels of PGC1-a in mammals have shown increased mitochondrial density and activity during periods of energetic stress, but recent studies suggest that this role is partially restricted in multiple fish species. Many of these studies were primarily correlative as no previous studies have examined the gain or loss of function of PGC1-a. A large number of metabolic diseases appear to be associated with PGC1-a malfunction such as asthma, diabetes, heart failure, stroke, obesity, neurodegeneration and multiple forms of cancer and arthritis. Current biomedical models are limited in studying these associations due to their incompatibly with vigorous drug testing methods. One fish species, the zebrafish, has been shown to act as a powerful biomedical model due to transparency within early life, high fecundity and an extensively annotated genome. These features have identified the zebrafish as a powerful developmental model for both neurological and metabolic diseases with the added benefit of being suited for robust drug design. In an effort to utilize the strengths of the zebrafish to its maximum potential, I plan to knockout PGC1-a and other key metabolic regulators within the zebrafish to establish a novel biomedical model for the study treatment of metabolic diseases.

column36: Acceptability of bariatric surgery in young women with endometrial cancer: a qualitative study
column37: Obesity is a significant cause of uterine cancer. Uterine cancer used to be most prevalent in women over 60; however, as obesity has been rising across the population, an increasing rate of uterine cancer has been observed in women under 40. The standard treatment for uterine cancer is hysterectomy, or removal of the uterus. This radical treatment is devastating for women of reproductive age who still want to have children. In an effort to preserve fertility, hormone treatment with progestin has been explored as an alternative to hysterectomy. However, progestin does not address obesity, the true cause of uterine cancer. In addition, it causes weight gain and is associated with high chance of cancer recurrence. Weight loss is a promising new treatment for uterine cancer that preserves fertility while addressing the root cause of uterine cancer - obesity -thus preventing recurrence. For women with obesity and uterine cancer, significant weight loss is required on a timeline that can only be achieved realistically through weight-loss surgery, such as bariatric (stomach reduction) surgery. Weight loss through bariatric surgery has the potential to treat obesity, preserve fertility, and more effectively treat uterine cancer. The purpose of this study is to explore the perceptions and attitudes towards bariatric surgery as a fertility-preserving treatment for uterine cancer in younger women (40 years old and younger) who have both uterine cancer and obesity. The results of this study will inform clinical practice through more productive oncologist-patient conversations, and the development and design of a larger pilot study of bariatric surgery as a treatment for uterine cancer.

column36: Genetic Testing in Females with Ovarian Cancer: Impact of Reflexive Tumour Genetic Testing on Clinical Care
column37: Ovarian cancer is the deadliest of all gynecologic cancers and the 5th leading cause of cancer death in women. Ovarian cancers can be caused by genetic changes (mutations). Most mutations occur in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which are inherited from a parent (germline) or develop in a tumour (somatic). Genetic testing is very important in ovarian cancer because patients with germline or somatic BRCA mutations can have targeted treatment with drugs called PARP inhibitors. In Ontario, all ovarian cancer patients have reflexive BRCA tumour genetic testing (RTGT). This means that BRCA genetic testing is completed automatically on all ovarian tumours as part of ovarian cancer surgery. RTGT gives ovarian cancer patients genetic information quickly so their doctors can decide the best cancer treatment. A second germline genetic test (blood test) is still needed to tell patients if there is a hereditary cancer risk in their family. RTGT can improve cancer care but its effects on patient psychological response and use of germline genetic testing are unknown. This study will examine the quality of patient care associated with RTGT in a group of ovarian cancer patients. Researchers will measure the patient psychological impact of RTGT and examine the effect of RTGT on use of germline genetic testing. To measure the patient impact, ovarian cancer patients who received RTGT results will be asked to fill in surveys about their experience. To look at changes in the use of germline genetic testing, researchers will compare the rate of referral and patient uptake of germline genetic testing in the year before and after the start of RTGT. The results of this study will be used to develop RTGT processes at hospitals around the world to make sure ovarian cancer patients and their family members get the information and support they need. This will reduce gaps in the care of ovarian cancer patients, help to find families with a hereditary cancer risk, and prevent ovarian cancer.

column36: Uterine preservation versus hysterectomy for pelvic organ prolapse surgery: A mixed methods prospective cohort study exploring health outcomes and patient beliefs
column37: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a medical condition in females where pelvic organs, such as the uterus, bladder or bowel, fall out of normal position and press into the vagina. POP will affect up to half of Canadian women in their lifetime, usually in relation to older age, higher body weight, and birthing children. Affected women often experience urine leakage, physical discomfort, embarrassment, and decreased quality of life. Surgery to correct POP is common, and approaches can be broadly divided into those that keep the uterus intact and those that remove the uterus from the patient's body. At present, we do not have enough high quality scientific evidence on which approach can best fix POP and restore quality of life, nor on the reasons women prefer to keep or remove their uterus during surgery. Our study will follow over 200 patients at the Pelvic Floor Clinic in Calgary, Alberta from their initial visit to 8 weeks after surgery to evaluate health outcomes and compare decision-making experiences between women who choose to keep versus remove their uterus during POP surgery. Our diverse team of doctors, researchers, and patient partners will collect study data using medical charts, questionnaires, and one-on-one interviews. Data on health outcomes will be statistically analyzed, and data on patient experiences will be analyzed by identifying themes across responses. As the Canadian baby boom generation ages, the number of women with POP is expected to increase and research on POP is needed to guide decision-making. Our study will address this need, and will provide women contemplating surgery for POP and their care providers with trusted information on the risks and benefits of each surgical approach. Our findings will also help care providers understand how patients think about, and decide upon, whether to keep or remove their uterus, which may improve how they counsel and educate patients about surgical decisions.

column36: Exogenous estrogen exposure and cardiovascular risk in women

column36: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Sexual Concerns During the Menopausal Transition: A Low Risk Treatment Protocol

Hormone therapies, including estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone treatments, are currently the most commonly prescribed treatments for sexual concerns during menopause. However, these treatments are associated with potential health risks and side effects for some women. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is a psychological treatment that has been proposed as a low-risk alternative treatment for menopausal symptoms. Thus far, CBT has been shown to be effective for some menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, depression, anxiety, and poor sleep. However, sexual concerns have either not been targeted at all during these interventions or, when directly targeted, only modest improvements have been observed. This study will evaluate the efficacy of a new four-session CBT protocol designed specifically to target commonly reported sexual concerns among women during the menopausal transition. The impact of CBT on sexual concerns, related distress, and associated difficulties (e.g., anxiety, depression, body image, relationship satisfaction) will be evaluated. This study will be the first to investigate the efficacy of a low-risk alternative treatment program specifically tailored to address the unique sexual concerns that women report during menopause.

column36: Preventing unnecessary surgeries for endometriosis with the Central Sensitization Inventory
column37: Endometriosis affects 1 in 10 reproductive-aged women, or approximately 1 million women in Canada. It is defined as tissue from inside the uterus (womb), being able to grow as implants outside of the uterus, in other parts of the body. Endometriosis is a common cause of infertility and pelvic pain, including painful periods, painful sexual activity, and chronic pelvic pain. Treatment consists of hormonal medications or surgical removal of the implants. Historically, the endometriosis implants themselves were thought to be the primary cause of pain. However, recent research as shown that in many patients with endometriosis, the primary cause of pain consists of changes in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) -- known as central sensitization -- rather than the endometriosis implants themselves. In these patients with central sensitization, repeated surgery to try to remove endometriosis implants is unlikely to be helpful. The problem is that research methodologies to measure central sensitization are not practicable for the clinical setting. There is a need for a clinical tool that can easily identify central sensitization, thereby helping clinicians and patients to determine when surgery is not likely to be helpful. Recently, the Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI) -- a patient-reported questionnaire -- has been shown to be validly identify patients with central sensitization. In this proposal, we will use the CSI in an ongoing prospective registry for endometriosis. We will determine whether the CSI can predict whether endometriosis surgery is effective or not. A cut-off for the CSI score will be identified, which can be used by clinicians and patients in their shared decision making about whether to proceed with surgery. The goal will be to reduce unnecessary repeat surgeries for endometriosis in women. This will be achieved by promoting the CSI in the national clinical practice guidelines for endometriosis and for pelvic pain.

column37: La vulvodynie (douleur/inconfort vulvaire) est une problematique presente chez 8 a 16% de la population feminine et affecte donc une proportion importante de femmes au Canada. La vestibulodynie provoquee, caracterisee par une douleur a l'entree du vagin lors d'un toucher et/ou une penetration est la forme la plus frequente de vulvodynie. Elle limite la qualite de vie et les relations sexuelles de ces femmes. La vestibulodynie provoquee est souvent traitee par des applications de creme de lidocaine avec des resultats mitiges. Recemment, plusieurs evidences en recherche indiquent que des mecanismes au sein du systeme nerveux central contribueraient a cette condition. La methode de reeducation sensitive (MRSD) est une approche innovante et prometteuse pour le traitement des douleurs qui vise a influencer les mecanismes de perception sensitive du systeme nerveux central. Plus de quatre-vingt professionnels au Canada sont formes a la MRSD, qui a fait ses preuves avec d'autres clienteles presentant de la douleur. Tout recemment la MSRD a ete utilisee avec succes chez des cas de vulvodynies traites dans une clinique en Suisse. Cette methode recommande de diminuer le contact cutane avec la zone douloureuse et d'appliquer progressivement quotidiennement des stimulations confortables. La presente etude controlee et randomisee vise a comparer les effets de la MRSD a ceux de la lidocaine pour la vestibulodynie. Cinquante-deux participantes seront assignees aleatoirement a l'un des deux traitements pour une duree de 12 semaines pour en valider l'efficacite. Les evaluations, avant et apres l'intervention, documenteront les effets sur la douleur, la fonction sexuelle, la perception de changement, les variables psychologiques et la sensibilite vulvaire. Si les resultats sont concluants, les professionnels de la sante auront un nouvel outil pour ameliorer la vestibulodynie provoquee et ainsi ameliorer la qualite de vie de nombreuses canadiennes.

column36: Women Living with HIV: Severity and Treatment of Menopausal Symptoms
column37: People living with HIV across the world are aging. In 2030, it is estimated that ~70% of individuals with HIV will be over 50 years. In conjunction with this evolving landscape of HIV, the UNAIDS has called for a "new worldwide focus on persons living with HIV aged 50 or older." For women living with HIV (WLWH), one of the most important life events nearing this age is that of menopause, a time accompanied by changes in physiology that affect quality of life and aging processes. Preliminary research suggests that WLWH experience menopause differently than HIV-negative peers and some studies suggest symptoms are heightened and undertreated in WLWH compared to the general population. Key knowledge gaps exist in understanding menopausal symptoms in WLWH including their evolution, biologic basis and management. All of these gaps serve as barriers to provision of optimal patient-centred care for WLWH. To further understand the menopausal experience in HIV, we will conduct a series of studies using 2 large cohorts of Canadian WLWH throughout stages of menopause. We will assess menopausal symptoms and follow their progression longitudinally. We will then assess hormonal changes throughout menopause, comparing important sex hormone levels (such as estrogen) during the menopausal transition compared to controls, and relate these hormones to symptom experience. Finally, we will evaluate the largest population of menopause hormone therapy used in WLWH in order to elicit characteristics of and barriers to use, thereby adding to the limited collective experience of hormonal therapy use in HIV. It is imperative moving forward that health providers adopt a tailored approach to address the complexities of reproductive health in HIV care. Further elucidating differences in the menopause experience in HIV from its progression and hormonal basis to treatment implications is a crucial step toward adopting a holistic approach to one of life's most important transitions.

column36: Reducing delay in treatment of psychosis through rapid access: Awareness and implementation of the 72-hour recommendation for early intervention services (EIS) across Canada
column37: Background: Delay in treatment of a first episode psychosis leads to poorer clinical, functional, and quality of life outcomes. Shortening the duration of untreated psychosis reduces disruption of life activities, such as education and employment, and makes treatment in an early intervention service more effective. Available evidence recommends rapid access through offering the youth experiencing a first episode psychosis an assessment within 72 hours. Objective: To assess the level of implementation and awareness among mental health providers, program managers, and service users and their families of the 72-hour recommendation in early intervention programs across Canada. To identify the barriers and facilitators to achieving the 72-hour recommendation. To capture the experiences of youth and their families of rapid access in early intervention services. Method: Mental health providers and program managers in the Canadian Consortium for Early Intervention in Psychosis will complete a questionnaire assessing their awareness of recommendations and their program's current practice. We will conduct semi-structured interviews with these stakeholders, which include questions addressing awareness of recommendations, site-specific guidelines for contact, and barriers and facilitators to achieving the 72-hour recommendation. We will conduct semi-structured interviews with youth service users and their families to assess their awareness of the 72-hour recommendation and their experience with rapid access in early intervention services. Analyses: We will use frequency analyses to describe the prevalence of awareness of the 72-hour recommendation. We will code the mental health provider and program manager interviews to identify common barriers and facilitators to achieving the 72-hour recommendation. We will code the youth and family interviews using categories derived from the research aims, the interview questions, and those that emerge while reviewing the interviews.

column36: Cardiac Outcomes of Menopausal Women Prescribed Concurrent Hormonal and Statin Combination Regimens in British Columbia
column37: Heart disease continues to be the leading cause of premature death for women in Canada. Historically, much of what is known about the treatment and pathophysiology of the disease has been tested on men and then transferred to women. We know there are differences between men and women in the development, presentation and response to treatment for heart disease. Despite this, most heart disease research is not sex specific. A commonly used drug therapy to prevent heart disease is the cholesterol lowering drugs known as statins. Although found to be effective in preventing both first and consecutive heart attacks in men, these drugs have found to be significantly less effective in prevention of heart attacks in women. Also, many women who are diagnosed with heart disease are near the age or past menopause. Many women of this age group are prescribed hormone therapy to treat symptoms related to menopause. The interaction between hormonal therapy and statins is just beginning to be understood. One recent study found that the combination and of hormone therapy and statin drugs resulted in greater prevention of heart attacks in women than statin therapy alone. However, more research needs to be done to better understand why this may be happening as well as if combinations of different types of hormone therapy and statin drugs may show greater benefit than others. We will use a population-based data set to determine whether we can confirm the benefit of combined therapy and, we will search for specific hormone and statin combinations for superior benefit (e.g. simvastatin with estrogen alone)? This research has the potential to significantly impact the outcomes of heart disease in women as well as contribute to what is known about sex specificity of heart disease.

column36: CSPG targeting for lesion regeneration in multiple sclerosis.
column37: Primary phases of multiple sclerosis (MS) are quite well controlled by anti-inflammatory drugs. However, these early stages are invariably followed with disease longevity by an uncontrolled progressive form of the disease mostly due to the lack of pro-regeneration therapies. Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) are one family of molecules known to exert inhibition of axonal regeneration in preclinical models of brain trauma. Recently, Dr Yong's group described that CSPGS are potent inhibitors of remyelination in mouse MS models, and that aging mice showed an increased deposition of CSPGs in their lesions. Concurrently, Dr Huard's group discovered a new natural ligand for CSPGs, expressed in MS lesions, A proliferation inducing ligand (APRIL). Drs Yong and Huard have thus combined their expertise in this project to test whether CSPG inhibition by APRIL may help induce regeneration in multiple sclerosis lesions. If so, this will have a considerable impact on regenerative biology in general and MS in particular.

column36: Improving suicide assessment and intervention with children: A participatory action research project informed by children's experiences
column37: Children's suicide risk has dramatically increased over the past 40 years. According to Statistics Canada, in 2017, suicide represented the 7th leading cause of death in children between the ages of five and nine, and is the primary cause of death in children between the ages of 10 and 14. While suicide in children remains a persistent issue, this age group has received considerably less research attention than their adolescent and adult counterparts. In addition, few studies have examined the experiences of children regarding the care they received for suicide prevention. Since child patients are the receivers of care, they are in a unique position to comment on the effectiveness of suicide prevention care. They represent an untapped source of valuable knowledge to improve suicide prevention and mental health care. Furthermore, inquiring the insight of children will produce valuable information regarding their clinical needs, goals, and preferences to improve suicide prevention. The overall objective of this study is to gain a better understanding of the experiences of children who have received suicide prevention care and improve the care offered to children. We seek to: (1) Increase our understanding of the care received by children at risk for suicide; (2) Identify children's needs, goals and preferences in relation to suicide prevention care, from their own perspectives; (3) Inform the adaptation of a suicide assessment and intervention tool to children's needs, goals and preferences; and (4) Assess the tool. In the first year of the project, we will study children's experiences related to suicide care and adapt the tool for use with children. In the second year, we will implement the tool in a specific setting and study its effect. Throughout this project, we will work in partnership with children, parents and healthcare workers to better align the project to their needs.

column36: Microglia Modulation to Protect the Developing Brain after Injury
column37: Cerebellar growth is highly vulnerable during the third trimester of pregnancy and could be affected by diverse insults leading to cerebellar growth failure and atrophy. Up to 19% of infants born extremely preterm will be affected by cerebellar injuries during their hospitalization. Despite a dramatic improvement of their survival and a major decrease in severe brain injury, almost 50% of infants born extremely preterm will suffer of long-term neurological impairments. We have developed the first animal model mimicking the most frequent type of cerebellar haemorrhage diagnosed in infant born extremely preterm. Combined with other stressors, such as inflammation, we can actually translate multiple cerebellar hits and further understand how these insults will alter cerebellar growth and impair neurological outcomes. The overall focus of this proposal is to examine the key role of microglial cell responses to perinatal insult, which may protect from damages induced to the cerebellum and means by which we may provide neuroprotection in the face of that damage. At first, we will examine the role of the brain innate immune system, microglial cells, in hindering the cerebellum's resilience to insult and prevent long-term cerebellar deficits. In second, we will describe changes in inflammatory expression pattern from microglial cells induced by perinatal cerebellar injury. In third, we will test the potential therapeutic benefit of FDA-approved drugs known to modulate brain inflammation. The focus has been so far on protecting cerebral injury in infants born prematurely; preventing cerebellar insults is as important and will result in significant neurodevelopmental improvement. Currently there is no therapeutic agent given routinely to prevent cerebellar injury affecting around 11 000 infants born extremely preterm in North America per year. Achievement of our goals will lead to expand the repertoire of potential therapies available to protect the developing brain.

column36: Epigenetic changes linking prenatal exposures to tobacco or cannabis smoke with asthma risk
column37: We know that the environment influences our health, and that babies are particularly sensitive to environmental exposures in the womb. When babies are exposed in the womb to pollutants like tobacco or cannabis smoke, health effects that can arise years or decades beyond the exposure itself. In 2018, over 11% of women of child-bearing age in Canada smoked cannabis, and nearly 20% of men. Both first- and second-hand tobacco smoke during pregnancy puts babies at risk of developing asthma, but much less is known about the risks of prenatal exposure to cannabis smoke. Research shows that many believe cannabis smoke to be less harmful than cigarette smoke to developing children. However, many of the inhaled products of combustion are similar between cannabis and tobacco smoke, and to date there is no evidence that cannabis smoke has different effects on developing offspring than tobacco smoke. This project uses epigenetics to try and understand what marks are being left behind in the cell by tobacco and cannabis smoke exposure. Epigenetics is a kind of cellular memory, that helps cells remember what kind of cells they are, but also what environments they have been exposed to. If we understand what cellular memories are left behind by specific environments, we may be able to reverse them, or even prevent them from being laid down in the first place, to ensure that every child in Canada gets the best possible start in life.
