column36: The mental health impact and needs of those living with food allergy: Perceptions from children, parents and care providers to inform a needs-based multi-faceted support programs and policy
column37: For the 4-8% of Canadian children with food allergy, and thus their families, deciding what and where to eat can be challenging and costly. These decisions can also lead to acute and severe reactions which require emergency medicine. But, because food allergic reactions are potentially fatal, these decisions can also be a potential life-or-death choice. To prevent a reaction, allergic individuals must exclude the foods to which they are allergic. This can be challenging, socially limiting and costly. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms recognizes food allergy as a legal disability. Yet, at present, there are no national policies to support those living with food allergy. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a project that uses data from various sources to increase our understanding of these families' needs. Our group includes Canadian leaders in pediatric allergy, knowledge translation, mixed methods and child psychology. Manitoba is the ideal place to do this work because it is a leader in pediatric allergy patient education and engagement, and is home to the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy, which houses health administation data for nearly all registered residents in the province. The major goal of our work is to describe how food allergy impacts families. We will learn about this impact by talking to families, medical professionals and school staff, and by analysing healthcare records. Our other major goal is to create a needs-focused pediatric food allergy support programme for low-income Manitoba children and their families. We will use this information to develop the types of programs they believe would be most helpful. Our long term vision is to use the findings to help inform a national strategy for families with food allergic children, to help inform decisions for maximising available resources, to provide optimal care for those with food allergy, and to assist with future planning.

column36: Collaborative work on the effect of environmental factors on glycemic control between Dutch and Canadian investigators
column37: My research has been focused on how specific brain regions regulate blood sugar level as well as other functions of the body such as appetite and body weight control. I described that the gene called "POMC" is present in some nerve cells in the brain and the level of POMC is reduced in several animal models of obesity and type 2 diabetes. I have then created a unique experimental mouse model with increased POMC level in the brain. Elevated POMC level almost completely corrected abnormally elevated blood sugar level in the mouse model of type 2 diabetes. These findings contributed to critical evidence leading to our current understanding of the importance of this brain system in the regulation of blood sugar level. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes. My current research project focuses on the role of environmental factors in the regulation of brain function. In laboratory experiments, mice are usually maintained in small cages with very limited environmental stimuli. Environmental enrichment (giving animals toys, exercise, companions, etc.) is the experimental protocol that facilitates the expression of species-specific behaviors and promotes psychological well-being and overall health of the animals. Interestingly, research has shown that environmental enrichment improves disease conditions such as type 2 diabetes in animal experiments. I have recently found that mice maintained under the enrichment condition showed enhanced response of brain cells to signals that convey body's energy status (for example, blood sugar level). These findings open up new avenues towards understanding how environmental factors affect the brain mechanism that controls blood sugar level, thereby establishing interventions that can prevent or reverse type 2 diabetes. To achieve this goal, I plan to form a joint research program on type 2 diabetes with Dutch researchers.

column36: The Netherlands-Canada Type 2 Diabetes Research Consortium: The Right Timing to Prevent and Treat Type 2 Diabetes.
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) stems from dysfunctions of multiple organs in the body caused by complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors. Among the environmental factors linked to the development of T2D, lack of sleep, light exposure during usual sleep time, and mistimed food intake have been shown to play a role in pre-clinical models and epidemiological studies. Experimental studies in animal and humans have suggested that better timing of lifestyle interventions during the day-night cycle or normalization of neurohormonal cycles and light exposure patterns improve cellular regulation of energy metabolism and inflammation in several tissues, most notably brown and white fat tissues. However, there is limited knowledge of the clinical relevance of these findings as no comprehensive in vivo studies have been made to integrate energy metabolism changes in all relevant organs/systems during carefully performed timed-interventions in animals and humans. We propose to establish a Netherlands-Canada Consortium on Type 2 Diabetes Research leveraging 7 outstanding research groups from the Netherlands that received prior funding as part of the Diabetes II Breakthrough Projects competition and 3 renowned research groups from Quebec City, Toronto and Sherbrooke in the field of Type 2 Diabetes research. Together our Netherlands-Canada Consortium will regroup expertise in animal and human day-night regulation of metabolism, brain, muscle, adipose tissue, liver and gut physiology, lipids and carbohydrate metabolism, hormonal regulation, nutritional and exercise interventions, type 2 diabetes clinical management, patient engagement experts and patient partners. We will bring together our expertise in training and mentoring of young scientists, clinicians, and patient-partners to create a first-class multi-institutional and international environment that will accelerate knowledge transfer from the proposed investigations into clinical practices in both countries.

column36: Metabolic impact of intermittent fasting in early type 2 diabetes
column37: Background: Intermittent fasting (IF) interventions in which no food is consumed over a period of time have been recently studied in individuals with obesity and shown to be beneficial. column36: The Netherlands-Canada Type 2 Diabetes Research Consortium: The Right Timing to Prevent and Treat Type 2 Diabetes (T2D).
column37: As an Early Career Researcher, I hope to offer a unique perspective and methodological approaches to investigating the mechanisms that contribute to the development of T2D and identifying strategies for its prevention and treatment. Indeed our human experimentations include a unique integration of medical imaging (PET and MRI) combined with tools to measure tissue and whole-body metabolism and body composition. Our expertise and resources offer integrated mechanistic views into in energy metabolism under real-life conditions directly relevant for human T2D pathophysiology. This methodological approach has led to our most significant contributions to T2D research, being the first to show cold-induced brown adipose tissue (BAT) thermogenesis in humans without and with T2D and demonstrating the ability of cold exposure to remove circulating glucose and insulin. It has also led to the development of several fruitful collaborations, which required the implementation of our methodologies in laboratories in the USA (University of Colorado), Europe (University of Granada) and Canada (McMaster University). Other Team Grants have allowed us to integrate our methodological approaches within a broader research question and collaboration. Pr. P. Schrauwen and his colleagues, regrouping 7 of the 19 awardees of the Diabetes II Breakthrough Projects competition in the Netherlands approached me and my colleagues Andre Carpentier (Sherbrooke), Gary Lewis (Toronto) and Jean-Pierre Despres (Quebec City) to join them and build on our expertise in T2D research to develop a consortium focusing on interventions to prevent and treat T2D based on day-night cycle changes in neuroendocrine/metabolic regulation. We aim to participate in the symposium to meet with our colleagues and develop common scientific goals and protocols, training and mentoring, knowledge translation and patient engagement activities, and administrative aspects.

column36: AD_GRIDS - altered grid cell computations in entorhinal cortex as a unique window into preclinical Alzheimer's disease?
column37: Spatial navigation is a fundamental cognitive ability that is often impaired in advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease (AD). One central component of the brain's navigational system is the grid cell network in entorhinal cortex, whose discovery was awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine/Physiology in 2014. Given that entorhinal cortex is particularly vulnerable to neurodegenerative changes in the earliest stages of AD, deficits in grid cell function could provide a unique functional window into early AD pathology. This project will break new ground by investigating (i) the mechanisms that compromise the integrity of the grid cell network in mouse models of AD pathology and in patients with Subjective Cognitive Decline, and (ii) whether a behavioral readout of grid cell functioning can improve the detection of preclinical disease stages. To address these important questions, the team will employ an interdisciplinary methodological approach that combines advanced behavioral and neuroscientific approaches with innovative data analysis techniques. Moreover, we will employ cutting-edge user-interface design principles to establish a standardised test of grid cell functioning that fulfills the requirements of clinical settings. Together, AD_GRIDS has the potential to significantly advance the detection of early disease stages, the monitoring of disease progression and the assessment of treatment efficacy.

column36: Microbiome Regulation of Beta-Cell Autoimmunity and Type 1 Diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is caused by autoimmune inflammation of the pancreatic islets and destruction of beta cells, the only cell type that makes insulin. The incidence of this disease in developed countries has been rising at the rate of 3-5% per year over the past several decades. Similar trends have been observed for other autoimmune and allergic diseases. Our genes do not change this quickly suggesting the influence of changing environmental factors. The complex bacterial community in our intestines (the "microbiome") is essential for metabolism for development and function of our immune system. This project seeks to understand how environmental changes have influenced the gut microbiome in infants with defined genetic risk for T1D. There is also emerging evidence from observational studies in children at risk for T1D that the gut microbiome lacks the diversity of age-matched children who lack these genetic risk factors. However, we don't understand the mechanisms that link microbial activity and the human responses to gut microbes to this rise in T1D. Our project will use set of complementary approaches to determine how exposures to harmless intestinal bacteria can protect from or potentiate T1D, and to understand how the bacteria that confer these effects on the disease. Our project is focused on defining what these gut microbes do inside the developing infant, and to identify the immune responses in children at risk for diabetes that influence the development of the disease. The outcomes of this work will support new strategies for clinical trials to prevent and treat new onset T1D, identify microbes and their products with activity during early life and diabetes development, and advance the design and testing of new therapeutics.

column36: Autonomic and autoregulatory function in brain during post-exercise as a marker of sport-related concussion
column37: Concussion is an injury that affects everyone differently as displayed by the wide range of symptoms one may experience (headaches, dizziness, pressure in head, etc.). There is currently a debate the role exercise has within concussion rehabilitation. Some studies have shown a reduction in symptoms, whereas others have found no change or an increase post-exercise. It is thought a reduced ability of the brain to regulate normal blood flow (autoregulation) or an impairment within the unconscious control of heart rate and blood pressure (autonomic functioning) may be attributable to the different responses following exercise. Therefore, this study is seeking to determine if the group of concussed individuals who have increased symptoms following exercise also have greater impairments within the functions previously mentioned. Near-infrared spectroscopy is an imagining technique that is capable of capturing neuronal activity within the brain and how this changes during various tasks. This technique will be used to capture both autoregulation and autonomic function and will be used while participants exercise on a treadmill. Before the treadmill test, individuals will fill out a symptom scale to capture the severity of their concussion. This will be filled out immediately following and roughly 1-hour, 12-hours, and 24-hours after the exercise test. The results in those with a concussion will be compared to a healthy population to see if deficits exist. As concussion affects each individual differently, treatment must be given based upon the symptoms an individual presents with. Thus, this study is seeking to understand the underlying factors as to why some symptoms are present following concussion and will help guide future rehabilitation strategies.

column36: Reframing Children's Pain Memories for Vaccination With a Parent-Led Intervention
column37: Painful procedures are routine and common during childhood: Healthy children receive multiple vaccinations. How children remember pain sets the stage for future pain experiences well into adulthood. Remembering more pain from a needle than was initially reported, is related to more pain and distress at future needle procedures. These distressing memories for pain can be changed, especially in early childhood. Interventions to reframe pain memory have been shown to reduce children's distressing memories for pain and distress at future needle procedures. However, these studies did not use parents, who have been argued to be most influential in children's pain memory development. The current study will be the first to use a parent-led memory reframing intervention for a routine vaccination in a community health setting aimed at increasing children's positive/more accurate memories of vaccine-related pain and their perceived ability to cope with pain (self-efficacy). Young children will rate their vaccine-related self-efficacy before a scheduled vaccination. Immediately after the vaccine, children will report pain and pain-related fear. Families will then be randomly assigned into two groups. Parents in the intervention group will be trained to elaborate when reminiscing with their children about positive aspects, and prevent children from exaggerating negative aspects of the vaccination, as well as praise children's ability to cope with pain. The control group will participate in a play-based task. Two weeks later, children will recall their vaccine-related pain/self-efficacy. Vaccinations are one of children's first and repeated healthcare encounters; therefore, intervening in early childhood could have lasting positive effects for children's health outcomes.

column36: Identifying gaps and barriers in the continuum of care for eating disorders
column37: Eating disorders have the highest mortality rate of all psychiatric disorders, resulting in a wide-range of physical, psychological and potentially life-threatening consequences. Prevalence estimates of anorexia and bulimia in North America are 0.9% and 1.5%, respectively, in women, and 0.3% and 0.5% in men. Due to the complex nature of eating disorders, treatment often requires a multidisciplinary team of healthcare professionals in the continuum of care, which refers to the continuity of medical care delivered to the patient over a period of time. However, challenges are often raised in terms of the integration of services and collaboration among treatment team members to establish a comprehensive treatment plan for each patient. Furthermore, this is exacerbated by the fact that eating disorders are often associated with comorbidities such as anxiety disorders, depression, and personality disorders; thus, making them difficult to treat. Consequently, gaps have been identified in the continuum of care for eating disorders, however these findings are sparse and require further exploration. This study will aim to provide a greater understanding of how the treatment team cares for patients with eating disorders. This study is clinically relevant because it will help identify ways in which healthcare professionals can work collaboratively in assessment, treatment planning, and evaluation to more effectively and safely care for their patients. These findings will help advance knowledge in the fields of medicine, health services research, and healthcare professions education, encourage practitioners to screen more thoroughly for eating disordered behaviors, and provide more clarity in terms of treating individuals struggling with an eating disorder.

column36: Examining the Role of the Endocannabinoid System in State-Dependent Food Approach Behaviour
column37: Stimuli, or cues, in the environment have varying degrees of perceived value. Change in an animal's internal state can colour perception and trigger stimuli reappraisal; stimuli value can alter depending on the physiological state. Food deprivation increases the motivational value of food-paired cues - i.e., food cues become more prominent when hungry. Once the need is satisfied, the internal state is regulated, and the altered cue perception reverts to normal. The amygdala (AMY) is a brain region sensitive to food-related cues and is involved in emotional and stress processing. The AMY manages the attribution of value to cues, and in conjunction with other brain regions seems to be at the centre of regulating cue-value changes. However, the mechanisms controlling shifts within the AMY during internal state change are not well understood. The endocannabinoid (eCB) system is a neuromodulatory system expressed throughout the AMY. There is a complex relationship between eCBs, neurophysiological stress regulation, and feeding control in the brain. eCBs are well placed to modulate the rapid intra-AMY modifications occurring in response to changed internal state and resulting in changed cue-value associations. We hypothesize that the need for an animal to correct its internal state will cause that animal to tolerate greater risks and that the eCB system in the AMY is involved in the mechanisms regulating this behavioural change. To investigate this, we will measure food approach tendency in an aversive context in male and female animals either sated or food deprived. AMY eCBs will be measured and their role evaluated. Elucidating the influence of the eCB system on state-dependent value shifts can further elevate it as a therapeutic target for eating and depressive disorders.

column36: Development of an Individualized Risk Prediction Tool to Improve Emergency Department Cardiac Care
column37: Chest pain is a leading reason for visits to Canadian emergency departments (ED), and can be a sign of potentially deadly heart attack. Thanks to new, highly-sensitive blood tests, ED doctors can quickly identify heart attacks with very high accuracy. Approximately 85% of patients with chest pain have not had heart attacks and are typically discharged home. ED physicians use risk scores to predict which of these discharged patients might be at risk for another cardiac event, such as heart attack or death, shortly after their original ED visit. While less than 5% of the patients who are sent home are truly at risk for such an event, current clinical practice guidelines recommend that patients classified as low-risk undergo additional testing regardless. These practice guidelines, combined with low risk tolerance for missed diagnoses by ED physicians and poor performance of existing risk-stratification tools, leads to additional testing for 40-70% of low-risk patients. Ultimately, this creates stress and worry for patients and families while causing an inefficient allocation of valuable resources in the Canadian healthcare system. To address this issue, this project will develop a new, more personalized risk score that can more accurately differentiate low-risk patients from high-risk patients. This tool will be developed using data that has already been collected from over 2200 Canadian chest pain patients. Collaborators in Calgary and Hamilton will provide input into the analytical plan of the project. If more patients are accurately classified as low-risk using the new risk score, less will undergo stressful, potentially dangerous, and non-beneficial testing, thus achieving our goal of improving quality of care while simultaneously conserving healthcare resources.

column36: Modeling Bone Architecture and Fracture Risk In Liver Transplant Patients using Image-Based Finite Element Analysis
column37: Despite improvements in the survival rates of liver transplant patients, there has been an increase of poor bone health in these patients. These individuals are often at risk for osteopenia (reduced bone mass) and fractures. These outcomes are believed to be a result of pre- and post-liver transplant complications, which include poor liver function and mediations given to patients to prevent organ rejection. The method currently used to assess bone health, dual x-ray absorptiometry, requires a large sample size and multiple measurements over larger time period to detect change. These criteria are difficulty to obtain in this population. A more sensitive tool, high-resolution peripheral quantitative peripheral computed tomography (HR-pQCT), may be part of the solution as it is able to detect changes in bone density and microstructure in a shorter period of time, where the most significant changes to bone occur in liver transplant patients. HR-pQCT scan data can be used to develop computerized three-dimensional models on which biomechanical tests can be conducted, a technique called finite element analysis. Results from these biomechanical tests have shown to provide valuable information in terms of fracture prediction. The objective of this study is to measure bone density and architecture in liver transplant patients pre- and post-transplant using HR-pQCT and measure fracture risk using finite element analysis. The significance of this proposed research is that an accurate measure will allow clinicians to ensure liver transplant patients are started on the appropriate therapy before a clinical endpoint (e.g. fractures), as well as future researchers to examine the effectiveness of different therapies targeted to treating bone disease in liver transplant patients.

column36: Characterization of bacterial replication and metabolism in an animal model of ulcerative colitis
column37: This project seeks to determine the bacterial activity in the intestines of animal models of ulcerative colitis. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that mainly affects the colon, or large intestine. Symptoms include diarrhea, fatigue, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Existing therapies remain limited and focus on reducing the onset or severity of symptoms in patients. This disease results from a combination of genetic factors of the patient and environmental factors, which leads to an excessive response of our immune system to naturally occurring bacteria in our gut, the gut microbiota. Considering the central role of the gut microbiota in the development of ulcerative colitis, we want to determine "who does what" in this disease and compare this bacterial activity to that of the gut microbiota in healthy individuals. Specifically, we will determine which bacteria are active, which are replicating and how quickly, and which nutrients they metabolize. These essential characteristics have not yet been determined in the context of ulcerative colitis, and limit our capacity for appropriate treatments. Understanding how bacteria in the digestive system modify their activity during this disease will allow the development of more effective treatments and generalizable approaches to other intestinal diseases.

column36: Novel targeted therapeutics against acute myeloid leukemia stem cells
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive form of blood cancer defined by the accumulation of abnormal blood cells in the blood and bone marrow. In our bodies, blood cells have a limited lifespan and need to be continuously replaced by hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). This process is disrupted in patients with AML and leads to hematopoietic failure. Therapy for AML exists, however the standard drugs have not changed in the last 30 years and involve intensive and aggressive treatments. Although most patients respond to therapy, many relapse with a more aggressive form of the disease. Currently, up to 70% of adults and 30% of children do not survive beyond 5 years post-diagnosis due to treatment failure or relapse. This is partially driven by the chemo-resistant nature of the leukemic stem cells (LSCs) that evade treatment. To improve safety and efficacy, novel therapies need to preferentially target LSCs while sparing HSCs, however this is difficult as both cell types share similar biological characteristics. Through the use of established HSC and LSC gene signatures, our lab identified 12 compounds that can preferentially target LSCs while sparing HSCs in vitro. Our next step is to establish the preclinical usefulness of these compounds to understand how the LSCs are impacted, their biological targets in the body and toxicities. This will help establish better treatment plans to reduce relapse rate and increase patient survival. Finally, we aim to investigate their mechanisms of action to yield insight on the biology of these stem cells. Since most of these compounds have been FDA approved and are being used to treat other diseases, they have a high potential to be used in the clinical, thus accelerating regulatory approval and reducing costs for drug discovery.

column36: The effects of bisphenols on limb development using a murine limb bud culture system
column37: Today, environmental exposure to toxic chemical substances is a problem of growing concern. Many everyday items are made out of plastic and the chemicals used to create them can be harmful to human health. Bisphenol A (better known as BPA) belongs to a family of chemicals called bisphenols, and is widely used in the production of plastics found in food packaging, plastic containers and reusable plastic water bottles. Considering its variety of uses, exposure to BPA and other bisphenols is quite common in everyday life. Unfortunately, BPA has been found to disrupt the human endocrine system and studies have discovered links between BPA and the presence of birth defects. Therefore, the ultimate goal of the proposed research is to determine if the chemicals that are emerging as replacements for BPA in consumer goods are safer than BPA. To achieve this, the first objective is to study the effects of BPA on the development of the murine limb in an ex vivo model. The second objective is to compare the observed effects of BPA with the effects of other bisphenols that act as replacements, like BPAF, BPF and BPS. To address these goals, pregnant mice that express fluorescent markers of collagen will be euthanized and will have their embryos removed and used to visualize the growth of their forelimbs. Using a microscope, images of the forelimbs will be examined to assess the development of cartilage and bone and thus, the effects of bisphenols. This research will contribute to the critical need for a better understanding of the adverse health effects of bisphenols, and lead towards the identification of responsible replacements.

column36: Prospective validation of stair stepping and shuttle walking tests to assess breathlessness in the clinical setting of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Physical activity-related breathlessness is the most common and burdensome symptom experienced by people living with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Even though relief of breathlessness is a primary goal in the clinical management of COPD, current breathlessness assessment tools are not appropriate to use in the evaluation of interventional efficacy because they do not standardize the level of exertion at which breathlessness is measured. Recent work from our laboratory at McGill has shown that the 3-min constant-rate stair stepping (3MST) and shuttle walking tests (3MWT) produce a standardized exercise stimulus that provokes a reproducible level of physical activity-related breathlessness that is responsive to both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic therapy in COPD. The current method used to determine the movement cadence (exercise intensity) needed to provoke a level of breathlessness that is responsive to therapy during the 3MST and 3MWT for a given patient, requires that each patient complete multiple 3MST and 3MWTs. This method is time consuming, burdensome for the patient, and therefore not practical for use in the clinical setting. To address this issue, we recently developed equations to predict the movement cadence needed to provoke moderate-to-severe levels of breathlessness during the 3MST and 3MST based on a patient's unique physical and clinical characteristics. The aim of this project is to prospectively validate these equations in a cohort of 100 adults with moderate-to-very severe COPD. Prospective validation of these equations will facilitate use of the 3MST and 3MWT for individualized assessment of interventional efficacy COPD and help to optimize the clinical care of symptomatic adults with COPD.

column36: Comparison of performance of two clinical scales to assess the post-thrombotic syndrome: Secondary analysis of a multicenter RCT of pharmacomechanical catheter-directed thrombolysis for deep-vein thrombosis
column37: Finding the scoring system that best captures the doctor's evaluation and the individual's experience of the long term complications of blood clots In Canada, up to 90,000 people per year are affected by blood clots. Blood clots are treated using blood-thinning medications called anticoagulants. In certain cases, doctors may use a more intensive "clot busting treatment" involving a procedure to deliver clot dissolving medication near the clot and actively remove the clot. Despite treatment, 20-50% of people with blood clots face long term complications, notably post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS). PTS consists of pain, redness and swelling that occur 6 months or later after the initial blood clot. Two measures, the Villalta scale and the Venous Clinical Severity Score (VCSS) can diagnose and asses the severity of PTS. They capture two separate lists of problems seen in PTS reflecting the doctor's evaluation and the individual's experience. My project will look at 692 study participants at 56 U.S hospitals from the previously published ATTRACT trial, which examined whether the "clot busting treatment" was better at preventing PTS compared to anticoagulants alone. Throughout the ATTRACT trial, the Villalta scale and the VCSS questionnaires were used to detect PTS and follow its changes during the study. Concurrently, the participants completed questionnaires about the impact of PTS on their quality of life (QoL). My research aim is to determine the relationship of the more objective scores of the Villalta scare and VCSS, to the subjective experience depicted through the QoL questionnaires. I will thereby determine which measure best captures PTS and PTS severity over time, which will greatly help researchers and doctors in this field as well as individuals affected by PTS.

column36: Arresten: a potential biomarker and therapy for cancer
column37: The leading cause of cancer related deaths is due to metastasis of cancer, which is the spreading of cancer from a primary site to secondary sites. Additionally, detection of many types of cancer is difficult in early stages, and the cancer is usually not detected until it has metastasized. An essential component of metastasis is angiogenesis, which is the formation of new blood vessels, because forming new blood vessels allows for cancerous cells to spread to secondary sites in the body. Angiogenesis is influenced by many factors which either activate or inhibit the process. One factor that inhibits the process of angiogenesis is arresten. The level of arresten is activated by the protein p53. However, in many cancers, the gene encoding p53 is mutated which can limit the level or change the function of p53. As a result, the level of arresten changes and is limited, thereby limiting inhibition of angiogenesis. This study proposes investigating arresten protein levels in blood and urine samples from mice and humans, with and without cancer, to determine if arresten levels correlate with tumour prognosis and patient survival. If arresten levels do correlate with tumour prognosis and patient survival, then arresten has the potential to be used as a biomarker for cancer detection. Furthermore, this study proposes experiments to mutate the gene encoding arresten, in human cells, so that p53 can no longer affect arresten levels. These cells will be used for eventual injection into mice to create human tumours in mice to further characterize the effect of p53-dependent arresten on angiogenesis. If we can further characterize this effect, this research can be useful when determining if arresten could be used in cancer therapy.

column36: Multisensory Integration of Social and Non-Social Information in Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorders at Different Periods of Development
column37: Atypical sensory processing is a key characteristic of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD; APA, 2013). One specific sensory process, which allows individuals to experience the world as a coherent whole, involves the ability to efficiently integrate stimuli from multiple sensory modalities, or multisensory integration (MSI). Research suggests that altered MSI may partially underlie sensory-related behaviours in ASD (Iarocci & McDonald, 2006; Zhou et al., 2018). Prior research, using social stimuli, has provided evidence that individuals with ASD have impaired MSI; however, there is a lack of research investigating the impairment to non-social stimuli (Stevenson et al., 2014; Bao et al., 2017). This study will assess both social and non-social MSI in individuals with, and without, ASD at different periods of development. It is hypothesized that individuals with ASD will have less efficient MSI abilities for both types of information during childhood, but that this difference will decrease with age. Given that sensory processing is essential for higher-level cognitive, communicative, and social functioning in ASD, knowledge regarding their ability to process sensory information is necessary, for them to benefit maximally from interventions.

column37: Genomique et apprentissage profond Les progres recents en genomique et dans les domaines connexes exigent une grande puissance de calcul et des algorithmes intelligents afin d'analyser les donnees massives generees. L'apprentissage profond, un domaine en pleine explosion, s'avere un outil prometteur pour realiser ce type de taches. Le but de ce projet est de developper et d'appliquer des methodes d'apprentissage profond a des donnees biomedicales (donnees genetiques, environnementales et cliniques) dans une perspective de medecine personnalisee, c'est-a-dire pour determiner la predisposition des individus a des maladies complexes, maladies determinees par l'interaction de facteurs environnementaux et genetiques, telles que les maladies cardiovasculaires. Dans un premier temps, nous testerons des architectures d'apprentissage profond precedemment developpees pour la prediction de phenotypes medicaux a partir de donnees genetiques et cliniques, en tenant compte de la diversite ethnique presente au sein des populations humaines. Nous developperons egalement des strategies d'integration pouvant s'appliquer a de grands ensembles de donnees heterogenes afin de permettre l'utilisation efficace des donnees multi-omiques en science biomedicale. Ce projet devrait avoir un impact important dans le domaine de l'apprentissage profond, puisqu'il qu'il vise a developper des algorithmes capables de gerer les donnees massives, mais aussi dans le domaine medical par l'amelioration de la prediction de risque de maladies complexes qui sont actuellement responsables d'un nombre eleve de cas de morbidite et de mortalite.

column36: Does the absence of dystrophin during somitogenesis dysregulate myogenic progenitor cell divisions and differentiation in the mdx mouse
column37: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is a fatal muscle degenerative disease that afflicts 1 in 3500 male children. DMD is caused by a loss-in-function mutation to the protein Dystrophin which normally maintains muscle fibre structure and regulates the division kinetics of muscle stem cells (MuSCs). The result of Dystrophin deficiency is progressive weakening and breakdown of muscle that is thought to manifest at ~3-5 years of age. However, we recently demonstrated that Dystrophin is expressed in adult MuSCs and that Dystrophin deficient 2-week-old mice have an unusually low proportion of asymmetric cell divisions that precede the major regeneration and inflammatory phase thought to trigger DMD. Considering our findings, we hypothesize that dystrophin deficiency in embryogenesis is a major contributor to the disease manifestation. I propose a comparative study between mdx (a model for DMD) and wild type C57BL/10ScSn mouse embryos to elucidate the role of Dystrophin in muscle development and define the homeostatic dysregulation in myogenic progenitor MRF expression. I hypothesize that dystrophic embryos will express abnormal MRF expression, delayed cell migration, and decreased abilities to differentiate. Moreover, I will profile dystrophin deficient myogenic progenitor cells to understand the underlying mechanisms of aberrant muscle development that will highlight novel therapeutic intervention. In conclusion, my project will provide insight into the manifestation of DMD in utero that was not previously investigated and change the landscape of DMD research.

column36: Nurses and Doulas Working Together Towards Optimal Birth Outcomes: Exploring the Nurses' Perspectives
column37: Continuous support during labour and birth by a trained labour companion, or a doula, has been shown to have many benefits for mothers and their newborns. These include shorter labours, less need for medications to speed up labour, as well as increasing likelihood of vaginal delivery. Mothers who have a doula are also more likely to view their birth experience positively. Nurses and doulas provide support to mothers during labour at the hospital, however nurses have other duties and specific shifts. Doulas are typically hired during a mother's pregnancy. They are continuously present throughout the mother's labour and birth, only taking short toilet breaks. The doula's responsibility is to provide emotional, physical and informational support to the labouring mother and her family. Doulas and nurses work together to ensure that the mother feels safe. However, conflict can occur between nurses and doulas, even though they have common goals and mostly positive views of each other. When conflict occurs, mothers tend to lose trust in the hospital staff and may view their birth experience negatively. Though not yet evaluated, several suggestions have been made on how to decrease conflict, including increasing understanding of the doula role and increasing nurses' contact with doulas. Research on nurses and doulas views each other exists, but there is still little detail about how nurses form these attitudes and how some nurses work well with doulas and others have a greater challenge. This research project will explore nurses' perspectives on working with doulas, by hearing from nurses who are recognized for their ability to work well with doulas. This new information may help to create more specific interventions to help nurses and doulas work well together.

column36: Applying an SGBA+ lens to medical device lifecycle management
column37: Medical devices (i.e. pacemakers, joints, breast implants, birth control devices) are needed to extend and improve life. In Canada, the makers/distributors of new devices apply to Health Canada for a license to sell them. Health Canada makes that decision based on research provided by device makers/distributors showing that the new device is safe and effective. However, if research does not test devices on patients with different characteristics (i.e. women and men), they may not work properly in all patients, possibly leading to serious problems. The overall aim of this research is to partner with Health Canada to explore if they can improve the way they make and communicate decisions about licensing of devices by more openly considering whether device safety and effectiveness were tested for sex (women/men) or gender-related factors (i.e. age, education level, ethnic background, region of Canada, urban-/rural-dwelling). The objectives are to: (1) Visit web sites and speak with representatives of device licensing agencies in other countries (i.e. Australia, England, United States) to explore if they make/communicate licensing decisions based on whether devices are proven to be safe/effective for patients who differ by sex/gender-related factors; (2) Explore Health Canada decision-making processes to date by examining the content of licensing applications they received from makers/distributors, licensing decision documents, and instructions prepared for makers/distributors, patients or clinicians for a range of devices; and (3) Based on the results, prepare recommendations for Health Canada on information they should request of makers/distributors, and employ when they make, document and communicate decisions to makers/distributors, patients and clinicians. By adopting the recommendations, Health Canada can strengthen decision-making processes, leading to licensing of thoroughly tested devices, which are more likely to be safe and effective for all Canadians.

column36: Canadian Concussion Network
column37: Each year, an estimated 250,000 Canadians and more than 40 million people worldwide sustain a concussion. Children and adolescents account for 50% of concussions, mostly occurring during sport and recreational activities; in Canada, roughly 1 in 10 teens will seek medical care for a sport-related concussion annually. Approximately 15-30% of children and youth with concussion report persistent postconcussive symptoms; and many sustain recurrent concussions, which can result in acute, life threatening injury in rare instances and may have lifelong consequences. Despite this growing burden, evidence-informed approaches to prevent concussions, diagnose them rapidly and objectively, and treat them effectively are sorely lacking. Integrated, multidisciplinary, large-scale research programs on concussion are needed to address this challenge. Canada is home to an impressive array of scientists who are world leaders in concussion research; however, they remain siloed and uncoordinated, without a national network to establish and guide a national concussion research agenda. Along with a variety of stakeholders, including patients, clinicians, community organizations, government, and industry, Canadian concussion researchers have agreed to forge the Canadian Concussion Network (CCN). The CCN organizers represent multiple disciplines and institutions, and are leaders in national and international concussion initiatives. They co-created the plan for the CCN with a broad range of stakeholders and a multidisciplinary group of scientists and clinician-scientists. The CCN will promote innovative and collaborative research to improve the prevention, diagnosis/prognosis, and management of concussion, focusing on sport and youth. Through continuous engagement with our knowledge users, integrated knowledge translation, and development of highly qualified personnel, the CCN will drive a coordinated research agenda that will shape best practices and policies in Canada and internationally.

column36: Does flavivirus infection trigger mitochondrial antigen presentation and autoreactive T-cell response in parkinsonism?
column37: The exact cause of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unknown and there is currently no cure for the disease. This is why there is a critical need for clinically-relevant biomarkers new therapeutic avenues. In this project, we will explore new research aspects of PD and atypical parkinsonism, related to autoimmunity (the immune attack of the self) triggered by flaviviruses. Indeed, these types of viruses are endemic in regions where atypical parkinsonism is highly frequent (such as Guadeloupe and Martinique) and are particularly associated with Parkinsonian features. Moreover, flavivirus infection is also associated with major mitochondrial disorders. Mitochondria was originally described as the powerhouse of the cell. However, the recent discoveries have highlighted the major role of this organelle in the regulation of the immune response. Particularly, our team have recently shown that the presentation of the proteins from the mitochondria leads to autoimmunity and to PD in a murine model. Therefore, we hypothesize that flavivirus infection trigger autoimmune attacks of dopaminergic neurons (target neurons in PD) through the induction of mitochondrial antigen presentation. Not only this would greatly impact the scientific community because of the first evidence of autoimmunity in PD and atypical parkinsonism patients, but it would generate several promising biomarkers.

column36: Role of microbes in the pathogenesis of PIBD: From discovery, through causation, to novel treatments
column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic conditions that damage a person's intestines and cause lifelong pain. IBD is becoming more common in Canada, especially in children. Current treatments (drugs) suppress patient's immune systems and don't work all the time; even when they work they carry substantial risks. Therefore, we need to develop new treatments. While studying some of our patients, our Team of doctors and scientists has found several types of unusual bacteria in their intestines. These bacteria are able to attach to - or invade the cells lining the human gut, and trigger inflammation. These bacteria are also recognized by the patient's immune cells, suggesting these "pathobiont" bacteria are involved in either causing IBD, or making it worse, and thus removing these nasty bacteria could be a new treatment for IBD. Our Team is part of a national Network studying IBD in more than 1500 Canadian children. We plan to use the existing Network infrastructure to collect samples from these patients, including stool samples, intestinal washing, and tissues. We will use specialized techniques to identify potential "pathobionts" and grow them up in large numbers, allowing us to study them in great detail. We will test how they stick or invade human cells grown in the lab, as well as inject them into mice to see how they cause disease. As we gain a better understanding of how different "pathobiont" bacteria cause disease, we will develop new ways to target these bacteria and test these approaches in the lab, in mouse models, and ultimately in the patients themselves. For example, we will test if certain diets can starve these bacteria, if there are specific good bacteria we can give to patients in their food that can outcompete the pathobionts, or if we can use new drugs to kill, or flush away these harmful bacteria. Taken together, our studies will help develop new precise and personalized ways to treat children with IBD, and ultimately improve their lives.

column36: Scaling up public health chronic disease prevention (CDP) innovations
column37: Periodic assessment of the capacity for chronic disease prevention (CDP) in the public health system in Canada is fundamental to optimizing CDP. Specifically, we need to monitor capacity for planning, target-setting, implementation and scaling up, and assessing the impact of interventions and policies that aim to reduce the chronic disease burden. Numerous important CDP capacity-building initiatives have taken place in Canada since the 1980s, and the public health systems in all 10 Canadian provinces have undergone major health system restructuring and reforms. Considering these ongoing structural changes in the public health system, periodic assessment is key to understanding progress and achievements in expanding CDP capacity as we work towards implementing and scaling up effective CDP programming across Canada. To address the lack of nationally representative data on CDP capacity, our team developed the Public Health ORganizational CApacity STudy (PHORCAST), comprising two Canada-wide surveys of public health organizations engaged in CDP. In 2005 and 2010, we surveyed all organizations in Canada with mandates for population-level primary prevention of chronic disease (cancer, CVD, diabetes, chronic respiratory illness), healthy lifestyle promotion, or with a single-focus mandate for healthy eating, tobacco control or physical activity. PHORCAST has already provided unique empirical insights into Canada's preventive health system and identified areas that need improvement (human resource planning, development and training, monitoring changes over time in organizational capacity for CDP; evaluating CDP programs, policies and practices). We propose to conduct a third survey, now 10-15 years since the original surveys, using the same methods used in 2005 and 2010. Results will update the evidence base on organizational capacity for CDP to support strategic expansion of CDP interventions and policies to better respond to the growing chronic disease burden in Canada.

column36: Public health in a time of austerity: measuring the divestments in Ontario's public health system and evaluating their impacts on population health and health inequities
column37: Public health encompasses a broad range of policies, programs, and initiatives implemented to promote community health and well-being. In times of austerity, governments tend to divest in public health, which may have devastating consequences for population health. Evidence identifying the health impacts of cuts to public health spending is limited. Furthermore, understanding how the impact of public health cuts on health inequities is essential for better population health. The current climate of austerity in Ontario presents an important opportunity to study the impact of public health divestments on population health. Specifically, we will measure changes to public health financing and delivery by examining Annual Service and Budget Plans for each public health unit. Secondly, we will administer questionnaires and in-person interviews with the Medical Officers of Health to identify how each public health unit prioritizes programs in response to budget cuts. Finally, we will conduct natural experiments analyzing secondary data, such as the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), to determine the impact of budget cuts. The overall goal of this study is to establish an open access data system for tracking public health expenditures, governance and delivery over time in Ontario and to examine the relationship between public health financing and population health and health inequities. The project will involve working with the frontline public health sector, such as the Medical Officer of Health of Toronto Public Health, and the Ontario Public Health Association, to develop our research questions and methodology, and plan for dissemination of our findings. The research fills a critical gap regarding the impact of divesting in public health on population health and health inequities in Ontario. New evidence will be generated to inform government and policy makers on how to best fund public health and prioritize which public health policies and programs.

column36: Optimizing adult vaccination outcomes under public health budgetary constraints
column37: Public health spending made up only 6.4% of the overall health budget across Canadian provinces and territories in 2018, yet, governments continue to target public health for funding cuts. Finding a way to estimate the value of public health programs for decision makers is key to ensure funding from provincial governments. Across Canada, one of the key responsibilities of provincial/territorial public health departments is vaccination, including large-scale adult vaccination programs, such as shingles and influenza. These programs make up a large amount of public health budgets, and it is important for provincial/territorial governments to understand the direct benefits of these vaccines, and gather evidence on which large-scale adult vaccination programs they should fund. Therefore, we aim to determine what mix of adult vaccination programs give the best health outcomes under various potential budgets. We will estimate the health and monetary outcomes (e.g., deaths and hospitalization prevented, and the associated costs) that provincial governments could expect with changes to the adult vaccination budget. For example, with a budget reduction of $1 million dollars for adult vaccines, we would see an increase of X number of hospitalizations, and X number of deaths. This project will help governments determine which vaccines to focus on in the future, and directly see what they are losing when they choose to defund public health. We will also consider the impact on equity, by determining how policy-advisors value health outcomes for different sub-populations (e.g., age groups and sex) and the various diseases targeted for vaccination (e.g., common but mild vs. uncommon but severe), and how those values may impact the optimal mix of adult vaccination programs.

column36: Establishing a platform to monitor the performance of public health systems across Canada
column37: Strong public health systems are essential to improving population health and ensuring sustainable health systems. While there is robust evidence of effectiveness of public health interventions, there is little known about how performance of public health systems varies across the country. Our proposed project aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining and comparing changes to public health financing, governance and organization on health outcomes using case studies in Canada and by defining structure, process and outcome indicators to establish a platform for ongoing monitoring and evaluation research. Second, we will conduct case studies of a selection of provinces and territories using key informant interviews with public health decision makers and stakeholders to gain insight into how systems responded to major changes. Third, we will identify and prioritize structure, process and outcome measures to establish a platform for the routine monitoring and evaluation of the positive, negative and unintended impacts of changes to public health financing, governance, organization and workforce.

column36: Public health financing and structural transformation: evaluating the impacts of past changes and understanding policymakers' preferences for the future
column37: The Canadian public health landscape has been deeply transformed over the past 20 years, both in terms of governance, organization and financing. Furthermore, tighter government budgetary constraints have affected public health spending. However, all these transformations occurred without extensive monitoring of their effects on population health and health services, and without an understanding of the preferences of the public health policymakers involved in the implementation of these transformations. Our project has two interrelated objectives that precisely address these gaps in knowledge. First, we will compile and analyze a longitudinal dataset at the provincial/territorial level to estimate the effect of changes in public health spending, governance and organization on intermediate (e.g., smoking rates) and final (e.g., preventable mortality) public health outcomes, as well as trade-offs and spillover on health services outcomes (e.g., physicians spending). Second, we will quantitatively and qualitatively investigate the preferences of public health policymakers at the provincial/territorial and local levels across the country to understand their preferences for future changes to governance, organization and financing of public health, and their equity implications. Knowledge users who are public health decision makers will be involved throughout the research continuum. Overall, results from this research program will significantly advance knowledge on the positive, negative and unintended effects of the transformation to the structure of public health in Canada. Guided by evidence on the impact of previous changes and the preferences for future changes of the policymakers responsible for implementing the reforms, they will have important implications for the optimal allocation of resources and structuring of public health systems, and provide a foundation for more systematic monitoring of the effects of these transformations in the future.

column36: Molecular Mechanisms of Opening and Closing in Hyperpolarization-activated Cyclic Nucleotide-gated (HCN) Channels
column37: Ion channels are proteins that act as microscopic conduits of electricity within our cells. Hyperpolarization-activated Cyclic Nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels are a family of ion channels that control important biological functions such as heart rhythm and neural communication. Mutations in HCN channels are naturally-occurring changes in the atomic structure of the channel and are associated with diseases such as heart arrhythmia and epilepsy. Disease-associated HCN channel mutations have been found to alter how the channels open and close, or "gate." However, how gating actually occurs at the atomic and molecular levels is unclear, hindering medical and scientific progress in understanding how these mutations may contribute to disease and developing appropriate treatments. To better understand channel gating and how disease-associated mutations impact this process, I will combine measurements of channel gating with a mathematical model that breaks down the channel into pieces or modules that interact dynamically. Using preliminary data, I have constructed a mathematical model of HCN channel opening and closing that I will apply to examine both normal and mutant channel gating. I will use molecular biology techniques to generate HCN channel mutants whose electrical activity can be measured using approaches in the Accili lab. Then, I will apply mathematical models to help understand how the channels gate normally and how mutations might impact this process. The proposed studies will thus provide novel insights into both the fundamental mechanisms of gating in HCN channels and the role of HCN channel dysfunction in the development of disease.

column36: Investigating Sex Differences in Fetal Antiretroviral Drug Disposition
column37: Combination antiretroviral (ARV) therapy during pregnancy is increasingly effective in reducing risk of vertical human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) transmission, however the fetal toxicity of widely administered ARV drugs remains poorly described and existing literature often fails to account for sex as a variable. Evidence of sex-linked toxicities in ARV exposed children suggests differing drug disposition between male and female subjects that may be explained by variable expression of drug transporters. These transporters are expressed at tissue barriers throughout the body and highly regulate the ARV drug exposure of vital tissues, such as the brain. Furthermore, sex and age have been identified as important factors influencing drug transporter expression in human and animal models. Using an ARV drug exposed mouse model, my research aims to compare male and female fetal expression of multi-drug transporters and penetration of ARV drugs into fetal tissues, in order to better understand sex-linked toxicities of antiretroviral therapy, and highlight the need for more effective design of HIV treatment regimens during pregnancy.

column37: The Indigenous Primary Health Care and Policy Research (IPHCPR) Network will support researchers, health system leadership, health service providers and Indigenous community to come together to build knowledge for improving primary health care (PHC) for Indigenous peoples. column36: Holistic Indigenous Mental Health and Wellness: Transforming Health Care Strengths and Solutions
column37: Indigenous peoples with serious mental illness face unique health care barriers due to racism, oppression, and intergenerational trauma of residential school and child welfare systems. Indigenous mental health is complex; research shows that challenges of cultural identity, food insecurity, environmental health, career, education, culture clash between biomedicine and Indigenous healing, and failure of Canada's health policy are mediating factors. Currently there are thousands of Indigenous youth and adults searching for healing, often stuck in cycles of mental health crisis that include lack of mental health service, extreme addictive behaviours, severe anxiety and depression, and chronic suicidality. Current mental health services focus on crisis and short term mental health programs; this network will move the focus to holistic culturally-based interventions that prevent illness and strengthen individuals' chances of successful wellness. There is a lack of national research networking among academics and communities in Indigenous health generally and specifically in holistic Indigenous mental health. The team will develop a cultural evidence-based Indigenous research network to improve mental wellness by generating data that shows that illness and crisis can be prevented with traditional knowledges, cultural safety, and Indigenous science, when applied to health systems. There are 6 research themes: Cultural safety; Indigenous holistic prevention and early intervention; Land based and planetary health solutions; Healing from trauma and reducing addictions; Enhancing wellbeing and eliminating suicide; and Translating Indigenous knowledges data to practice and policy. An Elders steering committees will govern the network. An Indigenous knowledges framework for mental health service and policy will be developed and results will have national and international impact for future generations toward ending Indigenous mental illness.

column36: Kishaadigeh: Indigenous Self Determination through Research for our Future Generations - Manitoba NEIHR
column37: Indigenous Peoples and communities have a long, often challenging relationship around research. In recent years, these relationships have healed and many communities and organizations have become leaders around self-determination in research. At the same time, Indigenous health researchers, many of whom are Indigenous women, have become emboldened and armored with ethical and effective approaches to Indigenous health research fostered by a growing network of scholars. This proposal, entitled Kishaadigeh, or "she who guards the lodge" is led primarily by Indigenous scholars, mostly women and Indigenous organizations who have a long history of being supported by and participating in the ACADRE/NEAHR programs. Due in part to the success of the ACADRE/NEAHR programs, Indigenous health scholars are now flourishing across campuses and in Indigenous organizations as the leaders and the ones who "guard the lodge". In many of our Indigenous communities, we see the responsibilities of "guarding of the lodge" as also guarding our stories and knowledge, a role often undertaken by women. The Manitoba NEIHR will develop a pathway for existing and upcoming Indigenous scholars (both men and women) to work with Indigenous organizations to clear the path for self-determination over research resulting in meaningful engagement that is ethical and impactful. The Manitoba NEIHR grant develop research lodges at the Indigenous community level with four Indigenous organizations which includes the First Nations Health and Social Secretariat of Manitoba (FNHSSM), the Manitoba Association for Friendship Centres (MAC), the Manitoba Inuit Association (MIA), and Aboriginal Youth Opportunities (AYO). column36: A proposal for a Network Environment for Indigenous Health Research in Nunavut
column37: For almost 15 years our organizations have been implementing community-led research through Inuit-governed non-profit research centres, and we are ready to elevate our research models, methodological approaches, and mentorship capacity to the next level. The Nunavut NEIHR will be a centre of excellence for Inuit methods, approaches, and tools, and provide training and support to the next generation of Inuit students and scholars in Nunavut. Each of the 4 'hubs' identified in this proposal are leaders in research and interventions that build on Inuit pathways to wellbeing. By coming together under the rubric of the NEIHR, we will elevate that research and these approaches to a national and international level. We will also formally coordinate and share our capacity and infrastructure to foster a learning environment for Inuit scholarship that will be unparalleled in Canada. With regard to feasibility: Since our inception, we have brought Inuit research methods into the forefront of discourse pertaining to Inuit health, and we have collectively brought more than 25 million dollars into the territory to strengthen the capacity of our communities to lead research. Qaujigiartiit, as the host institution, has a demonstrated record of excellence in the management of federal monies for the purposes of research and training, has an independent ethics review board, and has the administrative capacity to oversee the NEIHR.

column36: Youth Engagement in Mental Health & Substance Use Research: A Critical Component of a National Training Entity in Patient Engagement
column37: Engaging youth in research is valuable across the disciplines, including health and wellbeing, health promotion, and mental health. Youth are often underrepresented in mental health and/or substance use (MHSU) research and service development initiatives, limiting the ability to address the unique needs of this developmental stage. Reflecting a commitment to youth-engaged research, the Margaret and Wallace McCain Centre for Child, Youth & Family Mental Health co-developed the McCain Model of Youth Engagement together with youth with lived experience of MHSU challenges. Leveraging the team's commitment, we then collaborated with pan-Canadian partners, including youth, on the INNOVATE Research project, in which we co-developed with youth a thorough youth engagement curriculum for researchers. We then delivered the training in full-day workshops, together with coaching sessions and a webinar, to researchers across Canada. Given this experience, we are poised and ready to bring a Youth MHSU Component to the NTE as an essential ingredient. By specifically including a youth MHSU component, SPOR will ensure that this often overlooked population is directly targeted by national capacity development endeavors. This component will leverage a strong existing team that has made substantial progress in moving toward the goals of the NTE, in an important population subset. This project will also enable established national leaders and emerging researchers to expand upon and enhance their leadership role in transforming youth-engaged MHSU research processes and agendas. The team will collaborate with the winning applicants to integrate youth engagement into the NTE as a whole and to examine how our learnings intersect with or build upon engagement in other spheres. We will also rapidly scale up the existing INNOVATE Research training platform and establish a national networking forum for youth-engaged researchers to share their experiences and build new collaborations.

Establishing and applying best practices in academic, professional, and experiential education in implementation science and solutions-based research; 2. Developing a core and interdisciplinary set of competencies among learners (trainees and knowledge users) that can be applied to diverse challenges facing cities; 3. Creating and fostering a national, and internationally-recognized, community of practice of experienced mentors; 4. Ensuring the multidimensional career readiness of learners; 5. Facilitating opportunities for interagency networking and intersectoral partnerships. Equity: By focusing on growing environmental, social, and health inequities between and within Canadian cities, BUILD takes an intersectional approach, integrating inclusion of populations excluded at societal and community levels based on intersecting race; sex, gender, and sexual orientation; religion; migration status; socioeconomic status; disability; and geographical location. BUILD prioritizes inclusion of these populations at all levels of the platform, including in leadership, team, partnership development plan for engaging partners and collaborators, approaches, design, curriculum, instructors, learners (trainees and knowledge users), and evaluation.

column36: Healthy Cities of Tomorrow Research and Training Platform
column37: This project aims to train a generation of researchers and professionals who will help Canadian cities foster human health, reduce social inequity, and protect the environment. We will develop a training platform that reinforces urban planning and public health as interdependent disciplines, like they used to be more than a century ago. The platform will unite professors, health professionals, urban planning organizations, and other partners to develop a research training platform that will: 1) train students in a new interdisciplinary field that integrates urban planning, geography, engineering, public health, and environmental sciences; 2) produce a systematic framework that details best practices for urban projects like light rail, which are associated with better health and environmental outcomes; and 3) generate and maintain an accredited, freely accessible online course on healthy cities. The unifying hallmark of these activities will be the investigation of the environmental, health-related behavioural, and social impacts of large urban infrastructure projects across Canada. The 'low carbon transport' theme will examine best practices for implementing transport projects that balance environmental sustainability and promote human health. The 'healthy neighbourhoods' theme will focus on the interplay between social and built environments and cardio-metabolic health. The 'sustainable urban natural environments' theme will consider the multi-level impacts of urban environmental exposures in a changing climate. The platform's training program will include opportunities for students to study within the key theme areas, pursue internships with project partners, participate in an annual 'Building Healthy Cities' workshop with peers and mentors, and collaboratively build an online 'super-course,' which will eventually serve as a repository of knowledge, freely accessible to all.

column36: Healthy Cities Training Initiative (HCTI): an intelligent urban health and resilient monitoring, assessment, and management Platform and Network for Resilient, Healthy Canadian Cities
column37: Canadian cities and their residents face significant challenges due to climate change and the rising frequency and severity of disasters that couple with the aging infrastructures and technological disruption. The socio-economic and environmental resilience of Canadian cities requires enabling conditions where healthy individuals and communities can thrive, and where institutions, organizations and infrastructures can adapt swiftly and appropriately to the new and emerging conditions through timely and embedded adaptation, mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery strategies that are science and evidence-based. Such conditions are not automatic but rely on political decisions, democratic process and community involvement at all stages of design and implementation. Today's challenges require a new generation of highly qualified personnel (HQP) equipped with skills and training to be able to facilitate and conduct collaboration across sectors, services and professional or disciplinary silos, as well as an enhanced ability to work directly with urban residents, decision-makers, and other stakeholders. We will develop a Healthy Cities Training Initiative, whose Network and Platform will interact synergistically to produce a new generation of leadership and innovations to enable the conditions for resilient, healthy Canadian cities. We will create a Network of academics and their collaborating stakeholders across municipal, provincial and federal levels to mentor and develop trainees for development of an effective, data driven, intelligent health and resilience monitoring, assessment, and management Platform. The Platform will draw on causal mapping, state-of -the-art artificial intelligence and big data technologies to create targeted analytics and goal oriented Data Dashboards, and for complexity agent-based simulation and Scenario Planning. Such innovations will then be applied to the social, environmental and health challenges faced by Canadian cities.

column37: The Training for Healthy INterdisciplinary Knowledge in Cities (THINK-Cities) Research Training Platform is a national initiative to develop a new generation of leaders with interdisciplinary expertise in implementation of research-based approaches to improve health and reduce health inequalities in cities. The THINK-Cities framework is built around three core domains: housing, mobility, neighborhoods, four overarching themes essential to achieving healthier communities: scale of implementation, sociopolitical context, sustainability, and equity, and two nodes addressing "mid-sized/small cities" and "global cities". The team is led by three established researchers and the Urban Public Health Network (UPHN). UPHN has 15 years of successful collaboration with Medical Health Officers across Canada to address public health in urban populations. The leadership team brings diversity in disciplinary expertise, gender, career stage, and are based within Canada's three largest cities. The team brings decades of experience implementing solutions-based research with partners in Canadian communities. Our program will recruit leading trainees from health, social science/humanities, and natural sciences/engineering to gain specific cross-cutting competencies in a team-focused, solution-based training initiative. Trainees will develop skills to address challenges faced by municipalities by viewing cities as complex systems (engineering lens), as communities (social science/planning lens) and as opportunities for health-enabling design, planning and delivery of services (population health lens). Our training program will focus not only on absolute health, but health disparities within cities and will emphasize sociopolitical context, geospatial approaches and cross-cultural considerations explaining these disparities. After their experience with our team, trainees will be ready to tackle challenges affecting health and health inequalities in cities across Canada and globally.

column36: Identifying the role of a novel protein in the regulation of connections in the brain
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder, are manifested in early childhood and have limited treatment options (Thapar et al., 2017). It is thought that they arise from the abnormal development of the cerebral cortex, yet our understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms remain rudimentary. Our lab recently discovered a novel mouse mutant involving the Mllt11 gene (myeloid/lymphoid or mixed-lineage leukemia; translocated to chromosome 11) (Yamanda et al., 2014) that models neurodevelopmental disorders. I will explore the role of Mllt11 in the regulation of connections in the brain, and in so doing reveal mechanisms underlying cognitive disorders. I will use in vitro and in vivo approaches to manipulate the levels of Mllt11 gene dosage and explore its effect on the formation of cortical neurons. My thesis research program will take advantage of the ease at which mouse embryonic stem cells can be converted to specific classes of neurons using defined conditions, and test whether the loss of Mllt11 mutant mice alters the formation of a cortical projection neuron phenotype. If Mllt11 affects the formation of projection neurons, then I expect to see a reduction in the formation of certain cortical projection neurons over time. A complimentary approach will involve an in vivo analysis of Mllt11 loss within subclasses of projection neurons by conditional mutagenesis. As the destabilization of projection neurons may play a role in cognitive disorders (Yamanda et al., 2014), my thesis work will provide insight into the molecular causes of these disorders. These disorders are highly prevalent and display a large socioeconomic impact (Vasiliadis et al., 2017), the limited treatment options and growing burden necessitates further research in this field.
