column36: Exploring how the experience of birth trauma impacts birthing parents in their first postpartum year
column37: Increasingly, women perceive childbirth as a traumatic event. Consequently, some women live with psychological distress that is undiagnosed, untreated, and poorly understood by their family, friends, and healthcare providers (HCPs). This proposed research aims to explore how the experience of birth trauma (BT) impacts the lives of women in their first postpartum year. BT is commonly described as 'psychological distress that occurs in the postpartum period due to perceived traumatic events during childbirth'. Approximately 4-18.5% of women are diagnosed with post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in their postpartum period, with 20-48% exhibiting at least one symptom of PTSD but not formally diagnosed. Further, 30% of women perceive their birth as traumatic and will develop stress reactions after childbirth. Symptoms of BT include intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, nightmares, anxiety, depression, feelings of guilt, and decreased attachment to baby. Risk factors for BT include pre-existing mental illness, complications with mother or baby, negative interactions with HCPs, preterm birth, and cesarean birth. While much is known about the etiology, prevalence, and women's perceptions of traumatic birth, little is known about how women function after a traumatic birth experience. This proposed research will utilize feminist phenomenology to explore the complexities of living with BT, using interviews to get to the core of this experience. The proposed research is the first of its kind in Canada and aims to develop understanding of the social implications of living with BT, and uncover strategies for treatment and recovery in conjunction with women. Further, this proposed research will inform HCP education and change in healthcare practice with the goal of reducing cases of BT.

column36: Predictors and Motivation for Vaping Cannabis in Canadian Youth and Young Adults
column37: Electronic cigarettes (e-cigs) or vaping machines can be used to vaporize cannabis and are gaining popularity as an alternative to smoking. With legalization of cannabis in Canada in 2018, there is likely a marked increase in e-cig use to vape cannabis. Any existing findings may become outdated if the impact of legalization shifts vaping practices at the population level. Since it is not a risk-free alternative and rigorous studies on health outcomes are severely lacking, vaping cannabis is vital to understand given CIHR's recently published Lower Risk Cannabis Use Guidelines (LRCUG), which endorses safer practices for using cannabis; one recommendation is to use non-combustible methods of cannabis ingestion such as vaping. Young adults are a key target vulnerable demographic for cannabis use; this study will examine risk factors and motivations among a Canadian student population (i.e., ages 18-25). This project will address the following research questions, which will determine: (1) predictors of e-cig cannabis use (i.e., lifetime cannabis vaporization, past-month cannabis vaporization, cannabis vaping frequency) in young adults, and (2) motivations for using e-cigs to vape cannabis. A logistic regression to examine factors associated with cannabis vaporization use will be conducted. This will be the first study examining how motivations for using and habits related to cannabis vaping change in a young adult population post-legalization. Academic outputs have the potential to determine risk factors of using e-cigs to vape cannabis, especially as the harms and benefits of vaping are currently unknown. Knowledge exchange will be supported through disseminating results in a reputable addiction journal and presenting findings at an international substance use conference.

column36: Dyslexia in English-French Bilinguals: Temporal Sampling and Audio-Visual Integration
column37: Dyslexia is a reading disorder that affects 5-10% of the population, yet the underlying causes of this disorder are still unclear. Recent brain imaging studies reveal that dyslexia may involve deficits in both phonological and visual areas. However, the extent to which these two faculties interact during reading is still an area in need of research, as the task of integrating auditory information (phonology) to visual information (orthography) is paramount to reading ability. Furthermore, very little is known about how a secondary language, which differs in speech rhythm (prosody) and orthographic depth from the primary language, impacts the dyslexic reader's ability to form these auditory-visual associations. This proposed study aims to investigate the underlying causes of dyslexia by assessing the relationships between prosodic sensitivity, auditory-visual integration, and reading proficiency in English and French monolinguals versus English-French bilingual dyslexic readers. It is hypothesized that a cross-linguistic deficit in prosodic sensitivity and auditory-visual integration will adversely affect bilingual reading skills. If the results of this study suggest prosodic sensitivity to be correlated with auditory-visual processing and reading abilities across both languages, a cross-linguistic dyslexia diagnostic tool able to capture these deficits could potentially be developed. This diagnostic tool would be especially relevant to the English-French Canadian school systems. Additionally, a future study would aim to develop a musical rhythm-based, letter-sound mapping training paradigm as a cross-linguistic reading remediation tool. This rhythmic auditory-visual integration training could potentially be developed into a patentable computer treatment program.

column36: Analyzing muscle loss and myosteatosis after surgical prehabilitation in lung cancer patients
column37: Myosteatosis (fat infiltration into muscle) and muscle loss are prevalent in individuals with lung cancer and can predict higher mortality in these patients. This research will be a component of a larger multimodal intervention looking at the effects of a nutritional supplement and exercise in patients with lung cancer before and after surgery. The study will analyze myosteatosis in both the abdomen and leg of lung cancer patients throughout the intervention. Patients with stage I, II or IIIa non-small cell lung cancer will be placed in one of two arms; the exercise and nutritional supplement cohort (SUPP) or the exercise only control cohort (CTRL). Approximately 40 patients from the large intervention will undergo a computed tomography (CT) scan on their abdominal region and a peripheral quantitative CT (pQCT) scan on their dominant foreleg. The scans will be analyzed to determine the relationship between amount of fat that has infiltrated the muscle in the abdomen, to that of the leg. It is hypothesized that patients in the SUPP cohort will have less myosteatosis in both the abdomen and leg in comparison to those in the CTRL cohort. This is largely hypothesized due to omega-3 fatty acids in the supplement previously demonstrating a protective role in muscle loss and myosteatosis in lung cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. Muscles in the abdominal region are expected to have more fat infiltration than muscles of the leg, simply because they are surrounded by more visceral fat and are less solicited by physical exercise. This study will contribute to knowledge about muscle loss and myosteatosis in cancer patients after surgery. The results may be applied to both prehabilitation and rehabilitation to ultimately increase quality of life for lung cancer patients.

column36: The role of reassurance seeking in the maintenance of body dysmorphic disorder
column37: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a severely impairing yet common disorder characterized by a preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance that drives an individual to perform repetitive behaviours or mental acts (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). There is a paucity of research on the behaviours involved in the maintenance of the disorder. Understanding the behaviours, their function and their effect is essential to the improvement of our treatment methods. This study seeks to examine the frequency, purpose, stopping criteria and triggers of reassurance seeking (RS) in BDD compared to healthy controls using an ecologically valid daily diary method. This study also seeks to examine how RS relates to BDD symptom severity and how individuals who engage in RS differ from those who do not. A sample of forty individuals with BDD and forty healthy controls will be recruited. Using a daily diary over 14 days, data will be gathered on the frequency, the triggers, the function, the success, and the termination criteria for RS as well as information on the perceived quality of the reassurance. It is hypothesized that individuals who have BDD will engage in significantly more RS than controls overall, especially for appearance-related triggers. Greater frequency of reassurance seeking will be associated with greater symptom severity in clinical and nonclinical groups. This study will be the first to examine RS in BDD and to utilize daily diaries in obsessive-compulsive related disorders. It will inform studies on behavioural maintenance factors in the course of BDD and will elucidate targets for intervention with families and significant others, with the goal of delivering positive, long-term treatment outcomes.

column36: Costs and Cascade Health Service Use as a Consequence of Whole Genome Sequencing in Children with a Cardiomyopathy and their Families
column37: Whole exome sequencing (WES) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) are able to identify a wide range of genetic abnormalities, and as such are powerful new tools in human and medical genetics research. However, WES/WGS raises a multitude of ethical difficulties because, by its nature, it generates secondary findings - supplemental data not relevant to the initial diagnostic query. The challenges posed by these secondary findings are exacerbated in the paediatric context, where patients are often unable to give informed consent. There have been no economic analyses conducted specifically for the generation and return of secondary findings from paediatric WES/WGS, nor have there been economic studies of the effects of cascading genetic tests in family members of a child with a positive WES/WGS. The Genome Clinic at the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) already returns secondary results from paediatric WGS to parents, however there is little consideration of the impact of downstream cascade testing and service use on the health care system. We will fill this knowledge gap by conducting an economic analysis using the tools and methods of Health Technology Assessment, exploring the cascade use of health services and costs as a consequence of whole genome sequencing in the paediatric cardiomyopathy population.

column36: Building resources for Safer Opioid Supply prescribing to address the opioid overdose crisis in Ontario
column37: Canada is in a devastating opioid overdose crisis - 4 Ontarians die every day from overdose. While opioid agonist treatment provides protection from overdose-related mortality, retention is a major issue. SOS aim to offer low-threshold option on a spectrum of care for people who are immediate risk of overdose from the illicit opioid supply. Implemented in primary care settings, SOS patients also receive comprehensive primary care and wrap-around harm reduction programming. column36: Modelling Different Ethical Criteria of Health Equity to Inform Population Health Interventions
column37: This study sought to empirically model population-level interventions for diabetes according to distinct ethical criteria of health equity in order to understand the realistic consequences of adopting different ethical views about what health equity requires for public health. Using the validated Diabetes Population Risk Tool (DPoRT), ten-year diabetes risk was calculated for respondents to the nationally representative 2015-16 Canadian Community Health Survey (n=67,867). The number of diabetes cases prevented or delayed was estimated across low, medium, and high education categories according to two ethical criteria: 1) 'Equality' (equalizing diabetes risk); 2) 'Sufficiency' (reducing diabetes risk below the DPoRT high-risk threshold (over 16.5), beyond which remaining inequalities are not considered ethically important). Hypothetical percent weight-loss interventions in overweight and obese individuals were modeled for each ethical criterion. In total, 1,811,017 new diabetes cases were predicted for 2026. Education was inversely associated with baseline diabetes risk (risk ratio (RR)=1.68, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.63,1.73; low compared to high education). 'Equality' was achieved by implementing 20% and 15% weight-loss interventions in low and medium education groups. 'Sufficiency' was achieved by a 14% weight-loss intervention in high-risk individuals; however, large social inequalities in diabetes remained in this scenario (RR= 1.52, 95%CI: 1.48-1.56; low compared to high education). These interventions resulted in 246,923 and 267,690 diabetes cases prevented or delayed, respectively. This study is the first of its kind to illustrate how adopting different criteria of equity offered by public health ethicists could impact population health outcomes. As such, this study represents a promising program of research, the findings of which being poised to transform the ethical design of public health interventions which aim to 'reduce health inequities'.

column36: Exploring what interventions are needed in the Laurentians (Quebec, Canada) in the context of the opioid crisis: A mixed-methods study
column37: North America is facing an unprecedented wave of opioid-related overdoses, affecting both people who use drugs (PWUD) and those taking prescription opioids. There is little data currently available on the extent of the situation in the Laurentians (Quebec, Canada). The purpose of this study is to identify the best North American interventions, facilitators and barriers, as well as to understand the opioid crisis in the Laurentians region. A mixed-method design was developed by combining a literature review of systematic reviews and semi-structured interviews with stakeholders in the Laurentians. The nine systematic reviews revealed five categories of intervention: Those targeting opioid prescriptions, naloxone distribution, the use of psychosocial intervention in combination with opioid substitution therapy, medical cannabis in pain management and functional magnetic resonance imaging to study opioid use disorders. Naloxone distribution programs showed good evidence of effectiveness, but studies for other types of programs showed weak to no impact on the opioids-related harms. Four Laurentian stakeholders were interviewed: a public health officer, a PWUD, a community health physician and a community pharmacist. They presented their perspective according to five themes: the state of the situation in the Laurentians, the cause of the epidemic, the people at risk and the response to the crisis in the region, as well as future prospects. This study brings a new perspective on what is currently being done to address the opioid crisis in North America and how this knowledge can be applied to the opioid crisis in the Laurentians region and possibly in other Canadian regions.

column37: Unregulated cannabis products are currently being used by children with cancer for a variety of reasons including pain, sleep, nausea and as a cancer treatment. Without research evidence many doctors are hesitant to recommend cannabis products for children with cancer. Parents desperate for effective treatments and armed with anecdotal information from case reports and social media are obtaining cannabis products (e.g. online or storefront clinics). In order for doctors to feel confident in advising parents on the use and dose of cannabis they need better information on whether these products work and if they are safe. To address this goal, we established a national team of researchers, doctors, nurses, pharmacists, policy makers, youth and parents, called C4T. Our goal is to better understand the risks and potential benefits of medical cannabis use in children with cancer. Our diverse study team will determine how parents and youth are currently using cannabis products in cancer and what the reason for use is. C4T will review the literature and conduct a real-world study with children with cancer who are already using cannabis to try and establish a dose-response. C4T will use this information to create educational tools for doctors, youth and parents as well as to develop large scale studies to test the benefits and safety of medical cannabis products for children compared with existing treatments/standard of care. There is a large knowledge gap on if and when cannabis products can be used safely by children with cancer and other chronic health conditions. To ensure people can use our findings, we will create and update an online resource hut that is accessible to the public. Our research team is well equipped to fill this knowledge gap and continue to conduct high-quality research on cannabis for a variety of health conditions in children.

column36: Requirement of Bone Morphogenetic Protein-Activated Transcription Factors in Chondrogenesis
column37: Chondrogenesis, or the formation of cartilage, is an essential developmental process for formation of bones, joints, and other tissues. Failures in chondrogenesis are linked to both common diseases including osteoarthritis, and rarer genetic conditions including chondrodysplasia, with few available treatments for these diseases. Chondrogenesis is driven by a collection of proteins termed bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which are currently being investigated as therapeutic factors in bone and cartilage regeneration. However, progress is hampered by a poor understanding of how BMPs regulate their target genes, which comprise the network of genes that control chondrogenesis as a whole. Our lab has recently identified a set of BMP-activated proteins, which have been implicated in chondrogenesis-related diseases through patient sequencing data. None of these proteins currently have any known function in chondrogenesis. This project will identify the roles of these BMP-activated proteins during chondrogenesis by decreasing their expression levels in pre-cartilage cells, and observing loss of chondrogenesis. Our data will provide the first insight into the link between mutations in these BMP-activated proteins and their corresponding chondrogenic diseases, potentially revealing novel mechanisms regulating chondrogenesis, and opening new possibilities in bone and joint therapeutics.

column36: Drinking to cope: A prospective examination of transition-related risk in early adulthood
column37: Rates of alcohol and anxiety disorder comorbidity are high in adult populations. Yet, we know little about how risk unfolds early on. The undergraduate years are a time when alcohol misuse is commonplace, but most people mature out of heavy drinking when they take on adult roles. Evidence suggests that those who drink to cope are less likely to mature out, and this is concerning given that heavy drinking puts individuals at risk for alcohol use disorder. The goal of the proposed project is to examine anxiety as a predictor of impeded maturing out of alcohol misuse during the transition out of university. Behavioural theories offer a useful framework for thinking about anxiety-motivated drinking. The anxiety (behavioural inhibition) system is thought to lead to alcohol misuse, but the degree of this relationship depends on activation of the impulsive (behavioural approach) system. These systems are thought to influence alcohol attitudes (i.e., 'alcohol will reduce my tension'), which in turn promote risk. We hypothesize that young adults high in anxiety, who are also impulsive, will not mature out of alcohol misuse post-university graduation. A 12-month preliminary study, as part of a larger 6-year study, is proposed. One hundred and thirty undergraduates will complete baseline clinical assessments prior to graduation. Following graduation, participants will complete assessments online, three times, at three-month intervals. Transitioning out of university has inherent stressors. For those high in anxiety, this may be a period when patterns of problematic drinking are solidified. This research may have implications for how we think about, and thus intervene in, heavy drinking during periods of transition.

column36: Paved with good intentions: Gentrification and the health and equity impacts of urban change
column37: Urban renewal offers huge potential for improving population health in cities, but can also carry unintended consequences for health equity. While the lack of investments in disadvantaged neighbourhoods may perpetuate health inequities, so can gentrification processes. Limited evidence and ongoing debate about the definitions, perceptions, measurement, and consequences of gentrification create confusion for planners and policy makers trying to reimagine cities while optimizing health and equity. Given national interest in advancing solutions-oriented research on healthy cities and major government investments in urban infrastructure, the need to unpack the complex relationship between urban change, gentrification, and population health is a central challenge for both research and policy. Gentrification is of great interest to policy makers and population health researchers striving to improve urban environments while avoiding negative consequences like resident displacement. Currently, evidence on the definition, causes, and consequences of gentrification is mixed, limiting the ability of cities to maximize the health and equity benefits of urban renewal. This timely symposium will bring clarity to the gentrification debate by showcasing the latest research and thinking from a population health perspective. This interactive symposium will: 1) explore how diverse perspectives shape the meaning and measurement of gentrification, 2) propose a conceptual framework to illustrate how and for whom gentrification impacts health and wellbeing, and 3) engage participants in the design of a mixed-methods study to examine the mechanisms between urban interventions, gentrification, and population health. The symposium will conclude with a facilitated discussion to explore how gentrification is unfolding in Canadian cities and how urban revitalization strategies can be implemented in a way that is both impactful and equitable.

column36: "Why is it they're fixing the outside?": Rethinking the Role of the Built Environment in Promoting Health Among Marginalized Communities
column37: Neighbourhood built environment resources, such as green spaces and recreational facilities, have been associated with residents' health. Objective presence of such resources, however, does not equate to access, use, and a subsequent health improvement. In this study we explored (1) how individuals experienced their neighbourhood environment, and (2) how social factors interacted with the built environment to shape different groups' use of resources. Eight "go-along" focus groups were conducted with children, youth, adults, and seniors living in two marginalized neighbourhoods in Toronto, Canada. Participants led the interviewer on a walk through their neighbourhood. At each pre-identified stop, they discussed experiences they had with the place, what they (dis)liked about it, and facilitators and barriers to using the resources available. Informed by a relational approach to place, a content analysis of focus group transcripts, notes, and maps allowed for viewing resource use as emerging from the interaction between individuals and the environment. Go-along focus groups allow us to harness people's lived experiences of their neighbourhood. Aspects of the social environment, such as perceived safety considerations driven by the presence of people loitering or selling drugs on the property, emerged as a key barrier to using neighbourhood resources. Specific groups, such as working-age women, also identified broader social circumstances, such as having a low income, living in precarious housing, and having to care for relatives, as more important for their health than the built environment itself. Social factors interact with the built environment to complexify the relationship between the environment, resource use, and health. When designing built environment interventions to foster social inclusion and health equity, we should move beyond an exclusive focus on objective characteristics to also attend to the lived experiences people have of urban spaces.

column36: Competence in evidence-informed decision-making (EIDM): development and psychometric testing of a new EIDM competence measurement tool for public health nursing
column37: Evidence-informed decision-making is important for public health nurses because it has potential to improve outcomes for the clients and communities in which they work. The purpose of this study is to develop and test a new self-report tool among public health nurses to measure their competence in evidence-informed decision-making. The process used to develop the tool included a review of related literature and engaging international content experts and front line nurses to ensure content of the tool was relevant, and that it was easy to understand and use in daily practice. The tool is also being piloted with a larger group of nurses across different Ontario health units to assess its validity, reliability, and acceptability. The final tool can be used directly in practice to support front line nurses and administrators in assessing the status of evidence-informed decision-making competence to support professional development planning at the individual nurse or organizational level.

column36: Relationships between psychosocial stress and sedentary behavior during pregnancy among Canadian women: Results from a diverse cohort and a nationwide sample
column37: Introduction/contexte Past research shows that psychosocial stress and distress predict sedentary behavior, but few studies focus on pregnant women. Our objective was to analyze relationships between psychosocial stress and distress with sedentary behavior among pregnant women in Canada. Methode: We analyzed objectively-measured sedentary behavior at 16-18, 24-26 and 32-24 weeks gestation in a sociodemographically diverse cohort of 70 women in Montreal Canada. Participants completed the Perceived Stress Questionnaire, and wore an accelerometer for 3 days that quantified sitting time. We used univariate general linear models to analyze relationships between perceived stress and sedentary behavior at each evaluation period. To assess generalizability, we analyzed relationships between psychological distress with self-reported leisure-time sedentary behavior among a sample representative of 166,095 women in the Canadian Community Health Survey. Resultats et analyse: We observed positive association between perceived stress and sitting time in the Montreal cohort, with small to moderate effect sizes (partial n2=0.08-0.16). We observed similar relationships in the nationwide sample, but with smaller effect sizes (partial n2=0.02). Conclusions et repercussions concernant les politiques, la pratique ou le pistes de recherche: Despite recommendations to reduce sedentary behavior during pregnancy, sedentarity among pregnant women remains high. Psychosocial stress represents one risk factor. Results might guide the development of more comprehensive interventions targeting both stress and sedentarity

column36: A Spatiotemporal Analysis of the Effect of Vancouver's Bikeway Network on Commuting to Work by Bicycle
column37: Between 1996 and 2016, Vancouver made substantial investments to their bikeway network, adding over 200 km of bikeways for a total network of 291 km. This investment corresponded with increases in city-wide bicycle commuting: nearly a doubling from 3.3% in 1996 to 6.1% in 2016. Despite high investment in bicycle infrastructure and a growing bicycling mode share, no work to date has examined the long-term effect of bicycle infrastructure on commuting to work by bicycle. This study aims to understand whether residential access to bikeways in Vancouver influenced commuting to work by bicycle, and whether the type of bikeway implemented (local street bikeway, painted bike lane, protected bike lane) makes a difference. Over the 20-years, the proportion of commuters bicycling to work increased by 3.2%, with the largest growth concentrated around the downtown core. The proportion of neighbourhoods with any bicycle infrastructure increased from half in 1996 to nearly all neighbourhoods in 2016. We found that changes in the amount of local street bikeways in the residential neighbourhood were associated with bicycling to work, but changes in the amount of painted bike lanes or protected bike lanes were not. Our study provides insight into the effect of large-scale investments made by the City to encourage cycling, an important contribution to guide future investments.

column36: Towards a Comparative Study of City-Level Income-Related Health Inequalities in Canada
column37: Income-related health inequalities are an important indicator of health equity in Canada's cities. During the past two years, the Urban Public Health Network has been working with project partners and Canada's leading data stewards to develop a descriptive portrait of income-related health inequalities in the largest cities in each province using hospital administrative and survey data. We have found that: 1) income-related health inequalities are widespread in all cities we considered; 2) however, income-related health inequalities also vary considerably between them; 3) these between city differences are primarily driven by the health outcomes of poor neighbourhoods not rich; and 4) over time, inequalities overall have tended to stay the same or become worse. In the years to come, addressing health inequalities in Canada's cities is likely going to require making investments and policy choices that target and improve the health of poor neighbourhoods.

column36: Cultural adaptation of health and social interventions: a literature review of existing models
column37: Introduction: Significant gaps exist in the quality of health and healthcare across population groups in Canada and worldwide, with Indigenous and ethnocultural communities being particularly impacted. Cultural adaptation of programs or interventions is one way to take culture into consideration in the service provision in order to improve access to and outcomes of the health and social programs offered to improve their situation. This presentation aims to document the variety of models or frameworks that have been proposed for culturally adapting health and social programs intended for diverse populations. Methods: A systematic search was performed using 3 databases (CINAHL, Medline, and PsycInfo) to identify the academic literature on cultural adaptation models for interventions or programs. Documents were included if they were published between 2009 and 2019 either in English or French. Reference list of the included publications were also screened for additional documents. Findings: Over 20 models or frameworks found in the literature. Most of them were developed and used in the United States to adapt programs intended for Latinos and/or African Americans. Three frameworks were developed in the context of programs for indigenous populations. The models or frameworks help to answer the question 'What to adapt' (content-oriented) and/or 'How to adapt' (process-oriented). Their main limitations are that they focus almost exclusively on the program itself or its immediate context, and they rarely acknowledge organizational and community-level factors. Conclusions and implications: Existing cultural adaptation models and frameworks can assist program developers and implementers in making decisions about what and how to adapt their health and social interventions for diverse populations. Further research is needed to explore the way broader factors such as economic, social, policy, and organizational factors could be considered in such models.

column36: xacqanat ?itkinit (Many Ways of Working Together): Lessons Learned from Decolonized Co-Learning Between Ktunaxa Nation and Interior Health
column37: Over the last several years, Ktunaxa Nation and Interior Health Authority have formed a partnership to support co-learning processes to advance decolonizing health systems and services. Under the leadership of Ktunaxa Elders and Knowledge Holders, we developed xacqanat ?itkinit (Many Ways of Working Together), a locally-specific, culturally-informed and community-driven approach to co-learning and co-creation of knowledge. We piloted xacqanat ?itkinit through a series of community gatherings in Ktunaxa communities. We developed, piloted and validated xacqanat ?itkinit, with community members commenting that the process was "really meaningful, really powerful" and that being able to talk and listen embodied what it means to be a healthy community. The data from the pilot has informed the development of a Ktunaxa Model of Wellness that reflects Ktunaxa understandings of health and wellness. A significant outcome of this partnership is capacity building within Ktunaxa Nation for revitalizing, preserving and restoring traditional knowledge systems and knowledge sharing processes. Through relationship building and co-learning, we have learned: 1) real engagement starts before the work; 2) language matters; 3) Indigenous words break down differently than English; 4) the journey is a destination; and 5) no one knows everything. This partnership is paving a way forward for decolonized relationships between health systems and Indigenous communities, with the aim of reorienting health systems to learn from culturally-informed approaches to supporting wellness. This project can inform other relationship building processes, and offers insights for respectfully integrating Indigenous knowledge, languages and worldviews into health services, health policies and health research. Developing and piloting xacqanat ?itkinit was the formative first step along the pathway toward mutual long-term goals to support co-learning activities between Ktunaxa Nation and Interior Health.

column36: Canadian Users of Cannabis Smoke Study (CANUCKs): Impact on Lung Health via Clinical, Imaging, and Biologic Measures
column37: Almost 5 million Canadians smoke cannabis, but the effect that cannabis smoking has on their lungs is unclear. Some people think there is no harm caused by cannabis smoking, while others believe that cannabis smoking can significantly damage the lung like cigarette smoking does. Our study will look at a large population of around 1,200 Canadians to help settle the debate. We aim to describe what happens to the lung after cannabis smoking on multiple levels, looking at important health events and outcomes, breathing tests, imaging, and airway cells collected through a procedure called bronchoscopy. How all of these change in comparison to people who have never smoked and people who smoke cigarettes will be tested. The findings will help Canadians understand the long-term effects of cannabis smoking on their lungs. As well, they will help inform health care workers who will be counselling patients on cannabis smoking and potentially treating lung diseases that may be associated with cannabis smoking. Our analyses of the overall impact of cannabis smoking on the Canadian health care system from a cost and resource standpoint will also help to guide policy makers and health economists as to the burden of cannabis smoking on the Canadian health care system.

column36: Maternal-infant dyad health outcomes: infant neurodevelopment in the context of maternal cannabis use - a prospective cohort study
column37: In October 2018, recreational cannabis became legal in Canada; before then medical use was legal. Babies are exposed to cannabis their mothers use during pregnancy and through breastmilk. Research-informed information for parents and families is scarce and pregnant women receive mixed messages around the safety of cannabis. The Canadian government recommends avoiding it since there is no known safe level to use during pregnancy. Exposures have a higher risk of causing permanent health changes in growing and developing babies. Long term outcomes of cannabis exposure are not known. Some teens who use cannabis have permanent brain changes and an increased risk of mental health problems. Much less is known about second-hand cannabis exposure, especially in young children. We do not know whether cannabis smoke exposes children to biologically significant levels of cannabis. This study will follow women from early pregnancy until their babies are 18 months old. Mothers will report if, when and how they use cannabis. Their sleep, activity, mental and physical health and the baby's birth, development, behavior and health will be monitored, including a formal assessment at 18 months. The family will use an air quality monitor and passive environmental samplers for mothers and babies. They will also complete an environmental assessment. Breastmilk and urine will be tested for cannabis to see if babies absorb cannabis used by mothers. Passive sampler analyses will provide evidence of other exposures that could confuse the picture, like tobacco smoke and air pollution. Sleep and mood are related and impact development, so maternal and infant sleep will be monitored. Cannabis, used medically and for recreation, presents potential risks and benefits to expectant mothers and families. This study will provide valuable information to help families make informed choices about cannabis and set the stage for future research on the long term effects of cannabis exposure on children.

column36: Impact of Cannabis Use on Indigenous Peoples' Oral Health
column37: The legalization of non-medical cannabis in 2018 has raised many questions about the health effects associated with the drug's use. For instance, emerging evidence associates smoking cannabis with several oral diseases, including oral cancers. However, the effects of cannabis use on the oral health of Indigenous youth and adults are unknown. This study addresses stakeholder priorities and the impact increased cannabis use has on the already disproportionate burden of illness borne by Indigenous Peoples. Self-identified cannabis users and non-users, ages 18 to 44 years, will be recruited from partnering Indigenous communities and neighboring non-Indigenous communities, with each group followed for three years. Baseline and yearly comprehensive oral health examinations will be conducted by calibrated dentists. Saliva samples will be collected to monitor salivary constituents. Saliva and urine analyses will assess cannabis exposure. Non-invasive sensory tests will measure pain sensitivity in the orofacial region. Oral health outcomes will include: oral mucosal lesions, periodontitis, dental caries, changes in oral microbial composition, and abnormal sensory function. We hypothesize cannabis use in Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations is associated with: 1) a shift in the oral inflammatory signature that promotes the progression of pre-malignant lesions to oral cancers; 2) a distinctive salivary bacterial fingerprint; 3) a shift in the proteins in saliva reflecting a higher incidence of periodontitis and early-stage oral cancers, and; 4) oral and facial somatosensory changes dependent on drug use. The Indigenous Learning Circle model will be used throughout to share knowledge around the oral health risks of cannabis consumption and the drug's impact on Indigenous communities. The Circles will also be used to evaluate the research outcomes through the lens of the community so as to inform policy and recommend measures that promote cessation and harm reduction.

column36: A prospective translational model of the therapeutic potential of cannabidiol in reducing acute pain symptoms and opioid usage following traumatic injury.
column37: Recreational cannabis is legal in Canada since October 2018. Based on Colorado's experience, the first U.S. state to have legalized recreational cannabis in 2014, effects on Canadians' health are to be expected including: 1) increased recreational cannabis use; and 2) increased risk of traumatic injuries. Traumatic injuries are associated with an increased risk of chronic pain especially when peripheral orthopedic injuries (i.e., bone fracture) are combined with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Following a traumatic injury, opioid therapy is common despite the high risk of addiction/misuse/diversion as there is no other alternative to relieve severe pain. In parallel, cannabidiol (CBD) is emerging as a potent anti-inflammatory agent extracted from the cannabis plant which could promote pain relief and reduce opioid use after traumatic injuries. However, the low quality of clinical evidence on the safety and action mechanisms of CBD along with the lack of knowledge on interactions with opioids contribute to physicians' hesitation to adopt CBD as a regular therapeutic tool to relieve pain symptoms. The ongoing opioid crisis coupled with cannabis legalization in Canada therefore calls for an intersectoral strategy aiming to determine the potential of cannabinoids as co-analgesic agents for the treatment of pain, especially in vulnerable multi-trauma patients. To this end, expertise from 5 Canadian universities and a patient-expert partnership have led to an action plan with 4 main deliverables providing: 1) The first clinical assessment of the therapeutic potential of CBD for acute pain alleviation after multi-trauma; 2) A long-term assessment of CBD treatment effects on pain symptoms and trauma outcomes; 3) Using animal models of multi-trauma, assessment of interaction between CBD treatment and factors contributing to pain symptoms; 4) Scientific & clinical knowledge transfer strategy tailored to the needs of patients, practitioners, and key stakeholders.

column36: Cannabis-based precision medicine for osteoarthritis therapy
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of disability, in part due to a lack of effective treatment options. Cannabis offers a potential treatment for OA, however, little research has been done on this topic. Cannabinoids are the main active components in cannabis. The most abundant cannabinoids are delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and cannabidiol (CBD). There are many causes and types of OA, so it is likely that any therapeutic (or harmful) effect of cannabis will vary based on characteristics of the patient, and levels of cannabinoids in the cannabis strain used. We propose to study the characteristics of the patient and of the cannabis that predict how well cannabis works for treating OA. First, we will do studies in mice that have OA to examine the effect of different cannabinoids on different types of OA. column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease that manifests as relapses and/or progression. Multiple disease-modifying treatments (DMTs) are available to control the disease process. Lesser progress has been achieved to treat the multiple symptoms that MS can cause. Persons with MS PwMS, especially after 10 or more years of disease course, are frequently afflicted by a combination of leg weakness with spasticity, neuropathic pains, fatigue, sphincteric dysfunction, sleep disruption, and mood and cognition impairment. These are treated by muscle relaxants, neurotransmitter agents, tricyclics, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and CNS stimulants. The efficacy of these agents, which are fraught with side effects and drug-drug interactions, is often partial. Up to 49% of persons with MS (PwMS), have used cannabis, mostly for mood enhancing, to improve sleep, relieve pain and spasticity. A THC-CBD spray has been approved in Canada in 2005 for symptom improvement in adult PwMS with moderate to severe spasticity who have not responded adequately to other anti-spasticity medications. Now that the use of cannabis is legalized in Canada, the patient and medical communities expect the establishment of evidence-based guidelines for the proper use of cannabis. We are proposing to assess the clinical effects of THC and CBD positive and negative, in a carefully selected cohort of PwMS with single or multiple symptoms, enrolled in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, parallel groups trial of four weeks' duration. The main outcomes will be spasticity, with pain, sleep, mood and cognition, fatigue, and sphincteric function as secondary outcomes. The pharmacology of THC-CBD, as well as their effects on neuro-inflammation, will be explored. PwMS will be involved in all phases of the proposed study.

column36: Rewilding the human gut: Reintroduction of the species Lactobacillus reuteri
column37: The gut is home to trillions of bacteria, collectively known as the gut microbiome. A healthy microbiome is likely one that has a high diversity. However, industrialization has resulted in a loss of diversity, specifically of certain bacteria that may be important for health. It has also reduced the amount of dietary fibre we eat, which is the main source of nutrition for gut bacteria. Therefore, it is likely that our loss in bacterial diversity goes hand-in-hand with our reduced dietary fibre intake. Non-industrialized populations still consume plant-based diets that are rich in fibre, which likely supports the growth of bacteria not found in industrialized populations. Lactobacillus reuteri is a bacterial species that can benefit immunity and metabolic health. It is found in the gut microbiomes of non-industrialized populations, but rarely found in those living in industrialized countries. Therefore, the objective of this study is to provide L. reuteri as a probiotic to healthy adults along with a diet high in fibres known to facilitate its growth in an attempt to reintroduce this lost bacterial species to the gut microbiome. We will monitor if L. reuteri can be established in the gut by analyzing stool samples, and if there are associated immunological and metabolic benefits from both the reintroduction of L. reuteri and the consumption of a high-fibre diet. This study will be the first of its kind to provide evidence if a bacterium that was once lost can be reintroduced to the gut microbiome, and if this is of benefit to immunity and metabolic health. Further, this may inform personalized nutrition interventions, where individuals that are missing certain bacteria consume them as probiotics along with a high-fibre diet to unlock their health-promoting potential.

column36: Working Together: Using Social Network Analysis to Help Connect Mental Health and Addiction Services in London-Middlesex
column37: Introduction/Background: Those who face mental health, substance use, and addictions challenges require a dynamic system of care. Designing such a system presents significant challenges. Local providers continue to note that navigating this system is challenging for both providers and clients served. The first step to address these challenges is to develop a description of the system, which has not yet been done. Social network analysis provides a simple, yet comprehensive, representation of the system for local policy makers. Methods: An inventory of mental health programs, including independent practitioners, was created. An electronic survey was sent to programs asking them to list partners they work with, and rate the strength of and experience working with each partnership. Programs were also asked to list services they have difficulty accessing. Social network analyses were conducted to create maps of relationships at the program- and organization-levels. Results/Analysis: 435 programs representing 85 organizations were identified. In order of difficulty, the external support service categories identified as most difficult to connect with were: Housing (n=139), Counselling (n=84), Primary Care (n=68), Family and Caregiver Support (n=52), and Employment (n=37). On a scale of 1 to 7, 7 being "very strong", respondents reported an average relationship strength with partner organizations of 4.97. On a scale of 1 to 7, 7 being "very positive", respondents reported an average score of 5.32 when ranking their experience working with partners. Conclusions and implications for policy, practice, or additional research: The analysis provides a simple and comprehensive description of the local mental health services system. Intended to help identify strengths and gaps within London-Middlesex and provide recommendations to better connect services, the network maps form a foundation for important policy discussions.

column36: Student-Led and Gender-Equitable Active School Travel Interventions: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
column37: Active school travel (AST), such as walking, cycling, and rollerblading, improves children's health, air quality, and road safety. However, fewer North American children today, than in previous generations, use AST. While interventions promoting AST show improvements, the results also highlight gender inequities. At both baseline and post-intervention, boys are more likely than girls to have higher rates of AST. This research uses qualitative methods to explore children's preferences for AST interventions and identify how they differ among genders. Grade 5 and 6 students from two schools in London, Ontario were invited to participate in this study. In gender-based groups (n=30 groups, 5 students per group), students led researchers on a walk through their school neighbourhood (within 1 km). Throughout the walk, students took pictures and videos using Collector for ArcGIS to document their perceptions of barriers and enablers to AST. Students then used the five E's of road safety (i.e., education, encouragement, engineering, enforcement, and evaluation) as a guide to design an intervention targeting a barrier identified from the walk. Focus groups were then conducted, in which they explained and reflected on their intervention strategies. Focus groups were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and thematically analyzed in NVivo 12. Themes related to student-developed AST interventions will be discussed with a gender-focused lens. Girls tend to recommend interventions that aim to increase AST-related skills and change infrastructure in their environment. Whereas boys were more likely to suggest strategies addressing the social aspects of AST such as recreational facilities along the route. This research aims to address gender inequity by informing child-led and gender-based AST interventions. As AST interventions are gaining momentum and support, it is important to ensure that the interventions and programs being supported are effective and equitable among genders.

column36: Common Concerns and Insights into the Information Seeking Behaviours of Albertans who have Utilized an Online Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Virus Decision Aid Tool.
column37: HPV infection is a leading cause of preventable cancers. Since 2014, the Gardasil(R) vaccine has been available free of charge to Albertan children through school-based immunization programs, yet uptake remains suboptimal. In addition to challenges associated with overcoming vaccine hesitancy, research has also suggested gaps in knowledge about the health benefits and indications for the vaccine may be contributing to this trend. Decision aids have often proven effective for engaging target groups with unbiased information to support individual-decision making. In 2016, the Alberta Cancer Prevention Legacy Fund launched a version of our online HPV Vaccine Decision Aid Tool to increase immunization rates by supporting Albertans in making informed decisions about immunizing themselves and their children to protect against HPV infection. Between February 2017 and June 2019, we gathered data from visits to the tool by over 3000 unique individuals. Almost 70% of users of the HPV vaccine decision aid tool were individuals seeking the HPV vaccine for themselves, approximately 48% of whom were female. The most common concern selected by users of the tool was related to the cost of the HPV vaccine (50.5%). Once the sample was split into individuals and parents, it became clear that these two groups had very different concerns regarding the HPV vaccine. Parents were more concerned about risk-based concerns such as safety (61.5%), ingredients (45.7%) and side effects (57.7%). In contrast, individuals were more concerned about logistical issues such as the cost of the vaccine (62.0%), the number of injections (39.1%), and when they should receive the vaccine (47.6%). This information could be used to deliver targeted health marketing campaigns that address the leading concerns of different groups of Albertans considering obtaining the HPV vaccine who have not yet made a decision on whether to immunize but are actively seeking information.

column36: Accessing sexualized violence services and supports: Exploring the perspectives of women living in rural places
column37: Background: Women face significant barriers accessing formal services and informal supports in response to an experience of sexualized violence. These barriers include but are not limited to: victim blaming, stigma, and fear of a re-triggering or traumatic experience. Women living in rural places face unique barriers to accessing services and supports in response to an experience of sexualized violence. Rural areas may lack the services available in urban areas. Services that do exist may be limited in scope and/or difficult to access. The purpose of this study is to explore and understand the experiences of women living in rural Nova Scotia who have attempted to access or accessed formal and informal services and supports after experiencing sexualized violence. Results will identify what services and supports women who have experienced sexualized violence think are needed in rural places. Methods: Qualitative, one-on-one interviews with women who live in a rural place in Nova Scotia and who attempted to access or accessed formal services or informal supports in the past five years after any experiences of sexualized violence. Results and analysis: This research will identify several barriers and facilitators to accessing formal services and informal supports after experienced sexualized violence in a rural place, including travel, lack of trauma informed approaches, relationship between police and other services, a lack of support for survivors of historic trauma and the responsibility of women accessing services to navigate a complicated health service system. Conclusion: Women living in a rural place experience unique barriers and facilitators to accessing services and supports related to sexualized violence. Preliminary results will make recommendations for both polciy and program level changes to the delivery of sexualized violence services in rural areas.

column36: Improving birth outcomes for women who are substance using or have mental health conditions: a comparison of antenatal midwifery and physician models of care
column37: Background Studies have shown improved birth outcomes for women of low socioeconomic position (SEP) receiving antenatal midwifery versus physician care. To understand for whom and under what circumstances this applies, we examined whether substance use, mental illness, social assistance, residence in a neighbourhood of low/moderate SEP, and teen maternal age modified the association between model of care (midwifery vs. physician) and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) or preterm birth (PTB) for women of low SEP. Methods For this retrospective cohort study, maternity data from the British Columbia (BC) Perinatal Data Registry were linked with Medical Services Plan (MSP) billing data. We report adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals for SGA birth (< the 10th percentile) and PTB (< 37 weeks' completed gestation). For tests of interaction between antenatal models of care and psychosocial risk factors, p-values < 0.10 were considered statistically significant. Women were eligible for inclusion if they were residents of BC, carried a singleton fetus, had low to moderate medical/obstetric risk, birthed between April 1, 2008 and Dec. 31, 2012, and received an MSP subsidy (n=33,937). Results Midwifery vs. obstetrician patients had lower odds of PTB (aOR 0.53, 95% CI: 0.43-0.64). The difference was 31% lower among substance users (aOR 0.24, 95% CI: 0.11-0.54) compared to non-substance users (aOR 0.55, 95% CI: 0.44-0.68). For midwifery vs. obstetrician patients with both mental illness and substance use, odds of PTB were 34% lower (aOR 0.18, 95% CI: 0.06-0.55) compared to women with neither mental illness nor substance use (aOR 0.52, 95% CI: 0.41-.66). Effects were not statistically significantly different for midwifery vs. general practitioner patients with additional psychosocial risk. Conclusion Future studies should examine how antenatal models diverge in practice and if this systematically contributes to variation in birth outcomes.

column36: Understanding who does and does not respond to an interprofessional education and self-management model of care for chronic low back pain.
column37: Background: Low back pain (LBP) is the most common cause of disability in the world. Most LBP patients do not require costly imaging and specialist treatment. Current guidelines recommend education about the nature of LBP, advice to remain active and perform regular back exercises, and when necessary, management for the psychological effects of chronic pain such as depression. Since 2012, the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care has funded the Inter-professional Spine Assessment and Education Clinics (ISAEC: www.isaec.org), a program that coordinates timely, evidence-based care for patients with LBP persisting beyond 6 weeks. Patients referred to ISAEC receive rapid assessments from specially-trained allied health clinicians, who provide education and customized exercise plans to help patients manage their LBP. The ISAEC program has been shown to greatly reduce unnecessary spine imaging, and participants are highly satisfied with their care. Based on these findings alone, in 2018 the Ministry of Health began expanding the model across Ontario. However, ISAEC's impact on LBP outcomes specifically has not been fully evaluated. Methods: We plan to analyze data from 1,424 ISAEC patients, from whom pain and function measures were collected at their first ISAEC visit and six months afterwards. We will categorize outcomes as "successful" or "failed" depending on the degree of improvement, and use a variety of statistical approaches (including advanced artificial intelligence methods) to identify unique combinations of physical, psychological and social (e.g. type of work) characteristics related to successful or failed outcome. Impact: Identifying specific combinations of patient characteristics that predict LBP outcomes will help clinicians in ISAEC and other similar programs to promptly identify patients unlikely to benefit from education and exercise instructions alone, and provide additional support for more supervised and team-based LBP pain management.

column36: Evidence of health inequity in child survival: spatial and Bayesian network analyses of stillbirth rates in 194 countries
column37: Introduction: Stillbirths, at 2.6 million annually worldwide, remains stubbornly high; this is in contrast to neonatal and under-five mortality rates worldwide which has shown a decrease in recent years. Stillbirth is a neglected public health challenge globally. The global target of 9 stillbirths per 1000 total births, and national target of 12 per 1000 total births (especially in the Low and Middle Income Countries) by 2030 will be difficult to achieve at current rates. Studies heretofore have not quantified the relationship between stillbirth and its social determinants, leaving an evidence-gap for decision making, policy and practice. Main findings: Stillbirth rates varied across all countries with an average rate of 12.8 per 1000 total births. Thirty-seven countries (all from African continent) formed a cluster of high stillbirth rates (hot-spots); 13 countries formed a cluster of low stillbirth rates (cold spots), (from Central Asia and Canada). Society-wide gender inequality, anaemia in pregnancy were significant factors associated with higher stillbirth rates; while higher antenatal care coverage (ANC), skilled birth attendants during delivery were factors associated with lower stillbirth rates. A 44% improvement of stillbirth rate was associated with: skilled birth attendants during delivery increased from 70% to 88%, ANC coverage increased from 55% to 70%, prevalence of anaemia in pregnancy decreased from 27% to 11%, and gender inequality index decreased from 43% to 21%. Call to action: Recognizing the urgency in reducing stillbirths globally, multi-pronged strategies should be designed to promote gender equality and strengthen the reproductive and maternal health services-infrastructure in Africa, Eastern Mediterranean, and South Eastern Asia.Factors that place women at disadvantageous positions (low level education and literacy, economic insecurity, violence) are foundational and long-lasting solutions to address stillbirth rates.

column36: Defining the tumour-specific antigen landscape of lung cancer
column37: Cancer cells behave very differently from normal cells and employ multiple mechanisms to avoid recognition by the innate immune system. In addition to gain of function mutations that confer them a proliferative advantage, cancer cells also express non-coding variants that can disrupt chromatin structure and activate oncogenic transcription of proto-oncogenes. However, the search for tumour specific antigens (TSAs) presented by the major histocompatibility complex of cancer cells has produced less than a handful of putative candidates. This relatively meagre success is partly attributed to current search strategies that are often limited to the expression of source proteins originating from the canonical genome. Accordingly, we proposed here a novel proteogenomic approach that leverages high performance mass spectrometry and bioinformatics tools to uncover TSAs from coding and non-coding regions. We propose to apply this approach to the identification of TSAs from lung cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide with 1.8 million people being diagnosed every year. Given that lung cancer mutates at a high rate, we expect that lung tumour cells will express many of these unique antigens. In this project, we will be sequencing the genome of 40 tumours from 4 different classes of lung cancer to search for these TSAs. Finally, we will be classifying these components into two groups based on how they originated. The findings of such research could contribute to the development of a vaccine that makes use of these cancer-specific components to prime the immune system to attack cancer cells.

column36: Public Health Approaches to Homeless Health: Evidence Based Clinical Guidelines for Homeless, Vulnerably Housed and People with Lived Homelessness Experience and Their Relevance to Public Health Practitioners
column37: Homelessness is a critical social determinant of health and public health equity issue. People experiencing homelessness have high rates of morbidity and mortality, resulting in a life expectancy of 42 years for men, and 52 years for women. Stigma, trauma and discrimination contribute to marginalization of people who are homeless, particularly indigenous peoples, women, LGBTQI2S and racialized groups. The Evidence Based Clinical Guidelines for Homeless, Vulnerably Housed and People with Lived Homelessness Experience provide broad recommendations to support people experiencing homelessness with access to healthcare and housing. Because homelessness is a key health equity issue for the public health community, we utilize a prominent framework to examine public health roles as they pertain to the recent Evidence-Based Guidelines. Using the National Collaborating Center for Determinants of Health (NCCDH) framework "Public Health Roles for Improving Health Equity", we examine ways that public health is already and can further respond to homelessness including (1) assessing and reporting on inequities relating to homelessness, (2) modifying and orienting interventions to better serve this population, (3) partnering with other sectors and (4) participating in policy development. We use familiar public health examples including tuberculosis management, opioid strategy and adverse childhood experiences, to explore in detail how homelessness can be more effectively addressed by public health organizations. Application of these guidelines through this framework demonstrates how public health can act on this preventable cause of morbidity and mortality. We discuss how existing activities in public health are relevant to meeting this population's needs, and identify opportunities for public health to reduce barriers for homeless populations, and address determinants of poor health related to homelessness through program, organizational, and policy-level interventions.

column36: Service Mapping and Gap Analysis in Kee Tas Kee Now Tribal Council
column37: Kee Tas Kee Now Tribal Council (KTC), located in Treaty 8 territory, consists of five First Nations communities in northern Alberta. The findings from this service mapping and gap analysis will be used by front-line practitioners to increase awareness of available health services within and between communities. In addition, the barriers and gaps identified will be used to inform future direction and improve access to essential healthcare services. Further analysis needs to be conducted to identify relevant outcomes, including process and impact evaluations.

column36: Stroke Symptoms among the stroke-free older adults in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Ageing (CLSA): immigration, nutrition and implication for stroke prevention
column37: Introduction: Evaluating stroke symptoms is crucial for stroke prevention owing to the high risk of clinically undiagnosed stroke among older adults in Canada. This study assessed the prevalence and correlates of stroke symptoms in a stroke- and transient ischemic attack (TIA)-free population. Methods: Based on the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (2012-2014), multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed using a backward elimination approach. Stroke symptoms were assessed by the Questionnaire for Verifying Stroke-Free Status. Results: The study included 25,832 (16.2% immigrants, 1% refugees, 4.7% nonwhite, 50.9% female, mean age 62.37) participants who reported no stroke or TIA. The prevalence of stroke symptoms was 3.2% for one-sided sudden painless weakness, 4.7% for one-sided sudden numbness, 4.8% for sudden painless loss of vision in one or both eyes, 2.8% for sudden hemifield visual loss, 1.9% for sudden inability to understand speech, and 2.9% for sudden inability of linguistic expression. The prevalence of more than 1 symptoms was 13.3%. The adjusted odds (aOR) of stroke symptoms for non-refugee immigrants were 11% lower than the native-born Canadians (aOR=0.89, 95%CI: 0.80-0.99). Symptoms were more prevalent among those with lower income (aORs 1.29 to 2.22), lower education (aOR=1.23), smoking (aORs=1.10), multi-morbidities (aORs 1.79-4.08), chronic pain (aOR=1.35), high risk in waist-to-hip ratio (aOR=1.13), BMI above 25 (aOR 2.51 to 2.62), higher nutrition risk (aOR=1.29), daily intake of more than 5 fat sources (aOR=1.26), no intakes of calcium sources (aOR=1.14). Conclusion and implication for policy: Older adults with disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds, unhealthy behaviours and dietary intakes are at elevated risk of stroke symptoms that may have had clinically undetected. Aggressive stroke prophylaxis could be targeted to these identified high-risk populations to improve health equity for the aging population.

column36: Chronic conditions and executive function decline in aging adults
column37: Executive function is a set of cognitive skills, such as attention and reasoning, that allow persons to control and direct their abilities and behaviours. Having more chronic conditions has been linked to poorer executive function. People with poorer executive function, compared to others, are also at greater risk of dementia. However, few studies have looked at whether the amount of chronic conditions a person gains in a period of time is related to executive function. Therefore, this study explored the relationships between the number of and accumulation of chronic conditions on executive function overtime in aging adults. This study used data collected over a nine year period from the Survey of Midlife Development in the United States (MIDUS). Participants (2,532), aged 33-84 (mean age 55), completed telephone interviews, including a cognitive test, and questionnaires providing personal and health information. Twelve chronic conditions were included in the study: diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, heart disease, cancer (excluding skin), arthritis, asthma, obesity, neurological problems, stroke, depression and autoimmune disorders. Having a certain number of chronic conditions was not associated with executive function decline over time. However, people who had accumulated more chronic conditions in a ~9 year period were more likely to see executive function declines. This was also seen in those who were older, Black, and unemployed or retired. This research highlights high-risk groups that preventative efforts may want to focus on, as accumulation of chronic conditions may contribute to poorer cognitive health.

column36: Added, free and total sugar content and consumption of foods and beverages in Canada
column37: Background Consumption of sugars contributes to obesity and consequent chronic diseases. The World Health Organization and the US Department of Agriculture recommend consummation of added and free sugars not to exceed 10% of total energy intake (TEI). The added and free sugar content of foods and beverages consumed in Canada is not documente wd, and the sugar consumption and compliance with the above recommendation are unknown. Data and methods The added and free sugar content of 5,374 foods and beverages listed in the 24-hour dietary recalls of the 2015 Canadian Community Health Survey-Nutrition was calculated using established procedures. The distribution of usual intake of the added, free and total sugars by Canadians was estimated using the National Cancer Institution method. Results On average, Canadians consume 57.07 g/day added sugars, 66.62 g/day free sugars and 105.83 g/day total sugars in 2015. The average estimated added, free and total sugar intake contributed to 11.4%, 13.3% and 21.65% of TEI, respectively. Only 49.05% and 33.48% of Canadians consumed no more than 10% TEI from added and free sugars, respectively. The high sugars food groups included desserts and sweets, breakfast cereals, baked products, beverages and snacks. Desserts and sweets, and beverages contributed to most sugar intake in the Canadian diet. Interpretation Most Canadians consumed added and free sugars in excess of recommendations. Estimated values in this study will help policymakers articulate intervention targets and help researchers to evaluate the health and economic impacts of excessive sugar consumption.

column36: Impact of an advance practice physiotherapy model of care for older adults referred to neurosurgery for spinal pain: a prospective observational study from the CareAxis initiative
column37: Background: With the aging of the population, need for specialized care such as orthopaedics and neurosurgery, are rapidly increasing, resulting in long wait times. New models of care, involving advanced practice physiotherapy (APP) have been proposed as a potential solution. The CareAxis Group, a non-profit organization has developed with the support of several health charities an APP model of care for older adults referred to neurosurgery for spinal pain. In this program, the advanced practice physiotherapists assess and conservatively manage non-surgical patient in a one-hour session. The program was launched in January 2019 and showed promising results. However, the CareAxis group would like to offer a more comprehensive conservative rehabilitation intervention involving multiple sessions with the APP. To our knowledge, APP models comparing single to multiple consultations have not been evaluated. Objectives: The aim of this proposal is to perform a pragmatic randomized controlled trial to compare the effectiveness of the current CareAxis one session APP model compared to a multiple sessions APP model. Methods: This study will take place in nine physiotherapy CareAxis Group clinics in the Montreal region. One hundred and thirty-six older adults (65 years old or more) with neck or back pain will be recruited. Participants will be randomized in two groups: 1- a single session with the APP or 2- a group receiving multiple sessions with the APP (6 sessions over 5 months). Participants will be compared in terms of pain, function and quality of life. Economic analyses will be performed in order to compare the cost effectiveness of the two interventions. Significance: This study will contribute to the advancement of knowledge concerning APP models of care. Evidence-based development of APP models of care has the potential to profoundly impact access and quality of care for Canadians and is a novel model that may efficiently alleviate increasing health care demands.

column36: Primary care shared decision making for addressing painful chronic musculoskeletal conditions.
column37: Joint and muscle pain to the back, neck or knees are among the most common reasons for visiting a primary care physician. However, often patients are sent for several imaging tests, out of place specialist appointments or inappropriate surgery, and are given only pills for their pain with no rehabilitation to improve their mobility and long-term quality of life. Patients are rarely involved in deciding the best choices from among all possible options when they receive care for joint and muscle pain, and their values and preferences are rarely considered. Shared decision making between clinician and patient is known to improve patients' knowledge about their health problems and their confidence in the treatment chosen. Exercise therapy and pain education offered by rehabilitation professionals have proven useful for short- and long-term management of joint and muscle pain, but not all physicians and patients discuss this option or are even aware of it. A better conversation about options could reduce possibly harmful treatments. We will develop PRISM, an education program for physicians, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and psychologists to help them share decisions with patients about the best choices to diagnose and treat joint and muscle pain. We will test the program with a group of clinicians and patients to see if a larger study is feasible. We will assess clinicians' and patients' level of satisfaction with the program. We will assess patients' confidence that the options offered respect their preferences and that the chosen options improve their well-being. This project has great potential to improve communication among clinicians and patients and increase patients' knowledge, satisfaction and confidence about high-quality alternatives to advanced imaging and pills for their joint and muscle pain. This will contribute to a better experience with our healthcare system and improved quality of care for Canadians living with joint and muscle pain.

column36: Could brain stimulation alleviate chronic low back pain and potentiate the effect of exercises?
column37: Back pain produces the most years lived with disability in Canadian population. Despite continuous research effort, the prevalence of chronic back pain continues to grow, and the effect of conventional interventions on pain and disability is modest causing an enormous individual, social and economic burden. The prescription of stronger and more addictive drug, such as opioids, has leaded to a social crisis. It is then important to test novel non-pharmacological interventions that might be used to alleviate back pain. Brain stimulation techniques is known to reduce nerve pain but effect in people with chronic back pain is still unclear. In this project, we will test whether non-invasive brain stimulation techniques (repeated transcranial magnetic stimulation [rTMS]) can reduce back pain and enhance the effect of exercises on back pain and disability. Another objective is to determine if brain wiring and function may predict who will improve best following the interventions. State-of-the-art imaging techniques will screen the brain of the participants to search for potential markers predicting the best response to treatments. This project has the potential to provide the first available evidence of the effect of brain stimulation techniques in back pain and to better identify potential responders. These novel non-pharmacological techniques might help to reduce the personal, social and economic burden of back pain in Canada, and provide additional interventions to overturn the opioid crisis.
